The impact is financial: traders cannot retrieve earned rewards, effectively losing funds that were promised as part of the margin trading incentive program. The problem manifests whenever a trader initiates a withdrawal request; the transaction passes the reporter check but then fails to match the reward owner, resulting in no token transfer. To remediate, the contract should either remove the isIncentiveReporter restriction from withdrawReward or redesign the function to accept a recipient parameter and verify that the caller is either the recipient or an authorized manager, ensuring that the reward owner can successfully claim the funds. In short, the bug blocks reward distribution, violates the protocol’s accounting assumptions, and leaves users with missing payouts.
summary:
The rewards for a recipient in `IncentiveDistribution.sol` are stored in the storage mapping indexed by recipient `accruedReward[recipient]` and the recipient is the actual margin trader account, see `updateAccruedReward`.

These rewards are supposed to be withdrawn through the `withdrawReward` function but `msg.sender` is used here instead of a `recipient` (`withdrawer`) parameter. However, `msg.sender` is enforced to be the incentive reporter and can therefore not be the margin trader.

Nobody can withdraw the rewards.

Recommend removing the `isIncentiveReporter(msg.sender)` check from `withdrawReward` function.

title: lastUpdatedDay not initialized
content: The vulnerability originates from an uninitialized storage variable that tracks the last day on which incentive totals were updated. Because the contract never sets this "last updated day" value during deployment, it remains at its default of zero. The function responsible for distributing daily incentives iterates from the stored last updated day up to the current day, assuming the stored value represents a recent day index. With a zero start point, the loop attempts to walk through every day since the Unix epoch, resulting in an excessively large number of iterations. This can cause the transaction to run out of gas, preventing the update from completing, and if the loop were somehow allowed to finish, the routine would repeatedly overwrite the daily distribution variable, yielding a final amount that is far lower than the intended incentive. The issue manifests whenever the update routine is called after the contract has existed for more than a few days, effectively blocking the entire incentive distribution mechanism for all participants. Users expecting to receive their daily rewards may see no reward, a zero balance, or an unexpectedly small payout, violating the protocol’s economic assumptions. The problem was uncovered during a formal security audit, where the auditors observed that the loop condition relied on a variable that had never been set. Detecting the flaw can be difficult because the contract compiles without errors and the default zero value does not raise an immediate warning; the gas exhaustion only appears after the contract has been live for a sufficient period. To remediate the issue, the contract should initialize the last updated day to the current day at construction time, for example by assigning block.timestamp divided by one day to the variable, and the loop logic should be reviewed to ensure it caps iteration count or uses a safer incremental update pattern. Proper initialization restores the expected behavior of the incentive distribution, ensuring that rewards are calculated accurately and that the function can be executed without exceeding gas limits.
summary:
The variable lastUpdatedDay in IncentiveDistribution.sol is not (properly) initialized. This means the function updateDayTotals will end up in a very large loop which will lead to an out of gas error. Even if the loop would end, the variable currentDailyDistribution would be updated very often. Thus updateDayTotals cannot be performed.

The entire IncentiveDistribution does not work. If the loop would stop, the variable currentDailyDistribution is not accurate, resulting in a far lower incentive distribution than expected.

Recommend initializing lastUpdatedDay with something like block.timestamp / (1 days)

    uint256 lastUpdatedDay; # ==> lastUpdatedDay = 0

title: Impossible to call withdrawReward fails due to run out of gas
content: The vulnerability originates from an uninitialized state variable that is used as the starting point for a time‑based distribution loop inside the withdrawReward function. Because the variable that records the last day on which rewards were distributed (lastUpdatedDay) is never set during contract deployment, its default value is zero. When a user calls withdrawReward, the contract iterates over every day from day 0 up to the current day to compute the accrued reward. In a realistic scenario the day difference can be on the order of tens of thousands (the audit observed a difference of 18 724 days), and even with a very high gas limit (9.5 million) the loop exhausts the available gas after only a few hundred iterations, causing the transaction to revert. Additionally, the function iterates over an array of tranches (allTranches) that has no explicit upper bound; the owner can keep appending new tranches, and each additional element adds another inner loop iteration. As the array grows, the total gas consumption of withdrawReward grows linearly, eventually exceeding the block gas limit and making the function permanently uncallable. The practical impact is that users expecting to claim rewards see their transactions fail, receive no tokens, or observe that their balances remain unchanged despite having earned incentives. Funds that have been allocated to rewards become effectively locked in the contract because the only mechanism to retrieve them – withdrawReward – cannot complete. This affects any participant who holds incentive tokens, as well as the protocol itself, which loses credibility and may suffer economic loss if rewards cannot be distributed. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit where the tester invoked withdrawReward with a high gas allocation and observed that execution stopped at iteration 270, a symptom of the loop running far longer than intended. The problem is subtle because the contract compiles and seems correct at first glance; the missing initialization is not flagged by the compiler, and the unbounded array appears safe as only the owner can add elements, leading auditors to underestimate the potential loop size. To remediate the issue, the contract should initialize lastUpdatedDay to the deployment timestamp (or the current day) so that the daily loop starts from a realistic baseline. Moreover, the distribution logic should be refactored to avoid iterating over each day and each tranche on‑chain – for example by storing cumulative rewards per tranche, using a checkpointing scheme, or limiting the number of tranches that can be processed in a single call. Imposing a hard cap on the number of tranches, employing a pull‑based claim that processes a bounded batch, or migrating the accounting off‑chain are viable design changes that prevent out‑of‑gas failures and preserve users’ ability to retrieve their earned rewards.
summary:
The withdrawReward (https://github.com/code-423n4/marginswap/blob/main/contracts/IncentiveDistribution.sol#L224) fails due to the loop at https://github.com/code-423n4/marginswap/blob/main/contracts/IncentiveDistribution.sol#L269). Based on testing, the dayDiff would be 18724 and with a gasLimit of 9500000 it stops at iteration 270 due to the fact that lastUpdatedDay is not initialized so is 0. Other than that it could run out of gas also for the loop of allTranches (https://github.com/code-423n4/marginswap/blob/main/contracts/IncentiveDistribution.sol#L281) because it’s an unbounded array.

I’m not sure of the logic behind the shrinking of the daily distribution but i think that maybe you just missed to initialize the lastUpdatedDay to the day of deployment? If that’s the case it resolves partially the problem because allTranches is theoretically unbounded even though only the owner can add element to it and you should do deeply testing to understand how many elements it can have until it run out of gas. I read the comment that says you tried to shift the gas to the withdrawal people maybe you went too further and is it worth rethinking the design?

Exactly. we need to initialize lastUpdatedDay.

title: ERC-721 Enumerable Spec mismatch for index of `tokenByIndex`
content: The vulnerability is an off‑by‑one error in the ERC‑721 Enumerable extension’s `tokenByIndex` function. According to the ERC‑721 specification, token indices start at 0, allowing callers to retrieve the first token in the collection by passing 0 as the index. In this implementation the function includes a check that requires the supplied index to be greater than 0, effectively rejecting the valid index 0. The root cause is a misplaced inequality in the input validation logic, likely introduced by a misunderstanding of the enumeration contract’s requirements or by an arbitrary decision to index tokens from 1. An attacker or any external caller can exploit the bug simply by invoking `tokenByIndex(0)`, which will cause the transaction to revert. More subtly, legitimate users or integration platforms that iterate over a token collection from 0 up to `totalSupply‑1` will encounter a failure at the first iteration, preventing them from accessing the metadata, ownership information, or any other data associated with the token at index 0. The impact is that the first minted NFT becomes invisible to wallets, marketplaces, and analytics tools that rely on ERC‑721 enumeration, leading to missing balances, incomplete gallery displays, and potential loss of sales revenue. This condition manifests whenever a contract containing the faulty enumerable logic is queried for its tokens, especially during initial enumeration or when the collection contains a small number of items where the zero index is frequently accessed. The bug affects all token holders whose token resides at index 0, as well as third‑party platforms that assume full ERC‑721 compliance. It was discovered during a formal security audit that compared the contract’s behavior against the OpenZeppelin reference implementation of ERC‑721Enumerable. The issue can be hard to notice because many test suites start iteration at index 1 or only test with higher indices, and because most deployments may never mint a token that occupies index 0 in practice, masking the failure until a platform attempts full enumeration. To remediate the problem the input validation should be adjusted to accept index 0, for example by changing the require statement to `require(index >= 0 && index < totalSupply);` and ensuring that the bounds check correctly reflects the collection size. Conceptually, the fix restores compliance with the ERC‑721 Enumerable specification, allowing full enumeration of all tokens, preventing hidden or inaccessible NFTs, and aligning the contract with the expectations of the broader ecosystem.
summary:
Index starts at 0 for token array, but the implementation here requires index to be greater than 0. This will prevent querying of tokens at index 0.

See [reference implementation](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/blob/3ba2a1354f8f830d5a0e711537efdbdd8bcb109e/contracts/token/ERC721/extensions/ERC721Enumerable.sol#L21).

This will impact compatibility with NFT platforms that expect full conformity with ERC-721 specification.

Recommend accepting 0 index by changing to `require(index >= 0 && index < TOKEN_LIMIT);`.

Beebots indexes by 1 for whatever reason

title: Signature malleability of EVM’s `ecrecover` in `verify`
content: The vulnerability stems from the inherent malleability of the EVM's native ecrecover function, which can accept multiple distinct signatures that resolve to the same public key and message hash. In the contract's verify routine, a signed offer is validated using ecrecover, but no additional checks are made to enforce a canonical form of the signature (for example, limiting the s‑value to the lower half of the curve order or requiring a unique v). Because of this, an adversary can take a legitimately signed message, alter the signature components within the allowed malleable range, and produce a new, valid signature that the contract will also accept. The contract attempts to mitigate replay attacks by recording accepted offers and explicitly cancelling them after execution (as seen on line L645). However, this mitigation is tied to the current application logic; any future change that removes or bypasses the tracking step would re‑expose the system to replay attacks. Exploitation can therefore proceed in two phases: first, the attacker obtains a legitimate signed offer from a user; second, the attacker modifies the signature to a different but still valid representation and resubmits the offer. Because the contract still regards the altered signature as authentic, it will process the offer again, potentially transferring assets a second time, resulting in duplicated payouts or unauthorized withdrawals. The impact is severe: users may see their expected refunds or token allocations disappear, balances may be reduced unexpectedly, and the protocol's accounting assumptions—such as "each signed offer is executed at most once"—are broken. The issue manifests when the verify function is invoked with a signature that does not meet strict canonical criteria, especially in contexts where the contract assumes uniqueness of a signature without explicit enforcement. All participants who rely on the contract's integrity—users submitting offers, the protocol managing funds, and any downstream contracts assuming single‑use signatures—are affected. The flaw was identified during a formal audit (Code4rena) by reviewing the verification logic against known cryptographic best practices and cross‑referencing the SWC‑117 pattern for signature malleability. It may be hard to notice because the transaction appears to succeed, the signature verification returns true, and the contract's internal replay‑prevention flag may still be set correctly for the original signature, masking the duplicate execution under a different signature. To remediate, the contract should adopt a robust signature verification library such as OpenZeppelin's ECDSA, which enforces canonical signatures by rejecting high‑s values and ensuring a unique recovery identifier. Additionally, the contract should not solely rely on off‑chain tracking of processed offers; instead, it should embed a nonce or hash‑based identifier within the signed message that is stored on‑chain and checked atomically, guaranteeing that any replay—whether using the original or a malleated signature—fails. By normalizing the signature format and strengthening on‑chain state checks, the protocol can restore its guarantee that each signed intent is consumed exactly once, preventing funds from disappearing or being duplicated due to signature malleability.
summary:
EVM’s `ecrecover` is susceptible to signature malleability, which allows replay attacks, but that is mitigated here by tracking accepted offers and canceling them (on L645) specifically to prevent replays. However, if any application logic changes, it might make signature malleability a risk for replay attacks.

See [reference](https://swcregistry.io/docs/SWC-117).

Recommend using [OpenZeppelin’s ECDSA library](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/blob/master/contracts/utils/cryptography/ECDSA.sol)

title: Arbitrary Transfer of Unowned NFTs
content: The vulnerability consists of an arbitrary transfer flaw in a marketplace contract that allows an attacker to move any ERC‑721 token whose recorded owner address is the zero address. The root cause lies in the signature verification routine used by the `tradeValid` function, which calls a `verify` helper that relies on `ecrecover`. When an invalid signature is supplied, `ecrecover` returns the zero address. Because `verify` does not explicitly reject a zero‑address signer, the function incorrectly returns true, signalling that the signature is valid. Consequently, the surrounding `acceptTrade` logic proceeds with the transfer without confirming that the token actually belongs to a legitimate owner. The exploit works by crafting a trade request with an empty or malformed signature, causing the verification step to succeed and enabling the contract to transfer any NFT whose internal `idToOwner` mapping stores address(0). This includes tokens that have never been minted, as well as tokens that may have been burned and left with a zero owner. When the exploit is triggered, an attacker can claim ownership of these non‑existent or unowned NFTs, potentially receiving assets they never purchased and causing the marketplace to dispense funds for a transfer that has no underlying asset. The condition for the bug to appear is any call to `acceptTrade` where the offered NFT’s owner is the zero address, which is common for unminted token IDs. All participants in the marketplace—buyers, sellers, and the protocol itself—are affected because the accounting of token ownership becomes inconsistent, leading to lost trust, misplaced balances, and the risk of funds being paid out for phantom assets. The issue was discovered during a security audit by Code4rena when the auditors examined the signature validation logic and noticed the lack of a zero‑address check after `ecrecover`. It is subtle because the verification function returns true for a malformed signature, which may not raise an immediate error, making it easy to overlook during functional testing. To remediate the problem, the verification routine should explicitly reject a recovered signer of address(0) and the contract should also enforce that the token owner stored in `idToOwner` is a non‑zero address before allowing any transfer. Adding these checks restores the intended business logic that a trade can only occur between legitimate owners and prevents the creation of phantom NFT transfers that break the protocol’s accounting model.
summary:
Due to how the market functions are structured, it is possible to arbitrarily transfer any NFT that is not owned by any address.

The function in question is the `tradeValid` function invoked by `acceptTrade` before the trade is performed. It, in turn, validates the signature of a trade via `verify`, which does not account for the behavior of `ecrecover`.

When `ecrecover` is invoked with an invalid signature, the zero-address is returned by it, meaning that `verify` will yield `true` for the zero-address as long as the signature provided is invalid.

This can be exploited to transfer any NFT whose `idToOwner` is zero, including NFTs that have not been minted yet.

Recommend an additional check be imposed within `verify` that ensures the signer is not the zero-address which will alleviate this check. For more details, consult the [EIP721 implementation by OpenZeppelin](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/blob/v3.4.0/contracts/cryptography/ECDSA.sol#L53-L71).

title: `Beebots.TradeValid`
content: The vulnerability lies in the trade validation logic of the BeeBots contract suite. The function Beebots.verify() does not enforce that the supplied signer address is non‑zero. Because the Solidity ecrecover primitive returns address(0) when a signature does not match the expected signer, the verification routine simply compares the recovered address with the supplied signer. When the signer is set to address(0), ecrecover also returns address(0), causing the comparison to succeed regardless of the actual signature content. Consequently, Beebots.tradeValid() can be called with a maker value of address(0) and will still return true. In addition, the contract’s idToOwner mapping that tracks NFT ownership is implicitly initialized to address(0) for any token ID that has not yet been minted. The trade validation routine assumes that a zero‑address owner indicates a legitimate owner, and it does not check that the maker field is a real account. An attacker can therefore craft a trade request where maker is address(0) and makerIds reference any unminted NFT IDs. The contract will incorrectly deem the trade valid, allowing the attacker to execute actions that depend on a successful validation – for example moving assets, minting NFTs on behalf of the zero address, or bypassing fee and permission checks. The impact is the potential unauthorized transfer or creation of NFTs, loss of economic value, and a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees, as users may see trades reported as successful while no genuine ownership change occurs. This flaw is triggered whenever a trade involving unminted token IDs is processed, or when the caller intentionally supplies address(0) as the maker or signer. The issue was discovered during a static analysis audit by Code4rena, where the logic flow of signature verification and owner lookup was examined and the lack of explicit non‑zero checks was identified. The problem is subtle because a zero address is a valid Solidity value and mappings default to zero, so the contract appears to behave correctly under normal minted‑NFT scenarios, masking the flaw until edge‑case inputs are used. To remediate, the verification function should reject any signer that equals address(0), and trade validation must require that the maker address is non‑zero before proceeding. Adding explicit require statements for these conditions prevents ecrecover’s silent failure from being misinterpreted as a successful signature verification and stops the contract from treating unminted NFTs as owned by the zero address, thereby restoring the intended security guarantees.
summary:
`Beebots.TradeValid()` will erroneously return true when `maker` is set to `address(0)` and `makerIds` are set to the `tokenIds` of unminted beebot NFTs.

`Beebots.verify()` returns true no matter what signature is given when signer is set to `address(0)`. This means that `BeeBots.tradeValid()` will erroneously return true when `maker` is set to `address(0)`.

Finally, before an NFT has even been minted at all, it is assumed to have an owner of `address(0)` due to the `idToOwner` mapping being initialized to zero for all uninitialized slots, so an attacker can call `tradeValid()` with `maker` set to `address(0)` and `makerIds` set to the `tokenIds` of any unminted `nftIds`, and `tradeValid()` will erroneously return true.

  * (1) `Beebots.verify()` returns true no matter what signature is given when signer is set to `address(0)`.

    * (1a) `BeeBots.verify()` does not check to ensure that signer is not `address(0)`.
    * (1b) This is a problem because `ecrecover` fails silently if the signature does not match and returns zero.
    * (1c) So if an attacker passes in `address(0)` as the signer, then verify will return true no matter what signature is provided, since `ecrecover` will return `address(0)`, and the signer is `address(0)`, so verify will pass.
    * (1d) This means that `BeeBots.tradeValid()` will erroneously return true when maker is set to `address(0)`.
  * (2) Before an NFT has even been minted at all, it is assumed to have an owner of `address(0)` due to the `idToOwner` mapping being initialized to zero for all uninitialized slots

    * (2a) Solidity initializes all mappings to 0 for all slots that have not yet been set.
    * (2b) So for any NFT ID that has not yet been minted, the corresponding owner in the mapping `BeeBots.idToOwner` is `address(0)`, even though that NFT should not even exist.
    * (2c) This means that an attacker can call `tradeValid()` with maker set to `address(0)` and makerIds set to any unminted nftIds, and `tradeValid()` will erroneously return true.

(1) Recommend adding this check to `Beebots.verify()`: `require(signer != address(0), "Cannot verify signatures from 0x0");`

(2) Recommend adding this check to `Beebots.tradeValid()`: `require(maker != address(0), "Maker 0x0 not allowed");`

Wow, this exploit is absolutely stunning.

title: function `tokenByIndex` treats last index as invalid
content: The vulnerability is an off‑by‑one error in the ERC‑721 enumerable function `tokenByIndex`. NFTs are minted with identifiers that start at 1, because the contract adds one to the internal zero‑based counter (value.add(1)). Consequently, for a collection of N tokens the valid token IDs are 1 through N inclusive. However, `tokenByIndex` enforces a boundary check `require(index > 0 && index < TOKEN_LIMIT)`, where TOKEN_LIMIT equals the maximum token ID (N). This condition rejects the request when the caller supplies the highest valid index (N), because the comparison uses a strict “less than” instead of “less than or equal”. The root cause is a faulty logical condition that treats the last index as invalid. An attacker or any user who attempts to enumerate the collection by iterating from 1 to `totalSupply()` will encounter a revert on the final iteration, causing the enumeration call to fail. This can be exploited to cause a denial‑of‑service for marketplaces, wallets, or any dApp that relies on `tokenByIndex` to display or transfer the final token; the UI will stop rendering, often presenting an empty list, missing token, or a generic error. The impact includes missing visibility of the last NFT, inability to retrieve its metadata, potential failure to transfer or sell the token, and a break in the expected accounting that the contract holds exactly N tokens. The condition occurs whenever `tokenByIndex` is invoked with an index equal to the total supply, which is a common pattern when iterating over all tokens. All token owners, collectors, and protocol users are affected because they cannot correctly query the last token, and any third‑party service that lists the collection will present incomplete data, undermining trust in the protocol. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by reviewing the index handling logic and noticing the mismatch between the one‑based token IDs and the zero‑based range check. Off‑by‑one bugs are notoriously hard to notice because they often only surface at the boundary, which may be under‑tested; typical unit tests may check a few interior indices but omit the highest index. To remediate, the require statement should be changed to `require(index > 0 && index <= TOKEN_LIMIT)`, or the contract should adopt zero‑based indexing consistently across token ID generation and enumeration. The fix aligns the logical contract invariant that every valid token ID can be retrieved via `tokenByIndex`, restoring correct enumeration, accurate UI display, and reliable accounting of token balances.

title: NFT can be minted for free after sale ended
content: The vulnerability originates from a business‑logic flaw in the NFT sale contract where the function that calculates the mint price, getPrice(), returns a value of zero once the sale period has ended and the remaining supply is equal to SALE_LIMIT minus the number of NFTs already sold. Because the contract does not explicitly revert or block minting when the price is zero, users can invoke the mint function without sending any ether and obtain the leftover NFTs for free. This occurs after the intended sale window has closed, so the contract's accounting assumption that every minted token is paid for is violated. The issue was identified during a code audit that highlighted the unexpected zero return value and the lack of protective checks. From a user's perspective the symptom is that a transaction that should cost ether completes without any payment, resulting in the user receiving an NFT at no cost while the protocol loses expected revenue. An attacker can exploit the flaw by deploying a malicious contract that calls the mint function as soon as the sale ends, front‑running legitimate buyers and draining the remaining token supply without cost. The impact includes loss of funds for the project, reduction of scarcity for the collection, and potential reputational damage as users perceive the sale as broken or unfair. Detection is difficult because the function behaves syntactically correctly – it returns a valid uint256 – and without explicit documentation the zero price may be mistaken for a promotional offer. The proper remediation is to enforce a non‑zero price invariant: the getPrice() function should revert when the sale has concluded or when no paid supply remains, and the minting entry point must require a positive ether amount matching the calculated price. This class of bug falls under price calculation errors and missing guard conditions that break economic invariants of token sales.
summary:
The `getPrice()` function returned 0 after the sale ended and (`SALE_LIMIT - numSales`) NFT can be minted for free.

Without documentation, it’s not clear if this is the expected behavior or not. If it’s unexpected, it is recommended to revert instead of returning 0. If it’s expected behavior, it’s possible to create a smart contract and claim all the remaining NFT front-running the regular users.

title: Unhandled return value of transfer in `transferOut`
content: The vulnerability originates from the contract's handling of ERC20 token transfers in the `transferOut` function. The code invokes the standard `transfer` method on a token address that is supplied by a user or another contract, but it does not verify the boolean return value that some ERC20 implementations use to signal failure. While many tokens revert on error, a subset—including some malicious or non‑standard tokens—simply return `false`. Because the contract does not wrap the call in a `require` statement or use a safety library, it proceeds as if the transfer succeeded even when the token contract indicated failure. This discrepancy can be exploited when an attacker provides a token contract that deliberately returns `false` after accepting the call, causing the `transferOut` logic to believe that funds have been sent while they remain locked or unaltered in the vulnerable contract. The impact is that the protocol’s accounting becomes inconsistent: the contract’s internal ledger records a deduction, yet the external token balance is unchanged, leading to effective loss of user funds, potential over‑withdrawals, or stuck tokens that cannot be recovered. The condition occurs whenever `transferOut` is called with a token that does not follow the "revert on failure" convention, which is common for legacy or malicious ERC20 implementations. Users experience symptoms such as receiving no tokens after a withdrawal request, seeing their on‑chain balance reduced in the protocol’s UI while the actual token balance stays the same, or observing zero refunds where a payment was expected. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that reviewed the code paths for token transfers and noted the absence of return‑value checks, a pattern also highlighted in prior audits of similar protocols. It is difficult to notice because the transaction does not revert, producing no obvious error, and the failure is silent. The appropriate remediation is to enforce the transfer result by either wrapping the call in `require(token.transfer(...))` or, preferably, by employing OpenZeppelin's `SafeERC20` library, which automatically reverts on a false return. By treating the unverified transfer as a failure, the contract can maintain correct accounting and prevent malicious tokens from subverting withdrawals.
summary:
ERC20 implementations are not always consistent. Some implementations of transfer and `transferFrom` could return ‘false’ on failure instead of reverting. It is safer to wrap such calls into `require()` statements to handle these failures.

The transfer call [on L211](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-04-vader/blob/3041f20c920821b89d01f652867d5207d18c8703/vader-protocol/contracts/Pools.sol#L211) of `transferOut()` could be made on a user-supplied untrusted token address (from the different call sites) whose implementation can be malicious.

For reference, see similar finding from Consensys Diligence Audit of AAVE Protocol V2

Recommend requirements to check the return value and revert on 0/false or use OpenZeppelin’s SafeERC20 wrapper functions.

Not valid. Since the funds came in, and did not revert, they can leave. If the call passes, then the transferout is valid.

title: Flash attack mitigation does not work as intended in USDV.sol
content:
The vulnerability stems from an uninitialized `blockDelay` parameter in the USDV smart contract, which is intended to enforce a minimum number of blocks between successive calls from the same externally‑owned account (EOA) through the `flashProof` modifier. The contract checks `lastBlock[tx.origin] + blockDelay <= block.number` to determine whether a new call is occurring in a later block than the previous one. Because `blockDelay` defaults to zero when not set, the comparison effectively becomes `lastBlock[tx.origin] <= block.number`. After the first call in a block, `lastBlock[tx.origin]` is updated to the current block number, and any subsequent call in the same block still satisfies the condition (`block.number` is equal to `lastBlock[tx.origin]`). Consequently, the contract permits multiple interactions within a single block, negating the intended protection against flash‑loan style attacks.

The root cause is the omission of an explicit initialization of `blockDelay` (the developers intended a default of at least one block). The DAO‑only `setParams()` function could theoretically set the variable, but the DAO currently lacks the capability to invoke this function, leaving the variable at its zero default for the lifetime of the contract. Even if the DAO were able to update the value later, there would be a window of vulnerability from deployment until the DAO successfully votes and executes a parameter change, during which an attacker could exploit the flaw. Moreover, a malicious minority within the DAO could manipulate proposals to keep `blockDelay` at zero, further extending the attack surface.

An attacker can exploit this by issuing a sequence of calls in the same transaction or block that would normally be prevented. For example, they could borrow assets via a flash loan, interact with the USDV contract to manipulate price feeds or synthetic token balances, and then settle the loan—all within the same block—thereby extracting value or causing loss of funds for honest participants. From the user’s perspective this may manifest as unexpected loss of collateral, zeroed balances after a transaction, or missing refunds that the protocol should have returned.

The impact is high because the contract’s core economic assumptions—such as the immutability of price data within a block and the inability to execute rapid, intra‑block re‑entrancy—are violated. This can lead to funds disappearing from the protocol, incorrect accounting of synth positions, and overall erosion of trust in the system.

The issue was discovered during a security audit that compared the contract’s stated goal of preventing flash‑loan attacks with the actual logic of the `flashProof` modifier. The discrepancy between the intended behavior (blocking same‑block calls) and the actual code (allowing them due to a zero delay) is subtle and may be missed in regular testing because single‑block re‑entrancy does not surface in typical unit tests or simulations.

To remediate the problem, the `blockDelay` variable should be initialized to a non‑zero value (e.g., 1) at declaration or within the constructor, ensuring that the first check always requires the next block to be strictly greater than the previous one. Additionally, the protocol should guarantee that the DAO can set this parameter safely before the contract becomes operational, or make the delay immutable after deployment to avoid a mutable window of exposure.
summary:
One of the stated protocol (review) goals is to detect susceptibility to “Any attack vectors using flash loans on Anchor price, synths or lending.” As such, USDV contract aims to protect against flash attacks using `flashProof()` modifier which uses the following check in `isMature()` to determine if currently executing contract context is at least `blockDelay` duration ahead of the previous context: `lastBlock[tx.origin] + blockDelay <= block.number`

However, `blockDelay` state variable is not initialized which means it has a default uint value of 0. So unless it is set to >= 1 by `setParams()` which can be called only by the DAO (which currently does not have the capability to call `setParams()` function), `blockDelay` will be 0, which allows current executing context (`block.number`) to be the same as the previous one (`lastBlock[tx.origin]`). This effectively allows multiple calls on this contract to be executed in the same transaction of a block which enables flash attacks as opposed to what is expected as commented on [L41](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-04-vader/blob/3041f20c920821b89d01f652867d5207d18c8703/vader-protocol/contracts/USDV.sol#L140-L142): "// Stops an EOA from doing a flash attack in the same block"

Even if the DAO can call `setParams()` to change `blockDelay` to >= 1, there is a big window of opportunity for flash attacks until the DAO votes, finalizes and approves such a proposal. Moreover, such proposals can be cancelled by a DAO minority or replaced by a malicious DAO minority to launch flash attacks.

Recommend initalizing `blockDelay` to >= 1 at declaration or in constructor.

The actual issue is simply:

blockDelay state variable is not initialized

It is intended to be initialised to 1, so this is a bug. Severity: 2

title: Missing DAO functionality to call `changeDAO`
content: The vulnerability is a missing governance integration that prevents the DAO from updating the address of the DAO contract within the Vader protocol. The Vader contract contains a function, changeDAO(), that is restricted by a modifier to be callable only by the DAO address. However, the DAO contract itself does not implement any external function or interface that can invoke changeDAO(). Consequently, the protocol’s DAO address is effectively immutable after deployment. The root cause is a mismatch between the access control expectations of the Vader contract and the capabilities exposed by the DAO contract – the protocol assumes the DAO can call changeDAO(), but the DAO’s code provides no such entry point. This situation can be exploited indirectly: if the DAO address ever needs to be migrated because of a security breach, a governance upgrade, or an emergency shutdown, the missing call path makes it impossible to execute the required governance action. The impact is that the protocol may become permanently locked in its initial governance configuration, preventing token holders or governance participants from exercising any future DAO‑controlled functions that rely on an updated DAO address. This can lead to loss of control over protocol parameters, inability to enact security patches, and ultimately a situation where funds or protocol logic are stuck and cannot be rescued. The condition under which the issue manifests is any scenario where a governance decision requires the DAO address to change – for example, after a DAO contract upgrade, a multi‑sig replacement, or after a compromise that forces migration to a new DAO. All stakeholders who rely on the DAO for governance – token holders, developers, and protocol operators – are affected because the governance mechanism cannot be exercised as intended. The problem was discovered during a systematic code audit that cross‑checked the access‑controlled functions in Vader.sol against the public interface of the DAO contract and identified that no function exists that satisfies the required call pattern. The issue may be hard to notice because the changeDAO() function exists and appears correctly protected, giving the impression that the governance upgrade path is functional, yet no external contract can actually reach it, so the failure only becomes apparent when an upgrade is attempted. To remediate the problem, the DAO contract should be extended with a public function (e.g., updateVaderDAO(address newDAO)) that internally calls the changeDAO() function on the Vader contract, or the Vader contract’s access control should be adjusted to allow a designated upgrade mechanism. In essence, the fix restores the intended governance flow by providing a callable path for the DAO to modify its own reference inside the protocol, thereby re‑enabling future DAO‑driven upgrades and preventing the protocol from becoming permanently stuck.
summary:
`changeDAO()` is authorized to be called only from the DAO (per modifier) but DAO contract has no corresponding functionality to call `changeDAO()` function. As a result, DAO address cannot be changed ([L192-L196](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-04-vader/blob/3041f20c920821b89d01f652867d5207d18c8703/vader-protocol/contracts/Vader.sol#L192-L196)).

Recommend adding functionality to DAO to be able to call `changeDAO()` of Vader.sol.

[#46](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-04-vader-findings/issues/46)

Unlike in issues #140, #157, #158, & #159; without this functionality, missing functionality in the DAO becomes a very serious issue. As a result, this one is very high risk were it to be overlooked.

title: Proposals can be cancelled
content: The vulnerability lies in the DAO's proposal cancellation mechanism, which permits any actor to invoke the cancelProposal function with the same identifier for both the old and new proposal (oldProposalID == newProposalID). Because the function’s minority check only verifies that the proposal has not yet met the required approval threshold, and the check is bypassed when the proposal is already approved, the call succeeds and the proposal is marked as cancelled. This flawed logic stems from an absence of a validation that the old and new proposal IDs must differ, effectively allowing a self‑cancellation that sidesteps any access control or vote‑based restrictions. An attacker can exploit this by repeatedly calling cancelProposal on newly approved proposals, causing them to be cancelled before execution. The immediate impact is a denial‑of‑service condition on the DAO's governance process: proposals never reach the execution phase, funds or state changes tied to those proposals remain locked, and participants lose confidence in the protocol's ability to act on community decisions. The condition can be triggered at any point after a proposal has achieved approval, and it does not require any privileged role—any address on the blockchain can perform the cancellation. The issue was uncovered during a formal security audit that examined the governance contract’s control flow and identified that the minority check does not prevent a matching‑ID cancellation. Because the function appears to perform a sensible check at first glance, the flaw can be difficult to notice without a deep inspection of the branch that handles identical proposal IDs. From a user’s perspective, approved proposals suddenly disappear from the UI, execution buttons become disabled, and the DAO appears stalled, contradicting the expectation that an approved proposal will be carried out. This class of bug is a typical improper access control or logic validation error, often referred to as a "self‑cancel" or "proposal cancellation bypass" vulnerability. To remediate the issue, the contract should enforce a requirement that oldProposalID and newProposalID are not equal (e.g., require(oldProposalID != newProposalID)) and ideally restrict the cancellation ability to the original proposer or to addresses holding sufficient governance rights. By adding this check and tightening the access control, the DAO can ensure that only legitimate, intended cancellations occur, preserving the integrity of the governance process.
summary:
Anyone can cancel any proposals by calling `DAO.cancelProposal(id, id)` with `oldProposalID == newProposalID`. This always passes the minority check as the proposal was approved.

An attacker can launch a denial of service attack on the DAO governance and prevent any proposals from being executed.

Recommend checking that `oldProposalID` == `newProposalID`

This is valid, can fix with a `require()`

title: Flash loans can affect governance voting in DAO.sol
content: The vulnerability consists of a governance voting mechanism that determines a participant's voting power directly from the token balance held at the moment a vote is cast, without enforcing any historical snapshot or maximum cap on individual weight. Because the system does not differentiate between permanently held tokens and tokens that are merely borrowed for a single transaction, an attacker can obtain a large quantity of governance tokens through a flash loan, use the borrowed tokens to cast votes with an artificially inflated weight, and then repay the loan within the same transaction. This manipulation is possible whenever the voting function reads the current balance, the protocol permits flash loans of the governance token, and there is no restriction on how much voting power a single address may wield in a given proposal. The impact is that the outcome of any governance proposal – including changes to critical protocol parameters, fund allocations, or contract upgrades – can be steered by an entity that temporarily controls a majority of voting weight but does not possess that control outside the flash‑loan transaction. From a user’s point of view, proposals may pass or fail contrary to the expectations of legitimate token holders, leading to decisions that appear to have been made by the community but were actually driven by a transient, borrowed majority. The issue was identified during a security audit after observing a real‑world incident in MakerDAO where a flash loan was used to influence a governance vote, demonstrating that the problem is not merely theoretical. Detecting the exploit is difficult because the token balance reverts to its original state before the block is finalized, leaving no obvious ledger trace of the inflated voting power. To mitigate the flaw, the protocol should base voting weight on a snapshot of token holdings taken at the start of the voting period (or a previous block) and/or enforce a ceiling on the maximum weight any single address can contribute, thereby preventing temporary token spikes from affecting governance outcomes.
summary:
Flash loans can significantly increase a single voter’s weight and be used to impact the voting outcome. A voter can borrow a significant quantity of tokens to increase their voting weight in a transaction within which, they also deterministically influence the voting outcome to their choice.

This has already happened in the case of MakerDAO governance where [a flash loan was used to affect voting outcome](https://forum.makerdao.com/t/urgent-flash-loans-and-securing-the-maker-protocol/4901) and noted by the Maker team as: “a practical example for the community that flash loans can and may impact system governance”

Given that flash loans are a noted concern, the impact of it to DAO governance which can control all critical protocol parameters should be mitigated as in other places.

Recommend accounting for flash loans in `countMemberVotes()` by using weight from previous blocks or consider capping the weight of individual voters. ([L158-L163](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-04-vader/blob/3041f20c920821b89d01f652867d5207d18c8703/vader-protocol/contracts/DAO.sol#L158-L163))

Not valid. All pools use slip-based fees so flash loan attack by buying up USDV or synths is not going to work.

The funds to execute this attack do not need to come from a pool. It could be done as simply as malicious members pooling their funds in a flash loan contract, and each borrowing the funds in turn to vote.

title: Incorrect burn address in Vader.sol
content: The vulnerability resides in the token contract’s internal token transfer routine. The contract defines a private _transfer() helper that receives a sender address as an explicit parameter and uses it for the actual balance updates and fee calculations. However, when the routine subsequently calls the internal _burn() function to destroy the fee amount, it erroneously passes msg.sender as the burn address instead of the explicit sender argument. This mistake only aligns with the intended behaviour when the public transfer() function is used, because in that case msg.sender does equal the logical sender. When the public transferFrom() or transferTo() functions are used, the logical sender is supplied by a function argument (for transferFrom) or inferred from tx.origin (for transferTo). In those contexts msg.sender refers to an intermediate contract or the outer transaction origin, not the user whose tokens are actually being moved. Consequently, the fee tokens are burned from an unrelated account. The root cause is a flawed assumption that msg.sender always represents the token sender, leading to a mismatch between accounting and state updates. An attacker does not need to actively exploit the bug; any user invoking transferFrom() or transferTo() will cause the contract to debit the fee from the wrong address automatically. The impact is incorrect accounting: balances of contracts that happen to be the caller are reduced by the fee amount, while the true sender’s balance reflects only the transferred amount without the fee deduction. This can cause unexpected zero balances or missing funds for the affected contracts, break fee‑based economic models, and potentially lead to fund loss if the burned tokens were meant to be retained by the protocol. The condition under which the bug manifests is any execution path that reaches line 129 of Vader.sol while processing a transferFrom or transferTo call. All token holders who interact with those functions, as well as any contracts that act as intermediaries, are affected. The issue was discovered during a third‑party audit (Code4rena) by examining the flow of arguments through the internal functions and noticing the inconsistent use of msg.sender. It is subtle because the transfer appears to succeed and the burn event is emitted, so observers may assume the fee was correctly deducted from the sender’s balance, masking the accounting error. The flaw belongs to the class of “incorrect message context usage” or “misaligned authority propagation” bugs, where a contract incorrectly relies on msg.sender for permission or accounting decisions instead of using the explicit parameter that represents the logical actor. To remediate the problem the burn call should use the sender argument (or an equivalent variable that reflects the true token holder) as the address from which the fee is destroyed, thereby aligning the fee deduction with the actual participant in the transfer and restoring correct balance accounting.
summary:
The `internal _transfer()` function is called from external facing `transfer()`, `transferFrom()`, and `transferTo()` functions all of which have different sender addresses. It is `msg.sender` for `transfer()`, sender parameter for `transferFrom()` and `tx.origin` for `transferTo()`.

These different senders are reflected in the sender parameter of `_transfer()` function. While this sender parameter is correctly used for transfer of tokens within `_transfer`, the call to `_burn()` on L129 incorrectly uses `msg.sender` as the burn address which is correct only in the case of the `transfer()` caller’s context. This is incorrect for `transferFrom()` and `transferTo()` caller contexts.

This will incorrectly burn the fees from a different (intermediate contract) account for all users of the protocol interacting with the `transferTo()` and `transferFrom()` functions and lead to incorrect accounting of token balances or exceptional conditions. Protocol will break and lead to fund loss.

Recommend changing L129 to: `_burn(sender, _fee);`

Valid, disagree with severity though. Funds-not-at-risk. Recommend: 2

title: Wrong `calcAsymmetricShare` calculation
content:
The vulnerability lies in an incorrect implementation of the asymmetric share calculation, a core component used to translate user‑provided collateral into a base‑token value. The specification, as documented in an inline comment, defines the share as (u * U * (2 * A² - 2 * U * u + U²)) / U³, where A represents the asymmetric factor, u the user’s stake, and U the total stake. The actual code in Utils.calcAsymmetricShare implements (u*A * 2U² - 2uU + u²) / U³, omitting the A² term in the numerator and mis‑applying the multiplication order: the term P * part1 is associated incorrectly and part2 is never multiplied by P. This mismatch means the computed share can be significantly lower or higher than the spec intends, breaking the economic assumption that the collateral value fully covers the borrowed amount. 

Because the asymmetric share feeds the collateral‑valuation routine, an attacker who can supply crafted values for A, u, and U may cause the protocol to record an insufficient collateral requirement. In practice, a borrower could receive a larger loan than the value of the posted collateral, potentially leading to under‑collateralized positions and loss of funds for the protocol. The exploit becomes feasible whenever the faulty function is invoked during a loan or margin‑call operation; currently the function is not wired into the production flow, which is why immediate fund loss is unlikely, but the bug represents a high severity logical flaw that could be activated by future code changes. 

The issue was uncovered during a Code4rena audit by comparing the on‑chain implementation against the published mathematical spec and noticing the missing A² term and the incorrect associativity of multiplications. The problem is subtle because the function is not directly exposed in UI, the comment appears correct, and the arithmetic looks plausible at a glance, making it easy to miss in manual reviews or basic unit tests. 

To remediate, the implementation must be brought into exact alignment with the documented formula: (u * U * (2 * A² - 2 * U * u + U²)) / U³. The code should correctly compute the three sub‑terms, ensure that the P multiplier is applied to both parts of the expression, and include comprehensive test vectors that cover edge cases for A, u, and U. By doing so, the protocol restores the intended accounting guarantees that collateral always covers borrowed funds, eliminating the risk of economic exploitation.
summary:
The inline-comment defines the number of asymmetric shares as `(u * U * (2 * A^2 - 2 * U * u + U^2))/U^3` but the `Utils.calcAsymmetricShare` function computes `(uA * 2U^2 - 2uU + u^2) / U^3` which is not equivalent as can be seen from the `A^2` term in the first term which does not occur in the second one.

The associativity on `P * part1` is wrong, and `part2` is not multiplied by `P`.

The math from the spec is not correctly implemented and could lead to the protocol being economically exploited, as the asymmetric share (which is used to determine the collateral value in base tokens) could be wrong. For example, it might be possible to borrow more than the collateral put up.

Recommend clarifying if the comment or the code is correct and fix them if not.

Valid

Whilst the math is incorrect, in the current implementation it is not yet implemented, so disagree with Severity (funds not lost), recommend: 2

title: Wrong liquidity units calculation
content: The vulnerability consists of an incorrect implementation of the liquidity‑unit minting formula in the protocol’s utility library. According to the specification, the number of LP units that should be minted when a user adds liquidity is calculated as units = P * (a * B + A * b) / (2 * A * B) * slipAdjustment, where P is the price factor and slipAdjustment accounts for slippage. The actual code in Utils.calcLiquidityUnits evaluates the expression as ((P * part1) + part2) / part3 * slipAdjustment, omitting the multiplication of the second term (part2) by P and applying the multiplication in the wrong order. This associative error means the computed number of LP tokens deviates from the intended economic model. As a result, a user who supplies liquidity receives a quantity of LP tokens that does not correctly represent the value of the deposited assets. When those LP tokens are later redeemed, the protocol returns fewer underlying tokens than the provider originally supplied, effectively allowing an economic exploit where the protocol loses assets while the attacker can capture the surplus. The flaw is triggered whenever the calcLiquidityUnits function is invoked during liquidity provision, which is a routine operation for any liquidity provider. All participants who rely on the LP token’s proportional claim to the pool – including ordinary users, automated market makers, and other contracts interacting with the pool – are affected because the accounting invariant is broken. The issue was uncovered by a formal audit performed by Code4rena, which compared the implementation against the documented formula and identified the mismatch. The problem may be hard to detect in ordinary testing because the numerical discrepancy can be small for typical input sizes, and the symptoms manifest only when redemption is performed after multiple liquidity actions, making the loss appear as an incremental drift rather than an outright error. From a user’s perspective, the UI might show that a deposit succeeded, but later the user observes that the balance of withdrawn tokens is lower than expected, or that a refund amount appears to be zero when it should be positive. The bug belongs to the class of arithmetic‑logic errors, specifically incorrect order of operations and missing multiplicative factors in financial calculations. To remediate the issue, the utility function must be rewritten to follow the specification verbatim: both terms inside the parentheses must be multiplied by P before division by (2 * A * B), and the slipAdjustment factor must be applied to the final result. This correction restores the intended proportional relationship between deposited assets and minted LP tokens, preserving the economic integrity of the protocol.
summary:
The spec defines the number of LP units to be minted as `units = (P (a B + A b))/(2 A B) * slipAdjustment = P * (part1 + part2) / part3 * slipAdjustments` but the `Utils.calcLiquidityUnits` function computes `((P * part1) + part2) / part3 * slipAdjustments`.

The associativity on `P * part1` is wrong, and `part2` is not multiplied by `P`.

The math from the spec is not correctly implemented and could lead to the protocol being economically exploited, as redeeming the minted LP tokens does not result in the initial tokens anymore.

Recommend fixing the equation.

Valid, but funds not at risk.

title: Incorrect initialization gives IL protection of only 1 second instead of 100 days in Router.sol
content: The vulnerability stems from an incorrect initialization of the time constant that governs the Impermanent Loss (IL) protection schedule in the Router contract. The variable timeForFullProtection is set to 1 second, while the protocol specification and code comments state that full protection should be reached after 100 days (8640000 seconds). This discrepancy originates from a test configuration that was inadvertently left in the production code, and the only function capable of correcting the value – setParams() – is not currently callable by the DAO, meaning the erroneous setting persists on live deployments. The protection calculation in Utils.getProtection() linearly scales the protection percentage based on the elapsed time since a deposit divided by timeForFullProtection. With the constant set to 1 second, any user who waits more than a second after depositing will instantly receive 100 % IL protection. Consequently, when a withdrawal results in a loss relative to the original deposit, the protocol’s reserve is required to cover the entire deficit, eroding the reserve balance much faster than intended. This breaks the core economic promise of the Vader protocol: that protection ramps up slowly over roughly three months, allowing the system to manage risk and fee income. The bug manifests whenever a member deposits and later withdraws, as the UI will show a full‑protection percentage almost immediately, contradicting user expectations of a gradual increase. Affected parties include liquidity providers, token holders, and the DAO that relies on reserve stability. The issue was discovered during a code audit when reviewers compared the implementation against the documented 100‑day protection model and observed the mismatched constant. Because the variable is a simple uint256 with a plausible small value, the error can be easily missed in manual testing, especially if the test suite only exercises short‑duration scenarios. This class of flaw is a misconfiguration or improper constant initialization that leads to a logical error in time‑based incentive mechanisms. To remediate the problem, the contract should initialize timeForFullProtection to 8640000 seconds (or another correctly calibrated period) and ensure that the DAO can safely update the parameter through a controlled governance function. Adding explicit unit tests that assert the protection period matches the specification would further prevent recurrence. The overall impact is a potential drain of reserve funds, undermining the protocol’s sustainability and user trust.
summary:
Incorrect initialization of `timeForFullProtection` to 1 sec instead of 8640000 secs (100 days) as indicated in code comments, appears to be a test setting mistakenly carried over for deployment. Therefore, unless `timeForFullProtection` is reset to 100 days by `setParams()` (calling this function is a missing functionality in the DAO currently), the Impermanent Loss (IL) protection “rule” of 100 days will not apply in `Utils.getProtection()`.

This breaks a key value proposition of the Vader protocol which is IL protection as indicated in the specification:

“Impermanent Loss Protection: The deposit value for each member is recorded when they deposit. When they go to withdraw, the redemption value is computed. If it is less than the deposit value, the member is paid the deficit from the reserve. The protection issued increases from 0 to 100% linearly for 100 days.”

Recommend changing to “timeForFullProtection = 8640000; //100 days” on L84

It’s deliberately set to 1 second to conduct adequate testing.

title: Anyone can list anchors / curate tokens
content: The vulnerability resides in the router's anchor management functions, specifically Router.listAnchor and Router.replaceAnchor, which are intended to curate a limited set of token anchors that qualify for reward distribution. The contract only checks that a token is recognized as an anchor by calling require(iPOOLS(POOLS).isAnchor(token)). However, this flag is set opportunistically in Pools.addLiquidity when any user supplies a token to add liquidity, even if no actual tokens are transferred. Consequently, an attacker can call addLiquidity with a chosen token, trigger the internal _isAnchor[token] flag, and then invoke listAnchor to register that token as a curated anchor without any further validation. This flaw is exploitable while the anchorLimit has not been reached, and later via replaceAnchor, which also relies on the current reserves for its price‑range checks. By employing flash loans, an attacker can temporarily inflate the reserves of a malicious token, satisfy the reserve‑based checks, replace a legitimate anchor, and withdraw the associated rewards. The manipulated anchor can then be used to push a genuine anchor out of the acceptable price window, effectively stripping it of its reward eligibility. After the malicious anchor is in place, the attacker can withdraw the liquidity added during the flash‑loan, leaving the price of the new anchor vulnerable to further manipulation in the next block, which may open additional attack vectors such as price oracle skewing or fee exploitation. The impact is that the protocol’s reward distribution logic is subverted, honest token pools lose their reward share, and the overall economic incentives of the system can be distorted. Users who expect to earn rewards from anchored pools may see their earnings disappear or be redirected to the attacker’s controlled token. The issue was uncovered during a Code4rena audit through logical analysis of the anchor registration flow and testing of the addLiquidity pathway. It is subtle because the require statement appears to enforce a legitimate anchor check, masking the fact that the flag can be set arbitrarily. To remediate the problem, the listAnchor and replaceAnchor functions should be restricted to trusted governance (DAO‑only) and fortified against flash‑loan manipulation, for example by using time‑weighted average prices rather than instantaneous reserves for bounds checks. Additionally, the internal _isAnchor flag should only be set after robust verification of the token’s legitimacy, such as confirming sufficient on‑chain liquidity, token provenance, or a governance‑approved whitelist.
summary:
The `Router.listAnchor` function can be called by anyone and tokens can be added. The only check is that `require(iPOOLS(POOLS).isAnchor(token));` but this can easily be set by calling `Pools.addLiquidity(VADER, token, _)` once even without actually sending any tokens to the contract. This makes it an essentially useless check.

This only works initially as long as the `anchorLimit` has not been reached yet. However, the `replaceAnchor` can be used in the same way and flash loans can be used to get around the liquidity restrictions and push another anchor token out of the price range as these checks use the current reserves.

Anchored pools are automatically curated pools and determine if a pool receives rewards. An attacker can remove rewards of a curated pool this way and add rewards to their own pool with a custom token they control.

After a pool has been anchored through flash loans, liquidity can be withdrawn which could make the anchor price easy to manipulate in the next block and launch other attacks.

Recommend revisiting the `_isAnchor[token] = true;` statement in `addLiquidity`, it seems strange without any further checks. Consider making `listAnchor` / `replaceAnchor` DAO-only functions and make them flash-loan secure. One should probably use time-weighted prices for these pools for the bounds check.

The protocol is intended to be launched with 5 anchors so it can only be attacked by using `replaceAnchor()`, in which case slip-based fees apply for attacks and thwart the attack path.

title: Swap token can be traded as fake base token
content: The vulnerability resides in the pool contract’s swap routine, which assumes that the parameter named base will always represent one of the protocol’s designated base assets (typically USDV or VADER). The function does not enforce this assumption, allowing an attacker to supply any arbitrary ERC‑20 token as the base argument. When a user transfers a token to the pool and calls swap(token, token, member, toBase=false) while also setting base equal to that same token, the contract’s internal accounting misinterprets the transferred amount. Specifically, the helper _actualInput = getAddedAmount(base, token) returns the amount of the transferred token, but the subsequent price calculation uses the pool’s recorded base reserve (mapToken_baseAmount) as if it were the input reserve. This mismatched ratio (tokenIn / baseReserve * tokenReserve) produces an incorrect output amount, inflating the amount of the opposite asset that the attacker receives and simultaneously corrupting the pool’s balance sheets. Consequently, the pool’s token balance is reduced while its base balance is artificially increased, breaking the invariant that LPs rely on for accurate withdrawals. Under certain conditions—such as sending an amount equal to the current base reserve as the fake base token—an attacker can extract a disproportionate share of the genuine base asset, effectively stealing funds from the pool. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the swap logic and identified the missing validation. It is subtle because the function behaves correctly when the intended base tokens are used, so typical unit tests that only cover legitimate paths may not surface the flaw. The impact includes loss of user funds, inability for liquidity providers to redeem their correct share, and the potential for the pool to become insolvent. To remediate, the contract should enforce that the base argument belongs to an approved whitelist (e.g., USDV or VADER) and should separate the accounting of base and token reserves so that the input amount is always matched against the correct reserve. Conceptually, this is a whitelist‑validation bug leading to a swap‑ratio miscalculation, which violates the core accounting guarantees of an automated market maker and can cause funds to disappear or refunds to be zero when users expect a proper swap.
summary:
The `Pools.swap` function does not check if `base` is one of the base tokens. One can transfer `token`s to the pool and set `base=token` and call `swap(token, token, member, toBase=false)`

The `_actualInput = getAddedAmount(base, token);` will return the **token** amount added but use the ratio compared to the **base** reserve `calcSwapOutput(_actualInput=tokenInput, mapToken_baseAmount[token], mapToken_tokenAmount[token]); = tokenIn / baseAmount * tokenAmount` which yields a wrong swap result.

It breaks the accounting for the pool as `token`s are transferred in, but the `base` balance is increased (and `token` balance decreased). LPs cannot correctly withdraw again, and others cannot correctly swap again.

Another example scenario is that the token pool amount can be stolen. Send `tokenIn=baseAmount` of tokens to the pool and call `swap(base=token, token, member, toBase=false)`. Depending on the price of `token` relative to `base` this could be cheaper than trading with the base tokens.

Recommend checking that `base` is either `USDV` or `VADER`.

Valid, funds can be lost

title: `getAddedAmount` can return wrong results
content: The contract contains an accounting flaw in the function that calculates the amount added to a pool, referred to as getAddedAmount. The routine assumes that the token argument either matches the special VADER/USDV pair or is the same as the pool identifier. When the function is invoked with an arbitrary token that does not satisfy either condition, it mistakenly reads the balance of the supplied token and subtracts that value from a stored amount that belongs to a different token (the pool). This mismatch corrupts the internal map that tracks token amounts per pool. Because the contract does not verify that the token argument corresponds to the pool, an attacker can call the sync function with two unrelated token addresses—choosing token1 whose on‑chain balance is lower than the stored amount for token2. The sync logic then adds the difference to the stored amount for token2, inflating the pool’s recorded balance without moving any real tokens. Subsequent calls to the swap function can then exploit the inflated accounting to obtain tokens without providing the required payment, effectively allowing free swaps. The vulnerability manifests whenever getAddedAmount is called with a token that is not the pool, which can happen in normal user interactions or through crafted calls. All participants of the protocol—regular users, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself—are exposed because the corrupted accounting can lead to loss of funds, erroneous swap fees, and a breach of the expected invariant that pool balances reflect actual token holdings. The issue was uncovered during a security audit by Code4rena, where the auditors noted that the function works correctly only for a limited set of inputs and that the missing validation makes the bug subtle; the contract continues to operate but the internal accounting silently diverges from reality, making the problem difficult to detect through casual testing. To remediate the flaw, the contract should enforce that the token supplied to getAddedAmount matches the pool identifier before performing any arithmetic, for example by inserting a require statement that rejects mismatched arguments. A more robust fix would involve redesigning the accounting logic so that each token’s balance is always paired with its corresponding stored amount, eliminating any reliance on implicit token ordering. This change restores the invariant that the recorded pool amount equals the actual token balance, preventing free‑swap attacks and protecting user funds.
summary:
The `getAddedAmount` function only works correctly when called with `(VADER/USDV, pool)` or `(pool, pool)`. However, when called with (`token, pool)` where `token` is neither `VADER/USDV/pool`, it returns the wrong results:

  1. It gets the `token` balance
  2. And subtracts it from the stored `mapToken_tokenAmount[_pool]` amount which can be that of a completely different token

Anyone can break individual pairs by calling `sync(token1, token2)` where the `token1` balance is less than `mapToken_tokenAmount[token2]`. This will add the difference to `mapToken_tokenAmount[token2]` and break the accounting and result in a wrong swap logic.

Furthermore, this can also be used to swap tokens without having to pay anthing with `swap(token1, token2, member, toBase=false)`.

Recommend adding a require statement in the `else` branch that checks that `_token == _pool`.

Valid, funds can be lost

Would bundle this issue with: <https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-04-vader-findings/issues/205>

title: 4 Synths can be minted with fake base token
content: The vulnerability lies in the minting routine of a synthetic asset pool where the function that creates new synth tokens does not verify that the supplied base asset is one of the two authorized base tokens (USDV or VADER). Because the contract accepts any ERC‑20 token as the base parameter, an attacker can transfer an arbitrary token to the pool, set that token as the base argument, and invoke the minting function. The routine calculates the amount of synth to mint by taking the amount of the supplied token that was added to the pool and dividing it by the recorded reserve of the base token, then multiplying by the reserve of the target token. When the base argument is a token that is not actually a base, the contract mistakenly uses the reserve of the real base token (USDV/VADER) while the input amount comes from the attacker‑supplied token. This mismatch yields an inflated swap output, allowing the attacker to mint synths at a price far lower than the market rate. The pool’s accounting is broken: the attacker‑supplied token is credited as a base deposit, while the real base reserve remains unchanged, leading to an inconsistent internal balance sheet. The impact is that synthetic tokens can be created cheaply, diluting the pool’s value and potentially draining funds from honest participants who later trade or withdraw against the corrupted pool. The issue is triggered whenever mintSynth is called with a non‑base token as the base argument – a condition that cannot be prevented by the existing logic because there is no whitelist check. It was discovered during a security audit performed by Code4rena, where the auditors noticed that the function’s parameter validation was incomplete. The flaw is subtle because the contract still executes without reverting, and the incorrect accounting may not be evident until the pool’s balances diverge or users receive unexpected amounts of synths. To remediate, the mintSynth function should enforce that the base argument matches one of the known base token addresses (USDV or VADER) before proceeding, thereby restoring the intended price relationship and preserving accounting integrity. Conceptually this belongs to the class of "invalid asset role validation" bugs, where a contract fails to enforce that a parameter represents a specific economic role, leading to erroneous price calculations, fund leakage, and a breach of the protocol’s economic guarantees. From a user’s perspective, a user may observe that a mint transaction returns far more synthetic tokens than anticipated, or that later withdrawals from the pool yield zero or reduced balances, contradicting the expectation that depositing a known amount of base token should produce a proportional amount of synth. The bug violates the fundamental accounting assumption that each pool’s base reserve accurately reflects the total amount of base tokens deposited, breaking the invariant that synthetic supply tracks real collateral.
summary:
The `Pools.mintSynth` function does not check if `base` is one of the base tokens. One can transfer `token`s to the pool and set `base=token` and call `mintSynth(token, token, member)`.

The `_actualInput = getAddedAmount(base, token);` will return the **token** amount added but use the ratio compared to the **base** reserve `calcSwapOutput(_actualInput=tokenInput, mapToken_baseAmount[token], mapToken_tokenAmount[token]); = tokenIn / baseAmount * tokenAmount` which yields a wrong swap result.

It breaks the accounting for the pool as `token`s are transferred in, but the `base` balance is increased.

The amount that is minted could also be inflated (cheaper than sending the actual base tokens), especially if `token` is a high-precision token or worth less than base.

Recommend checking that `base` is either `USDV` or `VADER` in `mintSynth`.

Valid, funds can be lost.

would bundle this issue with: <https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-04-vader-findings/issues/205>

title: Missing access restriction on `lockUnits/unlockUnits`
content: The vulnerability is an authorization bypass in the pool contract's lockUnits and unlockUnits functions. Because there is no access control, any external address can invoke lockUnits and specify an arbitrary member address as the source of pool tokens. The contract will deduct the specified amount from the victim's internal balance and assign the same amount to msg.sender, effectively allowing an attacker to transfer pool tokens from any user without consent. This occurs whenever the lockUnits function is exposed as a public or external entry point, which the code currently permits. The root cause is the missing restriction that should limit calls to a trusted router, owner, or other authorized party. An adversary can exploit the bug by calling lockUnits with the victim's address and a chosen amount, causing the victim's balance to drop while the attacker’s balance rises. The impact is a direct theft of pooled assets, leading to unexpected zero or reduced balances for legitimate users, loss of confidence in the protocol, and potential financial loss for token holders. The issue was identified during a formal security audit (Code4rena) where the function signatures were examined and the lack of modifiers was noted. It can be hard to notice because the function name suggests internal usage and no explicit event is emitted indicating a transfer, so users may only observe their balance unexpectedly decreasing. The bug belongs to the class of access control vulnerabilities where privileged actions are exposed to unauthenticated callers, often resulting in token hijacking or unauthorized state changes.
