It was discovered by auditors during a post‑launch review of the competition code, shortly after the token‑shifting feature was added at the last minute. The issue is subtle because the contract does not revert on the first over‑shift; instead the erroneous state accumulates silently, making the bug hard to detect without deep state inspection. To remediate the problem, the contract should enforce that the sum of the amounts shifted away from both sides in the upcoming price interval does not exceed the user’s total staked balance, adding a combined‑balance check before performing any shift. This class of bug falls under “insufficient cumulative state validation” or “aggregate balance overflow”, where per‑call checks are insufficient to guarantee overall correctness. From a user’s perspective the symptom may appear as an unexpectedly high reward rate, a mismatch between displayed staked balances and actual token holdings, or a sudden change in issuance after a series of shift operations. Users expect that shifting tokens merely reallocates existing stake, not that it can inflate their effective position, and the discrepancy between expectation and reality can lead to confusion and loss of trust in the protocol.
summary:
The `shiftTokens` function of `Staker` checks whether the user has staked at least the number of tokens he wants to shift from one side to the other (line 885). A user could call the `shiftTokens` function multiple times before the next price update to shift the staker’s token from one side to the other with more than he has staked. [Staker.sol#L885](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-08-floatcapital/blob/main/contracts/contracts/Staker.sol#L885)

Recommend adding checks on `userNextPrice_amountStakedSyntheticToken_toShiftAwayFrom_long` and `userNextPrice_amountStakedSyntheticToken_toShiftAwayFrom_short` to ensure that the sum of the two variables does not exceed user’s stake balance.

Yes, spot on! We spotted this the next morning after launching the competition. Token shifting was a last minute addition to the codebase. Really glad someone spotted it, but only in the last few hours, phew!

This would allow a malicious user to completely shift all the tokens (even those not belonging to them to one side or the other!!) No funds could be stolen by the user directly (since the execution of those shifts would fail on the user level), but it could be done for personal gain (eg improving the users FLT issuance rate, or similar economic manipulation).

title: Potential DOS in Contracts Inheriting `UUPSUpgradeable.sol`
content: The vulnerability stems from deploying a proxy contract that uses the UUPSUpgradeable pattern while leaving the underlying implementation contract uninitialized. In the UUPS design, the implementation contract inherits an initializer that also sets the owner role used by the onlyOwner modifier. When the implementation’s initializer is never invoked, the contract’s owner variable remains unset, allowing any external address to call the initialize() function and claim ownership. Once an attacker gains the owner role, they can bypass the _authorizeUpgrade check that normally restricts upgrades to the contract owner. The attacker can then invoke upgradeToAndCall on the proxy, directing the proxy’s delegate call to a malicious contract whose fallback contains a self‑destruct operation. Because the proxy forwards all logic to the implementation via delegatecall, the self‑destruct executed in the context of the proxy eliminates the implementation’s bytecode, rendering the proxy unusable. From a user's perspective the token contract appears to stop working: balances read as zero, transfer attempts revert, and the UI shows no response from the ERC20 functions. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition that blocks all future interactions with the NoteERC20 token until a new implementation is deployed and re‑pointed, effectively freezing the token ecosystem and eroding trust. This scenario occurs only when deployment scripts fail to initialize the implementation contract before the proxy becomes accessible, a mistake highlighted in an OpenZeppelin advisory and demonstrated by a proof‑of‑concept exploit. The issue can be difficult to notice because the proxy operates correctly until an attacker deliberately triggers the upgrade, at which point the contract simply stops responding without obvious on‑chain error messages. To remediate, the implementation contract should be initialized immediately after deployment, setting a proper owner and preventing anyone else from calling initialize. Additionally, deployment processes can renounce ownership of the implementation, use constructor‑based initialization, or adopt a proxy pattern that does not expose the implementation’s initializer to external callers. By ensuring the implementation is locked down before the proxy is exposed, the upgrade path remains secure and the risk of a self‑destruct‑induced denial of service is eliminated.
summary:
There are a number of contracts which inherit `UUPSUpgradeable.sol`, namely; `GovernanceAction.sol`, `PauseRouter.sol` and `NoteERC20.sol`.

All these contracts are deployed using a proxy pattern whereby the implementation contract is used by the proxy contract for all its logic. The proxy contract will make delegate calls to the implementation contract. This helps to facilitate future upgrades by pointing the proxy contract to a new and upgraded implementation contract.

However, if the implementation contract is left uninitialized, it is possible for any user to gain ownership of the `onlyOwner` role in the implementation contract for `NoteERC20.sol`. Once the user has ownership they are able to perform an upgrade of the implementation contract’s logic contract and delegate call into any arbitrary contract, allowing them to self-destruct the proxy’s implementation contract. Consequently, this will prevent all `NoteERC20.sol` interactions until a new implementation contract is deployed.

Initial information about this issue was found [here](https://forum.openzeppelin.com/t/security-advisory-initialize-uups-implementation-contracts/15301).

Consider the following scenario:
  * Notional finance deploys their contracts using their deployment scripts. These deployment scripts leave the implementation contracts uninitialized. Specifically the contract in question is `NoteERC20.sol`.
  * This allows any arbitrary user to call `initialize()` on the `NoteERC20.sol` implementation contract.
  * Once a user has gained control over `NoteERC20.sol`’s implementation contract, they can bypass the `_authorizeUpgrade` check used to restrict upgrades to the `onlyOwner` role.
  * The malicious user then calls `UUPSUpgradeable.upgradeToAndCall()` shown [here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-08-notional/blob/main/contracts/proxy/utils/UUPSUpgradeable.sol#L40-L43) which in turn calls [this](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-08-notional/blob/main/contracts/proxy/ERC1967/ERC1967Upgrade.sol#L77-L107) function. The new implementation contract then points to their own contract containing a self-destruct call in its fallback function.
  * As a result, the implementation contract will be self-destructed due to the user-controlled delegate call shown [here](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/blob/v3.4.0-solc-0.7/contracts/utils/Address.sol#L163-L169), preventing all future calls to the `NoteERC20.sol` proxy contract until a new implementation contract has been deployed.

Recommend considering initializing the implementation contract for `NoteERC20.sol` and checking the correct permissions before deploying the proxy contract or performing any contract upgrades. This will help to ensure the implementation contract cannot be self-destructed.

Acknowledged, I don’t think this should be categorized high risk because the worst case is a denial of service and a redeployment of the ERC20 contract. As it stands, we’ve already successfully deployed our ERC20 contract so this is a non-issue.
I would categorize as `0 (Non-critical)`

Warden leastwood added this proof of concept to illustrate the vulnerability <https://gist.github.com/leastwood/b23d9e975883c817780116c2ceb785b8>

Ok I retract my previous statement, I misread the issue description. Up to you guys but do you want to pay out a full amount to someone who is reporting issues discovered elsewhere? OZ has already called initialize on our deployed contract for us.

@jeffywu (Notional) I think the question is whether the issue is valid based on the original code base. Given your initial response and change after his proof of concept, my read was there was value here in what he reported. Is that a correct understanding?

There was value added here but perhaps not at the same level as the other high risk issues.

title: Liquidity token value can be manipulated
content: The vulnerability originates from the way the protocol calculates the value of a liquidity provider (LP) token. The contract determines the LP token’s worth by summing the cash claim and the fCash claim, each of which is computed as a proportion of the pool’s current reserves (totalAssetCash and totalfCash) multiplied by the LP token amount and divided by the total liquidity supply. Because these calculations use the *instantaneous* reserve balances, the LP token price effectively reflects a spot price rather than a time‑weighted average. An attacker can therefore use a flash loan to deposit or withdraw a large amount of assets into the pool within a single transaction, temporarily shifting the reserve ratios. This manipulation inflates the apparent value of the LP token in the short term. When the manipulated LP token is used as collateral, the protocol’s free‑collateral computation applies a haircut to fCash claims (double‑haircut) but only a single haircut to cash claims. Consequently, although the raw LP token value rises, the *collateralized* value after haircuts can fall, potentially pushing a borrowing account below its required collateralisation threshold and making it eligible for liquidation. The exploit can be triggered when an attacker performs a large trade (either lending or borrowing) that skews the pool’s cash and fCash balances, then quickly supplies the inflated LP token to a borrowing position or uses it to trigger liquidation of an existing position. From the user’s perspective, this may manifest as a sudden loss of borrowing capacity, unexpected liquidation, or a discrepancy where the UI shows a healthy collateral ratio while the contract internally flags the account as under‑collateralised. The issue was identified during a security audit that examined the oracle design and observed that the LP token valuation re‑used the pool’s current reserves, a subtle foot‑gun previously exploited in other contracts. It is hard to detect because the LP token’s raw value appears to increase, which seems beneficial, while the hidden impact of haircuts on the collateral calculation is not obvious from surface‑level metrics. The root cause is the reliance on mutable, on‑chain reserve balances for pricing a financial instrument that should be priced using a price feed resistant to short‑term manipulation. To remediate, the protocol should stop using current reserves when computing LP token value and instead adopt a time‑weighted average price (TWAP) oracle for both the cash and fCash components, or directly price the LP token via its own TWAP. As an immediate mitigation, the system can restrict liquidity provision to trusted nToken accounts, which are not exposed to direct user deposits and therefore cannot be targeted by flash‑loan attacks. Long‑term, integrating dedicated LP‑token TWAP oracles will eliminate the spot‑price dependency and ensure that collateral valuations remain stable under rapid market movements.
summary:
The liquidity token value (`AssetHandler.getLiquidityTokenValue`) is the sum of the value of the individual claims on cash (underlying or rather cTokens) and fCash. The amount to redeem on each of these is computed as the LP token to redeem relative to the total LP tokens, see `AssetHandler.getCashClaims` / `AssetHandler.getHaircutCashClaims`:

```solidity
// @audit token.notional are the LP tokens to redeem
assetCash = market.totalAssetCash.mul(token.notional).div(market.totalLiquidity);
fCash = market.totalfCash.mul(token.notional).div(market.totalLiquidity);
```

This means the value depends on the **current market reserves** which can be manipulated. You’re essentially computing a spot price (even though the individual values use a TWAP price) because you use the current market reserves which can be manipulated.

See the “How do I tell if I’m using spot price?” section [here](https://shouldiusespotpriceasmyoracle.com/).

However, by doing this you’re actually incorporating the spot price because you’re still dependent on the reserve balances of the pool. This is an extremely subtle detail, and more than one project has been caught by it. You can read more about this [footgun](https://cmichel.io/pricing-lp-tokens/) in this writeup by @cmichelio.

The value of an LP token is computed as `assetCashClaim + assetRate.convertFromUnderlying( presentValue(fCashClaim) )`, where `(assetCashClaim, fCashClaim)` depends on the current market reserves which can be manipulated by an attacker via flashloans. Therefore, an attacker trading large amounts in the market can either increase or decrease the value of an LP token.

If the value decreases, they can try to liquidate users borrowing against their LP tokens / nTokens. If the value increases, they can borrow against it and potentially receive an under-collateralized borrow this way, making a profit.

The exact profitability of such an attack depends on the AMM as the initial reserve manipulation and restoring the reserves later incurs fees and slippage. In constant-product AMMs like Uniswap it’s profitable and several projects have already been exploited by this, like [warp.finance](https://cmichel.io/pricing-lp-tokens/). However, Notional Finance uses a more complicated AMM and the contest was too short for me to do a more thorough analysis. It seems like a similar attack could be possible here as described by the developers when talking about a different context of using TWAP oracles:

> “Oracle rate protects against short term price manipulation. Time window will be set to a value on the order of minutes to hours. This is to protect fCash valuations from market manipulation. For example, a trader could use a flash loan to dump a large amount of cash into the market and depress interest rates. Since we value fCash in portfolios based on these rates, portfolio values will decrease and they may then be liquidated.” - Market.sol L424

Recommend not using the current market reserves to determine the value of LP tokens. Also, think about how to implement a TWAP oracle for the LP tokens themselves, instead of combining it from the two TWAPs of the claimables.

It is true that a flash loan could be used to manipulate the value of a liquidity token’s cash and fCash claims. This issue can potentially cause accounts to be liquidated which shouldn’t be, but not for the reasons stated in this issue. I’ll explain what actually can go wrong, and why the fix is simple and non-invasive.

First, to restate the issue: The manipulator could borrow or lend a large amount to a liquidity pool, which would change the amount of cash and fCash sitting in that pool and the corresponding cash and fCash claims of a liquidity token associated with that pool. This could change the liquidity token’s net value within the space of a transaction despite the fact that the oracleRate used to value fCash is lagged and manipulation resistant.

But it is not true that this manipulation could decrease the value of a liquidity token - in fact it could only increase a liquidity token’s value. By borrowing or lending a large amount using a flash loan, the interest rate that the attacker would receive would deviate from the oracleRate in favor of the liquidity provider. If the attacker executed a large lend order, the interest rate on the loan would be significantly below the oracleRate. This would mean that the liquidity providers had borrowed at a below-market rate and that the net value of that trade would be positive for them. Conversely if the attacker executed a large borrow order, the interest rate on the loan would be significantly above the oracleRate. Again, this would mean that the net value of that trade would be positive for the liquidity providers because they would effectively be lending at an above-market rate. In either case, the value of the liquidity token would increase, not decrease.

However, even though the value of a liquidity token could only increase during such an attack, the collateral value of the liquidity token could decrease once the haircuts were applied in the free collateral calculation. The reason for this is that fCash claims are effectively double-haircut (once by the liquidity token haircut and once by the fCash haircut), whereas cash claims are only haircut once (by the liquidity token haircut). This means that even though the attack would increase the value of the liquidity token without haircuts, once you consider the haircuts applied in the free collateral calculation, the collateral value of the liquidity token can be decreased and accounts could become undercollateralized and eligible for liquidation.

**Remediation:** The immediate remediation for this issue is to restrict providing liquidity to the nToken account exclusively. In the longer term, we will plan to add TWAPs to determine the collateral value of liquidity token cash and fCash claims. This immediate remediation will be fine for now though, and will not degrade the system for two reasons:
  1. The team does not anticipate users providing liquidity directly outside of the nToken (we don’t even offer a way to do it within the UI for example). Only nToken holders receive NOTE incentives, not direct liquidity providers.
  2. The nToken accounts are safe from this attack because the maximum amount that an attacker could temporarily decrease the collateral value of liquidity tokens could never be enough to cause the nToken accounts to become undercollateralized, and therefore they would never be at risk of liquidation due to this attack. The TLDR here is that this attack can’t actually decrease the collateral value of liquidity tokens all that much, and so for an account to be vulnerable they would have to be running quite close to minimum collateralization. This will never happen for the nToken because it doesn’t borrow, it just provides liquidity and always maintains very healthy collateralization levels.

Again, I gave it some thought and I think that this is high risk. Keeping as is.

title: Self transfer can lead to unlimited mint
content: The vulnerability resides in a custom implementation of the token transfer function used by the Notional protocol. Unlike a standard ERC20 transfer, this function incorporates an incentive calculation that can produce a negative transfer amount when the sender and recipient are the same address (a self‑transfer). The code subsequently converts this negative amount back to a positive value before finalizing the transfer, effectively minting new tokens out of thin air. The root cause is the absence of a check that prevents a user from specifying the same address for both sender and recipient, combined with flawed arithmetic that treats a negative incentive as a legitimate positive mint. An attacker can invoke the transfer through the nTokenERC20Proxy, passing their own address as both sender and recipient. The contract then records a negative amount, flips its sign, and credits the attacker with additional tokens without any corresponding debit, allowing unlimited token creation. This manipulation breaks the token’s accounting model, inflates the attacker’s balance, and can erode the economic integrity of the entire protocol, harming all token holders and downstream applications that rely on the token’s fixed supply semantics. The issue was identified during a manual code audit that compared the function against the ERC20 specification and noticed the unconventional handling of self‑transfers. Because the transfer does not revert or emit an obvious error, the problem can remain hidden unless the balance changes are closely inspected. To remediate, the transfer logic should enforce a condition that the sender and recipient differ, or redesign the incentive accounting so that self‑transfers cannot generate a negative amount that is later reverted to positive. In broader terms, this bug belongs to the class of unchecked self‑transfer or arithmetic manipulation vulnerabilities, where malformed accounting enables unauthorized minting. From a user’s perspective, the symptoms may appear as unexpected balance increases, zero tokens being deducted while new tokens appear, or refunds that do not match the sent amount, contradicting the expectation that a transfer merely moves existing tokens between parties.
summary:
The implementation of the transfer function in [`nTokenAction.sol`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-08-notional/blob/main/contracts/external/actions/nTokenAction.sol) is different from the usual erc20 token transfer function.

This happens because it counts the incentive that the user gets, but with a self-transfer, it can lead to unlimited mint. In [L278](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-08-notional/blob/main/contracts/external/actions/nTokenAction.sol#_L278), it makes the amount negative, but in [L279](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-08-notional/blob/main/contracts/external/actions/nTokenAction.sol#L279), it returns the value to an amount that is not negative. So, in the [L281-282](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-08-notional/blob/main/contracts/external/actions/nTokenAction.sol#L281-282), it finalizes a positive value, only because the negative value is changed to the positive value.

You can interact with this transfer function through [nTokenERC20Proxy.sol](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-08-notional/blob/main/contracts/external/adapters/nTokenERC20Proxy.sol).

Recommend adding `(sender != recipient)`.

```solidity
// @audit sender can be passed in by the attacker
require(sender == address(this), "Unauthorized callback");
```

title: DAO proposals can be executed by anyone due to vulnerable `TimelockController`
content: The vulnerability resides in a governance contract that inherits from a TimelockController implementation with a flawed execution flow. The contract’s batch execution routine (_executeBatch) verifies that a proposal was scheduled only after it has already performed the calls in the batch. Because the state check is placed after execution, an attacker can embed a call that schedules the very same batch within the batch itself. When the custom executeProposal function omits the original queued‑state requirement, any user who can submit a proposal—meeting only the minimal proposal threshold—can trigger the batch without possessing the EXECUTOR_ROLE. By crafting a proposal that first grants themselves the TIMELOCK ADMIN, PROPOSER, and EXECUTOR roles, then reduces the timelock delay to zero, and finally calls a malicious contract that schedules the batch, the attacker escalates privileges and executes arbitrary transactions in a single transaction. This exploit can be carried out by anyone able to create a proposal, effectively turning the DAO’s GovernorAlpha into an open‑door for the attacker to act as the timelock admin. The impact is severe: the attacker can invoke any function the DAO controls, such as updating critical parameters like the globalTransferOperator or transferring all tokens out of the protocol, resulting in loss of funds and complete takeover of governance logic. The issue occurs only when the governance contract uses the vulnerable version of TimelockController (OpenZeppelin 3.4.0) and the custom executeProposal bypasses the queued‑state check. It was discovered during a formal security audit when the auditors noticed that the batch execution order allowed a self‑referential schedule call, and a proof‑of‑concept test confirmed the privilege escalation. The flaw is subtle because the contract still respects the timelock delay for normal operations, so the missing state check can be easily overlooked, especially when the UI shows proposals being executed as expected. To remediate, the contract should be upgraded to a patched TimelockController version (e.g., OpenZeppelin 4.3.1 or later) where the schedule verification occurs before execution, and the custom executeProposal should reinstate the queued‑state requirement. This aligns the implementation with the intended security model where only authorized proposer and executor roles may schedule and execute delayed operations, preserving the integrity of the DAO’s governance and preventing arbitrary fund transfers.
summary:
The `GovernorAlpha` inherits from a vulnerable `TimelockController`. This `TimelockController` allows an `EXECUTOR` role to escalate privileges and also gain the proposer role. See details on [OZ](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/security/advisories/GHSA-fg47-3c2x-m2wr) and the [fix here](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/compare/v4.3.0...v4.3.1).

The bug is that `_executeBatch` checks if the proposal was scheduled only **after** the transactions have been executed. This allows inserting a call into the batch that schedules the batch itself, and the entire batch will succeed. As the custom `GovernorAlpha.executeProposal` function removed the original “queued state check” (`require(state(proposalId) == ProposalState.Queued`), the attack can be executed by anyone, even without the `EXEUCTOR_ROLE`.

**Proof of concept** :
  1. Create a proposal using `propose`. The `calldata` will be explained in the next step. (This can be done by anyone passing the min `proposalThreshold`)
  2. Call `executeProposal(proposalId, ...)` such that the following calls are made:

    call-0: grantRole(TIME_LOCK_ADMIN, attackerContract)
    call-1: grantRole(EXECUTOR, attackerContract)
    call-2: grantRole(PROPOSER, attackerContract)
    call-3: updateDelay(0) // such that _afterCall "isOperationReady(id): timestamp[id] = block.timestamp + minDelay (0) <= block.timestamp" passes
    call-4: attackerContract.hello() // this calls timelock.schedule(args=[targets, values, datas, ...]) where args were previously already stored in contract. (this is necessary because id depends on this function's args and we may not be self-referential)
    // attackerContract is proposer & executor now and can directly call scheduleBatch & executeBatch without having to create a proposal

I already talked to Jeff Wu about this and he created a test case for it confirming this finding

The impact is that, anyone who can create a proposal can become `Timelock` admin (proposer & executor) and execute arbitrary transactions as the DAO-controlled `GovernorAlpha`. Note that this contract has severe privileges and an attacker can now do anything that previously required approval of the DAO. For example, they could update the `globalTransferOperator` and steal all tokens.

Recommend updating the vulnerable contract to `TimelockController v3.4.2` as it currently uses `OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts@3.4.0-solc-0.7`

title: `CompoundToNotionalV2.notionalCallback` ERC20 return values not checked
content: The vulnerability consists of an unchecked ERC‑20 token transfer pattern within the callback that the protocol uses to move underlying assets. The contract calls the standard IERC20.transferFrom function assuming that the token contract will return a boolean indicating success, as required by the current ERC‑20 specification. However, several widely used tokens, most notably USDT, implement an older version of the interface where the function returns no value (void) and instead reverts when the caller expects a return value. Because the callback does not verify the returned data nor employ a safe wrapper, the call to transferFrom will always trigger a revert when such a non‑standard token is supplied. This condition occurs whenever a user supplies a cToken whose underlying asset is a token that does not conform to the latest ERC‑20 spec. The immediate impact is that any operation that depends on moving that underlying token—such as supplying collateral, borrowing, or redeeming—fails, causing the transaction to revert and the user's funds to remain locked in the contract. From a user’s perspective the UI may display a generic "transaction failed" error, or the expected balance update never occurs, leading to confusion and the impression that funds have disappeared or that the protocol is broken. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit of the contract’s external token interactions, where the auditor observed that the code directly called IERC20.transferFrom without any safety checks. The flaw can be hard to notice because the source code looks correct at a glance; the missing return value is a subtle incompatibility that only manifests with certain tokens, and typical static analysis tools may not flag it as a failure. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of "unchecked external call" vulnerabilities where an assumed contract interface does not match the actual implementation, leading to unexpected reverts. To remediate the problem, the contract should replace raw transfer calls with a safe wrapper such as OpenZeppelin’s SafeERC20 library, using safeTransferFrom and safeTransfer which correctly handle tokens that return no value or that revert on failure. This ensures that the protocol gracefully handles both compliant and non‑compliant ERC‑20 tokens, preserving user funds and maintaining expected business logic for collateral movements.
summary:
Some tokens (like USDT) don’t correctly implement the EIP20 standard and their `transfer`/`transferFrom` functions return `void`, instead of a success boolean. Calling these functions with the correct EIP20 function signatures will always revert. See `CompoundToNotionalV2.notionalCallback`’s `IERC20(underlyingToken).transferFrom` call.

Tokens that don’t correctly implement the latest EIP20 spec, like USDT, will be unusable in the protocol as they revert the transaction because of the missing return value. The fact that there is a `cToken` with `USDT` as the underlying this issue directly applies to the protocol.

We recommend using OpenZeppelin’s `SafeERC20` versions with the `safeTransfer` and `safeTransferFrom` functions that handle the return value check as well as non-standard-compliant tokens.

title: Access restrictions on `CompoundToNotionalV2.notionalCallback` can be bypassed
content: The vulnerability resides in the `CompoundToNotionalV2.notionalCallback` function, which is intended to be invoked only by the contract that orchestrates the callback. The function attempts to enforce this restriction with the statement `require(sender == address(this), "Unauthorized callback");`. However, the `sender` variable is supplied as an external parameter to the function, meaning an attacker can choose any value for it when calling the function directly. Because the access check validates the caller‑provided `sender` rather than the actual `msg.sender`, the intended authentication is effectively bypassed. An attacker can therefore invoke `notionalCallback` themselves, supplying a victim’s address as the `account` argument. The victim must have previously approved the contract to transfer the relevant ERC‑20 token, which is a normal prerequisite for legitimate users who intend to interact with the outer protocol function. By front‑running the victim’s approval transaction, the attacker can call `notionalCallback` in the same block, causing the contract to execute `IERC20(underlyingToken).transferFrom(account, address(this), cTokenRepayAmount)`. This transfers the approved tokens from the victim to the contract. The subsequent call to `repayBorrowBehalf` can be supplied with a malicious cToken whose `repayBorrowBehalf` implementation does nothing, leaving the transferred assets locked inside the contract without any corresponding repayment. From the user’s point of view the approved tokens seemingly disappear; the UI shows a reduced balance or zero balance for the approved token, and the user receives no refund or acknowledgment of a successful operation. The impact is that funds become irretrievable (effectively burnt) and the protocol’s accounting invariants are broken because the expected free‑collateral check at the end of the callback is no longer valid. The flaw was identified during a Code4rena audit by examining the logical flow of the callback and noticing that the access control relies on a mutable argument rather than an immutable property of the call. The issue is difficult to notice because a superficial review sees a require statement that appears to protect the function, and the contract does not emit any events indicating an unauthorized transfer. Conceptually, this is an *improper authorization* or *access‑control bypass* bug, where a caller‑controlled parameter is trusted for security decisions. To remediate, the contract should replace the `sender` parameter with a check against `msg.sender`, enforce that only the designated orchestrating contract can call `notionalCallback`, and remove any reliance on externally supplied identifiers for authentication. Additional safeguards, such as validating the underlying token address and preventing arbitrary token transfers, would further mitigate the risk of token loss.

title: Access restrictions on `NotionalV1ToNotionalV2.notionalCallback` can be bypassed
content: The vulnerability resides in the callback function of the migration bridge between Notional V1 and V2, where the contract attempts to restrict who can invoke the `notionalCallback` by comparing a user‑supplied `sender` argument to its own address. Because `sender` is passed in as an external parameter, an attacker can call the function directly and arbitrarily set `sender` to the contract’s address, thereby bypassing the intended authorization check. Once the check is bypassed, the attacker can supply any `account` value, causing the bridge to treat the victim’s account as the source of funds. The attack flow consists of two steps: first, the attacker induces the victim to approve the bridge contract and then front‑runs a withdrawal transaction that moves the victim’s collateral (for example WBTC) into the bridge’s balance while simultaneously depositing an equivalent amount of a cheaper asset (such as DAI) on the V2 side; second, the attacker initiates a deposit transaction using the same callback but with `account` set to the attacker’s address, effectively re‑depositing the stolen collateral back into the V1 system under the attacker’s control. The impact is a complete loss of the victim’s migrated tokens, meaning users who attempt to migrate their positions may see their balances become zero or receive an unexpected asset, breaking the protocol’s accounting guarantees and violating the expectation that migration is a trustless operation. This condition can occur whenever a user initiates a migration and approves the bridge contract, providing an attack surface that is exploitable during the narrow time window between approval and the migration transaction, especially in a front‑running scenario. The vulnerability was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the access‑control logic of the callback and identified that the `require(sender == address(this))` condition relied on a mutable argument rather than an immutable source such as `msg.sender`. The flaw is subtle because the code superficially appears to enforce a restriction, yet the check does not actually verify the caller, making it easy to overlook during a superficial review. To remediate, the contract should eliminate the `sender` parameter entirely, enforce that only the trusted Notional V1 contract can invoke the callback by checking `msg.sender`, and/or use a dedicated access‑control modifier that references a hard‑coded whitelist. By grounding the authorization in the immutable caller identity rather than a mutable argument, the bridge can prevent unauthorized withdrawals and preserve users’ funds during migration.
summary:
The `NotionalV1ToNotionalV2.notionalCallback` is supposed to only be called from the verified contract that calls this callback but the access restrictions can be circumvented by simply providing `sender = this` as `sender` is a parameter of the function that can be chosen by the attacker.

```solidity
function notionalCallback(
    address sender,
    address account,
    bytes calldata callbackData
) external returns (uint256) {
    require(sender == address(this), "Unauthorized callback");
```

An attacker can call the function passing in an arbitrary `account` whose tokens can then be stolen. The `account` first has to approve this contract but this can happen with accounts that legitimately want to migrate their tokens and therefore have to send a first transaction to approve the contract, but then an attacker frontruns the actual migration transaction.

The attacker can steal the tokens by performing an attack similar to the following:
  * first transaction is used to withdraw the victim’s funds to the contract. This can be done by choosing `account=victim`, `v1RepayAmount=0`, `v1CollateralId=WBTC`, `v2CollateralId=DAI`. The [`NotionalV1Erc1155.batchOperationWithdraw`](https://github.com/notional-finance/contracts/blob/4bf7a85e6cf81cde4283e0efab0b03f21249ba00/contracts/ERC1155Trade.sol#L108) (not part of this contest) will withdraw the victim’s funds to this contract. Note that the attacker has to deposit the same `v2CollateralBalance = uint256(collateralBalance)` for the victim into the V2 version, but they can choose different cheaper collateral (for example, withdraw WBTC, deposit same amount of DAI).
  * second transaction is now used to deposit the victim funds in the contract into the user’s account. They use `account=attacker`, `v1DebtCurrencyId=WBTC`, `v1RepayAmount=amount` to deposit it into Notional V1. (They need to have a small `collateralBalance`, etc. to pass all checks).

Recommend fixing the authorization check.

title: `TokenHandler.safeTransferOut` does not work on non-standard compliant tokens like USDT
content: The vulnerability lies in the TokenHandler.safeTransferOut function, which attempts to move ERC‑20 tokens by calling token.transfer(account, amount) through the standard IERC20 interface and then runs a checkReturnCode routine intended to handle tokens that do not return a boolean value. The root cause is a mismatch between the assumed ERC‑20 compliance and the actual behavior of non‑standard tokens such as USDT, which implement transfer() without returning any data. Because the Solidity compiler expects a boolean return from the IERC20.transfer call, the lack of return data triggers an automatic revert before the custom checkReturnCode logic can execute. This defect can be exploited indirectly: any user attempting to deposit, withdraw, or otherwise move a non‑standard token through the affected contract will experience a transaction revert, effectively causing a denial‑of‑service for that asset. The impact is high, as deposits for USDT – a widely used stablecoin and a valid underlying for the cUSDT cToken – are broken, preventing users from interacting with the protocol as intended, and potentially leading to confusion when balances appear unchanged or disappear after a failed transaction. The condition occurs every time safeTransferOut is invoked with a token that does not conform to the ERC‑20 return‑value convention, which includes popular tokens like USDT. All participants who rely on the protocol to handle such assets – end‑users, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit, where the auditor observed that the fallback check never runs for non‑standard tokens because the call reverts earlier, a nuance that can be missed in standard testing suites that only use compliant mock tokens. The bug is subtle because the contract appears to handle return codes correctly, yet the underlying call fails silently from the developer’s perspective. To remediate the problem, the transfer should be performed via a library such as OpenZeppelin’s SafeERC20, which employs a low‑level call and explicitly checks for success without relying on a boolean return, thereby supporting both compliant and non‑compliant ERC‑20 implementations. In essence, this is a classic case of improper handling of non‑standard token interfaces, leading to broken business logic where expected refunds or deposits never materialize, causing user balances to remain zero despite the user’s expectation of a successful transfer.
summary:
The `TokenHandler.safeTransferOut` function uses the standard `IERC20` function for the transfer call and proceeds with a `checkReturnCode` function to handle non-standard compliant tokens that don’t return a return value. However, this does not work, as calling `token.transfer(account, amount)` already reverts if the token does not return a return value, as `token`’s `IERC20.transfer` is defined to always return a `boolean`.

The impact is that, when using any non-standard compliant token like USDT, the function will revert. Deposits for these tokens are broken, which is bad as `USDT` is a valid underlying for the `cUSDT` cToken.

We recommend using [OpenZeppelin’s `SafeERC20`](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/blob/release-v4.1/contracts/token/ERC20/utils/SafeERC20.sol#L74) versions with the `safeApprove` function that handles the return value check as well as non-standard-compliant tokens.

title: `TokenHandler.safeTransferIn` does not work on non-standard compliant tokens like USDT
content: The vulnerability resides in the TokenHandler.safeTransferIn function, which attempts to move ERC‑20 tokens into the protocol by calling token.transferFrom(account, amount) through the standard IERC20 interface and then running a checkReturnCode helper that is supposed to accommodate tokens that do not return a boolean value. The root cause is that the IERC20.transferFrom definition always expects a boolean return; when a non‑standard token such as USDT, which implements transferFrom without returning any value, is called, the Solidity compiler inserts a check that the call returns a boolean. Because USDT does not provide this return data, the low‑level call reverts before the custom checkReturnCode logic can execute. Consequently, any withdrawal operation that relies on safeTransferIn for a non‑standard token fails, reverting the whole transaction. This bug manifests when users attempt to withdraw USDT from the cUSDT market: the transaction reverts, the user’s UI may display an error or simply show no change in balance, and the expected refund never arrives. The impact is that funds become effectively locked for users holding non‑standard tokens, breaking the core functionality of the protocol’s lending market and potentially eroding trust. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined token handling paths and identified that the fallback return‑code check never triggered for tokens lacking a return value. It can be difficult to notice because the function name safeTransferIn suggests safety, and the revert appears as a generic transfer failure rather than an explicit incompatibility, leading developers to suspect other causes. This class of bug falls under ERC‑20 compatibility problems, specifically the mishandling of tokens that deviate from the ERC‑20 specification by omitting return values. To remediate, the contract should replace the direct IERC20 call with a wrapper that uses low‑level calls and explicitly checks success, such as OpenZeppelin’s SafeERC20 library, which safely handles both standard and non‑standard tokens by checking the call’s success flag and handling missing return data. By adopting such a pattern, the protocol can correctly process USDT and similar tokens, ensuring that withdrawals succeed and user balances are updated as expected.
summary:
The `TokenHandler.safeTransferIn` function uses the standard `IERC20` function for the transfer call and proceeds with a `checkReturnCode` function to handle non-standard compliant tokens that don’t return a return value. However, this does not work, as calling `token.transferFrom(account, amount)` already reverts if the token does not return a return value, as `token`’s `IERC20.transferFrom` is defined to always return a `boolean`.

When using any non-standard compliant token like USDT, the function will revert. Withdrawals for these tokens are broken, which is bad as `USDT` is a valid underlying for the `cUSDT` cToken.

We recommend using [OpenZeppelin’s `SafeERC20`](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/blob/release-v4.1/contracts/token/ERC20/utils/SafeERC20.sol#L74) versions with the `safeApprove` function that handles the return value check as well as non-standard-compliant tokens.

title: DOS by Frontrunning NoteERC20 `initialize`
content: The vulnerability is a front‑running initialization race condition that affects upgradeable ERC1967 proxy contracts, specifically the NoteERC20 token proxy used by the Notional protocol. The deployment script creates the proxy in one transaction and calls the contract’s initialise() function in a separate transaction. Because the initialise() function is not protected and is executed after the proxy has already been deployed, a malicious actor can monitor the mempool for the proxy‑creation transaction, detect that the implementation address matches the NoteERC20 bytecode, and submit a competing initialise() transaction with a higher gas price. By doing so the attacker becomes the owner of the proxy, taking control of the token contract. This ownership takeover prevents the legitimate deployer from completing the initialise() call, which in turn blocks the subsequent deployment of the GovernanceAlpha contract that depends on the token being correctly initialised. The result is a denial‑of‑service (DoS) situation where the protocol cannot be deployed, and the original deployer incurs unrecoverable gas costs. The issue occurs only when the deployment and initialisation steps are separated and when the initialise() function lacks an access‑control check such as onlyOwner or a constructor‑based admin assignment. It affects the protocol developers, the governance system, and any future token holders because the token contract never reaches a usable state. The flaw was discovered during a manual review of the Notional deployment scripts, where the auditor noted that the proxy creation and initialisation were performed in distinct transactions without any restriction on who could call initialise(). The problem is subtle because the proxy appears to be deployed successfully; however, without the initialise() call the contract’s state variables remain unset, and there are no obvious on‑chain signals that the contract is vulnerable until an attacker actually fronts‑runs the call. To remediate the issue, the deployment process should either combine proxy creation and initialise() into a single atomic transaction or enforce that only the deployer (or a pre‑designated admin) can invoke initialise(). This can be achieved by adding an access‑control modifier to initialise() or by passing the admin address to the proxy constructor, thereby eliminating the window where an attacker could intervene. The class of bug is a “proxy initialisation front‑run” or “upgradeable contract race condition”, which violates the expected business logic that the deployer retains ownership after deployment and that the token contract becomes operational immediately after deployment.
summary:
The `scripts/` folder outlines a number of deployment scripts used by the Notional team. Some of the contracts deployed utilize the ERC1967 upgradeable proxy standard. This standard involves first deploying an implementation contract and later a proxy contract which uses the implementation contract as its logic.

When users make calls to the proxy contract, the proxy contract will delegate call to the underlying implementation contract. `NoteERC20.sol` and `Router.sol` both implement an `initialize()` function which aims to replace the role of the `constructor()` when deploying proxy contracts. It is important that these proxy contracts are deployed and initialized in the same transaction to avoid any malicious front-running.

However, `scripts/deployment.py` does not follow this pattern when deploying `NoteERC20.sol`’s proxy contract. As a result, a malicious attacker could monitor the Ethereum blockchain for bytecode that matches the `NoteERC20` contract and front-run the `initialize()` transaction to gain ownership of the contract. This can be repeated as a Denial Of Service (DOS) type of attack, effectively preventing Notional’s contract deployment, leading to unrecoverable gas expenses. See [`deployment.py` L44-L60](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-08-notional/blob/main/scripts/deployment.py#L44-L60), and [`deploy_governance.py` L71-L105](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-08-notional/blob/main/scripts/mainnet/deploy_governance.py#L71-L105).

As the `GovernanceAlpha.sol` and `NoteERC20.sol` are co-dependent contracts in terms of deployment, it won’t be possible to deploy the governance contract before deploying and initializing the token contract. Therefore, it would be worthwhile to ensure the `NoteERC20.sol` proxy contract is deployed and initialized in the same transaction, or ensure the `initialize()` function is callable only by the deployer of the `NoteERC20.sol` contract. This could be set in the proxy contracts `constructor()`.

title: `findNewOwner` edgecase
content:
The vulnerability resides in the ownership‑selection routine of the RCOrderbook contract, specifically in the function that searches for a new owner after a rent payment (findNewOwner). The routine iterates over bids, removing them until either the foreclosure condition is no longer met or a configured deletion limit (maxDeletions) is reached. After the loop, the code decides whether the processing is finished by checking if the loop counter is different from the deletion limit. If the counter equals maxDeletions the implementation assumes that the search was stopped because the limit was hit, and therefore postpones ownership transfer to the next transaction. The root cause is an off‑by‑one logical error: the loop can finish exactly on the iteration where the last valid bidder is found, yet the post‑loop test still treats the situation as “limit reached” and discards the valid owner. This edge case occurs whenever the condition that stops the loop (foreclosureTimeUser < minimumTimeToOwnTo) becomes false on the same iteration that the loop counter reaches maxDeletions. Although the case is most obvious when maxDeletions equals one, it can manifest for any positive limit because the equality test does not distinguish between "stopped because limit reached" and "stopped because a valid owner was found".

Exploitation proceeds by arranging bids so that the final valid owner appears on the last allowed iteration. An attacker can place a series of low‑value, short‑duration bids (using Sybil accounts) that consume maxDeletions‑1 slots, wait for those bids to expire, and then submit a minimal bid that triggers rent collection. The findNewOwner loop will iterate exactly maxDeletions times, encounter the attacker’s low‑value bid on the final iteration, and mistakenly treat it as an incomplete search. Consequently the contract will not transfer ownership to the attacker in the current rent cycle, nor emit any event indicating a change. The UI continues to display the previous owner (or, if no previous owner existed, shows no owner), while the attacker silently accrues rental time at a price far below the market expectation. From the user’s perspective the symptom is that a card appears to remain owned by the higher‑bidding participant even though the contract’s internal state has moved the rental rights to another address without notification; the higher‑bidding user sees no refund, no ownership change, and may lose the ability to collect rent.

The impact includes incorrect accounting of ownership, potential loss of revenue for legitimate owners, and a distortion of the market price signal because cheaper bids can remain active without being challenged. Availability of the card for genuine bidders is reduced, as the UI suggests the card is still owned by the higher‑bidder while the contract allows cheaper usage. The bug is subtle because the contract does emit removal and foreclose events for the intermediate bids, so the abnormal behavior is hidden unless one inspects the post‑loop ownership logic or compares on‑chain state with UI displays. It was discovered during a manual audit of the order‑book logic, where the auditor noticed that the termination condition conflated two distinct reasons for exiting the loop.

To remediate, the termination check should be rewritten to explicitly consider both conditions: whether the loop stopped because a valid new owner was found or because the deletion limit was reached. A simple approach is to evaluate the ownership‑found flag inside the loop and break when it is true, regardless of the current loop counter, or to change the post‑loop condition to "if (foundValidOwner)" rather than comparing the counter against maxDeletions. Adding a safeguard that enforces maxDeletions be greater than one can reduce the likelihood of the edge case but does not eliminate it. The fix ensures that a valid owner is never skipped, preserving correct ownership transfer, accurate event emission, and consistent UI representation, thereby restoring the intended economic guarantees of the protocol.

title: `UberOwner` has too much power
content: The vulnerability is an excessive privileged authority granted to the Uber Owner role in the protocol. This role holds the capability to modify most of the contract's internal parameters, replace core logic, and execute functions that can halt the system or withdraw all user funds. The root cause stems from a design decision that places an unrestricted administrative key in the hands of a single external address (or a multisig that could be compromised). Because the contract’s upgrade and state‑changing functions are gated only by this Uber Owner check, any entity that gains control of that address can reprogram the prediction market, alter fee structures, pause trading, or invoke a so‑called “rug‑pull” routine that transfers all locked assets to the owner. Exploitation would involve an attacker either obtaining the private key of the Uber Owner or coercing the multisig signers, then calling the privileged functions to, for example, pause all activity while preventing withdrawals, or to directly move the treasury balance to an address under the attacker’s control. The immediate impact is the loss of user deposits, interruption of market operations, and a breach of the protocol’s promised decentralised governance model. This condition can manifest at any time the Uber Owner privileges are active, which, according to the code, is continuously throughout the contract’s lifecycle unless the role is deliberately relinquished. All participants – traders, liquidity providers, and anyone holding tokens in the system – are potentially affected because their funds become inaccessible or can be confiscated without any on‑chain warning. The issue was identified during a manual audit where the reviewer examined the access‑control modifiers and noted that the Uber Owner’s authority extends beyond typical parameter adjustments, effectively allowing a complete re‑programming of the protocol. Detecting this problem in normal operation can be difficult because the contract behaves correctly under honest administration; the dangerous capabilities are hidden behind a single address check and do not produce obvious error messages unless misused. To remediate, the privileged functions should be split into granular roles with limited scope, such as separating fee updates, contract upgrades, and emergency pauses, and each should be protected by multi‑signature or timelocked governance mechanisms. Additionally, an immutable pause‑only mode that allows withdrawals while blocking other state‑changing actions could mitigate rug‑pull scenarios. In generic terms, the bug belongs to the class of “over‑privileged admin” or “centralisation of control” vulnerabilities, where a single key can bypass the intended economic security model, leading to potential fund loss, unexpected contract behaviour, and erosion of trust in the platform.
summary:
The Uber Owner has too much power within the system. This makes the protocol closer to a centralized prediction market whose rules are determined by the Uber Owner. See issue page for referenced code

The above functions can be used by the Uber Owner to completely change the functionality of the system. This goes well beyond simple setting new constants and fees, the Uber Owner can basically reprogram how the entire protocol works. Not to mention if the address falls into the wrong hands.

Recommend limiting the permission of the Uber Owner to something more manageable and trustable. If upgrades to underlying contracts are required they can be done through a proxy instead, in the standard way.

This is a subjective opinion- there is always going to be a compromise between decentralisation and the ability to respond to potential problems. The latter is especially important with a protocol that is so new.

There is no correct answer here, but the current abilities of `uberOwner` were decided after a lot of thought and are in line with other DeFi protocols.

I’d just like to add that we did recognize the power of the UberOwner which is why it is separated from the Owner specifically so that we can add additional security to it (in the form of a multisig) and so that we can relinquish this control at the appropriate time. This was covered in the [readme](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-08-realitycards#mortar_board-governance-mortar_board). And also [commented](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-08-realitycards/blob/39d711fdd762c32378abf50dc56ec51a21592917/contracts/RCTreasury.sol#L288-L291) in the code.

I think the warden(s) have a valid point here. This is an incredible amount of power for a single address to yield over the protocol, even if backed by a multi-sig.

Is it no an option to 1) pause all activity, and unlock all funds allowing users to withdraw their own funds or 2) pause all activity besides withdraws and implement a time delay between that and the “rug pull” function being called.

The readme also states

`Alternatively we may wish for this to be a multisig but the normal owner to not be, for convenience.`

Without a multisig, I believe this absolutely qualifies as a high severity issue as a compromise of a single end user address compromises the entire system, with a multisig it potentially lowers the severity down to a medium, but its still a risk that is worth highlighting in the system and for the sponsor to scrutinize if there are indeed other mitigation paths that could be taken.

title: `CompositeMultiOracle` returns wrong decimals for prices?
content: The CompositeMultiOracle contract is intended to aggregate price data from multiple IOracle sources and return a single price with a fixed 18‑decimal precision. The implementation mistakenly uses the token‑decimal field of each source (source.decimals) when scaling intermediate price values, rather than the decimal precision reported by the underlying oracle contract (IOracle(source).decimals()). Because the contract assumes that the final price is always expressed in 18 decimals and divides the amount by 1e18, the intermediate scaling does not correctly compensate for token‑specific precision. As a result, when a price path involves tokens with differing decimal places—such as USDC (6 decimals) followed by DAI (18 decimals) and USDT (6 decimals)—the computed price is inflated by orders of magnitude. In the concrete example, a 1 USDC amount is transformed into a price of 1 e30, which after the final division yields an output of 1 e12 USDT, far exceeding the expected 1 USDT. The vulnerability can be exploited by any caller that relies on CompositeMultiOracle for price quotes or amount conversions, causing the protocol to over‑pay, mis‑price collateral, or incorrectly calculate swap amounts. The impact is a potential loss of funds or economic imbalance for users, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself because the oracle feeds incorrect values into downstream financial logic. The bug manifests whenever the oracle path includes assets with non‑18 decimals, which is common in many DeFi systems, and it is invisible to casual observers because the contract returns a value that appears syntactically correct (a uint256) and the erroneous scaling is hidden inside arithmetic that does not emit explicit warnings. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when the auditor traced the flow of the peek and get functions and observed that the scaling factor used was based on the token’s decimal count instead of the oracle’s decimal count, leading to a mismatch in expected precision. The difficulty in spotting the bug stems from the layered abstraction of price sourcing and the prevalence of hard‑coded 1e18 constants, which give a false impression that all intermediate values are already normalised. To remediate the problem, the oracle aggregation logic should consistently normalise every intermediate price to 18 decimals by dividing by the oracle’s declared decimals (IOracle(source).decimals()) rather than the token’s decimals, and the code should be refactored to remove hard‑coded scaling factors, replace them with dynamic queries of oracle precision, and add thorough documentation clarifying the scaling contract. By enforcing a uniform 18‑decimal output across all sources, the protocol can guarantee that price conversions remain accurate regardless of token‑specific decimal configurations, thereby preserving correct accounting and preventing inflated fund transfers.
summary:
The `CompositeMultiOracle.peek/get` functions seem to return wrong prices. It’s unclear what decimals `source.decimals` refers to in this case. Does it refer to `source.source` token decimals?

It chains the price arguments through `_peek` function calls and a single price is computed as:

```solidity
(priceOut, updateTimeOut) = IOracle(source.source).peek(base, quote, 10 ** source.decimals);   // Get price for one unit
// @audit shouldn't this divide by 10 ** IOracle(source.source).decimals() instead?
priceOut = priceIn * priceOut / (10 ** source.decimals);
```

Assume all oracles use 18 decimals (`oracle.decimals()` returns 18) and `source.decimals` refers to the _token decimals_ of `source.source`.

Then going from `USDC -> DAI -> USDT` (`path = [DAI]`) starts with a price of `1e18` in `peek`:

  * `_peek(USDC, DAI, 1e18)`: Gets the price of `1e6 USDC` (as USDC has 6 decimals) in DAI with 18 decimals precision (because all oracle precision is set to 18): `priceOut = priceIn * 1e18 / 1e6 = 1e18 * 1e18 / 1e6 = 1e30`
  * `_peek(DAI, USDT, 1e30)`: Gets the price of `1e18 DAI` (DAI has 18 decimals) with 18 decimals precision: `priceOut = priceIn * 1e18 / 1e18 = priceIn = 1e30`

It then uses `1e30` as the price to go from `USDC` to `USDT`: `value = price * amount / 1e18 = 1e30 * (1.0 USDC) / 1e18 = 1e30 * 1e6 / 1e18 = 1e18 = 1e12 * 1e6 = 1_000_000_000_000.0 USDT`. Inflating the actual `USDT` amount.

The issue is that `peek` assumes that the final price is in 18 decimals in the `value = price * amount / 1e18` division by `1e18`. But `_peek` (and `_get`) don’t enforce this.

Recommend that `_peek` should scale the prices to `1e18` by doing:

```solidity
(priceOut, updateTimeOut) = IOracle(source.source).get(base, quote, 10 ** source.decimals);
// priceOut will have same decimals as priceIn if we divide by oracle decimals
priceOut = priceIn * priceOut / (10 ** IOracle(source.source).decimals());
```

It does not need to divide by the `source.source` _token precision_ (`source.decimals`), but by the oracle precision (`IOracle(source.source).decimals()`).

It’s confusing to deal with all these decimals, I should at least comment the code better, and try to make it easier to understand.

It’s unclear what decimals source.decimals refers to in this case. Does it refer to source.source token decimals?

CompositeMultiOracle takes IOracle contracts as sources, so `source.decimals` refers to the token decimals of the oracle, not of the data source one level below.

It does not need to divide by the source.source token precision (source.decimals), but by the oracle precision (IOracle(source.source).decimals()).

The source.source token precision would be `IChainlinkAggregatorV3(source.source()).decimals()`, the source oracle precision is `source.decimals()`. CompositeMultiOracle cannot make an assumption on any fields present on `source.source`, and must work only with the underlying `source` IOracles.

I’m still not disputing this finding. I need to dig further to make sure the decimals are right when different IOracle sources have different decimals, and I’ve hardcoded a few `1e18` in there. Those are code smells.

**[alcueca (Yield) patched](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-08-yield-findings/issues/26#issuecomment-900850053):**

Sent me into a wild goose chase to support IOracle of multiple decimals as sources to CompositeMultiOracle, only to realize that we create all IOracles and we always create them with 18 decimals, converting from the underlying data source if needed.

Ended up making CompositeMultiOracle require that underlying oracles have 18 decimals. [Done](https://github.com/yieldprotocol/vault-v2/commit/621b680f893436f88f7668164b2942dbb94d1ca2).

**[alcueca (Yield) further patched](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-08-yield-findings/issues/26#issuecomment-900850053):**

Further [refactored all oracles so that decimals are handled properly](https://github.com/yieldprotocol/vault-v2/pull/276), and work on taking an amount of base as input, and returning an amount of quote as output. Our oracles don’t have decimals themselves anymore as a state variable, since the return values are in the decimals of quote. This means that CompositeMultiOracle is agnostic with regards to decimals, and doesn’t even need to know about them.

title: `ERC20Rewards` returns wrong rewards if no tokens initially exist
content: The vulnerability resides in the rewards accounting logic of the ERC20Rewards contract. The internal function that updates the accumulated rewards per token, _updateRewardsPerToken, contains a guard that returns immediately when the total token supply is zero. When this early‑return path is taken, the field that records the timestamp of the last rewards calculation (rewardsPerToken_.lastUpdated) is left unchanged. Consequently, if a reward period has already started but no tokens have been minted yet, the lastUpdated value remains set to the start of the period. When the first mint occurs, the contract records the new totalSupply and the user’s balance, but the rewards index still reflects the original start time. A subsequent claim call recomputes the elapsed time as the entire period (e.g., one month) and credits the caller with all pending rewards, even though the caller held no tokens during that interval. This bug allows an attacker or early participant to mint tokens and immediately claim the full reward allocation that was meant to be distributed over all holders for the elapsed time. The impact is a severe misallocation of incentive funds: the protocol loses the intended reward pool, legitimate users receive no rewards, and the economic assumptions of the system are broken. The condition occurs whenever the reward schedule is initialized before any tokens exist, which can happen with freshly deployed contracts, delayed launches, or when the setRewards function is used with a past start date. The issue is subtle because the contract’s UI may show a normal balance increase after minting, and the extra reward tokens may be indistinguishable from legitimate earnings, making the error hard to spot without inspecting the timestamp field. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the reward‑distribution flow and noticed that the early‑return path prevented the timestamp from advancing. To remediate the problem, the update routine must always advance rewardsPerToken_.lastUpdated to the current block timestamp (or the reward period end) even when totalSupply equals zero, and it should avoid performing the accumulated‑rewards arithmetic that would revert due to division by zero. By ensuring the time marker is refreshed, the contract will correctly calculate zero rewards for the period when no tokens were held, preserving the intended distribution among future token holders.
summary:
The `ERC20Rewards._updateRewardsPerToken` function exits without updating `rewardsPerToken_.lastUpdated` if `totalSupply` is zero, i.e., if there are no tokens initially.

This leads to an error if there is an active rewards period but no tokens have been minted yet.

**Example:** `rewardsPeriod.start: 1 month ago`, `rewardsPeriod.end: in 1 month`, `totalSupply == 0`.

The first mint leads to the user (mintee) receiving all rewards for the past period (50% of the total rewards in this case).

  * `_mint` is called, calls `_updateRewardsPerToken` which short-circuits. `rewardsPerToken.lastUpdated` is still set to `rewardsPeriod.start` from the constructor. Then `_updateUserRewards` is called and does not currently yield any rewards. (because both balance and the index diff are zero). User has now minted the tokens, `totalSupply` increases and user balance is set.
  * User performs a `claim`: `_updateRewardsPerToken` is called and `timeSinceLastUpdated = end - rewardsPerToken_.lastUpdated = block.timestamp - rewardsPeriod.start = 1 month`. Contract “issues” rewards for the past month. The first mintee receives all of it.

The first mintee receives all pending rewards when they should not receive any past rewards. This can easily happen if the token is new, the reward period has already been initialized and is running, but the protocol has not officially launched yet. Note that `setRewards` also allows setting a date in the past which would also be fatal in this case.

Recommend that the `rewardsPerToken_.lastUpdated` field must always be updated in `_updateRewardsPerToken` to the current time (or `end`) even if `_totalSupply == 0`. Don’t return early.

You are right, that’s a great finding. For the record, I think that this is what [this line in Unipool.sol](https://github.com/k06a/Unipool/blob/bb1843b454bbb10b3b1ccf48edf5e72a80b2acfe/contracts/Unipool.sol#L70) does:

```solidity
function rewardPerToken() public view returns (uint256) {
  if (totalSupply() == 0) {
    return rewardPerTokenStored;
  }
```

I’ll apply the mitigation step suggested, with a conditional to not do the `rewardsPerToken_.accumulated` math that would revert.

Now I know the feeling of the devs that fork a known project and leave a pesky conditional out, thanks again :D

title: `ERC20Rewards` breaks when setting a different token
content: The vulnerability resides in the reward distribution mechanism of a contract that allows the administrator to change the ERC‑20 token used for rewards through a function called setRewards. The contract stores each user’s pending reward as a raw integer amount that is interpreted according to the decimal precision of the token that was active when the reward was accrued. Because the stored amount is not normalised or converted when the reward token is swapped, a user who has not claimed their reward before the token change will later claim the same raw amount, but the contract will treat it as an amount of the new token. If the new token has a different number of decimals or a different market value, the user receives an amount that is dramatically higher or lower than intended. For example, a user owed 1e18 units of a token with 18 decimals (1 DAI) who waits until the contract switches to USDC, which has 6 decimals, will be able to claim 1e18 units of USDC – effectively 1 trillion USDC – because the contract does not adjust the scale. The flaw arises from the assumption that the numeric reward value is token‑agnostic, ignoring that ERC‑20 tokens may have differing decimal places and market values. Exploitation is straightforward: an attacker or any user with pending rewards deliberately delays the claim until after a token change, then calls the claim function and receives an inflated (or deflated) payout. The impact is a severe accounting error that can cause massive loss of funds for the protocol or unintended windfalls for users, violating the intended one‑to‑one reward mapping and breaking the economic model of the system. The condition for the bug to manifest is the existence of unclaimed rewards at the moment the reward token address is updated. All token holders who participated in the previous reward period are affected, as they may receive either far too many tokens or insufficient compensation. The issue was uncovered during a formal security audit where the reward‑token change path was examined and identified as a logical inconsistency. The bug is subtle because the contract correctly records the numeric amount; only when the token changes does the mismatch become visible, making it easy to overlook during testing. To remediate, the contract should either prohibit changing the reward token after any rewards have been accrued, or it must reset or recalculate each user’s pending balance whenever a token swap occurs, tracking the specific token associated with each pending reward. In essence, the problem belongs to the class of “token‑scale mismatch” or “reward‑unit conversion” bugs, where stored numeric values are interpreted with an incorrect decimal context after a token change, leading to erroneous payouts and broken accounting guarantees.
summary:
The `setRewards` function allows setting a different token. Holders of a previous reward period cannot all be paid out and will receive **their old reward amount** in the new token.

This leads to issues when the new token is more (less) valuable, or uses different decimals.

**Example:** Assume the first reward period paid out in `DAI` which has 18 decimals. Someone would have received `1.0 DAI = 1e18 DAI` if they called `claim` now. Instead, they wait until the new period starts with `USDC` (using only 6 decimals) and can `claim` their `1e18` reward amount in USDC which would equal `1e12 USDC`, one trillion USD.

Changing the reward token only works if old and new tokens use the same decimals and have the exact same value. Otherwise, users that claim too late/early will lose out.

Recommend disallowing changing the reward token, or clearing user’s pending rewards of the old token. The second approach requires more code changes and keeping track of what token a user last claimed.

Maybe I should have used stronger language: `// If changed in a new rewards program, any unclaimed rewards from the last one will be served in the new token`

The issue is known, but you are right in pointing it out. There are few situations in which changing the rewards token would make sense (such as replacing a faulty rewards token by a fixed one). I think it would be best to just disallow changing the token.
