title: Rewards accumulated can stay constant and often not increment
content: The vulnerability lies in the way the contract calculates the per‑token reward accumulator. The accumulator (rewardsPerToken_.accumulated) is updated with the expression `1e18 * timeSinceLastUpdated * rewardsPerToken_.rate / _totalSupply`. Because Solidity uses integer division, if the product of the scaled time interval and the reward rate is smaller than the total token supply, the division truncates to zero and the accumulator does not increase. The contract nevertheless updates rewardsPerToken_.lastUpdated, so time appears to advance while the recorded rewards remain unchanged. This situation occurs when the token supply is large (e.g., 1 billion tokens represented as 1e27 wei), the emissions rate is modest (rate < 1e9 wei per second), and the time between updates is very short. An attacker—or even a regular user—can keep the time delta tiny by repeatedly transferring, minting, or burning tokens every few seconds, especially on fast L2 networks, thereby forcing the reward increment to round down to zero on each call. As a result, token holders see their reward balances stay at zero despite the contract reporting that rewards are being accrued; the UI may show a growing timestamp but no increase in claimable amounts. The impact is a broken reward distribution mechanism: users receive no tokens, the protocol fails its economic promise, and the intended incentive model collapses. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the arithmetic of the accumulator and identified the rounding‑to‑zero condition. It is hard to spot because the contract appears to update state correctly, and the lack of reward growth may only become evident after prolonged observation or during testing with realistic token supplies. To fix the issue, the contract should avoid updating `lastUpdated` when the computed increment is zero, use a larger scaling factor or a different accounting strategy that preserves precision, and potentially redesign the reward formula to compute rewards on a per‑second basis before division, thereby eliminating the loss of precision caused by integer truncation. This class of bug is a classic precision or rounding error that prevents expected state changes in financial smart contracts.
summary:
`rewardsPerToken_.accumulated` can stay constant while `rewardsPerToken_.lastUpdated` is continually updated, leading to no actual rewards being distributed. I.e. No rewards accumulate.

Line 115, `rewardsPerToken_.accumulated` could stay constant if there are very quick update intervals, a relatively low `rewardsPerToken_.rate` and a decent supply of the ERC20 token.

I.e. imagine the token supply is 1 billion tokens (quite a common amount, note even if a supply of only say 1 million tokens this is still relevant). i.e. 1e27 wei.

Line 115 has

```solidity
1e18 * timeSinceLastUpdated * rewardsPerToken_.rate / _totalSupply
```

`timeSinceLastUpdated` can be crafted to be arbitrarily small by simply transferring or burning tokens, so lets exclude this term (it could be 10 seconds etc). Imagine total supply is 1e27 as mentioned.

Therefore, `1e18 * rewardsPerToken_.rate / 1e27`, which shows that if the `rewardsPerToken_.rate` is < 1e9, something which is very likely, then the accumulated amount won’t increment, as there are no decimals in solidity and this line of code will evaluate to adding zero. While this is rounded down to zero, critically, `rewardsPerToken_.lastUpdated = end;` is updated.

The reason I have labelled this as a high risk is the express purpose of this contract is to reward users with tokens, yet a user could potentially quite easily exploit this line to ensure no one ever gets rewards and the accumulated amount never increases.

Given a fairly large token supply, and a relatively low emissions rate is set, that satisfies the above equation, for the entire duration of the rewards period, the user simply sends tokens back and forth every couple seconds (gas limitations, but layer 2), to keep the delta `timeSinceLastUpdated` close to 1.

This way the accumulated amount will never tick up, but time keeps being counted.

Furthermore, I would say this is high risk as this wouldn’t even need an attacker. Given the transfer function is likely often being called by users, `timeSinceLastUpdated` will naturally be very low anyways.

Even if not so extreme as the above case, Alberto points out that “rounding can eat into the rewards” which is likely to be prevalent in the current scenario and make a big impact over time on the targeted vs actual distribution.

Again, this problem is more likely to occur in naturally liquid tokens where lots of transfer, mint or burn events occur.

As suggested by Alberto, the simplest it to probably not update the `rewardsPerToken_.lastUpdated` field if `rewardsPerToken_.accumulated` does not change. Although this change should be closely scrutinized to see it doesn’t introduce bugs elsewhere.

While the issue exists, it’s not as severe as portrayed, and doesn’t need fixing.

There is an error in the assessment, and it is that the `rate` refers to the rewards amount distributed per second among all token holders. It is not the rewards amount distributed per token per second (that’s dynamically calculated).

Also, it needs to be taken into account that `rewardsPerToken.accumulated` is stored scaled up by 1e18, to avoid losing much ground to rounding.

```solidity
struct RewardsPerToken {
  uint128 accumulated;                            // Accumulated rewards per token for the period, scaled up by 1e18
  uint32 lastUpdated;                             // Last time the rewards per token accumulator was updated
  uint96 rate;                                    // Wei rewarded per second among all token holders
}
```

One of the largest cap tokens is Dai, with a distribution close to 1e28. If ERC20Rewards were to distribute 1 cent/second among all token holders (which wouldn’t be very exciting), and block times were of 1 second, the accumulator would still accumulate.

`accumulator += 1e18 (scaling) * 1 (seconds per block) * 1e16 (Dai wei / second) / 1e28 (Dai total supply)` The increase to the `accumulator` is of 1e6, which gives plenty of precision. I would expect a rewards program on Dai holders would be at least 1e6 larger per second.

On the other hand, `accumulator` is an `uint128`, which holds amounts of up to 1e38. To overflow it we would need a low cap token (let’s say USDC, with 1e15), and a high distribution (1e12 per second, which is unreal), and we run the program for 3 years, or 1e9, to make it easy.

The accumulator at the end of the ten years would be: `accumulator = 1e18 (scaling) * 1e9 (seconds) * 1e12 (distribution) / 1e15 (supply) = 1e24` Which doesn’t overflow.

I’ll keep high risk as there should be no scenario where the math breaks.

title: Exchange rates from Compound are assumed with 18 decimals
content: The vulnerability lies in the way the CTokenMultiOracle contract interprets the exchange rate returned by Compound's cToken contracts. The oracle assumes that the exchange rate, which represents the borrowing price of the underlying asset, is always expressed with 18 decimal places. In reality, according to Compound’s specification, the exchange rate is scaled by the factor 10^(18 - 8 + underlying token decimals). Consequently, for underlying assets whose token decimals differ from 18 – for example USDC with 6 decimals or BUSD with 18 but a different scaling – the oracle reads a value that is either too large or too small. The root cause is the hard‑coded decimal assumption and the omission of a step that queries the underlying token’s decimal count when constructing a Source for the oracle. An attacker can exploit this mismatch by supplying a cToken whose underlying token has non‑standard decimals, causing the oracle to output an incorrect price. Because the Yield protocol relies on this price for collateral valuation, loan‑to‑value calculations, and token swaps, a distorted price can lead to under‑collateralisation, premature liquidations, or users receiving fewer tokens than expected when they perform a withdrawal or a swap. The impact becomes visible when a user attempts an operation that depends on the oracle’s price and receives an unexpectedly low amount, experiences a failed transaction due to insufficient collateral, or sees their balance mysteriously shrink. This condition manifests whenever the protocol queries Compound for a cToken that does not conform to the 18‑decimal expectation – a situation that can easily be overlooked because the numerical discrepancy may be subtle and appear only in edge‑case assets. The issue was discovered during a formal security audit when the auditors compared the oracle’s behavior against the official Compound documentation and noted the inconsistency in decimal handling. It is difficult to notice in routine testing because the contract still returns a value that looks plausible; the error only surfaces when the scaling factor diverges from 18, which can be masked by test environments that use tokens with 18 decimals. To remediate, the oracle should dynamically fetch the underlying token’s decimal count and apply the correct scaling factor as defined by Compound, ensuring that each Source stores the appropriate number of decimals for its specific cToken. By aligning the oracle’s calculation with the documented exchange‑rate formula, the protocol will produce accurate pricing, preserve correct collateralisation, and prevent users from receiving incorrect amounts or losing funds due to mis‑priced assets.
summary:
The `CTokenMultiOracle` contract assumes the exchange rates (borrowing rate) of Compound always have 18 decimals, while, however, which is not true. According to the [Compound documentation](https://compound.finance/docs/ctokens#exchange-rate), the exchange rate returned from the `exchangeRateCurrent` function is scaled by `1 * 10^(18 - 8 + Underlying Token Decimals)` (and so does `exchangeRateStored`). Using a wrong decimal number on the exchange rate could cause incorrect pricing on tokens. See [`CTokenMultiOracle.sol` #L110](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-08-yield/blob/main/contracts/oracles/compound/CTokenMultiOracle.sol#L110).

Recommend following the documentation and getting the decimals of the underlying tokens to set the correct decimal of a `Source`.

Thanks a lot for coming up with this. I had looked into how Compound defined the decimals and couldn’t find it.

[Fix](https://github.com/yieldprotocol/vault-v2/commit/e9c1ee5532c946e9ab2fc8912039829e190fbb64)

title: `veCVXStrategy.manualRebalance` has wrong logic
content: The vulnerability resides in the manual rebalancing routine of the veCVXStrategy contract. The function attempts to decide whether to lock additional CVX tokens by computing two values called `currentLockRatio` and `newLockRatio` and then comparing them with a simple less‑than-or‑equal check. The root cause is a mismatch in the semantics of these two values: `currentLockRatio` is calculated as `balanceInLock * 1e18 / totalCVXBalance`, which yields a percentage expressed with 18 decimal places (the maximum possible value is 1e18, representing 100%). In contrast, `newLockRatio` is derived as `totalCVXBalance * toLock / MAX_BPS`, which directly represents an amount of CVX tokens and is not bounded by 1e18. Because one operand is a scaled percentage and the other is an absolute token amount, the comparison `if (newLockRatio <= currentLockRatio)` does not reflect any meaningful business rule. An attacker or even a regular user could trigger the function and cause the contract to make an incorrect decision about how much CVX to lock or release. The impact is that the protocol may lock too few tokens, leaving user positions under‑collateralized, or lock an excessive amount, unnecessarily tying up capital. This mis‑allocation can manifest to users as missing rewards, unexpectedly low balances, or a failure to receive expected token allocations after a manual rebalance. The flaw appears only when the manualRebalance function is called, either by the contract owner or an authorized actor, and is triggered whenever `newLockRatio` and `currentLockRatio` differ numerically. The affected parties include token holders who rely on the strategy to maintain a target lock ratio, the protocol’s accounting layer, and any downstream contracts that assume the lock amount reflects the intended percentage. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where the auditors noted that the variable names suggested ratios but the underlying calculations produced unrelated units, making the logic obscure and difficult to verify through casual testing. The bug is hard to notice because both values are numeric and the comparison compiles without error; the error only surfaces in subtle economic mismatches that may not be revealed until a manual rebalance is performed. To remediate the problem, the contract should treat both operands consistently—either both as percentages or both as absolute CVX amounts. The recommended fix is to replace the percentage‑based `currentLockRatio` with the raw `balanceInLock` amount, rename the variables to reflect that they are balances rather than ratios, and adjust the subsequent arithmetic (e.g., `cvxToLock = newLockRatio - currentLockRatio`) accordingly. Alternatively, the entire manualRebalance function can be removed and its intended functionality implemented via more transparent, well‑tested helper functions such as `manualSendbCVXToVault`. By ensuring that the comparison operates on like‑for‑like units, the strategy will correctly enforce its lock policy, preserve user funds, and align with the protocol’s accounting assumptions.

title: Re-entrancy in `settleAuction` allow stealing all funds
content: The vulnerability is a re‑entrancy flaw in the `settleAuction` function of the Basket/Auction system. The function is intended to rebalance the basket after an auction by pulling a set of input tokens from the caller, transferring the appropriate amount of assets out of the basket, and then checking that the basket still holds the required token balances. The root cause is that the contract allows an attacker to supply any ERC‑20 token as an input, performs external token transfers before updating critical state variables, and does not use any re‑entrancy protection such as a mutex. Because the safety check that verifies the basket still holds a minimum amount of each token is executed only after the external transfer, an attacker can trigger a second call to `settleAuction` from within the first call (for example, by having the malicious input token’s transfer callback invoke `settleAuction` again). During the re‑entered call the contract recomputes the required token amounts using the current `ibRatio`. The first call lowers `ibRatio` (by setting a new ratio that is smaller than the previous one), which reduces the calculated `tokensNeeded`. When the re‑entered call finishes it again passes the safety check, but the basket’s token balances have already been drained further. By repeating this pattern, the attacker can continue to extract assets until the basket is effectively empty. This can be executed only when the time difference between `bondTimestamp` and `auctionStart` makes `newRatio` smaller than the current `ibRatio`, a condition that is normally reachable during a legitimate auction settlement. The affected parties are any users who have deposited tokens into the basket, the protocol itself because the basket’s capital is lost, and any downstream contracts that rely on the basket’s asset guarantees. The issue was uncovered during a formal security audit where the auditors noticed that `settleAuction` accepts untrusted token inputs, lacks a re‑entrancy guard, and violates the check‑effects‑interactions pattern. The bug can be subtle because the post‑transfer check appears to enforce that enough tokens remain, yet it can be bypassed through re‑entrancy, making the failure mode non‑obvious during casual testing. To remediate the problem, the function should be protected with a non‑reentrant modifier (e.g., OpenZeppelin’s `ReentrancyGuard`), move all state updates before any external calls, and restrict the set of acceptable input tokens to those that are part of the basket. Additionally, aligning the list of input tokens with the expected output tokens and eliminating the time‑dependent ratio manipulation would further close the attack surface. In practice, the exploit manifests as users seeing their expected refunds disappear, balances showing zero after settlement, or the basket becoming hollowed out despite the contract’s apparent safety checks.

title: `Basket.sol#auctionBurn`
content: The vulnerability resides in the auctionBurn() function of the Basket contract. When a failed auction is resolved, the function burns the bond tokens by calling _burn() but fails to adjust the ibRatio, a variable that represents the ratio between the basket's total supply and the underlying token holdings. The root cause is an omitted accounting step: after the totalSupply of basket tokens is reduced by the burned amount, ibRatio should be recomputed to reflect the new supply, yet the implementation leaves ibRatio unchanged. An attacker, or any participant who can trigger auctionBurn on a failed auction, can exploit this by burning bond tokens and then attempting to withdraw the proportional underlying assets. Because ibRatio still reflects the pre‑burn supply, the contract’s withdrawal logic believes the user’s share has already been accounted for, causing the underlying tokens (e.g., BTC and ETH) to become permanently locked in the contract. The impact is that users lose access to the underlying assets they expected to receive; the tokens appear to be frozen, and balances on the user interface may show zero or unchanged values despite the contract holding the assets. This condition occurs only after a failed auction when auctionBurn is called; any successful auction or normal mint/burn flow that correctly updates ibRatio does not exhibit the issue. The bug affects all participants who bond in auctions, the protocol’s overall fund safety, and any downstream applications that rely on accurate basket accounting. It was identified during a manual audit by Code4rena, where the mismatch between totalSupply and ibRatio was observed after executing the burn sequence. The problem is subtle because the burn transaction succeeds without reverting, and the ibRatio variable still holds a plausible value, making the freeze hard to detect without inspecting the underlying token balances. To remediate, the contract should recalculate ibRatio after burning, using the formula ibRatio = ibRatio * oldSupply / newSupply, and emit appropriate events to reflect the updated ratio. This fixes the accounting inconsistency, restores correct proportional withdrawal rights, and prevents funds from becoming irrevocably stuck. The issue is a classic example of an accounting/ratio desynchronization bug where a state variable dependent on token supply is not updated after supply changes, leading to loss of funds and violation of the protocol’s financial guarantees.
summary: Given the `auctionBurn()` function will `_burn()` the auction bond without updating the `ibRatio`. Once the bond of a failed auction is burned, the proportional underlying tokens won’t be able to be withdrawn, in other words, being frozen in the contract.

title: Reentrancy in settleAuction
content: The vulnerability is a classic re‑entrancy flaw located in the `settleAuction` function of the DeFi protocol’s basket contract. The function calls an external `withdrawBounty` routine, which in turn triggers a transfer of a bounty token using the ERC‑20 `transfer` method, before it updates the internal `auctionOngoing` flag to false. Because the state change (setting `auctionOngoing = false`) occurs after the external call, a malicious bounty token can re‑enter `settleAuction` during the transfer callback. The root cause is a violation of the Checks‑Effects‑Interactions pattern: the contract makes an external call prior to completing its own internal state updates. An attacker who controls the bounty token can craft a `transfer` implementation that invokes `settleAuction` again with crafted parameters. Since the first call has already satisfied all the prerequisite checks, the re‑entered call passes, invokes `setNewWeights`, and overwrites the pending weight structure with attacker‑chosen values. When the original `settleAuction` resumes, it again calls `setNewWeights`, now applying the malicious weights. The attacker then proceeds to burn all of his basket shares in the same transaction, causing the basket’s assets to be transferred to the attacker’s address. This sequence results in the complete draining of funds that were meant to be locked in the basket, effectively disappearing from the protocol’s balance. The issue surfaces only when a publisher—who is allowed to call the `onlyPublisher` functions such as `publishNewIndex`—submits a malicious bounty token alongside a legitimate auction settlement. Consequently, any user who holds basket shares or relies on the auction’s outcome can lose their value. The flaw was discovered during a Code4rena audit; the warden produced a proof‑of‑concept that demonstrated the re‑entrancy by deploying a malicious ERC‑20 token and invoking the vulnerable flow within a single transaction. The problem is subtle because the external token transfer appears innocuous and the state flag is updated later, making manual code reviews prone to overlooking the re‑entrancy window. To remediate the issue, the contract should adopt the Checks‑Effects‑Interactions pattern: move all external calls—including the bounty token transfer and `withdrawBounty`—to the end of `settleAuction`, and set `auctionOngoing = false` immediately after the initial checks. This ensures that any re‑entrant call finds the auction already marked as finished, blocking the secondary execution path. The fix also aligns with best practices for handling external token interactions, eliminating the state‑corruption window that allowed the attacker to manipulate pending weights and ultimately seize the basket’s assets.
summary: The `settleAuction()` function calls `withdrawBounty()` before setting `auctionOngoing = false`, thereby allowing reentrancy.

title: `PostAuctionLauncher.sol#finalize`
content: The vulnerability resides in the token sale finalisation function of the PostAuctionLauncher contract. The function `finalize()` is deliberately unrestricted – any address can invoke it – and it proceeds to mint liquidity tokens for a Uniswap‑style pair without first confirming whether the pair already exists or whether the supplied token amounts reflect the current market price of that pair. The root cause is a missing validation step: the contract calculates the amounts of token1 and token2 to add to the pool solely from the auction outcome, ignoring the existing reserves of the `tokenPair`. When an attacker creates the pair beforehand with a heavily skewed price (for example, a tiny amount of token1 against a large amount of token2), the `finalize()` call will still transfer the auction‑derived token amounts to the pair and invoke the pair's `mint()` routine. Because the `mint()` formula uses the current reserves to compute the amount of LP tokens, the attacker receives far fewer LP tokens than the value they supplied, while the contract’s tokens are added to the pool at the attacker‑controlled price. After the LP tokens are minted, the attacker can immediately withdraw the entire liquidity position, extracting a disproportionate share of the tokens that were intended for legitimate participants. This results in a direct fund loss for the protocol and any users expecting a fair distribution of liquidity. The issue manifests whenever the auction is successful, the pair already exists, and an external actor calls `finalize()`. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the control flow of the finalisation routine and identified the unchecked call to `IUniswapV2Pair.mint()` as a vector for price manipulation. The bug can be subtle because the transaction appears to succeed, the LP tokens are minted, and no error is thrown – the mispricing is only evident when the attacker removes liquidity and the protocol’s balances are drained. To remediate the problem, the contract should either restrict `finalize()` to privileged roles, enforce that the pair is freshly created by the launcher (preventing pre‑existing pools), or, at a minimum, verify that the token amounts being transferred align with the current reserve ratio of the pair before minting liquidity. This would ensure that LP tokens are issued at a fair market price and prevent an attacker from exploiting the price‑oracle‑free mint step to siphon funds.

title: SushiToken transfers are broken due to wrong delegates accounting on transfers
content: The vulnerability resides in the token contract’s accounting of delegated voting power during token minting, transfer, and burning operations. When a token holder has delegated their voting rights to another address, the contract stores the delegate address in a mapping called _delegates. The internal hook _beforeTokenTransfer is supposed to adjust the voting power of the delegate accounts to reflect the change in token balances. However, the implementation incorrectly calls the helper _moveDelegates with the literal from address instead of the delegate of the from address, i.e. it shifts votes from the token holder rather than from the address that actually holds the voting rights. This logical error originates from a mistaken assumption that the token holder and its delegate are the same, and it was carried over from a prior version of the contract where delegation was intentionally disabled. The bug manifests when a holder with a non‑zero delegate performs a transfer: the contract attempts to decrease voting power from an address that may not have any delegated votes, potentially causing an underflow or a failed internal check, which results in the whole transfer transaction reverting. From the user’s perspective the symptoms are confusing – a transfer that should succeed instead fails with no obvious error, balances appear unchanged, and the user may see their governance power disappear or be unchanged when it should have moved. The impact is twofold: token holders lose the ability to correctly transfer tokens while retaining delegated voting rights, and the governance layer may reflect inaccurate voting power, undermining the integrity of protocol decisions. The condition under which this occurs is any token transfer where the sender has previously set a delegate; if delegation is never used the contract behaves as expected, which makes the problem hard to detect during casual testing. The issue was discovered during a formal security audit that inspected the token’s governance logic and compared it with the reference implementation from Compound, noticing the mismatch in the delegate lookup. Because the delegating feature is not actively used in the current deployment, the bug remains latent and appears only when a user explicitly invokes delegation, which explains why it may go unnoticed in routine operation. To remediate the flaw, the contract must retrieve the correct delegate addresses for both the sender and the recipient and pass those values to _moveDelegates, ensuring that voting power is transferred from the delegated account of the sender to the delegated account of the recipient. This aligns the token’s accounting with the intended governance model and prevents unexpected reverts during legitimate transfers.
summary: When minting / transferring / burning tokens, the `SushiToken._beforeTokenTransfer` function is called and supposed to correctly shift the voting power due to the increase/decrease in tokens for the `from` and `to` accounts. However, it does not correctly do that, it tries to shift the votes from the `from` account, instead of the **`_delegates[from]`** account. This can lead to transfers reverting.

title: Last person to withdraw his tokens might not be able to do this, in Crowdsale
content: The vulnerability stems from an incomplete state transition check in a crowdsale contract. After a successful auction the contract’s finalize() function can be called as soon as the token sale reaches the required amount, even if the configured endTime has not yet passed. finalize() marks the sale as finalized, distributes the collected ether and any unsold tokens, and sets status.finalized to true. However, the commitment functions commitEth() and commitTokens() only verify that the current block timestamp lies within the auction window (between startTime and endTime) and do not check whether the auction has already ended or the contract has been finalized. Consequently, an attacker can construct an edge case where marketStatus.commitmentsTotal equals marketInfo.totalTokens minus one. In this situation auctionEnded() returns true, allowing the admin to call finalize() early, after which exactly one token remains unallocated in the contract. Because the commitment functions still accept new deposits, a malicious participant can submit a final commitment that purchases this last token before endTime expires. The contract’s accounting then records the purchase, but the token balance has already been transferred away during finalize, leaving the contract short of one token. When the buyer later invokes withdrawTokens(), the internal token transfer fails because there is no token left to transfer, and the revenue associated with that token remains locked since finalize() cannot be executed a second time. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after sending ether they receive no tokens and their balance appears to be zero, despite a successful contribution. The impact is loss of funds for the last purchaser and a breach of the crowdsale’s guarantee that all purchased tokens can be claimed, effectively breaking the accounting invariants of the sale. The issue was uncovered during a security audit that deliberately simulated the boundary condition of one token short of the total supply. It is difficult to notice because the contract’s public view functions report the auction as finished and the finalize flag as set, giving the impression that the sale is complete, while the internal commitment functions silently accept further deposits. The flaw belongs to the class of “missing state validation” or “post‑finalization state mutation” bugs, where functions that should be disabled after a finalization step remain callable due to inadequate checks. The proper remediation is to add explicit guards in _addCommitment() (and any other entry point that modifies commitments) to reject new contributions when auctionEnded() or status.finalized is true, thereby ensuring that once the sale is marked finalized no further token purchases are possible and the accounting balance remains consistent.
summary:
Suppose a Crowdsale is successful and enough commitments are made before the `marketInfo.endTime`. Suppose marketStatus.commitmentsTotal == marketInfo.totalTokens -1 // note this is an edge case, but can be constructed by an attacker Then the function `auctionEnded()` returns true Assume `auctionSuccessful()` is also true (might depend on the config of `marketPrice.goal` and `marketInfo.totalTokens`) Then an admin can call `finalize()` to finalize the Crowdsale. The function finalize distributes the funds and the unsold tokens and sets `status.finalized = true` so that finalized cannot be called again. Now we have “marketInfo.totalTokens -1” tokens left in the contract

However `commitEth()` or `commitTokens()` can still be called (they give no error message that the auction has ended) Then functions call `calculateCommitment`, which luckily prevent from buying too much, however 1 token can still be bought These functions also call `_addCommitment()`, which only checks for `marketInfo.endTime`, which hasn’t passed yet.

Now an extra token is sold and the contract has 1 token short. So the last person to withdraw his tokens cannot withdraw them (because you cannot specify how much you want to withdraw)

Also the revenues for the last token cannot be retrieved as `finalize()` cannot be called again.

title: Wrong inequality when adding/removing liquidity in current price range
content: The vulnerability stems from an off‑by‑one style mistake in the price‑range validation logic of the concentrated liquidity pool’s mint and burn functions. When a liquidity provider adds or removes liquidity, the contract checks that the current market price lies strictly between the lower and upper bounds of the provider’s price range, using the condition `priceLower < currentPrice && currentPrice < priceUpper`. This excludes the situation where the current price is exactly equal to the lower bound. As a result, if a user creates a position whose lower bound coincides with the market price, the contract incorrectly treats the position as out of range. Consequently, the mint operation may still accept the deposit but fails to correctly account for it, or the burn operation may refuse to withdraw the liquidity, leading to funds becoming effectively locked or, in the worst case, disappearing from the user’s balance. The flaw is triggered only when the market price matches the lower boundary of a newly added range, a circumstance that can be deliberately engineered through price manipulation or by selecting a precise tick during position creation. Liquidity providers, the protocol’s aggregate liquidity pool, and any downstream users depending on accurate accounting are affected because the pool’s invariant calculations become inconsistent, breaking the expected guarantee that deposited assets can always be retrieved. The issue was identified during a security audit when a reviewer noticed the strict inequality and later confirmed the exploit with a proof‑of‑concept that showed users losing funds when adding liquidity exactly at the lower price edge. The problem is subtle because the condition appears correct for most price movements, making it easy to miss during testing unless the exact boundary case is exercised. To remediate the bug, the validation should be changed to include the lower bound, i.e., `priceLower <= currentPrice && currentPrice < priceUpper`, and the same adjustment should be applied to any analogous checks in the burn path. This change aligns the contract’s logic with the intended economic model, ensuring that positions are considered active when the price sits on the lower edge, thus preserving users’ ability to retrieve their assets and maintaining the integrity of the pool’s accounting.
summary: The `ConcentratedLiquidityPool.mint/burn` functions add/remove `liquidity` when `(priceLower < currentPrice && currentPrice < priceUpper)`. Shouldn’t it also be changed if `priceLower == currentPrice`?

title: range fee growth underflow
content: The reported vulnerability is an unsigned integer underflow in the fee accounting routine of a concentrated liquidity pool. The contract calculates the fee accrued inside a price range by subtracting the fee growth below the lower bound and the fee growth above the upper bound from the global fee growth. When the pool price crosses a tick, the implementation updates only one of the two fee growth outside variables (either feeGrowthOutside0 or feeGrowthOutside1) depending on the direction of the crossing. Consequently, there are scenarios where the sum of feeGrowthBelow and feeGrowthAbove exceeds the stored global fee growth value. Because the subtraction is performed on unsigned integers, the excess causes an underflow, which triggers a Solidity revert. This revert stops the execution of the function that updates the fee growth and propagates to any external call that depends on a successful fee calculation, such as providing liquidity or burning liquidity positions. Users attempting to add or remove liquidity therefore see their transactions fail with a generic revert message, and any funds that were already deposited remain locked in the contract because the state cannot be progressed past the failing fee calculation. The issue manifests only when a tick crossing occurs that leaves one side of the fee‑growth‑outside mapping stale, a condition that is not obvious during normal operation and may only be observed under specific price movements. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the range fee‑growth logic and identified that the invariant feeGrowthBelow + feeGrowthAbove ≤ feeGrowthGlobal does not hold in all cases. The problem is subtle because the contract does not explicitly check for this condition, and the underflow only appears in edge‑case price paths, making it easy to miss in routine testing. The root cause is a logical flaw in the tick update algorithm: it fails to keep both fee‑growth‑outside values in sync with the global fee counter. Conceptually, the fix requires either redesigning the tick‑crossing algorithm to update both outside fee growth values or modifying the RangeFeeGrowth calculation to guard against underflow, for example by using a checked subtraction, saturating arithmetic, or by recomputing the fee using a different invariant that never results in a negative intermediate value. By ensuring that the fee calculation never underflows, liquidity providers will be able to add and withdraw positions as expected, and the contract will no longer revert, preserving user funds and maintaining the accounting guarantees of the protocol. From the user’s point of view, the symptom is a transaction that reverts when trying to interact with the pool, leaving the user’s balance unchanged while the contract shows the funds as still deposited, violating the expectation that liquidity operations succeed and that fees are correctly accounted.
summary:
The function `RangeFeeGrowth` ([ConcentratedLiquidityPool.sol#L601-L633](https://github.com/sushiswap/trident/blob/c405f3402a1ed336244053f8186742d2da5975e9/contracts/pool/concentrated/ConcentratedLiquidityPool.sol#L601-L633)) would revert the transaction in some cases.

When a pool cross a tick, it only updates either `feeGrowthOutside0` or `feeGrowthOutside1`. [Ticks.sol#L23-L53](https://github.com/sushiswap/trident/blob/c405f3402a1ed336244053f8186742d2da5975e9/contracts/libraries/concentratedPool/Ticks.sol#L23-L53)

`RangeFeeGrowth` calculates the fee as follow:

```solidity
feeGrowthInside0 = _feeGrowthGlobal0 - feeGrowthBelow0 - feeGrowthAbove0;
feeGrowthInside1 = _feeGrowthGlobal1 - feeGrowthBelow1 - feeGrowthAbove1;
```

`feeGrowthBelow + feeGrowthAbove` is not necessary smaller than `_feeGrowthGlobal`. Please see `POC`.

Users can not provide liquidity or burn liquidity. Fund will get stocked in the contract. I consider this is a high-risk issue.

title: `ConcentratedLiquidityPool.burn
content:
The vulnerability resides in the liquidity pool’s accounting logic that updates on token burns. When a liquidity provider redeems (burns) LP tokens, the contract must decrease its internal reserve variables to reflect the exact amount of underlying assets that are withdrawn from the pool. In the current implementation, the reserve values are reduced only by the fee amounts that are collected during the burn, while the full amount of tokens that leave the pool (principal plus fee) is not subtracted. As a result, the internal reserves (reserve0 and reserve1) become lower than the actual token balances held by the contract (balance0 and balance1). This discrepancy occurs because the update step uses the variables amount0fees and amount1fees instead of the total withdrawn amounts amount0 and amount1. The root cause is a misplaced subtraction in the accounting code, which fails to keep the reserve state in sync with the pool’s real holdings.

An attacker or a regular user can exploit this mismatch by performing a series of burns and mints that manipulate the stale reserve view. Because the reserves are used to calculate price quotes, swap ratios, and fee distribution, an under‑reported reserve causes the pool to appear less liquid than it actually is. Subsequent swaps will be priced incorrectly, potentially allowing a participant to obtain assets at a favorable rate or to drain value from the pool through arbitrage. The impact includes inaccurate pricing, loss of funds for honest participants, and erosion of trust in the protocol’s accounting guarantees. The issue manifests whenever a user burns LP tokens; any burn operation will leave the internal reserves lagging behind the true balances.

All participants who interact with the pool—liquidity providers, traders, and the protocol itself—are affected because the core invariant that "reserve equals token balance" is broken. The problem was uncovered during a formal security audit (Code4rena) that compared the state‑changing logic against the intended accounting model. It is subtle because the pool still holds the correct token amounts, so external balance queries appear normal, making the bug hard to detect through simple balance checks. However, any function that relies on the reserve variables for pricing or fee calculation will behave incorrectly.

To remediate the issue, the reserve update logic should subtract the full withdrawn amounts (amount0 and amount1) rather than only the fee portions. This change restores the invariant that reserves always match the contract's token balances after a burn, thereby re‑establishing correct price calculations and fee distributions. In broader terms, the bug belongs to the class of "state‑invariant violation" or "accounting mismatch" bugs, where internal bookkeeping does not faithfully reflect external asset movements, leading to economic distortion and potential fund loss.
summary:
The reserves should be updated once LP tokens are burned to match the actual total bento shares hold by the pool.

However, the current implementation only updated reserves with the fees subtracted.

Makes the `reserve0` and `reserve1` smaller than the current `balance0` and `balance1`.

title: ConcentratedLiquidityPool: incorrect `feeGrowthGlobal` accounting when crossing ticks
content: The vulnerability lies in the way the ConcentratedLiquidityPool contract records fee growth when a swap operation crosses a price tick. In a swap where token0 is exchanged for token1 (zeroForOne is true), the protocol correctly deducts fees from the output token1 and stores the cumulative fee amount in the global variable feeGrowthGlobal1. Conversely, when swapping in the opposite direction, fees are taken from token0 and stored in feeGrowthGlobal0. The root cause of the issue is a mismatch in the fee accounting logic inside the Ticks.cross() function: the implementation mistakenly updates feeGrowthOutside0 when zeroForOne is true and feeGrowthOutside1 when zeroForOne is false, effectively using the opposite token’s fee growth reference. This inversion causes the per‑tick fee snapshots to be calculated with the wrong fee growth index, leading to inaccurate fee attribution for liquidity providers whose positions span the crossed tick. Exploitation does not require a malicious actor; any legitimate swap that triggers a tick crossing will produce erroneous fee accounting. As a result, liquidity providers may receive less (or more) fee revenue than entitled, and the protocol’s accounting invariants break, potentially causing a mismatch between the total fees collected and the sum of fees distributed, which can manifest to users as missing refunds, balances that appear to shrink unexpectedly, or “funds disappearing” from the pool. The condition occurs whenever a swap traverses a tick boundary—specifically, any swap that changes the price enough to cross the next initialized tick. All participants in the pool, including traders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself, are affected because the fee distribution logic is central to the economic model. The issue was uncovered during a systematic audit by Code4rena, where the auditors compared the initialization of feeGrowthGlobal with the update logic in Ticks.cross() and observed the reversed token indices. The bug is subtle because the contract’s external behavior (swap execution) still succeeds, and the fee discrepancy may only become apparent after many swaps or when reviewing detailed fee accounting reports, making it easy to miss during surface‑level testing. To remediate the problem, the feeGrowthOutside update in Ticks.cross() should reference the same token index as feeGrowthGlobal—i.e., when zeroForOne is true, update feeGrowthOutside1 using feeGrowthGlobal1, and when false, update feeGrowthOutside0 using feeGrowthGlobal0. This correction aligns the per‑tick fee snapshot with the global fee growth used for fee calculation, restoring proper fee distribution and preserving the protocol’s accounting guarantees.

title: `ConcentratedLiquidityPool`: `secondsPerLiquidity` should be modified whenever pool liquidity changes
content:
The vulnerability resides in the accounting of time‑weighted liquidity for a concentrated liquidity pool. The pool maintains a variable called `secondsPerLiquidity` that is meant to capture the cumulative product of time elapsed and the inverse of the pool's total liquidity. The contract updates this variable using the expression `secondsPerLiquidity += uint160((diff << 128) / liquidity)`, where `diff` is the time since the last observation. The root cause is that the contract updates `secondsPerLiquidity` **after** the liquidity amount has already been altered by the `mint()` (add liquidity) or `burn()` (remove liquidity) functions, instead of updating it **before** the liquidity change when the current tick falls inside the newly added or removed position’s range (`lowerTick <= currentTick < upperTick`). Because the calculation uses the old liquidity value, the resulting `secondsPerLiquidity` lags behind the actual state of the pool.

When a liquidity provider adds or removes liquidity while the pool’s price is inside the affected tick range, the stale `secondsPerLiquidity` value is subsequently used by the pool’s observation logic (e.g., during tick insertion or price oracle queries). This leads to an inaccurate time‑weighted average price (TWAP) and fee‑growth tracking. An attacker can deliberately trigger mint or burn operations at strategic moments to distort the observation window, causing the oracle to report a price that is either higher or lower than the true market price. The attacker can then exploit the erroneous price in downstream contracts, perform arbitrage against other pools, or capture fees that should belong to honest liquidity providers.

The impact is therefore a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees: users may receive incorrect swap prices, experience unexpected slippage, or see their accrued fees reduced or disappear entirely. Liquidity providers are particularly affected because the fee‑distribution mechanism relies on an accurate `secondsPerLiquidity` value. The issue manifests only under the specific condition that the pool’s current tick lies inside the liquidity range being modified, which is a common scenario in active markets, making the bug both subtle and potentially high‑value.

The flaw was discovered during a formal security audit (Code4rena) that compared the implementation against the reference Uniswap V3 design, where the reference calls `observations.observeSingle()` to obtain the latest `secondsPerLiquidity` before updating a position. The problem is hard to notice because the variable is internal, its mis‑calculation does not immediately revert transactions, and standard unit tests may not cover the exact ordering of operations under varying price ranges.

To remediate, the contract must recompute the latest `secondsPerLiquidity` **prior** to adjusting the pool’s liquidity in both `mint()` and `burn()` whenever the price is within the position’s active range. Conceptually, the fix mirrors the Uniswap V3 approach: capture the current observation, update `secondsPerLiquidity` using the pre‑change liquidity, and only then apply the liquidity delta. This ensures that subsequent observations and fee calculations are based on a correct, up‑to‑date cumulative metric, restoring the integrity of the pool’s price oracle and fee accounting.
summary:
`secondsPerLiquidity` is updated as such: `secondsPerLiquidity += uint160((diff << 128) / liquidity);` where `diff = timestamp - uint256(lastObservation)`. Hence, whenever liquidity changes, `secondsPerLiquidity` should be updated prior to the change.

In particular, this affects the `mint()` and `burn()` functions, in the case where liquidity changes when `lowerTick <= currentTick < upperTick`.

In fact, the latest `secondsPerLiquidity` value should be calculated and used in `Ticks.insert()`. For comparison, notice how UniswapV3 fetches the latest value by calling `observations.observeSingle()` in its `_updatePosition()` function.

title: Burning does not update reserves
content: The vulnerability resides in the accounting logic of the pool's `burn` operation. When a liquidity provider removes liquidity, the contract correctly transfers the calculated `amount0` and `amount1` tokens back to the provider, but it updates the internal reserve variables using only the fee portions of those amounts (`amount0fees` and `amount1fees`). Consequently, the stored reserves are decreased by a value that is smaller than the actual tokens withdrawn. This mismatch means that after any burn transaction the on‑chain token balances of the pool are lower than the values held in the reserve state variables. The root cause is a mistaken assumption that only the fee portion should affect the pool's accounting, ignoring the principal amount that also leaves the contract. An attacker can exploit this inconsistency by performing a series of burns (or by combining burns with swaps) to create a state where the contract believes it holds more liquidity than it actually does. Subsequent operations that rely on the reserve variables – such as price calculations for swaps, minting new liquidity positions, or further burns – will be based on inflated numbers, enabling the attacker to receive more tokens than warranted or to drain the pool through arbitrage. The impact is a breach of the pool’s economic invariants: users may see their expected refunds reduced to zero, receive less than anticipated, or observe that the pool cannot honor withdrawals because the recorded reserves no longer match the real balances. This condition occurs each time the `burn` function is called, affecting all participants of the pool, including liquidity providers, traders, and the protocol itself. It was discovered during a manual audit of the contract's reserve‑updating code, where the auditor noted that the comment "decreases by fees only" contradicted the intended accounting behavior. The issue is subtle because the contract still passes basic balance checks, and the discrepancy only manifests after multiple burns or when interacting with other functions that assume correct reserves. To remediate the bug, the reserve variables must be reduced by the full amounts transferred out (`amount0` and `amount1`), not just the fee components, thereby restoring the invariant that `reserveX` reflects the actual token balance held by the pool. This class of bug falls under "incorrect internal accounting for token transfers" and violates the fundamental business logic that reserves must always equal the contract's token balances for accurate pricing and fair user expectations.

title: Unsafe cast in `ConcentratedLiquidityPool.burn` leads to attack
content: The vulnerability resides in the liquidity pool’s burn function, which accepts a caller‑controlled amount as an unsigned 128‑bit integer (uint128) and then casts it to a signed 128‑bit integer (int128) before applying a negation. Solidity 0.8.x does not automatically revert on such a cast; a value of 2**128‑1 (the maximum uint128) is interpreted as 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF, which as a signed integer represents -1. The subsequent negation (-(-1)) yields +1, so instead of removing the specified liquidity the contract adds a single liquidity unit to the caller’s position. Because the original unsigned amount is still used later to calculate the amounts of token0 and token1 to be transferred, the attacker can request an arbitrarily large unsigned amount, receive a trivial positive adjustment to the pool position, and then withdraw token amounts that correspond to the huge unsigned value. In practice this allows an attacker to mint LP tokens without providing any underlying assets and to redeem almost the entire pool reserves, effectively stealing the funds. The exploit is triggered when a user calls burn with a deliberately chosen amount and a tick range that satisfies the internal constraints of the _updatePosition routine. Any participant of the pool—including honest liquidity providers—may be affected because the pool’s total reserves can be drained, leading to unexpected zero balances for token0 or token1 and a mismatch between LP token supply and actual assets. The issue was uncovered during a Code4rena audit through manual inspection of the burn implementation and a proof‑of‑concept test that demonstrated the loss of up to 99 % of the pool’s token0 reserves. It is hard to notice because the function name and surrounding logic suggest a normal withdrawal, and the arithmetic operates on large numbers that may not overflow in the usual sense; the problem is a sign‑casting error rather than a classic overflow. The bug belongs to the class of unsafe type conversions where a unsigned integer is cast to a signed type without validation, causing sign‑extension and logical errors. From a user’s perspective the UI would show a successful burn transaction, yet the user’s LP token balance might increase unexpectedly, or other users would see their token balances drop to zero without any visible reason. The correct remediation is to avoid implicit casts by using a safe casting library such as OpenZeppelin’s SafeCast for every conversion between signed and unsigned integers, or to redesign the function to work exclusively with unsigned arithmetic and to explicitly validate that the signed value remains within the intended range before applying any negation.
summary:
The `ConcentratedLiquidityPool.burn` function performs an unsafe cast of a `uint128` type to a _signed_ integer.

```solidity
(uint256 amount0fees, uint256 amount1fees) = _updatePosition(msg.sender, lower, upper, -int128(amount));
```

Note that `amount` is chosen by the caller and when choosing `amount = 2**128 - 1`, this is interpreted as `0xFFFFFFFFF... = -1` as a signed integer. Thus `-(-1)=1` adds 1 liquidity unit to the position

This allows an attacker to not only mint LP tokens for free but as this is the `burn` function it also redeems token0/1 amounts according to the unmodified `uint128` `amount` which is an extremely large value.

title: Wrong usage of `positionId` in `ConcentratedLiquidityPoolManager`
content: The vulnerability resides in the reward‑handling logic of the ConcentratedLiquidityPoolManager contract. In the functions that manage subscription to incentives (subscribe) as well as reward retrieval (getReward and claimReward), the code looks up an incentive record using the identifier called `positionId`. The contract, however, maintains a separate counter named `incentiveId` that uniquely identifies each incentive added to a pool. Because `positionId` refers to a liquidity position rather than an incentive, the lookup `incentives[pool][positionId]` fetches either the wrong incentive entry or an entry that does not exist. When the fetched record does not match an active incentive, the subsequent check `block.timestamp < incentive.endTime` fails, causing the transaction to revert. This mis‑association means that a user who has correctly subscribed to an incentive may receive no reward, see a zero balance returned, or experience a failed claim transaction. The issue occurs whenever a caller provides a valid position identifier but the contract mistakenly uses it as the index of the incentive mapping. All liquidity providers and any party relying on the incentive distribution mechanism are affected because rewards can disappear or become inaccessible. The flaw was identified during a static audit when the mapping key used in the incentive lookup was examined and compared against the contract’s definition of incentive identifiers. The problem is subtle because the variable names `positionId` and `incentiveId` are syntactically similar and both are passed around in the same function signatures, making the misuse easy to overlook in a code review. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of "incorrect identifier usage" or "key‑collision logic errors" that break accounting assumptions: the contract assumes a one‑to‑one correspondence between a user’s position and an incentive, but the data model separates the two. From a user perspective, the UI may show that a subscription was successful, yet the reward claim button either returns 0 or throws an error, contradicting the expectation that a subscribed position will earn a payment. The impact is high because it prevents legitimate reward distribution and could lead to users losing earned incentive funds. The correct fix is to replace every occurrence of `positionId` that is used as a lookup key for the incentives mapping with the proper `incentiveId` counter, ensuring that incentive records are retrieved with the intended identifier and that reward calculations reference the correct time window and amount.
summary:
In the `subscribe` function of `ConcentratedLiquidityPoolManager`, the `incentive` to subscribed is determined as follows:

```solidity
Incentive memory incentive = incentives[pool][positionId];
```

However, `positionId` should be `incentiveId`, a counter that increases by one whenever a new incentive is added to the pool. The usage of `positionId` could cause the wrong incentive to be used, and in general, the incentive is not found, and the transaction reverts (the condition `block.timestamp < incentive.endTime` is not met). The `getReward` and `claimReward` functions have the bug of misusing `positionId` as the index of incentives.

title: `ConcentratedLiquidityPoolManager`’s incentives can be stolen
content: The vulnerability resides in the incentive handling logic of the ConcentratedLiquidityPoolManager contract. The contract stores the reward tokens for every incentive in a single global pool, and the function reclaimIncentive is intended to allow the incentive creator to withdraw any remaining unclaimed rewards after the incentive has expired. However, the implementation fails to modify the incentive's rewardsUnclaimed field when tokens are withdrawn. As a result, the on‑chain accounting entry that tracks how many reward tokens are still available remains unchanged after each successful call to reclaimIncentive. Because the contract only checks that the requested amount does not exceed rewardsUnclaimed, an attacker can repeatedly invoke reclaimIncentive with the same amount, effectively extracting the same tokens multiple times. The attack proceeds as follows: first, the attacker creates a malicious incentive that points to a dummy pool address, selects any ERC‑20 token with a non‑zero rewardsUnclaimed balance, and funds the incentive with that token. The incentive is configured with a short start and end time and an expiry far enough in the future to satisfy the contract’s temporal checks. After the incentive naturally expires, the attacker calls reclaimIncentive, specifying the full rewardsUnclaimed amount. Since the contract never decrements rewardsUnclaimed, the internal state still reports the full amount as available, permitting the attacker to call reclaimIncentive again and again until the contract’s token balance is completely drained. The impact is severe: any token that has been deposited as a reward in any incentive can be stolen, effectively emptying the incentive pool and depriving legitimate users of the promised rewards. This flaw affects all participants in the protocol who rely on incentive payouts, including liquidity providers and token holders, and it undermines the economic guarantees of the platform. The issue was identified during a systematic audit where the state‑update logic of the reclaimIncentive function was examined and found to be missing. The bug is subtle because the function appears to succeed – it transfers tokens and emits no error – yet the accounting variable that should reflect the reduced balance is untouched, making the problem invisible without a careful review of the contract’s storage updates. From a user's perspective the symptom is a disappearance of incentive tokens: users who expect to receive a refund or reward see their balances stay at zero, or previously visible reward pools suddenly become empty without explanation. Conceptually, this is an accounting double‑spend bug: the contract allows the same logical reward amount to be withdrawn multiple times because the internal ledger is not updated. The correct mitigation is to deduct the withdrawn amount from the incentive.rewardsUnclaimed field (or otherwise ensure that the state accurately reflects the remaining unclaimed rewards) before transferring tokens, thereby preventing repeated claims and preserving the integrity of the incentive accounting.
summary: The `ConcentratedLiquidityPoolManager` keeps all tokens for all incentives in the same contract. The `reclaimIncentive` function does not reduce the `incentive.rewardsUnclaimed` field and thus one can reclaim tokens several times. This allows anyone to steal all tokens from all incentives by creating an incentive themself, and once it’s expired, repeatedly claim the unclaimed rewards until the token balance is empty.

title: Overflow in the `mint` function of `ConcentratedLiquidityPool` causes LPs’ funds to be stolen
content: The vulnerability is an integer overflow in the mint routine of the ConcentratedLiquidityPool contract that breaks the fundamental accounting check intended to guarantee that a liquidity provider deposits at least the amount of tokens it claims to contribute. The root cause lies in an unchecked addition of two unsigned 256‑bit values that are first cast to 128‑bit variables (amount1Actual and reserve1) before being summed. Because the addition is performed inside an unchecked block, when the true sum exceeds the 128‑bit limit it wraps around to a small value, causing the subsequent comparison `_balance(token) >= amountActual + reserve` to evaluate to true even though the pool has received far fewer tokens than required. An attacker can trigger this condition by submitting a mint request where the current price equals the upper tick, selecting a carefully crafted amount1Desired that yields a large internal liquidity value but results in amount1Actual that is only slightly below the 128‑bit ceiling. When the pool’s existing reserve1 is greater than the difference between the ceiling and amount1Actual, the addition overflows, the balance check passes, and the attacker receives a disproportionately large amount of LP tokens for a minimal token deposit. The attacker can later burn this inflated liquidity position, retrieving the full value of the pool’s reserves and effectively stealing funds contributed by other liquidity providers. This exploit manifests only under the specific condition that the price tick matches the upper bound of the mint range and that the pool’s reserve for token1 exceeds the overflow threshold, making it non‑obvious during normal operation. Users affected are all participants in the pool: legitimate LPs see their balances reduced or disappear after the malicious mint, and the protocol suffers a loss of trust and capital. The issue was discovered during a focused audit that compared the mint logic to a similar overflow bug previously found in the IndexPool contract, revealing that the unchecked arithmetic was independent of another casting bug in the `_getAmountsForLiquidity` function. The problem is difficult to notice because the contract still reports a successful mint and the overflow produces a value that passes the balance check, masking the discrepancy from external observers. To remediate, the unchecked block should be removed and the addition should be performed using fully 256‑bit arithmetic or the operands should be explicitly cast back to uint256 before the sum, ensuring that any overflow triggers a revert. In broader terms, this is a classic unchecked arithmetic overflow that violates the invariant that deposited token amounts must be at least equal to the required liquidity contribution, leading to money disappearing from the pool and breaking the accounting guarantees of the protocol.
summary:
Similar to a previous finding in the `IndexPool` contract, the `mint` function of `ConcentratedLiquidityPool` allows integer overflows when checking the balance is larger or equal to the received amount of token plus the reserve. As a result, the attacker could get a large amount of liquidity but only provide a small number of tokens to the pool, effectively stealing other LPs’ funds when burning his liquidity.

Notice that this bug is independent of another bug of incorrect casting `uint256` type to `uint128` in the `_getAmountsForLiquidity` function. Even if the previously mentioned bug does not exist, the attacker could still steal the funds in the pool by exploiting this bug.

title: Incorrect usage of typecasting in `_getAmountsForLiquidity` lets an attacker steal funds from the pool
content: The vulnerability is an unchecked type‑casting error in the `_getAmountsForLiquidity` internal function of the ConcentratedLiquidityPool contract. The function takes the results of `DyDxMath.getDy` and `DyDxMath.getDx`, which are computed as `uint256`, and casts them directly to `uint128` without verifying that the values fit within the 128‑bit range. Because Solidity truncates the higher bits on such a cast, any value larger than `type(uint128).max` is silently reduced to its lower 128 bits. This overflow creates a discrepancy between the amount of liquidity that the contract believes it is issuing and the amount of token0 or token1 that the caller actually deposits. An attacker can exploit the bug by calling the `mint` entry point with a deliberately large `amount1Desired` (greater than 2^128) while setting `amount0Desired` to zero and selecting a price range where the current price equals the upper tick. The pool then calculates a very large liquidity value (`_liquidity`) based on the over‑sized `amount1Desired`. When the contract subsequently computes the actual amount of token1 to be taken from the caller, it calls `DyDxMath.getDy`, which returns a `uint256` value that far exceeds the maximum `uint128`. The unchecked cast truncates this value to a much smaller number, so the attacker only pays a tiny fraction of token1 while receiving a huge amount of liquidity tokens. The attacker can later burn those liquidity tokens to withdraw far more token1 than was paid, effectively stealing funds from other liquidity providers and potentially draining the pool. The issue occurs specifically during the minting process when the price is at the upper bound of the requested tick range and the attacker supplies a value that forces the intermediate calculation to overflow the 128‑bit limit. It affects anyone providing liquidity to the pool, as the pool’s accounting can be corrupted, leading to missing funds for honest participants. The bug was discovered by the Code4rena audit team through manual inspection and a crafted proof‑of‑concept that demonstrated the overflow and the resulting fund loss. The problem is subtle because the overflow does not generate a revert; the contract continues execution with a truncated amount, making the discrepancy hard to notice without detailed numeric analysis. To remediate, the contract should validate that the result of `DyDxMath.getDy` and `DyDxMath.getDx` does not exceed `type(uint128).max` before casting, or employ OpenZeppelin’s `SafeCast` library which reverts on overflow. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of unchecked integer casting leading to silent overflow and arithmetic truncation, which violates basic accounting assumptions that the amount taken from a user matches the amount recorded as deposited. From a user’s perspective the symptoms may appear as a situation where a user receives a large amount of liquidity tokens while their token balance is deducted by only a tiny amount, or where the pool’s total token balances shrink unexpectedly after a mint operation, contrary to the expectation that the pool’s token reserves should increase proportionally to the minted liquidity.
summary: The `_getAmountsForLiquidity` function of `ConcentratedLiquidityPool` explicitly converts the result of `DyDxMath.getDy` and `DyDxMath.getDx` from type `uint256` to type `uint128`. The explicit casting without checking whether the integer exceeds the maximum number (i.e., `type(uint128).max`) could cause incorrect results being used. Specifically, an attacker could exploit this bug to mint a large amount of liquidity but only pay a little of `token0` or `token1` to the pool and effectively steal other’s funds when burning his liquidity.

title: `ConcentratedLiquidityPosition.sol#collect
content: The vulnerability resides in the accounting of fee rewards for concentrated liquidity positions. When a liquidity provider calls the public collect() function to claim pending fees, the implementation calculates the owed amount using the pool's rangeFeeGrowth together with the position's feeGrowthInside values. If the Bento token balance of the contract already contains enough tokens to cover the calculated fee, the collect() routine skips a direct call to position.pool.collect(), assuming the fees are already available. However, the burn() function that removes liquidity implicitly triggers a call to position.pool.collect() as part of its execution. Consequently, a user who first invokes collect() when the internal balance is sufficient and then calls burn() ends up receiving the same fee amount twice: once from the explicit collect() call and a second time from the implicit collection performed during burn(). This double‑counting of fees results in an over‑issuance of reward tokens to the user, effectively creating extra tokens out of thin air. The issue manifests only when the contract’s token balance meets or exceeds the pending fee amount at the time of the first collect() call, a condition that can be met during normal operations where the pool has already transferred fees to the contract. The affected parties are liquidity providers who interact with the collect and burn functions, as well as the protocol itself, which suffers an economic loss equal to the duplicated fees. The bug was discovered during a formal audit that examined the interaction between fee collection and liquidity removal logic. It is subtle because each function individually appears to work correctly; only the specific sequence of calling collect() followed by burn() reveals the accounting flaw, making it hard to detect through simple unit tests or casual usage. To remediate the issue, the contract should ensure that fee collection is performed exactly once per fee accrual period. This can be achieved by making burn() invoke position.pool.collect() before the burn operation, or by converting collect() into an internal method that burn() calls after the pool’s burn, thereby preventing the double invocation of the pool’s fee collection routine. In essence, the fix enforces a single source of truth for fee accounting and eliminates the possibility of duplicated rewards, restoring the intended economic guarantees of the protocol.
summary:
When a user calls `ConcentratedLiquidityPosition.sol#collect()` to collect their yield, it calcuates the yield based on `position.pool.rangeFeeGrowth()` and `position.feeGrowthInside0, position.feeGrowthInside1`:

[`ConcentratedLiquidityPosition.sol#L75` L101](https://github.com/sushiswap/trident/blob/c405f3402a1ed336244053f8186742d2da5975e9/contracts/pool/concentrated/ConcentratedLiquidityPosition.sol#L75-L101)

When there are enough tokens in `bento.balanceOf`, it will not call `position.pool.collect()` to collect fees from the pool.

This makes the user who `collect()` their yield when there is enough balance to get double yield when they call `burn()` to remove liquidity. Because `burn()` will automatically collect fees on the pool contract.

title: `ConcentratedLiquidityPosition.sol#burn
content: The vulnerability resides in the burn workflow of a concentrated liquidity position contract. When a liquidity provider calls the burn function, the contract forwards a recipient address supplied by the caller to the pool’s internal burn routine. The pool’s internal _updatePosition routine calculates the total accrued fees for the entire tick range (lower and upper bounds) and transfers those fee amounts together with the withdrawn liquidity to the provided recipient. Because the fee accounting is performed per tick range rather than per individual position, any caller may trigger the fee distribution for the whole range regardless of who originally earned those fees. Consequently, an attacker can create a tiny position that uses the same tick bounds as a victim’s large position, invoke burn, and specify their own address as the recipient. The pool then incorrectly attributes the full amount of unclaimed fees – which may belong to honest liquidity providers – to the attacker, allowing the theft of accrued yield. This flaw occurs whenever multiple positions share identical tick boundaries and the burn function does not enforce that the recipient be the owner of the position. The affected parties include liquidity providers who expect their fees to be returned to them, the protocol’s fee accounting logic, and any users relying on correct distribution of pool earnings. The issue was uncovered during a manual audit of the contract’s source code, where the flow from ConcentratedLiquidityPosition.sol#burn to ConcentratedLiquidityPool.sol#burn was examined and the unchecked recipient parameter was identified. The bug is subtle because the burn interface appears to withdraw only the caller’s liquidity, and the aggregation of fees by tick range obscures the fact that the fees are not partitioned per depositor, making the misallocation easy to overlook. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after providing liquidity they may see their fee balance drop to zero or receive no fees, while an attacker can suddenly obtain a large amount of token0 and token1 that were never theirs. The problem belongs to the class of “incorrect fee attribution” or “unauthorized fee extraction” vulnerabilities, where shared accounting state is exposed to malicious manipulation. To remediate the issue the contract should either hard‑code the recipient to the position owner (e.g., using address(this) or msg.sender) or redesign the fee accounting so that fees are calculated and transferred on a per‑position basis, ensuring that only the rightful owner can claim the portion of fees proportional to their liquidity contribution.
summary:
When a user calls `ConcentratedLiquidityPosition.sol#burn()` to burn their liquidity, it calls `ConcentratedLiquidityPool.sol#burn()` -> `_updatePosition()`:

[`ConcentratedLiquidityPool.sol#L525` L553](https://github.com/sushiswap/trident/blob/c405f3402a1ed336244053f8186742d2da5975e9/contracts/pool/concentrated/ConcentratedLiquidityPool.sol#L525-L553)

The `_updatePosition()` function will return `amount0fees` and `amount1fees` of the whole position with the `lower` and `upper` tick and send them to the `recipient` alongside the burned liquidity amounts.

title: `ConcentratedLiquidityPool`: `initialPrice` should be checked to be within allowable range
content: The vulnerability originates from the constructor of a ConcentratedLiquidityPool where the provided initial price is not validated against the protocol‑defined bounds MIN_SQRT_RATIO and MAX_SQRT_RATIO. Because the contract trusts any arbitrary value for the initial sqrt price, an attacker or a careless deployer can initialise the pool with a price that lies below the minimum or above the maximum, for example a zero or an excessively large value. When the pool later attempts to compute the nearest tick using TickMath.getTickAtSqrtRatio, the out‑of‑range price causes the internal tick lookup to fail, triggering a revert in Ticks.insert() and consequently disabling the core operations of the pool – minting new liquidity positions, performing token swaps, and burning existing positions. From a user’s perspective the pool appears completely unusable: attempts to add liquidity are rejected without a clear error message, swap transactions revert, and any previously supplied funds remain locked with no visible balance updates, giving the impression that the funds have disappeared. The impact is broad – liquidity providers, traders and any other participants that rely on the pool are unable to interact with it, effectively freezing capital and undermining the economic assumptions of the protocol. The issue was discovered during a static analysis audit by Code4rena, where the absence of an input‑validation check in the constructor was noted while tracing the execution path of minting functions. It can be difficult to notice because the contract deploys successfully and the constructor does not emit any warning; the failure only becomes apparent when a user invokes a downstream function, at which point the revert may be generic and not point directly to the root cause. Conceptually, this is a classic case of missing input validation leading to invariant violation: a critical state variable is allowed to hold an illegal value, breaking the contract’s internal consistency. The recommended remediation is to enforce a require statement that ensures MIN_SQRT_RATIO <= initialPrice <= MAX_SQRT_RATIO during pool creation, thereby guaranteeing that all subsequent mathematical operations remain within the expected domain and restoring the normal behaviour of mint, swap and burn functionalities.
summary:
No check is performed for the initial price. This means that it can be set to be below the `MIN_SQRT_RATIO` or above `MAX_SQRT_RATIO` (Eg. zero value), which will prevent the usability of all other functions (minting, swapping, burning).

For example, `Ticks.insert()` would fail when attempting to calculate `actualNearestTick = TickMath.getTickAtSqrtRatio(currentPrice);`, which means no one will able to mint positions.

title: Flash swap call back prior to transferring tokens in `indexPool`
content: The vulnerability resides in the flash‑swap implementation of the IndexPool contract. A flash swap is expected to provide the caller with an amount of tokenOut before invoking the caller's callback, allowing the caller to perform arbitrary logic and then repay the pool with tokenIn. In the current code the contract invokes the callback ITridentCallee(msg.sender).tridentSwapCallback(context) **before** transferring tokenOut to the caller.
