In the examined DAI vault that partners with the NativeStrategyCurve3Crv strategy, the vault calculates its total value by summing the raw balances of all tokens it holds, implicitly assuming that each token unit has the same monetary value. Conversely, the controller’s balanceOf function only aggregates the amount of the strategy’s designated ‘want’ token (in this case the Curve 3CRV LP token) without applying any price conversion. This mismatched treatment of token values causes the reported vault value to be lower after the earn() function moves assets into the strategy. When earn() is called, the vault’s price per full share – the metric users rely on to gauge the worth of their holdings – drops by roughly two percent, meaning that shareholders lose money instead of earning yield. The impact is that everyday users who deposit DAI into the vault see a reduction in the value of their shares, experience missing or reduced refunds when withdrawing, and may observe their displayed balance shrink unexpectedly. The issue manifests specifically when a vault is configured to accept a base token (e.g., DAI) while the associated strategy operates on a different token (e.g., a Curve LP token) and earn() is invoked. It affects all depositors, the protocol’s economic model, and any external integrations that assume accurate share pricing. The flaw was uncovered during a Code4rena audit by reproducing the price drop with a simple web3.py script that recorded the price per full share before and after an earn() call. The problem is difficult to notice because the percentage loss per call is modest, the UI may continue to show a nominal APY, and the accounting discrepancy is hidden behind internal balance sheet calculations. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “price‑misalignment” or “asset accounting inconsistency” vulnerabilities, where contracts treat heterogeneous assets as if they were homogeneous, violating fundamental accounting assumptions. To remediate the issue, the protocol must define a single, consistent representation of the vault’s balance sheet and ensure that every component – the vault’s internal valuation and the controller’s external reporting – applies the same price conversion for all tokens. This can be achieved by either restricting the vault to a single token type that matches the strategy’s want token, or by modifying the controller’s balanceOf logic to multiply each token amount by its current market price before aggregation. By aligning the valuation methodology, the share price will no longer decrease after earn(), protecting users from inadvertent loss of funds.
summary:
For a dai vault that pairs with `NativeStrategyCurve3Crv`, every time `earn()` is called, shareholders would lose money. (about 2%)

There are two issues involved. The `Vault` contract and the `controller` contract doesn’t handle the price difference between the want token and other tokens.

At [Vault.sol L293](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-09-yaxis/blob/main/contracts/v3/Vault.sol#L293-L303), when a vault calculates its value, it sums up all tokens balance. However, when the controller calculates vaults’ value (at [Controller.sol L410-L436](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-09-yaxis/blob/main/contracts/v3/controllers/Controller.sol#L410-L436)), it only adds the amount of `strategy.want` it received. (in this case, it’s t3crv).

Under the current design, users who deposit dai to the vault would not get yield. Instead, they would keep losing money. I consider this a high-risk issue

title: `Vault.balance`
content: The vulnerability is a decimal‑normalization mismatch in the Vault contract’s balance aggregation routine. The function that reports the vault’s total holdings first iterates over each registered token, reads the on‑chain balance of the vault for that token, and then passes the raw amount through a helper that scales the value to 18 decimal places – a common convention that allows mixed‑decimals tokens to be summed uniformly. After processing all tokens, the function adds a second term obtained from the controller contract via IController(manager.controllers(address(this))).balanceOf(). This second term is taken directly from the controller’s internal accounting field, which stores raw token amounts without applying the same 18‑decimal normalization. Consequently, when a token such as USDC (which uses six decimals) is part of the controller’s balance, its value is added to the already‑scaled total as a six‑decimal figure, creating a systematic under‑ or over‑counting of assets depending on the token’s decimal configuration. The root cause is the inconsistent use of the _normalizeDecimals helper: it is applied to token balances read from the vault but omitted for the controller‑derived balance. Exploitation is straightforward – an attacker who can influence the controller’s reported balance (for example by depositing a low‑decimal token) can cause the aggregated vault balance to appear smaller than the actual assets, potentially inflating share values, misleading fee calculations, or creating a scenario where withdrawals succeed with insufficient collateral. The impact is a breach of accounting integrity that can distort user dashboards (showing a lower or higher total balance than reality), affect yield calculations, and open avenues for profit‑draining attacks. This condition manifests whenever the vault holds at least one token with a decimal count different from 18 and also relies on the controller’s balanceOf method for its total. Affected parties include token holders, liquidity providers, and any protocol components that depend on the reported total for fee distribution or risk assessment. The issue was uncovered during a formal static analysis audit by Code4rena, which flagged the mixed‑decimal addition as a high‑severity accounting flaw. It may be difficult to notice because individual token balances are displayed correctly, while the aggregated total – often shown in a single UI element – deviates subtly, especially for tokens with fewer decimals. The recommended remediation is to apply the same 18‑decimal normalization to the controller’s balance before adding it to the vault total, ensuring a consistent accounting pathway throughout the contract. This aligns the code with the principle of uniform decimal handling, eliminates the mis‑reporting bug, and restores trust in the protocol’s financial reporting.

title: `Vault.withdraw` mixes normalized and standard amounts
content: The vulnerability resides in the way the Vault contract handles token amounts that have different decimal precisions. The contract provides a `balance()` helper that normalizes every token balance to 18 decimals by calling an internal `_normalizeDecimals` routine. However, elsewhere in the contract – most notably in the `Vault.withdraw` function – the code mixes these normalized values with raw token balances that retain their native decimal format. When a user initiates a withdrawal, the requested amount (`_amount`) is calculated using the normalized 18‑decimal representation, while the current on‑chain token balance (`_balance = IERC20(_output).balanceOf(address(this))`) is taken directly from the token contract without any scaling. The function then compares the unscaled `_balance` against the scaled `_amount` and even subtracts the two, assuming they are expressed in the same units. Because the two quantities are not comparable, the contract can incorrectly conclude that sufficient funds are available when they are not, or it may subtract a larger normalized amount from a smaller raw balance, leading to an under‑withdrawal or an arithmetic mismatch. This inconsistency can cause users to receive less than the amount they requested, or in certain edge cases allow a malicious caller to trigger a withdrawal path that leaves the vault with a deficit, breaking the accounting guarantees of the protocol. The bug is triggered whenever `vault.balanceOfThis()` or `vault.balance()` is used to derive a token amount that is later used without first denormalizing it back to the token’s native precision. It was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where the auditors noted the mismatch between the normalized and unnormalized branches of the code. The issue is subtle because the contract appears to enforce a balance check, but the hidden decimal conversion error makes the check ineffective, and the problem may only surface when tokens with non‑18‑decimal precisions are involved. To remediate the flaw, every amount obtained from the normalized balance helper must be converted back to the token’s native decimal representation before any comparison, subtraction, or external call, ensuring that all arithmetic operates on homogeneous units. Consistently applying `_normalizeDecimals` (or its inverse) across the entire codebase restores the intended accounting logic, prevents mismatched withdrawals, and protects user funds from disappearing or being incorrectly accounted for.

title: Use of tokenB’s price instead of tokenA in determining account health will lead to protocol mis-accounting and insolvency
content: The vulnerability is a calculation error in the credit‑supply routine of the lending pair contract. When the protocol computes the amount of token B that can be supplied as credit, it calls an internal conversion function with the price of token B (_priceB) as the last argument, even though the conversion should use the price of token A (_priceA). This typo causes the derived values for supplyB, creditB, and the aggregate creditUni to be severely understated or overstated, which in turn corrupts the totalAccountSupply figure used by the accountHealth() routine. Account health is the metric that determines whether a user’s collateral is sufficient to support their borrowings, withdrawals, transfers, and liquidations. Because the health calculation relies on the mis‑computed supply numbers, the protocol may incorrectly deem an under‑collateralised position as safe, allowing further borrowing or withdrawals that exceed the actual value of the deposited assets. Over time, this mis‑accounting can deplete the pool of assets, leading to partial or complete insolvency of the protocol. The flaw manifests whenever a user supplies token B via the _supplyCreditUni path, which is invoked during regular operations such as deposit, borrow, or liquidity provision. Any participant who interacts with the contract – lenders, borrowers, and liquidity providers – is affected because the inaccurate health check can cause unexpected loss of funds or failed liquidations. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the flow of price arguments through conversion helpers and identified the mismatched variable name at line 674 of the contract. It is easy to miss because the surrounding code appears logically correct and the price values are both unsigned integers, so a simple swap does not produce a compile‑time error. The symptom from a user’s perspective is that their account may appear healthy while the on‑chain balance of their collateral is insufficient, leading to situations where a withdrawal or borrow succeeds but later the protocol cannot honour redemption requests, effectively making funds disappear. This bug belongs to the class of accounting or logic‑mistake vulnerabilities where an incorrect parameter is propagated through financial calculations, violating the fundamental assumption that collateral value is accurately reflected in health checks. To remediate the issue, the contract should be updated so that the conversion function receives the correct price input (_priceA) when calculating the token B supply, ensuring that all downstream credit and health metrics are based on precise market values.
summary: In `_supplyCreditUni()`, the last argument of `_convertTokenValues()` on `L674` being `_priceB` instead of `_priceA` in the calculation of `supplyB` is a typo (should be `_priceA`) and therefore miscalculates `supplyB`, `creditB`, `creditUni` and therefore `totalAccountSupply` in function `accountHealth()` which affects the health of account/protocol determination that is used across all borrows/withdrawals/transfers/liquidations in the protocol. This miscalculation significantly affects all calculations in protocol and could therefore cause protocol insolvency.

title: Liquidation can be escaped by depositing a Uni v3 position with 0 liquidity
content: The vulnerability resides in the liquidation workflow of the lending protocol, which accepts Uniswap V3 position NFTs as collateral and attempts to unwrap them during a liquidation call. The protocol’s liquidateAccount() function invokes an internal helper that calls the Uniswap V3 NonfungiblePositionManager’s decreaseLiquidity() method to extract the underlying tokens from the deposited position. This call assumes that the position always holds a positive amount of liquidity. However, Uniswap V3 permits the creation of a position NFT that contains zero liquidity. When a borrower deposits such a zero‑liquidity NFT and later becomes under‑collateralized, the liquidator’s attempt to call decreaseLiquidity() reverts because there is no liquidity to decrease, as documented in the Uniswap V3 periphery contract. The revert aborts the entire liquidation transaction, meaning the protocol is unable to seize collateral or repay the outstanding debt. From the borrower’s perspective, an under‑collateralized loan remains active and no liquidation occurs, contrary to the expectation that the system would automatically enforce liquidation and protect lenders. This flaw was discovered during a formal audit when the auditors inspected the liquidation path and observed that the helper function lacked validation for the liquidity amount of the deposited position. The issue is difficult to notice because the NFT appears valid and may be displayed in user interfaces without indicating that its liquidity is zero, so users and auditors might assume it provides collateral value. The impact is that malicious actors can deliberately deposit zero‑liquidity positions to block liquidation, potentially leading to prolonged exposure of the protocol to bad debt and loss of funds for lenders. The bug belongs to the class of “unchecked external call” or “assumption violation” vulnerabilities, where a contract makes implicit assumptions about the state of an external asset without verifying it. To remediate the problem, the protocol should explicitly check that any Uniswap V3 position used as collateral has a non‑zero liquidity amount before attempting to unwrap it, or it should gracefully handle the revert by treating the position as having zero value and proceeding with liquidation using other collateral. Alternatively, the system could prohibit the deposit of zero‑liquidity positions altogether. By enforcing these safeguards, the liquidation logic will no longer be subverted, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions about collateral value will be restored.
summary:
When the liquidator is trying to liquidate a undercollateralized loan by calling `liquidateAccount()`, it calls `_unwrapUniPosition()` -> `uniV3Helper.removeLiquidity()` -> `positionManager.decreaseLiquidity()`.

However, when the Uni v3 position has 0 liquidity, `positionManager.decreaseLiquidity()` will fail.

See: <https://github.com/Uniswap/v3-periphery/blob/main/contracts/NonfungiblePositionManager.sol#L265>

Based on this, a malicious user can escape liquidation by depositing a Uni v3 position with 0 liquidity.

title: `Controller.setCap` sets wrong vault balance
content: The vulnerability resides in the controller contract’s setCap function, which is responsible for adjusting the maximum amount (cap) that a strategy may hold and for withdrawing any surplus tokens that exceed the new cap. When the function detects an excess amount, it calculates the difference (named _diff) between the current strategy balance and the newly set cap, and then transfers that surplus back to the vault. However, instead of updating the vault’s internal accounting by the amount actually withdrawn (_diff), the code erroneously subtracts the entire strategy balance (_balance) from the vault’s recorded balance. This mis‑subtraction causes the vault’s stored balance to be reduced far beyond the real amount of assets that left the strategy. The root cause is a simple logic error: the wrong variable is used in the arithmetic operation that updates the vault’s bookkeeping. An attacker or any user who can trigger a cap reduction can exploit this flaw by calling setCap with a lower cap, forcing the contract to execute the faulty subtraction. As a result, the vault’s internal ledger will reflect a deficit that does not correspond to any actual token movement, leading to inconsistent accounting, reduced apparent user balances, and potentially erroneous fee or reward calculations. Users may observe that after a cap change, their vault share value drops dramatically or that withdrawals are rejected because the protocol believes there are insufficient funds, even though the tokens are still held by the strategy. This issue manifests whenever the controller attempts to lower a strategy’s cap and withdraw excess assets, affecting all participants who rely on the vault’s balance for deposits, withdrawals, or reward distribution. The problem was discovered during a Code4rena audit, where a reviewer highlighted the incorrect subtraction with an inline comment. Because the erroneous update only affects an internal variable, the bug can be hard to detect through simple token balance checks; only the vault’s bookkeeping state reveals the discrepancy. To remediate the flaw, the contract should subtract the calculated excess amount (_diff) from the vault’s balance instead of the full strategy balance, ensuring that the internal accounting accurately mirrors the actual token flow. Implementing this change restores proper accounting, prevents unintended balance reductions, and aligns the protocol’s on‑chain state with its economic expectations, thereby protecting users from mistakenly losing access to their funds or receiving incorrect payouts.

title: `removeToken` would break the vault/protocol.
content: The vulnerability resides in the managerial function that allows an administrator to remove a supported token from a vault without performing any safety checks or state migrations. The root cause is an unchecked call to `removeToken` that directly deletes the token mapping for the vault while leaving the vault's share accounting untouched. When the function is invoked after the vault has already accumulated assets, the underlying token balance recorded in the vault drops to zero, yet the total supply of vault shares remains unchanged. Because share price is calculated as total value divided by total supply, the price collapses, effectively making every existing share worthless. The controller contract continues to report the old token balance because its internal `_vaultDetails[msg.sender].balance` field is never updated after the token removal, creating a discrepancy between the view of the protocol and the actual on‑chain state. Users attempting to withdraw their funds will receive nothing, as the vault no longer holds the token required for redemption. From a user’s perspective the UI may show that their shares are still present (the balance of shares is unchanged) but the underlying balance reads zero and the displayed price of each share plummets, leading to confusion and perceived loss of funds. This issue was discovered during a formal audit when the security team executed a proof‑of‑concept script that called `removeToken` and observed the vault’s balance become zero while totalSupply stayed constant. The bug is hard to notice because no transaction reverts; the state transition is silent and only manifests later when users attempt withdrawals or when analytics display abnormal share‑price metrics. The class of bug can be described as an unchecked token‑removal operation that violates accounting invariants and breaks the invariant that total vault value must remain proportional to total share supply. To remediate, the protocol should enforce a complete migration of the token out of all strategies, withdraw the token from the vault, optionally convert it to an allowed replacement token, and only then permit removal. Additional checks must verify that the vault’s balance for the token is zero and that the controller’s recorded balances are reconciled before allowing the admin call, thereby preserving accounting consistency and preventing loss of user funds.
summary:
There’s no safety check in Manager.sol’s `removeToken`. [Manager.sol#L454-L487](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-09-yaxis/blob/main/contracts/v3/Manager.sol#L454-L487)

1. The token would be locked in the original vault. Given the current design, the vault would keep a ratio of total amount to save the gas. Once the token is removed at manager contract, these token would lost.
2. Controller’s `balanceOf` would no longer reflects the real value. [Controller.sol#L488-L495](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-09-yaxis/blob/main/contracts/v3/controllers/Controller.sol#L488-L495) While `_vaultDetails[msg.sender].balance;` remains the same, user can no longer withdraw those amount.
3. Share price in the vault would decrease drastically. The share price is calculated as `totalValue / totalSupply` [Vault.sol#L217](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-09-yaxis/blob/main/contracts/v3/Vault.sol#L217). While the `totalSupply` of the share remains the same, the total balance has drastically decreased.

Calling `removeToken` way would almost break the whole protocol if the vault has already started. I consider this is a high-risk issue.

title: Prevent execution with invalid signatures
content: The vulnerability is an unchecked privilege assignment to the zero address (address(0)) that permits any caller to invoke the contract's execute() function with an invalid signature. In the Identity contract constructor a list of privileged addresses is accepted without validation; if a zero address is accidentally included, the mapping privileges[0] is set to a non‑zero value (typically 1). Later, when execute() is called, the contract recovers the signer address from the supplied signature using ecrecover (implemented as recoverAddrImpl). For malformed or deliberately invalid signatures ecrecover returns address(0). The contract then checks whether the recovered address has privileges by evaluating privileges[signer] != 0. Because privileges[0] == 1, this condition is satisfied, and the contract proceeds to execute the supplied transaction payload. Consequently, an attacker can submit any arbitrary calldata together with an invalid signature and the contract will treat the call as authorized, allowing execution of any state‑changing function, including fund transfers. The impact is a full privilege escalation: any user can trigger arbitrary logic, potentially draining assets, corrupting protocol state, or breaking the intended business rules. The bug manifests whenever the Identity contract is instantiated with a zero address among its initial privileged accounts, a situation that can occur through a simple mistake in deployment scripts or manual configuration. It also applies to any later function that sets privileges without preventing address(0) from being granted rights. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the constructor logic and noted that ecrecover may yield address(0) for invalid signatures, but the contract never filtered out that result. It is hard to notice because address(0) is rarely used in normal operation, and a failed signature often silently returns zero without raising an exception. To remediate the vulnerability, the constructor (and any other function that assigns privileges) should explicitly reject address(0) using a require statement, and the execute() logic should also verify that the recovered signer is not zero before checking the privileges mapping. This prevents the zero address from ever acquiring authority and ensures that only valid, properly signed transactions can be executed, restoring the intended access control guarantees of the Identity contract.
summary:
Suppose one of the supplied `addrs[i]` to the constructor of `Identity.sol` happens to be 0 ( by accident).

In that case: `privileges[0] = 1`

Now suppose you call `execute()` with an invalid signature, then `recoverAddrImpl` will return a value of 0 and thus signer=0. If you then check `privileges[signer] !=0` this will be true and anyone can perform any transaction.

This is clearly an unwanted situation.

title: An attacker can steal funds from multi-token vaults
content: The vulnerability resides in the accounting logic of a multi‑token vault that aggregates the balances of several ERC‑20 tokens. The contract calculates the total vault balance by iterating over each accepted token, normalising its decimals, and simply adding the raw token amounts together. This approach implicitly assumes that every token has an identical monetary value, ignoring the fact that market prices of the underlying assets can diverge. Because the price of each token is not incorporated into the balance calculation, the vault’s reported total balance can be substantially overstated or understated relative to the true USD (or reference) value of the assets held. An attacker can exploit this mismatch by depositing a token that is temporarily undervalued relative to the other tokens in the vault and then withdrawing an equivalent share of the vault’s reported balance, which will be satisfied with the higher‑valued tokens. In the proof‑of‑concept scenario, the attacker deposits a large amount of USDT when its market price is below parity, then withdraws the corresponding shares and receives DAI and USDC whose combined market value exceeds the original USDT deposit. The exploit results in a net profit for the attacker while other depositors experience a loss of value, effectively draining funds from the vault. The flaw manifests whenever the vault accepts more than one token whose market prices are not perfectly aligned, and when the protocol permits users to deposit and withdraw based on the naïve total balance. All users holding shares in the vault, as well as the protocol’s governance and liquidity providers, are affected because the accounting inconsistency undermines the fundamental guarantee that each share corresponds to a fixed amount of value. The issue was uncovered during a formal security audit (Code4rena) by analysing the balanceOfThis function and recognizing that its implementation mirrors a known pattern that led to the Yearn finance exploit. The problem is subtle because the contract’s public balance function appears to return a sensible numeric total, and the UI may display share prices that seem correct, while the underlying valuation is flawed. To remediate, the vault must incorporate token price information—such as using a virtual price index, an oracle‑based weighted sum, or by restricting the vault to a single LP token whose price is well defined—so that the total balance reflects true economic value rather than raw token quantities. This change restores the integrity of accounting, prevents arbitrage based on price differentials, and protects users from unexpected loss of funds.

title: `QuickAccManager.sol#cancel
content: The vulnerability resides in the cancel function of the QuickAccManager contract. The function tries to locate a previously scheduled transaction by recomputing a transaction identifier called hashTx. However, the identifier is built with abi.encode(address(this), block.chainid, accHash, nonce, txns) – it omits the final boolean flag that is part of the identifier stored when the transaction was originally scheduled. Because the stored key in the scheduled mapping includes that missing flag, the recomputed hash never matches any entry, causing the require statement `scheduled[hashTx] != 0 && block.timestamp < scheduled[hashTx]` to fail and reverting with the error “TOO_LATE”. The root cause is a mismatch between the hash construction used at scheduling time and the hash construction used at cancellation time, i.e., a missing parameter in the hash computation. This mismatch can be exploited by preventing legitimate users from cancelling their own scheduled transactions; the contract will always treat the cancellation request as referring to a non‑existent or already‑executed transaction. Consequently, funds that were intended to be reversible become locked until the scheduled execution time passes, breaking the expected workflow where a user can rescind a pending operation. The issue manifests whenever a user calls cancel with a correctly signed request – the transaction reverts even though the signature is valid and the transaction is still pending. Affected parties include any wallet holder or dApp that relies on the QuickAccManager’s ability to cancel scheduled actions, potentially leading to loss of control over funds. The problem was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s logic, where the auditor noticed that the cancel function’s hash calculation differed from the one used in the scheduling path. The bug is subtle because both hash constructions look superficially similar, and the scheduled mapping is only accessed via the hash, so static analysis may not flag the missing argument without a detailed comparison of the two code paths. To remediate the issue, the cancel function should recompute the identifier using exactly the same encoding as the scheduling routine, including the boolean flag (or alternatively store the original hash when scheduling and compare directly). Aligning the hash generation ensures that the `require` condition can correctly locate the pending entry, restoring the ability for users to cancel transactions as designed.

title: Usage of an incorrect version of `Ownable` library can potentially malfunction all `onlyOwner` functions
content: The vulnerability stems from an upgradeability mismatch between the DelegatedStaking contract and the OpenZeppelin Ownable library it imports. The contract is intended to be deployed behind a proxy and therefore follows the initializer pattern instead of using a constructor. However, the source imports the standard, non‑upgradeable Ownable contract, whose constructor assigns the deployer as the owner. Because upgradeable proxies prohibit constructors, the constructor in the imported Ownable contract never runs, leaving the internal owner slot unset (typically the zero address). As a result, every function guarded by the onlyOwner modifier reverts, effectively making all administrative actions – such as parameter updates, emergency withdrawals, or any privileged operation – inaccessible. This condition manifests whenever the DelegatedStaking proxy is initialized; the contract appears to compile and deploy correctly, yet runtime checks reveal that the owner is missing. Users and protocol operators expecting the owner to manage the contract are instead met with silent failure: calls to admin functions return “caller is not the owner”, and any logic that depends on owner‑only actions cannot be executed, potentially freezing funds or preventing crucial upgrades. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by inspecting the import statements and recognizing that the upgradeable pattern was not paired with the matching OwnableUpgradeable contract. The bug can be hard to notice because compilation succeeds and there is no explicit warning; only runtime tests of onlyOwner functions expose the problem. Conceptually, the fix is to replace the non‑upgradeable Ownable with OwnableUpgradeable (or a comparable AccessControlUpgradeable) and to invoke its initialization routine (e.g., __Ownable_init()) inside the contract’s initialize function, ensuring the owner variable is correctly set before any onlyOwner functions are used. This correction restores proper access control, allowing the designated owner to perform privileged actions and preventing the accidental loss of administrative capability.
summary:
[`DelegatedStaking.sol` L62-L63](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-10-covalent/blob/ded3aeb2476da553e8bb1fe43358b73334434737/contracts/DelegatedStaking.sol#L62-L63)

```solidity
// this is used to have the contract upgradeable
function initialize(uint128 minStakedRequired) public initializer {
```

Based on the context and comments in the code, the `DelegatedStaking.sol` contract is designed to be deployed as an upgradeable proxy contract.

However, the current implementation is using a non-upgradeable version of the `Ownable` library: `@openzeppelin/contracts/access/Ownable.sol` instead of the upgradeable version: `@openzeppelin/contracts-upgradeable/access/OwnableUpgradeable.sol`.

A regular, non-upgradeable `Ownable` library will make the deployer the default owner in the constructor. Due to a requirement of the proxy-based upgradeability system, no constructors can be used in upgradeable contracts. Therefore, there will be no owner when the contract is deployed as a proxy contract.

As a result, all the `onlyOwner` functions will be inaccessible.

title: `unstake` should update exchange rates first
content: The vulnerability resides in the unstake routine of the staking contract, where the function computes the number of validator shares to remove using the exchange rate that is still stale at the moment of calculation. Specifically, the contract first calls a conversion helper to transform the requested token amount into shares based on the current v.exchangeRate, then, only after this conversion, it updates the global exchange rate and the validator-specific rate if the validator is not disabled. Because the exchange rate can increase after each epoch as rewards accrue, calculating the share reduction with the old rate causes the contract to burn a larger amount of shares than necessary. The user’s stake is deducted correctly in token terms, but the share balance is reduced according to the outdated rate, effectively erasing the user’s entitlement to the accrued rewards. When the user later attempts to claim rewards via redeemAllRewards, the contract reports zero rewards because the shares that would have generated those rewards were unintentionally removed. This bug manifests whenever a user invokes unstake after one or more reward‑generating epochs without first redeeming their rewards, and only when the validator is active (i.e., not disabled). It was uncovered during a formal audit performed by Code4rena, where test scenarios demonstrated that a staker who deposited 1000 tokens and expected a total payout of 2000 tokens after rewards only received the principal amount, with their share balance reset to zero, making subsequent reward claims impossible. The issue is subtle because the contract does not revert or throw an error; the transaction succeeds, leading users to believe the operation completed correctly, while silently degrading their economic position. The root cause is a ordering mistake: the exchange rates must be refreshed before any share calculations are performed. To remediate the flaw, the contract should call updateGlobalExchangeRate() and updateValidator(v) at the very start of the unstake function, ensuring that the conversion from tokens to shares reflects the most recent rate and preserving the correct share balance and reward entitlement. This class of bug is an accounting‑logic error where stale state is used for financial calculations, resulting in unintended loss of funds and broken accounting assumptions.

title: Signature replay attacks for different identities
content: The vulnerability is a signature replay attack that arises when a single QuickAccount contract is used as the privileged signer for multiple distinct identity contracts. The contract’s manager function `send` validates a signed message by reconstructing a hash that incorporates a nonce, the signer’s accHash, and other transaction parameters, but it deliberately omits the identity address from that hash. Because the nonce counter is stored per identity rather than per accHash, two fresh identities that share the same QuickAccount both start with a nonce value of zero. Consequently, the same signature that authorises a transfer for identity 1 produces an identical hash for identity 2. An attacker who observes a legitimate `send` call from identity 1 can simply replay the exact same parameters, substituting the second identity’s address, and the verification will succeed. This enables the attacker to execute arbitrary transactions on identity 2, such as moving funds, without the legitimate owner’s consent. The issue manifests whenever a QuickAccount is purposefully linked to more than one identity, a pattern that is encouraged by a comment in the source code, and when the manager does not embed the caller’s address into the signed payload. Users see unexpected withdrawals or transfers from an account they never authorized, effectively experiencing “funds disappear” or “unauthorized transaction” symptoms. The problem is subtle because the signature itself appears valid, the nonce values look correct, and the contract’s logic assumes that the signer (the QuickAccount) uniquely binds the operation, overlooking the fact that the same signer can be referenced by multiple identities. To remediate the flaw, the nonce should be tied to the accHash rather than the identity, ensuring a single replay‑prevention counter per signer, and the identity address must be included in the signed hash so that each signed message is intrinsically bound to a specific identity. This aligns the security model with standard replay‑protection practices and prevents cross‑identity reuse of signatures.
summary:
A single `QuickAccount` can serve as the “privilege” for multiple identities, see the comment in `QuickAccManager.sol`:

NOTE: a single accHash can control multiple identities, as long as those identities set it’s hash in privileges[address(this)]. this is by design

If there exist two different identities that _both share the same QuickAccount_ (`identity1.privileges(address(this)) == identity2.privileges(address(this)) == accHash`) the following attack is possible in `QuickAccManager.send`:

Upon observing a valid `send` on the first identity, the same transactions can be replayed on the second identity by an attacker calling `send` with the same arguments and just changing the `identity` to the second identity.

This is because the `identity` is not part of the `hash`. Including the **nonce of** the identity in the hash is not enough.

Two fresh identities will both take on nonces on zero and lead to the same hash.

title: `QuickAccManager` Smart Contract signature verification can be exploited
content: The vulnerability lies in the way the QuickAccManager contract validates signatures supplied to the Identity.execute function. When a caller provides a signature, the contract forwards the raw signature bytes to the SignatureValidator library, which recovers an address (the signer) and then checks the signer against a privileges mapping. The critical flaw is that the signature itself contains an attacker‑controlled address (the "id" contract) that is later used for the privilege check. Because the contract blindly trusts the id value extracted from the signature, an attacker can deploy a malicious contract that implements a privileges function returning any chosen bytes32 value. By encoding this malicious contract address into a signature of type SignatureMode.SmartWallet, the attacker can cause QuickAccManager.isValidSignature to call the attacker’s privileges function, receive a value that matches the expected account hash, and consequently pass the privilege check. This bypass allows arbitrary transactions to be executed through Identity.execute without genuine authorization. The exploit can be carried out whenever the SmartWallet signature mode is used, the Identity contract forwards the signature to QuickAccManager, and the privileges mapping contains a non‑zero entry for the targeted account – conditions that are common in the Ambire adex protocol where a single QuickAccManager instance manages many user accounts. The affected parties are the users of the protocol whose funds are stored in accounts managed by QuickAccManager, as well as the protocol itself, because the attacker can move or drain assets from any account whose privileges entry can be mimicked. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by analysing the signature handling logic and noticing that the id parameter is not validated and can be any contract address. It is hard to notice because the ERC‑1271 standard assumes one contract per wallet, and the singleton design of QuickAccManager violates that assumption; the signature appears valid on‑chain and no explicit error is emitted, so the misbehaviour blends with normal operation. From a user’s perspective, a transaction that should have been rejected may succeed, leading to symptoms such as balances suddenly dropping to zero, refunds not being received, or funds disappearing without any visible error. The root cause is the unchecked trust of external contract calls derived from signature data, effectively an authorization bypass. To remediate, the contract should stop trusting the id supplied in the signature and instead use msg.sender (or another verified source) as the identity, enforce that only trusted identity contracts can be consulted, or redesign the signature validation to avoid mixing ERC‑1271 semantics with a singleton manager. In essence, the fix requires ensuring that the contract does not call arbitrary external contracts for privilege checks and that the privilege mapping is consulted only for verified, immutable identities.

title: The design of `wibBTC` is not fully compatible with the current Curve StableSwap pool
content: The vulnerability originates from the incompatibility between the dynamic‑balance design of the wibBTC token and the accounting model used by Curve’s StableSwap pools. wibBTC is a rebasing‑style ERC20 whose internal "pricePerShare" variable causes each holder’s token balance to increase automatically as the underlying asset appreciates, without any explicit transfer. Curve StableSwap, on the other hand, assumes that token balances are static between transactions and records the amount of each coin in the pool based solely on the net of deposits, withdrawals and swaps performed by users. Because the pool contract does not include a mechanism equivalent to Uniswap V2’s sync() function, the reserves stored in the pool diverge from the true on‑chain balances of wibBTC whenever pricePerShare rises. This divergence can occur at any point after a user deposits wibBTC into the pool, i.e., as soon as the token’s automatic balance adjustment takes effect. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that the amount of wibBTC they receive back after a swap or withdrawal is lower than expected, sometimes appearing as if the pool “eats” their tokens or returns zero, despite the token contract showing a higher balance. The impact is that the pool’s pricing algorithm operates on stale reserve data, leading to incorrect swap rates, potential arbitrage opportunities for an attacker, and ultimately the loss or locking of user funds. The issue was identified during a security audit that compared the documented token model to the actual implementation of the Curve pool, noting that the pool lacks any function to resynchronize its internal accounting with the token’s rebasing behavior. The problem is hard to spot because wibBTC presents a standard ERC20 interface, so developers may not immediately recognize the hidden, automatic balance changes. To remediate the problem the protocol should either replace wibBTC with a non‑rebasing token for the pool or redesign the StableSwap contract to explicitly handle dynamic balances, for example by adding a sync‑like routine that updates stored reserves after each pricePerShare change, or by building a custom pool that incorporates the token’s rate‑multiplier logic into its invariant calculations. In essence, the bug is a classic case of a token’s internal accounting model conflicting with a DeFi primitive that assumes static balances, violating the core business logic that pool reserves must accurately reflect the actual token quantities held.
summary:
Per the documentation, `wibBTC` is designed for a Curve StableSwap pool. However, the design of `wibBTC` makes the balances change dynamically and automatically. This is unusual for an ERC20 token, and it’s not fully compatible with the current Curve StableSwap pool.

Specifically, a Curve StableSwap pool will maintain the balances of its `coins` based on the amount of tokens added, removed, and exchanged each time. In another word, it can not adopt the dynamic changes of the balances that happened automatically.

The pool’s actual dynamic balance of `wibBTC` will deviate from the recorded balance in the pool contract as the `pricePerShare` increases.

Furthermore, there is no such way in Curve StableSwap similar to the `sync()` function of UNI v2, which will force sync the stored `reserves` to match the balances.

title: Approved spender can spend too many tokens
content: The vulnerability resides in the way the ERC‑20‑like rebasing token tracks allowances for third‑party spenders. When a token holder calls `approve(spender, amount)` the contract stores the allowance in terms of *shares* rather than the current token amount. Because the token’s price per share (`pricePerShare`) can change over time due to rebasing, the numerical value of the stored allowance effectively grows whenever the price per share increases. Most contracts that interact with this token calculate the approval amount based on the number of tokens they intend to move in a subsequent `transferFrom` call, and they pass exactly that same number to `approve`. After a price‑per‑share increase, the same share allowance now corresponds to a larger token balance, allowing the approved spender to call `transferFrom` and withdraw more tokens than the holder originally intended. The root cause is that the `_allowances` mapping records the allowance in a rebasing unit and the `transferFrom` implementation subtracts the *share* amount (`amountInShares`) instead of the actual token amount transferred. Consequently, the allowance is not reduced by the correct amount and can be repeatedly exploited as the token rebalances. This flaw can be exploited by a malicious spender who waits for a positive rebasing event, then invokes `transferFrom` using the stale, oversized allowance to pull excess tokens from the holder’s balance. The impact is a potential drain of funds from any user who has granted an allowance, undermining the protocol’s accounting assumptions that an allowance limits the exact token quantity. The issue manifests only in contracts that use the rebasing token and rely on the standard `approve`/`transferFrom` flow; it is invisible to users because the UI shows the approved amount at the time of approval, while the underlying allowance silently expands with each rebasing. The bug was discovered during a Code4rena audit through a logical examination of the allowance handling logic. It is hard to notice because the contract does not emit events indicating a change in allowance value after rebasing, and the allowance variable appears unchanged when inspected directly. To remediate the problem, the allowance mapping should be expressed in a stable, rebased unit that does not increase with `pricePerShare`, and the `transferFrom` routine must decrease the allowance by the actual token amount transferred, not by the share amount. Conceptually, the contract should treat the allowance as a fixed token quantity that remains constant regardless of rebasing, ensuring that a spender can never move more than the explicitly approved amount. This class of bug falls under "allowance inflation" in rebasing token implementations, where accounting units diverge from user‑visible token balances, leading to unexpected token loss or "funds disappearing" scenarios for token holders.
summary:
The approved spender may spend more tokens than desired. In fact, the approved amount that can be transferred keeps growing with `pricePerShare`.

Many contracts also use the same amount for the `approve` call as for the amount they want to have transferred in a subsequent `transferFrom` call, and in this case, they approve an amount that is too large (as the approved `shares` amount yields a higher rebalanced amount).

title: `WrappedIbbtcEth` contract will use stalled price for mint/burn if `updatePricePerShare` wasn’t run properly
content: The WrappedIbbtcEth contract relies on a single on‑chain variable called pricePerShare to translate between the underlying ibBTC/Eth asset and its wrapped token representation. This variable is refreshed only by an external off‑chain script that calls the updatePricePerShare function, which emits a SetPricePerShare event. Because the contract does not enforce any freshness check, the pricePerShare can become stale if the off‑chain updater fails to run for an extended period (due to bugs, network outages, or other operational issues). When the market price of the underlying asset moves while pricePerShare remains outdated, a malicious actor can observe that the last SetPricePerShare event is old, then call mint() using the stale price to receive wrapped tokens at a undervalued rate. After the price is finally updated by the external script, the attacker can invoke burn() to redeem the wrapped tokens at the new, higher price per share, extracting a risk‑free profit that is paid from the contract’s reserves. The impact is a direct loss of value from the contract’s holdings, effectively draining funds from honest users who rely on accurate accounting. This vulnerability manifests only under the condition that the price update mechanism stalls, and it is hard to notice because the contract’s functions appear to work correctly in isolation; the error is only revealed over time when the stale price is exploited for arbitrage. The root cause is a design flaw that places trust in an off‑chain process without on‑chain safeguards and omits any staleness validation before using pricePerShare in mint, burn, or transfer calculations. The issue can be classified as a stale oracle or price‑feed vulnerability, where outdated data leads to incorrect financial calculations and accounting breaches. From a user’s perspective, the symptom may be that after depositing ibBTC/Eth they receive fewer wrapped tokens than expected, or that after burning they receive more underlying assets than justified by the market price, effectively seeing “funds disappear” from the pool while they profit. To mitigate the risk, the contract should enforce a maximum allowed time since the last price update (a max‑staleness threshold) and either revert operations that rely on stale data or trigger an on‑chain price refresh before proceeding. Alternative mitigations include integrating an on‑chain price oracle, making price updates mandatory within each state‑changing function, or providing a fallback mechanism that updates pricePerShare automatically when it becomes too old. By ensuring that pricePerShare reflects the current market value before any mint, burn, or transfer, the contract can preserve its economic invariants and protect user funds.
summary: Malicious user can monitor `SetPricePerShare` event and, if it was run long enough time ago and market moved, but, since there were no `SetPricePerShare` fired, the contract’s `pricePerShare` is outdated, so a user can `mint()` with `pricePerShare` that is current for contract, but outdated for market, then wait for price update and `burn()` with updated `pricePerShare`, yielding risk-free profit at expense of contract holdings.

title: `WrappedIbbtc` and `WrappedIbbtcEth` contracts do not filter out price feed outliers
content: The vulnerability in the WrappedIbbtc and WrappedIbbtcEth contracts stemsfrom an unchecked reliance on a single price feed that is updated by an external function without any sanity‑checking or outlier filtering. The contracts expose a public `updatePricePerShare` method that directly overwrites the `pricePerShare` variable, which is subsequently used by the conversion routine `balanceToShares` during mint, burn and transfer operations. Because the new price is accepted verbatim, an attacker who can influence the underlying oracle—or who can temporarily push a manipulated price through a flash‑loan attack—can cause the price to spike or drop dramatically. When the price is artificially high, a user depositing the underlying asset receives an inflated amount of wrapped tokens; conversely, when the price is artificially low, a user attempting to withdraw receives fewer underlying assets than expected. The contract does not keep a historical median, a moving‑average, or a deviation threshold, so it cannot distinguish a legitimate market movement from a transient outlier. This flaw is exploitable at any moment the price update function is called, which makes the attack surface continuous and independent of the contract’s internal state. The impact includes loss of collateral, users receiving zero or unexpectedly large balances, and the protocol becoming under‑collateralized, thereby jeopardizing the economic guarantees of the wrapped token. The issue was discovered during a security audit that reviewed the logic flow of minting and burning and noted the absence of any validation of the price feed before it is used for accounting. It is difficult to notice in normal operation because the price variable appears normal and the contract’s events do not flag abnormal conversions; the symptoms only become evident when users observe unexpected token amounts after a deposit or withdrawal. The proper mitigation is to decouple user‑initiated fund movements from immediate price‑dependent accounting and to introduce a scheduled mint/burn process that checks the new price against a window of recent prices, accepting the operation only when the price lies within a predefined threshold (for example, within 10 % of the median of the last ten observations). This can be implemented via a keeper‑style off‑chain script that records recent prices, computes a median, and triggers mint or redeem only on “calm” market conditions, thereby preventing flash‑loan‑driven price distortions from having immediate effect. In addition, employing time‑weighted average price (TWAP) or requiring multiple independent oracle sources would further harden the contract against single‑source manipulation.
summary: If price feed is manipulated in any way or there is any malfunction based volatility on the market, both contracts will pass it on a user. In the same time it’s possible to construct mitigation mechanics for such cases, so user economics would be affected by sustainable price movements only. As price outrages provide a substantial attack surface for the project it’s worth adding some complexity to the implementation.

title: Vault fails to track debt correctly that leads to bad debt
content:
The vulnerability lies in the accounting logic of a lending vault that issues a stablecoin against collateral. When a borrower requests a loan, the protocol intentionally adds a 0.5 % fee to the principal, calculating an *increasing debt* value as amount × 1.005. However, the contract records the aggregate debt for the vault using the raw borrowed amount instead of the fee‑adjusted amount. Consequently, the per‑user debt entry (the user’s debtIndex and debt fields) diverges from the global debt variable maintained by the vault. This discrepancy is introduced by an arithmetic mistake in the update function: the total debt is incremented with _amount, while the user‑specific debt is updated with the fee‑adjusted value. The root cause is inconsistent use of two different formulas for the same financial quantity, leading to an under‑reported total debt.

Because the vault’s global debt is lower than the sum of individual debts, later operations that rely on the global figure – such as liquidation – calculate the wrong repayment amount. In the illustrated scenario, a single borrower deposits collateral, borrows 1 M USDM, and incurs a fee that raises the personal debt to 1.005 M. The vault’s internal debt remains at 1 M. When the price of the underlying collateral drops by 20 % and a liquidator attempts to settle the position, the protocol tries to subtract 1.005 M from a global debt of only 1 M, causing an arithmetic underflow and triggering a transaction revert. This failure blocks liquidation, leaves the position under‑collateralized, and may ultimately cause the vault to hold bad debt that cannot be recovered.

The impact is severe: users may see their collateral locked with no possibility of liquidation, the protocol’s accounting invariants break, and the vault can become insolvent over time as the hidden fee bias accumulates with each loan. Affected parties include borrowers, liquidators, and any participant relying on the vault’s health metrics. The issue was discovered during a security audit that compared the loan‑fee computation with the debt‑tracking code and observed that the two did not align, a subtle bug that is hard to notice because the contract still records a positive debt and only fails under specific price‑movement and liquidation conditions.

From a user’s perspective, the symptoms are confusing: after depositing collateral and borrowing, the UI may show a normal loan amount, but when a price drop occurs, liquidation attempts simply revert with a generic “transaction failed” error, and the user’s balance may appear unchanged while the protocol flags the position as active. Expectations that the vault will automatically liquidate undercollateralized loans are violated, leading to potential loss of funds.

The vulnerability belongs to the class of *inconsistent accounting / arithmetic mismatch* bugs, where two related state variables are updated with different formulas, causing divergence between local and global views of the same quantity. To remediate the issue, the contract should consistently apply the fee‑adjusted debt computation whenever the total debt is modified, ensuring that both the per‑user debt and the vault‑wide debt reflect the same amount. A conceptual fix involves replacing the raw _amount usage with the previously calculated increasingDebt variable throughout all debt‑update paths, and adding invariant checks that validate that the sum of individual debts never exceeds the stored total debt.
summary:
It's similar to the issue "misuse amount as increasing debt in the vault contract". Similar issue in a different place that leads to different exploit patterns and severity.

When users borrow usdm from a vault, the debt increases by the amount * 1.005.
    
        uint256 increasingDebt = (_amount * 1005) / 1000;

However, when the contract records the total debt it uses `_amount` instead of `increasingDebt`.
    
    details[_id].debtIndex =
        (details[_id].debtIndex * (totalDebt)) /
        (details[_id].debt + _amount);
    details[_id].debt = totalDebt;
    details[_id].status = Status.Active;
    debts += _amount;

[MochiVault.sol L242-L249](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-10-mochi/blob/main/projects/mochi-core/contracts/vault/MochiVault.sol#L242-L249)

The contract’s debt is inconsistent with the total sum of all users’ debt. The bias increases overtime and would break the vault at the end.

For simplicity, we assume there's only one user in the vault. Example:

  1. User deposits 1.2 M worth of BTC and borrows 1M USDM.
  2. The user’s debt (`details[_id].debt`) would be 1.005 M as there's a .5 percent fee.
  3. The contract’s debt is 1M.
  4. BTC price decrease by 20 percent
  5. The liquidator tries to liquidate the position.
  6. The liquidator repays 1.005 M and the contract tries to sub the debt by 1.005 M
  7. The transaction is reverted as `details[_id].debt -= _usdm;` would raise exception.

inaccurate accounting would lead to serious issues. I consider this a high-risk issue.

title: `FeePoolV0.sol#distributeMochi
content: The vulnerability resides in the fee distribution routine of the FeePoolV0 contract. When the public function distributeMochi() is invoked, it internally calls _buyMochi() to convert the accumulated mochiShare into Mochi tokens and then calls _shareMochi() to allocate those tokens between the vMochi Vault and the veCRV reward pool. The intention of the design is that only the mochiShare balance is split, while any amount stored in treasuryShare – the portion of fees that should be routed to the protocol treasury – remains untouched for later collection. However, the implementation of _shareMochi() mistakenly resets treasuryShare to zero after the token transfers, without ever sending the corresponding funds to the treasury. The root cause is a logical error in the internal accounting: the code treats treasuryShare as if it were part of the same distribution path and clears it alongside mochiShare, despite the comment stating it should be left untouched. An attacker or any user who can trigger distributeMochi() can therefore cause the protocol’s treasury balance to be erased on each call. The exploitation flow is straightforward: (1) the caller initiates distributeMochi(); (2) the contract converts mochiShare to Mochi tokens; (3) _shareMochi() transfers the appropriate fractions to the vMochi Vault and the veCRV holders; (4) the function then sets both mochiShare and treasuryShare to zero. Because treasuryShare is never transferred, the protocol’s fee revenue is silently dropped from the accounting ledger. The impact is that the protocol loses visibility and access to its fee income, effectively making the funds disappear from the treasury’s perspective. This can degrade the economic security of the system, reduce incentives for stakeholders, and break the accounting assumptions that the treasury will receive a defined share of collected fees. The issue manifests only when distributeMochi() is called; under normal operation the UI may still display the expected fee accruals, but the underlying treasury balance will not increase, leading to a mismatch between displayed and actual funds. The bug is subtle because the function correctly handles token transfers, and the zeroing of treasuryShare does not emit an event or affect external token balances, making it easy to overlook during testing. The proper remediation is to remove the line that resets treasuryShare, and instead add logic that transfers the treasuryShare amount to the designated treasury address before clearing the variable, thereby preserving the intended fee flow. In summary, this is a classic accounting‑logic flaw where an internal state variable representing protocol fees is unintentionally cleared, resulting in lost revenue and a breach of the protocol’s financial guarantees.

title: `ReferralFeePoolV0.sol#claimRewardAsMochi
content: The contract provides a function that lets a user claim a reward that is stored in USDM and automatically swaps it for the native Mochi token via a Uniswap router. The implementation builds a path array intended to contain three addresses – the USDM token, the wrapped Ether (WETH) intermediate, and the Mochi token – but the array is allocated with a fixed length of two. When the code later writes to path[2], it accesses memory outside the allocated bounds, causing an out‑of‑bounds exception that reverts the entire transaction. This flaw originates from an off‑by‑one error in the array initialization, a classic array‑size mismatch bug. Because the revert happens before any token transfer is completed, a user attempting to claim their reward will receive no tokens; the UI will appear to accept the claim request but the balance remains unchanged, leading to confusion and the impression that rewards are missing. The condition under which the vulnerability manifests is any execution of the claimRewardAsMochi function, regardless of the amount of reward or the state of the router. All users of the ReferralFeePoolV0 contract are affected, as none can successfully claim their accrued rewards, effectively freezing their funds in the pool. The issue was discovered during a static audit that inspected the source code and identified the mismatch between the declared array size and the number of elements assigned. It is easy to overlook because the code compiles; the runtime exception only appears when the function is called, making the bug subtle in testing environments that may not trigger the path preparation. To remediate, the path array should be instantiated with a length of three, matching the three token addresses that are required for the swap, or the swap should be restructured to use a two‑element path if an intermediate token is not needed. Correcting the array size restores the intended flow: the contract approves the router, swaps the exact amount of USDM for Mochi, and transfers the resulting tokens to the caller, thereby preserving the business rule that users receive their entitled rewards and preventing a denial‑of‑service condition where funds become inaccessible.

title: `registerAsset
content: The vulnerability resides in the public function registerAsset() of the MochiProfileV0 contract, which allows any address to invoke the routine without any access control or existence check. When an asset has already been registered, the contract stores its classification in a mapping called _assetClass. The registerAsset() function overwrites this entry and forces the asset class to the enum value AssetClass.Sigma. Because the asset class is used as a key for several risk‑related view functions—liquidationFactor(), riskFactor(), maxCollateralFactor(), liquidationFee(), keeperFee() and maxFee()—changing the class silently alters the numeric parameters that govern the vault’s health calculations. As a result, the liquidation threshold for positions backed by the affected asset can shift dramatically, potentially causing a liquidation event for a position that would otherwise be safe under the original parameters. The root cause is a missing require statement that should ensure the asset has not been previously registered (or that the caller is authorised). An attacker can exploit this by first confirming that the asset’s liquidity pool contains sufficient funds to satisfy the function’s internal checks, then calling registerAsset() with the address of the already‑registered asset. The contract will reset the asset’s class to Sigma, the risk parameters will instantly change, and any open vaults that rely on the previous parameters may fall below the new liquidation ratio. Users observing their vaults will see unexpected liquidations, sudden loss of collateral, or a reduction in the displayed collateral factor, even though they have not performed any action. The impact is a direct financial loss for asset holders, liquidity providers, and any participants who rely on the protocol’s risk model, as well as reputational damage to the protocol. This flaw appears only under the condition that the asset is already present in the registry and that an attacker can invoke the function; it is not obvious in normal operation because the function name suggests a one‑time registration and the contract provides no visible warning when the asset class changes. The issue was uncovered during a manual audit that identified the absence of a guard against re‑registration. Because the changed parameters are read‑only functions, the bug may be difficult to notice without tracing state changes or inspecting the mapping directly. The recommended remediation is to add a check such as require(_assetClass[_asset] == 0, "Already exists") or to restrict registerAsset() to a privileged role, ensuring that once an asset is registered its classification cannot be altered arbitrarily. In broader terms, this is an authorization/ownership flaw that enables an attacker to mutate critical protocol state, leading to mis‑calculated risk metrics and unintended liquidations, effectively violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions that each asset’s risk parameters remain constant after registration.
summary:
Everyone can call the function `registerAsset()` of MochiProfileV0.sol Assuming the liquidity for the asset is sufficient, `registerAsset()` will reset the _assetClass of an already registered asset to `AssetClass.Sigma`.

When the _assetClass is changed to `AssetClass.Sigma` then `liquidationFactor()`, `riskFactor()`, `maxCollateralFactor()`, `liquidationFee()` `keeperFee()` `maxFee()` will also return a different value. Then the entire vault will behave differently. The threshold for liquidation will also be different, possibly leading to a liquidation that isn't supposed to happen.

title: `debts` calculation is not accurate
content:
The vulnerability consists of an accounting inconsistency in the MochiVault contract where the global debt counter (named `debts`) is updated with different formulas depending on the operation performed. When a user calls the `borrow()` function, the contract adds only the principal amount (`_amount`) to `debts`, deliberately excluding the stability fee that is stored in the loan's `details[_id].debt` field as `totalDebt`. In contrast, the `repay()` and `liquidate()` functions subtract from `debts` using the same value that is removed from the per‑loan debt entry, which already includes the fee. As a result, the aggregate `debts` variable under‑reports the true outstanding debt by the amount of accrued fees. This discrepancy can cause `debts` to drift towards negative values when all positions are fully repaid, although the `repay()` function contains a safeguard that prevents the variable from actually becoming negative. The root cause is the mismatched accounting logic: an inconsistent addition of fee‑free principal versus subtraction of fee‑inclusive amounts.

The inaccuracy propagates to any calculation that relies on the global debt counter. Functions such as `utilizationRatio()`, `stabilityFee()`, and `calculateFeeIndex()` in the profile contract, as well as `liveDebtIndex()`, `accrueDebt()`, and `currentDebt()` in the vault contract, all depend on the value of `debts`. Consequently, utilization ratios may appear lower than they truly are, stability fees can be mis‑computed, and the index used for rewarding lenders may be skewed. From a user perspective this manifests as unexpected outcomes: a borrower may see a lower utilization ratio after borrowing, a liquidator may observe a position that appears healthy when it is not, and lenders may receive smaller claimable rewards than deserved. The bug violates the fundamental accounting assumption that the sum of individual loan debts must equal the aggregate debt counter.

The issue was identified during a Code4rena audit, where the auditors compared the arithmetic used in the three functions and noted the inconsistency. It can be difficult to notice because the contract prevents the aggregate debt from becoming negative, and the numerical discrepancy is limited to the size of the fee, which may be relatively small compared to large loan amounts. Nevertheless, the cumulative effect across many loans can distort protocol economics and open doors for exploitation. An attacker could take advantage of the understated `debts` value to inflate the apparent utilization ratio, potentially borrowing additional funds or avoiding liquidation triggers, thereby gaining a financial advantage at the expense of other participants.

The appropriate remediation is to ensure that the same definition of debt is used for all state updates. Specifically, the `borrow()` function should increase `debts` by the total debt amount (principal plus fee) rather than by the principal alone. This change brings the addition operation in line with the subtraction performed by `repay()` and `liquidate()`, restoring consistency across the contract’s accounting logic and eliminating the inaccurate fee calculations.
summary:
The value of the global variable `debts` in the contract `MochiVault.sol` is calculated in an inconsistent way.

In the function `borrow()` the variable `debts` is increased with a value excluding the fee. However in `repay()` and `liquidate()` it is decreased with the same value as `details[_id].debt` is decreased, which is including the fee.

This would mean that `debts` will end up in a negative value when all debts are repay-ed. Luckily the function `repay()` prevents this from happening.

In the meantime the value of `debts` isn't accurate. This value is used directly or indirectly in:

  * `utilizationRatio()`,`stabilityFee()` `calculateFeeIndex()` of `MochiProfileV0.sol`
  * `liveDebtIndex()`, `accrueDebt()`, `currentDebt()` of `MochiVault.sol`

This means the entire debt and claimable calculations are slightly off.

title: Bonding mechanism allows malicious user to DOS auctions
content: The vulnerability lies in the bonding mechanism that protects the settlement of a basket auction. The contract requires a participant to post a bond before they are allowed to settle the auction, and the bond can only be burned after a fixed 24‑hour lock‑up period. Because the contract does not limit who may post a bond, a malicious actor can monitor the mempool for the event that signals the start of a new auction, submit a bond transaction immediately, and become the exclusive settler for that auction. Once the bond is posted, the protocol logic prevents any other user from bonding or settling until the bond is burned, which cannot happen before the 24‑hour timeout. Consequently, the auction cannot be settled for the full lock‑up period, and the funds that should be re‑balanced or claimed by honest participants remain frozen in the basket. The attacker loses the amount of the bond when it is finally burned, but the loss is relatively small compared to the denial‑of‑service impact: every auction round is delayed by at least one day, and users observing the UI see no settlement, no change in balances, and potentially missed opportunities to claim rewards. This issue was discovered during a manual code audit that examined the bonding functions and the settlement flow, noting that the only restriction on who can bond is the timing of the event, not the identity of the caller. The problem is subtle because the bond transaction appears legitimate and no error is emitted; the contract simply enforces the lock‑up rule, making it difficult for users to understand why the auction is stuck. The root cause is the combination of (1) unrestricted bonding rights, (2) a non‑cancellable bond with a long immutable delay, and (3) the settlement function being gated exclusively by the presence of a bond. To remediate the issue, the design should either allow multiple users to bond concurrently, remove the bond requirement entirely, or modify the bond so that it can be cleared or overridden without a prohibitive delay, thereby ensuring that the auction can progress even if a malicious bond is posted. In essence, the bug is a classic denial‑of‑service through resource‑locking: an attacker locks a critical protocol primitive (the auction settlement) by monopolizing a privileged role (the bonder) and exploiting a time‑based lock that cannot be bypassed, leading to funds being unavailable and the protocol’s intended economic behavior being broken.
summary:
A malicious user can listen to the mempool and immediately bond when an auction starts, without aim of settling the auction. As no one can cancel his bond in less than 24h, this will freeze user funds and auction settlement for 24h until his bond is burned and the new index is deleted. The malicious user can then repeat this when a new auction starts.

While the malicious user will have to pay by having his bond burned, it might not be enough of a detriment for the DOS of the basket.

title: Referrer can drain `ReferralFeePoolV0`
content: The vulnerability resides in the reward‑claiming routine of the ReferralFeePoolV0 contract. The function that allows a referrer to claim a reward for referring users fails to update the internal accounting after a payout. Specifically, the contract records the amount owed to each referrer in a mapping but never subtracts the claimed amount from that balance nor resets the balance to zero when the claim is executed. As a result, the same reward amount remains recorded as claimable, enabling the referrer to invoke the claim function repeatedly and drain the total fee pool. The root cause is an improper state transition: the contract does not enforce a decrease of the reward balance after a successful transfer, violating basic accounting invariants that a claimed amount must be removed from the creditor’s ledger. Exploitation is straightforward – a malicious referrer can call the claim function in a loop, each call receiving the full amount that was originally allocated to them, while the contract’s total pool is reduced each time until it reaches zero. The impact is a complete loss of referral fees that were intended to be distributed among participants, potentially emptying the pool and depriving honest referrers of any compensation. This condition occurs whenever a referrer invokes the claimRewardAsMochi function; there is no guard or check that prevents subsequent calls after the first successful claim. The affected parties include the protocol that relies on referral incentives, the referrers who expect a single payout, and any users whose referral rewards are effectively stolen. The issue was discovered during a static analysis audit that compared the function’s external effects (a token transfer) with its internal state changes and noticed the absence of a balance decrement. It can be hard to notice because the function appears to succeed – the transaction does not revert and the referrer receives the tokens, giving the impression of correct behavior, while the hidden accounting error silently accumulates. The correct mitigation is to update the rewards mapping after each payout, typically by subtracting the claimed amount from the stored balance and resetting the user’s pending reward to zero, thereby restoring the invariant that total pending rewards equal the sum of individual balances. In broader terms, this is an instance of an accounting or state‑management bug where a contract fails to synchronize external token transfers with internal ledger updates, leading to double‑spending of allocated funds. From a user’s perspective, a referrer sees repeated reward payouts that should have occurred only once, while other participants notice that their referral pool is depleted and that expected refunds or incentives never materialize. The discrepancy between the expected single payout and the reality of multiple claims constitutes a breach of the protocol’s business logic and financial guarantees.
summary:
```solidity
function claimRewardAsMochi in ReferralFeePoolV0.sol did not reduce user reward balance, allowing referrer to claim the same reward repeatedly and thus draining the fee pool.
```

title: Liquidation will never work with non-zero discounts
content: The vulnerability resides in the liquidation workflow of the Mochi Vault system when a discount profile that applies a positive discount to the debt is used.
