The root cause is a mismatch between the way the contract calculates the current debt of a position and the way the liquidation routine expects the debt amount. The function `vault.currentDebt(_nftId)` returns a discounted value based on the active discount profile, but the `triggerLiquidation` function forwards the undiscounted debt amount (`_usdm`) to the internal `vault.liquidate` call. Inside `vault.liquidate`, the `updateDebt` modifier recomputes the stored debt (`details[_id].debt`) using the same discounted formula, and then attempts to subtract the passed `_usdm` from this stored debt. Because the stored debt has already been reduced by the discount, the subtraction `details[_id].debt -= _usdm` underflows whenever the discount is greater than zero, causing the transaction to revert. An attacker does not need to craft any special input; merely invoking `triggerLiquidation` on any position that is subject to a non‑zero discount profile triggers the failure. The impact is that liquidation never succeeds, leaving positions permanently illiquid, collateral locked, and the protocol’s risk‑mitigation mechanism disabled. This condition can arise at any time a liquidator tries to rescue an under‑collateralised vault, effectively breaking a core economic invariant of the system. The bug primarily affects borrowers (who cannot be forced to repay), lenders (who cannot recover value from risky positions), and the protocol itself, which loses the ability to enforce solvency. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the discount implementation, where the auditor noticed that the only tested discount profile (`NoDiscountProfile`) performs no discount, masking the problem. It is difficult to spot because the underflow only manifests when a discount > 0 is configured, a scenario that may not be covered by standard unit tests. To remediate the flaw, the liquidation logic should either apply the same discount to the `_usdm` parameter or, more simply, set the stored debt to zero after a successful liquidation (`details[_id].debt = 0`). If no discount profiles other than the no‑discount variant are intended, the entire discount mechanism can be removed to eliminate the mismatch. In user‑facing terms, a user expecting a liquidation to free up collateral will see the transaction revert with an arithmetic error, and the collateral balance will appear unchanged, creating the impression that “funds disappear” or that the protocol is broken.
summary:
Right now, there is only one discount profile in the github repo: the "`NoDiscountProfile`" which does not discount the debt at all. This specific discount profile works correctly, but I claim that any other discount profile will result in liquidation never working.

Suppose that we instead have a discount profile where `discount()` returns any value strictly larger than 0. Now, suppose someone wants to trigger a liquidation on a position. First, `triggerLiquidation` will be called (within `DutchAuctionLiquidator.sol`). The variable “debt” is initialized as equal to `vault.currentDebt(_nftId)`. Notice that `currentDebt(_ndfId)` (within `MochiVault.sol`) simply scales the current debt of the position using the `liveDebtIndex()` function, but there is no discounting being done within the function - this will be important.

Back within the `triggerLiquidation` function, the variable “collateral” is simply calculated as the total collateral of the position. Then, the function calls `vault.liquidate(_nftId, collateral, debt)`, and I claim that this will never work due to underflow. Indeed, the liquidate function will first update the debt of the position (due to the `updateDebt(_id)` modifier). The debt of the position is thus updated using lines 99-107 in `MochiVault.sol`. We can see that the `details[_id].debt` is updated in the exact same way as the calculations for `currentDebt(_nftId)`, however, there is the extra subtraction of the `discountedDebt` on line 107.

Eventually we will reach line 293 in `MochiVault.sol`. However, since we discounted the debt in the calculation of `details[_id].debt`, but we did not discount the debt for the passed in parameter _usdm (and thus is strictly larger in value), line 293 will always error due to an underflow. In summary, any discount profile that actually discounts the debt of the position will result in all liquidations erroring out due to this underflow. Since no positions will be liquidatable, this represents a major flaw in the contract as then no collateral can be liquidated so the entire functionality of the contract is compromised.

title: Anyone can extend withdraw wait period by depositing zero collateral
content: The vulnerability resides in the deposit function of the MochiVault contract, where the function permits any caller to deposit collateral into an arbitrary position without validating that the deposited amount is non‑zero. When a caller invokes the function with amount = 0, the contract still updates the timestamp stored in the lastDeposit mapping for the targeted position. This timestamp is the sole factor that determines the waiting period a position owner must observe before being allowed to withdraw their collateral. By overwriting lastDeposit with the current block time while contributing no actual collateral, a malicious actor can arbitrarily extend the withdrawal delay for any position. The root cause is the absence of a guard that rejects zero‑value deposits and the lack of access control that restricts who may call the function on a given position. Exploitation is straightforward: an attacker identifies a position owned by a victim, calls deposit(positionId, 0) with minimal gas, and consequently resets the waiting timer to the moment of the attack. The victim then attempts to withdraw, but the contract reports that the required wait period has not elapsed, effectively locking the funds for the extended duration. This denial‑of‑service effect is especially damaging for positions that originally have long withdrawal delays, because the attacker can repeatedly reset the timer, preventing the owner from ever reaching the unlock point. The issue manifests whenever the protocol relies on the lastDeposit timestamp for withdrawal eligibility and when the deposit function is callable by any address on any position. All users who hold positions are affected, as their collateral becomes inaccessible, compromising the protocol’s core functionality and eroding trust. The flaw was uncovered during a manual audit of MochiVault.sol, where the auditor observed that the function does not enforce a positive amount and that the timestamp update occurs unconditionally. Because a zero‑value call does not produce any obvious on‑chain error or loss of assets, it can be easily overlooked during testing, making the bug subtle yet powerful. To remediate the issue, the contract should reject zero‑amount deposits (e.g., require(amount > 0, "zero")) and consider restricting the deposit operation to the position’s owner, ensuring that only legitimate users can modify the lastDeposit state. Conceptually, this is a timestamp‑manipulation denial‑of‑service class of bug, where an otherwise harmless state change is abused to break business logic that assumes the timestamp only advances when genuine collateral is added. From a user perspective, the symptoms are a suddenly longer waiting period displayed in the UI, a disabled withdraw button, or an error message indicating that the required lock‑up time has not expired, despite the user having deposited collateral recently. The expectation that a recent deposit should enable an immediate or shortly delayed withdrawal is violated, leading to frozen funds and a loss of confidence in the protocol’s safety.
summary: In `MochiVault.sol`, the deposit function allows anyone to deposit collateral into any position. A malicious user can call this function with amount = 0, which would reset the amount of time the owner has to wait before they can withdraw their collateral from their position. This is especially troublesome with longer delays, as a malicious user would only have to spend a little gas to lock out all other users from being able to withdraw from their positions, compromising the functionality of the contract altogether.

title: treasury is vulnerable to sandwich attack
content: The vulnerability resides in a permissionless function called veCRVlock within the MochiTreasury contract. Because the function lacks any access control, any external address can invoke it at any time. The logic of veCRVlock triggers the treasury to purchase CRV tokens based on the current market price obtained from a Uniswap pool. An attacker can exploit this unrestricted entry point by performing a flash‑loan, buying a large amount of CRV to artificially inflate its price on the pool, and then calling veCRVlock while the price is still elevated. The treasury consequently buys CRV at the manipulated high price, transferring a large amount of its native assets to the attacker. After the purchase, the attacker sells the newly acquired CRV at the market price, repays the flash‑loan and retains the profit, effectively draining the treasury’s funds. This attack is a classic sandwich or price‑manipulation attack that targets contracts that perform on‑chain asset acquisition without proper checks or price‑oracle safeguards. The impact is severe: the treasury’s balance can be dramatically reduced or even emptied, violating the expectation that the treasury safely holds and manages community funds. The issue manifests whenever an external actor can call veCRVlock while a flash‑loan based price swing is possible, typically in a highly liquid liquidity pool. All participants relying on the treasury—such as token holders, protocol users, and the governing team—are affected because the treasury’s assets are used to fund the protocol’s operations. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that identified the missing onlyOwner modifier and reasoned about how an attacker could combine a flash‑loan with a price‑impact trade. Detecting the problem in production can be difficult because the treasury transaction appears legitimate and the price manipulation may be short‑lived, leaving little on‑chain evidence beyond an unexpected large purchase at an inflated price. The appropriate mitigation is to restrict access to veCRVlock to a trusted role, such as the contract owner, and/or to incorporate price‑oracle validation and slippage checks before executing purchases. In generic terms, this is a permissionless state‑changing function that enables an economic manipulation attack, leading to funds disappearing from the treasury and breaking the accounting assumptions that the treasury only purchases assets at fair market rates.
summary:
There’s a permissionless function `veCRVlock` in `MochiTreasury`. Since everyone can trigger this function, the attacker can launch a sandwich attack with flashloan to steal the funds. [MochiTreasuryV0.sol#L73-L94](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-10-mochi/blob/main/projects/mochi-core/contracts/treasury/MochiTreasuryV0.sol#L73-L94)

Attackers can possibly steal all the funds in the treasury. I consider this is a high-risk issue.

title: Changing NFT contract in the `MochiEngine` would break the protocol
content: The vulnerability resides in an administrative function of the MochiEngine contract that permits the operator to replace the address of the NFT contract used by the protocol. Because the value stored in the engine determines which NFT contract each vault interacts with, changing this address re‑routes every vault to a completely different NFT implementation. The root cause is the contract’s design choice to keep the NFT contract reference mutable without any safeguard, allowing an authorized party (or a compromised operator key) to point the system to an arbitrary address. An attacker or a careless operator can invoke the function, set the NFT address to a malicious or empty contract, and consequently all existing user positions become detached from the original NFTs. Users attempting to view, transfer, or withdraw their positions will find that their balances appear to be zero or that the contract reports no ownership, effectively locking funds and breaking the core accounting logic of the protocol. This failure manifests whenever the mutable reference is altered, which can happen at any time after deployment, and it impacts every participant who holds a position in any vault, as well as the protocol’s overall integrity and reputation. The issue was identified during a security audit by reviewing the source code and noticing that the function to change the NFT contract address was publicly callable by the operator, a pattern that is rarely safe for a core component. Because the function does not emit a warning or require a multi‑step governance process, the risk can be easily overlooked, especially in UI layers that assume the NFT contract remains constant. The exploit does not require complex transaction ordering; a single call to the update function is sufficient to corrupt the state. The impact is severe: user assets become inaccessible, the protocol cannot fulfill withdrawals or display correct positions, and the overall system may become unusable. To remediate, the mutable reference should be eliminated; the NFT contract address should be set once at deployment and made immutable, or the function should be restricted behind a robust, time‑locked governance mechanism with proper event logging and community oversight. Removing the function entirely, as recommended, prevents the protocol from being broken by a single administrative action and aligns with best practices for immutable references in DeFi contracts.
summary:
`MochiEngine` allows the operator to change the NFT contract in [MochiEngine.sol#L91-L93](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-10-mochi/blob/main/projects/mochi-core/contracts/MochiEngine.sol#L91-L93)

All the vaults would point to a different NFT address. As a result, users would not be access their positions. The entire protocol would be broken.

IMHO, A function that would break the entire protocol shouldn’t exist.

I consider this is a high-risk issue.

title: `treasuryShare` is Overwritten in `FeePoolV0._shareMochi
content: The vulnerability resides in the fee distribution logic of the FeePoolV0 contract, which is responsible for splitting accrued USDM fees between the protocol treasury and the vMochi incentive mechanism. The contract maintains two internal variables – one representing the amount of USDM earmarked for the treasury (treasuryShare) and another for the amount to be converted into mochi tokens for veCRV holders (mochiShare). When the function distributeMochi() is invoked, it converts the mochiShare portion into mochi tokens and locks them in a Curve rewards pool for distribution. However, the implementation also contains a line that unconditionally resets treasuryShare to zero at the same time, regardless of whether any USDM tokens have been transferred to the treasury via sendToTreasury(). This premature flushing of treasuryShare occurs whenever distributeMochi() is called while there are still USDM tokens remaining in the contract. As a result, an attacker (or any veCRV holder) can call distributeMochi() before the treasury claim is settled, causing the treasury allocation to be erased. Subsequent calls to updateReserve() can then re‑allocate the leftover USDM, but because treasuryShare was already cleared, the re‑allocation effectively routes the entire remaining balance into the mochiShare pathway. Repeating this cycle allows the veCRV holder to repeatedly convert fees that were originally intended for the treasury into mochi tokens, ultimately draining the treasury of all its entitled funds. From a user perspective, the protocol appears to distribute rewards correctly, but the treasury balance silently drops to zero, leading to missing revenue and a breach of the protocol’s economic assumptions. The issue was identified during a manual audit of the contract’s accounting flow, where the auditors observed that the variable reset was unconditional and not guarded by any state check. The bug is subtle because the function’s primary purpose—distributing mochi—seems successful, hiding the fact that the treasury’s share is being silently discarded. To remediate the problem, the line that resets treasuryShare should be removed or guarded so that treasuryShare is only cleared after a successful call to sendToTreasury(). Additionally, the contract should enforce that distributeMochi() cannot be executed while treasuryShare is non‑zero, or it should separate the accounting of treasury and mochi shares into distinct, immutable snapshots to prevent accidental overwriting. By correcting the accounting logic, the protocol can ensure that fees are correctly split, preserving treasury revenue and maintaining the intended incentive structure.
summary: The `FeePoolV0.sol` contract accrues fees upon the liquidation of undercollaterised positions. These fees are split between treasury and `vMochi` contracts. However, when `distributeMochi()` is called to distribute `mochi` tokens to `veCRV` holders, both `mochiShare` and `treasuryShare` is flushed from the contract when there are still `usdm` tokens in the contract.

title: feePool is vulnerable to sandwich attack.
content: The vulnerability resides in a public, permissionless function named distributeMochi that distributes accrued fees from a pool to token holders. Because the function can be called by any address, it lacks any form of access control or slippage protection. The contract calculates the amount to transfer based on the current on‑chain price information, but it does not enforce a minimum return or compare the price against a time‑weighted average. An attacker can therefore perform a sandwich attack using a flash loan: first, the attacker takes a large flash loan and temporarily skews the market price, then calls distributeMochi while the price is artificial, causing the contract to transfer an inflated amount of assets to the attacker. After receiving the funds, the attacker repays the flash loan within the same transaction, leaving the pool drained. This exploit can be triggered whenever anyone calls distributeMochi, meaning that under normal operation a user expecting a regular fee distribution may instead see their pool balance drop to zero or observe that no rewards are received. The impact is severe because the attacker can potentially steal all assets held in the pool, compromising all users and the protocol’s financial integrity. The issue was identified during a manual security audit, with the auditors noting the similarity to known incidents such as the yDai harvest attack and the Mushrooms Finance theft, where lack of slippage checks in a harvest‑style function enabled flash‑loan‑based drains. The problem is hard to notice because the function appears to be a harmless accounting routine, and the malicious price manipulation occurs within the same transaction, leaving no obvious on‑chain trace of an external attacker. To remediate, the contract should introduce a minimum‑return check based on a time‑weighted average price (TWAP) or other oracle that cannot be manipulated within a single block, enforce slippage limits, or restrict calls to a trusted role. By ensuring that the amount distributed cannot be significantly altered by a single transaction, the protocol can prevent the sandwich vector and protect user funds from flash‑loan‑driven theft.
summary:
There’s a permissionless function `distributeMochi` in [FeePoolV0.sol L55-L62](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-10-mochi/blob/main/projects/mochi-core/contracts/feePool/FeePoolV0.sol#L55-L62). Since everyone can trigger this function, an attacker can launch a sandwich attack with flashloan to steal the funds.

The devs have mentioned this concern in the comment. An attacker can steal the funds with a flash loan attack.

Attackers can steal all the funds in the pool. I consider this is a high-risk issue.

title: Tokens Can Be Stolen By Frontrunning `VestedRewardPool.vest
content: The vulnerability is a front‑running race condition in the VestedRewardPool contract that allows an attacker to steal tokens that are supposed to vest for a beneficiary after a minimum 90‑day lock period. The root cause is that the vest() (and the analogous lock()) function does not perform the token transfer using a safeTransferFrom call or any other atomic transfer mechanism that ties the allocation of vested tokens to the execution of the function. Instead, the contract updates internal accounting and expects a later external token transfer to complete the vesting. Because the token movement is not protected against ordering, a malicious actor can observe a pending transaction that calls vest() on behalf of a legitimate recipient, and then submit their own transaction that invokes the same vest() (or lock()) function just before the victim’s transaction is mined. By front‑running the victim, the attacker can cause the contract to allocate the vested amount to the attacker’s address, effectively stealing the tokens that were meant to be released to the original recipient. The impact is that users who are waiting for their vested mochi tokens after the 90‑day period may receive nothing; their balance on the contract appears unchanged while the attacker’s balance increases by the stolen amount. This condition occurs whenever a user interacts directly with vest() or lock() without an intermediate safeguard that ensures the transfer is executed atomically with the vesting logic. The affected parties include token holders expecting a vesting schedule, the protocol that promises locked rewards, and any downstream contracts that rely on the correct distribution of those rewards. The issue was discovered during a formal security audit that examined the flow of token transfers and identified that the contract does not use safeTransferFrom in the vesting path, opening a window for transaction ordering attacks. It is hard to notice because the contract’s external view may show the correct vesting schedule and the internal state changes appear normal; only the token balances after the transaction reveal the misallocation. To remediate, the contract should combine the vesting accounting update and the token transfer into a single, atomic operation, preferably using a safeTransferFrom call that includes proper re‑entrancy guards, or expose a single external function that performs the accounting update, token transfer, and any locking in one transaction, thereby eliminating the race window. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of front‑running or race‑condition vulnerabilities where token transfers are not atomically coupled with state changes, breaking the business logic that vested tokens must be reliably delivered to the intended recipient.
summary: The `VestedRewardPool.sol` contract is a public facing contract aimed at vesting tokens for a minimum of 90 days before allowing the recipient to withdraw their `mochi`. The `vest()` function does not utilise `safeTransferFrom()` to ensure that vested tokens are correctly allocated to the recipient. As a result, it is possible to frontrun a call to `vest()` and effectively steal a recipient’s vested tokens. The same issue applies to the `lock()` function.

title: Miners Can Re-Roll the VRF Output to Game the Protocol
content: The vulnerability consists of a manipulation of the randomness source used by the PoolTogether protocol. The protocol requests a Verifiable Random Function (VRF) output from Chainlink and consumes the result in the same block to decide which participant wins the prize. Because the VRF output is derived from the block hash of the block that includes the request, a miner (or a well‑funded user who can pay miners) who is dissatisfied with the generated number can trigger a chain reorganization that excludes the original block and replaces it with a new block containing a different block hash. This new hash yields a different VRF output, thereby increasing the attacker’s probability of being selected as the winner. The root cause is the reliance on an immediately fulfilled VRF without any delay or confirmation period, which allows the block producer to influence the randomness source, and the potential for collusion between the VRF oracle operator and miners. Exploitation proceeds by submitting a VRF request, observing the returned number, and, if unfavorable, mining or incentivising a short‑range re‑org that replaces the block, causing the contract to read a fresh VRF result in a subsequent block. The impact is a breach of the protocol’s fairness guarantees: participants may be denied a legitimate prize while the attacker repeatedly wins, effectively draining the prize pool and eroding trust in the system. This condition can arise whenever the VRF request and its fulfillment occur within the same block, and the attacker controls at least a temporary majority of the hash power (51 % for guaranteed re‑orgs, or less for opportunistic short‑forks). All users of the PoolTogether pools are affected because the distribution of winnings can be biased, and the protocol’s reputation suffers. The issue was identified during a Code4rena audit that examined Chainlink’s VRF security considerations and observed that the contract does not enforce a sufficient block‑confirmation delay. The problem is subtle because the VRF proof still validates cryptographically; it only appears biased when statistical analysis of many draws reveals an abnormal win rate, making it hard to detect without extensive data. Mitigation should involve decoupling the request and fulfillment by adding a mandatory waiting period of several blocks (e.g., five) before the VRF result is used, thereby reducing the likelihood that a re‑org could replace the block containing the original output. Additional hardening could include upgrading to VRF 2.0, employing a commit‑reveal scheme, or using a decentralized randomness beacon that does not rely on a single block hash. In summary, the flaw is a classic “re‑roll” or “re‑org” attack on on‑chain randomness, where insufficient confirmation time lets miners or colluding parties bias the outcome, leading to unfair prize allocation and potential loss of funds for honest participants.
summary:
Miners are able to rewrite a chain’s history if they dislike the VRF output used by the protocol. Consider the following example:

  * A miner or well-funded user is participating in the PoolTogether protocol.
  * A VRF request is made and fulfilled in the same block.
  * The protocol participant does not benefit from the VRF output and therefore wants to increase their chances of winning by including the output in another block, producing an entirely new VRF output. This is done by re-orging the chain, i.e. following a new canonical chain where the VRF output has not been included in a block.
  * This attack can be continued as long as the attacker controls 51% of the network. The miner itself could control a much smaller proportion of the network and still be able to mine a few blocks in succession, although this is of low probability but entirely possible.
  * A well-funded user could also pay miners to re-org the chain on their behalf in the form of MEV to achieve the same benefit.

The PoolTogether team is aware of this issue but is yet to mitigate this attack vector fully.

title: Steal tokens from TempusController
content: The TempusController contract contains a function named _depositAndProvideLiquidity that is intended to accept a user‑specified TempusAMM, deposit tokens into the associated pool, and then provide liquidity on behalf of the caller. The vulnerability arises because the contract does not validate the TempusAMM argument or any of the data returned from the external AMM and vault contracts. By supplying a crafted fake AMM that returns arbitrary token addresses, balances, and share amounts, an attacker can manipulate the internal variables ammTokens, mintedShares and sharesUsed. At the end of the routine the contract executes ammTokens[0].safeTransfer(msg.sender, mintedShares - sharesUsed[0]);, which transfers the difference between mintedShares and sharesUsed[0] of the first token reported by the AMM. Because the AMM is under the attacker’s control, the attacker can make this difference correspond to any ERC20 token held by the TempusController, effectively withdrawing arbitrary tokens. The exploit can be performed whenever an attacker is able to call depositAndProvideLiquidity with a malicious TempusAMM contract; no additional permissions are required. From a user’s perspective the function appears to perform a normal deposit, but the attacker receives tokens that were never meant to be transferred, while the protocol’s dust balance is reduced unexpectedly. The issue was discovered during an audit when the test harness for TempusController demonstrated that the contract held ERC20 tokens and that a fake vault and pool could be used to satisfy the external calls. The problem is subtle because the amounts that can be stolen are usually small dust left after early redemptions, making the loss appear as normal rounding or leftover balance, and the code does not emit any warning or revert. This class of bug is an unchecked external contract trust vulnerability, where the protocol blindly trusts data from an unregulated external contract and uses that data to move funds. To remediate the flaw, the controller should enforce a whitelist of approved TempusAMM and TempusPool contracts, verify that returned token addresses belong to known assets, and ensure that the amount transferred cannot exceed the actual balance held for legitimate purposes. In addition, the safeTransfer call should be based on the contract’s real token balances rather than on values supplied by the caller, preventing arbitrary token extraction. The exploit violates the core business logic that only dust leftover from legitimate redemptions may be transferred, breaking accounting assumptions and potentially compromising user trust in the protocol.
summary:
The function `_depositAndProvideLiquidity` can be used go retrieve arbitrary ERC20 tokens from the TempusController.sol contract.

As the test contract of TempusController.sol <https://goerli.etherscan.io/address/0xd4330638b87f97ec1605d7ec7d67ea1de5dd7aaa> shows, it has indeed ERC20 tokens.

The problem is due to the fact that you supply an arbitrary tempusAMM to depositAndProvideLiquidity and thus to `_depositAndProvideLiquidity`. tempusAMM could be a fake contract that supplies values that are completely fake.

At the end of the function `_depositAndProvideLiquidity`, ERC20 tokens are send to the user. If you can manipulate the variables ammTokens, mintedShares and sharesUsed you can send back any tokens held in the contract “ammTokens[0].safeTransfer(msg.sender, mintedShares - sharesUsed[0]);”

The Proof of Concept shows an approach to do this.

title: Arbitrary contract call allows attackers to steal ERC20 from users’ wallets
content: The vulnerability originates from an uncontrolled external call inside the internal function fillZrxQuote. The function receives an arbitrary address (zrxTo) and raw calldata (zrxData) that are passed directly to a low‑level call without any validation or whitelisting. Because the address can point to any contract, an attacker can set it to an ERC20 token contract and craft calldata that invokes the token's transferFrom function. If a user has previously granted the Swap contract an allowance on that token, the malicious calldata will cause the token contract to move the approved tokens from the user’s balance to the attacker’s address. The root cause is the lack of access control and input sanitisation on the external call, which allows the contract to act as a proxy for arbitrary function invocations. Exploitation is straightforward: the attacker triggers a swap operation that calls fillZrxQuote, supplies the token contract as the destination, and provides calldata for transferFrom with the attacker as the recipient. The contract records its own token balance before the call, but that value is never used to enforce any safety checks after the call, so the stolen amount is not detected by the contract logic. The impact is a direct loss of user funds; users may see their token balances drop to zero or notice that expected refunds or trade results never arrive, while the attacker receives the withdrawn tokens. This condition occurs whenever the fillZrxQuote function is executed, which is part of the normal swapping workflow, making the flaw effectively hidden in regular user interactions. The issue was discovered through static analysis of the source code, noting the presence of an unrestricted call with user‑controlled parameters. It can be hard to notice because the call appears to be a legitimate integration point for a 0x exchange, and the function is internal, masking its exposure. To remediate the issue, the contract should restrict the destination address to a trusted set of contracts, validate the calldata to ensure only expected functions are invoked, or replace the low‑level call with a typed interface that only permits the intended exchange operation. In broader terms, this is an example of an arbitrary external call vulnerability that breaks the assumed trust boundary and enables unauthorized token transfers, violating the protocol’s accounting guarantees and user expectations of safe asset handling.

title: Wrong calculation of `erc20Delta` and `ethDelta`
content: The vulnerability resides in the accounting logic of the Swap contract's fillZrxQuote function, where the reported changes in ETH and ERC20 balances (ethDelta and erc20Delta) are calculated incorrectly. The function records the contract's ETH balance and the ERC20 token balance before calling an external ZRX quote execution. However, the recorded originalETHBalance already includes the msg.value sent by the caller, and the originalERC20Balance already includes any tokens that the caller has transferred into the contract as part of the swap. After the external call, the contract computes the deltas by subtracting the pre‑call balances from the post‑call balances using a subOrZero helper. Because the pre‑call balances already contain the incoming assets, the subtraction yields zero or a severely understated amount. For example, when a user swaps unwrapped ETH for an ERC20 token and receives a partial ETH refund, the function sees the original ETH balance as the sum of the contract's previous balance plus the user‑sent amount. If the contract ends up with the original balance plus the refund, the subtraction returns zero, causing ethDelta to be reported as zero even though ETH was actually received. A similar mis‑calculation occurs for ERC20 tokens when a user swaps a token for the same token (e.g., WBTC to WBTC) – the originalERC20Balance already includes the input amount, so the reported erc20Delta is far lower than the real increase. This flaw can be exploited by triggering swaps that rely on these deltas for downstream logic such as fee distribution, profit calculation, or state updates. An attacker could cause the protocol to believe that no assets were acquired, potentially preventing proper accounting, bypassing fee checks, or enabling arbitrage opportunities where the contract under‑reports received amounts. The impact is a breach of fundamental accounting assumptions: the contract's internal bookkeeping no longer reflects the true asset flow, leading to user-visible symptoms such as "my swap returned zero ETH" or "the token balance did not increase despite a successful trade". Users may see missing refunds, zero balances after a swap, or unexpected token amounts, undermining trust in the protocol. The issue manifests only in scenarios where the contract receives ETH or ERC20 tokens as part of the same transaction that it then measures, namely unwrapped ETH swaps and same‑token arbitrage swaps. It was discovered during a manual audit of the Swap.sol source code, where the auditor noticed that the balance snapshot includes the incoming value, a subtle logical error that does not raise a runtime exception and is therefore hard to spot in testing. To remediate the problem, the contract should capture the balance before the external call without the caller's incoming value – for ETH, subtract msg.value from the pre‑call balance or record the balance after the call and compute the delta relative to the expected post‑call state. For ERC20 tokens, the contract should query the token balance before the transfer is made inbound or adjust the delta calculation to add back the transferred amount. In essence, the accounting should be based on net inflow rather than raw balance differences, restoring accurate profit and fee calculations and preventing the described mis‑reporting.

title: `borrow` must `accrueInterest` first
content: The vulnerability originates from an incorrect ordering of state updates in the borrow function of the UToken contract. When a user initiates a borrow, the function first checks the user’s current borrow balance, the requested amount plus fee, and the credit limit against the maximum allowed borrow size. However, these checks are performed before the contract calls `accrueInterest()`, which updates the global `borrowIndex` and consequently the user’s effective borrow balance. As a result, the contract uses a stale borrow index – the old value that does not reflect interest accrued up to the moment of the transaction. This stale value can make the calculated `borrowBalanceView(msg.sender)` appear lower than the true balance, allowing the user to satisfy the `require` statements and borrow an amount that exceeds the real credit limit. The root cause is the placement of the `require(accrueInterest(), "UToken: accrue interest failed")` call at the end of the function instead of at the beginning, preventing the contract from accounting for the most recent interest before performing any further state‑changing logic. An attacker can exploit this by repeatedly borrowing just enough to stay within the outdated limits, effectively inflating their borrowing capacity without proper interest being deducted. The impact includes inaccurate accounting, potential over‑borrowing, and a scenario where the protocol’s total outstanding debt diverges from the expected value, which could lead to loss of funds or insolvency if unchecked. The issue manifests whenever a borrow transaction occurs after interest has accrued but before the contract has updated its internal accounting – typically during periods of high activity or when borrowers act immediately after a block that generates interest. All participants who rely on the protocol’s borrowing limits – lenders, borrowers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the protocol’s safety checks are bypassed. The flaw was discovered during a Code4rena audit where reviewers noted that the comment "this uses the old value" highlighted the misuse of an outdated borrow index. The problem is subtle because the contract may still emit seemingly correct events and external balances may appear consistent after the transaction, making the accounting discrepancy difficult to notice without deep inspection of the internal `borrowIndex` state. To remediate, the contract should invoke `accrueInterest()` at the very start of the borrow function, ensuring that the latest interest is applied before any balance or credit limit checks are performed. Conceptually, this aligns with the broader class of bugs where state‑dependent calculations are performed out of order, leading to stale data being used for authorization checks. From a user’s perspective, the symptoms may include being able to borrow more funds than expected, seeing their borrowed balance not reflect accrued interest, or encountering unexpected revert messages such as "UToken: amount larger than borrow size max" even when they believe they are within limits. Ultimately, the bug violates the protocol’s accounting invariants and the business rule that a borrower’s outstanding debt must always include all accrued interest before further borrowing is permitted.

title: Wrong implementation of `CreditLimitByMedian.sol#getLockedAmount`
content: The vulnerability resides in the function that calculates the new locked amount for a staker when a decrease operation is requested. Instead of reducing the stored locked amount by the amount the user wishes to unlock, the implementation always subtracts a constant value of one. This off‑by‑one error means the contract never correctly releases the requested portion of a user’s locked balance; if the user attempts to unlock more than a single unit, the function either returns a value that is one unit short or, when the stored amount is less than the requested amount, incorrectly returns zero without adjusting the real locked amount. The bug originates from a faulty conditional branch where `newLockedAmount = array[i].lockedAmount - 1;` is used instead of the correct `newLockedAmount = array[i].lockedAmount - amount;`. Exploitation is straightforward: any call to the contract’s update routine that tries to decrease a locker’s stake will invoke this faulty logic, resulting in the user’s funds staying locked despite the protocol indicating a successful unlock operation. From the user’s perspective, the UI may show that a withdrawal request was processed, yet the balance on‑chain remains unchanged or the unlocked portion is missing, leading to confusion and potentially loss of access to funds. The issue manifests whenever the `isIncrease` flag is false, i.e., during unlock attempts, and it affects all participants who rely on the CreditLimitByMedian model for managing their credit limits. The problem was identified during a manual code audit that highlighted the mismatched subtraction operation. It can be difficult to spot because typical test cases may only exercise a unit‑size unlock, which appears to work, masking the error for larger unlock amounts. To remediate, the subtraction should be changed to use the `amount` parameter, and the code should include proper underflow checks (e.g., using SafeMath or Solidity ^0.8 built‑in overflow protection) to ensure that the new locked amount never becomes negative. Correcting this logic restores the intended accounting behavior, allowing users to retrieve the exact amount they unlocked and preserving the protocol’s financial integrity.

title: Contract BasicSale is missing an approve
content: The vulnerability consists of a missing token allowance initialization in the BasicSale contract. The contract is designed to forward a portion of the received mainToken tokens to a separate Vesting contract by calling its vest() function, which internally invokes ERC20.transferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), _amount). For transferFrom to succeed, the BasicSale contract must first grant the Vesting contract an allowance via ERC20.approve. In the existing implementation the approve call is never executed, so the Vesting contract has a zero allowance for tokens owned by BasicSale. When a user invokes the public function _withdrawShare, the contract attempts to move tokens into the vesting schedule, triggering a transferFrom that fails with the revert message "ERC20: transfer amount exceeds allowance". As a result, the withdrawal reverts and the tokens that were previously sent to BasicSale become permanently locked in the contract with no mechanism for retrieval. This failure occurs each time _withdrawShare is called after any token deposit, affecting all users who expect to receive their vested shares and the overall protocol that relies on proper token distribution. The issue was discovered during a security audit when the auditors examined the call flow and observed that the Vesting contract’s vest() function performs a transferFrom from the BasicSale address, but the BasicSale constructor does not include a corresponding approve statement. The problem was not caught in earlier testing because the test suite used a mock Vesting contract whose vest() function was empty and therefore never attempted a transferFrom, allowing the contract to appear functional. The bug belongs to the class of initialization or allowance‑related defects where a contract fails to set required ERC20 approvals before attempting token transfers, leading to funds being irretrievably stuck. From a user’s perspective the UI would show a successful token purchase but later the expected vesting or refund transaction would revert, leaving balances unchanged or showing zero payouts despite having deposited assets. To remediate the issue, the contract should grant the Vesting contract an effectively unlimited allowance in its constructor (e.g., mainToken.approve(address(vestLock), type(uint256).max)), ensuring that subsequent transferFrom calls can succeed and that user funds are correctly vested and withdrawable.
summary:
As we can see in the contracts `AirdropDistribution` and `InvestorDistribution`, they both have the following `approve()` call: mainToken.approve(address(vestLock), 2**256-1);

  * <https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-bootfinance/blob/main/vesting/contracts/AirdropDistribution.sol#L499>
  * <https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-bootfinance/blob/main/vesting/contracts/InvestorDistribution.sol#L80>

This is necessary because both contracts transfer tokens to the vesting contract by calling its `vest()` function:

  * <https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-bootfinance/blob/main/vesting/contracts/AirdropDistribution.sol#L544>
  * <https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-bootfinance/blob/main/vesting/contracts/AirdropDistribution.sol#L569>
  * <https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-bootfinance/blob/main/vesting/contracts/InvestorDistribution.sol#L134>
  * <https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-bootfinance/blob/main/vesting/contracts/InvestorDistribution.sol#L158>

The code of the `vest()` function in the Vesting contract performs a transfer from `msg.sender` to Vesting contract address -> `vestingToken.transferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), _amount);` <https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-bootfinance/blob/main/vesting/contracts/Vesting.sol#L95>

Same is done in the BasicSale contract: <https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-bootfinance/blob/main/tge/contracts/PublicSale.sol#L225>

The problem is that this contract is missing the `approve()` call. For that reason, the contract is totally useless as the function `\_withdrawShare()` will always revert with the following message: revert reason: ERC20: transfer amount exceeds allowance. This means that all the `mainToken` sent to the contract would be stuck there forever. No way to retrieve them.

How this issue was not detected in the testing phase? Very simple. The mock used by the team has an empty `vest()` function that performs no transfer call. <https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-bootfinance/blob/main/tge/contracts/helper/MockVesting.sol#L10>

title: Can not update target price
content: The vulnerability resides in the price‑ramping logic of the custom swap contract. The function that updates the target price, rampTargetPrice, contains sanity checks that compare a future target price (futureTargetPricePrecise) with the current target price (initialTargetPricePrecise). The intention is to allow the price to move only within a bounded relative range defined by MAX_RELATIVE_PRICE_CHANGE. However, the mathematical expression used for the downward‑price case is incorrect: when futureTargetPricePrecise is lower than initialTargetPricePrecise, the contract requires futureTargetPricePrecise × MAX_RELATIVE_PRICE_CHANGE / WEI_UNIT >= initialTargetPricePrecise. Because futureTargetPricePrecise is already smaller, even after applying the allowed percentage increase the inequality cannot be satisfied, causing the require statement to revert. Consequently, the admin is unable to decrease the target price by any amount, even a single wei, and in practice cannot update the target price at all. This bug was discovered during a manual audit when the author attempted to invoke the ramping function with a minimal change and observed an unexpected revert. The issue is subtle because the code looks syntactically correct and the constant MAX_RELATIVE_PRICE_CHANGE suggests a permissive range; the failure only appears when the new price is lower than the current one. Exploitation is straightforward: an attacker (or any caller) can block the intended price‑adjustment process simply by submitting a legitimate ramp request that violates the broken check, preventing the contract from aligning the on‑chain price with external market data. The impact is that the swap’s pricing mechanism becomes static, breaking the economic model of the pool. Users may experience stale or incorrect exchange rates, leading to trades that execute at unfavorable prices, potential arbitrage opportunities for adversaries, and loss of confidence in the protocol. The bug affects the protocol’s governance (admin role) and any participant relying on the price‑ramping feature, including liquidity providers and traders. It manifests when the admin attempts to call rampTargetPrice after a market move that requires a lower target price, or during scheduled price updates. From a user’s perspective the UI would continue to display the old price, swaps would yield unexpected amounts, and balances could appear to change incorrectly. The root cause is an improper relative‑change comparison that does not account for the direction of price movement. To remediate, the sanity checks should incorporate the percentage tolerance on both sides of the inequality, for example by adding the WEI_UNIT to the multiplier (MAX_RELATIVE_PRICE_CHANGE + WEI_UNIT) before division, or by rearranging the logic to compare ratios rather than scaled absolute values. The fix restores the ability of the admin to adjust the target price within the intended bounds, ensuring that the accounting assumptions of the swap – that price updates remain within a limited relative delta – are upheld.

title: `setGuardian`
content: The vulnerability resides in two public functions named setGuardian that are intended to update a contract's guardian address. Instead of writing the supplied address to the guardian storage slot, the implementation mistakenly writes it to the governance variable, effectively overwriting the contract's administrator. The root cause is a copy‑and‑paste or naming error where the same state variable (governance) is used in both the access‑control check and the assignment, rather than the distinct guardian variable. Because the function is external and guarded only by the _onlyGovernance() modifier, any caller that currently holds the governance role can replace the governance address with an arbitrary address. Once an attacker has succeeded in calling setGuardian with their own address, they become the new governing entity and can subsequently invoke any privileged functions that were originally restricted to the legitimate governance address. This chain of events leads to a complete loss of control over the contract, allowing potential theft of funds, unauthorized parameter changes, or disruption of protocol logic. The flaw manifests whenever the setGuardian function is called, which may occur during routine upgrades, maintenance, or governance actions. All users of the contract, including token holders and integrators of the zap utilities, are affected because the compromised governance can alter the flow of assets, pause or resume operations, and modify critical contract behavior. The issue was discovered during a formal security audit performed by Code4rena, where reviewers compared the source code against the intended design and noticed the mismatched variable assignment. It can be difficult to notice in production because the function name and access modifier suggest correct behavior, and there is no immediate UI indication that the governance address has changed; only a deeper inspection of on‑chain storage reveals the swap. To remediate, the assignment should be corrected to target the guardian variable (guardian = _guardian) and the function should be renamed or its purpose clarified to avoid future confusion. Additionally, a separate dedicated access‑control check for guardian‑only actions would prevent accidental governance overwrites. The bug belongs to the class of "incorrect state variable assignment" or "privilege escalation through mis‑named storage writes," which violates the fundamental accounting assumption that only the designated administrator can change high‑level contract parameters. From a user’s perspective, actions that were expected to update the guardian simply leave the guardian unchanged while silently replacing the governance address, resulting in scenarios where users see no change in the guardian field but later experience unauthorized withdrawals or halted services.

title: Claim airdrop repeatedly
content: The vulnerability arises from an improper state‑reset in the airdrop distribution contract. When a beneficiary calls `claimExact()` and claims the final portion of their allocated airdrop, the contract correctly updates `airdrop[msg.sender].amount` to zero. The subsequent `validate()` function then checks `airdrop[msg.sender].amount == 0` to determine whether the user has already been validated. Because the amount is now zero, the check passes and the function proceeds to overwrite the existing `Airdrop` struct with a freshly constructed one, resetting the `claimed` field back to zero. This effectively re‑initialises the user’s airdrop entitlement while leaving the contract’s token balance untouched. An attacker can therefore repeat the cycle: claim the remaining tokens, invoke `validate()` to reset the record, and claim again as long as the contract still holds unclaimed tokens. The impact is a loss of funds from the airdrop pool, potentially allowing a single address to drain the entire allocation. The bug manifests only after a user’s balance reaches zero, a condition that is expected in normal operation, making the flaw subtle and easy to overlook during manual review. It affects any participant of the airdrop, the protocol’s token economics, and any downstream services that rely on the correctness of the distribution. The issue was discovered through static analysis of the contract’s state‑transition logic, noticing that the `validated` flag is set but never consulted on entry to `validate()`. The problem is hard to spot because the zero‑balance check appears legitimate and the contract does not emit an event or revert when the record is reset, so normal usage does not raise an alarm. To remediate the issue, the `validate()` function must enforce a guard that rejects callers who have already been validated, for example by requiring `validated[msg.sender] == 0` before resetting the airdrop struct, and by ensuring that a completed claim permanently marks the allocation as exhausted. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “state‑reset/re‑initialisation vulnerabilities” where a contract incorrectly re‑creates a data structure after it has been finalized, violating accounting assumptions that a zero balance signals finality.
summary:
Suppose someone claims the last part of his airdrop via `claimExact()` of `AirdropDistribution.sol`. Then `airdrop[msg.sender].amount` will be set to 0.

Suppose you then call validate() again. The check `airdrop[msg.sender].amount == 0` will allow you to continue, because amount has just be set to 0. In the next part of the function, `airdrop[msg.sender]` is overwritten with fresh values and `airdrop[msg.sender].claimed` will be reset to 0.

Now you can claim your airdrop again (as long as there are tokens present in the contract)

Note: The function `claim()` prevents this from happening via `assert(airdrop[msg.sender].amount - claimable != 0);`, which has its own problems, see other reported issues.

title: Anyone Can Arbitrarily Call `FSDVesting.updateVestedTokens`
content: The vulnerability is an authorization bypass in the vesting contract that permits any external address to invoke the `updateVestedTokens()` function and arbitrarily modify a user’s vested token balance. The function was designed to be called only by the core token contract (`FSD.sol`) when a beneficiary’s schedule is updated, and it contains a check that the supplied `_user` argument matches the beneficiary address. Because `_user` is a parameter supplied by the caller, an attacker can simply pass the intended beneficiary’s address, satisfy the equality check, and then execute the function without any additional verification of the caller’s identity. The root cause is the absence of a source‑authentication modifier (e.g., `onlyFSD`) and reliance on a mutable, user‑controlled argument for access control. An attacker can exploit this by calling `updateVestedTokens()` with a large `amount` value, inflating the recorded vested amount for any target beneficiary. Once the vested amount is artificially increased, the subsequent `calculateVestingClaim()` logic will consider the beneficiary fully vested, enabling an immediate withdrawal of the entire token allocation without waiting for the prescribed vesting period. Alternatively, an attacker can increase the vested amount beyond the contract’s token holdings, causing the `safeTransfer()` call inside `claimVestedTokens()` to revert due to insufficient balance; this effectively blocks legitimate beneficiaries from claiming their rightful tokens. The impact includes premature token extraction, loss of protocol‑controlled token reserves, and denial‑of‑service for other users. The issue manifests whenever the contract’s `updateVestedTokens()` function is exposed to the public, which is the default state in the current implementation, and can be triggered at any time by an arbitrary address. All beneficiaries, token holders, and the overall protocol are affected because the bug undermines the core accounting guarantees of the vesting schedule. The flaw was discovered during a systematic security audit that examined the contract’s external interfaces and identified missing access‑control guards. The problem is subtle because the function does perform a sanity check on the beneficiary address, which may give the false impression that the call is safe; however, without verifying the caller, the check can be bypassed. To remediate the issue, the contract should enforce a strict caller restriction, such as an `onlyFSD` role or a similar access‑control modifier, ensuring that only the designated token contract can modify vested balances. This aligns the implementation with the intended business logic that vesting updates are internal protocol actions, not user‑triggered operations. From a user’s perspective, the symptoms may appear as unexpected token balances (either excessively high or zero after a claim attempt), failed withdrawal attempts with error messages about insufficient contract balance, or simply the ability to claim the full allocation immediately, contrary to expectations of a gradual release schedule. The bug falls into the class of "improper access control" or "authorization bypass" vulnerabilities, where a function that should be restricted to a privileged contract is unintentionally exposed to any external caller, leading to accounting inconsistencies and potential fund loss.
summary:
The `updateVestedTokens()` function is intended to be called by the `FSD.sol` contract when updating a user’s vested token amount. A check is performed to ensure that `_user == beneficiary`, however, as `_user` is a user controlled argument, it is possible to spoof calls to `updateVestedTokens()` such that anyone can arbitrarily add any amount to the vested contract. Additionally, there is no check to ensure that the call originated from a trusted/whitelisted source.

There are two main reasons as to why the beneficiary or an attacker would want to call this function:

* To increase the vested amount such that `calculateVestingClaim()` allows them to withdraw their entire vested amount without waiting the entire duration.
* An attacker wishes to block withdrawals from other vested contracts by preventing successful calls to `claimVestedTokens()` by the beneficiary account. This can be done by increasing the vested amount such that `safeTransfer()` calls fail due to insufficient token balance within the contract.

title: `FSDVesting`: Claiming tributes should call FSD token’s corresponding functions
content: The vulnerability resides in the vesting contract’s reward‑claiming interface. When a beneficiary of a vested FSD token attempts to retrieve their staking or governance tribute through the `claimTribute()` or `claimGovernanceTribute()` functions, the contract calculates the amount of accrued tribute by querying the FSD token (`availableTribute` and `availableGovernanceTribute`) but never forwards the claim to the FSD token’s own `claimTribute` or `claimGovernanceTribute` methods. Consequently, the vesting contract never instructs the token contract to release the earned rewards, and the subsequent `safeTransfer` attempts to move tokens that are not actually allocated to the vesting contract. From a user’s perspective the transaction succeeds, no error is thrown, yet the user receives either zero tokens or an amount that does not reflect the true accrued tribute. The root cause is an omitted external call to the FSD token contract, combined with redundant internal bookkeeping (`_claimedTribute` and `_claimedGovernanceTribute`) that mirrors state already held in the token contract. The flaw can be exploited simply by invoking the claim functions; the attacker (any beneficiary) will be unable to collect their entitled rewards, effectively freezing or disappearing the tribute balance. This situation occurs during the vesting period for any beneficiary who expects to claim rewards, and it affects all users holding vested tokens, as well as the protocol’s governance economics because unclaimed governance tribute skews voting power distribution. The issue was uncovered during a systematic audit where the flow of function calls was traced and the missing calls were identified. It is subtle because the function signatures and event emissions give the impression of a successful claim, and there is no revert or explicit failure. The proper remediation is to insert the appropriate calls to `fsd.claimTribute(num)` and `fsd.claimGovernanceTribute(num)` inside the respective claim functions, and to delete the duplicated internal mappings that track claimed tribute, allowing the token contract to handle all accounting. This aligns the implementation with the intended business logic that a user’s tribute claim should trigger the token contract to release the funds, ensuring that users receive the expected refunds and the protocol’s accounting remains consistent.
summary: The claiming of staking and governance tributes for the a beneficiary’s vested tokens should be no different than other users / EOAs. However, the `claimTribute()` and `claimGovernanceTribute()` are missing the actual claiming calls to the corresponding functions of the FSD token contract. As a result, the accrued rewards are taken from the beneficiary’s vested token while not claiming (replenishing) from the FSD token contract.

title: Beneficiary cant get `fairSideConviction` NFT unless they only claim once, and only after it’s fully vested
content: The vulnerability concerns the distribution of the fairSideConviction NFT that is supposed to be granted to a vesting beneficiary after the full amount of vested tokens has been claimed. In the current implementation, the contract checks whether the amount of tokens claimed in a single transaction (tokenClaim) is equal to the total vesting amount (amount) before minting and transferring the NFT. This condition is evaluated inside the claimVestedTokens function immediately after a successful token transfer. Because tokenClaim reflects only the amount claimed in the current call, beneficiaries who claim any portion of their allocation before the vesting schedule is complete will never satisfy the equality test. Consequently, the NFT minting branch is never executed, even after the beneficiary eventually claims the remaining tokens in subsequent calls. The root cause is a logical error: the contract compares the per‑call claim amount rather than the cumulative amount of tokens claimed (totalClaimed) against the original vesting amount. The bug can be exploited unintentionally by any beneficiary who follows the intended incremental vesting pattern, effectively denying them the promised NFT reward. The impact is that users receive no NFT despite having fully vested their token allocation, leading to a breach of the protocol’s incentive promises, potential loss of perceived value, and user confusion when the UI shows a completed vesting but no NFT appears. The condition triggers only when the beneficiary attempts to claim the entire allocation in a single transaction after the vesting period; any earlier claim, even a single token, causes the NFT to be permanently inaccessible. This issue was discovered during a manual audit of the vesting contract, where the reviewer noted that the require clause used tokenClaim == amount, which does not align with the intended business logic of awarding the NFT after the total vested amount is exhausted. The flaw is subtle because the function still works correctly for token transfers, and the NFT minting logic is hidden behind a single equality check that many may assume is correct. To fix the issue, the contract should compare the cumulative totalClaimed variable to the original amount, or alternatively verify that the vesting schedule is complete (e.g., lastClaimAt >= vestingEnd) before triggering the NFT minting. This adjustment ensures that beneficiaries who claim incrementally still receive the NFT once the full vesting amount has been transferred, restoring the intended reward mechanism and preventing the silent failure that currently leaves users without their NFT.

title: Ideal balance is not calculated correctly when providing imbalanced liquidity
content: The vulnerability stems from an incorrect calculation of the "ideal balance" during the fee assessment that occurs when a liquidity provider adds imbalanced amounts of tokens to a custom‑price pool. In the current implementation the fee is derived from the raw token balances stored in the pool (self.balances). However, for pools that use a target price different from 1, the correct reference point is the virtual, price‑scaled balance obtained via the _xp function. By using the unscaled balances, the contract under‑estimates the ideal balance for the token that is over‑represented relative to the target price, which in turn reduces the fee charged for the deposit. As a result, a user who deposits a skewed ratio of tokens receives far more LP tokens than the proportional share they should obtain. For example, in a pool with a target price of 4, depositing DAI in a 10 : 1 DAI/LINK ratio yields approximately four times the expected amount of LP tokens. The impact is that the protocol can issue excessive LP tokens, effectively allowing an attacker to acquire a larger ownership stake of the underlying assets without paying the appropriate fee. When the attacker later withdraws or swaps, they can extract assets at the correct market ratios, causing loss of funds for other liquidity providers and reducing the protocol’s revenue. This issue appears only when the pool’s target price deviates from the 1 : 1 ratio and when liquidity is supplied in an imbalanced fashion, making it easy to overlook during casual testing because balanced deposits calculate fees correctly. It was discovered during a security audit by comparing the LP minted from two identical pools with different target prices and observing a four‑fold increase in LP for the imbalanced case. The bug is hard to notice because the fee computation itself does not throw an error; the mis‑calculation simply yields a lower fee, which is visible only under specific price‑ratio conditions. To remediate, the fee loop should replace the direct use of self.balances with the virtual balances returned by _xp(self, newBalances), aligning the ideal balance with the weighted‑price model used by similar protocols (e.g., Balancer's WeightedMath). This change restores correct fee assessment and prevents the over‑issuance of LP tokens, preserving the intended accounting invariants of the pool.
summary:
When a user provides imbalanced liquidity, the fee is calculated according to the ideal balance. In saddle finance, the optimal balance should be the same ratio as in the Pool.

Take, for example, if there’s 10000 USD and 10000 DAI in the saddle’s USD/DAI pool, the user should get the optimal lp if he provides lp with ratio = 1.

However, if the `customSwap` pool is created with a target price = 2. The user would get 2 times more lp if he deposits DAI. [SwapUtils.sol#L1227-L1245](https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-11-bootfinance/blob/main/customswap/contracts/SwapUtils.sol#L1227-L1245) The current implementation does not calculates ideal balance correctly.

If the target price is set to be 10, the ideal balance deviates by 10. The fee deviates a lot. I consider this is a high-risk issues.

title: ERC20ConvictionScore._writeCheckpoint` does not write to storage on same block
content: The vulnerability resides in the function responsible for recording a user’s conviction score on each update. When the contract attempts to overwrite an existing checkpoint that was created in the current block, it copies the checkpoint into a temporary variable declared with the `memory` keyword. The code then modifies the `convictionScore` field of this in‑memory copy, but never writes the updated structure back to the persistent `checkpoints` storage array. Because the modified data never reaches storage, only the first checkpoint written in a given block is ever persisted; any subsequent updates inside the same block are silently discarded. This occurs whenever a user’s score is updated multiple times within a single blockchain block, a scenario that can happen in high‑frequency voting, delegation, or batch‑execution contexts. The root cause is a classic storage‑vs‑memory confusion: a `memory` pointer is used instead of a `storage` pointer, so changes affect only a transient copy. An attacker, or even a regular user, can exploit the flaw by triggering multiple score updates in the same block—through rapid transactions, front‑running, or contract‑internal loops—expecting each update to be recorded. In practice the contract will appear to ignore later updates, causing the user’s displayed conviction score to remain at the initial value for that block. From the user’s point of view the UI may show the same score despite having performed actions that should increase or decrease it, leading to confusion such as “my voting power didn’t change” or “the protocol isn’t counting my last vote”. The impact is an incorrect accounting of conviction scores, which can affect voting outcomes, reward distributions, or any downstream logic that relies on an accurate snapshot of user stakes. This bug was discovered during a formal security audit that examined the checkpoint‑writing logic and noticed that the checkpoint variable was declared as `memory`. The issue can be subtle because the contract does not emit any event on the failed write, and the state appears consistent when only a single update per block occurs, making the defect easy to miss in regular testing. The appropriate remediation is to declare the checkpoint variable as a `storage` pointer so that modifications are written directly to the persistent data structure, ensuring that every update—regardless of block timing—is correctly saved. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of state‑persistence errors where mutable data is altered only in a temporary context, violating the contract’s business logic that assumes each conviction score change is durable and immediately reflected in on‑chain accounting.

title: `customPrecisionMultipliers` would be rounded to zero and break the pool
content: The vulnerability originates from the way the contract computes its custom precision multipliers during pool initialization. The multiplier for the first token is calculated as the original precision multiplier (typically 1 for 18‑decimal tokens) multiplied by the user‑provided target price and then divided by 10^18 using integer arithmetic. When the target price is expressed as a value smaller than 10^18 – for example 0.5 × 10^18 – the product of the original multiplier and the target price is still less than 10^18, and the subsequent integer division truncates the result to zero. Consequently the customPrecisionMultipliers[0] becomes zero. This zero multiplier is later used in price‑related calculations throughout the pool, causing division‑by‑zero style errors or effectively rendering the pool unable to compute correct swap amounts. As a result, users can still deposit assets into the pool, but any attempt to trade, withdraw, or rebalance will fail or produce nonsensical outcomes, effectively locking the funds. The issue occurs at contract construction (or any re‑initialisation path that sets the multipliers) whenever a target price lower than the scaling factor is supplied. Liquidity providers, traders, and any party interacting with the affected pool are impacted because their assets become inaccessible. The bug was identified during a manual audit that highlighted the integer division without proper scaling; a proof‑of‑concept demonstrates that setting the target price to 0.5 × 10^18 yields a zero multiplier and breaks the pool. The problem is subtle because the code compiles without warnings, the multiplier variable appears to hold a value, and standard unit tests that use default target prices (≥ 10^18) pass, making the failure mode easy to miss. To remediate the issue, the calculation should include an additional scaling factor of 10^18 before the division, ensuring that the multiplier retains its fractional precision and never collapses to zero. Alternatively, the contract could enforce a minimum positive multiplier via a require statement or redesign the pricing logic to avoid integer truncation altogether. Fixing the bug restores the expected behavior where a user deposits tokens, receives a correct share of the pool, and can later trade or withdraw without unexpected zero balances, aligning the implementation with the protocol’s accounting assumptions.
summary:
`CustomPrecisionMultipliers` are set in the constructor:

```solidity
customPrecisionMultipliers[0] = targetPriceStorage.originalPrecisionMultipliers[0].mul(_targetPrice).div(10 ** 18);
```

`originalPrecisionMultipliers` equal to 1 if the token’s decimal = 18. The targe price could only be an integer.

If the target price is bigger than 10**18, the user can deposit and trade in the pool. Though, the functionality would be far from the spec.

If the target price is set to be smaller than 10**18, the pool would be broken and all funds would be stuck.

I consider this is a high-risk issue.

title: Unable to claim vesting due to unbounded timelock loop
content: The vulnerability is an unbounded timelock loop that can be abused to deny beneficiaries the ability to claim their vested assets. In the Vesting contract each beneficiary is associated with an array of timelock entries that record individual vesting amounts and release timestamps. The contract’s vest() function does not verify that the caller is the intended beneficiary, allowing any address to push a new timelock entry into the timelocks[beneficiary] array on behalf of any other user. Because the array grows without any imposed limit, a malicious actor can repeatedly invoke vest() with minute vesting amounts, creating a very large list of entries for a target beneficiary. When the beneficiary later calls claim(), the claim() function invokes an internal helper, _claimableAmount(), that iterates over the entire timelocks[beneficiary] array to sum the amounts whose release time has passed. If the array has been inflated to a sufficient size, the loop exhausts the block gas limit, causing the claim transaction to revert. From the user’s perspective the contract appears to lock the funds: the beneficiary’s balance remains unchanged, the UI shows no claimable tokens, and attempts to claim result in out‑of‑gas errors or transaction failures. The impact is a denial‑of‑service on fund withdrawal that can affect any or all beneficiaries, effectively rendering vested tokens unrecoverable without a contract upgrade. The condition occurs whenever the timelock array for a beneficiary grows large enough to breach the gas budget, which can be triggered at any time by an attacker who does not need to be the beneficiary. This issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, which noted the missing beneficiary check in vest() and the unbounded iteration in _claimableAmount(). It can be difficult to notice because normal operation with a modest number of entries works as expected, and the problem only surfaces under deliberately adversarial conditions. The proper remediation is to enforce that only the beneficiary can add vesting entries (require(msg.sender == beneficiary)), optionally introduce a minimum vesting amount to discourage the creation of many tiny entries, and redesign the accounting logic to avoid iterating over an unbounded array—e.g., by aggregating vesting amounts per timestamp, using a cumulative balance, or imposing a hard cap on the array length. These changes restore the intended business logic that each beneficiary can reliably claim the amount that has vested according to the schedule, preventing funds from disappearing or becoming inaccessible due to a gas‑limit overflow.
summary:
The timelocks for any _beneficiary_ are unbounded, and can be vested by someone who is not the _beneficiary_. When the array becomes significantly big enough, the vestments will no longer be claimable for the _beneficiary_.

The `vest()` function in Vesting.sol does not check the _beneficiary_, hence anyone can vest for anyone else, pushing a new timelock to the `timelocks[_beneficiary]`. The `_claimableAmount()` function (used by `claim()` function), then loops through the `timelocks[_beneficiary]` to determine the amount to be claimed. A malicious actor can easy repeatedly call the `vest()` function with minute amounts to make the array large enough, such that when it comes to claiming, it will exceed the gas limit and revert, rendering the vestment for the beneficiary unclaimable. The malicious actor could do this to each _beneficiary_, locking up all the vestments.

title: addInvestor
content: The vulnerability resides in the investor onboarding function, which allows an administrator to allocate tokens to a new investor without verifying that the cumulative allocation stays within the predefined investor token supply limit. Because the function does not check the remaining balance of the investors_supply variable before increasing the total allocated amount, the contract can be instructed to assign tokens that exceed the intended cap.
