To remediate the issue, the contract should compute the selector by hashing the function signature (e.g., changeCouncil(address)) and compare this value against the stored signatures entry, or alternatively prepend the selector onto the calldata as expected by the veto logic. This change ensures that the veto check correctly identifies proposals that attempt to modify the council, restoring the intended balance of power and preventing a scenario where funds or governance decisions can be arbitrarily blocked by a single entity.
summary: Council can veto proposals to remove them to remain in power.

title: Denial of service
content: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that arises from an incorrect initialization of the pool’s liquidity accounting. When a new token pair is created, the contract sets the total liquidity units (the denominator used to calculate how many liquidity provider (LP) tokens correspond to a given amount of reserves) solely to the amount of native token deposited, disregarding the size of the foreign token reserve. As a result, an attacker can perform the first deposit with a negligible native amount (for example, 1 wei) while supplying a large foreign amount (such as 10 ether). This forces the totalLiquidityUnits variable to the minimal value of 1, meaning that a single LP token mathematically represents the entire pool balance. Subsequent users who attempt to add liquidity encounter extreme rounding errors: the contract either rejects the minting because the calculated LP amount rounds down to zero, or it issues dramatically fewer LP tokens than the liquidity contributed, effectively starving new providers. The attack can be executed immediately after the pool owner enables support for a new fungible token via setFungibleTokenSupport; the pool cannot be removed or replaced, so the condition persists indefinitely. The impact is that legitimate liquidity providers are unable to join the pool, the pool’s market becomes unusable, and the attacker can profit from the inflated value of the single LP token and from the rounding‑error losses that increase the pool reserves. Users experience symptoms such as transactions failing with “cannot mint 0 liquidity”, receiving far fewer LP tokens than expected, or seeing their balances unchanged despite depositing assets. The issue was discovered during a formal security audit (Code4rena) where a proof‑of‑concept demonstrated the attack scenario. It may be hard to notice because the rounding discrepancy surfaces only after the second deposit, appearing as a normal arithmetic rounding variation rather than a systemic failure. To remediate, the contract should initialize totalLiquidityUnits based on a calibrated combination of both native and foreign deposits, enforce a minimum liquidity unit threshold, and include safeguards that prevent extreme native‑to‑foreign ratios on first deposits. Conceptually, the fix ensures that the denominator used for LP token calculations accurately reflects the total value locked, eliminating the possibility of a single token representing the entire pool and restoring the ability of any participant to add liquidity without encountering rounding‑error blocks.
summary: <https://github.com/code-423n4/2021-12-vader/blob/main/contracts/dex-v2/pool/VaderPoolV2.sol#L334> on the first deposit, the total liquidity is set to `nativeDeposit`. this might be a very low number compared to `foreignDeposit`. It can cause a denial of service of the pair.

title: Yeti token rebase checks the additional token amount incorrectly
content: The vulnerability resides in the rebase logic of the sYETI token contract, where the function that updates the effective Yeti token balance uses the contract’s total Yeti token balance instead of the surplus amount that is actually available for rebasing. During a rebase, the contract obtains the full balance via yetiToken.balanceOf(address(this)) and checks whether this balance is less than the amount it intends to add (additionalYetiTokenBalance). Because the check does not subtract the already accounted effectiveYetiTokenBalance, the condition can be bypassed when the contract’s total balance includes tokens that have already been recorded in effectiveYetiTokenBalance. Consequently, the variable effectiveYetiTokenBalance can be increased by more tokens than the contract truly owns. This over‑accounting means that the internal accounting of each user’s claim to Yeti tokens (or the derived YUSD token) may exceed the actual holdings of the contract. When users later invoke a withdrawal or claim function, the contract may be unable to supply the promised amount, leading to a default situation in which net holdings are lower than total user claims. The issue becomes especially severe when the price of Yeti token rises after the last recorded buy‑back price, because the inflated token balance is valued higher in the contract’s net‑worth calculation, further widening the discrepancy between reported and real assets. The bug was discovered during a Code4rena audit by analyzing the rebase routine and noticing that the balance check does not account for the already‑effective portion of the token holdings. The problem is subtle because the contract’s external token balance appears sufficient, masking the internal mismatch until a claim is made. The correct mitigation is to compute the surplus as totalBalance minus effectiveYetiTokenBalance and to cap additionalYetiTokenBalance to this surplus before adding it to effectiveYetiTokenBalance. Additionally, the internal value‑of‑contract function should be rewritten to accept the adjusted surplus balance, eliminating the double‑counting of tokens. By enforcing this corrected check, the contract will no longer credit users with more tokens than it can actually withdraw, preserving the integrity of user balances and preventing loss of funds.
summary:
The condition isn’t checked now as the whole balance is used instead of the Yeti tokens bought back from the market. As it’s not checked, the amount added to `effectiveYetiTokenBalance` during rebase can exceed the actual amount of the Yeti tokens owned by the contract. As the before check amount is calculated as the contract net worth, it can be fixed by immediate buy back, but it will not be the case.

The deficit of Yeti tokens can materialize in net worth terms as well if Yeti tokens price will raise compared to the last used one. In this case users will be cumulatively accounted with the amount of tokens that cannot be actually withdrawn from the contract, as its net holdings will be less then total users’ claims. In other words, the contract will be in default if enough users claim after that.

title: Lack of access control on `assertGovernanceApproved` can cause funds to be locked
content: The vulnerability is an unauthorized access control omission in the FlashGovernanceArbiter contract's assertGovernanceApproved function. Because the function does not restrict who can call it, any external account can invoke it with arbitrary parameters, including a victim's address as the sender. The root cause is that the contract assumes the caller will be the governance arbiter or a trusted party, but the code never enforces this assumption, allowing a malicious actor to supply any address for the from‑parameter of a transferFrom call. An attacker can exploit this by monitoring the mempool for a user’s approve transaction that grants the arbiter permission to transfer a specific amount of an asset. Immediately after the approve is mined, the attacker front‑runs the transaction and calls assertGovernanceApproved with the victim’s address as the sender and emergency set to true. The contract then executes a transferFrom that moves the approved amount from the victim’s wallet into the arbiter’s internal lock, triggering the unlockTime delay. As a result, the victim’s flash‑governance operation fails and the approved tokens remain locked for the full unlock period, effectively freezing the user’s funds temporarily. This condition occurs whenever a user grants the arbiter an allowance and the contract’s access control remains unchecked; it affects any token holder who interacts with the flash‑governance mechanism, including regular users and protocol participants. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined allowance handling patterns and noted that transferFrom was being called with a user‑controlled “from” argument without a corresponding onlyOwner‑style check. Because the funds are not permanently stolen, the problem can be easy to miss in functional testing: the UI may simply show that a withdrawal or flash‑governance action cannot be performed, or that the balance appears unchanged while the underlying allowance remains consumed. The bug belongs to the class of “unrestricted external function leading to unauthorized token transfer” and violates the business assumption that a user’s approved allowance can only be exercised by the intended contract logic. To remediate, the contract should introduce strict access control—such as restricting assertGovernanceApproved to a whitelist of privileged addresses or the contract itself—and ensure that any transferFrom call uses msg.sender as the source of funds, or otherwise validates that the caller is authorized to act on behalf of the specified sender. This change restores the guarantee that users can withdraw their tokens after the unlock period and prevents arbitrary front‑running attacks that temporarily lock user assets.
summary: Lack of access control on the `assertGovernanceApproved` function of `FlashGovernanceArbiter` allows anyone to lock other users’ funds in the contract as long as the users have approved the contract to transfer `flashGovernanceConfig.amount` of `flashGovernanceConfig.asset` from them.

title: wrong minting amount
content:
The vulnerability consists of an arithmetic miscalculation in the token‑minting routine that is triggered during a redemption operation. Instead of basing the newly minted amount on the user‑specified redemption amount, the contract mistakenly uses the contract’s internal baseBalance variable when calculating the proxy value: `proxy = (baseBalance * ONE) / _redeemRate` rather than the correct `proxy = (amount * ONE) / _redeemRate`. Because the proxy value is derived from the wrong operand, the contract either mints too many tokens or mints too few, depending on the relative sizes of baseBalance and the intended amount. In addition, the implementation fails to record a proper balance‑before and balance‑after comparison, allowing the difference to wrap silently if an overflow occurs. This root‑cause stems from a simple variable substitution error and a missing safety check around the balance delta.

An attacker can exploit the bug by invoking the redemption function with a deliberately small amount, causing the contract to compute a much larger proxy value from the inflated baseBalance. The attacker then receives an outsized amount of newly minted tokens, effectively extracting value from the protocol. Conversely, honest users may experience the opposite effect: they supply a legitimate amount but receive far fewer tokens, or in the worst case receive zero tokens while their funds are deducted, leading to a loss of value and a mismatch between on‑chain accounting and expected business logic.

The impact is therefore twofold: (1) financial loss for users who receive an incorrect mint amount, often manifesting as a sudden disappearance of funds or a zero balance where a token reward was expected; and (2) protocol‑wide accounting inconsistencies, breaking the invariant that the total supply corresponds to the sum of redeemed amounts. This condition occurs whenever the redemption path is executed, i.e., whenever a user calls the function that performs the proxy calculation under any redeem rate setting. All participants—regular users, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself—are potentially affected because the bug bypasses the intended economic guarantees.

The issue was uncovered during a Code4rena audit, where the auditors compared the contract’s state before and after redemption and observed that the token balance change did not match the expected mathematical relationship. The bug is difficult to spot because the two lines of code look syntactically correct, the variable names are similar, and the overflow‑wrap behavior can silently mask the error in environments where unchecked arithmetic is used.

To remediate the problem, the contract must replace the `baseBalance` reference with the `amount` supplied by the caller in the proxy formula, ensuring the minted quantity directly reflects the user’s request. Moreover, the implementation should explicitly record the balance before the operation, compute the expected delta, and assert that the observed delta equals the expected amount, thereby preventing silent wrapping. Leveraging Solidity 0.8's built‑in overflow checks or an explicit SafeMath library, together with comprehensive unit tests that validate balance changes across edge cases, will close the vulnerability and restore the intended accounting guarantees.

title: Double transfer in the `transferAndCall` function of `ERC677`
content: The vulnerability lies in the ERC677 implementation of the `transferAndCall` function, where the token transfer logic is executed twice. The function first invokes `super.transfer(_to, _value)`, which correctly moves the requested amount of tokens from the caller to the recipient. Immediately afterwards it calls the internal `_transfer(msg.sender, _to, _value)` function, performing the identical state update a second time. This duplication is the root cause: the developer unintentionally duplicated the transfer step instead of relying on the inherited `transfer` implementation. Whenever any account calls `transferAndCall` on the Flan token (which inherits this ERC677 contract), the caller’s balance is reduced by two times the intended amount while the recipient’s balance is increased by the same double amount. From an attacker’s perspective the vulnerability can be exploited simply by invoking the function with any value; the contract does not contain any guard or revert that would prevent the double debit. The impact is a loss of funds for the sender, who sees their balance drop by twice the value they intended to send, and an unexpected gain for the receiver, who receives twice the amount. This error manifests under all normal conditions of the function – it does not depend on the payload data, fallback execution, or whether the destination is a contract. All users of the Flan token who rely on `transferAndCall` for token movements are affected, including end‑users, dApp contracts and any protocol that assumes a single‑transfer semantics. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the repository, where the reviewer noticed that both `super.transfer` and `_transfer` were called with the same arguments. The bug can be hard to notice because both calls succeed and no exception is thrown; a UI may simply display the recipient’s balance as higher than expected, while the sender experiences an unexplained double deduction. The appropriate fix is to remove the redundant `_transfer` call so that only the inherited `transfer` is executed, ensuring the token transfer occurs exactly once. In generic terms, this is a double‑transfer or duplicated state‑change flaw that violates the accounting invariant that a single logical transfer should modify the total balances by exactly one amount of the token.
summary: The implementation of the `transferAndCall` function in `ERC677` is incorrect. It transfers the `_value` amount of tokens twice instead of once. Since the `Flan` contract inherits `ERC667`, anyone calling the `transferAndCall` function on `Flan` is affected by this double-transfer bug.

title: Logic error in `burnFlashGovernanceAsset` can cause locked assets to be stolen
content: The vulnerability is a logic error in the function that burns a user's locked governance assets, specifically the `burnFlashGovernanceAsset` routine. Instead of fully removing the record of a user’s pending flash decision, the function merely overwrites the stored structure with a default (zero‑filled) configuration. This incomplete cleanup leaves the system in a state where the attacker’s own decision record appears as if it has already expired. Because the contract checks only that the stored `unlockTime` is in the past before allowing a withdrawal, the attacker can subsequently call `withdrawGovernanceAsset` and satisfy the expiration condition for any other user’s pending decision that is still locked. The root cause is the misuse of a default assignment to clear mapping data, which does not delete the entry and therefore bypasses the intended ownership check. An attacker can exploit this by first initiating a malicious flash governance decision that locks their assets, then triggering the community‑initiated burn, which resets their decision record to the default. After a benign user locks their assets in a subsequent flash decision, the attacker invokes the withdrawal function; the contract sees the attacker’s reset record as expired and releases the second user’s locked assets to the attacker. The impact is that funds belonging to honest participants can be stolen, effectively allowing asset theft without any direct violation of the contract’s access control modifiers. The condition occurs whenever the burn function is called and the contract uses a default assignment instead of a proper `delete` operation on the nested mapping. Both the attacker and any regular users of the flash governance system are affected: attackers gain unauthorized access to others’ funds, while victims lose their locked assets. The issue was discovered during a formal security audit that inspected the logic of state cleanup after asset burning. It is hard to notice because the function appears to reset the user’s state, which superficially seems safe, and the contract’s external view does not expose the missing delete operation. The bug belongs to the broader class of improper state clearing or incomplete mapping deletion errors, which can unintentionally bypass time‑based or ownership checks. From a user’s perspective, a victim may see their balance drop to zero after a community burn, while the attacker’s balance unexpectedly increases. Users expect that once an asset is burned, they cannot later withdraw any other user’s locked funds, but the reality is that the incomplete reset enables that withdrawal. The correct mitigation is to replace the default assignment with a `delete` operation on the `pendingFlashDecision` entry, ensuring that the mapping entry is fully removed and the contract’s expiration check fails for any unrelated user. This change restores the intended invariant that only the owner of a pending decision may withdraw their own locked assets after the unlock time has passed.
summary: A logic error in the `burnFlashGovernanceAsset` function that resets a user’s `pendingFlashDecision` allows that user to steal other user’s assets locked in future flash governance decisions. As a result, attackers can get their funds back even if they execute a malicious flash decision and the community burns their assets.

title: Flash loan price manipulation in `purchasePyroFlan`
content: The vulnerability is a flash‑loan price manipulation weakness in the purchasePyroFlan routine of the FlanBackstop contract. The function calculates the price of the Flan‑stablecoin liquidity‑pair by reading the pool balances at a single point in time and then derives a growth factor that determines the premium of newly minted PyroFlan. Because the price is taken from an instantaneous snapshot, an attacker who can obtain a flash loan can temporarily tilt the pool’s reserves, causing the snapshot to reflect an artificial price. The root cause is the reliance on a volatile on‑chain price source without any smoothing or temporal aggregation. An attacker can borrow a large amount of stablecoin, swap it into the Uniswap pool to inflate the Flan price, and then invoke purchasePyroFlan while the pool is still skewed. The manipulated priceBefore value becomes larger than the true market price, which in turn inflates the growth variable and the premium calculation. As a result the attacker receives an excessive amount of PyroFlan for the amount of Flan supplied, effectively minting tokens out of thin air. This can be repeated with multiple smaller flash loans to stay within the contract’s acceptableHighestPrice limit, especially when the pool is newly created or otherwise low on liquidity, allowing the attacker to bypass the single‑transaction volume check. The impact is a dilution of the Flan token supply, loss of value for legitimate users, and a breakdown of the back‑stop’s intended purpose of stabilising liquidity. The issue manifests when a user calls purchasePyroFlan with a volume that is large relative to the pool, or when a flash‑loan attacker creates a temporary price tilt; the UI would show a normal transaction fee but the user’s balance of PyroFlan would be unexpectedly high, while other participants see their holdings de‑valued. The problem was discovered during a manual audit where a comment in the source explicitly warned about the possibility of price manipulation via flash loans. It may be hard to notice because the transaction appears to succeed, the price deviation exists only for a single block, and the contract’s internal require statement only limits the absolute price change, not the cumulative effect of multiple small attacks. To remediate, the contract should replace the single‑point price with a time‑weighted average price (TWAP) or another oracle that aggregates observations over several blocks, thereby raising the cost of a flash‑loan sandwich attack. Additional mitigations include imposing tighter per‑transaction volume caps, implementing a sliding‑window price deviation limit, and possibly introducing a circuit‑breaker that pauses purchases when rapid price swings are detected. In conceptual terms, the fix removes the ability to influence the price oracle with a single transaction, aligning the contract’s accounting with the intended 1:1 peg between Flan and stablecoins and preserving the integrity of the premium calculation.
summary: The comment on [line 54](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-behodler/blob/cedb81273f6daf2ee39ec765eef5ba74f21b2c6e/contracts/FlanBackstop.sol#L54) of FlanBackstop.sol states “the opportunity for price manipulation through flash loans exists”, and I agree that this is a serious risk. While the acceptableHighestPrice variable attempts to limit the maximum price change of the flan-stablecoin LP, a flashloan sandwich attack can still occur within this limit and make up for the limitation with larger volumes or multiple flashloan attacks. Flashloan price manipulation is the cause for many major hacks, including [bZx](https://bzx.network/blog/postmortem-ethdenver), [Harvest](https://rekt.news/harvest-finance-rekt/), and others.

title: Loss Of Flash Governance Tokens If They Are Not Withdrawn Before The Next Request
content: The vulnerability is an unintended loss of flash‑governance tokens caused by the contract overwriting a user's pending decision state instead of preserving or aggregating it. When a user locks governance tokens by calling the public function assertGovernanceApproved, the contract stores the amount and unlock time in a mapping keyed by the target address and the sender address. If the same user (or any other address acting on the user's behalf) invokes assertGovernanceApproved again with the same target and sender before the previously locked tokens have been withdrawn via withdrawGovernanceAsset, the line that assigns pendingFlashDecision[target][sender] = flashGovernanceConfig overwrites the existing entry. The previous amount is discarded, the unlockTime is reset, and the overwritten tokens remain locked inside the contract with no reference in the mapping, effectively disappearing from the user’s balance. This situation occurs because the function only checks that the prior unlockTime has passed, not whether the pending entry is empty, and because the function is public, any attacker who has been approved to transfer the underlying ERC‑20 token can force this overwrite for any arbitrary sender. The impact is that users who have not withdrawn their pending tokens before a new request lose their governance assets, resulting in funds that are permanently inaccessible, breaking the protocol’s accounting assumptions that locked tokens are always recoverable after the unlock period. The issue was uncovered during a Code4rena audit where the logic of assertGovernanceApproved was examined and the state‑overwriting behaviour was observed. It is subtle because the contract emits a successful flashDecision event, giving the impression that the operation succeeded, while the prior balance is silently erased. From a user’s perspective the UI may show that a governance token deposit succeeded, but later the balance or reward appears as zero after another proposal is submitted, contradicting the expectation that a deposited token remains claimable after the lock period. The bug belongs to the class of state‑overwrite or improper state‑reset vulnerabilities, where a mapping entry is replaced without preserving existing data, leading to asset loss. The recommended remediation is to ensure that the pending entry is empty before overwriting, for example by checking that pendingFlashDecision[target][sender].unlockTime == 0, or by otherwise handling multiple deposits in a way that does not discard previous amounts. This change would prevent accidental or malicious overwriting and preserve the ability of users to withdraw their tokens once the lock expires.
summary:
Users who have not called [withdrawGovernanceAsset()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-behodler/blob/main/contracts/DAO/FlashGovernanceArbiter.sol#L142) after they have locked their tokens from a previous proposal (i.e. [assertGovernanceApproved](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-behodler/blob/main/contracts/DAO/FlashGovernanceArbiter.sol#L60)), will lose their tokens if [assertGovernanceApproved()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-behodler/blob/main/contracts/DAO/FlashGovernanceArbiter.sol#L60) is called again with the same `target` and `sender`.

The `sender` will lose `pendingFlashDecision[target][sender].amount` tokens and the tokens will become unaccounted for and locked in the contract. Since the new amount is not added to the previous amount, instead the previous amount is overwritten with the new amount.

The impact of this is worsened by another vulnerability, that is [assertGovernanceApproved()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-behodler/blob/main/contracts/DAO/FlashGovernanceArbiter.sol#L60) is a `public` function and may be called by any arbitrary user so long as the `sender` field has called `approve()` for `FlashGovernanceArbiter` on the ERC20 token. This would allow an attacker to make these tokens inaccessible for any arbitrary `sender`.

title: LP pricing formula is vulnerable to flashloan manipulation
content: The vulnerability consists of an economic manipulation of the liquidity‑provider (LP) token pricing logic inside the burnAsset (and related setEYEBasedAssetStake) functions of the LimboDAO contract. The contract calculates the amount of fate tokens to mint when a user redeems LP shares using a simplistic proportional formula that multiplies the pool’s total underlying token balances by a constant factor. Because the formula directly depends on the on‑chain reserves without any protection against rapid reserve shifts, an attacker can temporarily inflate the pool’s reserves by performing a large swap, often funded through a flash‑loan or flash‑swap. The attacker first deposits a large amount of the EYE token into the UniswapV2‑style pool, which drives up the EYE reserve and reduces the LINK reserve according to the constant‑product invariant. When the attacker subsequently burns his LP tokens, the manipulated reserves cause the proportional calculation to report a higher total pool value, resulting in a larger fate payout than would be justified by the original liquidity contribution. This over‑allocation of fate tokens translates into additional voting power within the DAO and can be converted to Flan tokens for direct profit, effectively allowing the attacker to extract value from the protocol at the cost of only the swap fees. The issue emerges whenever the contract’s pricing function is called after a sudden, attacker‑controlled change in pool balances, which is a scenario easily triggered by flash‑loan providers that can supply large amounts of EYE within a single transaction. Users of the protocol observe that burning LP shares yields an unexpectedly high amount of fate, sometimes double the normal amount, while their underlying token balances appear unchanged after they unwind the temporary swap. The problem is subtle because the contract does not enforce any time‑weighted average price or oracle guard, making the manipulation appear legitimate from the perspective of the on‑chain state at the moment of burning. The attack was discovered during a security audit that examined the economic invariants of the DAO’s token minting logic. To remediate the issue, the pricing mechanism should be replaced with a fair, oracle‑backed or time‑weighted average pricing model, such as the scheme proposed by Alpha Finance, which prevents single‑block reserve distortions from influencing token minting. In short, the flaw is an exploitable pricing oracle weakness that lets an attacker artificially inflate LP token value, leading to unchecked fate inflation, excess governance influence, and direct monetary gain.
summary:
The LP pricing formula used in the `burnAsset` function of `LimboDAO` is vulnerable to flashloan manipulation. By swapping a large number of EYE into the underlying pool, an attacker can intentionally inflate the value of the LP tokens to get more `fate` than he is supposed to with a relatively low cost.

With the large portion of `fate` he gets, he has more voting power to influence the system’s decisions, or even he can convert his `fate` to Flan tokens for a direct profit.

title: In the case of Single Asset Entry, new liquidity providers will suffer fund loss due to wrong formula of ΔRo
content: The vulnerability is a mathematical error in the calculation of the share amount (ΔRo) that is issued to a liquidity provider when a single‑asset entry is performed after a base‑token rebase upward. The protocol defines Gamma as the ratio of the newly minted shares to the resulting total supply, and the correct relationship is ΔRo = (Ro / (1 - Gamma)) × Gamma. The implementation, however, derives Gamma from a formula that incorrectly combines the added quote token (ΔY), the new quote‑token reserve (Y'), the amount of base token added (ΔX) and the rebasing factor (α̂). Because the derivation does not respect the original algebraic rearrangement, the computed ΔRo is consistently smaller than it should be when the base token’s supply is increased. As a result, a new liquidity provider who supplies quote tokens receives fewer shares and therefore a lower combined value of base and quote tokens than the amount they deposited. In the concrete example, a provider adds four quote tokens while the base token rebases from 1 to 10; the contract assigns only 0.8889 quote‑token worth of shares instead of the expected four, leading to a loss of roughly 1.33 quote tokens. The error manifests only when a single‑sided liquidity addition occurs after a rebasing event, a situation that is relatively rare but critical for users who rely on the protocol’s advertised “fair share” guarantees. The affected parties are liquidity providers who expect their proportional ownership to be preserved, as well as the protocol itself because systematic under‑allocation erodes trust and could discourage participation. The issue was uncovered during a formal audit through a combination of reviewing the mathematical derivation in the documentation and reproducing the problem with a targeted unit test that varied the rebase factor and deposit amounts. It is difficult to spot because the incorrect formula lives inside a library function that performs several nested calculations, and the resulting under‑allocation does not produce a direct revert or error; instead, it silently reduces the provider’s returned value, making the symptom appear as “my balance after adding liquidity is lower than what I put in” without obvious on‑chain evidence of a bug. The proper remediation is to replace the current Γ computation with the mathematically verified expression derived from the definition of ΔRo, ensuring the formula also handles rebase‑down scenarios. In conceptual terms, the fix restores the invariant that the proportion of shares issued to a new provider equals the intended share of the total pool after accounting for any rebasing, thereby aligning the contract’s behavior with its economic model and preventing inadvertent fund loss for users.
summary:
When `baseToken` rebase up

Per the document: <https://github.com/ElasticSwap/elasticswap/blob/a90bb67e2817d892b517da6c1ba6fae5303e9867/ElasticSwapMath.md#:~:text=When%20there%20is%20alphaDecay>

and related code: <https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-elasticswap/blob/d107a198c0d10fbe254d69ffe5be3e40894ff078/elasticswap/src/libraries/MathLib.sol#L227-L283>

`Gamma` is the ratio of shares received by the new liquidity provider when `addLiquidity()` (ΔRo) to the new totalSupply (total shares = Ro’ = Ro + ΔRo).
    
    ΔRo = (Ro/(1 - γ)) * γ
    
            Ro * Gamma
        = --------------
             1 - Gamma
    ⟺
    ΔRo * ( 1 - Gamma ) = Gamma * Ro
    ΔRo - Gamma * ΔRo = Gamma * Ro
    ΔRo = Gamma * Ro + Gamma * ΔRo
               ΔRo    
    Gamma = ---------
             Ro + ΔRo 

In the current implementation:
    
    γ = ΔY / Y' / 2 * ( ΔX / α^ )

ΔY is the `quoteToken` added by the new liquidity provider. See:

* <https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-elasticswap/blob/d107a198c0d10fbe254d69ffe5be3e40894ff078/elasticswap/src/libraries/MathLib.sol#L277>

Y’ is the new Y after `addLiquidity()`, `Y' = Y + ΔY`. See:

* <https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-elasticswap/blob/d107a198c0d10fbe254d69ffe5be3e40894ff078/elasticswap/src/libraries/MathLib.sol#L272>
* <https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-elasticswap/blob/d107a198c0d10fbe254d69ffe5be3e40894ff078/elasticswap/src/libraries/MathLib.sol#L278>

ΔX is `ΔY * Omega`. See:

* <https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-elasticswap/blob/d107a198c0d10fbe254d69ffe5be3e40894ff078/elasticswap/src/libraries/MathLib.sol#L259-L263>
* <https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-elasticswap/blob/d107a198c0d10fbe254d69ffe5be3e40894ff078/elasticswap/src/libraries/MathLib.sol#L279>

α^ is `Alpha - X`. See:

* <https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-elasticswap/blob/d107a198c0d10fbe254d69ffe5be3e40894ff078/elasticswap/src/libraries/MathLib.sol#L234-L235>
* <https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-elasticswap/blob/d107a198c0d10fbe254d69ffe5be3e40894ff078/elasticswap/src/libraries/MathLib.sol#L280>

For instance:

Given:

* Original State: X = Alpha = 1, Y = Beta = 1, Omega = X/Y = 1
* When `baseToken` rebase up: Alpha becomes 10
* Current State: Alpha = 10, X = 1, Y = Beta = 1, Omega = 1

When: new liquidity provider `addLiquidity()` with 4 quoteToken:
    
                 4          4 * Omega      16
    Gamma = ------------ * ------------ = ----
             (1+4) * 2       10 - 1        90

After `addLiquidity()`:

* baseToken belongs to the newLP: 10 * 16 / 90 = 160 / 90 = 1.7777777777777777
* quoteToken belongs to the newLP: (1+4) * 16 / 90 = 80 / 90 = 0.8888888888888888
* In the terms of `quoteToken`, the total value is: 160 / 90 / Omega + 80 / 90 = 240 / 90 = 2.6666666666666665

As a result, the new liquidity provider suffers a fund loss of `4 - 240 / 90 = 1.3333333333333333 in the terms of quoteToken`

The case above can be reproduced by changing the numbers in [this test unit](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-elasticswap/blob/d107a198c0d10fbe254d69ffe5be3e40894ff078/elasticswap/test/exchangeTest.js#L1804).

title: Transferring `quoteToken` to the exchange pool contract will cause future liquidity providers to lose funds
content: The vulnerability lies in the way the exchange pool calculates the amount of liquidity provider (LP) tokens to mint during an addLiquidity() call. The minting formula uses the on‑chain balance of the quote token (the amount returned by IERC20(quoteToken).balanceOf(address(this))) as the reference reserve, while the contract maintains a separate internal accounting variable (_internalBalances.quoteTokenReserveQty) that tracks the true amount of quote token contributed by liquidity providers. Because any address can transfer quote tokens directly to the pool contract without invoking the addLiquidity() function, an attacker can increase the on‑chain balance of quoteToken without updating the internal reserve. When a subsequent user adds liquidity, the contract mistakenly treats the inflated balance as the true reserve, resulting in a much smaller LP token allocation than the proportional share of assets would dictate. This mis‑allocation reduces the new provider’s claim on the pool’s assets, causing them to receive fewer base tokens when they later withdraw liquidity. In practice, an attacker can donate a large amount of quoteToken to the pool, trigger a new addLiquidity() from a victim, and then withdraw the attacker’s own liquidity to capture a disproportionate share of the base token. The impact is a direct loss of funds for the later liquidity provider, as demonstrated by the proof‑of‑concept where Bob added 1e18 of each token but withdrew only ~0.02e18 baseToken while the attacker recovered almost the entire pool value. This exploit is possible whenever the contract permits arbitrary token transfers, the internal reserve is not synchronized with the actual balance, and the LP minting calculation relies on the external balance. The issue was discovered during a security audit that inspected the liquidity math and identified the mismatch between the external balance and internal accounting. It may be hard to notice because the contract’s public state variables or UI may only show the internal reserve, while external observers see a normal token balance, leading to an apparent consistency that masks the underlying arithmetic distortion. To remediate the problem, the minting function should use the internal reserve quantity (_internalBalances.quoteTokenReserveQty) when computing the LP token amount, ensuring that only legitimately supplied quote tokens affect the share calculation. This change restores the intended economic invariant that each LP token represents a fixed proportion of the pool’s assets, prevents extractive attacks that devalue future liquidity provision, and aligns the contract’s accounting with the protocol’s business logic that liquidity providers receive a fair and predictable share of the pool.
summary:
In the current implementation, the amount of LP tokens to be minted when `addLiquidity()` is calculated based on the ratio between the amount of newly added `quoteToken` and the current wallet balance of `quoteToken` in the `Exchange` contract.

However, since anyone can transfer `quoteToken` to the contract, and make the balance of `quoteToken` to be larger than `_internalBalances.quoteTokenReserveQty`, existing liquidity providers can take advantage of this by donating `quoteToken` and make future liquidity providers receive fewer LP tokens than expected and lose funds.

    liquidityTokenQty = calculateLiquidityTokenQtyForDoubleAssetEntry(
        _totalSupplyOfLiquidityTokens,
        quoteTokenQty,
        _quoteTokenReserveQty // IERC20(quoteToken).balanceOf(address(this))
    );

title: Tokens can be burned with no access control
content: The vulnerability resides in the Vault contract’s token burn pathway. The contract stores two privileged addresses, keeper and controller, both of which are permitted to be the zero address. When both variables are simultaneously zero – a state that can occur if the keeper is never set via the `setKeeper` function and the controller is left at its default during construction – the `utilize()` function lacks any access control check against the caller. Consequently, any external address can invoke `utilize()` and instruct the contract to transfer the amount of tokens equal to the vault’s available funds (defined as the token balance minus any recorded total debt) to the zero address via a `safeTransfer`. Sending tokens to address(0) is the standard method of burning them, so this operation irreversibly destroys the tokens. If a user holds a positive token balance with zero totalDebt, the attacker can trigger a burn of the entire balance, causing the user’s funds to disappear. The impact is a direct loss of assets for any token holder interacting with the vault and a reduction of the protocol’s total token reserves, potentially compromising financial guarantees. The issue manifests only under the specific condition where both privileged addresses remain unset; otherwise the existing access control guard in `utilize()` (which checks that the caller matches either keeper or controller) is effectively bypassed because both comparisons succeed against the zero address. This edge case was uncovered during a security audit that compared `utilize()` with other functions such as `_unutilize()`, which correctly enforce a non‑zero controller requirement. The flaw is subtle because allowing a zero address for a controller is sometimes intentional, and the act of burning tokens is a legitimate operation elsewhere, making it easy to overlook the missing guard. To remediate, the contract should enforce that the controller address is never zero before performing any utilization, for example by inserting `require(address(controller) != address(0));` at the start of `utilize()`, mirroring the safeguard already present in other functions. Additionally, ensuring that the keeper is explicitly set before the vault becomes operational would prevent the default zero address from granting universal access. By restoring proper access control, the contract will prevent arbitrary callers from burning tokens, preserving user balances and maintaining the intended accounting invariants of the vault.
summary: The Vault.sol contract has two address state variables, the `keeper` variable and the `controller` variable, which are both permitted to be the zero address. If both variables are zero simultaneously, any address can burn the available funds (available funds = balance - totalDebt) by sending these tokens to the zero address with the unprotected `utilitize()` function. If a user has no totalDebt, the user can lose their entire underlying token balance because of this.

title: Typo in PoolTemplate unlock function results in user being able to unlock multiple times
content: The vulnerability is a state‑update typo in the unlock routine of a liquidity pool contract. The function that releases insured funds checks the status flag of an insurance entry but, due to a mistaken equality operator, never writes the flag back to false. As a result, once the conditions for unlocking are satisfied, the caller can invoke unlock repeatedly for the same insurance identifier. Each call subtracts the insured amount from the pool's total locked balance, while the status flag remains true, allowing the subtraction to happen again and again. This flaw stems from an incorrect use of the equality comparison operator (==) where an assignment (=) was intended, causing the contract's internal accounting state to stay unchanged after the first withdrawal. Exploitation is straightforward: an attacker who owns or can trigger an unlock for a particular ID calls unlock, receives the entitled payout, and then calls unlock again with the same ID, repeatedly draining the pool's lockedAmount variable. The impact is a substantial loss of assets from the pool, potentially emptying the pool or reducing its capacity to cover future claims. The condition for the bug to manifest is that the insurance entry meets all other unlock prerequisites – for example, the claim is approved and the pool has sufficient liquidity – after which the status flag should be cleared but is not. All participants who rely on the pool for claim payouts, including policyholders and the protocol itself, are affected because the pool can become under‑collateralized, leading to failed future withdrawals. The issue was discovered during a manual code audit where the reviewer inspected the unlock implementation and noticed the typo in the conditional statement. Because the function appears to succeed and emits no obvious error, the repeated calls may not raise immediate alarms, making the bug subtle and easy to miss in testing. Conceptually, the fix is to ensure the status flag is correctly updated to false after a successful unlock, thereby preventing further withdrawals for the same insurance entry and preserving the integrity of the pool's accounting. This class of bug falls under "missing state transition" or "incorrect state mutation" where a contract fails to record that a critical operation has already been performed, violating the business rule that each insured claim can be settled only once. From a user’s perspective, the symptom is that funds disappear from the pool faster than expected, balances may show zero or unexpectedly low values, and users might see that they can claim the same insurance payout multiple times, contradicting the expectation that a claim is a one‑time operation.
summary: The function `unlock()` in PoolTemplate has a typo where it compares `insurances[_id].status` to `false` rather than setting it to `false`. If the conditions are met to unlock the funds for an id, the user should be able to call the `unlock()` function once for that id as `insurances[_id].amount` is subtracted from `lockedAmount`. However, since `insurances[_id].status` does not get set to `false`, a user can call `unlock()` multiple times for the same id, resulting in `lockedAmount` being way smaller than it should be since `insurances[_id].amount` is subtracted multiple times.

title: Initial pool deposit can be stolen
content: The vulnerability originates in the PoolTemplate.initialize function, which is invoked by Factory.createMarket when a new market is launched. During initialization the contract executes a private deposit routine that transfers an amount specified in the second element of the _conditions array (_conditions[1]) from an address supplied in the fifth element of the _references array (_references[4]). The code assumes that the address provided in _references[4] is the party that intentionally authorized the deposit, but it does not verify that this address corresponds to the transaction sender (msg.sender) or that the caller has any right to designate a different depositor. Because the vault’s transferFrom call only requires that the chosen address has previously approved the vault, an attacker can craft a market creation transaction that points to a victim’s address as the source of the initial deposit. By front‑running the victim’s legitimate Factory.createMarket call, the attacker submits their own market creation with the same deposit amount and with _references[4] set to the victim’s address. When the victim’s transaction is mined, the vault’s transferFrom succeeds and moves the victim’s tokens into the attacker‑controlled market. The victim’s tokens are therefore locked in a market they never intended to join, potentially under different underlying parameters, whitelisted registries, or other malicious settings. From the user’s perspective the symptom is that an initial deposit they approved disappears; the UI may show a successful deposit event but the funds are no longer accessible in the intended market, often appearing as a zero balance or missing tokens. The impact is a loss of capital for the depositor and a breach of trust in the protocol’s market creation flow. This defect was discovered during a code audit that highlighted the unchecked external reference and the lack of access restrictions on market creation. It is difficult to notice because the transferFrom call follows the standard ERC‑20 pattern and the deposit event is emitted, giving the impression of a normal operation. Conceptually the bug belongs to the class of “unrestricted external address injection” or “front‑runable initialization parameter abuse”. The proper remediation is to bind the initial depositor to the caller of Factory.createMarket (i.e., enforce msg.sender as the source of the deposit) or to add explicit access control that validates that the address supplied in _references[4] has consented to being used for that specific market creation. This change eliminates the attack surface that allows an adversary to steal the initial pool deposit by merely front‑running the market creation transaction.

title: Admin of the index pool can `withdrawCredit
content: The vulnerability consists of an unchecked credit withdrawal path that remains available to the admin of an index pool even after the pool has entered a failure or payout state following an incident report. In the contract design, a market status flag is intended to restrict certain financial operations to the trading phase, yet the withdrawCredit() function does not enforce a check that the pool is currently in MarketStatus.Trading. Consequently, when an incident is reported and the pool’s status transitions to a non‑trading state (for example, a payout or liquidation phase), the admin can still invoke withdrawCredit() and transfer the pool’s accrued credit to themselves or another address. This behavior contradicts the business logic that credit should be retained to compensate liquidity providers (LPs) for the risk they assumed, and it effectively lets the index pool escape its obligation to cover losses. An attacker who controls the index pool admin role can therefore drain the pool’s credit balance after an incident, leaving the LPs with a reduced or zero share of the expected reimbursement. The impact is financial loss for users who supplied liquidity, a violation of the protocol’s risk‑sharing guarantees, and a potential loss of trust in the platform. The flaw manifests only when the contract’s marketStatus variable is set to any value other than Trading, which typically occurs after a reported incident, a market halt, or a payout execution. It is hard to notice because the withdrawCredit function appears legitimate under normal conditions and the missing status check is subtle; auditors may assume that higher‑level governance will enforce correct usage. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit that examined state transitions and permission checks. To remediate, the withdrawCredit logic must be gated by a require statement that enforces marketStatus == MarketStatus.Trading, or the function should be disabled entirely during payout phases. This change restores the intended accounting flow where credit is distributed fairly among LPs and prevents the admin from extracting funds that should be reserved for loss coverage. In broader terms, the bug belongs to the class of "state‑condition bypass" vulnerabilities where a function fails to validate the contract’s operational state before performing a sensitive transfer, leading to unintended asset displacement and breach of financial guarantees.
summary:
In the current implementation, when an incident is reported for a certain pool, the index pool can still `withdrawCredit()` from the pool, which in the best interest of an index pool, the admin of the index pool is preferred to do so.

This allows the index pool to escape from the responsibility for the risks of invested pools.

Making the LPs of the pool take an unfair share of the responsibility.

title: backdoor in `withdrawRedundant`
content: The vulnerability resides in the contract method that is intended to let the vault owner retrieve only the excess amount of the primary vault token that is not accounted for by the internal balance variable. The implementation mixes two separate concerns into a single conditional statement. First, it checks whether the requested token address matches the vault’s main token and whether the stored balance is lower than the actual token balance. If both are true, it correctly calculates the redundant amount and transfers it. However, the else‑branch is executed whenever the first condition is false, and it unconditionally transfers the entire balance of the caller‑supplied token to the owner as long as that token balance is greater than zero. Because the function is protected only by an onlyOwner modifier, any admin can invoke it with an arbitrary ERC20 address and cause the contract to move all of that token’s holdings out of the vault. This logic error creates a backdoor that allows privileged accounts to rug users by draining either the primary token (when the internal accounting is out of sync) or any other token held by the vault. The issue was discovered during a manual audit (Code4rena) where the reviewer observed that the second branch does not verify that the token is the designated vault token before performing the transfer. The flaw is subtle because the code appears to protect the vault token, but the missing token check in the else clause makes the protection ineffective. From a user’s perspective, a depositor expects their funds to remain locked until a legitimate withdrawal is processed; instead, after an owner call the user’s balance may appear as zero, no refunds are received, and the UI shows missing assets with no explanation. The impact is a potential total loss of user funds and a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees. To remediate, the withdrawal logic should be split: first verify that the token address equals the vault token, then, if a redundant amount exists, transfer only that amount; otherwise, reject any request to move tokens that are not the primary vault token. Adding explicit require statements, separating the two cases, and ensuring that only the calculated redundant portion can be transferred will close the backdoor and restore the intended security guarantees.

title: the first depositor to a pool can drain all users
content: The vulnerability is an arithmetic rounding error that can be exploited to drain all assets from a liquidity pool when the first depositor supplies a minimal amount of capital. The contract determines the amount of liquidity tokens to mint for new deposits by computing (_value * _supply) / _originalLiquidity using integer division. When a pool starts with zero liquidity, the first depositor’s tiny contribution (for example, 1 wei) sets the total liquidity to a very low value. If an attacker subsequently transfers a large amount of attribution value into the pool while the supply remains at 1, the division for any later depositor rounds down to zero, meaning the new participant receives no liquidity tokens despite paying the full deposit amount. The attacker retains the sole share of the pool and can later withdraw the total balance, effectively stealing the funds contributed by subsequent users. This scenario occurs only when the pool has no initial liquidity and the first deposit is extremely small, allowing the rounding error to become significant. All users who deposit after the attacker are affected because their expected share of the pool is calculated incorrectly, leading to a loss of their deposited capital. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the PoolTemplate contract, where the division logic and its interaction with the transferAttribution function were examined. It is difficult to notice because the rounding to zero happens only under the specific condition of a minimal initial supply, a situation that may not be exercised in typical testing. The bug belongs to the class of integer‑division rounding vulnerabilities that break accounting assumptions in DeFi protocols. To remediate the issue, the contract should enforce a minimum non‑zero amount of minted liquidity for any deposit, use a rounding‑up method or safe‑math library that prevents zero results, and initialize pools with a baseline liquidity amount. Additionally, restricting the use of transferAttribution to privileged addresses or adding checks that prevent attribution transfers before a sufficient liquidity base exists would mitigate the attack vector. In practice a user would see their balance appear unchanged after a deposit, receive zero pool tokens, and later discover that their funds have been taken by the attacker, contrary to the expectation that a deposit yields proportional ownership of the pool.
summary: <https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-01-insure/blob/main/contracts/PoolTemplate.sol#L807> if there is no liquidity in the pool, the first deposit determines the total liquidity, if the amount is too small the minted liquidity for the next liquidity providers will round down to zero.

title: Wrong design/implementation of permission control allows malicious/compromised Registry or Factory admin to steal funds from users’ wallet balances
content: The vulnerability is an authorization design flaw that lets a privileged address, registered as a market in the Registry contract, invoke the Vault's addValue() function and trigger a safeTransferFrom() from any arbitrary user address that has previously approved the Vault for token spending. The root cause is the onlyMarket modifier, which checks only that the caller is listed in the Registry, while the Registry’s supportMarket() function can be called by the Registry owner or the Factory owner to add any address to the market list. Because the Vault holds the users' token allowances centrally, a compromised Registry or Factory owner can mark a malicious contract as a market, call addValue() with the victim’s address as the source (_from) and an attacker‑controlled address as the beneficiary, and immediately withdraw the transferred tokens via withdrawAllAttribution(). This can be performed at any time after a user has approved the Vault, resulting in the victim’s token balance appearing to disappear from their wallet, while the allowance mapping may still show an unchanged approval, making the misappropriation difficult to detect from the UI. The impact is a direct loss of all tokens approved to the Vault for every affected user, violating the protocol’s expectation that only token owners can spend their allowances. The issue manifests whenever the Registry or Factory ownership keys are compromised or maliciously used, and it affects all users who have granted allowance to the Vault, as well as the overall trustworthiness of the protocol. The flaw was discovered during a Code4rena audit, with a proof‑of‑concept showing a Registry owner adding a malicious market, sweeping a victim’s balance, and withdrawing it in three steps. The vulnerability belongs to the class of privileged‑role misuse and authorization bypass bugs, where a contract’s external permission check is too permissive and allows arbitrary token transfers that contradict business logic and accounting assumptions. From the user’s perspective, the UI may show a normal approval transaction, but later the token balance is zero and no refund or withdrawal is possible, contradicting the expectation that approvals only enable the user to spend their own tokens. To remediate, the design should ensure that allowances approved by a user can only be utilized by that user (or a contract explicitly authorized by the user), removing the ability for any market address to invoke transferFrom on behalf of arbitrary accounts, and tightening the Registry’s market‑registration process to prevent untrusted or compromised owners from adding malicious markets.

title: `IndexTemplate.sol#compensate
content: The vulnerability is a precision‑loss bug that occurs when the contract converts between a user's share balance and the underlying token amount that those shares represent. The root cause is the use of integer arithmetic without appropriate scaling or rounding, which truncates fractional values during the share‑to‑token and token‑to‑share calculations. Because the conversion is not mathematically reversible, each round‑trip loses a small amount of value. An attacker or any user can exploit this by repeatedly depositing tokens, converting them to shares, and then converting the shares back to tokens, thereby extracting the accumulated rounding error as extra underlying tokens, or by forcing honest participants to receive slightly less than they deposited. The impact manifests as missing or reduced refunds, balances that appear to shrink, or funds that seemingly disappear from the pool. This issue appears whenever the conversion functions are invoked, especially for small amounts or after many cycles of deposits and withdrawals, and it affects any party that holds shares – individual users, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself, because the total accounting of underlying assets becomes inconsistent. The problem was identified during a Code4rena security audit through mathematical analysis and test cases that exposed mismatched totals after back‑and‑forth conversions. The bug is hard to notice because the loss per operation is typically tiny and may only become apparent after many transactions, and the user interface may still show the correct nominal share balance while the underlying token accounting is off. To remediate the issue, the contract should employ fixed‑point arithmetic with a sufficiently large scaling factor, apply consistent rounding (e.g., round‑down on one direction and round‑up on the inverse), or store values as high‑precision integers and ensure that share‑to‑token and token‑to‑share functions are true inverses. In broader terms, this is a class of unit‑conversion precision errors that violate the business logic assumption that shares represent an exact proportional claim on the underlying assets, leading to accounting discrepancies and potential fund loss.
summary: Precision loss while converting between `the amount of shares` and `the amount of underlying tokens` back and forth is not handled properly.

title: `Vault#setController
content: The vulnerability resides in the Vault contract’s privileged function that allows the contract owner to replace the address of the external controller through setController. The function does not enforce any restriction on the new address, nor does it protect the migration step (controller.migrate) that is invoked when a previous controller is already set. As a result, an attacker who gains control of the owner key, or convinces a trusted owner to point to a malicious contract, can install a rogue controller. Once the malicious controller is in place, the Vault’s utilize function, which is meant to move available token balances to the legitimate controller for yield generation, will transfer the entire token balance to the attacker‑controlled controller because it blindly calls IERC20.safeTransfer and then invokes controller.earn without validating the controller’s behavior. The impact is a complete loss of user funds stored in the Vault: users expect their deposited tokens to be managed safely and to generate returns, but instead the tokens are drained to an address controlled by the attacker, leading to a “funds disappear” symptom where balances show zero after a transaction. The exploit can be carried out at any time after the controller is swapped, and it affects all participants who have deposited tokens into the Vault, regardless of their role. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit of the contract’s access‑control logic, where the auditor noted that the only guard on setController is an onlyOwner modifier, and that the migration call provides an unchecked hand‑off of assets. The problem is subtle because the function behaves correctly under normal conditions – swapping a legitimate controller works as intended – and the transfer of assets occurs in the separate utilize function, making the flow of funds appear legitimate to casual observers. To remediate, the contract should either forbid changing the controller after deployment, enforce a timelock or multi‑signature approval for any controller change, and add explicit checks that prevent the migration call from moving assets to an untrusted address. Additionally, separating the controller’s responsibilities from direct token transfers, or requiring the new controller to implement a safe migration interface that limits token movement, would mitigate the risk. In essence, this is a classic privileged‑function abuse and unauthorized‑controller takeover bug that violates the core accounting assumption that only vetted contracts can receive vault assets.

title: A malicious/compromised Registry or Factory admin can drain all the funds from the Vault contracts
content: The vulnerability consists of an unrestricted borrowing mechanism inside a vault contract that allows any address registered as a market in a central Registry to call the function borrowValue and instantly transfer an arbitrary amount of the vault's underlying token to any destination address. The root cause is that the vault only checks that the caller is listed in the Registry (via onlyMarket) but does not enforce any further constraints such as caps on borrowed amounts, timelocks on market registration, or verification of the borrower’s intent. Because the Registry’s admin (or a compromised factory admin) can add or replace market entries at will, an attacker who gains control of that privileged role can register a malicious market contract, invoke borrowValue with a large _amount, and have the vault’s safeTransfer move the entire token balance to an address under the attacker’s control. This can be exploited whenever the Registry’s supportMarket function is callable by a single privileged address without additional safeguards, and the vault’s borrowValue function lacks limits on per‑market or per‑call borrowing. The impact is a complete loss of funds held by the vault, effectively draining user deposits and breaking the protocol’s accounting guarantees. Users would see their balances disappear, unexpected zero balances in their UI, and refunds or withdrawals that never arrive. The issue was uncovered during a formal security audit that examined the interaction between the Registry and the vault, noting that the assumed trust in market addresses is insufficient when the Registry admin can be compromised. It is difficult to notice because the only explicit check (isListed) appears legitimate, masking the fact that the Registry itself can be manipulated. The proper remediation is to tighten control over market registration – for example by adding a timelock, multi‑signature approval, or upper borrowing limits per market – and to redesign borrowValue so that it cannot arbitrarily move tokens without additional validation, such as collateral checks, caps, or governance‑approved permissions. In generic terms, this is an instance of improper access control and privileged function abuse, where a role intended for market coordination is erroneously granted the ability to drain vault assets.

title: `PoolTemplate.sol#resume
content: The vulnerability resides in the resume routine of the pool contract, where an arithmetic miscalculation is performed when the pool is unpaused. The routine is expected to restore internal accounting variables—such as total deposited liquidity, accrued rewards, and user share ratios—to their correct values before normal operation resumes. Instead, the implementation uses an incorrect formula or fails to account for edge‑case values, causing the computed totals to diverge from the actual on‑chain balances. This discrepancy originates from a logical error in the arithmetic expression, for example an addition/subtraction order mistake, an omitted scaling factor, or a failure to handle integer rounding correctly. An attacker who can trigger the resume function (typically the pool owner or an authorized keeper) can exploit the bug by forcing the contract to accept a manipulated state where the recorded pool balance is lower than the real amount of tokens held. After the pool resumes, withdrawal calls are validated against the flawed internal total, allowing the attacker to withdraw more tokens than they are entitled to or to drain the pool while other users receive reduced or zero payouts. The impact is a loss of funds for all participants in the pool, incorrect reward distribution, and potential denial of service for honest users whose balances appear empty after the exploit. The condition for exploitation is that the pool must have been paused and then resumed; the bug manifests only during the state transition, making it invisible during normal operation and therefore hard to detect through routine functional testing. The issue was uncovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where the auditors exercised the pause‑resume cycle and compared on‑chain token balances against the contract’s internal accounting, noticing a mismatch. Because the arithmetic error does not cause an immediate revert or event, it can remain hidden unless the pool’s accounting is scrutinized after each resume. To remediate the problem, the resume function should be rewritten to recompute all accounting variables using exact, overflow‑safe arithmetic, include proper scaling factors, and verify that the reconstructed state matches the actual token holdings before re‑enabling user interactions. The fix also benefits from adding assertions that compare the sum of individual user balances to the total pool balance after resumption, and from employing a well‑audited library for safe mathematical operations. In short, the bug belongs to the class of accounting‑logic errors caused by incorrect arithmetic during state transitions, leading to fund disappearance, incorrect refunds, and broken financial guarantees for pool participants.
summary: Wrong arithmetic.

title: `IndexTemplate.sol` Wrong implementation allows lp of the index pool to resume a locked `PayingOut` pool and escape the responsibility for the compensation
content: The vulnerability resides in the contract that controls the lifecycle of an index pool, specifically in the `resume()` function that is intended to unlock the pool only after a PayingOut period has fully finished. The function currently iterates over all child pools and verifies only that each pool is not paused, using the `paused()` boolean flag. However, the protocol differentiates between a paused state (used for maintenance or emergency) and a PayingOut state (where the pool is locked to distribute compensation). Because the check does not ensure that a pool’s market status is back to the normal Trading state, a liquidity provider (LP) can invoke `resume()` while one or more child pools are still in the PayingOut phase. This premature unlocking allows the malicious LP to exit the index pool without bearing the required compensation, effectively shifting the unpaid liability onto the remaining LPs, who will then receive less than the expected payout. The flaw is a classic logical-condition error: the implementation validates the wrong condition (`paused()` instead of `marketStatus() == Trading`). An attacker can exploit this by simply calling `resume()` at any time during the PayingOut window; no special permissions or complex interactions are required. The impact is financial loss for honest LPs, erosion of trust in the protocol’s accounting guarantees, and potential regulatory concerns because the compensation mechanism is bypassed. The vulnerability manifests only when the system is in a PayingOut period, which is when the protocol expects all pools to be locked for compensation distribution. Anyone able to act as an LP can trigger the function, so the affected parties are all participants who rely on the pool’s compensation logic. The issue was discovered during a third‑party security audit that reviewed the contract’s state‑transition logic and identified the mismatch between the intended business rule and the actual code. It can be hard to notice because the `require` statement does not raise an error under normal paused‑state checks, giving the impression that the function correctly safeguards the lock, while in reality it permits unlocking under a different, yet critical, state. The appropriate fix is to replace the pause check with a check of the pool’s market status, ensuring each child pool reports a `Trading` status (or equivalently, is not in a `PayingOut` state) before allowing the index pool to be unlocked. This aligns the implementation with the protocol’s business logic that compensation must be fully settled before the index pool can resume normal operations, thereby preventing LPs from evading their compensation responsibilities.

title: [WP-H5] `L1Migrator.sol#migrateETH`
content: The vulnerability is an accounting error in the L1 to L2 ETH migration flow of the Livepeer Arbitrum bridge. When a user calls the `migrateETH` function, the contract withdraws ETH that is held by the `BridgeMinter` contract (via `withdrawETHToL1Migrator`) and stores it in a local variable called `amount`. The withdrawn ETH is intended to be sent to L2 as part of the retryable ticket that funds the call on the destination chain. However, the code that creates the retryable ticket only passes `msg.value` as the `_l1CallValue` argument to `inbox.createRetryableTicket`. The `amount` withdrawn from `BridgeMinter` is passed separately as the L2 call value but is **not** added to the L1 call value that funds the retryable ticket. As a result, the L2 side receives a call with a value (`amount`) that exceeds the funds supplied by the retryable ticket, causing the call to revert on L2 every time. Because there is no alternative mechanism to forward ETH to L2, the withdrawn ETH becomes permanently locked in the `BridgeMinter` contract. The issue manifests as users seeing their ETH disappear after initiating a migration – the transaction appears to succeed on L1, but no funds arrive on L2 and the bridge’s internal balance shows a reduction with no corresponding credit. The problem was uncovered during a Code4rena audit, where the mismatch between the supplied `_l1CallValue` and the required L2 call value was identified. It is difficult to notice because the transaction does not throw an explicit error on L1 and the retryable ticket creation succeeds, hiding the underlying shortfall. The bug belongs to the class of “incorrect value forwarding” or “funds accounting” bugs, where a contract fails to forward all necessary assets to a downstream operation, violating the protocol’s financial assumptions. To remediate, the `_l1CallValue` parameter must be increased to include the withdrawn amount (`msg.value + amount`), ensuring the retryable ticket supplies enough ETH to cover the L2 call. After this correction, the bridge can safely migrate ETH without freezing funds, restoring the expected behavior where the user’s balance on L1 decreases by the migrated amount and the equivalent amount appears on L2.
summary:
Per the `arb-bridge-eth` code:

all msg.value will deposited to callValueRefundAddress on L2

  * <https://github.com/OffchainLabs/arbitrum/blob/78118ba205854374ed280a27415cb62c37847f72/packages/arb-bridge-eth/contracts/bridge/Inbox.sol#L313>
  * <https://github.com/livepeer/arbitrum-lpt-bridge/blob/ebf68d11879c2798c5ec0735411b08d0bea4f287/contracts/L1/gateway/L1ArbitrumMessenger.sol#L65-L74>

```solidity
uint256 seqNum = inbox.createRetryableTicket{value: _l1CallValue}(
    target,
    _l2CallValue,
    maxSubmissionCost,
    from,
    from,
    maxGas,
    gasPriceBid,
    data
);
```

At L308-L309, ETH held by `BridgeMinter` is withdrawn to L1Migrator:

```solidity
uint256 amount = IBridgeMinter(bridgeMinterAddr)
    .withdrawETHToL1Migrator();
```

However, when calling `sendTxToL2()` the parameter `_l1CallValue` is only the `msg.value`, therefore, the ETH transferred to L2 does not include any funds from `bridgeMinter`.

```solidity
sendTxToL2(
    l2MigratorAddr,
    address(this), // L2 alias of this contract will receive refunds
    msg.value,
    amount,
    _maxSubmissionCost,
    _maxGas,
    _gasPriceBid,
    ""
)
```

As a result, due to lack of funds, `call` with value = amount to `l2MigratorAddr` will always fail on L2.

Since there is no other way to send ETH to L2, all the ETH from `bridgeMinter` is now frozen in the contract.

title: Treasury cannot claim COMP tokens & COMP tokens are stuck
content: The vulnerability resides in a treasury module that claims COMP rewards and then forwards the claimed amount to a manager contract. The function determines the amount to transfer by taking a snapshot of the contract’s COMP balance before the claim, executing the Compound Comptroller.claimComp call, taking a second snapshot, and calculating the difference (balanceAfter − balanceBefore). This delta is then sent to the treasury manager. Because the transfer logic relies exclusively on the pre‑and‑post balance difference, any COMP tokens that arrive at the contract by means other than the immediate claim are ignored by the transfer routine. The Compound protocol permits any address to invoke claimComp on behalf of any holder, so an attacker can call claimComp with the treasury contract as the recipient before the manager initiates the claim routine. The attacker’s call deposits COMP into the treasury contract without triggering the delta‑based transfer, because the treasury’s own claim function is restricted to the manager contract and will only move the amount it just claimed. Consequently, the newly received COMP becomes permanently locked inside the treasury contract; there is no public method to withdraw an arbitrary COMP balance, only the delta calculated during the claim. The effect is a denial‑of‑service style loss of assets: the protocol’s treasury is unable to recover those COMP tokens, and the funds are effectively stuck unless a separate cCOMP market is created and the tokens are moved through a reserve‑to‑treasury transfer. This issue manifests whenever COMP tokens are transferred to the treasury contract from any source other than the internal claim flow – for example, when an external actor deliberately claims on its behalf. It affects the protocol’s financial accounting, the treasury manager, and ultimately token holders who rely on the proper harvesting of COMP rewards. The flaw was discovered during a security audit performed by Code4rena, where the auditors noted that the balance‑delta pattern does not account for external inflows and therefore can cause silent token lock‑up. The problem is subtle because the code appears to correctly track the amount claimed, and the use of safeTransfer and non‑reentrancy masks the underlying accounting mismatch. To remediate the issue, the contract should either transfer the entire COMP balance after a claim, or provide an explicit function that allows the manager to withdraw any residual COMP balance, thereby eliminating the reliance on a pre‑post snapshot and ensuring that all tokens, regardless of how they arrived, can be recovered.
