title: Any referrer can overwrite other
content: Any referrer can overwrite other traders' referral codes because the function setTraderReferralCodeByOwner only checks that the caller owns the code being set and does not verify that the trader has consented or that the caller is authorized to assign a code to that trader. As a result an attacker who registers a referral code can call this function with any trader address and replace the trader's existing code with the attacker’s code. When a trade is executed the protocol calculates a fee discount based on the stored referral code and sends the fee rebate to the address associated with that code. After the overwrite the trader receives the discount associated with the attacker’s tier (often a lower tier such as 5 %) and the rebate is credited to the attacker instead of the legitimate referrer. The vulnerability is triggered whenever the contract is not paused; there are no internal or external pre‑conditions limiting who may invoke the function. Affected parties include the trader, who experiences a reduced discount and may notice missing rebates, the original referrer, who loses the expected rebate, and the protocol, which may see reduced revenue or distorted accounting. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the referral module where the access‑control logic of setTraderReferralCodeByOwner was examined and found to lack proper authorization checks. The bug is subtle because the function name and the require statement suggest that only the code owner can act, yet the code does not restrict the target trader, so the overwrite can happen silently without any event emission. From a user perspective the UI may still display the original referral code while the on‑chain discount calculation uses the attacker’s code, leading to symptoms such as my fee discount is lower than expected or my rebate never arrives. The flaw belongs to the class of unauthorized state‑mutation vulnerabilities where an entity can modify another user’s configuration without consent. To remediate, the contract should either remove setTraderReferralCodeByOwner, restrict it to be callable only by the trader themselves, require explicit acceptance of a referral invitation, or allow a change only when the trader has not previously set a code. Adding proper access control and emitting an event on code changes would also improve detectability and prevent the diversion of fee rebates.

title: multiple times
content: The vulnerability originates in the trade unregistration logic of the leveraged trading contract. When a trader partially closes a position, the function receives the amount of collateral that is being withdrawn (_collateral) and releases the corresponding open‑interest by calling releaseBalance with _collateral multiplied by the trade leverage. However, the code contains a special branch that treats a partial close as a full close when the remaining collateral after the partial withdrawal is smaller than the total fees. In that branch the trade is marked as fully closed, the internal state is updated, and _collateral is overwritten with the trade's original initialPosToken. The releaseBalance call, however, is performed before this overwrite, using only the smaller partial amount. Consequently the protocol releases only the open‑interest associated with the withdrawn portion and leaves the remainder of the original reserved balance locked in the vault. The root cause is the mismatch between the condition that converts a partial close into a full close and the amount passed to the balance‑release routine. An attacker can exploit this by opening a high‑leverage position, then partially closing it with a withdrawal that leaves a dust amount of collateral smaller than the accrued fees. The contract will treat the trade as fully closed, but will only rebalance the partial amount, leaving a sizable chunk of the reserved open‑interest unreleased. Over time, especially with large positions and high leverage, the unreleased amount accumulates, reducing the protocol’s utilisation ratio and preventing liquidity providers from withdrawing their funds because the locked capital is no longer available for new trades. From a user’s perspective the UI may show the trade as closed and the expected refund received, yet the underlying vault still holds the missing funds, leading to confusion when balances appear lower than anticipated. Liquidity providers may notice that their withdrawable amount shrinks despite no change in their deposits. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the trade lifecycle functions, where the accounting of released balances did not match the expected values for edge‑case partial closes. It is hard to notice because the contract correctly updates trade state and emits events, masking the hidden accounting discrepancy. The proper fix is to ensure that when the partial‑to‑full conversion branch is taken, the releaseBalance call uses the full initialPosToken amount, or to invoke releaseBalance after the _collateral variable has been set to the original position size. In conceptual terms, the bug belongs to the class of “incorrect accounting on conditional trade closure” where the released collateral does not reflect the actual reserved open‑interest, violating the protocol’s financial invariants and leading to locked funds.
summary:
In the _unregisterTrade function, after a trade is partially or fully closed, the open interest reserved for the trade is released: storageT.vaultManager().releaseBalance(_collateral.mul(_trade.leverage)); For a partial trade, _collateral represents the amount of collateral the trader wants to close, while for a full trade close, it equals the initialPosToken of the trade. However, in some cases, when a trader partially closes a trade, any remaining dust collateral is also considered closed. This approach is intended to manage insignificant positions.  
if (_trade.initialPosToken == _collateral || (_collateral + totalFees >= _trade.initialPosToken)){  
storageT.unregisterTrade(_trade.trader, _trade.pairIndex, _trade.index);  
pairInfos.resetTradeInitialAccess(_trade.trader, _trade.pairIndex, _trade.index);  
_collateral = _trade.initialPosToken;  
}  
else {  
storageT.registerPartialTrade(_trade.trader, _trade.pairIndex, _trade.index, _collateral);  
}  
The problem arises because in such cases, the rebalance should consider the complete initialPosToken, not just the provided _collateral for the partial trade. As a result, the open interest corresponding to the remaining part is not released, even though the trade is effectively closed.  
This unreleased open interest accumulates and becomes unrecoverable, compounding the issue due to two factors:  
1. High leverage trades amplify the open interest value that remains stuck.  
2. For large trades where total fees on partial closes are high, the seized collateral is also high. This leads to a significantly higher open interest value being stuck. Due to this LPs would not be able to withdraw funds in some cases as utilisation ratio would go down gradually  
• In TradingCallbacks.sol:554 the releaseBalance function uses incorrect collateral amount when a partial trade is made but full trade is closed  
Internal pre-conditions  
External pre-conditions  
Attack Path  
1. A trader opens a long position in a BTC pair with the following parameters:  
• Collateral: 5000 USDC  
• Leverage: 100x  
• Opening price: 50,000 USDC  
2. Reserved amount = 5000 * 100 = 500,000 USDC  
3. The BTC price then rises to 55,000, allowing the trader to achieve a maximum profit of 500%.  
4. The trader decides to partially close the trade, withdrawing 4600 USDC.  
• Total fees for the partial trade amount to approximately 420 USDC.  
• Rebalance amount = 4600 * 100 = 460,000 USDC  
5. After the partial trade of 4600 USDC, the remaining 400 USDC collateral is less than the total fees of 420 USDC. Therefore, the remaining collateral will also be closed, and the trade will be registered as a full close.  
6. In this scenario, the rebalance should release the full 500,000 USDC, but it only rebalances 460,000 USDC.  
7. As a result, the stuck reserved open interest is:  
stuck reserved open interest = 500,000 - 460,000 = 40,000 USDC  
This causes significant amount of open interest to become unreservable, making it unavailable for other trades. LPs would not be able to withdraw funds as utilisation ratio would go down

title: FluidLocker::_getUnlockingPe
content: The vulnerability resides in the FluidLocker contract’s internal function that computes the unlocking percentage for a user’s locked Fluid tokens. The function uses a hard‑coded constant of 540 in the denominator of a square‑root expression, but the intended value is 540 days – a time‑based unit that is much larger. Because the code treats 540 as a plain integer, the denominator becomes far smaller than it should be, causing the calculated unlocking percentage (expressed in basis points) to exceed the maximum of 10,000 BP (100 %). When the percentage is larger than 10,000 BP, the subsequent arithmetic that derives the unlock flow rate multiplies the global flow rate by an out‑of‑range factor and then divides by the BP denominator. This overflow produces a value that is greater than the global flow rate, which triggers a revert when the contract attempts to compute the tax flow rate as the difference between the global flow rate and the oversized unlock flow rate. As a result, any user who tries to unlock their Fluid after the vesting period encounters a transaction failure, leaving their funds locked inside the contract. The only way to retrieve the assets is to perform an immediate unlock that incurs an 80 % penalty, effectively forcing users to surrender most of their balance or accept that their funds remain inaccessible. The bug occurs whenever the unlocking routine is invoked, regardless of the specific unlock period, because the mis‑scaled constant is used unconditionally. All participants who lock Fluid in the locker – individual users, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected, as the contract’s core accounting logic is broken. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the mathematical formulas used for vesting and identified a unit mismatch between a raw numeric constant and a time‑based value. The problem is subtle because the formula appears mathematically sound at a glance; the error only manifests when the computed percentage exceeds the logical maximum, which may not be obvious without testing extreme values. To remediate the flaw, the constant should be expressed in the correct time unit (e.g., 540 * 1 days) or the formula should be refactored to use a properly scaled maximum unlock period, ensuring that the unlocking percentage never exceeds 10,000 BP. This correction restores the intended linear unlocking curve, prevents underflow/overflow reverts, and allows users to retrieve their funds without an excessive penalty, aligning the contract’s behavior with its documented business logic of gradual vesting and fair unlocking.
summary:
FluidLocker::_getUnlockingPercentage() calculates the amount to unlock when unvesting via the FluidLocker. It incorrectly uses 540 instead of 540days, yielding a massive error such that the unlocking percentage will be much bigger than 10_000 and underflow.  
```solidity
function _getUnlockingPercentage(uint128 unlockPeriod) internal pure returns (uint256 unlockingPercentageBP) {
    unlockingPercentageBP = (
        _PERCENT_TO_BP
        * (
            ((80 * _SCALER) / Math.sqrt(540 * _SCALER)) *
            (Math.sqrt(unlockPeriod * _SCALER) / _SCALER)
            + 20 * _SCALER
        )
    ) / _SCALER;
}
```
In FluidLocker:388 it uses 540 instead of 540days.  
Internal pre-conditions  
None.  
External pre-conditions  
None.  
Attack Path  
1. User unlocks their Fluid from the FluidLocker, but it reverts because of the mentioned underflow. The funds within the locker will be stuck unless the user instantly unlocks and takes a 80% penalty.  
User is forced to take a 80% penalty or have the funds stuck.

title: Fontaine never stops the flows
content: The vulnerability resides in the Fontaine contract’s initialization routine, which creates Superfluid streams but never includes logic to stop those streams when the unlocking operation is completed. Superfluid streams automatically reserve a four‑hour buffer of the flow rate as a liquidation safeguard; when a stream is closed the reserved buffer is returned to the contract’s balance and can be redistributed to the intended recipients. Because Fontaine::initialize does not call the Superfluid host to delete or stop the flow, the reserved buffer remains locked inside the contract forever. An attacker (or any user) can trigger the condition by calling FluidLocker::unlock with a non‑zero unlocking period; the contract creates the unlocking flow to the recipient and a tax flow to the tax pool, but never stops them, so the buffered amount is never reclaimed. As a result the recipient and the tax distribution pool receive less than the expected amount – the user sees a shortfall in the transferred balance (for example, sending 10 000 e18 results in only 9 996.8 e18 being available). The loss is effectively funds disappear from the perspective of the user, violating the accounting assumption that the full deposited amount will be returned after unlocking. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the tester added console logs and observed that the contract balance after flow creation was lower than the initial deposit, and that the missing amount corresponded to the reserved buffer. The bug is subtle because the Superfluid framework handles the buffer internally and does not emit an explicit error; therefore developers may assume the buffer is automatically refunded when the flow ends. The proper fix is to add explicit termination of the created streams (e.g., calling deleteFlow or stopFlow) after the unlocking period expires, and to ensure the reserved buffer is transferred back to the contract before distributing funds. This class of bug can be described as a stream termination omission or resource‑leak in continuous payment protocols, where the protocol’s internal safety buffer is not reclaimed, leading to unintended fund loss.
summary:
Superfluid flows reserve 4 hours of the stream flow rate as a buffer for liquidations, and returns this when the flow is closed.  
However, Fontaine::initialize() never actually stops the flows, which means the deposit buffer will never be reclaimed, taking the recipient and the tax pool the loss.  
In Fontaine::initialize(), the flows are never stopped, which means the buffer will not be returned.  
Internal pre-conditions  
None.  
External pre-conditions  
None.  
Attack Path  
1. User unlocks their Fluid from the Locker by calling FluidLocker::unlock() with a non null unlocking period.  
The recipient and the tax distribution pool take the loss as they do not receive all their funds (the deposit buffer is never sent to them).

title: Anyone can call VVVVCTokenDist
content: The vulnerability is an authorization flaw in the token distribution contract where the claim function validates a signed ClaimParams structure but does not verify that the caller (msg.sender) matches the KYC address that is authorized to receive the reward. The root cause is the missing check that binds the signed parameters to the intended recipient, allowing any external account to submit a valid claim with the same signed data. An attacker can observe a legitimate user’s signed claim parameters, submit a transaction that calls claim before the user does (front‑running), and because the contract transfers the tokens to msg.sender, the attacker receives the full reward. After the transfer, the contract updates the nonce for the KYC address, which prevents the original user from submitting a second claim with the same nonce, effectively locking out the rightful recipient. This issue manifests whenever a user attempts to claim rewards using a signed message; the contract will accept the signature, update the nonce, and send the tokens to whoever called the function. The affected parties are the legitimate token recipients, the protocol’s users, and any downstream applications that rely on correct reward distribution. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that compared the signature verification logic with the token transfer destination and noticed the absence of a sender‑to‑recipient check. Because the contract appears to work correctly from a signature perspective, the problem can be subtle and may not be evident until a user reports missing funds. The impact is a loss of tokens for honest users and a potential drain of the distribution pool if attackers repeatedly front‑run claims. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of improper authentication or missing access control, where a function trusts data without confirming the caller’s identity. To remediate, the contract should transfer the tokens to the KYC address specified in the signed parameters rather than to msg.sender, or it should explicitly require that msg.sender equals the KYC address before proceeding. This change restores the intended business logic that rewards are delivered to the verified recipient and prevents unauthorized parties from hijacking the claim process.

title: Detaching HSG when there's non-unregistered owners who no longer own the hat would give them control over the multi-sig The protocol has acknowledged this issue. Found by bughuntoor
content: The vulnerability resides in the detachHSG function of the HatsSignerGate contract. When the contract is instructed to detach the Hats Signer Gate (HSG) from a Gnosis Safe, it removes the HSG as a guard and as a module but fails to verify that every current Safe owner still possesses the required hat that authorises them as a signer. Consequently, owners who have lost or transferred their hat remain recorded as owners inside the Safe, retaining full execution rights even though they are no longer recognised as valid signers by the protocol logic. The root cause is the absence of a validation step that checks hat ownership for each Safe owner during detachment, combined with the Safe’s owner list being updated only when removeSigner is explicitly called. An attacker who controls a hat that has administrative rights over another signer hat can exploit this by front‑running the detach transaction: they first transfer the lower‑level hat to a series of fresh addresses, claim each new address as a signer, and then allow the DAO’s detachHSG call to proceed. Because detachHSG does not prune these newly added owners, all of the attacker‑controlled addresses become permanent owners of the Safe after the gate is detached. This situation can give the attacker full custody of the Safe, enable them to overturn any pending multi‑sig proposals, or simply block the DAO from reaching quorum, effectively freezing or draining the funds held by the Safe. The issue manifests only after the detach operation; prior to detachment the Safe behaves as expected, making the problem hard to notice in routine testing or UI inspection, as the owners list still shows the attacker‑controlled addresses but the protocol no longer enforces hat‑based signing. The bug was discovered during a security audit (acknowledged by the protocol and reported by bughuntoor) and is classified as a privilege‑escalation and access‑control flaw. To remediate, the detachHSG routine should iterate over all current Safe owners and unregister any address that does not currently hold the required hat before completing the detachment, or alternatively prevent detachment while any owner lacks the appropriate hat. This ensures that only legitimate hat‑bearing signers retain ownership rights, preserving the intended multi‑sig security model and preventing unauthorized takeover of funds.

title: FluidLocker::_getUnlockingPe rcentage() incorrectly divides one of the components of the formula by S, leading to always having 80% penalty /issues/20 Found by 056Security, 0x73696d616f, Drynooo, IvanFitro, Kyosi, Z3R0, ke1caM, newspacexyz, redbeans, zhenyazhd
content: The vulnerability resides in the FluidLocker contract’s internal function that computes the unlocking percentage for a user’s locked assets. The function is intended to calculate a proportion of the locked amount that should be released to the user based on the chosen unlock period, while the remainder is redistributed to other stakers. However, the implementation mistakenly divides the term Math.sqrt(unlockPeriod*_SCALER) by the scaling constant _SCALER. Because _SCALER is a large fixed‑point factor (typically 1e18), this extra division reduces the term to a value that is effectively zero for any realistic unlockPeriod. Consequently the formula collapses to a constant 20 % unlocking percentage, imposing an 80 % penalty regardless of how long the user locks their fluid. The root cause is an arithmetic scaling error: an unnecessary division by the same scaling factor that was used to bring the square‑root term into fixed‑point representation. An attacker does not need to perform any special actions; any user who invokes the unlock routine with a positive duration will automatically receive only a fifth of the expected amount, with the remaining balance disappearing from their perspective. The impact is severe: users experience a substantial loss of funds, seeing their balances drop dramatically after an unlock transaction, contrary to the expectation that longer lock periods yield higher returns. This condition triggers every time the unlock function is called, with no external pre‑conditions required, affecting all participants of the FluidLocker system. The issue was uncovered during a comprehensive security audit by multiple independent researchers, who noted that the mathematical expression produced a near‑zero component and that the resulting unlocking percentage was constant. The bug is subtle because the surrounding arithmetic appears plausible and the scaling factor is commonly used throughout the codebase, making the mistake easy to overlook without detailed unit analysis. To remediate the problem, the extra division by _SCALER must be removed so that the square‑root term contributes correctly to the unlocking percentage calculation. This correction restores the intended variable unlocking rate, aligns the contract’s behavior with its economic design, and prevents the unintended 80 % penalty that currently causes funds to disappear from users’ accounts.
summary:
FluidLocker::_getUnlockingPercentage() calculates the percentage to unlock, which is the amount given to the user, while the remaining goes to other stakers. The formula incorrectly divides Math.sqrt(unlockPeriod*_SCALER) by SCALER:  
```solidity
function _getUnlockingPercentage(uint128 unlockPeriod) internal pure returns (uint256 unlockingPercentageBP) {
    unlockingPercentageBP = (
        _PERCENT_TO_BP
        * (
            ((80 * _SCALER) / Math.sqrt(540 * _SCALER)) *
            (Math.sqrt(unlockPeriod * _SCALER) / _SCALER)
            + 20 * _SCALER
        )
    ) / _SCALER;
}
```
In FluidLocker:388, it incorrectly divides the term (Math.sqrt(unlockPeriod*_SCALER) by _SCALER.  
Internal pre-conditions  
None.  
External pre-conditions  
None.  
Attack Path  
1. User unlocks their Fluid from the locker with a duration bigger than 0, unvesting it through the fountain.  
User suffers a big loss, even if they unlock with the maximum period, they will still get 80% penalty.

title: Lenders and borrowers can not
content: The vulnerability is an unchecked existence check for the receipt ERC721 token used as collateral in the liquidation flow of the Debita V3 loan protocol. When a veNFT auction is sold, the buyer becomes the holder of the receipt token and can later call veNFTVault.withdraw(), which burns the receipt token. The claim functions for lenders (claimCollateralAsNFTLender) and borrowers (claimCollateralNFTAsBorrower) rely on veNFTAerodrome.getDataByReceipt to obtain the token decimals needed for payment calculation. getDataByReceipt unconditionally calls ownerOf(receiptID) to retrieve the current owner, but if the receipt has been burned ownerOf reverts with ERC721NonexistentToken. Because this revert is not caught, the entire claim transaction aborts, leaving both lenders and borrowers unable to receive their liquidation tokens. From a user perspective the transaction simply fails, often showing a generic revert error or “transaction failed” message, and the expected liquidation token balance remains unchanged. The impact is that funds that should be distributed after liquidation become locked, breaking the protocol’s accounting assumptions and potentially causing loss of expected returns. The issue occurs only after the specific sequence where the auction buyer withdraws the veNFT after the auction, i.e., when the receipt token no longer exists. It was discovered during an audit when a test reproduced the failure by simulating the withdraw step followed by a claim attempt. The bug is hard to notice because the getDataByReceipt function appears to be a read‑only helper and the edge case of a burned receipt is not exercised in normal operation. Conceptually, the fix is to handle the non‑existent token case inside getDataByReceipt, for example by checking token existence before calling ownerOf or by providing a fallback value, or alternatively by obtaining the required decimals directly in the claim functions without depending on the receipt token. This class of bug falls under improper handling of external contract calls that may revert, leading to denial‑of‑service for legitimate users.

title: Nobody can buy the TaxTokenReceipt NFT from auction Found by 0x37, 0xPhantom2, KaplanLabs, KiroBrejka, bbl4de, dhank, dimulski, tmotfl, xiaoming90
content: The vulnerability originates from an overridden ERC721.transferFrom implementation that restricts token movement to addresses recognised as a BorrowOrder, a LendOrder or a Loan. The function computes two boolean flags – one for the sender (from) and one for the receiver (to) – and reverts unless at least one of the flags is true. This logic works for normal loan lifecycle transfers, where either the borrower, the lender or the loan contract participates, but it does not consider the auction contract that becomes the holder of the TaxTokenReceipt NFT after a borrower defaults. When a default triggers the auction, the NFT is transferred to the auction contract successfully because the from address (the loan) satisfies the check. However, the subsequent purchase step calls transferFrom with the auction contract as the from address and the buyer as the to address. Neither the auction contract nor the buyer matches the whitelist of BorrowOrder, LendOrder or Loan, causing the require statement to fail and the transaction to revert with the message "TaxTokensReceipts: Debita not involved". As a result, the NFT cannot be sold, the collateral token cannot be released, and lenders are unable to recover the value that backs the loan. The issue manifests only after a loan default and auction initiation, which is an edge case that may not be covered by standard unit tests, making it hard to notice during development. The bug was discovered during a security audit by tracing the transfer flow and noticing that the auction purchase path never satisfies the transfer restrictions. From a user perspective, attempts to buy the NFT from the auction UI result in a reverted transaction, no NFT is received, and the user’s ether or token balance remains unchanged apart from gas costs. This is an instance of an over‑restrictive access‑control bug where the whitelist of allowed participants is incomplete, leading to a dead‑lock of assets. To remediate the issue, the transfer logic should be extended to recognise an active auction as a valid participant, for example by checking that the from address is an authorized auction contract with a non‑zero auction index, or by providing a dedicated transfer pathway for auction sales that bypasses the strict BorrowOrder/LendOrder/Loan check. Such a change restores the intended business logic that collateral can be liquidated through auction, aligns the contract with accounting assumptions that defaulted loans can be recovered, and protects lenders from unexpected loss of funds.
summary:
Nobody can buy the TaxTokenReceipt NFT from auction due to the overrided transferFrom function. The transferFrom function is overrided with the following checks:
```solidity
function transferFrom(
    address from,
    address to,
    uint256 tokenId
) public virtual override(ERC721, IERC721) {
    bool isReceiverAddressDebita = IBorrowOrderFactory(borrowOrderFactory)
        .isBorrowOrderLegit(to) ||
        ILendOrderFactory(lendOrderFactory).isLendOrderLegit(to) ||
        IAggregator(Aggregator).isSenderALoan(to);
    bool isSenderAddressDebita = IBorrowOrderFactory(borrowOrderFactory)
        .isBorrowOrderLegit(from) ||
        ILendOrderFactory(lendOrderFactory).isLendOrderLegit(from) ||
        IAggregator(Aggregator).isSenderALoan(from);
    // Debita not involved --> revert
    require(
        isReceiverAddressDebita || isSenderAddressDebita,
        "TaxTokensReceipts: Debita not involved"
    );
```

This ensures that the transfer of the NFT, will go smoothly through the system, but one thing is missing. The thing is that if a borrower doesn't pay off his debt amount and the loan is auctioned, nobody will be able to buy the NFT off. This is because the transferFrom function requires for the from and to addresses to be either a BorrowOrder, LendOrder or a Loan to be able to transfer the receipt NFT. At the point when the NFT is in the Auction contract it will be too late because neither the Auction contract nor the msg.sender is or can be one of the listed. This means that it is impossible to get any amount of collateral token out of the NFT, which means that the lenders will experience a big loss of funds.  

The modifications of the ERC721::transferFrom function  

Internal pre-conditions  
TaxTokenReceipt being used as loan collateral  

External pre-conditions  
None  

Attack Path  
1. User makes BorrowOrder with TaxTokenReceipt NFT as collateral  
2. The offer is matched and a loan is now created.  
3. Borrower doesn't pay his loan off  
4. Loan is auctioned and the NFT is transferred to the created auction (Up to this moment everything is going smoothly because at least one address in the sequence meets the criteria of being either a BorrowOrder, LoanOrder or a Loan)  
5. At this point there is no eligible address since the Auction address doesn't meet the criteria and the msg.sender is just unable to meet it since neither the BorrowOrder nor the LendOrder can call Auction::buyNFT function.  

Lenders will experience big loss of funds, since the NFT can't be sold. Borrower will go off with their principle token and money that they should get in the form of NFT underlying are frozen forever.

title: Managed veAERO NFT can be withdrawn by owner after being used as collateral
content: The vulnerability concerns the use of a managed veAERO NFT (also called (m)veAERO) as collateral in lending or marketplace contracts. A managed veAERO NFT acts as a vault that holds an underlying unmanaged veAERO token; the owner can deposit the unmanaged token via Voter.depositManaged and later withdraw it with Voter.withdrawManaged, which changes the amount locked inside the vault. The protocol treats the NFT receipt representing the managed vault as a static asset and does not verify that the underlying balance remains intact after the receipt has been transferred to a loan or a sell order. Consequently, a malicious borrower can deposit his unmanaged veAERO into a managed vault, receive an NFT receipt, and use that receipt as collateral in a loan created through DebitaV3Aggregator.matchOffersV3. After the loan contract holds the NFT receipt, the borrower calls Voter.withdrawManaged to pull out the underlying veAERO, leaving the managed NFT empty while the loan still believes it is backed by one million AERO. When the borrower defaults, the loan’s liquidation process auctions the now‑worthless NFT receipt, and the lender receives no value, losing the borrowed USDC. The same pattern applies to any function that accepts a managed‑veAERO receipt, such as BuyOrder.sellNFT, where the seller can withdraw the locked amount after the receipt is sold, leaving the buyer with a non‑redeemable NFT. The issue is a classic “withdraw‑after‑collateralization” flaw: the system fails to enforce that assets used as collateral remain locked for the duration of the loan or sale. It is hard to notice because the NFT receipt appears valid on‑chain and in the UI, and there is no explicit check of the underlying veAERO balance at liquidation time. The impact is severe: lenders or buyers lose the value of their loan or purchase, effectively seeing their funds disappear. The bug was discovered during a manual audit of the Debita Finance V3 contracts, where the logical flow of depositManaged/withdrawManaged combined with collateral handling was examined. To remediate, the protocol should either prohibit withdrawals of the underlying veAERO while the managed NFT is pledged as collateral, lock the vault for the lifetime of the loan, or add runtime verification of the underlying balance before loan creation, liquidation, or NFT transfer. In user terms, a borrower may receive the expected USDC but later the collateral shown in the UI becomes empty, and a lender may see an auctioned NFT that yields no payout, contrary to the expectation that the NFT represents a valuable claim.
summary:
Internal pre-conditions  
External pre-conditions  
Attack Path  
Instance 1  
The Aerodrome's veAERO NFT can be an unmanaged veNFT OR managed veNFT. A managed veAERO NFT (also called (m)veAERO NFT) operates like a vault that allows users to deposit and withdraw their unmanaged veNFT into the managed veNFT via the Voter.depositManaged and Voter.withdrawManaged functions. Thus, the locked amount within the (m)veAERO NFT can increase or decrease.  
Bob, the malicious user, owns a (m)veAERO NFT and locks his unmanaged veNFT worth 1,000,000 AERO within it. He then converts it into an NFT receipt and uses it as collateral in his borrow offer. The borrow offer intends to exchange borrow 1,000,000 USDC at the price/ratio of 1 AERO = 1 USDC.  
Bob then matches his borrow order against other users' lending orders via the permissionless DebitaV3Aggregator.matchOffersV3 function himself. A new Loan contract is created, and 1,000,000 USDC is sent to Bob's wallet, and the (m)veAERO NFT is transferred into the Loan contract.  
Next, Bob calls the Voter.withdrawManaged function to withdraw his unmanaged veNFT, which is worth 1,000,000 AERO, from the (m)veAERO NFT. As a result, the (m)veAERO NFT collateral within the Loan becomes worthless now.  
Bob now holds 1,000,000 USDC and 1,000,000 AERO.  
Bob defaults on the Loan, and the (m)veAERO NFT will be auctioned. Since the (m)veAERO NFT is worthless, no one will purchase it, and the lender will not get any funds back and will lose 1,000,000 USDC.  

Instance 2  
Any mechanism that relies on NFT receipt will be vulnerable to such an issue by exploiting the managed veNFT.  
Another instance that is affected by a similar issue is the BuyOrder.sellNFT function, where the NFT receipt with managed veNFT is placed within a buy order and put up for sale. Once the NFT receipt is sold, the seller can proceed to withdraw all the locked amount within the NFT receipt, leaving the buyer with a worthless NFT receipt. Since the root cause is similar, the attack path will be omitted for brevity.  
High. Loss of assets for lenders and buyers.

title: No one can sell TaxTokensReceipts NFT receipt to the buy order The protocol has acknowledged this issue. Found by 0x37, KiroBrejka, bbl4de, dimulski, xiaoming90
content: The vulnerability concerns the transfer logic of the TaxTokensReceipts NFT, which is used to represent tax‑bearing tokens inside the Debita ecosystem. The contract overrides the standard ERC721 transferFrom function and restricts transfers to only those where either the sender or the receiver is one of three specific Debita contracts: a Borrow Order contract, a Lend Order contract, or a Loan contract. The newly introduced Buy Order (or Limit Order) feature creates a separate Buy Order contract that is intended to purchase these NFT receipts from users. When a holder calls buyOrder.sellNFT() the function attempts to move the NFT from the seller to the Buy Order contract via the overridden transferFrom. Because the Buy Order contract is not included in the whitelist check, the require statement in transferFrom fails and the transaction reverts with the message "TaxTokensReceipts: Debita not involved". Consequently, no user can sell a TaxTokensReceipts NFT to a buy order, rendering the buy‑order liquidity mechanism inoperable. The impact is that users expecting to sell their receipt for liquidity receive no transaction execution, their balances remain unchanged, and the protocol’s advertised feature of automated market making for tax‑token receipts is effectively broken. This condition occurs whenever a sellNFT call is made against a TaxTokensReceipts NFT while the Buy Order contract is the intended recipient. The affected parties are token holders who wish to liquidate their receipts, liquidity providers relying on the buy‑order market, and the overall Debita protocol which loses a core functionality. The issue was identified during a security audit when the auditors examined the transferFrom implementation and noticed that the Buy Order contract was omitted from the allowed address list. It can be hard to spot because the code follows a typical pattern of restricting transfers to known contracts, and the omission of the new contract does not raise a compiler warning. To remediate the problem, the transferFrom function should be extended to recognise the Buy Order contract (for example by adding an IBuyOrderFactory.isBuyOrderLegit check) or by redesigning the whitelist to include any contract that is part of the Debita protocol, thereby allowing the NFT to be transferred to a buy order. This change restores the intended behaviour where a user can sell a receipt to a buy order, enabling the protocol’s liquidity injection mechanism to function as designed.
summary:
Internal pre-conditions  
External pre-conditions  
Attack Path  
The TaxTokensReceipts NFT receipt exist to allow FOT to be used within the Debita ecosystem. If users have any tokens that charge a tax/fee on transfer, they must deposit them into the TaxTokensReceipts NFT receipt and use the NFT within the Debita ecosystem.  
The new Debita protocol has a new feature called ”Buy Order” or ”Limit Order” that allows users to create buy orders, providing a mechanism for injecting liquidity to purchase specific receipts at predetermined ratios. The receipts include the TaxTokensReceipts NFT receipt.  
Assume that Bob creates a new Buy Order to purchase TaxTokensReceipts NFT receipt. Alice, the holder of TaxTokensReceipts NFT receipt, decided to sell it to Bob's Buy Order. Thus, she called the buyOrder.sellNFT() function, and Line 99 below will attempt to transfer Alice's TaxTokensReceipts NFT receipt to the Buy Order contract.  
contracts/contracts/buyOrders/buyOrder.sol#L99  
File: buyOrder.sol  
```solidity

093:     require(buyInformation.isActive, "Buy order is not active");
094:     require(
095:         buyInformation.availableAmount > 0,
096:         "Buy order is not available"
097:     );
098:
099:     IERC721(buyInformation.wantedToken).transferFrom(
100:         msg.sender,
101:         address(this),
102:         receiptID
103:     );
```
However, the transfer will always revert because the transfer function has been overwritten, as shown below. The transfer function has been overwritten to only allow the transfer to proceed if the to or from involves the following three (3) contracts:  
1. Borrow Order Contract  
2. Lend Order Contract  
3. Loan Contract  
Since neither the Buy Order contract nor the seller (Alice) is the above three contracts, the transfer will always fail. Thus, there is no way for anyone to sell their TaxTokensReceipts NFT receipt to the buy order. Thus, this feature is effectively broken.  
contracts/contracts/Non-Fungible-Receipts/TaxTokensReceipts/TaxTokensReceipt.sol#L98  
File: TaxTokensReceipt.sol  
```solidity
093: function transferFrom(
094:     address from,

097: ) public virtual override(ERC721, IERC721) {
098:     bool isReceiverAddressDebita = IBorrowOrderFactory(borrowOrderFactory)
099:         .isBorrowOrderLegit(to) ||
100:         ILendOrderFactory(lendOrderFactory).isLendOrderLegit(to) ||
101:         IAggregator(Aggregator).isSenderALoan(to);
102:     bool isSenderAddressDebita = IBorrowOrderFactory(borrowOrderFactory)
103:         .isBorrowOrderLegit(from) ||
104:         ILendOrderFactory(lendOrderFactory).isLendOrderLegit(from) ||
105:         IAggregator(Aggregator).isSenderALoan(from);

```
Medium. Core protocol functionality (Buy Order/Limit Order) is broken.

title: After the buyOrder is completed, the NFT is not transferred to the order creator
content: The vulnerability consists of a missing NFT transfer after a buy order is fulfilled. When a user (the order creator) creates a buy order for a specific NFT, the protocol expects the seller to call the sellNFT function, receive the agreed buy token, and have the NFT transferred to the order creator. In the current implementation the sellNFT function only emits a completion event, updates internal bookkeeping and deletes the order, but it never calls the ERC‑721 transfer routine to move the token from the contract to the buyer. The root cause is a logical omission in the order‑finalisation flow: the contract assumes that ownership has already been handed over, or that emitting the event is sufficient, and therefore does not execute the safeTransferFrom call. An attacker (or any participant) can exploit this by simply completing a buy order; the seller receives payment while the NFT is transferred into the buyOrderContract address and becomes permanently locked because the contract provides no mechanism to withdraw it. From the user’s perspective the transaction appears successful – the event logs show order completion and the seller’s token balance increases – yet the buyer never receives the purchased NFT and the contract’s balance now holds an orphaned token. This breaks the fundamental business logic that a purchase should result in a one‑to‑one exchange of assets, leading to loss of value for the buyer and potential loss of the NFT for the seller if the contract does not allow later retrieval. The issue was discovered during a security audit when a test case asserted that the token owner after sellNFT was the contract address instead of the buyer. Because the contract does not revert or emit an explicit error, the problem can be hard to notice in production; only a manual inspection of token ownership or a missing NFT in the buyer’s wallet would reveal the discrepancy. The correct remediation is to add an explicit ERC‑721 transfer (e.g., receiptContract.safeTransferFrom(address(this), orderCreator, tokenId)) after the payment is sent, and to ensure that any failure to transfer reverts the whole transaction, thereby preserving atomicity and preventing assets from becoming stranded.

title: Some btc incoming transfers can fail due to invalid evm address parsing
content: The bridge component that moves BTC‑linked assets to other chains parses an EVM destination address from the rune runestone field "43". The code assumes the field always contains enough bytes to build a 20‑byte address and pads the intermediate byte slice only to a multiple of 16 bytes. When an attacker or a malformed transaction supplies a very short value – for example a single uint128 – the resulting byte slice is only 16 bytes long. The subsequent slice operation bs[:20] therefore triggers a runtime panic (slice bounds out of range). The panic is recovered by the surrounding goroutine, so the bridge process does not crash, but the current batch of up to 2500 UTXOs is left in an inconsistent state. The scanner repeatedly fails on the malformed entry and eventually skips it once the 2500‑UTXO window is exceeded. Because the scanner processes the latest 2500 entries as a block, other legitimate transfers that appear in the same window may also be skipped with high probability. From a user’s point of view a transfer that was expected to be forwarded to an EVM address simply never arrives; the user sees no refund or receipt and their balance on the destination chain remains unchanged. The root cause is insufficient validation and padding of the address byte array before slicing, combined with an unchecked assumption that the runestone field always provides at least 20 bytes. The issue was discovered during a security audit when a test case reproduced the panic by feeding a single‑uint128 value. It is hard to notice because the panic is caught and the bridge continues operating silently, leaving no explicit error logs for the failed transfers. The vulnerability belongs to the class of input‑parsing and slice‑bounds errors that lead to silent transaction loss. The recommended fix is to ensure the byte array is padded to at least 20 bytes for EVM targets, validate the length of the parsed address, and handle malformed fields gracefully – either by rejecting the transfer with a clear error or by skipping it without affecting other pending transfers.

title: Malicious user can trick bridge into spending rune UTXOs
content: The vulnerability resides in the bridge component that moves rune tokens from the Bitcoin chain to another chain. When the bridge prepares an outgoing Bitcoin transaction it scans the set of available UTXOs and selects those whose value exceeds a hard‑coded dust threshold (minimumDustThreshold). The code assumes that any UTXO with a value at or below this threshold is most likely a rune‑bearing UTXO originating from an inbound transfer, and therefore it skips those UTXOs. However, the logic does not verify whether a UTXO that is above the threshold actually carries rune data (a runestone). A malicious actor can craft a transaction that sends an output to the bridge’s address with a value just above the threshold, for example 10001 satoshis, and attach rune metadata to that output. Because the bridge’s selection routine only checks the numeric value, it treats this output as a regular spendable UTXO and later uses it to pay transaction fees or to create change outputs. The transaction that is built does not contain a runestone output for the attached runes, so the rune tokens associated with the 10001‑satoshi UTXO become permanently lost and unclaimable. From the user’s perspective the bridge appears to accept the transfer but the rune balance on the destination chain is reduced while the user receives the expected tokens on the other chain, effectively stealing rune value from the bridge. The issue manifests whenever the bridge processes outgoing transfers and constructs Bitcoin transactions, i.e., under normal operational conditions. It affects any party relying on the bridge’s accounting – the bridge itself becomes insolvent for the affected rune token, and users may see their rune balances disappear without any on‑chain indication. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the bridge’s source code, where the loop that filters UTXOs was examined and the lack of a rune‑presence check was noted. The problem is subtle because the value‑based filter is a common heuristic for dust avoidance, making the missing validation easy to overlook. To remediate the issue the bridge should explicitly verify that a candidate UTXO is not associated with a rune before using it for fee payment or change, for example by checking for the presence of a runestone or by maintaining a separate pool of pure‑bitcoin UTXOs. This change ensures that rune‑bearing outputs are never unintentionally spent, preserving the accounting integrity of the bridge and preventing silent loss of funds.
summary:
During outgoing rune transfers on the btc chain, the bridge logic checks which utxos can be used to spend value needed for the rune transfers (minimum dust 564 to associate with destination output and ”change” output, and tx fee). It skips the utxos having less than minimumDustThreshold because those are associated with incoming rune transfers. Unfortunately a malicious user can trick the bridge into using incoming rune transfers by associating a value of 10001 with a rune output. Since the constructed transaction will not have a runestone output, it means that the runes associated with that output will simply be lost and unclaimable by anyone, causing consequent losses for the bridge.

```go
for _, utxo := range utxos {
    value := StringToInt(utxo.Get("value"))
    if value <= minimumDustThreshold {
        continue // don't spend what is most likely to be a rune utxo
    }
}
```

External pre-conditions
Attack Path

The bridge will use that output at some point to pay for transaction fees, and will lose associated runes. The attacker does not lose anything since he is able to claim tokens on destination chain and roundtrip back on btc taking somebody else rune balance. As a result the bridge is insolvent in the targeted rune token.

title: Sol scan may be DoSed and locks
content: The vulnerabilityresides in the Solana‑to‑Ethereum bridge component that continuously polls Solana transaction signatures and decodes each instruction to create a Transfer record. For every lock or burn instruction the bridge extracts the transferred amount, the destination network, the destination address and a fee field. The implementation contains a hard‑coded validation that the fee must be at least 50,000,000 lamports; if the fee is lower the code triggers a panic with the message "sol fee paid to small to cover transaction cost". Because the panic is not caught, the Go routine that processes the signature crashes and is automatically restarted by the runtime. Upon restart the routine re‑examines the same signature, encounters the same insufficient‑fee condition and panics again, repeating this loop until the indexer’s polling window (a maximum of 100 signatures) is exhausted. When the window limit is reached the bridge silently discards the offending signature and moves on to newer ones. In periods of high transaction volume, many low‑fee signatures can be dropped, meaning that users who locked tokens with an under‑paid fee see their funds remain locked on Solana with no corresponding Transfer entry on the destination chain. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a pending lock, the balance on the destination chain stays unchanged, and no error is reported, creating the impression that the funds have vanished. The root cause is improper input validation combined with an unhandled exception that leads to a denial‑of‑service style loop and loss of state. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the reviewer noticed the panic condition and the retry logic in the source file chain_sol.go. It is difficult to notice in production because occasional skips can be mistaken for normal network latency or indexing delays, and the bridge does not emit an explicit failure event. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of unchecked exceptions causing service disruption and state loss. The recommended mitigation is to replace the panic with graceful error handling: record the transfer with an error or ignored status, emit an event, and continue processing subsequent signatures, thereby preventing the retry loop and preserving user funds.
summary:
The bridge uses polling of solana signatures to the address of the bridge ms. Inside these signature objects, individual instructions are parsed and parameters for transfers are extracted. One of these parameters is the native fee to be paid to the bridge. Unfortunately if the fee is insufficient a panic is triggered in the bridge code. Due to the recovery of the go routine, the bridge will attempt to iterate on the failed signature until reaching window limit of 100 (polling window of the indexer), at which point some signatures will be skipped during high usage.

```go
func (b *Bridge) solScanBurn(id, signer string, blockTime time.Time, decoder *SolanaDecoder, mint string) *Transfer {
    _ = decoder.String()
    amount := IntToBi(int64(decoder.Uint64()))
    fee := decoder.Uint64()
    targetNetwork := decoder.Uint8()
    targetAddress := decoder.String()
    if fee < 50000000 {
        panic(fmt.Sprintf("sol fee paid to small to cover transaction cost: %d", fee))
    }
    return &Transfer{
        ID: id,
        Target: int(targetNetwork),
        From: signer,
        To: targetAddress,
        Rune: mint,
        Amount: amount.String(),
        Created: blockTime,
    }
}
```

title: There is no mechanism in the EVM bridge to cover gas fees
content: The vulnerability is a missing gas‑fee‑coverage mechanism in the EVM side of a cross‑chain bridge that connects an EVM network with Solana. On the Solana side the bridge contract explicitly requires a fee that is transferred to a bridge‑signer address and that fee is validated to be at least 0.05 SOL, which is intended to pay the transaction cost of minting or unlocking tokens on Solana. The EVM implementation, however, provides burn and lock functions that do not accept any fee from the caller and do not enforce a minimum payment. As a result, when a user initiates a burn or lock on the EVM chain, the bridge protocol must create a separate transaction on the Solana chain to complete the mint or unlock, and the cost of that transaction is paid out of the protocol’s own treasury. The root cause is the asymmetry in fee handling: the Solana bridge enforces a fee, the EVM bridge does not, leaving the protocol exposed to un‑reimbursed gas expenses. An attacker can exploit this by repeatedly calling the EVM burn or lock functions with very small (dust) amounts, targeting a destination chain where the Solana transaction fee is high. Each call triggers the protocol to send a Solana transaction that consumes the required gas, and because the attacker pays nothing, the protocol’s funds are drained incrementally. The impact is a direct loss of treasury assets proportional to the number of bridge operations and the gas price on the target chain; in extreme cases the protocol could exhaust its reserve for cross‑chain operations. The condition for exploitation is any bridging operation from EVM to Solana, regardless of the amount transferred, and it occurs each time the bridge processes a burn or lock event. The parties affected are the protocol itself – its treasury and any users who rely on the bridge’s continued operation – while end‑users may not notice any fee on their transaction but may see missing tokens on the destination chain because the protocol cannot afford to complete the minting. The issue was discovered during a security audit that compared the fee logic of the two bridge implementations and identified the absence of a fee check in the EVM contract. It can be hard to notice because the user interface shows no fee, the amounts involved can be tiny, and the loss manifests as a gradual depletion of protocol funds rather than an immediate error. To remediate the problem the bridge should be redesigned to collect a fee from the caller on the EVM side, enforce a minimum fee comparable to the Solana requirement, or otherwise reimburse the protocol for the gas spent on the target chain. Adding validation to reject dust operations or implementing a rate‑limiting mechanism would also mitigate the economic incentive for an attacker to spam the bridge.

title: Nonce management vulnerability
content: The vulnerability is an improper nonce management flaw in the bridge's evmSend routine that can be exploited to cause a denial‑of‑service condition. The bridge maintains a cached variable called lastNonce for each target EVM network and uses it to compute the next transaction nonce. When a bridge transaction is front‑run by an attacker who submits a competing transaction with the same nonce, the bridge transaction reverts. Because the evmSend implementation does not update lastNonce after a failure, the stale nonce remains cached. Subsequent bridge calls therefore reuse the already‑used nonce, triggering the contract‑level check require(!nonces[nonce]) in the Multisig contract, which reverts each transaction. The attack path consists of observing a pending bridge transaction, front‑running it with the same nonce, causing the bridge transaction to fail, and then repeatedly sending new bridge transactions that all reuse the stale nonce, effectively halting all cross‑chain transfers for that network. From a user’s perspective, a transfer that appears to be submitted in the UI never completes; the UI may show a pending state that eventually fails, and the user sees no change in balances, contrary to the expectation that the assets would be moved across chains. The impact is a complete stoppage of bridge functionality for the affected network, preventing users from moving funds and disrupting the protocol’s cross‑chain operations. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the nonce handling logic and identified that lastNonce is only updated on successful transactions. The bug is subtle because occasional transaction failures can be attributed to network congestion, making the stale‑nonce condition hard to notice until an attacker deliberately exploits it. Conceptually, this is a nonce‑reuse vulnerability that violates the assumption that each transaction nonce is unique and monotonically increasing, breaking the accounting guarantees of the bridge. The recommended remediation is to ensure that lastNonce is updated regardless of transaction outcome, for example by using a defer/recover block that synchronizes the cached nonce with the contract’s highestNonce after a panic, or by eliminating the cache entirely and reading the highestNonce directly from the contract before each send, thereby guaranteeing that the next nonce is always fresh and preventing reuse of a used nonce.
summary:
The evmSend function in the bridge implementation is vulnerable to a Denial of Service (DoS) attack due to improper nonce management. When a transaction is front-run and reverts, the lastNonce variable is not updated, causing subsequent transactions to reuse an already used nonce. This leads to repeated failures, effectively halting the bridge's functionality.
1. Improper Nonce Handling in evmSend:
• The lastNonce for a target network is not updated when a transaction fails. hain_evm.go#L106
• Subsequent transactions reuse the stale lastNonce, leading to reverts due to the contract's nonces check. hain_evm.go#L88-L91
2. Contract-Level Nonce Validation:
• The bridge contract marks nonces as used after a successful or front-run transaction and update highest nonce. evm/Multisig.sol#L60-L62
• Reuse of a nonce results in reversion due to the contract's require(!nonces[nonce]) check. evm/Multisig.sol#L58
3. Faulty Logic in Nonce Calculation:
• The condition BiGte(BiFirst(lastNonce[transfer.Target]),nonce) assumes lastNonce is always up-to-date, which is not guaranteed after a failure. hain_evm.go#L89
Internal Pre-Conditions
• evmSend relies on lastNonce to calculate the next nonce.
• Transactions that fail due to front-running do not update lastNonce.
External Pre-Conditions
• An attacker front-runs the transaction by preemptively using the calculated nonce.
• The transaction reverts, leaving lastNonce stale.
Attack Path
1. The attacker observes the bridge transaction being broadcasted with a specific nonce.
2. The attacker front-runs the transaction by submitting their own with the same nonce.
3. The bridge transaction fails and does not update lastNonce.
4. Subsequent transactions from the bridge reuse the same nonce, repeatedly reverting.
5. The bridge becomes stuck, unable to process further transactions for the affected network.
This vulnerability allows a malicious actor to halt all bridge transactions for a specific EVM network, effectively rendering the bridge inoperable for that network. The issue constitutes a Denial of Service (DoS) attack, impacting users and disrupting cross-chain functionality.
Proof of Concept (PoC)
1. Set up a bridge instance and initiate a transfer to just one (bypassing to an attempt an EVM network.
2. Front-run the bridge transaction by submitting a transaction with the same nonce as the bridge.
3. Observe that the bridge transaction reverts due to the nonce being already used.
4. Initiate another transfer. Observe that the same nonce is reused, causing repeated reverts.
5. The bridge becomes non-functional for the target network.

title: Bypassing Multisig Execution Threshold with Duplicate Signatures Found by Atharv, KupiaSec, cergyk
content: The vulnerability is a multisignature threshold bypass that allows a transaction to be executed with fewer distinct admin approvals than the protocol requires. The contract is designed to require at least two out of three administrators to sign a payload before it can be executed, but the validation logic only counts the number of signatures that match known admin addresses without checking whether each signature is unique. During the verification loop the counter is incremented for every entry in the signatures array, even if the same signature appears multiple times. Consequently, an attacker can submit an array that contains a single valid admin signature repeated enough times to satisfy the condition n >= execN, causing the require statement to pass. Because the call function that performs the transaction is external and can be invoked by any address, a malicious party – either a compromised admin or an external user who can supply the duplicated signatures – can trigger the execution of arbitrary transactions that should have been blocked by the multisig guard. The impact is that unauthorized state changes, fund transfers, or contract upgrades can occur with only one admin’s consent, effectively nullifying the security guarantees of the multisig scheme. This flaw manifests whenever the contract processes a multisig execution request and does not enforce uniqueness of signers, which is typical for many threshold‑based designs that rely on simple counting. It was discovered during a manual audit by the team of Atharv, KupiaSec and cergyk, who noticed that the signature verification loop lacked a deduplication step. The issue can be hard to notice because the transaction receipt shows the required number of signatures, yet the underlying array may contain duplicates, giving a false sense of compliance. From a user’s perspective the UI may indicate that two approvals are needed, but the transaction succeeds after only one admin signs, leading to confusion such as “my transaction went through with a single signature”. The bug violates the fundamental accounting assumption that each distinct admin contributes an independent vote, breaking the intended multi‑party control. To remediate the problem the contract should enforce that each element in the signatures array corresponds to a unique admin address, for example by tracking seen signers in a mapping or by rejecting duplicate entries before counting, thereby ensuring that the threshold reflects distinct approvals only.

title: Cross-Chain Signature Replay
content: The vulnerability is a cross‑chain signature replay flaw that arises because the multisig contract’s signed payload does not contain any chain‑specific identifier. The contract builds the message to be signed by hashing the nonce, target address, ether value and calldata, then prefixes it with the standard Ethereum signed‑message header. Since the resulting hash is identical on every EVM‑compatible network, a signature that authorises a transaction on one chain (for example Bitlayer) is also valid on any other deployed instance of the same contract (such as Ethereum, Botanix or Core). An attacker who can observe a legitimate transaction – for instance by watching the Bridge contract that forwards signed calls – can copy the exact payload and the accompanying admin signatures and submit them to the multisig contract on a different chain. Because the verification routine only checks that the signature matches the payload, the call succeeds, allowing the attacker to execute arbitrary calls on the second chain. This can lead to unauthorized asset transfers, minting or unlocking of tokens, and potentially the loss of funds that are controlled by the multisig on the victim chain. The issue manifests whenever the multisig and bridge contracts are deployed on multiple networks without embedding a chain identifier in the signed message, which is a common pattern for cross‑chain projects that reuse the same Solidity code. It was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the signature verification logic and noticed the absence of a domain separator or chainId field. The flaw is subtle because the code appears to follow standard ECDSA verification practices, and the same hash function is used on all chains, making the problem invisible unless the auditor compares deployments across networks. To remediate the issue, the contract should adopt an EIP‑712 typed‑data scheme or otherwise include the chainId (or a unique network identifier) in the signed payload, ensuring that a signature is only valid on the chain for which it was created. This change binds the signature to a specific domain, preventing replay attacks across chains and restoring the intended security guarantees of the multisig governance model.
summary:
The protocol is deployed across multiple EVM-compatible chains (Bitlayer, Botanix, Core, and Ethereum) with separate instances of Multisig.sol and Bridge.sol. The Multisig.sol contract uses the call() function to execute transactions authenticated by admin signatures. However, the payload for these signatures is not chain-specific, making the signature valid across different chains.
This vulnerability allows an attacker to replay a valid signature from one chain to execute unauthorized transactions on another chain.
The payload hash used for signature creation and verification does not include chain-specific data, making signatures chain-agnostic:
```solidity
bytes32 payload = keccak256(abi.encode(nonce, target, value, data));
bytes32 hash = keccak256(abi.encodePacked("\x19Ethereum Signed Message:\n32", payload));
```
This design flaw allows a signature created on one chain to be reused for transaction execution on another chain.
Payload Signature Verification
Internal pre-conditions
External pre-conditions
Attack Path
1. Valid signatures are used by Bridge to call call() function on chain A.
2. Attacker sees the transaction data, signatures.
3. Use same signature and data on chain B.
1. Unauthorized transactions can be executed across chains using the same signatures.
2. Loss of funds if the target address on another chain contains different logic.
3. Unauthorized minting or unlocking of assets on other chains.

title: In setReward(), block.timestamp
content: The contract’s setReward function records the timestamp of the last reward update using block.timestamp instead of the configured startTime for a new reward schedule. When the owner creates a reward that is intended to begin in the future, the function still sets lastUpdateTime to the current block time. Consequently, the reward accounting logic treats the period between the current time and the future start as if rewards were already accruing. A staker who deposits tokens before the scheduled start will therefore receive a share of rewards for a time interval during which no reward was actually allocated. In the illustrated scenario, a user stakes at 1 PM, the owner schedules a reward to start at 2 PM and run for four hours, but because lastUpdateTime is set to 1 PM, the contract distributes roughly one‑hour’s worth of reward (25 tokens) immediately when the user claims at 2 PM. The impact is that the protocol’s reward pool is depleted faster than intended, causing users to obtain extra tokens and the contract to retain less than the promised amount, breaking the accounting assumptions of the staking system. This bug appears only when a future‑dated reward is set; if the reward starts immediately, the incorrect timestamp aligns with the intended start and the issue is not observable. The problem was discovered during a security audit through a unit test that simulated the described timing and observed an unexpected token balance for the staker. It can be hard to notice because the reward rate calculation itself looks correct and the extra distribution is hidden in the first claim, making the discrepancy subtle. The proper fix is to initialise lastUpdateTime with the reward’s startTime (or the maximum of the current time and startTime) so that reward accrual only begins when the schedule officially starts, thereby preserving the intended distribution schedule and preventing unearned reward payouts.
summary:
In setReward(), block.timestamp is used instead of startTime at lastUpdateTime. This results in reward distribution for the time, reward was not allocated for. In setReward(), owner can set rewards for present as well as future. Issue arises when owner sets rewards for future because at rewardData[rewardToken].lastUpdateTime, block.timestamp is used instead of startTime.
