None
External pre-conditions
None
Attack Path
For easier calculation, duration is taken in hours
1. Suppose its 1PM, Alice staked 5e18 tokens.
2. And owner wanted to distribute a rewardToken(amount = 100e18) starting at 2PM till 6PM ie duration = 4 hours. Therefore, rewardRate = 100e18 / 4 hours = 25e18 tokens/hour & lastUpdateTime = 1PM
3. Now, there should not be any reward from 1PM to 2PM because reward started from 2PM.
4. However, Alice will receive reward for 1PM to 2PM also
Users will receive reward for the time, reward was not allocated for. In above case, for 1PM to 2PM

title: Bonding curve logic can be exploited
content: The vulnerability resides in the pricing routine of a double‑sided bonding curve used by the ReputationMarket contract. The private function that computes the price of a vote multiplies the number of votes of the requested side (trust or distrust) by a constant base price and then divides by the total number of votes on both sides. Because the formula is purely proportional to the current vote distribution, an attacker can deliberately skew that distribution by buying cheap votes of the opposite side before purchasing the desired expensive votes. By alternating purchases of trust and distrust votes within the same block, the attacker forces the ratio of trust to distrust votes toward 1:1, which lowers the price of the next trust vote. After acquiring the target votes at a reduced cost, the attacker can sell the previously bought cheap votes at the higher price that results from the new distribution, netting a profit or obtaining additional voting power for less ether than expected. The exploit works whenever the same address can invoke buyVotes or sellVotes repeatedly without any temporal restriction, because the market state is updated instantly after each call and the price calculation does not incorporate any time‑weighted average, slippage protection, or minimum‑price floor. In practice the attacker observes that a normal purchase of twelve trust votes costs roughly 0.098 ETH, whereas the manipulated sequence of alternating trust and distrust purchases reduces the total cost to about 0.079 ETH – a saving of roughly 0.02 ETH. A similar pattern appears when an attacker first purchases a large batch of distrust votes before buying a large batch of trust votes, cutting the cost by about 0.28 ETH. The impact is that the reputation market no longer reflects true economic cost, allowing malicious participants to acquire voting power or extract value from the system, which can distort governance outcomes and erode confidence of honest users. The issue was uncovered during a security audit by constructing proof‑of‑concept test scripts that measured the ether spent in normal versus manipulated scenarios. Because the price deviation is modest and the market updates continuously, the problem can be difficult to spot without explicit testing of rapid trade sequences. To remediate the flaw, the contract should prevent immediate consecutive trades from the same address, for example by enforcing a minimum block or timestamp delay between buy or sell operations, or by redesigning the bonding curve to use a cumulative supply‑based pricing model that is resistant to short‑term manipulation. Such changes would restore the intended economic guarantees of the reputation market and protect users from losing funds or seeing their voting power unfairly altered.
summary:
Description & Impact
The _calcVotePrice() function uses the following bonding curve formula:
File: ethos/packages/contracts/contracts/ReputationMarket.sol
```solidity
/**
 * @notice Calculates the buy or sell price for votes based on market state
 * @dev Uses bonding curve formula: price = (votes * basePrice) / totalVotes
 * Markets are double sided, so the price of trust and distrust votes always sum to the base price
 * @param market The market state to calculate price for
 * @param isPositive Whether to calculate trust (true) or distrust (false) vote price
 * @return The calculated vote price
 */
function _calcVotePrice(Market memory market, bool isPositive) private pure returns (uint256) {
    uint256 totalVotes = market.votes[TRUST] + market.votes[DISTRUST];
    return (market.votes[isPositive ? TRUST : DISTRUST] * market.basePrice) / totalVotes;
}
```
This can be manipulated in the following ways:
Example1: ( coded in PoC1 )
• Normal Scenario:
– For a default market config, Alice decides to buy trust votes.
– She calls buyVotes() with 0.1 ETH of funds.
– This fetches her 12 trust votes and costs exactly 0.098439322450225045 ETH.
• Attack Scenario:
– For a default market config, Alice decides to buy 12 trust votes.
– She decides to alternate her buyVotes() call between 1 trust vote and 1 distrust vote.
– She repeats this 12 times.
– She sells all her distrust votes at the end.
– She ends up paying 0.079440616542537061 ETH, which is ￿0.02 ETH lesser than the normal scenario.
In fact in general, if Alice wishes to buy a higher-priced vote then it works in her favour to buy the lower-priced one first to make the vote ratio 1:1. At the end, this lower-priced purchase can be sold off for a net gain.
Example2: ( coded in PoC2 )
• Normal Scenario:
– For a default market config, Bob is sitting with 99 trust votes he bought a few moments ago.
– Alice wants to buy 100 trust votes. She calls buyVotes() with 1 ETH of funds.
– This fetches her 100 trust votes and costs exactly 0.993452851893538135 ETH.
• Attack Scenario:
– For a default market config, Bob is sitting with 99 trust votes he bought a few moments ago.
– Alice wants to buy 100 trust votes.
– She first buys 99 distrust votes.
– She now buys the 100 trust votes.
– She then sells all her distrust votes.
– She ends up paying 0.711616420426520863 ETH, which is ￿0.28 ETH lesser than the normal scenario.

title: Users could overpay fees when buying
content: The vulnerability is an over‑charging of protocol fees when a user purchases votes in the ReputationMarket contract. The root cause is that the previewFees function is called with the total amount of ETH supplied by the caller before the purchase loop runs, and the returned fee amount is added to the final fundsPaid regardless of how much of the supplied ETH is actually spent on votes. Because the price of each vote increases as votes are bought, the while‑loop may stop before all of the supplied funds are consumed, leaving a remainder that is never used to acquire additional votes. Nevertheless, the fee calculated on the original full amount is still charged, so the user ends up paying a fee on money that never contributed to a vote purchase. An attacker can exploit this by front‑running the transaction: if another user buys votes just before the victim’s transaction, the vote price rises, the loop terminates earlier, and the victim’s unused ETH is still subject to the full fee. The impact is that users receive fewer votes than expected while being charged a higher fee, effectively causing funds to disappear from the user’s balance without any corresponding benefit. This situation occurs whenever a buyVotes call is made with a fee preview that does not reflect the dynamic price changes that happen during the purchase loop, i.e., in any market where vote prices are not static. All participants who attempt to buy votes are affected, as the contract’s accounting logic violates the assumption that fees are proportional to the actual amount spent. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the fee calculation flow and identified the mismatch between fundsAvailable and fundsPaid. It can be hard to notice because the transaction succeeds and the fee appears correct at the moment of submission, while the leftover ETH is silently retained by the contract. The bug belongs to the class of fee miscalculation or accounting errors where fees are applied to an estimated amount rather than the realized amount. From a user’s perspective the UI may show that they sent a certain amount of ETH expecting a specific number of votes, but after execution they see only one vote and a larger fee deducted, with the remaining ETH seemingly vanished. The recommended remediation is to compute fees based on the actual amount of ETH that is spent on votes, or to redesign the buy interface so that callers specify the exact number of votes they want and the contract calculates the required payment and associated fees accordingly, ensuring that no unused funds are charged.

title: Market funds cannot be withdrawn
content: The vulnerability consists of an accounting error in the ReputationMarket contract where fees collected from vote purchases are transferred to the protocol treasury and the market owner's donation escrow, but the same fee amounts are not subtracted from the variable that records the total amount paid by the buyer (fundsPaid) before that value is added to the market's aggregate funds (marketFunds). As a result the protocol fee and donation fee are counted twice: once when they are sent out, and again when marketFunds is increased. This double‑counting occurs every time a user buys votes and the applyFees function is called, and it manifests when the market is graduated and the contract attempts to withdraw the recorded marketFunds. Because the recorded balance includes fees that no longer reside in the contract, the withdrawal reverts due to insufficient ether, leaving the market funds stuck or causing the contract to pull ether that belongs to other markets. The issue affects any participant who purchases votes, the market owner who expects to withdraw the correct amount, and the protocol treasury that relies on accurate accounting. It was discovered during a manual audit that traced the flow of funds from applyFees through the update of marketFunds and observed that the fee amounts were never deducted. The bug is hard to notice because the fee transfers succeed and the visible balances of the treasury and donation escrow appear correct, while the internal marketFunds ledger shows an inflated value that only surfaces during the graduation withdrawal. Conceptually the flaw belongs to the class of double‑counting or improper state update bugs where the same monetary amount is recorded in multiple places without proper reconciliation. From a user perspective the symptom is a withdrawal that fails with a revert or a situation where “my market funds disappear” after graduation, contrary to the expectation that the previously displayed market balance can be withdrawn. The correct fix is to adjust the accounting logic so that protocol fees and donation fees are deducted from fundsPaid before the amount is added to marketFunds, or to maintain a separate net‑funds variable that excludes already transferred fees.
summary:
```solidity
Funds withdrawal is blocked as fees are not deducted from fundsPaid when already being applied.
When votes are bought in ReputationMarket market, user has to pay fees:
• donation fees going to owner of the market
• protocol fees going to treasury
This is seen in applyFees function below:
function applyFees(
    uint256 protocolFee,
    uint256 donation,
    uint256 marketOwnerProfileId
) private returns (uint256 fees) {
    donationEscrow[donationRecipient[marketOwnerProfileId]] += donation; // donation fees are updated for market owner
    if (protocolFee > 0) {
        (bool success, ) = protocolFeeAddress.call{ value: protocolFee }(""); // protocolFees paid to treasury
        if (!success) revert FeeTransferFailed("Protocol fee deposit failed");
    }
    fees = protocolFee + donation;
}
```
Next, the total amount a user pays when votes are bought is managed by the fundsPaid variable. The amount consists of: cost of votes + protocol fees + donation fees.  
The vulnerability exists in the execution here:
1. send protocol fees to the treasury
2. add donations to market owner's escrow
3. marketOwner is able to withdraw donations via withdrawDonations()

In the buyVotes function, protocolFee and donation are paid first as seen below:  
```solidity
applyFees(protocolFee, donation, profileId);
```

Then, when tallying the market funds, marketFunds is updated with fundsPaid. This fundsPaid still includes the protocolFee and donation and has not been deducted.  
```solidity
marketFunds[profileId] += fundsPaid;
```

Hence, the protocolFee and donation has been counted twice.  
When a market graduates, because of the incorrect counting of marketFunds, the contract may not have enough funds to be withdrawn via ReputationMarket.withdrawGraduatedMarketFunds and results in transaction reverting.

title: A user can pay less in fees by
content: The vulnerability resides in the fee distribution logic of the EthosVouch contract. When a user creates a new voucher, a portion of the fee called vouchersPoolFee is meant to be shared among all existing vouchers. The implementation does not differentiate between a fresh vouch and a subsequent increase of an existing vouch, so the caller is treated as an existing voucher even during their own increaseVouch calls. As a result, a malicious user can split a large vouch amount into many small transactions, become an existing voucher after the first small deposit, and then repeatedly call increaseVouch. In each call the contract redistributes a share of vouchersPoolFee back to the caller, effectively reclaiming part of the fee that should have been paid to the protocol and to other voucher holders. The exploit works whenever there is at least one other voucher already present, because the pool fee is calculated based on the total of existing vouchers and then divided among them, including the attacker. From the user’s perspective the symptom is an unexpectedly high net vouch balance: a user who intends to lock 100 ETH expects to lose about 5.86 ETH in fees, but after splitting the deposit into ten 10 ETH increments they only lose roughly 3.32 ETH, saving around 2.54 ETH. The protocol loses the reclaimed fee revenue, and other voucher holders receive less than they should, breaking the economic assumptions of the fee model. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the fee calculation paths and noticed that the same redistribution function is called for both vouch and increaseVouch without excluding the caller. It is hard to notice because the contract still records a fee payment event, but the net effect on the attacker’s balance looks like a bonus rather than a bug. To remediate the problem the fee logic should be changed so that the caller is excluded from the vouchersPoolFee distribution during their own transactions, or a separate fee pool should be used for increases that does not reward the initiator. This change restores the intended fee structure and protects the protocol’s revenue and the fairness of the voucher system.
summary:
A vulnerability in the EthosVouch fee mechanism allows users to reduce fees when vouching a subject. By splitting their vouching process into multiple smaller transactions, users can partially reclaim vouchersPoolFee, resulting in significantly lower total fees compared to a single large transaction. This exploit undermines the intended fee structure and results in financial losses for other previous vouchers.  
The vouchersPoolFee is redistributed to existing vouchers. By vouching with a smaller value initially, a user becomes an existing voucher and subsequently benefits from vouchersPoolFee in subsequent EthosVouch::increaseVouch calls. The logic does not distinguish between fees for new vouches and subsequent increases, enabling fee circumvention.

Internal pre-conditions  
None

External pre-conditions  
1. There is at least one other existing voucher to receive part of the vouchersPoolFee.

Attack Path  
1. A user initially vouches with a smaller value (e.g., 10 ETH instead of the intended 100 ETH).  
2. The user becomes an existing voucher and receives part of the vouchersPoolFee.  
3. The user repeatedly calls increaseVouch in smaller increments (e.g., 10 ETH per transaction) to reach the intended total vouch value.  
4. In each increaseVouch call, the user reclaims part of the vouchersPoolFee, significantly reducing the total fees paid.  
5. Existing vouchers lose part of the intended fee revenue. In the provided example, the user saves approximately 2.54 ETH in fees for a 100 ETH vouch.

title: Unsafe Type Casting in Token
content: The vulnerability is an unsafe down‑casting oftoken amounts from a 256‑bit unsigned integer (uint256) to a 160‑bit unsigned integer (uint160) in several order‑handling functions. The contracts accept a user‑supplied amountIn as uint256, then directly cast it to uint160 when calling Permit2.transferFrom. Because Solidity 0.8.x only checks arithmetic overflow, it does not validate data loss during type conversion, so any amount larger than 2^160‑1 is silently truncated to the low 160 bits. When an attacker supplies an amount that exceeds the uint160 maximum, the cast produces a very small value (often the minimum position size) while the order bookkeeping still records the original large amount. The contract therefore transfers only a tiny token amount but believes it has received the full amount, allowing the attacker to later modify or cancel the order and withdraw the remaining tokens that were never locked. This mismatch can be exploited by creating an order with a malicious amount, relying on the overflow to pay almost nothing, and then draining the protocol’s token reserves. The impact is financial loss for the protocol and any users relying on correct accounting, as the protocol’s liquidity pool ends up under‑collateralized. The condition occurs in any function that performs the unsafe cast, such as createOrder, modifyOrder, and procureTokens in the StopLimit, Bracket, and OracleLess contracts, whenever the supplied amount exceeds type(uint160).max. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that flagged direct casts without safety checks. It is hard to notice because the transaction does not revert; it succeeds and appears to transfer the requested amount, while the internal accounting is wrong, leading to subtle balance discrepancies that only surface when orders are settled or modified. From a user’s perspective the UI may show an order with a large amount but the contract actually holds only a few tokens, resulting in unexpected zero refunds or missing balances. The bug belongs to the class of unsafe type‑casting or truncation vulnerabilities that cause data loss and accounting errors. The recommended remediation is to replace the raw cast with OpenZeppelin’s SafeCast library or explicit checks that ensure the amount fits within uint160 before casting, thereby preserving the intended amount and preventing the overflow from being exploited.

title: Splitter: Anyone can call incrementWindow to steal the tokens in the contract
content: The vulnerability lies in the Splitter contract’s incrementWindow function, which is intended to be triggered only when a legitimate RoyaltyVault deposits tokens into the contract. The function verifies that the caller implements the RoyaltyVault interface and that its getSplitter method returns the Splitter’s address, but it does not enforce that the caller is an authorized, specific vault contract. As a result, an attacker can deploy a counterfeit contract that pretends to be a RoyaltyVault, makes getSplitter return the correct Splitter address, and successfully call incrementWindow with an arbitrary royaltyAmount. The function then records this amount in the balanceForWindow array and advances the window counter without requiring the corresponding tokens to be present in the Splitter’s balance. Because the recorded per‑window balances can now exceed the actual token balance, any user who later invokes claim or claimForAllWindows will be able to withdraw more tokens than the contract holds, effectively allowing the attacker to steal the excess tokens. This flaw manifests whenever a malicious contract is able to call incrementWindow after the Splitter has been deployed, i.e., under any normal blockchain execution environment where the attacker can publish a contract. The primary victims are honest participants and the protocol itself, as they lose funds that they expected to be split according to the royalty logic. The issue was uncovered during a security audit that examined the access control of the function; it is subtle because the interface check appears reasonable and the contract’s state variables are updated in a way that looks consistent with token balances, making the discrepancy hard to notice without tracing the source of royaltyAmount values. To remediate the problem, the contract should restrict incrementWindow to calls from a known RoyaltyVault address, for example by adding an onlyRoyaltyVault modifier that checks msg.sender against a whitelist or immutable vault address, or by employing a robust access‑control pattern such as OpenZeppelin’s Ownable or AccessControl. By ensuring that only the intended vault can increment windows, the recorded balances will always reflect actual token deposits, preserving the accounting invariants and preventing unauthorized fund extraction. In user‑facing terms, a victim may observe that after attempting to claim their share, they receive more tokens than expected, or that the contract’s total balance suddenly drops to zero while claim transactions still succeed, indicating a breach of the expected “balance equals sum of windows” guarantee. The vulnerability belongs to the broader class of improper authorization or trust‑boundary bugs, where reliance on an interface identifier alone is insufficient to guarantee the caller’s authenticity.

title: DoS: `claimForAllWindows`
content:
The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition in the royalty distribution contract that arises from an unbounded iteration over all recorded royalty windows. The contract stores a monotonically increasing counter called `currentWindow` that represents the number of royalty periods for which funds have been deposited. The public function `claimForAllWindows()` loops from zero up to `currentWindow` and attempts to claim any unclaimed balance for the caller. Because the loop does not impose a hard limit or pagination, the gas required to iterate over the array grows linearly with the number of windows. When `currentWindow` becomes sufficiently large, the transaction exceeds the block gas limit and the function can no longer be executed, effectively locking out all legitimate royalty claimants.

The root cause is two‑fold. First, the contract permits the counter to be increased without a strict access control: any address that can satisfy a weak interface check (`IRoyaltyVault` support and matching splitter address) can call `incrementWindow()` and raise `currentWindow` by one, even if the caller only sends a trivial amount of WETH (as little as 1 wei). Second, the claim function assumes that iterating over every window is always feasible, which is not true once the counter grows beyond what a single transaction can afford.

An attacker can exploit this by repeatedly invoking `incrementWindow()`—either directly or by deploying multiple contracts that appear to implement the `IRoyaltyVault` interface—to inflate `currentWindow` to a very high value. Once the counter reaches a size that requires more gas than the block limit to process, any call to `claimForAllWindows()` will run out of gas and revert. Consequently, royalty recipients are unable to withdraw their funds, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions that all royalties can be claimed in one step are broken. From the user’s perspective the claim button appears to do nothing, transactions fail with out‑of‑gas errors, and balances shown in the UI remain unchanged, giving the impression that “funds disappear” or that “refunds are missing”.

The issue was discovered during a formal audit when the reviewers inspected the for‑loop in `claimForAllWindows()` and noticed that the loop bound is the mutable `currentWindow`. They also observed that the `incrementWindow()` function’s authorization checks can be bypassed by a contract that simply pretends to be a royalty vault, allowing an attacker to grow the counter at will. The problem is subtle because the function works correctly when the number of windows is small; only after many increments does the gas consumption become prohibitive, making the failure mode appear only after a period of normal operation.

To remediate the problem, the claim logic should be refactored to operate on a bounded range of windows supplied by the caller, for example `claimForWindows(uint256 startWindow, uint256 endWindow, ...)`, with a requirement that `endWindow` is less than `currentWindow`. This pagination limits the gas cost of each claim transaction. Additionally, the `incrementWindow()` function should enforce stricter access control, ensuring that only trusted royalty vault contracts can increase the window counter, or at least limit how frequently the counter can be incremented. By capping the number of windows processed per transaction and tightening authorization, the protocol restores the ability for users to claim royalties reliably and prevents the denial‑of‑service condition caused by an ever‑growing loop.
summary:
When the value of `currentWindow` is raised sufficiently high `Splitter.claimForAllWindows()` will not be able to be called due to the block gas limit.

`currentWindow` can only ever be incremented and thus will always increase. This value will naturally increase as royalties are paid into the contract.

Furthermore, an attacker can continually increment `currentWindow` by calling `incrementWindow()`. An attacker can impersonate a `IRoyaltyVault` and send 1 WEI worth of WETH to pass the required checks.

title: CoreCollection can be reinitialized
content: The contract contains a re‑initialization flaw in its CoreCollection module. The initialize function is designed to be called once to set up critical state variables such as the payableToken address, which governs the contract’s ability to withdraw all stored ether. Although the function marks an internal initialized flag, it does not enforce a check that prevents subsequent executions. Consequently, the owner can invoke initialize repeatedly, overwriting the previously stored values. This root cause stems from a missing onlyUninitialized guard, allowing the same code path to be executed after the contract has already been configured. An attacker with ownership privileges – either the legitimate owner acting mistakenly or with malicious intent – can exploit the flaw by calling initialize a second time and supplying a new payableToken address that points to an address under their control. Once the token reference is altered, any withdrawal routine that relies on payableToken will transfer the entire contract balance to the attacker‑controlled address, effectively draining funds. The impact is a total loss of user deposits and a breach of the protocol’s accounting assumptions that the payable token remains immutable after deployment. The vulnerability manifests only when the initialize function is called after the first successful run; normal operation before that point behaves as expected. All participants who trust the contract to safeguard their assets – end‑users, liquidity providers, and downstream protocol components – are affected because the contract’s core financial flow can be redirected without notice. The issue was identified during a security audit that reviewed the contract’s initialization logic and spotted the absence of a re‑entrancy‑style guard on the flag. It can be hard to notice because the function is protected by onlyOwner, leading reviewers to assume that owner‑only calls are benign, and because the contract may appear functional until a re‑initialization is performed. To remediate, the initialize routine should be guarded by a modifier that ensures it can be executed only when the initialized flag is false (e.g., onlyUninitialized) and should reject further calls after the first successful setup. This change restores the invariant that core variables such as payableToken are immutable after deployment, preserving the intended financial guarantees. From a user’s perspective, the symptom of this bug would be a sudden loss of funds where a withdrawal that previously returned the expected amount now sends zero or transfers the balance to an unknown address, contradicting the expectation that the contract will retain and correctly disburse funds. The bug belongs to the class of "unprotected re‑initialization" or "initialization‑override" vulnerabilities, which violate the assumption that contract configuration is a one‑time operation.
summary:
Reinitialization is possible for CoreCollection as `initialize` function sets `initialized` flag, but doesn’t control for it, so the function can be rerun multiple times.

Such types of issues tend to be critical as all core variables can be reset this way, for example `payableToken`, which provides a way to retrieve all the contract funds.

However, setting priority to be medium as `initialize` is `onlyOwner`. A run by an external attacker this way is prohibited, but the possibility of owner initiated reset either by mistake or with a malicious intent remains with the same range of system breaking consequences.

title: ERC20 transferFrom return values not checked
content:
The vulnerability consists of an unchecked boolean result from ERC20 transferFrom calls made by the contract when it attempts to collect payment before minting new tokens. In many ERC20 implementations a failed transfer causes the function to revert, which automatically aborts the surrounding transaction. However, a subset of tokens – for example EURS and BAT – follow the original ERC20 specification and simply return false when the transfer cannot be performed, without throwing. The contract’s logic assumes that a successful call will always indicate a completed transfer, but it never inspects the returned value. Consequently, if a caller supplies a token that returns false on a failed transfer, the contract proceeds as if the payment succeeded, allowing the minting function to execute and credit the user with newly minted assets while the expected payment never left the payer’s balance. This flaw is rooted in the omission of a safety check on an external call’s return data, a classic instance of an unchecked external call that can silently fail.

Exploitation is straightforward: an attacker or a malicious project creator can choose a payable token that either deliberately returns false on every transfer or fails under certain conditions (e.g., insufficient allowance). When the user invokes the minting operation, the contract calls transferFrom, receives false, ignores it, and still mints the requested amount. From the user’s perspective the UI shows a successful mint, the transaction receipt reports success, yet the user’s wallet shows no deduction of the payment token and the protocol’s accounting records reflect an unearned token issuance. The expected behavior – payment taken and token minted – is violated; the reality is a free token mint, causing revenue loss and breaking accounting invariants of the protocol.

The bug manifests only when the contract relies on ERC20 tokens that do not revert on failure. It affects any participant who attempts to acquire tokens through the payment pathway, the protocol’s revenue model, and any downstream contracts that trust the minted token supply to represent actual paid value. The issue was uncovered during a formal audit where the auditor noted that transferFrom return values were never evaluated, contrasting with a proper pattern where both transfer and transferFrom results are verified or wrapped in OpenZeppelin’s SafeERC20 library. The problem can be difficult to spot because many popular tokens do revert on failure, leading developers to assume this behavior is universal; static analysis tools may not flag the missing check as a vulnerability unless they have specific ERC20 heuristics.

Remediation requires adding explicit verification of the boolean returned by transferFrom (and transfer) or, preferably, replacing raw calls with SafeERC20.safeTransferFrom, which automatically reverts on false returns and also accommodates tokens that do not return any value. By ensuring that a failed transfer aborts the minting flow, the protocol restores its intended economic guarantees and prevents unauthorized token creation. The broader class of this bug is “unchecked return value from an external token transfer call,” which can lead to silent failures and unintended state changes across many smart‑contract systems.
summary:
The `transferFrom()` function returns a boolean value indicating success. This parameter needs to be checked to see if the transfer has been successful. Oddly, `transfer()` function calls were checked.

Some tokens like [EURS](https://etherscan.io/address/0xdb25f211ab05b1c97d595516f45794528a807ad8#code) and [BAT](https://etherscan.io/address/0x0d8775f648430679a709e98d2b0cb6250d2887ef#code) will **not** revert if the transfer failed but return `false` instead. Tokens that don’t actually perform the transfer and return `false` are still counted as a correct transfer.

title: Attackers can drain the
content: The vulnerability is an unchecked input flaw in the order creation and execution flow of the OracleLess contract. The createOrder function accepts any address as tokenIn without confirming that the address implements a standard ERC20 interface, and the fillOrder function similarly accepts arbitrary target addresses and raw transaction data (txData) without validation. Because of this, an attacker can deploy a malicious ERC20 token whose approve function contains side‑effects, such as transferring a small amount of WETH to the contract, and then craft an order that uses this token as the input asset. The attacker sets tokenOut to a legitimate stablecoin (for example USDT) and sets the minimum amount out to zero, then calls fillOrder with the target set to the USDT contract and txData crafted to transfer the entire USDT balance from the OracleLess contract to the attacker’s address. Inside fillOrder the execute helper records the pre‑execution balances, calls safeApprove on the malicious token (triggering the side‑effect), and then performs a low‑level call to the target with the attacker‑controlled txData. The call succeeds, moving all USDT out of the contract. After the call the accounting checks compare the final token balances against the recorded pre‑execution values; because the attacker set minAmountOut to zero and the malicious approve added a tiny amount of WETH, the require statements are satisfied and the function returns without reverting. The result is that the contract’s USDT balance is drained while the user‑facing behavior appears normal: a user who initiates a swap sees no refund, receives zero output, or notices that the contract’s USDT balance has vanished. The issue occurs whenever fillOrder is invoked with unvalidated tokenIn, target, or txData, meaning any attacker who can deploy a contract can exploit it. The affected parties are the protocol itself and any users who rely on the contract to safely swap assets, as their funds can disappear without warning. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the lack of whitelist or sanity checks in the order lifecycle functions. It is subtle because the contract’s accounting logic seems sound and the ERC20 interface is used, making the malicious behavior of approve easy to overlook. To remediate, the contract should enforce a whitelist of approved token contracts, restrict target addresses to known safe contracts, validate that txData corresponds to expected function signatures, and avoid using approve‑then‑call patterns for token transfers; instead, direct safeTransferFrom calls or a trusted router should be employed. This would prevent arbitrary code execution and stop attackers from draining assets through crafted orders.

title: Lack of nonReentrant modifier
content: The vulnerability is a missing reentrancy guard on the fillOrder and modifyOrder functions of the OracleLess contract, which allows an attacker to invoke fillOrder with a malicious target contract and arbitrary calldata, causing the target to call back into modifyOrder while the original execution is still in progress. The root cause is that both functions are public and lack the OpenZeppelin nonReentrant modifier, so the contract does not prevent nested calls that can alter order state before the outer call finishes. An attacker can create two orders that they control, set the recipient of each order to a contract they own, and then trigger fillOrder on the first order with calldata that executes a function in the malicious contract. Inside that function the attacker first calls modifyOrder to reduce the position of the first order, extracting most of the WETH deposited by the victim, then calls modifyOrder on the second order to increase its position and park the extracted WETH, while sending only a minimal amount of USDC back to satisfy the finalTokenIn >= initialTokenIn - order.amountIn check. After the re‑entered calls return, fillOrder continues, removes the first attacker order and returns the tiny USDC amount, leaving the victim’s order unchanged. The attacker then cancels the second order and withdraws the parked WETH, effectively stealing the victim’s funds without paying any fee. This attack works whenever fillOrder can be called by any address with a controllable target and calldata, and when modifyOrder is also callable without a reentrancy lock, which is the case in the current implementation. The affected parties are the naive users who place orders, the protocol’s liquidity pool, and any entity relying on the correctness of order execution. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that included a proof‑of‑concept test harness exercising reentrancy scenarios; it is hard to notice because the contract’s balance checks appear to succeed and the token transfers seem minimal, masking the underlying state manipulation. The bug belongs to the class of reentrancy vulnerabilities where state changes are performed after an external call without proper protection, violating the assumption that token balances remain consistent throughout execution. To remediate, the fillOrder and modifyOrder functions should be protected with a nonReentrant modifier or equivalent mutex, ensuring that any external call cannot re‑enter the contract and alter order state before the original call completes.
summary:
Root Causes:
1. OracleLess.sol::fillOrder() can be called by anyone with a malicious txData.
2. OracleLess.sol::fillOrder() lacks a nonReentrant modifier.
3. OracleLess.sol::modifyOrder() lacks a nonReentrant modifier.
Attack Path: (Please refer PoC for detailed execution flow)
1. Suppose the current pendingOrderIds looks like:
pendingOrderIds = [N,
A1,
A2]
(array indices)
Order-N is by the victim, a naive user. Orders A1 and A2 are by the attacker.
2. Attacker has made sure the Order-A1 and Order-A2 recipient is a contract with
address say, target.
3. Attacker's Order-A1 is in range so they call fillOrder() with malicious txData.
4. fillOrder() internally calls execute() which internally calls target.call(txData)
where both target and txData are attacker controlled.
5. From inside the target contract (let's say a function named attack()), they pull
tokenIn (WETH) of Order-A1 as they have the approval.
6. attack() then sends 1 wei tokenOut (USDC) or any minimum amount back. The
attacker will get this back later.
7. attack() then calls modifyOrder(Order-A1) and decreases the position size to the
minimum allowed. They are immediately credited say, M WETH.
8. attack() next calls modifyOrder(Order-A2) and increases the position size to park
this M WETH. This is done so that the overall WETH balance of OracleLess contract
is not affected by this theft and the following check about over-spend inside
execute() passes successfully:
require(finalTokenIn >= initialTokenIn - order.amountIn, "over spend");
9. The control now exits attack() and fillOrder() continues further. The code goes
ahead and removes Order-A1 from the pending order array and sends back the 1
wei USDC to target on L141. The attacker is at no loss & no gain right now.
10. The attacker now cancels Order-A2 and receives the M WETH back too, thus stealing
it from the rightful funds of the victim/protocol.
Bracket.sol::performUpkeep() as Bracket.sol::modifyOrder() is protected by the
nonReentrant modifier.
High. Victim & protocol funds can be stolen at no substantial cost to the attacker.

title: Users can modify a cancelled or-
content: The vulnerability is an order‑modification flaw that permits a user to change the parameters of an order after it has been cancelled, resulting in a double withdrawal of the order’s token collateral. The root cause is the absence of a state check in the modifyOrder logic of the Bracket, OracleLess and StopLimit contracts; the function does not verify whether the order’s cancelled flag is set before allowing changes to amountIn. An attacker can exploit this by first creating an order with a large amountIn, then calling the cancel function to withdraw the full token amount, and subsequently invoking modifyOrder to reduce amountIn to a minimal value (for example 1 wei). Because the contract still believes the order holds the original balance, the attacker can call the withdrawal routine again and extract the remaining tokens (original amount minus the tiny new amount). Repeating this cycle drains the contract’s entire token reserve. The impact is a complete loss of funds held by the protocol, affecting all participants who rely on the contract for order execution and token custody. The issue manifests when a user interacts with the order‑modification interface after cancelling an order; the UI may still display the order as editable, leading to unexpected token transfers. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the order lifecycle functions and noted that the cancelled state was never consulted before permitting modifications. The bug is subtle because the modify function appears legitimate and the cancelled flag is only used in the cancel routine, so developers may assume the order cannot be altered after cancellation. To remediate, the contract should enforce a check that rejects any modification request for orders whose cancelled flag is true, and optionally transition the order to a finalised state that disallows further interactions. This aligns the implementation with the intended business logic that a cancelled order should be immutable and that token withdrawals occur exactly once per order.
summary:
In Bracket, OracleLess and StopLimit a user can modify a canceled order, allowing them to withdraw the order tokens twice.
In Bracket, OracleLess and StopLimit there is no validation on whether an order has been canceled before allowing modifications. This allows users to cancel an order, withdrawing all of the tokens, and after that modifying it by reducing the amountIn to 1, withdrawing the rest of the tokens for a second time.
Internal pre-conditions
External pre-conditions
Attack Path
1. User creates an order with amountIn set to 1e18.
2. The user cancels the order, withdrawing 1e18 of the tokens.
3. Finally, they modify the order, decreasing amountIn to 1, withdrawing 1e18 - 1 of the already withdrawn tokens.
4. The attack can be performed several times until all of the contract's tokens are drained.
Bracket, OracleLess and StopLimit can be drained.

title: attacker can drain StopLimit con-
content: The vulnerability is an unlimited‑allowance bug that allows an attacker to drain all token balances held by the StopLimit contract. The root cause lies in the updateApproval function, which checks the current allowance of the Bracket contract for a given input token and, if it is lower than the required amount, calls safeIncreaseAllowance with type(uint256).max minus the current allowance. Because the amount parameter is treated as a delta, this calculation effectively raises the allowance to almost the maximum possible value for the Bracket contract. After a stop‑limit order is filled, the Bracket contract transfers the required input tokens from the StopLimit contract to itself, but the inflated allowance remains unchanged. An attacker can then craft a malicious order where the tokenOut field matches a token for which the Bracket contract already holds this near‑max allowance. By invoking performUpkeep on the Bracket contract with a target address set to the token contract and txData that calls transferFrom with the StopLimit contract as the source and the Bracket contract as the destination, the attacker triggers an external call that moves the entire token balance from the StopLimit contract to the Bracket contract. The execute function records the received amount as swapAmountOut, passes the fee check (feeBips set to zero), and finally transfers the swapped tokens to the attacker‑specified recipient. This sequence can be executed repeatedly for each token that received the inflated allowance, resulting in a complete drain of the StopLimit contract’s funds. The issue manifests whenever a stop‑limit order is successfully executed and the allowance update logic runs, which is after any order that calls fillStopLimitOrder. It affects all users of the protocol who rely on the StopLimit contract to hold their assets, as well as the protocol itself, because the accounting assumptions that token balances are only moved according to order logic are violated. The bug was discovered during a manual audit by reviewing the allowance‑increase code and tracing the flow of token transfers through the Bracket contract. It is hard to notice because the allowance increase appears to be a safety measure to ensure sufficient allowance for legitimate transfers, yet the use of type(uint256).max as a delta is unusual and not guarded by any caps or resets. To remediate, the StopLimit contract should only increase the allowance by the exact amount needed for the immediate fill operation, or reset/revoke the allowance after the transfer, avoiding the use of a near‑maximum allowance that can be abused to move arbitrary token amounts.

title: Failure to reset unspent approval
content: The vulnerability is an approval‑reset omission in the order execution routine. When the contract prepares to call an external target it grants the target an allowance equal to the full input token amount, but after the external call returns it never clears that allowance. Because the allowance remains non‑zero, a malicious target contract can later invoke transferFrom on the token and move any remaining approved tokens out of the order contract. The root cause is the missing safeApprove(target,0) statement after the external call, which violates the principle of least privilege and leaves a dangling permission. An attacker can exploit this by creating a contract that accepts the order, receives the approved tokens, and then calls transferFrom on the token to drain the leftover balance. The attack flow is: (1) attacker creates a malicious contract; (2) attacker creates an order with a small amount of input token and a minimal output requirement; (3) the order is filled using the malicious contract as the target; (4) the contract approves the target for the full input amount, the call succeeds, and the order logic refunds any unspent input; (5) because the approval is never revoked, the malicious contract calls transferFrom to pull the unspent tokens; (6) the attacker repeats the process, eventually emptying the contract’s token holdings. The impact is a complete loss of funds for the protocol and any users who placed orders, as the contract balance can be drained repeatedly. This occurs whenever an order is filled with a target that does not consume the full approved amount, which is common when the target contract’s logic is simple or when the order’s minAmountOut is set to a negligible value. All participants—order creators, the protocol’s treasury, and downstream users—are affected because their tokens can be stolen without any on‑chain indication other than a reduction in balance. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the execute function and noticed that the allowance was never reset after the external call. It is easy to miss because the contract’s accounting appears correct: the refund calculation uses balance differences, and the transaction does not revert, so the leftover allowance is invisible to standard tests that only check balances. The bug belongs to the class of “unrevoked token allowance” or “approval race” vulnerabilities, where a contract grants a spender more rights than necessary and fails to clean up, breaking the expected accounting invariants. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after filling an order they may see their token balance reduced dramatically or even to zero, while the transaction receipt shows a successful order and a refund amount that seems correct. The expectation that the contract will only spend the exact amount specified is violated, leading to funds disappearing. The proper fix is to reset the token allowance to zero immediately after the external call, or to use the ERC20 permit pattern or safeIncreaseAllowance/ safeDecreaseAllowance to limit the granted amount to the exact amount needed for the call, thereby restoring the principle of least privilege and preventing leftover approvals from being abused.

title: stopLimit Id collision with bracket
content: The vulnerability is an order identifier collision that occurs because both the StopLimit and Bracket contracts generate order IDs using a deterministic hash of only the current block number and the caller address. This hash provides no contract‑specific entropy, so when the same user creates orders in the two contracts within the same block, the resulting uint96 identifiers are identical. The root cause is the shared AutomationMaster function that lacks a per‑contract salt or a nonce, making the identifier predictable and repeatable across contracts. An attacker with MEV capabilities can exploit this by submitting a Bracket order and a StopLimit order in the same block, causing both to receive the same orderId. Because the Bracket contract stores orders in a mapping keyed by orderId, the StopLimit order later invokes the Bracket’s fill routine with the colliding identifier. When the attacker calls cancelOrder on the shared orderId, the Bracket contract processes the refund for the first order and, due to the collision, does not recognise that the order has already been settled. A second cancel call with the same identifier succeeds again, resulting in a double refund. The impact is a double‑spend of user funds, corruption of the protocol’s accounting state, and potential financial loss for the platform. The issue manifests only when two orders from the same address are created in the same block, a condition that can be orchestrated by an attacker who can control transaction ordering. All participants that rely on the order mapping – the protocol, its users, and any downstream contracts – are affected because the accounting invariants are broken. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the dual‑contract architecture, where the auditor noticed that the orderId generation did not incorporate any contract‑specific data. It is hard to notice because the identifier appears unique per user per block, and the mapping lookup succeeds, giving the illusion that the order is valid. The proper fix is to add contract address and a monotonically increasing nonce to the hash input, ensuring that each contract produces a distinct namespace for order IDs and that repeated calls cannot generate the same identifier. By separating the identifier space, the double‑refund path is eliminated and the accounting model remains sound. From a user perspective the symptom is that a refund may be received twice, balances may drop unexpectedly, or an order appears to be cancelled but still shows as active, contradicting the expectation that a single cancellation refunds the exact amount once.

title: Insecure calls to safeTransfer
content: The vulnerability is an insecure token transfer pattern in the order‑handling functions of the protocol. The contract calls the ERC‑1155 (or ERC‑20) safeTransferFrom method using an address supplied in the order data as the token source, rather than the transaction sender (msg.sender). Because the contract does not verify that the caller of createOrder or modifyOrder is the same address that is being debited, an attacker can craft an order that lists a victim’s address as the recipient/owner and specifies a transfer amount that is less than or equal to the victim’s previously granted allowance. When the protocol processes the order, it invokes safeTransferFrom and moves the victim’s tokens into the protocol’s vault. The attacker then immediately fills the order, receiving the transferred assets and profiting at the expense of the victim, whose token balance is reduced without any action on their part. This flaw arises from missing ownership checks and reliance on external allowance data instead of the caller’s identity. It can be exploited whenever a user has approved a token allowance that exceeds the amount needed for a legitimate trade, and the attacker can invoke the order‑creation or order‑modification functions. The impact is a direct loss of funds for the affected user, erosion of trust in the protocol, and potential financial liability for the platform. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that tokens disappear from their wallet after they have merely approved a contract, and an order appears to be filled without their consent, often showing a zero or unexpectedly low balance. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the call sites of safeTransferFrom in OracleLess.sol, StopLimit.sol and Bracket.sol and noted the absence of a msg.sender check. It is hard to notice because the token transfer itself succeeds and the allowance check is performed by the token contract, not the protocol, so the flow looks legitimate. The proper remediation is to enforce that the token source address equals msg.sender, either by passing msg.sender directly to safeTransferFrom or by adding explicit require statements that compare the order’s owner field with msg.sender before any transfer occurs. This change ensures that only the account that created or modified the order can have its tokens moved, eliminating the possibility of an attacker stealing tokens via a crafted order.

title: Lender group members can be
content: The vulnerability consists of an indefinite reset of the withdrawal delay mechanism in lender group contracts caused by zero‑value token transfers that invoke the afterTokenTransfer hook. The contract requires a lender to call prepareSharesForBurn, which records the amount of shares to withdraw and stores a timestamp. A separate function burn checks that the stored timestamp is older than the configured delay before allowing the withdrawal. However, the internal _afterTokenTransfer hook clears the prepared‑withdrawal amount and timestamp for the sender on every token transfer, without checking the transferred amount. Because OpenZeppelin ERC20.transferFrom does not reject a transfer of 0 tokens, an attacker can repeatedly call transferFrom(victim, attacker, 0) just before the countdown expires. Each call triggers the hook, resetting the victim’s timestamp and prepared amount, forcing the victim to re‑initiate the withdrawal process. By continuing this pattern, the attacker can keep the victim’s shares locked indefinitely, or until the victim pays a bribe to stop the attacks. The impact is that lender group members lose access to their earnings; the UI may show that a withdrawal request was prepared, but when the user attempts to claim the earnings the transaction reverts with a message such as "Shares not prepared for withdraw" or the request appears to have been cleared, leading to confusion because the user expects to receive funds after the delay but receives nothing. The issue occurs whenever a lender has called prepareSharesForBurn and any external address can invoke transferFrom on the share token. Affected parties are all lenders who rely on the delayed withdrawal mechanism to retrieve earnings. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the afterTokenTransfer hook and noted the absence of a zero‑value check, making the bug subtle because a zero‑value transfer does not change balances and therefore looks harmless in transaction logs, yet it still triggers state‑reset logic. This is a class of bug where an unchecked state reset is triggered by a side‑effect of a token‑transfer hook combined with missing input validation for zero amounts. To remediate, the hook should early‑return when amount == 0, or the contract should protect the prepared‑withdrawal state from being cleared by transfers that do not move value. Conceptually, the fix restores the invariant that a prepared withdrawal remains valid for the configured delay, preserving the accounting assumption that only actual share movements affect the withdrawal timer. From the user’s perspective the failure mode appears as a "withdrawal lockout" or "funds disappear" symptom, violating business logic that guarantees access to earnings after a known waiting period.

title: Malicious lender can pre- vent borrower from repayment due to try/catch block revert Source: Found by OpaBatyo, hash
content: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service flaw in the loan repayment flow that allows a malicious lender to block a borrower from repaying a loan. The contract stores an external address called a repayment listener and, when a borrower calls repayLoan, it invokes the listener via a try/catch block with a fixed gas stipend. Before the listener is set, the protocol checks that the address contains contract code by using extcodesize, and the try/catch is expected to catch any failure of the external call. However, the check is performed only at the moment the listener is registered. A lender can deploy a contract that includes a self‑destruct function, register this contract as the repayment listener, and then self‑destruct the contract in the same transaction. Because the self‑destruct removes the bytecode after the extcodesize check has passed, the subsequent try/catch call is made to a non‑contract address. In Solidity, a try/catch on an external call reverts when the target address has no code, so the call always reverts and the catch block is never reached. As a result, the borrower’s repayment transaction fails, the loan remains unpaid, and the protocol may treat the loan as defaulted, allowing the lender to claim the collateral. The issue occurs only when the lender controls the repayment listener and can destroy it within the same transaction, which is possible for any lender that can deploy arbitrary contracts. Borrowers are affected because they see their repayment transaction revert (often with a generic “NR gas” or other revert message) even though they have sufficient funds and gas, leading to unexpected zero balances or missing repayment records. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the TellerV2 contract by the auditor Sherlock, who noted that the extcodesize validation does not guarantee the listener remains a contract at call time. The problem is hard to notice because the try/catch construct appears to provide safety, and the extcodesize check seems to enforce a contract address, masking the timing window where the contract can disappear. To remediate, the protocol should avoid relying on try/catch for external callbacks and instead use a low‑level .call that returns a boolean success flag, or move the validation to the moment of the call, or eliminate the external listener altogether. Conceptually, the fix is to ensure that the repayment logic does not depend on an address that can become non‑contract between registration and execution, thereby restoring the borrower’s ability to repay and preserving the intended accounting guarantees of the loan system.

title: Using original principal amount
content: The vulnerability consists of an accounting error in the liquidation routine of a lending protocol. When a defaulted loan is liquidated the function liquidateDefaultedLoanWithIncentive retrieves the amount due by calling _getAmountOwedForBid, which returns the original principal amount recorded at loan creation. This value is used even if the borrower has already repaid part of the principal. Consequently the repayment callback later adds the repaid principal to totalPrincipalTokensRepaid, while the liquidation logic also treats the full original principal as still owed. The result is a double‑counting of principal in the global accounting variables totalPrincipalTokensRepaid and tokenDifferenceFromLiquidations. Because totalPrincipalTokensRepaid can become larger than totalPrincipalTokensLended, the expression totalPrincipalTokensLended‑totalPrincipalTokensRepaid underflows, causing new bids to revert and withdrawals to calculate a negative or zero available balance. In practice a lender may see that the contract holds tokens but the UI reports zero withdrawable amount, or attempts to withdraw trigger a revert or a division‑by‑zero error when estimated values collapse to zero. The bug is triggered only when a loan is partially repaid before it defaults; if the loan defaults without any prior repayment the accounting remains correct. The affected parties are lenders who expect to retrieve their deposited assets, borrowers who may be unable to close positions, and the protocol itself which can halt new loan creation and lose funds. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the liquidation path, where the auditor noticed that the amountDue variable was derived from the static loan summary rather than the dynamic remaining principal. The problem is subtle because the contract’s external balances appear unchanged, while internal counters diverge, making the failure visible only under specific repayment‑then‑default scenarios. The appropriate remediation is to compute the amount due as the remaining principal, i.e., original principal minus the amount already repaid, and to adjust the accounting updates so that totalPrincipalTokensRepaid never exceeds the total principal that has been lent. This brings the accounting back in line with the business logic that lenders should be able to withdraw the exact amount of assets that remain after repayments and liquidations.

title: A single depositor can grief other
content: The vulnerability is a logic error in the withdrawal flow of the Idle Credit Vault that allows a depositor to claim a withdrawal request immediately after it is made, even though the first epoch of the pool has not yet finished. The root cause is that the claimWithdrawRequest function checks the epoch end date and the epoch number against the lastWithdrawRequest mapping, but when the contract is first initialized the epochEndDate variable is zero. Because the condition "epochEndDate != 0 && (epochNumber <= lastWithdrawRequest[_user])" evaluates to false, the function does not block a claim made in the same epoch in which the request was created. An attacker can therefore deposit liquidity before the first epoch starts, request a full withdrawal, and call claimWithdrawRequest right away. The contract then pays out the principal plus the interest that would only have been earned after the epoch, and this extra amount is taken from the deposits of all other participants that are still waiting for the epoch to finish. The impact is that the pool’s total liquidity is drained, other users see their balances shrink or become zero, and the protocol loses trust because funds disappear without any explicit error. The exploit can be performed repeatedly: after each claim the attacker redeposits the received amount and repeats the request‑claim cycle, continuously siphoning liquidity from honest depositors. The vulnerability manifests only before any epoch has been started; once epochEndDate is set to a non‑zero timestamp the check works as intended. All depositors, the protocol’s liquidity providers, and any downstream users of the vault are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the tester wrote a proof‑of‑concept test that repeatedly deposited, requested, and claimed withdrawals before the first epoch, observing that the vault balance decreased while the attacker’s balance grew beyond the original deposit. The bug is subtle because the function appears to enforce a time lock, yet the uninitialized epochEndDate silently disables the protection, making it easy to miss in casual testing. To fix the problem the contract should initialise epochEndDate to the current block timestamp during deployment (or otherwise enforce that claimWithdrawRequest can only be called after the epoch end), ensuring that the early‑withdrawal guard is active from the start. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of “epoch timing bypass” or “premature claim” logic flaws where a state variable that controls access is left at its default value, allowing unauthorized actions that break the intended accounting guarantees of the system.

title: _requestedTip is not deduced
content: The vulnerability is an accounting omission in the GovernanceStaker contract where the bumpEarningPower function transfers a tip to a designated receiver but never deducts the requested tip amount from the depositor's unclaimed reward balance. The root cause is a missing state update after the SafeERC20.safeTransfer call; the contract checks that the depositor has sufficient unclaimed rewards to cover the tip, yet it does not adjust deposit.scaledUnclaimedRewardCheckpoint (or the equivalent reward accounting variable) to reflect the transferred tip. An attacker, typically a keeper, can exploit this by invoking bumpEarningPower with a non‑zero tip; the tip is sent out of the contract while the depositor’s internal reward counter remains unchanged, allowing the same rewards to be claimed later by the depositor or to be repeatedly siphoned by successive tip payments. Over time this leads to rewards insolvency: legitimate participants who have delegated to inactive delegatees may find that their expected rewards are unavailable, claim transactions revert with insufficient rewards, or the claimed amount is lower than displayed in the UI. The issue manifests whenever bumpEarningPower is called with a tip that passes the pre‑condition checks, affecting any depositor whose earnings are being bumped and any keeper who can trigger the function. It was discovered during a manual audit by Sherlock, who noted that the tip transfer succeeded but the accounting variable was never updated, a subtle bug that can be missed because external balances appear correct while internal bookkeeping diverges. The problem is hard to notice because the contract does not emit an explicit error; users only see a mismatch between the displayed reward balance and the amount they can actually claim. To remediate, the contract should subtract the tip from the depositor’s scaled unclaimed reward checkpoint (or the appropriate reward state) immediately after the transfer, ensuring that the total rewards pool remains consistent with the sum of individual balances. This class of bug falls under missing state mutation after an external token transfer, leading to double‑spending of reward tokens and violating the protocol’s accounting invariants that each depositor’s claimable amount must never exceed the total rewards allocated to them. From the user’s perspective, the UI may show a positive reward amount, the user expects to receive that amount, but the transaction either returns zero or a smaller amount, effectively causing funds to disappear or refunds to be missing.

title: Updating earning power for de-
content: The vulnerability is an accounting flaw that allows a participant to manipulate the reward distribution by changing the delegatee or claimer of a deposit without updating the global reward checkpoint. The root cause is that the internal functions responsible for altering a deposit’s delegatee (_alterDelegatee) and claimer (_alterClaimer) do not invoke the reward‑checkpointing logic that recalculates rewardsPerTokenAccumulated based on the current total earning power. When the earning power of the system changes – for example when a user temporarily delegates to a delegatee with zero eligibility score – the total earning power drops, but the global reward state is not refreshed. An attacker can exploit this by (1) delegating a sizable position to a zero‑score delegatee, (2) triggering a global reward checkpoint indirectly (such as by opening a tiny new position), (3) re‑delegating back to a valid delegatee, and (4) claiming rewards that were calculated with the artificially reduced total earning power. Because the rewards per token were computed on a lower denominator, the attacker receives a larger share than entitled, effectively draining the rewards that should have been allocated to all other participants. This can be repeated until the reward pool is exhausted. The impact is a loss of earned tokens for honest users, a breach of the protocol’s incentive guarantees, and a breakdown of the accounting assumptions that rewards are proportional to earning power. The issue manifests only when the BinaryEligibilityOracleEarningPowerCalculator is used and when there exist delegatees with a zero score, allowing the temporary reduction of total earning power. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are missing or unexpectedly low reward balances for regular participants, while the attacker may see an unusually high reward payout. The bug is difficult to notice because the sequence of delegatee changes is uncommon in normal operation and the reward numbers appear correct for the attacker, masking the loss for others. The flaw was discovered during a security audit when the reviewer observed that the reward‑checkpoint calls were omitted in the delegatee/claimer alteration paths. To remediate the issue the protocol should add calls to _checkpointGlobalReward and _checkpointReward inside both _alterDelegatee and _alterClaimer, ensuring that the reward state is updated before any delegatee or claimer change, thereby preserving the correct proportional distribution of rewards.
