title: Depositing to IdleCDO is vulnerable to inflation attacks
content: Depositing to the IdleCDO contract suffers from a share‑price inflation vulnerability that can be exploited when the total supply of a tranche token is zero. The contract determines the price of each tranche by dividing the contract’s token balance (obtained via balanceOf(address(this))) by the total supply of the tranche. Because the balance includes any tokens transferred directly to the contract, an attacker can first make a minimal deposit (for example 1 wei) to obtain a single share, then transfer a large amount of the underlying asset to the contract before another user’s deposit is processed. This external donation inflates the reported tranche price; when the subsequent user’s deposit is executed the _mintShares function calculates the number of shares as deposited amount divided by the inflated price, which can result in zero shares being minted. From the user’s perspective the transaction succeeds but the user receives no tranche tokens and their underlying assets are effectively lost, appearing as funds disappear or refund missing. The attack requires the tranche’s totalSupply to be zero, the attacker to be the first depositor, and the ability to front‑run the victim’s transaction, conditions that are common during the initial bootstrapping of a new tranche. The issue was discovered during a manual audit and reproduced with a test that donates assets after the first mint. It is hard to notice because the contract’s external view of total assets shows a higher value, giving the impression of healthy liquidity, while the internal accounting for share issuance is broken. The vulnerability belongs to the class of price‑manipulation or inflation attacks caused by using mutable on‑chain balances for price calculations without isolating external transfers. The impact includes loss of user deposits, distortion of accounting, and potential rounding losses for non‑integer multiples of the inflated price. Mitigation involves preventing the first mint from using a zero‑supply price, enforcing a minimum amount of shares to be minted on the initial deposit, or computing NAV based on internal accounting that excludes unsolicited token transfers. Implementing a minimum share burn or ignoring direct token donations in the price formula would close the attack vector.

title: H-01 | tradeRatio Rounded In Wrong Direction
content: The vulnerability is a rounding‑direction bug in the calculation of the trade ratio that is used for both the profit‑and‑loss (closePnL) and the amount of vETH that can be borrowed (borrowedVEth). The contract always applies the same rounding rule to the tradeRatioD18 value, rounding down when the position is long and rounding up otherwise, which is the opposite of the intended behaviour described in the design document. Because the same rounded value is reused for two distinct financial formulas, the protocol ends up borrowing less vETH than it could and simultaneously reporting a higher closePnL than it should. This bias creates a systematic shortfall that can lead to insolvency when a series of trades pushes the protocol’s collateral below the required level. The flaw is triggered whenever a trade is executed and the isLongDirection flag is evaluated; the incorrect rounding is applied before the protocol computes the vEthAmount to be borrowed and the closePnL to be credited. Users who open long positions see their expected borrowed vETH reduced, which may cause their positions to be under‑collateralised and potentially liquidated, while the protocol records an inflated profit that later has to be covered by other users. From a user‑interface perspective the symptom is that a trader receives less borrowed vETH than anticipated, or sees a profit that disappears later, and balances may unexpectedly drop to zero or become negative. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the implementation against the specification for rounding direction. It is hard to notice because the numerical difference is often a single unit of precision and only manifests under edge‑case price movements or large position sizes. The bug belongs to the class of arithmetic rounding bias vulnerabilities, where the choice of floor versus ceiling operations violates the accounting assumptions of the system. To remediate the problem the contract should maintain two separate trade ratios: one rounded down for calculations that need to minimise the credited amount (closePnL) and one rounded up for calculations that need to maximise the borrowed amount (borrowedVEth). Each vEthToZero and vEthFromZero computation must use the appropriate rounded ratio, and the logic that selects the final borrowedVEth should pick the larger absolute vEthFromZero while the logic that settles the position should pick the smaller absolute value, thereby aligning the implementation with the intended financial model.
summary: The recommendation of [H-03](https://www.notion.so/H-03-1348bda5828c810ba6bbe5baf4a7ed02?pvs=21) is to round up the trade ratio when going towards the long direction as a short. However, the fix implemented is the opposite - the trade ratio is being rounded down if isLongDirection and rounded up otherwise. Since the problem is not solved, the insolvency issue still exists. Currently, tradeRatioD18 is used to compute both closePnL and vEthAmount/borrowedVEth. Foil's goal should always be to maximize borrowedVEth and minimize closePnL and vEthAmount. Because of this, different rounding directions should be used depending on what's being calculated.

title: H-02 | Faulty Quoting With Small Amounts
content: The vulnerability is an off‑by‑one error in the calculation of the collateral required to mint a liquidity position when a new epoch is opened. The Vault first queries the quoting function to obtain the maximum amounts of token0 and token1 that can be deposited given the current reserves. It then calls Epoch.requiredCollateralForLiquidity(), which internally adds one wei to each of the quoted amounts before checking that the vault holds enough collateral. Because the quoted amounts were computed without this extra wei, the check can fail even though the vault’s balance exactly matches the quoted amounts. When the discrepancy occurs, the contract reverts with InsufficientCollateral(), preventing the epoch from being created. The bug appears with relatively small but realistic amounts (for example 1e17 wei) where the vault’s reserves are tight. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition: users attempting to open an epoch receive a transaction that reverts, the protocol cannot create new liquidity positions, and funds remain idle in the vault. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit that included fuzzing of the epoch‑creation path. Because the error is only one wei, it is easy to miss in manual testing and only surfaces when the vault’s balance exactly matches the quoted amounts, a situation that can be reproduced with modest collateral sizes. The correct fix is to remove the artificial +1 increment from the required‑collateral calculation, or alternatively to subtract one wei from the quoted amounts before performing the check, and to document the minimum‑collateral expectations so that future developers understand the edge case. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of rounding or off‑by‑one errors in financial calculations that break accounting invariants and cause unexpected reverts.
summary: When a new epoch is created, the Vault uses the assets in its reserves to deposit them as collateral in order to create a liquidity position. The vault will call quoteLiquidityPositionTokens to get the amount0 and amount1 that can be added as liquidity for the available collateral. However, Epoch.requiredCollateralForLiquidity() now adds 1 to loanAmount0 and loanAmount1. This means the actual required collateral for the position may exceed the available collateral in the vault. In result, the transaction will revert because of InsufficientCollateral() and the epoch creation will not be successful. This issue can occur with non-trivial amounts, for example 1e17.

title: H-01 | Last User Of Epoch Cannot Withdraw Collateral
content: The vulnerability originates from a rounding adjustment in the LiquidityModule._closeLiquidityPosition function. When aliquidity position is closed, the contract adds a constant of one wei to the collected amount in order to compensate for Uniswap’s rounding behavior when the position was originally opened. This adjustment is applied unconditionally, even in cases where the borrowed amount is zero and the collected amount itself may be zero – for example when liquidity is added above the current price tick and therefore only vGas is borrowed while no vETH is involved. By adding one wei to a zero‑valued collection, the contract records that the user has withdrawn more collateral than was actually supplied. Over the course of an epoch, each withdrawal that includes this extra wei reduces the pool’s total collateral by a tiny amount. The effect accumulates until the final user attempting to withdraw in that epoch finds that the contract’s remaining balance is short by a few wei, causing the withdrawal transaction to revert. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a legitimate liquidity provider sees their withdrawal fail with an out‑of‑gas or insufficient‑balance error, even though they expect to receive their full deposit. The impact is a loss of confidence in the protocol’s accounting, potential denial‑of‑service for the last participant in an epoch, and a subtle inflation of the protocol’s apparent collateral that can be abused. An attacker can exploit the bug by providing liquidity only above the current price tick, immediately removing that liquidity, and collecting the borrowed vGas together with the artificially added one wei of vETH. The extra wei is then added to the attacker’s recorded collateral and can be withdrawn, effectively stealing a wei of value while also contributing to the depletion of the pool for honest users. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by the Guardian team, who noticed that the rounding fix was applied without checking whether the collected amount was zero. Because the discrepancy is only a single wei, it is easy to overlook in testing and may not surface in typical transaction logs, making it hard to detect without precise accounting checks. The proper remediation is to conditionally apply the one‑wei adjustment only when the collected amount is non‑zero, and to modify the settlement logic so that if the contract’s balance is insufficient by a few wei, the remaining balance can still be paid out rather than causing the transaction to revert. This aligns the implementation with the intended accounting model and prevents the last‑user withdrawal failure while eliminating the opportunity for a malicious actor to extract value through the rounding hack.
summary: In LiquidityModule._closeLiquidityPosition, collected amounts are rounded up by adding 1 wei to offset Uniswap’s rounding when opening a position. However, borrowed amounts may be zero (e.g., when adding liquidity outside the current price tick), and collected amounts can also be zero, depending on the price tick. By adding 1 wei, users may withdraw more collateral than they initially deposited. Over time, this leads to the last user in an epoch being unable to withdraw due to insufficient collateral. This behavior can also be exploited by malicious users with the following steps: • Provide liquidity above the current price tick, so only vGas is borrowed and no vETH. • Immediately decrease liquidity, collecting all borrowed vGas plus 1 wei vETH. • The 1 wei of vETH is added to the user's deposited collateral and then withdrawn.

title: H-02 | Collateral Returned Despite Bad Debt
content: The vulnerability is an accounting error in the collateral settlement logic that occurs when a trader closes a position whose loss exceeds the amount of collateral originally deposited. The contract is supposed to reduce the trader’s deposited collateral to zero and require the trader to cover the shortfall (extra collateral) before returning any funds. However, the implementation only applies the extra‑collateral calculation when a new position is opened. When the position size is set to zero (i.e., the trader is closing), the code leaves the field that tracks deposited collateral unchanged, so the full amount is returned to the trader even though the protocol has incurred a bad‑debt loss. The root cause is a missing conditional branch that checks for a loss greater than the deposited collateral during the closing path, causing the protocol to absorb the loss instead of the trader. An attacker can exploit this by deliberately creating a losing trade that exceeds the collateral, then closing the position and receiving the entire collateral back, effectively extracting the loss amount from the protocol’s reserves. The impact is a direct drain of funds from the protocol’s liquidity pool, harming other traders and liquidity providers who rely on the pool’s solvency. This condition is triggered only when the closing function is called with a zero‑size position and a loss larger than the collateral; normal profitable or break‑even closures behave correctly, making the bug easy to miss during casual testing. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit that examined edge‑case settlement paths. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after a losing trade the UI shows the full collateral being returned, contradicting the expectation that the loss would be deducted, and the protocol’s total balance shrinks unexpectedly. The bug belongs to the class of “bad‑debt handling” or “collateral settlement” errors where accounting assumptions about loss coverage are violated. To remediate, the settlement logic must be updated so that when collateralLoss exceeds the previously deposited collateral, the contract sets the returned collateral amount to zero and calculates the extraCollateralRequired as the difference, thereby enforcing the trader to cover the shortfall before any funds are released.
summary: When a trader is closing out a position, if the loss exceeds collateral deposited then this case is entered. As bad debt has been incurred, the collateral should be reduced to zero but currently depositedCollateralAmount remains unchanged. The extraCollateralRequired would cover the losses, but however it is only taken into account if the trader is re-opening a new position. So, If the trader was closing the position (i.e. size = 0), then all deposited collateral is returned implying losses are borne by the protocol/other LPs and traders.

title: H-03 | Insolvency Because Of tradeRatio Rounding
content: The vulnerability is a rounding‑down error in the calculation of the trade ratio used as the fill price when a short position is closed. The contract computes the trade ratio with a decimal division function that always rounds toward zero. For long positions this conservative rounding is acceptable, but for shorts a lower fill price reduces the loss that the short trader should incur. Because the rounded‑down ratio understates the amount that must be repaid, the protocol records a smaller loss for the short trader and consequently retains less collateral in the Foil contract than required. When a short position that is fully funded by borrowed VGas is closed, the expected vEthToZero amount (the amount of virtual ETH that should be returned to zero) is slightly lower than the actual traded vEth amount. The shortfall remains in the system’s accounting, so later when liquidity providers attempt to settle or withdraw their earnings the contract tries to transfer more tokens than it holds, causing the ERC20 transfer to revert with “transfer amount exceeds balance”. The issue manifests only under specific conditions: the _quoteOrTrade function is invoked for a short, the position is being closed, and the rounding error accumulates enough to create a deficit. The affected parties are short traders who receive an unexpectedly small loss, liquidity providers who cannot collect their accrued rewards, and ultimately the protocol which may become insolvent. The bug was discovered during a fuzzing audit that exercised closing of short positions and observed the transfer revert. It is hard to notice because the rounding discrepancy is tiny and only appears when the position consists solely of borrowed gas and the trade ratio is rounded down; normal operations mask the loss. The vulnerability belongs to the class of precision‑loss or rounding‑error accounting bugs that break the invariant that total assets equal total liabilities. To remediate, the trade ratio for short positions should be rounded up (or calculated with ceiling division) so that the fill price is at least as unfavorable as the market price, ensuring that the protocol always retains sufficient collateral to cover settlements.
summary: When _quoteOrTrade is called and PnL is calculated, the tradeRatio experiences precision loss because of rounding down when performing divDecimal. While this is fine for longs, it's not for shorts. That's because the tradeRatio is a fill price and if the fill price is lower, shorts will have made a profit. In result, when the PnL for shorts is calculated the trader will experience a smaller loss, leaving the system with fewer funds available than it should have in order to operate. This can be most visible if a position has only borrowedVGas (short) and makes a trade to close the position. Because the entirety of the debt is being paid off, it would be expected that the vEthToZero would at least match the runtime.tradedVEth. However, the vEthToZero would be slightly less due to the tradeRatioD18 rounding, and less collateral being held in the Foil contract. Later, when LPs try to close or settle their position, they will not be able to do so. The contract will try to send them the amount they have earned, but this amount is not fully backed by the losses of the traders and the transaction will revert with ERC20: transfer amount exceeds balance.

title: H-04 | Settlement Failure Due To Underflow
content: The vulnerability is a settlement failure caused by an arithmetic underflow that originates from rounding down token amounts during the calculation of a liquidity position's current balances. When a position is settled, the protocol calls a helper routine that returns the amounts of virtual gas (vGas) and virtual ETH (vETH) tokens held by the position. These amounts are later used to rebalance the position by converting everything to ETH, adding the resulting value to the deposited collateral counter and subtracting the same amount from the borrowed collateral counter. The helper routine rounds the token amounts down to the nearest wei, which means that the summed value of the position – including the collateral that should back the loan – can become slightly smaller than the recorded debt. When the settlement logic then tries to set the internal variable representing the deposited collateral to the borrowed amount (self.depositedCollateralAmount = self.borrowedVEth), the contract detects that the new collateral value would be lower than the existing debt and triggers an underflow, causing the transaction to revert. This can be exploited by constructing a position with token amounts that sit just above a rounding boundary so that the floor operation reduces the effective collateral enough to make the debt appear larger than the collateral. An attacker does not need to directly manipulate the contract state; simply opening a position with the right size is sufficient to cause the settlement to fail. The impact is that legitimate users attempting to settle their positions receive a transaction revert, their balances appear unchanged, and the protocol may end up with locked or inconsistent accounting data. The bug manifests only when the calculated token amounts are such that the rounding error pushes the total value below the debt, which typically occurs with small or precisely tuned position sizes. Liquidity providers, borrowers, and any party relying on the settlement mechanism are affected because they may lose the ability to retrieve their collateral or repay their loan. The issue was discovered during a systematic fuzzing audit that generated many random position configurations and observed a pattern of reverts linked to the rounding step. Because the rounding discrepancy is on the order of a single wei, it is easy to miss in manual reviews and only surfaces under specific numeric conditions, making it a subtle accounting flaw. To remediate the problem, the protocol should incorporate rounding safety margins when computing the required collateral, for example by rounding up instead of down or by adding a one‑wei buffer to the loan amounts, ensuring that the deposited collateral can never be less than the recorded debt. In broader terms, this is an instance of a rounding‑induced under‑collateralization bug, where floor division leads to insufficient collateral checks and subsequent arithmetic underflow during state updates. From a user’s perspective the expected outcome – a successful settlement returning their ETH – is replaced by a failed transaction with no funds transferred, often described as “my refund came back as zero” or “the settlement just reverted”. The discrepancy violates the core business logic that collateral must always cover the borrowed amount, breaking the protocol’s accounting guarantees.
summary: When settling a liquidity position, getCurrentPositionTokenAmounts is called to retrieve the corresponding vGas and vETH token amounts of the position, which are then later rebalanced during position.settle. The rebalancing process converts everything to ETH, adding all value to depositedCollateral and subtracting all debt from depositedCollateral. However, the calculation during getCurrentPositionTokenAmounts rounds down, which can cause the total value of the position (including the collateral) to be less than the total debt in some cases. This results in the settlement reverting due to an underflow in the following line: self.depositedCollateralAmount = self.borrowedVEth.

title: H-01 | Users Incorrectly Credited WIth NFT Ownership At lzReceive Time
content: The vulnerability is a time‑dependent ownership mismatch that occurs during the cross‑chain claim process. When a user calls requestClaim, the contract records that the caller owns a specific NFT and is entitled to a vested amount of tokens. However, the actual token amount is calculated later in the lzReceive function using the current block.timestamp instead of the timestamp captured at the request time. Because the claim execution can be delayed by at least eight blocks (approximately 96 seconds) and potentially much longer during network outages or contract pauses, the original claimer can transfer the NFT to another address after the request but before lzReceive finalises. The contract then still credits the vested tokens to the original caller, even though ownership has changed. This results in funds being allocated to the wrong party, violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions that vested rewards correspond to the current NFT holder. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by Guardian, who identified that the _vested function relies on a stale ownership snapshot. It is hard to notice because the token transfer appears successful and the NFT transfer is a separate operation; only a detailed analysis of timestamps reveals the mismatch. The impact is that new NFT owners may receive no reward while previous owners collect undeserved tokens, leading to financial loss for users and erosion of trust in the protocol. The bug belongs to the class of race‑condition or stale‑state vulnerabilities where a contract uses a mutable global variable (block.timestamp) instead of a stored, immutable claim parameter. From a user’s perspective, the expected behaviour is that after selling an NFT they should no longer receive vesting rewards; instead they may see an unexpected increase in their balance, and the buyer may see a missing reward. To remediate, the claim request should embed the original timestamp (or a snapshot of ownership) into the ClaimParameters associated with the claimNonce, and the vested calculation in lzReceive must use this stored timestamp rather than the current block time, ensuring that rewards are only paid to the NFT holder at the moment of the request. Additional safeguards such as re‑checking ownership at lzReceive or enforcing atomic claim execution can further mitigate the risk.
summary: In the _claimBatch function after the claim has been validated by the l1 state at the timestamp of the requestClaim call, the claimer is awarded with the vested amount computed by the _vested function. However the _vested function determines the user’s vested amount based upon the current block.timestamp of the lzReceive action. This is however not the same timestamp that the claimer was veriﬁed to be authorized to claim at. The claimer could have sold their NFT to another user after the block.timestamp of the requestClaim call and thus received vested amounts which should have gone to the new owner of the NFT. There is a 8 block confirmation threshold currently conﬁgured, meaning that roughly 96 seconds will have to occur at minimum between the requestClaim call and the lzReceive which fulﬁlls the claim. This delay period could be made even more severe during a DVN outage or if a claim has passed all DVN checks but the lzReceive function reverts for some time until the revert is resolved (e.g. claim contract is paused and unpaused, or the daily withdrawal threshold has been met for the day) and then the lzReceive function is invoked again successfully passing a significant amount of time later.

title: H-02 | Collector Allocations Errantly Validated
content: The AnimeClaimer contract contains a cross‑chain validation flaw that allows a vesting allocation to be granted to a collector address on L2 without confirming that the same entity controls that address on L1. The contract checks that the caller is the designated collector for a collector vest, but after this check it simply transfers the vested amount to the collector address on L2. No additional ownership verification is performed, so if the collector address is a smart‑contract wallet or multisig that has been transferred on L1 to a new owner, the old owner may still retain control of a contract deployed at the identical address on L2. An attacker who controls the L2 address can therefore receive the tokens that were intended for the current L1 owner. This situation arises whenever a vest is claimed by a collector address that is not an externally owned account on both chains, or when the ownership of a contract wallet diverges between L1 and L2. The affected parties include the intended token holder, the protocol’s accounting logic, and any users relying on the claim UI to reflect their balance. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the claim flow, where the lack of a cross‑chain ownership check was noted. It can be difficult to notice because the transaction appears successful, the emitted events show the correct amount, and the address format matches on both chains, giving the false impression that the funds have been correctly allocated. From the user’s perspective the claim transaction succeeds, but the expected increase in their L2 balance does not occur; instead another address receives the tokens, leading to symptoms such as “my balance stays at zero after claiming” or “the vest was claimed but I got nothing”. The root cause is the missing verification that the collector address on L2 is owned by the same entity as on L1. To remediate, the contract should enforce that collector addresses are externally owned accounts on both chains, or implement a robust cross‑chain ownership proof (for example, requiring a signed message from the L1 owner, a mapping of L1 owner to L2 address, or using a trusted bridge to confirm control). By adding this additional validation the protocol can ensure that vested amounts are transferred only to the rightful owner, preserving accounting integrity and preventing unintended fund diversion.
summary: In the AnimeClaimer contract when the claimer is the collector for a collector vest then there is no further validation performed on the vest and the vested amount is granted to the collector address on the L2. However the owner of the collector address on the L2 may be different then the owner of the collector address on the L1. For example, a smart contract wallet/multisig could have been transferred from Alice to Bob on the L1, but Alice may have kept ownership of a smart contract wallet/multisig deployed at the same address on the L2.

title: H-01 | Ownership Cannot Be Synced To Base Chain
content: The vulnerability resides in the _updateOwnership routine of the cross‑chain NFT shadow system. The function unconditionally invokes executeCallback on the address stored in the _shadow variable, regardless of whether the NFT collection being processed is native to the current blockchain. When the collection is native, the _shadow address is actually the address of the real NFT contract, which does not implement the executeCallback interface. Consequently, any lzRead request that attempts to synchronize ownership back to the base chain triggers a call to a non‑existent function, causing the transaction to revert. This revert prevents the ownership state from being propagated to the base chain, breaking the fundamental assumption that cross‑chain ownership information is always consistent. The bug manifests only when isNative is true, i.e., when the collection resides on the same chain as the caller, and therefore may be overlooked during normal local operations because the faulty path is exercised only during cross‑chain read operations. Users attempting to view or transfer their NFT on the base chain experience failures such as missing ownership data, UI messages indicating that the owner cannot be determined, or outright transaction reverts. The impact is high because it can freeze cross‑chain functionality, lead to user confusion, and potentially lock assets in a state where they cannot be transferred across chains until the contract is patched. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the ownership synchronization logic. It is difficult to notice because the contract behaves correctly for native operations and only fails when the specific cross‑chain callback is executed. To remediate, the executeCallback call should be guarded by a condition that checks the isNative flag and only performs the callback when the collection is not native (i.e., when isNative is false). This change aligns the implementation with the intended design of invoking callbacks solely on shadow contracts that implement the required interface, thereby restoring reliable ownership syncing across chains.
summary: In the _updateOwnership function the executeCallback function is always invoked on the _shadow address, even when the collection is native to the current chain. In the case that the collection is native to the current chain the _shadow contract address is the address of the actual NFT collection, which does not implement the executeCallback function. As a result receptions of lzRead requests on the base collection chain will always revert, thus preventing the syncing of ownership to the base chain.

title: H-02 | Reorgs Invalidate The Locked Invariant
content: The vulnerability is a cross‑chain state‑inconsistency that arises when a blockchain reorganization (reorg) on the origin chain reverses a token lock that was created as part of a bridge operation. The bridge function releaseOnEid moves an NFT from its original owner on the source chain into a Beacon contract, delegates the ownership rights back to the original owner, and then initiates a LayerZero send that results in a shadow NFT being minted on the destination chain. Under normal operation the original NFT is locked on the source chain and the shadow NFT is owned by the beneficiary on the target chain, preserving a one‑to‑one ownership invariant. However, if a reorg occurs on the source chain after the lock transaction has been included but before the chain reaches a sufficient finality depth, the lock transaction can be dropped or replaced. When this happens the original NFT becomes unlocked again on the source chain, while the shadow NFT remains minted and owned on the destination chain. The result is that the same asset appears to be owned simultaneously on two chains, breaking the protocol’s accounting assumptions and enabling double‑spending or unauthorized transfer of the asset. From a user’s perspective the bridge appears to have succeeded – the user sees the shadow NFT in their wallet on the destination chain – but later the original NFT reappears in the owner’s balance on the source chain, leading to confusion such as “my NFT is suddenly back in my wallet even though I already transferred it” or “the bridge shows my NFT on both chains”. The issue is discovered during a security audit that examined the bridge’s state‑transition logic and identified that the lock relies on a single block confirmation without accounting for possible chain reorganizations. It is hard to notice in testing because reorgs are rare and the bridge UI typically shows only the final destination ownership, masking the hidden source‑chain state. To remediate the problem the protocol should enforce a sufficient finality window (e.g., wait for a configurable number of confirmations) before considering the lock final, use immutable proofs that survive reorgs, or implement a challenge/rollback mechanism that can revert the shadow NFT if the source lock is undone. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of “cross‑chain invariant violation due to insufficient finality” and can lead to loss of uniqueness, potential theft, and erosion of trust in the bridging service.

function releaseOnEid() transfers token from origin chain owner to the Beacon.sol contract, then delegates the rights to the owner, completing the lzSend() -> lzReceive() request on the destination chain. For completed request the NFTShadow is minted and is now owned by the beneficiary on the destination chain. In the case of a reorg on the base chain, the NFT ownership will revert back to the original owner, become unlocked on the origin chain and the destination chain. Example:

title: H-02 | Reorgs Invalidate The Locked Invariant
content: The vulnerability is a cross‑chain finality flaw that allows a blockchain reorganization on the destination chain to break the protocol’s locked‑invariant. The bridge logic releases the native token on the origin chain (Ethereum) immediately after sending a LayerZero message, while the ownership update of the shadow NFT on the destination chain (Polygon) is assumed to be final after only a few blocks. Because Polygon provides only probabilistic finality, a short‑range reorg of three or more blocks can rewrite the destination state, assigning the shadow NFT to a different address or rendering it irredeemable. An attacker who can trigger or wait for such a reorg can end up with the original token still in their wallet on Ethereum while the shadow NFT is either lost or transferred to another party, effectively violating the accounting assumption that the token is locked until the shadow NFT is securely minted. The issue manifests when a user initiates a bridge from Ethereum to Polygon, the bridge contract calls lzSend with releaseOnEid and triggerOwnershipUpdate, and the Polygon side processes the message but later experiences a reorg before the required confirmation depth is reached. From the user’s perspective the UI shows a successful bridge, the Ethereum balance is reduced as expected, but the corresponding NFT either disappears from their Polygon wallet or appears under a different owner, leading to confusion and potential loss of value. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the bridge’s finality handling and noted that the code does not wait for a sufficient number of confirmations on the destination chain before releasing assets on the source chain. It is difficult to notice because reorgs are infrequent and the bridge does not emit explicit warnings when the destination state is later reverted. To remediate, the protocol should enforce probabilistic finality on the origin chain before releasing assets, for example by configuring an appropriate confirmations threshold that reflects the safety margin of the destination chain, or by using a checkpoint or proof‑of‑finality mechanism that guarantees the shadow NFT’s ownership update is immutable before the native token is unlocked. This change restores the invariant that the token remains locked until the shadow NFT is irrevocably assigned to the intended beneficiary, preventing double‑spend scenarios and ensuring that users receive the expected asset on both chains.

title: Instant withdrawals in priority pool can result in loss of funds for StakingProxy contract
content: The vulnerability is an omission of a state update in the priority pool’s internal withdrawal routine when instant withdrawals are permitted. When a user calls the StakingProxy withdraw function, the proxy burns the user's liquid staking tokens (LSTs) and forwards the request to the PriorityPool. The pool first processes any queued withdrawals, correctly recording the amount in a local variable named withdrawn. If instant withdrawals are enabled and there are no pending queued withdrawals, the pool calls the underlying staking pool to pull the requested tokens. However, after this call the code fails to add the amount taken from the staking pool to the withdrawn variable. As a result the contract believes that no tokens have been withdrawn and therefore does not transfer the underlying tokens to the StakingProxy. From the user’s perspective the transaction appears successful – the LST balance decreases to zero – but the underlying token balance of the proxy does not increase, and the tokens remain locked inside the PriorityPool. This mismatch violates the accounting assumption that the sum of burned LSTs equals the amount of underlying tokens transferred out, effectively causing permanent loss of funds for any staker who uses instant withdrawals while the pool has no queued withdrawals. The condition occurs only when the allowInstantWithdrawals flag is true and the withdrawal queue is empty; under normal queued‑withdrawal paths the bug is not triggered. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the _withdraw function and noticed that the withdrawn variable is not updated after the stakingPool.withdraw call. Because the function does not emit an explicit error and the transaction does not revert, the problem can be hard to notice without checking post‑withdrawal balances. The fix consists of updating the withdrawn variable (e.g., adding the amount withdrawn from the staking pool) before the function continues, ensuring that the token transfer logic recognises the withdrawn amount and releases the tokens to the StakingProxy. In generic terms this is a state‑update omission leading to an accounting inconsistency, a class of bugs where a variable tracking transferred value is not correctly modified, causing funds to become inaccessible.

title: H-01 | Match Withdrawal Donation Underflow
content: The vulnerability is an arithmetic underflow in the withdrawal matching logic of a donation‑enabled withdrawal request. When a withdrawal request that includes a donation is partially filled, the contract fails to reduce the stored donation amount by the portion that has been satisfied. Consequently the remaining donation value can become larger than the residual withdrawal amount. On the next attempt to match the request the code subtracts the donation from the remaining amount, causing an unsigned integer underflow and triggering a panic revert. This revert stops the execution of the match function, preventing the user’s pending withdrawal from ever being completed. The bug appears only after a specific sequence: a partial fill followed by another match operation, and it affects any user who has created a withdrawal request with an attached donation. From the user’s perspective the expected outcome – a successful withdrawal of funds – is replaced by a transaction that reverts with a generic panic error, leaving the user’s balance unchanged and the request stuck indefinitely. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the accounting of donation amounts in the matchWithdrawRequest routine. It is difficult to notice because the contract behaves correctly for full withdrawals and only fails for the edge case where the donation exceeds the leftover amount, producing a low‑level arithmetic error rather than an explicit error message. The flaw violates the protocol’s accounting assumptions that the sum of the withdrawn amount and the donated amount never exceeds the original request. To remediate the problem the donation portion should be calculated proportionally to the original request amount, for example by applying a ratio of request.donation to the total requested amount, and the donation value should be decreased accordingly on each partial fill. This ensures that the subtraction never underflows and that withdrawal requests can be fulfilled safely.
summary:
In the matchWithdrawRequest the donation amount is not deducted from the withdrawal request
when the transaction is a partial withdrawal fill.
In this case the donation amount can be larger than the remaining amount for the withdrawal
request and lead to an underflow panic revert on the subsequent withdrawal match. This prevents
the user’s withdrawal request from being filled after this case has been reached.

title: H-01 | Sqrt Price Compared With Price
content: The vulnerability originates from a unit mismatch in the _getUtilizationRate routine of the contract. The function derives a variable called priceAdj by taking the square‑root of the market price using TickMath.getSqrtRatioAtTick and then dividing by FixedPoint96.Q96. This operation yields a value expressed in sqrt‑price units, not in absolute price units. Later in the same routine the code compares priceAdj directly with the output of getBLV, which returns a normal price value. Because a sqrt‑price is being treated as a full price, the subsequent premiumRatio calculation is mathematically incorrect. The root cause is the failure to convert the sqrt‑price to a regular price before the comparison – the code should square priceAdj (or otherwise convert units) to obtain a true price. An attacker who can influence the activeTickAdj parameter can manipulate the sqrt‑price, causing the premiumRatio to be severely mis‑estimated. This mis‑estimation can lead to users receiving a premium that is too high or too low, effectively allowing a malicious party to over‑charge borrowers or under‑pay lenders, resulting in loss of funds or unintended profit. The issue manifests every time _getUtilizationRate is invoked, which typically occurs during loan issuance, margin calls, or any operation that relies on utilization metrics. All participants that depend on correct premium calculations – borrowers, lenders, and the protocol’s treasury – are affected. The problem was discovered during a manual audit when the auditor noticed that the variable names suggested a price but the underlying computation produced a sqrt‑price, a subtle discrepancy that does not raise compiler warnings and can easily slip past basic unit tests. Because both values are numeric and appear plausible, the bug may remain hidden until financial anomalies surface, such as users seeing unexpectedly high fees or missing expected payouts. To remediate the issue, the contract should either square the priceAdj value before it is compared with the price from getBLV, or replace the current computation with a direct price calculation that maintains consistent units throughout the function. This correction restores the intended accounting logic, ensuring that premiumRatio reflects the true market price and that the protocol’s financial guarantees remain intact.
summary:
In the _getUtilizationRate function the priceAdj is computed as:
FixedPointMathLib.divWad(TickMath.getSqrtRatioAtTick(activeTickAdj), FixedPoint96.Q96);
Which has units of the square root of the price. However the priceAdj is compared against the result
of getBLV to compute the premiumRatio.
The result of getBLV is a price, instead of a square root price. Therefore the premiumRatio is
incorrect.

title: H-02 | Liquidity Rebalance Arbitrage
content: The vulnerability is an arbitrage opportunity that arises from the way the contract’s liquidity rebalance routine updates price ticks between two liquidity zones, called the Anchor range and the Discovery range. The root cause is that the _updateTicks logic only prevents new bAsset minting when the anchor range would receive additional liquidity after a large sell executed through the discovery range, but it does not protect the symmetric scenario where a large sell is performed from the top of the Anchor range. When the Anchor liquidity is initially lower than the Discovery liquidity, an attacker can sell a substantial amount of bAssets from the Anchor side, causing the rebalance algorithm to shift the Discovery range closer to the new market price. This shift effectively increases the amount of Discovery liquidity relative to the amount sold, so the attacker can subsequently buy back the same quantity of bAssets at a lower average price because the price impact is now diluted by the higher Discovery liquidity. The exploit can be carried out whenever the difference between Anchor and Discovery liquidity is sufficient and the leveraging factor of the Anchor position does not exceed that difference, allowing the price distortion to be profitable. From a user perspective the symptom is that the protocol appears to lose value: the price of bAssets drifts unfavorably, liquidity providers see their share diluted, and the protocol may end up with a net loss of assets because the attacker extracts value without any explicit token transfer. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the rebalance logic and identified that only one direction of the trade flow was guarded. It is hard to notice because the code seems to enforce a safety check for the “sell‑through‑discovery” path, giving a false sense of security while the opposite path remains unchecked. The bug belongs to the class of “imbalanced liquidity rebalance arbitrage” where asymmetric liquidity adjustments enable price manipulation. To remediate the problem the contract should enforce a limit on how many price ticks can be dropped in a single rebalance, effectively throttling the magnitude of the liquidity shift, and should add symmetric checks that prevent large sells from the Anchor side from causing disproportionate discovery‑range movement. In conceptual terms the fix requires bounding the rebalancing step size and ensuring that any liquidity addition or removal respects the relative sizes of the two ranges, thereby removing the profit‑making window for an attacker.
summary:
The _updateTicks logic intentionally assigns the anchorTick such that new bAssets are not minted
within the anchor range when the bAssets minted would be in addition to the liquidity in the
discovery range.
This is to avoid the following arbitrage attack:
• Anchor liquidity < Discovery liquidity
• An attacker makes a large sell through the discovery range and the anchor range
• Due to the instantaneous large sell, and the leveraging of the anchor liquidity, the anchor liquidity
becomes greater than the Discovery liquidity
• Now the attacker can buy back the same amount of bAssets but at a lower average price because
of the increased Anchor liquidity relative to the liquidity they sold through.
There is however another similar arbitrage attack which is not protected against:
• Anchor liquidity < Discovery liquidity
• Instead of selling through the discovery range, the attacker sells from the top of the Anchor range
• After the sell, the rebalance causes the higher liquidity discovery range to come down closer to the
new price
• Now the attacker can buy back the same amount of bAssets but at a lower average price because
of the increased Discovery liquidity relative to the liquidity they sold through.
• As long as the leveraging of the Anchor position is not greater than the liquidity difference between
the Anchor and Discovery then this arbitrage is profitable.

title: H-03 | Third Party Liquidity Results In DoS
content: The vulnerability originates from a mismatch between fee accounting and token burning in the liquidity removal routine of a pool contract. When a caller invokes the removeAllFrom function with a liquidity amount that exceeds the pool's current liquidity, the function reports the entire excess as bAsset fees (bAssetFees_) even though the excess tokens are subsequently destroyed (burned) from the caller in the internal _removeLiquidity routine. This double‑counting causes the calling contract to believe it holds more bAssets than are actually present in the pool. During a rebalance operation the protocol attempts to transfer the reported fee amount to the designated fee receiver. Because the pool no longer contains the over‑reported tokens, the transfer triggers an arithmetic underflow, causing the transaction to revert. The result is a denial‑of‑service condition that blocks further rebalancing and can lock user funds. The issue appears only when third‑party liquidity removal exceeds the pool's current liquidity, a situation that can be triggered intentionally by an attacker or unintentionally during normal operations. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the interaction between removeAllFrom and _removeLiquidity and noticed that the fee calculation does not account for the burn step. The bug is subtle because the fee amount is reported as a positive value, so on the surface the accounting looks correct, yet the actual token balance is lower, leading to hidden underflow errors that surface later in the workflow. To remediate the problem the fee calculation must be adjusted so that any excess liquidity that is burned is not included in the fee total, or the burn step should be removed entirely for third‑party removals. In essence, the contract must ensure that the sum of reported fees never exceeds the pool's real token holdings, preserving arithmetic safety and preventing the DoS scenario where users see transactions fail, balances appear unchanged, and expected refunds or fee payouts never arrive.
summary:
The removeAllFrom function in the BPOOL contract reports the entirety of third party liquidity as fees
when the liquidityToRemove > currentLiquidity, however the excess liquidity is burned from the
msg.sender in the _removeLiquidity function.
This means that the calling contract will think it has more bAssets than it does because the reported
bAssetFees_ includes an amount that was burnt from the sender.
During rebalances this results in an underflow DoS when ultimately attempting to send more
bAssets than the contract holds to the fee receiver for bAssetFees_.

title: H-02 | ExitVaultEntryPoint.transferFrom Can Be Abused By The Vault Owner To Prevent A User From Withdrawing
content: The vulnerability resides in theExitVaultEntryPoint contract where the transferFrom function permits the current vault owner to hand over ownership of the vault to another address without resetting the internal accounting variables that track the original owner’s share balances. Specifically, the state fields that store the initial GMX and GLP share amounts (s.ownerInitialGMX and s.ownerInitialGLP) are only written when the caller matches the stored owner address during a withdrawal request. When the original owner completes a full withdrawal, those fields are set to zero because all of the owner’s shares have been claimed. If the owner then transfers the vault NFT to a new user, the contract’s owner variable is updated but the initial‑share variables remain zero. When the new owner later invokes matchWithdrawRequest to claim their portion of the vault, the logic attempts to use the stale zero values as a basis for arithmetic that expects a positive balance, causing an under‑flow error that aborts the withdrawal. From a user’s perspective the new owner sees their withdrawal transaction revert, their UI shows no funds received, and the vault balance appears unchanged, contradicting the expectation that ownership transfer also transfers the right to withdraw. The issue is triggered only after a full withdrawal by the first owner followed by an ownership transfer, making it easy to miss during normal testing because the contract behaves correctly for the initial owner. The bug effectively blocks the new owner from extracting any funds, potentially leaving assets permanently locked in the vault. It was identified during a security audit by the Guardian team, who noted that the owner‑initial share variables add no functional benefit and can be abused in this way. Because the under‑flow occurs deep inside a matchWithdrawRequest call, the failure may surface as a generic revert without a clear error message, further obscuring the root cause. The recommended remediation is to eliminate the s.ownerInitialGMX and s.ownerInitialGLP variables entirely or to redesign the withdrawal logic so that ownership transfer resets or correctly accounts for these values, thereby restoring the ability of a new owner to withdraw their rightful share.

title: H-01 | Claimable Collateral Cannot Be Claimed
content: The vulnerability consists of an absent implementation of the function that transfers claimable collateral from the internal claimable pool to the user. In the GMX V2 position manager, when a trade experiences a negative price impact that is capped, the protocol deposits the excess amount into a dedicated claimable collateral pool. The design documentation states that the user must later invoke ExchangeRouter.claimCollateral to retrieve those funds. However, the contract does not contain any code for this function; the selector exists but the body is empty or missing, so any call reverts or does nothing. As a result, users who have earned claimable collateral are unable to receive it. The root cause is a missing or incomplete implementation of the claim‑withdrawal pathway, likely introduced during a refactor where the function signature was kept but the logic was omitted. An attacker does not need to actively exploit the bug; the mere occurrence of a capped negative price impact automatically places funds in the pool, and the user cannot claim them, effectively locking the assets. The impact is that legitimate users lose access to part of their collateral, leading to reduced confidence and potential financial loss. The condition occurs only when the price impact protection mechanism triggers, which may be infrequent but can affect any position that hits the cap. The affected parties are traders who close or reduce positions under such conditions, as well as the protocol itself because locked funds reduce available liquidity and may be considered a breach of the promised accounting model. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the PositionManager source code, where the expected claimCollateral call was referenced in the documentation but no corresponding implementation was found. The problem is subtle because the contract compiles and the function selector exists, so calls do not fail with a compile‑time error, making it easy to overlook during testing unless the specific claim path is exercised. The correct remediation is to implement the claimCollateral logic according to the GMX specification: read the amount owed from the claimable pool, transfer the tokens to the caller, and update internal accounting to prevent double claims. This aligns the contract with the intended business rule that all collateral, including excess from capped price impact, must be recoverable by the user. In user‑facing terms, a trader expects to receive a refund or additional collateral after a trade, but instead sees no change in balance, or the UI shows a claimable amount that cannot be withdrawn, creating the impression that funds have disappeared.
summary: The ExchangeRouter.claimCollateral is not implemented in the GmxV2PositionManager contract. Quoted from the GMX docs: If negative price impact is capped, the additional amount would be kept in the claimable collateral pool, this needs to be manually claimed using the ExchangeRouter.claimCollateral function.

title: H-02 | User Can Escape Cost Of Holding A Position
content: The vulnerability resides in the way the GmxV2PositionManager contract evaluates the monetary value of an open position. Instead of accounting for the full spectrum of costs that a trader incurs – including protocol fees, discount adjustments, funding payments, and price‑impact penalties – the contract only sums the deposited collateral and the raw profit‑and‑loss (PnL) figure. This omission creates a systematic mispricing of the user’s share of the position. Because the omitted costs are only settled when the position is closed, the share price can experience abrupt stepwise jumps at closure time. An attacker who can open, manipulate, or close positions can therefore capture the difference between the inflated on‑chain valuation and the true economic value, effectively escaping the cost of holding the position. The flaw is triggered whenever the contract’s internal valuation function is called, which includes every minting, burning, or settlement event for a position. All participants that rely on the PositionManager – individual traders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are exposed to potential loss of funds or unintended profit extraction. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by the Guardian team, which noted that the calculation ignored several fields present in the GMX Reader’s getPositionInfo output, such as totalCostAmount, pending funding fees, and settled but unclaimed funding amounts. The problem is subtle because the user interface typically displays only the net PnL, hiding the hidden fees; consequently, users may see a share price that appears correct until the position is closed, at which point the payout may be higher than expected for the attacker and lower than the protocol’s accounting. From a user’s perspective the symptom can manifest as a sudden, unexplained jump in the value of their position, a payout that does not match the displayed PnL, or a situation where closing a position yields a profit that seems to ignore any fees. This class of bug falls under valuation miscalculation and fee omission, a common accounting error in DeFi contracts where the economic model does not align with the on‑chain accounting. To remediate the issue, the contract should compute the position’s net value by incorporating the totalCostAmount returned by the GMX Reader’s getPositionInfo function, adding pending and settled funding fees (both claimableLongTokenAmount and claimableShortTokenAmount), and adjusting for price‑impact effects. In essence, the valuation must reflect the exact amount that would be transferred if the position were closed at that moment, ensuring that no fees are unintentionally bypassed and that the share price evolves smoothly without exploitable jumps.
summary: When calculating the value of the position the GmxV2PositionManager contract only takes into account the deposited collateral and the current PnL of the position. The calculation does not take Fees, discounts, funding & price impact into account. This will misprice the user's shares and can enable MEV opportunities as stepwise jumps in the share price will occur when the position is closed. Furthermore pending funding fees to be paid to the user and funding fees that have yet to be claimed but are no longer pending should be accounted for.

title: H-03 | Wrong Vault Beneﬁts From Funding Fee Claims
content: The vulnerability is a misallocation of funding fee rewards that occurs when a user holds a long position in a vault whose underlying asset is not USDC (for example the BTC vault) and the protocol distributes short‑side funding fees in USDC. The contract’s claim‑funding‑fees logic credits the USDC amount directly to the USDC vault instead of converting it to the long token and crediting the vault that actually holds the position. As a result, the user’s BTC vault receives no additional BTC yield from the short‑side fees, and the USDC vault accrues extra USDC that does not belong to its depositors. The root cause is a missing conversion step and an incorrect accounting entry: the code assumes that any claimed fee can be deposited into the same vault, ignoring that the fee token (USDC) differs from the vault’s base token. Exploitation is straightforward – any holder of a long position that is eligible for short‑side funding fees can trigger the claim function, and the protocol will silently route the USDC reward to the wrong vault. From the user’s perspective the symptom is that after claiming fees the balance of the BTC vault does not increase as expected, while the USDC vault shows an unexplained increase; users may see “my BTC balance stayed the same” or “my expected yield is missing”. The impact is a loss of yield for affected users and a distortion of the protocol’s accounting, potentially leading to under‑payment of rewards and erosion of trust. The issue manifests whenever the claimFundingFees (or equivalent) function is called for a long position that has accrued short‑side fees, i.e., under normal operation of the protocol. It was discovered during a manual audit by the Guardian team, who identified the logical flaw in the fee‑distribution routine. The problem can be hard to notice because the total USDC in the system still balances, and the UI may only display aggregate balances, hiding the per‑vault discrepancy. To remediate, the contract should swap the claimed USDC into the appropriate long token before crediting the user’s vault, and also ensure that any pending fee amount is recorded against the correct vault. This aligns the reward distribution with the intended economic model, restores correct yield calculations, and prevents funds from disappearing from the user’s expected vault.
summary: Long tokens can collect both long and short funding fees. Because short funding fees come in the form of USDC, those funding fees will be credited to the USDC vault instead of the vault that actually has the position. Leading to a loss of yield for users who have deposited into the BTC vault.

title: H-04 | Stepwise Jump From Claimable Funds Omitted
content: The vulnerability originates from an accounting mismatch in the vault’s positionMargin routine, which calculates a user’s margin without taking into account any funding fees or collateral that are currently claimable but not yet withdrawn. Because the function ignores these pending rewards, the reported margin is lower than the true economic value of the position. When a keeper later executes claimFundingFees or claimCollateral, the vault’s total assets jump upward in a single step, which directly raises the price‑per‑share (PPS) metric used to value each holder’s stake. An attacker can watch the blockchain for positions that have accumulated unclaimed fees or collateral, then deposit additional capital into the vault immediately before the claim transaction is processed. The deposit is evaluated against the stale, underestimated margin, allowing the attacker to acquire shares at a lower PPS. When the claim executes, the PPS increases, inflating the value of the attacker’s newly‑minted shares while the underlying assets belong to long‑term participants. The attacker can then withdraw the inflated shares and realize a profit that was generated by other users’ activity. This exploit requires no special permissions, relies only on the predictable timing of keeper‑driven claim calls, and scales with the amount of unclaimed fees or collateral. From a user’s perspective the symptoms may appear as an unexpected increase in share price after a claim, or a sudden loss of value when a deposit is made just before a claim, leading to confusion about why their balance seems to shrink or why they receive no additional yield despite depositing. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the PositionManager contract, where the omission of claimable amounts in the margin calculation was identified as a logical flaw. It is hard to notice because the function appears to return a correct margin based on the current on‑chain balances, while the hidden pending rewards are not visible in the immediate state. To remediate the problem the positionMargin logic should be amended to incorporate both claimable funding fees and claimable collateral, ensuring that the margin reflects the full economic value of the position before any claim is processed. By aligning the accounting with the actual assets, the stepwise PPS jump is eliminated and the protocol’s yield distribution remains fair to all participants.
summary: The positionMargin function fails to include claimable funding fees and claimable collateral. This omission creates opportunities for users to steal yield by timing their deposits before fee claims. The vulnerability exists because when these fees/rewards are later claimed, they cause a step increase in the vault's total value, which directly impacts the PPS (Price Per Share). This creates an exploitable scenario where users can: 1. Monitor positions for unclaimed fees/collateral 2. Deposit into the vault right before claims are processed 3. Capture a portion of the yield they didn't help generate 4. Exit with profits taken from legitimate long-term holders The impact is severe because: • Multiple claimable types are affected (funding, collateral) • Claims/Keepers are predictable • The attack requires no special permissions • Profit potential scales with unclaimed amounts

title: H-03 | Lack Of Incentives For Users To Match Withdrawals
content: The issue is an incentive misalignment that creates a withdrawal deadlock in the ExitVault contract. When a user initiates a withdrawal, the contract relies on another participant to match the request, take over the staking position and receive a portion of the shares as a donation. This donation is meant to be offset by future vesting rewards that arise from converting esGMX tokens into GMX. However, once the vault’s esGMX balance reaches the predefined limits (maxVestableAmountGmx and maxVestableAmountGlp), no additional esGMX can vest and therefore no further conversion rewards are generated. At that point a new matcher no longer receives any vesting benefit, making the donation the only compensation. Because the donation is typically small compared with the expected vesting reward, rational users have no economic reason to accept a matching request, even if a modest donation is offered. Consequently, existing users who have posted withdrawal requests find their requests stuck indefinitely, with no one willing to step in. From the user’s perspective the withdrawal transaction appears to succeed, but the balance remains unchanged and the UI shows a pending exit that never resolves, violating the expectation that a withdrawal will be fulfilled by a matching party. The problem was uncovered during a systematic audit that examined the withdrawal‑matching flow and identified that the incentive calculation becomes zero once the vesting cap is hit, a condition that only manifests after the vault has fully vested its esGMX supply. The bug is subtle because the contract behaves correctly during the normal vesting phase; only after the cap is reached does the incentive disappear, leaving no explicit error flag, which makes the deadlock hard to detect in routine testing. This situation can be classified as an economic denial‑of‑service or liquidity‑lock vulnerability, where the protocol’s accounting assumptions about continuous vesting rewards are broken, leading to funds being effectively locked inside the contract. To remediate the issue the contract should include a fallback mechanism that permits direct withdrawals when the vesting capacity is exhausted, or otherwise provide an alternative incentive (such as a fee pool or time‑based reward) that ensures there is always a reason for a participant to match a withdrawal request, thereby restoring the ability for users to exit their positions safely.
summary: In the ExitVault contract, withdrawals are fulfilled by other users who match these requests, taking over their staking positions and receiving a portion of their shares as donation for helping them exit. This donation is used to incentivize others to fulfill their withdrawal requests. However, once all the esGMX tokens have been fully vested (i.e., the vault reaches maxVestableAmountGmx and maxVestableAmountGlp), the vault cannot vest additional esGMX tokens. At this point, new users have no incentive to match withdrawal requests because they can no longer benefit from the vesting rewards as no more esGMX will be converted into GMX. This creates a scenario where existing users who wish to withdraw are unable to do so unless they find someone willing to match their withdrawal request without the prospect of earning vesting rewards. As matching a withdrawal request would not yield any benefits to the new participant, it's unlikely anyone would agree to fulfill such requests, even with a donation. This situation resembles the old "King of the Ether" game, where users are effectively locked into the contract with no viable means of exiting their positions unless someone else takes their place. The only option left is to offer increasingly higher donations to entice someone to take over, leading to an impractical and potentially infinite loop without resolution.

title: H-05 | ADL Returns Native ETH
content: The vulnerability occurs in the auto‑deleveraging (ADL) workflow of the GMX PositionManager when a position belonging to the WETH vault is closed by a keeper. According to the protocol documentation, if pending profits exceed a configured threshold the keeper may partially or fully close the position and the afterOrderExecution callback is invoked. The callback receives a flag (order.flags.shouldUnwrapNativeToken) that indicates whether the remaining collateral should be returned as native ETH. In the current implementation the callback does not check this flag; when the flag is true the contract unwraps the WETH collateral and leaves the resulting ETH in the vault without converting it back to WETH. The vault’s accounting routine AggregateVault.getVaultPPS, however, calculates the price‑per‑share (PPS) solely from the WETH balance, ignoring the native ETH that now resides in the vault. As a result the reported PPS experiences a sudden step‑wise increase because the total asset value appears larger than the accounted WETH amount. This mismatch allows a user to deposit or withdraw using an incorrect share price: a depositor may receive fewer shares than warranted, while a withdrawer may extract more value than they are entitled to. The issue is triggered only when an ADL event closes a WETH position with the unwrap flag set, i.e., when the market’s profit threshold is breached. All participants that interact with the WETH vault – liquidity providers, traders, and any downstream contracts – are potentially affected because the accounting error can lead to loss of funds for the protocol or unintended gains for an attacker who times deposits or withdrawals around the PPS jump. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the PositionManager’s ADL logic, where the auditor observed that the afterOrderExecution callback does not validate the unwrap flag and that getVaultPPS does not incorporate native ETH balances. The problem is subtle because the vault’s external UI may still display a balance that seems correct in ETH terms, while the internal share‑price calculation diverges, making the inconsistency hard to spot without deep inspection of the accounting code. To remediate the issue the contract should either pause deposits/withdrawals until the native ETH is wrapped back into WETH or explicitly include the ETH balance in the PPS calculation. In practice this means adding a check for order.flags.shouldUnwrapNativeToken in the afterOrderExecution flow and, when true, either converting the ETH to WETH before updating the vault state or adjusting getVaultPPS to account for both token forms. The bug belongs to the class of accounting mismatches caused by improper handling of token wrapping/unwrapping after external callbacks, which violates the protocol’s invariant that the total collateral value is accurately reflected in the share‑price metric. From a user’s perspective the symptoms may appear as an unexpected jump in the share price, deposits that yield fewer vault shares than expected, or withdrawals that return more ETH than the user believes they should receive, effectively causing “funds disappear” or “refund calculation error” scenarios.
summary: During auto deleveraging (ADL) scenarios, GMX keepers will automatically close positions. According to the docs, When the pending profits exceed the market's configured threshold, profitable positions may be partially or fully closed. The issue arises for the WETH vault, as ADL will return the remaining collateral in native ETH and not WETH. Therefore, the AggregateVault.getVaultPPS will have an invalid state as only WETH balance is accounted for, creating a big step wise jump, allowing users to deposit/withdraw with an incorrect share price calculation.

title: H-06 | GMX Callback Revert Due To Stale LLO Prices
content: The vulnerability originates from the way the protocol relies on Chainlink LLO price data inside the GMX afterOrderExecution callback, specifically when the GmxV2PositionManager.decreasePosition function calculates profit‑and‑loss (PnL) and position notional. The callback fetches the latest LLO price and checks that the price was updated in a recent block; if the stored price’s lastUpdatedBlockNumber is lower than a required minimum, the contract reverts with PriceOutsideTolerance. While the getVaultPPS function is protected because the protocol updates the LLO price at the opening and closing of a rebalance period, the decreasePosition path does not guarantee a fresh price before the callback runs. Consequently, when a user or an external actor triggers a position decrease after the price feed has become stale, the afterOrderExecution callback attempts to compute the position notional using the stale price, hits the block‑number check, and reverts. The revert aborts the caching of critical position data, most notably the parameter needed to compute positionMargin correctly. From a user’s perspective the transaction appears to fail silently: the user expects the position size to shrink and the margin to be adjusted, but the transaction reverts and the on‑chain state shows no change, leaving the position effectively locked and the user’s funds inaccessible for further operations. The impact is a denial‑of‑service style failure that can prevent legitimate position reductions, potentially causing funds to remain idle or be unable to be withdrawn, and it undermines the accounting assumptions that margin equals position value derived from up‑to‑date prices. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the flow of price data through the contract’s callbacks and identified that the stale‑price guard was applied inconsistently. It is hard to notice because the revert occurs deep inside a callback rather than in a user‑facing function, and the error message does not directly reference the user’s action, making debugging non‑trivial. To remediate, the contract should either remove the unnecessary pos.size calculation from the caching step in the afterOrderExecution callback—as it is not used elsewhere—or add logic that safely handles stale price data, such as falling back to a previously stored safe price or postponing the calculation until a fresh price is available. This change eliminates the revert condition and restores the ability to correctly cache position data and update margins, aligning the implementation with the intended business logic of accurate PnL accounting.
summary: Protocol uses Chainlink LLO pricing for critical calculations during rebalance period, like getVaultPPS which fetches GmxV2PositionManager.positionMargin. However, fetching LLO prices can revert if they are stale: if (priceDeets.lastUpdatedBlockNumber < minBlockNumber) revert PriceOutsideTolerance(); Although getVaultPPS is safe as the prices are updated when rebalance period is opened and closed, this is not the case for the GmxV2PositionManager.decreasePosition which uses LLO pricing for PnL calculations. Even if prices are updated just before decreasing a position, the GMX afterOrderExecution callback will likely revert when calculating position notional during _updatePositionCache. This issue will prevent position data to be cached, specially the key parameter used to correctly calculate positionMargin.

title: H-04 | Users Forfeit Their esGMX, bnGMX And GMX Rewards When Entering The Vault
content: The vulnerability is a reward‑distribution logic flaw in the ExitVault contract that allows the vault owner to capture all esGMX, bnGMX and GMX rewards generated by users’ GMX and GLP deposits while the vault is active, typically for at least one year. The root cause is that the contract never claims or forwards these rewards to the participants during the operational period; instead it accumulates them internally and only releases them to the owner when the earlyOwnerExit function is executed and the account transfer is accepted. An attacker who controls the vault owner role can therefore invoke the exit routine and withdraw the entire pool of accrued rewards, leaving ordinary users with only the modest portion of esGMX that vests according to the original design. The impact is that users who stake tokens expect to earn additional GMX‑related incentives, but they receive none of the generated rewards; from the user’s perspective the UI shows a zero or missing reward balance despite active staking, violating the economic assumptions of the protocol and effectively causing a loss of potentially valuable assets. This condition occurs for every user who participates in the vault during its active phase, regardless of when they later withdraw, and it is discovered through a manual audit that examined the reward‑claiming functions and identified that only the owner is authorized to collect the accumulated rewards. The issue can be hard to notice because the rewards are not emitted as events to external observers and the contract does not expose a public view of pending rewards for participants, so the discrepancy is hidden behind internal accounting.
