The core logic that selects the anchor tick compares the amount of anchor liquidity with the amount of discovery liquidity. When the anchor liquidity is larger than the discovery liquidity, the algorithm places the upper anchor tick below the current active tick while the price remains inside the discovery range. An attacker can exploit this deterministic behaviour by first buying a large quantity of the bToken, which pushes the market price upward within the discovery range, and then immediately invoking rebalance. The rebalance call shifts the tick range so that the newly added anchor liquidity now sits at a higher price level, allowing the attacker to sell the same amount of bToken at a higher average price. The reverse situation – anchor liquidity lower than discovery liquidity – enables a symmetric attack where the attacker sells first in a low‑liquidity environment, calls rebalance to move liquidity to a more favourable range, and then buys back at a lower price. This sequence creates a guaranteed‑profit arbitrage vector that extracts value from the protocol and its liquidity providers without any legitimate economic activity. The impact is that the protocol loses net liquidity and may experience abnormal price spikes, while honest users see their balances shrink or receive no expected refunds. The flaw manifests whenever the rebalance function is callable without restrictions and the relative sizes of anchor and discovery liquidity satisfy the described conditions. It was uncovered during a manual audit that examined the tick‑update algorithm and identified that the tick shift could be timed to capture price differentials. The issue is subtle because the rebalance operation appears to be a normal maintenance action; there is no explicit check that prevents a user from performing a large trade immediately before the tick adjustment, making the exploit easy to miss in routine testing. To remediate the problem, the protocol should limit how many ticks can be moved in a single rebalance, introduce a time‑delay or cooldown between large trades and tick updates, and add slippage or price‑impact checks that reject rebalances that would create a deterministic arbitrage opportunity. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of rebalancing‑induced price‑manipulation vulnerabilities where deterministic state changes can be front‑run for profit, violating the intended accounting invariants of the market‑making system.
summary:
The rebalance function removes the protocol-owned liquidity, updates ticks, and redeploys liquidity
using new tick ranges. The _updateTicks logic determines the anchorTick based on whether the
anchor liquidity is higher or lower than the discovery liquidity.
There are immediate arbitrage opportunities by using the rebalance functionality. When the anchor
liquidity is higher than the discovery liquidity:
• The upper anchor tick is below the active tick, and the current price is within the discovery range.
• User can buy a large amount of bToken, pushing the price even higher.
• Call rebalance, which updates ticks and range liquidities.
• Sell the same amount of bToken at a higher average price due to higher anchor liquidity.
A similar arbitrage opportunity can occur in the opposite direction as well. When anchor liquidity is
lower than discovery liquidity, the user can sell, rebalance, and buy back. This time, the user sells in a
low-liquidity environment and buys back in a high-liquidity environment.

title: H-01 | Working With Stale State Can Cause Invalid Delegation Rights
content: The vulnerability originates from a stale‑state read in the cross‑chain delegation logic of the NFT shadow system. When a user invokes the lzRead function to update delegation rights on the base chain or to mint an NFT on the shadow chain, the contract calls EVMCallComputeV1 with the current block timestamp. However, the lzMap component later relies on a delegatedOwners mapping that was populated using the timestamp captured at the moment of the EVM call. Because the _executeMessage routine may be executed after the underlying ownership on the shadow chain has already changed, the stored delegated owner can be outdated. In practice this means that the base chain continues to believe that User A is the delegated owner of a particular token even after the shadow chain has transferred ownership to User B or User C. When successive lzRead calls occur, the contract attempts to transfer delegation from the stale entry (User A) to the new owner, but it never revokes the previous delegation for User B before assigning it to User C. Consequently both User B and User C retain valid delegation rights simultaneously. The root cause is a time‑of‑check‑to‑time‑of‑use (TOCTOU) race condition where the contract checks the delegated owner using an old timestamp and then uses that stale value to perform state updates. Exploitation is straightforward: an attacker who can trigger ownership changes on the shadow chain between two lzRead calls can cause multiple parties to hold delegation rights, allowing unauthorized actions such as transferring or modifying the NFT. The impact is that the protocol’s accounting of delegation rights becomes inconsistent, breaking the guarantee that only the current owner (or a single delegated party) may act on the token. Users may notice that they can no longer rely on exclusive control; for example, a user who expects to be the sole delegate finds that another address can also execute privileged functions, leading to confusion, potential loss of assets, or unauthorized transfers. This condition occurs whenever delegation updates are performed via lzRead while the shadow chain’s ownership state changes faster than the base chain’s timestamp‑based snapshot. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by the Guardian team, who observed that the delegatedOwners mapping did not reflect the latest shadow‑chain owner after a series of lzRead calls. Because the contract does not emit explicit errors and the mapping still contains a valid address, the bug can remain hidden until multiple delegates are observed acting on the same token. To remediate the problem, the contract should avoid reading the stale owner from lzMap; instead it must retrieve the previous owner directly within the _updateOwnership routine, ensuring that delegation revocation is based on the most recent state. This change eliminates the TOCTOU window and restores the invariant that at any moment only one delegated address holds rights for a given token, aligning the implementation with the intended business logic of exclusive delegation.
summary:
When a user wants to update delegate rights on the base chain or mint an NFT on the shadow chain
they call lzread. However in lzread we use EVMCallComputeV1 with the current timestamp.
Meanwhile in lzmap we rely on a reading state that could potentially be outdated. This is because
the state is based on the timestamp set in EVMCallComputeV1 and by the time _executeMessage is
called that state may no longer be accurate.
Let's take example: (lzread from Base chain to Shadow chain). Initially, an NFT is locked on the base
chain but unlocked and owned by User A on Optimism, with lzRead delegating rights to User A. At
timestamp x, someone calls lzRead, and while the owner on Optimism has changed to User B, the
base chain still lists delegatedOwners[collectionAddress][tokenId] as User A at timestamp x.
At a later timestamp y, another lzRead call occurs, and now the owner on Optimism is User C, the
base chain still lists delegatedOwners[collectionAddress][tokenId] as User A at timestamp y. When
processing these updates, delegation rights are transferred from User A to User B for the ﬁrst call
and from User A to User C for the second call, leaving delegatedOwners[collectionAddress][tokenId]
set to User C. This creates an issue where both User B and User C have delegation rights, as the
delegation for User B cannot be properly revoked.

title: H-02 | If Beacon Delegates To Address(0) It Will Be Permanent
content: The vulnerability concerns a permanent delegation to the zero address (address(0)) that can be created by the Beacon contract when it processes delegation information coming from a remote chain. When the owner of an ERC‑721 token on the remote chain either burns the NFT or explicitly delegates it to address(0) via the IDelegateRegistry, the Beacon records this state by writing address(0) into its delegatedOwners mapping. The internal function _updateDelegations() contains a guard that refuses to clear a delegation if the staleOwner is address(0). Consequently, once a delegation to address(0) is stored, it can never be removed, even if the token later receives a new legitimate owner on the remote chain. The result is that the base‑chain Beacon ends up holding two active delegations for the same token: one to address(0) and another to the current owner. Projects that rely on a single active delegation for reward distribution, or that assume a delegation to address(0) means “no delegation”, may split rewards incorrectly, double‑count delegations, or fail to allocate rewards at all. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that rewards appear reduced, split, or missing even though the user still holds the NFT on the remote chain. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the delegation logic, and it is subtle because a zero‑address entry is often treated as a null value, yet the contract treats it as an active delegation that cannot be cleared. The root cause is the missing validation that prevents delegations to address(0) from being recorded, combined with the immutable check that blocks removal of such entries. To remediate, the contract should reject any attempt to set a new delegation to address(0) (for example by adding a require(newOwner != address(0)) check) and should also allow explicit clearing of a zero‑address delegation when the token changes ownership. This change restores the invariant that each token has at most one active delegation and prevents reward‑distribution logic from being confused by a permanent, meaningless delegation.
summary:
The Beacon can delegate to address(0) in case the owner on the remote chain have burned the NFT.
In this scenario the NFT remains unlocked and a read request from the base chain will set
delegatedOwners[collectionAddress][tokenId] to address(0). This will remove the active delegation
of the stale owner and will create a new delegation to address(0) via
IDelegateRegistry.delegateERC721.
There is another case where the owner of the NFT on the remote chain delegates to address(0) via
IDelegateRegistry.delegateERC721. Upon a read request the Beacon on the base chain will create an
active delegation to address(0) that it will not be able to remove ever again for this NFT since we
encounter this check in _updateDelegations() when the staleOwner is address(0): if (staleOwner =
address(0)) {.
This means that when the NFT gets a new owner on the remote chain from now on, the base chain
will have 2 active delegations. One to address(0) and one to the current owner. Having two active
delegations can confuse projects that implement logic for distributing rewards based on your
current active delegations (and split the rewards), require you to have 1 active delegation or does not
handle well delegation to address(0).

title: H-09 | oneRound Function Potentially Allows Negative Allocations
content: The vulnerability resides in the oneRound function of the allocation contract. The function relies on a helper routine called calculateXi to produce a set of allocation values for a given round. When calculateXi returns a negative value for any allocation, the inner processing loop detects the anomaly and breaks out of the iteration. However, the implementation continues to copy the partially built candidate array into the persistent bestXi storage even after the break. As a result, a negative allocation is recorded in mem.bestXi and later used as if it were a valid positive amount. This breaks the fundamental assumption of the allocation algorithm that all Xi values are non‑negative, leading to corrupted liquidity calculations, mismatched pool balances and incorrect cost accounting. The bug manifests only when the allocation logic encounters a situation that produces a negative Xi – for example an edge case in the pricing formula or an overflow that yields a signed underflow. Under those conditions the contract silently accepts the invalid data, so users and auditors may not notice the problem until they observe unexpected zero or negative shares, trades that fail due to insufficient liquidity, or overall pool accounting that does not reconcile. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that inspected the control flow of oneRound and identified that the bestCost and bestX update occurs unconditionally after the loop break. The problem is hard to spot because the break statement appears to handle the error, giving the impression that the round is aborted, yet the subsequent copy operation defeats that intention. To remediate the flaw the function should only update bestCost and the bestX array when the candidate allocations contain no negative entries; a guard clause or validation step must be added before the copy, and any round that produces a negative allocation should be discarded or corrected. In generic terms this is an allocation‑algorithm integrity bug where unchecked negative values propagate through state, violating the business rule that allocations must be non‑negative and causing accounting inconsistencies that can lead to loss of funds or incorrect user balances.
summary: Within the oneRound function, when a negative allocation is produced by calculateXi, the inner loop is broken but the partial candidate array is still copied into bestXi. This allows negative allocations to be stored and subsequently used, totally breaking the purpose of the allocation algorithm logic. Once a negative allocation is propagated into mem.bestXi and then allocated it will corrupt the overall allocation logic, causing mismatched liquidity calculations.

title: H-01 | Auto-Compounding Can Lead To Liquidations
content: The vulnerability resides in the auto‑compounding (reinvest) routine of a lending protocol that automatically converts fees earned on a Uniswap pool back into collateral for an outstanding loan. The routine rewards the caller with a bounty, but it does not perform any safety verification of the loan’s health after the collateral value has been altered. Because the reinvest operation reduces the net collateral that backs the borrower’s position, the health factor can fall below the liquidation threshold. When this happens, any external actor can trigger liquidation of the position, or the reinvest call itself can cause an immediate liquidation. The flaw is a classic missing post‑operation health check combined with an incentive misalignment: the system encourages third‑party callers to execute the function for profit without protecting the borrower’s collateral. Exploitation is straightforward – an attacker (or any user) calls the reinvest function on a marginally healthy loan, receives the bounty, and the collateral reduction pushes the loan into a liquidatable state. The protocol then allows the attacker or a liquidator to seize the collateral, resulting in loss of funds for the borrower. This can occur at any time a loan is close to the required collateralization ratio, especially when the borrower relies on the auto‑compounding feature for capital efficiency. The affected parties are borrowers whose positions are auto‑compounded, the protocol that loses trust, and any users who expect their collateral to remain safe after a reinvest. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the reinvest flow and noticed the absence of a health‑factor assertion after the bounty transfer. It is easy to miss because the function appears to add value (reinvesting fees) and the bounty seems benign, so developers may assume the loan remains safe without explicitly checking. From a user’s perspective the UI may show the collateral amount decreasing unexpectedly, the health factor dropping, or the loan becoming liquidatable immediately after a reinvest transaction, contrary to the expectation that auto‑compounding only improves capital efficiency. The bug belongs to the class of “post‑action invariant violation” where state changes break critical accounting assumptions. To remediate, the contract should re‑evaluate the loan’s health after the reinvest and revert the transaction if the position becomes under‑collateralized. Additionally, giving borrowers the ability to set a maximum auto‑compounding limit or to opt‑out of external callers receiving bounties would align incentives and prevent third‑party actors from pushing positions to the edge of liquidation.
summary: The auto-compounding feature should help borrowers be more capital efficient by automatically reinvesting fees earned on uniswap. As the caller of the reinvest function receives a bounty for doing the work, the position's collateral value decreases through auto-compounding. The reinvest function does not implement safety checks for the position's health. Therefore, it is possible that calling the reinvest function leads to positions being liquidatable, which is definitely not in the borrower's interest and should therefore be prevented. It is also possible to auto-compound liquidatable positions and therefore potentially make them go underwater.

title: H-02 | Oracle Price DoS
content: The vulnerability resides in the oraclePriceSqrtX96 routine, which aggregates time‑weighted average prices (TWAP) from a list of Uniswap pools that share a given token pair. The function assumes that each pool in the list can provide a historical observation at least ORACLE_T seconds old via Uniswap's observeSingle call. This assumption is the root cause: newly created pools, or pools that have not yet accumulated enough price observations, do not satisfy the required observation window. When observeSingle is invoked on such a pool, Uniswap deliberately reverts with the message "dev Reverts if an observation at or before the desired observation timestamp does not exist". Because the oracle routine does not handle this exception, the revert propagates and aborts the entire price calculation. An attacker can exploit this by deploying a new pool with a different fee tier for the same token pair, ensuring that the pool is added to the poolsList. The presence of the new pool forces oraclePriceSqrtX96 to call observeSingle on a pool that lacks the needed historical data, causing the whole oracle to fail. The impact is a denial‑of‑service on the price oracle: any downstream logic that depends on a valid price—such as the isUnderwater check, positionData retrieval, or the restructureBadDebt routine—cannot execute, effectively freezing liquidation, debt restructuring, and potentially other user‑facing actions. From a user perspective, transactions that rely on price data revert, the UI may show missing or zero prices, and users may see messages like "oracle price calculation failed" or experience unexpected zeros in their balance calculations. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the pre‑conditions of oraclePriceSqrtX96 and identified the unchecked external call to Uniswap. It can be hard to notice because the revert only occurs when a pool without sufficient history is introduced, a scenario that may not be exercised in typical testing. The bug belongs to the class of unchecked external call failures leading to denial‑of‑service, specifically an oracle aggregation routine that does not gracefully handle missing data. To remediate, the contract should catch the revert from each observeSingle invocation—using a try‑catch block or equivalent error handling—and exclude failing pools from the averaging calculation, adjusting the divisor accordingly. This change ensures that the oracle can continue to provide a price based on the remaining valid pools, preserving protocol functionality even when some pools are unsuitable for observation.
summary: The function oraclePriceSqrtX96 aims to calculate the oracle price by gathering the TWAP across all Uniswap pools with a specific (token0, token1) pair and calculating the mean. The pre-condition for a successful call to oraclePriceSqrtX96 is that for each Uniswap pool in the poolsList, the consult function does not revert. However, if a pool was just created, there would not be an observation that was ORACLE_T seconds ago and Uniswap's observeSingle would revert: "dev Reverts if an observation at or before the desired observation timestamp does not exist" Ultimately, a user can DoS the calculation of oracle pricing for an entire period just by deploying a different fee tier, which would prevent positionData retrieval and DoS other areas of the codebase such as function isUnderwater and consequently restructureBadDebt.

title: H-03 | Restructure Debt Locks Up Funds
content: The vulnerability concerns the handling of positions that undergo debt restructuring in a lending protocol. When a position’s debt is restructured, the protocol forgives the outstanding debt and distributes the loss across participants, after which the position remains recorded in the system. In some scenarios the restructured position becomes liquidatable because its collateral value is still insufficient relative to the (now zero) debt, yet the protocol does not automatically trigger liquidation. In other cases the position appears fully healthy and stays open. This inconsistent post‑restructuring behavior can be unexpected for the protocol because it effectively provides a bail‑out to certain underwater borrowers while keeping the associated lender funds locked inside the contract indefinitely. The root cause is a missing or incorrect state transition that fails to enforce liquidation or removal of positions that remain under‑collateralized after debt forgiveness. An attacker can exploit this by deliberately causing a position to become underwater, invoking the restructuring function to erase the debt, and then relying on the protocol’s failure to liquidate the still‑under‑collateralized position, thereby preventing lenders from withdrawing their collateral. The impact is that lenders’ assets may remain frozen for an unbounded period, reducing capital efficiency and potentially jeopardizing the protocol’s solvency if many positions are abused in this way. The issue manifests whenever a position is underwater and the restructuring routine is called; it is not limited to a specific token or market pair. All parties that provide liquidity – lenders, borrowers, and the protocol governance – are affected because the accounting assumptions of the system (that debt forgiveness either restores a healthy position or leads to liquidation) are violated. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the restructuring flow and noticed that the liquidation check was not re‑executed after debt forgiveness. It can be hard to notice because the UI may still display the position as active with a zero debt balance, giving the impression that the funds are safe, while the underlying collateral remains locked and may be flagged as liquidatable in the contract state. To remediate, the protocol should either prevent underwater positions from remaining in the system after restructuring, enforce an immediate liquidation when a restructured position is still under‑collateralized, or redesign the restructuring logic to ensure that debt forgiveness does not create a scenario where collateral can be indefinitely trapped. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of accounting‑logic errors where state transitions after a financial operation are incomplete, leading to funds disappearing from user access despite appearing normal on the front‑end.
summary: When a position’s debt is restructured, the debt is forgiven, the losses socialized, and the position remains in the system. In certain cases, the position can become liquidatable after restructuring and be liquidated, and other times the position can become fully healthy and remain. This incongruent behavior may be unexpected for the protocol, since some positions will effectively get a bail-out and remain. This can be used by malicious borrower’s to keep lender’s funds locked up indefinitely.

title: `GMXV2_Module` withdrawal functionality is broken due to missing callback implementation
content: The GMXV2_Module contract contains a critical withdrawal flaw: it registers itself as the callback contract for GMX V2 withdrawals but does not implement the required IWithdrawalCallbackReceiver interface. GMX V2 expects any contract supplied as a callback to expose two functions, afterWithdrawalExecution and afterWithdrawalCancellation, which are invoked by the GMX keeper after the withdrawal process. Because the module lacks these functions, the keeper’s call fails, causing the entire withdrawal transaction to revert. This revert happens every time the gmxv2_withdraw function is called, effectively locking any user funds that have been deposited in the protocol. The bug was discovered during a security audit when the code was examined and it was noted that the callbackContract field was set to address(this) without any corresponding implementation. The issue is subtle because unit tests that manually simulate token transfers can pass, masking the missing callback call that occurs only in the live GMX execution flow. From a user’s perspective, attempts to withdraw result in no funds being transferred, the UI may show a pending transaction that eventually fails, or simply display a zero balance change, contrary to the expectation that a withdrawal would return the deposited assets. The impact is severe: all withdrawal functionality is broken, preventing users from retrieving their assets and potentially leading to loss of confidence in the protocol. The vulnerability belongs to the class of missing external callback implementations, where a contract advertises a callback address but does not satisfy the required interface, violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions that post‑withdrawal logic will always execute. To remediate, the module should either remove the callback by setting callbackContract to the zero address when no post‑withdrawal processing is needed, or correctly implement the IWithdrawalCallbackReceiver interface and provide the two required functions. Either fix restores the expected flow, allowing the keeper to call the callbacks successfully and enabling users to withdraw their funds as intended.

title: `PRIVATE_KEY` exposed in `makefile` file and other sensitive data
content: The vulnerability consists of hard‑coded sensitive credentials, including a private key, RPC endpoint URLs with API keys, and several Etherscan API keys, being stored directly in the project's Makefile. This exposure occurs because the build configuration file is committed to the repository without any secret‑management safeguards, allowing anyone who can view the source code to read the credentials. An attacker who obtains the private key gains full control over the associated address; they can sign arbitrary transactions, withdraw any ether or tokens held by that wallet, and impersonate the protocol by deploying contracts that appear legitimate, such as fake vaults. The leaked RPC endpoints and API keys enable unauthorized calls to blockchain nodes and third‑party services, potentially incurring unexpected costs, exhausting rate limits, or disrupting production services. The impact is therefore two‑fold: direct financial loss if the compromised address holds funds, and indirect damage to the protocol’s reputation and operational stability through impersonation or service abuse. The issue manifests when the repository is cloned or inspected, for example during a public audit, code review, or by any third party with read access; the credentials are visible in plain text and may not be immediately obvious because a Makefile is typically viewed as a build script rather than a secret store. The discovery was made during a security audit that examined repository files for secret leakage. The problem is hard to notice because the credentials are embedded in a non‑executable configuration file and may not trigger compiler warnings or runtime errors. To remediate, all exposed secrets must be removed from the source, the compromised private key should be rotated and any assets transferred to a new secure address, contract permissions granted to the old address must be revoked, and all API keys regenerated. Future deployments should use secure secret‑management practices such as environment variables, encrypted vaults, or dedicated key‑management services, ensuring that no private keys or API tokens are ever committed to version control. From a user perspective, the symptoms could include unexpected zero balances, transactions appearing from an address the user never used, or the appearance of unauthorized vault contracts, all of which violate the expected accounting guarantees of the protocol.
summary:
** The project's Makefile contains hardcoded sensitive credentials including:

- A private key used for contract deployments
- Multiple RPC endpoint URLs with API keys
- Several Etherscan API keys for different networks

** Although no customer funds were at risk and the deployer key had no admin rights on any of the deployed strategies, this exposure is critical because:

1. The private key grants complete control over the associated address, including:
    - Full access to any funds held by the wallet
    - Impersonate the protocol and deploy fake vaults
2. The RPC endpoints could be used to:
    - Execute unauthorized API calls
    - Potentially incur costs to the project
    - Exceed rate limits affecting production services

title: Users may lose value when transferring ERC-4626 Vault tokens cross-chain
content: The vulnerability is a share‑value distortion that occurs when ERC‑4626 vault tokens are transferred across chains using the Mint/Burn pattern required by the LayerZero OFT standard. In this design the _debit function burns the sender’s shares on the source chain, which reduces the vault’s totalSupply while the underlying assets remain locked in the contract. Because ERC‑4626 defines the value of each share as assets divided by totalSupply, the reduction of totalSupply inflates the exchange rate for the remaining shares. Consequently, any user who keeps their tokens on the original chain sees a higher previewRedeem amount, but that increase is artificial: the extra value actually belongs to the shares that were burned and are still in transit. If another participant withdraws during this window, they receive a portion of the assets that should have been claimable by the transferred user. When the burned shares are later minted on the destination chain, the recipient finds that their shares are worth zero assets because the underlying pool has already been depleted. The impact is that users who initiate a cross‑chain transfer can lose part or all of their deposited value, and the protocol’s accounting invariants are broken, leading to potential fund loss and loss of trust. The issue manifests only while a transfer is pending; it is hard to notice because the share price appears to increase, which may be interpreted as a positive gain. The flaw was discovered during a security audit by observing that the previewRedeem value changes after a send call and that a later redeem by the original holder reverts with ZERO_ASSETS. To remediate, the vault should avoid burning shares for cross‑chain moves—using a lock/unlock mechanism that keeps totalSupply constant—or adjust the accounting to preserve the assets‑per‑share ratio during transit. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of accounting distortion in tokenized vaults caused by improper handling of share supply during cross‑chain operations.

title: Reward claiming fails for Berachain RewardVaults due to incorrect interface
content: The vulnerability is an interface mismatch between the D2 module that attempts to claim rewards from a Berachain RewardVault and the actual RewardVault contract implementation. The module calls IVault.getReward(address) while the deployed RewardVault expects a function signature getReward(address account, address recipient). Because the second parameter is missing, the low‑level call is encoded with the wrong calldata, causing the external call to revert at runtime. This mismatch occurs whenever the function bera_vault_get_reward is invoked, which is restricted to the EXECUTOR_ROLE but can be called by any authorized executor. As a result, any attempt to claim $BGT rewards fails, leaving the rewards unclaimed and the caller receiving no tokens. From a user perspective the claim transaction reverts, the UI may show an error or simply no change in balance, and users see that their expected reward amount remains zero despite having earned rewards. The issue was discovered during a security audit when a test that expected a successful claim instead triggered an expectRevert, confirming that the call could not succeed. The bug is hard to notice because the Solidity code compiles without errors—the interface definition matches the compiler’s expectations—but the runtime ABI does not match the on‑chain contract, leading to silent failures only observable at execution time. This class of bug falls under incorrect interface or ABI mismatch, which violates the accounting assumption that a successful claim transfers earned tokens to the caller. To remediate, the interface definition must be updated to include the recipient argument and the call should pass address(this) for both parameters, aligning the calldata with the actual contract signature. After fixing, reward claims will succeed, restoring the protocol’s incentive mechanism and allowing liquidity providers to receive their earned $BGT tokens.

title: H-01 | Invalid Remaining Reserves Calculation
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect calculation of the remaining reserves in the MarketMaking contract that governs capacity bumps. The contract attempts to simulate an increase in the blvTick and checks that the bumped capacity does not exceed the circulating supply. To compute the bumped floor capacity it calls a helper that returns a value called remainingReserves, which is derived from the virtual reserves plus the token balance held by the BPOOL contract. The root cause is that the BPOOL balance reflects the total reserves of the market, because all reserves have been removed from the active price ranges before the simulation. Consequently, the remainingReserves variable actually equals the total reserves instead of the reserves that are still free after accounting for the anchor range. This mis‑calculation allows the protocol to believe that more free reserves exist than actually do, so it may approve a capacity bump that exceeds the true available liquidity. An attacker or a malicious actor could trigger a bump when the contract thinks there is sufficient reserve, causing the protocol to allocate more tokens than it can back. The impact is a potential shortfall in the pool: users may later experience missing refunds, zero balances, or failed withdrawals because the contract has over‑committed its reserves. The bug manifests whenever the market‑making logic attempts to increase the blvTick and relies on the bumpedFloorCapacity check, i.e., during any rebalancing or expansion operation. All participants that rely on the market‑making contract – liquidity providers, token holders, and the protocol itself – are affected because the accounting assumptions of the system are broken. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the intended accounting model with the actual on‑chain state and noticed that the BPOOL balance was being used without subtracting the reserves already allocated to the anchor range. It is hard to notice because the code appears to read a balance and add virtual reserves, which seems reasonable, and the discrepancy only surfaces under specific rebalancing scenarios. The proper fix is to subtract the amount of reserves that have been locked into the anchor range before adding the BPOOL balance, thereby calculating the true remaining free reserves. In conceptual terms the bug belongs to the class of “incorrect reserve accounting” or “capacity over‑estimation” bugs, where a contract uses a total‑balance metric instead of a net‑available metric, leading to financial mis‑allocation and potential loss of funds.
summary: The MarketMaking contract verifies if the protocol can bump by simulating an increase in the blvTick, and later validating some conditions, like bumpedCapacity > circulating. The bumpedAnchorCapacity is calculated based on the _getAnchorReserves. However, the bumpedFloorCapacity is mistakenly uses the remainingReserves as follows: int256 remainingReserves = _getVirtualReserves() + reserve.balanceOf(address(BPOOL)); However, the balance of the BPOOL contains all reserves, as they were all removed from the ranges, so remainingReserves is actually equal to totalReserves.

title: H-02 | DoS Of Deployment
content: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that appears during the deployment phase of a contract that relies on a Uniswap V3 pool for rebalancing. The root cause is that the deployment script uses vm.startBroadcast(), which causes each initialization call (such as token distribution, liquidity provision, and the first call to rebalance()) to be sent as separate transactions rather than a single atomic transaction. Because the calls are not atomic, a user who already holds the newly minted bTokens can front‑run the deployment and interact with the Uniswap pool before the contract’s first rebalance is executed. By adding liquidity in a range that lies below the intended baseline value (BLV) and then performing a swap that moves the pool’s active tick into that lower range, the attacker forces the pool’s current active tick to be below the BLV tick. When the contract later invokes rebalance(), it attempts to set the lower bound of its anchor range to the BLV tick and calculates the upper bound based on the current active tick. Since the active tick is now lower than the BLV tick, the calculated tick range is invalid and the internal setTicks() function reverts with an InvalidTickRange error. This revert stops the rebalance logic, effectively freezing the contract’s ability to manage liquidity and rendering the deployment unusable. From a user’s perspective the contract appears to have been deployed successfully, but any subsequent attempt to rebalance results in a transaction that fails with no obvious error message, leading to missing or zero balances where users expect their positions to be adjusted. The impact is a denial of service: the protocol cannot perform its core accounting function, funds may become stuck, and the intended economic behavior of the system is broken. The issue is discovered during a security audit that included a proof‑of‑concept test where the attacker deliberately manipulated the pool before the rebalance call. It can be hard to notice because the deployment script itself does not throw errors; the problem only surfaces later when the contract’s rebalance function is called. The bug belongs to the class of “non‑atomic initialization leading to front‑running vulnerabilities” and violates the business assumption that the pool’s tick state will be within the expected range at the moment of the first rebalance. To remediate the issue the deployment should be performed inside a single smart‑contract function (for example, via a factory contract) so that all initialization steps execute atomically in one transaction, preventing any external actor from intervening between the steps. This ensures that the active tick cannot be moved out of the expected range before the contract sets its anchor ticks, eliminating the InvalidTickRange revert and restoring the protocol’s ability to manage liquidity safely.
summary: Deploying with vm.startBroadcast() will lead to each call happening as a separate transaction. This gives a user who was distributed bTokens the opportunity to interact with the Uniswap pool prior to the first rebalance occurring. A malicious user can deploy liquidity below the desired BLV. Then, they can swap to their new deployed liquidity range. This will mean the active tick is below the BLV tick. When rebalance() is invoked, it will attempt to set the lower tick of the anchor range to the BLV tick and the upper tick will be calculated using the current active tick. Since the current active tick is below the BLV tick, setTicks() will revert due to InvalidTickRange. This will DoS the deployment after the tokens are distributed and the contract has been deployed.

title: H-03 | Extend Interest Stolen
content: The vulnerability originates from the extend function of the CreditFacility contract, which accrues interest that is intended to be held temporarily until the designated fee recipient withdraws it with explicit approval. Instead of isolating the accrued interest, the internal _swapExactOut routine indiscriminately transfers the entire ether balance of the CreditFacility contract to the BPOOL liquidity contract. Because the accrued interest remains in the CreditFacility balance, the bulk transfer unintentionally moves those fee amounts into the protocol’s liquidity pool, making them unavailable for the fee recipient. This misdirection occurs whenever the extend function is used and a subsequent swap operation invokes _swapExactOut, effectively stealing the interest that should have been collectible. From a user perspective, the expected outcome – a fee recipient receiving a positive interest payout – is replaced by a silent reduction of the contract’s balance, often observed as a zero or unexpectedly low fee amount after the transaction. The impact is that the protocol loses revenue that was meant for fee recipients, and users may see their balances disappear without an obvious error, violating the accounting assumption that accrued interest remains separate until withdrawal. The issue was identified during a security audit performed by Guardian, who noted that the full‑balance transfer masks the loss of the fee amounts, making it difficult to detect through casual testing because the contract still appears to function normally after the swap. To remediate the problem, the extend logic should be altered so that the reserve amount (including the accrued interest) is sent directly to the fee recipient rather than being deposited into the CreditFacility contract, and any other code paths that leave reserves in the CreditFacility should be reviewed and corrected to avoid similar full‑balance transfers. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of improper fund routing where a contract’s balance is swept wholesale, causing unintended loss of earmarked funds.
summary: The Interest accrued from the extend function sits in the CreditFacility contract until the fee recipient removes it with their approval. However this poses an issue because the _swapExactOut function transfers the entire contract balance of the CreditFacility to the BPOOL contract. As a result these fee amounts which are sitting in the CreditFacility contract will be deployed into the protocol liquidity instead of collectable.

title: H-04 | All Credit Interests Are Deployed As Liquidity
content: The vulnerability is that the credit facility's reserve‑sending routine does not actually transfer the accrued interest to the designated fee recipient. The routine calls removeAllFrom, which only withdraws tokens from the internal accounting but leaves the withdrawn amount inside the BPOOL contract. As a result, the interest that should be collected as protocol fees is automatically re‑added to the liquidity pool instead of being sent to the feeRecipient. This occurs whenever the _sendReserves function is executed after interest has been accrued. The root cause is the misuse of the removeAllFrom helper, which does not perform an external token transfer, combined with missing logic to move the tokens to the feeRecipient. From a user perspective, the protocol appears to retain the same total liquidity, but the expected fee distribution never materialises; feeRecipient balances stay unchanged and users may see lower returns because the protocol does not capture the interest. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the credit facility contract. It is subtle because the pool’s total token count does not change, so the missing fee transfer can be overlooked unless the feeRecipient’s balance is inspected. The bug belongs to the class of “incorrect token routing” or “misdirected fund transfer” vulnerabilities, where funds are sent to the wrong contract or retained in an internal pool instead of the intended beneficiary. Exploitation does not require an attacker; the protocol itself loses revenue each time interest is generated. To remediate, the _sendReserves function should explicitly call BPOOL.transferToken(reserve, feeRecipient, _interest) so that the interest is moved out of the pool to the feeRecipient, and the obsolete feeRecipient approval logic can be removed. This correction restores the intended accounting invariant that interest reserves are collectible by the fee receiver and prevents silent erosion of protocol fees.
summary: The CreditFacility _sendReserves function used to keep the interest reserves amount in the CreditFacility contract so that this amount could be removed by the fee receiver which is approved for the CreditFacility. However now, because the removeAllFrom function leaves all removed tokens in the BPOOL contract, the interest amount is not collected by the protocol and will instead be deployed back into the liquidity structure.

title: H-01 | withdraw2Contract Crosschain Flow Pays Withdrawal Fee Twice
content: In the withdraw2Contract cross‑chain withdrawal flow the protocol records the withdrawal fee twice in the Ledger. The fee collector’s account is credited once when the withdrawal is initiated in the executeWithdraw2Contract step, where the user’s funds are frozen and the fee amount is deducted. A second credit occurs later in the accountWithDrawFinish step, which finalises the withdrawal and again adds the same fee amount to the collector’s balance. The root cause is that both steps contain logic that unconditionally credits the fee without checking whether it has already been accounted for. An attacker does not need to interact specially; any normal user withdrawal triggers the double credit, so the vulnerability can be exploited simply by performing a standard withdrawal. The impact is that the user is effectively charged twice for a single withdrawal, receiving less net amount than expected, while the fee collector’s balance is inflated with funds that never existed. This accounting error violates the protocol’s business logic that each withdrawal should incur exactly one fee and breaks the accounting invariants that total fees collected must equal the sum of fees deducted from users. The condition under which it occurs is any cross‑chain withdrawal that follows the withdraw2Contract path; it does not depend on specific input values. All users who withdraw, as well as the protocol’s financial reporting and any auditors, are affected because the ledger shows an incorrect distribution of funds. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s withdrawal functions, where the auditor noticed that the fee collector’s balance increased by an amount larger than the sum of fees taken from users. The bug can be hard to notice because the UI typically displays only the fee deducted once, masking the second hidden credit that only appears in the internal ledger. To remediate, the fee should be credited exactly once – either at the execution stage or at the final settlement stage – and the redundant credit in the other function must be removed or guarded by a flag that records whether the fee has already been applied. This class of bug is a double‑charging or duplicate accounting error, common in systems where state updates are performed in multiple phases without proper idempotency checks.
summary: In the withdraw2Contract crosschain flow, the Ledger credits the fee collector’s account with the withdrawal fee in executeWithdraw2Contract, then credits the same fee again in accountWithDrawFinish. As a result, a single user withdrawal leads to a double fee charge in the Ledger’s accounting, once when the funds are initially frozen and again when the ledger finalizes the withdrawal. This inflates the fee collector’s balance with inexistent funds.

title: H-02 | depositToStrategy Function Will Always Revert
content: The vulnerability is a missing token allowance step in the depositToStrategy function of the ProtocolVault contract. When the function attempts to forward a deposit request to an external DexVault by calling IDexVault(dexVault).depositTo(...), it expects the DexVault to pull the specified ERC‑20 tokens (USDC or any other token) from the ProtocolVault using transferFrom. However, the ProtocolVault never calls the ERC‑20 approve method to grant the DexVault permission to transfer those tokens on its behalf. Because the allowance is zero, the DexVault’s transferFrom call fails, causing the entire deposit transaction to revert. This is a classic missing‑allowance or approval bug, where a contract assumes an external party can move its tokens without first setting an allowance. The issue can be triggered every time a user or an automated process invokes depositToStrategy, regardless of the amount being deposited, leading to a deterministic revert. From the user’s perspective the UI will report a failed deposit, often showing a generic “transaction reverted” message, and the user’s token balance will remain unchanged, creating the impression that the deposit did nothing or that the contract is malicious. The impact is a denial‑of‑service for the deposit functionality: users cannot add liquidity, the vault cannot receive funds, and any business logic that depends on successful deposits (such as share issuance or fee accrual) is broken. The bug was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the flow of tokens between contracts and noticed the absence of an approve call before the external call. It can be hard to notice because the revert does not provide a specific error string; developers may mistakenly attribute the failure to other causes. To remediate, the contract should explicitly call token.approve(dexVault, amount) (or use safeIncreaseAllowance) before invoking the DexVault’s depositTo function, or redesign the interaction so that the DexVault pulls tokens only after the allowance has been set. This change restores the expected behavior where a user’s deposit is transferred, recorded, and reflected in their balance, aligning the implementation with the intended accounting model of the vault.
summary: The depositToStrategy function sends a deposit request to the dexVault via IDexVault(dexVault).depositTo(...), transferring USDC (or another token) in the process. However, there is no approval step for the vault to pull tokens from this contract. Without an ERC-20 approve call, the dexVault has no permission to transfer tokens on behalf of the ProtocolVault. As a result, the deposit call will always revert.

title: H-03 | Newly Added Strategy Provider Will Not Receive LP Deposits
content: The vulnerability is an allocation logic flaw in the vault’s proportional deposit routine that prevents a newly added strategy provider from ever receiving LP (liquidity provider) deposits. The contract distributes newly deposited LP assets among strategies based on the amount of main‑vault shares each strategy holds (mainShares). When a strategy is added after the vault has already been operating, its mainShares start at zero. Because the allocation formula multiplies the pending LP amount by the ratio of a strategy’s main assets to the total main assets, a zero main share yields a zero portion for the new strategy. Consequently, the new strategy never accrues any main‑vault capital automatically, even if the strategy provider contributes its own capital, because that capital is minted as strategy‑provider shares rather than main shares and does not affect the distribution ratio. The impact is that LP deposits are silently routed only to existing strategies, leaving the new strategy with a perpetual zero balance. From a user’s perspective, an LP depositor expects their funds to be spread across all active strategies to diversify risk and earn yield, but the UI will show the new strategy holding no assets despite being listed as active, leading to confusion and potentially lower overall returns. The issue manifests whenever a strategy is introduced in a later period (e.g., period 5) after the vault has already accumulated main shares for earlier strategies. It affects the protocol’s capital efficiency, the expectations of LP providers, and the operator’s ability to onboard new strategies. The flaw was discovered during a systematic audit of the allocation function, where the edge case of a zero‑share strategy was not covered by existing tests. It can be hard to notice because the allocation code appears mathematically correct for the typical case where all strategies already have non‑zero shares; the zero‑share scenario only surfaces when a strategy is added later. To remediate, the protocol should provide a mechanism for the operator to seed the new strategy with an initial amount of main‑vault capital, for example by rebalancing assets from existing strategies or allowing a manual allocation of main shares, thereby ensuring the new strategy participates in future LP deposit splits. This class of bug is a proportional‑allocation edge‑case where the denominator includes only existing participants, causing newcomers with zero weight to be excluded from future distributions, violating the intended accounting assumption that all active strategies share incoming liquidity proportionally.
summary: Under the current proportional deposit logic in allocatToFunds, the contract allocates newly deposited LP assets among strategies based solely on the main vault’s existing shares (i.e., mainShares). When a new strategy provider is introduced at a later period (for example, in the period 5), it starts with zero main shares. Consequently, the formula: portionForThisStrategy = pendingLpDepositAssets * (mainAssetsInFund / totalMainAssetsInFund) will yield zero for that strategy. The new strategy never accumulates any main vault capital automatically, as it isn’t part of the existing distribution ratio (which depends on mainShares). Even if the new strategy invests its own capital (SP deposit), that action mints strategy provider shares, not main shares, thus it does not affect the main vault ratio or future LP deposit splits. As a result, this new strategy remains perpetually excluded from LP inflows.

title: H-04 | Wrong Cross-chain Manager Usage
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect contract address reference inside the LedgerImplC contract that handles cross‑chain withdrawals. The contract stores two addresses: crossChainManagerV2Address, which is the manager for Solana withdrawals, and crossChainManagerAddress, which implements the withdraw2Contract function used for withdrawals to other contracts. While the executeWithdrawSolAction() function correctly calls the Solana manager via crossChainManagerV2Address, the executeWithdraw2Contract() function mistakenly reuses the same V2 address instead of the proper crossChainManagerAddress. Because the V2 manager does not implement the withdraw2Contract interface, any call to executeWithdraw2Contract() results in a call to a contract that lacks the expected function, causing the transaction to revert or silently fail. This bug can be exploited by any user who attempts a withdraw‑to‑contract operation: the transaction will appear to be submitted, but the funds never leave the LedgerImplC contract and the user receives no confirmation of a successful transfer. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a pending transaction that later fails, or simply no change in balance, leading to confusion as the expected refund or transfer never arrives. The impact is a denial‑of‑service for the withdraw2Contract feature and potential loss of funds if the caller does not handle the failure correctly, effectively making the protocol unable to honor certain cross‑chain withdrawals. The condition under which the bug manifests is any invocation of executeWithdraw2Contract(), which is triggered when a user requests a withdrawal to a contract address. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the intended contract interfaces with the actual address variables used in the code. It is hard to notice because both address variables have similar names and the compiler does not flag the mismatch; the failure only occurs at runtime when the called contract does not contain the expected function selector. The bug belongs to the class of “incorrect contract address usage” or “miswired dependency” bugs, where a contract calls an external contract using the wrong reference, violating the business logic that each manager should handle a specific withdrawal type. To remediate the issue, the code should replace crossChainManagerV2Address with crossChainManagerAddress inside executeWithdraw2Contract(), ensuring that the call is directed to the contract that actually implements withdraw2Contract, thereby restoring the intended withdrawal flow and preventing failed transactions.
summary: LedgerImplC holds the logic for Solana withdrawals and withdraw2Contract withdrawals. It correctly uses crossChainManagerV2Address inside executeWithdrawSolAction() to execute a Solana withdrawal. However, it uses the same crossChainManagerV2Address inside executeWithdraw2Contract() while the withdraw2Contract() function is implemented in crossChainManagerAddress. In result, withdraw2Contract() will always fail.

title: H-05 | DOS Of updateLPAndStrategyFund
content: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service (DoS) condition in the updateLPAndStrategyFund workflow ofthe vault contract. It originates from a timing inconsistency between the internal functions that handle liquidity‑provider (LP) and strategy‑provider (SP) withdrawals. When a user initiates a withdrawal, the contract first checks that the requested amount plus any already frozen shares does not exceed the user’s total share balance via _checkWithdraw. If the check passes, the amount is recorded in frozenShares and later subtracted from pendingShares and frozenShares in _handleLpWithdraw. However, the actual share balance (account.shares) is only refreshed later by settleAccounts, which copies pendingShares into shares. Between the execution of _handleLpWithdraw and the subsequent settleAccounts call, frozenShares is decreased while the official share balance remains unchanged. During this window a second withdrawal request can pass the same _checkWithdraw test because the contract still sees enough shares, leading to an additional increase in frozenShares. When the next period’s _handleLpWithdraw runs, it attempts to subtract the newly requested amount from pendingShares, which no longer contains enough shares to cover it, causing a revert. The revert aborts the updateLPAndStrategyFund function, effectively freezing the vault’s accounting cycle and preventing further LP or SP operations. The impact is that legitimate users cannot withdraw or interact with the vault, funds become temporarily inaccessible, and the protocol’s liquidity management is halted. The issue affects any participant who holds withdrawable shares, the vault’s governance, and any downstream contracts that rely on successful fund updates. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the withdrawal logic and state transitions. The bug is hard to notice because the contract appears to accept the withdrawal request and emits no immediate error; the failure only surfaces later when the accounting state is reconciled, making the problem manifest as an unexpected transaction revert rather than a straightforward validation error. To remediate the issue, the contract should prevent new withdrawal requests while the account’s share balance is out of sync, for example by disabling withdrawals in the window between _handleLpWithdraw and settleAccounts, or by adjusting the _checkWithdraw logic to also consider pendingShares or by updating the share balance before decreasing frozenShares. In user‑facing terms, a user may see a withdrawal transaction that seems to succeed, only to receive a later error message and find that their balance remains unchanged or that the vault UI reports a failure, violating the expectation that a successful transaction results in a reduced balance and received funds.
summary: LP_WITHDRAW and SP_WITHDRAW inside ProtocolVaultLedger.handleOpFromVault() should only be allowed if the user has enough withdrawable shares. This is handled by _checkWithdraw() - it ensures the amount to be withdrawn added to the current frozen amount doesn't surpass the share balance of the account. After that, the amount to be withdrawn is added towards frozenShares so checkWithdrawal will continue to work properly for further withdrawal requests. The withdrawal request will be handled by _handleLpWithdraw() and the amount to be withdrawn will be subtracted by the user's pendingShares and frozenShares. After some time, settleAccounts() will update the user's actual shares by setting them to pendingShares. This creates a window between _handleLpWithdraw() and settleAccounts() where frozenShares is decreased, but account.shares is not updated. Any withdrawal request in that window will successfully performed if it doesn't exceed the user's shares because _checkWithdraw() won't stop it. This will result in an increase in frozenShares, potentially doubling the current value. The withdrawal request inside this window will be processed inside _handleLpWithdraw() for the next period. The amount to be withdrawn will be subtracted from pendingShares again, however this time pendingShares will not cover it causing a revert and DOS of the updateLPAndStrategyFund function.

title: H-06 | Withdraw Message Sent Even If _validReceiver Check Fails
content: The vulnerability resides in the withdraw routine of the vault contract. When a user initiates a withdrawal, the contract first forwards a cross‑chain message to the IVaultCrossChainManager by calling withdraw(vaultWithdrawData) and only afterwards checks whether the supplied receiver address is accepted by the internal _validReceiver function. If the receiver validation fails, the contract emits a WithdrawFailed event and does not transfer any tokens to the ProtocolVault, but the earlier cross‑chain call has already been sent. The external ledger interprets this message as a successful withdrawal and records a final \"withdraw finish\" state. Consequently the ledger believes the user’s funds have been moved while the on‑chain vault retains the tokens, creating a mismatch between off‑chain accounting and on‑chain balances. This mismatch can strand user funds, cause the ledger to display a completed withdrawal even though the user receives nothing, and may require manual off‑chain reconciliation. The issue occurs whenever _validReceiver returns false, which can happen for unsupported token contracts, black‑listed addresses, or malformed receiver data. It affects any user attempting to withdraw to an invalid destination, as well as the protocol that relies on the ledger’s state for accounting and security guarantees. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the order of operations in the withdraw function. It is subtle because the contract does emit a failure event, but the external system does not listen to that event and instead trusts the cross‑chain message that was already dispatched. The bug belongs to the class of state‑inconsistent cross‑chain calls caused by improper ordering of validation and external messaging. To remediate, the contract should perform the receiver validation before any cross‑chain call, or, if validation fails, send an explicit \"withdraw failure\" message back to the ledger (or simply omit the success message) so that both sides maintain a consistent view of the withdrawal outcome. This ensures that users see the expected result – either the tokens arrive in their destination or the withdrawal is reported as failed – and prevents the ledger from recording a phantom transfer.
summary: In the Vault.withdraw function IVaultCrossChainManager(crossChainManagerAddress).withdraw(vaultWithdrawData) is called before verifying that the receiver is valid. Consequently, if _validReceiver(data.receiver, address(tokenAddress)) returns false, the vault still sends a cross‐chain message to the ledger acknowledging a “successful” withdrawal. Meanwhile, the local code emits only a WithdrawFailed event and never transfers the tokens to the ProtocolVault. This leaves the ledger believing the user’s withdrawal went through, while in reality no tokens were actually delivered. As a result, the user’s ledger state and on-chain vault state become out of sync. The ledger sees a final “withdraw finish,” but the vault never transferred tokens if the receiver check fails. This scenario could strand the user’s funds or require an off-chain correction.

title: MergeTgt has no handling if TGT _TO_ EXCHANGE is exceeded during the exchange period
content: The MergeTgt contract contains a hard‑coded ceiling for the amount of TGT that can be exchanged, defined as 579,000,000 tokens, and a corresponding hard‑coded amount of TITN that is deposited to be claimed by users. The contract calculates the exchange rate using the ratio of these two constants, but it does not enforce any check that the total amount of TGT deposited by all participants stays below the hard‑coded ceiling. As a result, when the cumulative TGT deposits exceed the limit, the internal accounting assumes that a matching amount of TITN is available, while in reality the MergeTgt contract holds less TITN than required. This mismatch leads to two concrete failures. First, users who attempt to claim their TITN after the limit is breached receive a revert because the contract’s balance of TITN is insufficient; from the user’s perspective the claim transaction fails and the expected refund is missing, often showing a zero balance or an error such as ERC20InsufficientBalance. Second, the function withdrawRemainingTitn performs an unchecked subtraction: it computes unclaimedTitn as remainingTitnAfter1Year minus initialTotalClaimable. When the TGT limit is exceeded, remainingTitnAfter1Year becomes smaller than initialTotalClaimable, causing an unsigned integer underflow (effectively an overflow) that reverts the transaction. The root cause is a missing validation of the total TGT deposited against the hard‑coded cap and the use of unsafe arithmetic without safeguards. The vulnerability is triggered only when the total TGT supplied by all users surpasses the 579 million threshold; blockchain explorers show that the combined supply of ARB and ETH tokens already exceeds this value, making the condition realistic. All participants of the MergeTgt protocol—depositors, claimers, and the protocol itself—are affected because the bug can lock funds, cause claim failures, and break the accounting invariants that the protocol relies on. The issue was uncovered during a Code4rena audit by modifying the test suite to artificially increase the TGT total supply above the hard‑coded limit and observing that the final claim reverted with an ERC20InsufficientBalance error. Because the contract behaves correctly for normal deposit amounts, the problem can be difficult to notice without stress‑testing edge cases. To remediate the issue, the contract should enforce a check that prevents total TGT deposits from exceeding the predefined ceiling, or dynamically adjust the claimable TITN amount based on the actual TITN balance. Additionally, arithmetic operations that involve subtraction of potentially larger values should be protected with safe‑math checks or use Solidity 0.8+ built‑in overflow protection, and a fallback mechanism should be added to refund excess TGT or allow users to withdraw safely if the contract cannot honor their claims.
summary:
MergeTgt has hardcoded amounts of TGT _TO_ EXCHANGE and TITN _ARB. Their ratio is used for rate calculation and TITN_ARB amount of TITN is deposited to be claimed.

The contract has no actual logic which would limit the deposited Tgt to MergeTgt. This means if this amount is crossed, any last claimers will not be able to do so or retrieve their Tgt back.

This same vulnerability also introduces an overflow in `withdrawRemainingTitn`. Since TGT is allowed to exceed the hardcoded value, the claimable TINT exceeds the actual mergeTgt contract TITN balance.

And this line overflows, as `remainingTitnAfter1Year` becomes less than the `initialTotalClaimable`.
    
    uint256 unclaimedTitn = remainingTitnAfter1Year - initialTotalClaimable;

Likelihood: Medium - The total Tgt of all users has to exceed TGT _TO_ EXCHANGE. According to blockchain explorers, ARB has 447,034,102 and ETH has 897,791,792, which is more than double the TGT _TO_ EXCHANGE of 579,000,000, so quite likely.

Impact: High - loss of user funds and breaking contract logic (revert on claim).

title: The user can send tokens to any address by using two bridge transfers, even when transfers are restricted.
content: The contract implements a transfer lock that is intended to prevent regular users from moving their bridged tokens to arbitrary addresses when the flag isBridgedTokensTransferLocked is true. The lock works by overriding the ERC20 transfer and transferFrom functions and calling an internal _validateTransfer routine that reverts unless the sender or receiver is the contract owner, the designated transferAllowedContract, or the LayerZero endpoint. The root cause of the vulnerability is that the bridge mechanism does not use these overridden functions; instead it moves tokens across chains by minting new tokens on the destination chain and burning them on the source chain. Because the mint/burn path bypasses the _validateTransfer check, a user can effectively transfer tokens to any address by performing two consecutive bridge operations: first sending the tokens to their own address on another chain, then sending them again to a third party’s address on the original chain. This circumvents the intended invariant that, when the lock is enabled, only the admin or the allowed contract may receive bridged tokens. In practice the exploit looks like a normal bridge send, but the result is that the recipient’s balance increases even though a direct transfer would have been rejected. The impact is that the protocol’s accounting guarantees are broken, allowing malicious actors to move or drain tokens despite the lock, and users may see tokens appear in unexpected wallets, violating trust in the system. The issue manifests only when the lock flag is true and the token holder is recognized as a bridged token holder (or the chain is Arbitrum, as coded). It affects all regular token holders, the protocol’s security model, and any downstream contracts that rely on the lock for compliance. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the transfer restrictions and then exercised the bridge functions, revealing that the lock does not apply to mint/burn operations. Because the bridge code is separate from the ERC20 transfer logic, the problem can be subtle and may not be caught by simple function‑level testing. To remediate, the same validation logic should be applied to the bridge’s mint/burn pathways, or the bridge should be disabled while the lock is active, ensuring that no token movement can occur outside the approved contracts when the restriction is enabled.
summary:
When `isBridgedTokensTransferLocked` is set to true, regular users’ `transfer` and `transferFrom` operations will be restricted. Regular users should not send their tokens to any address other than the `transferAllowedContract` and `lzEndpoint`. However, since bridge operations are not subject to this restriction, users can send tokens to any address by performing two bridge transfers.  
This breaks the primary invariant: _Unless enabled (or the user is the admin), users who merge their TGT to TITN should not be able to transfer them to any address other than the LayerZero endpoint or a specified contract address (`transferAllowedContract`)._

title: Reliance on `lifiData.receivingAssetId` can cause loss of funds
content: The vulnerability originates from an incorrect trust relationship between the output‑asset identifier supplied in the LiFiData struct and the actual asset identifier produced by the series of swaps executed in the swapTokensGeneric() function. The function records the pre‑swap balance of the asset referenced by LiFiData.receivingAssetId, performs an arbitrary number of swaps using the SwapData array, and then calculates the post‑swap balance by again querying the balance of LiFiData.receivingAssetId. Finally, it transfers the difference to the caller. Because the swapping logic itself does not use LiFiData.receivingAssetId – it relies on each SwapData element’s receivingAssetId – a mismatch between the two identifiers means that the balance of the token the contract believes it should have increased never does. Consequently, postSwapBalance is zero and the transfer sends nothing, leaving the swapped tokens stranded in the contract. This can be exploited by a caller who deliberately provides an incorrect receivingAssetId in the LiFiData argument, or by any user who unintentionally supplies a wrong value. The impact is that users who initiate a swap receive no tokens despite the transaction completing successfully; the funds are effectively locked in the contract and become unrecoverable without a contract upgrade or admin intervention. The issue manifests whenever the final asset ID expected by the caller does not match the receivingAssetId of the last element in the SwapData array, which can happen for single‑swap or multi‑swap calls alike. All participants that rely on swapTokensGeneric – end‑users, integrators, and the protocol itself – are affected because the business logic assumes that the token sent to the user is the one recorded in LiFiData.receivingAssetId. The problem was discovered during a manual audit when the code was traced and it became clear that the variable used for the final balance check had no functional role in the swap execution. The bug is subtle because the transaction does not revert, and no explicit error is emitted; from a user’s perspective the UI shows a successful swap but the wallet balance remains unchanged, creating the impression that the contract “eats” the funds. This class of bug can be described as an asset‑identifier mismatch or misuse of a parameter for accounting purposes without proper validation. The recommended mitigation is to either verify that LiFiData.receivingAssetId equals the receivingAssetId of the last SwapData entry before the transfer or, more robustly, to derive the token to be transferred directly from the SwapData array, thereby eliminating the reliance on an external identifier that is not involved in the swapping process.
summary:
[GenericSwapFacet.sol#L23-L30](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-lifinance/blob/699c2305fcfb6fe8862b75b26d1d8a2f46a551e6/src/Facets/GenericSwapFacet.sol#L23-L30)  

In the `swapTokensGeneric()` function, an arbitrary number of swaps can be performed from and to various tokens. However, the final balance that is sent to the user relies on `_lifiData.receivingAssetId` which has no use in the swapping functionality. LifiData is claimed to be used purely for analytical reasons per the comments to this function. If this value is input incorrectly, the swapped tokens will simply sit in the contract and be lost to the user.

title: All swapping functions lack checks for returned tokens
content: The vulnerability resides in the generic token swapping facet of the Li.Fi protocol. Every public swapping function that originates from the GenericSwapFacet contract forwards a swap request to an external decentralized exchange router via the LibSwap library. The LibSwap.swap() routine only checks that the low‑level call to the router returns a success flag and that the call does not revert. It does not verify that the router actually transferred any amount of the destination token back to the contract. Consequently, the outer function GenericSwapFacet.swapTokensGeneric() also lacks a final balance assertion that would confirm receipt of at least one unit of the expected receiving asset. The root cause is the omission of an output validation step after an external call, combined with reliance on a simple boolean success indicator rather than on concrete token balance changes. An attacker can exploit this by supplying a router address that implements a function with the same signature as a swap, such as getAmountsOut(), which returns true without performing any token transfer. When the contract invokes this function, the call succeeds, the user’s source tokens are already deposited in the contract, but no destination tokens are credited. From the user’s perspective the transaction appears successful, yet the expected output balance remains unchanged, leading to a scenario where the user receives nothing, their funds appear to be locked, or the contract’s balance is unexpectedly reduced. This flaw can manifest whenever the swap functions are used with untrusted or malicious router contracts, or when the calldata is crafted to invoke a non‑swap function that merely returns a success flag. The impact is high: users lose the value of the source tokens they supplied for swapping, and the protocol may be forced to hold or potentially lose those funds. The issue was discovered by the Code4rena audit team during a systematic review of the swap logic, noting that no post‑call balance check existed. It is difficult to spot because the external call does not revert and the transaction receipt shows a successful execution, giving the false impression that the swap succeeded. To remediate the problem, the contract should enforce a concrete verification that the receiving token balance after the call is greater than the balance before the call, for example by requiring `LibAsset.getOwnBalance(_swapData.receivingAssetId) - toAmount > 0`. Additionally, employing a whitelist of allowed function signatures or restricting router addresses to a known safe list would prevent accidental or malicious invocation of non‑swap functions. By adding these checks, the protocol restores the invariant that a successful swap must result in an increase of the destination token balance, aligning execution with the business logic that users expect to receive the swapped assets.
summary:
[GenericSwapFacet.sol#L23-L30](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-lifinance/blob/699c2305fcfb6fe8862b75b26d1d8a2f46a551e6/src/Facets/GenericSwapFacet.sol#L23-L30)  
[LibSwap.sol#L48](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-lifinance/blob/699c2305fcfb6fe8862b75b26d1d8a2f46a551e6/src/Libraries/LibSwap.sol#L48)
