The bug is subtle because the low‑debt guard appears protective at first glance and typical unit tests may not cover the edge case where debt shrinks below the minimum after the position is already unhealthy. To remediate, the MIN_DEBT validation should be removed from the generic isPositionHealthy routine and instead be enforced only in the borrow and repay entry points of the PositionManager, where the intent is to prevent creating positions with trivially small debt. By separating the concerns, the liquidation path can correctly assess health based on collateralisation alone, allowing under‑collateralised positions to be liquidated and preserving the protocol’s economic guarantees. From a user perspective, a liquidation transaction would unexpectedly revert with a “DebtTooLow” error, the user would see no collateral seized, and the position would appear to remain unchanged despite being flagged as unsafe, leading to confusion and potential loss of funds.
summary:
Users can borrow funds from pools using the PositionManager contract, as long as the position remains healthy, verified by riskEngine.isPositionHealthy(position).
The isPositionHealthy function has a flaw, as it has a condition where it can revert:
if (totalDebtValue != 0 && totalDebtValue < MIN_DEBT) revert RiskModule_DebtTooLow(position, totalDebtValue);
The liquidate function uses isPositionHealthy to avoid liquidating healthy positions, but if the position is not healthy and the totalDebtValue is less than MIN_DEBT, the liquidation fails.
Although isPositionHealthy is checked when a position borrows assets, the eth value of the debt can decrease below MIN_DEBT.

title: H-18 | feeRecipient Set To Zero Blocks Functionality
content: The vulnerability consists of an unchecked feeRecipient address in a SuperPool contract. During deployment and later through the setFeeRecipient function the contract stores an address that receives minted pool shares whenever interest is accrued. Because the code does not validate that the supplied address is non‑zero, a pool owner (or an attacker who gains ownership) can set feeRecipient to the zero address (0x0000000000000000000000000000000000000000). The accrue routine, which is invoked by most pool operations, attempts to mint new shares to feeRecipient. The internal _mint implementation reverts when the recipient is the zero address, causing the entire accrue call – and therefore any function that triggers it – to fail. This results in transactions that would normally succeed (deposits, withdrawals, interest claims) reverting with no explicit error message other than a generic failure, effectively freezing the pool and preventing users from interacting with their funds. The impact is high because all participants of the affected pool are unable to perform core actions, leading to a loss of usability and potential loss of access to deposited assets until the feeRecipient is corrected. The condition occurs whenever the feeRecipient is set to zero, either accidentally during deployment or maliciously by an owner with the ability to call setFeeRecipient. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined state‑changing functions for proper input validation. It can be hard to notice because the zero address is a valid Solidity address type and the contract does not emit a specific error; only downstream minting failures surface, which may be attributed to other causes. The proper mitigation is to add a require statement in both the deployment helper and the setFeeRecipient function that rejects a zero address when the fee amount is greater than zero, ensuring that feeRecipient always points to a valid account capable of receiving minted shares. Conceptually, this is a missing input validation bug that leads to a denial‑of‑service condition by violating the accounting assumption that fees are always credited to a real address. From a user’s perspective the UI would show transactions failing, balances remaining unchanged, and no fees being credited, contrary to the expectation that deposits accrue interest and fees are distributed.
summary:
The feeRecipient is initially set during the deployment of a SuperPool and can also be changed using the setFeeRecipient function in the SuperPool contract. This address receives fees when interest is accrued, which are minted as SuperPool shares to the feeRecipient.
The issue is that there is no restriction on the address to which the feeRecipient can be set. As a result, a SuperPool owner could inadvertently or maliciously set the feeRecipient to the zero address.
This will cause the accrue function, which is called in most operations, to revert, as the SuperPool _mint function will revert when the recipient address is zero.

title: H-01 | setFee Honeypot Attack
content: The vulnerability is an unrestricted fee parameter that can be modified by the pool owner at any time without any upper bound or delay. Because the contract does not enforce a maximum fee nor a timelock, an attacker who creates a SuperPool can initially set a modest fee (e.g., 1 %) to attract deposits. After users have deposited, the attacker can instantly change the fee to a value greater than 100 %, which causes the contract’s accounting of pending interest to credit the attacker with an amount that equals or exceeds the total assets held. The attacker can then call the withdraw function and drain all funds, leaving depositors with a zero balance. This attack is a classic honeypot: the pool appears legitimate at first, but the fee can be abused later. The issue occurs whenever the contract’s fee setter is callable by an address with owner privileges and there is no validation of the new fee value or a delay before the change takes effect. Users, depositors, and the protocol’s reputation are affected because deposited assets can disappear without warning. The problem was discovered during a security audit that examined the fee‑adjustment logic and noted the absence of constraints. The bug is hard to notice because the fee looks normal during the initial period and the malicious change can happen in a single transaction, giving no visible warning before the withdrawal. To remediate, the contract should enforce minimum and maximum fee limits (e.g., 0 %–100 %) and introduce a timelock or governance delay for any fee update, ensuring that users have a window to react before a potentially abusive change is applied. This class of vulnerability falls under “unbounded privileged parameter modification” and can lead to fund loss, broken accounting, and loss of trust.
summary:
SuperPool owners can adjust the fee anytime instantly and no boundaries for the fee are set. This enables a honeypot attack:
• Attacker creates a SuperPool with a 1% fee
• Users deposit into the pool
• The attacker sets the fee way above 100%
• A few seconds pass and the pending interest for the attacker is >= all assets in the contract
• Attacker withdraws all funds of the SuperPool

title: H-19 | Missing onlyFactory Check In SuperPool
content: The vulnerability consists of the absence of a factory‑only restriction in the constructor of the SuperPool contract. SuperPools are intended to be created exclusively through a dedicated factory so that every instance references the same singleton pool implementation, preserving a uniform asset management logic. Because the constructor does not verify that the caller is the authorized factory, any external account can invoke the constructor directly and deploy a SuperPool that points to an arbitrary base pool contract. An attacker can therefore publish a malicious SuperPool that appears identical to legitimate ones – for example by using the same asset symbol or name – while the underlying pool logic may redirect deposits, withdrawals, or reward calculations to an address controlled by the attacker. This situation can be exploited when a user selects a SuperPool from a list of pools containing the same asset; the user may unintentionally interact with the malicious instance, causing their tokens to be transferred to the attacker’s contract or to be locked in a pool that does not honor withdrawals. The impact is the potential loss of user funds, erosion of trust in the protocol, and difficulty for ordinary users to distinguish between authentic and counterfeit pools because the UI typically shows only high‑level identifiers. The condition under which the bug manifests is any deployment of a SuperPool that is not performed by the factory – a scenario that can be triggered by a simple transaction calling the SuperPool constructor with a crafted base pool address. The affected parties include any user who interacts with SuperPools, the protocol’s reputation, and any downstream contracts that assume a single, trusted pool implementation. The issue was discovered during a manual audit where the code was examined for proper access control; the missing onlyFactory check was noted as a logical omission rather than a syntactic error, making it easy to overlook because the contract otherwise compiles and functions correctly when deployed through the factory. The bug is hard to notice in normal operation because the malicious pool can be made to look identical to legitimate ones, and the contract does not emit any warning when instantiated by an unauthorized address. To remediate, the constructor should include a check that the msg.sender equals the known factory address (or use a modifier such as onlyFactory) so that deployment is restricted to the authorized factory contract. Conceptually, this belongs to the class of “missing access‑control on contract creation” vulnerabilities, which break the assumption that only trusted code can instantiate critical components, leading to accounting mismatches, unexpected zero balances for users, and loss of funds that were expected to be safely stored in a pool.
summary:
All pools exist within the singleton pool contract, with one singleton contract per SuperPool factory.
Developer comments indicate that SuperPools should only be deployed through the factory contract to ensure they all point to the same singleton pool implementation.
However, the constructor of the SuperPool lacks a check to confirm it is being called by the factory.
This opens the possibility for users to deploy a SuperPool that points to a malicious base pool. With multiple SuperPools containing the same asset, distinguishing between malicious SuperPools and regular ones becomes challenging for ordinary users.

title: H-02 | Malicious RateModel Attack
content: The vulnerability is an unchecked external RateModel injection that enables a malicious contract to fabricate arbitrary interest accrual and drain all assets from a SuperPool. The root cause is that the SuperPool architecture permits any address to be supplied as a RateModel when a BasePool is created, and the SuperPool owner can freely add a BasePool to the pool queue and reallocate the entire capital to that BasePool at any time. Because the RateModel is trusted to compute legitimate interest, the protocol does not validate its code or restrict its address, allowing an attacker to deploy a RateModel that reports an excessively large amount of accrued tokens. Exploitation proceeds as follows: the attacker (who may also be the SuperPool owner) creates a BasePool with a malicious RateModel, mints a small number of shares in that BasePool, adds the BasePool to the SuperPool’s queue, and then triggers a reallocation that moves all SuperPool funds into the malicious BasePool. The attacker then calls the accrue function; the malicious RateModel returns a fabricated interest amount that far exceeds the actual capital. Finally, the attacker withdraws the entire balance from the BasePool using the few shares originally minted, leaving the SuperPool’s legitimate users with zero remaining assets. The impact is a total loss of user funds, a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees, and a loss of confidence in the platform. This condition occurs whenever a SuperPool owner has permission to add arbitrary BasePools and reallocate funds, and there is no whitelist or governance check on the RateModel address. All participants who have deposited into the SuperPool—individual token holders, liquidity providers, and downstream contracts—are affected because their balances can be erased without warning. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the pool‑management functions and identified that the RateModel parameter is not constrained. The problem is subtle because the RateModel is an external contract whose logic is not executed within the SuperPool, so a malicious return value can appear legitimate and the protocol does not have a secondary verification step. To remediate, the protocol should prohibit arbitrary RateModel addresses, enforce a whitelist of vetted models, or require governance approval before a new RateModel can be linked to a BasePool. This class of bug falls under untrusted external contract injection and oracle manipulation, where a contract assumes correctness of an external component without proper validation, leading to fabricated accounting data and loss of funds. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after a withdrawal their balance shows zero or the expected refund is missing, contrary to the expectation that their shares would return the proportional amount of the pool’s assets. The failure mode is effectively “money disappears” because the protocol’s accounting trusts a malicious formula that inflates interest and then empties the pool.
summary:
• Anyone can create a BasePool with an arbitrary contract as RateModel
• Anyone can create a SuperPool
• The owner of a SuperPool can add a new BasePool to a SuperPool and reallocate all funds to it any time
These conditions allow the following attack:
• SuperPool owner creates a BasePool with a malicious RateModel and mints some shares
• SuperPool owner adds the BasePool to the queue of the SuperPool
• SuperPool owner reallocates all funds to the malicious BasePool
• The malicious actor calls accrue on the BasePool and the malicious RateModel returns that a lot of tokens in interest were accrued
• The malicious actor withdraws all funds in the BasePool with the few shares minted in the beginning and the users of the SuperPool lose everything

title: H-03 | Protocol Fees Are Donations
content: The vulnerability consists of an unchecked fee configuration in the BasePool contract. The protocol defines two fees, interestFee and originationFee, that are intended to be collected by the protocol on each loan. However, the constructor of BasePool allows any caller to specify arbitrary values for these fees when creating a new pool, and there is no validation that the values are non‑zero or that the caller is authorized to set them. As a result, an attacker can deploy a pool with both fees set to zero, effectively turning the protocol’s revenue mechanism into a donation. The exploit is straightforward: the attacker calls the pool creation function, passes 0 for interestFee and originationFee, and the contract records these values without restriction. Subsequent loan operations will therefore not transfer any fee to the protocol, causing the protocol to lose expected income. This condition occurs every time a new BasePool is instantiated, because the fee parameters are user‑controlled and not enforced by any access control or minimum‑fee check. The parties affected are the protocol itself, its token holders, and any users who rely on the protocol’s fee model for sustainability; they may notice that no fees are deducted from loan repayments, which appears as “no fee taken” or “fees disappear”. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the pool‑creation logic and identified the absence of fee validation. It can be hard to notice because the contract does not emit warnings when fees are zero, and the UI may simply display the configured fee values without indicating that they are ineffective. To remediate, the contract should enforce that interestFee and originationFee meet the protocol‑defined minimums and should restrict fee configuration to the protocol’s governance or a privileged role, ensuring that every pool contributes the intended revenue. In broader terms, this is a classic missing‑validation or fee‑bypass bug that violates the economic assumptions of the system, allowing users to create “free” pools that donate protocol fees.
summary:
• The interestFee and originationFee are fees that go to the protocol.
• Anyone can create a new BasePool and set the interestFee and originationFee while doing so.
Therefore the protocol fees are not enforced and act like donations instead. As it makes no economic sense for the BasePool owner to set these fees above 0 the protocol will probably lose a lot of money.

title: H-04 | Reallocating Can Freeze Funds
content: The vulnerability is a missing validation in the contract’s reallocate function that allows an owner to direct deposited assets to a pool that is not registered in the deposit/withdraw queue. Because the queue defines which pools are eligible for withdrawals, funds moved to an unregistered pool become effectively locked; the contract’s withdrawal logic will not recognise the pool, so users attempting to withdraw see no balance or receive zero despite the contract holding the assets. The root cause is the absence of a check that the destination pool identifier belongs to the active queue before the reallocation is performed. An attacker who controls a SuperPool can call reallocate with a malicious pool address, causing user deposits to be rerouted into that pool. The funds remain on-chain but are inaccessible through the normal user interface, creating a situation where users experience “nothing comes out” or “balance stays the same” when trying to withdraw. The attacker can then claim that the only way to unfreeze the assets is to pay an additional amount, possibly via a separate contract, and after receiving the payment the attacker can add the hidden pool to the queue or move the assets back, thereby releasing the funds. This attack can be carried out at any time the reallocate function is invoked, and it affects every participant who has deposited into the affected SuperPool, including regular users and any downstream contracts that rely on the pool’s liquidity. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the reallocate logic and noticed the lack of queue membership verification. Because the funds are still present on-chain, the problem may not be obvious from a simple balance view, making it hard to detect without tracing the internal pool mappings. The appropriate mitigation is to enforce that both source and destination pools are members of the deposit/withdraw queue before any reallocation, and to emit an event when an invalid pool is supplied. This change restores the invariant that only queued pools can hold user‑controllable assets, preventing the freeze and the associated extortion scenario. The bug belongs to the class of “missing access‑control / invariant validation” vulnerabilities that break accounting assumptions and allow assets to become unrecoverable through the intended interface.
summary:
In the reallocate function it is not checked if the given pools to deposit to are part of the deposit/withdraw queue.
Therefore malicious SuperPool owners can deposit funds into a pool that is not in the queue, which will freeze funds for the users of the SuperPool.
The owner could then spread on social media that users need to pay X amount of funds to unfreeze it (this could be even done with a contract).
When the users pay the amount, the owner can unfreeze the funds by adding the new pool to the queue or reallocating the funds back to the original pool.

title: H-05 | DoS On Setting The LTV Of a Token To Zero
content: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that arises when the contract owner of a BasePool is allowed to set the loan‑to‑value (LTV) parameter of a listed token to zero. The root cause is that the health‑check routine isPositionHealthy assumes any token with a non‑zero LTV can be evaluated, and it simply reverts when it encounters a token whose LTV equals zero. Because the contract does not forbid the owner from assigning a zero LTV, an attacker who controls the owner role can change the LTV of a token that is already used as collateral in an active borrowing position. Once the LTV is zero, any subsequent call to the PositionManager that touches the affected position – including repayment, liquidation, or collateral withdrawal – triggers the revert in isPositionHealthy, effectively freezing the position. From a user’s perspective the borrowed amount continues to accrue interest, but the borrower sees no way to repay, cannot be liquidated by the protocol, and cannot retrieve the locked collateral, leading to a situation where funds appear to disappear or become permanently inaccessible. This condition occurs only after the owner deliberately sets the LTV to zero while there exists at least one position holding that token; it does not affect tokens with positive LTV. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the logic of LTV handling and health checks. It can be hard to notice because zero is a mathematically valid value and the contract does not contain explicit validation against it, so the code path that reverts is only exercised in the specific edge case of a zero LTV. The bug belongs to the class of “parameter‑validation denial‑of‑service” or “invalid‑state revert” vulnerabilities, where a privileged role can push a protocol parameter into a state that breaks core accounting logic. To remediate the problem the contract should enforce a minimum LTV greater than zero for any token, or redesign isPositionHealthy to return a false health status instead of reverting when LTV is zero, thereby allowing the protocol to handle the situation gracefully and preserving the ability to repay or liquidate the position.
summary:
• The owner of a BasePool can set the LTV of a token to zero.
• The isPositionHealthy function will revert if a position holds a token in the asset list and this token has an LTV of zero.
Therefore if the owner updates the LTV of a token to zero and any position holds this token any interaction with it through the PositionManager will revert.
This has multiple bad consequences:
• Borrowers debt increases but they are not able to repay
• Borrowers can not be liquidated
• Borrowers are not able to get their collateral back
• The owner of a base pool can create unliquidatable positions
Unliquidatable positions:
• Owner sets the LTV of a token above 0
• The owner creates a position adds this token as collateral, borrows funds, and does something risky with them
• The owner sets the LTV for this token to 0
• Now the position is not liquidatable till the owner sets the LTV back to a value above 0

title: H-06 | _reorderQueue Does Not Work As Expected
content: The vulnerability resides in the queue‑reordering routine of the SuperPool contract, which maintains separate deposit and withdrawal queues whose processing order is critical for correct fund allocation. The contract exposes a private function, _reorderQueue, that is intended to let the contract owner supply an array of indexes describing a new ordering of the existing queue entries. However, the implementation mistakenly copies the original queue into a new temporary array using the statement newQueue[i] = queue[i] for each position, completely ignoring the supplied indexes array. As a result, any call to _reorderQueue leaves the queue order unchanged, preventing the owner from reshaping the processing sequence. This logical error arises from a simple copy‑and‑paste mistake where the mapping between the input indexes and the new positions was never applied. An attacker does not need to craft a special payload; the mere fact that the owner cannot reorder the queue means that users who rely on a reordered priority—such as high‑value withdrawers or time‑sensitive depositors—will continue to be served in the original order. Consequently, a user who expects their withdrawal to be moved forward after the owner invokes a reordering will instead experience the same delay, potentially leading to missed deadlines, loss of expected returns, or even fund lock‑up if the original order becomes unfavorable. The impact is high because the protocol’s business logic assumes that the owner can enforce a fair or strategic ordering; the broken function violates that assumption, breaking accounting guarantees and undermining trust in the system. The issue manifests whenever the owner attempts to call _reorderQueue with any non‑trivial index array, which is any situation where the protocol needs to adjust queue priorities, such as after a large deposit burst or during emergency shutdown procedures. All participants—contract owner, depositors, withdrawers, and any downstream protocol that depends on correct queue sequencing—are affected. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that compared the function’s signature and comments with its body, revealing that the indexes parameter was never used. Because the function does not revert or emit an error, the bug can be subtle and may only be noticed when expected ordering changes do not take effect, making it hard to detect through simple unit tests that only check for successful calls. The proper remediation is to replace the copy statement with newQueue[i] = queue[indexes[i]], thereby applying the caller‑provided permutation to the queue before writing it back to storage. This change restores the intended ability for the owner to reorder queues, aligns the contract’s behavior with its documented business logic, and prevents users from experiencing unexpected delays or missing funds due to an immutable queue order.
summary:
SuperPool contract has deposit and withdrawal queues. Order of these queues are important since deposits and withdrawals are done based on the order, which is supposed to be arranged by the owner.
However, due to incorrect implementation of the _reorderQueue function, the owner can not change queue orders. This function takes a new order as an indexes array, and is supposed to rearrange the order based on indexes. But it only copies the previous order as is with the newQueue[i] = queue[i] line.

title: H-07 | DoS In _removePool By Force Feeding
content: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition in the internal _removePool routine of the SentimentV2 contract. The function is designed to delete a pool only after the associated SuperPool no longer holds any assets. The contract allows any external account to deposit assets into a BasePool and to specify an arbitrary SuperPool as the recipient of those assets. Because the deposit operation is unrestricted, a malicious actor can front‑run the transaction that calls _removePool, deposit a single wei (or any minimal amount) into the SuperPool that is slated for removal, and thereby ensure that the SuperPool still reports a non‑zero balance at the moment _removePool performs its ownership check. When the check detects remaining assets, the function reverts, causing the entire removal transaction to fail. This behavior leads to a denial‑of‑service where legitimate pool owners are unable to cleanly remove or reallocate their pools, effectively locking the pool’s state and preventing further administrative actions. The impact is that funds become inaccessible for removal, users may see transaction failures with messages indicating that the SuperPool still owns assets, and the protocol’s governance or upgrade mechanisms that rely on pool removal may be stalled. The condition occurs only when an attacker can insert a tiny deposit between the initiation of the removal call and its execution, which is feasible in a public mempool where transactions can be reordered. All participants who rely on the ability to remove pools—typically pool owners, protocol administrators, and downstream contracts—are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the asset‑ownership checks in _removePool and identified that the check does not account for external deposits occurring after the call is scheduled. Because the extra wei is negligible, it may not be obvious during routine testing or simulation, making the bug hard to detect without explicit adversarial scenarios. The appropriate mitigation is to redesign the removal logic so that asset reallocation and pool deletion are performed atomically within a single transaction, eliminating the window where external deposits can intervene. More generally, the bug belongs to the class of front‑running‑induced denial‑of‑service vulnerabilities where state‑dependent checks can be subverted by a preceding transaction that alters the required condition. From a user perspective the symptom is a transaction that reverts with a generic “SuperPool still owns assets” error, even though the user did not intentionally send any tokens, leading to confusion and the perception that funds have disappeared or that the protocol is malfunctioning.
summary:
• The _removePool function reverts if the SuperPool still owns assets in the given pool.
• Anyone can deposit into a BasePool and set any SuperPool as the receiver of the assets.
This enables a malicious actor the possibility to front run a _removePool call and deposit one wei of assets into the SuperPool to DoS the call.

title: H-08 | Reentrancy In SuperPool
content: The vulnerability is a classic reentrancy flaw that appears in the withdrawal routine of the SuperPool contract. When a user initiates a withdrawal, the contract first burns the caller's share tokens, then transfers the underlying assets to the caller, and finally updates the internal accounting variable that records the last total assets of the pool. Because the external token transfer is performed before the lastTotalAssets value is reduced, a malicious caller can re‑enter the contract during the token receipt callback. At the moment of re‑entry the share balance has already been decreased, but the pool’s total asset counter still reflects the pre‑withdrawal amount. The contract’s interest‑accrual logic, which runs at the beginning of each deposit or withdrawal, uses the stale lastTotalAssets value to compute earned interest. The re‑entered call therefore sees an artificial surplus that is interpreted as interest, and the attacker is credited with additional fees. By repeatedly depositing, withdrawing, and re‑entering on each token receipt, the attacker can harvest these phantom fees over and over until the pool’s asset reserve is exhausted. The impact is a complete drain of user funds from the pool, loss of confidence for all participants, and a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees that assets equal shares. The issue manifests only when a contract or address can trigger a callback during the token transfer – for example, when the token implements a payable fallback or when the pool uses a non‑standard ERC‑20 that invokes external code on transfer. It was uncovered during a manual security audit that examined the ordering of state updates and external calls. The flaw is hard to notice because the three steps appear logically correct in isolation; only the combination of an external call before a critical state change reveals the inconsistency. From a user’s perspective the UI would show a successful withdrawal while the pool balance unexpectedly drops to zero, or a user might see their share balance disappear without receiving the expected amount of assets. The contract violates the fundamental business rule that the sum of all shares must always be backed by an equal amount of assets. To remediate the issue the safeTransfer (or any external call) should be moved to the very end of the withdrawal flow, after lastTotalAssets has been updated, and a reentrancy guard (such as OpenZeppelin’s nonReentrant modifier) should be applied to the withdraw and deposit functions to block recursive entry. This combination restores the invariant that asset accounting is performed before any external interaction, eliminating the opportunity for an attacker to claim phantom interest.
summary:
The last three actions in the withdrawal flow of the SuperPool are:
• Burning the share tokens
• Transferring the funds to the user
• Reducing the lastTotalAssets value
Therefore if the attacker reenters on receiving the tokens the total amount of shares is already reduced, but the total amount of assets is not.
The first action in withdraw/deposit is accruing interest calculated based on the saved lastTotalAssets value and the current total amount. Therefore the given difference on reentering (as lastTotalAssets is not reduced yet) is seen as interest and the owner of the pool receives fees on this interest.
This enables the following attack path:
• SuperPool owner deposits tokens into the own pool
• SuperPool owner withdraws the tokens and reenters on receiving them over and over again
• Every time the difference is seen as interest and the owner receives fees
• Owner withdraws the gained fees
• The owner repeats this process over and over again till the SuperPool is drained completely

title: H-01 | Incorrect Debt Update During Migration
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect debt update that occurs during the migration of a V2 staker when the preferred Spartan Council pool is backed by multiple collateral vaults. The root cause is that the AssociateDebt module, which is responsible for drawing the appropriate amount of debt from the backing vaults, only reduces the debt from a single vault instead of proportionally from all vaults that share the market’s liquidity. When a user migrates, the protocol is supposed to split the user’s outstanding debt across the vaults according to each vault’s share of the market (for example 50 % from the USDe vault and 50 % from the SNX vault). Because the implementation deducts the full debt amount from only the SNX vault, the USDe vault – and any delegators that have supplied liquidity to it – are left carrying the remaining half of the debt. An attacker does not need to perform any special action; the bug is triggered automatically for any migration transaction that involves a pool with more than one backing vault. The impact is that honest delegators experience an unexpected loss of value: their balances appear reduced, refunds may be missing, and the accounting of the market no longer matches the intended economic model. This situation occurs only during the migration step and only when the pool configuration includes multiple collateral types. Users who have supplied liquidity to the unaffected vault see their funds disappear or their expected returns drop, while the migrating staker may not notice any direct loss because the debt is still recorded against their account. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the migration logic, where the auditor observed that the reportedDebt delta was not fully accounted for across all vaults. It can be hard to notice because the migration transaction itself succeeds and the migrating user’s own balance may look correct, while the loss is distributed silently to other participants. To fix the problem the debt reduction logic must be changed to iterate over all backing vaults and subtract from each vault an amount proportional to its share of the market’s liquidity, ensuring that the total debt removed matches the user’s outstanding debt. This correction restores the intended invariant that the sum of debts across all vaults equals the total market debt, prevents unintended loss for delegators, and aligns the protocol’s accounting with its business rules about collateral backing and debt distribution.
summary: When the preferred Spartan Council pool contains multiple supported collateral type vaults the migration of a V2 staker's debt incorrectly deducts all of their associated debt from the collateral vault of the staker. However other collateral vaults may burden a portion of the reportedDebt delta which was experienced by the LegacyMarket when the staker migrated. For example (contrived example for simplicity): • User A migrates their account which has X debt • Upon a normal debt distribution X/2 of this debt would go to the USDe vault and X/2 to the SNX vault • The Spartan Pool has two vaults: USDe and SNX, split 50%/50% in terms of backing liquidity for the Legacy Market • The AssociateDebt module however deducts X debt from only the SNX vault with distributeDebtToAccounts • As a result the USDe vault delegators experience a loss due to the burden of X/2 debt which should have been corrected for.

title: H-02 | convertUSD DOS Because Of Share Rounding
content: The vulnerability resides in the convertUSD function of the legacy market contract, which burns a specified amount of synthetic USD (sUSD) from the caller’s account and then checks that the actual burnt amount differs from the user‑provided target by no more than one wei of sUSD. The check assumes that the burn operation performed by the Synthetix Issuer contract will produce an exact share‑to‑USD conversion. In reality the Issuer’s internal accounting rounds the number of debt shares when burning, and a second rounding step occurs when the contract reads the remaining SDS balance. When the debt‑shares‑per‑USD ratio exceeds one share per dollar, these rounding steps can produce a shortfall of more than one wei of sUSD, but the shortfall is expressed in shares rather than in the USD unit that the legacy market validates. Because the legacy market’s validation logic tolerates only a one‑wei deviation in sUSD, any transaction that triggers the larger share rounding error causes the entire convertUSD call to revert. An attacker can deliberately craft a conversion request that pushes the debt‑share ratio into the problematic range, causing the function to fail every time and effectively denying service to legitimate users. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition: users attempting to convert their sUSD receive a transaction revert, their balances remain unchanged, and the market becomes unusable for further conversions, potentially locking funds that should be migratable. The issue manifests only when the market’s debt‑share ratio is above the 1 USD‑per‑share threshold, a condition that may not be obvious during normal operation and therefore can be missed in routine testing. The problem was discovered during a manual audit by the Guardian team, who noticed that the rounding logic in the Issuer contract could produce a discrepancy larger than the one‑wei tolerance enforced by the legacy market. The bug is subtle because the rounding error is extremely small (on the order of a single wei) and only appears under specific accounting states, making it difficult to reproduce without targeted probing. To remediate the issue, the contract should relax the tolerance check to allow a one‑wei deviation in the share amount rather than in the USD amount, or otherwise adjust the validation to account for the known rounding behavior of the Issuer. This change aligns the contract’s expectations with the actual precision of the underlying Synthetix accounting, eliminating the unintended revert and restoring the ability for users to convert their synths without loss of funds.
summary: [LegacyMarket.convertUSD()](https://github.com/GuardianAudits/legacy-1/blob/636dc48c91b18807adf6ae71ac8eb45e22fc9ea9/markets/legacy-market/contracts/LegacyMarket.sol#L164-L167) burns synths from the converter's account and enforces a maximum difference between the actual burnt amount and the amount specified by the user to be no more than 1 unit of sUSD. However, when the [Issuer](https://github.com/Synthetixio/synthetix/blob/987f18e4f73fbfee3b984fd56934780e1df1508d/contracts/Issuer.sol#L1027-L1028) does the burning of the SDS, there is some rounding which happens on the shares. This means the end result can be with 1 unit less of a share, not sUSD. Furthermore, additional rounding can happen on [this line](https://github.com/Synthetixio/synthetix/blob/987f18e4f73fbfee3b984fd56934780e1df1508d/contracts/Issuer.sol#L300) when querying the SDS balance which will increase the margin of error. As a result, the burnt amount may deviate slightly more than 1 wei of sUSD when the debtShares ratio is above 1$ of debt per share. As the LegacyMarket does not tolerate this amount of inaccuracy, the whole transaction will revert and converting will not be possible.

title: H-03 | Liquidation Of Contract Accounts May Be Blocked
content: The vulnerability concerns the liquidation pathway for accounts that become under‑collateralised on the V2X version of the protocol. When an account is identified as liquidatable, the system is designed to forcibly migrate the account to the newer V3 system before performing the liquidation. The migration process relies on transferring an ERC‑721 token that represents the account position, and this transfer requires the destination contract to implement the ERC721Receiver interface, specifically the onERC721Received callback. If the liquidatable account is itself a smart contract that does not implement this callback, the safe transfer reverts and the migration aborts. Because the migration never completes, the subsequent liquidation step is never reached, leaving the debt associated with the account un‑settled within V2X. An attacker can deliberately create a contract without the required callback, deposit assets, and then allow the account to become under‑collateralised. When the protocol attempts to liquidate, the migration fails silently, the account remains in a liquidatable state, and the protocol accrues bad debt because the owed amount is never recovered. From a user perspective the symptoms are that a contract that should be liquidated shows no liquidation event, balances appear unchanged, and any expected repayment or collateral seizure never occurs, effectively causing funds to be stuck or lost. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the migration‑and‑liquidation flow and identified the missing interface check as a logical flaw. It is hard to notice because the failure occurs inside an internal migration call; no external error is emitted and the protocol simply proceeds without performing liquidation, making the problem appear as a silent “no‑action” rather than an explicit revert. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of transfer‑blocking or callback‑dependency failures that prevent state transitions required for financial enforcement. To remediate the issue the protocol should decouple liquidation from the ERC‑721 transfer requirement, for example by allowing migration to proceed without moving the token or by providing a fallback claim mechanism that lets the account owner recover any remaining funds after a failed migration, thereby ensuring that liquidations can always be completed and bad debt is avoided.
summary: If an account is liquidatable on V2X, it is expected to be forcibly migrated to the V3 system where it will be liquidated. It cannot be liquidated on V2X. However, if the account is a contract that does not implement onERC721Received, then the V3 account cannot be transferred and the migration would fail. This allows contract accounts to avoid liquidation and create bad debt within the V2X system.

title: H-04 | Debt Burden After Vault Liquidation
content: The vulnerability concerns the accounting of debt shares in a single‑vault migration pool when the vault is liquidated. The migration entry point migrateOnBehalf can be invoked by any address, and it does not enforce that the vault’s collateralisation ratio stays above the configured liquidation threshold after the migrated positions are added. An attacker can therefore migrate a carefully chosen set of V2 positions so that the combined collateral‑to‑debt ratio (c‑ratio) of the vault falls below collateralConfig.liquidationRatioD18. Once the ratio is below the threshold, a liquidator can trigger a vault liquidation, repaying the entire V3 debt and seizing all collateral that was in the vault. Because the pool contains only one vault, the liquidation removes the collateral that was backing the debt shares held by the Legacy market, leaving the vault with outstanding debt shares but no collateral. The protocol’s accounting assumes that every debt share is fully collateralised, so after liquidation the debt shares remain in the system and any subsequent user who calls migrateOnBehalf inherits the full amount of debt that now has no backing. If the value of debt shares rises during the interval between liquidation and the next migration, the new migrator will be assigned the extra debt, often becoming instantly liquidatable even though they did not generate that debt themselves. This creates a situation where users see their expected debt balance explode, their position is immediately flagged for liquidation, or they receive no collateral after migration. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the interaction between migration, vault c‑ratio checks, and the liquidation flow. It is hard to notice because the liquidation appears profitable for the liquidator and the vault’s empty collateral state does not raise an obvious error flag; the accounting inconsistency only surfaces when a later migrator’s debt calculation deviates from expectations. The root cause is the lack of safeguards that prevent migrations from pushing the vault into a liquidatable state and the failure to reset or re‑allocate debt shares after a liquidation event. To remediate, the contract should enforce that a sufficient volume of healthy accounts is migrated before allowing any migration that could endanger the vault’s collateralisation, reject migrations that would cause the c‑ratio to drop below the liquidation threshold, and implement logic that either clears or correctly re‑balances debt shares after a vault liquidation so that subsequent users are not unfairly burdened with debt that has no collateral backing.
summary: Vault liquidations are quite profitable for the liquidator who pays back the V3 debt but receives all collateral in the vault. As migrateOnBehalf can be called by anyone, an attacker may be able to put the SNX vault in a liquidatable state by migrating the right positions from V2, which would result in the c-ratio of the vault dropping below the collateralConfig.liquidationRatioD18 and become open for vault liquidation. This would be especially possible if only a handful of small accounts were migrated to V3, and then a big liquidatable account is force migrated to make the entire vault liquidatable. In the event of a vault liquidation, all debts are settled and the liquidator takes all collateral from the vault. Assuming there is only one vault in the pool, then there would be no collateral backing the debt shares that the Legacy market holds. This state in itself is somewhat peculiar and should be examined further. One concern would be during the period after vault liquidation till the next time another user migrate. If debt shares increase in value during that period, then the next user to migrate take on all extra debt. In many cases, any subsequent migrators/delegators would become immediately liquidatable by unfairly taking on debt that did not belong to them.

title: H-05 | Migrations Can Be Executed Even If Paused
content: The vulnerability is a missing pause guard on the public migrateOnBehalf function of the legacy market contract. The contract is designed to allow users to migrate their positions to a new market, and a global flag pauseMigration is intended to stop all migrations when the protocol is paused for upgrades or emergency. The internal _migrate routine checks this flag, and the direct migrate function correctly reverts when pauseMigration is true. However, migrateOnBehalf forwards the call to _migrate without performing the same pause check, meaning any address can invoke it and force a migration even while the system is officially paused. This occurs because the developer duplicated migration logic but omitted the pause guard, creating an inconsistency in access control. An attacker can exploit the flaw by calling migrateOnBehalf with a victim’s address as the target, causing the victim’s position to be moved without consent while the protocol is supposed to be frozen. The impact is that the intended safety window provided by pausing migrations is bypassed, potentially leading to unexpected asset transfers, state inconsistencies, or loss of funds if the new market behaves differently during a paused state. The bug manifests only when the pauseMigration flag is set to true; under normal operation the two functions behave similarly, making the issue easy to miss during casual testing because the primary migrate function appears safe. It was discovered during a manual audit that compared the implementations of migrate and migrateOnBehalf and noticed the missing require statement. The problem is hard to notice because both functions call the same internal routine and the pause flag is only checked in one entry point, giving a false sense of security. To remediate, the pause check should be moved into the shared internal _migrate function or duplicated in migrateOnBehalf so that any migration path respects the paused state. Conceptually this is a classic missing access‑control or guard condition bug, where a privileged state (paused) is not enforced on all external entry points, allowing unauthorized state changes. From a user’s perspective, a trader who expects that their positions cannot be moved while the protocol is paused may see their assets suddenly migrated, resulting in unexpected balance changes, missing positions, or funds appearing in an unintended market. The discrepancy violates the protocol’s business rule that pausing should freeze all migration activity, breaking accounting assumptions and potentially exposing users to risk.
summary: [LegacyMarket.migrate()](https://github.com/Synthetixio/synthetix-v3/blob/2ea4dd99d5344b38df7b695f255216958bf3b086/markets/legacy-market/contracts/LegacyMarket.sol#L179C1-L181C10) reverts if pauseMigration = true. However, there is another function for migrations which lacks this check - [migrateOnBehalf()](https://github.com/Synthetixio/synthetix-v3/blob/2ea4dd99d5344b38df7b695f255216958bf3b086/markets/legacy-market/contracts/LegacyMarket.sol#L189C1-L192C1). Anyone can call migrateOnBehalf and pass their address to execute a migration even when they are paused.

title: H-06 | Prevention Of convertUSD Via Bridge Migrations
content: The vulnerability resides in the convertUSD function, which internally invokes the burnSynths routine of the V2 system. BurnSynths contains a safeguard that reverts the transaction if the minimum stake time – a one‑week interval – has not elapsed since the staker’s last issuance event. The protocol records the timestamp of the most recent issuance per market, and this timestamp can be overwritten when sUSD is migrated across the L2‑to‑L1 bridge. By directing a bridge migration to the legacy market address, an attacker can set the legacy market’s last‑issuance timestamp to the current block time. Consequently, any subsequent call to convertUSD on that market will fail the minimum‑stake‑time check and revert, effectively denying the service for up to a week. Because the bridge can be used again after the week passes, the attacker can repeat the operation indefinitely, creating a near‑permanent denial‑of‑service condition. The same mechanism also blocks users from burning synths to restore healthy collateralisation, meaning positions that rely on burning may become stuck. This issue was uncovered during a security audit that examined the interaction between bridge migration logic and the V2 staking constraints; the problem is subtle because bridge migrations are expected to move balances, not to manipulate internal timestamps, making the bug easy to overlook. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that attempts to convert USD or burn synths simply revert, leaving balances unchanged and providing no error message beyond a generic revert. Users expect their convertUSD transaction to succeed and their balances to update, but instead they receive no funds and see no change, which violates the protocol’s accounting assumptions that a user can always convert or burn after the minimum stake period. The root cause is the reliance on a mutable timestamp that can be set by an external bridge call without proper validation. To remediate the issue the protocol should either disable the minimum‑stake‑time requirement after migration (by setting the corresponding setting to zero) or explicitly forbid bridge migrations that target the legacy market, thereby preventing the timestamp from being tampered with and restoring the intended convertUSD functionality.
summary: The convertUSD function calls burnSynths in the V2 system which will revert if the minimum stake time has not passed since the last issuance event of the staker. By bridging sUSD from an L2 to the L1 chain with the legacy market as the destination address, anyone can set the last issuance event of the legacy market to the current block time and therefore DoS the convertUSD function for one week. This call can be repeated once per week which can make DOS permanent. Notice also that this same attack vector could be used to prevent users from burning to make their positions healthy.

title: H-07 | Partial Vault Liquidations Ignore Rebalance
content: The vulnerability concerns the handling of partial vault liquidations in a multi‑market protocol. When a vault is liquidated only partially, the contract that seizes the liquidated collateral does not invoke the routine that recalculates the vault's effective collateral and rebalance the markets that rely on that information. As a result, the markets – such as the BFP market and the Perps market – continue to operate with an outdated view of the vault's credit capacity. They therefore cannot correctly evaluate the minimumCredit threshold that governs whether increase orders are permitted. This stale state may allow the protocol to accept new orders even though the vault’s actual collateral after liquidation would be insufficient, creating a situation where the system believes there is enough credit while in reality the vault is under‑collateralized. In addition, the vault’s debt distribution shares are not updated after the collateral value changes, causing the accounting of credit and debt across all vaults to become inconsistent. The issue manifests only when a partial liquidation occurs; full liquidations trigger the proper recalculation path, so the bug can be difficult to notice during routine testing that focuses on complete liquidations. Users experience symptoms such as being able to place increase orders that should be rejected, seeing no change in their reported collateral after a partial liquidation, or observing that their debt share remains unchanged despite a reduction in collateral. The root cause is the omission of a call to the recalculateVaultCollateral function in the partial liquidation code path, leaving the market’s internal creditCapacity and the vault’s debt distribution out of sync with the actual state. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the liquidation workflow and identified that the rebalance step was skipped. To remediate the issue, the protocol should ensure that after any reduction of collateral – whether full or partial – the vault’s collateral is recomputed and the markets are notified, typically by invoking the recalculateVaultCollateral routine before exiting the liquidation function. This will restore accurate minimumCredit checks, keep debt distribution consistent, and prevent the protocol from mistakenly allowing orders that could lead to over‑leveraged positions or loss of funds.
summary: When liquidating a vault partially the markets are not rebalanced after the collateralLiquidated is seized by the liquidator. Therefore markets are not aware of this reduction in creditCapacity and cannot accurately determine if they are below the minimumCredit threshold, which may be likely if a vault has been partially liquidated. For example, BFP market and Perps Market rely on minimumCredit validations to decide whether increase orders should be allowed. Additionally, the vaultsDebtDistribution shares are not updated for the vault after the collateral value changes, which can lead to further mis-accounting of credit and debt spread across vaults.

title: Users redeeming early will with-
content: The vulnerability is an accounting mismatch in the early‑redemption flow of the Vault contract. When a user calls Vault.redeemEarlyLv the function VaultLib._redeemCtDsAndSellExcessCt invokes PsmLib.lvRedeemRaWithCtDs to burn the corresponding Ct and Ds tokens and to transfer the underlying Ra to the caller. The logical expectation is that the amount of Ra that leaves the vault is also removed from the internal locked‑Ra counter maintained by RedemptionAssetManagerLib. However, the implementation of lvRedeemRaWithCtDs never calls RedemptionAssetManagerLib.decLocked, so the locked‑Ra balance remains unchanged even though the actual Ra has been sent to the user. Because the locked‑Ra figure is later used by PsmLib._separateLiquidity to compute the exchange rate for subsequent withdrawals or for the issuance of new Ds, the protocol assumes more Ra is available than really is. As a result, the first users who redeem early receive a larger amount of Ra than the protocol’s accounting permits, while later users encounter insufficient liquidity and may receive zero or a reduced amount. The bug manifests only when the early‑redemption path is exercised or when an admin triggers issueNewDs, which also relies on the same locked‑Ra accounting. Affected parties include any user of the vault, the protocol’s liquidity pool, and the overall stability of the system because the checkpoint for Ra and Pa becomes inaccurate. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the state changes of the locked‑Ra counter with the actual token transfers and noticed that the counter was never decremented. It is hard to notice because the free‑Ra balance may still appear positive, masking the fact that the locked portion is stale; only after several early redemptions does the shortage become visible as failed withdrawals. The correct mitigation is to decrement the locked‑Ra amount inside lvRedeemRaWithCtDs, i.e., call self.psm.balances.ra.decLocked(amount) before burning the Ct/Ds tokens. This restores the invariant that the sum of locked and free Ra equals the total Ra held by the vault, preventing over‑issuance and ensuring that users receive the amount they are entitled to according to the protocol’s accounting rules.
summary: VaultLib::redeemEarly() is called when users redeem early via Vault::redeemEarlyLv(), which allows users to redeem Lv for Ra and pay a fee. In the process, the Vault burns Ct and Ds in VaultLib::_redeemCtDsAndSellExcessCt() for Ra, by calling PsmLib::PsmLibrary.lvRedeemRaWithCtDs(). However, it never calls RedemptionAssetManagerLib::decLocked() to decrease the tracked locked Ra, but the Ra leaves the Vault for the user redeeming. This means that when a new Ds is issued in the PsmLib or users call PsmLib::redeemWithCt(), PsmLib::_separateLiquidity() will be called and it will calculated the exchange rate to withdraw Ra and Pa as if the Ra amount withdrawn earlier was still there. When it calls self.psm.balances.ra.convertAllToFree(), it converts the locked amount to free and assumes these funds are available, when in reality they have been withdrawn earlier. As such, the Ra and Pa checkpoint will be incorrect and users will redeem more Ra than they should, such that the last users will not be able to withdraw and the first ones will profit. In PsmLib.sol:125, self.psm.balances.ra.decLocked(amount); is not called. Internal pre-conditions None. External pre-conditions None. Attack Path 1. User calls Vault::redeemEarlyLv() or ModuleCore::issueNewDs() is called by the admin. Users withdraw more funds then they should via PsmLib::redeemWithCt() meaning the last users can not withdraw.

title: VaultPoolLib::reserve() will store the Pa not attributed to user with- drawals incorrectly and leave in untracked once it expires again The protocol has acknowledged this issue. Found by 0x73696d616f, 0xNirix, dimulski, sakshamguruji
content: VaultPoolLib::reserve incorrectly records the protocol asset (PA) that belongs to the automated market maker (AMM) in the field stagnatedPaBalance instead of the field attributedToAmm. Because the subsequent function VaultPoolLib::rationedToAmm only reads the RA (reserve asset) balance and never touches the PA balance, the PA amount remains forever idle after the vault expires. The bug is triggered whenever the vault liquidation path _liquidatedLP calls reserve, which happens when a user redeems expired liquidity‑vault shares or when an admin initiates a new issuance. At that moment the contract thinks the PA has been allocated, but in reality it is stored in an untracked slot and is never rationed or made available for withdrawal. From a user perspective the expected refund or liquidity share is missing; the UI may show a normal vault balance while the underlying PA amount is silently lost, leading to a situation where funds appear to disappear. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by multiple researchers and is hard to notice because the contract treats PA the same as RA and does not emit events or perform checks on the stagnatedPaBalance field. The impact is high because any PA that becomes stuck reduces the total assets backing user shares, potentially causing under‑collateralisation and loss of value for all participants. The vulnerability belongs to the class of accounting‑logic errors where a token balance is recorded in the wrong storage location and never reconciled. To remediate the problem the protocol should either distribute the stuck PA to users proportionally to their vault shares or convert the PA into RA and feed it back into the liquidity pool during the next issuance, ensuring that the amount is properly tracked and can be withdrawn.
summary: VaultPoolLib::reserve() stores the Pa attributed to withdrawals in self.withdrawalPool.stagnatedPaBalance instead of storing the amount attributedToAmm. Additionally, this amount of Pa, the one attributed to the Amm is never dealt with and leads to stuck PA. // FIXME : this is only temporary, for now // we trate PA the same as RA, thus we also separate PA // the difference is the PA here isn't being used as anything // and for now will just sit there until rationed again at next expiry. But it is incorrect as it is never rationed again, just forgotten. The VaultPoolLib::rationedToAmm() function only uses the Ra balance, not the Pa, which is effectively left untracked. In VaultPoolLib:170, the leftover non attributed Pa is not dealt with. Internal pre-conditions None. External pre-conditions None. Attack Path 1. VaultPoolLib::reserve() is called when liquidating the lp position of the Vault via VaultLib::_liquidatedLP(), triggered by users when redeeming expired liquidity vault shares or on the admin trigerring a new issuance. The Pa in the Vault is stuck.

title: Lack of slippage protection leads to loss of protocol funds Found by 0x6a70, 0x73696d616f, 0xjoi, 0xnbvc, 4b, 4gontuk, Abhan1041, MohammedRizwan, Pheonix, StraawHaat, alphacipher, boringslav, ivanonchain, sakshamguruji, vinica_boy
content: The vulnerability consists of missing slippage protection in two core AMM interactions performed by the vault library when a liquidity‑provider token holder redeems early or when the protocol liquidates a portion of its LP position. In the early‑redeem path the contract calls swapExactTokensForTokens with a minimum‑output argument of zero and a deadline equal to block.timestamp, meaning the swap will execute regardless of how much the output token price moves. Similarly, during partial liquidation the contract calls removeLiquidity with both minimum‑amount arguments set to zero and the same block.timestamp deadline, allowing the AMM to return arbitrarily low amounts of the underlying tokens. Because the contract does not enforce a minimum acceptable price, an attacker who observes the pending transaction in the mempool can front‑run it, trade against the same pool to shift the price, or even manipulate the block timestamp by being a miner, causing the protocol’s swap or liquidity removal to suffer extreme slippage. The result is that the vault receives fewer RA or CT tokens than expected, effectively draining protocol funds and reducing the yield that users later receive. This condition manifests to users as unexpectedly low or zero refunds when they redeem, or as a sudden drop in their reported balances after a withdrawal. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the vault library where the function signatures were examined and the hard‑coded zero values for minAmount parameters were noted. It can be hard to notice because the calls succeed on‑chain and no revert occurs; the loss is only visible in the accounting of the vault’s asset balances. The bug belongs to the class of “missing slippage protection” or “price‑manipulation” vulnerabilities common in DeFi contracts that interact with AMMs without specifying acceptable price bounds. To remediate, the contract should supply a reasonable minimum‑output amount based on a slippage tolerance (e.g., 1‑2 % of the expected amount) and use a future timestamp as a deadline, thereby preventing front‑running and miner‑controlled timing attacks. Implementing these checks restores the intended economic guarantees and protects user funds from being unintentionally lost.
summary:
There is no slippage protection while removing liquidity and swap tokens from AMM. There are 2 instances where slippage protection is missing which are as below: 1. When LV token holder redeem before expiry vaultLib::redeemEarly function is called in which _liquidateLpPartial function and in that _redeemCtDsAndSellExcessCt function CT tokens are swapped for RA tokens in AMM as below:
```solidity
ra += ammRouter.swapExactTokensForTokens(ctSellAmount, 0, path, address(this), block.timestamp)[1];
```
As stated above, swapExactTokensForTokens function's 2nd parameter is 0 which shows that there is no slippage protection for this swap and also deadline is block.timestamp. 2. In vaultLib::_liquidateLpPartial function __liquidateUnchecked is called in which liquidity is removed from AMM of RA-CT token pair by burning LP tokens of protocol as below:
```solidity
(raReceived, ctReceived) = ammRouter.removeLiquidity(raAddress, ctAddress, lp, 0, 0, address(this), block.timestamp);
```
As stated above, removeLiquidity function's 4th & 5th parameter is 0 which shows that there is no slippage protection for this swap and also deadline is block.timestamp. In such cases, an attacker can frontrun the transaction by seeing it in the mempool and manipulate the price such that protocol transaction have to bear heavy slippage which will leads to loss of protocol funds. Also, there is block.timestamp as deadline so malicious node can prevent transaction to execute temporary and execute the transaction when there is high slippage which will also leads to loss of protocol funds. Loss of protocol funds which will reduce the yield of users.

title: Strategy Migration May Leave Tokens in the Old Strategy Impacting Share Calculations
content: The vulnerability concerns the migration routine of a yield‑aggregating contract that moves user capital from one strategy to another. The core issue is that the routine assumes the old strategy can withdraw the full amount of tokens that it reports as its total value. In practice, many yield protocols lend deposited assets to borrowers, and the amount of liquid tokens available for withdrawal can be lower than the reported balance. When the migration function calls the old strategy’s withdraw method with the full reported balance, the call may succeed while only transferring the liquid portion, leaving a residual amount of tokens locked inside the old strategy contract. Because the migration code does not verify that the old strategy’s balance has been reduced to zero, the controller’s totalValue() function later reports only the tokens now held in the new strategy. This under‑reporting skews the accounting used during deposit operations: the share calculation performed in Collateral.deposit() uses the stale totalValue() as the denominator, which results in a higher share count being allocated to the depositor than their contribution actually warrants. Consequently, a user who deposits immediately after a migration may receive more shares than entitled. If the migration is later reversed to the original strategy, the previously omitted tokens reappear in totalValue(), causing the same user’s withdrawal to be over‑credited, while earlier participants who deposited before the migration experience a proportional loss of value because the total supply of shares now represents a larger pool of tokens than originally accounted for. The flaw manifests only when a strategy cannot fully satisfy a withdraw request, which is an edge case but can be triggered by normal operation of lending‑based yield platforms. It affects all participants of the protocol: recent depositors gain an unintended advantage, and earlier depositors suffer a dilution of their holdings. The issue was uncovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, which examined the migration logic and identified the missing verification of residual token balances. The problem is subtle because the withdraw call does not revert on partial payout, making the incomplete transfer appear successful, and the subsequent accounting step silently produces incorrect share ratios. To remediate the defect, the migration routine should enforce that the old strategy’s totalValue() is zero after the withdraw call, for example by adding a require statement that checks the post‑withdraw balance, and by ensuring any residual tokens are explicitly transferred to the new strategy before completing the migration. This approach restores the invariant that totalValue() always reflects the total tokens managed by the controller, preserving correct share calculations and preventing inadvertent over‑issuance or loss of funds.
summary:
If a strategy does not have sufficient funds to `withdraw()` for the full amount then it is possible that tokens will be left in this yield contract during `migrate()`.

It is common for withdrawal from a strategy to withdraw less than a user’s balance. The reason is that these yield protocols may lend the deposited funds to borrowers, if there is less funds in the pool than the withdrawal amount the withdrawal may succeed but only transfer the funds available rather than the full withdrawal amount.

The impact of tokens remaining in the old strategy is that when we call `StrategyController.totalValue()` this will only account for the tokens deposited in the new strategy and not those stuck in the previous strategy. Therefore `totalValue()` is undervalued.

Thus, when a user calls `Collateral.deposit()` the share calculations `_shares = (_amountToDeposit * totalSupply()) / (_valueBefore);` will be over stated (note: `uint256 _valueBefore = _strategyController.totalValue();`). Hence, the user will receive more shares than they should.

The old tokens may be recovered by calling `migrate()` back to the old strategy. If this is done then `totalValue()` will now include the tokens previously stuck. The recent depositer may now withdraw and will be owed `(_strategyController.totalValue() * _amount) / totalSupply()`. Since `totalValue()` is now includes the previously stuck tokens `_owed` will be overstated and the user will receive more collateral than they should.

The remaining users who had deposited before `migrate()` will lose tokens proportional to their share of the `totalSupply()`.

title: First depositor can break minting of shares
content: The vulnerability is a share‑dilution flaw that allows the first depositor, or any user who can inject a large amount of assets into the strategy controller before any shares exist, to manipulate the total asset balance such that the minting formula computes zero new shares for subsequent deposits. The root cause lies in the contract’s share‑minting logic, which calculates newly minted shares as a proportion of the deposited amount over the existing total assets multiplied by the current total supply. When totalSupply() equals zero, the divisor becomes zero, and the contract does not enforce a non‑zero share amount, allowing an attacker to deposit the minimum amount required to pass the fee check and receive the first share. By then transferring an exorbitant amount of tokens to the strategy controller, the attacker inflates the observed total assets dramatically. Any later user who deposits a reasonable amount triggers the same proportional calculation, but because the total assets have been artificially inflated while totalSupply() remains one, the computed share amount rounds down to zero. From the user’s perspective this appears as a deposit that succeeds on‑chain yet yields no share balance – the UI may show a successful transaction, the token balance remains unchanged, and the user receives nothing in exchange for their funds, effectively losing the deposited capital. The impact is high because the attacker keeps the sole share and can later withdraw the inflated assets, draining funds from honest participants. The condition for exploitation is that the contract’s initialization or first deposit occurs before any safeguards against zero‑share minting are applied, and that the attacker can make a large “donation” to the strategy controller before other users interact. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when a test case reproduced a scenario in which the first depositor sent only 2 wei, the contract minted one share, and a subsequent deposit of 10 000 ether resulted in zero shares. The problem is hard to notice because the transaction does not revert; it merely mints zero shares, which may be interpreted as a normal zero‑balance situation rather than a security breach. Conceptually, the fix is to prevent share minting when totalSupply() is zero from producing a zero‑share outcome: either by burning the first batch of shares (as Uniswap V2 does by sending them to the zero address), enforcing a require check that minted shares be non‑zero, or initializing the pool with a minimal non‑zero share supply through an atomic wrapper that calls initialize() and deposit() together. This class of bug falls under “initial share dilution” or “zero‑share minting” attacks, where economic assumptions about proportional ownership break down due to manipulated total assets.
summary:
[Collateral.sol#L82-L91](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-prepo/blob/main/contracts/core/Collateral.sol#L82-L91)  

The attack vector and impact is the same as [TOB-YEARN-003](https://github.com/yearn/yearn-security/blob/master/audits/20210719_ToB_yearn_vaultsv2/ToB_-_Yearn_Vault_v_2_Smart_Contracts_Audit_Report.pdf), where users may not receive shares in exchange for their deposits if the total asset amount has been manipulated through a large “donation”.

title: Withdrawal delay can be circumvented
content: The vulnerability consists of a circumvention of the intended delayed‑withdrawal mechanism in the Collateral token contract. When a user calls `initiateWithdrawal`, the contract records a withdrawal request that should lock the user’s collateral for a fixed number of blocks (the `_delayedWithdrawalExpiry`). However, the contract does not prevent the token holder from transferring the same amount of tokens to another address while the request is still pending. Because the withdrawal request is stored per account, the receiving address has no pending request and can immediately create its own withdrawal request, effectively resetting the waiting period. By repeatedly alternating the withdrawal request between two (or more) accounts and moving the tokens back and forth, an attacker can ensure that at least one account is always within a valid withdrawal window, allowing the full amount to be withdrawn at any time, even in the same block in which the tokens were originally purchased. The root cause is the lack of a transfer‑restriction check that ties token movement to an active withdrawal request; the contract only checks the request when a withdrawal is executed, not when tokens are transferred. Exploitation requires the attacker to own the collateral, create one or more auxiliary accounts, and orchestrate a sequence of `initiateWithdrawal` calls interleaved with token transfers every few blocks. The impact is severe: the protocol’s economic guarantees that rely on a mandatory waiting period (for example, to allow liquidators to act or to prevent flash‑loan attacks) are broken, and an attacker can effectively drain the collateral pool faster than intended. This condition occurs whenever a withdrawal request exists (`_accountToWithdrawalRequest[owner].blockNumber > 0`) and the owner is allowed to transfer tokens, which the contract currently permits. All token holders, the protocol’s risk management module, and any downstream users that rely on the delayed withdrawal guarantee are affected. The issue was discovered during a formal code audit that inspected the withdrawal flow and noticed that the `beforeTransfer` hook does not consider pending withdrawal requests. It may be hard to notice because token balances and transfer events appear normal; only the internal mapping of pending withdrawals reveals the inconsistency, and typical UI components only display the “withdrawal pending” status without warning about transferable balance. To remediate, the contract should lock the entire balance of any account that has an active withdrawal request for the duration of the defined expiry period, rejecting any outbound transfers until the window expires. Conceptually, this means coupling token transferability to the withdrawal state, ensuring that once a withdrawal is initiated the corresponding tokens cannot be reassigned or reused until the delay has elapsed. From the user’s perspective, the expectation is that after initiating a withdrawal they must wait the prescribed number of blocks before receiving funds; instead, they can move the tokens elsewhere and withdraw instantly, leading to confusion such as “my withdrawal is supposed to take 20 blocks but I got the money right away” or “my balance disappears after I initiate withdrawal despite the UI saying I must wait”. This breach violates the core business logic that the delayed withdrawal provides a safety buffer, effectively allowing funds to disappear from the protocol’s accounting earlier than designed.
summary:
[Collateral.sol#L97](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-prepo/blob/f63584133a0329781609e3f14c3004c1ca293e71/contracts/core/Collateral.sol#L97)  

After initiating a withdrawal with `initiateWithdrawal`, it’s still possible to transfer the collateral tokens. This can be used to create a second account, transfer the accounts to them and initiate withdrawals at a different time frame such that one of the accounts is always in a valid withdrawal window, no matter what time it is.
