If the token owner now wants to withdraw they just transfer the funds to the account that is currently in a valid withdrawal window.

Also, note that each account can withdraw the specified `amount`. Creating several accounts and circling & initiating withdrawals with all of them allows withdrawing larger amounts **even at the same block** as they are purchased in the future.

I consider this high severity because it breaks core functionality of the Collateral token.

title: FlashSwapRouter::emptyReserve()
content: The vulnerability resides in the FlashSwapRouter contract where the functions emptyReserve and emptyReservePartial are used to withdraw the DS token reserve after a liquidation step. Both functions transfer the full amount of DS to a target address and then return the value of self.ds[dsId].reserve after the subtraction. Consequently emptyReserve always returns 0 and emptyReservePartial returns the remaining reserve instead of the amount that was actually transferred. The VaultLib::_liquidatedLp and VaultLib::_redeemCtDsAndSellExcessCt logic rely on the returned value to calculate how much CT can be paired with DS to redeem RA tokens. Because the returned value is wrong, the protocol assumes that no DS is available, skips the intended CT‑DS pairing, and attempts to redeem RA and PA tokens with an incorrect CT amount. In the liquidation path this leads to the PSM receiving all CT from the AMM pair and issuing far more PA tokens than intended, while the LV holder receives zero RA tokens. In the early‑redeem path the calculation of ctSellAmount becomes larger than the actual CT balance, causing the swapExactTokensForTokens call to revert. The end result is that a user who calls redeemEarlyLv or who relies on the normal liquidation flow receives no RA tokens, the transaction fails, and the RA/CT tokens remain locked in the contract. The issue manifests after the first DS and CT tokens for a pair have expired and the protocol attempts to issue new DS tokens, or whenever a user tries to redeem LV tokens before the pair is fully settled. It affects all LV token holders, the protocol’s accounting, and any external participants that expect to receive their redeemed assets. The bug was discovered during a security audit when a test that expected a successful early redemption reverted with a transfer failure, revealing that the emptyReserve functions were returning an unexpected zero. The problem is subtle because the functions appear to correctly transfer the tokens; the incorrect return value is only used later in accounting calculations, making it easy to overlook. The proper fix is to change emptyReserve to return the amount that was transferred (or to return the pre‑transfer reserve) and to adjust emptyReservePartial to return the transferred amount as well, ensuring that the downstream calculations receive the correct DS balance. This restores the intended CT‑DS pairing, prevents the over‑issuance of PA tokens, and allows users to successfully redeem their LV tokens without locking funds.

title: LV token holders receive proportional fees incorrectly
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect fee accrual mechanism for the Liquidity Vault (LV) token. The contract distributes protocol fees to LV token holders without taking into account when each holder minted or redeemed their LV tokens. Because the system does not record a snapshot of fee balances at the moment a user deposits, any fee that is added to the underlying AMM pair or collected by the protocol is divided equally among all existing LV tokens, regardless of how long each holder has owned them. An attacker can exploit this by waiting until the last moment before a fee distribution or before the CT/DS tokens expire, depositing a new LV token, immediately requesting redemption, and then claiming the same amount of fees that early depositors would have earned. The impact is that early participants receive a reduced share of fees, while late participants effectively steal fees that should belong to the former. This occurs whenever fees are generated after a user has already deposited but before a new user deposits, and the protocol does not update per‑holder accounting. All LV token holders, the protocol’s revenue model, and any user relying on the promised proportional fee share are affected. The issue was discovered during an audit by injecting synthetic fees into the Uniswap V2 pair and observing that two users who deposited at different times received identical WETH balances after redemption. The bug is subtle because the UI shows a simple “fees per LV token” figure and does not expose the missing time‑weighting, making the unfair distribution easy to miss. The correct fix is to introduce a per‑holder fee accounting scheme, such as maintaining a cumulative fee per token snapshot at each distribution, updating individual balances on deposit and redemption, or using a checkpoint system that records the fee index at the moment of minting. This ensures that only fees generated after a holder’s deposit are credited to that holder, preserving the intended proportional revenue sharing.
summary:
The Corc protocol claims that the LV token holders should accrue fees that the protocol generates, from the docs: In our design we envision several mechanisms through which the Liquidity Vault will generate revenues. Some of these are from protocol fees that will flow to the Liquidity Vault and accrue to Liquidity Vault tokenholders. However, the fee accrual is incorrect, a user can deposit just before fees are about to be distributed to LV holders, and still receive the same amount of fees as a user who deposited tokens in the beginning. There is one LV token per RA:PA pair, however the CT and DS tokens expire and there may be several CT and DS tokens issued by the protocol. Users can mint an LV token via the Vault::depositLv() function, by depositing the corresponding RA asset. The first issue is that if User A mints a LV token, and request to redeem it, then some fees from swapping in the AMM pair for the CT and RA token are generated, or the protocol collects fees from users utilizing its functionality, then a User B mints a LV token, and request to redeem it, both users will accrue the same amount of fees generated by the protocol, when this shouldn't be the case. As the first users has had his request for redeem for a much longer period, risking the price of the RA token dropping significantly, while User B may just call the Vault::depositLv() function the last block before the CT and DS tokens expire, and request a redeem immediately. Then in the next block when the CT and DS tokens have already expired he can claim the same amount of fees as User A, this is demonstrated in the first POC. To better illustrate the second problem consider the following example  
• User A and User B minted LV tokens while the first issued CT and DS tokens were still not expired  
• The UniV2 pair generated some fees  
• The protocol collects fees, from users utilizing its functionality  
• The issued CT and DS tokens expired  
• The protocol issued new CT and DS tokens  
• User C mints some LV tokens  
• The UniV2 pair generates some more fees,  
The fees will be split equally between all the users (of course taking into account the amount of LV tokens they hold).  
The protocol doesn't implement any mechanism to track when users minted LV tokens, or when they requested a redemption of their LV tokens, or what rewards were accrued to the current LV holders.  

Internal pre-conditions  
External pre-conditions  
Attack Path  
Fees are distrusted incorrectly, users who have held LV tokens since the beginning will receive an equal amount of fees with users who deposit much later, even if no fees are generated by the protocol since the last user deposited. The last users to deposit are effectively stealing fees from the users who deposited earlier.

title: Incorrect redeemAmount Is Accounted as RA
content: The vulnerability is an accounting mismatch that treats the amount returned from a liquidation or flash‑swap operation as if it were already expressed in Redemption Assets (RA) when, in fact, it is still denominated in the combined Cover Token/Depeg Swap (Ct/Ds) unit. During the liquidateLP routine the contract empties the DS reserve, pairs it with the CT amount received from the AMM and records this combined Ct/Ds quantity as an increase in the RA balance. Because the protocol’s exchange rate – the factor that converts Ct/Ds to RA and vice‑versa – is not applied, the RA reserve is updated with an incorrect value. The same mistake propagates to other modules such as PsmLib, FlashSwapRouter and additional points in VaultLib where redeemAmount is used directly as RA. This error occurs whenever a liquidation, flash‑swap, or any function that credits or debits RA based on a Ct/Ds amount is executed. As a result, the protocol believes it has reserved more (or less) RA than it actually does, which can cause users to receive fewer redemption assets than expected, see their balances unexpectedly drop to zero, or allow an attacker to withdraw an excess amount of RA by exploiting the inflated reserve accounting. The impact is high because the mismatch can lead to loss of funds, under‑collateralisation of the vault, and a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the logical flow of asset conversion against the code and noticed that the exchange rate was never applied in several accounting statements. It is hard to notice because the variable names (redeemAmount, dsAttributed, etc.) suggest they already represent RA, and the conversion logic is hidden in the protocol’s economic model rather than in explicit code. To remediate, every place where a Ct/Ds quantity is credited to or debited from the RA balance must first be multiplied or divided by the current exchange rate, ensuring a consistent unit conversion across the entire code base. This conceptual fix restores the integrity of the accounting model, aligns on‑chain balances with user‑visible expectations, and prevents the protocol from mistakenly reserving or releasing the wrong amount of redemption assets.
summary:
When Liquidating LP , DS and CT are paired , then that amount is used to redeem RA . But the accounting for RA has been done incorrectly since it does not account for exchange rate.  
1.) Inside Liquidate LP we empty out the DS reserve and pair it up with the CT amount returned from the AMM -> ntracts/libraries/VaultLib.sol#L376  
This is the amount of CtDs being redeemed.  
2.) This same amount has been accounted for the increment in RA -> ntracts/libraries/VaultLib.sol#L390  
But this is incorrect , this is because redeemAmount is an amount in Ct/Ds not in RA , to make it into RA we need to apply the exchange rate over it(exchange rate is how many Redemption Assets you need to deposit to receive 1 Cover Token + 1 Depeg Swap and how many Redemption Assets you receive when redeeming 1 Pegged Asset + 1 Depeg Swap , read more in the Dealing with non-rebasing Pegged Assets section -> https://corkfi.notion.site/Cork-Protocol-Litepaper-f21a57d5c19d48209dfa0f0c2ab776c4).  
3.) Therefore incorrect RA amount has been accounted and incorrect amount of RA would be reserved -> ntracts/libraries/VaultLib.sol#L392  
meaning , incorrect amount of RA attributed to be withdrawn/redeemed.  
4.) This inconsistency is found at multiple places , and instead of making separate reports im listing them here ->  
contracts/libraries/PsmLib.sol#L122  
The amount here is in RA and we are issuing DS/CT with it.  
contracts/core/flash-swaps/FlashSwapRouter.sol#L368  
dsAttributed is in DS and we are depositing RA.  
contracts/libraries/VaultLib.sol#L331  
redeemAmount is in Ct/Ds here

title: Incoming Redemption Assets not being tracked when repurchase is called Found by 0x73696d616f, 0xNirix, Ace-30, KupiaSec, Pheonix, dimulski, sakshamguruji, steadyman, vinica_boy
content: During the redemption workflow the contract maintains a PsmRedemptionAssetManager struct with fields locked and free that record how many redemption assets (RA) have been received and are available for later accounting. The repurchase() function is supposed to receive RA from a user and return a combination of DepegSwap and a pegged asset. However, instead of calling the accounting‑aware lockFrom method, repurchase() transfers the incoming RA using lockUnchecked(), which bypasses the update of the locked counter. As a result the external token transfer succeeds but the internal variable that tracks total RA remains unchanged. The mismatch is harmless while the system is operating before expiry, but after the DepegSwap expiry the protocol calls _separateLiquidity() to archive the accumulated RA and pegged asset balances. That function reads the locked amount, archives it, and then resets the balances to zero. Because the locked counter does not reflect the RA that arrived through repurchase, the archived amount is lower than the actual token balance held by the contract. The surplus RA stays in the contract with no entry in the accounting tables, effectively becoming unrecoverable. Users who have previously used the repurchase path see their expected refund or balance disappear; the UI may show that they received the correct DepegSwap and pegged asset, but later their redemption asset balance is zero while the contract still holds the tokens. The vulnerability was discovered during a comprehensive audit by several independent researchers who traced the state changes of the PsmRedemptionAssetManager and noticed that lockUnchecked was used. The bug is difficult to spot because the token transfer does not revert and there is no immediate error; the inconsistency only manifests after the expiry‑triggered liquidity separation, a code path that may be exercised rarely. The issue belongs to the class of accounting or state‑tracking bugs where external asset movements are not reflected in internal bookkeeping, leading to asset loss. To remediate the problem the repurchase() implementation should update the locked counter, for example by invoking lockFrom instead of lockUnchecked, or by adding an explicit increment of the locked field after the transfer. Ensuring that every incoming RA is recorded restores the invariant that the sum of locked and free matches the actual token balance, preventing funds from becoming permanently stuck.

title: Users will steal excess funds from the Vault due to VaultPoolLib::redeem() not always decreasing self.withdrawalPool.raBalance and self.withdrawalPool.paBalance The protocol has acknowledged this issue. Found by 0x73696d616f, sakshamguruji
content: The vulnerability is an accounting inconsistency in the vault’s redemption logic that allows a user to withdraw more assets than they are entitled to. When a user calls the function that redeems expired liquidity (redeemExpiredLv), the internal library function that handles excess redemption from the automated market maker pool reduces only the AMM pool balance. It fails to decrement the corresponding withdrawal‑pool balances (raBalance and paBalance) that track how much of each asset has already been taken out. Because those balances remain unchanged, the next issuance round calculates the total withdrawal pool by adding the unchanged balances to the newly available liquidity, effectively counting the same funds twice. This double counting inflates the exchange rates used for subsequent redemptions, so a user who repeats the exploit can receive an amount that exceeds their original share, eventually draining the vault and leaving other depositors with insufficient funds or a zero balance. The flaw occurs whenever a user’s eligible redemption amount is larger than the amount they actually request, triggering the excess‑redeem path; no external pre‑conditions are required, meaning any participant can invoke the function. The issue was discovered during a security audit by the researchers 0x73696d616f and sakshamguruji, who noted that the state updates for the withdrawal pool were missing. It is hard to notice because the immediate transaction appears to succeed and the balances displayed after the call still look correct, while the hidden accounting error only manifests in the next issuance when the inflated exchange rates cause the vault to become insolvent. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “missing state update” or “double‑spend through accounting error” where a balance is not reduced after a transfer, leading to an over‑allocation of assets. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a normal redemption receipt, but the user receives more tokens than expected, while other users later see their balances unchanged or become unable to withdraw any funds. The expected behavior is that the withdrawal‑pool balances are reduced in tandem with any amount taken from the AMM pool; the fix is to replace the try‑redeem helper with the proper redeem function that updates raBalance and paBalance, or to add explicit subtraction of those balances when excess redemption occurs, thereby ensuring the accounting remains consistent and preventing double counting of funds.
summary:
Vault::redeemExpiredLv() calls VaultLib::redeemExpired(), which allows users to withdraw funds after expiry, even if they have not requested a redemption. This redemption happens in VaultPoolLib::redeem(), when userEligible < amount, it calls internally __redeemExcessFromAmmPool(), where only self.ammLiquidityPool.balance is reduced, but not self.withdrawalPool.raBalance and self.withdrawalPool.paBalance. As such, when calculating the withdrawal pool balance in the next issuance on VaultPoolLibrary::reserve(), it will double count all the already withdraw self.withdrawalPool.raBalance and self.withdrawalPool.paBalance, allowing users to withdraw the same funds twice.  
In VaultPoolLib::__redeemExcessFromAmmPool(), self.withdrawalPool.raBalance and self.withdrawalPool.paBalance are not decreased, but ra and pa are also withdrawn from the withdrawal pool when the user has partially requested redemption.  

Internal pre-conditions  
1. User requests redemption of an amount smaller than the total withdrawn in VaultLib::redeemExpired(), that is, userEligible<amount.  

External pre-conditions  
None.  

Attack Path  
1. User calls Vault::redeemExpiredLv(), withdrawing from the withdrawal pool, but self.withdrawalPool.raBalance and self.withdrawalPool.paBalance are not decreased.  
2. A new issuance starts, and in VaultPoolLib::reserve(), the funds are double counted as not all withdrawals were reduced.  
3. As such, self.withdrawalPool.raExchangeRate and self.withdrawalPool.paExchangeRate will be inflated by double the funds and users will redeem more funds than they should, leading to the insolvency of the Vault.  
Users steal funds while unaware users will not be able to withdraw.

title: Wrong accounting of locked RA
content: The vulnerability is an accounting inconsistency in the repurchase flow of the protocol where the amount of redemption asset (RA) that is considered locked is inflated. When a user supplies RA to repurchase DS and PA, the contract first records the full amount of RA as locked. A fee is taken from this amount and later used to mint CT and DS tokens for providing liquidity to an AMM pair. The function that provides liquidity calls unsafeIssueToLv, which again increments the locked RA counter by the amount of CT minted. Because the fee amount (or a portion of it) has already been counted as locked in the initial step, adding it a second time results in double‑counting. The root cause is the misuse of lockUnchecked followed by an additional incLocked call for the same fee‑derived amount. An attacker does not need to craft a special transaction; the bug is triggered automatically each time a user executes the repurchase function, which is a normal user operation. The inflated locked balance makes the protocol believe it holds more RA than it actually does, leading to over‑distribution of rewards to early users. Consequently, later users may attempt to redeem their assets and receive less than expected or nothing at all because the real RA pool has been depleted. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a successful repurchase and a higher reward balance, but when trying to redeem the contract returns zero or fails, violating the expectation that deposited RA can always be reclaimed. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s state‑update logic, where the auditor noticed that the locked RA value after providing liquidity exceeded the sum of previously locked amounts. It can be hard to notice because the contract’s external balances still appear correct at the moment of the transaction, and only after multiple repurchases does the discrepancy become visible through failed redemptions. The bug belongs to the class of state‑inconsistency or double‑counting accounting errors, which break fundamental financial invariants of the system. To remediate, the contract should either avoid counting the fee when initially locking RA or refrain from incrementing the locked counter during the liquidity‑minting step, ensuring that the locked RA total always matches the actual token holdings. This correction restores the guarantee that every locked RA can be redeemed and prevents unintended reward inflation.

title: Admin new issuance or user calling Vault::redeemExpiredLv() after Psm::redeemWithCt() will lead to stuck funds when trying to withdraw Found by 0x73696d616f
content: The vulnerability is an accounting mismatch that occurs when the vault attempts to redeem RA (the protocol’s primary asset) for CT (the collateral token) after the PSM (Pegged Stablecoin Module) has already performed a liquidity separation. The PSM library function _separateLiquidity records a checkpoint of the total CT supply and the amounts of RA and PA (the protocol’s secondary asset) that are available at that moment. Later, VaultLib::_liquidatedLp calls PsmLibrary.lvRedeemRaWithCtDs to redeem RA using CT and DS (a debt token) without checking whether the liquidity has already been separated. Because the checkpointed CT total no longer matches the actual CT balance after the earlier separation, the vault ends up withdrawing more RA than it should and fails to withdraw the PA that it is entitled to. This mismatch leaves a portion of PA permanently locked in the vault and causes the subsequent redeem operation to revert, meaning users cannot exchange their CT for the expected RA and PA. The bug can be triggered in two ways: an admin can call ModuleCore::issueNewDs, which internally invokes PsmLibrary.onNewIssuance before VaultLibrary.onNewIssuance, or a regular user can call Psm::redeemWithCT before Vault::redeemExpiredLv. In both cases the pre‑condition that _separateLiquidity has already been executed is satisfied, but the vault does not skip the redundant redemption step. The impact is high: funds become stuck, users see their balances unchanged or receive a transaction revert, and the protocol’s accounting guarantees are broken. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that traced the flow of state between the PSM and the vault and noticed that the liquiditySeparated flag was never consulted before the redemption call. It is subtle because the code paths appear independent and the error only manifests after a specific sequence of calls, making it easy to miss in routine testing. The correct mitigation is to add a guard that checks the liquiditySeparated flag and skips the lvRedeemRaWithCtDs call when liquidity has already been separated, thereby preserving the integrity of the RA/PA accounting and preventing funds from becoming unrecoverable.
summary:
VaultLib::_liquidatedLp() calls PsmLib::lvRedeemRaWithCtDs(), which redeems ra with ct and ds. However, if PsmLib::_separateLiquidity() has already been called, this will lead to an incorrect tracking of funds as PsmLib::_separateLiquidity() checkpointed the total supply of ct, but the Vault will redeem some of it using PsmLib::lvRedeemRaWithCtDs(), leading to some pa that will never be withdrawn and the vault withdraws too many Ra, which means users will not be able to redeem their ct for ra and pa as ra has been withdrawn already and it reverts.  
In VaultLib.sol:377, it calls PsmLib::lvRedeemRaWithCtDs() even if PsmLib::_separateLiquidity() has already been called. It should skip it in this case.  

Internal pre-conditions  
1. PsmLib::_separateLiquidity() needs to be called before VaultLib::_liquidatedLp(), which may be done on a new issuance when the admin calls ModuleCore::issueNewDs() or by users calling Psm::redeemWithCT() before Vault::redeemExpiredLv().  

External pre-conditions  
None.  

Attack Path  
1. Admin calls ModuleCore::issueNewDs(). Or users call Psm::redeemWithCT() before Vault::redeemExpiredLv().  
As the Vault withdraws Ra after the checkpoint and burns the corresponding Ct tokens, it will withdraw too many ra and not withdraw the pa it was entitled to.

title: Attackers will steal the reserve
content: The vulnerability is a misdirection of the liquidity fee token (Ra) in the FlashSwapRouter contract, allowing an attacker to extract the reserve that should remain locked in the Vault. The root cause is that the internal flash‑swap routine encodes msg.sender as the recipient of the fee and later transfers the Ra amount to that address in __afterFlashswapSell, instead of sending it to the Vault (the contract owner). Because swapRaforDs is a public entry point with no access control, any user can invoke it, triggering the flash‑swap flow: the router calls __swapDsforRa, which invokes __flashSwap, which calls UniswapV2Pair.swap. The pair then executes uniswapV2Call, decodes the caller address, and finally __afterFlashswapSell transfers the Ra tokens to the caller. This sequence means the fee that the Vault expects to retain is handed to the transaction originator, effectively stealing the reserve. The impact is that the Vault’s liquidity can be drained completely, causing loss of funds for token holders and breaking the protocol’s accounting assumptions. The issue manifests when a user calls swapRaforDs and receives an unexpected amount of Ra; from the user’s perspective the UI may show a normal swap but the Vault balance drops to zero, contradicting the expectation that the fee stays in the protocol. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit by tracing the data flow through the flash‑swap functions and noticing that the fee transfer uses the caller variable. It is hard to notice because the transfer appears legitimate and the contract does not emit a warning that the fee is being sent out of the Vault. To remediate, the flash‑swap function should be rewritten to accept a designated recipient (the Vault owner) and ensure that the Ra fee is transferred to that address, or the logic should be changed so that the Vault itself receives the fee instead of the external caller. This class of bug is an improper handling of privileged assets in a flash‑swap, essentially a fee‑misallocation or fund‑misrouting vulnerability that violates the protocol’s business logic of retaining fees for liquidity provision.
summary: FlashSwapRouter::__swapDsforRa() is called as part of FlashSwapRouter::_swapRaforDs() whenever the reserve is sold and the resulting Ra is used to provide liquidity to the Vault by calling Vault::provideLiquidityWithFlashSwapFee(). However, if we follow the code, FlashSwapRouter::__swapDsforRa() calls FlashSwapRouter::__flashSwap(), which calls UniswapV2Pair::swap(). Then, the Uniswap pair calls uniswapV2Call(), which calls FlashSwapRouter::__afterFlashswapSell() and sends the Ra to the caller. Thus, the vault is providing a fee, but does not use the acquired funds to fund it, but the already existing Ra in the contract. The Ra meant for the liquidity fee is sent to the user calling FlashSwapRouter::_swapRaforDs(). In FlashSwapRouter.sol:124, FlashSwapRouter::__swapDsforRa() is called, which ultimately sends the Ra to the msg.sender. Internal pre-conditions None. External pre-conditions None. Attack Path 1. User calls swapRaforDs() and ends up receiving Ra which was intended for the Vault. Users can steal all reserve from the Vault.

title: Boost buyback burns incorrect
content: The vulnerability resides in the public _unfarmBuyBurn function of the V3AMO contract, which is intended to withdraw liquidity from a Uniswap V3 style pool, use the extracted USD to purchase boost tokens and then burn those tokens to support the peg. The function estimates the amount of liquidity to burn by reading the token reserves of the pool and applying a formula that assumes both tokens contribute equally to the totalLiquidity value, a calculation that is correct for Uniswap V2 but invalid for V3 pools. In V3 pools single‑sided liquidity positions are allowed, meaning a user can add only one of the two assets (for example only USD or only boost) while the totalLiquidity counter still increases. Because the reserves do not change proportionally, the reserve‑based formula can return zero liquidity when the pool contains asymmetric single‑sided positions, or it can dramatically overestimate the required liquidity when a large amount of boost‑only liquidity is present. When the computed liquidity is zero the transaction reverts, preventing the intended buy‑back. When the computation is too high the contract burns more LP tokens than necessary, uses excess USD to buy boost, and pushes the boost price above the intended peg. An attacker can deliberately add boost‑only liquidity, trigger the function, and then buy boost before the price spike and sell after, extracting profit from the artificial price inflation. The impact is that token holders may see the boost price deviate far above the peg, the protocol’s price‑stabilisation mechanism fails, and burned boost tokens are permanently lost, reducing overall token supply without the intended economic effect. The bug manifests whenever any user can supply single‑sided liquidity to the pool, which is allowed by the V3 design, and then any user (including the attacker) can call the public function. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the auditor noticed that the liquidity calculation referenced reserve balances rather than a price‑aware quote function, a mismatch that is subtle because the code compiles and appears similar to V2 implementations. It is hard to detect in testing because normal V2‑style pools would not expose the problem, and the function may only misbehave under specific liquidity configurations. The recommended remediation is to replace the reserve‑based estimate with a price‑quote based calculation, such as using the quoteSwap function to determine exactly how much USD must be swapped to reach the target peg, thereby eliminating reliance on reserve totals that are unreliable in V3 environments.
summary: The function _unfarmBuyBurn in the V3AMO contract is a public function open to everyone and calculates the amount of liquidity to burn from the pool. This function basically burns LP positions to take out liquidity and uses the usd to buy up boost tokens and burns them to raise the price of boost tokens. The issue is in the _unfarmBuyBurn function when it tries to estimate how much liquidity needs to be taken out. V3AMO.sol#L320-L326 As seen above, first the token reserves of the pool are checked. Then, the liquidity to be burnt is calculated from the difference of the reserves. liquidity = (totalLiquidity * (boostBalance - usdBalance)) / (boostBalance + usdBalance); liquidity = (liquidity * LIQUIDITY_COEFF) / FACTOR; However, this calculation is not valid for V3/CL pools. This is because in V3 pools, single sided liquidity is allowed which adds to the totalLiquidity count, but increases the reserves of only 1 token. If a user adds liquidity at a tick lower than the current price, they will be adding only usd to the pool. For example, lets say the price currently is below peg, at 0.9. Say there are 1000 boost and 900 usd tokens in the pool, similar to a V2 composition. Now, since its a V3 pool, a user can come in and add 100 usd to the pool at a price of 0.5. Since this price is lower than the spot price, only usd will be needed to open this position. Now, the total reserves of both boost and usd are 1000 each, so the calculated liquidity amount to be removed will be 0. Thus the liquidity calculated in the contract has absolutely no meaning since it uses the reserves to calculate it, which is not valid for V3 pools. In the best case scenario, this will cause the function to revert and not work. In the worst case scenario, the liquidity calculated will be overestimated and the price will be pushed up even above the peg price. This is possible if users add single sided boost to the pool, increasing the liquidity amount calculated without changing the price. In this case, the contract assets will be used to force the boost token above peg, and malicious actors can buy the boost token before and sell it after for a handy profit. The main cause is that liquidity is calculated from the reserves. This is not valid for V3, since it can have single sided liquidity, and thus the reserves does not serve as an indicator of price or in this case the deviation from the peg. Internal pre-conditions None External pre-conditions Any user can add boost-only liquidity to make the contract overestimate the amount of liquidity it needs to burn Attack Path Users can add boost-only liquidity to make the contract overestimate the amount of liquidity it needs to burn. When extra liquidity is burnt and extra boost is bought back and burnt, the price will be pushed up even above the peg price. Users can buy before trigerring this and sell after for profit. Price can be pushed above the peg price

title: V2AMO is not compatible with
content: The vulnerability concerns the incompatibility of the V2 Automated Market Operations (V2AMO) contract with the Aerodrome and Velodrome decentralized exchanges. The V2AMO implementation assumes a specific interface for both the gauge contract that distributes rewards and the router contract that performs token swaps. For the gauge, V2AMO expects three overloaded getReward functions, including one that accepts an address and an array of token addresses, while Aerodrome’s gauge only provides a single getReward(address) function. For the router, V2AMO calls a pairFor function that takes two token addresses and a stability flag, but Aerodrome’s router defines a poolFor function that additionally requires a factory address parameter. Because the V2AMO code calls functions that do not exist on the Aerodrome/Velodrome contracts, the calls revert at runtime. This mismatch prevents the V2AMO contract from claiming rewards from the gauge and from locating the correct liquidity pool for swaps, effectively breaking the core functionality of the AMO. Users attempting to deposit, withdraw, or claim rewards experience symptoms such as receiving no tokens, seeing their balances remain unchanged, or observing that reward claims return zero. The issue manifests whenever V2AMO interacts with Aerodrome or Velodrome pools, i.e., during reward harvesting or token swapping operations. The affected parties include liquidity providers, end‑users of the V2AMO service, and the protocol that relies on these DEX integrations for yield generation. The problem was discovered during a security audit that compared the documented interface expectations with the actual contract ABIs of Aerodrome and Velodrome. It can be hard to notice because the Solidity compiler does not flag mismatched external interfaces; the contract compiles successfully, and the failure only appears at execution time when external calls revert. To remediate the issue, the V2AMO contract must be updated to match the exact function signatures of the target DEXes: replace calls to getReward(address, address[]) with getReward(address) or implement a wrapper that conforms to the DEX’s interface, and modify router interactions to use poolFor with the required factory argument instead of pairFor. Aligning the interface definitions and adapting the call logic will restore compatibility, allowing rewards to be claimed and swaps to execute as intended, thereby preventing funds from becoming inaccessible and ensuring the protocol’s accounting assumptions remain valid.

title: V3AMO integration with V3 does not collect LP fees when burning liq- uidity. Found by pkqs90
content: The vulnerability is an omission of LP fee collection in the V3 fork used by the V3AMO integration when a liquidity provider burns their position through the unfarmBuyBurn flow. In the original UniswapV3 design the pool contract updates and stores accrued fees for each position and the burnAndCollect function both removes liquidity and transfers those fees to the caller. In the V3 fork the fee‑update logic that would normally add the earned fees to the position’s tokensOwed fields has been removed from Position.sol, and the protocol documentation states that all fees are now routed through a separate RewardsDistributor contract that requires a merkle‑proof claim. Consequently, when V3AMO calls burnAndCollect the function only burns liquidity and returns the underlying token amounts; the accrued LP fees remain locked inside the pool and are never transferred to the caller. From a user’s point of view the transaction appears successful – the Burn event is emitted and the expected token amounts are received – but the expected fee payout is missing, leading to a situation where “funds disappear” or “refund is zero” despite having earned fees. The issue manifests every time a V3AMO liquidity position is burned, affecting any liquidity provider that expects to receive their share of pool fees, and it also reduces the protocol’s revenue because fees are not accounted for or distributed. The problem was discovered during a manual audit by comparing the V3 implementation of burnAndCollect with the reference UniswapV3 code and noticing that the fee‑update step is absent, a subtle bug that can be overlooked because the function still executes without reverting and emits normal events. The bug belongs to the class of accounting or state‑update omissions where a critical side‑effect (fee accrual) is not performed, violating the business logic that LP fees should be collectible on burn. To remediate the issue the contract should be extended with a call to the RewardsDistributor (or a dedicated collectFees function) after burning, ensuring that any pending fees are claimed and transferred to the caller, thereby restoring the intended fee‑distribution semantics.

title: Liquidity is incorrectly calcu- lated during addLiquidity() for V3AMO, causing DoS. Found by 0x37, pkqs90, s1ce, spark1
content: An incorrect liquidity calculation is performed in the addLiquidity function of the V3AMO contract. The code computes the amount of liquidity to mint as (usdAmount * currentLiquidity) / IERC20Upgradeable(usd).balanceOf(pool). This formula assumes that the pool’s total liquidity is represented by a single price range, which is true for a simple Uniswap V2 pool but not for Uniswap V3 where multiple tick ranges can overlap the current price. Because the contract does not take the tickLower/tickUpper bounds into account, the computed liquidity can be dramatically inflated when the pool already contains an unbalanced position that holds a large amount of the BOOST token but very little USD. An attacker can create such a position at no cost to the protocol, because the BOOST/USD pair is designed to stay at a 1:1 peg and therefore does not suffer impermanent loss. By depositing a heavily BOOST‑biased LP, the attacker raises the pool’s total liquidity while the USD balance of the pool remains unchanged. Subsequent calls to addLiquidity use the inflated pool.liquidity() value, causing the formula to demand more USD than the caller has approved. The mint operation then reverts, effectively denying any further liquidity addition. This denial‑of‑service condition also breaks the mintSellFarm workflow that relies on successful liquidity provision, so users attempting to add liquidity or sell farmed tokens see their transactions fail or receive no tokens, even though they supplied the correct amount of USD. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the testers observed that a deliberately unbalanced LP caused addLiquidity to revert despite sufficient USD approval. The bug is subtle because the contract does not check that the USD balance of the pool matches the proportion of total liquidity, and the failure only appears when the pool already contains a skewed position. The proper fix is to replace the custom formula with the official Uniswap V3 LiquidityAmounts library, which calculates liquidity based on the current sqrt price, the lower and upper tick bounds, and the actual token amounts supplied. Using the library ensures that the required USD amount reflects the true price range and prevents an attacker from inflating the liquidity denominator. In summary, the vulnerability is a mis‑calculated liquidity amount that enables an attacker to DoS the addLiquidity function by adding an unbalanced LP, leading to failed transactions, loss of expected liquidity, and potential disruption of the protocol’s peg mechanism.

title: Anyone can steal all funds from the market
content: The vulnerability is an account‑health aggregation flaw that allows an attacker to create multiple pending intents (signed position orders) that are each evaluated in isolation when the market checks collateral requirements. The root cause is that the health‑check logic only adds the profit‑and‑loss (PnL) adjustment of the *current* intent to the account’s collateral, while ignoring the PnL impact of any other pending intents that belong to the same account. Because each intent is processed separately, an attacker can submit a series of intents with prices deliberately chosen near the protocol’s maximum price‑deviation limit. Individually each intent appears to keep the account healthy – the collateral calculation adds a small positive margin – but when all intents are settled together the cumulative price adjustments become large enough to drive the account’s collateral deeply negative. The market’s invariant that collateral must remain non‑negative is therefore bypassed, and the attacker can withdraw the inflated profit from the counter‑party account, effectively stealing all market funds. This can be exploited at any time because intents can be created by any user without pre‑conditions; the attack works within a single epoch so that the pending intents remain unsettled until the attacker triggers settlement. All participants of the market are affected: the protocol loses its collateral pool, users may see their balances drop to zero or become negative, and the UI may show no warning because the health check reports a healthy state for each individual intent. The issue was discovered during a security audit when testing invariant violations with multiple intents; it is hard to notice because each intent passes the health check, masking the aggregate risk. To fix the problem the protocol must aggregate the price adjustments of *all* pending guarantees (from the latest price up to the current one) and include the total adjustment when validating the margin requirement, ensuring that the account’s overall collateral reflects the combined effect of all pending intents.
summary:
When user opens position from signed intent, pending orders are created for 2 accounts (intent taker and maker) with user-specified price. Upon settlement, there is some pnl realized to both accounts due to difference of intent price and market price. The intent price is specified by the user and can be any number within the limits set by the protocols off the latest commited price. The issue is that this pnl is accounted for in account health only for one (current) intent. If there are multiple intents pending for the same account, then all the other intents are ignored and thus attacker can send multiple intents, each of which keeps account healthy, but all of them combined put account into highly negative collateral, which is ignored by health check. This allows attacker to withdraw inflated profit from the other account, stealing all funds from the market.
When account health is checked, collateral is adjusted for only current intent erennial-v2-update-3-panprog/blob/ac46a2fc8baf6c827ee20c69eecae66561a5c65f/pe rennial-v2/packages/perennial/contracts/types/Guarantee.sol#L71
All the other intents (at this, or previous pending orders) are ignored.
Internal Pre-conditions
None.
External Pre-conditions
None.
Attack Path
Since intents can be easily created by any user, there are no pre-conditions for the attack. The scenario is as following:
• Attacker deposits some collateral into account1 and account2 (for example, 40)
• Attacker signs intent with some position (like long 1) and a price which is much higher than latest oracle price, but inside the protocol's max price deviation limit (say, of 120 when current price is 100) from account1
• Attacker uses account2 to calls market.update with the signed intent from account1. This is accepted, as account1 collateral when checking update invariant is 40 + 1 * (100 - 120) = 40 - 20 = 20
• The same intent is signed again from account1 and account2 submits it again. This is accepted again, as account1 collateral when checking update invariant is again 40 + 1 * (100 - 120) = 40 - 20 = 20 (it only accounts the 2nd intent, ignoring the 1st intent). However, if this is settled (both intents), the collateral will be 40 + 2 * (100 - 120) = 40 - 40 = 0.
• The same intent is signed again from account1 and account2 submits it again. This is accepted again, as account1 collateral when checking update invariant is again 40 + 1 * (100 - 120) = 40 - 20 = 20 (it only accounts the 3rd intent, ignoring the 1st and the 2nd intents). However, if this is settled (all 3 intents), the collateral will be 40 + 3 * (100 - 120) = 40 - 60 = -20.
• This is repeated as many times as necessary (everything in the same epoch, so that all intents are not settled)
• After the settlement, sum of all intents causes account1 to be in highly negative collateral, while account2 will be in the same profit.
• Attacker withdraws all funds which market has.
All market collateral token balance is stolen.

title: InvariantLib uses current position for multiple times
content: The vulnerability stems from an inconsistency in how the market contract validates margin requirements during normal updates versus liquidation checks. In a normal update the library InvariantLib.validate calls a margin‑check function that uses the currentPosition – the position that includes pending changes for the current epoch – to determine whether the user’s collateral is sufficient. During a liquidation (when the protected flag is true) the same library instead uses the latestPosition – the position that was last committed before any pending changes – to perform the maintenance‑ratio check. Because currentPosition and latestPosition can differ substantially, a trader can reduce a position and withdraw collateral based on the pending (smaller) position while the liquidation logic still evaluates the larger, previously committed position. This mismatch allows a user to appear healthy to the update logic but instantly become under‑collateralised under the liquidation logic, leading to an unexpected liquidation. The attack scenario is straightforward: a user (or an attacker) reduces a long position, withdraws enough collateral to keep the reduced position marginally safe, and then either a third‑party liquidator or the attacker themselves triggers a liquidation. The liquidation check sees the old larger position, deems the account under‑maintained, and liquidates it, causing the user to lose the withdrawn collateral and any accrued trading fees. In a self‑liquidation variant the attacker can close the position completely, withdraw all collateral (the margin check passes because currentPosition becomes zero), and then immediately liquidate the now empty account, earning the liquidation bonus while the original account ends up in bad debt. The impact can be a loss of 1 % or more of the user’s funds, and if the liquidation bonus exceeds typical trading fees the attacker could repeatedly drain market funds through profit‑making self‑liquidations. The bug appears only when a position is changed and a liquidation is attempted in the same epoch; normal tests that evaluate each check in isolation may not reveal the problem, making it hard to notice. It was discovered during an audit by Sherlock through an invariant test that simulated a reduced position followed by a liquidation, exposing the discrepancy between the two checks. The issue violates the core accounting assumption that margin and maintenance checks should be based on the same position snapshot, breaking the expected relationship between collateral, position size, and safety ratios. To remediate, the margin check should be performed against the latest committed position plus any pending positive adjustments (or use the same snapshot as the liquidation check), and the liquidation maintenance check should use the identical position value as the normal update check, ensuring both paths evaluate the same collateral‑to‑position ratio.
summary:
In normal update, the InvariantLib.validate uses the currentPosition for margin check:
```solidity
if (
    !PositionLib.margined(
        updateContext.currentPositionLocal.magnitude(),
        context.latestOracleVersion,
        context.riskParameter,
        updateContext.collateralization,
        context.local.collateral.add(newGuarantee.priceAdjustment(context.latestOracleVersion.price)) // apply price override adjustment from intent if present
    )
) revert IMarket.MarketInsufficientMarginError();
```
However, during liquidation (protected = true), latestPosition is used for maintenence check:
```solidity
if (context.latestPositionLocal.maintained(
    context.latestOracleVersion,
    context.riskParameter,
    context.local.collateral
)) return false; // latest position is properly maintained
```
The latest position is position at the last commited price, while current position is expected position when price is commited for the current epoch (latest + pending). These are 2 totally different values. Usage of currentPosition in margined check means that user is allowed to withdraw collateral based on ”pending” position (which might still be invalidated). This is wrong by itself, but usage of latestPosition in liquidation maintenence check means that normal updates and liquidations are disconnected: perfectly fine normal update can easily cause unexpected immediate liquidation after the user withdraws collateral.
Incorrect usage of currentPosition in margined check in InvariantLib.validate: al-v2/packages/core/contracts/libs/InvariantLib.sol#L87-L93
Additionally, liquidation uses latestPosition in maintenence check: al-v2/packages/core/contracts/libs/InvariantLib.sol#L124-L128
Internal pre-conditions
• User reduces position and withdraws collateral, keeping healthy collateral for new (reduced) position.
External pre-conditions
None.
Attack Path
Happens by itself:
• User reduces position (e.g., from 10 to 5) and withdraws collateral, keeping enough to keep new reduced position healthy (e.g. withdrawing half of collateral).
• User account becomes immediately liquidatable and user is liquidated by any liquidator.
• Result: user is unfairly liquidated, losing liquidation and trading fees
User crafts self-liquidation to steal liquidation fees (can be profitable depending on trading fees and liquidation fee):
• Attacker opens position from account1
• Awaits settlement
• Attacker then closes full position from account1 and withdraws all collateral (allowed, since currentPosition == 0, so 0 collateral needed in margined check)
• Attacker immediately liquidates account1 from account2.
• Result: account1 is in bad debt, account2 earns liquidation fees.
If user is unfairly liquidated: easily 1%+ funds loss from liquidation. For example:
• Margin ratio is 1.2%, maintenence ratio is 1%
• Trading fee is 0.3%
• Asset price = 1000
• User has position size = 10, collateral = 200 (margin = 200 / (10*1000) = 2%)
• User reduces position size to 5 (fee = 5000*0.3% = 15), withdraws collateral = 95. Remaining collateral = 90. Margin = 95 / (5 * 1000) = 1.8%
• But the position is immediately liquidated (because maintenence for liquidation purpose = 95 / (10 * 1000) = 0.95%)
• User has position unfairly liquidated and loses fee of 15, so his loss is 15 / 90 = 17%
If liquidation bonus for liquidator is higher than trading fees from the position, then attacker can repeatedly self-liquidate until all market funds are withdrawn via liquidation fees.

title: Intent orders are guaranteed to execute
content: The vulnerability originates from the market’s handling of Intent orders, which are designed to be guaranteed – meaning they cannot be invalidated even if the price for the corresponding epoch has not yet been committed. Because the contract treats these orders as having zero invalidation risk, it allows a user to open an Intent order and immediately close it, then withdraw the full amount of collateral without any fee deduction. The root cause is that trade fees are recorded as pending and are only applied to an account’s collateral when the epoch price is finally committed, a step that occurs after the withdrawal. During the margin and maintenance checks the pending fees are not subtracted from the guaranteed Intent orders, so the invariant that collateral must cover all liabilities is violated. An attacker can exploit this by funding two accounts, using one to create Intent orders that open and close a position, and using the second to execute those intents. After the intents are executed the attacker withdraws all collateral from both accounts, receiving back the exact amount deposited because the fees are still pending and ignored. When the epoch price is later committed, the pending fees are finally added to the attacker’s accounts, which now have zero collateral, creating a bad‑debt situation. The protocol then distributes those fees to the admin and a portion becomes claimable by the referrer; because the attacker also controls the referrer address, they can claim the newly generated fee amount. The impact is a complete loss of market funds: the attacker walks away with the deposited collateral plus the claimed referral fees, while the market is left with an abandoned account that owes the unpaid fees. This condition occurs whenever Intent orders are used to open and close positions within the same epoch before the price is committed, and there are no additional pre‑conditions required. All participants of the market – traders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the integrity of the fee accounting and collateral guarantees is broken. The issue was discovered during a systematic invariant‑checking audit that simulated complex order flows and observed that the collateral invariant could be violated after a price commit. It is hard to notice because the contract behaves correctly for normal orders and the fee deduction only happens later, making the exploit invisible at the time of withdrawal. The proper mitigation is to include pending fees from guaranteed Intent orders in the collateral‑maintenance calculation, effectively subtracting those fees before allowing a full withdrawal, thereby preserving the invariant that collateral always covers outstanding liabilities.
summary:
In normal update, all orders are pending and might be invalidated if invalid price is commited for the corresponding epoch (no pricefeed available or price commit timeout). However, when Intents are used, these orders are guaranteed to be accepted (invalidation = 0 for them). In particular, this feature allows to open and close orders via Intents even when open order epoch is not commited yet.
The issue is that the fees for the orders are pending and not included in collateral calculations. At the same time, since Intent orders are guaranteed, user can open them, close them and withdraw all collateral ignoring any pending fees. Then, after the price for the corresponding epoch is commited, the fees are added to user collateral (which is 0), thus user goes into bad debt. These fees taken are distributed to admin and part of them becomes claimable by the referrer.
This means that attacker can open, close, withdraw all collateral at 0 cost, and after epoch price is commited, the referrer (also controlled by attacker) can claim part of the fees. Essentially, attacker steals funds from the market via claiming fees which become bad debt of the abandoned account.
Trade fees are only applied to account collateral when advancing checkpoints (which happens after the epoch price is commited): al-v2/packages/core/contracts/libs/CheckpointLib.sol#L84-L92
At the same time, when all pending orders are guaranteed (from Intents, invalidation == 0), user is allowed to fully close the position, even if the opening is still pending (pending negative - which is pending closure - can exceed latest commited position): al-v2/packages/core/contracts/libs/InvariantLib.sol#L35-L38
Internal pre-conditions
None.
External pre-conditions
None.
Attack Path
1. Attacker funds account1 and account2
2. Attacker uses account1 to create 2 Intents to open and then close position with account3 as originator and referral.
3. Attacker uses account2 to execute both intents (to open and then immediately close position)
4. Attacker withdraws all collateral from account1 and account2, getting the same amount he has deposited, because fees are still pending and ignored at this time. execute the attack
5. Attacker waits until the epoch price is commited
6. Attacker call market.claimFee(account3) to get referral fees from the orders. Result: Attacker can steal all funds from the market.
All market funds are stolen by the Attacker.

title: When account is liquidated (protected)
content: The contract contains an invariant violation in the liquidation routine that allows a liquidator to increase, rather than decrease, an account's position when the account is in a pending‑close state. The original code enforced that a liquidation could only reduce the position size, but the check was removed and replaced with a condition that only verifies that the pending negative amount equals the magnitude of the latest position. When pendingLocal.neg() == latestPositionLocal.magnitude(), the function returns true and proceeds without any further validation. Because the liquidation path skips all collateral and position‑size checks, an attacker can trigger liquidation while the account’s position is pending closure, then supply an arbitrarily large positive delta that pushes the position up to the maximum representable value (2**62‑1). This artificial inflation of the position breaks market accounting: any subsequent price change creates an enormous profit or loss for the liquidated account and for counterparties, allowing the attacker to withdraw essentially all market funds. The exploit works when an account becomes liquidatable, the attacker closes the position (creating the pending zero‑cross condition), and then calls the liquidation function with a huge increase. After the price for the epoch is committed, the attacker can immediately submit a new price, realize the massive profit, and withdraw the collateral from either the attacked account or a counter‑party. The issue was discovered during a security audit by reviewing the invariant library and noticing the missing monotonicity check. It is hard to notice because liquidation is expected to shrink positions, so developers may not anticipate that the function could be called with a positive delta, and the large numeric overflow does not raise an error until accounting mismatches appear. The vulnerability belongs to the class of improper state validation in privileged operations, specifically a missing enforcement of a “only‑decrease” rule during liquidation. From a user perspective the symptoms are dramatic: the user’s collateral balance can become negative, the reported position size jumps to an astronomically large number, and expected refunds disappear, leading to the perception that funds have vanished. The correct mitigation is to re‑introduce a check that ensures any liquidation order can only reduce the absolute position size and to retain the usual collateral and size validations during liquidation, thereby preserving the market’s accounting invariants.
summary:
Previously, there was a check which enforced position to only decrease during liquidation. However, the check is gone and in the current code only the condition of pending.negative == latestPosition.magnitude:
```solidity
if (!context.pendingLocal.neg().eq(context.latestPositionLocal.magnitude())) return false; // no pending zero-cross, liquidate with full close
```
If account (before liquidation) is already in this state (for example, user has closed his position fully, but it's still pending - in this case pendingLocal.neg() will equal latestPositionLocal.magnitude() before the liquidation), then liquidator can increase position, and since it doesn't influence neither latest position nor pending negative (closing), it's allowed. Moreover, all collateral and position size checks are ignored during liquidation, so account position can be increased to any value, including max that can be stored: 2**62 - 1. If this is done, all market accounting is messed up as any slight price change will create huge profit or loss for makers and the liquidated account. This can be abused by attacker to steal all market funds.
Incorrect check when liquidating the account (lack of enforcement to only reduce the position): al-v2/packages/core/contracts/libs/InvariantLib.sol#L121
Internal pre-conditions
None.
External pre-conditions
None.
Attack Path
1. Attacker opens tiny long position from account1 with minimal collateral, and tiny maker position from account2.
2. Attacker awaits for the position to become liquidatable. He can also force liquidation himself, as described in another issue (close position and withdraw collateral, then position becomes liquidatable), but this is not necessary, just makes it easier.
3. Just before the position becomes liquidatable, attacker closes it fully (so that it's pending close), making pending.negative == latestPosition.magnitude
4. Attacker liquidates his position, increasing it to 2**62 - 1 or any other huge amount.
5. Attacker awaits commited price for the epoch of position increase (or commits himself).
6. Immediately after that, attacker commits any other price different from the previous commit with timestamp 1 second after the previous commit.
7. In the same transaction, attacker withdraws all market collateral either from account1 or account2 (depending on which account ends up in a huge profit due to price change). Result: Attacker steal all funds from the market.
All market funds are stolen by the Attacker.

title: USDC rewards will not be distributed if _-
content: The contract’s reward‑distribution logic suffers from a precision loss when the reward token has fewer than 18 decimal places, such as USDC (6 decimals). The function that updates per‑token rewards computes an increment as rewardRate × time × 1e18 divided by the total amount of SYMM staked, using integer division. Because rewardRate is expressed in USDC units, the product rewardRate × time is too small to survive the division by a large 1e18‑scaled supply, so the division truncates to zero on every call. Consequently, the perTokenStored variable never increases even though the lastUpdated timestamp moves forward, meaning that no USDC rewards are ever accrued for stakers. This condition is triggered whenever the update routine (_updateRewardsStates) is called frequently – for example, on every block via deposit, withdraw, claim or notifyRewardAmount – while the reward amount is modest relative to the staked supply. An attacker can deliberately call deposit or withdraw with a minimal amount each block, forcing the contract to execute the rounding‑to‑zero calculation repeatedly and preventing any reward accumulation. The impact is that legitimate stakers see their expected USDC rewards disappear; the contract holds the reward balance but users receive zero when they claim, effectively locking the funds. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the reviewer simulated a week‑long reward schedule of 1 209.6 USDC against a total SYMM stake of 1 000 000 e18 and observed that perTokenStored remained unchanged after many updates. The bug is subtle because the contract state appears to be updating (timestamps change) and no explicit error is thrown, making it easy to miss in casual testing. To remediate, the reward calculation should be up‑scaled, for example by introducing a 1e12 multiplier before the division and then down‑scaling when rewards are claimed, or by using a fixed‑point arithmetic library that matches the reward token’s decimal precision. This adjustment restores the ability of low‑decimal tokens to accrue rewards correctly, aligning the contract’s accounting with user expectations that a claimed reward should reflect the accrued amount rather than zero. From a user’s perspective the UI may show an increasing reward balance, yet the actual transfer on claim returns zero USDC, violating the business logic that staking should generate proportional returns.
summary:
```solidity
acts/staking/SymmStaking.sol#L402-L423
_updateRewardsStates can be triggered as often as each block (2 seconds) via deposit/withdraw/claim/notifyRewardAmount
```
e.g. if there's 1209.6e6 USDC rewards for one week (604800 seconds)
```solidity
acts/staking/SymmStaking.sol#L374
rate = 1209_600000 / 604800 = 2000 ”usdc units” per second
```
```solidity
acts/staking/SymmStaking.sol#L194-L202
if SYMM total staked supply is 1_000_000e18 (~26560 usd), and we call deposit each block, then perTokenStored will be increased by:
2 * 2000 * 1e18 / 1_000_000e18 = 4_000 / 1_000_000 = 0
```
Therefore, perTokenStored will not increase, but lastUpdated will be increased, therefore users will not receive any USDC rewards for staking.
In this particular example, triggering _updateRewardsStates once in 249 blocks would be sufficient, as it would still result in rewards rounding down to zero.
Lack of upscaling for tokens with less than 18 decimals for reward calculations.
Attack Path
1. Attacker calls deposit/withdraw/notifyRewardAmount with any non-zero amount every block (or less often as long as the calculation will still round down to zero)
High: stakers do not receive rewards in tokens with low decimals (e.g. USDC, USDT).

title: Attacker can DoS user withdrawals at no cost
content: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that arises when a user’s lockup record array grows without bound and the withdraw routine iterates over the entire array in a single transaction. Each time a user calls deposit or mint, the contract pushes a new LockedShares struct onto a per‑address array that stores the amount and an expiry timestamp. Because the deposit function accepts an arbitrary receiver address, an attacker can repeatedly call deposit on behalf of a victim, adding a large number of entries to the victim’s array while spending only the minimal amount required for the deposit. When the victim later attempts to withdraw or redeem, the internal updateUnlockedShares function loops over the whole userLockedShares array to unlock any expired entries and then calls a cleanup routine. The loop has no upper bound on the number of iterations, so a sufficiently large array causes the transaction to exceed the block gas limit and revert with an out‑of‑gas error. As a result the victim’s withdrawal fails, their assets remain locked in the contract, and the user sees no funds transferred – the UI may show a “withdraw failed” message or simply no change in balance. The issue occurs only when the contract allows deposits for arbitrary receivers and when the lockup period is non‑zero, because the expiry check is performed inside the loop. It affects any user whose lockup array has been artificially inflated, and an attacker can target many users with negligible cost beyond the deposits themselves. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that examined the flow of deposit and withdraw functions and identified the unbounded iteration as a potential gas‑limit bottleneck. The bug is hard to notice in normal operation because the array size remains small under typical usage, and the out‑of‑gas failure only appears after the array has been deliberately bloated. Conceptually, the flaw belongs to the class of unbounded loop DoS vulnerabilities in state‑ful contracts. The proper mitigation is to limit the number of iterations performed in a single call, for example by introducing a maximum‑entries parameter, processing entries in batches, or redesigning the lockup storage to avoid linear scans. By capping the loop or using a more gas‑efficient data structure, the contract can ensure that withdrawals remain executable even if an attacker attempts to fill the array.

title: Anyone who is approving BlueprintV5 can have their funds drained
content: The vulnerability is a public token transfer function that can be invoked by any address to move ERC20 tokens from an arbitrary user who has previously granted an allowance to the BlueprintV5 contract. The function payWithERC20 accepts a token address, an amount, a fromAddress and a toAddress, performs only basic sanity checks (different addresses, non‑zero amount) and then calls token.safeTransferFrom(fromAddress,toAddress,amount). Because the function is declared public and does not verify that fromAddress is the caller or that the caller is authorized, an attacker can supply a victim’s address as fromAddress, a token that the victim has approved for the BlueprintV5 contract, and the attacker’s own address as toAddress. When the victim has previously called BlueprintV5.addPaymentAddress and approved the contract to spend a sufficient amount of the token, the attacker’s call will succeed and the token contract will transfer the approved amount from the victim to the attacker. This drains the victim’s funds without any on‑chain indication that a payment was intended, leading to a loss of tokens, broken accounting, and loss of trust in the protocol. The issue manifests when a user interacts with BlueprintV5 (for example, creating an agent) and grants an allowance to the contract; later, any external actor can trigger the public function and steal the approved balance. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that inspected function visibility and noticed that a payment helper was unintentionally exposed. It can be hard to notice because the function appears to be a harmless utility for internal payments, and the token transfer itself follows the standard ERC20 safeTransferFrom pattern, which is normally safe when used correctly. To remediate, the function should be changed to internal or private, or protected by an access‑control modifier that restricts calls to the contract itself or to authorized roles. Additionally, the implementation should enforce that fromAddress equals msg.sender or that the caller is explicitly authorized, thereby preventing arbitrary third‑party transfers. Conceptually, this is an authorization bypass in a token transfer helper, a class of bugs where public functions expose privileged operations without proper checks, leading to unintended token drains and accounting failures.

title: MarketMaker.sol is vulnerable to inflation attacks
content: The vulnerability is an inflation attack that stems from the way the MarketMaker contract calculates the number of liquidity shares to mint when a user adds collateral. The function uses a ceiling division (ceilDiv) to compute sharesMinted as (collateralAdded * totalShares) divided by poolValue, rounding up to the next integer. Because the result is always rounded up, a depositor is guaranteed to receive at least one share even when the amount of collateral added is far smaller than the current pool value. An attacker can exploit this by first inflating the poolValue through a large collateral donation, then repeatedly depositing the minimum possible amount (one wei). Each tiny deposit mints one share, which dramatically increases the attacker’s share balance while diluting the proportionate ownership of existing liquidity providers. After accumulating a large number of shares, the attacker can withdraw the inflated share balance when the pool closes, extracting profit at the expense of honest participants. The attack works only when the pool already contains shares (totalShares > 0) and the poolValue is non‑zero, conditions that are normal for an active market. The issue was discovered during a security audit when the reviewer noticed the use of ceilDiv and recognised that guaranteeing a minimum share creates a rounding‑up bias. The bug is hard to notice because the minting of a single share for a one‑wei deposit appears harmless in isolation, and the rounding behavior is subtle. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are a sudden decrease in the value of their LP tokens, unexpected loss of funds after a withdrawal, or seeing that their share of the pool has been diluted without any obvious transaction. This class of bug belongs to share‑inflation or rounding‑up vulnerabilities that break the accounting assumptions of proportional ownership. The recommended mitigation is to replace the ceiling division with a floor division or to adopt a virtual offset mechanism as described in the OpenZeppelin ERC‑4626 reference, thereby preventing the guarantee of a minimum share and eliminating the inflation vector.

title: After migration, the old MarketFundingPool contract will fail to correctly distribute fees to new MarketFundingPool
content: The vulnerability originates from an accounting mismatch that appears after the protocol migrates liquidity from an old MarketFundingPool to a newly deployed MarketFundingPool. The old pool’s internal hook _beforeTokenTransfer is designed to claim any fees that have accrued while a liquidity provider (LP) holds LP tokens. When a user transfers LP tokens – which includes the operation of claiming shares in the new pool – the hook calls withdrawFees for the original holder. WithdrawFees sends the calculated fee amount to the old MarketFundingPool contract and expects the parent MarketMaker contract to be notified via its _afterFeesWithdrawn function so that the fee can be marked as paid and removed from the pool’s accounting. In the migrated system the new MarketFundingPool does not implement its own _afterFeesWithdrawn that forwards the notification to MarketMaker. Consequently, when fees are sent to the old pool they are never confirmed, and the MarketMaker’s internal accounting still believes those fees are outstanding. The unconfirmed fees are then redistributed across all remaining shares in the old pool, effectively diluting the yield of the user who initiated the transfer. From a user’s perspective the expected outcome – receiving the exact amount of accrued fees when moving to the new pool – does not happen; instead the user sees a lower or zero fee payout and may notice that their balance or expected yield is reduced unexpectedly. The bug manifests only when LP tokens are transferred after the migration event, meaning any liquidity provider who claims or moves their position will be affected. The issue was uncovered during a manual audit that examined the token transfer hook and the fee‑withdrawal flow, noticing that the call chain to MarketMaker#_afterFeesWithdrawn was missing in the new contract. Because the fee transfer itself succeeds, the problem can be subtle and may not raise an immediate error, making it hard to detect without inspecting the accounting state. The appropriate remediation is to implement the missing _afterFeesWithdrawn function in the new MarketFundingPool and ensure it forwards the fee‑withdrawn notification to MarketMaker#_afterFeesWithdrawn, thereby reconciling the fee accounting and preventing unintended redistribution of fees across other shareholders. This fix restores the intended business logic that fees earned by a specific LP holder are paid out to that holder alone, preserving the integrity of yield calculations and user expectations.

title: Precision error in _fetchTWAP causes vesting to be free after initial lockdrop period
content: The vulnerability originates from an incorrect conversion of the time‑weighted average price (TWAP) returned by the Uniswap V3 oracle. The oracle provides the price in a 64.96 fixed‑point format (Q64.96). The contract first adjusts the price for the difference in token decimals and then attempts to convert the value to a human‑readable number by dividing the adjusted _priceX96 by 2**96. Because the division is performed using integer arithmetic, any fractional component is discarded, resulting in a price that has zero decimal places instead of the expected 18‑decimal precision. The vesting logic later uses this truncated price to calculate how many stable‑asset units a user must provide to claim their vested BLB tokens. With the price effectively rounded down to an integer (often 1 or a very small number), the required payment becomes negligible, allowing any participant to vest the full allocation immediately after the initial lock‑drop period without spending the intended amount of stable assets. This flaw can be exploited simply by invoking the vest function after the lock‑drop ends; the transaction succeeds, the user’s stable‑asset balance remains unchanged, and the user receives the full token amount for free. The impact is a direct loss of value for the protocol, as the economic model that ties token vesting to a market‑based price is bypassed, leading to uncontrolled token distribution and potential market manipulation. The issue manifests only after the lock‑drop period when the vesting routine calls _fetchTWAP; before that, the price is not used for token release. All users, as well as the protocol’s treasury, are affected because the protocol’s accounting assumptions—namely that the price has 18‑decimal precision—are violated. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the price‑conversion code and compared the expected decimal scaling with the actual implementation. It is subtle because the returned price value appears plausible at a glance, and the UI may display a price without indicating the loss of precision, making the bug easy to overlook. The appropriate remediation is to perform the conversion with full‑precision arithmetic, for example by using FullMath.mulDiv to scale the Q64.96 value to 18 decimals before dividing by 2**96, as shown in the recommended code snippet. This ensures that the price retains its fractional component and that the vesting calculation enforces the correct payment amount, restoring the intended economic guarantees of the protocol.

title: Donations to MarketMaker will completely freeze all buy/sell capability of market
content: An assertion in the market‑maker contract checks that the internal token reserve is exactly zero before any pricing calculation is performed.
