The function getTargetBalance reads the current token balance (reserves()) and executes assert(localReserves == 0). Under normal operation the contract never holds a stray token because all incoming collateral is either allocated to liquidity or immediately sent back to the parent pool. However, the Ethereum token standard allows any address to transfer tokens to the contract without invoking its own logic. If an attacker or even an honest user sends a single wei of the underlying token directly to the MarketMaker contract, the reserve becomes non‑zero, the assert fails, and the transaction reverts. Because buyFor (and the analogous sell function) call getTargetBalance at the beginning of each trade, the revert aborts the entire trade flow, preventing any further buy or sell operations. The market therefore becomes effectively frozen: users attempting to place a bet receive a transaction failure, balances appear unchanged, and no refunds can be processed. The impact is a denial‑of‑service attack that can be launched with negligible cost, affecting all participants of the affected market, including the protocol’s liquidity providers and end‑users who expect to be able to trade. The vulnerability was discovered during a manual audit that examined the assumptions behind the reserve accounting logic. It is subtle because the assert looks harmless and the contract otherwise never manipulates the token balance directly, so a simple external token transfer is easy to overlook. The bug belongs to the class of “invariant violation caused by uncontrolled external state” or “assert‑based denial‑of‑service”. To remediate, the hard assert should be removed or replaced with a safe handling path that either ignores unexpected residual tokens or transfers them back to the parent pool before proceeding. Proper accounting should treat any non‑zero reserve as a recoverable surplus rather than a fatal error, ensuring that the market remains operational even if stray tokens are sent to it.

title: Frontrunning or reorg attacks can be used to corrupt initial pricing data to drain funds from MarketMaker
content: The vulnerability is an initialization-time price manipulation bug in the permissionless function prepareCondition. The function is designed to be callable by anyone to create a new condition and optionally set a price oracle address together with a packedPrices array that represents the initial market prices. Because there is no access control and the contract trusts the caller-provided pricing data, an attacker can front-run the legitimate transaction that prepares the condition or exploit a chain reorganization to replace the block containing the correct initialization. By submitting their own prepareCondition call before the intended one, the attacker can supply a priceOracle address they control and a packedPrices array whose values sum to the required divisor but are otherwise chosen to make the outcome prices extremely low (for example, setting most slots to zero). The contract accepts these values, emits the usual events, and records the corrupted pricing data. When users later interact with the market maker they see options priced at near-zero cost, purchase large quantities, and the liquidity pool is drained when the market settles because the pool had allocated far too little capital for the positions. From the user’s perspective the symptoms are unexpected zero-cost purchases, balances that suddenly drop to zero after a trade, or refunds that never arrive. The issue occurs only on the first preparation of a condition (when payoutNumerators[conditionId] is empty) and only when the caller also provides a non-zero priceOracle argument. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the idempotent nature of prepareCondition and noticed that price data is set without any verification of the oracle’s authenticity. The bug is hard to notice because the function emits legitimate events and the price validation only checks that the sum of packedPrices equals a constant divisor, which a malicious payload can satisfy. Conceptually the flaw belongs to the class of front-running or re-org attacks on permissionless initialization routines that allow arbitrary price injection. The recommended mitigation is to remove the ability to set initial pricing from the permissionless function, enforce that only a trusted price oracle can write prices after the condition is prepared, or add proper access control and commit-reveal mechanisms to ensure the integrity of the initial market data. By doing so the protocol prevents attackers from corrupting the initial pricing and protects users and liquidity providers from unexpected fund loss.

title: Payments for coupons to Booster are irretrievable
content: The vulnerability consists of a permanent loss of tokens when a user purchases a coupon through the Booster contract. The contract calculates a discounted price (couponPrice minus discount) and checks that the user’s token balance is at least this discounted amount, but it then calls safeTransferFrom with the full couponPrice instead of the discounted price. Because the contract does not implement any function to withdraw or forward the received tokens, the transferred amount becomes locked inside the contract forever. This occurs whenever a user invokes the buy function, under the condition that the contract’s code does not provide a recovery mechanism for the stored tokens. The root cause is a mismatch between the amount validated (discounted price) and the amount actually transferred (full price), combined with the absence of any withdrawal path for the contract’s token holdings. An attacker does not need to actively exploit the bug; any honest user who attempts to buy a coupon will unintentionally send more tokens than required and will never be able to retrieve them, leading to a reduction of their balance with no corresponding benefit. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a successful purchase event, but the user’s wallet balance drops by the full coupon price and no refund or further interaction can restore the lost funds, creating the symptom of “funds disappear” or “my balance is zero after buying a coupon”. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the Booster.sol source code, where the transfer line was examined and the lack of any withdrawal function was noted. The problem can be hard to notice because the transaction does not revert and the event emitted suggests a normal operation, masking the underlying accounting error. Conceptually the fix is to align the transferred amount with the validated discounted price and to provide a controlled mechanism—such as a configurable admin address or a withdrawal function—to allow the contract owner or a designated fee collector to retrieve the tokens, thereby preventing permanent token lock‑up and restoring the intended economic flow of the protocol.

title: BufferBinaryPool can permanently lock funds on early exercise
content: The vulnerability is an accounting mismatch that occurs when a binary option is exercised before its expiration. The contract calculates a profit based on a Black‑Scholes formula and then calls the pool’s send function with the profit amount. Inside the pool, the amount transferred to the user is also used to reduce the internal locked amount and premium counters. When the calculated profit is smaller than the total amount that was originally locked for the option, only the profit portion is unlocked while the remainder stays recorded as locked but is never transferred out. This mismatch means that a portion of the users’ deposited funds becomes permanently inaccessible to liquidity providers. The bug is triggered only in the early‑exercise branch (option.expiration > closingTime) where the price‑dependent profit can be less than the locked amount. It was discovered during a manual audit that compared the payout logic with the state updates in BufferBinaryPool. The issue is subtle because the transaction succeeds and the user receives a partial payout, so there is no revert or obvious error; the leftover locked balance is hidden from the UI and appears only in internal accounting, making it easy to overlook. The impact is that funds disappear from the pool’s withdrawable balance, reducing available liquidity and potentially harming LPs who cannot reclaim their capital. To fix the problem, the send routine should always clear the full locked amount and associated premium for the option, regardless of the actual payout, ensuring that the internal accounting matches the external transfer. This class of bug falls under partial‑unlock or accounting‑state inconsistency errors, where business logic assumes that the amount unlocked equals the amount transferred, violating the protocol’s expectation that exercising an option returns the full locked collateral or at least releases it for future withdrawals.

title: Market direction signature can be abused if privateKeeperMode is disabled
content: The vulnerability concerns the way market direction is verified in the BufferRouter contract when an option is exercised. The contract expects a cryptographic signature supplied by the option opener that declares the market direction (e.g., up or down). This signature is only checked at the moment of exercise, and the verification logic is gated by a flag called privateKeeperMode. When privateKeeperMode is disabled, the signature is not bound to the original trade creation and can be supplied, altered, or omitted by the user at a later time. As a result, a malicious user can manipulate the declared direction after the trade has been queued. Specifically, the attacker can (1) submit a direction that guarantees a winning outcome by changing it just before exercise, or (2) withhold the direction signature entirely, causing the contract to reject the exercise and leaving the liquidity‑provider (LP) funds locked indefinitely because the unlock logic never proceeds. The root cause is the reliance on a mutable off‑chain signature without a commitment scheme that ties the direction to the trade at the time of opening, combined with the lack of a restrictive keeper mode that would otherwise enforce proper authority. Exploitation occurs when the attacker opens a trade, then either submits a falsified direction signature or simply does not provide any signature when the exercise transaction is attempted. The impact is twofold: the attacker can secure a guaranteed profit by forcing the market direction to match their position, and honest LPs may see their capital frozen in the pool with no way to retrieve it until the contract is upgraded or an admin intervenes. This condition manifests only when privateKeeperMode is turned off; with the mode enabled, only authorized keepers could trigger the verification, preventing the user‑controlled abuse. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the BufferRouter source code, where the verification call Validator.verifyMarketDirection was observed to rely solely on a signature supplied at exercise time. The problem is subtle because the contract emits a failure event ("Router: Wrong market direction") but does not revert or unlock funds, making the lock appear as a normal failure rather than a malicious lock‑up. To remediate, the protocol should replace the runtime signature check with a commitment scheme: store a hash of the direction combined with a random salt when the trade is queued, and require the opener to reveal the salt and direction at closure, verifying the hash. This binds the direction to the trade immutably and prevents post‑hoc changes or omission. In generic terms, the bug belongs to the class of signature‑based authority misuse where verification is deferred and not cryptographically bound to the original state, leading to logical inconsistencies and fund‑locking vulnerabilities. From a user’s perspective, the symptoms include trades that always succeed for the opener regardless of market movement, LP balances that suddenly become zero or remain unchanged despite expected withdrawals, and error messages indicating a wrong market direction while funds stay locked. Expectations that a trade will be settled fairly are violated, and the accounting assumptions that each exercised option releases the corresponding liquidity are broken.

title: closeAnytime timestamp is never validated against current timestamp
content: The vulnerability consists of a missing validation of the exercise timestamp supplied to the option unlocking routine. When a user calls the router to exercise an option, the contract forwards a timestamp value taken from the keeper’s signed data directly into the options contract without checking that the value is close to the blockchain’s current time. Because the timestamp is not compared against block.timestamp, an attacker or a malicious keeper can provide an arbitrary past timestamp, causing the option to be considered exercised at a time when the underlying price would yield a higher payoff. This flaw originates from the router’s trust in external signed data and the absence of a guard clause that enforces a reasonable time window. Exploitation is straightforward: the attacker crafts a transaction that calls the unlock function with a deliberately older timestamp, causing the payoff calculation to use a more favorable price snapshot. The impact is that the option holder can obtain an inflated payout, effectively draining excess funds from the protocol’s liquidity pool and breaking the intended risk‑reward balance. The condition under which it occurs is any scenario where the private‑keeper mode is disabled, allowing public users to submit arbitrary timestamps. All participants who rely on the protocol’s fair pricing – option buyers, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the accounting assumptions about time‑based settlement are violated. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of BufferRouter.sol where the code path for early exercise was examined and the timestamp parameter was found to be passed unchecked. Because the contract does not emit any warning or revert on unusual timestamps, the bug can remain hidden; the UI may simply show a successful exercise with an unexpectedly high profit, making it difficult to spot without reviewing the source. The proper remediation is to add a validation step that requires the supplied timestamp to be within an acceptable margin of the current block timestamp, for example by asserting timestamp >= block.timestamp - delta and timestamp <= block.timestamp + delta, or by discarding external timestamps altogether and using block.timestamp directly. This class of bug is a time‑validation or oracle‑timestamp integrity issue, where the contract trusts an external time value without verification, leading to accounting errors such as “funds disappear” or “refund calculation error” when the protocol’s internal accounting no longer matches the expected temporal logic. From a user’s perspective the symptom may be that exercising an option yields a profit that seems too good to be true, or conversely that a claimed exercise results in no payout because the contract rejected the request after a later hard‑fork or timestamp mismatch. The discrepancy between the expected behavior (exercise at current time) and the actual behavior (exercise at arbitrary past time) breaks the business logic that options should be settled based on the price at the moment of exercise.

title: closeAnyTime timestamp is never validated against pricing timestamp
content: The vulnerability originates from the early‑exercise path of an option where the contract calls the unlock function with a timestamp taken directly from the pricing data (publisherSignInfo.timestamp) without any comparison to the timestamp that was originally signed in the closeAnytime request. Because the contract never validates that the two timestamps match, an attacker can supply a forged closeAnytime signature that contains an arbitrary timestamp. When the unlock call is executed, the pricing oracle is queried for the price at the attacker‑chosen timestamp, which may be dramatically different from the real time at which the holder intended to close the position. Consequently the option may be settled at an unfavorable price, causing the holder to receive less payout than expected or even to lose the entire position. The flaw is triggered whenever an option is exercised early via the closeAnytime function; it does not depend on the amount of the option or the specific asset. Users, option holders, and any keepers that interact with the contract are affected because the financial outcome of the settlement can be manipulated. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the flow of data between the signature verification and the pricing oracle and noticed the missing equality check. It is subtle because the transaction does not revert and the UI may still display the correct price feed, making the discrepancy appear as a normal loss rather than a contract bug. To remediate the problem the contract should enforce that the timestamp embedded in the closeAnytime signature is identical to the timestamp of the pricing data used for settlement, or at least that the two timestamps are within a short, predefined window. Adding an explicit require statement that compares the two values before calling unlock will prevent replay or manipulation of timestamps and restore the intended accounting guarantees of the protocol.
summary:
[BufferRouter.sol#L248-L258](https://github.com/Buffer-Finance/Buffer-Protocol-v2_5/blob/84b6060b4447b2550de595202e8820c7f515988b/contracts/core/BufferRouter.sol#L248-L258)
```solidity
    try
        optionsContract.unlock(
            params.optionId,
            params.closingPrice,
            publisherSignInfo.timestamp,
            params.isAbove
        )
    {} catch Error(string memory reason) {
        emit FailUnlock(params.optionId, params.targetContract, reason);
        continue;
    }
```
When an option is exercised early, it uses the timestamp of the pricing data without ever checking the timestamp of the closeAnytime signature. This can lead to 2 potential issues:
1) The user may receive less than expected due to the actual exercise timestamp being different than when they signed
2) If private keeper mode is disabled then transactions may be intercepted and the signature used by someone else to close the position with a much different timestamp

title: Sending child shares before burning shares allow reentrancy vulnerability in ParentFundingPool#removeChildShares
content: The vulnerability is a reentrancy flaw that occurs when a child share token is transferred to a user before the contract has finished updating its internal accounting and burning the corresponding shares. In the ParentFundingPool contract, the function removeChildShares first updates several state variables such as totalChildValueLocked and valueHighPoint, then calls childPool.safeTransfer to send the child shares to the caller, and only afterwards burns the parent shares with _burnSharesOf. The safeTransfer triggers an ERC1155 safeBatchTransferFrom call, which invokes onERC1155BatchReceived on the recipient contract. This callback gives the recipient arbitrary control of execution while the pool’s accounting state is still in an inconsistent intermediate state where the total value locked has been reduced but the shares representing that value have not yet been destroyed. Because the share valuation is calculated based on the current totalChildValueLocked divided by the remaining shares, the premature transfer creates a temporarily depressed share price. An attacker can exploit this window by reentering the contract, minting or withdrawing additional shares at the artificially low price, and then allowing the contract to finish its state updates, which restores the normal valuation and leaves the attacker with a disproportionate amount of assets. The impact is a potential drain of the pool’s collateral and conditional tokens, effectively stealing funds from all liquidity providers. The issue manifests only when a user removes child shares and the transfer occurs before the burn; it does not affect normal token transfers that do not involve the removeChildShares flow. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the ordering of state changes and external calls, noting that the external call precedes the critical burn operation. The bug is subtle because the transfer itself succeeds and appears correct from a UI perspective, but the underlying accounting inconsistency is hidden until the attacker exploits it. Users may notice that after withdrawing child shares they receive the expected tokens but later see the pool’s value drop or their own share balance become unexpectedly low, leading to missing refunds or zero balances where assets should exist. The class of bug is an unsafe external call before state finalisation, a classic reentrancy pattern that violates the “checks‑effects‑interactions” principle. The proper fix is to move the _burnSharesOf call (or any other state‑modifying effect) before the external safeTransfer, ensuring that the contract’s accounting reflects the final state before any untrusted code is executed. This eliminates the window where an attacker can manipulate share valuation and prevents the pool from being drained.

title: Shares of stUSDC can be lost/gained during cross chain transfers due to differing conversion rates across chains
content: The vulnerability is a conversion‑rate mismatch bug in the cross‑chain wrapper for stUSDC. The contract represents deposits as shares that are minted or burned based on the USD‑denominated amount at the moment of the operation. When a user initiates a cross‑chain transfer, the sending side burns shares calculated from the current conversion rate and records the USD amount that is being moved. The receiving side later mints shares from the amount that arrives, using the conversion rate that is current at that later moment. If the protocol’s internal price oracle (or the poke function that updates the rate) changes between the debit and the credit, the number of shares destroyed on the source chain will not equal the number of shares created on the destination chain. The mismatch can be positive (extra shares minted) or negative (fewer shares minted). A negative mismatch means the user’s balance on the destination chain is lower than expected; the protocol effectively loses the difference, and repeated negative mismatches can lead to under‑collateralisation of the whole pool. A positive mismatch inflates the user’s share balance, which may allow the user to withdraw more underlying assets than they deposited, also breaking the accounting guarantees of the system. The bug is triggered only when a rate update occurs while a transfer is in flight, i.e., between the moment the debit transaction is executed and the moment the credit transaction is finalized. It affects any user who relies on cross‑chain transfers of stUSDC, the protocol’s liquidity pool, and any downstream contracts that assume a 1‑to‑1 correspondence between burned and minted shares. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the cross‑chain bridge code, where the auditor noticed that the debit function uses the USD amount to compute shares, while the credit function recomputes shares from the received amount without preserving the original share count. The problem is subtle because the contract’s external interface reports only the transferred USD amount, so a user sees a successful transfer but may notice a discrepancy only when checking their share balance on the destination chain. The fix is to make the bridge transfer shares directly, i.e., encode the exact number of shares to be burned on the source chain and mint the same number on the destination chain, or otherwise lock the conversion rate for the duration of the transfer. By sending shares instead of value, the protocol eliminates the dependency on a mutable price oracle during the transfer window, preserving accounting integrity.

title: SUP rewards will be completely lost when depositing TBYs to stUSDC via wstUSDC
content: The vulnerability concerns the reward distribution logic when a user deposits a tokenized yield bearing (TBY) asset through the wrapped stUSDC (wstUSDC) contract. In the standard stUSDC flow, the depositTby function calculates the amount of stUSDC to mint, performs the mint, and then calls an internal _mintRewards routine that transfers reward tokens directly to msg.sender. When a user interacts with the wstUSDC contract, the wrapper forwards the TBY transfer to the underlying stUSDC contract and then calls stUSDC.depositTby. Because the wstUSDC contract itself becomes the caller of stUSDC, msg.sender inside the stUSDC reward routine is the wstUSDC contract, not the original external user. Consequently, the reward tokens are minted to the wstUSDC contract address and never forwarded to the user. The rewards become permanently locked because the wrapper does not expose any mechanism to withdraw them. This flaw originates from the wrapper’s failure to capture and re‑route the reward transfer after invoking the underlying deposit function. An attacker does not need to perform any special steps; any user who deposits TBY via wstUSDC will experience the loss of the expected reward tokens. The impact is a direct financial loss for users, as the promised incentive disappears, and it also undermines the economic assumptions of the protocol that rely on reward distribution to encourage deposits. The issue manifests only when the deposit path goes through wstUSDC; direct deposits to stUSDC work correctly. It was discovered during a manual audit that compared the two deposit implementations and noticed that the wrapper does not handle the reward transfer. The problem is subtle because the transaction does not revert and the user receives the wrapped token as expected, making the missing rewards easy to overlook. To remediate, the wstUSDC contract should detect any reward amount returned by the stUSDC call and explicitly transfer those rewards to the original caller, or redesign the reward mechanism so that rewards are minted to the user regardless of the intermediate wrapper. This class of bug is a reward‑forwarding omission in a wrapper contract, leading to funds disappearing from the user’s perspective while being trapped in the wrapper’s balance.

title: TBY#burn incorrectly burns id 0 for all burns causing complete loss of funds for lenders
content: The contract implements a burn function that is intended to destroy a specific token type identified by the parameter id. The function first reduces the total supply for the supplied id, then calls the internal _burn routine. However, the call passes a hard‑coded token identifier 0 instead of the supplied id. As a result, every burn operation removes tokens from the zero‑id bucket regardless of which token the caller requested to burn. During the first issuance round, when only id 0 exists, the function appears to work, but once additional token ids are minted, any attempt to redeem or burn those tokens silently burns id 0. Because the accounting for the requested id is not updated, the balance of the requested token remains unchanged while the underlying asset is transferred out, leaving the token effectively unredeemable. An attacker or any user who calls the function (restricted to onlyBloom, but the protocol itself may invoke it on behalf of lenders) can trigger the loss of funds by initiating a burn for a non‑zero id, causing the protocol to deduct the amount from the pool but not from the correct token ledger. The impact is a complete loss of the underlying assets for all lenders who hold the affected token ids, as the protocol can no longer match token balances to deposited funds. The condition occurs after the first round of token issuance when multiple ids exist; any subsequent burn will mis‑target id 0. The vulnerability was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s token accounting logic, where the mismatch between the id argument and the hard‑coded value was observed. The bug is subtle because the function emits a Burn event with the correct id, giving the impression that the correct token was burned, and the totalSupply for the requested id is decreased, masking the inconsistency. The issue belongs to the class of token accounting errors where a parameter is ignored in favor of a constant, leading to state desynchronisation and loss of assets. From a user perspective, a lender who expects to withdraw or redeem their TBY tokens sees their balance unchanged or receives zero payout, while the protocol’s internal accounting shows the tokens as burned. The expected behavior—burning the specified token id and reducing the corresponding balance—is violated, resulting in funds disappearing. The recommended fix is to pass the supplied id to the internal _burn call, ensuring that the token type being destroyed matches the caller’s intent, and to add tests that verify the id parameter is correctly propagated through all internal burn pathways.

title: BloomPool#redeemBorrower fails to decrement _idToTotalBorrowed leading to large portions of borrower funds being permanently trapped in the contract
content: The vulnerability resides in the borrower redemption logic of the BloomPool contract. When a borrower calls the redeem function, the contract calculates the reward as the borrower’s share of the total returns divided by the total amount that was originally borrowed for a given pool identifier. The calculation uses the stored variable that tracks the total amount borrowed (_idToTotalBorrowed) but, after a successful redemption, the contract only reduces the borrower‑specific amount and the pool’s remaining returns. It never decrements the total borrowed amount. As a result, the denominator in the reward formula stays artificially high after the first redemption, causing every subsequent borrower to receive a smaller fraction of the remaining returns. In a scenario with two equal borrowers and 100 units of returns, the first claim correctly yields 50 units, but the second claim only yields 25 units because the total borrowed value remains at the original 1000 instead of being reduced to 500. The leftover 25 units become permanently trapped in the contract because no further redemption can allocate them – the reward calculation will continue to underestimate the share. This bug originates from an accounting oversight: the state variable that represents the pool’s total borrowed balance is not updated when borrowers withdraw their share, violating the invariant that total borrowed plus total returns should reflect the remaining distributable amount. Exploitation is straightforward: any borrower can claim early, reducing the effective reward rate for later claimants and leaving a portion of the returns inaccessible. The impact is that borrowers receive less than the proportional amount they are entitled to, leading to missing funds, reduced yields, and a loss of confidence in the protocol’s fairness. The issue manifests whenever multiple borrowers redeem sequentially; a single redemption does not expose the problem, making it easy to miss during casual testing. It was discovered during a systematic audit of the redeemBorrower function where the state updates were examined and the missing decrement identified. Detecting the bug is difficult because the reward calculation appears mathematically sound for the first redemption, and the contract does not emit any warning when the reward becomes unexpectedly low. To remediate the flaw, the contract should decrement the total borrowed amount by the borrower’s redeemed amount (borrowAmount) at the same time it reduces the borrower‑specific balance and the pool’s remaining returns. This keeps the reward rate constant and ensures that all returns are fully distributable, restoring the intended accounting relationship and preventing funds from becoming permanently locked.

title: BloomPool#_normalize price will cause severe mis-pricing for RWAs that are not 18 dp
content: The vulnerability originates from an unnecessary scaling factor applied during the calculation of the normalized price for real‑world assets (RWAs) in the BloomPool contract. The function computes totalValue by multiplying existing collateral and the amount to be added by their respective 18‑decimal prices, then divides the sum by a variable called _rwaScalingFactor before dividing by totalCollateral to obtain the final price. Because both currentPrice and startPrice are already expressed with 18 decimal places and the collateral amounts share the same precision, the extra division by _rwaScalingFactor is redundant for assets that also use 18 decimals. However, when an RWA token uses fewer than 18 decimal places, the division by _rwaScalingFactor artificially reduces totalValue by a factor of 10^(18‑assetDecimals). This down‑scaled totalValue propagates through the price calculation, causing the returned price to be dramatically lower than the true market value. An attacker or a user who supplies a low‑decimal asset can therefore trigger a severe mis‑pricing: the protocol believes the asset is worth far less than it actually is, which may allow excessive borrowing against it, lead to under‑collateralisation, or cause users to receive far fewer tokens or refunds than expected. The issue manifests whenever the pool processes a RWA with a decimal precision different from 18, which is a common situation for many legacy tokens. It was discovered during a manual audit that compared the arithmetic flow against the intended accounting model; the bug is subtle because standard test cases using 18‑decimal assets produce correct results, masking the problem for other token precisions. From a user’s perspective the symptoms include seeing a zero or unexpectedly low price for a deposited asset, receiving no refund when withdrawing, or observing that their balance appears to shrink without an obvious on‑chain event. The root cause is the misuse of a scaling constant that should not be part of the totalValue formula. The recommended remediation is to remove _rwaScalingFactor from the totalValue computation entirely, ensuring that totalValue retains the same precision as totalCollateral and that the final price reflects the true value of the underlying asset. This correction restores the intended accounting invariants, prevents price distortion, and protects the protocol from potential under‑collateralisation attacks.

title: Malicious borrower can repeatedly fill then kill orders to permanently lock funds of lenders and other borrowers
content: The vulnerability is an order‑matching denial‑of‑service caused by the way matched orders are cleared for a borrower. When a borrower calls the kill function, the contract zeroes the collateral fields of the MatchOrder struct and overwrites the borrower address with the zero address, but it leaves the empty struct in the lender’s matches array. Because the array entry is not removed, a malicious borrower can repeatedly fill a new order, kill it, and cause another empty entry to be appended. Over time the matches array becomes arbitrarily large. Subsequent calls that iterate over the array to cancel or fill orders – for example the logic that walks the array until a requested amount is satisfied – must process every element, including the many zero‑filled entries. When the array grows beyond a reasonable size the iteration runs out of gas, producing an out‑of‑gas (OOG) revert. This OOG condition blocks the lender from matching or cancelling any of their open orders, effectively locking the lender’s collateral forever. The issue occurs only when a borrower is able to call killBorrowerMatch repeatedly and then re‑enter the matching flow, which is permitted because the contract does not enforce a single entry per borrower. The problem was discovered during a manual audit of the order‑matching functions, where the placeholder zero‑address entry was noted as never being cleaned up. It is hard to notice because the array still contains entries that appear empty, and the contract does not emit a clear warning when the array size becomes problematic; the failure only manifests as a transaction that suddenly runs out of gas after many iterations. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “array‑inflation denial‑of‑service” or “resource‑exhaustion via stale entries”. From a user’s perspective a lender may see that their order cannot be filled, that attempts to cancel return no effect, and that their balance remains unchanged despite expecting a refund or trade execution. The business logic that assumes every match can eventually be cleared is violated, because the stale entries prevent the accounting loop from completing. The recommended fix is to avoid clearing the borrower field to the zero address and instead either remove the entry from the array or keep the borrower address so that duplicate entries are not created. Using a mapping keyed by borrower or compacting the array after removal would also prevent uncontrolled growth and eliminate the OOG denial‑of‑service vector.

title: Yield spread cannot be decrease without causing significant loss to the stUSDC pool
content: The vulnerability originates from a contract‑wide variable called the spread that is used to adjust the rate returned by the getRate function for every TBY (tokenized bond yield). The spread can be modified at any time by the contract owner, and because the rate calculation applies the current spread to all existing TBY valuations, any change retroactively rewrites the value of every TBY that has already been minted. When the spread is decreased, the adjusted rate becomes lower, which directly reduces the aggregated value computed by the _liveTbyValue function that determines the worth of the stUSDC pool. Consequently, stUSDC holders experience an abrupt drop in the reported pool value and may receive less than expected when withdrawing or redeeming their shares. The issue is triggered whenever the owner invokes the function that updates the spread, which can happen at any block after users have deposited. All participants in the pool are affected because the valuation is shared across the entire pool, not per‑user. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that examined the rate calculation flow and noticed that the spread is a global mutable parameter rather than being fixed at TBY creation. It is difficult to notice in normal operation because the spread appears as a normal configuration value and does not emit explicit events indicating a retroactive revaluation, so users only see the pool balance change without a clear cause. The bug belongs to the class of “global mutable state affecting historical accounting” and violates the fundamental accounting assumption that once a token’s value is recorded, it should remain stable unless the token itself changes. From a user perspective the UI may show the stUSDC share price falling sharply, balances becoming lower than the amount originally deposited, or refunds returning zero when they were expected to be positive. The recommended remediation is to capture the spread value at the moment each TBY is minted and store it with the TBY metadata, ensuring that subsequent spread adjustments only affect newly minted TBY instances and do not alter the historic valuation of existing holdings.

title: The yield distribution methodology for stUSDC#poke will lead to substantial loss of yield due to MEV for both stUSDC and StakeUpStaking
content: The vulnerability is an economic manipulation flaw in the yield distribution mechanism of the stUSDC token. The contract’s poke function calculates the change in protocol value over the last 24 hours, computes a new USD‑per‑share value and distributes the entire increase to all current share holders in a single atomic step. Because the function does not enforce any timelock, deposit restriction or weighting based on the time a share has been held, an attacker who can obtain a large amount of USDC in a flash loan can deposit that amount, instantly own the majority of the global share count, call poke and capture almost the whole amount of newly generated yield. After receiving the inflated share value the attacker withdraws the underlying USDC, repays the flash loan and keeps the harvested yield. The root cause is the lack of a time‑weighted accounting model; the protocol treats the current global share balance as the sole determinant of reward entitlement, ignoring the fact that shares acquired moments before a distribution should not be eligible for the full period’s yield. The exploit can be carried out whenever the poke function is callable by anyone and there is no delay between a large deposit and the next distribution. Legitimate stUSDC holders, the StakeUpStaking contract and the protocol’s revenue are affected because the harvested yield is removed from the pool, reducing the expected APR for all other participants. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the poke implementation, where the atomic update of _lastUsdPerShare and the immediate processing of the performance fee revealed that the reward calculation can be gamed with a flash loan. The problem is hard to notice because the contract still reports a correct total value and the distribution appears normal for most users; only the disproportionate share taken by the attacker stands out after the transaction. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are a sudden drop in expected daily rewards, balances that do not grow despite the pool earning interest, and an apparent loss of yield that cannot be explained by market movements. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of flash‑loan‑driven MEV or “instantaneous reward distribution” vulnerabilities, where reward logic does not incorporate a delay or a per‑share accrual period. To remediate the issue the protocol should replace the single‑shot distribution with a gradual drip of yield over the 24‑hour window, update deposit accounting so that newly added shares only start accruing after the current period, and introduce a timelock or minimum holding period before a depositor becomes eligible for the next reward batch. Similar protections are required for the StakeUpStaking contract, which suffers from the same lack of deposit timing safeguards.

title: vePeg#deposit_for fails to increment perpetualLockAmount leading to incorrect supply values
content: The vulnerability resides in the deposit_for function of the vePeg contract, where the internal accounting variable that tracks the total amount of tokens locked forever, known as perpetualLockAmount, is not updated when a user adds more tokens to an existing lock. The function correctly validates that the added value is non‑zero, that a lock already exists, and that the lock has not expired, and then forwards the call to an internal routine that increases the locked balance. However, the routine does not increase perpetualLockAmount by the deposited amount. As a result, the contract’s reported total supply of voting points diverges from the actual amount of tokens held in perpetual locks. This discrepancy can be exploited by an attacker who repeatedly calls deposit_for on multiple token IDs, inflating the apparent supply of points without a corresponding increase in locked assets. The inflated supply may be used in downstream calculations such as reward distribution, voting weight, or token minting, leading to overall overallocation of protocol incentives and potential loss of value for honest participants. The issue manifests only when deposit_for is invoked on a lock that already has a positive amount and a future expiry; normal lock creation paths are unaffected. Users who expect their voting power or reward entitlement to grow proportionally to the added tokens will see no change in the displayed supply, and may observe that their balances appear unchanged or that rewards are lower than expected. The bug was discovered during a manual audit review of the vePeg source code, where the auditor noticed that the perpetualLockAmount variable was read for total‑supply calculations but never written to in the deposit path. Because the variable is used indirectly, the problem can be subtle and may not surface until the protocol performs accounting that relies on the total supply, making it hard to detect through simple functional tests. The proper remediation is to increment perpetualLockAmount by the deposited value inside the deposit_for execution flow, ensuring that the total supply accurately reflects all permanently locked tokens and that downstream accounting remains correct.

title: `InterestRateStrategyV1` ownership can be hijacked
content: The vulnerability is an ownership hijack in the InterestRateStrategyV1 contract, which is built on Solady's Ownable base and deployed as an upgradable proxy. Ownable includes an internal function _guardInitializeOwner that is intended to be overridden to return true, thereby preventing the initializer that sets the contract owner from being called more than once. Because InterestRateStrategyV1 does not override this guard, the default implementation returns false, allowing the initializeOwner routine to be executed repeatedly. An attacker can therefore call the initializer after the proxy has been deployed or after a legitimate upgrade and set themselves as the contract owner. Once in control, the attacker can perform malicious upgrades to the interest‑rate logic, for example imposing excessively high interest rates that instantly liquidate user positions or otherwise manipulate accounting to drain funds. This issue manifests when the contract is first deployed or after any upgrade that does not re‑initialize the owner, and it affects every participant that relies on the interest‑rate strategy – lenders, borrowers, and token holders. The problem was discovered during a security audit that compared the contract code against the Ownable documentation and noticed the missing override comment. It is subtle because the guard function is internal, pure, and never called directly in the public interface, so the lack of a return value can be easily missed. The bug belongs to the class of double‑initialization vulnerabilities in upgradable contracts, where ownership protection mechanisms are bypassed. From a user’s perspective the symptoms may include unexpected changes to interest rates, sudden liquidation of positions, or balances disappearing without any on‑chain error messages. The expected behavior is that only the original deployer can become owner and upgrade the contract, but the reality is that anyone can seize ownership. To remediate the issue the contract should override _guardInitializeOwner to return true, ensuring that the owner can only be set once and preventing any subsequent re‑initialization attacks.

title: `EmissionScheduler#epochEmission` lacks access control and can be called by anyone to cause epoch to mint no emissions
content: The vulnerability is an unauthorized‑access flaw in the epochEmission function of the EmissionScheduler contract. The function is intended to be called only by the designated minter to calculate and mint the token emissions for a new epoch. However, the code does not enforce any access control, allowing any external account to invoke it. When the function is called, it first reads the current epoch, compares it with the stored lastEpoch, and if they differ, it immediately updates lastEpoch to the current value before performing any emission calculations. Because the state update occurs before the emission logic, an attacker can call epochEmission ahead of the legitimate minter, causing lastEpoch to be set prematurely. Subsequent legitimate calls find that lastEpoch already matches the current epoch, trigger the early‑return branch, and return (0,0,0), effectively wiping out all emissions for that epoch. This can happen at any time an epoch is about to be processed, and it requires only a single external transaction from any address. The impact is that token holders, ve token participants, and the protocol team receive no newly minted tokens for the affected epoch, breaking the expected reward distribution and potentially undermining the economic incentives of the system. Users may notice that their balances do not increase after an epoch, that expected rewards are missing, or that the team allocation is zero, even though the protocol should have minted tokens. The issue was discovered during a manual audit review of the contract’s source code, where the lack of a onlyMinter modifier and the premature update of lastEpoch were observed. It is hard to notice because the function returns valid‑looking values and does not emit an event on unauthorized calls, so a zero‑emission result can be mistaken for a normal “no emission” condition. The bug belongs to the class of missing‑access‑control or authorization vulnerabilities that allow state manipulation. To fix the issue, the function should be restricted to the authorized minter (for example by adding an onlyMinter modifier) and the state update of lastEpoch should occur after the emission amounts have been successfully calculated and minted, ensuring that unauthorized callers cannot pre‑empt the emission schedule.

title: `RewardDistributor#claim` will revert for tokens with expired locks leading to loss of rewards
content: RewardDistributor.claim is intended to let a token holder retrieve accrued reward tokens. The function first calculates the last whole‑week timestamp, then calls an internal _claim routine which returns the amount of reward owed. After a non‑zero amount is obtained the function invokes IVotingEscrow(voting_escrow).deposit_for(_tokenId, amount) to re‑deposit the reward into the same ve token. The deposit_for implementation in vePeg requires that the lock associated with _tokenId is still active (locked.end > block.timestamp) and that the lock amount is non‑zero. If the lock has already expired, deposit_for reverts with "Cannot add to expired lock. Withdraw". Because RewardDistributor.claim does not check the lock status before making the call, any attempt to claim rewards after the underlying ve token’s lock period has ended causes the whole claim transaction to revert. Consequently the user receives no reward, the transaction fails, and the accrued reward balance remains locked inside the contract. Moreover, the vePeg contract does not allow an expired lock to be extended (increase_unlock_time also requires locked.end > block.timestamp), so once the lock expires the rewards become permanently inaccessible. The vulnerability manifests only when a token’s lock has passed its expiry, a condition that may be reached after weeks or months of normal operation, making it easy to miss during routine testing. It was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the call flow between RewardDistributor and vePeg and noticed the mismatched assumptions about lock validity. The issue is a classic case of improper handling of an external call that can fail, leading to a denial‑of‑service and potential loss of funds. From the user’s perspective the UI shows a “Claim” button, the transaction is submitted, but it reverts and the user sees no tokens transferred; the expectation that "my rewards will be sent to me" is violated and the reality is "the claim fails and the reward stays locked". The bug violates the business rule that rewards should be claimable at any time, regardless of the lock status of the underlying token. A correct fix would involve checking whether the lock is still active before calling deposit_for and, if it is expired, transferring the reward amount directly to the token owner (or another designated address) instead of attempting a deposit, thereby ensuring that rewards remain claimable even after lock expiry.

title: Incorrect strike price displayed in name/symbol of qToken
content: The vulnerability originates from an off‑by‑one error in a low‑level string utility function used to build the name and symbol of option tokens (qTokens). The internal function that extracts a substring – intended to take the decimal part of a strike price – incorrectly reads the source bytes with a constant offset (bytes(_s)[_start + 1]) instead of advancing with the loop index (bytes(_s)[_start + i]). As a result, the slice always returns the same character repeated, producing a string that consists of the first digit of the decimal portion followed by the original length of the slice. This malformed decimal string is then concatenated into the human‑readable token identifier, causing the displayed strike price to differ from the actual encoded price. The bug manifests only when the strike price includes a fractional component; if the remainder after scaling by the asset's decimals is zero, the name remains correct. Users interacting with wallets or DEX interfaces rely on the token name and symbol to understand the option’s terms. When the displayed strike price is inaccurate – potentially deviating by as much as 0.1 BUSD – a trader may believe they are buying or selling an option at a different price than intended, leading to confusion, mistaken trades, or perceived loss of value. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by Code4rena, where the auditors observed mismatched symbols for options with non‑zero decimals. Because the discrepancy is small and the token name still resembles a legitimate price, it can be easily overlooked, especially by non‑technical users who do not verify the underlying contract data. The root cause belongs to the class of off‑by‑one substring extraction bugs that result in incorrect data representation. To remediate the problem, the slice routine must be corrected to copy each byte using the loop variable (bytes(_s)[_start + i]) or replaced with a safe library function that reliably returns the requested substring. Ensuring that the generated token metadata precisely mirrors the encoded strike price restores the intended business logic that token identifiers faithfully convey option terms, eliminating user confusion and preserving trust in the protocol’s accounting conventions.
summary: `_slice()` in `options/QTokenStringUtils.sol` cut a string into `string[start:end]` However, while fetching bytes, it uses `bytes(_s)[_start+1]` instead of `bytes(_s)[_start+i]`. This causes the return string to be composed of `_s[start]*(_end-_start)`. The result of this function is then used to represent the decimal part of strike price in name/symbol of qToken, leading to potential confusion over the actual value of options.

title: PositionManager#setLiquidationManager fails to give allowances to new liquidation manager
content: The vulnerability resides in the PositionManager contract where the function setLiquidationManager allows the contract owner to replace the address of the liquidation manager without updating the ERC20 allowance that was originally granted to the previous manager during vault registration. When a vault is registered, PositionManager calls IVault(_vaultAddress).approve(address(liquidationManager), type(uint256).max) so that the liquidation manager can transfer the vault's asset in order to perform liquidations. The root cause is that setLiquidationManager only emits an event and updates the storage variable, but it never re‑approves the newly assigned liquidation manager for the vault assets. Consequently, after the manager address is changed, the new contract has no allowance to move the tokens needed for liquidation. An attacker who can call setLiquidationManager (typically the owner) could replace the legitimate manager with a malicious contract that either does nothing or deliberately blocks liquidations. Even without a malicious replacement, a legitimate manager upgrade would render the system unable to liquidate under‑collateralized positions, leading to accumulation of bad debt. The impact is that users who expect their positions to be liquidated when they fall below the minimum collateralization ratio will see no action; their balances remain unchanged, and the protocol may suffer unrecoverable losses as debt grows unchecked. This condition occurs whenever the owner invokes setLiquidationManager after one or more vaults have already been registered. All vault owners, lenders, and the protocol itself are affected because the accounting assumptions that liquidations will recover debt are violated. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the lifecycle of vault registration and manager updates; the missing approval call is silent and does not revert, making it easy to overlook in testing and UI monitoring. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are a vault that stays fully funded despite being under‑collateralized, or a liquidation transaction that completes without moving any assets, leading to confusion and potential loss of funds. The bug belongs to the class of authorization‑state‑inconsistency errors where a privileged role change is not accompanied by the necessary permission updates. To remediate, setLiquidationManager should include a call that grants the new liquidation manager maximal allowance for each registered vault’s asset (and optionally revokes the old manager’s allowance) so that the liquidation workflow remains functional after any manager upgrade.

title: Any bet can be refunded by supplying invalid `betBlob`
content: The vulnerability is an integrity check omission in the refund routine of a betting market contract. When a user calls requestRefund, the function extracts a market identifier (marketCommitment) from the supplied betBlob, but it never validates that the hash of this betBlob corresponds to the BetCommitment that was originally recorded in the BetRequest. Because of this missing verification, any arbitrary betBlob can be supplied, allowing the caller to point the refund logic to a market that has not yet revealed a result. The function only checks that the current block is past the refundStartBlock and that the market result is still null, which are satisfied for many markets that are still pending. Consequently, an attacker can craft a betBlob that references a fresh market, satisfy the null‑result condition, and trigger a safeTransfer of the full bet amount to the caller, even though the original bet may have been placed on a different market that could already be settled. This leads to unauthorized fund withdrawals, creating a shortfall in the protocol’s treasury and breaking the accounting assumptions that refunds are only possible for unresolved bets. The issue manifests whenever the refundStartBlock has passed and the market result for the supplied (or forged) market is still null. All participants who can invoke requestRefund are affected, as the protocol may lose funds and users may see their balances unexpectedly reduced. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the logical flow of the refund function and noticed that the betBlob’s commitment hash was never compared against the stored commitment. It is subtle because the function appears to perform reasonable checks (amount match, block number, result null) and therefore the missing integrity check can be overlooked. To remediate, the contract should compute the commitment hash of the provided betBlob and assert that it equals the BetCommitment stored in the original request, or alternatively eliminate the external betBlob parameter and rely solely on the stored commitment. This ensures that refunds can only be issued for the exact bet that was placed, preserving the intended business logic that refunds are only allowed for bets whose market outcome is still unknown.

title: Malicious request with `amount == 0` can be used to drain market
content: The vulnerability is an amount‑zero request bypass that allows an attacker to drain the market’s losing pot. When a bet is revealed the contract checks that the stored bet amount matches the amount supplied in the reveal request (betState.amount == request.amount) and then clears the stored amount by setting betState.amount to 0. After a legitimate reveal the stored amount is therefore zero. Because the contract does not forbid a reveal request with request.amount equal to zero, a malicious actor can submit a second reveal request with amount 0 once the original bet has been cleared. The validation passes because both sides are zero, and the attacker can provide an arbitrary betBlob. In the payout calculation the winningPotAmount is taken from request.amount (which is 0) but the losingPotAmount is computed as hiddenInfo.betWeight * resultInfo.losingTotalPot / resultInfo.winningTotalWeight. By choosing a large hiddenInfo.betWeight the attacker can make the losingPotAmount equal to the entire losing total pot, effectively stealing those funds. The impact is that market participants and the protocol lose the amount that should have been reserved for losers, while the attacker receives it without any legitimate stake. The bug occurs only after a bet has been successfully revealed and its amount cleared, i.e., in the window after the first reveal and before any further state reset. It affects any user who can submit a reveal request, the market creator, and any downstream contracts that rely on the market’s accounting. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the revealBet logic and noticed that the zero‑amount edge case was not handled. It is hard to notice because a zero amount looks harmless and the contract still emits a successful reveal event, while the payout function appears to use the request.amount only for the winning side, masking the fact that the losing side can be manipulated independently. The bug belongs to the class of “missing input validation / unchecked edge case” and “state‑clearing before full validation” vulnerabilities, where clearing a state variable enables a later request to satisfy a stale equality check. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a successful reveal with no winnings, yet the market’s total balance shrinks unexpectedly, leading to missing refunds or zero balances where funds should exist. To remediate, the revealBet function should reject any request where request.amount is zero, or the contract should perform the amount comparison before clearing the stored amount, or maintain an explicit revealed flag that prevents further reveals. Any of these conceptual fixes restores the invariant that only the original bet amount can be used to claim payouts, thereby preventing the market drain.

title: vePeg#delegate lacks any access control allowing all votes to be stolen through delegation
content: The vulnerability is an unrestricted delegation function that allows any caller to re‑assign the voting power of an arbitrary token holder. The root cause is the absence of an access‑control check that would normally verify that msg.sender is either the owner of the source address or an approved operator. Because the function is declared public and directly forwards to the internal _delegate routine without any require statement, an attacker can invoke delegate with a victim’s address as _from and the attacker’s address as _to. By doing so the attacker steals the entire voting weight of the victim, causing the victim’s on‑chain voting power to drop to zero while the attacker gains the same amount. This stolen voting power can be used to influence governance proposals, redirect reward distributions to a pool controlled by the attacker, or otherwise manipulate protocol decisions. The issue manifests whenever the contract is live and any user interacts with the delegation interface; there is no temporal restriction. All token holders, the governance system, and any reward mechanisms that rely on delegated voting power are affected. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the delegate function signature and noticed the missing permission check. Because delegation is often presented as a simple UI action, the lack of a check can be easy to overlook, especially if the front‑end does not display the caller address. The bug belongs to the class of “missing authorization” or “unrestricted state‑changing function” vulnerabilities, which violate the fundamental accounting assumption that only the token owner can move their voting rights. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are a sudden loss of voting power, inability to cast votes, and rewards being allocated to an unexpected address. The recommended remediation is to add a require that msg.sender equals _from or is approved by the owner of _from, following standard patterns such as ERC20Votes’ delegateBySig or OpenZeppelin’s AccessControl checks.

title: Potential issues that can arise from BGT being reward token
content: The vulnerability stems from the fact that the reward token used by the staking system is the Berachain Governance Token (BGT), which is deliberately designed as a non‑transferable ERC20. The token contract restricts the transfer function with an onlyApprovedSender modifier, meaning that only addresses that have been explicitly added to a whitelist can invoke transfer. The staking contract and its associated farming contract are not included in this whitelist. During normal operation the _preAction routine, collectRewards and setStakingStatus attempt to unstake BGT from a BerachainRewardsVault and then forward the claimed amount to the farming contract. Because the staking contract is not an approved sender, the call to BGT.transfer reverts, causing the claim transaction to fail or, if the failure is ignored, leaving the reward balance locked inside the vault or the staking contract. From a user perspective the expected outcome – a visible increase in their reward balance or a successful receipt of a refund – does not occur; users may see their balance remain unchanged or even appear to be reduced after a withdrawal, leading to confusion that funds disappeared. The issue is discovered during a security review that inspected the token’s transfer restrictions and traced the reward flow logic. It is hard to notice because the contract does not emit a specific error about whitelist failure and the UI may simply show a successful transaction hash while the reward amount is never credited. The impact is high: reward distribution is broken, accounting entries for earned BGT are missing, and the protocol cannot honor its incentive model, potentially eroding trust and causing loss of economic value for stakers. The bug belongs to the class of non‑transferable token misuse or whitelist‑restricted token transfer errors, where a contract assumes a token behaves like a standard ERC20 but the token enforces additional sender restrictions. The fix requires either adding the staking and farming contracts to the token’s approved‑sender list, or redesigning the reward handling code to check the whitelist status before attempting a transfer and to skip or revert the operation when the contract is not authorized. In practice this means introducing a require(isWhitelistedSender(address(this))) guard around reward transfers or restricting the setFarmingContract function to only accept contracts that are already whitelisted, thereby aligning the protocol’s business logic with the token’s transfer constraints.

title: H-1 Users' rewards can be lost if the incentive maker adds a new farming with the
content: The vulnerability is a reward‑loss bug that occurs when the contract’s incentive maker creates a new farming entry using a key that has already been used for a previous farming that has been detached from the pool. The contract does not enforce uniqueness of the farming identifier, so the new entry overwrites the storage slots that held the previous farming’s accounting data, including each user’s accrued reward balances. As a result, all users who had earned rewards in the detached farming suddenly find their reward balance equal to zero and are unable to claim any of the previously earned tokens. This situation can be triggered whenever a privileged maker removes a farming configuration and then, either intentionally or inadvertently, adds another farming with the same key. The impact is a loss of accrued rewards for every participant in the affected farm, potentially amounting to significant funds. The bug is discovered during a security audit by MixBytes, where the logical flow of farming creation and detachment was examined and the missing uniqueness check was identified. The issue is subtle because the contract does not emit an explicit error or event when the overwrite happens; users simply see their reward balance disappear, which may be interpreted as a normal state change or a UI glitch. To remediate the problem, the contract should enforce that each farming key is unique for the lifetime of the contract or at least until the previous farming is fully cleared, by adding a check that prevents the maker from creating a new farming with an identifier that already exists in the system. This change restores the accounting guarantees that rewards are preserved until they are explicitly claimed or the farming is properly terminated, aligning the implementation with the expected business logic that rewards cannot vanish without an explicit withdrawal or migration step.
summary:
If the incentive maker adds a new farming after the previous one was unattached by the pool, then all users' rewards will be lost.
AlgebraEternalFarming.sol#L113
AlgebraEternalFarming.sol#L303

title: H-2 The reward distributor can send funds to an unattached pool
content: The vulnerability is an unchecked reward allocation path in the addRewards() function of the Algebra farming contract. When the crossTo() call that links a virtual pool to its underlying Algebra pool reverts, the virtual pool remains detached but the contract does not verify this state before distributing rewards. As a result, the reward distributor can unintentionally send reward tokens to a virtual pool that is no longer attached to any active pool. This occurs because the function lacks a validation step that compares the stored virtual pool address with the currently attached virtual pool instance. An attacker or even an honest operator can trigger this condition by causing crossTo() to fail (for example, by providing malformed parameters or by exhausting gas), after which subsequent calls to addRewards() will still succeed and transfer funds into the orphaned virtual pool. The transferred funds become inaccessible: users who expect to receive rewards see no increase in their balances, and the protocol’s accounting shows a discrepancy where allocated rewards are missing. From a user’s perspective the UI may display a normal reward claim transaction, but the claimed amount is zero or the balance remains unchanged, leading to confusion and loss of confidence. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit performed by MixBytes, and it is subtle because the contract does not emit an explicit error when rewards are sent to a detached pool; the funds simply disappear from the protocol’s perspective. The bug belongs to the class of “reward misrouting” or “allocation to stale state” vulnerabilities, where state changes are not properly synchronized with external calls. To remediate the problem, the contract should introduce a check that retrieves the current virtual pool for the given key, compares its address with the incentive’s recorded virtualPoolAddress, and reverts if they differ, thereby preventing rewards from being sent to an unattached or stale pool. This ensures that reward distribution only occurs when the virtual pool is correctly linked, preserving the integrity of the accounting and preventing silent loss of funds.
summary:
There is no check in the addRewards() function that would stop the reward distributor from sending funds to a virtual pool that was unattached from the Algebra pool due to a revert in the crossTo() function.
AlgebraEternalFarming.sol#L186-L195

title: H-3 The creation of the incentive with zero rewards blocks the pool's incentive system
content: The vulnerability is an invariant violation in the incentive management logic of AlgebraEternalFarming. The contract permits the creation of an incentive record where the total reward amount is set to zero. Because later internal functions assume that every stored incentive has a positive reward balance, the helper _getIncentiveByKey reverts when it encounters a zero‑reward entry. As a result, any subsequent calls that need to locate the incentive – such as deactivateIncentive, decreaseRewardsAmount, or addRewards – also revert. This effectively freezes the incentive system for the affected pool: no new incentives can be added, existing bonus rewards cannot be withdrawn, and the pool appears to stop distributing any rewards. The bug is triggered when an attacker or a careless developer calls createEternalFarming with a reward amount of 0, which the contract does not guard against. The condition can be reproduced simply by submitting a transaction that creates a zero‑reward incentive and then attempting any management operation on that incentive. The impact is that the pool’s incentive mechanism is blocked, causing users to see empty reward balances, missing bonus payouts, and potentially losing access to previously allocated bonus tokens that become permanently locked. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the lifecycle of incentives and identified that the create function lacks a non‑zero check. It is subtle because the create function itself succeeds and does not emit an obvious error, so the problem only surfaces later when other functions unexpectedly revert, making it hard to trace back to the original zero‑reward creation. The bug belongs to the class of missing input validation / zero‑value edge case that breaks internal invariants. To fix the problem, the contract should enforce that the reward amount supplied to createEternalFarming is greater than zero, for example by adding a require statement, and optionally add defensive checks in the functions that retrieve incentives to handle zero‑reward entries gracefully. By restoring the invariant that every incentive holds a positive reward balance, the pool can continue to create, modify, and deactivate incentives without risk of the system becoming permanently blocked.
summary: It's possible to create an incentive with 0 rewards using AlgebraEternalFarming.createEternalFarming(): AlgebraEternalFarming.sol#L103. Later AlgebraEternalFarming._getIncentiveByKey() will revert for such incentives: AlgebraEternalFarming.sol#L418. So, it will be impossible to call AlgebraEternalFarming.deactivateIncentive(), AlgebraEternalFarming.decreaseRewardsAmount(), or AlgebraEternalFarming.addRewards(). So, the pool will be blocked from the creation of any incentive. If there are some bonus rewards for this incentive, they will be stuck forever.

title: H-1 Pool initialization can be front-run
content: The vulnerability concerns the creation and initialization of an Algebra pool. After the factory deploys a new pool contract, the required initialize() call is not executed automatically, leaving the pool in an uninitialized state where the price variables are still zero. Because the price can be set by any caller before any liquidity is added, a malicious actor can front‑run the first liquidity‑provider transaction and set an arbitrary initial price. The pool’s swap function does not enforce a minimum amount of input tokens when the swap occurs entirely within a tick range that currently holds zero liquidity, meaning a swap can be performed with no tokens transferred, solely to move the price. Moreover, the mint() function that adds liquidity does not accept amount0Max or amount1Max parameters, so it does not verify that the amounts of token0 and token1 received are within the provider’s expectations. An attacker can therefore execute a zero‑cost swap that pushes the price down, then let the legitimate LP’s mint transaction execute at the manipulated price, causing the LP to receive fewer token0 and more token1 than intended. The LP expects to deposit a balanced position but ends up with an unfavorable ratio, effectively losing value. After the LP’s position is minted, the attacker can reverse the price move with another swap, arbitraging the temporary price distortion and extracting profit. This sequence can be repeated to drain liquidity or to cause a denial‑of‑service by keeping the pool in a zero‑liquidity interval where price can be moved freely. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit of the Algebra core contracts, where the absence of an automatic initialize call and the lack of slippage checks in mint were identified as logical gaps. It is difficult to notice because the pool appears functional—functions can be called—but the economic invariants are broken only when the pool is still empty, a state that is rarely exercised in normal operation. To remediate, the factory’s createPool routine should invoke initialize() with a sensible price immediately after deployment, the swap function should reject or limit swaps that would end in a tick with zero liquidity unless a minimum token amount is supplied, and the mint function should include amount0Max and amount1Max checks or otherwise enforce price slippage limits. Adding a combined price‑move‑and‑liquidity‑add method would also prevent token‑free price manipulation when the pool has no liquidity. The vulnerability belongs to the class of initialization‑order and price‑manipulation bugs that arise from missing state‑validation checks in DeFi pool contracts.
summary:
After the pool deployment AlgebraFactory.sol#L95, the initialize function isn't called which allows anyone to set the initial price in the pool. The price setting can affect liquidity addition in the mint function. Initialization can also be front-run if the pool is created from the periphery, so this problem allows a malicious user to ddos any pool. Also, the swap function can be executed without any tokens from the msg.sender if it operates entirely within an interval with zero active liquidity. Concurrently, the mint function in the AlgebraPool contract does not include the amount0Max and amount1Max parameters making it vulnerable to undesirable price fluctuations. This creates a loophole that malicious actors can exploit capitalizing on price slippage to their advantage. For clarity, consider the following sequence of events (these events can also take place after the pool creation):
1. A liquidity provider (LP) initiates the mint transaction to the AlgebraPool with the current price set to P and the pool's actual liquidity standing at zero. The LP's intention is to set a position with the amount0 of token0 and amount1 of token1.
2. An exploiter front-runs this action by performing a swap which shifts the price to P' < P undervaluing token0. This operation costs the exploiter nothing in terms of token0 due to the absence of liquidity.
3. Subsequently, the LP mints the new position acquiring amount0' < amount0 of token0 and amount1' > amount1 of token1.
4. Then the exploiter conducts another swap acquiring token0 and reverting its price back to the prevalent market rate capitalizing on the arbitrage window.
5. These actions result in the LP contributing more of token1 than it was initially planned incurring a loss.
