This issue is classified as high severity. It offers bad actors an opportunity to exploit the lack of price slippage checks in the mint function. Even though conditions without amount0Max and amount1Max might be managed through the periphery, it still exposes the system to the near-zero cost of significant price shifts within intervals with zero active liquidity. This could potentially pave the way for DoS attacks targeting liquidity positions.

title: H-4 Unsynchronized positions in NonFungiblePositionManager and
content: The vulnerability is a state‑desynchronisation between the actual liquidity of a Uniswap‑style position and the accounting record kept by the AlgebraEternalFarming contract. When a user calls NonFungiblePositionManager.decreaseLiquidity, the manager invokes FarmingCenter._updatePosition, which internally calls exitFarming and then enterFarming. If the pool has been detached from its incentive, enterFarming reverts. The NonFungiblePositionManager implementation catches the revert and continues without propagating the error, so the liquidity is removed from the pool but the farming position is left unchanged. This mismatch allows the tokenId owner to keep collecting rewards based on the old, higher liquidity amount even though no liquidity remains in the pool. The bug occurs only when a pool is detached or deactivated and a decreaseLiquidity call is made on a position that is also farmed. It was discovered during a manual audit of the interaction between NonFungiblePositionManager and AlgebraEternalFarming, where the logical flow showed that a revert from FarmingCenter was ignored. The issue is hard to notice because the UI shows a successful liquidity removal and the reward balance continues to increase, giving the impression that the position is still providing liquidity. From a user perspective the symptom is that after withdrawing all tokens the contract still pays out farming rewards, i.e., 'I removed my liquidity but I still receive rewards'. The impact is an over‑payment of incentives, which can be exploited to earn free tokens: an attacker can flash‑loan assets, mint a position, enter farming, detach the pool, decrease liquidity to the minimum, and then collect rewards while the farming contract still believes the full amount is locked. Because the extra rewards are minted from the protocol’s incentive pool, the protocol suffers a loss of funds. The bug belongs to the class of unchecked external‑call failures that lead to inconsistent state across contracts. The recommended mitigation is to make the NonFungiblePositionManager propagate the revert from FarmingCenter._updatePosition, or to enforce a forced exit from the farming position whenever the update fails, thereby guaranteeing atomicity between liquidity changes and farming accounting.
summary:
If FarmingCenter._updatePosition reverts internally, NonFungiblePositionManager ignores that revert here: NonfungiblePositionManager.sol#L369 leading to unsynchronized positions between the actual position and the farming position. The _updatePosition function consists of sequential calls to the exitFarming and enterFarming functions within the AlgebraEternalFarming contract FarmingCenter.sol#L94. While the exitFarming function does not possess explicit revert statements, the enterFarming function can revert here: AlgebraEternalFarming.sol#L385. These reverts prevent the creation of farming positions in detached or deactivated farmings. Consequently, if a pool is detached, every call to NonFungiblePositionManager.decreaseLiquidity will revert within the FarmingCenter._updatePosition function. As a result, the actual liquidity of the position in the pool will decrease, but the liquidity in the farming position will remain unchanged, allowing the tokenId owner to continue collecting higher rewards than deserved. Furthermore, this vulnerability can be exploited by users who can find a way to manually detach the pool from its incentive. Consider the following scenario:
• The exploiter obtains a flashloan from an external project
• The exploiter mints a position in the pool using loaned tokens and enters farming
• The exploiter detaches the pool
• The exploiter decreases liquidity of the position to the minimum possible causing desynchronization in AlgebraEternalFarming which retains the liquidity of the flashloaned tokens.
• The exploiter repays the flashloan
In this scenario, the exploiter can collect rewards without maintaining an actual position.

title: H-5 Virtual pools detached from the corresponding AlgebraPool result in an
content: A virtual liquidity pool can become detached from its underlying AlgebraPool when the AlgebraPool invokes the crossTo function on the VirtualAlgebraPool and that call reverts. In that failure path the AlgebraPool resets its activeIncentive variable to the zero address but does not mark the virtual pool as deactivated nor set its rewardRates to zero. Consequently the virtual pool remains in an active state with non‑zero reward rates, while it stops receiving any further price updates because it is no longer linked to the real pool. Liquidity providers that continue to hold positions in the virtual pool therefore keep receiving incentive tokens that are calculated against a frozen price snapshot taken at the moment of detachment. From a user perspective the UI still shows normal reward accrual, but the amount earned does not reflect the current market price, leading to an over‑payment of rewards. The root cause is incomplete cleanup of the virtual pool’s state after a reverted cross‑contract call: only the incentive address is cleared, while the deactivation flag and reward parameters are left unchanged. The bug can be triggered deliberately by forcing the crossTo call to revert (for example by supplying malformed data or by a malicious contract) or may happen unintentionally during a failed migration. The impact is economic: the protocol distributes more incentive tokens than intended, diluting token value and potentially draining reserves, while liquidity providers receive unexpected extra tokens that may later be reclaimed or cause accounting mismatches. The issue was discovered during a systematic security audit by MixBytes, which examined the state‑transition logic of the farming contracts. It is hard to notice because the reward balances appear normal and no explicit error is emitted; only the underlying price feed is stale, which is not directly observable from the front‑end. To remediate the problem the detachment routine should explicitly set rewardRates to zero and flip the deactivated flag to true whenever the activeIncentive is cleared, ensuring that no further rewards are calculated on an outdated price. This aligns the virtual pool’s lifecycle with the intended incentive model and prevents reward accumulation based on a frozen price snapshot.
summary: In cases where AlgebraPool connected to VirtualAlgebraPool catches a revert during a call to the crossTo function, the pool will reset its activeIncentive parameter to the 0 address here: SwapCalculation.sol#L210. Subsequently, the virtual pool enters a state where it is not deactivated, its rewardRates remain non-zero, and the detached pool no longer updates subsequent price changes. As a result, current liquidity providers continue to collect rewards based on the "frozen" price present in the pool at the moment of detachment.

title: Alligator gives gas refunds but does not receive gas refunds
content: The vulnerability is a missing gas‑refund path in the AlligatorV2 contract when it forwards votes to an underlying DAO. The function castRefundableVotesWithReasonBatched records the initial gas, calls a helper that iterates over a list of authorities and invokes the DAO’s castVoteWithReason method, and finally refunds the caller based on the gas measured. The DAO, however, only issues a refund when its own castRefundableVote entry point is used. Because Alligator calls the non‑refundable castVoteWithReason, the DAO never sends any gas reimbursement back to Alligator. As a result Alligator can only refund users from its own balance and never receives the expected reimbursement, causing its internal treasury to be slowly depleted. This can be exploited by repeatedly invoking the batch voting function, which consumes gas for each vote; the contract refunds the user each time but does not get reimbursed, so an attacker can drain the contract’s funds over many calls. The issue occurs whenever a user calls castRefundableVotesWithReasonBatched, which internally uses the wrong DAO entry point. All users who rely on the promised gas refund are affected, as are the contract owners who must maintain a sufficient balance to continue providing refunds, and the broader protocol whose accounting assumptions about refundable voting are violated. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the Alligator implementation with the NounsLogicV2 reference and noticed the mismatch in function calls. It is hard to notice because refunds still reach the end user, masking the fact that the contract’s own balance is shrinking; no explicit error is thrown until the balance is exhausted. Conceptually the fix is to replace the call to castVoteWithReason with a call to the DAO’s castRefundableVote (or an equivalent refundable entry point) so that Alligator receives the gas refund before passing it on to the user, thereby preserving its treasury and maintaining correct accounting.

title: Gas refunds can be abused by batching transactions
content: The vulnerability stems from a gas‑refund mechanism that assumes a constant overhead of 36,000 gas for every refundable operation. The protocol adds this fixed amount to the gas actually spent and then sends the difference back to the caller as an ETH refund. Because the value is static, any situation where the real overhead is lower than 36 k results in a refund that exceeds the true cost of execution. This discrepancy becomes exploitable when several calls to the refundable voting function are packed into a single transaction. In a batched call the 20 k gas required to start a transaction is paid only once, and the destination address for the ETH refund is already “warm”, saving roughly another 2.5 k gas per call. Consequently each additional call in the batch consumes less than the assumed 36 k overhead, so the protocol over‑pays the caller. An attacker can split voting power across many delegated accounts, invoke the batched refundable vote repeatedly, and collect a net profit in ETH for each extra call. From the user’s perspective the transaction appears to succeed normally, but the caller’s balance increases after the vote – they receive more ETH than they spent on gas, contrary to the expectation that refunds only cover the exact gas cost. The impact is a direct loss of funds from the protocol treasury; in realistic scenarios with dozens of delegated tokens and multiple proposals the profit can amount to thousands of dollars. The issue manifests whenever the batched refundable‑vote function is used, especially when a user controls many delegations or can orchestrate multiple calls in one transaction. It affects token holders, delegators, and the overall economic model of the protocol because the incentive structure is broken. The flaw was uncovered during a security audit by constructing a test that called the function twice in a loop and measuring the gas before and after, revealing a surplus refund. The problem is subtle because the refund logic is intended to be a user‑friendly feature, and the over‑payment per call is small enough to be missed without systematic measurement. To remediate, the protocol should eliminate internal gas refunds and let the token contract handle any reimbursements, or at minimum restrict refunds to the original transaction sender (tx.origin) and prevent contracts from receiving them, ensuring that only one refund can be issued per block per address. This removes the economic incentive to batch calls for profit and restores the intended accounting balance.
summary:
The refund mechanism assumes a `REFUNDBASEGAS` value of 36k to account for the overhead gas that occurs outside of the tracked gas. Specifically, this accounts for the 20k gas to kick off the transaction, 7k for the ETH transfer, and other gas spent before `startGas` or within the `_refundGas()` function.

This is a fixed amount, which means that if less than 36k of overhead gas is used, the user is refunded more than the amount spent.

If multiple calls to `castRefundableVotesWithReasonBatched()` are batched into a single transaction, the actual gas spent per transaction will be lower than expected because:

1) The 20k transaction overhead will only be spent once, so will result in 20k gas profit each subsequent transaction.
2) The address for receiving ETH will be "warm", which will save an additional ~2.5k gas per transaction

A situation where a large number of these calls are batched could easily be created by a user splitting their Nouns across multiple accounts, and setting up different delegation paths for each. In this situation, separate calls could be made to vote with each Nouns and with each proposal.

title: Decimals not Handled by the Application Frontend
content: The vulnerability consists of the application’s front‑end accepting arbitrary decimal numbers as the deposit amount for a gaming session. The smart‑contract back‑end expects token amounts to be expressed as whole‑number integers (typically in the smallest token unit), but the UI does not enforce this restriction. When a user types a value such as 1.00000000000001 (14 decimal places) the JavaScript code converts the string to a Number and later formats it using exponential notation (for example 1e‑14). The session balance displayed to the user therefore shows an exponential value that does not correspond to the actual integer amount that will be sent to the contract. Because the displayed balance is wrong, the user may see insufficient balance warnings even though the wallet holds enough tokens, or conversely the contract may receive a value that is rounded down to zero, causing the user’s deposit to be rejected or silently lost. The issue is triggered whenever a user manually enters a decimal amount, when the front‑end parses the input with floating‑point arithmetic, or when the UI formats large or small numbers using scientific notation. The problem was discovered during a manual UI review of the AllYourBase virtual gaming platform, where the auditor observed that the session balance field displayed values in exponential form after entering a decimal deposit. The bug is subtle because the UI still accepts the input and the contract transaction may succeed, but the mismatch between displayed and actual amounts can lead to financial loss, failed bets, or unnecessary gas consumption as users repeatedly attempt to submit transactions that the front‑end believes are under‑funded. The vulnerability belongs to the class of input validation and numeric handling errors that arise from mixing floating‑point representations with integer‑only blockchain accounting. To remediate, the front‑end should restrict deposit inputs to integer values, validate that the parsed amount matches the expected token precision, and reject or round any decimal input before it is sent to the contract. Additionally, the UI should display amounts in a fixed‑point format consistent with the token’s decimals and provide clear feedback when a user attempts to enter unsupported fractional values. This would prevent the user‑visible symptoms of exponential balances, unexpected insufficient‑balance errors, and potential loss of funds due to rounding to zero.
summary:
In allyourbase.virtual.tech a user can manually enter 1.(decimal) numbers in the deposit amount. Consequently the frontend will display an exponential amount (see image) and the session balance will be displayed using this convention.
In the image: A user introduced a decimal value 1.0…0001(14 decimals) in the session balance. When submitting the app processes that amount as an exponential. If the user guesses an incorrect prediction the “Session balance” is still displaying the exponential value without any change.
Since the application relies on blockchain technology, these rounding errors could lead to issues in the calculations or even just gas griefing, as the backend might not be able to handle decimal values properly.
In the image: After finishing the session, the virtual balance is updated with exponentials.

In the image: Another example with 17 decimals.
In the image: The frontend is displaying at least 1 in session balance and the bet is for exactly $1. Hence, when hitting submit the app displays insufficient balance. The introduction of decimals are not handled by the app.

This particular finding is classified as high since it is related to gaming finance (at least from the frontend perspective), and the app is displaying amounts in decimals (something that might not be expected by the backend).

title: H-1 Farming can be deactivated by accident
content: The vulnerability consists of an accidental deactivation of the farming incentive mechanism in the virtual pool when a swap is executed without a tick change and the direction flag zeroToOne is false. The root cause is an overly permissive condition that checks only whether the current tick equals the previous tick together with zeroToOne being false before setting the farmingActive flag to false. Because the contract does not require a genuine price movement, a normal user or an attacker can trigger a swap that leaves the price unchanged, satisfying the condition and causing the deactivation logic to fire. When this happens the virtual pool is disconnected from the farming module, so subsequent reward calculations treat the pool as inactive and no further incentives are distributed to liquidity providers. The impact is that participants who expect continuous reward accrual see their earned‑rewards counter stop increasing, effectively losing potential earnings. This scenario occurs only when a swap occurs with zero price movement and the swap direction is from token1 to token0 (zeroToOne false). The affected parties are all users providing liquidity to the pool and any protocol component that relies on the farming rewards. The issue was discovered during a static analysis audit by MixBytes, which noted that the deactivation check could be satisfied unintentionally. Because the contract does not emit a distinct event when farming is turned off and the pool continues to accept swaps, the problem can be hard to notice; the UI may still show the pool as active and swaps succeed, yet the reward balance remains unchanged, which can be mistaken for a normal reward schedule. This bug belongs to the class of state‑transition logic errors where a feature‑enabling flag is cleared based on an insufficient condition, leading to unintended disabling of a core functionality. To remediate, the contract should verify that a genuine tick change has occurred before deactivating farming, for example by using the later check that also confirms the direction flag and ensures the price movement is non‑zero, or by moving the deactivation logic to a dedicated governance‑controlled function. From the user’s perspective the symptom is that after a swap the “earned rewards” display stays at zero or stops growing, contrary to the expectation that rewards continue to accrue, thereby violating the business assumption that farming incentives remain active as long as the pool is operational.
summary: The current check for farming deactivation can be triggered by accident if tick hasn't changed during the swap and zeroToOne is false EternalVirtualPool.sol#L131-L134. This action will disconnect farming from the pool and will affect incentive distribution for users.

title: H-2 Overﬂow will entirely block the plugin
content: The vulnerability is an integer overflow that occurs during the second initialization of a list inside the VolatilityOracle contract. When the contract attempts to re‑initialize the internal array or counter a second time, the arithmetic operation that increments the length or index wraps around the maximum uint256 value and resets to zero. This overflow is not guarded by any safety check, so the internal state becomes inconsistent and subsequent plugin updates that rely on the list fail silently. As a result, the volatility plugin can no longer push new data to the pool, effectively freezing the price‑feed mechanism. Users interacting with the pool notice that their balances do not change despite expected market movements, refunds are not issued, and the UI shows no new volatility information. The condition only manifests after the list has been initialized twice, a scenario that typical unit tests may not cover, making the bug hard to detect during development. The issue was uncovered during a manual security audit by MixBytes, which examined the initialization logic and identified the unchecked arithmetic as the root cause. Because the overflow corrupts the plugin’s state, only an admin‑only recovery function can reset the contract, meaning ordinary users cannot unfreeze the system themselves. The bug belongs to the class of unchecked arithmetic overflows that lead to state‑locking conditions, violating the protocol’s assumption that the plugin will always be able to accept new updates. To remediate, the contract should either prevent re‑initialization, reset the counter before a second use, or explicitly use an unchecked block only if the overflow is intentional and safely handled, but preferably incorporate overflow checks or SafeMath‑style guards to maintain correct accounting and ensure that plugin updates remain functional.
summary: Overﬂow will occur here on the second time of the list initialization VolatilityOracle.sol#L72-L74. This will block plugin updates that will affect the pool and further recovery can be executed by admin only.

title: Mint spread collateral-less and conjuring collateral claims out of thin air with implicit arithmetic rounding and flawed int to uint conversion
content:
The contract contains two related arithmetic defects that together enable a user to create or claim collateral that does not actually exist. The first defect is the use of plain integer division and multiplication in the fixed‑point library without an explicit rounding mode. Both the `mul` and `div` functions truncate the fractional part of the result, implicitly rounding down. When these operations are used to calculate the collateral required for a call credit spread in the `_mintSpread` flow, the rounding loss can reduce the computed collateral amount to zero even though a non‑zero amount of options is being minted. Because the subsequent `toScaledUint` routine only adds a rounding‑up correction after the scaling step, the earlier implicit round‑down is not compensated, allowing the protocol to accept a spread mint without any fee or collateral transfer. An attacker can therefore mint a spread with a negligible or zero collateral deposit, later neutralising the position and withdrawing the supposed collateral, effectively conjuring value from thin air.

The second defect resides in `SignedConverter.intToUint`, which is implemented as an absolute‑value conversion: it returns the absolute value of a signed integer as an unsigned integer, silently turning negative numbers into positive ones. This function is used in the collateral‑claim calculation (`calculateClaimableCollateral`). When the contract computes the payout for the short leg of a spread at expiry, the negative intermediate result produced by the rounding errors is turned positive, inflating the amount of collateral that the controller believes is returnable. By carefully choosing strike and expiry prices so that the short leg’s payout slightly exceeds the collateral requirement, the attacker can force the overall claimable collateral value to become negative before the `abs` conversion, which is then interpreted as a positive payout. The net effect is that the attacker can withdraw a small amount of the underlying asset (e.g., wei of WETH) that was never deposited.

Both bugs manifest only under specific numeric conditions: the implicit rounding loss becomes observable when the option amount is very small (on the order of 10⁻¹⁸ of a token) and the strike price difference is minimal, while the `intToUint` issue requires the expiry price to lie between the long and short strikes so that the short leg’s payout is positive but the collateral requirement is still lower. In practice the attacks require precise price prediction and large gas expenditure, which makes them costly on the current BNB chain, yet they demonstrate a violation of the protocol’s accounting assumptions – namely that the controller never loses tokens due to rounding and that collateral calculations cannot produce a negative claimable amount. The issues were discovered during a formal audit that examined the fixed‑point arithmetic pathways and the conversion utilities used throughout the QuantMath library. They are hard to notice because the rounding errors are hidden inside internal library calls and the `intToUint` function masquerades as a harmless type cast, while the protocol’s tests only exercised typical price ranges.

To remediate the problem, the `mul` and `div` functions should be rewritten to accept an explicit rounding direction (up or down) or to use a checked arithmetic library that guarantees no loss of precision. The scaling routine must then apply the chosen rounding consistently. The `intToUint` conversion should be replaced with a strict cast that reverts on negative inputs, or the function should be renamed and documented as an absolute‑value operation if that behavior is truly required. By eliminating implicit truncation and preventing negative values from being silently treated as positive, the protocol’s collateral accounting can once again guarantee that users receive exactly the amount of collateral they deposited, and that no unintended profit can be extracted from rounding artifacts.
summary:
[QuantMath.sol#L137](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-rolla/blob/main/quant-protocol/contracts/libraries/QuantMath.sol#L137)  
[QuantMath.sol#L151](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-rolla/blob/main/quant-protocol/contracts/libraries/QuantMath.sol#L151)  
[SignedConverter.sol#L28](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-03-rolla/blob/main/quant-protocol/contracts/libraries/SignedConverter.sol#L28)  

This report presents 2 different incorrect behaviour that can affect the correctness of math calculations:

1. Unattended Implicit rounding in QuantMath.sol `div` and `mul`
2. Inappropriate method of casting integer to unsigned integer in SignedConverter.sol `intToUint`

Bug 1 affects the correctness when calculating collateral required for `_mintSpread`. Bug 2 expands the attack surface and allows attackers to target the `_claimCollateral` phase instead. Both attacks may result in tokens being stolen from Controller in the worst case, but is most likely too costly to exploit under current BNB chain environment. The potential impact however, should not be taken lightly, since it is known that the ethereum environment in highly volatile and minor changes in the environment can suddenly make those bugs cheap to exploit.

title: Wrong implementation of `EIP712MetaTransaction`
content: The vulnerability resides in an improperly implemented EIP712 meta‑transaction utility contract that is meant to be inherited by application contracts. The contract defines an initialization function that uses OpenZeppelin’s `initializer` modifier, which is designed for a top‑level initializer that can only be executed once for the whole contract hierarchy. Because the utility contract is not abstract and its initializer is declared `public` with the `initializer` modifier, a derived contract that also contains an `initializer` will invoke the base initializer during its own initialization sequence. OpenZeppelin’s `initializer` logic interprets this call as a re‑entry attempt and triggers the `require` guard, causing the transaction to revert unless the call occurs inside a constructor. Consequently, the expected domain separator for EIP712 signatures is never set after deployment or after an upgrade, breaking the meta‑transaction verification flow. The root cause is the misuse of the `initializer` modifier instead of the intended `onlyInitializing` (or `internal` visibility) for utility contracts, combined with the failure to mark the contract as `abstract`. This design flaw makes the initialization routine non‑reusable across upgrades: the comment in the source claims the function can be called "once after every upgrade," but the `initializer` modifier enforces a single execution for the entire inheritance chain, so subsequent upgrades cannot re‑initialise the EIP712 domain. From a user perspective, attempts to interact with the protocol via meta‑transactions may suddenly revert with generic errors, leading to symptoms such as "transaction failed," "no receipt returned," or "signature verification failed" even though the user correctly signed the payload. The issue was identified during a manual audit of the contract’s inheritance structure and its compliance with OpenZeppelin’s upgradeable patterns. It is subtle because the code compiles without warnings and the mistake does not affect static analysis of the function body; only at runtime does the re‑entrancy guard abort the call. The impact is primarily functional: the protocol becomes unable to process signed meta‑transactions after deployment or after an upgrade, effectively freezing certain user flows and potentially causing loss of confidence or funds if users are unable to complete expected operations. The recommended fix is to declare the contract as `abstract`, change the initializer to `internal` (or `private`) visibility, replace the `initializer` modifier with `onlyInitializing`, and rename the function to follow the double‑underscore convention (`__EIP712MetaTransaction_init`). This aligns the utility contract with OpenZeppelin’s upgradeable patterns, ensures that the domain separator can be correctly set during the derived contract’s initialization, and restores the ability to re‑initialize after upgrades without triggering the re‑entrancy guard.

title: `EIP712MetaTransaction.executeMetaTransaction`
content: The vulnerability resides in the meta‑transaction execution flow of the EIP712MetaTransaction contract. The function first increments the caller’s nonce, then forwards the encoded action to the contract itself via a low‑level call, and finally requires the call to succeed. When the forwarded call reverts, the surrounding transaction also reverts, causing the earlier nonce increment to be rolled back. Because the nonce value stays unchanged, the original signed meta‑transaction, which includes the nonce as part of its signed payload, can be submitted again by any actor. The root cause is the placement of the nonce increment before the external call and the reliance on a require statement that triggers a full state revert on failure. This design flaw allows replay of any meta‑transaction that initially failed due to temporary conditions such as insufficient balance, time‑locks, or external state dependencies. An attacker can wait until those conditions change, resend the same signed payload, and cause the intended operation—such as minting options or transferring collateral—to succeed without the original signer’s consent. From the user’s perspective the symptom is a loss of funds or unexpected execution of an operation they believed had failed; the UI may initially show no change, but later the balance is reduced or an unexpected position is created. The issue affects every participant who relies on meta‑transactions for gas‑less interactions, including end users, protocol operators, and the overall financial integrity of the system. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the handling of failed low‑level calls and nonce management. The problem is subtle because the nonce appears to increase during execution, yet the revert undoes that change, making it easy to overlook during normal testing that only covers successful paths. To remediate, the contract should ensure that a nonce is consumed regardless of call success—by moving the nonce increment after the require, recording a used‑nonce flag, or using a non‑reverting pattern that still marks the signature as spent. Additionally, a gas‑payment check should be added to mitigate insufficient‑gas griefing attacks. By guaranteeing that each signed meta‑transaction can be used only once, the replay vector is eliminated and the protocol’s accounting assumptions are restored.

title: Token accounting can be permanently broken by malicious rebalancer
content: The vulnerability is an accounting invariant break in a vault that stores a virtual balance called nominals for each underlying asset. The system assumes that nominals multiplied by the total supply of the AMKT token, divided by a scalar, always equals the actual token balance held by the vault. This invariant is enforced when users issue or redeem tokens and when a rebalancer fulfills a bounty. During bounty fulfillment the contract calls an external rebalancer via a callback before the nominals values are updated. Because the contract has already calculated the amounts of assets to transfer based on the old nominals, a malicious rebalancer can invoke issue() or redeem() from within the callback. Those calls use the stale ratio, causing the vault to send assets at the previous rate and leaving the internal accounting out of sync with the real balances. The result is that the vault may end up with fewer underlying tokens than the formula predicts, permanently locking those assets and making future rebalancing or removal of an asset impossible. The problem is triggered only when the callback is executed, i.e., during the fullfillBounty function, and is exacerbated if the AMKT total supply changes during the callback. All token holders and the protocol are affected because the vault can no longer guarantee correct redemption values, leading to users receiving less than expected or seeing zero balances for assets that should exist. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the ordering of state updates and external calls. It is hard to notice because the invariant appears correct before and after the function call, and no explicit error is thrown; the mismatch only becomes visible when an asset is removed or a redemption yields an unexpected shortfall. The bug belongs to the class of reentrancy or stale‑state ordering flaws that break accounting invariants. To fix the problem the contract should either update the nominals before invoking the external callback or add a check that the AMKT total supply has not changed during the callback, thereby preventing the rebalancer from exploiting the stale state. In user‑facing terms a user may try to redeem their tokens and receive a smaller amount, or the UI may show an asset balance of zero even though the vault should hold value, indicating that funds have disappeared from the accounting perspective.
summary:
The `vault` holds a `nominals` value (also known as a virtual balance) for each asset. This value represents the amount of each asset that the vault should hold per 1e18 AMKT tokens. It is an invariant of the system that `nominals[asset] * totalSupply / 1e18` should always equal the asset's balance in the contract (unless someone sends ERC20 funds directly to the contract, in which case they are ignored to maintain this invariant).

This is maintained because, when a user calls `issue()` or `redeem()`, the amount of each asset that they send or receive is calculated based on the `nominals` value, keeping the ratio in line.

Similarly, when a user calls `fullfillBounty()` to rebalance the vault, the bounty `units` represent the new `nominals` values, and the tokens are exchanged precisely to bring the vault's balances into alignment with these values.

However, during the bounty fulfillment process, there is a callback to the rebalancer:
```solidity
try Rebalancer(msg.sender).rebalanceCallback() {} catch {
    revert BountyCallbackFailed();
}
```
At this point in the function, we have already decided on the numbers of tokens that need to be sent (based on the vault's total supply) in order to keep the `nominals` value in alignment with the actual balances.

However, since the `nominals` value has not been updated at the time of this callback, if we call `issue()` or `redeem()` from this callback, we will be sending assets at the previous ratio. This will throw off the math that was intended to ensure that `nominals[asset] * totalSupply / SCALAR = asset.balanceOf(vault)`.

The result is that, when the function is completed, this invariant will no longer hold.

This will create a situation where all tokens that were rebalanced in an upward direction during this bounty will have insufficient tokens in the vault to cover the calculated amount of value. This creates two major problems:

1) These assets are permanently locked as underlying tokens of the vault. If an asset is removed from the vault (`nominals[asset] = 0`), the rebalancing process will try to send `nominals[asset] * totalSupply / SCALAR` back to the rebalancer, but the vault will not hold that many tokens, so it will fail.

2) The accounting will permanently be off, as we expect that the value of the vault's underlying tokens can be calculated using the `nominals` value of all the assets, but this will no longer be the case.

title: If `feeScaled` is set too high in the constructor, the protocol will be bricked
content: The vulnerability is an unchecked initialization of the fee scaling factor in the contract constructor. The contract stores a variable feeScaled that represents a fee expressed as a fraction of 1e18 (the SCALAR constant). All runtime functions that rely on feeScaled first verify that the value does not exceed SCALAR by calling computeMultiplier, which reverts with MultiplierFeeTooHigh if the check fails. In the setter setFeeScaled the same check is performed before the value is updated, protecting later calls. However, the constructor assigns feeScaled directly from the supplied _feeScaled argument without any validation. If an attacker or a careless deployer passes a value larger than SCALAR, the invariant that feeScaled ≤ SCALAR is broken at deployment time. As soon as any function that invokes computeMultiplier—such as issue, redeem, fulfillBounty, or even setFeeScaled itself—executes, the internal check triggers a revert, causing every transaction that touches the vault to fail. From the user’s perspective, attempts to mint, withdraw, or claim rewards simply revert with no state change, giving the impression that the protocol is frozen or that their funds are missing. The protocol’s accounting logic assumes that feeScaled is always bounded; when the bound is violated the multiplier calculation cannot be performed, breaking the core accounting mechanism and effectively bricking the contract. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the reviewer noticed that the constructor lacked the same guard present in setFeeScaled and traced the execution path to computeMultiplier. Because the contract does not emit any explicit warning and the revert occurs only when a user interacts with the contract, the problem can be hard to notice until a transaction is attempted. The fix is to add the same upper‑bound check in the constructor, rejecting deployments with an oversized feeScaled, and optionally removing the redundant check in computeMultiplier once the invariant is guaranteed. This class of bug belongs to the category of missing input validation at contract initialization, leading to invariant violation and permanent denial‑of‑service.

title: Fees are sent to vault instead of feeRecipient
content: The vulnerability consists of an incorrect allocation of protocol fees that are generated during token issuance, redemption, or bounty fulfillment. The contract calls a function that checks whether a day has elapsed and, if so, calculates an inflation amount based on newly accrued fees. The calculated amount is then minted to the contract's own address (the vault) instead of being transferred to the configured feeRecipient. This misdirection occurs because the mint call uses address(this) as the destination and never includes a second mint to feeRecipient. As a result, the protocol's accounting assumes that fees have been paid to the intended recipient, while in reality the newly minted tokens remain locked in the vault, effectively removing them from the economic flow. An attacker or any user can trigger the inflation function by performing a token issuance, redemption, or bounty fulfillment after the required time interval, causing the vault to receive additional tokens that were supposed to be distributed. The impact is a loss of expected revenue for the feeRecipient, distortion of token supply metrics, and potential erosion of trust because users see lower payouts or missing refunds. The issue manifests whenever the daily inflation condition is satisfied and the contract mints a positive inflation amount. It affects all participants who rely on the feeRecipient receiving the correct amount, including token holders, bounty participants, and the protocol treasury. The bug was identified during a manual audit that compared the intended fee flow with the actual mint destinations and noticed that the feeRecipient address was never used. Because the function still returns a correct current multiplier, the problem can be subtle and may not raise immediate alarms; the vault simply holds extra tokens that are not visible in user‑facing balances. To remediate the issue, the mint operation should be split or redirected so that the calculated inflation amount is minted to the feeRecipient (or transferred from the vault to the feeRecipient) instead of, or in addition to, the vault. This aligns the on‑chain accounting with the protocol's economic design and prevents unintended token accumulation in the vault.

title: Recoveries of type SigMode.OnlySecond can be endlessly replayed
content: The vulnerability is an unlimited replay of account‑recovery operations when the contract is used with the SigMode.OnlySecond option. The contract stores a boolean flag in a mapping called recoveries to prevent a recovery payload from being executed more than once. The key for this mapping is built by hashing together the target account address, the recovery data and the entire SignatureMeta structure, which includes a string field called canonizedHeaders. In the OnlySecond mode the contract does not validate the contents of canonizedHeaders, so an attacker can change this string by adding a harmless character (for example a space or a newline) and obtain a different hash value. Because the mapping key changes, the contract treats the modified payload as a fresh recovery and allows it to be executed again, even though all other fields – including the newKeyToSet address that will gain control of the account – remain identical. This means that any recovery performed with SigMode.OnlySecond can be replayed an arbitrary number of times by simply tweaking the unvalidated string field. The impact is that a user who originally used the recovery to regain access to an AmbireAccount may later lose control permanently. After the user rotates their keys and discards the old ones, an attacker (or even the original user unintentionally) can replay the old recovery, granting control to the address stored in newKeyToSet – an address that the legitimate owner no longer controls. From the user’s perspective the wallet becomes inaccessible; the UI may show that the account exists but no transactions can be signed, and the user sees that a previously set recovery address still controls the account despite having rotated keys. The issue was discovered during a security audit when the reviewer noticed that the identifier used for replay protection incorporated a field that is not validated in all code paths. It is hard to notice because the mapping appears to block replays, yet the subtle change in a non‑critical string field bypasses the check without affecting the core recovery logic. The bug belongs to the class of replay attacks caused by weak identifier construction – using mutable or unchecked data to generate a uniqueness key. To remediate, the identifier should be derived only from fields that are strictly validated in every execution path, such as the account address, the recovery data and the immutable parts of SignatureMeta, or the contract should add explicit validation for canonizedHeaders before it is used in the hash. By ensuring that the replay‑prevention key cannot be altered by trivial modifications, the recovery can remain a one‑time operation as intended, preserving account safety and preventing permanent lock‑out.
summary:
The recoveries mapping in DKIMRecoverySigValidator is serving as a way to check if a recovery has been executed already, so it is a way to block recovery replays. The problem with this is that the key in that mapping is calculated from fields in a recovery payload that can be slightly changed (for example by adding a random character to a string or bytes typed field, examples are SignatureMeta.canonizedHeaders or SignatureMeta.key.pubKeyModulus) so you can execute a recovery payload where all other values are the same.

The concrete problem is here:
```solidity
bytes32 identifier = keccak256(abi.encode(accountAddr, data, sigMeta));
```
The identifier which is used as a key in the recoveries mapping, is using SignatureMeta sigMeta which has the string canonizedHeaders field. When SigMode.OnlySecond is used, the canonizedHeaders has no validation whatsoever, so it can be slightly changed and the identifier would be different, while all other values are the same and still valid. This means that all SigMode.OnlySecond recoveries can be replayed endlessly - as many times as desired, forever.

The problem is deflated by the fact that the SignatureMeta.newKeyToSet value can't be changed (it is validated when SigMode.onlySecond is used), so all of the mentioned replays will end up granting access to the same newKeyToSet address every time they are executed. Still, let's look at the following scenario:

1. Alice lost access to her AmbireAccount so she executes a recovery using DKIMRecoverySigValidator with SigMode.OnlySecond, which gives control over her AmbireAccount to the address she set in SignatureMeta.newKeyToSet

2. A year passes by, Alice rotates her keys and now throws away the old ones

3. Bob replays her previous recovery by slightly changing the canonizedHeaders field which results in that same address (which Alice now doesn't control) to control her AmbireAccount

4. Now Alice has lost control over her wallet and can't recover it, since the recovery is configured to work only for the previously set SignatureMeta.newKeyToSet

title: CompoundV2Connector#_convertSharesToAssets magnitude scalar can be too large and truncate the asset worth
content: The vulnerability resides in the conversion routine that translates cToken shares into an amount of the underlying asset. The routine computes a magnitude as 10 plus the number of decimals of the underlying token and then divides the product of the share balance and the stored exchange rate by 10**magnitude. For tokens such as ETH or DAI that have 18 decimals, magnitude becomes 28, so the division uses 10**28. However cTokens are defined with 8 decimals, meaning the correct divisor should be 10**18. The oversized divisor truncates the resulting asset amount by a factor of 10**10, causing the reported asset worth to be ten orders of magnitude smaller than the actual value. An attacker or any user invoking the redeem function receives far fewer underlying tokens than expected; the UI may show a successful redemption while the wallet balance increases only by a tiny fraction, often appearing as if the funds vanished or the refund is missing. The error manifests whenever the conversion function is called for an underlying token with 18 decimals, which includes the most common assets. It was uncovered during a formal audit by comparing the value computed with exchangeRateStored against the value obtained from exchangeRateCurrent in a Forge test; the logs revealed a consistent ten‑digit shortfall. The bug is subtle because the arithmetic uses large integers and the discrepancy can be mistaken for rounding noise, especially when only the final balance is observed. To remediate, the magnitude should be fixed to 10**18 or derived from the cToken’s fixed 8‑decimal precision rather than the underlying token’s decimals. This aligns the divisor with the token’s actual scaling factor and restores correct accounting of user balances, preventing loss of funds and ensuring that the protocol’s accounting assumptions hold.

title: Complete loss event counter resets to 0 on partial loss
content: The vulnerability is a logical accounting error in the yield calculation module. The function that updates the accumulated yield, loss amount and the counter of complete loss events fails to preserve the existing complete‑loss‑event count when the strategy experiences a partial loss. Because the variable that should hold the new complete‑loss‑event count is never assigned in the partial‑loss branch, it remains at its default value of zero. This mismatch between the strategy’s recorded complete‑loss‑event counter and the counter stored for each position breaks the invariant used by the balance‑calculation routine, which compares the two counters to decide how much yield to credit. The bug manifests only after a partial loss event – for example when a token is burned from the strategy but not fully depleted – and causes the counter to reset from a positive value to zero. From a user’s perspective the vault UI may suddenly show that no loss events have occurred, leading to unexpected balance values such as a zero accrued yield or a reduced payout when withdrawing. The impact is high because the protocol’s accounting assumptions are violated; users may receive less than their entitled amount or, conversely, the protocol may credit excess yield if other checks rely on the counter being monotonic. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit that simulated a series of deposits and alternating full and partial loss events; the test observed the completeLossEvents field moving from 3 to 4 and then unexpectedly to 0. The problem is subtle because the counter behaves correctly for full loss events, so the regression is not obvious in normal operation and may only appear after a specific sequence of partial losses. The correct fix is to ensure that in the partial‑loss path the new complete‑loss‑event counter is explicitly set to the previous counter value, preserving the monotonic property of the counter. In generic terms the bug belongs to the class of state‑reset or counter‑reset errors caused by missing state updates in conditional branches, which break accounting invariants and can lead to fund misallocation.
summary:
YieldMath.calculateAccum() is supposed to calculate updated yield accumulate, loss accumulate and complete loss event counter. However, on a partial loss event, this function doesn't set newStrategyCompleteLossEvents which is the updated complete loss event counter. Thus, it is implicitly set to 0.
This affects yield and balance calculation since YieldMath.calculateBalance() compares number of recorded complete loss events for the position with the number of complete loss events for the strategy.

title: The hint is not fetched properly from lido withdrawal queue and make all lido delayed withdraw revert
content: The vulnerability lies in the way the contract retrieves checkpoint hints for Lido delayed withdrawals. The function findCheckpointHints expects three parameters: a sorted array of request IDs, a first index greater than zero (because the checkpoint list is 1‑based), and a last index that must not exceed the current highest checkpoint index returned by getLastCheckpointIndex(). The calling code builds the last index as requestsToClaim.length + 1, assuming that the number of requests to claim is a safe upper bound. In practice the checkpoint list can be much larger (e.g., 562 checkpoints on mainnet) while the request array may contain only a few elements. When the supplied last index is smaller than the actual last checkpoint, the function returns a hint value of zero; when the supplied last index is larger than the real last checkpoint, the call reverts. Because the withdrawal logic relies on a non‑zero hint to locate the correct checkpoint, a zero hint causes the withdrawal transaction to revert, and a revert from the hint query aborts the whole operation. Consequently any user attempting a delayed withdrawal receives a transaction failure and sees no funds transferred, effectively locking their staked ETH. The issue manifests whenever the contract processes a batch of withdrawal requests whose length does not match the global checkpoint range, which is the typical case for most users. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that compared the documented requirements of findCheckpointHints with the actual parameters passed in the contract. It is subtle because the function call succeeds silently when the last index is too small, returning an empty hint that later triggers a revert deeper in the call stack, making the failure appear as a generic withdrawal error rather than a hint‑related problem. The root cause is an incorrect assumption about the relationship between the number of withdrawal requests and the checkpoint index range, combined with a missing validation that the last index respects getLastCheckpointIndex(). To remediate the issue, the calling code should first sort the request IDs, then pass getLastCheckpointIndex() as the _lastIndex argument (or otherwise ensure that the supplied last index is never greater than the actual checkpoint count). This change guarantees that findCheckpointHints returns a valid hint for each request, allowing withdrawals to complete as intended and preventing funds from becoming inaccessible.
summary:
```solidity
uint256[] memory hints = _queue.findCheckpointHints(requestsToClaim, 1, requestsToClaim.length + 1);
```
The hints is fetched using the code above. According to the code and docs:
```solidity
function findCheckpointHints(uint256[] _requestIds, uint256 _firstIndex, uint256 _lastIndex)
view
returns (uint256[] hintIds)
```
Requirements:
- Array of request ids must be sorted
- firstIndex must be greater than 0, because checkpoint list is 1-based array
- _lastIndex must be less than or equal to getLastCheckpointIndex()
Note how the _lastIndex is passed in. The last index is passed as requestsToClaim.length + 1, not getLastCheckpointIndex().
• Case 1: requestsToClaim.length < getLastCheckpointIndex():
Assume user wants to withdraw 5 requests and the requestsToClaim.length + 1 will be 6, but the current getLastCheckpointIndex() returns 562 (see contract 0x889edc...12f9b1 on Ethereum mainnet).
Then the hints will always be 0.
• Case 2: requestsToClaim.length > getLastCheckpointIndex():
This case is rare, but the transaction just reverts when querying the hint. We can work through an example (see transaction 0xcaee15...7f20ba on Ethereum mainnet).
This is a withdrawal transaction:
Request id: 59498
hints: 555
If we query findCheckpointsHints in the contract 0x889edc...12f9b1, we pass in:
Request id: 59498
first index: 1
last index: 2
we get 0, the last index is too short and we get no hints. The getLastCheckpointIndex() is 562. We pass in:
Request id: 59498
first index: 1
last index: 562
We get the hint value 555 correctly, which matches the withdrawal hint. But if we pass in:
Request id: 59498
first index: 1
last index: 600
In this case, last index > getLastCheckpointIndex(), the transaction query just reverts.

title: Donated reward token can overflow the yieldAccumulator and revert user withdraw transaction
content: The vulnerability resides in the accounting logic of the EarnVault contract where the variable that tracks accumulated rewards – often called a yieldAccumulator – is updated by adding the amount of newly donated reward tokens. Because the accumulator is stored in a fixed‑size unsigned integer, an excessively large reward amount can cause the addition to overflow the maximum representable value. When the overflow occurs the contract’s arithmetic check (or an implicit Solidity overflow check in newer compiler versions) triggers a revert, which aborts the subsequent withdraw call. This means that a legitimate user who attempts to withdraw their position after a large reward donation will see the transaction fail, their balance remain unchanged, and the UI may report that the withdrawal returned no funds or that the operation reverted. The issue is triggered only when the reward token amount is large enough to push the accumulator past its limit; normal reward sizes do not cause a problem. It was discovered during a unit‑test that deliberately minted a very high amount of a secondary ERC‑20 token (100 000 ether) and then performed a withdraw, causing the test to revert. The bug is subtle because the overflow only manifests under extreme reward conditions, which may not be exercised in routine operation, and the revert surface appears as a generic transaction failure rather than an obvious arithmetic error. Conceptually, the flaw belongs to the class of arithmetic overflow bugs in financial accounting contracts, where cumulative state variables are not protected against exceeding their numeric bounds. To remediate the issue the accumulator should be updated using safe‑math checks that cap the value at the maximum or switch to a larger integer type (e.g., uint256 with explicit overflow protection) and the contract should gracefully handle cases where the reward amount would exceed the accumulator capacity, perhaps by scaling down rewards or resetting the accumulator safely. Fixing the overflow restores the expected behavior where users receive their full withdrawable balance and the protocol’s accounting remains consistent with its business logic of rewarding depositors.

title: ExternalFee contract treats newly deposit vault share as yield and charge performance fee on user deposit amount immediately
content: The vulnerability resides in the fee handling logic of an ExternalFee contract that is attached to an ERC4626‑based vault. The contract is designed to charge a performance fee only on genuine yield generated by the strategy, but it mistakenly treats newly deposited vault shares as if they were already earned yield. When a user deposits ERC4626 shares directly (instead of depositing the underlying token), the fee routine queries the current balance of the underlying asset, which is zero because the strategy holds no assets yet. It then adds the amount of newly minted shares to this balance and records the sum as the new lastBalance. Immediately afterwards the contract calculates the performance fee based on the difference between the previous balance (zero) and the new balance (the full deposit amount). Consequently, the full deposit amount is considered profit and the performance fee – for example 500 basis points – is deducted from the user’s position at the moment of deposit. From the user’s perspective the expected behaviour is that the entire deposited amount is available for earning yield, yet the UI shows a reduced balance (e.g., a 5 % loss) and the user receives less than what was sent. The issue is triggered only when the performance fee parameter is non‑zero, the strategy holds no underlying assets, and the deposit is made using vault shares rather than the underlying token. It affects any depositor who uses the share‑deposit path, leading to immediate financial loss and a breach of the protocol’s accounting assumptions that fees apply only to actual profit. The flaw was uncovered during a formal audit by Spearbit, which added a mock performance fee of 500 bps and observed that the deposited amounts (100 000, 200 000, 50 000) were reduced to 93 389, 196 609, 49 999 respectively after the fee was applied. The problem is subtle because the fee calculation appears to work correctly for normal yield scenarios, making the mis‑charge easy to miss in routine testing. To remediate, the fee routine must be altered so that newly minted shares are excluded from the performance‑fee base – for instance by clearing the lastBalance before processing a share deposit, or by computing fees solely on the increase of the underlying asset balance, not on the share amount. This ensures that performance fees are only levied on genuine yield and that depositor balances reflect the amount actually contributed.

title: Users can manipulate the NFT chosen for the auction
content: The vulnerability allows a participant to influence which NFT is selected for an auction by manipulating the order and size of the auction queue between the moment a random number is requested and the moment the auction is created. The contract computes the index of the NFT to be auctioned as the remainder of the random number divided by the current length of the auction queue (randomIndex = uint256(randomNumber) % auctionQueue.length). Because the request for the random number and the actual receipt of that number occur in separate transactions, an attacker can front‑run the auction creation transaction and either add a new NFT to the queue or remove and re‑insert an existing NFT to change the queue length or the position of their own token. When the random number happens to be equal to the original queue length or one less than it, the modulo operation yields an index that points to the first or last element of the original queue. By increasing the queue length by one, the same modulo calculation now points to the newly added element, which can be the attacker’s NFT. In the second scenario the attacker moves his NFT to the last slot after the random number has been generated; the modulo result stays the same, so the attacker’s NFT is still selected. This manipulation can be performed without altering the random number itself, merely by changing the mutable state of the queue. The impact is that the auction no longer fairly selects a random NFT; instead the attacker can guarantee that his own NFT is the one being auctioned, potentially depriving other participants of expected assets and undermining the economic assumptions of the protocol. The issue manifests only under the specific edge cases where the random number equals the queue length or length‑1, making it easy to miss during testing because the modulo operation appears correct for typical values. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the interaction between random number generation and queue management logic. The bug is hard to notice because the code uses a standard modulo pattern, and the queue is assumed to be immutable during auction creation, an assumption that is violated by front‑running. To remediate, the contract should prevent any addition or removal of NFTs from the auction queue while an auction is being created, for example by locking the queue state during the _createAuction call, by moving the random number generation into the same transaction that finalises the queue, or by employing a commit‑reveal scheme that binds the queue composition before the random index is calculated. This eliminates the ability for an attacker to manipulate the selected NFT and restores the intended fairness of the auction process.
summary:
To create an auction, a random number is generated which is used to determine the index of the NFT auctioned off from the auctionQueue . If the random number is equal to the length of the auction queue or if the random number is 1 less than the length of the auction queue, users can manipulate the NFT chosen in their favor.
Firstly, let's imagine the first scenario:
An auction will be created with the random number 5 and there are 5 NFTs in the auction queue
Due to the line below, we will auction off the NFT with index of 0:
```solidity
uint256 randomIndex = uint256(randomNumber) % auctionQueue.length;
```
However, a user frontruns the auction creation and puts his NFT in the auction queue causing the index of the NFT to instead equal 5 % 6 = 5 which is his NFT
Now, let's imagine the other scenario:
An auction will be created with the random number of 5 and there are 6 NFTs in the auction queue
Due to the line above, the index of the to-be-auctioned NFT will be 5 % 6 = 5 or in other words, the last NFT will be auctioned off
However, a user who has already put his NFT in the queue frontruns the auction creation and does the following:
Take out his NFT from the queue
Put it back in
Now the NFT has gone from slot x in the queue to the last spot, the index of the to-be-auctioned NFT will still be the same which results in the user who conducted the sequence above, being the owner of the auctioned NFT.

title: The attacker can exit the queue after requesting a random
content: The vulnerability is an abuse of the auction queue logic that allows an attacker to trigger a random‑number request, then withdraw the queued NFT before the randomness is delivered, causing the contract to create an empty auction while still paying the Pyth fee. The root cause is that the contract does not lock a queued entry or enforce a fee when a participant exits the queue after a random request has been issued. An attacker can enqueue an NFT, call settleCurrentAndCreateNewAuction which requests entropy from Pyth, and, before Pyth calls back entropyCallback, call the function that removes the NFT from the queue. When the callback finally executes, the contract believes a valid auction should be created, but the queue is now empty, so the auction contains no assets. The contract has already spent the fee required to obtain the random number, so each cycle wastes funds and produces a useless auction. This can be repeated indefinitely with the same NFT, draining the contract’s balance allocated for randomness fees and effectively denying service to legitimate users. The issue occurs only when there are available seats in the auctionQueue, i.e., when the contract follows the first auction‑creation path that relies on Pyth randomness. Users are affected because they expect a new auction to contain their NFT and to be able to bid, but instead they see an auction with no items and notice that the contract’s treasury is slowly emptying. The problem was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the state transitions around queue management and entropy callbacks. It is hard to notice because the contract still creates an auction object, so the UI may simply show an empty auction without obvious error messages, and the fee loss is not directly visible on‑chain without detailed accounting. To remediate, the contract should either prevent participants from exiting the queue after a random request has been sent, or impose a penalty fee for such an exit, or redesign the flow so that the auction is only instantiated after confirming that the queued entry still exists. Conceptually, this is a race‑condition / state‑inconsistency bug where the contract’s accounting assumptions about queued assets are violated by an out‑of‑order state change, leading to fund loss and broken business logic around auction creation and fairness.
summary:
There are two situations when the ApiologyAuctionHouse contract creates an auction:
1. When there are seats in the auctionQueue , it will request a random number from Pyth. After Pyth generates the random number, it will call back the entropyCallback function to create the auction. The specific process is as follows.
1. (tx1) User calls ApiologyAuctionHouse.settleCurrentAndCreateNewAuction
2. (tx1) ApiologyAuctionHouse requests random numbers from Pyth and pay some fees to Pyth
3. (off-chain) Pyth generates random numbers
4. (tx2) Pyth calls ApiologyAuctionHouse.entropyCallback create the auction
2. When there are no seats in the auctionQueue , the auction is generated directly.
The problem exists in the first scenario. The attacker can put the NFT into the queue first, and then remove the NFT from the queue before Pyth generates the random number. This results in that every time settleCurrentAndCreateNewAuction is called, it will request a random number from Pyth, wasting the contract's funds and then creating an empty auction.
An attacker can use an NFT to repeatedly trigger this bug and consume the funds in the contract.

title: Incorrect usage of msg.value in iterative native token distribution
content: The vulnerability is an arithmetic miscalculation in the factory contract when distributing native token value across multiple cross‑chain messages during DAO creation. The function createERC20DAO iterates over the list of destination chain IDs and, for each iteration, forwards a portion of the transaction's msg.value to the communication layer using the expression (msg.value - fees) / (_depositChainIds.length - (i + 1)). This formula assumes that the full original msg.value (minus a static fee amount) is still available for every iteration, but it does not subtract the amount that has already been sent in previous loops. As a result, the remaining balance shrinks with each iteration while the divisor also changes, causing the calculated share to become progressively smaller than intended. When the number of destination chains is greater than one, later iterations may receive insufficient native token value, leading to failed sendMsg calls, incomplete cross‑chain messages, or under‑payment of required fees. The root cause is the failure to track and update the remaining native token pool after each distribution, a classic cumulative allocation bug. Exploitation is straightforward: an attacker or even an honest user can trigger the DAO creation with a modest msg.value that appears sufficient, but because the contract over‑estimates the available funds for later hops, the transaction reverts or silently drops messages on some chains. The impact includes partial DAO deployment, missing cross‑chain notifications, and potential loss of funds that are consumed as fees while the intended payload receives zero value. This condition occurs only when the deposit chain ID array contains more than one element and native token transfers are used; it does not affect single‑chain deployments. All participants who rely on the DAO being fully instantiated across the specified chains—depositors, DAO creators, and the protocol itself—are affected because the expected state consistency is broken. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit of factory.sol, where the loop logic and division expression were examined and identified as inconsistent with proper accounting. It can be hard to notice because the first few iterations may succeed, giving the impression that the operation works, while later iterations fail only after the transaction has already consumed gas and fees, producing a confusing partial‑success symptom. From a user’s perspective, the UI may report that the DAO was created, but the user sees no funds arriving on some target chains, or the transaction may revert after processing a subset of chains, leaving the user with a reduced balance and no clear error message. The bug belongs to the class of iterative fund distribution errors, where cumulative state is not correctly updated, leading to arithmetic under‑allocation. To remediate, the contract should store the remaining native token amount in a local variable, compute each iteration’s share based on that remaining balance, deduct the sent amount after each call, and use the updated remainder for the next iteration. This ensures that the total value sent across all iterations equals the original msg.value minus the required fees, preserving the intended accounting and preventing under‑funded cross‑chain messages.
summary:
In the factory::createERC20DAO function, when the _depositChainIds array has more than one element, the function iterates over the chain IDs to send messages using the commLayer::sendMsg function. A portion of the native token value (msg.value) is calculated and sent in each iteration using the formula (msg.value - fees) / (_depositChainIds.length - (i + 1)).
However, the calculation does not account for the diminishing msg.value as fees are deducted in each iteration. This might lead to incorrect fee distribution for the message transfers and possibly result in insufficient funds for subsequent message transfers.
File: factory.sol
```solidity
243: if (_depositChainIds.length > 1) {
244:     for (uint256 i; i < _depositChainIds.length - 1;) {
245:         require(_depositTokenAddress[i + 1] != NATIVE_TOKEN_ADDRESS, "Native not supported");
246:         bytes memory _payload = abi.encode(
247:             _commLayerId,
248:             _distributionAmount,
249:             amountToSD(_depositTokenAddress[0], _pricePerToken),
250:             amountToSD(_depositTokenAddress[0], _minDepositPerUser),
251:             amountToSD(_depositTokenAddress[0], _maxDepositPerUser),
252:             _ownerFeePerDepositPercent,
253:             _depositTime,
254:             _quorumPercent,
255:             _thresholdPercent,
256:             _safeThreshold,
257:             _depositChainIds,
258:             _daoAddress,
259:             _depositTokenAddress[i + 1],
260:             _admins,
261:             _onlyAllowWhitelist,
262:             _merkleRoot,
263:             0,
264:             msg.sender
265:         );
266:         ICommLayer(commLayer).sendMsg{value: (msg.value - fees) / (_depositChainIds.length - (i + 1))}(
267:             commLayer, _payload, abi.encode(_depositChainIds[i + 1], msg.sender)
268:         );
269:         unchecked {
270:             ++i;
271:         }
272:     }
274:     IEmitter(emitterAddress).createCCDao(_daoAddress, _depositChainIds);
275: }
```
Each call to sendMsg should account for the portion of msg.value that has already been distributed in previous iterations. Failing to do so can result in insufficient funds being sent for each subsequent message, leading to failures or incomplete operations.

title: Reversion in ApiologyDAOToken transfer due to insufficient governance tokens
content: The vulnerability originates from a mutable global parameter that defines how many governance tokens must be burned for each NFT transferred to the liquid backing treasury or auction house. The contract owner can change this parameter through a function that only checks that the new amount is greater than zero. During a transfer, the contract calls an internal burn routine that multiplies the current parameter by the number of NFTs being moved. If the owner raises the parameter, a user who holds an NFT may no longer possess enough governance tokens to satisfy the burn calculation. The ERC20 burn call then reverts due to insufficient balance, causing the entire NFT transfer to fail. This failure blocks the user from adding the NFT to the auction queue, effectively locking the asset because the auction mechanism is the sole path for selling. Conversely, if the owner lowers the parameter, the burn routine destroys fewer governance tokens than required by the original accounting model, leaving the user with excess governance tokens that should have been burned. The root cause is the reliance on a mutable constant for accounting without reconciling existing user balances or providing a safety check before burning. The issue is triggered whenever an NFT is transferred from a regular address to the treasury or auction house after the parameter has been altered. Affected parties include NFT holders, bidders, and any participant that relies on the auction house to liquidate assets, as well as the governance system that assumes a one‑to‑one relationship between NFTs and burned tokens. The problem was discovered during a security audit that examined the interaction between the parameter‑changing function and the burn logic. It can be hard to notice because the transaction simply reverts with a generic error, offering no clear indication that the failure is due to insufficient governance tokens. From a user perspective the UI shows a failed transfer, the NFT does not appear in the auction queue, and the governance token balance may either stay unchanged or retain extra tokens, contradicting the expectation that the transfer should succeed and the token balance should be correctly adjusted. This class of bug falls under mutable‑parameter accounting errors where a global variable influences token burning or minting, leading to under‑ or over‑burn conditions. To remediate, the contract should either prevent the owner from changing the parameter without first reconciling all user balances, implement a snapshot of each holder’s entitlement at the time of transfer, or add logic that automatically tops up or burns the exact amount required after a parameter change, ensuring that the burn operation never reverts due to insufficient balance and that governance token accounting remains consistent.

title: Potential overwriting of auction storage leading to loss of auctioned tokens
content: The vulnerability consists of an unchecked overwrite of the contract's auction storage when the entropyCallback function is invoked while a previous auction has not been settled. The contract relies on a random number supplied by an external Entropy contract to initialise a new auction; the callback creates a fresh AuctionV2 struct and assigns it directly to the single auctionStorage variable. Because the code does not verify that the existing auction is settled before writing the new struct, a second callback – which can be triggered in a separate transaction if the Entropy provider calls back more than once or if the owner repeatedly pauses and unpauses the contract – overwrites the previously stored token identifier, bid amount and other auction parameters. This race‑condition‑like behaviour leads to the loss of the token that was being auctioned and the associated bid funds, effectively making the funds disappear from the protocol's perspective. The issue manifests when the contract is unpaused, a random‑number request is pending, and the Entropy contract invokes the callback before the earlier auction has been marked as settled. Users experience a missing or empty auction UI, see a zero balance for the token they expected to be sold, and cannot retrieve their bid because the stored data has been erased. The problem was identified during a security audit that examined the flow of entropyCallback and noticed that the function does not guard against multiple invocations. It is hard to notice because the overwrite occurs silently without emitting an explicit error event; the contract simply presents a new, empty auction. The bug belongs to the class of state‑overwrite or race‑condition vulnerabilities where a critical storage slot is rewritten without proper state validation.
