The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined fee handling logic and noticed that the amount sent to the router did not match the net amount after fee deduction. It can be hard to notice because the discrepancy may be a few wei or token units, appearing as a rounding error rather than a systematic over‑payment. From a user perspective the UI may display the expected loan amount, yet the transaction results in the borrower receiving the full amount, creating confusion and potential distrust. The proper remediation is to adjust the transfer logic so that only the net amount (1‑np/dp)·T is sent to the router, ensuring the fee is correctly deducted before the borrower receives funds and preserving the protocol’s accounting guarantees.
summary:
totalBorrowed is the sum of all commitments[i].lienRequest.amount But if s.feeTo is set, some of funds/assets from the vaults get transferred to s.feeTo when _handleProtocolFee is called and only the remaining is sent to ROUTER(). So in this scenario, the total amount of assets sent to ROUTER() (so that it can be transferred to msg.sender) is up to rounding errors:  
(1 − np/dp)T  
Where:  
• T is the totalBorrowed  
• np is s.protocolFeeNumerator  
• dp is s.protocolFeeDenominator  
But we are transferring T to msg.sender which is more than we are supposed to send.

title: Withdraw proxy's claim() endpoint updates public vault's yIntercept incorrectly.
content: The vulnerability resides in the claim() function of the withdraw proxy, where the routine that updates the public vault's y‑intercept (y0) uses an incorrect arithmetic expression. The y‑intercept is a core accounting variable that tracks the net amount of assets that should be available to users after each epoch. The current implementation only adjusts y0 when the expression En‑1‑(Bn‑1‑Wn‑1) is positive and then subtracts a portion of En‑1, effectively ignoring the positive contribution of the assets transferred from the previous withdraw proxy to the public vault. As a result, y0 is decremented by max(0,En‑1‑(Bn‑1‑Wn‑1))·(1‑Sn‑1/Sv) instead of being updated with the mathematically correct formula y0 = y0 ‑ En‑1 + (Bn‑1‑Wn‑1)·(1‑Sn‑1/Sv). This mis‑calculation can cause the vault’s accounting to drift downward over successive epochs, leading to a situation where users who expect to receive a refund or withdrawable balance see a reduced amount, sometimes even zero, despite the contract having sufficient underlying assets. The bug manifests whenever claim() is called after an epoch transition, particularly when the amount received by the withdraw proxy (Bn‑1‑Wn‑1) exceeds the epoch‑specific liability En‑1 or when the condition En‑1‑(Bn‑1‑Wn‑1)>0 does not hold. Because the error is tied to a conditional subtraction and rounding effects, it may remain hidden during normal operation and only become apparent through careful balance reconciliation or when large liquidation auctions generate unusually high payments. The issue was discovered during a formal security audit (Spearbit) that compared the implemented formula against the protocol’s economic specification. It is hard to notice because the deviation can be small and may not trigger obvious revert messages; instead, it silently skews the internal accounting state. The impact is high risk: inaccurate y0 values can lead to under‑allocation of funds, users receiving less than they are owed, and potential insolvency of the public vault if the drift accumulates. To remediate, the claim() logic must be changed to apply the correct update expression, adding the transferred asset portion and subtracting the full epoch liability as specified, thereby preserving the intended accounting invariants and ensuring that users receive the correct balances.
summary:
Let:  
parameter description  
y0 the yIntercept of our public vault in the question.  
n the current epoch for the public vault.  
En−1 the expected storage parameter of the previous withdraw proxy.  
Bn−1 the asset balance of the previous withdraw proxy.  
Wn−1 the withdrawReserveReceived of the previous withdraw proxy.  
Sn−1 the total supply of the previous withdraw proxy.  
Sv the total supply of the public vault when processEpoch() was last called on the public vault.  
Bv the total balance of the public vault when processEpoch() was last called on the public vault.  
V the public vault.  
parameter description  
Pn−1 the previous withdraw proxy.

Then y0 is updated/decremented according to the formula (up to rounding errors due to division):  
y0 = y0 − max(0, En−1 − (Bn−1 − Wn−1))(1 − Sn−1/Sv)  
Whereas the amount (A) of assets transferred from Pn−1 to V is  
A = (Bn−1 − Wn−1)(1 − Sn−1/Sv)  
And the amount (B) of asset left in Pn−1 after this transfer would be:  
B = Wn−1 + (Bn−1 − Wn−1)Sn−1/Sv

(Bn−1 − Wn−1) is supposed to represent the payment withdrawal proxy receives from Seaport auctions plus the amount of assets transferred to it by external actors. So A represents the portion of this amount for users who have not withdrawn from the public vault on the previous epoch and it is transferred to V and so y0 should be compensated positively. Also note that this amount might be bigger than En−1 if a lien has a really high liquidationInitialAsk and its auction fulfills/matches near that price on Seaport. So it is possible that En−1 < A.  
The current update formula for updating the y0 has the following flaws:  
• It only considers updating y0 when En−1 − (Bn−1 − Wn−1) > 0 which is not always the case.  
• Decrements y0 by a portion of En−1.  
The correct updating formula for y0 should be:  
y0 = y0 − En−1 + (Bn−1 − Wn−1)(1 − Sn−1/Sv)  
Also note, if we let Bn−1 − Wn−1 = Xn−1 + ε, where Xn−1 is the payment received by the withdraw proxy from Seaport auction payments and ε (if Wn−1 updated correctly) be assets received from external actors by the previous withdraw proxy. Then:  
B = Wn−1 + (Xn−1 + ε)Sn−1/Sv = [max(0, Bv − En−1) + Xn−1 + ε]Sn−1/Sv  
The last equality comes from the fact that when the withdraw reserves is fully transferred from the public vault and the current withdraw proxy (if necessary) to the previous withdraw proxy the amount Wn−1 would hold should be max(0, Bv − En−1)Sn−1/Sv.  
Related Issue.

title: Public vault's yIntercept is not updated when the full amount owed is not paid out by a Seaport auction.
content: The vulnerability originates from an accounting inconsistency in the public vault implementation that uses a linear function characterised by a y‑intercept to compute the vault's total assets. When a collateral lien is settled through a Seaport auction, the ClearingHouse contract receives a callback containing the amount actually paid out. If the auction does not cover the full amount owed and the payee of the proceeds is a public vault, the contract fails to adjust the y‑intercept by the shortfall (amountOwed ‑ paymentReceived). Because the y‑intercept remains unchanged, the public vault’s totalAssets() function continues to report a value that assumes the full debt has been repaid, effectively inflating the reported balance. This flaw can be exploited by triggering a partial‑payment scenario—such as submitting a low bid to the auction—so that the vault believes it still holds the full amount owed. An attacker can then withdraw or claim assets based on the overstated balance, leading to a loss of funds for honest users and a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees. The issue only manifests when three conditions are met simultaneously: the payee is a public vault, the Seaport auction callback is executed, and the payment received is less than the amount owed. Users of the vault, including depositors and any role that can request withdrawals, are affected because they may see a higher balance than actually exists, experience unexpected token transfers, or find that their funds disappear after a malicious withdrawal. The bug was discovered during a manual security review by the Spearbit audit team, who noticed that the y‑intercept update logic was guarded by a condition that assumed full repayment. The problem is subtle because in normal operation where auctions fully satisfy the debt, the totalAssets calculation appears correct, making the discrepancy easy to miss unless a partial‑payment edge case is exercised. To remediate the issue, the contract should always invoke a decreaseYIntercept routine with the exact difference between the amount owed and the amount actually received whenever a partial payout occurs. Adding invariant checks that validate the consistency of totalAssets against the underlying debt after each callback would further reduce the risk of similar accounting errors. In summary, the bug is a classic case of an accounting state variable not being updated after a conditional financial event, leading to inflated asset reporting and potential fund loss.
summary: When the full amountOwed for a lien is not paid out during the callback from Seaport to a collateral's ClearingHouse and if the payee is a public vault, we would need to decrement the yIntercept, otherwise the payee.totalAssets() would reflect a wrong value.

title: LienToken payee not reset on transfer
content: The vulnerability is a state‑inconsistency bug in the LienToken ERC‑721 implementation where the address designated to receive lien payments (the payee) is stored separately from the token owner and is not automatically cleared or updated when the token is transferred. The root cause is that the transferFrom function does not reset the payee field in the lien metadata, leaving the previous owner’s address in the payee slot. An attacker can exploit this by first setting themselves as the payee while they still own the token, then selling or transferring the token to an unsuspecting buyer. Because the payee remains unchanged, all subsequent payment streams that the protocol routes to the lien are sent to the old owner’s address instead of the new owner. The impact is that the new token holder receives no funds, sees their expected payouts disappear, and may lose financial value associated with the lien, while the previous owner continues to collect the payments. This condition occurs every time a token is transferred without an explicit payee reset, regardless of whether the lien is in liquidation or not. The affected parties include token owners, lenders relying on the payment flow, and the overall protocol that assumes ownership and payment rights are aligned. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the separation of owner and payee state variables and noted the missing reset logic. It can be hard to notice because user interfaces typically display only the token owner, not the payee, so a buyer may not see that the payment address is still pointing to the seller. The bug violates the business logic that ownership transfer should also transfer the right to receive payments, breaking accounting assumptions and leading to funds disappearing from the new owner’s perspective. To remediate, the contract should clear the payee field (or set it to the new owner) during transfer, emit an appropriate PayeeChanged event, and enforce that any subsequent payment routing uses the updated payee address, thereby restoring the intended alignment between token ownership and payment rights.
summary:
payee and ownerOf are detached in that owners may set payee and owner may transfer the LienToken to a new owner. payee does not reset on transfer.  
Exploit scenario:  
• Owner of a LienToken sets themselves as payee  
• Owner of LienToken sells the lien to a new owner  
• New owner does not update payee  
• Payments go to address set by old owner

title: WithdrawProxy allows redemptions before PublicVault calls transferWithdrawReserve
content: The vulnerability resides in the WithdrawProxy contract’s redemption logic, which permits holders of WithdrawProxy shares to redeem their tokens as long as the contract reports a positive totalAssets() value and the auction end flag s.finalAuctionEnd is still zero. Under normal operation the PublicVault calls transferWithdrawReserve, which populates the withdraw reserve and makes totalAssets() reflect the true amount owed to each share. However, totalAssets() can also become non‑zero simply by any address sending WETH directly to the WithdrawProxy contract. An attacker can exploit this by depositing a small amount of WETH, causing totalAssets() to be greater than zero before the official reserve transfer occurs. A depositor who later redeems their shares—whether by accident or through a phishing trick—receives a proportion of the artificially inflated totalAssets, which is smaller than the amount they are entitled to because the real withdraw reserve has not yet been transferred. After the PublicVault eventually processes the epoch and sends the full withdraw reserve to WithdrawProxy, the remaining share holders receive an outsized portion, effectively compensating the earlier underpayment but at the expense of the early redeemer. The impact is a loss of value for users who redeem prematurely, breaking the accounting guarantees of the protocol and leading to an uneven distribution of funds. This condition occurs only when there is a pending withdrawal (i.e., WithdrawProxy shares exist) and the contract’s totalAssets() is made positive by an external WETH transfer before s.withdrawReserveReceived is set. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the state checks governing redemption. It is subtle because the presence of a positive totalAssets() appears to be a reasonable indicator that funds are available, masking the fact that the reserve has not been properly initialized. To remediate, the contract should require that the withdraw reserve has been received—e.g., by checking that s.withdrawReserveReceived is non‑zero—or otherwise ensure that redemption is only allowed after transferWithdrawReserve has been executed. This change prevents premature redemptions and preserves the intended one‑to‑one relationship between shares and underlying assets, eliminating the possibility of users receiving less than they are owed and maintaining the protocol’s financial integrity.
summary:
Anytime there is a withdraw pending (i.e. someone holds WithdrawProxy shares), shares may be redeemed so long as totalAssets() > 0 and s.finalAuctionEnd == 0.  
Under normal operating conditions totalAssets() becomes greater than 0 when the PublicVault calls transferWithdrawReserve.  
totalAssets() can also be increased to a non-zero value by anyone transferring WETH to the contract.  
If this occurs and a user attempts to redeem, they will receive a smaller share than they are owed.  
Exploit scenario:  
• Depositor redeems from PublicVault and receives WithdrawProxy shares.  
• Malicious actor deposits a small amount of WETH into the WithdrawProxy.  
• Depositor accidentally redeems, or is tricked into redeeming, from the WithdrawProxy while totalAssets() is smaller than it should be.  
• PublicVault properly processes epoch and full withdrawReserve is sent to WithdrawProxy.  
• All remaining holders of WithdrawProxy shares receive an outsized share as the previous shares were redeemed for the incorrect value.

title: VaultImplementation.buyoutLien does not update the new public vault's parameters and does not transfer assets between the vault and the borrower
content: The vulnerability resides in the buyoutLien function of the VaultImplementation contract. When a caller attempts to buy out an existing lien on a public vault, the function creates a new lien but fails to update the public vault's accounting parameters. Specifically the linear pricing variables slope and yIntercept, as well as the epoch‑specific counter of open liens (s.epochData[...].liensOpenForEpoch) for the epoch in which the new lien expires, remain unchanged. The code does update these fields for the payee of the swapped‑out lien via handleBuyoutLien, but it never performs the analogous update for the vault that executed buyoutLien. As a result the vault’s internal model of its exposure diverges from the actual state of its liens. In addition, the function pays the buyout amount directly from the vault but does not reconcile the net difference between the amount paid to the previous lien holder and the amount required for the newly created lien. If the buyout amount is higher than the new lien amount, the caller should transfer the excess wETH to the vault; if the new lien amount is higher, the vault should transfer the shortfall back to the caller. Because this settlement step is omitted, either the caller or the vault may retain or lose wETH without any on‑chain record of the transfer. The bug manifests only when buyoutLien is invoked on a public vault, a scenario that is common in protocols that allow third‑party participants to purchase liens. Users see a successful transaction and may receive the expected payout, but the vault’s parameters stay stale, leading to incorrect future calculations of interest, collateral requirements, or liquidation thresholds. Over time this accounting drift can cause the protocol to under‑collateralize positions, allow an attacker to exploit stale pricing, or simply lock funds that appear to have vanished from the user’s perspective. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the state‑transition logic of lien buyouts. It is hard to notice because the transaction does not revert and the UI reports a successful buyout, while the hidden accounting fields are silently incorrect. The proper remediation is to add explicit updates of slope, yIntercept, and the epoch‑level open‑lien counter for the public vault whenever a new lien is minted, and to introduce a settlement step that transfers the net difference between the buyout amount and the new lien amount between the caller and the vault, ensuring that the total wETH balance remains consistent with the recorded accounting.
summary: VaultImplementation.buyoutLien does not update the accounting for the vault (if it's public). The slope, yIntercept, and s.epochData[...].liensOpenForEpoch (for the new lien's end epoch) are not updated. They are updated for the payee of the swapped-out lien if the payee is a public vault by calling handleBuyoutLien. Also, the buyout amount is paid out by the vault itself. The difference between the new lien amount and the buyout amount is not worked out between the msg.sender and the new vault.

title: setPayee doesn't update y intercept or slope, allowing vault owner to steal all funds
content: The vulnerability originates from the setPayee() function, which changes the designated recipient of a lien payment without updating the accounting parameters that represent the vault’s financial position – specifically the y‑intercept and the slope used in the totalAssets() calculation. Because these parameters remain tied to the original vault even after the payee is switched to an external address, the vault’s reported total assets can be artificially inflated. An attacker who controls the vault can exploit this by creating a lien, calling setPayee() to point the lien to a non‑vault address, and then buying out the lien from another vault. The buyout operation increases the y‑intercept and slope of the counter‑party vault, but the original vault’s accounting values stay unchanged due to a check that only updates when the payee is a public vault. By repeating the cycle in both directions, the attacker can raise the totalAssets() of each involved vault to any desired amount. When the epoch settlement runs, withdrawal shares are converted to actual token amounts using the ratio totalAssets()/totalShares(). An inflated totalAssets() therefore yields a withdrawal rate that can exceed the real pool balance, allowing the vault owner to withdraw more than their proportional share and potentially drain the entire vault. This condition can be triggered at any epoch, especially when the attacker is the sole withdrawer in that epoch, making the exploit immediate and devastating. The issue affects vault owners, token holders who rely on correct accounting, and the overall protocol’s financial integrity. It was discovered during a manual security review that identified the mismatch between payee updates and accounting state. The bug is subtle because the vault’s external view of totalAssets() may still appear plausible, while the internal accounting is corrupted, making it hard to detect without deep inspection of the payee‑related state changes. The proper remediation is to adjust both the y‑intercept and the slope of the old payee and the new payee atomically whenever setPayee() is called, ensuring that the financial model stays consistent with the actual beneficiary of the lien. This class of bug falls under improper state synchronization after a role or beneficiary change, leading to accounting distortion and unauthorized fund extraction.
summary:
When setPayee() is called, the payment for the lien is no longer expected to go to the vault. However, this change doesn't impact the vault's y-intercept or slope, which are used to calculate the vault's totalAssets().  
This can be used maliciously by a vault owner to artificially increase their totalAssets() to any arbitrary amount:  
• Create a lien from the vault.  
• SetPayee to a non-vault address.  
• Buyout the lien from another vault (this will cause the other vault's y-int and slope to increase, but will not impact the y-int and slope of the original vault because it'll fail the check on L165 that payee is a public vault.  
• Repeat the process again going the other way, and repeat the full cycle until both vault's have desired totalAssets().  
For an existing vault, a vault owner can withdraw a small amount of assets each epoch. If, in any epoch, they are one of the only users withdrawing funds, they can perform this attack immediately before the epoch is processed. The result is that the withdrawal shares will by multiplied by totalAssets() / totalShares() to get the withdrawal rate, which can be made artificially high enough to wipe out the entire vault.

title: settleAuction() doesn't check if the auction was successful
content: The vulnerability resides in the settleAuction function, which is intended to be executed only after a Seaport auction for a collateralized NFT has been successfully completed. The function is invoked by the privileged LienToken.payDebtViaClearingHouse workflow, but it lacks any verification that the auction actually succeeded or that the collateral token still owns the underlying NFT. Because of this missing state validation, an attacker can craft a fake Seaport order that lists the CollateralToken as one of its consideration items and trigger settleAuction without a real auction outcome. When settleAuction runs, the protocol assumes the auction was successful and proceeds to transfer or release the collateral according to its internal accounting logic. This can result in the collateral being transferred to an unauthorized party, or the protocol marking the debt as settled while the borrower still retains the NFT, effectively breaking the accounting invariants of the system. The issue manifests whenever settleAuction is called, either directly or indirectly through payDebtViaClearingHouse, because there is no check that collateralIdToAuction[collateralId] is active or that the CollateralToken does not already own the NFT. Users experience symptoms such as their expected refund or collateral return being missing, balances appearing unchanged, or the protocol reporting a settled debt while the NFT remains in their wallet. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the business logic of the auction settlement flow and identified the absence of explicit success verification. It is difficult to notice because the function is privileged and developers may assume that external callers enforce the correct auction state, leading to a false sense of safety. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of missing state validation and improper business‑logic enforcement, where a function proceeds on an assumed condition that is never programmatically confirmed. To remediate the issue, the contract should enforce that the collateral token does not own the underlying NFT at settlement time and that the auction entry for the given collateral identifier is still marked as active and has reached a successful outcome before any state changes are performed. Adding these checks restores the intended invariant that only a genuinely successful auction can trigger the release or transfer of collateral, thereby protecting user funds and preserving protocol integrity.
summary: settleAuction() is a privileged functionality called by LienToken.payDebtViaClearingHouse(). settleAuction() is intended to be called on a successful auction, but it doesn't verify that that's indeed the case. Anyone can create a fake Seaport order with one of its considerations set as the CollateralToken as described in Issue 93. Another potential issue is if the Seaport orders can be "Restricted" in future, then there is a possibility for an authorized entity to force settleAuction on CollateralToken, and when SeaPort tries to call back on the zone to validate it would fail.

title: Accounts not properly removed from roles upon revoking
content: The vulnerability consists of an incomplete removal of an account from a role‑based access control set. When a role is revoked, the internal _revokeRole function calls the remove method of the AsSequentialSet library, which deletes the element from the underlying array but fails to clear the corresponding entry in the index mapping. The hasRole check later reads the index mapping to decide whether an address still holds the role; because the mapping entry remains non‑zero, the contract incorrectly reports that the account still possesses the role even though it has been removed from the array. This inconsistency arises from the removeAt routine only shifting and popping the array element without updating the index, and the has function only validates that the stored index is greater than zero and within the current array length. An attacker who has been revoked can therefore continue to call functions protected by the role modifier, gaining unauthorized access to privileged operations such as fund transfers or configuration changes. The impact is a breach of the intended permission model, potentially allowing theft of assets, manipulation of protocol parameters, or other malicious actions that compromise the security and trust of the system. The flaw manifests whenever a role revocation is performed and the contract later queries the role status, affecting any user whose role is revoked, the protocol’s overall integrity, and any downstream users who rely on correct access control. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the role management code, where the auditor noticed that the index mapping was never reset after removal, leading to a stale entry that fooled the hasRole view. It can be hard to notice because transaction logs show a RoleRevoked event and the array no longer contains the address, giving the impression that the revocation succeeded, while the contract’s internal state still grants the role. From a user perspective the UI may indicate that the privilege has been removed, yet the user can still execute privileged actions, creating a mismatch between expectation (“I should no longer be able to call admin functions”) and reality (“my calls still succeed”). This class of bug is a typical data‑structure inconsistency where auxiliary bookkeeping structures are not kept in sync after a delete operation, often referred to as a stale mapping or improper set cleanup. The recommended fix is to reset the index entry to zero before calling removeAt, or to replace the custom set implementation with a well‑tested library that atomically updates both the array and the index mapping, ensuring that hasRole returns false after a successful revocation.

title: Flash loan wrong balance check
content: The vulnerability is a logical error in the flashLoanSimple function where the contract records its token balance before transferring the loan amount out and then checks that the post‑execution balance increase is at least the total amount to be repaid (principal plus fee). Because the snapshot was taken before the loan was sent, the recorded balance does not include the transferred principal. After the borrower returns the loan, the contract’s balance rises only by the fee, while the check expects an increase of principal plus fee. Consequently the condition (asset.balanceOf(this) - balanceBefore) < toRepay is true for any non‑exempt borrower, causing the transaction to revert and forcing the borrower to supply an extra amount equal to the principal in order to satisfy the check. The root cause is the ordering of operations: balanceBefore is captured too early and the repayment verification uses the full repayment amount instead of just the fee. An attacker could trigger the revert by simply calling flashLoanSimple, effectively making the flash‑loan service unusable and potentially leading users to lose expected profit or to overpay if they manually add the principal. The impact is that users attempting to use the flash loan receive no funds, see a revert error, and may be forced to send back more tokens than they borrowed, violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions that only the fee should be owed after the loan. This condition occurs on every call to flashLoanSimple for addresses not listed in exemptionList, affecting any borrower, the protocol’s liquidity pool, and downstream contracts that rely on flash‑loan functionality. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit by the auditor Pashov, who noted that the balance check logic does not match the intended financial model. The bug is subtle because the code appears to compare the contract’s balance before and after the loan, a pattern that is common in flash‑loan implementations, making it easy to overlook the missing principal in the snapshot. To fix the issue the contract should either record balanceBefore after the safeTransferFrom call or simplify the check to compare only the fee (i.e., require that the balance increase is at least fee) and drop the toRepay variable. This correction aligns the repayment verification with the business rule that borrowers only need to return the fee, restoring correct flash‑loan behavior and preventing users from being overcharged.

title: Flash loan not working due to transferFrom Issue
content: The vulnerability is a misuse of the ERC20 transferFrom mechanism inside the flashLoanSimple function. The contract attempts to send the borrowed amount to the receiver by calling asset.safeTransferFrom(address(this), address(receiver), amount). For tokens that follow the standard ERC20 implementation, such as USDC, safeTransferFrom ultimately invokes transferFrom, which checks that the caller has an allowance from the source address (the contract itself) to move the specified amount. Because the contract never grants itself an allowance, the allowance mapping remains zero and the transferFrom call reverts with the message "ERC20: transfer amount exceeds allowance". This logical error prevents the flash loan from being issued, causing the entire flash loan transaction to fail before any funds are transferred. The impact is that borrowers cannot obtain flash loans, the protocol’s advertised functionality is broken, and users experience a mismatch between expectation (receiving a loan) and reality (receiving no funds and a revert). The issue manifests whenever the flash loan is requested with an ERC20 token that enforces allowance checks, such as USDC, and the contract has not pre‑approved itself. It affects any user or contract that tries to use the flash loan feature, as well as the protocol’s liquidity providers who rely on the flash loan revenue model. The problem was discovered during a manual code audit that highlighted the use of safeTransferFrom in a context where a simple transfer is required. The bug is subtle because the code compiles and the function signatures match, but the runtime allowance check is only triggered when the call is executed, making it easy to miss during testing if the specific token is not exercised. Conceptually, this is a class of allowance‑related token transfer bug where an internal contract attempts to move its own tokens using transferFrom without first setting an allowance, violating the ERC20 accounting assumptions. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a flash loan request that instantly fails, often with a generic error or no visible message, leaving the user confused as to why no funds were received. The correct remediation is to replace the safeTransferFrom call with safeTransfer, which does not require an allowance, or alternatively to set an explicit allowance for the contract to spend its own tokens before invoking transferFrom. Either approach restores the intended flow: the contract transfers the loan amount to the receiver, the receiver executes its operation, and the contract verifies repayment before emitting the FlashLoan event.

title: withdraw() worst price will distort sharePrice()
content: The contract implements a tokenized vault where each share represents a claim on the underlying assets. The vulnerability lies in the way the withdrawal function determines the price at which shares are redeemed. When a user initiates a redemption request, the contract stores the share price at the time of the request (request.sharePrice). During the actual withdraw, the code selects the worst (minimum) price between the stored request price and the last recorded global share price (last.sharePrice). This worst‑price logic is intended to protect against price drops, but the implementation fails to update last.sharePrice after the withdrawal is processed. Consequently, last.sharePrice continues to reflect the price before the withdrawal, while the actual assets have been reduced at the lower worst price. The sharePrice() view function later computes the current price using last.sharePrice, which now under‑states the true value of the remaining assets. The mismatch causes the reported share price to be artificially high for subsequent deposits and withdrawals, leading to unexpected slippage, reduced payouts, or apparent loss of funds. The issue manifests whenever a redemption request is made at a price lower than the current market price and the user later calls withdraw after the asset pool has grown. Users, depositors, and the protocol itself are affected because the accounting invariants of the vault are broken: the sum of share values no longer matches the underlying assets. The bug was discovered during a manual audit of the As4626 abstract contract by examining the state updates of last.sharePrice across deposit, withdraw, requestRedeem, and cancelRedeemRequest functions. It is subtle because the contract still updates last.sharePrice in several places, giving the impression that the price is always refreshed, yet the specific path taken by withdraw bypasses the correct update. Detecting the problem requires tracing the interaction between request.sharePrice, last.sharePrice, and the totalAccountedAssets calculation, which is not obvious from a superficial read. To remediate the issue, the contract should ensure that last.sharePrice is recomputed after any operation that changes the asset pool, including withdrawals that use the worst‑price path, so that sharePrice() always reflects the true post‑withdrawal asset balance. This aligns the accounting model with the intended ERC‑4626 semantics and prevents users from receiving less than the expected amount or from experiencing unexplained slippage on subsequent deposits.

title: Fee calculation mismatch in mint, deposit, redeem and withdraw
content: The contract implements four user‑facing entry points – mint, deposit, redeem and withdraw – that each rely on a preview function to calculate the amount of assets or shares involved and to apply a protocol fee expressed in basis points. For mint and redeem the preview logic is consistent with the intended economic model: mint calculates the required asset amount as convertToAssets(shares) plus the fee (addBp), and redeem calculates the net asset return as convertToAssets(shares) minus the fee (subBp). However, deposit and withdraw use the opposite approach on the wrong base value. In deposit the preview function computes the share amount as convertToShares(amount) minus the fee, where *amount* is the total value the user sends, which already includes the fee. By subtracting the fee from the gross amount the contract effectively charges the fee twice, causing the user to receive fewer shares than expected. Similarly, withdraw computes the share amount to burn as convertToShares(assets) plus the fee, where *assets* is the net amount the user wishes to receive. Adding the fee to the net amount again overcharges the user, requiring them to burn more shares than necessary. The root cause is the use of a simple addBp/subBp operation on a value that already incorporates the fee, instead of applying a proportional formula that isolates the net amount: net = gross * base / (base + fee). This logical flaw manifests whenever a user calls deposit() or withdraw(), leading to an over‑deduction of assets or shares. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are a mismatch between the amount they intended to deposit or withdraw and the actual shares received or burned – for example, a user who deposits 110 tokens receives only 99 shares, or a user who withdraws 100 tokens must surrender 110 shares. The impact is a systematic loss of user funds, erosion of trust, and distortion of the protocol’s accounting because the fee accounting no longer matches the economic assumptions of the system. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the fee calculations across the four entry points and identified the inconsistency in the preview logic. Because the mint and redeem paths appear correct, the bug can be subtle and may not be immediately obvious from UI balances alone; only a detailed inspection of the fee formulas reveals the over‑charging. To remediate the problem the fee for deposit should be calculated as convertToShares(amount) * base / (base + fee), and the fee for previewRedeem (and consequently withdraw) should be calculated as convertToAssets(shares) * base / (base + fee), thereby ensuring that the fee is applied to the net amount rather than the gross amount supplied by the user.
summary: When users calls mint(shares) code calls _deposit(previewMint(_shares), _shares and previewMint(shares) = convertToAssets(shares).addBp(). When users calls deposit(amount) code calls _deposit(_amount, previewDeposit(_amount) and previewDeposit(amount) = convertToShares(amount).subBp. Let's assume that price is 1:1 and fee is 10% and check the both case: 1. If user wants to mint 100 share then he would call mint(100) and code would calculate amount = previewMint(100) = convertToAssets(100).addBp(10%) = 110. So in the end user would pay 110 asset and receive 100 shares and 10 asset will be fee. 2. If users wants to deposit 110 asset then he would call deposit(110) and code would calculate share = previewDeposit(110) = convertToShare(110).subBp(10%) = 99. So in the end user would pay 11 asset and receive 99 share and 11 asset will be fee. As you can see the deposit() call overcharge the user. The reason is that code calculates fee based on user-specified amount by using subBp() but user-specified amount is supposed to be amount + fee so the calculation for fee should be .... * base / (base + fee). When users call redeem(shares) code calls _withdraw(previewRedeem(_shares), _shares) and previewRdeem(shares) = convertToAssets(_shares).subBp(). When users call withdraw() code calls _withdraw(_amount, previewWithdraw(_amount)) and previewWithdraw(_amount) = convertToShares(_assets).addBp(). Let's assume that asset to share price is 1:1 and fee is 10% and check both case: 1. If user wants to redeem 110 shares then he would call redeem(110) and code would calculate amount = previewRdeem(110) = convertToAssets(110).subBp(10%) = 99. So in the end user would burn 110 shares and receive 99 asset and 11 asset will be fee. 2. If user wants to withdraw 100 asset then he would call withdraw(100) and code would calculates shares = previewWithdraw(100) = convertToShares(100).addBp(10%) = 110. So in the end userwould burn 110 shares and receive 100 asset and 10 asset will be fee. So as you can see redeem() overcharges users. The reason is that code calculates fee based on user provided share with subBp() but the provided amount is total amount (burnAmount + fee) and calculation should be ..... * base / (base + fee).

title: Fee target mismatch in deposit, mint, withdraw, redeem and preview*** methods
content: The vulnerability is a fee‑target mismatch that appears in the deposit/mint and withdraw/redeem paths of the vault. The contract calculates the entry fee in the previewDeposit and previewMint view functions by applying the fee to msg.sender and either subtracting it from the returned share amount or adding it to the asset amount. However, when the internal _deposit function records the fee it uses the _receiver address, which can be supplied by the caller, to decide whether the fee is exempt and to add the fee amount to the claimableAssetFees accumulator. Because the exemption list is checked against a different address than the one used in the preview, an attacker can supply a fee‑exempt receiver while the caller itself is not exempt, causing the preview to show that no fee was taken while the contract still credits the fee to its internal pool. A symmetric problem exists in the withdrawal path: previewWithdraw and previewRedeem compute the exit fee based on msg.sender, but the internal _withdraw function adds the fee to claimableAssetFees using the _owner parameter, which may differ from the caller. By approving a fee‑exempt owner to a non‑exempt operator, the operator can trigger a withdrawal that returns the full asset amount to the caller while the protocol records an exit fee that was never paid. The result is an accounting inconsistency where claimableAssetFees grows without any user actually paying the fee, effectively a double‑spend of fee revenue. This issue manifests to users as a normal‑looking deposit, mint, withdraw or redeem where the UI shows the expected amount, but the protocol’s fee pool inflates unexpectedly. It is discovered during a manual audit of fee handling logic, and it can be hard to notice because the preview functions – which are often used to display expected fees – are consistent with the user’s view, while the internal state diverges. The bug belongs to the class of fee‑calculation and accounting mismatches, where the same logical condition (exemption) is evaluated against different actors in different parts of the code. To remediate, the contract should use the same address (msg.sender) for exemption checks and fee accumulation in both the preview and the internal functions, or explicitly pass the intended fee payer and ensure the exemption list is consulted consistently. Aligning the fee target eliminates the double‑counting and restores correct accounting of entry and exit fees.

title: Accounting issues after underlying asset change
content: The vulnerability originates from the pool’s handling of an underlying asset change. When the asset is updated, the contract continues to use previously cached pool price values for operations such as requestRedeem, withdraw, cancel request and fee calculation. These cached prices were stored at the time a redeem request was created and are later reused to determine the amount of assets to return, the price impact on withdrawal and the amount of tokens to burn when a request is cancelled. Because the cached values are never refreshed after the asset switch, the contract applies a price that no longer reflects the current underlying asset. In parallel, the claimableAssetFees variable, which tracks fees accrued in the old asset, is supposed to be cleared by the _collectFees function during updateAsset. However, _collectFees returns early when profit equals zero, leaving the old‑asset fee amount unchanged. The combination of stale price data and residual fee balances creates an accounting mismatch: users may receive too many or too few assets on withdrawal, be charged incorrect fees, see token burns based on an outdated price, or observe non‑zero claimable fees that belong to a previous asset. The issue manifests only after an asset update, a scenario that is common in pools that support dynamic underlying assets. It is difficult to notice because the cached values are internal and the UI typically shows the user’s balance after the operation, which may appear correct even though the underlying accounting is wrong. The impact is high because it can lead to loss of funds, incorrect fee distribution and a breach of the pool’s financial invariants. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the updateAsset flow and identified that price caches and fee state were not reset. To remediate, the contract should explicitly reset all cached price variables and recompute fees after an asset change, and the _collectFees routine should ensure that claimableAssetFees are cleared regardless of profit value, preventing leftover balances from the previous asset.
summary: In general updating underlying asset is very risky move in a pool. All the cached prices will be wrong. In the current code we have two cached prices(that I know of): In requestRedeem() code caches pool prices for requests. Code use it later in the withdraw and cancel request. (the price impact withdraw price and also burning tokens in cancel requests) In calculating fee, code caches pool price and use it to calculate fee later. (there may be other places the pool price is cached) ——— Another place that is asset amount is cached is claimableAssetFees. updateAsset() calls the _collectFees() to handle the claimableAssetFees and set it to zero but because of this line in the _collectFees() If (profit == 0) return; claimableAssetFees (which shows amount in old asset) could remain non-zero after asset update.

title: Cover premium rewards can be lost
content: The vulnerability is an accounting error in the premium reward distribution logic of the virtual pool. When the pool state is refreshed, the function VirtualPool::_refreshSlot0 first checks for initialized ticks that are crossed and updates the current tick, utilization and premium rate. After this crossing it immediately computes the liquidity index using the new utilization and premiumRate values and adds it to slot0.liquidityIndex. Because the reward for covers that expire between the previous tick and the new tick is calculated only after the tick crossing, the premiums that belong to those expired covers are never added to the liquidity index. Consequently any cover that is opened and closed, or that expires, within the interval between two calls to _refreshSlot0 will lose its entire premium reward. The bug manifests as cover holders receiving less or zero premium rewards and liquidity providers seeing a shortfall in accrued rewards, even though the UI may show that the cover was active and premiums were paid. The issue occurs on any transaction that triggers a pool‑utilisation change and therefore calls _refreshSlot0, such as deposits, withdrawals or claim settlements, when there are covers expiring in the processed tick range. It affects all participants who rely on the premium distribution: cover purchasers, who expect to be compensated for the risk they provided, and liquidity providers, who expect to earn the premiums from those covers. The problem was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s reward accounting, where the auditors noticed that the liquidity index is updated after the tick crossing instead of before, leading to a loss of rewards for the last interval. The bug is subtle because the normal operation distributes rewards correctly for most ticks; only the edge case where a cover’s lifetime fits entirely within a single refresh interval produces a zero‑reward outcome, which can be hard to detect in routine testing. To fix the issue the contract should calculate the liquidity index using the utilization and premium rate that existed before crossing the initialized tick, or otherwise apply the pending rewards for the expired cover before updating the index. This change restores the intended accounting invariant that all premiums paid by cover holders are fully accounted for and distributed to liquidity providers.

title: BetExpress is broken when a bet has a condition with more than one outcome
content: The vulnerability is a logic error in the bet construction and liquidity reservation code of the BetExpress contract. When a user creates a deposit for a condition that supports two or more possible outcomes, the contract records only a single payout entry in the condition.payouts array because the push operation is guarded by if (outcomeOrdinal == 0). At the same time the variable winningOutcomesCount correctly reflects the number of outcomes that can win, which is greater than one for multi‑outcome conditions. Later, the internal function _calcReserve calls Math.maxSum with the payouts array and the winningOutcomesCount as arguments. maxSum is designed to sum the n largest elements of an array, but it assumes that the array contains at least n elements. Because the payouts array contains only one element while n is at least two, the loop sorted[length - 1 - i] accesses an index that underflows when i reaches 1, causing a revert due to an arithmetic underflow. The exploit scenario is straightforward: an attacker does not need to do anything special; any user who attempts to place a bet on a market with multiple outcomes triggers the underflow and the transaction fails. From the user’s perspective the UI may show that the bet was submitted, but the transaction reverts, the user receives no confirmation, and only the gas fee is lost. The expected behavior—successful reservation of liquidity and acceptance of the bet—is violated, leading to a denial‑of‑service condition for all multi‑outcome markets. The bug appears only when the condition has more than one winning outcome, so tests that only cover single‑outcome markets may miss it, making it hard to notice during development. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s construction logic and reserve calculation, where the mismatch between condition.payouts length and winningOutcomesCount was observed. To fix the problem the contract must either populate the payouts array with a separate entry for each possible outcome, or modify maxSum (or the call site) to cap the number of items summed to the actual length of the array, and add explicit validation that n does not exceed a.length. This correction restores the intended accounting logic that reserves enough liquidity for every possible winning outcome and prevents unexpected reverts, thereby protecting users’ funds and preserving the protocol’s integrity.

title: Rounding direction in token rates leads to inconsistent price between addLiquidity and removeLiquidity
content: The vulnerability originates from the way the vault rounds token balances differently when liquidity is added versus when it is removed. When a user calls addLiquidity, the vault rounds the token balances upward; when the same user later calls removeLiquidity, the vault rounds the balances downward. This asymmetry is intentional to protect the protocol in most normal scenarios, but it also changes the effective price of each token in the pool because the invariant calculation depends on both the pool token price and the individual token rates. In pools that support token rate adapters, such as a stable‑coin paired with a wrapped asset that reports a rate slightly above one, the rounding can shift the ratio of the two assets. For example, if the rate‑adjusted token is represented as 2 units after rounding up during addLiquidity and as 1 unit after rounding down during removeLiquidity, the user effectively pays a higher price when depositing and receives a lower price when withdrawing. By supplying an extremely unbalanced amount of the cheap token and then withdrawing the expensive token, an attacker can create a profitable round‑trip where the minted BPT from the deposit exceeds the BPT burned on withdrawal, extracting value from the pool. The impact is most severe in pools where a tiny change in token balance dramatically moves the price, such as stable pools with high amplification factors; in edge cases the invariant may diverge, allowing the pool to be drained. The issue was discovered during a security audit that included manual tests with mock pools and fuzzing of invariant calculations, revealing that the rounding direction can produce a measurable profit in contrived but possible scenarios. The bug is subtle because the rounding logic is hidden inside internal vault functions and the price discrepancy is only visible when the pool is heavily unbalanced, making it easy to overlook during normal operation. To remediate the problem, the protocol should either enforce symmetric rounding for both add and remove paths, or introduce additional safeguards such as a minimum token balance threshold that prevents extreme imbalance, and clearly document the risk so that pool developers can decide whether to enable unbalanced liquidity. The class of bug can be described as an asymmetric rounding error in AMM invariant calculations that leads to inconsistent token pricing and potential value extraction through round‑trip liquidity operations.

title: H-1 Bypassing payment fees through various methods
content: The vulnerability resides in the fee‑collection mechanism of the SwapExecutor/SwapFacade swapping architecture. The contract assumes that a fee is implicitly paid by requiring a non‑zero amount of the final token (tokenToTransfer) to remain on the SwapExecutor after the swap, or by charging the fee in the token that appears at the end of the swap path. Because the fee logic does not enforce a fixed token or a minimum value independent of the token’s semantics, an attacker can manipulate the swap in three distinct ways to avoid paying any fee. First, the attacker can craft a swap that leaves only two wei of the output token on the executor, which satisfies the superficial check that some token remains, but the amount is too small to represent a meaningful fee, effectively allowing a fee‑free swap. Second, the attacker can append a malicious token that they control to the swap path; the contract then charges the fee in this attacker‑controlled token, which has no intrinsic value, so the protocol receives a worthless payment while the attacker receives the intended output. Third, the attacker can copy the SwapExecutor code, strip out the fee‑collection statements, and supply this custom executor to the SwapFacade via the swap() function, which accepts an arbitrary executor address. Because the facade does not validate that the executor implements the fee logic, the swap proceeds without any fee deduction. These methods can be executed whenever a user calls SwapFacade.swap() with a custom executor or a crafted path, meaning the vulnerability is present in any normal swap operation that does not involve the official executor. The impact is a loss of fee revenue for the protocol owners and a distortion of the economic model that relies on those fees to fund operations or incentivize participants. The issue was discovered during a security audit by MixBytes, which identified that the fee enforcement is based on token amount checks rather than a deterministic, token‑agnostic mechanism, making it easy to overlook because the contract still appears to transfer tokens correctly and the leftover amount passes superficial sanity checks. The bug is hard to notice because the contract does not emit explicit fee events, and the remaining token balance of two wei looks innocuous, while the poisonous token may be indistinguishable from legitimate assets. To remediate, the fee should be collected in a fixed, universally accepted token such as Ether, enforced before any token transfers, and the SwapFacade should restrict the executor to a known, immutable implementation, rejecting custom executors or paths that end with unverified tokens. This change would eliminate the ability to bypass fees by manipulating token amounts, token types, or contract code, restoring the intended economic guarantees of the swapping protocol.
summary:
SwapExecutor, a contract responsible for executing token swaps, is vulnerable to multiple methods of bypassing payment fees, allowing an attacker to perform swaps without paying the required fees.
The ﬁrst method involves specifying a personal transfer of all tokens in the ﬁnal swap, leaving only 2 wei of tokenToTransfer on the contract to avoid paying fees. This enables the attacker to evade payment and execute swaps at no cost.
• SwapExecutor.sol#L146
The second method involves passing a swap-path that ends with a poisonous token created by the attacker. The attacker pays fees in their own token, which is worthless, thus bypassing payment fees.
• SwapFacade.sol#L35
The third method involves copying the code of SwapExecutor and removing the payment logic, allowing the attacker to continue using the SwapFacade without paying any fees by passing the custom SwapExecutor to SwapFacade.swap().
• SwapFacade.sol#L29
Overall, these vulnerabilities allow attackers to perform swaps without paying the required fees, leading to potential ﬁnancial losses for the SwapExecutor owners.

title: H-2 Hashﬂow RFQ-integration
content: The vulnerability originates from the way the Hashflow RFQ integration handles a quote that is obtained off‑chain before the actual swap transaction is executed. The contract receives a HashflowQuote object containing a maximum allowable base token amount (quote.maxBaseTokenAmount). Because the quote is fetched prior to the transaction, the market price may change between the quote retrieval and the moment the transaction is mined. The code then compares the user‑supplied amount with the stale quote and, if the amount exceeds the quoted maximum, it emits an AmountExceedsQuote event and silently reduces the effective amount to quote.maxBaseTokenAmount instead of aborting the operation. This silent truncation means that part of the user’s funds remain locked in the SwapExecutor contract without any explicit error, leading to a situation where the user expects the full amount to be swapped but receives only a partial execution. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a successful trade while the balance of the user’s wallet is reduced by the full amount, yet the expected output token amount is lower than anticipated or appears to be missing entirely. The impact is that funds can become unrecoverable or stuck in the contract, breaking accounting assumptions and potentially causing a loss of confidence in the protocol. The issue manifests whenever the quote becomes outdated – for example during periods of high volatility or network congestion – and any caller that supplies an amount larger than the stale quote triggers the bug. It was discovered during a manual audit by MixBytes, where the logical flow of the quote handling was examined and the lack of a revert was identified as a flaw. The problem is hard to notice because the transaction does not revert; it only emits an event, so standard failure detection mechanisms may miss it. To remediate the issue the contract should enforce a strict check that reverts when the supplied amount exceeds quote.maxBaseTokenAmount, or it should obtain a fresh quote on‑chain just before execution, ensuring that the effective amount always matches the current market conditions. In broader terms this is a classic case of stale off‑chain data leading to a silent truncation bug that violates the expected financial invariants of a swap operation.

title: H-3 Swaps through an ERC777 token can lead to DoS of these swaps
content: The vulnerability originates from the combination of an unrestricted executeSwap function in the SwapExecutor contract and the ability of ERC777 tokens to invoke external hook contracts via the ERC1820 registry. ERC777 tokens call a user‑defined contract (the tokensReceived hook) before and after balance changes, and the address of this hook is stored in the ERC1820 registry using the setInterfaceImplementer function. Because executeSwap can be called by any address, an attacker can submit a transaction that makes the Executor contract invoke ERC1820Registry.setInterfaceImplementer with the attacker’s contract as the implementer for the ERC777 interface. Once the attacker’s contract is registered, any subsequent swap that routes an ERC777 token through the Executor will trigger the attacker’s hook when the token is transferred. The malicious hook can simply revert, causing the entire swap transaction to fail. This creates a denial‑of‑service condition for all swaps involving ERC777 tokens, and it also opens the possibility for the attacker to withdraw or manipulate the tokens that arrive in the Executor because the Executor believes the tokens belong to the attacker’s contract. The issue manifests when a legitimate user initiates a swap with an ERC777 token after the attacker has polluted the registry; the user’s transaction reverts, no tokens are received, and the user sees a generic “swap failed” error. From the protocol’s perspective, revenue from swaps is lost and the swapping functionality becomes unreliable. The problem was discovered during a security audit that examined the public accessibility of executeSwap and the interaction with ERC1820 hooks. It is difficult to notice because the revert appears as a normal transaction failure, and the underlying cause – a malicious hook registered in a global registry – is not obvious from the swap’s UI. To remediate, the Executor should only accept calls from the authorized Facade contract, a reentrancy guard should be added, and the contract should enforce a minimum return even for small swaps. Additionally, the protocol could validate the ERC1820 implementer before accepting ERC777 tokens or disable ERC777 hooks for swap operations, thereby preventing an attacker from injecting a malicious hook and causing a denial‑of‑service or token theft scenario.
summary:
ERC777 tokens allow hooks before and after balance changes.
Transfer _from and to can choose the exact receivers of these hooks via Registry.setInterfaceImplementer():
• 0x1820a4B7618BdE71Dce8cdc73aAB6C95905faD24
Also, Executor allows anyone to call executeSwap() and decide on the following targets and calldata.
1. An attacker uses executeSwap() so that Executor calls ERC1820Registry.setInterfaceImplementer(implementer=attacker).
2. User A swaps an ERC777 token to something with low minReturn. It must be at least one ERC777 among the list of tokens in swaps.
3. Executor receives ERC777 tokens from Facade (hook).
4. The attacker reverts on the hook.
As a result, any ERC777 token going through Executor will lead to DoS and swap will revert.
So, one of the attack flows can be like this:
1. Attacker uses executeSwap() so that Executor calls `ERC1820Registry.setInterfaceImplementer(implementer=attacker)`.
So, anytime Executor receives ERC777 tokens, a frontrunner contract will be called.
2. User A swaps the ERC777 tokens to something with low minReturn.
3. Executor receives the ERC777 tokens from Facade (hook).
4. Attacker contract enters Executor.executeSwap() and Executor thinks that current ERC777 tokens belong to Attacker. So, he can withdraw these tokens, or swap them to something.
Or at least Attacker can revert when recieving a call, not allowing a swap with this token at all.

title: H-1 Bypassing payment fees through various methods
content: The vulnerability resides in the fee collection mechanism of a token‑swap service that consists of a SwapFacade contract delegating execution to a SwapExecutor implementation. The contract assumes that a fee will be paid in the token that is transferred in the final step of the swap, but it does not enforce a fixed fee token, does not validate the amount beyond a minimal residual balance, and allows the executor implementation to be supplied by the caller. Because of these design choices an attacker can bypass the required payment in three distinct ways. First, the attacker crafts a swap where the final transfer moves all of the output tokens back to the caller except for a trivial amount (2 wei). The fee check only verifies that some amount of the token remains on the contract, so the fee is considered paid even though the effective fee is negligible, allowing the attacker to execute the swap at essentially no cost. Second, the attacker appends a malicious token that they control to the swap path. The fee is then paid in this attacker‑created token, which has no market value, so the protocol receives a worthless fee while the attacker still obtains the desired output token. Third, the attacker clones the SwapExecutor source code, removes the fee‑deduction logic, and passes this custom executor to SwapFacade.swap(). Since the facade does not restrict which executor can be used, the fee logic is completely omitted and the swap proceeds without any payment. These bypasses can be triggered whenever a user invokes SwapFacade.swap() with a crafted path, a minimal residual balance, or a custom executor, meaning the issue is present for any caller that can supply these parameters. The affected parties are the protocol owners who rely on fee revenue, token holders who expect fair pricing, and any user of the swap service who may see unexpected fee‑free swaps. The problem was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the fee verification code and identified logical gaps in the assumptions about token type and amount. The bug is subtle because the fee check appears to succeed for normal tokens and normal amounts, making the bypass invisible unless edge‑case values or attacker‑controlled tokens are used. To remediate the issue the fee should be collected in a fixed, immutable token such as Ether, the contract should enforce an exact fee amount, and the executor implementation should be immutable or at least validated to contain the fee logic. Additionally, the swap path should be validated to reject attacker‑controlled tokens as the final hop. In summary, the contract suffers from an under‑specified fee enforcement design that permits fee‑free swaps through minimal residual balances, poisonous tokens, or custom executor contracts, leading to loss of expected revenue and breaking the economic assumptions of the protocol.
summary:
SwapExecutor, a contract responsible for executing token swaps, is vulnerable to multiple methods of bypassing payment fees, allowing an attacker to perform swaps without paying the required fees.
The first method involves specifying a personal transfer of all tokens in the final swap, leaving only 2 wei of tokenToTransfer on the contract to avoid paying fees. This enables the attacker to evade payment and execute swaps at no cost.
• SwapExecutor.sol#L146
The second method involves passing a swap-path that ends with a poisonous token created by the attacker. The attacker pays fees in their own token, which is worthless, thus bypassing payment fees.
• SwapFacade.sol#L35
The third method involves copying the code of SwapExecutor and removing the payment logic, allowing the attacker to continue using the SwapFacade without paying any fees by passing the custom SwapExecutor to SwapFacade.swap().
• SwapFacade.sol#L29
Overall, these vulnerabilities allow attackers to perform swaps without paying the required fees, leading to potential financial losses for the SwapExecutor owners.

title: H-2 Hashﬂow RFQ-integration
content: The vulnerability is a stale‑quote validation flaw in the Hashflow RFQ integration. The contract receives a HashflowQuote object before the user‑initiated swap transaction is executed. Because the quote is fetched off‑chain and stored, the values inside the quote (especially maxBaseTokenAmount) may become outdated by the time the transaction is mined. The code that processes the user‑provided amount checks only whether the amount exceeds quote.maxBaseTokenAmount and, if it does, emits an AmountExceedsQuote event and silently reduces the effectiveBaseTokenAmount to the quoted maximum instead of reverting. As a result, any portion of the user's input that is larger than the stale maximum is not transferred to the intended counter‑party; the excess remains locked in the internal SwapExecutor contract. This behavior violates the expected accounting rule that the full amount supplied by the user should either be fully executed or the transaction should fail. From the user’s perspective the UI may show that the trade was submitted, but the received amount is lower than expected or the user’s balance appears reduced without a corresponding receipt, leading to confusion and perceived loss of funds. The issue can be triggered whenever the market moves between the time the quote is obtained and the time the transaction is mined, which is a realistic scenario in volatile markets. It affects any participant who relies on the RFQ integration, including regular traders and protocol users who trust the contract to execute the exact amount they specify. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the logic of quote handling and identified that the contract does not enforce a strict revert on mismatched amounts. The problem is subtle because the contract does emit an event, but the silent adjustment of the effective amount can be easily missed in normal testing, especially if the test suite does not simulate quote staleness. The bug belongs to the class of “stale data race” or “insufficient input validation” vulnerabilities, where external data used for on‑chain decisions is not re‑validated at execution time. To remediate the issue the contract should revert the transaction whenever the supplied amount does not match the current quote, or it should fetch a fresh quote inside the same transaction, ensuring that the effectiveBaseTokenAmount always equals the user‑provided amount. Alternatively, the contract could require the caller to explicitly acknowledge a partial fill, but this must be clearly communicated to the user. Until such a fix is applied, funds that exceed the stale quote may become permanently locked in the SwapExecutor, and users may experience missing refunds or reduced trade outputs.

title: H-3 Swaps through an ERC777 token can lead to DoS of these swaps
content: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service and potential token‑theft issue that arises when the SwapExecutor contract processes ERC777 tokens. ERC777 tokens support a callback mechanism (tokensReceived hook) that is looked up through the ERC1820 registry. The registry allows any address to declare itself as the implementer of the ERC777 interface for a given token by calling ERC1820Registry.setInterfaceImplementer. Because the Executor’s executeSwap function is public and accepts arbitrary calldata, an attacker can invoke executeSwap with a payload that registers the attacker’s contract as the ERC777 implementer. After this registration, whenever the Executor receives an ERC777 token as part of a swap, the token contract triggers the attacker’s hook. The attacker’s hook can deliberately revert, causing the whole swap transaction to fail, or it can execute malicious logic such as withdrawing the received tokens. Consequently, any swap that involves an ERC777 token becomes impossible (DoS) or may result in loss of funds. The problem occurs only when the swap flow includes an ERC777 token and the Executor is the recipient of that token, which is the case for all swaps listed in the protocol that allow ERC777 assets. Users experience a failed transaction, see no token received, or notice that their balance remains unchanged despite having initiated a swap. The issue was discovered during a security audit when the auditors observed that executeSwap does not restrict who can call it and that the ERC1820 registry can be manipulated without checks. It is hard to notice because the failure manifests as a generic swap revert, and the hook execution is invisible to the user. To remediate, the protocol should restrict executeSwap so that only the designated Facade contract can invoke it, add a reentrancy guard, enforce a sensible minReturn even for small swaps, and optionally validate that the ERC777 token’s implementer is a trusted contract before accepting callbacks. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of untrusted callback or hook injection, where external code is executed without proper access control, leading to denial‑of‑service or unauthorized asset movement.

Also, Executor allows anyone to call executeSwap() and decide on the following targets and calldata.
1. An attacker uses executeSwap() so that Executor calls ERC1820Registry.setInterfaceImplementer(implementer=attacker).
2. User A swaps an ERC777 token to something with low minReturn. It must be at least one ERC777 among the list of tokens in swaps.
3. Executor receives ERC777 tokens from Facade (hook).
4. The attacker reverts on the hook.
As a result, any ERC777 token going through Executor will lead to DoS and swap will revert.
So, one of the attack flows can be like this:
1. Attacker uses executeSwap() so that Executor calls `ERC1820Registry.setInterfaceImplementer(implementer=attacker)`.
So, anytime Executor receives ERC777 tokens, a frontrunner contract will be called.
2. User A swaps the ERC777 tokens to something with low minReturn.

title: Cross-chain smart contract calls can revert but source chain tokens remain burnt and are not refunded
content: The vulnerability is a missing rollback mechanism for cross‑chain token transfers performed through AxelarGateway.callContractWithToken. When a user initiates a cross‑chain call, the gateway first burns the specified ERC‑20 tokens on the source chain and then forwards a message to the destination chain where a contract is invoked. The design assumes the destination call will succeed, but it does not check the outcome. If the call on the destination chain reverts – for example because a required liquidity pool is empty, an assert fails, or any other business‑logic error occurs – the gateway never restores the burned tokens on the source chain. Consequently, the user's balance on the source chain permanently decreases while no assets are received on the destination chain. The root cause is the absence of a failure‑aware flow: the contract does not emit a failure event, nor does it trigger a re‑mint or refund when the downstream execution fails. Exploitation is straightforward: an attacker can craft a destination contract that always reverts, or can induce a revert by exhausting a required resource, causing any user who funds the cross‑chain call to lose the burnt tokens. The impact is loss of user funds and erosion of trust in the Axelar network, as users expect that a failed cross‑chain operation will either complete or be refunded, similar to a pending credit‑card transaction. The issue appears only when a token‑backed cross‑chain call is used; simple Ether calls revert correctly because the Ether is automatically returned by the EVM. From the user’s perspective the UI will show the token balance dropping to zero after the burn, but no subsequent credit appears on the target chain and no error is reported, leading to confusion and the perception that the protocol “stole” the funds. The problem was identified during a public audit where a test case deliberately caused a revert on the destination side by providing insufficient token B in a swap contract; the test confirmed that the source‑chain tokens remained burnt. This bug is hard to notice because the burn operation is a normal step and the EVM does not surface the remote revert to the caller. The proper fix is to treat the cross‑chain transfer as a two‑phase operation: after burning the tokens, the gateway should monitor the execution result on the destination chain, emit a failure event if the call reverts, and automatically re‑mint the original amount back to the user on the source chain. Implementing a pending state, explicit refund events, and a reliable off‑chain or on‑chain dispatcher to handle roll‑backs will align the behaviour with expected financial semantics and prevent permanent loss of assets.
summary:
Smart contract calls often revert. In such cases any ether sent along with the transaction is returned and sometimes the remaining gas (depending on whether an `assert` caused the reversion or not).

For contracts involving ERC20 tokens it is also expected that, should a contract call fail, one’s tokens are not lost/transferred elsewhere.

The [callContractWithToken](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-04-axelar/blob/dee2f2d352e8f20f20027977d511b19bfcca23a3/src/AxelarGateway.sol#L98-L115) function does not appear to take contract call failure on the destination chain into account, even though this could be quite a common occurrence.

Tokens are burned on [line 105](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-04-axelar/blob/dee2f2d352e8f20f20027977d511b19bfcca23a3/src/AxelarGateway.sol#L105) but there is no mechanism in the code base to return these burned tokens in the case that the contract call fails on the destination chain.

The impact is that users of the Axelar Network can lose funds.

title: Avoidance of Liquidation Via Malicious Oracle
content:
The vulnerability is an oracle‑validation flaw in the loan construction workflow. The contract accepts an arbitrary oracle address supplied by the borrower when a loan is created, but it never verifies that this oracle matches the one the lender expects to use for price feeds and liquidation checks. Because the oracle parameter is unchecked, a borrower can deliberately provide a malicious oracle that never returns a price that would trigger liquidation. When the loan reaches a state where the collateral should be liquidated—e.g., the NFT’s market value falls below the required threshold—the contract calls the supplied oracle’s get function. The malicious oracle can be programmed to always return a safe price, causing the liquidation condition to evaluate to false. Consequently, the lender is unable to invoke the removeCollateral function to seize the NFT, even though the loan is technically under‑collateralized. This creates a situation where the lender’s funds remain locked and the borrower effectively evades the protocol’s risk‑mitigation mechanisms.

The root cause is the lack of a requirement that the oracle used for price queries be pre‑approved or whitelisted by the lender, and the absence of a check that the oracle supplied at loan creation equals the lender‑agreed oracle. The contract assumes that any oracle address is trustworthy, which is not the case. Exploitation follows a simple flow: the borrower includes a malicious oracle address in the loan request, the lender accepts the loan without inspecting the oracle, the borrower’s oracle silently returns non‑liquidating rates, and the lender’s subsequent attempts to liquidate collateral fail the internal price‑check condition.
