content: The vulnerability consists of uninitialized storage variables that hold the address and balanceOfUnderlying for Unripe tokens, stored in s.sys.silo.unripeSettings, after a protocol migration. The migration contracts, known as reseed contracts, are responsible for populating these variables but they omit the initialization step, leaving the fields at their default zero values. Because many core modules read these settings to calculate Bean entitlement, perform Enroot deposits, and execute the Chop conversion from Unripe to Ripe tokens, the missing data causes those functions to operate on empty or zero addresses. As a result, entitlement calculations underestimate the amount of Beans a user should receive, EnrootDeposit calls silently fail or revert, and the Chop conversion logic cannot complete, effectively preventing users from converting their Unripe tokens. The impact is that holders of Unripe tokens see no reward, experience zero balances where they expect a positive amount, and may be unable to move their assets to the Ripe state, which can be perceived as funds being locked or disappearing. This condition manifests only after a migration event, when the reseed contracts run, and persists until the variables are correctly set. All users, the Silo module, and any downstream protocol component that relies on Unripe token accounting are affected. The issue was discovered during a security audit by CodeHawks, who noticed that the migration logic in the init folder does not write to s.sys.silo.unripeSettings. The bug is hard to notice because the faulty functions do not always revert; they may simply return zero values, leading to subtle accounting mismatches that are not obvious from the UI. To remediate, the migration code should be updated to explicitly assign the correct Unripe token address and its underlying balance to s.sys.silo.unripeSettings, and comprehensive tests should be added to verify that entitlement, Enroot, and Chop operations behave as expected after migration. This class of bug is an uninitialized storage variable after upgrade, which breaks business logic that assumes the presence of valid token metadata and accounting data.
summary:
Reseed contracts are responsible for setting storage variables during migration. Problem is that it forgets to initialize s.sys.silo.unripeSettings, i.e. address and balanceOfUnderlying of Unripe tokens. It has several consequences on different modules of Beanstalk

s.sys.silo.unripeSettings are not initialized after migration. All the contracts with migration logic are located in folder protocol/contracts/beanstalk/init/**

Values s.sys.silo.unripeSettings are used throughout a codebase. It has a lot of different impacts:
Invariable.sol underestimates Bean entitlement
EnrootFacet.enrootDeposit() doesn't work
Chop logic doesn't work, it means users can't convert Unripe tokens into Ripe tokens
And so on, I don’t see the point in listing everything. However I will add if necessary during post-judging period.

title: Tokens can get stuck during migration if the L2 side fails leading to loss of funds
content: The vulnerability is a loss‑of‑funds condition that occurs during the cross‑chain migration of Bean tokens from Layer 1 (L1) to Layer 2 (L2). The migration contract burns the user’s tokens on L1, then sends an asynchronous message to an L2 contract that is supposed to mint the same amount for the user. Because the burn and the mint are not performed atomically, the protocol relies on the external message succeeding. If the L2 call reverts – for example because the cumulative migrated amount would exceed a hard‑coded limit, because the supplied gas limit is insufficient, or because of any other contract‑specific check – the L2 mint never happens while the L1 tokens have already been destroyed. From the user’s perspective the balance on L1 becomes zero and the transaction receipt shows success, yet no tokens appear on L2, leading to the impression that the funds have simply disappeared. The issue was identified during a manual audit that examined the migration flow and noticed that there is no rollback or refund mechanism for failed L2 executions. It is difficult to detect because the L1 burn emits a normal event and the failure occurs on a different chain, so the user interface on L1 shows no error. The root cause is the lack of a two‑phase commit or escrow pattern that would guarantee either both sides succeed or both revert, combined with missing tracking of pending migration requests. The impact is permanent loss of tokens for any user whose migration triggers a revert, which can be induced deliberately by sending a request that exceeds the migration cap or by providing an intentionally low gas limit. To remediate, the protocol should record each migration request, allow a timeout‑based refund or retry, and only mark the migration as completed after the L2 mint succeeds. This transforms the bridge from a non‑atomic burn‑then‑mint design into a safe cross‑chain transfer that preserves accounting invariants and prevents funds from being irretrievably burnt.

title: Unfair Penalty Fees in Pipeline Convert
content: An unfair penalty fee is applied in the PipelineConvert function when a user contributes tokens toward the peg of a Well but the conversion capacity has not been exceeded. The root cause is that the calculation of the well’s token capacity (tokenWellCapacity) reads the capped reserves deltaB after the Basin pump has already updated the Well’s reserves within the same transaction. Because the cappedReservesDeltaB becomes zero after the update, the condition `pdCapacityToken > tokenWellCapacity` evaluates true even though the user’s contribution does not exceed the actual capacity. The contract then adds the full contribution amount to the cumulativePenalty, charging the user a fee that should be zero. This can be exploited by simply performing an advanced farm call that moves the Well’s deltaB from a negative value toward zero and then invoking pipelineConvert in the same transaction; the user will be deducted an amount equal to their contribution as a penalty. The impact is a loss of funds for honest participants who are trying to stabilize the peg, leading to unexpected balance reductions, zero refunds, or missing stalk rewards. The vulnerability manifests only when the reserve‑updating function (`readCappedReserves` via MultiflowPump) is called earlier in the transaction and the penalty calculation reads the updated capped reserves later. All users of the Beanstalk protocol who interact with the PipelineConvert facet are affected, as are the protocol’s economic incentives because the penalty discourages peg‑maintaining behavior. The issue was discovered during a security audit and reproduced with a targeted test that showed a penalty of 400 tokens when the expected penalty was zero. It is hard to notice because the code path appears correct and the penalty logic is only wrong under the specific ordering of state changes inside a single transaction. The proper fix is to capture the well’s capped deltaB before any reserve‑updating calls and pass that immutable value to the penalty calculation, ensuring the penalty is computed against the pre‑update capacity. In abstract terms, the bug is a state‑dependency timing error that leads to an incorrect accounting of conversion capacity and an unjust fee.

title: `ReseedSilo` does not set the necessary user variables
content: The vulnerability resides in the migration routine known as ReseedSilo, which is responsible for moving a user’s deposited assets from one accounting context to another. During this process the contract fails to write the user‑specific accounting fields that track the last time rewards were calculated – typically timestamps or counters such as lastUpdated, lastSop and lastRain. Because these variables remain at their default value of zero, the reward‑distribution formula, which assumes a non‑zero reference point, interprets the elapsed time as maximal. Consequently the protocol credits the migrating user with an inflated amount of the reward token (referred to as plenty) that far exceeds what the economic model permits. The flaw is triggered whenever a user invokes the ReseedSilo function; normal deposit or withdrawal paths that do not involve migration are unaffected. The impact is a systematic over‑allocation of rewards that can be repeatedly exploited by any participant who can trigger the migration, potentially draining the protocol’s reserve of reward tokens. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a surprisingly large reward balance after migration, or conversely the protocol may later run out of funds, causing withdrawals to fail or balances to appear empty. The issue was uncovered during a manual audit that examined state changes after migration calls and noticed that the expected fields were never updated. It is easy to miss because the function appears to succeed and emits no error, while the missing assignments are silent. The proper remediation is to ensure that the migration routine explicitly sets the user’s accounting variables to the correct current values before completing, or to redesign the reward calculation to handle zero‑initialized timestamps safely. In broader terms this is a classic state‑inconsistency bug where a critical piece of bookkeeping is omitted, leading to incorrect financial accounting and loss of funds.
summary:
ReseedSilo does not set the necessary user variables

When user deposits are migrated via ReseedSilo, user's storage variables such as lastUpdated, lastSop and lastRain are not set accordingly.

As these values would remain 0, this would allow users for unfair amounts of plenty

Loss of funds

title: Refunding ETH to the caller can be exploited using the Tractor component to call any arbitrary function on behalf of the publisher
content: The vulnerability resides in the Beanstalk protocol’s Tractor component, which is designed to let a publisher delegate a limited set of operations to an external executor via a signed blueprint. Certain functions executed through a blueprint – such as advancedPipe, etherPipe, wrapEth, L1TokenFacet.wrapEth, farm and advancedFarm – invoke an internal refundEth routine that transfers any remaining ETH in the contract to msg.sender using a low‑level call. Because the refund transfers execution control to the caller, the caller’s fallback function is executed while the protocol’s internal activePublisher variable still points to the original publisher. Consequently, the attacker who receives the ETH refund can continue to invoke arbitrary functions on the Beanstalk contract on behalf of the publisher, even though those functions were not authorized in the blueprint. The root cause is the combination of (1) sending ETH to msg.sender instead of the active publisher, (2) not clearing or updating the activePublisher state before the refund, and (3) allowing the refund to occur in the middle of a multi‑call transaction. An attacker can craft a blueprint signed by a victim, trigger one of the vulnerable functions, receive the ETH refund, and then, in the same transaction, call any other protocol function – for example token transfers, fertilizer withdrawals, or pod movements – as if they were the publisher. From the user’s perspective the expected refund arrives, but the victim’s balances may suddenly become zero or tokens may be moved without consent, violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions. The issue appears only when a blueprint includes a function that performs a refund, making it easy to miss during casual testing because the ETH transfer itself is a normal operation. It was discovered during a security audit that included a proof‑of‑concept test where the attacker’s fallback emitted the activePublisher address, confirming that the execution context remained that of the victim. Mitigation requires preventing the refund from being sent to msg.sender – for example by sending the ETH to the active publisher, setting the system flag s.sys.isFarm to block the refund, and adding re‑entrancy protection to the affected functions. By ensuring the activePublisher is cleared or the refund target is safe, the protocol can enforce that only explicitly authorized calls are executed on behalf of a publisher, restoring the intended security model.

title: All migrated silo users will receive less stalk accounted to their account during silo reseed
content: The vulnerability is an accounting error that occurs during the migration of Beanstalk from Layer 1 to Layer 2. When the migration script executes the reseed of the silo component, it reads the per‑BDV stalk issuance rate (stalkIssuedPerBdv) from the L2 state before the token‑whitelisting reseed has populated the asset settings for each token. Because the assetSettings entry for the migrated token is still zero at that moment, the calculation that adds stalk to each user’s account multiplies the user’s BDV by zero. Consequently, every migrated user receives less stalk than they owned on L1. The bug does not trigger a revert; the transaction completes successfully, but the resulting stalk balance is lower than expected. From a user’s perspective the UI will show the same deposited amount but a reduced stalk balance, leading to fewer future rewards or lower voting power. The root cause is the reliance on a state variable that is not yet initialized due to the ordering of reseed steps (silo reseed before token whitelist reseed). This ordering flaw is subtle because the contract does not emit an error and the discrepancy is only visible when comparing pre‑ and post‑migration stalk values. The impact is high because stalk is a core accounting metric that determines reward accrual; users effectively lose a portion of their earned value. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the migration flow and identified that the assetSettings entry is accessed before being set. To remediate, the reseed function should be made independent of external state by passing the correct stalkIssuedPerBdv value in the calldata, or the reseed order should be changed so that token whitelisting occurs before the silo reseed. Either approach ensures that the correct stalk issuance rate is applied and that migrated users retain the full amount of stalk they are entitled to.

title: User can steal all rewards due to checkpoint after transfer
content: The vulnerability arises from an incorrect ordering of operations in the StakerVault transfer function, where the contract updates a user's staked balance before invoking the reward‑checkpoint routine. The checkpoint (ILpGauge.userCheckpoint) is responsible for recording the amount of rewards that a user is entitled to based on their accumulated stake and the global reward integral (poolStakedIntegral). Because the checkpoint is executed after the balance transfer, the recipient’s reward share is calculated using the full transferred amount while the recipient’s previous per‑user integral is still zero. This allows the attacker to move the same tokens across multiple controlled addresses, repeatedly triggering a checkpoint that credits the full transferred amount as new reward entitlement each time. In practice, an adversary can stake a modest amount, transfer the entire balance to a fresh address, claim the newly minted rewards, repeat the transfer to another address, and claim again, draining the reward pool without reducing the underlying staked capital. The issue manifests whenever a user calls transfer, regardless of the source or destination, and it affects any participant who can control multiple accounts, as well as the protocol itself which loses reward tokens that were meant to be distributed proportionally over time. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of StakerVault.sol, where the auditor noticed that all other state‑changing functions invoke the checkpoint before mutating balances, but transfer does the opposite. Because the contract still updates balances correctly and does not revert, the problem is subtle and may be missed by simple testing that only checks token movement. The exploit violates the core accounting assumption that rewards are earned only on the duration of an active stake; instead, rewards are minted instantly after each transfer, effectively breaking the protocol’s economic model. The recommended remediation is to move the userCheckpoint call so that it occurs before the balance update, ensuring that rewards are accrued based on the pre‑transfer stake and preventing the artificial inflation of reward entitlement.
summary:
[StakerVault.sol#L112-L119](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-04-backd/blob/c856714a50437cb33240a5964b63687c9876275b/backd/contracts/StakerVault.sol#L112-L119)  

I believe this to be a high severity vulnerability that is potentially included in the currently deployed `StakerVault.sol` contract also. The team will be contacted immediately following the submission of this report.

In `StakerVault.sol`, the user checkpoints occur AFTER the balances are updated in the `transfer()` function. The user checkpoints update the amount of rewards claimable by the user. Since their rewards will be updated after transfer, a user can send funds between their own accounts and repeatedly claim maximum rewards since the pool’s inception.

In every actionable function except `transfer()` of `StakerVault.sol`, a call to `ILpGauge(lpGauge).userCheckpoint()` is correctly made BEFORE the action effects.

title: function `lockFunds` in `TopUpActionLibrary` can cause serious fund lose. fee and Capped bypass. It’s not calling `stakerVault.increaseActionLockedBalance` when transfers stakes.
content: The vulnerability resides in the TopUpActionLibrary.lockFunds function, which transfers a user’s staked LP tokens from the StakerVault to a TopUpAction position but fails to update the vault’s internal accounting of locked balances. Specifically, after calling stakerVault.transferFrom, the function does not invoke stakerVault.increaseActionLockedBalance for the payer. As a result, the mapping stakerVault.actionLockedBalances[payer] remains unchanged (typically zero) while the user’s tokens are actually locked in the TopUpAction contract. This discrepancy causes stakerVault.stakedAndActionLockedBalanceOf(payer) to return an incorrect, often zero, value. The incorrect balance propagates to several critical code paths: LiquidityPool.depositFor, which checks the user’s total deposits against a deposit cap; LiquidityPool._updateUserFeesOnDeposit, which calculates early‑withdrawal fees; and the userCheckpoint function, which determines reward allocations. Because the reported balance is zero, an attacker can bypass the deposit cap and avoid fee penalties, while legitimate users lose their expected rewards, effectively causing a loss of funds. The issue manifests whenever a user stakes LP tokens, approves the TopUpAction contract, and creates a position via TopUpAction.register. It was uncovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, and its subtlety makes it hard to spot: token transfers succeed and no revert occurs, yet the vault’s accounting state is silently inconsistent, leading to silent miscalculations rather than explicit failures. To remediate the issue, the lockFunds routine must call stakerVault.increaseActionLockedBalance(payer, amountLeft) immediately after the transfer, ensuring the vault’s locked‑balance mapping stays in sync with the actual locked tokens. This correction restores accurate balance queries, re‑enables proper fee enforcement, deposit‑cap validation, and reward distribution, and prevents the potential for fund theft or loss caused by the accounting mismatch.
summary:
[TopUpAction.sol#L57-L65](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-04-backd/blob/c856714a50437cb33240a5964b63687c9876275b/backd/contracts/actions/topup/TopUpAction.sol#L57-L65)  

In function TopUpActionLibrary.lockFunds when transfers stakes from payer it doesn’t call stakerVault.increaseActionLockedBalance for that payer so stakerVault.actionLockedBalances[payer] is not get updated for payer and stakerVault.stakedAndActionLockedBalanceOf(payer) is going to show wrong value and any calculation based on this function is gonna be wrong which will cause fund lose and theft and some restriction bypasses.

title: Customers cannot be `topUp`
content: The vulnerability originates from an incorrect use of OpenZeppelin's SafeERC20.safeApprove function in several top‑up handlers (CompoundHandler, AaveHandler, and TopUpAction). SafeERC20.safeApprove deliberately reverts when it attempts to set a non‑zero allowance while a non‑zero allowance already exists for the same spender, enforcing the pattern that allowances must be first set to zero before being changed to a new value. The contracts call safeApprove with a non‑zero amount each time a user performs a top‑up, without first resetting the existing allowance to zero or using the provided safeIncreaseAllowance / safeDecreaseAllowance helpers. As a result, the first top‑up for a given token succeeds (the allowance is initially zero), but any subsequent top‑up for the same token reverts with the error "SafeERC20: approve from non-zero to non-zero allowance". This failure occurs in the Compound-specific flow when approving the CToken, in the Aave-specific flow when approving the lending pool, and in the generic fee‑payment step when approving the fee handler. The impact is a denial‑of‑service for end‑users: they cannot add additional funds to their positions, the UI may show a successful transaction submission but the on‑chain state remains unchanged, leading to symptoms such as "balance stays at zero," "funds not deposited," or "refund amount is missing." The issue is discovered during a formal security audit that inspected the top‑up action logic and identified the repeated unsafe approve calls. It can be hard to notice because the revert only happens on the second attempt, so initial testing with a single top‑up may appear normal. The bug violates the accounting assumptions of the protocol, which expects that each top‑up will increase the user's collateral without interruption. To remediate, the contract should either reset the allowance to zero before each new approval (calling safeApprove(0) followed by safeApprove(newAmount)) or replace the calls with safeIncreaseAllowance / safeDecreaseAllowance, which safely adjust the allowance regardless of its current value. Implementing this change restores the ability for customers to repeatedly top‑up their positions and prevents unexpected transaction failures.

title: Incorrect calculation of `beanUsdPrice` in LibEvaluate::evalPrice
content: The vulnerability resides in the price evaluation routine of the Beanstalk protocol, specifically in the LibEvaluate.evalPrice function that determines the USD value of a bean token (beanUsdPrice). The code computes beanUsdPrice as 1e30 divided by the product of the USD‑per‑token price (usd/tkn) and the bean‑per‑token price (bean/tkn). Because both oracle values are already expressed as ratios, the correct conversion should multiply the bean‑per‑token price by a scaling factor and then divide by the USD‑per‑token price, not invert the product. This mathematical inversion is the root cause: the formula uses a division of a large constant by the product instead of a multiplication followed by a division, leading to an inverted and dramatically incorrect price. The bug is triggered whenever the function processes a positive deltaB (meaning a bean addition) and the bean‑to‑token price is greater than one, which is the normal path for updating protocol state. An attacker who can influence the underlying well reserves or the oracle‑provided usd/tkn and bean/tkn values can cause the computed beanUsdPrice to be far lower or higher than the true market price. As a result, the subsequent check against the excessivePriceThreshold may be bypassed, causing the function to return an incorrect caseId. This mis‑classification propagates to downstream logic that updates the protocol temperature, BeanToMaxLPRatio, rain handling, and soil issuance. From a user perspective the symptoms can appear as unexpected temperature values, rain events that never trigger, soil allocations that are missing or excessive, or bean balances that do not change after expected actions. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by CodeHawks, who noted that the price formula did not match the intended accounting model. The bug is subtle because the computed price may still be a numeric value that passes basic sanity checks, making it easy to overlook in testing. To remediate, the calculation should be rewritten to multiply the bean‑per‑token price by the scaling factor (1e18) and then divide by the USD‑per‑token price, or equivalently compute 1e30 divided by the product only after inverting one of the ratios. Using safe‑math operations and explicit comments clarifying the intended unit conversion will prevent the inversion error and restore correct protocol accounting.

title: Mint function mekHoneyJarWithETH will revert every time
content: The HoneyBox contract provides a public sale function that is intended to let users mint HoneyJar NFTs by sending Ether. The function calculates the required price using msg.value, which implies that the caller should transfer ETH along with the call. However, the function definition lacks the payable modifier, which is required in Solidity for any function that receives Ether. When a transaction includes a non‑zero msg.value and calls a non‑payable function, the EVM automatically reverts the call before any of the function’s logic executes. Consequently, every attempt to mint a HoneyJar with ETH triggers an immediate revert, the minting logic never runs, no NFT is minted, and the Ether is not transferred. From a user’s perspective the transaction fails with a generic revert error, the wallet shows a failed transaction, and the expected NFT never appears in the user’s balance, leading to confusion and loss of confidence in the sale. The issue is discovered during a security audit that examined the public sale interface and noticed the mismatch between the use of msg.value and the missing payable keyword. It can be hard to notice because the function signature appears correct and the revert occurs before any custom error messages are emitted, so only a generic failure is observed. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “missing payable modifier” bugs, where a contract unintentionally rejects incoming Ether, breaking business logic that assumes payment will be accepted. The impact is high because it disables the entire public sale, prevents users from acquiring NFTs, and may cause reputational damage to the protocol. The condition under which it occurs is any call to the minting function with a non‑zero Ether value; calls with zero value succeed but do not perform the intended purchase. The affected parties are all users attempting to participate in the sale, as well as the protocol that cannot collect funds. The correct remediation is to add the payable modifier to the function definition so that the EVM permits Ether transfers, allowing the price calculation and minting logic to execute as intended. After the change, calls with the appropriate Ether amount will succeed, mint the NFT, and transfer the funds to the contract, restoring the intended economic flow.
summary: The HoneyBox contract exposes a way for users to mint HoneyJar NFTs with ETH in a public sale by the mekHoneyJarWithETH method. The problem is that the method uses msg.value to calculate the expected price, as the name suggest, that would have been paid with ETH, but the method is missing the payable keyword. Every call with msg.value != 0 to the method will revert.

title: Admin account has a lot of power in the protocol and multiple ways to deny/steal users' rewards
content: The vulnerability is an over‑privileged admin role that can be used to manipulate core game mechanics, steal user rewards, and deny service. The root cause is a design that grants the GAME_ADMIN address unrestricted access to functions that change game state, pricing, randomness configuration and limits without any time‑delay or multi‑sig protection. Because the contract relies only on a comment that certain calls should not be made while a game is active, but does not enforce this through code, the admin can front‑run a user’s openHotBox call with a forceHoneyJarSearch call, causing the winner transaction to revert and effectively rugging the user’s reward. The admin can also call setVRFConfig to replace the trusted VRF contract with a custom one that returns deterministic numbers, allowing the admin to decide the outcome of each game. By invoking setMaxhoneyJar the admin can raise the maximum honey‑jar size to an arbitrarily large value, preventing the game from ever reaching a finishing condition; this creates a denial‑of‑service condition even though an isEnabled check exists, because the same admin can toggle the enabled flag via startGame and stopGame. Additionally, the admin can change the honey‑jar price through setHoneyJarPrice_ERC20 after users have granted unlimited token allowance, forcing users to pay a higher price and effectively stealing their tokens. These actions affect every participant who expects to receive a fair reward or to pay a known price; from the user’s perspective the UI may show a missing reward, a zero balance after a win, or a transaction that succeeds but results in a higher token deduction than anticipated. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the access‑control logic and identified that the privileged functions lack proper constraints and can be invoked at any time. The problem is hard to notice because the functions appear benign and the contract contains comments suggesting safe usage, yet no runtime checks enforce those expectations. To remediate, the protocol should remove or severely limit admin‑only functions, introduce a timelock or multi‑signature governance for any parameter changes, separate roles so that no single address can both start/stop games and modify critical parameters, and add explicit checks that prevent state‑changing calls during an active game. In essence, this is a classic case of privileged‑role abuse leading to economic manipulation, front‑running, and denial‑of‑service, violating the protocol’s core accounting assumptions that rewards are earned fairly and funds are transferred according to transparent pricing.
summary: There are multiple centralization flaws and attack vectors in the protocol: Game admin can make openHotBox revert by front-running it with a forceHoneyJarSearch call, essentially rugging game winner Game admin can call setVRFConfig and use his personally controlled VRF interface compliant contract and use a non-random number, essentially deciding the outcome of the game The setMaxhoneyJar method can be used so the game never finishes. Even though it has the isEnabled check, and there is a comment saying should not be called while a game is in progress to prevent hostage holding. this is not true, as the same address ( GAME_ADMIN role) that can call setMaxhoneyJar can call startGame and stopGame which set the enabled flag, so the admin can set the max to a huge number, essentially putting the game into a state of DoS Since game admin controls when a game is started or stopped, it can also front-run users with a call to setHoneyJarPrice_ERC20 and make them pay more if they put unlimited allowance, essentially stealing their tokens

title: H-1 EIP712 DOMAIN_SEPARATOR stored as immutable
content: The contract caches the EIP712 DOMAIN_SEPARATOR in an immutable variable that is calculated once at deployment using the chain ID that was current at that moment. Because the value is stored permanently, the contract never reads the actual chain ID from the CHAINID opcode when constructing the domain separator for later signatures. EIP712 is designed to bind a signed message to a specific blockchain by including the chain ID in the domain separator; if the separator does not reflect the real chain ID, a signature created on one network remains valid on any fork that reuses the same contract bytecode but has a different chain ID. An attacker can therefore take a legitimate order or approval signed on the original chain and replay it on a forked network, causing the contract to accept the message and execute the associated state changes without the original signer’s consent. When the contract also permits unlimited token approvals, the replayed order can move large amounts of assets, leading to unexpected balance reductions or complete loss of funds for the victim. From the user’s perspective the UI may show that an order was placed successfully on the forked network, yet the user’s token balance drops to zero or a refund that was expected never arrives, violating the assumption that a signed order is unique to its originating chain. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of BebopSigning.sol, where the DOMAIN_SEPARATOR was declared immutable and populated with a hard‑coded chain ID at construction, a pattern that deviates from the OpenZeppelin reference implementation. Because the bug relies on subtle EIP712 semantics, it can be overlooked by tests that only run on a single chain, making it hard to notice until a fork occurs. The recommended remediation is to compute the domain separator dynamically using the current chain ID each time a signature is verified, or to follow OpenZeppelin’s EIP712.sol pattern that stores the chain ID in a mutable variable that can be updated after a fork. This eliminates the cross‑chain replay risk and restores the intended security property that signatures cannot be reused on a different network. In generic terms, the vulnerability belongs to the class of static domain separator or chain‑ID mismatch bugs that break the cryptographic binding of messages to a specific blockchain, leading to replay attacks and financial loss.
summary: To prevent so-called "replay attacks", EIP712 incorporates the chain ID into the signed data. However, the audited BebopSigning.sol#L42 EIP712 implementation uses cached values (stored as immutable variables), independent of the actual chain ID which could be returned by the CHAINID EVM opcode. This approach is potentially unsafe as such signatures could be deemed valid in forked networks, thus creating a vulnerability to replay attacks. When combined with unlimited approvals (refer to Medium.1), orders placed on one network could be "replayed" on a forked network without the account owner's consent.

title: Accepting input after randomness is requested can be exploited
content: The vulnerability is a front‑running race condition that arises because the contract continues to accept user‑supplied inputs after a Chainlink VRF randomness request has been sent. In the BearCave game, the number of HoneyJar NFTs minted in a bundle is used inside the fulfillRandomWords callback to select the winning NFT. Because the contract does not lock or snapshot this mint count before the randomness request, an attacker can submit an additional mint transaction after the request but before the VRF callback is executed. The extra mint changes the bundle size, which in turn changes the index calculation that determines the winner. As a result, a participant who expected to be the winner based on the state at the time of the request may receive no reward, while the attacker’s NFT becomes the winner. This constitutes a griefing attack that breaks the economic assumption that the random draw is independent of later user actions. The issue was identified during a security review that referenced the VRF security considerations, which explicitly advise stopping user inputs after a randomness request. The bug is subtle because the contract appears to use a trusted randomness source, so developers may overlook the mutable state that feeds into the winner selection. The impact is limited to the fairness of the game: users can lose expected payouts, and the protocol’s reputation may suffer. The vulnerability affects any participant who relies on the mint count for winning, and it can be exploited by any address capable of front‑running the pending VRF request. To remediate, the contract should decouple the randomness request from mutable inputs: either snapshot the mint count at the moment the request is made, or reject further minting until the VRF callback has completed. Using only pre‑request user data eliminates the race condition and restores the intended guarantee that the random outcome cannot be manipulated after the request.
summary: The VRF security considerations docs explicitly mention that if an outcome in the contract depends on user-supplied inputs (in this case minting HoneyJar NFTs) and randomness, then the contract should stop accepting any additional user-supplied inputs after it submits the randomness request. The problem here is that in fulfillRandomWords the _setFermentedJars method is called where the number of HoneyJar NFTs minted for a bundle is used for the process of choosing the winning NFT - this means that the fulfillRandomWords transaction can be front-ran with a HoneyJar NFT mint and the winner will be different. This can result in a griefing attack for an expected winner of a game.

title: Rounding Issues
content: The vulnerability is a rounding inconsistency that arises because the contract’s deposit and withdraw functions accept arbitrary decimal values from users and immediately reflect those values in the session balance, while a separate rollup balance later aggregates the amounts using a different rounding strategy. The root cause is the lack of input validation that forces amounts to be whole‑unit values, combined with backend logic that does not normalise fractional units before accounting. An attacker can exploit this by submitting a deposit or withdrawal with a small fractional amount (for example 0.1 USDC). The session balance will show the fractional remainder, but when the rollup processes the same transaction it rounds the value differently, leaving a discrepancy such as a session balance of 0.1 USDC while the rollup reports a higher total (e.g., 5.0889 USDC). Over multiple games or transactions these tiny mismatches accumulate, effectively causing user funds to disappear from the visible balance or become locked in the contract without a clear way to retrieve them. The impact is a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees: users expect that the amount they deposit, wager, and withdraw will be tracked precisely, yet the rounding bug can lead to lost or unaccounted funds, undermining trust in the platform. The issue manifests whenever a user supplies a non‑integer amount, which the UI currently permits, and the backend does not enforce integer‑only arithmetic. It affects all participants who interact with the deposit/withdraw flow, the overall protocol’s financial integrity, and any downstream rollup that relies on accurate balances. The problem was discovered during a manual security review that compared on‑chain session balances with the aggregated rollup totals and noticed persistent fractional leftovers. Because the discrepancy is often only a few tenths of a token, it can be easy to overlook in normal operation, especially when UI elements round numbers for display. To remediate, the contract should either reject decimal inputs entirely or implement a consistent rounding scheme that is applied uniformly across session and rollup calculations, ensuring that every fractional unit is either accounted for or explicitly disallowed. This aligns the implementation with the business rule that bets are whole‑unit amounts and prevents the accounting drift that currently allows funds to vanish from the user’s perspective.
summary:
The application is accepting decimals in the Deposit and Withdraw function which is reflected immediately in the session balance (and rollup balance later on):

While the bets are always in rounded numbers, and the deposit, withdraw and finish seem to handle the decimals at the end of the game correctly, the reason this is classified as a High severity issue is that it might still present a potential issue of balance mishandling that the application is not expecting from the user input, considering it does not explicitly enforce the use of decimals and the backend might not be able to tackle the decimal rounding situations.
In the image: session balance 0.1 USDC remaining after playing.

In the image: rollup balance of 5.0889.

title: Tokens with less than 18 decimals allow for draining of funds
content: The contract implements a peer‑to‑peer lending pool where a borrower must provide collateral in a second token to receive a loan in the first token. The core safety check compares the amount of debt with the amount of collateral using a loan‑to‑value ratio (loanRatio) that is calculated under the assumption that both tokens have 18 decimal places. This assumption is hard‑coded in the arithmetic and no token‑specific scaling is performed. When a token with fewer than 18 decimals (for example USDC with 6 decimals or WBTC with 8 decimals) is used as the loan token, the raw integer values are interpreted as if they already contain 18 decimal places. Consequently the loanRatio becomes dramatically smaller than it should be, allowing a borrower to satisfy the maxLoanRatio condition with an almost negligible amount of collateral. An attacker can therefore open a pool, deposit a modest amount of a low‑decimal loan token, and then borrow the entire pool balance by supplying a tiny fraction of the collateral token (e.g., 0.00000001 WETH) that is worth only a few cents. The pool’s funds are transferred to the attacker while the collateral left in the pool is insufficient to cover the loss, effectively draining the pool. The vulnerability manifests whenever a pool is created with a loan token whose decimals are not 18, or when the collateral token has fewer decimals, which also breaks the ratio check and can block legitimate operations. It affects any user who supplies liquidity to such a pool, the protocol’s overall capital safety, and any downstream borrowers who rely on correct over‑collateralisation. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by constructing a test that created a USDC/WETH pool and observed that the borrower could extract the full USDC balance with a minuscule WETH deposit. Because the contract does not expose the decimal values of the tokens, the mis‑scaling is not obvious from the UI; users see that they can borrow large amounts with almost no collateral, which contradicts the expected economic model. The bug belongs to the class of “decimal‑handling or scaling errors” that arise when fixed‑point arithmetic assumes a uniform precision across heterogeneous ERC‑20 tokens. To remediate, the loanRatio calculation must be normalised by each token’s `decimals()` value, scaling the debt and collateral to a common 18‑decimal base before performing the division. This ensures that the ratio reflects the true monetary value of the assets and restores the intended over‑collateralisation guarantees.

title: Lender contract can be drained by re-entrancy in `repay`
content: The vulnerability is a classic re‑entrancy flaw that occurs in the repay function of the lending contract. When a borrower calls repay, the contract first transfers the outstanding loan amount and the protocol fee from the caller to itself using ERC20.transferFrom, then transfers the collateral back to the borrower, and only after these external calls does it delete the loan record. Because the loan data is removed after the token transfers, a malicious ERC20 token can execute code during its transferFrom hook (for example in _afterTokenTransfer) and call the repay function again before the original loan entry is cleared. By re‑entering repay multiple times, the attacker can cause the contract to transfer the same collateral repeatedly, effectively draining all tokens that were held as collateral. The bug is triggered whenever any token is used as the loan token and the token’s transfer implementation allows a callback, which is possible for custom ERC20 contracts. The impact is that the protocol’s collateral pool can be emptied, leaving legitimate borrowers without their pledged assets and causing the protocol’s accounting to break – users see their expected collateral return disappear and the contract balance drop to near zero. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the order of state changes and external calls, and it was demonstrated with a proof‑of‑concept exploit that creates a token with a transfer hook that re‑enters repay ten times. The flaw is subtle because ERC20.transferFrom is often assumed to be a simple value move without side effects, so developers may overlook the need for a re‑entrancy guard. To remediate, the contract should follow the Checks‑Effects‑Interactions pattern: delete or update the loan record before performing any external token transfers, and protect the function with a nonReentrant modifier or equivalent lock. This change ensures that even if a token’s transfer triggers a callback, the loan state is already finalized and cannot be abused, preserving the integrity of the collateral accounting.

title: Lender contract can be drained by re-entrancy in `setPool`
content: The vulnerability is a classic re‑entrancy flaw that appears in the Lender contract when it interacts with tokens that allow a callback during a transfer, such as ERC777 tokens with an _afterTokenTransfer hook. The contract’s setPool function compares the new pool balance with the current balance and, if the new balance is lower, it sends the difference to the lender before updating the internal pool mapping. Because the external token transfer is performed first, a malicious token can invoke its hook (tokensReceived) during the transfer and call back into setPool while the contract’s state still reflects the old, higher balance. The attacker can therefore manipulate the poolBalance value on the re‑entered call, causing the contract to believe it still owes funds and triggering another transfer. By repeatedly re‑entering in this way, the attacker can drain all tokens held by the Lender contract. The issue manifests only when the token used for the loan supports re‑entrant callbacks and when setPool is called with a poolBalance that is lower than the contract’s current token balance. It affects any lender, borrower, or token holder that relies on the Lender contract for safe custody of funds, as the contract’s accounting assumptions are broken and the expected invariant that the pool balance never exceeds the contract’s token holdings is violated. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that included testing with a custom token implementing a transfer hook, and it can be hard to notice because the transfer itself succeeds and the token appears to follow the ERC20 interface, masking the hidden callback. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are that after a pool update the contract’s token balance becomes zero, the lender receives no refund, and the attacker ends up with all the tokens, effectively making the funds disappear. The proper mitigation is to follow the Checks‑Effects‑Interactions (CEI) pattern: update the pool mapping (or any relevant state) before performing any external token transfer, and protect the function with a nonReentrant guard to block recursive calls. This eliminates the window where an external call can manipulate contract state and restores the intended accounting guarantees.

title: Sandwich attack to steal all ERC-20 tokens in the Fees contract
content: The vulnerability is a permissionless profit‑selling function that swaps any ERC‑20 token held by the Fees contract for WETH without enforcing any slippage protection. The function builds a Uniswap ExactInputSingle call with amountOutMinimum set to zero and sqrtPriceLimitX96 also set to zero, meaning the swap will execute at whatever price the pool offers at the moment of execution. Because the function can be called by any address and has no access control, an attacker can use a flash loan to manipulate the pool price, call the function, and extract all tokens that were meant to be retained as protocol fees. The root cause is the omission of a minimum‑output check or price ceiling, which allows a sandwich or front‑running attack to force the contract to sell its tokens at an artificially low rate. In a typical exploit, the attacker borrows a large amount of the target token (for example USDC) via a flash loan, uses part of the loan to buy WETH from the same Uniswap pool, thereby pushing the USDC/​WETH price upward. The attacker then invokes sellProfits, which swaps the entire USDC balance of the Fees contract for WETH at the now‑inflated price, receiving far fewer WETH than expected. The attacker immediately sells the acquired WETH back to the pool, restoring the original price, repays the flash loan, and keeps the drained USDC as profit. This sequence can be repeated for any ERC‑20 token held by the contract, such as DAI or CRV. The impact is the complete loss of protocol‑earned fees, leaving users with zero balances where they expected to see accrued rewards, and depriving the staking component of the WETH that should have been transferred. The issue manifests whenever sellProfits is called, which can happen at any time because the function is public and lacks any owner‑only restriction. It was discovered during a manual audit of the Fees.sol source, where the parameters amountOutMinimum and sqrtPriceLimitX96 were observed to be hard‑coded to zero, a pattern commonly associated with unchecked swaps. The problem is subtle because the function appears to perform a harmless conversion of profits, and the zero values may be mistakenly interpreted as “no limit” rather than “no protection”. To remediate, the function should be restricted to authorized callers (e.g., onlyOwner) and must enforce a reasonable amountOutMinimum based on market rates or an oracle, optionally also setting a sqrtPriceLimitX96 to cap the acceptable price range. This class of bug—unchecked external swaps with missing slippage safeguards—breaks the accounting assumptions of the protocol, allowing MEV bots to manipulate prices and steal funds that users expect to be safely stored.
summary:
The Fees::sellProfits() lacks slippage protection, resulting in being attacked by a sandwich attack to drain all locked ERC-20 tokens.

The sellProfits() is a permissionless function that can be called by anyone. The function lacks slippage protection (the parameters amountOutMinimum and sqrtPriceLimitX96 are set to 0) when swapping tokens through Uniswap's pools. 

In this way, an attacker can launch a sandwich attack with a flash loan to drain all ERC-20 tokens (e.g., USDC, DAI, CRV, etc.) locked in the Fees contract. 

For instance, to drain all USDC, consider the following proof-of-concept.
Attacker borrows a flash loan for USDC and buys WETH from Uniswap's WETH/USDC pool.
Attacker executes the sellProfits(USDC).
The sellProfits() will spend all locked USDC for buying WETH at a very high price.
Attacker sells the previously obtained WETH for USDC at the same pool and repays the flash loan.
Attacker takes all locked USDC as profit.

Moreover, an attacker can perform steps 1-5 above to steal other ERC-20 tokens locked in the Fees contract.

```solidity
    function sellProfits(address _profits) public {
        require(_profits != WETH, "not allowed");
        uint256 amount = IERC20(_profits).balanceOf(address(this));

        ISwapRouter.ExactInputSingleParams memory params = ISwapRouter
            .ExactInputSingleParams({
                tokenIn: _profits,
                tokenOut: WETH,
                fee: 3000,
                recipient: address(this),
                deadline: block.timestamp,
                amountIn: amount,
                amountOutMinimum: 0,
                sqrtPriceLimitX96: 0
            });

        amount = swapRouter.exactInputSingle(params);
        IERC20(WETH).transfer(staking, IERC20(WETH).balanceOf(address(this)));
    }
```

https://github.com/Cyfrin/2023-07-beedle/blob/658e046bda8b010a5b82d2d85e824f3823602d27/src/Fees.sol#L38-L39

An attacker can drain all ERC-20 tokens (e.g., USDC, DAI, CRV, etc.) locked in the Fees contract. Therefore, I consider this vulnerability a high-risk issue.

title: Borrower can use Refinance to cancel auctions so they can extend their loan indefinitely
content: The vulnerability is a logical flaw in the loan refinancing workflow that allows a borrower to cancel an active liquidation auction and keep the loan open indefinitely. When a lender initiates an auction on an overdue loan, the contract records an auction end timestamp based on the current block time plus a fixed auction length. The refinance function, however, resets this timestamp to the maximum uint256 value whenever the loan is moved to another pool, even if the new pool has identical parameters to the original one. Because the contract treats a timestamp of type(uint256).max as a sentinel meaning "no active auction", the ongoing auction is effectively cancelled. An attacker can exploit this by calling refinance during the auction, optionally followed by a giveLoan or a second refinance back to the original pool, which restores the loan without resetting the auction timer. This sequence can be repeated, allowing the borrower to extend the loan period forever, even when the loan is under‑collateralised. The impact is that lenders lose the ability to liquidate insolvent positions, leading to perpetual exposure to bad debt and potential loss of funds for the protocol. The issue manifests only when the borrower has permission to invoke refinance while an auction is live and when a compatible pool exists that matches the original loan specifications. It affects any lender or protocol participant relying on the auction mechanism for debt recovery. The flaw was discovered during a security audit by CodeHawks, who wrote a unit test that showed the auction timestamp being set to type(uint256).max after a refinance call. The problem is subtle because the refinance path is expected to transfer the loan, not to interfere with auction state, and the timestamp reset does not raise an explicit error, making it easy to miss in regular testing. To remediate, the contract should preserve the original auction timestamp when a loan is refinanced, or explicitly forbid refinancing while an auction is active, ensuring that the liquidation process cannot be bypassed. In broader terms, this is an instance of an auction‑cancellation bug caused by improper state reset during loan migration, violating the accounting assumption that a loan under auction remains subject to liquidation until the auction expires.

title: During refinance() new Pool balance debt is subtracted twice
content: During the refinance operation a borrower can move an existing loan from one liquidity pool to another with different lending terms. The contract first transfers the accrued interest from the loan back to the original pool, then attempts to transfer the outstanding debt amount to the target pool by decreasing the target pool's balance. However the implementation subtracts the debt amount from the target pool's balance twice: once through an internal helper call that updates the pool balance, and a second time by directly reducing the stored poolBalance variable. As a result the target pool's recorded balance is reduced by twice the debt, effectively removing funds that should belong to the lenders of that pool. The bug manifests whenever a refinance is executed, i.e., after the loan has accrued interest and the borrower calls refinance with a new pool identifier. Any borrower who successfully refinances a loan triggers the double subtraction, causing the lenders' pool to lose the amount of the transferred debt. From a user perspective the lenders see their pool balance drop unexpectedly, sometimes to zero, and borrowers may notice that the new pool reports a lower balance than expected, leading to missing funds for future borrowers. The issue was discovered during a manual audit and reproduced with a unit test that checks the pool balance before and after refinance, showing a discrepancy of two times the debt. The problem is subtle because the two statements appear in different parts of the function and both appear to be legitimate balance updates, making it easy to miss during code review. The vulnerability belongs to the class of accounting bugs where state variables are updated redundantly, causing double counting or double subtraction. To fix the issue the contract should ensure that the debt transfer updates the pool balance exactly once, either by using the helper function exclusively or by removing the direct subtraction, and adding a test that validates that the pool balance changes by exactly the debt amount. Proper invariant checks on pool balances before and after refinance would also help detect similar errors.
summary:
A borrower has the opportunity to move their loan to another pool under new lending conditions.

During refinancing interest from the loan is transferred to the old pool.

The debt is then transferred to the new pool however this subtraction occurs twice, resulting in loss of funds to the Lenders pool.

In refinance() the debt to the new pool is transferred at line 636

```solidity
_updatePoolBalance(poolId, pools[poolId].poolBalance - debt);
```

The debt is subtracted again at line 696

```solidity
pools[poolId].poolBalance -= debt;
```

title: Token spending by Uniswap router doesn't get approved
content: The vulnerability is a missing ERC20 allowance step in the sellProfits function of the contract. When the function attempts to swap a profit token for WETH through the Uniswap router, it calls swapRouter.exactInputSingle without first approving the router to transfer the token balance held by the contract. ERC20 tokens require an explicit allowance before a third‑party contract can move them; because no approve call is made, the router’s transferFrom reverts, causing the entire sellProfits transaction to fail. This failure occurs every time sellProfits is invoked with any ERC20 token other than WETH that the contract currently holds, effectively locking those tokens inside the contract forever. Users who send tokens to the contract expecting them to be sold for WETH see their transaction revert, receive no WETH, and find the token balance unchanged, which looks like a loss of funds. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the function logic and noticed the comment “@audit The tokens do not get approved”. It can be hard to notice because the function otherwise appears to construct a correct swap request, and the revert surface‑level error does not explicitly mention an allowance problem. The bug belongs to the class of missing‑approval or allowance‑related vulnerabilities, where a contract assumes it can move tokens without setting the required allowance. To remediate, the contract should call IERC20(_profits).approve(address(swapRouter), amount) (or the full balance) before invoking exactInputSingle, or alternatively pull the tokens from the user at the start of the call so that the contract never holds unapproved tokens. Proper error handling and checks for successful approval would also prevent the silent locking of assets and align the implementation with the expected business logic that profits are converted to WETH and transferred to the staking address.

title: Borrower can bypass maxLoanRatio's configuration of a pool via buyLoan()
content: The issue is a missing business‑logic validation in the buyLoan function of the lending protocol. When a loan is purchased from an auction, the contract calculates the loan‑to‑value ratio (loanRatio) but does not verify that this ratio is lower than the maxLoanRatio configured for the destination pool. As a result, a borrower can create a personal pool with an artificially high maxLoanRatio, borrow a loan using minimal collateral, start an auction, and then call buyLoan to transfer the loan to any other pool that has a lower maxLoanRatio. Because the buyLoan function lacks the ratio check that other functions enforce, the destination pool accepts the loan even though its LTV exceeds the pool’s risk parameters. This bypass can be performed by any caller, not only the borrower, so a lender may unknowingly acquire a high‑risk loan and suffer unexpected losses, such as collateral being insufficient to cover the debt or the loan being liquidated prematurely. The vulnerability manifests whenever buyLoan is invoked, regardless of the caller, and when the loan’s computed ratio exceeds the pool’s configured limit. It affects borrowers who can exploit the flaw, lenders who may receive loans with unacceptable risk, and the overall protocol integrity because accounting assumptions about loan safety are violated. The flaw was discovered during a security audit by CodeHawks through a crafted test case that minted a loan token, set up a pool with maxLoanRatio of five, borrowed with a 1:1 collateral‑debt ratio, and then successfully moved the loan to another pool with maxLoanRatio of one without any revert. The problem is subtle because the UI and transaction receipts show a successful loan purchase, and there is no explicit warning about the high LTV, making it hard for users to notice the discrepancy. To remediate, the contract should perform the same ratio validation used elsewhere: after computing loanRatio, compare it to pools[poolId].maxLoanRatio and revert with a RatioTooHigh error if the loan exceeds the allowed limit. This correction restores the intended risk controls and prevents borrowers from bypassing pool‑level LTV constraints, thereby protecting lenders from unexpected fund loss.
summary:
In buyLoan(), there is no validation if the loanRatio < pool.maxLoanRatio. Therefore, a lender can be given a loan with higher LTV than his pool which he doesn't want at all.

Since buyLoan() can be called by anyone, a malicious borrower can borrow a loan from his own pool with a pretty high maxLoanRatio so that he can put the least collateral possible to take the loan, then forcefully push this loan by calling buyLoan() with his own loan to a random pool with enough pool balance of the pairs. Doing this helps the borrower avoid the risk of high LTV.
Borrower can give his high LTV loan to any pool with enough balance by calling buyLoan() to escape the risk of high LTV.
Anyone or the new lender himself/herself can buy the loan via buyLoan() without noticing the high LTV in it, which may lead to fund losing.

title: Using forged/fake lending pools to steal any loan opening for auction
content: The vulnerability resides in the Lender contract’s buyLoan function, which allows a caller to specify an arbitrary pool identifier when purchasing a loan that is currently open for auction. The function does not verify that the loan’s original loanToken and collateralToken match the token pair associated with the supplied poolId. Because of this missing token‑compatibility check, an attacker can create or reference a forged pool that advertises a different loanToken or collateralToken, even a pair with zero market value, and pass its identifier to buyLoan. When the function executes, it deducts the total debt from the forged pool’s balance and records the attacker as the new lender, effectively transferring ownership of the loan and its associated debt without moving the genuine loanToken or collateralToken assets. This can be exploited by calling buyLoan with a pool that uses, for example, DAI as the loanToken while the original loan expects WETH, allowing the attacker to acquire a loan backed by high‑value collateral while paying only a negligible amount of DAI. The impact is severe: the borrower’s collateral may be left untouched while the loan’s debt is reassigned, causing the protocol’s accounting to become inconsistent and potentially rendering the entire system insolvent as the real loanToken and collateralToken are siphoned away. The flaw manifests whenever a loan is opened for auction and any participant invokes buyLoan; it does not depend on special permissions, making it exploitable by any external actor who can supply a crafted poolId. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the state updates in buyLoan and noticed the absence of any token‑pair validation before the pool balance adjustment. Because the function appears to work correctly from a superficial view—updating balances and loan metadata—the problem can be hard to spot without tracing the token flow. From a user’s perspective, a borrower may see that their loan has been transferred to an unknown lender, their expected repayment token balance remains unchanged, or the protocol UI may show a loan marked as sold while the underlying assets are missing, leading to confusion and loss of funds. This class of bug is an “incorrect asset‑type validation” or “token mismatch” vulnerability, where the contract assumes that the pool’s token configuration aligns with the loan’s configuration without enforcing it. To remediate, the buyLoan implementation should explicitly compare the loan’s loanToken and collateralToken against the pool’s declared tokens and revert the transaction if they differ, thereby preventing forged pools from being used to hijack loans.

title: Stealing any loan opening for auction through others' lending pool
content: The vulnerability is an authorization bypass in the loan purchase function. The contract allows any caller to invoke buyLoan and specify an arbitrary pool identifier. Because the function does not verify that msg.sender is the owner (lender) of the supplied pool, the caller can force a pool that does not belong to them to transfer the full loan debt from its balance to the caller’s address. The forced pool’s balance is reduced by the total debt and its outstandingLoans counter is increased, while the loan record is updated so that the attacker becomes the new lender. Later, when the borrower repays the loan, the repayment logic recomputes the pool identifier from the loan.lender field, which now points to the attacker’s pool. Consequently, the repayment amount—including principal and accrued interest—is credited to the attacker’s pool, effectively stealing the loan principal and interest from the original pool. This flaw can be exploited by any external account, including the current legitimate lender, by simply calling buyLoan with a victim’s poolId. The impact is a loss of funds for the victim pool, incorrect accounting of outstanding loans, and a breach of trust in the lending protocol. The issue manifests when a loan is opened for auction and the buyLoan function is executed; the victim observes an unexpected drop in pool balance and may later see that repayments are routed to an unknown address. The vulnerability was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the flow of pool balance updates and noticed the missing check for pool ownership. It is subtle because the function appears to perform a legitimate loan purchase, and the lack of an explicit require statement makes the misuse non‑obvious. The bug belongs to the class of access‑control/ownership validation errors that break financial invariants. To remediate, the contract should enforce that msg.sender matches the lender recorded for the pool before allowing a balance deduction, and should ensure that pool identifiers used in repayment are derived from a trusted source rather than a mutable loan field.

title: Attacker can steal a loan's collateral and break the protocol
content: The vulnerability is an authorization and token‑compatibility flaw in the loan‑purchase routine of the lending platform. The buyLoan function can be invoked by any address, regardless of whether the caller owns the pool identified by the supplied poolId, and it does not verify that the pool’s collateralToken and loanToken match the tokens of the loan being bought. Because of this, an attacker can create a fake pool that uses worthless ERC‑20 tokens, call buyLoan to acquire an auctioned loan, and later create a legitimate‑looking pool with the correct token pair only to satisfy the internal bookkeeping that updates the pool’s outstandingLoans. By doing so the attacker can invoke seizeLoan and transfer the entire collateral of the original borrower to themselves while paying only a tiny amount equal to loan.debt * borrowerFee/10 000. The attack proceeds as follows: an attacker creates a fake pool with arbitrary tokens, purchases the loan from the auction using that pool, then creates a real pool that matches the loan’s token pair but is funded only with the exact debt amount needed to avoid underflow checks. The attacker then auto‑borrows from this pool, starts a new auction, and finally calls seizeLoan, which moves the borrower’s collateral to the attacker’s address. The impact is that the original borrower loses their collateral, lenders attached to the loan cannot withdraw their loanToken balances, and the protocol’s accounting invariants are broken, leading to underflow reverts in repay or refinance functions. This condition occurs only when a loan is in auction state and the platform does not enforce pool ownership or token compatibility checks. All participants—borrowers, lenders, and the protocol itself—are affected because funds disappear and the protocol’s trust model is compromised. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the control flow of buyLoan and identified missing require statements. It is hard to notice because the function appears to work correctly for legitimate pools, and the mismatch of token addresses does not raise an error until later bookkeeping steps fail. To remediate, the contract must enforce that msg.sender is the owner of the pool identified by poolId and must require that pools[poolId].collateralToken equals loan.collateralToken and pools[poolId].loanToken equals loan.loanToken before allowing a purchase, thereby preventing unauthorized pool substitution and ensuring that only compatible token pairs can be used in loan auctions.
summary:
The platform allows an attacker to steal an auctioned loan's collateral. The result of the attack is that
At some point, some lender will not be able to withdraw the invested loanToken used to create the pool (or add balance to the pool)
The attacker has stolen the whole loan's collateral amount (minus protocol fee) by just spending (loan.debt * borrowerFee / 10_000)

The attack is pretty complex but is based on different issues that are present in the buyLoan function. This function allows
anyone to call the function even if msg.sender is not the owner of the poolId passed as parameter. The function at the very end will anyway set loan.lender = msg.sender and will update the newLoanPool.poolBalance and newLoanPool.outstandingLoans without the authorization of the newLoanPool real owner
do not check that the newLoanPool is compatible with the loan that will be bought. To be specific, the function does not check that newLoanPool.collateralToken == loan.collateralToken and newLoanPool.loanToken == loan.loanToken

We are in the current scenario
Alice creates alicePool with the following config
collateral token = collateralToken
loan token = loanToken
poolBalance = 1000 ether of loanToken 
the other part of the config is not relevant
Bob borrows 100 ether of loanToken and provides 100 ether of collateralToken as collateral. This operation generates a Loan identified with the id bobLoan
Some time passes by and Alice decides that she wants to auction bobLoan. Alice calls startAuction(bobLoan)

At this point, the attack starts. Let's call Paul our attacker.
Paul creates a fake pool called fakePool with the following configuration:
collateral token = fakeCollateralToken. This token is a fresh and value-less ERC20 token that Paul deployed just before the pool creation.
loan token = fakeLoanToken. This token is a fresh and value-less ERC20 token that Paul deployed just before the pool creation.
poolBalance = 1000 ether of fakeLoanToken 
interestRate = 1 wei. This allows Paul to be able to instantly buy the loan without waiting for the auction to decay the currentAuctionRate
the other part of the config is not relevant
Paul at this point has bought bobLoan spending value-less tokens by using a fakePool that uses tokens incompatible with alicePool and bobLoan

Already at this point, we have created a huge problem for the protocol because 
Bob will not be able to refinance or repay the loan to take back the collateral. Those function would try to update a pool identified by (paul, loan.loanToken, loan.collateralToken) but such pool does not exist because the loan has been "bought" by using fakePool identified as (paul, fakeLoanToken, fakeCollateralToken). Because the pool with the tokens used by the Loan do not exist, both repay and refinance will revert to an underflow error
At some point some Lender won't be able to withdraw their loanToken because Paul has not provided any loanToken to create the fakePool but only an amount of fakeLoanToken

Paul now performs the final step to steal the collateral that Bob has provided to open the borrow position. To do so, Paul needs to seize bobLoan. 

The only problem for Paul is that the function perform this operation at the very end

```solidity
bytes32 poolId = keccak256(
	abi.encode(loan.lender, loan.loanToken, loan.collateralToken)
);

// update the pool outstanding loans
pools[poolId].outstandingLoans -= loan.debt;
```

But at the moment pools[poolId] does not exist because Paul has only created a pool that uses the fake tokens. To be able to finish the attack, Paul needs to perform

1) Paul creates a real pool called paulPool with the following configuration
collateral token = collateralToken (equal to bobLoan.collateralToken)
loan token = loanToken. (equal to bobLoan.loanToken)
poolBalance = bobLoan.debt ether of loanToken. We just need to make the seizeLoan function not revert when it updates the paulPool.outstandingLoans state variable
interestRate = 1 wei. This allows Paul to be able to instantly buy the loan without waiting for the auction to decay the currentAuctionRate
minLoanSize <= bobLoan.debt. In this case, we can set it to 1 wei
maxLoanRatio = type(uint256).max. The attacker wants to be able to provide less collateral as possible to perform the needed debt
2) Paul perform an auto-borrow operation. Be borrows loanToken from his own paulPool to maximize the final profit, spending as less as possible. Paul borrows from paulPool bobLoan.debt tokens, providing only 1 wei of collateralToken. This is possible because paulPool.maxLoanRatio == type(uint256).max. By performing this operation, we now have paulPool.outstandingDebt == bobLoan.debt. At the end of the operation, Paul will have in his balance bobLoan.debt - borrowerProtocolFee of loanToken
3) Paul calls startAuction([bobLoan]) starting the loan auction
4) Paul calls seizeLoan([bobLoan]) that will seize bobLoan.collateral amount of collateralToken and will send them to the attacker (minus the protocol fee)

At the end of the attack, Paul has invested just bobLoan.debt * borrowerFee / 10_000 of loanToken to perform the needed borrow operation and has gained the whole bobLoan.collateral (minus the protocol fee).

The platform allows an attacker to steal an auctioned loan's collateral. The result of the attack is that
At some point, some lender will not be able to withdraw the invested loanToken used to create the pool (or add balance to the pool)
The attacker has stolen the whole loan's collateral amount (minus protocol fee) by just spending (loan.debt * borrowerFee / 10_000)

title: Fee on transfer tokens will cause users to lose funds
content: The vulnerability is an accounting mismatch that arises when the contract interacts with ERC20 tokens that charge a fee on each transfer, often called fee‑on‑transfer or tax‑on‑transfer tokens. In the deposit() function the contract calls transferFrom with the amount supplied by the caller and then blindly adds that same amount to the internal balances mapping, assuming the token transferred exactly the requested number of tokens. Because the token deducts a percentage as a fee, the contract actually receives less than the amount specified, but its internal accounting still records the full amount. Consequently the sum of the internal balances can exceed the real token balance held by the contract. An attacker can exploit this by depositing a fee‑on‑transfer token, inflating the pool’s reported balance, and then withdrawing the nominal amount, thereby siphoning the fee portion that belongs to other users. When an honest user later attempts to withdraw their recorded amount, the transfer call reverts due to insufficient token balance, leaving the user with a zero or stuck balance. The issue only manifests when a token that imposes a transfer fee is used and the contract does not verify the net amount received; it is hard to notice because the transfer call succeeds and no event signals the fee deduction, so the mismatch is only visible when withdrawals fail or when the contract’s total token balance does not match the sum of user balances. This bug violates the fundamental business logic that token transfers are fee‑free and that the amount sent equals the amount received, breaking accounting assumptions and allowing funds to disappear from honest participants. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract’s internal accounting with the actual token balance of the contract. To remediate, the contract should measure the token balance before and after each transfer (or use a token interface that returns the actual amount received) and update the internal accounting with the net amount, and also protect the function with a reentrancy guard. This class of issue is commonly referred to as a “fee‑on‑transfer token mismatch” or “incorrect handling of tokens with transfer fees”. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are that after depositing tokens the internal balance appears correct, but later a withdrawal either returns zero, reverts, or the pool’s total token balance is higher than the sum of individual balances, effectively causing funds to disappear.

title: update() not getting called right after a WETH amount has been sent will cause users to lose staking rewards
content: The vulnerability originates from a missing call to the Staking contract’s update() function immediately after a WETH reward is transferred from Fees.sol via sellProfits(). Staking.sol maintains a reward index that is recalculated whenever new WETH is added; the index is computed as (newWETH * 1e18) / totalStakedSupply and later used to determine each staker’s additional reward through the formula (stakedAmount * currentMultiplier) / 1e18. If update() is not executed right after the WETH transfer, the internal index remains stale while the contract’s total token supply changes when a new user deposits tokens. Consequently, when the next updateFor() call is performed, the multiplier is applied to an outdated supply figure, causing earlier stakers to receive a smaller share of the newly added rewards.
