summary: The code flow of Distributor.distributeFor is in charge of compensating validators with BGT tokens and additional vault specific tokens. During the flow of the function, it queries the nextActionableBlock, then it is transferring (using a potentially untrusted external call) the incentive tokens to the validator and only then increments the getNextActionableBlock to make sure the next transaction would not double-spend. The distributeFor is therefore violating the "Checks-Effects-Interactions" pattern since the external interaction is executed before the effects (incrementing the getNextActionableBlock). In case one of the incentive tokens implements an unsafe external call, the call flow can be hijacked to re-enter distributeFor repeatedly and by this drain the entire BGT and incentive tokens allocated. The reentrant call will have to provide the necessary parameters that were used originally for the call but this can be fetched by a front runner spotting the call to distributeFor in the mempool and writing the value to a contract that will be used through the reentrancy flow.

title: Validators can front run calls to addIncentive to drain the entire incentive allocation in return for validating a single block
content: The vulnerability is a front‑running manipulation of the permissionless addIncentive function that allows a validator to set the incentive rate under a specific edge case and then drain the entire incentive allocation in a single block. The root cause lies in the contract logic that permits any caller to change the incentiveRate whenever incentive.amountRemaining is less than or equal to minIncentiveRate, without requiring additional checks or isolation of the caller’s intent. Because the rate can be overwritten by anyone in this state, an attacker can monitor the mem‑pool, submit a tiny addIncentive transaction with the maximum allowed incentiveRate, and cause the contract to record a high rate while only adding a minimal amount of tokens. When a legitimate user later submits a larger addIncentive call expecting to set a lower rate, the condition on line 329 is bypassed, leaving the previously injected high rate in place and the amountRemaining just above the minimum threshold. The attacker then calls distributeFor, which calculates the reward as the minimum of the product of the emitted BGT amount and the inflated incentiveRate and the amountRemaining. Since the amountRemaining is now just above the minimum, the calculation yields the full token balance, allowing the attacker to claim the entire incentive pool for a single validated block. This results in the loss of incentive tokens, unfair reward distribution, and a breach of the protocol’s economic assumptions. The issue manifests only when the incentive pool is low – either on the first funding or after previous rewards have been exhausted – making it easy to miss during normal testing because the usual path (with sufficient amountRemaining) behaves correctly. The affected parties include validators who rely on predictable rewards, token holders whose incentives are depleted, and the protocol itself, which can no longer guarantee proper incentive accounting. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the addIncentive logic and identified that the incentiveRate could be set without proper permission checks. Detecting the exploit in production can be difficult because the contract does not emit explicit warnings when the rate is overwritten, and the UI may simply show a sudden drop of the incentive balance or a single validator receiving an unexpectedly large reward. To remediate, the contract should prevent arbitrary rate changes when the pool is low, for example by requiring that any rate adjustment be accompanied by a sufficient token deposit to cover the increase, by restricting rate changes to a privileged role, or by adopting a commit‑reveal or isolated‑per‑caller design similar to the Drips Protocol. The proposed code adds validation that only allows a rate reset when the pool is empty and otherwise requires the caller to provide enough tokens to justify the rate delta, thereby raising the cost of front‑running attacks and mitigating the incentive drain.

title: Attacker Can Redirect Funds To Staking Via Allowances
content: The vulnerability is an allowance misuse in the delegateStake function of the staking contract. The function calls ERC20.transferFrom with a caller‑supplied "from" address instead of restricting the source to the transaction sender. Because users and the contract owner must approve the staking contract before calling stake, delegateStake, createReward, repayment or depositRewardAmount, an attacker can watch for these approvals and then front‑run the next transaction. By invoking delegateStake on behalf of the approved address, the attacker can cause the contract to pull tokens from the victim’s balance and stake them under the attacker’s control or under a lock chosen by the attacker. This redirects funds that were meant to be distributed as rewards into a staking position that is subject to the contract’s lock period, effectively freezing the victim’s tokens until the lock expires. The issue occurs only after a legitimate approval has been granted and before the intended function call is mined, making the attack timing‑dependent. Any user who approves the contract, as well as the protocol owner who approves reward deposits, can be affected: users may see their expected reward balance disappear, owners may notice that reward tokens are locked instead of being available for distribution, and the staking parameters (such as lockId) can be altered without consent. The flaw was discovered during a manual security review that examined the flow of token approvals and noticed that the contract does not verify that the "from" address in transferFrom matches msg.sender. The problem is subtle because transferFrom is a standard ERC20 method and approvals are a normal prerequisite, so the misuse does not raise an immediate error and may only be observed as missing funds or unexpected lock states. To remediate, the contract should enforce that the source of the transferred tokens is the caller (e.g., use transferFrom(msg.sender, ...) or require that the supplied address equals msg.sender) and avoid using arbitrary addresses in allowance‑based transfers. This change restores the intended accounting logic where a user’s approved tokens are only moved when that user explicitly initiates the stake, preventing unauthorized redirection of rewards and preserving the expected behavior that a user receives a reward or can stake their own tokens without interference.
summary: In deligateStake() the transferFrom() function uses an arbitrary value for the from address. Before users or owner call stake(), deligateStake(), createReward(), repayment() or depositRewardAmount() they first approve the StakingKo contract. Once this is done the attacker can frontrun their next call and call deligateStake() on their behalf. This way funds that were intended to be added by the owner as rewards will be staked on behalf of the owner. The owner will then need to wait for the lock to expire and try again. In the case of users that try to stake in lockId 0, this lock can be changed to any other lock when the attacker stakes on behalf of the user. The attacker can redirect funds intended for rewards and stake them instead + he can change the settings of the stake for the users who try to stake.

title: Users Might Not Be Able To Fully Claim
content: The vulnerability is an exponential gas consumption problem that occurs when a user invokes the fullyClaimReward function. The function iterates over every lock and every reward token in a pool, performing a nested loop whose size equals the number of reward tokens multiplied by the number of locks. In addition, the internal _claimReward function is protected by an updateReward modifier that repeats the same double‑loop logic. Because the modifier is applied to each call of _claimReward, the total number of iterations grows quadratically: the outer updateReward loop runs once (e.g., 50 iterations for 10 tokens and 5 locks) and then each of the 50 internal _claimReward calls triggers another 50‑iteration loop, resulting in roughly 2,550 iterations for a single fullyClaimReward call. When the pool contains many tokens or locks, the iteration count can easily exceed the block gas limit, causing the transaction to run out of gas or become prohibitively expensive. This situation can be exploited by an attacker who deliberately creates a pool with a large number of reward tokens and locks, or simply by normal users as the protocol scales, leading to a denial‑of‑service where legitimate users are unable to claim their accrued rewards. The impact is that users see their claim transaction revert with an out‑of‑gas error, receive no rewards, and may observe unusually high gas fees or a complete inability to interact with the claim function. The issue manifests whenever fullyClaimReward is called on a pool that has more than a modest number of locks or reward tokens, and it affects any participant who expects to retrieve their earned tokens. The problem was discovered during a manual security review that examined the control flow of reward distribution and identified the redundant application of the updateReward modifier. It can be hard to notice because the function works correctly for small pools, and the gas cost only becomes apparent as the state grows, which may be overlooked during testing with limited data. The bug belongs to the class of gas‑limit exhaustion or loop‑explosion vulnerabilities, where algorithmic complexity leads to unbounded gas consumption. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a “claim” button that appears to work, but after confirming the transaction the wallet reports an out‑of‑gas failure or the transaction is mined with a very high fee and no tokens are transferred, contradicting the expectation that “my rewards will be claimed”. To remediate the issue the updateReward modifier should be removed from the internal _claimReward function, ensuring that the reward‑updating logic is executed only once before the outer loop, thereby reducing the overall complexity to linear rather than quadratic. This change restores the intended accounting behavior, prevents the denial‑of‑service scenario, and aligns the contract’s gas usage with realistic block limits.
summary:
The fullyClaimReward() function loops through all locks and all rewards for a pool. Let’s say we have 10 reward tokens and 5 locks. This is 10 reward tokens * 5 locks = 50 loops. In the updateReward() modifier we do the same 50 more loops. It looks like _claimReward() incorrectly has the updateReward modifier which makes the looping exponential:  
1. 50 loops in updateReward() before the execution of fullyClaimReward().  
2. 50 loops of _claimReward() * 50 loops for each _claimReward() due to updateReward() modifier: 50 * 50 = 2500 loops  
3. 50 + 2500 = 2550 loops for calling fullyClaimReward() once. This at some point could reach the block gas limit and prevent the user from calling fullyClaimReward() successfully. The fullyClaimReward() function can get DOSed or very expensive gas-wise.

title: Validators can manipulate incentive rates to receive more incentives than intended
content: The vulnerability resides in the reward‑distribution function of the BerachainRewardsVault contract, specifically the addIncentive routine that records a new incentiveRate for a given incentive token. The function permits any caller to set an arbitrary incentiveRate as long as three superficial checks are satisfied: the caller must transfer at least the protocol‑defined minimum incentive rate amount, the remaining incentive balance must be less than or equal to that minimum, and the new rate must not be lower than the minimum. Because the logic does not tie the amount of tokens transferred to the magnitude of the newly declared rate, a validator who knows that the upcoming block will emit a certain amount of BGT (bgtEmitted) can inflate the incentiveRate to a very high value, still satisfy the minimum‑transfer requirement, and then receive a reward calculated as bgtEmitted multiplied by the inflated rate. In practice the validator receives the full remaining incentive amount plus a refund of the tokens they were forced to transfer, effectively earning more tokens than the protocol intended. This manipulation occurs precisely when the incentive.amountRemaining is small (≤ minIncentiveRate) and before any other constraints are applied, allowing the attacker to exploit the timing of the block reward. The affected parties are the validators who can execute the attack and the broader protocol participants who lose incentive tokens, leading to distorted token economics and potential depletion of the incentive pool. The issue was uncovered during a security audit by Spearbit, where the conditional checks were examined and found to lack a proper coupling between transferred amount and new rate. The flaw is subtle because the function appears to enforce a minimum transfer and respects a minimum rate, yet it silently permits rate escalation that results in over‑payment; the automatic refund can mask the abnormal reward, making the problem hard to spot in normal operation. From a user perspective the symptom is an unexpectedly large reward display – a validator sees a reward far exceeding the amount predicted by the protocol’s calculator, while other users may notice a rapid drop in the remaining incentive balance. Conceptually, this is an economic‑logic bug often classified as incentive‑rate manipulation or unchecked parameter escalation. The recommended remediation is to restrict changes to the incentiveRate to situations where the remaining balance is zero, to allow only rate reductions when a balance exists, or to require that the transferred amount be at least equal to the newly proposed rate, thereby preventing arbitrary inflation of the reward multiplier.
summary:
In BerachainRewardsVault.addIncentive, it's possible for anyone to arbitrarily set the incentiveRate of an incentive token given the following requirements:  
• The caller must transfer in at least the incentive.minIncentiveRate amount of tokens.  
• The incentive.amountRemaining must be at most the incentive.minIncentiveRate.  
• The new incentive.incentiveRate must be at least the incentive.minIncentiveRate.  
Knowing that the distribution for the block that they validated is upcoming, if the incentive.amountRemaining will be less than or equal to the incentive.minIncentiveRate but the amount of incentives the validator will receive is less than the incentive.amountRemaining, a validator can exploit this logic by increasing the incentive.incentiveRate sufficiently that they will receive the full incentive.amountRemaining while also being refunded the tokens that they were forced to transfer in.  
Consider the following example (assuming 18 decimal tokens):  
• incentive.minIncentiveRate = 100e18  
• incentive.incentiveRate = 100e18  
• incentive.amountRemaining = 99e18  
• bgtEmitted = 0.5e18  
Normally, in this case the validator can expect to receive bgtEmitted * incentive.incentiveRate == 0.5e18 * 100e18 == 50e18 tokens.  
However, if the validator were to instead call addIncentive with an incentiveRate of 398e18, transferring in 100e18 tokens, they would instead receive a total of bgtEmitted * incentive.incentiveRate == 0.5e18 * 398e18 == 199e18 tokens, effectively receiving a full refund for the tokens they had to transfer in to increase the incentive.incentiveRate and also receiving the full incentive.amountRemaining of 99 tokens, receiving 44 tokens more than expected.

title: Stakers Can Lose Their Earned aSugar
content: The vulnerability is a reward‑accounting reset bug that causes stakers to lose unclaimed aSugar tokens when they perform a second stake without first calling fullyClaimReward(). The contract tracks reward accrual using a timestamp field (cheque.lastPrintedAt) that is updated each time a stake is recorded. Rewards are calculated as a function of the staked amount multiplied by the elapsed time between the current block timestamp and the stored lastPrintedAt value. When a user stakes a second time, the delegateStake (or deligateStake) function updates lastPrintedAt to the new block timestamp but does not mint the aSugar that had accumulated since the previous stake. Consequently, the pending reward balance is overwritten and effectively disappears. The issue also extends to third‑party calls: if a user has granted an allowance, an attacker or any other actor can invoke delegateStake on the user’s behalf, triggering the same timestamp reset and causing the user’s pending rewards to be lost without their consent. This flaw is triggered under the condition that a user stakes again before invoking the claim function, or when an authorized delegate performs a stake on their behalf. It primarily affects token holders who participate in the staking program, leading to a reduction of expected earnings and potentially significant financial loss. The problem was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the reward‑minting logic and identified that the contract does not account for pending rewards on re‑staking. The bug can be hard to notice because the user interface may still show the correct staked balance while the reward balance silently drops to zero, giving the impression that the protocol is functioning normally. The impact is classified as high risk because it directly erodes user funds and undermines trust in the protocol’s accounting guarantees. To remediate the issue, the contract should compute any accrued aSugar for the staker before updating lastPrintedAt in both the direct stake and delegateStake paths, and mint that amount together with the newly earned rewards. This ensures that reward accrual is continuous and that no pending amount is discarded, aligning the implementation with the intended business logic that rewards accrue over time and are claimable at any point.
summary:
Users who stake a second time without calling fullyClaimReward() will lose their accumulated unclaimed aSugar. Furthermore, the second stake could be executed by somebody else via deligateStake() if there is an active allowance.
Example:
The user stakes 100e18 of a token. He gets minted X amount of aSugar based on lock leverage and stakeToken price. cheque.lastPrintedAt gets updated to block.timestamp. This is very important since the accumulation of aSugar is based on the staked amount and the difference between the block.timestamp when calling fullyClaimReward() and cheque.lastPrintedAt.
Since cheque.lastPrintedAt gets updated in deligateStake() and the accumulated amount from previous stakes is not minted then the user loses this accumulation.
Flow:

1. User stakes

2. Time passes

3. User stakes again

4. Calls fullyClaimReward() but the aSugar generated between both stakes is lost.

Staker can lose aSugar unclaimed rewards if he stakes again before calling fullyClaimReward().

title: fallback() logic prevents hook's postCheck from getting executed
content: An issue exists in the fallback function of the Nexus account where the post‑check hook is never executed. The contract uses a withHook modifier that calls a hook contract’s preCheck before the function body and its postCheck after the function body. The fallback function forwards calls to external handler contracts using low‑level assembly blocks that end with a return opcode. In Solidity, the return opcode terminates the current call immediately, discarding any remaining code in the surrounding function, including the code that the modifier would execute after the underscore. Consequently, when the external handler call succeeds and the assembly block returns, control never reaches the IHook.postCheck call placed after the underscore in the modifier. The preCheck runs, but the postCheck, which is supposed to enforce constraints such as balance validation, re‑entrancy protection, or custom business rules, is skipped. This bug appears only for calls that are routed through the fallback handler; direct calls to other functions are unaffected because they do not use the assembly return pattern. The impact is that any security or accounting logic implemented in the hook’s postCheck is bypassed, allowing malicious handlers to execute actions that would otherwise be rejected. Users interacting with the account may see a transaction succeed and receive the expected return data, yet the underlying safety checks have not been performed, potentially leading to unauthorized fund transfers or state corruption. The problem was discovered during a manual security audit when the auditor noticed that the fallback’s assembly blocks used return statements and that the modifier’s postCheck was never reached. The issue is subtle because the return opcode is a legitimate way to forward data, making the missing postCheck easy to overlook in code review. The proper fix is to avoid terminating the call inside the fallback; instead the fallback should capture the returned data in memory, allow execution to continue to the postCheck, and only after the postCheck completes should the data be returned to the caller. This can be achieved by replacing the direct assembly return with a memory copy followed by a final assembly block that returns the cached data, or by restructuring the logic to call preCheck and postCheck explicitly inside the fallback rather than relying on the modifier.

title: Enable Mode Signature can be replayed
content: The vulnerability concerns the enable‑mode signature used when a smart contract wallet installs a new validator module. In the current design the enable‑mode data – consisting of the module address, its type, initialization data and a dedicated enableModeSignature – is packed into the user operation (userOp) signature field, but this field is not part of the userOpHash that the EntryPoint contract signs and checks. Consequently the enable‑mode signature is not bound to any unique identifier of the user operation such as the nonce or the userOpHash. Because the EntryPoint only protects the outer userOp nonce, an attacker (or a malicious bundler) can reuse the same enable‑mode signature in a different user operation, even after the original module has been uninstalled, on a different chain, or on another smart account that shares the same owner address. The replay is possible simply by copying the previously signed enable‑mode tuple into a new userOp, because the EntryPoint validation of the outer signature still succeeds as long as the enable‑mode bit and the validator address encoded in the nonce match. From a user’s perspective the wallet may appear to have installed a trusted validator, yet the underlying module may have been re‑enabled without the owner’s consent, potentially granting the attacker privileged actions such as fund transfers or contract upgrades. The impact is high because it breaks the assumption that installing a module is a one‑time, consented action; it allows unauthorized re‑installation and can lead to loss of control over the account or theft of assets. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the flow of enable‑mode validation and noticed that the enable‑mode signature lacked any replay protection mechanism. It is subtle because the enable‑mode data lives inside the userOp.signature, which is not hashed for replay checks, making the problem invisible to standard nonce‑based replay detection. To remediate, the enable‑mode validator should incorporate a unique identifier of the user operation – for example the userOpHash or the nonce – into the data that is signed off‑chain, and verify this binding on‑chain. By signing over the userOpHash, each enable‑mode signature becomes tied to a single user operation, inheriting the EntryPoint’s replay protection and preventing reuse across different operations, chains, or accounts. This change aligns the enable‑mode signature with the broader replay‑resistance guarantees of the account abstraction framework and restores the intended security guarantees of module installation.
summary:
During enable mode, two validators are used.
1. validator: The module to be installed as any module type that can be defined. It must be a validator either already before the user op or after enabling it as a validator in enable mode. This validator will be used to validate the final userOp.
2. enableModeSigValidator: This validator is used in _checkEnableModeSignature to check the _getEnableModeDataHash(validator, initData) for enabling the first validator.
Note that these two validators are independent of each other and might have different trust assumptions and privileges.
While a user operation has a nonce field (that is used in the userOpHash and its signature) and the entrypoint checks and increments this nonce to avoid replaying a user operation, the inner enableModeSignature does not have any such replay protection.
The same module, moduleInitData, enableModeSignature can be used in a different user operation to install the module a second time, for example, after the user uninstalled the module already.
As the entire enable mode data is encoded in the userOp.signature that is not part of userOpHash, a bundler can replace the enable mode data with a different previously signed one without invalidating the user operation (as long as the enable mode bit and the validator encoded in the userOp.nonce match).
op.signature = (moduleType, moduleInitData, enableModeValidator, enableModeSignature, userOpSignature)
This signature can also be replayed across another chain, as well as on another smart account on the same chain with the same owner.

title: Enable Mode Signature ignores module type
content: The vulnerability concerns the enable‑mode workflow used to install a validator module in a modular smart‑contract system. In this workflow a user operation (userOp) carries a signature that is meant to authorize the installation of a specific validator (the "validator") together with an optional initialization payload (initData). A second validator, called enableModeSigValidator, checks the signature against a hash produced by _getEnableModeDataHash which only incorporates the validator address and initData. Crucially, the hash does not include the moduleType field that determines how the validator will be registered (for example as a regular validator, a hook, or a multi‑type validator). Because the moduleType is omitted from the signed data, an attacker who can submit a userOp can arbitrarily change the moduleType value without invalidating the signature. The attacker therefore forges the enable‑mode data, keeping the original signature valid, and causes the system to register the same validator contract under a different, potentially more privileged, type. This can be exploited by submitting a crafted userOp that installs a malicious validator as an admin‑type module or by upgrading a benign validator to a multi‑type role that grants additional permissions. The impact is a privilege escalation that may allow the attacker to execute privileged functions, modify contract state, or drain funds, depending on the privileges associated with the forged moduleType. The issue manifests whenever the enable‑mode path is used to add a validator and the signature verification step does not bind the moduleType. All participants that rely on the enable‑mode signature for trust – including end users, protocol operators, and third‑party integrators – are affected because the assumed security guarantee (that the signed data uniquely defines the installed module) is broken. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the data flow of enable‑mode signatures and noticed that the moduleType field is never hashed. It can be hard to notice because the signature verification succeeds, the transaction does not revert, and the UI typically only displays the validator address, not the type, so users see no immediate error. To remediate, the enable‑mode hash function should be extended to include the moduleType (or any other attribute that influences the validator’s privileges) so that the signature uniquely commits to the full installation intent. This change restores the intended binding between the signed data and the resulting module registration, preventing the forgery of module types and the associated privilege escalation.
summary:
During enable mode, two validators are used.
1. validator: The module to be installed as any module type that can be defined. It must be a validator either already before the user op or after enabling it as a validator in enable mode. This validator will be used to validate the final userOp.
2. enableModeSigValidator: This validator is used in _checkEnableModeSignature to check the _getEnableModeDataHash(validator, initData) for enabling the first validator.
Note that these two validators are independent of each other and might have different trust assumptions and privileges.
The enableModeSigValidator owner might only want to produce a signature for a specific module type. However, the signature is only over the module (validator) and initData fields, not over the moduleType that the module will be installed as. The user op submitter can forge the module type without invalidating the enable mode signature.
(As the entire enable mode data is encoded in the userOp.signature that is not part of userOpHash).
They can then create a user op with the forged enable mode module type to install the module as any type they want.
A multi-type validator can be installed as all of its types.

title: ERC-7484 registry checks missing on calls to modules
content: The vulnerability consists of a missing runtime verification of module legitimacy against an ERC‑7484 registry when a smart account executes validators, hooks or fallback handlers. The contract is designed to allow the account owner to opt‑in to a registry by setting a registry address and then uses a withRegistry modifier that calls _checkRegistry during module installation and when an executor module is used. However, the same check is not performed when the account later invokes a validator during user‑operation validation, when a hook is called, or when a fallback handler processes a call. The root cause is that the developer applied the withRegistry modifier only to a subset of functions, leaving the execution paths for other module types unchecked. If a module initially satisfies the registry’s attestation threshold and is installed, it will be accepted. Should the attesters later revoke their attestation because the module is discovered to be unsafe, the registry will reject the module on a subsequent check, but because no check is performed at execution time the account will continue to use the now‑untrusted module. An attacker who can cause a module to lose its attestation – for example by compromising an attester or by submitting a revocation – can therefore keep the module active and exploit its malicious behaviour, such as authorising unauthorized transfers, bypassing security checks, or returning incorrect data. The impact is high because the smart account owner and any users of the account may lose funds or experience unexpected behaviour; the protocol that relies on the registry’s guarantee of safety is also undermined. The issue manifests only after a module’s attestation status changes; during normal operation the contract appears to work correctly, making the problem hard to notice because no revert or error is emitted when the unsafe module is called. From a user perspective the symptoms can be transactions that succeed but result in funds disappearing, a validator that should reject a malicious operation but does not, or a fallback handler that processes calls it should no longer handle. This class of bug is a runtime authorization bypass caused by incomplete enforcement of external registry checks. To remediate, every function that invokes a module – including validateUserOp, any hook pre‑check, and the fallback handler – must call _checkRegistry (or apply the withRegistry modifier) before the external call, ensuring that the registry’s current attestation state is respected at execution time. This aligns the implementation with the ERC‑7579 requirement that the adapter revert the transaction flow whenever the registry reverts, thereby restoring the intended safety guarantees.

title: Owner Cannot Claim Token Fees
content: The vulnerability is a fee‑claim logic error in the staking contract that prevents the contract owner from receiving token fees that have been accrued for each lock. Each lock maintains a tokenFeeBalance that represents the portion of the staked amount taken as a fee according to a configurable tokenFeeRate. The contract provides a claimTokenFee() function that is supposed to transfer the accumulated tokenFeeBalance to the owner. However, the implementation first resets lock.tokenFeeBalance to zero and only afterwards attempts to transfer the balance using safeTransfer(msg.sender, lock.tokenFeeBalance). Because the balance variable has already been cleared, the transfer amount is always zero, so the owner receives no tokens even though fees have been recorded. The root cause is the incorrect ordering of state mutation and external call, violating the Checks‑Effects‑Interactions pattern. An attacker does not need to perform any special actions; simply invoking claimTokenFee() results in a no‑op transfer, effectively locking the fees inside the contract forever. The impact is that the protocol’s revenue stream is broken: the owner cannot collect fees, users may see fees accumulating without ever being paid out, and the contract’s accounting assumptions about fee distribution are violated. This condition occurs whenever a lock has a non‑zero tokenFeeBalance and the owner calls the claim function. The affected parties are the contract owner (who cannot retrieve earned fees), the protocol (which loses expected income), and potentially users who rely on fee redistribution. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the claimTokenFee() implementation and noticed the balance being cleared before the transfer. It can be hard to notice because the code appears to perform a transfer, and no revert or error is emitted; the transaction succeeds but moves zero tokens, giving a false impression of success. The correct fix is to cache the current tokenFeeBalance in a local variable, perform the safeTransfer using that cached amount, and only after a successful transfer set the stored balance to zero. This follows the Checks‑Effects‑Interactions pattern and ensures that the actual fee amount is transferred before the state is mutated. From a user’s perspective, the owner expects to receive a token payout after calling claim, but the UI may show a successful claim while the balance remains unchanged, leading to confusion and the perception that “funds disappear” or “refund calculation error”. The bug belongs to the class of state‑mutation‑before‑external‑call errors that result in zero‑value transfers and broken accounting logic.

title: Users Can Steal Part of Protocol Fees Through Referrals to Their Own Addresses
content: The vulnerability is an unrestricted referral address parameter in the functions that handle buying and selling passes. Because the contract allows the caller to supply any non‑zero address as the referral, the fee distribution logic deducts a portion of the protocol fee (calculated as price multiplied by a referral fee percentage) and transfers it to the supplied address. The root cause is the absence of access control or whitelist enforcement on the referral address, which means the protocol cannot verify whether the address belongs to an authorized partner or the treasury. An attacker can exploit this by calling buyPasses or sellPasses with a referral address that they control, causing the contract to subtract the referral fee from the protocol fee and credit the attacker’s address. This results in the protocol losing part of its intended revenue on every affected transaction while the attacker receives an unexpected reward. The issue manifests whenever a user initiates a purchase or sale and provides a non‑zero referral address; it therefore affects all participants who interact with the fee‑bearing functions, the protocol’s treasury, and any stakeholders relying on the fee model for sustainability. The flaw was discovered during a manual security review that examined the fee calculation and noticed that the referral address was taken directly from user input without any restriction. It can be hard to notice because the code appears to correctly compute a referral fee and the UI may display a legitimate‑looking referral reward, masking the fact that the reward can be directed to any address. To remediate, the contract should restrict the referral address to a set of admin‑approved addresses, or move the referral distribution to a separate, permissioned module. Additionally, the protocol fee should be calculated and transferred before any referral deduction, and the referral mechanism should be documented as a whitelist‑only feature. From a user perspective, an attacker may see an unexpected increase in their balance after a transaction, while the protocol’s fee balance appears lower than expected, violating the business rule that protocol fees must be retained by the treasury for funding operations and incentives.
summary:
Users can steal part of the protocol fee by setting referral to addresses they control. buyPasses and sellPasses allows the caller to specify the referral address where the referralFee is paid to.

Part of the protocol fees can be stolen.

title: Missing nonce in `_getEnableModeDataHash()` allows signature replay
content: The vulnerability is a replayable enable-mode signature caused by the function that builds the EIP-712 digest for installing a validator module not incorporating any nonce or other unique per-operation value. When a Nexus account owner signs a message to enable a validator, the contract hashes only the module address and its initialization data. Because the resulting digest is identical for every installation of the same validator, the same signature can be presented to the contract multiple times. After the owner later uninstalls the validator, a malicious relayer or bundler can submit a new user operation that includes the previously recorded signature, causing the contract to reinstall the validator without a fresh approval. This replay attack violates the intended access-control model: the owner's explicit consent is required for each module installation, but the missing nonce allows the consent to be reused indefinitely. The bug manifests when the account's module list changes; the user interface may show a validator reappearing after it was removed, or transactions may be executed by an unexpected module, leading to unauthorized actions and potential loss of funds. The issue was identified during a formal security audit (CodeHawks) by inspecting the data that is signed for enable-mode operations and noticing the absence of a nonce field. Because the signature verification itself succeeds, the problem is subtle and may not be evident until an attacker deliberately replays a stale signature. The appropriate remediation is to include a nonce, a timestamp, or any other unique identifier in the typed data hash used by _getEnableModeDataHash, ensuring that each enable-mode request produces a distinct digest that cannot be reused. This class of bug is a typical replay-signature vulnerability where the signed message lacks sufficient freshness guarantees, breaking the accounting assumption that each approval is one-time only.

title: User may lose funds when creating Nexus account or executing user operations
content: The vulnerability is a value‑forwarding omission that occurs in three core entrypoints of the Nexus account system. When a user sends Ether together with a call to deployWithFactory on the BiconomyMetaFactory, the function forwards the calldata to a user‑provided factory contract using a low‑level call, but it does not include the msg.value field in the call parameters. Consequently the factory receives a call with zero value while the user’s transaction has already deducted the Ether, leading to a situation where the sent funds are neither transferred to the intended contract nor returned to the sender. The same omission exists in the executeUserOp function of the Nexus contract: the EntryPoint extracts the inner call data from a user operation and invokes the target contract with target.call(data) without attaching msg.value, even though the outer function is payable. If the inner call expects a payment, it will either reject the call or accept it without receiving the Ether, causing the user’s funds to be lost or the transaction to revert. A third occurrence is in the fallback handler invoked when a single‑call fallback is used; the assembly block performs a low‑level call to the handler without passing callvalue, again discarding any Ether attached to the original transaction. The bug manifests whenever a user includes Ether in a transaction that relies on these pathways – for example when creating a Nexus account, executing a user operation that involves a payment, or invoking a fallback handler. Affected parties include any end‑user who attempts to fund these operations, as well as the protocol itself because the loss of funds undermines its economic guarantees. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected payable functions and noticed that the low‑level calls omitted the {value: msg.value} syntax. It can be hard to notice because the functions are marked payable and the surrounding code appears to handle calls correctly, yet the omission is subtle and only visible when a transaction actually includes Ether. The impact ranges from silent loss of Ether (the user receives no refund and sees a zero balance change) to outright transaction reverts, which also waste gas. This class of bug is commonly referred to as a “msg.value forwarding omission” or “value‑loss due to missing call value”, a subset of improper handling of payable low‑level calls. To remediate the issue, each low‑level call that is intended to forward Ether must be rewritten to include the callvalue, e.g., factory.call{value: msg.value}(factoryData) and target.call{value: msg.value}(data), and the assembly fallback should use callvalue() in the call opcode. Proper forwarding ensures that the contract’s accounting matches user expectations: a user who sends Ether expects the amount to be transferred to the target contract or, at minimum, to be returned if the call fails.

title: Registry is never called when setting up modules using the `Bootstrap` contract
content: The vulnerability is an ordering flaw in the Bootstrap contract that installs modules before the module registry is configured, violating the requirement of EIP‑7484 that the registry be queried at least once before or during the first call to a module. The root cause is that the internal function _configureRegistry is invoked only after the call to _installValidator (or other install functions), so the withHook modifier that performs the registry check sees a zero address for the registry and skips the check. An attacker can exploit this by calling initNexusWithSingleValidator (or initNexus, initNexusScoped) to install a malicious validator or other module that has not been registered, because the registry check never runs. The impact is that unauthorized modules can be attached to a smart account, bypassing the intended access‑control and attestation logic, potentially allowing the module to execute arbitrary code, steal funds, or corrupt account state. The condition occurs whenever a user or a contract uses the Bootstrap contract to set up a smart account in a single transaction; the bug is triggered during the installation step before the registry is set. All users of the affected smart account framework are affected, including account owners, developers, and any parties relying on the registry to enforce security policies. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the Bootstrap contract where the sequence of internal calls was examined against the EIP‑7484 specification. It can be hard to notice because the transaction does not revert and the installed module appears to work, so the missing registry verification is silent and only visible by reviewing the code flow. From a user perspective the symptom is that a validator is accepted even though it is not listed in the registry, leading to unexpected behavior such as missing attestations, thresholds not being enforced, or funds being transferred without proper authorization. The bug belongs to the class of “registry bypass” or “initialization order” vulnerabilities where a security check is skipped due to improper sequencing of state‑setting calls. To remediate the issue the Bootstrap contract should call _configureRegistry before any module installation functions, ensuring that the registry variable is populated when the withHook modifier invokes _checkRegistry, thereby restoring compliance with EIP‑7484 and re‑enabling the intended access‑control checks.

title: Installing validators with enable mode in `validateUserOp()` doesn't check `moduleType`
content: The issue is an authorization bypass in the enable‑mode flow of Nexus smart accounts. When an account owner wants to add a new validator by calling enableMode, the contract extracts the module address, the module initialization data and the module type from the packed user operation. It then builds a hash of the module address and the keccak256 of the init data, verifies that this hash is signed by the owner, and finally calls installModule with the supplied module type. Because the module type is not part of the signed hash, a malicious relayer can replace the legitimate MODULETYPEVALIDATOR with any other type, such as MODULETYPEEXECUTOR, while keeping the same module address and init data. The owner’s signature still validates, so the contract installs the module under an unauthorized type. This allows an attacker to turn a benign validator into an executor that can perform delegatecalls on behalf of the account, potentially draining funds or executing arbitrary logic. The bug manifests only when the owner uses enable mode to install a validator; it is invisible to the user because the UI shows a successful validator installation and the signature check appears to succeed. From the user’s perspective the account may suddenly execute unexpected calls, balances may drop to zero, or refunds may fail, leading to confusion and loss of trust. The root cause is the omission of the moduleType field from the data that is hashed and signed in _getEnableModeDataHash, resulting in an incomplete authorization check. The vulnerability was discovered during a manual audit that traced the enable‑mode data flow and noticed the missing parameter. It is hard to notice because the signature verification logic looks correct at a glance, and the contract does not emit explicit events about the module type change. To remediate, the installModule call should be forced to use MODULETYPEVALIDATOR when enableMode is intended for validators, or the moduleType should be added to the hash that the owner signs, ensuring that the owner explicitly authorises the specific module category. This aligns the implementation with the intended security model and prevents privilege escalation through manipulated enable‑mode signatures.

title: StakedCitadel doesn’t use correct balance for internal accounting
content: The vulnerability resides in the vault’s internal accounting of total assets. The contract’s `balance()` view function is intended to report the combined token holdings of the vault itself and the underlying strategy to which the vault forwards the majority of deposited funds. However, the implementation mistakenly returns only the vault’s own token balance, omitting the strategy’s holdings. This root‑cause stems from an oversight in the balance calculation, where the function queries the ERC‑20 balance of the vault contract instead of aggregating the strategy’s balance as well. Because the reported pool size is used directly to compute the number of shares that must be minted on deposit and the number of shares that must be burned on withdrawal, the erroneous balance leads to two exploitable failure modes. First, after the initial deposit the vault forwards the tokens to the strategy, leaving the vault’s token balance at zero while the total assets are still positive. When a second user attempts to deposit, the contract divides by the reported pool size (which is zero) and the transaction reverts with a division‑by‑zero error, preventing further deposits. Second, an attacker can deliberately deposit a tiny amount of tokens after the vault’s balance has been drained to manipulate the denominator in the share‑minting formula. By adding a single token to the vault’s balance, the attacker inflates the share allocation dramatically – for example, depositing five tokens while the reported balance is one yields fifty shares instead of the expected five. The inflated shares can later be redeemed for a proportionally larger amount of underlying tokens, allowing the attacker to withdraw more value than contributed and effectively siphon funds from honest participants. The impact is severe: users experience unexpected transaction failures, receive an abnormal number of shares, or see the vault’s accounting break down, potentially resulting in loss of funds for the protocol and its users. This condition occurs whenever the vault has transferred its token holdings to the strategy – i.e., after any successful deposit that moves assets out of the vault – and any subsequent deposit triggers the faulty calculation. All depositors, the protocol’s token holders, and the governance of the vault are affected. The issue was discovered during a security audit by Code4rena, where the auditors compared the `balance()` implementation against the intended specification and observed the inconsistency during simulated deposits. It may be hard to notice in normal operation because the UI typically displays the total value managed by the vault, masking the internal misreporting of the balance; only edge‑case interactions such as a second deposit or an unusually high share count reveal the bug. To remediate the problem, the `balance()` function should be corrected to return the sum of the vault’s token balance and the strategy’s token balance, aligning the reported pool size with the actual assets under management. This change restores correct proportional minting and burning of shares, preserving the integrity of the accounting logic and preventing share inflation or division‑by‑zero failures. In broader terms, the bug belongs to the class of accounting errors where the total asset view used for share calculations is incomplete, leading to mis‑allocation of ownership stakes and violation of the protocol’s financial invariants.
summary:
The StakedCitadel contract’s `balance()` function is supposed to return the balance of the vault + the balance of the strategy. But, it only returns the balance of the vault. The balance is used to determine the number of shares that should be minted when depositing funds into the vault and the number of shares that should be burned when withdrawing funds from it.

Since most of the funds will be located in the strategy, the vault’s balance will be very low. Some of the issues that arise from this:

**You can’t deposit to a vault that already minted shares but has no balance of the underlying token** :

1. fresh vault with 0 funds and 0 shares
2. Alice deposits 10 tokens. She receives 10 shares back (<https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-04-badger-citadel/blob/main/src/StakedCitadel.sol#L887-L888>)
3. Vault’s tokens are deposited into the strategy (now `balance == 0` and `totalSupply == 10`)
4. Bob tries to deposit but the transaction fails because the contract tries to divide by zero: <https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-04-badger-citadel/blob/main/src/StakedCitadel.sol#L890> (`pool == balance()`)

**You get more shares than you should**

1. fresh vault with 0 funds and 0 shares
2. Alice deposits 10 tokens. She receives 10 shares back (<https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-04-badger-citadel/blob/main/src/StakedCitadel.sol#L887-L888>)
3. Vault’s tokens are deposited into the strategy (now `balance == 0` and `totalSupply == 10`)
4. Bob now first transfers 1 token to the vault so that the balance is now `1` instead of `0`.
5. Bob deposits 5 tokens. He receives `5 * 10 / 1 == 50` shares: <https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-04-badger-citadel/blob/main/src/StakedCitadel.sol#L890>

Now, the vault received 15 tokens. 10 from Alice and 5 from Bob. But Alice only has 10 shares while Bob has 50. Thus, Bob can withdraw more tokens than he should be able to.

It simply breaks the whole accounting of the vault.

title: StakedCitadel: wrong setupVesting function name
content: The vulnerability resides in the token withdrawal flow of the StakedCitadel system. When a user invokes the `_withdraw` function of the StakedCitadel contract, the code attempts to call a vesting routine on an external contract referred to as `vesting`. Specifically, the call is made to `IVesting(vesting).setupVesting(msg.sender, _amount, block.timestamp)`. However, the actual vesting contract deployed at that address implements a function named `vest`, not `setupVesting`. Because the interface used by StakedCitadel does not match the concrete implementation, the external call fails with an “undefined function” error, causing the entire `_withdraw` transaction to revert. As a result, the token transfer that should move the user’s withdrawn amount to the vesting contract never occurs, and the user receives no tokens despite a successful request. The root cause is a mismatch between the declared interface and the real contract’s function signature, a classic case of an incorrect external call or API contract mismatch. This can be exploited simply by any user attempting to withdraw: the transaction will revert, leaving the user’s balance unchanged and giving the impression that the withdrawal request succeeded when, in fact, no funds are transferred. The impact is severe because it blocks legitimate users from retrieving their staked assets, effectively freezing their funds and undermining trust in the protocol. The condition occurs every time the `_withdraw` path is executed – that is, whenever a user calls the public or internal withdrawal function – and it affects all holders of the staked token, as the bug resides in shared contract logic, not in a per‑address condition. The issue was discovered during a systematic security audit by Code4rena, where the auditors compared the interface definitions against the actual contract code and identified the naming discrepancy. The problem may be hard to notice in functional testing because the withdrawal call reverts without a clear error message; a developer might misinterpret the failure as a generic require‑statement error rather than an interface mismatch. To resolve the issue, the StakedCitadel contract must be updated to reference the correct function name (`vest`) in its interface, and the call should be changed to `IVesting(vesting).vest(msg.sender, _amount, block.timestamp)`. This aligns the interface with the deployed contract, allowing the external call to succeed and the token transfer to complete. The bug belongs to the broader class of "incorrect external contract interface" or "API mismatch" vulnerabilities, where a caller invokes a non‑existent function on a target contract, leading to transaction failure and loss of functionality. From a user’s perspective, the symptom is that after pressing the withdraw button, the UI may display a transaction hash but the on‑chain state shows no change: the user's token balance remains the same, no new vesting schedule appears, and no refund is received, contrary to the expectation that the withdrawal should unlock the tokens. This violation of the business logic – which assumes that withdrawing automatically vests the tokens – breaks accounting assumptions and can cause funds to appear "stuck" in the protocol.

title: StakedCitadel depositors can be attacked by the first depositor with depressing of vault token denomination
content: The StakedCitadel contract suffers from a precision‑loss vulnerability that can be exploited by the very first depositor of a freshly deployed vault. The root cause lies in the deposit logic, which does not enforce a minimum deposit amount and mints vault shares based on a simple division of the total pool balance by the total number of issued shares. When the contract is empty, the first deposit of a single wei of Citadel creates one vault token representing the entire pool. An attacker can then send a massive amount of Citadel (for example 10⁶ × 10¹⁸ ‑ 1 tokens) to the vault. Because only one share exists, the price per share is driven to an extreme value (≈ 10⁶ Citadel per share). Subsequent users who deposit after the attacker trigger the same division, but the integer‑division rounding causes their deposits to be rounded down to the nearest whole share. The remainder of each large deposit is automatically allocated to the existing share holders – in this case the attacker – effectively stealing a proportion of every later deposit. From a user’s point of view, a depositor may send a substantial amount of Citadel and receive only one vault token, seeing their balance after withdrawal far lower than expected, or noticing that the refund amount is unexpectedly small. The impact is a loss of principal for almost all later depositors while the attacker retains 100 % of the pool’s shares and can remain staked indefinitely, collecting the remainder of every new deposit. The flaw only manifests when the contract is brand new with a zero balance and an attacker can be the first depositor; it is difficult to notice because rounding errors are commonly small and the contract appears to function normally under ordinary conditions. The issue was identified during a Code4rena audit by reviewing the deposit lifecycle and noticing the absence of any safeguard against an initial tiny deposit. To remediate, the contract should enforce a minimum deposit size, require the first depositor to lock a sufficient amount of liquidity, or initialize the share‑to‑value ratio in a way that prevents extreme price per share values. These measures remove the economic incentive for the attack and ensure that later depositors receive a fair share of the pool, preserving the intended accounting guarantees of the vault.
summary:
An attacker can become the first depositor for a recently created StakedCitadel contract, providing a tiny amount of Citadel tokens by calling `deposit(1)` (raw values here, `1` is `1 wei`, `1e18` is `1 Citadel` as it has 18 decimals). Then the attacker can directly transfer, for example, `10^6*1e18 - 1` Citadel to StakedCitadel, effectively setting the cost of `1` of the vault token to be `10^6 * 1e18` Citadel. The attacker will still own 100% of the StakedCitadel’s pool being the only depositor.

All subsequent depositors will have their Citadel token investments rounded to `10^6 * 1e18`, due to the lack of precision which initial tiny deposit caused, with the remainder divided between all current depositors, i.e. the subsequent depositors lose value to the attacker.

For example, if the second depositor brings in `1.9*10^6 * 1e18` Citadel, only `1` of new vault to be issued as `1.9*10^6 * 1e18` divided by `10^6 * 1e18` will yield just `1`, which means that `2.9*10^6 * 1e18` total Citadel pool will be divided 50/50 between the second depositor and the attacker, as each have 1 wei of the total 2 wei of vault tokens, i.e. the depositor lost and the attacker gained `0.45*10^6 * 1e18` Citadel tokens.

As there are no penalties to exit with StakedCitadel.withdraw(), the attacker can remain staked for an arbitrary time, gathering the share of all new deposits’ remainder amounts.

Placing severity to be high as this is principal funds loss scenario for many users (most of depositors), easily executable, albeit only for the new StakedCitadel contract.

title: Participants can join knowing they'll win
content: The vulnerability stems from the way the lottery and auction contracts determine winners after a verifiable random function (VRF) value has already been revealed. The contract stores a list of eligible participants and, when the seller calls selectWinners, it shuffles this list using the publicly known randomNumber and then picks the first numberOfTickets entries as winners. Because the randomNumber is known to everyone before selectWinners is executed, an attacker can observe the exact ordering that the shuffle will produce. By joining the lottery after the VRF result is available but before the seller invokes selectWinners, the attacker can add themselves to the end of the eligibleParticipants array and calculate whether that new position will fall within the winning slice. If the calculation shows that the last slot will be a winner, the attacker can submit a deposit (or multiple deposits) to guarantee a win, or conversely withdraw if the position would be a loser. This manipulation is possible because the contract allows deposits to be made while the randomness is already fixed, effectively letting participants influence the participant list after the random seed is known. The impact is a breach of the fundamental fairness assumption of the lottery: some users can secure a win with certainty, depriving other honest participants of a chance to win and potentially draining the prize pool. The issue manifests whenever the deposit function remains open after the VRF request has been fulfilled and before selectWinners is called, which is the case in the current implementation. All participants, especially the last ones to join, are affected because they can gain an informational advantage that the protocol does not intend to provide. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the ordering of operations and the visibility of the random seed. It can be difficult to notice because the shuffle algorithm appears random at first glance, and the UI typically does not warn users that the participant list is still mutable after randomness is known. To remediate the problem, the contract should lock the participant list before requesting the VRF value, or require all deposits to be completed before the lottery starts, ensuring that the random seed is generated only after the final set of participants is fixed. Alternative mitigations include using a commit‑reveal scheme for randomness or generating the random seed after the deposit period ends, thereby preventing any post‑randomness manipulation of the winner selection process.

title: Buyer can request randomness multiple times
content: The vulnerability allows a lottery participant to obtain multiple independent randomness draws for the price of a single ticket, thereby inflating their probability of winning. The contract’s deposit function only verifies that the caller’s rolled number is zero before issuing a VRF request, but it does not check whether a randomness request is already pending or whether the caller has already recorded a deposit. Because the VRF service processes requests asynchronously, an attacker can submit several deposit transactions in rapid succession while the first request is still awaiting fulfillment. Each deposit, even with a dust amount, triggers a new _requestRandomness call, resulting in multiple random numbers being stored for the same participant when the VRF callbacks are finally executed. The attacker’s multiple rolls are all evaluated against the winning number, and any successful roll adds the attacker to the winners list, effectively granting them many tickets for a single payment. This breaks the core business rule that each ticket costs a fixed amount and yields exactly one draw, leading to an unfair advantage, reduced expected returns for honest participants, and potential loss of revenue for the protocol. The issue manifests when the VRF latency is non‑zero and the contract does not maintain a flag for pending requests. From a user’s perspective the UI may indicate that a single ticket was purchased, yet the backend records several entries, causing unexpected wins or, conversely, other users seeing their odds diminish. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined state checks around the randomness request logic; it is subtle because the contract emits the usual events and does not revert, making the extra draws invisible to casual observers. The bug belongs to the class of insufficient state validation and request replay vulnerabilities, where a function can be called repeatedly before a prior asynchronous operation completes. To remediate, the contract should enforce that a randomness request is sent only when both the participant’s rolled number and deposit balance are zero, or maintain an explicit pending‑request flag, ensuring exactly one draw per ticket purchase.

title: Initializing the pool in uniswap will lock all ETH in bridge
content: The vulnerability is a front‑running initialization flaw in the bridge contract that relies on a Uniswap V3 pool being created only when the admin calls closeMint. The contract splits the ETH collected from NFT sales and, during closeMint, it calls a private function that mints an initial liquidity position with a hard‑coded slippage tolerance of ninety percent of the desired amounts. Because the pool is not pre‑initialized, any external actor can call the Uniswap non‑fungible position manager to create and initialize the pool beforehand with an arbitrary price. When the admin later invokes closeMint, the Uniswap mint call checks the current price against the expected price and, due to the attacker‑set price, the slippage check fails and the whole transaction reverts. As a result the bridge remains permanently in the open‑minting state, the BLERB tokens are never minted, and the ETH that was supposed to be used as initial liquidity stays locked in the contract. The issue occurs after NFTs have been minted but before the admin finalises the minting process, and it affects every participant who expects to receive BLERB tokens or to see their ETH converted into liquidity. It was discovered during a security audit when a test demonstrated that calling createAndInitializePoolIfNecessary with a high sqrt price caused closeMint to revert with a price slippage error. The problem is subtle because the failure only appears at the finalisation step, presenting as a generic slippage revert rather than an obvious pool‑initialisation problem, making it easy to miss in normal operation. The bug belongs to the class of initialization‑order and price‑manipulation vulnerabilities where a contract trusts external state that can be set by anyone. From a user perspective the UI would show that the minting transaction fails, no BLERB tokens appear in the wallet, and the ETH that was paid for the NFT seems to disappear or remain locked. To remediate the issue the protocol should initialise the Uniswap pool deterministically at deployment or immediately after token creation, enforce that only the bridge contract can initialise the pool, or remove the reliance on a slippage check that can be triggered by an attacker‑controlled price. By fixing the initialization order the bridge can guarantee that the price used for the first liquidity position is the intended one and that the closeMint function will not be blocked by external manipulation.

title: The protocol does not implement slippage checks on swaps
content: The vulnerability consists of the absence of any slippage protection in the protocol's swap facility. The contract that performs token swaps does not verify that the amount of output tokens received is at least a minimum threshold expected by the caller. The root cause is that the SwapFacility::_swap function lacks a parameter such as minOutAmount and therefore never checks the actual execution price against the price quoted when the transaction was submitted. An attacker or market volatility can be exploited by submitting a swap transaction that is placed in the mempool and then allowing the price to move significantly before the transaction is mined. Because the contract does not revert when the received amount is lower than expected, the swap completes and the caller receives substantially fewer tokens than anticipated, effectively causing a value loss for both the user and the protocol's liquidity pool. This situation occurs when there is a delay between transaction submission and execution, for example during network congestion or when a front‑runner deliberately manipulates the market price. All participants who rely on the swap facility – regular users, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the accounting assumptions that a swap will preserve value are broken. The issue was discovered during a security audit that compared the README documentation, which explicitly states that the SwapFacility must implement slippage checks, with the actual Solidity implementation that omitted any such verification. The bug can be hard to notice because the transaction does not fail; it simply returns a lower amount, which may be interpreted as a normal market outcome rather than a contract flaw. To remediate the problem, the swap function should be extended to accept a minimum acceptable output amount and should revert if the actual output falls below this threshold, thereby enforcing slippage limits and aligning the contract behaviour with the documented expectations. In generic terms, this is a classic case of missing input validation or unchecked external state, leading to a financial accounting error where funds disappear or refunds are insufficient, violating the protocol's business logic that swaps should be executed at a predictable rate.
summary: The protocol mentions in its README file that the SwapFacility has to implement slippage checks, but it doesn't. If a swap transaction is sent to the mempool, but it takes a while until it is executed, it is possible that there was big price movement and the swap returned value is substantially lower than what it was initially expected to be, which will be a value loss for the protocol & its users.

title: MJR-1 Potential safeApprove blocking
content: The vulnerability is a classic allowance‑reset issue that appears when the contract uses a safeApprove helper to set a new ERC20 allowance for Uniswap calls. SafeApprove follows the OpenZeppelin pattern that requires the current allowance to be zero before a non‑zero amount can be approved. In the audited code the contract first grants a large allowance to the Uniswap router, then calls a Uniswap function that may consume only part of that allowance. Because the remaining allowance is non‑zero, the next invocation of safeApprove attempts to set a new allowance without first resetting the old value to zero. The safeApprove call reverts, which blocks the subsequent logic that depends on the allowance being updated. This can happen repeatedly whenever a Uniswap swap does not use the full approved amount, causing a cascade of failed transactions. The impact is that users attempting to invest, buy back tokens, claim profits or interact with the market maker may see their transactions revert with an “ERC20: approve from non‑zero to non‑zero allowance” error, effectively freezing their ability to move funds through the affected functions. From a user perspective the UI may show “transaction failed” or “insufficient allowance” even though the user still holds the tokens, leading to confusion and potential loss of confidence. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s interaction with Uniswap, where the auditor noticed repeated safeApprove calls after partial swaps. It is hard to notice because the failure only occurs after a specific usage pattern (partial consumption of allowance) and the revert message is generic, not directly pointing to a business‑logic problem. The bug belongs to the broader class of allowance‑reset or race‑condition vulnerabilities in ERC20 token approvals. To remediate, the contract should always reset the allowance to zero before setting a new non‑zero amount, for example by calling safeApprove(token, spender, 0) followed by safeApprove(token, spender, newAmount), or by using the increaseAllowance/decreaseAllowance pattern that does not require a zero‑balance precondition. By ensuring the allowance is cleared, subsequent Uniswap calls will succeed regardless of how much of the previous allowance was spent, restoring expected functionality and preventing funds from becoming effectively locked in the contract.
summary:
At several places, e.g. Investment.sol#L182 contract perform safeApprove before uniswap's function call, however in case if uniswap doesn't use full provided allowance that can lead to blocking next safeApprove call because safeApprove requires zero allowance.
Another lines with same issue:
Market.sol#L248
Buyback.sol#L125
ProfitSplitter.sol#L195
ProfitSplitter.sol#L204
UniswapMarketMaker.sol#L116
UniswapMarketMaker.sol#L124
UniswapMarketMaker.sol#L125
UniswapMarketMaker.sol#L151
UniswapMarketMaker.sol#L152
UniswapMarketMaker.sol#L181

title: MJR-2 Wrongly calculated ETH amount to transfer
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect calculation of the ETH amount that the contract attempts to transfer when it needs to cover a shortfall between its current ETH balance and a required payout amount. The contract first checks whether the incoming token balance (splitterIncomingBalance) can be swapped for enough ETH to fill the gap between the existing ETH balance (splitterEthBalance) and the target amount. If the token balance is insufficient, it swaps the entire incoming balance to ETH and stores the resulting ETH amount in amountsOut[1]. However, instead of adding this newly obtained ETH to the already‑available ETH balance, the code mistakenly assigns amount = amountsOut[1] only. The root cause is a missing addition of splitterEthBalance to the swapped amount, i.e., the logic should set amount = splitterEthBalance + amountsOut[1]. This miscalculation can be exploited by triggering the swap path where the contract already holds some ETH; the contract will then believe it has enough ETH to satisfy the payout, but in reality it will transfer a smaller amount than required. The impact is that users or downstream contracts receive less ETH than expected, balances appear inconsistent, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions are violated – for example, a user may request a refund and receive zero or a reduced amount, or a profit‑splitting operation may leave the contract with a residual ETH deficit. The condition under which the bug manifests is when splitterIncomingBalance is insufficient to fully cover the gap, causing the contract to execute the fallback swap logic. It is hard to notice because the code path is only exercised in edge cases where the contract already holds some ETH, and the resulting shortfall may be subtle, showing up as occasional missing funds rather than a blatant failure. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the ProfitSplitter contract, where the auditor identified that the amount variable was derived from the swap output without accounting for the existing ETH balance. To fix the problem, the assignment should be changed to amount = splitterEthBalance.add(amountsOut[1]) (or the equivalent arithmetic in Solidity), ensuring the total ETH available after the swap is correctly reflected before any transfer is performed. This correction restores the intended business logic that the contract must always transfer the full required amount, preserving user expectations and maintaining correct financial accounting.
summary: At lines ProfitSplitter.sol#L198-L205 contract swaps whole splitterIncomingBalance to ETH if splitterIncomingBalance insufficient to cover gap between splitterEthBalance and amount, in other words contract try to get as much as closer to amount ETH amount. However as we can see in this block of code contract assigns amountsOut[1] to amount, it's wrong because we need to assign splitterEthBalance.add(amountsOut[1])

title: MJR-3 Potential re-entrancy problem
content: The vulnerability is a classic re‑entrancy issue in the profit‑splitting contract. At the point where the contract transfers incoming tokens to the designated recipient, it performs an external call before updating the internal accounting that records how much each participant is owed. Because the state change occurs after the external call, a malicious recipient contract can execute a fallback or receive function that calls back into the profit‑splitting function, causing the same transfer logic to run again before the balance is reduced. This loop can be repeated until the contract’s token reserve is exhausted. The root cause is the violation of the Checks‑Effects‑Interactions pattern and the absence of a re‑entrancy guard such as a nonReentrant modifier. An attacker would need to deploy a contract that implements a token‑receiving callback and, when invoked by the splitter, immediately invokes the splitter’s withdraw or split function again. Under these conditions the attacker can siphon funds that were meant to be split among legitimate participants. The impact is that users who initiate a split may see their expected refund disappear, their balance become zero, or receive less than the calculated share, effectively losing funds. The problem manifests whenever the recipient is a contract capable of executing code on token receipt, which includes many ERC20 implementations that invoke a callback on transfer. All token holders and any party relying on the correct accounting of the splitter are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit by MixBytes, which flagged the line as a potential re‑entrancy point. It can be hard to notice because the external call looks like a normal token transfer and typical unit tests may not include a malicious callback contract. To remediate, the contract should follow the Checks‑Effects‑Interactions pattern by updating balances before making external calls, or it should protect the vulnerable function with a re‑entrancy guard that blocks nested entries. This class of bug is known as a re‑entrancy vulnerability, which breaks the assumption that accounting state is updated atomically with respect to external interactions, leading to money disappearing or refunds failing.
summary: At the line ProfitSplitter.sol#L227 contract transfers incoming tokens to recipient, however that place can be re-entered in case of callbacks from incoming contract.

title: MJR-4 Blocked LP tokens on contract
content: The vulnerability is that the market‑maker contract allows the incoming token to be changed without first ensuring that any liquidity‑provider (LP) tokens that were previously minted and remain in the contract are removed.
