The code that performs the token switch simply forwards all remaining balance of the new incoming token to the designated recipient, but it never checks whether the contract still holds LP tokens of the old pair. Because there is no rescue path for those tokens, they become permanently locked once the incoming token variable is overwritten. This situation can be triggered whenever the function that updates the incoming token is called while the contract still holds LP tokens – for example, after a liquidity provider has added liquidity and the owner later decides to switch the market to a different token. An attacker or even the contract owner could deliberately invoke the token‑change function after liquidity has been supplied, causing the LP tokens to be stranded. The impact is that the value represented by the LP tokens is effectively lost; liquidity providers see their balances drop to zero, refunds or withdrawals no longer work, and the protocol loses the expected liquidity depth. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the UniswapMarketMaker.sol source, where the line that changes the incoming token (L85) was examined and the lack of a check for leftover LP tokens was noted. The bug is subtle because the contract does not emit any warning or revert, and the UI may simply show that the contract holds no supported token, hiding the fact that unsupported LP tokens are still present. To remediate, the contract should enforce that all LP tokens are withdrawn before the incoming token variable is altered, or it should include a generic rescue function that can transfer any ERC‑20 token (including LP tokens) held by the contract to a designated safe address. In broader terms, this is a classic case of improper state transition handling where a contract assumes that changing a configuration parameter automatically discards all previous state, leading to asset lock‑up.
summary: At the line UniswapMarketMaker.sol#L85 contract changes incoming token to another one, while transferring contract sends all remaining incoming tokens to _recipient, but contract never check remaining incoming <> support LP tokens on contract side. That tokens cannot be rescued anymore after changing incoming.

title: H-01 | Incorrect Calculation Of totalFees In updateNav
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect calculation of the totalFees variable that is performed during a net asset value (NAV) update in the vault contract. The totalFees field is supposed to represent the fees that must be transferred between the vault and the manager for the current accounting epoch. In the existing implementation the contract adds the cumulative manager performance fees (accruedManagerPerformanceFees) and cumulative manager TVL fees (accruedManagerTvlFees) together with the fee that is generated only for the current epoch (brktTvlFee). Because the manager fees are already accumulated from previous epochs, adding them again results in a double‑counting of fees that have already been locked in the vault’s balance. Consequently the totalFees value is larger than it should be for the current epoch. This mis‑calculation is used later to compute totalDebit = withdrawalAssets + totalFees inside the internal _processDepositsWithdrawals function, which determines how much the manager must transfer to the vault (or receive from it). When the manager transfers the amount based on the inflated totalFees, the vault either receives insufficient funds to cover withdrawals or the manager is forced to send more than necessary, breaking the intended fee‑locking mechanism. The impact is that the vault can become under‑funded, causing user withdrawals to fail or be partially fulfilled, and the accounting invariants of the protocol are violated – the protocol may appear to have enough assets while in reality the fee pool is depleted. The bug manifests whenever the NAV is updated after the first epoch, i.e., any time there are previously accrued manager fees and a new brktTvlFee is applied. All participants that rely on correct fee accounting – the vault, the manager, and ultimately the end‑users who expect to withdraw their assets – are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the updateNav logic, where the auditor noticed that the fee variables used in the totalFees expression had mismatched semantics (cumulative versus per‑epoch). The problem is subtle because the vault’s balance may still look reasonable at a glance; the double‑counted fees are hidden inside the totalFees computation and only surface when a withdrawal is processed. The bug belongs to the class of accounting or fee‑calculation errors where cumulative state is mixed with per‑epoch values, leading to incorrect financial flows. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are missing or zero withdrawals, unexpected “insufficient vault balance” errors, or a vault balance that seems to shrink without a clear reason. The correct fix is to compute totalFees using only the fees that are generated in the current epoch – managerPerformanceFee, managerTvlFee and brktTvlFee – thereby ensuring that previously accrued fees remain locked in the vault and are not double‑counted. This aligns the fee transfer logic with the intended business rule that the manager only needs to cover the net asset flow for the epoch plus the new fees, preserving the integrity of the protocol’s accounting model.
summary:
The totalFees variable is intended to represent the total fees affecting the asset flow between the vault and the manager during an NAV update. However, the calculation is inconsistent:
• accruedManagerPerformanceFees and accruedManagerTvlFees are cumulative (including fees from all previous epochs plus the current epoch's managerPerformanceFee and managerTvlFee).
• brktTvlFee is the new fee for the current epoch only, not the cumulative accruedBrktTvlFees.
This inconsistency leads to an incorrect totalFees value. Since totalFees is used in totalDebit = withdrawalAssets + totalFees within _processDepositsWithdrawals, it determines how much the manager must transfer to the vault (or receive from it). Using cumulative fees for manager fees is incorrect.
Expected Behavior: As the fees are now "locked on the vault's balance" the vault should retain all accrued fees and the manager should only need to cover the net asset flow (withdrawalAssets - depositAssets) plus the new fees for the current epoch. The previously accrued fees are already in the vault and can be used to pay withdrawals or claimed fees.
Example:
• Epoch 1: brktTvlFee = 5, so accruedBrktTvlFees = 5.
• Epoch 2: brktTvlFee = 3, so accruedBrktTvlFees = 8. Current code computes totalFees = accruedManagerFees + accruedManagerTvlFees + 3, ignoring the prior 5 in accruedBrktTvlFees. It should use only new fees (managerPerformanceFee + managerTvlFee + brktTvlFee).

title: H-02 | Incorrect Subtraction Of totalFees
content: An incorrect subtraction of accrued fees from the manager's available balance is present in the _getManagerAvailableBalance function. The function is intended to compute how much of the manager's token can be transferred to the vault when the amount to be deposited is lower than the total debit. It takes the minimum of the manager's token balance and the allowance granted to the vault, and then subtracts totalFees, which represent all fees that have already been accrued in the vault. The root cause is a misunderstanding of where those fees are stored: the fees are locked inside the vault's balance, not inside the manager's token balance. Consequently, the manager's token.balanceOf(manager) does not include the fee amount, and subtracting totalFees artificially reduces the amount the manager is considered able to transfer. This mis‑calculation can be exploited indirectly: when totalFees is non‑zero, the function may report an available balance that is lower than the true transferable amount, causing the vault to revert the transfer with an InsufficientManagerFunds error. The impact is that legitimate deposits may fail, users see transaction reverts, and the protocol may be unable to accept new assets, effectively freezing revenue streams. The condition under which the bug manifests is when depositAssets is less than totalDebit and the vault has accrued fees greater than zero. The affected parties include the manager role, any user attempting to deposit assets, and the overall protocol that relies on continuous inflow of funds. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the accounting logic of the vault. It is hard to notice because the subtraction looks plausible from a superficial accounting perspective, yet it violates the invariant that fees are held separately and should not be deducted from the manager's transferable balance. The bug belongs to the class of accounting or balance‑calculation errors where locked funds are incorrectly accounted for, leading to under‑estimation of available liquidity. From a user’s point of view the symptom is a failed deposit transaction with an error message such as 'InsufficientManagerFunds', even though the manager’s wallet actually holds enough tokens. Users expect the deposit to succeed and the vault to receive the full amount, but instead the transaction reverts and no funds move. The correct fix is to remove the subtraction of totalFees from the calculation, allowing the manager’s available balance to be simply the minimum of its token balance and the granted allowance. This aligns the accounting model with the reality that fees are stored in the vault and claimed separately, restoring the ability of the manager to transfer the full amount it controls.
summary:
The _getManagerAvailableBalance function calculates the manager's available balance for transferring funds to the vault when depositAssets < totalDebit. It subtracts totalFees (all accrued fees) from the minimum of the manager's balance and allowance.
However, this is illogical because:
• The accrued fees are locked in the vault's balance, not the manager's. The manager's token.balanceOf(manager) does not include these fees.
• Subtracting totalFees underestimates the manager's ability to transfer funds, potentially causing unnecessary reverts with InsufficientManagerFunds.
The manager's available balance should be the full amount it can transfer to the vault, limited only by its balance and allowance. Since fees are held in the vault and claimed separately (claimManagerFees, claimBrktTvlFees), they do not reduce the manager's available balance.
Example:
• Manager balance = 100, allowance = 100, accruedFees = 10 in the vault.
• Current code: available = min(100, 100) - 10 = 90.
• Actual: Manager can transfer up to 100, as the 10 in fees is in the vault.

title: MJR-5 Missed depositary check
content: The vulnerability resides in the market contract function that swaps collateral tokens for stable tokens. The function assumes that the address used as the depositary for the incoming collateral is always one of the authorised depositaries defined by the token issuer. However, the code does not verify that the supplied depositary belongs to the approved list before performing the exchange. As a result, if a caller provides an incorrect or malicious depositary address, the contract will still accept the collateral, execute the internal rebalance routine and complete the purchase without reverting. Because the rebalance call is deliberately fault‑tolerant, the transaction succeeds even though the collateral has been routed to an unexpected location. This creates a collateralisation disbalance: the protocol’s accounting records show that the required amount of collateral has been deposited, while in reality the funds are held by an unauthorised address. Users therefore experience symptoms such as receiving fewer stable tokens than expected, seeing their collateral balance appear unchanged or zero, or being unable to redeem their positions because the protocol believes it is fully collateralised when it is not. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s business logic, where the lack of a depositary whitelist check was noted as a deviation from the issuer’s specification that mandates an exact list of depositaries. The problem is subtle because the transaction does not revert and no explicit error is emitted, making it easy to miss during functional testing. The root cause is a missing validation step – a classic example of an unchecked input leading to a business‑logic violation. To remediate, the contract should enforce a check that the depositary address is present in the authorised list before proceeding with the token exchange, and should revert the transaction if the check fails. This ensures that the accounting invariants for collateralisation remain intact and prevents funds from being unintentionally diverted, preserving the protocol’s financial guarantees.
summary: In function buy defined at CollateralMarket.sol#L120 contract exchanges collateral tokens to stable tokens. But in case of wrong depositary that code will lead to collateralization disbalance, that is bad even you have manual depositary changing mechanism because issuer requires exact list of depositaries and transaction wont fail because rebalance call is fault tolerance.

title: MJR-6 Invalid depositary add/remove logic
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect existence check in the depositary management functions of the contract. A mapping called depositariesIndex stores the position of each depositary inside an array, but the code treats a stored value of zero as meaning "not present". Because Solidity mappings return 0 for keys that have never been set, the first depositary that is added receives index 0, which satisfies the condition depositariesIndex[depositary] == 0 used to guard against duplicate additions. As a result the contract allows the same depositary to be added multiple times, creating duplicate entries in the depositaries array. Conversely, the removal function checks that depositariesIndex[depositary] != 0 before allowing a removal, which prevents the removal of a depositary that resides at index 0. The bug occurs whenever a depositary is added for the first time (index 0) or when an attempt is made to remove that first entry. It affects any participant that relies on correct depositary bookkeeping, including users whose funds are allocated through these depositaries and the protocol that assumes a one‑to‑one relationship between depositary identifiers and array positions. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the add and remove logic and noticed the contradictory use of zero as both a valid index and a sentinel value. It can be hard to notice because the contract may appear to work for most depositaries, and only the first entry exhibits the removal problem, while duplicate entries may not immediately cause visible errors until accounting functions process the list. Exploitation could involve repeatedly adding the same depositary to inflate the array, potentially leading to double counting of balances, incorrect distribution of funds, or denial of service by preventing legitimate removal of the first depositary. The impact ranges from accounting inconsistencies to possible loss or misdirection of user funds. The proper fix is to redesign the existence check: either store index+1 in the mapping so that zero unequivocally means "not present", or maintain a separate boolean mapping that records whether a depositary has been added. The removal logic should then reference the same reliable indicator, allowing the first depositary to be removed correctly. In summary, the bug is a classic sentinel‑value misuse in a mapping that leads to duplicate entries and inability to delete the initial element, violating the protocol's accounting assumptions and requiring a conceptual redesign of the depositary tracking mechanism.
summary: At lines AgregateDepositaryBalanceView.sol#L49, AgregateDepositaryBalanceView.sol#L62 are defined functions to add or remove depositaries, depositariesIndex map contains depositary indexes added to depositaries array. At line AgregateDepositaryBalanceView.sol#L50 contract requires that depositariesIndex[depositary] == 0, that check allow to add already added depositary that have 0 index. Same error at line AgregateDepositaryBalanceView.sol#L64 that don't allow to remove depositary that have index 0

title: MJR-7 Wrongly used safeApprove
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect use of the safeApprove function from the OpenZeppelin SafeERC20 library within the Treasury contract. The contract calls safeApprove to set a token allowance for a recipient without first ensuring that the existing allowance for that spender is zero. SafeERC20’s safeApprove implementation deliberately reverts when the current allowance is non‑zero and the caller attempts to set a new non‑zero allowance, as a mitigation against the well‑known ERC20 race‑condition where a spender could use both the old and the new allowance. Because the Treasury contract does not reset the allowance to zero before assigning a new value, any subsequent call to safeApprove after an initial approval will fail. This failure manifests as a transaction revert, which from a user’s perspective appears as a generic “approval failed” or “transaction reverted” error, often without a clear message. Users attempting to deposit, withdraw, or otherwise interact with the Treasury may see their balances unchanged, receive no tokens, or experience missing refunds, leading to the impression that funds have disappeared. The impact is that token transfers that rely on the approval step cannot be executed, effectively locking assets that the protocol needs to move and breaking core business logic such as fund distribution or reward payouts. The condition occurs whenever an account already has a non‑zero allowance for the token in question, which is common after the first successful approval. The affected parties include token holders interacting with the Treasury, the protocol’s operational contracts that depend on the allowance, and any downstream services that assume successful token transfers. The issue was discovered during a manual code audit that highlighted the safeApprove call without a preceding allowance reset. It can be hard to notice because the revert does not provide a specific error code; developers may attribute the failure to network issues or other unrelated bugs. The proper fix is to follow the recommended pattern: first call safeApprove(recipient,0) to clear any existing allowance, then call safeApprove(recipient,desiredAmount), or alternatively use safeIncreaseAllowance / safeDecreaseAllowance or ERC20Permit where appropriate. This aligns the contract with the standard safe approval pattern and eliminates the race‑condition vulnerability, ensuring that token approvals succeed consistently and that funds are not unintentionally locked.
summary: At line Treasury.sol#L51 contract call safeApprove method, however that method fails if account have remaining allowed tokens.

title: MJR-8 Budget payment blocking
content: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service (DoS) condition caused by the contract’s pay function iterating over a list of recipients and sending Ether with the Solidity transfer primitive. Transfer forwards a fixed stipend of 2300 gas to the recipient’s fallback or receive function. If any recipient implements a payable fallback that consumes more than 2300 gas, or deliberately reverts, the transfer call will fail and revert the entire transaction, preventing the loop from completing. Consequently, all subsequent payments are blocked and the contract’s intended distribution of funds does not occur. This issue appears when the contract is executed under normal conditions where at least one recipient is a contract with a non‑trivial fallback, which is common in composable DeFi ecosystems. The affected parties include the contract’s owner, any users expecting their share of a budget, and the protocol that relies on timely payouts. The problem was identified during a manual audit that examined the payment logic and recognized the unsafe use of transfer in a batch payment context. It can be hard to notice because transfer is often considered a safe way to send Ether, yet the fixed gas stipend is insufficient for many modern contracts, and the failure manifests only when a malicious or misbehaving recipient is present. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a user who should receive a payment sees no change in balance, while other users may also receive nothing because the whole function reverts. The business logic that assumes all recipients will be paid is violated, breaking accounting guarantees and potentially leading to funds being locked in the contract. The recommended mitigation is to replace the push‑payment model with a pull‑payment (claimable) pattern, or to use low‑level call with proper error handling and sufficient gas, ensuring that a single failing recipient cannot halt the entire distribution.
summary: In pay function of Budget.sol contract defined at Budget.sol#L109 contract sends ETH to recipients in loop using transfer method. As we know transfer method limited by 2300 gas, so any single recipient with payable fallback method can block whole pay function execution

title: H-01 | Incorrect stethAmount Used
content: The vulnerability originates from an incorrect interpretation of the value returned by Lido's submit function inside the _lidoEthToBrktETH routine. The submit call returns the number of newly minted stETH shares, not the actual quantity of stETH tokens that were transferred to the router contract. The router mistakenly treats this share count as the amount of stETH received and proceeds to wrap it directly into wstETH before minting the corresponding brktETH. Because the share count can be significantly lower than the true token balance change, a portion of the stETH remains idle in the router contract after the conversion step. From a user's perspective the transaction appears to succeed, but the expected brktETH amount is lower than it should be, often resulting in the user receiving little or no brktETH for the deposited stETH. This accounting mismatch occurs whenever the router invokes the submit function and relies on its return value instead of measuring the before‑and‑after stETH balances. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract's internal accounting with the external token balances and noticed that stETH was left stranded in the router after a conversion. The bug is subtle because the transaction does not revert and no explicit error is emitted; the loss manifests only as a discrepancy between the amount the user supplied and the amount of brktETH minted, which can be hard to spot without detailed balance tracing. The impact is that users effectively lose part of their deposited assets, reducing the protocol’s economic guarantees and potentially eroding trust. The affected parties include any user who deposits stETH through the router, the protocol’s liquidity pool that relies on accurate accounting, and any downstream contracts that assume a one‑to‑one conversion rate. To remediate the flaw, the router should compute the actual stETH received by recording the stETH balance before calling submit, then subtracting the balance after the call, and use this delta as the amount to wrap and mint brktETH. This approach aligns the accounting with the true token flow and prevents leftover stETH from being trapped in the router, restoring the intended business logic that each deposited stETH yields a proportional amount of brktETH.
summary: In the _lidoEthToBrktETH function the return value from the submit function is used as the stEth amount gained from the submit call. However the return value represents the amount of stEth shares, not the amount of stEth which were gained from the submit call. As a result a significant portion of stEth will be left in the router contract and the user will not receive brktEth for this amount.

title: GG-2 | Reenter Dividends
content: The vulnerability is a classic reentrancy flaw that appears in the dividend distribution routine of the contract. When a user requests a dividend payout, the contract first performs an external call that transfers BNB to the caller and only afterwards updates the internal recordthat tracks how much dividend the caller has already received. Because the state change occurs after the external call, a malicious contract can implement a fallback function that re‑enters the dividend function before the record is updated. Each re‑entry triggers another transfer of the same dividend amount, allowing the attacker to repeatedly drain BNB from the contract. This exploit can be carried out whenever a dividend claim is made, so any legitimate user who initiates a claim may unintentionally trigger the re‑entrancy if the caller is a contract under attacker control. The impact is a loss of funds from the dividend pool, resulting in reduced or missing payouts for honest participants and a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees that dividends should be distributed exactly once per entitlement period. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the order of operations in the payout function and noticed that the balance update was placed after the external call, a pattern known to be vulnerable to re‑entrancy. The bug can be hard to notice because the function appears to send the correct amount and may work correctly for externally owned accounts, masking the problem until a contract with a malicious fallback is used. To remediate the flaw, the contract should follow the check‑effects‑interactions pattern by updating the dividend ledger before any external call, or it should protect the function with a nonReentrant modifier from OpenZeppelin’s ReentrancyGuard, ensuring that a second entry cannot occur until the first execution finishes. Fixing the issue restores the intended business logic that each user receives exactly their entitled dividend and prevents the contract’s funds from being siphoned away through repeated re‑entries.
summary: Because the dividends paid to a user is only updated after the external call sending them funds, it is possible for a malicious contract to re-enter and keep draining div amount of BNB on each call.

title: PAIR-1 | Duplicate Dividends
content: In this contract the dividend distribution mechanism relies on a list of token holders called the users list. The list is populated in the mint function: whenever an address calls mint and its current token balance is zero, the address is appended to the users array. The contract never removes an address from the array when the holder transfers or burns its BridgesPair tokens, and the mint function does not check whether the address is already present. Consequently, a holder can mint tokens, transfer or burn the entire balance, and then mint again. Each mint operation adds a new entry for the same address, so the same holder appears multiple times in the users list. The distributeDividends function iterates over the users array and sends a dividend share to every entry, assuming each entry corresponds to a distinct holder. Because duplicate entries exist, the contract pays the same holder multiple dividend shares for a single entitlement. This logical flaw leads to over‑payment of dividends, draining the dividend pool and breaking the intended accounting invariant that total dividends distributed equal the pool amount. The vulnerability is triggered whenever a holder with a zero balance mints, then later empties its balance and mints again; it does not depend on any special permissions, so any token holder can exploit it. The impact is that malicious users can repeatedly inflate their dividend receipts, causing loss of funds for honest participants and potentially exhausting the contract’s reserves. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the conditions for adding and removing addresses from the users list and noticed that the removal step was missing. It can be hard to notice because the users array may contain duplicate addresses that are not visible in typical UI views, and the contract still appears to function correctly for single‑entry holders. To remediate, the contract should enforce uniqueness when inserting into the users list, for example by checking a mapping that tracks membership, and it should remove an address when its balance drops to zero or when it transfers all tokens. This change restores the one‑to‑one relationship between holders and dividend entries and prevents the over‑payment bug.
summary:
In the mint function, the only precondition for adding an address to the users list is if the balance of the address is 0. Additionally, an address is not removed from the users list if it transfers it’s balance of the BridgesPair token.
This way an address can continually mint and transfer/burn it’s tokens to enter the users list multiple times. Multiple entries in the users list will result in multiple dividends being paid out in the distributeDividends function.

title: Excess Payment When Plugin Owner Reduces Price
content: The vulnerability is an over‑payment flaw in the payable click function of a multicall contract that forwards funds to a plugin. The function calculates the required amount by multiplying the current entry fee returned by the plugin with the number of clicks, but it never checks that the ether sent with the transaction (msg.value) matches this calculated price. Because the entry fee is stored in the plugin and can be changed by the plugin owner at any time, a user may sign and broadcast a transaction based on an old fee, while the owner reduces the fee before the transaction is mined. When the transaction executes, the contract uses the new lower price for the deposit call, consumes only part of the sent ether, and leaves the surplus ether locked in the contract with no refund mechanism. This occurs whenever the plugin owner modifies the entry fee between the time a user determines the payment amount and the moment the transaction is included in a block. The affected parties are the end‑users who pay for clicks, the protocol that expects correct accounting of received funds, and any token minting logic that assumes a one‑to‑one relationship between payment and minted amount. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the flow of payable functions and identified that msg.value was never compared to the computed price. It can be hard to notice because the transaction does not revert; it simply succeeds, and the excess ether silently accumulates in the contract balance, making the contract appear to have more funds than expected. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “missing payment validation” or “price manipulation after user commitment” vulnerabilities, where business logic assumes a fixed price at the moment of user consent. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a successful click, but the user’s wallet balance drops by more than the amount that is actually used for the operation, leading to a symptom such as “my ETH disappeared” or “I paid 10 ETH but only got the service for 5 ETH”. The root cause is the lack of a check that msg.value equals the price and the ability of the plugin owner to change the entry fee unilaterally. The recommended remediation is to enforce that msg.value matches the calculated price, to revert the transaction if it does not, or to automatically refund any surplus ether back to the sender. Alternatively, the contract could lock the price at the time of user intent via an off‑chain signature or use a pull‑payment model where the contract only pulls the exact amount needed. Fixing the issue restores the intended accounting invariant that the amount of ether received equals the amount required for the requested service, preventing funds from being unintentionally locked and preserving user trust in the protocol.

title: Share price increases can lead to sandwiching attacks when using only one vault
content: The vulnerability is a pricing‑logic flaw that can enable sandwich attacks when the Bunni protocoluses only a single vault to manage liquidity for one side of a token pair. The root cause lies in the _shouldSurgeFromVaults routine inside BunniHookLogic, which only evaluates a surge in total liquidity when both vaults are active. The code assumes that with a single vault the overall pool liquidity remains constant, but this assumption breaks when the pool’s token balances are uneven and the vault that holds the token with lower liquidity experiences a share‑price increase. Such an increase, triggered by mechanisms like LDF updates, rehypothecation yield accrual, or autonomous rebalances, actually raises the total pool liquidity even though only one vault is used. An attacker can observe this impending share‑price rise, submit a transaction that inflates the price before the victim’s swap (the “front‑run” leg), let the victim’s transaction execute at the now‑worse rate, and then reverse the position (the “back‑run” leg) to capture the price differential. From a user’s perspective the swap appears to execute with excessive slippage: the user expects a fair amount of output tokens but receives noticeably less, or sees a sudden drop in the quoted price. The impact is a loss of value for the user and a distortion of the protocol’s accounting, potentially eroding trust in the pricing oracle and the overall liquidity‑provision model. The issue manifests only when the pool is unbalanced, only one vault is active, and a share‑price increase occurs – conditions that are not uncommon in dynamic yield‑bearing environments. It was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the interaction between autonomous liquidity modifications and the surge‑fee protection logic. The bug is subtle because the code path that checks for surges is simply bypassed, leaving no obvious error flag, and the price deviation may be attributed to normal market movement. To remediate, the surge‑detection logic must be extended to evaluate liquidity changes even when a single vault is in use, and the same correction should be mirrored in BunniQuoter so that quoted prices reflect the true risk of a surge. By enforcing a consistent surge check across both single‑ and dual‑vault scenarios, the protocol can prevent the price manipulation vector that currently enables sandwich attacks.
summary:
The surge fee is a mechanism to avoid sandwiching attacks during autonomous liquidity modifications, which can happen due to LDF updates, rehypothecation yields, or autonomous rebalances.

The beforeSwap function in BunniHookLogic checks for these changes in liquidity and the check for changes in rehypothecation yields is done in the _shouldSurgeFromVaults function. This function performs the check only when both vaults are being used, assuming that when using only one vault, the total liquidity will not change. However, in case the tokens in the pool are unbalanced and only the token with less liquidity uses a vault, an increase in the share price of its vault will increase the total liquidity, which can lead to a sandwiching attack.

title: Function poolManager.sync called before the unlock process
content: The vulnerability consists of invoking the pool manager’s sync function before the unlock process has been started during the execution of the rebalanceOrderPostHook in the BunniHook contract. The sync function is protected by the onlyWhenUnlocked modifier, which checks that the global lock state is already unlocked; if the lock is not active the call reverts with a ManagerLocked error. Because the unlock call is only issued later in the same hook (at line 505), the earlier sync call (line 501) always fails when the hook is executed. This ordering mistake causes the entire rebalance transaction to revert, preventing the pool’s internal accounting from being updated. As a result, the pool can become unbalanced: liquidity providers see no change in their balances, the UI may report a successful rebalance while the on‑chain state remains unchanged, and subsequent operations that rely on correct reserves may behave incorrectly. The issue is triggered whenever a rebalance post‑hook is run, i.e., for any user or automated actor attempting to rebalance the pool. It affects all participants of the pool, including liquidity providers and the protocol itself, because the failure can lead to stuck funds or denial‑of‑service conditions. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that examined the call flow of the hook and identified that the sync call precedes the unlock, violating the contract’s lock‑state assumptions. The bug is subtle because the revert surface is a generic lock error rather than an explicit “sync called too early” message, making it easy to misinterpret as a network or gas issue. Conceptually, this is a state‑ordering vulnerability where a function that requires a particular contract state is called before that state is established. The correct mitigation is to move the sync invocation (and any associated safeTransfer) into the callback that is executed after the unlock has been initiated, ensuring the lock condition is satisfied before sync runs. This adjustment restores the intended execution order, prevents the revert, and maintains proper pool balance and accounting integrity.

title: amAMM manager can capture fees from the protocol and referrers
content: The vulnerability is a fee‑capture manipulation in a decentralized automated market maker where a privileged manager contract can arbitrarily set the swap fee of the underlying Bunni protocol. The root cause is that the manager contract holds the authority to change the protocol fee and can act as a proxy for user swaps. By temporarily setting the protocol fee to zero, performing a swap on behalf of a user, and then resetting the fee to its maximum value, the manager can keep the entire fee amount for itself while presenting a lower fee to the user. This flow allows the manager to receive the full fee revenue that should have been split between the protocol and any referrer contracts. The exploit is carried out by the manager receiving the input token, overriding the protocol fee to zero, executing the swap without any fee deduction, retaining the fee internally, sending the net output token to the user, and finally restoring the protocol fee to its maximum. The impact is a loss of expected revenue for the protocol and its referrers, as they receive no fees, and a distortion of the accounting model that assumes a fixed fee share. The condition for the attack is that the manager has permission to adjust the protocol fee and that users route swaps through the manager’s proxy contract, which is likely if a canonical proxy swapper is deployed. Users may notice that the swap appears to have a low or zero fee, but the protocol’s fee balance remains unchanged and referrers receive no compensation, violating the business logic that fees are distributed proportionally. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined privileged fee‑setting functions and identified the possibility of a fee‑override abuse. It can be hard to notice because the transaction logs show a fee‑free swap, masking the fact that the manager is siphoning the fee after the fact. The recommended remediation is to base any hook‑fee calculations on the immutable fee override or a dynamic swap fee that cannot be set to zero by the manager, ensuring that fee distribution always reflects the protocol’s intended fee schedule and preventing the manager from capturing the full fee amount.
summary:
The amAMM manager is allowed to set and adjust swap fees to maximize revenue. A percentage of the fees captured by the manager is distributed to the protocol and referrers.

However, the manager can retain all the fees by acting as a proxy between the swapper and the Bunni protocol. By setting the swap fee in the Bunni protocol to the maximum and offering a lower fee in swaps executed through his proxy contract, users might be incentivized to always interact with the manager contract.

The flow for swaps in the manager contract would be as follows:  
Receive the input token from the swapper.  
Set the swap fee in the Bunni protocol to 0 and perform the swap without fees.  
Manage the fee retention inside the manager contract itself and send the due output token amount to the swapper.  
Set the swap fee in the Bunni protocol to max value.

As a result, protocol and referrers receive no fees and the manager captures the full amount of swap fees.

It can be argued that having to interact with a different manager contract depending on the pool and the current topBid will reduce the likelihood of users interacting with the manager contract. However, it is likely that a canonical proxy swapper contract will be created to allow managers to perform this strategy and attract all the users to interact with it.

title: Attacker can DOS the rebalance mechanism
content: An on-chain rebalance hook validates that the contract’s token balance after a pre-hook call is exactly equal to the amount supplied in the rebalance arguments. The check is implemented as if (args.currency.balanceOfSelf() != args.amount) revert … . The logic assumes that the contract’s balance changes only by the amount transferred in the rebalance operation. However, when the AMM is configured with manager fees, the contract may already hold a fee balance, and any external token transfer – for example a small donation from an attacker – increases the total balance without changing the intended rebalance amount. Because the condition compares the total balance to args.amount, the presence of any extra tokens makes the equality fail and the transaction reverts. An attacker can deliberately send a minimal amount of the target token to the hook contract before the rebalance is triggered, causing the post-condition to be false and preventing the rebalance from completing. This denial-of-service (DoS) vector can be exercised repeatedly, effectively freezing the protocol’s rebalancing mechanism. The impact is that the protocol may be unable to maintain its target asset allocations, users may see failed transactions or missing expected yield, and funds could become locked in an unbalanced state. The vulnerability appears only when the manager fee feature is enabled and when the contract does not restrict external token transfers. It was discovered during a manual audit of the BunniHook contract where the post-condition was examined without considering external balance changes. The issue is subtle because the check looks correct in isolation and does not emit any warning when extra tokens are present, making it easy to overlook during testing. The proper fix is to verify that the increase in the contract’s token balance during the hook execution equals args.amount, for example by recording the balance before the operation and ensuring balanceAfter - balanceBefore == args.amount, or by using internal accounting that excludes fee balances and external deposits. This change ensures that only the intended rebalance amount is considered, preventing an attacker from causing a false revert and restoring the ability of the protocol to rebalance safely.

title: Using the same block number as nonce for permit2 order
content: The vulnerability originates from the way the Bunni rebalance contract constructs a Permit2 order. The order struct includes a field called nonce, which is populated with the current block number (block.number). Permit2 uses the nonce as a replay‑protection mechanism: each distinct order must present a unique nonce, otherwise the internal Permit2 logic rejects the transfer. Because the block number is shared by all transactions that are mined in the same block, any two rebalance orders created within that block will carry identical nonces. When the first order is processed, Permit2 records the nonce as used; any subsequent order in the same block attempts to reuse the same nonce and is therefore rejected by the permitWitnessTransferFrom / _permitTransferFrom call. The immediate effect is that only one rebalance can succeed per block, while the others silently fail. From a user’s perspective this manifests as a pool that does not rebalance when expected: balances remain unchanged, the UI may show a rebalance transaction pending or completed but the token amounts do not move, and the pool may become out‑of‑balance. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit of the Bunni contract where the auditor observed the nonce assignment and verified Permit2’s nonce‑uniqueness requirement. It is hard to notice because the failure does not revert the transaction; the contract simply does not execute the token transfer, leaving no obvious error flag. The root cause is a design flaw: using a globally shared, low‑entropy value (the block number) as a unique identifier for a cryptographic permit. This belongs to the broader class of nonce‑reuse or replay‑protection bugs, where insufficient uniqueness of a nonce allows legitimate operations to be blocked or replayed. An attacker can exploit the flaw by submitting a fake rebalance order for a pool they control in every block, thereby consuming the block‑number nonce and preventing legitimate pools from rebalancing. Front‑running a legitimate rebalance with a malicious order that uses the same nonce achieves the same effect. The impact is high because it can halt the core rebalancing mechanism of the protocol, leading to stale pricing, potential arbitrage opportunities, and loss of expected yield for users. The affected parties include any pool that relies on the Bunni rebalance logic, the protocol’s overall health, and ultimately the end‑users who expect their funds to be reallocated correctly. To remediate, the nonce should be derived from a source that guarantees uniqueness per order, such as a combination of the pool identifier and the block timestamp, or a monotonically increasing counter stored in contract state. This change restores proper replay protection, ensures that multiple rebalances can coexist within a single block, and eliminates the attack surface that allows denial‑of‑service through nonce exhaustion.
summary:
```solidity
IFloodPlain.Order memory order = IFloodPlain.Order({
    offerer: address(this),
    zone: address(env.floodZone),
    recipient: address(this),
    offer: offer,
    consideration: consideration,
    deadline: block.timestamp + rebalanceOrderTTL,
    nonce: block.number,
    preHooks: preHooks,
    postHooks: postHooks
});
```
The issue is that if in the same block there were multiple rebalance orders only one of them will be executed as Permit2 won't allow to use same nonce twice. Flood uses permitWitnessTransferFrom() / _permitTransferFrom() function in Permit2 to transfer tokens and they won't allow for the same nonce to be used twice. Because BunniHook handles all the pools rebalance orders so this issue won't let two rebalance happen in the same block and without any attack some rebalances won't happen. Also attacker can use this issue and prevent pools from rebalancing by creating a rebalance for their fake pool in each block (or attacker can front-run rebalance creations and create rebalance for their pool).

title: joinRecurPool can incorrectly increment userPoolCounts
content: joinRecurPool function is intended to let a user add more stake to an existing recurring pool or join a new pool for the first time. The implementation keeps a per‑user counter (userPoolCounts) that records how many distinct stake tokens a user is participating in. The counter is incremented unconditionally after the balance update, using an unchecked ++ operation. Because the code does not verify whether the user’s previous staked balance for that token was zero, the counter is also increased when the call is merely updating an existing stake. The unlocking logic elsewhere expects the counter to reflect the number of distinct pools a user has joined; when the counter is larger than the actual number of pools, the contract treats the user as still being enrolled and refuses to release the locked tokens. An attacker or any user can trigger the bug simply by calling joinRecurPool with a higher token balance after already being in the pool. The impact is that the user’s tokens become permanently locked, appearing as a zero balance on the UI or as “cannot withdraw” errors, even though the contract still holds the funds. The condition occurs only when a user with a non‑zero existing stake calls joinRecurPool with an increased balance; users who join for the first time are not affected. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the increment of userPoolCounts and noticed the missing zero‑balance check. It is easy to miss because the function emits a normal JoinRecurPool event and does not revert, so the state change looks benign until the unlock step fails. The correct mitigation is to increment userPoolCounts only when the previous staked balance for that token is zero, i.e., when the user is joining the pool for the first time. This change restores the invariant that the counter matches the actual number of pools a user participates in, allowing the unlocking mechanism to work as intended and preventing funds from disappearing from the user’s perspective.

title: _settleCurrency does not properly interact with the poolManager when calling settle
content: The contract contains an accounting flaw in its internal settlement routine. When the contract owes the pool manager a negative amount of an ERC20 token, the function transfers the required tokens to the pool manager but never invokes the pool manager’s settle() method that finalises the accounting entry. The pool manager therefore still records an outstanding debt even though the tokens have already been moved, creating a mismatch between on‑chain token balances and the pool manager’s internal ledger. This mismatch can be triggered whenever _settleCurrency is called with a negative amount for a non‑native currency. Because the settlement call is omitted, the protocol believes the contract still owes tokens, which may allow a malicious actor to later invoke take() or other withdrawal paths to extract additional tokens, or cause legitimate users to see their refunds disappear or become zero. From a user’s perspective the UI may indicate that a settlement succeeded and that a refund was processed, yet the expected balance does not appear, or funds seem to be missing. The issue was discovered during a manual security review where an auditor noted a comment suggesting that poolManager.settle() should be used and observed a misplaced else‑if block that prevents the positive‑balance branch from executing correctly. The bug is subtle because the token transfer itself does not revert and no explicit error is emitted, making the accounting inconsistency hard to detect without inspecting the pool manager’s state. The proper fix is to call poolManager.settle() after transferring ERC20 tokens and to restructure the conditional logic so that the positive‑balance case is reachable and correctly updates the pool manager’s records. In broader terms this is a classic settlement‑or‑accounting bug where external state is not synchronised after a token transfer, violating the protocol’s invariant that token balances on both sides must remain consistent.

title: Lack of receive() function
content: The contract implements an unwrapEthOutput function that calls the WETH token’s withdraw method to convert all wrapped Ether held by the contract into native Ether. The withdraw call attempts to send Ether to the contract address itself. Because the contract does not define a receive() or payable fallback function, it is unable to accept incoming Ether transfers. When the WETH contract executes the low‑level call that delivers Ether, the call reverts due to the lack of a payable entry point, causing the entire unwrapEthOutput transaction to fail. This failure prevents users from receiving the expected Ether, effectively locking the converted funds inside the contract. The issue originates from a missing payable fallback, a common class of bug where contracts are not prepared to handle plain Ether transfers. It manifests whenever the unwrap function is invoked, or any other operation that results in the contract receiving Ether, such as direct transfers or other token withdrawals. Users attempting to unwrap their WETH see their transaction revert, receive no Ether, and may observe that their balance remains unchanged despite a successful WETH withdrawal call. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the contract’s external functions and noted the absence of a receive() implementation. Because the revert occurs only at runtime, it can be difficult to spot without testing the withdrawal path, and the UI may simply report a generic failure without indicating the underlying cause. To remediate the issue, the contract should include a receive() external payable {} (or a payable fallback) so that it can accept Ether sent by the WETH contract, allowing the unwrap operation to complete and funds to be released to the caller. Adding this payable entry point restores the intended business logic of converting WETH to Ether and prevents denial‑of‑service conditions where funds become permanently inaccessible.

title: Missing transfer of tokens before island.mint()
content: The vulnerability consists of a missing token transfer step in the Burve contract's mint function. When a user calls Burve.mint(recipient, liq) the function iterates over a distribution array, calculates per‑range liquidity amounts and finally invokes _mint(recipient, liq) on the island pool. However, the contract never moves the required underlying tokens from the caller to the pool before invoking island.mint. The root cause is the omission of a token.transferFrom (or equivalent safeTransfer) call and the associated allowance check. Because the pool expects the caller to have supplied the tokens, the internal mint operation reverts due to insufficient balance, causing the whole transaction to fail. From a user's perspective the UI may display a successful submission, but the transaction ends with a generic revert and the user receives no liquidity tokens, their balance remains unchanged and any previously approved allowance stays untouched. This denial‑of‑service condition affects every liquidity provider that interacts with the Burve contract, reducing the pool's ability to attract capital and potentially harming the protocol's economic model. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that compared the expected token flow with the actual code. It can be hard to notice because the revert does not explicitly mention a missing transfer, and the contract does not emit an event indicating the failure. The bug belongs to the class of “missing pre‑condition enforcement” or “incomplete asset handling” bugs, where a contract assumes that external assets have been moved without actually performing the transfer. To remediate, the mint function should first call the underlying ERC‑20 token's transferFrom (or safeTransferFrom) to pull the required amount from the caller, verify that the transfer succeeded, and only then proceed to call island.mint and _mint. Proper checks for allowance and balance, as well as emitting an event after a successful transfer, would align the implementation with the intended business logic of providing liquidity in exchange for tokens.

title: Normalizing token weights can result in a revert
content: The vulnerability originates from the weight‑normalisation routine that multiplies each stored weight by the total weight using the FullMath.mulDivX256 helper. The helper contains a safety check require(denominator > num, "0") that aborts the call when the denominator is not strictly greater than the numerator. When the token array contains only a single element, that element’s weight is equal to the totalWeight, causing the denominator and numerator to be identical. Consequently the require condition fails and the transaction reverts. This situation can be triggered whenever a pool is created with a single asset or when all but one asset are removed, leading to a state where the normalisation step is executed on a solitary weight entry. From a user perspective the contract appears to reject weight updates, deposits or swaps with a generic revert message, often showing no change in balances or a zero‑value return, which can be confusing. The impact is that the affected functions become unusable, potentially freezing user funds or preventing further interactions with the pool until the weight is manually corrected. The bug was discovered during a systematic audit of the arithmetic utilities, where the auditor noticed that the denominator‑greater‑than‑numerator guard could be violated in edge‑case configurations. Because the revert occurs deep inside a library call, the root cause may be hard to spot from the UI or transaction logs alone; developers may only see a generic failure without understanding that the equality of weight and totalWeight is the trigger. The issue belongs to the class of arithmetic‑validation bugs where input assumptions (denominator > numerator) are not enforced for all logical states, leading to unexpected reverts. To remediate the problem the normalisation logic should detect the equality case and assign the maximum uint256 value (2**256‑1) to the weight, or otherwise bypass the mulDivX256 call when denominator equals numerator. This ensures the mathematical operation remains valid and the contract continues to function even when only one weight entry exists, preserving expected behaviour such as successful deposits, swaps and balance updates.
summary:
```solidity
self.weights[i] = FullMath.mulDivX256(
    self.weights[i],
    self.totalWeight
```
The issue is that if there is a single element in the array, then that element will equal the totalWeight which results in a revert when calling mulDivX256() as we have the following check there:
```solidity
require(denominator > num, "0");
```
As they are equal, we will revert.

title: Incorrect recipient results in the inability to properly redeem a position
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect recipient address used when minting island shares. When the contract mints shares for a user, it passes the user‑provided recipient to island.mint, but later the burn() function expects the shares to be owned by the Burve contract itself because the burn call is executed by the contract. Since the shares were minted to the external user, the contract does not hold any shares and the subsequent burn reverts. This mismatch between minting and burning logic constitutes a logic error in the accounting of share ownership. It can be exploited by any user who tries to redeem their position: the transaction will fail, leaving the liquidity locked and the user unable to receive the expected funds. The impact is that users see no redemption, their balances appear unchanged, and they may need to perform an extra step of transferring the minted shares to the contract before burning, or they must burn directly on the island, which still leaves them with Burve shares that cannot be used elsewhere. The bug occurs whenever the minting path for the island is taken (i.e., when range.lower and range.upper are both zero). It affects all participants who provide a recipient address, the Burve protocol, and any downstream contracts that rely on successful redemption. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the mint and burn flows and noticed that the recipient argument was inconsistent. Because the failure only appears at burn time, the contract appears to work during minting, making the problem subtle and easy to miss. The correct fix is to mint the island shares to the contract itself (address(this)) so that the contract holds the shares and can later burn them without reverting. This aligns the minting and burning ownership model and restores the intended accounting behavior. In generic terms, the bug is a mismatch of token ownership between creation and destruction phases, leading to a denial‑of‑service style failure where funds cannot be redeemed.

title: DoS on mint() and burn() due to overestimation of available liquidity
content: The Burve contract implements a multi‑range liquidity provision mechanism where mint() and burn() invoke compoundV3Ranges() to collect fees and then allocate new liquidity across several weighted price ranges. The vulnerability arises from the way the contract estimates how much liquidity can be minted from the token balances it holds. After collecting fees, the function collectAndCalcCompound() scales the available token0 and token1 balances by a large constant (2^64) and divides by the per‑range token requirements derived from the weight distribution. It then caps the resulting nominal liquidity to the minimum of the two token‑specific values and applies a small rounding adjustment. This calculation assumes that the scaled token amounts can be split proportionally across all ranges, but it ignores the fact that the actual pool liquidity distribution may not follow the same proportions. When the real distribution cannot satisfy the scaled amounts – for example, when the contract holds only a single wei of each token and the weight distribution is split evenly across two ranges – the algorithm overestimates the amount of liquidity that can be minted. The over‑estimated nominal liquidity (e.g., 14 units) is larger than the true available liquidity (zero), causing the subsequent mint or burn operation to revert. The issue manifests as a denial‑of‑service condition: legitimate users attempting to mint or burn receive a generic revert, see no change in their balances, and are forced to donate additional token0 or token1 to make the calculation fit, which may be impractical. An attacker can exploit this by front‑running a legitimate transaction and donating a small amount of token that deliberately skews the balance, ensuring the over‑estimation persists and causing the transaction to fail. This attack vector does not require any special permissions and can be repeated to keep the contract unusable. The bug affects any participant who relies on the mint() or burn() functions – liquidity providers, traders, and the protocol itself – because it prevents normal liquidity management and can lock funds in a non‑functional state. The problem was discovered during a security audit when the auditors examined the compoundV3Ranges() flow and tested edge cases with minimal token balances, revealing that the rounding and scaling logic could produce impossible liquidity values. The flaw is subtle because the arithmetic appears correct in isolation; the error only surfaces when the distribution of scaled tokens diverges from the actual pool distribution, and the contract does not emit a clear error indicating insufficient liquidity. To remediate the issue, the contract should either compute the optimal mintable liquidity off‑chain and require the caller to submit this verified amount, or redesign the on‑chain calculation to respect per‑range liquidity caps, iteratively checking each range and limiting the mint amount to the smallest feasible value. Such a fix would align the accounting with the real pool state, eliminate the over‑estimation, and restore the ability of users to mint and burn without needing to provide extra tokens or risk transaction reverts. In summary, the vulnerability is a mis‑accounting of multi‑range liquidity that leads to an over‑estimation bug, causing denial‑of‑service symptoms such as transaction failures, unchanged balances, and the perception that funds have disappeared, even though the contract logic is at fault rather than an external attack on the assets.
summary:
In the Burve contract, compoundV3Ranges() is executed when mint() or burn() are called. This function performs the following actions:
1. Collects fees from the UniswapV3 pool for all ranges.
2. Calculates the total liquidity that can be minted with the available balance of token0 and token1.
3. Calculates the liquidity that can be minted for each range, according to their weight distribution.
4. Mints the respective liquidity for each range.
Step 2) is performed by the collectAndCalcCompound() function and these are the steps followed:
1. Obtains the balance of token0 and token1 in the Burve contract.
2. Calculates the amounts of token0 and token1 required to mint 2^64 liquidity given the weight distribution of the ranges.
3. Calculates the nominal liquidity for each token by scaling up by 2^64 the amounts of token0 and token1 and dividing by the amounts calculated in the previous step.
4. Caps the nominal liquidity to the minimum of the liquidity for token0 and token1, and adjusts for rounding errors in minting.
However, it is not taken into account that the distribution of the scaled distribution might not match the distribution of the actual liquidity in the pool, which overestimates the amount of liquidity that can be minted, causing the transaction to fail.
Let's consider the following example:
The Burve contract has two ranges with equal weight distribution.
On burn, the balance of token0 and token1 is 1.
amount0InUnitLiqX64 and amount1InUnitLiqX64 are calculated to be 1e18.
We have that nominalLiq0 = (1 << 64) / 1e18 = 18 (same for nominalLiq1).
mintNominalLiq adjust for rounding errors, giving mintNominalLiq = 18 - 2 * 2 = 14.
The real liquidity available is 0, though, as the 1 wei cannot be split into the two ranges.
As a result, the mint() and burn() functions will revert. The users will be forced to donate to the contract an amount of token0 or token1 such that the calculation of the nominal liquidity is not overestimated. Note, however, that a malicious attacker can also front-run their transaction by donating an amount that will cause the transaction to revert, causing a denial of service attack.

title: First deposit front-running attack
content: The vulnerability is a front‑running manipulation of the share‑minting formula that is common to many ERC‑4626 vault implementations. When a user makes the first deposit, the contract calculates the number of shares to mint using the expression mintNominalLiq * totalShares / totalNominalLiq. Because totalShares is initially very small (often one dead share) and totalNominalLiq is low, an attacker can submit a transaction just before the user’s deposit that mints a single share and immediately donates an amount equal to half of the user’s intended liquidity. This donation inflates totalNominalLiq, so when the user’s transaction is processed the division is truncated and the user receives only one share regardless of the amount deposited (x * 1 / (0.5x + 1) = 1). After the user’s deposit the attacker burns his share and withdraws roughly half of the total liquidity, effectively stealing a portion of the user’s funds. The attack can be carried out whenever the vault has a minimal share supply and the attacker can front‑run the first deposit, which is typical for newly deployed vaults or after a period of inactivity. The affected parties are any liquidity provider who attempts to be the first depositor, the protocol’s overall fund pool, and any downstream users who rely on correct share accounting. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the ERC‑4626 share‑minting logic and identified the lack of protection against state changes between the share‑calculation and the actual deposit. It is hard to notice because the contract’s arithmetic appears correct on its own and the front‑run transaction is indistinguishable from a legitimate deposit, making the loss manifest only as an unexpected reduction in minted shares or missing funds after withdrawal. From a user’s perspective the UI may show that a large amount of liquidity was supplied but only a single share appears in the balance, or the user may see their balance drop after the attacker withdraws, leading to confusion and the perception that “funds disappeared”. The bug belongs to the class of price‑manipulation or deposit‑front‑run vulnerabilities that break the accounting invariant that each share represents a proportional claim on the vault’s assets. To remediate the problem the contract should decouple share calculation from the current total nominal liquidity, for example by introducing dead shares at deployment or by using a virtual deposit amount as implemented in OpenZeppelin’s ERC‑4626, which records the intended deposit amount before any external state changes can affect the share ratio. These mitigations ensure that the first depositor receives the correct share amount even if an attacker attempts to manipulate the vault’s liquidity state immediately before the deposit.
summary:
The Burve contract is subject to a common issue of ERC-4626 vaults, where the first deposit is front-run by an attacker.
1. A user will add liquidity into the contract to mint shares.
2. The attacker front-runs the user's transaction by minting one share and donating 50% of the liquidity provided by the user.
3. The user transaction is executed, and the shares minted are calculated as mintNominalLiq * totalShares / totalNominalLiq. As compoundV3Ranges() is executed, totalNominalLiq is inflated by the attacker's donation, so the division is truncated, and the user mints only 1 share: x * 1 / (0.5x + 1) = 1.
4. The attacker burns his share, receiving half of the liquidity of the contract.

title: Island shares ownership not updated on Burve token transfer
content: The vulnerability is a synchronization flaw between Burve token ownership and the associated island share accounting. When a user mints Burve tokens, a portion of the provided liquidity is used to create island shares that are deposited into the StationProxy contract under the recipient’s address and the islandSharesPerOwner mapping is updated to reflect this ownership. However, the token transfer logic does not invoke any update of the island share records. Consequently, if the token holder transfers Burve tokens to another address, the island shares remain recorded under the original sender both in the StationProxy contract and in the islandSharesPerOwner mapping. From the user’s perspective this manifests as a situation where the new token holder sees the correct Burve balance but is unable to harvest any rewards or burn the island shares for the underlying liquidity; reward functions return zero and burn attempts revert because the contract believes the caller owns no shares. The root cause is the missing state transition in the transfer path – the _update() hook is not overridden to re‑allocate the proportional LP tokens and to adjust the islandSharesPerOwner entries for both the sender and the receiver. The bug can be exploited to create a denial‑of‑service condition for the new owner, and it also allows the original owner to continue harvesting rewards after relinquishing the tokens, breaking the accounting assumptions that token balance and share entitlement are aligned. This issue appears only after a token transfer; it is not obvious during minting because the initial allocation works correctly. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the lifecycle of mint, transfer, and reward functions and noticed that the transfer path does not touch the island share state. The problem is hard to notice because the token balance updates normally and no event signals the mismatch, so users may assume they are entitled to rewards when they are not. The appropriate remediation is to override the _update() function so that on every Burve token transfer the contract withdraws the proportional amount of LP tokens from the StationProxy under the old owner, redeposits them under the new owner, and updates the islandSharesPerOwner mapping for both parties, thereby keeping token ownership and share ownership in sync.
summary:
When a Kodiak island contract is set in the Burve, on mint() a portion of the liquidity will be used to mint island shares, which will then be deposited into the station proxy at the name of the recipient, and the islandSharesPerOwner mapping will be updated for the recipient. The recipient will also receive Burve tokens (shares) for the liquidity provided to the Uniswap pools.
However, if the recipient transfers the Burve tokens to another address, the island shares are still assigned to him, both in StationProxy and in the Burve's islandSharesPerOwner mapping. This means that after the transfer, the new owner of the Burve tokens will not be able to harvest the rewards in StationProxy, nor will he be able to burn the island shares in exchange for the underlying liquidity.

title: Manipulatable oracle and breaking slippage protection
content: The vulnerability is that the contract determines the amount of BEAM tokens it should receive by calling UniswapV2Router02.getAmountsOut with a path that reflects the current reserves of the involved pools. Because the router query reads the live on‑chain reserves, any external actor can change those reserves immediately before the call. An attacker can front‑run the protocol’s buy transaction with a large swap that skews the price in one or more pools, causing getAmountsOut to return an artificially low output amount. The contract then applies a fixed slippagePercent to compute a minimum acceptable amount, but because the slippage value is static and does not incorporate any time‑weighted average or protection against rapid reserve changes, the calculated minimum can be satisfied even when the real market price has been driven down to near zero. Consequently the protocol may execute a purchase that delivers almost no BEAM tokens while still paying the full input amount, effectively losing value. This can be exploited as a sandwich attack: the attacker swaps a large amount of the input token before the protocol’s transaction, then optionally reverses the swap after the protocol’s purchase, extracting the difference between the manipulated price and the true market price. The impact is that the protocol’s funds are drained or its token balance is depleted, users see their expected BEAM allocation disappear, and the overall accounting of the system becomes inconsistent. The condition occurs whenever the contract performs a buy using the getAmountsOut oracle without any time‑weighted averaging or price sanity checks, i.e., on every call to the buy function. All parties that rely on the protocol’s token acquisition – the protocol itself, its users, and token holders – are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that highlighted the reliance on a spot price oracle and the static slippage calculation. It is hard to notice because the transaction appears to respect the configured slippage limit, yet the underlying price source is fully manipulable, so the failure manifests only under adversarial market conditions. To remediate, the contract should replace the spot price query with a less manipulatable oracle such as a TWAP derived from the same pools, or an external price feed like Chainlink, and/or compute the expected output amount directly from the buy() logic rather than applying a fixed slippage percentage. Adding a price sanity check, a dynamic slippage bound, or a delay between price observation and execution would also mitigate the attack surface.

title: Last buyer in the BondingCurve contract can experience significant fund losses if he overpays for remaining tokens
content: The vulnerability is an over‑payment loss that occurs when the final buyer of a bonding‑curve token contract sends more ether than is required to purchase the remaining tokens. The contract’s buy function calculates the number of tokens to mint using a solveForN routine that rounds down and caps the result at the maximum token supply. Because the subsequent require check only verifies that the new token count does not exceed the hard cap (using a <= comparison), the check always passes even when the caller has supplied excess ether. Consequently, the function never executes a refund path and the surplus ether remains locked in the contract. An attacker or any user who happens to be the last purchaser can exploit this by deliberately sending a larger ether amount than the exact price returned by the ethForN pricing function; the contract will mint the maximum number of tokens and retain the extra ether with no way for the sender to retrieve it. The impact is a direct loss of funds for the last buyer, erosion of trust in the token economics, and a breach of the protocol’s accounting invariant that total ether collected should equal the price of minted tokens. The condition under which the bug manifests is when the total supply is about to reach the predefined MAX_MILLION_TOKENS limit and the buyer’s transaction includes more ether than the exact amount needed for the final allocation. All participants who might become the final purchaser are affected, while earlier buyers are not. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by ThreeSigma, who noted that the rounding behavior of solveForN combined with the always‑true require statement prevented detection of over‑payment. The problem is subtle because the transaction succeeds without reverting and no explicit error is emitted, making the loss appear as a silent deduction from the sender’s balance. To remediate, the solveForN algorithm should be adjusted to return the precise maximum token count only when the supplied ether matches the exact price, eliminating the rounding‑down bias. Additionally, the buy function must include explicit logic that compares the ether sent with the exact cost for the calculated token amount and, if a surplus exists, transfers the excess back to the caller before finalizing the purchase. This ensures that the contract respects the expected refund behavior and preserves the integrity of its financial accounting.
summary: The buy() function does not refund overpayments to the last buyer in a situation where he transfers more ETH than needed to complete the sale. This issue arises from the incorrect interaction between the solveForN() function and the following require check: require(newN <= MAX_MILLION_TOKENS * 1e18, "Max token supply reached"); The value returned by solveForN() will always be less than or equal to MAX_MILLION_TOKENS * 1e18 due to internal rounding down and the fact that the result is constrained to the maximum MAX_MILLION_TOKENS * 1e18. Therefore, the require statement using the <= comparison is always satisfied. In cases where the last buyer transfers more ETH to the buy() function than calculated by the ethForN() function, the excess funds will be lost as there is no refund mechanism to handle overpayments.

title: Uninitialized maxTransaction and maxWallet variables prevent trading for non-excluded users
content: The vulnerability is an uninitialized limit configuration in the token contract that unintentionally blocks all trades for users who are not explicitly excluded from transaction and wallet size checks. The contract defines two state variables, maxTransaction and maxWallet, which are meant to cap the size of a single purchase and the total balance a regular address may hold during the first ten minutes after trading is enabled. These caps are only enforced when the boolean flag maxBuyStat1, set to true in the constructor, is active.
