It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the flash‑loan integration and noted the missing re‑entrancy‑style guard. The flaw is subtle because the contract appears to follow the standard Aave flash‑loan pattern, and the msg.sender check gives a false sense of security, making the problem easy to overlook without a deeper analysis of the call flow. To remediate, the contract should record when it initiates a flash loan (for example, setting an isFlash boolean to true) and require that executeOperation can only proceed when this flag is set, resetting it after repayment. Additionally, the contract should validate or whitelist the DEX routers used in aggregatorSwap and avoid accepting arbitrary calldata from external sources. By enforcing these controls, the vault would reject unauthorized flash‑loan callbacks and prevent the attacker from forcing harmful swaps, thereby preserving user balances and maintaining protocol integrity.
summary: According to Aave documentation, when requesting flash-loan, it’s possible to specify a `receiver`, so function `executeOperation()` of that `receiver` will be called by `lendingPool`. <https://docs.aave.com/developers/v/2.0/guides/flash-loans> In the `SuperVault` there is no check to prevent this attack so attacker can use this and perform `griefing attack` and make miner contract lose all its funds. or he can create specifically crafted `params` so when `executeOperation()` is called by `lendingPool`, attacker could steal vault’s user funds.

title: Beacon chain withdrawals that occur at lastwithdrawaltimestamp will be lost Submitted by hash
content: The vulnerability is an off‑by‑one timestamp check in the withdrawal processing logic of an EigenPod contract that interacts with the Beacon Chain. The contract stores the most recent withdrawal timestamp in mostRecentWithdrawalTimestamp and only allows the verification function _verifyAndProcessWithdrawal to be called for timestamps strictly greater than this value (require(timestamp > mostRecentWithdrawalTimestamp)). When a user calls activateRestaking, the internal function _processWithdrawalBeforeRestaking sets mostRecentWithdrawalTimestamp to the current block timestamp and then sends the contract’s ETH balance to the pod owner. Because Beacon Chain withdrawals are executed after all user‑initiated transactions in the same block (as defined by EIP‑4895), a withdrawal that is included in the same block as activateRestaking will be credited to the contract only after the timestamp has already been recorded. Consequently the withdrawal’s timestamp is equal to mostRecentWithdrawalTimestamp, causing the strict > check to reject the proof. The funds are therefore never processed and become permanently inaccessible through the contract’s withdrawal path. The impact is loss of user funds that were supposed to be withdrawn from the Beacon Chain in that block; the user sees no ETH transferred, their balance appears unchanged, and subsequent attempts to withdraw fail with a timestamp‑validation error. This condition occurs only when a withdrawal and a restaking activation happen in the same block, which can be triggered deliberately by an attacker who front‑runs the activation or unintentionally by a user who does not understand the ordering. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the timestamp validation modifier and the ordering of Beacon Chain withdrawal execution relative to contract calls. It is hard to notice because the contract behaves correctly for all other timestamps and the missing funds are only observable when the specific timing condition is met, which may not appear in routine tests. The bug belongs to the class of off‑by‑one or strict inequality logic errors that break accounting assumptions about monotonic timestamps. To fix the problem the contract should accept withdrawals whose timestamp is greater than or equal to mostRecentWithdrawalTimestamp (i.e., change the require to >=) or otherwise adjust the accounting so that withdrawals occurring in the same block are processed before the timestamp is updated. This ensures that the contract’s internal state remains consistent with the Beacon Chain’s post‑transaction withdrawal semantics and prevents funds from disappearing.

title: A malicious early user/attacker can manipulate the vault’s `pricePerShare` to take an unfair share of future users’ deposits
content: The vulnerability resides in the way the vault calculates and stores its price per share (PPS) using the aToken balance as the denominator without any safeguards for the initial state. When the contract is first deployed its total supply of shares is zero, and the _tokenToShares function mints a one‑to‑one amount of shares for the first depositor. An attacker can exploit this by depositing the smallest possible amount of the underlying asset (1 wei) and receiving an equal amount of share tokens. Because the contract does not enforce a minimum share issuance, the attacker then transfers a huge amount of aToken directly to the vault (for example 10 000 e18 − 1 tokens). This inflates the aToken balance while the share supply remains unchanged, causing the PPS to jump from roughly 1 to an astronomically high value (around 1 e22). Future users who deposit normal amounts of the underlying asset are converted to shares using the inflated PPS, so their deposits are divided by a massive denominator and they receive only a negligible number of shares – often as little as 1 wei for a deposit of 19 999 e18. When these users attempt to redeem their tokens, the contract computes the amount of underlying assets to return based on the tiny share amount, resulting in a loss of roughly half of their deposited funds, or even a complete loss if the PPS is high enough that the redemption calculation rounds down to zero. Additionally, because the PPS is extreme, the attacker can redeem a large amount of underlying tokens while burning zero shares, due to precision loss in the division. The issue manifests when the contract is fresh, has no minimum share rule, and an adversary can move aToken into the vault after the first mint. It affects any depositor after the attacker, the protocol’s vault balance, and ultimately the DAO that relies on correct accounting. The flaw was discovered during a Code4rena audit as a known pattern of price‑per‑share manipulation in newly‑initialized yield contracts. It can be difficult to notice because the PPS appears as a large number on‑chain, and user interfaces may not highlight that a deposit yielded almost no share tokens, making the loss appear as a silent reduction of balance. The recommended mitigation is to enforce a non‑zero share amount for the first mint, reserve a portion of the initial liquidity to the DAO, and add explicit checks that prevent burning zero shares. More generally, contracts should avoid using a mutable external balance as the sole basis for PPS calculations without constraints, and should implement safeguards against initialisation attacks and precision‑loss exploits.

title: Anyone can vote multiple times by using multiple addresses and transferring a voting token if private mode is off Submitted by stiglitz, also found by jesjupyter, Rotciv Egaf, nmirchev8, Haxatron, PENGUN and Said
content: The vulnerability is a voting‑power inflation flaw that arises because the voting token (DToken) can be freely transferred when the contract’s private mode is disabled, while the voting power calculation reads the current token balance each time a voter calls the updatePower function. The root cause is that the private‑mode flag only blocks the token’s transfer functions, but does not prevent the voting contract from re‑reading the balance after a transfer, nor does it lock or snapshot the voting power at the moment a vote is cast. An attacker can exploit this by moving the same amount of DToken between multiple addresses and invoking updatePower on each address, causing the same token balance to be counted repeatedly in the vote tally (vote.attackerPower += power or vote.defenderPower += power). In practice, a user who holds X tokens calls updatePower, transfers all X tokens to another address, and then the second address calls updatePower again, resulting in X being added twice; by repeating the process with n addresses the attacker can multiply their influence n‑fold. The impact is a distortion of governance outcomes: proposals may be approved or rejected based on artificially inflated voting power, undermining the protocol’s decision‑making integrity and potentially harming honest participants who expect one vote per token. The condition for exploitation is that the DToken contract is not in private mode; the exact circumstances under which private mode is toggled are unclear, but whenever it is off the flaw is present. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the interaction between the private‑mode flag and the voting logic. It can be hard to notice because token transfers appear legitimate and the private‑mode flag gives a false sense of protection, while the voting contract does not enforce any snapshot or lock‑in of voting power. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a vote count may be unexpectedly high or that an address with zero token balance after a transfer still contributed voting power, contradicting the expectation that each token can be used only once per voting round. The bug belongs to the class of “double‑counting voting power” or “snapshot‑missing governance” vulnerabilities. To remediate, the protocol should either keep the token permanently non‑transferable during voting periods, enforce private mode whenever voting is active, or implement a proper snapshot mechanism that records each holder’s balance at the start of the voting window and prevents subsequent transfers from affecting the recorded power. Additionally, the voting contract should track whether a particular token amount has already been accounted for, ensuring that each token contributes to the tally at most once.
summary:
The token used for voting is the DToken (based on the deployment script). The PERC contract (inherited by DToken) implements so-called private mode. If the contract is in private mode, transfer functions are not callable. However, if the mode is off, there is a place for voting manipulation. I am not sure when or in what type of circumstances the private mode will be on/off. However because the functionality is there and transfers are not banned completely, I chose the likelihood medium.

Exploit scenario:
• DToken is not in private mode.
• User A who has an amount X of DToken calls Voting::updatePower. It will take the DToken balance of user A and use it as a voting power.
• User A transfer X amount of DToken to user B.
• User A now has 0 amount. User B now has X amount.
• User B who has amount X of DToken calls Voting::updatePower. It will take the DToken balance of user B and use it as a voting power.

This way the voting power of X amount of DToken will be used twice in vote.attackerPower += power or vote.defenderPower += power;. User A can create n addresses to make his power n times stronger.

title: _updatesponsor implementation contradicts sponsor role in pool and open's backrunning attack vectors Submitted by Spearmint, also found by ast3ros
content: The contract’s internal function that decides which address is the pool’s sponsor contains a logical flaw that breaks two core protocol guarantees. First, the protocol documentation states that the first sponsor – the “early sponsor” – should be protected for a short period after they become the sponsor, preventing an attacker from immediately out‑bidding them with a negligible amount of additional stake. The implementation does not enforce any such protection; it simply compares the new staker’s raw token balance (stakerDTokenBalance) against a calculated sponsorPower that adds a time‑based bonus to the current sponsor’s balance. Because the bonus is capped by a maximum time window, an attacker who submits a transaction that is mined after the early sponsor’s transaction can add a tiny amount of stake (as little as a few wei of wstETH) and satisfy the condition stakerDTokenBalance > sponsorPower, causing the sponsor role to be transferred. This back‑running attack allows the attacker to hijack the sponsor position and any associated rewards or governance rights with almost no cost. Second, the sponsor definition in the protocol states that the sponsor must be the staker with the highest staking power. The current formula for sponsorPower (sponsorDTokenBalance + sponsorBonus) does not correctly reflect the true staking power because the bonus is a linear function of elapsed time rather than the actual amount staked. Consequently, a staker who contributes a much larger amount of tokens may still be considered weaker than the current sponsor if the sponsor’s time‑based bonus remains high. The test suite demonstrates this by showing that even after a competitor stakes six times more, the original sponsor remains unchanged, violating the intended business logic. The vulnerability manifests whenever a stake transaction is processed after another user’s stake, especially in environments where transaction ordering can be manipulated (e.g., via front‑running or back‑running bots). It affects all participants of the pool because the sponsor role controls reward distribution and may confer governance privileges; users may see their expected rewards disappear or be redirected to an attacker. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by reproducing the scenario in a Foundry test that back‑runs a stake transaction with a minimal extra amount. It is subtle because the contract does not emit explicit warnings and the sponsor change appears legitimate from the contract’s perspective, making it easy to miss during casual testing. To remediate, the sponsor update logic should be rewritten to (i) enforce a protection window for the early sponsor, preventing any sponsor change within that period regardless of marginal stake differences, and (ii) compute sponsorPower based on the actual staking amount without an artificial time‑based multiplier, or at least ensure the calculation aligns with the definition of “highest staking power”. This would restore the intended fairness and prevent attackers from hijacking the sponsor role with negligible stake.

title: If pool owner withdraws 100% of earnings, poolusers will be permanently blocked from withdrawing staked funds Submitted by Spearmint
content: The vulnerability is a division‑by‑zero arithmetic error that occurs when the pool owner withdraws the entire amount of earned fees from a staking pool. The contract stores the earnings balance (earningBalance_) and uses it to compute a scaling factor Fs via a pure function that returns a percentage of the earnings relative to a maximum. When the owner withdraws 100 % of the earnings, earningBalance_ becomes zero, causing the function to return the minimum percentage (DEM I) and consequently set Fs to zero. Fs is then used in a second pure function that calculates the lock duration for each user’s stake. Because Fs equals zero, the duration formula reduces to zero, and the subsequent withdrawal routine divides the total locked amount by this duration (total * pastTime / duration). The division by zero triggers a Solidity panic (error code 0x12), causing the transaction to revert. As a result, any pool user who attempts to withdraw their locked ETH receives a revert error and their funds remain locked indefinitely. This situation can be reproduced simply by the pool owner calling the earnings withdrawal function with the full earnings amount; no special permissions or edge‑case conditions are required. The impact is that users lose access to their staked assets, violating the core business logic that staked funds must be withdrawable after the lock period. The issue was discovered during a formal audit that included unit‑test execution; the test showed that after the owner’s full earnings withdrawal, a subsequent user withdrawal reverted with a division‑by‑zero panic. The bug is hard to notice because the contract does not explicitly guard against a zero duration, and the arithmetic appears correct for typical non‑zero earnings. The vulnerability belongs to the class of unchecked arithmetic errors where a denominator can become zero due to state changes, leading to a runtime exception. From the user’s perspective the UI would show a “transaction failed” message, the balance would remain unchanged, and the expected refund of locked ETH would be missing. The contract should protect the duration calculation by handling the zero‑Fs case, for example by bypassing the duration‑based formula and allowing a direct withdrawal when Fs is zero, or by enforcing a minimum non‑zero duration. This fix restores the guarantee that users can always retrieve their staked funds, even if the pool owner extracts all earnings.

title: Malicious poolowner can withdraw earnings without affecting trust score Submitted by Spearmint
content: The vulnerability is a manipulation of the protocol’s reputation mechanism that allows a pool owner to extract all of their earned rewards while keeping their Trust Score unchanged. The root cause lies in the way the Trust Score is updated: it is decreased only when earnings are withdrawn directly from the owner’s own pool, but the system does not account for earnings that are first reinvested into another pool where the owner controls an extremely high Owner% (for example 99%). By creating a secondary account, configuring its pool with a near‑full Owner share, and using the reinvestEarnings function to move the original earnings into that pool, the attacker receives almost the entire amount as new earnings in the secondary pool (the protocol’s dev team receives the remaining 1%). The attacker can then call the standard withdrawal function on the secondary pool and transfer the funds to their main wallet. Because the Trust Score calculation does not consider the reinvest‑and‑withdraw flow, the score remains exactly the same as before the operation. This attack can be executed with negligible cost and does not require any special privileges; any user can follow the described steps. From a user’s point of view the protocol promises that withdrawing earnings will lower the Trust Score, signalling reduced reputation, yet the victim sees their Trust Score stay high while their balance is emptied, violating the expected accounting logic of the system. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that included a Foundry test reproducing the attack scenario, confirming that the Trust Score before and after the reinvest‑withdraw sequence is identical. The bug is hard to notice because the contract’s state variables that track Trust Score are updated only on direct withdrawals, and the reinvest function does not emit any warning that the earnings are being redirected to a pool with an abnormal Owner share. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “reward‑reinvestment bypass” or “trust‑score manipulation” bugs, where economic incentives are sidestepped by exploiting mismatched accounting rules. To remediate the problem the protocol should enforce a reasonable upper bound on the Owner% (and possibly the combined Owner% + User% for a pool) so that no pool can allocate almost all earnings to a single owner, and the Trust Score logic should be extended to treat earnings moved via reinvest as a withdrawal for reputation purposes. In short, the flaw lets a malicious pool owner withdraw all earnings without any penalty to their reputation, breaking the core promise of the system as a reputation‑standard platform.
summary:
There is a way for a malicious user to withdraw their earnings without affecting their trust score at all. It involves the following steps:
1. Use a second account to create a pool.
2. Configure the pool to have an Owner% of 99%.
3. When you want to withdraw earnings from the main account use the reinvestEarnings function to stake the earnings into the second account's pool.
4. Now since the pool has a 99% owner percentage, the second account's owner will receive 99% of the staked amount as earnings (dev team gets 1%).
5. Now withdraw the earnings from second account to main account's wallet.
6. This will not compromise the trust score at all, even though the pool owner has withdrawn all their earnings. See the proof of concept.
Impact: The issue breaks the core function of the protocol being a "reputation standard" and I have shown a simple way how a user can effectively withdraw their earnings without affecting the trust score. The "Trust Score" cannot be trusted if it can be manipulated like this by bad actors.
Likelihood: It is a very simple attack to execute and any user could easily do this with negligible cost, see the proof of concept.

title: Anyone can steal protocol's llido assets and ether balance using its distributive functions Submitted by 0xumarkhatab
content: The vulnerability consists of two publicly callable functions that allow unrestricted withdrawal of the protocol’s LLido reserves and native Ether balance. Because the functions do not verify the caller’s authority, any address can invoke them and cause the contract to transfer all available assets either directly to msg.sender or to an address supplied as a parameter. The first function, intended to distribute a revenue share to the development team, calls an internal claim routine, converts LLido tokens to Ether, and then executes a plain transfer of the contract’s entire Ether balance to the caller. The second function performs a series of internal accounting clean‑ups and distribution calls before optionally converting a portion of the wrapped token holdings to Ether and sending the full balance to a bounty address chosen by the caller. Since there is no require‑style access control, the logic proceeds regardless of who initiates the transaction. An attacker can therefore trigger these functions when the contract holds any amount of LLido‑derived Ether or raw Ether, resulting in a complete drain of funds. The impact is a total loss of user‑deposited assets, zeroing out the contract’s balance and breaking the protocol’s revenue‑sharing and bounty mechanisms. The issue manifests whenever a legitimate user or automated process calls the functions, because a front‑running MEV bot can observe the pending transaction, simulate the profit, and submit a competing transaction with higher gas fees, causing the legitimate call to fail while the attacker extracts the assets. All participants that rely on the protocol’s financial guarantees – developers, pool owners, bounty participants, and end‑users – are affected because the expected payouts never arrive and balances disappear from the UI, showing zero or missing funds. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that highlighted the absence of any access‑control modifiers on the external functions and the direct transfer of the contract’s balance without checks. It can be hard to notice because the functions appear to perform legitimate accounting work and the transfers succeed silently, making the loss observable only after the balance is unexpectedly empty. The proper remediation is to introduce strict authorization checks (e.g., only the designated governance or a specific role may call these functions) and to validate that any address supplied as a parameter is authorized, thereby preventing arbitrary callers from draining assets. This class of bug is an unauthenticated external call or unrestricted withdrawal vulnerability that violates the fundamental accounting assumption that only privileged entities can move protocol funds.

title: A malicious user can prevent vote creation at almost no cost Submitted by b0g0
content: A malicious staker can prevent the creation of a reputation challenge vote in the GOAT protocol by exploiting the way the contract determines the amount of wstETH that the attacker has locked. The vulnerability originates from a check that reads the contract's current wstETH balance (aEthValue) directly from storage and compares it with the defender's earnings that the challenger wants to freeze (dEthValue). Because the balance is taken from the contract address itself, an attacker can front‑run the createVote transaction, send a small amount of wstETH to the Controller contract so that the observed aEthValue becomes larger than the defender's dEthValue, and cause the require statement to revert. After the revert the attacker immediately calls the earningWithdraw function, which unwraps the temporarily deposited wstETH and transfers it back to the attacker, leaving only the gas cost of two transactions. From a user’s perspective the attempt to create a vote fails with the error message "aEthValue invalid", no vote is recorded, and the expected frozen earnings on the defender never appear. The impact is a denial‑of‑service on the reputation‑challenge mechanism: legitimate stakers are unable to challenge other stakers, the protocol’s governance and trust model are weakened, and the attacker can disrupt the normal accounting of frozen earnings without spending any significant funds. The condition for exploitation is that the attacker can send wstETH to the Controller contract in the same block (or just before) the victim’s createVote call and then withdraw it immediately afterwards. All stakers who rely on the ability to open a vote are affected, as are any downstream contracts that assume the challenge will be created. The issue was discovered during a manual audit and reproduced with a Foundry fork test that simulated the front‑run and withdrawal sequence. It is hard to notice because the revert looks like a normal validation failure, yet the underlying cause is an external balance manipulation that is not part of the contract’s internal state logic. The recommended mitigation is to stop deriving aEthValue from the contract’s balance. Instead, the attacker’s locked amount should be supplied as an explicit function argument that is validated against the amount transferred via a safe transferFrom call, or the contract should lock the required wstETH before performing the check, ensuring that external balance changes cannot influence the validation. By making the locked amount immutable to external transfers, the protocol regains its intended accounting guarantees and prevents the cheap denial‑of‑service attack.

title: The swapexactinputsinglehop function in the llido library consistently fails Submitted by merlin, also found by 0xrex, zigtur, deth, hals, Rotciv Egaf, 0xRizwan, Spearmint, ast3ros, smbv19192323, 0xblackskull, Said and 0xluckyy
content: The vulnerability originates from a missing deadline parameter in the LLido library function swapExactInputSingleHop, which builds an ISwapRouter.ExactInputSingleParams struct without supplying a value for the deadline field. In Uniswap V3's router, the exactInputSingle function is guarded by a checkDeadline modifier that requires the current block timestamp to be less than or equal to the supplied deadline; if the deadline is zero (the default value when omitted), the condition fails and the transaction reverts with the generic error message "Transaction too old". This logical omission propagates to every higher‑level controller function that relies on the swap, such as ethStake, earningPulls, lockWithdraw, and earningWithdraw. When a user initiates a stake or withdrawal, the contract attempts to perform the token swap, the router rejects the call, and the whole operation aborts. From the user’s perspective the UI may show that a stake or withdrawal was submitted but the balance remains unchanged, or that a refund amount is zero, leading to confusion and the impression that the protocol is broken or possibly malicious. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the controller’s flow, where the auditor noticed that the deadline line in the params struct was commented out and that calls consistently reverted with the deadline error. Because the revert message does not reference the missing field directly, the problem can be hard to spot; developers may attribute the failure to network congestion or gas limits instead of a contract‑level logic error. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition: no user can successfully execute staking, withdrawing, or any operation that depends on the swap, effectively freezing funds that are already in the contract. No funds are transferred out of the contract, so there is no direct theft vector, but the protocol’s core functionality is unusable until the bug is fixed. The appropriate remediation is to pass a realistic deadline value—typically block.timestamp plus a reasonable buffer—when constructing the ExactInputSingleParams, or to redesign the library to accept a deadline argument from callers. This class of bug falls under missing‑parameter validation or deadline misconfiguration, where a required time‑bound check is bypassed, causing systematic transaction failures and breaking business logic that assumes successful token swaps.

title: During voting the attacker's refund is vulnerable to a sandwich attack Submitted by Spearmint, also found by PENGUN, 0xRajkumar, Bauer, zigtur, hals, Bauchibred and Tripathi
content: The vulnerability resides in the refund routine of the voting contract, where the contract attempts to convert a calculated amount of wrapped stETH (wstETH) back to native ETH in order to pay the attacker after a vote is finalized. The core issue is that the contract performs this conversion through a Uniswap swap without any slippage or price‑impact checks, effectively trusting the market price at the exact moment of execution. Because the swap is executed inside the same transaction that finalizes the vote, a malicious participant can intervene with a flash‑loan‑driven price manipulation, commonly known as a sandwich attack. The attacker first identifies a vote that has reached quorum but has not yet been finalized, then waits until the voting period ends. At that moment they borrow a large amount of capital, swap wstETH for WETH to artificially inflate the WETH price, and immediately trigger the contract’s _tryFinalize function. When the contract executes the refund, it sells the attacker’s wstETH at the inflated price, receiving far fewer WETH (and consequently less ETH) than the theoretical amount. The contract then forwards the reduced ETH balance to the attacker, while the malicious user can reverse the price distortion and profit from the difference, effectively stealing from the intended refund recipient. From a user’s perspective the refund transaction appears to succeed – the contract sends ETH – but the amount received is unexpectedly low or even zero, contradicting the expectation that the refund should equal the original deposit minus the win value. This discrepancy is hard to notice because there is no explicit verification of the swap outcome; the contract merely checks that it has a non‑zero balance before sending it. The bug belongs to the class of price‑manipulation or sandwich attacks caused by unchecked external swaps. It violates the protocol’s accounting assumptions that refunds are deterministic and fully recoverable. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the finalization logic and identified the missing slippage protection. To remediate the problem the contract should enforce a maximum acceptable slippage on the wstETH‑to‑WETH conversion, use a trusted price oracle, or defer the refund until after the price impact window has passed, thereby ensuring that the amount sent to the attacker matches the intended refund calculation.

title: Premature unlocking of goat tokens upon transfer of lock Submitted by Vijay, also found by etherhood and Haxatron
content: Vester.sol contains a function transferLock that allows the contract admin to move an existing token lock from one investor address to another. The function copies the lock parameters but fails to copy or reset the startedAt timestamp for the destination lock. Because startedAt remains zero for the new holder, the restDuration calculation treats the lock as already fully elapsed: pastTime = block.timestamp - 0 equals the current time, which is always greater than the lock duration, so the function returns zero remaining time. Consequently, when the Unlock function is called, the entire locked amount is considered vested and can be withdrawn immediately, bypassing the intended vesting schedule. This bug can be triggered by any admin who invokes transferLock, effectively allowing premature unlocking of any investor’s Goat tokens. The impact is that investors lose the protection of the vesting schedule, potentially leading to sudden token dumps, distortion of tokenomics, and loss of trust in the protocol. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the vesting logic, where the missing assignment of startedAt was noted. It is subtle because the transferLock function appears to only reassign ownership, and the timestamp field is not part of the public interface, so the premature release may not be obvious in normal operation. The vulnerability belongs to the class of vesting‑schedule bypass bugs caused by incorrect handling of time‑based state during ownership transfer. To remediate, the transferLock implementation should set lockData.startedAt to the current block.timestamp (or preserve the original start time) for the recipient, ensuring that the restDuration calculation reflects the correct remaining vesting period. After fixing, the Unlock function will correctly enforce the remaining duration before releasing tokens.

title: A user calling controller::dctstake can bypass tax by ﬁrst transferring the tokens to be staked in a separate transaction
content: The vulnerability is a tax‑avoidance flaw in the controller contract’s dctStake function. The function is intended to apply a 1 % tax on the amount of DCT tokens a user stakes, but the tax calculation relies solely on the amount parameter supplied to dctStake. Because the contract does not verify that the amount of tokens actually transferred to the contract matches this parameter, a malicious user can first transfer the desired stake amount directly to the controller in a separate transaction and then invoke dctStake with a zero amount. The contract then moves the previously transferred tokens to the locker without applying the tax, effectively bypassing the fee. This can be exploited by any participant who can call the controller, and it results in the protocol losing the expected tax revenue, breaking the tokenomics assumptions that a 1 % fee is always collected on stakes. The issue occurs whenever a user separates the token transfer from the staking call and supplies a zero amount to dctStake, which the contract treats as a valid stake request. It was discovered through a targeted unit test that performed the two‑step transfer and observed that the locker balance matched the full transferred amount, confirming that no tax was deducted. The bug is subtle because the contract’s external interface appears to accept a legitimate stake amount, and the zero‑amount call does not raise an error, making the fee omission easy to miss during casual testing. To remediate, the contract should base the tax calculation on the original intended stake amount, enforce that the transferred token balance equals this amount, and reject calls where the supplied amount does not reflect the actual tokens received. Conceptually, this belongs to the class of “incorrect input validation” or “fee‑calculation bypass” bugs where economic parameters are derived from untrusted caller‑provided values rather than on‑chain state. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after staking, the expected 1 % deduction never appears; the locker shows the full transferred balance, contradicting the expectation that a small portion would be taken as tax. This discrepancy can lead to unfair advantage for attackers and erosion of protocol revenue if left unaddressed.
summary: A user calling controller::dctstake can bypass tax by ﬁrst transferring the tokens to be staked in a separate transaction

title: When stake eth in earningreinvest, the reduction of maxearning may not work Submitted by cccz
content: The vulnerability originates from an incorrect ordering of state updates in the earningReinvest workflow of the protocol. When a user stakes ETH earnings through earningReinvest, the function first reads the current maxEarning value for the caller, calculates a reduction proportional to the amount being reinvested and the effective lock duration, and writes the reduced value back to the earnings contract. The intention of this reduction is to preserve financial stability by limiting the maximum future earnings a user can claim. However, immediately after this reduction the function invokes earningWithdraw, which internally calls shareCommission. The shareCommission routine updates the shared amount (_sharedA) and, if the shared amount exceeds the stored maxEarning, it calls _updateMaxEarning to raise maxEarning to the new shared total. Because shareCommission runs after the manual reduction, it overwrites the reduced maxEarning with a larger value derived from the commission calculation. Consequently, the intended reduction is effectively cancelled. This flaw manifests when a user calls earningReinvest with ETH, supplies an amount equal to or close to their current maxEarning, and uses the maximum allowed lock duration. Under these conditions the protocol records a temporary maxEarning of zero, but the subsequent withdraw restores it to a value higher than zero (for example 1090 in the illustrated scenario). The restored maxEarning is then used in the staking logic to compute the poolOwner’s score (fs), leading to an unexpectedly low score (e.g., 0.1) and an inaccurate representation of the pool’s health. From a user perspective the symptoms are subtle: the UI may show that the reinvestment succeeded, but the poolOwner’s reputation or reward multiplier drops dramatically without an obvious cause, and the accounting numbers no longer match the expected financial model. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by Spearbit, who noticed that the maxEarning reduction appeared to have no lasting effect. It is hard to detect because the contract does not emit explicit events for the intermediate reduction, and the final state after the withdraw looks plausible, masking the logical inconsistency. The bug belongs to the class of state‑invalidation or ordering bugs where a later internal call unintentionally reverts a prior state change. To remediate the problem the reduction of maxEarning must be performed after the withdraw (or the withdraw must be modified not to adjust maxEarning), ensuring that the final stored maxEarning reflects the intended lower bound. This change restores the accounting invariants, prevents unintended score reductions, and preserves the protocol’s financial stability guarantees.

title: _recalep2pdbalance should be called before p2udtoken.burn/mint, not after Submitted by cccz
content: The vulnerability is an ordering flaw in the reward distribution logic of a staking protocol that separates two token types: a pool‑share token (p2UDtoken) and a global reward token (eP2PDToken). The contract is supposed to distribute accumulated GOAT mining rewards to each pool based on the users' p2UDtoken balances before those balances are changed. In the current implementation, when a user stakes ETH, the contract first mints additional p2UDtoken to increase the user’s share, and only afterwards calls the internal function that recalculates and distributes the eP2PDToken rewards. Because the reward calculation uses the updated p2UDtoken total supply and the user’s new balance, the global reward pool is allocated as if the user already owned the larger share. Consequently, the user receives a proportion of the global reward that is higher than the proportion of power they actually contributed at the moment the reward was earned. This mis‑allocation can be observed when a user’s reward amount jumps from, for example, 50 % of the pool’s reward to 60 % after a single stake, even though the global reward pool has not changed. The impact is that the pool’s reward balance is drained faster than intended, other participants receive less than their fair share, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions about proportional distribution are violated. The bug manifests whenever p2UDtoken.mint or p2UDtoken.burn is executed before the distributor’s claim function is invoked, i.e., during staking, unstaking, or lock‑withdraw operations. It affects all participants in the affected pools, the protocol’s overall reward economics, and any downstream contracts that rely on correct reward accounting. The issue was discovered during a security audit by Spearbit, who noted that the reward distribution hook (_beforeTokenTransfer) is called before balance updates, but the higher‑level staking flow calls mint first and only later triggers the reward recalculation, breaking the intended order. The problem is subtle because the contract does emit reward events and the balances appear consistent on a per‑transaction basis; only a careful analysis of the sequence of state changes reveals the over‑allocation. To remediate, the protocol should pull (claim and distribute) the pending GOAT rewards before any p2UDtoken mint or burn operation, ensuring that the reward calculation always uses the pre‑action balances. This change restores the invariant that rewards are allocated based on the share of power held at the time of distribution, preventing users from receiving more than their entitled portion and preserving the integrity of the pool’s reward accounting.

title: When _dp2pdtoken.athbalance() is increased, the power of almost all pools becomes stale Submitted by cccz
content: The vulnerability is a stale‑state bug in the calculation of a pool's booster factor, which is used to determine the pool's voting power and reward share. The booster is defined as 1 plus the ratio of a pool's own _dP2PDToken balance to the highest _dP2PDToken balance observed across all pools (the athBalance). The contract recomputes the booster only when a specific pool performs a staking or withdrawal operation, calling the internal function _reCalBooster. When another pool increases its token balance and thereby raises the global athBalance, the stored booster values of all other pools are not automatically updated. Consequently, those pools continue to use an outdated, higher booster value that was calculated against the previous, lower athBalance. This mismatch can be exploited by an attacker who deposits a large amount of tokens into any pool, causing the athBalance to rise. Because other pools' boosters remain inflated, they receive a larger share of the protocol’s reward distribution than they are entitled to, effectively siphoning rewards away from honest participants. The impact is incorrect reward allocation, potential loss of funds for the protocol, and unfair advantage for the attacker. The issue manifests whenever the maximum token balance across pools changes – i.e., when any pool’s balance exceeds the prior athBalance – and persists until the affected pools trigger a stake or withdraw action that forces a recalculation. All pool participants, the protocol’s accounting logic, and any downstream token holders are affected because the accounting assumptions that rewards are proportional to current power are violated. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that examined the relationship between athBalance and booster updates and noticed that the booster is only refreshed on per‑pool actions, not on global state changes. It is hard to notice from a user interface because balances appear correct while reward payouts are subtly skewed, and there is no explicit error flag. The proper fix is to ensure that any change to athBalance triggers a recomputation of the booster for every pool, either by iterating over all pools or by exposing a public function that anyone can call to recalculate a specific pool’s booster and power after athBalance changes. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of stale‑cache or out‑of‑sync state vulnerabilities, where a dependent value is not refreshed after its source variable changes, leading to incorrect business logic execution.

title: When the poolowner gets shared earnings, the power of that pool becomes stale Submitted by cccz
content: The vulnerability is a stale‑state accounting bug in the pool power calculation. The pool’s power relies on a financial‑stability factor (fs) defined as the ratio of the pool’s current ETH earnings to its historical maximum ETH earnings. The contract recomputes fs in the internal function _reCalFs, which is invoked only during staking and withdrawal operations. When the pool owner receives shared commission through the public shareCommission function, both the current earnings balance and the recorded maximum earnings may increase, but _reCalFs is not called. Consequently the stored fs value remains at its old ratio, causing the pool’s power to be outdated (stale). This stale value is later used in reward distribution, so the pool receives a lower share of rewards than it is entitled to, leading to under‑payment of participants and an inaccurate ranking of pools. The issue manifests whenever a pool owner’s earnings are increased by the commission‑sharing mechanism without a subsequent explicit fs recalculation. It affects all participants that rely on the pool’s power for reward allocation, including delegators and the protocol’s overall fairness guarantees. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that traced the flow of earnings updates and noticed that the fs update hook was missing after shareCommission execution. It can be hard to notice because balances appear correct on‑chain and the contract emits the expected commission events, yet the hidden power metric does not reflect the new balance, producing subtle reward mismatches that only become evident over multiple epochs. The root cause is a logical omission: the state‑changing path of shareCommission does not trigger the accounting routine that maintains the invariant fs = earnings / maxEarnings. To remediate, the contract should expose a public or external function that recomputes fs for any pool and invoke it after shared earnings are credited, or integrate the fs recalculation directly into shareCommission so that the financial‑stability factor is always consistent with the latest earnings. This correction restores the intended accounting relationship and ensures that reward distribution matches the actual economic contribution of each pool.

title: Missing access control on update() function in Earning.sol opens up many attack vectors Submitted by Spearmint, also found by 0xRajkumar, nmirchev8, sashik-eth, ladboy233 and Charles
content: The vulnerability is an unauthorized access control omission in the update function of the Earning contract. Because the function lacks the onlyAdmin modifier, any address can invoke it. The root cause is that the contract does not restrict who can call update, which is intended to be an admin‑only operation that records earnings derived from staking activity. An attacker, typically a pool owner, can call update after sending wstETH directly to the contract, causing the internal ETH_Earning variable to be increased artificially. By doing so the attacker can withdraw the inflated earnings, reset their Fs (trust score factor), and later redeposit the same amount to restore the earnings without suffering the intended penalty for withdrawing a large portion of rewards. This manipulation breaks the protocol’s reputation model, which assumes that a pool owner’s trust score decreases when a majority of earnings are withdrawn and recovers only slowly through additional staking or mining rewards. The exploit can be performed at any time because the function is publicly callable; no special conditions are required beyond possessing the ability to send tokens to the contract. All pool owners and any external user are affected because the trust scores displayed to delegators become unreliable, and the system’s guarantee of honest reputation is compromised. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the intended access restrictions with the actual function visibility. It is hard to notice because the contract still updates balances correctly, so normal operation appears functional, while the hidden path for arbitrary earnings inflation does not generate explicit errors. The fix is to enforce proper access control, for example by adding the onlyAdmin modifier to the update function, ensuring that only authorized administrators can modify earnings. In generic terms this is a classic missing‑access‑control bug that permits unauthorized state changes, leading to reward manipulation, inflated balances, and a broken trust‑score calculation.
summary:
The update() function in Earning.sol is callable by anyone as it is lacking the onlyAdmin modifier.

This allows poolOwner's to directly send in wsteth to the Earning.sol contract and call the update() function to increase their ETH_Earning. A poolOwner's ETH_Earning normally increase by users staking in their pool and the poolOwner getting a % of the stake. It does not make sense to allow poolOwners to update their earnings by depositing into it.

The fact that a poolOwner can easily withdraw their ETH_Earning (drop their Fs) then come back later and deposit it back in directly (increasing it back to normal) defeats the purpose of the system that measures trustworthiness based on "not withdrawing majority of earnings".

Normally to recover the trust score poolOwners would need more people to stake in their pool and/or sit and wait to collect more mining reward to make up the earnings. Both of these take significantly longer and thus until the earnings recover the poolOwner would have a lowered Fs and therefore lower Trust Score since Fs is proportional to Trust score. This period of lower Trust Score is meant to be the punishment for withdrawing the majority of earnings.

Impact: The issue breaks the core function of the protocol being a "reputation standard" AND I have shown ways how malicious users can manipulate their earnings to dodge the reputation penalty.

Likelihood: These attacks are quite simple to execute. The core protocol functionality of being a reputation standard is broken as the key metric for trustworthiness can be manipulated by bad actors.

title: The pool owner can manipulate users to steal all of their stake amounts by using code edge case Submitted by 0xRajkumar
content:
The vulnerability is a configuration‑code collision in the staking pool contract. The contract builds a numeric identifier called poolConfigCode_ by multiplying the owner’s fee percentage (ownerPercent_) by a constant DEMI (10000) and adding the user’s fee percentage (userPercent_). Because this is a simple linear combination, two distinct pairs of percentages can produce the same identifier. For example, (ownerPercent=1, userPercent=0) and (ownerPercent=0, userPercent=10000) both yield the code 10000. The contract uses this identifier to verify that the pool configuration has not been altered after the transaction is created, assuming that a matching code guarantees unchanged percentages. The root cause is the lack of a collision‑resistant encoding; the identifier does not uniquely bind the two percentage values.

An attacker who controls the pool owner can exploit the collision by first creating a pool with a benign configuration (ownerPercent=1, userPercent=0) to attract users. While users are staking, the owner monitors pending transactions and front‑runs a second transaction that re‑configures the pool with the colliding configuration (ownerPercent=0, userPercent=10000). Because the poolConfigCode_ remains identical, the contract’s validation logic accepts the new configuration as unchanged. The altered percentages redirect the reward distribution: the owner’s share becomes 100 % of the minted p2UDtoken supply, while the user’s share becomes 0. Consequently, users who expected to earn tokens receive none, and the value of their staked Geth is effectively transferred to the owner’s distributor address. From the user’s point of view the balance of earned tokens stays at zero, the UI shows no reward, and the staked amount appears to have vanished.

The attack succeeds only when the pool is not locked in a default‑only mode (inDefaultOnlyMode is false) and when the owner is willing to act maliciously. It also requires the ability to submit a transaction that is mined before the user’s staking transaction, which is realistic for a well‑funded owner running a front‑running bot. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the validation logic and identified the arithmetic collision.

Because the code comparison is performed on a value that can be duplicated, the problem is subtle and may not be obvious during testing; the contract appears to reject any change to the configuration, yet the underlying percentages can be swapped without changing the identifier. The bug belongs to the class of “identifier collision” or “non‑unique hash” vulnerabilities, where a simplistic encoding is used to represent a set of parameters.

To remediate the issue the contract should generate the configuration identifier using a cryptographic hash such as keccak256 over the full set of parameters (ownerPercent, userPercent, and any other relevant fields). A hash function makes collisions computationally infeasible, ensuring that any change to the percentages results in a different identifier and will be rejected by the validation logic. Additionally, the contract could enforce immutability of the percentages after pool creation or require explicit owner consent for any re‑configuration, further reducing the attack surface.
summary:
poolConfigCode_ is used to validate that users staking in the pool have the same code as when transaction was created, and the owner has not changed it, providing protection that ownerPercent and userPercent have not changed. However, there is an edge case where different configurations can have the same code. Let's see how the code is generated:

```solidity
ownerPercent_ * LPercentage.DEMI + userPercent_
```

Here the DEMI is 10000. We can actually find two different ownerPercent and userPercent inputs that have the same code:

- First example:
  - ownerPercent = 1
  - userPercent = 0
  - code = 1*10000 + 0 = 10000

- Second example:
  - ownerPercent = 0
  - userPercent = 10000
  - code = 0*10000 + 10000 = 10000

We can also validate the sum because of 1 and 0, and the sum of 0 and 10000 is actually valid:
```solidity
function validatePercent(uint percent_) internal pure {
    // 100% == DEMI == 10000
    require(percent_ <= DEMI, "invalid percent");
}
```

We are assuming two things:
1. Pool owner is actually having bad intention and he want to take advantage of this edge cases.
2. inDefaultOnlyMode is false.

Both are possible.

Now let's see how the owner can take advantage of it.
1. First, they will need to create a pool by staking some Geth and earning some p2UDtoken.
2. As inDefaultOnlyMode is false, he will set ownerPercent = 1 and userPercent = 0 to attract users.
3. He will run a bot that will constantly monitor transactions and will frontrun with configPool ownerPercent = 0 and userPercent = 10000.
4. As the code will be the same, user funds will be transferred to pool.ethDistributor, and since p2UDtoken will have all the supply, he will earn all the Geth. Users will not earn any p2UDtoken tokens.

title: Attacker can take advantage of multiplier when there's only one second left, allowing them to fraudulently gain voting power Submitted by 0xRajkumar
content: The contract contains a logic flaw in the calculation of staking power that allows an attacker to obtain an outsized amount of voting power by staking a large amount of tokens for an extremely short remaining lock duration. The function that mints staking power checks only that the remaining duration (rd) of an existing lock is greater than zero when the new lock time (lockTime_) is zero, but it does not enforce a minimum remaining duration. Because the multiplier used to compute voting power is based on the sum of the new lock time and the remaining duration, an attacker can wait until the existing lock has only one second left, then call the staking function with lockTime_ set to zero. The multiplier for a one‑second remaining duration is still relatively high (approximately 0.88), so the attacker receives a large amount of minted power for a negligible amount of time. The attacker can then use this inflated power to vote on governance proposals and earn reward tokens, after which they withdraw the staked tokens using a forced‑withdraw flag that incurs only a small penalty for the one‑second early exit. If the reward earned from the vote exceeds the penalty and any loan fee, the attacker profits, effectively buying voting influence for a fraction of the cost. This vulnerability manifests only when there is an existing lock with a very small remaining duration and the contract permits staking with lockTime_ equal to zero. Any user who can obtain a short‑term loan of tokens can exploit the bug, compromising the integrity of the governance process and allowing disproportionate reward extraction. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that noticed the missing duration check in calMintStakingPower. It is hard to notice because the require statement appears to protect against unlocking already expired locks, yet it does not guard against the edge case of a near‑expired lock, and the multiplier formula seems reasonable for normal durations. The bug belongs to the class of “insufficient input validation leading to economic manipulation” and violates the protocol’s assumption that voting power is proportional to the amount and length of a lock. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are unexpected spikes in voting weight when staking a token amount for only a second, and the ability to withdraw almost immediately with only a tiny loss. The contract should enforce that the remaining duration used in the multiplier calculation is above a safe threshold (for example, greater than one week) or redesign the multiplier to depend solely on the new lock time, thereby preventing the exploitation of near‑expired locks.

title: Multiple ways for reentrancy in InfinityPoolsPeriphery through both swapForwarders could lead to loss of funds Submitted by ktl, also found by yttriumzz, joicygiore, Nyxaris, ZC002 and Spearmint
content: The vulnerability is a reentrancy flaw in the InfinityPoolsPeriphery contract that can be triggered during a collateral swap operation (payment type COLLATERAL_SWAP). The periphery contract delegates the actual token swap to a configurable swap forwarder contract. Becausethe forwarder address and the calldata passed to it are supplied by the caller, an attacker can deploy a malicious forwarder (GeneralSwapForwarder or UniV2SwapForwarder) and encode a callback that is executed after the swap payment is made. Inside this callback the attacker calls a function that increases the periphery's internal token balance – in the proof‑of‑concept the attacker invokes depositERC20 – before the original payment callback finishes its accounting. The periphery therefore records the same tokens twice: once in the normal accounting path (line 129 of InfinityPoolsPeriphery.sol) and again when depositERC20 updates the collateral mapping (lines 173 or 180). This double accounting inflates the attacker’s collateral balance, allowing the attacker to later withdraw more tokens than were actually supplied, effectively draining funds from the pool. The bug occurs only when a user initiates a collateral swap and the contract’s addOrRemoveSwapForwarder function has previously whitelisted a forwarder that the attacker controls; the reentrancy is triggered by the external call to the forwarder’s swap function, which can be crafted to invoke any arbitrary function on the periphery. The issue was discovered during a security audit when the researchers built a test that added a malicious forwarder, performed a newLoan call with a crafted SwapInfo, and observed that the collateral and deposit values reported by the periphery were larger than expected after the callback. The problem is hard to notice because the contract’s external view functions report the inflated balances as if they were legitimate, and the reentrancy happens deep inside a callback where typical static analysis may not flag a state‑changing external call. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are unexpected changes in collateral: after a swap the user may see their collateral amount increase dramatically, or later notice that the pool’s total token reserves have shrunk without any obvious withdrawal. The bug violates the core accounting assumption that each token transfer is accounted exactly once, breaking the protocol’s financial integrity. To remediate the issue the contract should follow the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern, moving all state updates that affect collateral before any external call, and should protect the functions that modify balances with a reentrancy guard. Additionally, the periphery should restrict which forwarder contracts can be used, validate the calldata supplied to them, or at least ensure that callbacks cannot re‑enter functions that modify the same accounting variables. In short, the flaw is a classic reentrancy where attacker‑controlled external code re‑enters a balance‑updating function, leading to double accounting and potential loss of funds for honest participants.
summary:
In InfinityPoolsPeriphery.infinityPoolPaymentCallback() when there is a swap of type PaymentType.COLLATERAL_SWAP, a user can specify one of the two swapForwarders in src/periphery/swapForwarders to handle the swap with attacker controlled data.  
1. For src/periphery/swapForwarders/GeneralSwapForwarder.sol attacker controls both to and data.  
2. For src/periphery/swapForwarders/UniV2SwapForwarder.sol attacker controls path given to the uniswap router, an attacker can specify a path that goes through a malicious token he creates as uniswap pool creation is permissionless.  
Once the attacker has control flow, he pays for the swap and then calls any function that would increase the InfinityPoolsPeriphery's token balance (in the proof of concept the attacker calls InfinityPoolsPeriphery.depositERC20()), this will be double accounted in InfinityPoolsPeriphery.sol#L129 or the next line. This would be later added to the attacker's collateral in InfinityPoolsPeriphery.sol#L173 or InfinityPoolsPeriphery.sol#L180 (depending on token0 and token1).  
The below proof of concept is for the attack vector through GeneralSwapForwarder as the attack vector through UniV2SwapForwarder is too complex as it involves deploying a malicious token for reentrancy and creating a uniswap pool, but it should be very similar.

title: An attacker can re-enter the InfinityPool contract to double account when adding liquidity Submitted by Spearmint, also found by ktl, yttriumzz, zigtur, joicygiore, Boraicho, ZC002, ustas, anonymousjoe and J4X
content: The vulnerability is a re‑entrancy flaw in the InfinityPool contract that allows an attacker to double the amount of liquidity recorded for a position when adding liquidity through the pour() function. The pour() function accepts an optional data parameter; if data is supplied the contract makes an external call to the sender’s infinityPoolPaymentCallback. Inside this callback the attacker can invoke the pool’s doActions() function, which itself calls back into the pool to perform another pour operation. Because doActions() is not protected by a non‑reentrant guard, the second pour executes before the original pour finishes its balance checks. The contract records the token balances before the callback and expects the post‑callback balances to increase by the exact amounts supplied. By re‑entering and adding liquidity a second time, the attacker inflates the contract’s token balance, satisfies the balance checks, and later withdraws liquidity from both the original and the re‑entered positions. This results in the attacker receiving the original liquidity provider’s tokens in addition to their own, effectively stealing funds from honest LPs. The attack can be carried out whenever a user adds liquidity with a non‑empty data field, which triggers the callback, and the pool’s doActions() function lacks a re‑entrancy protection. The issue was discovered during a security audit and demonstrated with a concrete proof‑of‑concept test that shows the pool balance doubling after the malicious callback and the attacker’s final collection of the victim’s tokens. The bug is subtle because the balance verification logic only checks that the contract’s token balances have increased by at least the expected amounts, which the attacker can satisfy by manipulating the balance during the re‑entrancy. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are that after providing liquidity the pool’s token balance unexpectedly grows, and later the user’s deposited tokens disappear while the attacker’s balance increases. This violates the core accounting assumption that each liquidity addition corresponds to a one‑to‑one increase in pool balance and that withdrawals return only the provider’s own share. The recommended mitigation is to apply a nonReentrant modifier (or an equivalent re‑entrancy guard) to the doActions() function, or to restructure the code so that external calls are performed after all internal state updates, thereby preventing the contract from being re‑entered during the callback.

title: Incorrect WETH Deposit in wrapAndDepositWETH Function leads to loss of funds Submitted by Spearmint, also found by 0xRaz, lian886, ktl and Joshuajee
content: The InfinityPoolsPeriphery contract provides a helper called wrapAndDepositWETH that is intended to convert any leftover native Ether held by the periphery into Wrapped Ether (WETH) and immediately credit the caller’s deposit balance. The implementation calls IWETH9.deposit with the contract’s current Ether balance, which correctly creates WETH, but then it queries address(this).balance to determine how many WETH tokens were minted. Because the deposit call consumes the Ether, the balance of the contract is zero at that point, so the function records a deposit amount of zero. As a result the newly minted WETH remains in the periphery contract with no accounting entry, while the user receives no WETH credit. This bug can be triggered whenever a user adds liquidity with native Ether, leaves excess Ether in the periphery, and subsequently invokes wrapAndDepositWETH. From the user’s perspective the transaction succeeds, but the expected refund or deposit of WETH never appears; the UI may show a zero WETH balance or a missing refund, and the user’s Ether appears to have vanished. The impact is a permanent loss of the wrapped amount because the contract does not provide a mechanism to withdraw the orphaned WETH, effectively locking the funds. The issue was discovered during a security audit and reproduced with a unit test that logged the periphery’s Ether balance before wrapping, the resulting WETH balance after the call, and the user’s deposit record, confirming that the user’s balance stayed at zero while the contract held the WETH. The bug is subtle because the function does not revert or emit an error; it silently records an incorrect amount, making it easy to overlook during manual testing. The vulnerability belongs to the class of accounting‑logic errors where a contract uses a post‑operation state variable to calculate a transfer amount, leading to a zero‑value transfer and locked assets. The proper fix is to capture the Ether balance in a local variable before calling the WETH deposit, then use that stored value both for the deposit call and for the subsequent ERC20 accounting, ensuring that the exact amount of newly minted WETH is credited to the user. Adding comprehensive unit tests for the wrapAndDepositWETH path would also help prevent regression.
summary:
The InfinityPoolsPeriphery contract implements a wrapAndDepositWETH function. The purpose of the function according to the code comments is as follows:
This function is to help user get back the leftover ETH at the end of a transactions. The wrapAndDepositWETH function correctly wraps Ether into WETH using IWETH9.deposit, but due to using address(this).balance after the deposit, the function will account 0 WETH instead of the deposited amount. This results in the user receiving 0 WETH despite their Ether being wrapped. This WETH remains permanently locked in the contract.

title: Insufficient access control in the batchActionsOnSwappers() function Submitted by Spearmint, also found by ZC002 and Saksham seth
content: The vulnerability is an authorization bypass in the batchActionsOnSwappers function of the InfinityPoolsPeriphery contract. The function is intended to allow an operator who has been granted permission over a specific NFT (or all NFTs of an owner) to perform actions such as reflow, unwind or newLoan on that NFT. However, the implementation only verifies that the caller is approved for the first tokenId supplied in the batch and then assumes the same approval applies to every subsequent tokenId, checking only that the caller is the owner of those tokens. Because ERC‑721 defines an operator as someone approved for all tokenIds of an owner, the correct check must be performed for each tokenId individually using isApprovedForAll or the standard _isApprovedOrOwner logic. The root cause is a faulty loop that skips the per‑token approval verification after the first element. An attacker can exploit this by obtaining approval for a single NFT from a victim and then calling batchActionsOnSwappers with a list that includes many other tokenIds owned by the same victim. The attacker can invoke reflow, unwind, or any other swapper action on all of the victim’s positions, effectively taking control of collateral, forcing unwanted rebalances, or draining funds. The impact is that the victim’s positions may be altered without consent, leading to loss of collateral, unexpected token transfers, or disruption of the protocol’s accounting. This condition occurs whenever a batch operation is executed with more than one tokenId and the caller has operator rights for only the first ID. All NFT owners who rely on the per‑token approval model are affected, as are the protocol’s overall security guarantees and any users’ funds locked in those positions. The issue was discovered during a security audit and reproduced with a concrete proof‑of‑concept test that demonstrated an approved operator manipulating unrelated positions. The bug is subtle because the function name suggests a batch operation and developers may assume that a single approval check suffices for the whole batch, making the missing per‑token verification easy to overlook. To remediate, the contract should iterate over each tokenId in the batch and verify that the caller is either the owner or an approved operator for that specific tokenId, using the ERC‑721 isApprovedForAll or _isApprovedOrOwner checks for every element. This ensures that only authorized parties can act on each individual position and restores the intended access control model.
summary:
The docs clearly state under the permissions subheading the following:
InfinityPoolsPeriphery ensures that only authorized users can manipulate a position associated with a specific tokenId. Either the caller must be the NFT owner, or the owner must have assigned the caller as the NFT operator.
The definition for an NFT operator according to ERC-721 is as follows:
The operator can manage all NFTs of the owner.
The NFT operator is someone that has been granted approval over ALL tokenIds of the owner. The issue is that in the batchActionsOnSwappers() function, it only checks if the msg.sender is approved over the first tokenId in the list. For all subsequent tokenIds it simply checks that the owner is the same even if they are not approved to the msg.sender.
This opens up the following attack vector:
1. Alice opens 10 swapper positions.
2. Alice approves bob over position 1.
3. Bob now calls reflow, unwind etc. on ALL of Alice's positions even though he is only approved for one of them.

title: Wrong reward distribution formula, YT holders can get more rewards for themselves by just collecting accrued YBT yield Submitted by Catowice
content: The vulnerability is a mis‑calculation in the reward distribution logic for Yield Tokens (YT) that allows a holder who claims the underlying Yield‑Bearing Token (YBT) early to receive the same proportional share of future rewards while also keeping the rewards generated by the claimed YBT. The root cause is that the contract computes each holder’s entitlement solely as YT balance divided by the total YT supply at the moment of claim, ignoring the fact that part of the YT value may already have been converted into claimed YBT that continues to accrue its own rewards. An attacker can exploit this by claiming their accrued YBT as soon as it becomes available, then waiting for the exchange rate to increase; the contract still treats the attacker’s YT balance as representing the same share of the total reward pool, so the attacker receives rewards for both the previously claimed YBT and the remaining YT share. This results in an unfair advantage: the early claimer receives more total rewards than entitled, while other YT holders receive fewer rewards and the overall reward pool distributes less than the intended amount, effectively causing “funds disappear” from the perspective of honest participants. The issue manifests whenever a YT holder performs a claim before the next exchange‑rate update, which is a normal operation in the protocol’s yield‑harvesting cycle. All users holding YT, the protocol’s reward accounting, and the overall token economics are affected because the accounting assumptions that rewards are split proportionally to current YT holdings are violated. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that compared two scenarios – one with no early claims and one with an early claim – and observed a discrepancy in total rewards distributed. It is hard to notice because the contract still distributes rewards and the formula appears reasonable at a glance; only a detailed balance‑sheet analysis reveals that the early claimer’s YBT continues to generate rewards that are double‑counted. The correct fix is to base reward shares on the amount of unclaimed YBT yield plus the YT value expressed as YT balance divided by the current exchange rate, i.e., the actual YBT amount that the YT represents, and to use the total YBT held by the protocol as the denominator. This ensures that once YBT is claimed, it no longer contributes to future reward shares, restoring fair distribution and preventing the double‑dip effect.
summary:
Impact Explanation:
• Users can get an unfair advantage in the reward distribution, by having the claimed YBT itself generates rewards all for themselves, and still having the same YT shares in relation to the total YT supply.
• All other YT holders will receive reduced rewards speed as a result due to the PT holding less YBTs.
Proof of concept (textual): We provide two scenarios for comparison. In each scenario we use the same setting:
• We start at exchange rate 1.
• We end at exchange rate 2.
• The YBT's interest and reward amount are constant: 50 reward tokens are distributed for every +1 exchange rate.
• Scenario 1: No one claims any yield:
– Let the initial exchange rate be 1. The PT pool holds 100 YBT tokens.
– Alice and Bob holds 50 YT tokens each, so each holds 50% of the YT supply.
– Exchange rate goes to 3. The 100 YBT is entitled to 100 reward tokens.
– The YTs are entitled to 66.6 YBT, and 100 reward tokens are distributed to YT holders. Since Alice and Bob hold 50% of the YT shares, they are entitled to 33.3 YBT and 50 reward tokens each.
• Scenario 2: Alice claims early:
– Let the initial exchange rate be 1. The PT pool holds 100 YBT tokens.
– Alice and Bob holds 50 YT tokens each, so each holds 50% of the YT supply.
– Exchange rate goes to 2. The 100 YBT is entitled to 50 reward tokens.
– The YTs are entitled to 50 YBT, and 50 reward tokens are distributed to YT holders.
* This amount is distributed 50/50 to YT holders. Alice and Bob are entitled to 25 YBT and 25 rewards each.
Alice claims at this point. The balances at this point are:
– Alice: 50 YT, 25 YBT, 25 reward.
* Unclaimed: 0 YBT, 0 reward.
– Bob: 50 YT, 0 YBT, 0 reward.
* Unclaimed: 25 YBT, 25 reward.
– PT holdings: 75 YBT, 25 reward.
We continue on reaching the exchange rate of 3:
– Exchange rate goes to 3. The 75 YBT left is entitled to 37.5 reward tokens.
– The YTs are entitled to 16.66 YBT, and 37.5 reward tokens are distributed to YT holders.
* This amount is distributed 50/50 to YT holders. Alice and Bob are entitled to 8.33 YBT and 18.75 rewards each.
At this point:
– Alice: 50 YT, 25 YBT, 25 reward.
* Unclaimed: 8.33 YBT, 18.75 reward.
– Bob: 50 YT, 0 YBT, 0 reward.
* Unclaimed: 33.33 YBT, 43.75 reward.
– PT holdings: 75 YBT, 62.5 reward.
Note the difference against the ﬁrst case. Bob is still entitled to 33.33 YBT, but only 43.75 rewards in total, instead of 50. Furthermore, the total claimable rewards are only 25 + 18.75 + 43.75 = 87.5, contrary to the 100 rewards earlier.
This is because the 25 claimed YBT by Alice also yields rewards. By taking away some of the YBT in the form of shares, Alice still has the same 50% shares of accrued reward, but also the same. In other words, Alice has less unclaimed YBT compared to others, but are still subject to the same rewards share.
– In fact, the 25 YBT claimed by Alice earlier has yielded the missing 12.5 rewards. Alice is entitled to 43.75 rewards from holding the YT, 12.5 rewards for claiming the interest YBT early and taking the rewards for herself, for a total of 43.75 + 12.5 = 56.25 rewards.

title: Ineffective slippage control Submitted by 99Crits
content: An insufficient slippage control flaw exists in the Lockbox V2 deposit instruction. The function accepts token_max_a and token_max_b and derives the amount of liquidity to request by converting token_max_a using the current on‑chain sqrt price of the pool. Because the calculation does not incorporate any slippage tolerance or a user‑provided liquidity target, an attacker who can temporarily move the pool price can cause the derived liquidity to be dramatically lower than the depositor expects. The attack proceeds by first buying a large amount of token B, which pushes the pool’s price down and reduces the sqrt_price_lower value used in the get_liquidity_from_token_a formula. When the victim’s deposit transaction is executed, the contract computes a smaller liquidity_amount based on the manipulated price, then calls Orca’s increase_liquidity with that reduced amount. The victim therefore receives far fewer LP shares than anticipated, often seeing a near‑zero increase in their position or a balance that appears unchanged. After the deposit, the attacker sells the previously bought token B back into the pool at the restored price, capturing a profit from the price swing.
