It was discovered during a manual security audit that highlighted the absence of any require(msg.sender == authorized) or similar guard. The problem is subtle because the function executes without reverting and appears to work normally, so unauthorized proposals may go unnoticed until the state diverges from expectations. To remediate, the contract should enforce a whitelist of proposer addresses or adopt a role‑based access control mechanism, rejecting any call from an unapproved sender before forwarding the proposal to the settlement contract. This restores the intended trust model where only designated entities can drive state updates, preserving accounting integrity and preventing funds from disappearing due to rogue proposals.

title: Inability to claim various protocol rewards due to missing implementation
content: The vulnerability consists of a missing reward‑claiming mechanism in the protocol’s core contracts. Because the contract that holds the underlying assets never invokes the claim functions provided by external reward controllers (such as claimAllRewards on the Aave RewardsController or allowClaimOnBehalf on the EigenLayer RewardsCoordinator), any incentive tokens that accrue to the protocol remain permanently unclaimed. The root cause is an incomplete integration: the code that should forward reward‑claim calls to the respective controllers was never written, leaving the wrapped rebasing token wrapper without any path to retrieve earned AAVE, ARB, OP, ZKSYNC, SNX or EigenLayer tokens. When the protocol accumulates rewards, the expected flow – reward accrual, claim, and redistribution or reinvestment – is broken, so the rewards are effectively locked inside the contract. An attacker does not need to actively exploit the contract; the mere existence of the missing function prevents legitimate participants from receiving their entitled incentives. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that balances displayed on dashboards do not increase after a reward period, users receive zero or no reward notifications, and the protocol’s total value appears lower than expected. The issue manifests whenever the protocol holds assets that are eligible for external incentive programs, which is a regular condition for many DeFi platforms. All participants who rely on the reward distribution – token holders, liquidity providers, and governance voters – are affected because they lose the additional yield that the incentives were meant to provide. The problem was discovered during a systematic audit that compared the protocol’s reward‑earning contracts against the documented reward‑claim interfaces of the integrated platforms. It can be hard to notice because the contracts compile and function correctly for core operations; the missing claim logic does not generate a revert or error, it simply results in silent omission of reward payouts. To remediate the issue the protocol should implement explicit calls to the external reward controllers for each supported incentive source, handle the returned token amounts, and then either reinvest them into the protocol, distribute them to eligible users, or allow authorized actors to withdraw them. Proper test coverage must be added to verify that rewards are correctly claimed, accounted for, and transferred according to the protocol’s economic model, thereby restoring the intended incentive flow and preventing future reward lockout bugs.
summary: The current implementation lacks mechanisms to claim various rewards that accrue to the protocol from different sources. This affects: • Aave Protocol Rewards: – Staked AAVE tokens rewards. – Chain-specific incentive campaign rewards (ARB, OP, ZKSYNC tokens). – Protocol integration specific incentives (e.g., SNX incentives for providing sUSD). – Other protocol-specific rewards. • Reserve Manager Contract Rewards: – EigenLayer rewards. Rewards accrue to the wrapped rebasing token wrapper contract as it holds the underlying funds. There is no implementation to call claimAllRewards or utilize allowClaimOnBehalf functions on the RewardsController contract for aave and RewardsCoordinator for eigenlayer Impact: • Accrued rewards become effectively locked in the protocol. • Loss of value for protocol participants who should benefit from these reward mechanisms. • Reduced protocol efficiency as incentive mechanisms cannot be fully utilized. • Potential compound effect as unclaimed rewards may also miss out on additional yield opportunities.

title: Insufficient slippage protection in mintlvlUSD
content: The vulnerability resides in the mintlvlUSD function of the LevelBaseReserveManager contract, where the parameter that should protect a user against slippage – the minimum lvlUSDAmount – is incorrectly calculated. Instead of reducing the originally expected mint amount by the allowed slippage, the code overwrites the minimum amount with the slippage value itself. This happens because the assignment `lvlUSDAmount = lvlUSDAmount.mulDiv(maxSlippageThresholdBasisPoints,MAX_BASIS_POINTS)` replaces the original expected amount rather than subtracting the slippage component. As a result, the minimum amount that the protocol promises to deliver can become negligibly small, effectively removing any slippage protection. An attacker or any caller providing collateral can therefore trigger a mint operation that succeeds while the receiver obtains far fewer lvlUSD tokens than anticipated, potentially receiving zero tokens for the supplied collateral. The impact is a direct loss of value for the collateral provider, breaking the economic assumption that the minted lvlUSD will be roughly proportional to the collateral and that the protocol will not mint at a severe discount. This condition occurs on every execution of mintlvlUSD while the maxSlippageThresholdBasisPoints variable is set (e.g., 5 basis points, representing 0.05%). The affected parties include any user who supplies collateral, the protocol’s liquidity pool, and downstream applications that rely on the minted lvlUSD amount. The issue was uncovered during a manual security audit performed by Spearbit, who noted that the slippage logic does not enforce a lower bound but instead lowers it. The bug can be hard to notice because the code appears to apply a slippage limit, yet it does not cause a revert or emit an obvious warning; the transaction completes and the user simply receives less than expected, which may be interpreted as normal market variation. To remediate the problem, the contract should compute the minimum acceptable mint amount by subtracting the slippage allowance from the original expected amount, for example `lvlUSDAmount -= lvlUSDAmount.mulDiv(maxSlippageThresholdBasisPoints,MAX_BASIS_POINTS)`, thereby restoring the intended protection. Conceptually, this belongs to the class of “incorrect slippage calculation” or “minimum‑output protection bypass” bugs, where a safety check is overwritten rather than enforced, leading to potential fund loss and accounting inconsistencies.

title: USDT cannot be withdrawn from AaveV3YieldManager
content: The vulnerability is that the withdraw function of AaveV3YieldManager attempts to transfer USDT using the standard IERC20.transfer interface, which expects a boolean return value. USDT, however, implements a non‑standard ERC20 where transfer does not return any value. Solidity therefore tries to decode a non‑existent return value, causing the call to revert. As a result, any user who calls withdraw with token address USDT experiences a transaction failure and receives no tokens, even though the preceding steps (wrapping, unwrapping, and Aave withdrawal) may have succeeded. The root cause is the reliance on the raw ERC20 interface instead of the SafeERC20 library that handles tokens with missing return values. The issue manifests only when the token argument is USDT (or any other token that does not follow the ERC20 spec) and the withdraw function is executed. Users, token holders, and the protocol are affected because funds become effectively locked in the contract, breaking the intended flow of depositing, earning interest, and withdrawing. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the withdraw implementation and compared token behaviours. It can be hard to notice because most popular tokens conform to the ERC20 standard and the code compiles without warnings; the revert only appears at runtime for the specific non‑standard token. The impact is high risk: users cannot retrieve their USDT, and the protocol must resort to manual unwrapping and off‑chain processes to return funds. To fix the issue, the contract should replace direct calls to IERC20.transfer (and similar functions) with the SafeERC20 library’s safeTransfer, safeTransferFrom, and safeApprove methods, or implement a low‑level call that does not expect a return value, thereby supporting non‑standard tokens. This class of bug is commonly referred to as non‑standard ERC20 handling or missing return value bug, which violates the accounting assumption that a token transfer either succeeds or fails based on a boolean flag. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a withdrawal request but the transaction reverts, leaving the balance unchanged or showing zero received, contrary to the expectation of receiving the requested USDT amount.

title: DoS due to not accepting native ETH transfer
content: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that occurs when a contract that manages deposits into an external staking vault or strategy receives native Ether transfers that it is not programmed to accept. The root cause is the absence of a receive or fallback function in the contract, which means any incoming Ether sent by the underlying vault or strategy triggers an automatic revert. This situation can be exploited when the external protocol distributes rewards or returns staked Ether in native form; the contract attempts to withdraw those funds, the Ether transfer fails, and the whole withdrawal transaction reverts. As a result, users who try to redeem their stake see their transaction fail, their balances appear unchanged, and the funds become effectively locked in the contract. The issue manifests only when the underlying vault or strategy is capable of sending native Ether back to the caller, which may happen intermittently depending on reward accrual or when the protocol redeems positions. All participants who interact with the staking interface – depositors, withdrawers, and the protocol’s reserve manager – are affected because the contract cannot complete the expected accounting flow. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that examined the contract’s external calls and noted that the transferEther helper assumes the contract can receive Ether, yet no payable fallback was present. It is subtle because the contract may work correctly for ERC‑20 rewards, leading testers to miss the failure mode unless they simulate an Ether‑based reward path. To remediate, the contract should implement a receive or fallback function that safely accepts Ether, preferably guarded by access control to prevent unintended transfers, or the protocol should explicitly document that it will never interact with vaults or strategies that send native Ether. By aligning the contract’s interface with the expected Ether flow, the denial‑of‑service condition is eliminated and users can reliably withdraw their funds without encountering unexpected reverts.
summary: When depositing into underlying staking protocol, which is either vault or strategy which delegates to operator. If strategy / vault supports native staking or accrues rewards in ETH then contract will revert when withdrawing from such strategy / vault because it doesn't implement receive or fallback function. The protocol correctly implements transferEther to remove the ETH out of contract once it is redeemed by reserve manager.

title: Lombard unstake functionality currently not working as expected
content: The vulnerability resides in the Lombard protocol's unstake validation routine, specifically the function that checks the outputs of a Bitcoin‑style unstake transaction. The validator enforces a strict equality between the sum of all output values and the sum of the input values (totalOut == totalIn). Because Bitcoin transactions must leave a difference between inputs and outputs to pay the miner fee, this equality leaves no room for any fee at all. As a result, any unstake request that includes a realistic miner fee is rejected by the validation step, causing the entire unstake flow to fail. The root cause is an overly strict condition introduced in a recent mitigation commit, which unintentionally removed the allowance for the fee margin. An attacker does not need to craft a special payload; simply submitting a normal unstake request triggers the rejection, leading to a denial‑of‑service condition where legitimate users cannot retrieve their BTC. The impact is that users see their unstake transaction remain pending or disappear from the mempool, their balances appear unchanged, and they receive no BTC back despite having initiated a withdrawal. No funds are permanently lost because the transaction never leaves the protocol, but the stuck UTXO remains in the mempool and cannot be confirmed until the validation logic is corrected. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the post‑mitigation code path and observed that the validator rejected all requests that included any fee. It is hard to notice because the transaction looks syntactically correct and the UI may simply show a pending state without an explicit error. To fix the problem, the validation should be relaxed to allow totalOut to be less than or equal to totalIn, ensuring that the difference can cover a reasonable miner fee, and the fee calculation should be explicitly verified rather than assuming zero. This class of bug is a fee‑validation mismatch common in cross‑chain bridges that handle Bitcoin‑style UTXO transactions, where the accounting assumptions of “inputs must equal outputs” conflict with the necessity of a miner fee, leading to refund calculation errors and funds appearing to disappear from the user’s perspective.
summary:
validateUnstakingOutputs is too strict and currently DOS the whole Lombard unstake functionality. A recent mitigation (commit-SHA 1fac8baea) seems to have broken Lombard unstake as a whole, as not allowing any room for the miner fee during the validation process of unstake MFA request, which should result in almost all the Lombard unstake request to be rejected (lombard_unstake.go#L28), assuming here that the proposer would be proposing "valid" request which include a miner fee. If this assumption would be wrong, that would also be an important negative impact (but no fund loss, once the issue is fixed those transactions can be re-submitted), as transaction would be broadcasted to BTC, but since those doesn't include miner fee would likely remain stuck in the mempool indefinitely, preventing the user to get his BTC back. A BTC UTXO is structured as follow:
• Input(s) to spent (which point to an output from a previous UTXO).
• Output(s) (which need to cover fully this Input(s) - fee for miner).
– Output (Part of the input).
– Change (The remaining part minus fees).
So the sums of outputs values must be less then total of inputs, as what remains is the miner fee, the cost to include this transaction in the block. In the current function, there is no room for the fees (if totalOut != totalIn; lombard_unstake.go#L108). Here is a typical example. Previous Transaction:
Output 0: 1 BTC to Address A
Output 1: 2 BTC to Address B
New Transaction:
If you want to spend Output 0 (1 BTC), you must use all of it:
- You can't just use 0.5 BTC from it
- If you only want to send 0.5 BTC to someone, you need to:
1. Use the entire 1 BTC input
2. Create two outputs:
- 0.5 BTC to recipient
- ~0.499 BTC back to yourself as change (minus transaction fee)

title: `Minter.sol#startInflation`
content: The contract contains an initialization flaw in its inflation mechanism. Two state variables, lastEvent and lastInflationDecay, are meant to track when inflation started and when the last decay period occurred, but they are never set in the constructor. As a result, both variables default to zero. The function startInflation is supposed to be called by governance to set these timestamps, yet the public executeInflationRateUpdate function does not verify that they have been initialized before using them. If an attacker calls executeInflationRateUpdate before startInflation, the subtraction (block.timestamp - lastEvent) treats lastEvent as zero, causing the calculation totalAvailableToNow += currentTotalInflation * (block.timestamp - 0) to inflate the available mintable supply by roughly currentTotalInflation multiplied by the full elapsed time since blockchain inception (approximately 52 years). Simultaneously, the check for the decay period sees that block.timestamp >= lastInflationDecay + _INFLATION_DECAY_PERIOD is true because lastInflationDecay is also zero, immediately setting the initialPeriodEnded flag and applying decay logic that was intended only after a real inflation period. This mis‑calculation corrupts the accounting invariant that totalMintedToNow must never exceed totalAvailableToNow, allowing the _mint function to bypass the intended cap and mint arbitrarily large amounts of tokens. The impact is that any user or malicious actor can trigger an uncontrolled increase in the token supply, effectively draining the economic model, breaking the sponsor’s emission goals, and compromising the protocol’s monetary policy. The vulnerability manifests when executeInflationRateUpdate is invoked before the governance‑only startInflation call, a scenario that may not be obvious because the function appears permission‑less and successful execution returns true. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when the logic of startInflation and the lack of initialization checks were examined. It can be hard to notice because the variables hold the default zero value, which passes basic type checks, and the overflow of totalAvailableToNow may not be immediately visible in UI components that only display current balances. To remediate, the contract should either initialize lastEvent and lastInflationDecay to the deployment timestamp in the constructor or add explicit require statements in executeInflationRateUpdate that reject calls while the timestamps are still zero. Ensuring that inflation cannot be started without proper governance approval restores the intended accounting guarantees and prevents the token supply from ballooning unexpectedly.

title: Total Supply is not guaranteed and is not deterministic.
content: The vulnerability lies in the way the token contract calculates the cumulative amount of tokens that can be minted (the total supply) across inflation periods. The contract updates the available supply by applying the current inflation rate to the elapsed time since the last update, but it performs this calculation before checking whether the elapsed time has crossed the predefined inflation decay boundary. Consequently, if the function that triggers the inflation update, _executeInflationRateUpdate, is not called for a duration that spans the decay point, the contract will apply the old (higher) inflation rate to the entire interval, including the portion that should have been subject to a reduced rate. This timing dependence makes the total supply effectively random and nondeterministic, allowing the supply to exceed the advertised hard cap of 268,435,456 tokens. An attacker can deliberately postpone calls to the update function, creating a window in which the contract mints more tokens than intended, thereby inflating the token supply and diluting the value for all holders. The impact is a breach of the protocol’s economic invariant, potential loss of confidence in the token, and the possibility for malicious actors to capture the surplus tokens. The issue was uncovered during a code audit that compared the tokenomics documentation, which guarantees a fixed cap, with the actual minting logic in the Minter contract. Because the overshoot only manifests after a period of inactivity, it may not be evident from ordinary UI observations, making it hard to detect without thorough testing of edge‑case timing scenarios. To remediate, the inflation update logic must first determine whether the elapsed time crosses the decay period and then apply the appropriate rate for each sub‑interval, ensuring that the calculated mint amount never exceeds the theoretical maximum defined by the cap. In essence, the contract must enforce a deterministic, bounded inflation schedule that respects the decay boundary before minting any new tokens, thereby restoring the guarantee of a fixed total supply.
summary: The actual total supply of the token is random and depends on when `_executeInflationRateUpdate` is executed.

title: DSPC.set can bypass the cfg.step constraint by including the same id multiple times in the updates array and continuously increase the bps
content: The vulnerability resides in the function that allows a privileged actor (called a bud) to modify protocol rates such as the stability fee for collateral. The contract stores a configuration object that defines a minimum, maximum and a step value for each rate. The step value is intended to limit how much a rate can increase in a single transaction. The implementation calculates the absolute difference between the current rate and the new rate for each entry in an array of updates and checks that this delta does not exceed the step limit. However, the function processes the updates sequentially and updates the stored rate after each iteration. If the same identifier appears multiple times in the updates array, each iteration treats the rate that was just written as the old rate for the next iteration. By repeating the same id, an attacker can add the step amount repeatedly within a single call, effectively bypassing the step constraint and raising the rate to its maximum allowed value in one transaction. This bypass can be triggered whenever a bud supplies a crafted updates array containing duplicate ids, which is not prevented by the current logic. The impact is that the stability fee or other rates can be arbitrarily increased, breaking the economic assumptions of the protocol, potentially leading to excessive fees for users, loss of collateral value, or destabilisation of the system. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the loop logic and the delta check. It is subtle because each individual delta passes the step check, so the contract appears to enforce the limit on a per‑iteration basis, masking the cumulative effect. To remediate, the function should enforce uniqueness of identifiers in the updates array, for example by sorting the array and rejecting duplicates, or by computing the delta against the original rate before any modifications. Conceptually the bug belongs to the class of “batch update with mutable state leading to cumulative constraint bypass” and violates the intended accounting rule that a rate may only move by a bounded step per transaction. From a user perspective the symptom is a sudden, unexpected increase in fees or a missing refund, where the user expects a modest change but observes a large jump or a zero balance where funds should remain.

title: Morpho rewards can not be claimed due to missing claimRewardsForToken implementation
content: The vulnerability is a reward‑claiming dead‑end in the MorphoVaultRouter integration with ERC4626Kandel. The router contract, which supplies capital to a Morpho vault, automatically receives MORPHO token rewards on behalf of its depositors. A dedicated function claimRewardsForToken, guarded by onlyAdmin, is required to forward those rewards to a chosen receiver. When a router is instantiated for a specific Kandel, the router’s admin role is transferred to the ERC4626Kandel contract so that the Kandel can later withdraw assets via adminWithdrawTokens. However, ERC4626Kandel does not expose any mechanism to invoke claimRewardsForToken on the router, and the router does not automatically forward rewards during adminWithdrawTokens. Consequently, MORPHO rewards accumulate in the router but cannot be claimed or transferred, effectively becoming inaccessible. This situation occurs whenever a Morpho vault is used through the router‑Kandel pattern and rewards have been generated; it affects every depositor who expects to receive MORPHO incentives, as well as the protocol’s economic model that relies on those incentives. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the admin flow and reward distribution logic. It is subtle because the primary asset balances appear correct, the router still holds the underlying tokens, and the missing reward token transfer is not reflected in standard balance checks or UI displays, leading users to believe rewards are being handled correctly. The impact is a loss of reward tokens for users, a breach of the promised incentive scheme, and potential erosion of trust in the protocol’s accounting. To remediate, the design should be altered so that the Kandel contract can call claimRewardsForToken, either by adding a public wrapper in the router that forwards the call, by extending ERC4626Kandel with a specific claimRewardsForToken interface, or by integrating the reward claim into the existing adminWithdrawTokens flow, thereby ensuring that accrued MORPHO tokens can be transferred to the intended recipients.

title: Morpho rewards cannot be claimed due to ﬂawed integration with rewards distributor
content: The vulnerability resides in the claimRewardsForToken function of the MorphoVaultRouter contract, which is designed to let an admin retrieve token rewards from Morpho's rewards distributor and forward them to a chosen receiver. Instead of passing the router’s own address to the distributor’s claim method, the function incorrectly supplies msg.sender – the admin’s external account – as the first argument. Because the distributor sends the reward tokens to the address supplied, the tokens are transferred to the admin rather than to the router contract. Consequently, when the router subsequently attempts to transfer the received tokens to the receiver, it holds no balance and the transfer inevitably fails. This logical mismatch causes the entire claiming workflow to break, leaving rewards permanently locked in the distributor or effectively inaccessible through the router. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the integration flow between the router and the external rewards contract; the flaw is subtle because the initial external call succeeds and does not revert, giving the impression that the claim succeeded, while the final token transfer silently fails. The impact is that administrators cannot claim accrued rewards, leading to missing incentive payouts, potential loss of confidence from token holders, and a deviation from the protocol’s economic assumptions that rewards are claimable and distributable. The bug belongs to the class of incorrect caller‑address integration errors, where a contract assumes it will be the recipient of an external call but passes a different address, breaking accounting logic. From a user perspective the UI may show a successful claim transaction but the expected token balance remains unchanged, creating confusion and the perception that “my rewards disappeared” or “the refund is missing”. The condition under which it occurs is any invocation of claimRewardsForToken by the admin; no special state is required. To remediate, the function should be modified to pass address(this) – the router’s own address – to the distributor’s claim method, ensuring the router receives the tokens before forwarding them. Additional integration tests should be added to verify that the router’s balance increases after the claim and that the subsequent transfer succeeds, thereby restoring the intended reward flow and aligning the contract with its business logic.
summary: The claimRewardsForToken function of the MorphoVaultRouter contract is intended for the admin to claim token rewards from Morpho's rewards distributor. To do this, the function ﬁrst intends to call IMorphoRewardDistributor::claim and then transfer the received tokens to a receiver account passed as parameter by the admin. However, the ﬁrst argument passed to claim is msg.sender - that is, the admin's account. As a consequence, the MorphoVaultRouter never receives the tokens from the distributor, and the token transfer after the call to claim will inevitably fail. Thus breaking the whole claiming process.

title: DoSing the launch ﬁnalization process
content: An attacker can invoke the UniswapV3Pool.initialize() function before the official launch sequence has completed. The pool contract expects initialization to occur only during creation, but the function is publicly accessible and does not enforce a launch‑completed flag. By calling initialize early, the contract transitions to an initialized state while required launch parameters are still unset. Subsequent calls to the finalization routine, which normally completes the launch and enables trading, fail because the contract believes it is already initialized. This creates a denial‑of‑service condition: users attempting to add liquidity or trade after the intended launch find the pool stuck in an unfinalized state, receiving errors or zero‑output transactions. The impact is that the protocol cannot be launched, funds that would be deposited during the launch remain locked, and the overall project timeline is delayed. The issue appears only when an external actor interacts with the pool before the launch manager calls the finalization step; in normal operation the function would be called automatically during pool creation, so the bug can be missed during testing if the launch flow is not exercised with adversarial calls. The vulnerability belongs to the class of improper state‑transition checks leading to a denial‑of‑service. It was discovered during a manual audit of the pool lifecycle code, where the auditor noticed that initialize() lacks a guard against being called after deployment but before finalization. Because the function does not revert or emit a clear error when called out of order, the failure may be subtle: the UI simply shows that the pool is not ready, without indicating that an attacker blocked the process. The recommended fix is to restrict initialize() to the constructor or to a privileged role and to add a check that the launch has not yet been finalized before allowing the call. In conceptual terms, the contract should enforce a single‑use initialization that cannot be triggered by arbitrary callers after deployment. Users would otherwise expect the pool to become tradeable after the launch, but instead they see no liquidity, transactions revert, or the pool appears permanently inactive. This violates the business logic that the launch finalization must be the sole gatekeeper for enabling trading.
summary: The UniswapV3Pool.initialize() function can be called before the launch is complete, DOS-ing ﬁnalization process.

title: MarginalV1LBLiquidityReceiver.mintMarginalV1() refunds to treasury, instead of liquidity owner
content: The vulnerability resides in the liquidity‑receiver contract that mints Marginal V1 liquidity on behalf of a user. After the minting process the contract attempts to return any leftover token amounts to a hard‑coded treasury address. This logic is incorrect because the contract does not keep track of the original liquidity provider – the address that deployed the LB pool and supplied the initial liquidity – and therefore refunds the residual balances to the treasury instead of the rightful owner. The root cause is a design flaw in the refund routine: it unconditionally calls the internal pay function with params.treasuryAddress as the recipient, ignoring the caller’s identity. Exploitation is straightforward: whenever the minting operation leaves unused token balances – a situation that frequently occurs due to price slippage, delayed deposits to Uniswap V3, partial swaps, or delayed finalisation of the LB pool – those tokens are automatically transferred to the treasury. From the user’s perspective the expected behaviour is that any excess tokens are returned to their wallet, but the UI shows no refund and the user’s balance is reduced by the amount that silently disappears. The impact can be severe because the leftover amounts may be significant, effectively stealing funds from liquidity providers and breaking the accounting assumptions of the protocol that all unspent assets belong to the provider. The issue manifests only after a successful call to mintMarginalV1 when the contract’s internal token balances are non‑zero; it does not affect cases where the mint consumes the exact supplied amounts. The bug was discovered during a manual audit by Spearbit, which identified the mismatch between the intended refund destination and the actual hard‑coded address. It can be hard to notice because the refund amount varies per transaction and the protocol does not emit a specific event indicating the beneficiary of the refund, so users may not realize that the treasury is receiving their leftover tokens. To remediate the problem the contract should record the address that supplied the initial liquidity and use that address as the recipient of any residual balances, or make the refund destination configurable and validated against the caller. In generic terms this is a “wrong beneficiary” or “misdirected refund” class of bug, where residual funds are sent to an unintended party, violating business logic that expects refunds to be returned to the liquidity provider and causing unexpected loss of assets.

title: Unbalanced or single-sided liquidity leaves tokens locked in MarginalV1LBLiquidityReceiver
content: The vulnerability is an unbalanced or single‑sided liquidity lock in the MarginalV1LBLiquidityReceiver contract. The contract’s mintUniswapV3 function deposits token0 and token1 to a Uniswap V3 pool at the pool’s current price and expects the two amounts to be balanced according to that price. Because the LB pool may be finalized at a price that differs from the Uniswap pool price at the moment of deposit, the amounts supplied can become unbalanced. Uniswap only accepts the smaller of the two amounts and silently leaves the excess token in the receiver contract. The receiver does not provide any method to refund or withdraw the leftover amount, and the subsequent mintMarginalV1 function also requires a balanced liquidity, so the excess cannot be moved forward. In a rarer case, if the LB pool is finalized with only one side of liquidity (no swaps performed), the entire deposit is single‑sided. Uniswap rejects single‑sided liquidity at the current price, causing mintUniswapV3 to revert and leaving the whole deposit locked. Because the contract lacks a refund mechanism, the tokens remain trapped for the duration of the lock period, and users see their balances reduced or zero without receiving the expected liquidity tokens or refunds. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the flow of funds from LB finalization to Uniswap and Marginal. It is hard to notice because the contract does not emit an explicit error for the leftover tokens and the UI may simply show a successful transaction while the funds are silently retained. The impact is that users may lose part or all of their deposited liquidity, violating the protocol’s accounting assumption that deposited amounts are always fully transferable. The vulnerability manifests when there is a price mismatch between the LB pool and the Uniswap pool, or when liquidity is provided only on one side. The affected parties are liquidity providers who interact with the MarginalV1LBLiquidityReceiver, the protocol that relies on those funds, and any downstream contracts that expect the liquidity to be available. The recommended fix is to add a refund path, such as a freeReserves function that can be called after the lock duration to transfer any remaining token balances back to a designated refund address, and to allow withdrawals before liquidity is supplied to Uniswap.
summary:
After MarginalV1LBLiquidityReceiver.mintUniswapV3() was called, some amount of tokens can be left locked in the contract without the ability to be withdrawn or deposited to Marginal.  
The MarginalV1LBLiquidityReceiver.mintUniswapV3() function is used to deposit funds to Uniswap V3 after a pool was finalized. The funds are deposited as pool liquidity at the current price of the pool, which requires that the deposited amounts are balanced, relative to the price.  
Since there can be a delay between the LB pool finalization and depositing to Uniswap V3, the current price in the Uniswap pool can be different from the final price of the LB pool. As a result, the amounts deposited to Uniswap will be balanced differently, resulting in a leftover of one of the amounts (Uniswap takes the smaller liquidity when minting, thus not asking for more tokens). It won't be possible to deposit this leftover to Marginal via the MarginalV1LBLiquidityReceiver.mintMarginalV1(), because it also requires a balanced liquidity.  
However, the receiver contract doesn't allow to refund of tokens left after providing liquidity to Uniswap. Thus the tokens will be left in the contract.  
In an alternative and rare scenario, when an LB pool is finalized with the full initial liquidity (i.e. no swaps were made in the contract), the entire liquidity in the receiver contract is single-sided. Since Uniswap doesn't allow adding single-sided liquidity at the current price, the call to MarginalV1LBLiquidityReceiver.mintUniswapV3() will fail, leaving the entire liquidity locked in the contract.  
MarginalV1LBLiquidityReceiver.mintMarginalV1() will also fail because it requires that liquidity was previously added to Uniswap.  
Impact: There's a risk of locking all or a portion of liquidity in the receiver contract.  
Likelihood: The vulnerability impacts the normal flow of events in the protocol, but not all scenarios. E.g. when there's no price difference between the LB and the Uniswap pools, there will be no leftover token amounts.

title: Borrower can choose Loan migration arguments or perform a noop migration
content: The vulnerability resides in the loan contract’s upgrade mechanism, where the function that upgrades the loan implementation accepts an arbitrary calldata argument supplied by the caller. Because the borrower is granted permission to invoke this upgrade function, they can provide migration arguments that are interpreted by the migrator contract. By crafting these arguments, the borrower can manipulate the migration logic to their advantage, for example by inflating the principal amount, reducing the interest rate, or by encoding a payload that bypasses the migrator’s fallback function entirely, resulting in a no‑operation upgrade while the proxy points to a newer implementation. This flaw originates from the lack of validation or restriction on the arguments passed to the upgrade routine, effectively allowing any caller with upgrade rights to dictate the behaviour of the migration code. An attacker can exploit the issue by calling upgrade with a specially encoded arguments_ value that either triggers a favourable state change in the loan storage or simply skips the migration logic, leaving the loan in its original state but under a newer contract version. The impact is a breach of the protocol’s financial assumptions: lenders may receive less interest or see the loan balance altered without consent, while the borrower gains an unintended advantage. The condition for exploitation is that the borrower (or any entity with the same upgrade role) initiates the upgrade; the vulnerability is hidden because the upgrade interface appears standard and the arguments field is often ignored by front‑ends, making the malicious payload invisible to users. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the upgrade path and identified that the arguments parameter was not constrained. Detecting the problem can be difficult because the contract’s state after a no‑op upgrade looks identical to a legitimate upgrade, and the financial effects may only become apparent later when loan accounting mismatches occur. To remediate, the upgrade function should be refactored to remove the arguments parameter entirely, with migration data hard‑coded in the migrator contract, and the permission to call upgrade should be limited to a trusted security admin rather than the borrower, thereby restoring the intended business logic and preventing unauthorized manipulation of loan terms.
summary: The MapleLoan.upgrade(uint256 toVersion_, bytes calldata arguments_) function can be called by the borrower (and the security admin). The borrower can choose migration arguments for future migrations that are in their favor, like increasing principal or decreasing interest rates. The borrower can also skip running the migration code but still upgrade to the latest loan version by encoding arguments that would not call the fallback function on the migrator. For example, for the old MapleLoanV4Migrator they could have chosen arguments that call encodeArguments(0), skipping the migration code in the fallback (the proxy would still point to the new implementation code).

title: Specified amount is not updated after clamping, causing a lock of funds
content: The vulnerability is an over‑payment and fund‑locking bug that occurs in the swap function of a concentrated‑liquidity pool when the target price is clamped to the lower or upper bound. The contract computes a next price using a price‑clamping routine, which may reduce the amount of input tokens required to reach the target. However, the code does not recalculate the amountSpecified after this clamping step, so the swap proceeds with the original input amount even though a smaller amount would have been sufficient. As a result the trader pays more tokens than needed, and when the pool is later finalized the withdrawal logic only accounts for the amount required to move the price within the range. The surplus tokens remain in the contract because there is no mechanism to withdraw them, effectively locking a portion of user funds. This issue manifests when a swap reaches the final price and the price calculation is clamped; users see that they sent the full amount they specified but receive a smaller amount out, and after pool finalization the contract balance contains unexpected leftover tokens. The bug was discovered through functional tests that compared the emitted swap amounts with the computed clamped price, revealing a mismatch. It can be hard to notice because the swap still succeeds and the pool appears to function, but the hidden surplus is only observable by inspecting contract balances after finalization. The problem belongs to the class of accounting‑logic errors where post‑condition values are not updated after a constraint adjustment, leading to incorrect fund accounting. To fix the issue the swap routine should recompute the required input amount after price clamping and use those adjusted values for the transfer and for the finalization calculations, ensuring that the amount withdrawn matches the amount actually paid.

title: Token transfer logic is incorrect for some tokens
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect handling of ERC20 token transfers that affects tokens which deviate from the standard specification, such as USDT and fee‑on‑transfer tokens. The contract assumes that the transfer and transferFrom functions return a boolean value indicating success and that the amount transferred equals the amount requested. This assumption is the root cause: the code uses a plain require statement on the return value of token.transferFrom, which fails for tokens that do not return a bool, and it does not verify the actual token balance after the call, which fails for tokens that deduct a fee on transfer. An attacker can exploit this by supplying a token that either does not return a value or that charges a transfer fee. In the first case the require statement reverts, preventing the function from executing and effectively locking the user out of purchasing tickets or depositing liquidity. In the second case the contract receives less than the expected amount, yet it records the full amount as deposited. This mismatch leads to accounting errors: the contract’s internal accounting believes it holds more tokens than it actually does, causing later withdrawals or prize payouts to be short‑changed or to fail entirely. From a user’s perspective the transaction appears successful – the UI shows a confirmation and the user’s balance is deducted – but later the user may see a zero or reduced balance when trying to claim a refund or withdraw winnings, creating the impression that “funds disappeared” or that “my refund is missing”. The issue manifests whenever the contract calls token.transfer or token.transferFrom, notably in the purchaseTickets and lpDeposit functions, and also when the contract attempts to send tokens out. All participants who interact with the contract – regular users, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the contract’s token accounting becomes unreliable. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract’s transfer logic against the OpenZeppelin SafeERC20 library and identified the missing safety checks. It is hard to notice because the transaction does not revert and no explicit error is emitted; the discrepancy only becomes visible later when balances are queried or withdrawals fail. To remediate the issue the contract should replace raw transfer calls with OpenZeppelin’s safeTransfer and safeTransferFrom, which correctly handle tokens that do not return a boolean. Additionally, for fee‑on‑transfer tokens the contract should record the pre‑transfer balance, perform the transfer, then compute the actual received amount by checking the post‑transfer balance and compare it against the expected value, rejecting the operation if the amounts differ. The contract should also enforce that only tokens adhering to the ERC20 specification without rebasing or unconventional fee mechanisms are accepted, or otherwise implement token‑specific handling logic. By applying these safeguards the contract will maintain accurate accounting, prevent unexpected reverts, and ensure that users receive the correct amounts when depositing, purchasing tickets, or withdrawing funds.
summary:
The current transfer funds logic has multiple issues:
1. Tokens like USDT does not return a bool value on transfer/transferFrom function. This means below require check will fail.
```solidity
require(
    token.transferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), value),
    "ERC20: transfer failed"
);
```
2. In case of fee on transfer tokens, contract will actually receive lesser amount. Since contract code does not check if amount received is expected amount, contract will lack expected funds.

title: getOraclePrice is prone to manipulation
content: The vulnerability resides in the getOraclePrice function, which is intended to fetch the most recent price from a Velodrome liquidity pool. The implementation makes a faulty assumption: it treats any observation whose timestamp differs from the current block timestamp as trustworthy, returning the spot price and tick without performing additional validation. Velodrome pools only write price observations every fifteen seconds, meaning that an observation can be up to fifteen seconds stale. An attacker who can influence the pool price within that window can cause the contract to read a deliberately outdated observation, effectively feeding a manipulated price into downstream calculations such as APR, reward distribution, or collateral valuation. The exploit works by submitting a transaction that triggers getOraclePrice after the pool has recorded a price but before the next observation is written; the function sees a timestamp mismatch, skips further checks, and returns the stale, attacker‑controlled price. The impact is that users may receive incorrect pricing information, leading to over‑payment, under‑payment, or loss of funds when the contract settles trades, calculates rewards, or enforces liquidation thresholds. This condition occurs whenever the contract calls getOraclePrice within the fifteen‑second observation interval, which is common in time‑sensitive DeFi operations. All participants who rely on the price – traders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the business logic assumes price integrity. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the oracle integration logic and identified the missing freshness check. It can be hard to notice because the contract still returns a plausible price and the discrepancy may only manifest as occasional mismatches in expected rewards or unexpected slippage, which are often attributed to market volatility rather than a systematic bug. To remediate, the contract should only accept an observation as final after the pool’s fifteen‑second interval has elapsed, or it should explicitly verify that the observation timestamp is recent (for example, require that the current block timestamp exceeds the observation timestamp by at least fifteen seconds) before using the price. This aligns the oracle usage with the pool’s update cadence and restores confidence that the price cannot be deliberately stale, thereby preserving the intended accounting guarantees of the protocol.

title: avgBorrowRate can blow-up for small linearVariation
content: The vulnerability lies in the calculation of the average borrow rate (avgBorrowRate) used by the interest rate model. The contract computes avgBorrowRate by dividing the difference between the new borrow rate and the borrow rate after a jump (newBorrowRate‑borrowRateAfterJump) by a parameter called linearVariation. When linearVariation is a very small non‑zero value, the division operation amplifies the rounding errors that are inherent in the fixed‑point arithmetic library (MathLib). The library’s exponential approximation wExp(x) is accurate for small x only up to a term proportional to x, but the subsequent rounding adjustments (ε0, ε2, ε3, ε4) become dominant when the denominator is tiny. As a result, an error term E, which contains components such as –A·ε2 and 10^18·ε0·x, grows dramatically, causing the computed avgBorrowRate to deviate far from the mathematically expected value. In practice this means that for markets where linearVariation is close to zero – for example when the jump multiplier or variation multiplier produce only a slight change – the protocol may report an average borrow rate that is orders of magnitude higher or lower than it should be. An attacker who can influence the market parameters to keep linearVariation small can therefore manipulate the interest calculation: borrowers may be charged far less interest than intended, lenders receive less return, and the protocol’s accounting can become inconsistent, potentially leading to loss of funds or unfair profit extraction. The issue manifests only under the condition |linearVariation| < LN2_INT/2, a range that is easy to miss because the rates still appear plausible and the error is hidden inside rounding noise. It was discovered during a formal audit by Spearbit, who traced the mathematical derivation of the avgBorrowRate formula and identified the amplification of rounding errors. The bug is hard to notice because it does not cause outright reverts or obvious overflow; instead it subtly skews financial outcomes, which may only be observed as unexpected small differences in accrued interest or as a mismatch between expected and actual balances. To remediate the problem the calculation should avoid dividing by a small linearVariation. The recommended fix is to detect the small‑variation regime and compute avgBorrowRate with a mulDivDown expression that incorporates the linearVariation into the numerator (borrowRateAfterJump * (2*WAD + linearVariation) / (2*WAD)), thereby eliminating the division by a near‑zero value and reducing the error term. This change restores the intended linear relationship between rates and ensures that users receive the correct interest amounts, preserving protocol integrity and financial correctness.

title: Incorrect upper bound check in wExp(x) can produce an overflown result
content: The vulnerability resides in the exponential helper function wExp(x) which is intended to compute e^x for a fixed‑point input expressed with 18 decimals. The implementation protects against overflow by requiring the input x to be less than or equal to 177.44567822334599921 ether, a limit derived from the natural logarithm of 2^256‑1. However, because the function works with 18‑decimal fixed‑point numbers, the true safe upper bound is much lower – roughly 135.306 ether when the same scaling is applied. The root cause is an incorrect calculation of the maximum admissible exponent, which ignores the fixed‑point scaling factor and the second‑order Taylor approximation used internally. An attacker can exploit this by supplying an exponent value that is just above the real safe limit but still below the overly permissive 177‑ether check. When such a value is processed, the internal multiplication overflows the 256‑bit integer space, causing the result to wrap around to a much smaller number or to zero. From a user’s perspective the contract may return a dramatically smaller exponential value than expected, leading to zero or negligible interest, missing rewards, or incorrect pricing in downstream calculations. The impact can be severe because many financial primitives – such as interest rate calculations, bonding curves, or token minting formulas – rely on the correctness of wExp. If the function silently returns an incorrect value, funds may be allocated incorrectly, balances may appear unchanged, or the protocol could become under‑collateralised. The bug manifests only when the exponent approaches the upper region of the function’s domain; normal small inputs behave correctly, making the issue hard to notice during casual testing. The problem was discovered during a formal audit when the auditor performed a binary‑search test around the theoretical limit and observed that inputs like 135.999582271169154766 ether caused the output to collapse, while a slightly smaller input produced the correct large number. To remediate the issue the upper‑bound check must be tightened to a value that guarantees no overflow for the given fixed‑point representation, for example the conservative bound 196 * LN2 or the mathematically derived 135.306 ether. The new limit should be documented together with a proof that any input below it cannot cause overflow, and the function’s comments should explain the scaling considerations. By enforcing a correct bound, the exponential calculation will remain within the 256‑bit range, preserving the integrity of all downstream financial logic.

title: Withdrawal roots can be specifically crafted such that multiple withdrawals are possible
content: The vulnerability is a flawed Merkle‑proof verification routine that can be used to generate a valid root without correctly incorporating the leaf index. The function that reconstructs the Merkle root from a leaf, its index, the total number of leaves and a proof array ignores the leaf_idx when calculating the root. When the proof array is empty or the loop is skipped because leaves_len equals one, the routine simply returns the hash of the leaf itself, effectively treating any leaf as a valid root. This happens because the algorithm does not enforce that the supplied leaf position matches the path taken through the tree, and it does not assert that leaves_len is greater than leaf_idx. An attacker can therefore craft a withdrawal request with a deliberately empty or mismatched proof, causing the contract to accept the request as if the proof were correct. The impact is that the contract’s withdrawal logic, which relies on Merkle proofs to prove entitlement to funds, can be bypassed, allowing multiple or unauthorized withdrawals and resulting in loss of funds for honest participants. The issue manifests whenever a user attempts to withdraw using the vulnerable function, especially when the proof length is zero or when the leaf index is out of range. All parties that rely on the contract’s accounting – users, the protocol’s treasury, and any downstream services – are affected because the contract may release funds that should remain locked. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the proof‑verification loop and noticed that the leaf_idx variable is never used in the hash computation and that the final assertion only checks proof length, not the relationship between leaf_idx and leaves_len. The bug is subtle because the function still returns a hash that looks syntactically correct, so superficial testing that only checks for a non‑zero proof may miss the problem. To remediate, the implementation must incorporate the leaf index into the hash chaining logic, enforce that leaves_len is greater than leaf_idx, and reject empty proofs unless the tree truly contains a single leaf. In broader terms, this is a class of Merkle‑proof validation errors where the positional information of a leaf is omitted, leading to incorrect root reconstruction and potential unauthorized asset release. From a user’s perspective the contract may appear to accept a withdrawal request that should have failed, resulting in unexpected balance changes such as “my balance decreased twice” or “I received a refund even though I provided no proof”. The discrepancy between the expected proof‑based security check and the actual behavior violates the fundamental accounting assumption that only holders of a valid Merkle proof can claim funds.

title: Block finalization is immediate and permissionless
content: The vulnerability is an immediate and permissionless block finalization mechanism. After the operator proposes a new block, the contract permits any address to call the finalize_block function without any waiting period or validation step. The root cause is the absence of a challenge or validity‑proof phase that would normally allow validators to inspect the block contents, verify the correctness of the withdrawal root, and reject malformed or malicious data before the block is considered final. Because finalization can be triggered instantly, a malicious operator can embed a specially crafted withdrawal root that authorises the transfer of funds to an attacker. As soon as the block is proposed, an attacker (or any participant) can invoke finalize_block, causing the contract to execute the withdrawal logic based on the fraudulent root. This results in unauthorized fund movement, effectively allowing funds to disappear from the protocol treasury or from user balances. The issue manifests whenever a block is proposed; there is no conditional check on the caller’s role, no time‑based delay, and no proof‑of‑validity requirement, so the exploit can be performed in a single transaction after block proposal. All participants who rely on the protocol’s accounting – token holders, liquidity providers, and downstream applications – are affected because the protocol’s accounting assumptions (that withdrawals are only processed after consensus validation) are violated. The problem was discovered during a security audit that examined the block lifecycle and identified that the finalize_block entry point lacks any access control or challenge window. It can be hard to notice in normal operation because the UI may simply show a block being finalized instantly, giving the impression of normal progress, while the underlying state transition has already moved funds to an attacker. To remediate, the design should be changed to introduce a challenge period during which validators can submit a proof of block validity or raise objections, and only after this period should the block be allowed to finalize. This aligns the contract with standard finality models where consensus validation precedes state changes, preventing immediate malicious withdrawals.
summary: Once a block is proposed by the operator, which might malicious e.g. containing a specifically crafted withdrawal root, anyone can immediately invoke the finalize_block instruction to finalize it. Consequently, a malicious withdrawal can be performed immediately after proposing such a block.

title: TransferLib.transferFromERC721 doesn't support CryptoKitties, so a range of protocol oper- ations are unavailable for them
content: The vulnerability is an incompatibility in the TransferLib.transferFromERC721 helper function. The function assumes that every ERC721 token implements the standard safeTransferFrom(address,address,uint256) method and builds a low‑level call with that signature. CryptoKitties, however, implements only the older transferFrom(address,address,uint256) function and does not provide safeTransferFrom. When the library is used with a CryptoKitties contract address, the generated call targets a non‑existent function, the low‑level call returns false and the require statement reverts the transaction. This makes any protocol operation that relies on TransferLib—such as depositing a CryptoKitty into an NFTX vault, selling it through the router, adding liquidity with it, creating a vault via the zap, or swapping it in the marketplace router—unavailable for CryptoKitties owners. The root cause is a missing branch in the transfer helper that handles non‑standard ERC721 implementations. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the TransferLib source code, where the developer noticed the special‑case handling for CryptoPunks but no equivalent handling for CryptoKitties. Because the failure occurs only when the asset address matches the CryptoKitties contract, it can be easy to miss in testing if the test suite does not include that token. From a user’s perspective the transaction simply reverts with an error like 'transfer failed', the expected balance update never happens, and the user sees no change in their wallet or protocol position, contrary to the expectation that the deposit or sale would succeed. The bug belongs to the class of 'ERC721 interface incompatibility' or 'missing fallback for alternative transfer functions'. It violates the protocol’s business logic that any ERC721 token can be deposited, swapped, or used as liquidity, breaking accounting assumptions and preventing users from accessing the value of their CryptoKitties. The recommended remediation is to extend TransferLib.transferFromERC721 with a CryptoKitties‑specific branch that encodes a call to transferFrom(address,address,uint256) instead of safeTransferFrom, mirroring the implementation already present in NFTXVaultUpgradeableV3.

title: NFT sale price is calculated as WETH spent on vTokens purchase and is overstated this way in royalty deductions
content: The vulnerability is an accounting mis‑calculation in the NFT marketplace router that overestimates the sale price when deducting royalties. The contract swaps the user’s incoming WETH for vTokens, records the amount of WETH that left the contract (wethSpent) and later uses this value as the effective sale price for royalty calculation. However, the swap can produce more vTokens than are required to redeem the requested NFTs because the vToken balance is uncapped. The excess vTokens remain in the contract but are not reflected in the sale price, yet the royalty logic still assumes the entire wethSpent contributed to the purchase. Consequently, the _deductRoyalty and _deductRoyalty1155 functions compute a royalty amount that is higher than what the actual transaction warrants. An attacker does not need to act actively; any user who purchases NFTs through the router will automatically lose the over‑deducted royalty amount. The impact is a systematic loss of funds for buyers, who receive less net proceeds than expected, and the protocol may appear to charge excessive royalties. This condition occurs whenever the swap generates surplus vTokens – a situation that can be arbitrarily large because the vToken amount is not capped by the number of NFTs being bought. The bug was discovered during a manual audit of the MarketplaceUniversalRouterZap contract, where the auditor noticed that wethSpent is derived from the total WETH swapped rather than the portion actually spent on the NFTs. The issue is subtle because the contract emits a Buy event that includes the inflated royalty amount, making the discrepancy easy to overlook in normal UI displays. To fix the problem, the router should compute the exact amount of WETH that corresponds to the vTokens actually used for the NFT redemption, for example by measuring the vToken amount required for the purchase and scaling wethSpent accordingly before calling the royalty deduction routine. This aligns the royalty calculation with the true sale price, restores correct accounting, and prevents users from losing funds due to an overstated royalty deduction.

title: When creating the vault, the forceTimelock parameter of inventoryStaking.deposit should be false.
content: The vulnerability is a logical error in the vault creation flow where the contract forces a timelock on deposits to the inventory staking module even when the minting operation does not generate a mint fee. The root cause is that the code unconditionally passes the boolean flag forceTimelock as true to inventoryStaking.deposit, assuming that every mint of vTokens requires a fee‑neutralising lock period. In reality, the very first mint of a newly created vault does not charge a mint fee because there is no associated pool and the time‑weighted average price returns zero. Consequently, the deposit does not need to be locked, but the contract still enforces a timelock, preventing the user from withdrawing the deposited vTokens for the configured lock duration. An attacker does not need to actively exploit the bug; the issue manifests automatically for any user who creates a vault via Factory.createVault, mints vTokens, and then attempts to deposit those vTokens into inventoryStaking. The impact is that legitimate users are unexpectedly locked out of their funds, losing the ability to move liquidity or respond to market changes during the lock period, which can be especially damaging in fast‑moving DeFi environments. The condition occurs only on the initial vault creation when mintFee is zero, making it a subtle edge‑case that can be missed by standard testing that focuses on later deposits where fees are present. The affected parties are end‑users who provide NFTs as liquidity and the protocol itself, because the unnecessary lock reduces usability and may deter participation. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit performed by Spearbit, who noted that the forceTimelock flag is set to true without checking whether a fee actually applies. It is hard to notice because the timelock flag is a simple boolean and the code path is only exercised in the first‑mint scenario, which many test suites do not cover. To remediate, the contract should conditionally set forceTimelock to false whenever the deposited vToken amount is above the minimum inventory liquidity and the mint fee is known to be zero, as shown in the recommended code change. This adjustment aligns the timelock enforcement with the business rule that only fee‑charged mints require a lock, restoring the expected behavior where users receive their deposited tokens immediately after the transaction.
summary:
When creating the Vault, the user can provide NFTs to add liquidity to the Pool or deposit to inventoryStaking. The problem here is that adding liquidity does not require timelock, while depositing to inventoryStaking forces timelock.

        tickLower: tickLower,
        tickUpper: tickUpper,
        fee: params.liquidityParams.fee,
        sqrtPriceX96: currentSqrtPriceX96,
        vTokenMin: params.liquidityParams.vTokenMin,
        wethMin: params.liquidityParams.wethMin,
        deadline: params.liquidityParams.deadline,
        forceTimelock: false
    })
);
...
inventoryStaking.deposit(
    vaultId,
    vTokensBalance,
    msg.sender,
    "",
    false,
    true // forceTimelock as we minted the vTokens with NFTs
Since the ﬁrst mint of the Vault doesn't charge mintFee (because there is no corresponding pool and getTwapX96 returns 0), the initial add liquidity or deposit to inventoryStaking does not require timelock to neutralize mintFee. And if the user creates the Vault via Factory.createVault and then mints VToken, mintFee will not be charged, and later deposits to inventoryStaking also does not need to be locked.
This would cause the user to have to lock for some time when depositing to inventoryStaking, which is considered high risk due to the high likelihood and medium impact.

title: Fee calculation in _sendDeposits is done for overall msg.value instead of bridged value
content: The vulnerability is an over‑charging fee bug in the OmniXMultisender contract's _sendDeposits function. The contract is supposed to charge a flat 1 % fee on the amount of native token that is being bridged via LayerZero's airdrop mechanism. However, the implementation mistakenly computes the fee on the entire msg.value that the caller sends, which includes not only the bridged token amount but also the LayerZero verification network (DVN) fee and the relayer fee required for the airdrop. Because the fee calculation does not separate these components, the contract deducts a percentage that is larger than the intended 1 % of the bridged amount. This can be exploited whenever a user calls sendDeposits with any non‑zero overhead; the contract will automatically retain the excess portion as fee, effectively stealing funds from the user. The impact is that users receive fewer bridged tokens than expected, see their balance reduced unexpectedly, and may be charged several percent more than advertised. The condition for the bug to manifest is any deposit transaction where msg.value > bridged amount, which is the normal case because LayerZero requires additional fees. All users of the service, including those who hold discount‑eligible NFTs, are affected because the discount is applied to the already inflated fee. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit performed by Spearbit, who noted that the fee formula uses msg.value directly instead of the variable representing the bridged token amount. The problem is subtle because the contract does not emit a separate event for the fee breakdown, and the UI only displays the advertised 1 % rate, making the over‑charge hard to detect without inspecting the contract code. To remediate, the fee logic should be rewritten to calculate 1 % of the actual bridged token value, obtained from the parameter that represents the amount being sent, and then apply any NFT‑based discount to that figure before transferring the remainder. This change restores the intended economic model, prevents users from losing extra funds, and aligns the on‑chain behavior with the protocol’s public fee policy.
summary:
The OmniXMultisender contract implements a function sendDeposits to utilize Layerzero's native airdrop functionality to bridge gas tokens.
To offer such a service, Omni X charges a ﬂat 1% fee on all transfers, which is discounted based on the number of Omni X NFTs the user holds.
So, in such a deposit scenario, the msg.value included two values: the value to pay Layerzero veriﬁcation network / DVN and the relayer fees, including the native airdrop value. The fee calculation, instead of calculating 1% of the native token the user is bridging, calculates for the overall msg.value, hence overestimating it.
Impact: Likelihood: HIGH and impact: HIGH; hence, this is considered a HIGH severity bug.

title: Checking for message expiration after receipt processing prevents pruning indexes, increase resources
content: The vulnerability consists of an incorrect ordering of the expiration validation for cross-chain messages in the Optimism op-program. The implementation retrieves the full receipt data for a block before checking whether the originating message timestamp is older than the configured expiration period. Because the receipt is accessed prior to the expiration test, nodes that prune old receipt indexes are forced to keep every receipt indefinitely in order to be able to perform the later check. This defeats the intended design where expired messages should be discardable without retaining their receipts, and it causes nodes to require unbounded storage and processing resources. An attacker can exploit the flaw by submitting a message with a timestamp far in the past; when a validating node processes the block it will be compelled to fetch the corresponding receipt from archival storage, potentially exhausting memory or I/O bandwidth and preventing the node from completing synchronization. The impact is that full-node operators experience excessive disk usage, increased sync times, and may be unable to validate state transitions after pruning, which undermines network reliability and could lead to denial-of-service conditions. The issue manifests whenever a block is fetched and the op-program attempts to validate a message; the condition is independent of the specific message content and occurs for any expired message. All participants that run a pruning-enabled node—validators, relayers, and end-users—are affected because the protocol’s correctness relies on being able to prove state transitions without historic receipts. The problem was discovered during a security audit that examined the message validation flow and identified that the expiration check was placed after receipt retrieval, a subtle ordering mistake that does not produce immediate functional errors but creates hidden resource costs. The bug is hard to notice because the validation still succeeds and the contract logic appears correct; only the performance and storage characteristics reveal the flaw. The appropriate remediation is to move the expiration verification to the earliest possible point, such as immediately after the block header is obtained in CanonBlockByNumber or Contains, before any receipt data is accessed. By performing the timestamp comparison first, nodes can safely prune receipts for expired messages, restoring the intended resource guarantees and preventing the excessive indexing problem.
summary:
In the present implementation the initiating message/s timestamp is checked for expiration after the message is retrieved from the block. This defeats the purpose of limiting the need of keeping receipts indexed forever -- and actually make nodes that prune their indexes unable to prove a state transition.  
Running the op-program would require having all receipts from all blocks available regardless of expiration settings, since any message from any receipt from any block might need to be retrieved for validation.

title: The same message can be marked as executing multiple times without being executed
content: The vulnerability consists of a logic flaw in the cross‑layer message inbox where the contract that records the execution of a cross‑chain message is allowed to emit the same execution log more than once without actually performing the underlying message logic. The root cause is that the inbox contract does not enforce a uniqueness constraint on the ExecutingMessage event; it simply emits the event whenever a caller invokes the function that signals execution, regardless of whether the message state has already been marked as executed. Because the off‑chain op‑program relies on parsing block receipts and collecting ExecutingMessage logs to decide which messages need further processing, duplicate logs are interpreted as distinct executions. An attacker, or even a benign user, can trigger the emission of the same execution log repeatedly – for example by calling a wrapper function or by replaying a transaction that only emits the event – causing the op‑program to process the same message multiple times. The impact is that the same state‑changing operation (such as a token transfer, withdrawal, or state update) may be applied more than once, leading to double spending, unintended fund movement, or corrupted accounting. This can happen whenever the inbox contract is called to signal execution and there is no guard against re‑emitting the same event, i.e., under normal operation of the protocol as well as under malicious replay attempts. All participants that rely on the op‑program’s correct accounting – users, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because their balances may be altered incorrectly or funds may disappear from the system. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the op‑program’s message‑processing pipeline, where the auditor noticed that the log‑parsing routine collected duplicate entries without any corresponding state change in the inbox contract. The bug is subtle because the contract’s external behavior (the actual execution of the message) appears unchanged; only the emitted logs are duplicated, which can be overlooked when only functional tests are run. To remediate, the inbox contract should enforce a one‑time emission rule for each message identifier, for example by storing a flag that marks a message as already executed before emitting the log. Alternatively, the op‑program can add a deduplication step that discards repeated ExecutingMessage logs based on their unique identifiers. In either case, the fix restores the invariant that each cross‑layer message is processed exactly once, preserving accounting integrity and preventing double execution attacks. From a user’s perspective the symptom may be that an expected operation (such as a withdrawal) appears to succeed multiple times, resulting in a sudden loss of funds or an unexpected zero balance, contrary to the expectation that the operation would be performed only once.
summary: Currently, the op-program retrieves executing messages by parsing logs from the block receipts. Each log in the block is passed to DecodeExecutingMessageLog. If an ExecutingMessage log coming from the CrossL2Inbox contract is found, it is collected in execMsgs for processing. However, the current implementation of CrossL2Inbox allows emitting multiple times the same ExecutingMessage log without actually executing the message.

title: DoS in claim Function Due to init Constraint on an Already Initialized Account
content: The vulnerability is an improper use of the init constraint on the Position account inside the claim instruction. The Position PDA is created and initialized during the stake instruction, so when the claim instruction is later called the runtime attempts to re‑initialize an already existing account. Anchor treats the init flag as a request to allocate a fresh account; because the account already exists, the instruction aborts with an account already initialized error. This error occurs every time a user tries to claim accrued rewards after the first staking operation, effectively preventing any further claim calls.
