The impact is severe: an attacker can gain complete control of the proxy for the duration of the call, enabling theft of funds, unauthorized cancellation of streams, or any other owner‑only operation, effectively breaking the accounting guarantees of the protocol. Users may notice that expected refunds are missing, balances become zero, or streams are cancelled without explanation, while the contract state appears unchanged after the transaction. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the storage handling of delegatecalls and identified that the owner check does not protect against intermediate modifications. The bug is hard to detect because the final state of the owner variable is correct, so standard tests that only inspect end‑state values will not reveal the transient takeover. To remediate, the proxy’s ownership model should be redesigned so that the owner cannot be altered by delegatecall code, for example by making the owner immutable, storing it in a separate contract (such as a registry) that is queried for authority checks, or by preventing delegatecalls from accessing the storage slot that holds the owner. In any case, the fix must ensure that ownership cannot be changed at any point during the execution of a delegated call.

title: Malicious asset can be used to inject Javascript into Sablier front end
content: An attacker can inject arbitrary JavaScript into the Sablier front‑end by supplying a malicious ERC20 (or other asset) contract whose symbol field contains a long string that includes SVG‑compatible script tags. The NFT descriptor contract reads the symbol via a low‑level staticcall and, if the returned data is longer than 64 bytes, returns it unchanged. No validation, length‑based filtering, or HTML/SVG escaping is performed before the symbol is concatenated into an SVG <text> element that is later rendered by any web UI displaying Sablier NFTs. Because SVG images are allowed to contain <script> elements, a crafted symbol such as <script>…</script> can execute code in the victim’s browser when the SVG is rendered. The exploit works whenever a user opens the NFT view for a stream that uses the malicious asset, causing the front‑end to run the injected script. From the user’s point of view the NFT appears normal, but instead of seeing a plain asset symbol the browser runs hidden JavaScript that could display a fake Metamask signature request, steal private keys, or perform other phishing actions. The vulnerability was discovered during a security audit that examined how external data is incorporated into on‑chain SVG generation and recognised that the safeAssetSymbol function only checks the length of the returned bytes, not its content. The issue is difficult to notice because the symbol field is normally a short alphanumeric string, so developers may assume it is safe to embed directly. This class of bug is a DOM‑based cross‑site scripting (XSS) vector caused by unsanitized user‑controlled data being inserted into an SVG document. To remediate, the contract should enforce a reasonable maximum length for the symbol (for example 16 characters), whitelist allowed characters (letters and digits), and escape or strip any characters that could form HTML or SVG tags such as <, >, ', ", ;. Adding proper sanitisation prevents an attacker from embedding executable code and restores the intended behaviour that the SVG only displays static text.

title: Wrapped native asset address can be freely chosen and is assumed to return equal amount of tokens on deposit
content: The vulnerability resides in the wrapAndCreate* functions of the SablierV2ProxyTarget contract where the caller can supply an arbitrary address for the wrapped native asset. The code assumes that calling deposit() on the supplied contract will mint an amount of ERC‑20 tokens equal to the ETH sent (msg.value) and then approves the Sablier lockup contract to spend that exact amount. Because the contract does not verify the number of tokens actually received, an attacker can deploy a malicious ERC‑20 contract whose deposit() function accepts ETH but returns fewer tokens than the amount deposited. When a user invokes wrapAndCreateWithDurations with the malicious address, the proxy wraps the ETH, receives a shortfall of tokens, then executes an infinite approval for the token contract and creates a stream with totalAmount set to msg.value. The lockup contract will pull the full msg.value amount from the proxy’s balance, effectively taking the missing tokens from the proxy and crediting them to the stream. This results in a loss of tokens from the proxy, while the user sees a stream that appears to have been funded with the expected amount, creating a discrepancy between the displayed stream amount and the actual token balance of the proxy. The issue occurs whenever wrapAndCreate* is called with a non‑trusted asset address and a non‑zero msg.value, affecting any user of the proxy and the protocol’s overall token accounting. It was discovered during a security audit that highlighted the unchecked external call and the lack of validation of the token amount returned by deposit(). The bug is subtle because the transaction does not revert; the stream is created successfully, and only the proxy’s token balance is reduced, making the problem easy to miss in normal operation. The class of bug can be described as an unchecked external contract interaction leading to a deposit‑return mismatch, a form of wrapped‑asset amount manipulation. From a user perspective the symptoms are that after sending ETH they receive fewer wrapped tokens than expected, the UI may show the correct stream amount but the underlying token balance of the contract is lower, effectively causing funds to disappear. To remediate the issue the contract should restrict the wrapped native asset to a known safe implementation via an allow‑list or immutable variable, and it should verify that the token balance increase after deposit matches the ETH amount before granting any approvals. This ensures that the proxy cannot be tricked into approving and transferring more tokens than it actually holds, preserving the intended accounting guarantees of the protocol.

title: Any plugins using permit2 can steal funds with frontrunning attack
content: The vulnerability is an authorization‑binding flaw in contracts that forward a Permit2 signature to plugin modules. Permit2 signatures are created by a token holder to allow a specific spender address to move a defined amount of a given token, but the signature data (PermitSingle) only records the spender, token address, amount, expiration and nonce – it does not record the ultimate target contract or the function that the spender intends to call. In the SablierV2ProxyTarget design the proxy calls permit2.permit and then permit2.transferFrom to move funds on behalf of the user, and it forwards the same Permit2 parameters to any installed plugin. Because the signature lacks any witness of the intended plugin or action, a malicious actor can observe a user’s transaction that includes the Permit2 signature, copy the same signature and front‑run the proxy’s call. By submitting a transaction that invokes permit2.transferFrom before the legitimate proxy transaction is mined, the attacker can cause the Permit2 contract to transfer the authorized amount to an address of the attacker’s choosing. This results in the user’s tokens being drained without any explicit approval for that destination. The flaw occurs whenever a proxy permits plugins to use raw Permit2 signatures without additional intent verification, and it is especially exploitable in environments where transactions are publicly visible before inclusion (e.g., Ethereum mempool). The affected parties are the token owners who interact with the proxy, the proxy contract itself, any downstream protocol that relies on the proxy for scheduled payments, and ultimately the users of those protocols. The issue was discovered during a security audit of the cantina_sablier contract by Spearbit, who noted that the Permit2 documentation advises callers to check the signer’s intent, a step that the proxy does not enforce. The problem is subtle because the Permit2 call succeeds and the token transfer appears legitimate; there is no on‑chain evidence that the signature was meant for a particular plugin, making the mis‑use hard to detect from logs alone. To remediate, the proxy should reject raw Permit2 usage in plugins and instead employ the more restrictive permitWitnessTransferFrom function, which allows the signer to embed a witness (such as the target contract address, function selector, and possibly parameters) that the proxy can verify before forwarding the call. A dedicated executeWithPermit2 entry point that extracts and validates the witness data would bind the authorization to the intended action, preventing an attacker from reusing the signature for a different purpose. In abstract terms, this is a class of “missing intent verification” or “unbound delegation” bug, where an authorization token is not cryptographically tied to the specific operation it is meant to enable, leading to unauthorized fund transfers, unexpected zero balances, and a breach of the protocol’s accounting assumptions.

title: Lack of reasonable value check in setMinGasReserve() can lead to bricked proxy
content: The contract implements a configurable gas reserve that is subtracted from the remaining gas before performing a delegatecall to a target or plugin contract. The function setMinGasReserve allows an authorized account to write a new value, but the implementation does not validate that the supplied value is reasonable. Because the reserve is subtracted from gasleft() to compute the stipend, an attacker or a careless admin can set minGasReserve to a value that is close to or larger than the total gas available for the transaction. When the subsequent _safeDelegateCall is executed, the calculated stipend becomes zero or negative, causing the delegatecall to be sent with insufficient gas. The EVM will then either revert due to out‑of‑gas or, if the stipend is still positive but too small, the call will fail and the proxy will be unable to forward any further calls. In the worst case the required gas exceeds the block gas limit, meaning the transaction can never be included, effectively bricking the proxy contract. Because the minGasReserve is stored in a regular storage slot, a malicious plugin or target contract that can write to that slot (for example via a delegatecall that modifies storage) can overwrite it with an extreme value, achieving the same denial‑of‑service without direct access to setMinGasReserve. From a user’s point of view the proxy appears to accept a transaction, then immediately reverts with an out‑of‑gas error, or later becomes completely unresponsive, leaving all funds locked in the proxy with no way to withdraw them. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the gas handling logic and noticed the absence of bounds checking. It is hard to notice because the contract will behave normally for typical reserve values, and the failure only manifests when an extreme value is set, which may not be exercised in standard tests. The vulnerability belongs to the class of unchecked configuration parameter leading to denial‑of‑service and specifically to gas‑reserve mis‑management. The recommended mitigation is to either eliminate the manual gas reserve and rely on the EVM’s built‑in 1/64th gas safety margin, or to enforce a maximum allowed minGasReserve (for example a few hundred thousand gas) when the value is updated, and to protect the storage slot from being overwritten by external contracts, for instance by moving it to a dedicated external storage contract. By applying such checks, the proxy will retain the ability to forward calls and users will be able to retrieve their funds.

title: Any envoy with access to SablierV2ProxyTarget can steal all funds in proxy
content: The vulnerability is an unchecked external contract address in the proxy’s stream creation path. When a proxy owner grants an envoy permission on the SablierV2ProxyTarget, the envoy can call the createStream function which internally invokes a helper that accepts a Permit2Params struct supplied by the caller. This struct contains the address of a Permit2 contract used to call permit and transferFrom before approving the Sablier contract to spend the asset. Because the helper does not verify that the Permit2 address is a trusted implementation, a malicious envoy can deploy a dummy contract that implements the expected functions but does nothing, returning success. The helper then proceeds to approve the Sablier contract and creates a stream that directs the proxy’s assets to the attacker’s address. The stream may be uncancellable and can drain the proxy’s balance over a short period, effectively stealing all funds. The root cause is the assumption that any Permit2 contract supplied by an authorized envoy is safe, which breaks the trust boundary between the proxy and external contracts. Exploitation requires only that the owner has given the envoy permission on the target; no additional signatures or approvals are needed. The impact is loss of funds for the proxy owner and any users relying on the proxy, while the protocol’s accounting assumptions are violated because assets disappear without a legitimate transfer. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the permission model and noticed that the Permit2 address is not validated. It can be hard to notice because the transaction succeeds, the dummy contract mimics the expected interface, and there is no revert or error. The bug belongs to the class of unchecked external contract address or external call injection vulnerabilities, where a contract trusts an arbitrary external address without verification. From a user perspective the UI may show a newly created stream that appears normal, but the balance drops to zero or the expected refund never arrives. The expected behavior is that only streams backed by a legitimate Permit2 order can be created, yet the reality is that any contract can be supplied, allowing asset theft. The recommended mitigation is to maintain a whitelist of approved Permit2 contracts and enforce that the supplied address matches an entry in this list before performing the permit and transferFrom calls, or to hard‑code the known Permit2 implementation, thereby restoring the intended trust model.

title: Recipient can block the sender's cancel by sending the NFT to an address known to revert the transfer of the underlying ERC20
content: The vulnerability arises from the way the cancel function of the SablierV2LockupDynamic and SablierV2LockupLinear contracts handles the final distribution of funds. When a sender initiates a cancel, the internal _cancel() routine attempts to transfer the remaining balances to both the recipient and the sender in a single atomic operation using the safeTransfer helper of the underlying ERC20 token. SafeTransfer reverts if the token transfer fails for any reason. Because the recipient address is derived from ownership of the Sablier NFT, a malicious or disgruntled recipient can front‑run the cancel transaction by first calling withdraw() to claim all owed tokens and then transferring the NFT to an address that the underlying token deliberately rejects (for example, an address on USDC’s blocklist). When the sender later calls cancel, the contract tries to send the recipient’s portion to the blocked address; the safeTransfer call fails and the whole transaction reverts, preventing the sender’s funds from being returned. This situation can occur whenever the recipient is able to move the NFT to a revert‑prone address before the sender’s cancel is mined. The affected parties are the sender, who expects the cancel to release their remaining balance, and the protocol, which loses the guarantee that funds can always be reclaimed. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the flow of cancel logic and identified that the recipient’s address is not immutable during cancellation. It is subtle because the cancel function appears to correctly compute amounts and uses a standard safeTransfer pattern; only when the token implements address‑based transfer restrictions does the problem surface, making it easy to miss in typical testing. The impact is that a sender’s attempt to cancel a stream can be blocked, effectively bricking the sender’s funds until the protocol is upgraded or the recipient releases the NFT. Conceptually, this is a denial‑of‑service style bug where a counter‑party can manipulate ownership metadata to cause a downstream token transfer to revert, breaking the atomicity of the cancel operation. The recommended mitigation is to separate the cancel process into two distinct steps: first, an accounting step that records the cancellation and allows the initiator to withdraw their portion, and second, a separate withdrawal step for the other party. By decoupling the two transfers, a failure in the recipient’s transfer cannot prevent the sender from retrieving their funds, restoring the intended financial guarantees of the protocol.

title: If MAX_FEE is set too high, user may be able to underﬂow deposit value to steal all funds
content: The vulnerability is an arithmetic underflow/overflow bug in the stream creation logic that occurs when the contract’s MAX_FEE constant is set to the maximum possible value (1e18). The contract calculates broker fee and protocol fee and then asserts that totalAmount > protocolFee + brokerFee inside an unchecked block. Because the addition of protocolFee and brokerFee can overflow, the assertion incorrectly passes, and the subsequent subtraction underflows, producing a deposit amount that wraps around to a very large value close to the uint128 maximum. This inflated deposit is then transferred to the contract, allowing an attacker who can flash‑mint the maximum uint128 amount of a token to create a stream with a past start time, withdraw the entire inflated deposit, and thereby drain funds that belong to other users. The attack requires three conditions: MAX_FEE equal to 1e18, a token that supports flash minting up to type(uint128).max, and a very low protocol fee. When these conditions hold, the attacker can flash‑mint the maximum amount, create a stream with brokerFee set to MAX_FEE‑protocolFee+1, trigger the overflow, and then call withdraw to extract the wrapped deposit. The impact is total loss of user balances stored in the contract, as the attacker can repeatedly withdraw the inflated deposit and also profit from subsequent streams. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined fee calculations and noticed that critical assertions were placed inside unchecked blocks for gas optimisation. Because the overflow only occurs with extreme values, it may not be evident during normal testing, making it hard to notice. The bug belongs to the class of unchecked arithmetic leading to incorrect invariant checks, specifically an underflow/overflow that bypasses safety assertions. To fix the problem, the contract should enforce a reasonable upper bound on MAX_FEE (e.g., below 0.2e18) and move the fee‑related assertions out of unchecked blocks or replace them with safe arithmetic that reverts on overflow. Additionally, using Solidity's built‑in overflow checks or a safe‑math library for critical calculations would prevent the deposit from wrapping to a huge value. Users would notice that after creating a stream they can withdraw far more tokens than they deposited, or that balances disappear from the contract unexpectedly. The vulnerability violates the accounting assumption that the sum of protocol fee, broker fee and deposit never exceeds the total amount, and it enables a malicious actor to steal all funds stored in the stream contract.
summary:
This vulnerability has some narrow constraints that make it unlikely to occur at the moment but would result in theft of all user funds, so are important to address.  
There are three constraints required for this attack:  
• MAX_FEE is set to 1e18 (which is the only value explicitly called out in the comments)  
• There is a token that allows ﬂash mints of up to type(uint128).max (currently DAI allows 500mme18, but this possibility seems likely at some point)  
• This token has a protocol fee that is set extremely low  
If those constraints are met, we are able to use them to create a stream with parameters that will underﬂow deposits and allow them to steal all funds.  
Here is a walkthrough of the attack:  
1) Take a ﬂash mint of type(uint128).max This is a precondition of the attack, which does not seem to be possible with any mainstream tokens at the moment. However, there is no reason to assume this will continue to be the case.  
2) Create a new stream with this full amount We create a new stream with type(uint128).max as the totalAmount, our own address as the broker, broker fee set to 1e18 - protocolFee + 1, and a start time in the past. (Note that the totalAmount value can be adjusted slightly to ensure less liquidity is wasted to protocolFees, but we will use these simple values for this proof of concept.)  
The function then calls out to Helpers.checkAndCalculateFees() to get the exact amounts:  
• The function checks that brokerFee < maxFee, which will pass if MAX_FEE = 1e18.  
• We calculate the broker payment amount (which will be slightly below the max uint128).  
• Then the following check is performed:
```solidity
unchecked {
    assert(totalAmount > amounts.protocolFee + amounts.brokerFee);
    // Calculate the deposit amount (the amount to stream, net of fees).
    amounts.deposit = totalAmount - amounts.protocolFee - amounts.brokerFee;
}
```
• Because this check is performed in an unchecked block, protocolFee + brokerFee will overﬂow and pass the assertion.  
• Then deposit will be calculated as total - protocol - brokerFee, which will underﬂow and result in a value slightly under the max uint128.  
Once these values are returned, assets are transferred:  
• deposit + protocolFee is transferred into the contract, which is also in an unchecked block and will overﬂow, leading to a value of protocolFee - 1.  
• brokerAmount is transferred to another account we own.  
3) Steal all user funds At this point, we have the following values:  
• protocolFee is in the contract (small value)  
• brokerFee is in another account we own  
• deposit value on the contract is close to type(uint128).max  
Since our start time was set to the past, some portion of that deposit value is available for immediate withdrawal. (We could even set endTime in the past so that the full amount is available.) Since our deposit value is now extremely high, we can pass the assertions meant to keep the protocol safe, such as:
```solidity
assert(stream.amounts.deposit >= stream.amounts.withdrawn);
```
We can simply call the withdraw() function with the total amount of the asset owned by the contract, and we will pass all checks to be able to withdraw these assets (which belong to other users).  
4) Pay back ﬂash mint As long as stolenMoney > protocolFee, we will have more money than we initially deposited. At this point, we can pay back the ﬂash mint and keep the proﬁts.  
5) Continue to monitor the contract This attack completes with a large leftover deposit balance. If any other user creates a stream using the same asset in the future, it will be trivial to withdraw some portion of the deposit balance, emptying the contract of the asset and stealing their stream.

title: PRBMath pow() function can return inconsistent values
content:
The vulnerability resides in the mathematical library PRBMath, specifically in the pow() function that computes x raised to the power y for signed fixed‑point numbers. The function delegates the actual exponentiation to an internal exp2() routine, which builds the result by multiplying a series of pre‑computed constants that represent 2 raised to fractional powers. In the current implementation a constant used for one of the bit‑mask positions is wrong: the code uses 0xFF00000000 where the correct value should be 0xFF000000. This off‑by‑one error corrupts the binary representation of the multiplier for a particular bit, causing the exp2() calculation to produce a slightly larger (or smaller) factor than mathematically intended. As a consequence the overall pow() result can violate the monotonicity invariant that for any non‑negative exponent a, if x ≥ y then x⁽ᵃ⁾ ≥ y⁽ᵃ⁾. In practice this means that for two inputs where the base value increases, the computed power may unexpectedly decrease.

The issue was discovered during a formal audit of the Sablier V2 dynamic lockup contract, where pow() is used to translate elapsed time into a cumulative streamed amount. A test case demonstrated that a higher base (representing a later timestamp) produced a lower streamed amount than a lower base, breaking the expectation that the streamed total should only grow as block.timestamp advances. The root cause was traced to the incorrect constant in exp2() at Common.sol line 170, introduced in a pull request on 17 April 2022.

Exploitation does not require on‑chain manipulation beyond calling the vulnerable pow() with crafted arguments. An attacker who can influence the parameters of a stream—such as the start time, duration, or rate—can select values that trigger the faulty bit mask. When the contract later computes the streamed amount, it may report a smaller value than the actual time would dictate. From the user’s perspective this manifests as a missing or reduced balance: a recipient expects to see their accrued tokens increase over time, but the UI shows a stagnant or even decreasing amount, and withdrawals may fail or return less than anticipated. The protocol’s accounting assumptions are broken, potentially leading to under‑payment of beneficiaries and loss of trust in the streaming service.

Detecting the bug can be difficult because the numerical discrepancy is subtle; the result is still a plausible fixed‑point number, and only a careful invariant check (monotonicity) reveals the inconsistency. Standard unit tests that compare against known values may not cover the specific range of inputs that expose the error.

The conceptual fix is to correct the constant used in the exp2() bit‑mask table so that each fractional power of two is represented accurately. After the constant is fixed, the exp2() routine will generate the proper scaling factor, restoring the monotonic relationship of pow() and ensuring that streamed amounts increase monotonically with time. Re‑running the invariant tests should then pass, confirming that x ≥ y implies x⁽ᵃ⁾ ≥ y⁽ᵃ⁾ for all non‑negative a, and the protocol’s financial logic will behave as intended.

title: Sender can brick stream by forcing overﬂow in debt calculation
content: The vulnerability is an arithmetic overflow in the internal debt‑calculation routine of a token streaming contract. The routine computes the ongoing debt by multiplying the elapsed time since the last snapshot by the per‑second rate, storing the product in a uint128 variable. Because both operands are uint128, any product that exceeds the 128‑bit limit wraps around and triggers a revert when the value is later used. The overflow can be triggered simply by setting the ratePerSecond to a very large value – a parameter that the stream sender controls – and allowing any non‑zero amount of time to pass. When the multiplication overflows, every function that relies on the debt calculation – withdraw, refund, pause, or rate adjustment – reverts, effectively freezing the stream. From the user’s perspective the recipient sees transactions fail with generic revert messages, receives no funds despite the passage of time, and the UI may show the balance unchanged. The sender also cannot pause or modify the stream, leaving the deposited tokens permanently locked. This situation violates the core business logic that streamed funds become claimable over time and that both parties retain the ability to manage the stream. The issue was discovered during a security audit that included a proof‑of‑concept test where a maximal uint128 rate caused the contract to revert on totalDebtOf, pause and withdraw calls. The bug is hard to notice because the overflow does not occur at contract creation; it only manifests after time has elapsed, and the revert does not explicitly indicate an arithmetic problem. The flaw belongs to the class of integer‑overflow bugs caused by insufficient width for intermediate calculations. The recommended remediation is to perform the multiplication in a uint256, propagate that type through the debt‑calculation path, and only down‑cast to uint128 after comparing against the token balance, thereby preventing overflow while preserving the original storage constraints.
summary:
The _ongoingDebtOf() internal function is used to calculate the amount of funds owed to the stream recipient since the last snapshot. As a part of these calculations, the scaledOngoingDebt is calculated by multiplying the seconds that have passed since the last snapshot by the rate per second.
```solidity
uint128 scaledOngoingDebt = elapsedTime * ratePerSecond;
```
Since elapsedTime and scaledOngoingDebt are both uint128, any result of the multiplication that is greater than uint128 will overﬂow and cause a revert.
Note that this multiplication does not require an unrealistically high balance of the token, only for ratePerSecond to be set to a high value, which is completely in the control of the sender.
This is a major concern because, once this calculation overﬂows, any calls to withdraw(), refund(), or to adjust the rate back down will all fail, because they all rely on this function. As a result, once this change happens, there is nothing anyone can do to receive funds from the stream, and all funds will permanently be stuck.
This fact could lead to problems in two situations:
1. It could be abused by a sender who is angry with a recipient to lock all previously streamed funds that have not yet been withdrawn, which should be the property of the recipient.
2. It could occur because a ratePerSecond is set to too high of a value accidentally, and then cannot be recovered by either party.

title: Permissionless route creation leads to contract DoS and token theft
content: The vulnerability is a permissionless route creation function that lacks any access control or input validation, allowing any address to call route() with arbitrary parameters. Because the function does not bound the timelock argument, an attacker can supply the maximum uint256 value, which puts the forwarder contract into a perpetual settlement state. While the contract is considered settled, the admin transfer() function reverts, effectively denying service token withdrawals and causing a denial‑of‑service condition that can persist for centuries. In addition, the function does not require the hashlock to be non‑zero nor verify that the supplied token contract address is valid, so an attacker can create a route with a hashlock that corresponds to a preimage they already know. By calling settle() with that preimage, the attacker can immediately satisfy the hashlock condition and trigger the release of the locked tokens to an address of their choice, resulting in theft of the service tokens held in the forwarder. The issue manifests when a malicious user invokes route() with a false incoming flag, an absurd timelock, and either an empty or a crafted hashlock, after which legitimate admins find that their balance reads correctly but any attempt to transfer out fails or the balance disappears after settlement. The affected parties include the contract owner, any admin responsible for moving service tokens, and token holders who rely on the forwarder for timed releases. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the state transitions of ForwarderHashedTimelockERC20 and noticed that the contract does not enforce any constraints on the parameters that drive those transitions. Because the function appears to be a normal routing helper, the lack of validation is not obvious from the UI or typical usage patterns, making the problem easy to overlook until an attacker exploits it. To remediate, the contract should enforce access control on route() or, if the design intends it to remain open, it must implement strict input sanitisation: cap the timelock to a reasonable future timestamp, reject zero hashlocks, reject a zero token address, and validate that the amount is positive and consistent with the direction of the route. Additionally, a safe‑reset mechanism that sweeps any remaining tokens to a treasury before redeploying a new forwarder can mitigate the impact of a successful attack.
summary:
The route() function of ForwarderHashedTimelockERC20.sol enables users to create a route for incoming or outgoing transactions, provided that the preceding transaction is either settled or refunded and the contract remains in its initial state.
Because of the function's permissionless design and absence of input validations, a malicious actor can create routes with infinite timelocks, effectively blocking admins' ability to transfer tokens. They can also steal those tokens by creating malicious routes.
Impact:
• Permanently DoS the ForwarderHashedTimelockERC20.sol contract, forcing the project to deploy new forwarders.
• Block recovery of service tokens held in the forwarder by admin through the transfer function.
• Steal the service tokens in the forwarder by creating a route with a hashlock and a known preimage.

title: TokenPayAndSettleIncoming will process incoming transfer with incorrect hash lock
content: The vulnerability resides in the TokenPayAndSettleIncoming component that handles incoming transfers from an EVM‑based channel. The code performs a basic sanity check that the supplied hashlock is not the zero‑filled 32‑byte value, but it fails to verify that the hashlock actually matches the hashlock that the caller expects for the specific transfer. This missing equality check constitutes an incomplete input‑validation bug. Because the contract only rejects a hashlock of all zeros, any non‑zero hashlock – even one that does not correspond to the pre‑agreed secret – will be accepted and the transfer will be processed. An attacker can therefore craft a malicious transfer with an arbitrary hashlock, submit it to the bridge, and cause the plugin to settle the transfer based on a wrong secret. The exploit works whenever an incoming transfer is received from the EVM side and the hashlock field is populated with any non‑zero value; no additional conditions are required. The impact is that funds may be released to unintended parties, locked indefinitely, or accounted for incorrectly, breaking the accounting guarantees of the bridge and potentially leading to loss of user assets. Users experience symptoms such as their balance not reflecting the expected incoming amount, refunds that never arrive, or funds disappearing from the bridge without a clear on‑chain error. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the validation logic of the incoming transfer path. It is hard to notice because the contract does not emit an explicit error when the hashlock is mismatched; the only visible check (non‑zero) passes for most inputs, so the bug can remain silent until an exploit is attempted. To remediate, the implementation must compare the hashlock provided by the EVM contract with the hashlock supplied in the request parameters and reject the transfer unless the two values are identical. This hardens the integrity check, ensuring that only transfers with the correct cryptographic commitment are settled, restoring the intended business logic that a hashlock must correspond to a previously agreed secret before funds are moved.
summary: The TokenPayAndSettleIncoming functionality processes incoming transfer from EVM. It implements multiple checks on the expected fields. However, one of these checks is insufficient. The EVM channel checks that the hashlock value is not [0u8; 32] before processing the transfer. This check must be hardened to ensure that the hashlock value corresponds to the expected hashlock. This can lead the plugin to process invalid transfers.

title: no-revert-on-transfer ERC20 tokens can be drained
content: The vulnerability arises from the contract’s handling of token transfers when initializing a vault. Certain ERC20 tokens, such as ZRX, do not revert when a transfer fails; instead they return a boolean false. The createVault() function assumes that a failed transfer will cause a transaction revert, but it calls the standard ERC20 transferFrom() without checking the returned value. Because the function does not verify the boolean result, a transfer that returns false is silently accepted, allowing the vault to be recorded with a specified token amount even though no tokens have actually been moved into the contract. The bug is amplified by the fact that the vault’s token type can be declared as ERC721, causing the code path to use transferFrom() instead of the safer safeTransferFrom() that would revert on an unsupported interface. An attacker can exploit this by creating a vault with a non‑reverting ERC20 token while indicating the token type as ERC721. The vault appears to hold the declared amount of tokens, but the contract’s balance for that token remains zero. When another user later purchases and exercises the option linked to this vault, the contract dutifully transfers the buyer’s Ether (premium and strike) but does not deliver any underlying tokens, because none are present. From the buyer’s perspective the UI shows a successful purchase and exercise, yet the token balance they receive is zero, resulting in a direct loss of Ether. The impact is a loss of funds for option buyers and a breach of the protocol’s economic guarantees, potentially damaging user trust. This condition only manifests when the token’s transfer function returns false rather than reverting, and when the vault creation logic does not enforce a check on that return value. The issue was uncovered during a security audit that included a forked‑mainnet test using the ZRX token contract, demonstrating that the vault could be created without any token deposits. The flaw is subtle because the transaction receipt shows success and no explicit error is emitted, making it easy to miss in normal testing. To remediate, token transfers should be performed through a safety wrapper such as OpenZeppelin’s SafeERC20 library, which asserts that the call succeeds and reverts otherwise, or by using safeTransferFrom() for ERC721 tokens. Additionally, the contract should enforce that the token type matches the interface being called, rejecting mismatched type declarations. By ensuring any failed transfer triggers a revert, the vault cannot be initialized without the required token collateral, thereby preserving the intended accounting and preventing fund drains.
summary:
Some ERC20 tokens don’t throw but just return false when a transfer fails. This can be abused to trick the `createVault()` function to initialize the vault without providing any tokens. A good example of such a token is _ZRX_ : [Etherscan code](https://etherscan.io/address/0xe41d2489571d322189246dafa5ebde1f4699f498#code#L64)

When such a vault is initialized, another user can both buy and exercise the option without ever receiving any funds. The creator of the vault does receive the buyer’s Ether tho. So it can cause a loss of funds.

title: Inefficiency in the Dutch Auction due to lower duration
content: The reported vulnerability is a mis‑calculation in the Dutch auction pricing logic of the Cally protocol. The contract stores a fixed auction duration of 24 hours and a reserve strike price that is never zero. The function that derives the current auction strike uses the remaining time (auctionEnd‑timestamp) as the basis for the price decay. Because the price is computed as a function of the remaining time, the price reaches the reserve strike well before the 24‑hour deadline when the gap between the starting strike and the reserve strike is large. Once the reserve is reached, the price stays constant for the rest of the auction, leaving the remaining time unused and allowing the auction to be completed at a price that is substantially lower than the creator expected. This effect can be observed with examples such as a starting strike of 55 and a reserve of 13.5, where the price hits the reserve after roughly 12 hours, wasting the second half of the auction. The root cause is the use of a decreasing linear (or quadratic) progress variable based on time left instead of time elapsed, which makes the price drop faster than intended. An attacker or a careless vault creator can deliberately choose a wide spread between start and reserve, causing the auction to hit the floor early; participants can then purchase options at a price that is far below the market expectation, causing the vault creator to lose value. The impact is primarily financial loss for the vault creator and a distortion of the protocol’s pricing guarantees, potentially eroding trust in the auction mechanism. The bug manifests whenever a vault is instantiated with a non‑zero reserve strike that is significantly lower than the starting strike, which is a common configuration. It was discovered during a third‑party audit where the auditors compared the intended price curve against the actual on‑chain behavior. The issue is subtle because the UI only shows a steadily falling price and does not indicate that the price will flatten prematurely; users may assume the price will continue to decline until the end of the auction, leading to mismatched expectations. The correct fix is to base the progress calculation on elapsed time (or equivalently on the complement of the remaining time) so that the price reaches the reserve exactly at the 24‑hour mark, for example by squaring the ratio of elapsed time over the total duration and adding the reserve thereafter. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of "time‑based pricing miscalculations" in Dutch auctions, where the floor price is applied too early, resulting in wasted auction time and unintended price floors.
summary:
The vulnerability or bug is in the implementation of the function getDutchAuctionStrike() The AUCTION_DURATION is defined as 24 hours, and consider that the dutchAuctionReserveStrike (or reserveStrike) will never be set to 0 by user.

Now if a vault is created with startingStrike value of 55 and reserveStrike of 13.5 , the auction price will drop from 55 to 13.5 midway at ~12 hours. So, after 12 hours from start of auction, the rate will be constant at reserveStrike of 13.5, and remaining time of 12 hours of auction is a waste.

Some other examples :

startStrike, reserveStrike, time-to-reach-reserveStrike
55 , 13.5  , ~12 hours
55 , 5     , ~16.7 hours
55 , 1.5   , ~20 hours
5  , 1.5   , ~11 hours

title: [WP-H0] Fake balances can be created for not-yet-existing ERC20 tokens, which allows attackers to set traps to steal funds from future users
content: The vulnerability originates from the use of solmate’s SafeTransferLib for pulling ERC20 tokens into a newly created vault. SafeTransferLib does not verify that the supplied token address actually contains contract code before attempting a transfer. Consequently, if the address passed to createVault() points to a location with no deployed contract, the safeTransferFrom call succeeds silently, and the vault’s internal accounting records a balance for a token that does not yet exist. This creates a phantom balance – a ‘fake’ token balance – that can later be abused. The problem becomes exploitable when a legitimate ERC20 token is subsequently deployed to the same address, a situation that is common for multi‑chain projects that reuse the same deployer nonce to obtain identical token addresses across networks. An attacker can pre‑emptively create vaults using the yet‑undeployed token address and claim a large amount of that token in the vault’s accounting. When the real token contract is finally deployed, unsuspecting users will deposit the genuine token into the vault, trusting the recorded balance. At withdrawal time the protocol will honor the bogus balance, allowing the attacker to invoke withdraw() and siphon away the amount that was previously entered as a fake balance. From the user’s point of view the expectation is that depositing 11,000 tokens will later allow them to withdraw the same amount, but they may instead receive only a portion of their funds or see their balance disappear entirely. The impact is a direct loss of user funds and a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees. The issue was identified during an audit that referenced the well‑known qBridge hack, which demonstrated that missing code checks can be used to set traps for future token deployments. Detecting the bug is difficult because the transaction that creates the vault does not revert and no error is emitted; the contract’s state simply records a balance for a token that currently has no on‑chain representation. To remediate the issue, the contract should enforce a check that the token address contains contract code before attempting any transfer, for example by switching to OpenZeppelin’s SafeERC20 library, which performs such a verification, or by adding an explicit `require(token.code.length > 0)` guard. This class of bug is generally known as a “missing contract‑code validation” or “phantom token balance” vulnerability, where accounting logic assumes the existence of an external token contract without confirming it, leading to potential fund theft when the contract is later deployed at the expected address.

title: LibClone: Length overﬂow allows corruption of created proxy
content: The vulnerability resides in a library function that creates immutable proxy contracts by concatenating a small header with user‑supplied initialization data. The implementation assumes that the length of the supplied byte array plus a constant offset will always fit into a 2‑byte unsigned integer, but this assumption is never validated. When the data length exceeds 65,535 bytes, the calculated length overflows the 2‑byte field and is left‑shifted by 15 bytes before being OR‑ed into the bytecode template. Because the overflow is not truncated, the high‑order bits of the length become part of the opcode stream, effectively mutating the first PUSH2 opcode into a larger PUSH<n> opcode (for example PUSH4, PUSH6, etc.). This mutation changes the semantics of the subsequent bytes, turning what should be logical opcodes into data that is pushed onto the stack, or even into destructive opcodes such as SELFDESTRUCT. As a result, the deployed proxy may contain malformed runtime bytecode: it can either revert during deployment or, more subtly, result in a contract with no executable code at all. From a user’s perspective the proxy appears to be successfully created – the address is non‑zero and the transaction does not revert – but the contract’s code size is zero. Any ether sent to that address is accepted by the fallback function but becomes permanently inaccessible because there is no code to execute a withdrawal. The impact is loss of funds and a false sense of security for developers who rely on the library’s clone functions to deploy functional proxies. The issue manifests whenever a caller provides an initialization payload larger than the 2‑byte limit, which can be achieved with a single large bytes array (approximately 0.9 MiB) that still fits within main‑net gas constraints. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the cloning routine, where the arithmetic that computes the extra length was examined and found to lack a bounds check. The problem is hard to notice because the deployment transaction succeeds and the address can be predicted, yet the contract’s bytecode is empty – a condition that is not automatically flagged by typical tooling. To remediate the issue, the library should enforce a strict upper bound on the length of the initialization data such that the final runtime size never exceeds the 2‑byte limit (for example, capping the data at 65,435 bytes, which together with the constant header stays below 65,535). This check prevents the length overflow and ensures that the generated bytecode remains well‑formed, preserving the intended proxy behavior and protecting user funds.
summary:
When creating an immutable proxy with args with either the clone(address, bytes memory) or cloneDeterministic(address, bytes memory, bytes32) functions it's assumed that the length of the bytes input +100 (0x62 + 2) will fit in 2-bytes.
Excerpt from clone(address, bytes) (both the non-create2 & create2 variants of this clone function have the same logic & flaw):
```solidity
let extraLength := add(dataLength, 2)
mstore(
    sub(data, 0x5a),
    or(shl(0x78, add(extraLength, 0x62)), 0x6100003d81600a3d39f336602c57343d527f)
)
```
The assumption that "The inserted data length will fit in 2-bytes" is not explicitly checked anywhere. A final length that is larger than 2-bytes is not truncated either, being first bit shifted to the left by 15-bytes (0x78 bits) and then bitwise OR-ed with the data for insertion. This means that a final length requiring 3 or more non-zero bytes (≥65536) would actually change the meaning of the final bytecode:
- OR(0x6100003d81, 0x0001230000) = 0x6101233d81 => `PUSH2 0x0123 RETURNDATASIZE DUP2 ...`
+ OR(0x6100003d81, 0x0200230000) = 0x6300233d81 => `PUSH4 0x00233d81 ...`
This allows you to modify the PUSH2 byte (0x61) into a different opcode while still resulting in runnable code.
Speciﬁcally the ﬁrst PUSH2 can be changed into any even PUSH<n> opcode (PUSH4, PUSH6, PUSH8, PUSH10, ...) depending on the length in the resulting inserted length. Extending the length of the initial push opcode means that subsequent opcodes will be turned from logical operations into part of the word that'll get pushed onto the stack as part of execution. If suﬃciently extended it'll consume the op-byte of other subsequent push opcodes, turning their "value bytes" into logical opcodes, e.g.:
- 6101023d8160ff => PUSH2 0x01 0x02 RETURNDATASIZE DUP2 PUSH1 0xff
+ 6401023d8160ff => PUSH5 0x01 0x02 0x3d 0x81 0x60 SELFDESTRUCT
In the clone{Deterministic} functions this can be used to achieve 1 of 2 things:
1. Cause a proxy deployment to fail that would otherwise be considered valid (predictDeterministicAddress would still compute an address for the undeployable contract).
2. Cause a valid, empty contract (no bytecode) to deployed
Action 2. might be especially harmful as a library consumer may assume that if the cloning does not revert it must've been successful. Any funds sent to such a contract would be permanently forever lost & inaccessible.

title: Calls to AccessHub.setFeeSplit will revert due to _feeSplits having the wrong type
content: The vulnerability is a type‑mismatch in the AccessHub.setFeeSplit function that allows the privileged role SWAP_FEE_SETTER to configure fee distribution percentages for each pool. The function receives an array named _feeSplits declared as uint8[], which can store values only up to 255. In the protocol's accounting model a full 100 % fee split is represented by the integer 10 000 (basis points). Consequently any intended split larger than 2.55 % (255/10 000) cannot be represented. When a caller supplies a value greater than 255 the transaction reverts because the value does not fit into the uint8 type, and when a caller supplies a value within the uint8 range the contract records a much smaller percentage than intended, leaving the majority of fees unallocated. This bug originates from an incorrect choice of data type for a monetary parameter, causing overflow or truncation. An attacker or a mis‑configured admin can exploit the situation by submitting a split that triggers a revert, effectively preventing the protocol from distributing fees to a pool, or by submitting a low split that silently reduces the pool's revenue. The impact is loss of expected fee revenue for pool operators, liquidity providers and the protocol treasury; users see transactions that appear to succeed while their pools receive little or no fees, or they encounter unexpected revert messages when trying to set fee splits. The condition occurs whenever the setFeeSplit function is called for non‑CL pools where the desired split exceeds 2.55 %. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the declared type of _feeSplits with the documented fee‑split representation. It can be hard to notice because small splits work correctly and the revert message does not explain the underlying overflow. The proper fix is to change the parameter type to a larger unsigned integer such as uint256[] (or at least uint16[]) so that the full range of basis‑point values up to 10 000 can be stored, and to adjust any related logic accordingly. This class of bug is a numeric overflow/under‑allocation error caused by an inappropriate data type, which breaks the accounting assumptions that a fee split of 100 % can be expressed and leads to missing or unclaimed funds.
summary:
AccessHub.setFeeSplit is a function that allows SWAP_FEE_SETTER to set the fee splits for pools (CL or not). _feeSplits is an array that represent percentages. In the case of non CL pairs (managed by poolFactory), 100% is represented as 10,000, but as we can see _feeSplits is uint8[] which means it can only facilitate a percentage of 255/10,000 = 2.55% per pool which will cause some fees to be unclaimed.
To summarize, calls to the function will either revert or will leave unclaimed tokens.

title: Missing checkpoint on APY change will create unfair interest and rewards
content: The vulnerability originates from the contract’s interest‑accrual logic, which relies on a stored APY value and a timestamp called lastCheckpoint to compute pending token‑per‑share (TPS) for lenders and pending interest for borrowers. When the APY is changed through the internal _setApy function, the code simply overwrites the stored APY without first advancing the checkpoint. Consequently, the formulas that use block.timestamp‑lastCheckpoint continue to apply the new APY retroactively to the entire period since the previous checkpoint. This creates an accounting mismatch: lenders receive rewards that are calculated with a rate that did not apply during earlier blocks, and borrowers are charged interest as if the higher (or lower) rate had been in effect for the whole loan duration. The issue manifests only after an APY update and after some time has elapsed, making it easy to miss during a quick balance inspection because the current TPS value looks plausible. It was discovered during a manual audit of the staking module where the auditor noticed that the _setApy routine does not invoke the checkpoint routine that normally records accrued rewards before a parameter change. The impact can be severe: lenders may see their expected returns reduced or inflated, borrowers may be over‑charged, and the overall pool accounting can become inconsistent, potentially leading to fund loss or insolvency if the pool pays out more than it has accrued. The affected parties are all participants in the staking pool – lenders, borrowers, and any protocol that relies on the correct distribution of interest and rewards. To remediate the problem, the contract should record a checkpoint (or otherwise settle accrued TPS) before any APY modification, and it should keep a history of APY values with associated timestamps so that interest can be calculated piece‑wise for each interval. This ensures that interest calculations respect the rate that was actually in force at each point in time, preserving the intended business logic that rewards and repayments are based on the correct, time‑bound APY.

title: Subsequent rounds of winner selection is blocked for a pot
content: The vulnerability concerns the inability torun a second round of winner selection for a given pot. The contract function rotateLiquidity is intended to be called repeatedly to select a new winner for each round, but the second invocation reverts because it calls entropy.reveal with a sequenceNumber that has already been consumed. The entropy contract clears a request after it is revealed, and any subsequent reveal using the same sequenceNumber triggers a revert. This design flaw means that once a pot has performed its first winner selection, the same pot cannot be used again to select another winner, effectively locking the pot and preventing further participation. Exploitation is straightforward: an attacker or any user can trigger the first round, causing the entropy request to be fulfilled, and then the contract becomes permanently unable to process further rounds. As a result, funds that remain in the pot after the first round cannot be redistributed, users see no winner, balances may appear unchanged or zeroed, and the UI may display error messages or simply show that the pot is closed. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the flow of rotateLiquidity and the interaction with the entropy contract. It is subtle because the first round works as expected, so developers may assume the mechanism is sound; the failure only appears on the second call, which can be missed in basic testing. The bug belongs to the class of state‑reuse errors where a one‑time request identifier is reused without regeneration, leading to denial‑of‑service conditions. To remediate, the contract should generate a fresh sequenceNumber for each round of winner selection, or redesign the pot logic to allow only a single winner selection per pot and prevent re‑joining after a round is completed. This ensures that entropy.reveal always receives a valid, unused identifier and that the pot can either be safely closed after one round or continue operating with proper sequence management.
summary: Second call to rotateLiquidity() for a pot reverts due to the call to entropy.reveal(). Once a sequenceNumber is used, entropy reverts if it's used again as it clears the request. Hence, a pot cannot be used to select a winner again.

title: potCreator can block liquidity rotation
content: The vulnerability is a centralized access‑control flaw that makes the liquidity rotation step of the pot contract callable only by the address that created the pot (potCreator). The contract logic requires the potCreator to call rotateLiquidity after a random number is revealed; this function moves the locked deposits into the next stage and ultimately enables participants to withdraw their winnings. Because no alternative path exists, if the potCreator never invokes rotateLiquidity—whether due to loss of the private key, negligence, or malicious intent—the funds remain permanently locked inside the contract. The root cause is the combination of a single‑owner privileged function and a hard dependency on the same address to reveal entropy, which causes a single point of failure. An attacker or a benign but unavailable potCreator can therefore prevent the contract from progressing, resulting in user deposits that appear to be accepted but never become withdrawable. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a successful deposit, yet later the balance shown for the user remains unchanged or becomes zero when they expect a refund or prize. The impact is high because participants lose access to their funds and the protocol’s economic guarantees are broken; the locked capital cannot be recovered without a contract upgrade. This condition occurs after a pot is created and before rotateLiquidity is called, and it affects every participant who deposited into that pot as well as the overall trustworthiness of the protocol. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that highlighted the lack of a fallback withdrawal mechanism and the reliance on the potCreator for entropy revelation. It is hard to notice because the contract does not emit explicit warnings when rotateLiquidity is not called, and the normal flow appears functional until the withdrawal step is attempted. The bug belongs to the class of privileged‑function‑only‑access and liquidity‑lock bugs, where business logic assumes a single trusted actor to perform a critical state transition. To remediate, the contract should introduce a time‑based escape hatch: after a reasonable period, rotateLiquidity should become unavailable and participants should be allowed to withdraw their deposits directly, or the rotation function should be opened to any caller who can provide a valid proof of the random number, thereby removing the single point of failure.
summary: Only potCreator can call rotateLiquidity(). If potCreator for any reason doesn't call this function, funds are permanently locked. The only way to withdraw it would be to use the merkle tree which we have recommended to change to so that it can't access user funds. potCreator may not call rotateLiquidity() for multiple reasons like losing the private key, or maliciousness. This require check can't be removed as only the requestor of the random number in createPot() should reveal the random number used to declare winner, otherwise the call to entropy.reveal() reverts.

title: potCreator can participate in multiple rounds and lose rewards
content: The contract implements a lottery‑style pot where each round selects a single winner and records the reward for that address. Business logic assumes that an address can win only once, so the reward for a winner is expected to be claimable after the round ends. However, the implementation automatically adds the potCreator address as a participant in every new round without checking whether that address has already won. Consequently, if the potCreator wins a round, the reward stored for that address is later overwritten when the potCreator is added again and wins a subsequent round. The earlier reward becomes inaccessible because the contract’s accounting overwrites the previous entry instead of preserving it or aggregating multiple rewards. This flaw can be triggered simply by starting a new round after the potCreator has already won; the contract does not enforce a has‑won flag for the creator, so the creator can repeatedly re‑enter and win. The impact is that funds that should have been claimable from earlier rounds disappear from the user’s perspective – the UI may show a zero balance or a missing payout even though the contract technically holds the ether. Affected parties include the potCreator (who loses previously earned rewards), any participants who rely on the guarantee that each winner receives a unique payout, and the overall protocol reputation because the fairness assumption is broken. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the participant‑addition logic and noticed the missing check against pot.hasWon. It is subtle because the contract does not emit explicit errors when a reward is overwritten; only when a user attempts to claim the earlier reward will they see an empty balance, which can be mistaken for a normal zero‑payout scenario. To remediate, the contract should verify that potCreator (or any address) has not already won before adding it as a participant in a new round, for example by checking a hasWon flag or by excluding the creator from the participant list after a win. Additionally, reward accounting should be designed to either accumulate multiple rewards per address or store them per round to avoid accidental overwriting, thereby preserving the intended one‑time‑win guarantee and ensuring that all earned funds remain claimable.
summary: The intention of the team is to not let the winner enter the round again. However, the potCreator always becomes participant in the next round. Hence, if potCreator is a winner, it breaks assumptions taken for the winner that an address wins only once in a pot. If potCreator wins again, the reward won in a future round overwrites all the rewards won in past rounds making it unclaimable.

title: Signature can be reused
content: The vulnerability is a signature replay flaw that allows an authenticated address to join a round multiple times by reusing the same signed message and nonce. The contract expects the nonce supplied with the signature to guarantee uniqueness, but because the nonce is only passed as a function argument and not stored or checked for prior use, the same nonce can be submitted repeatedly. An attacker can therefore replay a valid signature, causing the contract to treat each replay as a distinct participant entry. This can be exploited by submitting the same signed join request up to numParticipants‑1 times, effectively crowding out other legitimate participants and giving the attacker a majority of entries. When the round is settled, the attacker’s overwhelming share of entries makes it highly probable that the attacker will be selected as the winner, allowing them to claim the entire pot and deprive honest users of their contributions. The issue manifests whenever a user attempts to join a round; the contract does not enforce a one‑time‑only rule for each address or nonce, so repeated joins are accepted. All participants, especially those who rely on fair competition, are affected because their chances of winning are reduced and their funds may be lost. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the join logic and identified that the nonce parameter was not persisted or validated against replay. Because the contract does not emit explicit warnings and the UI may simply show that the join succeeded, the problem can be hard to notice until a round ends with an unexpected winner or missing funds. The bug belongs to the class of replay attacks caused by improper nonce handling and insufficient state tracking. From a user perspective the symptom is that after a few joins the interface may stop accepting new participants, or a user may see that their contribution disappears after the round, contrary to the expectation that each address can join only once and that the pot will be fairly distributed. To remediate the issue the contract should record each used nonce or maintain a mapping of addresses that have already joined a given round, rejecting any subsequent join attempts from the same address or with a previously used nonce, thereby ensuring that each authenticated participant can enter at most once.
summary: An authenticated address (say A) can join multiple times due to signature replay attack. The nonce used here also comes as an argument, hence can be reused. This has two issues: It blocks other authenticated addresses to participate. A can enter into the pot so many times that it becomes the majority in participants (up to numParticipants - 1 times). So with very high probability, it wins the pot effectively guaranteeing winning and taking other participants' contributions.

title: createPot() reverts due to incorrect condition on fee
content: The contract function responsible for creating a new betting pot requires the caller to send a fixed fee together with the transaction. The implementation uses a require statement that checks the condition msg.value < fee and reverts with the message "Insufficient fee" when the condition is false. Because require only passes when the condition evaluates to true, the current logic actually rejects any call where the sent value is equal to or greater than the required fee. As a result, a legitimate user who supplies exactly the fee – which is the intended usage – triggers a revert, and the pot is never created. The root cause is a simple inequality mistake: the contract validates the payment with the wrong relational operator, effectively enforcing a fee that is lower than the required amount instead of matching it. An attacker does not need to exploit a complex flaw; simply attempting to use the function causes a denial‑of‑service condition, preventing honest participants from creating pots and halting the protocol’s core functionality. The impact is that users see a transaction failure with the "Insufficient fee" error, the UI reports that the pot could not be created, and no funds are locked or transferred, but the protocol cannot generate revenue from fees and may appear broken to participants. This condition occurs every time createPot() is called with msg.value equal to the fee (the normal case) or higher, which is any realistic scenario. All users, as well as the protocol’s business logic that depends on successful pot creation, are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the payment validation logic. It can be hard to notice because the error message "Insufficient fee" seems appropriate, masking the fact that the inequality is reversed; developers may assume the check is correct without testing the exact fee amount. The vulnerability belongs to the class of payment‑validation bugs where the contract enforces an incorrect condition on msg.value, leading to unintended reverts. To remediate, the require should be changed to require(msg.value == fee) so that the transaction only succeeds when the exact fee is supplied, or alternatively require(msg.value >= fee) with additional logic to refund any excess amount, thereby aligning the contract’s behavior with the intended economic model and preventing the denial‑of‑service scenario.
summary: entropy needs fee amount to be sent as msg.value, but createPot() doesn't let the caller send fee value along with the call due to this require condition: require(msg.value < fee, "Insufficient fee"); Thus, the call reverts blocking the creation of a pot.

title: riskPoolBalance is overwritten
content: The vulnerability consists of an incorrect update to the contract's risk pool balance. Instead of accumulating the new risk amount with the existing pool, the code reassigns the variable, effectively overwriting the previously stored value. The root cause is a simple assignment statement that copies the current locked balance back into the storage slot rather than adding the new contribution. This logic executes at the end of each game round, particularly when no new player joins the next round. Because the overwritten value discards any previously aggregated risk, the protocol loses the ability to carry forward funds that should be available for future payouts. From a user's perspective the symptom is that a contribution that was expected to remain in the pool either disappears or results in a zero balance when a round ends without new participants, leading to missing refunds or reduced payouts. The impact is a loss of funds that were meant to be retained, breaking the accounting assumptions of the game and potentially causing the protocol to under‑pay winners or retain unclaimed assets. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the state‑update logic of the risk pool. It can be hard to notice because the variable name suggests a balance and the assignment looks syntactically correct, yet the semantic effect is a silent reset of the pool. The bug belongs to the class of state‑overwrites where a cumulative variable is mistakenly reassigned, a common source of accounting errors in smart contracts. To remediate the problem the update should use an additive operation, accumulating the new amount onto the existing balance rather than overwriting it, thereby preserving the intended risk pool across rounds.
summary: riskPoolBalance is reassigned instead of adding it to the new amount: pot.riskPoolBalance = riskPoolBalance; riskPoolBalance currently is locked but the intention is to reuse it in later rounds if a player doesn't join. In that case, the aggregated risk pool won't be used since it only stores the latest value.

title: rotateLiquidity() can revert if all participants don't join a pot
content: The vulnerability resides in a function that selects a winner for a liquidity‑rotation pot. The contract stores the expected number of participants in a variable (pot.numParticipants) and also keeps an array of actual participant addresses (pot.participants). The winner is chosen by computing a random index as uint256(randomNumber) % pot.numParticipants and then reading pot.participants[winnerIndex]. If, for any reason, fewer users actually join the pot than the value recorded in pot.numParticipants, the length of the participants array becomes smaller than pot.numParticipants. In that situation the modulo operation can produce an index that is larger than the highest valid array index, causing an out‑of‑bounds read. Solidity treats this as a runtime error and the transaction reverts. The root cause is a mismatch between the declared participant count and the real size of the participants list, which is not validated before the index calculation. An attacker or a careless user could trigger the condition by withdrawing or failing to join after the pot has been created, leading to a state where pot.participants.length < pot.numParticipants. When rotateLiquidity() is called under those conditions, the contract reverts, preventing the rotation from completing. The impact is a denial‑of‑service: users who expect their liquidity to be rotated or to receive a potential reward see the transaction fail, their balances remain unchanged, and the UI may display an unexpected error or a missing winner. Funds are not stolen, but they become temporarily inaccessible because the rotation cannot proceed. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by Spearbit, who noticed that the code uses pot.numParticipants for the modulo instead of the actual array length. It can be hard to notice because the failure only occurs when the participant count is not fully met, a scenario that may not appear in normal test runs. To remediate, the winner index should be derived from the actual participants array length (uint256(randomNumber) % pot.participants.length) or the contract should enforce that pot.numParticipants always equals pot.participants.length before the selection logic runs. This aligns the selection algorithm with the true state of the array and eliminates the out‑of‑bounds access, restoring correct behavior and preventing the denial‑of‑service condition.

title: User funds can be withdraw without their permission
content: The contract contains a function called claimFunds that is intended to let participants claim the yield generated by a shared USDB pot. The function verifies a Merkle proof that a leaf’s claimAmount matches the amount recorded in the tree, but it does not enforce any relationship between the claimed amount and the actual yield earned by each participant. Because the contract owner can set the Merkle root arbitrarily, the owner can construct a Merkle tree whose leaves sum to the total amount of USDB deposited by all participants. When the owner calls claimFunds with a proof that matches this malicious tree, the contract treats the request as a legitimate claim and transfers the entire balance to the owner. This flaw arises from a missing invariant that the claimed amount must be bounded by the accrued interest, not by the total deposits. Exploitation is straightforward: the owner creates a crafted Merkle tree, generates a valid proof for the total deposit amount, and invokes claimFunds, causing all user funds to be withdrawn without any user interaction. The impact is severe: participants see their balances drop to zero, expected refunds or yield payments never arrive, and the protocol loses trust and potentially becomes insolvent. The vulnerability manifests whenever the owner calls claimFunds, which can happen at any time because there is no time‑based or role‑based restriction beyond the owner’s ability to set the Merkle root. All users who have deposited USDB are affected, as their funds can be taken without consent. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the logical flow of claimFunds and noticed that the function only checks Merkle proof validity but never checks that the amount being claimed is limited to earned yield. Because the function appears to perform a standard Merkle‑based claim, the problem can be subtle and may not be caught by simple unit tests that only cover normal yield‑claim scenarios. To remediate, the contract should enforce that claimAmount is never greater than the net interest accrued for the claimant, separate user principal from yield in storage, and restrict withdrawals to the yield component only. Additionally, the owner should not be able to arbitrarily set the Merkle root; a trusted off‑chain process or a decentralized oracle should manage the root, and proper access controls should be added to prevent unauthorized manipulation. In user‑facing terms, a participant who expects to receive a small interest payment may instead find that their entire deposited balance has vanished, with the UI showing a zero balance and no transaction history of a personal withdrawal.
summary: claimFunds() enables the owner to withdraw all USDB funds in the contract. So pot participants funds can be withdrawn without their permission: Owner creates a merkle tree with leaves such that the total claimAmount in leaves equal to the deposits made by pot participants. claimFunds() is called and withdraws all funds.

title: Claimed gas is locked forever
content: The vulnerability is a logic flaw that causes gas accumulated by the contract to be transferred back into the contract itself instead of being sent to an external address that can later withdraw it. The root cause is that the claim function deposits the claimed amount into the contract’s own balance and the contract does not provide any subsequent withdraw mechanism. An attacker or any user who invokes the claim function can trigger the transfer, but because there is no function to move the funds out of the contract, the claimed gas becomes permanently locked inside the contract’s internal accounting. This can be exploited simply by calling the claim function; the transaction succeeds, the contract’s internal gas counter is reduced, and the ether is added to the contract’s balance, but no one can ever retrieve it. The impact is that legitimate users who expect to recover unused gas end up with zero payable amount, effectively losing the value of the gas they thought they could claim. The condition occurs whenever the claim function is executed, regardless of who calls it, because the contract lacks a withdrawal path. All participants who rely on the contract’s gas reimbursement mechanism are affected, including end‑users, the protocol’s economic model, and any party that assumes the claimed gas will be payable. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the flow of the claim function and noticed the absence of any external transfer or withdraw routine. It may be hard to notice because the function does not revert and appears to succeed, giving the impression that the claim was processed correctly, while the funds are silently trapped. The appropriate remediation is to redesign the claim logic so that the claimed gas is sent to a designated recipient (for example, the caller or a treasury address) and to implement a withdraw function that allows the contract owner or authorized parties to retrieve any residual balance.
