This class of bug is commonly referred to as a replay‑or‑double‑execution vulnerability caused by inconsistent state updates across different transaction entry points, and it breaks the fundamental accounting assumption that each transaction consumes a unique nonce.

title: H-1 Front-running for the bid() method
content: The vulnerability is a front‑running weakness in the auction contract’s bid() function. The contract accepts a new bid if it is higher than the current highest bid and finalises the winner based on the last transaction that reaches the auction end time. Because the contract does not separate the bidding phase from the resolution phase, an attacker can observe a legitimate bidder’s transaction in the mempool and submit a slightly higher bid with a higher gas price so that it is mined just before the auction deadline. This timing advantage allows the attacker to become the winner even though the original bidder offered a valid amount. The root cause is the reliance on a simple comparison of bid values against the current highest bid and the use of the block timestamp to determine the auction end without any commit‑reveal scheme, delay buffer, or resolution step that would lock in bids from a previous block. Exploitation is straightforward: a malicious participant monitors pending bids, crafts a transaction that increases the bid by the smallest possible increment (often one unit), and ensures it is included in the block that closes the auction. The impact is that the auction’s fairness is compromised, legitimate participants may lose the chance to win, and funds can be transferred to an attacker who did not earn the win through genuine competition. This occurs specifically when the auction is close to its end, i.e., during the final few seconds or minutes of the bidding period. All users who intend to place a bid are affected, as are the protocol’s reputation and any downstream logic that assumes the highest bid reflects honest competition. The issue was identified during a manual security audit that examined the auction lifecycle and noticed that the bid() call can be front‑run or back‑run without any protection. The problem is subtle because the contract behaves correctly under normal conditions; only the ordering of transactions near the deadline reveals the flaw, making it easy to miss in functional testing. To remediate the issue, the contract should separate the bidding phase from the resolution phase, for example by taking the highest bid from the previous block during a resolveAuction step, or by employing a commit‑reveal scheme, a minimum time buffer after each new bid, or a sealed‑bid auction design that prevents an attacker from reacting to a pending bid. Conceptually, the fix ensures that once a block is mined, the set of bids considered for the winner cannot be altered by later transactions in the same block, thereby restoring the intended economic guarantees of the auction.
summary: The bid() transaction (Auction.sol#L105) with a slightly higher bid can be sent right before the end of an auction. The winner can be the one who bids a unit more at the last moment. Every bid transaction can be front-run or back-run. Thus, a legitimate bidder can be prevented from making a proper bid.

title: H-2 Rejected auction is always in default state
content: The vulnerability consists of a pool that becomes permanently stuck after an auction is rejected. When the auction resolver is called with a false flag, the pool’s internal status is left in a default state that indicates a rejected auction, but the contract does not provide any transition that allows the pool owner or participants to close the pool or withdraw funds. As a result, any subsequent call to the pool’s allowWithdrawalAfterNoAuction or close functions reverts, preventing the pool from being removed from the factory’s registry and leaving the assets locked indefinitely. The root cause is the missing handling of the rejected‑auction branch in the pool lifecycle logic; the state machine only permits closure when an auction succeeds or when other explicit conditions are met, and it never accounts for the false outcome. An attacker or a benign user can trigger the rejected path simply by causing the auction to fail, for example by not meeting the minimum bid or by deliberately calling resolveAuction with false. Once this path is taken, the pool cannot be closed, so the funds remain inaccessible, the UI continues to display the pool as active, and users see no withdrawal option or balance updates. This situation violates the protocol’s accounting assumptions that every pool will eventually resolve to either a successful auction or a clean closure, and it breaks the expectation that users can always retrieve their deposits after an auction ends. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the pool lifecycle functions and noticed that the revert messages were triggered after a rejected auction, indicating an unreachable state. Because the pool appears to exist normally in the factory’s list, the problem can be hard to notice until a user attempts to close it and encounters an unexpected revert. The recommended remediation is to extend the state machine to include a transition that allows a pool in the rejected‑auction state to be closed, or to document the existence of this state in the protocol’s whitepaper so that users are aware of the limitation. Implementing a conditional check in the close function (for example at PoolBase.sol line 180) that permits closure when the auction flag is false would resolve the issue and restore the ability for owners and participants to withdraw their funds.

title: H-3 Protect CPOOLs in PoolFactory
content: The vulnerability resides in the PoolFactory contract where a generic sweep function is exposed that permits the caller to transfer any ERC20 token held by the factory, including the CPOOL token that is used to pay user rewards. The root cause is the lack of a restriction or access control that distinguishes between stray tokens and the reward token; the sweep logic simply iterates over a token address supplied by the caller and moves the entire balance to the caller’s address. An attacker who can invoke this function—typically the contract owner or any address granted the sweep role—can call it with the CPOOL token address after the factory has accumulated reward balances. By doing so the attacker withdraws all CPOOL tokens from the factory, effectively emptying the pool of reward funds. When a legitimate user later attempts to claim their reward, the claim transaction either returns zero tokens or reverts because the factory no longer holds any CPOOL to distribute. From the user’s perspective the UI shows that a reward is pending but the received amount is zero, or the claim button fails without a clear error, leading to confusion and loss of expected earnings. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the factory’s token management functions, where the auditor noted that the sweep routine does not filter out the protocol’s own reward token. This bug can be hard to notice because sweep functions are commonly used for recovering accidentally sent tokens, and developers may assume that only non‑essential tokens will be targeted. The flaw violates the accounting assumption that reward tokens remain locked in the factory until distributed, breaking the protocol’s economic guarantees. To remediate, the sweep function should either be removed or hardened by adding an explicit check that rejects the CPOOL token address, and by limiting the caller to a highly trusted role with multi‑sig or timelock protection. In broader terms, this is a classic “unrestricted token sweep” or “withdrawal of privileged assets” bug where privileged assets are mistakenly treated as generic recoverable tokens, leading to potential fund loss and broken reward logic.
summary: The rewards, which will be paid to the user, are at the factory. Sweep allows to withdraw CPOOL tokens and block the possibility of claiming by users. • PoolFactory.sol#L393

title: H-4 Infinite Block Auction
content: The vulnerability is an improper access‑control design in the auction contract that restricts the resolveAuction function to the contract owner only. Because resolveAuction is the only mechanism that finalises the auction, distributes the winning bid and triggers any associated insurance payout, the owner’s exclusive right creates a denial‑of‑service condition. When the auction end time has passed, any user who placed a lastBid expects the contract to resolve automatically or to be able to invoke the function themselves. Instead, the contract requires the owner to call resolveAuction, and there is no alternative path for users or a time‑based fallback. This root cause – a missing public exit or timeout guard – allows the owner, either intentionally or inadvertently, to withhold the call indefinitely. An attacker controlling the owner role can therefore block the lastBid of a participant, prevent the pool’s users from receiving their insurance or bid refunds, and manipulate market outcomes by keeping the auction open forever. From a user’s perspective the UI will continue to display the auction as active even after the deadline, the user’s balance will not change, and attempts to claim a refund or insurance will fail silently. The impact includes locked funds, loss of expected payouts, erosion of trust in the protocol, and potential market manipulation. The issue was discovered during a security audit performed by MixBytes, which noted that the contract lacks any mechanism for non‑owner callers to resolve the auction after the timeout, making the problem subtle and easy to miss in functional testing because the function works correctly when the owner calls it. To remediate, the contract should allow any participant (or at least the highest bidder) to invoke resolveAuction after the auction end timestamp, or implement an automatic resolution triggered by block time, while preserving proper checks to prevent re‑entrancy or other abuses. This change restores the intended flow where the auction can always be finalised, ensuring that users receive their refunds or insurance payouts and that the market cannot be held hostage by a single privileged address.
summary: The owner may not call resolveAuction (Auction.sol#L139): • to block lastBid of a user on the Auction contract and there is no mechanism to bypass that; • to prevent the pool's users from getting an insurance or bid after the auction; • to manipulate the market.

title: H-5 Double-Adding Pool Vulnerability
content: The vulnerability is a logical duplication flaw in the pool management component of the protocol. When the factory function that registers existing pools for a market is invoked, it appends the pool address to the marketPools array without first checking whether that address is already present. Consequently, if the function is called more than once—whether by an operator mistake, a scripted batch, or a malicious re‑entry—the same pool can be inserted multiple times. The removal routine is written to delete only the first matching entry and does not iterate to eliminate additional duplicates, so a second call to remove the same pool fails to clean the array completely. This situation arises during normal initialization or any subsequent re‑initialization of market pools. Users of the protocol are affected because the UI that reads the marketPools array will display duplicate entries, leading to confusion (e.g., a pool appears twice in the list, making users think there are more options than actually exist). Moreover, every iteration over the array—such as when calculating rewards, aggregating liquidity, or performing batch updates—will process the duplicated entry, consuming extra gas and potentially skewing accounting calculations if the code assumes each pool is unique. The impact is primarily economic: higher transaction costs for anyone interacting with the affected functions and a degraded user experience due to misleading information. The issue was discovered during a manual code audit that highlighted the absence of a uniqueness guard in the initializeExistingPoolsByMarket function and the limited removal logic in the corresponding delete function. It can be hard to notice because the duplicate entries do not immediately cause a revert or loss of funds; they only manifest as subtle UI anomalies and increased gas usage, which may be attributed to normal network conditions. To remediate the problem, the initialization routine should assert or require that the pool address is not already stored in the marketPools array before pushing it, and the removal routine should be updated to eliminate all occurrences of the target address or to enforce a one‑to‑one mapping between pools and array slots. In generic terms, this is a duplicate‑entry bug in a collection data structure that violates the invariant that each element must be unique, breaking business logic that relies on a one‑per‑pool representation and leading to accounting inconsistencies and unnecessary gas consumption.
summary: The PoolFactory.sol#L214 function may add a pool to the marketPools array more than once if the function is called multiple times. This can occur if the function is called by mistake. The PoolFactory.sol#L402 function is unable to remove more than one instance of the same pool from the marketPools array and cannot be called twice for the same pool. As a result, the pool will remain in the array misleading users and also consuming gas when the array is iterated through.

title: H-6 Close active pools via resolveAuctionWithoutGoverment
content: The vulnerability resides in the function resolveAuctionWithoutGoverment, which is intended to finalize an auction only after the auction has legitimately ended and a valid pool has been identified. In the current implementation the function performs only three superficial checks: it requires that the stored tokenId equals zero, that the stored end timestamp equals zero, and that the current block timestamp is at least six days after the stored end timestamp. Because the default values for a newly created auction are zero for both tokenId and end, these checks are trivially satisfied even when no real auction has been started. Moreover, the function proceeds to transfer the last bid amount to the last bidder using currency.safeTransfer. When both lastBidder and lastBid are their default values (address(0) and 0), many ERC‑20 implementations (for example WETH or USDT) allow a transfer of zero tokens to the zero address without reverting. Consequently the function reaches the code that marks the auction as closed (setting auctionInfo[pool].tokenId to type(uint96).max) and invokes IPoolMaster(pool).processDebtClaim(), effectively allowing any caller to close an active pool and trigger a debt‑claim routine without any governance or time‑based restriction. An attacker can exploit this by calling resolveAuctionWithoutGoverment with an arbitrary pool identifier; the missing validation of pool existence and of a non‑zero auction state lets the call succeed. The impact is that active pools can be terminated prematurely, debt claims can be processed without a proper auction outcome, and funds may be redistributed according to the contract’s internal accounting rather than the intended auction result. Users expecting their bids to be honored see their balances unchanged or, in the worst case, see the protocol’s accounting become inconsistent, leading to potential loss of funds or unfair allocation. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that highlighted the absence of robust state checks and the reliance on default zero values. It is difficult to notice because the function does not revert on zero‑value transfers, and the checks appear to enforce a time delay, giving a false sense of security. To remediate the problem the contract should enforce that the pool address is non‑zero and corresponds to a registered pool, that the auction’s tokenId is non‑zero (indicating an active auction), that the auction end timestamp is set and has truly passed, and that lastBidder is a valid address with a positive lastBid amount before any transfer is attempted. Additionally, the contract should reject zero‑value transfers to the zero address or use explicit require statements to guard against such edge cases, and the governance pathway should be re‑introduced to ensure only authorized entities can close auctions.
summary: In commit 68820cb61c8e3fa1714be0aca161d9916c8ac9d3 resolveAuctionWithoutGoverment is called without a pool and time filtering. These checks can be passed by the user (Auction.sol#L266): by default currentAuction.tokenId = 0 require(currentAuction.tokenId == 0, "AC"); by default currentAuction.end = 0 require(block.timestamp >= currentAuction.end, "ANF"); block.timestamp >= 6 days require(block.timestamp - currentAuction.end >= 6 days, "TNP"); lastBidder = 0x0, lastBid = 0 some erc-20 tokens allow to transfer(0x0, 0) currency.safeTransfer( currentAuction.lastBidder, currentAuction.lastBid ); So, anyone can close an active pool at any time and call (Auction.sol#L288): ... auctionInfo[pool].tokenId = type(uint96).max; ... IPoolMaster(pool).processDebtClaim(); ...

title: In PCLBaseSwapInside::_compoundRewards(), if the sellPortion is smaller than rewardSwapThreshold, some of the rewards will move to keepPortion
content: The vulnerability resides in the reward‑compounding routine of the PCLBaseSwapInside contract, specifically in the internal function _compoundRewards. The function separates a portion of newly earned rewards into a "sellPortion" that should be swapped for the underlying token pair (tokens 0 and 1) and a "keepPortion" that is retained for future compounding. A business rule requires the sellPortion to be larger than a configurable rewardSwapThreshold before the swap is executed. The implementation, however, never records the amount of sellPortion that is calculated when the threshold is not met. Consequently, when the sellPortion is smaller than the threshold, the function simply skips the swap and, on the next invocation of _compoundRewards, adds that previously unsold amount to the keepPortion. Over repeated calls, especially when the contract is invoked frequently and the reward accrual per call remains below the threshold, the sellPortion may never be swapped and will continuously be re‑assigned to the keepPortion. This results in rewards that should have been compounded being effectively diverted away from the compounding shares, reducing the expected growth of those shares. From a user perspective, an investor who expects their rewards to be automatically reinvested will see their balance stagnate or even appear to shrink, because the UI shows the reward amount but the underlying compounding calculation does not reflect the expected increase. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the reward distribution logic, where the auditor noticed that the variable representing the sell portion was never persisted or used after a threshold check. The bug is subtle because the contract still executes without reverting and the overall reward flow appears to function; only the accounting of unsold rewards is incorrect, making it easy to miss in functional testing. The root cause is a missing accounting step – the sellPortion is calculated but not stored or accounted for when below the threshold. The impact is a high‑severity loss of expected yield for all participants, potentially leading to lower protocol incentives and user dissatisfaction. To remediate, the contract should introduce a state variable that records the pending sell portion and ensures that any amount that fails the threshold check is either carried forward for the next swap attempt or directly added to the compounding balance, thereby preserving the intended reward economics. In broader terms, this is a classic case of improper state handling in conditional reward‑distribution logic, where a branch skips a critical accounting update, leading to systematic under‑allocation of rewards.
summary:
Rewards allocated to compounding shares are only swapped to tokens 0 and 1 if the sellPortion exceeds the rewardSwapThreshold. However, the allocated sell portion is not accounted for anywhere, which means that if the rewards are not sold due to being smaller than the threshold, a portion of them will go to the keepPortion the next time _compoundRewards() is called.
In the worst scenario, sell portion may always be smaller than the threshold if _compoundRewards() is called frequently enough and no rewards will be allocated to compounding shares.

title: PHyperLPoolSwapInside::_rebalance() checks the price manipulation before and after the swap with the same price threshold
content: The vulnerability resides in the rebalancing routine of the PHyperLPoolSwapInside contract, where a single priceThreshold parameter is reused for two distinct safety checks: a pre‑swap price manipulation test intended to block sandwich attacks, and a post‑swap slippage verification meant to ensure the trade stays within acceptable price deviation. Because the same threshold is applied to both checks, the contract must tolerate a large threshold when a rebalancing operation moves a substantial amount relative to the pool’s liquidity. This large tolerance weakens the pre‑swap anti‑sandwich test, allowing an attacker to front‑run the transaction, execute a small trade that moves the price, and then let the victim’s large rebalancing execute at a manipulated price. The attacker profits from the price difference while the victim receives a worse rate or even loses value. The issue manifests when the pool is asked to rebalance a large volume, i.e., when the amount to be swapped is comparable to the pool’s depth, causing significant slippage. Under those conditions the priceThreshold must be inflated, which inadvertently opens a window for price manipulation. Users experience symptoms such as receiving far fewer tokens than expected, seeing their balances shrink unexpectedly, or observing that a seemingly successful swap leaves them with a poor exchange rate. The problem was identified during a manual audit that examined the logic of the _rebalance function and noticed that the same variable governed both checks, a pattern that can easily hide the mismatch between anti‑sandwich protection and slippage tolerance. The bug is subtle because the contract does perform a price check, so a superficial test may not reveal the weakness unless large‑volume rebalances are simulated. Conceptually, the fix is to separate the concerns: introduce a tighter threshold for the pre‑swap price‑manipulation guard to guarantee that no sandwich attack can succeed, and a separate, possibly looser, threshold for the post‑swap slippage check that reflects the expected market impact of a large trade. This decoupling restores proper validation of both attack vectors and aligns the contract’s behavior with its intended economic guarantees.
summary: PHyperLPoolSwapInside::_rebalance() checks price manipulation before swapping to prevent sandwich attacks and after swapping as a way to mitigate slippage. The same priceThreshold is used for both checks, which means that when rebalancing a large amount in comparison to the pool's liquidity, which would lead to significant slippage, an equally large priceThreshold would need to be used. This means that the PHyperLPoolSwapInside would be vulnerable to sandwich attacks.

title: Missing owner check on from when transferring tokens
content: The vulnerability is a missing ownership verification in the internal token transfer routine of an ERC‑721 style contract. When a caller invokes transferFrom or safeTransferFrom, the contract checks that msg.sender is either approved or the owner of the token via _isApprovedOrOwner, but it never confirms that the address supplied in the from parameter actually owns the token being transferred. As a result, an attacker can craft a call where from is set to a victim’s address, to is the attacker’s address, and tokenId is an NFT that the attacker already owns. The approval check passes because the attacker is the owner of tokenId, and the internal _transfer function proceeds to decrement the balance of the from address without verifying ownership. This causes the victim’s NFT balance to decrease incorrectly, potentially to zero, even though the victim still holds the token. The impact is a denial‑of‑service style loss of accounting integrity: users may be unable to cancel or claim their NFTs, and funds associated with those NFTs become effectively locked. The bug manifests whenever transferFrom or safeTransferFrom is called, under any circumstances where the caller can supply an arbitrary from address. All token holders and the protocol that relies on correct balance accounting are affected. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the logical flow of token transfers and identified the absent owner check as a deviation from the ERC‑721 specification. It can be hard to notice because the transaction does not revert; it appears successful, yet the balances become inconsistent, leading to UI symptoms such as a user seeing a missing or zero balance after a seemingly valid transfer. To remediate, the contract should enforce that the from argument matches the actual owner of tokenId, typically by adding require(ownerOf(tokenId) == from) in the internal _transfer function. This aligns the implementation with the expected ownership model and prevents balance manipulation attacks. The flaw belongs to the class of authorization bypass bugs where insufficient validation of input parameters allows state corruption, specifically an ownership‑verification omission in token transfer logic.
summary: The OrderNFT.transferFrom/safeTransferFrom use the internal _transfer function. While they check approvals on msg.sender through _isApprovedOrOwner(msg.sender, tokenId), it is never checked that the specified from parameter is actually the owner of the NFT. An attacker can decrease other users' NFT balances, making them unable to cancel or claim their NFTs and locking users' funds. The attacker transfers their own NFT passing the victim as from by calling transferFrom(from=victim, to=attackerAccount, tokenId=attackerTokenId). This passes the _isApprovedOrOwner check, but reduces from's balance.

title: Wrong minimum net fee check
content: The vulnerability is a logical error in the fee validation routine of the market factory contract. The protocol defines a minimum net fee (minNetFee) that must be collected from each trade, calculated as the sum of the taker fee and the maker fee. The contract, however, checks the fee pair using an incorrect condition that does not enforce takerFee + makerFee >= minNetFee. As a result, fee configurations that satisfy the protocol’s minimum are mistakenly rejected, while configurations that fall below the minimum are accepted. This flaw can be exploited by a market creator who deploys a market with deliberately low or zero taker and maker fees, thereby bypassing the protocol’s fee collection mechanism. When such a market is used, trades generate no protocol revenue, causing the protocol’s fee pool to remain unchanged while users continue to trade. The impact is a loss of expected fee income for the protocol and a potential unfair advantage for market creators who avoid paying fees. The issue manifests whenever a market is created, because the factory performs the faulty check at deployment time. All participants that rely on the protocol’s fee model—protocol treasury, token holders, and other market participants—are affected. The problem was discovered during a manual security review that compared the intended fee policy with the actual Solidity require statement. Because the check uses a signed‑integer cast and compares the raw taker fee value instead of the summed net fee, the bug can be subtle and may not produce obvious runtime errors; the contract still compiles and markets can be created, making the issue easy to overlook. To remediate, the validation should compute the net fee as the arithmetic sum of takerFee and makerFee (converted to a signed integer) and require that this sum be greater than or equal to minNetFee before allowing market creation. This aligns the implementation with the protocol’s accounting assumptions that every trade must contribute at least the minimum net fee, restoring correct fee collection and preventing market creators from evading fees.
summary: A minimum net fee was introduced that all markets should comply by such that the protocol earns fees. The protocol fees are computed takerFee + makerFee and the market factory computes the wrong check. Fee pairs that should be accepted are currently not accepted, and even worse, fee pairs that should be rejected are currently accepted. Market creators can avoid collecting protocol fees this way.

title: Rounding up of taker fees of constituent orders may exceed collected fee
content: The vulnerability is a rounding error in the fee accounting logic of a decentralized order‑book contract. When a taker fills multiple maker orders, the contract first computes the total taker fee on the summed trade amount and rounds the result up to the nearest wei. It then computes each individual maker order fee separately, also rounding each result up. Because each rounding operation can add up to one wei, the sum of the individually rounded maker fees can exceed the single rounded taker fee by up to the number of filled orders. This discrepancy means the contract’s internal fee balance records more wei than were actually transferred from the taker, leading to a mismatch between the recorded fee balance and the real token balance. The issue can be exploited by constructing a transaction that fills many small orders, inflating the accounted fee and causing the subsequent fee‑collection call to revert with an “ERC20: transfer amount exceeds balance” error. The impact is twofold: the protocol’s accounting becomes inaccurate, potentially hiding revenue loss, and the fee‑collection process can be blocked, resulting in a denial‑of‑service condition for fee withdrawals. The bug manifests only when multiple orders are taken in a single claim and the taker fee percentage is such that the division produces a fractional wei that is rounded up. Users see a fee balance that is higher than the token balance, and attempts to collect fees fail, which may appear as missing funds or a contract that “doesn’t pay out”. The problem was discovered through a unit test written in Foundry that deliberately exercised the claim path with two identical orders and observed the off‑by‑one wei discrepancy. Because the error is only a few wei per order, it can be easily overlooked in normal operation, especially when large volumes mask the small mismatch. The recommended remediation is to use a consistent rounding direction—preferably rounding down (floor) for the taker fee—or to compute the fee once and distribute it without per‑order rounding, thereby ensuring that the recorded fee balance never exceeds the actual transferred amount. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of integer‑division rounding errors that break financial invariants in smart contracts, violating the assumption that fees collected equal fees accounted for and leading to accounting breaks and potential loss of trust in the protocol.

title: Drain tokens condition due to reentrancy in collectFees
content: The vulnerability is a re‑entrancy flaw in the fee‑collection routine of a decentralized exchange pool. The collectFees function transfers accumulated protocol fees to the DAO and to the caller without first locking the contract state or updating the internal fee counters. Because the function does not employ a re‑entrancy guard or follow the check‑effect‑interaction pattern, a malicious token that implements a callback (for example a token with a transfer hook or a token that executes arbitrary code on receipt) can re‑enter collectFees during the external transfer. When re‑entered, the attacker can invoke collectFees again before the original call finishes, causing the contract to transfer the same fee balance multiple times. This condition allows the attacker to drain tokens from the trading pool beyond the recorded fee amount, effectively emptying the pool or stealing fees that should belong to the DAO. The issue manifests when a fee collection is triggered while at least one of the pooled tokens is a contract capable of executing code on transfer. Users observing the UI may see their expected fee balance disappear, receive zero refunds, or notice that the pool’s total liquidity has unexpectedly dropped to zero. The bug was identified during a manual security review that flagged the absence of a re‑entrancy guard in the collectFees implementation. It can be hard to notice because the function appears to succeed and emit normal events, while the underlying state is being manipulated repeatedly in the same transaction. The proper mitigation is to protect the function with a re‑entrancy lock (e.g., OpenZeppelin’s nonReentrant modifier) or to restructure the code so that the fee counters are updated before any external token transfer, thereby eliminating the window for re‑entrancy. This class of bug falls under the broader category of re‑entrancy vulnerabilities that break accounting assumptions and allow an attacker to extract more assets than the contract’s internal accounting permits.
summary: collectFees function is not guarded by a re-entrancy guard. In case a transfer of at least one of the tokens in a trading pair allows to invoke arbitrary code (e.g. token implementing callbacks/hooks), it is possible for a malicious host to drain trading pools. The re-entrancy condition allows to transfer collected fees multiple times to both DAO and the host beyond the actual fee counter.

title: marketOrder() with expendOutput reverts with SlippageError with max tolerance
content: The vulnerability resides in the marketOrder function of the Clober decentralized exchange where the slippage validation logic uses the expendOutput value incorrectly. When a user submits a market order, the contract calculates the amount that will be spent (expendOutput) and compares it against a slippage tolerance parameter supplied by the caller. The implementation mistakenly applies the tolerance check to the wrong side of the inequality, causing the transaction to revert with a SlippageError even when the caller has set the maximum possible tolerance (for example 100%). This logical error means that the order cannot be executed under any circumstances, effectively creating a denial‑of‑service condition for market orders. The bug was discovered during a security audit performed by Spearbit, who noted that the function reverts consistently despite the tolerance being set to its maximum. Because the failure occurs deep inside the order execution path, it may not be obvious from the user interface; users simply see their transaction fail with a generic slippage error and may assume a network issue or a malicious contract. The impact is that traders are unable to place market orders, leading to lost trading opportunities, potential fee loss for liquidity providers, and a perception that the protocol is unreliable. Funds are not actually transferred or stolen; the transaction is reverted, but users still incur gas costs. The issue affects any participant who attempts to trade on the platform, including regular users, market makers, and protocol operators. It is hard to notice because the error only surfaces when the slippage tolerance is explicitly set to its maximum, a scenario that many test suites do not cover. The proper fix is to correct the slippage comparison so that the contract validates the actual output against the tolerance in the intended direction, ensuring that a market order only reverts when the real slippage exceeds the user‑specified limit. Conceptually, this is a logical validation bug in the slippage checking routine, a class of errors where business rules are implemented incorrectly, leading to unintended reverts and broken accounting assumptions.
summary: During the audit the Clober team raised this issue. Added here to track the fixes.

title: H-1 _execute allows you to execute unsuccessful tasks in the future
content: The vulnerability resides in a multisignature wallet where the internal execution routine attempts to perform a low‑level call to a target address and checks the returned success flag. If the call fails, the routine reverts with an error that includes the returned data. However, the contract does not invalidate the transaction record after a revert; the permission to execute that transaction remains stored and can be invoked again later when external conditions change. This design flaw allows an attacker or any authorized executor to re‑trigger a previously failed transaction after a delay, for example after the expirationTime window has passed or after market conditions such as slippage have shifted. The root cause is the absence of a state flag that marks a transaction as permanently failed, combined with a logic path that permits execution of pending transactions without re‑checking the original failure reason. Exploitation proceeds by first submitting a transaction that is expected to fail (e.g., a token swap with a tight slippage limit). The call reverts, but the transaction entry stays in the pending queue. Later, when the price moves or the expiration deadline is reached, the executor calls the same execution function; the contract sees the transaction as still pending and attempts the call again, this time succeeding because the external condition now satisfies the call. The impact includes unintended state changes, loss of funds, or execution of economic actions that the signers did not intend at the original time, such as a swap that should have been aborted but is later performed at an unfavorable rate. The issue manifests whenever a transaction can be retried after a revert, which is especially dangerous for time‑sensitive operations like swaps with slippage protection, token approvals that rely on a deadline, or owner configuration functions that should be one‑shot. All participants who rely on the multisig – token holders, protocol users, and the contract owners – are affected because the wallet no longer guarantees that a reverted transaction is dead. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the execution flow and noticed that the revert path does not clear the pending flag. It can be hard to notice because the contract still emits a revert event, giving the impression that the transaction is fully cancelled, while the internal bookkeeping silently keeps the entry alive. To remediate, the contract should mark a transaction as permanently failed after a revert, preventing any future execution attempts, or it should delete the transaction record entirely. Alternatively, the execution function could include a check that the transaction has not previously failed before allowing a retry. This class of bug falls under “incomplete transaction finalisation” or “re‑executable failed operation”, where business logic assumes a revert equals cancellation, but the implementation does not enforce that invariant. From a user perspective the wallet may show a transaction that initially reported an error, yet later the funds move unexpectedly, balances appear to change without a new user‑initiated action, or a swap that was supposed to be aborted is finally executed, violating the expectation that a failed operation does not affect the account.

title: H-2 A transaction doesn't have the sequence information
content: The vulnerability consists of the absence of a nonce or sequence identifier in the multisignature wallet’s transaction model, which allows any owner with execution rights to arbitrarily reorder a set of previously approved transactions before they are executed. Because the contract stores each approved transaction without an immutable ordering field, the execution routine simply iterates over the pending list and does not verify that the order matches the order in which the owners signed off. This design flaw becomes critical when multiple transactions are intended to be performed as a coordinated sequence, such as a DeFi workflow that requires swapping a token, then providing liquidity, then withdrawing rewards. In such scenarios the economic outcome depends on the precise ordering; an owner who can reorder the calls may front‑run, sandwich, or otherwise extract additional value by executing the steps in a more profitable permutation. The wallet also restricts each transaction to a single target call, forcing complex interactions to be split across several separate transactions. When those separate calls are reordered, the overall logic can break, leading to unexpected token balances, failed trades, or loss of funds. The issue manifests when a batch of approved transactions is pending execution; any owner can trigger the execution in any order, and the contract will happily process each call, giving the false impression that everything succeeded while the final state diverges from the signers’ expectations. Affected parties include the multisig owners, any protocol that relies on the wallet for governance or fund management, and end‑users whose assets are controlled by the wallet. The problem was uncovered during a manual security audit that inspected the transaction handling code and noted the missing nonce field and the single‑target limitation. It can be difficult to detect because the contract does not revert or emit explicit errors; the only symptoms are subtle accounting mismatches such as a balance becoming zero, a refund not arriving, or a DeFi operation yielding less profit than anticipated. To remediate, the wallet should embed a monotonically increasing nonce (or sequence number) with each approved transaction and enforce that the nonce of the transaction being executed matches the next expected value, thereby preventing reordering. Additionally, the contract should support an array of target calls per transaction so that multi‑step DeFi interactions can be performed atomically, preserving the intended business logic and protecting against value‑extraction attacks.
summary:
In case of multiple transactions are approved any owner is able to choose the sequense of transactions. In some cases this owner can extract additional beneﬁts from choosing the ordering.
In addition, transactions allow only one target call per transaction - it may be not enough for DeFi interactions. Complex DeFi interactions require making a few approved transactions, so beneﬁts from sequencing can arise.
• IMultiSigWallet.sol#L11-L18
• MultiSigWalletBase.sol#L378

title: minLiquidityRate formula
content: The vulnerability originates from the way the protocol calculates the minimum liquidity rate (minLiquidityRate) for a mini‑pool borrow when the Mproxy does not hold enough underlying assets. The contract mints debt for the user and a corresponding lending share for the mini‑pool, then expects the mini‑pool’s share (A2) to be sufficient to repay the borrowing debt owed to the main lending pool (A0). The calculation relies on a series of Ray‑precision multiplications that are not mathematically associative; swapping the order of the components introduces tiny rounding errors. The code assumes that the set of interactions with the lending pool (J) and the set of interactions with the mini‑pool (K) coincide and that the time delta between them is bounded by a fixed margin (Δt). Under these assumptions the inequality A0 ≤ A2 (or the stronger A0 ≤ A2 ≤ A1) is believed to hold. However, when the interest rates of the reserve and the mini‑pool diverge, or when there are many more lending‑pool interactions than mini‑pool interactions, the accumulated rounding error and the difference between rL and rB can cause A2 to be smaller than A0. Consequently the mini‑pool cannot fully repay the borrowed amount, leaving the protocol under‑collateralised. From a user’s perspective the borrow transaction may succeed but later the user receives less than expected, or the protocol may revert or lock funds, effectively causing “funds disappear” or “refund calculation error”. The issue is subtle because the discrepancy is only a few Ray units and only manifests after several interactions or over the Δt window, making it hard to detect through simple testing. The flaw was discovered during a formal audit that examined the mathematical model of the minLiquidityRate formula and identified that the code does not compare the computed fmax against the minimum liquidity rate, nor does it enforce the J ⊆ K relationship robustly. To remediate the problem the protocol should enforce that the interest rates of the reserve are synchronised with the mini‑pool’s tranched reserves, explicitly compare the minimum liquidity rate against the maximum of f(0) and f(Δt), and ensure that the time delta between any lending‑pool and mini‑pool interaction never exceeds the allowed margin. Additionally, using a mathematically associative arithmetic representation or increasing precision can mitigate the rounding‑error accumulation, guaranteeing that the repayment inequality holds and preventing loss of liquidity.

title: RewardsController uses inconsistent scaling in handleAction and can lead to transfer DoS to/from minipool market
content: RewardsController.handleAction mixes two different scaling conventions when processing a minipool market (ERC6909 aToken). The function reads IAERC6909(user).scaledTotalSupply, which is expressed in units that incorporate the minipool liquidity index, but later combines this value with balances that are scaled only with the main lending pool index. Because the two indices diverge, the subtraction totalSupplyAsset - userBalance can underflow, causing the internal _totalDiff calculation to wrap and the subsequent _updateUserRewardsPerAssetInternal call to revert. In practice a user who deposits assets into the main pool, moves the resulting aTokens into a minipool, and then tries to withdraw will see the withdrawal transaction fail with no funds transferred, even though the UI shows the expected balance. The bug was discovered during a manual audit of the RewardsController logic, where the special‑case branch for ERC6909 tokens was examined and the mismatch of scaling functions was identified. The issue is subtle because the numbers involved are close and the underflow only appears when the minipool index is higher than the main pool index, a condition that is not obvious from the contract’s public interface. The vulnerability belongs to the class of accounting‑scale mismatches that break reward calculations and can lead to a denial‑of‑service on token transfers. Affected parties include any user of the minipool market, the protocol’s reward distribution mechanism, and potentially the overall liquidity of the platform. The recommended fix is to replace the call to scaledTotalSupply with totalSupply, which returns the raw supply without applying the minipool index, thereby keeping the units consistent across the reward calculation. After the change the diff computation will use comparable units, preventing the underflow and allowing withdrawals to succeed.

title: Index can reach type(uint104).max when asset totalSupply is dust and DoS aToken transfers indefinitely
content: The vulnerability is an arithmetic overflow in the reward‑distribution index used by the RewardsDistributor contracts. The index, which records cumulative rewards per unit of aToken, is stored in a uint104 variable under the assumption that the underlying asset’s total supply will always be at least 10**decimals. The update formula multiplies the global emission rate per second by the elapsed time and by 10**decimals, then divides by the total balance of the asset before adding the result to the current index. When the total balance becomes extremely small – for example when the asset supply is reduced to dust – the division denominator shrinks dramatically and the numerator can exceed the maximum value representable in 104 bits. The require statement that checks newIndex <= type(uint104).max then triggers, causing the transaction that attempts to update rewards to revert. This situation can be triggered deliberately by an attacker who forces the asset supply to drop below a safe threshold, for instance by withdrawing almost all tokens or by deploying a new token with a tiny supply, and then waiting a few seconds for the index calculation to overflow. Once the overflow condition is reached, any subsequent call that tries to accrue or claim rewards for that asset will revert, effectively denying service to all participants. The impact is that users who expect to earn or claim rewards see no accrual; the UI may display zero pending rewards, reward‑claim transactions fail with an “Index overflow” error, and the protocol’s incentive mechanism is broken, potentially eroding trust and leaving allocated reward funds unclaimed. The bug occurs only when the totalSupply is dust and a non‑zero amount of time passes, conditions that are rare in normal operation and therefore easy to miss during testing. It was discovered during a formal audit by Spearbit, which identified the unsafe assumption about totalSupply size and the lack of a guard against tiny balances. The issue belongs to the class of integer‑width overflow bugs in financial accounting logic, where insufficient bit‑width combined with a division by a very small denominator leads to a wrap‑around or revert that can be exploited for denial‑of‑service. To remediate, the index should be stored in a larger integer type (e.g., uint140) that can accommodate extreme values, or the contract should skip index updates when totalBalance falls below a predefined safe threshold, or allow the index to wrap safely because only differences are used in reward calculations. Adding explicit checks for zero or dust balances before performing the multiplication would also prevent the overflow and restore reliable reward distribution.

title: In updateAToken and updateVariableDebtToken of the LendingPoolConfigurator encodedCall is constructed incorrectly
content: The vulnerability originates in the configuration functions that update the aToken and variable debt token contracts of a lending pool. When the configurator builds the calldata for the proxy upgrade, it uses abi.encodeWithSelector and assembles the argument list in the wrong order. Specifically, after encoding the token decimals, the required reserveType argument is omitted, causing the subsequent fields – reserve type, token name, symbol and additional parameters – to be shifted one position left. As a result, the proxy contracts receive malformed data and store an incorrect reserve type together with mismatched name, symbol and configuration parameters. This mismatch means that any later call that references a reserve by its underlying asset and expected reserve type will actually address a different, incorrectly typed reserve. Users interacting with the affected market may see unexpected behavior such as zero balances, missing or wrong token symbols in the UI, or failed withdrawals because the protocol is querying the wrong reserve data. The impact is high because the error propagates to all functions that rely on the reserve metadata, potentially breaking accounting, preventing deposits or withdrawals, and exposing the pool to misallocation of interest or collateral. The bug manifests whenever a new market is added or an existing market is reconfigured through the affected functions, i.e., during pool upgrades or when the configurator is invoked. It affects all participants of the lending pool – borrowers, lenders, and the protocol itself – because the core accounting assumptions about reserve identity are violated. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that inspected the calldata construction logic and identified the missing parameter. It can be hard to notice because the contract still compiles and the proxy upgrade succeeds, but the resulting state inconsistency only appears later when higher‑level operations produce incorrect results. To remediate the problem, the configurator must insert the missing reserveType argument in the correct position and preferably switch to abi.encodeCall, which enforces compile‑time checking of argument order and types, thereby preventing similar mistakes in the future. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “incorrect calldata encoding” or “parameter misalignment” vulnerabilities, where a mismatch between the expected function signature and the supplied arguments leads to corrupted state and broken business logic.
summary:
In updateAToken and updateVariableDebtToken of the LendingPoolConfigurator encodedCall is constructed incorrectly:
```solidity
bytes memory encodedCall = abi.encodeWithSelector(
    /*...*/ selector,
    cachedPool,
    // ...
    input.asset,
    input.incentivesController,
    decimals, // <--- `reserveType` is missing after here
    input.name,
    input.symbol,
    input.params
);
```
and thus RESERVE_TYPE, name, symbol and params will be set incorrectly in the proxy contracts. This will cause all the following calls to query or update data for a wrong reserve in the lending pool: pool.function(_underlyingAsset, RESERVE_TYPE, /*...*/ )

title: ATokenERC6909.totalSupply for debt tokens uses the liquidity index
content: The vulnerability resides in the totalSupply function of the ERC‑6909 token implementation used by the protocol. The function retrieves the scaled total supply from the parent contract and then multiplies it by a pool index that is obtained via POOL.getReserveNormalizedIncome. This logic assumes that the supplied token identifier always corresponds to an aToken, which represents supplied assets. However, the same function is also called for debt tokens (variable debt tokens) where the correct index should be the normalized variable debt index obtained from POOL.getReserveNormalizedVariableDebt. Because the function does not distinguish between aToken and debt token identifiers, it applies the income index to debt token supplies. The root cause is a missing type check that would select the appropriate index based on the token class. When a debt token identifier is passed, the function returns a value that is inflated or deflated depending on the relationship between the income index and the variable debt index. This incorrect totalSupply value propagates to several critical calculations: the utilisation rate used by MiniPoolPiReserveInterestRateStrategy, the oldSupply parameter supplied to the incentives controller in _afterTokenTransfer, and any off‑chain or on‑chain agents that query totalSupply for debt token balances. From a user perspective the symptoms may appear as a mismatch between the displayed variable debt amount and the actual borrowed amount, unexpected zero or unusually high utilisation rates, and incentives that seem to be allocated incorrectly. The issue is subtle because the function still returns a non‑zero number, so a simple sanity check does not reveal the problem; only a deeper audit of the index selection logic uncovers the mismatch. The bug violates the protocol’s accounting assumptions that totalSupply for each token type is scaled by its respective index, leading to inaccurate interest‑rate calculations and potentially mis‑distributed rewards. The flaw was discovered during a security review where the auditor compared the totalSupply implementation against the expected behaviour for debt tokens. To remediate, the totalSupply function must first determine whether the supplied id corresponds to a debt token or an aToken and then apply the correct pool index – POOL.getReserveNormalizedVariableDebt for debt tokens and POOL.getReserveNormalizedIncome for aTokens – before performing the ray multiplication. This change restores correct accounting for both token classes and prevents downstream miscalculations.

title: Minipools can borrow from lending pool reserves that are not borrowable
content: The vulnerability consists of a missing validation step in the mini‑pool borrowing routine of a lending protocol. When a mini‑pool invokes the borrow function, the implementation does not verify that the target reserve is active, not frozen, and that borrowing is enabled in the reserve configuration. It also skips the usual checks that ensure the caller has sufficient collateral, that the health factor of the position is above the required threshold, and that the amount requested respects the aggregate loan‑to‑value limits derived from the supplied collateral. Because these safeguards are omitted, a mini‑pool can request an unbacked loan from any reserve, even one that has been frozen or marked as non‑borrowable. An attacker can trigger the executeMiniPoolBorrow entry point with arbitrary parameters, causing the protocol to transfer assets out of the reserve without creating a corresponding debt entry or updating accounting balances. The immediate impact is that funds may disappear from the lending pool, users receive no assets in return, and the protocol’s accounting invariants are violated, potentially leading to insolvency of the pool. This condition occurs whenever the mini‑pool borrowing path is used, regardless of the reserve’s state, and affects any participant whose assets are held in the affected reserves, including lenders, borrowers, and the protocol itself. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that compared the mini‑pool borrow flow with the standard lending pool borrow flow and identified the absent checks. It can be hard to notice because the code path appears similar to the regular borrow function, and the missing assertions are not obvious without side‑by‑side comparison. To remediate, the borrow routine must be updated to include the same reserve‑status verification (checking that the reserve is not frozen and that borrowingEnabled is true), enforce collateral presence, validate the health factor, and enforce LTV‑based borrowing limits, thereby restoring the intended economic guarantees of the lending pool.
summary:
In this context unlike the borrow flow of the lending pool we don't check whether:
• The reserve is not frozen. This check is later performed when one deposits assets into the lending pool again when calling:
```solidity
ILendingPool(vars.LendingPool).deposit(
    underlying, true, vars.amountReceived, address(this)
);
```
• The reserve can be borrowed from.
And also based on the assumption that it is an unbacked borrow the following checks are omitted:
• Checking that there are some collaterals.
• The position of the mini pool is healthy (checking the health factor).
• The amount being borrowed does not exceed what is allowed based on the total collateral and average LTV and the total borrowed amount.

title: Mix of scaled and non-scaled parameters in _afterTokenTransfer
content: The vulnerability is a unit‑mixing arithmetic error that occurs in the _afterTokenTransfer hook of an ERC6909‑based token. The function receives the transfer amount already expressed in scaled units (shares) because the ERC6909 base contract normalises the value by dividing by the token’s index. However, the hook reads the previous total supply and the sender and receiver balances using the unscaled getters totalSupply(id) and balanceOf(address,id). Those values are expressed in raw token units, not in shares. When the code later adds or subtracts the scaled amount from these unscaled values – for example oldToBalance = oldToBalance - amount – the arithmetic mixes two different units. The mixed‑unit values are then forwarded to the INCENTIVES_CONTROLLER.handleAction call, which assumes all inputs are in the same scaled representation. Because of the mismatch, the incentives controller records an incorrect snapshot of supply and balances, leading to wrong reward calculations. An attacker can trigger a mint, burn or ordinary transfer to cause the controller to credit too few incentives or, conversely, to over‑credit rewards that can be harvested later. The impact is a distortion of the protocol’s accounting: users may see their expected reward amount drop to zero, receive a smaller amount than promised, or the protocol may unintentionally distribute excess tokens, jeopardising economic security. The bug manifests whenever _afterTokenTransfer is executed – i.e., on every token mint, burn or transfer – and affects all token holders, the incentives controller, and any downstream contracts that rely on accurate reward data. It was discovered during a manual security audit that inspected the arithmetic in the hook and noticed the inconsistent use of scaled versus unscaled values. The problem is subtle because the token balances themselves appear correct on‑chain; only the incentive accounting is wrong, making it easy to miss in functional tests that only check balance transfers. The proper fix is to ensure that all values supplied to the incentives controller are consistently scaled. This can be achieved by reading the supply and balances through the parent contract’s scaled getters (e.g., super.totalSupply and super.balanceOf) or by explicitly converting unscaled values to shares before arithmetic. Using Solidity’s type system or wrapper libraries to enforce unit safety at compile time would also prevent future mixing errors. In summary, the bug belongs to the class of “unit‑mixing arithmetic” or “scale mismatch” vulnerabilities, where calculations combine values expressed in different units, leading to incorrect financial outcomes such as missing or inflated rewards, which violates the protocol’s accounting assumptions and user expectations of receiving correct incentives after a transfer.

title: DoSing vault rehypothecation through flashloans
content: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that appears when the AToken contract processes a flash‑loan request. The flash‑loan entry point calls transferUnderlyingTo, which withdraws the requested amount from the vault, updates the internal accounting variable _underlyingAmount by subtracting the amount, and then sends the tokens to the borrower. After the borrower’s callback finishes, the borrower returns the same amount of underlying tokens to the AToken contract. The repayment handler, handleRepayment, only increments _underlyingAmount by the repaid amount and does not invoke the internal _rebalance routine that would reconcile the contract’s token balance with its accounting state. Because the rebalance step is omitted, the vault’s external token balance can become zero while the internal accounting still reports a positive balance. Subsequent operations that rely on the vault’s ability to rehypothecate assets – for example, other flash‑loans or liquidation calls – will see an empty token pool and revert, effectively locking the vault and preventing any further borrowing. The root cause is the asymmetric handling of state: withdrawal updates both the balance and the accounting, but repayment updates only the accounting, leaving the two out of sync. The issue is triggered only during flash‑loan execution, when the contract is expected to temporarily move tokens out and back in, and it is exposed even when the vault is otherwise healthy (not paused and below its deposit cap). Users experience the problem as failed transactions or “rehypothecation unavailable” errors, often seeing no funds returned or a sudden revert without an obvious on‑chain error. The bug was uncovered by a fuzzing campaign performed by the Cod3x team, which repeatedly exercised the flash‑loan flow and observed the mismatch. It is difficult to notice because the internal variable _underlyingAmount appears correct, masking the fact that the actual ERC‑20 balance is empty. To remediate the issue, the contract should ensure that _rebalance is called after any repayment that changes the token balance, or restrict rebalance calls to the flash‑loan path only, as suggested in the recommendation. By keeping the accounting and the real token balance synchronized, the vault can safely accept repayments and continue to provide rehypothecation services without risking a denial of service.

title: Significant rounding errors due to gameETH not having precision
content: The vulnerability is a precision loss caused by integer division when converting a raw token amount into the internal accounting unit called gameETH. In the functions that add gameETH and reinvest, the contract computes gameETH as amount divided by gameETHPrice, where gameETHPrice can be a very large integer (for example 1e12 in the test suite). Because Solidity integer division truncates toward zero, any fractional part of the division is discarded, creating a rounding error that can be as large as gameETHPrice‑1. With a price of 1e12 this translates to a loss of up to roughly 0.0023 USD per operation, and the error scales linearly with the price, so higher prices produce proportionally larger monetary loss. The bug appears whenever a user deposits, upgrades, or reinvests funds, because each of those paths invokes the same division without applying additional scaling or fixed‑point arithmetic. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that the expected refund, upgrade credit, or reinvested balance is slightly lower than anticipated; in extreme cases the rounding can reduce a small deposit to zero, making the user see no balance change or a missing few cents. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the arithmetic in up::addGameETH and Codeup::reinvest and noticed the absence of any precision‑enhancing helpers such as _getUpgradePrice or _getYield. It is hard to notice because the per‑transaction discrepancy is tiny and may be dismissed as normal gas cost or rounding noise, yet it accumulates over many operations and can lead to a measurable erosion of user funds. This precision loss violates the protocol’s accounting assumptions that the internal representation of value is lossless and that users receive the exact amount they contributed or are entitled to. An attacker could repeatedly trigger the vulnerable paths to amplify the rounding loss, effectively draining small amounts from many users over time. The recommended remediation is to introduce a scaling factor (for example using a fixed‑point library or multiplying the numerator before division) so that gameETH calculations retain sufficient decimal places, and to adjust all related price‑retrieval functions to operate with the same precision. By doing so the contract will preserve the intended value across conversions and eliminate the systematic under‑payment that currently harms users.
summary: UP-H01 Significant rounding errors due to gameETH not having precision up::addGameETH() and Codeup::reinvest(), gameETH is obtained as gameETH = amount / gameETHPrice, which means there may be rounding errors. gameETH has no up::_getUpgradePrice() and up::_getYield(), which have no extra precision. Thus, as gameETHPrice may be a big value - currently 1e12 in the tests, the rounding error may be up to 1e12 - 1, which is approx 0.0023 USD. If the price is increased, the rounding error grow to bigger values causing significant loss of funds for users. up::_getUpgradePrice() and Codeup::_getYield() and decreasing the gameETHPrice so gameETH inherits the decimals of ETH.

title: Permissions can drain approvals given to certain paymasters
content: The vulnerability stems from the fact that the Smart Wallet Permissions system only verifies that a paymaster is allowlisted during the execution phase (the beforeCalls function) and does not perform this check during the validation phase of an ERC‑4337 user operation. Because the validation step can succeed even when a non‑allowlisted paymaster is supplied, a permission can trigger a paymaster that is authorized to debit the wallet (for example an ERC20 paymaster that withdraws tokens to cover gas) during validation. The paymaster will charge the account regardless of whether the subsequent execution phase succeeds or the beforeCalls check later reverts. An attacker can craft a permission that references such a paymaster and optionally inflate the gas limit, causing the paymaster to withdraw the pre‑approved token balance rapidly. This results in the user’s balance being drained, often without any visible error in the UI – the transaction may appear to have failed while the funds have already been taken, leading to symptoms such as a zero balance, missing refunds, or unexpected token loss. The issue affects any user of the Smart Wallet Permissions system who has previously approved a paymaster outside the allowlist, as well as protocol operators who rely on the allowlist to enforce trust boundaries. It was discovered during a security audit (Spearbit) that highlighted the misplaced allowlist check. The problem is hard to notice because the charge occurs before the execution revert, so standard revert‑based debugging does not reveal the loss. Conceptually, this is an authorization‑check ordering bug where a critical permission is enforced in the wrong phase, allowing privilege escalation and fund draining. The recommended mitigation is to move the paymaster allowlist verification into the validation phase, for example by embedding the allowed paymaster address directly in the Permission struct or by redesigning the validation logic to respect the isPaymasterEnabled mapping, thereby ensuring that only approved paymasters can participate at any stage of the user operation.

title: Staking.earned calculates the rewards wrongly
content: The vulnerability resides in the reward‑calculation routine of a staking contract. The function that reports a user’s earned rewards computes a proportional share of the contract’s token balance based on the user’s stake and the total amount staked. When the contract’s token balance is lower than the total amount staked – a situation that occurs after the contract suffers a loss, for example when a game round pays out more than it receives – the routine returns the user’s proportional share instead of zero. This logic error means that even though the contract is in deficit, the function still reports a positive reward and the privileged giveReward() call distributes those tokens to the user. An attacker who can trigger giveReward (typically the contract owner or a manager) after a loss can therefore cause the contract to hand out tokens that do not actually exist in surplus, draining the remaining balance. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a reward amount even though the pool has shrunk, leading to unexpected token transfers or, conversely, to a sudden disappearance of funds when the contract becomes insolvent. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the edge case where totalTokenBalance < totalStaked. It is subtle because the main calculation appears mathematically correct for the normal case; only the conditional branch that handles a deficit is flawed, making it easy to overlook during testing. The bug belongs to the class of “incorrect accounting under negative balance” or “reward calculation with insufficient funds”. To remediate, the function should explicitly return zero when the contract balance is lower than the total staked amount, or otherwise ensure that rewards are only paid from surplus tokens. This change restores the invariant that rewards cannot exceed the net profit of the staking pool, preserving protocol economics and preventing unintended token loss.

title: giveReward() does not update the stake balances
content: The vulnerability resides in the staking contract’s giveReward() function, which is intended to distribute a profit amount to a specific staker when called by the contract owner or manager. The function transfers the reward but fails to adjust the internal accounting variables that represent the individual staker’s balance and the aggregate totalStaked amount. Because the stake balance is not increased, the protocol’s accounting continues to treat the staker’s contribution as unchanged, while the reward pool is reduced. Consequently, when future rewards are calculated proportionally to each staker’s share of the total stake, the missing update causes a portion of the rewards that should belong to other participants to be incorrectly allocated to the staker whose reward was just given. This misallocation can be exploited by repeatedly invoking giveReward() for a chosen address, allowing the owner or manager to siphon rewards away from the broader pool without any direct transfer of tokens from the victim’s balance. The impact is a reduction in expected earnings for honest stakers, potentially leading to a net loss of funds for the community and erosion of trust in the protocol’s fairness. The issue manifests each time giveReward() is executed, under the condition that the caller has the privileged role required to invoke the function. All participants who have deposited tokens into the staking pool are affected because the proportional reward calculation becomes inaccurate. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the state‑mutation logic of reward distribution and noticed that the stake balance and totalStaked variables were never updated after a reward transfer. The problem is subtle because the reward transfer itself succeeds, so a user may see a token transfer in their wallet and assume the accounting is correct, while the contract’s internal ledger silently diverges. Detecting the discrepancy requires inspecting the contract’s storage values before and after reward distribution, which is not obvious from the UI. To remediate the issue, the giveReward() implementation should be amended to increment the targeted staker’s recorded balance and the global totalStaked amount by the reward value, or alternatively to adjust the reward accounting logic so that the total stake reflects the newly added tokens. This change restores the invariant that the sum of all individual balances equals the totalStaked value and ensures that future reward calculations distribute profits fairly according to each participant’s actual stake.
summary: In the Staking contract, the giveReward() function can be called by the owner or the manager to distribute the profit of a staker. However, this function does not update the stake balance of the staker and the total staked amount. As a result, a portion of other stakers' rewards will be distributed to the staker whose reward is being given.

title: Users can potentially steal other user's staking rewards
content: The contract implements a staking mechanism where a user’s staked balance is recorded at the moment of deposit and later used to compute a proportional share of the contract’s token holdings during an unstake. The vulnerability arises because the share calculation in the unstake function uses the current total token balance divided by the total amount of tokens recorded as staked, without accounting for rewards that have accrued to the pool since earlier users deposited. As a result, when the contract’s token balance grows (for example through external reward distributions) and an earlier staker has not yet withdrawn, a later staker can deposit additional tokens, increase the totalStaked counter, and then call unstake. The later staker’s share is computed against the inflated pool balance, allowing them to withdraw more than their proportional contribution and effectively siphon the rewards that belong to the earlier participants. This can be exploited by simply waiting for the pool to earn rewards, making a small additional stake, and then withdrawing the full calculated share, which includes the earlier user’s accrued rewards. The impact is a loss of expected rewards for the first staker, a reduction of their effective balance, and a potential erosion of trust in the protocol’s accounting logic. The condition for the exploit is that the pool’s token balance must increase while the original staker’s position remains unclaimed, and the contract must allow new stakes before the original user withdraws. All users who stake before rewards are distributed are affected, as their earned returns can be stolen by subsequent participants. The issue was identified during a manual audit of the share‑calculation logic, where the relationship between totalStaked and the actual token balance was found to be inconsistent. It is subtle because the arithmetic appears correct at a glance – the division yields a proportional amount – yet it ignores that totalStaked does not reflect the accrued rewards, leading to an over‑allocation of shares. To remediate, the contract should adjust the accounting model so that the share calculation reflects both the principal and any earned rewards, for example by minting virtual shares that represent the total pool value, updating totalStaked to match the contract’s token balance, or using a snapshot mechanism that records each user’s entitled share at the time of reward accrual. In user‑facing terms, a participant may see their balance unexpectedly drop to zero after staking, or notice that another user receives a larger payout than expected, indicating that rewards have been diverted. The bug belongs to the class of “proportional share mis‑allocation” or “reward dilution” vulnerabilities, where the accounting of pooled assets does not correctly isolate individual entitlements.

title: Executor and AssetLogic deals with the native tokens inconsistently that breaks execute()
content: The vulnerability stems from an inconsistent representation of native tokens across the BridgeFacet, AssetLogic library and the Executor contract. When the BridgeFacet processes a cross‑chain transaction that involves a native asset, it calls AssetLogic.transferAssetFromContract to move the liquidity to the Executor before invoking Executor.execute. AssetLogic explicitly rejects a zero address as an asset identifier, reverting with AssetLogic__transferAssetFromContract_notNative if the supplied _assetId equals address(0). In contrast, the Executor determines that a call involves a native token by checking if the assetId field in its arguments equals address(0). Consequently, when the BridgeFacet attempts to forward a native token, it supplies address(0) as the asset identifier, which triggers the AssetLogic revert before the Executor can perform its logic. This mismatch causes the execute() call to fail, preventing the intended transfer of native tokens. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the flow of assets between the BridgeFacet and the Executor and noticed that the native‑token sentinel value was handled differently in the two components. The bug is subtle because the same code paths work correctly for ERC20 tokens, so the failure only appears when a user initiates a bridge of ETH or another native coin. From a user’s perspective the transaction appears to revert or succeed without delivering any funds; the UI may show an execution error, the user’s balance on the source chain may be deducted while the destination balance remains unchanged, and the expected refund or receipt never arrives.
