The function will accept the root, mark it as processed, and forward it to the RootManager via aggregate, thereby inserting a fraudulent state update into the cross-chain accounting system. The processed mapping prevents a duplicate update from being applied twice, but it does not stop the initial malicious insertion. This can be exploited after a legitimate fast-path message has been processed, or even in isolation, allowing the attacker to manipulate the set of roots that the RootManager aggregates. The impact is that the protocol’s cross-chain state can be corrupted, leading to incorrect asset balances, failed withdrawals, or other accounting errors that affect users and the protocol’s integrity. The bug manifests when a message is received from the AMB on the slow path; under those conditions the contract does not verify the source domain, so any entity that can trigger the call may inject a fake root. The issue was discovered during a formal security audit when reviewers observed that _processMessage lacks a mirrorConnector check. Because the function appears to be internal and is only called in two places, the missing check is not obvious from the surface, making the flaw easy to overlook. To remediate, the second (slow-path) invocation should be removed entirely, or the function should enforce that only the authorized mirror connector on the expected domain can call it, restoring the intended trust boundary. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of unchecked external calls or missing access control, where a privileged internal function can be reached without proper authentication, leading to potential state manipulation.

title: Renouncing ownership or admin role could affect the normal operation of Connext
content: The vulnerability stems from the presence of unrestricted renounceOwnership and revokeRole functions in several core contracts of the Connext protocol. These contracts inherit a standard ownership pattern that allows the current owner to call renounceOwnership, permanently removing the owner address, and inherit a role‑based access control that permits an admin to call revokeRole, which can be used to drop the admin role. Because there is no safeguard that ensures at least one privileged account remains, an owner or admin can unintentionally or maliciously relinquish all authority, leaving the contract without any entity capable of performing owner‑only or admin‑only actions. When this occurs, critical operations such as unpausing the message bridge after a fraud dispute, re‑adding a connector, or withdrawing accumulated swap admin fees become impossible. From a user perspective, the system may appear frozen: messages that were expected to be processed remain stuck, swaps complete but the advertised admin fee cannot be claimed, and attempts to recover from a fraudulent transfer fail because the contract cannot be unpaused. The impact is high because the protocol loses its ability to enforce security guarantees and to manage revenue, potentially resulting in funds that are effectively locked forever. The condition for exploitation is simply that the current owner or admin invokes the renounce or revoke function; no special permissions or external calls are required beyond the existing privileged role. All participants who rely on the protocol—liquidity providers, traders, and the protocol itself—are affected because the loss of administrative control can halt normal operation and prevent fee extraction. The issue was identified during a manual security review that highlighted the inheritance hierarchy and the lack of constraints on these privileged functions. It is difficult to notice because the functions are part of standard OpenZeppelin‑style contracts and are often retained for decentralisation purposes, yet the audit revealed that in this specific deployment they introduce a single‑point‑of‑failure. To remediate, the renounceOwnership function should be removed or disabled on contracts where ownership is required for ongoing management, and the revokeRole logic should be altered to enforce that at least one admin remains, for example by requiring a multi‑signature or by preventing the last admin from being removed. Conceptually, the fix is to enforce a non‑empty set of privileged actors so that essential protocol logic can always be executed, preserving the ability to recover from fraud, withdraw fees, and maintain operational continuity.
summary:
Consider the following scenarios.
• Instance 1 - Renouncing ownership
All the contracts that extend from ProposedOwnable or ProposedOwnableUpgradeable inherit a method called renounceOwnership. The owner of the contract can use this method to give up their ownership, thereby leaving the contract without an owner. If that were to happen, it would not be possible to perform any owner-specific functionality on that contract anymore.
The following is a summary of the affected contracts and their impact if the ownership has been renounced.
One of the most significant impacts is that Connext's message system cannot recover after a fraud has been resolved since there is no way to unpause and add the connector back to the system.
• Instance 2 - Renouncing admin role
All the contracts that extend from ProposedOwnableFacet inherit a method called revokeRole.
1. Assume that the Owner has renounced its power and the only Admin remaining used revokeRole to renounce its Admin role.
2. Now the contract is left with Zero Owner & Admin.
3. All swap operations collect adminFees via SwapUtils.sol contract. In absence of any Admin & Owner, these fees will get stuck in the contract with no way to retrieve them. Normally it would have been withdrawn using withdrawSwapAdminFees|SwapAdminFacet.sol.
4. This is simply one example, there are multiple other critical functionalities impacted once both Admin and Owner revoke their roles.

title: No way of removing Fraudulent Roots
content: The vulnerability is a missing removal mechanism for fraudulent Merkle roots in the cross-chain message queue of the Connext/Nxtp bridge. When the Watcher contract detects that a submitted root is fraudulent, it marks the root but the main bridge contract does not provide any function to purge that entry from the pending-root queue. Because the queue is immutable after insertion, the flagged root remains in the list and is subsequently relayed to every connected chain during the normal processing cycle. An attacker can therefore submit a crafted root that contains malicious transfer instructions; the Watcher will flag it, but the bridge will still propagate the root, causing the malicious instructions to be executed on each destination chain. This can lead to unauthorized token transfers, loss of user balances, or the execution of arbitrary calls, effectively making funds disappear from user accounts. The issue manifests when the contract is operating normally or even when it is paused, because there is no owner-only cleanup path. Users may notice that a transfer they initiated never resolves, their balance becomes zero, or refunds are not received, while the UI continues to show the operation as pending. The bug was discovered during a manual security review by Spearbit, who noted that the contract’s state-machine lacks a transition to delete or invalidate a fraudulent root. The problem is hard to spot because the Watcher’s flag is an internal variable that does not surface in the public interface, and the normal flow of root processing masks the fact that a bad root is still present. Conceptually, the fix is to add an owner-restricted method that can be called when the contract is paused to remove any root that has been marked as fraudulent, thereby preventing its further propagation and restoring the integrity of the message queue. This class of bug belongs to missing state-cleanup or queue-purge vulnerabilities, where invalid entries cannot be removed, breaking the accounting assumptions of the protocol and allowing malicious state transitions.
summary: Fraudulent Roots cannot be removed once fraud is detected by the Watcher. This means that Fraud Roots will be propagated to each chain.

title: `_aggregateValidFulfillmentOfferItems
content: The vulnerability resides in the Seaport contract's internal function that aggregates offer items for a fulfillment. The function uses a temporary integer called errorBuffer to record two distinct validation failures: a missing item amount (represented by bit 0) and an arithmetic overflow of a consideration amount (represented by bit 1). After processing all items, a switch statement reverts the transaction when errorBuffer equals 1 (missing amount) or 2 (overflow). However, the logic does not handle the case when both conditions occur simultaneously, which yields an errorBuffer value of 3 (binary 11). Because the switch lacks a case for 3, the function treats the combined error as a successful validation and continues execution. An attacker can exploit this by constructing an order that contains at least one item with a zero amount and another item whose amount calculation overflows the 256‑bit integer limit. When the contract processes such an order, errorBuffer becomes 3, the missing‑amount and overflow checks are silently bypassed, and the order is fulfilled with a consideration that may be essentially zero. From the user's perspective, a seller may observe that their NFT was transferred while the received payment is far lower than expected, often appearing as a zero or negligible balance update, contradicting the expectation of receiving the full listed price. The impact is a direct loss of funds for the seller and a distortion of the protocol's accounting, allowing assets to be acquired for a fraction of the price. This issue was discovered during a security audit when a test case demonstrated buying an NFT for 1 DAI instead of the intended 1000 DAI. The bug is subtle because the error handling appears correct for isolated failures, making the combined failure mode easy to miss during code review. To remediate the problem, the validation logic should be extended to explicitly handle the errorBuffer value of 3, or an early abort should be introduced whenever errorBuffer is non‑zero, ensuring that any combination of missing amounts and overflows triggers a revert. In essence, the contract needs to treat the error buffer as a bitmask and reject any non‑zero state rather than assuming only singular error codes are possible.
summary:
[FulfillmentApplier.sol#L406](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-opensea-seaport/blob/main/contracts/lib/FulfillmentApplier.sol#L406)  

The `_aggregateValidFulfillmentOfferItems()` function aims to revert on orders with zero value or where a total consideration amount overflows. Internally this is accomplished by having a temporary variable `errorBuffer`, accumulating issues found, and only reverting once all the items are processed in case there was a problem found. This code is optimistic for valid inputs.

Note: there is a similar issue in `_aggregateValidFulfillmentConsiderationItems()`, which is reported separately.

The problem lies in how this `errorBuffer` is updated:
    
    errorBuffer := or(
      errorBuffer,
      or(
        shl(1, lt(newAmount, amount)),
        iszero(mload(amountPtr))
      )
    )

The final error handling code:
    
    switch errorBuffer
    case 1 {
        mstore(0, MissingItemAmount_error_signature)
        revert(0, MissingItemAmount_error_len)
    }
    case 2 {
        throwOverflow()
    }

While the expected value is `0` (success), `1` or `2` (failure), it is possible to set it to `3`, which is unhandled and considered as a “success”. This can be easily accomplished by having both an overflowing item and a zero item in the order list.

This validation error could lead to fulfilling an order with a consideration (potentially ~0) lower than expected.

title: Truncation in `OrderValidator` can lead to resetting the fill and selling more tokens
content: The vulnerability resides in the order‑validation logic of the Seaport marketplace where the fill progress of a partially fillable order is tracked using a numerator and denominator stored in a uint120 variable. When a filler supplies a new fractional fill, the contract combines the previously recorded fraction with the new one by cross‑multiplying the denominators and adding the resulting numerators. If the intermediate product exceeds the 120‑bit limit, Solidity silently truncates the value to the lower 120 bits, which in the examined scenario can reduce both the numerator and denominator to zero. This truncation effectively resets the recorded fill amount, making the contract believe that no part of the order has been filled. An attacker can exploit this by first submitting a large fill expressed as a high‑power‑of‑two fraction (e.g., 2**118/2**119) that brings the stored numerator close to the maximum value, and then supplying a small additional fraction such as 1/10. The cross‑multiplication of these two fractions overflows the uint120 range, causing the stored numerator and denominator to wrap to zero. Once the fill counters are reset, the attacker can continue to invoke fill calls and drain any tokens that the original maker has approved to the marketplace, far exceeding the amount originally offered for sale while still receiving the same consideration amount. From a user’s perspective the seller may see their ERC1155 balance drop to zero or to a much lower amount than expected, while the payment received remains unchanged, violating the basic accounting assumption that the amount of assets transferred matches the agreed‑upon portion of the order. This bug appears only when a PARTIAL_OPEN order is used with fractional fills that can cause the internal arithmetic to exceed the uint120 capacity; it is invisible under normal fills that stay within the range, making it difficult to detect through routine testing. The issue was discovered during a formal security audit performed by Code4rena, which reproduced the overflow using a crafted proof‑of‑concept that demonstrated the reset of the fill state and subsequent token drain. The root cause is insufficient overflow protection on the arithmetic that updates the fill fraction, combined with an unsafe cast to a fixed‑size integer type. To remediate the flaw, the contract should validate that the intermediate numerator and denominator never exceed the uint120 maximum before casting, revert on overflow, and consider redesigning the fill‑tracking mechanism to use a larger integer size or a different accounting approach that does not rely on cross‑multiplication of potentially large fractions. In broader terms, this is an instance of an integer overflow/truncation bug that leads to state reset and enables unauthorized asset extraction, undermining the trust model of the marketplace and exposing token owners to unexpected loss of holdings.
summary:
[OrderValidator.sol#L228](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-opensea-seaport/blob/4140473b1f85d0df602548ad260b1739ddd734a5/contracts/lib/OrderValidator.sol#L228)  
[OrderValidator.sol#L231](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-opensea-seaport/blob/4140473b1f85d0df602548ad260b1739ddd734a5/contracts/lib/OrderValidator.sol#L231)  
[OrderValidator.sol#L237](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-opensea-seaport/blob/4140473b1f85d0df602548ad260b1739ddd734a5/contracts/lib/OrderValidator.sol#L237)  
[OrderValidator.sol#L238](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-opensea-seaport/blob/4140473b1f85d0df602548ad260b1739ddd734a5/contracts/lib/OrderValidator.sol#L238)  

A partial order’s fractions (`numerator` and `denominator`) can be reset to `0` due to a truncation. This can be used to craft malicious orders:

  1. Consider user Alice, who has 100 ERC1155 tokens, who approved all of their tokens to the `marketplaceContract`.
  2. Alice places a `PARTIAL_OPEN` order with 10 ERC1155 tokens and consideration of ETH.
  3. Malory tries to fill the order in the following way:

     1. Malory tries to fill 50% of the order, but instead of providing the fraction `1 / 2`, Bob provides `2**118 / 2**119`. This sets the `totalFilled` to `2**118` and `totalSize` to `2**119`.
     2. Malory tries to fill 10% of the order, by providing `1 / 10`. The computation `2**118 / 2**119 + 1 / 10` is done by “cross multiplying” the denominators, leading to the acutal fraction being `numerator = (2**118 * 10 + 2**119)` and `denominator = 2**119 * 10`.
     3. Because of the `uint120` truncation in [OrderValidator.sol#L228-L248](https://github.com/ProjectOpenSea/seaport/blob/6c24d09fc4be9bbecf749e6a7a592c8f7b659405/contracts/lib/OrderValidator.sol#L228-L248), the `numerator` and `denominator` are truncated to `0` and `0` respectively.
     4. Bob can now continue filling the order and draining any approved (1000 tokens in total) of the above ERC1155 tokens, for the same consideration amount!

title: MJR-1 Unstable gauge version check
content: The vulnerability resides in the way the ShashFactory contract determines the version of a Curve gauge before creating a stash. Instead of using a static whitelist or an explicit version identifier, the contract performs a series of low‑level call probes that inspect the presence of functions such as rewardedToken() or rewardTokens(uint256) on the gauge contract. This dynamic probing works for the current set of ~40 known gauges, but it assumes that every future gauge will expose the same set of functions with identical semantics. If Curve later deploys a new gauge version that either adds, removes, or changes the behaviour of these functions, the probe logic can mis‑classify the gauge’s version. Consequently, ShashFactory may accept a gauge that it believes to be compatible while the underlying contract follows a different reward‑distribution logic. An attacker or an unwitting developer could therefore create a stash linked to an incompatible gauge, causing the reward‑calculation code in Convex to operate on unexpected data. From a user’s perspective this may manifest as missing or zero rewards, balances that appear to be frozen, or refunds that never arrive despite successful deposits. The impact is primarily logical: accounting invariants break, reward distribution becomes incorrect, and funds may become effectively unrecoverable because the protocol can no longer reconcile the stash state with the gauge’s actual state. The issue appears only when a new gauge version is introduced; under the existing gauge set the checks pass, making the bug hard to notice during routine testing. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the version‑checking code and identified the reliance on function‑presence probes as a brittle pattern. To remediate the problem, the contract should replace the probe‑based detection with a deterministic whitelist of known gauge addresses or explicit version identifiers supplied by Curve, ensuring that only vetted gauges can be used. This eliminates the risk of mis‑classification and restores confidence that reward calculations align with the intended gauge logic. The flaw belongs to the class of “dynamic interface probing” bugs, where contracts infer contract type from optional functions, leading to unsafe assumptions when interfaces evolve.
summary: ShashFactory contract have gauge version check based on call probes defined at StashFactory.sol#L51-L61, that approach is very dangerous in case of new version added to curve. E.g if curve will add new version of gauge that have rewardedtoken() or rewardtokens(uint256) and with different behavior, then version checker will wrongly classify version and allow to create stash with invalid version. That can lead to broken logic.

title: MJR-2 Wrong logic in withdrawAll
content: The vulnerability is an accounting logic error in the withdrawAll function of the protocol’s proxy contract. Instead of calculating the total amount of tokens that can be withdrawn as the sum of the gauge’s pooled balance and any tokens that are already held by the proxy contract, the implementation only queries balanceOfPool(_gauge). Consequently, when the system is shut down via shutdownSystem, any token balance that resides directly in the proxy contract is ignored and remains locked. The root cause is a missing addition of IERC20(token).balanceOf(address(this)) to the withdrawal amount, which violates the expected accounting invariant that the contract’s total token holdings equal the sum of the gauge balance and the contract’s own balance. An attacker does not gain direct access to the omitted tokens, but the bug can be exploited by a malicious operator who triggers shutdown and then claims that all assets have been withdrawn while a portion stays trapped, effectively reducing the available liquidity for users. The impact is that users may see a zero balance or receive no refund after a shutdown, yet the tokens are still present in the contract, leading to apparent loss of funds, broken accounting, and potential loss of confidence in the protocol. The condition under which the issue manifests is any execution of withdrawAll during or after a shutdown, where the proxy contract holds a non‑zero token balance outside the gauge. All participants that rely on the shutdown process – token holders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the protocol cannot correctly report or return the full amount of assets. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the withdrawal logic and identified the mismatch between the intended formula and the actual code. Because the symptom is that funds simply do not leave the contract, it can be hard to notice without inspecting the internal token balances, especially if the UI only shows a successful shutdown message. The recommended fix is to modify withdrawAll so that it computes the withdrawable amount as balanceOfPool(gauge) plus the token balance held by the contract, thereby restoring the correct accounting and ensuring that all assets are transferred out during shutdown. This type of bug belongs to the class of withdrawal or accounting miscalculations where the contract fails to aggregate all sources of token holdings before performing a transfer, leading to funds appearing to disappear or refunds being zero when they are actually still locked in the contract.
summary: At the moment withdrawAll counts balance as: balanceOfPool(_gauge) (VoterProxy.sol#L92) Correct logic should be: balanceOfPool(gauge).add(IERC20(token).balanceOf(address(this))). The withdrawAll method is used by shutdownSystem so potentially some tokens could remain in the contract.

title: MJR-3 Zero gauge could be added via addPool
content: The vulnerability originates from the function that registers a new liquidity pool in the Booster contract. When a caller invokes the pool‑addition routine, the supplied gauge address is stored without any validation that it is a non‑zero, contract‑type address. Because the internal helper that enumerates existing gauges returns a fixed‑size array that may contain empty slots, a caller can deliberately pass the zero address (0x0000000000000000000000000000000000000000) as the gauge parameter. The Booster contract then records this zero gauge and later invokes the StashFactory to create a stash for the pool. The StashFactory performs a low‑level call to the gauge address using address(0).call.value(0)(data). In the Ethereum Virtual Machine a call to the zero address with zero value does not revert; it simply returns true. Consequently, the Booster logic interprets the call as a successful stash creation even though no real contract was interacted with. An attacker who can add a pool with a zero gauge can therefore trigger erroneous execution paths, bypass the intended accounting of rewards, and potentially cause funds to be mis‑routed, locked, or lost. The impact is considered major because the protocol’s reward distribution and stash management rely on the assumption that every gauge is a valid contract that will execute the expected logic. The bug manifests whenever the addPool function is called with a gauge argument that is zero, which can happen either accidentally or maliciously because there is no explicit check. All participants that rely on correct reward accounting – including liquidity providers, the protocol’s treasury, and any downstream contracts – are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the Booster contract’s input validation and noticed the absence of a non‑zero gauge requirement. It is subtle because the zero‑address call succeeds silently, providing no error signal, and the surrounding code does not emit an event or revert, making the problem easy to overlook in testing. To remediate the issue, the contract should enforce that the gauge address supplied to addPool is non‑zero and points to a contract that implements the expected interface. Additionally, the StashFactory should verify the success of the low‑level call by checking that the target address contains code, or by using a higher‑level interface that reverts on failure. By adding these checks, the protocol can prevent the creation of invalid stashes and preserve the integrity of reward calculations, ensuring that users receive the expected refunds and that balances do not unexpectedly become zero.
summary: In addPool defined at Booster.sol#L160 there is no check for _gauge variable. For example during this call booster.addPool(threeCrvSwap, "0x0000000000000000000000000000000000000000", 0) Gauge will be found because get_gauges returns array like [address1, address2, 0x0, 0x0, ...]. Intruder can call some errors in Booster logic. It's major because at the moment StashFactory call address(0x0).call.value(0)(data) (StashFactory.sol#L53) and due to specific of EVM there is true.

title: MJR-1 Error while calculating the value
content: The vulnerability is a scaling error in the price‑per‑share calculation of a yDAI token wrapper. The function that should return the price per full share multiplies the raw share value by the fixed‑point factor 1e18 but fails to divide the result by the same factor before returning it. As a result the reported price is inflated by exactly 1e18 times the correct value. This mistake originates from an incorrect handling of the token’s 18‑decimal precision, a common pitfall when mixing integer arithmetic with fixed‑point scaling. Any contract that relies on this function – for example the flash‑loan borrower implementation that calls getPricePerFullShare at several points – will receive a massively overstated share price and will therefore compute token amounts that are off by the same factor. An attacker or a careless developer can exploit the bug by triggering a transaction that uses the erroneous price to request or repay assets, causing the protocol to transfer far more tokens than intended or to believe a repayment has been satisfied when it has not. The impact includes potential loss of funds, incorrect accounting, and failure of flash‑loan repayment logic, which may leave user balances empty or cause the protocol to become under‑collateralised. The condition occurs every time the price‑per‑share getter is invoked, which in the audited code happens in the CoverFlashBorrower contract at the indicated lines. All participants that interact with the yDAI wrapper – borrowers, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the bug corrupts the fundamental accounting invariant that one share equals a fixed amount of underlying assets. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit performed by MixBytes, who noted the mismatch between the multiplication and the missing division. The bug can be subtle because the returned number is still a valid uint256 and may be used in subsequent calculations that also apply a 1e18 scaling, thereby masking the error until a concrete mismatch in token balances appears. To remediate the problem the getter should either divide the multiplied value by 1e18 before returning it or, alternatively, avoid the unnecessary multiplication altogether and keep the value in its native fixed‑point representation. In broader terms the flaw belongs to the class of decimal‑scaling or unit‑conversion bugs that break financial invariants and lead to erroneous token transfers, refund failures, or balance disappearances.
summary: The getPricePerFullShare() function for a yDAI token contract returns the value multiplied by a factor of 1e18. But it doesn't divided by 1e18: CoverFlashBorrower.sol#L90 CoverFlashBorrower.sol#L155 CoverFlashBorrower.sol#L182

title: MJR-2 Wrongly used safeApprove
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect use of the safeApprove function from the OpenZeppelin SafeERC20 library. The contract calls safeApprove(recipient, amount) without first resetting the existing allowance to zero. SafeERC20’s safeApprove internally checks that the current allowance for the spender is either zero or that the new allowance is zero; if the allowance is non‑zero and the new value is non‑zero, the call reverts. Consequently, when the contract or a user has previously granted a non‑zero allowance to the same token contract, any subsequent attempt to increase or change that allowance fails, causing the transaction to revert, which can be exploited by an attacker who can pre‑set a non‑zero allowance (for example by calling approve directly) and then trigger a function that relies on safeApprove to set a new allowance, causing the function to fail and potentially locking funds or preventing a flash‑loan operation that depends on the approval. The impact is that legitimate users may see their transactions revert with no obvious error, balances may appear unchanged, and flash‑loan borrowers may be unable to execute the loan, effectively “funds disappear” from the perspective of the user because the intended operation does not happen. The condition occurs whenever the contract executes the approval line (CoverFlashBorrower.sol line 351) and the token already has a non‑zero allowance for the recipient. The affected parties are token holders, borrowers, and any protocol component that relies on dynamic approvals, such as the flash‑loan module. The issue was discovered during a manual code review by the MixBytes audit team, who noted the unsafe pattern. It is hard to notice because the revert message from SafeERC20 is generic (“ERC20: approve from non‑zero to non‑zero allowance”) and may be swallowed by higher‑level error handling, making the failure appear as a silent “nothing happened”. The proper fix is to follow the standard two‑step allowance change: first call safeApprove(recipient, 0) to clear the existing allowance, then call safeApprove(recipient, newAmount) to set the desired value, or use safeIncreaseAllowance / safeDecreaseAllowance where appropriate. This aligns with the ERC20 allowance change best practice and prevents the revert. In abstract terms, the bug belongs to the class of “incorrect ERC20 allowance reset” or “unsafe approve pattern” vulnerabilities, where a contract assumes it can overwrite an existing allowance without resetting it first, violating the token’s accounting assumptions and breaking expected business logic of token transfers.
summary: At the line CoverFlashBorrower.sol#L351 contract call safeApprove method, however that method fails if account have remaining allowed tokens.

title: MJR-1 It is possible to carry out attacks to manipulate pools within one
content: The vulnerability is a flash‑loan‑driven liquidity manipulation bug present in the CoverRouter and Rollover contracts. The contracts allow any address to add liquidity, remove liquidity and perform token swaps without any per‑transaction or per‑block restrictions. Because the contracts do not keep track of the origin of a swap or enforce a delay between successive liquidity operations, an attacker can obtain a large amount of capital through a flash loan, inject that capital into a pool, execute a series of swaps or liquidity additions/removals within the same transaction, and then withdraw the manipulated assets before the transaction is settled. The root cause is the absence of a protection mechanism that ties a user’s actions to a specific block (for example, a mapping that records the last block in which the address performed a swap) and the lack of any flash‑loan detection or reentrancy‑style guard. Exploitation proceeds as follows: (1) the attacker borrows a flash loan; (2) the attacker adds a large amount of liquidity to a pool, artificially inflating the pool’s balance; (3) the attacker performs one or more swaps that shift the pool’s price curve in the attacker’s favor; (4) the attacker removes the previously added liquidity, capturing the price distortion as profit; (5) the transaction completes, leaving the pool with an altered token ratio that harms other users who later trade or withdraw. The impact is a direct loss of funds for honest liquidity providers and traders, as the pool may dispense fewer tokens than expected, causing refunds to be zero or balances to be unexpectedly reduced. The issue manifests whenever a user can call the addLiquidity, removeLiquidity or swap functions in rapid succession within a single block, which is permitted by the current contract logic. All participants who rely on the pool’s pricing – including regular users, other liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected. The flaw was discovered during a formal security audit performed by MixBytes, which noted that the contracts lack any safeguard against same‑transaction token manipulation. Because the manipulation happens entirely inside one atomic transaction, the abnormal state is not observable on‑chain until after the damage is done, making it hard to detect through ordinary monitoring. To remediate the problem, the contracts should record the block number of the last swap or liquidity operation for each origin address and reject further operations from the same address within the same block, as illustrated by the sample mapping _lastSwapBlock and the _preventSameTxOrigin check. Additional mitigations may include limiting the amount of liquidity that can be added or removed per block, integrating flash‑loan detection, or employing a more comprehensive reentrancy guard. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of “same‑transaction price manipulation” or “flash‑loan liquidity attack” vulnerabilities, where unchecked rapid state changes enable an attacker to profit at the expense of other participants.
summary: In contracts CoverRouter.sol and Rollover.sol, any user can exchange tokens with a contract. Any user can add and remove liquidity. An attacker can take a flash loan and perform multiple liquidity manipulations within a single transaction. These manipulations can lead to a loss of funds for other users.

title: MJR-2 Possibility to steal tokens from the contract balance
content: The vulnerability resides in the addCoverAndCreatePools function, which accepts arbitrary protocol and collateral token addresses and then calls an internal addCover routine thatunconditionally grants the supplied protocol an unlimited allowance of the collateral token using token.approve(spender, uint256(-1)). Because the function does not validate that the protocol address corresponds to a trusted contract, an attacker can supply a malicious protocol contract that, once approved, can invoke transferFrom to move any amount of the collateral tokens held by the CoverRouter. Additionally, the contract assumes an optimistic flow in which the router’s token balance should remain zero after a successful call, but it does not enforce this invariant nor does it check the boolean return value of _protocol.addCover. If the external addCover call fails and returns false, the transaction does not revert, leaving the user’s deposited tokens stranded in the router’s balance. The root cause is a combination of missing address validation, the use of an unlimited token approval pattern, and inadequate error handling that fails to enforce the zero‑balance invariant. An attacker can exploit the flaw by calling addCoverAndCreatePools with a malicious protocol address, causing the router to approve unlimited tokens to the attacker’s contract, which can then drain the router’s balance. The impact includes complete loss of user‑deposited collateral, funds becoming irretrievable, and a breach of trust in the protocol’s accounting logic. The issue manifests when a user initiates a cover addition; the transaction appears successful, but the user’s tokens disappear or remain locked in the router, contradicting the expectation that the tokens are transferred to a newly created pool. This bug was discovered during a security audit by MixBytes, which noted the unchecked external address and the unsafe approve call. It can be difficult to notice because the approve pattern is common and the transaction does not revert on failure, giving a false sense of success. To remediate, the contract should stop using unlimited approvals, instead approving only the exact amount required, implement strict validation or whitelisting of protocol addresses, and enforce that addCover returns true, reverting otherwise, thereby preserving the zero‑balance invariant and preventing token theft.
summary: Method addCoverAndCreatePools defined at CoverRouter.sol#L128 accepts _protocol and collateral addresses as arguments, then call addCover that makes approve for protocol an unlimited amount of collateral tokens and call _protocol.addCover. There are no checks of protocol and collateral validity, so an attacker can pass malicious protocol and get unlimited approval of collateral tokens: if (token.allowance(address(this), spender) < _amount) { token.approve(spender, uint256(-1)); } According to the contract logic in an optimistic flow a contract shouldn't have any tokens in balance, but this invariant not fully checked, e.g. if _protocol.addCover at Rollover.sol#L75 fails and returns false, then the transaction will be executed successfully, but the user's funds will be left on the CoverRouter balance.

title: MJR-1 Incorrect check of timeWindow
content: The vulnerability concerns an incorrect validation of the claim time window in thecontract that governs claim periods. The contract is supposed to enforce a minimum duration of three days for any new claim window that can be set by privileged callers. However, the implemented check compares the supplied _newTimeWindow against the threshold using an inappropriate condition, allowing values that are shorter than the intended three‑day minimum to pass. This logical error originates from a faulty comparison operator or missing boundary condition in the require statement. An attacker who can invoke the function that updates the claim window can therefore set an arbitrarily short window, even zero, which collapses the intended claim period. By shortening the window, the attacker can either prevent legitimate users from submitting claims within the expected timeframe or, if the claim logic permits immediate execution, claim the funds before others have a chance. The impact is that users expecting a three‑day claim period may see their refunds or payouts disappear, balances remain unchanged, or the UI shows a claim window that never actually allows a claim. The bug manifests whenever the function that updates the time window is called, which may be during normal protocol governance or administrative actions. It affects all participants who rely on the claim mechanism, including token holders, claimants, and the protocol itself, because the accounting assumptions about a minimum claim period are violated. The issue was discovered during a formal security audit performed by MixBytes, where the auditors identified that the require statement did not correctly enforce the intended lower bound. Because the check looks syntactically correct, the problem can be subtle and may not be caught by simple testing unless edge‑case windows are exercised. To remediate, the contract should enforce the condition require(_newTimeWindow >= 3 days, "CC: window too short"); ensuring that any new time window is at least three days long, thereby restoring the intended claim period and preventing premature or impossible claim scenarios.
summary: At the line ClaimConfig.sol#L50 there is incorrect check of _newTimeWindow.

title: MJR-2 Lack of claim validation
content: The contract's claim management function accepts three parameters: coverPool, nonce, and an index that selects a claim from an internal array. The code does not verify that the supplied index is within the bounds of the stored claim list. Consequently, a caller can pass an out‑of‑range index, causing the function to read uninitialized storage or a different claim. The require statement that checks other conditions does not include an index bounds check, so the transaction proceeds and the claim state is set to Validated and the cover‑pool claim fee is reset even though the claim data is invalid. This bug belongs to the class of unchecked array‑index vulnerabilities and improper input validation. An attacker can exploit it by submitting a transaction with a deliberately wrong index, causing the contract to mark a non‑existent or unrelated claim as validated, potentially resetting fees, mis‑accounting, or allowing the attacker to claim rewards they are not entitled to. The impact includes incorrect accounting, loss of fee revenue for the protocol, and possible denial of service if the state machine becomes inconsistent. The issue manifests whenever the claim function is called with any index that is not less than the length of the claim array for the given coverPool and nonce. All participants that rely on correct claim processing – policy holders, claim submitters, and the protocol itself – are affected because the protocol may think a claim has been settled when it has not. The flaw was discovered during a manual code audit that highlighted the missing bounds check. Because the function still passes its internal require, the bug can be subtle and may not produce an obvious revert; instead the contract state silently diverges from expected accounting, making it hard to notice without explicit testing of edge cases. The proper fix is to add an explicit require that the index is smaller than the length of the claim array (e.g., require(index < coverPoolClaims[coverPool][_nonce].length, 'bad indexes')), ensuring that only existing claims can be processed. This restores the invariant that a claim can only be validated if it actually exists, preserving the protocol’s accounting guarantees.
summary: At lines: ClaimManagement.sol#L112 ClaimManagement.sol#L145 ClaimManagement.sol#L176 the claim is taken by coverPool, nonce, _index, however caller may send incorrect indexes to the method. At the line ClaimManagement.sol#L114 even the flow with invalid claim will pass the require condition and go to claim.state = ClaimState.Validated; resetCoverPoolClaimFee(coverPool); this is unexpected behavior and potentially can lead to the contract misfunctioning.

title: Global connection limit vulnerable to DoS attacks
content: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition caused by a globally shared connection counter that caps the total number of simultaneous active connections at a fixed value (one thousand). The root cause is that the middleware tracks connections in a single static variable without distinguishing the source of each connection, so there is no per‑IP or per‑client rate limiting. An attacker can exploit this by opening many parallel connections from one or multiple IP addresses until the global counter reaches the maximum, after which any further connection attempts – including those from legitimate users – are rejected. The impact is that honest participants see connection failures, error messages such as "service unavailable" or simply experience a timeout, and are unable to interact with the contract or game, effectively freezing access to the platform. This condition occurs whenever the service is under load and the attacker is able to sustain enough concurrent connections to fill the quota; it is not dependent on specific contract functions but on the networking layer. All users of the front‑end, including players and API clients, are affected because the block is applied before any business logic runs. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that inspected the connections.ts middleware and identified the use of a single static limit without any per‑IP safeguards. Because the symptom is simply a failure to connect, it can be hard to notice that the cause is a resource‑exhaustion bug rather than a network outage or a bug in the UI. The bug belongs to the class of resource‑exhaustion or global‑state denial‑of‑service vulnerabilities, where a shared counter is used to enforce a limit that can be saturated by a single actor. From a user’s perspective the expectation is that the application will accept new connections as long as the service is healthy, but in reality the connection request is dropped once the global limit is reached, leading to a situation where funds may be locked in the contract because users cannot place bets or claim rewards. The recommended remediation is to replace the global counter with per‑IP or per‑client connection tracking, enforce rate limits at the edge (for example using a Web Application Firewall such as Cloudflare), and optionally add a mechanism to gracefully reject new connections with a clear error message when limits are exceeded. This change restores availability by preventing a single entity from monopolising all connection slots and aligns the implementation with standard best practices for protecting against DoS attacks.
summary: The application implements a global connection limit in the connections.ts middleware: private static readonly MAX_ACTIVE_CONNECTIONS = 1000 While limiting connections is a good practice, the current implementation tracks connections globally rather (DoS) attack by creating multiple connections until the maximum limit is reached, preventing legitimate users from connecting. The lack of per-IP rate limiting at this layer makes it trivial for a malicious actor to consume all available connection slots.

title: MJR-1 Excess reserve amount
content: The vulnerability originates from an accounting error in the CCapableErc20 contract where two state variables, internalCash and totalReserves, are updated incorrectly when a user pays a fee. Specifically, the contract adds the full amount of totalFee to internalCash and also adds the full amount of reservesFee to totalReserves. Because reservesFee is derived from the same user‑paid totalFee, the net effect is that the protocol’s recorded assets increase by the sum of totalFee and reservesFee, even though the user only transferred totalFee. This creates an uncollateralized reserve amount – the protocol appears to hold more reserves than it actually received. The root cause is a misplaced accounting rule: the fee should be split between cash and reserves, not added to both independently. An attacker could exploit this discrepancy by triggering fee‑related operations repeatedly, causing the protocol’s reserve balance to inflate artificially and potentially allowing withdrawal of funds that were never deposited. The impact includes inflated reserve metrics, broken accounting invariants, and a risk that legitimate users’ withdrawals could be denied or that the protocol could become under‑collateralized, leading to loss of funds. The condition occurs whenever the fee‑processing function at lines 250‑252 is executed, typically during flash‑loan repayments or other fee‑bearing actions. All participants that rely on the protocol’s reserve accounting – lenders, borrowers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the internal accounting no longer reflects reality. The issue was discovered during a manual security review by MixBytes, who noted the mismatch between fee inflow and reserve growth. It is subtle because the contract still records a positive cash flow, so the bug does not produce an outright revert or obvious error; instead, it silently skews the accounting numbers, making it hard to detect without detailed balance tracing. To remediate, the fee handling logic should be revised so that the incoming totalFee is partitioned appropriately: a portion should increase internalCash while the complementary portion should be recorded as reserves, ensuring that the sum of internalCash and totalReserves grows exactly by totalFee, not by totalFee plus reservesFee. This correction restores the invariant that total assets equal the sum of cash and reserves, eliminating the uncollateralized reserve surplus and preserving the protocol’s financial integrity.
summary: At lines CCapableErc20.sol#L250-L252 contract increases internalCash and totalReserves values, but it's so strange that internalCash increased by totalFee and totalReserves increased by reservesFee so we totally increased assets amount by reservesFee + totalFee however user paid only totalFee . It seems there are some uncollateralized reservesFee . May be there totalFee paid by user should be splitted to internalCash and totalReserves ?

title: Balancer Read-Only Reentrancy Vulnerability (Changes from dev team added to audit.)
content: The vulnerability is a read‑only reentrancy bug in Balancer‑based contracts used by Cron‑Fi's TWAMM. Although the affected functions are declared as view, they perform external calls (for example to price oracles) that allow an attacker to re‑enter the contract before the original call finishes. Because the contract does not update any persistent state in those functions, the original developers assumed they were safe, but the re‑entrancy can be used to manipulate the virtual reserve calculations that feed the TWAMM's pricing algorithm. An attacker can trigger the view function, cause a callback that invokes the same function again, and read inconsistent intermediate values. By doing so they can craft a sequence of calls that cause the virtual price oracle to return a manipulated price, or cause executeVirtualOrdersToBlock to process orders based on stale or fabricated reserve data. The impact is that the TWAMM may execute trades at incorrect prices, leading to users receiving less than expected, or the protocol may record wrong virtual reserves, breaking accounting and potentially allowing loss of funds. The bug manifests when a contract or externally owned account calls the view functions while a malicious contract is able to perform a low‑gas re‑entrancy check, as the Balancer team added a mitigation that forces a minimum gas stipend to trigger the built‑in re‑entrancy guard. If the mitigation is omitted, the re‑entrancy guard may not fire because the call is considered view, allowing the attack. The vulnerability was discovered during a security audit of Cron‑Fi, where the auditors noted that the Balancer library had recently expanded its re‑entrancy scope and that the affected functions were still marked view. The issue is subtle because view functions are typically assumed to be read‑only and safe from re‑entrancy, so developers may not add re‑entrancy protection. To remediate, the functions should be changed from view to non‑view (for example external) and the Balancer mitigation (minimum gas stipend) should be retained, or the code should be tested to confirm that re‑entrancy cannot affect the outcome and the mitigation can be safely removed. In practice, converting the functions to non‑view makes the re‑entrancy guard trigger automatically, ensuring that any external call cannot re‑enter before the first call completes. This aligns the implementation with the intended security model and prevents the virtual reserve and price oracle calculations from being tampered with.
summary:
Balancer's read-only reentrancy vulnerability potentially effects the following Cron-Fi TWAMM functions:
• getVirtualReserves
• getVirtualPriceOracle
• executeVirtualOrdersToBlock A mitigation was provided by the Balancer team that uses a minimum amount of gas to trigger a reentrancy check. The Balancer vulnerability is discussed in greater detail here:
• reentrancy-vulnerability-scope-expanded/4345

title: Overpayment of one side of LP Pair onJoinPool due to sandwich or user error
content: The vulnerability is an over‑payment of one side of a liquidity‑provider (LP) pair when a user calls the joinPool function. The contract calculates the amount of pool tokens to mint by taking the minimum of two ratios that involve the amounts of token0 and token1 supplied and the current reserves. Because the calculation uses the reserves at the moment the transaction is executed, it does not protect against price changes that may occur between the time the user signs the transaction and the time it is mined. If the price of the pair shifts – for example due to a front‑running swap (a sandwich attack) or because the user supplied an unbalanced amount – the min() function will select the lower‑valued side, causing the contract to consume more of the higher‑valued token than is reflected in the minted LP tokens. The result is that the liquidity provider over‑pays with one token while receiving LP tokens that represent a smaller combined value. An attacker can exploit this by submitting a large swap just before the victim’s join transaction, moving the price, and then reversing the swap after the victim’s transaction has been mined, capturing the excess tokens that the victim unintentionally contributed. From the user’s perspective the symptoms are confusing: the join transaction appears successful, LP tokens are minted, but after exiting the pool the user receives far fewer underlying tokens than they originally deposited, sometimes even zero balance for one of the assets. The impact is a direct loss of funds for the liquidity provider and a distortion of the pool’s accounting, which undermines trust in the protocol. The issue occurs whenever there is any price movement between transaction submission and inclusion – a condition that is common in volatile markets or when an attacker can front‑run. It affects any participant who adds liquidity, the protocol’s overall liquidity health, and ultimately token holders who rely on accurate pool accounting. The bug was discovered during a security audit by Spearbit, where a test harness simulated a sandwich scenario and observed that the victim’s token balances were dramatically reduced while the attacker profited. The problem is hard to notice because the contract does not revert; it simply mints LP tokens based on the lower side of the ratio, making the loss appear as a normal outcome of the join operation. The appropriate mitigation is to introduce slippage tolerance checks on both join and exit paths, similar to the protection implemented in UniswapV2Router02, so that the transaction reverts if the actual token amounts required deviate beyond an acceptable threshold. This change restores the expected economic behavior that a user who supplies X of token0 and Y of token1 should receive LP tokens representing roughly the same combined value, and prevents attackers from extracting value through price manipulation.

title: Loss of Long-Term Swap Proceeds Likely in Pools With Decimal or Price Imbalances
content: The vulnerability is an overflow of the 128‑bit 'scaled proceeds' counters used by the TWAMM implementation to track long‑term swap earnings. The contract stores the accumulated proceeds for each token in a single 256‑bit slot, allocating 128 bits to each token and updates these counters with unchecked arithmetic. A scaling factor of 2^64 is applied to keep precision, and the increment added each order‑block interval (OBI) is computed as (quantity purchased) × 2^64 / (sales rate). Because the addition is unchecked, if the 128‑bit counter wraps more than once between two claims, the difference calculation used to determine the withdrawable amount becomes incorrect, effectively locking the proceeds in the contract. This situation is especially likely when the two pool tokens have very different decimal places or price magnitudes, such as a DAI‑GUSD pair (18 vs 2 decimals) or DAI‑WBTC (8 decimals and a price gap of four orders of magnitude). In those cases the increment per OBI can be on the order of 10^37, causing the 128‑bit counter to overflow after only a few dozen OBIs – roughly six hours for DAI‑GUSD and about twelve days for DAI‑WBTC. When a user does not withdraw before the second overflow occurs, the contract computes a negative or zero delta and the user receives no proceeds, even though the swap should have generated profit. From the user’s perspective the expected refund or accrued balance is missing; the UI may show the same balance as before or a zero claim amount, leading to confusion and perceived loss of funds. The bug was discovered during a security audit by Spearbit, who noted that the unchecked arithmetic was intentional to save gas but that the design assumes at most one overflow per claim period – an assumption that breaks under realistic pool configurations. The issue is hard to notice because the contract does not revert or emit an error; the overflow silently corrupts the accounting state, and the loss only becomes apparent when a withdrawal returns less than expected after a long‑running order. The root cause is the combination of limited 128‑bit storage, a fixed scaling factor that does not account for token decimal or price disparity, and unchecked arithmetic that allows multiple wraps. To remediate, the scaling factor should be adjusted per token pair based on their decimal differences, or the counters should be stored in 256‑bit variables to eliminate the overflow risk, albeit at higher gas cost. Alternatively, making the scaling factor configurable at pool creation or using separate scaling factors for each token can mitigate the problem. Until such changes are applied, long‑term swap participants in pools with imbalanced decimals are at risk of losing their accrued proceeds.
summary:
This TWAMM implementation tracks the proceeds of long-term swaps efficiently via accumulated values called "scaled proceeds" for each token. In every order block interval (OBI), the scaled proceeds for e.g. the sale of token 0 are incremented by
(quantity of token 1 purchased during the OBI) × 2^64 / (sales rate of token 0 during the OBI)
Then the proceeds of any specific long-term swap can be computed as the product of the difference between the scaled proceeds at the current block (or the expiration block of the order if filled) and the last block for which proceeds were claimed for the order and the order's sales rate, divided by 2^64:
last := min(currentBlock, orderExpiryBlock)
prev := block of last proceeds collection, or block order was placed in if this is the first withdrawal
LT swap proceeds = (scaledProceeds_last − scaledProceeds_prev) × (order_sales_rate) / 2^64
The value 2^64 is referred to as the "scaling factor" and is intended to reduce precision loss in the division to determine the increment to the scaled proceeds.
The addition to increment the scaled proceeds and the subtraction to compute its net change is both intentionally done with unchecked arithmetic--since only the difference matters, so long as at most one overflow occurs between claim-of-proceeds events for any given order, the computed proceeds will be correct (up to rounding errors). If two or more overflows occur, however, funds will be lost by the swapper (unclaimable and locked in the contract).
Additionally, to cut down on gas costs, the scaled proceeds for the two tokens are packed into a single storage slot, so that only 128 bits are available for each value. This makes multiple overflows within the lifetime of a single order more likely. The CronFi team was aware of this at the start of the audit and specifically requested it be investigated, though they expected a maximum order length of 5 years to be sufficient to avoid the issue in practice.
The scaling factor of 2^64 is approximately 1.8 × 10^19, close to the unit size of an 18-decimal token. It indeed works well if both pool tokens have similar decimals and relative prices that do not differ by too many orders of magnitude, as the quantity purchased and the sales rate will then be of similar magnitude, canceling to within a few powers of ten (2^128 ≈ 3.4 × 10^38, leaving around 19 orders of magnitude after accounting for the scaling factor). However, in pools with large disparities in price, decimals, or both, numerical issues are easy to encounter.
The most extreme, realistic example would be a DAI-GUSD pool. DAI has 18 decimals while GUSD has only 2. We will treat the price of DAI and GUSD as equal for this analysis, as they are both stablecoins, and arbitrage of the TWAMM pool should prevent large deviations. Selling GUSD at a rate of 1000 per block, with an OBI of 64 (the stable pool order block interval in the audited commit) results in an increment of the scaled proceeds per OBI of:
increment = (64 × 1000 × 10^18) × 2^64 / (1000 × 10^2) = 1.18 × 10^37
This will overflow an unsigned 128 bit integer after 29 OBIs; at 12 seconds per block, this means the first overflow occurs after 12 × 64 × 29 = 22272 seconds or about 6.2 hours, and thus the first double overflow (and hence irrevocable loss of proceeds if a withdrawal is not executed in time) will occur within about 12.4 hours (slightly but not meaningfully longer if the price is pushed a bit below 1:1, assuming a deep enough pool or reasonably efficient arbitrage). Since the TWAMM is intended to support swaps that take days, weeks, months, or even years to fill, without requiring constant vigilance from every long-term swapper, this is a strong violation of safety.
A less extreme but more market-relevant example would be a DAI-WBTC pool. WBTC has 8 instead of 2 decimals, but it is also more than four orders of magnitude more valuable per token than DAI, making it only about 2 orders of magnitude "safer" than a DAI-GUSD pool. Imitating the above calculation with 20_000 DAI = 1 WBTC and selling 0.0025 WBTC (~$50) per block with a 257 block OBI yields:
increment = (257 × 50 × 10^18) × 2^64 / (0.0025 × 10^8) = 9.48 × 10^35
OBI to overflow = ceiling(2^128 / (9.48 × 10^35)) = 359
time to overflow = 12 × 257 × 359 = 1107156 seconds = 307 hours = 12.8 days
or a little more than a day to encounter the second overflow. While less bad than the DAI-GUSD example, this is still likely of significant concern given that the CronFi team indicated these are parameters under which the TWAMM should be able to function safely and DAI-WBTC is a pair of interest for the v1 product. It is worth noting that these calculations are not directly dependent on the quantity being sold so long as the price stays roughly constant--any change in the selling rate will be compensated by a proportional change in the proceeds quantity as their ratio is determined by price. Thus the analysis depends only on relative price and relative decimals, to a good approximation--so a WBTC-DAI pool can be expected to experience an overflow roughly every two weeks at prevailing market prices, so long as the net selling rate is non-zero.

title: An attacker can block any address from joining the Pool and minting BLP Tokens by filling the joinEventMap mapping
content: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that allows an attacker to prevent any address from minting Balancer Liquidity Provider (BLP) tokens in the CronV1Pool contract. The root cause is a hard‑coded maximum number of join events (MAX_JOIN_EVENTS) enforced by the JoinEventLib library and a public function that lets any caller transfer join events to an arbitrary address without checking whether the target’s join‑event storage has already reached the global limit. An attacker can exploit this by repeatedly minting BLP tokens from a large set of distinct addresses, then calling the pool’s transfer and transferJoinEvent functions to move both the tokens and the associated join events to the victim address. Because each transfer of join events consumes one slot in the joinEventMap mapping, after the attacker has filled the mapping with the maximum number of entries (50 in the current implementation) the victim’s subsequent attempt to join the pool fails – the contract rejects the minting call, the user receives no new BLP tokens and the balance of the user remains unchanged. This situation occurs when the attacker can orchestrate transfers over multiple blocks (the example uses 50 blocks, roughly ten minutes) and when the pool does not enforce per‑address limits or require that join events be moved together with the token transfer. The affected parties are any legitimate liquidity providers who expect to be able to add liquidity and receive BLP tokens; from their perspective the UI shows a failed transaction, a zero token balance after an attempted deposit, or a missing refund of liquidity shares. The issue was discovered during a security audit that included a proof‑of‑concept script which systematically filled the joinEventMap using 50 dummy addresses. The bug is subtle because the limit is hidden in a library and the transferJoinEvent function appears innocuous, so developers may not anticipate that external actors can exhaust the storage space. To remediate the problem the contract should either move join events together with the token transfer (for example by overriding the internal _move function of the BalancerPoolToken contract) or redesign the join‑event accounting to enforce per‑address limits, allow dynamic resizing, or reject external join‑event transfers that would exceed the capacity. By ensuring that join events cannot be arbitrarily injected into a victim’s account, the protocol restores the expected business logic that every user can join the pool and receive the correct amount of BLP tokens.

title: The executeVirtualOrdersToBlock function updates the oracle with the wrong block.number
content: The vulnerability resides in an externally callable function that processes virtual orders up to a supplied block limit. The function accepts a parameter representing the maximum block number (_maxBlock) and then invokes an internal oracle‑update routine that relies on the current block timestamp and implicitly assumes that the reserves being recorded belong to the present block. Because the caller can supply any _maxBlock value, including a number that is lower than the actual block.number, the oracle is forced to record reserve data that does not correspond to the current blockchain state. This mismatch causes the price oracle to emit stale or incorrect price information. An attacker can exploit the flaw by invoking the function with a deliberately low _maxBlock, causing the oracle to be updated with outdated reserve values. The resulting incorrect price feed can be used to manipulate trades, trigger liquidations, or extract value from users who rely on the oracle for accurate pricing. The impact is a breach of the protocol’s accounting assumptions: users expect that the oracle reflects the most recent market state, but instead they receive prices that are artificially shifted, potentially leading to loss of funds, failed transactions, or unexpected zero refunds. The issue manifests whenever any external account calls the function with a _maxBlock that is not equal to or greater than the current block, which is always possible because the function is public and lacks access control. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the interaction between virtual order execution and oracle updates, noting that the internal update routine does not receive an explicit block identifier and therefore trusts the global block context. The bug is subtle because the function appears to perform a legitimate bookkeeping task, and the incorrect block reference does not raise an immediate error; the oracle simply records a value that looks plausible but is temporally inaccurate. To remediate the problem, the oracle‑update routine should be refactored to accept the intended block number as an explicit argument, or the external function should enforce that _maxBlock is never less than the current block, or restrict its visibility to trusted actors. By decoupling the oracle update from the implicit block context, the protocol can guarantee that price calculations are based on up‑to‑date reserve data, preserving the integrity of user balances and the overall financial logic of the system.
summary:
The executeVirtualOrdersToBlock is external, meaning anyone can call this function to execute virtual orders.
The _maxBlock parameter can be lower block.number which will make the oracle malfunction as the oracle update function _updateOracle uses the block.timestamp and assumes that the update was called with the reserves at the current block.
This will make the oracle update with an incorrect value when _maxBlock can be lower than block.number.

title: Unclaimed User Staking Rewards Are Going to Get Lost on Each Call to stake() Function in StakedCSX Contract
content: The vulnerability resides in the staking contract’s stake() function, which updates reward accrual for three separate reward tokens by invoking an internal routine that overwrites the caller’s reward rate instead of preserving the already earned amount. The root cause is the misuse of the _updateRewardRate() helper: each call resets the stored reward rate for the user, effectively discarding any rewards that have accumulated but not yet been claimed. When a user who already has pending rewards calls stake() to add more CSX tokens, the contract silently clears those pending balances, so the user’s unclaimed rewards become zero. This can be exploited simply by invoking stake() with any non‑zero amount; the attacker does not need special permissions because the function is public and the loss occurs to the caller’s own account. The impact is a loss of value for stakers: users expect their pending rewards to remain available, but after staking they see their reward balances drop to zero and later attempts to claim return nothing, resulting in funds that appear to disappear from the protocol’s accounting. The condition under which the bug manifests is any call to stake() after the user has earned rewards that have not been claimed. All participants who stake CSX are affected, including regular users and any downstream applications that rely on accurate reward accounting. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the reward‑updating logic and noticed that the function name suggested an update rather than a claim, leading to the realization that the reward state was being overwritten. The problem is subtle because the contract emits a Stake event and the UI may still display the user’s total staked amount, masking the fact that the reward balance has been reset; there is no explicit error or revert, so the loss can go unnoticed until a user attempts to claim. To remediate the flaw, the contract should replace the three _updateRewardRate() calls with a single _claimToCredit() invocation (or an equivalent routine) that first records the accrued rewards into a credit mapping and then updates the reward rate for future accruals. This ensures that previously earned rewards are preserved and can be claimed later, aligning the implementation with the intended business logic that rewards accrue continuously and are only transferred when explicitly claimed. In broader terms, the bug belongs to the class of accounting reset or state‑overwrite vulnerabilities where a function unintentionally clears pending balances instead of aggregating them, violating the protocol’s guarantee that rewards are cumulative and recoverable.
summary:
The current implementation of the stake() function in StakedCSX.sol calls _updateRewardRate() internally for all three reward tokens. This is incorrect as it will just reset the reward rates of the caller, leading to the loss of all of their unclaimed staking rewards.

Users are going to lose all of their unclaimed rewards whenever they stake additional CSX tokens.

title: The USDT Reward Claiming Functionality of VestedStaking Can Be DoSed Due to a Logical Error
content: The vulnerability resides in the USDT reward‑claiming path of the VestedStaking contract. When a user calls claimRewards with claimUsdt set to true and a non‑zero usdtAmount, the function records the contract’s own USDT balance in a variable called beforeBalance, then transfers the requested amount to the caller and finally recomputes usdtAmount as the difference between the caller’s post‑transfer balance and the previously stored beforeBalance. Because beforeBalance was taken from the contract instead of the caller, the subtraction uses mismatched sources: it subtracts the contract’s balance from the caller’s balance. In normal situations where the contract holds enough USDT, the error may go unnoticed, but when the contract’s balance is zero or lower than the amount being transferred – for example after an attacker deliberately sends a tiny excess of USDT to the contract or when transfer fees are enabled and exceed the contract’s holdings – the subtraction underflows, triggering Solidity’s panic code 0x11 (arithmetic under/overflow). The transaction then reverts, effectively denying any user the ability to claim their USDT rewards. From the user’s perspective the claim either fails with a low‑level panic or succeeds but the emitted Claim event reports an incorrect USDT amount, often zero, while the user’s wallet shows no new tokens. The root cause is an accounting mistake: the code intended to measure the recipient’s balance before the transfer, but mistakenly measured the contract’s balance, breaking the invariant that the difference equals the transferred amount. This logical flaw was discovered during a security audit by Shiedify, which also provided a proof‑of‑concept test that forces the underflow by depositing a single wei‑scale USDT amount greater than the vester’s balance. The issue is hard to spot because the transfer itself appears successful and the bug only manifests under specific low‑balance conditions, which may not be exercised in routine testing. The vulnerability belongs to the class of balance‑mismanagement bugs that lead to arithmetic underflows and denial‑of‑service of reward functions. To remediate, the contract should record the caller’s balance (msg.sender) before the transfer, or avoid recomputing usdtAmount altogether and rely on the known usdtAmount value. Correcting the address used for the balance query restores proper accounting, prevents the underflow, and ensures that users receive the expected USDT rewards and that the Claim event reflects the true transferred amount.

title: H-1 Addresses for oracles should be whitelisted
content: The vulnerability consists of allowing any address to be used as a price oracle when a new stable pool is created through the factory contract. Because the factory does not restrict or validate the oracle address, a malicious actor can supply an oracle that returns arbitrary prices. The root cause is the absence of an access control or whitelist for oracle contracts, combined with the assumption that the oracle will always provide a correct, monotonic price feed. An attacker can deploy a pool with a deliberately manipulated oracle, then perform swaps or liquidity removals while the oracle reports inflated or deflated asset values. This creates a price imbalance inside the pool, enabling the attacker to extract assets at a favorable rate. The impact is that liquidity providers who deposit into such a pool experience a reduction of their token balances, effectively losing value, and end users may receive incorrect swap amounts or see their balances drop unexpectedly. The condition under which the bug manifests is any time a new pool is instantiated with a user‑supplied oracle address; no further checks are performed before the pool becomes operational. The affected parties include the protocol because the integrity of its pools is compromised, third‑party integrations that rely on the pool’s price stability, and any LPs or traders interacting with a maliciously created pool. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the factory’s pool‑creation logic and identified that the oracle parameter is not validated. Because the pool may appear normal at first glance—its contract code is standard and the oracle can be a seemingly legitimate contract—the problem can be hard to notice until abnormal price movements or unexpected loss of funds are observed. From a user perspective the symptoms are a sudden drop of LP token value, swaps returning far less than expected, or balances becoming zero after a removal. The expectation that a stable pool will preserve value is violated, leading to money disappearing and accounting breaking. To remediate, the factory should maintain a whitelist of approved oracle contracts, or otherwise enforce that only oracles meeting predefined security criteria can be used. This prevents arbitrary price manipulation and aligns with the business logic that pools must maintain a stable, predictable price relationship. In practice the fix involves adding a mapping of allowed oracle addresses and checking it during pool creation, with governance processes to add or remove entries. The bug belongs to the class of untrusted external contract injection or oracle address whitelisting omission, which can lead to price manipulation and fund loss in DeFi protocols.
summary:
The current implementation of the Pools Factory allows users to create pools with user-supplied oracles to determine prices of assets:
CurveStableSwapFactoryNG.vy#L531
CurveStableSwapFactoryNG.vy#L657
This allows malicious users to create pools with oracles that can change their returned values. This could lead to imbalanced pools where a malicious user can steal assets via swaps or liquidity removes. However, the pools created by malicious users should not accumulate any liquidity since these pools will not be accepted by the community and LPs in these pools will not be rewarded with CRV tokens.
But there is one more dangerous scenario that can lead to lost value by Curve users. Let's imagine a situation where a new protocol builds an integration with Curve and deploys a stable pool with some custom mechanics, which is allowed because of the user-supplied oracles. But developers didn't pay enough attention to the security of their price oracle, and a hack took place with the manipulation of the price oracle (flashloan manipulation, donation attack, price control in the pool, etc.) set by that team in the pool. In this case, Curve LPs will lose value.
In our opinion, it is impossible to control the quality of price oracles in an automated way (it is impossible to build this type of check inside any function) which is why we recommend adding a whitelist for oracles so the community can assess the quality of new oracles. Moreover, pools with volatile oracles will lead to permanent losses for LPs (if someone decides to create a wETH/wBTC pool with an oracle that sets the price from wETH to wBTC).

title: H-2 Incorrect storage update
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect accounting bug in the meta‑pool component of a stable‑swap implementation. When liquidity is added through the meta_add_liquidity routine, the contract receives a net amount of the underlying token that may be reduced by protocol‑level fees applied during the addition.
