However, the storage variable that tracks the pool's balance of the meta‑coin is updated with the full fee amount (dx_w_fee) instead of the net amount actually transferred in. This mismatch means the internal accounting state diverges from the real token balances held by the contract. The bug manifests after a call to exchange_underlying, which internally invokes meta_add_liquidity and then attempts to update stored_balances. Because the stored balance is inflated, the subsequent call to exchange_received, which relies on the invariant that stored balances reflect true holdings, fails or produces incorrect results. From a user perspective, a swap may appear to succeed once, but any following swap or withdrawal returns zero or an unexpected amount, leading to missing refunds or balances that suddenly become zero. The impact is high: the pool can become unusable after a single operation, potentially locking user funds or causing loss of expected returns. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the Curve StableSwapNG codebase, where the auditor noticed that the variable update did not account for possible fees on liquidity addition. It is subtle because the contract still accepts the transaction and does not revert, so the failure only becomes visible on subsequent operations, making it hard to detect through simple testing. The root cause is a logical error in the accounting formula: using the raw fee value instead of the net amount after fee deduction. To remediate, the storage update should be changed to add the actual amount returned from meta_add_liquidity, i.e., the net increase after fees, ensuring that the on‑chain balance and the internal accounting remain consistent. This class of bug falls under incorrect state update or accounting inconsistency, which violates the fundamental business logic that pool balances must always match the tokens held, breaking the guarantee of accurate swaps and refunds.
summary: stored_balances is increased by dx_w_fee for metacoin in meta_pool here CurveStableSwapMetaNG.vy#L1065 but actually it should be increased by dx_w_fee that returned from the meta_add_liquidity because the actual increase in metacoin balance will be less than dx_w_fee from transfer_in due to possible fees on liquidity addition. This finding is classified as HIGH because the current implementation of the meta_pool will become broken after one call of the exchange_underlying() function (exchange_received will not work after this).

title: H-3 Incorrect work for the base_pool swap
content: The vulnerability is an accounting error in a Curve metapool implementation that occurs when a user attempts to swap a token that belongs to the underlying base pool through the metapool interface. The contract’s transfer_in routine incorrectly updates the internal stored_balances mapping for the base‑pool token, even though the balance of that token should be managed by the base pool itself. Because the stored_balances entry is altered, the invariant that the pool’s accounting reflects the true token reserves is broken. When the subsequent exchange_received function checks the pool’s state, the mismatch triggers a revert, causing the whole swap transaction to fail. This bug manifests only for the specific path of swapping base‑pool tokens via the metapool; regular swaps of the metapool’s own tokens are unaffected. Users experience a failed transaction where they receive no output tokens, their wallet balance remains unchanged, and the UI may show a generic error or a silent revert. The impact is that the pool becomes unusable for that token pair after the first erroneous swap, effectively locking liquidity and preventing further trades, which can erode confidence in the protocol. The issue was discovered during a formal security audit that examined the token transfer logic of the metapool contract. It is hard to notice because the faulty code path is rarely exercised in normal operation and the failure appears later in the exchange_received call, making the root cause non‑obvious. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of state‑inconsistency or double‑accounting errors where a contract updates a balance that should be delegated to another contract. To remediate, the contract should either prohibit swaps of base‑pool tokens through the metapool or adjust the transfer logic so that stored_balances is not modified for those tokens, thereby preserving the correct accounting invariant and preventing the revert cascade.
summary: Metapool incorrectly updates stored_balances when a user tries to swap tokens in base_pool from the metapool. CurveStableSwapMetaNG.vy#L1087-L1089 In the case of swap basepool tokens from metapool, stored_balances shouldn't be updated in transfer_in. Because of this update, the pool will become broken and always revert on the exchange_received call.

title: Game fee locked in earlyEndGame
content: The vulnerability concerns the earlyEndGame function of a gaming smart contract. When the function is executed, the contract calculates a game fee based on a take‑rate and subtracts that amount from the player’s payout. However, after the subtraction the fee is never transferred to the designated treasury address; instead it remains trapped in the contract’s balance. This accounting omission means that every time earlyEndGame is called, the contract’s internal ether pool grows with fees that cannot be reclaimed, while the treasury receives no revenue. The issue originates from missing transfer logic after the fee deduction step, a classic fee‑locking or accounting‑omission bug. An attacker or any caller with admin rights can trigger earlyEndGame repeatedly, causing the contract to accumulate unrecoverable funds. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that the payout they receive is lower than expected, yet there is no visible error and the missing amount silently disappears into the contract’s balance. The protocol’s economic model is violated because fees that should be routed to the treasury are instead locked, potentially leading to a shortfall in reward pools or treasury funding. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the payout flow and noticed that the fee variable was never used in a call to the treasury. It can be hard to notice because the contract does not emit an event for the fee transfer and the balance increase is not directly observable by end‑users. The proper remediation is to add a transfer (or call) to the treasury address after the fee is calculated and deducted, and to handle any failure of that transfer gracefully, ensuring that the fee is either sent or the transaction reverts. This restores the intended accounting flow where the fee is collected and the treasury is compensated, preventing funds from becoming permanently locked in the contract.
summary: In the earlyEndGame function, there is an issue where the game fee deducted from a player's payout is not subsequently transferred to the treasury address. Instead, the fee is subtracted from the player's payout and remains in the contract. This results in the funds being locked within the contract without a dedicated method available to transfer these collected fees to the treasury.

title: H-4 An incorrect rate update
content: The vulnerability is a timing or ordering flaw in the CRV reward gauge contract where the reward rate is read from storage before the epoch transition logic has been executed. Because the contract fetches the rate prior to updating the epoch, it records a value that reflects the previous epoch’s parameters instead of the newly‑calculated rate for the current epoch. This mismatch can be triggered whenever the epoch update function is called, which typically occurs at the start of a new reward period. An attacker or any user who initiates the update at a strategic moment can cause the contract to store an incorrect rate, leading to an inaccurate amount of CRV tokens being minted and distributed to liquidity providers. The impact is that users may receive more or fewer CRV tokens than the protocol’s economic model intends, breaking the accounting guarantees of the system and potentially draining or inflating the token supply. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit performed by MixBytes, who noted that the rate‑fetching line appears before the epoch‑update call in the LiquidityGauge contract. The bug is subtle because the contract still updates a rate value, so on‑chain observers see a change, but the value is offset by one epoch, making the discrepancy hard to spot without comparing expected versus actual reward calculations. From a user’s perspective the symptoms can include receiving a zero or unexpectedly low CRV reward after staking, seeing their balance remain unchanged despite a new epoch, or observing that the total CRV minted does not match the protocol’s published emission schedule. The root cause is a logical error in the sequence of operations: the contract should first perform the epoch transition, which may adjust parameters such as total supply or voting power, and only then compute and store the new reward rate based on the updated state. The recommended remediation is to reorder the calls so that the rate is fetched after the epoch update, ensuring that the stored rate accurately reflects the current epoch’s conditions and preserving the intended distribution mechanics.
summary: rate is fetched before epoch update in the CRV contract LiquidityGauge.vy#L237-L238 which can lead to an incorrect rate being saved to the storage. This finding is classified as HIGH severity because an incorrect rate update will lead to incorrect CRV distribution to users.

title: H-5 Incorrect rewards distribution
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect rewards distribution logic in the liquidity gauge contract. When a reward token is deposited while the gauge has no staked tokens (totalSupply == 0), the contract still updates the internal timestamp variable last_update. Because the reward accounting formula uses last_update to calculate accrued rewards per share, advancing the timestamp without any shares causes the newly deposited reward amount to be recorded as already distributed, even though there are no participants to receive it. As a result the reward balance is moved into an internal accounting bucket that can never be claimed, effectively locking those tokens inside the contract. An attacker or any user can trigger the condition simply by calling the reward deposit function when the gauge is empty, which may happen after all users have withdrawn their liquidity or before any deposits have been made. The impact is that a portion of the reward pool becomes permanently unrecoverable, reducing the overall incentive for liquidity providers and potentially causing a loss of funds for the protocol’s reward distributor. The issue occurs only when totalSupply is zero at the time of reward deposit; otherwise the distribution works as intended. It affects any party that relies on the gauge to receive rewards, including liquidity providers, the protocol’s treasury, and any third‑party integrators that expect correct reward accounting. The bug was discovered during a manual code review of the reward distribution function, where the auditor noticed that last_update is unconditionally set regardless of the presence of staked tokens. Because the contract does not emit an explicit error or revert, the problem can be subtle and may only be observed as missing rewards or a shrinking reward balance after a deposit to an empty gauge. From a user’s perspective the UI may show that a reward deposit succeeded, but later the expected reward claim returns zero, leading to confusion that funds disappeared or rewards are missing. This class of bug belongs to accounting or state‑update errors where a bookkeeping variable is modified without the necessary pre‑condition, breaking the invariant that rewards are only accrued when there are active shares. To remediate the issue the contract should guard the update of last_update (and any related per‑share calculations) with a condition that totalSupply > 0, or alternatively skip the reward distribution logic entirely when the gauge is empty. Ensuring that reward deposits are either rejected or deferred until at least one share exists will prevent the locking of tokens and restore correct reward accounting.
summary: Some of the rewards will be blocked on the contract if they were deposited to the empty gauge (when totalSupply == 0) LiquidityGauge.vy#L318 This happens because last_update will be updated nevertheless totalSupply is zero. This finding is classified as HIGH severity since the reward distributor will block some rewards on the contract without a possibility to retrieve them.

title: H-1 An inﬂated fee in the AMM leads to a partial AMM DOS
content: The vulnerability is an accounting error in the automated market maker (AMM) withdraw logic where the admin fee for the borrowed token (adminfeesx) is increased without scaling by the token’s precision constant (BORROWED_PRECISION). The root cause is a missing division operation when the contract transfers the remaining dust from a tick to the protocol’s fee pool. Because the borrowed token may have a lower decimal precision (for example WBTC with 8 decimals) the unchecked addition inflates the recorded fee by up to ten orders of magnitude. An attacker can exploit this by deliberately inflating the share price of a tick so that the dust amount becomes large, then triggering the final‑withdraw path. The inflated adminfeesx value can be harvested through the public collect_fees() function, which sends the entire borrowed‑token balance of the AMM to the factory’s fee_receiver. When the fee_receiver is functional, the AMM loses essentially all of its borrowed‑token liquidity, preventing any further withdrawals from that tick and causing a partial denial‑of‑service for users. The issue manifests only when a withdrawal empties a tick and dust is present; it does not depend on the configured ADMIN_FEE parameter. It affects all participants who rely on the AMM to retrieve their borrowed assets, including lenders, borrowers, and any downstream protocol that routes through the AMM. The bug was discovered during a manual security audit by MixBytes, where the logical flow of the withdraw() function was examined and the missing division was identified. It is hard to notice because the fee accounting appears normal under typical usage and the overflow only becomes evident when the dust conversion is triggered, a scenario that may not occur in routine tests. Conceptually, the fix is to apply the same precision scaling used for the collateral side: divide the raw fee amount x by BORROWED_PRECISION before adding it to adminfeesx, ensuring that fee accounting respects the token’s decimal representation. This correction restores the intended invariant that fees are a small proportion of the total balance, prevents fee inflation, and eliminates the possibility of draining the AMM’s borrowed‑token pool, thereby preserving normal withdrawal functionality and protecting user funds.
summary:
The adminfeesx variable is not divided by BORROWED_PRECISION in AMM withdraw():
If withdrawal is the last one - transfer dust to admin fees
if new_shares == 0:
if x > 0:
self.adminfeesx += x
if y > 0:
self.adminfeesy += unsafediv(y, COLLATERALPRECISION)
AMM.vy#L794
If borrowed_token is WBTC (decimals=8), then the error in fee accrual will be on the order of 10 magnitudes. A hacker could perform an inﬂation attack on the nearest available tick to trigger this piece of code and inﬂate adminfeesx to the total amount of the borrowed_token balance in the AMM, while losing 10 magnitudes less funds than the ﬁnal inﬂation amount. If the hacker then calls collect_fees(), which is a public method, all borrowed tokens from the AMM will be sent to FACTORY.fee_receiver(). This will lead to a partial DOS of the AMM, as users will lose the ability to withdraw borrowed tokens from ticks, as there simply won't be any funds in the AMM for this.
There are a few notes on this:
1. This attack does not depend on ADMIN_FEE; the code is always activated when there is dust in the tick. In order to execute the attack, the hacker needs to inﬂate the share price in the tick, causing the dust to have a large value.
2. AMM uses dead shares, but price inﬂation is still possible via the exchange() method or other means. It's just not proﬁtable for the hacker.
3. Currently, collectfees() reverts as Vault does not have a feereceiver() method which is called by the collectfees() method. Still, if the collectfees() revert issue is addressed by introducing a fee_receiver() in the factory, then the fee inﬂation bug will arise.

title: H-2 An incorrect last_tvl state after the price pair removal
content: The vulnerability resides in a price‑aggregation contract that maintains a historical total‑value‑locked (TVL) record in an array called last_tvl. When a price pair is removed through the contract’s removal routine, the implementation fails to delete the corresponding entry from the last_tvl array. As a result, the array continues to contain stale TVL data for a pair that no longer exists. This mismatch causes the contract to compute an inaccurate aggregate TVL and to publish incorrect price information for the remaining pairs. The root cause is a missing state‑cleanup step: the removal function updates the mapping of active price pairs but does not synchronize the auxiliary accounting array. An attacker or any user observing the contract can exploit the bug simply by triggering the removal of a price pair (or by waiting for a legitimate removal) and then reading the aggregated TVL value, which will be inflated or deflated depending on the stale entry. The impact includes misleading TVL figures displayed on dashboards, potential mispricing of loans or deposits that rely on the aggregated price, and erosion of trust in the protocol’s accounting. The condition occurs whenever the protocol removes a price pair – a routine that may be invoked periodically as markets evolve or as governance decisions are enacted. All participants that depend on the contract’s TVL output – lenders, borrowers, front‑end interfaces, and analytics services – are affected because they receive a distorted view of the total assets under management. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit of the contract’s state‑transition logic, where the auditor noticed that the array length remained unchanged after a removal call. The bug can be hard to notice because the contract still reports a numeric TVL value; the discrepancy only becomes apparent when comparing the TVL against known asset balances or when a removed pair’s contribution is expected to disappear. To remediate, the removal routine should be extended to locate and delete the matching entry in the last_tvl array, or to rebuild the array without the removed pair, ensuring that the TVL aggregation reflects only active price pairs. Conceptually, this is a state‑inconsistency or stale‑data bug, where auxiliary bookkeeping structures are not kept in sync with the primary data set, violating the protocol’s accounting invariants and leading to user‑visible symptoms such as “TVL shows a higher amount than my deposited balance” or “price feed appears unchanged after a pair was removed.”
summary:
• AggregateStablePrice2.vy#L108
The AggregateStablePrice contract doesn't remove the corresponding entry in the last_tvl array during the removepricepair() call. This may result in inaccurate TVL calculations and incorrect price aggregations.

title: H-1 Withdrawal of tokens with debt as zero
content: The vulnerability is a rounding error in the liquidation routine that can reduce the recorded debt to zero, allowing an attacker to withdraw the full amount of collateral without repaying any portion of the loan. The root cause is the use of integer division (unsafe_div) on the product of the current debt and a fractional parameter (frac) where the denominator is 10**18. Because Solidity integer division truncates toward zero, if debt * frac is smaller than 10**18 the division result becomes zero. When this occurs the contract updates the loan’s debt to zero and proceeds with the collateral transfer, effectively erasing the borrower’s obligation. An attacker can exploit this by creating a loan with a small debt amount and then calling the extended liquidation function with frac set to a value just below 10**18 (for example 10**18‑1). The multiplication debt*frac then falls below the denominator, the division yields zero, and the liquidation logic treats the loan as fully repaid. The attacker receives the entire collateral balance while the stablecoin balance remains unchanged, which from a user’s perspective looks like “my collateral increased for free” or “I got tokens without paying anything”. The impact is a direct loss of collateral value for the protocol and any lenders, as the protocol’s accounting assumptions that debt must be positive before collateral can be seized are violated. This condition only occurs when the debt is sufficiently small relative to the chosen fraction, so larger loans are not directly affected, but the bug undermines the fundamental guarantee of debt repayment in liquidation. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by MixBytes, and it can be hard to notice because the zero‑debt state may appear impossible under normal operation, and the gas cost of the exploit is modest, making it easy to overlook in testing. To remediate, the contract should enforce that the resulting debt after the division is non‑zero, or use a ceiling division or explicit minimum repayment check, ensuring that a liquidation cannot clear the debt entirely when the calculated repayment would be zero. This fixes the rounding bug and restores the intended economic invariant that collateral can only be seized after an actual debt repayment.
summary:
This code allows you not to spend debt in liquidation (
Controller.vy#L990):
```solidity
debt = unsafe_div(debt * frac, 10**18)
```
If debt * frac is less than 10**18, then you don't have to pay for the liquidation part. We especially have
the ability to eliminate the entire collateral by passing frac as 1. Example:
```solidity
l_amount = 1
collateral_token.mint_for_testing(user, c_amount)
market_controller.create_loan(c_amount, l_amount, n)
market_controller.liquidate_extended(user, 0, 10**18 - 1,
True, ZERO_ADDRESS, [])
d_debt = 0
xy[0] = 0
xy[1] = 1000
PROFIT stablecoin.balanceOf(user) +0
PROFIT collateral_token.balanceOf(user) +1000
```
In this case, the attack is disadvantageous due to the gas.

title: H-2 AMM.exchange() produces negative fees
content: The vulnerability consists of a fee‑calculation error in the AMM exchange() routine that can produce negative fees when the configured AMM fee (and admin fee) are very low. The root cause is an inaccurate computation of the constant‑product invariant that does not correctly account for fee subtraction, allowing rounding or precision loss to turn the fee amount negative. An attacker can exploit this by performing a back‑and‑forth swap across many price ticks inside a single transaction. Each tick yields a tiny profit (on the order of 0.000000000136353050% of the traded amount) because the fee is effectively subtracted from the pool instead of being added. By repeating the cycle thousands of times, especially on a sidechain with cheap gas, the accumulated profit can become large enough to drain a significant portion of the pool’s stablecoin reserves. The impact is that funds disappear from the AMM: liquidity providers see their balances shrink, users receive more tokens than expected in a single swap but the pool overall loses value, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions that fees are non‑negative are violated. The condition for the bug to manifest is that the AMM fee is set between zero and 650,000 (the attack fails when the fee is 1,000,000 or higher). It is most relevant on networks with low transaction costs where the gas expense is lower than the per‑tick profit. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by MixBytes, which identified the mathematical inconsistency in the fee formula. The problem is hard to notice because the per‑tick profit is extremely small and may be masked by gas costs on mainnet, only becoming apparent when gas is cheap and the attack is amplified through many iterations. The recommended mitigation is to enforce a minimum AMM fee of at least 1,000,000 or to redesign the fee calculation to guarantee non‑negative fees and proper invariant preservation. This class of bug belongs to fee‑underflow or negative‑fee rounding errors common in constant‑product AMMs, where the business logic assumes that a round‑trip trade cannot generate profit without external arbitrage. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are unexpected extra tokens received in a single swap, or more critically, a gradual reduction of the pool’s total balance without any visible external trades, leading to loss of funds for liquidity providers.
summary:
Using exchange() back-and-forth can generate profit without losing stablecoins. This occurs due to
inaccuracies in calculating the invariant when AMM fees are low.
The profit generated from each tick is small (approximately 0.000000000136353050%), but under certain
circumstances it can be significant enough for a hacker to execute an attack.
For example, let's assume that there are 100 billion USD spread across 1000 ticks and both the AMM fee
and AMM admin fee are equal to zero. In this case, during a single back-and-forth pass, the hacker would
earn 0.000000000136353050% from each tick and their total profit from the 100 billion would be
approximately 0.136 USD.
If we consider that such a back-and-forth pass would take 833,333 gas, then at the current gas prices on
the Ethereum mainnet, such an attack would not be economically feasible.
However, the attack may become more relevant in the future if it is executed on a sidechain with low gas
fees. For example, at a gas price of 130 gwei on the Polygon MATIC network (1 MATIC = $0.93), the hacker
would spend approximately $0.10 on the attack but earn $0.136. The hacker can repeat the back-and-forth
passes in a cycle within a single transaction 1000 times in a cycle and will get a net profit of $36 from a
single transaction. By repeating this attack over and over again, they would be able to drain a significant
portion of the funds available in the AMM.
The attack works with an AMM fee ranging from 0 to 650,000. Starting from an AMM fee of 1,000,000, the
attack fails.

title: RubiconRouter: Offers created through offerWithETH
content: The RubiconRouter contract provides a convenience function called offerWithETH that allows a user to create a market offer while sending Ether in a single transaction. Internally this function forwards the call to the RubiconMarket contract's offer function. The market contract records the address of the caller (msg.sender) as the offer owner. Because the call originates from the router, the router contract's own address is recorded as the owner of the newly created offer instead of the original external user. This misassignment of ownership creates a privilege‑escalation flaw: the cancelForETH function in RubiconRouter is designed to let the offer owner cancel the offer and retrieve the locked Ether. Since the stored owner is the router contract itself, the cancelForETH function does not verify the identity of the external caller against the original user. Consequently, any address can invoke cancelForETH on an offer that was created through offerWithETH and siphon the Ether that was supposed to be held for the legitimate offer maker. The vulnerability manifests only for offers created via the router's offerWithETH path; offers created through other entry points retain the correct owner. Affected parties include any user who creates an ETH‑backed offer through the router, the Rubicon protocol which loses trust in its settlement logic, and ultimately the funds that disappear from the expected escrow. The issue was uncovered during a formal security audit that traced the ownership flow across contract boundaries and observed that the router address was being written to the offer struct. It is subtle because the router contract appears to be a neutral middle‑man and no explicit error is emitted; the mistake is hidden in the implicit use of msg.sender across contracts. To remediate the defect, the router must explicitly forward the original caller's address to the market contract, for example by passing msg.sender as an explicit owner parameter or by having the market contract accept a designated owner argument. Additionally, the cancelForETH function should verify that the caller matches the recorded offer owner, ensuring that only the true creator can cancel the offer. This class of bug falls under "misaligned access control" or "incorrect ownership propagation" and results in a refund calculation error where users receive nothing and an attacker receives the full ETH amount, violating the protocol's accounting assumptions that locked funds remain under the control of the offer initiator.
summary:
```solidity
When a user creates an offer through the offerWithETH function of the RubiconRouter contract, the offer function of the RubiconMarket contract is called, and the RubiconRouter contract address is set to offer.owner in the offer function.

This means that anyone can call the cancelForETH function of the RubiconRouter contract to cancel the offer and get the ether.
```

title: RubiconRouter: Offers created through offerForETH cannot be cancelled
content: The vulnerability resides in the RubiconRouter contract's handling of offers created through its offerForETH function. When a user invokes offerForETH, the router forwards the call to RubiconMarket's offer function and records the router contract’s own address as the offer owner instead of the caller’s address. Because the RubiconRouter does not expose any method that can cancel an offer whose owner is the router, a user who creates an ETH‑based offer has no means to withdraw the locked funds if the offer is never matched. The root cause is a mismatch between the logical owner of the offer (the user) and the on‑chain owner stored in the market (the router), combined with the absence of a cancellation entry point in the router. Exploitation is straightforward: a user creates an offer, the ETH is transferred to the router and then locked in the market contract, and because no cancelForERC or equivalent function exists, the ETH remains unrecoverable until another party accepts the offer. The impact is that user balances can disappear from the user's perspective – the UI will show the user’s ETH as deposited but never returned, leading to a situation where funds are effectively frozen. This condition occurs every time an offer is created via offerForETH and remains unfilled; it does not depend on any special attacker actions, making it a systemic risk for any participant. The affected parties include ordinary users who intend to provide liquidity with ETH, as well as the protocol itself, which may accumulate dead capital and suffer reputational damage. The issue was discovered during a formal audit, where the lack of a cancellation pathway was observed while reviewing the router’s public interface and ownership handling logic. It can be hard to notice because most other offer creation functions do implement cancellation, so developers may assume symmetry without verifying the ETH‑specific path. To remediate the problem, the router should record the message sender (msg.sender) as the offer owner when calling market.offer, and a corresponding cancelForERC (or cancelWithETH) function should be added that validates the caller against the stored owner and invokes the market’s cancel routine. This change restores the expected economic invariant that users can always retrieve their assets when an order is not executed, aligning the implementation with standard market behavior and preventing funds from becoming permanently locked.
summary:
```solidity
When a user creates an offer through the offerForETH function of the RubiconRouter contract, the offer function of the RubiconMarket contract is called, and the RubiconRouter contract address is set to offer.owner in the offer function.

But the RubiconRouter contract does not implement a function to cancel this offer. This means that if no one accepts the offer, the user’s tokens will be locked in the contract.
```

title: Attacker could steal almost all the bonus tokens in BathBuddy Vesting Wallet
content: The vulnerability resides in the way the BathBuddy Vesting Wallet calculates a user’s entitlement to bonus tokens. The contract determines the reward amount at the moment of withdrawal by multiplying the total releasable bonus tokens by the caller’s current (spot) share of the pool and dividing by the initial total supply of shares. Because the calculation uses the instantaneous share balance rather than a historically‑locked snapshot, an attacker can temporarily acquire an overwhelming proportion of the pool, claim the reward, and then relinquish that position in the same transaction. In practice, an adversary can perform a flash‑loan to borrow a large amount of the underlying asset, deposit it into the BathToken pool just before the vesting period ends, and immediately withdraw both the deposited liquidity and the associated bonus tokens. The withdraw call triggers the reward distribution, and the attacker’s inflated share causes the contract to allocate almost the entire remaining bonus token balance to them, leaving only a negligible dust amount for legitimate participants. This attack can be executed atomically, meaning the pool’s share distribution is manipulated within a single block, making the exploit difficult to detect during normal operation. The impact is severe: honest users who later withdraw receive dramatically reduced bonuses, effectively losing the majority of the incentive rewards that were intended for them. The issue affects all participants of the BathBuddy vesting scheme, including token holders, liquidity providers, and the protocol’s economic model, as it undermines the fairness and accounting assumptions underlying the reward system. The flaw was discovered during a security audit and reproduced in a test suite that demonstrated an attacker draining roughly 997 DAI of a 1000 DAI bonus pool while legitimate users received less than one DAI. The problem is subtle because the contract’s code appears to correctly compute a proportional share, yet it fails to account for the temporal dimension of share ownership. The recommended mitigation is to replace the spot‑share calculation with a checkpointing mechanism that records each user’s share balance at the end of the previous block (or at the start of the vesting interval) before rewards are allocated, thereby preventing flash‑loan manipulation and ensuring rewards are distributed according to the actual historical stake. Implementing a reward distribution pattern similar to Synthetix’s StakingRewards contract, which accrues rewards over time per share, would resolve the issue and restore the intended economic fairness.
summary:
```solidity
BathBuddy is a Vesting Wallet that payout withdrawers any `bonusTokens` they may have accrued while staking in the Bath Token (e.g. network incentives/governance tokens).

BathBuddy Vesting Wallet releases a user their relative share of the pool’s total vested bonus token during the withdraw call on BathToken.sol. This vesting occurs linearly over Unix time.

It was observed that an attacker could steal almost all the `bonusTokens` in the BathBuddy Vesting Wallet.
```

title: Decimals not Handled by the Application Frontend
content: The vulnerability is a mismatch between the user‑interface handling of wager amounts and the underlying accounting logic of the coin‑flip game. The frontend allows users to type fractional values such as 0.001 for the wager, but it formats the displayed win or loss amount by rounding any value smaller than one whole unit to $0. Consequently, when a flip is executed the UI reports a $0 result while the smart‑contract‑backed session balance is updated with the exact decimal amount entered, and the Recent Flips table records the same fractional change. This discrepancy arises because the application does not enforce integer‑only inputs nor does it communicate to the user that sub‑unit wagers are unsupported. An attacker or any user can exploit the bug simply by entering a decimal wager; the contract will accept the value, adjust the balance accordingly, but the UI will hide the monetary effect, making it appear that no money was won or lost. The impact includes silent loss or gain of small amounts that accumulate over many flips, breaking the expected accounting invariants of the game, potentially allowing an adversary to manipulate the contract’s state without visible feedback, and causing gas‑griefing if the backend repeatedly processes tiny values it was not designed for. The issue manifests whenever the wager input field is set to “Other” and a user supplies a non‑integer amount, which can happen in any session where the UI does not validate the input. All participants—players, the protocol operator, and auditors—are affected because the financial ledger no longer reflects the user‑perceived outcomes, violating trust and the business rule that a displayed win/loss should correspond to the actual balance change. The flaw was discovered during a manual security review of the frontend, where the tester entered a decimal wager and observed the UI showing $0 while the on‑chain balance changed. It is hard to notice because the UI appears to work correctly for whole‑unit bets, and the discrepancy only surfaces for fractional inputs that many users may never try. To remediate, the application should enforce integer‑only wager validation, reject or round decimal inputs before they reach the contract, and clearly inform users that only whole‑unit amounts are accepted, thereby aligning the displayed result with the actual balance update and preserving the accounting integrity of the game.
summary:
In dedprz.virtual.tech a user can manually enter 0.(decimal) numbers in the wager amount. Consequently, when a user flips the coin, the result will always show that the user either lost or won $0 (the front end rounds it to 0). Despite this, the session balance will be updated with the decimal values entered, and the Recent Flips table will also reflect these changes.
Since the application relies on blockchain technology, these rounding errors could lead to issues in the calculations or even just gas griefing, as the backend might not be able to handle decimal values properly.
This particular finding is classified as high since it is related to gaming finance (at least from the frontend perspective), and the app is displaying amounts in decimals (something that might not be expected by the backend).
Figure 1: In the image: A user introduced a decimal value 0.001 in the wager amount. The application still processes that amount when flipping the coin but reports 0$ win/loss Session balance and Recent Flips are still updated according to the decimals added/subtracted.

title: Sale token amount is not adjusted per its decimals
content: The vulnerability is an arithmetic scaling error in the token sale contract that converts a stablecoin contribution into the amount of sale tokens to be vested. The conversion routine assumes the sale token has six decimal places, matching the USDC precision, and therefore does not apply an additional factor for tokens that use a larger decimal count such as the common 18‑decimal ERC20. Because the function returns ((_amountUSDC * 1e18) / _price) without multiplying by 10^(tokenDecimals‑6), the computed token quantity is smaller by a factor of 10^(tokenDecimals‑6). For an 18‑decimal token this factor is 10^12, meaning a user who expects to receive one million tokens will instead be allocated only one‑thousandth of a token, often appearing as dust or even zero in the user interface. The bug originates from a mismatch between the comment that claims the result is scaled for future token decimals and the actual implementation that omits the scaling step. It is triggered whenever a participant deposits USDC during the public sale and the sale token’s decimals exceed six. The affected parties are contributors who rely on the advertised token price; they receive far fewer tokens than paid for, leading to a loss of economic value and a breach of the protocol’s promised token distribution logic. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the documented scaling formula with the on‑chain code and identified the missing multiplication. It can be hard to notice because the contract still mints a non‑zero amount, so the transaction does not revert, and the UI may simply show a very small balance without obvious error messages. Exploitation does not require malicious intent; any honest user will be under‑allocated, effectively allowing the sale contract to retain the excess value. To remediate, the conversion function should query the token’s decimals via the ERC20 decimals() view and multiply the raw result by 10^(tokenDecimals‑6) (or equivalently by 1e12 for an 18‑decimal token). This adjustment restores the intended one‑to‑one price relationship and ensures that contributors receive the correct amount of tokens as advertised.

title: Withdrawal shares of msg.sender are burnt incorrectly in _removeLiquidity flow
content: The vulnerability originates from an inconsistency in the liquidity removal flow of the contract. When a caller invokes the internal function that removes liquidity, the contract creates (mints) a specific amount of withdrawal share tokens and assigns them to the address supplied in the options structure (the intended recipient of the withdrawal). This minting step correctly records the entitlement of the chosen destination to later claim the underlying assets. However, later in the same overall operation, the contract calls a separate internal routine that redeems excess idle assets and then destroys (burns) a portion of the withdrawal share tokens. The burn operation mistakenly references msg.sender – the address that initiated the transaction – instead of the destination address that originally received the minted shares. Because the burn target does not match the mint target, the shares that were supposed to be held by the destination are either left untouched or incorrectly removed from the caller’s balance. This mismatch can lead to a situation where the intended recipient cannot later redeem their shares, effectively locking or losing the value associated with those shares. The bug is a classic example of a logical accounting error where token accounting (mint vs burn) is performed on different principals, violating the invariant that every minted share must be burned from the same holder. Exploitation does not require sophisticated techniques; an attacker can simply call the liquidity removal function with a destination address different from their own, then trigger the redemption step, causing the contract to burn shares from the attacker while the destination never loses its shares, resulting in a denial of service for the destination or a loss of accounting integrity. The impact is high because users may see their withdrawal balances become zero or receive no funds despite having initiated a withdrawal, and the protocol’s accounting guarantees are broken, potentially leading to locked funds and loss of trust. The condition occurs whenever the remove‑liquidity flow is used with a non‑zero destination address – a common pattern for forwarding withdrawals to another wallet or contract. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the token accounting logic across the two functions. It can be hard to notice because the mint and burn calls are separated into different internal functions, and the variable names do not immediately reveal that they refer to different principals. To remediate the problem, the burn call should be changed to target the same address that received the minted withdrawal shares (the options.destination), ensuring that the accounting invariant holds and that users receive the expected funds after redemption. This correction restores the logical consistency of the withdrawal share lifecycle and prevents accidental loss or locking of user assets.
summary:
When _removeLiquidity is called, the _lpShares of AssetId._WITHDRAWAL_SHARE_ASSET_ID is minted for _options.destination.
```solidity
_mint(
    AssetId._WITHDRAWAL_SHARE_ASSET_ID,
    _options.destination, // <---
    _lpShares
);
```
But after distributing the excess idle in _redeemWithdrawalSharesInternal we burn the clamped amount of withdrawal shares for the msg.sender and not the _options.destination:
```solidity
_burn(
    AssetId._WITHDRAWAL_SHARE_ASSET_ID,
    msg.sender, // <---
    withdrawalSharesRedeemed
);
```
Note that burning for the msg.sender in _redeemWithdrawalShares makes sense.

title: Closing netted, non-matured shorts can lead to insolvency
content: The vulnerability originates from the contract's short‑closing routine when it is invoked before the short reaches its maturity date. In a typical netted position a user holds an equal amount of long and short tokens, so the pool’s net exposure appears balanced. The implementation updates the long exposure when a short is closed, but it does not perform a solvency verification after this update for non‑matured shorts. Consequently, if a user first opens a netted long‑short pair, then opens an additional un‑netted long, and finally closes the short before maturity, the long exposure of the pool increases while the short exposure disappears. The pool now holds more outstanding long positions than it has assets to satisfy at maturity. Because the contract skips the required solvency check in this scenario, the protocol can enter a state where it cannot honour all long redemptions, effectively becoming insolvent. From a user’s perspective the short closure appears to succeed and returns the expected proceeds, but later attempts to close the long positions either return zero or fail, leading to missing balances and funds that seemingly disappear. The issue is triggered only when closeShort is called on a short that is still before its maturity while there exist additional non‑netted longs; closing shorts at maturity does not suffer from this problem because the netted long exposure created by the short closure is immediately offset by the simultaneous closure of the corresponding matured longs. The flaw was uncovered during a formal audit by reproducing the scenario in a test that opened netted positions, added an extra long, advanced time to a partial‑term point, and then called closeShort, which caused the pool to become insolvent without any error. The problem is subtle because the netted balances initially look equal, masking the hidden increase in long exposure until the short is closed. To remediate, the contract should enforce a solvency check after updating long exposure in the internal _closeShort routine for any short that is closed before maturity, or otherwise restrict early closure of netted shorts, ensuring that the pool always retains enough assets to satisfy all outstanding long positions at the time of maturity.
summary: Closing netted shorts can increase the long exposure in case the now non-netted longs are not also closed. This happens when calling closeShort before maturity. As the long exposure increases, a solvency check is required so that all outstanding longs can be fulfilled at maturity. This is not done in closeShort and the protocol can end up insolvent.

title: H-1 Incorrect last_tvl state after price pair removal
content: The vulnerability resides in the AggregateStablePrice contract where the function responsible for removing a price pair does not also delete the associated entry in the last_tvl array. As a result, the contract continues to retain a stale TVL (total value locked) snapshot for a pair that has been logically removed. This mismatch between the active price pairs and the stored TVL data leads to inaccurate TVL calculations and consequently incorrect price aggregation results. The root cause is an incomplete state update: the removepricepair() routine updates the mapping of price pairs but neglects to keep the parallel last_tvl array in sync. An attacker or a malicious actor could exploit this inconsistency by triggering the removal of a price pair and then reading or using the outdated TVL entry to manipulate on‑chain metrics, such as inflating reported TVL to earn higher rewards or to mislead users about the health of the protocol. The impact includes distorted accounting, potential over‑payment of incentives, and loss of trust from users who see their balances or rewards calculated incorrectly. The bug manifests whenever removepricepair() is called, which typically occurs during governance actions that retire a stablecoin pair or during automated maintenance. All participants that rely on the TVL figure—liquidity providers, reward distributors, and external dashboards—are affected because they receive misleading information. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit by MixBytes, where the auditors compared the expected length of the last_tvl array with the active price pair list and observed a discrepancy. Because the contract still functions and does not revert, the problem can be subtle and may only be noticed when TVL‑dependent calculations produce unexpected results, such as zero rewards despite a healthy deposit. To remediate, the removepricepair() function should be extended to locate and delete the corresponding element in the last_tvl array, ensuring that both data structures remain consistent after a pair is removed. This fix restores the invariant that every active price pair has a matching TVL entry, thereby preventing accounting errors, preserving correct incentive distribution, and aligning on‑chain data with user expectations.
summary:
• AggregateStablePrice.vy#L90-L100
The AggregateStablePrice contract doesn't remove the corresponding entry in the last_tvl array during removepricepair() call.
This may result in inaccurate TVL calculations and incorrect price aggregations.

title: addLiquidity(...) can be griefed
content: The vulnerability resides in the addLiquidity function of the Hyperdrive contract, where an attacker can deny service to a legitimate liquidity provider by manipulating the internal APR calculation. The root cause is that the APR formula depends on a variable representing the short position size (denoted as z) without enforcing a lower bound, allowing z to be driven arbitrarily close to zero when the market has few or no outstanding long positions. When an attacker front‑runs a pending addLiquidity transaction and opens the maximum possible short, the ratio z/y becomes extremely small or even zero. This causes the expression (1‑z/y)^(ts/tnorm_pos) / (z/y)^ts to explode to a very large number or to trigger a division‑by‑zero error inside HyperdriveMath.calculateAPRFromReserves. The subsequent APR check against the user‑supplied _maxApr fails, or the contract reverts directly due to a zero denominator. Even if the user sets _maxApr to the maximum uint256 value, the division‑by‑zero case still forces a revert, and if the division is avoided the calculation of lpShares later underflows because endingPresentValue becomes smaller than startingPresentValue, leading to another revert. From the user’s perspective the transaction simply fails: no LP tokens are minted, the call returns an error such as InvalidApr or a generic arithmetic revert, and the gas spent is lost. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition for liquidity providers; they cannot add liquidity while the attacker maintains the manipulated short position, potentially discouraging participation and harming the pool’s health. The issue manifests only when an attacker can front‑run a transaction and when the market state permits a short that drives z near zero, conditions that are realistic in a high‑frequency trading environment. The bug was uncovered during a security audit by Spearbit, who noted its similarity to other sandwich‑style attacks that exploit extreme short positions. It is difficult to detect because the APR calculation normally yields reasonable values, and the extreme case only appears under a precise sequence of actions that may not be exercised in routine testing. To remediate the problem the contract should enforce a minimum bound on z (or on the shareReserves ratio), add explicit checks for a zero denominator before performing the APR calculation, and consider requiring a non‑zero _minApr value so that the APR check cannot be bypassed. Additionally, the lpShares computation should guard against underflow by verifying that endingPresentValue is not less than startingPresentValue, and the overall design should avoid relying on variables that can be driven to pathological extremes for critical financial formulas.
summary:
An attacker can DoS/block another use to provide liquidity to the Hyperdrive. The attack works as follows:
1. The attacker frontruns a transaction that would call addLiquidity(...) by opening the maximum possible short. In case of no or small outstanding longs ( L0_c ≈ 0 ), the attacker can reduce the z to a number close to 0 such that:
APR = (1 - z/y)^(ts/tnorm_pos) / (z/y)^ts
blows up to a really big number since the denominator or z/y^ts would be a really small number such the apr = HyperdriveMath.calculateAPRFromReserves(...) would not be less than or equal to _maxApr provided by the user in the next transaction. The attacker might also be able to trigger division by z/y = 0 revert.
2. The user's transaction of calling addLiquidity(...) would be processed and reverted due to above. Even if the user sets _maxApr = type(uint256).max, the attacker can take advantage of the division by 0 case or if that is not possible the following calculation of lpShares would underflow and revert due to the fact that endingPresentValue < startingPresentValue:
lpShares = (endingPresentValue - startingPresentValue).mulDivDown(
    lpTotalSupply,
    startingPresentValue
);
This line of attack is similar to the ones used in the below issues where the attacker tries to open a short with the maximum possible amount:
• Sandwich a call to addLiquidity(...) for profit
• Drain pool by sandwiching matured shorts

title: Applying checkpoint can revert
content: The vulnerability is that the function that applies a checkpoint to the AMM can revert when the pool’s share reserves become extremely low and a large share update is applied. The root cause is that the contract scales the bond reserves by the ratio of the new share reserves to the previous share reserves and then casts the result to a uint128. When the previous share reserves are close to zero, the ratio can become very large, causing the intermediate uint256 value to exceed the maximum value that fits into a uint128. The safe‑cast therefore reverts. An attacker can trigger this situation by opening a large short position that drains the share reserves to (or near) zero, then allowing an existing short to mature so that the checkpoint logic attempts to rebalance the reserves. The exploit results in the checkpoint function reverting, which prevents any subsequent trade from being processed because every trade first calls applyCheckpoint. Consequently, the pool becomes permanently stuck: liquidity providers and traders cannot close their positions or withdraw funds, effectively locking the assets in the contract. The condition occurs only when the pool is in a temporary state with near‑zero share reserves, which can happen after aggressive shorting or liquidity removal, and it is reproduced by the provided test that opens a maximal short and then advances time to maturity. The issue is subtle because the contract checks that reserves fit into uint128, a check that normally passes, and the overflow only appears under extreme but feasible reserve ratios, making it easy to miss during normal testing. The proper fix is to avoid casting large intermediate values to uint128 without verifying that the ratio will not overflow, for example by using a larger integer type for the intermediate calculation, adding explicit overflow guards, or redesigning the reserve‑scaling logic to handle near‑zero share reserves safely. This class of bug is an arithmetic overflow caused by unsafe down‑casting after a division by a very small denominator, leading to a denial‑of‑service condition where funds appear to “disappear” from the user’s perspective because they can no longer be traded or withdrawn.

title: First LP can steal subsequent LP provisions
content: An attacker who is the first liquidity provider can manipulate the pool’s accounting by donating a large amount of the underlying asset before another user’s addLiquidity transaction is mined. The contracts compute the number of yield shares to mint with the expression newShares = totalShares.mulDivDown(amount, assets). Because the assets variable can be increased by an external donation, the ratio amount / assets can become smaller than one unit, and the mulDivDown function, which rounds down, returns zero. When zero yield shares are allocated, the corresponding ERC4626 LP shares are also zero, so the victim’s deposit does not increase their LP token balance. The attacker then redeems their own shares, which now represent the entire pool balance including the victim’s contribution, effectively stealing the funds. This situation occurs when the totalSupply of LP shares is very low (often a single share) and the contract does not protect against virtual balance inflation. It affects any liquidity provider that attempts to add liquidity after the pool has been initialized with minimal liquidity, and it undermines the economic guarantees of the protocol because users expect to receive LP tokens proportional to their deposit. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the share‑minting logic of AaveHyperdrive and DsrHyperdrive and noticed that assets could be arbitrarily increased without corresponding share issuance. The bug is subtle because the zero‑share result is a consequence of integer rounding and may not be obvious from the UI, where a user sees a transaction succeed but receives no new LP tokens and later finds the pool balance reduced. To remediate, the contract should prevent virtual balance manipulation, for example by using OpenZeppelin’s ERC4626 virtual‑balance protection or by minting a fixed amount of initial LP shares to a dead address and locking them, thereby ensuring a minimum liquidity baseline and avoiding a share price reset to the initial value when totalSupply reaches zero. Changing the share calculation to avoid floor rounding to zero or adding explicit checks that newShares is non‑zero before proceeding would also close the attack surface.
summary:
The AaveHyperdrive and DsrHyperdrive compute the yield share contribution of LPs in _deposit as uint256 newShares = totalShares_.mulDivDown(amount, assets);. Furthermore, the assets can be artificially inflated by donating to the contract. The first depositor can use this to steal subsequent LP provisions by frontrunning them with a donation and making them mint 0 yield shares. The 0 yield shares contribution also translates to 0 minted LP shares as Hyperdrive's present value does not change. The attacker can afterward redeem their own shares for the entirety of the assets, including the assets of the victim LP.
Example:
• Victim calls AaveHyperdrive.addLiquidity with a contribution of 1e6 * 1e18 DAI. The transaction is pending in the mem pool.
• The attacker (the first and sole LP) removes their liquidity (or adds liquidity) such that the totalSupply is 1. For example, assume totalSupply = totalAssets = 1 with a sharePrice = 1e18.
• The attacker donates 1e6 * 1e18 DAI to the pool, totalSupply = 1, totalAssets = 1e24 + 1.
• The victim transaction is mined, _deposit calculates newShares = totalShares_.mulDivDown(amount, assets) = 1 * 1e24 / (1e24 + 1) = 0. totalSupply = 1, totalAssets = 2e24 + 1.
• The attacker withdraws and receives the totalAssets = 2e24 + 1 with a profit of the victim's contribution.

title: pow function silently overflows and yields wrong results
content: The vulnerability resides in a fixed‑point exponentiation routine that computes x**y by first calculating the product y·ln(x) (named ylnx) and then applying the exponential function. The implementation casts the unsigned exponent y to a signed integer and multiplies it with the signed natural logarithm of x without any overflow protection. When the magnitude of y·ln(x) exceeds the range of a signed 256‑bit integer, the multiplication silently wraps around, producing a value that is close to zero. The subsequent call to the exponential function therefore evaluates exp(0) and returns the neutral fixed‑point value 1e18, even though the mathematically correct result should be astronomically large. This flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the FixedPointMath library, where a test case deliberately chose y as the maximum uint256 divided by ln(2e18) plus one, causing the intermediate product to overflow and the final result to be incorrect. Because the function does not revert or emit an error, the wrong output can be indistinguishable from a legitimate value, making the bug hard to notice in production. The overflow can be triggered whenever a caller supplies a very large exponent together with a base whose logarithm is non‑trivial, a situation that occurs in several higher‑level contracts such as HyperdriveMath and YieldSpaceMath that rely on the pow routine for pricing, interest accrual, and token minting calculations. From a user’s perspective the protocol may appear to return a normal amount (e.g., 1e18 tokens) when a much larger amount was expected, leading to under‑payment, incorrect pricing, or loss of potential earnings. The affected parties include any participants who interact with functions that depend on the pow calculation – liquidity providers, borrowers, and token holders – because the financial accounting performed by the protocol becomes inaccurate. To remediate the issue the multiplication should be performed with overflow‑checked arithmetic, the unsafe cast from uint256 to int256 should be eliminated or replaced with a safe conversion, and the intermediate result should be validated before being passed to the exponential function. In essence, the pow implementation must enforce proper bounds checking or use a larger numeric type to guarantee that the intermediate y·ln(x) cannot wrap around, thereby preserving the intended mathematical semantics and preventing silent mis‑calculations.

title: Governance fees are part of share reserves when opening shorts
content: The vulnerability consists of an accounting error in the short‑position opening flow where governance fees are unintentionally added to the pool's share reserves. In the openShort routine the contract first computes the amount of shares to be removed from the reserves (shareReservesDelta) by calling a curve‑based calculation and then subtracts the total curve fee. The total curve fee, however, already contains the governance fee component. After this subtraction the contract updates the market state by decreasing shareReserves by shareReservesDelta. Because the governance fee was part of the fee that was subtracted earlier, the subsequent subtraction of shareReservesDelta effectively adds the governance fee back into the share reserves. As a result the governance fee becomes part of the tradable share balance, allowing anyone who holds short positions to trade those shares and drain the fee amount. The issue can be exploited by opening a short position, which triggers the faulty shareReserves update, and then selling the newly created shares that include the governance fee, thereby preventing the protocol’s governance module from ever claiming its entitled fees. The impact is a loss of revenue for governance, a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees, and a potential erosion of trust because fees that should be locked for the protocol become freely tradable. The bug manifests only during the execution of openShort when totalCurveFee includes a non‑zero governance fee; if the governance fee is zero the problem is invisible. The affected parties are the governance contract (which cannot collect its fees), token holders who rely on those fees for incentives, and the overall protocol economics. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the short‑position logic, where the auditor noticed that the share reserve adjustment did not explicitly remove the governance portion of the fee. It is subtle because the code appears to correctly deduct the total fee, but the composition of that fee is not considered, making the error easy to overlook in a superficial review. The correct mitigation is to ensure that only the non‑governance portion of the curve fee is added back to the share reserves, for example by subtracting totalGovernanceFee from the fee that is re‑added, or by directly reducing shareReserves by totalGovernanceFee after the main fee adjustment. This restores the intended invariant that governance fees remain separate from the pool’s tradable share balance and preserves the protocol’s fee accounting model.

title: Governance fees are part of share reserves when closing non-matured longs
content: The vulnerability consists of an accounting flaw in the closing logic for non‑matured long positions where governance fees are unintentionally added to the pool's share reserves. In the normal fee model, governance fees are collected in a separate storage variable and are never meant to be part of the tradable share balance. However, during the closeLong flow the contract first subtracts the total curve fee from the shareReservesDelta, then reduces shareProceeds by the sum of totalCurveFee and totalFlatFee. Because totalGovernanceFee is included in the totalCurveFee+totalFlatFee bundle and the code never removes it from the share reserves, the net effect is that the governance fee amount is added back into the shareReserves state variable. Consequently, the fee becomes indistinguishable from regular share tokens and can be transferred or traded by any participant. The bug is triggered only when a user closes a long position before its maturity date; matured positions follow a different fee path that does not suffer from this issue. The affected parties are the protocol’s governance (which loses the ability to claim its fees), liquidity providers who rely on accurate accounting, and any user who may inadvertently receive or trade shares that actually represent governance fees. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by Spearbit, where the auditors traced the variable flow and observed that totalGovernanceFee is never read except when it is added to the governance fee storage, yet it re‑appears in the updated share reserves. The problem is subtle because share reserves are an internal accounting figure and the extra shares are not displayed as a separate fee line, making the loss of governance revenue hard to notice without deep inspection. Exploitation can be performed by opening a non‑matured long, closing it to inject the governance fee into the share pool, and then swapping or transferring those shares to extract value that rightfully belongs to governance. The impact is a reduction of the protocol’s fee revenue and a breach of the accounting invariants that guarantee that only genuine liquidity shares are tradable. To remediate the flaw, the contract should explicitly deduct totalGovernanceFee from the share reserves when applying the closeLong operation, for example by passing a reduced _shareProceeds value that subtracts the governance fee, and by ensuring that any LP fee logic for matured positions remains correct. This adjustment restores the separation between fee collection and share liquidity, preventing governance fees from being unintentionally tradable.

title: No LP fees when closing matured longs/shorts
content: The vulnerability is an accounting defect that causes liquidity‑provider (LP) fees to disappear when a matured long or short position is closed. The contract’s checkpoint routine (_applyCheckpoint) automatically settles matured positions and updates the share and bond reserves by calling updateLiquidity with a negative shareProceeds value. However, this routine does not deduct the flat LP fee from the shareProceeds nor add the fee back into the pool’s share reserves. Later, when a trader explicitly closes the position via closeLong (or the analogous short function), the contract subtracts the totalFlatFee – which includes the LP portion and a governance portion – from the trader’s proceeds. The governance portion is correctly accounted for, but the LP portion is never reinvested into the pool, so the fee is effectively burned. The bug occurs only for matured positions that are settled through the checkpoint path; non‑matured closures that bypass the checkpoint do apply the fee correctly. As a result, LPs receive less compensation than the protocol’s fee schedule promises, while traders see a reduced payout and may assume the fee has been distributed. This discrepancy is hard to notice because the UI typically shows only the trader’s net proceeds and does not expose the internal reserve balances; the missing fee does not generate an explicit error or revert. The issue was discovered during a security audit (Spearbit) that examined the fee‑handling logic across checkpoint and close functions. Exploitation can be passive – every time a position matures, the LP fee is silently omitted – or active, where an attacker forces many checkpoints to be processed, accelerating the loss of fees from the pool. The impact is a systematic under‑payment of LPs, erosion of expected yield, and a breach of the protocol’s economic assumptions that fees are reinvested for liquidity providers. To remediate, the checkpoint routine should deduct the flat LP fee at the moment it processes matured bonds, add the net LP fee (totalFlatFee minus totalGovernanceFee) back into the share reserves, and record the governance fee separately. The closeLong logic must be adjusted to avoid double‑counting fees for matured and non‑matured paths, ensuring that LPs receive their entitled share immediately after a position is settled, regardless of who initiates the closure.
summary:
When closing matured longs through closeLong or checkpoint, _applyCheckpoint is first run which closes the matured longs/shorts for this checkpoint. This function, however, does not take a fee on the shareProceeds. The share (and bond) reserves are updated by updateLiquidity(-shareProceeds) which reduces the share proceeds by the fee-exclusive shareProceeds.
When traders now close their positions by calling closeLong, their own shareProceeds are reduced by the totalFlatFee but this fee is never added back to the share reserves, i.e., never reinvested for the LPs.
Note that the same issue also applies to closing shorts.

title: apr circuit breaker can be avoided
content: The vulnerability is a circuit‑breaker bypass in the liquidity‑addition path of the Hyperdrive pool. The contract enforces a slippage guard by calculating the current spot APR and comparing it to the weighted spot APR stored in the most recent checkpoint. The check only uses the weightedSpotPrice of the latest checkpoint, which is a time‑averaged value that does not include price movements that occur immediately before the checkpoint start. An attacker can open a very large short position exactly at the moment a new checkpoint begins, causing a sharp drop in the spot price and a corresponding spike in the spot APR. Because the weightedSpotPrice for that checkpoint is computed after the short is executed, the weightedSpotAPR reflects the post‑short price. If the attacker then waits a single block (or the smallest possible delay) and adds liquidity, the spot APR calculated for the addLiquidity call matches the weightedSpotAPR within the allowed delta, so the circuit‑breaker condition is not triggered. This timing‑window attack allows the attacker to add liquidity under an artificially high APR without the intended protection, effectively bypassing the slippage guard. The impact is that the pool can be exposed to extreme APR values, leading to unfair pricing, potential loss of value for honest liquidity providers, and erosion of the pool’s economic guarantees. The issue occurs whenever large price movements happen at the boundary of a checkpoint and a subsequent addLiquidity transaction is submitted within the same checkpoint interval, which can be as short as one block. Users who provide liquidity expect the circuit‑breaker to reject trades that deviate beyond the configured tolerance; instead they may see their liquidity added at a rate that does not reflect the true market conditions, resulting in lower returns or even loss of capital. The bug was discovered during an integration test (SandwichTest) that deliberately performed a max short at the checkpoint start, waited a block, performed a tiny trade, and then called addLiquidity; the test showed that the circuit‑breaker revert never occurred. The problem is hard to notice because the weightedSpotPrice calculation appears correct in normal operation and the checkpoint logic is trusted; only edge‑case timing interactions expose the flaw. Conceptually, the fix is to use a moving‑window weighted average of spot APR or to incorporate the APR of the previous checkpoint into the circuit‑breaker comparison, ensuring that rapid price changes across checkpoint boundaries are captured. This change would close the timing gap and restore the intended protection against extreme slippage. In summary, the vulnerability is a timing‑dependent circuit‑breaker bypass caused by an insufficient averaging window in the APR guard, allowing an attacker to add liquidity after a large short without triggering the safety check, which can lead to unfair pricing and potential loss for honest participants.

title: withdraw_tokens fails to adjust claimed_supply locking tokens permanently
content: The vulnerability is that the withdraw_tokens (withdraw_token_handler) function refunds a user's payment tokens when the launch's revenue does not reach the minimum threshold, but it fails to update the contract's accounting of the tokens that were originally allocated to that user. Specifically, the function marks the user's stats as claimed and transfers the payment token refund, yet it never subtracts the user’s tokens_purchased from the global claimed_supply variable nor returns the corresponding launch tokens to the authority account. As a result, the tokens that should become available for other participants remain permanently locked in the contract. This occurs after the launch end time, only when the launch is marked as launched, the revenue is below the min_threshold, and the user has not already claimed. An attacker (or any legitimate user) can trigger the withdrawal, receive the refund, and unintentionally cause a portion of the total token supply to be inaccessible, reducing the effective supply that others can claim. From a user’s point of view the refund succeeds, but the expected increase in available tokens does not happen; other users may see fewer tokens available for purchase or claim, and the protocol’s accounting shows a discrepancy between claimed_supply and the actual tokens held. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the launchpad contract logic, where the lack of state updates after a refund was observed. It can be hard to notice because the function emits no error and the monetary refund appears correct, while the token locking bug manifests only as missing tokens in subsequent claims. The bug belongs to the class of accounting or state‑inconsistency vulnerabilities where a financial operation updates one balance but neglects related internal accounting, leading to permanent asset lock‑up. To remediate, the contract should decrement claimed_supply by the user’s tokens_purchased and transfer the same amount of launch tokens back to the authority (or otherwise make them claimable), ensuring that the token supply reflects the refund and no tokens remain permanently locked.

title: claim_revenue lets admin block user withdrawals below min threshold
content: The vulnerability is a logical flaw in the revenue‑claiming workflow of a launchpad contract that allows the contract administrator to call the claim_revenue function immediately after the sale period ends, even when the total collected revenue is below the predefined minimum threshold. The withdraw_token function, which users rely on to reclaim the payment tokens they contributed, contains a guard that only permits withdrawals when the recorded revenue is strictly lower than the min_threshold. Because claim_revenue does not enforce the same threshold check, an admin can transfer the collected revenue out of the contract before users have a chance to withdraw. Once the admin’s transfer is executed, the internal accounting (e.g., the balance of the stats_pay_token account) no longer matches the expected revenue value, causing the withdraw_token guard to fail and effectively blocking users from retrieving their funds. Conversely, if a user withdraws part of their payment tokens first, the remaining balance may fall below the recorded revenue amount, making a subsequent admin claim fail due to insufficient funds. This race condition creates a situation where either the admin or the users can be locked out of their rightful assets depending on the order of operations. The impact is that legitimate participants may be unable to receive a refund of their contribution, leading to lost or frozen funds and eroding trust in the platform. The issue manifests after the sale has closed, before any user‑initiated withdrawals have occurred, and it affects all contributors as well as the protocol’s reputation. It was discovered during a manual security audit that compared the pre‑conditions of claim_revenue and withdraw_token and identified the missing invariant that both functions should respect the same minimum‑revenue rule. The bug is subtle because both functions appear to work correctly in isolation; only when the admin exercises the claim function early does the inconsistency surface, which may not be covered by typical unit tests. To remediate the problem, the contract should either forbid claim_revenue when the revenue is below the min_threshold, introduce a cooldown period that gives users a reasonable window to withdraw after the sale ends, or redesign claim_revenue to transfer only the surplus amount that remains after all user withdrawals have been satisfied. In essence, the fix restores the invariant that revenue can only be claimed by the admin after users have been allowed to reclaim their payment tokens, thereby preventing the accidental or malicious freezing of user funds.

title: H-1 TheControllerV2 implementation can be destroyed by an attacker
content: The vulnerability is an unsafe initialization function in an upgradeable contract architecture.
