In conceptual terms the fix is to ensure that all internal links between short records and their representing NFTs are fully cleared when the short record is removed, thereby preventing a previous owner from exercising control over an NFT that has already been transferred.

title: Flag can be overriden by another user
content: The vulnerability is a flagger‑identifier reuse bug that allows a malicious participant to replace the original flagger of a short position and seize the exclusive liquidation right. The contract stores a flaggerId that grants the holder the ability to liquidate a flagged short after a first liquidation window (firstLiquidationTime) has elapsed. In the setFlagger routine the code checks whether the elapsed time (timeDiff) is greater than firstLiquidationTime and, if so, deletes the existing flaggerId and assigns the supplied flaggerHint to the short. Because the same time condition also governs when a new flagger may initially flag a short, an attacker can call flagShort with the flaggerHint of an already‑active flagger exactly when the first liquidation window opens. The contract mistakenly treats the previous flagger as inactive and overwrites its mapping, effectively transferring liquidation authority to the attacker. This can be exploited by observing the moment a short becomes liquidatable, then submitting a flagShort transaction that reuses the active flagger’s identifier. The attacker then calls liquidate and receives the liquidation reward, while the original flagger’s transaction reverts with MarginCallIneligibleWindow, causing loss of gas and expected reward. The impact is a loss of economic incentive for legitimate flaggers, potential front‑running of liquidation rights, and a breach of the protocol’s accounting assumptions that each flagged short has a unique, immutable flagger during its liquidation window. The bug manifests only after the first liquidation period has passed and when the flaggerHint supplied corresponds to an active flagger; otherwise the reuse logic works as intended for truly inactive flaggers. All parties that rely on the flagger reward – flaggers, short position owners, and the protocol’s reward distribution – are affected. The issue was discovered during a security audit when a unit test reproduced the scenario: after skipping ten hours the test showed that flagger2 could replace flagger1’s identifier and later liquidate the short that flagger1 was supposed to liquidate. The problem is subtle because the reuse check is meant for reclaimed identifiers, yet the timing overlap makes the condition true for active flaggers as well, which is not obvious from a surface review. The recommended fix is to compare the elapsed time against the second liquidation window (secondLiquidationTime) instead of the first, or to add an explicit guard that prevents overwriting a flaggerId that is still within its active liquidation period. This ensures that a flagger’s rights remain exclusive until both liquidation windows have expired, preserving the intended reward flow and protocol integrity.

title: Margin callers can drain the TAPP during liquidation by willingly increase gas costs with the shortHintArray
content: The vulnerability is an unchecked length on the short‑hint array that is supplied to the liquidation routine. The protocol expects this array to contain a small set of order‑book identifiers that help locate short positions above the oracle price, thereby saving gas. Because the contract does not validate the size of the array, a caller can pass an arbitrarily long list of bogus hints. The liquidation function iterates over every element of the array, performing a small amount of work for each entry. When the array is excessively large, the cumulative gas consumption grows proportionally. During primary liquidation the Treasury Asset Protection Pool (TAPP) is programmed to reimburse the gas fees of the forced‑bid operation, so the inflated gas cost is charged to the TAPP instead of the caller. By deliberately providing a huge short‑hint array, an attacker can cause the TAPP to spend far more ether than intended, eventually exhausting its balance. When the TAPP runs out of funds it can no longer cover the gas fees required for future liquidations; under‑collateralised short positions then remain un‑liquidated, the protocol’s accounting invariants break, the market may be forced to shut down and users can lose their deposits. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the liquidation path, where the loop over shortHintArray was observed without any length guard. It is subtle because the array is meant to be a performance optimisation, so developers may assume it cannot be abused, and the gas cost is paid by a separate pool, masking the direct impact on the caller. The fix is to enforce a reasonable maximum length on the short‑hint array or to reject empty or malformed hint lists, and to ensure that gas reimbursement logic does not rely on unbounded external input. In user‑facing terms, a trader attempting to liquidate a position may see the transaction succeed but later notice that the protocol’s pool has been drained, resulting in missing refunds, zero balances in the protection pool, and potentially a halted market where further liquidations are impossible. This class of bug falls under unchecked external array length leading to gas‑cost inflation and denial‑of‑service of a critical financial reserve.

title: User's can loose collateral when exiting a short
content: The vulnerability is an accounting and state‑cleanup flaw that can cause a user to lose the collateral that backs a short position when they try to exit that short. The root cause lies in the exitShort logic, which deletes a ShortRecord as soon as the debt reported in the exit call (e.ercDebt) equals the amount of debt that was actually filled (e.ercFilled). When the user’s own short order happens to be the cheapest order on the book, the forced bid created by exitShort matches against that same order. The matching routine adds the newly bought‑back debt and the associated collateral to the existing ShortRecord before the deletion check runs. Because the check only compares e.ercDebt and e.ercFilled, it does not verify that the ShortRecord’s original debt (short.ercDebt) has been fully repaid. Consequently the ShortRecord is removed while it still holds the freshly added collateral, making that collateral unrecoverable. An attacker – or even an honest user – can trigger the condition simply by exiting a short when their own order is the best match, which is a realistic scenario in a decentralized order‑book environment. The impact is that the user’s escrowed ETH (or other collateral) is reduced unexpectedly; from the UI the user sees a partial refund or a balance that is lower than expected, often described as “funds disappear” or “collateral missing”. The bug affects any participant who opens a short and later exits it, and it also undermines the protocol’s accounting guarantees because the total collateral accounting no longer matches the recorded debt. The issue was discovered during a manual audit and reproduced with a targeted unit test that showed the ShortRecord being deleted and the user ending up with only half of the original escrowed amount. It is hard to notice because the transaction completes without reverting, the debt appears to be fully repaid, and the missing collateral is not emitted in an event. The proper fix is to ensure that the ShortRecord is only deleted when the original short’s debt is fully repaid and no new collateral has been added, for example by adding a condition that short.ercDebt == e.ercDebt before calling deleteShortRecord, or by preventing a short from matching against its own order during exit. This change prevents the accidental loss of collateral and restores the intended accounting behavior where a full exit returns all collateral to the user.

title: H-3 Price manipulation by calling updatePhase with different symbols
content: The vulnerability is a manipulation of the price calculation algorithm caused by improper handling of the asset symbol parameter in the updatePhase function. The function updates internal state used for price aggregation, but the endRoundId value that determines which Chainlink round is considered final is calculated without taking the supplied symbol into account. Because endRoundId is stored globally rather than per‑symbol, an attacker can invoke updatePhase with a symbol that does not correspond to the current market asset, causing the contract to record an incorrect round identifier. This altered identifier is then used in the subsequent price computation, producing a wrong price feed that feeds into the battle income logic. The impact is that participants in the battle may receive an income that is either lower or higher than the correct amount, effectively allowing an attacker to siphon value or inflate rewards. The flaw can be exploited only during the one‑hour window that follows a change of the Chainlink phase, when the contract expects a new round to be finalized. During this period the attacker can submit a crafted updatePhase call with a mismatched symbol, manipulate endRoundId, and cause the price algorithm to use a stale or unrelated round. Users experience symptoms such as unexpected zero or inflated battle payouts, missing refunds, or balances that do not match the expected outcome of the game. The issue was discovered during a formal security audit by MixBytes, which identified that the endRoundId variable is not bound to the asset identifier, a classic case of insufficient input validation and state isolation. The bug is subtle because the function signature appears legitimate and the symbol argument is not used elsewhere, making the manipulation hard to notice without deep inspection of the state transition logic. To remediate, the algorithm that interacts with Chainlink should be redesigned so that each asset symbol maintains its own round identifier, or the updatePhase function should enforce that the symbol matches the currently tracked asset before updating any global state. In broader terms, this is a state‑corruption vulnerability in oracle integration that violates the accounting assumption that price data is uniquely tied to a specific asset, leading to incorrect financial calculations.
summary:
In the audited commit 29a0ccb5fc7ac838bd44c75c0afc398b84be267a, the endRoundId value is not dependent on the asset symbol. By calling the updatePhase function with a different symbol argument, an attacker may manipulate the endRoundId values. This could violate the correctness of the price calculation algorithm, leading to incorrect battle income.  
Although this is a critical flaw, it is only exploitable during a 1-hour period after a Chainlink phase has been changed. Given its critical impact but low likelihood, this issue is assigned a HIGH severity rating.

title: H-4 Price manipulation by calling updatePhase prematurely
content: The vulnerability is a phase‑transition manipulation that allows an attacker to call the contract’s updatePhase function before the current pricing phase has naturally ended. The root cause is that updatePhase does not enforce a check that the current phase’s end time or round identifier has been reached, so it records the endRoundId parameter based on the caller’s request rather than the actual last round of the Chainlink price feed. Because the price calculation for the next phase relies on the stored endRoundId, an early call can force the contract to use a deliberately chosen round that contains a manipulated price. Conversely, if updatePhase is never called after the legitimate phase end, the contract continues to use an outdated endRoundId, causing the price formula to reference stale or incorrect data. An attacker can therefore trigger the function at a convenient moment, supply a round identifier that reflects an artificially inflated or deflated price, and cause the protocol’s pricing logic to compute wrong token amounts, liquidation thresholds, or fee rates. The impact is critical: users may receive fewer tokens than expected, be liquidated unfairly, or see their balances reduced without a clear on‑chain error. The issue manifests whenever the protocol depends on Chainlink round IDs to anchor price calculations and the phase‑transition function is callable by any external account without temporal restrictions. All participants who rely on accurate pricing – lenders, borrowers, traders, and token holders – are affected because the economic guarantees of the system are broken. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit performed by MixBytes, which noted that the updatePhase logic does not validate the phase’s completion and therefore can be abused. The problem is subtle because the contract does not revert or emit an obvious error; the price simply deviates from the true market value, making it hard to detect without deep inspection of round IDs. To remediate, the algorithm that interacts with the Chainlink oracle should be redesigned to enforce that updatePhase can only be executed after the official phase end, verify that the supplied endRoundId matches the latest confirmed round, and include fallback or sanity checks that reject out‑of‑range price data. In broader terms, this is a classic example of an unchecked state transition combined with reliance on external oracle data, leading to price manipulation and accounting inconsistencies.
summary:
When updatePhase is called before the current phase has ended, it records an incorrect endRoundId value. Additionally, if updatePhase is not called after the phase has ended, the price calculation will be compromised in a manner similar to issue High.3.  
This issue is even less exploitable than the previous one, but the impact is still critical, hence we assign it a HIGH severity rating.

title: H-1 The startSqrtPriceX96 manipulation
content: The vulnerability consists of an unchecked user‑controlled initialization of the starting price for a battle in the Divergence Protocol. When a battle is created the contract accepts an arbitrary startSqrtPriceX96 value supplied by the caller and stores it as the initial price for the pool. Because this value is not tied to the battle identifier or validated against any market reference, an attacker can specify a deliberately skewed price. The root cause is the lack of constraints on a critical economic parameter that should be immutable or derived from deterministic data. An attacker can exploit the flaw by calling the battle‑creation function with a manipulated start price, then allowing other participants to join the battle under the assumption that the price reflects a fair market rate. Once the battle is active the attacker can execute trades that profit from the artificial price gap or simply cause trades to yield zero or far‑below‑expected returns, effectively griefing honest users. The impact is that users may receive no refund, see their balances shrink unexpectedly, or lose funds that were locked in the battle. This occurs every time a new battle is instantiated, i.e., under any condition where the startSqrtPriceX96 argument is supplied by an external account. All participants in the affected battle, as well as the protocol’s reputation and any funds locked in the battle, are potentially harmed. The issue was discovered during a systematic security audit that examined the initialization logic of the battle contract. It is difficult to notice in normal operation because the start price is an internal variable that does not appear directly in the UI; the price may appear reasonable after the first trade, masking the initial manipulation. The bug belongs to the class of parameter‑tampering or unchecked initialization vulnerabilities that break economic assumptions. From a user’s point of view the expectation is that the battle starts with a fair market price, but in reality the price may be set to an extreme value, leading to outcomes such as “my trade returned zero”, “my balance became zero after joining”, or “I received far less than expected”. To remediate the issue the startSqrtPriceX96 should be incorporated into the battle identifier or derived deterministically from immutable data, and the contract should enforce validation rules that prevent arbitrary price setting, thereby restoring the invariant that the initial price reflects a legitimate market condition.
summary: The starting price Battle.sol#L102 is an arbitrary, user-defined value. For the given battle key, an attacker can specify their unfair price to grief other users or even to make profits from unfair trade conditions. Such attacks can't be avoided without redeploying the system's smart-contract.

title: H-2 Empty trades
content: The vulnerability is an empty‑trade flaw in the trade function of the Battle contract. When a caller supplies a price limit that is reached while the liquidity curve is empty, the function exits the execution loop without moving any tokens, yet it still updates the stored current price variable. This occurs because the contract performs a balance check that can be satisfied by sending a single token back in the tradeCallback, allowing the execution path to continue even though no actual exchange of assets takes place. An attacker can exploit this by deploying a malicious contract that invokes trade with a crafted price limit, satisfies the balance check with a token sent in the callback, and thereby forces the protocol to record a price change without any token flow. The impact is that the attacker can manipulate the on‑chain price, create artificial price spikes or drops, and effectively block or disrupt liquidity providers who rely on a stable price curve to add liquidity. The condition under which this happens is when the price limit falls into a region of the tick space that contains no liquidity (an empty area), causing the trade loop to terminate early while still writing the new price. Users experience symptoms such as the displayed price moving unexpectedly while their token balances remain unchanged, and attempts to add liquidity may fail because the price is no longer aligned with the expected range. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the trade logic and identified that the price update is performed unconditionally after the loop, regardless of whether any token transfer occurred. It is hard to notice because standard event logs show a successful trade and a price update, but there is no accompanying transfer event, making the discrepancy subtle. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “state‑update‑without‑effect” or “price‑only‑state‑mutation” vulnerabilities, where protocol state is altered without the corresponding economic action. To remediate, the contract should either revert any trade that results in zero token movement (i.e., enforce a non‑zero transfer requirement) or restructure the workflow so that the price is only updated after a successful exchange, possibly by introducing an initialization step that moves the price into a valid liquidity region before allowing liquidity addition. This would restore the invariant that price changes are always backed by real token swaps, preventing price manipulation and ensuring that liquidity providers can reliably add liquidity.
summary:
The trade function allows you to specify a price limit, upon reaching which the cycle will be exited without performing any movement of tokens at line Battle.sol#L286, but with a change of the current price at line Battle.sol#L359.  
An attacker creates a contract that calls the trade function of the Battle contract with a price limit. To get passed the balance check, the attacker sends one token to the contract inside tradeCallback.  
This ability to perform empty exchanges in empty areas of liquidity creates the possibility of price manipulation. This capability can be used by an attacker to attack liquidity providers in order to block the addition of liquidity.  
LiquidityManagement.sol#L43  
To resolve this, it is necessary to resort to non-standard actions, for example, adding liquidity over the entire tick interval.  
This error is marked as HIGH as the contract is blocked by the attacker.

title: The bid function will revert because of a wrong check
content: The vulnerability is a logical error in the bid function of an auction contract. The function first checks that the amount sent in the current transaction (msg.value) is greater than the current highest bid before it adds the sender’s previous bid amount to compute a new total. If a participant who already has a bid wants to increase it by an amount that is smaller than the current highest bid, the first require fails even though the sum of the previous bid and the new amount would exceed the highest bid. This causes the transaction to revert unnecessarily. The root cause is the ordering of validation checks: the contract validates the incremental amount instead of the cumulative total. An honest bidder can trigger the revert by submitting a modest additional amount after being outbid, preventing the contract from accepting a higher total bid. The impact is that legitimate bidders may be unable to raise their standing, leading to loss of auction participation and wasted gas. The condition occurs whenever a bidder who already has a non‑zero balance attempts to add funds that are individually lower than the highest bid but together would surpass it. Users, the auction protocol, and any funds locked in the contract are affected because the contract’s business logic – that the highest total bid wins – is broken. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the require statements and their logical relationship. It can be hard to notice because the two require statements appear reasonable in isolation; only the interaction between them reveals the flaw. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a successful bid attempt but the transaction fails with a message indicating the bid is not high enough, and the user sees no change in their bid status or balance, contrary to the expectation that adding more ETH should increase their total. The bug belongs to the class of incorrect validation order or cumulative amount check bypass where a contract validates a partial value instead of the intended aggregate. To fix the issue the contract should compute the new total first, then verify that the total exceeds the current highest bid, while still enforcing the minimum‑bid rule on the incoming amount. Removing or re‑ordering the first require eliminates the false revert and restores the intended auction behavior.

title: No protection implemented against listing clone NFTs
content: The vulnerability is a lack of uniqueness enforcement when an NFT is listed on the marketplace. The list function accepts arbitrary name, symbol and description values and deploys a new ERC‑721 token with those parameters, but it never checks whether an identical asset has already been listed in the same round. Because the selection algorithm prefers the lowest price, a malicious seller can copy the metadata of any previously listed NFT, deploy a clone contract, and list it for just one wei less than the original. When the system evaluates the pool of candidates, the cloned asset will be chosen, allowing the attacker to capture the sale without creating any original content. This situation can occur whenever a seller calls the list function during the Sell phase; there are no additional guards such as metadata hashing, creator address verification, or per‑round uniqueness constraints. The impact is that the protocol’s core promise of unique, creator‑driven NFTs is broken: users see multiple listings with identical name, symbol and description, each undercutting the previous price, leading to a race‑to‑the‑bottom where the cheapest clone wins. From a user’s perspective the UI may display many entries that look the same, and the expected unique artwork is replaced by a duplicate that costs almost nothing, causing confusion and potential loss of value. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the list function’s logic and noticed the absence of any duplicate‑detection mechanism. It can be hard to notice because the cloned NFTs are syntactically valid and the price difference is minimal, so automated tools may not flag them as malicious. To remediate, the contract should enforce that each asset’s metadata (or a hash of it) is unique within a round, reject listings that match an existing name‑symbol pair, or require the original creator’s address to be recorded and checked. Implementing a loop that scans existing listings or, more efficiently, maintaining a mapping of metadata hashes to prevent duplicates would close the attack surface, albeit with some gas cost considerations. In summary, the bug belongs to the class of duplicate‑asset or clone‑listing vulnerabilities, where insufficient validation allows adversaries to undercut genuine listings, violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions and expected economic behavior.

title: Subtraction in `variance()` will revert due to underflow
content: The vulnerability resides in a statistical helper routine that calculates variance on an array of unsigned integers. The routine first computes the arithmetic mean, then iterates over each element and subtracts the mean from the element using the expression `data[i] - mean`. Because both operands are of type `uint256`, the subtraction is performed in unsigned arithmetic; if any element is smaller than the calculated mean the operation underflows, producing a very large unsigned value and causing the transaction to revert due to Solidity’s built‑in overflow check (available since version 0.8). This underflow condition is triggered whenever the dataset is not perfectly uniform – that is, when at least one value differs from the average – which is the typical case for real‑world data. The function is invoked by `finalizeValidation()` at the end of a validation workflow, meaning that any call to the public `validate()` entry point will propagate the revert and abort the whole process. From a user perspective the symptom is a silent failure: a transaction that is expected to complete validation and possibly lock or release funds instead reverts, leaving the caller with no state change and often no clear error message beyond a generic revert. The impact is that the protocol’s validation mechanism becomes unusable, preventing users or validators from completing required actions, potentially freezing funds or breaking business logic that relies on successful validation. The issue was uncovered during a formal audit and reproduced with a Foundry test that deliberately supplies distinct numbers and expects a revert. It is easy to miss because the code appears mathematically correct and the subtraction looks innocuous; only when the data set contains variance does the unsigned subtraction reveal the flaw. The bug belongs to the class of arithmetic underflow/overflow errors caused by inappropriate use of unsigned types for operations that may yield negative intermediate results. To remediate, the subtraction should be performed in a signed integer domain (e.g., casting both operands to `int256` before subtraction) or the algorithm should be rewritten to avoid negative values altogether, such as by using absolute differences or by rearranging the variance formula to work with only non‑negative intermediate values. After fixing, the function will correctly compute variance for heterogeneous data sets without causing transaction reverts, restoring the intended validation flow and preserving protocol functionality.

title: Missing transferable Check in send
content: The vulnerability consists of an absent transferability guard in the token contract's public send function. The contract is intended to restrict token movement unless a global flag transfersEnabled is true or the caller is the designated controller, a rule that is enforced elsewhere through a transferable modifier that checks require(msg.sender == controller || transfersEnabled, "NON_TRANSFERABLE"). However, the send function directly invokes the internal _transfer routine without applying this modifier, meaning the require check is completely bypassed. As a result, any address can call send and move tokens even when the contract owner has deliberately disabled transfers, violating the contract's core invariant that token transfers are only permitted under controlled conditions. An attacker can exploit this by simply calling send with arbitrary recipient and amount while transfersEnabled is false, causing tokens to be transferred away from holders who believe their assets are frozen. The impact includes loss of expected transfer restrictions, potential unauthorized draining of user balances, and erosion of trust in the protocol's governance model. This condition occurs whenever the contract is in a state where transfers are disabled but the send function is still accessible, which is true for all callers because there is no access control on that entry point. All token holders, the protocol’s governance, and any third‑party integrations that rely on the transfer lock are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that compared the implementation of the transferable modifier against all external‑facing functions and noticed the omission in send. It can be hard to spot because the function appears to perform a normal token transfer and emits the expected events, giving the impression that normal checks are in place, while the critical require statement is simply missing. To remediate, the send function should be protected by the same transferable modifier (or an equivalent explicit require) so that only the controller or callers when transfersEnabled is true can execute the transfer, thereby restoring the intended access control and preserving the contract’s accounting guarantees.

title: All of the pairings' timestamps will be updated for epoch 0
content: The contract is intended to keep timestamps separated by epoch so that each predefined time window has its own record for every trading pair. A state variable called epochCount is declared and initialized to zero, but the code never updates this variable anywhere in the system. As a result, every call to the function that stores a timestamp passes the constant value 0 as the epoch argument. The internal setTimestamp function writes the value into a mapping indexed by trading pair and epoch, so all timestamps are written to the slot [pair][0]. This design flaw means that timestamps for all epochs are overwritten on the same storage location, effectively erasing any historical data and breaking any logic that relies on epoch separation, such as tribe re‑organization, price‑feed validation, or time‑based reward calculations. An attacker or any actor that can trigger the processCluster function can supply a new timestamp for any pair and cause the stored value for epoch 0 to be replaced, leading to incorrect accounting, unexpected zero balances, missing refunds, or other business‑logic violations. From the user’s perspective the UI may display a current timestamp that looks correct, but queries that expect epoch‑specific values return empty or stale data, causing confusion when a user expects a refund for a previous epoch but receives nothing. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the SupraSValueFeedVerifier contract where the epochCount variable was found to be static. Because the bug resides in a simple assignment and no events are emitted when timestamps are written, it can remain unnoticed until epoch‑dependent features fail. The vulnerability belongs to the class of state‑variable‑not‑updated bugs that lead to data‑overwrites across logical partitions. To remediate, the protocol must implement a mechanism that increments epochCount according to the specification—such as after a fixed number of processed clusters or after a defined time interval—and ensure that all timestamp writes use the current epoch value. This restores proper epoch isolation, prevents accidental overwriting of prior data, and aligns the implementation with the documented business logic.

title: Fees are not burnt on losing games
content: The vulnerability consists of an asymmetric fee‑burning logic in the reward‑distribution function of a betting game. The contract is supposed to charge a 10 % house fee on every bet, convert 80 % of that fee into USDT, and later swap the collected USDT for MONT tokens that are burned, thereby creating buying pressure that offsets the token’s selling pressure. However, the implementation only executes the USDT transfer to the burner when the player is declared a winner. The code calculates a burnAmount based on the houseEdge and then, inside an if‑statement that checks _isPlayerWinner, sends both the player’s reward and the burnAmount to the burner. When the player loses, the function skips the burner transfer entirely, yet the MontRewardManager continues to mint and distribute MONT rewards as if the fee had been burned. The root cause is the misplaced conditional: the burn transfer is tied to the winner branch instead of being unconditional. An attacker can exploit this by deliberately losing bets to receive MONT rewards without any corresponding fee being burned, inflating the token supply and reducing the intended buying pressure. The impact is primarily economic: the protocol’s tokenomics are broken, leading to a mismatch between selling pressure (from users withdrawing or trading MONT) and the expected compensating buying pressure from burned tokens. Over time this can dilute token value, undermine confidence in the platform, and potentially expose users to lower returns or loss of value. The issue manifests whenever a bet results in a loss; the user sees no USDT being sent to the burner, yet still receives MONT rewards, which may appear as “extra” tokens. Affected parties include all participants of the betting game, the protocol’s token economy, and any stakeholders relying on the promised fee‑burn mechanism. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the reward‑distribution flow, where the auditor noticed that the burn transfer was inside the winner branch and that the reward manager still emitted rewards on losing bets. The problem can be subtle because the UI may still show that rewards are being given, masking the missing burn operation, and the USDT burn may not be directly visible to users. To remediate, the burn transfer should be moved outside the conditional so that the fee is always sent to the burner regardless of the game outcome, and the event emission should reflect the correct flow. Conceptually, this belongs to the class of “conditional fee handling” or “incorrect accounting of fees” bugs, where fee logic is tied to a success condition instead of being applied uniformly, leading to accounting inconsistencies and economic distortion.

title: Mont price can be manipulated to earn more rewards
content: The vulnerability originates from the way the MontRewardManager contract calculates player rewards using the current on‑chain price of the MONT token obtained from Uniswap’s quoteExactInputSingle function. The contract calls getMontPrice, which directly queries the pool for the price of one MONT in USDT at the exact moment the reward is transferred. Because this price is taken from the instantaneous pool state, an attacker can manipulate it by executing trades immediately before the operator’s revealCard transaction. In a typical attack scenario the player first predicts or front‑runs the time when the operator will call revealCard after a guessCard call. The attacker then swaps a large amount of MONT for USDT (or vice‑versa) to push the pool price down (or up). When the operator’s revealCard transaction executes, getMontPrice returns the artificially low price, causing the reward formula reward = ((houseFeeFixedPoint * 8) / 10) / price to produce a much larger reward amount. The contract then credits the player’s balance with this inflated reward, which the attacker can later claim and optionally swap back to USDT after the price normalises. The impact is that the attacker can earn extra MONT tokens at the expense of the protocol’s economics, while other honest players may receive reduced rewards if the price is pushed up. This issue occurs whenever the reward calculation is performed in the same block as a price‑sensitive trade and the operator’s transaction timing is predictable. It affects any user who participates in the guessing game, the protocol’s token economics, and any stakeholder relying on fair reward distribution. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the reward flow and identified the reliance on a volatile price source. The problem is subtle because the price returned by the quoter appears legitimate and the contract does not perform any sanity checks, making the manipulation hard to detect without analysing transaction ordering. To remediate the issue the contract should replace the direct pool quote with a price feed that is resistant to short‑term manipulation, such as a time‑weighted average price (TWAP) oracle, or commit the price ahead of time and use a delay window before rewards are calculated. This change removes the ability for an attacker to profit from immediate price swings and restores the intended accounting logic where rewards are proportional to a stable market price.

title: Initialization of DyadXPv2 is impossible
content: The DyadXPv2 contract contains an initialization routine that iterates over the entire supply of DNFT tokens to populate an array of note data structures. For each token index the code writes a NoteXPData entry with timestamps, deposited assets, and XP values. Because the DNFT supply currently stands at 882, the loop executes hundreds of iterations. Each iteration consumes a measurable amount of gas; the audit measured roughly 3.13 million gas for 88 iterations, which extrapolates to at least 31.3 million gas for the full supply. This exceeds the typical block gas limit of 30 million, meaning that when the initialize() function is called the transaction will run out of gas and revert. The root cause is an unbounded on‑chain loop that depends on a mutable external token supply, turning a seemingly simple initialization into a gas‑intensive operation. An attacker does not need to exploit the contract; the vulnerability manifests simply by calling initialize, which cannot complete, leaving the contract in an uninitialized state. As a result the protocol cannot record any XP data, users cannot earn or claim rewards, and any funds that would be managed by DyadXPv2 remain inaccessible. The issue appears only when the DNFT supply grows beyond a modest threshold (approximately ninety tokens) and is therefore hard to notice during early development when the supply is small. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that measured gas consumption per loop iteration. Because the failure occurs at deployment or first‑use time, developers may assume the contract works until a transaction consistently reverts, leading to confusion and loss of confidence. To remediate the issue the initialization should avoid iterating over the full token set in a single transaction; alternatives include lazy‑initializing entries on demand, using a batch‑processing pattern with multiple transactions, or storing only aggregate data that does not require per‑token loops. By redesigning the initialization logic the contract can stay within block gas limits, allowing the protocol to function as intended and preventing funds from becoming permanently locked.

title: Users cannot stake in UniV3Staking
content: The vulnerability is a missing ERC721 receiver implementation in the UniswapV3Staking contract, which causes the stake() function to revert whenever it attempts to pull a position NFT from a user. The contract calls safeTransferFrom(msg.sender,address(this),tokenId) to move the NFT, and safeTransferFrom requires the recipient contract to implement onERC721Received and return the expected selector. Because the staking contract does not define this function, the ERC721 transfer fails, the call reverts, and the staking transaction is aborted. This bug belongs to the class of ERC721 receiver interface violations, where a contract that is intended to accept NFTs does not conform to the ERC721Receiver standard. An attacker does not need to exploit any hidden backdoor; any user who tries to stake experiences a failed transaction, which effectively constitutes a denial‑of‑service on the staking feature. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a “Stake” button, but after confirming the transaction the wallet reports a revert or “execution failed” error and the NFT remains in the user’s wallet, contrary to the expectation that the NFT would be deposited and start earning rewards. The issue occurs every time stake() is called, i.e., under normal usage conditions, and affects all participants who wish to lock their Uniswap V3 position NFTs in the protocol. It was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the staking flow and noticed the absence of the required onERC721Received callback. The problem can be hard to notice because the contract compiles without errors and the NFT does not appear to be transferred, so the failure only surfaces at runtime when the safeTransferFrom call reverts. The impact is that the staking service is unusable, preventing users from earning incentives and potentially reducing protocol revenue. The correct remediation is to implement the ERC721Receiver interface by adding an onERC721Received function that returns the selector (bytes4(keccak256("onERC721Received(address,address,uint256,bytes)"))), thereby allowing safeTransferFrom to succeed and enabling the staking mechanism to function as intended.
summary:
UniswapV3Staking.stake() pulls NFTs from the user in the following way:
```solidity
positionManager.safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), tokenId);
```
However, this will end up calling the onERC721Received() function on the UniswapV3Staking contract, and expect a return value. However since that function is not implemented in this contract, the ERC721 transfer will fail, reverting the execution of stake().

title: Staking rewards should be claimed before each balanceOfNote changing
content: The vulnerability originates from a missing reward‑claim step in a staking contract where rewards are calculated based on the current balance of a note (balanceOfNote). The contract’s internal reward calculation multiplies the elapsed time, a rewards rate, the staked liquidity and the note’s balance (xp). Because the function that claims pending rewards is never invoked before any operation that changes the note’s balance – such as deposit, withdraw, mintDyad, burnDyad or liquidation – the reward amount is computed using a stale balance value. Consequently, when a user later claims rewards, the contract may credit an amount that does not reflect the actual time‑weighted stake, either inflating the reward (if the balance was increased after the last claim) or deflating it (if the balance was decreased). This mis‑alignment can lead to significant asset loss for the protocol, as users may receive fewer tokens than they are entitled to, or, conversely, an attacker could manipulate the balance to harvest excess rewards. The issue manifests whenever a staked note’s balance changes without a preceding claimRewards call, which is the typical flow for most user‑initiated actions. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that expected rewards are missing or appear incorrect – for example, a user who deposited additional tokens expects a higher reward but receives zero, or a user who withdraws sees their reward balance reset unexpectedly. The problem is subtle because the contract does not emit an explicit error; the reward calculation is performed on‑chain only when the claim function is called, so the discrepancy is only observable after the fact. The root cause is a logical omission in the contract’s workflow: the protocol assumes that rewards are automatically updated on balance changes, but the implementation never triggers the update. To remediate, the contract should invoke the reward‑claim routine for any note that is currently staked before any state‑changing operation that affects balanceOfNote, ensuring that rewards are settled with the correct balance snapshot. This aligns the accounting with the business rule that rewards are proportional to the time‑weighted stake and prevents unintended loss of funds.

title: The redeemDyad() Function Does Not Adjust Decimals Prop- erly
content: The vulnerability resides in the redeemDyad() function that is responsible for burning DYAD tokens and releasing the underlying collateral to the caller. The function computes the amount of collateral to withdraw using the formula asset = amount * 10**oracle.decimals() / assetPrice, which implicitly assumes that the collateral token has 18 decimal places – the same precision used by DYAD. When the vault’s asset uses a different decimal precision, such as USDC with 6 decimals or WBTC with 8 decimals, the calculation omits the necessary scaling factor for the asset’s own decimals. As a result the contract over‑estimates the amount of collateral to transfer, often by a factor of 10^(18‑assetDecimals). For example, redeeming 100 DYAD (100e18) against a USDC vault with a price feed of 1e8 would incorrectly compute 100e18 USDC instead of the intended 100e6, causing the contract to attempt to withdraw an astronomically larger amount. This mis‑calculation can lead to three observable failure modes: the transaction may revert because the vault does not hold enough of the over‑estimated asset, the caller may receive far more tokens than expected (appearing as a “free” payout), or the vault’s collateral pool can be drained, exposing the protocol to unintended liquidations. The bug is triggered every time redeemDyad() is called for a vault whose underlying asset does not use 18 decimals, affecting any DYAD holder who redeems, as well as the broader protocol that relies on the integrity of its collateral accounting. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the arithmetic against assets of varying decimal precision and identified the missing asset‑decimal factor as a logical flaw. It is subtle because the on‑chain numbers are syntactically correct and the UI may display the correct DYAD amount burned, while the collateral amount appears unusually large only after the transaction succeeds, making the error easy to overlook. To remediate the problem the redemption logic must normalize both the oracle precision and the asset’s own decimal precision before dividing by the price, for instance by multiplying by 10**(oracle.decimals + asset.decimals) and then dividing by assetPrice and the DYAD base unit (1e18). This adjustment restores proper accounting, prevents over‑withdrawals, and aligns the contract’s behavior with the expected business logic that a user who burns a given amount of DYAD receives a proportional amount of collateral, no more and no less.

title: Insufficient Exogenous Collateral Check in VaultManagerV2::liquidate() function
content: An insufficient exogenous collateral verification in the VaultManagerV2 liquidate function allows a vault to avoid liquidation when the value of the external collateral falls below the required 100 % backing, even though the combined collateral ratio (external plus kerosene) remains above the minimum 150 % threshold. The contract only checks the overall collateral ratio with the statement if (collatRatio(id) >= MIN_COLLAT_RATIO) revert CrTooHigh();, which means the separate external‑collateral ratio is never evaluated. When the price of the external asset drops, the external‑collateral backing can dip to, for example, 95 % while the kerosene buffer keeps the total ratio at 155 %. Because the total ratio is still above 150 %, the liquidation routine does not trigger, leaving the vault effectively under‑collateralized with respect to the rule that external collateral must back each DYAD token one‑to‑one. An attacker or a market participant can exploit this by allowing the external price to fall, then withdrawing or closing vaults, which reduces total value locked and pushes the system toward a fractionally collateralized stablecoin similar to FRAX or DEI. The impact is that DYAD may lose its full‑collateral guarantee, causing a de‑peg, loss of confidence, and potential loss of user funds. The condition occurs whenever external collateral price declines while enough kerosene remains to keep the aggregate ratio above the minimum. All vault owners, DYAD holders, and lenders are affected because the protocol’s accounting assumptions are broken. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit (issue #338) by observing that liquidation never fires in scenarios where external collateral is insufficient but total collateral looks healthy. It is hard to notice because the UI typically displays only the overall collateral ratio, which appears safe, masking the underlying deficiency. The recommended mitigation is to add a separate check that external collateral backing stays at or above 100 % before allowing a vault to escape liquidation, or to permit liquidation whenever the external‑collateral ratio falls below the required level regardless of the total ratio. This change restores the intended business logic that each minted DYAD must be fully backed by external assets and prevents the system from unintentionally becoming fractionally collateralized.
summary:
Code4rena issue #338 linked here. The issue shows that liquidations do not go through if the exogenous collateral does not sufficiently back the DYAD minted. The protocol lays down 2 ground rules:

1. Exo collateral backs DYAD at least 1:1 (100%)

2. Kerosene can be used to keep the minimum backing to 150%.

So for this to function properly, a user must have exo-backing of 100% and exo+kerosene backing of 150%. But if a user’s exo-backing falls below 100% but their exo+kerosene backing is still above 150%, they won’t get liquidated:
```solidity
if (collatRatio(id) >= MIN_COLLAT_RATIO) revert CrTooHigh();
```
This can lead to systematic problems with collateral backing. For instance, if there is 1 million USD worth of exo collateral, and 1 million DYAD minted. Let’s also say 600k USD worth of kerosene is in the vaults as well. Now, Exo collateral backing = 1 million / 1 million = 100% Total backing = 1.6 / 1 = 160%. Now, say the price of the exo collateral drops so there is only 950k USD worth of exo collateral left. Exo collateral backing = 950k / 1 million = 95% Total backing = 1.55 / 1 = 155%. If this was a single vault, this wouldn’t be liquidatable since the CR is still above 150%. The overall backing of the system is not 100% with exo collateral anymore. This can lead to people closing and withdrawing funds from their vaults, which further reduces the TVL of the system. The main idea is that the system and individual vaults can reach a state where some of the DYAD is backed by kerosene, and not by other exo collateral. This would make it a fractionally collateralized stablecoin, like FRAX or DEI, both of which had stability issues and FRAX later voted to fully collateralize itself.

title: Users will get 1/100 of the intended accrual rate
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect scaling factor in the XP accrual calculation of the DyadXPv2 contract. The documentation states that the base accrual rate should be 1e9, but the implementation multiplies the accrualRateModifier by 1e7, resulting in a rate that is two orders of magnitude smaller than intended. This mismatch causes every user who deposits to receive only about one hundredth of the XP they expect. The root cause is a simple constant typo that went unnoticed because the contract still compiles and the function executes without reverting, making the bug subtle. Exploitation does not require an attacker; any normal user invoking the accrual function will experience the reduced yield automatically. The impact is economic: users see their XP balances grow far slower, leading to disappointment, potential loss of trust, and reduced incentive to lock funds. The condition under which it occurs is any call to the internal _computeXP routine, which is used whenever deposits are made or rewards are claimed. All participants—depositors, reward claimers, and the protocol that relies on accurate XP accounting—are affected. The issue was discovered during a security audit that compared the contract code against the published specifications and noticed the discrepancy between the documented 1e9 factor and the 1e7 factor in code. Because the bug does not produce a runtime error, it can be hard to notice without explicit testing of reward amounts. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a normal deposit transaction but the displayed XP balance increases only marginally, or appears unchanged after a period where growth was expected. Users expect a proportional increase in XP based on the advertised rate, but reality delivers a much smaller increment, effectively making the reward calculation wrong. This class of bug belongs to the category of incorrect constant scaling or mis‑configured economic parameter which violates the business logic that rewards should be calculated with a predefined rate. To remediate the issue the contract should be updated so that the adjusted accrual rate multiplies the modifier by 1e9 instead of 1e7, aligning the on‑chain calculation with the documented specification.
summary:
The base accrual rate, as described in the documentation, should be 1e9. However, in DyadXPv2._computeXP it is set to 1e7:
```solidity
uint256 adjustedAccrualRate = accrualRateModifier * 1e7;
```
As such, users will get a meager yield for their deposit (2 orders of magnitude less than the intended value).

title: totalXP is wrongly calculated for existing users
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect calculation of the totalXP value for existing users that is performed during the contract upgrade initialization. The initialize function iterates over all DNFT tokens and populates each NoteXPData struct, but it assigns totalXP the value of lastXP without applying the _computeXP formula that accounts for the elapsed time and the bonus derived from deposited kerosene and minted DYAD. Because the time between a user’s last action and the upgrade is typically non‑zero, the accrued bonus is omitted, causing totalXP to be lower than it should be. An attacker or any user can exploit this by triggering the upgrade (or relying on the upgrade that already occurred) and then invoking functions that use totalXP to compute the accrualRateModifier and subsequent reward amounts. Since accrualRateModifier is inversely proportional to the logarithm of totalXP, a smaller totalXP yields a larger modifier, which inflates the adjusted accrual rate and results in higher XP or reward accrual than intended. From the user’s perspective the UI may show the same XP balance after the upgrade or a sudden, unexpected increase in rewards later, contradicting the expectation that XP grows proportionally with time. The bug affects all existing DNFT holders and any protocol component that relies on totalXP for accounting, such as Uniswap position reward calculations. It was discovered during a security audit when the reviewer compared the initialize logic with the _computeXP implementation and noticed that the bonus term was never added. The issue is subtle because the contract still records a non‑zero lastXP and the UI may not display the internal totalXP field directly, making the discrepancy easy to miss. The proper fix is to recompute totalXP for each user during initialization by calling the same _computeXP routine that is used in normal operation, thereby including the elapsed time and bonus in the stored value. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of state‑migration miscalculations where upgrade code fails to preserve derived state, leading to accounting errors and potential economic manipulation.

title: updateXP can be omitted during liquidation
content: The vulnerability is that the liquidation routine fails to update the experience points (XP) of a note when the note does not contain the special KEROSENE_VAULT or when the vault reports a deposit amount of zero. The root cause is a conditional call to dyadXP.updateXP that is placed inside a block that only executes for the KEROSENE_VAULT and after a non‑zero deposit check. As a result, after the dyad.burn call reduces the debt, the XP accounting remains unchanged. An attacker can trigger liquidation on a note that lacks the KEROSENE_VAULT, causing the contract to skip the XP update while still burning debt. This leaves the note’s recorded XP higher than it should be, breaking the accounting assumptions that XP reflects the current state of the note. Users may notice that after a liquidation their XP balance appears unchanged or inconsistent with the expected reduction, leading to confusion when rewards or governance power are calculated from XP. The issue appears only when the liquidation path reaches the for‑loop and either the vault list does not contain the KEROSENE_VAULT or the vault’s depositAmount is zero, conditions that are common for notes that hold only collateral without the special vault. The bug was identified during a manual audit of the liquidate function, where the conditional update was observed and flagged as a logical omission. Because the XP update is silent, the problem can be hard to notice unless the developer checks the XP state before and after liquidation. The proper remediation is to move the dyadXP.updateXP calls outside the vault‑specific conditional, ensuring that both the liquidated note and the recipient note have their XP refreshed after the debt change, regardless of vault composition.

title: Lack of slippage control can lead to sandwich attacks
content: The vulnerability is that the contract hard‑codes the minimum amount of output tokens (amountOutMin) to zero when calling the UniswapV2Router function swapExactTokensForETHSupportingFeeOnTransferTokens and also when adding liquidity. Because amountOutMin is zero, the router will accept any amount of ETH in return, even if the actual output is far below the amount the user expects, effectively allowing 100% slippage. This lack of slippage protection enables a sandwich attack: an attacker front‑runs the victim’s swap with a large trade that moves the price, then the victim’s transaction executes with amountOutMin = 0 and receives a severely reduced amount of ETH (potentially zero), after which the attacker back‑runs and restores the price, capturing the difference. The impact is that users who initiate a token‑to‑ETH swap or add liquidity may end up receiving far less ETH than anticipated, effectively losing funds. The condition occurs on every call to swapTokensForEth() or addLiquidity() because the parameter is hard‑coded; any transaction that reaches the public mempool can be targeted by MEV bots using flash loans. The affected parties are token holders who trust the contract to perform swaps or provide liquidity, as well as the protocol that may lose reputation and capital. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that inspected the router calls and noticed the amountOutMin argument set to a literal zero instead of being derived from user input or off‑chain price data. Because the contract does not emit any warning and the swap still succeeds, the problem can be subtle: the transaction appears successful while the user’s balance may drop unexpectedly, making it hard to detect without comparing pre‑ and post‑swap balances. The bug belongs to the class of missing slippage protection or unbounded slippage vulnerabilities, where a contract accepts any price for a trade. To remediate, the contract should accept an amountOutMin value supplied by the caller (or calculated off‑chain) and pass it to the router, optionally enforcing a reasonable maximum slippage percentage. Adding validation that the received ETH is at least a certain fraction of the expected amount prevents the attacker from extracting value via sandwich attacks.
summary:
The amountOutMin parameter in swapExactTokensForETHSupportingFeeOnTransferTokens is
hard coded to 0 in swapTokensForEth():
function swapTokensForEth(uint256 tokenAmount) private lockTheSwap {
path[1] = uniswapV2Router.WETH();
uniswapV2Router.swapExactTokensForETHSupportingFeeOnTransferTokens(
tokenAmount,
0,
path,
block.timestamp
This basically allows for 100% slippage as the call agrees to receive 0 amount of ETH for the swap. This can
be done through a sandwich attack. The same applies to the addLiquidity function:
function addLiquidity(uint256 tokenAmount, uint256 ethAmount) private {
tokenAmount, 0, 0, owner(), block.timestamp);
This is a very easy target for MEV and bots to do a flash loan sandwich attack and can be done on every call
if the trade transaction goes through a public mempool.

title: Ineffective deadline check
content: The vulnerability is an ineffective deadline check in the UniswapV2Router02 functions swapExactTokensForETHSupportingFeeOnTransferTokens and addLiquidityETH that are invoked by the protocol’s swapTokensForEth and addLiquidity helpers. The contract passes block.timestamp directly as the deadline argument, and the router’s ensure modifier only requires deadline >= block.timestamp. Because the supplied value is exactly equal to the current block timestamp, the require condition is always satisfied and the transaction never expires. The root cause is the hard‑coded use of the current block time instead of a user‑supplied future timestamp, which eliminates the intended time‑lock protection. An attacker or a validator can keep the transaction in the mempool for an arbitrarily long period by offering a low gas price; the transaction will remain pending without reverting. During this delay the market price of the traded assets may move, so when the transaction finally executes the user may receive a much worse rate, effectively losing value. From the user’s perspective the swap may stay pending for hours or days, the UI shows no error, but the received ETH amount is lower than expected or the added liquidity is priced unfavorably. The issue affects any user who relies on the deadline parameter to protect against price slippage, including traders and liquidity providers. It was discovered during a manual security audit that inspected the router calls and noticed the deadline being set to block.timestamp. The bug is subtle because the deadline parameter exists and the require statement appears correct, yet the logic never triggers an expiration, making it easy to overlook. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “ineffective time‑lock” or “deadline bypass” bugs, where a protective deadline is rendered moot by improper parameter handling. To remediate, the protocol should expose a deadline field that callers can set to a future timestamp, and the router should enforce that the supplied deadline is greater than the current block time, optionally with a minimum buffer. This restores the intended protection against prolonged pending transactions and mitigates the risk of users receiving unfavorable prices.
summary:
The deadline parameter in swapExactTokensForETHSupportingFeeOnTransferTokens() and
addLiquidityETH() which are called in swapTokensForEth() and addLiquidity() is hard coded to
block.timestamp.
Example in addLiquidity():
function addLiquidity(uint256 tokenAmount, uint256 ethAmount) private {
tokenAmount, 0, 0, owner(), block.timestamp); ///@audit here is the
problem
The addLiquidityETH() in UniswapV2Router02 contract:
function addLiquidityETH(
uint amountTokenDesired,
uint amountTokenMin,
uint amountETHMin,
uint deadline
) external virtual override payable ensure(deadline) returns (uint
amountToken, uint amountETH, uint liquidity)
The deadline parameter enforces a time limit by which the transaction must be executed otherwise it will
revert.
Lets take a look at a modifier which is present in the functions you are calling in UniswapV2Router02
contract:
modifier ensure(uint deadline) {
require(deadline >= block.timestamp, 'UniswapV2Router: EXPIRED');
Now when the deadline is hardcoded as block.timestamp, the transaction will not revert because the
require statement will always be fulfilled by block.timestamp == block.timestamp.
If a user chose a transaction fee that is too low for miners to be interested in including the transaction in a
block, the transaction stays pending in the mempool for extended periods, which could be hours, days,
weeks, or even longer.
This could lead to users getting a worse price, because a validator can just hold onto the transaction.

title: Wrong total supply amount leads to problems with the fees
content: The contract defines a fixed total supply variable that is intended to represent ten billion tokens, but the source code mistakenly sets the value to one hundred million tokens (uint256 private _tTotal = 100_000_000 * 10 ** 9). This discrepancy between the documented tokenomics and the on‑chain constant is the root cause of the vulnerability. Because many protocol parameters – such as the maximum transaction amount, fee calculations, and other limits – are expressed as a proportion of the total supply, the undersized supply inflates those limits relative to the actual circulating amount. For example, the setter for the maximum transaction amount requires a value greater than ten million tokens and then scales it by 10 ** 9. With a true supply of only one hundred million tokens, the minimum allowed maxTxAmount represents at least ten percent of the entire supply. If a user or the owner attempts to set or use such a large transaction size, the trade will move a substantial portion of the market, causing extreme price impact, massive slippage, and potentially triggering anti‑whale or anti‑bot mechanisms. The issue manifests whenever the contract enforces the require(maxTxAmount > 10_000_000) check or when fee distribution logic assumes a larger pool of tokens; under the wrong supply the calculations become inaccurate, leading to unexpected fee amounts or failed transfers. All token holders, traders, and the protocol itself are affected because the economic guarantees described in the white‑paper no longer hold, and users may see their balances reduced unexpectedly or receive zero tokens after a transfer due to fee overflow. The problem was discovered during a manual audit by comparing the documented tokenomics (10 billion) with the hard‑coded constant in the Solidity source. It is easy to miss because the contract compiles without errors and the variable name does not hint at the magnitude; only a careful review of the numbers reveals the mismatch. To remediate, the constant should be corrected to reflect the intended supply (uint256 private _tTotal = 10_000_000_000 * 10 ** 9), and any dependent calculations should be re‑validated against the updated supply. This class of bug falls under “incorrect immutable parameter” or “misconfigured tokenomics”, where a hard‑coded economic constant does not match the protocol specification, leading to broken business logic and potential financial loss.

title: If insider deposits and unlocks in quick succession, attacker can steal their NFT and their deposit funds
content: The vulnerability is a logical flaw in the dNFT contract that permits an insider NFT to be unlocked before any deposit is attached, and the contract does not enforce a safety check that a deposit must exist prior to unlocking. Because insider NFTs are minted without an initial deposit and start in a locked state, the protocol expects the owner to first unlock the NFT and then make a deposit before the NFT becomes eligible for liquidation. However, the unlock() function only verifies that the token is currently locked and does not verify that a non‑zero deposit (shared balance) is present. This omission creates a window where an attacker can exploit the ordering of transactions. If an insider submits an unlock transaction followed shortly by a deposit transaction, both may sit in the mempool simultaneously. A malicious actor can submit a liquidation transaction that is sandwiched between the unlock and deposit using a flash‑bots bundle or other front‑running technique. The liquidation succeeds because the NFT is unlocked and has no deposit protecting it, allowing the attacker to seize the NFT. When the subsequent deposit transaction is finally mined, it credits the ETH to the now‑stolen NFT, effectively transferring the insider’s funds to the attacker. The impact is that the insider loses both the NFT and the deposited ETH, while the attacker gains ownership of the NFT and the associated funds. This issue affects any user who mints an insider NFT, expects to unlock it and then fund it, and relies on the protocol’s implicit assumption that a deposit will always precede unlocking. It was discovered during a manual audit that highlighted the missing validation in the unlock() logic. The bug is subtle because the normal user flow (unlock then deposit) works correctly when no adversary interferes, making the problem hard to notice without deliberately testing for front‑running scenarios. From the user’s perspective, the UI may show a successful unlock, followed by a successful deposit, yet the NFT disappears from their wallet and their balance appears unchanged or reduced, contradicting the expectation that they would retain the NFT after funding it. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “missing state validation” or “order‑dependency” bugs where contract functions assume a certain sequence without enforcing it, leading to race‑condition exploits. To remediate, the unlock() function should include a check that the NFT has a non‑zero deposit (e.g., require shared balance > 0) before allowing the lock to be released, or the protocol should enforce that deposits must be made before unlocking, thereby eliminating the exploitable window.
summary:
The dNFT contract allows the owner to mint a predefined quantity of "insider" NFTs without any deposit attached to them. These NFTs begin in a locked state, which stops them from being immediately liquidated due to their lack of deposits.

The protocol enforces that, in order for insider's to mint any DYAD, they must unlock their NFTs (so that they will be subject to liquidation, like all other users).

However, there is no safety check for the opposite case, where an insider unlocks their NFT before making a deposit. In this situation, any user could liquidate them and steal their NFT.

This is especially dangerous because if a user calls both of these functions in quick succession, they may both be in the mempool at the same time. If this is the case, a malicious attacker can create a flashbots bundle to sandwich their liquidation transaction between the unlock() and deposit() transactions, with the result that:
The attacker will successfully liquidate and steal the insider's NFT
The deposit transaction will deposit the insider's ETH to the stolen NFT, securing it for the attacker

title: Current liquidation mechanism is ineffective and dangerous
content: The vulnerability lies in the liquidation logic of the protocol that issues dNFTs representing a share of the collateral pool. The contract treats a dNFT as liquidatable when the number of shares attributed to that token falls below a hard‑coded threshold of 0.1 %. At that moment any external address can call the liquidation function, supply enough ETH to raise the share count above the threshold, and in return receive ownership of the dNFT together with all shares that were previously assigned to it. Because the protocol does not enforce a per‑token collateralisation invariant – it only checks a global ratio that is not kept as a strict invariant – the act of pushing the share count back up does not restore the original over‑collateralised state. Consequently a liquidator can repeatedly trigger the condition, inject ETH, and walk away with the dNFT and its underlying value while the original holder loses the token and any claim to the deposited collateral. The flaw originates from the design choice of using a very low share‑percentage trigger and from the absence of a check that the total deposited ETH multiplied by the current ETH price equals the contract balance. Exploitation is straightforward: an attacker monitors the share ratio of each dNFT, waits until it dips below the 0.1 % mark, sends a minimal amount of ETH to satisfy the threshold, and then calls the liquidation routine to claim the dNFT. The user experience is that a holder who expected to retain their dNFT and to be able to withdraw DYAD or ETH suddenly sees the token disappear from their wallet, their balance become zero, and any subsequent withdrawal attempts fail. The impact is a loss of ownership, potential under‑collateralisation of the protocol, and an unfair advantage for the first liquidator, which can lead to systemic risk if many dNFTs are drained. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the liquidation path and identified that the global collateral invariant is not enforced and that the low threshold enables manipulation. The problem is subtle because the ETH sent by the liquidator is indistinguishable from a normal deposit and the contract does not emit a clear warning that ownership has been transferred. To remediate the bug the protocol should enforce an over‑collateralisation ratio on each individual dNFT, track the amount of DYAD withdrawn per token, and verify that after any redeem or withdraw operation the value of the remaining shares divided by the withdrawn amount remains above a minimum collateralisation ratio. Additionally, the rebasing logic should be adjusted so that totalDeposit × ETH price always equals the contract’s ETH balance, making the invariant observable and enforceable. By making liquidation a function of the token holder’s own collateral state rather than an externally manipulable share percentage, the protocol can restore its intended safety guarantees.
summary:
The liquidation mechanism is intended to keep the protocol overcollateralized. However, the current mechanism design seems inherently unstable and doesn't accomplish the objective.

Currently, the logic for liquidation is as follows:
The shares held by a specific dNFT falls below a certain threshold (currently 0.1%)
A Liquidator sends sufficient ETH to push that dNFT's shares above the threshold
The Liquidator gets possession of the dNFT, as well as all the shares that it previously owned
There are a number of issues I see with this. I'll go into details below, and then share some thoughts on how this might look in the Recommendations section.

title: Collateralization ratio can be broken by users redeeming deposits for ETH
content: The vulnerability consists of a missing collateralization check when users redeem ETH from the DYAD vault. The DYAD system is designed to keep a 300% collateralization ratio, meaning that the USD value of ETH held in the contract must be at least three times the total DYAD supply. This invariant is enforced in the withdraw() function, which prevents minting additional DYAD if the resulting ratio would fall below the minimum. However, the redeemDeposit() function, which allows users to withdraw ETH that they previously deposited, does not perform the same ratio calculation before releasing the funds. The root cause is that the invariant enforcement logic is only applied to the minting path and not to the redemption path, leaving a gap in the accounting of the vault’s collateral. An attacker can exploit this by first depositing ETH, minting a portion of DYAD, and then calling redeemDeposit to withdraw the remaining ETH without any ratio check. Because the contract’s balance is reduced while the DYAD supply remains unchanged, the collateralization ratio can drop from the intended 3:1 to as low as 1:1, effectively breaking the economic guarantee of the stablecoin. The impact is that the protocol becomes under‑collateralized, which can lead to loss of confidence, potential de‑pegging of the token, and exposure of token holders to loss of value. The condition under which this occurs is any situation where a user with a non‑zero deposit calls redeemDeposit after minting DYAD; the bug is triggered regardless of the amount redeemed as long as the contract’s balance falls below the required threshold. All DYAD holders, the protocol’s governance, and any downstream applications that rely on the stablecoin’s backing are affected because the system no longer guarantees the promised collateral ratio. The issue was discovered during a security audit when a test case demonstrated that after withdrawing a portion of the deposited ETH, the subsequent call to redeemDeposit could reduce the ratio to 1:1 without any revert. The bug is subtle because the contract does not emit an error; the ratio appears correct after the initial mint, and only after redemption does the invariant break, making it easy to miss in manual reviews. The recommended fix is to abstract the collateralization logic into a shared modifier that is applied to both withdraw() and redeemDeposit(), ensuring that any change to the vault’s ETH balance is evaluated against the DYAD supply before the operation proceeds. The modifier should also handle the edge case where the total DYAD supply is zero to avoid division‑by‑zero errors. By enforcing the check on both paths, the protocol maintains its economic guarantees and prevents the under‑collateralization scenario that currently allows funds to disappear from the backing pool.

title: Middleware can Deny Withdrawls by Revoking Slashing Prior to Queueing Withdrawal
content: The vulnerability arises from the interaction between the middleware (slasher) contract and the StrategyManager withdrawal logic. A middleware that has been granted slashing rights for an operator can call a function that records the last stake update and simultaneously revokes its own slashing ability. When an operator is configured with only a single approved middleware, this revocation changes the internal update record used by StrategyManager._completeQueuedWithdrawal. The withdrawal completion routine checks two conditions via Slasher.canWithdraw: (1) the withdrawal must have been queued before the latest update block recorded by the slasher, and (2) the current timestamp must be later than the slasher’s serving period. If the middleware revokes its slashing rights before the user queues a withdrawal, condition (1) fails because the latest update block is now newer than the withdrawal start block. Consequently, the user’s queued withdrawal can never satisfy the canWithdraw check, and the withdrawal remains permanently stuck. This edge case occurs only when the operator relies on a single middleware; with multiple middlewares the revocation of one does not affect the overall frozen status. The impact is that stakers are unable to retrieve their funds, leading to a situation where the UI shows a pending withdrawal that never resolves, balances appear unchanged, and users may perceive that their funds have disappeared.
