The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the modifier onlyNotFrozen and the logic that updates frozenStatus based on middleware actions. It is difficult to notice because the normal flow of slashing and withdrawal works correctly, and the failure only manifests under the specific sequence of revoking rights before queuing a withdrawal. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of state‑dependency errors where a contract’s permission state is altered in a way that invalidates previously recorded user intents. To remediate, the protocol should relax the first canWithdraw condition when there is exactly one approved middleware, or otherwise ensure that revoking slashing ability does not retroactively invalidate already queued withdrawals, thereby preserving the user’s right to withdraw funds.
summary:
The slasher.sol contract manages middleware rights and capabilities for a given operator, whilst the StrategyManager.sol relies on this contract to determine if withdrawals are allowed. If a given slasher (middleware) revokes their own rights to slash for an operator using Slasher.recordLastStakeUpdateAndRevokeSlashingAbility(), a staker will be unable to queue withdrawals. A condition for this edge case is that a staker maintains only one middleware.
The StrategyManager.queueWithdrawal() leverages the function modifier onlyNotFrozen(msg.sender) to determine if a user is able to initiate a withdrawal. Rejecting withdrawals is managed by updating the frozenStatus[operator] and can only be done by an approved middleware that the operator has opted into slashing. Once a withdrawal is queued, a staker can complete the withdrawal by calling StrategyManager.completeQueuedWithdrawl().
The StrategyManager._completeQueuedWithdrawal() checks the Slasher.canWithdraw() which requires the following conditions to be met:
1. withdrawalStartBlock < update.stalestUpdateBlock: requiring the withdrawal to be initiated prior the latest update from the slasher.
2. uint32(block.timestamp) > update.latestServeUntil: requiring the withdrawal to be completed after the slasher’s serving period has elapsed.
These two conditions are valid and required for the system to function under normal circumstances. However, in the event that a middleware operates maliciously, or accidentally revokes their slashing ability by calling Slasher.recordLastStakeUpdateAndRevokeSlashingAbility() prior to a withdrawal being queued, condition (1) above will fail. Effectively preventing the completion of queued withdrawals.

title: withdrawalDelayBlocks Cannot Be Initialised After M2 Upgrade
content: The vulnerability consists of a missing initialization of the withdrawal delay parameter after the M2 upgrade of the EigenLayer system. In the original design the variable withdrawalDelayBlocks, which defines how many blocks must pass before a withdrawal can be completed, lived in the StrategyManager contract and was set during its initialize() call. The M2 upgrade moved this storage slot to the DelegationManager contract, but the DelegationManager instance had already been initialized earlier, and its initialize() function cannot be called again. As a result the new variable remains at its default value of zero, meaning that withdrawals are processed without any enforced block delay. This occurs whenever a user or an operator initiates a withdrawal through DelegationManager after the upgrade. The bug was discovered during a security audit that examined storage layout changes across upgrades. It is subtle because the contract compiles and runs, and the missing delay does not produce an explicit error; the only symptom is that withdrawals complete instantly, contrary to the protocol’s expectation of a waiting period. The impact is that malicious restaked operators, especially when integrated with an AVS (Attestation Verification Service), could withdraw funds in the same block they are restaked, preventing the AVS from reacting to potentially fraudulent activity. Users may notice that their balances are reduced immediately after a withdrawal request, and the protocol’s risk model that assumes a delay for slashing or challenge periods is violated. The issue belongs to the class of upgrade‑induced storage mis‑initialization bugs, where a variable is relocated to a new contract but the initialization path is no longer reachable. To remediate the problem the recommended approaches are to deploy a fresh DelegationManager proxy that can be initialized with a proper withdrawalDelayBlocks value, or to add a re‑initializable function protected by a reinitialize modifier that explicitly sets the delay after the upgrade. Both solutions restore the intended block‑based withdrawal latency and re‑align the protocol’s security guarantees with its design assumptions.
summary:
The withdrawalDelayBlocks storage variable will not be able to be initialised, hence there will be no delay on completing withdrawals in DelegationManager.
In the M2 upgrade, the withdrawalDelayBlocks storage variable has been moved from StrategyManager to the DelegationManager. However, withdrawalDelayBlocks can only be initialised in the initialize() function, which cannot be called again as the DelegationManager contract has already been initialised.
It is worth noting that currently risk to funds on EigenLayer Beacon Chain Strategy might not be present, though depending on future integrations with an AVS, default values for withdrawalDelayBlocks may prevent an AVS from responding to same block withdrawals of malicious restaked operators. This would significantly increase the severity of this bug from what is reported currently.

title: Priority operation reexecution for ERA chain in GW and L1 when migrating from GW to L1
content: The vulnerability originates from a mismatch between the priority‑operation bookkeeping structures that exist on the Layer‑1 (L1) settlement contract and the Gateway (GW) contract after the ERA chain is migrated from GW back to L1. During the initial migration to the GW, the upgrade routine creates a priority tree and records a startIndex equal to the current tail of the priority queue on L1 (for example 3,268,282). However, the GW does not receive the corresponding head (firstUnprocessedPriorityTx) value from the L1 priority queue, so on the GW the head remains zero. When a new priority operation is submitted on the GW, the contract checks whether the stored startIndex is greater than the GW’s firstUnprocessedPriorityTx; because startIndex is large and the GW head is zero, the condition is true and the code pushes a duplicate entry into both the GW priority queue and the priority tree. This process repeats for every operation, causing millions of redundant priority entries to be recorded on the GW while the tree’s unprocessedIndex never advances. If the ERA chain is later migrated back to L1, the L1 contract still sees its unprocessedIndex at zero even though many priority operations have already been executed on the GW. Consequently, L1 treats those already‑executed operations as pending and re‑executes them, leading to double execution of the same priority transaction. From a user perspective this can manifest as a withdrawal that appears to succeed twice, a balance that unexpectedly drops to zero, or a refund that never arrives because the same operation is being processed again. The root cause is the failure to synchronize the unprocessedIndex (or the head of the priority queue) across the two layers during migration, resulting in a logical inconsistency rather than a direct code injection. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the upgrade path and the interaction between s.priorityTree.setup and the writePriorityOpHash logic. It is hard to notice because both layers maintain separate data structures that appear correct in isolation; the problem only surfaces when the chain is moved back and the indices diverge. The impact is high because duplicated priority operations can cause double‑spending, inconsistent state, and potential loss of funds. The recommended mitigation is to ensure that the unprocessedIndex of the priority tree is updated whenever a priority operation is processed on the GW, or to transfer the head index from L1 to GW during migration so that startIndex and firstUnprocessedPriorityTx remain aligned. By keeping the indices consistent, the system will correctly recognise which operations have already been executed and will not re‑execute them after a migration, preserving the intended accounting guarantees of the protocol.

title: Device wallet creation can be DoSed, making the whole protocol obsolete
content: The vulnerability resides in a public wallet‑creation function that can be called by anyone without any access control. The function receives a device identifier and an owner key, checks a registry mapping to see whether a wallet with that identifier already exists, and then deploys a new wallet. Because the check only looks at the identifier and does not bind the deployment to the caller or to the owner key, a malicious actor can submit a transaction that uses the same identifier as a legitimate user or as the admin‑restricted deployment routine, but supplies a different owner key. By broadcasting this transaction slightly earlier (front‑running), the attacker causes the registry to record a wallet that is owned by the attacker instead of the intended user. Subsequent legitimate attempts to create a wallet with the same identifier either fail silently or create a second wallet that collides with the registry’s expectations, effectively preventing the rightful owner from using the device wallet. The protocol relies on the uniqueness of the identifier for later operations such as batchPopulateHistory and deployLazyWalletAndSetESIMIdentifier; when the identifier is already occupied by an attacker‑controlled wallet, those functions revert or consume excessive gas, leading to a denial‑of‑service condition. The issue is discovered during a security audit that examined the permission model of the factory contract and noticed that the admin‑only deployment path internally calls the same public function, making it vulnerable to front‑running. It is hard to notice because the transaction appears successful – a wallet address is returned – yet the wallet is owned by an unexpected party, and the UI may simply show that a wallet exists without indicating the ownership mismatch. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after attempting to register a device, the wallet either shows a zero balance, refuses further interactions, or the UI reports “device not found” even though the transaction succeeded. The impact is that users cannot create or use their device wallets, effectively rendering the protocol unusable and potentially locking any funds that would be deposited. The class of bug is a front‑running race condition combined with insufficient access control and identifier collision, often referred to as an identifier‑squatting denial‑of‑service. To remediate, the creation routine should be restricted to authorized callers, the unique identifier should be bound to the caller’s address (for example by incorporating msg.sender into the salt), and the contract should enforce that a wallet with the given identifier cannot be re‑registered with a different owner. Additionally, the mapping could be redesigned to include the owner key or a deterministic address scheme that prevents collisions, and the admin deployment path should not rely on the same public function without proper checks.

title: The deployLazyWalletAndSetESIMIdentifier function won't send ETH to the registry and will revert, resulting in a core protocol functionality not working
content: The vulnerability resides in an admin‑only function that is intended to deploy a device wallet and an eSIM wallet while locking a user‑specified ETH deposit. The function is marked payable and asserts that the ether sent with the transaction (msg.value) matches the _depositAmount argument. However, when the function forwards the call to the RegistryHelper.deployLazyWallet routine, it does so without attaching any ether. Consequently, the RegistryHelper contract receives a call that expects a non‑zero balance but gets none, causing an internal require or transfer to fail and the whole transaction to revert. The root cause is the omission of the {value: msg.value} forwarding syntax in the external call, which means the deposited ether never leaves the caller contract. An attacker does not need to craft a malicious payload; any legitimate admin who attempts to create a wallet with a positive deposit will trigger the revert, effectively blocking the core onboarding flow of the protocol. The impact is that device owners cannot obtain their lazy wallets, the intended deposit is never locked, and the protocol’s eSIM provisioning mechanism becomes unusable. This condition occurs whenever the admin invokes deployLazyWalletAndSetESIMIdentifier with _depositAmount greater than zero, which is the normal case for most users. The affected parties include the protocol administrators, end‑users who expect their wallets to be created, and any downstream services that rely on the existence of those wallets. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the payable semantics of the function and noticed that the ether was never forwarded. It can be hard to notice because the function compiles without errors, the payable modifier is present, and the require check on msg.value passes, so only the downstream call fails, which may be overlooked if only zero‑deposit scenarios are tested. To remediate, the call to the registry should explicitly forward the received ether, for example using registry.deployLazyWallet{value:msg.value}(...), and the RegistryHelper should also ensure that any further calls to factory contracts propagate the value as needed. This aligns the implementation with the intended business logic that a user’s deposit is locked at deployment, preventing the “funds disappear” symptom where the transaction reverts and no wallet is created despite the user sending ether.

title: PegStabilityModule assumes underlying has 18 decimals
content: The vulnerability resides in a module that handles peg stability swaps. The module calculates swap amounts using the same decimal precision as the synthetic token, which is fixed at 18 decimals. This assumption is hard‑coded and not adjusted for the actual decimal count of the underlying asset being swapped. When the underlying token uses a different number of decimals – for example 6 or 8 – the quoted amount is either overstated or understated relative to the true value of the asset. The root cause is a missing scaling factor that should convert between the synthetic token’s 18‑decimal representation and the underlying token’s native decimal representation. An attacker can exploit this mismatch by initiating a swap where the contract believes it is sending or receiving a certain amount, while the real amount transferred is larger or smaller due to the decimal discrepancy. By carefully choosing the direction of the swap, the attacker can extract profit from the protocol, effectively draining value from the peg stability pool. The impact is a loss of funds for the protocol and its users, as the pool’s accounting becomes inaccurate and the protocol may become under‑collateralised. The issue manifests whenever a peg‑stable token is backed by an underlying asset whose decimals differ from 18, which can happen in deployments that support multiple assets. All participants that rely on the peg stability module – liquidity providers, borrowers, and end‑users – are affected because the module will report incorrect balances and may deliver zero or unexpected amounts to users. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that compared the module’s arithmetic against the ERC‑20 specification of token decimals, revealing that the code never reads the underlying token’s decimals field. Because the error does not cause an outright revert, it can be subtle and may only be noticed when abnormal profit appears or when balances diverge from expectations. To remediate, the contract should retrieve the decimals of each token involved in a swap and apply a scaling factor so that quoted amounts are expressed in the correct base units for both assets. This change restores proper accounting, ensures that users receive the amount they expect, and prevents profit extraction through decimal‑based arbitrage. The bug belongs to the class of “decimal‑mismatch pricing errors” that break financial invariants and can lead to silent fund loss.
summary: The swap amounts in the PegStabilityModule are quoted in the same decimals as the synth, which is always 18. It is therefore only compatible with underlying's of 18 decimals. If the pegged underlying has different decimals, it's profitable to perform the swap.

title: Self-liquidations of leveraged positions can be profitable
content:
The vulnerability is a profitable self‑liquidation scenario that arises from the interaction between leveraged borrowing, oracle price updates, and the liquidation discount mechanism. An attacker can open a highly leveraged position by flash‑loaning collateral and borrowing the maximum amount of the debt token allowed by the protocol’s loan‑to‑value (LTV) ratio. Because the protocol permits an external price oracle to be updated within the same block, the attacker can sandwich a price change: after taking the leveraged position, they trigger or front‑run a price update that lowers the reported value of the collateral relative to the debt. Immediately afterwards the attacker initiates a liquidation of the same position from a different sub‑account. The liquidation logic applies a discount on the collateral that is higher than the loss incurred by the price drop, so the liquidator (the attacker) receives more value than they need to repay the debt, resulting in a net profit. This profit is realized without any external market risk and effectively extracts value from the protocol’s collateral pool.
The root cause is the combination of (1) an oracle that can be updated atomically with user actions, (2) a liquidation discount factor that is not tightly bound to the LTV configuration, and (3) the ability for the same entity to act as both borrower and liquidator in the same transaction or block. When the discount factor exceeds the threshold defined by 1‑sqrt(LTV), the liquidation reward becomes larger than the loss caused by the price deviation, making self‑liquidation economically attractive.
Exploitation proceeds step‑by‑step: (i) the attacker flash‑loans enough assets to provide collateral, (ii) they borrow the maximum debt permitted, (iii) they cause or front‑run a price oracle update that reduces the collateral’s reported price, (iv) they call the liquidation function from a separate sub‑account, receiving the discounted collateral and repaying the debt, and (v) the difference between the discounted collateral value and the repaid debt is kept as profit. Because all actions can be packed into a single transaction or executed within the same block, the attack does not require waiting for external market movements.
The impact is a direct loss of funds from the protocol’s collateral reserves, erosion of the economic safety margin, and potential loss of confidence among users and investors. Any participant who can open leveraged positions and access the oracle update mechanism is a potential attacker; the protocol itself, its governance token holders, and honest borrowers are all affected by the drained collateral.
The condition for the attack to succeed is that the oracle update can be front‑run or sandwiched and that the protocol’s discount factor is set above the safe bound relative to the LTV. This situation is subtle because liquidation is a legitimate operation and the profit appears as a normal liquidation reward, making it difficult to detect through routine monitoring. The issue was discovered during a security audit by Spearbit, where the logical flow of leveraged borrowing and liquidation was examined and the profit‑making loop was identified.
To remediate the problem, the protocol should align the maximum discount factor with the chosen LTV configuration, ensuring that the discount never exceeds 1‑sqrt(LTV). Governance can enforce a tighter oracle update threshold (e.g., requiring the price deviation to be smaller than 1‑sqrt(LTV)) or introduce a delay between price updates and liquidation eligibility. Additional mitigations include restricting self‑liquidation, requiring an external third‑party liquidator, or redesigning the liquidation incentive model so that no profitable arbitrage exists when the price feed changes. These changes would close the economic incentive for self‑liquidation while preserving legitimate liquidation functionality.
summary:
An attacker can perform the following attack by sandwiching a price oracle update:
1. Taking on a leveraged position by flashloaning collateral and max-borrowing the debt token.
2. Performing the price update.
3. Liquidating themself (from another subaccount).

title: H-1 Double-counting of the Migrated Stake
content: The vulnerability is a double‑counting accounting error that occurs in the internal _delegateStake function of the stake delegator contract. When a user’s stake is migrated from an account to its owner via the internal _migrateStake call, the function returns the amount that was migrated. The original implementation then adds this returned amount to the amount argument that was already supplied for delegation, effectively counting the same stake twice. The root cause is a logical mistake: the migrated stake is treated as additional new stake instead of being recognized as already accounted for, leading to an inflated total delegated amount. An attacker or any user who triggers a delegation after a migration can exploit this by causing the contract to record a larger stake than actually deposited, which in turn results in the reward vault distributing more rewards than it should. The impact includes over‑allocation of rewards, distorted stake balances, and potential loss of value for other participants because the protocol’s accounting assumptions are broken. The bug manifests only when a delegation follows a migration – i.e., when the account has a non‑zero owner and _migrateStake is executed – and therefore affects users who have previously migrated stakes as well as the protocol’s overall reward distribution logic. It was discovered during a manual security audit by MixBytes, who noted that the addition of the migrated amount to the original amount was inconsistent with the intended accounting model. The issue can be hard to notice because the contract still compiles and appears to delegate stake correctly; the inflated numbers only become apparent when comparing expected versus actual reward payouts or when auditing stake balances. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are a stake balance that appears larger than the deposited amount and rewards that are unexpectedly high, contradicting the expectation that rewards are proportional to the actual stake. The recommended fix is to separate the migration step from the delegation step and to pass only the original amount to the reward vault after migration, removing the erroneous addition of the migrated amount. This aligns the contract with the intended single‑count accounting model and restores correct reward calculations.
summary:
There is an issue with HookTargetStakeDelegator.sol#L283 inside the _delegateStake function.
_migrateStake internally delegates the stake from the account to the owner and returns the
delegated amount. This amount is then added to the amount value originally passed to the
_delegateStake function.
The issue is classified as High severity because it leads to double-accounting for the delegated
value from the account to the owner address, which is incorrectly added to the original amount,
which was subject to delegation.

title: H-1 DOS of pool adapters via positive allowance
content: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition affecting pool adapters that expose a public swap() function. The swap implementation calls OpenZeppelin's SafeERC20.safeIncreaseAllowance to grant the pool contract permission to transfer the input token. In older versions of OpenZeppelin, safeIncreaseAllowance simply adds the desired amount to the current allowance by invoking token.approve(spender, currentAllowance+amount) without first resetting the allowance to zero. Certain ERC‑20 tokens, most notably USDT, implement a non‑standard rule that rejects any approve call that attempts to set a non‑zero allowance when the existing allowance is already non‑zero. Consequently, when the swap() function is executed with such a token and the allowance is already non‑zero, the approve call reverts, causing the entire swap transaction to fail. Additionally, the swap code contains a conditional check where if the caller‑provided minAmountOut is greater than the pool‑computed minDy, the function transfers the full amountIn to an emergency address and returns zero output. An attacker can deliberately craft a swap call that triggers this branch, leaving the allowance unchanged (or zeroed) and causing subsequent legitimate swaps to be blocked because the pool adapter can no longer obtain the required allowance. The impact is that users attempting to trade the affected token receive no output, may see their input tokens transferred to an unexpected address, and the protocol’s liquidity for that token becomes unusable, effectively a funds‑availability denial‑of‑service. This condition occurs only when the token exhibits the approve‑revert behaviour and the contract uses the outdated safeIncreaseAllowance implementation. It primarily affects users, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself because the pool can no longer process trades for the impacted token. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the pool adapter code, where the auditor noted the public swap entry point and the reliance on safeIncreaseAllowance, then cross‑checked token behaviours and identified the incompatibility with USDT‑style tokens. The bug is subtle because the swap function appears to succeed from a transaction‑status perspective, yet the business logic fails silently, returning zero output and moving funds to an emergency address, which may be overlooked without detailed testing of edge‑case token contracts. To remediate, the project should upgrade its OpenZeppelin dependencies to a version where safeIncreaseAllowance first sets the allowance to zero before assigning the new value, or replace the allowance logic with a custom implementation that handles tokens requiring a zero‑first pattern. This change restores the ability of the pool adapter to increase allowances safely, eliminating the denial‑of‑service vector and ensuring that swap operations behave as users expect—receiving the correct amount of output tokens or reverting with a clear error rather than silently failing.

title: H-2 Signature veriﬁcation bypass
content: An attacker can bypass the signature verification in the router by exploiting the way the raw data that is signed is constructed. The _getRawData function builds a byte stream by simply appending the encoded operation identifiers and their parameter arrays one after another without any delimiter. Because the concatenation is ambiguous, different sets of parameters can produce exactly the same byte sequence. The signature verification routine hashes this raw byte stream and checks it against the signer’s public key, but it cannot tell whether the bytes correspond to the intended grouping of parameters. Moreover, the subsequent abi.decode call silently discards any surplus bytes, so a payload that contains extra arguments does not cause a revert at the decoding stage. An attacker can therefore rearrange or split the original parameter list into alternative groupings that still match the signed hash, submit the manipulated payload to RouterV2.start, and cause the router to execute operations with arguments that were never approved by the signer. In practice the attacker may craft a swap operation with a favorable slippage setting and redirect the output tokens to an address they control before the later operation that expects a different argument set fails and reverts the transaction. The vulnerability appears when the router processes multi‑operation batches that rely on a single signature for the whole batch. Users who trust the router to enforce the signed intent may see their funds transferred to an unexpected address, experience a transaction that reverts after partially executing, or notice that a swap returned less than expected. The issue was discovered during a manual code audit that highlighted the lack of separators in the raw data construction and the permissive behaviour of abi.decode. It is hard to notice because the signature itself appears valid and the transaction does not fail until after some state changes have already occurred. The bug belongs to the class of signature‑binding or message‑format ambiguities, where the signed message is not uniquely parsable. The proper fix is to introduce unambiguous delimiters or length prefixes between each operation identifier and its parameter list, or to use a structured encoding such as ABI‑encoded tuples that preserve boundaries, ensuring that any change in the grouping of parameters results in a different hash and therefore an invalid signature.
summary:
• BaseRouter.sol#L271-L272
The BaseRouter._getRawData() function concatenates operations and parameters without separators. This allows a hacker to feed operations to the RouterV2.start() with different parameters while maintaining the same signature.
For example, given the operations [op1, op2] and parameters [[a, b], [c, d]], the BaseRouter._checkSignature() method cannot distinguish between [[a, b], [c, d]] and [[a], [b, c, d]] or [[a, b, c], [d]], because _getRawData() will always concatenate parameters into a single stream of [a, b, c, d].
Moreover, there will also be no errors with unpacking the parameters, because abi.decode() does not revert when provided with excess data; it discards extra bytes.
Consequently, while the backend may sign legitimate data, an attacker could reorganize this data in such a way that the operations will execute with entirely different arguments. Although this manipulation will eventually cause a revert due to missing arguments in the ﬁnal operations, an attacker could potentially extract funds prior to the revert by initiating a swap with slippage, directing funds to an emergency address controlled by the attacker.

title: H-3 BURNUNLOCKCODE does not validate p.tokenIn
content: The vulnerability is located in the BURNUNLOCKCODE function of the router contract, where the input parameter p.tokenIn is accepted without any validation of its authenticity or interface compliance. Because the function does not verify that tokenIn points to a trusted token contract, an attacker who can influence the data supplied to the function – for example by compromising the off‑chain backend that assembles the p struct – can inject an arbitrary contract address as tokenIn. The router stores this address in a variable called possibleAdapter and later invokes possibleAdapter.originalToken() and other adapter methods without additional checks. A malicious contract can therefore return crafted values that cause the router to treat the operation as successful while bypassing the intended monetary cost, allowing the attacker to unlock tokens on subsequent chains without burning or locking the required amount. This results in funds disappearing from users who expect their tokens to be burned or locked, and it breaks the accounting guarantees of the cross‑chain bridge. The issue manifests whenever BURNUNLOCKCODE is called with a p struct that originates from an untrusted source, which is common in designs where transaction data is prepared off‑chain. All participants – token holders, bridge operators, and downstream contracts – are affected because the integrity of the token flow is compromised. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that highlighted the absence of any require or assert statement checking the tokenIn address against a whitelist or confirming that it implements the expected adapter interface. Because the function proceeds silently with a malicious contract, the problem can be subtle and may only become apparent when an attacker successfully exploits it, making it hard to notice during normal operation. The recommended remediation is to enforce strict validation of the tokenIn parameter: verify that the address belongs to a known, whitelisted token contract, confirm that it implements the required adapter interface, and optionally require a signed attestation from a trusted authority. Adding these checks prevents arbitrary contracts from being injected, restores the intended economic guarantees, and eliminates the possibility of fee‑less token unlocking that leads to fund loss.
summary:
• RouterV2.sol#L120
The BURNUNLOCKCODE function does not validate p.tokenIn, which can lead to the theft of funds. If the backend is compromised, an attacker could insert a malicious contract as the p.tokenIn parameter into the BURNUNLOCKCODE operation. This would result in the possibleAdapter being set to the fake p.tokenIn, enabling all subsequent calls to it to proceed without any monetary cost. This vulnerability could allow an attacker to unlock any token on subsequent chains, provided it is returned from the possibleAdapter.originalToken() function.

title: H-1 Incorrect logic in GaugeV1.notifyRewardAmount()
content: The vulnerability resides in the reward notification routine of a gauge contract that is responsible for creating Merkle‑based reward campaigns. The function receives an explicit amount parameter that callers expect to be the quantity of reward tokens to distribute, but instead the implementation reads the contract's own token balance (balanceOf(address(this))) and uses that value when constructing the campaign. Because the gauge contract never receives the tokens – it only calls approve on the token contract without a subsequent transferFrom from the escrow manager – the approved amount is never moved into the gauge. After the approval step the code also clears the mapping that tracks claimable rewards for the gauge, effectively erasing any previously accumulated reward balance. As a result, when the escrow manager triggers a distribution, the gauge appears to have created a campaign, but the underlying token balance is either zero or unchanged, and users attempting to claim rewards receive nothing. The impact is a loss of reward funds for all participants of the gauge, a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees, and a potential avenue for a malicious actor to sabotage reward distribution by invoking the function with arbitrary parameters. The bug occurs whenever an authorized escrow manager calls the notification function, which is the only allowed caller, and the gauge contract holds no tokens at that moment. It was discovered during a manual audit that compared the function signature with its internal logic and noticed the mismatch between the amount_ argument and the variable used, as well as the absence of a token transfer after the approve call. The issue is subtle because the transaction does not revert and the UI may still show a successful campaign creation, making it hard for users to realize that their rewards have been silently wiped. To remediate, the contract should use the supplied amount_ value, invoke transferFrom (or a safe transfer) from the escrow manager to move the exact reward tokens into the gauge before approving the distribution creator, and avoid deleting the claimable rewards mapping until after a successful transfer. This correction restores the intended accounting flow where rewards are securely transferred, recorded, and claimable by participants, aligning the implementation with the business logic that rewards must be funded before a campaign is announced.

title: H-2 Incorrect ProposalManager.CLOCK() behaviour
content: The vulnerability originates from the ProposalManager contract assuming that the EscrowManager token implements the standard CLOCK() and CLOCK_MODE() view functions used to obtain a reliable time source. In reality EscrowManager does not provide these methods, so when ProposalManager.propose() calls the clock() function the call fails and is caught by a try‑catch block. The catch clause returns the current block number instead of a timestamp. Because the governance logic later computes the proposal snapshot as the returned clock value plus the configured votingDelay (which is expressed in seconds, e.g., two days), the snapshot becomes block.number+votingDelay. Since block.number grows only by one per mined block, the added votingDelay contributes only a few extra blocks, producing a snapshot that is far earlier than the intended future time. This mis‑calculation propagates to Governor.castVote() and ProposalManager.state(), causing these functions to read an incorrect snapshot and therefore report wrong proposal states. From a user perspective a newly created proposal appears to be ready for voting almost immediately, or conversely the proposal may remain stuck in an unexpected state, leading to situations where a user expects a voting delay of days but receives a proposal that can be voted on within a few seconds or blocks, or where votes are ignored because the contract believes the voting window has not started. The root cause is the fallback to block.number, a value that does not share the same unit (blocks vs seconds) as the expected timestamp, and the lack of proper interface implementation in EscrowManager. The issue was discovered during a security audit by MixBytes, which highlighted that the try‑catch pattern silently masks the missing function and returns a plausible‑looking value, making the bug hard to notice without inspecting the interface contract. Exploitation is possible: an attacker can submit a malicious proposal, rely on the artificially short snapshot to bypass the intended voting delay, and cast votes or trigger execution before honest participants have a chance to react, potentially compromising the DAO’s governance decisions. The affected parties include all DAO token holders, governance participants, and any external contracts that rely on the correct proposal lifecycle. To remediate, the catch block should return block.timestamp, aligning the returned value with the time‑based votingDelay, or the EscrowManager should be upgraded to implement the full CLOCK() and CLOCK_MODE() interface. Additionally, the governance code should avoid silent fallbacks and explicitly verify that the clock source provides timestamps, ensuring that accounting assumptions about time‑based delays remain valid.
summary:
The ProposalManager contract interacts with EscrowManager as a token, but the EscrowManager contract does not implement the CLOCK() and CLOCK_MODE() methods.
When attempting to create a proposal using ProposalManager.propose(), the clock() method is invoked. The call to this method fails within the try block, causing the execution to enter the catch block. In the catch block, block.number is returned.
https://gitlab.ubertech.dev/blockchainlaboratory/eywa-dao/-/blob/29465033f28c8d3f09cbc6722e08e44f443bd3b2/contracts/ProposalManager.sol#L161
The snapshot is calculated as block.number + votingDelay. With the current votingDelay set to 2 days, this results in a very small snapshot value, which is not aligned with expected behavior. The proposalSnapshot then used in Governor.castVote() and ProposalManager.state() methods returns incorrect values due to this miscalculation.

title: H-3 Protocol DoS via EscrowVoteManagerV1.poke()
content: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition in the EscrowVoteManagerV1 contract caused by the public poke(uint256 tokenId) function accepting any token identifier without verifying that the caller owns the token. The root cause is the absence of an ownership check before the function marks the token as being in a voting state. When an attacker calls poke with a tokenId that either does not exist yet or belongs to another user, the contract records the token as locked for voting. Subsequent operations in the EscrowManager contract – such as mint(), burn() and transfer() – invoke an internal _update() routine that expects tokens to be in an unlocked state. Because the token is incorrectly flagged as voting, these operations revert with the custom error LockCurrentlyVoting, effectively preventing legitimate users from creating new locks, transferring NFTs, or performing other core actions. The impact is that the protocol’s core functionality is halted: users cannot lock assets, cannot receive expected voting power, and the DAO’s governance flow is disrupted. This condition occurs whenever an adversary can submit a transaction to poke with an arbitrary tokenId, which is possible at any time because the function is unrestricted. All participants who rely on the escrow mechanism – token holders, stakers, and the DAO itself – are affected, as their funds remain locked and their expected interactions fail. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit that included functional tests; a test case demonstrated that after a random user called poke on tokenId 2, a subsequent createLock call reverted with LockCurrentlyVoting, confirming the DoS scenario. The bug is subtle because the poke function is documented as a helper for legitimate voting‑power adjustments, so developers may assume it is safe to call with any tokenId. However, the side‑effect of marking a token as voting is not reversible without additional logic, making the problem hard to notice until an operation fails. To remediate, the contract should enforce that only the owner of the tokenId (or an authorized manager) can invoke poke, typically by adding a require statement that checks msg.sender against the token’s owner mapping before changing the voting state. This restriction restores the intended invariant that only token holders can trigger voting‑state transitions, eliminating the DoS vector and preserving the protocol’s accounting guarantees that locked tokens can be freely minted, transferred, or burned when not voting.

title: H-4 svotesByPool[mpool] persists indefinitely, leading to rewards
content: The vulnerability resides in the EscrowVoteManagerV1 contract where the aggregate voting power for a pool, stored in svotesByPool[mpool], is only increased when a user casts a vote and never automatically decreased when the user’s lock expires. The contract relies on explicit calls to vote(), poke() or reset() to adjust the stored value, so if a user’s lock runs out and the user does not interact with any of those functions, the stale voting power remains recorded indefinitely. Because the gauge index is refreshed each time new rewards are transferred to the manager, the pool continues to be treated as if it still holds the original voting weight and therefore keeps receiving a share of the newly minted or transferred rewards. An attacker can exploit this by creating a lock, voting once, allowing the lock to expire, and then simply walking away; the pool will keep earning rewards that should have been re‑allocated to active voters. The impact is a systematic over‑allocation of rewards, inflation of the reward token supply, and an unfair advantage for the attacker that can erode the economic incentives of honest participants. The issue manifests whenever a lock expires without the owner calling any of the maintenance functions, and it is amplified when getVotesByTokenId(tokenId) returns zero, because the contract reverts on attempts to clear a zero‑vote entry, preventing any later cleanup of the stale entry. This bug was discovered during a manual code review by the MixBytes audit team, who noticed that the vote‑tracking mapping never gets cleared on expiry and that the zero‑entry revert blocks any automatic nullification. The problem is subtle because the external behavior – rewards being distributed – appears normal, while the internal accounting silently retains outdated voting power, making it hard to spot without inspecting the state variables. To remediate, the contract should track votes on a per‑epoch basis or otherwise automatically decrement or delete svotesByPool entries when a lock’s expiry is reached, mirroring the logic used in the IncentiveRewardsDistributor and RebaseRewardsDistributorV1 contracts. Additionally, the zero‑entry guard should be removed or replaced with logic that safely handles a zero vote count, allowing the system to purge expired votes. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a pool seems to earn more rewards than expected, or that the overall reward distribution feels skewed, while the protocol’s accounting assumptions about voting power and reward entitlement are violated.
summary:
When a user votes in the EscrowVoteManagerV1 contract, the value of svotesByPool[mpool] is incremented by the user's voting power.
https://gitlab.ubertech.dev/blockchainlaboratory/eywa-dao/blob/29465033f28c8d3f09cbc6722e08e44f443bd3b2/contracts/EscrowVoteManagerV1.sol#L307
However, this value does not decrease when the user's lock expires. Instead, it remains unchanged until the user explicitly interacts with one of the following functions.
1. EscrowVoteManagerV1.vote()
2. EscrowVoteManagerV1.poke()
3. EscrowVoteManagerV1.reset()
This behavior allows a user to create a lock, vote once, and ensure that the corresponding pool continues to benefit from their voting power indefinitely, even after the lock has expired. This occurs because the votes are not adjusted or re-evaluated unless the user takes further action.
Additionally, the gauge index is updated whenever new rewards are transferred to EscrowVoteManagerV1, which ensures that the gauge tied to the pool continues to receive rewards. This creates an inconsistency where expired locks still influence reward distribution.
https://gitlab.ubertech.dev/blockchainlaboratory/eywa-dao/-/blob/29465033f28c8d3f09cbc6722e08e44f443bd3b2/contracts/EscrowVoteManagerV1.sol#L356
It was also found that if calling sescrowManager.getVotesByTokenId(tokenId) (https://gitlab.ubertech.dev/blockchainlaboratory/eywa-dao/-/blob/29465033f28c8d3f09cbc6722e08e44f443bd3b2/contracts/EscrowVoteManagerV1.sol#L198) returns 0, then no one can nullify the user's votes, due to the following revert (https://gitlab.ubertech.dev/blockchainlaboratory/eywa-dao/-/blob/29465033f28c8d3f09cbc6722e08e44f443bd3b2/contracts/EscrowVoteManagerV1.sol#L303):
if (m_votesForPool == 0) {
    revert ZeroEntry();
}
This way, the user will forever have votes for pools in EscrowVoteManagerV1.

title: H-5 Incorrect transfer of ERC-20 tokens to non-compatible contract
content: The vulnerability consists of an incorrect transfer of ERC‑20 tokens to a contract that is not built to receive or manage such tokens. In the EscrowVoteManagerV1 contract a call is made to IERC20(seywa).safeTransfer(semissionManager,m_claimableRewards) where s_emissionManager (referred to as semissionManager) is a contract that only handles internal accounting and does not implement any ERC‑20 token handling functions such as a fallback or a token recovery mechanism. Because the target contract lacks the ability to accept ERC‑20 tokens, the safeTransfer call succeeds from the caller’s perspective – it only checks that the token contract returns a true value – but the tokens are effectively locked inside s_emissionManager with no way for the protocol or users to retrieve them. This situation can be triggered whenever a user or the protocol attempts to claim reward tokens that are meant to be sent to the emission manager, causing the claimed amount to disappear from the user’s balance while the transaction appears successful. The impact is a loss of claimable reward funds for any participant who triggers the transfer, violating the expectation that rewards are credited after a vote. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s reward distribution logic, where the auditor noted that the emission manager does not contain any ERC‑20 handling code. The problem is subtle because the transfer does not revert and emits the usual Transfer event, making it appear normal in transaction logs, yet the tokens become irretrievable. To remediate, the contract should either prevent ERC‑20 transfers to the emission manager unless the manager is upgraded to include proper token receipt and withdrawal functions, or the reward distribution logic should be rewritten to send tokens directly to an address that can handle them, such as the user’s wallet or a dedicated treasury contract. This class of bug falls under “token lock due to incompatible contract interface” and breaks the accounting assumptions of the DAO by allowing money to disappear silently.
summary:
• https://gitlab.ubertech.dev/blockchainlaboratory/eywa-dao/-/blob/29465033f28c8d3f09cbc6722e08e44f443bd3b2/contracts/EscrowVoteManagerV1.sol#L136
It was discovered that the s_emissionManager contract does not handle ERC20 tokens. However, the following code attempts to transfer ERC20 tokens to this contract:
IERC20(seywa).safeTransfer(semissionManager, m_claimableRewards);
Since s_emissionManager is not designed to accept or manage ERC20 tokens, any tokens sent to it may become irretrievable.

title: H-6 Incorrect math in EscrowManager.getPastVotes()
content: The vulnerability resides in the function that returns a user’s historical voting power, which incorrectly computes past votes by applying the current decay rate to the elapsed time even when the query refers to a timestamp that has already passed. The protocol defines voting weight as decreasing over time at a fixed rate that is derived from the user’s current deposit. When a user’s deposit changes after the queried time—such as by adding more tokens—the current rate no longer matches the rate that applied in the past. The function therefore adds or subtracts an amount based on a rate that was not valid at the earlier moment, causing the returned past voting weight to be either higher or lower than the true value the user possessed at that block. This discrepancy appears when the governance module (ProposalManager) retrieves a user’s voting power for proposals created in a previous epoch, relying on getPastVotes to enforce eligibility or calculate proposal weight. An attacker can exploit the flaw by depositing or withdrawing tokens after a proposal is opened, causing the contract to report an altered historical voting power and potentially influencing the outcome of the proposal. The impact is that governance decisions may be based on inaccurate accounting, breaking the assumption that past voting power is immutable except for legitimate rate changes, and allowing manipulation of proposal support. The issue was discovered during a security audit when auditors observed that after a deposit, the value returned by getPastVotes for a timestamp that had already elapsed decreased, contrary to the expected invariant that past votes should remain unchanged unless the underlying rate at that past time changes. The bug is subtle because the deviation may be small relative to large integer values, making it easy to miss in routine testing and UI displays. To remediate, the contract should store the decay rate (or the deposit amount) at each epoch boundary and use that historical rate when reconstructing past voting weight, or maintain explicit snapshots of voting power per user per block. This ensures that getPastVotes reflects the true historical voting power and that governance logic remains sound. In broader terms, the flaw is an incorrect historical state calculation caused by using a mutable current parameter to reconstruct past values, a common pitfall in time‑weighted accounting systems.

title: H-7 Unchecked voting status in moveVotes() allows vote power
content: The vulnerability resides in the EscrowManager contract where the moveVotes() function fails to verify whether a token has already participated in a vote. The contract maintains a mapping called s_hasVotedByTokenId that records if a particular token identifier has cast a vote. In the normal voting flow, the _update() routine checks this flag and reverts if the token is already marked as having voted. However, moveVotes() does not perform the same validation, allowing a token that has already voted to be moved again through the DelegationManager. An attacker can therefore follow a three‑step loop: first, cast a vote with a token; second, invoke moveVotes() to transfer the voting power to another address or delegate; third, repeat the process with the same token. Because the s_hasVotedByTokenId flag is never cleared or checked during the move, each iteration adds the same voting weight to the attacker’s total, artificially inflating their influence in subsequent governance decisions. This manipulation can distort proposal outcomes, enable a malicious participant to sway votes, and potentially compromise the integrity of the DAO’s governance. The issue appears only when a token holder who has already voted calls moveVotes, which is a legitimate operation for delegating voting power, making the bug subtle and easy to overlook in normal UI interactions. From a user’s perspective the symptom may be that their voting power appears to increase without any additional token acquisition, or that proposals pass with unexpectedly high vote counts. The problem was identified during a formal security audit performed by MixBytes, which compared the logic of moveVotes against the existing _update() checks and noted the missing guard. Detecting the flaw can be difficult because the function does not revert or emit an error, and the contract’s public interface does not expose the internal voting flag. To remediate the issue, the moveVotes() implementation should include a check similar to if (s_hasVotedByTokenId[tokenId]) { revert LockCurrentlyVoting(); } thereby preventing any token that has already voted from being moved again. Additionally, the contract should ensure that the voting status is appropriately cleared or that delegation does not bypass the voting guard, aligning moveVotes with the same safety guarantees as other vote‑related functions. This class of bug falls under unchecked state validation, where a critical flag governing access control is omitted, leading to double‑spending of voting power.
summary:
• https://gitlab.ubertech.dev/blockchainlaboratory/eywa-dao/blob/39fba4bee623a3e60a529416f93d76e73658440d/contracts/EscrowManager.sol#L396
The moveVotes() method in EscrowManager does not validate whether the token has already voted by checking the s_hasVotedByTokenId mapping.
Because there is no check of shasVotedByTokenId[tokenId] within moveVotes(), an attacker (or any user) can:
1. Cast a vote.
2. Call moveVotes() to move their votes (via DELEGATION_MANAGER).
3. Repeat the above sequence.
By doing so, the user could artificially inflate their voting power, effectively manipulating voting outcomes.

title: H-4 FantiumNFTV1.owners shadows ERC721Upgradeable.owners
content: The vulnerability is a storage‑variable shadowing bug that occurs in the FantiumNFTV1 contract, which inherits from ERC721Upgradeable. The child contract declares its own mapping(uint256 => address) internal _owners, which has the same name and type as the private _owners mapping defined in the ERC721Upgradeable base. Because Solidity resolves variable names to the most derived definition, the child’s _owners completely hides the parent’s mapping. The public exists(uint256 _tokenId) function reads from the shadowed mapping (owners[tokenId]) instead of the canonical ERC721 storage that actually tracks token ownership. As a result, the function can return false even when a token is already minted, or return true for a token that has never been minted if the child mapping is unintentionally populated. This discrepancy can be exploited by callers that rely on exists() to guard critical actions such as minting, transferring, or burning. An attacker could invoke a mint function that checks exists(tokenId) before creating a new token; because exists() may incorrectly report that the token does not exist, the attacker can mint a duplicate token ID, thereby overwriting ownership data, breaking the uniqueness guarantee of ERC721, and potentially stealing or locking funds. The impact includes loss of token uniqueness, incorrect UI displays (users see “token does not exist” or a zero balance), failed transfers, and a breach of the protocol’s accounting assumptions that each token ID maps to a single owner. The bug manifests whenever the contract’s logic calls exists() or any other function that directly accesses the shadowed _owners mapping, which includes any custom checks added by the developer. All token holders and any downstream applications that query token existence are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit performed by MixBytes, and it is subtle because the Solidity compiler does not emit a warning for variable shadowing, and the two mappings have identical signatures, making the mistake easy to overlook during code review. To remediate the problem, the redundant _owners mapping should be removed from FantiumNFTV1, and all existence checks should be rewritten to use the standard ERC721Upgradeable.ownerOf() function or the internal _ownerOf() logic provided by the base contract. This eliminates the shadowing, restores a single source of truth for token ownership, and ensures that existence queries reflect the true state of the ledger.

title: H-1 Contract works with non-existent collections and tokens
content: The vulnerability consists of missing existence validation for collection identifiers and token identifiers in several public view and state‑changing functions. Functions such as getRoyalties and tokenURI accept a collectionId or tokenId without first confirming that the identifier corresponds to a minted collection or token. As a result the contract returns a royalty structure that contains placeholder addresses and zero basis points for collections that have never been created. Likewise, privileged roles (Athlete and Platform Manager) are able to invoke updateCollectionAthleteAddress and similar setters on a collectionId that does not exist, effectively writing arbitrary data into storage slots that are never used by a real collection. In addition, the mint function in FantiumMinterV1 permits a caller to request minting of a collectionId that has not been instantiated; if the maxInvocations field is set, the function bypasses payment checks and mints a token for free. The root cause is the absence of a require(_exists(tokenId)) or similar guard before accessing collection‑specific state. An attacker can exploit this by calling getRoyalties with any arbitrary collectionId to retrieve fabricated royalty data, by altering athlete addresses for phantom collections, or by repeatedly invoking mint with non‑existent collectionIds to obtain free tokens, thereby inflating supply and potentially draining protocol incentives. The impact includes incorrect royalty information being displayed to users, unauthorized modification of collection metadata, and unintended token creation that can distort the economic model, leading to loss of revenue for legitimate creators and confusion for users who see unexpected balances or zero‑value refunds. The bug manifests whenever a function is called with an identifier that has not been minted; it does not require any special permissions beyond those already granted to the caller (any user can call the view functions, and any user can call mint). The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the control flow of collection‑related functions and noted the lack of existence checks. Because the contract still returns syntactically valid data, the problem can be hard to notice unless the caller cross‑checks the collectionId against a registry or observes anomalous royalty payouts. The appropriate remediation is to add explicit existence validation before any read or write of collection‑specific state, for example by invoking _requireMinted(tokenId) or require(collectionExists(collectionId), 'Nonexistent collection') in each affected function. This aligns the contract with the standard pattern for ERC‑721 and ERC‑1155 tokens and restores the invariant that only existing collections can be queried or modified, preventing phantom royalty data, unauthorized parameter changes, and free minting of non‑existent assets.
summary:
1. View methods (getRoyalties(), tokenURI()) work with non-existent collections. In this example, incorrect royalty is returned for a non-existent collection:
```solidity
await nftContract.getRoyalties(0);
```
returns:
```json
recipients: [
    '0x3C44CdDdB6a900fa2b585dd299e03d12FA4293BC',
    '0x0000000000000000000000000000000000000000'
],
bps: [
    BigNumber { value: "250" },
    BigNumber { value: "0" }
]
```
2. Athletes and Platform Manager can change parameters for non-existent collections. For example, function updateCollectionAthleteAddress (FantiumNFTV1.sol#L308). 3. A user can try to mint non-existent collections for free via FantiumMinterV1.mint() if maxInvocations is set. (FantiumMinterV1.sol#L241)

title: H-2 Undeﬁned behavior for mint
content: The vulnerability resides in the mint function of the FantiumMinterV1 contract. The function accepts an address parameter that is intended to designate the future owner of the newly minted NFT, but the implementation ignores this parameter and instead assigns ownership to the caller (msg.sender). This mismatch between the documented interface and the actual behavior is caused by the internal call to the NFT contract’s mint routine, which defaults to using msg.sender as the recipient. An attacker or any user can exploit this by invoking mint with a third‑party address while the token is silently credited to their own wallet, effectively allowing them to mint tokens on behalf of others without the intended recipient ever receiving them. The impact is that users expecting a token to be transferred to a specified address (for example, an athlete) receive nothing, while the caller’s balance unexpectedly increases. The bug manifests every time the mint function is called with a non‑zero address argument, regardless of the amount of ether sent. All participants who rely on the contract to correctly allocate NFTs – including end users, the protocol’s accounting layer, and any downstream applications – are affected. The issue was uncovered during a manual code review by the MixBytes audit team, who noticed that the _to argument was never used in the minting call. Because the transaction does not revert and the UI reports a successful mint, the problem can be hard to detect; the only symptom is that the token appears under the caller’s address instead of the intended recipient. To remediate, the contract should forward the supplied address to the NFT contract’s mintTo function (e.g., fantiumNFTContract.mintTo(_to, tokenId)) and optionally add checks that the _to argument is not the zero address. This aligns the contract’s behavior with its specification, restores correct ownership semantics, and prevents unintended token allocation.

title: H-3 An intruder can block any users
content: The vulnerability resides in the mint function of the FantiumMinterV1 contract, which accepts an arbitrary destination address parameter (_to) without performing any validation or access‑control checks. Because the function proceeds to modify the permit state of the supplied address after the minting logic, an attacker who can invoke mint can supply the address of any legitimate user and cause the contract to alter that user’s permit, effectively revoking or changing their allow‑list status. This flaw originates from a missing validation step that should ensure only authorized recipients (for example, the platform manager or a pre‑approved list) can be passed to mint, and from conflating token minting with permission management in a single routine. Exploitation is straightforward: the attacker calls mint with the victim’s address as _to, the contract mints tokens (or performs a no‑op) and then updates the victim’s permit entry, causing the victim to be blocked from future protocol actions such as deposits, withdrawals, or further minting. The impact is that any user on the platform can be arbitrarily disabled, leading to loss of access to funds, inability to interact with the protocol, and potential financial loss if the blocked user cannot retrieve deposited assets. The condition for the attack is simply the ability to call the public mint function; no special role or permission is required because the function does not restrict callers. All users, especially those relying on the allow‑list for participation, are affected. The issue was uncovered during a manual security audit that examined the flow of data through mint and identified that the _to argument was never checked before being used to modify permission state. Because the mint function appears benign and the permission change is hidden behind a standard token‑minting call, the bug can be hard to notice without a deep code review. To remediate, the contract should separate minting from permission updates, enforce strict validation of the _to address (e.g., require it to be the caller, a platform manager, or an address on an approved list), and restrict any permit‑changing logic to callers with the onlyPlatformManager role. This aligns the implementation with the intended business logic that only authorized entities can alter user permissions, preventing arbitrary blocking of users.
summary: FantiumMinterV1.mint() allows passing _to, which is not validated. After this line (FantiumMinterV1.sol#L266), we can change the permit of some users. In a common way we need to have the onlyPlatformManager permission for this action.

title: H-1 Some distribution parameters cannot be updated after funds sending
content: The vulnerability consists of allowing critical distribution parameters—such as the tournament distribution amount, the other distribution amount and the list of collection identifiers—to be modified after the contract has already transferred funds for a given distribution event. The root cause is the absence of a guard that checks whether the distribution event has been settled (the amountPaidIn flag). Because the contract does not prevent updates once payouts have begun, an administrator or any entity with permission to call the update function can change the amounts or the collection set after some participants have already claimed their share. An attacker can exploit this by increasing the allocated amount for a subset of users before they claim, then decreasing the remaining amount or removing collections before other users attempt to claim. As a result, later claimants may receive zero or a reduced amount, effectively losing the funds they were entitled to. The impact is that users experience a mismatch between expected and actual payouts: a user who expects a refund or reward sees the claim transaction succeed but returns a zero balance, or the UI shows a claim button that yields no tokens. This situation occurs only when the distribution event has already been marked as paid in, but the contract still permits parameter updates. All participants of the affected distribution event are impacted, including token holders, liquidity providers and any downstream protocol that relies on correct accounting of rewards. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that identified the missing require statement in the update function. It can be hard to notice because the UI does not expose the internal flag, and the contract will not revert; instead it silently returns an empty allocation, leading users to think the contract is malfunctioning rather than being maliciously altered. The bug belongs to the class of post‑settlement state‑mutation vulnerabilities, where mutable configuration is changed after an irreversible financial operation, breaking accounting invariants. To remediate, the contract should enforce an immutable state after the first payout by checking that distributionEvents[_distributionEventId].amountPaidIn is false before allowing any changes to tournamentDistributionAmount, otherDistributionAmount or collectionIds. This lock ensures that once funds are sent, the distribution parameters cannot be altered, preserving the integrity of the claim process and preventing users from receiving nothing or an incorrect amount.
summary:
The updating of tournamentDistributionAmount, otherDistributionAmount and
collectionIds could lead to the situation when some users would be unable to claim their funds,
because the funds had already been claimed by other users.
FantiumClaimingV1.sol#L300-L302
FantiumClaimingV1.sol#L315

title: H-10 Funds sent by an athlete to a closed distribution are impossible to return
content: The vulnerability consists of an ability to deposit funds into a distribution that has already been marked as closed, after which the deposited amount becomes permanently unrecoverable. The root cause is the absence of a state check in the function that adds distribution amounts; the contract does not verify that the target distribution is still open before accepting the transfer. An attacker, or any athlete, can call the addDistributionAmount method with the identifier of a distribution that the manager has previously closed. The call succeeds, the contract records the incoming ether against the closed distribution, and the distribution’s closed flag prevents the closeDistribution function from being invoked again. Because there is no separate withdrawal or refund path for a closed distribution, the funds remain locked in the contract with no way for the athlete or the manager to retrieve them. This situation typically occurs when a manager creates a distribution, closes it, possibly recreates a new distribution with a different identifier, and an athlete mistakenly references the old closed identifier when sending funds. The affected parties are the athletes who expect their contribution to be allocated to an active distribution and the protocol itself, which loses accounting integrity and may expose users to loss of assets. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined state transitions and identified that the addDistributionAmount function does not enforce the expected invariant that only open distributions may receive funds. The bug can be hard to notice because the function appears to accept ether without reverting, giving the impression that the deposit succeeded, while the UI may later show a zero balance or missing refund, contradicting user expectations. From a user perspective, an athlete may see a transaction receipt confirming the transfer, but later when attempting to claim a reward or request a refund, the contract returns no balance, effectively making the funds disappear. The vulnerability belongs to the class of state‑validation errors where a function fails to enforce proper lifecycle constraints, leading to locked assets and broken business logic. To remediate the issue, the contract should include an explicit check that the distribution is not closed before accepting additional funds, typically by requiring !distribution.closed in the addDistributionAmount implementation, thereby preserving the invariant that only active distributions can receive deposits.
summary:
It's possible for an athlete to send funds to a closed distribution with
FantiumClaimingV1.addDistributionAmount() if they were not sent before
(FantiumClaimingV1.sol#L253). After that it will be impossible to return them to the athlete (it's possible to
call FantiumClaimingV1.closeDistribution() only for non-closed distributions). For example, it
can happen if the incorrect distribution was created by the manager, the manager closed the distribution
and recreated it. And by mistake the athlete called FantiumClaimingV1.addDistributionAmount()
with an id of the closed one.

title: H-11 Updating a token version can cause a jump of tokens between collections
content: The contract implements a collection of non‑fungible tokens where each collection can hold up to one million token identifiers and each token version is limited to ten thousand identifiers. The upgrade mechanism increments a token's version and stores the new version in the same collection until the per‑version capacity is exhausted. Because the per‑version limit (10,000) multiplied by the maximum number of versions (100) equals the total collection capacity (1,000,000), a token can be upgraded only a hundred times before the next version would exceed the collection's storage bounds. When the hundredth upgrade is attempted, the internal accounting moves the token identifier to the next collection rather than keeping it in the original one. This jump is not reflected in the user interface, so the token appears to remain owned by the user, but the underlying contract state points to a different collection where the token is either inaccessible or considered burned. The root cause is an implicit assumption that the collection can accommodate an unlimited number of version upgrades, while the code enforces a hard cap on the number of identifiers per version without checking for overflow across collections. Exploitation consists of repeatedly invoking the version‑upgrade function until the limit is reached; the attacker can then trigger the overflow and cause the token to disappear from the expected collection, potentially leading to loss of ownership, inability to transfer, or failure of downstream logic that assumes the token resides in its original collection. The impact is high because token holders may lose access to their NFTs, marketplaces may reject transfers, and the protocol’s accounting guarantees are broken. The condition occurs only after a token has been upgraded exactly one hundred times, a scenario that may be rare in normal use but can be forced by a malicious actor or by a user repeatedly upgrading a token for cosmetic or functional reasons. The vulnerability was discovered during a systematic audit of the token‑versioning logic, where the auditors identified the fixed size of the version‑specific identifier range and the lack of a boundary check before assigning a new version. The issue is subtle because the contract does not emit an explicit error when the overflow happens; instead it silently reassigns the token to a different collection, making the problem hard to detect without deep state inspection. To remediate, the upgrade function should be redesigned to either remove the per‑version identifier cap, allow unlimited upgrades by dynamically expanding storage, or explicitly prevent upgrades that would cause a collection jump by checking the remaining capacity before incrementing the version. In addition, a guard should be added to ensure that tokenVersionUpgrade never results in a token being stored outside its intended collection, and appropriate events should be emitted when an upgrade fails due to capacity limits. This class of bug falls under the broader category of storage‑capacity overflow and improper state migration, where assumptions about fixed‑size containers lead to unexpected token relocation and loss of assets.
summary:
One collection can store only 1000000 token ids and one version can store maximum 10_000 of token ids
that means a token version can be updated only 100 times. Moreover, updating the token version the 100th
time will cause a jump of this token to the next collections.

title: H-12 Inconsistent shares upgrade
content: The vulnerability concerns an inconsistent handling of share values after a share‑upgrade operation in the Fantium NFT contract. When the contract owner updates the distribution shares for a specific collection, the function correctly writes the new values to the global variables tournamentDistributionAmount and otherDistributionAmount, but it fails to propagate those new values to every previously recorded distribution event belonging to that collection. As a result, the claim calculation for older distributions continues to use stale share percentages while newer distributions use the updated ones. This mismatch creates a logical inconsistency in the accounting of claimable amounts. An attacker or a malicious participant can exploit the inconsistency by submitting a claim for a distribution that was recorded before the share change, causing the contract to compute an incorrect payout – either under‑paying legitimate claimants or, depending on the direction of the share change, over‑paying a claimant who can craft a claim that references the outdated share data. The impact is a breach of the protocol’s financial guarantees: users may receive less than they are entitled to, or the protocol may lose funds to over‑payment, breaking trust in the revenue‑sharing model. The bug manifests only after a share‑upgrade transaction has been executed and there exist pending claims for distributions created before that upgrade. All participants who rely on the claim function – token holders, tournament participants, and any role that receives a share of the revenue – are potentially affected. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the flow of share updates and claim calculations, noting that the share values used in the claim function were read from global state rather than from the immutable snapshot stored at distribution time. Because the UI typically shows only the total amount available for claim, the discrepancy can be subtle and may only be observed when a user’s received amount deviates from the expected proportion, for example when a user expects a refund or reward but receives a lower amount or zero. The bug belongs to the class of “state‑inconsistent accounting” or “share‑snapshot mismatch” vulnerabilities, where mutable configuration data is incorrectly referenced in historical financial calculations. To remediate the issue, the contract should capture the share percentages at the moment each distribution event is emitted and store them alongside the event data, then reference those immutable snapshots during claim calculations. Alternatively, the contract could enforce a re‑evaluation of all pending claims whenever the share configuration changes, ensuring that every claim uses the same version of the share parameters. This approach restores deterministic accounting, aligns user expectations with actual payouts, and prevents inadvertent fund loss or over‑payment.
summary:
After shares update in the NFT contract FantiumNFTV3.sol#L638-L640
tournamentDistributionAmount and otherDistributionAmount should be updated for all
distributions for the speciﬁc collection, otherwise, there will be inconsistency in the calculations of the
amount for the claim.

title: H-13 An incorrect check
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect state validation in the function that updates the total earnings amounts for a distribution event.
