Instead of verifying the actual distribution amounts that will be paid out – namely the tournamentDistributionAmount and otherDistributionAmount – the code checks two unrelated internal accounting variables (_totalTournamentEarnings and _totalOtherEarnings). This check is performed after the contract takes a snapshot of the claiming state via triggerClaimingSnapshot, but the snapshot does not modify the distribution amounts, so the wrong variables are still being examined. The root cause is a copy‑and‑paste or logic error where the developer reused a check that was appropriate for a different context, failing to update it for the new flow. An attacker who controls the manager role can deliberately lower the tournamentDistributionAmount or otherDistributionAmount before the snapshot is taken. Because the contract does not validate these amounts after the snapshot, the reduced values pass the faulty check, allowing the manager to effectively block the distribution. When the distribution is blocked, athletes (the end users who are supposed to receive tokens) are unable to add their earned tokens to the distribution and the distribution may be closed prematurely. From the user’s point of view the UI will show that a claim period is open, but attempts to add tokens result in no change to their balance, and the distribution may appear to have ended with zero payout. The impact is a denial‑of‑service for legitimate participants and potential loss of expected earnings, which is especially severe in a high‑value sports or tournament reward system. The issue manifests whenever the manager updates earnings totals and then calls updateDistribtionTotalEarningsAmounts without the proper post‑snapshot validation. It was discovered during a manual security audit by MixBytes, who noted the mismatch between the variables being checked and the variables that actually determine payout amounts. The bug is subtle because the function still compiles and runs, and the incorrect check does not revert; it merely allows an inconsistent state that only becomes apparent when users try to claim or add tokens. To remediate, the contract should replace the check on _totalTournamentEarnings and _totalOtherEarnings with a check on tournamentDistributionAmount and otherDistributionAmount after the snapshot is taken. The same corrected validation should be added to any other function that updates distribution event collection identifiers, ensuring that the actual payout amounts are always verified before the distribution is considered active. This aligns the contract’s business logic – that distribution amounts must be non‑zero and consistent – with its implementation, preventing managers from unintentionally or maliciously blocking payouts.
summary:
There is an incorrect check in the updateDistribtionTotalEarningsAmounts() function
FantiumClaimingV1.sol#L326-L327. Instead of a check for _totalTournamentEarnings and
_totalOtherEarnings there should be a check for tournamentDistributionAmount and
otherDistributionAmount after calling the triggerClaimingSnapshot function. Otherwise, the
manager could reduce tournamentDistributionAmount and otherDistributionAmount by
mistake and block the distribution (the athlete will not be able to add tokens and will also close the
distribution).

title: H-14 It's possible to top up a closed distribution
content: The vulnerability is a missing state validation in the FantiumClaimingV1 contract that allows a privileged manager to invoke updateDistributionTotalEarningsAmounts or updateDistributionEventCollectionIds on a distribution that has already been marked as closed. Because the contract does not check the closed flag before performing these updates, the functions will accept additional earnings amounts and will transfer the athlete's funds into the internal accounting of a distribution that can no longer be closed. The root cause is the absence of a require(!distributionEvents[_id].closed) guard, which means the contract assumes the distribution is still open when it may already be finalized. An attacker with manager privileges can exploit this by calling either function after the distribution has been closed, causing the contract to top up the closed distribution with athlete funds. Since the distribution cannot be closed again, the added funds become permanently locked; there is no mechanism to reopen the distribution or withdraw the stuck amount. The impact is that athletes who expect to claim earnings may see their claimable balance remain zero, effectively losing access to the funds that were unintentionally deposited. This situation occurs only when the manager mistakenly or maliciously triggers the update functions after the distribution lifecycle has ended, and it affects any participant who relies on the distribution for payouts, including athletes and downstream protocol users. The issue was discovered during a MixBytes security audit, where the auditors identified that the closed state was not validated before state‑changing calls. It can be hard to notice because the functions appear to be harmless bookkeeping operations and the UI typically shows the distribution as closed, so users may not see any immediate error; the symptom is a missing or unchanged balance despite a successful transaction. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of improper state validation or missing invariant checks that lead to locked assets. The recommended remediation is to add an explicit check that the distribution is not closed before allowing any update to total earnings amounts or event collection identifiers, thereby preventing further modifications to a finalized distribution and ensuring that funds cannot be inadvertently trapped.
summary:
If the manager calls by mistake updateDistribtionTotalEarningsAmounts() or
updateDistributionEventCollectionIds() for a closed distribution, it will be topped up using the
athlete's funds. These funds will be stuck because it's impossible to close the already closed distribution
again.
FantiumClaimingV1.sol#L318
FantiumClaimingV1.sol#L342

title: H-15 Distribution parameters shouldn't be updated after the ﬁrst claim
content: The vulnerability consists of the ability to modify the parameters of a token distribution event after the first claim has been processed. The contract design permits the athlete or manager to change collection identifiers or the total amount of earnings allocated to the distribution while the claiming contract has already transferred tokens to early claimers. Because the contract does not take a snapshot of the distribution state before any claim, the mutable parameters are read on each claim. An attacker can therefore update the collection IDs or reduce distributionTotalEarningAmounts during the claim window. The first users to call the claim function will receive rewards based on the original parameters and will consume a portion of the token pool. Subsequent users, whose claims are evaluated against the altered parameters, may receive a reduced amount or nothing at all, leading to an unequal and potentially unfair distribution of funds. This situation can occur whenever the distribution event is active, tokens have been sent from the claiming contract, and the owner retains permission to modify the distribution configuration. All participants who rely on the advertised reward amounts—athletes, managers, and regular users—are affected because some may lose expected payouts while others receive more than intended. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the lifecycle of the distribution contract and identified that the function takeClaimingSnapshot is not enforced before the first claim, allowing state changes afterwards. The problem is subtle because the UI may still display the total reward amount correctly, yet individual users experience missing or reduced balances, making the bug hard to notice without detailed testing. To remediate the flaw, the contract should lock the distribution parameters permanently after the first successful claim or require an explicit snapshot that freezes the state before any claim can be processed. By treating the mutable configuration as immutable once the distribution starts, the protocol restores the intended accounting guarantees that the total allocated earnings are distributed fairly among all eligible claimants.
summary:
If the athlete/manager decides to update the parameters of the distribution event after the tokens have
been sent from the claiming contract, it may lead to an unequal distribution of tokens among users. This
outcome is inherent in the design. For example, updating the collection IDs while the claiming process is in
progress implies that an individual from the previous collection could claim the rewards for themselves
and expend some funds from the distribution. Consequently, someone from the new collection may be
unable to claim rewards. Updating the distributionTotalEarningAmounts signiﬁes that a person
who has already claimed rewards might receive lower rewards than those who claimed them later.

title: H-2 Some tokens could be left on the contract
content: The vulnerability is a logical flaw that allows the privileged manager role to change the ERC20 token address used by the claim contract before the distribution of all allocated tokens is finished. Because the contract does not verify that the current distribution round is closed or that the contract balance for the original token is zero, changing the token address while a residual balance remains locks those tokens inside the contract. The contract will subsequently attempt to transfer the newly set token, which may have no balance, causing the original tokens to become unrecoverable. At the same time, fans who invoke the claim function after the address change may receive tokens from a different distribution, leading to unexpected token types or amounts. From a user’s point of view, a fan may see that their claim returns zero tokens, or they may receive a token they did not expect, violating the expectation that each fan receives the correct allocation. The impact includes potential loss of funds for token holders, misallocation of assets, and a breach of the protocol’s accounting assumptions that each distribution round is atomic and final. The issue occurs whenever the manager calls the address‑update function before the distribution is fully settled, which can happen in normal operational workflows if the manager mistakenly or maliciously updates the address early. It was discovered during a security audit by MixBytes, where the auditors identified that the update function lacks a guard checking the distribution state. The bug is hard to notice because the function appears to be a simple administrative change and does not emit obvious errors; the token loss only becomes apparent when users attempt to claim and receive nothing or the wrong token. To remediate, the contract should enforce that the token address can only be changed after all tokens have been distributed or the distribution round has been explicitly closed, or the ability to change the token address should be removed entirely, ensuring that leftover tokens cannot be stranded and that claimants always receive the intended token.
summary:
The manager can update the token address before all tokens were distributed among fans. This can block
some tokens on the contract and fans can receive tokens from other distributions.
FantiumClaimingV1.sol#L614

title: H-3 TransferFrom from address(this) will not work for most of the tokens
content: The vulnerability originates from an incorrect use of the ERC20 allowance mechanism. The contract calls transferFrom(address(this), recipient, amount) to move tokens that are already owned by the contract itself. In the ERC20 standard, transferFrom requires that the caller has been granted an allowance by the token holder (the from address). Because the contract does not call approve to give itself an allowance over its own balance, most token implementations will reject the call, causing the transaction to revert or silently fail. This mistake means that whenever the contract attempts to distribute or refund tokens – for example during a claim or withdrawal operation – the expected token transfer does not occur. From the user’s perspective the UI may show that a claim was submitted, but the user receives no tokens, their balance appears unchanged or zero, and no error message is displayed on the front‑end. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit when the auditors observed a transferFrom invocation with address(this) as the source without a preceding approve. It can be hard to notice because some tokens do not enforce the allowance check strictly, allowing the call to succeed in limited cases, which gives a false sense of correctness. The root cause is a misunderstanding of the ERC20 transfer semantics: transfer should be used when moving tokens owned by the caller, while transferFrom is intended for third‑party transfers that require an explicit allowance. The impact is a functional denial‑of‑service for token distribution, potentially leading to lost refunds, stuck funds, and a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees. The bug belongs to the class of allowance‑related misuse bugs, where developers invoke transferFrom on an address that has not granted the necessary allowance. To remediate the issue the contract should replace the transferFrom call with a direct safeTransfer (or SafeERC20.safeTransfer) call, or alternatively set an allowance for itself via approve before invoking transferFrom. Either approach restores the intended token movement and aligns the implementation with ERC20 specifications, ensuring that users receive the tokens they are owed and that the protocol’s financial logic remains sound.
summary:
Here transferFrom(address(this),...) is used which will not work with most of the tokens without
calling approve.
FantiumClaimingV1.sol#L647-L651

title: H-4 Not enough checks for collections shares
content: The contract implements a reward claiming mechanism that distributes tournament and other token rewards based on per‑user share values expressed in basis points multiplied by 1e7. The intended business rule is that the sum of all individual shares for a given token type must never exceed the total basis‑point allocation configured for the tournament (tournamentBPS) or for other tokens (otherBPS). The code, however, does not enforce this invariant. As a result, if the aggregate of tournamentTokenShare1e7_i values is greater than 1e7 * tournamentBPS / 10000, the internal accounting assumes more reward entitlement than the contract actually holds. When a user calls the claim function, the contract attempts to allocate rewards based on the pre‑computed share, but because the total share pool is oversized, the division of the available token balance yields zero or insufficient amounts for some participants. Consequently, affected users see their claim transaction succeed but receive no tokens, or they receive a smaller amount than expected, effectively losing their reward. The flaw originates from missing validation checks on the sum of share variables before rewards are recorded, a classic example of an unchecked arithmetic constraint leading to an accounting inconsistency. Exploitation does not require malicious input; it can be triggered simply by having many participants or by configuring share values that collectively exceed the allowed limit. The impact is a denial‑of‑service for reward claims and potential loss of funds for honest users, as the contract may retain tokens that cannot be claimed. The issue manifests whenever the share configuration is updated or when new participants are added without a guard that enforces the total share ceiling. It affects all users of the protocol who are entitled to claim tournament or other token rewards, as well as the protocol itself because undistributed tokens remain locked, breaking the expected economic model. The vulnerability was discovered during a manual security audit that reviewed the reward distribution logic and identified the absence of sum‑checks. It can be hard to notice because the contract does not revert or emit an error; the claim transaction appears successful, yet the user’s balance does not change, which may be interpreted as a UI glitch rather than a contract bug. To remediate, the contract should include explicit assertions that the sum of tournamentTokenShare1e7_i does not exceed 1e7 * tournamentBPS / 10000 and that the sum of otherTokenShare1e7_i does not exceed 1e7 * otherBPS / 10000 before any reward allocation occurs. Adding these checks restores the invariant that total allocated shares never surpass the available token pool, ensuring that every eligible user can claim the correct amount of rewards and that the protocol’s accounting remains sound.
summary:
There are not enough checks on the collections shares (tournament and others) which could lead to an
unfair distribution of rewards for users. If sum(tournamentTokenShare1e7_i) > 1e7 *
tournamentBPS / 10_000 , then not all users will be able to claim rewards.
FantiumClaimingV1.sol#L225-L232

title: H-5 athleteSecondarySalesBPS and fantiumSecondarySalesBPS should be restricted
content: The contract stores two basis‑point parameters, athleteSecondarySalesBPS and fantiumSecondarySalesBPS, which are later combined to compute the royalty percentage applied to secondary sales of NFTs. The royalty formula assumes a base point of 1/10 000, meaning that the sum of the two parameters must never exceed 10 000 (100 %). The code does not enforce this upper bound, so an administrator or a malicious actor could set the values such that their sum is greater than 10 000. When the royalty calculation uses a value above 100 %, the resulting payment amount exceeds the total sale price, causing the transaction to revert due to insufficient funds. This situation can be triggered during any secondary sale that relies on the royalty calculation, leading to a failed purchase, loss of gas, and a broken user experience. The impact is that legitimate buyers receive a revert error instead of the expected NFT, and the protocol’s revenue‑sharing mechanism becomes unusable. The vulnerability was discovered during a manual audit of the FantiumNFTV3 contract, where the lack of a validation check on the combined basis‑point values was noted. Because the parameters are stored as simple unsigned integers without constraints, the issue may remain hidden until an extreme configuration is applied, making it difficult to detect through normal testing. The bug belongs to the class of unchecked arithmetic or parameter validation errors that violate business logic assumptions about percentage limits. To remediate the issue, the contract should include an explicit require statement that enforces athleteSecondarySalesBPS + fantiumSecondarySalesBPS <= 10 000 before the values are used in royalty calculations, thereby guaranteeing that the royalty never exceeds 100 % and preventing transaction reverts.
summary:
athleteSecondarySalesBPS and fantiumSecondarySalesBPS should be restricted because they
will be used in other contracts to calculate royalties with base point = 1 / 10_000, so if
athleteSecondarySalesBPS + fantiumSecondarySalesBPS > 10_000, the royalty will be >
100%. Due to this all transactions with royalty payments will revert.
FantiumNFTV3.sol#L526-L527
FantiumNFTV3.sol#L544-L545
FantiumNFTV3.sol#L658-L659
FantiumNFTV3.sol#L752-L753

title: H-6 maxInvocations should be limited
content: The vulnerability originates from an unchecked parameter that defines the upper bound for token numbers within a non‑fungible token contract. Each token identifier is built by concatenating a collection identifier, a version identifier, and a token number. The business logic assumes that the token number component will never exceed 9,999 so that the version identifier can be correctly extracted from the combined value. Because the contract does not enforce a limit on the maxInvocations variable, an attacker or careless deployer can set this limit to 10,000 or higher. When tokens are minted with a tokenNumber equal to or greater than 10,000, the encoding of the tokenId overflows the bits reserved for the versionId, causing the versionId extraction routine to produce incorrect results. This breaks the intended accounting model: token metadata may be fetched from the wrong version, token identifiers can collide, and downstream contracts that rely on the versionId may behave unpredictably. From a user’s perspective the symptoms can include seeing unexpected token IDs, receiving wrong metadata, or observing that a token they expected to belong to a certain version appears under a different version, effectively making the token appear invalid or “missing”. The issue is discovered during a manual audit that examined the tokenId construction and noticed the absence of a guard on maxInvocations. It is subtle because normal operation with token numbers below the threshold behaves correctly, so the bug only manifests when large token numbers are minted, which may not be exercised in typical test suites. The impact ranges from loss of token uniqueness, potential financial loss if tokens are sold based on incorrect versioning, to protocol‑level accounting errors that could be exploited to create counterfeit tokens. The recommended remediation is to add an explicit validation that maxInvocations is strictly less than 10,000 at the point where the value is set, ensuring that the tokenNumber component always fits within the expected range and preserving the integrity of the versionId logic.
summary:
TokenId contains collactionId, versionId and tokenNumber. maxInvocations is a parameter that
determines the max tokenNumber. Due to using versionId, tokenNumber should be < 10_000, otherwise the
versionId logic would be broken.
FantiumNFTV3.sol#L528
FantiumNFTV3.sol#L691

title: H-7 trustedForwarder can be used to impersonate any account or contract
content: The contract overrides the standard _msgSender() function so that a designated trustedForwarder address can supply an arbitrary address as the apparent caller. Because the forwarder is a single address controlled by its owner, the owner can make the contract believe that any user or contract is the transaction sender. Critical functions such as upgradeTokenVersion and the mint routine rely on _msgSender() for permission checks and allowance verification. When the forwarder is compromised, an attacker can impersonate any participant, trigger token upgrades without consent, mint NFTs using another user’s allowance, and potentially cause loss of funds. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the inheritance hierarchy and the meta‑transaction pattern, where the overridden _msgSender() appeared to follow a familiar OpenZeppelin Context design, making the deviation easy to overlook. This class of bug is an untrusted forwarder impersonation or meta‑transaction sender spoofing vulnerability. From a user’s perspective the symptoms may include unexpected NFT upgrades, newly minted tokens appearing in their wallet without any action, or a reduction in their allowance or balance after a seemingly legitimate transaction. The protocol’s accounting assumptions that the caller identity matches the genuine participant are violated, breaking trust and enabling fund drainage. The recommended remediation is to protect the trustedForwarder with a multisignature wallet, add explicit signature verification for forwarded calls, or eliminate reliance on _msgSender() in privileged functions, thereby restoring proper access control and preserving the integrity of the accounting model.
summary:
There is an overriden _msgSender() function FantiumNFTV3.sol#L993 which allows the
trustedForwarder address owner to specify any address being used as sender. This function is used
at some of the key parts of the protocol. For example, in the upgradeTokenVersion function -
FantiumNFTV3.sol#L790. Someone's address and allowance can also be used during mint -
FantiumNFTV3.sol#L350. In case trustedForwarder is compromised, it can lead to the funds loss.

title: H-8 An incorrect expression inside require leads to a revert
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect conditional expression inside a require statement that causes an unconditional revert when the protocol manager attempts to close a distribution event and transfer the remaining balance to the athlete. The root cause is the use of an assignment operator (=) instead of a logical equality operator (==) when checking the closed flag of the distribution. This mistake overwrites the flag with a false value and then passes that false value to require, which always fails and aborts the transaction. A second require in the same function suffers from a similar operator misuse, reinforcing the failure path. Exploitation is straightforward: any call to the closeDistribution function, even by an authorized manager, will hit the malformed require and revert, preventing the state change that marks the distribution as closed and blocking the transfer of leftover funds. The impact is that the athlete never receives the expected payout, the distribution remains in an open state, and the protocol’s accounting becomes inconsistent because the contract believes the event is still active while the UI may indicate otherwise. This occurs whenever the manager invokes the closure routine, regardless of input values, because the condition is hard‑coded to evaluate to false. All participants who rely on the distribution closure – the athlete, the manager, and downstream users – are affected, as funds become effectively locked and the protocol’s business logic (closing an event and disbursing remaining assets) is violated. The issue was discovered during a manual code audit that flagged the require line as using an assignment where a comparison was intended; such a mistake can be hard to notice because the code compiles without error and the variable name suggests a boolean check, yet the logic never succeeds. The proper fix is to replace the assignment operator with a logical equality operator (==) in both require statements, ensuring the condition evaluates the actual state of the closed flag instead of overwriting it. Conceptually, this belongs to the class of “incorrect conditional checks” or “logic operator misuse” bugs that lead to unintended reverts and broken control flow, breaking the contract’s guarantee that a distribution can be safely closed and remaining funds transferred.
summary:
There is a closeDistribution function - FantiumClaimingV1.sol#L624. It is used by the protocol
manager to close a distribution event and transfer the remaining funds to the athlete. But the ﬁrst require
here FantiumClaimingV1.sol#L632 uses an assignment operator instead of a logic operator. It always
assigns a false closed parameter on a distribution event and uses false as a require argument that
leads to an unconditional revert. There is also a second require check FantiumClaimingV1.sol#L636
which uses an incorrect operator too.

title: H-9 Not checking the ERC20 transfer result on depositing funds by an athlete
content: The vulnerability is a missing verification of the ERC20 transferFrom result when an athlete deposits tokens into the protocol via the addDistributionAmount function. The contract calls transferFrom on the payout token but does not check the boolean return value or enforce a revert on failure. This design assumes that a compliant ERC20 will either succeed or revert, however many tokens follow the older ERC20 pattern of returning false on failure without reverting. Consequently, if a token (or a malicious wrapper) returns false, the contract proceeds as if the transfer succeeded, marking the event as amountPaidIn and updating internal accounting. An attacker controlling the athlete role can exploit this by approving the contract and then invoking addDistributionAmount with a token that silently fails, causing the protocol to record a deposit that never arrived. The protocol will later distribute funds based on the false assumption that it holds the deposited amount, leading to over‑payment to other participants and a net loss of assets. The issue manifests whenever the payoutToken does not revert on a failed transfer – for example, when the token has insufficient balance, insufficient allowance, or is deliberately crafted to return false. All parties that rely on the protocol’s accounting – the athletes, downstream beneficiaries, and the protocol itself – are affected because the internal ledger no longer matches the actual token balances. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit by MixBytes, which noted the absence of a require statement or SafeERC20 usage. It can be hard to notice because the transaction does not revert, no error event is emitted, and the UI may display a successful deposit while the token balance remains unchanged. From a user perspective the athlete sees a confirmation that the deposit succeeded but the contract’s token balance stays the same, and later users may receive zero or reduced payouts because the protocol has over‑committed funds. The bug belongs to the class of unchecked external calls or missing return‑value validation for ERC20 operations. The recommended remediation is to replace the raw transferFrom call with OpenZeppelin’s SafeERC20.safeTransferFrom, or at minimum to check the boolean result and revert if it is false, ensuring that any failed token transfer aborts the deposit logic and keeps the accounting consistent.
summary:
There is an addDistributionAmount function which transfers funds from an athlete to the protocol. It
uses the transferFrom function here - FantiumClaimingV1.sol#L277. If payoutToken which returns
false/true instead of reverting on an unsuccessful transfer would be used there, then an athlete would be
able to mark the event as amountPaidIn without depositing any tokens.

title: secondsPerLiquidityCumulativesDelta calculation can overflow
content: The vulnerability originates from the subtraction of two uint160 cumulative values that represent seconds per liquidity inside a Uniswap V3 tick range. In the original Uniswap V3 library, which was written for Solidity 0.6, arithmetic overflow and underflow silently wrap, so the expression secondsPerLiquidityCumulativeX128s[1] - secondsPerLiquidityCumulativeX128s[0] could produce a wrapped result without reverting. The audited contract, however, is compiled with Solidity 0.8 where unchecked arithmetic is no longer the default; any underflow or overflow triggers an automatic revert. When the later cumulative value is smaller than the earlier one – a situation that can occur when the internal 128‑bit fixed‑point counter wraps or when the pool reports a decreasing value due to fee growth calculations – the subtraction underflows, causing the consult() function to revert. This revert propagates to any logic that depends on the harmonicMeanLiquidity calculation, including fee distribution in the _fees() routine where a similar unchecked subtraction is performed on poolFeeGrowthInside. From a user’s perspective the contract appears to stop paying out rewards: liquidity providers see their expected refunds or fee accruals become zero, the UI may show missing balances, and the protocol’s accounting no longer matches the business expectation that fees are continuously collected. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract’s implementation to the reference Uniswap V3 library and noted the change in Solidity version semantics. It is hard to notice because the overflow only manifests after the cumulative counter wraps, which may take a long time or require specific pool activity, so normal testing may not trigger it. The impact is high because it can halt fee collection, effectively freezing revenue for liquidity providers and potentially undermining confidence in the protocol. The proper mitigation is to perform the subtraction in an unchecked block or to explicitly handle the wrap‑around case, thereby restoring the original wrap‑around semantics, or alternatively to compile the contract with a Solidity version that does not enforce overflow checks. Conceptually, the fix restores the intended arithmetic behavior of the cumulative counters, ensuring that fee calculations remain correct and that users receive the rewards they expect.

title: Calculations in solverMetaTryCatch() non consistent
content: The vulnerability resides in the function that settles a solver operation, where the contract computes a start balance, an end balance and an extra‑ETH amount using the same variable names for different purposes. The logic assumes that the contract begins with a zero ETH balance and that the solver has an allowance to pull ERC20 tokens, but these assumptions are not enforced. When the flag that inverts the bid value is true, the code deliberately sets the ETH start balance to zero and then subtracts the end balance from it, which causes an under‑flow or a revert because a negative value is attempted on an unsigned integer. In the opposite case, the end balance is reused to calculate an extra‑ETH contribution, but the calculation does not subtract the initial balance, so the extra amount is either always zero or includes the solver’s own value, leading to an incorrect accounting of funds. For ERC20 tokens the same pattern appears: the pre‑operation hook is expected to provide tokens, yet no allowance is granted, so the solver cannot retrieve the required amount and the balance checks become inconsistent. These inconsistencies mean that a user who expects a refund or a correct payout may receive nothing, see their balance drop to zero, or experience a transaction revert. The issue manifests only when the solverMetaTryCatch routine is invoked with specific flag combinations (invertsBidValue true/false together with bidFind true/false) and when the contract already holds ETH or ERC20 tokens before the call. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that compared the intended accounting model with the actual Solidity statements and noticed that the same variable was being repurposed without proper re‑initialisation. It is hard to spot because the code paths look similar and the reuse of variables masks the fact that the start balance is never populated for certain branches. To remediate the problem the contract should separate the variables used for the initial and final balances, compute the extra‑ETH amount as (endBalance‑startBalance)‑bidAmount, initialise the start balance with the actual contract balance, enforce that the solver has an ERC20 allowance before attempting a pull, and remove the assumption that the contract starts with zero ETH. By aligning the calculations across the bidFind true and false branches and documenting the pre‑operation expectations, the accounting logic becomes consistent and the risk of lost or mis‑allocated funds is eliminated.

title: bypassSignatoryApproval skips important checks
content: The vulnerability originates from a boolean flag named bypassSignatoryApproval that is used to return early from the internal _verifyDApp function after only the signature check has been performed. Because the early return is placed before several critical validation steps, the function skips the control‑address verification (ensuring that dAppOp.control matches the expected destination) and the nonce handling logic that prevents replay or out‑of‑order execution. The root cause is a logical ordering mistake: the developer assumed that when bypassSignatoryApproval is true the remaining checks are optional, but in reality those checks enforce fundamental business rules such as authorized control flow and unique transaction ordering. An attacker who can trigger the bypass flag – for example by calling the function in simulation mode or by supplying a specially crafted dAppOperation – can submit a transaction that passes the signature test yet bypasses the control address check, allowing arbitrary contracts to be targeted, and can also reuse a previously consumed nonce, effectively replaying a transaction or executing operations in an unexpected sequence. This can lead to unauthorized state changes, loss of funds, or protocol corruption because the system no longer guarantees that only the designated control address can be used and that each nonce is consumed exactly once. The issue manifests when the bypassSignatoryApproval flag is set to true; under those conditions the function returns (true, ValidCallsResult.Valid) immediately after the signature verification, ignoring the later safeguards. Users of the protocol experience transactions that appear to succeed even though the sender is not authorized to act as the auctioneer or bundler, or they see duplicate actions being accepted, which contradicts the expectation that the contract will reject such calls. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that highlighted the misplaced early return and the fact that essential checks were conditionally omitted. It is difficult to notice because the signature validation still succeeds, giving a false impression that the operation is fully vetted. To remediate the issue, the control‑address equality check and the call to the nonce handling routine should be moved before any early return based on bypassSignatoryApproval, ensuring they are always executed regardless of the flag. In broader terms, this is an improper authorization bypass where security‑critical logic is conditionally skipped, a class of bugs that can undermine trust and accounting guarantees in smart‑contract systems.

title: Incorrect indexing for bid sorting algorithm
content: The vulnerability is an off‑by‑one indexing error in the on‑chain sorting routine that orders solver operations by their simulated bid amount when exPostBids is enabled. The algorithm builds two parallel arrays, one for the indices of the operations (sortedOps) and one for the corresponding bid amounts (bidAmounts). A counter j tracks how many operations have a zero bid and are skipped. For each operation the inner loop starts with k = i - j + 1 and writes to sortedOps[k] and sortedOps[k-1]. If no operation is skipped (j stays zero) the expression i - j + 1 evaluates to i + 1, which for the first iteration (i = 0) yields k = 1. Because sortedOps was allocated with length equal to the number of operations, the highest valid index is length‑1. When i equals the last index, k becomes length, which is out of bounds and triggers a revert. In addition, the algorithm may never write to index 0, leaving it unset and causing the first operation to be considered twice later in the execution phase. The root cause is the incorrect calculation of the insertion point in the insertion‑sort style loop, mixing the number of skipped entries with the current loop index. An attacker or a benign user can trigger the bug simply by submitting a batch of operations where all simulated bids are non‑zero. The contract will attempt to sort the bids, hit the out‑of‑bounds write, and revert the whole transaction. From the user’s perspective the transaction fails with no explicit error message; the expected outcome – a successful solver operation selected by the highest bid – never occurs, and the user may see that no funds are transferred or that the operation appears to have been ignored. The protocol’s auction mechanism therefore loses its ability to choose the most profitable solver, potentially leaving the system idle or forcing a fallback path that may be less efficient or more expensive. The issue was discovered during a manual security review of the Fastlane contract suite, where the auditor noticed that the inner loop uses i‑j+1 as the starting index and reasoned that when j is zero the index can exceed the array bounds. A proof‑of‑concept contract reproduces the revert by initializing two non‑zero bids and executing the same sorting logic. Because the failure occurs only when all bids are non‑zero, it can be hard to notice in routine testing that includes zero‑bid cases. The revert does not emit a custom error, so developers may misinterpret the failure as a generic out‑of‑gas or network issue. Moreover, the subtle duplication of the first operation can lead to inconsistent execution ordering that is not obvious from logs. The correct fix is to compute the insertion point without the extra “+1” and to shift existing entries only while the target position is greater than zero and the new bid is larger than the previous entry. A safe implementation uses a while loop that starts at k = i - j and moves elements one position to the right until the proper place is found, then writes the current index at k. Re‑architecting the sorting routine to use a standard insertion sort or a library function would also eliminate the off‑by‑one error and make the code easier to audit.

title: userOp validation is skipped in simulation mode for smart contract user accounts
content: The vulnerability is avalidation bypass that occurs when a user operation (userOp) is simulated for a smart contract based account. In the validation routine the code returns the logical OR of a simulation flag (isSimulation) and the result of the account's validateUserOp function. Because the expression is written as (isSimulation || validSmartWallet), a true simulation flag forces the whole check to succeed even if the account explicitly rejects the operation by returning a non‑zero value. The root cause is the misplaced trust in the simulation mode, which is intended only for estimating gas and not for enforcing permission checks. An attacker or a careless developer can craft a userOp that would be rejected by the account’s validation logic, but during simulation the system believes the operation is allowed. When the same userOp is later submitted on‑chain, the validation fails, the transaction reverts and the bundler that included the operation loses the gas spent on execution. The impact is a denial‑of‑service style loss of gas for bundlers and a misleading user experience where a simulation shows a successful operation while the real execution fails. This condition occurs only when the isSimulation flag is true, typically during off‑chain simulation calls made by bundlers or wallets. All participants that rely on the simulation result – bundlers, wallet developers, and end users – are affected because they may assume the operation is valid and proceed to include it in a block. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the validation flow of account contracts and noticed that the simulation shortcut short‑circuits the permission check. It can be hard to notice because simulations often succeed and developers may not test the on‑chain path with a rejecting account. The bug belongs to the class of “simulation‑mode validation bypass” or “false‑positive permission check” where business logic that should enforce user consent is unintentionally disabled. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a preview of a successful transaction, but once submitted the transaction reverts and no funds are transferred, leading to confusion and wasted gas fees. The correct remediation is to remove the isSimulation shortcut and require the validateUserOp call to succeed regardless of simulation mode, i.e., return only validSmartWallet without the OR condition. This ensures that both simulated and on‑chain executions enforce the same permission checks and prevents bundlers from incurring unnecessary gas costs.
summary:
It can happen that user has not allowed this userOp (ie, returning validateUserOp() returns false), but during simulation it's falsely believed that the user has allowed it since isSimulation is true:  

```solidity
bool validSmartWallet =
    IAccount(userOp.from).validateUserOp{ gas: 30_000 }(userOp, _getProofHash(userOp), 0) == 0;
return (isSimulation || validSmartWallet);
```

If this userOp goes onchain, it leads to a revert wasting gas for the bundler.

title: ExecutionEnvironment deployment can be incorrectly skipped
content: The vulnerability concerns the conditional deployment of the ExecutionEnvironment contract. The deployment logic checks the target address' codehash and proceeds only if the codehash equals zero, assuming that a zero value indicates an empty account. According to EIP‑161 an account is considered empty when it has no code, zero nonce and zero balance, and EIP‑1052 specifies that an account without code returns the keccak256 hash of empty data (c5d2460186f7233c927e7db2dcc703c0e500b653ca82273b7bfad8045d85a470) rather than zero. Consequently, if an attacker front‑runs the deployment transaction and sends any amount of ether to the target address before the check is performed, the address will still have no code but will now have a non‑zero balance, causing its codehash to be the non‑zero empty‑code hash. The deployment condition therefore fails and the ExecutionEnvironment contract is never created. This can be exploited by submitting a small ETH transfer to the address in the same block, ensuring the codehash check returns a non‑zero value and skipping the deployment. The impact is that the protocol’s expected execution environment is missing, leading to failed calls, broken business logic, and potentially locked funds or denied services for users who rely on that component. The issue manifests only when the deployment transaction is pending and the address is still empty; it does not appear if the address is pre‑funded or if the codehash check is bypassed. All participants that interact with the protocol – developers, auditors, end‑users and any contracts that expect the ExecutionEnvironment to exist – are affected because the protocol may silently stop working without an obvious error message. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that cross‑referenced the EIP‑161 and EIP‑1052 specifications and identified the mismatch between the intended empty‑account check and the actual semantics of codehash. It is hard to notice because the address indeed has no bytecode, so a superficial inspection may assume the check is sufficient, overlooking the fact that a non‑zero balance changes the codehash result. To remediate the issue, the deployment logic should verify that the target address contains no bytecode by using extcodesize (or checking executionEnvironment.code.length) instead of relying on codehash, or it should also ensure the balance is zero before proceeding. By using a proper emptiness test, the contract can guarantee that the ExecutionEnvironment is deployed exactly once and cannot be blocked by a simple ETH transfer, preserving the intended accounting and functional guarantees of the protocol.
summary:
ExecutionEnvironment is deployed iff the address executionEnvironment, at which it's going to be deployed, has no code. The is checked by ensuring executionEnvironment.codehash is 0. However, someone can frontrun this transaction by sending some ETH to this address. Now codehash returns a non-zero hash and executionEnvironment is never deployed.  
An address which doesn't have code but has any non-zero ether balance returns keccak256("") as its codehash.  
This is as per the following EIPs:  
• From https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-161:  
An account is considered empty when it has no code and zero nonce and zero balance.  
• From https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-1052:  
In case the account does not exist or is empty (as defined by EIP-161) 0 is pushed to the stack.  
In case the account does not have code the keccak256 hash of empty data (i.e. c5d2460186f7233c927e7db2dcc703c0e500b653ca82273b7bfad8045d85a470) is pushed to the stack.

title: Wrong ERC20 token transferred
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect ERC20 token transfer in the settlement logic of an auction contract. The code checks that the auction base‑currency balance is greater than zero and then calls safeTransfer on the token identified by swapIntent.tokenUserBuys, passing the amount auctionBaseCurrencyBalance. The intention, however, is to return the auction base currency to the user, which should be the token identified by swapIntent.auctionBaseCurrency. Because the wrong token identifier is used, the contract sends the base‑currency amount using the wrong ERC20 contract. This mismatch can cause the user to receive an unexpected token, receive a token amount that does not correspond to its market value, or receive nothing if the token address is zero or not approved. The bug originates from a copy‑paste or naming error where the variable representing the token the user intends to buy is reused instead of the variable representing the currency used for the auction. It can be exploited whenever the settlement function is executed – any participant who triggers the transfer will obtain the wrong asset, and the contract may retain the intended base‑currency tokens, effectively locking funds. The impact is high because it breaks the accounting guarantees of the auction: users expect to be refunded in the same currency they paid, but they may end up with a different token or with a zero balance, leading to loss of value and loss of trust in the protocol. The condition occurs only when auctionBaseCurrencyBalance > 0, i.e., when there is a non‑zero amount to be returned. All users of the auction, as well as the protocol that relies on correct settlement, are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that compared the intended token flow with the actual transfer statements. It can be hard to notice because the transfer succeeds on the blockchain – there is no revert – and the token address may be a valid ERC20 contract, so the transaction appears normal even though the economic outcome is wrong. The proper fix is to replace the token identifier in the safeTransfer call with swapIntent.auctionBaseCurrency, ensuring that the amount is sent using the correct ERC20 contract. In generic terms, this is a token‑misdirection bug where the contract transfers assets using an incorrect token reference, violating the business rule that refunds must be issued in the same asset that was originally deposited.

title: Borrow()s after validateBalances()
content: The vulnerability consists of the borrow() function being callable after the protocol has already performed its balance validation step, specifically during the AllocateValue and PostOps execution phases. The contract’s design assumes that all borrowing occurs before validateBalances() runs, after which the internal _settle() routine is responsible for reconciling any outstanding debt. Because borrow() remains accessible after validateBalances(), a malicious actor can trigger an additional borrow in those later phases. At that point the solver no longer controls the transaction flow, so the extra amount must be repaid during _settle() without the solver having received any compensating assets. This creates a griefing scenario where the solver is forced to cover the debt, potentially losing funds or causing a settlement failure. The impact is a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees: funds may disappear from a solver’s balance, refunds may be missing, and the expected invariant that borrowing only happens before balance checks is violated. The condition arises from inadequate phase‑based access control; the SafetyBits mechanism that normally restricts borrow() relies on a variable key that is not exposed at the Atlas level, preventing the contract from correctly detecting that it is in AllocateValue or PostOps. The issue was uncovered during a security audit that examined the execution‑phase state machine and identified that borrow() lacked proper phase restrictions. It is difficult to notice because the function still executes successfully, but its adverse effect only becomes visible later during settlement, making functional tests that stop after validateBalances() insufficient. Conceptually, the fix is to enforce a phase check that blocks borrow() calls after validateBalances(), either by moving the execution phase tracking to a level visible to borrow() or by redesigning the access‑control logic to use a shared variable. This class of bug falls under “post‑validation state manipulation” or “phase‑restricted function misuse,” where a financial‑state‑changing function is allowed after safety checks have been performed. From the user’s perspective, a solver may see their balance unexpectedly reduced or a transaction that appears successful but results in a zero or missing refund, contradicting the expectation that the protocol will honor their funds after a trade. The protocol’s business logic that assumes all borrowing is settled before balance validation is therefore broken, leading to potential fund loss and reduced trust in the system.
summary:
The function borrow() can still be called in the AllocateValue and PostOps phases. As this is after validateBalances() the solver has to pay for this in _settle(). However the solver is no longer in control and would be griefed this way.  
Another risk is highlighted in the issue "Circumvent AtlETH unbonding period".

title: validControl / onlyAtlasEnvironment are not effective in delegatecall situation
content: The vulnerability consists of an ineffective access‑control pattern in the ExecutionEnvironment/DappControl architecture. The contract uses two modifiers, validControl and onlyAtlasEnvironment, to restrict which contracts may invoke privileged hooks. Both modifiers rely on the value of msg.sender being the Atlas core contract and on a stored control address matching the expected DappControl instance. When the ExecutionEnvironment performs a delegatecall to an arbitrary user contract, the call is executed in the context of the ExecutionEnvironment’s storage but the original msg.sender (the Atlas contract) is preserved. Because the onlyAtlasEnvironment modifier only checks that msg.sender equals atlas, the check passes even though the call originated from a user‑supplied contract. Likewise, the validControl modifier compares a constant CONTROL variable with the result of an internal _control() function; when invoked via delegatecall the storage slot read by _control() can be manipulated by the caller, allowing the comparison to be bypassed. As a result, a malicious user contract can invoke any DappControl hook, re‑enter the ExecutionEnvironment, adjust configuration parameters, call solver contracts, and withdraw ERC20 or Ether funds that are otherwise protected. The exploit can be triggered whenever the ExecutionEnvironment delegates to external code – for example during pre‑operation hooks or any DappControl‑registered callback. The attacker supplies crafted calldata that appends additional arguments after the expected selector, causing the delegatecall to execute the hook with attacker‑controlled parameters while still satisfying the access checks. From a user’s perspective the symptoms may appear as unexpected zero balances, missing refunds, or withdrawals that occur without explicit permission. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that examined the logic of the modifiers and observed that delegatecall does not change msg.sender, allowing the checks to be bypassed. The bug is subtle because the modifiers appear to enforce strict access control, yet the underlying EVM semantics of delegatecall invalidate those assumptions, making the problem easy to overlook in code reviews. To remediate, the protocol should obtain the authoritative control address and execution phase directly from the Atlas core contract rather than from storage that can be altered via delegatecall, add explicit re‑entrancy guards around privileged functions, and enforce that calls to DappControl hooks originate from the Atlas contract via a low‑level call that does not preserve msg.sender, or use a pattern such as onlyOwner with tx.origin checks. In short, the vulnerability is a delegatecall‑based access‑control bypass that enables unauthorized execution of privileged hooks and potential fund loss.

title: reconcile() creates deposits out of thin air
content: The vulnerability resides in the reconcile function of the Fastlane contract, where the routine adds a value called maxApprovedGasSpend to the internal deposits accounting without any corresponding reservation or later subtraction. The code computes a surplus as deposits + maxApprovedGasSpend + msg.value and then overwrites deposits with this surplus whenever either msg.value or maxApprovedGasSpend is non‑zero. Because maxApprovedGasSpend is supplied by the caller and only bounded by the solver’s bonded balance, the function can increase the recorded deposits even though no actual ether or token has been transferred to back that increase. The root cause is a missing accounting step: the contract never records the intention to spend the solver’s bonded balance and never deducts it later, despite comments suggesting a subtraction will occur. An attacker can exploit this by calling reconcile with a large maxApprovedGasSpend that fits within the solver’s bonded balance; the function will inflate the deposits variable, and later logic that credits the solver based on deposits will effectively mint funds out of thin air. This can be done by any address because reconcile is publicly callable and the surrounding checks do not prevent arbitrary callers. The impact is that the protocol’s accounting invariants break – solvers may receive more atlETH than they actually supplied, the protocol’s treasury can be drained, and users may see incorrect balances or missing refunds. The issue manifests whenever reconcile is invoked with a non‑zero maxApprovedGasSpend (or msg.value) and the caller’s address is not restricted; the condition that maxApprovedGasSpend is capped by the bonded balance gives a false sense of safety, but the bonded balance is never decremented. The affected parties include solvers who may be over‑credited, users whose deposits appear inflated, and the overall protocol which loses financial integrity. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that highlighted inconsistent accounting and the lack of a corresponding subtraction step. It is hard to notice because the code appears to simply add a legitimate amount (msg.value) to deposits, and the variable names do not reveal that maxApprovedGasSpend is a phantom reservation. To remediate, the function should explicitly register the reserved gas spend, deduct the reserved amount from the solver’s bonded balance at the appropriate point, and restrict who can call reconcile or add additional validation to ensure that only legitimate gas spend reservations are recorded. In broader terms, this is a classic accounting‑oriented bug where internal state is increased without a matching outflow, leading to creation of unbacked assets and violation of the protocol’s financial guarantees.

title: Flag _solverFulfilled is unreliable
content: The vulnerability concerns an internal flag named _solverFulfilled that is used to indicate that a solver’s duty has been completed and that the contract’s financial state is healthy. The flag is set inside the reconcile function after a simple check that deposits plus the maximum approved gas spend and any incoming ether (surplus) are at least as large as the sum of outstanding claims and withdrawals (deficit). The problem arises because the flag is stored without a final verification of the actual balances after the reconcile call returns. Subsequent external calls such as _borrow or _contribute can modify the deposits or withdrawals variables within the same transaction or in a later callback, thereby changing the deficit/surplus relationship after the flag has already been set. The validateBalances view function later reads the flag from solverLockData and, if the flag is true, assumes the contract is fully funded without performing an additional balance comparison. Consequently, an attacker who can trigger a callback that invokes reconcile and then immediately changes the accounting state can cause the contract to believe it is solvent while it is actually under‑collateralised. This can lead to a situation where users attempting to withdraw or claim refunds receive less than expected, or where the protocol loses funds because the accounting invariant is broken. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the logical flow of state flags and balance checks. It is subtle because the flag appears to provide a convenient shortcut for the view function, and the code does not emit any warning or revert when the underlying balances become inconsistent after the flag is set. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a withdrawal may return zero or a smaller amount than anticipated, even though the UI shows that the contract is “fulfilled”. The bug belongs to the class of state‑inconsistency or flag‑reliability errors, where a boolean indicator is trusted without re‑evaluating the condition it represents. To remediate the issue the contract should stop using the _solverFulfilled flag as a proxy for balance health and instead recompute the deposits ≥ claims + withdrawals condition each time validateBalances is called, or enforce that no state‑changing operations can occur after the flag is set within the same transaction. Removing the flag from reconcile and performing the final accounting check in validateBalances restores the intended invariant and prevents the protocol from mistakenly reporting a fulfilled state while funds are missing.

title: Nonce logic is skipped for smart contract wallets
content: The vulnerability is a missing nonce verification step for smart‑contract based user accounts in the entry point contract. When a UserOperation is submitted and the from address is a contract, the internal function _verifyUser calls the contract’s validateUserOp (or isValidSignature) and immediately returns the boolean result. Because the return occurs before the subsequent call to _handleNonces, the nonce that should guarantee each operation is unique is never checked. Most contract‑based validation functions do not implement their own nonce logic and rely on the caller to enforce it, so the early return effectively disables replay protection for contract wallets. An attacker who can obtain a valid signature for a legitimate operation can replay the same UserOperation indefinitely, because the same nonce value will be accepted each time. This can lead to unauthorized execution of transactions, loss of funds, or unintended state changes. The flaw manifests only when the from address is a contract and the validation function returns true; ordinary externally owned accounts are unaffected because their nonce is handled elsewhere. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that traced the control flow of _verifyUser and noticed that the call to _handleNonces was placed after the early return. It is easy to miss because the code appears to return a success flag, which is a common pattern, and the missing nonce check does not produce an explicit error. To remediate, the control flow should be reordered so that _handleNonces is executed before the function returns, or the nonce check should be incorporated into the contract’s validateUserOp implementation. In either case the system must ensure that every UserOperation, regardless of the wallet type, is subject to a unique, monotonically increasing nonce check, thereby restoring replay protection and preserving the accounting guarantees of the protocol.
summary:
If the userOp.from address is a smart contract, the _verifyUser() function makes a call to the user's validateUserOp() function. This call is expected to return a success bool value, which is instantly returned.
Since this return happens before the code reaches _handleNonces(), there is no nonce validation for smart contract wallets. Most smart contract validation functions (e.g. validateUserOp() in the case of ERC4337 or isValidSignature() in the case of ERC1271) do not manage nonces themselves, and rely on the caller for this. As a result, signatures can be replayed and nonces can be reused when the user is a smart contract wallet.
Also see the issue titled "Call to validateUserOp() won't work", which suggests replacing validateUserOp() with isValidSignature().

title: _releaseSolverLock() doesn't undo all the actions of _trySolverLock()
content: The contract contains a lock‑release routine that fails to fully reverse the state changes performed when a solver attempts to lock the system. When a solver operation is submitted, the internal function _trySolverLock records the caller address in a variable that acts as a lock and increments a withdrawals counter after borrowing the requested ETH amount. The counterpart function _releaseSolverLock is supposed to clear the lock and restore the withdrawals counter, but it leaves the lock variable set to the last solver and never decrements the withdrawals counter. As a result the lock remains active after the operation has finished, allowing later hooks such as AllocateValue and PostOps to see a stale lock value and permitting the reconcile function to be invoked by any participant even though the operation was already authorized. Moreover, each failed solver attempt leaves an unrecovered withdrawal entry, causing the withdrawals total to grow beyond the contract’s actual balance. When the accumulated withdrawals exceed the contract’s ether holdings, subsequent calls to _borrow will reject legitimate solver requests, effectively halting the protocol. The bug can also be triggered when _releaseSolverLock is called without a preceding _trySolverLock, or when it is omitted entirely, leading to inconsistent accounting of gas usage and lock state. From a user perspective the symptoms include unexpected reverts of solver submissions, missing refunds, or the contract refusing new solver operations despite having sufficient funds. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that traced the lock lifecycle and observed that the lock flag was never cleared and that withdrawals were not rolled back on revert. It is hard to notice because the contract does not emit explicit events for lock release or withdrawal adjustments, and the balance checks in _borrow mask the underlying accounting drift until the balance becomes insufficient. The vulnerability belongs to the class of incomplete state‑rollback bugs where cleanup functions do not fully undo prior mutations, breaking invariants and enabling unauthorized actions. To remediate the problem the release function should explicitly reset the lock variable to the unlocked sentinel value and subtract the previously borrowed amount from the withdrawals counter, preferably moving the borrowing logic into the execution wrapper so that a revert automatically restores the original state. Renaming the release function to reflect its dual role of unlocking and gas accounting would also improve code clarity and reduce the risk of future misuse.

title: solverMetaTryCatch() assumes there is no pre-existing ETH in contract
content: The vulnerability resides in the solverMetaTryCatch function of the ExecutionEnvironment contract. The function asserts that the contract's ETH balance exactly matches the value specified in the solver operation (solverOp.value) by using require(address(this).balance == solverOp.value, \"ERR-CE05 IncorrectValue\"). This assumption is incorrect because the contract's balance can be altered by external transactions before the solver call. An attacker can front‑run the intended transaction and send a small amount of ETH to the ExecutionEnvironment contract, causing address(this).balance to become greater than solverOp.value. When the solverMetaTryCatch call is executed, the balance check fails, the require statement reverts, and the surrounding wrapper interprets the failure as an EVMError. As a result the solver transaction is aborted and the caller must still pay the gas consumed by the revert. The impact is a denial‑of‑service style condition where legitimate solvers cannot be executed unless the contract balance is exactly the expected amount, and the gas cost is wasted. This issue affects any participant that relies on the solver execution, including protocol operators, users submitting operations, and the overall economic model of the system. The problem was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the logic of value handling and identified that the balance check does not consider pre‑existing ETH. The bug is subtle because checking the contract balance is a common pattern and may appear correct in isolation; however, it ignores the possibility of external deposits and front‑running. The vulnerability belongs to the class of improper balance verification or value‑dependency bugs, where contract state is assumed to be immutable between calls. From a user perspective the transaction simply fails with an \"IncorrectValue\" error, no funds are transferred, and the UI may show that the operation did not complete while the user's ETH balance is reduced only by the gas fee. To remediate the issue the code should compare the amount of ETH sent with the operation (msg.value) rather than the contract's total balance, and the internal accounting of startBalance should be derived from address(this).balance minus msg.value. This change eliminates the reliance on a mutable contract balance and prevents front‑run attacks that inject extra ETH.
summary:
```solidity
solverMetaTryCatch()
requires ExecutionEnvironment's balance to be the same as solverOp.value:
require(address(this).balance == solverOp.value, "ERR-CE05 IncorrectValue");
```
However, someone can frontrun this transaction and send some ETH to ExecutionEnvironment making its balance non-zero. This leads to the solverMetaTryCatch() call reverting, since the call is sent with an ETH amount equal to solverOp.value. This makes address(this).balance > solverOp.value. Since the error would be treated as SolverOutcome.EVMError in the _solverOpWrapper(), the solver would be forced to pay the gas costs for this revert.

title: Bid tokens aren't enforced to be the same
content: The vulnerability consists of a lack of on‑chain enforcement that the token used for bids is identical across all places where the token is referenced in the Atlas auction system. The contract stores the expected bid token in the DAppConfig and also records a token address inside each SolverOperation that is submitted by the auctioneer or a bundler. Because the verifySolverOp logic does not compare the token address in the SolverOperation with the token returned by getBidFormat, a transaction can contain mismatched token identifiers. When this occurs the internal comparison of bid amounts, which assumes a common token, produces incorrect ordering, and the allocateValueCall function, which transfers the winning token to the winner, receives arguments that do not correspond to the expected token. As a result the auction may silently select a winner based on an unrelated token, transfer the wrong asset, or fail to transfer any asset at all, leaving bidders with missing or zero balances. The issue manifests only when the auctioneer or a malicious bundler deliberately or accidentally includes a SolverOperation that references a different ERC‑20 token than the one configured in DAppConfig. Honest users who place bids see their expected refunds or allocations disappear, often without an explicit revert or error message, making the problem hard to notice during normal operation. The flaw was discovered during a manual security review of the Fastlane codebase, where the auditor observed that the token field appears in multiple structs but no require statement validates their equality. The bug belongs to the class of “inconsistent state validation” or “cross‑parameter mismatch” vulnerabilities, where related parameters are not synchronised, leading to logical errors in accounting. To remediate the issue, a check should be added in the verifySolverOp function (or an equivalent validation hook) that asserts the token address in each SolverOperation matches the token returned by DAppConfig.getBidFormat, and that any deviation causes the transaction to revert. This ensures that bid amount calculations and allocation calls always operate on the same token, preserving the intended economic guarantees of the auction.
summary:
In Atlas, bid tokens are specified in multiple locations:
1. Within the DAppConfig (specifically from the getBidFormat() function).
2. Within each SolverOperation.
Currently, it's not enforced on-chain that these values are all consistent with each other. If the auctioneer or bundler includes different tokens in a transaction, the bid amount comparisons and the allocateValueCall() function would silently break, which could lead to unexpected results.

title: No slippage protection for UniswapV2 swaps
content: The vulnerability consists of the absence of any slippage protection when the contract performs a UniswapV2 swap. In UniswapV2 the amount of input tokens that must be sent (amount0In or amount1In) is calculated from the current reserves of the pool and the requested amount‑out. Because the contract does not enforce a maximum acceptable amount‑in, an attacker can execute a sandwich attack: first a front‑running transaction changes the pool reserves, then the victim’s swap is executed with a much higher required input, and finally a back‑running transaction restores the original price. The victim therefore ends up sending far more tokens than expected, potentially draining the entire balance of the user. This situation occurs whenever a user initiates a swap without specifying a slippage tolerance, and the pool is exposed to rapid price changes caused by other participants. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that highlighted the missing check on amount‑in versus a user‑defined limit. It can be hard to notice because the transaction may still succeed and emit normal swap events, while the user’s balance silently decreases. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a successful swap, but the received token amount is zero or far lower than expected, and the user’s original token balance may become zero. The impact is a loss of funds for any user who relies on the contract to perform swaps, and it undermines the economic guarantees of the protocol. The bug belongs to the class of “missing slippage protection” or “unchecked price impact” vulnerabilities, where the contract trusts external price calculations without bounding the worst‑case input. To remediate, the contract should enforce a maximum acceptable amount‑in (or minimum amount‑out) based on a user‑provided slippage tolerance, or at least document the lack of protection so callers can add their own checks.
summary:
amount0In and amount1In values are dependent on UniswapV2 pool's current token balance and on amount-out values. Someone can sandwich Atlas transaction to imbalance the pool leading to high amount-in value which is then transferred from user to the pool.
The attacker makes a profit through this sandwich and thus it's likely that all the token balance of the user is transferred to the pool.

title: Hard-coded slippage may freeze user funds during market turbulence
content: The vulnerability consists of a hard‑coded slippage limit of 99 % (i.e., only 1 % deviation allowed) that is embedded in the GeneralVault contract and inherited by specialised vaults such as the LidoVault. This rigid parameter is used when the vault attempts to swap a yield token (for example stETH) for the underlying asset (ETH) during a withdrawal. The root cause is the absence of any mechanism for users or operators to adjust the maximum acceptable slippage, combined with the fact that the contract enforces the limit with a require statement that compares the expected receive amount against the hard‑coded threshold. When market conditions become volatile and the price of the yield token drops—such as during a sudden de‑peg of a stablecoin or a sharp decline in stETH's price relative to ETH—the actual amount received from the swap can fall below the 99 % threshold. At that point the require check fails, the withdrawal transaction reverts, and the user’s funds remain locked inside the vault. From a user’s perspective the UI will show that the withdraw button is unresponsive or that the transaction fails, leaving the displayed balance unchanged and giving the impression that the funds have vanished or are frozen. The impact is that users cannot retrieve their holdings when they need them most, potentially leading to loss of confidence in the protocol and, in extreme cases, to an inability to recover the locked assets without external intervention. The issue manifests only under specific market turbulence; under normal price conditions the contract behaves as expected, which makes the bug hard to notice during routine testing. It was uncovered during a security audit that simulated adverse price movements, revealing that the static slippage control could cause withdrawals to fail. To remediate the problem the slippage constraint should be made configurable: either expose a min‑receive amount parameter that callers can set according to current market rates, or allow an authorized operator to update the maximum slippage setting through a controlled governance function. Additionally, providing an alternative withdrawal path that returns the original yield token (e.g., stETH) instead of forcing an immediate conversion to ETH would give users a safe fallback when the swap market is illiquid. Implementing these changes restores alignment with the protocol’s accounting assumptions, ensures that users receive the funds they expect, and eliminates the risk of funds becoming permanently inaccessible.
summary:
[GeneralVault.sol#L125](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-sturdy/blob/main/smart-contracts/GeneralVault.sol#L125)  
GeneralVault set a hardcoded slippage control of 99%. However, the underlying yield tokens price may go down.  
If Luna/UST things happen again, users’ funds may get locked.  

[LidoVault.sol#L130-L137](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-sturdy/blob/main/smart-contracts/LidoVault.sol#L130-L137)  
Moreover, the withdrawal of the lidoVault takes a swap from the curve pool. 1 stEth worth 0.98 ETH at the time of writing.  
The vault can not withdraw at the current market.  

Given that users’ funds would be locked in the lidoVault, I consider this a high-risk issue.

title: The check for value transfer success is made after the return statement in `_withdrawFromYieldPool` of `LidoVault`
content:
The vulnerability resides in the withdrawal routine of the LidoVault contract, specifically in the internal function `_withdrawFromYieldPool`. The function attempts to transfer a calculated amount of collateral back to a user and then returns the transferred amount. However, the contract performs the `require` check that validates whether the low‑level call succeeded only after the `return` statement. Because the `return` ends execution immediately, the `require(sent, Errors.VT_COLLATERAL_WITHDRAW_INVALID)` line is never reached. As a result, if the external call that sends the funds fails – for example due to the recipient being a contract that reverts, out‑of‑gas, or refusing the transfer – the function still reports a successful withdrawal and exits without reverting.
