The root cause is that the removal routine only rewires the previous node's next reference but neglects to adjust the tail reference when the removed node equals the tail. Exploitation is possible whenever a user or an attacker can trigger the removal of a credit account that happens to be the tail; after the operation the list is malformed and later accounting, reward distribution, liquidation or balance‑query calls that walk the list may miss the stale tail or fail entirely. The impact is a logical error that can make funds appear to disappear, prevent users from seeing their accounts, or cause zero balances to be reported even though assets remain locked in the contract. This condition occurs only when the function that extracts a credit account is invoked with the tail account as argument. All users holding credit accounts and the protocol itself are affected because the protocol assumes a well‑formed list for correct accounting. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit by MixBytes, who observed that the tail variable is never reassigned after a removal operation. The bug can be hard to notice because normal removals of non‑tail accounts work correctly, and the corrupted tail may only surface during infrequent operations that iterate to the end of the list. The appropriate remediation is to add logic that, when the removed account equals the current tail, updates the tail pointer to the previous node or clears it if the list becomes empty. This is a classic linked‑list pointer update error, often classified as an incorrect tail handling or list‑corruption bug. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after closing an account the UI may no longer display the account, balance queries return zero, or withdrawal attempts revert, giving the impression that funds have vanished. The bug violates the protocol’s business logic that assumes the account list is always intact, breaking accounting invariants and potentially locking assets. Updating the tail correctly restores list integrity and prevents these erroneous behaviours.
summary:
If creditAccount == tail then tail is not updated properly and this will break the list of accounts:
AccountFactory.sol#L260

title: MJR-11 Incorrect minting
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect minting bug that occurs when the protocol mints Diesel tokens based on the amount of USDT that a user is expected to transfer, without accounting for the transfer fee that USDT deducts in its transferFrom function. The root cause is the assumption that a fee‑on‑transfer token will move the full requested amount, leading the contract to calculate the mint amount from a value that does not match the actual balance increase. An attacker or any user can exploit this by initiating a mint operation with USDT; because USDT subtracts a fee, the contract receives less USDT than recorded, and consequently mints fewer Diesel tokens than the user paid for. The impact is that users receive a smaller token balance than expected, effectively losing value, and the protocol’s accounting invariants are broken because the total Diesel supply no longer reflects the true USDT collateral held. This condition manifests whenever the mint function is called with USDT, i.e., under normal usage of the protocol’s deposit‑and‑mint flow. The affected parties are users who mint Diesel with USDT and the protocol itself, which may suffer reputational damage and financial imbalance. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined token transfer handling and identified that the USDT implementation charges a fee, a detail that was not reflected in the minting logic. The bug can be hard to notice because the UI may simply show a successful transaction, while the user’s Diesel balance is lower than anticipated, and the discrepancy may be attributed to market fluctuations rather than a contract error. To fix the problem, the contract should determine the actual amount of USDT received by measuring the balance before and after the transfer (balance difference) and use that precise value to calculate the number of Diesel tokens to mint, thereby eliminating reliance on the nominal transfer amount. This class of bug falls under fee‑on‑transfer token handling errors, where contracts fail to adjust for token‑level transfer fees, leading to incorrect accounting and token supply mismatches. From a user’s perspective the symptom is a missing or reduced Diesel balance after a successful USDT deposit, contrary to the expectation that the deposited amount translates one‑to‑one into newly minted tokens.
summary:
Because of fees in transferFrom function in USDT, contract would have less than amount:
PoolService.sol#L155

title: MJR-12 Impossible liquidity removing
content: The vulnerability concerns a liquidity pool contract that becomes unable to return assets to users when the pool’s capital is almost entirely borrowed. The root cause is an accounting mismatch: the contract assumes that the on‑chain token balance (balanceOf(address(this))) is always sufficient to cover a user’s withdrawal request (amountSent). When a large portion of the pool’s funds are lent out, the on‑chain balance drops below the amount a user tries to withdraw, causing the condition amountSent > balanceOf(address(this)) and the transaction to revert. This situation can be triggered by a malicious borrower who deliberately drains the pool’s available liquidity, effectively locking other users’ funds and creating a denial‑of‑service scenario. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a withdrawal or liquidity removal transaction fails, the UI shows an error or simply does not complete, and the user sees no tokens returned despite having a positive balance in the protocol. The impact is that legitimate liquidity providers may be unable to retrieve their capital, leading to funds being effectively frozen and eroding trust in the protocol. The issue was discovered during a formal security audit performed by MixBytes, and it is subtle because it only manifests under extreme borrowing conditions that may not be exercised in routine testing. The bug belongs to the class of “liquidity‑locking” or “insufficient‑reserve” defects, where the contract’s business logic does not enforce a minimum reserve or provide a fallback path for withdrawals when the internal balance is insufficient. To remediate the problem the contract should implement a safe‑exit mechanism, such as a function that allows the protocol to close an account and force‑return the remaining assets to liquidity providers, or enforce borrowing limits that guarantee a reserve sufficient to satisfy any pending withdrawal request. By ensuring that either the borrowed amount can be reclaimed before a withdrawal or that a fallback path exists, the protocol can avoid the situation where users expect a refund but receive zero, and the accounting invariants of the pool remain intact.
summary:
In case all funds were borrowed (big part of funds), users can't return their assets (amountSent > balanceOf(address(this))):
PoolService.sol#L182

title: MJR-13 Calculation can be incorrect
content: The vulnerability is an accounting mis‑calculation in the pool’s liquidity logic where the variable that represents the expected liquidity of a pool is derived by adding the pool’s actual token balance to a “pseudo‑balance” that originates from borrowers’ accrued interest. This blending of real assets with interest that has not yet been realized causes the contract to over‑estimate the amount of funds that are actually available for liquidity providers (LPs) and other protocol operations. The root cause is the use of a single aggregate figure for expectedLiquidity that does not distinguish between on‑chain token holdings and off‑chain interest obligations, violating the fundamental accounting assumption that a pool’s reported liquidity must equal the sum of assets that can be immediately withdrawn. An attacker or a malicious borrower can trigger a situation where the protocol believes more liquidity exists than is truly present, allowing them to request withdrawals, swaps, or other actions that draw down the pool beyond its real balance. Because the excess amount is only a bookkeeping artifact, the protocol may later be unable to satisfy legitimate LP redemption requests, leading to missing or zero balances for users, unexpected shortfalls in refunds, or complete loss of funds for LPs. The issue manifests whenever borrowers accrue interest and the pool’s expectedLiquidity is consulted – for example during LP withdrawal, fee distribution, or forced closure of accounts. All participants who rely on the pool’s reported liquidity – LPs, borrowers, and the protocol itself – are affected. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the PoolService contract and identified that the line computing expectedLiquidity mixes real balance with pseudo‑balance from borrowers’ interest. The problem is subtle because the numbers may appear reasonable on the surface; the over‑statement is hidden in the interest component, making it difficult to detect through simple balance checks. To remediate, the contract should separate the real token balance from any interest accruals, ensuring that expectedLiquidity reflects only assets that can be immediately transferred. Additionally, providing a mechanism to force‑close accounts and settle all outstanding balances for LPs would prevent the protocol from operating on inflated liquidity figures. In summary, the bug belongs to the class of “incorrect financial accounting” or “liquidity over‑estimation” vulnerabilities, where a contract’s internal accounting diverges from the actual on‑chain token holdings, leading to potential fund loss, failed refunds, and broken business logic.
summary:
expectedLiquidity contains real balance + pseudo balance from borrowers interest:
PoolService.sol#L396

title: MJR-14 Impossible liquidation of broken account
content: The vulnerability is an accounting inconsistency that arises when a token transfer, intended to be used as collateral, reverts. In the CreditManager contract the total collateral value (tv) and the weighted total value (tvw) are updated unconditionally, even if the underlying ERC20 transfer fails. As a result the protocol believes the account holds a certain amount of the token, while the token balance is actually zero. When a liquidator attempts to liquidate the position, the protocol still charges the liquidation fee for the missing token and expects to receive the token, but the transfer cannot be completed. This creates a situation where an under‑collateralised account appears to be sufficiently collateralised on‑chain, making liquidation impossible or causing the liquidator to lose the fee. The impact is that funds can become stuck, risk parameters are violated, and a malicious borrower could deliberately trigger a revert (for example by using a token that reverts on transfer) to protect an unhealthy position. The bug occurs during any operation that updates collateral accounting – typically when adding collateral or during the liquidation routine – and only manifests when the transfer call returns false or throws. It was discovered by the MixBytes audit team while reviewing the lines that accumulate tv and tvw in CreditManager.sol; the logic does not check the transfer result before adjusting the accounting variables, which makes the problem easy to miss because the UI shows the expected collateral value and no error is emitted. To remediate, the contract should only increase tv and tvw after a successful transfer, or revert the accounting changes if the transfer fails, and it must also skip charging the liquidation fee for tokens that were not actually transferred. In broader terms this is a classic “failed transfer accounting” bug, a subclass of improper state updates that break the invariant that recorded collateral matches on‑chain balances, leading to broken liquidation logic and potential loss of funds.
summary:
In case transfer was reverted, then specific token can't be accounted as collateral, and also liquidator must not pay the fee for this token:
CreditManager.sol#L593-L594

title: MJR-15 Using tokens with whitelist function
content: The vulnerability originates from the liquidation routine of the Gearbox CreditManager contract, specifically the internal function that moves collateral tokens to a recipient during a credit account liquidation. The protocol assumes that any token used as collateral implements an off‑chain whitelist mechanism (for example USDC or USDT) and that a transfer will always succeed when the whitelist permits it. When a token is blocked off‑chain, the low‑level safe transfer call silently fails, but the function continues to add the token’s reported value (tv) and weighted value (tvw) to the cumulative totals that are later used to decide whether the liquidation succeeded. Consequently the contract reports a higher totalValue than was actually transferred. This mismatch can be triggered whenever the liquidation path iterates over enabled tokens, finds a token with a non‑zero balance (amount > 1) and attempts to transfer it while the token is blocked. The affected parties are borrowers whose credit accounts are liquidated, lenders who rely on correct collateral accounting, and the protocol itself because the accounting invariant that transferred value equals reported value is broken. The issue was discovered during a MixBytes audit by analysing the _transferAssetsTo loop and observing that the return values are updated unconditionally after the transfer call. It is hard to notice because the function does not revert on failure, no event signals the transfer problem, and the UI may still display a successful liquidation with the expected totalValue, giving the impression that assets have been moved when they have not. The impact includes potential loss of collateral, incorrect liquidation incentives, and a state where the protocol believes a credit account has been cleared while the underlying tokens remain locked, which could be exploited to claim liquidation rewards without actually providing the assets. To remediate, the contract should only increase totalValue and totalWeightedValue after confirming that the token transfer succeeded, for example by checking the return flag of the safe transfer or by reverting on failure, and by adding an on‑chain whitelist check so that blocked tokens cannot be processed at all. In abstract terms the bug belongs to the class of accounting‑value‑mismatch vulnerabilities where a contract records asset value without guaranteeing the physical movement of those assets, violating the fundamental business logic that transferred collateral equals accounted collateral.
summary:
At line: CreditManager.sol#L584-L593
The Gearbox protocol is assumed to use some tokens which have whitelist function (ex. USDC, USDT) like a collateral. If this token will be blocked off-chain the Liquidates credit account function member of the CreditManager contract (CreditManager.sol#L300) will not work correctly because the internal function _transferAssetsTo() (CreditManager.sol#L584-L591) returns incorrect return value totalValue.

title: MJR-16 Looping a linked list
content: The vulnerability is an improper handling of a singly‑linked list that stores credit account addresses in the _nextCreditAccount mapping. When a credit account is removed from the list by the takeOut() function, the contract does not clear the pointer that links the removed node to its successor. Consequently, the removed address retains its old next pointer value. If the same address is later re‑added to the tail of the list, the stale pointer creates a cycle, causing the list to loop back on itself. This loop can be triggered when the internal helper _countCreditAccountsInStock iterates over the list to count available credit accounts; the iteration will follow the cycle indefinitely, eventually exhausting the block gas limit. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition that prevents the protocol from correctly accounting for credit accounts, potentially blocking new credit allocations and causing user‑facing operations such as withdrawals or refunds to fail with out‑of‑gas errors. The issue occurs whenever takeOut() is called without resetting _nextCreditAccount[creditAccount] to address(0) and the same credit account is later re‑inserted at the tail. All participants that rely on the credit‑account pool – including borrowers, lenders, and the credit manager – are affected because the protocol can no longer reliably track available accounts. The bug was discovered during a manual audit of the AccountFactory contract where the auditor noticed that the linked‑list removal logic omitted a step to nullify the next pointer, and that the counting routine could enter an infinite loop. The problem is subtle because the list still appears structurally correct for a few operations; only when the list is traversed repeatedly does the cycle manifest, making it hard to detect through simple unit tests. To fix the issue, the contract should explicitly clear the next pointer of the removed node (e.g., _nextCreditAccount[creditAccount] = address(0)) before re‑adding the node to the tail, thereby breaking any potential cycle and restoring linear traversal. This class of bug is a linked‑list pointer mismanagement leading to a cycle, a common issue in data‑structure implementations that violates the invariant that a singly‑linked list must be acyclic. From a user’s perspective, transactions that rely on counting or iterating over credit accounts may hang, return zero results, or consume all gas, contrary to the expectation that the system will promptly report the number of available accounts or process withdrawals.
summary:
At the line: AccountFactory.sol#L40 there's a linked list called _nextCreditAccount.
In this list, the account address refers to the address of the next account. Thus, a chain of addresses linked to each other is formed.
At the lines contracts/core/AccountFactory.sol#L248-L263 there's a takeOut() function.
It takes the credit account address from anywhere on the list and attaches it to the credit manager.
At the lines: AccountFactory.sol#L186-L199 there's a function returnCreditAccount(). It returns the credit account address in the tail of the _nextCreditAccount linked list.
In the takeOut() function there is no logic for checking and zeroing the link to the next account from the taken account address.
When the taken address is returned to the tail of the list, it will contain the old value of the address. Loop through the list may occur when the function _countCreditAccountsInStock() is used for the line: AccountFactory.sol#L352-L365.

title: MJR-17 No checking of element properties when returning it to the list
content: The vulnerability resides in the AccountFactory contract’s returnCreditAccount function, which is responsible for handing out the address of the credit account located at the tail of an internal linked list (_nextCreditAccount). The function performs a single validation step: it checks that the credit account’s since() timestamp is not equal to the current block number. For a freshly deployed or never‑registered credit account the since() value is zero, which satisfies the condition because zero is not equal to block.number. Consequently the function can return an address that has never been added to the creditAccounts array and therefore is not tracked by the factory’s accounting logic. The root cause is an incomplete sanity check – the code does not verify that the account has been initialized (since() > 0) nor that the address actually exists in the creditAccounts collection. An attacker or a careless user can invoke returnCreditAccount and receive this unregistered address, then interact with it under the assumption that it is a valid credit account. Because the factory believes the address is part of its managed set while the protocol’s bookkeeping does not, funds may be sent to an address that is not recorded, leading to missing balances, failed refunds, or accounting inconsistencies. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a credit account being allocated but subsequent operations return zero balances or revert, creating the impression that “my funds disappeared” or “the refund is missing”. The issue manifests whenever the tail pointer of the linked list points to an element that has never been registered – for example after a removal operation that does not correctly update the tail or when the factory is queried before any accounts have been created. The bug was discovered during a systematic audit by MixBytes, which identified that the linked‑list management lacked a proper existence check. It is subtle because the function appears to return a legitimate address and the failing condition (since() != block.number) does not raise an error for an uninitialized contract, making the problem easy to overlook during testing. To remediate the issue the contract should enforce that the returned address satisfies both since() != block.number and since() > 0, ensuring that only accounts that have been created and recorded in the creditAccounts array can be returned. Additionally, the factory should verify that the tail pointer references an element present in the array or reset the pointer when the list becomes empty, thereby restoring the integrity of the credit‑account management logic.
summary:
At the lines: AccountFactory.sol#L186-L199 there's a function returnCreditAccount(). It returns the credit account address in the tail of the _nextCreditAccount linked list.
For the line: AccountFactory.sol#L192, the check is made that the value of since() is not equal to block.number.
If the address has never been registered in an AccountFactory it will pass this check too.
But this address will not be added to the creditAccounts array and the logic of the entire contract will be violated.

title: MJR-2 Incorrect change of state
content: The vulnerability concerns an improper state transition in the CreditFilter component of the Gearbox protocol. A boolean flag that determines whether a token is permitted to interact with the protocol can be switched to true directly through a function that was intended only for disabling a token. The root cause is the absence of a validation step and missing access control when setting the flag to true; the correct pathway for enabling a token is the dedicated allowToken() routine, which performs necessary checks such as token verification and risk assessment. Because the flag can be set to true without invoking allowToken(), an attacker or any caller with access to the faulty function can mark an arbitrary token as allowed. Once the flag is true, the protocol will treat the token as trusted, allowing deposits, loans, or other financial operations with that token. This can lead to the protocol accepting malicious or unsupported assets, breaking accounting assumptions, and potentially causing loss of user funds or incorrect collateral valuation. The issue manifests when the state‑changing function is called under normal operation; there is no immediate UI symptom, but later users may experience unexpected behavior such as deposits being accepted for a token that should be disabled, or refunds failing because the protocol treats the token as valid when it is not. The bug was discovered during a formal security audit performed by MixBytes, who noted that the state change to true bypasses the intended allowToken() workflow. It can be hard to notice because the boolean assignment looks innocuous and does not emit an event, so observers may not realize that a token has been inadvertently whitelisted. To remediate, the contract should restrict the state‑changing function to only allow setting the flag to false, and enforce that any transition to true must occur exclusively through allowToken(), which includes all required validation logic and emits appropriate events. This aligns the implementation with the intended security model, ensuring that only vetted tokens become usable and preserving the protocol’s financial integrity.
summary:
Changing state to true is incorrect and must be done via allowToken():
CreditFilter.sol#L398

title: MJR-3 creditManager isn't checked
content: The vulnerability is an unchecked reference to the credit manager contract when granting token allowances. In the leverage action routine the contract calls an ERC20 approve function and passes the address supplied as the credit manager without verifying that this address belongs to a trusted system component. The root cause is the absence of a validation step that ensures the credit manager is a known, immutable system contract. An attacker can supply a malicious contract in place of the expected credit manager, causing the protocol to execute an unlimited approve call that authorises the attacker’s contract to transfer any amount of the underlying token on behalf of the protocol. Exploitation proceeds by the attacker deploying a contract that implements the expected interface, then invoking the leverage function with the address of this malicious contract. Because the protocol does not check the contract’s provenance, the approve call succeeds and the attacker gains an allowance that can be used to drain token balances. The impact is the potential loss of user funds or protocol assets, as the attacker can move tokens without restriction, effectively making funds disappear from user balances or from the protocol’s vault. This condition occurs whenever the leverage action is executed with a user‑controlled credit manager parameter, which is allowed by the current implementation. All participants that rely on the protocol’s accounting – lenders, borrowers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the accounting assumptions that only the system can move tokens are violated. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the flow of privileged parameters and identified that the credit manager address was not validated against a whitelist of system contracts. The bug can be subtle because the approve call itself is a standard ERC20 operation and may not raise an error; the malicious allowance is invisible until a token transfer is attempted, making it hard to notice through normal testing. The recommended remediation is to add an explicit check that the supplied credit manager address matches a contract that is registered as a system component, for example by consulting a registry or by using an immutable address constant, before performing the approve. Conceptually this belongs to the class of “missing access‑control validation” or “unrestricted delegate contract reference” bugs, where a privileged operation is performed on an untrusted contract. From a user’s perspective the symptom would be that after a transaction they see their token balance reduced unexpectedly or that a withdrawal returns zero tokens despite a successful transaction. The expectation that the protocol only authorises its own credit manager is broken, leading to a scenario where funds can be siphoned away without the user’s consent.
summary:
It is possible to give unlimited approve to poisoned contract:
LeverageActions.sol#L222

title: MJR-4 Uncounted fees in USDT
content: The vulnerability originates from the contract’s reliance on the ERC‑20 transferFrom function to move an exact amount of USDT from a user to the protocol, while USDT implements a fee‑on‑transfer mechanism that reduces the amount actually received. Because the contract does not account for this fee, it may end up holding fewer tokens than the amountIn parameter supplied by the caller. This discrepancy can occur whenever openCreditAccount invokes transferFrom on USDT, which is expected to credit the contract with the full requested amount. The root cause is the assumption that transferFrom will always transfer the precise value, an assumption that holds for standard ERC‑20 tokens but not for fee‑on‑transfer tokens such as USDT. An attacker or any user can trigger the condition simply by depositing USDT, causing the contract to believe it has sufficient collateral while the real balance is lower. The impact includes failed credit‑account openings, potential under‑collateralisation of leveraged positions, and unexpected reverts or loss of funds for users who expect their full deposit to be usable. From the user’s perspective the UI may show that the deposit was accepted, but later actions (e.g., opening a leveraged position) revert or result in zero usable balance, leading to confusion when “my funds disappeared” or “the refund is missing”. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the auditors observed that the contract’s balance after a transferFrom call was consistently lower than the amount requested, a symptom that is easy to miss because the transferFrom call returns true and does not revert. Detecting the problem requires checking the actual token balance after the transfer, which the current implementation omits. To remediate, the protocol should either query the contract’s USDT balance after the transfer and use that value when opening a credit account, or adjust the amountIn to include the expected fee, or restrict usage to fee‑free tokens. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “fee‑on‑transfer token handling errors”, where accounting assumptions about token transfers are violated, leading to mismatched accounting and potential financial loss.
summary:
Contract can have less than amountIn because of fees in transferFrom function in USDT:
LeverageActions.sol#L232
LeverageActions.sol#L324

title: MJR-5 Possible loss of assets by mistake
content: The vulnerability is an unchecked destination address in a liquidation function of the CreditManager contract. When a liquidator invokes the function with the parameter `to` set to the zero address (address(0)) and the `force` flag set to true, the contract proceeds to transfer or burn the assets without any validation, resulting in the complete loss of the assets that were supposed to be transferred. The root cause is the absence of a guard clause that ensures the target address is non‑zero before executing the asset movement logic. An attacker or an accidental user can exploit this by deliberately passing address(0) together with the force flag, causing the contract to send the funds to the zero address, which is effectively an unrecoverable burn. The impact is that all assets held for the affected credit position disappear, leaving the liquidator, borrowers, and the protocol without those funds. This condition occurs only when the function is called with a zero destination and the force option enabled; under normal calls with a valid address the bug does not manifest. The parties affected include any user who relies on the liquidation process to recover collateral, the protocol’s overall capital pool, and any third‑party liquidators who might mistakenly trigger the call. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the liquidation flow and identified the missing address check. Because address(0) is a syntactically valid address, the problem can be subtle and may not produce an obvious error message, making it hard to notice until assets are irretrievably lost. From a user perspective the symptom is that after initiating liquidation the expected transfer never arrives; balances appear unchanged or the protocol reports a successful liquidation while the funds have vanished. The bug belongs to the class of unchecked address validation or asset‑burn bugs that violate the accounting assumption that transferred assets must end up in a controllable account. To remediate, the contract should include an explicit require statement that rejects a zero destination address, reverting the transaction when `to == address(0)`. This ensures that assets cannot be unintentionally burned and preserves the integrity of the protocol’s financial logic.
summary: If a liquidator calls this function by mistake with the next parameters: to = address(0), force = true, then he loses all assets: CreditManager.sol#L302

title: MJR-6 Broken account must be deleted
content: The vulnerability concerns a broken account state that persists when a token transfer initiated by the protocol fails and is reverted. The root cause is the absence of cleanup logic after a failed transfer; the contract does not delete or deactivate the user’s accounting record even though the underlying token operation did not succeed. An attacker or any user can trigger a transfer that reverts – for example by using a token that rejects the transfer, has insufficient allowance, or contains a custom require that fails – and the protocol will leave the account entry in its internal ledger unchanged. Because the account is still considered active, subsequent operations that rely on the account’s balance or debt position may behave incorrectly, leading to accounting mismatches, inability to withdraw or claim rewards, and potentially a denial‑of‑service condition where the protocol cannot process further actions for that user. From the user’s point of view the symptom is that after attempting a withdrawal or reward claim the UI shows no change, the balance appears unchanged or zero, and the expected funds never arrive. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit by MixBytes, which noted that the code path at the point where token transfers are performed does not include a branch to remove the account when the external call reverts. The bug is subtle because the transaction itself does not revert – only the internal token call does – so the overall transaction may appear successful while the internal state is left inconsistent. To remediate the problem the contract should incorporate explicit error handling: if a token transfer returns false or throws, the protocol must either roll back the entire operation or, if partial state changes are acceptable, delete or deactivate the affected account and emit an event indicating the cleanup. This ensures that the accounting model remains sound, users do not lose access to their funds, and the protocol’s financial invariants are preserved. The class of bug is a state‑inconsistency after external call failure, commonly referred to as improper cleanup of stale accounts or broken accounting entries.
summary: In case if some tokens cannot be transferred from the account, then this account must be deleted: CreditManager.sol#L451

title: MJR-1 Deposit will be unavailable if lending pool address will be
content: The vulnerability is a stale token allowance problem that makes the deposit function of the Aave integration contract unusable when the underlying lending pool address changes. The contract calls safeApprove only once during its constructor, granting the initial pool contract permission to transfer the user's token. The deposit routine later assumes that this approval is still valid and does not re‑verify or refresh the allowance. Aave may upgrade or replace the pool address, which means the previously approved address no longer matches the current pool contract. When a user invokes deposit after such a change, the token transfer call fails because the allowance for the new pool address is zero, causing the deposit transaction to revert. This results in a denial‑of‑service condition: users see their deposit attempts revert or silently fail, balances remain unchanged, and the contract appears to be broken until the allowance is updated or the contract is redeployed. The issue was discovered during a static code audit that noted the safeApprove call at line 49 and the lack of any subsequent allowance management before the deposit call at line 132. It can be hard to notice because the contract works correctly on first deployment and only exhibits the problem after an external upgrade of the Aave pool, which may be infrequent. The impact is that funds cannot be deposited, users may lose confidence, and the protocol’s promised functionality is broken, violating the business assumption that deposits are always possible. The affected parties are token holders trying to deposit, the protocol relying on continuous liquidity, and any downstream contracts that expect successful deposits. To remediate, the contract should either call safeApprove each time before a deposit or implement a mechanism that detects changes to the pool address and refreshes the allowance accordingly, ensuring that the token transfer permission always matches the current pool contract.
summary: At line GenericAave.sol#L132 the deposit function assumes recent approval of token transfer. However, the safeApprove() is called once during contract initialization(GenericAave.sol#L49) and possible changes of lending pool address is not tracked properly. If lending pool address is updated by AAVE, the deposit() will be unavailable/reverted until contract replacement.

title: MJR-7 Possible transfer of bad account
content: The vulnerability concerns the ability to transfer a credit account that is already under‑collateralised, i.e., its health factor (Hf) is below the safety threshold of 1, without any prior liquidation or explicit consent from the receiving party. The root cause is the lack of a validation step in the transfer function that checks the health factor of the source account before allowing the ownership change. Because the protocol does not enforce an approval or consent mechanism, a user who holds a bad account can invoke the transfer routine and assign the same account to another address. An attacker can therefore off‑load a risky position to an unsuspecting participant, who will inherit the under‑collateralised state and may be forced into liquidation at the next block. The impact is that the recipient may lose collateral, see their balance drop to zero, or experience unexpected liquidation events, effectively causing funds to disappear from their perspective. This situation occurs whenever an account’s health factor falls below 1 but the liquidation bot has not yet acted, and the contract’s transfer logic is called. All users of the CreditManager who rely on the ability to transfer accounts are affected, especially those who assume that transferred accounts are healthy. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the Gearbox Protocol codebase, where the auditor noticed that the transfer path does not include any health‑factor guard or receiver approval. The bug is subtle because the transfer succeeds syntactically and the protocol does not emit a warning, so users may not realise they have inherited a failing position until liquidation occurs. To remediate, the contract should introduce an explicit approval step (e.g., an `approveTransfer` call) that requires the destination address to accept the account, and the transfer function should reject any account with Hf < 1 unless a special emergency flag is set. This aligns the implementation with the business logic that an account transfer should only occur for healthy positions, preserving accounting integrity and preventing accidental loss of funds.
summary: User can have bad account with Hf < 1 but not liquidated yet, and transfer it to another user: CreditManager.sol#L954

title: processValidators() Function Can Be Prevented Funds Get Stuck
content: The vulnerability resides in the validator processing routine of the Geode finance contract, specifically the processValidators function that attempts to settle exited validators by burning a quantity of gETH. When the contract’s internal queue does not contain enough gETH to satisfy the amount required for the pending validator exits, the burn operation is executed before the balance check, causing the transaction to revert. Because the revert aborts the entire processing step, any validators that have already signaled exit remain unprocessed and the associated funds stay locked in the contract. Consequently, pool owners and operator accounts do not receive the fees they are entitled to, and users observing the UI see exited validators with no corresponding refunds or fee payouts, creating the impression that funds have vanished. The issue occurs only under the condition that the gETH balance earmarked for processing is insufficient, which may happen intermittently as deposits arrive asynchronously. It was discovered during a collaborative security review with the core development team, where the auditors noticed that the contract could not advance when the queue was empty, leading to stuck funds. The problem is subtle because the contract does not emit a distinct error message for the insufficient‑balance case; instead it simply reverts, making it easy to miss during routine testing unless the specific edge case is exercised. This class of bug can be described as an improper ordering of state‑changing operations combined with an inadequate pre‑condition check, a common pattern in accounting‑logic contracts where balance validation must precede token burns or transfers. To remediate the issue, the burn of gETH should be moved out of the internal _realizeProcessedEther routine and performed only after the contract has confirmed that the required amount is available, for example within the _fulfill and _fulfillBatch functions where the actual fulfillment logic resides. By restructuring the flow so that the balance verification happens before any irreversible token destruction, the contract can safely process whatever amount is currently available, record the shortfall, and later complete the remaining portion when additional gETH arrives, thereby preventing funds from becoming permanently inaccessible and ensuring that operator fees are correctly distributed.
summary: When there is not enough gETH enqueued to process validators, it causes a revert and it is not possible to processValidators. Thus, there can be stuck funds even though there are exited validators. Additionally this prevents operators and pool owners from getting their fee. This is a serious problem. We need to process the amount already requested. But it creates a problem to track the rest and process when more gETH comes. This finding has been identified in close collaboration with the Geode core developer team.

title: MJR-8 Unnecessary allowance
content: The vulnerability consists of an unnecessary ERC20 allowance being granted by the vault contract during a withdrawal operation. In the YearnV2 implementation the withdraw function is designed to burn the caller’s share tokens rather than transfer the underlying asset, which means the contract never needs to move ERC20 tokens on behalf of the user. However, the code still calls the token’s approve method and sets an allowance for the vault to spend the user’s tokens. The root cause is a logical mismatch: the developer assumed a transfer would be required and therefore added an allowance, but the actual business logic only burns shares. Because the allowance remains active, any address that can call the token’s transferFrom function with the vault’s allowance can move the underlying tokens out of the vault without the user’s consent. An attacker who obtains the allowance (for example by being the vault or by exploiting a separate contract that can invoke transferFrom) can drain the vault’s token balance, resulting in loss of funds for all depositors. This issue manifests whenever a user initiates a withdrawal; the contract silently creates an allowance that is never used for the intended burn operation, exposing the token balance to potential misuse. All users who have deposited tokens into the vault, as well as the protocol that relies on the vault’s accounting, are affected because the unexpected allowance breaks the assumption that only the vault can manage its own assets. The problem was discovered during a manual security audit that compared the withdraw logic with the allowance handling and identified the redundant approve call. It can be hard to notice because the approve call does not produce an immediate error and the allowance may appear harmless in normal operation, yet it opens a hidden attack surface. To remediate the issue, the contract should stop granting any ERC20 allowance during withdrawal, removing the approve call entirely, or ensure that no external address can invoke transferFrom with that allowance. This aligns the implementation with the intended accounting model where shares are burned and no token transfer is required, eliminating the risk of unauthorized token movement and preserving the integrity of user balances.
summary: Vault's withdraw function burns shares, so allowance is unnecessary: YearnV2.sol#L130

title: MJR-9 Incorrect usage of function returned value
content: The vulnerability resides in the vault contract’s withdraw function, which is intended to return the number of vault shares that were burned when a user redeems their tokens. Instead, the implementation returns the raw amount of underlying tokens that were transferred to the caller. This mismatch between the documented API contract and the actual return value constitutes an incorrect‑return‑value bug, a class of accounting errors where a function reports a value that does not reflect the operation performed. The root cause is a developer oversight: the function captures and returns the token transfer amount rather than the share amount calculated by the vault’s accounting logic. Because the function still transfers the correct token amount, the error is not immediately visible on the user interface; however, any external contract, script, or off‑chain service that relies on the returned value to update its internal bookkeeping will record an inaccurate share balance. An attacker or a careless developer could exploit this by assuming they received a larger share balance than they actually hold, leading to subsequent operations (such as further withdrawals or voting) being authorized on an inflated balance. The impact includes potential loss of funds, broken accounting invariants, and user confusion where the UI shows a successful withdrawal but the reported share balance remains unchanged or becomes zero. The bug manifests every time the withdraw function is called, affecting all users of the vault and any protocol components that integrate with it. It was discovered during a formal security audit performed by MixBytes, and its subtle nature makes it hard to notice because the token transfer succeeds and no revert occurs; only the return data is wrong, which many callers may ignore. The proper remediation is to modify the withdraw implementation so that it returns the exact number of shares burned, or to remove the return value entirely if it is not required, thereby aligning the function’s observable behavior with its intended specification and restoring correct accounting across the protocol.
summary: Vault's withdraw function returns amount of tokens which was transferred, not shares: YearnV2.sol#L145

title: User rewards stop accruing after any `_writeCheckpoint` calling action
content: The vulnerability is an off‑by‑one error in the checkpoint‑writing routine of the gauge contract that incorrectly records the voting status for newly created balance checkpoints. When a user who has previously voted performs any balance‑affecting operation – such as depositing more tokens, withdrawing, or claiming rewards – the internal function _writeCheckpoint creates a new checkpoint. Because the code reads the voted flag from checkpoints[account][_nCheckPoints] instead of the last existing checkpoint at checkpoints[account][_nCheckPoints‑1], the newly stored checkpoint always receives a voted flag of false. The reward‑calculation logic later iterates over checkpoints and only credits rewards for periods where the checkpoint’s voted flag is true. Consequently, any checkpoint created after the balance change is treated as a non‑voted period, causing the contract to skip reward accrual for the entire interval until the user casts another vote. From the user’s point of view, expected rewards disappear: after a deposit or withdrawal the UI may show a sudden drop to zero pending rewards, even though the user’s voting status has not changed. This mismatch violates the protocol’s economic model, which assumes that rewards continue to accrue for voted users regardless of ordinary balance updates. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when the reviewers examined the _writeCheckpoint implementation and observed that the vote status was never carried over to the new checkpoint. It can be hard to notice because the balance updates succeed and no explicit error is thrown; the symptom is simply a loss of expected yield. The flaw belongs to the class of checkpoint‑state mis‑assignment bugs, where an incorrect index or missing range check leads to wrong flag propagation, breaking downstream accounting logic. To remediate, the code should retrieve the previous checkpoint’s voted flag using the index _nCheckPoints‑1, ensuring that the new checkpoint inherits the correct voting status. This change restores proper reward accrual for all periods between balance‑changing actions, aligning contract behavior with the intended incentive design.
summary:
Any user balance affecting action, i.e. deposit, withdraw/withdrawToken or getReward, calls _writeCheckpoint to update the balance records used for the earned reward estimation. The issue is that _writeCheckpoint always sets false to `voted` flag for the each new checkpoint due to wrong index used in the mapping access, while only voted periods are eligible for accruing the rewards.

This way any balance changing action of a voted user will lead to stopping of the rewards accrual for the user, until next vote will be cast. I.e. any action that has no relation to voting and should have only balance change as the reward accruing process impact, in fact removes any future rewards from the user until the next vote.

Setting the severity to be high as the impact here violates system logic and means next periods accrued rewards loss for a user.

title: Bribe Rewards Struck In Contract If Deposited During First Epoch
content: The vulnerability consists of bribe rewards that are deposited into the Bribe contract during the first epoch (day 0) becoming permanently unclaimable. The root cause is a timing mismatch: the contract allows bribes to be added immediately after deployment, but the internal logic that permits voters to claim those bribes requires a minimum amount of reward tokens to be available, which only accrues after a seven‑day delay tied to the VELO emission schedule. Because the claim‑ability check is performed against the reward balance, any bribe added before the first reward emission fails the check and the contract never provides a path to release the deposited tokens. An attacker or any user who adds bribes during this initial window can therefore lock tokens in the contract with no mechanism to withdraw them. The impact is that funds disappear from the perspective of the depositor – the UI may show a successful transfer, but the claimable balance remains zero and the tokens remain stranded in the Bribe contract indefinitely. This situation occurs only for the first week after a Bribe contract (and its associated Gauge) is deployed, but because new Bribes and Gauges can be created permissionlessly, the bug can be reproduced for every new pair of contracts, potentially affecting any protocol that wishes to seed rewards immediately. The issue was identified during a security audit through logical analysis of the reward‑distribution flow. It is hard to notice because the lockup only manifests in the very early stage of a contract’s lifecycle, a period that may be overlooked during functional testing. To remediate the bug, the contract should either prevent bribe deposits before the reward emission begins, align the start of the bribe period with the VELO reward schedule, or add an administrative rescue function that can recover tokens inadvertently locked during the first epoch. In abstract terms, the flaw is a classic edge‑case timing error that violates the accounting assumption that rewards are always available when bribes are claimable, resulting in a permanent loss of funds for anyone who provides bribes during the first epoch.
summary: Bribe rewards added to the `Bribe` contract in the first epoch will not be claimable by any voters, and the rewards will struck in the `Bribe` contract.

title: Voting overwrites `checkpoint.voted` in last checkpoint, so users can just vote right before claiming rewards
content:
The vulnerability resides in the gauge contract’s reward accounting mechanism, where the `voted` flag of the most recent checkpoint is overwritten instead of a new checkpoint being created when a user’s voting status changes. The `earned` function checks the `voted` flag of the latest checkpoint (cp0) to decide whether to credit the caller with rewards for the elapsed period. Because the contract does not preserve historical voting status, a user can set the `voted` flag to true immediately before invoking the reward claim, satisfy the `if (cp0.voted)` condition, and receive rewards that are calculated for the entire time since the user’s last interaction with the gauge. After the claim, the user can immediately call `voter.reset` (or an equivalent function) to clear the voting status in the same transaction, effectively erasing any evidence of having voted throughout the reward interval.

The root cause is the lack of a checkpoint per vote‑status transition, causing the contract to treat the latest flag as evidence of continuous voting. Exploitation is straightforward: an attacker (or any participant) votes for the gauge right before calling `earned`/`claim`, passes the `voted` check, receives the full period reward, and then resets the vote, all within one transaction. This bypasses the intended economic incentive that should reward only those who keep their escrowed VELO voted for the gauge over time.

When this condition occurs—specifically when a user calls a function that triggers `gauge.earned` after having toggled their vote status in the same block—the protocol distributes rewards to a user who has practically not provided voting weight for the majority of the reward window. The impact is a dilution of reward value for honest participants, potential depletion of the reward pool, and a break in the protocol’s accounting assumptions that voting participation correlates with reward entitlement. Users who expect to earn proportional rewards based on their voting duration may see unusually high payouts without having maintained a vote, leading to confusion and perceived unfairness. The issue was uncovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, which included a proof‑of‑concept test where two accounts—one that voted continuously for six days and another that voted only immediately before claiming—received identical non‑zero reward amounts.

Because the reward calculation appears correct on the surface, the problem is subtle and may go unnoticed unless the historical voting status is examined. The symptom from a user’s perspective is that the UI shows a normal reward amount but the underlying logic allowed the reward to be claimed without any prior voting activity; balances may be reduced more quickly than anticipated, and the protocol’s incentive model no longer aligns with its design.

A conceptual fix involves creating a distinct checkpoint each time a user’s voting status changes (`setVoteStatus`), preserving the historical `voted` flag rather than overwriting it. Additionally, the reward eligibility check should reference the voting status at the start of the reward period or maintain a cumulative voting weight over time, ensuring that only participants who have been continuously voting earn the full period reward. The patched mainnet deployment removed the `voted` logic entirely, illustrating that a redesign of the incentive scheme is required to restore proper accounting and prevent reward sidestepping.

[Gauge.sol#L195](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-05-velodrome/blob/7fda97c570b758bbfa7dd6724a336c43d4041740/contracts/contracts/Gauge.sol#L195)

title: Attacker can block LayerZero channel
content: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that arises from the default blocking behavior of LayerZero messaging. When a cross‑chain transaction sent to a destination contract fails, LayerZero stores the failed message and automatically blocks the entire channel for the source‑destination pair until the message is successfully retried. The contracts under review – a RedemptionSender and its corresponding RedemptionReceiver – forward messages without implementing the non‑blocking pattern recommended by LayerZero, nor do they expose the forceResumeReceive function that allows an administrator to clear a stuck message. Because the receiver does not guard against arbitrary callers and does not verify the integrity of incoming payloads, any attacker can craft a payload that forces the receiver to revert. Once the receiver reverts, the offending message is marked as failed and stored, causing the channel between the Fantom (FTM) source and Optimism destination to become blocked. As a result, all subsequent legitimate cross‑chain calls from the same source address are prevented from being delivered, effectively bricking the redemption functionality. This issue can be triggered at any time the attacker can invoke the LayerZero sendMessage function, which is publicly accessible according to the documentation. The impact is that users attempting to redeem assets across chains receive no response, see balances unchanged or even reduced if partial state changes occurred before the revert, and the protocol loses the ability to process future redemptions, potentially locking funds forever. The problem was discovered during a security audit that compared the contract’s implementation against LayerZero’s guidance on message ordering and non‑blocking designs. It is difficult to notice because normal operation proceeds without error; only after a deliberately failing transaction does the channel become immobile, manifesting as missing updates or silent failures in the UI. To remediate the issue, the contracts should adopt the non‑blocking LzApp pattern, implement proper exception handling for incoming messages, and expose the forceResumeReceive (or forceReceive) hook so that administrators can purge or retry failed messages. Additionally, the contract should restrict who can invoke the sendMessage function or validate payloads before processing, thereby preventing untrusted callers from deliberately causing a revert. By addressing these design flaws, the protocol can preserve message throughput, avoid permanent channel blockage, and ensure that cross‑chain fund movements remain reliable.
summary:
According to the LayerZero docs, the default behavior is that when a transaction on the destination application fails, the channel between the src and dst app is blocked. Before any new transactions can be executed, the failed transaction has to be retried until it succeeds.

See <https://layerzero.gitbook.io/docs/faq/messaging-properties#message-ordering> & <https://layerzero.gitbook.io/docs/guides/advanced/nonblockinglzapp>

So an attacker is able to initiate a transaction they know will fail to block the channel between FTM and Optimism. The RedemptionSender & Receiver won’t be usable anymore.

title: User’s Staked ETH Can Be Stuck in the Protocol Through Two Cases
content: The contract suite allows a user to stake ETH through a deposit() function that imposes no lower bound on the amount deposited, while the corresponding withdrawal mechanism requires a minimum request size of 0.05 ETH. This asymmetry creates a logical inconsistency: a staker who initially deposits less than 0.05 ETH can later be prevented from adding the missing amount because the pool may become private or the Portal contract may be paused, both of which block further deposits. In the first scenario the pool owner changes the pool visibility to private after the small deposit, so the user cannot increase the stake to meet the withdrawal threshold. In the second scenario the contract is paused, which also disables deposits. When the user subsequently attempts to enqueue a withdrawal, the call reverts with the minimum‑size error, and because the user cannot make an additional deposit, the originally staked ETH remains locked in the pool with no way to retrieve it. The impact is financial: the affected user’s funds are effectively frozen, and the protocol’s reputation suffers because users cannot rely on the ability to withdraw their stake. The vulnerability is discovered during a security audit that exercised edge‑case flows and observed the mismatch between deposit and withdrawal constraints. It is hard to notice in normal operation because the deposit succeeds and the UI may not warn that a later change in pool visibility or a pause will make the funds unrecoverable. The bug belongs to the class of “minimum‑withdrawal‑size mismatch” or “state‑dependent lock‑up” defects, where business logic assumes that users can always satisfy a minimum withdrawal amount, but protocol state changes invalidate that assumption. To remediate, the protocol should either enforce the same minimum deposit amount as the withdrawal request, remove the minimum‑withdrawal requirement, or adjust the visibility and pause logic to allow users to top‑up their stake after a pool becomes private or the contract is paused, thereby ensuring that funds can always be withdrawn according to the advertised rules.
summary:
The deposit() function in the Portal.sol contract allows users to stake their ETH into any staking pool that is created. If the user wants to unstake his ETH he must make a withdrawal request to the WithdrawalContract.sol contract of the given staking pool by calling the enqueue() function. Note: When a staking pool is created, a separate contract is deployed for that staking pool called WithdrawalContract.sol. The impact is primarily financial, as the current implementation for enqueue() function in WithdrawalContract.sol compels users to initiate a withdrawal with a minimum of 0.05 ETH.

In contrast Portal.sol, the deposit() function lacks any restrictions on the amount of ETH that can be added to a staking pool. The following two scenarios show two Proof of Concepts of how user’s funds can be stuck in the protocol.

title: AaveV3 RewardsController provides rewards in any token, should be handled separately
content: The vulnerability originates from the assumption that rewards distributed by the Aave V3 RewardsController are always a single, known token (typically WAVAX). In reality the RewardsController can emit rewards in any ERC‑20 token, and these reward tokens are accounted for separately from the protocol’s yield. The strategy contract treats the rewards as if they were always WAVAX and does not provide a dedicated mechanism to claim, convert, or otherwise manage arbitrary reward tokens. Consequently, when a reward token other than WAVAX is received, it is deposited into the ReservePool without being swapped or forwarded to the network wallet. This mismatch can cause the ReservePool to hold unexpected token balances, leading to accounting inconsistencies, inability to use the rewards for intended purposes, and potential loss of value if the tokens cannot be swapped or are left idle. The issue can be exploited by simply triggering a reward distribution in a non‑WAVAX token; the protocol will silently accept the token, but downstream logic that expects only WAVAX will fail to process it, resulting in funds that appear to disappear from the network’s perspective. The impact is that users and the protocol may see lower network balances, missing refunds, or zero‑value rewards despite a successful distribution event. The problem manifests whenever the RewardsController emits a token that the strategy does not explicitly handle, which can happen at any time the Aave market adds a new incentive token or when an existing incentive changes its reward asset. All participants that rely on the ReservePool’s balance – including liquidity providers, network operators, and auditors – are affected because the protocol’s accounting assumptions are violated. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the interaction between the AaveV3Strategy and the ReservePool and noted that the code only references WAVAX when processing rewards. It is subtle because the contract does not revert or emit an obvious error; the unexpected token simply sits in the pool, making the problem easy to overlook during normal operation. To remediate, the strategy should implement a separate claim‑rewards function that can retrieve any reward token, and the ReservePool should either forward those tokens to a designated network wallet for conversion or include a generic swap routine that converts non‑WAVAX assets into WAVAX, handling failures gracefully. This class of bug falls under improper token handling or reward‑asset assumption errors, where the contract’s logic is tightly coupled to a specific token type instead of being token‑agnostic. From a user’s perspective, a participant may expect to receive a reward in WAVAX but sees no increase in their balance, or they may notice stray token contracts appearing in the pool’s holdings, leading to confusion and the perception that “funds disappeared” or “rewards are missing”.
summary: The RewardsController from AaveV3 rewards are separate from the yield accrued and can be several different tokens. Thus, they should be handled differently.

title: Not updating MINT_COUNT_CID and BURN_COUNT_CID
content: The vulnerability resides in the batch minting and burning functions of the GameItems contract. These functions invoke the internal _mintBatch and _burnBatch routines to create or destroy multiple token IDs in a single call, but they omit any update to the accounting variables that track the total number of items minted (MINT_COUNT_CID) and burned (BURN_COUNT_CID). Because the contract relies on these counters to calculate the overall supply of each game item, the omission causes the reported supply to diverge from the actual on‑chain balances. The root cause is a missing state‑update step in the batch pathways; the single‑item mint and burn functions correctly adjust the counters, while the batch variants were implemented without mirroring that logic. An attacker who possesses the MINTER_ROLE or the GAME_LOGIC_CONTRACT_ROLE can invoke mintBatch or burnBatch with arbitrarily large arrays, inflating the token supply without the counters reflecting the change. This discrepancy can be exploited to mislead users, break rarity calculations, and potentially allow economic attacks such as over‑minting rare items while the protocol’s accounting reports a normal supply. The impact is high because the protocol’s tokenomics, rarity tiers, and any features that depend on accurate total supply (e.g., marketplace pricing, reward distribution) become unreliable, eroding trust and possibly leading to financial loss for players. The flaw manifests whenever batch operations are executed, which is allowed during normal gameplay when the authorized roles call these functions. All token holders, game designers, and any external services that query the supply are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that compared the behavior of single‑item and batch functions and noticed that the supply‑tracking variables were never touched in the batch paths. It can be hard to notice because the contract may still emit Transfer events and appear to work correctly on a per‑transaction basis, while the aggregate accounting remains wrong; typical unit tests that only check individual minting may not cover batch scenarios. The proper remediation is to add explicit logic inside mintBatch and burnBatch that iterates over the provided ids and amounts, incrementing MINT_COUNT_CID for each minted amount and BURN_COUNT_CID for each burned amount, thereby keeping the global supply counters in sync with the actual token balances. In broader terms, this is a classic example of an accounting or state‑synchronization bug where batch processing bypasses essential bookkeeping, leading to supply misreporting and potential economic manipulation.

title: Unauthorized access to update() function
content: An unauthorized access vulnerability exists in the update() function of the GigaNameNFTBeforeUpdateHandler and GigaNoobNFTBeforeUpdateHandler contracts. The function is invoked by GameNFT._update() during mint, transfer, or burn, and it updates the datastore in AccountSystem by removing the previous owner record and inserting a new owner record. Because the update() function lacks any access control, any external address can call it directly with arbitrary tokenContract, to, and tokenId parameters. An attacker can therefore invoke update() on an already minted token, causing the original owner's entry to be deleted and replaced with an attacker‑controlled address. The AccountSystem later checks whether an address already has an account before allowing mintWithEth(); after the unauthorized update the original owner’s record is missing, while the attacker’s address appears to already own an account, so subsequent legitimate mint attempts by the rightful owner revert with the error "User already has an account". This effect manifests when a user tries to mint a GigaNoobNFT after their token has been transferred or burned, but the datastore has been tampered with. The impact is that legitimate users are blocked from minting new NFTs, potentially losing access to game features and causing loss of expected value. The vulnerability was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the handler contracts and noticed the absence of modifiers such as onlyRole or onlyOwner on the update() entry point. Because the function does not emit obvious events and the datastore manipulation is internal, the issue can be hard to notice until users encounter unexpected revert messages. The bug belongs to the class of access‑control bypass or unauthorized state mutation vulnerabilities, where a public function that should be restricted can be called by anyone to corrupt critical protocol state. From a user perspective the UI shows a transaction failure with "User already has an account" even though the user has never created an account, leading to confusion and perceived loss of funds. The proper mitigation is to restrict the update() function so that only the corresponding NFT contract (GigaNameNFT or GigaNoobNFT) can invoke it, typically by adding a role‑based check (e.g., onlyRole(GAME_LOGIC_CONTRACT_ROLE)) or an onlyOwner modifier that validates the caller against the expected contract address. This restores the integrity of the ownership datastore and prevents unauthorized overwriting of owner records.

title: Soulbound tokens cannot be minted or burnt due to an invalid check
content: The vulnerability resides in the overridden _update function of the GameNFT contract, which is shared by the GigaNoobNFT and GigaNameNFT contracts. When a token is minted, transferred, or burnt, the function is invoked to perform bookkeeping. Inside the function a boolean flag isSoulbound is obtained from token metadata and a require statement unconditionally rejects any operation on a token that is marked as soulbound: require(!isSoulbound, "GameNFT: Token is soulbound"). Because the check does not differentiate between a normal transfer, a mint (where the previous owner should be address(0)), or a burn (where the recipient should be address(0)), the contract erroneously reverts minting and burning of soulbound tokens. The root cause is an invalid conditional that treats the soulbound flag as a blanket prohibition rather than a rule that should only apply to transfers after the token exists. An attacker or a careless developer can trigger the bug simply by flagging a token as soulbound before attempting to mint it, causing the transaction to revert and effectively denying service for that token type. Legitimate users experience the failure as a transaction that reverts with the message "GameNFT: Token is soulbound", resulting in no token being created or destroyed and only the gas cost being lost. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s inheritance hierarchy and the overridden _update logic, where the auditor noticed that the soulbound check was placed before any verification of the operation context. The bug is subtle because the same _update function is used for all token lifecycle events, and developers may assume that the soulbound flag only blocks transfers, not minting or burning. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition for any token intended to be soulbound: such tokens cannot be minted, cannot be burned, and therefore cannot be used in the game’s economy, breaking accounting assumptions that soulbound assets are unique, non‑transferable, but still creatable and destroyable when needed. To remediate, the _update function should first determine the nature of the operation – by checking that the previous owner is address(0) for minting or that the recipient address is address(0) for burning – and only then enforce the soulbound restriction for regular transfers. This conceptual fix restores the intended behavior where soulbound tokens are immutable after creation but can still be minted and burnt according to the protocol’s rules.

title: Stuck ETH in GigaNameNFT contract
content: The vulnerability is a permanent fund‑locking condition in the GigaNameNFT contract. The contract is designed to accept ether when an authorized minter calls the mintUsername function to create a new NFT, but it does not provide any mechanism—neither in the contract itself nor in its parent GameNFT contract—for the manager or owner to retrieve the collected ether. The root cause is the absence of a withdrawal function or any payable fallback that forwards the balance to a designated treasury address. As a result, every time mintUsername is invoked with a non‑zero value, the ether is deposited into the contract’s balance and becomes inaccessible because there is no code path that can move those funds out. This can be exploited indirectly: an attacker or any user can send ether to the contract (intentionally via minting or accidentally via a direct transfer) and the funds will be locked forever, effectively stealing the value from the payer and depriving the protocol of expected revenue. The impact is that users who pay for minting receive no refund or benefit beyond the NFT, the protocol’s treasury never receives the collected fees, and the locked ether reduces overall liquidity, potentially affecting downstream economic assumptions. The condition occurs each time the payable mintUsername function is called, or whenever ether is sent to the contract address by any means. All parties that rely on the contract’s ability to forward or withdraw funds—namely the protocol’s manager, the treasury, and the users who paid for the NFT—are affected. The issue was discovered during a systematic security audit that examined the contract’s payable functions and identified the missing withdrawal logic. It can be hard to notice because the contract compiles and runs without errors; transactions succeed, and the contract balance simply grows, which may be interpreted as normal activity rather than a bug. From a user’s perspective, the symptom is that after paying ether to mint an NFT, the expected outcome (the treasury receiving the payment or the user being able to retrieve excess funds) does not happen; the UI may show a successful mint but the protocol’s revenue dashboard shows no incoming funds, and the contract balance appears to hold ether with no visible way to extract it. This class of bug belongs to the “inaccessible funds” or “missing withdrawal” category, where business logic assumes that collected payments can be moved to a designated address, but the implementation fails to provide the necessary function. To remediate, the contract should be updated to include a secure withdrawal method—restricted to an authorized role such as the manager or owner—that uses a low‑level call or transfer to send the entire balance (or a specified amount) to the treasury address, and it should follow best practices such as re‑entrancy guards and proper event emission. Implementing this will align the contract’s behavior with the intended accounting model, ensuring that ether paid for minting is correctly accounted for and can be retrieved by the protocol.
summary: The GigaNameNFT contract is supposed to receive ETH when the minter role calls mintUsername() to mint a GigaNameNFT for a player, however, this contract doesn't implement a mechanism to enable the manager from withdrawing collected ETH (nor does the parent GameNFT contract), which would result in permanently locking the collected ETH in the contract.

title: Zero Username price when it is minted with mintUsername()
content: The vulnerability is a price‑bypass bug that allows an account to be minted without paying the intended Ether fee. The contract architecture stores the mint price in a table identified by the constant ETH_MINT_PRICE_CID. The AccountSystem contract correctly reads this value from its own table and enforces the payment in the mintWithEth function, while the manager can update the price via setMintPrice. However, the GigaNameNFT contract implements an alternative entry point, mintUsername, that also checks the same constant but reads the value from the GigaNameNFT’s own table. Because this table is initialized to zero and the contract provides no setter to change it, the required payment is always zero. Consequently, any caller can invoke mintUsername with no Ether and satisfy the require statement, resulting in a free account creation. This can be exploited simply by calling mintUsername with msg.value set to zero, which passes the insufficient‑payment check and triggers confirmMint, allocating a new username to the caller. The impact is that the protocol loses the revenue it expects from username sales, opens the system to spam or abuse by mass‑minting free accounts, and undermines the economic assumptions of the platform. The bug manifests whenever the GigaNameNFT table’s ETH_MINT_PRICE_CID entry remains at its default zero, which is the case because no function exists to modify it. All users are affected because anyone can obtain a username without paying, and the protocol’s manager cannot enforce the intended fee. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the two minting paths and noticed the divergent price source. It is easy to miss because the require statement appears identical in both contracts, giving the false impression that the same price is being enforced. To remediate, the mintUsername function should reference the same price stored in the AccountSystem table, or the GigaNameNFT contract should expose a setter to keep its price in sync with the manager’s configuration, or the free‑mint path should be removed entirely. In user‑facing terms, a user expecting to pay a fee sees the transaction succeed with zero Ether, leading to a situation where “my username was minted for free” contrary to the advertised cost, effectively causing “funds disappear” from the protocol’s expected revenue stream.

title: increaseNetworkTotal() allows big arbitrage opportunities by depositing before an increase transaction
