Under these conditions the require statements pass, the calculation yields a positive vestedAmount, and the transfer is performed without any check against previously claimed tokens. Users observing their balances may notice that the total supply of tokens allocated to them shrinks unexpectedly, or that the team wallet receives far more tokens than the schedule would allow, leading to a mismatch between expected and actual token distribution. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the function logic with the intended vesting model and identified the missing state variable for tracking claimed tokens. It can be hard to notice because the function appears to respect the vesting timeline and emits a TokensWithdrawn event, giving the impression that only newly vested tokens are being transferred. The root cause is a missing accounting invariant: the contract does not maintain a cumulative claimed amount, which is a classic example of a “vesting double‑spend” or “unbounded claim” bug. To remediate, the contract should introduce a storage variable (e.g., claimedTeamTokens), update it after each successful transfer, and compute the claimable amount as the vested amount minus claimedTeamTokens, ensuring that the team can only withdraw tokens they are entitled to at any point in time.

title: User deposit balance incorrectly zeroed after partial token claim
content: The vulnerability is an improper state update in the token claim routine of a presale contract. When a participant calls the claimTokens function, the contract correctly computes the amount of tokens that have vested based on the user’s original deposit, the total allocation, and the elapsed time. However, immediately after the transfer, the implementation unconditionally sets the user’s deposit balance to zero, regardless of whether the claim represents the full entitlement or only a partial portion of the vested amount. This logic error originates from the absence of a mechanism to track how many tokens have already been withdrawn; the contract treats the deposit as a one‑time claim flag instead of a mutable accounting record. An attacker – or any honest user – can trigger the bug simply by invoking claimTokens after the presale has succeeded. If the user claims before the vesting schedule is complete, they receive the currently vested tokens, but the contract then erases the remaining deposit, preventing any future claims. The impact is that users lose the right to receive the rest of their vested tokens, effectively causing funds to disappear from their perspective. The issue manifests only after the presale is marked successful and the claim function is reachable; it does not affect users who never call claimTokens or who wait until full vesting, although the latter case still suffers from a broken accounting model. The affected parties are all participants who deposited tokens and intend to claim them over time, as well as the protocol that promises a linear vesting schedule. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the claimTokens implementation, where the auditor noted that the deposit mapping was cleared without considering partial withdrawals – a subtle mistake that can be missed because the function appears to transfer the correct vested amount on each call. From a user’s point of view the UI would show a successful token transfer followed by a zero balance, leading to confusion such as “I expected to claim more later but my deposit is now zero”. This violates the business logic that deposits should be decremented only by the amount actually withdrawn, preserving the remaining entitlement. The bug belongs to the class of balance‑reset or accounting‑state bugs, where a contract incorrectly overwrites a persistent balance after a partial operation. To remediate, the contract should maintain a separate record of the amount already claimed (or the remaining deposit) and update that record incrementally, rather than zeroing the entire deposit. This change restores the ability for users to claim their tokens gradually according to the vesting schedule and aligns the on‑chain accounting with the expected financial model.

title: Uniswap V2 pair poisoning DoS vulnerability in liquidity migration
content: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that arises during the liquidity migration step of a token presale when the contract creates a new Uniswap V2 pair with zero initial reserves for both the token and WETH. Because the pair starts with (0,0) reserves, an attacker can send a single wei of WETH to the pair and immediately call the pair’s sync function, which updates the stored reserves to (0,1 wei). The presale’s migration logic later relies on Uniswap V2’s router library function quote, which contains a require statement that both reserveA and reserveB are greater than zero. With the token reserve still equal to zero, any attempt to add liquidity through the router triggers the require and reverts with the message “UniswapV2Library: INSUFFICIENT_LIQUIDITY”. This revert blocks the minting of LP tokens, preventing the presale from completing its transition to the trading phase. From a user’s perspective the presale appears stuck, no liquidity is created, and users are forced to withdraw their contributions, effectively losing the opportunity to trade the token. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the migration flow, where the auditor noticed that the router’s quote function would be called on a freshly created pair without any token balance. The problem is subtle because the pair contract itself does not reject the tiny WETH deposit, and the UI shows no obvious error until the router call fails. The root cause is the assumption that a newly created pair will have non‑zero reserves for both assets, an assumption violated by the attacker’s “poisoning” of the reserve state. The vulnerability belongs to the class of liquidity‑pool poisoning or reserve‑manipulation DoS bugs, where an adversary corrupts internal accounting to make subsequent operations fail. The recommended mitigation is to avoid using the router for the migration and instead transfer the required token and ETH amounts directly to the pair contract and invoke the pair’s mint function, which does not depend on the quote calculation and therefore cannot be blocked by zero‑reserve checks.

title: BPS_TO_DECIMAL conversion is wrong, leading users to dramatically overpay for options
content: The vulnerability is a unit‑conversion error in the constant used to translate basis‑points (bips) into the 18‑decimal fixed‑point format required by the Black‑Scholes pricing routine. The contract defines BPSTODECIMAL as 10e14, which evaluates to 1e15. The correct scaling factor for converting 10 000 bips (1 %) to the 18‑decimal representation is 1e14. Because the constant is ten times larger, every value that is multiplied by BPSTODECIMAL – notably the volatilityDecimal and rateDecimal parameters – becomes ten‑fold inflated. These inflated parameters are fed into the Black‑Scholes algorithm, which computes an option price that is dramatically higher than the true market price. When the contract subsequently uses this price to generate the ask and bid values for an option, the bid that a user must pay is over‑estimated, often by two orders of magnitude, causing users to overpay for the same option. The bug manifests whenever the _computeOptionAskAndBid function is called, i.e., during any option creation or pricing request. It affects all participants who rely on the contract to obtain fair option pricing, leading to loss of funds for buyers and potentially unfair profit for the protocol or malicious actors who can exploit the inflated pricing. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the tester compared the on‑chain price against a reference Black‑Scholes implementation and observed a 200× discrepancy; a simple public test exposing the internal computation confirmed the scaling error. The problem is subtle because the numbers involved are large 18‑decimal integers, and a ten‑fold error does not cause an overflow or revert, only a mis‑priced output that may appear plausible at a glance. The vulnerability belongs to the class of arithmetic scaling bugs where a constant representing a unit conversion is incorrectly defined, leading to systematic mis‑calculation of financial parameters. From a user’s perspective the UI would show a normal option listing, but when the user attempts to purchase the option the required premium is far higher than expected, sometimes resulting in a zero‑profit trade or an unaffordable price. The expected behavior is that the premium reflects the true volatility and risk‑free rate; the actual behavior is that the premium is inflated, breaking the accounting assumptions of the option market. The recommended fix is to correct the constant to 1e14, thereby restoring the proper conversion factor and ensuring that volatility and rate values are accurately represented in the pricing formula.
summary:
The constant value used to convert bips to decimals is defined as:
```solidity
uint256 constant BPSTODECIMAL = 10e14;
```
`10e14` is equivalent to `1e15`, which when multiplied by `10_000 bips` equals `1e19`, which is 10x higher than it should be. The result is that the `decimalVol` and `rateDecimal` values calculated using this value are 10x inflated. When these values are passed into the Black Scholes algorithm, they result in incorrect bids, which automatically clear as approved by the user. Because the volatility number increases the price of options more dramatically than the risk free rate decreases it, the result is (in most cases) a substantially increased option price.

title: Incorrect adjustment for decimals in maxStrikePriceMultiple check
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect decimal scaling in the validation of the maxStrikePriceMultiple parameter for option orders. The contract attempts to compare the user‑provided maxStrikePriceMultiple against the actual multiple by which the strike price exceeds the current asset price. To perform this comparison it multiplies the strike price (expressed with decimals) by the literal 10e18 before dividing by the asset price. The literal 10e18 evaluates to 1e19, which is ten times larger than the intended scaling factor of 1e18. Because of this off‑by‑order‑of‑magnitude error the computed price multiple is always inflated by a factor of ten. Consequently the condition "computed multiple < maxStrikePriceMultiple" frequently fails, causing legitimate orders to be rejected with the error message "option is too far out of the money" even when the strike price is well within the allowed range. The root cause is a misuse of scientific notation in Solidity where 10e18 does not mean ten times 10^18 but rather ten multiplied by 10^18, i.e., 10^19. The bug manifests during the order‑creation or order‑execution path whenever the contract validates the strike‑price relationship. Users who attempt to create or trade options experience transaction reverts, see zero options minted, or notice that their funds are locked in a failed transaction. The affected parties are option creators, traders, and ultimately the protocol because the intended risk‑limit enforcement is broken, potentially leading to loss of trading opportunities or denial‑of‑service for certain price ranges. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the arithmetic expressions and identified the mismatched scaling factor. It can be hard to notice because the literal looks syntactically correct and typical unit‑tests may not cover extreme strike‑price scenarios where the ten‑fold error becomes visible. To remediate the problem the multiplication should use the correct scaling constant 1e18, aligning the computed multiple with the intended decimal precision and restoring the proper comparison logic. In broader terms this is a classic decimal‑handling bug where an incorrect magnitude constant leads to miscalculated financial ratios, breaking business logic that assumes accurate accounting of price differentials.
summary:
When comparing `order.maxStrikePriceMultiple` to the actual multiple by which the strike price exceeds the asset price, the calculation is performed as follows:
```solidity
require(
    order.maxStrikePriceMultiple == 0 || 
    (strikePricedecimal * 10e18) / assetPrice < order.maxStrikePriceMultiple,
    "option is too far out of the money"
);
```
As we can see, the difference in price is multiplied by `10e18` before being divided by the current price. `10e18` is equivalent to `1e19`, which is 10x higher than the intended value. The result is that the multiple representing the gap between the strike price and asset price will always be overrepresented by 10x, causing it to fail the comparison to the `maxStrikePriceMultiple`.

title: Incorrect fee calculation and token accounting in sellToken function
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect fee calculation and token accounting in the sellToken function of the HotCurves contract. The function is supposed to convert a user‑provided amount of tokens into ETH, deduct a referrer fee and a protocol fee, and update the virtual liquidity pool variables. However, the implementation calls the conversion routine multiple times on the same token amount: once to compute the referrer fee, once for the protocol fee, and again for the net amount sent to the seller. Because each call uses the current curve state, the same token slice is converted repeatedly, inflating the ETH values that are transferred to the fee recipients. At the same time, the accounting variables virtualTokenLp, virtualEthLp and realEthLp are updated only for the portion of the tokens that is not subject to fees, meaning the pool’s internal accounting does not reflect the full token inflow or the full ETH outflow. The root cause is a logical error in the order of operations: fees are calculated on the token side before the total ETH equivalent is determined, and the liquidity‑pool state is adjusted inconsistently. An attacker can exploit this by calling sellToken with any token amount; the contract will over‑pay the referrer and fee address, effectively creating ETH out of thin air. The impact is that the protocol loses ETH, users may receive less ETH than expected, and the pool’s invariant is broken, potentially leading to further price distortion or depletion of funds. The bug manifests whenever a user sells tokens, i.e., any execution of sellToken, and affects all participants: token holders who sell, referrers who receive inflated fees, and the protocol that holds the fee address. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the fee‑distribution logic and the updates to virtual liquidity variables. The issue is subtle because the function still returns a positive ETH amount to the seller, so the over‑payment is not obvious from the transaction receipt alone; only a careful comparison of expected versus actual fee amounts reveals the discrepancy. To fix the problem, the function should first compute the total ETH amount corresponding to the full token amount using a single call to the conversion routine, then derive the referrer and protocol fees as percentages of that ETH amount, distribute those fees, and finally send the remaining ETH to the seller. After the transfer, the virtualTokenLp must be increased by the full token amount, and both virtualEthLp and realEthLp must be decreased by the total ETH amount, ensuring the pool’s accounting stays consistent. This class of bug belongs to “incorrect fee calculation and liquidity‑pool accounting” where fees are derived from an intermediate conversion rather than the final value, leading to double‑counting and state inconsistency.
summary: The sellToken function in the HotCurves contract is designed to facilitate the sale of tokens by users, applying fees and distributing them to a referrer and a designated fee address. However, the current implementation contains a flaw in the fee calculation and token accounting logic. The function incorrectly computes the conversion from tokens to ETH multiple times: once for the referrer fee, once for the fee address, and once for the remaining token amount. This repeated conversion over the same portion of the curve leads to inflated ETH amounts being calculated and distributed, resulting in financial discrepancies. Additionally, the virtualTokenLp is only increased by the portion of tokens not related to the fees, which is incorrect. The entire _amount of tokens should be accounted for in the liquidity pool, as all tokens are effectively entering the pool. Similarly, virtualEthLp and realEthLp are only decreased by the eth amount unrelated to the fees, which is also incorrect.

title: Lack of slippage protection in buyToken() and sellToken() leads to sandwich attacks and potential loss of funds
content: The vulnerability stems from the absence of any slippage protection in the contract functions that handle token purchases and sales on a constant‑product bonding curve. The contract calculates token prices using the standard k = x * y formula, which naturally causes the price to rise when a user buys tokens and to fall when a user sells them. Because the buyToken() and sellToken() functions do not enforce a minimum amount of tokens that must be received (or a maximum amount of ETH that may be spent), an attacker who can observe a pending transaction in the mempool can front‑run it, execute a trade that artificially moves the curve price, and then let the victim’s transaction execute at the manipulated price. The victim therefore receives fewer tokens than expected for the same amount of ETH, or pays more ETH than necessary when selling, resulting in an unexpected loss of value. The attacker then reverses the price impact by selling the tokens acquired in the front‑run, capturing a risk‑free profit. This attack can be carried out on both buy and sell paths and only requires the attacker to have the ability to submit a transaction with higher gas priority. The issue affects any user of the contract, the overall token economics of the protocol, and any party that relies on the bonding curve for fair pricing. It was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the price‑calculation logic and noted the lack of a slippage check. The problem is subtle because price movement is an inherent property of bonding curves, so a user may attribute a poor trade outcome to market volatility rather than a malicious manipulation. To remediate the issue, the contract should introduce a slippage‑limit parameter, such as a minimum token amount that must be received (or a maximum acceptable price), and revert the transaction if the actual outcome falls outside this bound. This change restores the expected economic guarantees of the bonding curve and prevents attackers from extracting profit through sandwich attacks.
summary:
The HotCurves contract utilizes a bonding curve with the standard constant product formula (k = x * y) to determine token prices during buy and sell transactions. This means that when tokens are purchased, their price increases, and when they are sold, their price decreases. The buyToken() and sellToken() functions lack slippage protection, making transactions vulnerable to sandwich attacks where a malicious user can manipulate the execution price, leading to unexpectedly high costs or loss of funds for regular users. The following is an example of how such an attack occurs:  
1) A malicious user detects a buy transaction in the mempool. They frontrun this transaction by executing their own purchase first, artificially inflating the token price.  
2) The regular user's transaction is then executed, but at a higher price, causing them to receive fewer tokens for their ETH than expected and potentially incurring significant financial loss.  
3) The malicious user sells the tokens acquired in step 1 at the inflated price, securing a risk-free profit at the expense of the regular user, who has overpaid due to the manipulated price.  
Such an attack can also be executed during token sales.

title: Restriction of transfer can be circumvented by using approve + transferFrom
content: The vulnerability originates from the fact that TrancheVault and FirstLossCover deliberately disable the standard ERC20 transfer function to enforce that tranche shares can only be moved by addresses holding a specific LENDER_ROLE. However, both contracts inherit from ERC20Upgradeable, which still provides the approve and transferFrom functions. Because only the transfer function is overridden to revert, the approve/transferFrom pathway remains operational and can be used to move tokens without triggering the role‑based checks. An attacker or any user can call approve on their own balance, granting another address permission to call transferFrom and relocate the shares to an arbitrary account, including accounts that do not possess the LENDER_ROLE. This circumvention also bypasses the checkLiquidityRequirementForRedemption logic, which is intended to ensure that only accounts linked to the poolOwnerTreasury or evaluationAgent can redeem shares. By approving a transfer to a newly created account that is not subject to this check, the attacker can subsequently redeem the shares and extract value that should have been locked. Furthermore, the flaw enables a lender who has opted into reinvestment to transfer their principal amount to a non‑reinvesting lender; the protocol’s processYieldForLenders function then treats the transferred principal as yield, allowing the recipient to redeem it immediately. The impact is that tranche shares, which are supposed to be non‑transferable and tightly accounted for, can be moved arbitrarily, leading to unauthorized redistribution of principal and yield, violation of accounting assumptions, and potential loss of funds for legitimate lenders. The issue manifests whenever a user or contract interacts with the approve function or when a malicious contract is built to automate the approve‑then‑transferFrom sequence; it does not require any special privileges beyond ownership of the tokens. The affected parties include all lenders, the protocol’s risk‑management layer, and any downstream users who rely on the immutability of share ownership. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the inheritance hierarchy and identified that only transfer was overridden while transferFrom remained functional. It can be difficult to notice because the UI and typical test suites focus on the transfer function, and the approve/transferFrom path is often overlooked in permission‑restricted token designs. To remediate, the contract should either disable transferFrom entirely, override it to include the same role and liquidity checks as transfer, or replace the ERC20 base with an implementation that enforces non‑transferability across all token movement functions. In practice, users may observe that after approving another address, their tranche balance unexpectedly drops to zero, or they receive shares they did not anticipate, and they may be able to redeem more yield than they originally contributed, contradicting the expected behavior that shares are locked and only redeemable under strict conditions.
summary:
In TrancheVault and FirstLossCover, transfer is disabled. However, those inherit from ERC20Upgradeable which includes approve and transferFrom functions that can circumvent this restriction. Here are the following issues that may arise through the use of approve + transferFrom:  
1. TrancheVault shares, intended only for addresses with the LENDER_ROLE, can be sent to an address without this role. A trustless smart contract can be built to make this functionality available as well.  
2. The checkLiquidityRequirementForRedemption check can be bypassed by approving and calling transferFrom() to a new account not associated with poolOwnerTreasury or evaluationAgent, followed by redeeming these shares.  
3. Lender's principal amount can be converted into yield which is readily redeemable, circumventing the redemption process. This is done by transferring the principal amount from a reinvesting lender's account to a non-reinvesting lender's account. The excess amount is treated as yield by the processYieldForLenders function.

title: _getStartOfNextHalfYear does not update year correctly for the second half of the year
content: The contract contains a date‑calculation bug in the internal helper that determines the start timestamp of the next half‑year period. The routine extracts the calendar year and month from a supplied Unix timestamp and then builds a new timestamp for either July 1st or January 1st of the following period. The logic correctly chooses January when the current month is greater than six, but it forgets to increment the year value in that branch. As a result, for any timestamp that falls in the second half of a calendar year (July 1 – December 31), the function returns a timestamp that points to January 1 of the same year instead of January 1 of the next year. The root cause is an off‑by‑one error in the year handling of the date conversion routine. This mis‑calculation can be exploited by any actor who can influence the timestamp supplied to the function or who can trigger a contract operation that relies on the returned period start. For example, a vesting contract that releases tokens when the next half‑year begins will believe the period started earlier than it actually does, allowing a user to claim tokens prematurely or, conversely, causing the contract to delay releases and lock funds longer than intended. The impact is therefore a breach of the intended accounting logic: rewards, interest, or lock‑up schedules may be computed against an incorrect start date, leading to either loss of funds for the protocol or unintended gains for an attacker. The bug manifests only when the input timestamp belongs to the second half of a year; timestamps in the first half behave correctly, which makes the problem easy to miss during casual testing. It was discovered during a formal security audit that highlighted missing unit‑test coverage for the edge case where month > 6. Because the function is pure and does not emit events, the error does not generate obvious on‑chain warnings, and the contract’s UI may simply show a “next period starts today” message while the underlying schedule is actually a year off. Users may notice that a “next half‑year” claim window opens immediately after a July‑date, or that balances that should have been locked until the following January remain unlocked. The vulnerability belongs to the class of calendar‑logic errors, specifically incorrect handling of year rollover in period‑boundary calculations. To remediate, the implementation must explicitly increment the year when the month exceeds six before constructing the new timestamp, and comprehensive unit tests should be added for timestamps at the boundary of the year (e.g., a zero timestamp representing the Unix epoch and a timestamp in December). This correction restores the intended business rule that the next half‑year always begins on either July 1 or January 1 of the following calendar year, preserving the integrity of time‑based accounting and fund release mechanisms.

title: Calling splitValue when token index is not the latest will overwrite other claims' storage
content: The vulnerability resides in the splitValue routine that creates new token identifiers by incrementing a global token counter (_tokenID) without taking the token type’s current maximum index into account. When a holder calls splitValue on a token that is not the most recent identifier for its type, the function computes the new IDs as ++currentID, where currentID is initialized from the global counter. Because other tokens of the same type may already occupy those sequential IDs, the newly generated IDs collide with existing ones. As a result, the mapping that stores each token’s value (tokenValues) is overwritten with the split amounts, effectively replacing the original holder’s balance with the split values. In the illustrated scenario, Alice splits her token 1 into two tokens of 5 units each. The algorithm assigns the new IDs 2 and 3, but token 2 already belongs to Bob and holds 100 units. The assignment tokenValues[2] = 5 overwrites Bob’s balance, reducing his token to 5 units, while Alice’s newly minted tokens are mistakenly associated with Bob’s token type. This mis‑allocation can be exploited by any user who can trigger splitValue on a non‑latest token, causing other users’ balances to be reduced or redirected without their consent. The impact includes loss of value for honest participants, incorrect accounting in the protocol, and potential confusion for users who see their token balances shrink or receive unexpected token types. The bug manifests only when the token being split is not the highest index for its type; if the token is the latest, the collision does not occur. All token holders, the protocol’s accounting layer, and any downstream applications that rely on tokenValues are affected. The issue was uncovered during a manual security audit that examined the logic of _splitValue and identified the misuse of the global counter. It is subtle because the minting operation still succeeds and the token IDs appear valid, making the overwritten values hard to detect without explicit state inspection. To remediate, the contract should compute new token IDs based on the type‑specific maximum index (e.g., _typeID + ++maxIndex[_typeID]) rather than the global counter, ensuring that each newly minted token receives a unique identifier that does not clash with existing tokens. This change restores the invariant that tokenValues entries are never overwritten by split operations, preserving correct balances and preventing accidental fund loss.

title: TransferFrom is incorrectly treated as a view function
content: The vulnerability originates from an incorrect classification of the token TransferFrom operation inside the MultiCurrencyPrecompile module. The execute function uses a check_function_modifier routine to label each selector with a FunctionModifier that tells the execution environment whether the call is payable, non‑payable, or view‑only. Because the match statement only lists Function::Transfer as NonPayable and falls back to FunctionModifier::View for all other selectors, the TransferFrom selector is mistakenly treated as a view function. TransferFrom is defined by the ERC20 standard as a state‑changing operation that moves tokens from one account to another using an allowance; it must be allowed to modify storage and therefore requires a NonPayable modifier. When the runtime interprets TransferFrom as view, it blocks any state mutation, causing the call to either revert or silently succeed without updating balances. From a user perspective this manifests as a transaction that appears to have been mined but results in no token movement – balances remain unchanged, refunds are missing, or the UI shows a zero balance after an attempted transfer. The bug is discovered during a manual security audit when the reviewer noticed the missing case in the selector match. It is hard to notice because the function signature is syntactically correct and the contract compiles without warnings; only when a TransferFrom call is exercised does the mismatch surface, often only in environments that enforce view‑only contexts. The impact is high because any workflow that relies on TransferFrom – such as delegated payments, escrow releases, or automated token swaps – may fail, leading to loss of expected functionality, user frustration, and potential financial loss if callers assume the transfer succeeded. The issue belongs to the class of function‑modifier misclassification bugs, where a state‑changing function is incorrectly labeled as read‑only, violating business logic that assumes token balances are updated after the call. To remediate, the match statement should be extended to include Function::TransferFrom and assign it FunctionModifier::NonPayable, aligning the modifier with the function’s intended side effects and restoring correct state transition behavior.

title: Improper use of locked funds as liquidity in PositionInteractionFacet
content: The vulnerability resides in the way the PositionInteractionFacet contract accounts for token liquidity when settling Call options. When a holder exercises a Call option, the contract is supposed to pay the profit (pnl) from tokens that are freely available, i.e., not already earmarked for other obligations. Instead, the internal _payout function reads the field rewardsByToken[pos.buyToken].totalRewards and treats this amount as liquid pool balance. Because the reward system updates indexes as soon as rewards accrue, those tokens are already considered distributed to users, even if they have not been claimed. Consequently the contract mistakenly believes it can draw from these rewards to cover the Call payout. No explicit reservation of the portion of the buyToken that is locked for future Put option settlements exists, so the same tokens are double‑counted: once as locked collateral and again as free liquidity. An attacker can trigger the flaw by exercising a Call option when the totalRewards value is large enough that the required payout exceeds the truly free balance. The contract will then pull the shortfall from the locked pool, reducing the reserve that backs Put options. This can lead to a situation where later Put holders receive less than their entitled payout, or the contract may revert because the pool amount becomes negative. From a user’s perspective the symptom is a missing or reduced refund: a Call exerciser receives the expected profit, but a subsequent Put holder sees a zero or unexpectedly low balance, or the UI may still display a healthy pool balance while the underlying accounting is broken. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the accounting model of rewards with the actual token transfers. It is hard to notice because the ledger’s totalRewards field appears as a positive balance, giving the impression of ample liquidity, while the logical reservation of those tokens is hidden in the reward index mechanism. The bug belongs to the class of “incorrect liquidity accounting” or “double‑counting of reserved assets”. To remediate the problem the contract should separate available and locked balances for each token, avoid using reward totals as a source of payout, and instead swap the underlying assets or use a dedicated liquidity pool that respects the lockedUsd invariant. By introducing explicit checks that ensure only truly free tokens are used for Call payouts, the protocol can preserve the collateral needed for Put settlements and prevent funds from disappearing unexpectedly.

title: Vulnerability in PositionInteractionFacet slippage control due to spot price
content: The vulnerability is a price‑manipulation weakness in the contract function that swaps one asset for another during position exercise or liquidation. The function obtains the spot price directly from a Uniswap pool via a quote call and then applies a slippage tolerance to the quoted amountInMaximum. Because the contract trusts the instantaneous pool price, an attacker who can observe the pending transaction can front‑run it and trade against the same pool to shift the spot price in their favour. When the contract subsequently queries the pool, it receives a manipulated price, calculates a higher amountInMaximum, and after applying the slippage buffer it ends up approving and spending more input tokens than necessary. The attacker therefore receives a better exchange rate, while the protocol loses value – the contract swaps at an unfavorable rate, resulting in a net loss of funds or a reduced output amount for the user. This issue occurs whenever the contract performs a swap as part of exerciseOrLiquidatePosition, i.e., during liquidation or position closure, and any external actor with the ability to submit a transaction before the contract’s swap can exploit it. The affected parties include the protocol itself, token holders whose positions are liquidated, and any users expecting a fair swap rate. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the flow of the swap function and identified the reliance on a single‑block spot price without protection against manipulation. The problem is subtle because the slippage check appears to provide safety, yet it merely widens the margin for error after the price has already been tampered with, making the abnormal loss easy to miss in normal operation. To remediate, the contract should replace the direct spot‑price quote with a price source that is resistant to short‑term manipulation, such as a time‑weighted average price (TWAP) oracle, a trusted external price feed, or by setting a strict sqrtPriceLimitX96 bound that limits how far the price can move within a single swap. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of oracle‑or price‑feed manipulation vulnerabilities where on‑chain price data is used without sufficient sanitisation, leading to front‑running and sandwich attacks that break the expected accounting logic of the protocol, causing users to receive less than expected or see balances unexpectedly reduced.

title: payOff() underflow in OperationalTreasury locks assets permanently
content: The vulnerability resides in the payoff routine of the OperationalTreasury contract. The function calculates a fee amount (feesUSD) by multiplying the full position size by a fee percentage and the current market price, without taking the actual profit‑and‑loss (pnl) of the position into account. When the market price is only marginally higher than the strike price, the pnl – which is the difference between the current price and the strike price multiplied by the position amount – can be smaller than the fee that is charged. The code then subtracts feesUSD from pnl to obtain a net amount. Because Solidity 0.8+ reverts on arithmetic underflow, the expression pnl‑feesUSD triggers a revert whenever feesUSD exceeds pnl. The revert occurs before the contract calls the external exerciseOrLiquidatePosition function that would normally release the underlying assets from the pool. As a result, the assets remain locked in the pool forever, effectively making the user’s funds inaccessible. This condition appears only in edge cases where the price movement is tiny, so it may be missed during normal testing and can look like a generic transaction failure. The issue was identified during a manual security audit that examined the payoff logic and fee calculation. It is hard to notice because the contract does not emit a specific error message for the underflow; the transaction simply fails. The impact is that any trader whose position closes with a small profit may lose the ability to withdraw their collateral, harming users and reducing the protocol’s liquidity. The affected parties include position owners, the treasury, and any participants relying on the pool’s solvency. To remediate, the fee calculation must be bounded by the actual pnl – for example by capping feesUSD to the pnl value before subtraction – or by deriving fees directly from the pnl rather than from the gross position size. This change prevents the underflow, ensures the liquidation call is always executed, and guarantees that assets are either returned to the user or correctly accounted for as fees.

title: Option premium calculation underprices options
content: The vulnerability is a pricing mismatch that causes option contracts to be underpriced because the premium is calculated with the user‑provided period in seconds while the actual expiry timestamp is rounded up to the end of the day. The root cause lies in two separate functions: the premium calculation routine uses the raw period value to feed the Black‑Scholes formula, whereas the maturity date computation adds the same period to the current block timestamp and then aligns the result to the next midnight, effectively extending the real duration by up to 86,399 seconds (just under one full day). An attacker or trader can exploit this discrepancy by selecting a short‑term period, for example seven days, and receiving an option that actually lasts almost eight days while paying a premium that reflects only seven days. The impact is a systematic under‑payment of the time value component of the option price, which can lead to a significant loss of revenue for the protocol, especially for high‑volatility assets or short‑duration contracts where the time value is a large proportion of the premium. The condition occurs whenever the requested period does not end exactly at 23:59:59 UTC, which is true for virtually all user‑specified periods that are not a multiple of a full day. All participants who purchase options – traders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the accounting assumptions of the option pricing model no longer match the actual contract terms. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the premium calculation in the internal _calculatePremium function with the maturity date logic in _computeMaturityDate, revealing a gap of up to one day between the two values. The bug is subtle because the difference is less than a day and may appear negligible, yet it manifests as a noticeable premium shortfall (approximately 23 % in the provided example) and can be missed by casual testing that does not examine boundary‑condition timestamps. To remediate the problem, the premium calculation should be based on the true time‑to‑expiry derived from the rounded maturity timestamp, or the maturity computation should be changed to use the exact period without rounding, ensuring that the pricing model and the contract’s expiry are consistent. This class of vulnerability can be described as a time‑value misalignment or pricing logic error that violates the fundamental accounting principle that the premium must reflect the actual time remaining until expiry. From the user’s perspective the UI may show an option that expires later than requested while the amount paid appears lower than expected, leading to confusion when the trader expects a 7‑day premium but receives an 8‑day contract at a reduced cost.
summary:
The option premium is calculated using the input period, while the actual duration until the maturity date is rounded up to the end of the day which is typically longer than the given period. This allows traders to get longer option durations than what they pay for.  
The premium calculation in Strategy._calculatePremium() uses the input period in seconds to calculate the option price:  
```solidity
function _calculatePremium(
    uint256 amount,
    uint256 period,
    uint256 preciseCurrentPrice,
    uint256 strike,
    uint256 iv
) internal returns (uint256 premium) {
    (uint256 callPremium, uint256 putPremium) =
        StrategyStorage.layout().setUp.base.bs.optionPrices(
            period, iv, preciseCurrentPrice, strike, 0);
}
```
However, the maturity date is rounded up to the end of the day in PositionParams._computeMaturityDate():  
```solidity
function _computeMaturityDate(uint256 period) internal view returns (uint32) {
    uint256 maturityTimestamp = block.timestamp + period;
    maturityTimestamp -= (maturityTimestamp % 1 days);
    maturityTimestamp += 1 days - 1;
    return uint32(maturityTimestamp);
}
```
Therefore, the gap between the input period and the actual duration until maturity date can be up to 86399 seconds, which can be a significant difference for short-period positions.  
Consider the following scenario:  
1. Current time: 1743638400 (Thu Apr 03 2025 00:00:00).  
2. User inputs period = 7 days = 604800 seconds.  
3. Actual maturity: 1744329599 (Thu Apr 10 2025 23:59:59).  
Input period: 604800 seconds  
Actual period: 1744329599 - 1743638400 = 691199 seconds (7 days + 86399 seconds ≈ 8 days).  
The premium is calculated using the input period (604800 seconds) in the Black-Scholes formula, resulting in a lower premium as it underestimates the time until maturity.  
Below is an example output for a 7-day CALL option (3500 USD spot price, 10% relative strike, 48.9% IV). This results in approximately 23% underpricing for this CALL option position.  
Logs:  
Period: 604800 sec  
Maturity: 1744329599  
Actual Period: 691199 sec  
--- Premium: period ---  
call: 8963759233891000000  
put: 358963759233891000000  
--- Premium: maturity - uint32(block.timestamp)---  
call: 11675104193168500000  
put: 361675104193168500000  
Premium difference: 2711344959277500000

title: Insufficient liquidity checks for PUT may cause exercise failures
content: The vulnerability is an insufficient per‑asset liquidity validation for PUT options in a multi‑stablecoin pool. The contract validates that the total USD value of all stablecoins in the pool is greater than or equal to the sum of already locked USD and the size of a new PUT position, but it does not verify that the specific stablecoin required for the PUT payout (the buyToken) is actually available in sufficient quantity. This mismatch between aggregate pool valuation and per‑token availability creates a situation where a PUT position can be opened even though the pool holds zero balance of the payout token. The root cause is the use of a single pool‑wide liquidity check (_checkEnoughLiquidity) that only considers a combined USD metric and the absence of tracking of locked amounts per buyToken. An attacker or any user can exploit this by opening a PUT when the pool contains other stablecoins but no USDC, or by allowing a liquidity provider to withdraw the USDC after the position is opened, reducing the USDC balance to zero while the aggregate pool value remains above the locked threshold. When the holder later attempts to exercise the PUT, the internal _payout function tries to deduct the payout amount from the USDC balance, finds it insufficient, and reverts, causing the transaction to fail. The impact is that option holders receive no payout despite the pool appearing solvent, leading to locked funds, loss of expected returns, and erosion of trust in the protocol. This condition occurs whenever the pool supports multiple stablecoins, PUT positions require a specific token, and withdrawals or initial pool composition leave the required token balance at zero. Affected parties include option buyers, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the liquidity checks and withdrawal impact logic and noticed that the lockedUSD variable is not associated with a particular token. The bug is hard to notice because standard pool health metrics show sufficient total value, masking the per‑token shortfall. To remediate, the protocol should maintain a locked amount for each buyToken and enforce that both position opening and withdrawal impact checks compare the required token’s balance against its locked amount, preventing withdrawals that would render a PUT unexercisable. This class of bug can be described as an accounting mismatch or insufficient per‑asset liquidity validation, where business logic assumes any stablecoin can satisfy a payout that is actually token‑specific, violating the protocol’s financial guarantees. From a user’s perspective the UI would show an “exercise” button that reverts, the user receives no USDC, and their balance remains unchanged, contrary to the expectation of receiving a refund or profit from the option.

title: Inaccurate accounting in removeLiquidity() overstating liquidity
content: The vulnerability resides in the liquidity removal routine of a decentralized exchange contract. When a user calls the removeLiquidity function, the protocol calculates the total amount of tokens to be withdrawn (outAmount) and separates a protocol fee (pFee) from that amount, leaving a net amount (netOutAmount) that is actually transferred to the user after the fee is taken. The contract then updates its internal accounting by adding the fee to a dedicated protocolFee ledger but only subtracts the netOutAmount from the pool’s recorded token balance (poolAmount). Because the full outAmount (netOutAmount + pFee) is physically taken from the pool’s token holdings while only netOutAmount is deducted from the accounting variable, the poolAmount value becomes inflated by the fee amount. This discrepancy originates from a mismatch between the physical token movement and the logical state update – the fee is recorded separately but not removed from the pool’s balance, violating the invariant that poolAmount must always equal the actual token reserve. The flaw can be exploited by repeatedly invoking removeLiquidity with any non‑zero fee. Each call leaves the fee hidden inside the poolAmount, causing the contract to believe it holds more liquidity than it really does. An attacker can then perform additional withdrawals, swaps, or other operations that rely on the overstated balance, effectively extracting more value than entitled or causing severe pricing errors for honest users. The impact includes distorted pool pricing, potential loss of funds for liquidity providers, and a risk of the protocol becoming insolvent because the accounting no longer reflects reality. The condition for the bug to manifest is any execution of removeLiquidity where the protocol fee is greater than zero; it does not depend on special inputs or external contracts. All participants that rely on the pool’s reported liquidity – liquidity providers, traders, and the protocol itself – are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that compared the token transfer logic with the state‑update logic and identified the missing deduction. It is hard to notice because the UI typically shows the user‑visible token balances, while the internal poolAmount variable is not directly exposed, allowing the inconsistency to remain hidden until it causes observable anomalies such as unexpected swap rates or missing refunds. From a user’s perspective, after a removal transaction the pool may still display a higher available liquidity than the actual token balance, leading to situations where a user expects a refund or a correct swap price but receives less or sees the pool “run out” of tokens unexpectedly. The bug belongs to the class of accounting mismatches or invariant violations where fees are double‑counted or not properly accounted for. To remediate the issue, the contract should deduct the full outAmount (netOutAmount + pFee) from poolAmount while still crediting pFee to the protocolFee ledger, thereby keeping the accounting consistent with the physical token movement. This correction restores the invariant that the recorded pool balance matches the real token reserve and prevents the inflation of liquidity that enables the exploit.

title: Attacker can make his vePeg NFT unpokeable
content: The vulnerability originates from the way the voting contract updates the weight of a vePeg NFT when its balance decays over time. vePeg NFTs have a linear decay, so their effective voting power must be refreshed periodically through a "poke" operation that recomputes each pool’s share as _weights[i] * _weight / _totalVoteWeight. The implementation contains a require(_poolWeight != 0) guard that aborts the whole poke if any individual pool weight rounds down to zero. An attacker can deliberately create a so‑called dust vote by assigning an almost‑entire weight (for example 10e18‑1) to one preferred pool and a single unit of weight to a second, arbitrary pool. After even a short decay interval the total vePeg balance drops slightly below the original value, causing the tiny allocation to be multiplied by a slightly smaller numerator. Because Solidity integer division truncates toward zero, the expression for the dust pool evaluates to zero, triggering the require check and reverting the transaction. As a result the NFT becomes "unpokeable": any subsequent attempt to refresh its voting weight fails, leaving the NFT’s vote locked at the stale, pre‑decay value. This stale vote continues to influence governance decisions, potentially skewing outcomes in favor of the attacker and disadvantaging honest participants. The issue is hard to notice because a dust vote looks harmless and the zero‑weight condition only appears after the balance has decayed, a state that may not be exercised in normal testing. The bug belongs to the class of rounding‑error‑induced reverts in weighted voting systems. To remediate, the poke routine should not revert when a computed pool weight is zero; instead it should simply skip that pool or treat a zero weight as a no‑op, ensuring that the overall poke can succeed and the NFT’s voting power can be updated correctly. From a user’s perspective the expected behaviour – a successful poke that updates their voting power – is replaced by a transaction that reverts with no visible change, leading to confusion and the perception that the system is broken or possibly manipulated.

title: Gauge Rewards Stuck In `VoterProxy` Contract When `ExtraRewardStashV3` Is Used Within Angle Deployment
content: The vulnerability concerns the handling of gauge rewards for the Angle protocol when the ExtraRewardStashV3 contract is used in a deployment that relies on the VeToken (VoterProxy) architecture. The contract assumes that the claim of the veAsset token (ANGLE) and the claim of any additional reward tokens (for example DAI) are performed by separate function calls and that each call will direct the respective tokens to the appropriate receiver contract. In practice, Angle's LiquidityGaugeV4 implements a single claim_rewards() function that returns both the veAsset and all extra reward tokens in one transaction. During the Booster._earmarkRewards routine the first operation calls IStaker.claimVeAsset, which internally invokes IGauge.claim_rewards and therefore pulls all reward tokens from the gauge and forwards them to the VoterProxy contract. The second operation then calls ExtraRewardStashV3.claimRewards, expecting only the extra rewards to be available, but because the gauge redirection was never configured to point to the stash (the deployment omitted a call to Booster.setGaugeRedirect), the extra reward tokens have already been sent to VoterProxy and are not transferred to the stash. As a result, the extra rewards remain locked inside VoterProxy, never reaching the user‑facing reward pool, and the processStash step cannot resolve them. This issue manifests whenever Angle gauges are integrated without explicitly setting gauge redirection during deployment, which is the default configuration in the current code base. Users experience a discrepancy where the gauge reports earned rewards (e.g., DAI) but the user interface shows a zero balance or missing payout, violating the expectation that claimed rewards are deposited to their account. The bug breaks a core accounting invariant of the system – that veAsset and additional rewards are handled independently – and therefore constitutes a logical flaw in the reward routing logic, classifiable as an incentive‑distribution or accounting‑routing vulnerability. The problem was discovered during a security audit that traced the call flow of _earmarkRewards and identified that the extra reward stash was never receiving the tokens due to the missing redirection configuration. The issue is subtle because the gauge still reports successful claims, and there are no explicit error messages; the funds appear to be "claimed" but are silently trapped in an internal contract. To remediate, the deployment script should invoke Booster.setGaugeRedirect to point the gauge to the ExtraRewardStashV3 contract before any rewards are claimed, ensuring that both veAsset and extra rewards are routed correctly. Alternatively, the internal _earmarkRewards logic can be refactored to claim all rewards through the stash contract first, eliminating the need for separate veAsset claims and guaranteeing that the stash processes both token types. Adding comprehensive tests for extra reward claiming, alongside the existing veAsset tests, would also help prevent regression. Once the redirection is set, the previously stuck tokens can be recovered by an admin calling processStash, restoring the expected reward flow and fixing the broken accounting assumption.
summary: Note: This report aims to discuss the issue encountered when `ExtraRewardStashV3` is used within Angle Deployment. There is also another issue when `ExtraRewardStashV2` is used within Angle Deployment, but I will raise it in a separate report since `ExtraRewardStashV2` and `ExtraRewardStashV3` operate differently, and the proof-of-concept and mitigation are different too.

title: DeployUsdxlUtils does not transfer ownership of usdxlToken to admin
content: The vulnerability is that after deploying the USDXL token via a TransparentUpgradeableProxy, the contract's "initialize" function is called with the deployer's address, which makes the deployer the token's owner. The deployment script never transfers this ownership to the intended admin address. As a result, the deployer retains privileged admin rights such as upgrading the implementation, minting, pausing, or any owner‑only functions. This can be exploited by the deployer or anyone who gains control of the deployer's private key to modify token behavior, issue arbitrary tokens, or freeze the system, contrary to user expectations that the protocol admin controls the token. The issue occurs whenever the _deployUsdxl function is executed, i.e., during the initial deployment of the protocol. Users may notice that token‑related actions that should be governed by the protocol admin are instead controlled by an unexpected address, or that upgrade attempts by the admin fail because they are not the token owner. The problem was discovered during a manual audit of the deployment code, where the absence of a transferOwnership call after initialization was observed. Because ownership is stored in the token's own state rather than the proxy admin, the mismatch can be subtle and not visible in standard proxy admin interfaces, making it hard to detect. The correct fix is to add a call that transfers token ownership from the deployer to the designated admin after the proxy is initialized, or to initialize the token directly with the admin address. This class of bug falls under improper initialization and ownership mis‑assignment, which violates the protocol's trust model and accounting assumptions by allowing an unintended party to control token supply and upgrade logic.

title: Deployer does not transfer ownership of CapAutomator to admin
content: The vulnerability is that the CapAutomator contract, which is intended to be managed by a designated admin, is deployed with ownership automatically assigned to the transaction sender (the deployer) because the constructor of Ownable is called with msg.sender. The deployment script (DeployCapAutomator.run) never calls transferOwnership to hand over control to the admin address. As a result, the deployer – which may be an external account or a malicious actor – retains exclusive rights to execute onlyOwner functions such as adjusting the borrowing cap. This mismatch between the expected governance model and the actual ownership can be exploited by the deployer to arbitrarily raise or lower caps, potentially allowing excessive borrowing, draining liquidity, or preventing legitimate admin actions. The issue manifests immediately after deployment, before any admin interaction, and affects any user or protocol component that relies on the cap limits being enforced by the trusted admin. It was discovered during a manual audit of the deployment script, where the ownership transfer step was missing. The problem is subtle because the contract inherits Ownable and the owner variable is correctly set, but the UI or documentation may indicate that the admin is the owner, leading to a false sense of security. The fix is to add a call to transferOwnership(admin) after the CapAutomator instance is created, or to modify the constructor to accept the admin address and set it as the initial owner. This aligns the on‑chain ownership with the intended off‑chain governance and prevents unauthorized cap manipulation.

title: Faulty deposit_for() check
content: The vulnerability is a logical error in the reward distribution flow of the RewardsDistributor contract. The claim() function decides whether to transfer rewards directly or to call vePeg.deposit_for() based on the lock status. For locks that are marked as perpetual, the contract stores an end timestamp of zero. The deposit_for() implementation checks only that locked.end > block.timestamp and reverts with Cannot add to expired lock. Withdraw when the condition is false. Because zero is never greater than the current timestamp, the check incorrectly treats a perpetual lock as expired, causing the deposit_for() call to revert. As a result, rewards that should be added to a perpetual lock are never deposited, preventing the lock’s voting power from increasing and leaving the user with no visible reward balance. The bug manifests only when a user with a perpetual lock invokes claim() while the lock remains unexpired; normal time‑limited locks work as intended. It was discovered during a manual audit of the claim() logic, where the auditor noticed that the perpetual‑locked branch called deposit_for() without a corresponding exception for the zero‑end case. The issue is subtle because perpetual locks are a legitimate feature and the end field being zero is a valid sentinel value, so a simple expired check appears reasonable at first glance. The impact is high for affected users because they cannot claim rewards, effectively losing potential token accrual and associated voting power, although no funds are stolen. The fix is to modify deposit_for() to accept perpetual locks by adding a condition that allows _locked.perpetuallyLocked or by handling the zero‑end case explicitly, and to update the perpetual‑locked balance accordingly. This change restores the intended accounting where rewards increase the lock’s balance and voting weight, aligning the contract’s behavior with its business logic that perpetual locks should continue to earn rewards.

title: Losing voting power in rewards distribution
content: The vulnerability lies in the way the rewards distribution contracts compute voting power for perpetual locks. Both the RewardsDistributor and TokenRewardsDistributor use a linear decay formula (bias - slope * time) to derive voting power, but perpetual locks are initialized with bias set to zero and slope set to zero. Because the formula multiplies the slope by elapsed time, a zero slope yields a result of zero voting power regardless of how long the lock has been held. Voting power is the core metric that determines how many reward tokens an account is entitled to, so a perpetual lock that should provide a constant, non‑zero voting power ends up being treated as having no voting power at all. As a consequence, when the contract functions ve_for_at, _checkpoint_total_supply, _claim and _claimable are invoked, the system calculates a claimable amount of zero for any address that holds a perpetual lock. The bug was discovered during a manual audit of the reward contracts, where the auditor noticed that the perpetual‑lock branch never updates bias or slope and therefore always returns zero. The issue is subtle because no transaction reverts and no explicit error is emitted; users simply see that their claim transaction returns zero tokens, which can be mistaken for a normal period of no rewards. The impact is that token holders who lock their tokens permanently lose the expected continuous accrual of rewards, undermining the incentive model of the protocol and potentially eroding trust. The problem occurs whenever a user creates a lock without an expiration date and later attempts to claim rewards; the contract’s accounting logic mistakenly treats the lock as having no voting power. Affected parties include any user with a perpetual lock, the protocol’s reward pool, and downstream contracts that rely on accurate voting‑power based accounting. This is a class of bug where a special‑case state (perpetual lock) is not handled correctly in a mathematical model, leading to a zero‑value calculation that violates the business assumption that an active lock always contributes positive voting power. From the user’s perspective the UI may display “No rewards available” or the claim transaction may return 0 tokens even though the lock is still active, contrary to the expectation that a perpetual lock continuously earns rewards. The failure mode can be described as a reward‑distribution logic error that causes funds to disappear from the user’s perspective. To remediate, the implementation should detect perpetual locks (for example by checking if the lock end timestamp is zero) and assign a constant voting power equal to the locked amount, bypassing the decay formula. This ensures that reward calculations use the correct, non‑zero voting power and that perpetual lock holders can claim their entitled rewards.
summary:
Both RewardsDistributor and TokenRewardsDistributor contracts lack of properly account for perpetual locks in their voting power and rewards calculations. The contracts calculate voting power using the linear decay formula ( bias - slope * time ), which incorrectly handle the perpetual locks as that perpetual locks should maintain constant voting power over time. This issue affects the following functions in both contracts:
ve_for_at()
_checkpoint_total_supply()
_claim()
_claimable()
Since perpetual locks are initialized with bias = 0 and slope = 0, the current reward logic calculates zero voting power for them.
As a result, users with perpetual locks unable to claim their rewards, despite having an active and constant lock. The only way for such users to receive rewards is to first convert their perpetual lock into a normal lock.

title: Non-perpetual locks gaining extra delegation power
content: The vePeg contract implements a delegation mechanism that is supposed to allow only tokens locked permanently (perpetual locks) to transfer their voting power to another address. The public _delegate function enforces this rule by checking the perpetualLocked flag of the token being delegated. However, the internal helper _moveAllDelegates, which is invoked by _delegate, iterates over the complete list of token IDs owned by the delegator and assigns each of them to the new delegate without testing whether the token is a perpetual lock. This mismatch creates a bypass: when a user delegates a perpetual lock, the contract unintentionally also moves every non‑perpetual lock owned by that user, granting the delegate additional voting weight that should not exist. The root cause is the missing filter on the perpetualLocked property inside the token‑movement loop. An attacker can exploit the bug by creating short‑term locks, then delegating a single perpetual lock; the contract will automatically attach the short‑term locks to the delegate, inflating the delegate’s voting power and potentially swaying governance proposals. The impact is a distortion of the protocol’s voting calculus, allowing parties to gain influence they are not entitled to, which undermines the integrity of governance decisions and may lead to malicious parameter changes. The vulnerability manifests whenever a user calls the delegation function – the check passes for the chosen token, but the subsequent internal call moves all tokens, regardless of lock type. Token holders, delegators, and the overall governance system are affected because the accounting assumptions that only perpetual locks contribute to voting are violated. The issue was uncovered during a manual security audit that traced the delegation flow and observed that the loop over ownerTokenCount did not discriminate between lock types, a detail that is easy to miss because the external interface appears to enforce the correct rule. From a user’s perspective the symptom is an unexpectedly high voting power for a delegate or a sudden change in a user’s governance score, while the user expects only permanent locks to count. The bug belongs to the class of delegation bypass or privilege escalation caused by insufficient state validation. To remediate, the contract should either replace the call to _moveAllDelegates with a token‑specific delegation routine that moves only the intended token, or modify _moveAllDelegates to filter out non‑perpetual locks before adding them to the delegate’s balance, thereby aligning the implementation with the intended business logic that only perpetual locks have voting rights.

title: Incorrect proxy address tracking misconfigures USDXL pool tokens
content: The vulnerability consists of an incorrect address tracking logic in the deployment utilities for the USDXL pool. The internal helper functions that are supposed to return the proxy contracts for the AToken and the VariableDebtToken instead return the addresses of the underlying implementation contracts. Because the pool interacts only with the proxy instances, any configuration that is sent to the implementation address never reaches the live token contracts. As a result, during the reserve initialization the exported deployment artifacts contain the wrong addresses, the pool configurator does not set the AToken and VariableDebtToken parameters, the facilitator entity is not linked to the correct token, and the discount token and strategy settings are left pointing to empty or default contracts. The root cause is the use of the variable usdxlAToken (which holds the implementation) instead of a newly stored variable that captures the proxy address returned by the pool’s getReserveData call. The bug is discovered through static analysis of the deployment scripts and a manual review of the address handling logic. It is subtle because the returned addresses are syntactically valid contract addresses, so the deployment appears to succeed and no immediate runtime error is thrown. From a user’s perspective the USDXL pool behaves as if the token contracts are missing: interest accrual does not happen, users see zero balances for their deposited USDXL, refunds or withdrawals may fail, and the treasury cannot receive fees. The impact is high because the core accounting layer of the protocol is effectively disabled, potentially leading to loss of funds or inability to interact with the pool. The issue can be exploited by an attacker who relies on the assumption that the pool’s tokens are correctly configured; they could deposit funds that never earn interest or trigger unexpected reverts. The proper fix is to query the pool after reserve creation, store the proxy addresses returned in reserveData.aTokenAddress and reserveData.variableDebtTokenAddress, and use those stored proxy addresses in all subsequent configuration calls and artifact exports. This ensures that the pool’s token contracts are correctly initialized, the facilitator entity is linked, and the discount strategy operates on the intended contracts.

title: Mint price will be inaccurate for quantities that jumped more than one price
content: The vulnerability resides in the mint‑price calculation routine that determines how much ether a user must send when minting a batch of tokens. The function receives a starting token identifier and a quantity, then fetches the price associated with the first token (starting tier) and the price associated with the last token (ending tier). It assumes that the price is constant across the whole range or that at most one tier change occurs. When the requested quantity spans more than one price tier, the algorithm only multiplies the starting tier price by the number of tokens that belong to the first tier and the ending tier price by the remaining tokens, completely ignoring any intermediate tiers. This logical oversight originates from the use of only two price look‑ups and a single calculation of the number of tokens belonging to the first tier, without iterating over all tiers crossed by the range. An attacker or any user can exploit the flaw by requesting a mint that jumps across multiple tiers in a single transaction; the contract will apply the higher ending‑tier price to tokens that should have been priced at the intermediate tier, resulting in an over‑charge. Conversely, if the ending tier is cheaper than an intermediate tier, the user could be under‑charged. The impact is monetary mispricing: users may pay more than the protocol’s advertised price, leading to loss of funds, or may pay less, allowing free acquisition of tokens and revenue loss for the protocol. The condition under which the bug manifests is any mint call where the quantity causes the token id range to cross more than one pricing tier – for example, starting at the last id of tier 1 and minting enough tokens to reach tier 3. All participants who rely on the public mint function are affected, but the effect is most severe for large batch minting operations. The issue was identified during a manual security review that inspected the pricing logic and observed that the comment “@audit - this will not work properly if jump more than 1 tier” accurately described the flaw. The bug is subtle because the function returns a single numeric price without exposing the tier breakdown, making the miscalculation hard to detect without cross‑checking against a step‑wise price aggregation. To remediate, the pricing routine should iterate over each tier intersected by the mint range, summing the product of each tier’s price and the number of tokens belonging to that tier, or the contract should enforce a maximum quantity that guarantees at most one tier transition per call. This class of bug is a tier‑boundary pricing miscalculation, common in systems that apply piecewise‑linear pricing without proper aggregation across intervals. From a user’s perspective the UI may display the expected total cost based on the advertised tier schedule, but after the transaction the wallet shows a higher (or lower) deduction, or the minted token balance does not match the amount paid, violating the expectation that “pay X ether to receive Y tokens at the listed price”.

title: Missing payable function
content: The vulnerability consists of a missing payable capability in a set of contracts that are expected to forward native blockchain tokens (e.g., ETH) using a low‑level .call with a value field. The internal _call function builds a call request that includes a non‑zero value and invokes the target address with .call{value: _callRequest.value}(_callRequest.data). However, none of the contracts involved – including the main wallet contract, the pre‑authorized calls module, the session calls module, the generic calls module, and the controller module – declare any functions as payable nor provide a receive() or payable fallback function. Consequently, when a call request carries a positive value, the EVM reverts the transfer because the destination contract is not allowed to accept native tokens. The root cause is the omission of the payable modifier and the absence of a receive/fallback entry point, which violates the basic requirement that a contract must be explicitly marked to accept value transfers. An attacker or a legitimate user can exploit this by crafting a call request with a non‑zero value; the low‑level call will return false, but the surrounding code does not check the success flag, so the transaction may appear to succeed while the intended token transfer silently fails. This leads to a mismatch between expected and actual behavior: users anticipate that their funds will be forwarded to the target contract or that a refund will be issued, but instead the funds remain locked in the caller or are simply not delivered, resulting in missing balances, zero refunds, or failed business logic that depends on successful payment. The issue manifests whenever the wallet attempts to execute a payable operation, such as sending ETH to a third‑party contract, a DeFi protocol, or a user‑controlled address. All participants – end‑users, protocol operators, and auditors – are affected because the core accounting assumptions of the wallet (that a call with value will transfer the specified amount) are broken. The problem was discovered during a manual security audit that inspected the Calls.sol module and noticed that the _call function includes a value parameter but the contract hierarchy lacks any payable functions. The bug can be hard to notice because the call does not revert the whole transaction; the success flag is ignored, so the surrounding logic may continue as if the transfer succeeded, masking the failure. To remediate, the contracts should be updated to include the payable modifier on any function that may receive native tokens, and a receive() or payable fallback function should be added to accept unsolicited value transfers. This change restores the expected accounting flow, ensures that value‑bearing calls either succeed or properly revert, and aligns the implementation with the intended business logic of forwarding funds and processing refunds.
summary:
_call() could send native token via .call{ value: _callRequest.value }, however, none of the contracts can receive native token, including Main.sol, PreauthorizedCalls.sol, SessionCalls.sol, Calls.sol, Controllers.sol.
File: contracts\modules\Calls\Calls.sol
```solidity
80: function _call
(CallsStructs.CallRequest calldata _callRequest) internal returns (bytes memory) {
81: (
bool success,
bytes memory result
) = _callRequest.target.call{ value: _callRequest.value }(_callRequest.data
```

title: Threshold conflicts with removing controllers
content: The vulnerability is a threshold‑weight inconsistency that allows a controller to lower the voting threshold and then remove another controller in the same atomic call, thereby gaining exclusive control of the wallet. The contract stores each controller’s voting weight, the sum of all weights (totalWeight) and a required threshold. When a controller is removed, the internal function subtracts the controller’s weight from totalWeight and then checks that totalWeight is still greater than or equal to the stored threshold. The check does not consider that the threshold may have been changed earlier in the same transaction. Because any controller can call updateControlThreshold to set a new threshold that is lower than the current totalWeight, an attacker can first obtain a legitimate signature from another controller to lower the threshold to its own weight, and then, in the same multicall, invoke _removeController to delete the other controller. After the removal, totalWeight equals the attacker’s weight, which satisfies the lowered threshold, so the wallet ends up with a single controller that can unilaterally approve all actions. The exploit works when there are at least two controllers whose combined weight equals the original threshold, and when the contract permits threshold updates without requiring that the new threshold be enforceable after any subsequent removal. From a user perspective the wallet may appear to reject a controller‑removal transaction with a “ThresholdImpossible” error, or after the attack the UI may show only one controller and the previous controller is unable to sign any further transactions, effectively stealing the funds.
