An attacker or any actor who can trigger a Vault operation that invokes _accrueFee (for example a deposit, withdrawal, or harvest) while at least one IonPool is paused can cause the protocol to allocate more fee shares than justified, effectively siphoning value from depositors to the fee recipient. The impact is a systematic over‑charging of fees, distortion of accounting invariants, and potential erosion of user balances, which may eventually compromise the protocol’s solvency. This condition occurs only when the pause flag on an IonPool is active and the Vault’s fee‑accrual path is executed; it does not require any special permissions beyond the ability to interact with the Vault. The affected parties include ordinary users who deposit assets, the designated fee recipient who receives an inflated share of fees, and the protocol itself, which may lose trust due to accounting inconsistencies. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the interaction between the pause mechanism and the fee‑accrual code, noting that the pause flag was not propagated to the totalAssets calculation. The bug is subtle because the Vault still reports a non‑zero asset balance and the fee‑minting transaction appears normal, making the over‑allocation of fees hard to detect without detailed accounting analysis. From a user’s perspective, the symptom may manifest as an unexpected reduction in the value of their shares, a higher than anticipated fee deduction, or a situation where the protocol seems to “keep more fees” even though no interest was earned during the pause. This class of bug can be described as a pause‑bypass accounting error where fee calculations rely on a view that does not respect the paused state, leading to incorrect fee distribution. To remediate the issue, the Vault should either query a pause‑aware view that returns the unaccrued underlying claim (for example a new getTotalUnderlyingClaimsUnaccrued function) or explicitly check the paused flag of each IonPool before including its balance in totalAssets. If a pool is paused, its contribution should be excluded from fee calculations, or the entire fee‑accrual process should be deferred until all pools are unpaused, thereby ensuring that fees are only minted on legitimately accrued interest.

title: Sale creator can possibly steal bidders' claimable tokens
content: The vulnerability is an authorization bypass that allows the creator of a StakedVestedCrowdSale or VestedCrowdSale to steal the tokens that bidders are supposed to receive after the auction. The contract design permits the sale creator to supply arbitrary addresses for the TokenVesting and TimelockedToken contracts that are used to lock and vest the auction token. During settlement the sale contract automatically approves the supplied TimelockedToken contract to spend the entire amount of auction tokens that should be claimable by bidders. If the creator supplies a malicious contract that inherits from TokenVesting or TimelockedToken and adds a function to transfer any approved tokens, the approved contract can immediately pull the locked tokens and forward them to an address controlled by the creator. This results in bidders attempting to claim their tokens and receiving nothing, their balances appearing as zero, and a total loss of the value of the auction tokens. The issue occurs only when the sale creator is malicious and provides a custom vesting or timelocked contract; it is triggered at the moment of settlement when the approval is granted. All participants who have placed bids are affected because they cannot retrieve the tokens they purchased, breaking the fundamental accounting assumption that locked tokens will be released to the rightful owners after the vesting period. The problem was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the flow of token approvals and the trust model around external contracts. It is difficult to notice because the approval of an external contract is a common pattern and the contract does not verify the bytecode of the supplied address, leading auditors to assume the vesting contract behaves correctly. To remediate, the sale contract should only accept vesting and timelocked contracts that are deployed internally from a known implementation or verified against a whitelist of bytecode hashes, thereby preventing user‑supplied contracts from being granted spend authority over auction tokens. In conceptual terms the bug belongs to the class of “untrusted contract injection” or “external contract approval abuse”, where a privileged role can inject malicious logic that bypasses intended token lock mechanisms, causing funds to disappear and the protocol’s financial guarantees to be violated.
summary: In StakedVestedCrowdSale the sale creator can give the address to his own TokenVesting & TimelockedToken contracts. Same in VestedCrowdSale but only for TimelockedToken. Now if the sale creator is malicious he can give the addresses of his own deployed contracts that inherit from either TokenVesting or TimelockedToken but add functionality to pull the funds out on demand, while they are still locked in them. This is even worse when it comes to the token locking logic in VestedCrowdSale, where on sale settlement the TimelockedToken contract is approved to spend all the auctionToken that should be claimed, meaning if it has the functionality it can just pull the funds and transfer them out of the contract on demand. This will result in inability for bidders to claim their tokens and 100% loss of their value.

title: User can prevent balance updates by withdrawing
content: The vulnerability is an accounting mismatch in the node withdrawal routine. When the function finishWithdraw is executed, the contract transfers the requested ETH amount from the node's native balance to the caller, but it never reduces the internal variable that records how much ETH has already been credited to that node (creditedNodeETH). As a result the recorded credited amount remains higher than the actual on‑chain balance. Later, when the protocol takes a snapshot of node balances, it computes the unattributed node balance as nodeAddress.balance minus creditedNodeETH. Because creditedNodeETH is overstated, the subtraction can underflow, causing the internal _startSnapshot call to revert. This can be triggered by any user who performs a withdrawal, and a malicious actor can deliberately withdraw repeatedly to keep the internal accounting out of sync, especially after a beacon‑chain slashing event where the node's real balance has been reduced. The impact is that the protocol’s accounting state becomes inconsistent: snapshots fail, rewards may not be distributed, and funds can become effectively locked because the contract believes the node still holds more ETH than it actually does. Users see their withdrawal succeed on the UI, but subsequent operations that rely on correct snapshots report errors or show zero rewards. The bug is hard to notice because the transfer itself succeeds and the visible balance may appear correct, while the hidden internal counter is wrong. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that inspected the finishWithdraw implementation and the snapshot logic. To remediate, the contract must update the creditedNodeETH variable by subtracting the withdrawn amount before completing the transfer, ensuring that the internal accounting always matches the external balance. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of state‑inconsistent accounting errors where a contract updates external balances without synchronizing internal bookkeeping, leading to underflow/overflow conditions and broken business logic.
summary:
When finishWithdraw() is called the ETH amount is transferred from the native node contract's balance but the code doesn't decrease the value of the creditedNodeETH so its value would be higher than it should be and _startSnapshot() would revert because of underflow:
```solidity
// Calculate unattributed node balance
uint256 nodeBalanceWei = node.nodeAddress.balance - node.creditedNode
```

The issue would happen to all users who withdraw tokens and malicious users can do it intentionally to prevent balance updates (when they are slashed in the beacon chain)

title: Broken balance update if a slash event happens
content: The vulnerability is an accounting error that occurs when a slash event is processed. The function that transfers the slashed ETH moves the funds out of the node contract’s balance but fails to decrement the internal variable that records how much ETH has already been credited to the node (creditedNodeETH). Because the credited amount is left unchanged, the subsequent calculation of the node’s unattributed balance adds the full contract balance to an outdated credit value. When the protocol later calls the snapshot routine, it computes nodeBalanceWei as contractBalance minus creditedNodeETH; the stale credit value makes this subtraction underflow, causing the snapshot function to revert. This can be triggered whenever a slash is executed, affecting any node operator whose contract is subject to penalties. From a user perspective the node’s balance appears higher than it should be, the UI may still show a credit after a penalty, and attempts to finalize a snapshot result in a transaction failure with an underflow error. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the slash handling logic, where the auditor noticed that the creditedNodeETH variable was never updated after the transfer. The bug is hard to notice because the contract still holds the correct amount of ETH; only the internal accounting diverges, and the failure only surfaces later in a separate function. The root cause is a missing state update, a classic example of an accounting‑balance mismatch that leads to arithmetic underflow. The recommended fix is to subtract the slashed amount from creditedNodeETH within the _transferToSlashStore() routine, ensuring that the internal credit reflects the actual funds remaining. After the fix, the snapshot calculation will produce a correct non‑negative balance, preventing reverts and preserving protocol liveness.
summary:
When _transferToSlashStore() is called the slash ETH amount is transferred from the native node contract's balance but the code doesn't decrease the value of the creditedNodeETH so its value would be higher than it should be and _startSnapshot() would revert because of underflow:
```solidity
// Calculate unattributed node balance
uint256 nodeBalanceWei = node.nodeAddress.balance - node.creditedNode
```

title: Denial of Service Risk Due to Frozen token_escrow in ONFT::Adapter
content: During the initialization of an ONFT that uses the Adapter pattern, the contract stores the address of a token mint without checking whether the mint has a freeze authority. SPL tokens can be configured with a freeze authority that allows the token issuer or an authorized account to freeze any token account, including the escrow account used by the ONFT to lock transferred tokens. If the escrow account is frozen, the subsequent call to token_interface::transfer_checked in the send instruction reverts, because the token program rejects transfers to a frozen destination. As a result, the ONFT becomes unable to lock new tokens, effectively causing a denial-of-service condition. The vulnerability is triggered when a token with a freeze authority is supplied during init_ONft, or when the freeze authority is exercised after deployment. Users attempting to send their tokens see a transaction failure, often reported as "InvalidTokenEscrow" or a generic revert, and their balances remain unchanged, contrary to the expectation that the token will be locked in the escrow. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the init_ONft logic and noticed the absence of any validation of the mint’s freeze_authority flag. Because freeze authority is an optional feature, developers may not anticipate that a token such as USDC, which deliberately includes a freeze authority for regulatory purposes, could be used to freeze the escrow and halt the protocol. The problem is hard to notice in normal operation because the token appears functional until the freeze is applied, at which point the failure manifests only when a transfer is attempted. The bug belongs to the class of token-freeze based denial-of-service vulnerabilities, where missing checks on token properties allow an external authority to render a critical contract function unusable. To remediate, the init_ONft function should explicitly verify that the supplied mint does not have a freeze authority and reject the initialization, or the protocol should maintain an allowlist of trusted tokens and display a clear UI warning when a token with freeze authority is used. If a freeze does occur, the locked tokens cannot be moved by the contract until the authority unfreezes the escrow, meaning funds may remain inaccessible for the duration of the freeze.

title: activeValidatorCount is never set or increased
content: The vulnerability resides in the NativeVault contract where the field activeValidatorCount, intended to reflect the number of validators that currently have active withdrawal credentials for a given node, is never initialized or incremented. The contract decreases this counter when a validator balance reaches zero, but because it never starts with a positive value, the counter remains at its default zero. When a snapshot is started, the contract copies activeValidatorCount into the remainingProofs field of the Snapshot struct. Consequently remainingProofs is always zero. The subsequent validation routine iterates over the supplied balance proofs and unconditionally decrements remainingProofs; with an initial value of zero this triggers a Solidity underflow revert. Moreover, the logic that finalizes a snapshot checks if remainingProofs equals zero to decide whether to credit the node’s ETH balance. Since the condition is true immediately, the node’s creditedNodeETH is updated at the start of the snapshot and again when validateSnapshotProofs is called with an empty proof array, resulting in a double credit. From a user perspective the symptoms include unexpected reverts when submitting proofs, the node’s balance appearing to increase twice, or the node’s balance remaining unchanged despite having active validators. The bug affects any node operator or delegator who relies on accurate accounting of validator rewards and withdrawals, potentially leading to loss of funds or over‑payment that must later be corrected. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that traced the flow of activeValidatorCount and noticed the absence of any assignment or increment operation. It is subtle because the counter is stored in a mapping and the contract does not expose it directly, so the problem does not surface until the snapshot logic is exercised. The proper fix is to set activeValidatorCount to one (or increment it) whenever a validator with active withdrawal credentials is added, and to ensure the counter is correctly decremented only when a validator is withdrawn, thereby aligning the remainingProofs value with the actual number of validators that need proof submission. In abstract terms the bug belongs to the class of state‑initialization and counter‑management errors that cause accounting mismatches and premature termination of multi‑step processes.

title: MJR-1 Incorrect calculation of rewardPerLiquidity
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect calculation of the per‑liquidity reward amount in a staking rewards contract. The contract updates a variable called rewardPerLiquidity based on the elapsed time since the last update, assuming that the elapsed time can be up to the full reward duration. When the first user deposits an NFT after the reward period has already been started by a call to notify(), the expression (lastTimeRewardApplicable() - lastUpdateTime) becomes smaller than the configured DURATION. Because the formula multiplies the reward rate by this time delta, the resulting rewardPerLiquidity value is either zero or far lower than intended. As a consequence the contract does not allocate any reward tokens to the staked liquidity, effectively freezing the tokens that were meant to be distributed as incentives. This situation occurs only under the specific timing condition where the initial deposit happens after the reward period has begun and before any other deposit has updated the accounting state. Users who stake NFTs expect to earn reward tokens proportional to their share of liquidity, but they receive nothing, seeing their reward balance remain at zero while the contract holds undistributed tokens. The issue was discovered during a formal security audit performed by MixBytes, where the auditors traced the reward calculation logic and identified that the time‑difference term can be less than the full duration, breaking the accounting assumptions. The bug is subtle because normal operation—where deposits occur early in the reward period—does not expose the problem, making it easy to miss in testing. It belongs to the class of accounting or reward‑distribution bugs where a formula incorrectly handles edge‑case timing, leading to locked funds and broken incentive economics. To remediate the issue the rewardPerLiquidity computation should be revised to correctly handle cases where the elapsed time is less than the full duration, for example by using the actual elapsed time without assuming it reaches DURATION, or by initializing lastUpdateTime appropriately so that the delta never becomes negative or zero when rewards should be accruing. A proper fix restores the intended reward flow, ensuring that users receive the correct amount of tokens and that no funds remain unintentionally frozen in the contract.
summary:
If the first user deposits NFT after some time from notify() call, then (lastTimeRewardApplicable() - lastUpdateTime) always will be less than DURATION which leads to freezing some funds on the contract:
StakingRewardsV3-1.sol#L156

title: _increaseBalance() mints fewer shares than expected
content: The vulnerability resides in the internal function that updates a node owner's balance in the vault. The function first adds the deposited assets to the global totalAssets variable and only afterwards converts the deposited amount to vault shares. Because the conversion routine uses totalAssets as part of its calculation, increasing totalAssets before the conversion inflates the denominator, causing the computed share amount to be smaller than it should be. As a result, when a user deposits ETH (or other native asset) they receive fewer vault shares than the protocol’s accounting rules promise. The bug is triggered every time _increaseBalance is called with a non‑zero assets value, i.e., on any normal deposit, and it is deterministic under the current implementation. From a user’s point of view the UI may show that the deposit succeeded, but the displayed share balance grows less than expected, or the user later receives a smaller amount when withdrawing, effectively losing part of the deposited value. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the NativeVault contract by inspecting the order of state updates and reasoning about the share conversion formula. It is easy to miss because the transaction does not revert and the emitted event only reports the updated totalRestakedETH, not the minted share amount, so the discrepancy is hidden unless the share balance is compared against the deposit amount. The bug belongs to the class of accounting‑order‑of‑operations errors where a mutable global state is modified before a dependent calculation, breaking the invariant that shares represent a proportional claim on total assets. Exploitation does not require malicious code; any honest user making a deposit will be short‑changed, and a malicious actor could repeatedly trigger deposits on behalf of victims to erode their share holdings. The impact is high because it directly reduces users’ ownership stakes and can lead to loss of funds when withdrawals are performed. The correct fix is to compute the number of shares to mint before mutating totalAssets, then mint the shares, and finally update totalAssets and the per‑owner accounting fields. This restores the intended accounting relationship and ensures that the share amount matches the deposited assets.

title: MJR-2 Possible ddos attack
content: The vulnerability is a front‑running price manipulation in the withdraw() function of the staking rewards contract. The contract calculates a user’s reward based on the current pool price at the moment withdraw is called. Because the price is derived from mutable pool state that can be altered by any participant before the withdraw transaction is mined, a malicious actor can submit a transaction that changes the price just before the victim’s withdraw is executed. By doing so the attacker forces the price to a value that reduces the computed reward to zero or a negligible amount, causing the legitimate staker to receive no rewards despite having accrued them. This attack can be carried out whenever a user initiates a withdrawal and the network’s transaction ordering allows the attacker to place a preceding transaction, i.e., under normal Ethereum mempool conditions. The affected parties are stakers who expect to receive proportional rewards; they see their balance unchanged or a missing reward after the transaction. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the StakingRewardsV3 contract, where the price‑dependent reward logic was identified as relying on a single instantaneous pool price without any smoothing or averaging. Because the price can be moved by a single transaction, the problem may not be obvious from static analysis; it only manifests when an attacker deliberately reorders transactions, making it hard to detect without dynamic testing. The bug belongs to the class of oracle manipulation or front‑running vulnerabilities where on‑chain state used for accounting can be tampered with by adversaries. From a user’s perspective the UI shows a successful withdrawal but the reward amount displayed is zero, contradicting the expectation that the user receives their earned tokens. The business logic that rewards are proportional to the time‑weighted average price is violated, breaking accounting guarantees. A proper mitigation is to compute the price using an average over a recent block window or a time‑weighted moving average, or to use a trusted external price oracle, thereby preventing a single transaction from drastically shifting the price used for reward calculation. Implementing such an averaging mechanism removes the ability for an attacker to front‑run the withdraw and ensures that rewards are calculated on a stable price reference.
summary:
Malicious user can front run withdraw() function to change the current price in pool, so user can lost all his rewards:
StakingRewardsV3-1.sol#L195

title: User can close a vault that should be liquidated
content: The vulnerability resides in the vault‑closing routine of the protocol. The closeVault function is intended to allow a user to terminate a healthy vault and receive the locked collateral back after the associated debt is burned. However, the implementation does not verify whether the vault satisfies the minimum collateralisation requirement (MCR) before permitting the closure. As a result, a vault that is under‑collateralised – i.e., one that should be flagged for liquidation – can be closed by its owner. The root cause is a missing eligibility check: the function proceeds directly to burn the debt tokens, adjust global accounting variables and transfer the collateral without first confirming that the vault’s collateral‑to‑debt ratio is above the required threshold. An attacker can exploit this by calling closeVault on an insolvent vault, thereby receiving the full collateral while the protocol records a reduction in total debt but also a reduction in total collateral, leaving a net negative equity position (bad debt). By front‑running a legitimate liquidation transaction, the attacker can bypass the liquidation mechanism entirely, causing the protocol to retain unrecoverable debt and increasing the risk of insolvency. The impact is that the protocol’s accounting invariants are broken, other users’ funds become exposed to loss, and the intended safety net of liquidation is rendered ineffective. This condition occurs whenever a vault’s collateral value falls below the liquidation threshold and the owner invokes closeVault, either deliberately or unintentionally. The affected parties include the vault owner (who may receive collateral they are not entitled to), the protocol (which accrues bad debt), and all participants who rely on the protocol’s solvency. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit performed by CD Security, where the audit team noted the absence of a liquidation‑eligibility guard in the closeVault flow. The problem can be subtle because the function appears to perform all expected state updates – burning debt, transferring collateral, emitting an event – and therefore may not raise an immediate error, making the logical flaw easy to overlook. To remediate, the contract should enforce a check that the vault’s collateralisation ratio meets or exceeds the MCR before allowing closure, or require the user to add sufficient collateral to bring the vault back into a healthy state prior to closing. This aligns the function with the intended business logic that only solvent vaults may be voluntarily closed, preserving the integrity of the liquidation process and preventing the creation of unrecoverable bad debt. The bug belongs to the class of missing business‑logic validation or state‑transition errors that enable liquidation bypass and accounting inconsistencies, leading to symptoms such as users receiving collateral from an underwater vault, the protocol’s total collateral dropping unexpectedly, and the overall health metric of the system deteriorating.

title: Transferring NativeVault tokens can break some functionalities
content: The vulnerability resides in the NativeVault token, which represents shares of a staking node and is implemented as an ERC20‑compatible asset. Because the token’s transfer and transferFrom functions are not overridden, holders can move their shares to any address. The contract’s internal accounting assumes that a node owner’s token balance always reflects the amount of ETH restaked in the node (node.totalRestakedETH). When a transfer occurs, the balance of the original owner decreases while the node’s totalRestakedETH value remains unchanged. This mismatch leads to two distinct problems. First, during a slashing event the contract computes the amount of ETH to slash as node.totalRestakedETH minus the ETH equivalent of the owner’s current token balance (convertToAssets(balanceOf(owner))). If the owner has transferred away shares, the balance used in the formula is lower than the actual stake, causing the contract to slash more ETH than the owner is entitled to, effectively stealing assets. Second, if the recipient of the transferred shares is not a node owner with a matching node record, the shares become non‑functional: the holder cannot withdraw ETH or participate in any protocol operation, turning the tokens into a useless asset. Moreover, if the recipient is a node owner and a slashing event has already occurred, the balance may have increased (due to received shares) while node.totalRestakedETH has not been updated, which can cause the slashedAssets calculation to underflow. This underflow can be exploited to block the execution of validateExpiredSnapshot, preventing the protocol from processing slashing evidence for that validator. The issue manifests whenever a token transfer is performed, especially before or after a slashing event, and it affects node owners, token holders, and the overall protocol integrity because the accounting invariants are broken. The bug was discovered during a manual security review of the NativeVault.sol source, where the auditor noticed that the internal _transferToSlashStore function relied on balanceOf without protecting against external transfers. The problem is subtle because the token behaves like a normal ERC20 on the surface, and the incorrect accounting only appears under specific slashing scenarios, making it easy to miss in routine testing. To remediate, the contract should disable arbitrary transfers by overriding transfer and transferFrom to revert, thereby preserving the invariant that a node owner’s token balance always matches the node’s restaked ETH. This class of bug can be described as an accounting mismatch caused by unrestricted token transfer, leading to incorrect slashing calculations, loss of withdrawable funds, and potential denial‑of‑service of protocol functions.

title: finishWithdrawal() doesn't remove withdrawal info
content: The vulnerability is a missing state cleanup in the withdrawal lifecycle of the contract. When a user creates a withdrawal request, the contract stores the amount and timestamps the request, enforcing a MIN_WITHDRAWAL_DELAY before the user may call finishWithdrawal to receive the funds. The intended logic is that each request can be settled exactly once after the delay, after which the stored withdrawal information should be removed so that the request is considered completed. However, the finishWithdrawal implementation does not delete or reset the stored withdrawal record after transferring the requested amount. As a result, the contract continues to believe that a valid withdrawal request exists, allowing the same user (or any party with the request data) to invoke finishWithdrawal repeatedly without waiting for the delay again. This can be exploited by calling finishWithdrawal in a loop after the initial delay, each call triggering another transfer of the same amount. The impact is that an attacker can drain the contract’s funds by repeatedly withdrawing the same amount, effectively creating an unlimited payout channel. The condition for exploitation is simply that a withdrawal request has been made and the MIN_WITHDRAWAL_DELAY has elapsed; no additional permissions or re‑entrancy tricks are required. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that examined the withdrawal flow and noticed that the state variable holding the request was never cleared. It may be hard to notice because the function appears to succeed and emit the expected transfer event, giving the impression that the operation is final, while the persistent data silently enables further calls. From a user’s perspective, the UI may still show the withdrawal request as pending even after the user receives the funds, and the user may be able to call the withdraw button again and receive money a second time, contrary to the expectation that the request is fulfilled only once. This violates the fundamental accounting assumption that each withdrawal request corresponds to a single debit of the contract’s balance. The proper fix is to delete or zero‑out the withdrawal record (for example, by removing the mapping entry or setting the amount to zero) immediately after the transfer succeeds, and optionally emit an event indicating completion. This ensures that subsequent calls to finishWithdrawal will revert because no pending request exists, restoring the intended one‑time withdrawal semantics.
summary:
In order to withdraw funds, the user needs to make a withdrawal request. This will store information about the amount that the user wants to withdraw and the request will be queued for execution.

After MIN_WITHDRAWAL_DELAY passes, the user has the ability to call finishWithdrawal to get funds. The reason why the user needs to wait MIN_WITHDRAWAL_DELAY is to make sure the user can't avoid slashing by frontrunning the slash action.

The problem is that finishWithdrawal function doesn't delete information about withdrawal after it's executed and as a result, the user can execute it as many times as he wishes and he doesn't need to wait MIN_WITHDRAWAL_DELAY anymore.

title: Code should use state root to validate withdraw credentials
content: The vulnerability consists ofan incorrect verification of withdrawal credentials during validator onboarding. The contract calls a function that is supposed to validate a proof against the beacon chain state root, but the implementation mistakenly passes the block root derived from the same timestamp instead of the beaconStateRoot. As a result, the Merkle proof that contains the validator’s information is checked against the wrong root, causing the proof verification to always fail. Consequently, any attempt to add a new validator is silently rejected: the transaction may appear to succeed, the caller’s balance is deducted, but the validator is never recorded in the system. This mismatch originates from a confusion between two distinct data structures – the beacon state root, which stores validator sets, and the block root, which represents the block header. The bug manifests whenever the validateWithdrawalCredentials function is invoked, i.e., during every validator addition. Users, staking operators, and the protocol itself are affected because new validators cannot be onboarded, effectively halting the growth of the staking set and potentially freezing funds that were intended for staking. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that compared the intended verification logic with the actual code. It is hard to notice because the function compiles, no revert is emitted, and the surrounding logic does not raise an explicit error, making the failure appear as a silent logical flaw rather than a runtime exception. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition for validator enrollment and a breach of the protocol’s accounting assumptions: funds are deducted but never reflected in the validator registry, violating the expectation that a successful transaction results in a registered validator. To remediate, the call to validateWithdrawalCredentials must be supplied with the beaconStateRoot proof (or the correct state root) instead of the block root, ensuring that the proof is verified against the data structure that actually contains the validator information. This correction aligns the verification step with the intended Merkle‑tree root and restores proper validator registration.
summary:
In the function validateWithdrawalCredentials() code validates the state root's proof but then it uses the block's root to verify the validator's information:
```solidity
totalRestakedWei += self.validateWithdrawalCredentials(
    nodeOwner,
    beaconStateRootProof.timestamp,
    _getParentBlockRoot(beaconStateRootProof.timestamp),
    validatorFieldsProofs[i]
);
```

Because of this issue, no validator can be added to the system.

title: H-1 Excessive rights for the MANAGER role
content: The vulnerability is an excessive‑rights issue in the role‑based access control of the LRT system. The MANAGER role, which is intended to be a limited administrative account, is granted permissions that allow it to modify the list of supported assets, change the price oracle for any asset, move tokens from NodeDelegator contracts and perform unrestricted swaps inside the deposit pool. Because these functions are not restricted to the DEFAULT_ADMIN role, a holder of the MANAGER role can introduce a malicious ERC‑20 token, register a fake price fetcher for that token, transfer all tokens held by the NodeDelegator contracts into the deposit pool and then execute swapAssetWithinDepositPool to exchange the malicious token for any other token and withdraw the proceeds. The root cause is a mis‑configuration of access control where critical asset‑management functions are exposed to a role that is assumed to be semi‑trusted. An attacker who obtains the MANAGER role can exploit the flaw by following a sequence: (1) call addNewSupportedAsset to add a token they control, (2) call updatePriceOracleFor to point the new token to a price oracle they control, (3) invoke transferFromNodeDelegator to move all pool assets into the deposit pool, (4) call swapAssetWithinDepositPool to swap the malicious token for a legitimate token and withdraw the funds. This results in the complete draining of user deposits, leaving user balances at zero, refunds unavailable and the protocol’s total assets depleted. The issue manifests whenever the MANAGER role is assigned to an address that is not the ultimate admin, for example a governance‑controlled multisig or a third‑party operator. All participants who rely on the protocol to safeguard their tokens – individual users, liquidity providers and the protocol itself – are affected. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the contract’s role definitions and identified that the MANAGER role overlaps with functions that should be exclusive to the admin. Because the permissions are granted through OpenZeppelin’s AccessControl and the functions appear to be benign (adding a token or updating an oracle), the problem can be easy to overlook in testing, especially if the audit does not simulate a malicious manager. The vulnerability belongs to the class of excessive privileges or over‑privileged role bugs, where a non‑owner role can perform actions that compromise asset integrity. To remediate, the privileged functions addNewSupportedAsset, updatePriceOracleFor and swapAssetWithinDepositPool should be restricted to the DEFAULT_ADMIN role (or a similarly trusted role), and the MANAGER role should be limited to read‑only or non‑financial operations. Additional safeguards such as multi‑signature approval for asset addition and oracle updates can further reduce the attack surface. In practice, users would notice that after a transaction their wallet shows no balance in the protocol, attempts to claim refunds return zero, and the UI reports no assets available. The expectation that a manager can only configure parameters is violated, leading to a breach of the protocol’s accounting assumptions and loss of funds.
summary:
The current system conﬁguration grants the MANAGER role extensive rights giving its owner the possibility to withdraw all the tokens from the contract. Speciﬁcally, the MANAGER is authorized to:  
• Swap the supported tokens within the LRTDepositPool.sol#L355.  
• Introduce new supported tokens to the LRTConﬁg.sol#L60 contract.  
• Set the IPriceFetcher oracles to the LRTOracle.sol#L93 for the supported tokens.  
• Transfer assets from the NodeDelegator contracts to the NodeDelegator.sol#L103.  
Advantaging these permissions, a manager is able to add their own ERC-20 token and PriceFetcher for it to the system, transfer all the available tokens from the NodeDelegator contracts to DepositorPool, and then withdraw them using swapAssetWithinDepositPool.  
While the MANAGER role acts as a sort of restricted administrative account, the fact that the MANAGER and DEFAULT_ADMIN roles are separated is the evidence that, by design, this role is not considered to be absolutely trustworthy.

title: H-2 An arbitrage opportunity in the rsETH price calculation for MANAGER role
content: The vulnerability is an arbitrage flaw in the multi‑asset deposit pool that allows an account holding the MANAGER role to extract value by calling the swapAssetWithinDepositPool function. The root cause is an incorrect internal price calculation for rsETH that relies on a static or otherwise inaccurate price oracle instead of a market‑driven pricing mechanism. Because the contract trusts the oracle value when determining the exchange rate, the calculated rate can diverge from the true market price, creating a systematic mispricing. A manager can invoke swapAssetWithinDepositPool, specify an amount of one asset, and receive the counterpart asset at a rate that is more favorable than the external market, thereby generating a profit without any risk. This can be exploited whenever the MANAGER permission to call swapAssetWithinDepositPool is retained, even if other manager privileges have been revoked. The impact is that liquidity providers and other participants see their pool balances shrink, expected returns disappear, and overall protocol funds may be drained, undermining confidence in the system. The issue manifests during normal deposit‑pool operations when a manager initiates a swap; from a user’s perspective the pool may appear to lose assets, withdrawals may return zero or far less than expected, and accounting reports show unexplained deficits. The flaw was discovered during a security audit performed by MixBytes, which highlighted that the price‑oracle‑based exchange rate is unsuitable for internal asset swaps. The problem is hard to notice because the function itself appears benign and the price discrepancy may only become evident after a manager repeatedly exploits it, making the loss look like normal market variance. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of pricing‑logic or oracle‑dependency vulnerabilities that enable arbitrage. To remediate, the contract should replace the oracle‑driven rate with a collateral‑debt model or an automated market maker (AMM) liquidity pool that derives prices from on‑chain supply and demand, thereby eliminating the deterministic mispricing that the manager can exploit.
summary: There is an arbitrage opportunity for the MANAGER role using the swapAssetWithinDepositPool function. Even if some MANAGER permissions are revoked, the permission to call swapAssetWithinDepositPool is enough to perform proﬁtable arbitrage.

title: H-3 Potential withdraw credentials overwritting by a malicious node operator
content: The vulnerability is an overwrite of withdrawal credentials that occurs when a malicious node operator front‑runs a legitimate deposit on the EigenLayer NodeDelegator contract. The root cause lies in the Ethereum 2.0 deposit contract’s inability to clearly distinguish an initial validator deposit from a subsequent top‑up deposit. Because the contract only checks the deposit root without verifying whether a public key already has an initial deposit, an attacker can submit an initial deposit for the same validator public key immediately before a target project such as KelpDAO submits its deposit. The target’s deposit is then interpreted as a top‑up of the attacker’s validator, causing the withdrawal credentials stored for the validator to remain those of the attacker. An attacker can therefore claim the deposited Ether when withdrawing, while the intended depositor sees no balance and cannot retrieve the funds. This can be exploited by monitoring pending deposit transactions, broadcasting a competing initial deposit with a higher gas price, and ensuring the attacker’s deposit is mined first. The impact is a permanent loss of liquidity for the affected project, as the stolen Ether is accounted for under the attacker’s validator and the legitimate depositor receives nothing. The condition for the exploit is the presence of a public key that has not yet been used for an initial deposit and the ability to front‑run the transaction; it is most relevant when using the stake function of NodeDelegator.sol around line 185 on mainnet. The affected parties include the DAO or protocol that performs the deposit, its users who expect to receive a corresponding tokenized stake, and any downstream contracts that rely on correct withdrawal credentials. The issue was discovered during a security audit performed by MixBytes, and it is subtle because the deposit root appears valid and the contract does not emit an explicit error when a top‑up is mistakenly applied to an attacker’s validator. Detecting the problem requires correlating on‑chain deposit events with off‑chain knowledge of which public keys already have an initial deposit, which is not trivial. Conceptually, the fix is to enforce a check that the deposit root matches an expected state calculated off‑chain, rejecting the transaction if a prior initial deposit for the same public key exists. This prevents the attacker’s initial deposit from being silently overwritten by a later top‑up, ensuring that withdrawal credentials correspond to the entity that performed the original deposit and preserving the intended accounting of funds.
summary: While performing a stake into the EigenLayer NodeDelegator.sol#L185, the Ether could be stolen. The speciﬁcation of ETH2.0 staking allows for two types of deposits: the initial deposit and the top-up deposit, which increases the balance of a previously made initial deposit. Unfortunately, the current implementation of the mainnet deposit contract does not sufﬁciently distinguish between these types of deposits. This oversight allows an attacker to front-run a KelpDAO's deposit with their own initial deposit causing KelpDAO's deposit to be treated as a top-up of the attacker's deposit. Consequently, KelpDAO's withdrawal credentials will be ignored, and the assets will be accounted for on behalf of the attacker. This issue has been classiﬁed as high severity due to the potential for permanent loss of project liquidity. The classiﬁcation also takes into consideration the developers' statement that all validator nodes are permissioned and have passed KYC, mitigating the overall risk assessment.

title: H-4 The reward calculation may be blocked until contract upgrade
content: The vulnerability is a hard‑coded reward‑withdrawal guard that reverts the initiateWithdrawRewards function whenever the total balance of the associated EigenPod exceeds 16 ETH. The guard was introduced as a temporary measure to differentiate normal staking rewards (expected to be below 16 ETH) from a full validator stake withdrawal, which should be handled manually. Because the check is hard‑coded and the contract does not contain any fallback path, any situation in which the accumulated rewards grow beyond the 16 ETH threshold—such as a period of high reward accrual or an unexpected validator‑initiated withdrawal—causes the function to revert. When the revert occurs, the reward calculation and withdrawal flow are blocked, preventing users from claiming their earned rewards. The impact is that legitimate reward funds become inaccessible until a contract upgrade is performed to replace or remove the guard. This condition can persist indefinitely because the contract lacks an on‑chain mechanism to bypass the check, and the only remediation path is a manual upgrade, which may be delayed or never executed. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the withdraw‑rewards logic and identified the hard‑coded limit as an ad‑hoc solution. It is difficult to notice in normal operation because most reward periods stay below the threshold, so the revert only appears under edge‑case reward growth, making it easy to miss during routine testing. The bug belongs to the class of “hard‑coded business‑logic limits that cause functional freeze” and violates the accounting assumption that rewards are always claimable. From a user’s perspective, a transaction to claim rewards fails with a revert, the UI shows no change in balance, and the user receives no funds despite expecting a payout. The expected behavior (reward claim succeeds) diverges from reality (transaction reverts, funds stay locked). To remediate, the contract should be refactored to use a dynamic, upgrade‑safe accounting model that distinguishes stake withdrawals from reward payouts without relying on a static ETH threshold, and the logic should be made upgradable or include an emergency bypass that allows reward claims even when the balance exceeds the previous limit.
summary: Currently, the NodeDelegator.initiateWithdrawRewards() will revert NodeDelegator.sol#L232 if the balance of the EigenPod exceeds 16 ETH. This is intended to distinguish between the staking rewards and the stake withdrawal. It is expected that rewards will be less than 16 ETH; otherwise, something unexpected has occurred (i.e., the validator initiated the withdrawal) and should be resolved manually. It is an ad-hoc temporary solution that will require a contract upgrade by design. This ﬁnding is rated HIGH as the reward calculation may be blocked until a manual contract upgrade.

title: Users can set feeOn > 1 to avoid fees
content: The vulnerability originates from the way the contract interprets the user‑supplied feeOn parameter during a swap operation. feeOn is intended to be a binary flag where the value 0 selects feeIn (charging a fee on the input amount) and the value 1 selects feeOut (charging a fee on the output amount). The implementation uses a conditional expression that sets (bool feeIn, bool feeOut) based on feeOn only when the global fee variable is greater than zero. However, there is no validation that feeOn is limited to the values 0 or 1. When a caller provides a feeOn value greater than 1, the expression evaluates to (false, false), meaning that both feeIn and feeOut are disabled even though the fee variable is non‑zero. As a result, the contract skips the fee calculation and does not accrue any fee for that swap. This can be exploited by any user who can control the feeOn argument: they simply pass a value such as 2 (or any integer larger than 1) when initiating a swap, and the transaction proceeds without any fee being deducted. The impact is that the protocol loses expected revenue, users can trade for free, and the tokenomics that rely on fee collection are undermined. The issue occurs whenever the fee mechanism is active (fee > 0) and the contract accepts an unchecked uint8 feeOn from the caller. All participants who perform swaps are affected – honest users may see an unexpected fee‑free trade, while the protocol and token holders suffer reduced fee income. The flaw was discovered during a manual code review that highlighted the missing range check on feeOn; it is subtle because the parameter is documented as a boolean flag, yet the tests only exercised the valid values 0 and 1, allowing the bug to remain hidden. Detecting the problem in production can be difficult because the contract still behaves correctly for the documented inputs, and the absence of a fee may be interpreted as a favorable outcome rather than a security issue. To remediate, the contract should enforce that feeOn can only be 0 or 1, either by changing the type to a boolean or by adding an explicit require statement that validates the range before the fee logic is executed. This ensures that the fee calculation path is always taken when a fee is configured, preserving the intended economic model and preventing fee‑free swaps.
summary: feeOn is indicated by users on every swap and is responsible for choosing between feeIn and feeOut . feeOn == 0, means feeIn true and feeOut false. feeOn == 1, means feeIn false and feeOut true. (bool feeIn, bool feeOut) = fee > 0 ? (feeOn == 0, feeOn == 1) : (false, false); But if feeOn is above 1, both feeIn and feeOut will be false, even if fee is set. As a result, fees will not be accrued.

title: LPS-1 | Rewards May Be Stolen
content: The vulnerability resides in the interaction between the LPStaker contract and the Uniswap V3 Staker contract. The Uniswap V3 Staker permits any address to invoke the unstakeToken function for any depositor after the incentive key's endTime. When an attacker calls unstakeToken directly on the Uniswap V3 Staker for a position that was originally deposited through the LPStaker, the Uniswap V3 Staker updates the reward accounting for the LPStaker contract, but the LPStaker does not forward those rewards to the original user. Consequently, the attacker can subsequently call the LPStaker's claimRewards function and receive the newly accrued rewards, which actually belong to the victim. This can be exploited after the incentive period has expired, i.e., when endTime has passed, and only if the LPStaker contract does not enforce that the caller of unstakeToken matches the original depositor. The impact is that malicious actors can siphon reward tokens that were meant for honest liquidity providers, effectively stealing a portion of the incentive pool. Users see their expected reward balance remain unchanged or become zero, while the attacker’s balance increases unexpectedly. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the LPStaker’s integration with Uniswap V3 Staker, where the auditor noticed that the unstake function does not verify the msg.sender against the original depositor. The bug is subtle because the Uniswap V3 Staker itself is trusted and the reward increment appears to be correctly recorded for the LPStaker, masking the fact that the rewards are not tied to a specific user. To remediate, the LPStaker (or a fork of Uniswap V3 Staker) should enforce that only the original depositor can trigger an unstake after the incentive period, or the reward accounting should be tied to the depositor’s address before any claim is allowed. Managing incentive keys so that they never reach endTime while users are still staked is another mitigation, but the robust fix is to add depositor verification or redesign the reward flow to prevent third‑party unstaking.
summary: The uniswapV3Staker contract which the LPStaker interacts with allows any arbitrary address to directly call the unstakeToken function and unstake for any depositor after the incentive key endTime. When a deposit is unstaked from an incentive key directly from the uniswapV3Staker, those rewards will be incremented for the LPStaker contract, but not credited towards the user who staked. Therefore malicious stakers may unstake for other stakers and immediately claim their rewards as their own by unstaking through the LPStaker contract.

title: STK-1 | Reward Compounds Are Sandwichable
content: The vulnerability is that the staking contract allows a user to start staking immediately before the reward‑compounding function runs and receive a proportional share of rewards that were intended for existing stakers. Because there is no fee, no lock‑up, and no warm‑up period, the attacker can sandwich the reward update: first deposit (stake) just before the update, then after the update claim the newly minted rewards, immediately unstake and sell the underlying token. This results in other stakers receiving less reward than expected, effectively stealing value from them. The root cause is the absence of a mechanism that delays reward accrual for newly‑staked positions, combined with the reward distribution being calculated based on total staked amount at the moment of the update without distinguishing between old and new stakes. The exploit can be performed by monitoring pending reward updates, submitting a stake transaction with a higher gas price to be mined just before the updateAllRewardsForTransferReceiverAndTransferFee call, then after the call executing a claimRewards and unstake transaction. The impact is a reduction of earned rewards for honest participants, loss of expected yield, and potential erosion of trust in the protocol's fairness. The condition occurs whenever the contract’s updateAllRewards... function is called, which is typically triggered by transfers or other state changes; any time this function runs, an attacker can insert a stake just before it. All stakers, including regular users and institutional participants, are affected because the total reward pool is diluted by the attacker’s share. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the reward‑distribution logic and noted the lack of a warm‑up or fee mechanism. It may be hard to notice because the contract’s external behavior (users can stake and claim rewards) appears normal, and the loss of rewards is only observable as a slight shortfall in expected returns, which can be attributed to market variance. To remediate, the contract should enforce a minimum staking period before rewards are eligible, introduce a staking fee that reduces the immediate reward share, or redesign the reward calculation to exclude newly‑staked balances from the current compounding cycle. This class of bug is commonly known as a sandwichable reward distribution or front‑runable staking reward flaw, where the reward accounting does not differentiate between existing and newly‑added stake during a compounding event. From a user’s perspective, a regular staker may notice that after a reward cycle their claimed amount is lower than the projected amount, or that the protocol’s APY appears to drop unexpectedly. The expectation that staking immediately yields a proportional share of the current reward pool is violated, leading to funds disappear or rewards stolen symptoms.
summary: There exists no fee or lockup period associated with staking to receive a portion of the rewards compounded during the updateAllRewardsForTransferReceiverAndTransferFee function. A malicious actor may simply buy GMXKey and stake right before the updateAllRewardsForTransferReceiverAndTransferFee function to immediately accrue a portion of the collected rewards that were meant to be attributed to other stakers. The malicious actor can then immediately claim these rewards, unstake and sell GMXKey after the reward compound, therefore stealing rewards from other stakers.

title: TREC-1 | Lost WETH Rewards Upon Upgrade
content: The vulnerability is a reward‑migration logic error that occurs when a user upgrades their account to a new TransferReceiver contract. The system is supposed to move the user’s staked balance and any accumulated WETH rewards to the new contract. However, the RewardRouter component fails to invoke the claim function for the fee‑tracker that holds the pending WETH rewards before the balance transfer. As a result, the pending rewards remain locked in the old tracker and are never injected into the new Rewards contract. When the new TransferReceiver attempts to mint reward tokens, the calculation that determines the amount to mint uses the transferred‑out staked balance as a denominator. Because the balance has already been moved out while the reward amount is zero, the arithmetic underflows, causing the transaction to revert. This means the user’s accrued WETH rewards disappear from the system and the upgrade transaction fails, leaving the user with no way to claim the rewards. The issue is triggered only during an upgrade path that involves the TransferReceiver’s upgrade function; normal staking or reward claiming operations are unaffected. It primarily affects token holders who try to migrate their position, the protocol’s reward accounting, and any downstream contracts that rely on the minted reward amount. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the upgrade flow, where the auditor observed that the claimForAccount call was missing and that the amount‑to‑mint formula could underflow after a balance transfer. Because the failure manifests as a transaction revert without an obvious error message, it can be hard for users to understand why their rewards are missing. The correct mitigation is to ensure that all pending rewards are claimed and transferred into the new reward pool before the staked balance is moved, or to adjust the minting calculation to handle a zero‑reward case safely. In generic terms, this is a state‑migration bug where reward state is not synchronized with balance state, leading to loss of funds and broken accounting logic. From the user’s perspective, after initiating an upgrade they may see the transaction fail, their reward balance stay at zero, and the expected WETH payout never arrive, contrary to the expectation that the upgrade preserves all earned rewards.
summary: During the account transfer process, the RewardRouterV2 does not claimForAccount from the feeGMXTracker. Therefore any accrued WETH rewards will not be transferred to the new address upon upgrade of the TransferReceiver. The TransferReceiver will then have no means of claiming these WETH rewards and injecting them into the Rewards system as the amountToMint calculation will underflow and revert since the receiver’s staked balances have been transferred out.

title: H-1 The SponsorPaymaster owner should be restricted to withdraw
content: The vulnerability is an accounting inconsistency in the SponsorPaymaster contract that allows the contract owner to withdraw ETH that should remain available to sponsor accounts. The root cause lies in the _postOp function, which after each UserOperation deducts the gas cost (ethCost) from the sponsoring account’s internal balance, records the spent amount, and then incorrectly adds the same ethCost to the owner’s internal balance. Because the total of all internal balances is kept constant, the sum of sponsor balances reported by the paymaster does not reflect the actual ETH held in the EntryPoint’s deposit mapping, which is reduced by the same ethCost when the operation is executed. When the owner later calls withdrawTokensTo, the owner’s balance is reduced and the corresponding ETH is transferred out of the EntryPoint, but the internal balances of the other sponsors are left unchanged. Consequently, the EntryPoint’s deposit for the paymaster can become zero while the paymaster still reports non‑zero balances for individual sponsors. This mismatch causes subsequent UserOperations that rely on a positive paymaster deposit to fail, effectively locking sponsor funds and preventing withdrawals. The issue manifests whenever the SponsorPaymaster is used and the owner performs a withdrawal; it affects all sponsors who have deposited ETH through the paymaster, as well as any users whose transactions depend on the paymaster’s funding. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the invariant that the sum of all sponsor balances should equal the EntryPoint’s deposit for the paymaster and observed that the invariant was broken after owner withdrawals. The bug is subtle because each individual sponsor’s balance appears correct, so the error only becomes visible when the global deposit is exhausted, leading to unexpected “insufficient balance” reverts. To remediate, the line that credits the owner’s balance (balances[owner()] += ethCost) should be removed or replaced with a proper accounting mechanism that does not alter the total of sponsor balances, ensuring that withdrawals only affect the owner’s own entitlement and that the paymaster’s deposit in the EntryPoint always matches the sum of sponsor balances.

title: H-2 Draining SponsorPaymaster.balances with spam operations
content: The vulnerability is an unchecked gas‑payment mechanism in the SponsorPaymaster contract that allows an attacker to deplete the balance associated with any address that has been pre‑funded in SponsorPaymaster.balances[]. The contract deducts gas costs from SponsorPaymaster.balances[account] where *account* is the destination address supplied to KintoWallet.execute() or executeBatch(). Because the UserOp.account that initiates the transaction is not required to pay for the gas, an adversary can craft a UserOp whose target address is a KintoWallet that holds a sponsor balance and invoke any function, even a read‑only view function. The call still consumes gas, which is silently taken from the sponsor’s balance, while the attacker pays nothing. This design flaw stems from the assumption that the destination address will always be the same as the sponsor or that only state‑changing calls need to be charged, which is not enforced. Exploitation proceeds by submitting a large number of UserOps with malicious calldata that points to a sponsored wallet; each operation drains a small amount of the sponsor’s balance, and the attacker can repeat the process until the balance is exhausted. The impact is a loss of funds for the sponsor account, potential denial‑of‑service for users who rely on the sponsor’s gas coverage, and erosion of trust in the protocol’s sponsorship model. The issue manifests whenever a UserOp is processed for a destination address that has a non‑zero entry in SponsorPaymaster.balances[], regardless of whether the called function modifies state. Affected parties include the sponsors (any address with a balance in the paymaster), the owners of the sponsored KintoWallets, and the protocol that promises gas‑free transactions. The problem was discovered during a security audit by MixBytes, where the logical flow of gas accounting was examined and the missing charge to the caller was identified. Because the operations appear harmless on the UI—no token transfers, no state changes, and no error messages—the balance drain can go unnoticed until the sponsor’s funds are significantly reduced. To remediate, the paymaster should require that the UserOp.account (the caller) contributes to the gas cost, or at least verify that the destination address is authorized to consume the sponsor’s balance. Introducing a per‑operation fee, adding explicit checks that the target is not a sponsored wallet, or redesigning the accounting so that only approved, state‑changing calls are charged would close the attack vector and align the implementation with the intended business logic of sponsored gas payments.
summary: Currently, users are not charged for their operations. Gas compensations are taken from SponsorPaymaster.balances[account], where account is the destination address in KintoWallet.execute() or KintoWallet.executeBatch(). These accounts are charged with their SponsorPaymaster.balances[]. As a result, users can spam multiple UserOps, and gas costs will be compensated from these account balances. This attack has no cost, but results in losses for account if actively used. Moreover, these accounts can be other KintoWallets if they have some balance on SponsorPaymaster.balances[]. An attacker should build a calldata where the target address is another KintoWallet and the function signature is some read-only function on the target KintoWallet.

title: H-3 DoS of an account using frontrun
content: The vulnerability is a front‑run denial‑of‑service condition in the KintoWalletFactory contract. An attacker can call the factory’s deployContract function with a chosen salt before a legitimate user invokes createAccount. Because deployContract creates a proxy instance of the wallet without initializing the internal wallet timestamp (walletTs), the subsequent createAccount call detects that a contract already exists at the deterministic address and therefore skips the CREATE2 deployment step. The result is a wallet that is technically deployed but has a zero timestamp and lacks the metadata required by the recovery mechanism. If a user later sends tokens to this wallet, the funds become permanently inaccessible: the EntryPoint cannot invoke any owner‑controlled function, and the built‑in recovery path cannot locate a valid timestamp to trigger a rescue. The issue occurs whenever an adversary can front‑run the user’s transaction and knows the salt used for CREATE2, which is typical in public mempools. All participants who rely on KintoWalletFactory to create accounts are affected, including individual users, the protocol’s accounting layer, and any downstream services that assume wallets are recoverable. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the interaction between deployContract and createAccount and identified that the factory does not enforce a unique creation path for KintoWallet accounts. It is subtle because the wallet contract appears valid on‑chain; there is no explicit error flag, and the UI may simply show the wallet address as existing, leading users to believe the account is functional. The denial‑of‑service manifests as tokens sent to the address never being withdrawable, effectively disappearing from the user’s perspective. To remediate, the factory should prohibit the creation of KintoWallet instances via deployContract, enforce that only createAccount can instantiate wallets, or add a check that the wallet timestamp is set during deployment. Alternatively, a commit‑reveal scheme for the salt or a guard that rejects deployments when a wallet already exists would prevent the front‑run scenario. In short, the bug is a classic front‑runable contract‑creation race that results in a wallet with missing initialization data, causing funds to be locked and the recovery process to fail.

title: H-4 DoS KintoWallet contract
content: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition in the KintoWallet contract that arises when the resetSigners function is used to set an owners array whose length is smaller than the current signerPolicy. The contract stores a signerPolicy value that indicates how many distinct signatures are required to approve a user operation. ResetSigners, however, does not validate that the new list of owners satisfies this policy. Consequently, a user (or an attacker) can call resetSigners with a single owner while the signerPolicy remains set to two or more. During signature validation the contract iterates over the owners array and expects a matching signature for each owner. Because the owners length is less than the required number of signers, the requiredSigners counter never reaches zero and the _validateSignature routine returns an error for every transaction. The wallet therefore becomes unusable: any attempt to execute a user operation fails with a signature‑validation error, and the only way to restore functionality is to wait for the built‑in 7‑day recovery period and invoke finishRecovery. This issue was discovered during a security audit performed by MixBytes. It can be hard to notice because the resetSigners function appears to accept any array of addresses, and the UI does not warn the user that the new owner set violates the existing policy. The impact is that funds locked in the wallet cannot be moved, users see no transaction execution, and balances appear unchanged while the wallet is effectively frozen. The affected parties are all owners of the wallet and any protocol that relies on the wallet for fund management. To remediate the problem the contract should enforce that the number of owners after a reset is greater than or equal to the signerPolicy, or automatically lower the policy to match the new owner count, and revert the transaction if the condition is violated. This fixes the class of bug known as a policy‑owner mismatch leading to signature‑validation failure and prevents the wallet from being rendered inoperable.

title: H-5 Incorrect signature validation for different signer policies
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect signature validation logic in a multi‑owner smart‑wallet that supports several signer policies. The root cause is that the function responsible for checking signatures calculates the number of required signatures based on the selected policy but fails to enforce a minimum when the policy is set to a minus‑one signer configuration, and it only verifies the first owner when the policy is single‑signer. Additionally, the validation routine checks the KYC status of the first owner exclusively, and it can return values greater than one, which are interpreted incorrectly by the ERC‑4337 entry point. An attacker can exploit the minus‑one signer case by setting the wallet to a single‑owner configuration; the validation then requires zero signatures, allowing any actor to submit a withdrawal transaction that will be accepted without a valid signature, resulting in loss of funds. In the single‑signer case, if the first owner loses their private key or fails KYC, the contract rejects all signatures from the remaining owners, causing a denial‑of‑service where legitimate owners cannot execute any transaction. The return of a number larger than one may cause the entry point to treat the transaction as having an aggregator, leading to unexpected acceptance or rejection of operations. From a user perspective the symptoms include unexpected successful withdrawals without a signature, inability to send transactions despite having other owners, and error messages when trying to execute actions after a policy change. The issue affects all wallet participants, the protocol that relies on the wallet for fund custody, and any funds locked in the contract. It was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the signature validation routine and policy‑changing functions. The flaw is subtle because the code appears to enforce the intended policies, yet the off‑by‑one calculation and the hard‑coded owner index hide the bypass. To remediate the problem the validation should be constrained to return only 0 (invalid) or 1 (valid), the required‑signer calculation must never result in zero, the single‑signer policy should accept a signature from any listed owner rather than only the first, and KYC checks should be applied to the signer that actually provided the signature. Moreover, the function must conform to ERC‑4337 expectations by never returning values that could be misinterpreted as an aggregator signature.

title: H-6 Signature issues in KintoID and Faucet
content: The vulnerability is a signature replay flaw that allows a privileged KYC node to destroy a user’s KintoID after the user has signed a legitimate minting request. The contract builds the signed message by hashing a fixed set of fields – the signer address, the contract address, the target account, the token identifier, an expiration timestamp, a nonce taken from the signer’s entry in a mapping, and the chain identifier – but it omits the function selector that identifies which operation the signature is intended for. After the signature is verified, the contract mistakenly increments the nonce associated with the target account instead of the signer, leaving the signer’s nonce unchanged. Because the nonce does not advance, the same signature remains valid for any function that uses the same hashing scheme. Consequently, a node that holds the KYCPROVIDERROLE can reuse a signature that was originally created for mintIndividualKyc() to call burnKYC() and permanently remove the user’s KintoID. This can be performed at any later time, without further consent from the user. The impact is the unauthorized burning of identity tokens, which may revoke access rights, break downstream protocol logic, and cause users to see their KintoID disappear from the UI even though they expected it to persist after minting. The issue manifests whenever a user signs a mint transaction, the contract checks the signature using the flawed hash, and the privileged node decides to invoke the burn function with the same signature. It affects all users of the KintoID system and any contracts that rely on the existence of those IDs, such as the Faucet contract, which contains the same flawed logic. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the signature verification flow and noticed the mismatch between the nonce that is hashed and the nonce that is incremented, as well as the absence of a domain separator for the function name. The problem is subtle because the signature appears cryptographically correct and the contract does not emit an explicit error, making the replay attack hard to detect without reviewing the hashing code. To remediate, the contract should increment the nonce belonging to the signer, ensure that the nonce is tied to the signer’s address, and incorporate the function selector (or a unique operation identifier) into the hashed data so that a signature is bound to a single intended action. This class of bug falls under improper nonce management and missing domain separation in off‑chain signatures, which can lead to replay attacks across different contract functions.
summary:
• KintoID.sol#L371-L399  
• Faucet.sol#L90-L114  
In the current implementation, it is assumed that a KYC node can issue a user a KintoID and cannot burn it unless the user signs such a transaction. Incorrect handling of nonces and non-standard construction of the hash for signature lead to the situation where a node with the KYCPROVIDERROLE can at any time burn a user's KintoID.  

The SignatureData struct has fields signer and account. Signer is the one who makes the signature. Account is the one to whom the KintoID is issued. The minting and burning functions check the signature of the following structure:  
```solidity
keccak256(
    abi.encodePacked(
        '\x19\x01', // EIP-191 header
        keccak256(abi.encode(
            _signature.signer,
            address(this),
            _signature.account,
            _id,
            _signature.expiresAt,
            nonces[_signature.signer],
            bytes32(block.chainid)
        ))
    )
)
```
It can be noticed that nonces[_signature.signer] is hashed. However, after the signature check, nonces[_signature.account] is increased, which is incorrect.  

Furthermore, in building the hash, the name of the function for which the signature is given is missing. This allows the same signature to be used to call any of the functions, such as mintIndividualKyc(), as well as burnKYC().  

As the nonce for the signature effectively does not change, the KYC node can subsequently use the same signature that was applied for the mintIndividualKyc() function to burn the KintoID through burnKYC().  
It should be noted that similar problems are present in the Faucet contract.

title: gameEndTime is incorrectly updated during unpause
content: The contract implements a pause/unpause feature for a timed button‑press game but updates the deadline incorrectly when the game is resumed. The root cause is that the unpause logic recomputes the game end timestamp as the moment the last button press occurred (pausedAt) plus the remaining countdown, instead of adding the remaining time to the current block timestamp. Because the pause duration is not subtracted from the countdown, any pause that lasts longer than the remaining time makes the stored gameEndTime lie in the past. When the owner calls unpause, the contract sees the current block.timestamp greater than the stale gameEndTime and immediately triggers the end‑game routine, declaring the player who made the last press before the pause as the winner. An attacker who can trigger a pause (or who colludes with the pauser) can therefore force the game to finish instantly after the pause, denying other participants the chance to act and potentially capturing the reward unfairly. The bug manifests only when the game is paused after at least one press and the pause lasts longer than the remaining countdown; in normal short pauses the deadline appears correct, which makes the problem easy to miss during casual testing. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit of the pause handling code, where the mismatch between the stored duration and the calculation on unpause was identified. From a user perspective the UI shows the game resuming, but the contract instantly emits a win event and the balance of the last player is transferred, while other players see no opportunity to submit a move and may wonder why the game ended “out of nowhere”. This is a classic time‑accounting bug where the paused state is not accounted for in deadline calculations, similar to “deadline not extended after pause” vulnerabilities. The proper fix is to capture the remaining time (gameEndTime‑block.timestamp) at the moment of pause, store it in a dedicated variable, and on unpause set gameEndTime to block.timestamp plus that stored remaining time, then clear the temporary variable. This ensures the countdown continues from where it left off, preserving the intended game duration and preventing an immediate win after a long pause.
