summary: The pause/unpause mechanism fails to adjust the game end time to account for elapsed time during pauses. When unpausing, the contract calculates gameEndTime using pausedAt + countdown instead of considering the actual pause duration. If a game is paused long enough, it will end immediately upon unpausing, declaring the last player before pause as the winner without giving other players the chance to participate. Consider the following scenario: 1. Game starts at timestamp 1000 with gameStartTime = 1000 and countdown = 300 seconds 2. Initial gameEndTime = 1300 3. At timestamp 1005, Player A presses the button - countdown decreases to 270 seconds (after 30-second decrement) - gameEndTime is updated to 1005 + 270 = 1275 - lastPlayer = Player A 4. At timestamp 1010, the game is paused for maintenance - pausedAt = 1005 (timestamp of last press) 5. The game remains paused for 500 seconds until timestamp 1510 6. At timestamp 1510, the game is unpaused - gameEndTime is incorrectly set to pausedAt + countdown = 1005 + 270 = 1275 7. Since timestamp 1510 > gameEndTime 1275, the game immediately ends 8. Player A is declared the winner without other players having a chance to compete

title: A malicious actor can prevent sending messages through the executor and
content: The vulnerability is an unrestricted access control on the function that updates the deny‑list used by the executor’s access‑control list (ACL). The executor program checks the ACL before allowing a quote request, which is required for the Ultra Light Node (ULN) to calculate the fee and forward a cross‑chain message. The SetDenylist routine iterates over a caller‑supplied array and adds each address to the deny‑list, but it does not verify that the caller is the contract owner or any privileged role. Because there is no permission check, any external account can invoke this routine and insert arbitrary sender addresses – including the address of an OApp that the ULN relies on for quoting – into the deny‑list. When a sender is denied, the subsequent call to the quote function fails the ACL assertion, causing the executor to reject the fee quotation. The ULN, which automatically calls the quote function before paying the executor, then receives no fee estimate and aborts the send operation. This results in a denial‑of‑service condition where legitimate cross‑chain messages cannot be dispatched, effectively “blocking” the protocol’s messaging layer. The impact is that users or applications attempting to send messages experience silent failures: the UI may show no fee estimate, the transaction may revert with an ACL error, or the message simply never leaves the source chain, leading to funds being locked or delayed. The issue manifests whenever an attacker submits a SetDenylist transaction with the target sender’s address, and it persists as long as the deny‑list entry remains because only the contract owner can later remove it. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the executor’s permission checks, where the absence of a has_one or similar owner constraint on the SetDenylist instruction stood out as a logical oversight. It can be hard to notice because the function appears innocuous and the deny‑list is stored in a configuration account that is otherwise only read during normal operation; the failure only surfaces when a denied sender attempts to use the executor. To remediate, the SetDenylist instruction should enforce that only the designated owner (or another authorized role) can modify the deny‑list, for example by adding a has_one = owner constraint to the config account or by explicitly checking the caller’s signature against the stored owner address before mutating the ACL. This change restores the intended trust model, prevents arbitrary denial of service, and aligns the contract’s behavior with the business logic that only privileged entities may restrict message senders.

title: protocol/WETHGateway.sol: contract can be griefed not allowing borrowing
content: The vulnerability is a grief‑grabbing condition in the WETHGateway contract that blocks the borrow function when the contract holds an unexpected dust amount of WETH. The contract asserts that its WETH balance exactly matches the amount it has just borrowed from the market (assert(_weth.balanceOf(address(this)) == amount)). Because the check uses strict equality, any extra wei – for example a single wei sent by an attacker to the contract – makes the assertion fail and forces the borrow transaction to revert on every call. This happens because the contract does not tolerate a non‑zero residual balance; it assumes that the only WETH it holds is the amount it just borrowed. An attacker can exploit this by sending a minimal amount of ETH (which is automatically wrapped to WETH) to the contract before a legitimate user initiates a borrow. The tiny dust is enough to break the equality test, causing the borrow operation to revert every time, effectively denying service to all users who rely on the gateway for borrowing ETH. The impact is a denial‑of‑service on the borrowing path: users see transactions fail, receive no funds, and experience a broken front‑end experience, even though their assets remain safe because the transaction reverts before any transfer occurs. The condition occurs whenever the contract’s WETH balance is not exactly the borrowed amount, which can be triggered at any time by anyone who can call depositTradingPool() or otherwise transfer a single wei to the contract. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the balance assertion logic. It is hard to notice because a one‑wei discrepancy is invisible in normal operation and does not affect the contract’s normal accounting, yet it completely disables borrowing. The proper fix is to remove the strict equality assertion or replace it with a more tolerant check (e.g., require the balance to be at least the borrowed amount) and rely on the market.borrow call to handle failures. In broader terms, this is a classic example of a “dust‑sensitivity” or “balance‑equality” bug that enables a griefing attack by introducing minimal token dust, violating the protocol’s expectation that balances remain clean and causing user‑facing symptoms such as “borrow transaction reverts”, “no funds received”, and “frontend shows error”.
summary:
The borrow operation of the WETHGateway contract can be rendered useless if someone sends 1 wei to the contract (causing it to always revert on line 117):
```solidity
assert(_weth.balanceOf(address(this)) == amount);
```
This issue is not critical since the WETHGateway contract is just a router which simplifies operations with eth (by converting it to weth), however, the severity is still high since it is used by the front end, so this exploit could significantly harm user experience.

title: WithdrawDonation can incur max slippage
content: The vulnerability resides in a public withdrawDonation function that moves donated assets from a remote chain to a designated receiver. The function accepts a slippage protection argument called minAmount, which is supplied by the caller. Because the function is permissionless, any external account can invoke it and set minAmount to zero. This effectively disables the slippage guard, allowing the transfer to proceed even if the received amount on the destination chain falls far below the expected donation amount due to price volatility, bridge fees, or other on‑chain losses. An attacker can therefore trigger a donation withdrawal at a moment when market conditions cause severe slippage, causing the donationReceiver to obtain far less than the donor intended, or in extreme cases to receive nothing while the donor’s funds are burned or locked in the bridge. The issue appears when the contract relies on the caller‑provided minAmount to enforce a lower bound on the received value, but does not restrict who may set this parameter. It affects all participants who rely on the donation mechanism: donors expect their full contribution to be delivered, the receiver expects a guaranteed minimum, and the protocol’s reputation is harmed because donations can be arbitrarily reduced. The flaw was identified during a security audit that examined the access control model of the contract and noticed that the slippage parameter was not validated. It can be difficult to notice in normal operation because a zero minAmount does not raise an error; the transaction succeeds and only the final received amount reveals the loss, which may be hidden behind normal bridge fee variance. To remediate, the withdrawDonation function should be restricted to trusted callers (e.g., only the contract owner or the designated receiver) or the minAmount parameter should be validated to enforce a sensible lower bound, ensuring that slippage protection cannot be disabled arbitrarily. Conceptually, this is a classic case of unchecked user‑controlled parameters combined with missing access control, leading to a slippage‑protection bypass that violates the accounting assumption that the transferred amount will not fall below a predefined threshold. From a user’s perspective, the UI may still show the original donation amount, but the receiver’s balance may be unexpectedly low or zero, contradicting the expectation that the full donation arrives.

title: _lzReceive reverts when there is a fee refund
content: The vulnerability is a missing payable fallback (receive) function in the ClaimLocal contract that prevents it from accepting native ETH refunds. When a user initiates a cross‑chain claim, the LayerZero endpoint calculates a messaging fee and, if the supplied fee exceeds the exact amount required, the surplus is automatically sent back to the caller address – in this case the ClaimLocal contract. Because ClaimLocal does not implement a receive() external payable or a fallback() external payable function, the low‑level call performed by Transfer.native reverts with Transfer_NativeFailed. Consequently the internal _lzReceive handler reverts every time a fee refund is attempted, aborting the entire claim flow. The impact is that users cannot successfully claim their ZRO tokens on remote chains; the transaction fails, no tokens are transferred, and the user sees no change in balance despite having paid a fee. The issue manifests only when the supplied msg.value is larger than the exact fee, which is a common situation when callers over‑estimate fees to guarantee delivery. It affects any user attempting to claim tokens across chains and also harms the protocol’s reliability because the claim mechanism is effectively broken. The bug was discovered during a security audit that inspected the interaction between the ClaimLocal contract and LayerZero’s SendLibrary, noticing that the refund path had no payable entry point. It is hard to notice because the revert occurs deep inside a library call and surfaces as a generic transfer failure rather than an obvious missing function. The class of bug is a payable fallback omission leading to native token transfer failure, a subtype of improper handling of external ETH refunds. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a “claim” button that appears to submit, but after confirmation the token balance remains unchanged and no refund is received, contradicting the expectation that the claim succeeds and any excess fee is returned. To remediate, the contract should implement a receive() external payable (or a fallback payable) function so that the refund can be accepted, allowing the _lzReceive logic to complete and the token claim event to be emitted as intended.

title: MJR-1 Possible incorrect scaledTotalSupply calculation
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect calculation of the scaled total supply in the AStETH contract. The contract stores a variable representing shares as a signed integer. When the share balance becomes negative, the code later casts this signed value to an unsigned uint256 without checking its sign. Because Solidity performs a two's‑complement conversion, a negative number is interpreted as a very large positive integer, causing an overflow. The overflow propagates to the scaledTotalSupply variable, which is used to represent the total amount of stETH that corresponds to the underlying assets. As a result, the reported total supply can be dramatically higher or lower than the actual amount of assets held by the contract. This mis‑calculation can be triggered whenever a user’s share balance drops below zero, for example after a withdrawal that exceeds the recorded share amount due to rounding errors or edge‑case logic. An attacker who can cause a negative share balance can therefore manipulate the scaled total supply, potentially inflating their own share of the pool or causing other users to receive fewer tokens than expected. From a user’s perspective the symptoms may appear as missing or unexpectedly reduced balances, refunds that are zero, or a total supply displayed in the UI that does not match the sum of individual holdings. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit by MixBytes, where the auditors noted the unchecked conversion at line 595 of AStETH.sol. The bug is subtle because the transaction does not revert; the overflow silently corrupts accounting data, making it hard to detect without deep inspection of the supply calculation logic. The class of bug is a signed‑to‑unsigned casting overflow, a common arithmetic error that violates the protocol’s accounting invariants. To remediate the problem the contract should validate that the share value is non‑negative before casting, or use a safe casting library that reverts on negative inputs, thereby ensuring that scaledTotalSupply always reflects the true amount of assets. Proper checks will restore the integrity of the supply accounting and prevent users from experiencing lost or incorrect token balances.
summary: At the line AStETH.sol#L595 if the shares are below zero then value may overflow and scaled total supply calculation will be wrong.

title: MJR-1 Token Bridging doesn't work with Wormhole fees
content: The vulnerability is a fee‑handling mismatch in the token bridging flow of the Lido Anchor collateral system. The Bridge contract exposes a payable function transferTokens that forwards the caller‑provided ether (msg.value) to an internal logTransfer routine, which in turn calls a Wormhole implementation’s publishMessage function that enforces a strict fee requirement via require(msg.value == messageFee(),"invalid fee"). However, the higher‑level BridgeConnectorWormhole contract invokes transferTokens from its own transferasset function without declaring the function payable and without forwarding any ether. As a result, when a user or another contract attempts to bridge MJR‑1 tokens, msg.value reaches publishMessage as zero, causing the require check to fail and the transaction to revert with an "invalid fee" error. This failure propagates to the AnchorVault contract, preventing the submit and collect_rewards functions from executing because they depend on a successful bridge that includes the Wormhole commission. The impact is that users cannot move their tokens across chains, cannot claim expected rewards, and may see UI symptoms such as a missing or zero balance after a bridge attempt, or a failed transaction message. The bug occurs whenever transferasset is called through BridgeConnectorWormhole, i.e., any bridging operation that does not supply the Wormhole fee. It affects token holders, the bridging service, and any protocol component that relies on successful cross‑chain transfers. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that traced the flow of payable parameters and identified the missing @payable modifier and fee forwarding. It can be hard to notice because the payable attribute is present on the low‑level function, giving the impression that the system handles fees, while the higher‑level caller silently omits them. Conceptually, this is a classic payable‑mismatch or fee‑forwarding bug, where a contract expects a payment but the caller does not provide it, violating the accounting assumption that the fee will be collected before message publication. To remediate, the transferasset function (or its caller) should be marked payable and should forward the exact amount returned by messageFee() to the Bridge contract, or the internal require should be adjusted to accept a zero fee if the protocol intends to subsidize the Wormhole cost. Proper validation and documentation of fee requirements would prevent the discrepancy and restore the intended bridging and reward‑collection functionality.
summary:
Line Bridge.sol#L93 has a transferTokens () function of type payable. In the body of this function, on line 133, a call to the internal function logTransfer () is made and one of the parameters msg.value is passed.
At line Bridge.sol#L151 from the logTransfer() function, the publishMessage() function is called.
The publishMessage() function of type payable on the line: Implementation.sol#L21 the condition for payment of the commission must be met. require(msg.value == messageFee(), "invalid fee");
In the checked contract, at line BridgeConnectorWormhole.vy#L49 a call to the transferTokens() function from the transferasset() function is made.
But there is no @payable modifier anywhere and no msg.value value handling.
Therefore, the transferasset() function will not work.
As a result, the submit () and collect_rewards () functions will not work in the AnchorVault.vy contract, because there is no commission fee for the Wormhole system.

title: MJR-1 Changing the shared variable can affect previous votes
content: The vulnerability consists of a single mutable contract‑level variable that defines the duration of every voting instance, called voteTime. Because the same variable is read by all active votes, a privileged function named unsafelyChangeVoteTime can modify this value after one or more votes have already been created. The root cause is the design choice to store the voting period as a global parameter instead of embedding it in each Vote struct, which means the contract does not keep a snapshot of the intended duration for a specific proposal. An attacker or any account with permission to call the change function can therefore extend or shorten the remaining voting window of an ongoing proposal. By shortening the period, voters may be cut off before they can cast a vote, causing their preferences to be ignored; by lengthening it, an adversary can keep a proposal open indefinitely to wait for a favorable vote or to stall the decision process. The impact is that governance outcomes can be manipulated, leading to decisions that do not reflect the original community intent, potential misallocation of protocol funds, and loss of trust in the voting mechanism. This condition occurs whenever the contract allows the voteTime variable to be altered while at least one vote is active, and it affects all participants who rely on the voting schedule – token holders, proposal creators, and the protocol itself. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the logic of vote creation and noticed that the same variable is used for both new and existing votes. It can be hard to notice because the variable appears to be a harmless configuration parameter and typical unit tests may only check the default voting period, not the effect of changing it after a vote has started. To remediate, the contract should store the intended voting duration inside each Vote struct, similar to how supportRequiredPct and minAcceptQuorumPct are handled, and the function that changes the default should only affect future votes. From a user’s perspective the symptom is a proposal that closes earlier than expected or stays open far longer than advertised, resulting in “my vote didn’t count” or “the voting window disappeared” messages, which contradicts the expectation that a vote’s deadline is fixed once the proposal is submitted. This class of bug is a mutable‑state‑shared‑parameter flaw that violates the accounting assumption that a voting period is immutable after creation, thereby breaking the integrity of the governance process.
summary:
At the lines Voting.sol#L126-L133 in the unsafelyChangeVoteTime() method is a change in the common for all voting variable voteTime.
Changing this variable will extend or shorten the voting time on existing voting.
This will affect the voting results, because the process will not go as planned when creating a vote.
So this action is potentially dangerous and may bring the unexpected side effects.

title: MJR-2 Fix gas cost ETH transfer
content: The vulnerability originates from the use of a fixed 2300‑gas stipend when transferring Ether, typically via Solidity's transfer or send functions. This design assumes that the recipient’s fallback or receive function will always fit within the limited gas amount, an assumption that was valid before certain protocol upgrades but is no longer reliable. After hard forks such as Istanbul, the gas cost of several opcodes increased, meaning that even a simple fallback may now exceed the 2300‑gas limit. When the contract attempts to send ETH using this fixed stipend, the call can run out of gas and revert, causing the transfer to fail. An attacker can exploit this by deploying a contract with a fallback that deliberately consumes more than 2300 gas, causing any ETH sent to it via transfer to revert and effectively locking the funds in the sending contract. The impact is that users expecting to receive a refund, withdrawal, or any ETH payment may see no change in their balance, experience transaction reverts, or observe that their deposited funds remain stuck. This situation occurs whenever the contract sends ETH to an address that is a contract with a non‑trivial fallback, or when network gas costs rise beyond the hard‑coded limit. All participants who interact with the contract – depositors, withdrawers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the business logic that assumes successful ETH transfers no longer holds. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that flagged the hard‑coded gas amount as a potential future failure point. It can be hard to notice because the code compiles without warnings and the transfer appears to succeed in simple test cases; only when the recipient’s fallback grows or gas costs change does the failure surface. To remediate, the contract should replace transfer/send with a low‑level call that forwards all available gas (or a configurable amount) and explicitly checks the returned success flag, handling failures gracefully. This change aligns the contract with the modern best practice of using call for ETH transfers, eliminating the fixed‑gas limitation and restoring reliable fund movement.
summary: ETH sending at this line Lido.sol#L301 uses 2300 gas amount, but gas price can be vary and it is possible that in future it may exceed gas limit.

title: MJR-1 Public access to all functions
content: The vulnerability consists of missing access control on every external function of the Controller contract. Because each function is declared public without any modifier, any external account can invoke them. The root cause is that the developer did not restrict privileged operations such as setting parameters, pausing the system, or moving assets. An attacker can call these functions directly, for example by invoking the function that changes the address of a critical component or that triggers a withdrawal, thereby altering protocol state, redirecting funds, or disabling safety mechanisms. This can happen at any time after deployment, as there is no role check; the condition is simply that the caller is an EOA or contract. Users of the protocol are affected because the controller may be manipulated to send tokens to an attacker, freeze deposits, or change fee structures, leading to loss of funds or denial of service. The issue was discovered during a manual source‑code audit where the auditor observed that no access modifiers such as onlyOwner, onlyAdmin, or role‑based checks were present on any function. The problem can be subtle because the functions compile and appear to work correctly for legitimate callers, so a casual test may not reveal the over‑exposure. The appropriate remediation is to introduce proper access control, for example by adding OpenZeppelin's Ownable or AccessControl modifiers to restrict privileged functions to authorized accounts, and to review each function to ensure that only intended callers can execute it. In generic terms this is an “unrestricted public function” bug, a class of access‑control flaw that violates the principle that only trusted actors may perform administrative actions. From a user’s perspective the symptom may be that a transaction they did not initiate appears to have changed protocol parameters, that their balance suddenly drops to zero, or that a withdrawal they expected never arrives because the controller has been hijacked. The mismatch between the expected behavior (only the protocol owner can change settings) and the actual behavior (anyone can) breaks the accounting assumptions of the system and can lead to funds disappearing or the protocol becoming unusable.
summary: In contract Controller all functions have public access which can be exploited: Controller.sol

title: MJR-2 Controller can be initialized several times
content: The vulnerability is a re‑initialization flaw in the Controller contract where the public initialize function can be invoked more than once. The root cause is the absence of a protection mechanism such as the OpenZeppelin initializer modifier or an explicit boolean flag that would restrict the function to a single execution. Because the contract relies on an initialize routine to set critical state variables—typically the owner, admin address, fee parameters, or other privileged settings—an attacker who discovers that the function is unrestricted can call it after deployment and overwrite those variables with attacker‑controlled values. Exploitation proceeds by sending a transaction that calls initialize with malicious arguments; the contract accepts the call, updates its storage, and effectively hands over control of the protocol logic to the attacker. The impact includes loss of administrative control, the ability to change protocol parameters arbitrarily, and potential theft or freezing of user funds, as the new controller can redirect withdrawals or disable essential functions. This condition occurs whenever the contract is deployed without a constructor and expects initialize to be called exactly once, but no guard is present to enforce that expectation. All participants that rely on the controller—protocol governance, token holders, and end‑users—are affected because the security guarantees of the system are broken. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected upgradeable contract patterns and flagged the missing initializer protection as a known anti‑pattern. The flaw can be hard to notice because the initialize function may appear innocuous, emits no special events, and the contract may operate normally until an attacker triggers a re‑initialization, at which point the state change can be subtle or only observable through unexpected behavior such as sudden loss of privileges or zeroed balances. To remediate, the initialize function should be marked with the initializer modifier or wrapped in a custom one‑time guard that records whether it has already been executed and reverts on subsequent calls, thereby ensuring the initialization logic runs only once as intended.
summary: In contract Controller the initialize function can be called several times: Controller.sol#L140

title: MJR-3 Incorrect condition
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect logical condition inside a loop of the Lido contract that can cause the loop to never terminate. The root cause is the use of a logical OR (||) where a logical AND (&&) is required, meaning the exit criteria are evaluated incorrectly. When the contract reaches this point, the loop condition remains true for a combination of state variables that should have caused it to stop, so the execution continues indefinitely until the transaction runs out of gas. An attacker or any user can trigger the problematic path by providing inputs that satisfy one side of the OR while the other side never becomes false, causing the contract to enter the infinite loop. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition: the transaction reverts only after exhausting gas, the caller loses the gas fee, and the contract’s functionality that depends on this loop becomes unavailable for all users until the state is manually corrected. This occurs whenever the function containing the loop is called with values that make the faulty condition true, which can happen in normal operation if the contract’s internal accounting reaches certain edge cases. All participants of the protocol—delegators, node operators, and any external callers—are affected because the contract may become unresponsive, preventing deposits, withdrawals, or reward calculations. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit by MixBytes, who identified the logical operator mismatch while reviewing the control flow. It is hard to notice because the code compiles and passes basic tests; the loop only fails under specific state combinations that are not exercised in typical unit tests, and the symptom—transactions hanging or consuming all gas—may be attributed to other causes. The proper fix is to replace the OR operator with an AND operator so that the loop exits when either of the intended conditions is no longer satisfied, restoring the correct termination logic. Conceptually, this is a classic infinite‑loop or denial‑of‑service bug caused by an incorrect boolean expression, which violates the contract’s business logic that expects the loop to terminate after processing a bounded set of items. From a user’s perspective, a transaction that should complete (for example, a deposit or withdrawal) instead stalls, the UI shows a pending state for an unusually long time, and eventually the transaction fails with an out‑of‑gas error, leaving the user with a lost gas fee and no state change. The expectation that the operation will finish is broken, leading to funds appearing to “disappear” in the sense that the operation never finalizes.
summary: The condition is incorrect here that can lead to an infinite loop: Lido.sol#L748

title: MJR-4 Possible burn of zero shares
content: The vulnerability is a rounding‑precision error that can cause the burn operation in the staking contract to calculate zero shares to be burned. The root cause is integer division or rounding logic that truncates fractional share amounts, so when a user attempts to burn a very small amount of underlying tokens the computed share quantity may round down to zero. An attacker can invoke the burn function with such a small amount, the contract will accept the call, emit the burn event and possibly transfer the underlying tokens, but the internal accounting will not decrease the caller’s share balance because zero shares were recorded as burned. This mismatch allows the caller to retain the original share balance while the contract believes a burn has occurred, potentially enabling the user to later claim additional rewards or withdraw more assets than entitled. The issue manifests only when the calculated share amount is less than one whole share, which typically happens for tiny withdrawal requests or when the total supply of shares is large relative to the amount being burned. All participants who hold shares are affected because the accounting invariant that total shares equal total underlying assets can be broken, leading to inaccurate reward distribution and possible fund loss for honest users. The bug was discovered during a formal security audit where the auditors examined the burn logic and identified that the rounding could produce a zero‑share result. It is hard to notice in normal operation because most users interact with amounts that round to at least one share, and the contract does not explicitly reject zero‑share burns, so the transaction appears successful even though no state change occurs. To remediate the issue the contract should add an explicit check that the number of shares to be burned is greater than zero before proceeding, or adjust the rounding method to ensure that any positive amount results in at least one share being burned, possibly by using ceiling division or by requiring a minimum burn amount. This class of bug falls under rounding or precision errors that lead to zero‑value operations, a common source of accounting inconsistencies in financial smart contracts. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after calling the burn function the displayed share balance remains unchanged, the expected reduction does not happen, and the user may see a successful transaction receipt despite receiving no refund or reduction, violating the expectation that burning tokens always reduces the share balance.
summary: Due to rounding errors a user can burn zero shares: Lido.sol#L522

title: MJR-5 Possible division by zero
content: The vulnerability is an unchecked division operation that can trigger a division‑by‑zero exception in the Lido staking contract. The root cause is a calculation that divides a value representing a user’s stake by the total amount of shares without first verifying that the total shares variable is non‑zero. When the contract’s overall shares balance reaches zero – for example after all participants have withdrawn or a rebase reduces the share count – the denominator becomes zero and the Solidity runtime throws a revert. An attacker or any user can deliberately or unintentionally bring the share total to zero and then invoke the function that performs the division, causing the transaction to fail. This failure can be exploited as a denial‑of‑service vector: legitimate deposits, withdrawals, or reward distributions that rely on the same calculation will revert, preventing users from interacting with the protocol and potentially locking funds in the contract. The impact is that users expect their stake to be calculated and their funds to be transferred, but instead receive no transaction receipt and see no change in balances, effectively experiencing a “funds disappear” symptom because the operation never completes. The condition occurs only in the edge case where the total shares amount equals zero, which is rarely exercised in standard testing, making the bug hard to notice until the edge case is triggered. The issue was discovered by MixBytes during a static analysis audit of the Lido codebase, where the lines performing the division were flagged as potentially unsafe. To remediate, the contract should include a guard that checks the denominator before performing the division and, if the total shares are zero, set the resulting stake to zero or revert with a clear error message. This aligns with the general class of arithmetic‑related vulnerabilities where unchecked division can cause runtime exceptions and break business logic, violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions that a stake must always be derived from a positive share pool.
summary: In some cases division by zero can take place here: Lido.sol#L658 Lido.sol#L708

title: MJR-6 Insufficient xcKSm balance on Lido
content: The vulnerability is an insufficient token balance check in the Lido contract when it attempts to transfer xcKSM tokens. The contract maintains an internal counter called _readyToClaim that represents the amount it intends to send to users, but it does not verify that its actual xcKSM balance is at least that amount before performing the transfer. This mismatch can arise when external events such as slashing, token withdrawals, or previous failed transfers reduce the contract's balance without updating the internal accounting. An attacker or any user can trigger the claim function while the contract holds fewer tokens than _readyToClaim, causing the transfer to revert or to send a smaller amount than expected. From the user's perspective the UI may show a pending claim, but the received amount is zero or lower than promised, leading to confusion and perceived loss of funds. The issue belongs to the classic class of “insufficient balance” or “unchecked external call” bugs, where a contract assumes it has enough tokens without enforcing that invariant. It was discovered during a manual audit of Lido.sol at line 563, where the code reads the internal counter but lacks a require statement that checks the contract's xcKSM balance against _readyToClaim. The problem can be hard to notice because the contract’s internal accounting may still indicate a positive claim even though the token balance is depleted, and the failure only surfaces under specific state conditions. The proper fix is to add an explicit check that the contract’s xcKSM balance is greater than or equal to the amount it is about to transfer, and to handle the case where the balance is insufficient, for example by reverting with a clear error or by adjusting the claim amount. By enforcing this invariant, the protocol restores the guarantee that users receive the full amount they are owed, preserving accounting integrity and preventing funds from disappearing.
summary: It is possible that Lido can have less than _readyToClaim : Lido.sol#L563

title: MJR-7 Possible zero balance on Lido
content: The vulnerability concerns the reward distribution mechanism of the Lido contract, where the function responsible for allocating accrued rewards can be executed even when the contract’s reward pool holds a zero token balance. The root cause is the absence of a guard condition that verifies the pool contains a positive amount before proceeding with the transfer logic. Because the contract does not check for a non‑zero balance, an external caller can trigger the distribution routine at any time, including moments when the pool is empty due to prior withdrawals, mis‑configuration, or simply because no rewards have been accrued yet. When this occurs, the routine completes successfully but transfers zero tokens to the intended recipients. From a user’s perspective the transaction appears to have succeeded – no revert is emitted, gas is spent, and an event may be emitted – yet the staker’s balance does not increase and the expected reward is missing. This mismatch between expectation (receiving a reward) and reality (receiving nothing) can lead to confusion, loss of trust, and accounting inconsistencies, because the protocol’s internal accounting may record that a distribution event occurred while the actual token flow was nil. The issue was identified during a MixBytes security audit of the Lido KSM implementation, where the auditors noted that the reward distribution code at line 588 lacks a balance‑greater‑than‑zero check. The bug is subtle because the function does not revert or emit an explicit error; it simply performs a no‑op transfer, making it easy to overlook during testing unless the specific scenario of an empty reward pool is exercised. To remediate the problem, the contract should include an explicit validation such as require(rewardPoolBalance > 0) before executing the transfer, ensuring that distribution can only occur when there are actual rewards to allocate. This change restores the intended business logic that rewards are only distributed when they exist, prevents users from receiving empty payouts, and aligns on‑chain accounting with the protocol’s economic guarantees.
summary: It is possible that Lido can have zero balance on reward distribution: Lido.sol#L588

title: MJR-8 Possible underflow
content: The vulnerability is an arithmetic underflow that can occur when the protocol records the free balance for a new era. The contract assumes that the free balance reported for the current era will never be lower than the free balance recorded for the previous era. Because there is no explicit check enforcing this monotonicity, a situation may arise where the reported free balance is smaller than the prior value. When the contract later calculates the amount to be bonded or transferred using a subtraction that expects a non‑negative result, the subtraction can underflow, wrapping around to a very large unsigned integer. This can be exploited by an attacker who manipulates the reported free balance (for example by triggering a state transition that yields a lower balance) and then initiates a bonding or withdrawal operation that relies on the faulty subtraction. The impact is that the protocol may credit the attacker with an inflated bonded amount or allow withdrawals that exceed the actual holdings, effectively draining funds or breaking the accounting guarantees of the staking system. The condition occurs at the boundary between eras, specifically at the point where the ledger updates the free balance (see Ledger.sol line 297). Any participant whose balance is tracked by the ledger – including regular stakers, delegators, and the protocol itself – can be affected because the accounting error propagates to subsequent reward calculations and bond management. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the Lido KSM smart‑contract code, where the auditor noticed that the free‑balance update logic did not enforce a non‑decreasing invariant and that the subsequent bonding calculation performed an unchecked subtraction. The bug can be hard to notice because the underflow only manifests when a rare state transition produces a lower free balance, which may not happen under normal operation, and the resulting huge number may be interpreted as a legitimate value by downstream logic. To fix the problem, the contract should introduce an explicit variable or flag that determines the exact amount to be bonded for the next era and should add a validation step that ensures the new free balance is not less than the previous one, or that uses safe arithmetic (e.g., SafeMath) with proper revert on underflow. In user‑facing terms, a staker might see their balance unexpectedly drop to zero or see a refund that is far larger than expected, contradicting the expectation that their funds are safely accounted for. This class of bug falls under unchecked arithmetic underflow in state‑transition logic, violating the fundamental accounting assumption that balances cannot become negative.
summary: It is possible that free balance from the report can be less than free balance from the previous era: Ledger.sol#L297

title: H-1 Opportunity to add bufferedETH without submitting to LIDO
content: The vulnerability consists of an unrestricted ETH injection path into the LidoMevTxFeeVault contract. The contract is designed to collect transaction fees and forward them to Lido’s staking contract when an off‑chain oracle signals that the vault balance should be transferred for reward distribution. Because the receive function (or fallback) does not restrict the sender, any external address can send arbitrary amounts of ETH directly to the vault. When the oracle later triggers the transfer, the injected ETH is treated as legitimate fee revenue and is converted into Lido shares (stETH). This extra supply dilutes the value of existing shares, causing the price per share to fluctuate unexpectedly. The root cause is the lack of access control on the ETH‑receiving entry point and the absence of limits on the withdrawRewards() routine that moves the collected ETH to Lido. An attacker can exploit the bug by depositing a large amount of ETH, waiting for the oracle to trigger the payout, and thereby artificially inflating the reward pool. The inflated pool changes the accounting of rewards, leading to a lower reward per share for honest participants. The impact is a potential loss of value for stETH holders, distorted reward calculations, and a breach of the protocol’s economic assumptions that only legitimate fees contribute to rewards. The condition under which the issue manifests is any time the oracle reports that the vault should forward its balance; the malicious deposit will be included in that balance. All users who hold Lido shares, delegators, and the protocol itself are affected because the share price may drop and the reward distribution becomes unfair. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the LidoMevTxFeeVault source code, where the auditor noted the missing sender verification and the unrestricted reward withdrawal logic. The problem can be hard to notice because the contract’s external behavior (receiving ETH and forwarding it) appears normal, and the price impact may be attributed to market movements rather than a contract bug. To remediate, the contract should enforce that only authorized addresses (e.g., the Lido protocol or a designated fee collector) can send ETH to the vault, and the withdrawRewards() function should include caps or checks that prevent excessive or unexpected transfers. This aligns the implementation with the intended security model of fee collection and preserves the integrity of share pricing and reward accounting.
summary:
It is possible to send ETH to the LidoMevTxFeeVault contract and when the oracle reports contract sends ETH to LIDO, which will be used to rewards, it may fluctuate the price of lido shares.
LidoMevTxFeeVault.sol#L79

title: H-1 stETH liquidity problem
content: The vulnerability resides in the L2ERC20Bridge component that handles the conversion between wrapped stETH (wstETH) and native stETH on the Optimism layer‑2 network. When a user bridges wstETH from L1 to L2 and then invokes the bridge to receive stETH, the bridge contract mints the requested amount of stETH but fails to mint a matching amount of wstETH on L2. Consequently the L2 stETH contract can end up holding more stETH than the corresponding wstETH balance it is supposed to back, breaking the one‑to‑one accounting invariant that each stETH token must be fully collateralised by a wstETH token. The root cause is a missing mint operation for wstETH in the L2ERC20ExtendedTokensBridge implementation at line 172, which leaves the wstETH supply unchanged while increasing the stETH supply. An attacker can deliberately trigger this path without incurring any loss, for example by repeatedly bridging wstETH and requesting stETH, thereby creating a state where the L2 stETH contract’s balance of wstETH is insufficient. When this condition occurs, users who have wrapped wstETH to stETH on L2 find that they cannot unwrap their stETH back into wstETH on the same layer. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a normal stETH balance, but attempts to convert back to wstETH either fail or return zero, leading to the symptom “funds disappear” or “refund calculation error”. The impact is that users must perform a multi‑step workaround: transfer the stETH back to L1, wrap it into wstETH on L1, and then transfer the wstETH back to L2, incurring additional gas costs and latency. This breaks the expected business logic that a user’s wrapped token can be freely converted back and forth on the same chain, violating accounting assumptions of full collateralisation. The issue was uncovered during a security audit by MixBytes, and because the mismatch only manifests when a user attempts the reverse conversion, it can be difficult to notice during normal operation. The recommended remediation is to modify the bridge so that it mints the corresponding amount of wstETH on L2, locks those wstETH tokens within the stETH contract, and then transfers the newly minted stETH to the user, thereby preserving the invariant that stETH is always fully backed by wstETH on the same layer.
summary: L2ERC20Bridge mints stETH without minting a corresponding amount of wstETH on L2 L2ERC20ExtendedTokensBridge.sol#L172. This can lead to insolvency issues, affecting users who have bridged wstETH on L2 and wrapped them to stETH. There is a chance (this can be forced by a malicious user without any losses) that the stETH contract on L2 might lack wstETH in its balance. This will require users who wrapped wstETH to stETH on L2 to: • transfer stETH from L2 to L1; • wrap stETH to wstETH on L1; • transfer wstETH from L1 to L2.

title: MJR-1 Possible blocking of the contract
content: The vulnerability is an ownership initialization flaw where the contract assigns a new owner address without verifying that the supplied value is non‑zero. Because the code does not include a check such as require(newOwner != address(0)), an attacker or a mistaken transaction can set the owner variable to the zero address. When the owner becomes address(0) the contract’s access‑controlled functions that rely on a valid owner – including setOwner, setNodeOperatorsRegistry, setPauseIntentValidityPeriodBlocks, setMaxDeposits, setMinDepositBlockDistance, setGuardianQuorum, addGuardian, addGuardians, removeGuardian and unpauseDeposits – effectively stop working. These functions either revert due to implicit checks that the caller must be the owner, or they become no‑ops because the contract treats the zero address as an invalid authority. The impact is that the protocol’s administrative controls are frozen, preventing updates to deposit parameters, pausing or unpausing deposits, and managing guardians. From a user’s perspective deposits may suddenly stop being accepted, or previously set limits cannot be changed, leading to a perception that the contract is “blocked” or “broken”. The condition occurs whenever the owner variable is set to zero, which can happen during contract initialization, an upgrade, or a malicious call to setOwner if the function is exposed without proper validation. The issue was discovered during a formal security audit by MixBytes, who noted the missing zero‑address guard. It can be hard to notice because the Solidity compiler does not reject a zero address assignment and no explicit revert is triggered at the point of assignment; the failure only becomes apparent later when owner‑only functions are called. The proper remediation is to add an explicit validation step before assigning the new owner, for example require(newOwner != address(0)), and to follow a well‑tested Ownable pattern that enforces non‑zero ownership throughout the contract lifecycle.
summary: At the line DepositSecurityModule.sol#L123 initializes the owner variable without checking the new value of the variable. If the value of the variable is equal to zero, then the following functions will stop working: setOwner(), setNodeOperatorsRegistry(), setPauseIntentValidityPeriodBlocks(), setMaxDeposits(), setMinDepositBlockDistance(), setGuardianQuorum(), addGuardian(), addGuardians(), removeGuardian(), unpauseDeposits().

title: Receiver doesn't always reset allowance
content: The vulnerability is an allowance‑reset bug in the bridge receiver contract. After an ERC20 transfer the function _swapAndCompleteBridgeTokens increases the executor’s allowance to the transferred amount, but it attempts to clear that allowance with a safeApprove(0) only after the external call to the executor. If the contract is configured to reserve gas for a recovery path (reserveRecoverGas) and the remaining gas (gasleft()) falls below a predefined threshold (_recoverGas), the code takes an early return before executing the safeApprove(0). Consequently the executor retains a non‑zero allowance on the token contract. An attacker controlling the executor can later invoke transferFrom on any ERC20 tokens that remain in the Receiver, effectively stealing them. The impact is loss of user funds: a user expects the bridge to return the exact amount of tokens, but the token balance may become zero or reduced because the executor can drain the leftover tokens. The bug manifests only when the low‑gas condition is met, which may be rare and therefore hard to notice during normal testing. It was discovered during a security audit by Spearbit, who observed that the allowance reset is conditional on gas availability and not guaranteed. The issue is subtle because the allowance appears to be cleared in the normal execution path, and the early‑return path is only taken under specific gas constraints, making it easy to miss in functional tests. To remediate, the contract should ensure that the allowance is increased only when sufficient gas remains to later reset it, or it should move the allowance reset before any possible early return, or use a pattern that always clears the allowance regardless of gas state. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of improper permission revocation, where an approval is left open due to conditional logic, violating the accounting assumption that temporary approvals are always revoked after use, leading to unauthorized token transfers and potential fund loss.

title: CelerIMFacet incorrectly sets RelayerCelerIM as receiver
content: The vulnerability originates from the way Solidity handles memory copies of structs. When the function _startBridge creates a local variable bridgeDataAdjusted by assigning it the value of the incoming _bridgeData struct, both variables reference the same memory location. Consequently, modifying bridgeDataAdjusted.receiver also mutates _bridgeData.receiver because they are aliases rather than independent copies. In the current implementation the code sets bridgeDataAdjusted.receiver to the relayer address before calling the relayer’s sendTokenTransfer function. Because of the aliasing, the original _bridgeData.receiver is overwritten with the relayer address as well. The subsequent call to relayer.forwardSendMessageWithTransfer uses _bridgeData.receiver as the destination address on the target chain, which now incorrectly points to the relayer instead of the intended user. This misdirection causes the bridged tokens to be credited to the relayer’s account on the destination chain, effectively diverting funds away from the legitimate recipient. The impact is a loss of user funds and a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees, as the bridge no longer delivers assets to the address specified by the user. The bug manifests whenever the bridge is executed in the code path that adjusts the receiver field – in the provided example this is the “yes” case that performs both a token transfer and a message‑bus call. It is discovered through static analysis and a simple unit test that demonstrates that assigning one memory struct to another does not create a deep copy; changing a field in the copy reflects in the original. The issue can be hard to notice because the UI may still display the correct receiver address before the transaction is sent, and the transaction itself does not revert – it simply routes the funds to an unexpected address. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are that after initiating a bridge the user’s balance on the source chain is reduced, the destination chain shows a receipt for the relayer address, and the intended recipient receives nothing, leading to confusion and potential loss of trust. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “shallow memory copy” or “reference aliasing” errors that break the intended isolation of data structures. The correct fix is to avoid creating a separate bridgeDataAdjusted variable that shares memory with the original. Instead, the code should temporarily store the original receiver address, overwrite the receiver field in the original _bridgeData only for the call to the relayer, and then restore the original value after the message‑bus call. This ensures that the destination‑chain call receives the proper receiver address while the relayer still acts as the intermediary for the token transfer, preserving the intended accounting logic and preventing unintended fund diversion.

title: Max approval to any address is possible
content: The vulnerability is an unrestricted token approval function that allows any caller to grant an unlimited ERC20 allowance to an arbitrary address for any token held by the Diamond contract. The root cause is the absence of an access‑control check in the setApprovalForBridges function; it is declared external but does not enforce that only the contract owner or a privileged role may invoke it. An attacker can exploit this by calling setApprovalForBridges with a list containing their own address as a bridge and the addresses of tokens stored in the contract. The function then executes LibAsset.maxApproveERC20 with type(uint256).max, giving the attacker permission to transfer the full token balance via transferFrom. This results in the loss of all tokens that were deposited in the Diamond, effectively stealing funds. The issue manifests whenever the function is invoked, which can happen at any time because there is no restriction on the caller. All users, token holders, and the protocol itself are affected because any ERC20 token left in the contract can be drained without consent. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the contract’s permission model and identified that setApprovalForBridges lacked any owner check. Because the function appears to be a legitimate administrative utility, the missing restriction may not be obvious during casual testing, making the bug hard to notice until an audit or a malicious transaction occurs. From a user perspective the symptom is that token balances suddenly become zero or missing after an unexpected transaction, contradicting the expectation that deposited funds remain safe. Conceptually, this is a classic case of missing access control leading to unrestricted token allowance, a class of bug that violates fundamental accounting assumptions that only the contract owner can authorize token movements. The recommended remediation is to add an authorization guard such as LibDiamond.enforceIsContractOwner() or any appropriate onlyOwner modifier so that only a trusted entity can call setApprovalForBridges, thereby preventing arbitrary parties from granting themselves unlimited token approvals.

title: Return value of low-level .call() not checked
content: The vulnerability is an unchecked low‑level call used to transfer native cryptocurrency from a contract to an external address. In Solidity, the .call() primitive returns a boolean indicating whether the called function completed without reverting, but it does not automatically propagate a revert to the caller. When the return value is ignored, the caller assumes the transfer succeeded even if the callee reverted. This mismatch occurs because the contract does not evaluate the success flag returned by .call(). An attacker or a misbehaving receiver can deliberately cause its fallback or receive function to revert, causing the low‑level call to fail silently. The caller then proceeds as if the ETH was sent, leaving the funds locked inside the contract. From a user’s perspective the UI may report a successful transaction, yet the expected balance on the receiving side remains unchanged, or the sender’s balance appears unchanged because the contract still holds the ETH. The impact is the loss of accessibility to the transferred amount, effectively freezing funds and breaking the accounting assumptions of the protocol that assume successful payouts. The condition manifests whenever the contract attempts to send ETH using a low‑level call without checking the returned success flag, which is typical in contracts that prefer .call() over .transfer() for gas‑forwarding reasons. The issue was discovered during a security audit that inspected the code paths for external value transfers and noted the absence of a require(success) check after the call. It can be hard to notice because the transaction receipt shows no revert, and the contract’s internal state does not change in an obvious way; only the external balance of the intended recipient stays unchanged. The bug belongs to the class of unchecked low‑level call vulnerabilities, where error handling is omitted, leading to silent failures. To remediate, the contract should capture the boolean result of the call and explicitly revert if the call returned false, for example by using (bool success, ) = receiver.call{value: amount}(''); require(success); This ensures that any revert in the callee propagates back to the caller, preventing funds from becoming permanently locked and preserving the intended financial flow of the protocol.
summary: Low-level primitive .call() doesn't revert in caller's context when the callee reverts. If its return value is not checked, it can lead the caller to falsely believe that the call was successful. Receiver.sol uses .call() to transfer the native token to receiver. If receiver reverts, this can lead to locked ETH in Receiver contract.

title: Hardcode bridge addresses via immutable
content: The vulnerability stems from the way bridge contracts are referenced in the LiFi diamond architecture. Functions that initiate cross‑chain transfers, such as startBridgeTokensViaOmniBridge, accept a BridgeData structure that contains a bridge address supplied by the caller. This address is then cast to an interface (IOmniBridge) and used to invoke a hard‑coded function signature (wrapAndRelayTokens or relayTokens). Because the address is not fixed in the contract code, any arbitrary address can be passed, allowing an attacker to supply a malicious contract that implements the same function selector. Even though the selector is hard‑coded, Solidity permits different functions to share the same 4‑byte selector, so a colliding function in a malicious contract could be executed instead of the intended bridge logic. Consequently, a user who signs a transaction believing they are interacting with the official LiFi bridge may unintentionally approve a call to a rogue contract that can steal or lock the transferred assets. The issue manifests whenever a bridge‑initiating function is called with a user‑controlled bridge address, which can happen in normal usage because the address is taken from calldata without validation. The impact is severe: funds can be redirected, wrapped, or relayed to an attacker‑controlled contract, leading to loss of tokens or failure of the cross‑chain operation. The problem is subtle because the external call appears to target a known interface and the function selector matches the expected one, making it difficult to detect through simple static analysis or UI inspection. The bug belongs to the class of “unrestricted external contract calls with unchecked addresses” and is closely related to arbitrary‑address approval vulnerabilities. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a transaction that should result in a successful bridge either completes with no tokens arriving on the destination chain or the user’s balance on the source chain is reduced while the destination receives nothing. The protocol’s accounting assumptions—that the bridge address is trustworthy and that the called function behaves as specified—are violated. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the flow of bridge address parameters and identified the lack of immutability or validation. To remediate the flaw, the bridge addresses should be set once in the contract’s constructor (or an immutable initializer) and stored in immutable state variables, eliminating the need to pass them via calldata. This approach prevents address tampering, reduces gas costs compared with repeated SLOADs, and works correctly with delegatecall patterns used in the diamond architecture. Additionally, the contract could enforce a whitelist of approved bridge contracts or verify that the target address implements the expected interface before invoking any external call.

title: Tokens are left in the protocol when the swap at the destination chain fails
content: The vulnerability consists of tokens becoming stranded in the LiFi protocol contract when a cross‑chain swap that is supposed to execute on the destination chain fails. The root cause is that the protocol design uses its own address as the receiver for bridge callbacks, and some bridge services (for example Stargate, Amarok and NXTP) implement a try‑catch pattern that, on failure, directly transfers the bridged tokens to the receiver address instead of reverting the whole transaction. Because the receiver is the LiFi contract itself, the tokens are deposited into the protocol’s balance and no further logic is executed to return them to the user or to a safe escrow. An attacker can exploit this by forcing the destination swap to revert – for instance by manipulating market prices in a sandwich attack – causing the bridge call to fail. The bridge then sends the tokens to the LiFi contract, where the attacker, who may have permission to call a pull function on the protocol or on the associated Executor contract, can withdraw the stranded assets. The impact is loss of user funds: a user who initiates a swap expects to receive the swapped token on the destination chain, but instead sees no balance change or a zero balance, while the protocol holds the tokens. This situation occurs only when the selected bridge service follows the described error‑handling pattern and the swap execution on the destination chain fails. It affects any user of the LiFi protocol who relies on those bridges for cross‑chain swaps, as well as the protocol itself because the stranded tokens can be swept by anyone with access to the pull function. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the flow of bridge callbacks and identified that the protocol address was being used as a fallback receiver without proper post‑failure handling. The bug is subtle because the transaction may still be reported as successful on the source chain, and the UI may show a completed swap, while the funds are silently held in the contract. The class of bug is an improper handling of failed external calls leading to token loss, essentially an accounting inconsistency caused by missing fallback logic. To remediate, the protocol should avoid using its own address as the receiver for bridge callbacks; instead a dedicated receiver contract should be employed that can safely handle the case where the bridge sends tokens back on failure, either by forwarding them to the original user or by allowing only authorized recovery. The receiver should also clear allowances and avoid unsafe external calls, ensuring that no tokens remain locked in the protocol after a failed swap.
summary:
```solidity
LiFi protocol finds the best bridge route for users. In some cases, it helps users do a swap at
the destination chain. With the help of the bridge protocols, LiFi protocol helps users trigger swapAndComplete-
BridgeTokensVia{Services} or CompleteBridgeTokensVia{Services} at the destination chain to do the swap.
Some bridge services will send the tokens directly to the receiver address when the execution fails. For example,
Stargate, Amarok and NXTP do the external call in a try-catch clause and send the tokens directly to the receiver
when it fails. The tokens will stay in the LiFi protocol’s in this scenario. If the receiver is the Executor contract,
users can freely pull the tokens. Note: Exploiters can pull the tokens from LiFi protocol, Please refer to the issue
Remaining tokens can be sweeped from the LiFi Diamond or the Executor , Issue #82
Exploiters can take a more aggressive strategy and force the victims swap to revert. A possible exploit scenario:
• A victim wants to swap 10K optimism’s BTC into Ethereum mainnet USDC.
• Since dexs on mainnet have the best liquidity, LiFi protocol helps users to the swap on mainnet
• The transaction on the source chain (optimism) suceed and the Bridge services try to call Complete-
BridgeTokensVia{Services} on mainnet.
• The exploiter builds a sandwich attack to pump the BTC price. The CompleteBridgeTokens fails since the
price is bad.
• The bridge service does not revert the whole transaction. Instead, it sends the BTC on the mainnet to the
receiver (LiFi protocol).
• The exploiter pulls tokens from the LiFi protocol.
```

title: Tokens transferred with Axelar can get lost if the destination transaction can’t be executed
content: The vulnerability concerns the handling of token transfers that are routed through the Axelar cross‑chain messaging system. When the contract's internal function that executes a token‑bearing call (commonly named _executeWithToken) forwards the call to a destination contract using a low‑level call, it first transfers the tokens to the executor contract and then attempts to invoke the target logic. If the low‑level call returns false and the function reverts with an ExecutionFailed error, the contract does not contain any logic to return the transferred tokens to the sender or to redirect them to a recovery address. The root cause is the absence of a fallback or recovery pathway for tokens after a failed external execution, effectively leaving the tokens locked in the executor contract with no accessible owner. An attacker or a malformed payload can deliberately cause the destination call to revert—for example by providing invalid calldata, insufficient gas, or by deploying a malicious contract that always reverts—thereby triggering the loss condition. The impact is that users who initiate a cross‑chain transfer expect their tokens to appear on the destination chain, but instead the tokens become unrecoverable, resulting in a loss of funds. This situation occurs only when the external call fails; successful calls behave as intended. The affected parties include any token holder using the bridge, the protocol that advertises reliable cross‑chain transfers, and any downstream applications that rely on the transferred assets. The issue was identified during a security audit that examined the execution flow and noted that the revert path does not include any token‑return logic, making the bug subtle because the transaction may still be reported as “executed” on‑chain while the assets are silently trapped. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a successful transaction hash, yet the balance on the target chain remains unchanged, leading to confusion and perceived loss of funds. This class of bug falls under the broader category of “asset‑locking due to missing error‑handling” or “failed external call without token recovery”. To remediate, the contract should implement a recovery mechanism such as forwarding the tokens to a designated recovery address, allowing the contract owner or an authorized role to withdraw stuck tokens, or using a safe‑transfer pattern that only moves tokens after the external call succeeds. Adding such logic restores the accounting guarantees of the bridge and aligns the actual behavior with user expectations that funds are either delivered or safely returned in case of failure.

title: Use the getStorage() / NAMESPACE pattern instead of global variables
content: The vulnerability is a storage collision caused by declaring a global state variable (appStorage) directly in multiple facets of a Diamond contract. In the DexManagerFacet and the Swapper facet the variable is placed in the first storage slot, so the two facets share the same slot. Because Diamond upgrades use delegatecall, any facet that is added later and also declares a global variable will occupy the same slot unless a unique namespace is used. This overlap can overwrite critical data such as access‑control flags, admin addresses or balances. An attacker who can propose or add a malicious facet could define a variable that collides with the existing appStorage and, through a delegatecall, modify the overwritten slot to gain unauthorized privileges or redirect funds. The impact is that the protocol’s permission checks may be bypassed, allowing arbitrary callers to execute privileged functions, potentially leading to fund theft or protocol takeover. The issue manifests when a new facet is introduced or when an existing facet is upgraded without isolating its storage layout; it is difficult to notice because the Solidity compiler does not warn about overlapping slots and the contract may continue to operate normally until a conflicting facet is executed. The bug belongs to the class of storage‑collision vulnerabilities in upgradeable proxy or Diamond patterns. From a user’s perspective the symptoms can include unexpected rejections of privileged actions, balances appearing unchanged after a transaction, or the UI showing zero balance despite deposits. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the storage layout of each facet and identified the direct declaration of a global variable on the same slot. To remediate, the contract should stop using direct state variables in facets and instead retrieve a dedicated storage struct via a getStorage() function that uses a unique namespace (for example a keccak256 hash) for each facet, ensuring that each piece of data resides in its own isolated slot. This pattern eliminates accidental overwrites and preserves the integrity of access control and accounting logic.
summary:
```solidity
The facet DexManagerFacet and the inherited contracts Swapper.sol / SwapperV2.sol define a
global variable appStorage on the first storage slot. These two overlap, which in this case is intentional.
However it is dangerous to use this construction in a Diamond contract as this uses delegatecall. If any other
contract uses a global variable it will overlap with appStorage with unpredictable results. This is especially impor-
tant because it involves access control.
For example if the contract IAxelarExecutable.sol were to be inherited in a facet, then its global variable gateway
would overlap. Luckily this is currently not the case.
contract DexManagerFacet {
...
LibStorage internal appStorage;
...
}
contract Swapper is ILiFi {
...
LibStorage internal appStorage; // overlaps with DexManagerFacet which is intentional
...
}
```

title: Decrease allowance when it is already set a non-zero value
content: The vulnerability originates from the use of the ERC20 approve function to set a spender allowance without first resetting the existing allowance to zero. Certain non‑standard tokens, most notably USDT, enforce a rule that a call to approve must not change an allowance from a non‑zero value to another non‑zero value; attempting to do so causes the transaction to revert. In the examined contracts, approve is called directly and the return value is not checked, meaning that a revert is not explicitly handled and the caller may assume the allowance was updated when it was not. This pattern also opens a front‑running window: an attacker who observes a pending approve transaction can submit a transaction that spends the current allowance before the approve executes, or can manipulate the allowance change to their advantage. The impact is that users attempting to grant permission to a contract may see their transaction fail silently, resulting in a missing or unchanged allowance, which in turn prevents the contract from pulling tokens and can cause funds to remain locked or be unintentionally transferred if the attacker exploits the race condition. The issue manifests whenever a contract tries to increase an allowance that is already non‑zero, especially when interacting with tokens that implement the non‑zero‑to‑non‑zero restriction. It affects any user or protocol component that relies on standard ERC20 approve semantics, including token holders, DeFi aggregators, and bridge contracts. The problem was discovered during a security audit that inspected token handling code and identified direct calls to approve without safety checks. Because the failure occurs at the token contract level, it may be difficult to notice from the calling contract’s perspective; the calling contract receives no explicit error and the UI may simply show a successful transaction while the allowance remains unchanged. To remediate, the contract should either reset the allowance to zero before setting a new value, use OpenZeppelin’s safeApprove which enforces the zero‑to‑zero rule, or employ safeIncreaseAllowance/safeDecreaseAllowance which adjust the allowance atomically. This aligns the code with the expected ERC20 allowance management pattern and eliminates the front‑running risk associated with direct overwrites. The bug belongs to the class of allowance‑management flaws where improper handling of token approval semantics leads to transaction reverts, unexpected zero balances, and potential loss of control over funds.
summary:
```solidity
Non-standard tokens like USDT will revert the transaction when a contract or a user tries to approve
an allowance when the spender allowance is already set to a non zero value.
For that reason, the previous
allowance should be decreased before increasing allowance in the related function.
• Performing a direct overwrite of the value in the allowances mapping is susceptible to front-running scenarios
by an attacker (e.g., an approved spender).
As an Openzeppelin mentioned, safeApprove should only be called when setting an initial allowance or when
resetting it to zero.
function safeApprove(
IERC20 token,
address spender,
uint256 value
) internal {
// safeApprove should only be called when setting an initial allowance,
// or when resetting it to zero. To increase and decrease it, use
// 'safeIncreaseAllowance' and 'safeDecreaseAllowance'
require(
(value == 0) || (token.allowance(address(this), spender) == 0),
"SafeERC20: approve from non-zero to non-zero allowance"
);
_callOptionalReturn(token, abi.encodeWithSelector(token.approve.selector, spender, value));
}
There are four instance of this issue:
• AxelarFacet.sol is directly using approve function which does not check return value of an external function.
The faucet should utilize LibAsset.maxApproveERC20() function like the other faucets.
• LibAsset’s LibAsset.maxApproveERC20() function is used on the other faucets. For instance, USDT’s ap-
proval mechanism reverts if current allowance is nonzero. From that reason, the function can approve with
zero first or safeIncreaseAllowance can be utilized.
• FusePoolZap.sol is also using approve function which does not check return value. The contract does not
import any other libraries, that being the case, the contract should use safeApprove function with approving
zero.
• Executor.sol is directly using approve function which does not check return value of an external function.
The contract should utilize LibAsset.maxApproveERC20() function like the other contracts.
```

title: Too generic calls in GenericBridgeFacet allow stealing of tokens
content: The vulnerability resides in the GenericBridgeFacet contract where two internal functions – swapAndStartBridgeTokensGeneric (which forwards to LibSwap.swap) and _startBridge – perform low‑level .call operations with caller‑supplied address and calldata without any validation or whitelist. Because the call data is taken directly from user‑controlled structures, an attacker can craft a payload that invokes any function on any contract reachable from the LiFi diamond, including ERC‑20 transferFrom on a token for which the LiFi contract already holds a large allowance from a user. When the malicious call is executed, the token contract transfers the approved amount to the attacker’s address, effectively stealing the user’s funds. The same unrestricted call pattern also permits calls back into the LiFi diamond itself, bypassing functions that lack a nonReentrant guard, potentially cancelling other users’ transfers or invoking privileged functions such as completeBridgeTokensViaStargate.
