The issue manifests whenever a user initiates a bridge transaction that uses the generic facet; the attacker does not need any special permissions beyond the ability to submit a transaction with crafted swap data. Users who have previously approved the LiFi contract for token transfers are affected because their allowances can be abused, leading to loss of tokens, missing balances on the UI, and a bridge operation that appears successful but delivers no assets on the destination chain. The flaw was discovered during a security audit (Spearbit) by reviewing the code paths that forward arbitrary call data and noting the absence of address or selector restrictions. It is difficult to notice because low‑level calls are a common pattern in Solidity, and the token transfer may be indistinguishable from a legitimate bridge operation, especially when the UI reports success. To remediate, the contract should enforce a strict whitelist of allowed external contract addresses and function selectors for both swap and bridge calls, replace generic .call with typed interface calls, ensure that all external interactions are protected by a reentrancy guard, and consider removing the generic facet from the LiFi diamond altogether. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of unchecked external call vulnerabilities that break the trust model of token allowances and allow arbitrary code execution, leading to fund theft and broken accounting assumptions.

title: LiFi protocol isn’t hardened
content: The vulnerability is a design flaw in the LiFi bridging protocol where critical parameters such as token amounts, fees, limits, chain identifiers and contract addresses are supplied exclusively by off‑chain APIs and are not verified on‑chain. Because the smart contracts trust these external values without signature checks, whitelist enforcement or any access‑control mechanism, an attacker who can tamper with the API response, compromise the front‑end, or host a malicious website can feed false data to the contracts. This enables several attack vectors: the emitted LiFiTransferStarted event can be generated with values that do not correspond to any actual bridge transaction, allowing the event log to be spoofed; fee payments to the FeeCollector can be bypassed by calling the bridge functions directly with manipulated fee fields; the periphery contracts referenced in the on‑chain registry can be mismatched with the contracts actually used, breaking the intended accounting relationship. When a user initiates a bridge through a compromised UI, the transaction may appear successful, the UI may show a transfer started, but the tokens are either sent to an attacker‑controlled address or remain locked, resulting in a user‑facing symptom of receiving nothing, seeing a zero balance, or observing that the expected fee was not deducted. The issue manifests whenever LiFi functions are invoked either via the official front‑end, through other smart contracts, or directly by users, because the protocol does not enforce that the data originates from a trusted source. The audit team discovered the flaw during a systematic security review that examined the data flow between off‑chain services and on‑chain logic, noting the absence of any cryptographic verification or caller restrictions. The problem is hard to notice because the on‑chain state may look normal – events are emitted, and transactions succeed – while the underlying accounting is inconsistent, and users may only notice the loss after the fact. To remediate, the protocol should either be hardened for on‑chain usage by adding signature verification of API payloads, whitelisting of authorized callers, and strict checks that fees and destination addresses match the expected values, or, if on‑chain integration is not desired, it must enforce access controls and verification in every bridge function to ensure that only data signed by the trusted LiFi backend is accepted. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of “trusting off‑chain data without verification” and “missing access‑control checks”, which can lead to token loss, fee circumvention, and broken accounting assumptions.
summary:
```solidity
The usage of the LiFi protocol depends largely on off chain APIs. It takes all values, fees, limits,
chain ids and addresses to be called from the APIs and doesn’t verify them. Several elements are not connected
via smart contracts but via the API, for example:
• the emits of LiFiTransferStarted versus the bridge transactions.
• the fees paid to the FeeCollector versus the bridge transactions.
• the Periphery contracts as defined in the PeripheryRegistryFacet versus the rest.
In case the API and or frontend contain errors or are hacked then tokens could be easily lost. Also, when calling
the LiFi contracts directly or via other smart contracts, it is rather trivial to commit mistakes and loose tokens.
Emit data can be easily disturbed by malicious actors, making it unusable. The payment of fees can be easily
circumvented by accessing the contracts directly. It is easy to make fake websites which trick users into signing
transactions which seem to be for LiFi but result in loosing tokens.
With the current design, the power of smart contracts isn’t used and it introduces numerous risks as described in
the rest of this report.
```

title: Bridge with Axelar can be stolen with malicious external call
content: The vulnerability resides in the Executor contract used by Li‑Fi to perform cross‑chain swaps. The contract permits a user to supply an arbitrary external‑call payload and only blocks calls to a single hard‑coded address (the erc20Proxy). Because the payload is later executed by the contract that inherits IAxelarExecutable, an attacker can craft a payload that calls the Axelar gateway’s validateContractCallAndMint function. When the gateway receives a valid payload hash it mints the requested tokens to the receiver address, which in the normal flow is the Executor contract itself. An attacker can observe a victim’s bridge transaction, submit the same payload (or a maliciously crafted one) to trigger the gateway validation, causing the gateway to mint the tokens directly to the Executor. The Executor contract has previously granted the attacker an unlimited allowance on the minted token, so the attacker can immediately transfer the newly minted tokens out, effectively stealing the funds that the victim expected to receive on the destination chain. From the user’s perspective the bridge appears to have succeeded on the source chain, but on the destination chain the user’s balance is zero, no refund is received and the expected tokens never arrive. The issue occurs whenever a user sets the Executor contract as the receiver address to obtain the best price, which is a standard Li‑Fi usage pattern. The problem was discovered during a security audit that examined the external‑call construction and the interaction with the Axelar gateway, and it is subtle because the contract seems to protect only a single address while the gateway itself is a privileged contract that can be invoked indirectly. This bug belongs to the class of unrestricted external‑call vulnerabilities combined with privileged contract mint‑on‑validate logic, allowing an attacker to hijack token minting and drain allowances. To remediate, the contract should enforce a whitelist of callable addresses that excludes the Axelar gateway, separate the IAxelarExecutable logic from the Executor, and never set the Executor as the receiver for cross‑chain calls. Additionally, any pre‑approved unlimited token allowance should be removed or tightly scoped, and the payload should be checked to ensure it has not already been executed before allowing further external calls.


title: Oracle.removeMember could, in the same epoch, allow members to vote multiple times and other members to not vote at all
content: The vulnerability originates from the way the oracle contract removes a member from its internal list. When an admin calls removeMember, the implementation deletes the entry by swapping the last element of the members array into the slot of the removed address and then popping the array. Vote tracking for the epoch is stored in a separate bitmap (ReportsPositions) that is indexed by the member’s position in the array, not by the member’s address. Because the bitmap entry is never cleared or updated when the array element is swapped, the vote flag remains attached to the original index. Consequently, after a removal the index that previously indicated that a member had already reported now belongs to a different member. This leads to two distinct problems in the same epoch: (1) the member that was removed can be re‑added by a corrupted admin and, because the bitmap entry for the old index is still true, the contract will treat the re‑added address as having already voted, allowing it to submit another report without triggering the AlreadyReported check; (2) a legitimate member whose address is moved into the swapped slot will find that ReportsPositions reports a true value for its new index, causing any attempt to call reportBeacon to revert with AlreadyReported even though the member has never voted. The bug manifests only after a removal operation within an active epoch and is more likely to affect honest members because removals are a normal administrative action. From a user perspective the symptoms are a transaction that reverts with the AlreadyReported error despite no prior vote, or a situation where a member appears to be able to submit multiple reports in the same epoch, breaking the one‑vote‑per‑member rule. The issue was discovered during a security audit by Spearbit through logical analysis and a reproducible test case that demonstrated the index mismatch. It is difficult to notice because the array‑swap pattern is a common and efficient way to delete items, and the vote‑tracking structure is separate, so the correlation between an address and its voting flag is not obvious without inspecting the removal path. The vulnerability violates the core business logic of the oracle, which assumes that each member can cast exactly one report per epoch and that every active member is able to participate. To remediate the problem the contract must clear the voting state associated with the removed member from both ReportsPositions and ReportsVariants. If clearing a single entry is not feasible, the safest approach is to reset the entire voting bitmap for the epoch, forcing all remaining members to vote again, thereby restoring the invariant that each index correctly reflects whether its current holder has reported.
summary:
The current implementation of removeMember is introducing an exploit that allows an oracle member to vote again and again (in the same epoch) and an oracle that has never voted is prevented from voting (in the same epoch). Because of how OracleMembers.deleteItem is implemented, it will swap the last item of the array with the one that will be deleted and pop the last element. Let's make an example: 
1) At T0 m0 to the list of members → members[0] = m0. 
2) At T1 m1 to the list of members → members[1] = m1. 
3) At T3 m0 call reportBeacon(...). By doing that, ReportsPositions.register(uint256(0)); will be called, registering that the member at index 0 has registered the vote. 
4) At T4, the oracle admin call removeMember(m0). This operation, as we said, will swap the member's address from the last position of the array of members with the position of the member that will be deleted. After doing that will pop the last position of the array. The state changes from members[0] = m0; members[1] = m1 to members[0] = m1;. At this point, the oracle member m1 will not be able to vote during this epoch because when he/she will call reportBeacon(...) the function will enter inside the check. 
```solidity
if (ReportsPositions.get(uint256(memberIndex))) {
    revert AlreadyReported(_epochId, msg.sender);
}
```
This is because int256 memberIndex = OracleMembers.indexOf(msg.sender); will return 0 (the position of the m0 member that have already voted) and ReportsPositions.get(uint256(0)) will return true. At this point, if for whatever reason an admin of the contract add again the deleted oracle, it would be added to the position 1 of the array of the members, allowing the same member that have already voted, to vote again. Note: while the scenario where a removed member can vote multiple time would involve a corrupted admin (that would re-add the same member) the second scenario that prevent a user to vote would be more common. Check the Appendix for a test case to reproduce this issue.

title: Order of calls to removeValidators can affect the resulting validator keys set
content: The vulnerability is a race‑condition in the removeValidators function that allows the final set of validator keys for an operator to depend on the order in which multiple removeValidators calls are mined. The root cause is that the function checks the supplied key index against the current operator.keys length without recording a snapshot of the validator set at the time the transaction is created. When two parties – for example an admin and an operator – submit removeValidators calls with different removal parameters, the blockchain may include them in either order. If the first transaction removes enough keys to shrink the operator.keys array, the second transaction may reference an index that is now out of bounds, triggering the InvalidIndexOutOfBounds revert. This can be exploited by an attacker who front‑runs a legitimate removal transaction, deliberately removing a large number of keys so that the victim’s transaction fails. The impact is that the intended validator keys are not removed, the operator may be unable to manage its validator set, and the protocol can be denied service because validators cannot be updated or withdrawn, potentially affecting staking rewards and overall system reliability. The condition occurs whenever multiple entities can call removeValidators without coordination, and it is hard to notice because transaction ordering is nondeterministic; occasional reverts may appear as random bugs rather than a systematic issue. The bug was discovered during a security audit that examined the logic of operator key management. From a user perspective the symptoms are a transaction that reverts with InvalidIndexOutOfBounds, or a UI that shows the validator still present after a removal attempt, leading to confusion and loss of expected functionality. The issue belongs to the class of concurrency or state‑inconsistency bugs where state changes are not protected against concurrent modifications. To fix the problem the contract should capture a snapshot block (or a version number) when the removal request is created and verify that the validator set has not changed since that snapshot before performing the removal, similar to the mechanism used for setOperatorLimits. This optimistic‑concurrency check ensures that a transaction will only succeed if the validator set remains unchanged, preventing front‑run‑induced reverts and preserving the integrity of the operator’s validator list.

title: _hasFundableKeys marks operators that have no more fundable validators as fundable.
content: The vulnerability resides in the function that determines whether an operator still has capacity to receive new validator slots, commonly named _hasFundableKeys. The routine evaluates a boolean expression that combines the operator's activity flag with a comparison involving the operator's limit, funded count, and stopped count. Because the logic was simplified to operator.active && operator.limit > (operator.funded - operator.stopped), an operator that has already reached its funding limit but also has one or more stopped validators incorrectly satisfies the condition. In practice this means that an operator whose funded count equals its limit (or even exceeds it when stopped validators are present) is still reported as having fundable keys. The root cause is an erroneous assumption that the stopped counter can be subtracted from funded without affecting the overall capacity, and that operator.limit is always greater than or equal to operator.funded. When stopped validators exist, the expression evaluates to true even though no additional validator slots are actually available. An attacker or a malicious contract can exploit this by invoking the funding routine for such an operator, causing the protocol to allocate validator slots beyond the intended maximum. This can lead to out‑of‑bounds writes in the ValidatorKeys array, mis‑allocation of staking funds, or the creation of validators that never become active, effectively causing user funds to be locked or lost. The impact is high because the protocol’s accounting guarantees are broken: users expect that a funded operator will receive exactly the number of validators they paid for, but the bug may result in refunds that never happen, balances that appear to disappear, or validators that cannot be activated. The condition manifests whenever an operator is active, has a non‑zero stopped counter, and its funded count is equal to its limit – a scenario that can arise during normal operation when validators are slashed or voluntarily stopped. All participants that rely on the operator registry – delegators, node operators, and the overall protocol – are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the logical relationships between the operator’s counters and identified that the simplified return expression does not reflect the intended business rule. It is subtle because the function returns true for many legitimate cases, making the false‑positive cases hard to spot without testing edge conditions. To remediate the problem the function should be rewritten to reflect the true capacity check, for example by returning operator.active && operator.limit > operator.funded, or by incorporating a correct accounting of stopped validators in the capacity calculation. Additionally, any downstream logic that relies on _hasFundableKeys, such as the _getNextValidatorsFromActiveOperators routine, must be reviewed to ensure consistency with the corrected condition. The fix restores the invariant that an operator cannot be considered fundable once its funded count reaches its declared limit, thereby preserving the protocol’s accounting guarantees and preventing unintended loss or misallocation of funds.
summary: Since operator.keys >= operator.limit (based on the checks when operator.keys has been set), we can simplify _hasFundableKeys's return expression to: operator.active && operator.limit > (operator.funded - operator.stopped) Also based on the assumption at Non-zero operator.limit should always be greater than or equal to operator.funded, if true: operator.limit >= operator.funded This means an active operator that has at least one stopped validator would pass the test (_hasFundableKeys(operator) == true) (stop, funded, limit, keys) = (s, F, L, K) // where s > 0 Even operators that have their funded equal to their limit: (stop, funded, limit, keys) = (s, F, F, K) // where s > 0 Although they are maxed out for further funding. For these cases _hasFundableKeys returns true. So based on these findings it would make sense to have this function return: operator.active && (operator.limit > operator.funded) Unless some other changes are applied to OperatorResgistry.1.sol, specially its _getNextValidatorsFromActiveOperators function. Also, note that funded, limit, and keys are not only counters for the operator's struct, but also they define ranges in ValidatorKeys for the operator (based on the way that they have been used in OperatorResgistry.1.sol). And this is one of the main differences between these 3 fields and the stopped field. The stopped field is only used as a counter.

title: Non-zero operator.limit should always be greater than or equal to operator.funded
content: The vulnerability originates from an arithmetic assumption in the OperatorsRegistry contract where the code subtracts the amount of funds already allocated (operators[selectedOperatorIndex].funded) from the operator's capacity limit (operators[selectedOperatorIndex].limit). The logic expects limit to be greater than or equal to funded, otherwise the subtraction would underflow on an unsigned integer and cause a revert. This expectation is not enforced when the setOperatorLimits function is called, allowing an administrator or malicious actor to set a non‑zero limit that is lower than the amount already funded for that operator. When later operations attempt to compute the remaining capacity using the unchecked subtraction, the underflow produces a very large integer value, breaking the accounting invariants of the protocol. Exploitation can occur by deliberately configuring an operator with limit < funded, which either blocks further interactions (denial‑of‑service) because the transaction reverts, or, depending on downstream logic, may cause the contract to believe the operator has an enormous remaining capacity, potentially enabling unauthorized withdrawals or misallocation of funds. The impact is high because it compromises the core accounting guarantees of the collective, can lead to loss of user deposits, and may allow an attacker to manipulate operator limits to extract value or freeze the protocol. The condition manifests whenever setOperatorLimits is invoked without a validation check and the chosen limit is non‑zero but smaller than the current funded amount. All participants who rely on correct operator capacity – including token holders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that identified the missing invariant check in the limit‑setting function. It can be hard to notice because the contract compiles and runs correctly until a specific limit configuration triggers the underflow, which may only appear in edge‑case testing or after a governance action. To remediate, the setOperatorLimits function should enforce that any new limit is either zero (indicating a disabled operator) or at least as large as the already funded amount, thereby preserving the invariant limit >= funded. This aligns the implementation with the intended business rule that an operator cannot be assigned a capacity smaller than the funds it already holds, preventing accounting anomalies and ensuring that refunds, withdrawals, and capacity checks behave as users expect (e.g., a user expects a refund but receives zero because the contract reverts). The bug belongs to the class of unchecked arithmetic invariants and improper input validation that can cause underflow/overflow errors in financial smart contracts.
summary: For the subtraction operation in OperatorsRegistry.1.sol#L428-L430 to not underflow and revert, there should be an assumption that operators[selectedOperatorIndex].limit >= operators[selectedOperatorIndex].funded Perhaps this is a general assumption, but it is not enforced when setOperatorLimits is called with a new set of limits.

title: User's LsETH might be locked due to out-of-gas error during recursive calls
content: The vulnerability is an unbounded recursive claim mechanism in the LsETH redemption flow that can exhaust the transaction gas limit and permanently lock a user’s tokens. When a user submits a redeem request that is larger than the amount available in a single withdrawal event, the contract’s _claimRedeemRequest function processes the matching withdrawal event and, if the request is not fully satisfied, calls itself recursively with the next withdrawal event identifier. This recursion continues until the request amount is reduced to zero or no further withdrawal events exist. If the request is satisfied by many small withdrawal events – for example a 1000 LsETH request matched by dozens of <10 LsETH events – the recursion depth becomes large, each call consuming additional gas. Eventually the transaction runs out of gas and reverts, leaving the redeem request in an incomplete state. Because the contract does not provide a way to split the claim into smaller chunks or to resume the process after a failure, the user cannot retrieve the locked LsETH. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that traced the call stack of resolveRedeemRequests and _claimRedeemRequest and identified that the recursive pattern has no termination guard other than gas exhaustion. It is hard to notice because normal‑size requests complete successfully; only unusually large requests trigger the failure, and the revert appears as a generic out‑of‑gas error without a clear indication that the funds are locked. The impact is that users may lose access to their LsETH, the protocol’s liquidity pool can become fragmented, and confidence in the redemption process is undermined. Affected parties include any holder of LsETH who attempts to redeem a large amount, as well as the protocol that relies on accurate accounting of redeemed tokens. The root cause is the use of unbounded recursion for claim processing without gas‑aware limits or user‑controlled chunking. To remediate, the contract should be refactored to use an iterative loop or a batched claim approach that allows the caller to specify a maximum number of withdrawal events per transaction, enable partial claims, and provide a mechanism to resume after a failure. This eliminates the recursion depth problem, ensures that redemption requests can always be completed within gas limits, and restores the expected accounting invariant that a redeem request is either fully satisfied or safely revertible without locking funds.
summary:
Let W0, W1, ...W7 represent the withdrawal events in the withdrawal stack.
Let R0, R1, R2 represent the users' redeem requests in the redeem queue.
Assume that Alice is the owner of R1. When Alice called the resolveRedeemRequests function against R1, it will resolve to W1.
Next, Alice called the _claimRedeemRequest function with R1 and its corresponding W1.
The _claimRedeemRequest will first process W1. At the end of the function, it will check if W1 matches all the amounts of R1. If not, it will call the _claimRedeemRequest function recursively with the same request id (R1) but increment the withdrawal event id (W2 = W1 + 1).
The _claimRedeemRequest function recursively calls itself until all the amount of redeem request is "expended" or the next withdrawal event does not exist. In the above example, the _claimRedeemRequest will be called 7 times with W1...W7, until all the amount of R1 is "expended" (R1.amount == 0)
However, if the amount of a redeem request is large (e.g. 1000 LsETH), and this redeem request is satisfied by many small chunks of withdrawal events (e.g. one withdrawal event consists of less than 10 LsETH), then the recursion depth will be large. The function will keep calling itself recursively until an out-of-gas error happens. If this happens, there is no way to claim the redemption request, and the user's LsETH will be locked.
In the current implementation, users cannot break the claim into smaller chunks to overcome the gas limit. In the above example, if Alice attempts to break the claim into smaller chunks by first calling the _claimRedeemRequest function with R1 and its corresponding W5, the _isMatch function within it will revert.

title: Wrong refundExecutionFee in _handleReturn
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect reference to a deposit record when refunding the execution fee in the _handleReturn function of the PerpetualVault contract. The function receives a deposit identifier (depositId) that points to the user who initiated a withdrawal, but the refund logic mistakenly reads the executionFee from a different storage slot identified by the global counter variable. The root cause is a mismatched key: depositInfo[depositId] is used for the fee comparison, yet depositInfo[counter] is used for the actual refund call. This mismatch can be exploited whenever the refundFee flag is true, which occurs only in the runSwap path that a keeper can trigger manually. An attacker (or a careless keeper) can cause the contract to send the excess execution fee to the owner of the most recent deposit instead of the withdrawing user. The impact is that the original depositor receives a smaller refund than expected, while another user receives an unintended surplus, breaking the accounting guarantees of the vault and potentially leading to loss of funds for the affected user. The bug manifests under the condition that a withdrawal is processed with refundFee enabled, typically when the vault state is changed to WITHDRAW via setVaultState and runNextAction invokes runSwap. Users experience a discrepancy where the refund amount they expect (executionFee minus gas used) is either reduced or missing, and another user may see an unexpected credit. The issue was discovered during a manual code audit that highlighted the inconsistent use of the counter variable. It is hard to notice because the emitted events do not directly reveal the recipient of the refund, and the total fee balance of the contract may still appear correct. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of incorrect mapping key usage leading to misallocation of funds. The proper remediation is to replace the reference to depositInfo[counter] with depositInfo[depositId] in the refundExecutionFee call, ensuring the refund is calculated and sent to the correct depositor.

title: Deposits on long one leverage vault don't actually finalize the flow, leading to a Denial of Service (DoS)
content: The Gamma protocol uses a state machine with a "flow" variable and a "nextAction" selector to track the progress of deposit, withdraw and other operations. For a long one‑leverage vault the deposit function sets the flow to DEPOSIT and schedules an INCREASE_ACTION that is later executed by the keeper through runNextAction. In the normal path the keeper calls _runSwap, receives the swapped amount and then the contract calls _finalize to reset the flow to NONE, allowing a new deposit or withdrawal. However, when the vault is configured for a single‑DEX swap (metadata contains only a ParaSwap DEX entry) the _runSwap implementation returns true after minting the share tokens but the surrounding runNextAction code never invokes _finalize for this specific branch. As a result the flow variable remains stuck at DEPOSIT. Because the contract checks that no other flow is in progress before accepting a new deposit, any subsequent deposit attempts are rejected with the FlowInProgress error. From a user’s perspective a deposit appears to succeed (the transaction does not revert) but the share balance does not increase and later attempts to deposit or withdraw simply fail, giving the impression that the vault is frozen or that funds have disappeared. The bug is a classic state‑machine mis‑transition: the contract fails to complete the state transition after a successful swap, leaving the vault in an intermediate state that blocks all further actions. It is triggered only for long one‑leverage vaults that use a single‑DEX swap path, so it can be hard to notice during normal testing where other vault configurations finalize correctly. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition: the vault becomes unusable, new users cannot add liquidity, and existing users cannot retrieve their positions, potentially leading to loss of revenue and user trust. The issue was discovered by the CodeHawks audit team through a targeted test that performed multiple deposits on a long one‑leverage vault and observed that the second deposit reverted because the flow never reset. Although the contract provides cancelFlow and setVaultState functions, they are not intended for this scenario and do not automatically resolve the stuck state. The proper fix is to ensure that after _runSwap completes for the long one‑leverage case, the contract explicitly calls the internal _finalize function (or otherwise resets the flow) before exiting runNextAction, thereby guaranteeing that the state machine returns to the idle state and subsequent operations can proceed. This correction restores the expected business logic that a successful deposit results in minted shares and a cleared flow, preventing the vault from being locked out of service.

title: Loss of fee refund due to premature state deletion in `PerpetualVault::_handleReturn` function
content: The vulnerability is that the PerpetualVault::_handleReturn function burns the deposit record before attempting to refund the execution fee. Because the internal _burn routine deletes depositInfo for the given depositId, the executionFee field is cleared and becomes zero. The subsequent refund logic checks if depositInfo[depositId].executionFee is greater than the used fee, a condition that can never be true after the deletion. As a result, when a flow ends with refundFee set to true – for example in withdraw or signal‑change flows – the user’s excess execution fee is never sent back and remains locked in the GmxProxy contract. An attacker or any user can deliberately over‑pay the execution fee via PerpetualVault::payExecutionFee, causing the contract to keep the entire amount. From the user’s perspective the transaction completes successfully, a Burned event is emitted, but the expected refund is missing, the user’s balance after the transaction is zero and the ether is stuck in the proxy. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that traced the order of operations and observed that the state deletion occurs before the refund calculation, making the refund condition unreachable. It is hard to notice because the contract does not revert and the flow appears normal, so the loss of funds is only visible by inspecting balances after execution. The bug belongs to the class of premature state deletion leading to lost refunds, a specific form of incorrect ordering of state updates that breaks accounting assumptions. The impact is loss of user funds, potential loss of trust in the protocol, and fees becoming unrecoverable without a special withdrawal function. The fix is to move the refund logic before the call to _burn, or to cache the execution fee in a temporary variable before deleting the depositInfo, ensuring the refund condition can be evaluated and the fee returned to the user.

title: If users withdraw while a position is in loss, the whole PNL of the position to their withdrawal amount instead of just their share of it.
content: The vulnerability occurs when a user attempts to withdraw from a vault that holds an open leveraged long or short position with more than 1x leverage. The withdraw routine calculates the user’s proportional collateral and fee based on the number of shares owned, but it obtains the profit‑and‑loss (PNL) of the position by calling an external reader contract with a boolean flag set to true. This flag tells the reader to use the full position size as the size delta, causing the reader to return the total PNL of the entire position instead of the PNL that corresponds to the user’s share. When the position is in loss, the returned negative PNL is subtracted from the user’s collateral amount. If the loss exceeds the user’s collateral, the subtraction underflows and the transaction reverts; if the collateral is sufficient, the user still absorbs the entire loss of the position rather than only their proportional share. From the user’s perspective the withdrawal either fails with an underflow error or succeeds but returns far less than expected, sometimes leaving the balance at zero or showing an unexpected loss. The issue is triggered only when a withdrawal is performed while a leveraged position is open and the position is underwater. It affects any participant who holds shares in the vault and tries to exit under those conditions, leading to potential loss of funds and denial of service for withdrawals. The bug was discovered during a manual security audit by CodeHawks, who traced the flow from the vault’s _withdraw function through VaultReader.getPnl and the GMX reader’s getPositionInfo, identifying the incorrect boolean argument as the root cause. The problem is subtle because the withdraw logic appears to allocate shares proportionally, while the PNL calculation is hidden in an external library, making the mis‑allocation difficult to spot without deep tracing. The recommended remediation is to pass false for the usePositionSizeAsSizeDeltaUsd argument when invoking the GMX reader, ensuring that the PNL is computed based on the user’s size delta rather than the whole position. This change restores the intended accounting semantics, prevents users from unintentionally inheriting the full loss of a position, and eliminates the underflow revert scenario.

title: Subtracting position fee in position net value will lead to incorrect share allocation
content: The vulnerability originates from the way the PerpetualVault contract computes the net value of a position when minting new shares for a user deposit. The contract subtracts the position fee from the position's net value inside the _totalAmount() helper, and then uses this reduced totalAmountBefore in the share formula _shares = amount * totalShares / totalAmountBefore. Because the position fee is already deducted from the user’s deposit amount during order execution (the fee is taken from the increase/decrease amounts), including it again in the net value causes the denominator to be artificially low. As a result, later depositors receive a larger share count than their proportional contribution warrants, while earlier depositors are diluted. This mis‑allocation can be exploited by repeatedly depositing after the fee has been applied, inflating share balances and effectively extracting value from the vault. The impact is an unfair distribution of ownership, potential loss of value for honest participants, and a breach of the protocol’s accounting invariants that assume shares represent a true proportion of the underlying collateral. The issue manifests whenever the position fee is non‑zero and multiple deposits occur in the same position, which is a common scenario in perpetual vaults. Users experience symptoms such as receiving more shares than expected for an identical deposit, seeing their share balance increase disproportionately, or observing that the total share supply grows faster than the total collateral. The bug was discovered during a manual audit of the share‑minting logic, where the auditor noticed that the net value calculation included the position fee despite the fee already being accounted for elsewhere. The problem is subtle because the share numbers still appear plausible on a per‑transaction basis, and the discrepancy only becomes evident after several deposits. To remediate, the position fee must be excluded from the net value used in the share calculation, i.e., the _totalAmount() function should return the gross position value without subtracting positionFee, or the share formula should be adjusted to use a fee‑adjusted denominator that reflects the true collateral increase. This correction restores the intended one‑to‑one relationship between deposited collateral and minted shares, preserving the economic integrity of the vault.

title: Borrowing interest is calculated inaccurately and can be manipulated
content: The vulnerability is an inaccurate interest accrual calculation that uses the current market utilization rate to compute interest for a past time interval, leading to over‑charging or under‑charging borrowers. The root cause is that each loan stores only a last‑update timestamp and the contract reads the global utilization rate at the moment of the next user action, assuming the rate has been constant during the elapsed delay. Because other participants can change total borrows or cash, the utilization rate can vary arbitrarily between the two timestamps, so the formula applies a wrong rate to the whole delay. An attacker can manipulate the utilization rate just before repaying: by minting a large amount of interest‑bearing tokens (or withdrawing cash) they push utilization down, causing the contract to compute a near‑minimum rate for the repayment period and thus avoid paying the proper interest, then unwind the position and keep the saved amount. A legitimate user experiences the same problem when another borrower changes the market state; they may see a higher than expected repayment amount, or see their balance reduced unexpectedly after a repayment. The impact is financial loss for borrowers and distortion of the protocol’s economic model; over‑charged interest can erode user trust and under‑charged interest can be exploited to siphon value. The condition occurs whenever a user’s debt is updated after a period in which the market’s utilization rate has changed, which is the normal operation of any lending market with multiple participants. All borrowers, lenders and the protocol itself are affected because the accounting invariants are broken. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the intended accounting model with the actual implementation and identified that the contract does not snapshot the utilization rate per user. It is hard to notice because the contract still records a non‑zero interest value and the discrepancy may be small for short intervals, making it appear as normal rounding noise. The bug belongs to the class of “state‑dependent arithmetic errors” or “incorrect temporal snapshotting” where a variable that should be frozen for a period is instead read lazily. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a repayment amount that is higher than expected, or a balance that becomes zero after a repayment that should have left a residual. The expectation that “repaying my loan should cost exactly the accrued interest” is violated; instead the protocol charges interest based on a rate that was not in effect for most of the elapsed time. To fix the issue the contract should maintain a global borrow index that is updated whenever the utilization rate changes and each user should store an interest index; before any state‑changing action the protocol must accrue interest globally and then compute each user’s debt from the stored index, ensuring that past periods are charged at the rates that were actually in effect. This design mirrors Compound V2 and eliminates the need to recompute interest with a stale utilization rate.
summary: The system keeps track of each user's loan and the accrued interest individually. Each user has a corresponding last-update timestamp, which is compared with the current timestamp to calculate the newly accrued interest only when the user's position is updated, e.g., when borrowing funds or repaying debt. The accrued interest during a period is calculated as: interestAccrued = debt * (utilizationRate * baseRate + initRate) * delay / oneYearInMs where utilizationRate = TotalBorrows / (TotalBorrows + Cash), i.e., the market's current utilization rate. The delay variable represents the time difference between the user's current and last actions. However, using the current utilization rate to calculate the interest in the past delay period is incorrect. It assumes that the rate has not been changed since the last user's action, which, however, is not always the case because other users' actions can arbitrarily change the market's state. Consider the following example: 1. t = 0, User A borrows. The utilization rate is 50%. 2. t = 100, User B borrows. The utilization rate becomes 90%. 3. t = 101, User A repays. The interests are calculated using a rate of 90%, but it was 50% most of the time. User A ends up paying more interest. Additionally, an attacker could exploit this design to lower the interest rate to a number close to initRate. Before repaying their debt, they could mint a large number of oTokens with another account to decrease the market's utilization rate as much as possible. After repaying the debt, they redeem the underlying tokens without incurring a loss.

title: Incorrect Tag Parsing in Interest Sync
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect tag parsing in the interest synchronization routine of a loan protocol. The function syncInterests decides whether a message represents a repayment by checking msg.Tags.Action == "Repay", but the protocol defines repayment intent using the X-Action tag. Because the check looks at the wrong field, repayment messages are not recognised and the code falls into the generic else branch, which treats msg.From as the target for interest updates. In a repayment flow msg.From is the collateral token contract, not the borrower, so the interest balance of the actual borrower is never updated. As a result the borrower can repay the principal while the accrued interest remains unchanged, effectively allowing under‑payment or complete bypass of interest accrual. The bug also lacks validation of the address fields contained in msg.Tags.Sender or msg.Tags["X-On-Behalf"], meaning malformed or malicious tag values can be accepted and used as the interest update target, potentially causing inconsistent state or runtime errors. The issue manifests whenever a repayment notice is sent following the borrow‑loan‑interest‑sync‑dynamic pattern, i.e., during normal loan repayment operations. All participants that rely on correct interest accounting – borrowers, lenders, and the protocol’s risk engine – are affected because the accounting invariant that interest owed equals accrued interest is broken. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that compared the contract’s tag handling against the protocol specification and identified the mismatch. It is subtle because the contract still compiles and processes messages; the wrong branch simply updates a different account, which may not be immediately visible in UI unless the borrower checks their interest balance after repayment. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “incorrect protocol message parsing” or “mis‑routed state update” bugs, where business logic relies on specific metadata fields that are mis‑interpreted. From a user perspective the symptom is that after making a repayment the displayed interest owed remains unchanged or even shows zero while the loan principal is reduced, leading to a mismatch between expected and actual balances. The attack scenario consists of an adversary (or even an honest borrower) sending a repayment message that follows the standard format; the contract misinterprets the tags, updates the collateral contract’s interest record instead of the borrower’s, and leaves the borrower’s interest untouched, allowing the borrower to avoid paying interest. To remediate the issue the syncInterests logic should be changed to check msg.Tags["X-Action"] for the value Repay, combine this with the existing Action == Credit-Notice and msg.From == CollateralID checks, and validate that either msg.Tags["X-On-Behalf"] or msg.Tags.Sender contains a well‑formed address using the isAddress helper before performing any state change. This ensures that interest updates are applied to the correct borrower and that malformed tags are rejected, restoring the intended accounting guarantees.
summary: In the interest.lua contract, the syncInterests function incorrectly checks for a repayment action by evaluating msg.Tags.Action == "Repay". However, according to the messaging conventions established by the protocol (specifically the borrow-loan-interest-sync-dynamic pattern), the repayment intent is signaled via the X-Action tag, not the Action tag. As a result, the intended conditional branch for interest synchronization on repayments is bypassed, and execution falls through to the default else block. This default case uses msg.From as the interest update target, which in repayment flows refers to the collateral token process—not the borrower. Consequently, the system updates the interest balance for an incorrect user and skips the actual borrower, allowing them to underpay or bypass interest accrual entirely. Additionally, there is no validation to ensure that msg.Tags.Sender or msg.Tags["X-On-Behalf"] is a properly formed address before updating interest. This opens the door to further inconsistencies or even execution errors if unexpected data is received in those fields.

title: Partial liquidations allow position management blocking and liquidation prevention due to queue mechanism implementation
content: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service style flaw in the liquidation workflow of the LiquidOps protocol. The protocol supports partial liquidations and, when a liquidation is started, the borrower’s address is inserted into a LiquidationQueue. While an address is present in this queue the contract’s public functions – repayment, collateral withdrawal, and other management actions – first check the queue and reject the call with an “In‑Queue” response. Because the implementation does not enforce any minimum liquidation amount, an attacker (or the borrower themselves using multiple auxiliary accounts) can trigger a liquidation of an arbitrarily small portion of the debt. This tiny liquidation is sufficient to add the borrower to the queue, which immediately blocks the borrower from repaying the loan or moving collateral. The attacker can repeat the minimal liquidation or keep the borrower in the queue indefinitely, effectively preventing other legitimate liquidators from seizing the under‑collateralised position and from receiving the liquidation incentive. From the user’s perspective the UI shows that the transaction fails with an “In‑Queue” error, balances appear unchanged, and attempts to withdraw collateral return zero, leading to the impression that my funds are stuck or my repayment did nothing. The issue occurs whenever a partial liquidation is allowed and the queue‑check is performed, which is the default path for most state‑changing functions. It affects borrowers who are at risk of liquidation, external liquidators who rely on the incentive, and ultimately the protocol’s solvency because under‑collateralised loans may remain open. The flaw was discovered during a manual security review that traced the queue insertion logic and noted the absence of a lower bound on liquidation size. It is hard to notice because the queue mechanism is intended as a safety feature, and a single tiny liquidation does not raise obvious red flags in transaction logs. The vulnerability belongs to the class of resource‑locking denial‑of‑service bugs where a contract’s internal lock can be abused without cost. The recommended mitigation is to introduce a minimum liquidation threshold expressed as a percentage of the total outstanding debt (for example 20 %) so that only economically meaningful liquidations can trigger the queue, thereby making the attack prohibitively expensive. Additional hardening could include allowing repayment and collateral management even while the borrower is queued, or removing the queue lock entirely.
summary: The LiquidOps protocol allows partial liquidations where only a portion of a loan is liquidated. When a liquidation is initiated, the target user is added to a LiquidationQueue to prevent duplicate liquidations: -- Add the target to the liquidation queue to lock further liquidations table.insert(LiquidationQueue, target) The user remains in this queue until the liquidation is complete, at which point they are removed: -- Remove target from liquidation queue to allow further liquidations LiquidationQueue = utils.filter( function (v) return v ~= target end, LiquidationQueue ) While a user is in the LiquidationQueue, they are prevented from performing certain operations, as many protocol actions check if the user is queued: -- check-queue handler -- the user is queued if they're either in the collateral -- or the liquidation queues return msg.reply({ ["In-Queue"] = json.encode( utils.includes(user, CollateralQueue) or utils.includes(user, LiquidationQueue) ) }) Due to lack of minimum liquidation size requirements, this implementation allows for two attack vectors: 1. An attacker could liquidate a minimal amount of a user's position to forcefully add them to the queue, temporarily preventing them from performing critical actions such as repaying loans or managing collateral. 2. Users at risk of liquidation could create multiple accounts to perform minimal self-liquidations (as direct self-liquidation is not allowed from the protocol), effectively preventing other liquidators from capturing the full liquidation incentives and potentially preventing the liquidation of undercollateralized positions.

title: Attacker can call sweepRewardToken
content: The vulnerability resides in a reward‑sweeping routine that moves any unprotected token balance held by the contract to a designated bribes processor address. The routine is invoked through a public function that first checks that the caller is either governance or a strategist and that the token is not on a protected list, then obtains the full token balance of the contract and forwards it to an internal handler. The handler decides, based on the token type, whether to route the amount to a Badger‑tree or, for all other tokens, to the bribes processor via a low‑level safeTransfer call. Crucially, the code does not verify that the bribes processor address is non‑zero before performing the transfer. Because the bribes processor variable is initialised to the zero address and can be explicitly set to zero by the governance role, there exists a state in which the address equals 0x0. When that state is reached, any execution of the sweep function will cause the contract to transfer its entire reward token balance to the zero address, effectively burning the tokens. An attacker who can trigger the sweep while the processor address is zero can therefore cause a total loss of the accumulated rewards. The root cause is a missing validation of an external address prior to a token transfer, combined with the ability for a privileged role to set the address to an unsafe value. This flaw is subtle because ERC‑20 transfers to address(0) are technically allowed; they simply result in token destruction without emitting a distinct warning, and the contract only logs a generic RewardsCollected event, making the loss difficult to detect from the contract’s perspective. The impact is the disappearance of all reward tokens that users expect to receive, breaking the accounting assumptions of the protocol and diminishing the value of the reward pool. The issue manifests whenever the bribes processor variable is zero—either by default or after an intentional governance change—and the sweep function is called. It primarily affects token holders and the protocol’s economic guarantees. The flaw was uncovered during a security audit when the logic of the sweep function and the default value of the bribes processor variable were examined. To remediate the issue, the contract should enforce a non‑zero address check before any transfer to the bribes processor, either by adding a require statement in the internal _sendTokenToBribesProcessor function or by initializing the processor to a safe, immutable address. Alternatively, the sweep function could be restricted to a role that cannot set the processor to zero, or the transfer could be guarded with a fallback that redirects tokens to a safe vault when the target address is invalid. Implementing such validation restores the intended accounting flow and prevents accidental or malicious token burns.
summary: If the value of `bribesProcessor` was `0x0` (the default is `0x0` and `governance()` can set to `0x0`) then attacker can call `sweepRewardToken()` make contract to send his total balance in attacker specified token to `0x0` address.

title: Underlying asset price oracle for `CToken` in `BaseV1-periphery` is inaccurate
content: The vulnerability is an inaccurate price oracle for the cNOTE token in the BaseV1‑periphery contract. Instead of returning a correctly scaled price of 10**18 (the standard 1e18 fixed‑point representation), the getUnderlyingPrice function returns the literal integer 1 when the caller is the Comptroller and the token symbol matches "cNOTE". This developer mistake originates from a hard‑coded return value that treats 1 as a full price, ignoring the 18‑decimal scaling used throughout the protocol. Because all downstream calculations – notably the diff computation in NoteInterest.sol that determines accrued interest – rely on the oracle price being expressed in 1e18 units, the erroneous return of 1 collapses the price to a near‑zero value. Consequently the diff term becomes zero for every block, causing the protocol to calculate interest solely from the baseRatePerYear and effectively eliminating any variable component of the rate. The bug manifests whenever the Comptroller queries the price of cNOTE, which happens during every borrow, repay, or supply operation involving that market. Users who supply cNOTE expect their balance to grow with accrued interest, but they observe a static balance and zero earned interest, despite the protocol’s UI showing a positive base rate. Lenders, borrowers, and any party relying on accurate interest accrual are therefore affected, as the protocol may distribute insufficient rewards or, conversely, allow borrowers to repay less than they should, potentially leading to under‑collateralisation and loss of protocol funds. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when the code was examined and the static return value was noted as inconsistent with the documented scaling convention. Detecting the problem is difficult because the function compiles and returns a non‑zero value, and the error only becomes apparent when interest calculations yield unexpectedly flat results. To remediate, the hard‑coded return should be replaced with the correct fixed‑point value of 10**18, or, preferably, the oracle should fetch the true market price from a reliable source and return it in the standard 1e18 format. This aligns the price with the protocol’s accounting assumptions, restores correct interest accrual, and prevents the economic distortion caused by a zero diff term.
summary: Underlying asset price oracle for CToken in BaseV1-periphery is inaccurate.

title: Oracle `periodSize` is very low allowing the TWAP price to be easily manipulated
content: The vulnerability is a mis‑configuration of the time‑weighted average price (TWAP) oracle where the constant `periodSize` is set to zero. Because the oracle uses this value to determine the interval between price observations, a zero period forces the oracle to take a new price observation on every single block, effectively turning the intended TWAP into a spot price that reflects the most recent price update only. This happens due to a coding mistake that left the period constant at zero, despite comments indicating the intention to use a non‑zero interval (commonly 1800 seconds). An attacker can exploit the situation by flooding the price feed or by executing a flash‑loan that briefly manipulates the underlying asset’s price immediately before the oracle records the price for that block. Since the oracle reports the manipulated spot price, any downstream calculation that relies on `getUnderlyingPrice`, such as collateral valuation, borrowing limits, or liquidation thresholds, will be based on a falsified value. The impact may include incorrect pricing, unintended liquidations, loss of collateral, and overall erosion of trust in the protocol. The condition for exploitation is any scenario where an adversary can influence the price source within a single block window, which is always possible when `periodSize` equals zero. All users of the protocol – lenders, borrowers, and token holders – are affected because the protocol’s accounting assumptions that prices are smoothed over a reasonable window are violated. The issue was discovered during a formal audit, where reviewers noted the constant set to zero and highlighted that comments suggested it was an error. It is hard to notice because the oracle appears to function correctly on a per‑block basis, so quick manual checks may not reveal the lack of averaging. To remediate, the contract should be updated so that `periodSize` is a non‑zero, configurable constant (e.g., 1800 seconds) and the oracle must compute the average over multiple observations rather than a single block, restoring the intended TWAP behavior. This class of bug is a timing‑or‑configuration error in oracle design that leads to price manipulation, causing symptoms such as users receiving zero refunds, balances becoming unexpectedly low, or positions being liquidated despite unchanged market conditions.
summary: TWAP oracle easily manipulated.

title: The LP pair underlying price quote could be manipulated
content: The vulnerability originates from the way the contract derives the value of a liquidity‑provider (LP) token by simply adding the market value of the underlying assets as measured by the pool’s total value locked (TVL). The code fetches a quoted price for each token against USDC, multiplies those quotes by the amount of each token that one LP token can redeem (derived from the pool’s reserves), and sums the results to obtain a single price. This approach assumes that the reserves reported by the pool are a faithful representation of the market price at the moment of calculation. However, because the reserves can be altered arbitrarily within a single block, a malicious actor can deposit a large amount of any token into the pool just before the price query, artificially inflating the TVL and consequently the computed LP price. The attacker can then exploit the inflated valuation by, for example, minting or withdrawing LP tokens at the exaggerated price, swapping against the pool, or providing collateral based on the overstated value, ultimately extracting funds from honest participants. The impact manifests as a discrepancy between the expected and actual value of LP tokens: users who think their LP token is worth a certain amount may receive far less after redemption, or the protocol may suffer a net loss of assets that appear to have “disappeared” from its balance sheet. This condition can be triggered in any block where an attacker can move enough capital to sway the pool’s reserves, which is feasible with flash‑loan techniques or large token holdings. The issue was uncovered during a Code4rena audit, referencing a previously documented incident (Warp Finance) where similar mis‑pricing led to total loss of funds. Detecting the problem in production is difficult because the price computation itself looks mathematically sound and the resulting LP price may not immediately appear abnormal; the manipulation occurs within a single block and can be reverted by normal market activity, masking the exploit. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “price oracle manipulation via on‑chain state” where the oracle trusts a mutable on‑chain variable (the pool’s reserve) without protective smoothing or external validation. To remediate, the pricing logic should be replaced with a method that does not rely on instantaneous TVL, such as using time‑weighted average prices, external price feeds, or a formula that accounts for the invariant of the pool rather than raw reserve totals, as described in the referenced guide on correct LP token pricing. By adopting a robust pricing mechanism, the protocol can prevent an attacker from inflating the LP token value within a single block and protect users from unexpected losses.
summary:
The underlying price for LP pool pair can be manipulated. This kind of price mainpulation happened before, can be found here: [Warp Fincance event](https://rekt.news/warp-finance-rekt/).

Which may lead to the exploit of the pool by a malicious user.

title: `getBorrowRate` returns rate per year instead of per block
content: The vulnerability consists of a unit‑conversion error in the interest‑rate model used by the protocol. According to the documented Interface of InterestRateModel, the function getBorrowRate must return the borrow rate expressed on a per‑block basis, because the CToken contract directly forwards this value to its internal borrowRatePerBlock variable. In the NoteInterest implementation, however, the function returns a rate that is calculated on a per‑year basis. As a result, the CToken contract interprets an annual percentage as if it were the per‑block percentage, effectively multiplying the intended rate by the number of blocks produced in a year (approximately two million). This mismatch inflates the effective interest charged to borrowers by several orders of magnitude and produces misleading yield figures for lenders. The root cause is the absence of a conversion from annual to block units, i.e., the model returns baseRatePerYear instead of baseRatePerBlock. The flaw can be exploited simply by interacting with the market as normal; any borrowing activity will cause the debt to grow at a dramatically accelerated pace, potentially draining the borrower’s balance and causing liquidations, while lenders may see an advertised APY that does not correspond to any real earnings. The impact includes loss of value for users, incorrect accounting, distorted yields, and overall reduction of confidence in the protocol’s financial guarantees. The condition under which the bug manifests is whenever the NoteInterest model is supplied to a CToken that relies on getBorrowRate for per‑block calculations, which is the default configuration for the affected markets. Affected parties are borrowers, lenders, the protocol treasury, and any participants that depend on accurate interest calculations. The issue was discovered during a formal security audit performed by Code4rena, where auditors compared the contract’s implementation against the specification and observed the unit mismatch. Because the contract compiles and runs without reverting, the problem does not generate obvious runtime errors, making it difficult to detect without dedicated testing of interest accrual over realistic block intervals. The recommended remediation is to adjust the model so that getBorrowRate returns a value expressed per block, either by converting the annual rate using the known number of blocks per year or by directly returning the stored baseRatePerBlock variable. This type of bug belongs to the broader class of “unit conversion errors” in financial smart contracts, where a numeric value is interpreted with an incorrect time unit, breaking accounting assumptions such as “interest accrued per block”. From a user’s perspective, borrowers may notice that their debt grows far faster than expected, sometimes reducing their balance to zero within a few blocks, while lenders may observe that the displayed interest rates do not match the actual earned interest. Expectations of reasonable borrowing costs and accurate yield reporting are therefore violated, undermining the protocol’s reliability.
summary: According to the documentation in `InterestRateModel`, `getBorrowRate` has to return the borrow rate per block and the function `borrowRatePerBlock` in `CToken` directly returns the value of `getBorrowRate`. However, the rate per year is returned for `NoteInterest`. Therefore, using `NoteInterest` as an interest model will result in completely wrong values.

title: Deny of service in `AccountantDelegate.sweepInterest`
content: The AccountantDelegate contract contains a denial‑of‑service flaw in its sweepInterest function. The routine is designed to collect accrued cNote interest by transferring a calculated amount (amtToSweep) to a designated treasury, invoking the treasury’s redeem method, and then asserting that the treasury’s cNote balance is exactly zero. This zero‑balance check is an invariant that assumes the treasury holds no cNote tokens after redemption. The root cause is that the invariant is enforced without any protection against external token transfers to the treasury address. An attacker can simply send a single cNote token directly to the treasury; because the sweepInterest logic derives amtToSweep solely from the contract’s own balance, the extra token remains in the treasury after the transfer and redemption steps. When the function reaches the require statement checking for a zero balance, the condition fails and the transaction reverts, aborting the sweep. Since the function does not provide an alternative mechanism to withdraw or clear the unexpected token, the invariant can never be satisfied again, permanently bricking sweepInterest. The impact is that the protocol’s interest‑sweeping mechanism becomes inoperable, causing loss of yield for lenders and potentially harming the treasury’s accounting integrity. The vulnerability manifests whenever the treasury address holds any non‑zero cNote balance prior to calling sweepInterest, which can be induced by any external party. It was discovered during a manual audit by Code4rena, where the team identified the incorrect invariant and demonstrated that a single external token transfer is sufficient to lock the function. The issue is subtle because the function behaves correctly under normal conditions and the require statement appears legitimate, making the denial of service invisible until the unexpected token is present. To remediate, the contract should either remove the strict zero‑balance requirement, include logic that safely handles surplus tokens (for example by returning them to the sender or to a recovery address), or provide an alternative withdrawal path that can clear the treasury’s balance before the invariant is checked. By treating the zero‑balance check as a soft assertion rather than a hard invariant, the protocol can maintain correct accounting while preventing a malicious actor from permanently disabling interest sweeps.
summary:
<https://github.dev/Plex-Engineer/lending-market-v2/blob/2646a7676b721db8a7754bf5503dcd712eab2f8a/contracts/Accountant/AccountantDelegate.sol#L101>

The `sweepInterest` method is susceptible to denial of service.

title: AccountantDelegate: The sweepInterest function sweeps an incorrect number of cnote
content: The vulnerability resides in the sweepInterest function of the AccountantDelegate contract, where the logic that moves accrued interest from the contract to the protocol treasury mixes up two distinct units of value. The function first calculates amtToSweep as the amount of interest expressed in the base token (Note) and then derives cNoteToSweep, the corresponding amount of interest expressed in the wrapped token (cNote), by dividing amtToSweep by the current exchange rate. The intention is to transfer cNoteToSweep cNote tokens to the treasury and then redeem them for the underlying Note amount. However, the implementation mistakenly passes amtToSweep – the larger Note‑valued amount – to the cnote.transfer call and to the Treasury.redeem call. Because cNoteToSweep is typically much smaller than amtToSweep, the contract attempts to move an amount of cNote tokens that does not exist, causing the ERC‑20 transfer to fail and the function to revert. When the transfer reverts, the accrued interest remains locked inside the AccountantDelegate contract, breaking the protocol’s accounting assumptions that interest is periodically swept to the treasury. This failure manifests to users as missing or delayed refunds: a user who expects to see their accrued interest reflected in the treasury balance instead observes no change, or the UI may show that interest is still pending despite the sweep being invoked. The bug is a classic unit‑mismatch or arithmetic‑misuse error that belongs to the class of “incorrect token amount handling” vulnerabilities. It occurs whenever there is a non‑zero interest balance (cNoteAmt > noteDiff) and the sweepInterest function is called. The affected parties include the protocol treasury, token holders who rely on timely interest distribution, and any downstream contracts that assume the treasury’s balance is up‑to‑date. The issue was discovered during a manual code audit performed by Code4rena, where the auditor compared the variables used in the transfer and redeem statements and identified that the wrong variable was being supplied. The problem is subtle because the code compiles without errors and the variable names are similar; only a logical inspection of the arithmetic relationship reveals the discrepancy. To remediate the flaw, the contract should use cNoteToSweep – the correctly scaled amount – as the transfer amount to the treasury and as the argument to the redeem call. This change aligns the units, prevents unnecessary reverts, and ensures that interest can be swept out of the contract, restoring the intended flow of funds and preserving the integrity of the protocol’s financial accounting.

title: auraBAL can be stuck into the Strategy contract
content: The vulnerability originates from the way the Strategy contract calculates reward earnings in its internal _harvest()routine. When the contract wants to claim auraBAL from the Aura locker it invokes LOCKER.getReward(address(this)) and then determines how much auraBAL was earned by measuring the token balance before the call and after the call, using the difference as the reward amount. Because the reward‑claim function is public, any external address may trigger getReward on behalf of the Strategy contract at any time. If an attacker (or any third party) calls getReward before the Strategy’s own _harvest() execution, the locker will transfer auraBAL to the Strategy contract outside of the expected claim window. When _harvest() later runs, the pre‑call balance already includes the previously transferred tokens, so the measured delta is zero and the contract incorrectly assumes that no auraBAL was earned. The mistakenly transferred auraBAL then sits in the Strategy’s balance but is classified as a protected token and cannot be swept or exchanged by the contract’s normal logic. Consequently, those funds become effectively stuck, reducing the protocol’s yield and depriving users of expected refunds or conversions. A similar issue exists in claimBribesFromHiddenHand(): the input array of claims can be front‑run, causing a third party to invoke hiddenHandDistributor.claim(_claims) for the Strategy address before the legitimate call. Tokens received in that pre‑emptive claim are not accounted for by the subsequent processing, and because the notification step (_notifyBribesProcessor) may never be triggered, the rewards remain unprocessed. The bug is a classic accounting‑logic error where reward amounts are derived from a balance delta rather than an absolute post‑claim balance, making the system vulnerable to timing attacks. It manifests whenever external callers can invoke the public reward functions before the Strategy’s scheduled harvest or bribe‑claim functions, which can happen at any block. The affected parties are the Strategy contract itself, its investors, and ultimately the Badger protocol that relies on these reward conversions for proper accounting. The issue was uncovered during a Code4rena audit by analyzing the reward‑claim flow and testing edge cases where rewards were sent outside the expected window. It is difficult to spot in normal operation because no exception is thrown; the contract’s balance simply contains extra auraBAL that never gets swapped, leading to a silent loss of assets. The recommended remediation is to stop using a balance‑before/balance‑after delta and instead read the absolute token balance directly after the claim, treating the entire balance as the reward amount. This eliminates the timing window where external calls can steal the accounting of earned rewards and ensures that all received tokens are correctly processed or become sweepable. In broader terms, the flaw belongs to the class of reward‑distribution accounting bugs where reliance on mutable state snapshots creates exploitable race conditions, breaking the contract’s invariants that “earned rewards must be fully accounted for and convertible”.
summary:
The internal `_harvest()` function defined is responsible to claim auraBAL from the aura locker and within the function it swaps them to auraBAL -> BAL/ETH BPT -> WETH -> AURA, finally it locks AURA to the locker to increase the position. For claiming auraBAL it calls `LOCKER.getReward(address(this))` and it calculates the tokes earned, checking the balance before and after the claiming.

The function to get the rewards is public and any address can call it for the strategy address, and it will transfer all rewards tokens to the strategy, but in this scenario the auraBAL will remain in stuck into the contract, because they won’t be counted as auraBAL earned during the next `_harvest()`. Also they could not sweep because auraBAL is a protected token.

Also, the aura Locker will be able to add other token as reward apart of auraBAL, but the harvest function won’t be able to manage them, so they will need to be sweep every time.

The same scenario can happen during the `claimBribesFromHiddenHand()` call, the `IRewardDistributor.Claim[] calldata _claims` pass as input parameters could be frontrunned, and another address can call the `hiddenHandDistributor.claim(_claims)` (except for ETH rewards) for the strategy address, and like during the `_harvest()` only the tokens received during the call will be counted as earned. However every token, except auraBAL can be sweep, but the `_notifyBribesProcessor()` may never be called.

title: Total supply can be incorrect in `ERC20`
content: The vulnerability concerns an ERC‑20 token implementation in which the contract’s internal variable that tracks the total token supply is initialized to a non‑zero value directly in the constructor. Instead of starting at zero and increasing the supply through a standard minting routine that also emits the required Transfer event, the constructor assigns an _initialSupply amount to the _totalSupply storage slot and credits the deployer’s balance without invoking the proper mint logic. This design flaw creates a discrepancy between the amount of tokens that actually exist in user balances and the value returned by the totalSupply() view function. The root cause is the omission of a call to the ERC‑20 compliant _mint helper, which both updates the total supply and triggers the Transfer event, and the direct manipulation of the private _totalSupply variable. An attacker does not gain direct access to funds, but the inconsistency can be exploited by downstream contracts, analytics platforms, or off‑chain services that rely on totalSupply() to compute market capitalisation, enforce caps, or reward distributions. If the constructor is invoked with an _initialSupply of 1,000 tokens, the contract will forever report a total supply that is 1,000 tokens higher than the actual circulating amount, causing integrations that query totalSupply to report inflated values, potentially leading to incorrect financial calculations, failed assertions in other contracts, or misleading data displayed to users. The issue manifests whenever the token is deployed with a non‑zero initial supply and persists throughout the lifetime of the contract because the total supply is never adjusted again. It primarily affects token holders, integrators, and any protocol components that depend on accurate accounting of the token’s supply.
