It is hard to notice because the bug only manifests under extreme front‑running conditions and with minimal deposit amounts, which are rarely covered by standard unit tests. To remediate, the contract should enforce a minimum initial share mint that is burned to a dead address, reducing the number of shares actually allocated to the depositor and ensuring that the cost of obtaining a share is not profitable for an attacker. Alternatively, the share calculation could be performed with rounding up or by requiring a minimum deposit size, thereby eliminating the rounding window that enables the exploit. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of initialization‑time rounding or precision attacks that allow front‑runners to dilute the first legitimate depositor’s share allocation and extract value from the pool.
summary: The first deposit with a totalSupply of zero shares will mint shares equal to the deposited amount. This makes it possible to deposit the smallest unit of a token and profit off a rounding issue in the computation for the minted shares of the next depositor: (shares_ * totalAssets()) / totalSupply_ Example: • The first depositor (victim) wants to deposit 2M USDC (2e12) and submits the transaction. • The attacker front runs the victim's transaction by calling deposit(1) to get 1 share. They then transfer 1M USDC (1e12) to the contract, such that totalAssets = 1e12 + 1, totalSupply = 1. • When the victim's transaction is mined, they receive 2e12 / (1e12 + 1) * totalSupply = 1 shares (rounded down from 1.9999...). • The attacker withdraws their 1 share and gets 3M USDC * 1 / 2 = 1.5M USDC, making a 0.5M profit. During the migration, an _initialSupply of shares to be airdropped are already minted at initialization and are not affected by this attack.

title: Comptroller uses the wrong address for the WETH contract
content: The vulnerability is that the Comptroller contract contains a hard‑coded address for the WETH token which actually points to the mainnet COMP contract rather than the correct WETH contract on the deployed network. Because the reward‑distribution functions – grantCompInternal and claimComp – retrieve the token address via getWETHAddress and then invoke balanceOf and transfer on that address, any call that attempts to distribute or claim COMP tokens interacts with a contract that does not implement the expected ERC‑20 interface. If the address contains no contract, the calls succeed but have no effect; if it contains a contract with a different interface, the calls revert. In both cases the user receives no COMP rewards despite having accrued them. The bug originates from leftover code copied from the original Compound repository where the address was appropriate for the original chain, but it was never updated for the target deployment. The issue manifests whenever a user or the protocol triggers reward distribution – typically when a user calls claimComp or when the system internally calls grantCompInternal. Affected parties include any lender or borrower who expects COMP incentives, and the protocol’s economic model because undistributed rewards undermine the incentive structure. The problem is subtle because the UI may still display a claim button and show accrued rewards, yet the transaction either reverts silently or completes without moving tokens, leading to user confusion and apparent loss of funds. The vulnerability was discovered during a code audit that traced the hard‑coded address and observed its mismatch with the network’s WETH address. Fixing the issue requires removing the hard‑coded constant and making the token address configurable – for example by passing the correct WETH address through the constructor or an administrator function – and then upgrading or redeploying the Comptroller so that grantCompInternal and claimComp interact with the proper ERC‑20 contract.
summary: The Comptroller contract uses a hardcoded address for the WETH contract which is not the correct one. Because of that, it will be impossible to claim COMP rewards. That results in a loss of funds so I rate it as HIGH.

title: `lending-market/Note.sol` Wrong implementation of access control
content: The vulnerability is an improper implementation of access control in the Note contract of the lending‑market system. The contract stores two privileged roles: an admin and an accountant, and it provides a function _mint_to_Accountant that is supposed to allow only the designated accountant to mint a token amount equal to the maximum uint value. The root cause is a logical error in the internal helper _setAccountantAddress: it only verifies that the caller is the admin when the accountant variable is already set (accountant != address(0)). When the contract is freshly deployed, accountant is initially zero, so the admin check is skipped. Consequently, the first call to _mint_to_Accountant triggers _setAccountantAddress, which sets accountant to msg.sender without any restriction. The subsequent require statement in _mint_to_Accountant then trivially succeeds because msg.sender has just been recorded as the accountant, allowing the caller to mint the full uint supply to themselves. An attacker can exploit this by front‑running the transaction that is intended to initialize the accountant, calling _mint_to_Accountant first, thereby seizing the accountant role and creating an effectively infinite token balance. The impact is that a malicious actor can arbitrarily inflate the token supply, diluting existing balances, breaking accounting assumptions, and potentially destabilizing the entire lending protocol. This condition occurs whenever the contract has not yet set an accountant, i.e., during its initialization phase, and any externally owned account can trigger the flaw. All users of the protocol, the token holders, and the protocol’s economic model are affected because the total supply can be corrupted. The issue was discovered during a formal security audit (Code4rena) when the auditors examined the control flow of the setter function and identified that the admin guard is never enforced on first use, and then demonstrated a front‑run scenario that allows privilege escalation. Because the bug resides in a simple conditional that appears innocuous, it can be hard to notice during casual review or testing, especially if the contract is already deployed with a proper accountant and the initialization path is not exercised. The flaw belongs to the broader class of access‑control bypass vulnerabilities caused by improper role initialization and missing validation checks. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are unexpected token balances appearing out of thin air, legitimate users seeing their holdings reduced or their refunds becoming zero, and the protocol’s UI showing a total supply that suddenly jumps to an astronomically large number. In conceptual terms the fix is to enforce the admin‑only restriction unconditionally when setting the accountant, to separate initialization from regular updates, and to ensure that the accountant role cannot be overwritten without explicit, authorized governance. Proper role assignment, a clear initialization step, and immutable access checks would restore the intended invariant that only the designated accountant can mint tokens.

title: In `ERC20`, `TotalSupply` is broken
content: The vulnerability concerns an accounting flaw in an ERC‑20 implementation where the contract’s total supply variable is not correctly initialized before token minting. The constructor accepts a parameter (often called _initialSupply) and additionally mints the same amount of tokens, but the internal _totalSupply counter is left at its default uninitialized value instead of being set to zero. As a result, the totalSupply() view returns a value that includes both the initial parameter and the minted amount, effectively double‑counting the supply. This happens whenever the contract is deployed with a non‑zero initial supply and later any minting operation is performed. The bug is discovered during a security audit (Code4rena) by inspecting the constructor logic and noticing that the totalSupply returned 1000 immediately after deployment with an initialSupply of 1000, and grew to 2000 after minting another 1000 tokens, which contradicts the expected accounting where totalSupply should match the exact number of tokens minted. Exploitation does not require a malicious attacker; the incorrect totalSupply value can be observed by any user or third‑party service that queries the token contract. Because many DeFi protocols, market‑cap calculators, price oracles and analytics dashboards rely on the totalSupply value to compute ratios, liquidity, or governance thresholds, the inflated number can lead to wrong market‑cap calculations, mis‑allocation of rewards, and faulty governance decisions. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that the token explorer or wallet UI displays a total supply that is higher than the amount of tokens circulating, and expectations that a 1000‑token deployment should show 1000 are violated – the UI may show 2000 after a single mint. The issue belongs to the class of "incorrect accounting" or "state initialization" bugs, where a storage variable is left in an undefined state and later updated in a way that does not reflect the intended invariant. It can be hard to notice because the contract still allows minting and transfers, and the discrepancy appears only in the totalSupply view, which may not be directly exercised in functional tests. The conceptual fix is to ensure that the totalSupply counter is initialized to zero in the constructor before any minting, or to eliminate the redundant initialSupply parameter and rely exclusively on the mint function to set the correct supply. By resetting the counter or removing the extra parameter, the totalSupply function will faithfully reflect the true amount of tokens minted, restoring correct accounting for downstream integrations.
summary: For an obscure reason as it’s not commented, `_totalSupply` is not initialized to 0, leading to an inaccurate total supply, which could easily break integrations, computations of market cap, etc.

title: It’s not possible to execute governance proposals through the `GovernorBravoDelegate` contract
content: The vulnerability consists of an incorrect handling of the proposal lifecycle flag within the GovernorBravoDelegate contract. When a governance proposal is queued, the contract erroneously sets the internal `executed` flag to true. This flag is intended to indicate that a proposal has already been carried out, and it should remain false until the `execute()` function successfully runs the queued actions. Because the flag is true prematurely, the `state()` function reports the proposal as Executed rather than Queued, causing the `execute()` routine to reject the proposal as if it had already been processed. The root cause is a misplaced assignment in the queueing logic that violates the expected state transition model for governance proposals. An attacker or any user attempting to trigger execution will find that no proposal can ever reach the execution phase; the contract will consistently reject calls with a state mismatch. Consequently, the governance mechanism becomes unusable, and any assets deposited for use by proposals – such as funds earmarked for distribution, upgrades, or parameter changes – may become permanently inaccessible, effectively locking them in the contract. This condition manifests whenever a proposal is moved from the pending to the queued stage, which is a routine operation in normal protocol governance. The issue was uncovered during a security audit by Code4rena, where the auditors compared the implementation against the reference Compound GovernorBravo contract and observed that the `executed` flag was set to true at the wrong point in the lifecycle. It is subtle because the flag change occurs early, and the contract does not emit a distinctive error unless an execution attempt is made, making it easy to miss during functional testing. To remediate the problem, the assignment that sets `executed` to true during queueing must be removed so that the flag remains false until the proposal is truly executed; this aligns the contract with the standard governance state machine and restores the ability to carry out proposals, preventing fund lock‑up and reinstating the protocol’s intended governance functionality.
summary:
It’s not possible to execute a proposal through the GovernorBravoDelegate contract because the `executed` property of it is set to `true` when it’s queued up.

Since this means that the governance contract is unusable, it might result in locked-up funds if those were transferred to the contract before the issue comes up. Because of that I’d rate it as HIGH.

title: `WETH.allowance`
content: The vulnerability resides in the public view function that reports token allowances in the Wrapped Ether (WETH) contract. Instead of returning the value stored in the internal allowance mapping, the function omits the return statement and therefore always yields the default value of zero. This developer oversight causes the contract to misreport the amount that an owner has approved for a spender, regardless of any prior successful calls to the approve method. The root cause is a missing return keyword that prevents the stored _allowance[owner][spender] value from being emitted to the caller. As a result, any external contract or user querying the allowance will observe a zero balance, even though the approval may have been recorded on-chain. This discrepancy can be exploited to cause a denial‑of‑service condition: downstream protocols that rely on a non‑zero allowance to execute transferFrom operations will fail, leading to reverted transactions, stuck funds, or unexpected loss of functionality. Users expecting that their approved spending limits are respected will instead see their allowances reported as zero, experience failed token transfers, and may interpret the behavior as a contract bug or a malicious restriction. The issue manifests whenever the allowance view is called – which is a standard step in ERC‑20 interactions – and therefore affects all token holders, DeFi applications, and any smart contract that depends on WETH's allowance semantics. The problem was uncovered during a formal security audit by Code4rena, where static analysis highlighted the missing return line. Because the bug does not trigger an error or revert, it can remain unnoticed unless tests explicitly compare expected allowance values against the contract’s response. The underlying business logic of ERC‑20 token accounting, which assumes that allowance reflects the approved amount, is violated, breaking trust and potentially causing financial loss. The recommended remediation is to modify the function to return the value stored in the allowance mapping, i.e., `return _allowance[owner][spender];`. Restoring the correct return behavior realigns the contract with ERC‑20 specifications and prevents the zero‑allowance illusion that currently undermines user expectations and protocol integrations.
summary:
WETH.allowance() returns wrong result.  
I can’t find other contracts that use this function but WETH.sol is a base contract and it should be fixed properly.

title: Fixed term loans can be deployed with a wrong fee manager and possibly steal all funds.
content: In Maple Finance the loan initialization contract accepts an arbitrary address for the fee manager when deploying a fixed‑term loan. The code does not verify that the supplied fee manager belongs to the set of trusted managers maintained by the global configuration. Because the fee manager is not whitelisted, an attacker can submit a transaction that mirrors a legitimate loan creation request – using the same borrower, delegate, principal amount and other parameters – but replaces the fee manager address with one that the attacker controls. The attacker can also choose a deployment salt that makes the first bytes of the malicious loan contract match those of the genuine loan contract, making the contract appear identical to the pool delegate. When the delegate later funds the loan, it reads the loan address from the initializer output and transfers the principal to that address, which now points to the attacker‑controlled contract. The result is that the full loan amount is transferred to the attacker, leaving the borrower with no funds and the protocol with a missing balance. This vulnerability is a classic instance of missing whitelist validation or unauthorized address injection, where a critical external dependency is not constrained. It can be exploited whenever a borrower and delegate agree on loan terms and the delegate relies on the initializer’s output without performing an additional check on the fee manager. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the MapleLoanInitializer source, where the absence of an isInstanceOf check against MapleGlobals was noted. Because the loan creation flow appears normal and the contract bytecode may look identical, the problem can be hard to notice until funds are unexpectedly missing. The fix is to enforce that the fee manager address is an instance of the registered FeeManager contract, typically by adding a whitelist or isInstanceOf verification in the global configuration before the loan contract is deployed. By ensuring only approved fee manager contracts can be used, the protocol restores its accounting guarantees and prevents the malicious redirection of loan principal.

title: Pool Delegates can set a really high origination fee and steal all pool funds.
content: The vulnerability is an unchecked origination fee that can be set to an arbitrarily high value by a pool delegate at any time, combined with the fact that any address is allowed to deploy a loan against the pool. The root cause is the absence of access‑control checks and upper‑bound validation on the fee‑setting function, as well as missing restrictions on who may create a loan. An attacker who controls the delegate role can first accumulate legitimate deposits in the pool using the normal, low‑fee configuration. Once the pool holds a sufficient balance, the attacker calls the fee‑update routine and raises the origination fee to the pool’s total amount minus the platform‑level fee (which may be zero when the loan is created with a single payment interval and a single payment). Because loan creation is open to anyone, the attacker then initiates a loan, causing the contract to transfer the entire loan principal to the delegate as an origination fee. This drains the pool, leaving lenders with no remaining balance and borrowers receiving a loan that is immediately siphoned away. The impact is a total loss of pooled capital, erosion of user trust, and potential legal exposure for the protocol. The exploit can be triggered whenever a delegate has the ability to modify the fee and the pool contains enough funds; it does not require any special permissions beyond the delegate role. The affected parties include pool delegates, lenders who deposited funds, borrowers who expect to receive a loan, and the overall protocol governance. The issue was discovered during a systematic security audit by ThreeSigma, where the logical flaw of unrestricted fee manipulation was identified. It is hard to notice because the fee parameter is presented as a normal configurable value, and the UI may not highlight that the fee can be set to 100 % of the pool balance; users typically expect a modest fee and therefore may not scrutinize large fee changes. The bug belongs to the class of economic vulnerabilities caused by improper access control and missing parameter bounds, often referred to as fee‑manipulation or unchecked parameter bugs. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are striking: after a loan is created the pool balance drops to zero, the user receives no repayment, and the displayed origination fee appears unusually high or simply disappears from the UI. To remediate the issue the contract should enforce a maximum origination fee, restrict fee changes to a governance‑approved process, add a timelock or minimum withdrawal period before a fee can be altered, and require explicit permission for loan deployment rather than allowing any address to create a loan. These measures restore the intended economic guarantees and prevent a delegate from stealing the entire pool.
summary:
The delegate origination fee can be set to any value at any time and anyone can deploy a loan, so the delegate can receive all the funds of a loan.
Exploit scenario
• gather funds to a pool with a regular origination fee
• given enough funds, increase the origination fee to the pool amount minus the platformOriginationFee (which can be close to zero if the delegate creates the loan with 1 payment interval and 1 number of payments)
• create a fake loan (anyone can deploy a loan) and fund it

title: Pool Delegates can steal all the pool's funds by setting a malicious Withdrawal Manager.
content: The vulnerability is an unchecked ability for the pool manager role to replace the contract that governs token withdrawals, known as the withdrawal manager, through the setWithdrawalManager() function. Because the function lacks any access control, validation, or timelock, a pool delegate who already possesses the pool manager permission can point the pool to a malicious withdrawal manager contract that it controls. The root cause is the absence of safeguards that ensure only a trusted entity can modify the component responsible for holding redeemable tokens and informing the pool about which tokens are eligible for redemption. An attacker can exploit this by first depositing a minimal amount of token to obtain a single share in the pool, then calling setWithdrawalManager() to install a crafted contract that reports the entire pool balance as redeemable for that single share. When the attacker subsequently calls the redeem function, the malicious withdrawal manager authorizes the transfer of the full pool balance to the attacker, effectively stealing all funds. The impact is a total loss of assets for all other pool participants, as their balances become zero while the attacker walks away with the entire pool. This scenario occurs whenever the pool manager role is granted to an entity that can invoke setWithdrawalManager() without restriction, which is typical in many decentralized finance pools where the manager is a delegate address. The affected parties include ordinary users who deposit into the pool, the protocol that relies on the pool’s integrity, and any downstream contracts that assume correct accounting of pool shares. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the governance and upgrade paths of the pool contracts; the function appeared benign and therefore did not raise immediate red flags, making the flaw hard to notice in routine testing. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after a normal redemption they receive far more tokens than expected, while other users see their balances disappear. The bug belongs to the class of “unrestricted contract upgrade/manager replacement” vulnerabilities, where critical logic can be swapped without verification, breaking accounting assumptions and allowing arbitrary fund extraction. To remediate, the setWithdrawalManager() function should be removed entirely, or at minimum be protected by a robust access control mechanism, a multi‑signature governance process, or a timelocked pause that prevents immediate malicious swaps. Additionally, any future design should enforce that the withdrawal manager contract is immutable or only upgradable through a vetted governance procedure, thereby preserving the invariant that a share can only redeem a proportional portion of the pool’s assets.
summary:
The current PoolManager contract allows the pool manager to change the withdrawalManager contract without any checks using the setWithdrawalManager() function. Since the withdrawal manager is responsible for holding the redeemable tokens and informing the pool which tokens can be redeemed, corrupting this contract gives complete control of the pool's funds to the pool delegate.
Exploit scenario
• Pool delegate deposits one token into the Pool to get a single share
• Pool delegate sets a malicious withdrawal manager, allowing them to redeem a single share for the entire pool balance
• Pool delegate redeems their share and receives all the funds in the pool

title: MJR-1 Possible withdraw unavailiability
content: The vulnerability is an accounting error in the vault contract that manages token deposits and withdrawals. When a user initiates a withdrawal, the contract transfers the requested tokens but fails to update the internal vault state that records the total amount of tokens held. Because the stored balance is not decremented, the contract believes more tokens are still available than actually are. Subsequent withdrawal attempts therefore request an amount that exceeds the real token balance, causing the transaction to revert. This situation can occur after any successful withdrawal and persists until the state is corrected, meaning users may see a positive balance in the UI but are unable to retrieve their funds. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract’s external token transfers with its internal accounting variables and noticed the mismatch. It is hard to notice because the contract does not emit explicit error messages about insufficient vault liquidity; instead, the generic revert hides the underlying accounting flaw. The impact is that legitimate users cannot withdraw their assets, effectively locking funds and breaking the expected deposit‑withdraw lifecycle. The bug belongs to the class of state‑management or accounting bugs where internal bookkeeping does not reflect external token movements. To fix the problem, the withdraw function must correctly decrement the vault’s stored balance (or otherwise reconcile the internal accounting) after each successful transfer, ensuring that future withdrawal calculations are based on the actual remaining token pool. Proper checks should be added to prevent withdrawals that would exceed the real token balance, and comprehensive tests should verify that the internal state matches the external token balances after every deposit and withdrawal operation.
summary: The amount of transferred out tokens are not accounted at the vault state while processing user withdrawals. This will cause attempt to withdraw incorrect (too large) amount and probable almost any withdrawals attempts will be reverted.

title: H-1 Calls via .call() to internal functions _deleteProposal,
content: The vulnerability originates from a mismatch between function visibility and the way those functions are invoked during DAO proposal execution. Several functions that implement critical governance actions – such as deleting a proposal – are declared as internal, meaning they can only be called from within the same contract context. However, the proposal creation logic builds calldata that encodes calls to these internal functions and later executes the calldata using a low‑level .call() operation. Because .call() performs an external call, the EVM expects the target function to be externally visible. When the call reaches an internal function, the call fails and returns false, often without reverting the transaction. This failure prevents the intended state changes, such as removing a proposal or updating grant parameters, from occurring. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the DAO’s implant contract, where the auditor observed that the encoded function selectors corresponded to internal functions and that the surrounding code did not check the success flag of the .call(). The bug is subtle because a failed .call() does not automatically throw an exception; if the return value is ignored, the contract appears to execute normally while silently skipping the critical logic. From a user’s perspective, a proposal that should delete a stale entry or adjust a grant simply does nothing – the UI may show the proposal as executed, but the underlying data remains unchanged, leading to confusion such as “my proposal was accepted but the proposal still exists” or “funds that should be reclaimed stay locked”. The impact is high: governance participants cannot rely on the DAO’s veto or grant mechanisms, proposals may become permanently stuck, and funds associated with those proposals may remain inaccessible, undermining the protocol’s economic security. The vulnerability belongs to the class of visibility‑mismatch or improper low‑level call usage bugs, where internal functions are mistakenly targeted by external call mechanisms. To remediate the issue, the affected functions should be changed to external visibility and protected with a modifier that restricts calls to the same implant contract (for example, an onlyThis modifier). This ensures that the low‑level .call() can successfully reach the function while preserving access control, and the contract should also verify the boolean result of .call() and revert on failure to avoid silent skips.
summary: There is an issue at the lines: daoVetoGrantImplant.sol#L195, daoVetoGrantImplant.sol#L375, daoVetoGrantImplant.sol#L391, daoVetoGrantImplant.sol#L433. These functions are declared internal, but during the creation of proposals, calldata is created which encodes calls to the mentioned functions. During proposal execution, .call() is performed to invoke functions execution. Such calls will fail.

title: H-2 Proposal duration is not set
content: The vulnerability is a governance timing flaw where the proposal duration field is never initialized when a new proposal is created. The contract’s execution logic checks that the current block timestamp is greater than or equal to the proposal start time plus the stored duration before allowing execution. Because the duration remains at its default value of zero, the condition is satisfied immediately after the proposal is recorded, so any proposal can be executed in the same transaction that creates it. This happens because the constructor or initialization routine that populates the proposal struct only assigns the identifier, the start timestamp, and the calldata, but omits the assignment of the intended voting or waiting period. An attacker or any user can therefore submit a malicious proposal and trigger its effects without giving token holders a chance to vote or react, effectively bypassing the DAO’s intended governance delay. The impact is that funds or state changes that should be subject to community approval can be moved instantly, undermining the security model of the DAO and exposing token holders to unauthorized asset transfers. The issue manifests whenever a proposal is created; there is no conditional path that restores a proper duration later, so every proposal is vulnerable from inception. All participants in the DAO, including token holders, proposal submitters, and any external contracts that rely on the proposal outcome, are affected because the governance process no longer enforces its promised time‑bound decision window. The flaw was discovered during a manual code audit that examined the proposal lifecycle and noticed that the duration variable was never set, leading to the immediate pass of the time check. It can be hard to notice in practice because the UI may simply show a proposal appearing and being executed in rapid succession, which could be interpreted as normal fast processing rather than a security breach. To remediate, the contract should assign a non‑zero duration at proposal creation, validate that the duration meets a minimum expected value, and ensure that the execution guard correctly references this field so that proposals cannot be executed until the prescribed waiting period has elapsed. This correction restores the intended governance delay and prevents instant, unauthorized execution of proposals.
summary: There is an issue at the lines: daoVetoGrantImplant.sol#L236, daoVetoGrantImplant.sol#L288, and daoVetoGrantImplant.sol#L346. New proposals are created and initialized with the id, start time, and calldata. But the proposal duration is not set, which will lead to the passing check at line daoVetoGrantImplant.sol#L174. All created proposals can be executed instantly without waiting for duration time.

title: H-3 DoS of cooldown
content: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service (DoS) condition affecting the cooldown mechanism of a BORG_SAFE multisignature wallet. A public function named checkTransaction is intended to act as a guard that validates transaction parameters and updates the timestamp of the last successful execution. Because the function is declared public, any external account can invoke it directly. When called, the function unconditionally resets the stored last‑execution timestamp, which is later used by the contract’s cooldown logic to determine whether a new transaction may be processed. The root cause is the lack of access control on a state‑changing function that should only be callable by the BORG_SAFE core contract. An attacker can exploit this by calling checkTransaction immediately before a legitimate proposal is executed, thereby resetting the timestamp and causing the cooldown check to fail. The legitimate transaction then reverts, and the multisig becomes effectively frozen because subsequent proposals will also fail the cooldown test until the attacker stops interfering. This situation occurs whenever a user attempts to submit a valid transaction while the attacker continuously front‑runs the guard function, which can be done repeatedly because the function is open to anyone. All participants of the multisig – owners, signers, and any downstream contracts that rely on the wallet – are affected because they lose the ability to execute approved actions and may see funds become inaccessible. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s access control and transaction flow, where the auditor noted that the guard function lacked any restriction and that it directly manipulates the cooldown timestamp. The problem can be hard to notice because the function does not emit obvious events and the failure manifests as a generic “cooldown not satisfied” revert, which may be misinterpreted as a business‑logic error rather than an external interference. To remediate the issue, the checkTransaction function should be restricted so that only the BORG_SAFE core contract can invoke it, typically by adding an onlyOwner or internal modifier, or by making the function internal and calling it from within the authorized execution path. This change restores the intended invariant that only legitimate transaction processing updates the cooldown timer, preventing arbitrary actors from resetting it and eliminating the DoS vector. The bug belongs to the class of unauthorized state‑change vulnerabilities where public functions modify critical protocol parameters without proper access control, leading to denial of service and loss of functionality.
summary:
The checkTransaction function serves as a guard for the BORG_SAFE multisig and checks the call's parameters for it. Currently, this function is publicly accessible, making it possible for any actor to call it. The function resets the last execution timestamp, which affects the cooldown check. Therefore, any actor can front-run any BORG SAFE transaction, causing it to fail and blocking the BORG SAFE:  
• borgCore.sol#L153  
• borgCore.sol#L166.

title: H-4 Reentrancy in optimisticGrantImplant
content: The vulnerability is a classic re‑entrancy flaw that occurs in the function responsible for creating a direct grant. The function initiates an external call to transfer Ether or an ERC‑20 token before it updates the internal accounting that tracks how much of the approved grant has been spent. Because the state change (the reduction of the remaining grant amount) is performed after the external call, a malicious contract that controls the recipient address can re‑enter the grant‑creation function during the transfer callback. By re‑entering, the attacker can trigger the same external transfer again while the contract still believes the grant has not been exhausted, allowing the attacker to drain a much larger portion of the allocated funds than the optimistic grant limits permit. This breaks the business rule that a grant may only spend up to a predefined amount, effectively bypassing the accounting checks. The issue is discovered during a manual security audit that examined the order of operations and identified that the check‑effect‑interaction pattern was not followed. It can be hard to notice because the external call appears legitimate and the contract does not revert on the first transfer, giving the impression that the grant logic works correctly. From a user’s perspective, a grant that should transfer a modest amount may instead result in the recipient receiving far more Ether or tokens, or the grant balance appearing to be unchanged while the protocol’s total funds shrink unexpectedly. The impact is high: funds can be siphoned from the protocol, grant limits become meaningless, and the overall trust in the optimistic grant mechanism is compromised. The flaw manifests whenever a grant is created and the recipient is a contract capable of executing code on receipt of funds. Any owner of a BORG_SAFE contract that can act as a malicious recipient can exploit this path. To remediate, the function should be rewritten to follow the check‑effect‑interaction pattern: first verify that the grant has sufficient remaining amount, then update the spent amount, and finally perform the external transfer. Adding a nonReentrant modifier or using a pull‑payment model would also prevent the re‑entrancy window. In summary, the bug is a re‑entrancy class vulnerability caused by updating critical accounting state after an external call, leading to potential over‑payment, loss of funds, and violation of the protocol’s accounting guarantees.
summary: The createDirectGrant function makes external calls (ETH or ERC20 transfer) before updating the approvedToken.amountSpent, which allows malicious owners of BORG_SAFE to transfer a much larger part of the funds and break the logic of the optimistic grant restrictions. optimisticGrantImplant.sol#L128

title: H-5 Incorrect function signature in
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect function signature used when encoding a call to executeAdvancedGrant via abi.encodeWithSignature in the proposeAdvancedGrant functions of two implant contracts. The code supplies a short, mismatched signature string instead of the full canonical signature that includes all nested tuple types. Because the selector is derived from the supplied string, the resulting selector embedded in the proposalBytecode does not match the actual selector of executeAdvancedGrant. When the DAO later attempts to execute the advanced grant proposal, the call is routed to a non‑existent function selector, causing the call to fail or be silently ignored. This makes any advanced grant proposal impossible to execute, effectively locking the funds allocated to the proposal and breaking the intended governance flow. The issue occurs whenever a user creates an advanced grant proposal through daoVoteGrantImplant.proposeAdvancedGrant or daoVetoGrantImplant.proposeAdvancedGrant, which both rely on the faulty encoding. Affected parties include DAO participants, grant recipients, and any protocol component that depends on successful execution of advanced grants. The bug was discovered during a manual security audit that inspected the encoding logic and compared the expected function selector with the one actually generated. It is hard to notice because the Solidity compiler does not validate the string passed to abi.encodeWithSignature, and the proposal transaction itself appears successful, masking the underlying selector mismatch. The impact is a denial‑of‑service on the advanced grant mechanism, leading to funds that cannot be released and a breach of the protocol’s accounting assumptions that a granted amount will be transferred after a successful vote. To remediate, the encodeWithSignature call must be updated to use the exact canonical signature of executeAdvancedGrant, including the full nested tuple definition, so that the correct selector is embedded and the execution path works as intended. This class of bug is a function selector mismatch caused by an inaccurate ABI encoding string, which violates the contract’s business logic that proposals should be executable after voting.
summary: An incorrect function signature executeAdvancedGrant(MetaVesT.MetaVesTDetails) is used for abi.encodeWithSignature() in daoVoteGrantImplant.proposeAdvancedGrant() and daoVetoGrantImplant.proposeAdvancedGrant(). The selector in the proposalBytecode will be calculated incorrectly, and the future call to executeAdvancedGrant() will be impossible. daoVoteGrantImplant.sol#L234, daoVetoGrantImplant.sol#L344

title: H-6 Incorrect loop boundary inside removeContract
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect loop boundary in the function that removes a contract’s policy entries. The code iterates over the array of method signatures using the current length of the array as the upper bound, but inside the loop it calls a helper that deletes an element from the same array, thereby shrinking the array while it is being traversed. Because the loop condition is evaluated against the decreasing length, some indices are never visited and the corresponding method selectors are not removed. This classic “modify‑while‑iterate” bug means that after a contract is supposedly deregistered, a subset of its previously authorized function selectors remain in the policy mapping. An attacker who knows those selectors can still invoke the protected functions, bypassing the intended revocation and potentially stealing funds or manipulating protocol state. The issue manifests only when the removal routine is executed; if the contract never calls the removal path, the bug is dormant. It affects any user or role that relies on the policy enforcement to block calls from a removed contract, including token holders, liquidity providers, and governance participants. The problem was discovered during a manual security audit by MixBytes, who noticed that the loop uses policy[_contract].methodSignatures.length while the helper _removePolicyMethodSelector shortens that array. The bug is subtle because the transaction does not revert and no explicit error is emitted; the loop simply finishes early, leaving the system in an inconsistent state that is hard to detect without deep inspection of the policy data after removal. To fix the issue, the removal logic should not alter the array length while iterating. Common remedies are to cache the original length before the loop, iterate backwards, or move the deletion to a separate pass after the iteration completes, ensuring that every method selector is processed and fully cleared. This correction restores the intended security guarantee that removing a contract revokes all of its method permissions, preventing unauthorized calls and protecting user assets.
summary: There is an issue at borgCore.sol#L269. policy[_contract].methodSignatures.length is used as a loop boundary, but the length of the policy[_contract].methodSignatures is reduced inside the _removePolicyMethodSelector function. It leads to the missing loop iterations, which means that not all methodSelector is removed.

title: H-7 Always failing check inside the checkCondition for
content: The vulnerability is a time‑based validation error in the contract’s price‑oracle condition function. The code retrieves the updatedAt timestamp from Chainlink’s latestRoundData call, which records the moment the price was last reported, and then compares it directly with block.timestamp, expecting the current block time to be less than or equal to the oracle timestamp. Because block.timestamp always advances and is always greater than a past oracle timestamp, the condition evaluates to false on every invocation, causing the function to revert. This bug originates from a misunderstanding of the semantics of the oracle’s timestamp field; the developer treated it as a future or current marker rather than a historical one. An attacker does not gain direct financial advantage, but can trigger a denial‑of‑service by repeatedly invoking the affected function, causing legitimate users’ transactions to fail and potentially freezing a critical workflow such as price‑dependent trades or settlements. The impact is that users see transaction reverts, error messages in the UI, and expected actions (e.g., trade execution, fund release) do not occur, leaving balances unchanged and creating confusion about missing refunds or failed operations. The condition fails under any normal network conditions because the comparison logic is inherently flawed; it does not depend on specific inputs or edge cases. All participants who rely on the price check—traders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself—are affected because the contract cannot progress past the stale‑data guard. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the oracle integration and identified the misuse of the updatedAt field. It can be hard to notice in unit tests that mock timestamps to match the oracle value, masking the problem until deployment on a live chain where real block timestamps diverge. The appropriate remediation is to replace the direct equality/inequality check with a duration‑based validation, such as requiring that block.timestamp minus updatedAt be less than or equal to an acceptable freshness window. This aligns the contract’s expectations with the reality that oracle data is always slightly stale and restores correct business logic, allowing the function to succeed when the price data is recent enough. The bug belongs to the class of stale‑data or improper timestamp comparison vulnerabilities, which violate accounting assumptions that price information must be current at the moment of execution.
summary: There is an issue at chainlinkOracleCondition.sol#L59. updatedAt value fetched from the Chainlink latestRoundData() is the time in the past when the price was reported. block.timestamp would always be bigger than that value, which will lead to condition revert.

title: H-1 Possible Reverts Due to Underflow in Case if vestingRate or unlockRate was
content: The vulnerability is an arithmetic underflow/revert condition that arises when the contract’s vestingRate or unlockRate is reduced after some options have already been exercised or some tokens have been withdrawn. The contract calculates the amount of tokens that are vested or unlocked by multiplying the total allocation by the current rate. When the rate is lowered, the recalculated vested or unlocked amount can become smaller than the amount already exercised, withdrawn or claimed. Subsequent functions such as getAmountWithdrawable, getUnlockedTokenAmount and terminate subtract the already exercised or withdrawn amount from the newly calculated amount. If the subtraction results in a negative value, the Solidity compiler (or explicit require) triggers a revert due to underflow. This can also appear in the RestrictedTokenAllocation contract in a similar function. The bug is triggered only when a rate reduction occurs after partial exercise, which makes it easy to miss in static tests that assume rates are monotonic. From a user’s perspective the contract appears to lock their tokens: a withdrawal transaction reverts, no tokens are transferred, and the user sees an error or a zero balance change despite having a vested entitlement. The impact is a denial‑of‑service style failure that prevents token holders from claiming their vested or unlocked tokens, effectively freezing funds. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the arithmetic of vesting and unlock calculations. It is hard to notice because the revert only happens under specific state transitions involving rate changes, which are not exercised in typical unit tests. The proper mitigation is to forbid decreasing vestingRate or unlockRate after deployment, or to add explicit checks that the new rate never makes the recalculated vested or unlocked amount smaller than any already exercised, withdrawn or claimed amount. Using safe‑math checks or redesigning the accounting to store cumulative vested amounts independent of mutable rates also resolves the problem. In short, the bug is a classic underflow caused by mutable rate parameters that break accounting assumptions, leading to unexpected reverts and locked funds.
summary: The issue was identified within the TokenOptionAllocation.sol#L180 of the TokenOptionAllocation contract. If vestingRate is reduced, the calculated _tokensVested may lead to a revert at TokenOptionAllocation.sol#L193 as there could be more tokensExercised than the recalculated vested amount. Another issue was identified within the same TokenOptionAllocation contract. If unlockRate is reduced, then a call to the TokenOptionAllocation.sol#L213 function will return a smaller value, which may be less than tokensExercised and tokensWithdrawn, leading to an underflow during subtraction. This issue is classified as High severity because it will lead to unexpected reverts in the getAmountWithdrawable(), getUnlockedTokenAmount(), and terminate() functions. A similar issue is also present in the RestrictedTokenAllocation.sol#L230 function of the RestrictedTokenAllocation contract. The only way to resolve the issue is by increasing both the vestingRate and the unlockRate.

title: H-2 Voting Logic Issue: Lack of Handling for Amendments without Reached Quorum
content: The vulnerability is a governance lockout caused by missing quorum handling in the amendment voting process. When an amendment is opened, the contract expects a quorum of votes to be reached before the end of a one‑week voting window. The code does not define any fallback when the quorum is never met; after the deadline the amendment state is marked as 'locked' and the associated set cannot be modified. As a result, any subsequent actions that rely on that set – adding or removing grants, deleting the set, or proposing a new amendment – are rejected. This can be triggered simply by allowing a vote to expire without sufficient participation, which may happen naturally if token holders are inactive or deliberately if an attacker withholds votes. The impact is a permanent governance gridlock for the affected set, effectively freezing the protocol’s ability to allocate or reallocate funds, update parameters, or execute future proposals. The condition occurs whenever the voting period exceeds the allowed one‑week timeframe and the quorum threshold is not satisfied. All participants who rely on the set – token holders, grant recipients, and the protocol itself – are affected because expected actions never happen; users may see that their proposals are rejected with no error message, or that the UI shows the set as immutable. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the MetaVesTController contract, where the absence of a quorum‑failure branch was noted. It is subtle because the contract does not revert or emit an explicit error; it merely changes an internal flag, making the lockout appear as a normal state transition rather than a bug. The correct mitigation is to add logic that automatically cancels or removes amendments that fail to reach quorum after the voting deadline, resetting the set to an active state and allowing new proposals. In broader terms, this is a classic case of missing fallback handling for unmet quorum in a time‑bounded voting mechanism, leading to a denial‑of‑service style failure of the governance layer.
summary: This issue has been identified in the voteOnMetaVesTAmendment function of the MetaVesTController.sol#L598-L618 contract. Currently, if the voting period for an amendment extends beyond the allowed one-week timeframe without reaching the required quorum, the associated set becomes locked. This situation prevents any further changes, such as adding or removing grants, deleting the set, or proposing a new amendment, effectively blocking future governance actions for that set. The issue is classified as High severity because it can lead to governance gridlock and prevent the proper functioning of the contract's voting mechanism, causing potential disruptions in decision-making.

title: H-3 Missing Call to _resetAmendmentParams in setMetaVesTGovVariables
content: The vulnerability consists of a missing internal cleanup call in the governance controller contract. Specifically, the function that updates the core governing variables does not invoke the private routine that clears any previously stored amendment parameters. The root cause is an oversight in the implementation of the variable‑setting function, which fails to reset the amendment state after a prior amendment has been processed. Because the stale amendment data remains in storage, subsequent attempts to create or process a new amendment are rejected by the contract’s internal checks that expect a clean state. An attacker or even a legitimate governance participant can trigger the issue simply by invoking the variable‑update function after a prior amendment has been made; the contract will then refuse new amendments, effectively causing a governance dead‑lock. The impact is that the protocol’s ability to adjust critical parameters – such as fee rates, timelocks, or quorum thresholds – can be halted, preventing the community from responding to market conditions or security incidents. This condition occurs whenever setMetaVesTGovVariables is called following any amendment that altered the governing variables, and it affects all roles that rely on the amendment mechanism, including token holders, proposal creators, and the protocol’s admin. The flaw was discovered during a systematic security audit that examined the flow of amendment handling and identified that the expected reset routine was never called. The problem can be hard to notice because the function appears to succeed and emits the usual events, while the UI may still show the old parameters as unchanged, leading users to assume the transaction failed for unrelated reasons. To remediate the issue, the contract should be updated to include a call to the internal reset routine at the end of the variable‑setting function, ensuring that any residual amendment data is cleared before new proposals are accepted. This type of bug belongs to the class of state‑management errors where leftover mutable state prevents correct operation of a protocol component, analogous to missing cleanup in configuration‑update functions. From a user perspective, the symptoms include proposals being rejected without clear error messages, governance dashboards showing no pending amendments despite recent activity, and expectations that a parameter change will take effect being contradicted by the unchanged on‑chain values. The failure violates the fundamental accounting assumption that each amendment starts from a clean slate, breaking the protocol’s governance logic and potentially leading to a situation where critical updates cannot be performed until the contract is patched or redeployed.
summary:
This issue has been identified in the setMetaVesTGovVariables function of the MetaVesTController.sol#L507-L509 contract.
The function does not call _resetAmendmentParams, which could lead to a situation where amendments cannot be created or processed properly if a previous amendment to update the governing variables was made. This oversight may result in inconsistencies or hinder the inability to proceed with governance updates as intended.
The issue is classified as High severity because it affects the ability to manage and update governance parameters, potentially leading to governance gridlock or an inability to adjust critical parameters.

title: H-4 Incorrect Handling of tokensRepurchased in repurchaseTokens
content: The vulnerability is an accounting error in the token repurchase mechanism of the RestrictedTokenAllocation contract. The function that reports how many tokens can still be bought back, getAmountRepurchasable, calculates the remaining amount without subtracting the tokens that have already been repurchased, stored in the tokensRepurchased state variable. As a result, after the first successful repurchase the reported amount remains unchanged, giving a misleading impression that the full original pool is still available. This discrepancy can be exploited by calling repurchaseTokens repeatedly; each call sees the same inflated available amount and can therefore withdraw more tokens than the contract intended to allow. The impact is that token accounting becomes inconsistent, potentially inflating the total supply of repurchased tokens, breaking the protocol’s invariant that the sum of repurchased tokens never exceeds the allocated pool, and causing users to receive unexpected extra tokens or see balances that do not match the UI. The bug manifests only after at least one repurchase has occurred, because tokensRepurchased is initially zero. It affects any participant that interacts with the repurchase feature, including token holders, the protocol’s treasury, and downstream contracts that rely on accurate token accounting. The issue was uncovered during a professional security audit performed by MixBytes, which examined the logical flow of the repurchase functions and identified the missing variable in the calculation. The problem is subtle because the contract does not revert or emit an obvious error; the UI simply shows a number that appears plausible, making the over‑repurchase easy to miss in casual testing. To remediate the flaw, the getAmountRepurchasable function should be updated to incorporate tokensRepurchased (or an equivalent decrement) so that the returned value truly reflects the remaining pool, thereby restoring the intended accounting guarantees and preventing unintended token extraction.
summary:
This issue has been identified in the repurchaseTokens function of the RestrictedTokenAllocation.sol#L138-L153 contract.
The tokensRepurchased variable is not properly accounted for in the getAmountRepurchasable calculation. After the first repurchase, the getAmountRepurchasable function will display an incorrect amount because it does not consider the tokens that have already been repurchased. This can lead to a misleading view of the number of tokens available for repurchase and potentially allow attempts to repurchase more tokens than are actually available.
The issue is classified as High severity because it affects the accuracy of the token repurchase logic, leading to potential miscalculations and incorrect token handling.

title: H-5 Issues with MetaVesTs Having Different Decimals in the Same Set
content: The vulnerability consists of an arithmetic inconsistency that arises when MetaVesT tokens with different decimal precisions are grouped together in a single voting set. MetaVesTController calculates voting weight by scaling token balances according to the token's declared decimals. Because the calculation multiplies the raw balance by 10**decimals, a token that uses 18 decimals contributes a value that is orders of magnitude larger than a token that uses 6 decimals, even when the underlying economic value is identical. This mismatch gives MetaVesTs with higher decimals an exponential advantage in the voting process. The problem also propagates to auxiliary functions that adjust exercise or repurchase price, unlock rate, and vesting rate; these functions assume a uniform decimal base and therefore produce incorrect rates or revert when the set mixes decimals. An attacker can exploit the flaw by creating or acquiring a MetaVesT with a larger decimal setting, adding it to a governance set, and then casting votes that outweigh all other participants, potentially forcing proposals to pass or be blocked. The impact is a corrupted governance outcome, loss of trust in the protocol, and possible financial loss if decisions affect fund allocation. The condition occurs whenever the contract owner or a governance admin creates a set that includes MetaVesTs with heterogeneous decimal definitions; the bug is not obvious because the UI shows token symbols and balances correctly, but the voting power displayed may not reflect the real economic stake, leading users to see proposals pass unexpectedly or their votes appear ineffective. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit of the MetaVesTController logic, where the auditor observed that the weight calculation used a direct multiplication by 10**decimals without normalisation. The flaw is hard to notice because token balances are typically displayed in human‑readable format, masking the underlying scaling factor, and because the contract does not emit explicit warnings when mixing decimals. The correct mitigation is to enforce a single decimal precision for all MetaVesTs within a set, or to normalise all balances to a common base before computing voting weight and before applying price or rate updates. This change removes the exponential advantage and ensures that voting power is proportional to the true economic value of each MetaVesT. The bug belongs to the class of “inconsistent numeric scaling” or “decimal mismatch” vulnerabilities that affect token‑based governance systems.
summary:
If MetaVesTs with different decimals are included in the same set, metavests with higher decimals will have an exponential advantage over those with lower decimals MetaVesTController.sol#L583-L589, resulting in an incorrect voting process. Additionally, using updateExerciseOrRepurchasePrice(), updateMetavestUnlockRate(), and updateMetavestVestingRate() in the case of sets with different decimals may lead to errors.
This issue is classified as High, as the voting functionality works incorrectly in certain cases, and fixing it requires redeployment.

title: H-6 Exercised but Not Unlocked Tokens Will Be Sent to Authority During
content: The vulnerability resides in the token recovery routine of the TokenOptionAllocation contract. After a vesting schedule is terminated, the authority can invoke recoverForfeitTokens to pull back any tokens that remain in the contract. The implementation calculates the amount to recover by taking the entire token balance of the contract, without excluding tokens that have already been exercised by the grantee but are still locked. Because exercised tokens are considered withdrawable only after they become unlocked, they remain part of the contract balance until that moment. The function therefore mistakenly treats those exercised‑but‑still‑locked tokens as forfeitable and transfers them to the authority’s address. An attacker who controls the authority role can call recoverForfeitTokens after termination and cause the contract to send the exercised tokens back to the authority, even though the grantee has already paid for them. The impact is that the grantee loses the tokens they expected to receive after exercising their options, effectively paying for nothing, while the authority receives extra tokens that must later be compensated manually. This situation occurs only after a vesting termination and when the authority executes the recovery function; it does not affect tokens that are already withdrawable (unexercised or unlocked). The affected parties are the option grantee, who suffers a loss of value, and the protocol’s authority, which unintentionally acquires tokens it should not. The issue was identified during a formal security audit by MixBytes, and it can be subtle because the function name and purpose suggest it only reclaims forfeited tokens, making the inclusion of exercised tokens easy to overlook. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after exercising options the user’s balance remains zero and no tokens are received, contrary to the expectation that exercising yields tokens. The bug belongs to the class of accounting‑logic errors where the recovery calculation does not correctly filter out already‑exercised assets, violating the business rule that exercised tokens should only be transferred to the grantee once they are unlocked. The recommended fix is to compute the recoverable amount as the contract’s token balance minus the amount already exercised, ensuring that only truly forfeitable tokens are reclaimed.
summary:
If the authority calls TokenOptionAllocation.recoverForfeitTokens() for a given vesting after the termination, all tokens, except for those that are currently withdrawable, TokenOptionAllocation.sol#L174 to the authority's address. Withdrawable includes all unwithdrawn exercised and unlocked tokens. As a result, the authority will also receive tokens that have already been exercised by the grantee (the grantee has paid for them) but have not yet been unlocked.
This issue has a High severity level because the grantee will spend money but not receive the exercised tokens. The authority will then have to manually compensate the grantee for the tokens sent to the authority's address.

title: Lost nfts due to smart wallets having different addresses on different chains
content: The vulnerability originates from a design assumption that the address invoking a token transfer function (send()) is also the intended recipient of the NFT. In many multi‑chain deployments the caller may be a smart contract wallet whose address is not identical on every blockchain – for example a wallet that is deployed separately on Ethereum, Polygon, or other EVM‑compatible chains. Because the contract unconditionally forwards the NFT to msg.sender, the token is minted or moved to the caller’s address on the current chain, which may be an address that the user does not control on that chain. This mismatch can cause the NFT to be locked in an inaccessible account, effectively disappearing from the user’s portfolio. The issue is triggered whenever a user interacts with the contract through a smart‑contract wallet that has distinct addresses across chains, such as a wallet created by a factory contract or a wallet that uses different address‑generation schemes per chain. From the user’s perspective the transaction appears successful – the UI shows a “transfer completed” message – but the NFT balance shown in the wallet becomes zero or the NFT never appears in the expected account. The problem is subtle because the contract does not emit an explicit error and the blockchain records a valid transfer to the caller’s address, making it difficult to detect without manually checking the address mapping on each chain. The impact is loss of ownership of the NFT, which may represent significant monetary value, and it undermines the protocol’s accounting guarantees that each user’s assets remain under their control. The flaw was identified during a manual audit that examined the token‑transfer logic and recognized that the code does not account for cross‑chain address variance. To remediate the issue the contract should not rely on msg.sender as the destination; instead it should allow the caller to explicitly specify a destination address, or resolve the correct address through a trusted registry that maps a user’s universal identifier to the appropriate chain‑specific address. By decoupling the transfer destination from the caller, the contract ensures that NFTs are sent to an address the user actually controls, preserving asset integrity across all supported chains.
summary: send() sends the tokens to the same address that called the function. Some smart contract wallets may have different addresses on different chains (or even chains with different address generation).

title: feesAccrued or staker principal may be sent as rewards if rewardRate and emissionEnd are not properly calculated
content: The vulnerability is an over‑allocation of staking rewards that allows a participant to withdraw more tokens than are actually available in the contract, potentially taking fees that belong to other users or even part of another staker’s principal. The root cause is that the contract computes the total amount of rewards that can be distributed as the product of emissionEnd and rewardRate, but it never checks that this theoretical amount is bounded by the real token balance held by the staking contract. Because emissionEnd can be changed after deployment and rewardRate, although only set in the constructor, can be chosen arbitrarily, an attacker can arrange a situation where emissionEnd × rewardRate exceeds the number of basicToken units transferred to the contract. When a user calls the function that claims rewards or withdraws their stake, the contract simply transfers the recorded reward amount without verifying that the contract still holds enough tokens after accounting for the total staked amount and the feesAccrued field. Consequently the contract may send out feesAccrued as if they were rewards, or it may pull a portion of another staker’s principal, effectively draining the pool. This bug manifests when the token balance of the contract becomes lower than the calculated reward entitlement, which can happen after a large emission period is set, after the rewardRate is set too high, or after the contract receives fewer tokens than expected. All stakers are affected: a malicious participant can claim excess rewards, honest users may see their balances shrink unexpectedly, and the protocol loses trust because the accounting assumptions that rewards are always covered by the contract’s balance are violated. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the reward‑distribution logic and noticed the missing cap on claimable rewards. It is hard to notice in normal operation because the UI shows the accrued reward amount correctly, but the underlying token balance is not displayed, so the contract appears to work until a large withdrawal reveals the shortfall. To fix the problem the reward‑claiming function should be limited to the actual available token balance minus the sum of totalStaked and feesAccrued, ensuring that no more tokens can be transferred than the contract truly holds. A simpler design is to separate the unstake operation from reward claiming: unstake only reduces the staked amount, while rewards remain stored in a per‑user reward field that can be claimed later, and the claim function should decrement the stored reward by the amount actually withdrawn rather than deleting it entirely. This prevents feesAccrued from being mis‑treated as rewards and guarantees that the contract never distributes more tokens than it possesses, preserving user funds and protocol integrity.
summary: As emissionEnd and rewardRate can be freely set (although rewardRate only in the constructor), if emissionEnd x rewardRate is bigger than the amount of tokens sent to the staking contract, stakers may withdraw feesAccrued or other stakers' principal as rewards.

title: Participating in raffle with multiple tickets does not work
content: The vulnerability is a business‑logic flaw in the raffle redemption flow where a participant who holds more than one winning ticket is limited to claiming a single NFT. The contract records a boolean flag in a mapping keyed by the caller address (claimed[msg.sender]) and checks this flag before allowing the initialSale function to transfer the prize. Because the flag is not tied to individual ticket identifiers or to the specific tokenId being claimed, the verification step only proves that the caller is a winner, not how many winning tickets they own. Consequently, when a user who has secured multiple winning tickets attempts to redeem each ticket, the first successful call sets claimed[msg.sender] to true and the subsequent calls are rejected by the require statement, even though the user is entitled to multiple NFTs. This can be exploited simply by purchasing several tickets in the raffle; if the random draw assigns more than one winning slot to the same address, the user can only receive one NFT, effectively losing the value of the other winning tickets. The impact is a loss of expected assets for legitimate participants, a breach of the advertised “multiple tickets = multiple chances” promise, and potential reputational damage for the protocol. The condition occurs during the redemption phase after the Chainlink VRF has selected the winners, specifically when the initialSale function is called with a valid proof for a tokenId that the caller already claimed. All participants who buy multiple tickets are affected, as are the protocol operators who must honor the raffle rules. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the raffle’s intended mechanics with the actual contract logic, revealing that the claimed mapping does not reflect per‑ticket state. It is subtle because the contract correctly enforces a one‑claim‑per‑address rule, which may appear reasonable at first glance, masking the mismatch with the multi‑ticket design. To remediate, the contract should track claims per ticket or per tokenId—e.g., using a mapping from address to a counter of claimed tickets, or a mapping from tokenId to a claimed flag—so that each winning ticket can be redeemed independently. Alternatively, the Merkle proof could be extended to include a unique identifier for each ticket, and the claimed state should be recorded against that identifier rather than the address alone. This adjustment restores the intended economic outcome where each winning ticket yields a distinct NFT, aligning the smart contract behavior with the raffle’s advertised rules.

title: The total supply of NFTs might not be fully minted
content: The contract implements a two‑mode minting function for a fixed collection of 150 NFTs. One mode (batch) mints exactly ten tokens per call and is limited to ten batches, while the other mode (release) allows a variable quantity up to ten tokens per call and is limited by a counter that may only be incremented six times. The vulnerability arises because the release branch enforces a hard cap on the number of releases (totalReleases <= 5) without tying this limit to the overall supply, and because the batch branch checks the remaining amount against the batch‑specific supply (BATCH_SUPPLY) instead of the global TOTAL_SUPPLY. As a result, an attacker or any user can deliberately mint a small number of tokens through the release path, exhausting the release counter before the batch path is used. Once the release counter is exhausted, the batch logic may still reject further minting because totalMinted may already exceed BATCH_SUPPLY, even though the global total of 150 tokens has not been reached. Consequently up to fifty tokens can become permanently unmintable. From a user perspective this manifests as a transaction that reverts with “Exceeds total releases” or “All batches have been minted” despite the fact that the collection still has available token IDs, leading to confusion, missing expected NFTs, and reduced revenue for the protocol. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the logical constraints of each branch and identified the inconsistency between the release counter and the total supply check. It is hard to notice because each branch individually contains a supply guard, giving the impression that the total supply is always enforced. The proper fix is to remove the artificial release‑count limit and to make the batch branch validate against TOTAL_SUPPLY rather than BATCH_SUPPLY, allowing the existing totalMinted check to guarantee that no more than 150 NFTs can ever be minted while ensuring that all tokens remain reachable.

title: NFT ids do not correspond to their position in the nfts array
content: The vulnerability consists of a mismatch between the token identifier (NFT id) and the position at which the NFT struct is stored in the contract's internal array. When a token is minted the contract increments a counter and assigns the resulting value as the token id, starting at 1, while the array that holds the NFT data is zero‑based. Consequently the first token is stored at index 0 but is referenced by id 1. The problem is compounded for the breeding mechanism: a separate counter named length is initialized to 150 (the size of the pre‑minted 0th generation). When a new NFT is created by breeding, the contract assigns the current value of length as the token id and then increments length. Because breeding can occur before all 150 original tokens have been minted, the newly created NFT may be pushed into the array at an index lower than 150 while its id is greater than 150. All functions that later retrieve an NFT by treating the id as an array index therefore read the wrong element, read out‑of‑bounds data, or fail with a revert. This logical inconsistency breaks core protocol operations such as ownership lookup, transfer, breeding eligibility checks and any accounting that assumes a one‑to‑one mapping between id and storage slot. The root cause is the assumption that a sequential numeric identifier can be used directly as an array index without accounting for the zero‑based nature of Solidity arrays and for the asynchronous order in which NFTs are created. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the minting and breeding functions and traced the flow of the id variable to array accesses. Exploitation is straightforward: an attacker can invoke a function that expects id = index to retrieve a different NFT, manipulate its state, or cause a revert that halts the contract. For example, by calling transfer with a token id that actually resides at a different index, the contract may transfer ownership of an unintended NFT or fail, leaving the attacker able to lock assets. The impact includes loss of correct ownership information, inability to transfer or breed NFTs, and potential financial loss for users who cannot access their assets. The issue manifests whenever a token id is used to index the nfts array – i.e., during minting, breeding, transfer, and any view functions that rely on the mapping. All participants are affected: token owners experience missing or incorrect NFTs, the protocol cannot enforce its business rules, and the overall system integrity is compromised. Because the mismatch is subtle, the contract appears to work for the first 150 pre‑minted tokens, making the bug hard to notice until a bred token is created early. The symptom from a user’s perspective is that a newly minted or bred NFT either shows no metadata, appears as a different token, or the transaction reverts with an 'index out of bounds' error. The appropriate remediation is to replace the array with a mapping from token id to NFT struct, or to maintain a separate mapping that records the exact array index for each id. This eliminates the false assumption that id equals index and restores a reliable lookup mechanism. In generic terms the bug belongs to the class of identifier‑to‑storage mismatches, often referred to as off‑by‑one or indexing errors, which violate the accounting invariant that each token id uniquely identifies a single stored NFT.
summary: When a new NFT is minted it is assigned an id which is pushed in the nfts array. Afterward, NFTs are accessed in that array by id as if the id corresponds to the NFT index in the array.
