There are two problems with this logic. First, the array index starts at 0 and the first NFT id is 1, because the counter is first incremented and assigned as id to the newly minted NFT after that. Hence it would equal 1. The second issue is with the generation after the initial one. Basically, the protocol mints only the 0th generation which is 150 NFTs and every single one after is minted only by breeding. When a new NFT is born it is assigned an id from a new state variable counter called length, which is initially equal to 150. The problem here is that a NFT can be born before all NFTs from the 0th generation are minted. Hence it would be added to the array and be at an index below 150 but its id would be above 150. This discrepancy between NFT id in the contract and in the array index completely breaks all the protocol logic.

title: NFT marked as sold on initial sale can lead to losing funds
content: The vulnerability is a state‑tracking error in the marketplace’s handling of an NFT’s first sale. When a user purchases one of the initial Ghost NFTs, the contract executes the initialSale path but fails to set the nftSold flag for that token. Because the flag remains false, any subsequent sale or auction of the same token is mistakenly treated as another first‑sale transaction. The marketplace therefore routes the proceeds to the protocol‑controlled wallets instead of the current owner’s address. This occurs because the mapping update (nftSold[contract][tokenId] = true) is omitted in the initialSale function, a simple oversight that breaks the intended resale logic. An attacker or any seller can trigger the bug simply by listing the NFT for resale; the marketplace will call the resale branch, see the flag still false, and execute the initial‑sale payment flow, sending the buyer’s funds to the protocol rather than the seller. The impact is that legitimate sellers receive no payment, effectively losing the sale proceeds, while the protocol unintentionally accrues extra funds. Users who expect to receive payment after a resale see their balance unchanged or receive zero, creating confusion and loss of trust. The issue manifests only for NFTs that were part of the raffle‑based initial sale and were not correctly marked as sold; subsequent sales of other tokens behave correctly. It was discovered during a manual audit of the marketplace logic, where the auditor noticed that the nftSold flag was never written in the initialSale path. The bug is subtle because the surrounding code appears to handle first‑sale and resale correctly, and the missing line does not produce a compile‑time error. To remediate, the initialSale function must update the nftSold mapping to true for the specific NFT address and token ID immediately after processing the initial payment, ensuring that future sales follow the resale branch and transfer funds to the seller. This correction restores the intended accounting model where the protocol receives fees only on the first sale and sellers receive proceeds on all later transfers, aligning contract behavior with user expectations and business logic.

title: Users can place bets on canceled auctions
content: The vulnerability consists of a logical flaw in the auction lifecycle that permits users to place bids on auctions that have already been cancelled. The protocol allows a seller to call cancelAuction before the auction starts, which only changes the auction status to CANCELLED and transfers the NFT back to the seller, but it does not remove the auction record or prevent later functions from interacting with it. Because the bidPlace and resultAuction functions do not verify that the auction status is still ACTIVE, they accept new bids and later attempt to settle the auction even though the underlying NFT is no longer held by the contract. When resultAuction is finally invoked, the contract tries to transfer the NFT that is no longer owned, causing the transaction to revert. The revert leaves the last bidder’s ether locked inside the contract with no automatic refund path. This issue can be triggered whenever a seller cancels an auction before it begins and a malicious or unaware participant subsequently places a bid. The affected parties are the bidders who lose access to their funds, the seller who may be blamed for a broken auction, and the overall protocol which suffers from locked capital and broken accounting. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that examined state transitions and noticed the missing status checks. It is subtle because the UI may still show a “place bid” button after cancellation, and the contract does not emit an explicit error until settlement, making the loss of funds appear as a silent disappearance. To remediate the problem the contract should either delete the auction data entirely when cancelling or, at a minimum, add explicit require statements in bidPlace and resultAuction that enforce the auction status to be ACTIVE before proceeding. This ensures that cancelled auctions cannot be interacted with, preventing bids on non‑existent sales and guaranteeing that funds are either correctly refunded or never accepted in the first place. The bug belongs to the class of state‑inconsistent logic errors where a contract’s internal status is not enforced across all entry points, leading to accounting violations and potential fund loss.
summary: The protocol lets users create auctions and sell off their NFTs. Sellers can also cancel the auction but only if it is before the auction has started. This is achieved via the cancelAuction function and only the auction status is updated to CANCELLED and the NFT is transferred back to the owner. In the bidPlace and resultAuction functions there is no check whether the auction was canceled. That lets users freely bet on canceled auctions and when the time comes to close the auction the transaction will revert because the NFT was sent back to the owner when canceling. The last bidder's funds would get stuck in the contract.

title: acceptOfferNFT can be frontrun to scam the seller
content: The vulnerability resides in the acceptOfferNFT function that lets a seller accept an existing offer for an NFT. The function checks only that an offer exists for the given token and that the caller is the seller, but it does not bind the acceptance to a specific offer identifier or lock the offered price at the moment the seller decides to accept. Because the offer data is stored in a mutable mapping, an attacker who monitors the mempool can see the seller’s transaction, then submit two transactions before the seller’s transaction is mined: one that cancels the original high‑value offer and another that creates a new offer with a negligible amount (for example 1 wei). When the seller’s transaction finally executes, the require checks still pass, the contract reads the now‑modified offer entry and proceeds to transfer the NFT for the low price. From the seller’s perspective the UI shows a successful sale, but the received payment is far below the expected amount, effectively robbing the seller of the NFT’s value. The impact is a loss of funds for the seller and a breach of trust in the marketplace protocol, as any participant can manipulate offers between the decision and execution phases. The issue occurs whenever the marketplace allows acceptance of an offer without an immutable reference to that offer – typically in any “first‑come‑first‑served” design that relies on mutable state. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the flow of offer acceptance and noticed that the offer mapping can be altered between the time the seller initiates the call and the time the transaction is mined. The bug is subtle because the transaction does not revert; it simply processes a different offer, making the problem easy to miss in testing. To remediate, the contract should introduce a unique offer identifier that is passed to acceptOfferNFT and verified against the stored offer, or employ a commit‑reveal scheme or signed off‑chain offer that cannot be overwritten after the seller signals intent. Additionally, a minimumAmount parameter can be enforced to guarantee that the seller receives at least the price they intended. This class of flaw is a front‑running or race‑condition vulnerability in mutable marketplace state, where the business logic assumes the offer remains unchanged after the seller decides to accept it, violating the accounting assumption that the price at acceptance equals the price at offer creation.

title: Making more than 1 offer on an item will cause loss of eth
content: The vulnerability is a logical accounting flaw in the marketplace contract that allows a user to lose previously deposited Ether when making more than one offer on the same NFT. The contract stores each offer in a three‑dimensional mapping keyed by the NFT contract address, token identifier and the offerer address, but the value is a single OfferNFT struct. When the same address calls the payable offerNFT function a second time for the same token, the new OfferNFT struct overwrites the existing entry. Because the previous struct, which contained the amount of Ether sent with the first offer, is deleted, there is no reference to that amount any more. The cancelOfferNFT function reads the current mapping entry and refunds only the amount stored in the overwritten struct, so the earlier deposit becomes unrecoverable. This can be exploited simply by submitting a higher offer after an initial lower one; the attacker does not need any special permissions, only the ability to call the function. The impact is that honest users who try to improve their bid lose the Ether they originally sent, effectively causing funds to disappear from their wallet with no way to retrieve them. The condition under which the loss occurs is when a user who already has an active, unaccepted offer on a particular NFT makes another offer on the same NFT. All participants who can place offers – buyers, bidders, and any address interacting with the marketplace – are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the state handling of offers and noticed that the mapping does not support multiple entries per user per token. It is easy to miss because the function appears to accept any number of offers and the contract does not emit any warning or error when an existing offer is overwritten; the UI may simply show the latest offer amount, giving a false impression that the previous funds were automatically reclaimed. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “state overwrite leading to fund lock” or “single‑slot accounting for multiple bids”. The correct fix is to either prevent a second offer from being created while a previous one is still pending, or to redesign the storage so that each address can hold a list of offers (for example, using an array or a mapping of offer IDs) and ensure that each deposited amount can be individually withdrawn. This would preserve the accounting integrity of the marketplace and guarantee that users can always retrieve the exact amount they sent, matching the expectation that a cancelled offer returns the full deposited Ether.

title: Direct theft of initial sale NFT
content: The vulnerability resides in the initialSale function that sells the first ten NFTs to whitelisted users. The function checks that the caller has not claimed before and that the caller is on the Merkle whitelist, but it never verifies whether the specific tokenId being transferred has already been sold or is owned by the expected seller. Because the contract relies only on a per‑address claimed flag, an attacker who has been granted approval to move the victim’s NFT (for example via ERC721 setApprovalForAll) can invoke initialSale with the victim’s address supplied as the _ownerAddress and the tokenId that the victim already owns. The Merkle proof will still succeed for the attacker, the price check passes, and the contract will call safeTransferFrom(_ownerAddress, msg.sender, _tokenId), moving the token from the victim to the attacker even though the token was previously claimed. This results in direct theft of the NFT, causing the victim to lose ownership of a potentially valuable asset while the attacker receives it for free. The issue occurs only during the initial sale phase for token IDs 0‑9 and requires that the contract has been approved to transfer the victim’s token. It was discovered during a manual audit that focused on logical flow rather than arithmetic errors. The bug is subtle because the function appears to enforce whitelist and payment constraints, masking the missing ownership validation. To remediate, the contract should track which token IDs have been sold, enforce that the token’s current owner matches the expected seller (typically the contract itself), or mint the NFT directly instead of transferring from an external address. In essence, the flaw is a missing “token already claimed” check, a class of access‑control/ownership validation errors that can lead to unauthorized asset transfer, violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions that each NFT can be sold only once.

title: Increasing emissionEnd after the previous emissionEnd ended will yield full rewards according to newEmissionEnd - prevEmissionEnd
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect reward-distribution logic that appears when the contract’s emissionEnd timestamp has already been reached and the owner later extends this timestamp. The contract’s function lastApplicableTime() is defined to return the minimum of block.timestamp and emissionEnd; after emissionEnd has passed, it always returns emissionEnd. Consequently, when a new emissionEnd is set to a later value, the calculation of pending rewards for every staker uses the same reference point (the previous emissionEnd) regardless of when the stake was made. As a result, a user who stakes after the original emission period ends receives the same amount of reward as a user who has been staking since the beginning, because the rewardDebt stored for the new staker is based on (newEmissionEnd – previousEmissionEnd) instead of the actual elapsed staking time. An attacker can exploit this by calling setEmissionDetails() to increase emissionEnd after it has elapsed and then either front‑run a stake transaction or rely on other users to stake, causing all participants to be credited with the full additional reward pool. The impact is an unintended inflation of token rewards, which can drain the protocol’s reward reserve, break the intended pro‑rata distribution, and undermine trust in the staking mechanism. The bug manifests only under the specific condition that emissionEnd is extended after it has already been reached; under normal operation the reward rate works as designed. Users affected are any stakers, especially those who interact with the contract after the emission period, as they may see their balance increase unexpectedly or receive rewards they did not earn. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined edge‑case timing logic; it is subtle because the reward calculation appears correct for the majority of timestamps and only fails when the emissionEnd is modified post‑expiry, a scenario that typical unit tests may not cover. The problem is hard to notice because the contract does not emit explicit warnings and the reward increase is indistinguishable from legitimate earnings. To remediate, the contract should either forbid changing emissionEnd after it has passed, or adjust the reward‑calculation algorithm to use the current timestamp as the reference point for new stakes, ensuring that pending rewards are proportional to the actual staking duration. In other words, the reward distribution must be tied to each user’s individual staking interval rather than a global delta that can be arbitrarily extended.
summary: Rewards are emitted at a certain rewardRate, which means stakers that have been staking for longer receive more rewards. However, there is an edge case in which this does not happen. When the emissionEnd is reached, lastApplicableTime() will always be emissionEnd. This means that anyone who stakes after emissionEnd, no matter how much time after it, will have the same rewardDebt stored. Thus, if the emissionEnd is increased after it has ended, every staker will receive the same rewards according to newEmissionEnd - prevEmissionEnd, even if they have staked in the same block that the emissionEnd was increased. Putting this thought into numbers, if emissionEnd = 10, and if at block.timestamp = 15, a new emissionEnd is set to 20, stakers that staked from the beginning will get rewards pro-rata to 15-10 at the current timestamp, the same as stakers who staked at the current block.timestamp = 15, if they frontrun the setEmissionDetails() call.

title: Send should revert if the gas limit has not been set for a destination chain (peer)
content: The vulnerability is a missing validation in the cross‑chain messaging function send(). The function permits a user to initiate a message to a destination chain even when the contract’s internal gasLimit mapping does not contain an entry for that destination peer. Because the mapping entry is absent, the function defaults the gas limit to zero and proceeds without reverting. This occurs because the implementation does not check whether a gas limit has been configured before constructing the outbound message. An attacker or any user can exploit this by sending a message to a newly added or unconfigured peer; the destination chain receives a message that specifies a gas limit of zero, which is insufficient to execute any logic on the target. Consequently, the transaction on the destination chain reverts, leaving the message unprocessed. From the user’s perspective the source transaction appears successful – the fee is deducted and the transaction receipt shows a success – but the expected outcome on the destination side never materialises. Users may observe symptoms such as a pending or failed status in the UI, missing refunds, or a complete lack of any observable effect on the target chain despite having paid the sending fee. The impact is high because funds paid for cross‑chain delivery are effectively lost or locked, and the protocol’s reliability is compromised; subsequent messages to the same peer will continue to fail until a proper gas limit is set. The issue is discovered during a security audit that examined the handling of gas limits for each peer and noticed that the contract does not enforce a non‑zero requirement. It can be hard to notice because the source transaction does not revert and no explicit error is emitted, so developers may assume the message was delivered correctly. The bug belongs to the class of unchecked input or missing pre‑condition validation, specifically an “uninitialized configuration” flaw that leads to downstream execution failure. To remediate, the contract should explicitly revert when a caller attempts to send a message to a destination whose gas limit has not been recorded, forcing the caller to set the appropriate gas limit via the protocol’s configuration function before any messages are dispatched. This ensures that every outbound message carries a sufficient gas budget, preserving the intended accounting guarantees and preventing silent loss of user funds.
summary: send() allows users to send messages with 0 gas limit if the gasLimit mapping has not been seen for a certain peer. This will likely make the transaction revert on the destination chain,

title: buyNFT does not check if a listing id was canceled
content: The vulnerability resides in the marketplace contract’s buyNFT function, which processes a purchase based solely on the existence of a listing identifier and the sold flag, but fails to verify whether the listing has been cancelled. When a seller cancels a listing, the contract typically marks the entry as cancelled or removes it from the active set, yet the underlying data structure (listNfts mapping) still retains the record. Because the buyNFT function does not include a check for a cancelled status, an attacker can supply the stale listing identifier, satisfy the price requirement with the old (lower) price, and trigger the purchase flow. The function then marks the listing as sold and transfers ownership, even though the seller intended the listing to be inactive and possibly relisted at a higher price. This logical omission allows a malicious buyer to acquire the NFT for less than the intended price, resulting in financial loss for the seller and undermining the marketplace’s pricing guarantees. The issue manifests when a seller cancels a listing and subsequently creates a new listing for the same token; the old identifier remains usable until explicitly invalidated. Users experience symptoms such as an NFT being transferred despite the seller believing the original offer was withdrawn, or the seller seeing a sale at an unexpected low price while the UI may no longer display the cancelled listing. The bug belongs to the class of missing state validation or stale identifier misuse, where business logic assumes that a cancelled listing cannot be acted upon, but the contract does not enforce this invariant. It was discovered during a security audit by CD Security, where the logical flow of the buyNFT function was examined and the absence of a cancelled‑listing guard was noted. The problem can be hard to notice because the function appears to enforce price and sold checks, and the UI typically hides cancelled listings, giving a false sense of safety. To remediate, the contract should introduce an explicit requirement that the listing is not cancelled (for example, require(!listedNft.canceled) or checking a status enum) before proceeding with the purchase, and optionally purge or invalidate the mapping entry when a listing is cancelled to prevent reuse of stale identifiers. This correction restores the intended accounting model, ensuring that only active, non‑cancelled listings can be bought and that sellers receive the correct compensation for their assets.

title: The bonding curve implementation can not be fully changed
content: The vulnerability concerns a bonding‑curve token contract where the price‑calculation routine is hard‑coded in the token implementation instead of being delegated to the upgradable bonding‑curve logic. The factory function updateBondingCurve is intended to replace the entire bonding‑curve formula by pointing the token to a new AMMFormula contract, but the getOutputPrice function remains defined directly in the ContinuosBondingERC20Token contract. Because the function is compiled into the token bytecode, changing the bonding‑curve implementation does not affect the price calculation. This design flaw creates a mismatch between the intended formula and the actual one used at runtime. An attacker or a careless user can exploit the situation by assuming that the updated curve will be applied throughout the whole price range, while in reality the token price at the high‑end of the curve is still computed by the old, hard‑coded expression. The old formula tends to over‑estimate the price when the output reserve is nearly depleted, causing the denominator (outputReserve‑outputAmount) to become very small and the returned price to spike incorrectly. Consequently, a buyer who expects to receive a certain amount of tokens for a given input amount may be charged more than the intended price, or may receive fewer tokens than anticipated. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a normal price for most trades but suddenly display an unexpectedly high cost or a zero‑output situation when trying to purchase the last few tokens, leading to confusion such as “my transaction cost far more than before” or “I got no tokens even though I sent ETH”. The impact is financial loss for token purchasers and a distortion of the market price, which can undermine confidence in the protocol and potentially allow a malicious actor to profit from the price discrepancy. The issue manifests only after the factory’s updateBondingCurve call has been executed; before the upgrade the hard‑coded function matches the original formula, so the bug is not obvious during normal operation. It was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the upgrade path and noticed that getOutputPrice is not part of the upgradable interface. The problem is subtle because the function works for the majority of the curve and only deviates near the curve’s end, making it easy to miss in routine testing. To remediate the issue the price calculation should be moved into the AMMFormula contract (or another upgradable module) and the token should call that external contract via an interface or delegatecall. This ensures that any future updateBondingCurve operation truly replaces the pricing logic, keeping the on‑chain price consistent with the intended bonding‑curve formula and preventing incorrect high‑price calculations.

title: Bonding token transfers DOS after the pair was created
content: The contract implements a bonding ERC‑20 token that blocks all normal transfers until a liquidity goal is reached. The blocking logic lives in the overridden _update function, which reverts with TransferNotAllowedUntilLiquidityGoalReached when the liquidityGoalReached() view returns false and the transfer is not a mint or burn. The liquidityGoalReached() function determines success by comparing the current reserve of the token/WETH pair (getReserve()) with the difference between the maximum token supply and the amount of tokens still available for purchase (MAX_TOTAL_SUPPLY‑availableTokenBalance). After the initial sale finishes, the pair is created, getReserve() becomes zero and the condition evaluates to true, so transfers are allowed. However, the check does not also verify that the pair has already been created. An attacker can exploit this by sending a large amount of tokens directly to the token contract itself, which reduces availableTokenBalance. This manipulation makes the expression (MAX_TOTAL_SUPPLY‑availableTokenBalance) grow, causing liquidityGoalReached() to flip back to false even though the pair already exists. Because the _update guard no longer distinguishes the post‑creation state, every subsequent transfer – including legitimate user transfers or contract‑initiated moves – triggers the revert, effectively creating a denial‑of‑service condition on token movement. From a user’s perspective the token appears frozen: attempts to send tokens result in a transaction that reverts with TransferNotAllowedUntilLiquidityGoalReached, balances remain unchanged, and no funds can be transferred out of the contract. The impact is severe because token holders lose the ability to move or trade their assets, and the protocol’s liquidity mechanisms become unusable. The issue was discovered during a security audit when a test case deliberately transferred MAX_TOTAL_SUPPLY‑availableTokenBalance+1 tokens to the token contract and observed that further transfers reverted. The bug is subtle because the original intention of the guard – to prevent transfers before the sale ends – is correct; the missing isLpCreated guard makes the condition unintentionally re‑activate after the pair is created, a scenario that is not obvious during casual testing. The proper fix is to augment the transfer restriction with an explicit check that the liquidity pair has already been created (e.g., && !isLpCreated) so that once the pair exists the transfer guard is disabled regardless of the liquidityGoalReached() result. This change restores normal token transfer functionality while preserving the intended pre‑sale protection, and eliminates the DoS vector caused by manipulating the available token balance.

title: Lack of slippage control can lead to sandwich attacks
content: The vulnerability consists of missing slippage protection in the token‑to‑ETH swap functions. Both swapTokensForEth and openTrade call the Uniswap router with the amountOutMin argument hard‑coded to zero, which tells the router that any amount of ETH, even none, is acceptable as output. This design flaw allows an attacker to execute a front‑running sandwich attack: the attacker first performs a large trade that pushes the price unfavourably, then the victim’s transaction is mined, receiving far less ETH than expected (often zero), and finally the attacker reverses the price impact with a second trade to capture the profit. The exploit works whenever the contract’s swap functions are invoked, especially when the transaction is broadcast to a public mempool where bots can observe and react. Affected parties include any user or the contract owner who initiates a trade, as the business logic assumes that swapping tokens will yield a minimum amount of ETH. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit by CD Security, which flagged the hard‑coded zero as a lack of slippage control. It can be hard to notice because the transaction does not revert; it appears successful on‑chain, yet the user may receive no ETH or a dramatically reduced amount, leading to a discrepancy between expected and actual balances. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a completed swap while the wallet balance remains unchanged, creating confusion and potential loss of funds. The bug belongs to the class of unchecked output amount or missing slippage protection vulnerabilities that break accounting assumptions and open the contract to MEV exploitation. To remediate, the contract should accept a user‑supplied amountOutMin parameter calculated off‑chain based on current market rates, or otherwise enforce a reasonable slippage limit through oracle checks or router functions that reject trades delivering less than the expected minimum.
summary:
The amountOutMin parameter in swapExactTokensForETHSupportingFeeOnTransferTokens is
hard coded to 0 in swapTokensForEth():
```solidity
function swapTokensForEth(uint256 tokenAmount) private {
    // make the swap
    uniswapV2Router.swapExactTokensForETHSupportingFeeOnTransferTokens(
        tokenAmount,
        0, // accept any amount of ETH //@audit no slippage protection
        path,
        block.timestamp
    );
}
```
This basically allows for 100% slippage as the call agrees to receive 0 amount of ETH for the swap. This can
be done through a sandwich attack. The same applies to the openTrade function:
```solidity
function openTrade() external payable onlyOwner {
    0, //uint amountTokenMin, //@audit both inputs here should be
    user supplied parameters, not hardcoded to 0
    0, //uint amountETHMin,
    owner(),
    block.timestamp
}
```
This is a very easy target for MEV and bots to do a flash loan sandwich attack and can be done on every call
if the trade transaction goes through a public mempool.

title: Deadline check is not effective
content: The vulnerability consists of an ineffective deadline check in functions that interact with UniswapV2Router02, specifically swapExactTokensForETHSupportingFeeOnTransferTokens and addLiquidityETH when they are invoked through the contract's swapTokensForEth and openTrade helpers. The code hard‑codes the deadline argument to block.timestamp, which means the ensure modifier that requires deadline >= block.timestamp will always succeed because the two values are identical at execution time. The root cause is a misuse of the deadline parameter: instead of allowing a user‑supplied future timestamp that defines an expiration window, the contract forces the deadline to be the current block time, effectively disabling the time‑limit protection. An attacker, miner, or any validator can exploit this by submitting the transaction with a very low gas price, causing it to linger in the mempool for an extended period—minutes, hours, or even days. Because the deadline never expires, the transaction will eventually be mined regardless of how long it waits, and during that waiting period the market price of the traded assets may move unfavorably. Consequently, the user may receive far less ETH than expected, experience severe slippage, or see the swap execute at a price that results in a net loss. The impact is a breach of the economic assumptions of the swap: users expect the deadline to protect them from price drift and front‑running, but the contract provides no such guarantee, exposing them to arbitrage or sandwich attacks. This condition occurs whenever a user initiates a trade without specifying a custom deadline and the network is congested or the gas price is set too low. All participants who interact with the AMM functions—regular users, liquidity providers, and the protocol owner—are affected because the flaw resides in the shared router interface. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the parameter handling of deadline in the router calls and noticed that the modifier ensure would never revert. It is hard to notice because the transaction does not fail; instead it silently proceeds after an unpredictable delay, making the problem appear only as an unexpected price outcome rather than a direct error. To remediate, the contract should accept a deadline supplied by the caller that is greater than the current block timestamp, and the ensure modifier will then correctly enforce expiration. Adding optional slippage limits can further protect users from adverse price movements. In abstract terms, this is a time‑based validation bypass, a class of bugs where expiration checks are rendered ineffective by using the current time as both the reference and the limit. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a pending transaction for an unusually long time, and after confirmation the received amount may be zero or dramatically lower than anticipated, violating the expectation that the swap executes at the quoted rate within a reasonable window.
summary:
The deadline parameter in swapExactTokensForETHSupportingFeeOnTransferTokens() and
addLiquidityETH() which are called in swapTokensForEth() and openTrade() is hardcoded to
block.timestamp.
Example in openTrade():
```solidity
function openTrade() external payable onlyOwner {
    0, //uint amountTokenMin,
    0, //uint amountETHMin,
    owner(),
    block.timestamp
}
```
The addLiquidityETH() in UniswapV2Router02 contract:
```solidity
function addLiquidityETH(
    uint amountTokenDesired,
    uint amountTokenMin,
    uint amountETHMin,
    uint deadline
) external virtual override payable ensure(deadline) returns (uint amountToken, uint amountETH, uint liquidity)
```
The deadline parameter enforces a time limit by which the transaction must be executed otherwise it will
revert.
Let's take a look at a modifier that is present in the functions you are calling in UniswapV2Router02
contract:
```solidity
modifier ensure(uint deadline) {
    require(deadline >= block.timestamp, 'UniswapV2Router: EXPIRED');
}
```
Now when the deadline is hardcoded as block.timestamp, the transaction will not revert because the
require statement will always be fulfilled by block.timestamp == block.timestamp.
If a user chooses a transaction fee that is too low for miners to be interested in including the transaction in a
block, the transaction stays pending in the mempool for extended periods, which could be hours, days,
weeks, or even longer.
This could lead to users getting a worse price because a validator can just hold onto the transaction.
Recommendations
Protocols should let users who interact with AMMs set expiration deadlines. Without this, there's a risk of a
serious loss of funds for anyone starting a swap, especially if there's no slippage parameter.
Use a user-supplied deadline instead of block.timestamp.

title: The _transfer function will not work for normal users
content: The vulnerability is a fee‑calculation underflow in the token’s internal _transfer routine. The contract determines a dynamic fee that decreases over time and is supposed to reach zero after a fixed period (90 days for private‑sale participants and 120 days for angel‑sale participants). The current fee is stored in a uint256 variable and is computed as initialFee minus daysPassed × dailyDecrease. Because uint256 cannot represent negative numbers, when daysPassed × dailyDecrease exceeds initialFee the subtraction underflows, causing the EVM to revert before the subsequent if‑statement that would clamp the fee to zero can execute. This revert occurs only when the transfer is subject to fees – i.e., when either the sender or the recipient is an automated market‑maker pair and the takeFee flag is true. After the designated period has elapsed, any normal user who is not fee‑exempt attempts a transfer and the transaction fails with a generic “revert” error. From the user’s perspective the UI reports a failed transaction or “out of gas” without indicating that the fee logic is the cause, and the token balance remains unchanged, contrary to the expectation that the transfer should succeed. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition: funds become effectively immobile for affected holders, liquidity pools cannot be updated, and the protocol’s trading functionality is broken. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the fee‑adjustment functions, where the arithmetic was examined and the unsigned type was identified as unsafe for a decreasing fee that can become negative. The bug is subtle because the code includes an explicit check to set the fee to zero, which gives the impression that the calculation is safe, yet the compiler’s built‑in overflow/underflow protection triggers earlier. To remediate, the fee calculation should be performed using a signed integer type (int256) or guarded with a max‑zero clamp before the subtraction, ensuring that the result never underflows, or the logic should be rewritten to return zero directly when the elapsed days exceed the fee‑duration threshold. This change restores the intended behavior where fees gradually drop to zero and normal transfers work after the fee period ends.

title: `PortalFacet.repayAavePortal`
content: The vulnerability resides in the `repayAavePortal` function of the PortalFacet contract. The function is intended to allow a router to repay an Aave loan by swapping a local asset into the adopted asset and then decrementing the router's stored balance. The root cause is the use of an unchecked subtraction on the router's balance after a swap operation that can return a user‑controlled amount. When the local asset passed to the function is the same as the adopted asset, the helper `AssetLogic.swapFromLocalAssetIfNeededForExactOut` short‑circuits and returns the exact `totalAmount` (the sum of `_backingAmount` and `_feeAmount`) as `amountIn`. Because the contract only checks that `routerBalance` is greater than or equal to `_maxIn`, an attacker can pass a `totalAmount` that exceeds the actual router balance, causing `amountIn` to be larger than the stored balance. The subsequent unchecked line `s.routerBalances[msg.sender][_local] -= amountIn;` then underflows, wrapping around the unsigned integer and resulting in an arbitrarily large positive balance for the attacker. This can be exploited by calling `repayAavePortal` with `_local` set to the adopted asset, providing `_backingAmount` and `_feeAmount` that together exceed the router's current balance, and setting `_maxIn` high enough to pass the initial sanity check. The impact is that the attacker’s router balance inflates without depositing any assets, breaking the protocol’s accounting invariants and potentially allowing the attacker to withdraw the artificially created funds. The issue occurs only when the local and adopted assets are identical and the subtraction is performed in an unchecked context, a condition that is not obvious from the external UI and may go unnoticed because the function appears to succeed without error. It was discovered during a manual audit that traced the flow of values from the swap helper back to the balance update and noted the lack of safe arithmetic. The bug belongs to the class of unchecked arithmetic underflow/overflow vulnerabilities, often manifested as “balance inflation” or “credit injection”. From a user’s perspective the router balance may suddenly jump to a very high number, contrary to the expectation that the balance would decrease by the amount repaid. To remediate, the contract should verify that the router’s balance is at least `amountIn` after the swap and before the subtraction, or perform the subtraction with checked arithmetic, ensuring that an underflow cannot occur. Adding a condition such as `require(routerBalance >= amountIn);` after the swap resolves the flaw and restores the intended accounting behavior.
summary:
[PortalFacet.sol#L80-L113](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-06-connext/blob/main/contracts/contracts/core/connext/facets/PortalFacet.sol#L80-L113)  

The caller of `repayAavePortal()` can trigger an underflow to arbitrarily increase the caller’s balance through an underflow.

title: Wrong implementation of `withdrawAdminFees`
content: The vulnerability resides in the admin fee withdrawal routine of a swap contract. The function iterates over each pooled token, reads the stored fee amount from an array, and if the amount is non‑zero it transfers that amount to a destination address. However, after performing the transfer the contract never clears the stored fee balance. Because the fee accounting variable is left unchanged, the same fee amount remains recorded and can be transferred again on any subsequent call to the same function. This omission of a state reset is the root cause: the contract does not update its internal accounting after dispensing fees. An attacker who controls the admin role can repeatedly invoke the withdrawal function, each time receiving the identical fee amount, effectively draining the pool of fees that should have been accounted for only once. The impact is a systematic erosion of liquidity provider value and a breach of the protocol’s economic model, where fees are expected to be collected a single time per swap. The condition for exploitation is simply the ability to call the internal withdrawAdminFees routine, which is typically exposed to the contract owner or an authorized admin; no additional permissions or complex triggers are required. The issue was uncovered during a manual code audit that highlighted the missing reset of the adminFees array. It can be hard to notice because the transfer succeeds and no explicit error is emitted, so observers see only successful fee payouts without realizing the accounting entry remains unchanged. From a user’s perspective, LPs may notice their share of the pool diminishing over time, or see that expected fee accruals are not reflected in their balance, leading to confusion when their earnings appear lower than anticipated. The bug belongs to the class of "state‑inconsistent accounting" vulnerabilities, where a contract fails to synchronize on‑chain state with external actions, violating the invariant that fees are deducted exactly once. To remediate the issue, the contract should atomically reset the stored fee amount to zero before transferring tokens, ensuring that each fee is withdrawn only once and that the accounting state mirrors the performed payout. This correction restores the intended economic behavior and prevents repeated siphoning of fees by the admin.

title: Router Owner Could Steal All The Funds Within `SponsorVault`
content: The vulnerability resides in the SponsorVault fee‑reimbursement mechanism of the Connext bridge. SponsorVault is designed to subsidize the liquidity fee that routers charge for fast transfers by paying a fixed percentage (50 % in the example) of the fee back to the router after the cross‑chain message is reconciled. The root cause is a missing validation that the router receiving the reimbursement is not the same entity that supplied the liquidity for the transfer, nor that the fee being reimbursed originated from a third‑party sponsor. Because the protocol trusts any router to provide liquidity and later reimburses a portion of the fee based solely on the amount of liquidity used, a malicious router owner can deliberately become the sole provider of liquidity for a large transfer, collect the expected user‑paid fee, and then receive an additional sponsorship reimbursement that effectively creates new tokens out of thin air. In practice, an attacker who controls a router with sufficient balance can craft a transfer that exceeds the liquidity of all other routers, forcing the sequencer to select the attacker’s router. The router supplies the required 95 % of the amount (the 5 % fee is withheld), and after the bridge reconciliation the SponsorVault automatically credits the router with 50 % of the fee, even though the fee was already covered by the router’s own funds. The net result is a profit for the attacker equal to half of the fee (25 000 USDC in the scenario) and a corresponding loss for the SponsorVault. This exploit can be repeated for each large transfer, potentially draining the entire sponsor pool. The issue manifests as users receiving the correct amount of bridged tokens, while the sponsor’s balance diminishes unnoticed; from a user perspective the UI shows the expected transfer amount and no error, making the problem hard to detect. The flaw was uncovered during a security audit by Code4rena, which highlighted the logical inconsistency in the reimbursement flow. Because the protocol assumes honest routers and does not enforce any separation of duties, the bug blends into normal accounting and may only be spotted by analyzing the net change in sponsor balances over many transactions. To remediate the problem, the reimbursement logic should be re‑designed to verify that the reimbursed fee originates from external sponsor funds and not from the router’s own liquidity, enforce per‑router caps, restrict reimbursement to pre‑approved routers, or eliminate the automatic subsidy altogether. In essence, the vulnerability is a classic incentive‑misalignment and double‑spending style bug where a privileged participant can game a subsidy mechanism to extract value from a pool that is meant to benefit end users.
summary:
[BridgeFacet.sol#L541](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-06-connext/blob/4dd6149748b635f95460d4c3924c7e3fb6716967/contracts/contracts/core/connext/facets/BridgeFacet.sol#L541)  
[SponsorVault.sol#L196](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-06-connext/blob/4dd6149748b635f95460d4c3924c7e3fb6716967/contracts/contracts/core/connext/helpers/SponsorVault.sol#L196)  

Assume the following:

* For simplicity sake, only two (2) routers exist within Connext. Gas, relayer, callback fees and slippage are ignored.
* An attacker owns Router A. Router A has `1,000,000` oUSDC on Optimism Domain/Chain
* Router B has only `100` oUSDC on Optimism Domain/Chain
* The liquidity fee is 5% for fast transfer service
* SponsorVault will reimburse 50% of the liquidity fee incurred by the users

At this point, attacker balances are as follows (2,000,000 USDC in total)

Attacker’s wallet in Ethereum = `1,000,000` USDC

Attacker’s wallet in Optimism = `0` oUSDC

Attacker’s router in Optimism = `1,000,000` oUSDC

First, the attacker attempts to transfer an extremely large amount - `1,000,000` USDC from attacker’s address in Ethereum to attacker’s address in Optimism Chain. The transfer amount should be much larger than the rest of the router’s liquidity so that only attacker’s router is capable of providing the liquidity.

In our example, since Router B does not have sufficient liquidity to facilitate the fast transfer, Router B will not be selected by the Sequencer. Since only Router A has sufficient liquidity, Router A, which is owned by the attacker, will facilitate the fast transfer and selected by the Sequencer.

Since the liquidity fee is 5%, Router A only need to supply `950,000` oUSDC on `execute`. The Sponsor will then reimburse 50% of the liquidity fee, which is `25,000` oUSDC in total. The final amount of oUSDC sent to the attacker’s wallet address in Optimism will be `975,000` oUSDC.

At this point, attacker balances are as follows (1,025,000 USDC in total)

Attacker’s wallet in Ethereum = `0` USDC

Attacker’s wallet in Optimism = `975,000` oUSDC

Attacker’s router in Optimism = `50,000` oUSDC

When the nomad message arrives, the attacker will be reimbursed `1,000,000` oUSDC when [`BridgeFacet._reconcile`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-06-connext/blob/4dd6149748b635f95460d4c3924c7e3fb6716967/contracts/contracts/core/connext/facets/BridgeFacet.sol#L541) is triggered.

At this point, attacker balances are as follows (2,025,000 USDC in total)

Attacker’s wallet in Ethereum = `0` USDC

Attacker’s wallet in Optimism = `975,000` oUSDC

Attacker’s router in Optimism = `50,000` + `1,000,000` oUSDC

Attacker earned `25,000` USDC, and SponsorVault lost `25,000` USDC.

title: Market interest is not always accrued
content: The vulnerability is that the strategy contract does not always trigger the market's interest accrual before performing operations that depend on the total asset amount. The market contract maintains an internal interest counter that updates totalAssets() when markets.accrueInterest() is called. Because the strategy only calls accrueInterest() inside the _withdraw() function after it has already calculated the number of shares to return, any interest that accumulated between the previous call and the current withdrawal is ignored. The same omission occurs on deposit/mint, where shares are calculated before the market interest is accrued, and in view functions such as totalAssets(), expectedAmountsToWithdraw() and maxWithdraw(), which return values that do not reflect the latest accrued interest. The root cause is the missing pre‑action call to markets.accrueInterest() and the lack of a read‑only interface to fetch the pending interest. An attacker or a regular user can exploit this by timing deposits or withdrawals after periods of high interest accrual; the contract will compute shares or withdrawal amounts based on stale asset totals, causing users to receive fewer tokens than they are entitled to, or conversely allowing a malicious actor to claim more than their proportional share if the contract later corrects the balance. The impact is financial loss for users, inaccurate accounting for the protocol, and potential erosion of trust because the UI may display a balance that does not match the amount actually withdrawable. The bug manifests whenever the market has accrued interest since the last explicit call to markets.accrueInterest(), which can happen in any block where the market's interest rate is non‑zero. All participants who interact with the strategy – depositors, withdrawers, and anyone relying on view functions for off‑chain calculations – are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the expected accounting model with the implementation and noticed that interest was only applied after share calculations. It is hard to notice because the discrepancy may be small per block and only becomes apparent after multiple accrual periods, making UI balances appear correct while the underlying accounting is off. The proper fix is to invoke markets.accrueInterest() before any state‑changing operation that reads or writes total assets, and to add a view‑compatible method (or expose the pending interest) so that read‑only functions can return values that include the most recent interest. This aligns the contract with the intended business logic that interest should be earned on the full asset amount before any share or withdrawal computation.
summary:
```solidity
The market accrues interest, which changes totalAssets() in theLoopStrategy. Thus, everytime there is some action that modifies the amount of assets, interest should always be accrued first. However, markets.accrueInterest() in only called on _withdraw(), post shares/assets calculation, which will lead to an incorrect asset withdrawal.
On deposit/mint, it also does not accrue market interest before calculating the shares to receive.
In the view functions, such as totalAssets(), expectedAmountsToWithdraw() or maxWithdraw(), it also does not consider the accrued interest from the market.
```

title: Distribution.getCurrentPoolRate() function will revert after block.timestamp reaches the maximum end time causing unrecoverable DoS
content: The vulnerability is an arithmetic underflow that occurs in the reward‑distribution logic of a linear decreasing interval contract. The contract calculates the amount of reward that remains for a given period by subtracting a decreasing amount (decreaseAmount multiplied by the number of elapsed intervals) from the initial reward amount. When the start time of a user‑requested period falls inside the last interval of the distribution and the initial amount is not an exact multiple of the decrease amount, the computed decreaseRewardAmount can become equal to or larger than the initialAmount. The subtraction then underflows, causing the internal function that determines the current pool rate to revert. This revert propagates to the public functions that rely on the pool rate – stake, withdraw, claim and edit – making them permanently unusable once block.timestamp reaches or exceeds the maximum end time of the distribution. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the LinearDistributionIntervalDecrease library, where the auditor observed that the division‑ceil helper could round up and produce an interval count that exceeds the reward budget. Because the revert only happens at a specific time boundary, the contract appears to work correctly for most of its lifetime, making the bug hard to notice without testing edge cases near the final distribution day. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are that transactions that previously succeeded now fail with a generic revert, balances appear unchanged, and expected rewards or refunds are never received. The bug belongs to the class of “reward‑calculation underflow leading to denial‑of‑service” errors, where a mathematical assumption (initialAmount divisible by decreaseAmount) is violated, breaking accounting invariants. An attacker does not need to interact directly; the contract will self‑destruct its functionality when the blockchain reaches the cutoff timestamp, effectively locking all funds. The correct mitigation is to guard the subtraction by checking whether decreaseRewardAmount is greater than or equal to initialAmount and, in that case, return a zero reward instead of performing the subtraction, or to redesign the formula so that it never produces a negative intermediate value regardless of divisibility. This change restores the ability of the contract to report a pool rate of zero after the distribution ends, preventing the unintended revert and preserving the ability to withdraw or claim remaining tokens.

title: All claimed rewards will be lost for the users using the account abstraction wallet
content: The vulnerability originates from the cross‑chain reward distribution logic that assumes a user’s address is identical on every EVM‑compatible chain. In the claim() function the contract forwards the caller’s L1 address directly to the L2 minting routine via a LayerZero message. The L2 receiver decodes the payload and mints the pending reward to the address contained in the payload. For users who employ an account abstraction (AA) wallet, the address that represents the same logical account differs between L1 and L2 because AA wallets generate a new contract address on each chain. Consequently, when a claim is executed for an AA wallet, the mint operation on L2 credits an address that is not owned by the intended user. The transaction does not revert; the mint succeeds, but the tokens are sent to an address with no private key, making the rewards permanently unrecoverable. An attacker who discovers this pattern can trigger claim() for many AA users, effectively griefing them by draining their pending rewards without any on‑chain error. The issue manifests when the claim() function is called for any account whose L1 address does not map to a valid L2 address, which is the case for all AA wallet holders. Affected parties include the AA wallet users, the protocol’s reward pool, and any stakeholders relying on accurate accounting of distributed assets. The problem was uncovered during a manual audit of the Distribution.sol contract by tracing the flow of the user address through the LayerZero send and receive functions. It is subtle because the mint call on L2 appears successful, and the UI may simply show that the user’s reward balance remains unchanged, leading to confusion rather than an explicit failure. To remediate, the contract should not rely on the L1 address as the sole recipient. Instead, it should allow the user to provide an explicit L2 recipient address (for example, by adding an l2Recipient field to the stored user data) and enforce that this address is used for minting. Additionally, documentation should warn AA wallet holders that their L1 address cannot be reused on L2. This change aligns the reward distribution with the actual ownership of the target address and prevents permanent loss of funds.

title: Accounting issue when repaying P2P fees while having a borrow delta
content: The vulnerability is an accounting inconsistency that occurs when a borrower repays P2P fees while a positive borrow delta is present in the Morpho protocol. The root cause is that the function which decreases the borrow delta clears the scaledDelta value but postpones the update of the scaledP2PAmount (scaledP2PTotal) until the end of the repay routine. The subsequent call that calculates the repayable fee reads the stale scaledP2PAmount, which leads to an over‑estimation of the fee that can be repaid. An attacker or any borrower can trigger this path by invoking a repayment that first matches the borrow delta and then immediately calls the fee‑repayment logic; the contract will think a larger fee is outstanding and will accept a higher repayment amount. The excess fee is transferred into the contract without being accounted for – it is not used to promote borrowers, increase idle supply, or demote suppliers as the business logic requires. Consequently, the internal accounting state diverges from the expected invariant: P2P suppliers that should have been demoted remain marked as active even though they have no counter‑party, and the protocol’s view of total P2P exposure becomes incorrect. This situation can lead to incorrect interest distribution, potential loss of funds, and overall instability of the lending market. The bug manifests only when a borrow delta exists and a fee repayment is performed in the same transaction, making it easy to miss because the contract does not revert or emit an error; the surplus fee simply disappears from the accounting view while the external balances appear unchanged. The issue was discovered during a security audit by Spearbit through logical analysis of the repay flow and delta handling. It is hard to notice because the symptom is a silent mismatch in internal variables rather than an obvious user‑visible error. To fix the problem, the decreaseDelta routine should also reduce the scaledP2PAmount by the amount that was matched, or the order of operations should be rearranged so that the fee calculation always uses the updated value. Adding dedicated tests that cover scenarios with both a positive borrow delta and fee repayment would help prevent regression. From a user perspective, the bug may appear as a situation where after repaying fees the supplied balance does not increase as expected, or where the protocol seems to retain extra fees without any benefit, violating the expectation that fees are redistributed to borrowers or suppliers according to the protocol’s accounting rules. This class of bug can be described as a stale‑state or order‑of‑operations accounting flaw in financial smart contracts.
summary:
When repaying debt on Morpho, any potential borrow delta is matched first. Repaying the delta should involve both decreasing the scaledDelta as well as decreasing the scaledP2PAmount by the matched amount. However, the scaledP2PAmount update is delayed until the end of the repay function. The following repayFee call then reads the un-updated market.deltas.borrow.scaledP2PAmount storage variable leading to a larger estimation of the P2P fees that can be repaid.
The excess fee that is repaid will stay in the contract and not be accounted for, when it should have been used to promote borrowers, increase idle supply or demote suppliers. For example, there could now be P2P suppliers that should have been demoted but are not and in reality don't have any P2P counterparty, leaving the entire accounting system in a broken state.
• Example (all values are in underlying amounts for brevity.)
Imagine a borrow delta of 1000, borrow.scaledP2PTotal = 10,000 supply.scaledP2PTotal = 8,000, so the repayable fee should be (10,000 - 1000) - (8,000 - 0) = 1,000. Now a P2P borrower wants to repay 3000 debt:
1. Pool repay: no pool repay as they have no pool borrow balance.
2. Decrease p2p borrow delta: decreaseDelta is called which sets market.deltas.borrow.scaledDelta = 0 (but does not update market.deltas.borrow.scaledP2PAmount yet!) and returns matchedBorrowDelta = 1000
3. repayFee is called and it computes (10,000 - 0) - (8,000 - 1,000) = 2,000. They repay more than the actual fee.

title: Repaying with ETH does not refund excess
content: The vulnerability concerns the repayment flow of WETH Morpho positions when a borrower uses the WETHGateway to repay with native ETH. The gateway wraps the supplied ETH into WETH and forwards the amount to Morpho’s repay function. Morpho’s internal logic, however, only accepts the minimum of the caller‑specified amount and the actual outstanding borrow balance, effectively capping the repayment to the exact debt. Because the gateway does not check whether the amount sent exceeds the debt, any surplus ETH that is wrapped into WETH remains locked inside the WETHGateway contract after the repayment succeeds. This situation arises whenever a user over‑estimates the amount needed to clear their debt – a common practice when users want to be sure they cover principal and accrued interest – and submits the transaction through the ETH‑based gateway. The affected parties are the individual borrowers who lose the excess ETH, as well as the protocol which ends up holding unrecoverable native balances that break accounting assumptions. The issue was identified during a security audit that compared the behaviour of the standard Morpho.repay function (which does not suffer from this problem) with the gateway‑based variant. It is difficult to notice because the transaction does not revert; it appears successful, yet the user’s wallet balance is reduced by more than the debt cleared, and no error is emitted. From a user‑experience perspective the expectation is that any over‑payment is returned, but instead the user receives nothing back and may see their balance unexpectedly drop to zero for the excess amount. Conceptually, this is an asset‑leakage bug caused by missing refund logic after an over‑payment, a class of vulnerabilities where contracts fail to return surplus funds after a capped operation. The business logic of loan repayment – that the borrower should either repay exactly what is owed or receive any surplus – is violated, leading to potential loss of funds and inaccurate protocol accounting. The recommended remediation is to calculate the difference between the ETH supplied and the amount actually consumed by Morpho’s repay call, then unwrap and transfer the excess back to the sender. Additionally, implementing a skim or rescue function that can sweep any stranded ERC20 or native tokens to a designated recovery address would prevent permanent loss of assets.
summary:
Users can repay WETH Morpho positions with ETH using the WETHGateway. The specified repay amount will be wrapped to WETH before calling the Morpho function to repay the WETH debt. However, the Morpho repay function only pulls in Math.min(_getUserBorrowBalanceFromIndexes(underlying, onBehalf, indexes), amount). If the user specified an amount larger than their debt balance, the excess will be stuck in the WETHGateway contract.
This might be especially confusing for users because the standard Morpho.repay function does not have this issue and they might be used to specifying a large, round value to be sure to repay all principal and accrued debt once the transaction is mined.

title: Morpho can end up in isolation mode
content: The vulnerability originates from Morpho's integration with Aave V3 where the protocol maintains a single shared Aave position for all of its users. Aave V3 introduces the concept of isolated assets and isolation mode: when an isolated asset is supplied as collateral, the entire Aave position is switched into isolation mode and all non‑isolated assets are no longer recognised as collateral, while borrowing is limited to a specific stablecoin debt ceiling. Morpho's internal logic assumes that any supplied token, regardless of its isolation status, can be used as collateral for its users. Consequently, if the Morpho contract ever holds an isolated asset as collateral, Aave silently marks the whole position as isolated, but Morpho continues to treat the non‑isolated assets as usable collateral. This mismatch can be exploited in several ways. An attacker can pre‑send an isolated asset to the contract address before deployment, because Aave marks assets as collateral on transfer, causing the contract to start in isolation mode immediately. The same effect occurs if the first supplier after deployment provides an isolated asset, or later when all non‑isolated collateral is withdrawn or liquidated leaving only an isolated asset. When isolation mode is active, users attempting to borrow stablecoins against their supplied tokens may experience transaction reverts, receive zero amounts, or see their balances unchanged despite a successful supply operation. The impact is that users cannot obtain the expected credit, the protocol may breach its risk parameters, and liquidity could be locked or forced into liquidation. All Morpho participants, including lenders and borrowers, are affected because the shared Aave position governs the entire system. The issue was discovered during a security audit of Morpho's Aave V3 integration, where the auditor noted that the contract never explicitly disables collateral for isolated assets. The problem is hard to notice because the contract's token balances appear normal in the UI, while Aave's internal collateral flag changes without visible indication, leading to a discrepancy between expected and actual borrowing capability. To remediate, the contract should ensure it never holds isolated assets as collateral: for example, supply a known non‑isolated asset at deployment, explicitly call setReserveAsCollateral to turn off collateral for any isolated asset, and add safeguards that reject isolated asset deposits. This class of bug can be described as an isolation‑mode misconfiguration or collateral‑flag mismatch, where business logic assumes universal collateral eligibility but the underlying lending platform enforces stricter isolation rules, resulting in funds appearing to disappear or borrowing failing contrary to user expectations.
summary:
Aave-v3 introduced isolation assets and isolation mode for users:
"Borrowers supplying an isolated asset as collateral cannot supply other assets as collateral (though they can still supply to capture yield). Only stablecoins that have been permitted by Aave governance to be borrowable in isolation the mode can be borrowed by users utilizing isolated collateral up to a specified debt ceiling."
The Morpho contract has a single Aave position for all its users and does therefore not want to end up in isolation mode due to its restrictions. The Morpho code would still treat the supplied non-isolation assets as collateral for their Morpho users, allowing them to borrow against them, but the Aave position does not treat them as collateral anymore. Furthermore, Morpho can only borrow stablecoins up to a certain debt ceiling.
Morpho can be brought into isolation mode:
• Up to deployment, an attacker maliciously sends an isolated asset to the address of the proxy. Aave sets assets as collateral when transferred, such that the Morpho contract already starts out in isolation mode.
This can even happen before deployment by precomputing addresses or simply frontrunning the deployment.
This attack also works if Morpho does not intend to create a market for the isolated asset.
• Upon deployment and market creation: An attacker or unknowing user is the first to supply an asset and this asset is an isolated asset, Morpho's Aave position automatically enters isolation mode.
• At any time if an isolated asset is the only collateral asset. This can happen when collateral assets are turned off on Aave, for example, by withdrawing (or liquidating) the entire balance.

title: Morpho's logic to handle LTV = 0 AToken diverges from the Aave logic and could decrease the user's HF/borrowing power compared to what the same user would have on Aave
content: Morpho implements a special case for assets whose Loan‑to‑Value (LTV) parameter is set to zero on the underlying Aave V3 market. In the current code the function that gathers liquidity data checks the LTV value and, when it equals zero, forces the asset to be treated as non‑collateral by returning a liquidation threshold of zero. This effectively removes the asset from the user’s collateral basket and forces the health‑factor calculation to ignore it. The root cause is a design decision that conflates two distinct Aave states: (1) a zero liquidation threshold, which legitimately disables the asset as collateral, and (2) a zero LTV while the liquidation threshold remains positive, a situation where Aave still counts the asset as collateral but does not increase borrowing power. By applying the same “disable collateral” rule to the second case, Morpho reduces the user’s borrowing capacity, may block legitimate collateral withdrawals, and can push the health factor below safe levels, making the position appear liquidatable even though the same position on Aave would be healthy. An attacker could supply an LTV‑zero token to a Morpho market, causing downstream supply, borrow or liquidation calls to fail for honest users. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are confusing: attempts to withdraw collateral are rejected with no clear error, borrow transactions are denied despite apparent available liquidity, and the health‑factor displayed in the UI drops unexpectedly, sometimes to a value that triggers full‑collateral seizure by a liquidator. The issue was discovered during a security audit (Spearbit) that compared Morpho’s liquidity calculations against Aave’s reference implementation and identified the divergent handling of the LTV‑zero edge case. Because the code path is only exercised for assets with a zero LTV, it may remain unnoticed in normal operation and only surface when such an asset is introduced, making it a subtle accounting bug rather than an outright contract flaw. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “incorrect collateral accounting” bugs, where the protocol’s internal accounting of collateral versus borrowing power does not match the intended financial model. To remediate the problem, Morpho should align its logic with Aave’s specification: when LTV is zero but the liquidation threshold is positive, the asset should remain part of the collateral pool with a zero contribution to the average LTV, preserving withdrawal rights and preventing unnecessary health‑factor degradation. If a different approach is required, the protocol must provide thorough documentation and user warnings describing the edge‑case behavior, so that participants understand the reduced borrowing power and potential liquidation risk associated with LTV‑zero assets.

title: RewardsManager does not take in account users that have supplied collateral directly to the pool
content: The vulnerability resides in the RewardsManager contract, specifically in the internal function that aggregates a user’s asset balances for reward calculation. The function determines the amount of supplied and borrowed assets by querying Morpho’s scaled pool supply balance, but it deliberately omits the separate scaled collateral balance that a user may have deposited directly into the underlying Aave pool. This omission constitutes a logical error: when the asset being evaluated is the market’s aToken, the code should sum both the pool supply balance and the collateral balance, yet it only returns the pool supply component. Consequently, any user who supplies assets solely as collateral – or who holds a significant portion of their position as collateral – is counted as having a lower supplied balance than they actually own. The reward algorithm therefore allocates fewer rewards, and in extreme cases where the user’s only exposure is collateral, the system reports a zero reward entitlement. The bug manifests under the condition that a user’s collateral is recorded in Aave but not mirrored in Morpho’s internal accounting, which is precisely the scenario the RewardsManager is supposed to handle. Affected parties include all participants of the Morpho protocol who rely on accurate reward distribution, particularly lenders who use collateral to secure borrowing. The issue was uncovered during a security audit that examined the reward accounting logic and identified the missing call to the scaledCollateralBalance function. It can be difficult to notice because the UI may simply display a lower or null reward amount without indicating a calculation error, and the user’s collateral remains locked, giving the false impression that the protocol is functioning correctly. The impact is economic: users receive fewer tokens than they are entitled to, eroding trust and potentially causing financial loss. To remediate the problem, the reward calculation should be amended so that when the asset equals the market’s aToken, the user’s balance is computed as the sum of both the scaled pool supply balance and the scaled collateral balance, ensuring that all supplied assets are accounted for in the reward formula. This correction aligns the implementation with the intended accounting model, where every unit of collateral contributes proportionally to reward eligibility, and restores the expected behavior that users receive rewards commensurate with their total supplied value.
summary: Inside RewardsManager._getUserAssetBalances Morpho is calculating the amount of the supplied and borrowed balance for a specific user. In the current implementation, Morpho is ignoring the amount that the user has supplied as collateral directly into the Aave pool. As a consequence, the user will be eligible for fewer rewards or even zero in the case where he/she has supplied only collateral.

title: FullMath requires overflow behavior
content: The vulnerability is an arithmetic overflow handling mismatch introduced when FullMath.sol, originally written for Solidity versions that performed unchecked arithmetic, was copied into a contract compiled with Solidity 0.8. Solidity 0.8 automatically inserts overflow checks and reverts the transaction when a uint256 operation exceeds its maximum value. FullMath’s internal mulDiv and other helper functions rely on the natural wrap‑around of uint256 to produce correct results for very large intermediate values. Because the migrated code does not wrap the critical calculations in an unchecked block, any overflow causes an unexpected revert. This can be triggered during normal operation of the SwapManagerUniV3 contract when it calculates the amount of token out for a given amount in, especially for large trade sizes or when price ticks are extreme. When the overflow occurs, the transaction aborts, the swap does not complete, and the user sees no token received while the input token may have already been transferred, effectively resulting in a loss of funds or a stuck transaction. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the original FullMath implementation with the migrated version and noticed the missing unchecked statements. It is hard to notice because the contract behaves correctly for typical trade sizes; only edge‑case values cause the revert, which may be reproduced only with specially crafted inputs. The bug belongs to the class of unchecked arithmetic required after migration or overflow‑dependent logic broken by compiler safety checks. To fix the problem the FullMath library should be imported from the official 0.8 branch where the arithmetic that may overflow is explicitly placed inside an unchecked { … } block, or the developer should add unchecked blocks around the vulnerable calculations. After fixing, swaps will no longer revert on overflow, the expected output amount will be returned, and users will receive the correct token balances as advertised.
summary: UniswapV3’s FullMath.sol is copied and migrated from an old solidity version to version 0.8 which reverts on overflows but the old FullMath relies on the implicit overflow behavior. The current code will revert on overflows when it should not, breaking the SwapManagerUniV3 contract.

title: Morpho’s USDT mainnet market can end up in broken state
content: The vulnerability is a token‑allowance handling flaw that can leave Morpho’s USDT market on Ethereum in a permanently broken state. USDT is a non‑standard ERC20 implementation that requires an allowance to be reset to zero before it can be changed to a new non‑zero value. In the internal function that repays ERC20 tokens to the Aave pool, the contract first calls approve for the full amount that the caller wants to repay. Immediately afterwards the code reduces the actual transfer amount with a Math.min operation, so the token transfer may be smaller than the approved amount. Because the allowance is now larger than the amount actually moved, a non‑zero allowance remains on the USDT token contract. Any subsequent call that tries to adjust the allowance – for example another repay or a supply operation – triggers USDT’s strict approve logic, which reverts when the current allowance is non‑zero. As a result, users are unable to call most functions of the Morpho USDT market; transactions revert with an approval‑reset error, the UI shows failed actions, and balances appear unchanged even though the user attempted an operation. The issue occurs only when the repay (or supply) path reduces the transferred amount compared to the approved amount, which is common for USDT because of its rounding or fee behavior. It affects every participant that interacts with the USDT market – lenders, borrowers, and the protocol itself – because the market becomes unusable and funds may become effectively locked. The flaw was discovered during a manual security review that examined token‑specific behavior and identified that the code assumed standard ERC20 semantics. It is hard to notice because the first approve call succeeds, and the failure only appears on a later transaction that tries to modify the allowance again, producing a generic revert that does not clearly point to the allowance issue.
