The proper mitigation is to use a safe‑approve pattern: before setting a new allowance, first reset the existing allowance to zero, or ensure that the exact amount approved is always transferred so that the allowance is cleared automatically. Alternatively, the contract could use increaseAllowance/decreaseAllowance functions or a pull‑based transfer that does not rely on changing allowances for USDT. Implementing one of these fixes restores the ability for users to repay, supply, or withdraw without hitting the approval‑reset restriction, thereby preserving the intended business logic of accurate accounting and fund availability.
summary: Note that USDT on Ethereum mainnet is non-standard and requires resetting the approval to zero (see USDT L199) before being able to change it again. In _repayERC20ToPool, it could be that _amount is approved but then _amount = Math.min(...) only repays a smaller amount, meaning there remains a non-zero approval for Aave. Any further _repayERC20ToPool/_supplyERC20ToPool calls will then revert in the approve call. Users cannot interact with most functions of the Morpho USDT market anymore.

title: Wrong reserve factor computation on P2P rates
content: The vulnerability consists of an incorrect application of the reserve factor when calculating peer‑to‑peer (P2P) supply and borrow rates in the Morpho protocol. Instead of applying the reserve factor only to the spread between the underlying pool’s supply and borrow rates, the code multiplies the entire mean rate (meanSPY) by a factor that includes the reserve factor. The faulty formulas are: supplyP2PSPY = (meanSPY * (MAX_BASIS_POINTS - reserveFactor)) / MAX_BASIS_POINTS and borrowP2PSPY = (meanSPY * (MAX_BASIS_POINTS + reserveFactor)) / MAX_BASIS_POINTS. Because the reserve factor is applied to the whole rate, suppliers are charged a higher fee and borrowers receive a higher cost than intended, resulting in P2P rates that can be worse than the raw pool rates. This miscalculation can be exploited simply by interacting with the protocol as usual: any user who supplies assets will earn a lower APY than advertised, and any borrower will pay a higher APR than expected, without any explicit malicious transaction. The impact is economic loss for both lenders and borrowers, eroding the incentive to use Morpho’s P2P market and potentially reducing overall protocol adoption. The bug manifests whenever the protocol computes P2P rates, i.e., on each supply or borrow operation across all markets that use the reserve factor. It affects all participants—individual users, liquidity providers, and borrowers—who rely on the protocol’s promise of better rates than the underlying pool. The issue was discovered during a security audit performed by Spearbit, which identified the logical error in the rate‑calculation routine. The problem is subtle because the displayed rates may still appear reasonable, and the discrepancy only becomes evident when comparing the effective return or cost against the pool’s baseline rates; users may notice their balances growing slower or their borrowing costs higher, but the UI does not highlight the mis‑applied fee. The bug belongs to the class of fee‑miscalculation or scaling‑factor errors, where a parameter intended to affect only a margin is mistakenly applied to the full value, breaking accounting assumptions that the reserve factor should only reduce the spread. To remediate, the computation should be rewritten so that the reserve factor is applied exclusively to the difference between the pool’s supply and borrow rates, preserving the intended fee structure while keeping the base mean rate unchanged. Conceptually, the fix involves calculating the spread, applying the reserve factor to that spread, and then adjusting the supply and borrow rates accordingly, ensuring that suppliers receive at least the pool supply rate minus the appropriate fee and borrowers pay at most the pool borrow rate plus the appropriate fee. This correction restores the economic guarantees of the protocol and aligns user expectations with actual outcomes.
summary:
The reserve factor is taken on the entire P2P supply and borrow rates instead of just on the spread of the pool rates. It’s currently overcharging suppliers and borrowers and making it possible to earn a worse rate on Morpho than the pool rates.
```solidity
supplyP2PSPY[_marketAddress] =
(meanSPY * (MAX_BASIS_POINTS - reserveFactor[_marketAddress])) /
MAX_BASIS_POINTS;
borrowP2PSPY[_marketAddress] =
(meanSPY * (MAX_BASIS_POINTS + reserveFactor[_marketAddress])) /
MAX_BASIS_POINTS;
```

title: SwapManager assumes Morpho token is token0 of every token pair
content: The vulnerability resides in the price‑consultation routine of the SwapManager contract, which calculates the expected amount of Morpho tokens when a user claims rewards. The routine makes a hard‑coded assumption that the Morpho token is always the first token (token0) in the Uniswap‑style token pair that also contains the reward token. This assumption is the root cause of the bug: the contract never checks the actual ordering of the two tokens in the pair, nor does it retrieve the correct reserve values based on the real token0/token1 layout. Because of this, when a pair is deployed where Morpho is token1, the consult function reads the reserves in the wrong direction and produces an inverted price. The inverted price is then fed into a slippage check that expects the amountOut to be within a certain tolerance. Since the calculated amount is far from the true value, the slippage check fails and the transaction reverts. An attacker or a careless deployer can therefore create or select a pair with Morpho as token1, causing any call to the reward‑claiming path to revert. From the user’s perspective the claim transaction simply fails, often with a generic “revert” error, and the expected reward never arrives, leaving the user’s balance unchanged. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition for reward claims, which can effectively freeze users’ earned Morpho tokens and undermine confidence in the protocol. The issue appears only when the token ordering does not match the hard‑coded expectation, making it easy to miss during testing if only one pair configuration is examined. It was discovered during a manual security audit that compared the consult implementation with the reference UniswapV2 oracle pattern. To remediate, the contract should dynamically determine which reserve corresponds to Morpho by querying token0 and token1 of the pair, then compute the price using the correct reserve values, following the UniswapV2 oracle example. Callers of the consult function must also be updated to handle the corrected amountOut semantics, ensuring that the returned value represents Morpho tokens regardless of token ordering. This class of bug—an incorrect assumption about token ordering in a pair—can lead to price inversion, slippage failures, and ultimately a loss of functionality for users expecting to receive rewards.
summary: The consult function wrongly assumes that the Morpho token is always the first token (token0) in the Morpho <> Reward token token pair. This could lead to inverted prices and a denial of service attack when claiming rewards as the wrongly calculated expected amount slippage check reverts.

title: SwapManager fails at updating TWAP
content: The vulnerability is a logical error in the time‑weighted average price (TWAP) update routine of the SwapManager contract. The update function checks the elapsed time since the last TWAP calculation and returns early when the elapsed time is greater than or equal to the configured TWAP period. Because the condition is inverted, once the elapsed time exceeds the period the function exits without recomputing the TWAP, leaving the stored price permanently stale. This stale price is later used in the reward‑claiming path to compute the expected amount of tokens and to enforce a slippage check. When the TWAP no longer reflects the current market, the calculated expected amount deviates from the actual amount, causing the slippage verification to fail and the transaction to revert. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition: users attempting to claim accrued rewards experience a revert with a slippage error, effectively preventing them from receiving any rewards despite having earned them. The issue manifests only after the first full TWAP period has elapsed without an update, which can happen naturally as time passes or be accelerated by an attacker who deliberately avoids calling the update function. All participants who rely on reward claims – token holders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the protocol cannot distribute rewards, breaking its economic incentives. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the update logic and identified the inverted time comparison as a deviation from the intended design. It can be hard to notice because the contract continues to operate normally until the period expires, at which point the failure appears as a generic slippage revert rather than an obvious TWAP‑staleness bug. The correct fix is to invert the condition so that the function proceeds only when at least one full period has elapsed, ensuring the TWAP is refreshed before it is used for reward calculations. In broader terms, this is a class of time‑based state‑staleness bugs where an early‑return guard prevents essential state updates, leading to incorrect accounting and potential denial‑of‑service. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a non‑zero pending reward balance, but the transaction to claim those rewards reverts with a slippage error, violating the expectation that rewards can be claimed at any time.
summary: The update function returns early without updating the TWAP if the elapsed time is past the TWAP period. Meaning, once the TWAP period passed the TWAP is stale and forever represents an old value. This could lead to a denial of service attack when claiming rewards as the wrongly calculated expected amount slippage check reverts.

title: P2P rate can be manipulated as it’s a lazy-updated snapshot
content: The vulnerability concerns the way the Morpho protocol derives its peer‑to‑peer (P2P) interest rate from Aave. The contract stores a snapshot of the Aave supply and borrow rates and only recomputes the P2P rate when a user interacts with Morpho. The snapshot is calculated by taking the instantaneous liquidity rate and variable borrow rate from Aave, averaging them and dividing by the number of seconds in a year. Because the snapshot is lazy‑updated, an attacker can temporarily distort the underlying Aave rates – for example by depositing a large amount of capital to raise the liquidity rate or by borrowing heavily to push the variable borrow rate upward – and then trigger a Morpho interaction that calls the internal _updateSPYs function. At that moment the manipulated rates are captured and become the new P2P rate. The attacker can then open or refinance P2P positions at an artificially inflated rate, earning excess interest while other users receive lower returns than advertised. The impact is a mis‑allocation of interest, potential loss of protocol revenue, and users seeing an APY that looks attractive but later reverts, causing their balances to grow slower than expected or even to shrink relative to the promised rate. The issue appears mainly in markets with low activity, where the snapshot may remain unchanged for long periods, giving an attacker ample time to manipulate the rates before the next update. It affects any participant that supplies or borrows through Morpho, as well as the protocol’s overall financial health. The problem was discovered during a security audit that examined the rate‑updating logic and noticed that the contract trusts a single, instantaneous Aave snapshot instead of a time‑averaged value. The bug is subtle because the UI shows the current P2P APY, which may look correct at the moment of manipulation, and there is no obvious on‑chain flag indicating that the rate is based on a stale or manipulated snapshot. To remediate, the protocol should replace the instantaneous snapshot with a time‑weighted average rate (TWAR) oracle that aggregates Aave rates over a defined window, and it should ensure that the P2P rate is refreshed regularly, independent of user interactions, so that it cannot diverge from the underlying market for extended periods.

title: Liquidating Morpho’s Aave position leads to state desynchronization
content: The vulnerability is a state‑synchronization bug that occurs when Morpho’s single aggregated position on Aave is liquidated. Morpho aggregates all individual user deposits and borrows into one Aave loan, and it keeps an internal ledger that maps each user’s collateral and debt to that aggregated loan. The liquidation routine that interacts with Aave only updates the external Aave position and does not correctly adjust the internal per‑user accounting. As a result, after a liquidation event the internal ledger still reflects the pre‑liquidation amounts while the actual Aave loan has been reduced or closed. This mismatch can be triggered whenever the aggregated position becomes under‑collateralised and a liquidator calls the Aave liquidation function. An attacker can deliberately cause the liquidation, then attempt a second liquidation on the same stale state to extract additional profit (double‑liquidation). For honest users the symptom is that attempts to withdraw collateral or repay debt through Morpho either revert or return zero, even though the UI shows a positive balance. Users expect to be able to retrieve their funds after repayment, but the protocol silently blocks the operation because the internal state no longer matches the real Aave position. The issue was discovered during a security audit by Spearbit, which noticed that the liquidation path does not invoke the internal state‑update hooks. The bug is hard to notice because the aggregated position appears healthy on‑chain and the per‑user balances look correct until a withdrawal or repayment is attempted. The class of bug is an accounting desynchronization after an external protocol interaction, similar to “state inconsistency” or “invariant violation” bugs. To remediate, the liquidation logic must be extended to reconcile the internal ledger with the external Aave state, or the protocol should prevent liquidation of the aggregated position from breaking core user functions. Proper checks, re‑entrancy‑safe updates, and tests that verify per‑user balances after any external liquidation are required to ensure that user funds remain accessible and that double‑liquidation cannot be performed.
summary: Morpho has a single position on Aave that encompasses all of Morpho’s individual user positions that are on the pool. When this Aave Morpho position is liquidated the user position state tracked in Morpho desynchronize from the actual Aave position. This leads to issues when users try to withdraw their collateral or repay their debt from Morpho. It’s also possible to double-liquidate for a profit.

title: Liquidating Morpho's Aave position leads to state desync
content: The vulnerability is a state‑desynchronisation bug that appears when Morpho’s aggregated Aave position is liquidated. Morpho aggregates all individual user deposits and borrows into a single Aave loan and keeps an internal ledger that mirrors the Aave balance for each user. When the aggregated position is liquidated, Aave updates its own collateral and debt values, but Morpho does not adjust its internal accounting to reflect those changes. As a result the internal user‑state (how much collateral each user is entitled to withdraw and how much debt they owe) no longer matches the real Aave position. This mismatch can be triggered by an attacker who forces liquidation – for example by manipulating the price feed that determines the health factor – and then exploits the stale internal balances. Because Morpho believes the user still owns collateral that has already been seized by the liquidator, the attacker can request a withdrawal that either returns zero or, in the worst case, can trigger a second liquidation on the same underlying assets for additional profit (double‑liquidation). The impact is that honest users may be unable to withdraw their collateral, may see their debt incorrectly reported, or may lose funds altogether, while the protocol may suffer financial loss from over‑ or under‑liquidation. The bug manifests only after a liquidation event; under normal deposit/withdraw cycles the internal and external states stay aligned, making the problem hard to notice without deliberately testing liquidation paths. The issue was discovered during a security audit by Spearbit, which identified that the core functionality of Morpho – allowing users to withdraw or repay – breaks when the underlying Aave position is liquidated. The root cause is an accounting inconsistency: Morpho assumes the aggregated Aave position is immutable with respect to liquidation, while Aave’s liquidation logic can change the underlying balances without notifying Morpho. From a user’s perspective the symptom is a failed withdrawal (the UI shows “insufficient collateral” or returns zero) or an unexpected debt amount after a liquidation event, contrary to the expectation that their funds remain accessible. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of cross‑protocol state‑sync failures, where a contract’s internal representation diverges from the external protocol after an event such as liquidation, flash loan, or re‑balancing. To remediate the issue Morpho should either prevent the aggregated Aave position from being liquidated, or implement a robust sync routine that updates every user’s internal balance immediately after any external state change, including liquidation, ensuring that withdrawal and repayment logic always reflects the true on‑chain state.
summary: Morpho has a single position on Aave that encompasses all of Morpho's individual user positions that are on the pool. When this Aave Morpho position is liquidated the user position state tracked in Morpho desyncs from the actual Aave position. This leads to issues when users try to withdraw their collateral or repay their debt from Morpho. It's also possible to double-liquidate for a profit.

title: Anyone can use or steal ArbitrumSwaps native asset balance
content: The vulnerability is an unauthorized withdrawal of the native asset balance held by the ArbitrumSwaps router contract. Theroot cause is that the stargateSwap function forwards the refund address parameter to the Stargate router as address(this), causing any native asset that is refunded by the external router to be deposited into the ArbitrumSwaps contract itself. The contract was designed under the assumption that it would never hold native assets, so no protective checks are in place for outgoing transfers of that balance. An attacker can exploit this by first triggering a swap that generates a refund, which is automatically credited to the router contract, and then immediately back‑running a call to the arbitrumSwaps method with the steps WETH_DEPOSIT and WETH_WITHDRAW, supplying a malicious destination address. Because the contract treats its own balance as freely withdrawable, the call transfers the entire native asset balance to the attacker‑controlled address. The impact is the loss of any native assets that happen to be held by the router, effectively making funds disappear from the protocol’s accounting and leaving users without the expected refund. This condition occurs whenever the stargateSwap function is used with the default refund address set to the contract itself, which is the current implementation. All participants that rely on the router for swaps – including end‑users, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the contract’s balance can be drained without authorization. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the refund handling logic and identified the mismatch between the contract’s assumed statelessness and its actual stateful balance. The problem is subtle because the router is not expected to display a native balance, so a non‑zero balance may go unnoticed, and there are no explicit events or checks that flag an unexpected transfer. To remediate the issue, the refund address should be changed from address(this) to msg.sender, ensuring that any refunded native assets are sent directly back to the caller rather than being retained by the router. Additionally, the contract could include explicit safeguards that reject outgoing transfers when the balance originates from a refund, or enforce that the router never holds native assets. This class of bug falls under improper handling of external refunds and unauthorized asset extraction, where business logic assumes a stateless contract but the implementation inadvertently creates a stateful balance that can be abused.
summary: An attacker can steal the ArbitrumSwaps native asset balance by doing a call to the arbitrumSwaps method with steps WETH_DEPOSIT and WETH_WITHDRAW - this will send over the whole contract balance to a caller-supplied address. This shouldn't be a problem, because the contract is a "swap router" and is not expected to hold any native asset balance at any time. Well this assumption does not hold, because in the stargateSwap method the _refundAddress argument of the swap method call to the stargateRouter is address(this). This means that all of the native asset that is refunded will be held by the ArbitrumSwaps contract and an attacker can back-run this refund and steal the balance.

title: Last NFT from the supply can't be minted
content: The vulnerability is an off‑by‑one error in the supply‑cap check of the mint and mintPhysical functions. The contract uses the condition nextId + amount >= MAX_SUPPLY to decide whether to revert with ExceedsMaxSupply. Because the comparison includes the equal sign, a transaction that would exactly fill the remaining supply (for example when nextId equals MAX_SUPPLY‑1 and amount is 1) is incorrectly rejected. The root cause is a boundary‑condition mistake: the logic should allow the sum to be equal to MAX_SUPPLY and only revert when it exceeds the maximum. An attacker or any user can trigger the bug simply by attempting to mint the last available NFT; the transaction reverts, the user receives no token, and the expected minting event does not occur. The impact is that the contract can never reach its declared maximum supply, leading to a permanent shortfall of tokens, potential loss of revenue for the protocol, and a poor user experience where a user expects to receive the final NFT but gets a revert error. The issue occurs only under the specific condition where the next token identifier is one less than the maximum and the mint amount is exactly one, making it easy to miss in casual testing but detectable with edge‑case unit tests. All participants who intend to acquire the final token—regular users, collectors, and the protocol itself—are affected because the contract’s accounting assumes that MAX_SUPPLY tokens can be minted, which is violated by this bug. The problem was discovered during a security audit when a test case attempted to mint all but one token and then the last one, observing the unexpected revert. It is hard to notice because typical minting flows rarely target the exact boundary, and the revert message ExceedsMaxSupply appears legitimate, masking the logical flaw. The correct fix is to change the comparison to nextId + amount > MAX_SUPPLY, thereby allowing the final token to be minted while still preventing any overflow beyond the declared cap. This class of bug belongs to off‑by‑one or boundary‑condition errors in supply‑limit enforcement, which can cause accounting inconsistencies and denial‑of‑service style failures where legitimate minting requests are blocked.
summary: Currently both the mint and mintPhysical methods have the following check: if (nextId + amount >= MAX_SUPPLY) revert ExceedsMaxSupply(); This is incorrect, as even when the nextId is MAX_SUPPLY - 1 then an amount of 1 should be allowed but with the current check the code will revert. This is due to the equal sign in the check, which shouldn't be there. Here is a Proof of Concept unit test demonstrating the issue (add it to MuseumOfMahomes.t.sol): function testNotAllNFTsCanBeMinted() public { museum.setPrice(PRICE); uint256 allButOneNFTSupply = 3089; // mint all but one from the NFT `MAX_SUPPLY` (3090) museum.mint{value: allButOneNFTSupply * PRICE}(address(this), allButOneNFTSupply); require(allButOneNFTSupply == museum.balanceOf(address(this)), "Mint did not work"); // try to mint the last NFT from the supply, but it doesn't work vm.expectRevert(MuseumOfMahomes.ExceedsMaxSupply.selector); museum.mint{value: PRICE}(address(this), 1);

title: Lack of deadline in PowerToken.buy can lead to user's cashToken being distributed through ZeroToken holders
content: The vulnerability resides in the PowerToken.buy function, which implements a Dutch‑auction style token purchase but does not enforce any deadline on when the transaction must be executed. Because the price of the token is a deterministic function of block.timestamp, the absence of a deadline allows a transaction that is signed and approved by a user to remain pending in the mempool indefinitely and later be mined in a completely different auction round where the price has risen dramatically. The root cause is the missing timestamp check; the contract assumes that a call will be executed in the same auction in which it was submitted, but it never validates that the current block time is still within the intended auction window. An attacker, typically a holder of ZeroToken who benefits from fees collected in the vault, can monitor the mempool for stuck buy transactions, wait until a new auction starts with a much higher price, and then include the original transaction in a Flashbots bundle. When the transaction finally executes, the user’s approved cashToken (e.g., WETH) is transferred at the new, higher price, often many times the amount the user expected. The WETH is deposited into a vault that distributes fees among ZeroToken holders, so the user suffers a large loss while the attacker and other ZeroToken holders receive a proportional share. This scenario can occur whenever a user submits a buy order with a low gas price or during network congestion, causing the transaction to linger for hours, days, or even weeks. All participants who rely on the buy function – individual traders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the economic model of the auction is broken; users expect to pay a price that was visible at the time of submission, but the contract delivers a different outcome. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the function’s parameters and identified the lack of a deadline field. It is hard to notice because the transaction may still emit a successful purchase event, yet the user’s wallet shows a far larger deduction than anticipated, and the UI may not highlight the price discrepancy. To remediate, the function should accept a deadline argument and enforce block.timestamp < deadline, optionally also checking that the cost does not exceed a user‑specified maximum amount. This change restores the intended invariant that a purchase must be executed within the same auction window, preventing replay in later auctions and protecting users from unintended overpayment.
summary:
The function PowerToken.buy is used to purchase tokens in auction. The price of those tokens decreases with time, following a dutch auction model. Because there's no deadline parameter in the function call, it's possible to retain this transaction and execute it in a subsequent auction at a steeper price, potentially resulting in a significant loss to the user, considering the price in an auction starts at 2^99 wei per supply basis point. Here's a likely scenario:
1. Auction A starts. Let's assume that cashToken is WETH.
2. Nobody buys the tokens until the price becomes more reasonable. For example, 1 ether per bps.
3. Alice max-approves the spending of her WETH for the PowerToken contract to transfer them. Alice holds 100 WETH in her wallet.
4. Alice tries to buy the tokens, but ends up paying a very low fee and the transaction ends up not being picked up for execution. In the meantime, market fees rise and the transaction gets stuck in the mempool. This is not uncommon, and there are thousands of mempool transactions with over a month.
5. A new auction B eventually starts. Starting price is the same.
6. A ZeroToken holder Bob submits Alice's transaction inside a flashbots bundle. Bob does this when the price is 100 ether per bps.
7. Alice ends up buying the desired amount of PowerToken. However, the price was much larger than she wanted, and she ended up spending 100 times more.
8. The WETH falls into the vault, where both Bob and the other ZeroToken holders will be able to claim their fair share. It should be noted that, in theory, all ZeroToken holders have an economic incentive to be on the look for these buying attempts that get stuck on the mempool.

title: Validator signature with zero timestamp can always be replayed
content: The vulnerability consists of a replayable validator signature when the signed timestamp is zero. The contract’s updateCollateral function relies on the smallest timestamp among a set of validator signatures to enforce a staleness check, rejecting updates that appear older than the last recorded update. However, the signature verification routine explicitly ignores zero values when computing the minimum timestamp, treating them as absent. Consequently, if all (or a sufficient number of) validator signatures contain a zero timestamp, the computed minimum defaults to the current block timestamp, which always satisfies the staleness condition. This logical flaw allows a minter to reuse the same set of signatures to repeatedly claim that its collateral amount remains unchanged, even after the real‑world collateral has been withdrawn. An attacker can therefore add a large amount of off‑chain collateral, record it on‑chain via updateCollateral with zero‑timestamp signatures, later redeem the off‑chain assets, and then replay the same signatures to convince the protocol that the collateral is still present. The protocol will then permit the minter to mint the maximum allowed amount of the associated token, effectively creating tokens backed by no actual collateral. The issue manifests whenever updateCollateral is called with validator signatures that include a zero timestamp, which the protocol currently permits. It affects any minter who can obtain such signatures, the overall protocol’s economic security, and token holders who rely on the collateralisation guarantees. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit by ThreeSigma, where the interaction between the min‑timestamp calculation and the zero‑timestamp handling was examined. The problem is subtle because the zero timestamp is technically a valid value according to the signature schema, and the staleness check appears to function correctly for non‑zero timestamps, making the replay possibility easy to overlook. To remediate, the contract should reject any validator signature that carries a zero timestamp, for example by adding an explicit revert when a zero timestamp is encountered during signature verification. Enforcing a non‑zero timestamp restores the intended monotonic increase of the update timestamp and prevents replay attacks, thereby preserving the integrity of the collateral accounting and the token’s backing.
summary:
When calling MinterGateway.updateCollateral, an array of timestamps gets passed. That is because the digest signed by a validator includes an updating timestamp. The minimum timestamp between the signatures will be used as the new collateral update timestamp. This is used to check for staleness, which also has the side effect of preventing replaying a set of signatures: function _updateCollateral(address minter_, uint240 amount_, uint40 newTimestamp_) internal { uint40 lastUpdateTimestamp_ = _minterStates[minter_].updateTimestamp; // MinterGateway already has more recent collateral update if (newTimestamp_ < lastUpdateTimestamp_) revert StaleCollateralUpdate(newTimestamp_, lastUpdateTimestamp_); _minterStates[minter_].collateral = amount_; _minterStates[minter_].updateTimestamp = newTimestamp_; } The issue arises when a timestamp signed by a validator is zero. This is explicitly allowed by the validator signature verification, which ignores zero values: // Find minimum between all valid timestamps for valid signatures. minTimestamp_ = UIntMath.min40IgnoreZero(minTimestamp_, UIntMath.safe40(timestamps_[index_])); In the extreme scenario where every validator signature of the array has a zero timestamp, minTimestamp_ will be block.timestamp, which will always pass the staleness check. This means that an array of signatures with zero timestamps can be replayed as many times as a minter wants, thus achieving a way for updating its collateral to that same value in the future, regardless of whether or not that's still true in the off-chain world. A minter could do the following:
1. Add a very large amount of real world collateral. Let's say $10M.
2. Call updateCollateral with the right amount. Let's assume validators will have signed with a zero timestamp, which is explicitly allowed by the protocol.
3. Redeem the entire real world collateral.
4. Call updateCollateral by replaying the original validator signatures. The protocol will still think the minter has all the collateral.
5. Mint the maximum allowed amount of MToken. Sell them somewhere at market price. In a less extreme scenario where only 1 validator signs with a zero timestamp, we can still say that this specific signature can be reused anytime in the future, as long as the same collateral value is being used and that validator continues being approved by the TTG. The previous scenario can still be achieved if a minter rightfully calls updateCollateral multiple times with the same amount and rotates the validators until they finally get enough zero timestamp signatures from different validators.

title: Malicious user can easily make the protocol revert on every USDT swap on Uniswap
content: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that occurs when the contract attempts to approve USDT tokens using the contract’s current USDT balance as the allowance amount. USDT implements a non‑standard ERC20 approve function that only allows a non‑zero allowance to be set when the previous allowance is exactly zero; otherwise the call reverts. The contract’s swap logic in UniswapAdapter.sol calls TransferHelper.safeApprove with IERC20(token).balanceOf(address(this)) as the amount, which for USDT becomes the exact token balance held by the contract. An attacker can exploit this by sending a single wei of USDT to the contract and then invoking a swap. The first swap succeeds because the allowance is set from zero to one wei (plus a negligible epsilon). After the swap, the contract’s USDT balance remains one wei, so the next call to safeApprove tries to set the allowance to the same non‑zero value while the existing allowance is already non‑zero. USDT’s approve implementation rejects this and the transaction reverts, causing every subsequent USDT swap on Uniswap to fail. This effect is a classic approval race condition that results in a protocol‑wide denial of service for USDT swaps. The impact is that any user attempting to swap USDT through the ArbitrumSwaps contract will see their transaction revert, receiving no output and potentially losing confidence in the protocol. The issue manifests only after a malicious user performs the described steps; under normal operation with no external USDT deposits the contract behaves correctly, which makes the bug hard to notice during standard testing. The root cause is the use of the token’s balance as the approved allowance instead of the intended amountIn parameter, violating USDT’s special approval rules. The bug was discovered during a security audit that examined token interaction patterns and identified the known USDT approve edge case. To remediate, the contract should approve either the exact amountIn supplied by the caller or a maximum allowance (type(uint256).max) after first resetting any existing allowance to zero, thereby complying with USDT’s approve semantics and preventing the denial‑of‑service scenario. This class of bug falls under improper token allowance handling for non‑standard ERC20 implementations, where using dynamic values such as balances can lead to unexpected reverts and broken business logic, such as missing refunds or zero‑output swaps that contradict user expectations.
summary:
A malicious user can get the ArbitrumSwaps contract to revert on each USDT swap on Uniswap, because of a well-known attack vector of the token implementation. The problem is in the following code from UniswapAdapter.sol and is present in both swapExactInputSingle and swapExactInputMultihop TransferHelper.safeApprove( swapParams.token1, address(swapRouter), IERC20(swapParams.token1).balanceOf(address(this)) Here is how the attack can be done:
1. Malicious user transfers manually 1 wei of USDT to ArbitrumSwaps
2. Now he calls ArbitrumSwaps::arbitrumSwaps with step == UNI_SINGLE to swap 1 USDT
3. Now swapExactInputSingle approves 1 + 1e-18 USDT, because of the balanceOf call
4. Transaction will complete successfully, but next time anyone wants to swap USDT on Uniswap the transaction will revert, because of USDT approval race condition - to do an approve call the allowance should be either 0 or type(uint256).max, which is not the case because allowance is 1 wei

title: Cool-off period for deposits in swap pools can be bypassed
content: The vulnerability concerns a swap pool that imposes a cool‑off period on newly deposited liquidity before the tokens become withdrawable through a backstop pool. The contract records the block number of the last deposit for each address, but it does not update this timestamp when the LP tokens are transferred to another address. As a result, an attacker or any user can deposit liquidity, receive LP tokens, and then immediately transfer those tokens to a different address. Because the recipient’s latestDepositAtBlockNo value remains unchanged, the backstop pool treats the transferred tokens as if they were never subject to the cool‑off, allowing an instant withdrawal. This bypass defeats the intended economic safeguard that prevents rapid exit after a deposit, effectively letting users withdraw funds without waiting the prescribed number of blocks. The impact is that funds can be drained from the pool much faster than expected, breaking the accounting assumptions of the protocol and potentially leading to liquidity shortages or unfair advantage for users who exploit the transfer. The issue manifests whenever a deposit is followed by an LP token transfer before the cool‑off expires, affecting any participant who holds or receives LP tokens. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the interaction between the deposit logic and the ERC‑20 transfer mechanism, noting that the internal _transfer hook does not propagate the deposit timestamp. The bug is subtle because the contract still enforces the cool‑off for direct withdrawals by the original depositor, so casual testing that only checks the depositor’s own balance may not reveal the problem. To remediate, the contract should either override the token transfer function to also update the recipient’s latestDepositAtBlockNo, or, more robustly, maintain a per‑address accounting of the amount of tokens that are currently in cool‑off together with the block number of the most recent deposit or inbound transfer. This ensures that any address receiving LP tokens inherits the appropriate waiting period, preserving the intended withdrawal restrictions and preventing immediate backstop withdrawals after a transfer. The fix must be implemented in a way that does not open a denial‑of‑service vector where tiny token amounts could be used to block legitimate withdrawals. Overall, the bug belongs to the class of “state‑inconsistent token transfer” vulnerabilities where auxiliary accounting data is not synchronized with token ownership changes, leading to bypasses of time‑based restrictions and unintended fund loss.
summary: Deposits into the swap pool are subject to a cool-off period before being available for withdrawal via the backstop pool. However, this restriction can be bypassed by transferring the LP tokens received from the deposit to another address.

title: Stale share price usage leading to fund loss and unfair distribution
content: The vulnerability is a stale share‑price usage bug that appears in the deposit and withdrawal logic of the ETH and USD vault contracts. The contracts keep a single sharePrice variable that reflects the value of one share in terms of the underlying asset. This variable is updated only when external yield events are processed, but the internal functions that handle user deposits, withdrawals, and LayerZero fee quotations do not refresh sharePrice before performing arithmetic. As a result, when a user initiates a withdrawal after the protocol has earned additional yield – for example, Lido rewards for ETH or interest on sDAI for USD – the contract still uses the old sharePrice to compute the amount of assets to return. The user therefore receives fewer tokens than they are mathematically entitled to, creating a shortfall that accumulates over time and leads to unfair distribution of shares among participants. The issue is discovered during a manual audit that compared the timing of reward accruals with the share‑price calculations in the code. It is hard to notice because the contract does not emit explicit warnings when the price is outdated, and the discrepancy may be small on a per‑transaction basis, only becoming evident after many withdrawals. The impact is a loss of funds for honest users, a distortion of the accounting model that assumes each share represents a constant proportion of the pool, and a potential erosion of trust in the protocol. The bug manifests whenever a user action that depends on sharePrice occurs without a preceding update – i.e., during deposits, withdrawals, or when quoting LayerZero fees – and the pool’s underlying assets have changed in value between the request and execution. Affected parties include any depositor or withdrawer, the protocol’s revenue model, and any downstream contracts that rely on correct share accounting. To remediate, the contract should recalculate and store the current sharePrice at the beginning of every function that performs share‑based arithmetic, or alternatively use a view function that fetches the latest price from a reliable source each time. This aligns the implementation with the intended business logic that each share always represents the up‑to‑date value of the underlying assets, preventing fund disappearance and ensuring fair distribution.

title: Arithmetic underflow in total balance calculation
content: The vulnerability is an arithmetic underflow in the calculation of the total ETH balance that is used to derive the share price for deposited assets. The contract computes the balance with the expression "ethDeposited - ethWithdrawn + rewardsClaimed" which, due to left‑to‑right evaluation of unsigned integers, first subtracts the amount withdrawn from the amount deposited. When the withdrawn amount exceeds the deposited amount – a situation that naturally occurs as users withdraw both principal and earned rewards – the subtraction underflows to a very large number before the rewards are added back. This underflow corrupts the total balance, causing the subsequent share price formula to use an incorrect denominator. The root cause is the ordering of arithmetic operations on unsigned 256‑bit integers without protective checks, a classic precedence‑related underflow bug. An attacker or any user who triggers a state where ethWithdrawn > ethDeposited can cause the share price to become either zero or astronomically high, depending on how the underflow wraps, which in turn leads to incorrect minting or redemption of protocol tokens. The impact includes mis‑allocation of shares, potential loss of user funds, and a breach of the protocol’s accounting invariants – the protocol may think it holds more value than it actually does, or users may receive fewer tokens than expected. The condition occurs during normal protocol operation after enough withdrawals have accumulated, making it hard to notice because the share price may still appear plausible until a boundary is crossed. All participants – depositors, withdrawers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the bug violates the fundamental business logic that the total balance equals deposited funds plus earned rewards minus withdrawals. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the internal accounting functions and identified the unsafe arithmetic ordering. It is difficult to spot in testing because the underflow only manifests after a specific sequence of deposits and withdrawals, which may not be covered by typical unit tests. The recommended remediation is to reorder the operations so that addition occurs before subtraction, i.e., compute the total balance as "ethDeposited + rewardsClaimed - ethWithdrawn", or to use checked arithmetic libraries that revert on underflow. Conceptually, the fix ensures that the total balance is always non‑negative and that the share price calculation reflects the true economic state of the contract. From a user’s perspective the bug can manifest as a situation where a user expects a normal share price on deposit but receives zero or an unexpectedly large value, leading to missing tokens or apparent loss of funds, which contradicts the expectation that deposited ETH is fully accounted for.

title: Share price manipulation
content: The vulnerability is a share‑price manipulation flaw that allows an attacker to force the internal share price of both the ETH and USD vaults to zero, causing every subsequent user deposit to be recorded without any corresponding shares and resulting in a total loss of the deposited funds. The root cause lies in the share‑price calculation, which multiplies the total number of minted shares (nETHMinted) by a base point and divides by the total ETH balance that includes deposited ETH, withdrawn ETH and claimed rewards. When the vault is freshly deployed, nETHMinted is zero. By making a tiny initial deposit and then calling the reward‑update function, the attacker can inject a small amount of rewards (through a donation‑style call to getRewards) so that rewardsClaimed becomes positive while nETHMinted remains zero. The contract’s _updateSharePrice routine then computes sharePrice as (0 * BASE_POINT) / (positive balance) which evaluates to zero. Because the share price is stored as zero, the later deposit functions calculate the number of shares to mint as (sharePrice * depositAmount) / BASE_POINT, which also yields zero. From the user’s perspective the transaction appears to succeed – the contract accepts the ETH – but the user receives no nETH shares, sees no increase in their balance, and cannot later withdraw the funds because the accounting assumes no ownership. This attack can be carried out only before any legitimate shares have been minted, i.e., when the vault is in its initial state, and it exploits the lack of a guard against a zero share price and the permissive reward‑donation logic that allows an external address to hold more tokens than the strategy’s recorded balance. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the interaction between the reward‑claiming logic and the share‑price update. It is difficult to notice because the contract does not emit an explicit error; the UI may simply show a successful deposit while the internal share count remains zero, leading users to assume their funds are safe. The bug belongs to the class of initialization and arithmetic errors where a division by a non‑zero denominator with a zero numerator produces a zero price, breaking the fundamental accounting invariant that each share represents a proportional claim on the vault’s assets. To remediate the problem the protocol should ensure that an initial non‑zero amount of shares is minted by the admin or that the share‑price update function rejects a zero‑share scenario, and it should prevent external reward donations before any shares exist, for example by adding a check that rewardsClaimed can only increase after nETHMinted is greater than zero.

title: Incorrect access control logic in onlyDeposit modifier
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect access‑control modifier named onlyDeposit. The modifier checks that msg.sender is either the ETH deposit contract or the USD deposit contract, but it uses the logical OR operator (||) between two inequality checks: if(msg.sender != depositETH || msg.sender != depositUSD) revert. Because an address can never be equal to both deposit contracts simultaneously, at least one of the two comparisons is always true, making the whole condition always true. Consequently every call to any function protected by onlyDeposit, such as sendMessage, will revert with NotDepositContract, even when the caller is a legitimate deposit contract. The root cause is a Boolean logic error: using OR where AND is required for a whitelist check. The bug can be exploited trivially by any caller: the function is effectively dead, leading to a denial‑of‑service where legitimate users cannot send messages or trigger any downstream logic that depends on the modifier. The impact is high because the core messaging functionality becomes unusable, breaking the protocol’s business logic and potentially causing users to lose confidence or be unable to interact with the system. The condition triggers on every invocation, regardless of the caller, so the failure occurs under all normal operating conditions. Both deposit contracts and any external actors are affected: deposit contracts cannot perform their intended actions, and users attempting to use the protocol receive immediate transaction reverts with the NotDepositContract error. The issue was discovered during a manual code review where the auditor noticed the contradictory logic in the modifier. It can be hard to notice because the code compiles without warnings and the revert message may be interpreted as a permission problem rather than a logical flaw. The fix is to replace the OR with an AND, i.e., require that msg.sender is not equal to both authorized addresses before reverting, which correctly implements a whitelist check. This class of bug belongs to improper access‑control conditions, often described as “always‑true require statements” or “incorrect boolean operator in whitelist checks”. From a user’s perspective the UI will show transactions failing instantly, balances remaining unchanged, and no messages being delivered, contrary to the expectation that a deposit contract can trigger sendMessage. The accounting assumptions of the protocol—that authorized contracts can invoke certain functions—are violated, leading to a broken workflow where funds appear to be locked or operations are silently dropped.

title: Lack of approval before depositing DAI into DSR contract
content: The vulnerability is a missing ERC20 allowance step in the DSRStrategy contract's deposit function. The function attempts to call the DSR contract's deposit method, which internally tries to transfer DAI from the strategy contract using transferFrom. Because the strategy contract never calls approve on the DAI token for the DSR contract, the allowance remains zero and the transferFrom call reverts. This is a classic missing approval bug, a subclass of token handling errors where a contract assumes it can move tokens without first granting permission. An attacker does not gain direct access to funds, but any user invoking deposit will experience a transaction revert, meaning the DAI never leaves the user's wallet, no sDAI is minted, and the expected interest‑earning position is never created. The impact is high because the core functionality of depositing into the savings rate is unusable, breaking the protocol's business logic that users deposit DAI to earn interest. The issue manifests whenever the deposit function is called without a prior allowance, which is the default state after deployment. It was discovered during a manual code review that inspected the flow of tokens and noticed the absence of an approve call before the external deposit invocation. The bug can be hard to notice because the function compiles and the external call signature appears correct; only at runtime does the ERC20 transfer revert, which may be attributed to other causes if not examined closely. From a user perspective the UI may show a “deposit” button, the transaction is submitted, then it fails with a generic revert message, leaving the user with no change in balance and no receipt of sDAI, contrary to the expectation that the deposit succeeds and starts earning interest. To remediate, the contract should include an explicit call to the DAI token's approve method granting the DSR contract permission to transfer the specified amount before invoking the deposit, or use a safeTransferFrom pattern that ensures allowance is set. This aligns the implementation with the ERC20 standard and restores the intended accounting flow where deposited DAI is converted to sDAI and interest accrues.

title: Lack of withdrawal functionality in strategy contracts
content: The vulnerability consists of a missing withdrawalpath in the two strategy contracts that manage the protocol’s yield‑earning assets – the LidoStrategy for ETH and the DSRStrategy for DAI. The contracts are designed to accept deposits from the DepositETH and DepositUSD front‑ends, forward those funds to external yield providers (Lido and sDAI) and let the accrued rewards accumulate, but they do not expose any function that can pull the principal together with the earned interest back into the protocol. The root cause is a design omission: the strategy interfaces and the delegatecall execution loop expect each strategy to implement a complete lifecycle (deposit, earn, withdraw), yet the code base only implements the deposit side. Because the withdrawal functions are absent, when the protocol’s reserve manager or a user attempts to redeem their share, the manager calls executeStrategies which iterates over the strategies and invokes the supplied calldata. Since no calldata exists for a withdraw operation, the delegatecall succeeds on deposit‑only functions but fails to provide any exit mechanism. An attacker does not need to actively exploit a code flaw; the risk is systemic – the protocol simply cannot retrieve the locked assets, so any redemption request will either revert or return zero, leaving users unable to access their funds. The impact is that the protocol’s liquidity pool cannot be replenished, reserves may fall below the required threshold, and users may see their balances stay unchanged or be shown as “pending” while the underlying assets remain trapped inside Lido or the DSR contract. This condition occurs whenever a user initiates a share redemption, when the protocol needs to rebalance its holdings, or during emergency withdrawals. All participants who rely on the DepositETH or DepositUSD contracts – end‑users, liquidity providers, and the protocol’s governance – are affected because the promised “withdraw” functionality is effectively a dead‑end. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the strategy manager’s delegatecall loop, where the auditor noticed that the strategy contracts lack any public or external method for withdrawing assets and that the documentation assumes such a method exists. The problem is subtle because the contracts compile without errors, deposits succeed, and the yield accrues, so the missing exit path does not raise compiler warnings and may only become apparent under redemption scenarios. To remediate the issue, the strategy contracts should be extended with a withdrawal interface that correctly interacts with the external protocols: for Lido, the contract must submit a withdrawal request to Lido’s primary market queue, wait for the claim period, and then retrieve the ETH, or alternatively use the secondary market to liquidate the stETH tokens; for DSR, the contract must call the DSR’s withdraw function to pull DAI and accrued interest. The withdrawal logic must also update internal accounting so that the protocol’s share ledger reflects the returned assets and rewards. In generic terms, this is a “missing exit function” or “withdrawal deadlock” bug, where an asset‑management component implements only the inbound flow and neglects the outbound flow, violating the fundamental accounting invariant that every deposited token must be recoverable on demand. From the user’s perspective, a redemption attempt results in a UI that shows no change in balance, an error message, or a perpetual pending state, contrary to the expectation that the protocol will return the deposited ETH or DAI together with earned rewards. The bug therefore breaks the business logic that users’ funds are liquid and withdrawable, and it can lead to loss of confidence or actual loss of access to funds if the protocol cannot be upgraded to add the missing functions.

title: In `execute
content: The vulnerability originates in the bridge contract’s handling of transfer amounts across the three phases of a cross‑chain transaction: the initial user call (xcall), the reconciliation of the received message (_reconcile), and the execution of fast‑liquidity routing (_handleExecuteLiquidity). When a user initiates a transfer, the contract records the amount the user signed in the XCallArgs structure ( _args.amount ) and uses this value to compute the transfer identifier (transferId). At the same time, the contract swaps the received asset to the local representation token, a step that can be affected by token‑level fees (deflationary tokens) or market slippage. The result of this swap, called bridgedAmt, is the amount that is actually sent across the Nomad bridge and later used in the reconciliation message. Because the transferId is derived from the original user‑signed amount rather than the bridgedAmt, the amount stored in the message and the amount that routers are expected to cover during fast‑liquidity execution can diverge. In the execute path, routers are required to provide liquidity equal to the user‑signed amount ( _args.amount ), which may be larger than the real bridged amount after slippage. During reconciliation, routers are reimbursed based on the smaller bridgedAmt, leaving them with a shortfall equal to the difference between the two values. An attacker can deliberately trigger this mismatch by using a deflationary token that burns a fraction on transfer, or by configuring a swap that incurs high slippage, thereby causing the bridgedAmt to be materially lower than the signed amount. The router therefore fronts more liquidity than it will ever receive back, potentially draining its balance after repeated attacks, especially on low‑liquidity assets. The issue is observable from a router’s perspective as a gradual reduction of its recorded balance despite seemingly successful transfers; users, however, receive the full amount they expect, which masks the problem. This mismatch is subtle because the protocol’s external events (XCalled and Reconciled) both report successful transfer amounts, and the discrepancy resides only in the internal accounting of router liquidity. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that traced the flow of amount variables through the bridge’s core functions and noticed that the transfer identifier and router settlement logic were based on different sources of truth. To remediate the issue, the contract should generate the transfer identifier from the actual bridged amount, adjust router accounting to credit them based on the amount they truly provided (the bridgedAmt), and incorporate explicit handling of token‑level fees and slippage tolerance when calculating router obligations. By aligning the amount used for transferId generation, reconciliation, and liquidity deduction, the protocol can ensure that routers are compensated fairly and that no unintended fund loss occurs.
summary:
[BridgeFacet.sol#L526-L616](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-06-connext/blob/b4532655071566b33c41eac46e75be29b4a381ed/contracts/contracts/core/connext/facets/BridgeFacet.sol#L526-L616)  
[BridgeFacet.sol#L753-L803](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-06-connext/blob/b4532655071566b33c41eac46e75be29b4a381ed/contracts/contracts/core/connext/facets/BridgeFacet.sol#L753-L803)  
[BridgeFacet.sol#L398-L428](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-06-connext/blob/b4532655071566b33c41eac46e75be29b4a381ed/contracts/contracts/core/connext/facets/BridgeFacet.sol#L398-L428)  
[BridgeFacet.sol#L345-L351](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-06-connext/blob/b4532655071566b33c41eac46e75be29b4a381ed/contracts/contracts/core/connext/facets/BridgeFacet.sol#L345-L351)  

Routers pay for transaction in destination domain then nomad messages come and routers get paid again. but the amount routers pay in `execute()` are what transaction sender signed and the amount routers receive is what nomad sends and handles in `_reconcile()` but this two amount can be different because of slippage and swap that happens in `xcall()` because the amount sent in nomad message is the result of `swapToLocalAssetIfNeeded()`.  
So it’s possible for routers to lose funds if some slippage happens in that swap.

title: Routers are not Enforced to Repay AAVE Portal Loan
content: The vulnerability is a lack of on‑chain enforcement that a router must repay a loan taken from the Aave Portal when it is used to fund a cross‑chain bridge operation. The root cause is a design assumption that only trusted routers will act honestly; the BridgeFacet contract credits the router’s balance immediately after a bridge reconciliation (_reconcileProcessPortal) even if the subsequent AavePool.backUnbacked call fails, and there is no requirement or mechanism that forces the router to settle the outstanding loan. An attacker who controls a whitelisted router can exploit this by initiating a bridge transfer, receiving the loaned assets, and then refusing to trigger the repayment logic, effectively keeping the borrowed funds. This can be done especially when the swap or backUnbacked step reverts, because the contract still credits the router without escrow or repayment checks. The impact is a direct loss of funds from the protocol—potentially millions of stablecoins—as the loan remains unrepayed and the protocol’s accounting assumes the loan will be returned. The issue manifests when a router uses the Aave Portal for credit‑risk‑based bridging, under conditions where the reconciliation process encounters a failure but still records a credit for the router. Users may see their expected inbound transfer arrive, but the protocol’s balance sheet will be off, and in extreme cases the router’s balance may be inflated while the overall pool shrinks, leading to missing funds for other participants. The vulnerability was discovered during a security audit of the BridgeFacet.sol file, where the audit team observed that the repayment step is not enforced and that the code trusts the router owner’s integrity. It is hard to notice because the contract flow appears normal—funds are transferred and balances updated—yet there is no explicit check that the loan is fully repaid before the router can claim the credited amount. To remediate, the protocol should introduce an escrow or withdrawal pattern that holds the received assets until the loan repayment is verified on‑chain, enforce a repayment condition in the contract logic, or replace the single‑trusted router model with a multi‑signature or validation scheme that limits the ability of any single router to retain unrepayed loans. By making repayment deterministic and verifiable, the protocol can align incentives, prevent rogue routers from keeping the borrowed assets, and restore confidence in the bridge’s financial guarantees.
summary: [BridgeFacet.sol#L984](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-06-connext/blob/b4532655071566b33c41eac46e75be29b4a381ed/contracts/contracts/core/connext/facets/BridgeFacet.sol#L984)

title: Malicious Relayer can Replay Execute Calldata on Different Chains Causing Double-Spend Issue
content: The vulnerability is a cross‑domain replay flaw in Connext’s fast‑transfer bridge that allows a malicious relayer to reuse the same execute calldata on different destination domains. The root cause is that the bridge’s sanity checks verify the router’s signature and the transfer ID, but they do not confirm that the calldata’s destination domain (s.domain) matches the domain encoded in the transfer’s CallParams. Because the transfer ID is computed without the destination domain, the same signed message can be submitted to any chain where the same router provides liquidity, and the router’s signature will still be considered valid. An attacker who controls a relayer can therefore take a legitimate fast‑transfer request—e.g., a user sending 1,000 USDC from Ethereum to Optimism—relay the execute call to Optimism, receive the minted oUSDC, then modify the ExecuteArgs.local to reference the equivalent token on Polygon and replay the same execute call on Polygon. The bridge will accept the modified calldata, transfer another 1,000 POS‑USDC to the attacker’s address on Polygon, and the router will be unable to reclaim the funds on Polygon while still being able to claim back the Optimism funds. This results in a double‑spend condition where the same liquidity provision is consumed on multiple chains, effectively draining the router’s capital and violating the accounting assumption that each transfer can be settled only once. The issue manifests only for fast‑transfer paths, which lack the fraud‑proof challenge that protects slow‑transfer messages, and it requires that the same router is active on the target domains and that the same canonical token is registered on those domains. It was discovered during a security audit that inspected the BridgeFacet.execute implementation and noticed that the domain field was never compared against the CallParams.destinationDomain. The flaw can be hard to notice because on a single chain the replay protection works, and the absence of a cross‑domain check does not raise any immediate on‑chain error; the malicious behavior is observable only after funds appear on multiple chains. From the user’s perspective, a user expects to receive the transferred assets on a single destination chain, but instead sees the tokens appear on two different chains, potentially leading to confusion such as “I received my USDC on Optimism and also on Polygon, why is my balance doubled?” or “my router’s liquidity was drained without a visible claim.” To remediate the issue, the bridge should include the destination domain as part of the signed payload and verify that the execute calldata is intended for the current domain before processing. Additionally, the calldata should be signed by a trusted sequencer or router and the signature verified on‑chain, ensuring integrity against tampering by relayers. Enforcing a domain‑match check in the _executeSanityChecks function would prevent the cross‑domain replay and restore the intended one‑time settlement property of fast‑transfer operations.
summary:
[BridgeFacet.sol#L411](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-06-connext/blob/4dd6149748b635f95460d4c3924c7e3fb6716967/contracts/contracts/core/connext/facets/BridgeFacet.sol#L411)  

This issue is only applicable for fast-transfer. Slow transfer would not have this issue because of the built-in fraud-proof mechanism in Nomad.

First, the attacker will attempt to use Connext to send `1000 USDC` from Ethereum domain to Optimism domain.  

Assume that the attacker happens to be a relayer on the relayer network utilised by Connext, and the attacker’s relayer happens to be tasked to relay the above execute calldata to the Optimism’s Connext [`BridgeFacet.execute`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-06-connext/blob/4dd6149748b635f95460d4c3924c7e3fb6716967/contracts/contracts/core/connext/facets/BridgeFacet.sol#L411) function.  

Optimism’s Connext `BridgeFacet.execute` received the execute calldata and observed within the calldata that it is a fast-transfer and Router A is responsible for providing the liquidity. It will then check that the router signature is valid, and proceed to transfer `1000 oUSDC` to attacker wallet (0x123456) in Optimism.  

Next, attacker will update the `ExecuteArgs.local` within the execute calldata to a valid local representation of canonical token (USDC) used within Polygon. Attacker will then send the modified execute calldata to Polygon’s Connext `BridgeFacet.execute` function. Assume that the same Router A is also providing liquidity in Polygon. The `BridgeFacet.execute` function checks that the router signature is valid, and proceed to transfer `1000 POS-USDC` to atttack wallet (0x123456) in Polygon.  

At this point, the attacker has `1000 oUSDC` and `1000 POS-USDC` in his wallets. When the nomad message arrives at Optimism, Router A can claim the `1000 oUSDC` back from Connext. However, Router A is not able to claim back any fund in Polygon.  

Note that same wallet address exists on different chains. For instance, the wallet address on Etherum and Polygon is the same.

title: Incorrect IPETHNFTVault::borrow assumption breaks the protocol
content: The vulnerability originates from an incorrect assumption made by the NFT capsule contract when it interacts with the IPETHNFTVault borrow function. The capsule's depositNft routine requests a specific amount of PETH by passing a _borrowAmount parameter to the vault's borrow method, and later treats the returned value as if it were exactly the amount requested. However, the vault's borrow implementation always deducts a borrow fee and insurance from the requested amount, as documented in its NatSpec comment: the user will receive less than the amount requested because the fee and insurance are automatically removed. Consequently, the capsule contract ends up with a smaller PETH balance than it expects, but it still attempts to provide the full _borrowAmount as liquidity to a Curve pool. This mismatch causes the liquidity provision step to fail due to insufficient PETH, rendering the entire deposit and position‑opening workflow unusable. The issue manifests whenever a user deposits an NFT and the contract tries to open a new leveraged position, because the protocol relies on the borrowed PETH to fund the Curve pool. Although the current fee may be set to zero, the contract logic does not account for future fee changes, meaning the protocol can break at any time the fee is adjusted. The bug was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the flow of funds between the capsule and the vault and compared the documented behavior of the borrow function with the actual usage in the capsule code. It is subtle because the fee is presently zero, so the failure is not observable in a basic test, and the contract does not emit an explicit error indicating a fee mismatch. The impact is that users attempting to deposit NFTs receive no liquidity, their positions cannot be created, and the protocol may appear to be non‑functional, potentially leading to loss of confidence and financial loss if users are unable to recover or re‑deposit. To remediate the issue, the capsule should base its liquidity provision on the actual amount of PETH received from the borrow call, update its accounting fields (such as newPosition.amountBorrowed) to reflect the net amount, and apply the same correction to any other functions that increase the borrowed amount, ensuring that fee deductions are always considered in the protocol’s business logic.
summary:
The depositNft method in Capsule calls IPETHNFTVault::borrow with a
_borrowAmount argument. Later, the code actually tries using the
_borrowAmount value as the amount of PETH to provide as liquidity to a Curve
pool. The problem is that the borrow method of those vaults always takes a
fee, so Capsule will have received less than _borrowAmount of PETH. Quoted
from IPETHNFTVault::borrow's NatSpec:
/// @param _amount The amount of PUSD to be borrowed. Note that
the user will receive less than the amount requested,
/// the borrow fee and insurance automatically get removed from the amount
borrowed
This means that the liquidity provision will always fail due to insufficient
PETH balance, making the protocol unusable.
Even if the fee value is currently zero it can be changed and the protocol will
be broken.

title: Contract might not have enough balance for winner to claim prize
content: The vulnerability is a missing balance enforcement in the NFT lootbox contract that can leave the contract without sufficient stablecoin to satisfy a winner's claim. The root cause is that the createLootbox function records the USD value of each prize but never actually transfers the corresponding amount of stablecoin into the contract, nor does it enforce that the contract holds an equivalent amount for each NFT deposited as a reward. Because the contract does not verify that its on‑chain balance is at least the sum of all possible rewards, a situation can arise where a user wins a prize, initiates a claim, and the contract either reverts or returns zero value. This can be exploited by a malicious lootbox creator who declares large USD prizes, skips funding the contract, and then allows participants to claim, resulting in lost funds for winners. The impact is that users may receive nothing despite the UI indicating a prize, balances may appear to disappear, and the protocol loses trustlessness and capital efficiency. The condition occurs whenever a lootbox is created without an accompanying stablecoin transfer, or when an NFT is deposited without also depositing its USD‑valued counterpart. All participants who expect to receive either the NFT or its USD value are affected, including end‑users, the protocol’s reputation, and any token holders relying on the promised payouts. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the logical flow of reward handling and identified the absence of any balance check or escrow mechanism. It is hard to notice because the contract’s public view functions may still report the intended prize amounts, and the UI may show the reward, while the underlying balance remains insufficient. To remediate, the contract should enforce that the creator transfers the exact stablecoin amount equal to the declared USD prizes at lootbox creation, hold the NFT and its USD‑valued token in escrow, and include a runtime check that the contract balance never falls below the total value of all possible rewards, reverting any operation that would violate this invariant. This change restores trustlessness by guaranteeing that every advertised reward is always claimable.
summary:
The protocol doesn't enforce the actual balance in the NFTLootbox contract to
be enough to pay out rewards. The first issue comes in the createLootbox
method, where the code does
loot.usdPrizes = prizes;
but it doesn't actually transfer prizes amount of stablecoin into the contract -
it just expects it will have it as a balance, which is not enforcing it and is error-
prone. Also, the contract is expected to hold the value of each NFT supplied as
reward also in its USD value. So if a BAYC NFT was deposited as a reward,
not only the BAYC should be held by the contract but also its USD value in
stablecoin. Even though winners will be able to claim either the NFT itself or
its USD value, this way the capital efficiency gets cut in half. This is also not
enforced.
The situation currently is that the contract is not trustless - there might not be
enough rewards to pay winners.

title: Realized pnl not returned to trader on _mergeDecrease()
content: The vulnerability occurs in the function that merges a liquidator's position after a liquidation event. When a trader’s position is liquidated, the contract calculates a realized profit or loss (realizedPnl) for the liquidated position. The intended accounting flow is to add this realizedPnl to the amount of margin that the liquidator should receive (the marginToRemove variable) before the margin is transferred. However, the implementation mistakenly omits the addition of realizedPnl to marginToRemove, while still subtracting the realizedPnl from the openNotional accounting field. As a result, the liquidator’s margin does not include the profit that should have been credited, effectively causing a loss of yield for the liquidator. This bug is an accounting error that belongs to the class of “missing credit” or “incorrect settlement” vulnerabilities, where a value that should increase a balance is never applied. The issue can be exploited simply by triggering a liquidation of a position that yields a positive realizedPnl for the liquidator; the contract will then remove the profit from the openNotional but will not transfer it to the liquidator, causing the liquidator’s funds to disappear or be lower than expected. The impact is that liquidators receive less compensation than the protocol promises, leading to reduced incentives, potential loss of capital for participants who rely on liquidation rewards, and a breach of the economic assumptions of the perpetual market. The condition occurs whenever the _mergeDecrease() internal routine is called during a liquidation that results in a positive realizedPnl. Any user acting as a liquidator, as well as the overall protocol health, is affected because the missing payout undermines the fairness of the system. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s accounting logic, where the auditor noticed that the marginToRemove variable was never updated with the realizedPnl despite the openNotional being decreased. The bug can be hard to notice because the contract still updates other state variables, and the missing credit does not generate an explicit error; only a careful comparison of expected versus actual margin transfers reveals the discrepancy. From a user’s perspective, a liquidator may see a transaction succeed, but the expected reward amount is lower or even zero, leading to confusion such as “my balance didn’t increase after I liquidated a position”. The business logic that guarantees that liquidators are compensated for the risk they take is violated, breaking the accounting invariants of the system. The recommended fix is to modify the accounting line so that the realizedPnl is added to marginToRemove (e.g., marginToRemove += params.rpnl), ensuring that the profit is correctly transferred to the liquidator’s margin before the final settlement.
summary: On the merge of a liquidator position following a liquidation, the realizedPnl from the previous position is not added to the marginToRemove() variable, but it is removed from the openNotional, leading to loss of yield for the liquidator.
