The problem is subtle because the contract’s public functions appear to work correctly for many price ranges; only under specific price disparities does the truncation become visible, making it easy to miss during routine testing. To remediate the issue, the contract should avoid direct division of two 18‑decimal fixed‑point values. Instead, it should multiply the numerator by a scaling factor (e.g., 1e18) before dividing, or employ a well‑audited fixed‑point or full‑precision math library that preserves fractional bits throughout the calculation. By ensuring that the price ratio retains its full precision, the contract will prevent zero‑division reverts and will produce accurate reserve calculations, restoring correct economic behavior and protecting user funds.
summary: Price ratio was calculated by division of price0 and price1. Both prices are normalized to 18 decimal points. Division at best case would return 0 which would cause division by zero revert. At worst case it returns single digit which will make calculations of fair reserves incorrect.

title: Expanding reward token list right after linked YT expiration freezes the accumulated rewards
content: The vulnerability originates from the way the contract updates and distributes rewards after a yield token (YT) has expired. The contract maintains a list of reward tokens that can be expanded by calling updateRewardTokensList. When a new reward token is added after the YT expiration, the post‑expiry reward index for that token is never initialized and therefore remains zero. During reward distribution, the function _updateRewardIndex returns this zero index for the newly added token. The distribution routine then reads the user’s stored reward index, which is set to the constant INITIAL_REWARD_INDEX equal to one when the user has no prior record. Because the code calculates deltaIndex as index minus userIndex, the subtraction yields a negative value that underflows to a very large unsigned integer. The subsequent multiplication with the user’s share either produces an incorrect large number or, depending on the rounding function mulDown, results in zero reward delta. In either case the user’s accrued reward balance is never updated, effectively freezing any rewards associated with the newly added token. The rewardTokens array is append‑only and the post‑expiry data cannot be reset, so the frozen balances remain permanently locked in the contract. This situation can be triggered whenever (1) the standardized yield (SY) contract allows its reward token list to be expanded, (2) the YT has already reached its expiry, and (3) an external caller invokes updateRewardTokensList to add a new token. All users who hold the YT and are entitled to rewards for that token are affected; they will see their reward balance stay at zero despite having earned tokens, leading to a loss of expected payouts. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the interaction between reward token list expansion and the post‑expiry reward index logic. It is subtle because the contract does not revert or emit an error; the reward distribution simply skips the new token without any visible warning, making the bug easy to miss in normal testing. To remediate, the distribution logic should either ignore tokens whose post‑expiry index is zero, initialize the index for newly added tokens, or prohibit adding reward tokens after the YT has expired. Any of these approaches would prevent the mismatch between userIndex and index and ensure that rewards remain claimable.

title: User Can Be Permanently Denied from Purchasing New Penguins Due to Incorrect Alive Penguin Count Validation
content: The contract implements a purchase function that limits the number of living penguins a player may own. The limit is enforced by a modifier that counts the entries in a mapping that stores all penguins ever owned by the player, including those that have died. Because dead penguins are never removed from this array, the count grows even when the player’s alive penguin count is zero. As a result, after enough deaths the modifier believes the player has reached the maximum allowed number of alive penguins and blocks further calls to buyPenguin(). This creates a permanent denial‑of‑service where a user who has lost all penguins cannot acquire a replacement, effectively locking them out of the core gameplay. The bug originates from using the wrong data structure for the validation check – a classic “incorrect state tracking” or “logic error in access control” pattern. It can be exploited simply by playing the game normally until a penguin dies; no special transaction is required. The impact is loss of ability to purchase new assets, leading to stuck funds and reduced user engagement. The condition occurs whenever the contract’s maxAlivePenguins setting is low enough that the cumulative number of dead penguins can exceed it, which is typical in test environments with a limit of ten. All players are affected, but especially those who experience multiple deaths. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the intended accounting model with the actual code paths and noticed that the alive‑penguin mapping is updated while the owned‑penguin array is not. Because the UI still shows a zero balance of living penguins, the problem may be hard to notice without inspecting internal state, as the contract does not emit an explicit error explaining the denial. The fix is to replace the length check with a query on the alive‑penguin collection, ensuring that only currently living penguins are counted against the limit. More generally, the vulnerability belongs to the class of “incorrect accounting of mutable assets” where stale data is used for permission checks, leading to unintended denial of service. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after a series of activities the “Buy Penguin” button becomes permanently disabled, the wallet transaction reverts with a generic “max penguins reached” error, and the user sees no living penguins despite having funds to buy new ones. The contract’s business logic assumes that the count used for the limit reflects live assets; the bug violates that assumption and breaks the economic model of the game.
summary:
The vulnerability exists in the penguin purchase mechanism within the buyPenguin() function and its associated validation logic. The contract maintains two separate data structures to track penguin ownership: playerOwnedPenguins mapping, which stores all penguins ever owned by a player (including dead ones), and alivePenguins mapping, which should theoretically track only living penguins. However, the purchase validation logic incorrectly uses playerOwnedPenguins instead of alivePenguins to determine if a user can acquire additional penguins.  
The checkCanGetExtraPenguin modifier calls playerOwnedPenguins[owner].length to count the user’s penguins and compares this against settings.limits.maxAlivePenguins. This count includes all penguins that have ever been owned by the user, regardless of their current state. When penguins die during activities in the doActivity() function, they are correctly removed from the alivePenguins mapping via alivePenguins[params.player].remove(params.penguinId), but they remain in the playerOwnedPenguins array permanently. This creates a discrepancy where the validation logic considers dead penguins as part of the alive count, effectively reducing the user’s ability to purchase new penguins below the intended limit.  
In extreme scenarios, if the maximum alive penguin limit is set to a relatively low number (such as 10 as mentioned in test cases), users could find themselves completely unable to participate in the game after a series of unfortunate activity outcomes, despite the game’s intended design.  
This vulnerability creates a permanent denial of service condition that fundamentally breaks the core functionality of the penguin management system. Users who experience multiple penguin deaths through activities will progressively lose their ability to purchase replacement penguins, eventually reaching a state where they cannot acquire any new penguins despite having zero living ones. This effectively locks users out of the primary game mechanic permanently.

title: Predictable Randomness in Activity Outcomes
content: The contract PenguinManager.doActivity uses a pseudo‑random value that is derived from block.timestamp together with a salt and the penguin identifier supplied by the caller. Because block.timestamp can be influenced by the miner and the salt and penguinId are fully controlled by the user, the resulting numbers are deterministic for any given block. The function Game.doActivity validates only the signer of a message and does not enforce any expiration on the signature. An attacker can therefore obtain a valid signature from an authorized signer, deploy a malicious contract that reproduces the three keccak256 calculations, and simulate the outcome for the current or future timestamps. By looping over possible timestamps (or by using MEV tools such as flashbots) the attacker can identify a block where the computed deathChance is below the activity’s death threshold, the successChance is above the activity’s success threshold, and the dropChance yields a desired item. The contract then calls doActivity with the same parameters, guaranteeing that the penguin does not die, the activity succeeds, and the most valuable drop is awarded. Because the signature never expires, the attacker can repeat this process indefinitely, extracting maximum rewards while honest players receive normal, probabilistic outcomes. From a user perspective the bug manifests as 'my penguin never dies and I always get the best drop', breaking the intended randomness and creating an unfair advantage. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the randomness source and signature validation logic. It is difficult to notice because the on‑chain transactions appear successful and the random numbers look random, yet they are fully predictable given the inputs. The vulnerability belongs to the class of predictable‑randomness and replay‑able‑signature bugs. Mitigation requires replacing the deterministic formula with a source of unbiased randomness such as Chainlink VRF or a commit‑reveal scheme, and adding a timestamp or nonce expiration to signed messages so that an attacker cannot reuse a signature after the intended block.

title: Indexing issues in RebalancingLib lead to undefined rebalancing behavior
content: The vulnerability is an index misalignment bug in the RebalancingLib library that generates preview rebalancing orders for both normal and reserve rebalancing. The library maintains several counters – a generic chain counter (i), a prior‑chain counter (chainIndex), an active‑chain counter (activeChainIndex), a currency counter (j), an order counter (orderIndex) and a weight counter (weightIndex). The implementation mistakenly reuses the generic orderIndex when accessing data structures that are indexed by chain identifiers, such as the array of withdrawals, the array of currency sets and the destination chain identifier in each order. Because the new anatomy of chains is not a superset of the old anatomy, using the same index for both prior and active chains leads to withdrawals being written to the wrong slot, BitSets being created with an incorrect size, and OrderLib.OrderId being populated with a chainId that belongs to a different iteration. The loop increments both chainIndex and activeChainIndex only when the corresponding chain is active, but the orderIndex is always incremented, causing the three indexes to drift apart. When the preview functions are executed, the protocol may generate orders that point to the wrong destination chain or reference a withdrawal structure that does not correspond to the intended chain. From a user perspective this manifests as rebalancing transactions that never settle, balances that appear unchanged after a rebalance, or orders that are sent to an unexpected chain, effectively locking funds. The protocol does not immediately lose assets, but it enters an undefined state where further rebalancing steps can become stuck, requiring manual intervention by governance to rescue the situation. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the rebalancing logic, where the auditor noticed inconsistent use of indexes and mismatched array accesses. It is hard to notice in normal operation because no explicit revert occurs; the contract simply records data in the wrong slots, and the resulting mis‑routing only becomes apparent when a rebalance fails to complete. Conceptually, the fix consists of introducing a dedicated activeChainIndex variable, using the correct index when accessing withdrawals, BitSets, currency arrays and chain identifiers, and adjusting the increment logic so that each index stays aligned with its intended dimension. By ensuring that each data structure is addressed with the proper index, the rebalancing algorithm will generate correct orders, maintain consistent state, and prevent funds from becoming inaccessible.
summary: The RebalancingLib contains the previewRebalancingOrders() and previewReserveRebalancingOrders() functions. These functions generate the orders for the rebalancing and reserve rebalancing respectively. It is critical that both the rebalancing and reserve rebalancing algorithms use the correct indexes. Failing to do so doesn't result in an immediate loss of funds, but the protocol ends up in an undefined state. For example, orders can be sent to the wrong chains and the rebalancing can get stuck. In the best case, only significant action by the governance could save the protocol.

title: Rounding of sell amounts in RebalancingLib can make rebalancing stuck
content: The vulnerability is a rounding‑precision bug in the rebalancing logic that can cause the calculated sell amount for a reserve rebalancing order to become zero. The library builds orders on the local chain and then filters out any order whose sellAmount field equals zero before calling OrderLib.set(). Because the filter is unconditional, an order with a zero sellAmount never increments the incomingOrders counter on the destination chain. The incomingOrders counter is used by the protocol to determine when all expected orders have been processed; it must reach zero for the rebalancing round to be considered finished. When an attacker (or a careless user) creates a situation where the reserve balance is reduced to a dust amount, the division or rounding performed by RebalancingLib.previewReserveRebalancingOrders() yields a sellAmount of zero. The library currently checks only that reserveAmount > 0, not that the derived orderSellAmount > 0, so it still creates an order that is later discarded. As a result the incomingOrders counter is never decremented, the protocol believes there are still pending orders, and the rebalancing round remains stuck indefinitely. This can be triggered by front‑running an ongoing rebalancing transaction and leaving just enough reserve to cause the rounding to zero. The impact is that the protocol cannot complete its rebalancing cycle, potentially locking user funds in the reserve, breaking expected accounting guarantees, and preventing users from seeing their balances update or receiving expected refunds. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the order‑generation code and noticed the mismatch between reserveAmount and orderSellAmount checks. It is hard to notice because the zero‑sell orders are silently ignored; no explicit error is emitted and the UI may simply show that rebalancing is still in progress while balances appear unchanged. The bug belongs to the class of rounding or precision errors that lead to zero‑value transactions and accounting mismatches. To remediate, the code should verify that the computed orderSellAmount is greater than zero before creating or counting an order, replace the reserveAmount > 0 condition with orderSellAmount > 0 in previewReserveRebalancingOrders, and adjust the incomingOrders increment logic to only fire when sellAmount != 0. This ensures that the protocol’s accounting stays consistent and that rebalancing can always reach a terminal state.
summary: The RebalancingLib generates orders for the rebalancing and reserve rebalancing. It is important that orders with localChain != destinationChain and zero sellAmount do not increment incomingOrders. This is because on the local chain, such orders will be skipped in OrderLib.set().

title: Indexing issues in ConfigBuilder lead to corrupted anatomy data when rebalancing is finished
content: During the rebalancing process the ConfigBuilder contract builds a new anatomy that maps chain identifiers to their order and currency data. The implementation uses a BitSet to iterate over chain indexes and then accesses the array chainOrders[chainIndex] and results[chainIndex] based on the same index. However, the code mistakenly treats the chain identifier as a direct array index. When the set of chain IDs is sparse (for example IDs 0 and 2), the loop accesses chainOrders[2] while the array only contains entries at positions 0 and 1. This off‑by‑one / out‑of‑bounds indexing causes two distinct problems. In startRebalancing the erroneous access may read beyond the end of chainOrders, triggering a revert and aborting the rebalancing initiation. In finishRebalancing the same mistake leads to writing data from the wrong result slot into the anatomy structures (chainIds, currencyIdSets, currencies). As a result the protocol’s internal representation of the new anatomy becomes inconsistent: some chain IDs are associated with the wrong snapshot or currency set, and the resultIndexes bitmap no longer matches the actual result positions. The immediate symptom is that the rebalancing transaction gets stuck – the contract cannot progress to the next phase because the stored anatomy no longer satisfies the expected invariants. From a user perspective, funds that were supposed to be redistributed across chains may remain locked, balances may appear unchanged, or the UI may report that rebalancing is “in progress” forever. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the ConfigBuilder source, where the auditor noticed that the comment “say we have IDs 0 and 2, then we need to access chainOrders[0] and chainOrders[1], not chainOrders[0] and chainOrders[2]” did not match the actual code. Because the bug only manifests when the set of chain IDs is non‑contiguous, it can be hard to reproduce with simple test cases that use sequential IDs, making it easy to overlook. The root cause is an incorrect assumption that a chain’s identifier can be used directly as an array index, ignoring the fact that the underlying arrays are dense and indexed by position, not by identifier. The proper fix is to translate the chain identifier to its position in the dense array (for example by maintaining a mapping from chainId to array index) before accessing chainOrders or results, and to ensure that the resultIndexes bitmap is updated consistently with the actual result positions. After correcting the indexing, startRebalancing will no longer revert unexpectedly, and finishRebalancing will populate the anatomy with the correct data, allowing rebalancing to complete and preserving protocol state integrity.
summary: The wrong indexing is used in ConfigBuilder.startRebalancing() and ConfigBuilder.finishRebalancing(). In the ConfigBuilder.startRebalancing() function the wrong indexing simply causes the function to revert in some cases since chainOrders[chainIndex] accesses chainOrders with an out-of-bounds index. On the other hand, in the ConfigBuilder.finishRebalancing() function, wrong results can be assigned to the data structures that keep track of the new anatomy. This not only makes rebalancing get stuck, it also corrupts the protocol's data.

title: RedstoneChainlinkPriceOracle.valuation() can return outdated valuation and funds can be stolen from the index
content: The vulnerability resides in the price oracle’s valuation routine, which can return a stale or outdated valuation because the helper that extracts timestamps from calldata does not verify that the timestamp embedded in the supplied data is recent. The root cause is the absence of a legitimacy check on the timestamp field; the function only confirms that the calldata follows the expected binary layout. When the stored staticRedstoneData contains a price that was recorded hours or days earlier, an attacker can craft a calldata payload that passes the format check but carries the old timestamp. The oracle then uses this stale price to compute the reserve price and the overall valuation. Because the valuation is used directly in deposit() and redeem() operations of the index, the attacker can deposit funds while the oracle reports an inflated valuation, receiving more index shares than the amount of capital actually contributed. Conversely, the attacker can redeem shares when the valuation is artificially low, extracting a larger amount of underlying assets than entitled. This results in a direct loss for honest participants, as their share of the pool is diluted or their balances shrink unexpectedly. The flaw manifests whenever the oracle’s static data is not refreshed within the allowed update window and the contract does not enforce a freshness constraint. It was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the CalldataExtractor.extractTimestampsAndAssertAllAreEqual() logic and noticed the missing timestamp validation. The issue can be subtle because the function appears to succeed – it returns a numeric valuation without raising an error – so users and developers may assume the price is current. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a normal deposit transaction, but the user receives more shares than expected, or later sees their balance reduced because another participant extracted value from an outdated price. The bug belongs to the class of oracle‑freshness or stale‑data injection vulnerabilities, where the contract trusts external data without confirming its timeliness. To remediate, the valuation path must invoke a timestamp validation routine (for example RedstoneDefaultsLib.validateTimestamp) and revert the transaction if the timestamp is older than the permitted update frequency, thereby preventing outdated valuations from being used in any accounting calculation.
summary: The CalldataExtractor.extractTimestampsAndAssertAllAreEqual() function only checks the calldata format but not the legitimacy of the data or the timestamp. This means that if the oldest saved price in staticRedstoneData is say from 1 hour ago or even a week ago, an attacker can provide bytes calldata such that the outdated valuation is returned. An attacker can intentionally access the outdated valuation to deposit() into the Index and receive more shares than he is entitled to or redeem() from the Index and receive more constituents/reserve than he should be able to. This is a direct loss to the other users of the protocol.

title: retryRedeem() can be used to block the LayerZero pathway
content: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service flaw in the retryRedeem function of the HomechainOmnichainMessenger contract. The function forwards a cross‑chain message by calling the internal _lzSend routine and passes a user‑controlled bytes array called options (adapterParams) to the LayerZero endpoint. Because the code does not validate the contents of this options array, an attacker can craft a payload that specifies an extremely low extraGas value, effectively setting the gas limit for the relayer on the destination chain to a value that is insufficient for the lzReceive implementation. When the message arrives on the destination chain, the LayerZero endpoint attempts to execute lzReceive, runs out of gas, and reverts. The endpoint then stores the failed payload in its storedPayload mapping instead of discarding it. As long as this stored payload remains, the endpoint blocks the delivery of any subsequent messages for that endpoint, causing a complete halt of the LayerZero pathway for the affected chain pair. The impact is that users attempting to redeem or transfer assets across chains see their operations remain pending forever, balances appear unchanged, and the protocol cannot process any new cross‑chain messages, effectively freezing funds and breaking the expected business logic of seamless omnichain transfers. The condition occurs whenever retryRedeem is called with malicious options; any caller who can invoke the function can trigger the issue. The affected parties include all users of the messenger, token holders, and the protocol itself because the blockage is global for that channel. The flaw was discovered during a security audit when the auditors noticed the absence of any checks on the adapterParams length or the extraGas field. It is hard to notice because the source‑chain transaction succeeds and the failure manifests only on the remote chain, where the message simply never arrives and no explicit error is returned to the caller. The bug belongs to the class of insufficient input validation leading to out‑of‑gas denial‑of‑service in cross‑chain messaging. To remediate, the contract should enforce a minimum gas amount by validating the options array before calling _lzSend, rejecting values that do not meet a safe threshold, and optionally providing a mechanism to clear storedPayloads after a failure. This prevents an attacker from deliberately starving the relayer of gas and ensures that the LayerZero pathway remains operational.
summary: There is no validation of bytes passed as options to _lzSend() inside the retryRedeem() function. An attacker can encode the adapterParams and specify a very small gasLimit for the relayer to deliver the message to the destination chain. A transaction with such a small gas limit would revert inside the lzReceive() function due to out-of-gas exception. As a consequence, it would end up as storedPayload inside the Endpoint contract. This would block the delivery of all the subsequent messages until the payload is cleared.

title: ETH balances of home and remote messenger can be drained
content: The vulnerability consists of an unintended ability to drain the native ETH balance that is held by the HomechainOmnichainMessenger and RemoteOmnichainMessenger contracts. When an order is executed on a chain different from its final destination, the executeOrder function marks the order as outgoing and sets the messenger contract as the recipient of the trade output. If the output token of the trade is the native ETH, the protocol transfers that ETH into the messenger’s balance. Later, several public functions – such as retryRedeem, redeem, broadcastOrders, broadcastReserveOrders, sendCurrenciesHash and finishRebalancing – use the contract’s current ETH balance (address(this).balance) to pay LayerZero endpoint fees. These functions do not require the caller to provide sufficient msg.value, and after the fee payment they automatically refund any remaining balance to the caller. Consequently, a user can invoke a function with msg.value set to zero, causing the contract to spend its own ETH to cover the LayerZero fee and then return the leftover ETH to the caller. This flow effectively lets any caller withdraw the messenger’s native balance, draining funds that were meant to be reserved for cross‑chain swaps. The issue arises from improper accounting of native token balances, missing checks that the fee source is the caller’s payment, and the unconditional refund of any surplus balance. It is triggered whenever an outgoing order results in native ETH being held by the messenger and any of the affected functions are called without providing enough ETH for the fee. The parties impacted include the protocol (which loses the ETH needed for future cross‑chain operations), users who expect their swaps to be settled correctly, and governance that may unintentionally fund fee payments with the messenger’s balance. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the order execution and distribution logic, where the auditor observed that native balances were routed to the messenger and later used in fee‑payment calls without proper safeguards. The problem is subtle because the contract’s refund mechanism masks the loss of funds, making the drain appear as a normal refund. To remediate, the contract should record the pre‑call balance, ensure that only the msg.value supplied by the caller is used for LayerZero fees, and refund only any excess of that supplied amount. Additionally, access controls or explicit fee provision checks should be added to prevent arbitrary users from triggering fee payments that consume the contract’s own ETH. This class of bug can be described as an unauthorized native‑token withdrawal caused by improper balance handling during external fee payments, often referred to as a “balance leakage” or “native token drain” vulnerability.
summary: During the executeOrder() function execution, in case the orderId.finalDestinationChainId != block.chainid, the order is outgoing and the recipient of the token is the messenger contract. If the output token after the trade is ETH it will end up as the balance of the HomechainOmnichainMessenger or RemoteOmnichainMessenger contract.

title: depositWithCommand() undercounts deposited when reserve is ETH
content: The vulnerability is an accounting error in the depositWithCommand function of the index contract that causes the amount of native ether recorded as deposited to be lower than the actual amount sent by the user when the index reserve token is ETH. The root cause is that the function records the reserve balance before the user transfer (reserveBefore) without subtracting msg.value, while it correctly subtracts msg.value from the currency balance when the currency is native. Because the incoming ether is included in reserveBefore, the subsequent calculation of deposited as reserveAfter‑reserveBefore excludes the ether that was just sent, so the deposited value is under‑counted. An attacker can exploit this by calling depositWithCommand with a native ether reserve and also sending ether together with a token swap; the contract will credit only the portion of ether that remains after the swap, effectively stealing the rest of the ether because the protocol’s accounting will treat it as un‑deposited. The impact is that users see a smaller recorded deposit than they actually provided, leading to loss of funds, incorrect share allocation, and distorted protocol accounting. This condition occurs only when the reserve token of the index is a native blockchain token (e.g., ETH) and the caller includes a non‑zero msg.value in the same transaction. The affected parties are the depositing users, the index’s share holders, and any downstream contracts that rely on the recorded deposit amount for reward distribution or withdrawals. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the reserve balance before and after the call and noticed that the ether sent with the transaction was not accounted for in the deposited variable. It is hard to notice because the balance checks appear to succeed – the contract only reverts if the currency balance after the call is lower than the recorded balance, which is satisfied – and the missing subtraction is subtle when both reserve and currency can be native tokens. The bug belongs to the class of “under‑counting deposit” or “incorrect handling of native token transfers” accounting bugs, where the protocol assumes that the reserve balance does not change due to the incoming msg.value. From a user’s perspective the UI would show that the deposit amount or resulting share balance is lower than expected, for example a user expects to deposit 1 ETH and receives credit for only 0.5 ETH, or the displayed index balance does not increase by the full amount sent. To fix the issue the contract should subtract msg.value from reserveBefore when the reserve token is native, mirroring the adjustment already performed for the currency balance, thereby ensuring that the deposited calculation reflects the true amount of ether contributed.
summary:
IndexCommandsLib.depositWithCommand() has the following logic:
1. Records the index's current reserve and currency balance:
```solidity
uint256 reserveBefore = reserve.balanceOfSelf();
uint256 balanceBefore = commandParams.currency.balanceOfSelf();
if (commandParams.currency.isNative()) balanceBefore -= msg.value;
```
2. Transfers currency from the user into the contract and executes user-specified commands:
```solidity
commandParams.currency.selfDeposit(params.amount);
CommandLib.callCommand(
    commandParams.command,
    params.config.shared.metadata,
    CommandLib.BalanceState(commandParams.currency, balanceBefore)
);
```
3. Calculates deposited as the difference between the reserve balance after and the recorded reserve balance:
```solidity
if (commandParams.currency.balanceOfSelf() < balanceBefore) revert InvalidDepositData();
deposited = uint96(reserve.balanceOfSelf() - reserveBefore);
```
Since it is possible for reserve or currency to be native tokens, msg.value is subtracted from balanceBefore when commandParams.currency is native tokens. This ensures that the difference between commandParams.currency.balanceOfSelf() and balanceBefore afterwards will include msg.value. However, msg.value is not subtracted from reserveBefore, which means that any ETH sent along with the call will be included in reserveBefore. Consequently, the ETH sent will then be excluded from deposited, which is problematic as deposited represents the amount of funds deposited by the user into the index. This will undercount the user's deposit when reserve is native tokens, for example:
• Assume that reserve is ETH, and a user wants to deposit 1 ETH and 2000 USDC in one call.
• He calls Index.depositWithCommand() with:
  – msg.value = 1 ether
  – commandParams.currency as USDC, and params.amount = 2000e6
• In IndexCommandsLib.depositWithCommand():
  – reserveBefore = 1 ether, since it includes msg.value.
  – 2000 USDC is transferred into the contract and swapped to 1 ETH.
  – Afterwards, reserve.balanceOfSelf() = 2 ether, so deposited = 1 ether.
• As a result, his deposit is recorded as only 1 ETH, causing him to lose the other 1 ETH.

title: Reentrancy via callback from SKIM command leads to theft of Vault funds
content: The vulnerability is a reentrancy bug that occurs when the SKIM command processes a native currency and invokes an untrusted contract as part of its callback mechanism. The root cause lies in the line that computes the amount to be skimmed using the expression uint256 amount = currencyState.currency.balanceOf(msg.sender) - currencyState.minBalance; this calculation is performed after the external call returns, allowing the attacker to manipulate the reported balance of the Vault. An attacker can trigger the vulnerability by calling redeemK (or its L2 variant) which internally executes the SKIM command for the native currency. During the SKIM execution the protocol calls an attacker‑controlled contract; the attacker’s contract then deposits additional native tokens into the Vault (for example via a donate call) before the amount variable is read. Because the balance of the Vault has increased, the subsequent subtraction yields a larger amount than intended, and the protocol transfers this inflated amount to the attacker, effectively stealing funds. The impact is a direct loss of vault assets, observable to users as missing balances, zero refunds, or unexpected reductions in their holdings. The bug manifests only when the currency being skimmed is the native token and when the SKIM command processes multiple currencies, meaning that any path that leads to a native‑currency SKIM followed by a callback can be exploited. All users of the protocol, as well as the protocol’s overall liquidity, are affected because the stolen funds reduce the total assets backing the system. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that identified the unsafe ordering of external calls and state‑dependent calculations. It is hard to notice because the balance check appears legitimate and the external call is hidden inside a library function, making the reentrancy vector non‑obvious. The recommended mitigation is to apply a reentrancy guard (for example a nonReentrant modifier) to the functions that can be re‑entered – redeemK in both Index and L2Index contracts and the donate function in the Vault – or to restructure the code so that the amount is calculated before any external call and to follow the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern. By preventing the contract from being re‑entered during the SKIM operation, the protocol ensures that the balance used for the amount calculation cannot be artificially inflated, thereby protecting vault funds from theft.
summary: An attacker can get a callback from the CommandLib._call() function, since via the SKIM command, an untrusted contract can be called if currencyState.currency is the NATIVE currency.

title: MJR-1 Invalid setter function
content: The vulnerability consists of two setter functions that modify configuration variables without updating dependent state, leading to a logical inconsistency in the contract’s accounting and access control. The first function, setDefaultController, writes a new address into the defaultController storage slot but does not consider that the pool owner may have been previously set to the old defaultController address during a call to bakePie. Because the pool owner field is left unchanged, the pool continues to be governed by the previous controller even though the contract reports a different defaultController. This mismatch violates the expectation that changing the controller will immediately transfer management rights, causing users to interact with a pool that appears to be under a new address while actions are still executed by the old one. The second function, setFeeBeneficiary, updates the FeeBeneficiary address in storage but ignores that fee‑bearing tokens may have already been minted to the previous beneficiary in several token‑issuance paths. Consequently, fees that are supposed to be credited to the newly set beneficiary continue to be sent to the old address, breaking the accounting assumptions of the protocol and potentially diverting revenue. Both issues arise because the setters only change a single variable and lack any reconciliation logic that would re‑assign ownership or re‑allocate previously issued tokens. An attacker or a careless administrator could exploit the inconsistency by calling setDefaultController to point to a malicious address while the pool still operates under the original owner, allowing the original owner to retain control and the new address to gain no authority. Similarly, an attacker could change the fee beneficiary to an address they control, but because earlier token issuances remain tied to the old address, the protocol may continue to send fees to the old beneficiary, causing loss of expected revenue for the new beneficiary. The impact includes loss of trust, potential misdirection of fees, and a breach of the protocol’s governance model, affecting pool participants, fee recipients, and any parties relying on correct ownership semantics. The condition occurs whenever the setter functions are invoked after the pool has been initialized or after fees have been minted, which is the typical operational flow of the system. The affected parties are pool owners, fee beneficiaries, and end‑users who expect correct fee distribution and proper controller authority. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined state‑transition logic and identified that the setters do not propagate changes to related storage structures. The bug is subtle because the contract does not revert or emit an error; the state appears to have been updated, yet downstream logic still references stale addresses, making the problem hard to notice without tracing the full execution path. To remediate, the setter functions should include additional logic that either (a) updates the pool owner to match the new defaultController, or (b) emits an event and requires an explicit migration step, and (c) re‑assigns any previously minted fee tokens or updates the fee distribution mechanism to reference the new FeeBeneficiary. In essence, the setters must enforce consistency across all dependent variables to preserve the intended business rules of ownership transfer and fee allocation.
summary:
In the setDefaultController() function defined at line PieFactoryContract.sol#L34, the new value is assigned to the defaultController variable. But it is not taken into account that earlier using the bakePie() function, the pool owner could be changed to address of defaultController. Thus, as a result of the work of the setDefaultController() function, the pool owner will remain the same, while it is expected that the pool will be managed from a different address.
In the setFeeBeneficiary() function defined at line BasketFacet.sol#L87, the LibBasketStorage.basketStorage().FeeBeneficiary variable is assigned a new value. But it is not taken into account that earlier tokens could be issued to this address in the following places: BasketFacet.sol#L141, BasketFacet.sol#L175, BasketFacet.sol#L216.

title: MJR-2 Incorrect logic when burning and minting tokens
content: The vulnerability is an accounting inconsistency in the ERC‑20 implementation where the mint and burn functions modify only the holder balances but fail to adjust the global totalSupply variable. According to the ERC‑20 specification, totalSupply must reflect the sum of all minted tokens and be reduced when tokens are burned. Because the contract omits these updates, any logic that relies on totalSupply – such as price‑per‑share calculations, basket valuations, or proportional distribution of rewards – operates on a stale value. An attacker or any user can trigger the mint or burn functions, causing balances to change while totalSupply remains unchanged; subsequent calls to functions in BasketFacet that read totalSupply will produce incorrect results, potentially leading to under‑ or over‑allocation of assets, loss of value for token holders, or manipulation of protocol economics. The issue manifests when a user mints new tokens expecting the overall supply to increase, but the UI or downstream calculations still report the old supply, resulting in unexpected zero or reduced share values. It also appears when burning tokens, where the holder’s balance decreases but the protocol’s accounting still assumes the same total amount of tokens in circulation. The bug was discovered during a manual security audit that compared the contract code against the ERC‑20 standard and identified that the totalSupply variable is never modified in the mint or burn paths, despite being used in seven separate calculations in another facet. The problem is subtle because balance changes appear correct, so casual testing may not reveal the discrepancy; only operations that depend on totalSupply expose the flaw. To fix the issue, the mint function should increment totalSupply by the minted amount and the burn function should decrement totalSupply by the burned amount, ensuring that all accounting invariants hold and that downstream calculations reflect the true token supply. This class of bug is commonly referred to as an “incorrect totalSupply accounting” or “missing supply update” in ERC‑20 tokens.
summary:
The mint() function defined at the line ERC20Facet.sol#L44 is for minting new tokens.
The amount of tokens is increased on the wallet with the address _receiver.
But the ERC-20 specification also uses the value of the totalSupply variable.
This variable is not incremented here.
At line: ERC20Facet.sol#L48. The burn() function is for burning tokens. The amount of tokens is reduced on the wallet with the address _from.
But the ERC-20 specification also uses the value of the totalSupply variable.
The value of this variable is not decremented here.
At the same time, the value of the variable totalSupply is used 7 times for calculations in this smart contract: BasketFacet.sol.

title: MJR-3 Approve / TransferFrom multiple withdrawal attack
content: The vulnerability is a race condition in the standard token allowance mechanism that allows a spender to withdraw more tokens than the token holder intended when the holder changes the allowance. The root cause is that the approve function overwrites the existing allowance without requiring the current allowance to be cleared first, and the contract does not enforce any ordering between the approval transaction and a pending transferFrom call. An attacker can observe the token holder’s second approval transaction in the mempool, submit a transferFrom transaction that consumes the original allowance, and if the attacker’s transaction is mined before the holder’s transaction, the original allowance is spent. After the holder’s transaction is mined, the new allowance becomes active, enabling the attacker to immediately spend the new amount as well. The result is that the spender can transfer the sum of the old and the new allowances (N+M) even though the holder only intended to allow either N or M, but not both. This impact manifests as an unexpected loss of tokens for the token holder, potentially draining the entire balance if the attacker repeats the pattern. The condition occurs whenever a token holder attempts to change an existing non‑zero allowance to another non‑zero value and the spender monitors the network for the pending approval transaction. Any user, protocol, or contract that relies on the ERC‑20 approve/transferFrom pattern is affected, especially those that grant third‑party spenders permission to move funds. The issue was discovered through analysis of the ERC‑20 standard and documented in the Ethereum Improvement Proposal discussion (EIP‑738). It can be hard to notice because the token holder’s UI typically shows only the final allowance value, not the intermediate state where the spender may have already consumed the previous allowance. The bug violates the accounting assumption that the allowance value represents the total amount a spender may move at any point in time; the contract incorrectly allows two separate allowances to be active sequentially without resetting the first. To remediate, the approve function should require that either the new allowance is zero or the current allowance is zero before setting a new value, or developers should use the increaseAllowance and decreaseAllowance helper functions that adjust the allowance atomically. Conceptually, the fix enforces a clear‑then‑set pattern or uses safe arithmetic to prevent overlapping allowances, thereby eliminating the possibility of double withdrawal.
summary:
This known issue is documented here: https://github.com/ethereum/EIPs/issues/738.
Summary / example of the attack:
1. Alice allows Bob to transfer N of Alice's tokens (N>0) by calling approve method on Token smart contract passing Bob's address and N as method arguments
2. After some time, Alice decides to change from N to M (M>0) the number of Alice's tokens Bob is allowed to transfer, so she calls approve method again, this time passing Bob's address and M as method arguments
3. Bob notices Alice's second transaction before it was mined and quickly sends another transaction that calls transferFrom method to transfer N Alice's tokens somewhere
4. If Bob's transaction is executed before Alice's transaction, then Bob will successfully transfer N Alice's tokens and will gain an ability to transfer another M tokens
5. Before Alice noticed that something went wrong, Bob calls transferFrom method again, this time to transfer M Alice's tokens.
So, Alice's attempt to change Bob's allowance from N to M (N>0 and M>0) made it possible for Bob to transfer N+M of Alice's tokens, while Alice never wanted to allow so many of her tokens to be transferred by Bob.

title: MJR-4 Gas overflow during iteration (DoS)
content: During execution of several functions in the PieDAO contracts, the code iterates over dynamic arrays without any upper bound. Each iteration consumes a fixed amount of gas, and the total gas required grows linearly with the number of elements. When the array length exceeds the amount of gas that can be supplied in a single block, the transaction runs out of gas and the whole loop reverts. Because the loop is part of core operations such as creating a new pie, calling a facet, or updating a basket, the failure blocks those functions entirely, effectively creating a denial‑of‑service condition. The problem appears in PieFactoryContract at line 72 and in CallFacet and BasketFacet at several lines where for‑loops walk through arrays of calls, assets or basket items. The root cause is an unbounded iteration over user‑controlled data structures; there is no check that limits the maximum number of elements that can be stored. An attacker can inflate the arrays by repeatedly adding entries (for example, by creating many pies or by submitting many calls) until the gas needed to process the next operation exceeds the block gas limit. At that point any subsequent transaction that triggers the same loop will revert with an out‑of‑gas error, leaving users unable to perform expected actions such as adding a new basket, executing a call, or withdrawing funds. From a user’s perspective the transaction simply fails with a generic “out of gas” or “intrinsic gas too low” message, balances remain unchanged, and the UI may show no error details, creating confusion and loss of confidence. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by MixBytes, which identified the unbounded loops as a potential gas overflow risk. The bug is hard to notice in normal testing because typical array sizes are small and the gas limit is rarely reached; only when the contract state grows large does the problem surface. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “unbounded loop gas exhaustion” or “DoS via block gas limit”. To remediate, the contract should enforce a maximum allowed length for each array, reject operations that would exceed that limit, or refactor the logic to avoid iterating over large collections in a single transaction (e.g., by using mappings, pagination, or external batch processing). Adding such checks restores the guarantee that each function can complete within the block gas budget and prevents the denial‑of‑service scenario.
summary:
Each iteration of the cycle requires a gas flow.
A moment may come when more gas is required than it is allocated to record one block. In this case, all iterations of the loop will fail.
Affected lines:
PieFactoryContract.sol#L72
CallFacet.sol#L43
CallFacet.sol#L67
CallFacet.sol#L81
BasketFacet.sol on lines 45, 126, 158, 274, 296

title: MJR-5 Global Protection of malicious backward calls in raw methods
content: The vulnerability is an unchecked execution of arbitrary external code via low‑level calls in several manager contracts. Because the contracts do not enforce a one‑directional call graph, a malicious target contract can invoke back‑calls into the caller or other contracts during the same transaction. This lack of protection stems from the absence of a global counter or reentrancy guard that would detect additional calls made while a raw call is in progress. An attacker can craft a contract that, when called by the manager, triggers a callback that re‑enters the manager’s functions, modifies internal accounting variables, or initiates further calls before the original call returns. Exploiting this requires the attacker to be able to supply a target address to the manager’s raw call functions (e.g., at lines 44,70,102,114 in LendingManager.sol and lines 94,131 in RSIManager.sol). Once the malicious contract is invoked, it can execute arbitrary logic, potentially causing funds to be transferred out, balances to be set to zero, or refunds to be omitted. The impact includes loss of user funds, broken accounting, and violation of the protocol’s business logic that assumes a linear execution flow. The issue manifests when a user initiates an operation that triggers a low‑level call; from the UI the user may see that a deposit or loan request appears to succeed but later the balance is reduced unexpectedly or a refund is missing. The vulnerability was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the call graph and noted that the contracts do not record the number of internal calls before and after a raw call. Because the contracts rely on external calls without a guard, the problem can be subtle and may not surface in simple unit tests, making it hard to notice. The recommended mitigation is to introduce a contract‑wide call counter (or a reentrancy lock) that is captured before the low‑level call and verified after it returns, rejecting the transaction if the counter has changed. This ensures that no additional calls were made during the execution of the target method, restoring the intended one‑way execution model and protecting against reentrancy or malicious backward calls.
summary:
At the lines: LendingManager.sol#L44, LendingManager.sol#L70, LendingManager.sol#L102, LendingManager.sol#L114, RSIManager.sol#94, RSIManager.sol#131 anything can happen in target methods execution.
We expect one-way class methods execution-graph like:
A.method1 -> B.method2 -> C.method3
So it is better to ensure it.

title: AdapterV1.sol Contract Always Uses the Entire Balance of PSM of the Adapter, Which Can Lead to Weak Slippage
content: The vulnerability resides in the AdapterV1 contract when it processes a portal‑energy sell operation in mode one. The function first swaps a user‑provided amount of PSM for WETH via the 1inch router and then adds liquidity to a Ramses pool using the remaining PSM and the received WETH. The contract determines how much PSM to supply to the pool by reading the entire PSM balance of the adapter after the swap (PSM.balanceOf(address(this))). However, 1inch may not consume the full amount of PSM supplied for the swap; any surplus is automatically refunded to the caller. In the adapter code this refund is only executed when the internal flag _forLiquidity is false. During the sellPortalEnergy flow the flag is set to true, so the surplus PSM stays in the adapter contract. Because the subsequent liquidity‑addition routine uses the full contract balance, the amount of PSM considered for the pool is larger than the user anticipated. This mismatch inflates the effective slippage: the user specifies a minimum acceptable PSM amount (minPSM) based on the expected input, but the contract supplies a higher amount, causing the transaction to execute at a worse price than the user intended. The issue can be exploited by influencing market conditions or the 1inch router to return a partial refund, thereby causing the adapter to over‑allocate PSM to the pool and allowing the transaction to pass with a price drop that exceeds the user’s tolerance. The impact is that users may lose value, receiving fewer WETH or a lower‑valued liquidity position than expected, while the protocol’s accounting assumptions about token ratios are violated. The bug occurs only when the swap is performed with forLiquidity set to true, which is the normal path for sellPortalEnergy, and when 1inch does not fully consume the supplied PSM – a situation that cannot be predicted in advance. It was discovered during a manual security review that highlighted the discrepancy between the refund logic and the balance‑based calculation. The problem is subtle because the contract does return unused tokens in other contexts, so the missing refund in this specific flow is not obvious from a superficial inspection. To remediate, the contract should always return any unused PSM from the 1inch swap before calculating liquidity amounts, or it should compute the liquidity contribution based on the exact amount intended for the pool rather than the total contract balance. This correction restores predictable slippage behavior and aligns the on‑chain accounting with the user’s expectations, eliminating the class of bugs where leftover tokens are unintentionally consumed, leading to inflated slippage and potential fund loss.
summary:
When setPortalEnergy is called with mode = 1 the protocol will first swap PSM for WETH using 1inch, then use PSM and WETH to add liquidity to a Ramses pair. In order to do this, the user has to specify 2 slippages, 1 for the 1inch swap and 1 when calculating how much liquidity needs to be added to the Ramses pair.

Let’s go over the code one step at a time. First, we have to sell our portal tokens to get PSM which is sent to the adapter. Second, we do a swap using 1inch which will swap some amount of the received PSM for WETH, when the swap is done the WETH is received in the adapter. Third, we get PSMBalance and WETHBalance which are then passed to _addLiquidity() which will calculate amountPSM and amountWETH which need to be transferred to the Ramses pair.

1inch has a case, where the tokens that were used for the swap were actually more than necessary, so the unspent amount is refunded to msg.sender. This is what this part of the code is used for.

```solidity
// @dev Send remaining tokens back to the user if not called from addLiquidity
if (!_forLiquidity) {
    uint256 remainAmount = _swap.psmAmount - spentAmount_;
    if (remainAmount > 0) PSM.safeTransfer(msg.sender, remainAmount);
}
```

This will refund any amount that wasn’t used to msg.sender, but this only happens if forLiquidity = false, but when we call sellPortalEnergy(), we use forLiquidity = true which won’t refund any unused amount.

If 1inch refunds any PSM, it will later be used when calling _addLiquidity(), as we use PSMBalance = PSM.balanceOf(address(this)), which uses the entire PSM balance of the contract.

This is the actual problem because the tokens aren’t refunded to msg.sender, _addLiquidity() will be called with a larger PSMBalance than the user expected, which will drastically affect his slippage minPSM because now the amount of PSM that will be used to add liquidity is larger than he expected.

There is no way to know if 1inch will use up all of the PSM for the swap, due to market conditions and when the tx will be executed, so there is no way to predict minPSM in the case where 1inch refunds PSM to the Adapter.

Inflated/unfair slippage used for user

Attack Scenario  
To better visualize this, I’ll give an example. The correlation between PSM and WETH is simplified to better understand the issue.

1. Alice wants to sell her portal tokens and then add liquidity in the Ramses pair.

2. She calls sellPortalTokens().

3. She sells 200 PSM worth of portal tokens and she wants to use 100 PSM to swap for 1 WETH, the other 100 she wants to use to add liquidity to the pool.

4. 1inch uses up only 50 PSM for 1 WETH, so the other 50 PSM are refunded directly to the Adapter.

5. PSMBalance is now 150, as the code uses the entire balance of the Adapter to calculate how much liquidity needs to be added.

6. Alice specified 90 PSM as minPSM, as she expected only 100 PSM to be used to add liquidity, but now 150 is used.

7. Due to market conditions, amountPSM = 100, but PSMBalance is 150, meaning that the price dropped a lot more than Alice would have wanted.

8. Because Alice specified minPSM = 90 the tx goes through and Alice let a tx which slipped in price a lot more than she would have agreed to if she knew that the 150 PSM would be used to add liquidity instead of 100 PSM.

title: Users Fund Loss When Adding Liquidity to Ramses Since Re- maining Tokens Are Not Paid Out
content: When a user sells portal energy and selects the liquidity‑addition mode (mode == 1), the contract swaps a portion of the received PSM tokens for WETH and then attempts to provide both assets to the Ramses WETH‑PSM pool. The contract assumes that after the internal _addLiquidity call all of the tokens it holds will be transferred to the pool and that its own balance will be zero. However, the _addLiquidity routine calculates optimal amounts based on current pool reserves and a user‑provided slippage floor. If the optimal amount of one token is lower than the amount actually held, the function transfers only the optimal portion and leaves the remainder in the contract. Because the contract does not include a step that refunds any leftover balance to the caller, the residual tokens remain locked in the contract. An attacker can exploit this by manipulating the price in the Ramses pool between the swap and the liquidity addition, causing the optimal calculation to leave a non‑zero remainder. The attacker can then trigger a subsequent function that performs a 1inch swap on the contract’s residual tokens, effectively draining the leftover amount. From a user’s perspective the transaction appears successful, the LP tokens are minted, but the user receives less than the expected refund – often seeing a small amount of PSM or WETH disappear from their wallet with no error message. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the flow of token balances after liquidity provision and noticed that the contract’s invariant “no token should remain after minting” was violated. The bug is subtle because the contract does not emit an explicit warning and the leftover amount can be very small, making it easy to overlook in normal testing. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “incomplete token accounting after liquidity provision” or “unrefunded residual balance” bugs, where a contract’s internal accounting does not reconcile all incoming assets before completing an operation. To remediate, the contract should explicitly transfer any remaining PSM or WETH back to the original user after the mint call, or redesign the liquidity‑addition logic to ensure that the full balance is always consumed, for example by adjusting the slippage parameters or by performing a final sweep of the contract’s token holdings.

title: The expiry of the parent node can be smaller than the one of a child node, violating the guarantee policy
content: The vulnerability resides in the ENS NameWrapper contract’s expiry handling logic. By design, a child node’s expiration timestamp must never exceed the current expiration of its parent node, allowing users to reason about guarantees simply by looking at the name they own. The contract implements this rule in the internal function `_getDataAndNormaliseExpiry`, which reads the parent’s expiry (`maxExpiry`) and the child’s previous expiry (`oldExpiry`) and then normalises the new expiry so it cannot be set higher than `maxExpiry`. The flaw appears when a parent node that already has one or more sub‑nodes is unwrapped (i.e., burned). During the unwrapping process the stored expiry for the parent node is cleared to zero, regardless of whether the node still has active children. Consequently, when the same parent later calls `setSubnodeOwner` or `setSubnodeRecord`, the function sees `oldExpiry == 0` and therefore skips the comparison against the child’s expiry. An attacker who controls a domain can therefore create a deep hierarchy (e.g., `sub1.base.eth` and `sub2.sub1.base.eth`), ensure the deepest node has a long expiry, unwrap the intermediate node, and re‑wrap it with a deliberately shorter expiry. The new parent expiry can be smaller than the already‑set expiry of its descendant, violating the ENS guarantee policy that parent expiry bounds all descendants. From a user’s perspective the system may show a sub‑domain that appears to be valid for years while the immediate parent is set to expire much sooner, potentially leading to unexpected loss of control, inability to renew the child, or confusion when the parent expires and the child becomes inaccessible despite its own longer expiry. The issue was discovered during a security audit that traced the expiry normalisation logic and identified the missing constraint when `oldExpiry` is reset to zero on unwrapping. The bug is subtle because the zero expiry is a valid state for an unwrapped node, and developers normally assume that unwrapping a node with children is either prohibited or harmless. However, ENS contracts do not enforce such a check, making the problem easy to miss in casual testing. To remediate the issue, the contract should either prevent unwrapping of a node that still owns sub‑nodes, propagate the maximum child expiry to the parent when unwrapping, or require the `CANNOT_UNWRAP` fuse to be burned before allowing a parent’s expiry to be set via `setSubnodeOwner`/`setSubnodeRecord`. In essence, the fix must ensure that the parent’s expiry can never be reduced below any existing child’s expiry, thereby restoring the intended hierarchical guarantee and protecting users from unexpected expiration behavior.
summary:
[NameWrapper.sol#L504](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-07-ens/blob/ff6e59b9415d0ead7daf31c2ed06e86d9061ae22/contracts/wrapper/NameWrapper.sol#L504)  
[NameWrapper.sol#L356](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-07-ens/blob/ff6e59b9415d0ead7daf31c2ed06e86d9061ae22/contracts/wrapper/NameWrapper.sol#L356)  

By design, the child node’s expiry can only be extended up to the parent’s current one. Adding these restrictions means that the ENS users only have to look at the name itself’s fuses and expiry (without traversing the hierarchy) to understand what guarantees the users have.

When a parent node tries to `setSubnodeOwner` / `setSubnodeRecord`, the following code is used to guarantee that the new expiry can only be extended up to the current one.

```solidity
function _getDataAndNormaliseExpiry(
    bytes32 parentNode,
    bytes32 node,
    uint64 expiry
)
    internal
    view
    returns (
        address owner,
        uint32 fuses,
        uint64
    )
{
    uint64 oldExpiry;
    (owner, fuses, oldExpiry) = getData(uint256(node));
    (, , uint64 maxExpiry) = getData(uint256(parentNode));
    expiry = _normaliseExpiry(expiry, oldExpiry, maxExpiry);
    return (owner, fuses, expiry);
}
```

However, the problem shows when

  * The sub-domain (e.g., `sub1.base.eth`) has its own sub-sub-domain (e.g., `sub2.sub1.base.eth`)
  * The sub-domain is unwrapped later, and thus its `oldExpiry` becomes zero.
  * When `base.eth` calls `NameWrapper.setSubnodeOwner`, there is not constraint of `sub1.base.eth`’s expiry, since `oldExpiry == 0`. As a result, the new expiry of `sub1.base.eth` can be arbitrary and smaller than the one of `sub2.sub1.base.eth`

The point here is that the `oldExpiry` will be set as 0 when unwrapping the node even it holds child nodes, relaxing the constraint.

Specifically, considering the following scenario

  * The hacker owns a domain (or a 2LD), e.g., `base.eth`
  * The hacker assigns a sub-domain to himself, e.g., `sub1.base.eth`

    * The expiry should be as large as possible
  * Hacker assigns a sub-sub-domain, e.g., `sub2.sub1.base.eth`

    * The expiry should be as large as possible
  * The hacker unwraps his sub-domain, i.e., `sub1.base.eth`
  * The hacker re-wraps his sub-domain via `NameWrapper.setSubnodeOwner`

    * The expiry can be small than the one of sub2.sub1.base.eth

The root cause _seems_ that we should not zero out the expiry when burning a node if the node holds any subnode.

title: `PARENT_CANNOT_CONTROL` can be bypassed by maliciously unwrapping parent node
content: The vulnerability concerns the ENS NameWrapper contract’s fuse mechanism designed to prevent a parent node from regaining control over a protected subdomain after the subdomain’s PARENT_CANNOT_CONTROL fuse has been burnt. By design, once a subdomain burns the PARENT_CANNOT_CONTROL fuse, the parent should be unable to modify the subdomain’s owner or reset its fuses. The flaw arises because the parent node can first unwrap its own wrapped domain, then call ENSRegistry.setSubnodeOwner on the protected subdomain to re‑assign itself as the owner, and finally invoke NameWrapper.wrap to rewrite the fuse set and ownership of the subdomain. This sequence bypasses the intended protection: the parent’s unwrapping does not automatically burn the CANNOT_UNWRAP fuse on the subdomain, so the registry call is still permitted and the wrapper can be reapplied with a fresh fuse configuration. An attacker who controls a parent domain (e.g., "hack.poc.eth") can therefore steal a victim’s sub‑subdomain (e.g., "victim.hack.poc.eth") even after the victim has explicitly burnt PARENT_CANNOT_CONTROL, expecting immutability. The impact is a loss of control over subdomains, potential seizure of assets linked to those names, and a breach of trust in the ENS name‑wrapping system, which many protocols rely on for immutable naming and access control. The issue manifests when the parent node remains wrapped, the subdomain’s PARENT_CANNOT_CONTROL fuse is burnt, but the CANNOT_UNWRAP fuse is not simultaneously burnt, allowing the parent to later unwrap and rewrap. It affects ENS name owners, developers integrating ENS names, and any users whose subdomains are expected to remain under their sole authority. The bug was discovered during a security audit that exercised the fuse‑burning logic and observed that unwrapping a parent node could reset ownership of a child node. It is subtle because the contract only checks fuse state locally and does not perform a costly root‑to‑leaf verification, making the bypass non‑obvious in normal operation. To remediate, the contract should automatically burn the CANNOT_UNWRAP fuse whenever any descendant burns PARENT_CANNOT_CONTROL, or enforce that unwrapping cannot be used to override existing fuse states unless the name has expired, and any re‑wrap operation should validate the previous fuse configuration before allowing changes. From a user’s perspective, a subdomain that was believed to be permanently owned may suddenly show a different owner in the UI, balances tied to that name disappear, and expected refunds or permissions no longer work, violating the fundamental accounting assumption that once a fuse is burnt, control cannot be reclaimed by the parent.
summary:
[NameWrapper.sol#L356](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-07-ens/blob/ff6e59b9415d0ead7daf31c2ed06e86d9061ae22/contracts/wrapper/NameWrapper.sol#L356)  
[NameWrapper.sol#L295](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-07-ens/blob/ff6e59b9415d0ead7daf31c2ed06e86d9061ae22/contracts/wrapper/NameWrapper.sol#L295)  
[ENSRegistry.sol#L74](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-07-ens/blob/ff6e59b9415d0ead7daf31c2ed06e86d9061ae22/contracts/registry/ENSRegistry.sol#L74)  

By design, for any subdomain, as long as its `PARENT_CANNOT_CONTROL` fuse is burnt (and does not expire), its parent should not be able to burn its fuses or change its owner.

However, this contraint can be bypassed by a parent node maliciously unwrapping itself. As long as the hacker becomes the ENS owner of the parent node, he can leverage `ENSRegistry::setSubnodeOwner` to re-set himself as the ENS owner of the subdomain, and thus re-invoking `NameWrapper.wrap` can rewrite the fuses and wrapper owner of the given subdoamin.

Considering the following attack scenario:

  * Someone owns a domain (or a 2LD), e.g., _poc.eth_
  * The domain owner assigns a sub-domain to the hacker, e.g., _hack.poc.eth_

    * This sub-domain should not burn `CANNOT_UNWRAP`
    * This sub-domain can burn `PARENT_CANNOT_CONTROL`
  * Hacker assigns a sub-sub-domain to a victim user, e.g., _victim.hack.poc.eth_
  * The victim user burns arbitrary fuses, including `PARENT_CANNOT_CONTROL`

    * The hacker should not be able to change the owner and the fuses of `victim.hack.poc.eth` ideally
  * However, the hacker then unwraps his sub-domain, i.e., _hack.poc.eth_
  * The hacker invokes `ENSRegistry::setSubnodeOwner(hacker.poc.eth, victim)` on the sub-sub-domain

    * He can reassign himself as the owner of the _victim.hack.poc.eth_
  * The hacker invokes `NameWrapper.wrap(victim.hacker.poc.eth)` to over-write the fuses and owner of the sub-sub-domain, i.e., _victim.hacker.poc.eth_

The root cause here is that, for any node, when one of its subdomains burns `PARENT_CANNOT_CONTROL`, the node itself fails to burn `CANNOT_UNWRAP`. Theoretically, this should check to the root, which however is very gas-consuming.

title: ValueCanBeExtractedFromThePoolByCombiningTheBurning of bToken and the Buying/Selling of Portal Energy
content: The vulnerability is a price‑manipulation flaw that arises from the interaction between the burning of liquidity‑provider tokens (bToken) and the pricing function for portal energy in the virtual liquidity pool. The pool determines the amount of portal energy that can be bought using the quoteBuyPortalEnergy view function, which calculates the portal energy reserve as a constant product divided by the current PSM token balance held by the pool. When a user who holds bToken calls burnBtokens, the contract transfers the underlying PSM tokens back to the user, instantly reducing the PSM balance that the pricing formula relies on. Because the price quote does not account for this imminent reserve change, an attacker can first sell portal energy at the pre‑burn price, then burn a large amount of bToken to withdraw PSM, causing the PSM reserve to drop and the portal‑energy price to fall dramatically. The attacker can then immediately buy portal energy with the same or a larger amount of PSM, receiving more portal energy than before and extracting net value from the pool. This exploit works whenever the pool is active, the attacker can acquire a substantial quantity of bToken, and the LP protection hurdle only reduces the input amount of the trade but does not mitigate the reserve shift caused by the burn. The impact is that the attacker can profit in portal‑energy units, effectively stealing value that should belong to other liquidity providers and the protocol, while ordinary users may see their portal‑energy holdings devalue or experience unexpected zero‑balance outcomes. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the PortalV2MultiAsset contract, where the reviewer noticed that the quoteBuyPortalEnergy function uses the live PSM balance without any safeguard against simultaneous withdrawals. The flaw is subtle because the arithmetic of the constant‑product formula appears correct in isolation, and the LP protection hurdle gives a false sense of security, making the manipulation hard to spot in routine testing. To remediate, the protocol should limit the amount of bToken that can be burned in a single transaction or introduce a time‑based replenishment limit, thereby preventing large, instantaneous reserve shifts. Alternatively, the pricing function could be decoupled from the immediate PSM balance or incorporate a virtual reserve that smooths out abrupt changes, ensuring that the price quote remains stable even when liquidity is withdrawn. In practice, users would notice that after burning bToken the price of portal energy drops, allowing them to buy more energy for the same PSM amount, while other participants may see their expected refunds or balances disappear, violating the economic assumptions of the pool.

title: Unsafe type-casting
content: The vulnerability is an unsafe down‑casting of signed integers that allows values larger than the target type to overflow silently. In the contract’s swap routine an invariant value calculated as a signed 256‑bit integer is explicitly cast to a signed 128‑bit integer before being stored in a struct. The cast assumes the value fits into 128 bits; if the invariant grows beyond the 2^127‑1 limit the high bits are discarded and the stored value wraps around. The same pattern appears in the settlement logic where the net balance is computed as the difference between the contract’s ether balance and an internal accounting balance, both cast to int256. If the internal balance itself exceeds the maximum int256 value, the subtraction overflows to a negative number, causing the settlement function to credit the caller with the entire physical balance. Additional encoding and decoding helpers also perform unchecked casts that truncate large numbers, which can be triggered by supplying specially crafted data that exceeds the expected size. An attacker can exploit these flaws by performing extremely large swaps or allocations that push the invariant or internal balance beyond the safe range, or by feeding maliciously encoded instructions that cause overflow in fee calculations or pool initialization. The impact is that the protocol’s accounting invariants break, leading to situations where users receive no tokens, balances become zero, or the attacker walks away with more funds than they should, effectively causing funds to disappear from the pool. The issue manifests only when values approach the limits of the integer types, making it hard to detect in normal testing because typical transaction sizes stay well within range. The bug was discovered during a manual security review that inspected type conversions and identified missing range checks. To remediate, all casts from a larger signed integer to a smaller one should be replaced with safe casting utilities that verify the value fits within the destination range and revert otherwise, or the code should retain the larger type throughout the computation and eliminate unnecessary down‑casts. Removing the int128 cast in the swap event and adding explicit overflow checks in settlement and encoding functions would restore the intended accounting guarantees and prevent the protocol from crediting users incorrectly.
summary: Throughout the contract we’ve encountered various unsafe type-castings. • invariant Within the _swap function, the next invariant is a int256 variable and is calculated within the checkInvariant function implemented in the RMM01Portfolio. This variable then is dangerously typecasted to int128 and assigned to a int256 variable in the iteration struct (L539). The down-casting from int256 to int128 assumes that the nextInvariantWad fits in a int128, in case it won’t fit, it will overflow. The updated iteration object is passed to the _feeSavingEffects function, which based on the RMM implementation can lead to bad consequences. • iteration.nextInvariant • _getLatestInvariantAndVirtualPrice • getNetBalance During account settlement, getNetBalance is called to compute the difference between the "physical reserves" (contract balance) and the internal reserves: net = int256(physicalBalance) - int256(internalBalance). If the internalBalance > int256.max, it overflows into a negative value and the attacker is credited the entire physical balance + overflow upon settlement (and doesn’t have to pay anything in settle). This might happen if an attacker allocates or swaps in very high amounts before settlement is called. Consider doing a safe typecast here as a legitimate possible revert would cause less issues than an actual overflow. • getNetBalance • Encoding / Decoding functions The encoding and decoding functions in FVMLib perform many unsafe typecasts and will truncate values. This can result in a user calling functions with unexpected parameters if they use a custom encoding.
