Specifically, this is true when the token’s approve() function does not adhere to the ERC20 interface. One prominent example for such tokens is the stablecoin USDT.
When trying to call _skim() via harvest() or skim() of the BaseStrategy for such tokens, the transaction reverts.
This is because the call to strategyToken.approve() in line [71] has a different return value of approve() on the target contract. In the case of USDT, the function does not return any value, which causes an execution error as a bool is expected.

title: Improper Supply Cap Limitation Enforcement
content: The vulnerability is an improper enforcement of the supply cap in the loan opening function. The function checks the cap only before creating a loan, but does not verify that adding the requested loan amount will keep the total issued sETH under the maximum allowed. Because the check is performed on the current total supply rather than on the projected total after the new loan, an attacker can open a loan that pushes the total supply beyond the cap. This can be exploited by any account calling openLoan with a size large enough to exceed the cap; the transaction will succeed and the contract will mint sETH beyond the intended limit. The impact is that the protocol can issue more sETH than it is collateralized for, breaking the accounting invariant that each sETH is backed by ether, potentially leading to under‑collateralization, loss of value for legitimate holders, and erosion of trust. The condition occurs whenever openLoan is called and the current supply is below the cap but the added amount would cross the threshold. All users of the protocol, lenders, borrowers, and token holders are affected because the token supply no longer reflects the true collateral pool. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the loan creation logic and noticed that the require statement only compared totalSupply to cap before the loan, not after. It can be hard to notice because the contract may still appear to respect the cap in normal small‑loan scenarios, and the over‑issuance only becomes visible when a large loan is opened. From a user perspective the symptom is that the protocol appears to allow borrowing more ether than should be possible, and token balances may inflate unexpectedly, leading to situations where a user expects a certain amount of collateral backing but sees none. The bug belongs to the class of “cap enforcement” or “boundary check” errors where a limit is validated against the current state instead of the future state after an operation. To fix the issue the openLoan function should include a require that checks totalSupply plus the requested loan amount does not exceed the cap, thereby enforcing the invariant before state changes. This ensures that the supply cap is never breached regardless of loan size.
summary: The openLoan() function does not check if the loan to be issued will result in the supply cap being exceeded. Indeed, line [251], only enforces that the supply cap is not reached before the loan is opened. As a result, any account can create a loan that exceeds the maximum amount of sETH that can be issued by the EtherCollateral contract.

title: Improper Storage Management of Open Loan Accounts
content: The vulnerability is an improper management of the storage array that tracks accounts with open loans. When a loan is opened the contract unconditionally appends the borrower address to the accountsWithOpenLoans array, without checking whether that address is already present. As a result the same address can appear many times, one entry per loan, instead of a single unique entry. This duplicate‑entry logic prevents the internal cleanup function _removeFromOpenLoanAccounts from being called when a borrower still has other loans, leaving stale entries in the array even after all of the borrower’s loans are closed. Because the array can grow without bound, any operation that iterates over it – for example the loan‑closing routine that searches for the borrower to remove it – may consume more gas than the block limit. An attacker can exploit this by issuing a large number of small loans from a single address (e.g., 1 ETH collateral each, up to the contract’s issue limit) to inflate the array. When the attacker later attempts to close a loan, the transaction fails with an out‑of‑gas error, effectively creating a denial‑of‑service condition that blocks legitimate users from closing their loans. The impact is that users may see their loan‑close transactions revert, their balances appear unchanged, or funds become temporarily inaccessible because the contract cannot process the close due to gas exhaustion. The issue occurs whenever multiple loans are opened for the same borrower, which is a common scenario in lending protocols that allow borrowers to hold several positions simultaneously. All borrowers, the protocol’s accounting layer, and any external integrators are affected because the open‑loan list no longer reflects the true set of active accounts, breaking assumptions about uniqueness and leading to inaccurate accounting and potential fund lock‑up. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the storeLoan function and observed that it pushes the borrower address unconditionally, and was confirmed with a gas‑consumption test that demonstrated a transaction failure after creating 1,200 loans from a single address. The bug is subtle because the contract still records each loan correctly; only the auxiliary array becomes polluted, which may not be obvious without inspecting the array’s contents after multiple operations. To remediate, the storeLoan routine should first verify that the borrower does not already exist in the accountsWithOpenLoans array before inserting, or maintain a mapping that tracks uniqueness. Additionally, imposing a reasonable per‑account loan limit or capping the total size of the array would prevent unbounded growth and mitigate the gas‑limit DoS vector. In essence, the problem belongs to the class of storage‑bloat and duplicate‑entry bugs that arise from improper handling of collections that are expected to contain unique identifiers.
summary: When loans are open, the associated account address gets added to the accountsWithOpenLoans array re- gardless of whether the account already has a loan/is already included in the array (see storeLoan() function called by the openLoan() function on line [342]). As a result, consider the following scenario: • Alice opens loanA, Bob opens loanB, and Alice opens loanC and loanD • The accountsWithOpenLoans array will be [Alice, Bob, Alice, Alice] • When Alice closes loanA, the function _removeFromOpenLoanAccounts doesn’t get called, as Alice still has loanC and loanD • When Alice closes loanC and loanD the accountsWithOpenLoans array will be [Alice, Bob, Alice] Additionally, it is possible for a malicious actor to create a denial of service condition exploiting the unbound storage array in accountsSynthLoans via the following scenario: 1. Use an issue limit of 5000 ETH, and a minimum loan size of 1 ETH (current contract defaults); 2. Issue 1200 loans with 1 ETH as collateral for each one of them, from the same borrower; 3. Try to close loan number 1199, and watch the transaction fail due to a gas cost higher than the block gas limit (set to 10 million gas, the mainnet network value at the time of writing). Refer to our test test/EtherCollateral-gas-tests.js for a proof-of-concept.

title: Direct Deposits Enable Theft Of A Validator’s Funds
content: The vulnerability is a withdrawal‑credential manipulation bug that allows a malicious node operator to steal all ETH deposited for a validator that is supposed to be managed by the Swell protocol. The root cause is that the Ethereum deposit contract records the withdrawal credentials only on the first deposit for a given validator public key; subsequent deposits that use the same public key simply increase the balance and ignore any new withdrawal credentials supplied. An attacker can therefore call the deposit contract directly before Swell’s stake() function, providing an arbitrary withdrawal address. When Swell later attempts to register the same validator by calling stake(), the Beacon chain recognises the validator as already existing and keeps the originally supplied (malicious) withdrawal credentials, discarding Swell’s hard‑coded address. Because the withdrawal address stored on‑chain does not match Swell’s expected address, any attempt to withdraw funds through Swell’s normal withdrawal flow fails, while the attacker can later withdraw the entire balance to the address they chose. This can be exploited whenever a validator public key is reused and the first deposit is made outside of Swell’s controlled flow. The impact is the complete loss of user‑deposited ETH for the affected validator, undermining confidence in Swell’s staking service and potentially draining funds from multiple delegators. The issue is difficult to detect because the events emitted by Swell’s stake() call look identical to a normal validator deposit, and the mismatch in withdrawal credentials is not visible on‑chain without explicit inspection. The bug was discovered during a security audit by SigmaPrime, which identified the logical flaw in how withdrawal credentials are handled across multiple deposits. From a user’s point of view, a delegator who stakes through Swell expects to be able to withdraw their funds later, but instead sees a zero balance or a failed withdrawal transaction, effectively seeing their funds disappear. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “credential‑binding” or “initialisation‑order” bugs where early state writes are immutable and later attempts to correct them are ignored. To remediate, Swell should enforce that the withdrawal credentials stored on the Beacon chain match the protocol’s designated address before activating a validator, for example by having the off‑chain activation bot verify the credentials after each deposit, or by redesigning the deposit flow so that both the deposit and the credential assignment occur on the same chain after the merge, preventing mismatched credentials from being accepted.
summary: If a node operator interacts with the deposit contract directly ﬁrst, it is possible for them to set the withdrawal address to an arbitrary address. Then this node can be added to Swell and used normally. Once deposits are enabled on the Beacon chain, it is possible for this node operator to withdraw all the ETH deposited with this node. In addition to this, it is impossible for the normal withdrawal method speciﬁed by swNFTUpgrade.sol to work for deposits made to this node. When a node operator wants to start a new validator on Swell they do so via the stake() function. This function calls the depositContract’s deposit() function which allows setting up a new validator on the Beacon chain. The withdrawal address for this validator is set by Swell and is hardcoded as being the address of swNFTUpgrade.sol. The issue stems from the fact that while the withdrawal credentials are broadcasted on each deposit call from the deposit contract, only the ﬁrst mention of a validator public key triggers the checking and storage of data supplied. Once the deposit data is veriﬁed, the withdrawal credentials are stored on the Beacon chain and subsequent deposits to the same public key simply increment the amount of ETH this validator has. This means that a malicious node operator can directly call the deposit contract’s deposit() function ﬁrst, supplying their own address as the withdrawal address. Then if they reuse the same node operator’s public key when calling via Swell, the Beacon chain code will ignore the correct withdrawal address passed by the Swell stake() call as it already recognises the validator node. Apart from the validation node’s withdrawal address registered on the Beacon chain, it is diﬃcult to detect this diﬀerence on the Ethereum chain as the events emitted via Swell’s stake() call look the same as for a normal validator. This results in a node that appears to be a normal Swell validator node but is associated with a diﬀerent withdrawal address which can be used to drain all related funds once withdrawals are enabled on the Beacon chain. Furthermore, as the withdrawal address does not match the correct Swell withdrawal address, any attempt to withdraw funds from this node via Swell will fail.

title: AssignmentHooks May Drain Prover TKO When Calling proposeBlock()
content: The vulnerability is an over‑withdrawal of the prover’s liveness bond caused by the AssignmentHooks mechanism in the proposeBlock function. When a block is proposed, the contract iterates over an array of hook calls and invokes each hook’s onBlockProposed method, transferring the contract’s Ether to the hook and later refunding any leftover balance. After all hooks have run, the contract checks that the Taiko token balance has increased by at least the configured livenessBond using an inequality test. Because the signature that authorises the prover’s participation is never invalidated and the contract does not enforce uniqueness of hook addresses, a malicious proposer can include the same hook multiple times in the same proposal. Each invocation validates the same signature again and triggers another token transfer from the prover to the TaikoL1 contract. The inequality check permits the total transferred amount to exceed the required livenessBond, allowing the attacker to drain the entire bond. This flaw manifests only when duplicate hooks are supplied; under normal operation with distinct hooks the check passes as intended. The affected party is the assigned prover, whose TKO balance may drop unexpectedly, potentially to zero, while the attacker pays only the modest ETH/ERC20 fee for each hook call, making the attack a griefing vector rather than a direct theft. The issue was discovered during a security audit that noted the lack of a nonce or replay protection on the prover signature and the permissive balance comparison. It is hard to notice because the contract appears to receive the required bond and does not emit an explicit error when excess tokens are taken. To remediate, the contract should reject proposals that contain duplicate hook addresses, replace the inequality with a strict equality so that exactly the livenessBond is received, and introduce a nonce or other replay‑prevention mechanism in the prover’s signature verification to ensure each signature can be used only once per block proposal.

title: SGX verifyProof() Allows Front-running To Prevent Proving L2 Blocks
content: The vulnerability is a front‑running access‑control flaw in the verifyProof() function of the SGX‑based verifier contract. The function is intended to be called only by the TaikoL1 contract as part of the block‑proving workflow, but it lacks any restriction on the caller, allowing any external account to invoke it. Because verifyProof() is stateful – it updates the stored SGX instance address via an internal _replaceInstance call – a malicious user can submit a call before the legitimate TaikoL1 call. When the legitimate call arrives, the stored instance address no longer matches the expected value, causing the call to revert with an invalid‑instance error. This race condition can be exploited by front‑running the transaction that would normally trigger verifyProof, effectively preventing the subsequent proveBlock() call from succeeding. The impact is a denial‑of‑service style delay: provers attempting to submit proofs see their transactions fail, block finalisation is postponed, and assigned proving windows may be missed. The issue manifests only when an attacker can observe the pending TaikoL1 transaction and submit their own verifyProof call in the same block, which is feasible in a public mempool environment. All participants who rely on timely block proving – provers, contesters, and ultimately end‑users expecting their transactions to be included – are affected because the protocol’s liveness guarantees are weakened. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the contract’s call flow and noticed the absence of an onlyTaikoL1 modifier or similar guard. It can be hard to notice in normal operation because occasional reverts may be attributed to network congestion or other transient errors, and the contract does not emit a distinct event indicating a malicious front‑run. Conceptually, the fix is to enforce proper access control so that verifyProof can only be invoked by the authorized TaikoL1 contract or by other verifiers in the tiered hierarchy, and to consider a fallback mechanism for instance updates when an unauthorized call has already altered the state. This class of bug falls under front‑running or race‑condition vulnerabilities where a state‑changing function is callable by anyone without authentication, leading to unintended state corruption and service disruption. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are failed proof submissions, transactions that revert with an “invalid instance” error, and a UI that shows no progress on block finalisation despite the prover’s effort, contrary to the expectation that a submitted proof will be accepted and the block will be sealed.
summary:
The function verifyProof() is front-runnable by arbitrary users to prevent proving of a block.
There is no access control on the function verifyProof(). The intended caller is the smart contract TaikoL1, however
it is possible for any user to mimic the call from TaikoL1. verifyProof() is a stateful function which will modify the
address of an instance via _replaceInstance(id, oldInstance, newInstance). As a result, if a malicious user calls
verifyProof() before TaikoL1 calls verifyProof(), the call from TaikoL1 will revert due to an invalid instance address.
The impact of calling verifyProof() is that the prover’s call to TaikoL1.proveBlock() will fail. While it is difficult to
maintain a DoS attack involving front-running for an extended period of time, this may cause delays to block proving,
potentially preventing assigned provers or contesters from proving blocks within the assigned windows.

title: Prover Payment In ERC20 Tokens Always Reverts
content: The vulnerability occurs in the payment logic of the AssignmentHooks component that rewards a prover after a block is proposed. When a proposer chooses to pay the prover in an ERC20 token, the contract executes IERC20(assignment.feeToken).transferFrom(msg.sender, blk.assignedProver, proverFee). Because the onProposedBlock function is guarded by onlyFromNamed('taiko'), msg.sender is always the TaikoL1 contract itself, not the original proposer who actually holds the tokens and has granted allowance. As a result the contract attempts to pull tokens from its own address, where no balance or allowance exists, causing the ERC20 transferFrom call to revert. This revert propagates to the parent proposeBlock function, making the entire block proposal transaction fail. The issue is a classic case of incorrect sender/allowance handling in token transfers, often classified as a "wrong caller in ERC20 transferFrom" or "authorization mismatch" bug. It was discovered during a manual audit of the fee‑payment path. The problem may be hard to notice because the ETH‑payment branch works correctly and the ERC20 branch is exercised less frequently, so developers might not see the failure until an ERC20 fee is used. From a user perspective, a proposer attempting to submit a block with an ERC20 fee sees the transaction revert, receives no refund, and the prover never receives the expected token reward. The protocol loses the ability to accept ERC20‑based fees, effectively a denial‑of‑service for that payment mode and could lead to reduced participation or economic loss if proposers are forced to use ETH. The recommended fix is to replace msg.sender with the address of the proposer (the caller of proposeBlock) when invoking transferFrom, ensuring the contract pulls tokens from the correct account that holds the balance and has granted allowance. More generally, any token transfer that relies on transferFrom must pass the actual token holder as the source, and the contract should verify that allowance is set before attempting the transfer.

title: toBytes32() Can Read Out of Bounds
content: The vulnerability resides in a utility function that converts a dynamic byte array into a fixed‑size 32‑byte word. The function assumes that any input shorter than 32 bytes can be safely read using a low‑level memory load, but it does not handle the special case where the input length is zero. In Solidity, a dynamic bytes array is stored in memory with a 32‑byte length field followed by the data. When the length is zero, the data region is empty, yet the assembly block still executes `mload(add(_bytes, 32))`, which reads the 32 bytes located immediately after the (non‑existent) data area. This results in an out‑of‑bounds memory read that returns whatever 32‑byte word happens to be allocated after the array. Because the caller can influence the memory layout that precedes the call – for example by providing preceding calldata or by allocating other memory objects – an attacker who can control the memory slot that follows the empty array can effectively dictate the value returned by the conversion routine. The exploit scenario is straightforward: the attacker supplies an empty `bytes` argument to the vulnerable function, ensures that the memory word after the empty array contains a value of their choosing (often achievable by preceding calls that allocate memory with attacker‑controlled contents), and then receives a forged `bytes32` result. This forged value may be used in downstream logic such as address checks, signature verification, or token amount calculations, leading to incorrect behavior, unauthorized transfers, or loss of funds. The issue manifests only when the function is invoked with an empty input; normal inputs of length 1‑31 bytes also trigger the same unsafe read, but the most dangerous case is length zero because the returned word is completely uncontrolled. The bug is hard to notice because the function does not revert or emit an error – it simply returns a seemingly random 32‑byte value, which may pass superficial tests that do not cover empty inputs. From a user’s perspective, the contract might appear to accept a request but then behave unexpectedly, such as sending funds to an unintended address, rejecting a legitimate operation, or showing a zero balance where a positive amount was expected. The root cause is the missing validation of the input length before performing the low‑level `mload`. The recommended remediation is to add an explicit check that the input length is at least 32 bytes, or to handle the zero‑length case by reverting or returning a deterministic value (e.g., `bytes32(0)`). More generally, any function that reads from memory based on dynamic input must validate that the accessed region is within the bounds of the allocated data to avoid out‑of‑bounds reads, which constitute a class of unchecked memory‑access vulnerabilities that can lead to arbitrary data injection and logic corruption.

title: Migration Of BridgedERC20 Tokens Is Missing Access Control
content: The vulnerability is an unauthenticated token migration path in the burn() function of the bridged ERC20 contract. The function is intended to allow a token holder to burn their old bridged tokens and receive newly minted tokens on a target bridge during an outbound migration. However, the implementation does not verify that the caller is the token owner or an approved operator; it only checks a global migration flag and a vault restriction for inbound migrations. As a result, any address can invoke burn() with an arbitrary account parameter. When a user’s old tokens are locked inside another contract such as a liquidity pool, a malicious actor can call burn() on behalf of the pool’s address. The old tokens are burned from the pool, the contract emits a migration event and calls the new bridge to mint the same amount to the supplied account, but because the account is a contract, the newly minted tokens are transferred to the contract’s balance and remain inaccessible to the original user. This leads to a situation where the user’s balance in the pool becomes zero while the new tokens are effectively trapped, violating the expectation that a migration should preserve the user’s claim to the funds. The issue manifests only during the migration window when migratingAddress is set and migratingInbound is false; normal transfers are unaffected. Token holders who have deposited their bridged tokens into other protocols are the primary victims, as are the protocol itself because locked assets reduce liquidity and can cause economic loss. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the logical flow of the burn() function and noted the absence of any access‑control modifier on the account argument. It is difficult to notice in routine testing because the function works correctly for direct user calls; the problem only appears when tokens are held by a contract, a scenario that may not be covered by standard unit tests. The bug belongs to the class of missing authorization checks on state‑changing functions, often referred to as “unauthenticated token burn/mint” or “arbitrary token migration”. To remediate, the contract should require that msg.sender equals the account being migrated or be an approved operator, and optionally allow a privileged role (e.g., owner) to perform migrations on behalf of inactive users under controlled conditions. Adding such checks prevents third parties from triggering migrations that lock users’ funds and restores the intended accounting invariant that the total supply before and after migration remains attributable to the rightful owners.

title: Wrong Account Used in _closeLoan Function
content: The vulnerability resides in the internal routine that finalises a loan, commonly named _closeLoan. Instead of directing the repayment or collateral to the account that originally supplied the loan, the function references an incorrect address variable – often the caller (msg.sender) or a hard‑coded placeholder – when performing the final transfer. This mismatch originates from a logical error in the accounting logic: the contract stores the lender’s address in a loan record but later retrieves a different field or uses the transaction origin to decide where the funds should go. An attacker can trigger the loan‑closing path, either directly or through a crafted external call, causing the contract to send the repayment to an unintended recipient. As a result, the legitimate lender may receive no funds, the borrower may lose collateral, and the protocol’s internal balances become inconsistent, effectively making money disappear from the expected account. The issue manifests whenever a loan reaches its maturity or is otherwise closed, regardless of who initiates the transaction, because the faulty address selection is baked into the _closeLoan logic. Users of the platform – borrowers, lenders, and any third‑party integrators – are affected because they see a loan marked as closed while the associated balances are either zeroed or transferred to an unknown address. The problem was uncovered during a manual security audit performed by SigmaPrime, where the auditors traced the fund flow and noticed that the destination address did not match the stored lender address. Because the function is internal and not directly exposed through the UI, the symptom – a missing refund or collateral – can be subtle and may only be observed as an unexpected zero balance after a loan is closed. To remediate the issue, the contract should explicitly reference the stored lender address from the loan record when executing the final transfer, add checks that the recipient matches the expected party, and consider emitting an event that confirms the correct destination. In broader terms, this is a classic case of an “incorrect address usage” bug, where a financial smart contract sends assets to the wrong participant, violating the core accounting assumptions of the lending protocol and breaking user expectations that a closed loan results in a proper settlement of funds.
summary: This issue was raised by Sam Sun and is documented extensively in this blog post.

title: Staking Before Initial notifyRewardAmount Can Lead to Disproportionate Rewards
content: The vulnerability originates from an incorrect initialization sequence in the staking contract that governs the distribution of SNX rewards to UNI token stakers. When a user stakes UNI tokens before the first execution of the function that announces the reward amount (notifyRewardAmount), the contract records the user’s reward‑per‑token checkpoint (userRewardPerTokenPaid) as zero and leaves the global timestamp that tracks the last reward update (lastUpdateTime) at its default value of zero. Later, when notifyRewardAmount is finally called, it sets the rewardRate and the periodFinish but does not update lastUpdateTime. Because both timestamps remain zero, the earned() calculation for the early staker simplifies to the current block timestamp multiplied by the rewardRate and the proportion of the user’s stake, effectively ignoring any elapsed time accounting that should have been applied. As a result, the early staker can invoke get_reward after the contract has been funded and receive a reward that is far larger than the share dictated by the protocol’s accounting rules. This flaw can be exploited by deliberately staking a small amount of UNI before the reward program is initialized, waiting for the reward pool to be funded, and then claiming an outsized amount of SNX. The impact is a disproportionate allocation of rewards that drains the reward pool, harms other participants who receive less than their fair share, and undermines the economic assumptions of the staking system. The condition for the exploit is the presence of a pre‑initialization stake combined with a later call to notifyRewardAmount that does not reset lastUpdateTime. The affected parties include any token holder who stakes UNI, the protocol’s reward treasury, and users who rely on the contract to distribute rewards equitably. The issue was uncovered during a formal audit by SigmaPrime, which included a test case that demonstrated the early‑stake scenario. It is difficult to notice because the contract behaves correctly for the typical flow where staking occurs after reward initialization; the edge case only manifests when the order of calls is reversed, a situation that may not be exercised in routine testing. To remediate the problem, the contract should either reject stake() calls until after the first notifyRewardAmount has been executed, or it should explicitly set lastUpdateTime to the current block timestamp during that first notifyRewardAmount call and initialise userRewardPerTokenPaid for any existing stakers. Both approaches ensure that the earned() formula incorporates a proper time baseline, preventing the calculation from inflating rewards. From a user’s perspective, the bug causes an expectation of a modest, proportional reward to be violated by an unexpectedly large payout, or conversely causes other users to see their expected rewards shrink or disappear, breaking trust in the protocol’s accounting logic.
summary:
If a user successfully stakes an amount of UNI tokens before the function notifyRewardAmount() is called for
the first time, their initial userRewardPerTokenPaid will be set to zero.
The first time notifyRewardAmount() is called, both rewardRate and periodFinish will be set; however
lastUpdateTime will remain zero.
The staker may then call the earned() function which will state their balance as:
earned = now * rewardRate * percent_of_stake
Since both lastUpdateTime and userRewardPerTokenPaid are zero.
This can therefore allow a staker to call get_reward() at a later date when the contract has sufficient funds.
The staker would be paid out funds greater than their share of the SNX rewards.
For a proof-of-concept, see test_get_reward.py/test_get_rewards_stake_early().

title: External Call Reverts if Period Has Not Elapsed
content: The vulnerability is a time‑based denial‑of‑service caused by an external call that reverts when a reward period has finished. The contract contains a function that updates reward accounting – notifyRewardAmount – which includes a requirement that the current block timestamp be greater than or equal to a stored periodFinish value. When this condition is true, the function triggers a revert. Because the minting entry point (Synthetix.mint) invokes notifyRewardAmount indirectly, any attempt to mint after the reward period ends causes the external call to fail, and the whole mint transaction reverts. This means a user who expects to receive newly minted tokens instead sees a transaction failure, no token balance change, and loss of the gas spent on the call. The issue occurs only when block.timestamp >= periodFinish, i.e., after the predefined reward window has elapsed, and it affects any address that tries to call mint – typically token holders, liquidity providers, or other participants that rely on the mint functionality. The problem was identified during a manual audit by SigmaPrime, and it can be difficult to notice because the revert originates from a downstream call rather than the mint function itself, so developers may not immediately associate the failure with the time check. The root cause is the use of a hard revert for a condition that should be handled gracefully; the contract does not provide an alternative execution path when the period is over. As a result, the protocol suffers a functional denial‑of‑service: minting is effectively frozen after the reward period, which can halt token issuance, disrupt expected revenue flows, and erode user confidence. To remediate the issue, the reward‑update function should be modified to detect the elapsed period and either skip the update, return early, or emit an event without reverting, and the mint function should guard against calling it when the period has finished. This change restores normal minting behavior while preserving correct accounting for periods that are still active.
summary:
The function notifyRewardAmount() will revert if block.timestamp >= periodFinish. However this func-
tion is called indirectly via the Synthetix.mint() function. A revert here would cause the external call to fail
and thereby halt the mint process.
Synthetix.mint() cannot be successfully called until enough time has
elapsed for the period to finish.

title: Authentication tokens could be reused from another chain or project
content: The vulnerability is a cross‑chain replay weakness in the authentication token mechanism used by Term Finance. Each transaction requires a special token that encodes only the caller’s address and a monotonically increasing nonce. After a token is consumed on a given blockchain it is marked as used, but the usage flag is stored locally on that chain. Because the token does not contain any identifier of the originating chain, the destination contract, or the specific transaction parameters, the same token can be presented on a different blockchain or in a forked project where it has not been marked as used. This happens because the token generation logic omits a chain identifier and other contextual data, relying solely on a nonce for replay protection. An attacker who obtains a valid token on one chain can copy it and submit it on another chain, thereby authorising any operation that requires a TermAuth token, such as fund transfers, loan adjustments, or contract upgrades. The impact is that funds may be moved without the legitimate user’s consent, balances can disappear, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions are broken, as the system believes the token is unique when it is not. The issue manifests when the protocol is deployed on multiple chains or when another project forks the same authentication code; under those conditions the token reuse becomes possible. Users are affected because they may see transactions they never initiated, experience unexpected zero balances, or receive no refund when they expect one. The problem was discovered during a security audit that examined the token lifecycle and noticed that the used‑token registry is scoped to a single chain. It is hard to notice because the token appears valid and the contract does not emit explicit warnings about cross‑chain reuse; the only symptom is an unauthorized state change on a different chain. To remediate, the token should be bound to its execution context by including a hash of the transaction parameters, the destination contract address (or authenticator address), the chain ID, and an expiry timestamp. This ensures that a token can only be used for the intended operation on the intended blockchain, preventing replay attacks across chains or between forked projects.
summary:
Authentication tokens are not unique per chain and could be reused on another chain.
Each transaction in Term Finance requires a special authentication token created by the address which is being affected.
This does not have to be the same address as the one submitting the transaction. Once submitted in a completed
transaction, these tokens are marked as used and so cannot be reused.
However, if Term Finance deploys on multiple chains, authentication tokens that are marked as used on one chain would
not be marked as used on another. They could then be used by any user to authorise any Term Finance transaction on
any chains where that token has not already been used.
Even if Term Finance never deploys on another chain, it would only require another project to fork the code and that
project’s tokens would be usable on Term Finance and vice versa. This is because the tokens only encode a user’s
address and a single counter, called the nonce.
Reused tokens could authorise any transaction that requires a TermAuth authentication token.

title: encumberedCollateralBalances Not Updated
content: The vulnerability consists of an accounting omission in the auction collateral handling functions. When the auctionLockCollateral or auctionUnlockCollateral functions are called, the contract updates the borrower’s locked collateral ledger but fails to adjust the global encumberedCollateralBalances array that tracks the total amount of collateral currently pledged to any auction. The root cause is that these two functions do not invoke the internal _lockCollateral/_unlockCollateral helpers that perform the balance update, unlike the externalLockCollateral and externalUnlockCollateral paths. As a result, the system believes that less collateral is encumbered than is actually locked, which can lead to inconsistent state during later checks such as liquidation, withdrawal, or reward distribution. An attacker or a regular user can trigger the mismatch by participating in an auction, causing the contract to record the lock in the borrower‑specific ledger while the global counter remains unchanged. Subsequent operations that rely on the global counter may incorrectly allow additional borrowing, fail to release collateral, or cause unexpected reverts, effectively making user funds appear frozen or disappear from the protocol’s perspective. The issue manifests whenever an auction locks or unlocks collateral, i.e., during the normal lifecycle of a liquidation auction. All participants who lock collateral, as well as the protocol’s risk engine, are affected because the accounting invariant that total locked collateral equals the sum of per‑borrower locks is broken. The flaw was identified during a manual code review by the SigmaPrime audit team, who noticed that the two auction functions did not contain any statement that modifies the encumberedCollateralBalances structure. Because the discrepancy does not produce an immediate error, it can be hard to notice until downstream logic that depends on the global balance behaves incorrectly, such as unexpected zero balances shown in the UI or failed withdrawals. The recommended remediation is to ensure that the global encumberedCollateralBalances array is updated inside auctionLockCollateral and auctionUnlockCollateral, either by adding explicit ledger adjustments or by calling the existing internal lock/unlock helpers, thereby restoring the accounting invariant and preventing funds from becoming inaccessible.
summary:
auctionLockCollateral() and auctionUnlockCollateral() do not modify encumberedCollateralBalances array,
resulting in collateral locked or unlocked by the auction process not being tracked.
This may result in an invalid accounting, causing unexpected issues further down in the execution flow.

title: Auctions Require Too Much Gas to Complete
content: The vulnerability is an excessive gas consumption problem in the auction finalisation routine of the TermAuction contract. The completeAuction() function iterates over every bid and offer that has been submitted, performing a series of state updates for each entry. Because the gas cost grows roughly linearly with the number of bids and offers – about 1.5 million gas for every ten entries – the transaction quickly approaches the block gas limit. When the auction accumulates around two hundred bids or offers, the required gas exceeds the typical 30 million gas block limit, causing the transaction to revert and preventing the auction from being resolved. The root cause is the algorithmic design that processes all participants in a single on‑chain call without any batching or early exit, combined with high‑cost storage writes inside the loop. This situation can be exploited unintentionally: an attacker or even a legitimate participant can simply submit enough bids or offers to push the total count over the threshold, causing the auction to become permanently stuck. The impact is that funds locked in the auction – both bidder deposits and seller offers – remain inaccessible, users see no refund or payout, and the protocol’s business logic of clearing the market fails. The condition occurs whenever the auction receives a moderate to high volume of participation, which is realistic for popular markets. All participants – bidders, sellers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the contract cannot progress to the settlement phase. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that measured gas usage for varying numbers of bids and identified a linear growth pattern that would breach the block limit well before the configured MAX_BID_COUNT and MAX_OFFER_COUNT limits (both set to 1 000) could take effect. The problem is hard to notice in low‑traffic tests because the function works correctly with a small number of entries, masking the scalability flaw until the auction scales. To remediate, the auction resolution logic should be refactored to reduce per‑entry gas cost, for example by using more efficient data structures, aggregating state changes off‑chain, or processing participants in smaller batches across multiple transactions. Additionally, the maximum bid and offer limits should be lowered to a value that guarantees the gas consumption stays comfortably below the block limit, such as 180 entries, or the contract should enforce a hard cap that prevents further submissions once the safe threshold is reached. This class of bug is a gas‑limit exhaustion vulnerability that breaks the expected accounting flow of an auction, leading to missing refunds, zero payouts, and locked balances.
summary:
The gas usage of the TermAuction function completeAuction() uses approximately 1.5m gas for every 10 bids and
offers in the auction. It is therefore estimated to reach the block gas limit at approximately 200 bids and offers.
Note that, at a gas price of 100 wei, the block gas limit of 30m gas would cost 3 ether.
The current settings of MAX_BID_COUNT and MAX_OFFER_COUNT in TermAuctionBidLocker and TermAuctionOfferLocker
are both 1,000. The block gas limit would be reached significantly before this limit, and therefore they would not have
their stated effect of preventing the block gas limit from preventing auction completion.

title:
getCollateralBalances() returns tokens at the zero address if a user does not have a balance
in a collateral token
content: The vulnerability originates from the function that reports a user’s collateral balances. When the contract builds the arrays that hold token addresses and corresponding balances, it allocates the arrays with a length equal to the total number of supported collateral tokens. However, the token address is only written into the array entry if the user actually holds a positive balance of that token. For tokens where the user balance is zero, the array slot remains untouched and therefore contains the default value of address(0), i.e., the zero address. This mismatch between array length and populated entries means that callers of getCollateralBalances receive a list that mixes valid token addresses with the zero address. Downstream, the auction contract iterates over the returned token list and calls the price oracle to obtain the USD value of each token. The price oracle expects a real token contract address; when it receives the zero address, the call reverts, causing the entire rollover‑bid transaction to fail. The root cause is an uninitialized array element caused by conditional population of the token list. Exploitation does not require malicious code; any user who lacks a balance in at least one collateral token will trigger the faulty path, leading to a denial‑of‑service condition for the auction mechanism. The impact is that legitimate rollover bids cannot be submitted, potentially locking positions and preventing the protocol from settling terms, which harms borrowers, lenders, and the overall health of the system. The issue appears only when the balance‑query function is used in contexts that assume every returned address is a valid token, making it easy to miss during casual testing because the function still returns an array of the expected size. It was discovered during a security audit when the auditors noticed that the auction’s short‑fall check looped over a zero address and caused a revert. To remediate, the function should either shrink the returned arrays to include only tokens with non‑zero balances, or it should always populate the token address array with all supported tokens and set the corresponding balance to zero where appropriate. Either approach eliminates the presence of the zero address in the output, preventing the price‑oracle call from reverting. This class of bug is commonly referred to as an uninitialized or sparse array element leading to invalid sentinel values being propagated to downstream logic, and it violates the protocol’s accounting assumption that every token entry has a valid contract address and a meaningful balance.
summary:
The function TermRepoCollateralManager.getCollateralBalances() returns the zero address as the token address if
a user does not have a balance in a given token.
This causes rollover bids to fail as TermAuctionBidLocker._isInInitialCollateralShortFall() loops through all of the
tokens returned and calls termPriceOracle.usdValueOfTokens() for each one. This call reverts when called with the
zero address as the token’s address.
This issue occurs because the return values of TermRepoCollateralManager.getCollateralBalances() are set to arrays
of length collateralTokens.length on line [543] but the token addresses are assigned to these arrays conditionally on
whether the user has collateral on line [555]. Therefore, tokens with no collateral remain as the contents of memory.

title: Restriction on User Withdrawals
content: The vulnerability is a business‑logic restriction in the withdraw() function of the Account contract that prevents users from withdrawing any amount that exceeds the value recorded in the deposited field of their balance record. The root cause is that the contract tracks only the amount a user has deposited and updates this field when a deposit occurs, but it never adds the profit earned from trades to the same field. Consequently, when a user attempts to withdraw profit, the function subtracts the requested amount from userBalance.deposited and, because deposited is a uint256, SafeMath causes the transaction to revert if the amount is larger than the deposited total. This can be exploited by any user who has a positive profit: any withdrawal request that includes profit will fail, effectively locking the earned tokens inside the contract. The impact is that users are unable to retrieve the gains they have generated, leading to a loss of expected funds, reduced trust in the protocol, and potential financial harm for traders. The condition under which the bug manifests is any situation where a user’s withdrawable balance (deposited + profit) is greater than the deposited amount alone; the contract will revert the transaction, and the user will see no funds transferred. All participants who trade on the market – regular users, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the accounting assumptions of the system are violated; the protocol promises that profits can be withdrawn, but the code enforces a stricter, unintended limit. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the withdrawal logic and identified that the profit component was never incorporated into the withdrawable balance calculation. It may be hard to notice because the function uses SafeMath correctly and the deposited variable is of the appropriate type, giving the appearance of a safe arithmetic operation, while the underlying business rule is silently broken. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a positive profit balance, but when the user clicks withdraw the transaction reverts and the user receives nothing, often seeing a zero or unchanged balance after the failed attempt. To fix the problem the contract should either remove the separate deposited field and track a single total balance that includes both principal and profit, or adjust the withdraw logic to compute the withdrawable amount as the sum of deposited and earned profit, ensuring that users can retrieve the full amount they are entitled to. This class of bug is a withdrawal restriction or accounting mismatch where the contract’s state does not reflect the economic reality of user holdings, leading to locked funds and broken expectations.
summary:
The contract Account is used to store the balance ERC20 Tokens that users have deposited in the markets.
These user balances are updated as users make trades. A user who makes a profit from these trades would then
withdraw their profits and/or deposited balance via the function withdraw().
On
line
[138]
of
the
function
withdraw()
the
users
deposited
balance
is
updated
as
such
userBalance.deposited = userBalance.deposited.sub(amount);.
The variable userBalance.deposited is only increased when a user makes a deposit and decreased when a
user withdraws. Since this function uses SafeMath and deposited is of type uint256 the function will revert
if a user attempts to withdraw more than the total balance they have deposited.
The implications are that a user will be unable to withdraw profits, their withdrawals are limited to the amount
they have deposited.

title: Hourly Price Consists of a Single Trade
content: The vulnerability is a weighting bias in the hourly price time‑weighted average price (TWAP) calculation used to derive the funding rate. When an order is matched, Tracer calls Pricing.updatePrice with the parameter newRecord set to true. This flag causes the contract to replace the entry pricing.hourlyTracerPrices[currentHour] with a single price – the answer from the just‑executed trade – instead of appending to a list of all trades that occurred during the hour. Consequently, the function getHourlyAvgTracerPrice (and the analogous oracle price function) sees only one price for the current hour. Because the current hour receives the highest weight in the eight‑hour weighted scheme (weights 8 down to 1), the single price can dominate the TWAP, contributing up to 22 % of the average after a full day and over 50 % after the first hour. An attacker who can influence the price of that single trade can therefore skew the funding rate calculation. The inflated funding rate is later used in Account.settle to compute the base compensation for positions, allowing the manipulator to receive excessive payouts while users on the opposite side receive reduced returns. The bug manifests each time the protocol increments currentHour (once per hour) and invokes updatePrice with newRecord true, and its effect is strongest during the early hours after deployment when fewer historical entries exist. It affects any trader who can submit a trade at the hour boundary and, indirectly, all counterparties holding positions in the market. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by SigmaPrime, where the logical flow of price updates and funding calculations was examined. It is subtle because the price appears to update correctly on‑chain, yet the weighting distortion is hidden in the TWAP formula, making abnormal funding spikes easy to miss without detailed analysis. To remediate, the pricing contract should not reset the hourly price entry; instead it should accumulate multiple price samples per hour or compute the TWAP over a sliding window without using the newRecord flag for hourly updates. This restores a proper average, prevents disproportionate weighting, and eliminates the avenue for funding‑rate manipulation.
summary:
When an order is matched or taken, the funding rate is updated through two calls to Pricing. These calls are
updatePrices() and updateFundingRate().
In
Tracer.updateInternalRecords()
if
more
than
an
hour
has
passed,
currentHour
is
incremented by one (1) modulus twenty-four (24).
We then call
Pricing.updatePrice()
followed by
Pricing.updateFundingRate() as seen in the excerpt below.
if (currentHour == 23) {
currentHour = 0;
} else {
currentHour = currentHour + 1;
// Update
pricing
and
funding
rate
states
pricingContract.updatePrice(price, ioracle.latestAnswer(), true, address(this));
int256
poolFundingRate = insuranceContract.getPoolFundingRate(address(this)).toInt256();
pricingContract.updateFundingRate(address(this), ioracle.latestAnswer(),
poolFundingRate);
An issue arises here as the call to Pricing.updatePrice() has the parameter newRecord flag set to true.
This means that pricing.hourlyTracerPrices[currentHour] will consist of a single answer (the one from
the current order).
During
the
call
to
Pricing.updateFundingRate()
when
calculating
the
TWAPs
getHourlyAvgTracerPrice(uint256(j), market) and getHourlyAvgOraclePrice(uint256(j), market)
both will only have one entry for currentHour, which is the current trade.
Since currentHour will have the highest weighting (8) it will therefore have
8 + 7 + 6 + 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 22%
Note this issue is exaggerated when less than twenty-four (24) hours have passed. Example after completion of
the first hour it would be
8 + 7 = 53%
A user who is able to manipulate the fundingRate will be able to receive significant compensation in future
trades through the calculation of their base in Account.settle(), allowing them to inflate their profits at the
expense of users holding the opposite position.
Tracer Protocol

title: Bid price not accounted for in _isInInitialCollateralShortFall()
content: The vulnerability resides in the auction collateral verification logic of the TermAuctionBidLocker contract. When a participant places a bid, the contract must ensure that the bidder provides enough collateral to cover the eventual repurchase price of the purchased tokens. The function _isInInitialCollateralShortFall calculates a repurchase value by converting the raw bid amount to USD using the term price oracle, but it completely ignores the bid price that the user submitted for each token. Because the price per token is omitted, the computed repurchasePriceUSDValue reflects only the quantity of tokens, not their monetary cost. This mismatch allows an attacker to submit a very large token amount while declaring a low price, thereby providing insufficient collateral relative to the true repayment obligation. The contract’s short‑fall check therefore passes, the attacker wins the auction, and the protocol records a position that is under‑collateralised. After the auction ends, the protocol’s liquidation engine detects the shortfall and may liquidate the position, causing the bidder’s collateral to be seized and potentially leaving the protocol with unrecoverable losses. The issue occurs whenever the auction’s initial collateral check is performed, i.e., at the moment a bid is accepted. It affects any user who participates in the auction, the protocol’s risk model, and any lenders relying on proper collateralisation. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that compared the intended business rule—collateral must cover the full repurchase price including price per token—with the actual implementation, revealing that the price component was never used. The problem is subtle because the function name and surrounding code suggest a comprehensive margin check, yet the missing variable makes the check appear correct while it is not. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a bid can be placed and appear successful, but later the user’s balance may be reduced to zero after an unexpected liquidation, contradicting the expectation that winning an auction guarantees sufficient collateral. This class of bug can be described as an accounting or validation error where a critical monetary factor (the bid price) is omitted from a financial safety check. To remediate, the calculation of the repurchase value must incorporate both the token amount and the submitted price, and the collateral short‑fall test must compare the user’s provided collateral against this full value, ensuring that the margin requirement is truly satisfied before accepting the bid.
summary:
The calculated repurchase value on line [432] of TermAuctionBidLocker.sol does not take into account the submitted
bid price. The check is only performed on the bid amount:
Exp memory repurchasePriceUSDValue = termPriceOracle.usdValueOfTokens(
purchaseToken,
bidAmount
As a result, a user could submit a large bid without providing sufficient collateral to service the interest on their loan,
and thereby win an auction.
Note, this would make them under immediate threat of liquidation after conclusion of the auction, but nonetheless
they would be able to participate in and complete the auction successfully.

title: Accounting discrepancy in rollover bids
content: An accounting discrepancy exists in the rollover‑bid flow of the TermAuction system. When a rollover bid is transferred to a new TermRepoCollateralManager, the auction contract calls acceptRolloverCollateral after moving the collateral tokens. The function updates the internal ledger that records how much collateral is locked for a borrower (lockedCollateralLedger[borrower][collateralToken]) but it does not adjust the global counter that tracks how much collateral is currently encumbered (encumberedCollateralBalances[collateralToken]). The missing update means the two sources of truth diverge: the ledger shows a higher locked amount while the encumbered total remains unchanged. This mismatch is detected later when _unlockCollateral attempts to decrease encumberedCollateralBalances based on the ledger entry; because the global counter was never increased, the subtraction can drive the balance below zero, causing a revert. The bug can be triggered whenever a rollover bid is accepted, i.e., during normal operation of the protocol when borrowers roll over positions. Any borrower, lender, or user who relies on the ability to unlock or withdraw collateral may experience failed transactions, loss of expected refunds, or collateral that appears to be stuck. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s accounting logic, where the auditor noticed that acceptRolloverCollateral does not call the same internal routine (_lockCollateral) used elsewhere to update both structures. The problem is subtle because the token transfer itself succeeds and the ledger entry looks correct, so the error only surfaces later in a different function, making it easy to miss in functional testing. The vulnerability belongs to the class of state‑inconsistency bugs where two related accounting variables are not kept in sync, leading to arithmetic under‑flow and unexpected reverts. From a user’s perspective the UI may show that a bid was placed successfully, but subsequent attempts to claim or withdraw collateral revert with an “underflow” or “balance below zero” error, and the user sees no funds returned. The protocol’s business logic assumes that the total amount of encumbered collateral always equals the sum of all locked ledger entries; this assumption is violated, breaking the accounting guarantees of the system. The recommended fix is to modify acceptRolloverCollateral so that it also increments encumberedCollateralBalances[collateralToken] by the same amount that is added to lockedCollateralLedger, or to reuse the existing _lockCollateral routine that already performs both updates. Aligning the two balances restores the invariant that locked collateral never exceeds encumbered collateral and prevents the under‑flow revert.
summary:
Discrepancy between balances of
lockedCollateralLedger and
encumberedCollateralBalances could lead to accounting errors and unexpected reverts.
When
a
rollover
bid
is
transferred
to
a
new
TermRepoCollateralManager,
TermAuction
calls
TermRepoCollateralManager.acceptRolloverCollateral()
after transferring the collateral tokens.
However,
acceptRolloverCollateral()
only modifies the value of
lockedCollateralLedger[borrower][collateralToken].
It does not increase
encumberedCollateralBalances[collateralToken]
by the same amount, as it occurs in
_lockCollateral.
This could lead to an accounting error that could lead to reverts when _unlockCollateral() is called for the borrower
and encumberedCollateralBalances[collateralToken] could be reduced below zero.

title: Predictable price hashes
content: The contract uses a price‑locking mechanism where a bidder submits a hash of the offered price. The hash is computed with keccak256(abi.encode(price)). Because the hash function is deterministic and only the raw price is encoded, the same numeric price always produces the same hash. An attacker can therefore pre‑compute a table of hashes for a realistic price range and compare any submitted hash against that table to recover the hidden price. This also reveals whether a rollover bid re‑uses the same price, because the hash will be identical. The vulnerability stems from insufficient entropy in the commitment scheme; no nonce, timestamp, bidder address or random salt is mixed into the hash. Exploitation consists of generating the lookup table, submitting a bid, reading the on‑chain hash, and performing a reverse lookup to obtain the clear‑text price. Once the price is known, an adversary can front‑run the bid, adjust their own offers, or manipulate market dynamics, effectively breaking the intended privacy of the auction. The issue appears whenever a bid or offer is created, i.e., on every call that invokes the price‑hash function, and it affects all participants who rely on price confidentiality, including regular users, market makers, and the protocol itself because price leakage can lead to economic loss. The problem was identified during a manual code review that highlighted the deterministic hash generation. It is easy to miss because the hash looks cryptographically strong, yet the input space is small and predictable, making brute‑force enumeration feasible. The proper mitigation is to turn the commitment into a true commitment scheme by mixing unpredictable data such as a per‑bid nonce, the sender’s address, a block‑timestamp, or a securely generated random salt, and by ensuring the hash changes for each bid even if the price repeats. This adds entropy, prevents a single lookup table from being useful, and restores the privacy guarantees of the auction mechanism.
summary:
Generated price hashes are easy to guess.
Bids and offers send a hash of their price as a mechanism for locking in a price whilst not revealing the price publicly.
The method of generating these hashes is predictable, the same price will always result in the same hash. Because of
this, it is easy to generate lists of all price hashes and test them against submitted hashes, thereby discovering hidden
bid prices.
Similarly, rollover bids are likely to use the same price, and it will be clear if this is the case as the price hash would be
unchanged.
A price hash is generated by the simple code:
hash = keccak256(abi.encode(price))
This code can be reproduced and run quickly to test a large range of potential prices. Once a realistic range has been
compiled, a simple script would be able to look up any given price hash in a database of price hashes.

title: Risk Free Negative Price Trades
content: The vulnerability is a margin‑validation bypass that occurs when a tracer market permits a negative fair price (pricefair). The contract computes the notional value as the absolute quote amount multiplied by pricefair; when pricefair is negative the resulting notional becomes negative. The required minimum margin (minMargin) is derived as a proportion of this notional, so it also becomes negative. The function marginIsValid() checks that the supplied margin is greater than minMargin. Because a user can open a trade with zero deposited margin, the margin value of zero is greater than a negative minMargin, causing the check to succeed even though no collateral has been provided. Consequently a trader can place a position without any deposit, immediately withdraw any previously deposited funds, and still retain the position, effectively creating a risk‑free trade. This flaw is triggered only in markets where the pricing logic allows pricefair to drop below zero, and it was identified during a security audit by SigmaPrime. The issue is subtle because the margin check appears to pass and the UI may display a required margin of zero, leading users to believe the trade is legitimate. The impact is that an attacker can repeatedly open such zero‑margin positions, extract profits from price movements, and potentially drain protocol funds or undermine liquidation mechanisms. To remediate, the protocol must enforce non‑negative notional and minMargin values, reject or clamp negative pricefair inputs, and ensure that marginIsValid() requires a strictly positive collateral amount regardless of price sign, thereby restoring the intended economic guarantees of the system.
summary:
The tracer markets are designed to allow for negative price trades. However users can make trades without making deposits (or can make a trade and then withdraw their initial deposit (see Maximum Withdrawal Observations for a simple analysis)).
The issue occurs due to the calculations of notional value, |quote| ∗ pricefair. Thus if pricefair < 0 notional value will be less than zero. Since minMargin is a portion of the notional value it will also be negative (excluding potential liquidation gas costs).
Now if we take an order at the pricefair then our margin will be zero.
Thus, the check margin > minMargin in marginIsValid() will always pass even though as user has made no deposits.

title: Signature Use in Alternate Markets
content: The vulnerability is a market‑mismatch flaw in the Trader contract that allows a signed limit order to be executed on a different market than the one the user originally approved. The root cause is that the executeTrade function receives a market identifier as a parameter but never checks that this identifier matches the targetTracer field stored inside the signed order. Because the order hash that the user signs does not incorporate the market argument, the signature remains valid even when the caller supplies a different market value. An attacker can therefore reuse a legitimate user signature that was intended for market A, call executeTrade with market B, and cause the trade to be settled at the price of market B. This can lead to highly unprofitable outcomes for the user, as the price on the unintended market may be far worse, and a malicious counter‑party can take the opposite side to capture the loss. The issue manifests whenever executeTrade is invoked with a market argument that does not equal the order’s targetTracer, provided the user has granted the Trader contract permission in both markets, the user’s margin remains sufficient after the trade, and the transaction nonce is correct. All users who rely on the Trader contract to execute off‑chain orders are affected, because they may see a trade appear to have been placed correctly while the underlying market is wrong, resulting in unexpected balance reductions or missing expected refunds. The flaw was discovered during a security audit by SigmaPrime, where the logical omission of the market‑to‑order consistency check was identified. It can be hard to notice because the signature verification passes and the UI typically displays the order details without indicating the market mismatch, so the user may not realize the trade was routed to a different market. To remediate, the contract should bind the market identifier to the signed order, either by including the market in the order hash or by explicitly checking that order.targetTracer equals the market argument before executing the trade. This class of bug falls under authorization/context‑binding errors where signatures are replayable across distinct execution contexts, breaking the accounting assumption that a signed order applies only to the market it was created for, and can cause funds to disappear or be exchanged at an unintended price.
summary:
The Trader contract makes trades on behalf of users. The purpose is that it is an oﬀ-chain order book system which can execute orders on-chain on a user’s behalf.
It proves a user requested an order by having them sign the hashOrder() of a LimitOrder. This ensures that the details of the order match those desired by the user.
The LimitOrder contains the field targetTracer which links the order to a specific market. However, the function executeTrade(makers, takers, market) does not ensure that the function parameter market matches the variable targetTracer in the order.
The impact is that a user may call executeOrder() using signatures that were intended for a different market.
Since different markets will have different prices this will result in users creating highly unprofitable trades. A malicious user may capitalise on this by taking the opposite side of these trades.
This attack would require the user to have given permission to the Trader in both markets, for the user’s margin to be valid after the trade and finally for the transaction to have a valid nonce.

title: Insurance Funding Rate Increases Indefinitely
content: The vulnerability is an unbounded upward drift in the insurance funding rate used by the protocol. The rate is calculated in Insurance.getPoolFundingRate() as a non‑negative uint256 that reflects the gap between leveraged notional exposure and the amount of capital held in the insurance pool. When the protocol updates the rate in Pricing.updateFundingRate() it reads the current rate as a signed int256, adds the freshly computed pool funding rate (which is always >=0) and stores the sum as the new rate. Because the added component can never be negative, each update can only increase the stored rate; there is no mechanism to decrease it even when the pool has already reached its target size. This design flaw originates from treating the funding rate as an accumulating value rather than a snapshot of the pool’s current state. An attacker or even normal market dynamics can trigger the update function repeatedly, causing the rate to climb indefinitely. As the rate grows, every user interaction that incurs an insurance fee pays a larger amount, eventually draining user balances or making the service prohibitively expensive. The problem manifests on every funding‑rate update cycle, typically after each market settlement or price refresh, and affects all participants who must pay the insurance fee – traders, liquidity providers, and any holder of the protocol’s token. The issue was discovered during a manual code audit that highlighted the additive update pattern and the lack of a ceiling or decay logic. It can be difficult to notice because the rate remains a positive number, which matches the expectation that insurance fees should be non‑negative; however, the monotonic increase is subtle and may only become apparent after several periods when fees appear unusually high. To remediate the bug, the update logic should replace the additive step with a direct assignment of the pool funding rate, or compute a delta that can be positive or negative, ensuring the stored rate can move downward when the pool is sufficiently funded. In essence, the contract should treat the insurance funding rate as a recalculated snapshot rather than an ever‑growing accumulator, thereby preventing users from being overcharged and preserving the intended economic balance of the protocol.
summary:
The insurance funding rate is calculated in Insurance.getPoolFundingRate() to be proportional to the difference between the leveraged notional value and pool holdings. The value returned from this function is a uint256 as the insurance funding rate should be non-negative.
When the insurance funding rate is being updated in Pricing.updateFundingRate() the following occurs.
int256 currentInsuranceFundingRateValue = getOnlyInsuranceFundingRateValue(market, fundingIndex);
int256 IPoolFundingRateValue = currentInsuranceFundingRateValue.add(IPoolFundingRate);
Here IPoolFundingRate = Insurance.getPoolFundingRate() and thus is always greater than or equal to zero (0).
The value IPoolFundingRateValue which adds IPoolFundingRate and the currentInsuranceFundingRateValue then becomes the new insurance funding rate value.
Since we are taking the current insurance funding rate value and adding a number that is greater than or equal to zero, the new insurance funding rate value may only ever increase.
The impact here is that users will have to pay significant fees to the insurance pool even when the pool has reached the target amount.

title: Double Voting by Delegaters
content: The vulnerability is a double‑voting flaw in a governance contract that permits a token holder who has delegated voting power to another address to cast the same voting weight more than once on a single proposal. The root cause is the absence of any restriction on withdrawing delegated stake after a vote has been recorded and the lack of a lock‑up or cooldown period for tokens that are restaked during an active voting window. Because the contract only checks the current voting power at the moment a vote is submitted, it does not track whether the same tokens have already been used to vote on the same proposal. An attacker can exploit this by first delegating their tokens to a delegate, allowing the delegate to vote with the combined stake, then, while the proposal is still open, withdrawing the delegated tokens, transferring them to a new address, restaking, and voting again. This sequence results in the same economic stake being counted twice, inflating the Yes (or No) tally and potentially causing a proposal to pass or fail incorrectly. The impact is a breach of the fundamental accounting assumption that each token may contribute at most one vote per proposal, leading to governance manipulation, loss of trust, and decisions that do not reflect the true intent of token holders. The condition under which this occurs is any active proposal where the warm‑up period has elapsed, the delegator’s stake is still withdrawable, and the contract permits immediate voting after restaking. All participants who rely on the integrity of the voting process—token holders, protocol developers, and downstream applications—are affected because the outcome of governance actions can be arbitrarily altered. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when a test case (test_withdraw_double_vote) demonstrated that after delegating and voting, the delegator could withdraw, restake, and vote again on the same proposal. The bug is subtle because the contract correctly records the vote weight at each call, so there is no obvious error flag; only a careful analysis of token flow across proposals reveals the double counting. To remediate, the contract should enforce that a token’s voting power is locked for the duration of any proposal it participates in, prevent withdrawal of delegated stake after a vote has been cast, and maintain a per‑proposal record of which token IDs (or address‑stake combinations) have already contributed a vote. Implementing a cooldown period for staking and unstaking, or restricting voting to accounts that were already staked before the proposal was created, would also close the attack vector. From a user’s perspective, the symptom is that a proposal may be approved even though the user believes they voted only once, or the UI may display an unexpected increase in vote weight, contradicting the expectation that each token can vote only a single time per proposal.
summary:
If a user has delegated their voting rights to another member of the governance network, the recipient of these rights is able to propose/vote with the combined value of their stake plus any delegated stake. However, as there are no restrictions on withdrawing delegated stake once a vote has already been made, a user is able to double vote by transferring this stake to another account and voting on the same proposal.
This process can be further outlined in the following scenario:
1. Alice and Bob both decide they want to stake their governance tokens.
2. Bob delegates his stake to Alice, relinquishing him of his voting rights until he decides to remove Alice as his delegate.
3. Alice submits an arbitrary proposal, whereby her entire stake (including any delegated stake) is counted as a Yes vote.
4. Alice and Bob both wait some time for the warm up period to pass and then Bob proceeds to withdraw his stake while the proposal is still actively being voted on.
5. Bob then transfers his governance token to an arbitrary account controlled by him and restakes his governance tokens.
6. With no cooldown on voting after staking, Bob is able to vote on the same proposal, effectively double voting.
Refer to the test test_withdraw_double_vote() in test_gov.py for a proof of concept.

title: Keeper Rewards Are Not Scaled Down to Settlement Token Decimals
content: The vulnerability is an arithmetic scaling error in the keeper reward calculation of a perpetual pools protocol. The contract obtains the price of the settlement token from an oracle and scales it to 18 decimal places, which is the standard precision used by the protocol. It then adds gas cost, overhead and an incremental incentive and converts this sum into an amount of the settlement token. However, the implementation never scales the resulting reward amount back to the actual number of decimals of the settlement token, which may be lower than 18.
