Because the reward is expressed in the token's smallest unit (wei) but interpreted as having the token’s native decimal precision, the protocol over‑pays keepers when the token has fewer than 18 decimals. The bug can be exploited by any participant who can trigger an upkeep; the caller receives a reward that is larger than intended, draining the pool’s balance and ultimately costing the leveraged pool’s users. The overpayment occurs each time an upkeep is performed on a pool that uses a low‑decimal settlement token, and it is deterministic rather than random. Users of the protocol see their pool balances decrease unexpectedly while keepers receive unusually large payouts, a symptom that may be missed because the UI often displays token amounts without exposing the underlying decimal mismatch. The issue was discovered during a formal audit that examined the reward‑calculation logic and identified the missing decimal‑adjustment step. It is hard to notice because the contract still reports a reward value that appears correct in token units, yet the internal conversion inflates the actual amount transferred. This class of bug belongs to unit‑conversion or decimal‑handling errors, where mismatched precision leads to incorrect financial accounting. To remediate the problem the keeperReward function should apply a scaling factor that reduces the computed wadRewardValue to the settlement token’s decimal precision before transferring the reward, ensuring that the amount paid matches the intended economic incentive.
summary:
The perpetual pools protocol utilises keepers to upkeep leveraged pools. An upkeep can be performed by anyone and is incentivized through small payments denominated in the pool’s settlement token.
As settlement tokens can contain any arbitrary number of decimals fewer than 18, the KeeperRewards.sol contract will scale the price of the token retrieved by querying the oracle. Using this scaled amount, {gas cost + overhead + incremental incentive} is converted to the settlement token amount, but this is not scaled back to the settlement token’s decimals.
As a result, if a settlement token uses any number of decimals fewer than 18, the protocol will severely overpay keeper rewards at a net cost to the leveraged pool and its users.

title: Protocol Fees Can be Double Claimed
content: The vulnerability is a double‑claim of protocol fees that occurs because the feeTransfer() routine both sends the calculated fees to the primary and secondary accounts and simultaneously increments the stored counters secondaryFees and primaryFees. After this transfer, the contract also exposes claimPrimaryFees() and claimSecondaryFees() functions that read the same counters and issue another safeTransfer to the same accounts without resetting the counters or checking whether the fees have already been paid. The root cause is the misplaced transfer logic: fees are paid twice – once directly in feeTransfer() and again when any caller invokes the claim functions. An attacker, or even any external user, can trigger the claim functions after each upkeep interval, causing the protocol to disburse the same fee amount a second time. This can be exploited repeatedly, draining the fee pool and resulting in funds disappearing from the protocol’s accounting. The impact is a loss of revenue for the protocol, broken accounting assumptions (the protocol assumes fees are transferred exactly once per interval), and potential insolvency of the fee reserve. The condition under which it occurs is any time the keeper performs an upkeep that calls feeTransfer() followed by a later call to claimPrimaryFees() or claimSecondaryFees() before the next interval. All participants that rely on the fee distribution – the primary and secondary beneficiaries, token holders, and the protocol itself – are affected because the expected fee payout is higher than the actual amount retained. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by SigmaPrime, where the logical flow of fee handling was examined and the redundant transfer was identified. It may be hard to notice because the contract still appears to transfer fees correctly on the surface; only a careful review of state updates versus external transfers reveals the double payout. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that the protocol’s fee balance shrinks faster than expected, or that a user who expects a single fee payout sees the same amount being sent twice, effectively “money disappears” from the pool. The bug belongs to the class of accounting or double‑spend logic errors where state variables are not cleared after a transfer. To remediate, the feeTransfer() function should stop performing the safeTransfer and instead only record the fee amounts, leaving the actual transfer to be performed exclusively by the claimPrimaryFees() and claimSecondaryFees() functions, or the claim functions should reset the counters after a successful payout and include guards to prevent re‑entrancy or repeated claims.
summary:
On each update interval, a keeper will perform an upkeep which executes a price change in the asset being tracked before transferring the associated fees to the primary and secondary accounts. The feeTransfer() function handles how fee amounts are paid, however, the logic has been altered with the addition of the claimPrimaryFees() and claimSecondaryFees() functions.
feeTransfer() will transfer fees to the respective accounts and increment two storage variables, secondaryFees and primaryFees. As a result, if anyone subsequently calls claimPrimaryFees() or claimSecondaryFees(), fees will be paid out to these accounts again.

title: Flip Commitments Are Not Charged Their Respective Mint And Burn Fee
content: The vulnerability consists of a fee‑omission bug in the pool commitment logic. When a user creates a flip commitment – a request that converts short exposure tokens into long exposure tokens or vice‑versa – the contract does not apply the standard mint or burn fee that is charged for all other commitment types. The root cause is that the fee‑calculation routine is bypassed for the newly added flip path, while the rest of the PoolCommitter.sol contract correctly deducts fees for mint and burn operations. An attacker can exploit this by repeatedly submitting flip commitments to rebalance a portfolio without incurring any fee, effectively performing cost‑free arbitrage or continuous rebalancing. The impact is a loss of expected revenue for the protocol, distortion of the token’s economic model, and potential manipulation of pool balances because the protocol’s accounting assumes that every exposure change is taxed. This condition occurs whenever a user invokes the flip function; no additional state or external condition is required. Both regular users and the protocol are affected: users benefit from free rebalancing, while the protocol and token holders suffer reduced fee income and possible imbalance. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit of the PoolCommitter.sol source, where the fee logic was compared across different commit types and the flip path was found to be inconsistent. Because the contract still appears to accept the flip request and the UI shows a successful operation, the omission can be subtle and may not raise immediate alarms. The bug belongs to the class of accounting or fee‑enforcement errors where a transaction that should be charged is mistakenly exempted. From a user’s perspective the UI indicates that the flip succeeded, but the expected fee deduction never appears, leading to a situation where “my balance stays the same after flipping” instead of “a small fee is taken”. To remediate the issue the fee‑calculation should be integrated into the flip commit flow, ensuring that the same mint/burn fee is deducted regardless of the direction of the exposure change, or an explicit fee rule should be documented and enforced. This correction restores the intended economic guarantees and prevents free rebalancing from eroding protocol revenue.
summary:
Users are charged a fee on their tokens whenever they commit to mint or burn short or long tokens. A new commit type was introduced to allow users to flip their short tokens to long tokens and vice-versa. While it might be intended that fees should not be charged when a user flips their commit type (as the tokens remain within the protocol), it is not consistent with the implementation shown in other areas of the PoolCommitter.sol contract.
As a result, users can constantly rebalance their portfolio without incurring any additional cost.

title: Pool Keepers Can Re-Enter poolUpkeep() if Tokens With Callbacks Are Used
content: The vulnerability is a re‑entrancy flaw in the poolUpkeep() routine of a leveraged pool contract. The function is intended to run at fixed intervals, checking that the update interval has elapsed before applying a price change and distributing fees. Because the implementation does not follow the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern, the contract updates its lastPriceTimestamp only after it has transferred fees to the primary and secondary fee addresses. If the settlement token used by the pool implements a transfer callback – for example an ERC777 token that invokes a hook on the recipient – the secondary fee address can execute code during the fee transfer. That code can call back into poolUpkeep() before the timestamp is updated, causing the intervalPassed() condition to be true again. The attacker can therefore trigger the fee‑distribution logic repeatedly within a single upkeep cycle, collecting fees multiple times and ultimately draining the pool’s assets. The issue manifests when a keeper invokes poolUpkeep() during a normal update interval while the pool holds a token with a callback mechanism. Users of the pool, the protocol itself, and any parties relying on the pool’s financial integrity are affected because the pool’s capital can be siphoned away, leading to loss of user balances and broken accounting assumptions. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit by SigmaPrime, which noted the missing state update before the external call. It is subtle because most ERC20 tokens do not have callbacks, so the re‑entrancy vector is not obvious during casual testing, and the timestamp update appears later in the function, giving a false sense of safety. To remediate, the contract should update the lastPriceTimestamp (or otherwise lock the function) before any external token transfer, or move fee distribution to a separate non‑re‑enterable function that does not allow the secondary fee address to control execution flow. Applying the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern or a re‑entrancy guard will prevent the secondary fee address from re‑entering poolUpkeep() and ensure that fees are transferred only once per interval, preserving the pool’s financial correctness.
summary:
Pool upkeeps are performed on each update interval by the protocol’s keepers. The poolUpkeep() function will check if the pool’s update interval has passed before executing a price change. However, because this function does not implement the checks-effects-interactions pattern, it is possible to re-enter the function and satisfy the intervalPassed() check again.
If we assume that the settlement token may contain a callback on transfers (typical for ERC777 standard tokens), the secondary fee account can re-enter poolUpkeep() and receive fees again. This can be repeated to effectively drain the leveraged pool of its funds.

title: Lack of withdrawal limits check
content: The vulnerability consists of a missing enforcement of withdrawal limits when collateral is moved between accounts or when collateral shares are updated. In the original design, a dedicated check function validates that a withdrawal does not exceed the per‑account or global limits defined by the protocol’s collateral configuration. However, the recent code change relocated the limit verification from the central CollateralConfiguration.checkWithdrawLimits routine to the AccountCollateral.updateBalance routine, and the functions that perform direct share transfers – namely the internal transferFunds routine and the externally exposed updateCollateralShares method – bypass updateBalance entirely. As a result, an actor can invoke these pathways to transfer arbitrary amounts of collateral shares without triggering any limit validation. Exploitation is straightforward: an attacker calls transferFunds or updateCollateralShares with a large positive delta for a target account, causing the contract to debit the source account and credit the destination account without any guard on the maximum allowable withdrawal. This can lead to over‑drawn balances, effectively draining collateral from vulnerable accounts, and may cause the protocol’s accounting invariants to break, resulting in lost funds or incorrect collateral ratios. The issue manifests whenever a user or contract interacts with the affected functions, which are reachable through normal contract calls and do not require special privileges. All participants that hold collateral – individual users, liquidity providers, or other protocol modules – are potentially affected because the missing check applies to every collateral type listed in the global configuration. The flaw was uncovered during a manual security review that compared the call flow of withdrawal‑related functions and noticed that the limit‑checking routine was omitted from the transfer paths. Because the functions appear to perform legitimate balance updates, the absence of a limit check can be subtle and may not raise immediate alarms, especially if the UI does not display explicit error messages for over‑withdrawals. To remediate the issue, the protocol should reinstate the withdrawal‑limit validation in every code path that modifies collateral shares, either by routing all share updates through a common function that includes the check or by explicitly invoking the limit‑checking routine inside transferFunds and updateCollateralShares. Restoring these checks will re‑align the contract’s behavior with its intended accounting model and prevent unauthorized depletion of collateral.

title: Ignoring withdrawal limits during accounts merging
content: The vulnerability originates in the merge routine of a collateral management contract where a child pool is combined into a parent pool. The function correctly transfers the collateral shares from the child to the parent, but it completely ignores the withdrawal limits that are associated with the child pool. Because the limits are not copied or re‑applied to the parent after the merge, the parent pool inherits the child’s collateral balance while retaining its own (often higher) withdrawal constraints, effectively allowing an actor to withdraw the full amount of the merged collateral immediately after the operation. This situation can be triggered whenever the protocol permits merging of pools that have non‑zero collateral shares and distinct withdrawal caps. An attacker can create or use a child pool with a very low withdrawal ceiling, merge it into a larger parent pool, and then call the standard withdrawal function on the parent to extract funds that would otherwise be blocked by the child’s limit. From a user perspective the UI may show the expected balance in the parent pool, but the withdrawal button works without the usual restriction, leading to unexpected zero balances or missing funds after a withdrawal. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the merge logic and noticed that only collateral shares were updated while the limit‑related state variables were untouched. It is subtle because the merge appears to be a benign accounting operation and the missing limit transfer does not generate an explicit error, making it easy to overlook during testing. The bug violates the protocol’s accounting assumptions that withdrawal limits are enforced per pool, breaking the guarantee that users cannot extract more collateral than allowed. To remediate the problem the merge implementation should also transfer, aggregate, or re‑enforce the withdrawal limits of the child pool onto the parent, ensuring that the combined pool respects the most restrictive limit or a correctly calculated aggregate limit before any withdrawal is permitted.

title: Incorrect increment of signature nonce
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect handling of the signature replay‑prevention nonce in the executeBySig function and related permission‑by‑signature functions. The contract is designed to increment a nonce that is tied to the signer of a meta‑transaction so that each signed message can be used only once. However, the implementation mistakenly increments the nonce that belongs to the account owner regardless of which address actually produced the signature. This root cause stems from calling the nonce‑increment routine with the stored owner address instead of the recovered signer address. Because the nonce is advanced even when an attacker supplies a signature from any arbitrary address, an attacker can repeatedly invoke executeBySig with an empty command list, causing the owner’s nonce to increase far beyond the value used when legitimate signatures were created. When the owner later tries to submit a valid transaction, the contract recomputes the expected nonce, finds a mismatch, and rejects the signature as a replay, effectively locking the account. The impact is a denial‑of‑service: users cannot execute withdrawals, permission grants, or revocations, and funds remain trapped in the contract. The attack can be carried out without paying gas, as the Reya Network relays meta‑transactions for free, allowing an attacker to spam the function at negligible cost. The issue is discovered during a manual audit that highlighted the nonce increment line and noted that the increment should reference the recovered address. It is hard to notice because the function still executes and returns normally for the attacker, and there is no explicit error when the wrong nonce is incremented. From a user’s perspective the UI may show that a withdrawal request fails with no error message, or that a permission change appears to be ignored, leading to confusion when expected actions produce no effect. The bug belongs to the class of replay‑nonce mis‑binding errors, where the accounting of used nonces does not match the signer identity, breaking the fundamental assumption that each signature is tied to a unique, monotonically increasing counter. The correct fix is to replace the owner‑based nonce increment with an increment of the nonce associated with the recovered signer address, ensuring that only the actual author of a signature consumes a nonce and that unrelated callers cannot advance the owner’s counter.

title: principle not updated in rebase() leading to underflow and withdrawal failures
content: The vulnerability is a state‑inconsistency bug in the staking token contract where the internal variable that records the total amount of underlying assets, called principle, is not updated when the contract performs a rebase that changes the total token supply. The root cause is that the rebase function adjusts the supply to reflect accrued rewards but leaves principle unchanged, creating a mismatch between the recorded principal amount and the actual supply. When a user later initiates an unstake, the contract calculates the remaining principal by subtracting the requested amount from the stored principle. Because principle still holds the old lower value, the subtraction can underflow, triggering an arithmetic error and causing the transaction to revert. This can be exploited simply by performing a rebase that increases supply and then attempting to withdraw; the attacker does not need to craft special inputs, the contract’s own logic will fail. The impact is that users are unable to withdraw their funds after a positive rebase, effectively locking their assets and creating a denial‑of‑service condition, especially for the last users trying to withdraw. The condition occurs whenever the REBASE_ROLE is exercised to increase totalSupply without a corresponding update to principle, and it affects any holder who tries to request an unstake after such a rebase. The issue was discovered during a security audit that exercised a rebase followed by a deposit and an unstake request, revealing that the approveUnstakeRequest function reverted with an arithmetic error. The bug is hard to notice because the contract’s balance and token supply appear correct on‑chain, and the UI may still display a positive balance, while the underlying accounting state is inconsistent. The flaw belongs to the class of accounting‑logic errors where a critical state variable is not kept in sync with derived values, leading to arithmetic underflow. From a user’s perspective the symptom is a normal‑looking balance that cannot be redeemed; attempts to claim result in a transaction that fails with an “arithmetic error” or simply returns zero assets. To remediate the issue the principle variable must be synchronized with the new total supply inside the rebase function, ensuring that all subsequent calculations that depend on principle reflect the updated supply and preventing underflow during withdrawal calculations.

title: User can lose tokens during deposit fallback bridging
content: The vulnerability residesin a cross‑chain fallback mechanism that attempts to return a user’s tokens when a deposit transaction reverts. The module responsible for this fallback assumes that the address supplied as the deposit owner on the source chain is controlled by the same entity on the destination (Reya) chain. This assumption is false for certain wallet designs, such as account‑abstraction contracts and legacy Safe multisignature wallets, where the logical owner on one chain may be a contract that does not exist or is not owned by the same private key on the other chain. When a deposit fails, the fallback code catches the exception and calls a bridging utility, passing the original owner address as the receiver for the bridged tokens. Because the address may not be owned on the source chain, the bridging transaction sends the tokens to an address that cannot be accessed, effectively locking or burning the funds. From a user’s perspective the expected behaviour – a reverted deposit with a refund – is replaced by a silent loss: the user sees no tokens returned, their balance on the source chain drops to zero, and the UI shows no error beyond the original revert. The impact is high because the protocol may lose user funds permanently and users lose trust in the bridging service. The issue only manifests when a deposit reverts and the fallback path is executed; normal successful deposits do not trigger the faulty logic, making the bug easy to miss during routine testing. It was discovered during a security audit that examined error‑handling paths and identified the unsafe assumption about address equivalence across chains. The bug belongs to the class of cross‑chain address‑mismatch or receiver‑validation errors, where a contract blindly forwards assets to an address without confirming ownership on the target chain. To remediate, the fallback data structure should include an explicit receiver field supplied by the caller, and the bridging call must use this field instead of the original owner address, ensuring that tokens are sent to an address that the user actually controls on the source chain.
summary:
```solidity
DepositsFallbackModule handles situations where a deposit reverts and
initiates bridging back of users' funds. Note that it uses the address receiver
of the deposit on the Reya chain to bridge back funds on the source chain:
try DepositsModule(address(this)).depositPassivePool(inputs) { }
catch {
    BridgingUtils.executeBridging({
        withdrawToken: usdc,
        socketConnector: fallbackData.socketConnector,
        socketMsgGasLimit: fallbackData.socketMsgGasLimit,
        tokenAmount: inputs.amount,
        receiver: inputs.owner,
        socketPayloadSize: fallbackData.socketPayloadSize
    });
}
```
It incorrectly assumes that the address inputs.owner on the source chain is
owned by the same person on Reya chain. There are 2 cases when the
assumption is not guaranteed:
1. Account Abstraction wallet implementations
2. old version of Safe multisigs https://rekt.news/wintermute-rekt/

title: Slashing isn't supported in the rebasing mechanism
content: The vulnerability originates from a rebasing mechanism that only implements an upward adjustment of the share price through the rebase() function. This design assumes that the only change to the underlying asset value is a positive staking reward, and therefore lacks any logic to decrease the share price when negative events occur. In networks where staked tokens can be slashed, such as Commume or Bittensor, or where tokens may be lost or stolen during bridging, the protocol must be able to reflect a reduction in the total value backing each share. Because the current implementation cannot lower the share price, the accounting model continues to treat the total value as unchanged, causing the protocol to over‑state each holder’s entitlement. An attacker or a malicious bridge operator could trigger a slashing event or cause token loss, and the contract would still allow users to redeem shares at the previous higher price, effectively granting them more assets than the protocol actually holds. This mismatch can lead to insolvency, loss of funds for honest participants, and a breach of the economic guarantees promised by the system. The issue manifests whenever a negative event that reduces the underlying token pool occurs; the rebase function is never called with a negative factor, so the share price remains static. Users may notice that after a slashing incident their displayed balance does not decrease, or that they can still claim the same amount of tokens despite a known loss, creating confusion and a false sense of security. The problem was discovered during a security audit that examined the rebase logic and identified the absence of a downward adjustment path. It is hard to notice because normal operation only triggers positive rebases, and negative events are relatively rare, so the bug does not surface in routine testing. To remediate, the contract should be extended to support a downward rebase that can safely reduce the share price in proportion to any loss, slashing, or theft, with appropriate access controls, event emission, and safeguards to prevent underflow or manipulation. This change restores the invariant that the total value of shares always matches the actual token pool, preserving protocol integrity and user trust.
summary: The function rebase() has been used to increase the share price and apply staking rewards. The issue is that staking has its own risks and stake amounts can be slashed (In Commume or Bittensor network) and current logic doesn't support decreasing the share price. Also, some tokens can be stolen or lost when bridging so it would be necessary to have the ability to decrease the share price to adjust the share price according to those events.

title: Owner can not set the `ve` address via `RewardDistributor.addVoteEscrow`
content: The vulnerability resides in the RewardDistributor contract's addVoteEscrow function, where the developer intended to allow the contract owner to initialise or update the address of the vote‑escrow (ve) contract. Instead of assigning the supplied function parameter _voteEscrow to the storage variable ve, the implementation mistakenly reads from a different storage slot, pendingVoteEscrow, which is uninitialised and therefore holds address(0) on the first call. Because pendingVoteEscrow is never set before this branch executes, the conditional block always assigns ve = VE(address(0)), leaving ve permanently equal to the zero address. Subsequent calls to multiStakerClaim check that ve is not address(0) and revert with "VE not added yet" if the check fails. As a result, veNFT holders – the users who own NFTs representing locked voting power – are unable to claim any reward tokens or Ether that the protocol distributes. The bug manifests only on the initial execution of addVoteEscrow before ve has been set; any later attempt to change the vote‑escrow address follows a different branch that stores the new address in pendingVoteEscrow but never assigns it to ve because the first branch never succeeded. This logical error was uncovered during a formal audit when the reviewer compared the function documentation, which describes the owner’s ability to set ve without a timelock, against the actual source code and observed that the parameter was ignored. The issue is subtle because the contract compiles without warnings, the addVoteEscrow function is restricted to the owner, and there is no immediate on‑chain indication that ve is mis‑initialised except for the revert message during reward claims. From a user perspective, attempts to claim rewards result in a transaction that reverts, leaving the expected reward balance unchanged and giving the impression that rewards have vanished or that the protocol is withholding funds. The class of bug is an incorrect state‑variable assignment (using the wrong storage variable) that leads to a denial‑of‑service condition for reward distribution. To remediate the problem, the function should assign ve using the provided _voteEscrow argument, enforce the documented timelock logic only when updating an existing ve address, and initialise pendingVoteEscrow appropriately or remove it entirely. By correcting the assignment and ensuring that ve is set to a valid contract address, the protocol restores the ability of veNFT holders to claim their entitled rewards and aligns the on‑chain behaviour with the intended business logic of reward distribution.
summary:
On the initial `RewardDistributor.addVoteEscrow` call, the owner of the contract can set the `ve` address without a timelock (which is as intended according to the function documentation). However, as the function parameter `_voteEscrow` is not used for the assignment, instead the storage variable `pendingVoteEscrow` (which is not initialized, hence `address(0)`) is used, the `ve` storage variable can not be set to the provided `_voteEscrow` address.

This prevents setting the `ve` address (`ve` is set to `address(0)`) and therefore prevents `veNFT` holders to claim reward tokens and Ether rewards via `RewardDistributor.multiStakerClaim`.

title: `VoteEscrowDelegation._writeCheckpoint` fails when `nCheckpoints` is 0
content: The issue resides in the delegation mechanism of the VoteEscrowDelegation contract. When a token holder calls the delegate function for the first time, the contract calculates the current number of checkpoints (nCheckpoints) for the destination token ID. Because no delegation has been recorded yet, nCheckpoints is zero. The internal helper _writeCheckpoint is then invoked with nCheckpoints equal to zero. Inside _writeCheckpoint the code unconditionally reads checkpoints[toTokenId][nCheckpoints - 1] to obtain the previous checkpoint. In Solidity 0.8.x this subtraction underflows, causing the array index to wrap to a very large value and the transaction to revert. As a result, the first delegation attempt always fails, preventing any user from creating a delegation. The root cause is an off‑by‑one error and a missing guard for the case where the checkpoint list is empty. The bug can be exploited simply by submitting a delegation transaction when no prior checkpoints exist; the contract will revert and the user’s delegation will never be recorded. The impact is functional: token owners who wish to delegate their voting power cannot do so, leading to a broken user experience, missing delegation events, and potentially locked voting power that cannot be transferred or utilized by the protocol. The failure occurs only on the initial delegation for a given token ID, which makes it easy to miss during testing if the test suite only covers subsequent delegations. The affected parties are all token holders and the protocol itself, because the delegation feature is integral to its governance model. The problem was discovered during an external audit by Code4rena, where the auditors observed a revert when invoking delegate on a fresh token. The issue is subtle because the code path for nCheckpoints > 0 works correctly, so only the edge case of zero checkpoints triggers the underflow. To remediate the bug, _writeCheckpoint must be rewritten to handle the zero‑checkpoint case separately: when nCheckpoints is zero it should create a new checkpoint at index 0 instead of trying to read a non‑existent previous entry, and only attempt to read the last checkpoint when nCheckpoints > 0. This aligns the implementation with the intended accounting logic, ensures that the delegatedTokenIds array is stored correctly, and restores the ability for users to delegate their voting power. In broader terms, the vulnerability is an initialization‑logic error common in contracts that maintain rolling checkpoint histories, where the absence of a prior entry is not accounted for, leading to array‑index underflow and transaction failure.
summary: When a user call `VoteEscrowDelegation.delegate` to make a delegation, it calls `VoteEscrowDelegation._writeCheckpoint` to update the checkpoint of `toTokenId`. However, if `nCheckpoints` is 0, `_writeCheckpoint` always reverts. What’s worse, `nCheckpoints` would be zero before any delegation has been made. In conclusion, users cannot make any delegation.

title: Users are likely to lose their bid if purchaseToken is a low-decimals token
content: The vulnerability is an integer‑division rounding error that can cause a bidder to lose the entire amount of their bid when the auction settles. In the commitBid function a user supplies a volume of purchaseToken and a price expressed in reserveToken. When the auction window expires the fulfillWindow routine calculates the amount of reserveToken to be credited to the bidder as volume / price. Because Solidity performs integer division, any fractional part is discarded. If the purchaseToken has fewer decimals than the reserveToken – for example USDC (6 decimals) against an 18‑decimal reserveToken – the division often truncates to zero, especially when the bid size is small relative to the price. The same effect occurs even with equal‑decimal tokens when the supplied volume is lower than the price. As a result the auction owner receives the full bid amount while the bidder’s claim entry records a zero reserveToken payout, effectively making the bidder’s funds disappear. This condition is triggered only during the settlement phase after the auction window closes, and it affects any participant who places a low‑volume bid with a low‑decimal purchase token. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that examined the arithmetic of the settlement logic. It is hard to notice because the transaction does not revert; the UI may show a successful bid and a successful claim, yet the user’s balance of reserveToken remains unchanged, leading to confusion and loss of trust. The bug belongs to the class of precision‑loss or rounding‑down vulnerabilities caused by mismatched token decimals and unchecked integer division. To remediate, the contract should enforce that the bid volume is at least equal to the price, or require that both tokens share the same decimal precision, and preferably perform the calculation using fixed‑point arithmetic (e.g., multiply before dividing) to avoid truncation. By ensuring proper scaling or validation, the protocol can guarantee that bidders receive a non‑zero amount of reserveToken proportional to their bid, preserving the intended economic guarantees of the auction.

title: Overwriting collateral breaks collateral gains logic
content: The vulnerability resides in the StabilityPool contract's handling of collateral lifecycle. After a collateral type reaches its sunset period (180 days) the protocol allows a new collateral to be enabled, which overwrites the previous entry. During this overwrite the internal mapping that tracks cumulative sums per epoch and scale (epochToScaleToSums) is reset, but the mappings that store each depositor's pending gains (collateralGainsByDepositor) and the per‑epoch deposit totals (depositSums) are left untouched. Consequently, gains that were accrued for the retired collateral remain recorded and are later interpreted as gains for the newly enabled collateral. This state‑contamination bug causes several downstream problems. When a user later triggers the internal function _accrueDepositorCollateralGain, the contract computes a portion as sums[i] - depSums[i]; if the stale sums are larger than the cleared deposit sums, the subtraction underflows, reverting the transaction and effectively denying service to any function that relies on that calculation (DoS). Even when the transaction does not revert, the stale pending gains are added to the new collateral pool, allowing a depositor to claim collateral that never existed for the new asset, thereby stealing value from other participants. In other cases the pool may not contain enough of the new collateral to satisfy the inflated claim, causing legitimate users to receive zero or a reduced amount, contrary to the expectation that they receive their earned gains. The issue appears only after the sunset period has elapsed and a replacement collateral is enabled; it does not affect normal operation before that point. All depositors, the protocol’s stability mechanism, and any users relying on accurate collateral rewards are affected. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s state‑reset logic, where the auditor noticed that only a subset of storage variables were cleared on collateral replacement. Because the incorrect values are hidden inside mappings and only surface when a claim is made, the problem can be difficult to detect through routine testing that does not simulate the full sunset‑and‑replace lifecycle. The bug belongs to the class of “incomplete state cleanup after asset replacement” or “stale accounting data reuse”, which violates the fundamental accounting assumption that gains are tied to a specific collateral type. The correct mitigation is to avoid overwriting a sunset collateral altogether and to provide a dedicated function that disables the collateral after the expiry without reusing its storage slots, or to explicitly reset all related accounting mappings (collateralGainsByDepositor, depositSums, and any other per‑collateral aggregates) before a new collateral is introduced. From the user’s perspective the symptoms may include: a transaction that reverts with an underflow error when trying to claim rewards, a claim that returns zero collateral despite a positive balance shown in the UI, or a claim that returns more collateral than expected, effectively draining other users’ balances. These behaviors contradict the protocol’s promise that deposited collateral earns proportional gains and that claims are settled accurately.
summary:
In the StabilityPool contract, when 180 days have passed since the sunset of a collateral, enabling a new collateral overwrites the previous one. In this process, the epochToScaleToSums mapping is cleared, but not the collateralGainsByDepositor and depositSums mappings. This means that the pending gains for the old collateral will be counted as gains for the new collateral.  
As a result, the collateral gains logic is broken, leading to different situations, such as:  
DoS on functions that execute _accrueDepositorCollateralGain due to underflow on uint256 firstPortion = sums[i] - depSums[i]; .  
Users being unable to claim their collateral gains because there is not enough collateral in the pool.  
Users claiming more gains than they should, taking them from other users (see proof of concept).  
Additionally, the current overwriting system requires that a new collateral is enabled in order to disable the sunset collateral, which is not ideal.

title: Stale totalActiveDebt used in openTrove causing incorrect debt update
content: The vulnerability is a stale‑value bug in the TroveManager.openTrove function where the global accounting variable that tracks the total active debt is cached before the contract accrues interest for the current block. The function stores totalActiveDebt in a local variable (named supply) and then calls an internal routine that updates totalActiveDebt with newly accrued interest. After the interest accrual finishes, the code proceeds to compute the new total debt by adding the user‑requested composite debt to the previously cached supply value, completely ignoring the interest that was just added. As a result, the totalActiveDebt recorded after the transaction underestimates the true debt by the amount of interest accrued in the same call. This under‑estimation can occur whenever a user opens a trove while the system is performing an interest accrual, which is the normal path for openTrove. The bug was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the ordering of state updates and identified that the cached value was used after the state had already changed. It is hard to notice because the contract still updates totalActiveDebt, but the new value is silently lower than it should be, so surface‑level checks may appear to pass. The impact is that the protocol’s global debt limit (maxSystemDebt) may be breached without detection, allowing users to open larger positions than intended, potentially leading to insufficient collateralisation, unexpected liquidations, or accounting mismatches that affect all participants. From a user’s perspective the symptoms can manifest as a trove appearing to have a healthier collateral‑to‑debt ratio than reality, or the system rejecting later operations because the recorded debt does not match the actual economic state. The issue belongs to the class of “stale state variable” or “incorrect accounting after side‑effect” bugs, where a mutable global variable is read before a side‑effect and then written back using the stale snapshot. The correct mitigation is to avoid caching totalActiveDebt before the interest accrual, or to recompute the new total debt using the updated totalActiveDebt after _accrueActiveInterests returns, ensuring that the interest component is always included in the final accounting.
summary:
In the TroveManager::openTrove function, the totalActiveDebt is cached into a local variable supply before the _accrueActiveInterests function is called. The _accrueActiveInterests function itself updates the totalActiveDebt to reflect accrued interest. However, the openTrove function subsequently updates totalActiveDebt using the cached supply value instead of the potentially updated totalActiveDebt.  
Specifically, the code caches totalActiveDebt in line 754:  
File: TroveManager.sol  
```solidity
uint256 supply = totalActiveDebt;
```
Then, interest is accrued, potentially updating totalActiveDebt in line 761 by calling _accrueActiveInterests():  
File: TroveManager.sol  
```solidity
uint256 currentInterestIndex = _accrueActiveInterests();
```
Inside _accrueActiveInterests, totalActiveDebt is updated:  
File: TroveManager.sol  
```solidity
totalActiveDebt = currentDebt + activeInterests;
```
Finally, in line 776, totalActiveDebt is updated using the cached supply value:  
```solidity
uint256 _newTotalDebt = supply + _compositeDebt;
require(
    _newTotalDebt + defaultedDebt <= maxSystemDebt,
    "Collateraldebtlimitreached"
);
totalActiveDebt = _newTotalDebt;
```
Because supply is the value of totalActiveDebt before interest accrual in _accrueActiveInterests, the update in line 776 does not incorporate the interest accrued within the same openTrove transaction. This means the totalActiveDebt may be incorrectly updated, potentially underestimating the actual debt in the system.  
Consider the next scenario:  
Initial state:  
totalActiveDebt = 1000  
Interest rate is such that _accrueActiveInterests() will increase totalActiveDebt by 100.  
openTrove call:  
User calls openTrove with _compositeDebt = 500 .  
Line 754: supply = totalActiveDebt; => supply = 1000 (cached value).  
Line 761: _accrueActiveInterests() is called. Inside _accrueActiveInterests() (line 1183): totalActiveDebt is updated to 1000 + 100 = 1100 .  
Line 776: totalActiveDebt = _newTotalDebt; where _newTotalDebt = supply + _compositeDebt = 1000 + 500 = 1500 .  
totalActiveDebt is set to 1500 .  
Expected vs. actual totalActiveDebt :  
Expected totalActiveDebt : Initial debt (1000) + accrued interest (100) + new debt (500) = 1600 .  
Actual totalActiveDebt after openTrove : 1500 .  
The totalActiveDebt is underestimated by 100 (the accrued interest within the same transaction).

title: Incorrect boost management leads to staking reward loss
content: The vulnerability is a logical error in the boost management of a staking system that prevents the proper reduction of boosted rewards when a user redeems or changes validators. The contract provides a queueDropBoost function that records a pending boost reduction together with the block number at which the request was made. The dropBoost function then checks this queue entry and, after a configurable delay, removes the specified amount of boost. However, the Staker contract calls dropBoost directly from its _redeemRewards and setValidator functions without first invoking queueDropBoost, leaving the dropBoostQueue empty. Because the queue entry is missing, the amount read from the queue is zero and the time‑check fails, causing dropBoost to return false silently. As a result, the boosted balance is never decreased, reward calculations that depend on the updated boost amount are inaccurate, and users receive less than the expected reward or see no change in their boost after a redemption. The issue manifests whenever a staker attempts to claim rewards or switch validators, affecting all participants who rely on the boost mechanism. It was discovered during a manual audit that compared the intended flow of queueing a boost drop with the actual calls made by the Staker contract. The bug is hard to notice because the function does not revert or emit an error; it simply returns false, so the front‑end may display a successful transaction while the underlying accounting remains unchanged. Conceptually, this is a state‑management flaw where a prerequisite operation is omitted, leading to dead code execution. To fix the problem, the Staker contract must be updated to call rewardCache.queueDropBoost with the appropriate amount before invoking rewardCache.dropBoost, or the dropBoost logic should be redesigned to operate without requiring a queued entry. Correcting the flow restores the intended accounting invariant that boosted balances are reduced after the delay, ensuring users receive the correct reward amounts and that the protocol’s accounting assumptions remain sound.

title: Borrowers fail to claim their surplus collateral
content: The vulnerability is an improper withdrawal mechanism for surplus collateral that remains after a liquidation in recovery mode. When the Total Collateral Ratio (TCR) falls below the Critical Collateral Ratio (CCR), the protocol enters recovery mode and may liquidate positions even if their Individual Collateral Ratio (ICR) is above the Minimum Collateral Ratio (MCR). During such a liquidation the contract calculates the exact amount of collateral required to cover the debt at MCR and records any excess as a collateral surplus (collSurplus). This surplus is stored in a mapping called surplusBalances via the addCollateralSurplus function. The intended user flow is that the borrower calls claimCollateral to retrieve the surplus. However, the claimCollateral implementation attempts to transfer the surplus directly from the TroveManager contract using safeTransfer, while the actual collateral tokens are held in a separate Staker contract because all collateral is automatically staked to earn rewards. Because the TroveManager does not own the tokens, the transfer call reverts, preventing the borrower from receiving any of the surplus. The bug therefore makes the surplus permanently inaccessible until the contract logic is corrected. It occurs only when a liquidation leaves a surplus, which is a situation specific to recovery mode, and it is triggered by the borrower’s claim attempt. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the liquidation and claim paths. It can be hard to notice because the claimCollateral function appears to work in normal operation where no surplus exists, and the failure only manifests when the surplus is non‑zero. The impact is that users who expect to receive leftover collateral after liquidation see a transaction revert, leading to missing funds, zero balances where a positive amount should appear, and a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees. To fix the problem the claim routine must first withdraw the surplus from the Staker contract—using the Staker’s onWithdrawal interface—or otherwise route the transfer through the contract that actually holds the tokens, ensuring that the recorded surplus can be safely transferred to the borrower.

title: Incorrect activateBoost interface is
content: The Staker contract attempts to increase a queued boost by calling an external contract (BGT) through the function activateBoost. The code uses an interface that declares activateBoost(address validator) external, but the actual BGT implementation expects activateBoost(address user, bytes calldata pubkey) external returns (bool). Because the interface signature does not match the real contract, the call is encoded with the wrong arguments: the user address is supplied where the contract expects a user address followed by a public key, and the required second parameter is omitted entirely. As a result, the external call either reverts or silently fails, meaning the boost is never activated even when the internal condition (queued > 0 and blockDelta > 8191) is satisfied. This mismatch is triggered inside the internal function _tryToBoost, which itself is called by _updateRewardIntegral during reward calculations. Consequently, any logic that depends on a successful boost – including reward distribution in TroveManager and other protocol functions – operates on stale or incorrect state. From a user’s perspective, stakers see no increase in their boosted rewards; balances appear unchanged and expected higher returns never materialize, leading to confusion when the UI shows a pending boost but the on‑chain state shows none. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s source code, where the interface definition was compared against the BGT contract’s ABI. It can be hard to notice because the transaction that calls activateBoost does not necessarily revert; it may succeed from the caller’s perspective while the boost logic inside BGT never executes, leaving no obvious error logs. The root cause is a classic ABI mismatch – an interface that does not reflect the target contract’s function signature – which violates the protocol’s accounting assumptions that a boost will be applied when the conditions are met. To remediate, the Staker contract must import the correct interface definition, pass both the user address and the required public key, and handle the boolean return value to ensure the boost succeeded. This aligns the call with the BGT contract’s expectations and restores the intended reward‑boosting behavior.

title: BGT stake rewards are locked
content: The vulnerability consists of a missing reward‑claiming interface in the Staker contract that prevents users from retrieving the HONEY tokens earned through a boost operation. When a user stakes collateral in the Staker contract they receive BGT reward tokens. Those BGT tokens can be “boosted”, which triggers the BGT contract to call the external BGTStaker contract and stake the BGT tokens there. The BGTStaker contract, in turn, generates HONEY rewards that are intended to be claimable through its public getReward() function. However, the Staker contract never forwards a call to BGTStaker’s getReward, nor does it expose any method for the original user to withdraw the accrued HONEY. As a result, the HONEY rewards become effectively locked inside the BGTStaker contract after a boost. The root cause is an omission in the contract’s interface design: the developer added the boost logic but forgot to add a corresponding reward‑withdrawal function. Exploitation is straightforward – any user who performs a boost will see their HONEY balance increase in the BGTStaker contract, but any subsequent attempt to claim or view the reward through the Staker contract will return zero or revert, leaving the funds inaccessible. The impact is that users lose access to earned rewards, which can be a significant financial loss and erodes trust in the protocol’s incentive model. This condition occurs whenever the internal _tryToBoost function activates a boost (queued > 0 and blockDelta > 8191) and the BGT contract stakes the tokens in BGTStaker. All participants who rely on the boost feature – regular stakers, delegators, and the protocol’s reward distribution system – are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the external interfaces of the Staker and BGTStaker contracts and noticed the absence of a getReward call in the former. The problem can be subtle because the contracts compile without errors and the boost transaction succeeds, giving the false impression that rewards are being handled correctly; only when users attempt to withdraw do they encounter empty balances. To remediate, the Staker contract should implement a public function that forwards the getReward call to the BGTStaker contract (for example, a claimBoostRewards() method that invokes BGTStaker.getReward(msg.sender) and transfers the returned HONEY to the caller). This aligns the contract’s external API with its internal reward‑generation logic and restores users’ ability to claim earned tokens. The bug belongs to the class of “missing withdrawal interface” or “reward lock” vulnerabilities, where a contract generates value but provides no mechanism for the rightful owner to retrieve it, violating basic accounting assumptions that earned assets must be claimable.

title: Error in preview rate calculation results in users losing rewards or offers not being allocated
content: The vulnerability resides in the previewRateAfterDeposit function, which is intended to calculate the reward rate a user would obtain after depositing assets. The function contains a logical check that incorrectly treats the active reward interval as if it were outside the valid period. Specifically, the condition uses a comparison that returns a zero rate when the current block timestamp falls between the start and end of the rewards interval, while it returns a non‑zero rate before the interval begins. This inverted logic causes the previewed rate to be zero during an active reward period and non‑zero beforehand. As a result, two harmful behaviours emerge. First, an attacker can submit a deposit during the active period, see a zero previewed rate, and still allocate the assets to the incentivized vault because the contract does not reject the operation based on the preview. The attacker can then cancel the reward period and retrieve the deposited assets, leaving the original user with no rewards and effectively stealing the incentive. Second, legitimate users attempting to allocate offers after the reward period has started receive a previewed rate of zero, causing the allocation to fail even though the reward is active and the rate should be positive. The impact is a loss of expected rewards for users, failed offer allocations, and potential economic loss for the protocol. The bug manifests whenever block.timestamp is greater than or equal to rewardsInterval.start and less than rewardsInterval.end, i.e., during the active reward window. All participants who rely on the previewed rate—depositors, reward claimants, and vault operators—are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit by Spearbit, where the logical condition was identified as inconsistent with the intended business rule. Because the function is a view that only returns a rate, the problem may not be obvious from transaction logs, making it hard to detect without inspecting the source. To remediate the issue, the condition should be changed to treat timestamps before the start as invalid (start > block.timestamp) and timestamps at or after the end as invalid (block.timestamp >= end), thereby ensuring that a zero rate is only returned outside the active interval. This correction aligns the preview calculation with the protocol’s accounting assumptions that rewards are only available during the defined interval, preventing both the exploit and the unintended allocation failures.
summary:
The previewRateAfterDeposit() function calculates the rate a user would receive in rewards after depositing assets. However, the incorrect implementation of a check causes the function to return a zero rate for an active reward period, and non-zero before the period starts.
An attacker can exploit this error to allocate user's assets to the incentivized vault even though the reward has not started yet, and subsequently get refunded by canceling the reward period. Users will end up getting no rewards at all.
On the other hand, users' offer will fail to be allocated to the vaults even though the reward period has started and the rate is high enough because the previewed rate is always zero.

title: Malicious markets can be injected into orders in the event of a re-org
content: The vulnerability stems from the way weiroll markets are identified and referenced within the protocol. Markets are created permissionlessly through a function that increments a sequential counter (numMarkets) and the resulting identifier, targetMarketID, is stored in offers to indicate which market should be used for fulfillment. Because the identifier is based solely on the order of creation and not on any immutable cryptographic hash, a chain re‑organization that reverts the block containing the original market creation can erase the market from the canonical history while leaving the numeric identifier unchanged. An attacker can then create a new market in the reorganized chain that reuses the same targetMarketID but contains a malicious deposit recipe. When an existing offer, which was created before the re‑org and still references the original targetMarketID, is later fulfilled, the protocol resolves the identifier to the newly injected market. The malicious recipe can divert deposited funds to the attacker, violating the offerer’s original intent. This attack can be triggered whenever the protocol permits permissionless market creation, relies on a mutable numeric ID, and operates on a blockchain where re‑orgs are possible. The impact includes loss of funds for honest offer creators and fulfillers, erosion of trust in the marketplace, and the potential for strategic re‑org attacks to be used as a profit‑making vector. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the interaction between market creation and offer fulfillment logic. It is difficult to notice because the market identifier displayed to users does not change, so the UI shows the same market ID before and after the re‑org, giving the false impression that the same market logic is being executed. From a user’s perspective, an order may appear to be fulfilled successfully, yet the expected deposit or refund never arrives, leaving balances unexpectedly zero. The bug belongs to the class of “state‑inconsistent identifier reuse” or “re‑org‑induced market injection” vulnerabilities, where mutable identifiers allow an attacker to replace contract logic after a re‑org. To remediate, the protocol should not rely solely on a sequential numeric ID; instead it must verify that the market’s code or state hash matches the one recorded at offer creation, or bind the market to an immutable reference such as a transaction hash or a Merkle root that cannot be altered by a re‑org. Adding a cryptographic integrity check before fulfillment ensures that any divergence caused by a re‑org is detected and the offer is rejected, thereby preserving the intended economic guarantees.
summary:
Recipe markets can be instantiated permissionlessly in createMarket() and is indexed by numMarkets which increases for each new instance. AP and IP offers can be created using targetMarketID to indicate which weiroll market to execute the fulfillment. However, during a chain re-org, it becomes possible to inject a completely different weiroll market instance that references the same targetMarketID that the IP/AP offer was initially created on. In this case, the offer can be fulfilled such that a malicious deposit recipe is executed, breaching the offerer's intended commitment to fulfill the order according to the parameters defined prior to the re-org.
Consider the following example:
• A weiroll market is created with valid inputs.
• An honest actor creates a valid IP or AP offer referencing targetMarketID as the newly created market they intend to deposit into.
• At some point before or after order fulfillment, if a chain re-org occurs and reverts state up and until market creation, then it becomes possible to inject a malicious market.
• A malicious actor sees this and quickly creates a new market which has the same targetMarketID as the market prior to the chain re-org.
• This market contains a malicious deposit recipe which when re-executing offer creation, the same malicious actor can fulfill the order and steal funds.
This also incentivizes intentional re-orgs as strategies emerge to create attractive IP offers which lure fulfillers and then the above scenario plays out profitably for the malicious actor.

title: Setting and refunding intervals enable owner theft and other problems
content: The vulnerability is an interval management flaw that allows the contract owner to lock and subsequently steal reward tokens. The contract uses setRewardsInterval to create a reward campaign and transfers the reward amount to the contract at the time the interval is defined. When an interval has been scheduled but has not yet started, the function does not revert and overwrites the stored interval data. Because the previously transferred tokens remain in the contract but the bookkeeping for the old interval is lost, those tokens become inaccessible to users. The refundRewardsInterval function is intended to return the unused reward tokens to the owner, but it only transfers the tokens and fails to clear or update the stored interval information. As a result the contract still believes an interval is active even after the refund, causing claimRewards to revert for that token and preventing any new interval from being created until the stale interval expires. An attacker who controls the owner role can exploit this by (1) adding a vault token as a reward, (2) setting an interval, (3) allowing the interval to pass so that users accrue unclaimed rewards, (4) setting a new interval for the same token, (5) calling refundRewardsInterval to retrieve the originally transferred amount, and (6) calling refundRewardsInterval again to capture the unclaimed rewards that remain owed to users. The impact is that users see their expected reward balance stay at zero, receive no payouts after a campaign ends, and the protocol loses funds that were supposed to be distributed. The bug manifests only when an interval is scheduled in the future and is either overwritten or refunded without proper state cleanup; it does not appear during normal operation of a single, uninterrupted interval. The affected parties are the regular users who deposit into the vault and expect rewards, as well as the protocol itself because the accounting invariants are broken. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the logic of interval creation and refund, and it is subtle because the contract does not emit explicit errors when the accounting mismatch occurs – the functions simply revert on claim, making the loss of rewards appear as a normal “no reward” condition. To remediate the problem the contract should prevent overwriting a pending interval, update or delete the interval record when a refund is performed, and disallow the vault token from being added as a reward token. Additional safeguards such as resetting internal timestamps when an interval is cleared and adding early‑return checks in reward‑per‑token calculations would close the accounting gap and restore the expected behavior that users receive their entitled rewards.

title: Protocol will miss part of it's fee
content: The vulnerability resides in the withdraw logic of a variable‑staking vault that interacts with Lido. When a variable staker calls withdraw during the ongoing stage, the contract calculates the user’s share of accumulated staking earnings (ethAmountOwed) based on the total earnings and the user’s bearer token balance. After the amount is determined, the contract deducts the protocol fee from ethAmountOwed and stores the net amount in withdrawnStakingEarnings while also updating a per‑user mapping variableToWithdrawnStakingEarnings with the net amount (currentState‑protocolFee). The root cause is that the stored value does not include the protocol fee that was taken from the user’s earnings. On a subsequent withdrawal, the helper function calculateVariableWithdrawState uses variableToWithdrawnStakingEarnings[msg.sender] as the previousWithdrawnAmount argument. Because this value excludes the fee, the fee amount from the previous withdrawal is mistakenly treated as part of the user’s still‑unwithdrawn earnings. Consequently, ethAmountOwed is inflated, causing the user to receive more ETH than they are entitled to and the protocol to miss part of its fee. This mis‑calculation only manifests when a user withdraws earnings more than once while the vault is still active and a non‑zero protocol fee is configured; a single withdrawal appears correct, making the bug subtle and hard to detect during casual testing. The impact is a systematic under‑collection of protocol fees and an over‑payment to users, breaking the accounting assumptions of the vault and potentially draining protocol revenue over time. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the withdraw function, where the interaction between fee subtraction and the subsequent state‑update logic was examined. To remediate, the contract should either store the total withdrawn amount inclusive of the protocol fee or adjust the calculation of the previousWithdrawnAmount to account for the fee, for example by scaling the stored value with the factor 10000/(10000‑protocolFeeBps). This ensures that future calls to calculateVariableWithdrawState correctly reflect the net earnings already taken and that the protocol fee is consistently applied.

title: finalizeVaultEndedWithdrawals() will fail when last withdrawal request is less than 100 wei
content: The vulnerability occurs in the withdrawal routine of a Lido‑integrated vault when the contract attempts to finalize vault‑end withdrawals. The function that splits a requested stETH amount into multiple withdrawal requests enforces a maximum per request of 1,000 stETH and a minimum per request of 100 wei. When the total balance to withdraw is not an exact multiple of the maximum, the algorithm creates a final chunk that contains the remainder. If that remainder is smaller than the protocol‑defined minimum of 100 wei, the call to Lido's withdrawal queue (requestWithdrawals) reverts because the queue contract rejects any request below the minimum. This revert aborts the entire finalizeVaultEndedWithdrawals execution, leaving the whole stETH balance locked inside the LidoAdapter contract. The root cause is the naive splitting loop that does not verify that the last chunk satisfies the minimum‑withdrawal constraint, violating the assumption that any positive amount can be submitted. Exploitation is straightforward: any vault end that results in a remainder below 100 wei triggers the failure, effectively preventing the vault from converting its stETH holdings into ETH. The impact is that users who expect their vault to close and receive ETH see no funds transferred; the UI may show the vault as ended while the on‑chain balance remains unchanged, creating the impression that money has disappeared. This condition occurs only when the vault’s total stETH balance modulo 1,000 stETH yields a value less than 100 wei, a rare edge case that can be missed during testing because the majority of balances are larger. All participants who rely on the vault – token holders, protocol governance, and any downstream contracts – are affected because the locked assets cannot be used elsewhere, reducing liquidity and potentially harming protocol economics. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the withdrawal logic and identified the mismatch between the maximum‑chunk loop and the minimum‑withdrawal requirement. It is hard to notice because the revert only happens for an extremely small remainder, which may not appear in typical test scenarios. To remediate, the splitting algorithm must guarantee that every generated withdrawal request meets the minimum threshold, for example by aggregating the remainder with the previous chunk, rounding up the final request, or adding a guard that adjusts the chunk sizes before calling the withdrawal queue. In conceptual terms, the bug belongs to the class of “boundary‑condition arithmetic errors” where protocol‑level constraints on input sizes are violated by a naïve chunking implementation, leading to a denial‑of‑service style lockup of funds.

title: finalizeVaultEndedWithdrawals would be DOSed if at least one fixed participant would withdraw from the ongoing vault
content: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that occurs when a fixed‑rate participant withdraws from an ongoing vault and later the contract attempts to finalize withdrawals after the vault has ended. The root cause is the use of the Solidity delete operator on an element of the fixedOngoingWithdrawalUsers array. Deleting an array element only resets the value to its default (address(0)) but does not shrink the array or remove the slot, so the array length stays unchanged and a zero address remains in the list. When finalizeVaultEndedWithdrawals iterates over the entire fixedOngoingWithdrawalUsers array, it calls claimFixedVaultOngoingWithdrawal for each entry, including the stale address(0). The claim function expects a non‑empty withdrawal request and reverts with an error when the requestIds array is empty, which is always true for address(0). Consequently the whole finalizeVaultEndedWithdrawals call reverts, preventing any further withdrawals from being processed. This can be exploited by any fixed participant who simply performs a normal withdrawal before the vault ends; their withdrawal creates the zero‑address entry that later blocks the batch finalization. The impact is that all users, including those who have not withdrawn, are unable to claim their funds after the vault ends, effectively locking the assets in the contract. The condition occurs only for fixed‑rate participants and only after the vault has transitioned to the ended state, but it affects the entire protocol because the admin‑only settlement function is required to recover the flow. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the withdrawal logic, where the array manipulation pattern was examined and the mismatch between delete semantics and iteration was identified. It is hard to notice because the array still reports the original length, so tests that only check the number of entries may pass, and the zero address does not cause an immediate error until the batch finalization is invoked. The bug belongs to the class of array‑element‑removal errors that lead to stale entries and subsequent out‑of‑bounds or empty‑data checks, a common source of denial‑of‑service in smart contracts. From a user’s perspective the contract appears to accept a withdrawal request, but later when they try to finalize withdrawals they receive a transaction revert and see no funds transferred, contrary to the expectation that their balance would be returned. The correct fix is to modify claimFixedVaultOngoingWithdrawal so that it safely handles a zero address (for example by returning zero without reverting) or, better, to remove the element from the array entirely (e.g., by swapping with the last element and popping) so that no stale entries remain. This eliminates the DOS condition and restores the intended accounting flow where users receive their withdrawn amounts after the vault ends.

title: Fixed participants will be incorrectly penalized during adminSettleDebt timelock period
content: The vulnerability concerns the fee calculation applied to fixed‑rate participants when the contract is in the adminSettleDebt timelock state. When an admin calls initiatingAdminSettleDebt, a three‑day lock period starts before the admin is allowed to execute adminSettleDebt and transfer the remaining stETH balance. The purpose of this lock is to give fixed participants a safe window to withdraw their deposits without suffering a penalty if the admin attempts to settle the debt with an unfavorable amount. However, the internal function calculateFixedEarlyExitFees is invoked for any withdrawal that occurs after initiatingAdminSettleDebt, and the function always adds a scaling fee based on the quadratic earlyExitFeeBps factor. Because the function does not check whether the timelock is active, the scaling fee is applied even during the protected window. As a result, a participant who withdraws during the timelock is charged an early‑exit penalty that the protocol intended to waive, leading to under‑compensation. An attacker controlling the admin role can deliberately trigger initiatingAdminSettleDebt with a settleDebtAmount that leaves a shortfall, then wait for participants to withdraw and collect the extra fees, effectively stealing value from fixed participants. The issue manifests only after the timelock is started and before it expires, so normal withdrawals outside this window behave correctly and the bug can be hard to notice during routine testing. The impact is financial loss for fixed‑rate depositors, erosion of trust in the protocol’s promised safety guarantees, and potential regulatory concerns because the contract violates its own accounting assumptions about fee exemption during the lock period. The flaw was discovered during a manual security review of the Saffron contract by auditor Pashov, who observed that calculateFixedEarlyExitFees is called unconditionally and does not consider the adminSettleDebtLockPeriod flag. To remediate, the fee calculation should be gated by a condition that disables the scaling component while the timelock is active, or the function should be bypassed entirely for withdrawals during that period. This class of bug is a timelock‑aware fee‑misapplication error, where business logic that should exempt users from penalties under a privileged state is incorrectly enforced, causing users to see unexpected deductions, zero or reduced refunds, and a mismatch between expected and actual balances.

title: Fixed participants will earn full premium even when vault ends early from debt settlement
content: The vulnerability concerns the handling of premium payouts when a vault is terminated early by the adminSettleDebt function. In the intended design, if the vault ends before its scheduled duration, fixed‑rate participants should receive their original deposit plus a premium that is proportional to the time the vault actually ran, while variable‑rate participants should receive their earnings and a partial premium that reflects the remaining unused time. The contract’s vaultEndedWithdraw routine, however, omits the calculation that reduces the fixed‑rate participants’ premium according to the shortened period. As a result, when the vault is closed early, fixed participants are allowed to withdraw both their full deposit and the full fixed premium, even though part of that premium should have been returned to variable participants. This omission creates a financial imbalance: variable participants receive less than they are owed, effectively losing the premium that should have been allocated to them. The flaw is triggered only when the admin invokes adminSettleDebt before the vault’s natural expiration and then finalizes withdrawals via finalizeVaultEndedWithdrawals. An attacker who controls the admin role can deliberately deposit as a fixed participant, force an early settlement, and then call vaultEndedWithdraw to extract the entire premium without any deduction, thereby earning an unjust profit. From a user’s perspective, a fixed participant sees a larger than expected payout – the full premium appears “for free” – while a variable participant observes a shortfall or even a zero premium return, contrary to the expectation that they should receive a proportional share. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the premium accounting logic with the withdrawal implementation and noticed that the variable‑side repayment calculation was never applied in the early‑exit path. It is subtle because the withdrawal function correctly burns tokens and transfers the calculated amount, giving the impression that balances are consistent, yet the underlying accounting of premium obligations is incomplete. To remediate the problem, the contract should adjust vaultEndedFixedDepositsFunds by the amount of premium that must be returned to variable participants, or otherwise incorporate a proportional premium reduction into the sendAmount calculation for fixed participants when the vault ends early. This change restores the intended economic invariants, ensuring that both fixed and variable participants receive payouts that match the actual time the vault was active and preventing malicious exploitation of early settlement.

title: Funds in vault can be temporarily locked by spamming dust deposits and withdrawals
content: The vulnerability is an unbounded iteration over a dynamic list of users that have ongoing fixed withdrawals. The contract function that finalizes all fixed withdrawals, finalizeVaultEndedWithdrawals, loops through the array fixedOngoingWithdrawalUsers without any size check. An attacker can inflate this array by creating a large number of dust deposits – for example 100 wei fixed deposits from many externally‑owned accounts – and then withdrawing those tiny amounts while the vault is still in the ongoing state. Because each deposit adds an entry to the array, the attacker can make the array arbitrarily large at almost no cost. When the vault later reaches its end state and the admin calls finalizeVaultEndedWithdrawals, the function must iterate over every entry. The gas required grows linearly with the array length and can exceed the block gas limit, causing the transaction to run out of gas and revert. As a result the finalisation never completes, withdrawals remain blocked and the vault funds become effectively locked.
