A related effect occurs before the vault starts: an attacker can spam many 1‑wei variable deposits and then front‑run the last legitimate depositor to withdraw one of the dust entries, reducing the available capacity below the required minimum and preventing the vault from entering the active state. The impact is that honest participants cannot retrieve their assets after the vault ends, and the protocol may never become operational, which undermines user trust and can lead to loss of funds if no admin recovery mechanism is used. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the control flow of the vault lifecycle and identified that the array used for tracking ongoing withdrawals is not bounded. It is hard to notice because the individual deposits are tiny and appear harmless, and the loop looks innocuous until the array is deliberately bloated. The bug belongs to the class of gas‑limit denial‑of‑service vulnerabilities caused by unbounded loops over user‑controlled data structures. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a “withdrawal pending” status forever, or the balance displayed after the vault ends may remain unchanged even though the user expects a refund. The contract violates the business logic that all deposited funds should become withdrawable after the vault ends. A conceptual fix is to prevent the array from growing without bound: enforce a reasonable minimum deposit amount, limit the number of entries processed per transaction, or replace the array with a mapping and a counter that can be iterated in smaller batches. Additionally, the protocol should include safeguards that reject dust deposits or cap the total number of active withdrawal entries, thereby raising the cost of a DoS attack and ensuring that finalisation can always complete.
summary: finalizeVaultEndedWithdrawals() is required to be called to finalize all fixed withdrawals, including on-going fixed withdrawals. The issue is that it iterates through fixedOngoingWithdrawalUsers, which can be manipulated and become unbounded. An attacker can make fixedOngoingWithdrawalUsers extremely large by spamming dust fixed deposits of 100 wei (with multiple EOA) and then withdraw them when vault is on-going. This will cause finalizeVaultEndedWithdrawals() to be DoS, which prevents withdrawals when vault ends, resulting in the vault funds locked. I have classified this as Medium impact as admin can recover the issue with settle debt function. Another issue that can occur with dust deposits and withdrawals is that an attacker can prevent vault from starting. The attack can conducted by spamming multiple 1 wei variable deposits and then withdraw one of them whenever vault is going to start by frontrunning the last depositor.

title: Variable participants could lose their fee earnings
content: The contract contains a withdrawal calculation flaw in the function that determines how much ETH a variable‑bearer participant is owed. The function computes the participant's share of total earnings by multiplying the holder's token balance with the total earnings and dividing by the total token supply, then subtracts the amount the participant has already withdrawn. This logic assumes that the computed share will always be greater than or equal to the previously withdrawn amount. In practice, edge cases such as a negative rebase of the earnings or an admin‑initiated debt settlement that reduces totalEarnings after earlier withdrawals can make the participant's share smaller than what was already withdrawn. Because Solidity 0.8 reverts on unsigned integer underflow, the subtraction triggers a revert, causing the higher‑level vaultEndedWithdraw routine to fail. When this happens, the affected participant cannot complete the withdrawal of both staking earnings and fee earnings, effectively locking their funds in the contract. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the arithmetic assumptions of the withdrawal path. It is subtle because the revert only occurs under specific state transitions that are not part of the normal happy‑path flow, making it easy to miss in standard testing. The bug violates the accounting invariant that a participant’s cumulative withdrawn amount must never exceed their proportional share of earnings, leading to a situation where users see their balances unchanged or reduced to zero despite having earned fees. The recommended mitigation is to guard the subtraction by checking whether the previousWithdrawnAmount is greater than or equal to the calculated share and, in that case, set the owed amount to zero before returning the updated state. This restores the invariant and prevents the contract from reverting, allowing participants to withdraw any remaining earnings safely.

title: Lack of frontrunning protection in resolveCondition allows unfair advantage
content: The vulnerability is a front‑running weakness in the contract function that resolves a betting condition. Because the function does not verify that the betting period has ended before it determines the winning outcome, an attacker can watch the transaction pool for a pending resolve call, read the outcome that will be recorded, and then submit a large bet on that outcome before the resolution transaction is mined. This race condition arises from the missing end‑time check and the absence of any mechanism that blocks new bets once the outcome is about to be fixed. An attacker exploits the timing gap by submitting a transaction with higher gas price, causing it to be mined before the legitimate resolve transaction, thereby capturing the winning odds with a disproportionate stake. The impact is that honest participants may see the odds shift dramatically, place bets that are effectively guaranteed to lose, and experience unexpected loss of funds, while the attacker profits from the unfair advantage. The issue manifests whenever a resolveCondition call is broadcast while the betting window is still technically open, which can happen frequently in live prediction markets where outcomes are resolved shortly after the event ends. All users who place bets during this window, as well as the protocol’s overall fairness guarantees, are affected. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the state transitions of the betting lifecycle and identified that the resolve function lacked a guard against pending bets. Because the exploit relies on observing mempool activity and does not produce an obvious on‑chain error, it can be difficult to notice without detailed transaction‑ordering analysis. To remediate, the resolution logic should be split: one step must first close the betting window and prevent any further wagers, and a second step should record the winning outcome. Additional safeguards such as commit‑reveal schemes or time‑locked state changes can also mitigate the race condition. In user terms, a participant expects to place a bet and receive a fair chance of winning, but instead may see their balance drop to zero or receive no payout because an attacker front‑ran the resolution and captured the winning outcome. This constitutes a classic front‑running or race‑condition class of bug that breaks the accounting assumptions of the prediction market, allowing funds to disappear or be unfairly redistributed.
summary: The EnhancedSportsPrediction::resolveCondition function can be frontrun by malicious users. Since there is no check for endTime, a user can monitor the mempool for a resolveCondition transaction, extract the winningOutcome, and place a large bet on it before the condition is resolved.

title: An allowed signer can sign mints with malicious parameters
content: The vulnerability consists of an authorization bypass in the minting flow of a SeaDrop‑based ERC721 contract. The contract maintains a list of allowed signers that can produce off‑chain signatures authorising mint operations. When a signature from an allowed signer is presented, the contract trusts the signed mint parameters without independently verifying that the protocol fee fields obey the intended business rules. Specifically, a signer can embed a feeBps value of zero, which eliminates the protocol fee entirely, or can set a custom feeRecipient while also setting restrictFeeRecipients to false, thereby bypassing the on‑chain check that would normally enforce that fees are sent only to the protocol‑designated address. Because the owner of the ERC721SeaDrop contract can add or replace signers through the updateSigner function, the owner (or any party that gains signer privileges) can deliberately craft mint parameters that divert or suppress fees. An attacker who controls an allowed signer therefore signs a mint transaction with these malicious parameters and submits it; the contract processes the mint as usual, but the fee calculation either yields zero or routes the fee to an address chosen by the attacker. From a user’s perspective the mint appears to succeed, the NFT is received, but the expected protocol fee is missing or is sent to an unexpected address, effectively causing revenue loss for the protocol. The issue was discovered during a security audit by Spearbit, where the logical assumption that signers would respect fee constraints was found to be unchecked. The flaw is subtle because the mint transaction itself is valid and the UI typically does not expose the feeBps or feeRecipient fields, making the fee manipulation hard to notice without deep inspection of the signed payload. To remediate, the contract should enforce feeBps > 0 and require restrictFeeRecipients to be true at the point of mint execution, regardless of who signed the request, or restrict signers to only sign fee‑compliant parameters and add explicit on‑chain validation of fee fields. This would restore the intended accounting guarantees and prevent fee diversion or loss.
summary:
An allowed signer (SeaDrop.sol#L318-L319) can sign mints that have either:
• mintParams.feeBps equal to 0.
• A custom feeRecipient with mintParams.restrictFeeRecipients equal to false to circumvent the check at SeaDrop.sol#L469.
And thus avoid the protocol fee being paid or allow the protocol fee to be sent to a desired address decided by the signer. Note that the ERC721SeaDrop owner can allow signers by calling ERC721SeaDrop.updateSigner. Therefore, the owner can allow an address they control as a signer and sign mints that have either one of the above features.

title: ERC721SeaDrop's modifier onlyOwnerOrAdministrator would allow either the owner or the admin to override the other person's config parameters.
content: ERC721SeaDrop contract includes a modifier onlyOwnerOrAdministrator that is applied to four external configuration functions. The modifier permits either the contract owner or an address designated as administrator to call the function, without distinguishing which caller may change which parameter. As a result the two privileged parties can overwrite each other's settings. The root cause is that the access control logic treats owner and administrator as interchangeable for configuration updates, rather than enforcing a separation of duties. An attacker who controls either role can later be overridden by the other role, allowing a malicious party to replace critical data such as the merkle root used for allow‑list verification, the drop URI, the allowed SeaDrop implementation address, or the authorized signer. Exploitation proceeds by first having the legitimate administrator set a correct allow‑list merkle root and emit the expected parameters, after which the owner (or a compromised owner) calls the same updateAllowList function with a new merkle root that encodes leaves where the fee basis points field is zero. Minters who obtain a proof from the latest allow‑list can then submit mint transactions with feeBps set to 0, causing the SeaDrop mintAllowList endpoint to skip the protocol fee that would normally be sent to the creator payment address. The impact is that the protocol fee revenue is eliminated for those mints, effectively allowing the privileged party to steal fee revenue or to give users free minting, which undermines the economic model of the SeaDrop system. The condition occurs whenever the contract is deployed with both an owner and an administrator and the onlyOwnerOrAdministrator modifier is used on configuration functions, which is the default in the audited implementation. All parties that rely on the fee collection – the protocol, creators, and users expecting correct fee deductions – are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that examined the access control patterns and identified that the modifier does not enforce exclusive rights, leading to a potential conflict of interest. The bug can be hard to notice because the functions appear to be protected and emit events that look normal; however, the underlying data can be silently replaced without obvious on‑chain alerts, and the fee bypass only manifests as missing fee deductions in transaction receipts. To remediate, the contract should enforce a strict separation of duties: either restrict configuration updates to a single privileged role, or split the functions so that the owner can change only certain parameters (e.g., allowed SeaDrop address) while the administrator can change others (e.g., allow‑list data), and add explicit checks that prevent overwriting of critical fee‑related fields without consensus. Additionally, emitting a distinct event when fee‑related parameters are changed and requiring multi‑signature approval for such changes would mitigate the risk. In summary, the vulnerability is a role‑conflict configuration override that enables a privileged party to replace critical contract settings and bypass protocol fee logic, leading to potential loss of revenue and violation of the intended accounting guarantees of the SeaDrop protocol.
summary:
The following 4 external functions in ERC721SeaDrop have the onlyOwnerOrAdministrator modifier which allows either one to override the other person's work.
• updateAllowedSeaDrop
• updateAllowList
• updateDropURI
• updateSigner
That means there should be some sort of off-chain trust established between these 2 entities. Otherwise, there are possible vectors of attack. Here is an example of how the owner can override AllowListData.merkleRoot and the other fields within AllowListData to generate proofs for any allowed SeaDrop's mintAllowList endpoint that would have MintParams.feeBps equal to 0:
1. The admin calls updateAllowList to set the Merkle root for an allowed SeaDrop implementation for this contract and emit the other parameters as logs. The SeaDrop endpoint being called by ERC721SeaDrop.updateAllowList: SeaDrop.sol#L827
2. The owner calls updateAllowList but this time with new parameters, specifically a new Merkle root that is computed from leaves that have MintParams.feeBps == 0.
3. Users/minters use the generated proof corresponding to the latest allow list update and pass their mintParams.feeBps as 0. And thus avoiding the protocol fee deduction for the creatorPaymentAddress (SeaDrop.sol#L187-L194).

title: Reentrancy of fee payment can be used to circumvent max mints per wallet check
content: During a public mint, the contract first checks that the caller has not exceeded the maxMintsPerWallet limit. The check is performed in an internal function _checkMintQuantity before the mint is executed. After the mint, the contract distributes a fee to the address supplied as feeRecipient by calling an external address with a low‑level call. Because the fee transfer is performed without a re‑entrancy guard, a malicious feeRecipient can execute code in its fallback function that calls mintPublic again before the original call finishes. The second call reaches the same _checkMintQuantity function while the internal counter that records how many tokens the wallet has minted has not yet been updated for the first call, allowing the attacker to bypass the maxMintsPerWallet restriction. When PublicDrop.restrictFeeRecipients is false, any address can be used as feeRecipient, so an attacker can repeatedly re‑enter and mint unlimited tokens. If restrictFeeRecipients is true, only addresses that are whitelisted as allowed fee recipients can perform the attack, which still represents a privilege escalation but with a higher barrier. The impact is that a user can receive more NFTs than the protocol intends, breaking the economic model, depriving honest participants of scarce tokens, and potentially allowing the attacker to extract additional revenue or manipulate supply. The bug is discovered during a security audit that examined the fee dispersal path and noticed that the state update for minted count occurs after the external call. It is hard to notice because the re‑entrancy occurs in a seemingly unrelated fee payment step and the contract does not use a non‑reentrant modifier on that path. To remediate, the fee‑payment code should be protected with a re‑entrancy lock (e.g., using OpenZeppelin’s nonReentrant modifier) or the transfer should be performed with .transfer which forwards only a limited amount of gas, preventing the fallback from executing a second mint. However, using .transfer may break contracts that rely on receiving more gas. In summary, the vulnerability is a re‑entrancy flaw in the fee distribution that allows circumvention of per‑wallet mint limits, leading to unexpected extra mints and loss of protocol guarantees.

title: GolomTrader’s `_settleBalances` double counts protocol fee, reducing taker’s payout for a NFT sold
content: The vulnerability resides in the settlement routine that distributes proceeds after a NFT sale. When the contract processes a batch of NFTs (the `amount` parameter greater than one), it calculates the protocol fee as a percentage of the order total, but then multiplies that fee by the batch size twice: once when the fee amount is stored in a local variable and again when the fee is subtracted from the total payable to the taker. This double‑counting of the protocol fee leads to an excessive deduction from the taker’s share. For example, if the fee per unit is 1 ETH and six units are sold, the contract should remove only 6 ETH from the taker’s payout, but the erroneous formula removes 1 ETH × 6 × 6 = 36 ETH, freezing the extra 30 ETH in the contract balance. The root cause is an arithmetic mistake where the `amount` multiplier is applied to the protocol‑fee term both inside the fee variable and again inside the final payout expression. The bug can be exploited by anyone who can track the contract state and withdraw the surplus balance that remains unintentionally locked, effectively stealing the funds that should have gone to the seller. The impact is a reduction of the taker’s expected proceeds, causing funds to disappear from the user’s perspective; a seller who expects to receive the full net amount after fees may instead receive a smaller amount or, in extreme cases, nothing at all. The condition under which the issue manifests is any sale where `amount > 1`, i.e., batch sales or multiple‑unit fills. The affected parties are the buyers/takers of NFTs and, indirectly, any participants relying on the protocol’s accounting integrity. The problem was uncovered during a Code4rena audit by reviewing the `_settleBalances` implementation and noticing the mismatched arithmetic. It is subtle because the fee formula looks syntactically correct and only deviates when larger batch sizes are used, making it easy to miss in basic tests. To remediate, the protocol fee should be calculated once and multiplied by `amount` only a single time, and the taker payout formula should subtract exactly that fee quantity, not an amount‑scaled version of it. This belongs to the broader class of fee‑miscalculation bugs where fees are double‑counted or incorrectly scaled, leading to accounting errors and unintended fund lock‑up.
summary:
Currently `((o.totalAmt * 50) / 10000)` protocol fee share is multiplied by `amount` twice when being accounted for as a deduction from the total in amount due to the `msg.sender` taker calculations in _settleBalances(), which is called by fillBid() and fillCriteriaBid() to handle the payouts.

Setting the severity to be high as reduced payouts is a fund loss impact for taker, which receives less than it’s due whenever `amount > 1`.

Notice that the amount lost to the taker is left on the contract balance and currently is subject to other vulnerabilities, i.e. can be easily stolen by an attacker that knowns these specifics and tracks contract state. When these issues be fixed this amount to be permanently frozen on the GolomTrader’s balance as it’s unaccounted for in all subsequent calculations (i.e. all the transfers are done with regard to the accounts recorded, this extra sum is unaccounted, there is no general native funds rescue function, so when all other mechanics be fixed the impact will be permanent freeze of the part of taker’s funds).

title: Old delegatee not deleted when delegating to new tokenId
content: The vulnerability occurs in the delegation logic of the VoteEscrowDelegation contract. When a token holder calls the delegate function to assign its voting power to a new delegatee, the implementation adds the token ID to the new delegatee’s list but fails to remove the same token ID from the previous delegatee’s list. This omission creates a state inconsistency where the same token ID is recorded as delegated to multiple addresses at the same time. The root cause is that the delegate routine does not invoke the removal helper (removeDelegation) or otherwise update the old delegatee’s delegatedTokenIds array before inserting the new entry. An attacker can exploit the bug by repeatedly delegating the same token ID to different addresses, effectively multiplying the token’s voting weight across several delegatees. Each delegatee will be counted by the governance system as possessing the full voting power of the token, inflating the total voting supply and allowing the attacker to sway proposals, block legitimate decisions, or crash quorum calculations. The impact is a compromised governance process where votes no longer reflect the true distribution of token holdings, potentially leading to malicious proposals being accepted or legitimate ones being rejected. The condition under which the issue manifests is any call to delegate after a token has already been delegated once; the contract does not check or clean up prior delegations. All token holders and participants in the protocol’s governance are affected because the inflated voting power can distort outcomes that should be decided by the genuine token distribution. The flaw was identified during a formal security audit by Code4rena, where the auditors observed that the delegatedTokenIds mapping for the old delegatee was never cleared, leading to an over‑count of voting power. The problem is subtle because the delegation transaction itself succeeds and appears to work from a UI perspective – a user sees that their token is delegated to the new address, but the system silently retains the previous entry, making the inconsistency hard to detect without inspecting internal state. To fix the issue, the delegate function should first remove the token ID from the current delegatee’s delegatedTokenIds array, either by calling the existing removeDelegation helper or by directly updating the mapping, ensuring that each token ID is associated with at most one delegatee at any time. This correction restores the one‑to‑one relationship required for accurate vote accounting and prevents the multiplication of voting power. In summary, the bug belongs to the class of state‑inconsistency delegation vulnerabilities where outdated references are not purged, leading to double counting and governance manipulation.
summary:
[VoteEscrowDelegation.sol#L80](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-07-golom/blob/8f198624b97addbbe9602a451c908ea51bd3357c/contracts/vote-escrow/VoteEscrowDelegation.sol#L80)  

In `delegate`, when a user delegates to a new tokenId, the tokenId is not removed from the current delegatee. Therefore, one user can easily multiply his voting power, which makes the toking useless for voting / governance decisions.

title: `addFee` will stop accumulating fee once `rewardToken` has reached max supply
content: The vulnerability lies in the fee‑distribution routine of the RewardDistributor contract, specifically in the addFee function. When the total supply of the protocol's reward token reaches the hard‑coded cap of one billion tokens (adjusted for decimals), the function executes a branch that emits a NewEpoch event with zero token emission and bypasses the logic that converts the accumulated protocol fees (held as native ETH) into WETH and credits them to stakers. Because the fee‑handling code—including the weth.deposit call and the update of the previous epoch's fee balance—is only executed in the else‑branch (when the supply is below the cap), any fees collected after the cap is hit remain locked in the contract's ETH balance and are never reflected in the staker reward accounting. This happens at the moment an epoch transition is triggered (block.timestamp exceeding startTime plus epoch·secsInDay) and only after the token supply surpasses the maximum. As a result, users who have staked tokens, such as Alice in the proof‑of‑concept, stop receiving fee rewards despite the protocol continuing to collect fees from traders. From the user's perspective the UI may show that fees are being taken from trades, but the expected reward balance stays unchanged or becomes zero, creating a discrepancy between expected and actual payouts. The issue was uncovered during a Code4rena audit by inspecting the conditional flow of addFee and reproducing the scenario where the reward token supply reaches its limit. It is subtle because the contract still records fee amounts in epochTotalFee, yet the downstream conversion to WETH and distribution is silently omitted, making the problem easy to miss unless transaction traces are examined. To remediate, the fee‑distribution logic must be decoupled from the token‑minting condition so that fee handling (WETH deposit, fee accounting, and event emission) continues even when no new reward tokens are minted, or the condition should be revised to only skip token emission while preserving fee processing. This adjustment restores the intended accounting guarantees and ensures that stakers receive their entitled fees regardless of the token supply state.
summary: `RewardDistributor` will stop accumulating fees for staker rewards once `rewardToken` supply has reached the maximum supply (1 billion).

title: NFT transferring won’t work because of the external call to `removeDelegation`.
content: The vulnerability resides in the NFT delegation contract where the internal transfer routine `_transferFrom` invokes the function `removeDelegation` via `this.removeDelegation(_tokenId)`. Because `removeDelegation` is declared as an external function, the call through the contract’s own address changes the execution context: `msg.sender` becomes the contract address instead of the external account that initiated the transfer. Inside `removeDelegation` there is an access‑control check `require(ownerOf(tokenId) == msg.sender, 'VEDelegation: Not allowed');` which expects the caller to be the current owner of the token. When the call is performed through `this`, the contract itself is not the token owner, causing the require statement to revert. Consequently, any attempt to move a delegated NFT through the public `_transferFrom` path fails, effectively locking the token for the legitimate owner. The issue manifests whenever a token holder tries to transfer their delegated NFT, for example through a marketplace or a wallet UI, and the transaction is reverted with the error message "VEDelegation: Not allowed". Users experience a sudden inability to move their assets, seeing no balance change and often receiving a generic revert reason, which can be mistaken for a broader protocol failure. The bug belongs to the class of access‑control failures caused by incorrect use of external calls that alter `msg.sender`, a subtle problem that is easy to miss during code review because the call syntactically appears valid and the failure only surfaces at runtime when the ownership check is evaluated. The issue was discovered during a security audit that inspected the delegation logic and traced the flow of `msg.sender` across internal and external calls. Fixing the problem requires removing the external call through `this`; the recommended approach is to make `removeDelegation` a public (or internal) function that can be invoked directly without changing the caller context, thereby preserving the original `msg.sender` and allowing the ownership check to succeed. By correcting the call semantics, the contract regains its intended behavior: owners can transfer delegated NFTs, balances update correctly, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions about token ownership remain intact.
summary:
The `VoteEscrowDelegation._transferFrom` function won’t work because it calls `this.removeDelegation(_tokenId)`. The `removeDelegation` function is external, so when the call is done by `this.removeDelegation(_tokenId)` msg.sender changes to the contract address.

This causes the check in the `` function to (most likely) fail because the contract is not the owner of the NFT, and that will make the function revert.  
`require(ownerOf(tokenId) == msg.sender, 'VEDelegation: Not allowed');`

title: `_writeCheckpoint` does not write to storage on same block
content: The vulnerability resides in the VoteEscrowDelegation contract’s internal function `_writeCheckpoint`, which is responsible for updating delegation checkpoints for a given token ID. When the contract attempts to overwrite an existing checkpoint within the same block, it creates a temporary copy of the latest checkpoint in memory (`Checkpoint memory oldCheckpoint = checkpoints[toTokenId][nCheckpoints - 1];`). The subsequent modification of `oldCheckpoint.delegatedTokenIds` only changes this in‑memory copy; the original storage entry is never updated because the variable points to memory, not to storage. As a result, any delegation change that occurs in the same block after an initial delegation – for example, removing a delegation or delegating the same token to a different delegate – is silently ignored, and the contract retains the earlier delegation record. This behavior can be exploited by an attacker who performs a delegation and then a removal (or a second delegation) within a single block, typically by bundling the two calls in one transaction through a helper contract. The removal transaction appears successful from the caller’s perspective, but the checkpoint does not persist, allowing the attacker’s voting power to be multiplied indefinitely with each repeated cycle. The impact is that the protocol’s accounting of delegated voting power becomes incorrect, potentially inflating governance influence, breaking expectations for token holders who believe a delegation has been withdrawn, and undermining the integrity of any mechanisms that rely on accurate delegation totals. The issue manifests only when two `_writeCheckpoint` calls affect the same token ID in the same block; under normal usage with separate blocks the bug remains hidden, which explains why it is easy to miss in standard testing. It was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the checkpoint‑writing logic and noticed the use of a memory variable where a storage reference was required. The fix consists of changing the declaration of `oldCheckpoint` to a storage pointer (`Checkpoint storage oldCheckpoint = checkpoints[toTokenId][nCheckpoints - 1];`), ensuring that updates affect the persisted state. Conceptually, this is a classic example of a state‑update bug caused by improper handling of reference types, leading to a mismatch between expected on‑chain state and actual stored data, and it violates the protocol’s fundamental accounting assumptions that each delegation change is reflected immediately and accurately.

title: Users can avoid paying fees while trading trustlessly & using Golom’s network effects
content: The vulnerability is a fee‑bypass flaw in the Golom marketplace trade logic. The contract calculates trading fees and royalty cuts from the order field `o.totalAmt`. Because the fee checks only compare the payment amount `p.paymentAmt` against a function of `o.totalAmt`, a maker can set `o.totalAmt` to zero and hide the true amount they wish to receive inside the otherwise unrelated `order.root` (or `deadline`) field. By deploying a malicious contract and listing it as the order's `reservedAddress`, the maker ensures that the marketplace will only execute the trade through this contract, which re‑creates the same checks but with `o.totalAmt` equal to zero. As a result, the condition `require(o.totalAmt * amount * 15/100 >= p.paymentAmt)` becomes `require(0 >= p.paymentAmt)`, which is trivially satisfied when `p.paymentAmt` is also zero‑checked against the hidden root value, allowing the trade to proceed without the expected 15% fee or any pre‑payment royalty. The exploit can be performed by any user who can craft a signed order with these manipulated fields and invoke the `fillAsk` function through the malicious contract. When executed, the maker receives the full sale price of their NFT while the protocol collects no fees, effectively diverting revenue that should have been distributed to the exchange, pre‑payment pool, and the platform. This situation occurs only when the order’s `totalAmt` is deliberately set to zero and the hidden amount is encoded in a field that is not validated, and when the contract’s `reservedAddress` check is satisfied. The affected parties are the protocol (loss of fee revenue), other traders (unfair marketplace conditions), and potentially users who rely on correct fee accounting. The issue was uncovered during a manual audit that included a proof‑of‑concept contract named `AvoidsFeesContract`. It is subtle because the fee calculation appears correct at first glance and the `totalAmt` field is normally expected to be non‑zero, so a zero value does not raise an alarm. The bug falls under the class of "fee calculation bypass" or "unchecked arithmetic based on mutable input fields". From a user’s perspective, a trade completes successfully, the NFT is transferred, but the expected fee deduction never occurs; the protocol’s UI may still show the trade as normal, masking the loss. To remediate, the contract must enforce that `o.totalAmt` is strictly greater than zero and that `p.paymentAmt` (or any amount derived from hidden fields) cannot exceed `o.totalAmt`. An explicit check such as `require(o.totalAmt > p.paymentAmt && o.totalAmt > 0)` should be added, and the reliance on `reservedAddress` for fee enforcement should be re‑examined to prevent contracts from arbitrarily overriding fee logic.
summary:
* If a maker makes below mentioned `AvoidsFeesContract` a [reservedAddress](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-07-golom/blob/main/contracts/core/GolomTrader.sol#L220) and hides the info about how much they want their NFT in [order.root](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-07-golom/blob/main/contracts/core/GolomTrader.sol#L58), they can avoid paying fees while trading trustlessly and using the network effects of golom maketplace with 0 [o.totalAmt](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-07-golom/blob/main/contracts/core/GolomTrader.sol#L52). See POC to get a better idea.
  * Here the maker uses order.root to hide the amount they want to get paid because it is much cleaner for a POC.

    * But since golom does not have an API where user can submit a signature without using the frontend, they will use something like deadline to hide the amount they want to get paid.
    * Reason they would use deadline is because that is something they can control in the golom NFT frontend
    * They can pack the information about deadline and amount they want to get paid, in one uint256 as a deadline and then the check in the contract would look different

title: Repeated calls to `multiStakerClaim` in the same block leads to loss of funds
content: The vulnerability consists of an ability to claim the same epoch reward multiple times by exploiting the way the RewardDistributor contract calculates a staker’s entitlement. The contract’s multiStakerClaim function checks a per‑token‑ID flag to ensure a reward for a given epoch has not already been claimed, but the reward amount is derived from the current balance of the lock token at the moment the epoch changes (epochBeginTime). Because the underlying vote‑escrow (VE) token permits locks to be merged and a new lock receives a fresh token ID while preserving the exact amount of staked tokens, an attacker can create a new lock in the same block, merge the original lock into the new one, and then invoke multiStakerClaim again with the new token ID. The require statement sees a different token ID and therefore permits the second claim, even though the underlying economic position has not changed. This attack can be orchestrated by bundling the necessary transactions (initial claim, creation of a new lock, merge, second claim) into a single block, typically using services such as Flashbots to guarantee inclusion in the block that also triggers the epoch change via an addFee call. When executed, the attacker repeatedly drains the WETH balance held by the RewardDistributor, effectively stealing all pending reward funds. The bug manifests only when an epoch transition occurs and multiple contract calls are processed within the same block; otherwise the normal per‑epoch accounting works as intended. The affected parties include any staker who expects to receive rewards, the protocol that relies on the RewardDistributor to fairly allocate WETH, and ultimately the users whose funds are at risk of disappearance. The issue was discovered during a security audit of the Golom protocol when the auditor observed that the reward calculation referenced live lock balances rather than a snapshot taken at epoch start, and a proof‑of‑concept demonstrated the double‑claim using flash‑bot bundles. The flaw is subtle because the require check appears to protect against double claims, yet it only validates the token identifier, not the underlying economic stake, and typical testing does not execute multiple transactions in the same block. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that expected rewards are not received or the contract’s WETH balance suddenly drops to zero, contradicting the expectation that claimed rewards are transferred to the user. Conceptually the bug is a reward‑snapshot race condition combined with mutable token identifiers, leading to a double‑spend of rewards. The recommended mitigation is to replace the live‑balance query with a per‑epoch snapshot of each lock’s balance, to record claimed epochs per economic position rather than per token ID, and to prevent multiple claim calls within a single block or to disallow lock merging for reward purposes. Implementing a checkpointing mechanism ensures that rewards are calculated from immutable data captured at epoch start, restoring the intended integrity of the reward distribution logic.
summary:
A malicious user can repeatedly claim the same staker reward for an epoch, provided the transactions all happen in the same block. This can effectively be done using services like [Flashbots bundles](https://docs.flashbots.net/Flashbots-auction/searchers/faq/#can-you-give-a-step-by-step-description-of-how-flashbots-works-for-a-searcher-today) and will result in the draining of the WETH balance of the `RewardDistributor` contract.

The idea is to bypass the require statement [line 185](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-07-golom/blob/e5efa8f9d6dda92a90b8b2c4902320acf0c26816/contracts/rewards/RewardDistributor.sol#L185) which checks if a claim has been already done for the epoch, **for a specific token ID**. By moving the locked tokens in a new lock, a new token ID will be generated and can be used to claim the rewards again, **if the transaction happens in the same block for which the epoch is updated**.

Indeed, when `multiStakerClaim()` is called, the `rewardETH` will be calculated from the amount of tokens locked in `tokenids[tindex]` at the block that triggered the epoch change (variable `epochBeginTime`). If, during this time, an attacker transfers its staked tokens to a new vault using the [`merge`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-07-golom/blob/e5efa8f9d6dda92a90b8b2c4902320acf0c26816/contracts/vote-escrow/VoteEscrowCore.sol#L893) function of the VE token, the function will calculate the amount of staked tokens for the newly created tokenID **as the same as the original tokenID reward**.

A example abuse will look like this (pseudo-code adapted from the PoC) :
```solidity
lockID = voteEscrow.create_lock(amount, 1 week); // Create lock #1 before
// IN THE BLOCK OF EPOCH CHANGE
rewardDistributor.multiStakerClaim([lockId], [0]); // Claim epoch 0 rewards for lock #1
voteEscrow.create_lock(1, 1 week); // Create lock #2 (requires 1 Golom token, could be created in advance)
voteEscrow.merge(lockId, lockId + 1); // Transfer lock #1 tokens to lock #2
rewardDistributor.multiStakerClaim([lockId + 1], [0]); // Claim same epoch rewards for lock #2
// repeat ...
```
To abuse this, the attacker needs to follow this steps:

  * Have some locked Golom tokens.
  * Wait for a `addFee` call that will trigger an epoch change (this can be monitored by looking at the mempool or predicted from block timestamps). Services like Flashbots also [allows for specifying a range of blocks for bundles](https://docs.flashbots.net/Flashbots-auction/searchers/faq/#how-do-i-target-a-timestamp-range-instead-of-a-block-number-when-submitting-a-bundle) for better targeting.
  * Send a bundle of transactions to be included with the block containing the epoch changing transaction (see the PoC for an example of transactions).

Note that this needs to succeed only once to allow an attacker to drain all WETH funds so if the bundle isn’t included for a particular epoch, given the frequency of epoch changes, the bundle will eventually be included and trigger the exploit.

title: Upon changing of delegate, `VoteDelegation` updates both the previous and the current checkpoint
content: The vulnerability resides in the vote‑delegation logic of the contract that tracks voting power through a series of checkpoints. When a token holder changes or removes a delegate, the implementation reads the most recent checkpoint using a storage reference, mutates that checkpoint by adding or removing a token ID, and then forwards the modified structure to the internal `_writeCheckpoint` routine. Because the checkpoint was obtained as a storage pointer, the mutation also alters the historic checkpoint that should remain immutable. `_writeCheckpoint` subsequently creates a new checkpoint for the current block, copying the already‑modified token list, which means that both the previous checkpoint and the newly created one now contain the same token ID. The root cause is the misuse of a `storage` variable where a `memory` copy should be used, causing retroactive modification of past voting power records. An attacker who controls delegation can therefore inflate their voting power for earlier blocks, effectively rewriting the voting history. This manipulation can change the outcome of past governance proposals, corrupt quorum calculations, and undermine the integrity of any protocol component that relies on the historical voting snapshot. The flaw manifests whenever a delegate is assigned to an address that already holds one or more checkpoints, or when an existing delegation is removed, because both paths read and mutate the latest checkpoint in storage. All token holders and the governance process are affected, as the voting power of delegates may be reported incorrectly. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that inspected the delegation flow and observed that the same token ID appeared in both the old and new checkpoint after a delegation change. It is subtle because checkpoints are internal data structures not directly exposed to users; the bug does not produce an immediate runtime error, but the resulting vote tallies are silently wrong, making it difficult to detect without deep inspection of the checkpoint history. To remediate the problem, the contract should retrieve the latest checkpoint into a temporary `memory` variable, modify that copy, and then write the updated data to a new checkpoint, ensuring that historic checkpoints remain unchanged. In abstract terms, the bug belongs to the class of state‑mutation‑through‑aliasing errors, where a reference to persistent storage is unintentionally altered, leading to retroactive state corruption. From a user’s perspective, a delegator may notice that their voting power appears higher than expected for previous periods, or that proposals they did not vote on seem to have been decided differently, contrary to the expectation that delegation only affects future votes. This breach of accounting assumptions violates the core business rule that voting power snapshots must be immutable once recorded.
summary: The contract is accidently editing both the previous and current checkpoint when changing/removing a delegate.

title: Untrusted ERC-20 decimals() Return Values Could Be Mutated, Uncached Access Shouldn’t Be Considered Reliable
content: The vulnerability stems from the contract’s reliance on the ERC‑20 decimals() function as if it were an immutable constant. In many places the code calls decimals() on a token address repeatedly and uses the returned value in arithmetic that determines how many token units are transferred, how interest is calculated, or how balances are displayed. Because the ERC‑20 standard does not enforce that decimals() must return the same value for the lifetime of a token, a malicious or poorly‑implemented token can return different numbers on each call, even within a single transaction. An attacker can therefore deploy a token whose decimals() implementation varies with block.timestamp, block.number, or any other mutable state. When the victim contract queries decimals() multiple times, each query may yield a different divisor, causing the contract to mis‑scale amounts. For example, a transfer that should move 1 token (with 18 decimals) could be interpreted as 1 × 10⁶ units if decimals() suddenly reports 6, resulting in an over‑payment to the attacker or an under‑payment to a legitimate user. From the user’s point of view the UI may show a normal deposit, but the received balance becomes unexpectedly low or even zero, violating the expectation that “the amount I deposited should appear in my account”. The impact includes incorrect accounting, potential loss of funds, and broken protocol invariants such as collateral ratios or reward calculations. The issue appears whenever the contract interacts with an untrusted ERC‑20 token without caching the decimals value or without validating that the token adheres to the expected metadata. It was discovered during a security audit that highlighted repeated external calls to decimals() and demonstrated a proof‑of‑concept token that returns block.timestamp % 18 as its decimal count. The bug is subtle because decimals() is a view function and developers normally assume it is constant, so the problem does not raise compiler warnings or obvious runtime errors. To remediate, the contract should treat any external token metadata as untrusted: it must call decimals() once, verify that the value lies within a reasonable range (e.g., 0‑18), store the result in an immutable storage slot, and reuse that cached value for all subsequent calculations. Alternatively, the protocol can restrict interactions to whitelisted tokens whose metadata is known, or use a separate adapter that enforces the constant‑ness of decimals. By eliminating repeated uncached calls, the protocol restores correct scaling of token amounts and prevents attackers from manipulating arithmetic through mutable metadata.

title: LP Oracle Should Enforce 18 Decimals Or Use Decimal Flexible Fixed Point Math
content: The vulnerability is a mis‑valuation bug in the liquidity‑pool (LP) oracle that assumes every priced token uses 18 decimal places. The oracle multiplies token balances by a fixed‑point scaling factor based on 10^18 (WAD) without taking the token’s own decimals into account. When a token with fewer than 18 decimals, such as USDC (6 decimals), is supplied, the scaling factor is too large and the computed value is artificially low, causing the LP token to be undervalued. Conversely, tokens with more than 18 decimals produce an overvalued LP token. This discrepancy can be exploited by creating permission‑less pools that deliberately include non‑18‑decimal tokens, allowing an attacker to mint LP shares that appear to represent a larger stake than they actually do, then withdraw the underlying assets and leave other participants with fewer or no tokens. The attack may also involve a malicious ERC‑20 contract that reports a legitimate decimals() value during normal operation but returns a manipulated value when the oracle queries it, further skewing the price calculation. The issue manifests whenever the oracle’s price function is called with a token whose decimals differ from 18, which includes many stablecoins and user‑created tokens. Users experience symptoms such as receiving LP tokens that appear to have zero or negligible value, seeing their balance drop unexpectedly after joining a pool, or observing that the reported pool value does not match the sum of its constituent assets. The problem was discovered during a security audit that examined the assumptions of the price‑calculation routine and identified the hard‑coded reliance on 18‑decimal scaling. It can be hard to notice because the contract does not explicitly check token decimals, and the arithmetic still succeeds without overflow, giving a false sense of correctness. The recommended remediation is to either enforce that only tokens with 18 decimals are accepted, adding a runtime check of the decimals() value, or to adapt the fixed‑point math to use each token’s own decimal count as the scaling factor, caching the value securely in an adapter to prevent manipulation. By aligning the scaling factor with the actual token precision, the oracle will produce accurate valuations and eliminate the avenue for undervaluation or overvaluation attacks.
summary:
Situation:
This calculation assumes all priced tokens have 18 decimals. This can be implicitly enforced with Zero tokens which can be deployed at 18 decimals every time. However, target tokens exist that are not 18 decimals, such as USDC (6 decimals) or any user-created ERC-20 could set decimals to uint8 bounds.
If a target token lower than 18 decimals is passed, this would yield the calculation to return an undervaluing of the LP tokens. If the target token was greater than 18 decimals, it could yield an overvalue.
Both of these could lead to attacks. According to the documentation, the creation of Zeroes and Fuse pools is intended to become permissionless. This means that users could build malicious pools that purposely undervalue or overvalue to steal the tokens of other users that join it.

title: Intra-Transaction Oracle Tampering Possible With LP Pricing Using Flashloans
content: The vulnerability is an intra‑transaction oracle manipulation that arises when a contract derives token prices directly from the current balances of a liquidity pool and uses those instantaneous values inside the same transaction for critical calculations such as collateral valuation, liquidation thresholds or token swaps. The root cause is the reliance on a price source that reflects the pool state at a single point in time without any time‑weighted averaging, liquidity safeguards, or cross‑checking against independent feeds. Because the pool balances can be altered arbitrarily by a flash‑loan borrower within the same block, an attacker can borrow a large amount of one token, inject it into the pool, and thereby inflate or deflate the apparent price that the oracle reads. The manipulated price is then used by the protocol to, for example, compute how many tokens can be withdrawn or liquidated, allowing the attacker to drain the remaining assets from the contract. This attack can be executed entirely within one transaction, so the price appears correct before and after the transaction, making the mis‑behaviour hard to notice from external monitoring. The impact includes loss of user funds, depletion of the protocol’s reserves, and a breach of the accounting assumptions that the protocol’s business logic relies on, such as “the price reflects a fair market value”. The condition for exploitation is a pool that has low or insufficient liquidity, an oracle that is enabled on that pool, and the absence of a time‑weighted average price (TWAP) or multi‑source verification. Any user, liquidity provider, or token holder interacting with the affected contract may suffer loss, and the protocol itself may become untrustworthy. The issue was discovered during a security audit that compared the oracle implementation against known attack patterns on similar systems such as Fuse and Compound adapters, where prior flash‑loan attacks have caused millions of dollars of loss. The bug is subtle because the price deviation exists only for the duration of the attacker’s transaction; after the flash loan is repaid, the pool balances revert, and the oracle returns to normal, leaving no persistent on‑chain evidence of the manipulation. To remediate, the contract should avoid using instantaneous pool balances as a price source; instead it should employ a time‑weighted average over multiple blocks, enforce a minimum liquidity threshold before enabling the pool as an oracle, and require consensus among several independent on‑chain price feeds with acceptable error margins. These measures raise the cost and time required for an attacker, forcing the manipulation to span multiple blocks where arbitrageurs can correct the price, thereby protecting user funds and preserving protocol integrity.
summary:
Situation:
This utilizes the current balances of the respective tokens within the LP. As these are current balances, they are trivial to manipulate via a flash loan.
By setting arbitrary pool values only true for a certain point of the transaction, an attacker could potentially tamper with the price.
An attacker could also exploit this to create a skewed price of one of the tokens in the fuse pool and then drain the contract of the rest. Recent similar attacks have been done in the wild on Fuse. This resulted from weak Oracles, even in the case of ones with TWAP.
The associated Zero price should have a TWAP backing it according to the current commit hash, when it is completed and working. However, if the oracle is enabled on a pool without sufficiently safe liquidity, it may too be vulnerable to flash loan attacks, even with the TWAP.
The target price, which will be the other token used in the calculation, may also be manipulable.
This token also does not appear to be a TWAP based on the 2 current adapter implementations. Therefore, it is even more trivial to manipulate, even with sufficient liquidity. This is true except in the case that a constant pricing is used, i.e. for CETH.
Compound-based adapters will likely use their built-in Oracle pricing. Prior implementations have been exploited in the past, even with stablecoins such as DAI leading to millions in losses.

title: Avoid External Calls To Transient Or Unverified External Contracts
content: The vulnerability consists of an external call made by the contract’s _deployMarket function to a Comptroller contract that is itself a proxy (FuseAdminProxy). The proxy’s implementation contract is not verified on Etherscan and can be replaced at any time by the proxy admin. Because the implementation source code is missing, the logic that governs the deployment and control of Fuse pool tokens is opaque. This creates a classic upgradeable‑proxy risk: the contract places a high degree of trust in an external, transient contract whose behavior can be altered maliciously after the initial deployment. An attacker who gains control of the proxy admin, or a malicious upgrade performed by a trusted party, could change the implementation to execute arbitrary code, steal tokens, block withdrawals, or otherwise break the accounting assumptions of the protocol. The exploit would be triggered when the _deployMarket function invokes setComptroller, which forwards the call to the proxy; at that moment the proxy forwards the call to whatever implementation is currently set. If the implementation has been swapped for a malicious version, the call may redirect funds, modify internal state, or disable expected functionality. The impact is that users of the protocol may see their deposited assets disappear, receive zero refunds, or be unable to interact with the newly created market. The issue manifests only under the condition that the proxy’s implementation is upgraded to a harmful contract; otherwise the system may appear to work correctly, making the problem hard to detect during normal testing. The audit discovered the problem by inspecting the call flow and noticing that the Comptroller address points to an upgradeable proxy whose implementation is unverified and transient. Because the proxy can be changed without any on‑chain verification, the risk is subtle and may only become apparent after a malicious upgrade has been performed. To remediate, the code should restrict interactions to contracts with publicly verified source code, avoid reliance on upgradeable proxies for critical logic, or at minimum enforce a governance mechanism that requires user opt‑in or multi‑sig approval before any implementation change. In summary, the bug belongs to the class of “untrusted external contract call via upgradeable proxy” and violates the protocol’s expectation that token accounting and market deployment remain immutable and trustworthy.
summary:
Situation:
External calls take place via the _deployMarket function through the set Comptroller. Rari Capital’s on-chain Ethereum mainnet Comptroller calls out to a contract called FuseAdminProxy. This contract’s implementation can be transient and it’s underlying implementation source code is missing as well as unverified on Etherscan. It handles the deployment and potential control of fuse pool derived tokens.
Interacting with transient, unverified contracts on-chain can be quite dangerous, as its underlying logic could turn malicious at some point. Due to the difficulty in verifying states or effects, interacting with unverified/missing contracts could lead to some malicious contract interactions.
Below are the listed on-chain contracts as reference points with links to their respective Etherscan page.
• FuseAdmin proxy contracts (AdminUpgradabilityProxy.sol) on Etherscan
• Unverified Implementation used by proxy on Etherscan
• Unitroller is directly called here, which is an upgradeable proxy contract on Etherscan
Currently, the above point to the following Comptroller implementation on Etherscan.

title: The Variable maxscale Is Not Saved
content: The vulnerability is a state‑persistence bug in the internal _collect function of the Divider contract. The function reads a Series struct from storage into a local memory variable called _series, updates the maxscale field of that memory copy, and then uses the updated value to write a per‑user scale entry (lscales). However, because _series resides in memory, the modified maxscale is never written back to the persistent storage slot series[adapter][maturity]. As a result, the contract does not remember the highest scale that has ever been observed for a given series. The root cause is the misuse of a memory reference where a storage reference is required, combined with the omission of an explicit write‑back for the updated field. An attacker or any user can exploit this by triggering a collection with a larger cscale value; the contract will temporarily record the larger maxscale for that transaction, but the value will be lost after the function returns. Subsequent collections will therefore operate with an outdated maxscale, causing the scaling calculation to be performed with a lower factor than intended. This mis‑calculation can lead to users receiving less than their entitled amount, or conversely, the protocol may credit more than it should, breaking the accounting invariants of the system. The impact is high because the bug affects the core accounting logic of the protocol, potentially resulting in systematic under‑payment of users, loss of trust, and financial loss if the protocol’s token economics rely on accurate scaling. The condition under which the bug manifests is any call to _collect where the current scale (cscale) exceeds the previously stored maxscale; the temporary update is applied but never persisted. All participants that rely on correct scaling – token holders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined storage handling patterns and identified that the Series struct was declared as memory instead of storage, and that no explicit assignment back to the storage mapping was performed. The bug is subtle because the function appears to update maxscale correctly, and the per‑user mapping receives the new value, giving the impression that the state is consistent, while the global maxscale remains stale. To fix the issue, the Series variable should be declared as a storage pointer so that any field modifications are automatically persisted, or an explicit assignment such as series[adapter][maturity].maxscale = _series.maxscale should be added at the end of the function to ensure the updated maxscale is saved. This correction restores the intended invariant that the contract always tracks the highest observed scale, preventing accounting errors and protecting user funds.

title: Check zeroParams and lpTokenParams Is Not Empty
content: The contract contains a missing validation bug in the public function addSeries. Unlike addTarget, which explicitly checks that the targetParams structure has been populated before it is used, addSeries does not verify that the zeroParams and lpTokenParams structures have been initialized via setParams. Both structures hold critical configuration values such as irModel and collateralFactor that are later encoded and passed to the Comptroller’s internal _deployMarket routine. Because addSeries can be called by any address, an attacker can invoke it before the contract owner has set these parameters, causing the encoded data to contain default zero values (e.g., irModel == address(0)). The Comptroller may either reject the deployment, revert, or create a market with an invalid interest rate model, effectively rendering the market unusable. This results in a griefing or denial‑of‑service condition: legitimate users attempting to interact with the newly created series will encounter missing or broken markets, see no balances, or receive error messages when trying to deposit or withdraw. The impact is high because the protocol’s accounting assumptions rely on each market having a valid irModel; a market with a zero address breaks interest calculations and can lock funds or prevent future deposits. The vulnerability was discovered during a manual audit that compared the validation logic of addTarget and addSeries and noticed the asymmetry. It is subtle because the code paths look similar and the missing checks are not obvious without a side‑by‑side review. To remediate, the addSeries implementation should include explicit require statements that verify zeroParams.irModel and lpTokenParams.irModel (and any other essential fields) are non‑zero before they are encoded and passed to the Comptroller. This restores the invariant that every deployed market is configured with a valid interest‑rate model, preventing griefing attacks and preserving protocol integrity.

title: Use safeMath for Space contract
content: The vulnerability is an unchecked arithmetic flaw in the onJoinPool function of the Space contract, which inherits logic from Balancer and is compiled with Solidity 0.7.x. Because Solidity 0.7.x does not automatically revert on overflow or underflow, the contract performs addition, subtraction, multiplication and division operations without any safety checks. The root cause is the absence of a library such as OpenZeppelin SafeMath or Balancer Math that would enforce bounds on numeric calculations. An attacker can trigger onJoinPool with crafted input values that cause the internal token‑minting calculation to overflow, resulting in the contract minting an unexpectedly large amount of tokens. This can be exploited by submitting a join request that pushes the total supply variable past its maximum representable value, causing the arithmetic to wrap around to a low number and then continue minting, effectively allowing the attacker to create tokens out of thin air. The impact is severe: token holders see their balances diluted, the economic model of the pool is broken, and the protocol may lose trust because the token supply can be arbitrarily inflated. The condition for exploitation is any call to onJoinPool where the supplied token amounts or the resulting internal calculations exceed the 256‑bit limit, which is possible because the function does not validate the size of the inputs. All participants in the pool, including regular users and liquidity providers, are affected because the inflated supply can devalue their holdings and disrupt reward distribution. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that highlighted the high‑risk nature of the minting path and the lack of protective arithmetic. It is hard to notice because the contract will not revert; instead, the numbers silently wrap, making the bug invisible in normal operation unless extreme values are tested. To remediate, the contract should replace every raw arithmetic operation in the minting and accounting logic with calls to a vetted SafeMath implementation that checks for overflow and underflow, thereby ensuring that any attempt to exceed the numeric limits will cause a transaction revert. This aligns the contract with standard best practices for arithmetic safety in Solidity 0.7.x and restores confidence that token supply cannot be manipulated through arithmetic bugs.
summary:
Situation:
onJoinPool() is high risk, as it could mint a large amount of tokens and other locations in Space.sol.
The safe contract builds on Balancer contracts and thus uses solidity 0.7.x.
However, the math operations in solidity 0.7.x can underflow and overflow. The safe contract doesn’t have sufficient protection against this.

title: Wrong Amount in sponsorSeries
content: The vulnerability resides in the sponsorSeries function of the contract. The function transfers a sponsor's stake token into the contract using safeTransferFrom with an amount that is first converted to the token's base units by applying the token's decimal count. Immediately afterwards the same token is approved for the Divider contract using safeApprove, but the approval amount is the raw stakeSize value without applying the same decimal conversion. When the stake token does not use the standard 18 decimals, the two amounts diverge: for a token with fewer decimals the approved amount is larger than the transferred amount, and for a token with more decimals the approved amount is smaller. This mismatch can be exploited because the Divider contract is allowed to pull the approved amount from the contract. An attacker controlling the Divider could withdraw more tokens than were actually transferred, effectively stealing funds, or could cause legitimate withdrawals to fail, leaving sponsor funds locked. The issue appears only when the stake token's decimals differ from 18, which is common for stablecoins such as USDC (6 decimals) or other assets. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that compared the two code paths and noticed the inconsistent handling of token decimals. It is subtle because most ERC20 tokens use 18‑decimal tokens, so typical unit tests that only cover 18‑decimal tokens would not reveal the problem. To remediate, the contract should apply the same decimal conversion to both the transfer and the approval, or store the converted amount in a variable and reuse it, and unit tests should be added for tokens with non‑standard decimal counts. The impact is that sponsors may see their balances reduced unexpectedly, refunds may be missing, or the protocol may lose accounting integrity, violating the expectation that the amount transferred equals the amount approved for withdrawal.

title: Return value missing in wrapUnderlying() WstETHAdapter
content: The vulnerability is a missing return value in the wrapUnderlying function of the WstETHAdapter contract. The function is declared to return a uint256 amount of wrapped tokens, but it never executes a return statement, so the EVM implicitly returns 0. The Periphery contract calls wrapUnderlying and stores the result in a variable that is later used to add liquidity. Because the returned value is always 0, the Periphery believes that no wrapped tokens were received and proceeds to add zero liquidity, even though the adapter has actually transferred wstETH to the caller. This mismatch breaks the accounting logic of the protocol: users see a successful transaction and receive the wrapped token, but the protocol records a zero balance for the added liquidity, leading to missing or incorrect pool shares, potential loss of rewards, and confusion in UI displays where a user expects a positive liquidity amount but sees none. The root cause is a simple implementation oversight: the adapter follows the same interface as other adapters (such as CAdapter) but omits the return statement that CAdapter includes. The issue is triggered whenever Periphery interacts with WstETHAdapter, i.e., any call to addLiquidityFromUnderlying that relies on wrapUnderlying’s output. All participants who provide underlying assets through this path—regular users, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself—are affected because the protocol’s state diverges from reality. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared adapter implementations and noticed that the WstETHAdapter version did not return the transferred amount. It can be hard to notice because the transaction does not revert, the token transfer succeeds, and no explicit error is emitted; only the downstream zero‑value liquidity addition reveals the inconsistency. To remediate, the wrapUnderlying function should explicitly return the amount of wstETH transferred (return wstETH) so that Periphery receives the correct value and updates its accounting accordingly. Adding unit tests that verify the return value for each adapter would prevent similar regressions. This class of bug is an interface contract mismatch where a function’s declared return type is not honored, leading to silent logical errors in downstream callers.

title: Send Reward And Stake Once
content: The vulnerability is an improper accounting flaw that allows the reward and stake associated with a series to be transferred more than once. The contract contains two functions that can move these assets: settleSeries and backfillScale. settleSeries includes a guard (_canBeSettled) that ensures it can only be executed a single time for a given series, but backfillScale lacks any comparable protection. Because backfillScale does not record whether the reward and stake have already been sent, an attacker who can invoke backfillScale repeatedly can trigger ERC20.safeTransferFrom calls each time, draining the adapter’s token balance and the protocol’s stake pool. The root cause is the missing state flag or clearing of the reward amount after the first successful transfer, which makes the function non‑idempotent. Exploitation consists of calling backfillScale in a loop or from multiple trusted contracts, each call causing another transfer of the full reward amount and the full stake size to the attacker‑controlled destination addresses. The impact is a loss of funds that were intended to be paid out only once, breaking the protocol’s accounting assumptions, potentially emptying the reward pool and reducing the stake backing the series. This condition occurs whenever backfillScale is invoked after a series has been settled, because the function does not check the settlement status. The affected parties include the protocol’s token holders, any users expecting a single reward, and the overall economic security of the series. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that compared the control flow of settleSeries and backfillScale and noticed the absence of a re‑entrancy‑style guard in the latter. It can be hard to notice because each transfer appears legitimate and emits the standard ERC20 Transfer event, so observers may not see that the same amount is being sent repeatedly unless they audit the state changes. The recommended remediation is to make backfillScale idempotent by setting a boolean flag (e.g., rewardSent) after the first transfer, clearing the stored reward amount, or otherwise ensuring that subsequent calls skip the transfer logic. This aligns the function with the intended business rule that a reward and its associated stake are distributed only once, preserving the protocol’s accounting integrity and preventing fund leakage.

title: Many 0x transformations ignore outputToken, returning unaccounted for tokens to account and risking liquidations
content: The vulnerability originates from the way Sentiment’s TransformController interacts with the 0x transformERC20 function. The controller assumes that the only token that will be returned after a series of transformations is the explicit outputToken supplied to the call, and it validates the result solely by checking that the caller’s balance of that token has increased by at least minOutputTokenAmount. In reality, many 0x transformers (for example PositiveSlippageFeeTransformer, PayTakerTransformer and AffiliateFeeTransformer) are written without any awareness of the inputToken or outputToken parameters. Instead of sending any acquired assets back to the temporary state.wallet contract, they forward tokens directly to the original caller (msg.sender). Consequently, when such a transformer is included in the transformations array, tokens other than the declared outputToken can be transferred to the user’s address, while the state.wallet never receives them. The controller’s post‑call accounting therefore records zero tokensIn and zero tokensOut, because it only inspects the balance change of the expected outputToken. This mismatch means that a user may actually receive a token (e.g., WETH) that is not reflected in the protocol’s accounting, leading to an understated collateral balance. Under normal operation the user expects to receive only the outputToken; instead they see an unexpected token appear in their wallet, yet the protocol still believes their balance is lower than it truly is. When the risk engine later evaluates the user’s position, it may trigger a liquidation despite the hidden token that could have prevented it. The issue is most likely to be triggered when the caller sets minOutputTokenAmount to zero or a very low value, or when the transformation list includes any of the aforementioned fee‑or‑slippage transformers that send assets directly to the caller. The bug was uncovered during a security audit by constructing a test that calls transformERC20 with a PayTakerTransformer that returns WETH; the controller reported no output tokens while the wallet’s WETH balance increased. The problem is subtle because the expected outputToken balance does change as required, so a superficial check passes, and the extra token may be overlooked in UI displays that only show the primary asset. This class of flaw can be described as improper accounting of external token transfers or unchecked return values in composable DeFi pipelines. To remediate, the controller should either restrict the set of allowed transformers to those that reliably route all assets through the state.wallet, or it must decode each transformer’s calldata and explicitly verify that any token transferred out is captured and recorded in the tokenIn/tokenOut arrays. In addition, the post‑call validation should be extended to ensure that the total value of all tokens received meets the intended minimum, not just the balance of a single outputToken. Implementing these safeguards will prevent hidden token flows, preserve accurate collateral accounting, and eliminate the risk of unfair liquidations.
summary:
When we call `transformERC20()` on the 0x contract, the following inputs are included as arguments:
```solidity
function transformERC20(
    address inputToken,
    address outputToken,
    uint256 inputTokenAmount,
    uint256 minOutputTokenAmount,
    Transformation[] calldata transformations
) external payable returns (uint256 outputTokenAmount);
```
`TransformController.sol` assumes that `outputToken` will be the only token returned.

However, if we look at the implementation of the function on 0x, we see the following flow:
all tokens are transferred into the `state.wallet` contract
we execute all the transformations based on our specified parameters
after the transformations, if the `state.wallet` has any of our output token, it is transferred back to us
we ensure that our balance of `outputToken` has increased by at least `minOutputTokenAmount`

If we look at the specific transformer implementations, we can see that they take their data from the `transformations` params and do not have visibility into the `inputToken` or `outputToken`. In addition, many of them transfer the assets directly back to the caller, rather than to the `state.wallet` contract.

As a few examples:
[PositiveSlippageFeeTransformer.sol](https://github.com/0xProject/protocol/blob/198d986fdc8c65eb7de718dbc277c097cd7a53b7/contracts/zero-ex/contracts/src/transformers/PositiveSlippageFeeTransformer.sol) allows you to send a token, an amount and a recipient, and it will send any balance it holds over the amount to that recipient.
[PayTakerTransformer.sol](https://github.com/0xProject/protocol/blob/198d986fdc8c65eb7de718dbc277c097cd7a53b7/contracts/zero-ex/contracts/src/transformers/PayTakerTransformer.sol) allows you to specify a list of tokens and amounts, and it will send that amount of each token to the `msg.sender` of the original call.
[AffiliateFeeTransformer.sol](https://github.com/0xProject/protocol/blob/198d986fdc8c65eb7de718dbc277c097cd7a53b7/contracts/zero-ex/contracts/src/transformers/AffiliateFeeTransformer.sol) takes a list of tokens, amounts and recipients and sends the specified amount of each token to the matching recipient.

In each of these cases, there will be no assets sent back to the `state.wallet` contract.

However, the `transformERC20()` function still checks that our balance of the `outputToken` has increased by at least `minOutputTokenAmount`. However, it is highly possible that other transformations will have caused this increase, or that a user will input `0` for this parameter since it often doesn't matter.
