Because the fee manager later checks only the amount that is returned from the route against the service charge and relayer refund, the attacker can return a deliberately small amount of token, satisfying the condition that the returned amount is greater than serviceCharge + relayerRefund. Consequently, the protocol’s fee calculation is bypassed and the attacker receives the original assets without paying the intended fees. This flaw can be exploited whenever a user invokes exchange with a custom route, which is allowed by design, and the attacker controls at least one element of that route. The impact is a loss of revenue for the protocol and its relayers, as well as a potential erosion of trust because users may observe that fees are not being collected as advertised. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the logic of calculateFee and noted the absence of address validation for pool or zap entries. It is subtle because the route abstraction hides the fact that arbitrary contracts can be called, and the fee check appears to succeed, making the problem easy to miss in functional testing. To remediate, the contract should enforce fee deduction at the point where assetIn is released rather than after the route execution, and it should validate that each pool or zap identifier corresponds to a known, trusted contract, ensuring that the fee manager cannot be tricked by a malicious swap contract. In essence, this is a classic unchecked external call leading to fee‑bypass, a class of bug where business logic assumes honest participants in a composable call chain but fails to enforce that assumption.
summary: CurveMultiExchangeAssetManager::exchange() allows sending any route, which is of type Array of [initial token, pool or zap, token, pool or zap, token, ...]. The pool or zap chosen indexes are not validated, which means any contract can be specified. Thus, users can create a contract with the same interface as pool or zap and receive the amountIn there. Then, only send back a very small amount of token out to bypass the fee manager check in calculateFee() of the amount being bigger than serviceCharge + relayerRefund. The service fees will be very small and the user will get the funds right away. The poc for issue #13 contains an example of a malicious swap contract.

title: Anyone can deposit to DarkpoolAssetManager as the owner can be freely chosen without any implication
content: The vulnerability resides in the deposit functions of the asset manager contract, specifically depositETH() and depositERC20(). Both functions accept an address parameter that designates the owner of the deposited funds, but they do not enforce any relationship between this owner argument and the caller (msg.sender). As a result, any external account can invoke the functions and arbitrarily assign the deposit to any address while the caller still supplies the value and receives the corresponding receipt token. The root cause is the missing access‑control check or signature verification for the supplied owner field, allowing the owner to be freely chosen. An attacker can exploit this by calling the deposit function with a victim’s address as the owner, thereby crediting the victim’s internal balance while the attacker retains the external token or receipt. Later, if the protocol permits withdrawals based solely on the internal balance mapping, the attacker may be able to trigger a withdrawal on behalf of the victim or cause double‑spending by moving the same funds through multiple owner entries. The impact includes mis‑attribution of assets, potential loss of funds for honest users, corrupted accounting, and a breach of the protocol’s financial integrity. The condition under which the bug manifests is any execution of the deposit functions; there is no conditional guard that restricts the owner argument. All participants of the pool—depositors, token holders, and the protocol itself—are affected because the internal ledger can be polluted with false ownership records. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit performed by ThreeSigma, which flagged the owner parameter as unchecked. It can be hard to notice because the transaction appears to succeed, the UI may display the deposited amount for the chosen owner, and the contract does not emit an explicit warning about the mismatch between sender and owner. To remediate, the contract should either set the owner implicitly to msg.sender or require a cryptographic signature from the declared owner that proves consent, thereby binding the deposit to a verified party. This change restores the intended invariant that only the depositor can credit their own balance, preserving correct accounting and preventing unauthorized fund attribution.
summary: DarkpoolAssetManager::depositETH() and DarkpoolAssetManager::depositERC20() allow choosing any owner, while the msg.sender still receives the deposit.

title: Attackers can include other users nullifiers to make their funds stuck when adding liquidity to curve
content: An attacker can cause other users' funds to become permanently locked when they add liquidity through the CurveLiquidityAssetManager contract. The function curveAddLiquidity always consumes the supplied nullifiers regardless of the amount being added. In the zero‑amount branch the circuit skips the verification that each nullifier is signed by the owner, so an attacker can embed nullifiers belonging to unrelated users in a single transaction. When the transaction is executed the contract treats those nullifiers as spent, but because no signature was checked the protocol does not credit the corresponding balances, effectively removing the users' ability to withdraw the locked assets. This flaw occurs only when the liquidity amount parameter is zero; otherwise the normal signature check prevents misuse. The vulnerability was discovered during a manual audit of the asset manager’s add‑liquidity flow, where the post‑withdraw step was observed to run unconditionally. It is easy to miss because the zero‑amount path is rarely exercised in normal operation and the contract does not emit explicit error messages when nullifiers are consumed without a matching signature. The impact is that any user whose nullifier is injected can see their balance become zero and be unable to retrieve the funds, leading to a loss of value and breaking the accounting guarantees of the protocol. The affected parties are liquidity providers and any participant relying on the contract to safeguard their deposits. To remediate, the add‑liquidity implementation should bypass the post‑withdraw (nullifier‑spending) logic when the amount is zero, ensuring that nullifiers are only marked as spent after a successful signature verification. This class of bug is an authorization bypass combined with improper handling of no‑op inputs, where a security check is omitted for a special case, allowing malicious inclusion of other users' identifiers. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a successful liquidity addition while the user’s balance unexpectedly drops to zero or the expected refund never arrives, contradicting the expectation that adding zero liquidity should have no effect. The failure mode violates the protocol’s accounting assumptions that each nullifier corresponds to a unique, authorized deposit, and it enables an attacker to lock away funds without any visible on‑chain error.
summary: CurveLiquidityAssetManager::curveAddLiquidity() always spends the nullifiers, even if the amounts used are 0. In the circuit, if the amount is 0, it does not validate the nullifier against the user signature, making it possible to include nullifiers from other users in the same transaction and losing their funds forever. Here is the poc.

title: _addLiquidity() slippage is incorrectly set
content: The vulnerability resides in the liquidity‑addition routine where the contract attempts to protect users against price slippage but does so using a flawed calculation. The function computes the amount of pool tokens (mintAmount) by calling the pool’s price‑calculation routine after the user‑supplied token amounts have already been applied to the pool’s pricing curve. It then reduces this value by a hard‑coded 95 % factor (mintAmount = (mintAmount/100)*95). Because the price‑calculation is performed on the already‑manipulated state, any attacker who can influence the pool’s price immediately before the call can force the returned mintAmount to be artificially low. The hard‑coded 95 % multiplier further masks the problem by giving the illusion of a 5 % slippage buffer, while in reality the buffer is applied to a value that may already be compromised. An attacker can therefore submit a transaction that first skews the pool’s price (for example by a large swap) and then triggers the add‑liquidity function, causing the contract to mint far fewer pool tokens than the liquidity provider expects. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a successful liquidity addition, but the received LP token balance is much smaller than anticipated, or in extreme cases may be zero, leading to a loss of deposited assets. The issue is discovered during a manual audit that examined the slippage logic and noticed that the minimum‑mint calculation used post‑price data and a static 95 % factor. It is hard to notice because the code appears to enforce a slippage limit, yet the limit is applied after the price has already been altered, so the protection is ineffective. The bug belongs to the class of “incorrect slippage enforcement” or “post‑price manipulation mint amount calculation”. To remediate, the contract should accept a user‑provided minimum mint amount (or a maximum acceptable slippage) as an argument and verify that the actual mint amount meets this threshold before minting. Alternatively, the contract could obtain a trusted price reference from an off‑chain oracle such as Chainlink and compute the expected mint amount on that basis, removing the reliance on a hard‑coded percentage. By ensuring the slippage check is performed on a price that cannot be manipulated within the same transaction, the protocol restores the intended protection and prevents users from receiving fewer tokens than they paid for.
summary:
The slippage is computed as:
```solidity
mintAmount = _args.isLegacy & 12 == 12 ?
    IPools(_args.pool).calc_token_amount(curveInputAmounts)
    : IPools(_args.pool).calc_token_amount(curveInputAmounts, true);
mintAmount = (mintAmount / 100) * 95;
```
This gets the mintAmount value post price manipulation, rendering the slippage protection useless. Also, hardcoding a parameter of 95% slippage is not ideal. Here is a similar finding.

title: Anyone can frontrun a relayer interaction with the same arguments but a much higher/lower relayer fee
content: The vulnerability is a missing validation of the relayer fee parameter in the contract’s execution path, which allows any actor to submit a transaction with the same functional arguments as a legitimate user‑initiated request but with a deliberately altered relayer fee. The root cause is that the code never checks that the fee supplied in the calldata matches the fee that the user signed off‑chain, nor does it restrict the fee to be set only by the designated relayer address. Because the fee field is treated as an ordinary input, an attacker can front‑run the pending legitimate transaction, copy its payload, and replace the fee with a much lower value (stealing revenue from the relayer) or a much higher value (inflating the cost for the user). Exploitation proceeds by monitoring the mempool for a pending relayer call, broadcasting a competing transaction with identical arguments but a modified fee, and ensuring the attacker’s transaction is mined first. The impact is financial loss: the relayer may receive far less compensation than expected, while the user may be over‑charged or under‑compensated depending on the direction of the fee manipulation. This occurs whenever the contract processes a relayed operation that includes a fee argument, which is currently unchecked. All participants who rely on the fee mechanism – relayers, users, and the protocol that assumes correct accounting – are affected. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit that examined the handling of signed messages and identified that the relayer address is not enforced as msg.sender and that the fee value is not bounded or signed. Because the fee is just another integer in the calldata, the problem does not manifest as an outright revert or error, making it easy to miss during functional testing; the transaction appears successful while the economic outcome is wrong. The bug belongs to the class of “unchecked fee manipulation” or “parameter tampering” vulnerabilities, where a critical economic parameter is not cryptographically bound to the signer or the authorized actor. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a successful operation but the relayer’s balance does not increase by the expected amount, or the user’s wallet shows a higher than anticipated deduction. The expectation that the signed fee will be honored is violated, leading to a discrepancy between the promised and actual payment. To remediate, the contract should enforce that the relayer fee is either part of the signed message, that the relayer address is required to be msg.sender, and that the fee is constrained within reasonable bounds, thereby preventing arbitrary fee changes by third parties.
summary: The relayer fee used throughout the codebase is not enforced anywhere, such that it's possible to frontrun a legit transaction and set a much lower/higher relayer fee, harming the relayer/user.

title: Early self liquidations receive a portion of future fees to be paid by other creditors
content: The vulnerability is an economic misallocation that occurs during early self‑liquidations of a debt position that has multiple creditors. When a creditor detects that the total debt of a position exceeds the collateral backing it, the protocol allows that creditor to perform a self‑liquidation in order to realise the loss. The liquidation routine first checks eligibility, then charges the borrower a repay fee that is split pro‑rata among all creditors based on their share of the face value, and finally computes the amount of collateral to assign to the liquidating creditor. The flaw lies in the function that calculates the assigned collateral: it uses the raw total collateral of the debt position without subtracting the repay fees that will later be owed by other creditors. Because the repay fee is paid by the borrower but is allocated to all creditors, the first creditor that self‑liquidates receives a share of the collateral that implicitly includes the portion of fees that should belong to later creditors. In practice this means the early liquidator captures not only their rightful collateral but also a slice of future fee revenue, leaving the remaining creditors with less collateral than the protocol’s accounting assumes. The impact is a distortion of the intended loss‑sharing mechanism, potential loss of funds for later creditors, and an incentive for malicious actors to front‑run self‑liquidations to harvest extra value. The condition for exploitation is the presence of multiple creditors on an under‑collateralised position and the ability of a creditor to trigger self‑liquidation before others have acted. All creditors, borrowers (who may see higher effective fees) and the protocol’s economic integrity are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the fee distribution logic and identified that the collateral assignment routine ignored pending fees. It can be hard to notice because the function appears to allocate collateral proportionally, and simple unit tests with a single creditor do not expose the over‑allocation. The recommended remediation is to modify the collateral calculation so that the repay fee is deducted from the collateral pool before the pro‑rata split, ensuring that each creditor receives only the net collateral that remains after accounting for all fees. This aligns the implementation with the intended accounting model where fees are paid separately and not bundled into the collateral share, preventing early liquidators from unintentionally receiving future fee revenue.
summary:
Self liquidations are permitted when a creditor is at loss. Put simply, this means when the total debt of a position exceeds it's share of collateral then creditors may self liquidate to realize the loss instead of being further exposed to the borrower. The flow of self liquidation looks like the following:
• Liquidation eligibility is checked on the debt position.
• Repay fees are paid pro-rata by the borrower in proportion to the creditor's contribution of debtPosition.faceValue.
• assignedCollateral is calculated based off of creditPosition in a pro-rata fashion.
assignedCollateral utilizes the debt position's total collateral and does not consider fees that other creditors will pay when they perform their respective liquidations. In effect, the first creditor has a percentage claim on all collateral which includes unpaid fees.

title: Validation of APR in BuyMarketCredit leads to underestimation of borrower requirements
content: The vulnerability originates from an incorrect validation of the annual percentage rate (APR) in the BuyMarketCredit action. The contract currently checks only that the APR does not exceed a configured maximum (maxAPR) before allowing a lending operation. Business requirements, however, dictate that the APR must also stay above a minimum threshold (minAPR) to guarantee a reasonable return for the lender. Because the lower‑bound check is missing or incorrectly implemented, a borrower can request credit at an APR that is arbitrarily low, as long as it is below the maximum limit. This mismatch allows transactions to be approved that do not satisfy the lender’s intended yield expectations. An attacker or opportunistic borrower can exploit the flaw by submitting a loan request with a very low APR; the contract will accept it, the loan will be funded, and the lender will receive far less interest than anticipated, potentially reducing overall profitability or even resulting in a net loss if the APR is close to zero. The impact is primarily on lenders who rely on the protocol’s guarantees of a minimum return; their expected revenue is eroded, and the economic model of the market may become unsustainable. The issue manifests whenever the APR calculation for a given due date yields a value below the intended minAPR but still passes the existing maxAPR check. All participants who interact with the BuyMarketCredit function are affected, but the financial harm is borne by lenders. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that compared the contract’s code against the documented business logic and identified the missing lower‑bound validation. It can be difficult to notice because the transaction still succeeds, no explicit error is thrown, and the UI may simply display a successful loan without highlighting the unexpectedly low return, leading users to assume the loan is normal. To remediate the problem, the contract should be updated to include a check that reverts when the computed APR falls below a defined minAPR, and the error message should clearly indicate that the APR is lower than the acceptable minimum. This change aligns the implementation with the intended economic guarantees, preventing loans that would under‑compensate lenders and preserving the integrity of the protocol’s accounting assumptions.
summary:
The implementation of the BuyMarketCredit checks if the APR exceeds maxAPR to decide whether to proceed with a lending operation. However, the intention, as deduced from the business logic, seems to focus on ensuring that the APR should not fall below a certain threshold, which is beneficial for the lender in terms of returns.
The current implementation may lead to transactions that do not satisfy the lender's intended minimum yield.

title: DarkpoolAssetManager::Split() into 2 equal amounts leads to lost funds
content: The vulnerability resides in the DarkpoolAssetManager Split function which creates two output notes from a single input note. The implementation does not verify that the two resulting notes are distinct. When the split produces two notes with identical values and identifiers, the nullifier that is consumed to spend the first note is also applied to the second note. Because the nullifier is already marked as spent, the second note cannot be redeemed in any later transaction, effectively locking the assets represented by that note. This situation occurs whenever the caller requests a split that yields equal amounts, for example splitting an even amount into two halves without any additional randomness or differentiation. The root cause is a missing inequality check between the two output notes. An attacker or an unwary user can trigger the condition by selecting an amount that divides evenly, causing half of the intended funds to become inaccessible. From a user perspective the UI may show a successful split and display both notes, but attempts to withdraw or transfer the second note fail silently, leading to confusion such as my balance is lower than expected or the second half is missing. The impact is high because the affected funds are effectively lost unless the contract is upgraded or an admin manually intervenes. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the Split logic and identified the absence of a _noteOut1 != _noteOut2 requirement. The bug is subtle because the function does not revert or emit an error, so the failure is only observable when the second note is later used. The appropriate fix is to add a check that the two output notes are not equal before completing the split, ensuring each note has a unique nullifier and can be spent independently. This class of bug can be described as a nullifier collision or duplicate output vulnerability that breaks the accounting assumptions of one‑to‑one correspondence between notes and spendable rights.
summary: When using DarkpoolAssetManager::Split(), there is no check to make sure that the 2 resulting notes are not equal, making it impossible to use the second note after the first one as the nullifier will be used by then. Check the poc here.

title: MJR-1 "Sandwich attack" on user withdrawal
content: The vulnerability is a classic sandwich attack that can be triggered during a user‑initiated withdrawal when the strategy contract performs an automated market maker (AMM) token swap inside the same transaction. The root cause is that the swap is executed without any slippage protection or price verification, allowing an attacker who observes the pending withdrawal to place a trade that moves the market price just before the user’s swap (front‑run) and then reverse the trade immediately after (back‑run). By doing so the attacker inflates the price the user receives, causing the user’s withdrawal to be settled at an unfavorable rate. This can result in the user receiving less of the expected token, or in extreme cases the protocol losing value because the swap extracts value from the pool. The attack can only be carried out when the withdrawal path includes a direct AMM swap and when the attacker can monitor the mempool and act within the same block, conditions that are relatively rare but not impossible. All users who request a withdrawal are affected, as they may see their balance reduced unexpectedly, and the protocol’s overall liquidity can be eroded over time. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the flow of funds in the withdrawal function and identified the lack of slippage checks. It is hard to notice because the failure manifests only under specific market conditions and the user interface typically shows a successful transaction without indicating that the received amount is lower than expected. To remediate the problem the swap operation should be protected with a maximum slippage parameter, use a trusted price oracle, or be moved out of the user‑controlled transaction so that the price cannot be manipulated by a front‑runner. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of price‑manipulation vulnerabilities caused by unchecked AMM interactions within privileged functions, leading to a mismatch between expected and actual refund amounts and breaking the accounting assumptions of the protocol.
summary: In some rare conditions, the strategy is using AMM DEX to Strategy.sol#L348 inside of the user-handled transaction. This is vulnerable to the "sandwich attack".

title: Signatures can be replayed using different addresses
content: The vulnerability is a replayable signature flaw in the commitToMint function. The function builds a hash from collectionId, spins, a per‑sender nonce, msg.value and a minter address, then recovers a signer address from a supplied ECDSA signature. Because the hash does not contain the address that actually executes the transaction (msg.sender), the same signature can be submitted by any other account that currently holds the same nonce value. An attacker can monitor the blockchain, copy a legitimate signature that a user submitted, and call commitToMint from a different address that has a matching nonce (starting from zero and incrementing with each call). The contract will accept the signature as long as the recovered signer matches the authorized signer, and will mint a ticket for the attacker’s chosen minter. This allows unauthorized minting without the original user’s consent, potentially inflating the supply of minted assets and causing loss of revenue for the protocol. The issue appears only when the caller is not the privileged commitController; the code path that verifies the signature is executed for any external caller. Because the signature verification succeeds, the transaction does not revert, making the problem subtle and easy to miss during testing. The bug belongs to the class of “signature replay” or “missing signer binding” vulnerabilities, where a signed message is not tied to a unique context such as the sender address or a domain separator. From a user’s perspective the symptom may be that minted tickets appear to be claimed by unknown addresses, or that the protocol’s token economics are disturbed because extra tickets are created without payment. The root cause is the omission of msg.sender (or an equivalent unique identifier) from the signed payload, combined with a per‑address nonce that does not prevent cross‑address reuse. The recommended mitigation is to include the executor address in the hash, or to adopt a standard signing scheme such as EIP‑712 that incorporates the caller’s address and a domain separator, thereby ensuring that a signature is only valid for the intended sender. Fixing the issue restores the intended security property that only the address that generated the signature can use it, preventing replay attacks and preserving the integrity of the minting process.

title: Use of msg.value inside a loop
content: The vulnerability resides in the batchCommitToMint function, which iterates over an array of mint requests and calls the payable commitToMint function for each element. The commitToMint function expects the caller to provide ether via msg.value for the specific mint operation. In the batch version, the same msg.value supplied to batchCommitToMint is reused on every iteration. During the first iteration the ether is transferred successfully, but after that the contract’s balance for the call is depleted, so subsequent calls attempt to forward ether that no longer exists. This causes the internal transfer to fail and the whole transaction reverts due to insufficient funds. The bug manifests only when the batch array length is greater than one; a single call works as intended, making the issue easy to miss during code review. Users invoking batchCommitToMint expect to receive multiple minted tokens in a single transaction and to have their payment cover all items. Instead they experience a reverted transaction, no tokens are minted, and only the gas cost is lost. The impact is high because it prevents the intended batch minting feature, can lead to user frustration, and may be exploited by an attacker who forces repeated calls to drain gas or cause denial of service. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that examined the flow of payable values inside loops. It is hard to notice because the function compiles without warnings and the single‑mint path is correct; the failure only appears at runtime when the loop executes more than once. The issue belongs to the class of “reusing msg.value in a loop” or “double‑accounting of payable ether” bugs, where a contract incorrectly assumes that msg.value is replenished for each internal call. To remediate, the contract should either make commitToMint internal and handle the payment once outside the loop, pass the required ether amount explicitly to each iteration, or redesign the batch function to require the total ether equal to the sum of individual mint prices and forward the appropriate slice of value per call. By ensuring that each payable call receives its own dedicated ether amount, the contract will honor its accounting assumptions and prevent the insufficient‑funds revert.

title: order.amount not accounted when filling
content: The vulnerability consists of an accounting mismatch in the single‑order fill functions of a marketplace contract. In the functions that handle a single ask or bid order, the implementation forwards only the order.price amount of ether to the pool’s swap routine, while the order.amount field – which indicates how many tokens or NFTs are being purchased – is ignored. The code builds a one‑element amounts array containing order.amount, but the value sent to the pool is hard‑coded to order.price, assuming that order.amount will always be one. When a user or an attacker creates an order with amount greater than one, the contract still transfers only price wei, effectively underpaying for the additional units. This discrepancy can be exploited by submitting a multi‑unit order and calling fillAskOrder or fillBidOrder, receiving more assets than the ether paid. The impact is a loss of funds for the protocol and a breach of the accounting invariants that price multiplied by amount should equal the total payment. The bug manifests only when the order.amount field is not equal to one, a scenario that may be missed during testing because many examples use a single unit. The affected parties include any trader attempting to fill multi‑unit orders, the liquidity pool that loses assets, and ultimately the protocol’s users who may see their balances reduced unexpectedly. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the single‑order fill logic with the multi‑order function fulfillMultipleOrders, which correctly multiplies price by amount. The problem is subtle because the UI may still display a successful fill, and the user may not notice that they received extra tokens for less payment, or conversely that the pool’s balance is drained. To remediate, the fill functions must incorporate order.amount into the value sent to the pool (i.e., use order.price * order.amount) and ensure that any accounting events reflect the total amount paid. This aligns the single‑order path with the multi‑order logic and restores the invariant that total payment equals price per unit times quantity, preventing funds from disappearing and preserving correct accounting.

title: Large centralization attack surface
content: The vulnerability is a centralization and governance‑related attack surface in the pool contract. The contract allows a single owner of the governance module to add an arbitrary number of operator addresses. Because the epoch‑proposal function iterates over the full operator list, an attacker who controls the owner can inflate the list to a size that makes the transaction exceed the block gas limit, effectively causing a denial‑of‑service where no new epochs can be proposed. In addition, each operator is entitled to claim a fee that is calculated from the pool’s total balance. If a group of operators colludes they can submit votes and claims that drain the entire pool balance as fees. The contract also stores reward withdrawals in a Merkle tree; operators are able to insert arbitrary leaf entries, which means they can add an address that is not registered in the system and allow that address to claim rewards that never belonged to it. Finally, the owner can transfer ownership of the pool contract to an address they control and then invoke the epoch‑update function directly, which again permits the owner to withdraw the whole contract balance as a fee. The impact is that users who have deposited funds expecting to earn rewards may see their balances become zero, receive no rewards, or see the pool stop advancing epochs. From a user’s point of view the UI would show that the pool is stuck, that rewards are not being distributed, or that the total pool value suddenly drops to zero. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that examined the governance flow and the fee‑distribution logic. It is hard to notice because the functions appear to work correctly when a small number of operators are present, and the fee‑withdrawal logic is not obviously malicious when executed by a legitimate operator. The root cause is the lack of any constraints on the number of operators, the unrestricted ability of operators to manipulate the Merkle‑tree of withdrawals, and the fact that ownership of the pool can be transferred without any timelock or multi‑signature protection. To remediate the problem the governance contract should be owned by a multi‑signature wallet behind a timelock, a hard cap on the number of operators should be enforced (for example fifty), and additional checks should be added to prevent operators from adding arbitrary reward recipients or from claiming more than their proportional share. In summary, the bug belongs to the class of centralization‑induced governance and accounting flaws that allow a privileged party to cause a denial‑of‑service, to siphon funds, and to bypass reward eligibility checks.
summary:
1. The owner of PoolGovernance can add a big number of operators, resulting in a block gas limit DoS of proposeEpoch, because the method loops over all operators
2. Operators can group their voting and claim all of SmoothlyPool's balance as a fee
3. Operators can allow an unregistered account to claim rewards from SmoothlyPool by adding it to one of the withdrawals Merkle tree leafs
4. The owner of PoolGovernance can transfer ownership of SmoothlyPool to an account he controls and directly call updateEpoch, withdrawing the whole contract balance as the fee

title: Unsound assumption about structure of calldata arrays
content: The vulnerability originates from an unsound assumption about the layout of calldata arrays when they are accessed inside inline assembly. In Solidity, a calldata array is represented as a struct with two fields: an offset pointing to the first element of the array and a length indicating how many elements are present. The ABI encoding places the length word immediately before the first element, so a naïve copy that starts 32 bytes before the reported offset will capture the length word followed by the array data. This works for external functions that receive a direct calldata array, but it fails when the function receives a slice of an array or a manually constructed calldata pointer. A slice is created by taking a sub‑range of an existing array, which results in a new calldata pointer whose offset points somewhere inside the original data while its length reflects only the slice size. Similarly, inline‑assembly can craft arbitrary calldata pointers with mismatched offset and length. When code such as `calldatacopy(add(m, 0xc0), sub(data.offset, 0x20), add(0x20, data.length))` is used under these conditions, the copy operation reads the word preceding the slice as if it were the array length. Because that word does not contain the true length, the copied data may be truncated, padded with unrelated bytes, or otherwise corrupted. An attacker can exploit this by supplying a sliced calldata argument to a function that performs the bulk copy, causing downstream logic that expects a correctly encoded array to operate on malformed data. The impact includes incorrect processing of user‑provided data, potential loss of funds if the corrupted array is used for token transfers, refunds, or permission checks, and a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees. The bug manifests whenever a non‑external function or a function that accepts a sliced calldata array invokes the bulk copy optimisation. Users, developers, and auditors are affected because the contract may silently accept malformed inputs and produce unexpected results, such as zero refunds or truncated payloads. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that examined the assembly‑based calldata handling and identified that the code relied on the offset‑length invariant without verifying that the pointer referenced the start of the original array. The problem is subtle because the contract compiles without warnings and the behaviour appears correct for typical external calls, making it easy to miss during testing. The recommended mitigation is to avoid the one‑shot copy that assumes the length word is located directly before the data. Instead, the implementation should write the length field explicitly to memory and then copy only the actual data bytes, or use higher‑level Solidity constructs that handle calldata safely. Additionally, tests should include cases where calldata pointers are created via slicing or manual assembly to ensure the code behaves correctly under those conditions. This class of bug falls under the broader category of unsafe calldata manipulation and incorrect assumptions about ABI encoding layout, which can lead to data corruption and financial loss.
summary:
When accessing calldata arrays in inline assembly (e.g. myArray) it's essentially a struct with 2 fields myArray.offset and myArray.length. The .offset property gives you the direct calldata offset of the first value in the array while the .length gives you the length of the array. When ABI encoding an array it's encoded as enc(array_len) ++ enc(tuple(array[0], array[1], ...)) meaning that in this case the offset given by the calldata pointer, points to the word right after the array's length. This opens the path to some clever optimizations in the case where you need to re-encode an array in memory from calldata. e.g. in Solady's Lifebuoy.sol:
```solidity
// Copies the length and actual data of the `bytes calldata` into memory by starting the copy 32 bytes before the offset
calldatacopy(add(m, 0xc0), sub(data.offset, 0x20), add(0x20, data.length))
```
However the critical flaw in this assumption is that unless these methods are marked external you cannot guarantee that they have this structure. The two major exceptions are:
- Slices: When you take the slice of an array via myArray[start:end] it creates a new calldata pointer where .length = end - start and .offset = myArray.offset + start * itemSizeBytes.
- Manually created calldata objects: Using inline-assembly you can manually manipulate calldata pointer and assign arbitrary offsets & lengths.
In both cases you can reasonably create calldata pointers that no longer point to the beginning byte of the original array and can only reliably retrieve their length via the .length property. In such cases the referenced code sections would incorrectly copy the word preceding the slice as the the length for the encoded array. This could lead to truncation or extension of the array with other bytes causing downstream code to receive incorrect and potentially tampered data.

title: Incorrect placement of ERC7579 modeSelector
content: The vulnerability originates from an incorrect layout of the 32‑byte mode field defined by the ERC7579 standard. According to the specification, the mode field must be composed of a 1‑byte callType, a 1‑byte execType, four reserved bytes (unused), a 4‑byte modeSelector, and a 22‑byte modePayload, in that exact order. The library implementation (LibERC7579) violates this ordering by writing the modeSelector directly after the execType and before the reserved bytes, and by extracting the selector with a left‑shift of only 16 bits instead of the required 48 bits. This mismatch causes any contract that relies on the library to encode or decode the mode incorrectly: the selector bits are interpreted as part of the reserved region, and the actual selector is shifted out of its intended position. As a result, when a caller supplies a specific execution mode—such as a delegatecall that should not revert on failure—the contract will read a different modeSelector, causing it to perform a staticcall, a batch call, or an unintended error‑handling path. From a user’s perspective the transaction may appear to succeed while the expected behavior (for example, a state‑changing delegatecall or a refund) does not occur, leading to missing balances, zero‑value returns, or funds that seem to disappear. The bug is triggered whenever the encodeMode or getSelector functions are used, which is typical for any ERC7579‑compatible contract that employs LibERC7579 for mode handling. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that compared the library’s assembly layout against the ERC7579 reference specification; the discrepancy is subtle because the byte‑wise operations succeed without reverting, making the problem hard to detect through ordinary testing. The root cause is a simple ordering mistake in the assembly code and an incorrect bit‑shift constant. To remediate the problem the encoding routine must write four zero bytes after execType before storing the selector, and the selector extraction must shift the 32‑byte word left by 48 bits (instead of 16) before truncating to four bytes. Correcting the layout restores compliance with the ERC7579 mode definition, ensuring that contracts execute with the intended call type and error‑handling semantics, and prevents the silent mis‑execution that can lead to loss of funds or broken business logic.

title: Changing _initializableSlot() can cause _disableInitializers() to actually enable initializers
content: The vulnerability is an initializer bypass caused by overriding the internal _initializableSlot function in contracts that inherit Initializable. The library expects the storage slot used for the initialization version and flag to have its most significant 8 bytes set to 0xffffffffffffffff. _disableInitializers reads those upper bytes to compute the maximum uint64 value (2**64‑1) and writes it to the version field, thereby preventing any future calls to initializer functions. When a developer overrides _initializableSlot to return a custom constant that does not contain the required 0xffff… pattern, the calculation of the maximum version becomes incorrect; the function ends up writing a zero version instead of the maximum. As a result, the call to _disableInitializers in the implementation contract’s constructor does not lock the contract but effectively re‑enables initializers. An attacker can exploit this by deploying an implementation that overrides the slot, allowing the initializer to be called on the implementation contract itself. Because the implementation is often used as the logic target for proxy contracts, the attacker can then initialize the proxy, set themselves as owner, or execute privileged functions, leading to loss of control and potentially loss of funds. The issue appears only when the slot is overridden, which is uncommon and therefore easy to miss during testing; the default slot works correctly, so the bug is hidden unless a custom slot is used. The problem violates the fundamental assumption that the initialization version storage layout is immutable, breaking the contract’s upgrade‑ability safety guarantees. To fix the issue the library should not rely on a fixed upper‑byte pattern; _disableInitializers should compute the maximum version in a way that works for any slot, or the contract should enforce that overrides preserve the required pattern. In practice this means adding a check on the returned slot or redesigning the initializer guard so that it does not depend on hard‑coded slot bits. From a user perspective the contract that is supposed to be locked may still accept an initialize call, resulting in unexpected ownership changes or missing refunds, i.e., “the contract should be frozen but I can still call initialize and become owner”. This class of bug is a storage‑slot misalignment leading to initializer bypass.

title: Rounding issue in price formula
content: The vulnerability is a precision loss and rounding error in the on‑chain price calculation formula. The contract computes a price using three terms that involve integer division on 1e18‑scaled values. Because Solidity performs integer division that truncates toward zero, the first term (totalSupply * curveFactor) / (totalSupply - x) is rounded down when both numerator and denominator are already expressed with 18‑decimal precision. The second term is mathematically equivalent to curveFactor, yet the implementation still performs a division that discards the fractional part, wasting gas and adding unnecessary rounding. The third term, initialPriceFactor / 1000 * x, suffers from two problems: initialPriceFactor is bounded between 100 and 1000, so the division by 1000 yields a value less than one, which is then truncated to zero before being multiplied by x, and the term is not scaled to 1e18 like the other terms. As a result the overall expression can under‑flow or produce a price that is significantly lower than intended. The bug can be exploited by submitting a purchase request with a value of x that pushes (totalSupply - x) close to totalSupply, causing the first term to be heavily rounded down while the third term contributes nothing. An attacker can therefore acquire tokens at a price far below the economic model, draining protocol funds or receiving fewer tokens than expected. The impact is that users may see a price that is too low, leading to unexpected token allocations, or conversely the protocol may record a negative or zero price, breaking accounting logic and potentially causing funds to disappear from the treasury. The condition occurs every time the price function is called, especially for large x values, and affects any participant who relies on the price output – buyers, sellers, and the protocol itself. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the arithmetic expressions and identified the mismatched scaling and unnecessary divisions. It is hard to notice because the differences are subtle; the contract still returns a numeric value, and small rounding errors may not be obvious without precise test vectors. The proper fix is to perform the multiplication before division to preserve 1e18 precision, remove the redundant division in the second term, and reorder the operations in the third term so that the scaling factor is applied after multiplication, as shown in the recommended code. This aligns all terms to the same fixed‑point representation, eliminates truncation, and restores the intended economic behavior of the price function.
summary:
Here is current formula:
```solidity
return (
    (totalSupply * curveFactor) / (totalSupply - x) -
    (totalSupply * curveFactor) / totalSupply
    - initialPriceFactor / 1000 * x
) * 1 ether;
```
There are several issues:
1. First parameter (totalSupply * curveFactor) / (totalSupply - x) is rounded down, because both numerator and denominator are 1e18 numbers.
2. Second parameter (totalSupply * curveFactor) / totalSupply can be simply reduced to curveFactor.
3. Third parameter initialPriceFactor / 1000 * x is always round down to 0 because initialPriceFactor is in range [100, 1000]. And also this parameter is meant to be in terms of 1e18, but previous parameters are just numbers. So in the end there will be underflow after fix.

title: Incorrect fee growth initialisation causes incorrect reward distribution
content: The vulnerability originates from an incorrect initialisation of the reward growth value that is stored for each price tick in the pool contract. In a correctly designed system the value called rewardGrowthOutside must be set to the global growth‑outside amount at the moment a tick is first used, which guarantees the invariant that for any two ticks with tickA > tickB the stored growthOutside[tickA] is greater than or equal to growthOutside[tickB]. The examined implementation deviates from this rule and allows the rewardGrowthOutside field to be re‑initialised when a tick is already considered initialised. As a result, when a user creates several liquidity positions that share the same lower tick but have different upper ticks within the same block, the contract may assign a non‑zero rewardGrowthOutside to the later‑created position even though no fees have been accrued for that range. This breaks the accounting logic: a newly opened position that should start with zero pending rewards can appear to have earned rewards, leading to an over‑payment of protocol fees or token rewards. From the user’s perspective the UI may display a positive reward amount for a brand‑new position, contradicting the expectation that rewards are zero until the pool generates fees. The impact is high because it distorts the distribution of fees, gives an unfair advantage to attackers who can deliberately open positions in the vulnerable pattern, and can cause the protocol to lose funds or to allocate rewards incorrectly. The bug is triggered only when multiple positions are opened in the same block with identical uninitialised lower ticks but differing upper ticks, a situation that is not obvious during normal operation and therefore easy to miss in casual testing. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when a test case demonstrated that a position with an upper tick of 300 received a non‑zero reward while a position with an upper tick of 180 correctly received zero, violating the expected invariant. Fixing the problem requires changing the initialisation logic to match the reference implementation used by Uniswap: rewardGrowthOutside should be set to the current global growth‑outside value at the moment of first use, and the related calculations for feeGrowthInside and pastRewards must be updated accordingly to preserve the monotonicity invariant across ticks. By restoring the correct initialisation, newly created positions will start with zero pending rewards, the accounting will remain consistent, and the protocol will no longer distribute unintended rewards.
summary:
```solidity
The initialisation of the rewardGrowthOutside of a tick differs from Uniswap's. It is set to maintain the following invariant:
for all ticks: if (tick > current_tick) then
for all ticks: if (tick' > tick) then
growthOutside[tick] >= growthOutside[tick']
However, it is possible to re-initialise the rewardGrowthOutside when it shouldn't. For instance, one could create multiple positions with the same uninitialised lower tick, but different upper ticks that may have different growth outside values in the same block. This results in being able to create a new position being initialised with non-zero rewards.
```

title: Incorrect extraFeeAsset0 fee accounting
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect accounting of the extraFeeAsset0 fee in a token swap contract. The fee is applied inconsistently depending on the swap direction (zeroForOne vs oneForZero) and whether the caller specifies an exact input amount or an exact output amount. For a zeroForOne swap with an exact input, the contract subtracts the extra fee from the amount of asset0 taken from the user, meaning the user pays less asset0 while also receiving less asset1 than expected. For a zeroForOne swap with an exact output, the extra fee is subtracted from the required asset0 payable, which can make the net change of asset0 in the bundle negative and trigger a BundleChangeNetNegative() revert, causing the order to be dropped from the bundle. In the oneForZero direction the exact‑input case is handled correctly, but the exact‑output case again mis‑applies the fee: the user receives fewer asset0 tokens than requested while also paying a reduced amount of asset1, violating the expected one‑to‑one fee relationship. The root cause is that the fee is applied before the conversion between input and output amounts in some branches, and after conversion in others, without a unified rule for the sign and placement of the fee. An attacker could craft swaps that deliberately trigger the negative bundle delta, causing legitimate orders to be excluded from a batch transaction or forcing the whole bundle to revert, effectively a denial‑of‑service on the swapping service. Even when the transaction does not revert, users see a mismatch between the amount they expected to receive and the amount actually transferred – they may notice that “my balance is lower than expected” or “the swap gave me less tokens than I asked for”. The issue is high‑risk because it can lead to loss of protocol revenue, unexpected user losses, and transaction failures that are hard to debug. It occurs only under specific combinations of direction and exact‑specification, which makes it easy to miss in standard testing that often covers only the most common path. The problem was discovered during a manual security audit by Spearbit, which highlighted the inconsistent fee handling as a logical flaw. The bug is a classic example of asymmetric fee calculation or sign‑error in financial smart contracts, where the accounting assumptions (that fees are always taken from the payer or always deducted from the output) are violated. To fix the issue, the contract should first compute the exact input or output amount based on the price conversion, and only afterwards apply the extraFeeAsset0 in a direction‑agnostic way: add the fee to the input amount for zeroForOne swaps, or subtract it from the output amount for oneForZero swaps, as shown in the recommended code snippet. This ensures that the fee is always taken from the party that should pay it and that the net asset delta remains non‑negative, preserving both user expectations and protocol accounting integrity.
summary:
```solidity
The application of extraFeeAsset0 is inconsistent depending on the direction & specification of the swap:
• zeroForOne:
– Exact input: extraFeeAsset0 is subtracted from quantityIn, which means the less asset0 is taken from the user, although less asset1 is given.
– Exact output: For the specified asset1, extraFeeAsset0 is subtracted from the required asset0 payable. Likely to cause the order to be excluded from the bundle because it would cause the asset0 bundle delta to be negative and thus the bundle transaction to revert with the BundleChangeNetNegative() error.
• oneForZero:
– Exact input: Correctly implemented.
– Exact output: The user receives less than the specified quantity, but will pay less as well.
```

title: SwapCallLib.call() incorrectly uses return() instead of revert() on failed calls
content: The vulnerability resides in the low‑level call wrapper used by the swap module. When the contract attempts to execute a swap on Uniswap V4, it performs a raw call and checks the returned success flag. If the call fails, the code copies the returned error data and executes the EVM return opcode instead of the revert opcode. The return opcode terminates execution but does not trigger a state‑reverting exception; all state modifications that occurred before the failed call remain persisted. This behavior violates the expected atomicity of a swap operation, where a failure should roll back any token transfers, balance updates, or bookkeeping performed earlier in the transaction. The root cause is the misuse of return() where revert() is required, a pattern that can appear when developers copy low‑level call handling snippets without adjusting the error‑propagation semantics. An attacker can exploit this by crafting a bundle that includes a deliberately failing swap; because the contract does not revert, the bundle continues and the attacker can keep any state changes that were already applied, such as token deductions or position openings, while the swap itself yields no output. The impact includes potential loss of user funds, inconsistent protocol accounting, and the ability for malicious actors to submit invalid bundles that appear successful from the blockchain’s perspective. The issue manifests whenever a swap call returns false – for example, due to insufficient liquidity, slippage limits, or a deliberately malformed payload – and the surrounding code follows the faulty return path. All participants that rely on the swap module – end users, liquidity providers, and the protocol’s risk engine – are affected because the protocol may record an executed swap that never actually transferred assets. The problem was discovered during a manual security review that inspected the assembly implementation of the call helper and noticed the use of return() instead of revert(). It can be hard to notice because the transaction still completes with a successful status, and the on‑chain logs may not clearly indicate that the swap failed, leading to silent state corruption. The correct mitigation is to replace the return opcode with revert, ensuring that any failure in the external call triggers a full transaction revert and restores the pre‑call state. Conceptually, this belongs to the class of “failure‑to‑revert on external call” bugs, which break the atomicity guarantees of composable DeFi operations. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are a missing or zero refund after a swap, balances that appear unchanged despite a transaction receipt, or a UI that shows a successful swap while no tokens were received. The expectation that a failed swap should undo all prior changes is violated, resulting in money disappearing or accounting mismatches.

title: Anyone can frontrun fixed price signature mints to waste claim ticket
content: The vulnerability resides in the FixedPriceSignatureMinterV2 contract where a signed claim ticket is used to authorize minting of a specific quantity of NFTs. The contract builds the signed digest from the buyer address, mint identifier, claim ticket, signed quantity and affiliate, but when the mintTo function is executed it does not bind the signature to the caller (msg.sender) nor does it enforce that the exact signed quantity is minted. Consequently any external actor can copy a valid signature from the mempool, submit a transaction with the same claim ticket, and request any amount x such that 0 < x <= signedQuantity. The first transaction that succeeds consumes the claim ticket, marking it as used, and prevents the original user from receiving the remaining NFTs they were entitled to. This flaw can be exploited by a front‑runner who monitors pending transactions, replays the signature with a smaller mint amount (often just one NFT) and pays only the gas cost, especially attractive in free or low‑price mints where the economic loss to the victim is high while the attacker’s expense is minimal. The impact is that users may see their transaction succeed but receive fewer or no NFTs, their claim ticket becomes invalid, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions that a signed ticket guarantees a specific allocation are broken. The issue manifests whenever a user calls mintTo with a signed ticket, regardless of price, and is particularly dangerous for large‑quantity claims because the incentive to front‑run increases. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the signature verification logic and noticed the absence of msg.sender and exact quantity checks. The problem is subtle because the transaction still appears successful and the signature itself is valid; only the mismatch between expected and actual minted amount reveals the exploit. To remediate, the contract should include the caller’s address in the signed payload, enforce that the minted amount equals the signed quantity, or redesign the claim ticket representation to track individual NFT indices so that each ticket can only be used for its specific token. Such changes would bind the authorization to the intended recipient and prevent replay attacks, restoring the intended economic guarantees of the minting process.
summary:
When NFTs are minted using the `FixedPriceSignatureMinterV2.sol` contract, the user is able to input any quantity to mint. As long as this amount is less than the quantity that has been signed for, the transaction will succeed and the claim ticket will be used up.

The signed ticket includes the following details:
Buyer
Mint ID
Claim Ticket
Signed Quantity
Affiliate

When `mintTo()` is called, these values are all filled in entirely from the arguments passed to the function, as we can see here:
```solidity
bytes32 digest = keccak256(
    abi.encodePacked(
        "\x19\x01",
        DOMAIN_SEPARATOR(),
        keccak256(abi.encode(MINT_TYPEHASH, to, mintId, claimTicket, signedQuantity, affiliate))
    )
);
```
This leaves us with two facts:

1) The signature used by Alice to claim her NFTs could equally have been used by Bob to send NFTs to Alice, because there is no reference to who the `msg.sender` is when checking the signature.

2) The signature used to claim `signedQuantity` NFTs could also have been used to claim any amount `x` (where 0 < `x` <= `signedQuantity`), because there is no reference to the quantity claimed in the signature.

As a result, any user who is claiming a large number of NFTs is vulnerable to being frontrun. Bob can watch the mempool for Alice's transaction, copy the signature, and replay his own version of the transaction, sending just 1 NFT to Alice instead of the full `signedQuantity`.

Once this action has been taken, Alice's ticket will be claimed, and she will be unable to claim the additional NFTs she was entitled to.

This attack does require Bob to pay for Alice's NFT, but it because especially harmful in free or low price NFT mints, where there are likely large quantities that will be minted by top users and the attack can be performed for only the gas cost.

title: Keys for _balances mapping are inverted in _settleOrderIn() and _settleOrderOut()
content: The vulnerability originates from an inverted key order in a nested balance mapping used by the Settlement contract. The contract defines a private mapping that stores balances as asset => owner => amount, meaning the first key should be the token address and the second key the user address. However, the internal functions that settle orders – _settleOrderIn and _settleOrderOut – mistakenly access the mapping as if it were owner => asset. Specifically they execute _balances[from][asset] -= amount and _balances[to][asset] += amount, swapping the intended dimensions. This mismatch causes the contract to debit and credit balances in a location that does not correspond to the actual asset holder, effectively writing to a completely different storage slot. When an order is settled, the protocol believes it has moved the correct amount of a given token from one participant to another, but the stored balances remain unchanged for the real asset-owner pair while unrelated entries are altered. From a user perspective this manifests as missing or unchanged token balances after a trade, refunds that never arrive, or a zero balance where funds should exist. The impact is high because the accounting layer of the protocol is broken; users cannot rely on internal balances for withdrawals or further trades, and an attacker could trigger settlements to corrupt the ledger, potentially leading to permanent loss of funds. The issue occurs every time the settlement functions are invoked, which is any time an order is executed or cancelled. All participants, including token holders and the protocol itself, are affected because the core invariant that total deposited assets equal the sum of internal balances no longer holds. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that inspected the storage layout and the logic of the settlement functions; the error is subtle because Solidity does not emit warnings for incorrect mapping key ordering, and the code compiles without errors, making it easy to overlook during testing. To remediate the problem the mapping accesses must be corrected to respect the declared order: the asset address should be the first index and the owner address the second, i.e., replace _balances[from][asset] with _balances[asset][from] and similarly for the destination address. This adjustment restores the intended accounting semantics, ensuring that balances are updated for the correct asset-owner pair and that users see the expected token amounts after trades or refunds. The bug belongs to the class of “incorrect mapping key ordering” or “nested mapping misuse” which can lead to silent state corruption and financial loss in smart contracts that rely on multi‑dimensional mappings for accounting.

title: deposit() can be used to inﬂate a user's balance for not-yet-deployed tokens
content: The vulnerability resides in the deposit functions of the Settlement contract, which accept an arbitrary ERC‑20 token address and increase an internal balance after calling SafeTransferLib.safeTransferFrom. SafeTransferLib deliberately does not verify that the supplied token address contains contract code before performing the low‑level call, delegating that responsibility to the caller. Consequently, when a caller provides an address that has no deployed contract (for example, a placeholder address or a token that is scheduled to be deployed later), the safeTransferFrom call succeeds silently because the call does not revert on a non‑existent contract. The contract then adds the requested amount to the caller’s internal balance without any actual token transfer occurring. An attacker can exploit this by front‑running a token deployment: they submit a deposit transaction referencing the future token’s address before the token contract is deployed, inflating their balance with an arbitrary amount (even type(uint256).max as demonstrated in the test). When the token is eventually deployed, the protocol’s accounting reflects a balance that was never backed by real tokens, allowing the attacker to later withdraw assets they never supplied, effectively stealing funds from the protocol. This issue manifests whenever deposit() is called with an asset address that lacks bytecode, which can happen unintentionally if a user mistypes an address or deliberately if an adversary chooses a non‑contract address. The problem is hard to notice because the external token transfer appears successful (no revert) and the internal ledger simply records the amount, giving the false impression that a legitimate deposit occurred. The root cause is the missing validation of the asset address’s code size before performing the transfer. To remediate, the deposit functions should explicitly check that the asset address contains contract code (e.g., require(asset.code.length > 0, "asset must be a contract")) or use a transfer library that enforces this check. By ensuring that only real ERC‑20 contracts can be used, the protocol prevents balance inflation, preserves accounting integrity, and protects user funds from being artificially created.

title: Oracle data feed can be outdated yet used anyways which will impact payment logic
content: The vulnerability is an oracle staleness flaw in the Juicebox protocol where the price feed contract (JBChainlinkV3PriceFeed) fetches the latest answer from a Chainlink data feed but never validates the accompanying timestamp fields (updatedAt or latestTimestamp). Because the contract assumes the answer is fresh, an outdated or out‑of‑bounds price can be injected into the downstream pricing logic (JBPrices.priceFor) and subsequently used by the payment terminal store functions that record payments, distributions, allowance usage, overflow calculations, and total overflow queries. The root cause is the omission of a freshness check on the oracle data, which violates the recommended Chainlink pattern of comparing the data timestamp against a reasonable heartbeat. An attacker, or even a benign market condition that causes the feed to stop updating (e.g., network congestion, upstream outage, or a long‑configured heartbeat), can cause the contract to continue using a stale price for an indefinite period. When this occurs, the payment terminal miscalculates token amounts to mint, the recorded distributed amount, the used allowance, and overflow limits, leading to incorrect token balances and potentially rewarding or penalizing participants based on obsolete market prices. From a user’s perspective, the expected outcome—such as receiving a proportional amount of project tokens for a contribution or seeing the correct project balance after a distribution—may not materialize; users might see zero or unexpectedly low token allocations, balances that do not reflect their contributions, or over‑ or under‑reported overflow values. The issue was discovered during a formal security audit (Code4rena) where auditors traced the data flow from the oracle to the payment terminal functions and identified the lack of timestamp validation as a logical flaw that could be exploited under conditions of feed delay. The bug is subtle because the contract does not revert or emit explicit error messages when the price is stale; it simply proceeds with the stale value, making the misbehavior hard to notice without detailed accounting checks. The flaw belongs to the class of “oracle staleness” or “price feed freshness” bugs, where reliance on external data without proper timeliness validation leads to accounting inconsistencies. The recommended mitigation is to enforce a tolerance check on the updatedAt timestamp against the block timestamp, pause operations or switch to a fallback oracle when the feed is stale, and possibly integrate additional redundant oracles (e.g., Uniswap) to cross‑verify prices. By adding these checks, the protocol can ensure that only recent and reliable price data influences payment calculations, preserving the integrity of token issuance and balance accounting.
summary:
The current implementation of `JBChainlinkV3PriceFeed` is used by the protocol to showcase how the feed will be retrieved via Chainlink Data Feeds. The feed is used to retrieve the `currentPrice`, which is also used afterwards by `JBPrices.priceFor()`, then by `JBSingleTokenPaymentTerminalStore.recordPaymentFrom()`, `JBSingleTokenPaymentTerminalStore.recordDistributionFor`, `JBSingleTokenPaymentTerminalStore.recordUsedAllowanceOf`, `JBSingleTokenPaymentTerminalStore._overflowDuring` and `JBSingleTokenPaymentTerminalStore._currentTotalOverflowOf`. Although the current feeds are calculated by a non implemented IJBPriceFeed, if the implementation of the price feed is the same as the showcased in`JBChainlinkV3PriceFeed`, the retrieved data can be outdated or out of bounds.

It is important to remember that the sponsor said on the dedicated Discord Channel that also oracle pricing and data retrieval is inside the scope.

title: Token Change Can Be Frontrun, Blocking Token
content: The vulnerability arises from an inadequate authorization check during the token migration process of Juicebox projects. When a project admin transfers ownership of a token contract to the JBTokenStore prior to invoking the changeToken (or changeTokenOf) function, the system does not verify that the caller of the migration function is the current owner of the token. As a result, a malicious actor can observe the pending ownership transfer and submit a competing transaction that calls changeTokenFor (or the newer changeTokenOf) before the legitimate admin’s transaction is mined, effectively frontrunning the migration. In the first step the attacker links the token to one of their own projects, and in a subsequent step they set themselves as the new token owner by supplying their address as the _newOwner parameter. Because many Juicebox‑based tokens, such as JBToken, restrict minting to the contract’s owner, gaining ownership enables the attacker to mint an arbitrary amount of the token that was intended to be transferred. This attack blocks legitimate users from changing the project token, hijacks token ownership, and allows unchecked inflation of the token supply, diluting existing holders’ balances and potentially compromising the financial integrity of the project. The flaw manifests only when the token’s ownership is transferred to the JBTokenStore before the changeToken call, a pattern recommended in Juicebox’s own post‑mortem guidance. The affected parties include project administrators, token holders, and any downstream protocols that rely on the token’s accounting. The issue was uncovered during a Code4rena audit that examined the migration workflow and identified that the contract trusted the caller without confirming ownership. The problem is subtle because the ownership transfer appears legitimate and the migration transaction itself succeeds, making the theft of ownership difficult to detect without explicit inspection of the token’s owner field. The recommended remediation is to enforce that the caller of the change‑token function is the current token owner, or to maintain a whitelist of trusted legacy directories and require explicit approval from the project owner before a token can be set. Additionally, the migration flow should be reordered so that the token change happens before ownership is handed over to the token store, eliminating the window where an attacker can intervene. By ensuring proper ownership verification and sequencing, the protocol can prevent unauthorized token control and the resulting arbitrary minting.
summary: This vulnerability allows malicious actors to block other users from changing tokens of their projects. Furthermore if ownership over the token contract is transferred to the `JBTokenStore` contract prior to the change, as suggested in the [recourse section of Juicebox’s 24.05.2022 post-mortem update](https://github.com/jbx-protocol/juice-contracts-v2-code4rena/blob/main/security/postmortem/5.24.2022.md#Recourse), this vulnerability would allow an attacker to become the owner of tokens being transferred. For `JBToken` based tokens this would allow an attacker to begin issuing arbitrary amounts the token that was meant to be transferred.

title: Golden Egg will continue to change throughout SAM
content: The vulnerability concerns the calculation of the Golden Egg token identifier that determines which address receives a percentage of all sales generated by the bonding curve after a fixed‑price sale ends and a SAM (Split Auction Mechanism) begins. The contract obtains the token ID by calling a metadata module function that computes the ID as (mintRandomness % editionMaxMintable) + 1. The root cause is that editionMaxMintable is not a constant value; after the editionCutoffTime it returns the total number of tokens minted so far, clamped between a lower and an upper bound. Because the total minted count continues to increase as the bonding curve mints new tokens, editionMaxMintable changes on each subsequent SAM mint. Consequently the modulo operation yields a different tokenId each time, meaning the Golden Egg winner can shift after the sale has already been declared. An attacker who can trigger additional mints during the SAM period can therefore alter the tokenId and redirect the fee share to an address they control, or simply cause the intended recipient to receive less than expected. The impact is a misallocation of revenue: users who expect to receive a percentage of sales may see their balance stay at zero or receive a smaller amount, while the protocol may unintentionally pay fees to an unintended holder. This condition occurs only while the edition has not yet reached its maximum mintable upper limit; once that limit is hit the value freezes and the bug no longer manifests. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the SAM contract and the OpenGoldenEggMetadata module, where the dynamic nature of editionMaxMintable was observed. It is hard to notice because the token ID appears deterministic at first glance, and the UI typically shows the winner of the Golden Egg without revealing that the underlying fee recipient can change later. To remediate, the contract should capture a snapshot of the total minted count the first time samMint is called and use that fixed value for all subsequent Golden Egg calculations, effectively locking the tokenId after the initial sale. This aligns the implementation with the intended business logic that the Golden Egg winner is fixed once the fixed‑price sale ends, preserving correct fee distribution and preventing revenue leakage.

title: The same signature can be used in different `distribution` implementation causing that the caller who owns the signature, can distribute on unauthorized implementations
content: The vulnerability is a signature replay issue across different distribution implementations in the ProxyFactory contract. The contract’s deployProxyAndDistributeBySignature function verifies a signed digest that only includes the contest identifier and the distribution data, but it deliberately omits the address of the distribution implementation. Because the implementation address is not part of the signed message, a signature that was created for one implementation can be reused to authorize a distribution on any other implementation that later gets registered for the same contest identifier. The root cause is the construction of the EIP‑712 digest at line 159, which calls _hashTypedDataV4(keccak256(abi.encode(contestId, data))) and therefore does not bind the implementation parameter. An attacker who possesses a valid organizer signature can call deployProxyAndDistributeBySignature with a different implementation address after the owner has re‑registered the contest with a new distributor. The function will compute the same digest, recover the organizer’s address, and then deploy a proxy that points to the new implementation, finally invoking the distribution logic. This allows the attacker to move prize funds to recipients defined by the new implementation without the organizer’s explicit consent. The impact is that prize money can be transferred under an unauthorized contract, breaking the accounting assumptions of the contest, potentially causing loss of funds, misallocation of rewards, and erosion of trust in the protocol. The bug manifests whenever a contest is re‑configured with a new distributor after a signature has already been issued; the condition is that the salt used for registration includes the implementation, but the signature verification does not, so the check passes. The affected parties are the contest organizer, participants expecting a legitimate payout, sponsors funding the prizes, and the overall protocol that relies on correct distribution logic. The issue was discovered during a security audit when a test demonstrated that the same signature could be used to trigger distribution on a newly set implementation.
