It is hard to notice because the transaction appears to be correctly signed by the organizer and the contest is registered, so no obvious error is raised. The proper fix is to include the implementation address in the signed digest, for example by changing the hash to _hashTypedDataV4(keccak256(abi.encode(contestId, implementation, data))) so that each implementation requires a fresh organizer signature. This change binds the signature to the specific distribution contract, eliminating the replay vector and restoring the intended authorization model.

title: If any Splits Wallet sets up incentives on Warehouse, all funds can be stolen
content: The vulnerability is an economic drain that arises when a SplitsWalletV2 enables incentives on the associated SplitsWarehouse while the warehouse withdrawal configuration remains unpaused, which is the default state. The root cause is that both the warehouse.withdraw function and the wallet.depositToWarehouse function are declared public and lack any access control, allowing any external account to invoke them directly. Because the warehouse rewards an incentive on each successful withdrawal, an attacker can repeatedly call withdraw to claim the incentive together with the full token amount, and then immediately call depositToWarehouse to move the withdrawn tokens back into the wallet. By looping this cycle many times, the attacker extracts the incentive on every iteration, gradually draining almost the entire balance from the user’s split. The impact is that the user’s token balance in the split can drop to near zero, while the attacker’s address accumulates the stolen funds; the protocol’s accounting assumptions that incentives are paid only on legitimate distributions are violated. This condition occurs whenever a split has any incentive configured on the warehouse and the withdrawal config is not paused, which is true for most deployments. All token holders that rely on the split for revenue sharing are affected because their funds can be silently siphoned away. The issue was discovered during a security audit by writing a test that performed thousands of withdraw‑deposit cycles and observed that more than 99.999% of the initial assets were transferred to the attacker. The problem is hard to notice because each individual incentive is small and the functions appear benign, so the drain happens gradually and may be mistaken for normal fee accrual or rounding loss. The bug belongs to the class of permissionless incentive‑drain vulnerabilities where unrestricted external calls combined with reward logic enable an economic attack. From the user’s perspective the UI would show the expected balance disappearing after a distribution, or a refund that should be received turning into zero, contradicting the expectation that funds remain safe. To remediate, the depositToWarehouse function should be restricted so that only the internal distribute mechanism can call it, or otherwise protected by proper access control, and the warehouse withdraw incentive should be disabled or gated behind a paused state to prevent arbitrary external withdrawals.
summary:
There are two forms of incentives that can be added for distributions. On the `SplitsWarehouse`, incentives are added to the WithdrawConfig, and on the `SplitsWalletV2`, incentives are baked into the Split struct.

In the event that a Splits Wallet sets up any incentives on the Warehouse (and has their withdrawal config set to unpaused, which is the default state), this can be used to drain all funds from a user.

This is the case because the `warehouse.withdraw()` function and the `wallet.depositToWarehouse()` functions are public and permissionless. This means any user can withdraw, claiming the incentive, and force the wallet to immediately redeposit the funds. After enough cycles, the attacker will have claimed almost all of the assets.

title: Split ownership can be spoofed using `execCalls()`
content: The vulnerability is an ownership spoofing flaw that arises because the onlyOwner access control permits calls originating from the contract’s own address (address(this)). This design choice allows the execCalls function, which can batch arbitrary internal calls, to invoke any function protected by onlyOwner, including transferOwnership. An attacker can start an execCalls transaction, pass the onlyOwner check, and then within the same transaction temporarily change the split’s owner to any address, such as address(0) to satisfy immutability checks, perform external calls that rely on the owner being immutable, and finally restore ownership to the attacker’s address. The root cause is the combination of a permissive onlyOwner modifier and the ability of execCalls to chain privileged calls without re‑validating ownership after each step. Exploitation proceeds by (1) invoking execCalls, (2) calling transferOwnership to set the owner to the required value, (3) triggering the external protocol’s ownership‑based validation (for example, a require(split.owner() == address(0)) check), and (4) reverting ownership back to the attacker. This can be carried out by any contract that can call execCalls, meaning that protocols which trust split ownership as a guarantee of immutability or revenue entitlement may be deceived. The impact is that a protocol may register a split as immutable and allocate at least half of its revenue to itself, yet the split’s parameters can later be altered, causing loss of expected funds or unauthorized revenue diversion. The issue manifests only when a split’s ownership is used as a security assumption; otherwise the contract behaves normally. It affects any user or protocol that relies on split ownership checks, including revenue‑sharing platforms and DeFi aggregators. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the interaction between execCalls and the onlyOwner modifier. It is subtle because the transaction appears to be initiated by the contract itself, so external observers see a legitimate internal call chain and may not notice the temporary ownership change. To remediate, the contract should either forbid execCalls from invoking transferOwnership, enforce an ownership re‑check before each privileged operation, or clearly document that ownership checks cannot be trusted when execCalls is used. Conceptually, the fix removes the ability to bypass ownership validation by ensuring that ownership state cannot be altered mid‑transaction without detection, thereby preserving the integrity of immutability guarantees and protecting revenue streams.

title: UniV3 Oracle unsafe on L2s in event of Sequencer downtime
content: The vulnerability originates from the way the Uniswap V3 time‑weighted average price (TWAP) oracle is used on layer‑2 networks. The contract calls the library function consult() which internally invokes getSurroundingObservations. This helper assumes that if the requested target timestamp (secondsAgo) is older than the newest stored observation, the most recent observation can be reused for both the before and after points, effectively extrapolating the previous price forward in time. When a sequencer on an L2 such as Arbitrum experiences downtime, no new blocks are produced and the pool does not record fresh observations. Because the oracle does not verify that a recent observation actually exists for the requested interval, it continues to return the stale price that was recorded before the outage. An attacker can exploit this gap by submitting a transaction that relies on the outdated TWAP – for example a swap, liquidation or any operation that uses the price as a reference – and, on Arbitrum, can force the transaction through the delayed inbox to guarantee inclusion while the sequencer is offline. The transaction then executes at the old price, allowing the attacker to obtain a better rate or trigger a liquidation that would not have been possible with the current market price. The impact is that users may receive less output than expected, experience unexpected liquidations, or see their balances reduced because the protocol priced assets incorrectly. This situation occurs only when the sequencer is down long enough that the oracle’s secondsAgo window exceeds the time since the last observation, and when no other participants are submitting transactions that would update the pool’s price during the outage. All users and the protocol that depend on the oracle for pricing are affected, including traders, liquidity providers and token holders. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the oracle integration and noticed the optimistic fallback to the newest observation without a freshness check. It is hard to notice because the price appears to drift slowly back to the correct value once the sequencer resumes, masking the brief period of manipulation, and because the Uniswap V3 Oracle library is widely trusted. The bug belongs to the class of oracle data‑availability failures where a TWAP calculation extrapolates stale data when observations are missing. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are trades executed at an old price, unexpected loss of funds, or liquidations that seem to happen “out of nowhere”. The expected behavior – a price that reflects the current market – is violated by the oracle’s assumption that the last known price remains valid. A proper mitigation is to replace the Uniswap V3 oracle on L2s with a source that guarantees fresh data, such as Chainlink, or to add a safeguard that rejects price queries when the time since the last observation exceeds a safe threshold, or to pause dependent functionality during sequencer downtime.

title: Incorrect Assumptions About Chain Native Token Will Heavily Skew Protocol Pricing Mechanism
content: The vulnerability stems from hard‑coded assumptions about the value of the chain’s native token when defining the protocol’s ante and maximum ante parameters. The contracts express these limits in ether units (e.g., 0.01 ether) under the expectation that the native token will have a high market price similar to Ethereum, where 1 ether is worth thousands of dollars. When the same bytecode is deployed on a network whose native token is cheap – in this case Berachain’s BERA, priced at roughly six dollars per ether – the numeric values translate into a collateral requirement of only a few cents. This mismatch is the root cause: the pricing model treats the ante as a fixed amount of native token rather than a fixed USD‑equivalent value, and the code does not adjust the limits based on the actual market price. An attacker can exploit the situation by opening debt positions with the minimal ante of roughly $0.06, which is far below the intended risk barrier. Because the ante is so low, many users can borrow large amounts of protocol assets with negligible collateral, quickly generating bad debt. The protocol’s warning mechanism, which pays out either a quarter of the ante or the contract balance, also becomes ineffective – the payout is too small to incentivize anyone to issue a warning before liquidation. Consequently, liquidations are delayed or omitted, allowing the bad debt to grow unchecked. The impact is a distortion of the protocol’s economic incentives: borrowers are over‑leveraged, lenders may lose funds, and the overall health of the market can deteriorate. This condition occurs whenever the contract is deployed on a chain where the native token’s price deviates significantly from the price assumed during development, and it affects every participant that relies on the ante to provide a safety margin – borrowers, lenders, and the governance body. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the hard‑coded ante values against the actual market price of BERA, revealing that the intended $0.06 collateral was far lower than expected. The problem is subtle because the code compiles without errors and the receive/payable functions work as designed; only a cross‑chain price check exposes the flaw. To remediate, the ante and its maximum should be made configurable through a governance function or, preferably, derived from a reliable price oracle so that the collateral requirement remains consistent in fiat terms regardless of the underlying token’s market value. This change restores the intended economic barrier, re‑aligns incentives for warnings and liquidations, and prevents the protocol from being gamed by cheap‑token deployments.
summary:
In various parts of the contract, the native token is meant to be used. Contracts have payable receive functions, etc. The ante constant is set to an amount that otherwise would be reasonable, were the contracts to be deployed on a chain with an expensive native token like ETH. But the contracts are to be deployed on Berachain. Its native token is BERA, which at the time of writing, costs about $6.29 per ether. Compared to ETH which costs $2371 per ether, there is a very large price discrepancy which skews protocol pricing mechanisms, disincentivizes warnings, and liquidations, encourages bad debt, etc.

The default ante is 0.01 ether, which, based on our above pricing assumptions, is about $0.06 or 6 cents. Our max ante therefore will be about $3.14.

The main impact here revolves around protocol pricing. Since the ante determines the minimum amount required to take on debt, having it as low as $0.06 strongly incentivizes borrowing, which can quickly lead to significant bad debt. Even if governance adjusts the ante upwards, governMarketConfig() enforces a cap CONSTRAINT_ANTE_MAX of just $3—still relatively low. On top of that, the warning mechanism isn’t compelling enough; with a minimum payout of either ante/4 or the contract balance, warners won’t be properly incentivized. As a result, liquidations won’t happen as frequently as needed, since warnings must occur before liquidation can take place.

title: The feeProtocol Calculation in the VolatilityOracle::_getPoolMetadata() Is Flawed
content: The vulnerability resides in the feeProtocol calculation performed inside the VolatilityOracle::_getPoolMetadata() function. The contract stores feeProtocol as a 32‑bit unsigned integer where the upper 16 bits represent the protocol fee for token1 and the lower 16 bits represent the fee for token0, expressed in basis points (e.g., a value of 3500 corresponds to a 35 % fee). The existing implementation mistakenly treats feeProtocol as an 8‑bit field by applying a modulo 16 operation and a right‑shift of four bits, mirroring the logic used in UniswapV3 where the fee is encoded as a denominator. Because Kodiak pools encode fees differently, the calculation `metadata.gamma0 -= uint24(fee / (feeProtocol % 16))` and the analogous line for gamma1 use only the least‑significant 8 bits of each 16‑bit segment. This misinterpretation leads to an incorrect protocol fee deduction, producing wrong values for gamma0 and gamma1, which are later used to compute implied volatility. When a new market is created, the defaultFeeProtocol set in the KodiakV3Factory (for example 229379500, which corresponds to 3500 basis points for each token) is fed into this flawed logic, causing the VolatilityOracle to emit inaccurate implied volatility numbers. Those numbers flow into Borrower::getPrices(), and any function that relies on those prices – such as modify(), liquidate(), warn() and clear() – receives distorted price data. From a user perspective this may appear as unexpected liquidation, zero or wildly inaccurate price quotes, or failure of borrowing operations that should otherwise succeed. The bug is hard to notice because the price deviation can be subtle and the faulty arithmetic occurs deep inside the oracle, not at the UI layer. It was discovered during a manual audit by Shiedify, who compared the fee encoding expectations of Kodiak with the actual bit‑masking logic. Exploitation is possible by creating a market with a feeProtocol value that triggers the incorrect division, allowing an attacker to manipulate the implied volatility and consequently the price feed, potentially causing wrongful liquidations or profit extraction. The affected parties include borrowers, lenders, and any protocol component that depends on the oracle’s price output. To remediate the issue the calculation should be rewritten to extract the full 16‑bit segments, interpret them as basis points, and apply the fee proportionally (for example `metadata.gamma0 -= uint24(fee * feeProtocolLow / 10000)`). This change aligns the arithmetic with the intended fee representation and restores correct price calculations throughout the system.
summary:
The feeProtocol calculation in the VolatilityOracle::_getPoolMetadata() is erroneous:
```solidity
unchecked {
    if (feeProtocol % 16 != 0) metadata.gamma0 -= uint24(fee / (feeProtocol % 16));
    if (feeProtocol >> 4 != 0) metadata.gamma1 -= uint24(fee / (feeProtocol >> 4));
}
```
The feeProtocol is given in uint32 and the first 16 bits are for token1 and the lower 16 bits are for token0. But the above calculation uses only 8 bits for the protocolFee calculation, similar to UniswapV3, but that is wrong with regard to Kodiak.

Furthermore, the KodiakV3Factory contract is deployed at 0xD84CBf0B02636E7f53dB9E5e45A616E05d710990 in Berachain. In the constructor, the defaultFeeProtocol is given as:
```solidity
defaultFeeProtocol = 229379500; //35%, 35%
```
Hence, this is equal to 3500, 3500 after converting to hexadecimal and then again to decimal for two tokens (token1 and token0). Hence the feeProtocol is given in basis points and not as a denominator as with UniswapV3 Pools.

This will lead to wrong protocol fee calculation during the new market creation and these erroneous values will result in providing wrong ImpliedVolatility values in the VolatilityOracle. This will result in erroneous price values being given as output of the Borrower::getPrices() function. Hence the critical function execution in the Borrower contract, which uses the getPrices() such as the modify(), liquidate(), warn() and clear(), will be broken.

title: A user can steal an already transfered and bridged reSDL lock because of approval
content: The vulnerability is an authorization persistence flaw in the reSDL token bridge. When a user bridges a reSDL lock to another chain, the handleOutgoingRESDL function updates the lock state but fails to clear the ERC‑721 style approval that was previously granted for that lock identifier. Because the approval mapping (tokenApprovals) is left untouched, the original approver retains the right to transfer the NFT even after the lock has been transferred to a new owner on the destination chain. An attacker can exploit this by pre‑approving a malicious address for a lock they intend to bridge, then allowing a victim to purchase or receive the lock on the target chain. When the victim later attempts to bridge the same lock back, the stale approval remains attached to the lock identifier. The attacker can then call transferFrom using the approved address and move the NFT from the victim back to themselves, effectively stealing the lock. The impact is the loss of ownership of a reSDL lock, which represents a valuable asset; the victim sees the NFT disappear from their account while the attacker gains control. This condition occurs whenever handleOutgoingRESDL is invoked without deleting tokenApprovals, i.e., for any bridge operation that moves a lock across supported chains. The affected parties are lock owners, buyers, and any protocol participants relying on the bridge to safely transfer ownership. The issue was discovered during a security audit when a test case demonstrated that after bridging, the getApproved query still returned the original approver, and the attacker could subsequently invoke transferFrom to reclaim the lock. The bug is subtle because the UI typically shows the lock as belonging to the new owner, and approvals are not prominently displayed, making the lingering permission easy to overlook. Conceptually, the fix is to treat the approval as part of the lock’s mutable state and clear it whenever the lock is moved out of the current chain, similar to how ERC‑721 implementations clear approvals on transfer. Deleting tokenApprovals[_lockId] inside handleOutgoingRESDL restores the intended invariant that only the current owner can authorize transfers, thereby preventing the described theft scenario.

title: Not Update Rewards in `handleIncomingUpdate` Function of `SDLPoolPrimary` Leads to Incorrect Reward Calculations
content: The vulnerability is a reward‑accounting error that occurs when the primary pool contract processes an incoming update from a secondary chain but fails to update the pending rewards before adjusting the effective balance of the cross‑chain controller. The root cause is that the handleIncomingUpdate function modifies the effectiveBalances mapping and totalEffectiveBalance for the CCIP controller without first invoking the internal reward‑update routine that would recalculate rewardPerToken based on the current totalEffectiveBalance. Because rewardPerToken is derived from the ratio of total rewards to totalEffectiveBalance, changing the balance without a prior reward snapshot inflates the controller’s share of future rewards. An attacker or any participant can trigger the bug simply by causing a supply change on the secondary chain – for example, by staking additional tokens on the secondary side – which results in a positive totalRESDLSupplyChange being forwarded to the primary pool. When the primary pool receives this message, it adds the supply change to the controller’s effective balance while leaving the stored rewardPerToken unchanged. Consequently, the next call to distributeRewards calculates a controller reward that exceeds the actual token balance held in the rewardsPool. Users experience this as missing or unclaimable rewards: the UI may show a positive withdrawableRewards amount for the controller, but the withdraw operation reverts due to insufficient pool balance, and legitimate stakers receive less than expected or see their reward claim fail. The issue manifests whenever an incoming update with a non‑zero supply change is processed, which is a normal operation in the cross‑chain staking flow, affecting all stakers and the protocol’s reward distribution logic. It was discovered during a functional test that simulated cross‑chain messages; the test observed that after an incoming update the sum of withdrawable rewards for the controller and a regular staker exceeded the total rewards held in the rewardsPool, causing the distributeRewards call to revert. The bug is subtle because the contract’s state variables appear to be updated correctly, and the reward calculation code is otherwise sound; the missing call to update rewards is easy to overlook in a complex cross‑chain flow. To remediate, the handleIncomingUpdate function should invoke the reward‑update routine (e.g., updateReward or similar) before mutating effectiveBalances, ensuring that rewardPerToken is recomputed with the old balance and that the controller’s accrued rewards are settled prior to the balance change. This aligns the accounting with the intended invariant that total rewards never exceed the pool balance and restores correct reward distribution for all participants.

title: Incorrect fee calculation occurs on bonding curve buys
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect fee calculation that occurs during bonding curve purchase operations when the requested order size (trueOrderSize) exceeds the number of tokens that remain available (maxRemainingTokens). The root cause is that the contract recomputes the fee after truncating the order size, but it bases the fee on the original totalCost (msg.value) rather than on the actual ETH required to acquire the reduced number of tokens (ethNeeded). Consequently the fee is systematically underestimated for this edge‑case path. An attacker can exploit the bug by deliberately submitting a buy order that would overshoot the remaining supply; the contract will cap the order size, compute a lower fee than should be charged, and then refund any excess ETH based on the underestimated totalCost. This results in the protocol receiving less fee revenue than intended while the user may obtain more tokens for a lower effective cost. The impact is economic: fee revenue is reduced, token pricing assumptions are violated, and repeated exploitation could erode the protocol’s financial model. The condition under which the bug manifests is when trueOrderSize > maxRemainingTokens, i.e., when the purchase would exhaust the curve’s remaining liquidity. All participants that rely on correct fee accounting – the protocol owners, token holders, and users – are affected because the accounting invariants of the bonding curve are broken. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the bonding‑curve buy logic, where the fee calculation block was examined and the mismatch between ethNeeded and totalCost became apparent. It is hard to notice because normal purchases (where the order size fits within the remaining supply) calculate the fee correctly; only the rare overshoot scenario triggers the faulty path. The bug belongs to the class of arithmetic/logic errors where a variable is recomputed without updating dependent values, leading to an under‑charged fee. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are confusing: a user sends a certain amount of ETH expecting a fee proportional to the purchase, but receives a larger token amount or a refund that does not match the expected fee deduction, effectively seeing “my fee is too low” or “my refund is larger than I thought”. The expectation that the fee equals (totalCost * feeBps) / 10000 is violated; the reality is that the fee is calculated on a smaller base, causing the protocol to lose revenue. The recommended fix is to recompute totalCost using a fee‑inclusive formula (totalCost = (10000 * ethNeeded) / (10000 - feeBps)) and then derive the fee as the difference between totalCost and ethNeeded, ensuring the fee reflects the actual amount of ETH needed for the capped order size. This correction restores proper accounting and prevents fee underestimation.

title: Malicious dao owner can break lz communication
content:
The vulnerability is an out‑of‑gas denial‑of‑service condition that can be triggered by a malicious DAO owner when the contract processes an excessively large list of tokens during a cross‑chain purchase. The LayerZeroImpl contract relies on the NonBlockingLzApp pattern: when a message arrives it calls an internal _blockingLzReceive function which forwards the call to nonblockingLzReceive using the full amount of gas reported by gasleft(). Because of the EVM 63/64 rule, only one‑sixty‑fourth of the remaining gas is left for the code that runs after the call, which includes the logic that stores a failed message in case the receive call reverts. Storing a failed payload requires a zero‑to‑non‑zero SSTORE operation that costs roughly 22 k gas. When the nonblockingLzReceive function itself consumes almost all of the supplied gas – for example because it loops over a large token array supplied by the DAO owner – the leftover gas drops to around 9 k, insufficient for the storage write. The attempt to record the failed payload then reverts, and the revert propagates out of the Endpoint try/catch block, leaving the communication channel in a blocked state.

The root cause is the combination of (1) an unbounded token list that can make the cross‑chain minting logic arbitrarily expensive, and (2) the fixed gas allocation strategy of the LayerZero SDK that does not guarantee enough gas for the failure‑handling path. The issue manifests when a DAO owner deliberately adds a large number of tokens to the token‑gating configuration and then initiates a cross‑chain buy. The call stack proceeds through commLayer.sendMsg, endpoint.send, commLayer.lzReceive, lzReceive, _nonblockingLzReceive, and finally factory.crossChainMint, where the large loop triggers an out‑of‑gas error. Because the subsequent _blockingLzReceive cannot store the failed message, the endpoint’s catch block fails, and the message channel becomes permanently blocked until the state is manually corrected.

From a user’s perspective the transaction appears to be submitted but no DAO tokens are received; the user’s balance remains unchanged and the UI may show a generic “transaction failed” or “out of gas” error without indicating that the cross‑chain bridge is stuck. The protocol’s accounting assumptions – that every cross‑chain message will either succeed or be safely stored for retry – are violated, leading to potential loss of liquidity and inability to perform further cross‑chain operations.

The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the LayerZero integration and identified that the gas limit passed to the endpoint (600 k) combined with the 63/64 rule left an insufficient safety margin for the failure‑handling path. The problem is subtle because the SDK’s non‑blocking pattern normally masks failures, and the out‑of‑gas condition only appears when the payload processing becomes unusually heavy, which may not be exercised in normal testing.

To remediate the issue the contract should enforce a reasonable upper bound on the number of tokens that can be added to the gating list, thereby limiting the worst‑case gas consumption of the cross‑chain mint loop. Additional mitigations could include increasing the gas buffer supplied to the endpoint or redesigning the failure‑handling logic to avoid costly storage writes when gas is scarce. By constraining the token array size, the contract ensures that the non‑blocking receive always retains enough gas to store a failed message, preserving the intended retry mechanism and preventing a malicious owner from permanently blocking the communication channel.

title: Incorrect value will get sent to the commLayer
content: The vulnerability resides in the cross‑chain DAO factory’s createERC20DAO (and createERC721DAO) function, which is responsible for forwarding a user‑provided ether amount (msg.value) to a communication layer that relays the deposit to secondary chains. The implementation mistakenly divides the total ether by the full length of the _depositChainIds array, which includes the primary chain, and then repeatedly applies the same division in a loop while the remaining value is reduced on each iteration. As a result, the amount sent to each secondary chain is smaller than intended and a residual ether balance remains locked in the factory contract. This residual balance can only be withdrawn by the contract owner, effectively trapping user funds. The bug occurs whenever a user creates a DAO that spans more than one chain and supplies a non‑zero msg.value. Users expect the full amount they specify to be distributed evenly among the selected secondary chains; instead they observe that only a fraction reaches the intended destinations, while the rest disappears from their wallet and does not appear in any DAO balance. From a user‑interface perspective the symptom is a missing or reduced refund: the transaction succeeds, but the user’s wallet shows a lower balance than expected and no funds are visible on the newly created DAO on the secondary chains. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the value calculation logic and identified that the divisor used (_depositChainIds.length) does not reflect the number of secondary chains (length‑1) and that the loop’s decreasing value leads to cumulative loss. The problem is subtle because the contract does not revert or emit an explicit error; the ether simply stays in the factory, making the loss appear as a silent shortfall. Conceptually, the fix is to adjust the division to use the remaining number of target chains for each iteration, i.e., divide by (_depositChainIds.length‑(i+1)) after subtracting any protocol fees, ensuring that each secondary chain receives the correct share and no ether is left stranded. This class of bug falls under incorrect financial accounting and mis‑allocation of funds in multi‑chain smart contracts, violating the protocol’s assumption that the sum of forwarded amounts equals the user‑provided deposit.
summary:
The factory.createERC20DAO() function creates cross-chain DAOs using LayerZero. Users can specify msg.value, which is distributed across multiple chains. For example, if there are 5 chains and msg.value is 1000, each chain receives 200. This value is forwarded to the commLayer. The _depositChainIds array is intended to manage the distribution across chains. For instance, if a user wants to create a DAO on the primary chain and 2 secondary chains: Bob wants to create a DAO on the primary chain (Ethereum) and 2 secondary chains (Binance and Arbitrum One). Bob wants to forward 250 value to each secondary chain, so he must pass the depositChainIds array would be:
```solidity
uint256[] memory depositChainIds = new uint256[](3);
depositChainIds[0] = 1; // Ethereum
depositChainIds[1] = 56; // Binance
depositChainIds[2] = 42161; // Arbitrum One
```
However, there are two issues:
1. Incorrect Division: The value calculation divides by 3 instead of 2, incorrectly including the primary chain.
2. Decreasing Value: The value shrinks with each iteration, while _depositChainIds.length remains constant. For example:
First Iteration:
i = 0 (i < _depositChainIds.length - 1)
value = msg.value / _depositChainIds.length = 500 / 3 = 166
Second Iteration:
i = 1 (i < _depositChainIds.length - 1)
value = msg.value / _depositChainIds.length = 334 / 3 = 111
Only 277 (166 + 111) is forwarded instead of the intended 500. The remaining 223 is left in the factory, withdrawable only by the owner.

title: Token-gated airdrops don't work with ERC20 DAOs
content: The vulnerability is a denial-of-service logic error in the token-gated airdrop claim function. The contract attempts to verify that the DAO token used for gating implements a specific interface by calling IERC20Extended(...).supportsInterface(0xd9b67a26). ERC20 DAO contracts do not inherit ERC165, so they do not provide a supportsInterface function. When the claim function executes for a holder of an ERC20 DAO token, the call to supportsInterface reverts, causing the entire claim transaction to revert before any balance check or token transfer occurs. As a result, eligible users who possess the required amount of DAO tokens see their claim transaction fail with an InsufficientBalance error (or a generic revert), even though their token balance satisfies the gating condition. The issue occurs only when the permission mode is set to TokenGated and the daoToken is an ERC20 DAO; ERC721 DAO tokens work because they inherit ERC165 and therefore implement supportsInterface correctly. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that examined the conditional logic of the claim function. It is hard to notice because interface detection via supportsInterface is common for ERC721 tokens, leading developers to assume the same pattern works for ERC20 tokens. The impact is that the airdrop distribution mechanism cannot serve ERC20 DAO holders, effectively locking the intended reward and breaking the protocol’s business logic that ties token ownership to airdrop eligibility. To remediate, the ERC20 DAO contract should inherit ERC165Upgradeable so that supportsInterface is present, or the claim contract should replace the direct supportsInterface call with a safe check such as ERC165Checker::supportsERC165, which returns false instead of reverting when the token does not implement ERC165. This change restores the expected behavior where the contract checks the holder’s balance and, if sufficient, transfers the airdropped tokens.

title: Imprecise validation of deposit amounts
content: The vulnerability is an imprecise validation of deposit amounts in the minting functions of the DAO contracts. The code checks that the sum of the current DAO token balance (daoBalance) and the incoming deposit (_totalAmount) does not exceed a calculated maximum based on price per token and distribution amount. However, daoBalance is obtained from the contract's current token balance, which is a transient value that can increase when tokens are received or decrease when tokens are transferred out, and in some configurations the deposited tokens are never held by the DAO but by an external Safe wallet, causing daoBalance to be zero. Because the validation relies on this volatile balance instead of a cumulative total of all tokens ever deposited, an attacker can bypass the fundraising cap by moving tokens out of the DAO before making a large deposit or by exploiting the Safe‑wallet configuration where the balance check never applies. This allows minting of governance tokens beyond the intended supply limit, inflating the token total, breaking economic assumptions, and potentially harming token holders and the protocol’s governance. The issue manifests when a user expects a deposit to be rejected after the cap is reached, but the transaction succeeds and the user receives more tokens than should exist, while the UI may show no error and the token supply grows unexpectedly. The bug was discovered during a security audit that examined the minting logic and noticed that the invariant (total raised must not exceed the cap) was enforced using a variable that does not represent the total amount raised over time. The problem is hard to notice because the balance at a single point in time often appears correct, and tests may not cover scenarios where tokens are moved out or sent to a different address. To remediate, the contract should maintain a dedicated storage variable that records the cumulative amount of tokens deposited and use this immutable counter for cap checks, ensuring that the limit cannot be circumvented regardless of token movements or address configurations. This class of bug falls under incorrect accounting or misuse of transient state for invariant enforcement, leading to a mismatch between business logic (fundraising limit) and implementation (balance‑based check).

title: Cross-chain deposits will fail when the deposit token is the native token
content: The vulnerability is a cross‑chain deposit failure that occurs when the DAO is configured to accept the native blockchain token as its deposit asset. The crossChainMint() routine calculates the DAO’s token balance by invoking IERC20(_daoDetails.depositTokenAddress).balanceOf(_daoAddress). This call assumes that the deposit token implements the ERC‑20 interface. However, when the deposit token is the native currency, the contract uses a sentinel address (0xEeeeeEeeeEeEeeEeEeEeeEEEeeeeEeeeeeeeEEeE) that does not correspond to a deployed contract. As a result, the balanceOf() call reverts because there is no contract code at that address. The root cause is the unchecked use of a generic ERC‑20 balance query without a special‑case for native token handling. An attacker does not need to perform any complex steps; any user attempting to buy cross‑chain DAO tokens with the native token will trigger the revert, causing the entire cross‑chain mint transaction on the destination chain to fail. The impact is that legitimate deposits are rejected, users lose the gas spent on the failed transaction, and the protocol’s cross‑chain functionality is effectively disabled for native‑token deposits, undermining user trust and potentially leading to a denial‑of‑service condition for that DAO. The bug manifests only when the DAO’s configuration specifies the native token; for standard ERC‑20 tokens the function works as intended. All participants who rely on cross‑chain minting – token buyers, DAO members, and the protocol itself – are affected. The issue was identified during a manual security audit that examined the token‑handling logic and noticed the hard‑coded sentinel address. It can be hard to spot because the code compiles without errors and the sentinel address is often used as a placeholder for native assets, so developers may assume it behaves like a contract. To remediate, the implementation should detect the sentinel address and, instead of calling balanceOf(), query the native balance of the DAO address using address(_daoAddress).balance (or an equivalent payable check). This conditional handling ensures that both ERC‑20 tokens and the native currency are supported correctly, restoring the expected behavior where a user deposits native tokens and receives the corresponding cross‑chain DAO tokens without transaction reverts.
summary:
The crossChainMint() function calculates the _daoBalance as:
```solidity
uint256 _daoBalance = IERC20(_daoDetails.depositTokenAddress).balanceOf(_daoAddress);
```
The problem is that the cross-chain DAO can be deployed with the native token (defined in the contract as address: 0xEeeeeEeeeEeEeeEeEeEeeEEEeeeeEeeeeeeeEEeE). So, anytime a user tries to buy cross-chain DAO tokens, they will deposit tokens but the transaction on the destination chain will always revert as it will try to perform a balanceOf() call on a non-existing contract.

title: DAO creators can avoid paying creation fees
content: The vulnerability is an fee‑bypass condition in the DAO creation functions createERC20DAO() and createERC721DAO(). Both functions call an internal routine that calculates the required creation fee as createFees multiplied by the length of the _depositChainIds array and then checks that msg.value is at least that amount. However, the contract does not enforce that the array contains at least one element. When a caller supplies an empty array, the length is zero, the calculated fee becomes zero, and the require statement trivially passes because any non‑negative msg.value satisfies the condition. The code later contains an explicit guard that only executes a loop when _depositChainIds.length != 0, which prevents out‑of‑bounds errors but also means the fee check is never re‑evaluated for the empty‑array case. As a result, a malicious or careless user can deploy a DAO on the source chain without sending any native tokens, effectively avoiding the creation fee that the protocol intends to collect. This occurs whenever the creation transaction includes an empty deposit‑chain identifier list, a situation that is not prevented by any input validation. The affected parties are the protocol’s revenue model, DAO creators who expect to pay a fee, and any downstream users who rely on the fee as a deterrent against spam or malicious DAO deployments. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the fee‑verification logic and noticed the missing length check. It can be hard to notice because the fee check itself succeeds (msg.value >= 0) and no revert is triggered, so the transaction appears normal from a user‑interface perspective; the UI may display the expected fee amount while the blockchain records a zero‑fee payment. The impact is a loss of expected fee revenue and the potential for an attacker to flood the system with free DAOs, undermining economic assumptions of the protocol. Conceptually, this is a classic missing‑validation or edge‑case bug where a zero‑length input bypasses a monetary guard. To remediate, the contract should enforce that _depositChainIds.length is greater than zero before calculating or accepting fees, for example by adding require(_depositChainIds.length > 0) or by restructuring the fee logic to charge a minimum fee regardless of array length. This ensures that every DAO creation incurs the intended cost and restores the intended economic protection.

title: Bypassing maxTokensPerUser limits for ERC721 DAO
content: The vulnerability is a reentrancy flaw in the function that sells governance ERC721 tokens. The contract first checks that a caller does not exceed a per‑user token cap, then proceeds to mint the requested tokens one by one using the ERC721 _safeMint routine. Because _safeMint triggers the ERC721 receiver hook on the destination address, a malicious caller can execute code in that hook that calls back into the same purchase function before the internal counters (_tokenIdTracker and the recipient’s balance) are updated. This re‑entry bypasses the cap check, allowing the attacker to acquire additional governance NFTs beyond the intended maximum. The root cause is the classic check‑effect‑interact anti‑pattern: the contract performs the cap verification, then makes an external call (the safe‑mint hook) before it records the state change. The issue manifests only when the minting process invokes an external callback, which is typical for ERC721 safe transfers. From a user’s perspective the contract promises a limit on how many governance tokens a single address may hold, but an attacker can end up with far more, inflating their voting power and potentially draining the token supply intended for the DAO. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the purchase flow and noticed the absence of a reentrancy guard or state update before the external call. It can be hard to notice because the minting appears atomic and the cap check seems to be enforced, yet the hook provides a hidden entry point. To remediate, the contract should either apply a non‑reentrant modifier, move all state updates (incrementing the token ID tracker and adjusting the recipient’s balance) before invoking any external code, or replace _safeMint with a minting method that does not trigger external callbacks. Implementing the check‑effect‑interact pattern or using OpenZeppelin’s ReentrancyGuard will close the reentrancy window and ensure the per‑user limit cannot be circumvented.
summary: When users call buyGovernanceTokenERC721DAO() code performs max cap checks and then calls mintToken(). The issue is that there's no reentrancy guard and when code wants to mint tokens one by one by using _safeMint() user can reenter the Factory contract again in ERC721's hook function and call buyGovernanceTokenERC721DAO() and buy more while bypassing the checks because _tokenIdTracker and balanceOf(_to) are still not updated fully.

title: It is possible to override DAO details
content: The vulnerability is a deterministic address collision that occurs when a DAO token contract is deployed using the CREATE opcode from a Deployer contract whose own address and deployment nonce are the only inputs to the address calculation. Because CREATE derives the new contract address solely from the creator’s address and its current nonce, two separate blockchains that happen to have an identical Deployer contract address will generate the same DAO contract address when the Deployer creates a DAO on each chain. In a multi‑chain deployment scenario, a user may intend to launch the same DAO on chain 1 and chain 2, expecting each instance to be independent. If an attacker can deploy a malicious DAO on chain 2 that reuses the identical address, the cross‑chain factory logic may send a message to chain 1 to instantiate the attacker‑controlled DAO at the exact address that the legitimate user’s DAO occupies. This overwrites the original DAO’s stored details in the factory on chain 1, effectively replacing the user’s DAO metadata with the attacker’s data. The impact is that the legitimate DAO’s governance parameters, token metadata, or other critical information can be silently altered, leading to loss of control, potential fund misdirection, and erosion of trust in the protocol’s cross‑chain guarantees. The condition required is that the Deployer contract address is the same on both chains and that the deployment nonce has not diverged, which is plausible when the same contract bytecode is deployed at the same address on multiple networks. The affected parties include DAO creators, token holders, and any protocol components that rely on the uniqueness of DAO addresses across chains. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the address generation logic and cross‑chain messaging flow. It is hard to notice because the address collision occurs only across chains, not within a single chain, and typical unit tests or on‑chain explorers do not compare addresses between networks. To remediate, the protocol should ensure that DAO contracts receive unique addresses on each chain, for example by incorporating the chain identifier into the address derivation, using CREATE2 with a chain‑specific salt, or deploying a distinct Deployer contract per chain. By guaranteeing that the same DAO cannot be instantiated at the same address on different chains, the overwrite scenario is prevented and the integrity of cross‑chain DAO deployments is preserved.
summary:
Code uses create to deploy DAO token in Deployer contract, so the DAO address only depends on Deployer contract addresses and its deployment nonce. If two chains have the same Deployer contract address then DAO created in those chains would have the same addresses. This would cause congestion when some DAOs deploy on both of those chains. An attacker can use this to override the DAO's details in the other chain. So when a DAO uses multi-chain deployments it would be possible to deploy the same DAO in the cross-chain and the result would be that the real DAO's information in the factory can be overwritten. This is the POC:
1. User1 wants to deploy his DAO in chain1 and chain2. He creates a tx deploys his DAO in chain1 and uses chain2 as the second chain. The DAO address will be determined only by the result of create opcode which is based on Deployer contract address and its deployment nonce.
2. If Chain1 and Chain2 had the same Deployer contract address then the attacker can create a DAO in chain2 whose addresses would be the same and the attacker would set chain1 as a side chain for his DAO.
3. As a result the Factory contract in chain2 would send a message to Chain1 to deploy the attacker-specified DAO in the chain1 in the same DAO address of the User1 and it would cause a rewrite of the User1's DAO.

title: Users can break the lz communication
content: The vulnerability is a gas‑exhaustion failure in the LayerZero communication layer that prevents the contract from recording a failed cross‑chain message. The contract uses the NonBlockingLzApp pattern: when a message is received it calls nonblockingLzReceive via an excessivelySafeCall that forwards the remaining gas (gasleft()) to the receiver. Because of the EVM 63/64 rule, only 1/64 of the gas remains after the call, and the implementation also forwards a fixed 600 000 gas to the endpoint. If the downstream contract’s onERC721Received hook deliberately consumes all of the supplied gas, the call to _blockingLzReceive runs out of gas before it can execute the _storeFailedMessage SSTORE, which costs more than the ~9 000 gas that is left. The SSTORE reverts, the try/catch in the endpoint catches the error and marks the channel as blocked, so subsequent cross‑chain messages are dropped. This can be triggered by a malicious contract that participates as the recipient of a cross‑chain token mint (e.g., a contract that calls crossChainBuy and implements a gas‑wasting onERC721Received). The impact is that a user who attempts to buy DAO tokens across chains sees the transaction revert, the token is not minted, and the cross‑chain pathway becomes permanently blocked until the contract is upgraded or the stored payload is manually cleared. Funds sent with the cross‑chain call may be locked in the contract because the refund address receives no refund when the endpoint reverts. The issue occurs only when the recipient is a contract with a malicious ERC721 receiver hook; honest users who receive tokens in an EOA are not affected. The bug was discovered during a security audit that traced the call stack from commLayer.sendMsg through endpoint.send to the ERC721 safe mint logic and identified the insufficient gas left for the failure‑handling SSTORE. It is hard to notice because the failure happens deep inside the LayerZero SDK and manifests as a generic “payload stored” event rather than an obvious out‑of‑gas error at the user level. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “insufficient gas for error handling” or “gas‑driven denial‑of‑service” bugs, where a contract assumes that enough gas will always be available to record a failure but the EVM gas‑forwarding semantics invalidate that assumption. From the user’s perspective the UI shows a transaction that appears to succeed until the cross‑chain step, then the token balance remains unchanged and no refund is received, leading to confusion and loss of funds. The recommended fix is to avoid using safeMint, which triggers the onERC721Received hook, and instead use a direct mint that does not invoke external code, thereby guaranteeing that the failure‑handling path always has sufficient gas. Alternatively, the contract could increase the gas buffer supplied to the endpoint or redesign the failure storage to use a cheaper operation. In short, the contract must not rely on the assumption that the non‑blocking receive path will always have enough gas to store a failed payload; it must either provide a larger gas stipend or eliminate the external call that can be abused.

title: User address may not be accessible on other chains
content: The vulnerability stems from an incorrect assumption that a smart‑wallet or contract address generated on one blockchain will be identically controllable on another blockchain when using cross‑chain functions. This assumption fails because deterministic address creation mechanisms such as CREATE2 rely on the deployer address, the salt, and chain‑specific rules; any variation—such as the deployer not existing on the destination chain, an unavailable or different salt, or chain‑specific address derivation (for example zkSync always produces a different address even with identical parameters)—can cause the resulting address to differ. When a user invokes crossChainBuy, the function sets the receiver of newly minted DAO tokens to msg.sender, expecting that the same address on the destination chain is owned by the caller. If the address does not resolve to a key the user controls, the tokens are transferred to an address that the user cannot access, effectively making the funds disappear. Similarly, createERC20DAO and createERC721DAO copy the admin list from the source chain to the destination chain’s Safe contract; if those admin addresses are not owned on the destination chain, the admins lose the ability to manage the Safe, preventing withdrawals or any other privileged actions and locking the DAO’s assets. The impact is loss of tokens, inability to control DAO funds, and a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees, which can erode user trust. The issue manifests only when cross‑chain operations are performed on chains where address equivalence is not guaranteed, making it hard to notice during single‑chain testing because the same code works correctly on the source chain. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the cross‑chain logic and identified the mismatch between address generation assumptions and actual blockchain behaviour. Mitigation requires either restricting cross‑chain operations to externally owned accounts that can guarantee address equivalence, or allowing callers to explicitly specify a receiver address for each destination chain. For DAO creation, the protocol should let the creator provide a distinct admin set per chain rather than copying the source‑chain admin list. By removing the implicit reliance on identical addresses, the protocol can ensure that tokens are sent to addresses the user controls and that admin functions remain accessible, preserving the intended financial flows and governance capabilities.
summary: A smart wallet is deployed in one chain and has a specific address. But it is possible that trying to deploy a smart wallet with the same address won't be possible on other chains. For example, if the deployer is not available on the destination chain, or if it is not possible to set the same salt/noce. Also on chains like zkSync that create operations will always lead to different addresses with the same deployment parameters. In any of these cases, the user won't be able to control the same address on both chains. Some cross-chain functions assume that the same address in the source chain will also be controlled on the destination chain. crossChainBuy() sets the receiver of the DAO tokens to msg.sender. The tokens might be sent to an address they don't control. createERC20DAO() and createERC721DAO() set the same admins as the source chain for their cross-chain Safe. So admins might not be able to control the Safe, and not be able to transfer locked funds in the DAO (among other admin functions).

title: No refund nor retry mechanism for failing cross-chain transactions
content: The vulnerability is an absence of a refund or retry mechanism for cross‑chain transactions that can revert on the destination chain. When a user calls crossChainBuy on the source chain, they lock tokens and pay fees. The protocol then forwards a message to the destination chain where crossChainMint attempts to mint DAO tokens. If any of the destination‑chain validation rules (such as insufficient DAO balance, exceeding per‑user token caps, distribution limits, whitelist checks, token‑gating, or an invalid deposit token address) cause crossChainMint to revert, the message is dropped and the user’s locked tokens remain on the source chain with no way to retrieve them. The root cause is that the contract assumes the off‑chain validation performed before sending the message is sufficient, while the true source of truth resides on the destination chain; there is no on‑chain escrow release or retry logic tied to the message status. An attacker or even an honest user can trigger the revert simply by providing values that become invalid after state changes on the destination chain, for example when another user’s earlier transaction consumes the remaining DAO supply or when the per‑user cap is reached. Exploitation consists of submitting a cross‑chain buy that appears valid at submission time, then waiting for the destination chain state to change (or deliberately causing it) so that the mint reverts. The user sees no DAO tokens appear, their balance on the source chain is reduced, and the UI may show a successful deposit but no received tokens, leading to “funds disappear” or “refund missing” symptoms. The impact is loss of user funds and erosion of trust in the protocol, as users cannot recover the deposited tokens and cannot retry the operation. The condition occurs whenever cross‑chain messages are processed without a guarantee of atomicity or a fallback path, which is typical for many bridge‑style designs that rely on optimistic execution. All participants—regular users, token holders, and the DAO itself—are affected because the protocol’s accounting becomes inconsistent: total deposited tokens no longer match minted DAO tokens. The issue was discovered during a manual security review that compared source‑chain validation logic with destination‑chain minting requirements and identified the mismatch. It is hard to notice because the transaction on the source chain reports success, the UI may not display an error, and the revert happens on a different chain where the user does not directly observe the failure. The recommended remediation is to introduce a deterministic escrow that can be released back to the sender when the destination‑chain mint fails, and to add a retry mechanism that re‑queues the message or allows the user to invoke a retry function after the revert condition clears. In generic terms, this is a cross‑chain atomicity violation and a missing compensation path, a class of bug where state changes on one chain are not safely rolled back on another, leading to unrecoverable asset loss.
summary: When performing cross-chain transactions, the transaction may always revert to the destination chain under certain circumstances or for certain values. Users will deposit tokens or pay fees in the source chain that will be lost when those reverts occur on the destination chain and can't be recovered by them. For the cross-chain buy operation: The user will deposit tokens on the source chain via crossChainBuy(). If crossChainMint() reverts, no DAO token will be minted. This may happen for different reasons: If the amount is not valid (depends on DAO balance, token price, and distribution amount in the DAO chain). If maxTokensPerUser would be surpassed. If distributionAmount would be surpassed. If the total deposit for the user is below or above a limit. If the user is not whitelisted. If token gating is applied. User errors. It is important to note that most of these conditions depend on moving values, and any off-chain validation might be true when sending the source chain transaction, but may not hold when the cross-chain transaction is executed. Validations on the source chain would not be sufficient, as the source of truth is ultimately on the chain to which the DAO contract was deployed. In addition, this could theoretically happen for cross-chain DAO deployments too, but not likely. A possible revert might be on an invalid _depositTokenAddress that can't be queried for its decimals() (although the deployment wouldn't make sense with an invalid address). Other checks are performed in _createERC20DAO() or _createERC721DAO(), but with the same values as for the source chain, so they would have reverted on the original transaction. Other statements in the destination chain should not revert but bear in mind that they would lead to the scenario described in this report.

title: Adversary can block the counterpart deployment of cross-chain DAOs
content: The vulnerability is a nonce‑collision race condition that allows an attacker to block the creation of a cross‑chain DAO counterpart. The deploySAFE() function attempts to create a Gnosis Safe proxy on the destination chain by calling SafeProxyFactory.createProxyWithNonce() inside a try/catch block. If a Safe with the same nonce already exists, the call reverts and the catch block re‑throws the error, causing the whole transaction to fail. The root cause is that the nonce used for the proxy is derived deterministically from the DAO address and is therefore predictable. An adversary can pre‑emptively call SafeProxyFactory.createProxyWithNonce() with the same nonce and identical initializer parameters while the LayerZero cross‑chain message is in flight. Because the proxy address is already occupied, the subsequent call from deploySAFE() hits the catch clause and reverts, preventing the Safe from being deployed on the destination chain. This makes the cross‑chain DAO creation transaction revert, so the counterpart DAO never appears and users on that chain cannot interact with the DAO (e.g., they cannot buy the ERC‑20 token). The attack can also be used as a griefing vector on the source chain by front‑running the deployment transaction, causing the DAO creation to fail on both chains. The issue primarily affects DAO creators, token holders, and any protocol component that relies on the automatic deployment of the Safe proxy across chains. It was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the control flow of the deploySAFE() function and noticed that a revert inside a catch block propagates to the outer transaction. The problem is subtle because the failure manifests as a generic “Safe proxy creation failed” error, which may be interpreted as a transient bug rather than an active attack. To remediate, the contract should avoid the try/catch pattern, pre‑compute the expected proxy address, check whether code already exists at that address, and only invoke createProxyWithNonce() when the address is empty. This eliminates the reliance on a mutable nonce and prevents an attacker from forcing a revert by pre‑deploying the proxy. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of deterministic‑nonce replay attacks that break cross‑chain contract orchestration, leading to missing contracts, zero balances where a DAO should exist, and a broken user experience where a user expects a newly created DAO but sees nothing on the destination chain.
summary: The deploySAFE() function in Deployer attempts to create a Safe for the DAO via SafeProxyFactory::createProxyWithNonce(). It uses a try/catch pattern, but it will always revert if another Safe with the same nonce was created beforehand on that chain. Notice how a revert inside a catch block will make the whole transaction revert: uint256 nonce = getNonce(_daoAddress); try ISafe(safe).createProxyWithNonce(singleton, _initializer, nonce) returns (address _deployedSafe) { SAFE = _deployedSafe; } catch Error(string memory reason) { nonce = getNonce(_daoAddress); revert SafeProxyCreationFailed(reason); } catch { revert SafeProxyCreationFailed("Safe proxy creation failed"); } while (SAFE == address(0)); An adversary can directly call SafeProxyFactory::createProxyWithNonce() on the destination chain while the cross-chain transaction is being processed by LayerZero. Using the same nonce generated for the victim _daoAddress() and the same initialize parameters will guarantee it will create a Safe with the same address. This is problematic since it will make the cross-chain transaction revert when trying to execute deploySAFE() in createCrossChainERC20DAO(): function createCrossChainERC20DAO(...) { address _safe = IDeployer(deployer).deploySAFE(_admins, _safeThreshold, _daoAddress); _createERC20DAO(...); ccDetails[_daoAddress] = CrossChainDetails(_commLayerId, _depositChainIds, false, msg.sender, _onlyAllowWhitelist); It will be impossible to finish the creation of the DAO counterpart on the destination chain, and buy operations will not be available there. Note: There's also a secondary, less severe impact of this finding that involves frontrunning the transaction on the source chain, and preventing the creation of any DAO altogether. In this case, there is no risk as no DAO was created on any chain, but it can be considered a griefing attack. The recommendation covers this scenario as well.

title: Block of GMXVault by using GMX UI fee
content: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that allows an attacker to permanently block the GMXVault contract by abusing the UI fee receiver mechanism on the GMX protocol. The root cause is that the GMXVault’s processDepositFailure routine builds a withdrawal request that inherits the current refundee address (self.refundee) as the UI fee receiver for the GMX removeLiquidity call. This refundee is set to the original depositor when the deposit succeeds and is never overwritten when a deposit later fails. Because the UI fee receiver is paid a percentage of the swapped tokens during a withdrawal, an attacker can register his own address as the UI fee receiver and configure an arbitrarily high fee percentage. When a deposit is marked as failed, the keeper invokes processDepositFailure, which calculates the expected tokenA and tokenB amounts from the LP tokens, applies the slippage check, and then calls GMXWorker.removeLiquidity. The high UI fee reduces the net amount received from the swap, causing the slippage check to fail and the GMX withdrawal to revert. The revert leaves the vault in the Deposit_Failed state, preventing any further deposits, withdrawals, or emergency actions, effectively freezing all user funds in the vault. This condition occurs only when a deposit fails and the processDepositFailure path is executed, but an attacker can deliberately trigger a failed deposit or wait for a natural failure to exploit the bug. All users of the protocol, including depositors and liquidity providers, are affected because their assets become inaccessible and the vault cannot process new operations. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the interaction between GMXVault and the GMX UI fee logic, and it is subtle because the UI fee receiver is not normally considered part of the slippage calculation, making the bug easy to overlook in functional testing. To remediate the problem, the contract should avoid using the UI fee receiver for withdrawal requests, for example by setting the UI fee receiver address to the zero address for both deposits and withdrawals, or by resetting the refundee before calling removeLiquidity so that the fee does not interfere with the slippage check. This change eliminates the ability for an attacker to manipulate the fee percentage and restores the vault’s ability to recover from failed deposits without becoming permanently blocked.
summary:
Attacker can block GMXVault by setting registering himself as ui fee receiver on GMX and causing slippage check to always revert, when processDepositFailure is called.
In case if deposit has decided to be failed, that means that processDepositFailure function will be called by keeper in order to withdraw already deposited LP tokens and send received tokens to the depositor.
processDepositFailure function calculates amount of tokenA and tokenB that it can get in exchange of LP tokens and also consider slippage. So in case if smaller amount will be received when GMX will do swap, then GMX withdrawal will revert. In order to send request to GMX removeLiquidity function is called, which will eventually call GMXWorker.removeLiquidity. This function sets self.refundee as uiFeeReceiver to the GMX withdraw request. In this case, self.refundee will be previous depositor, as this value is not changed by processDepositFailure function.
Now let's check what is uiFeeReceiver on GMX. This is actually entity that will receive percentage of your swaps on GMX. For withdrawing it will receive fee for both long and short tokens. Amount of fee depends on what ui fee receiver has provided to himself.
So attacker can register himself as ui fee recipient and set his percentage high enough, so when processDepositFailure is called on his deposit, then created withdrawal request will always revert with slippage error. As result system will stuck in Deposit_Failed status and will not be able work normally and emergency operations will be needed.
GMXVault will be blocked.

title: try-catch does not store the state when it is reverted
content: An issue exists in the withdrawal flow of a GMX‑based vault where the repayment of borrowed assets is performed inside a try‑catch block. When the post‑withdrawal checks (afterWithdrawChecks) revert, the EVM rolls back all state changes that occurred inside the try‑catch, including the repayment of the loan. The vault’s status is updated to Withdraw_Failed, but the borrowed amount remains outstanding. A keeper is then expected to call a recovery function (processWithdrawFailure) that, according to the current implementation, attempts to borrow the same amounts again from the lending vaults before trying to restore the withdrawn tokens. Because the original repayment never happened, this second borrowing creates additional debt that is never repaid, inflating the vault’s leverage. An attacker can deliberately cause the afterWithdrawChecks to revert by submitting an unrealistically high minimum withdrawal amount, causing the revert every time. By repeatedly invoking the failure‑handling routine, the attacker can force the vault to borrow repeatedly, draining the liquidity of the lending vaults, raising utilization rates and borrowing costs, and potentially leaving other users with reduced borrowing capacity. The vulnerability was discovered during a functional audit that exercised edge‑case withdrawal parameters and observed that the vault’s debt increased after a failed withdrawal. The bug is subtle because the revert only affects the internal try‑catch scope, while the external status flag suggests the operation failed, leading developers to assume the loan was already repaid. The proper fix is to remove the borrowing logic from the failure‑handling path or to ensure that repayment is performed outside of any revertible context, so that a failed after‑withdrawal check does not trigger an additional loan. In summary, the contract suffers from a state‑reset on revert combined with erroneous re‑borrowing, which allows an attacker to artificially increase debt and leverage, effectively stealing liquidity from the lending vaults.

title: `GMXVault` can be blocked by a malicious actor
content: The issue is a denial‑of‑service condition that can permanently block a GMXVault when a deposit is cancelled and the contract attempts to push a refund to an address that cannot receive native ether. The vulnerability originates from the depositNative workflow: a user calls the payable function, the contract forwards the ether to the WNT wrapper and then marks the vault status as Deposit before invoking the external GMX exchange router to add liquidity. If the router rejects the operation – for example because the caller supplied an extreme slippage value – the router calls back into the vault’s processDepositCancellation routine. That routine tries to return the original ether to the depositor using a low‑level call (self.depositCache.user.call{value: address(this).balance}('')). When the depositor is a contract that deliberately rejects incoming ether (an unpayable contract), the call returns false, the require statement reverts, and the vault never reaches the code that would reset its status to Open. As a result the vault remains stuck in the Deposit state, preventing any further deposits or withdrawals. The impact is that the vault becomes unusable, locking user funds that are already inside the vault and halting any new liquidity provision for the protocol. The condition occurs only when a deposit is cancelled – typically due to a high slippage setting – and the refund recipient cannot accept ether. The affected parties are the vault’s users, the protocol that relies on the vault for liquidity, and any downstream contracts that expect the vault to be operational. The problem was uncovered during a security audit that included a crafted test contract (BlockerContract) that cannot receive ether; the test demonstrated that after a cancelled deposit the vault status stayed at Deposit and the contract’s balance decreased because the refund failed. The bug is subtle because the vault appears normal during successful deposits, and the status flag is only examined after a failure, making the lock‑up easy to miss in routine operation. To remediate the issue the refund logic should be changed from a push model to a pull model, allowing the depositor to withdraw the refunded ether at their own convenience, and the vault should ensure that its status is reset to Open even if the refund transfer fails, for example by using a safe‑transfer pattern or by catching the failure and proceeding with status restoration.
summary:
GMXVault can be blocked by malicious actor if he made a depositNative call with unpayable contract and the deposit then cancelled by the GMX exchange router (3rd party).
Users can deposit native tokens in vaults that either of its token pair is a WNT (wrapped native token) by calling GMXVault.depositNative payable function with the required deposit parameters (such as token, amount, minimum share amount, slippage & execution fees), then this function will invoke GMXDeposit.deposit with a msg.value equals the amount that the user wants to deposit + execution fees.
In GMXDeposit.deposit: various checks are made to ensure the sanity of the deposit parameters and the elligibility of the user to deposit, and to calculate the required tokenA & tokenB needed to deposit in the GMX protocol, then the sent native tokens are deposited in the WNT contract and an equivalent amount of WNT is transferred to the vault.
And before the call is made to the GMXManager.addLiquidity (where a call is going to be made to the GMX.exchangeRouter contract) to add liquidity; the status of the vault is checked if it's Open, if yes; then the status of the vault is set to Deposit so that no more deposits or withdrawls can be made (the vault will be blocked until the operation succeeds).
So if the operation succeeds in the GMX exchange router; the vault callback will invoke preocessDeposit function to finish the process and update the vault status to Open.
And if the operation of adding liquidity is cancelled by the GMX exchange router (3rd party); the vault callback will invoke processDepositCancellation function to rollback the process by repaying the lendingVaults debts and paying back the native tokens sent by the user, then update the vault status to Open so that the vault is open again for deposits and withdrawals.
Usually the deposit (liquidity addition to GMX protocol) fails if the user sets a very high slippage parameter when making a deposit (dp.slippage).

How can this be exploited to block the vault?
Imagine the following scenario:
If a malicious user deploys an unpayable contract (doesn't receive native tokens) and makes a call to the GMXVault.depositNative function with a very high slippage to ensure that the deposit will be cancelled by the GMX exchange router.
So when the deposit is cancelled and the vault callback processDepositCancellation function is invoked by the router; it will revert as it will try to send back the native tokens to the user who tried to make the deposit (which is the unpayable contract in our case).
And the status of the vault will be stuck in the Deposit state; so no more deposits or withdrawals can be made and the vault will be disabled.
The same scenario will happen if the user got blocklisted later by the deposited token contract (tokenA or tokenB), but the propability of this happening is very low as the GMX exchange router will add liquidity in two transactions with a small time separation between them!

The vault will be blocked as it will be stuck in the Deposit state; so no more deposits or withdrawals can be made.

title: Incorrect Execution Fee Refund address on Failed Deposits or withdrawals in Strategy Vaults
content: The vulnerability is a misdirection of the execution‑fee refund when a deposit or withdrawal in a Strategy Vault fails. The contract stores the address that should receive any leftover execution fee in a variable called refundee. During a normal deposit the refundee is set to the original caller (the depositor) because that caller also pays the fee. However, when the deposit or withdrawal later fails a keeper – an off‑chain actor that monitors the vault – calls a failure‑handling function (processDepositFailure or processWithdrawFailure) and pays the gas for the reversal. The failure‑handling code never updates the refundee variable, so the contract still thinks the original depositor (or withdrawer) is the rightful recipient. Consequently the excess execution fee that the keeper has just spent is sent back to the user instead of the keeper. The root cause is the omission of a self.refundee = payable(msg.sender) assignment in the failure paths, leaving the beneficiary unchanged from the initial deposit call. An attacker does not need to craft special inputs; the bug is triggered automatically whenever a deposit or withdrawal fails the vault‑health check and a keeper invokes the failure function. The impact is a systematic loss of execution‑fee refunds for keepers, which reduces their incentive to monitor the vault and can lead to under‑compensation for the gas they spend. Users may notice an unexpected increase in their balance (a small fee credit) that does not correspond to any action they performed, while keepers see a shortfall in the fee they expected to be reimbursed.
