The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the reward accounting logic with the intended vesting model and identified that the contract assumes every user started staking when rewardPerToken was zero. It is subtle because the contract still updates claimableRewards and appears to respect vesting rates, so the over‑payment is not obvious from a superficial inspection or from normal UI output; users simply see a large reward balance after claiming, which may be interpreted as a bonus rather than a bug. The bug belongs to the class of “reward‑per‑token accounting errors” or “incorrect reward debt handling” where the reward debt (the amount of reward per token already accounted for) is not recorded for new participants. To fix the issue, the contract should store a snapshot of the current rewardPerToken at the moment a user stakes (often called rewardDebt or userRewardDebt) and subtract this snapshot from future per‑token calculations, ensuring that only newly accrued rewards are credited to the staker. This adjustment aligns the reward calculation with the intended business logic that rewards accrue only after a stake, restores fairness, and prevents the protocol from unintentionally distributing historic rewards to newcomers.

title: Blacklisted User Can Transfer Tokens via Approved Addresses
content: The vulnerability is an incomplete blacklist enforcement in the token contract’s transferFrom function. The contract is designed to prevent blacklisted addresses from moving tokens, but the implementation only verifies that the caller (msg.sender) is not blacklisted. It does not check the actual token owner specified by the from parameter. As a result, a user who has been added to the blacklist can still have their tokens transferred if they previously granted an allowance to another address. The approved spender, which is not blacklisted, can invoke transferFrom and move the blacklisted user’s balance because the contract’s notBlacklisted modifier validates only the caller. This flaw arises from a missing subject check in the authorization logic, a classic case of incomplete access‑control validation. Exploitation proceeds as follows: (1) a legitimate token holder approves a third‑party address to spend a certain amount; (2) the holder is later blacklisted; (3) the approved address calls transferFrom, passing the blacklisted holder as the from address; (4) the contract checks only that the caller is not blacklisted, allowing the transfer to succeed. The impact is that the intended freeze of blacklisted funds is ineffective; blacklisted tokens can still be moved, undermining anti‑money‑laundering measures, enabling stolen assets to be drained, and breaking the protocol’s security guarantees. The issue manifests whenever an allowance exists for a blacklisted account and the contract relies on a single‑parameter blacklist check. Users who expect their tokens to be frozen will see unexpected balance reductions or see tokens appear in other accounts, contradicting the promised behavior. The problem was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s blacklist modifiers, where the reviewer noticed that transferFrom did not reference the from address in the notBlacklisted check. Because the function already performs allowance verification, the missing blacklist check can be easily overlooked, making the bug subtle. To remediate, the transferFrom logic should be updated so that both the caller and the token owner are validated against the blacklist, either by extending the notBlacklisted modifier to accept two addresses or by adding an explicit require statement that rejects transfers when the from address is blacklisted. This brings the contract in line with the intended security model, ensuring that blacklisted accounts cannot move tokens directly or indirectly through approved spenders.
summary:
The contract implements a blacklist mechanism to prevent certain addresses from performing to-
ken transfers. However, the implementation contains a critical flaw in the transferFrom() function
where it only checks if the caller (msg.sender) is blacklisted, not the actual token owner (from ad-
dress). This allows a blacklisted user to transfer tokens if they had previously approved another ad-
dress before being blacklisted. The approved address can then call transferFrom() to move the
blacklisted user’s tokens, since the modifier only verifies the caller’s status. The vulnerability stems
from incomplete blacklist checks in the transfer authorization logic.

This vulnerability severely compromises the effectiveness of the blacklist feature. Malicious actors
who get blacklisted can still move their funds through pre-approved addresses, defeating the pur-
pose of the security measure. In scenarios where tokens need to be frozen, this flaw allows contin-
ued token movement, potentially enabling money laundering or helping attackers escape with stolen
funds.

title: Non monotonic L2 block timestamps
content: The vulnerability consists of non‑monotonic block timestamps on the layer‑2 chain. The L2 protocol derives timestamps from two independent sources: timestamps attached to sequencer‑generated blueprint blocks, which the sequencer can set arbitrarily, and timestamps copied from the underlying L1 block for blocks that originate from the delayed inbox. Because the delayed‑inbox blocks are inserted after a sequencer blueprint block, the L1 timestamp may be lower than the previously recorded blueprint timestamp, breaking the requirement that block timestamps be strictly increasing. This inconsistency is the root cause: the protocol does not enforce a monotonic ordering when merging the two timestamp streams. An attacker who controls or influences the sequencer can deliberately set a high timestamp for a blueprint block and then allow a delayed‑inbox block with a lower L1 timestamp to be appended, creating a backward jump in time. Any smart contract that relies on block.timestamp or block.number to enforce time‑based conditions—such as vesting schedules, token lock‑ups, auctions, interest accrual, or deadline checks—may observe a timestamp that appears to move backwards. When this happens the contract logic can incorrectly consider a deadline already passed, release funds early, or, conversely, prevent a function from executing because the required time has not been reached. From the user’s perspective the symptoms are visible as unexpected behavior: a user may receive no payout from a vesting contract, an auction may close prematurely, or a time‑locked withdrawal may fail with “deadline passed” even though the wall‑clock time has not advanced. The issue manifests whenever a delayed‑inbox block follows a sequencer blueprint block, which is a common situation in normal operation of the L2. All participants—regular users, token holders, and protocol operators—are potentially affected because the bug violates the fundamental accounting assumption that time only moves forward. The problem was discovered during a formal security audit that examined the timestamp handling logic and identified the lack of a strict‑greater‑than check between successive blocks. The bug can be hard to notice because most blockchain explorers display timestamps without highlighting non‑monotonic sequences, and many contracts only fail under specific edge‑case timing conditions. The recommended mitigation is to enforce a strict monotonic increase for every new block timestamp, for example by using the previous block’s timestamp as a lower bound and allowing only values greater than that (or at most previous timestamp plus one). This aligns the L2 implementation with the Ethereum specification that requires strictly increasing timestamps, eliminating the possibility of time‑regression attacks and restoring correct behavior for all time‑dependent smart contracts.
summary:
The L2 blocks use two different sources for the block timestamps:
• The blocks produced from the sequencer's blueprints use the blueprint timestamp, which are set arbitrary by the sequencer.
• The blocks produced from the delayed inbox base on the L1 block timestamp.
It is almost certain that the blocks produced from the delayed inbox break monotonicity of block timestamps.

title: Missing Incident Response Plan
content: The vulnerability consists of the absence of a documented incident response (IR) framework for the Thala protocol. Because no formal procedures, playbooks, or communication templates exist, the team lacks a predefined way to detect, contain, and remediate security events that require rapid, coordinated action. This gap originates from a missing governance artifact rather than a code defect, and it manifests when an incident such as a smart‑contract exploit, private‑key compromise, front‑end malicious deployment, or social‑media account takeover occurs. In such time‑critical situations the lack of a war‑room structure, role assignments, and clear escalation paths leads to delayed detection, uncoordinated team actions, inconsistent external communications, and missed opportunities to freeze contracts or recover funds. From a user perspective the symptoms may include unexpected downtime, no notification that a contract has been paused, funds becoming inaccessible, or refunds not being processed, creating a perception that the protocol is unreliable or even malicious. The issue was identified during a security audit that reviewed operational readiness and noted that the organization had no written IR plan, making the risk hard to spot because the smart‑contract code itself appears functional; the weakness only becomes apparent under stress‑testing or real‑world attacks. The problem belongs to the class of governance and operational security deficiencies where procedural controls are missing, violating the business assumption that incidents can be handled promptly and transparently. To remediate, the protocol should adopt a comprehensive, documented incident response plan that defines war‑room procedures, role‑based responsibilities, communication protocols, containment and recovery steps, and post‑incident review processes, and should be exercised regularly through tabletop drills to ensure the team can act effectively when an actual breach occurs.
summary:
Thala lacks documented incident response procedures and playbooks. The lack of formal procedures increases risk of delayed or ineffective response during time-critical situations, especially for incidents requiring different handling than past experiences.
Without documented procedures, the team faces increased risks of:
• Delayed detection and response to security incidents.
• Uncoordinated team actions during critical moments.
• Inconsistent external communications.
• Missed opportunities for fund recovery.
• Extended downtime from delayed decisions.
• Impaired judgment under high-stress situations.

title: Alert System Coverage and Classification
content: The vulnerability consists of an insufficiently designed monitoring and alerting framework that fails to reliably detect and prioritize critical protocol actions. The root cause is a loosely defined classification scheme that mixes high‑severity events such as administrative function calls, pool creation, and balance invariant violations with low‑importance informational messages, and routes them through shared communication channels without clear escalation rules. Because the system does not generate alerts for several key actions, an attacker or a faulty contract can modify protocol state— for example by creating a new pool or invoking an admin function that changes total value locked— without triggering any immediate notification. This lack of coverage allows the malicious change to persist unnoticed until a manual check occurs, potentially leading to a rapid TVL drop or other financial impact. The impact is observed as a sudden decrease in reported TVL, missing or delayed warnings, and users seeing their balances appear unchanged while the protocol’s underlying state has been altered. The condition occurs whenever a critical event happens in the protocol while the alert system is configured to treat all messages equally, resulting in alert fatigue and delayed response. All participants— token holders, liquidity providers, and the protocol operators—are affected because the delayed detection can cause loss of funds, reduced confidence, and operational downtime. The issue was discovered during a post‑mortem of a November 2024 incident where TVL‑drop alerts were incorrectly classified as routine changes, causing a several‑hour investigation lag. The problem is hard to notice because the alert channels continue to receive messages, giving a false sense of coverage, and because the misclassification does not raise an obvious error flag. Conceptually, the fix requires implementing comprehensive alert coverage for both critical and informational events, establishing a structured classification hierarchy that separates urgent alerts from routine notifications, defining clear triage and escalation procedures, and enforcing evidence‑based closure of critical alerts. By aligning the monitoring system with the business logic that expects immediate detection of state‑changing actions, the protocol can prevent silent fund disappearance, ensure that refunds or balance updates are correctly reported, and maintain trust in the system’s accounting integrity.
summary:
The system lacks monitoring for several protocol actions:
• Administrative function calls.
• Pool creation and management.
• Balance invariant violations.
Thala's alert system could be improved with a more structured classification and triage system. The November 2024 incident highlighted how TVL drop alerts were mistakenly misclassified as routine changes, delaying investigation by several hours. At the time of the incident, alerts were split between alerts-activity and alerts-protocol channels without clear prioritization or investigation requirements.
Additionally, alerts in the protocol channel mix critical and non-critical items, contributing to alert fatigue and reducing effectiveness of the notification system.

title: Rewards can be drained because of lack of access control
content: The vulnerability resides in the reward distribution functionof the liquidation pool, which is declared as an external payable method without any access control. Because the function can be invoked by any address, an attacker can call it directly and supply a crafted list of asset descriptors that bypass the normal validation performed during a legitimate liquidation. The root cause is the missing onlyManager (or similar) modifier that should restrict calls to the pool manager contract, combined with the fact that the function trusts the supplied asset data for price feeds and token addresses. An attacker who holds a negligible stake can construct fake asset entries whose token contract address and Chainlink price feed address point to the attacker’s contract, set the collateral rate to one and the hundred‑percent parameter to zero, and calculate asset amounts that are proportional to the total stake divided by the attacker’s tiny stake. This manipulation inflates the portion variable, causing the rewards mapping to be credited with amounts far larger than the pool’s actual balances. The attacker then calls the claimRewards function and drains virtually all assets from the pool, leaving other stakers with little or no reward. The exploit can be performed after any liquidation event, because the pool’s assets become available for distribution and the distributeAssets function is publicly callable. All participants who have staked in the pool – including regular users, delegators, and the protocol itself – are affected because the expected reward distribution is subverted and the pool’s capital is depleted. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the liquidation flow and noticed that the distributeAssets function lacked any restriction on the caller, a pattern that is easy to overlook when the function is only used internally by the manager contract. The bug is hard to notice in normal operation because the function works correctly when called by the manager, and the abnormal call path is not exercised in typical usage. To remediate the problem, the function should be protected with an onlyManager modifier (or equivalent access control), and additional validation should be added to ensure that asset token addresses and price feed contracts correspond to known, trusted contracts before performing calculations. This prevents arbitrary payloads from being used to manipulate reward calculations and restores the integrity of the accounting logic that guarantees each staker receives a share of the liquidation proceeds proportional to their stake.

title: Looping over unbounded `pendingStakes` array can lead to permanent DoS and frozen funds
content: The vulnerability is an unbounded iteration over the contract's pendingStakes array that can be filled with arbitrarily many tiny entries, causing gas exhaustion and a permanent denial-of-service that freezes user funds. The root cause is the use of a dynamic array to store pending stakes together with functions such as consolidatePendingStakes, distributeFees and decreasePosition that iterate over the entire array without any size limit or pagination. Each iteration also performs a costly delete operation that shifts the remaining elements, making the gas cost grow linearly with the number of entries. An attacker can exploit this by repeatedly calling increasePosition with a minimal amount (for example 1 wei) from many addresses, thereby spamming the pendingStakes array with dust entries. When a legitimate user later calls decreasePosition to withdraw their stake, the contract must first run consolidatePendingStakes and distributeFees, which now have to loop over a very large array. The block gas limit is reached, the transaction reverts, and the user receives no tokens even though the UI may show a pending withdrawal. The impact is that all users of the liquidation pool are unable to retrieve their funds, effectively locking the assets in the contract and undermining confidence in the protocol. The issue occurs whenever the pendingStakes length grows beyond what can be processed within a single block, which can be triggered at any time by a malicious actor. It affects every participant holding positions, as well as the protocol operators who rely on the ability to settle stakes. The problem was discovered during a security audit by CodeHawks, who created a proof-of-concept test that fills the array with 100 dust entries and observes an out-of-gas failure. The bug is hard to notice in normal testing because small deposits appear harmless and the loops work correctly with a modest number of entries; only when the array becomes large does the gas limit manifest. This class of bug is commonly referred to as an unbounded loop or gas-griefing vulnerability, where on-chain data structures are iterated without bounds. From a user perspective the symptoms are failed withdrawals, out-of-gas reverts, and balances that remain unchanged despite a pending stake. The contract violates the business logic that users should be able to withdraw their deposited assets at any time. A proper fix would replace the array with a mapping or another data structure that allows constant-time access, introduce pagination or batch processing for any required iteration, add a minimum deposit check to prevent dust spamming, and expose a dedicated external function to clean up old pending stakes without incurring the full withdrawal gas cost.

title: swap fees going to the liquidation pool manager contract will be accounted for as part of the liquidation amount
content: The vulnerability is an accounting miscalculation in the liquidation workflow where swap fees that are transferred to the liquidation pool manager contract are mistakenly added to the amount declared as liquidated assets. This occurs because the fee handling logic does not separate earned swap fees from the principal collateral that is supposed to be liquidated, causing the protocol to treat the fee balance as part of the borrower’s debt. An attacker or any participant who can trigger a liquidation can exploit this by initiating a liquidation transaction; the contract will compute the liquidation amount using the inflated balance that includes the swap fees, and the liquidator will receive a payout that contains both the legitimate collateral and the erroneously counted fees. The impact is a net loss for the protocol: funds that should remain in the fee pool are transferred out as if they were part of the borrower’s debt, leading to a reduction of the protocol’s revenue and a distortion of its accounting invariants. The issue manifests whenever a liquidation is performed after swap activity that generated fees, i.e., when the liquidation pool manager holds a non‑zero fee balance. All parties that rely on correct accounting – the protocol treasury, liquidity providers, and users expecting accurate liquidation outcomes – are affected. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the liquidation amount calculation and noticed that the fee variable was included in the total debt without proper segregation. Because the symptom is a subtle shift in the liquidation payout rather than an outright failure, it can be hard to notice without detailed balance checks or comparison against expected fee accruals. Conceptually, the fix is to treat swap fees as a separate accounting bucket and exclude them from the liquidation amount calculation, ensuring that only the borrower’s outstanding collateral is considered for liquidation. This class of bug belongs to fee double‑counting or liquidation amount inflation, which violates the protocol’s accounting assumptions that fees are earned revenue and should not be reclaimed during debt enforcement. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a higher liquidation reward than anticipated, or the protocol’s total fee balance may appear to shrink after a liquidation, contradicting the expectation that fees are retained for future distribution.
summary: This miscalculation leads to the unintended distribution of swap fees as part of liquidated assets causing losses to the protocol. Furthermore, an incorrectly inflated liquidation amount can disrupt the protocol's accounting balance and potentially give rise to further complications.

title: Malicious users can honeypot other users by minting all the ``EURO`` tokens that the vault's ``collateralRate`` allows right before sale
content: The vulnerability is a front‑running honeypot scenario that arises when a Smart Vault is represented by an NFT and the owner lists that NFT for sale without first disabling the vault’s minting capability. The vault contract grants the vault address MINTER_ROLE for the EURO stable‑coin, allowing the vault to mint new EURO tokens up to the amount permitted by its collateralRate. Because the mint() function can be called by the current vault owner at any time, a malicious seller can observe a pending purchase transaction in the mempool, submit a competing transaction that mints the full amount of EUROs the vault is entitled to, and then let the buyer’s transaction complete. The buyer receives the NFT and the underlying vault, but the vault’s mintable balance has been drained, so the new owner cannot mint any further EUROs without providing additional collateral. From the buyer’s perspective the UI may show that the vault was purchased successfully, yet attempts to mint or withdraw EUROs return zero, leading to confusion and apparent loss of value. The impact is that the buyer pays the agreed price (for example $800) while the seller walks away with both the sale proceeds and the freshly minted EURO tokens (for example 1,000 EURO), effectively stealing value from the buyer and undermining trust in the marketplace. This condition occurs only when the vault is over‑collateralized enough to allow minting and when the owner does not pause vault interactions before listing the NFT. The affected parties include any user attempting to buy a listed Smart Vault, the protocol that issues the EURO token, and any downstream applications that rely on the vault’s accounting guarantees. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the lifecycle of the vault NFT and identified that the contract does not enforce any state change on listing. It can be hard to notice because the front‑run transaction may be indistinguishable from normal minting activity and the loss manifests only after the purchase, when the new owner finds the mintable balance unexpectedly zero. The bug belongs to the class of “state‑inconsistent asset transfer” or “mint‑before‑transfer” vulnerabilities, where privileged actions are allowed after an asset has been transferred but before the transfer is finalized. To remediate, the protocol should introduce a mechanism that automatically pauses or disables minting (and possibly other privileged actions) when the vault’s NFT is put up for sale, or require that minting can only be performed by the current owner after the transfer has been confirmed. This ensures that the economic state of the vault cannot be altered by the seller after a buyer has committed funds, preserving the expected accounting relationship between collateral, mintable EUROs, and ownership.

title: H-1 An attacker can steal the StabilityPool depositors profit
content: The vulnerability allows an attacker who can obtain a flash loan to temporarily inject collateral into the StabilityPool, trigger a batch of liquidations, and then claim the resulting collateral gains as if they were a legitimate depositor. The root cause is that the liquidation and profit‑distribution logic does not distinguish between collateral that has been provided for a sustained period and collateral that is supplied and withdrawn within the same atomic transaction. Because the protocol calculates each depositor’s share of liquidation profits solely on the current pool balance, an attacker can satisfy the condition Lsum < SPusd + FLusd and a fee inequality, deposit the flash‑loaned collateral, call the liquidateTroves function, move the earned collateral gains to their own trove, close the trove and repay the flash loan, leaving the excess profit permanently taken from other StabilityPool participants. The exploit can be carried out in a single block, making it difficult to detect; the profit loss appears only as a reduction in expected gains for honest depositors, who may notice that their ThUSD balance does not increase after a liquidation event or that their collateral reward is unexpectedly zero. The attack occurs whenever the system’s collateral‑ratio check allows liquidation while the pool contains enough total ThUSD to satisfy the attacker’s flash‑loan‑derived balance, and when the fee required to open a trove is lower than the proportional fee derived from the liquidated amount. All users who have deposited into the StabilityPool, as well as the protocol itself, are affected because the stolen profit reduces the economic incentive to provide stability and may eventually cause the Threshold USD peg to break. The issue was identified during a security audit performed by MixBytes, which highlighted that the profit‑sharing mechanism lacks a time‑based restriction on newly added collateral. Because the attack does not rely on a visible re‑entrancy or a contract‑level bug, it can remain unnoticed until depositors experience unexplained loss of expected returns. The recommended mitigation is to incorporate a time factor or a minimum‑deposit duration before newly added collateral becomes eligible for liquidation rewards, thereby preventing flash‑loan‑based profit extraction. In conceptual terms, the fix requires the protocol to treat freshly deposited collateral as locked for a period or to weight profit distribution by the length of time each deposit has been present, ensuring that only genuine, long‑standing providers receive liquidation gains.
summary:
The liquidation flow of the protocol is supposed to be as follows:  
• users open troves and join StabilityPool  
• anyone calls the liquidateTroves function that iterates the given troves and liquidates them one by one  
• StabilityPool depositors move collateral gains to their troves and increase the StabilityPool ThUSD balance by getting more ThUSD.  
By using a flash loan any user can bypass the provision of liquidity to the protocol for a long time and steal some of the StabilityPool provider's profit taking the following steps:  
1. Let's wait for liquidation opportunities. The following notions are to be introduced: Lsum is the total liquidatable amount of ThUSD and FLusd is the amount of ThUSD that can be accumulated after depositing flashloaned collateral to the protocol; FLfee is the fees the attacker should pay for opening a trove, SPusd is the total ThUSD amount in StabilityPool.  
The conditions for an attack are:  
Lsum < SPusd + FLusd  
FLfee < Lsum * FLusd / SPusd  
2. An attacker gets a flash loan and swaps the Lsum equivalent of the collateral token to ThUSD.  
3. The attacker makes a deposit of all remaining collateral tokens to StabilityPool.  
4. The attacker calls the TroveManager.sol#L464 function to liquidate the troves. If the CR system is lower than 150%, the amount of liquidated troves can be significantly bigger.  
5. The attacker calls StabilityPool.sol#L283 then StabilityPool.sol#L310 of StabilityPool to move collateral to the attacker's trove. The CR System here has to be more than 150%.  
The attacker's trove here contains the initial collateral and collateral gain.  
6. The attacker closes the trove providing the rest of ThUSD plus the Lsum equivalent from step 1.  
7. The attacker returns the flash loan.  
The attack's impact:  
• loss of profit from liquidations by StabilityPool providers  
• decreased motivation to use the Stability Pool which may cause Threshold USD to unpeg

title: xPYT auto-compound does not take pounder reward into account
content: The vulnerability resides in the auto‑compound routine of the xPYT vault, specifically in the accounting of the pounder reward that is paid out to the caller after the compound operation. The function correctly updates the internal assetBalance for the yield claim, the purchase of xPYT, the redemption of those shares and the subsequent deposit, but it fails to subtract the PYT amount that is transferred to the caller as a reward. As a result the contract’s recorded assetBalance becomes larger than the actual PYT held by the vault. This mismatch causes the exchange ratio (assets per share) to be artificially inflated because the share supply is reduced by the burned xPYT while the asset total is overstated. Under normal operation, later depositors are forced to compensate for the missing assets when the sweep routine reconciles the two values, and withdrawers can redeem more PYT than they are entitled to until the final withdrawer is left with worthless xPYT. The issue is triggered whenever the pound function is called with a non‑zero pounderReward, which is typical for any auto‑compound call that includes a fee or incentive. All participants – depositors, withdrawers and the protocol itself – are affected because the accounting error can lead to loss of funds for honest users and an unfair advantage for callers who repeatedly trigger the function. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract’s internal assetBalance variable with the actual token balances after a compound cycle and noticed that the reward transfer was not reflected in the accounting. It is subtle because the contract’s external view of total assets still appears to increase, masking the fact that part of that increase is owed to the caller and not retained by the vault. To remediate the bug, the assetBalance update must be amended to subtract the pounderReward in the same transaction that adds the yield amount, ensuring that the internal accounting always mirrors the real token holdings. Adding unit tests that verify the balance before and after the reward payout would help prevent regression. This class of bug is an accounting mismatch where outgoing transfers are not reflected in the internal state, leading to inflated share prices and potential fund loss.
summary:
Conceptually, the xPYT.pound function performs the following steps:  
1. Claims yieldAmount yield for itself, deposits the yield back to receive more PYT/NYT (Gate.claimYieldEnter).  
2. Buys xPYT with the NYT.  
3. Performs a ERC4626.redeem(xPYT) with the bought amount, burning xPYT and receiving pytAmountRedeemed PYT.  
4. Performs a ERC4626.deposit(pytAmountRedeemed + yieldAmount = pytCompounded).  
5. Pays out a reward in PYT to the caller.  
The assetBalance is correctly updated for the first four steps but does not decrease by the pounder reward which is transferred out in the last step.  
The impact is that the contract has a smaller assets (PYT) balance than what is tracked in assetBalance.  
1. Future depositors will have to make up for it as sweep computes the difference between these two values.  
2. The xPYT exchange ratio is wrongly updated and withdrawers can redeem xPYT for more assets than they should until the last withdrawer is left holding valueless xPYT.  
Consider the following example and assume 100% fees for simplicity i.e. pounderReward = pytCompounded.  
• Vault total: 1k assets, 1k shares total supply.  
• pound with 100% fee:  
  – claims Y PYT/NYT.  
  – swaps Y NYT to X xPYT.  
  – redeems X xPYT for X PYT by burning X xPYT (supply -= X, exchange ratio is 1-to-1 in example).  
  – assetBalance is increased by claimed Y PYT  
  – pounder receives a pounder reward of X + Y PYT but does not decrease assetBalance by pounder reward X+Y.  
• Vault totals should be 1k-X assets, 1k-X shares, keeping the same share price.  
• Nevertheless, vault totals actually are 1k+Y assets, 1k-X shares. Although pounder receives 100% of pounding rewards the xPYT price (assets / shares) increased.

title: Loss of fees due to rounding down
content: The vulnerability is a precision loss caused by integer rounding when the contract calculates accumulated fees per share of liquidity. The contract stores fees using a fixed‑point scale factor of 1e12. For tokens that have a low decimal count, such as USDC with six decimals, the amount contributed by a single token unit can be as small as 1e6 (the smallest representable amount). When the total liquidity is large – the liquidity variable is a uint128 and can reach values on the order of 1e38 – the expression amount * SCALE_FACTOR / liquidity can evaluate to a value far below one, for example 1e6 * 1e12 / 1e38 ≈ 1e‑20. Because Solidity performs integer division, any fractional result is truncated to zero. Consequently the incremental fee per share that should be added to the accumulator becomes zero. This rounding to zero means that a portion of the fees that should be credited to liquidity providers never enters the accounting state and is therefore permanently unclaimable. The bug manifests whenever the fee amount for a low‑decimal token is small relative to the total liquidity, which can happen even with liquidity far below the maximum uint128 range (e.g., liquidity greater than 1e18). The contract’s updateFarm function can be called by any address, and a malicious actor can repeatedly invoke it while the fee per share remains zero, forcing the contract to “collect” fees that are effectively zero and preventing later legitimate harvests from receiving the missing amount. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are that after providing liquidity and attempting to harvest, the UI shows no increase in the reward balance, or the balance appears to stay at zero despite the expectation that fees should accrue. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the fee‑accumulation formula and identified the mismatch between the scale factor precision and the token decimal precision. It is hard to notice because the contract still records fee events and the UI may display a non‑zero total fee pool, yet individual users receive nothing due to the per‑share rounding. The bug belongs to the class of fixed‑point rounding errors in financial smart contracts, where an insufficient scaling constant leads to loss of fractional value. To remediate the problem the scale factor should be increased to a higher precision, such as 1e18, so that the multiplication retains enough significant digits before division, preventing the fee per share from being rounded down to zero. Alternatively, the contract could switch to a library that performs safe decimal arithmetic with dynamic scaling based on token decimals. Implementing the fix restores the invariant that all accrued fees are eventually distributable to liquidity providers, aligning the contract’s behavior with the expected accounting model.

title: MJR-1 Wrongly increased participants amount
content: The vulnerability is a logical accounting error in the staking contract where the counter that tracks the number of participants is incremented even when a user stakes zero tokens. The root cause is a condition that only checks whether the caller’s existing stake amount is zero before increasing the participants count, without verifying that the amount being added (_amountToStake) is greater than zero. An attacker can exploit this by repeatedly calling the stakeTokens function with a zero stake while their current balance is also zero, causing the participants counter to grow indefinitely. This inflated participant count can break downstream assumptions that rely on an accurate number of active stakers, such as reward distribution formulas, governance voting weight calculations, or any logic that divides rewards by the participant count. When the counter is artificially high, legitimate participants may receive a smaller share of rewards, or the protocol may encounter division‑by‑zero or overflow errors if the count exceeds expected limits. The issue manifests only when a user with no prior stake invokes stakeTokens with a zero amount; under normal staking operations with a positive amount the counter behaves correctly. All users of the protocol are affected because the displayed number of participants may be misleading, and the economic outcomes for stakers can be altered without any visible transaction. The flaw was discovered during a manual code audit by MixBytes, where the logic of the participant‑incrementing statement was examined and found to lack a proper amount check. It can be hard to notice because a zero‑value stake appears to be a no‑op, yet the contract still records a new participant, making the discrepancy subtle in UI dashboards that only show total participants. To remediate, the contract should only increase the participants counter when the incoming stake amount is strictly greater than zero, ensuring that the counter reflects only accounts that actually hold a positive stake. This aligns the implementation with the intended business rule that participants are users who have contributed funds, preserving correct accounting, reward calculations, and governance integrity.
summary:
```solidity
At line StakingPool.sol#L120 contract increases participants amount, that happens if user.amount is zero, however if user will provide zero _amountToStake participants also will increased. So somebody can increase participants infinitely by calling stakeTokens with zero stake.
```

title: MJR-2 Potentially differentiating message senders
content: The vulnerability is an inconsistent use of the Ethereum transaction origin identifier, where some functions read the caller from the built‑in variable msg.sender while other functions obtain the caller through a wrapper such as _msgSender(). This inconsistency creates a class of access‑control bugs that appear when the contract is used with relayed calls or meta‑transactions. The root cause is that msg.sender always returns the immediate caller (for example a relayer contract), whereas _msgSender() is designed to return the original user that signed the meta‑transaction. When a function that protects a privileged operation checks msg.sender but the surrounding logic or inherited contracts expect _msgSender(), the contract may grant or deny rights to the wrong address. An attacker can exploit this by submitting a transaction through a trusted relayer or a meta‑transaction forwarder, causing the contract to treat the relayer as the authorized sender. This can lead to unauthorized minting, fee collection, or ownership changes, effectively allowing the attacker to move or lock funds that belong to honest users. The issue manifests only when the contract is called via a forwarding mechanism; direct calls from an EOA will appear normal, making the bug hard to notice in standard unit tests. Users may experience symptoms such as fees not being deducted, withdrawals appearing to succeed while balances remain unchanged, or unexpected loss of token control. The affected parties include token holders, the protocol’s governance, and any role that relies on correct sender verification. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that highlighted lines where msg.sender and _msgSender() were mixed. Because both identifiers are valid addresses, the inconsistency does not raise compiler warnings and can remain hidden until a meta‑transaction is used. To remediate, the contract should adopt a single, consistent method for retrieving the caller—preferably the context‑aware _msgSender() provided by an AccessControl or Context base contract—and replace every direct msg.sender reference. This eliminates double‑ownership or mis‑ownership scenarios and restores the intended security model.
summary:
```solidity
This warning is about inconsistent message sender address source (msg.sender and _msgSender()) usage in here: FeeToken.sol#L37, FeeToken.sol#L39, FeeToken.sol#L40.
This can lead to the incorrect message sender address choice in case, for example, particular function call was a relayed call or meta-transaction-related call.
```

title: No price scaling in SMAOracle
content: The vulnerability is a missing price scaling step in the SMAOracle contract. Although the constructor creates a scaler based on the difference between the maximum supported decimals (MAX_DECIMALS) and the spot price oracle’s native decimal precision, the update() function never applies this scaler to the latestPrice value retrieved from the underlying spot oracle. As a result, the price returned by SMAOracle remains in the original decimal format instead of being normalised to the protocol’s 18‑decimal standard. This discrepancy originates from an implementation oversight: the code that should convert the raw price using toWad() or multiply by the scaler is absent, while the companion ChainlinkOracleWrapper correctly performs the conversion. When SMAOracle.update() is called, it fetches the raw price, stores it in the price observer, and propagates it to downstream contracts without any adjustment. Consequently, any component that relies on SMAOracle for price information receives a value that can be off by a factor of 10^(MAX_DECIMALS‑spotDecimals). Under conditions where the spot oracle reports prices with fewer than 18 decimals, the protocol will underestimate asset values, potentially triggering premature liquidations, incorrect fee calculations, or allowing an attacker to manipulate the underlying oracle and profit from the mis‑priced data. Users experience symptoms such as collateral appearing to have zero or dramatically reduced value, trades executing at unexpected rates, or loans being liquidated instantly. The issue was discovered during a security audit by Spearbit, which compared the scaling logic of SMAOracle with that of ChainlinkOracleWrapper and noted the absence of the scaling operation. The bug is subtle because the raw price may still look plausible when the decimal mismatch is small, making it easy to overlook in functional testing. To remediate the problem, the SMAOracle contract should re‑introduce the toWad() conversion or explicitly multiply the retrieved latestPrice by the previously calculated scaler before storing or returning it, thereby ensuring all prices are expressed in the expected 18‑decimal format and preserving the protocol’s accounting invariants.

title: Two different invariantCheck variables used in PoolFactory.deployPool()
content: The vulnerability resides in the PoolFactory.deployPool function where two distinct invariantCheck variables are referenced: a state variable defined on the factory contract and a field named invariantCheck that is part of the PoolDeployment struct supplied as a calldata argument. The function mistakenly forwards the struct field to the poolCommitter.initialize call instead of the factory’s own invariantCheck address. This mismatch originates from a naming collision and a failure to enforce a single source of truth for the invariant verification contract. An attacker who can control the deploymentParameters struct – for example by submitting a crafted transaction to the factory – can supply an arbitrary address for invariantCheck. Because the factory trusts the supplied value, the newly created pool will be initialized with a malicious or disabled invariant contract, allowing the pool’s internal accounting rules to be bypassed. The exploit can be carried out during the pool creation step, which is typically performed by a trusted pool committer but may be open to any caller depending on the factory’s access control. If the invariantCheck is replaced with a contract that always returns true, or with a contract that reverts only under specific conditions, the pool may accept invalid state transitions, leading to loss of user funds, incorrect reward distribution, or complete breakdown of the pool’s economic guarantees. From a user’s perspective the symptoms can appear as missing refunds, balances that unexpectedly become zero, or pools that accept deposits without performing the expected safety checks. The issue was uncovered during a manual security review where the auditor noticed the duplicate variable name and the inconsistent usage in the initialization call. It is subtle because the code compiles and the function signature appears correct; the bug only manifests when the struct field is populated with a value that differs from the intended invariant contract, making it easy to overlook during testing. The proper remediation is to remove the invariantCheck field from the PoolDeployment struct entirely and ensure that the factory’s invariantCheck state variable is the sole source passed to poolCommitter.initialize. This eliminates the naming collision and guarantees that every deployed pool uses the verified invariant contract, restoring the intended security guarantees.
summary:
```solidity
The deployPool() function in the PoolFactory contract uses two different invariantCheck variables: the one defined as a contract’s instance variable and the one supplied as a parameter.
```

title: Duplicate user payments for long commits when paid from balance
content: The vulnerability is a duplicate payment logic error that occurs when a user calls the commit function to mint long‑position pool tokens while indicating that the payment should be taken from their internal aggregate balance. The contract receives a flag (fromAggregateBalance) that tells it to use the user’s stored balance instead of pulling tokens via a transfer. However, the second conditional statement that decides whether to invoke the token transfer is written incorrectly. It checks only the commit type and does not properly exclude the case where the payment is already covered by the internal balance. As a result, when the commit type is LongMint and fromAggregateBalance is true, the contract still executes a quoteTokenTransferFrom call, pulling the same amount of quote tokens from the user’s external wallet in addition to deducting the amount from the internal balance. This leads to users paying twice for a single mint operation. The issue can be exploited simply by submitting a commit transaction with CommitType.LongMint and fromAggregateBalance set to true; the contract will automatically debit the user twice without any additional action required. The impact is a loss of funds for any participant who uses this payment mode, as their token balance is reduced by twice the intended amount, potentially causing unexpected zero balances or insufficient funds for subsequent operations. The condition is triggered every time the specific combination of parameters is used, so it occurs under normal usage patterns rather than requiring a special edge case. All users of the protocol who rely on internal balance payments for long‑mint commits are affected, while short‑mint commits remain unaffected because the condition for them is correctly guarded. The flaw was discovered during a manual code audit that examined the logical flow of the commit function and identified that the boolean expression did not correctly reflect the intended payment semantics. The bug is subtle because the transaction may still succeed from the contract’s perspective, and the UI typically only reports a successful commit, making the double deduction easy to miss unless the user closely monitors their wallet balances. From a user’s point of view the symptom is that after a successful long‑mint commit they see their token balance reduced by twice the amount they expected, or that a refund that should have been zero appears as a missing amount. This violates the core accounting assumption that a single mint operation should correspond to a single payment, breaking the protocol’s financial integrity. The recommended fix is to rewrite the conditional so that the token transfer is performed only when the payment is not covered by the internal balance, i.e., combine the commit type checks with a negated fromAggregateBalance flag. Conceptually, the fix ensures that the contract respects the user’s choice of payment source and prevents any double‑charging logic from being executed.
summary:
```solidity
When minting pool tokens in commit(), the fromAggregateBalance parameter indicates if the user wants to pay from their internal balances or by transferring the tokens. The second if condition is wrong and leads to users having to pay twice when calling commit() with CommitType.LongMint and fromAggregateBalance = true.
```

title: Initial executionPrice is too high
content: The vulnerability originates from an inconsistency in how the execution price of a leveraged pool is initialised versus how it is updated later. When a pool is first created, the contract reads the oracle price (firstPrice) and multiplies it by a fixed‑point constant of 1e18 before storing it as executionPrice. Subsequent price updates retrieve the latest price from the oracle wrapper and store it directly without applying the same scaling factor. Because the initial price is artificially inflated, the funding rate calculation, which compares the current executionPrice to the latest price, always yields a negative rate for long token holders. As a result, the funding payments are consistently routed to short token holders, causing long positions to lose value even though the market price may be stable. This effect is observed immediately after a user opens a long position: the expected funding reward is missing, the token balance may appear to drop or even reach zero, and the user receives no compensation. The issue manifests only at pool deployment, when the first executionPrice is set, and persists for the lifetime of the pool because the inflated baseline skews all future funding calculations. All participants who hold long tokens are affected, while short token holders receive unintended gains. The problem was discovered during a security audit that compared the initialisation logic with the regular upkeep logic and identified the mismatched scaling as a logical flaw. It can be hard to notice because the contract behaves normally after the first update; the abnormal loss is attributed to market movements rather than a coding error. To remediate the issue, the scaling factor should be removed from the initial executionPrice assignment so that the same unit representation is used throughout the contract, ensuring that funding rates are calculated on a consistent basis and that long token holders receive the correct payments.

title: Paused state can’t be set and therefore withdrawQuote() can’t be executed
content: The vulnerability consists of an unreachable pause state in the leveraged pool and its associated commit contract. The contracts use modifiers that invoke an invariant‑checking routine before and after each public function. When the invariant check detects a violation it calls a pause function on the pool contracts. However, each modifier immediately executes a require(!paused, \"Pool is paused\") statement after the call. Because the pause function sets the boolean paused to true, the subsequent require fails, causing the whole transaction to revert. The revert also rolls back the state change that set paused, so the paused flag is cleared again. Since only the invariant‑check contract is authorized to call pause, there is no other path to set the flag, making the pause condition permanently false. The withdrawQuote function is written to be callable only when the contract is paused, therefore it can never be executed. As a result, quote tokens that should be returned to users remain locked in the pool even when the accounting invariants are broken, and all other actions are blocked by the invariant checks. The issue manifests whenever the invariant‑checking logic determines that the pool’s internal balances are inconsistent, which can happen under extreme market movements or due to bugs in the pool’s accounting. All users, liquidity providers and the protocol itself are affected because they cannot retrieve their funds and the protocol’s safety mechanism is ineffective. The bug was discovered during a manual audit by inspecting the pause modifiers and noticing that the require statement undoes the pause state. It is difficult to notice in normal operation because the pause event may be emitted, yet the on‑chain paused variable never becomes true, so external callers see no obvious error until they attempt a withdrawal and receive zero. The root cause is the ordering of state changes and the unconditional revert that rolls back the pause flag. To remediate, the pause logic should be decoupled from the function modifiers, for example by storing the pause flag in a separate contract or by using a try/catch pattern that allows the invariant check to revert without undoing the pause state. Alternatively, the dead pause code can be removed to avoid misleading developers. Fixing the issue restores the intended safety valve, allowing withdrawQuote to execute when invariants fail and ensuring that users can recover their quote tokens.

title: Delegators can Avoid Lock Commitments if they can Reliably get Themselves Blocked when Needed
content: The vulnerability concerns the emergency undelegation mechanism of a voting escrow contract, where a delegator’s lock period can be shortened after delegation without preserving the original commitment. The root cause is that the function invoked during a block event—forceUndelegate—does not enforce that the delegator’s lock end remains at least as long as the delegatee’s lock end. Consequently, an attacker who can reliably trigger a block on an account can cause that account’s lock to expire immediately, withdraw the underlying tokens, and retain the voting power associated with the delegatee’s still‑active long lock. In practice, an attacker can use two accounts: a “Rider” that holds a large token balance and locks for a short period, and a “Horse” that holds a token of negligible value but locks for the maximum duration. The Rider delegates its voting power to the Horse. When the attacker forces the Rider to be blocked, the protocol calls forceUndelegate, which clears Rider’s lock and makes it eligible for immediate withdrawal. The attacker withdraws the large token balance while the Horse continues to enjoy the maximised voting power because its lock remains unchanged. By repeating this process with fresh Rider accounts, the attacker can repeatedly extract tokens while inflating voting power, undermining the incentive model and potentially enabling malicious governance proposals. The issue manifests only when the attacker can satisfy the protocol’s blocklist conditions, such as being flagged for a bannable offence; the blocklist logic itself is out of scope, but the exploit assumes such a pathway exists. This flaw is difficult to notice because forceUndelegate appears to be a benign administrative utility, and the contract’s invariants only check that delegatee lock periods are not shorter than delegator lock periods at the moment of delegation, not after a forced undelegation. The impact is a breach of the accounting assumptions of the system: token holders expect that delegating their locked tokens commits those tokens for the duration of the lock, yet the attacker can bypass that commitment, causing "funds disappear" from the protocol’s perspective and inflating voting power beyond what the economic model allows. The vulnerability was discovered during a security audit (Code4rena) and demonstrated with a proof‑of‑concept posted by the researcher warden. To remediate, the contract should ensure that forceUndelegate either preserves the original lock end (e.g., by setting locked_.end to the delegator’s previous end) or, as the eventual fix implemented, copies the delegatee’s lock endpoint when re‑delegating to self, thereby guaranteeing that any forced undelegation cannot reduce the lock duration below the delegatee’s lock. Additional safeguards could include prohibiting forced undelegation from shortening locks, or limiting blocklist‑triggered withdrawals to accounts whose lock has truly expired.
summary: Users can enjoy the voting power of long lock times whilst not committing their tokens. This could cause the entire system to break down as the incentives don’t work any more.

title: Bypass of EntityType check when null attribute is returned by Quadrata
content: The vulnerability is a logic bypass in the KYC verification module that checks an investor's EntityType (Individual or Business) before allowing participation in a deal. The check relies on a business attribute returned by the Quadrata oracle; when the oracle supplies a null value (all bytes set to zero) for the business attribute while the DID attribute is non‑zero, the boolean expression that determines whether the account is a business evaluates to false and, because the expression uses a short‑circuit &&, the auxiliary _isExpired function is never called. As a result the flag that indicates a business entity is never set to true, and the subsequent conditional blocks that would reject a mismatched EntityType are never reached. Consequently an account that should be rejected – for example an individual trying to satisfy a Business‑only requirement – passes the verification unchecked. This can be exploited by an attacker who simply ensures that the Quadrata response for the business attribute is the zeroed placeholder, which can be done by not setting the attribute or by submitting a deliberately empty attestation. The impact is that deals that are intended to be limited to a specific entity class may admit any participant, breaking regulatory compliance, exposing the protocol to legal risk, and potentially allowing malicious actors to obtain privileged token allocations or financial benefits. The bypass occurs only when the business attribute is null and the DID attribute is present; it does not affect cases where the attribute contains a valid non‑zero value. The affected parties include the protocol that enforces KYC rules, its investors who rely on proper eligibility checks, and any compliance officer or regulator expecting the EntityType constraint to be enforced. The issue was discovered during a security audit when a test case that omitted the business status attribute still allowed the verifyEligibility function to succeed. It is subtle because the code appears to perform the correct comparison, yet the short‑circuit logic silently skips the expiration validation and the final rejection branches, making the bug easy to miss in manual review. To remediate, the verifier should explicitly reject null or zeroed business attributes, or treat a zeroed attribute as an invalid response and fail the check. Adding a validation step that confirms the attribute is not bytes32(0) before using it in the isBusinessEqual comparison restores the intended behavior and prevents the EntityType requirement from being bypassed. In user‑facing terms, a participant who expects to be blocked from a Business‑only sale may instead be allowed to purchase, leading to confusion when the UI shows a successful eligibility message despite the user not meeting the stated criteria. This class of bug falls under attribute‑validation and short‑circuit logic bypasses, where missing or default data causes security checks to be unintentionally skipped.

title: AML requirement checks skipped if no AML attribute for user
content: The vulnerability is a logic flaw in the AML eligibility verification where a missing AML attribute is treated as a valid, non‑expired attribute, allowing investors who have never completed KYC/AML to satisfy a deal’s AML requirement. The root cause is the _isExpired helper returning false when attribute.epoch equals 0; the function only checks that epoch > 0 before comparing to the allowed age, so a null attribute (epoch == 0) is considered not expired. The AML check combines a risk‑score comparison with the _isExpired result, and because both sub‑conditions evaluate to false for a zeroed attribute, the require statement never reverts. An attacker can simply call the investment function without having any AML attribute stored by a Quadrata issuer and still pass the check, thereby investing in deals that explicitly require an AML risk score of 5 or lower. The impact is that the protocol can admit non‑compliant participants, breaking regulatory assumptions, exposing the platform to money‑laundering risk, and potentially causing legal or reputational damage. This condition occurs whenever a user’s AML attribute has never been set (epoch == 0), which is common for new users or for assets that do not enforce mandatory KYC at onboarding. The affected parties include the protocol’s compliance team, investors who expect only verified participants, and any deal that relies on the AML guard. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the verifyEligibility function and noticed that the revert path was never reached for zeroed attributes, a subtle bug because the code appears to perform a check but silently accepts default values. It is hard to notice because the contract does not emit an error or warning; the transaction simply succeeds, giving the impression that the user is compliant. To remediate, the _isExpired function should treat a null attribute as expired (for example return attribute.epoch == 0 || attribute.epoch < block.timestamp - maxAttributeAge) or the eligibility logic should explicitly revert when an expected attribute is missing. This change restores the intended business rule that a user without a recorded AML score must be rejected, aligning the contract’s behavior with regulatory expectations and preventing funds from being allocated to unverified participants.

title: InvestmentManager::_deleteOffer should subtract escrowAmount instead of $.offers[id].amount
content: The vulnerability resides in the escrow accounting logic of the InvestmentManager contract, specifically in the private function that removes an offer after the review period expires. When an investor creates an offer, the contract escrows the total amount required for the deal, which includes the principal amount plus any applicable fees (the escrowAmount). If the originator does not review the offer within the configured offerEscrowPeriod, the investor may call withdrawOffer to retrieve the funds. The withdrawal path invokes a helper that calls _deleteOffer, which is supposed to reduce the global escrowedAmount counter by the amount that is being released. However, the implementation mistakenly subtracts only the principal amount (offers[id].amount) instead of the full escrowAmount (principal plus fees). As a result, the fee portion remains recorded as still escrowed even though the investor has received the principal back. This creates a discrepancy between the contract’s internal accounting of escrowed funds and the actual token balance, causing the fee to become permanently locked in the contract. The issue can be exploited simply by waiting for the offer to expire and then withdrawing; the attacker does not need to craft any special transaction – the contract’s own logic will lock the fee. The impact is that investors lose the fee portion of their escrow, effectively reducing their expected refund and decreasing overall liquidity. The problem manifests only when an offer is not reviewed within the escrow period and the investor triggers a withdrawal; offers that are accepted or cancelled through other paths do not exhibit the bug. The affected parties are the investors who place offers, the protocol’s overall fund pool, and any admin trying to assess available funds via hasSufficientAvailableFunds, which will incorrectly consider the locked fees as still withdrawable. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the accounting flow of escrowed funds. It is subtle because the contract’s external balance still shows the total tokens, and the missing fee is relatively small, making it easy to overlook during routine testing. To remediate the issue, the subtraction should use the full escrowAmount stored for the offer, thereby correctly updating the escrowedAmount counter and releasing the entire escrowed value back to the investor. This correction aligns the contract’s internal accounting with its external token balance and restores the intended economic behavior where no fees are retained when an offer expires without acceptance.
summary:
When an investor submits an offer to DealManager, the payment is initially escrowed, waiting for the offer to be reviewed by an Originator. If, after a delay of offerEscrowPeriod (initially 5 days), the offer is not reviewed, the investor can call withdrawOffer to get his funds back.
However the accounting is incorrect in that case, since amount is deducted from the escrowed funds, whereas escrowAmount (amount + fees) has been escrowed.
The surplus amount (equivalent to the fee), stays locked in the contract.
hasSufficientAvailableFunds would deduct escrowedAmount from current contract balance to determine the funds which can be distributed or withdrawn by admin.

title: TradableSideVault: accepted tokens cannot be activated, deactivated or deleted
content: The vulnerability resides in the way the TradableSideVault processes cross‑chain messages received via LayerZero. When a message is sent to activate (aat+), deactivate (aat-), or delete (dat) an accepted token, the payload is encoded as a string identifying the operation followed by the token address. Inside the vault’s _nonblockingLzReceive function the payload is decoded only as an address, extracting the first 20 bytes of the encoded data. Those bytes do not correspond to the original token address, resulting in a mismatched address that does not exist in the vault’s registry. Because the activation, deactivation and deletion functions first verify that the token is present, the calls revert, effectively preventing any accepted token from being managed through the cross‑chain bridge. The root cause is an incorrect abi.decode call that ignores the string component of the payload. Exploitation is straightforward: an attacker or honest user sends a correctly formatted message, but the vault always interprets the token address incorrectly, causing the transaction to fail. The impact is that token owners cannot add new tokens, remove obsolete ones, or pause trading for a specific token, which may lead to frozen liquidity, unexpected zero balances in UI, or inability to withdraw funds that rely on token activation status. The bug manifests only when the functions are invoked via LayerZero; local calls that pass the address directly work, making the issue hard to notice during unit testing. It was discovered during a manual audit of the cross‑chain messaging logic, where the auditor observed that the decoded address was a constant low‑value placeholder (0x...60) rather than the expected token address. The problem is subtle because the payload appears correctly formed and the revert message does not reveal the decoding mistake. To remediate, the payload must be decoded as a tuple containing both the operation string and the address, for example (, address token) = abi.decode(payload,(string,address)). After fixing the decoding, the vault will correctly recognize the token and allow activation, deactivation and deletion as intended, restoring expected behavior where users can see tokens appear in their list, be removed, or be paused without unexpected failures.
summary:
The current implementation of the TradableSideVault, doesn't allow the following operations:
- aat+ - activate accepted token
- aat- - deactivate accepted token
- dat - delete accepted token
This is due to a bug in the decoding of the message payload on the sideVault. In function _nonblockingLzReceive(), the payload (which contains the messageType string and the token address) is only being decoded to an address, which will be set to the first 20 bytes of the payload, a value that has nothing to do with the token address. Since the functions to activate, deactivate and delete tokens require that the token exists, these calls will revert when called through layerZero.
Take a look at the following code:
```solidity
function test() external {
    address token = address(this); // 0x9d83e140330758a8fF…
    bytes memory payload = abi.encode("aat", token);
    (string memory messageType) = abi.decode(payload, (string)); // returns "aat"
    (address token_) = abi.decode(payload, (address)); // returns 0x0000000000000000000000000000000000000060
}
```
Here, the value for the decoded token address has nothing to do with the value that was encoded.

title: Contracts do not support tokens with fees or rebasing tokens
content: The vulnerability stems from the contract’s assumption that the payment currency behaves like a standard ERC20 token with no transfer fees or automatic balance adjustments. In the capital‑call answer routine the code calls safeTransferFrom for the exact amount specified (cc.amount) and then mints deal tokens based on that same amount, without checking how many tokens actually arrived in the recipient’s balance. When a fee‑on‑transfer token such as USDT is used, a portion of the transferred amount is taken as a fee and never reaches the capital recipient, yet the contract still records the full cc.amount and mints deal tokens as if the full amount was received. The same mismatch occurs for the fee transfer: the feeRecipient receives less than cc.feeAmount, but the event logs the intended fee amount. Consequently the protocol’s accounting becomes inconsistent – investors may receive more deal tokens than their net contribution warrants, or the protocol may think it has collected more capital than it actually has. This discrepancy can be exploited by an attacker who deliberately supplies a fee‑on‑transfer token, causing the system to over‑issue deal tokens and dilute other participants, or by causing under‑funding that leaves the deal under‑capitalized. The bug manifests whenever a capital call is answered with a token that charges a transfer fee or that rebases its supply, because the internal logic never validates the post‑transfer balance. All parties that interact with the capital‑call flow – investors, fee recipients, and the protocol itself – are affected, as the financial guarantees and token economics rely on precise accounting. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined token handling assumptions and noticed that the code does not verify actual received amounts. It is hard to notice because the transfer succeeds, no revert occurs, and the UI may simply show that the transaction completed, while the hidden accounting tables are wrong. From a user perspective the symptoms include receiving fewer underlying tokens than expected, seeing deal tokens that do not correspond to the net contribution, or observing that the fee recipient gets a smaller fee than shown in the event. The bug violates the core business logic that each unit of contributed capital should map to a proportional amount of deal tokens and that fees should be accurately accounted for. The recommended remediation is to avoid supporting fee‑on‑transfer or rebasing tokens altogether, or to modify the flow to measure the actual amount received (for example by checking balances before and after the transfer) and to adjust the minting and fee calculations accordingly, thereby restoring the integrity of the accounting model.

title: Distribute is permissionless, allowing malicious users to specify 0 slippage and sandwich the swap
content: The vulnerability resides in a reward distribution function that can be called by any address without any access restriction. The function accepts a parameter that defines the minimum amount of output tokens expected from a swap, which is intended to protect against slippage. Because the function is permissionless, an attacker can invoke it and set this slippage parameter to zero, effectively disabling any safeguard against price movement. When the swap executes at an unfavorable rate, the attacker can sandwich the transaction – either by front‑running with a trade that moves the price before the distribution call and then back‑running after it – and capture the excess value that should have gone to legitimate reward recipients. This flaw occurs whenever the contract attempts to convert accrued rewards into another token via a decentralized exchange and relies on the caller‑provided slippage limit. Users who expect to receive a certain amount of reward tokens may instead receive nothing or a reduced amount, while the protocol’s reward pool can be drained or depleted. The issue was identified during a manual audit that examined function visibility and parameter validation. It is subtle because the function appears to perform a routine accounting operation, and a zero‑minimum output does not cause a revert, so the loss may only be observed as missing rewards after the fact. To remediate the problem, the contract should enforce an authorized keeper role for calling the distribution routine and should enforce a sensible minimum slippage threshold or use an on‑chain price oracle to validate the swap rate before execution. In essence, the bug is a classic case of missing access control combined with unchecked user‑controlled slippage, leading to potential fund loss and broken accounting guarantees.
summary: distribute() uses the argument amountOutMinimum as slippage control, but the function is permissionless, so malicious users can trigger swaps with 0 minimum amount out.

title: TradableSettings: tokens can only be added in one chain
content: The vulnerability is a logical restriction in the token registration workflow of the TradableSettings contract. The contract maintains a single list of accepted token addresses and, before adding a new token, it checks that the address does not already exist with require(!tokenExists(_token)). Because the same ERC‑20 address can be deployed on several side chains, the first successful call to addAcceptedToken registers the token for the first sideVault and then permanently blocks any subsequent call that tries to register the identical address for a different sideVault on another chain. The check is performed in addAcceptedToken and also in deleteAcceptedToken, so the token cannot be removed and re‑added on a different chain either. This condition occurs whenever a token that is intended to be tradable on multiple chains shares the same contract address across those chains. Users attempting to add the token on a second chain receive a “!token‑already‑exists” revert, see no trading pair appear in the UI, and may be left with a missing or zero balance for that asset on the new chain. The impact is a denial‑of‑service style failure: liquidity providers cannot list the token on additional chains, traders cannot execute swaps, and the protocol’s cross‑chain offering is effectively reduced. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the token management functions, where the auditor noticed that tokenExists iterates over a single list and that the require statement prevents duplicate entries. Because the symptom is simply a revert message, it can be easy to overlook; the contract appears to work correctly for the first chain, and the failure only manifests on later attempts, which may be interpreted as a configuration error rather than a bug. The root cause is the use of a global token registry without distinguishing per‑chain contexts, treating the token address as a unique identifier across the entire system. To fix the problem, the contract should either remove the global uniqueness check or maintain separate token registries for each sideVault/chain, allowing the same address to be accepted on multiple chains. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “incorrect global state sharing” or “cross‑chain token registration collision” bugs, where a data structure intended for a single domain is incorrectly reused across multiple isolated domains.

title: CircuitBreaker can not incentivize users
content: The vulnerability consists of a missing payable entry point in the CircuitBreaker contract, which prevents the contract from ever receiving Ether despite the documentation stating that calls to tripBreaker and setValue are incentivized with a reward. The root cause is that the Solidity source does not define a receive() function, a fallback() function marked payable, or any other payable function that could accept Ether, while a withdraw() function exists, indicating an original intention to hold funds. Because the contract cannot hold Ether, any reward that the protocol intends to send to the caller is never funded; the caller therefore receives no payment and only incurs the gas cost of the transaction. This can be exploited simply by invoking the incentivized functions – the attacker (or any user) will spend gas without receiving the promised compensation, leading to a loss of funds from the user’s perspective. The impact is that users are discouraged from exercising the core functionality of the contract (tripping the breaker), which may render the circuit‑breaker mechanism ineffective and could cause the protocol to remain in an unsafe state. The condition occurs whenever a user calls tripBreaker or setValue, regardless of the input parameters, because the contract’s balance is always zero.
