All participants who are expected to be rewarded – typically external callers or bots that monitor the contract – are affected, as they experience a mismatch between expected reward and actual outcome. The issue was discovered during a security audit when the auditors compared the public documentation with the source code and noticed the absence of any payable function despite the presence of a withdraw method. The problem is subtle because the contract compiles and functions without reverting; the missing reward is only observable through the lack of incoming Ether, which may be overlooked if the tester does not check the contract’s balance after calls. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of incentive‑funding failures caused by missing payable entry points, leading to a reward‑distribution breakdown. From a user’s point of view the UI may show a successful transaction but the user’s wallet balance does not increase, or the expected refund amount appears as zero, contradicting the expectation that the protocol pays for the action. To remediate the issue the contract should be modified to include a receive() or payable fallback function, or otherwise make the functions that dispense rewards payable, and ensure that sufficient Ether is deposited into the contract before rewards are promised. This change aligns the implementation with the documented incentive model and restores the economic motivation for users to call the circuit‑breaker functions.
summary:
It is stated in the docs that calls to the methods tripBreaker and setValue are incentivized in order to make them work trustlessly and autonomously. However CircuitBreaker.sol has no receive(), no fallback() or payable function which means that there is no way ETH to be sent to the contract.
Because of this, whoever calls tripBreaker or setValue won't receive the expected reward which will lead to discouraging users to call the tripBreaker which is the main functionality of the contract. Thus, instead of not receiving reward, the users will be at loss because of the gas fee. In addition a withdraw method is present in the contract which shows that the initial intention for CircuitBreaker is to be able to receive ETH yet this is not possible.

title: The setValue() will revert because of a wrong time unit
content: The vulnerability is a time‑unit mismatch in the setValue function of the CircuitBreaker contract. The function reads a timestamp from a Chainlink oracle (updatedAt) and compares the elapsed time since the last update (lastTimestamp) with a hard‑coded constant 1000*60*60*12. This expression evaluates to 43,200,000, which represents twelve hours only when the unit is milliseconds. However, the timestamps supplied by the oracle are expressed in seconds, so the comparison is effectively checking whether at least 43,200,000 seconds (about 500 days) have passed. Because the required interval is far larger than the actual twelve‑hour window, the require statement fails on every call after a legitimate update, causing the transaction to revert with the message 'The value can only be updated after 12 hours'. The root cause is the incorrect assumption about the time unit of the oracle timestamps, leading to a logical error in the time‑based guard. An attacker does not need to do anything special to exploit this; simply invoking setValue after a normal update will always hit the require and revert, resulting in a denial‑of‑service condition where the circuit breaker cannot be refreshed and the oracle floor value remains stale. This impacts any user or protocol component that relies on timely updates of the floor value, potentially locking funds or preventing risk mitigation mechanisms from triggering. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the arithmetic of the time check and noticed the discrepancy between milliseconds and seconds. It can be hard to notice because the revert message correctly mentions a twelve‑hour delay, giving the impression that the logic is sound, while the underlying unit conversion error is subtle. To remediate, the contract should store the intended interval in seconds (e.g., a constant of 12 hours = 43,200 seconds) or use Solidity’s built‑in time units (12 hours) and compare against timestamps measured in the same unit. Conceptually, the fix is to align the units of both sides of the comparison so that the guard enforces the intended twelve‑hour window. From a user’s perspective, the UI will show a transaction failure with the revert string, even though the required twelve hours have already elapsed, leading to confusion because the expected behavior (price update after twelve hours) does not occur. This bug belongs to the class of time‑unit conversion errors that break business logic assumptions about timing and can cause funds to become effectively inaccessible until the contract is patched.
summary:
The function setValue in CircuitBreaker.sol allows you to update the oracle floor value by reading the Chainlink oracle.
Now lets take a look at the second require statement in it:
```solidity
require(updatedAt - lastTimestamp > 1000*60*60*12, "The value can only be updated after 12 hours. If the price moves a lot before 12 hours have passed, the breaker should be called");
```
The math 1000*60*60*12 is equal to 43,200,000 which is expected to be 12 hours like the revert string says. And yes it is 12 hours but in milliseconds and we are comparing it to a unix timestamp values taken from the oracle updateAt and lastTimestamp which are in seconds. So 43,200,000 seconds will be equal to 500 days and not 12 hours. Which will DOS the function because it will revert every time if the oracle is fetching the right data.

title: An off-by-one error can DoS the bribe method
content: The vulnerability is an off‑by‑one error in the payable bribe function that validates the amount of ether sent by the caller. The function requires that msg.value be strictly greater than a predefined bribeAmount (initially 0.01 ether). Because the comparison uses the > operator instead of >=, a transaction that sends exactly the required amount fails the require check and reverts. The revert message explicitly states the required bribe amount, which misleads users into thinking they sent insufficient funds even though they sent the exact amount. This bug can be exploited simply by honest users repeatedly attempting to pay the exact bribe amount; each attempt will revert, effectively preventing any successful bribe. The impact is a denial‑of‑service on the bribe mechanism: holders of TradFiLines NFTs cannot trade their tokens for an extra trading hour outside normal market hours, and the protocol’s advertised feature becomes unusable. The condition occurs whenever the function is called with msg.value equal to the current bribeAmount, which is a common scenario because users typically send the exact quoted price. All participants who rely on the bribe feature—NFT holders, traders, and the protocol itself—are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual code audit that flagged the require statement as an off‑by‑one error. It may be hard to notice because the revert message appears correct, and the failure only happens at the exact boundary value, which can be overlooked during testing that uses higher amounts. To fix the problem, the require should be changed to accept values greater than or equal to the required amount (msg.value >= bribeAmount), thereby aligning the contract logic with user expectations and restoring the intended functionality. This class of bug belongs to boundary‑condition validation errors, where an inequality operator is incorrectly chosen, leading to unexpected reverts and potential service disruption. From a user’s perspective the UI will show a failed transaction with a message indicating the required bribe amount, while the user’s balance remains unchanged, creating confusion and discouraging further attempts.

title: Using an oracle for another collection can DoS the trading
content: The contract implements a circuit‑breaker that is supposed to stop trading of a specific NFT collection when the collection’s own floor price moves beyond a configured percentage threshold. The implementation obtains the latest floor price by calling the Chainlink oracle for the Bored Ape Yacht Club (BAYC) collection and then compares the derived percentageChange against the haltPercentage. Because the oracle source is unrelated to the target collection (TradFiLines), the percentageChange is calculated from a price that has no logical connection to the TradFiLines floor. This mismatch is the root cause: an external oracle feeds data that the business logic assumes represents the TradFiLines market, while in reality it reflects BAYC volatility. An attacker (or any user) can trigger the tripBreaker function whenever the BAYC floor price fluctuates enough to make the computed percentageChange exceed the halt threshold, even if the TradFiLines floor price is stable. By doing so, the caller can halt trading for the entire protocol for at least one day, potentially for many consecutive days if BAYC remains volatile. The impact is a denial‑of‑service: users attempting to buy, sell or list TradFiLines NFTs receive transaction reverts or see the market marked as halted, leading to loss of trading opportunities and possible financial loss if time‑sensitive strategies are blocked. The condition occurs whenever the tripBreaker function is called and the oracle returns a value that pushes the computed change above the threshold; no additional checks verify that the oracle data belongs to the correct collection. The vulnerability was discovered during a manual audit that compared the price histories of BAYC and TradFiLines and noticed that the two series are independent. It can be hard to notice because the contract compiles and the function call succeeds; only the business‑logic mismatch causes the unexpected halt, which may be attributed to a “normal” market pause rather than a bug. The issue belongs to the class of oracle‑misuse or external‑dependency coupling bugs, where a contract relies on an off‑chain data source that does not correspond to the intended asset. From a user’s perspective the UI would show the market as “trading halted” or “no orders can be placed”, contradicting the expectation that trading should continue when the collection’s own floor price is stable. To remediate, the contract should either obtain a dedicated oracle that reports the floor price of the TradFiLines collection, or remove the ability to halt trading based on external price data altogether, adding internal safeguards that do not depend on unrelated market feeds. In short, the bug allows an attacker to exploit price volatility of an unrelated NFT collection to deny service to the target protocol.

title: Wrong active pumper bonus calculation
content: The vulnerability is an arithmetic scaling error in the calculation of the extra reward granted to participants classified as "active pumpers". According to the protocol specification, an active pumper should receive an additional three percent (3%) on top of the standard guardian bonus. The contract, however, derives the bonus percentage from a constant that is divided by ten, producing a value of three hundredths of a percent (0.03%). This incorrect value is then applied in a formula that uses a denominator of 10,000, which is appropriate for basis‑point arithmetic but not for a plain percent. As a result, the multiplier becomes (10000 + 0.03) / 10000 instead of the intended (100 + 3) / 100, yielding a negligible increase in the payout. The root cause is a mismatch between the unit used in the white‑paper (percent) and the unit implemented in code (basis points), combined with an erroneous divisor. The bug is triggered each time the private function that allocates top‑contributor bonuses runs for a cycle and the helper that checks active‑pumper status returns true. Any user who qualifies as an active pumper therefore receives only a 0.03 % uplift rather than the promised 3 %, which translates into a loss of roughly ninety‑nine percent of the expected extra earnings. From the user’s perspective the UI may display a bonus entry, but the balance increment is far smaller than anticipated, leading to confusion such as “my reward didn’t increase” or “I expected a larger refund but got almost nothing”. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that compared the on‑chain calculation with the white‑paper description and identified the scaling mismatch. Because the contract still adds a positive amount, the problem can be subtle and may go unnoticed unless the actual payout is audited against the specification. The bug belongs to the class of unit‑conversion or scaling bugs, where a percentage is mistakenly treated as basis points, causing an incorrect formula. To remediate the problem the calculation should be rewritten to use a percent‑based denominator (100) and to define the active‑pumper bonus constant as the intended three percent value, for example: bonus = bonus * (100 + ACTIVE_PUMPERS_BONUS_PERCENTAGE) / 100. This aligns the on‑chain logic with the protocol’s economic model and restores the intended incentive structure.

title: DoS on the pump function due to excessively low slippage tolerance
content: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition in the pump function of the ULTI protocol caused by an excessively low slippage tolerance. The contract defines a constant MAX_SWAP_SLIPPAGE_BPS equal to 99 basis points (0.99 %), which is used to compute the minimum amount of ULTI tokens that must be received when the contract swaps a portion of its input tokens for ULTI. Because the Uniswap pool that the contract interacts with charges a 1 % fee, any realistic swap will incur at least that amount of price impact, meaning the calculated minimum amount is always higher than what the pool can deliver. Consequently the internal slippage check fails and the swap transaction reverts, preventing the pump process from completing. The root cause is the static slippage limit that does not account for the pool fee, pool liquidity, or possible divergence between the time‑weighted average price (TWAP) and the spot price. The issue can be exploited simply by invoking the pump function; the transaction will revert with a “slippage too high” error, leaving the ULTI contract unable to perform its core price‑adjustment operation. The impact is that the protocol’s primary economic mechanism is blocked, users cannot trigger a pump, token balances remain unchanged, and the UI may display an unexpected failure message. This condition occurs whenever the contract holds any amount of input tokens and attempts to execute the pump, regardless of market conditions, because the slippage check is deterministic. All participants who rely on the pump – token holders, liquidity providers, and the protocol governance – are affected because the system cannot progress as designed. The problem was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the slippage calculation logic and compared it against the known pool fee. It is subtle because the transaction simply reverts with a generic slippage error, which could be mistaken for a normal market condition, and because another bug that under‑estimates the expected ULTI amount currently masks the failure; once that bug is fixed, the DoS becomes observable. To remediate the issue the slippage protection should be redesigned to allow a maximum slippage that exceeds the pool fee and includes a safety margin for TWAP deviation, pool size, and potential future fee changes. A dynamic calculation based on the actual pool fee or a higher constant (e.g., >100 bps) would prevent the automatic revert and restore the ability of the pump function to execute as intended.

title: DoS on deposits during the early bird period
content: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that affects deposits during the first 24 hours after the contract launch, often called the early‑bird period. The contract calculates a fixed deposit price based on the initial pool ratio instead of using the current time‑weighted average price (TWAP). When a user deposits, the contract determines the amount of ULTI tokens to mint for liquidity by dividing the input token amount by this static price, then checks that the actual amounts added to the pool do not deviate by more than MAX_ADD_LP_SLIPPAGE_BPS from the expected values. Because the price is fixed, any change in the pool’s spot price caused by swaps will create a difference between the static deposit price and the live market price. If that difference exceeds the allowed slippage, the minUltiAmount and minInputTokenAmount checks fail and the transaction reverts. This situation occurs only while the early‑bird timer is active; after the period ends the contract switches to the TWAP price and the problem disappears. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the interaction between the early‑bird pricing logic and the slippage guard. It can be hard to notice because the deposit function appears to work correctly at launch, but later price movements silently cause all subsequent deposits to revert, giving users the impression that the contract is broken without an obvious error message. From a user’s perspective, an attempt to deposit results in a transaction that reverts, leaving the user’s balance unchanged and only incurring gas costs, contrary to the expectation that the deposit should succeed and provide LP tokens. A malicious actor can exploit this by making a single deposit at the favorable early‑bird price and then performing a large swap that moves the spot price enough to exceed the slippage threshold, thereby preventing any other user from depositing until the early‑bird window closes. The attacker can then sell the cheaply acquired ULTI tokens at a higher price after the period ends, gaining an unfair profit while the protocol suffers reduced adoption and loss of credibility. The root cause is the use of a static price in combination with a strict slippage check, which together create a condition where normal market activity can unintentionally lock the main functionality of the contract. To remediate the issue, the contract should compute the ULTI amount using the current spot price (or TWAP) even during the early‑bird period, or relax the slippage constraint for that window, ensuring that deposits remain possible regardless of price fluctuations.

title: GLOBAL-2 | Centralization Risk
content: The vulnerability is a centralization risk arising from privileged roles such as admins and oracles that have unchecked authority over critical contract functions. The root cause is the use of a custom admin access‑control model that allows any single privileged address to execute actions that affect user holdings, combined with a treasury contract that can be manipulated by a principal admin who is able to force a quorum on the in‑house MultiSig. Because the model does not require multiple independent approvals for sensitive operations, an attacker who compromises or colludes with one admin or oracle can arbitrarily move funds, change parameters, or block legitimate user actions. Exploitation is straightforward: the malicious privileged address calls the privileged function (for example a withdrawal or parameter update) and the contract accepts it without additional checks, resulting in immediate transfer of assets to the attacker or denial of service for honest users. The impact includes loss of user funds, inability to claim winnings or refunds, and erosion of trust in the protocol, as users may see their balances become zero or expected payouts disappear. The condition occurs at any time the contract relies on the custom admin model, especially when the number of admins or oracles grows, because the attack surface expands linearly with each added privileged address. All participants—regular users, bettors, and token holders—are affected because the privileged actors can alter the state that determines payouts and treasury balances. The issue was discovered during a systematic security audit that examined role‑based access controls and identified that the admin model lacks multi‑signature enforcement and timelock safeguards. The problem is hard to notice in normal operation because the contract behaves correctly when admins act honestly; only malicious or compromised admins trigger the failure, which may appear as an unexplained loss of funds rather than a code bug. To remediate, privileged functions should be gated behind a true multi‑signature scheme or a timelocked governance process, reducing the ability of any single actor to act unilaterally. Additionally, limiting the number of admin/oracle addresses and employing transparent KYC procedures can further mitigate the risk. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of “centralized privileged‑role abuse” where insufficient decentralization of authority enables fund misappropriation and violates the protocol’s accounting assumptions that only the protocol logic, not individual operators, controls asset movement.
summary:
Throughout the contracts there is a risk of admins and oracles using their privilege to beneﬁt
themselves or act malicious toward user’s holdings. Contracts utilizing the CustomAdmin access
control model face more risk as the number of admins or oracles increase because it only takes one
to act mischievous.
Additionally, the treasury which is under the in-house MultiSig.sol contract can be can be
manipulated by the principal admin who can unethically force a quorum.

title: UB-1 | DoS Attack
content: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition caused by unboundedgrowth of the bettor storage arrays in a betting contract. When a user calls the placeBet function, the contract records the caller’s address in either the YesBettors or the NoBettors array. Because the function does not limit the number of distinct callers or the amount of ether each caller can send, a malicious actor can repeatedly invoke placeBet from many different addresses, each sending only a tiny amount of ETH. Each call appends a new entry to one of the arrays, so the total length of the arrays can increase without bound. Later, when the contract owner or an authorized party calls reportResult, the implementation iterates over the entire YesBettors and NoBettors arrays with a for‑loop to distribute winnings. As the arrays become very large, the gas required to execute the loop approaches or exceeds the block gas limit, or the transaction becomes prohibitively expensive. At that point the reportResult function cannot be executed, preventing the contract from settling bets and effectively locking all funds. The impact is that legitimate users cannot claim winnings or refunds, the protocol becomes unusable, and the locked ether remains inaccessible until the contract is upgraded or the arrays are manually cleared. The condition occurs whenever the contract receives a high volume of distinct placeBet calls, especially when the attacker can create many fresh addresses cheaply. All participants—bettors, the contract owner, and any downstream services—are affected because the core business logic (bet resolution) is blocked. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the control flow of placeBet and reportResult and identified the unbounded loop as a classic DoS vector. It can be hard to notice because each individual bet appears legitimate and the gas cost of a single placeBet call is low; only the cumulative effect manifests later when the settlement function is invoked. The bug belongs to the class of “unbounded iteration” or “gas exhaustion” vulnerabilities, where on‑chain data structures grow without a cap and are later processed in a single transaction. From a user’s perspective the UI may show that a bet has been placed successfully, but when the outcome is announced the contract reports a transaction failure, and users see that their expected payout is missing or that the contract appears frozen. To remediate the issue the contract should avoid iterating over dynamic arrays in a single transaction. A pull‑over‑push withdrawal pattern can be used: instead of distributing winnings inside reportResult, the contract should record each bettor’s entitlement in a mapping and let each participant withdraw their own funds in separate calls. Alternatively, the contract could limit the number of bettors, use a more scalable data structure, or split the settlement into multiple smaller transactions. Implementing these changes removes the unbounded loop, prevents gas‑limit exhaustion, and restores the ability for users to claim their rightful balances.
summary:
A malicious actor can call placeBet with different addresses, sending a tiny amount of ETH per call.
As a result, the YesBettors array and NoBettors array will expand to the point where it either exceeds
the block gas limit, or costs too much to reportResult. This will render the function inoperable.

title: UB-2 | DoS Attack
content: The vulnerability is an arithmetic underflow in the fee calculation of a betting contract. The contract determines the fee for a bettor (feeBettorBet) by taking the sum of the bettor’s total stake – both the amount placed on the winning side and the amount placed on the losing side – and applying a percentage. When a participant wagers a larger amount on the losing side than on the winning side, the computed fee can become larger than the amount that should be paid out from the winning side. Because the contract uses unsigned integer arithmetic, subtracting a larger fee from a smaller winning payout triggers an underflow, causing the transaction to revert. The revert happens inside the reportResult function, which is responsible for distributing winnings after a match is settled. As a result, every call to reportResult fails, preventing any user from receiving their expected winnings and effectively freezing the contract’s payout mechanism. This denial‑of‑service condition can be deliberately triggered by an attacker who places a heavy losing bet and then forces the settlement function to run, causing the underflow on purpose. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the fee logic and identified that the fee was not bounded by the actual winning amount. It is subtle because the fee calculation appears correct for typical cases where the winning stake dominates, so the bug may remain hidden until an extreme betting pattern occurs. The impact is that users see no payout, balances appear unchanged, and the protocol’s promised reward distribution breaks, undermining trust. To remediate, the fee should be calculated solely from the amount the user has on the winning side, or a hard cap should be introduced so the fee never exceeds the payable winning amount, thereby eliminating the possibility of an underflow and restoring reliable payout behavior.
summary:
feeBettorBet is calculated based on total amount bet for a user i.e. winning side + losing side.
If the user bet more on the losing side, it is possible for the feeBettorBet to exceed the amount bet
on the winning side, causing a subtraction underﬂow which will revert. Therefore, reportResult will
consistently fail and users will not get their winnings.

title: UB-3 | Lost Funds On Cancel
content: The vulnerability is a loss‑of‑funds bug that occurs when a binary market event is cancelled. The contract allows a participant to place bets on both possible outcomes, a pattern that is useful for arbitrage. When the protocol triggers an emergency cancellation, the cancellation routine resets the stored stake for both outcomes to zero, but the withdrawal function that users call after a cancel only reads the amount associated with one side of the position. As a result the amount that was wagered on the opposite side becomes permanently inaccessible and cannot be reclaimed. The root cause is a mismatch between the state‑reset logic (which clears both sides) and the claim logic (which only considers a single side), violating the invariant that all deposited funds must be fully recoverable after any terminal state of the market. An attacker does not need to act maliciously; any user who has opened a dual‑side position can experience the loss simply by waiting for the contract to cancel the event or by invoking the emergency cancel function if they have the permission. The exploitation flow is: (1) user places bets on both outcomes; (2) the market is cancelled; (3) the contract zeroes both balances; (4) user calls the withdraw function; (5) the function returns only the amount from one side, leaving the other side’s funds locked. From the user’s perspective the UI may indicate that the cancellation succeeded, but the wallet balance shows a shortfall: the expected refund is partially missing, often appearing as “refund is zero” for one side while the other side is returned correctly. This symptom can be confusing because normal resolution paths (when the event resolves) correctly pay out both sides, so the asymmetry only appears in the rare cancel path, making it hard to notice during routine testing. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s settlement and cancellation flow, where the auditor observed that the withdraw routine references only one side after a cancel. The bug belongs to the class of asymmetric state‑reset or partial‑withdrawal bugs that break accounting assumptions. To remediate, the contract should either forbid users from opening positions on both sides simultaneously, or adjust the cancellation logic to record refundable amounts for each side and modify the withdrawal function to allow claiming both amounts. In conceptual terms the fix restores the invariant that total deposited funds are always fully recoverable, eliminating the scenario where “funds disappear” or “refund calculation error” occurs after an emergency cancellation.
summary:
The contract allows placing bets on both sides which makes sense if the user would like to perform
arbitrage. If the event is canceled upon an emergency, a user can only withdraw funds from one side.
If they were betting on both sides for arbitrage, they lose the amount they bet on the other side.

title: MS-1 | Principal Admin Abuse
content: The vulnerability consists of an unchecked ability for the principal admin to call the function that registers new approver addresses, allowing the admin to add as many addresses as needed to satisfy the quorum required for transaction approval. The root cause is the lack of proper access control and quorum enforcement on the setApproverAddr routine; the contract does not require existing approvers to consent to the addition of new ones, nor does it limit the number of addresses that can be added by a single privileged account. An attacker who controls the principal admin can therefore create a set of approvers that are all under their control, reach the quorum threshold, and approve any arbitrary treasury transaction without any independent verification. This defeats the intended multi‑signature security model, turning what should be a decentralized decision process into a single‑point‑of‑failure. The impact is that funds can be moved out of the treasury without the consent of other admins or the community, leading to potential theft, loss of trust, and violation of the protocol’s governance assumptions. The condition under which this occurs is any time the principal admin invokes setApproverAddr, which can be done repeatedly and at will. All participants who rely on the multi‑sig guarantee—token holders, users, and the protocol itself—are affected because the treasury’s safety is compromised. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the governance flow and identified that the admin could manipulate the approver list without restriction. It may be hard to notice because the function appears benign, simply adding addresses, and the contract does not emit warnings or checks that the added addresses are distinct or that a majority of existing admins have approved the change. To remediate, the contract should enforce that any addition or removal of an approver requires approval from a majority of the current approvers, enforce a reasonable limit on the total number of approvers, and ensure that the quorum cannot be satisfied by addresses controlled by a single admin, thereby restoring a true multi‑signature governance model.
summary:
The principalAdmin can keep calling setApproverAddr to add as many addresses as needed to reach
quorum and approve any arbitrary transaction. This is not a true multi-sig if a principal admin can
obtain all the power and decision making.

title: 721A-1 | Wrong Token Sent
content: The vulnerability is an off‑by‑one error in the token transfer logic of an ERC721A‑style contract. The function that is supposed to hand over a specific NFT first validates that the supplied tokenId belongs to the caller by checking that the tokenId maps to msg.sender. After this verification the contract mistakenly calls the internal transfer routine with tokenId+1 instead of the verified tokenId. Because the check and the actual transfer use different identifiers, the contract can send a token that the caller does not own, or even a token that has not been minted yet. This mismatch can be exploited by a malicious actor who triggers the function expecting to receive a known token but receives the next token in the sequence, potentially allowing the attacker to acquire an NFT without proper authorization or to cause the intended token to become locked in an inconsistent state. The impact includes loss of ownership for honest users, unexpected changes in token balances, and a breach of the protocol’s accounting assumptions that each token is uniquely tied to its owner. The bug manifests whenever the vulnerable function is invoked – typically during a claim, withdrawal, or mint‑to‑user operation – because the condition that checks ownership is satisfied but the subsequent transfer uses the wrong identifier. All token holders and any downstream logic that relies on correct token ownership are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by the Guardian team, who noticed that the verification step referenced tokenId while the transfer step referenced tokenId+1. The problem is subtle because the transferred token may still be a valid token, so the UI may simply show a different token ID without obvious error messages, making it hard for users to notice that they received the wrong asset. To remediate the issue, the contract should be updated to pass the verified tokenId to the transfer routine, ensuring that the token that was checked against the caller’s address is the one actually transferred. This aligns the verification and execution paths and restores the intended one‑to‑one relationship between a user and their NFT, eliminating the risk of unintended token movement and preserving the integrity of the platform’s accounting model.
summary:
The tokenId+1 is sent to the caller although it was not used in the check for a valid leaf. Instead,
tokenId was veriﬁed to correspond with the msg.sender.

title: SQDF-1 | Winner Can Be Changed
content: The vulnerability is a mutable result flaw that allows the declared winner of a betting event to be altered after the event has been marked as finished. The root cause is that the contract’s reportResult function does not record whether a result has already been submitted, nor does it enforce a single‑time update. Because the function lacks a guard flag or a check that the result is immutable once set, a malicious oracle can invoke reportResult repeatedly after the event closure and flip the winning side at will. An attacker can exploit this by calling reportResult with a different outcome each time, causing the contract’s internal winner variable to be overwritten. The impact is that payouts may be redirected to the attacker or to an unintended party, users who originally won may lose their expected reward, and the overall accounting of the protocol becomes unreliable. This condition occurs whenever the event lifecycle reaches the finished state but the contract does not lock the result, meaning any entity with permission to call reportResult (typically the oracle) can continue to modify it. All participants who placed bets on the event are affected because the final settlement may not reflect the true outcome, leading to lost or incorrectly distributed funds. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that identified the missing state‑change protection. It can be hard to notice because the function may appear to be called only once in normal operation, and there may be no explicit event emitted to signal a result change, so the problem only surfaces under adversarial repeated calls. The bug belongs to the class of “state‑reentrancy after finalization” or “result tampering” vulnerabilities, where business logic assumes immutability after a certain phase but the code does not enforce it. From a user’s perspective the contract may show that they have won, but later their balance drops to zero or the payout is sent to another address, violating the expectation that a declared winner receives the prize. To remediate, the contract should introduce a boolean flag (e.g., resultReported) that is set the first time reportResult is executed and reject any subsequent calls, or otherwise enforce that the winner can be set only once through access control or commit‑reveal schemes, thereby preserving the integrity of the settlement logic.
summary:
Once the event is ﬁnished, it is possible to for a malicious oracle to repeatedly call reportResult to
modify which side is the winner.

title: SQDF-2 | Weak Source of Randomness
content: The vulnerability is a weak source of on‑chain randomness used by the pickWinner function, which allows an attacker to influence the selection of the competition winner. The root cause is that the contract derives randomness from predictable block variables such as block.timestamp, block.difficulty or similar values that miners or validators can manipulate. Because these inputs are not cryptographically secure, a validator who can control or predict the block attributes can craft a transaction that makes the computed random number favorable to an address they control. In addition, the contract does not enforce a single execution of pickWinner; after a winner is reported the admin can call pickWinner again, then call reportResult to reset the isCompetitionEnded flag, and repeat the process until the random outcome matches an address they own. This repeated‑call loophole effectively lets the admin brute‑force the winner selection. The impact is that the intended fairness of the betting protocol is broken: users expect a random, unbiased winner and a timely payout, but the attacker can consistently win or prevent others from receiving their prize. From a user’s perspective the UI may show that a competition has ended, yet the prize balance remains unchanged or the same address repeatedly appears as the winner, leading to missing refunds or zero payouts. The issue manifests whenever pickWinner is invoked, especially in blocks where the attacker can influence the block header, and when the contract logic does not track whether a winner has already been chosen. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the randomness generation and state‑transition logic, noting the absence of a guard against multiple winner selections. It can be hard to notice because the contract still produces a number that looks random on the surface, and the repeated‑call pattern does not revert or emit obvious errors; only careful inspection of the state flag and the randomness source reveals the problem. To remediate, the contract should replace the weak on‑chain variables with a strong randomness source such as a verifiable random function (VRF) or a trusted oracle, and it must record that a winner has been selected so that subsequent calls to pickWinner are rejected. This aligns the implementation with the generic class of bugs known as insecure randomness and unchecked state transitions, which violate the business logic that each competition must have exactly one unbiased winner and that funds must be distributed according to that outcome.
summary:
pickWinner uses weak sources of on-chain randomness. A validator can exploit this in order to
obtain a winner that is beneﬁcial to themselves.
In addition, an Admin can keep calling pickWinner, then reportResult to clear isCompetitionEnded,
then call pickWinner again and so on until the winner is favorable to them.

title: SQPR-2 | Winners Can’t Get Prize
content: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that occurs when the contract attempts to distribute prize money to a large set of winners in a single transaction. The root cause is an unbounded iteration over the list of winners that can require more gas than the block gas limit permits. When the number of winners grows, the cumulative gas needed for the loop exceeds the maximum gas that can be included in a block, causing the entire payout transaction to revert. An attacker or even a legitimate user can trigger the payout function, but the transaction will fail with an out‑of‑gas error, preventing any winner from receiving their prize. The impact is that funds allocated for prizes become effectively locked in the contract, users see their expected balances remain zero, and the user interface may display that a prize was awarded while the on‑chain state shows no transfer. This condition occurs only under the circumstance that the winner set is sufficiently large; small winner sets succeed, making the problem easy to miss during normal testing. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the prize distribution logic and identified the potential for gas exhaustion. It is hard to notice because the contract behaves correctly for typical cases, and the failure only manifests at scale. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “mass‑payout” or “unbounded loop” vulnerabilities that violate the assumption that a contract can safely push funds to an arbitrary number of recipients in one call. From a user’s perspective, a winner may attempt to claim a reward and receive a transaction failure, see no change in their balance, or receive a message that the prize could not be claimed. The recommended mitigation is to replace the push‑style payout with a pull‑over‑push withdrawal pattern, allowing each winner to individually withdraw their prize in separate transactions that stay within the gas limit, thereby preserving the accounting guarantees and preventing funds from becoming inaccessible.
summary:
If there are a large amount of winners, the amount of gas can exceed the block limit and winners will
not be able to get the prize money.

title: GLOBAL-2 | Centralization Risk
content: The vulnerability is a centralization risk arising from the use of a custom admin access‑control model that grants privileged rights to a set of admin and oracle addresses. The root cause is that the contract design allows any single admin or oracle to invoke critical functions – such as changing betting parameters, updating price feeds, or transferring assets – without additional safeguards like multi‑signature approval or timelocked execution. Because the model does not enforce collective decision‑making, a malicious or compromised privileged address can act unilaterally. An attacker who controls one of these privileged accounts can exploit the flaw by calling the privileged functions to alter odds, freeze or cancel bets, or directly withdraw user balances, leading to loss of funds or incorrect settlement. The impact is that users may see their expected payouts disappear, balances become zero, or bets resolve in an unexpected way, eroding trust in the protocol. This risk materialises whenever the contract relies on admin‑controlled parameters or oracle data – essentially any time a bet is placed or settled – and it is amplified as the number of privileged addresses grows, because the probability that at least one of them behaves maliciously increases. All participants – bettors, token holders, and the broader community – are affected because the protocol’s core financial logic can be subverted. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the access‑control patterns and identified that the custom admin model lacks multi‑sig or timelock constraints. It can be hard to notice in normal operation because the contracts behave correctly when admins act honestly; there is no on‑chain alarm when a privileged function is called, so malicious actions may only become apparent after funds are missing or outcomes are inconsistent with expectations. To remediate, the privileged roles should be migrated to a multi‑signature wallet or a timelocked governance contract, the number of admins should be minimised, and oracle data should be sourced from a decentralized, verifiable mechanism. These changes enforce community oversight, reduce the chance of a single point of failure, and align the protocol with its intended trust‑less design. In summary, the bug belongs to the class of “centralized privileged‑role abuse” where insufficient checks on admin/oracle actions allow unilateral manipulation of protocol state, leading to potential fund loss and broken business logic such as incorrect refund calculations or missing payouts.
summary:
Throughout the contracts there is a risk of admins and oracles using their privilege to beneﬁt
themselves or act malicious toward user’s holdings. Contracts utilizing the CustomAdmin access
control model face more risk as the number of admins or oracles increase because it only takes one
to act mischievous.

title: UB-2 | Order of Operations
content: The vulnerability is an arithmetic mis‑calculation caused by an incorrect order of operations when using SafeMath functions to compute a bettor's gain. The contract chains SafeMath calls as add then mul then div, which forces the addition to be performed before the multiplication and division. The intended formula is to first calculate the proportion of the loser’s stake that belongs to the winner (loserStake * winnerBet / winnerStake) and then add that amount to the winner’s original bet. Because SafeMath evaluates left‑to‑right, the expression 3.add(10).mul(3).div(6) yields 6, whereas the mathematically correct evaluation 3 + 10 * 3 / 6 yields 8. This discrepancy arises from the root cause that SafeMath does not respect conventional arithmetic precedence; it simply applies each operation sequentially. An attacker or honest participant can trigger the bug whenever a bet settlement uses this chained expression, causing the winner to receive less than the expected payout. The impact is a systematic under‑payment to winners and an over‑retention of funds by the protocol, breaking the economic assumptions of fair reward distribution. The condition occurs during the settlement phase of any match where the contract calculates the winner’s gain using the flawed SafeMath chain. All participants who place bets are affected because the contract may return an incorrect amount, leading to user‑facing symptoms such as “my balance is lower than expected” or “the refund amount is zero when it should be positive”. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the arithmetic logic and compared the on‑chain calculation with the intended mathematical model. It can be hard to notice because the code compiles and runs without errors, and the discrepancy only appears when specific numeric values produce a noticeable difference between the two evaluation orders. To fix the problem, the calculation should be rewritten to enforce the correct precedence, for example by computing the product and division first and then adding the winner’s original stake, or by using explicit parentheses or separate variables to avoid SafeMath’s left‑to‑right chaining. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of “order‑of‑operations errors in safe arithmetic libraries”, which can lead to subtle financial inaccuracies in smart contracts that rely on chained library calls for complex formulas.
summary: The logic does not correctly calculate the gain due to the SafeMath order of operations. With the SafeMath operations the addition is performed first, but what is needed is to first calculate the winner’s part of the loser funds and then finally adding it to BettorBetWinner. For example: 3.add(10).mul(3).div(6) = 6 3 + 10 * 3 / 6 = 8

title: Withdrawing funds can lead to wrong accounting
content: The vulnerability is an accounting inconsistency that occurs when a user withdraws an amount larger than the currently unstaked balance (totalUnstaked) from the Vault. The withdrawal function calculates an immediateAmount that can be paid out immediately and a delayedAmount that is supposed to be paid after the underlying stake is unstaked. The implementation reduces totalUnstaked by the immediateAmount and, crucially, also subtracts the delayedAmount from totalStaked while merely recording the delayedAmount in a pending withdrawals mapping. Because the contract does not actually exit the validator or unstake the delayed portion at that moment, the funds remain locked in the staking protocol and continue to earn rewards. Consequently, the contract’s internal totalStaked figure becomes smaller than the real amount that is still staked. This discrepancy can be repeatedly triggered by requesting many small withdrawals that exceed totalUnstaked by a tiny margin, causing the pending withdrawals to accumulate while totalStaked is steadily under‑counted. From a user’s perspective the UI may show the expected immediate payout, but the overall protocol dashboard will display a lower total stake than should exist, potentially leading to incorrect reward calculations, insufficient collateral for slashing, or false assumptions about the health of the system. The issue was discovered during a security audit when the auditors noticed that totalStaked was decreased before the stake was actually released, a logical flaw that is easy to miss because the contract still honors the withdrawal after a delay and rewards keep flowing. The bug belongs to the class of premature state‑mutation accounting errors, where a balance is adjusted before the underlying asset is truly transferred. To remediate the problem the contract should only decrement totalStaked when the delayed amount has been successfully unstaked and transferred to the Vault, or maintain a separate accounting entry for pending withdrawals without touching totalStaked until the exit is finalised.
summary: The users can withdraw their funds from the Vault and if there is not enough LYX in the contract (totalUnstaked), a delayedAmount will be deducted from totalStaked and be assigned to _pendingWithdrawals[beneficiary]: nonReentrant whenNotPaused { uint256 immediateAmount = amount > totalUnstaked ? totalUnstaked : amount; uint256 delayedAmount = amount - immediateAmount; totalUnstaked -= immediateAmount; totalStaked -= delayedAmount; //@audit totalStaked is decreased _pendingWithdrawals[beneficiary] += delayedAmount; This means that when LYX is unstaked and a validator is exited, the user will be able to claim the delayedAmount which is already deducted from the totalStaked. However, the LYX is still staked and the validator is running until it is exited. However, as mentioned above, rewards are constantly sent to the Vault automatically. This can lead to a scenario when the _pendingWithdrawals[beneficiary] is a small amount and it is beneficial for the Vault to wait few days and to accrue rewards instead of exiting a validator. As mentioned in the docs, a withdrawal can take up to 8 days. Let's look at an example: -. A user wants to withdraw 10 LYX but totalUnstaked = 9.5 LYX. /. 0.5 LYX is deducted from totalStaked and _pendingWithdrawals[beneficiary] += 0.5 LYX. 0. Instead of exiting validator, there are enough rewards so the user can claim the delayedAmount which is 0.5. 1. Now, the totalStaked is 0.5 less than it should be because the funds were deducted beforehand. In the long run, this will seriously mess up the whole internal accounting if this happens a lot of times which is quite likely for small amounts.

title: Exiting a validator will not be noticed by the Vault
content: The vulnerability is a logical accounting error in the Vault contract that governs deposits of LYX tokens. The contract enforces a depositLimit by calculating a value called newTotalDeposits as the larger of two quantities – the product of the number of registered validators and a constant DEPOSIT_AMOUNT, and the sum of totalStaked and totalUnstaked – then adding the incoming deposit amount. The root cause is that the internal validators counter is never decremented when a validator exits the system. Consequently, after some validators leave because users withdraw their stakes, the expression validators * DEPOSIT_AMOUNT continues to reflect the original, higher validator count, while the actual token balance represented by totalStaked + totalUnstaked drops. When newTotalDeposits is compared against the depositLimit, the stale validator‑based term can dominate the max calculation, causing the check to falsely indicate that the limit has been reached. An attacker or any user can therefore trigger a denial‑of‑service condition: once enough validators have exited, the contract will reject all further deposits with a DepositLimitExceeded revert, even though the vault still holds far fewer tokens than the limit permits. This situation is observable from the user’s perspective as a failed deposit transaction, often accompanied by an error message stating that the deposit limit was exceeded, while the UI may still show a low vault balance. The impact is primarily on availability – legitimate users are unable to add liquidity, which can stall staking operations and reduce protocol utility. The bug was discovered during a security audit that examined the deposit logic and state updates. It can be hard to notice because the contract’s accounting variables appear consistent individually; only the interaction between the stale validator count and the deposit limit reveals the inconsistency. To remediate the issue, the contract should either base the deposit limit solely on the actual token balance (totalStaked + totalUnstaked) or ensure that the validators variable is correctly decremented whenever a validator exits. This correction restores the intended invariant that the deposit limit reflects the real amount of tokens held in the vault, preventing false reverts and preserving the protocol’s expected deposit functionality.
summary: The Vault has a depositLimit that ensures no more LYX can be deposited when a certain number is reached. Inside deposit, there is the following check: uint256 newTotalDeposits = Math.max(validators * DEPOSIT_AMOUNT, totalStaked + totalUnstaked) + amount; if (newTotalDeposits > depositLimit) { revert DepositLimitExceeded(newTotalDeposits, depositLimit); The newTotalDeposits take the higher number between validators * DEPOSIT_AMOUNT and totalStaked + totalUnstaked, adds the amount, and compares it to the depositLimit. The problem is that when a validator is exited, the validators variable inside the Vault is not decreased as it should be. For example, if 10 validators are registered and after some time 5 of them are exited because of user withdrawals the validators * DEPOSIT_AMOUNT will be still equal to 320 while the totalStaked + totalUnstaked will be much smaller because of funds exiting the Vault. For simplicity, if the depositLimit is set to 320, no more users will be able to deposit LYX even though the funds in the Vault are much less than the limit.

title: SQDF-5 | Weak Source of Randomness
content: The vulnerability is a weak source of randomness used in the contract's pickWinner function. The function relies on on‑chain values such as block.timestamp, block.difficulty, or blockhash to derive a pseudo‑random number. Because these values can be influenced or predicted by a validator or miner, the randomness is not cryptographically secure. An attacker who controls block production can manipulate the inputs so that the computed winner address is one they control or otherwise beneficial. Exploitation proceeds by the validator observing the pending transaction that calls pickWinner, adjusting the block parameters within the allowed range, and then mining a block that yields a favorable random value. When the contract subsequently selects the winner, the manipulated value causes the contract to transfer the prize to the attacker instead of a truly random participant. The impact is that the lottery or betting protocol loses its fairness guarantee; users may see their expected winnings disappear, and the protocol's reputation is damaged. The condition occurs whenever the contract calls pickWinner without an external verifiable random function; any validator or miner with sufficient stake can bias the outcome. All participants who entered the bet are affected because the prize may be diverted. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that flagged the use of deterministic on‑chain variables for randomness. Because the contract appears to work correctly on the surface—winners are still selected and funds are transferred—the flaw can be hard to notice without inspecting the source of entropy. The proper mitigation is to replace the weak on‑chain values with a strong source of randomness, such as the blockhash of a future block combined with an oracle like Chainlink VRF, or any provably unpredictable randomness pattern. This class of bug is commonly known as a predictable or manipulable randomness vulnerability and violates the fundamental business logic that a lottery must select a winner uniformly at random. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a winner being announced, but the user who expected a fair draw may receive nothing or see the same address win repeatedly, leading to confusion and loss of trust. The failure mode is that funds that should be be distributed randomly instead disappear into an attacker‑controlled account.
summary: pickWinner uses weak sources of on-chain randomness. A validator can exploit this in order to obtain a winner that is beneficial to themselves.

title: MaliciousUserCanMintUnlimitedAmountofNFTsDuetoReentrancy in whitelistMint() and FCFSMint()
content: The contract contains a reentrancy weakness in its whitelistMint and FCFSMint functions. Both functions invoke the ERC721 _safeMint routine, which performs an external call to the recipient contract’s onERC721Received hook. Because the contract updates its internal accounting variables (such as the number of minted tokens or whitelist allowances) only after the _safeMint call, a malicious recipient can exploit the callback to re‑enter the same mint function before those variables are changed. By repeatedly re‑entering, the attacker can cause the mint logic to execute many times with the same allowance, effectively minting an unlimited number of NFTs. This flaw arises from the classic Checks‑Effects‑Interactions anti‑pattern: the contract checks the caller’s eligibility, then makes an external call, and only afterwards applies the effect of reducing the allowance. The vulnerability is discovered during a manual audit that flagged the absence of a reentrancy guard on these entry points. It can be difficult to spot because the external call is hidden inside the library function _safeMint, making the flow appear safe at first glance. When exploited, the token supply can be exhausted or heavily inflated, breaking the economic model of the protocol, devaluing existing tokens, and potentially allowing the attacker to sell the over‑minted NFTs for profit. Users who expect a limited collection may receive unexpected extra tokens, and the protocol’s reputation can suffer. The issue belongs to the broader class of reentrancy bugs in minting functions. To remediate, the contract should either move all state updates (such as decrementing the whitelist quota or incrementing the total supply counter) to occur before the external _safeMint call, or protect the functions with a nonReentrant modifier from OpenZeppelin’s ReentrancyGuard, thereby preventing nested calls from re‑entering the mint logic.
summary:
```solidity
// whitelistMint() and FCFSMint() are vulnerable to reentrancy
```
The whitelistMint() and FCFSMint() functions are vulnerable to reentrancy. We can see that the function fails to apply a reentrancy modifier. When a malicious user calls them, they can do a reentrancy attack via the _safeMint() function that is called. We can see that absolutely all variables are updated afterwards. Thus, a malicious user can mint as many NFTs as he wants.

title: FCFSMint() Can Be Called By Anyone, Not Only By Whitelisted Users
content: The vulnerability is an unauthorized access control flaw in the FCFSMint function of the contract. The function is intended, according to the project documentation, to be callable only by wallets that have been added to a whitelist, allowing each whitelisted participant to mint up to two additional NFTs during the First‑Come‑First‑Serve (FCFS) phase. However, the contract code does not contain any verification that the caller is actually whitelisted, meaning that any address can invoke FCFSMint and receive the privileged minting rights. This occurs because the developer omitted a require statement or similar check that would compare the caller against a stored whitelist mapping, resulting in a missing authorization gate. An attacker can simply send a transaction calling FCFSMint, receive the two extra NFTs, and repeat the call as many times as desired, effectively flooding the supply. The impact is a dilution of the NFT collection’s scarcity, loss of revenue for the project, and potential devaluation of existing tokens, as users who expected a limited allocation may receive more than intended or see their assets lose value. The issue manifests whenever the FCFS minting window is open and any user interacts with the contract, regardless of their whitelist status. All participants, including legitimate whitelisted users, are affected because the economic model assumes a capped mint per address; the breach breaks that assumption. The flaw was discovered during a security review that compared the contract’s public interface against the README specifications and noted the absence of any access‑control logic. Because the function appears to work correctly from a functional standpoint—minting NFTs without reverting—the problem can be subtle and may not be caught by simple transaction testing unless the whitelist requirement is explicitly verified. To remediate, the contract should enforce a whitelist check before allowing the mint, typically by adding a require statement that validates msg.sender against a stored whitelist mapping, and by emitting an event when a non‑whitelisted call is attempted. This class of bug is commonly referred to as an “missing access control” or “authorization bypass” vulnerability, which violates the intended business logic of restricted participation and can lead to unintended token creation and financial loss.
summary: From the ReadMe, we can see that the FCFSMint() function should be called only by whitelisted users: Ability to participate in the FCFS phase where every whitelisted wallet can mint two additional NFTs But as we can see in the functions thus verification is completely missing.

title: levelUP doesn't actually increase the level
content: The vulnerability resides in the levelUP function that is intended to let an NFT owner spend accumulated experience points (XP) to raise the NFT's level. The function checks the current NFTLevel (1 or 2) and, after deducting the appropriate XP amount, increments a field called balance instead of the NFTLevel field. Because the level variable never changes, the contract records the XP expenditure but leaves the NFT at its original level, violating the expected business logic that a successful level‑up should increase the NFT's level. This logical error originates from a mistaken state update – the developer updated the wrong storage slot, confusing a generic balance counter with the specific level counter. An attacker does not need to craft a special payload; any user who calls levelUP with a valid NFT will experience the bug. The exploitation flow is straightforward: the user initiates levelUP, the contract calls spendXP which transfers the required XP from the user, then the contract executes stakedNFTs[msg.sender][index].balance++ instead of NFTLevel++. From the user’s perspective the UI still shows the same level, while the XP balance has decreased, leading to confusion and potential loss of valuable XP that cannot be reclaimed. The impact is high because users are effectively paying for a service that never materializes, eroding trust and possibly causing economic loss if the XP has monetary value or is required for further protocol interactions. The condition under which the bug manifests is any call to levelUP when the NFT is at level 1 or 2; calls for higher levels revert correctly. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the intended state changes with the actual code. It can be hard to notice because the balance field may be unrelated to leveling, and the contract does not emit an explicit event indicating a level change, so observers see no error. To remediate, the function should increment the NFTLevel field instead of balance, and optionally emit a LevelUp event to make the state transition observable. This class of bug is a logical state‑update mistake, often categorized as an “incorrect variable assignment” or “business‑logic violation” where the contract updates the wrong storage variable, breaking accounting assumptions and user expectations that spending XP results in a higher NFT level.

title: spend/addXP will not add or spend correctly
content: The contract implements a function that spends experience points (XP) from a collection of staked NFTs belonging to a user. The intended behaviour is to deduct the requested amount proportionally from each NFT, zeroing an NFT’s balance only when its XP is fully consumed and adding the amount actually spent to a running total. The vulnerability arises because the code clears an NFT’s balance before adding that balance to the spent accumulator. As a result, when an NFT does not have enough XP to cover the remaining request, its balance is set to zero but the spent variable is not increased, leaving the accumulator lower than the true amount removed. Later, the algorithm computes a delta as the original request minus the spent total and subtracts this delta from the last NFT in the list. Because spent is understated, the delta is larger than the remaining XP, causing the contract to believe it has spent more XP than it actually did. This mis‑calculation can occur whenever a user tries to spend an amount that requires draining more than one NFT, especially when the second (or later) NFT’s balance is insufficient. From a user’s perspective the transaction appears to succeed, but the on‑chain state shows an inconsistent XP accounting: the user may see one NFT with a reduced balance, another NFT at zero, and the contract’s internal accounting still expects additional XP to be deducted. The impact is that users can lose visibility of their XP, experience unexpected reverts on subsequent spend attempts, or have their XP effectively “disappear” because the contract’s bookkeeping is out of sync with the actual balances. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the spendXP logic and identified the incorrect ordering of operations. It is hard to notice because the transaction does not revert and the balance changes look plausible at a glance; only a detailed trace of the spent accumulator reveals the mismatch. The proper fix is to update the spent accumulator before zeroing the NFT’s balance, or to redesign the algorithm to compute a proportional deduction for each NFT and then apply any remaining delta in a second pass, ensuring that the total amount deducted matches the requested spend. In generic terms, this is a state‑update ordering bug that breaks accounting invariants and leads to incorrect resource accounting in a multi‑asset spend routine.

title: spendXP fails if the last NFT lacks balance
content: The contract implements a function called spendXP that is intended to deduct a user‑specified amount of experience points (XP) from each NFT a user has staked. The implementation first computes a uniform share amountPerNFT by dividing the total amount by the number of staked NFTs. It then iterates over the list, reducing each NFT’s balance by amountPerNFT when the NFT has enough XP, or setting the balance to zero when it does not. While this loop tracks how much XP has actually been spent in the variable spent, the function finishes with a final line that subtracts the remaining delta (amount‑spent) from the balance of the last NFT in the array. The root cause of the vulnerability is that the final subtraction assumes the last NFT still holds enough XP, but the earlier loop may have already reduced that NFT’s balance to zero when it lacked sufficient XP. Consequently, when the last NFT’s balance is zero and amount‑spent is less than the requested amount, the expression (amount‑spent) is a positive value that is subtracted from a zero balance, triggering an under‑flow revert in Solidity. This bug manifests only when the user’s most recently added NFT – which the contract treats as the last element – has less XP than the proportional share, a situation that is common because newer NFTs typically start with low XP. Any user who tries to spend XP under these conditions will see the transaction fail, receiving an error instead of the expected XP deduction. From the user’s perspective the UI may display “spend failed” or simply not update the XP balance, contradicting the expectation that the requested amount is deducted proportionally. The impact is a denial‑of‑service on the spendXP functionality: users cannot spend XP, rewards that depend on XP may be blocked, and the protocol’s accounting logic is broken because the intended deduction never occurs. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the arithmetic flow of the spendXP routine and identified the unsafe final subtraction. It is hard to notice because the loop appears to handle insufficient balances correctly, masking the fact that the residual amount is later applied without a safety check. To remediate the problem the algorithm should be redesigned so that the residual amount is allocated to an NFT that actually has enough XP, or the proportional deduction should be calculated based on each NFT’s current balance (for example, using (amount * nftBalance) / totalBalance) and a second pass should distribute any leftover amount to the first NFT with sufficient balance. Additionally, explicit checks before any subtraction and the use of safe‑math patterns would prevent the under‑flow revert.

title: Level XP multiplier isn't updated on NFT level
content: The contract allows users to stake NFTs and earn experience points (XP) that can be spent on raffles or to level up the NFTs. Each NFT level is supposed to grant a higher XP multiplier, defined by the variables levelTwoMultiplier (value 2) and LevelThreeMultiplier (value 3). The levelUP function correctly deducts the required XP and increments the NFT balance, but it never updates the NFTXPMultiplier field that is used in later XP calculations. As a result, after an NFT is promoted from level 1 to level 2 (or from level 2 to level 3), the on‑chain record of the multiplier remains at its previous value. Consequently, the XP earned after leveling is calculated with the old, lower multiplier, so the user receives less XP than expected. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a higher NFT level, yet the XP accrual rate appears unchanged or even lower, leading to confusion such as “my NFT is level 2 but I still get the same XP as before” or “my raffle entries did not increase after leveling”. The bug originates from a logical omission: the state variables that store the multiplier are never written to during the level‑up process, and the contract does not derive the multiplier dynamically from the NFTLevel field. This condition is triggered every time a user calls levelUP, i.e., whenever an NFT is upgraded, and it affects all NFT owners who rely on XP for participation in the protocol’s economic mechanisms. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the levelUP implementation and noticed that the multiplier variables were declared but never referenced. It can be hard to notice because there is no explicit error; the contract continues to function, but the expected increase in XP is silently missing, which may only be observed through abnormal XP balances or reduced raffle chances. The vulnerability violates the business logic that higher NFT levels should provide proportionally higher rewards, breaking the accounting assumptions of the system. To remediate, the levelUP function should assign the appropriate multiplier to the NFTXPMultiplier field after a successful upgrade (e.g., setting it to levelTwoMultiplier for a level‑2 NFT and to LevelThreeMultiplier for a level‑3 NFT), or alternatively compute the multiplier on‑the‑fly from the NFTLevel value, ensuring that future XP calculations reflect the new level correctly.

title: returnLoserTicketXPs uses wrong price
content: The contract contains an off‑by‑one indexing error in the function that refunds experience points (XP) to participants of a raffle that did not win. The function receives a raffle identifier `id` that is treated as a 1‑based value, so it computes a zero‑based `index = id‑1` for accessing the `raffles` array. While the end‑time check correctly uses `raffles[index]`, the calculation of the XP amount later references `raffles[id]` instead of `raffles[index]`. Because the `raffles` array is zero‑based, `raffles[id]` points to the next raffle entry, causing the price from a different raffle to be applied when computing `valueToReturn`. This mismatch can lead to participants receiving either too many or too few XP points depending on the price difference between the intended raffle and the adjacent one. The bug is triggered whenever the owner calls `returnLoserTicketXPs` for any raffle, which is a privileged operation but still part of normal protocol flow. Users may notice that their XP balance suddenly jumps to an unexpected value or that they receive no XP when they should have been refunded, breaking the expectation that the XP reward matches the ticket price of the specific raffle they entered. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected array indexing patterns and identified inconsistent use of `id` versus `index`. It can be hard to spot because the XP accounting is internal and does not directly affect token transfers, so visual UI cues may not highlight the discrepancy. The proper fix is to use the same zero‑based index for every access to the `raffles` array, replacing `raffles[id].price` with `raffles[index].price` (or alternatively make `id` zero‑based throughout). Aligning the indexing eliminates the price mismatch, ensuring that XP refunds are calculated correctly and that the protocol’s accounting assumptions remain intact.

title: Raffles cannot be created
content: The contract implements a raffle registry using a dynamic array called raffles. When a new raffle is created the code attempts to store the raffle struct at index raffleCounter-1 by direct assignment. In Solidity a dynamic array does not automatically allocate storage for an index that does not yet exist; the array length must be increased before an element can be written. Because the code writes to an index that is outside the current length, the EVM throws an out-of-bounds panic and the transaction reverts. This bug appears as “Raffles cannot be created” – any call that tries to add a raffle fails, the UI reports an error, and no raffle is recorded. The root cause is a misuse of array indexing (C-06 rule) instead of using the push() method or increasing the length first. An attacker does not need to exploit a hidden backdoor; the vulnerability is triggered simply by invoking the normal createRaffle function, which makes the contract effectively unusable for its primary purpose. The impact is a denial-of-service on the raffle feature: users cannot launch new raffles, the protocol cannot collect entry fees, and any funds that might have been sent before the revert are returned to the sender, but the business logic is broken because the expected raffle list never grows. The condition occurs whenever raffleCounter is zero (the first raffle) or when the counter is incremented after the failed assignment, leading to an index that is always one position beyond the current array length. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that checked for Solidity anti-pattern C-06. It can be hard to notice because the contract compiles without warnings and the panic only appears at runtime, often only when a user attempts to create the first raffle. The correct fix is to replace the direct index assignment with a push of the newly constructed raffle struct, and then increment the counter, ensuring the array length is increased before the element is stored. This aligns the implementation with the expected dynamic-array semantics and restores the ability to create raffles, eliminating the out-of-bounds revert.
summary:
Similar to C-06 in solidity you cannot add elements to an array by assigning that index:
```solidity
raffles[raffleCounter - 1] = raffle(
    raffleCounter,
    _raffleName,
    _rewardAmount,
    block.timestamp,
    _endTime,
    _price,
    0,
    _image
);
```
This causes an array out-of-bounds panic.

title: leading to loss of funds
content: The vulnerability originates from the cumulativeDepositsMultiplierX18 variable, which is intended to represent a scaling factor for all deposits in the protocol. When a spot account is socialized – meaning the borrowed amount is removed from a short position and redistributed to other depositors – the contract updates this multiplier. However, the update logic does not enforce a lower bound, allowing the multiplier to drop to zero or even become negative. If the multiplier reaches zero, every subsequent deposit call triggers a revert because the contract attempts to multiply the deposit amount by zero, effectively rejecting the transaction and leaving the user’s funds stuck in the contract. If the multiplier becomes negative, the arithmetic treats the deposit as a short position; deposits are then processed without any health‑check, exposing the depositor to liquidation despite having supplied funds. This flaw can be exploited simply by triggering a socialization event that drives the multiplier to an extreme value, after which any user attempting to deposit will either see their transaction fail silently or unintentionally open a short position that can be liquidated. The impact is a loss of user funds: users may see their balances disappear, receive no tokens in return for a deposit, or be forced into liquidation without warning.
