The attacker can set themselves as the beneficiary, choose a short non‑revokable duration, and effectively capture the funds that were intended for the original schedule. This occurs when two separate transactions are required – one to move tokens into the contract and another to register the schedule – and there is no atomic transfer inside createVestingSchedule. The impact is that funds disappear from the intended beneficiary’s balance and appear in the attacker’s vesting schedule, violating the accounting assumptions that each transferred amount is locked for the specified recipient. Users expect that after sending tokens to the vesting contract, the subsequent schedule creation will lock those tokens for the chosen beneficiary; instead they may see zero balance or missing refunds. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined role management and the flow of token transfers, and it can be hard to notice because the contract does not emit explicit warnings when the balance is insufficient at schedule creation, and the front‑running transaction can be indistinguishable from a legitimate schedule creation. To remediate, the contract should either perform the token transfer internally within createVestingSchedule (so the transfer and schedule registration happen atomically) or restrict the permission to a single trusted address, eliminating the possibility of competing schedule creations. This class of bug is commonly referred to as a front‑runable race condition in permissioned functions that rely on external state changes.
summary: The createVestingSchedule method of TokenVestingV2 expects to have a pre-transferred balance before initializing a vesting schedule. The problem with the current contract version is that multiple accounts can hold the ROLE_CREATE_SCHEDULE role. Since two transactions are expected to create a vesting schedule (transferring funds to the TokenVestingV2 contract and then calling createVestingSchedule) this means that between them another holder of the role can come in and create a vesting schedule of his own (with himself as beneficiary for example, non-revokable with just 7 days of duration) and in this way steal the funds of the other role holder.

title: MJR-1 Correct migration
content: The vulnerability originates from the strategy contract’s constructor, where it grants unlimited spend allowances (approve) for external token contracts such as CRV and USDC. These allowances are intended to enable the strategy to manage its assets while it is active. However, when the strategy is migrated to a new implementation, the migration routine does not revoke or reset those allowances. As a result, the old strategy contract retains the right to move the tokens that remain in its balance after migration. An attacker who can trigger a transferFrom call on the token contracts, or a malicious new strategy that re‑uses the old allowance, can drain the assets that were supposed to be transferred to the new strategy. The impact is that users who have deposited funds into the vault may see their balances reduced or completely emptied after a migration that appears to have succeeded. The issue manifests only during or after a migration operation, specifically when the prepareMigration function is executed without clearing the previously granted approvals. Token holders, the vault’s governance, and any downstream protocol that relies on the migrated strategy are affected because the accounting assumptions that the old contract no longer has control over the assets are violated. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit performed by MixBytes, which noted that the constructor’s approve calls were never paired with a corresponding reset in the migration path. Because approvals are stored on the token contracts and not reflected in the strategy’s UI, the problem can be difficult to notice; the migration may look successful while the hidden allowance still exists. To remediate the issue, the migration routine should explicitly set the allowances for all previously approved tokens back to zero, claim any pending rewards, transfer any residual token balances to the new strategy, and finally revoke the vault’s own approvals. This ensures that after migration the old contract no longer possesses any authority to move user funds, restoring the intended accounting invariants and preventing unauthorized token transfers.
summary: In constructor, rights are granted to spend tokens, which should be canceled when migrating the strategy. Strategy.sol#L171

title: Inadequate Checking of `isIncreasing` when trader adjusts position size
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect classification of position‑size changes in the perpetual futures engine. The library function that determines whether a trader is increasing a position only looks at the sign of the size delta relative to the current position size, and it treats a zero‑size position as an increase. It does not consider the sign of the resulting position after applying the delta (self.size + sizeDelta). Consequently, when a trader with an existing long position submits a negative sizeDelta that is larger in magnitude than the current size, the new position becomes short, but the function still reports that the operation is not an increase. This mis‑classification bypasses the checks that block order creation and filling when the market and settlement modules are disabled. The protocol intends to prevent new positions or increases while allowing decreases or closures, but the flawed logic lets a trader reverse the position direction and effectively increase the position size in the opposite direction. Because the order is treated as a decrease, the contract applies the lower maintenance‑margin requirement instead of the higher initial‑margin requirement that should apply to an increase. Under market‑disabled conditions this can leave the trader under‑collateralised and subject to liquidation, or allow the trader to open a new position when the protocol explicitly forbids it. The issue manifests when the owner disables a market and its settlement configuration, a trader already holds a position, and then submits an order with a sizeDelta that flips the sign of the position. The affected parties are any traders holding positions in a disabled market, as well as the protocol that may suffer unexpected liquidations or loss of trust. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit by CodeHawks, who wrote a test that showed a trader could close a long position and immediately open a short position despite the market being disabled, while another trader could achieve the same by submitting a single order with a large negative delta. The problem is subtle because the function name and its simple checks give the impression that it correctly identifies increases, making the sign‑flip case easy to overlook. The recommended fix is to modify the isIncreasing routine to also evaluate the sign of the resulting position (self.size + sizeDelta) and treat a sign change as an increase, ensuring that the proper margin checks are enforced and that disabled markets truly block position increases. This bug belongs to the class of business‑logic errors where sign handling of financial deltas is incorrect, leading to privilege escalation and margin‑requirement bypass.

title: Positive PnL is lost for all parties when liquidating an account, potentially causing that the MarginCollateralRecipient ends up receiving way less USD value than what it could have received.
content: The vulnerability is a loss of positive unrealized profit‑and‑loss (PnL) during the liquidation of a trading account. When an account that holds profitable open positions becomes under‑collateralised, the liquidation routine closes the positions but fails to mint the positive PnL as USD‑denominated collateral before deducting the required maintenance margin. The root cause is that the LiquidationBranch.liquidateAccounts function calculates the margin balance using only the existing collateral balance, ignoring the unrealized profit that would normally be converted into USDZ tokens and added to the account’s collateralMarginBalance. Because the positive PnL is not minted, the margin that can be seized from the account is limited to the raw collateral value, which may be lower than the required maintenance margin. An attacker (or any liquidator) can therefore trigger liquidation on a profitable account, causing the account to lose the entire amount of its unrealised profit while the marginCollateralRecipient receives less USD than it should. The impact is two‑fold: the liquidated trader sees their profit disappear and receives no compensation for it, and the protocol’s liquidator reward pool is under‑funded because the transferred collateral is short of the expected amount. This situation occurs only when an account is liquidated while its unrealised PnL is positive and the required maintenance margin exceeds the raw collateral but would be satisfied if the PnL were treated as collateral. The affected parties are the traders whose positions are liquidated, the liquidators who receive the margin collateral, and the protocol that relies on accurate accounting of rewards. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by CodeHawks, who traced the liquidation flow and observed that the positive PnL was never minted before the deductAccountMargin call. The bug is subtle because the liquidation transaction still succeeds, but the amounts transferred are lower than expected, making the discrepancy easy to miss in normal operation and only visible when comparing the account’s total market value before and after liquidation. To remediate the problem, the liquidation logic should first check whether the account’s unrealised PnL is positive and, if so, deposit that amount as USDZ into the account and mint the corresponding tokens in the PerpetualEngine contract. Only after this step should the required maintenance margin be deducted, ensuring that the positive PnL is treated as part of the collateral balance and that the correct amount is transferred to the marginCollateralRecipient. This fix aligns the liquidation process with the intended accounting model where profits are converted into usable collateral before any margin seizure.

title: `SettlementBranch._fillOrder` does not guarantee the collateral of a position is enough to pay the future liquidation fee.
content: SettlementBranch._fillOrder contains a logical accounting flaw that allows a position to be opened with collateral that is sufficient to cover the opening fee but insufficient to cover the liquidation fee that may be charged later. The function deducts the opening fee from the trader's margin balance but does not subsequently verify that the remaining collateral can satisfy the protocol‑defined liquidation fee. Because TradingAccount.deductAccountMargin pays the liquidation fee before any profit‑and‑loss (PnL) is transferred to the market‑making engine, a trader can deliberately supply a minimal amount of collateral, open a position, and then become liquidated with the liquidation fee consuming the entire remaining balance. From the user’s perspective the trade appears to succeed, but when the market price moves against the position the account is liquidated and the user’s balance drops to zero, while the market maker receives no PnL because the liquidation fee has already been taken. The impact is a loss of funds for the trader and a potential distortion of market‑making incentives, as the engine receives no compensation for the trade. The vulnerability manifests whenever the margin after opening‑fee deduction is lower than the required liquidation fee, which can be triggered by small‑collateral positions or by manipulating the fee parameters. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the fee‑deduction flow and identified that the contract never validates the post‑fee margin against the liquidation‑fee requirement. The issue is subtle because the contract does not revert; instead it silently allows the liquidation to proceed, making the loss appear as a normal market event. The bug belongs to the class of insufficient‑collateral‑validation or fee‑ordering vulnerabilities, where the order of accounting operations violates the business rule that a position must always retain enough collateral to cover its worst‑case liquidation cost. The recommended fix is to add an explicit margin‑requirement check after the opening fee is deducted, ensuring that the sum of the order fee and the liquidation fee can be covered by the remaining margin before the position is accepted. This restores the intended accounting invariant and prevents traders from opening under‑collateralised positions that can be liquidated with zero residual balance.
summary:
SettlementBranch._fillOrder does not guarantee the collateral of a position is enough to pay the future liquidation fee.

SettlementBranch._fillOrder does not check the collateral of a position is enough to pay the future liquidation fee after paying the fee for opening a position.

Traders may put too small collateral to pay the whole liquidation fee to exploit the imbalance between expected profit and loss. TradingAccount.deductAccountMargin pays liquidation fee first, so market making engine also receives 0 from pnl.

https://github.com/Cyfrin/2024-07-zaros/blob/7439d79e627286ade431d4ea02805715e46ccf42/src/perpetuals/leaves/TradingAccount.sol#L528-L566

title: Incorrect logic for checking isFillPriceValid
content: The contract contains an incorrect validation routine for off‑chain order execution, specifically the isFillPriceValid check inside the fillOffchainOrders function. The routine is intended to ensure that a trader’s target price (used for take‑profit or stop‑loss) is compatible with the market fill price at the moment the order is processed. However, the logic is inverted: for a buy order the code requires the target price to be less than or equal to the fill price, and for a sell order it requires the target price to be greater than or equal to the fill price. In a typical trading scenario the opposite relationship is required – a buyer wants the fill price to be at or below the target price, and a seller wants the fill price to be at or above the target price. Because of this reversal the condition evaluates to false for any realistic combination of fill price and target price, causing ctx.isFillPriceValid to be false for every order. The function does not revert when the check fails; it simply continues to the next order, so the failing order is silently skipped. As a result, traders are unable to set effective take‑profit or stop‑loss levels; off‑chain orders that include a target price never complete, and users see no execution or error messages, only the absence of the expected trade. The impact is that funds remain locked in the trader’s account without the intended protective or profit‑taking actions, breaking the business logic that assumes a valid target price will trigger an order. This bug manifests whenever an off‑chain order is submitted with a non‑zero target price, regardless of market direction, and it affects any user who relies on the off‑chain order mechanism, including market makers and liquidity providers. The issue was discovered during a security audit by CodeHawks, where the test suite showed that orders were being skipped without a revert, indicating a logical flaw rather than a runtime exception. The problem is subtle because the contract’s control flow does not raise an error, making the failure easy to miss in standard tests that only check for reverts. To remediate the issue, the comparison operators must be inverted: for buy orders the target price should be greater than or equal to the fill price, and for sell orders the target price should be less than or equal to the fill price. This correction restores the intended validation, allowing off‑chain orders with proper target prices to be executed and re‑establishes the expected accounting guarantees of the protocol.

title: Market Disruption and Financial Loss Post-Liquidation
content: The vulnerability resides in the liquidation routine of the perpetual market contract. When an account is liquidated the code calls the generic updateOpenInterest function with values that have been calculated without preserving the existing open interest (OI) and skew of the market. Instead of subtracting only the size of the liquidated position, the implementation overwrites the market’s OI and skew with zero. This mistake originates from a comment that intended to bypass cap checks during liquidation, but the actual arithmetic clears the whole state. As a result, after a single liquidation the market reports zero skew, zero total open interest, and consequently all derived metrics – funding velocity, funding rate, mark price, order fee and accrued funding – collapse to zero or incorrect values. Any subsequent attempt to modify a position triggers the open‑interest limit check, which now sees a current OI of zero and attempts to subtract the old position size, causing an arithmetic underflow and a transaction revert. The protocol therefore experiences a denial‑of‑service condition: traders cannot increase margin, cannot open or modify positions, and the funding mechanism stops working. From a user’s perspective the UI would show that the market has no open interest, funding rates are flat, order fees are zero and attempts to trade revert with an “arithmetic underflow” error, effectively making funds appear to disappear or become locked. The issue was discovered during a manual audit and reproduced with a proof‑of‑concept test that liquidated a single account and observed the OI and skew reset to zero, followed by a failing transaction when trying to update a position. The bug is hard to notice because zero values may be interpreted as a dormant market rather than a corrupted state, and the comment in the code masks the intention. The proper fix is to adjust the liquidation path so that it only deducts the liquidated position from the existing OI and skew, preserving the rest of the market state. A dedicated updateOpenInterestLiquidation function can perform the subtraction safely, after which the regular updateOpenInterest call can be retained for other operations. This restores correct funding calculations, prevents underflow, and eliminates the denial‑of‑service scenario, ensuring that traders retain accurate interest, price impact and fee information after liquidations.

title: Any borrower with bad debt can be liquidated multiple times to lock funds in the lending pair
content: The vulnerability resides in the liquidation routine of a lending pair where the function responsible for cleaning up bad debt, `liquidateClean`, subtracts the cleared shares only from the global pair totals while leaving the borrower’s individual borrowed‑share counter untouched. As a result, after an initial liquidation that drains the borrower’s collateral, the borrower may still retain a non‑zero share balance that represents leftover debt. The protocol treats this leftover balance as insolvent, but the function permits subsequent calls with `_sharesToLiquidate` set to zero. Each of these zero‑share calls erroneously reduces the pair’s total borrowed shares and total asset amounts without moving any assets from the borrower or rewarding the liquidator. This repeated reduction corrupts the accounting state: total assets shrink, total borrow amounts under‑flow, and the pool’s bookkeeping no longer reflects any real collateral. The impact is that borrowers can no longer repay debt because the recorded borrow totals become inconsistent, while lenders see their withdrawable balances dramatically reduced, often to near‑zero, effectively locking the pool. The issue manifests only when a borrower becomes insolvent (bad debt) and a liquidator invokes `liquidateClean` on the remaining shares. It was discovered during a security audit and reproduced with an end‑to‑end test that called the function repeatedly after an initial liquidation. The bug is subtle because the function appears to succeed, emits no error, and the borrower’s share counter still shows a positive value, making it easy to miss during casual testing. From the user's perspective, a borrower may notice that after liquidation their collateral is gone but the debt line still shows a residual amount that cannot be cleared, while lenders may observe that their deposited assets have vanished or that withdrawal attempts return far less than expected, contrary to the expectation that only the liquidated portion should be lost. Conceptually, the flaw belongs to the class of accounting‑state inconsistencies where a global accounting variable is updated without synchronizing the corresponding per‑user state, leading to phantom reductions of total supply. The recommended fix is to ensure that any leftover shares identified during liquidation are also deducted from the borrower’s debt record, for example by adding `_sharesToLiquidate += _sharesToAdjust;` so that the borrower’s share balance is properly reduced together with the pair totals, restoring consistency between global and user‑level accounting.
summary:
Leftover shares in `liquidateClean` are only subtracted from pair totals, but not from user’s borrowed shares. This means that after `liquidateClean`, borrower’s shares will be greater than `0` (leftover shares after liquidations), but the user is still insolvent and can be liquidated again and again (with `_sharesToLiquidate` set to `0`). Each subsequent liquidation will write off the bad debt (reduce pair totals by borrower leftover shares/amounts), but doesn’t take anything from liquidator nor borrower (since `_sharesToLiquidate == 0`).

This messes up the whole pair accounting, with total asset amounts reducing and total borrow amounts and shares reducing. This will make it impossible for borrowers to repay debt (or be liquidated), because borrow totals will underflow, and lenders amount to withdraw will reduce a lot (they will share non-existant huge bad debt).

Reducing pair totals scenario:

1. Alice borrows `1000 FRAX` (`1000` shares) against `1.5 ETH` collateral (`1 ETH = 1000`, `Max LTV` = `75%`)
2. ETH drops to `500` very quickly with liquidators being unable to liquidate Alice due to network congestion
3. At ETH = `500`, Alice collateral is worth `750` against `1000 FRAX` debt, making Alice insolvent and in a bad debt
4. Liquidator calls `liquidateClean` for `800` shares, which cleans up all available collateral of `1.5 ETH`.
5. At this point Alice has `200` shares debt with `0` collateral
6. Liquidator repeatedly calls `liquidateClean` with `0` shares to liquidate. Each call pair totals are reduced by `200` shares (and total borrow amount by a corresponding amount).
7. When pair totals reach close to `0`, the pool is effectively locked. Borrowers can’t repay, lenders can withdraw severly reduced amounts.

title: `liquidate
content: The vulnerability originates from a flaw in the liquidation workflow of a lending pair where the function used to liquidate a borrower’s position does not clear any existing bad debt. Bad debt occurs when the borrower’s collateral falls below the outstanding loan value, but the protocol fails to subtract that shortfall from the reported total assets. As a result, the contract’s `totalAssets.amount` continues to reflect the original loan amount plus accrued interest, even though the actual solvent assets are lower. This mismatch means that lenders who redeem their share tokens early receive a larger portion of the inflated asset pool, while lenders who wait until after the bad debt would have been cleared are left with reduced or zero returns. The issue becomes noticeable when a borrower’s collateral is fully depleted or close to zero, yet the protocol still reports a high total asset balance because the liquidation call (`liquidate()`) does not invoke the accounting routine that marks off the bad debt. Under these conditions, a malicious or opportunistic liquidator can trigger liquidation, collect fees, and leave the pool with a large amount of unaccounted bad debt. Subsequent lenders who attempt to redeem later find that the pool’s assets are insufficient to cover their shares, leading to partial repayments or total loss of principal. The impact is a financial loss for later lenders, a distortion of the protocol’s accounting guarantees, and erosion of trust in the system’s fairness. The flaw was identified during a formal audit when reviewers simulated extreme price drops and observed that the `totalAssets` variable remained overstated after a liquidation that left near‑zero collateral. The problem is subtle because the contract’s public view functions still report a seemingly healthy asset balance, masking the underlying insolvency until redemption attempts expose the shortfall. To remediate the issue, the protocol should ensure that any liquidation that reduces collateral to zero or a negligible amount also invokes the bad‑debt‑clearing routine (or an equivalent `liquidateClean()` path) so that the total asset accounting accurately reflects the remaining solvency. This adjustment restores the invariant that total assets always equal the sum of collateral value plus accrued interest minus any recognized bad debt, protecting all lenders from being disadvantaged by timing of redemption. The bug belongs to the broader class of accounting‑consistency vulnerabilities where state variables that represent aggregate balances are not updated in tandem with state‑changing actions, leading to overstated balances and exploitable profit differentials. From a user’s perspective, an early redeemer may see an unexpectedly large payout (“I got more than my share of interest”), while a later redeemer experiences a surprising shortfall or a completely empty balance (“my redemption returned almost nothing”). The discrepancy violates the protocol’s business logic that each lender’s share should be proportional to the actual solvable assets, and it can be exploited by timing redemptions to occur before the bad debt is recognized.
summary:
When there’s bad debt which wasn’t marked off yet, the `totalAssets.amount` is higher than the actual (solvent) amount the pair has, meaning that lenders who redeem their tokens earlier will get more in return, at the expense of lenders who leave later. Therefore bad debt should be marked off as soon as possible, the later it’s done the more interest it accumulates and the higher the chances are that some of the lenders will notice and redeem their shares before the bad debt is subtracted from the total assets amount.

Having the option to liquidate via the `liquidate()` function (which doesn’t mark off bad debt) can lead to users using that function and leaving bad debt alongside zero collateral or near-zero collateral (giving no motivation for other users to liquidate the rest).

Marking off the remaining of the bad debt via `liquidateClean()` with 0 shares might be possible (not always, some tokens [don’t allow 0 transfers](https://github.com/d-xo/weird-erc20#revert-on-zero-value-transfers)), however there’s no motivation for outside users to do so. And as for the lenders - redeeming their tokens before the bad debt is subtracted from the total amount might be more profitable than staying and marking off the bad debt.

title: `LiquidationBranch::checkLiquidatableAccounts()` executes `for` loop with wrong values, causing array out of bounds to be recovered, the program will not work as expected
content: The vulnerability resides in the function that scans a range of trading accounts to determine which ones can be liquidated. The function allocates an output array whose length is the difference between the upper and lower bounds (upperBound‑lowerBound). However, the for‑loop that populates the array starts its counter at lowerBound and writes the result directly to liquidatableAccountsIds[i]. When lowerBound is greater than zero, the index i can be larger than the highest valid index of the newly created array (which is upperBound‑lowerBound‑1). As a result, the contract attempts to write to an out‑of‑bounds slot, causing the EVM to trigger a panic (error code 0x32) and revert the whole call. This bug was discovered during a security audit and confirmed with an integration test that deliberately supplies lowerBound = 10 and upperBound = 20, expecting the panic. The issue is subtle because the size of the array appears correct at allocation time, and the code does not contain an explicit bounds check before the write. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that the liquidation keeper receives an empty or zero‑filled list of liquidatable accounts, so positions that should be liquidated remain open, potentially leading to under‑collateralized accounts and loss of protocol safety. The affected parties include any trader whose position becomes under‑collateralized, liquidators who rely on the keeper to trigger liquidation, and the protocol itself because missed liquidations can erode capital reserves. The bug belongs to the class of array index out‑of‑bounds errors, a common source of runtime reverts in Solidity. It violates the business logic that the function should return a compact list of IDs; instead it either reverts or returns an array padded with default zeros. The exploit scenario is straightforward: an attacker (or even a benign caller) can invoke the function with a non‑zero lowerBound, causing the revert and preventing the keeper from performing any liquidation work. The fix consists of decoupling the external index from the internal array position, for example by using a separate counter (i‑lowerBound or an explicit count variable) when writing into liquidatableAccountsIds, and by trimming trailing zero entries after the loop. Additionally, the implementation should filter out zero values before the array is returned to the keeper. Applying these changes restores correct behaviour, prevents unexpected reverts, and ensures that liquidations are processed as intended.

title: Wrong parameter passed in `TradingAccount::deductAccountMargin` function that results in excess margin withdrawal
content: The vulnerability is an accounting error that occurs during the liquidation of a trading account. In the liquidation routine the contract calls TradingAccount::deductAccountMargin and supplies a parameter named pnlUsdX18, which is supposed to represent the account's total unrealized profit‑and‑loss. Instead of passing the actual unrealized PnL, the code mistakenly passes the required maintenance margin value (requiredMaintenanceMarginUsdX18). Because the required maintenance margin is typically a positive number that represents the minimum collateral needed, using it as the PnL causes the margin balance to be inflated rather than reduced. When the function later withdraws margin, the inflated marginBalanceUsdX18 leads to a smaller token transfer to the designated margin collateral recipient and leaves an excess amount in the trader’s account that can be withdrawn. The impact is that a trader who is liquidated can receive additional funds – for example a long position opened with 75,000 USDz may allow the trader to withdraw an extra 7,102 USDz, while the protocol’s collateral recipient receives 7,102 USDz less. This bug manifests only during liquidation when the account is marked liquidatable and the deductAccountMargin call is executed. It affects any user whose position is liquidated, the protocol’s margin pool, and any party relying on correct collateral accounting. The issue was discovered during a security audit by inspecting the call arguments in LiquidationBranch::liquidateAccounts and confirming the mismatch with a proof‑of‑concept test that showed the unexpected margin increase. The bug is subtle because the function signatures match and the wrong variable name does not raise a compiler warning; the accounting discrepancy only becomes visible after liquidation when balances are logged. It belongs to the class of “incorrect parameter usage leading to accounting mis‑calculation”. From a user’s perspective the UI would show a higher available margin after liquidation, an unexpected increase in token balance, and a lower amount transferred to the protocol’s fee collector. The expected behavior is that liquidation reduces the margin balance by the unrealized loss and transfers the correct collateral to the fee recipient; the reality is the opposite due to the wrong argument. The proper fix is to pass the absolute value of the account’s total unrealized PnL (accountTotalUnrealizedPnlUsdX18.abs()) to the pnlUsdX18 parameter, ensuring the margin balance is adjusted correctly and the correct amount of tokens is transferred to the collateral recipient.

title: Draining the protocol fully
content: The vulnerability is an economic manipulation flaw in the perpetual futures margining logic that allows an attacker to artificially inflate the reported collateral balance by repeatedly creating and filling large long orders. The root cause is that the protocol adds unrealized profit from an open position directly to the margin‑collateral balance, and then uses this inflated balance to satisfy the initial‑margin check for subsequent orders. Because each new order increases the market skew, the mark price rises, generating additional unrealized profit on the existing position. This profit is immediately credited to the collateral pool, making the account appear to have more margin than it truly possesses. An attacker can exploit this by depositing a modest amount of collateral, opening a first large position, and then repeatedly opening additional positions that push the mark price higher. After each fill the unrealized profit is harvested into the collateral balance, allowing the next order to pass the margin requirement even though the underlying account is under‑collateralised. As the process repeats, the account’s notional size approaches the protocol’s maximum open‑interest limit, while the apparent collateral balance grows to many times the original deposit. Eventually the account becomes liquidatable because the true maintenance margin (computed from the actual position value) is far lower than the inflated collateral balance. When liquidation occurs the protocol deducts only the required maintenance margin and fees, leaving a large residual amount in the attacker’s collateral account. The attacker can then withdraw this residual amount, effectively draining the protocol of funds that were never legitimately supplied. The attack occurs under normal market conditions whenever the contract permits unrealized profit to be counted as usable margin for new orders and does not block order creation for accounts that are already under‑collateralised. It affects any user who can open large positions, the protocol’s overall liquidity pool, and any external parties relying on the integrity of the perpetual market. The issue was discovered through a systematic audit that included a proof‑of‑concept test reproducing the exploit step‑by‑step, revealing that the margin check logic does not distinguish between realised and unrealised equity. The bug is subtle because the protocol’s accounting appears correct at a glance – the collateral balance increases as expected after a profitable trade – but the increase is improperly used to satisfy future margin checks, violating the economic assumption that only realised funds should be spendable. To remediate, the margin‑validation routine should separate unrealised P&L from the usable collateral when evaluating initial and maintenance margin, and should prevent order creation when an account is already below the required maintenance margin, even if unrealised profit temporarily inflates the balance. This change restores the intended safety guarantees and stops the feedback loop that lets an attacker pump the mark price and siphon funds.
summary:
Attacker deposits a large collateral, and creates an order with large size delta. Later, it fills. Then, the attacker creates second order, and later it fills. The second order will increase the mark price, so the old position will gain large unrealized profit. This profit will be added to the collateral balance, and makes the margin balance larger. Now that the margin balance is larger (thanks to the unrealized profit), it allows creating another order again. The attacker repeats this, until reaching to the maximum allowed open interest. Now the attacker has a huge collateral balance and position size. Now the attacker's account is liquidatable. After it is liquidated, huge amount of fund will be remained as collateral in the attacker's account. Attacker can now easily withdraw them. <https://github.com/Cyfrin/2024-07-zaros/blob/main/src/perpetuals/branches/SettlementBranch.sol#L435> <https://github.com/Cyfrin/2024-07-zaros/blob/main/src/perpetuals/leaves/TradingAccount.sol#L200>

The following scenario is implemented in the PoC. It can be verified easily by running the PoC. Attacker deposits 1\000\000 USDz as collateral in ETH market where its index price is 1000\$. Attack creates a long position order with size 92\_000. This order will be filled at mark price 1004.6\$. The attacker creates another long position order with size 60\000. It is expected that it reverts because very simply the final position size would be 152\000 each with minimum price of 1000\$. So, the final position value would be 152_000 * 1000 = 152M, and its required initial margin would be 0.01 * 152M = 1.52M, while the collateral worths only 1M, which is less than the initial required margin. But the protocol is implemented differently, and this order will be filled successfully. Because, when the new order 60\000 is created, the mark price will increase to 1012.2 (this is because the skew increases). Then, the unrealized profit associated to the old position will be added to the collateral which is equal to 92000 * (1012.2 - 1004.6) = 699200$, so the collateral would be equal to 1000000 + 699200 = 1.699M by ignoring the fees for simplicity (the PoC demonstrates the real case). It can be seen that since collateral is higher than initial required margin 1.52M, it allows the order to be created and later filled. Now, the attacker has a long position with size 152\_000, while the original collateral was 1M. The attacker repeats this scenario again. I.e. he again creates another long position order with size 60\_000, and it later be filled. He repeats this until it reaches to the maxOpenInterest (maximum profit of the attacker is when reaching to this limit, that is why some iterations are done. Without any iteration, the attacker would steal less fund). The PoC shows that 15 iterations are enough to reach to this limit. The following table shows each step in real case (including fees).

```solidity
                        sizeDelta       markPrice       newSkew     marginCollateralBalance  
befor order creation    0               1000            0           1000000                    
first order             92k             1004.6          92k         926_059
iteration 1             60k             1012.2          152k        1576671    
iteration 2             60k             1018.2          212k        2439796         
iteration 3             60k             1024.2          272k        3662632 
iteration 4             60k             1030.2          332k        5245180
iteration 5             60k             1036.2          392k        7187441
iteration 6             60k             1042.2          452k        9489413
iteration 7             60k             1048.2          512k        12151097
iteration 8             60k             1054.2          572k        15172494
iteration 9             60k             1060.2          632k        18553602
iteration 10            60k             1066.2          692k        22294422 
iteration 11            60k             1072.2          752k        26394954
iteration 12            60k             1078.2          812k        30855198
iteration 13            60k             1084.2          872k        35675153
iteration 14            60k             1090.2          932k        40854821
iteration 15            60k             1096.2          992k        46394200                                                                              

The table shows that after the final order being filled, the marginCollateralBalance is equal to 46394200. For sure this account is liquidatable because the requiredMaintenanceMarginUsdX18 is equal to 992k * 1049.6 * 0.005 = 5206016 (where 1049.6 is the mark price when closing the entire position). While the marginBalanceUsdX18 is just equal to 46394200 - (1096.2 - 1049.6) * 992k = 167_000. When this account is liquidated, the requiredMaintenanceMarginUsdX18 will be deducted from marginCollateralBalance, so the remaining would be 46394200 - 5206016 - liquidation fee = 41188179. Moreover, the position would be entirely closed. Now, the attack can withdraw the remaining marginCollateralBalance which is equal to 41188179. So, the attacker just paid 1M, but he could steal almost 41M, equal to 40M profit. Note that after the second iteration, the account is liquidatable. If after the second iteration, it is liquidated, the attacker would steal 1368555$, equal to 368_555$ profit.

title: The unlockExponent does not work as intended when it is ≠ 1
content: The contract implements a time‑based token release mechanism that relies on an "unlockExponent" parameter to shape the unlocking curve. The intended behavior, as documented, is that when unlockExponent equals zero the entire locked amount becomes claimable immediately after the configured unlockDelaySec, and when the exponent is greater than one the release should be slower than linear. In practice the calculation of the unlock factor is flawed. The function computes a normalized time delta (deltaTimeNormalized) by multiplying the elapsed time by a large precision constant (1e8) and dividing by the total unlock period. It then raises this normalized value to the power of unlockExponent to obtain a factor, which is subsequently capped at the same precision value. The total amount that can be withdrawn is calculated as (totalAmount * factor) / precision. Because factor is derived from a value that already includes the precision scaling, two critical errors arise. First, when unlockExponent is zero the exponentiation yields a factor of one, which is far smaller than the precision constant. The division by precision therefore reduces the unlockable amount to totalAmount / 1e8, meaning users can only ever withdraw a tiny fraction of their deposit regardless of how much time has passed. Second, when unlockExponent is greater than one the exponentiation can quickly produce a value that exceeds the precision threshold, causing the capping logic to set factor equal to precision. This makes the division cancel out, resulting in totalAmount being fully unlocked after only a tiny fraction of the unlock period (for example, 0.1 % of the period when the exponent is two). The root cause is the misuse of a fixed‑point precision multiplier together with exponentiation and an overly aggressive cap, which together break the intended linear or sub‑linear release curve. An attacker or a misconfigured deployment can therefore cause either permanent token lock‑up (exponent = 0) or premature full release (exponent > 1). The impact is severe: legitimate users may see their balances remain effectively zero when they expect a full refund, or conversely they may be able to withdraw all locked tokens far earlier than the protocol’s economic model assumes, leading to potential loss of value or incentive misalignment. The bug manifests after the unlockDelaySec has elapsed and any subsequent call to the withdraw calculation uses the flawed factor, so it is not a one‑time glitch but a persistent accounting error. It affects every participant who locks tokens in the Zerem protocol, including end‑users, liquidity providers, and the protocol’s overall token accounting. The issue was discovered during a security audit by comparing the documented unlock curve against the actual on‑chain math and observing that the computed withdrawable amount never matched expectations. Because the error is hidden inside a seemingly innocuous exponentiation and scaling step, it can be difficult to notice without explicit testing of edge cases such as exponent = 0 or values greater than one. To remediate the problem the unlockExponent logic should be redesigned: either enforce a linear release by fixing the exponent to one, or rewrite the factor computation to use proper fixed‑point arithmetic without double‑scaling, and remove the blanket cap that forces early full unlocks. The corrected implementation must ensure that when the elapsed time reaches the unlock period the user can claim the full amount, and that intermediate times produce a proportionate, predictable release according to the chosen curve.

title: Transaction processing doesn’t reject malleable signatures
content: The vulnerability consists of the transaction validation logic accepting ECDSA signatures that use a high‑s value, i.e., an s component larger than the curve order divided by two. According to the Ethereum protocol (EIP‑2) and the Yellow Paper, a transaction signature must be in the low‑s range (s ≤ secp256k1n/2) to prevent signature malleability. The root cause is that the processing routine forwards the raw (r,s) pair to the ecrecover precompile, which only checks that r and s lie in the full field range [1, secp256k1n‑1] and does not enforce the low‑s restriction required for transaction signatures. As a result, a malicious actor can craft a transaction with a high‑s signature that the network accepts as valid. Because the same public key can be recovered from a low‑s counterpart of the same signature, the attacker can later replace the original transaction hash with a different hash that still authorises the same operation. This malleability breaks the assumption that a transaction hash uniquely identifies a signed action, leading to potential replay attacks, double‑spending, or confusion for off‑chain services that rely on the hash for tracking, auditing, or nonce management. Users may notice that a transaction they submitted appears to be processed, but later a different transaction hash shows up for the same operation, or that refunds and balance updates are recorded under an unexpected identifier, effectively making funds seem to disappear from the expected view. The issue manifests whenever the zkEVM implementation processes a transaction whose signature contains a high‑s value; it does not depend on contract logic or specific function calls, only on the signature format. The affected parties include any wallet holder submitting transactions, relayers, explorers, and the protocol itself because the integrity of transaction ordering and accounting can be undermined. The flaw was discovered during a formal security audit by Spearbit, who compared the implementation against the specification in Appendix F of the Yellow Paper and observed that the low‑s check was missing. The problem is subtle because the transaction executes correctly and the signature verification succeeds, so typical testing that only checks for successful execution will not reveal the malleability. To remediate, the transaction validation step must explicitly reject signatures with s > secp256k1n/2, thereby enforcing the low‑s rule and restoring the guarantee that each transaction hash is unique and non‑malleable. This fix aligns the implementation with the EIP‑2 requirement and prevents the described attack vectors.
summary:
Signatures with high S values were restricted in EIP-2 (i.e. the Homestead upgrade):
All transaction signatures whose s-value is greater than secp256k1n/2 are now considered invalid. The ECDSA recover precompiled contract remains unchanged and will keep accepting high s-values; this is useful e.g. if a contract recovers old Bitcoin signatures.
The transaction processing code in processTx passes down the raw signature details to ecrecover, which only performs validation of r in [1, secp256k1n - 1] and s in [1, secp256k1n - 1]. Since the ecrecover code is used for the precompile, this is expected there, however for transaction processing the valid range is s in [1, secp256k1n / 2].
See also the Appendix F of the Yellow Paper.

title: `MIMOEmptyVault.sol executeOperation`
content: The vulnerability resides in the empty‑vault action contract of the MIMO protocol, specifically in the function that executes a flash‑loan‑based rebalance (executeOperation). The function is intended to repay the flash loan and then return any surplus collateral to the vault owner or to the MIMOProxy that orchestrates the operation. However, after satisfying the flash‑loan repayment, the implementation does not perform any transfer of the remaining token balance. Instead, it simply returns true, leaving the surplus tokens locked inside the action contract. The root cause is a logical omission: the contract increases the allowance for the lending pool to cover the exact repayment amount but never moves the excess collateral out of its own address. This can be exploited whenever the flash‑loan repayment amount is lower than the total collateral held by the vault, which is a normal situation when the vault contains more assets than necessary to cover the debt. An attacker does not need to craft special inputs; any user who invokes the empty‑vault operation under these conditions will see the leftover assets become inaccessible. The impact is that funds that should be returned to the user disappear from their wallet and are trapped in the contract, effectively causing a loss of collateral. The issue manifests only when the empty‑vault action is called with a flash‑loan repayment that does not consume the full vault balance—i.e., when the vault holds surplus collateral after the debt is cleared. The affected parties are the vault owners, delegators, and any participants relying on the protocol to safely return their assets after a rebalance. The bug was discovered during a security audit and reproduced with an integration test that logged the contract’s balance before and after the operation, revealing a non‑zero balance remaining in the contract despite a successful transaction. The problem is subtle because the transaction does not revert, emits no error, and the UI may simply show a successful empty‑vault call, making it easy to overlook the missing funds. To remediate the issue the contract should be modified to transfer exactly the amount needed to repay the flash loan to the lending pool and then explicitly send the residual token balance back to the vault owner or to the MIMOProxy. In abstract terms, the bug belongs to the class of asset‑leakage errors caused by incomplete post‑operation fund redistribution, violating the business logic that all collateral must either service the debt or be returned to the rightful owner.
summary: `MIMOEmptyVault.sol executeAction()` is supposed to pay off the debt and return the leftover assets to the owner of the Vault. But in fact the emptyVault contract, after executing the executionOperation(), only pays back the flash loan, and does not transfer the leftover assets to the owner, and locked in the emptyVault contract.

title: Automation / management can be set for not yet existing vault
content: The vulnerability stems from an insufficient existence check when configuring automation or management parameters for a vault in the MIMO protocol. The contract determines whether the caller is authorized by comparing the vault owner address returned by `vaultOwner(vaultId)` with the proxy address returned by `proxyRegistry.getCurrentProxy(msg.sender)`. For a vault that has not yet been created, `vaultOwner` returns the zero address, and for a user that has not deployed a proxy, `getCurrentProxy` also returns the zero address. Because both values are equal, the access‑control condition `vaultOwner == mimoProxy` mistakenly evaluates to true, allowing any caller to invoke `setAutomation` or `setManagement` on a non‑existent vault. An attacker can therefore pre‑configure a vault with arbitrarily high automation fees before the legitimate user ever creates the vault. When the user later creates the vault, the stored automation settings become active immediately, causing the protocol to charge the user excessive fees on every automated action. The impact is a loss of funds for the victim, potentially complete depletion of the vault balance if the attacker sets fees high enough. This flaw occurs only when the vault identifier has not been initialized and the caller does not yet have a registered proxy, a scenario that is common during the first interaction with a new vault. All participants who create new vaults – individual users, liquidity providers, or downstream contracts – are affected because the automated fee schedule can be hijacked without their knowledge. The issue was discovered during a security audit by Code4rena, where the wardens noticed that the access‑control check passed for zero addresses, a condition that is normally reserved for uninitialized state. The bug is subtle because comparing two zero addresses is syntactically correct and does not raise an obvious red flag; developers may assume that a zero address simply indicates “no owner” and not consider it an exploitable authentication path. To remediate, the contract must explicitly verify that the vault owner is not the zero address before accepting automation or management settings, effectively rejecting any attempt to configure a vault that has not been created. This change restores the intended invariant that only existing, owned vaults can be managed, preventing attackers from pre‑loading malicious fee structures. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “uninitialized‑object access control bypass” bugs, where missing existence checks enable unauthorized configuration of future objects, leading to financial loss and violation of the protocol’s accounting guarantees.
summary:
`vaultOwner` returns zero for a non-existing `vaultId`. Similarly, `proxyRegistry.getCurrentProxy(msg.sender)` returns zero when `msg.sender` has not deployed a proxy yet. Those two facts can be combined to set automation for a vault ID that does not exist yet. When this is done by a user without a proxy, it will succeed, as both `vaultOwner` and `mimoProxy` are `address(0)`, i.e. we have `vaultOwner == mimoProxy`.

The consequences of this are quite severe. As soon as the vault is created, it will be an automated vault (with potentially very high fees). An attacker can exploit this by setting very high fees before the creation of the vault and then performing actions for the automated vault, which leads to a loss of funds for the user.

The same attack is possible for `setManagement`.

title: Registry.sol fails to deliver expected functionality
content: The vulnerability resides in the proxy registry and factory architecture used by the MIMO protocol. The system is designed so that each user (owner) can have exactly one proxy contract, with the registry keeping a mapping from owner address to proxy address. In practice, the proxy contract also stores its own owner state and provides a transferOwnership function. Because the registry does not listen to or update its records when the proxy’s internal owner changes, the two sources of truth can diverge. An owner can invoke transferOwnership on the proxy, causing the proxy to recognize a new owner while the registry still points to the old owner. Consequently, the old owner retains privileged access to automation actions (such as vault emptying, leverage, or rebalancing) while the new owner loses the ability to control their own proxy and any funds associated with it. Additionally, the factory contract exposes deploy() and deployFor() functions to any caller without registering the newly created proxy in the registry, allowing an attacker to create multiple proxies for the same owner or to create proxies on behalf of others. These flaws break the fundamental business assumption that each owner has a single, reliably tracked proxy, leading to a situation where funds may become inaccessible to the rightful owner or, conversely, where an unauthorized party retains control over actions that move or lock assets. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are confusing: a user may attempt to interact with their vault and find that transactions are rejected, or they may observe that their proxy address shown in the UI no longer corresponds to the one that actually holds authority, resulting in “nothing happens” or “my funds are stuck”. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit when wardens compared the ownership data stored in MIMOProxy and MIMOProxyRegistry and noticed that ownership transfers were not propagated. The problem is subtle because both contracts appear to function correctly in isolation, and the mismatch only manifests when ownership is transferred or when proxies are deployed without proper registration. The recommended remediation is to eliminate the owner variable and transferOwnership function from the proxy, restrict the factory’s deploy functions to authorized callers, and centralize ownership management in a single contract (the factory) that updates the registry atomically. This ensures a single source of truth for proxy ownership, prevents multiple proxies per owner, and guarantees that only the current owner can execute privileged actions, thereby restoring the intended security guarantees of the protocol.
summary:
The description of Registry.sol is following:

/// Deploys new proxies via the factory and keeps a registry of owners to proxies. Owners can only /// have one proxy at a time. But it is not. There are multiple problems:

  1. Proxy owner can change and will not be registered
  2. There many ways for an owner to have many proxies:
  3. A few other proxy owners transferOwnership() to one address.
  4. Registry tracks last deployments and does not guarantee ownership.
  5. Factory.sol allows calling deployFor() to anyone, without any checks and registrations.

title: Incorrect implementation of access control in MIMOProxy:execute
content: The vulnerability resides in the access‑control logic of the proxy contract’s execute function. Instead of extracting the function selector from the supplied calldata payload, the contract reads the first four bytes starting at the dynamic data offset (data.offset). When the caller passes an empty bytes array, Solidity still permits additional trailing bytes in the overall transaction calldata, and the calldataload instruction will read those trailing bytes rather than the intended empty payload. Consequently, an attacker who already possesses permission for any single selector can craft a call where data.length is zero but extra bytes are appended after the encoded parameters. The selector read from the trailing bytes will be arbitrary, allowing the permission check to be bypassed and the delegatecall to be performed with essentially no calldata. This enables the caller to invoke the fallback function of the target contract or any other function that does not require a selector match, violating the intended permission model. The impact is that any user who has been granted at least one allowed selector can execute arbitrary code on the target contract, potentially stealing funds, altering state, or disrupting protocol logic. The bug manifests only when the execute function is invoked with an empty data argument; under normal non‑empty payloads the selector is read correctly. It is difficult to notice because Solidity does not automatically reject excess calldata beyond the declared parameters, and the selector extraction uses a low‑level assembly read that silently consumes whatever bytes happen to be present at the calculated offset. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that included a proof‑of‑concept showing that appending a four‑byte value after an empty data array allowed the check to be circumvented. To remediate the flaw, the contract should validate that the calldata contains at least four bytes for the selector (e.g., require(data.length >= 4)) or extract the selector from the data array itself rather than from the raw calldata offset. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of improper calldata handling and insecure selector extraction, where assumptions about calldata layout are violated, leading to authorization bypass and unintended execution paths.

title: ERC721Checkpointable: delegateBySig allows the user to vote to address 0, which causes the user to permanently lose his vote and cannot transfer his NFT.
content: The vulnerability resides in the ERC721Checkpointable contract’s off‑chain delegation mechanism, specifically the `delegateBySig` function. Unlike the on‑chain `delegate` function, which sanitises the `delegatee` argument by redirecting a zero address to the caller, `delegateBySig` lacks any check that prevents a caller from submitting a signed delegation to the zero address (0x0). When a holder executes `delegateBySig` with `delegatee = address(0)`, the internal `_delegate` routine stores this zero address directly in the `_delegates` mapping. The public `delegates` view function later interprets a stored zero as a fallback to the delegator only for calls that go through `delegate`, but because the zero value is now persisted, subsequent calls to `_moveDelegates`—which update voting checkpoints during transfers or further delegations—receive an invalid source representative. The arithmetic in `_moveDelegates` attempts to subtract the transferred amount from a source vote count that is already zero, triggering an underflow overflow (`sub96` reverts). This revert aborts the transfer logic, effectively locking the NFT: the holder can no longer transfer, delegate to another address, or even burn the token. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are a sudden disappearance of voting power (the UI shows zero votes), transaction failures with generic “amount underflows” errors, and an inability to move or destroy the NFT. The issue was uncovered during a Code4rena audit by analysing the logical divergence between `delegate` and `delegateBySig`. It is hard to notice because the contract does not emit a distinct error for delegating to zero; the failure only surfaces later when a state‑changing operation attempts to move votes. The bug belongs to the class of input‑validation errors that lead to inconsistent internal state and arithmetic underflow. The recommended remediation is to add a `require(delegatee != address(0))` guard to `delegateBySig`, or to adjust the internal delegate handling so that a zero address is treated the same as in `delegate`. While the contract is already deployed and not upgradable, the fix would prevent future occurrences of permanent vote loss and transfer blockage.

title: In `Governance.sol`, it might be impossible to activate a new proposal forever after failed to execute the previous active proposal.
content: The vulnerability is a governance dead‑lock caused by the combination of a strict endorsement threshold for activating new proposals and the permanent locking of voting tokens while a proposal remains active. In the contract, activating a proposal requires that at least 20 % of the total voting power endorse it. When an active proposal gathers more than 80 % of the total votes, the remaining 20 % (or less) is insufficient to meet the endorsement requirement for any subsequent proposal. At the same time, the voting tokens of the majority that supported the active proposal are transferred to the contract and cannot be reclaimed until the proposal is either executed successfully or replaced after a grace period. Because the execution of the active proposal also depends on a separate quorum condition (the difference between ‘yes’ and ‘no’ votes must exceed a fixed percentage), it is possible for the active proposal to fail to meet that condition while still holding the majority of votes. In this state, the contract holds the majority of tokens, no user can reclaim their locked votes, and no new proposal can achieve the 20 % endorsement threshold, effectively freezing the governance process forever. The impact is that the protocol’s governance cannot be updated, new proposals cannot be activated, and token holders are unable to move or recover their voting tokens, leading to a loss of control over the system and a potential erosion of user trust. This condition occurs only when a proposal attracts > 80 % of the total voting power and simultaneously fails the execution quorum, an edge case that can be difficult to spot during normal testing because the logic for activation and execution appears correct in isolation. The issue was identified during a formal audit by reviewing the proposal activation flow and the vote‑locking mechanics, revealing that the contract lacks a timeout or reclamation mechanism for votes locked in an active but unexecutable proposal. The problem belongs to the class of "governance lock" or "dead‑lock" bugs, where state variables prevent any further state transitions. From a user’s perspective, the UI will indicate that an active proposal remains forever, the “activate proposal” button stays disabled, and attempts to reclaim voting tokens return an error. Users expect to be able to submit and activate new proposals after voting, but instead their tokens appear to disappear and new governance actions are impossible. To remediate the issue, the contract should introduce a bounded execution period (for example, an EXECUTION_EXPIRE constant of two weeks) after which voters can reclaim their locked tokens even if the proposal is still marked active. This timeout would break the dead‑lock by allowing the remaining voting power to become available again, restoring the ability to endorse and activate new proposals and preserving the intended governance lifecycle.
summary:
Currently, if users vote for the active proposal, the `VOTES` are transferred to the contract so that users can’t vote or endorse other proposals while the voted proposal is active.

And the active proposal can be replaced only when the proposal is executed successfully or another proposal is activated after `GRACE_PERIOD`.

But `activateProposal()` requires at least 20% endorsements [here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-08-olympus/blob/2a0b515012b4a40076f6eac487f7816aafb8724a/src/policies/Governance.sol#L216-L221), so it might be impossible to activate a new proposal forever if the current active proposal involves more than 80% of total votes.

title: Anyone can pass any proposal alone before first `VOTES` are minted
content: The vulnerability is an unguarded governance path that allows any address to submit, endorse, activate and execute a proposal before the VOTES token has a non‑zero totalSupply. The root cause is that the Governance contract validates proposal execution only against the result of VOTES.totalSupply(), and treats a value of zero as a valid condition for proceeding, effectively bypassing any quorum or voting requirement. This check is performed at several points in the contract (including the proposal activation and execution functions). Because the contract does not enforce a minimum supply of voting tokens, an attacker who acts in the window between contract deployment and the first minting of VOTES can craft a malicious proposal that changes the Kernel’s admin and executor roles. The attacker first submits a proposal containing instructions to set the admin and executor to an address they control, endorses the proposal (which requires no votes), activates it, waits for the required delay, and then executes it. Once the Kernel’s admin and executor are under the attacker’s control, they can upgrade any module, call permissioned functions, and drain treasury funds. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a proposal passing with zero votes, and later the protocol’s admin address may appear to have changed without any visible voting activity. Users may notice that funds are no longer withdrawable or that the governance page lists a proposal that was approved instantly, contradicting the expectation that a proposal needs community backing. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where a test case was added that omitted the VOTES minting step and demonstrated that the proposal could be passed and executed immediately. The problem is subtle because the code superficially appears to enforce voting; however, the condition VOTES.totalSupply() == 0 is true only before token distribution, making the check ineffective during the initialization phase. The impact is high: an attacker can seize control of the protocol’s administrative functions and potentially steal all assets held by the treasury, violating the core security assumptions of the governance model. To remediate, the contract should enforce that VOTES.totalSupply() is greater than zero before allowing any proposal lifecycle step, enforce a minimum quorum of votes, and prevent the executor role from being granted before the voting token is minted. In broader terms, this is a classic initialization‑time governance bypass, a class of bugs where access control checks rely on a mutable state that is initially empty, allowing an attacker to exploit the empty‑state window to gain privileged rights.
summary: Before any `VOTES` are minted anyone can activate and execute an arbitrary proposal even with 0 votes cast. So an attacker can pass any proposal (i.e. change the `executor` + `admin` of the `Kernel`, gaining access to all permissioned functions and to funds held).

title: TRSRY: front-runnable `setApprovalFor`
content: The vulnerability is a front‑running race condition in the treasury’s approval mechanism. The contract allows a privileged role to set a withdrawal allowance for a specific address and token by directly overwriting the stored approval amount. Because the function simply assigns a new value without first checking or reducing the existing allowance, an attacker who already holds a positive approval can observe a transaction that intends to lower that allowance, submit a competing transaction that spends the current allowance before the reduction is processed, and then also spend the newly set lower allowance. In practice the attacker can front‑run the custodian’s call that reduces the allowance, withdraw the full original amount, and subsequently withdraw the reduced amount as well, effectively extracting the sum of both allowances. This flaw occurs whenever the treasury custodian attempts to decrease an existing approval; it is exploitable whenever the network’s mempool is public and transaction ordering can be manipulated by a malicious actor. The parties affected are the treasury’s funds and any stakeholders relying on the treasury’s integrity; the attacker gains unauthorized access to additional tokens, while honest users see unexpected reductions or disappearance of treasury balance. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the allowance‑setting logic and identified that the function does not enforce a monotonic decrease or verify that the previous approval has been spent before allowing a lower value. The problem is subtle because the function appears to correctly emit an approval event, and a simple test of decreasing an allowance may not reveal the race unless a concurrent withdrawal is simulated. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “allowance race” or “front‑running mutable state” vulnerabilities, where state is overwritten without atomic checks, violating the accounting assumption that total authorized withdrawals never exceed the sum of outstanding approvals. From a user perspective the symptom is that funds can disappear from the treasury without any visible error, or a user who expects to be limited to a new lower amount can still withdraw the old, larger amount, leading to “more tokens withdrawn than intended” and a mismatch between expected and actual balances. The recommended fix is to redesign the approval function to modify allowances incrementally—either by increasing or decreasing relative to the current value—and to include checks that ensure the new allowance does not exceed the previous allowance unless the previous allowance has been fully spent. Using a decrease‑only pattern that requires the caller to supply the current allowance and validates it against the stored value can prevent the front‑run, or alternatively employing a two‑step commit‑reveal or time‑locked update can make the change atomic with respect to withdrawals.
summary: An attacker may be able to withdraw more than intended

title: Untyped data signing
content: The vulnerability stems from the way the Rigor contracts handle off‑chain signatures. Throughout the codebase, arbitrary application data is hashed and signed without any type‑information, domain separator, or chain identifier. Because the signed payload consists only of generic fields such as two addresses, a byte and two unsigned integers, the resulting signature is not uniquely tied to a particular project, blockchain, or contract function. Consequently, an attacker can replay a valid signature in a different context – for example, by taking a signature that a project owner used to update the hash of Project A and submitting it to update the hash of Project B, which may share the same owner and start with a nonce of zero. The same lack of binding allows the signature to be reused on another chain (e.g., Ethereum vs. Polygon) because the chain ID is not part of the signed message, and it also permits cross‑function reuse, where data intended for an invitation can be supplied to a task‑completion function. Moreover, an adversary could craft a phishing DApp that requests a signature in the same generic format, tricking a user into signing data that later authorises unwanted actions on their Rigor project. The issue is discovered during a manual audit that inspected the signature verification logic and noted the absence of EIP‑712 style domain separation. It is hard to spot because the signatures appear cryptographically valid and the contract does not emit explicit warnings when a replayed signature is accepted. When exploited, the impact can range from unauthorized state changes – such as unintended contractor invitations, task completions, or project hash updates – to potential loss of control over a project’s funds or governance. The affected parties are project owners, contractors, and any participants relying on the integrity of the project’s lifecycle. To remediate, the contracts should adopt a standards‑based signing scheme like EIP‑712, which incorporates a domain separator containing the contract address and chain ID, and a type hash that uniquely identifies each function’s parameters. By binding each signature to its specific contract, chain, and function, replay attacks across projects, chains, or unrelated DApps become impossible, restoring the intended security guarantees.

title: Builder can halve the interest paid to a community owner due to arithmetic rounding
content: The vulnerability originates from an arithmetic rounding error in the routine that calculates accrued interest for a community loan. The contract determines the number of whole days that have passed since the last interest update by subtracting the stored timestamp from the current block timestamp and dividing the result by the number of seconds in a day (86,400). Because Solidity performs integer division, any fractional component of the day is discarded. When a builder (the borrower) repays a negligible amount of tokens just shy of a full two‑day interval—specifically, at a time of lastTimestamp + 2 × 86400 − 1 seconds—the division yields a value of 1 instead of the expected 2. The contract then records this truncated day count as the period for which interest is calculated, but it still overwrites the stored timestamp with the current block timestamp. Consequently, the system records only one day of interest for a span that actually covered almost two days. This truncation halves the effective APR that the community owner (the lender) receives, turning an expected 10 % annual rate into roughly 5 % for that interval. The issue can be triggered repeatedly, allowing a malicious or merely careless builder to systematically under‑pay interest while still advertising high APR figures to attract funding. From the user’s perspective, a community owner may notice that the expected daily reward (for example, 136.9 tokens) is consistently lower (around 136 tokens) despite the passage of nearly two days, leading to missing or reduced refunds. The problem does not require sophisticated exploitation; merely timing a small repayment at the wrong moment is sufficient. The root cause is the reliance on whole‑day integer division without accounting for partial days, combined with the unconditional update of the last‑interest timestamp. This makes the bug subtle because the discrepancy is small on a per‑interval basis and may be dismissed as a rounding artifact, yet it accumulates into significant revenue loss over time. To remediate the issue, the calculation should either retain higher precision by multiplying the elapsed time by a large scalar before division, ensuring that the fractional component becomes negligible, or the contract should eliminate the separate day‑count variable altogether and compute interest directly using the exact timestamp delta, thereby avoiding any truncation. Properly fixing the rounding logic will align the actual interest paid with the advertised APR, preserving the economic expectations of community owners and maintaining trust in the protocol’s financial accounting.
summary:
[Community.sol#L685-L686](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-08-rigor/blob/5ab7ea84a1516cb726421ef690af5bc41029f88f/contracts/Community.sol#L685-L686)  

Due to arithmetic rounding in `returnToLender()`, a builder can halve the APR paid to a community owner by paying every 1.9999 days. This allows a builder to drastically decrease the amount of interest paid to a community owner, which in turn allows them to advertise very high APR rates to secure funding, most of which they will not pay.

This issue occurs in the calculation of `noOfDays` in `returnToLender()` which calculates the number of days since interest has last been calculated. If a builder repays a very small amount of tokens every 1.9999 days, then the `noOfDays` will be rounded down to `1 days` however `lastTimestamp` is updated to the current timestamp anyway, so the builder essentially accumulates only 1 day of interest after 2 days.

I believe this is high severity because a community owner can have a drastic decrease in interest gained from a loan which counts as lost rewards. Additionally, this problem does not require a malicious builder because if a builder pays at a wrong time, the loaner receives less interest anyway.

title: Builder can call `Community.escrow` again to reduce debt further using same signatures
content: The vulnerability resides in the escrow mechanism that allows a project builder to reduce the outstanding debt owed to a lender. The function that processes escrow repayments verifies a signature against a hash derived from several parameters, but it fails to include any unique replay‑prevention identifier such as a nonce.
