The impact is a denial‑of‑service on liquidation for any account that uses NFTs (excluding UniswapV3 NFTs) as collateral, allowing malicious actors to protect their own positions or sabotage competitors by timing the feeder removal to coincide with an imminent liquidation. The issue manifests only after the feeders have been removed and the price data has aged beyond the configured expiration period; before that, price queries succeed, making the problem easy to miss during routine testing. The vulnerability was discovered through a code audit that compared the function comments with the actual implementation and identified the missing onlyRole(DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE) restriction. It falls into the class of unchecked access control leading to oracle denial of service, which in turn breaks critical business logic such as liquidation. To remediate, the removeFeeder() function should be protected with an appropriate access‑control modifier (e.g., onlyRole(DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE)) so that only authorized administrators can modify the feeder set, preventing unauthorized removal of price updaters and ensuring that liquidation logic can always obtain a valid price feed.
summary: Contrary to what the function comments say, `removeFeeder()` is able to be called by anyone, not just the owner. By removing all feeders (i.e. floor twap price oracle keepers), a malicious user can cause all queries for the price of NFTs reliant on the `NFTFloorOracle` (all NFTs except for the UniswapV3 ones), to revert, which will cause all calls to `liquidateERC721()` to revert.

title: Attacker can manipulate low TVL Uniswap V3 pool to borrow and swap to make Lending Pool in loss
content: The vulnerability exists in the way Paraspace values a Uniswap V3 position that is offered as collateral. The protocol calls a function that reads the on‑chain liquidity of a specific Uniswap V3 pool, calculates the amounts of token0 and token1 that belong to the position, adds any accrued fee amounts, multiplies those amounts by the price data returned by an oracle associated with the same pool, and then sums the two values to obtain the collateral worth. Because the calculation does not verify how much total value is locked in the pool, an attacker can create a new pool for a supported token pair with almost no other liquidity, deposit a single‑owner position, and then present that position as collateral. By supplying a tiny amount of liquidity, the attacker can later manipulate the pool’s price through a large swap that moves the pool far from the initial price. The oracle, which is fed solely by the low‑TVL pool, will still report the inflated value of the attacker’s position at the time of borrowing, allowing the attacker to draw a maximum loan against an apparently over‑collateralised asset. After the loan is taken, the attacker swaps within the same pool, causing the price to collapse and the value of the deposited position to drop dramatically. Paraspace continues to hold the now‑devalued collateral, resulting in a net loss equal to the borrowed amount. This attack can be carried out whenever a token pair has at least one Uniswap V3 pool with very low total liquidity and the protocol does not restrict which pools may be used for collateral. The issue was discovered during a code audit that examined the getTokenPrice implementation and noted the comment that the calculation “can be easily manipulated with low TVL pool”. It is subtle because the function appears to use a standard price feed, and the existence of multiple fee‑tier pools for the same pair is a native feature of Uniswap V3, making a low‑liquidity pool seem innocuous. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are that a borrower can deposit a position, receive a large amount of borrowed tokens, and later see the collateral value reported by the protocol drop to near zero, leading to an unexpected loss of funds. The class of bug is an oracle manipulation caused by insufficient liquidity checks and lack of pool whitelisting. Conceptually the fix requires the protocol to enforce a minimum total value locked threshold for any pool used in price calculations, to maintain a whitelist of trusted pools, or to aggregate price data across multiple pools or external sources so that a single, manipulable pool cannot dominate the valuation. By ensuring that only pools with sufficient depth are accepted, the protocol restores the expected relationship between deposited collateral and borrowable amount and prevents the described loss scenario.

title: Discrepency in the Uniswap V3 position price calculation because of decimals
content: The vulnerability is a mis‑scaled price calculation in the Uniswap V3 oracle wrapper used by the Paraspace protocol. When the contract derives the square‑root price of a liquidity position, it applies a hard‑coded denominator of 1 × 10⁹ (1E9) regardless of the difference between the decimal count of token0 and token1. This assumption is only correct when both tokens have the same number of decimals. If token1 has more decimals than token0, the denominator is too small, which inflates the computed square‑root price by up to several orders of magnitude. The root cause is the omission of a decimal‑delta factor in the division step of the price formula; the code does not adjust the scaling factor to compensate for the relative precision of the two assets. An attacker or a careless user can trigger the bug by providing a position where token1.decimals > token0.decimals. In that scenario the wrapper’s `_getOracleData()` function returns an excessively high sqrtPriceX96 value, which is then fed into `getAmountsForLiquidity()` and `getTokenPrice()`. Those downstream calculations use the inflated sqrt price to compute token amounts and a token price that are dramatically oversized. From a user’s perspective this manifests as a “price” that is many times larger than expected, or a situation where a supplied amount of liquidity appears to yield far more token0 or token1 than should be possible, potentially causing the protocol to accept an incorrect collateral valuation or to allocate insufficient funds to a user’s withdrawal. The impact is high because the protocol relies on the oracle for margin checks, liquidation triggers and repayment calculations; an inflated price can lead to under‑collateralisation, unauthorized liquidations, or loss of funds when the protocol executes trades based on the wrong valuation. The defect surfaces only when token pairs have mismatched decimal precision, a condition that is not obvious during casual testing and may go unnoticed because the calculated price, while numerically large, is still a valid uint160 and does not cause immediate reverts. The issue was discovered during a security audit that inspected the oracle wrapper’s price‑derivation logic and identified the static scaling factor as a source of inaccuracy. To remediate the problem the denominator should be dynamically scaled by 10^(9 + |token1Decimal − token0Decimal|) and the numerator should be multiplied by the corresponding power of ten to align both assets to the same precision before taking the square root, as illustrated in the supplied patch. This correction ensures that the sqrt price remains correctly normalised irrespective of decimal differences, preserving the integrity of downstream amount and price calculations and preventing the protocol from operating on a distorted market view.
summary:
When the squared root of the Uniswap V3 position is calculated from the [`_getOracleData()` function](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-11-paraspace/blob/main/paraspace-core/contracts/misc/UniswapV3OracleWrapper.sol#L221-L280), the price may return a very high number (in the case that the token1 decimals are strictly superior to the token0 decimals). See: <https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-11-paraspace/blob/main/paraspace-core/contracts/misc/UniswapV3OracleWrapper.sol#L249-L260>

The reason is that at the denominator, the `1E9` (10**9) value is hard-coded, but should take into account the delta between both decimals.  
As a result, in the case of `token1Decimal > token0Decimal`, the [`getAmountsForLiquidity()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-11-paraspace/blob/main/paraspace-core/contracts/dependencies/uniswap/LiquidityAmounts.sol#L172-L205) is going to return a huge value for the amount of token0 and token1 as the user position liquidity.

The [`getTokenPrice()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-11-paraspace/blob/main/paraspace-core/contracts/misc/UniswapV3OracleWrapper.sol#L156), using this amount of liquidity to [calculate the token price](https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-11-paraspace/blob/main/paraspace-core/contracts/misc/UniswapV3OracleWrapper.sol#L176-L180) is as its turn going to return a huge value.

title: User can pass auction recovery health check easily with flashloan
content: The vulnerability resides in the auction recovery mechanism of the protocol, which allows a borrower to invalidate an already‑started liquidation auction by merely raising the health factor above a recovery threshold at the moment a transaction is executed. The root cause is an instantaneous health‑factor check that does not enforce any temporal commitment; it validates the borrower’s collateralisation only for the single block in which the function call occurs. Because the check is performed before the auction validity time is updated, a user can artificially inflate the health factor with a flash‑loan, call the function that sets the auction validity time to the current block timestamp, and then unwind the temporary capital, all within a single transaction sequence. This sequence of actions—depositing flash‑loaned assets, invoking the auction‑cancellation function, withdrawing the assets, and repaying the flash loan—effectively bypasses the intended recovery safeguard. The exploit is viable whenever an auction has already begun, the health factor is below the liquidation threshold, and the attacker can acquire sufficient short‑term liquidity to push the health factor above the recovery factor (typically 1.5). The affected parties include borrowers who attempt to recover their positions, lenders who rely on timely liquidations, and the protocol itself, which may suffer delayed liquidations and potential loss of collateral value. The issue was discovered during a security audit (Code4rena) that examined the logic of the auction‑recovery flow. It can be difficult to detect because the transaction appears to satisfy all on‑chain checks; the health factor momentarily meets the required level, and the reentrancy guard does not intervene since each step completes before the next begins. From a user’s perspective, the symptom is that an auction that should have proceeded disappears, the user’s NFT remains in their wallet, and the protocol’s liquidation timeline is altered, contradicting the expectation that providing sufficient collateral would simply pause liquidation rather than fully cancel it. This violates the business logic that recovery funds must be stable and verifiable, not transient. The recommended remediation is to enforce a time‑locked recovery window—holding the borrower’s assets for a minimum period (e.g., five minutes) before allowing auction invalidation, thereby ensuring that the health factor remains above the recovery threshold for a sustained duration and preventing flash‑loan‑based circumvention.

title: NFTFloorOracle’s asset and feeder structures can be corrupted
content: The NFTFloorOracle contract uses two dynamic arrays – one for registered NFT asset contracts and another for price feeder contracts – together with mappings that store the position of each element inside the arrays. The position fields are defined as uint8, which can only represent values from 0 to 255. When a new asset or feeder is added, the contract records the index using a cast to uint8 (uint8(assets.length - 1) or uint8(feeders.length - 1)). At the same time, the contract never shrinks the assets array; removal of an asset only deletes the entry in place, leaving a zero‑filled slot while the array length stays unchanged. Over time, as the protocol supports many NFT collections and multiple price feeders, the length of the assets array (and potentially the feeders array) will exceed 255. Once the length passes this threshold, the cast to uint8 silently truncates the higher bits, causing the stored index to wrap around modulo 256. This integer truncation corrupts the mapping entries: the stored index no longer points to the correct element, and subsequent calls to _removeAsset() or _removeFeeder() use the wrong index to delete items. As a result, the contract may delete an unrelated asset or feeder, leave stale entries, or lose price information, breaking the accounting logic that aggregates floor prices for NFTs. Users who rely on the oracle for pricing see incorrect or missing price data, potentially receiving zero price reports or stale values, which violates the expected business rule that each registered asset always has an up‑to‑date floor price. The vulnerability manifests only after a prolonged system lifetime when the cumulative number of distinct assets or feeders exceeds the 8‑bit limit, a condition that is realistic given the growing diversity of NFT collections. It was discovered during a formal security audit (Code4rena) where the auditors inspected the add/remove logic and noted the mismatch between array growth and index size. The bug is subtle because the use of delete on the array element appears to remove the asset, yet the underlying array length does not shrink, making the overflow invisible until the index wraps. The issue belongs to the class of integer truncation/overflow leading to storage corruption and broken invariant maintenance. To remediate, the index fields should be widened to at least uint32 (or uint256) to accommodate long‑term growth, and asset removal should follow the same swap‑pop pattern used for feeders, ensuring the array length reflects the actual number of active entries and preventing index mismatches. This conceptual fix restores the invariant that each mapping entry correctly references a live array element and preserves the integrity of the price aggregation mechanism.
summary:
NFTFloorOracle’s `_addAsset()` and `_addFeeder()` truncate the `assets` and `feeders` arrays indices to 255, both using `uint8 index` field in the corresponding structures and performing `uint8(assets.length - 1)` truncation on the new element addition.

`2^8 - 1` looks to be too tight as an **all time** element count limit. It can be realistically surpassed in a couple years time, especially given multi-asset and multi-feeder nature of the protocol. This way this isn’t a theoretical unsafe truncation, but an accounting malfunction that is practically reachable given long enough system lifespan, without any additional requirements as asset/feeder turnaround is a going concern state of the system.

title: UniswapV3 tokens of certain pairs will be wrongly valued, leading to liquidations
content: The vulnerability originates from an arithmetic ordering mistake in the oracle that derives the square‑root price (sqrtPriceX96) for a Uniswap V3 liquidity token used as collateral. When the two tokens in the pair share the same number of decimals, the contract computes an intermediate price ratio by multiplying token0Price by 10^18 and then dividing by token1Price. Because Solidity performs integer division, the expression becomes zero whenever token1Price is larger than token0Price multiplied by 10^18 – a situation that can easily arise when the tokens have vastly different market values, such as WETH versus a low‑price token like BTT. The zero result is later scaled by 2⁹⁶, but the scaling occurs after the division, so the final sqrtPriceX96 remains zero. This zero sqrtPriceX96 is fed into the Uniswap V3 library function getAmountsForLiquidity, which interprets a zero price as being below the lower tick bound and therefore treats the entire liquidity as amount0 and amount1 as zero. Consequently, the calculated value of the LP position is dramatically understated. The protocol’s health‑factor calculation then uses this undervalued amount, causing the borrower’s collateral to appear insufficient and triggering a liquidation event even though the actual market value of the position is healthy. The bug manifests only when the price ratio exceeds the 10^18 threshold, so it may remain hidden during normal operation and is difficult to notice because the oracle still returns a non‑reverting value; the mis‑valuation appears as an unexpected drop in the user’s health factor or a sudden liquidation notice. Affected parties include any user who supplies Uniswap V3 NFT positions as collateral, the liquidators who may profit from premature liquidations, and the protocol itself which could lose trust due to erroneous collateral assessments. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the price‑oracle logic and identified the integer‑division‑before‑scaling pattern as a source of precision loss. To remediate, the calculation should apply the 2⁹⁶ scaling factor before performing the division, or otherwise use a fixed‑point arithmetic library that preserves precision throughout the computation. In abstract terms, this is a classic fixed‑point precision bug caused by premature integer truncation, leading to a mis‑valuation of assets and a violation of the protocol’s accounting invariants. From a user’s perspective, the symptoms are a health factor that suddenly falls to a very low number, a liquidation alert despite no change in the underlying position, and the disappearance of the NFT collateral after liquidation, contrary to the expectation that their collateral remains safe as long as market prices are stable.

title: Attacker can drain pool using `executeBuyWithCredit` with malicious marketplace payload
content: The vulnerability resides in the way Paraspace’s leveraged NFT purchase flow validates the price of an order when executing a buyWithCredit call through a marketplace adapter. When a user invokes buyWithCredit, the supplied calldata is decoded by the LooksRareAdapter’s getAskOrderInfo function, which extracts both a MakerOrder (the seller’s ask) and a TakerOrder (the buyer’s bid). The adapter constructs an OrderInfo object that records the consideration amount using only the MakerOrder’s price field, while completely ignoring the price supplied in the TakerOrder. During the subsequent pool‑side execution, the contract checks that the token address of the consideration matches the credit token and that the start and end amounts are equal, but it never verifies that the maker price equals the taker price. The LooksRare exchange contract, when matching the orders, ultimately transfers the funds based on the taker price (the amount the pool is instructed to pay) rather than the maker price (the amount the user is expected to pay). Because the attacker controls both the maker and taker order in the payload, they can set a low maker price that satisfies the pool’s price check while advertising a much higher taker price that is actually transferred from the pool’s liquidity. The exploit can be performed with a credit loan amount of zero, leveraging early returns in the pool’s _borrowTo and _repay functions, which means the pool’s own funds are used to cover the difference. In practice the attacker funds a small down‑payment (e.g., 10 DAI), supplies a taker order for the full pool balance (e.g., 1000 DAI), and the pool automatically moves the extra 990 DAI from its reserves to the maker, draining the pool and leaving the attacker with both the stolen funds and the purchased NFT. From a user’s perspective the expected outcome – paying only the quoted maker price and receiving the NFT – is violated; instead the pool’s balance drops to zero and the attacker walks away with the full amount. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by constructing a malicious payload that deliberately mismatches maker and taker prices and observing that the pool’s funds were depleted. The flaw is subtle because the validation logic appears to ensure that the credit token matches the order token and that amounts are consistent, yet it overlooks the critical equality between maker and taker pricing, making the bug easy to miss in a manual review. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “price manipulation via mismatched order fields” or “incorrect price validation in delegated marketplace calls”. To remediate the problem the adapter must enforce that the price field of the maker order is identical to the price field of the taker order before constructing the OrderInfo, thereby guaranteeing that the amount charged to the pool matches the amount the user agrees to pay. This change would align the business logic of leveraged purchases with the accounting assumption that the pool’s outflow exactly equals the user‑specified price, restoring trust in the protocol’s financial integrity.

title: The `redeem` related functions are likely to be blocked
content: The vulnerability concerns a set of redemption functions that allow users to retrieve GLP tokens from the Pirex contract. The root cause is an external cooldown mechanism enforced by the GlpManager contract of the GMX protocol. GlpManager requires that the time elapsed between a liquidity addition (deposit) and a liquidity removal (redeem) be greater than a configurable cooldownDuration. If any deposit operation has occurred within the cooldown window, a call to the removal function will revert. The Pirex contract forwards user redemption requests directly to GlpManager without checking whether a recent deposit by the same contract or by an attacker has reset the cooldown timer. Consequently, whenever a deposit is made shortly before a user attempts to redeem, the redemption call fails and the user receives no tokens, effectively locking the funds. In normal operation the average interval between deposits on GMX is on the order of seconds, while the cooldownDuration is set to fifteen minutes. Statistical analysis shows that, for a modest share of the GLP market (e.g., ten percent), the probability that a redemption attempt is blocked exceeds ninety‑five percent. An attacker can exploit this denial‑of‑service condition by making tiny, inexpensive deposits (as little as one wei) at the cadence of the cooldown, paying only a few dollars per day to keep the redemption path perpetually unavailable. If the underlying protocol changes cooldownDuration to a larger value (up to two days), the blockage becomes even more certain. The impact is that legitimate users of Pirex see their balances remain unchanged, receive a transaction failure, and cannot withdraw their assets, violating the core business promise of fund accessibility. The issue was discovered during a code review of the Pirex contract when the auditors examined the interaction with GlpManager and noted the absence of any logic to respect or wait for the cooldown period. The problem can be hard to notice because the functions operate correctly in isolation; only when a recent deposit coincides with a redemption does the failure surface, leading to intermittent and non‑deterministic errors that may be dismissed as random bugs. To mitigate the risk, the contract should enforce a redemption schedule that guarantees a sufficient gap after the last deposit before allowing a withdraw, for example by reserving a specific time window (e.g., one day out of every seven) for redemption, or by programmatically checking the timestamp of the most recent deposit and delaying the call until the cooldown has elapsed. Alternative mitigations include using a separate liquidity pool without a cooldown, or negotiating with the GMX protocol to adjust the parameter for contracts that provide redemption services. Properly addressing the issue restores users' expectation that a redeem request will result in a successful transfer of tokens and eliminates the possibility of funds being effectively frozen by a low‑cost, automated attack.

title: Users Receive Less Rewards Due To Miscalculations
content: The vulnerability resides in the reward distribution mechanism of the PirexRewards contract, where the amount of reward tokens a user can claim is calculated using the formula (rewardState * userRewards) / globalRewards. This design assumes a constant emission rate and that globalRewards accurately reflects the total accrued rewards across all users. However, the actual emission rate of reward tokens such as esGMX or WETH is dynamic, depending on governance‑determined allocations and the total amount of producer tokens staked by the community. Because the contract updates globalRewards only when there is a change in total supply or last update timestamp, the globalRewards figure can drift away from the true sum of individual user accruals when the emission rate varies over time. Consequently, the proportional calculation for each user becomes inaccurate: users who accrued rewards during high‑emission periods receive fewer tokens than they earned, while users who accrued during low‑emission periods may receive more than they are entitled to. The discrepancy is amplified by integer division rounding, which truncates fractional rewards and further skews the distribution. Exploitation occurs naturally during normal claim operations: a user calls claim(), the contract executes the flawed proportionate formula, and the user receives an amount that does not match the actual rewards they should have earned based on the time‑weighted emission schedule. The impact is an unfair redistribution of value—some participants see their balances shrink unexpectedly, receiving less than anticipated, while others receive excess tokens, breaking the intended accounting guarantees of the protocol. This condition manifests whenever the emission rate changes, the total staked supply fluctuates, or the global and user states are out‑of‑sync, which can happen frequently in a live system with variable governance parameters. The issue was uncovered by the Code4rena audit team through manual calculation of expected rewards versus on‑chain results, revealing that the rewardState and globalRewards values did not align with the dynamic emission model. The bug is subtle because the total rewardState appears correct and the contract still distributes tokens, making the misallocation easy to miss without detailed per‑user accounting checks. To remediate, the contract should adopt a reward‑per‑token accounting pattern, such as the cumulative RewardPerToken approach used in Flywheel‑v2 or Synthetix staking contracts, which correctly handles variable emission rates and avoids rounding bias. By tracking a global cumulative reward index and applying it to each user's balance at the time of claim, the protocol can ensure that every user receives precisely the amount they earned, preserving the economic integrity of the system.

title: Malicious Users Can Drain The Assets Of Auto Compound Vault
content: The vulnerability is a rounding‑down error in the share‑to‑asset conversion logic of an ERC‑4626 based auto‑compound vault. The contract calculates the number of vault shares that must be burned to cover a withdrawal by multiplying the requested asset amount by the total share supply and dividing by the total assets under management, using a function that rounds the result down (mulDivDown). When the calculated value is less than one share, Solidity truncates the fractional part to zero, causing the previewWithdraw function to return zero shares for certain withdrawal amounts. Consequently, the withdraw function proceeds without burning any shares and transfers the requested assets to the receiver. This flaw allows a malicious user to request a withdrawal that mathematically maps to fewer than one share, receive the assets for free, and repeat the operation until the vault’s assets are exhausted. The issue manifests when the withdrawal amount is small relative to the pool size or when the total supply of shares is low, as demonstrated with a vault holding 1,000 WETH and 10 shares where a request for 99 WETH results in a zero‑share requirement. The problem was uncovered during a systematic audit of the contract’s accounting functions, where the rounding behavior of convertToShares was examined. It is subtle because the previewWithdraw function appears to return a plausible share amount, yet under specific inputs it silently yields zero, making the bug easy to miss during casual testing or code review. The impact is a total loss of funds for the protocol and its honest participants, as the contract’s accounting guarantees no free asset extraction are broken. To remediate, the share calculation should be performed with a rounding‑up operation (mulDivUp) or the contract should enforce a minimum burn of one share regardless of the computed value, ensuring that every withdrawal reduces the share supply and preserves the invariant that assets and shares remain proportional. This class of bug falls under arithmetic rounding errors in financial smart contracts, specifically where down‑rounding leads to zero‑share edge cases that violate the intended accounting logic, allowing assets to be withdrawn without proper share redemption.
summary: Malicious users can withdraw the assets from the vault for free, effectively allowing them to drain the assets of the vault.

title: User’s Accrued Rewards Will Be Lost
content: The vulnerability resides in the reward‑claiming logic of the PirexRewards contract. When a user calls the claim function, the contract computes the amount of each reward token to transfer by multiplying the total reward state of the token by the user’s accrued reward balance and then dividing by the global reward balance. Because Solidity performs integer division, any fractional component of the division is truncated. If the user’s accrued reward balance (userRewards) is small relative to the total amount of rewards that have been accumulated across all participants (globalRewards), the product rewardState * userRewards may be lower than globalRewards, causing the division to round down to zero. The function, however, clears the user’s accrued reward record before the transfer loop, setting p.userStates[user].rewards to zero unconditionally. As a result, a user with a modest stake who has earned a non‑zero amount of rewards will receive a transfer amount of zero, lose the recorded accrued amount, and subsequently start accruing from zero. The leftover tokens remain in the contract and can be claimed by other participants, effectively redistributing the small user’s rewards to larger stakeholders. This condition occurs during any claim where userRewards / globalRewards is less than the smallest unit that can be represented after the multiplication, which is typical for users who deposit a very low amount of GMX compared to the total supply of pxGMX. The issue was uncovered during a Code4rena audit through static analysis of the claim implementation and a concrete example involving two users, Alice and Bob, where Alice’s tiny stake produced a zero claim amount despite her theoretical entitlement of 1.2 esGMX tokens. The flaw is subtle because the function does not revert on a zero amount; it merely emits a Claim event and proceeds, making the loss appear as a normal claim with no obvious error. To remediate the bug, the contract should either avoid truncating the division by using a higher‑precision arithmetic method (for example, scaling the numerator before division or employing a library that supports fixed‑point math), or it should postpone clearing the user’s accrued rewards until after a successful transfer, and include a safeguard that prevents clearing when the calculated amount is zero. In essence, the problem is a classic rounding‑error or integer‑division bug that violates the accounting assumption that accrued rewards are fully transferred on claim, leading to unexpected disappearance of funds for users with small balances.

title: Underlying assets stealing in `AutoPxGmx` and `AutoPxGlp` via share price manipulation
content: The vulnerability is a share‑price manipulation flaw in the ERC‑4626 vault implementation used by the AutoPxGmx and AutoPxGlp contracts. The root cause is the way the `convertToShares` function computes the number of shares when the total supply of shares is zero: it returns the raw asset amount, effectively giving the first depositor a 1 : 1 mapping between assets and shares. An attacker can exploit this by being the first depositor with a microscopic amount (for example, 1 wei), receiving a single share, and then inflating the vault’s underlying asset balance by sending a large quantity of the underlying token directly to the vault. Because the share supply remains tiny, the calculated share price (assets per share) skyrockets. Subsequent honest users who deposit larger amounts receive only a handful of shares due to the integer division and rounding in `convertToShares`. When the attacker later redeems their single share, they receive a disproportionate portion of the total assets, effectively stealing tokens from later depositors. The impact is that users who trusted the vault to hold their assets receive less than they supplied; the protocol’s accounting is broken, leading to loss of funds and erosion of trust. The attack can be triggered whenever the vault is initialized without a seeded balance or without a minimum‑deposit safeguard, i.e., on the first deposit after contract deployment. All depositors, especially those who deposit after the attacker, are affected, as are the protocol’s revenue model and any users relying on correct redemption values. The issue was discovered during a formal audit that referenced a known problem in Solmate’s ERC‑4626 implementation, and it is subtle because the rounding error may appear insignificant and the share price may look reasonable at a glance, making the theft difficult to detect without examining the share‑to‑asset ratio after the first deposit. To remediate, the contract should enforce a sufficiently large initial deposit or mint a fixed, high number of shares on the first deposit, seed the vault with a substantial asset balance during deployment, or burn a small amount of shares (e.g., sending 1000 wei to the zero address) to raise the cost of manipulating the share price. These mitigations raise the share supply, reduce rounding error, and prevent an attacker from setting an artificial price with a negligible share amount, thereby aligning the protocol’s accounting with its expected financial invariants.
summary: pxGMX and pxGLP tokens can be stolen from depositors in `AutoPxGmx` and `AutoPxGlp` vaults by manipulating the price of a share.

title: fee loss in AutoPxGmx and AutoPxGlp and reward loss in AutoPxGlp by calling `PirexRewards.claim
content: The vulnerability resides in the way the AutoPxGmx and AutoPxGlp vault contracts calculate protocol fees and user reward accruals. Both contracts rely on a single function, `compound()`, to collect pending rewards from the PirexRewards module, measure the amount received by comparing token balances before and after the `claim()` calls, compute a platform fee on that delta, and finally update the reward accounting by calling internal harvest functions. Because the fee and reward logic is tied exclusively to the execution of `compound()`, any reward that arrives in the vault without that function being invoked remains invisible to the accounting code. The PirexRewards contract exposes a public `claim(address token, address user)` method that can be called by anyone for any user address. An attacker can therefore call `PirexRewards.claim(pxGmx, AutoPxGlp)` (and similarly for the GMX reward) directly, causing the reward tokens to be transferred into the AutoPxGlp contract without triggering `compound()`. As a result, the vault’s internal balance‑delta calculations see no change in `totalAssets()` or `pxGmx` balance during a later `compound()` call, so the platform fee (`totalPxGlpFee` and `totalPxGmxFee`) is calculated as zero and never transferred to the owner. Moreover, the `_harvest()` function that updates the per‑user `pxGmx` reward accrual is only called inside `compound()` when `pxGmxAmountOut` is non‑zero; bypassing this path means that the newly received `pxGmx` rewards are never harvested, leaving users without the expected reward distribution. From a user’s perspective, the vault appears to have received additional tokens, yet no fee is paid to the protocol and the expected reward payouts are missing – users may see their reward balance stay unchanged or even drop, and the protocol owner loses the fee that should have been collected. The issue manifests whenever there are pending rewards in the PirexRewards module and an attacker can invoke `claim()` directly, which is possible because the contract does not restrict the caller or enforce a callback mechanism. This bug was discovered during a security audit that examined the reward‑collection flow and noticed that `compound()` is the sole place where reward deltas are measured, while the external `claim()` function is publicly accessible. The problem is difficult to spot in ordinary testing because the token balances do increase, but the fee transfer events are absent and no error is thrown, making the loss appear as a silent accounting discrepancy. To remediate the issue, the contracts should maintain a persistent record of the vault’s token balances and update this record not only inside `compound()` but also after any direct token receipt, such as through a dedicated synchronization function or by restricting `claim()` to be callable only by the vault itself. Additionally, the fee‑calculation logic should be decoupled from the specific `compound()` flow and be triggered whenever the token balance of the vault changes, ensuring that protocol fees are always accounted for and that user reward accruals are properly harvested regardless of how the rewards are transferred.
summary: Function `compound()` in `AutoPxGmx` and `AutoPxGlp` contracts is for compounding `pxGLP` (and additionally `pxGMX`) rewards. it works by calling `PirexGmx.claim(px*, this)` to collect the rewards of the vault and then swap the received amount (to calculate the reward, contract save the balance of a contract in that reward token before and after the call to the `claim()` and by subtracting them finds the received reward amount) and deposit them in `PirexGmx` again for compounding and in doing so it calculates fee based on what it received and in `AutoPxGlp` case it calculates `pxGMX` rewards too based on the extra amount contract receives during the execution of `claim()`. But attacker can call `PirexGmx.claim(px*, PirexGlp)` directly and make `PirexGmx` contract to transfer (`gmxBaseReward` and `pxGmx`) rewards to `AutoPxGlp` and in this case the logics of fee calculation and reward calculation in `compound()` function won’t get executed and contract won’t get it’s fee from rewards and users won’t get their `pxGmx` reward. So this bug would cause fee loss in `AutoPxGmx` and `AutoPxGlp` for contract and `pxGmx`’s reward loss for users in `AutoPxGlp`.

title: Bidders might fail to withdraw their unused funds after the auction was finalized because the contract doesn’t have enough balance.
content: The vulnerability is an accounting mismatch that can lock bidders' unused quote tokens after an auction has been finalized. The contract calculates the amount of quote tokens owed to the seller by multiplying the cleared base amount with the cleared quote price and then rounding the result down. Each bidder’s refund is also calculated by rounding down the product of the bidder’s base amount and the lowest quote price. Because the rounding down operation is performed separately for the seller and for each bidder, the total quote amount that the seller receives can be larger than the sum of the quote amounts actually offered by all bidders. When this happens the auction contract ends up holding fewer quote tokens than required to satisfy the refund calculations for the last bidders. As a result, a call to the withdraw function reverts due to insufficient contract balance, and the affected bidders cannot retrieve the unused portion of their quote tokens. This condition occurs only after the auction is finalized, when there are multiple bidders and the rounding error accumulates, and it is especially problematic when the same quote token is not used in other auctions that could replenish the contract’s balance. The issue was discovered during a security audit by reproducing a test case in which the seller claimed more quote tokens than the bidders had supplied, causing the final bidder’s withdrawal to fail. The problem is hard to notice because the rounding discrepancy is small on a per‑bidder basis and the contract’s balance check passes before the withdrawal attempt, making the failure appear only at the moment of refund. The impact is that funds become effectively locked for the affected bidders, violating the expectation that a user can always withdraw any unspent quote tokens after an auction. The bug belongs to the class of rounding‑error or accounting‑mismatch vulnerabilities that break financial invariants. To remediate the issue the contract should track the exact amount of quote tokens filled for the seller (for example by adding a filledQuote field) and use this precise value for settlement, thereby avoiding multiple round‑down operations and ensuring that the contract always retains enough balance to cover all refunds.
summary:
Bidders might fail to withdraw their unused funds after the auction was finalized because the contract doesn’t have enough balance.

The main flaw is the seller might receive more quote tokens than the bidders offer after the auction was finalized.

If there is no other auctions to use the same quote token, the last bidder will fail to withdraw his funds because the contract doesn’t have enough balance of quote token.

title: Attacker can steal any funds in the contract by state confusion
content: The vulnerability is a state‑confusion bug that arises from using the variable lowestQuote as a sentinel to indicate whether an auction has been finalized. In the contract the atState modifier determines the current auction phase by checking the block timestamp and, after the end time, by inspecting whether lowestQuote still equals the maximum uint128 value. The code assumes that once finalize() is called the sentinel will be replaced by a real price, but finalize() accepts user‑controlled inputs for clearingBase and clearingQuote and does not forbid setting them to the maximum uint128 value. An attacker can therefore call finalize() with clearingQuote and clearingBase both equal to 2**128‑1, which satisfies the internal checks and triggers the transfer of unsold base tokens to the seller and the matched quote tokens to the seller as well. Because lowestQuote remains at the sentinel value, the contract still believes the auction is not finalized. Consequently the seller (or any attacker controlling the seller address) can invoke cancelAuction(), which resets the end timestamp to the maximum uint32 value and refunds the total base amount, and the buyer can subsequently call cancelBid() and receive a refund of the quote amount. The net effect is that the attacker receives both the quote tokens that were transferred during finalize and the quote tokens refunded by cancelBid, effectively creating tokens out of thin air. This can be performed without any preconditions; the attacker only needs to craft an auction with specific parameters that satisfy the inequality checks in createAuction, bid and finalize, such as setting the clearing price to the maximum uint128 value and matching base and quote amounts. From a user’s perspective the UI may show an auction that appears to have been finalized, yet the seller can still cancel it and both parties receive funds they should not have. The impact is a loss of funds from the protocol’s treasury and a breach of the accounting guarantees that each token is transferred exactly once. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that examined the state machine logic and identified that the sentinel value could be overwritten, a subtle condition that is easy to miss because the maximum uint128 value is a legitimate numeric constant and the code does not explicitly track a finalized flag. The issue is hard to notice because the contract’s state transitions are implicit and rely on a mutable variable rather than an explicit enum, allowing the state to be misinterpreted after an attacker manipulates the sentinel. The recommended fix is to stop using lowestQuote as a proxy for the auction state and instead introduce a dedicated state variable (e.g., an enum) that is set atomically when finalize() succeeds, and to reject any finalize call that attempts to set the price to the sentinel value. This eliminates the ambiguity and prevents the state‑confusion that enables the double‑withdrawal attack.

title: Any user being the first to claim rewards from `GiantMevAndFeesPool` can unexepectedly collect them all
content: The vulnerability resides in the reward distribution logic of the GiantMevAndFeesPool contract. The pool tracks accumulated ETH per liquidity‑provider share (accumulatedETHPerLPShare) and a per‑address claimed amount, but the interaction between these two state variables is flawed. When a user invokes the claim function for the first time, the contract calculates the claimable amount based on the current accumulatedETHPerLPShare without correctly subtracting any previously distributed rewards for that address because the claimed mapping is still zero. As a result, the first caller receives the entire pool of ETH that has been accrued since the pool’s inception, regardless of how much liquidity that caller actually supplied or whether they contributed to generating the rewards. This over‑claim can be triggered simply by being the first address to call claim after any period of reward accumulation. The impact is severe: the attacker drains all pending rewards, leaving subsequent legitimate claimants with zero payouts, effectively stealing funds that belong to other participants. Users experience a situation where they expect to receive a proportional share of fees or MEV rewards, but instead see the pool balance drop to zero after the first claim, and later users receive nothing. The bug was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where test cases reproduced the scenario by calling claim from a fresh address and observing the full balance transfer. The issue is subtle because the contract’s accounting appears correct at a glance; the variables are named intuitively and the arithmetic seems standard, making the over‑claim easy to miss without explicit tests for first‑claim behavior. To remediate, the accounting of claimed rewards must be restructured so that each address’s entitlement is calculated against the accumulated per‑share value at the moment they first provide liquidity, and subsequent claims must correctly offset the already‑claimed portion. In practice this means initializing the claimed mapping with the current accumulatedETHPerLPShare when a user first stakes, or using a checkpoint system that records each user’s last seen per‑share value. The bug belongs to the class of “incorrect reward accounting” or “share‑based distribution mis‑initialization” vulnerabilities, where the initial state for a participant is not properly recorded, leading to an exploitable over‑payment. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a normal reward balance, but after claiming the first time the displayed balance becomes zero for everyone else, contradicting the expectation that each participant receives only their share of the pool’s earnings.
summary: Any user being the first to claim rewards from GiantMevAndFeesPool, can get all the previously generated rewards whatever the amount and even if he did not participate to generate those rewards…

title: Rewards of `GiantMevAndFeesPool` can be locked for all users
content: The vulnerability resides in the reward distribution mechanism of the GiantMevAndFeesPool contract. The pool relies on ERC20‑derived tokens (GiantLP and LPToken) that implement before‑ and after‑transfer hooks to update internal accounting for pending rewards. Because the standard ERC20 transfer function is not protected by any access control, any holder can invoke it directly, which triggers those hooks outside the intended pool context. When a malicious actor performs an arbitrary transfer, the hooks are executed with a corrupted state, causing the pool’s reward ledger to be marked as settled or to reference an invalid balance. As a result, the rewards that should be claimable by every participant become effectively locked – users see their reward balances in the UI but attempts to claim return zero or revert, creating the impression that funds have disappeared. The flaw occurs whenever a token transfer is possible outside the pool’s own functions, i.e., any time a user can call transfer on GiantLP or LPToken. It affects all users of the protocol who are entitled to MEV and fee rewards, as well as the protocol’s economic model that assumes continuous reward availability. The issue was uncovered by the Code4rena audit team through a reproducible test that performed a direct transfer and observed that subsequent reward claims failed for all accounts. Detecting the problem is difficult because the transfer itself succeeds and does not emit any obvious error; only the downstream reward claim behaves unexpectedly, which may be attributed to a temporary “no rewards” condition rather than a systemic lock. Conceptually, the bug is a classic case of unprotected token hooks leading to state corruption, similar to re‑entrancy or accounting bypass vulnerabilities. To remediate, the contract should restrict external calls to transfer‑related functions that affect reward accounting, either by adding proper modifiers (e.g., onlyOwner or onlyPool) to the ERC20 transfer functions, by disabling the hooks for external callers, or by redesigning the reward update logic so that it cannot be triggered by arbitrary token movements. This ensures that reward balances remain accurate and claimable, preserving the protocol’s financial guarantees.
summary: Any malicious user could make the rewards in GiantMevAndFeesPool inaccessible to all other users…

title: Theft of ETH of free floating SLOT holders
content: The vulnerability is an accounting flaw that allows a malicious participant to drain all ETH that is pending claim for holders of free‑floating SLOT tokens. The root cause is an incorrect update of the per‑share accrued reward variable: the contract uses a direct assignment ( = ) when it should increment the existing value ( += ). Because the function that refreshes the reward state – updateAccruedETHPerShares – is invoked lazily, the stored per‑share amount can be overwritten with a value that does not reflect previously earned rewards. An attacker can trigger the lazy update at a moment when the contract’s internal accounting is out of sync, cause the assignment to reset the accrued amount to a lower value, and then claim the difference, effectively stealing the ETH that should belong to other SLOT holders. This exploit can be carried out by calling the public claim function after manipulating the reward update, and it works whenever the lazy update path is taken, i.e., after any operation that does not immediately refresh the reward state. The affected parties are all users who hold free‑floating SLOT tokens and expect to receive their proportional share of ETH rewards; they may see their pending balance disappear or receive zero when attempting to claim. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where the complex reward‑tracking logic and the lazy call pattern raised suspicion and were reproduced with a proof‑of‑concept test using Forge. The bug is subtle because the contract appears to track rewards correctly in most cases, and the incorrect assignment only manifests when the lazy update is triggered, making it easy to miss during casual testing. To remediate, the contract should replace the assignment with an additive update so that new rewards are accumulated rather than overwriting existing ones, and the reward state should be refreshed after each operation that changes shares or distributes rewards, eliminating the reliance on a lazy update. This class of bug falls under improper state mutation and reward‑distribution miscalculation, leading to a situation where funds disappear from the protocol’s accounting and legitimate claimants receive nothing, violating the core business logic that each SLOT holder is entitled to a proportional share of accrued ETH.
summary: A malicious user can steal all claimable ETH belonging to free floating SLOT holders…

title: Unstaking does not update the mapping `sETHUserClaimForKnot`
content: The vulnerability is an accounting inconsistency that occurs when a user partially unstakes their staked sETH tokens. The contract records the amount of ETH a user is entitled to claim in a mapping that is calculated based on the total staked balance at the moment of the last claim. When the user later calls the unstake function to withdraw only a portion of their stake, the contract correctly reduces the staked balance mapping but fails to update the claim‑entitlement mapping to reflect the reduced balance. As a result the stored claim amount remains tied to the original larger stake. When the user later attempts to claim ETH, the contract computes the unclaimed share using the current (smaller) staked balance and subtracts the stale claim amount, which can produce a negative or zero result. Consequently the user receives no ETH even though they are still entitled to a proportional share of the accumulated rewards. This bug manifests only after a partial unstake; a full withdrawal would reset the claim amount, masking the problem. It affects any staker who reduces their position, leading to lost rewards and a mismatch between expected and actual payouts. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when the auditors examined the state updates in the unstake and claim functions and noticed that the claim‑tracking variable was not refreshed. Because the symptom is that a claim transaction simply returns zero without an explicit error, it can be hard to notice during normal usage. The flaw belongs to the class of state‑inconsistency or accounting bugs where derived values are not kept in sync with their base variables. To fix the problem the contract should recompute and store the updated claim entitlement for the user after every unstake, using the same formula that is applied during a claim but based on the new staked balance. Updating the mapping ensures that future claim calculations use a correct baseline, restoring the expected relationship between remaining stake and reward entitlement.
summary: If a user stakes some sETH, and after some time decides to unstake some amount of sETH, later s/he will not be qualified or be less qualified to claim ETH on the remaining staked sETH.

title: Reentrancy in `LiquidStakingManager.sol#withdrawETHForKnow` leads to loss of fund from smart wallet
content: The contract LiquidStakingManager exposes a function withdrawETHForKnot that allows a node runner to pull a fixed amount of 4 ether from the smart wallet that backs a registered KNOT. The function first validates the caller, checks that the associated smart wallet holds enough balance and that the BLS public key is in the INITIALS_REGISTERED lifecycle state. After these checks it performs an external call to the smart wallet via IOwnableSmartWallet.rawExecute, sending 4 ether to the address supplied as _recipient. Only after this external call does the contract update the bannedBLSPublicKeys mapping, effectively marking the BLS key as used and preventing further withdrawals. Because the state change (banning the key) occurs after the external call, a malicious contract supplied as the _recipient can execute code in its fallback/receive function and invoke withdrawETHForKnot again before the mapping is updated. This classic checks‑effects‑interactions violation creates a reentrancy window that lets the attacker repeat the 4 ether transfer multiple times, draining the smart wallet of twice the intended amount (or more if the fallback loops). The vulnerability is triggered only when the recipient is a contract, the node runner is not banned, the smart wallet balance is at least 4 ether, and the lifecycle status of the BLS key is INITIALS_REGISTERED. The impact is a loss of funds from the protocol’s smart wallet, breaking the accounting assumption that each KNOT can withdraw exactly one fixed payout. Users (node runners) expecting a single refund receive more ether than allowed, while the protocol suffers a net outflow and potential under‑collateralisation. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where a proof‑of‑concept contract (NonEOARepresentative) was written to register a BLS key, call withdrawETHForKnot, and re‑enter the function from its receive hook, demonstrating that the balance after withdrawal doubled from the expected 4 ether to 8 ether. The bug can be hard to notice because the external call is deliberately placed before any state mutation, a pattern that often looks harmless in simple reading, and the reentrancy only manifests when a contract is used as the recipient. To remediate, the contract should follow the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern: update the bannedBLSPublicKeys mapping (or any other state that prevents further withdrawals) before performing the external call, and optionally protect the function with OpenZeppelin’s nonReentrant modifier. This eliminates the reentrancy window and ensures that each KNOT can withdraw at most the intended amount, preserving protocol accounting and user expectations.

title: `BringUnusedETHBackIntoGiantPool` can cause stuck ether funds in Giant Pool
content: The vulnerability is an accounting flaw in the Giant Pool contracts where the internal variable that tracks the amount of idle Ether (idleETH) is not updated after the function withdrawUnusedETHToGiantPool moves Ether from the staking vault back into the pool. The root cause is a missing state mutation: the contract deducts the withdrawn amount from the vault but never subtracts the same amount from idleETH. Because idleETH is the only source used to validate subsequent deposit and withdrawal operations, its value becomes artificially high and eventually underflows when the contract later attempts to increase it, causing the idleETH counter to wrap around to a very large number. This underflow makes the contract believe that no idle Ether is available, so any later call to depositETHForStaking or withdrawETH reverts with an arithmetic error. The exploit scenario is straightforward: an attacker (or any user) can trigger bringUnusedETHBackIntoGiantPool after a deposit has been made while the staking knot is still in the INITIALS_REGISTERED state. The function calls withdrawUnusedETHToGiantPool, which transfers the Ether but leaves idleETH unchanged. Subsequent attempts to interact with the pool fail, effectively locking the Ether inside the vault forever. The impact is that users who have deposited Ether see their balances disappear from the pool UI, attempts to withdraw return a revert, and new deposits are blocked, leading to a loss of usability and potential loss of funds if the contract cannot be upgraded. The condition under which this occurs is when staking has not yet commenced and the idleETH accounting path is exercised. All participants who rely on the pool – depositors, node runners, and the protocol itself – are affected because the pool can no longer accept or release funds. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when the auditors wrote a test that called bringUnusedETHBackIntoGiantPool and observed an underflow in idleETH that caused subsequent operations to revert. The bug is hard to notice because idleETH is an internal bookkeeping variable that does not surface in external events; the symptom only appears as unexpected reverts or missing balances. To fix the problem the contract must update idleETH whenever Ether is withdrawn back to the pool, preferably using safe arithmetic checks, and ensure that the accounting invariant that idleETH equals the pool’s available Ether is maintained after every state‑changing operation. In user‑facing terms, a depositor expects to see their Ether reflected in the pool and to be able to withdraw it later, but instead the pool balance stays unchanged, withdrawal attempts fail, and the deposited funds appear to have vanished, even though they remain locked in the vault due to the faulty accounting logic.
summary: `withdrawUnusedETHToGiantPool` will withdraw any eth from the vault if staking has not commenced(knot status is `INITIALS_REGISTERED`), the eth will be drawn successful to the giant pool. However, idleETH variable is not updated. idleETH is the available ETH for withdrawing and depositing eth for staking. Since there is no other places that updates idleETH other than depositing eth for staking and withdrawing eth, the eth withdrawn from the vault will be stuck forever.

title: GiantLP with a `transferHookProcessor` cant be burned, users’ funds will be stuck in the Giant Pool
content: The vulnerability is a zero‑address validation failure that occurs when the GiantLP token, which is configured with a transferHookProcessor, is burned as part of a withdrawal operation. In ERC20 the internal _burn function transfers tokens to address(0). The transferHookProcessor’s beforeTokenTransfer hook is invoked with the destination set to the zero address. Inside the hook the GiantMevAndFeesPool calls the SyndicateRewardsProcessor._distributeETHRewardsToUserForToken function, which begins with a require(_recipient != address(0), "Zero address") check. Because the recipient is the zero address during a burn, the require statement reverts, causing the entire burn (and therefore the withdrawETH call) to fail. As a result, the ETH that the user deposited into the Giant pool remains locked in the pool contract, and the user receives no funds despite a successful deposit. The issue manifests whenever a user attempts to withdraw ETH, which internally burns their GiantLP tokens, or any other flow that triggers a token burn while the transferHookProcessor is active. It affects all participants who hold GiantLP tokens and rely on the withdraw functionality, effectively making their funds irretrievable until the contract logic is changed. The bug was discovered during a unit test that called GiantMevAndFeesPool.withdrawETH; the test reverted with a Zero address error, confirming that the hook prevents successful burns. The problem is subtle because the zero‑address check is a legitimate safety guard in many contexts, and developers may not anticipate that a burn operation uses address(0) as the recipient. The bug belongs to the class of “hook‑induced revert on token burn” or “zero‑address validation in transfer hooks” vulnerabilities, where external logic attached to token transfers does not correctly handle the special case of burning. From a user’s perspective the UI shows a successful deposit, but the withdrawal transaction fails silently, leaving the balance unchanged and the user confused. The expected behavior is that the user’s ETH is returned; the actual behavior is a revert and locked funds. The recommended fix is to modify the beforeTokenTransfer hook (or the rewards distribution function) to skip the zero‑address check when the destination is address(0), or to guard the call with a condition that only updates rewards for non‑zero recipients. Implementing this change restores the ability to burn LP tokens and withdraw ETH, aligning the contract with its intended accounting logic.
summary:
The GiantLP with a transferHookProcessor will call `transferHookProcessor.beforeTokenTransfer(_from, _to, _amount)` when it’s transferred / minted / burned.

But the `to` address is address(0x00) in the erc20 `_burn` function. The GiantMevAndFeesPool.beforeTokenTransfer will call the function `SyndicateRewardsProcessor._distributeETHRewardsToUserForToken` will a zero address check in the first line:
```solidity
function _distributeETHRewardsToUserForToken(...) internal {
    require(_recipient != address(0), "Zero address");
```
So any withdraw function with a operation of burning the GiantLP token with a transferHookProcessor will revert because of the zero address check. The users’ funds will be stuck in the Giant Pool contracts.

title: function `withdrawETH` from `GiantMevAndFeesPool` can steal most of eth because of idleETH is reduced before burning token
content: The vulnerability resides in the GiantMevAndFeesPool contract where the function withdrawETH reduces the idleETH accounting variable before burning the lpTokenETH. The contract overrides totalRewardsReceived to return the pool balance plus totalClaimed minus idleETH. This value is used by the reward processor to compute the amount of unprocessed rewards as received minus totalETHSeen. When withdrawETH is called, idleETH is decreased first, which lowers the reported totalRewardsReceived. Immediately afterwards the burn of lpTokenETH triggers the beforeTokenTransfer hook, which calls _updateAccumulatedETHPerLP. Because idleETH has already been reduced, the calculation of unprocessed rewards becomes artificially larger, causing the accumulatedETHPerLPShare to increase without any real ETH being added to the pool. The attacker’s withdraw call therefore receives more ETH than they are entitled to, effectively creating ETH out of thin air. The exploit works whenever a user invokes withdrawETH while idleETH is non‑zero; the token burn hook distributes the inflated rewards to the caller. Honest users see their balances reduced or even become zero, while the attacker’s balance grows. The issue was discovered during a security audit when a test showed that after two users deposited 4 ether each, the attacker could withdraw 6 ether while the pool retained only 2 ether. The bug is subtle because idleETH is intended to track unallocated ETH, and its premature reduction is not obvious in the reward‑distribution logic, making the extra reward appear as a normal accounting update. To remediate, the contract should update idleETH after the lpTokenETH burn, or otherwise ensure that totalRewardsReceived reflects the true pool balance before any reward distribution hook runs. This restores the invariant that the sum of claimed rewards and idleETH never exceeds the contract’s ETH balance, preventing the creation of phantom ETH and protecting all LP token holders from loss.

title: Incorrect accounting in `SyndicateRewardsProcessor` results in any LP token holder being able to steal other LP tokens holder’s ETH from the fees and MEV vault
content: The vulnerability is an accounting error in the rewards distribution logic of the SyndicateRewardsProcessor contract that allows any holder of LP tokens to repeatedly claim ETH rewards that belong to the shared fee and MEV vault. The root cause is that the internal bookkeeping variable that tracks how much reward a user has already claimed (the claimed mapping) is overwritten with the amount due for the current claim instead of being incremented. Consequently, after a user makes a first successful claim, the contract records only the most recent claim amount; when additional ETH is later deposited into the vault and the same user calls the claim function again, the calculation of the new due amount subtracts only the last recorded claim, effectively treating the entire newly‑available balance as unclaimed. An attacker can therefore invoke claimRewards repeatedly after each deposit, draining the vault until little or no ETH remains for other LP holders. This flaw manifests only when the vault receives new ETH after a claim, and it is triggered by the external claimRewards function that forwards the call to the faulty internal _distributeETHRewardsToUserForToken routine. All LP token holders are affected because the shared reward pool is depleted, leading to loss of expected fee and MEV earnings for honest participants. The issue was uncovered during a formal audit by reproducing a test that repeatedly called claimRewards after funding the vault, revealing that the claimed amount never accumulated and the vault balance could be emptied. The bug is subtle because the first claim behaves correctly and the contract’s state variables appear consistent; only after multiple cycles does the discrepancy become evident, making it easy to miss in casual testing. To remediate the problem, the contract should update the claimed mapping by adding the newly‑earned amount (claimed[user][token] += due) rather than overwriting it, ensuring cumulative accounting of rewards and preventing repeated extraction of the same funds. This class of bug falls under improper state update or accounting mis‑management, where cumulative totals are reset instead of aggregated, violating the protocol’s financial invariants and allowing unauthorized depletion of shared assets.

title: `GiantMevAndFeesPool.bringUnusedETHBackIntoGiantPool` function loses the addition of the idleETH which allows attackers to steal most of eth from the Giant Pool
content: The vulnerability resides in the accounting logic of the GiantMevAndFeesPool contract. The pool tracks a variable called idleETH, which represents ETH that is temporarily held while LP tokens are staked. When users deposit ETH, idleETH is decreased accordingly in batchDepositETHForStaking, reflecting that the funds are now allocated to the staking vault. However, when the function bringUnusedETHBackIntoGiantPool is called to retrieve ETH that was not used for staking, the contract correctly transfers the ETH back to the pool but fails to increase the idleETH counter. The totalRewardsReceived view function computes the pool’s effective reward balance as the contract balance plus totalClaimed minus idleETH. Because idleETH is not restored, the subtraction is smaller than it should be, causing totalRewardsReceived to appear larger than the actual ETH held. This inflated value is later used by SyndicateRewardsProcessor._updateAccumulatedETHPerLP to calculate unprocessed rewards and to update accumulatedETHPerLPShare. As a result, the per‑share reward metric is increased “out of thin air”, allowing any caller of claimRewards to receive more ETH than they are entitled to. An attacker can trigger bringUnusedETHBackIntoGiantPool after a staking round, then immediately call claimRewards, stealing ETH from the pool. The impact is a direct loss of funds: the pool’s balance decreases while the attacker’s balance grows, effectively making funds disappear from the protocol’s accounting. The bug manifests when idleETH is decreased on deposit but never increased on return, and when the reward calculation relies on the stale idleETH value. All participants who rely on correct reward distribution – LP token holders, fee and MEV collectors, and end‑users – are affected because the protocol violates its accounting assumptions and promises of fair reward allocation. The issue was uncovered during a Code4rena audit by writing a test that performed a deposit, a staking round, a call to bringUnusedETHBackIntoGiantPool, and then a claimRewards call; the test logs showed the attacker receiving two extra ETH and the pool balance shrinking accordingly. The problem is subtle because the UI may still show normal deposit and withdrawal actions, while the internal accounting mismatch is hidden, making it hard to notice without detailed balance checks. The appropriate remediation is to update the idleETH variable when ETH is returned, for example by adding idleETH += _amounts[i] before burning LP tokens in bringUnusedETHBackIntoGiantPool, thereby restoring the correct accounting and preventing reward over‑allocation. This class of bug is an accounting mismatch or missing state update that leads to reward calculation errors and can be generalized to any contract where a balance‑tracking variable is not correctly reconciled after a transfer.

title: Protocol insolvent - Permanent freeze of funds
content: The vulnerability is a permanent freeze of user funds caused by a combination of a cross‑function reentrancy bug and improper accounting of ETH deposited by node runners for each BLS key. The root cause is that the withdrawETHForKnot function sends ETH to the node runner’s smart wallet before marking the BLS public key as banned, allowing the external call to re‑enter the LiquidStakingManager contract and invoke the stake function while the key is still considered unbanned. Because the stake function checks only that the key is not banned and that the overall smart‑wallet balance meets a minimum threshold, the re‑entered call passes all assertions even though the funds for the specific validator are insufficient. After the stake completes, control returns to withdrawETHForKnot, which then bans the key and updates the lifecycle status to DEPOSIT_COMPLETE. In this inconsistent state the key is banned while the lifecycle status indicates that the deposit phase is finished, which disables all downstream operations such as mintDerivatives, burnLPToken and rotateLPTokens. Consequently users who deposited ETH for staking cannot receive their original deposits, cannot claim rewards, cannot mint derivative tokens, cannot burn LP tokens to withdraw, and cannot rotate to other tokens. From the user’s perspective balances appear to be zero, minting attempts return “BLS public key is banned”, and withdrawal attempts fail with “Cannot burn LP tokens”. The protocol becomes effectively insolvent because the accounting assumes that deposited ETH can always be withdrawn or used for staking, an assumption broken by the reentrancy ordering and the use of a single wallet balance check instead of per‑key accounting. The issue manifests when a node runner invokes withdrawETHForKnot while the contract is still in the INITIALS_REGISTERED state and then re‑enters stake before the key is banned. It was discovered during a Code4rena audit through manual inspection of the contract’s state machine and testing of reentrancy scenarios. The bug is hard to notice because the external call is to a trusted smart wallet, the state transition appears correct at a glance, and the balance checks succeed, masking the underlying inconsistency. To remediate the problem the contract should introduce a reentrancy guard on withdrawETHForKnot and stake, move the banning of the BLS key before any external call, and maintain accurate per‑key accounting of node‑runner deposits so that balance checks reflect the actual funds available for each validator. Implementing these fixes restores the expected lifecycle flow, prevents permanent fund lock‑up, and re‑establishes confidence that deposited ETH can be withdrawn or used for staking as intended.
summary:
* Permanent freeze of funds - users who deposited ETH for staking will not be able to receive their funds, rewards or rotate to another token. The protocol becomes insolvent, it cannot pay anything to the users.
  * Protocol’s LifecycleStatus state machine is broken

Other impacts:

  * Users deposit funds to an unstakable validator (node runner has already took out his funds)

Impact is also on the Giant Pools that give liquidity to the vaults.

A competitor or malicious actor can cause bad PR for the protocol by causing permanent freeze of user funds at LSD stakehouse.

title: Sender transferring `GiantMevAndFeesPool` tokens can afterward experience pool DOS and orphaning of future rewards
content: The vulnerability resides in the reward accounting logic of the GiantMevAndFeesPool contract. When a holder transfers a portion of their pool tokens, the contract’s afterTokenTransfer hook updates the token balance but fails to adjust the corresponding entry in the claimed[] mapping for the sender. Consequently, the claimed amount recorded for the sender remains tied to the original, larger token balance. When the pool later distributes ETH rewards, the calculation of a user’s due reward subtracts the stale claimed value from the newly computed accumulated reward per share. Because the claimed value is now higher than the maximum possible reward for the reduced share, the subtraction underflows, causing an integer overflow that reverts the transaction. This overflow manifests in functions such as _previewAccumulatedETH and _distributeETHRewardsToUserForToken, which are invoked during reward preview, claim, and token transfer callbacks. The immediate effect is a denial‑of‑service condition: the affected user cannot preview their pending rewards, cannot claim rewards, and even simple token transfers revert. Over time, any rewards that accrue for that user become orphaned in the pool because the contract believes they have already been claimed, while in reality the user is unable to retrieve them. The bug appears only after a token transfer that reduces the holder’s balance; it is not triggered for users who never transfer. Users experience symptoms such as “my transfer reverts with an overflow error”, “preview shows zero rewards even though the pool received ETH”, and “my balance is correct but I cannot claim any rewards”. The issue was uncovered during a Code4rena audit by reproducing the failure in a unit test that transferred tokens and then attempted to claim rewards, observing the revert. It is difficult to spot because the claimed[] entry looks valid when inspected against the original balance, and the UI may still display the correct token balance, masking the hidden accounting inconsistency. The flaw belongs to the class of reward‑distribution accounting bugs where state is not kept in sync with token balances, leading to stale accounting data and overflow/underflow errors. To remediate, the contract must adjust the claimed[] entry on the sender side during token transfers, either by reducing it proportionally to the transferred amount or by redesigning the accounting to track claimed rewards on a per‑share basis rather than a total amount, thereby ensuring that claimed values always reflect the current token holdings.
summary: When a user transfers away GiantMevAndFeesPool tokens, the pool’s claimed[] computed is left unchanged and still corresponds to what they had claimed with their old (higher) number of tokens. (See GiantMevAndFeesPool afterTokenTransfer() - no adjustment is made to claimed[] on the from side.) As a result, their claimed[] may be higher than the max amount they could possibly have claimed for their new (smaller) number of tokens. The erroneous claimed value can cause an integer overflow when the claimed[] value is subtracted, leading to inability for this user to access some functions of the GiantMevAndFeesPool - including such things as being able to transfer their tokens (overflow is triggered in a callback attempting to pay out their rewards). These overflows will occur in SyndicateRewardsProcessor’s _previewAccumulatedETH() and _distributeETHRewardsToUserForToken(), the latter of which is called in a number of places. When rewards are later accumulated in the pool, the user will not be able to claim certain rewards owed to them because of the incorrect (high) claimed[] value.
