To remediate the problem, the contract should replace the single lastUserPeriodReset variable with a mapping from address to timestamp (e.g., mapping(address => uint256) private lastUserPeriodReset) and adjust the logic so that each user’s withdrawn amount is reset independently when their personal period expires. This change aligns the implementation with the intended design, eliminates the possibility of users being blocked by others, and restores the expected behaviour where every user can withdraw up to the limit after each epoch.
summary:
To withdraw, a user needs to convert his collateral for the base token. This is done in the **withdraw** function in Collateral.

The WithdrawHook has some security mechanics that can be activated like a global max withdraw in a specific timeframe, also for users to have a withdraw limit for them in a specific timeframe. It also collects the fees.

The check for the user withdraw is wrongly implemented and can lead to an unepexted delay for a user with a position > userWithdrawLimitPerPeriod. To withdraw all his funds he needs to be the first in every first new epoch (lastUserPeriodReset + userPeriodLength) to get his amount out. If he is not the first transaction in the new epoch, he needs to wait for a complete new epoch and depending on the timeframe from lastUserPeriodReset + userPeriodLength this can get a long delay to get his funds out.

The documentation says, that after every epoch all the user withdraws will be reset and they can withdraw the next set.

65:    * be evaluated against. Every time `userPeriodLength` seconds passes, the
66:    * amount withdrawn for all users will be reset to 0. This amount is only

But the implementation only resets the amount for the first user that interacts with the contract in the new epoch and leaves all other users with their old limit. This can lead to a delay for every user that is on his limit from a previous epoch until they manage to be the first to interact with the contract in the new epoch.

title: A whale user is able to cause freeze of funds of other users by bypassing withdraw limit
content: The vulnerability resides in the withdrawal throttling mechanism of the Collateral contract. Users withdraw underlying tokens through a function that, after burning the user's share, calls an external withdrawHook. The hook maintains two period counters – a global period and a per‑user period – each with a reset timestamp and a cumulative amount withdrawn during the current window. When the current block timestamp exceeds the configured period length, the hook resets the timestamp and sets the cumulative amount to the amount of the current withdrawal, but it does not perform any check that this amount respects the globalWithdrawLimitPerPeriod or the userWithdrawLimitPerPeriod. Consequently, the very first withdrawal after a period reset can specify an arbitrarily large amount, bypassing the intended limits. A malicious or “whale” user can deliberately wait until both the global and user periods have elapsed, then submit a withdrawal that drains the entire token reserve held by the contract. After this large withdrawal, the cumulative counters are set to the drained amount, so any subsequent withdrawal attempts by other users exceed the stored limits and are rejected, effectively freezing their funds until the contract is replenished. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the logic of the withdrawHook and noticed that the reset branch lacked the require statements present in the normal branch. The bug is subtle because the reset path appears legitimate – it updates timestamps and amounts – and developers may assume that resetting the period implicitly enforces limits. However, the missing validation allows a single transaction to overflow the limits. This flaw belongs to the class of period‑based rate‑limiting bypasses, where a throttling mechanism can be circumvented by exploiting a state‑reset edge case. From a user’s perspective, a regular user expects to be able to withdraw up to the per‑period allowance and to see their balance reduced by the withdrawn amount, but instead they receive a transaction revert or simply see that no funds are available, leading to confusion and loss of access to their assets. The proper remediation is to enforce the same limit checks in the reset branch, ensuring that even the first withdrawal after a period reset cannot exceed the configured global or per‑user limits, or to redesign the accounting so that the period reset does not overwrite the cumulative amount without validation.

title: Funds are permanently stuck in OptimisticListingSeaport.sol contract if active proposal is executed after new proposal is pending.
content: The contract OptimisticListingSeaport.sol allows a vault to propose a listing, creates an order structure and stores the resulting order hash in a global mapping vaultOrderHash keyed only by the vault address. When a proposal is promoted to an active listing, the same hash is later used by the internal function _verifySale to confirm that the Seaport order has been fully filled before the cash() function can release the seller’s collateral. The vulnerability arises because the contract does not protect the stored order hash after a proposal becomes active. If any user calls propose() again for the same vault while the active listing is still awaiting settlement, the new call overwrites vaultOrderHash with a fresh hash that reflects the new block.timestamp and other parameters. Consequently, when the original order is finally fulfilled on OpenSea, _verifySale queries the overwritten hash, which points to an order that has never been filled. The check therefore fails, cash() reverts with NotSold, and the collateral remains locked in the contract forever. This situation can be triggered simply by submitting a second proposal – either maliciously or unintentionally – before the seller calls cash() after a successful sale. From the user’s perspective the UI will indicate that the NFT has been sold, but the expected ETH payout never arrives; attempts to withdraw revert with a generic error, giving the impression that the sale did not complete. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the lifecycle of order hashes and noticed that the single‑per‑vault storage allowed accidental overwriting. It is hard to notice because the revert does not expose the underlying mismatch and the contract emits no explicit event about the hash being replaced. The bug belongs to the class of state‑collision or hash‑overwrites where mutable global state is reused for distinct logical entities, breaking accounting assumptions that each sale has a unique immutable identifier. The recommended fix is to move the order hash into the Listing struct so that each active and proposed listing maintains its own immutable hash, or otherwise prevent propose() from being called while an active listing exists. By keeping the hash tied to the specific listing, _verifySale will always reference the correct order, allowing cash() to succeed and ensuring that funds are not permanently trapped.

title: User loses collateral converted to pendingBalance when `cash`
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect update of the pending balance mapping in the OptimisticListingOpensea contract. When a proposer’s collateral is transferred to the pendingBalances structure during the cash() or list() functions, the code uses the assignment operator (=) instead of the additive operator (+=). As a result, any existing amount that was already stored for the same proposer and vault is overwritten rather than accumulated. The root cause is a simple arithmetic mistake: the contract assumes the pending balance is always zero at the moment of the transfer, which is not true because previous proposals, rejected listings, or earlier cash calls can leave a non‑zero pending balance. An attacker or honest user can exploit this by first creating a proposal that deposits collateral, then either proposing again or triggering a cash() after a sale. When cash() executes, it writes the current collateral value to pendingBalances, erasing the earlier amount. The impact is that a portion of the user’s collateral becomes permanently locked in the contract, effectively disappearing from the user’s perspective. This occurs whenever cash() or list() is called while pendingBalances already contains funds for the same vault‑proposer pair, which can happen after multiple proposals or after a reject path that also writes to pendingBalances. The affected parties are the proposers who provide collateral, any users relying on the contract to return their full collateral, and the protocol itself because the accounting invariants are broken – the total collateral accounted for by the contract no longer matches the sum of pending balances and active listings. The issue was discovered during a formal security audit (Code4rena) where the auditors noticed that the pendingBalances entry was being set rather than incremented, and they reproduced the loss of funds in a proof‑of‑concept scenario. The bug is subtle because the contract does not emit an explicit error; the balance simply drops after a cash() call, making it look like a normal state transition. To fix the problem, the assignment statements in both cash() and list() should be replaced with additive updates (pendingBalances[...][...] += collateral) so that existing pending amounts are preserved and the total pending balance correctly reflects all collateral that has not yet been withdrawn. This correction restores the intended accounting model where each collateral deposit is accumulated until the user explicitly withdraws it, preventing accidental loss of funds.

title: GroupBuy does not check return value of call
content: The vulnerability is an unchecked low‑level call used to transfer Ether from the GroupBuy contract to a contributor. The contract invokes payable(msg.sender).call{value:amount}("") twice – once for a regular contribution refund and once for a final balance payout – but it never inspects the boolean success flag returned by call. Because the call is assumed to always succeed, the contract proceeds to set the contributor’s stored balance to zero or delete the contribution record regardless of whether the Ether actually left the contract. This logic flaw originates from the fact that low‑level calls do not automatically revert on failure; they only return false when the callee’s receive or fallback function reverts or runs out of gas. An attacker can exploit the issue by deploying a malicious contract whose receive function deliberately reverts (or runs out of gas) when it receives Ether. When a legitimate user later triggers a withdrawal or refund, the GroupBuy contract will execute the call, the malicious contract will reject the transfer, the call will return false, but GroupBuy will ignore the result, clear the user’s balance and emit a success event. From the user’s perspective the UI may indicate that the withdrawal succeeded, the on‑chain transaction is mined, yet the user’s wallet receives no funds and the recorded contribution disappears, effectively causing a loss of funds. The impact is a breach of accounting guarantees: the protocol believes it has paid out, while the contributor’s assets remain locked in the contract, leading to potential financial loss for any participant and undermining trust in the protocol’s refund mechanism. The condition under which this occurs is any situation where the recipient is a contract that can revert in its receive function – for example, a contract that temporarily disables receiving Ether or that contains a require statement that fails. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that flagged the missing require(success) after each call. It is hard to notice because the transaction does not revert; the call failure is silent, and standard testing may not include a malicious recipient. The proper remediation is to capture the boolean returned by call and enforce success with require(success) or to replace the low‑level call with a safer transfer pattern that automatically reverts on failure, or to adopt a pull‑payment model where users withdraw funds themselves after the contract confirms the transfer. In short, the bug belongs to the class of unchecked low‑level calls leading to silent Ether loss, violating the protocol’s expectation that a successful withdrawal results in the user receiving the exact amount of Ether they are owed.
summary:
Both usages of `call` do not check if the transfer of ETH was successful:
```solidity
payable(msg.sender).call{value: contribution}("");
...
payable(msg.sender).call{value: balance}("");
```

This can become very problematic when the recipient is a smart contract that reverts (for instance, temporarily) in its `receive` function. Then, `GroupBuy` still assumes that this ETH was transferred out and sets the balance to 0 or deletes `userContributions[_poolId][msg.sender]`, although no ETH was transferred. This leads to a loss of funds for the recipient.

title: GroupBuy: Lost ETH when the NFT is bought for less than the minimum reserve price
content: The vulnerability originates from a mismatch between the price validation performed during the purchase of a fractional NFT and the accounting logic used when a participant later claims their contribution. In the purchase function the contract only checks that the total amount sent (_price) does not exceed the product of the pool’s minimum reserve price and the number of units filled (minReservePrices[_poolId] * filledQuantities[_poolId]). The condition deliberately allows the transaction to succeed with a lower amount, because paying more than the reserve price would be undesirable. However, the claim function later assumes that the buyer has paid exactly the minimum reserve price per unit. It reduces the stored contribution by quantity * reservePrice, where reservePrice is taken from the immutable minReservePrices mapping, and then refunds any remaining balance to the user. When the actual purchase price is smaller than the expected reserve price, the subtraction removes more ether than was actually contributed, leaving a negative remainder that is never returned. Consequently the buyer loses the difference between the expected reserve price and the discounted price, effectively causing ETH to disappear from the contract with no recovery path. This defect manifests only when an NFT is bought for less than the calculated minimum reserve amount, a situation that can be triggered intentionally by a malicious buyer or unintentionally by a user who submits a lower price. The affected parties are the purchasers of the fractional NFT, the protocol that relies on correct accounting for each pool, and any downstream participants who may see reduced pool balances. The issue was uncovered during a formal security audit that examined the logical flow between purchase and claim and noticed that the refund calculation does not reflect the actual amount paid. It is subtle because the price check appears reasonable at first glance and the contract does not emit any warning when the refund is smaller than expected; users simply receive less ETH than they believe they are entitled to, often seeing a zero or unexpectedly low balance after claiming. The bug belongs to the class of accounting or under‑payment handling errors, where the contract’s internal state assumes a higher payment than was actually received, leading to an incorrect refund formula. To remediate the problem the contract should record the actual price paid for each pool and use that recorded value when computing the contribution reduction, or alternatively adjust the stored minimum reserve price after a purchase to reflect the real per‑unit price (price / filledQuantities). By aligning the claim logic with the true amount transferred, the protocol can ensure that users receive the correct refund and that no funds are unintentionally lost.

title: Groupbuy: `_verifyUnsuccessfulState` and `_verifySuccessfulState` both can return true when block.timestamp == pool.terminationPeriod
content: The contract implements two internal verification functions, `_verifyUnsuccessfulState` and `_verifySuccessfulState`, that are intended to be mutually exclusive: when one permits execution, the other must revert. The intended invariant is that exactly one of the two states – successful or unsuccessful – can be true at any point in time. However, when the pool has not succeeded (`pool.success == false`) and the blockchain timestamp is exactly equal to the pool's termination period (`block.timestamp == pool.terminationPeriod`), both checks evaluate to false. In `_verifyUnsuccessfulState` the condition `if (pool.success || block.timestamp > pool.terminationPeriod) revert InvalidState();` does not trigger because `pool.success` is false and the timestamp is not greater than the termination period. Likewise, in `_verifySuccessfulState` the condition `if (!pool.success && block.timestamp < pool.terminationPeriod) revert InvalidState();` also does not trigger because the timestamp is not less than the termination period. This equality edge case breaks the fundamental invariant that the contract’s state machine should never allow both verification paths to succeed simultaneously. An attacker can exploit this by calling `claim` to retrieve their full contribution when the contract incorrectly treats the state as successful, and then immediately place a new higher bid, effectively withdrawing the same funds multiple times. The impact is a potential loss of pool assets, as contributors may be able to extract more value than they originally deposited, undermining the financial guarantees of the group‑buy protocol. The bug manifests only when the block timestamp matches the termination period, a situation that occurs with non‑trivial probability on Ethereum mainnet because block timestamps advance in roughly 12‑second increments, giving an approximate 1/12 (≈8.3 %) chance per block that the equality condition is met. This edge case is hard to notice during casual testing because most test scenarios use timestamps that are strictly before or after the termination period, and the logic appears correct for the common `>` and `<` comparisons. The issue was discovered during a formal security audit by Code4rena, which highlighted the broken invariant and the potential for double‑claim exploitation. To remediate the problem, the comparison in `_verifySuccessfulState` should be changed from `<` to `<=`, ensuring that the equality case is handled consistently and that exactly one verification function reverts at any given timestamp. This correction restores the intended exclusive state behavior, prevents double withdrawals, and aligns the contract with its intended accounting logic, where a user expects either a refund or a successful claim, but never both.
summary:
The functions `_verifyUnsuccessfulState` and `_verifySuccessfulState` should always have a differing behavior with regards to reversion, i.e. when one does not revert, the other should revert. In one condition, this is not true. Namely, when we have `pool.success == false` and `block.timestamp == pool.terminationPeriod`, this check within `_verifyUnsuccessfulState` is `false`:
```solidity
if (pool.success || block.timestamp > pool.terminationPeriod) revert InvalidState();
```

Similarly, this check within `_verifySuccessfulState` is also `false`:
```solidity
if (!pool.success && block.timestamp < pool.terminationPeriod) revert InvalidState();
```

Because this breaks a fundamental invariant of the contract, there are probably multiple ways to exploit it. One way an attacker can exploit is by calling `claim` (to get his contribution back completely), bidding again with a higher value than his previous contributions (to get his contributions back again).

title: OptimisticListingSeaport.propose sets pendingBalances of newly added proposer instead of previous one
content: The vulnerability resides in the propose function of the OptimisticListingSeaport contract where the pendingBalances mapping is updated after the contract overwrites the storage variable that holds the previous proposal. The function is intended to credit the collateral of the previous proposer so that they can later withdraw it, but the code calls _setListing first, which replaces the proposedListing struct with the new listing data. Immediately after this call, the line pendingBalances[_vault][proposedListing.proposer] += proposedListing.collateral; uses the now‑updated proposedListing, meaning the collateral is credited to the new proposer instead of the old one. This ordering mistake causes the original proposer to lose access to their locked collateral, while the new proposer can submit proposals without paying any effective collateral. The issue can be exploited by any participant who submits a proposal after another user’s proposal is pending: the attacker’s proposal overwrites the stored proposer address, and the contract mistakenly attributes the previous collateral to the attacker’s address. As a result, the victim sees their pending balance remain zero and cannot withdraw the funds they expected, effectively losing their collateral. The bug manifests whenever a new proposal is made while a previous proposal with collateral is still recorded, affecting all proposers and undermining the economic incentive model of the protocol. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the state transitions of the propose function; the logic appeared correct at a glance, making the flaw subtle and easy to miss because the variable name proposedListing is reused and the pendingBalances update looks syntactically correct. The problem belongs to a class of fund‑misallocation bugs caused by incorrect ordering of state updates and stale references after a storage variable is overwritten. To remediate, the pendingBalances update should be performed before the call to _setListing, or the contract should store the old proposer address in a temporary variable before overwriting the struct and then credit the collateral to that saved address. This ensures that the original proposer’s collateral remains withdrawable and that new proposers must provide the required collateral, preserving the intended security and accounting guarantees of the system.

title: Attacker can DOS OptimisticListing with very low cost
content: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition in the OptimisticListing mechanism where a new proposal is accepted only if its price per token is strictly lower than the current active or previously proposed listing. The contract does not enforce any meaningful constraint on the amount of collateral supplied with the proposal, aside from rejecting a zero collateral value. Because of this, an attacker can submit a proposal with the minimum possible collateral (for example, a single token) and a price that is only marginally lower than the existing price. The price‑per‑token check passes, the collateral check passes, and the proposal is recorded. The attacker can then immediately reject the proposal or simply let it sit, effectively preventing any subsequent legitimate proposal from meeting the lower‑price requirement. When the total supply of the underlying token is large, the price per token becomes very small, making it cheap for an attacker to create such a blocking proposal. This results in a situation where a vault cannot be bought at a reasonable price, violating the business rule that a user should not be able to hold a vault hostage. From a user’s perspective, attempts to list or purchase a vault either revert with a NotLower error or appear to succeed but never result in a sale, leaving the vault stuck and balances unchanged. The impact is that legitimate participants lose the ability to trade the asset, potentially causing loss of liquidity and trust in the protocol. The issue was discovered during a security audit using a Foundry proof‑of‑concept test that attempted to propose a lower‑price listing with a collateral of one and observed that the contract did not revert as expected. The bug is subtle because the price check alone seems sufficient at first glance, and the collateral requirement appears to be a harmless non‑zero guard. To remediate, the contract should require that the total value of the new collateral (collateral amount multiplied by its price) be greater than the total value of the previous proposal, or enforce a minimum collateral amount that scales with the token supply. This change ensures that an attacker cannot cheaply block the marketplace by submitting a minimal‑collateral, lower‑price proposal, restoring the intended economic guarantees of the system.
summary:
The only check on a new proposal is that it is priced lower than the existing proposal. It does not constrain on the `_collateral` supplied (except it will revert in `_verifyBalance` if set to 0). Anyone can block normal proposal creation by creating a proposal with lower price but `_collateral == 1`. When a high total supply is used, the price of each Rae is negligible and enables an attacker to DOS the protocol.

This violated the `prevent a user from holding a vault hostage and never letting the piece be reasonably bought` requirement.

title: Attacker can steal the amount collected so far in the GroupBuy for NFT purchase.
content: The vulnerability is an unchecked external market contract parameter that allows an attacker to supply a malicious contract as the _market argument when executing a GroupBuy purchase. The function forwards the purchase price to the market contract, receives back an address (named vault) that is assumed to be a newly deployed vault holding the purchased NFT, and then checks that this vault owns the token. Because the _market address is not validated, an attacker can deploy a contract that simply forwards the received ETH to themselves and returns their own address as the vault. The ownership check then succeeds because the attacker’s contract reports that it owns the NFT, even though the NFT was never transferred to a legitimate vault or the attacker may have already transferred it to their own wallet. The root cause is the lack of whitelisting or registry verification for the market contract and the returned vault address, allowing arbitrary code execution and spoofing of ownership. Exploitation proceeds by calling the purchase function with a malicious market contract, causing the protocol to accept the attacker’s address as the vault, thereby granting the attacker the NFT without contributing any funds and enabling them to siphon the pooled ETH. The impact is that contributors to the GroupBuy lose the ETH they deposited and receive no NFT, effectively stealing the funds and the asset. This occurs whenever the purchase function is invoked with a user‑controlled _market parameter, which any participant can do. All users who contribute to the GroupBuy, as well as the protocol’s economic model, are affected because the accounting assumptions that the vault holds the purchased NFT and that the funds are used for that purchase are violated. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by reviewing the purchase flow and noticing that the external contract address is never validated. It is hard to notice because the code includes an explicit ownership check that appears to guarantee correctness, masking the fact that the check can be satisfied by a malicious contract. To remediate, the protocol should restrict the _market argument to a whitelist of trusted market contracts, or require that the returned vault be registered in a VaultRegistry that only trusted factories can populate, ensuring that the vault is a legitimate contract and not an attacker‑controlled address. This change restores the intended invariant that the pooled funds are used to acquire the NFT and that the NFT is held in a secure vault, preventing unauthorized diversion of assets.

title: GroupBuy can be drained of all ETH.
content: The vulnerability is a re‑entrancy flaw in the purchase routine of the GroupBuy contract that allows an attacker to repeatedly invoke the function before the contract marks the pool as successful. The root cause is that the contract performs an external call to a market buyer contract (execute) and only sets the pool.success flag after the call returns, without any re‑entrancy guard. Because the external call can be controlled by the attacker, the attacker can re‑enter purchase, trigger another execute, and repeat the process, each time withdrawing the maximum allowed amount of ETH defined by the pool’s reserve price. By chaining these re‑entrancy calls the attacker can drain the entire ETH balance held by the GroupBuy contract, exceeding the intended cap of minReservePrices * filledQuantities. The exploit works when the attacker supplies a malicious market address or abuses a market that forwards control to a user address in the purchase order. It occurs during the execution of purchase, after contributions have reached the required threshold, and before the termination period expires. All contributors to the pool are affected because the drained funds belong to them, and the protocol loses the ability to deliver the purchased NFT. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the interaction between purchase and the market buyer contract and noticed that the success flag is updated only at the end of the function. The problem is subtle because the contract appears to succeed and emit a Purchase event, masking the fact that funds have been siphoned out. To fix the issue the contract should update the pool state to successful before making any external calls and should also employ a standard re‑entrancy guard (e.g., the OpenZeppelin nonReentrant modifier) around the purchase function. This prevents recursive entry and ensures that the contract cannot be called again while it is in the middle of processing a purchase, thereby protecting the pooled ETH from being drained.

title: Lock.sol: assets deposited with Lock.extendLock function are lost
content: The vulnerability is an accounting mismatch in the Lock contract that manages bond deposits. The contract keeps a global mapping totalLocked per asset that records the total amount currently locked. When a user creates a new bond with the lock function, totalLocked is increased by the deposited amount. The extendLock function is intended to either lengthen the lock period, increase the locked amount, or both. However, the implementation fails to add the additional amount to totalLocked. As a result, the internal accounting records only the original amount deposited via lock. When the bond expires and the release function is called, it subtracts the full locked amount (including any extensions) from totalLocked. Because totalLocked does not contain the extra amount, the subtraction underflows, causing the transaction to revert. Users therefore cannot retrieve the extra assets they added through extendLock; the funds remain permanently locked in the contract. The issue manifests only after a user has extended a bond and then attempts to release it after expiry. It affects any participant who relies on extendLock to add more capital, as their expected refund of the full principal is not delivered. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that examined the accounting flow of lock, extendLock, and release and identified that totalLocked is never updated in the extension path. The problem is subtle because the extendLock function does not emit any warning or error, and the UI may still show a successful extension, making the loss of funds hard to notice until the release step fails. The class of bug is an accounting inconsistency leading to integer underflow, a common pattern in smart contracts where state variables are not kept in sync across related functions. To fix the issue, the extendLock logic must increment totalLocked by the additional amount, ensuring that the release subtraction matches the total amount ever locked. After the fix, users will be able to retrieve the full amount they deposited, and the contract will maintain correct accounting invariants.
summary:
The `Lock` contract (<https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-tigris/blob/496e1974ee3838be8759e7b4096dbee1b8795593/contracts/Lock.sol#L10>) allows end-users to interact with bonds.

There are two functions that allow to lock some amount of assets. The first function is `Lock.lock` (<https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-tigris/blob/496e1974ee3838be8759e7b4096dbee1b8795593/contracts/Lock.sol#L61-L76>) which creates a new bond. The second function is `Lock.extendLock` (<https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-tigris/blob/496e1974ee3838be8759e7b4096dbee1b8795593/contracts/Lock.sol#L84-L92>). This function extends the lock for some `_period` and / or increases the locked amount by some `_amount`.

The issue is that the `Lock.extendLock` function does not increase the value in `totalLocked[_asset]`. This however is necessary because `totalLocked[_asset]` is reduced when `Lock.release` (<https://github.com/code-423n4/2022-12-tigris/blob/496e1974ee3838be8759e7b4096dbee1b8795593/contracts/Lock.sol#L98-L105>) is called.

Therefore only the amount of assets deposited via `Lock.lock` can be released again. The amount of assets deposited using `Lock.extendLock` can never be released again because reducing `totalLocked[_asset]` will cause a revert due to underflow.

So the amount of assets deposited using `Lock.extendLock` is lost.

title: Riskless trades due to delay check
content: The vulnerability originates from the way the limitClose function validates the block delay before allowing a position to be closed. The function calls an internal _checkDelay routine that only verifies whether the required number of blocks have passed since the position was opened. Because the delay check does not also consider the state of the stop‑loss, a trader can repeatedly call addToPosition with a trivial amount (for example 1 wei) just before the delay expires. Each call to addToPosition resets the internal timer, effectively extending the delay indefinitely. As a result, even if the market price falls below the stop‑loss, the position remains open and cannot be closed by the trader, by bots, or by the liquidation mechanism. This creates a scenario where a trader can capture price rises by raising the stop‑loss while simultaneously preventing any loss when the price drops, achieving a risk‑free trade. The impact is that the protocol’s core accounting assumptions – that a stop‑loss will eventually close an underwater position – are broken, allowing an attacker to lock in profit without exposure and to block other participants from closing or liquidating the position. The issue manifests whenever a position is created with a non‑zero blockDelay and the trader has permission to call addToPosition; it is observable from the user interface as a position that never closes despite the market price being below the stop‑loss, and bots attempting to close or liquidate the trade receive a revert error (often "0" from the delay check). The bug was discovered during a formal audit by reproducing the behavior in a test script that repeatedly refreshed the delay and observed that limitClose and liquidatePosition calls were consistently rejected. The problem is subtle because the delay logic appears harmless in isolation and the ability to add a negligible amount to a position does not change the economic state, making the exploit easy to overlook. To remediate the issue the delay verification must be extended to also enforce that a position cannot remain open when its price is under the stop‑loss, or the contract should prevent the delay timer from being reset once the position is underwater. In essence, the contract should treat the stop‑loss condition as a hard invariant that overrides any delay‑based timing mechanism, thereby restoring the intended risk model and preventing risk‑less trades.
summary: `Trading.limitClose()` uses `_checkDelay()`. This allows for riskless trades, by capturing price rises through increasing the stop-loss, while preventing the underwater position to be closed in case of the price dropping by continuously increasing the delay.

title: Certain fee configuration enables vaults to be drained
content: The vulnerability is an unchecked arithmetic overflow in the profit‑and‑loss (PnL) calculation performed by TradingLibrary.pnl(). The function uses an unchecked block when applying fee parameters to the raw PnL value, allowing the intermediate unsigned 256‑bit integer to wrap around the 2^256 limit if the inputs are crafted to be large enough. A specific fee configuration – a non‑zero DAO fee combined with a non‑zero referral fee while other fees are set to zero – creates the conditions under which the overflow can be triggered. An attacker can open a limit order with a modest margin, high leverage and an extreme take‑profit price, then close the position after the price feed is supplied. Because the overflow turns a negative PnL into a very large positive number, the contract records an enormous profit for the trader. When the trader calls the close function, the vault believes it must transfer this inflated profit to the user, effectively draining all assets from the stable vault. The exploit occurs only when the fee parameters are set to the vulnerable values and when the attacker can supply the trade parameters that push the PnL calculation beyond the uint256 range. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by feeding extreme values into the library and observing that the unchecked block allowed the result to wrap without reverting. It is difficult to notice because the contract does not emit an explicit error; the user interface simply shows a normal trade execution and, after closing, the user’s balance jumps to an unexpectedly large amount while the vault balance drops to zero, contradicting the expectation that the user receives only the earned profit. The impact is the loss of all funds stored in the vault, affecting any participant who relies on the vault for stable‑token custody. The bug belongs to the class of unchecked arithmetic overflow leading to incorrect accounting, where a mathematical assumption about bounded values is violated and money disappears from the system. To remediate, the unchecked block must be removed or replaced with safe arithmetic (e.g., Solidity’s built‑in overflow checks or OpenZeppelin’s SafeMath) and fee validation should be added to ensure that fee configurations cannot cause the PnL calculation to exceed the uint256 range. In short, the contract incorrectly calculates profit due to an overflow, causing the vault to think it must pay out an astronomically large amount, which results in funds vanishing from the protocol.
summary: An overflow in `TradingLibrary.pnl()` enables all funds from the vault contracts to be drained given a certain fee configuration is present.

title: Bypass the maximum PnL check to take extra profit
content: The vulnerability is a missing validation of the maximum profit‑and‑loss (PnL) limit in the addToPosition function of the Tigris trading contract. The protocol specifies a hard cap of +500% profit on any position, but the implementation only checks this cap when a position is closed. Because addToPosition does not recompute or enforce the PnL limit, an attacker can increase the margin of an already profitable position after the price has moved enough to reach the cap, and then close the position to collect a payout that exceeds the intended 500% ceiling. This bypass allows the attacker to extract additional profit – in the provided proof‑of‑concept the extra profit is more than $2,600 on a $9,900 trade – which is paid out of the liquidity providers’ funds and the protocol’s treasury. The issue occurs when a position has already achieved the maximum allowed profit, the price remains favorable, and the attacker calls addToPosition before closing. It affects any user who opens leveraged positions, the LPs that fund the vault, and the overall protocol safety because the profit‑cap mechanism is meant to protect stakers from extreme payouts. The flaw was discovered during a security audit by Code4rena, which reproduced the scenario with a test that first closed a position normally and then repeated the profit collection after calling addToPosition, showing that the contract does not enforce the cap on margin additions. The problem is subtle because the contract correctly limits profit on close, so a casual review may miss the missing check on intermediate state changes, and the extra profit only appears when the attacker deliberately manipulates the position flow. To remediate, the addToPosition (and related functions such as addMargin and removeMargin) should recompute the current PnL and revert if the resulting profit would be equal to or exceed the configured maxPnL percentage, thereby forcing users to close the order to realize profit and preserving the intended safety margin. This class of bug is a business‑rule enforcement omission, where a critical accounting constraint is not applied consistently across all state‑changing functions, leading to a profit‑cap bypass and potential fund loss.
summary:
To protect the fund of vault, the protocol has a security mechanism which limits:
    
    Maximum PnL is +500%. 

source: <https://docs.tigris.trade/protocol/trading-and-fees#limitations>

But the implementation is missing to check this limitation while `addToPosition()`, an attacker can exploit it to get more profit than expected.

title: Malicious user can steal all assets in BondNFT
content: The vulnerability is an invariant violation in the reward accounting of the BondNFT contract that allows a malicious actor to repeatedly call the public claim function on an expired bond and artificially inflate the global accumulator accRewardsPerShare. The root cause is an inconsistent implementation of bond state changes: the claim function does not reject expired bonds and, when invoked, recalculates accRewardsPerShare using a delta that should only be applied to active bonds. Because the function updates the accumulator even though the expired bond receives zero reward, each call increases the pending reward of every other bond proportionally to its share. An attacker can create a bond that expires early, repeatedly invoke claim on that bond while it remains unreleased, and thereby drive the pending rewards of a second bond arbitrarily close to the total asset balance held by the contract. When the attacker finally claims the second bond, they can drain essentially all assets from the BondNFT contract, leaving other depositors with no rewards and a depleted balance. The exploit occurs only while the expired bond has not been released; the contract permits unlimited calls to claim on such bonds, making the bug hard to notice because each individual claim appears to transfer zero tokens, giving the false impression that the function is harmless. The issue was discovered during a security audit when the warden observed that repeated claims on an expired bond caused the accumulator to grow and the contract’s token balance to shrink. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are unexpected growth of pending rewards for some bonds, followed by a sudden disappearance of the contract’s token balance and zero rewards for legitimate users. This class of bug falls under reward‑distribution logic errors and state‑transition inconsistencies, where an expired entity is allowed to affect global accounting. The proper mitigation is to enforce that claim on an expired bond either reverts or forces the bond to be released before any reward calculation, and to separate the internal _claim logic so that only active bonds can modify accRewardsPerShare. By restoring the invariant that only unexpired bonds participate in reward distribution, the contract regains its intended accounting guarantees and prevents any single user from draining the pool.
summary: Malicious user can drain all assets in BondNFT, and other users will lose their rewards.

title: Incorrect calculation of new price while adding position
content: The vulnerability resides in the addToPosition function of the Trading contract where the new average entry price for a leveraged position is calculated with an incorrect arithmetic formula. Instead of using a weighted harmonic average that reflects the total USD exposure divided by the total base‑asset amount, the code combines the old price and the new price linearly weighted by their respective margins. This mis‑calculation causes the resulting _newPrice to be slightly lower than it should be, which in turn reduces the payout that traders receive when they add additional margin to an existing position. The root cause is a faulty algebraic expression: _newPrice = oldPrice * oldMargin / newMargin + newPrice * addedMargin / newMargin, which does not preserve the invariant that total position value equals the sum of individual sub‑positions. The correct expression is _newPrice = oldPrice * newPrice * totalMargin / (oldMargin * newPrice + addedMargin * oldPrice). The bug manifests whenever a trader calls addToPosition with a non‑zero additional margin, regardless of whether the market price moves up or down. Exploitation is straightforward: an attacker can repeatedly add margin to a position and systematically receive a payout that is marginally less than the mathematically expected amount, leading to a gradual erosion of funds. In practice users observe that after adding margin their profit or refund is off by a few wei (for example, a payout of 1999.99999 instead of the expected 2000), or that the balance displayed in the UI is lower than anticipated. The impact is a loss of user funds and a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees, as the total position value no longer matches the sum of its components. This issue affects any participant who uses the addToPosition feature, including regular traders and liquidity providers, and it undermines confidence in the platform’s financial correctness. The problem was discovered during a security audit when unit tests compared expected PnL outcomes with actual contract results and identified consistent under‑payment. The discrepancy is subtle because the error is small and can be mistaken for normal rounding, making it hard to detect without precise testing. To remediate the issue, the contract must replace the faulty formula with the mathematically correct one that computes the new average price as the product of the old and new prices multiplied by the total margin, divided by the sum of the cross‑products of margins and opposite prices. This change restores proper accounting, ensures that added margin does not unintentionally diminish user payouts, and aligns the contract with standard financial math practices. The vulnerability belongs to the class of financial‑logic arithmetic bugs, specifically incorrect weighted‑average calculations that violate expected invariants in leveraged trading systems.
summary:
The formula used for calculating `_newPrice` in `addToPosition()` function of Trading.sol is not correct, users will lose part of their funds/profit while using this function.

The wrong formula

```solidity
uint _newPrice = _trade.price*_trade.margin/_newMargin + _price*_addMargin/_newMargin;
```

The correct formula is

```solidity
uint _newPrice = _trade.price * _price * _newMargin /  (_trade.margin * _price + _addMargin * _trade.price);
```

Why this works?

Given

```
P1 = _trade.price
P2 = _price
P = _newPrice
M1 = _trade.margin
M2 = _addMargin
M =  M1 + M2 = _newMargin
L = _trade.leverage
U1 = M1 * L  = old position in USD
U2 = M2 * L = new position in USD
U = U1 + U2 = total position in USD
E1 = U1 / P1 = old position of base asset, such as ETH, of the pair
E2 = U2 / P2 = new position of base asset of the pair
E = E1 + E2 = total position of base asset of the pair
```

Then

```
P = U / E
  = (U1 + U2) / (E1 + E2)
  = (M1 * L + M2 * L) / (U1 / P1 + U2 / P2)
  = P1 * P2 * (M1 * L + M2 * L) / (U1 * P2 + U2 * P1)
  = P1 * P2 * (M1 + M2) * L / (M1 * L * P2 + M2 * L * P1)
  = P1 * P2 * (M1 + M2) * L / [(M1 * P2 + M2 * P1) * L]
  = P1 * P2 * M / (M1 * P2 + M2 * P1)
```

proven.

title: reentrancy attack during `mint
content: The vulnerability is a reentrancy flaw that occurs in the Position.mint function of the trading protocol. The function creates a new ERC721 token by calling _safeMint, which triggers an external call to the recipient's onERC721Received hook before any of the contract's internal state variables such as _limitOrders, _limitOrderIndexes, initId, _openPositions and related index mappings are updated. Because the contract does not follow the check‑effect‑interaction pattern, an attacker that controls the receiving address can reenter the trading contract during this external call. By invoking functions like cancelLimitOrder or addToPosition before the original mint logic finishes, the attacker can manipulate storage that has not yet been correctly set. In the limit‑order scenario the attacker creates a limit order, reenters via onERC721Received, calls cancelLimitOrder for the same order id, and the burn routine removes the element at index 0 of the limit‑order array, which belongs to an innocent user, effectively deleting another user’s order. In the market‑order scenario the attacker opens a position with a small margin, reenters, calls addToPosition with a larger margin, and then the original mint logic overwrites initId with the low‑margin value. The profit calculation later uses the higher margin but the stored initId is based on the low margin, causing the contract to compute an inflated accrued interest and payout an excessive profit to the attacker. The impact includes loss of other users’ limit orders, inconsistent contract state, and unauthorized extraction of funds through inflated profit payouts. The issue manifests when a contract that can receive ERC721 tokens is used as the order owner and when the attacker can bypass the _checkDelay validation, which is not required for opening actions. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the ordering of state updates relative to external calls. The bug is hard to notice because the state variables appear to be correctly set after the function returns, masking the transient inconsistency that exists during reentrancy. The proper mitigation is to move all state modifications before the external call, apply a reentrancy guard, and generally adhere to the check‑effect‑interaction pattern. This class of bug is a reentrancy vulnerability caused by improper ordering of external calls and state updates, violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions that a position’s initId reflects the margin at creation. From a user perspective the symptoms are missing limit orders, unexpected zero balances for orders that should exist, and unusually large profit payouts that do not match the supplied margin.
summary:
Function `Position.mint()` has been used in `initiateLimitOrder()` and `initiateMarketOrder()` and it doesn’t follow check-effect-interaction pattern and code updates the values of `_limitOrders`, `initId`, `_openPositions` and `position _tokenIds` variables after making external call by using `safeMint()`. This would give the attacker opportunity to reenter the Trading contract logics and perform malicious actions while the contract storage state is wrong. The only limitation of the attacker is that he needs to bypass `_checkDelay()` checks. Attacker can perform this action:

1. Call `initiateLimitOrder()` and create limit order with id equal to ID1 reenter (while `_limitOrders` for ID1 is not yet settled) with `cancelLimitOrder(ID1)` (no `checkDelay()` check) and remove other users limit orders because code would try to remove `_limitOrderIndexes[_asset][ID1]` position but the value is 0 and code would remove limit order in the index 0 which belongs to another user in the `Position.burn()` code.
2. Call `initiateMarketOrder()` and create a position with ID1 and while `initId[ID1]` has not yet settled reenter the Trading with `addToPosition(ID1)` function (bypass `checkDelay()` because both action is opening) and increase the position size which would set `initId[ID1]` according to new position values but then when code execution returns to rest of `mint()` logic `initId[ID1]` would set by initial values of the positions which is very lower than what it should be and `initId[ID1]` has been used for calculating `accuredInterest` of the position which is calculated for profit and loss of position and contract would calculate more profit for position and would pay attacker more profit from contract balances.

title: Incorrect Assumption of Stablecoin Market Stability
content: The vulnerability consists of an incorrect assumption that all supported stablecoins maintain a perfect 1‑to‑1 USD value. The StableVault contract groups USDC, USDT and other stablecoins under a single internal token and allows users to deposit any supported stablecoin, mint the internal token at a 1:1 rate, and later withdraw any other stablecoin at the same 1:1 rate with zero slippage. This design ignores the fact that market prices of stablecoins can deviate slightly from one another, as demonstrated by Curve 3‑pool rates and Chainlink oracle feeds where USDC traded at 0.99994853 USD while USDT traded at exactly 1.00000000 USD. Because the contract treats the assets as interchangeable, an attacker can deposit a lower‑priced stablecoin, receive the internal token, and withdraw a higher‑priced stablecoin, effectively extracting the price differential. The exploit can be performed in a single transaction using a flash loan to provide the initial capital, swapping the received higher‑priced stablecoin back to the lower‑priced one on an external market, and repaying the loan while keeping the surplus. The impact is a loss of value for honest depositors: they expect to receive a stablecoin worth the same USD amount they supplied, but the vault delivers a token that is worth less, resulting in reduced balances or zero refunds in extreme cases. The issue manifests whenever the price gap between any two supported stablecoins is non‑zero and the contract’s 0 % slippage exchange is used. All users who interact with the deposit or withdraw functions are affected, as are the protocol’s overall liquidity and token holders who rely on the vault’s accounting. The problem was discovered during a security audit that compared the contract’s internal accounting with external price feeds and observed that the vault’s balance sheet could be arbitraged. It is difficult to notice because stablecoins are commonly perceived as perfectly pegged, so a 1:1 exchange appears reasonable at first glance. The proper mitigation is to stop treating all stablecoins as identical; the contract should query a reliable price oracle such as Chainlink for each asset, calculate the USD value of deposits and withdrawals, and enforce a fair exchange rate that reflects the current market price, optionally adding a slippage buffer. By normalising each asset to its neutral USD value, the vault eliminates the arbitrage window and protects depositor funds.
summary:
The `StableVault` contract attempts to group all types of stablecoins under a single token which can be minted for any of the stablecoins supported by the system as well as burned for any of them.

This is at minimum a medium-severity vulnerability as the balance sheet of the `StableVault` will consist of multiple assets which do not have a one-to-one exchange ratio between them as can be observed by trading pools such as [Curve](https://curve.fi/#/ethereum/pools/3pool/deposit) as well as the [Chainlink oracle reported prices themselves](https://data.chain.link/ethereum/mainnet/stablecoins/usdc-usd).

Given that the contract exposes a 0% slippage 1-to-1 exchange between assets that in reality have varying prices, the balance sheet of the contract can be arbitraged (especially by flash-loans) to swap an undesirable asset (i.e. USDC which at the time of submission was valued at `0.99994853` USD) for a more desirable asset (i.e. USDT which at the time of submission was valued at `1.00000000` USD) acquiring an arbitrage in the price by selling the traded asset.

title: Users can bypass the `maxWinPercent` limit using a partially closing
content: The vulnerability is a logic error in the contract’s profit‑capping mechanism that allows a trader to receive more than the configured maximum win percentage (maxWinPercent) by repeatedly closing only a portion of an open position. The root cause is that the contract checks the maxWinPercent limit against the full margin of the trade rather than against the margin that is actually being closed in a partial‑close operation. Because the check uses the total margin value, each partial close is evaluated as if the entire position were being settled, so the calculated payout is capped only by the partial margin multiplied by maxWinPercent. An attacker can open a position with a large unrealised profit, then close, for example, 50 % of the position repeatedly. After each partial close the contract mints tokens up to maxWinPercent of the partial margin, which in practice equals the full allowed profit for the original margin. The remaining margin is reduced, but the unrealised profit stays, allowing the attacker to repeat the step until almost the entire profit is extracted. From a user’s point of view the UI may show a payout that far exceeds the documented +500 % limit, or the trader may notice that the balance increases dramatically after each partial close, contrary to the expectation that the protocol would cap total winnings at 500 % of the initial margin. The condition for exploitation is that maxWinPercent is greater than zero, the contract permits partial closing, and the limit check is performed against the full trade margin instead of the partial margin being closed. This bug primarily harms liquidity providers and the protocol’s accounting invariants, as the excess payouts drain funds that should have been reserved for LPs. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, which demonstrated the exploit with a proof‑of‑concept that repeatedly closed 50 % of a position and harvested nearly the entire profit. The flaw is subtle because the limit appears to work correctly for full position closures, making it easy to overlook the partial‑close path. To remediate, the contract should compute the maximum allowable payout based on the margin actually being closed (partialMarginToClose) and enforce the cap against that value, or otherwise track cumulative payouts to ensure the overall profit never exceeds maxWinPercent of the original margin. Implementing this check restores the intended business rule that a trader cannot earn more than the configured percentage of their initial margin, preserving LP safety and protocol integrity.
summary:
Users can bypass the `maxWinPercent` limit using a partial closing.

As a result, users can receive more funds than their upper limit from the protocol.

title: User can abuse tight stop losses and high leverage to make risk free trades
content: The vulnerability is a stop‑loss execution flaw that allows a trader to close a leveraged position at the price that was originally stored in the stop‑loss field instead of the current market price. The contract treats the user‑provided stop‑loss price as the settlement price when the stop condition is met, rather than using it only as a trigger threshold. This design mistake originates from a logic error in the limit‑close routine where the variable _limitPrice is assigned directly from _trade.slPrice for stop‑loss closures. Because the stop‑loss price is typically set very close to the entry price, an attacker can open a high‑leverage long (or short) position with a stop‑loss placed a few cents below (or above) the market. If the price moves against the position immediately, the stop condition is satisfied, but the contract settles the trade at the stored stop‑loss price, which is essentially the entry price. The trader therefore incurs only the opening and closing fees while the market price may have moved dramatically, resulting in a near‑risk‑free loss for the attacker. Conversely, if the market moves in the trader’s favor before the stop is triggered, the trader can realize a large profit because the stop‑loss does not limit downside risk as intended. The impact is a breach of the fundamental invariant that a stop‑loss caps a trader’s maximum loss at the prevailing market price; instead, the loss is capped at the user‑defined price, allowing the attacker to extract value from the liquidity pool. This issue manifests whenever a stop‑loss order is executed, which is any time a position is closed through the limitClose function with the _tp flag set to false. All participants who provide liquidity to the pool are affected because the protocol’s accounting assumes that stop‑losses protect against adverse price movements, and the exploit drains funds from the pool to the attacker. The flaw was discovered during a security audit by the Code4rena warden, who noted that the stop‑loss price is used as the settlement price rather than as a trigger. The problem can be subtle because the contract does not revert or emit an obvious error; the trade simply closes at an unexpected price, which may appear as a normal execution from the UI perspective. From a user’s point of view the symptom is that a trade that should have been stopped out at the current market price instead closes at the stop‑loss price, leading to either an unexpectedly small loss (or a profit) and a discrepancy between the displayed market price and the execution price. The correct mitigation is to replace the stored stop‑loss value with the current market price when performing the settlement, i.e., use the market price as the execution price after the stop condition is satisfied, while keeping the user‑defined price only as a trigger check. This change restores the intended risk‑limiting behavior and protects liquidity providers from loss caused by the exploit.
summary: User can abuse how stop losses are priced to open high leverage trades with huge upside and very little downside.

title: Not enough margin pulled or burned from user when adding to a position
content: The vulnerability is an under‑collateralisation bug that occurs when a trader adds margin to an existing position through the Trading.addToPosition function. The contract calculates a fee that is minted to referrers and the protocol, but then mistakenly subtracts that fee from the amount passed to the internal _handleDeposit call. As a result the protocol records that the full _addMargin amount has been locked, while in reality only _addMargin minus the fee is taken from the user’s wallet (or burned when using tigAsset). This mismatch lowers the actual collateralisation ratio of the tigAsset position, breaking the invariant that a position must be fully backed by the declared margin. The bug can be exploited by opening a leveraged position with less real collateral than the contract believes, allowing an attacker to obtain higher leverage, increase the chance of liquidation, or cause the protocol to lose value because fees are effectively double‑counted. The issue manifests whenever addToPosition is called, i.e., any time a user tries to increase margin on a position, and it affects all participants who rely on correct margin accounting – traders, lenders, and the protocol itself. It was discovered during a manual audit by Code4rena when the fee handling logic was compared with the correct pattern used in initiateMarketOrder, revealing that the fee was being deducted from the deposited amount instead of being accounted for separately. The problem is subtle because the UI continues to display the expected margin amount and the position size appears correct, so users may not notice that less collateral is actually locked until an unexpected liquidation or a missing refund occurs. From a user perspective the symptoms are a position that seems properly funded but later gets liquidated prematurely, or a situation where a refund or remaining balance is lower than expected. The bug belongs to the class of margin‑accounting errors or fee double‑counting bugs that violate the business logic that each unit of margin must be fully backed. The recommended fix is to invoke _handleDeposit with the full _addMargin value, removing the subtraction of _fee, and to handle fee minting as a separate step that does not reduce the amount of collateral taken from the user. This restores the correct collateralisation ratio and prevents the protocol from being exposed to unintended leverage.
summary: When adding to a position, the amount of margin pulled from the user is not as much as it should be, which leaks value from the protocol, lowering the collateralization ratio of `tigAsset`.

title: Bank run is possible when the product is insolvent.
content: The vulnerability is a systemic insolvency handling flaw in a financial product contract where withdrawals are processed without accounting for any accumulated shortfall. When one or more participant accounts become bankrupt, the product records a shortfall – the total assets are lower than the total liabilities – but the withdrawal function continues to allow users to withdraw their full recorded balance. The root cause is the absence of any logic that reduces a withdrawing user’s payout proportionally to the outstanding shortfall, and the lack of a mechanism that forces the protocol owner or a backer to resolve the deficit before later withdrawals are executed. An attacker or any user can exploit this by being among the early withdrawers, receiving their full balance while later users, especially the last ones, receive only a partial amount or nothing at all because the remaining assets have already been depleted. The impact is a classic bank‑run scenario: users see their expected refunds disappear, balances become unexpectedly zero, and confidence in the protocol erodes, potentially leading to a cascade of withdrawals that the contract cannot satisfy. This condition occurs only when the product becomes insolvent – i.e., shortfall > 0 – and the contract’s withdrawal path does not check the shortfall state. All participants of the product, including regular users, protocol owners, and any insurance or re‑insurance backers, are affected because the shortfall may never be resolved in time, leaving some users under‑compensated. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the product’s accounting invariants and noticed that the OptimisticLedger never reflects a negative balance caused by bankrupt accounts. It is hard to notice in normal operation because the contract behaves correctly while assets exceed liabilities; the problem only surfaces under stress when insolvency occurs, a scenario that may not be covered by routine tests. To remediate, the withdrawal routine should first compute the proportion of the shortfall attributable to each user’s open position and deduct that amount from the payout, updating the ledger accordingly. The shortfall should be expressed per unit of open position rather than per unit of collateral, ensuring that users who hold only idle collateral are not unfairly penalised. This change restores the accounting invariant that total withdrawals cannot exceed remaining assets, preventing the bank‑run condition and aligning the contract’s behavior with the expected business logic that every user’s balance can be fully withdrawn only when the product is solvent.
summary: When a product becomes insolvent, the last user(s) will not be able to withdraw their full balance. When one or more accounts go bankrupt, the bad debt will be accumulated in the product as the shortfall. When shortfall > 0 it means the product is now insolvent i.e. the total assets (product.total) is lower than the total liabilities (sum of all takers and makers' product accounts). If a protocol becomes insolvent, the protocol owner (or a backer e.g. re-insurance fund) has the responsibility to resolve the shortfall, but there is nothing in the protocol to guarantee the protocol’s shortfall to be resolved in time for all users’ withdrawals to be made whole. Furthermore, when a user withdraws, the product’s shortfall is not taken into consideration. Early withdrawals will be able to close their position without being impacted by the insolvency but the protocol may not have sufficient funds for later withdrawals of the insolvent product. Therefore early users can be made whole as there are still enough assets for them to exit, but late users or at least the last user will not be able to withdraw their entire balance. This will make the users of the insolvent product rush to withdraw their balances, i.e. a bank run scenario.

title: Unconventional PnL settlement can cause unexpected user liquidation.
content: The vulnerability consists of a permissionless profit‑and‑loss (PnL) settlement mechanism that treats unrealized PnL as if it were realized and writes it directly to a trader’s collateral balance each time the internal settleAccount function is invoked. Because the function can be called by any address, an attacker or any third party can trigger settlement for a user at any moment, even while the user’s position is still open. The protocol does not distinguish between unrealized and realized gains or losses, so a negative unrealized PnL is immediately deducted from the user’s collateral. The liquidation check later uses the updated collateral amount, which may fall below the maintenance margin requirement, causing the position to be liquidated even though the user has not closed the position and has not received any liquidation warning. The issue appears when the market price moves against an open leveraged position and an external actor invokes settlement, causing the user’s balance to drop below the required maintenance threshold. Users experience symptoms such as a sudden reduction of their collateral balance, a missing liquidation alert, and an unexpected liquidation of an otherwise healthy position. The problem was discovered during a manual audit of the Perennial perpetual futures contract, where the auditor observed that the settleAccount flow is public and that the PnL accounting logic writes directly to the collateral without an unrealized‑PnL buffer. The bug is subtle because the contract’s documentation states that PnL is settled “every oracle version globally,” which can be interpreted as normal behavior, and because the liquidation logic still works correctly when the balance is accurate, making the flaw easy to miss in functional tests. To remediate, the protocol should separate unrealized PnL from realized collateral, either by deferring settlement until a position is closed or by restricting the settlement function to be callable only by privileged internal calls triggered by position updates or liquidation processes. Additionally, the liquidation check should be performed against the collateral that excludes pending unrealized losses, and the UI should clearly communicate that liquidation price is computed with the protocol‑specific formula and may differ from traditional perpetual futures. Implementing these changes would prevent third parties from forcing premature liquidation and would align the protocol’s behavior with trader expectations.
summary: P&L is settled directly to the user's account and can be triggered by anyone which could lead to unexpected liquidations. As per the documentation: “P&L is settled every oracle version globally on a per-position basis. Account-level P&L is synced when a user makes any position-related updates to their account (i.e. opening or closing a position).” In conventional perpetual futures markets, PnL will only be settled when positions are closed. For open positions, “unrealized” PnLs are tracked and accounted for, but only realized/settled upon closing of positions. However, the current implementation of Perennial protocol settles PnL directly to the user's account every time settleAccountInternal is called (by anyone), without differentiating between unrealized and realized PnL. Furthermore, settleAccount flow is permissionless which means that anyone can trigger PnL settlement for anyone else. This combination could lead to unexpected liquidations. Example Scenario: Let’s say that the product is ETH3x. Maintenance is 0.5 (50%) and the current price of the product is $3000 (3 * 1000). 1. Alice deposits $2000 into her collateral account 2. Alice opens a maker (short) position of 1 ETH3x 3. As an experienced perpetual futures trader, Alice sets an alert for the liquidation price of $4000 for ETH3x or ~$1333 for ETH 4. After a few rounds, the price of ETH3x rises to $3600 (ETH price: $1200) 5. Mallory calls settleAccount(Alice) and the PnL of Alice's open position $-600 was settled to Alice's collateral account, and the updated balance is $1400 6. Alice's position gets liquidated due to insufficient maintenance collateral $1800 ($3600 * 0.5) which is > Alice’s balance of $1400 7. After a few rounds, the price of ETH3x plunges to $2400 8. Alice returns to check her earnings prepared to close the position and collect the profit when she discovers that her position had already been liquidated 9. Alice's liquidation alert was never triggered but Alice's position has been liquidated Users get unexpectedly liquidated if they assume that Perennial protocol behaves similar to conventional perpetual futures market.

title: Missing accumulatedFee debit on the paying side may make the product insolvent.
content: The vulnerability is a missing debit of the platform fee component (accumulatedFee) on the side that is supposed to pay it during funding settlement. The contract calculates a funding fee that consists of a funding portion and a platform fee, but only the funding portion is transferred between maker and taker accounts. The platform fee is subtracted from the product’s total asset pool (product.total) without being credited to any participant’s balance. This creates a mismatch where the sum of all maker and taker account balances (the total liabilities) remains unchanged while the product’s recorded assets are reduced by the fee amount. The root cause is the omission of a line that should debit the paying side – either the maker or the taker depending on the sign of the accumulated funding – for the accumulatedFee. An attacker does not need to craft a special transaction; the bug manifests automatically on every settlement where a fee is charged. After settlement the product becomes insolvent: the total assets recorded by the contract are lower than the total liabilities owed to users. From a user’s perspective the balances shown in their wallets appear correct, but the underlying product can no longer honor withdrawals because the accounting books do not balance. This condition can lead to loss of funds, inability to settle future trades, and erosion of trust in the protocol. The issue appears only when the funding fee includes a non‑zero platform fee and the settlement logic executes; it is invisible in normal operation because the UI typically displays individual account balances, not the aggregate product total. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the expected accounting equation (assets = sum of liabilities) with the actual state after settlement. It is hard to notice because the discrepancy is a single unit of value per settlement and does not trigger an explicit error flag. The correct fix is to debit the accumulatedFee from the side that pays the fee – subtract the fee from the maker’s accumulatedFunding when the funding sign is negative, otherwise subtract it from the taker’s accumulatedFunding – ensuring that the fee is transferred from a participant to the platform and that the product’s total assets remain consistent with the sum of participant balances. This brings the contract back into the class of accounting‑consistent funding mechanisms where every fee charged is matched by a corresponding debit, preventing insolvency and preserving the integrity of the product’s financial state.
summary: The platform/product fee (accumulatedFee) component of the funding fee (accumulatedFunding) is missing a debit on the paying side. The current implementation does not debit the platform/product fee accumulatedFee on the paying side. Given: Example scenario: Alice is the only Maker of the product, holding a position of 20 with a collateral of 100; Bob is the only Taker, holding a position of 10 with a collateral of 100; rateAccumulated = 10%; The price is 10; product.total = 200; FundingFeeRate is 0.1 (10%); In product.settle(): takerNotional = 10 * 10 == 100; fundingAccumulated = 100 * 10% == 10; accumulatedFee = 10 * 0.1 == 1; fundingIncludingFee = +(10-1) == 9; Total accumulatedFunding on the maker side is 9; total accumulatedFunding on the taker side is -9; As a result: product.total = 199; Alice's account = 100+9 == 109; Bob's account = 100-9 == 91; The product is now insolvent as the total liabilities is 109 + 91 == 200, but the total assets is only 199. The product will become insolvent right after the product is settled because the accumulatedFee will be deducted from the total assets (product.total) but the total liabilities (sum of all takers and makers' product accounts) remain unchanged. In other words, a fee is taken from the product but no one is paying for that.

title: Untitled
content: The vulnerability is a manipulation of the price feed median calculation caused by the ability of a malicious actor to filter the set of validator signatures down to the minimum number required (minSigners) before calling transmit(). Because transmit() is not restricted to validators and signatures do not carry timestamps, an attacker observing the mempool can select any subset of valid signatures, submit a transaction that includes only those signatures, and cause the contract to compute the median from an incomplete and potentially biased set of answers. This results in a median price that can deviate significantly from the true median that would be obtained if all validator answers were considered. The issue occurs whenever the number of validators exceeds minSigners, timestamps are omitted, and the transmit function is publicly callable. Users of the feed, downstream protocols that rely on the price, and token holders are affected because they may receive a price that is artificially low or high, leading to incorrect settlements, liquidations, or arbitrage losses. The problem was discovered during a security audit that constructed a proof‑of‑concept where six validators submitted [1,5,8,10,10,10] giving a median of 9, but an attacker front‑ran the transaction with only three signatures [1,5,8] producing a median of 5. The manipulation is hard to notice because the contract does not record which signatures were omitted and the resulting median may still appear plausible, so no obvious error is emitted.
