content: The vulnerability is a logical error in the increaseLock() function of the TimeLockPool contract where the code loads the deposit information of the caller (msg.sender) instead of the intended receiver when calculating the remaining lock duration. The root cause is the use of depositsOf[_msgSender()][_depositId] rather than depositsOf[_receiver][_depositId] to obtain the userDeposit struct. This incorrect reference leads to an inaccurate remainingDuration value, which is then used to compute a multiplier for the amount of new shares (mintAmount) that the receiver will obtain. Because the multiplier is based on the caller’s longer lock period, a receiver can be granted many more shares than justified, or conversely fewer shares if the caller’s lock is shorter. The exploit scenario is straightforward: an attacker calls increaseLock() on behalf of another user, supplying a depositId that belongs to the victim, while the attacker’s own deposit has a much longer remaining duration. The contract mistakenly applies the attacker’s duration to the victim’s mint calculation, inflating the victim’s share balance by a factor proportional to the duration mismatch (for example, a 4‑year remaining lock versus a 10‑minute lock can produce a five‑fold increase). This results in unintended token inflation, dilution of existing shareholders, and a breach of the protocol’s accounting assumptions that share issuance is proportional to lock time. The issue manifests only when the caller’s deposit has a different remaining duration than the receiver’s deposit; in cases where both durations match, the bug remains hidden, making it hard to detect through casual testing. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the flow of data in increaseLock() and identified the mismatched index usage. From a user’s perspective, the expected behavior is that a user receives a share amount that reflects their own remaining lock period; instead, they may see an unexpectedly large (or small) share balance after the operation, with no visible error message. This class of bug falls under “incorrect state reference leading to arithmetic miscalculation” and violates the business logic that ties token rewards to time‑locked deposits. The recommended fix is to replace the line that reads the deposit with the correct mapping key, i.e., use depositsOf[_receiver][_depositId] when constructing the userDeposit variable, ensuring that the remainingDuration and multiplier are calculated from the receiver’s actual deposit.
summary:
TimeLockPool.sol L203 should read depositsOf[_receiver][_depositId] as userDeposit.  
TimeLockPool.sol L230 in increaseLock() is loading depositsOf[_msgSender()][_depositId] as userDeposit, which will later be used to check if the deposit has expired (L206-208) and calculating the remainingDuration (L213).  
This remainingDuration will be used to calculate the multiplier for the mintAmount at L215.  
As a result, the _receiver can receive a much larger shares.  
For example, if the receiver only has 10 mins left in depositsOf[_receiver][_depositId], but depositsOf[_msgSender()][_depositId] have 4 years left. The mintAmount will be 5x than expected.  
Or fewer shares than expected when the caller's deposit's remainingDuration is shorter than the receiver's.

title: Unit isn't recalculated on curve modification
content: The TimeLockPool contract uses a variable called unit to translate a lock duration into an index on a reward‑bonus curve. Unit is calculated as maxLockDuration divided by (curve.length‑1) and is refreshed only during contract initialization and when the whole curve is replaced via setCurve(). The function setCurvePoint() allows a privileged account (onlyGov) to add, replace or remove a single point in the curve, thereby changing the curve length. However, setCurvePoint() does not recompute unit after the length changes. As a result, the mapping between lock duration and curve index becomes stale: if the curve is shortened, unit remains based on the old longer length, causing getMultiplier() to treat a relatively short lock as if it were near the end of the curve, and if the curve is lengthened, unit stays too small, causing the multiplier to be capped prematurely. This mismatch leads to incorrect share calculations – users may receive more shares than the protocol intends when the curve is shortened, or fewer shares when it is lengthened. The impact is monetary: the reward multiplier, which directly determines token allocations, can be inflated or deflated, effectively creating or destroying value for users. The bug manifests only after a governance transaction that calls setCurvePoint() to modify the curve length; normal operations that use setCurve() or the constructor keep unit consistent. It was discovered during a manual audit by the researcher Sherlock, who noticed that unit is never updated in setCurvePoint() despite the comment that the function can change the curve size. The issue is subtle because unit is an internal bookkeeping variable; the contract does not emit an event or revert when the multiplier is wrong, so the UI may still display a multiplier value that appears plausible, while the underlying token accounting is off. From a user perspective the symptoms are a mismatch between expected and actual rewards – for example, a user who locks for half of the maximum duration may see the maximum bonus applied, or a user may see their reward drop to zero unexpectedly after a curve extension. This class of bug is a state‑invariant violation caused by a stale derived variable, often referred to as a “stale cache” or “incorrect derived state” vulnerability. To remediate, the contract should recalculate unit every time the curve length changes, either by updating unit inside setCurvePoint() after push or pop operations, or by extracting the calculation into a private helper that is called after any modification of the curve array. Ensuring that unit always reflects the current curve length restores the correct relationship between lock duration and multiplier, preventing unintended creation or loss of funds.

title: Surplus auction cannot be cancelled
content: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition in the surplus‑auction cancellation flow of the protocol. When a caller attempts to cancel an active surplus auction, the contract invokes the ERC‑20 token’s transferFrom function to move the winning bid back to the auction recipient. TransferFrom requires that the caller have a non‑zero allowance set by the token holder (the contract itself in this case). Because the contract never grants itself an allowance, the internal allowance check fails and the transaction reverts with \"ERC20: transfer amount exceeds allowance\". Consequently the cancellation transaction cannot succeed and the auction remains open indefinitely. The root cause is a misuse of the ERC‑20 transferFrom API: the developers assumed that a contract could pull its own tokens without an explicit approval, which is contrary to the OpenZeppelin ERC‑20 implementation that enforces allowance checks even when the sender and the caller are the same address. An attacker or any user who triggers the cancel function can therefore block the auction, preventing the protocol from reclaiming surplus funds. This may lead to funds being locked in the auction contract, users seeing no refund or payout, and the overall accounting of the system becoming inconsistent because expected surplus balances never clear. The issue appears only when the cancel path is exercised; normal auction creation and bidding work because they do not call transferFrom. It was discovered during a manual security audit that inspected the cancelAuction logic and compared it against the ERC‑20 token contract. The problem is subtle because transferFrom is a common pattern for moving tokens and developers may overlook the allowance requirement when the contract itself is the token holder. To remediate, the contract should replace the transferFrom call with a direct transfer (or OpenZeppelin’s safeTransfer) which does not require an allowance, thereby allowing the contract to move its own tokens and successfully cancel the auction. This change restores the intended business logic that surplus auctions can be cancelled and that surplus funds are returned to the designated recipient, aligning the implementation with the protocol’s accounting assumptions.

title: Stale price can be disputed but still accepted
content: The vulnerability is a stale‑price acceptance flaw in the OptimisticChainlinkOracle contract. The shift() function allows a proposer to create a new price proposal that is syntactically valid but originates from an old Chainlink round because it does not enforce that the proposal is submitted within the designated proposeWindow or that its timestamp is newer than the previously accepted round. An attacker can therefore submit a proposal containing a price that is days old. When another participant disputes this proposal, the dispute() routine calls validate() which only checks the nonce and deliberately skips a fresh fetch of the underlying Chainlink price as long as the nonce is still valid. Consequently the stale price is treated as the correct value and is passed to the internal settlement function _settleDispute(). The dispute also creates a new proposal on behalf of the OptimisticChainlinkOracle contract itself, but this auto‑generated proposal carries no bond, so it may escape further challenges and be shifted into the Collybus shortly after the dispute. From a user perspective the system records a price that is far from the current market rate, causing the Collybus to provide incorrect valuations. This can lead to under‑collateralized positions, unexpected liquidations, refunds that are zero or far too low, and overall loss of funds for traders, lenders, or any party that relies on the oracle for settlement. The issue manifests when a proposal is submitted after the normal update interval but before the dispute window expires, and when the dispute validation path is taken. It was discovered during a manual audit of the shift() and dispute() logic, where the lack of a timestamp or proposeWindow check was observed. The bug is subtle because the proposal passes all signature, nonce, and basic validity checks, and the price appears to be a legitimate Chainlink value, so routine monitoring may not flag it as abnormal. The recommended remediation is to require that any new proposal be created within the proposeWindow or to enforce that its round timestamp be newer than the last accepted round, and to make dispute validation re‑fetch the latest price from the Chainlink feed. Adding a keeper that pushes the most recent Chainlink round whenever a lag is detected can also prevent stale prices from being accepted. This class of bug belongs to the “stale data acceptance” or “time‑of‑use validation missing” category, where outdated oracle data is accepted as authoritative, violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions that prices reflect the current market.
summary:
The shift() function has no validation that stops a proposer from creating a new proposal with valid but outdated price data.  
Oct 3rd to Oct 5th.  
If an attacker submitted a proposal with the price from a long time ago, say 10 days, this proposal can and will be disputed.  
However, dispute()->validate() won't refetch the new price data as long as nonceIsValid (L183-198), so that the price from 10 days ago will be passed to _settleDispute() as the validValue (OptimisticChainlinkOracle.sol#L191, OptimisticOracle.sol#L188,207).  
Even though the dispute() won't push the stale price to the Collybus immediately, instead, it creates a new proposal in the name of the OptimisticChainlinkOracle contract itself as the proposer. But since this proposal is not bonded, it may not get disputed, so the stale price can likely be shifted to the collybus soon after the dispute.

title: nonce could be malicious in OptimisticOracle.s
content: The vulnerability resides in the OptimisticOracle contract where the proposer supplies a nonce that encodes both a Chainlink round identifier (roundId) and a round timestamp (roundTimestamp) without any verification. Because the contract does not validate that the nonce corresponds to the actual data returned by the Chainlink feed, a malicious proposer can craft a nonce containing an arbitrary roundId or a timestamp that lies outside the expected dispute window. By doing so the proposer can either skip the dispute window entirely, allowing a proposal to become final without the opportunity for challengers, or force the ChainlinkValidator.validate function to accept stale or manipulated price data from an old round. This mismatch between the encoded timestamp and the on‑chain feed timestamp breaks the core accounting assumption that price feeds are fresh and trustworthy. An attacker can therefore push incorrect price values into the FIAT protocol, causing downstream contracts to settle trades, mint or burn tokens, or calculate collateral based on a falsified rate. From a user’s perspective the protocol may display a price that is dramatically higher or lower than the market, leading to unexpected losses, zero refunds, or funds that appear to disappear after a transaction. The issue manifests whenever a proposer calls OptimisticOracle.shift (or dispute) with a user‑controlled nonce; it is not limited to a specific function signature but is a class of nonce‑validation flaw. The flaw was uncovered during a security audit by Sherlock, who noted that the lack of checks makes the bug subtle – the nonce is a 32‑byte opaque value, so the contract appears to accept it without error, and the incorrect price only becomes visible later when settlements occur. To remediate, the contract should either generate the nonce internally or enforce that the roundTimestamp extracted from the nonce matches the timestamp reported by the Chainlink round, and that the roundId is the latest valid round. Additional checks should ensure the dispute window is applied to the verified timestamp and that old round identifiers cannot be reused. By binding the nonce to verified on‑chain data, the protocol restores the integrity of its price oracle and prevents malicious manipulation of financial outcomes.
summary:
Proposers can use malicious nonce in OptimisticOracle.shift, since there is no check for nonce.
nonce is provided by the proposer. Thus, roundId and roundTimestamp can be malicious.
1. A malicious roundTimestamp can skip disputeWindow due to this issue https://github.com/SherlockAudit/fiat-dao/issues/31
2. A malicious roundId can cheat ChainlinkValidator.validate, e.g. Use old roundId, then ChainlinkValidator.validate can accept old value (which could be a bad value in the current round).
Proposers can use malicious nonce to set bad values. Bad values will be pushed to FIAT. It could lead to a big disaster in FIAT protocol.

title: SurplusAuction.sol#closeAuction()will revert as
content: The contract implements a surplus auction where the winner’s bid is supposed to be transferred back to a designated recipient when the auction is closed. In the current implementation the closeAuction function attempts to transfer the bid amount using token.transfer(address(0), auctions[auctionId].bid). Because the ERC‑20 token contract rejects transfers to the zero address, the call reverts and the whole closeAuction execution fails. The root cause is a hard‑coded zero address used as the destination for the token transfer, which violates the token’s invariant that the zero address cannot be a recipient. The function is only reachable after the auction has expired (bidExpiry or auctionExpiry passed) and the contract is live, so an attacker or any user who calls closeAuction after a legitimate auction ends will trigger the revert. As a result the auction state is never cleared, the bid funds remain locked in the contract, and the intended recipient never receives the tokens. From a user’s perspective the expectation is that after the auction ends they will receive their bid back or see the auction marked as closed, but instead the transaction fails silently and the UI may continue to show the auction as open with no balance change. This denial‑of‑service style bug can be hard to notice because the code appears to follow the usual pattern of deleting the auction after the transfer, and developers may mistakenly assume that sending to address(0) is a burn operation, not realizing the token contract forbids it. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the SurplusAuction.sol source where the transfer line was inspected and the token’s transfer restrictions were cross‑checked. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “invalid address transfer” or “zero‑address transfer denial‑of‑service” bugs, where an incorrect recipient address causes a transaction to revert and locks assets. To remediate the problem the contract should replace the zero address with a valid recipient, such as the governance address, or implement a proper burn mechanism that the token contract supports. This change ensures that the token transfer succeeds, the auction state can be cleared, and users receive the expected outcome without funds disappearing.

title: OptimisticOracle.unbond can be tricked by malicious users
content: The vulnerability resides in the unbond function of the OptimisticOracle contract. The function is supposed to prevent a proposer from retrieving the bond while a proposal is still within the dispute window. To enforce this, the code recomputes a proposal identifier (proposalId) from the caller address (msg.sender), the rate identifier, the bond value and a nonce, and then checks whether the stored proposal identifier for the given rate (proposals[rateId]) matches the recomputed one. If the identifiers match and a validator is configured, the call is reverted with OptimisticOracle__unbond_isProposing. Because the proposal identifier is derived from msg.sender, a malicious proposer can supply a different value or nonce that yields a different proposalId, causing the equality test to fail. Consequently the revert condition is bypassed and the function proceeds to release the bond even though the dispute window has not elapsed. The root cause is the reliance on a caller‑controlled identifier for the protection check instead of a stable record of who created the active proposal. The exploit can be carried out by any user who has previously submitted a proposal and still holds the bonded tokens; during the dispute period they simply call unbond with crafted parameters, the check does not trigger, and the contract releases the bonded tokens back to the attacker. The impact is that the economic guarantee that bonds provide against dishonest proposals is broken: attackers can reclaim their stake without waiting for the dispute window, potentially allowing them to submit multiple proposals without risk, undermining the oracle’s security model and exposing honest participants to loss of confidence and possible financial harm. The bug manifests only when a rate configuration includes a validator (rateConfig.validator != address(0)) and the validator reports that the proposal is still disputable (canDispute returns true). Under those conditions, the unbond function’s protective clause is ineffective. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit by the researcher Sherlock, who noticed that the proposal identifier is computed using msg.sender and therefore can be manipulated. It is subtle because the revert logic appears correct at a glance and typical unit tests may not vary the value or nonce parameters, making the bypass hard to detect in ordinary testing. To remediate the problem, the contract should store the proposer’s address in a dedicated mapping (e.g., proposer[rateId]) when a proposal is created and then compare msg.sender directly against that stored address in the unbond function, rather than recomputing a proposal identifier. This change ensures that the check cannot be evaded by altering input parameters, restoring the intended bond‑locking behavior and preserving the protocol’s economic security.

title: Incorrect translation of require checks to revert
content: The vulnerability is a logic inversion error that occurs when translating Solidity require statements into custom error revert checks. In the original library a condition such as require(x.length > 0) ensures that the input array is non‑empty; the correct translation to a custom error is to revert only when the length is zero (if(x.length == 0) revert...). However the audit found that the condition was mistakenly inverted to if(x.length != 0) revert..., meaning the contract now reverts whenever the array is non‑empty and accepts empty inputs. This mistake appears in several utility functions that decode compact representations and validate RLP items. Because the guard is flipped, legitimate calls that provide required data are rejected, while calls with missing data pass through, potentially leading to malformed state, failed proofs, or downstream contract failures. An attacker can exploit this by simply providing a correctly sized input, causing the transaction to revert and thereby creating a denial‑of‑service condition for honest users. The impact is high because core verification routines become unusable, preventing users from submitting valid proofs, withdrawing funds, or interacting with the protocol, effectively freezing functionality. The bug manifests whenever a function that relies on the affected guards is invoked, which includes Merkle‑Patricia proof verification and RLP decoding. All participants—users submitting proofs, relayers, and the protocol itself—are affected because their transactions will fail unexpectedly. The issue was discovered during a manual code review that compared the new implementation against the original library and noticed that the logical negation was applied incorrectly. The problem is subtle because the code still compiles and the revert messages are generic, so developers may not immediately see that the condition is reversed; only a careful inspection of the intended semantics reveals the mismatch. The proper fix is to restore the original logical intent by changing each inverted guard to check for the zero or invalid condition (e.g., if(compact.length == 0) revert ...) and to use the appropriate custom error. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of condition inversion or improper error handling when refactoring require statements to custom errors. From a user perspective, transactions that should succeed now revert with an error, leading to confusion such as 'my proof was rejected even though it is valid' or 'the contract returned zero balance after I tried to withdraw'. The expectation that a non‑empty input is accepted is violated, resulting in lost time, possible gas waste, and a temporary loss of service.
summary:
There are a number of instances where the require checks in the original libraries were incorrectly translated to revert conditions.
One of the changes to the utils libraries from the referenced ones were the use of custom errors instead of require statements. This means that conditions and checks have to be inverted. For instance, require(x==0) is to be replaced with if(x!=0)revertCustomError().
One of these conditions was inverted incorrectly. The original statement require(x.length>0); should have been converted to if(x.length==0)revertCustomError(), but was incorrectly converted to if(x.length!=0)revertCustomError() instead.
Broken functionality.

title: The implied value of a public vault can be impaired
content: During a partial repayment of a lien in a public vault the contract updates the stored lien amount with accrued interest before calling the vault's beforePayment hook. The beforePayment hook reads the current slope by invoking calculateSlope, which internally recomputes the owed amount using the same accrued interest that has already been added to lien.amount. Because the timestamp stored in lien.last is not refreshed before the slope calculation, the interest for the elapsed period is counted twice. The duplicated interest inflates or deflates the lien slope, which is then subtracted from the vault's slope accumulator. The vault uses this accumulator to derive its implied value (totalAssets) that backs LP shares. When the slope is wrong, the implied value can become smaller than the actual underlying assets, causing liquidity providers to receive less than their share, or larger than the assets, allowing early withdrawers to take more than they are entitled to while later providers are left with a shortfall. The bug manifests only when a borrower repays only part of a lien; full repayment resets the slope correctly. It is difficult to detect because the vault's balance remains unchanged and the error appears only in the conversion of shares to assets during redemption. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that traced the flow of partial payments and observed that lien.last was not updated before slope calculation. The proper fix is to postpone the update of lien.amount until after the beforePayment call, or to refresh lien.last before calculating the slope, ensuring that interest is accounted exactly once.

title: Lien buyout with new terms does not update the slope
content: The vulnerability consists of an accounting inconsistency that occurs when a lien on a public vault is bought out with new terms. A lien defines a repayment schedule through parameters such as last payment timestamp, start time, interest rate and duration, which together determine a slope – the rate at which the lien’s accrued value grows. In the buyoutLien function the contract updates the lien parameters to reflect the new agreement, but it fails to adjust the public vault’s stored slope to match the changed terms. Consequently the vault continues to use the old slope for subsequent calculations. This mismatch manifests during liquidation: the liquidation routine adjusts the vault’s slope by the lien’s slope, assuming the stored slope is current. When the lien has been previously bought out, the stored slope is stale, causing the adjustment to be incorrect and the liquidation function to revert. In addition, the public vault’s implied value, which is derived from the slope, becomes outdated, leading to over‑ or undervaluation of vault shares. Users therefore experience failed liquidation transactions, unexpected share values, or balances that appear to disappear. The issue is triggered only when a public vault contains a lien that has been bought out with altered terms; private vaults or unchanged liens are unaffected. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the interaction between VaultImplementation.buyoutLien and PublicVault.updateVaultAfterLiquidation. The bug is subtle because the slope is an internal accounting variable that is not exposed directly to users, so the problem only surfaces as transaction reverts or incorrect accounting numbers, which can be mistaken for network congestion or user error. To remediate, the implementation should capture the current slope before modifying the lien, subtract that value from the vault’s stored slope, apply the updated lien terms, recompute the new slope, and add the new value back to the vault’s slope. This ensures that the vault’s accounting stays consistent with the lien’s actual repayment schedule, preventing liquidation failures and preserving accurate vault valuations.
summary:
Lien buyout with new terms does not update the slope of public vaults leading to reverts and potential insolvency of vaults. In the VaultImplementation.buyoutLien function, a lien is bought out with new terms. Terms of a lien (last, start, rate, duration) will have changed after a buyout. This changes the slope calculation, however, after the buyout, the slope for the public vault is not updated. There are multiple parts of the code affected by this.
1) When liquidating, the vault slope is adjusted by the liens slope (see https://git85-L387). In case of a single lien, the PublicVault.updateVaultAfterLiquidation function can revert if the lien terms have changed previously due to a buyout.sol#L532). Hence, liquidations with a public vault involved, will revert.
2) The PublicVault contract calculates the implied value of a vault (ie. value can be outdated, this leads to undervalue or overvalue of a public vault and thus vault share calculations will be incorrect.

title: Auction bid that partially pays back an expired lien reverts
content: The vulnerability is a logic error in the auction liquidation flow that causes a transaction to revert when a bidder attempts to partially repay an expired lien. The root cause is that the contract updates the timestamp field lien.last to the current block time even after the lien has passed its expiration (lien.start + lien.duration). When a partial payment is made, the _payment function follows a branch that sets lien.last to block.timestamp, which is now greater than the original end time of the auction. Later the code computes a divisor end - lien.last; because lien.last exceeds end, the subtraction underflows to zero or a negative value, causing the mulDivDown arithmetic to revert. An attacker or honest participant can exploit this by submitting a bid that does not fully cover the outstanding amount of an expired lien; the transaction will fail, preventing the bid from being recorded. The impact is a denial‑of‑service on the auction mechanism: partial bids are blocked, the auction cannot progress, and liquidity providers lose expected revenue because their funds remain locked. The condition occurs only for liens that have already expired and are being repaid only partially; full repayment bypasses the problematic branch because lien.last is not updated in that case. All users interacting with the auction, including bidders, lien owners, and LPs, are affected because the auction may stall and funds may be stranded. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the Astaria protocol where the auditor traced the flow of afterPayment, slope calculation and the final return expression and observed that the timestamp update could push lien.last beyond the auction end, leading to a revert. The bug is subtle because the same timestamp update is used in multiple places for valid liquidations, so the erroneous path is only triggered by a specific partial‑payment scenario that is not exercised in normal tests. It violates the accounting assumption that the time interval (end - lien.last) is always positive, breaking the linear decay formula used to compute owed amounts. To fix the issue the protocol should separate the handling of expired liens from active ones, ensuring that lien.last is not advanced past the auction end during a partial repayment, or adjust the divisor calculation to guard against a zero or negative denominator, for example by capping the subtraction at zero or by refusing to update lien.last until the lien is fully settled.

title: LIEN_TOKEN.ownerOf(i) should be LIEN_TOKEN.ownerOf(liensRemaining[i])
content: The vulnerability is an accounting and ownership mismatch that occurs in the endAuction routine of the protocol. During the loop that processes remaining lien tokens, the contract uses the loop index i as the identifier for the lien token when calling LIEN_TOKEN.ownerOf(i). The correct identifier is stored in the array liensRemaining, so the call should be LIEN_TOKEN.ownerOf(liensRemaining[i]). Because the wrong token id is queried, the contract checks ownership against an unrelated token, which can cause a legitimate lien holder to be treated as non‑owner. At the same time the amount associated with each vault lien is recorded using the same incorrect index, so the YIntercept (the accounting variable that aggregates lien values) is updated with wrong numbers. The cumulative effect is that totalAssets, the on‑chain representation of the protocol’s holdings, becomes inaccurate. When users expect to receive a refund or a payout after an auction, they may see a zero or reduced balance, or the UI may display missing collateral. The bug is triggered each time endAuction is executed after an auction finishes, specifically when the contract iterates over the liensRemaining array. All participants who hold lien tokens, as well as the protocol itself, are affected because the mis‑recorded amounts can lead to loss of funds or incorrect distribution. The issue was uncovered during a manual security audit performed by the auditor Sherlock, who noticed that the owner check referenced the wrong identifier and that the accounting variables did not reflect the actual lien amounts. Because the contract does not revert on the mismatch, the problem can remain hidden until a discrepancy in totalAssets is observed, making it hard to notice during normal operation. To remediate the flaw, the code should be changed to query the owner using the actual token id from liensRemaining (LIEN_TOKEN.ownerOf(liensRemaining[i])) and to record the lien amount based on that id, ensuring that the YIntercept and totalAssets calculations reflect the true state of the vaults. This correction restores proper ownership verification and accurate accounting, preventing potential fund loss and aligning the contract’s behavior with its intended business logic.
summary: In endAuction(), the check for public vault owner is referred to the wrong lien token id. And the actual vault lien amount is not properly recorded. The lien token id should be queried is liensRemaining[i] instead of i. YIntercept will not be correctly recorded. The accounting for LienToken amounts will be wrong. Hence the totalAssets on book will be wrong, eventually the contract and users could lose fund due to the wrong accounting.

title: Anyone can deposit and mint withdrawal proxy shares
content: The vulnerability is an unauthorized minting flaw in the WithdrawProxy contract, which inherits the ERC4626Cloned vault implementation. Because the proxy does not override the afterDeposit hook, the public deposit and mint functions of the base ERC4626Cloned contract remain callable by any address. An attacker can therefore interact directly with the proxy, deposit WETH, and receive withdrawal proxy shares without going through the intended PublicVault.redeemFutureEpoch flow that is supposed to restrict share creation to epoch‑locked liquidity providers. Once assets are transferred into the withdraw reserve by PublicVault.transferWithdrawReserve or LiquidationAccountant.claim, the attacker can redeem the freshly minted shares for WETH that now includes the borrower’s interest yield. This yields on‑demand profit for the attacker while the legitimate LPs see their returns diluted because the total share supply has been inflated by unauthorized mints. The issue occurs whenever the proxy’s deposit or mint functions are publicly accessible and assets are later added to the reserve, which is the normal operation of the protocol. It affects all participants: legitimate liquidity providers experience reduced yields, the protocol’s accounting assumptions about share supply and asset backing are broken, and borrowers may indirectly suffer from altered incentive structures. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the inheritance hierarchy and noticed that afterDeposit was left unimplemented, leaving the base contract’s public entry points exposed. The problem is subtle because the proxy still behaves like a standard ERC4626 vault – users can successfully deposit and receive shares, so the unexpected share creation does not raise immediate alarms. To remediate, the contract should override afterDeposit (or otherwise block) to revert any direct deposit or mint calls, or restrict those functions to only be callable by the PublicVault contract, thereby restoring the intended share‑minting pathway and preserving the integrity of the protocol’s accounting model.
summary: Anyone can deposit and mint Withdrawal proxy shares by directly interacting with the base ERC4626Cloned contract's functions, allowing them to capture distributed yield from borrower interests. The WithdrawProxy contract extends the ERC4626Cloned vault contract implementation. The ERC4626Cloned contract has the functionality to deposit and mint vault shares. Usually, withdrawal proxy shares are only distributed via the WithdrawProxy.mint function, which is only called by the PublicVault.redeemFutureEpoch function. Anyone can deposit WETH into a deployed Withdraw proxy to receive shares, wait until assets (WETH) are deposited via the PublicVault.transferWithdrawReserve or LiquidationAccountant.claim function and then redeem their shares for WETH assets. By depositing/minting directly to the Withdraw proxy, one can get interest yield on-demand without being an LP and having capital locked for epoch(s). This may potentially be timed in a way to deposit/mint only when we know that interest yields are being paid by a borrower who is not defaulting on their loan. The returns are diluted for the LPs at the expense of someone who directly interacts with the underlying proxy.

title: Epochs can be progressed during ongoing auctions
content: The vulnerability consists of allowing the protocol epoch to be progressed while a liquidation auction is still active, which breaks the intended accounting guarantees of the liquidation module. The root cause is an incorrect calculation of the auction end timestamp (finalAuctionEnd) inside the liquidation accountant. The handleNewLiquidation routine adds a fixed offset of two days plus an extra day instead of using the exact auctionWindow value returned by the collateral token, and the contract does not enforce a check that prevents PublicVault.processEpoch from being called when an auction is ongoing. Because claim() on the LiquidationAccountant can only be executed when finalAuctionEnd is zero or the current block timestamp exceeds finalAuctionEnd, advancing the epoch before the auction truly ends leaves finalAuctionEnd in an inconsistent state. An attacker or any user who can trigger a liquidation can start an auction, then invoke processEpoch to move to the next epoch. This action resets or bypasses the finalAuctionEnd check, causing the claim function to remain permanently blocked. As a result, liquidity‑provider (LP) funds that should be claimable after liquidation become locked, and the associated collateral may remain trapped in the auction contract. The impact is a potential loss of LP capital and a breakdown of the protocol’s accounting logic, which can lead to collateral lockup and reduced confidence in the system. The issue manifests only when a liquidation accountant is deployed for the current epoch, an auction is active, and the epoch‑progression function is called – a combination that is not obvious during normal operation. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the logical flow between AstariaRouter.liquidate, LiquidationAccountant.handleNewLiquidation and PublicVault.processEpoch, revealing that the timestamp arithmetic does not enforce the intended end‑of‑auction constraint. The bug is subtle because the auctionWindow value appears reasonable and the epoch‑progression function seems harmless, making the failure mode easy to miss in testing. To remediate, the contract should (1) compute finalAuctionEnd as the current block timestamp plus the exact auctionWindow without arbitrary offsets, (2) add an explicit require in PublicVault.processEpoch that reverts if any liquidation auction is still open, and (3) ensure that claim() can only be called after the true auction end, possibly by resetting finalAuctionEnd only after a successful claim. These changes restore the invariant that epochs cannot be advanced while liquidation auctions are pending, thereby protecting LP funds and preserving correct collateral accounting.
summary: The currentEpoch can be progressed while having an ongoing auction which will completely mess up the liquidation logic to potentially cause LP fund loss and collateral lockup. The LiquidationAccountant.claim() function is only callable if finalAuctionEnd is set to 0 or the block.timestamp is greater than finalAuctionEnd (i.e. auction has ended). Furthermore, PublicVault.processEpoch should only be callable if there is no ongoing auction if a liquidation accountant is deployed in the current epoch. finalAuctionEnd is set within the LiquidationAccountant.handleNewLiquidation function, which is called from the AstariaRouter.liquidate function. However, instead of providing a timestamp of the auction end, a value of 2 days + 1 days is given because COLLATERAL_TOKEN.auctionWindow() returns 2 days. This does not achieve the intended constraint on checking for the end of the epochs can be progressed during ongoing auctions to completely mess up the liquidation logic to potentially cause LP fund loss and collateral lockup.

title: Public vault depositors will receive fewer vault shares
content: The vulnerability resides in the way the public vault computes its total assets before any payment has been made. The contract stores a variable called last, which is initialized to zero and is used by the totalAssets function to return the current ERC‑20 token balance (WETH) held by the vault. Because the vault also performs borrowing operations, the on‑chain token balance is reduced by the amount that has been borrowed. When no payment (i.e., no yield distribution) has occurred yet, the last variable remains zero, so totalAssets simply reflects the reduced token balance rather than the true economic value of the vault. Share minting logic typically uses totalAssets divided by totalSupply to determine how many vault shares to issue to a depositor. Consequently, the lower totalAssets figure causes the contract to mint fewer shares than a user expects for a given deposit amount. From the user’s perspective this manifests as a discrepancy between the number of shares shown in the UI and the amount of assets they deposited – users may see a smaller share balance, or even a zero increase, despite having transferred tokens. The issue only appears for deposits that happen before the first payment is recorded; once a payment updates the last variable, the totalAssets calculation aligns with the intended accounting model. The bug was discovered during a security audit that examined the accounting flow and identified that the totalAssets function does not account for borrowed funds when last is zero. It is subtle because the vault still accepts deposits and the token balance appears correct, so the error is not obvious without inspecting the share‑minting formula. The impact is a violation of the protocol’s financial guarantees: users receive fewer shares, effectively losing a portion of their ownership stake, which can translate into reduced future earnings. To remediate the problem the contract should update the last variable whenever the yIntercept or slope parameters change, or otherwise adjust totalAssets to include the borrowed amount when calculating share issuance. In broader terms this is a mis‑calculation of asset valuation that leads to an under‑allocation of ownership tokens, a class of bug often seen in yield‑bearing vaults that rely on lazy accounting of accrued interest.
summary: Public vault total asset calculation is incorrect until the first payment, leading to depositors receiving fewer vault shares than expected. As long as PublicVault.last is set to 0, the PublicVault.totalAssets function returns the actual ERC-20 token balance (WETH) of the public vault. Due to borrowing, this balance is reduced by the borrowed amount. Therefore, as there is no payment, this leads to depositors receiving fewer vault shares than expected. PoC: https://gist.github.com/berndartmueller/8a71ff76c7eb8207e1f01a154a873b2c Public vault depositors will receive fewer vault shares until the first payment.

title: Payments and liquidations of multiple liens revert
content: The vulnerability is an array‑index shifting bug in the contract that stores debt positions (liens) in a dynamic array. When a lien is fully repaid the contract deletes the corresponding entry from the array, which shortens the array and changes the numeric indexes of all remaining liens. Because the payment and liquidation logic later references liens by their position in the array, the stale indexes become invalid. If a borrower or liquidator attempts to process several liens in a loop, a deletion that occurs earlier in the loop causes the subsequent iteration to address the wrong element or to read past the end of the array, triggering an out‑of‑bounds revert. An attacker can exploit this by front‑running a payment or liquidation, repaying a senior lien that is about to be cleared, thereby shrinking the array and shifting the target index. The borrower then unintentionally pays the attacker’s junior lien, or the whole batch of operations reverts, leaving the collateral NFT permanently locked. The impact is loss of expected refunds, inability to liquidate positions, and potential diversion of funds to a malicious lien holder. The bug manifests whenever multiple liens are processed in a single transaction or when a lien is cleared in a preceding transaction before the loop finishes. All participants that rely on correct payment routing – borrowers, senior and junior lien holders, and the protocol itself – are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the logic for adding, traversing, and deleting entries in the liens array. It is hard to notice because the array manipulation is internal and tests that only cover single‑lien scenarios do not expose the shifting indexes; the contract appears to work correctly until a multi‑lien batch is executed. The root cause is the use of mutable array positions as stable identifiers, a pattern known as an “unstable reference” or “array index shifting after deletion” bug. To remediate, the contract should stop using the array index as the lien identifier. A common fix is to store liens in a mapping keyed by a unique ID, or to iterate over a snapshot of the array and perform deletions only after the loop completes. Additionally, the code should validate that an index is still within bounds before accessing it and emit clear error messages. By decoupling the logical identifier from the physical array position, the protocol can guarantee that payments and liquidations always target the intended lien, preserving user expectations that a payment to a specific debt will be honoured and that collateral can be reclaimed without unexpected reverts.
summary: The liens array and its indexes are changed whenever a lien is fully paid back. Therefore, referencing liens by their position in the array is broken because indices change. Payments and liquidations of multiple liens within a loop will revert and can be exploited by sandwiching liens to force a payment to the attacker's lien. Whenever a lien position is fully paid back, the lien is deleted from the liens array. This means that the array is shortened and the indices of the remaining liens are changed. This is problematic when paying back liens in a loop because the indices of the remaining liens are changed which will cause revert with an index out-of-bounds error. One can be exploited to pay for a different (attacker's) lien position because the lien array gets shortened when another payment (by the attacker or someone else) beforehand causes a deleted lien position. Liquidations of multiple liens and payments against a collateral token and all its liens will revert. This will result in the collateral NFT being locked forever. Exploit scenario: A malicious junior debt holder can buy out a senior debt (sandwich the original borrower effectively) to trigger this sequence of actions. For e.g., if the liens array is [1, 5, 3] where the malicious junior lien holder of 3 also buys out 1 and front-runs the borrower's intended payment for 5 by repaying 1 and forcing the array to shorten to [5, 3] will make the borrower pay off their lien of 3 instead of borrower's lien of 5. Effectively, a lien holder can "force" a payment to their own lien instead of another one.

title: Loans can exceed the maximum potential debt
content: The vulnerability is an accounting flaw that allows a borrower to create new liens on a collateral token that push the total outstanding debt above the protocol‑defined maxPotentialDebt limit. The contract’s LienToken.createLien function is supposed to enforce this ceiling by calling getTotalDebtForCollateralToken, which sums the debt of all existing liens stored in the liens[collateralId] array. However, the new lien that is being created in the same transaction has not yet been inserted into the array when the total‑debt query is performed, so the function returns a value that excludes the pending lien. As a result, the check believes the vault is still within the allowed limit and permits the loan. An attacker can repeat this process, opening multiple liens sequentially; each individual check passes because the previous lien’s debt is counted but the current one is omitted, eventually causing the aggregate debt to exceed maxPotentialDebt. This condition can occur whenever a new lien is created and the limit‑enforcement logic runs before the state mutation that records the lien. The affected parties are liquidity providers (LPs) who fund the public vault, the protocol that relies on the debt ceiling to stay solvent, and borrowers who may unintentionally trigger insolvency. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the loan‑creation flow and identified that the debt‑limit verification does not consider the newly added lien. It is subtle because the code appears to perform a proper check, yet the ordering of operations creates an off‑by‑one error that is easy to miss in testing. From a user’s perspective, LPs may see their deposited balances shrink unexpectedly or become zero after a borrower obtains multiple loans, even though the UI shows the max debt limit as unchanged. The business logic that guarantees that total debt never exceeds the collateral’s capacity is violated, breaking accounting assumptions and exposing the vault to insolvency risk. The recommended remediation is to perform the maxPotentialDebt verification after the new lien has been added to the liens[collateralId] array, or to recalculate the total debt including the pending lien before allowing the loan, thereby ensuring that the protocol’s safety invariant is correctly enforced.
summary:
Missing to account for the new lien can allow loans on a collateral to exceed maximum potential debt leading to vault insolvency and potential loss of LP funds. The LienToken.createLien function tries to prevent loans and the total potential debt from surpassing the defined params.terms.maxPotentialDebt limit. When the getTotalDebtForCollateralToken function is called, the new lien (which will be created within this transaction) is not yet added to the liens[collateralId] array. However, the getTotalDebtForCollateralToken function iterates over this very same array and will return the total debt without considering the new lien being added and for which this check is being performed. The strategist's defined max potential debt limit can be exceeded, which changes/increases the risk for LPs, as it imposes a higher debt to the public vault. This could lead to vault insolvency and loss of LP funds. PoC: https://gist.github.com/berndartmueller/8b0f870962acc4c999822d742e89151b Example exploit: Given a public vault and a lien with a max potential debt amount of 50 ETH (that's the default standardLien in TestHelpers.t.sol)
1. 100 ETH have been deposited in the public vault by LPs
2. Bob borrows 50 ETH with his 1st NFT -> success
3. Bob borrows another 50 ETH with his 2nd NFT -> successful as well even though theirs a limit of 50 ETH
4. Bob now has 100 ETH -> The max potential debt limit is exceeded by 50 ETH

title: Triggering liquidations ahead of expected time
content: The vulnerability consists of an early‑liquidation path that can be triggered for a collateral after one of its liens has passed its loan duration but before the protocol‑defined auction window (by default two days) expires at the end of an epoch. The root cause is that the liquidation routine does not perform two essential state updates when the remaining time to the epoch end exceeds the auction window: it fails to decrement the count of active liens for the epoch and it does not instantiate the liquidation accountant that is responsible for collecting auction proceeds on behalf of the lien owners. Because the auction logic is still executed, the auction runs with an incomplete accounting state. An attacker (or any caller) can therefore invoke the liquidation function at this precise moment, causing the auction to complete while the epoch’s lien bookkeeping remains unchanged. The immediate effect is that the proceeds of the auction are sent directly to the lien owners instead of being routed through the liquidation accountant, resulting in a loss of funds for the protocol or other participants. Moreover, because the epoch’s lien count is never reduced, the epoch cannot advance to the next stage, effectively locking all funds associated with that epoch and halting further protocol activity. This situation can be observed from a user’s perspective as a collateral being liquidated earlier than expected, the user receiving no refund or seeing their balance drop to zero, and the UI indicating that the epoch is stuck or that no new auctions are being created. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the interaction between the liquidation trigger, the auction window, and epoch progression logic. It is difficult to notice because the transaction does not revert; the auction appears to succeed, yet the internal accounting state is inconsistent, leading to subtle financial loss and a protocol stall. To remediate the problem the liquidation code must be revised so that, regardless of the time remaining to epoch end, it always updates the epoch lien count and creates the liquidation accountant before starting the auction, or alternatively it should reject liquidation attempts that occur before the auction window has elapsed. In essence, the bug belongs to the class of “state‑inconsistent liquidation” or “premature auction trigger” defects where critical bookkeeping steps are omitted, breaking the protocol’s accounting invariants and causing funds to disappear or become unrecoverable.
summary: Triggering liquidations for a collateral after one of its liens has expired but before the auction window (default 2 days) at epoch end leads to loss and lock of funds. Liquidations are allowed to be triggered for a collateral if any of its liens have exceeded their loan duration with outstanding payments. However, the liquidation logic does not execute the decrease of lien count and setting up of liquidation accountant if the time to epoch end is greater than the auction window (default 2 days). The auction proceeds nevertheless. If liquidations are triggered before the auction window at epoch end, they will proceed to auctions without decreasing epoch lien count, without setting up the liquidation accountant for the lien and other related logic. This will, at a minimum, lead to auction proceeds going to lien owners directly instead of via the liquidation accountants (loss of funds) and the epoch unable to proceed to the next on (lock of funds and protocol halt).

title: Lack of access control in transferWithdrawReserve
content: The vulnerability is an unrestricted public function called transferWithdrawReserve in the PublicVault contract that moves funds from the vault to a WithdrawProxy. Because the function lacks any access‑control modifier, any address can invoke it repeatedly. The root cause is the omission of a permission check and the absence of a guard that the withdrawProxy address must be non‑zero before adjusting state. When the proxy has not yet been created, its address is address(0). The function attempts to transfer assets, but the low‑level call fails silently; nevertheless the code still executes a branch that reduces the withdrawReserve variable according to the requested withdraw amount. An attacker can therefore call transferWithdrawReserve many times before the proxy is set, each call decrementing withdrawReserve even though no assets leave the vault. By repeating the call until withdrawReserve reaches zero, the attacker effectively drains the reserve that legitimate users rely on for withdrawals. This can occur any time the contract is deployed before the withdrawProxy is initialized or if the proxy address is later reset to zero. All users of the vault, as well as the protocol that depends on the reserve for liquidity, are affected because their expected balance becomes unavailable; from a user’s perspective a withdrawal attempt returns zero or fails silently, leading to missing funds and a perception that the contract “eats” their money. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that inspected function visibility and state updates. It is hard to notice because the function is public and appears to perform a normal transfer, yet the failure path does not revert and silently mutates accounting state. The bug belongs to the class of unauthorized state‑changing functions and improper handling of external call failures, which violates the accounting invariant that withdrawReserve should never be reduced unless a corresponding transfer succeeds. To remediate, the function should be protected with an appropriate access‑control modifier (for example requestAuth or onlyOwner) and should explicitly revert when the withdrawProxy address is zero, ensuring that no state change occurs unless a successful transfer is guaranteed.

title: LienToken.buyoutLien will always revert
content: The vulnerability is that the function buyoutLien in the LienToken contract always reverts because the contract stores a buyout fee denominator that is never initialized and has no setter. When buyoutLien calls getBuyoutFee, the denominator is zero, causing a division‑by‑zero or require check to fail, which triggers a revert. As a result, borrowers cannot execute the buyoutLien flow that is required for refinancing a loan. The protocol expects borrowers to be able to refinance when a better interest rate or longer duration is offered; instead the transaction fails and the borrower is locked into the existing loan. This can lead to funds being effectively inaccessible because the borrower cannot move to a more favorable loan and may be forced to keep paying a higher rate. The issue occurs whenever a borrower attempts to call buyoutLien, which is a core user‑initiated operation. It affects any user holding a lien token, the protocol’s liquidity pool, and the overall health of the lending market. The bug was discovered during a manual audit of the AstariaRouter and LienToken contracts, where the auditor noticed that the buyout fee denominator variable was declared but never assigned a non‑zero value and that no external function existed to modify it. Because the revert happens inside a low‑level call, the failure may appear only as a generic transaction failure without a clear error message, making it hard for users to understand why refinancing is impossible. The class of bug is an uninitialized state variable leading to a division‑by‑zero or require failure, combined with missing setter logic, which violates the business rule that refinancing must be possible under improved terms. To remediate, the contract should initialize both the buyout fee numerator and denominator to sensible non‑zero defaults in the router’s constructor and expose setter functions that can be called by the appropriate governance role to adjust the fee parameters. After fixing, the buyoutLien function will compute the fee correctly, allow the buyout transaction to succeed, and restore the intended refinancing pathway, preventing users from losing access to better loan conditions.
summary: buyoutLien() will always revert, preventing the borrower from refinancing. buyoutFeeDenominator is 0 without a setter which will cause getBuyoutFee() to revert in the buyoutLien() flow. Refinancing is a crucial feature of the protocol to allow a borrower to refinance their loan if a certain minimum improvement of interest rate or duration is offered. The reverting buyoutLien() flow will prevent the borrower from refinancing and effectively lead to loss of their funds due to lock-in into currently held loans when better terms are available.

title: Lien count per epoch is not updated ultimately
content: The vulnerability originates from an inconsistency in the way the PublicVault contract tracks the number of open liens for each epoch. The contract maintains a mapping called liensOpenForEpoch that is incremented when a new lien is created and decremented when a lien is fully repaid or liquidated. When a lien is bought out, the lien’s start timestamp and duration are reset to the current block time and the newly supplied duration, effectively moving the lien into a future epoch. However, the code that updates the epoch‑specific lien count is never invoked for this scenario. Consequently, the lien count for the new epoch remains zero while the lien itself is considered open. When the borrower later attempts to make a payment or trigger a liquidation, the LienToken._payment function calculates the current epoch based on the updated start time and calls IPublicVault(lienOwner).decreaseEpochLienCount. Because the count for that epoch was never increased, the decrease operation reverts, causing the payment or liquidation transaction to fail. The failure prevents the borrower from reducing the debt, and the collateralized NFT becomes permanently locked because the protocol cannot progress to auction the collateral even when the liquidation window expires. This issue manifests only after a lien buyout that shifts the lien into a later epoch; normal lien creation and repayment paths work correctly. The bug was discovered during a manual audit of the Astaria protocol where the auditor traced the flow of lien buyouts and observed that the internal accounting function _increaseOpenLiens was never called for bought‑out liens. The problem is subtle because the contract does not emit explicit warnings; the only symptom is a revert on payment or liquidation calls, which may be misinterpreted as a generic transaction failure. The impact is high: borrowers lose the ability to repay, lenders cannot recover their position, and the protocol’s collateral may remain idle, violating the business assumption that every open lien is accounted for in the epoch ledger. To remediate the issue, the contract should increment liensOpenForEpoch whenever a lien is bought out and its duration spans a future epoch, ensuring that decreaseEpochLienCount can succeed. In broader terms, the bug belongs to the class of state‑inconsistency errors where accounting variables are not kept in sync with lifecycle events, leading to reversible operations that lock assets.
summary: The lien count per epoch is not updated, causing payments to the lien and liquidation of the lien to revert. The PublicVault contract keeps track of open liens per epoch to prevent starting a new epoch with open liens. The lien count for a given epoch is decreased whenever a lien is fully paid back (either through a regular payment or a liquidation payment). However, if a lien is bought out, the lien start will be set to the current block.timestamp and the duration to the newly provided duration. If the borrower now wants to make a payment to this lien, the LienToken._payment function will evaluate the lien's current epoch and will use a different epoch as when the lien was initially created. The attempt to then call IPublicVault(lienOwner).decreaseEpochLienCount will fail, as the lien count for the new epoch has not been increased yet. The same will happen for liquidations. After a lien buyout, payments to the lien and liquidating the lien will revert, which will ultimately lock the collateralized NFT. This will certainly prevent the borrower from making payments towards that future-epoch lien in the current epoch because decreaseEpochLienCount() will revert. However, even after the epoch progresses to the next one via processEpoch(), the liensOpenForEpoch for the new epoch still does not account for the previously bought out lien aligned to this new epoch because liensOpenForEpoch is only updated in two places: 1. _increaseOpenLiens() which is not called by anyone 2. _afterCommitToLien() <- commitToLien() <-- <-- commitToLiens() which happens only for new lien commitments This will prevent the borrower from making payments towards the previously bought lien that aligns to the current epoch, which will force a liquidation on exceeding lien duration. Depending on when the liquidation can be triggered, if this condition is satisfied PublicVault(owner).timeToEpochEnd() <= COLLATERAL_TOKEN.auctionWindow() then decreaseEpochLienCount() will revert to prevent auctioning and lock the borrower's collateral in the protocol.

title: Purchaser of a lien token may not receive future payments after buyout
content: The contract allows a lien token to be bought out through the buyoutLien function, which transfers ownership of the lien to a new purchaser. However, the function does not modify the stored payee address associated with the lien (lienData[lienId].payee). The payment routine (_payment) determines the recipient by calling getPayee, which returns the explicit payee if it is non‑zero, otherwise it falls back to the current owner. When a previous lien holder has previously called setPayee to redirect payments to an arbitrary address, that address remains stored after the buyout. Consequently, even though the ownership record shows the new buyer as the lien holder, all subsequent payments are still sent to the old payee. This mismatch can be exploited by a malicious seller who deliberately sets the payee to their own address before selling the lien; the buyer, unaware of the need to reset the payee, receives no future payments. The impact is a loss of expected revenue for the purchaser, effectively causing funds to disappear from the buyer’s perspective while the seller continues to collect them. The condition for the bug to manifest is two‑fold: the original owner must have invoked setPayee, and the new owner must not invoke setPayee after the buyout. The affected parties are any users purchasing lien tokens, the protocol’s accounting logic, and any downstream participants relying on correct payment distribution. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the state transitions of lien ownership and payment routing. It is subtle because the ownership transfer succeeds and the UI may display the new owner correctly, giving no immediate indication that payments are being diverted. The bug belongs to the class of improper state reset or payment routing errors, where critical mutable state is not updated after a change of authority. From a user’s point of view, the symptom is that after buying a lien they see their balance remain at zero and receive no refunds or interest, contrary to the expectation that they should start receiving payments immediately. To remediate the problem, the buyoutLien function should explicitly reset lienData[lienId].payee to either the zero address (so that getPayee falls back to the new owner) or directly assign the new owner’s address, ensuring that future payments are correctly routed to the purchaser.
summary: A purchaser who buys out an existing lien via buyoutLien() will not receive future payments made to that lien holder if the seller had changed the lien payee via setPayee() and if they do not change it themselves after buying. buyoutLien() does not reset lienData[lienId].payee to either 0 or to the new owner. While the ownership is transferred, the payments made in _payment() get their payee via getPayee() which returns the owner only if the lienData[lienId].payee is set to the zero address but returns lienData[lienId].payee otherwise. This will still have the value set by the previous owner who will continue to receive the payments. The purchaser who buys out an existing lien via buyoutLien() will not receive future payments if the previous owner had set the payee but they do not change it via setPayee() themselves after buying. Given that setPayee() is considered optional flow, this will lead to a loss of purchaser's anticipated payments until they realize and reset the lien payee. Exploit Scenario: A malicious lien seller can use setPayee() to set the payee to their address of choice and continue to receive payments, even after selling, if the buyer does not realize that they have to change the payee address to themselves after buying.

title: A payment made towards multiple liens causes funds to be lost
content: An over‑payment logic error occurs when a borrower calls the bulk payment function makePayment with a paymentAmount intended to settle several open liens on a collateral. The function iterates over the list of liens and, for each lien, calls an internal _payment routine passing the full remaining paymentAmount. Because the code does not reduce paymentAmount after a lien is satisfied, the first call to _payment transfers the entire amount to the first lien’s payee even if that amount exceeds the lien’s outstanding balance. The _payment routine returns the amount actually spent (capitalSpent) which equals the full paymentAmount, so the loop’s paymentAmount for subsequent liens becomes zero. Consequently only the first lien is marked as paid and the borrower’s funds are completely drained to that payee, while the remaining liens stay unpaid. The bug is a classic accounting mis‑allocation in batch payment processing, caused by failing to decrement the available capital after each partial settlement. It manifests only when a bulk payment is attempted; single‑liens payments work as expected. Borrowers experience the symptom of their wallet balance decreasing by the full paymentAmount while seeing only one lien cleared and the others unchanged, leading to apparent loss of funds. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the payment workflow, and it can be hard to notice because the transaction does not revert and the UI may report a successful payment without indicating which liens were actually settled. The proper fix is to adjust the else branch of the internal payment routine (or the loop logic) so that paymentAmount is reduced by the amount applied to each lien, ensuring that only the necessary portion of the capital is transferred to each payee and that remaining liens can be processed.
summary: A payment made towards multiple liens is entirely consumed for the first one causing the borrower to lose funds to the payee. A borrower can make a bulk payment against multiple liens for a collateral hoping to pay more than one at a time using makePayment (uint256 collateralId, uint256 paymentAmount) where the underlying _makePayment() loops over the open liens attempting to pay off more than one depending on the totalCapitalAvailable provided. However, the entire totalCapitalAvailable is provided via paymentAmount in the call to _payment() in the first iteration which transfers that completely to the payee in its logic even if it exceeds that lien.amount. That total amount is returned as capitalSpent which makes the paymentAmount for next iteration equal to 0. Only the first lien is paid off and the entire payment is sent to its payee. The remaining liens remain unpaid. The payment maker (i.e. borrower) loses funds to the payee.

title: LiquidationAccountant.claim() can be called by anyone
content: The vulnerability resides in the claim function of the LiquidationAccountant contract, which is invoked by a public vault during the epoch‑finalisation process. Because the function lacks any access‑control checks, any external address can call claim an unlimited number of times. After the final auction period has ended, the claim flow triggers a call to decreaseYIntercept on the vault’s accounting state. The y‑intercept represents the implied value of the vault’s assets; repeatedly lowering it reduces the reported value of the vault without moving any actual funds. An attacker can therefore call claim repeatedly after liquidations have been processed, forcing the vault’s accounting to show a lower balance and potentially rendering the vault insolvent in the eyes of the protocol. From a user perspective, liquidity providers may see their share price drop to zero or receive a reduced redemption amount, even though no tokens were transferred out of the vault. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the public interfaces of the liquidation accounting module. It is difficult to notice because the claim function does not directly transfer assets and appears to be a harmless bookkeeping call, yet it manipulates a critical accounting variable. The root cause is the missing authorization guard that should restrict claim to be callable only by the owning vault contract. To remediate, the contract should enforce that only the designated vault address (or an authorized role) can invoke claim, for example by adding a require statement that checks msg.sender against the vault address or by using OpenZeppelin’s Ownable/AccessControl patterns. By limiting who can trigger the y‑intercept adjustment, the protocol preserves the integrity of its accounting and prevents malicious actors from artificially decreasing the vault’s implied value.
summary: LiquidationAccountant.claim() can be called by anyone to reduce the implied value of a public vault. LiquidationAccountant.claim() is called by the PublicVault as part of the processEpoch() flow. But it has no access control and can be called by anyone and any number of times. If called after finalAuctionEnd, one will be able to trigger decreaseYIntercept() on the vault even if they cannot affect fund transfer to withdrawing liquidity providers and the PublicVault. This allows anyone to manipulate the yIntercept of a public vault by triggering the claim() flow after liquidations resulting in vault insolvency.

title: A malicious lien owner can exploit a reentrancy in auctions
content: The vulnerability is a reentrancy flaw that occurs during the finalisation of a liquidation auction in the Astaria protocol. When the auction house calls the external function decreaseYIntercept as part of endAuction, control is transferred to a contract that owns the lien token. Because the call is not protected by a reentrancy guard, the lien token owner can re‑enter the auction contract and invoke cancelAuction before the original endAuction logic finishes. By cancelling the auction, paying the reserve price plus any initiator fee, and then immediately taking a new loan against the same NFT collateral, the attacker causes the newly created lien token to be deleted when execution returns to endAuction. The root cause is the unchecked external call that allows the borrower (or any malicious lien token holder) to execute arbitrary logic that interferes with the auction’s state transition, combined with the protocol’s assumption that a lien token cannot be removed while an auction is being settled. An attacker can exploit this by following a sequence: create a public vault, provide liquidity, open a loan, buy out the lien, let the loan lapse, trigger endAuction, hijack the decreaseYIntercept callback to cancel the auction and release the NFT, then open a fresh loan of the full vault balance. When control returns to the original endAuction, the protocol deletes the new lien token, releases the NFT to the attacker and leaves the vault with a missing amount of ETH. The impact is a direct loss of liquidity provider funds – the vault’s balance is reduced by the amount of the second loan while no lien remains to claim it, effectively stealing the funds. The issue manifests when a malicious lien token owner initiates the endAuction function; from a user’s perspective the vault balance drops unexpectedly, liquidity providers see their deposited ETH disappear, and borrowers receive their NFT back without repaying any debt. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that identified the external call pattern and verified that the contract lacked a reentrancy protection mechanism. It is difficult to notice because the auction flow appears normal on the surface and the token deletion happens only after the external call returns, making the loss seem like a normal state transition. To remediate the problem the protocol should introduce a reentrancy guard around endAuction, prevent lien token owners from calling cancelAuction during the auction finalisation, maintain an explicit mapping of active public vaults to ensure that only authorised actions can modify auction state, and adjust the lien‑buyout logic to account for the possibility of malicious token owners. In short, the bug belongs to the class of reentrancy vulnerabilities that break accounting assumptions in liquidation auctions, leading to funds disappearing and the protocol’s financial guarantees being violated.
summary:
A malicious lien owner can exploit a reentrancy in auctions to have their liens removed without making their payments and thus stealing LP funds. A malicious lien owner can exploit a reentrancy from the callback to decreaseYIntercept() in endAuction() to call cancelAuction() and then take a new loan whose lien token is removed when control returns back to endAuction(). PoC: https://gist.github.com/lucyoa/901a7713fded73293b5e4f9452344c5a Exploit scenario sequence:
1. Strategist creates the public vault
2. Liquidity provider puts 50 ETH into vault
3. Malicious borrower takes a loan of 10 ETH by depositing NFT
4. Borrower buys out their own lien via _buyoutLien by paying 10ETH + fee
5. Borrower does not repay within lien duration to trigger liquidation
6. Borrower (or someone else) triggers endAuction()
7. Execution flow gets hijacked by borrower (lien token owner) inside call to decreaseYIntercept():
   - Borrower cancels auction by paying reservePrice+initiatorFee (this would also go to borrower if setPayee is set before the auction as the owner of that Lien token)
   - Borrower releases NFT to themselves
   - Borrower now takes another loan of 50 ETH with the same NFT, vault and commitment
8. Once control returns to AuctionHouse.endAuction, borrower's new loan's Lien token is deleted
9. CollateralToken.endAuction releases borrower's NFT to borrower
10. Malicious borrower steals 50 ETH from vault without any outstanding liens resulting in LP fund loss

title: VaultImplementation._validateCommitment may cause DoS
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect calculation of the potential debt in the function that validates a borrower commitment. The code multiplies seniorDebt by (rate + 1) and then by duration, which adds an extra factor of duration to the debt amount. It also omits the scaling factor INTEREST_DENOMINATOR and ignores the implied lien rate from other liens. As a result the computed potentialDebt can be many times larger than the real amount that would be owed.
