Issue: A malicious strategist can deny the repayment of loans by setting a extremely high vault fee during creation of a public vault. The high vault fee will cause a revert due to a failed integer conversion using SafeCastTo88(). This will lead to forced liquidation of the borrowers when the loans expire outstanding, making them lose their NFT collaterals. (Vault fee is an incentive awarded to strategist on each loan repayment, where a percentage of the interest payment is allocated to the strategist, in terms of vault shares.)

High Likelihood: The strategist could target borrowers by refinancing outstanding loans and transferring the loans to his high fee vault, which does not require the borrowers’ consents. This can be achieved as refinancing can be done by anyone and the logic only checks for better interest rate and duration, but not the vault fee. The borrowers will not be aware of the issue, until they attempt to repay the loan. Furthermore, the strategist could specifically target loans that are about to expire, giving little reaction time for borrowers to report the issue.

Financial gain: With the ability to force a liquidation, the strategist can possibly stand to gain financially (e.g. by refinancing the loans with a lower liquidationInitialAsk and then bid for the NFT collateral (with high gas fee) during liquidation.

Note: Even if there are no lenders willing to lend to the vault due to the high vault fee, the strategist still can lend to its own vault to facilitate the refinance.

title: Borrower can use liquidationInitialAsk to block future borrowers
content: The vulnerability originates from an incorrect validation of the liquidationInitialAsk parameter during the construction of a lien stack. When a new lien is added or an existing lien is bought out, the contract iterates backwards through the entire stack, accumulates the potential debt of each borrower, and checks that this cumulative amount does not exceed the liquidationInitialAsk of the current stack element. In practice only the first lien in the stack determines the auction’s starting price, because Router#liquidate reads stack[0].lien.details.liquidationInitialAsk. The additional per‑lien checks are therefore unnecessary and harmful. An attacker can exploit this by setting their own liquidationInitialAsk to exactly the amount of their loan. Because the validation requires futureBorrow + myBorrow <= myLiquidationInitialAsk, any non‑zero future borrow will cause potentialDebt to exceed the recorded ask, triggering a revert with InvalidState(INITIAL_ASK_EXCEEDED). The result is a denial‑of‑service condition: subsequent borrowers are unable to open new loans against the same collateral, receive a transaction failure, and see no funds transferred. From the user’s perspective the UI shows a generic “transaction reverted” or “initial ask exceeded” error, contrary to the expectation that they can borrow as long as the collateral is sufficient. The issue affects all participants that rely on the stack – borrowers, lenders, and any protocol component that expects continuous borrowing or refinancing – and can lock collateral until the offending lien is repaid or replaced. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that examined the stack‑building logic and noticed that liquidationInitialAsk is only meaningful for the first element, yet the code enforces it on every element. It is subtle because the check appears logical at first glance and does not affect the immediate price calculation, making it easy to overlook. The proper remediation is to remove the per‑lien liquidationInitialAsk comparison and instead verify that the total potential debt of the whole stack does not exceed the liquidationInitialAsk of the first lien only. This aligns the validation with the economic model of the auction and eliminates the unintended denial‑of‑service vector.

title: Anyone can wipe complete state of any collateral at any point
content: The vulnerability is an unauthorized state‑wipe that occurs when the Clearing House settlement function is invoked for a collateral that is not currently in an auction. The contract implements the settlement of an auction through an ERC1155 safeTransferFrom call, which internally calls settleAuction to delete the lien state hash, burn all lien tokens, clear the idToUnderlying mapping and finally burn the collateral token. The root cause is a logical error in the condition that checks whether an auction is active: the code uses a logical AND (&&) instead of a logical OR (||) when verifying that a collateralId has an associated auction and that the Clearing House owns the underlying asset. Because the first part of the condition (collateralIdToAuction[collateralId] == bytes32(0)) is false for a non‑auctioned collateral, the whole expression evaluates to false and the revert is not triggered. Consequently, an attacker can call safeTransferFrom with a payment amount of zero, causing the settlement routine to execute and wipe all lien records and burn the borrower’s collateral token without any payment. The exploit can be performed by any user who knows the collateralId of another user’s deposit; no special privileges are required. The impact is that the borrower loses all claim to their underlying NFT, the lien information disappears, and any funds that would have been returned to the borrower are never transferred, effectively making the collateral disappear. This situation occurs whenever safeTransferFrom is called on a collateral that has not entered an auction, i.e., before the auction start or after it has been cleared. All borrowers who have deposited collateral and all lenders holding liens on that collateral are affected. The issue was discovered during a security audit by Code4rena, where the logical condition was identified as incorrectly using &&. The bug is subtle because the settlement flow appears normal and the zero‑payment passes the existing checks, making it easy to miss during functional testing. To remediate, the condition should be changed to use an OR, ensuring that the function reverts whenever the collateral is not currently in an auction, thereby preventing unauthorized deletion of state. This class of bug falls under improper access control and missing state validation, where critical state‑mutating operations are performed without confirming the required pre‑conditions, leading to loss of assets and violation of the protocol’s accounting guarantees. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after initiating a transfer they see their collateral token balance drop to zero, receive no refund, and are unable to reclaim the underlying NFT, contrary to the expectation that a transfer only moves ownership after a successful auction.
summary:
The Clearing House is implemented as an ERC1155. This is used to settle up at the end of an auction. The Clearing House’s token is listed as one of the Consideration Items, and when Seaport goes to transfer it, it triggers the settlement process.

This settlement process includes deleting the collateral state hash from LienToken.sol, burning all lien tokens, deleting the idToUnderlying mapping, and burning the collateral token. **These changes effectively wipe out all record of the liens, as well as removing any claim the borrower has on their underlying collateral.**

After an auction, this works as intended. The function verifies that sufficient payment has been made to meet the auction criteria, and therefore all these variables should be zeroed out.

However, the issue is that there is no check that this safeTransferFrom function is being called after an auction has completed. In the case that it is called when there is no auction, all the auction criteria will be set to 0, and therefore the above deletions can be performed with a payment of 0.

This allows any user to call the `safeTransferFrom()` function for any other user’s collateral. This will wipe out all the liens on that collateral, and burn the borrower’s collateral token, and with it their ability to ever reclaim their collateral.

title: A malicious private vault can preempt the creation of a public vault by transferring lien tokens to the public vault, thereby preventing the borrower from repaying all loans
content: The vulnerability consists of a pre‑emptive transfer of lien tokens from a malicious private vault to the address of a public vault before the public vault contract is actually deployed. The transferFrom function in the LienToken contract is designed to reject transfers to an existing public vault, but it only checks the recipient against a stored list of known vaults and does not verify that the address already contains contract code. Because the Ethereum CREATE opcode generates contract addresses deterministically, an attacker can compute the future address of the public vault, send the lien token to that empty address, and later invoke the router to create the public vault at the predicted address. When the public vault finally exists, its internal counter for open liens (liensOpenForEpoch) is still zero, so when the borrower later calls makePayment the decreaseEpochLienCount call underflows, causing an arithmetic overflow that aborts the repayment logic and triggers liquidation of the collateral. This chain of events prevents the borrower from repaying the loan, leading to the automatic auction of the NFT used as collateral and a loss of funds for the borrower and the lending protocol. The issue occurs only when a private vault can predict the public vault address and is able to transfer lien tokens before the vault contract is created, affecting borrowers, lenders, and the overall protocol integrity. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the logical flow of lien token transfers and identified that the transferFrom guard does not consider future contract creation. The bug is subtle because the transfer succeeds without error, and the failure only manifests later during repayment, making it difficult to detect from normal transaction logs. The root cause is the reliance on a runtime check of the recipient’s vault status without confirming that the recipient is an already‑deployed contract, allowing a class of “pre‑deployment address hijacking” attacks. To remediate, the transfer function should require that the destination address contains bytecode (e.g., to.code.length > 0) or otherwise enforce that lien tokens can only be sent to existing, verified vault contracts, thereby preventing the pre‑emptive transfer and the subsequent underflow condition.

title: Wrong starting price when listing on Seaport for assets that has less than 18 decimals
summary:
According to Astaria’s docs:   
<https://docs.astaria.xyz/docs/protocol-mechanics/loanterms>

Liquidation initial ask: Should the NFT go into liquidation, the initial price of the auction will be set to this value. Note that this set as a starting point for a dutch auction, and the price will decrease over the liquidation period. This figure is should also be specified in 10^18 format.

The liquidation initial ask is specified in 18 decimals. This is then used as a starting price when the NFT goes under auction on OpenSea. However, if the asset has less than 18 decimals, then the starting price goes wrong to Seaport.

This results in listing the NFT with too high price that makes it unlikely to be sold.

title: When Public Vault A buys out Public Vault B’s lien tokens, it does not increase Public Vault A’s liensOpenForEpoch, which would result in the lien tokens not being repaid
content: The vulnerability originates from an accounting mismatch in the handling of public vaults that buy out lien tokens belonging to another public vault. When a public vault (Vault A) invokes the buyoutLien function to purchase the lien tokens of a second public vault (Vault B), the protocol correctly burns the original lien token and mints a new token for the buyer, but it only calls the handleBuyoutLien routine on the seller side. This routine decreases the seller’s internal counter called liensOpenForEpoch, which tracks how many lien tokens are still outstanding for the current epoch. The buyer’s counter, however, is never increased. Consequently, after the buyout the buyer’s liensOpenForEpoch remains zero even though it now holds an active lien token. Later, when the borrower repays the loan, the repayment logic attempts to decrease the buyer’s liensOpenForEpoch again. Because the counter is already zero, the unchecked subtraction underflows, wrapping to a very large value and causing the transaction to revert. The overflow also propagates to the liquidation path, where updateVaultAfterLiquidation also tries to decrement the same counter and fails. From a user perspective the borrower sees that a repayment transaction reverts with no clear error, the expected repayment amount is not transferred, and the collateral that should be auctioned remains locked. Depositors to the public vault experience a loss of expected returns because the vault cannot recover the collateral. The bug is a classic example of inconsistent state updates across related contracts – a missing increment in a counter that should mirror a decrement performed on the counterpart. It was discovered during a manual audit that traced the flow of buyoutLien and identified that the public‑vault specific bookkeeping was only applied to the seller. The issue is hard to notice because the immediate buyout succeeds and the token balances appear correct; the failure only surfaces later when the counter is decremented, at which point the underflow causes a revert that looks like a generic payment failure. The proper fix is to modify the buyout logic so that when the caller is a public vault, the protocol also calls the increase‑counter path on the buyer, or otherwise adjusts the accounting to keep the sum of open liens consistent across epochs. By ensuring that both the decrease on the seller and the corresponding increase on the buyer are performed, the underflow is avoided and the repayment and liquidation flows operate as intended.

title: Function `processEpoch`
content: The vulnerability is an arithmetic underflow that occurs when the PublicVault contract processes the end of an epoch while a large number of users are withdrawing their vault tokens through a WithdrawProxy. The contract calculates a new yIntercept value by subtracting the product of totalAssets() and the liquidationWithdrawRatio from the current yIntercept. Because totalAssets() is derived from the stored slope and yIntercept (totalAssets = slope*Δt + yIntercept), it can be larger than the stored yIntercept itself. When many users withdraw, the liquidationWithdrawRatio approaches 1, making the term totalAssets()*liquidationWithdrawRatio almost equal to totalAssets. If totalAssets exceeds yIntercept, the subtraction results in a negative number, which underflows in unsigned arithmetic and causes the transaction to revert. The root cause is that the epoch‑processing function does not first accrue pending interest or otherwise update the yIntercept before performing the subtraction, allowing stale accounting data to be used in the calculation. An attacker or a coordinated group of users can trigger the condition by withdrawing a large proportion of the vault’s supply in a single epoch, causing the contract to revert on the last withdrawals. The impact is that the affected users see their withdrawal transaction fail, receive no tokens, and their balances appear unchanged, while the vault’s epoch state becomes stuck and cannot advance to the next period. This effectively locks funds in the contract until the issue is resolved. The bug manifests only under extreme withdrawal pressure, which is why it may be missed during routine testing that uses typical withdrawal volumes. It was discovered during a formal audit that exercised edge‑case withdrawal scenarios. The problem belongs to the class of accounting‑logic underflow bugs where a derived value is subtracted from a stored baseline without guaranteeing the baseline is larger. To remediate, the contract should update its accounting state (for example by calling accrue() at the start of processEpoch) so that yIntercept reflects the latest accrued assets before the subtraction, or it should cap the liquidationWithdrawRatio or use safe arithmetic that checks for underflow before updating yIntercept. By ensuring the new yIntercept is never computed from a larger value than the current one, the vault can correctly process withdrawals, maintain epoch continuity, and prevent funds from becoming inaccessible.
summary: When users withdraw their vault tokens PublicVault mint WithdrawProxy’s shares token for them and at the end of the epoch PublicVault would calculated WithdrawProxy’s assets and update PublicVault assets and start the next epoch. if a lot of users withdraws their funds then the value of the `totalAssets().mulDivDown(s.liquidationWithdrawRatio, 1e18)` (the amount belongs to the WithdrawProxy) would be higher than `yIntercept` and code would revert because of the underflow when setting the new value of the `yIntercept`. This would cause last users to not be able to withdraw their funds and contract epoch system to be broken for a while.

title: `PublicVault.processEpoch` calculates `withdrawReserve` incorrectly; Users can lose funds
content: The vulnerability resides in the epoch‑finalisation routine of the PublicVault contract, specifically the calculation of the withdrawReserve variable inside processEpoch. The function is supposed to determine how much of the vault’s total assets should be transferred to the WithdrawProxy so that users can redeem their shares after an epoch ends. The code checks whether totalAssets() is greater than the amount expected from an ongoing auction (expected). If the condition is true, withdrawReserve is set to the surplus multiplied by the liquidationWithdrawRatio; otherwise it is forced to zero. This logic is flawed because when totalAssets() is exactly equal to expected – a situation that occurs when the withdraw ratio reaches 100 % (i.e., the WithdrawProxy holds all shares) or when an auction fully covers the vault’s assets – the contract incorrectly sets withdrawReserve to zero. As a result, no funds are sent to the WithdrawProxy even though the protocol’s accounting assumes that the entire vault balance should be transferred. Users attempting to withdraw after such an epoch receive less than they are entitled to, often nothing at all, while the vault retains the assets in a state that becomes inaccessible after the epoch counter is incremented. The impact is a loss of user funds, which is classified as high severity because it directly violates the core financial guarantees of the system. The bug manifests only under the precise condition totalAssets() <= expected, and is especially hidden when the equality case is not covered by typical test suites; developers may assume that a zero reserve is correct when assets are insufficient, overlooking the edge case where assets exactly match the expected amount. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by Code4rena, where the auditor examined the processEpoch flow and identified that the conditional zeroing of withdrawReserve contradicts the intended accounting model. It is difficult to notice because the surrounding logic appears reasonable and the faulty branch is rarely exercised in normal operation. To remediate the problem, the withdrawReserve calculation should not be conditioned on totalAssets() being greater than expected; instead it should always compute the amount based on the liquidationWithdrawRatio (for example, withdrawReserve = totalAssets().mulWadDown(liquidationWithdrawRatio)) or otherwise ensure that when the ratio is 100 % the full balance is transferred to the WithdrawProxy. This change restores the invariant that all assets are either allocated to the proxy or correctly accounted for, preventing silent fund loss.
summary: PublicVault.processEpoch calculates withdrawReserve incorrectly. As result user can receive less funds when totalAssets() <= expected from auction.

title: Vaults don’t verify that a strategy’s deadline has passed
content: The vulnerability is a missing time‑based validation in the vault contract that allows a borrower to create a loan commitment using a strategy whose deadline has already passed. The root cause is that the internal function VaultImplementation._validateCommitment does not check the strategy.deadline against the current block timestamp, while the corresponding router function does perform this check. Because the vault’s validation path skips the deadline test, an attacker can submit a commitment directly to the vault after the strategy’s expiry, causing the vault to accept the loan as if it were still valid. This can be exploited by crafting a commitment with an expired strategy signature and calling the vault’s loan entry point; the vault will verify the signature and authority but will not reject the request based on the expired deadline. The impact is that liquidity providers’ funds may be exposed to under‑collateralised positions or outright loss, since the economic assumptions of the strategy (such as repayment schedule) are no longer enforceable after expiry. The condition under which the bug manifests is any situation where a loan is taken directly from the vault rather than through the router, and the strategy’s deadline is in the past. The affected parties include borrowers who may receive a loan that later cannot be honoured, liquidity providers whose capital is at risk, and the protocol as a whole because the accounting model assumes that only active strategies are used. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when the auditors noticed that the deadline variable was never read in the vault’s validation logic, despite being checked in the router. It is easy to miss because the presence of the deadline check in the router gives a false impression that the entire system enforces the time constraint, and the vault’s code path is less frequently examined. To remediate, the vault’s _validateCommitment function should include a condition that reverts when block.timestamp exceeds the strategy.deadline, or it should delegate the deadline verification to the router’s validation routine. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of missing business‑logic constraints where critical temporal rules are omitted, leading to accounting inconsistencies such as funds disappearing or loans being issued without proper expiry enforcement. From a user’s perspective, a borrower may expect a loan to be valid but later find that the strategy is expired, while a liquidity provider may see their balance unexpectedly reduced or a collateral token locked with no repayment path, violating the expectation that only active, non‑expired strategies are used.
summary: The vault doesn’t verify that a deadline hasn’t passed when a commitment is validated. Users are able to take out loans using strategies that have already expired. Depending on the nature of the strategy that can cause a loss of funds for the LPs.

title: Deadlock in vaults with underlying token with less then 18 decimals
content: The vulnerability is a deadlock condition that appears in vault contracts when the underlying ERC‑20 token does not use the standard 18 decimal places. The contract logic that settles a liquidation epoch assumes that token amounts are expressed with 18 decimals and hard‑codes a scaling factor of 10**18 when calculating the amount that must be transferred to the WithdrawProxy during the claim step. If a token has fewer decimals – for example 8‑decimal WBTC or 6‑decimal stablecoins – the arithmetic performed in the claim function produces a value that is either zero or insufficient, causing the call to revert. Because the claim transaction is part of the epoch‑finalisation flow, a revert prevents the epoch from being processed, leaving all deposited funds locked both in the vault and in the associated WithdrawProxy. Users attempting to withdraw see no balance returned, the UI may display a generic “claim failed” error, and the expected refund amount is missing. The issue is triggered after a liquidation auction has completed, when the protocol calls withdrawProxy.claim() to distribute the proceeds. It affects any participant who deposited a low‑decimal token, the vault operator, and ultimately the protocol’s reputation and capital availability. The problem was discovered during a Code4rena audit by constructing an 8‑decimal test token, performing a liquidation, and observing that withdrawProxy.claim() reverted. The bug is subtle because most deployed tokens use 18 decimals, so standard unit tests that only cover 18‑decimal assets do not expose the failure. It belongs to the class of decimal‑precision mismatches that cause arithmetic under‑/overflow and can lead to deadlocks in financial smart contracts. To remediate, the contract should replace the hard‑coded 10**18 constant with a dynamic factor derived from the token’s decimals (e.g., 10**token.decimals()) or enforce that only 18‑decimal tokens are accepted, ensuring that claim calculations always produce a valid, non‑zero amount and that epoch processing can complete without reverting.
summary:
If underlying token for the vault would have less then 18 decimals, then after liquidation there would be no way to process epoch, because `claim` function in `WithdrawProxy.sol` would revert, this would lock all user out of their funds both in vault and in withdraw proxy. Alternatively, if there is more then 18 decimals, claim would leave much less funds than needed for withdraw, resulting in withdrawers losing funds.

To make report more concise, I would focus on tokens with less then 18 decimals, because they are much more frequent. For example, WBTC have 8 decimals and most stablecoins have 6.

title: Attacker can take loan for Victim
content: The vulnerability is an authorization bypass that allows an attacker who does not own or have explicit permission for a piece of collateral to initiate a loan on behalf of the legitimate owner. The root cause lies in the logical condition that validates who may request a loan. The contract checks that either the caller (msg.sender) is the collateral holder, the designated receiver is the holder, the receiver is the approved operator, or the caller is approved for all of the holder’s tokens. Because the condition combines these checks with logical AND, an attacker can satisfy the test simply by setting the receiver address to the actual owner of the collateral. In that case the sub‑condition `receiver != holder` evaluates to false, causing the whole `if` statement to be skipped even though the caller is neither the owner nor an approved operator. Consequently the signature verification proceeds and the loan is issued, charging fees to the unsuspecting owner. Exploitation proceeds as follows: (1) the attacker calls the loan‑creation function with a collateral identifier they do not control; (2) they set the `receiver` parameter to the true owner’s address; (3) the contract’s authority check evaluates to false because the receiver matches the holder; (4) the contract skips the revert and creates a lien, minting a loan and associated debt against the owner’s collateral. The impact is that the victim’s account accrues an unwanted loan, incurs interest and fees, and may face liquidation or loss of collateral value. Any user who holds ERC‑721 collateral, as well as the protocol’s overall accounting and lenders, can be affected because the protocol records debt that was never authorized. The issue was discovered during a security audit when the auditors examined the `_validateCommitment` function and noticed that the condition incorrectly mixes `msg.sender` and `receiver` checks, allowing the bypass. It is subtle because the code appears to protect the owner at first glance, but the logical operator ordering creates a loophole that is not obvious without tracing the exact evaluation path. To remediate, the contract should enforce that the caller is authorized independently of the receiver, for example by rejecting the request unless `msg.sender` is the holder, an approved operator, or approved for all, and additionally ensuring that the `receiver` is also authorized or equal to the caller. In other words, the authority check must be split into two distinct validations: one for the transaction initiator and one for the designated loan recipient, preventing an attacker from masquerading as the owner by merely setting the receiver field. This class of bug is an improper access control check, often referred to as an authorization bypass due to flawed logical conditions. From the user’s perspective the symptom is a sudden loan appearing on their account, a debt balance that was never requested, and unexpected fee deductions, contradicting the expectation that a loan is only created when they explicitly initiate it.
summary: An unapproved, non-owner of collateral can still take loan for the owner/operator of collateral even when owner did not needed any loan. This is happening due to incorrect checks as shown in POC. This leads to unintended loan and associated fees for users.

title: Destruction of the `SmartAccount` implementation
content: The vulnerability concerns the SmartAccount contract architecture where a proxy wallet points to a shared implementation contract. The implementation contract is deployed without being initialized, leaving its owner variable at the zero address. Because the contract’s initialization function can still be called, an attacker can invoke a delegatecall from a proxy wallet to a malicious contract whose fallback function executes the selfdestruct opcode. When the delegatecall is performed, the code of the malicious contract runs in the context of the implementation contract, causing the implementation to self‑destruct. The destruction of the implementation contract freezes every wallet that references it, because the proxy can no longer forward calls to a valid implementation and the Singleton upgrade mechanism is also removed. This situation arises only when the deployment script does not enforce an initialization step for the implementation, which is the case in the current scripts. Users of the affected wallets experience a complete loss of functionality: transactions appear to be submitted but never execute, balances remain displayed but cannot be moved, and the UI may show no response or “wallet frozen” messages. The impact is severe because funds remain locked in the proxy contracts and the protocol cannot be upgraded or repaired without redeploying a new implementation and migrating all wallets. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the deployment flow and the checkSignatures logic, noting that an uninitialized owner (address(0)) allows signature checks to be bypassed and that the implementation contract can be destroyed via delegatecall. The bug is subtle because the implementation contract looks normal and selfdestruct can only be triggered indirectly through delegatecall, which is not an obvious attack surface. To remediate, the implementation contract should be initialized at deployment (calling its init function) or protected by a constructor that sets the owner to a non‑zero sentinel value, thereby preventing any future initialization and blocking the delegatecall path to selfdestruct. Additionally, the deployment scripts should enforce this initialization step and the contract code could include explicit guards that reject delegatecalls to contracts containing selfdestruct logic, ensuring the implementation remains immutable and the wallets stay operational.

title: Theft of funds under relaying the transaction
content: The vulnerability resides in the gas‑refund mechanism of the execTransaction function of the SmartAccount contract. The function estimates the gas that the relayer will spend by adding a fixed 21000 base cost to a per‑byte cost calculated as msg.data.length multiplied by 8 gas. At the end of the call the contract computes the refund as the difference between the estimated startGas and the remaining gas, multiplied by the relayer’s fee rate. Because Solidity discards trailing zero bytes when decoding calldata, an attacker can prepend or append an arbitrary number of zero bytes to the calldata without affecting the successful execution of the function. Each zero byte costs only 4 gas to transmit, but the contract assumes 8 gas per byte when calculating the refund. By front‑running the legitimate transaction and supplying a calldata payload that contains a large block of zero bytes, the attacker causes the contract to believe that the relayer spent more gas than it actually did, resulting in an excessive refund that is paid out of the wallet’s balance. The impact is a direct loss of funds from any smart‑contract wallet that relies on this refund logic; the relayer receives a larger payment than justified and the wallet owner sees an unexpected reduction of their balance. The issue manifests whenever execTransaction is called with user‑controlled calldata, which is typical for meta‑transactions and relayed calls, and it can be triggered without any special permissions. It was discovered during a security audit when the auditors crafted a proof‑of‑concept that appended 100 000 zero bytes to the calldata and observed a refund increase of 400 000 gas units. The bug is hard to notice because the transaction still succeeds, the extra bytes are ignored by the ABI decoder, and the over‑refund appears as a normal payment to the relayer. To remediate, the contract should not rely on msg.data.length for gas estimation; instead it must compute the expected number of bytes from the known static and dynamic parameters, bound the length of the signatures field, and use the actual gas consumed (gasleft before and after execution) rather than an assumed per‑byte cost. This change eliminates the advantage of supplying non‑standard ABI encoding and restores the intended accounting guarantees of the refund mechanism.
summary:
[contracts/smart-contract-wallet/SmartAccount.sol#L200](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-01-biconomy/blob/main/scw-contracts/contracts/smart-contract-wallet/SmartAccount.sol#L200)  
[contracts/smart-contract-wallet/SmartAccount.sol#L239](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-01-biconomy/blob/main/scw-contracts/contracts/smart-contract-wallet/SmartAccount.sol#L239)  
[contracts/smart-contract-wallet/SmartAccount.sol#L248](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-01-biconomy/blob/main/scw-contracts/contracts/smart-contract-wallet/SmartAccount.sol#L248)

The `execTransaction` function is designed to accept a relayed transaction with a transaction cost refund. At the beginning of the function, the `startGas` value is calculated as the amount of gas that the relayer will approximately spend on the transaction initialization, including the base cost of `21000` gas and the cost per calldata byte of `msg.data.length * 8` gas. At the end of the function, the total consumed gas is calculated as `gasleft() - startGas` and the appropriate refund is sent to the relayer.

An attacker could manipulate the calldata to increase the refund amount while spending less gas than what is calculated by the contract. To do this, the attacker could provide calldata with zero padded bytes of arbitrary length. This would only cost 4 gas per zero byte, but the refund would be calculated as 8 gas per calldata byte. As a result, the refund amount would be higher than the gas amount spent by the relayer.

title: Attacker can gain control of counterfactual wallet
content: The vulnerability concerns a deterministic counterfactual wallet created by the SmartAccountFactory where the address is pre‑computed using CREATE2 with a salt that only incorporates the owner address and an index. Because the entrypoint parameter is supplied later to the init function and is not part of the salt or the creation code hash, the same address can be deployed with any arbitrary entrypoint. An attacker can therefore front‑run the legitimate user by deploying the wallet first, choosing a malicious entrypoint contract, and then invoking the wallet’s execFromEntryPoint function to transfer any ether that was sent to the pre‑generated address. This attack works whenever a user relies on the pre‑generated address to receive funds before the wallet is actually deployed, assuming the entrypoint is not validated during address generation. The impact is that the user’s funds disappear from the expected wallet address and are transferred to the attacker, breaking the accounting assumptions that the wallet will hold the deposited balance. The issue was discovered during a security audit that included a proof‑of‑concept test where the attacker funded the counterfactual address, deployed the wallet with a custom StealEntryPoint, and successfully drained the balance. The bug is subtle because the address appears correct and the deployment transaction does not revert, making it easy to miss in normal testing. From a user’s perspective the wallet shows a zero balance after deployment even though they previously sent ether, violating the expectation that the wallet will retain the funds. This class of bug is an insecure deterministic address generation where a critical parameter (the entrypoint) is not bound to the address, enabling takeover and fund theft. The recommended mitigation is to bind the entrypoint to the address computation, for example by including it in the CREATE2 salt or in the init code hash, and to enforce that the same entrypoint is used during deployment, thereby preventing an attacker from substituting a malicious entrypoint.

title: Arbitrary transactions possible due to insufficient signature validation
content: The vulnerability is an authorization bypass in a smart contract wallet that supports EIP‑1271 contract signatures. The wallet’s execTransaction function calls checkSignatures to validate the supplied signatures, but checkSignatures only verifies that the supplied signer contract returns the EIP1271 magic value and never confirms that the signer is an authorized owner of the wallet. Because the function does not enforce ownership, an attacker can deploy a malicious contract that implements isValidSignature to always return the magic value, craft a signature that points to this contract (using v=0 to indicate an EIP‑1271 signer), and satisfy all length checks. The crafted signature passes the validation logic, allowing the attacker to invoke execTransaction with arbitrary transaction data. By setting the transaction to a delegatecall to a self‑destructing contract, the attacker can destroy the proxy wallet and transfer all its native and ERC20 balances to themselves. Alternatively, the attacker can call the wallet’s updateImplementation function, replacing the implementation with a malicious contract that can further steal funds, unstake assets from protocols, or lock out the original externally owned account (EOA) from interacting with the wallet. The exploit works whenever the wallet is configured to accept contract signatures and the checkSignatures routine lacks an explicit owner check. It was discovered during a security audit and demonstrated with a Foundry proof‑of‑concept that executed a self‑destruct on a Goerli‑deployed proxy, after which the contract’s bytecode size was zero and any further calls reverted. The issue is hard to notice because the signature appears cryptographically valid and the transaction does not revert during execution, giving a false sense of security while the wallet’s state is silently compromised. From a user’s perspective the wallet balance may suddenly become zero, calls to the wallet may revert, and the UI may show that the wallet no longer exists. This bug belongs to the class of signature validation flaws that lead to arbitrary transaction execution and ownership bypass. To remediate, the contract should enforce that the signer address resolved from the signature is an authorized owner, restrict execTransaction and updateImplementation to calls from owners, and add explicit checks that EIP‑1271 signers are registered and trusted before allowing any state‑changing operation.

title: Paymaster ETH can be drained with malicious sender
content: The vulnerability is a replay‑attack weakness in the VerifyingSingletonPaymaster contract used by Biconomy. The contract’s validatePaymasterUserOp function accepts a signed UserOperation and a paymaster signature, but it does not keep any record of which operation hashes have already been processed. Because the function is not required to be view‑only by the ERC‑4337 specification, a malicious sender can call it repeatedly with the same user operation hash and the same paymaster signature. The root cause is the absence of a replay‑protection mechanism such as a used‑hash mapping or a nonce incorporated into the hash. An attacker who can control the sender contract – for example by upgrading a smart‑account to a malicious implementation that skips nonce checks – can submit the identical transaction over and over. Each submission is accepted as a fresh sponsored transaction, causing the paymaster to deduct the required pre‑fund from its deposit each time. Over many repetitions the paymaster’s ETH balance is drained, effectively stealing the sponsor’s funds. This situation occurs whenever a paymaster relies solely on a signature without tracking usage, and when an adversary can submit transactions from a contract that does not enforce its own replay protection. The affected parties are the paymaster (its deposited ETH disappears), the protocol that assumes sponsored transactions are safe, and any users who expect their transactions to be covered without cost. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit that included a proof‑of‑concept where a user upgraded their account to a malicious contract and replayed a previously valid signature, demonstrating that the paymaster’s deposits could be emptied. The bug is subtle because the function appears to perform a normal validation and does not emit obvious warnings; without explicit state changes it is easy to overlook that the same hash can be reused. To remediate, the paymaster should store a mapping of processed operation hashes (or include a unique nonce in the hash) and reject any operation whose hash has already been marked as used. This adds a simple replay‑prevention check, ensuring that each signature can fund only one transaction and preserving the intended accounting guarantees of the paymaster system.
summary:
[contracts/smart-contract-wallet/paymasters/verifying/singleton/VerifyingSingletonPaymaster.sol#L97-L111](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-01-biconomy/blob/53c8c3823175aeb26dee5529eeefa81240a406ba/scw-contracts/contracts/smart-contract-wallet/paymasters/verifying/singleton/VerifyingSingletonPaymaster.sol#L97-L111)

Paymaster’s signature can be replayed to drain their deposits.

title: `FeeRefund.tokenGasPriceFactor` is not included in signed transaction data allowing the submitter to steal funds
content: The vulnerability is an omission in the transaction signing process of the "SmartAccount" contract. When a user authorises a transaction that includes a fee‑refund in ERC20 tokens, the contract expects the submitter to provide three parameters—baseGas, gasPrice and tokenGasPriceFactor—to compute the token repayment. The user’s signature is verified against a hash that includes baseGas and gasPrice, but the tokenGasPriceFactor is not part of the signed data. Because the factor is omitted, a malicious relayer can present the user with a transaction that contains a reasonable tokenGasPriceFactor, obtain the user’s signature, and then replace the factor with a much smaller value (e.g., 1 instead of 18) when actually submitting the transaction. The repayment formula (gasUsed + baseGas) * gasPrice / tokenGasPriceFactor) therefore yields a payment that is up to the ratio of the original factor to the manipulated one, allowing the submitter to claim an excessive amount of tokens from the wallet. The exploit can be carried out whenever the wallet is used with ERC20 fee‑refunds and the owner relies on the signed parameters for security. The impact is a direct loss of funds from the wallet: the owner sees a token balance reduced by an amount far larger than the gas actually consumed, while the relayer receives the over‑paid tokens. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the SmartAccount contract by reviewing the encodeTransactionData function and noticing that tokenGasPriceFactor is omitted from the signed hash. It is hard to notice because the contract still performs a signature check and the payment logic appears correct; the missing field is subtle and does not raise compiler warnings. The bug belongs to the class of “missing‑parameter‑in‑signature‑verification” or “under‑validated payment calculation” vulnerabilities, where a value that influences monetary transfer is not covered by the user’s consent. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a normal transaction execution but the token balance drops unexpectedly or the refund amount is much higher than anticipated, violating the expectation that the refund equals the actual gas cost. The correct fix is to include tokenGasPriceFactor in the encoded transaction data that is hashed and signed, and to verify that the signed value matches the one used in handlePayment, thereby ensuring that the user explicitly authorises the exact factor used for the repayment calculation.
summary:
[contracts/smart-contract-wallet/SmartAccount.sol#L288](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-01-biconomy/blob/main/scw-contracts/contracts/smart-contract-wallet/SmartAccount.sol#L288)  
[contracts/smart-contract-wallet/SmartAccount.sol#L429-L444](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-01-biconomy/blob/main/scw-contracts/contracts/smart-contract-wallet/SmartAccount.sol#L429-L444)

The submitter of a transaction is paid back the transaction’s gas costs either in ETH or in ERC20 tokens. With ERC20 tokens the following formula is used: $(gasUsed + baseGas) \\* gasPrice / tokenGasPriceFactor$. `baseGas`, `gasPrice`, and `tokenGasPriceFactor` are values specified by the tx submitter. Since you don’t want the submitter to choose arbitrary values and pay themselves as much as they want, those values are supposed to be signed off by the owner of the wallet. The signature of the user is included in the tx so that the contract can verify that all the values are correct. But, the `tokenGasPriceFactor` value is not included in those checks. Thus, the submitter is able to simulate the tx with value $x$, get the user to sign that tx, and then submit it with $y$ for `tokenGasPriceFactor`. That way they can increase the actual gas repayment and steal the user’s funds.

title: Replay attack
content: The vulnerability is a replay attack affecting the SmartAccount wallet contract. The contract verifies a signed transaction by hashing the transaction data, but the hash calculation omits the batch identifier (batchId). Because batchId is not part of the signed message, an attacker can submit the same signed payload multiple times while varying the batchId value. The root cause is the missing batchId in the encodeTransactionData function, which means the signature does not bind to a unique execution context. An attacker who observes a valid signed transaction can call execTransaction with the original batchId to execute it once, and then call execTransaction again with a different batchId that shares the same nonce. The contract only checks that the nonce matches the stored value and does not verify that the batchId itself is unique, so the second call is accepted and the transaction is executed a second time. This can be exploited to double‑spend assets, for example by transferring tokens to a beneficiary twice when only a single transfer was intended. The impact is that funds can be moved repeatedly without the signer’s consent, breaking the accounting guarantees of the wallet and potentially draining user balances. The attack surface is present for any signed transaction; the first transaction in a series can be replayed indefinitely, while later transactions have a reduced but still non‑zero chance of replay. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, which included a proof‑of‑concept test that executed a token transfer, then replayed the same signed transaction with a different batchId, resulting in the recipient receiving double the amount. The bug is subtle because each execution emits a success event and does not revert, so users see no error and may only notice an unexpected balance change. From a user’s perspective, a user expects to send 10 tokens and see the recipient’s balance increase by 10, but after the replay the balance increases by 20, or the user may see their own balance decrease more than intended. This violates the fundamental business logic that a signed transaction should be executed exactly once. The recommended mitigation is to incorporate batchId into the transaction hash (e.g., by adding it to encodeTransactionData) so that each batchId produces a distinct signed message, preventing the same signature from being valid for multiple executions.

title: Attacker can frontrun a victim’s `mint`+`add` transaction to steal NFT
content: The vulnerability is a front‑running race condition in the CID protocol’s CidNFT contract that allows an attacker to steal subprotocol NFTs that a victim tries to attach during a combined mint‑and‑add transaction. The root cause is that the mint() function accepts an arbitrary list of calldata for the add() function and then executes each add() via delegatecall without binding the add operation to the newly minted token ID. The add() function only checks that the caller is the owner or an approved operator of the target CidNFT, but it does not verify that the target ID matches the token created in the same transaction. Because token IDs are allocated sequentially, an attacker can front‑run the victim’s transaction, mint the token ID the victim expects, and grant the victim approval for that token. When the victim’s transaction later executes, the mint call creates the next token ID, but the add calldata still references the attacker‑controlled token ID. Consequently the victim’s subprotocol NFT is transferred to the attacker’s CidNFT and can be removed by the attacker, effectively stealing the asset. The impact is loss of ownership of attached NFTs, breach of trust in the identity system, and potential financial loss for users who rely on the protocol to safeguard their traits. The condition for exploitation is that the victim uses the convenience of minting and attaching NFTs in a single transaction while the attacker can submit a transaction with a higher gas price to be mined first. All users who mint a CidNFT and attach traits are affected, as are the subprotocol NFT contracts whose tokens become mis‑assigned. The issue was discovered through manual code review and reproduced with a Forge test that demonstrated the exact sequence of calls. It is hard to notice because the victim’s transaction does not revert; the minted token is received, but the attached NFT is missing, which may appear as a silent loss in the UI. The bug belongs to the class of front‑running and insecure token binding vulnerabilities where identifiers supplied by the caller are not validated against the contract’s internal state. To remediate, the contract should enforce that add() can only target the token ID that was just minted, for example by passing the newly created token ID internally to add() or by separating mint and add into distinct, non‑interleavable steps, and by rejecting add calls that reference any other token ID. This would restore the intended business logic that a user’s subprotocol NFT becomes a trait of their own newly minted identity token, preventing unauthorized transfer of assets.

title: Drips that end after the current cycle but before its creation can allow users to profit from squeezing
content: The vulnerability is a timing‑logic flaw in the drips mechanism that allows a sender to create a drip whose declared end time occurs after the current accounting cycle but before the moment the drip is actually recorded, then immediately remove that drip. Because the contract calculates the dripped amount based only on the interval between the current cycle start and the drip’s end timestamp, it treats the interval as having zero length and therefore permits the sender to withdraw the full deposited balance without any assets being considered dripped. However, the receiver – which can be an address controlled by the attacker – is still able to invoke the squeeze function using a squeezeStartCap equal to the current cycle start and a squeezeEndCap equal to the removal time. The squeeze logic does not re‑validate that the drip’s end precedes its creation, so it incorrectly credits the receiver with the full amount that was supposedly withdrawn by the sender. This results in an arbitrary‑asset drain from the contract: the attacker’s controlled receiver obtains tokens that never should have been disbursed, while the sender believes they have reclaimed their entire balance. The issue manifests only when the attacker can schedule a drip with a start time earlier than the current cycle, set an end time that falls within the same cycle but before the transaction that registers the drip, and then remove the drip before the cycle ends. It affects any user capable of creating and removing drips, the protocol’s token pool, and any downstream applications that rely on correct drip accounting. The flaw was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, which supplied a proof‑of‑concept test that reproduces the exploit by creating a drip at the 5th second of a 10‑second cycle, removing it at the 6th second, and then squeezing the receiver for the full amount. The problem is subtle because the dripped amount appears to be zero, so the removal looks legitimate, yet the squeeze function still pays out, making the bug easy to overlook in casual testing. To remediate, the contract should enforce that the squeeze start cap cannot be earlier than the drip’s last update time, for example by clamping squeezeStartCap to the drips.updateTime after any modification, or by adding a validation that the drip’s end timestamp must be greater than or equal to its creation timestamp before allowing removal or squeezing. In essence, the bug is a mis‑ordered time‑window validation that breaks the accounting invariants of the drips protocol, leading to unexpected fund loss where users expect a removed drip to stop all future payouts but instead see the receiver still obtain the full amount.
summary:
By creating a drip that ends after the current cycle but before its creation time and immediately removing it, the sender doesn’t have to put in any assets but the receiver can still squeeze this drip.

By setting a receiver that the sender controls, the sender can drain an arbitrary asset from the contract.

title: Precision loss in the invariant function can lead to loss of funds
content: The vulnerability is a precision‑loss bug in the core invariant function that validates the balance relationship of a liquidity pool. The function computes two scaled reserve values by first dividing the raw token amounts by the total liquidity and then multiplying by a token‑specific scale factor. Because the division is performed before the multiplication, the intermediate result is rounded down, especially when the token has a low number of decimals (for example six decimals for USDC) and the liquidity amount has many more decimals. This rounding error can make the calculated invariant appear to be satisfied even when the actual reserves have diverged, allowing an attacker to execute a swap that extracts tokens without triggering the invariant check. The exploit works by submitting a trade that increases one reserve while the rounded invariant calculation still returns true, so the contract permits the withdrawal of excess value. The impact is that an attacker can withdraw a non‑zero amount of a low‑decimal token (e.g., 0.5 USDC in the demonstrated test) while the invariant remains zero, effectively stealing funds without any on‑chain error. The condition occurs whenever the pool contains a token with significantly fewer decimals than the liquidity precision, and the invariant function is called during swaps or liquidity updates. Users of the pool, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself are affected because their deposited assets can be silently drained. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when the auditors compared the invariant calculation with a reference implementation and observed that large changes in the reserve of the low‑decimal token did not affect the invariant result. The bug is subtle because the invariant still returns true, so no revert or error is emitted, making it hard to notice without detailed numeric analysis. The proper fix is to rearrange the arithmetic so that the multiplication by the token scale is performed before the division, eliminating the intermediate rounding and preserving full precision. Conceptually, the fix ensures that the invariant check uses exact scaled values rather than approximated ones, restoring the intended accounting guarantees of the protocol. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a pool may appear balanced in the UI while the actual token balance of the pool decreases, or a participant may receive tokens “for free” after a swap that should have cost nothing, contradicting the expectation that swaps are always balanced by the invariant.
summary:
[src/core/Pair.sol#L56](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-01-numoen/blob/2ad9a73d793ea23a25a381faadc86ae0c8cb5913/src/core/Pair.sol#L56)  

An attacker can steal the funds without affecting the invariant.

title: Loss of user funds when completing CASH redemptions
content: The vulnerability resides in the cash redemption workflow of the protocol. When the manager admin calls completeRedemptions, the function first determines how many CASH tokens were burned during the epoch and then subtracts any amount that was refunded to users via the internal _processRefund call. The resulting quantityBurned is used to compute each redeemer’s share of the collateral that will be transferred. However, the contract never writes the adjusted quantityBurned back to the epoch’s totalBurned storage variable. Consequently, if a refund occurs in the first call for a given epoch, the next call to completeRedemptions still sees the original totalBurned value, which includes the refunded tokens. This leads to an over‑estimation of the amount of CASH considered burned and an under‑allocation of collateral to later redeemers. The bug manifests only when multiple completeRedemptions calls are made for the same epoch and at least one of those calls processes a refund. Users who redeem after a refund receive less USDC than the proportional amount they expect, effectively losing part of their funds. The issue was uncovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where a test scenario with three participants (Alice, Bob and Charlie) demonstrated that Alice received the correct amount after a refund to Charlie, but Bob’s subsequent redemption was short‑changed because the previous refund was not accounted for in the stored totalBurned. The problem is subtle because each individual call appears to compute the correct share; the error only becomes visible when the state is examined across calls, making it easy to miss in casual testing. The root cause is an accounting mismatch – the protocol’s invariant that totalBurned reflects the net amount of tokens actually removed from circulation is violated. To remediate the issue, the contract should update redemptionInfoPerEpoch[epoch].totalBurned with the net burned amount after subtracting refunds, ensuring that subsequent calls operate on the corrected state. This change restores the accounting guarantees, prevents inadvertent loss of user funds, and aligns the on‑chain state with the expected business logic that each user’s redemption is proportional to the net burned supply for the epoch.

title: Any user can drain the entire reward fund in MultiRewardStaking due to incorrect calculation of `supplierDelta`
content: An arithmetic mismatch occurs when the contract calculates reward accrual using two different decimal bases. The internal reward index is scaled by the number of decimals of the staking token (typically 18) but later the per‑user delta is divided by a factor derived from the reward token’s own decimals. If the reward token has fewer decimals than the staking token, the division does not cancel the earlier multiplication, causing the per‑user reward amount to be multiplied by 10^(stakingDecimals‑rewardDecimals). As a result, a single block can inflate the computed reward by orders of magnitude. When a user calls the claim function, the contract attempts to transfer the inflated amount from the reward pool. Because the pool does not contain that amount, the transfer either reverts (denial‑of‑service) or, if the pool is funded with enough tokens, the user can withdraw far more than entitled, effectively draining the entire reward fund. The bug is triggered whenever a reward token with a different decimal precision is added to the staking contract, which is a common scenario (e.g., adding USDT with 6 decimals). Any participant can exploit the flaw simply by waiting one block after the reward token is added and then invoking the claim function, receiving an astronomically large reward. The impact ranges from a temporary inability to claim rewards to a total loss of all funds allocated for rewards, affecting all users, the protocol’s economic model, and any parties relying on the escrow mechanism. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by examining the arithmetic in the reward‑accrual functions and reproducing the behavior with a test that uses a 6‑decimal reward token against an 18‑decimal staking token. The problem is subtle because the code appears to use the same scaling factor in both places, but the implicit reliance on matching decimal counts is not documented, making the bug easy to overlook during code review. The correct mitigation is to ensure that the same decimal base is used for both the global reward index and the per‑user delta calculation, either by normalising all values to a common precision or by explicitly converting the reward token amount to the staking token’s decimal scale before performing arithmetic. By aligning the decimal handling, the inflated multiplier disappears and the reward accounting respects the intended economic assumptions, preventing users from receiving or draining more tokens than should be allocated.
summary:
Reward `deltaIndex` in `_accrueRewards()` is multiplied by `10**decimals()` but eventually divided by `rewards.ONE` (which is equal to `10**IERC20Metadata(address(rewardToken)).decimals()`) in `_accrueUser()`.

If the number of decimals in MultiRewardEscrow share token differs from the number of decimals in the reward token, then all rewards are multipled by `10 ** (decimals() - rewardToken.decimals())`.

Therefore, for example, if an admin adds USDT as the reward token with decimals=6, it will result in the reward for any user to be multiplied by `10**(18-6) = 1000000000000` on the next block. This will at best lead to a DOS where no one will be able to withdraw funds. But at worst, users will drain the entire reward fund due to inflated calculations in the next block.

title: `BeefyAdapter`
content: The BeefyAdapter contract allows the vault owner to supply an optional _beefyBooster address during initialization. The code decodes this address from user‑controlled input but does not verify that the booster contract is a legitimate, endorsed Beefy booster. After decoding, the adapter unconditionally calls IERC20(_beefyVault).approve(_beefyBooster, type(uint256).max) when a non‑zero booster is provided, granting the booster an unlimited allowance to transfer the vault token held by the adapter. Later, during a deposit, the adapter calls beefyBooster.stake(beefyVault.balanceOf(address(this))). A malicious booster can implement the stake function to invoke _beefyVault.transferFrom(this, attacker, amount), using the previously granted allowance to move all tokens out of the adapter. The root cause is the absence of a validation step for the booster address and the reckless approval of an unlimited token allowance to an untrusted contract. Exploitation requires a malicious vault owner (or any actor able to set the booster) to deploy a contract that pretends to be a valid booster, passes its address in the initialization data, and then, when a user deposits funds, the booster drains those funds. The impact is that user deposits disappear, balances shown in the UI become zero, and no refunds are received, effectively stealing the assets stored in the adapter. This condition occurs whenever the adapter is initialized with a non‑zero booster that is not verified against the permission registry, and the deposit flow is executed. All users of the adapter, the protocol that relies on the adapter for asset management, and any token holders are affected. The issue was discovered during a security audit that highlighted the missing endorsement check and the unlimited approve pattern as a logical flaw. It can be hard to notice because granting an allowance to a contract is a common pattern and the stake call appears benign, masking the malicious behavior. To remediate, the adapter should enforce that the booster address is endorsed by the permission registry, reject boosters whose stakedToken does not match the vault, and avoid granting unlimited allowances; instead, use a minimal allowance or a pull‑based pattern, and consider removing the approve call entirely. This aligns the implementation with the intended business logic that only trusted Beefy boosters may manage deposited tokens, preserving accounting integrity and preventing unauthorized token transfers.
summary: Malicious vault owner can use Malicious `_beefyBooster` to steal the adapter’s token.

title: Incorrect Reward Duration After Change in Reward Speed in MultiRewardStaking
content: The vulnerability resides in the reward‑duration accounting of a multi‑reward staking contract. When the contract owner calls the function that changes the per‑second reward rate, the code recomputes the new end timestamp by looking at the current token balance held by the contract. This balance, however, does not represent the amount of reward tokens that are still available for distribution because a portion of the tokens may already be owed to stakers who have not yet claimed their accrued rewards. Consequently the contract assumes more tokens are free than actually are, extends the reward period incorrectly, and allows users to keep earning rewards after the intended end of the program. The root cause is an accounting mismatch: the contract treats the on‑chain token balance as the pool of undistributed rewards, ignoring pending liabilities. An attacker (or any privileged caller) can trigger a reward‑speed increase after some rewards have accrued but before they are claimed. The contract will calculate a longer remaining time based on the inflated balance, effectively granting extra reward seconds. Stakers who deposit after the speed change can then claim rewards that exceed the total tokens originally funded, as demonstrated by a Foundry test where a second user received twenty ether of rewards while the contract only held ten ether. The impact is two‑fold: honest participants may receive less than expected because the contract runs out of tokens, and the protocol’s economic model is broken, potentially leading to insolvency. The bug manifests only when the reward speed is altered during an active reward period and there are unclaimed rewards; otherwise the balance and liability coincide and the error is invisible. Users notice the symptom as an unexpected surplus of rewards for some accounts and a sudden shortage or zero balance for the contract, contradicting the expectation that the total distributed rewards never exceed the funded amount. The issue belongs to the class of “reward schedule mis‑calculation” or “incorrect time‑extension due to pending liabilities”. It is hard to spot because the contract’s token balance appears sufficient, and the logic that updates the end timestamp is hidden behind a single arithmetic expression. The proper fix is to compute the remaining reward amount from the previously scheduled end time and the old per‑second rate, thereby accounting for rewards already owed, as shown in the recommended code snippet that uses the previous end timestamp and the unreleased reward remainder to derive the new end timestamp. This ensures the reward period shortens or extends only in line with the actual undistributed token pool, preserving the intended accounting guarantees.
summary: When the reward speed is changed in `MultiRewardStaking`, the new end time is calculated based off of the balance of the reward token owned by the contract. This, however, is not the same as the number of reward tokens that are left to be distributed since some of those tokens may be owed to users who have not collected their rewards yet. As a result, some users may benefit from earning rewards past the end of the intended reward period, and leaving the contract unable to pay the rewards it owes other users.

title: Staking rewards can be drained
content: The vulnerability is a reentrancy flaw in the reward‑claiming function of a multi‑reward staking contract that uses ERC777 tokens for reward distribution. The function iterates over a list of reward tokens, reads the accrued amount for a user, and then transfers the tokens before resetting the stored balance. Because ERC777 tokens support a recipient hook (tokensReceived) that can execute arbitrary code during the transfer, a malicious contract can register such a hook and re‑enter the claimRewards function while the original transfer is still in progress. The root cause is the failure to follow the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern: the contract updates the user’s accruedRewards mapping only after the external token transfer, allowing the attacker to invoke claimRewards again and read the same non‑zero balance repeatedly. This can be exploited by a hacker contract that first deposits staking tokens, then calls claimRewards; the ERC777 hook triggers a second call to claimRewards before the first call clears the reward balance, and this loop continues until the staking contract’s reward pool is emptied. The impact is that the entire reward balance held by the staking contract can be drained, effectively stealing funds that were meant to be distributed to legitimate stakers. The condition for exploitation is that at least one reward token follows the ERC777 standard and that the staking contract does not protect the claimRewards function with a reentrancy guard or proper state updates before external calls. Users are affected because they see their expected rewards disappear; from a UI perspective a user may see a “reward claimed” event but later notice that the contract’s reward balance is zero and that no further rewards are available. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by reviewing the claimRewards implementation and confirming that the accruedRewards entry is cleared after the transfer, then reproducing the attack with a test contract that registers an ERC777 hook. The bug is subtle because the transfer succeeds and emits the expected event, so casual testing may not reveal that the balance remains unchanged until after the call, and the reentrancy only manifests with ERC777 tokens, which are less common than ERC20. To remediate, the contract should clear the accruedRewards entry before performing the token transfer (checks‑effects‑interactions) and protect the function with a non‑reentrant modifier such as OpenZeppelin’s ReentrancyGuard. Conceptually, this is a classic reentrancy vulnerability where external calls are made before internal state is updated, allowing an attacker to manipulate accounting logic and drain funds.
summary: If ERC777 tokens are used for rewards, the entire balance of rewards in the staking contract can get drained by an attacker.

title: Malicious strategy can lead to loss of funds
content: The issue is a storage‑manipulation vulnerability that arises because the adapter contract invokes the strategy contract using delegatecall. Delegatecall executes the callee’s code in the context of the caller, which means the strategy gains unrestricted read and write access to the adapter’s storage layout. A malicious strategy can therefore overwrite critical state variables such as the performance fee, the high‑water‑mark, or any other storage slot defined in the adapter. The exploit is performed by deploying a strategy that implements the expected interface but contains malicious logic that, when the adapter calls functions like harvest via delegatecall, directly assigns new values to these variables. Because the adapter trusts the strategy to behave correctly, the malicious code runs without additional checks, allowing the attacker to set the fee to 100 % or lower the high‑water‑mark, effectively siphoning user funds or preventing legitimate fee collection. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are that after a harvest transaction the expected reward is missing, the fee taken appears unusually high, or the user’s balance is reduced to zero despite no explicit withdrawal. The impact is a loss of funds for any participant who interacts with the adapter‑strategy pair, and it undermines the economic assumptions of the protocol, breaking accounting guarantees and potentially eroding trust. The vulnerability manifests whenever the adapter delegates calls to an untrusted or unverified strategy, which is typical in designs that aim to mix and match adapters and strategies. It was discovered during a formal audit when the security team examined the delegatecall pattern and crafted a malicious strategy that altered storage slots, confirming that the adapter does not isolate its state from the strategy. The problem is subtle because delegatecall is a legitimate Solidity feature and the code appears to follow the intended modular architecture, making the malicious behavior hard to detect without explicit storage‑slot analysis. To remediate the issue the adapter should avoid using delegatecall for external strategy execution, treat strategies as separate contracts with isolated storage, and enforce granular approvals for each state‑changing operation. Re‑architecting the system to use call instead of delegatecall, or implementing a proxy pattern with strict storage slot protection, would eliminate the ability of a strategy to tamper with the adapter’s internal variables and restore the intended security boundaries.
summary: A malicious strategy has access to the adapter’s storage and can therefore freely change any values.

title: Lost Rewards in MultiRewardStaking Upon Third-Party Withdraw
content: The vulnerability resides in the MultiRewardStaking contract, which inherits the ERC4626Upgradeable interface. When a user (the owner) authorises a third‑party address to withdraw a portion of the staked assets and specifies a receiver that is not the owner, the internal reward accounting is performed only for the caller (the third‑party) and the receiver, while the actual owner’s reward balance is never updated. This omission occurs because the private _withdraw function calls _accrueRewards(caller, receiver) instead of _accrueRewards(owner, receiver). As a result, any rewards that have accrued for the owner during the staking period are not recorded and become permanently inaccessible. The bug can be exploited by an approved third‑party withdrawing to an address they control; the owner’s expected reward (for example, 1 ether of reward tokens after ten seconds) is never credited, and both the owner and the third‑party see zero claimable rewards. From a user’s perspective the UI would show that the stake has been withdrawn successfully, but the reward balance remains at zero, leading to a situation where “my rewards disappeared” or “I cannot claim any rewards after a delegated withdrawal”. The issue manifests whenever the ERC4626 withdraw(uint256 amount, address receiver, address owner) function is used without being overridden, which is the default behaviour of the contract. It affects any participant who relies on third‑party withdrawals – typically delegators, custodial services, or protocols that assume the standard ERC4626 semantics. The problem was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena when a reproducible test showed that both the owner and the third‑party reverted with a ZeroRewards error after a delegated withdrawal. The bug is subtle because the withdrawal itself succeeds and the staked balance is correctly transferred, so the missing rewards are not immediately obvious without inspecting the reward claim functions. To remediate the issue the contract should accrue rewards for the actual owner before the transfer, i.e., call _accrueRewards(owner, receiver) in the _withdraw path, and a corresponding test should be added to ensure that the owner can still claim the expected rewards after a third‑party withdrawal. This correction restores the accounting invariant that rewards earned by a staker are always credited to that staker, regardless of who initiates the withdrawal, thereby preventing permanent loss of reward tokens.
summary:
Affected contract: `MultiRewardStaking`

When assets are withdrawn for user `Alice` by an approved user `Bob` to a receiver that is not `Alice`, the rewards are never accrued and the resulting **staking rewards are lost forever**. This is because `accrueRewards` is called on `caller` and `receiver` but never `owner`.

Third-party withdrawals are allowed by the fact that `withdraw(uint256, address, address)` exists in `ERC4626Upgradeable` and is never overwritten by a method with the same signature. Protocols composing with Popcorn will assume by the nature of this contract being an `ERC4626` that this method is safe to use when it in fact costs the user significantly.

title: Anyone who uses same adapter has the ability to pause it
content: The vulnerability is that the pause function for adapters is gated only by a check that the caller is the creator or owner of a vault, not the creator or owner of the adapter itself. Because multiple vaults can reference the same adapter contract, any user who can create a vault that points to that shared adapter can invoke the pauseAdapters function and cause the adapter to be paused. The root cause is the misuse of _verifyCreatorOrOwner which compares msg.sender to the vault's creator and the contract owner, but then executes a pause on the adapter obtained from the vault address without confirming that the caller has authority over the adapter. An attacker can therefore create a malicious vault, select the same adapter used by legitimate vaults, and call pauseAdapters with the address of a victim vault. The call is forwarded through an admin proxy to the adapter's pause() selector, which succeeds because the proxy has permission to call any function on the adapter.
