When a user initiates a withdrawal through queueWithdraw, the contract burns the user’s liquidity tokens and records a request in the withdrawalQueue. Later, an authorized caller invokes processWithdraws, which iterates over the queue, checks that each request has satisfied the minimum delay, and then transfers the corresponding amount of SUSD to the address supplied in the original request. The SUSD token contract contains a safety check that rejects transfers to three special addresses – the zero address, the token contract itself, and the proxy implementation address – by reverting the call. If a queued withdrawal specifies one of these prohibited addresses, the internal SUSD transfer reverts. Because processWithdraws does not catch the revert or advance the queuedWithdrawalHead pointer when a transfer fails, the head index becomes stuck on the failing entry. Consequently, every subsequent request in the queue remains unprocessed, even though the users’ liquidity tokens have already been burned. From a user’s point of view, a withdrawal that was queued appears in the UI as pending, but the user never receives any SUSD and their pool share disappears, effectively losing funds. The issue is triggered whenever an attacker or a careless user submits a queueWithdraw request with the receiver set to the SUSD proxy or implementation contract, which can be done at any time or by front‑running a large legitimate request. The problem was uncovered during a formal audit by examining the token’s transfer logic and reproducing the failure with a mock ERC20 that reverts on the prohibited address. It is difficult to notice because the queue appears to function normally until the first bad entry, after which all later withdrawals silently fail, giving the impression of a stalled system rather than an outright exploit. The root cause is the lack of error handling for a reverting transfer inside the queue processing loop, combined with the immutable head pointer update. To remediate, the contract should protect the iteration by catching transfer failures, skipping the offending entry, or moving it to a separate failedWithdrawals list, and always advancing the head index so that the rest of the queue can continue to be processed. This change restores the expected business logic that queued withdrawals eventually deliver the user’s SUSD and prevents a single malformed request from blocking the entire withdrawal pipeline.
summary:
The preferred way for withdrawals of the Liquiditypool is to do this via a withdrawal queue. According to Polynomial:

Queuing will be the default deposit/withdraw mechanism (In the UI) and not planning to charge any fees for this mechanism  
Instant deposit / withdraw is mechanism is meant for external integrations in case if they don’t want to track status of the queued deposit or withdraw

It is also stimulated to use `queueWithdraw()` over `withdraw()` by charging a withdrawalFee for direct withdrawals.

QueuedWithdrawals work in two steps.

  1. A user initialtes the Withdrawal via `queueWithdraw()`. This burns the `liquidityTokens` and adds the request to the `withdrawalQueue`.
  2. `processWithdraws()` can be called to process requests in the `withdrawalQueue` that have passed `minWithdrawDelay` to transfer the SUSD tokens to the user.

If the processing of a `QueuedWithdraw` in the `withdrawalQueue` reverts, the `queuedWithdrawalHead` (`LiquidityPool.sol#LL331C13-L331C33`) will never increase and further processing of the queue will be impossible. This means that any users that have placed a QueuedWithdraw after the reverting entry will have lost their liquiditytokens without receiving their SUSD.

title: Exchange: `totalFunding` calculation should be done with a simple multiplication operation instead of a `wadMul` operation
content: The vulnerability originates from an incorrect arithmetic operation used to compute the cumulative funding adjustment in the Exchange contract. The contract stores the funding rate as a signed 18‑decimal fixed‑point number (wad) and correctly converts the per‑second rate by dividing the raw rate by 1 day. However, when the contract later multiplies this per‑second rate by the elapsed time since the last update, it uses the generic wadMul helper, which assumes both operands are 18‑decimal numbers. The elapsed time is a plain integer representing seconds and does not carry 18‑decimal precision, so wadMul implicitly divides the product by 1e18. This extra division yields a totalFunding value that is many orders of magnitude smaller than the true funding amount. The underestimated totalFunding is then subtracted from 1e18 to form a normalizationUpdate, which is fed into mulWadDown to adjust the normalizationFactor and ultimately the mark price. Because the normalization factor is wrong, the reported mark price deviates from the mathematically correct price. The deviation propagates to any downstream logic that relies on the mark price, such as liquidation checks, margin calculations, and fee assessments. From a user’s perspective, a trader may see a price that is unexpectedly low or high, may be liquidated when the position should be safe, or may notice that their expected funding payments never materialise, effectively causing funds to disappear or balances to be incorrectly adjusted. The bug manifests whenever getMarkPrice or _updateFundingRate is called after a non‑zero time interval, i.e., any normal operation of the protocol after the funding rate has been set. All participants—traders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself—are affected because the core accounting invariant that funding payments balance long and short positions is broken. The issue was identified during a formal security audit (Code4rena) by noticing that the wadMul call was applied to a raw timestamp difference, a pattern that does not match the intended fixed‑point semantics. It is subtle because the contract still compiles and runs, and the price error may only become apparent after several hours or days of operation, making it easy to attribute to market volatility rather than a calculation bug. The proper remediation is to replace the wadMul call with a plain integer multiplication (fundingRate * timeDelta) and keep the subsequent scaling consistent with the 18‑decimal representation of the funding rate. In conceptual terms, the fix removes the unintended 1e18 divisor, ensuring that totalFunding reflects the true cumulative funding amount, restoring correct normalizationFactor updates, and guaranteeing that the mark price aligns with the intended economic model. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of fixed‑point arithmetic misuse, where developers apply generic high‑precision multiplication to operands that are not uniformly scaled, leading to systematic under‑ or over‑flows in financial calculations.
summary:
`wad` operations are meant to be done with int/uint which represent numbers with 18 decimals.

While the funding rate follows this representation, a simple time difference does not.

In `Exchange.getMarkPrice` as well as in `Exchange._updateFundingRate` a `wadMul` operation is done to multiply the funding rate per second by a simple time difference, leading to wrong calculation of `normalizationFactor` and mark price, affecting critical parts of the protocol.

title: Inexpedient liquidatable logic that could have half liquidable position turns fully liquidable instantly
content: The vulnerability resides in the liquidation routine of the ShortCollateral contract, specifically in the function that determines the maximum amount of debt that can be liquidated (maxLiquidatableDebt). When a short position’s safety ratio – a metric derived from the collateral amount, collateral price, short amount, mark price and the protocol’s liquidation ratio – falls within the narrow band of 0.95e18 to 1e18, the contract classifies the position as only slightly unhealthy and permits a partial liquidation by setting maxDebt to half of the short amount. However, the liquidation process also applies a liquidation bonus that effectively reduces the remaining collateral more than proportionally to the debt reduction. As a result, after the partial liquidation the safety ratio drops below the WIPEOUT_CUTOFF (approximately 0.95e18), causing the same position to become fully liquidatable immediately. Because the contract executes the check atomically in two successive transactions, a liquidator can trigger the first partial liquidation and, in the same block, liquidate the remainder, draining the user’s entire collateral. The root cause is the overly aggressive slashing logic that does not ensure the post‑liquidation health of the position; the hard‑coded thresholds and the way the liquidation bonus is applied create a spiral where a barely unhealthy position becomes instantly fully liquidatable. This flaw was discovered during a Code4rena audit by analysing the ShortCollateral.sol source and reproducing the scenario in the accompanying test suite (ShortCollateral.t.sol). It is difficult to notice because the code appears to allow a safe partial liquidation, yet the subtle interaction between the safety‑ratio calculation and the bonus‑adjusted collateral reduction is not obvious at a glance. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are stark: a trader who expects only half of their debt to be removed sees their collateral balance drop to zero, receives no refund, and their position disappears despite being only marginally under‑collateralized. The issue belongs to the class of liquidation‑logic bugs where the accounting formula reduces debt less than the collateral loss, causing the health metric to cross the liquidation threshold again instantly. To remediate, the slashing logic should be restructured so that after a partial liquidation the remaining collateral ratio is restored above the safe threshold, for example by recalculating maxDebt based on the post‑liquidation safety ratio or by adjusting the liquidation bonus so that it does not push the ratio below the wipe‑out cutoff. Such a change would prevent the spiral effect and ensure that a position deemed only partially liquidatable cannot be drained in a single atomic sequence.
summary:
In ShortCollateral.sol, the slash logic of `maxLiquidatableDebt()` is specifically too harsh to the barely unhealthy positions because `maxDebt` will be half of the position to be liquidated if `0.95e18 <= safetyRatio <= 1e18`.

Additionally, once a position turns liquidatable, the position is deemed fully liquidatable atomically in two repeated transactions.

title: `LotteryMath.calculateNewProfit` returns wrong profit when there is no jackpot winner
content: The vulnerability resides in the profit‑updating routine of the lottery contract, specifically the function that computes the new net profit after a draw. When a draw finishes without a jackpot winner, the routine calculates the expected reward payout by multiplying the total ticket payout (ticketsSold × expectedPayout) with a multiplier derived from the excess pot. Instead of applying the multiplier as a percentage, the code multiplies the raw values directly, bypassing the PercentageMath utility that would correctly scale the amount. This arithmetic mistake causes the expectedRewardsOut value to be dramatically inflated or deflated, which in turn corrupts the currentNetProfit variable that is later used to determine individual rewards. The root cause is a logical error in the reward formula: the multiplier is treated as a raw factor rather than a percentage, leading to an incorrect profit delta. An attacker or any user can trigger a draw where no jackpot is won – a normal scenario in a lottery – and the contract will record a net profit that is far lower (or even negative) than it should be. As a result, subsequent reward calculations may under‑pay winners, produce zero payouts, or, conversely, allow the contract to over‑draw from the pot, effectively making funds disappear from the protocol’s accounting. From a user’s point of view the symptom is that a participant who expects a refund or a prize receives nothing or a much smaller amount than advertised, and the protocol’s balance may show unexpected deficits. The issue was uncovered during a formal audit by reproducing the calculation with a test harness that logged the intermediate values; the logged profit differed by several orders of magnitude from the mathematically expected result, confirming the mis‑calculation. Because the faulty variable is internal and only manifests as an accounting discrepancy, it can be hard to notice without explicit testing of the no‑jackpot path. The proper fix is to replace the direct multiplication with a percentage‑based computation, for example by using PercentageMath.getPercentage on the product of ticketsSold, expectedPayout and the multiplier, as illustrated in the recommended code snippet. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “incorrect financial scaling” or “percentage‑math misuse” bugs, where a factor intended to represent a percent is applied as a raw multiplier, breaking the economic invariants of the contract.

title: The call to `MsgValueSimulator` with non zero `msg.value` will call to sender itself which will bypass the `onlySelf` check
content: The vulnerability originates from the MsgValueSimulator system contract, which forwards an incoming call using the mimicCall opcode. When a caller supplies a non‑zero msg.value and sets the destination address (the "to" parameter) to the MsgValueSimulator contract itself, the simulator forwards the call back to its own fallback function. Because the fallback is invoked with the original calldata and the msg.value is propagated through low‑level registers, the contract ends up calling itself as if it were an external account. This self‑call bypasses any checks that rely on msg.sender being equal to address(this), such as the onlySelf modifier that requires msg.sender == address(this). The root cause is the lack of validation that the "to" address cannot be the MsgValueSimulator address, combined with the mimicCall implementation that does not preserve the original register layout and therefore allows the re‑entered call to appear legitimate. An attacker can exploit this by crafting a contract or a custom account that invokes MsgValueSimulator with a non‑zero value and the simulator’s own address as the recipient, optionally controlling the calldata to trigger arbitrary functions on the target contract. The exploit results in the target contract executing its own code under the guise of an external call, which can break accounting assumptions that treat msg.sender as a unique identifier, spoof the contract’s identity, and cause unexpected value transfers. In practice the impact may be a contract’s fallback function being called without intention, funds being sent to the simulator and becoming irretrievable, or security checks like onlySelf being circumvented, leading to potential loss of funds or violation of protocol invariants. The issue manifests whenever a contract uses MsgValueSimulator for value‑simulation patterns common in withdrawal functions or smart‑contract wallets, i.e., any situation where a contract forwards a call with value through the simulator. It was discovered during a security audit when the researchers reproduced the behavior with a test contract that called the simulator and observed the fallback being entered unexpectedly. The bug is subtle because the re‑entrancy occurs at the system‑contract level and the register manipulation is not visible in high‑level Solidity code, making it hard to notice without low‑level inspection. The recommended mitigation is to add an explicit check in MsgValueSimulator that rejects calls where the destination address equals the simulator’s own address, or to redesign the forwarding logic to avoid using mimicCall for value‑bearing calls, thereby preserving the intended msg.sender semantics and preventing self‑calls. This class of vulnerability can be described as a self‑call bypass or msg.sender spoofing through unchecked destination addresses in low‑level call forwarding, which violates the business logic that a contract should not be able to invoke its own functions unless explicitly programmed to do so.

title: Royalty receiver can drain a private pool
content: The vulnerability resides in the way the private pool contract calculates and pays ERC‑2981 royalties during a buy operation. The function first iterates over the requested token IDs, calls the internal _getRoyalty routine to sum the royalty amounts, and stores this total in a local variable. After this first loop the contract performs an external call that refunds any excess ETH to the caller. Because the refund is an untrusted external call, a malicious caller that is a contract can execute code during the refund and modify the royalty information of the tokens being purchased – for example by invoking a setter that changes the royalty fee from 0 % to 100 %. When execution returns to the contract, a second loop calls _getRoyalty again, this time using the newly‑changed royalty data, and transfers the calculated royalty fee directly to each royalty recipient. The net input amount that the buyer must provide was increased only by the original (lower) royalty total, so the pool ends up covering the difference between the original and the manipulated royalty amounts. Consequently the attacker receives the NFT while paying little or nothing, and the pool’s base‑token balance is drained as the royalty receiver extracts the full sale price. The flaw is a classic double‑fetch or inconsistent‑state bug amplified by a re‑entrancy window created by the refund call. It can be exploited whenever the royalty receiver is under the attacker’s control or when the royalty fee can be altered by the caller between the two _getRoyalty invocations. The impact is that the private pool can lose all of its funds, the attacker can acquire NFTs for free and later sell them back for profit, and users see their balances unexpectedly reduced or the pool’s liquidity disappear. The issue was discovered during a security audit that identified the duplicated royalty lookup and the external call that allowed state manipulation. It is hard to notice because the two royalty calculations appear correct in isolation and the refund logic is a common pattern, masking the inconsistency. The proper fix is to eliminate the second royalty lookup and ensure that the amount transferred to royalty recipients matches the amount accounted for in the initial calculation, typically by performing a single pass that both aggregates and pays royalties, or by moving the external call after all royalty transfers have been finalized. This class of bug falls under re‑entrancy‑related state‑inconsistency vulnerabilities where mutable external data is read multiple times across an untrusted call, leading to asset loss and violation of the protocol’s accounting guarantees. From a user’s perspective the expected behavior – paying the pool for an NFT while royalties are deducted from the same payment – is broken; instead the user may receive the NFT without any deduction, or see the pool’s balance drop to zero, contradicting the expectation that funds are safely held by the pool.

title: PrivatePool owner can steal all ERC20 and NFT from user via arbitrary execution
content: The vulnerability resides in the PrivatePool contract’s execute function, which is advertised as a helper for claiming airdrops but actually permits the pool owner to invoke an arbitrary call on any target contract with arbitrary calldata. The function is protected only by an onlyOwner modifier, assuming the owner is trustworthy, yet the protocol allows anyone to create a private pool and therefore the owner may be malicious. When a user interacts with the pool they must approve the pool to spend their ERC20 tokens or setApprovalForAll for their NFTs so that the pool can pull assets during buy, sell, or flash‑loan operations. Because execute does not validate the target address or the calldata, the owner can craft a payload that calls the token’s transferFrom (or an ERC721 safeTransferFrom) to move the approved assets from the user’s wallet directly to the attacker’s address. The exploit proceeds step‑by‑step: (1) the user grants the pool an unlimited allowance for a token; (2) the malicious owner calls execute, passing the token contract as the target and the selector for transferFrom together with the victim, attacker, and full allowance amount as arguments; (3) the token contract processes the call and transfers the entire approved balance to the attacker; (4) the user’s balance drops to zero while the pool’s internal accounting remains unchanged. This results in the user losing all approved ERC20 or NFT holdings, effectively “funds disappear” or “refund calculation error” from the user’s perspective. The impact is severe: users lose assets they never intended to deposit into the pool, the protocol’s trust model is broken, and the pool’s owner can repeatedly harvest approvals from multiple users. The issue is discovered during a security audit and demonstrated with a proof‑of‑concept test that shows a victim’s token balance falling from 100 000 MTK to zero after a single execute call. The flaw is subtle because the execute function appears legitimate for airdrop claims and does not emit any warning events, making it hard to notice without inspecting the calldata. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of unchecked arbitrary external call vulnerabilities where privileged code can be misused to bypass business‑logic constraints. To remediate, the contract should either remove the ability for the owner to perform arbitrary calls or enforce strict whitelisting that prevents execute from targeting token or NFT contracts, ensuring that only safe airdrop‑claim logic can be performed. This change restores the intended accounting guarantees and prevents the pool owner from stealing user‑approved assets.

title: Risk of silent overflow in reserves update
content: An overflow vulnerability exists in the pool contract when updating virtual reserves. The contract stores virtualBaseTokenReserves and virtualNftReserves as uint128, but the calculations that modify them use uint256 values (net input amount minus fees, weight sum, etc.). The code casts the uint256 result directly to uint128 without checking that the value fits. If the computed amount exceeds 2^128‑1, the cast silently truncates the high bits, causing the stored reserve to wrap around to a much smaller number. This break the invariant xy = k that underpins the constant‑product pricing formula. As a result the pool can report an incorrect price, allowing trades at far‑from‑market rates and potentially draining user funds. The overflow can happen during a buy or sell transaction when the base token has a very large decimal precision or when a large amount of tokens is transferred, as demonstrated by a test that uses a 30‑decimal ERC20 token and a pool initialized with 100 000 000 * 1e30 base tokens. From a user’s perspective the trade appears to succeed, but the pool’s internal accounting is corrupted: subsequent swaps may return zero or excessive amounts, balances may disappear, and the expected K constant changes unexpectedly. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where the auditors observed the unchecked cast and reproduced the overflow with a high‑precision token. The bug is subtle because the transaction does not revert and no event signals the overflow, making it hard to notice without inspecting the reserve values after the trade. The proper fix is to add explicit checks that the value to be cast does not exceed type(uint128).max before performing the cast, and to revert with an overflow error if it does. This restores the safety of the reserve updates and preserves the constant‑product invariant.

title: Slot and block number proofs not required for verification of withdrawal
content: The vulnerability is a missing input‑validation flaw in the EigenLayer withdrawal verification flow. The library function that checks beacon chain proofs, BeaconChainProofs.verifyWithdrawalProofs, accepts a struct containing several Merkle proofs, among them slotProof and blockNumberProof. The implementation only validates the length of the withdrawalProof and executionPayloadProof fields and does not enforce a minimum size for the slot and block number proofs. As a result, an attacker can supply empty byte arrays for these two proofs, causing the verification routine to treat the proof as valid. The contract later uses a modifier (proofIsForValidBlockNumber) that relies on the blockNumberRoot derived from the blockNumberProof; when the proof is empty, the modifier is effectively bypassed because the root is set to a value that passes the check. Consequently, the EigenPod.verifyAndProcessWithdrawal function processes withdrawals without confirming that the slot and block number correspond to a genuine beacon block. This enables several exploit scenarios: a malicious actor can submit a full withdrawal proof with empty slot and block number proofs and drain the entire balance; they can also submit partial withdrawal proofs repeatedly, because each partial claim is considered distinct when the slot proof is omitted, allowing the same funds to be withdrawn multiple times. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are unexpected loss of funds – a user may see their balance become zero after a single withdrawal, or notice that a partial withdrawal does not reduce the balance as expected, indicating that the protocol accounting is broken. The impact is high because the protocol’s accounting assumptions are violated, leading to potential double‑spend and loss of deposited assets for any pod owner or validator. The bug manifests whenever EigenPod.verifyAndProcessWithdrawal is called with a WithdrawalProofs struct that contains empty slotProof or blockNumberProof fields, which can be crafted by an attacker without needing to forge the other Merkle proofs. The issue was discovered during a security audit when test cases were altered to intentionally skip these proofs; the tests still passed, revealing that the library does not enforce the required proof length. The problem is hard to notice because the majority of the proof data appears correct and the contract emits no explicit error when the slot or block number proofs are missing. The recommended remediation is to add explicit require statements that enforce a non‑zero length (at least one 32‑byte element) for slotProof and blockNumberProof, or to reuse a generic Merkle proof validation routine that checks proof size. By ensuring that these proofs are present and correctly linked to the beacon state, the contract will correctly reject malformed withdrawal attempts and restore the intended accounting guarantees.
summary: Since this is a vulnerability that involves multiple in-scope contracts and leads to more than one impact, let’s start with a bug description from bottom to top.

title: It is impossible to slash queued withdrawals that contain a malicious strategy due to a misplacement of the ++i increment
content: The vulnerability resides in the slashQueuedWithdrawal function of the StrategyManager contract where the loop index i is only incremented inside the else branch. When the function receives an indicesToSkip array that marks a strategy as malicious, the code correctly detects the matching index and increments a separate indicesToSkipIndex counter, but it does not advance i. As a result the loop repeats the same position, falls through to the else block on the next iteration and attempts to call withdraw on the supposedly skipped strategy. If that strategy is crafted to revert on any withdraw call, the whole slash transaction reverts, making it impossible for the contract owner to slash the queued withdrawal. This bug is an off‑by‑one / loop‑control error that defeats the intended skip‑logic. An attacker can exploit it by creating a queued withdrawal that includes a malicious strategy, adding the strategy’s index to indicesToSkip, and then waiting for the owner to attempt a slash. Because the index is never advanced, the skip is ignored and the malicious strategy’s revert aborts the slash. Consequently the slashing mechanism, which is meant to burn shares of misbehaving strategies, is bypassed and the attacker can later complete the withdrawal and keep the funds. The issue manifests only when a skip list is used and at least one of the listed strategies reverts on withdraw; otherwise the function behaves as expected. It affects protocol owners, delegators and any user whose withdrawal could be slashed, undermining the security guarantees of the EigenLayer protocol. The problem was discovered during a formal audit by observing that the indicesToSkip parameter had no effect in a unit test that deliberately set the skip list to the only strategy. The bug is subtle because the for‑loop condition appears correct and the code compiles without warnings, yet the missing increment silently breaks the control flow. The proper fix is to move the unchecked ++i statement outside of the if/else construct so that i is increased on every loop iteration, or to restructure the loop to use a conventional for‑loop header. This ensures that strategies listed in indicesToSkip are truly bypassed and the slash operation can proceed safely, preserving the intended accounting logic where shares of malicious strategies are burned while honest strategies are still processed.
summary:
`StrategyManager::slashQueuedWithdrawal()` contains an `indicesToSkip` parameter to skip malicious strategies, as documented in the [function definition](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-eigenlayer/blob/main/src/contracts/core/StrategyManager.sol#L532-L534):

> so that, e.g., if the slashed `QueuedWithdrawal` contains a malicious strategy in the `strategies` array which always reverts on calls to its ‘withdraw’ function, then the malicious strategy can be skipped (with the shares in effect “burned”), while the non-malicious strategies are still called as normal.

The problem is, the function does not work as expected, and `indicesToSkip` is ignored. If the queued withdrawal contains a malicious strategy, it will make the slash always revert.

Owners won’t be able to slash queued withdrawals that contain a malicious strategy.

An adversary can take advantage of this and create withdrawal queues that won’t be able to be slashed, completely defeating the slash system. The adversary can later complete the withdrawal.

title: Challenges can be frontrun with de-leveraging to cause lossses for challengers
content: The vulnerability is a front‑running and price‑manipulation flaw in the challenge lifecycle of a DeFi position auction. When a user launches a challenge they deposit collateral that is supposed to be protected by a price‑based collateral check. The contract, however, allows the position owner to call an adjustPrice function after the challenge transaction has been submitted but before it is mined. Because the launchChallenge function does not record the price at the moment of submission, an attacker can front‑run the challenger, send enough ZCHF to repay the position, call adjustPrice with a value of zero, and thereby set the internal price variable to zero while the collateral check still uses the (now zero) price. The subsequent collateral verification condition (_bidAmountZCHF * ONE_DEC18 >= price * _collateralAmount) always succeeds when price is zero, so any bid – even a single wei – passes the check. The attacker then back‑runs the challenger’s transaction with a minimal bid, captures the challenger’s entire collateral, and the challenger loses their deposited funds. This sandwich attack can be repeated for any open position that permits price adjustment, leading to systematic loss of challenger collateral and erosion of trust in the protocol. The issue occurs only when a position is open, the owner retains the ability to lower the price, and the challenge is not yet closed; it is triggered by the ordering of transactions in a block. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the interaction between launchChallenge, adjustPrice, and the collateral verification logic. The problem is subtle because the price‑zero case satisfies the inequality and therefore does not raise an obvious error, making it easy to overlook during testing. To remediate, the protocol should lock the price at the moment a challenge is launched, require an expectedPrice parameter that must match the on‑chain price (acting as a slippage guard), and prevent price adjustments until the challenge is resolved. Alternatively, the collateral check could be rewritten to reference the price at the time of challenge creation rather than the mutable current price. Implementing these controls stops the front‑runner from forcing a zero price and ensures that challengers’ collateral remains protected under the intended economic assumptions.
summary:
Challenges, once created, cannot be closed. Thus once a challenge is created, the challenger has already transferred in a collateral amount and is thus open for losing their collateral to a bidding war which will most likely close below market price, since otherwise buying from the market would be cheaper for bidders.

Position owners can take advantage of this fact and frontrun a `launchChallenge` transaction with an `adjustPrice` transaction. The `adjustPrice` function lets the user lower the price of the position, and can pass the collateral check by sending collateral tokens externally.

As a worst case scenario, consider a case where a position is open with 1 ETH collateral and 1500 ZCHF minted. A challenger challenges the position and the owner frontruns the challenger by sending the contract 1500 ZCHF and calling `repay()` and then calling `adjustPrice` with value 0, all in one transaction with a contract. Now, the price in the contract is set to 0, and the collateral check passes since the outstanding minted amount is 0. The challenger’s transaction gets included next, and they are now bidding away their collateral, since any amount of bid will pass the avert collateral check.

The position owner themselves can backrun the same transaction with a bid of 1 wei and take all the challenger’s collateral, since every bid checks for the `tryAvertChallenge` condition.

```solidity
if (_bidAmountZCHF * ONE_DEC18 >= price * _collateralAmount)
```

Since price is set to 0, any bid passes this check. This sandwich attack causes immense losses to all challengers in the system, baiting them with bad positions and then sandwiching their challenges.

Since sandwich attacks are extremely commonplace, this is classified as high severity.

title: Double-entrypoint collateral token allows position owner to withdraw underlying collateral without repaying ZCHF
content: The vulnerability resides in the Position contract's withdraw function, which is intended to let a position owner retrieve any ERC20 token that may have been sent to the position address, while enforcing that collateral can only be withdrawn after the associated ZCHF debt is repaid. The implementation performs a token address comparison and, when the supplied token matches the stored collateral address, it calls an internal withdrawCollateral routine that checks the caller's debt balance before allowing the transfer. However, this logic assumes that the token address uniquely identifies the underlying asset. When the collateral token is a double‑entrypoint token – a legacy ERC20 contract that forwards its state‑changing calls to a newer contract while exposing two distinct contract addresses that share the same balance storage – the assumption breaks. The legacy token’s transfer and balance queries are delegated to the new contract, meaning that the Position contract sees the same underlying balance regardless of which of the two addresses is used. An attacker can therefore dust the position with a small amount of the legacy token, delegate the legacy contract to the new double‑entrypoint contract, and then call withdraw with the legacy address as the token argument. Because the withdraw function treats the legacy address as a non‑collateral token, it bypasses the debt‑repayment check and proceeds to transfer the full collateral balance to the caller. This exploit allows the position owner to extract the entire collateral without repaying any ZCHF, leaving the protocol under‑collateralised while the debt remains outstanding. The issue manifests only when the collateral token is, or can become, a double‑entrypoint token – a class of upgradeable or proxy‑style ERC20 contracts that are not easily detectable by static analysis. From a user’s perspective the expected behaviour is that a withdrawal of collateral requires prior debt settlement; instead the user receives the full collateral amount while the ZCHF balance stays unchanged, effectively causing funds to disappear from the protocol. The bug is hard to notice because the token conforms to the ERC20 interface, the balance checks succeed, and the double‑entrypoint nature is hidden behind delegation logic. The root cause is the reliance on a single token address for collateral identification without verifying that the token’s underlying balance has not been altered through a delegated contract. To remediate, the withdraw routine should validate that the collateral balance remains unchanged after any token transfer, enforce that only the designated collateral token address can be used for collateral withdrawals, and consider restricting or removing the generic withdraw function altogether. Adding explicit checks that compare pre‑ and post‑withdrawal collateral balances, as well as rejecting tokens that exhibit delegate behavior, would close the attack surface and restore the intended accounting guarantees.
summary:
`Position::withdraw` is intended to allow the position owner to withdraw any ERC20 token which might have ended up at position address. If the collateral address is passed as argument then `Position::withdrawCollateral` is called to perform the necessary checks and balances. However, this can be bypassed if the collateral token is a double-entrypoint token.

Such tokens are problematic because the legacy token delegates its logic to the new token, meaning that two separate addresses are used to interact with the same token. Previous examples include TUSD which resulted in [vulnerability when integrated into Compound](https://blog.openzeppelin.com/compound-tusd-integration-issue-retrospective/). This highlights the importance of carefully selecting the collateral token, especially as this type of vulnerability is not easily detectable. In addition, it is not unrealistic to expect that an upgradeable collateral token could become a double-entrypoint token in the future, e.g. USDT, so this must also be considered.

This vector involves the position owner dusting the contract with the collateral token’s legacy counterpart which allows them to withdraw the full collateral balance by calling `Position::withdraw` passing the legacy address as `token` argument. This behaviour is flawed as the position owner should repay the ZCHF debt before withdrawing their underlying collateral.

title: When the challenge is successful, the user can send tokens to the position to avoid the position’s cooldown period being extended
content: The vulnerability is a logical flaw in the challenge resolution flow that allows a malicious actor to prevent the intended extension of a position's cooldown period by depositing additional collateral immediately before the contract withdraws the existing collateral. The contract’s internalWithdrawCollateral function transfers the collateral out of the position and then checks the remaining balance; if the balance falls below the configured minimumCollateral the cooldown timestamp is set to the position’s expiration, effectively extending the lock‑up period. Because the balance check occurs after the transfer, an external account can send enough collateral to keep the balance at or above the minimum just before the withdrawal is executed. When this happens the condition balance < minimumCollateral evaluates to false, the cooldown is not extended, and the position becomes immediately usable again. An attacker can exploit this by front‑running the transaction that ends a successful challenge: after the challenge period has elapsed, the challenger calls end(), but a third party observes the pending transaction and quickly sends the required minimum collateral to the position. The contract then sees a sufficient balance, skips the cooldown extension, and the attacker can immediately mint new tokens or execute other privileged actions at the favorable price that was established during the challenge. The impact is that the economic safety window intended by the cooldown is bypassed, allowing profit extraction, market manipulation, and potential loss of value for honest participants who relied on the cooldown to protect against rapid price changes. This issue occurs only when a challenge succeeds, internalWithdrawCollateral is invoked, and the protocol permits external deposits to the position during the same block or transaction ordering window. All users who open positions, challenge them, or rely on the cooldown for security are affected because the protocol’s accounting assumptions about collateral sufficiency and time‑based lock‑up are violated. The flaw was discovered during a security audit by Code4rena, where the auditors identified that the cooldown logic depends on a post‑withdrawal balance that can be altered by a front‑run deposit, a scenario that typical unit tests may not cover. The problem is subtle because the contract emits no error and the balance appears correct, making it hard to notice without analyzing transaction ordering and state changes. To remediate, the cooldown extension should be based on the collateral amount that existed before the withdrawal, or the contract should forbid additional collateral deposits while a challenge is being resolved, or it should always extend the cooldown on a successful challenge regardless of the remaining balance. Implementing a mandatory one‑day cooldown after any successful challenge, as suggested by the auditors, would close the window for this exploit and restore the intended security guarantees.

title: Transfer position ownership to `addr
content: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that occurs when the owner of a position in the Frankencoin auction system transfers the position ownership to the zero address (address(0)). The contract logic in MintingHub.end assumes that the position owner is a valid address and attempts to refund any excess amount from the effective bid to the owner using an ERC20 transfer. Because the ERC20 implementation requires the recipient not be the zero address, the transfer reverts, causing the entire end() call to fail. This situation can be triggered after a challenge has succeeded and the effective bid exceeds the funds needed to cover the repayment and challenger reward, leaving only a small refund for the owner. The owner, seeing an unavoidable loss of collateral, can deliberately transfer ownership to address(0) and thereby cause the end() transaction to revert. The impact is that the successful bidder loses the bid funds that were supposed to be transferred, the challenger’s collateral remains locked and the challenger reward is not paid, and the protocol’s accounting invariants are broken because the expected refund never reaches the owner. The affected parties include the position owner, the winning bidder, the challenger, and any users relying on the auction’s correct settlement. The issue was discovered during a security audit that constructed a proof‑of‑concept scenario with specific collateral and bid values, demonstrating that the zero‑address transfer leads to a revert in the ERC20._transfer function. The bug is subtle because transferring ownership to address(0) is not prohibited elsewhere in the code, and the failure only manifests in the edge case where a refund is sent to the owner, making it easy to miss during normal testing. To remediate, the contract should disallow transferring position ownership to the zero address, or the end() function should include a guard that skips the refund when the owner is address(0) and handles the excess amount safely. In essence, this is a classic zero‑address transfer denial‑of‑service flaw that violates the protocol’s business logic that expects every successful auction to settle cleanly and return any surplus to the rightful owner.
summary:
If some challenge is about to succeed, the position owner will lose the collateral. Seeing the unavoidable loss, the owner can transfer the position ownership to `addr(0)`, fail the `end()` call of the challenge. At the end, the DoS in `end()` will have these impacts:

  * the successful bidder will lose bid fund.
  * the challenger’s collateral will be locked, and lose the challenge reward.

title: Position owners can deny liquidations
content: The vulnerability is an liquidation‑denial flaw that allows the owner of a position to prevent the protocol from liquidating that position by setting the reported price to the maximum uint256 value. The root cause is an unchecked arithmetic overflow in the function that evaluates whether a liquidation challenge can be averted; when the price is set to type(uint256).max, the calculation overflows and the call to tryAvertChallenge always reverts. An attacker can exploit this by calling the price‑adjustment function with the extreme value, after which any subsequent attempt by a challenger to bid on the liquidation or to end the challenge will fail with a revert. The impact is that the position remains under‑collateralized while the owner retains the synthetic asset (zchf) and the collateral becomes permanently locked, depriving challengers of their expected reward and breaking the protocol’s accounting guarantees. This condition occurs whenever a position owner can arbitrarily set the price, typically after a time delay, and chooses to use the maximum value, which may happen during market stress such as de‑pegs or runs on the bank. The affected parties include position owners who can abuse the bug, challengers who lose the ability to liquidate and claim rewards, and the overall protocol which loses confidence in its liquidation mechanism. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where a test case demonstrated that after adjusting the price to the maximum, calls to bid and end the challenge reverted, confirming the denial of liquidation. The bug is subtle because setting an extreme price may not be an obvious malicious action and the overflow manifests only in the internal liquidation logic, making it easy to miss in regular testing. To fix the problem, the contract should enforce a sensible upper bound on price values, use safe‑math checks that detect overflow before performing arithmetic, and ensure that the liquidation‑challenge routine can handle edge cases without reverting, thereby restoring the ability of challengers to liquidate under‑collateralized positions.
summary:
The owner of a vulnerable position can deny being liquidated by setting the price to be `type(uint256).max`, making every call to `tryAvertChallenge` fail due to an overflow.

This means that if it’s advantageous enough the owner can choose to keep `zchf` and leave the collateral stuck. This could happen in any scenario where a collateral is likely to loose it’s value, for example, de-pegs, runs on the bank, etc.

title: `CHALLENGER_REWARD` can be used to drain reserves and free mint
content: The vulnerability lies in the way the challenger reward is calculated and when a challenge can be launched. The protocol awards a CHALLENGER_REWARD equal to a percentage of the theoretical ZCHF volume that could be minted from the challenged collateral, where the volume is computed as price multiplied by the collateral size. Because the price of a Position can be set by its owner to an arbitrarily large value and the contract allows a challenge to be started immediately when the _challengeSeconds parameter is zero, an attacker can create a Position with an inflated price, launch a challenge before the position is considered valid, and then call the end() function. At the end of the challenge the reward formula (reward = volume * CHALLENGER_REWARD / 1_000_000) uses the inflated price, producing an enormous reward amount. If the reserve does not contain enough ZCHF to cover this reward, the protocol calls notifyLoss() which mints new ZCHF from thin air to satisfy the payment, effectively draining the reserve and creating an uncontrolled supply of tokens. From a user’s perspective the expected outcome is that the challenger receives back the small amount of collateral they posted, but instead they see a massive increase in their ZCHF balance while the reserve balance drops to zero and total supply spikes. The impact is a loss of economic backing for the token, potential de‑valuation of all holders, and the possibility for any attacker to empty the reserve in a single transaction. The issue occurs only when a Position can be opened with a very high price and when challenges are allowed before the position’s start time or when the challenge period is set to zero. It affects the protocol’s accounting assumptions that the reward is a modest percentage of a fair market price, breaking the invariant that ZCHF is always fully backed. The flaw was discovered during a security audit through systematic testing and a proof‑of‑concept script that demonstrated the reserve being drained and the total supply inflating to astronomic values. The problem is hard to notice because the reward percentage (2 %) looks harmless and the price parameter is not validated, so the reward calculation appears correct on the surface. To remediate the issue the protocol should restrict challenge initiation to only after a Position has a validated start time and a price that has not been artificially inflated, enforce a maximum change per price adjustment, cap the challenger reward to a safe absolute amount or to a percentage of the actual collateral value, and ensure that rewards are paid only from existing reserves without minting new tokens when the reserve is insufficient.
summary:
The goal of the auction mechanism is to determine the fair price of the collateral, so that Frankencoin (ZCHF) is always sufficiently backed and the system remains in balance.

If the challenge is successful, the bidder gets the collateral from the position and the position is closed, distributing excess proceeds to the reserve and paying a reward to the challenger.

The reward for the challenger is based on the user provided price and can be abused to have the protocol pay unlimited rewards.

title: Self-delgated users can have their delegation unknowingly hijacked during crowdfunding
content: The issue is an unintended delegation hijack that occurs when a contributor who has self‑delegated (by passing address(0) as the delegate) is later funded by a third party. The contract stores a delegationsByContributor entry that is initialised to address(0) for self‑delegation. In the internal _processContribution function the code checks "if (msg.sender == contributor || oldDelegate == address(0))" before updating the delegate. Because oldDelegate is zero for a self‑delegated user, the condition is true even when the caller is not the contributor. Consequently, an attacker who calls contribute on behalf of the victim can supply any delegate address, and the contract overwrites the victim’s self‑delegation with the attacker’s address. The root cause is the use of address(0) as both a sentinel for “no delegate” and as the signal for self‑delegation, combined with a permissive update rule that does not distinguish between a genuine owner‑initiated change and a third‑party contribution. Exploitation is straightforward: the attacker simply makes a minimal contribution for the target user, specifying their own address as the delegate. The impact is that the victim’s voting power, which would normally be attached to their own address or to a chosen delegate, is transferred to the attacker. In the ReraiseETHCrowdfund scenario, where party NFTs (and thus voting rights) are minted only after the crowdfund succeeds, the attacker can capture all of the newly minted votes, effectively stealing the user’s influence in the governance process. This bug is discovered during a security audit that examined the delegation logic and contribution flow. It can be hard to notice because the code appears to protect existing delegations by checking for a non‑zero oldDelegate, yet self‑delegation also results in a zero value, unintentionally satisfying the same condition. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after contributing with delegate set to zero, the user later finds that their NFTs are delegated to an unknown address, or that they receive no voting power despite having contributed the maximum amount. The expected behaviour is that a self‑delegated user retains control over their own votes, but the reality is that an attacker can hijack those votes. The vulnerability belongs to the class of delegation‑overwrite or authority‑confusion bugs, where a sentinel value is misinterpreted, allowing unauthorized state changes. To remediate, the contract should hard‑code self‑delegation by setting the delegate to the contributor’s own address when the supplied delegate is zero, and should reject delegate updates from callers that are not the contributor unless the existing delegate is already non‑zero, thereby preventing third‑party contributions from overwriting a self‑delegated entry.
summary: Self-delegation can be hijacked.

title: An attacker can contribute to the ETH crowdfund using a flash loan and control the party as he likes
content: The vulnerability is a flash‑loan‑enabled majority attack on the ETH crowdfund governance model. The contract calculates voting power directly from the amount of ETH contributed, and it finalises the crowdfund as soon as the total contributions reach the configured maximum. Because there is no cooldown or executionDelay enforced between finalisation and the ability to call the distribution function, an attacker can borrow a large amount of ETH in a single transaction, contribute it to the crowdfund, and cause the crowdfund to finalise in the same block. This extra contribution gives the attacker more than half of the total voting power (for example 55 % when contributing 10 ETH on top of an existing 10 ETH pool). With majority voting power the attacker can either submit a distribution proposal that executes immediately or, if the contract is configured to allow direct distribution without a vote, call the distribute() function directly in the same block. The attacker then withdraws a proportional share of the party’s ETH balance (e.g., 55 % of 19 ETH = 10.45 ETH), repays the flash loan and retains control over the party. From a user’s perspective the party balance suddenly drops, contributors see their expected refunds disappear, and the party’s funds appear to vanish. The issue occurs only when the party’s executionDelay is set to zero, which removes the intended waiting period before proposals can be executed. It was discovered during a formal audit when a test case demonstrated that the crowdfund could be finalised and funds distributed within a single block using a flash loan. The bug is hard to notice because the logic for finalisation and distribution appears correct in isolation, and the flash‑loan timing edge‑case is not obvious without explicit testing. The vulnerability belongs to the class of majority‑control and flash‑loan‑driven governance attacks, where economic power can be temporarily inflated to bypass intended safeguards. To remediate, the contract should enforce a cooldown after finalisation (e.g., store a partyStartedTime and require block.timestamp to exceed this value before allowing distribution), enforce a non‑zero executionDelay, and optionally require that all distributions go through a voted proposal, thereby preventing immediate fund extraction after a flash‑loan contribution.
summary: An attacker can have more than half of the total voting power using a flash loan and abuse other contributors.

title: Users wouldn’t refund from the lost ETH crowdfunds due to the lack of ETH
content: The vulnerability is a refund‑calculation error in the ETH crowdfund contract that can cause the contract to attempt to transfer more ether than it actually holds, causing the refund transaction to revert and leaving contributors unable to retrieve their funds. The root cause is a mismatch in rounding direction when the contract subtracts a funding‑split fee from a contribution and later adds the fee back during refund calculation. During contribution the fee amount is computed with integer division, which rounds down, and the net contribution is therefore rounded up. When a refund is processed the _calculateRefundAmount function multiplies the stored voting power by a factor and then divides by (1e4‑fundingSplitBps), effectively rounding up the fee component. This second rounding can produce a refund amount that is slightly larger than the original contribution, for example by one wei. When the crowdfund enters the Lost state and a contributor calls refund, the contract tries to send the inflated amount. Because the contract balance is only the actual contributed amount (which is lower by the rounding discrepancy), the transfer fails and the transaction reverts. The impact is that users see their refund calls revert, receive no ether, and their balances remain unchanged, contrary to the expectation that they would get back the exact amount they contributed. The issue occurs only when a funding split fee is configured (fundingSplitBps > 0) and the crowdfund has been marked as Lost, but it can affect any contributor because the rounding error is deterministic for the given fee percentage. The bug was discovered during a security audit that included a concrete test case reproducing the revert with a contribution of 1 ether‑1 wei and a 10 % fee. The problem is subtle because the contract’s balance appears correct at a glance, and the off‑by‑one error is hidden in integer arithmetic, making it hard to notice without precise accounting checks. To fix the issue the refund calculation should use the same rounding direction as the contribution subtraction, for example by applying the fee factor as amount * (1e4‑fundingSplitBps) / 1e4 when processing contributions and avoiding a second division that can round up. This ensures that the computed refund never exceeds the original contribution, preventing the contract from attempting to transfer more ether than it holds and restoring reliable refund behavior. The vulnerability belongs to the class of rounding‑error and accounting‑logic bugs that break financial invariants in smart contracts, leading to lost or locked funds and violating the protocol’s guarantee that contributors can retrieve their deposits after a failed crowdfund.
summary: After the ETH crowdfunds are lost, contributors wouldn’t refund their funds because the crowdfund contract doesn’t have enough ETH balance.

title: `ReraiseETHCrowdfund.sol`: Multiple scenarios how pending votes might not be claimable which is a complete loss of funds for a user
content: The vulnerability resides in the claim workflow of the ReraiseETHCrowdfund contract where a contributor’s pending voting power is converted back into an ETH contribution using a simple division by the exchange rate. This conversion ignores the funding fee that was deducted from the original contribution and also does not account for rounding effects, causing the derived contribution amount to fall outside the contract‑defined minimum and maximum contribution limits. When the calculated contribution exceeds maxContribution, the single‑claim function reverts with an AboveMaximumContributionsError; when it falls below minContribution, the multi‑claim function reverts with a BelowMinimumContributionsError. Because the contract enforces that all pending voting power must be claimed either in a single claim or split across multiple cards, a situation where the contribution cannot satisfy both bounds makes the claim permanently impossible. This can happen under normal, intended configurations of minContribution, maxContribution, minTotalContributions and maxTotalContributions, especially when a non‑zero fundingSplitBps fee is applied or when rounding losses occur. An attacker can deliberately contribute a small amount that pushes the victim’s pending voting power into a range that violates the bounds, effectively griefing the victim. The impact is that the affected user cannot retrieve their ETH, sees no tokens minted, and experiences transaction reverts, resulting in a complete loss of funds. The issue manifests after the crowdfund reaches the Finalized lifecycle and a contributor attempts to claim. It affects any participant who has pending voting power, the protocol’s economic guarantees, and the overall trustworthiness of the fundraising mechanism. The problem was discovered during a security audit by Code4rena through systematic testing of the claim functions with various parameter combinations, revealing that the invariant “contribution must lie within [minContribution, maxContribution]” is not preserved after fee deduction and rounding. The bug is subtle because the arithmetic appears correct at first glance and only fails for specific, non‑edge‑case configurations, making it hard to notice in casual testing. To remediate, the contribution calculation must be adjusted to add back the funding fee, ensuring the resulting amount respects the configured bounds, and the contract should either relax the claim‑blocking checks or enforce stricter configuration validation that guarantees a feasible claim path for any pending voting power. In broader terms, this is a parameter‑validation mismatch and rounding‑induced invariant violation that blocks a critical user‑facing operation, violating the expected business logic that contributors can always retrieve their funds after a successful crowdfund.
summary:
This issue is about how the [`ReraiseETHCrowdfund`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-party/blob/main/contracts/crowdfund/ReraiseETHCrowdfund.sol) claim functionality can be broken.

When the claim functionality is broken this means that a user cannot claim his voting power, resulting in a complete loss of funds.

The claim functionality is not broken in any case, i.e. with any configuration of the `ReraiseETHCrowdfund` contract.

However the contract can be configured in a way - and by configured I mean specifically the `minContribution`, `maxContribution`, `minTotalContributions` and `maxTotalContributions` variables - that the claim functionality breaks.

And the configurations under which it breaks are NOT edge cases. They represent the **intended use** of the contract as discussed with the sponsor.

The fact that when the contract is used as intended it can lead to a complete loss of funds for the users makes me estimate this to be “High” severity.

title: `ReraiseETHCrowdfund.sol`: party card transfer can be front-run by claiming pending voting power which results in a loss of the voting power
content: The vulnerability is a front‑run authorization flaw in the ReraiseETHCrowdfund.claim function that permits any address to claim pending voting power on behalf of any contributor and to add that power to an existing party card owned by the contributor. The root cause is that the function does not restrict the caller to the contributor when the caller supplies a non‑zero tokenId and the party card owner matches the contributor; it only checks that the caller is the owner of the token if the token already belongs to the contributor, but it does not require msg.sender to be the contributor. An attacker can exploit this by observing that a victim has pending voting power in the crowdfund and is about to transfer one of their party cards. The attacker front‑runs the victim’s transfer transaction, calls claim with the victim’s address as the contributor and the tokenId of the card that will be transferred, and thereby adds the pending voting power to that card before the transfer completes. When the victim’s transfer later executes, the card (now owned by the attacker) carries the voting power that originally belonged to the victim, leaving the victim with a transferred card that has no voting power. The impact is a loss of governance weight for the victim, which can be used as a griefing attack or, if the attacker is the recipient, as a direct gain of voting power. The attack can occur whenever a contributor has pending voting power (i.e., after a successful crowdfund) and initiates a transfer of a party card before the pending votes are claimed, and the attacker can submit a transaction that finalizes the crowdfund and calls claim before the transfer is mined. All users who hold party cards and have unclaimed voting power are affected, as voting power is the core asset of the Party protocol’s governance model. The issue was discovered during a security audit when the auditors wrote a test that demonstrated the front‑run scenario. It is hard to notice because the claim function appears to be a benign utility for contributors, and the loss of voting power only becomes visible after a transfer, which may be attributed to other reasons. The recommended fix is to restrict claim so that adding voting power to an existing card is only allowed when the caller is the contributor (msg.sender == contributor) or to disallow adding to existing cards altogether and always mint a new party card on claim. This aligns with the generic class of bugs where a function that should be limited to a privileged actor lacks proper access control, leading to asset misallocation. From the user’s perspective, they expect that after transferring a party card they retain the same amount of voting power, but instead the transferred card arrives with zero votes and the user’s governance weight disappears, violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions that pending voting power remains attached to the contributor until they claim it themselves.
summary:
In this report I show how an attacker can abuse the fact that anyone can call [`ReraiseETHCrowdfund.claim`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-party/blob/440aafacb0f15d037594cebc85fd471729bcb6d9/contracts/crowdfund/ReraiseETHCrowdfund.sol#L251-L303) for any user and add voting power to an existing party card.

The result can be a griefing attack whereby the victim loses voting power. In some cases the attacker can take advantage himself.

In short this is what needs to happen:

1. The victim sends a transaction to transfer one of his party cards
2. The transaction is front-run and pending voting power of the victim from the `ReraiseETHCrowdfund` contract is claimed to this party card that is transferred
3. The victim thereby loses the pending voting power

The fact that any user is at risk that has pending voting power and transfers a party card and that voting power is arguably the most important asset in the protocol makes me estimate this to be “High” severity.

title: `ETHCrowdfundBase.sol`: `totalVotingPower` is increased too much in the `_finalize` function
content: The vulnerability originates from the way the ETHCrowdfundBase contract updates the party's total voting power during finalisation. When a contributor sends ETH, the contract first deducts a funding fee and then calculates the contributor's individual voting power based on the net amount. However, the totalContributions variable that is later used to compute the party's total voting power is increased by the gross amount before the fee is subtracted. Consequently, the call to PartyGovernanceNFT.increaseTotalVotingPower adds an amount that reflects the full contributions rather than the net contributions that actually generated voting power. This mismatch inflates the total voting power stored in the governance contract while each user's recorded voting power is lower. The inflated total makes it mathematically impossible for the sum of all users' voting power to ever equal the reported total, meaning a unanimous vote – which is required for proposal execution – can never be reached. The issue appears only after the crowdfund is finalised and the fee is transferred, so it may be difficult to notice during normal operation because the total voting power is a hidden internal value. Users experience symptoms such as being unable to pass proposals despite holding what appears to be sufficient voting power, or seeing their votes count for less than expected. The impact is that proposals become dead‑locked, potentially locking funds or preventing protocol upgrades. The bug is a classic accounting inconsistency where a global aggregate is calculated from raw inputs while the per‑account values are derived from adjusted inputs, violating the invariant that total voting power equals the sum of individual voting powers. It was discovered during a security audit by reproducing the scenario with a test that contributed two accounts, each paying a 10 % fee, and observing that the contract reported a total voting power of 2 e18 while the two accounts together only held 1.8 e18. The recommended fix is to compute the new total voting power using the net contribution amount – i.e., subtract the funding fee from totalContributions before applying the exchange rate – ensuring that the aggregate matches the sum of the users' voting power and restoring the ability to achieve unanimous decisions.
summary:
This issue is about how the [`ETHCrowdfundBase._finalize`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-party/blob/440aafacb0f15d037594cebc85fd471729bcb6d9/contracts/crowdfund/ETHCrowdfundBase.sol#L273-L292) functions calls [`PartyGovernanceNFT.increaseTotalVotingPower`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-party/blob/440aafacb0f15d037594cebc85fd471729bcb6d9/contracts/party/PartyGovernanceNFT.sol#L193-L197) with an amount that does not reflect the sum of the individual users’ voting power.

Thereby it will become impossible to reach unanimous votes. In other words and more generally the users’ votes are worth less than they should be as the percentage is calculated against a total amount that is too big.

In short, this is how the issue is caused:

1. The voting power that a user receives is based on the amount they contribute MINUS funding fees
2. The amount of voting power by which `totalVotingPower` is increased is based on the total contributions WITHOUT subtracting funding fees

title: `InitialETHCrowdfund` + `ReraiseETHCrowdfund`: `batchContributeFor` function may not refund ETH which leads to loss of funds
content: The vulnerability resides in the batchContributeFor wrapper used by both the InitialETHCrowdfund and ReraiseETHCrowdfund contracts. The function is designed to forward a series of individual contributeFor calls while tracking the amount of ether that remains available for refund. The implementation subtracts the intended contribution amount from the local ethAvailable variable before each call, regardless of whether the call succeeds. When a contribution fails and the caller has set the revertOnFailure flag to false, the function does not revert the transaction and also does not restore the deducted amount to ethAvailable. Consequently, the final refund step only returns the ether that remained after the premature deductions, leaving the failed contribution amount permanently lost to the caller. The root cause is an accounting error: the contract assumes that all forwarded ether will be consumed, but it fails to roll back the accounting state on partial failure. An attacker or a careless user can trigger the bug by including at least one contribution that violates the minimum contribution requirement or any other condition that makes contributeFor revert, while explicitly disabling automatic reverts. Under these conditions the transaction appears successful, no error is emitted, but the caller’s balance is reduced by the amount of the failed contribution. The impact is a direct loss of user funds; the user may see their wallet balance drop unexpectedly, often to zero, even though the transaction receipt shows success. The issue affects any participant who uses batchContributeFor with revertOnFailure set to false, as well as the overall protocol because the accounting of total contributions becomes inaccurate. It was discovered during a security audit when a test case demonstrated that a sender who supplied 2.5 ether and included a failing contribution ended with a zero ether balance. The bug is subtle because the contract does not emit a revert or explicit error, making the loss appear as a silent shortfall rather than a failed transaction. The class of bug is an improper handling of partial failures in batch operations, specifically a refund logic error where deducted funds are not restored on failure. To remediate, the contract should only decrement ethAvailable after a successful contribution or should add the amount back to ethAvailable when a call fails, ensuring that any unused ether is correctly refunded to the caller. This change restores the intended accounting guarantees and prevents silent loss of funds.
summary:
This vulnerability exists in both the [`InitialETHCrowdfund`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-party/blob/main/contracts/crowdfund/InitialETHCrowdfund.sol) and [`ReraiseETHCrowdfund`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-party/blob/main/contracts/crowdfund/ReraiseETHCrowdfund.sol) contracts in exactly the same way.

I will continue this report by explaining the issue in only one contract. The mitigation section however contains the fix for both instances.

The [`batchContributeFor`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-party/blob/440aafacb0f15d037594cebc85fd471729bcb6d9/contracts/crowdfund/InitialETHCrowdfund.sol#L235-L268) function is a wrapper that allows to make multiple calls to `contributeFor` within one function call.

It is possible to specify that this function should not revert when one individual call to `contributeFor` fails by setting `args.revertOnFailure=false`.

The issue is that in this case the ETH for a failed contribution is not refunded which leads a loss of funds for the user calling the function.

Note:  
This issue also exists in the [`Crowdfund.batchContributeFor`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-party/blob/440aafacb0f15d037594cebc85fd471729bcb6d9/contracts/crowdfund/Crowdfund.sol#L367-L385) function which is out of scope. The sponsor knows about this and will fix it.

title: `VetoProposal`: User can veto multiple times so every proposal can be vetoed by any user that has a small amount of votes
content: The VetoProposal contract implements a veto mechanism where participants can call voteToVeto to add their voting power toward a threshold defined as a percentage of the party's total voting power. The contract does not record whether a particular address has already contributed to the veto count for a given proposal. Because of this missing has‑voted check, the same participant can invoke voteToVeto repeatedly, each call adding the full amount of their voting power again. An attacker who controls even a modest fraction of the total voting power (for example 1 % when the pass threshold is 10 %) can simply submit enough consecutive veto transactions to reach or exceed the required threshold, causing the proposal status to change from Voting to Defeated. The exploit works whenever the contract is in the Voting state and the caller is able to send multiple transactions before the proposal is finalized. The immediate impact is that any proposal can be blocked by a single user, effectively freezing the party's governance and preventing execution of approved actions. Users observing the UI will see proposals that should remain active suddenly marked as Defeated, with no indication that the veto came from multiple votes by the same address; they may expect a collective community decision but instead see a single participant silently vetoing. The issue was discovered during a code audit that examined the voteToVeto logic and noticed the absence of a per‑address tracking variable. It can be hard to notice in testing because a single address can still reach the threshold in a controlled environment, and the contract does not emit an event distinguishing repeated votes from distinct voters. The bug belongs to the class of “multiple‑vote” or “replay” vulnerabilities where state is not properly guarded against duplicate actions. The correct mitigation is to introduce a mapping that records, for each party, proposal and voter, whether the voter has already cast a veto, and to reject subsequent calls with an AlreadyVoted error. This ensures that each participant's voting power is counted at most once, preserving the intended quorum logic and preventing a single user from unilaterally disabling proposals.
summary:
The [`VetoProposal`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-party/blob/440aafacb0f15d037594cebc85fd471729bcb6d9/contracts/proposals/VetoProposal.sol#L8-L69) contract allows to veto proposals with the [`voteToVeto`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-04-party/blob/440aafacb0f15d037594cebc85fd471729bcb6d9/contracts/proposals/VetoProposal.sol#L19-L60) function.

When the amount of votes collected to veto a proposal exceeds a certain threshold (the `passThresholdBps`, which is determined upon initialization of the party), the proposal is vetoed, meaning it cannot execute anymore (its status becomes `Defeated`).

The `passThresholdBps` specifies a percentage of the `totalVotingPower` of the party.

E.g. `passThresholdBps=1000` means that 10% of the `totalVotingPower` must veto a proposal such that the veto goes through.

The issue is that the contract lacks the obvious check that a user has not vetoed before, thereby a user can veto multiple times.

So say a user holds 1% of `totalVotingPower` and in order for the veto to go through, 10% of `totalVotingPower` must veto.

The user can just veto 10 times to reach the 10% requirement.

The impact is obvious: Any user with a small amount of votes can veto any proposal. This is a critical bug since the party may become unable to perform any actions if there is a user that vetoes all proposals.

title: `RubiconMarket._buys` will not work for V1 offers due to the reversion in `cancel` method.
content: The vulnerability occurs in the RubiconMarket contract when the internal _buys function attempts to clean up a small remaining amount of the pay token (dust) after a partial fill of an offer. For V1 offers the owner field is deliberately set to the zero address, and the market expects the cancel routine to refund the remaining pay amount to the original recipient. However, RubiconMarket._buys triggers SimpleMarket.cancel with the caller (the buyer) as msg.sender, not the original recipient. SimpleMarket.cancel contains a conditional that checks whether the caller is the recipient; when the condition is false it treats the offer as a V2 offer and tries to transfer the dust amount to the owner address. Because the owner is address(0) for V1 offers, the ERC20 transfer call reverts (OpenZeppelin ERC20 blocks transfers to the null address).
