```solidity
[`VeryFastRouter::swap`](https://github.com/sudoswap/lssvm2/blob/78d38753b2042d7813132f26e5573c6699b605ef/src/VeryFastRouter.sol#L266) is the main entry point for a user to perform a batch of sell and buy orders on the new Sudoswap router, allowing partial fill conditions to be specified. Sell orders are executed first, followed by buy orders. The `LSSVMPair` contracts themselves are implemented in such a way that re-entrancy is not possible, but the same is not true of the `VeryFastRouter`. Assuming a user calls `VeryFastRouter::swap`, selling some NFTs and passing in some additional ETH value for subsequent buy orders, an attacker can re-enter this function under certain conditions to steal the original caller's funds. Given that this function does not check whether the user input contains valid pairs, an attacker can use this to manipulate the return values of `LSSVMPair::swapNFTsForToken` and `LSSVMPair::swapTokenForSpecificNFTs`, which interferes with internal accounting. In this way, the attacker can make it appear that a buy/sell order input/output more/less value than expected.

Consider the case where the attacker is a malicious royalty recipient, and their re-entrant swap order contains a single sell order and an empty array of buy orders. Calling out to their malicious pair gives control over the [`outputAmount`](https://github.com/sudoswap/lssvm2/blob/78d38753b2042d7813132f26e5573c6699b605ef/src/VeryFastRouter.sol#L296) value which is used in addition assignment to the [virtual balance](https://github.com/sudoswap/lssvm2/blob/78d38753b2042d7813132f26e5573c6699b605ef/src/VeryFastRouter.sol#L301-L302) `ethAmount` used to [transfer any remaining ETH](https://github.com/sudoswap/lssvm2/blob/78d38753b2042d7813132f26e5573c6699b605ef/src/VeryFastRouter.sol#L482-L486) after all orders have been executed, filled partially or otherwise. The current contract balance is the original caller's remaining ETH value, so the attacker would intend to have their malicious pair return this amount to drain the funds. However, without the introduction of a malicious pair contract to both the attacker's re-entrant order and the original caller's order, the attacker is prevented from stealing the remaining intermediate funds due to the safe ETH transfer of `ethAmount` as this will cause the original caller's transaction to revert at this same line - the contract is attempting to transfer balance that it no longer has. If this had instead been a transfer of the contract balance directly rather than a virtual balance, then the attacker could succeed in stealing the user's funds without baiting them into making a call to their malicious pair. Of course, calling a malicious pair allows it to steal any funds sent with the call, but given that this can manipulate internal accounting through an incorrect return value, as described above, calling this pair can impact other swap orders/partial fills, tricking the contract into thinking it has fewer funds than it does during the lifetime of the original caller's transaction such that the attacker can re-enter and make away with their ETH. Otherwise, the extent of this vulnerability is a DoS attack on calls to the router.

The steps to perform this exploit are as follows:

* Trick the caller into including an order on the attacker's malicious pair.
* The attacker re-enters, passing an order of sell orders and calling back to their malicious pair contract due to unvalidated user input. This inflates the `outputAmount`, which in turn inflates the `ethAmount` for their call.
* Excess ETH is sent to the attacker.
* The malicious pair manipulates `ethAmount` by returning a large `inputAmount`.
* Original caller has any additional partial buy orders fail to fill and receives no ETH in return for selling their NFTs.

The second exploit case is where the caller specifies the router contract as their token recipient, performing DIY recycle ETH functionality of sorts for subsequent buy orders, likely with zero input `msg.value`. This would allow an attacker to steal intermediate balances by re-entering the final sell order before any funds are consumed by buy orders, as these funds are not tracked by `ethAmount`, and so the final transfer will not revert. Independent of a malicious royalty recipient, this also means that any excess ETH sent not consumed by subsequent buy orders will remain locked in the contract if the caller specifies the router contract as their token recipient. Pool funds are safe due to the use of the factory re-entrancy guard, which prohibits calling into any of the pair swap functions that are responsible for transfers to the router. ETH value sent with ERC-20-based swaps due to user misconfiguration is also vulnerable in the case of malicious royalty recipient.
```
This vulnerability results in the loss of user funds, with high impact and medium likelihood, so we evaluate the severity to HIGH.

title: Linearity assumption on the royalty can lead to denial of service
content: The vulnerability originates from an incorrect assumption in the VeryFastRouter contract that the royalty amount returned by an external royalty information provider is linear with respect to the sale amount. The router’s internal binary‑search functions (_findMaxFillableAmtForSell and _findMaxFillableAmtForBuy) calculate a value called priceToFillAt, which is later passed as the minimum expected output to the pair’s swapNFTsForToken function. Line 598 subtracts a royalty amount from the current output using a simple linear formula (currentOutput -= currentOutput * royaltyAmount / BASE). If the royalty provider returns a royalty that varies non‑linearly—for example, higher royalties for larger sales or rounding‑induced step changes—the linear subtraction under‑estimates the true royalty cost. Consequently, priceToFillAt is set higher than the amount that can actually be obtained from the bonding curve. When the swap is executed, the pair contract checks that the actual output meets or exceeds priceToFillAt; because the estimate is too optimistic, the check fails and the transaction reverts. This manifests to the user as a failed swap where no tokens are received despite having sufficient NFT assets, effectively a denial‑of‑service condition. The issue occurs whenever a collection uses a royalty lookup that does not conform to the EIP‑2981 linearity guarantee, such as the KODAV2 royalty implementation where rounding creates a piecewise‑linear royalty curve. Both honest users and liquidity providers are affected because any legitimate sell or buy order that relies on the faulty priceToFillAt calculation will be rejected, leading to lost trading opportunities and potential loss of confidence in the protocol. The bug was discovered during a security audit that examined the router’s handling of royalty data and identified the linearity assumption as undocumented and unsafe. It is hard to notice because the royalty provider is an external contract; the router does not validate the shape of the returned royalty, and the binary‑search loop silently accepts the linear estimate. To remediate, the router should query the exact royalty amount for the specific sale quantity and use that precise value in the price calculation, or otherwise remove the linearity shortcut and incorporate a safe fallback that validates the royalty curve before proceeding. By aligning the royalty computation with the actual data, the protocol restores correct minimum‑output checks, prevents unnecessary reverts, and eliminates the denial‑of‑service vector caused by malicious or poorly‑implemented royalty providers.

title: DPCU-1 | priceImpactDiffUsd Unclaimable For Adjusted PnL
content: The vulnerability concerns the handling of a trader’s profit‑and‑loss (PnL) when a position is closed and a price‑impact fee, expressed as priceImpactDiffUsd, must be deducted from the realised PnL. The contract computes an adjustedPositionPnlUsd value that represents the PnL remaining after the price‑impact deduction. If the raw positionPnlUsd is positive but smaller than the required priceImpactDiffUsd, the logic forces adjustedPositionPnlUsd to zero. The subsequent step that makes any amount claimable for the user checks the condition adjustedPositionPnlUsd > 0 before calling incrementClaimableCollateralAmount. Because adjustedPositionPnlUsd is forced to zero in the described scenario, the condition fails and the contract never records the portion of PnL that was actually used to cover part of the price‑impact fee. Consequently, the user’s claimable collateral does not increase even though part of their PnL was consumed, leaving the user unable to withdraw the expected funds. This situation occurs only when priceImpactDiffUsd exceeds positionPnlUsd while the latter is still positive – a narrow edge case that can be missed during normal testing because the overall accounting balances and no explicit error is thrown. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a successful position close, but the expected refund or profit amount is missing, the claimable balance remains zero, and the user may see “no funds received” or “balance unchanged” after the transaction. The issue was discovered during a targeted audit where a proof‑of‑concept test reproduced the condition and demonstrated that the claimable amount stayed at zero. The bug belongs to the class of accounting‑logic errors where a conditional guard prevents a state update, effectively making earned funds unclaimable. To remediate the problem the contract should either relax the guard to adjustedPositionPnlUsd >= 0 or invoke the claimable‑collateral increment directly whenever the PnL is reduced by the price‑impact fee, ensuring that any portion of PnL used for the fee is still accounted for as claimable to the user.
summary: If the positionPnlUsd is positive but smaller than the priceImpactDiffUsd, the adjustedPositionPnlUsd is set to 0. However the condition for accounting for the pnlDiffAmount and making that amount claimable for the user is dependent on adjustedPositionPnlUsd > 0. Therefore, cases where the priceImpactDiffUsd cannot be entirely fulfilled by the positionPnlUsd result in the user being unable to claim their pnl that was used to cover a portion of the priceImpactDiffUsd.

title: Protocol's invariants can be broken
content: The vulnerability consists of a broken mathematical invariant in the constant‑function automated market maker implementation. The protocol assumes that at any moment the total amount of LP tokens reported by the contract (totalSupply) is exactly equal to the value returned by the well function that calculates the LP supply from the current token reserves (calcLpTokenSupply). Because the calculation functions do not specify a deterministic rounding direction, the two values can diverge after normal operations such as swaps or liquidity removal. When the invariant is violated, the removeLiquidity logic, which relies on the ratio of lpAmountIn to totalSupply, can produce token output amounts that are mathematically inconsistent with the actual reserves. This inconsistency manifests as under‑ or overflow errors, causing valid removal transactions to revert, LP balances to be burned without receiving the expected token amounts, and in extreme cases rendering the pool insolvent. The issue appears after a series of swaps that change the reserve ratios, especially when the last token in a multi‑token pool is withdrawn, because the contract calculates the output for the first n‑1 tokens using one formula and the final token using another that suffers from rounding mismatch. All liquidity providers, the protocol’s accounting layer, and any users attempting to withdraw funds are affected. The bug was discovered during a formal audit by Cyfrin, which added assertions that totalSupply must equal calcLpTokenSupply and observed mismatches in unit tests that logged differing values and caused arithmetic underflow. The problem is hard to notice because the differences are on the order of a few units in very large numbers, and the contract does not emit explicit error messages for invariant violations. To remediate, the contract should enforce a consistent rounding direction by adding a flag to the calculation functions, handle the final token withdrawal with the same rounding logic as the other tokens, and either relax the invariant to totalSupply >= calcLpTokenSupply or maintain a separate variable that always reflects the calculated supply for use in withdrawal calculations. By aligning the mathematical model with the on‑chain state, the protocol can prevent unexpected reverts, ensure that users receive the correct token amounts, and preserve overall solvency.
summary:
The protocol intends to provide a generalized framework for constant-function AMM liquidity pools.
We have identified some invariants that should hold at any given time. One of these invariants is `totalSupply() == calcLpTokenSupply(reserves)`, and we can interpret this as the pool's total LP supply should match the calculation of LP from the current `reserves` state values.

This invariant can be broken with valid transactions in the current implementation, leading to several problems. For example, valid liquidity removal might revert, as shown in the PoC test below.

The impact is HIGH because this discrepancy will lead to protocol insolvency (revert on valid transactions).

title: Each Well is responsible for ensuring that an `update` call cannot be made with a reserve of 0
content: An issue exists in the GeoEmaAndCumSmaPump component used by Beanstalk wells. The pump records a geometric exponential moving average (EMA) and a cumulative geometric simple moving average (SMA) for each token reserve. The implementation contains a comment that assumes every call to update() will be supplied with a non‑zero reserve value and that a zero reserve would set the geometric mean to zero. However, the Well contract does not enforce this assumption; it can legitimately call update() with a reserve of zero, for example after a remove‑liquidity‑one‑token operation that empties one side of the pool. When a zero reserve is passed, the pump silently writes zero into the EMA and SMA storage, causing the price oracle that reads these values to report a price of zero or otherwise distorted values. This distortion can be triggered by a normal user transaction and does not revert, making it exploitable by an attacker who can deliberately drive a reserve to zero and then rely on the corrupted oracle to manipulate downstream contracts that depend on the price feed. The impact includes incorrect price information, potential loss of funds for users who trade against a corrupted oracle, and increased MEV opportunities. The bug is discovered during a security audit by Cyfrin, where a test case demonstrated that after a series of swaps and a removal of liquidity, the second token reserve becomes zero and the subsequent pump update succeeds without reverting. The problem is hard to notice because a zero reserve may be a rare state and the contract does not emit an error; the only symptom is an unexpected zero or wildly inaccurate price. The correct mitigation is to add an explicit check in the pump’s update routine that reverts when any reserve argument is zero, thereby preventing the geometric mean from being set to zero and preserving the integrity of the oracle. In abstract terms, the vulnerability belongs to the class of invalid input handling leading to silent state corruption where a mathematical invariant (reserve > 0 for geometric mean) is violated without protection.
summary:
The current implementation of `GeoEmaAndCumSmaPump` assumes each well will call `update()` with non-zero reserves, as commented at the beginning of the file:
```solidity
/**
 * @title GeoEmaAndCumSmaPump
 * @author Publius
 * @notice Stores a geometric EMA and cumulative geometric SMA for each reserve.
 * @dev A Pump designed for use in Beanstalk with 2 tokens.
 *
 * This Pump has 3 main features:
 *  1. Multi-block MEV resistence reserves
 *  2. MEV-resistant Geometric EMA intended for instantaneous reserve queries
 *  3. MEV-resistant Cumulative Geometric intended for SMA reserve queries
 *
 * Note: If an `update` call is made with a reserve of 0, the Geometric mean oracles will be set to 0.
 * Each Well is responsible for ensuring that an `update` call cannot be made with a reserve of 0.
 */
```

However, there is no actual requirement in `Well` to enforce pump updates with valid reserve values. Given that `GeoEmaAndCumSmaPump` restricts values to a minimum of 1 to prevent issues with the geometric mean, that the TWA values are not truly representative of the reserves in the Well, we believe it is worse than reverting in this case, although a `ConstantProduct2` Well can have zero reserves for either token via valid transactions.
```solidity
for (uint i; i < length; ++i) {
    // Use a minimum of 1 for reserve. Geometric means will be set to 0 if a reserve is 0.
    b.lastReserves[i] =
        _capReserve(b.lastReserves[i], (reserves[i] > 0 ? reserves[i] : 1).fromUIntToLog2(), blocksPassed);
    b.emaReserves[i] = b.lastReserves[i].mul((ABDKMathQuad.ONE.sub(aN))).add(b.emaReserves[i].mul(aN));
    b.cumulativeReserves[i] = b.cumulativeReserves[i].add(b.lastReserves[i].mul(deltaTimestampBytes));
}
```

Updating pumps with zero reserve values can lead to the distortion of critical states likely to be utilized for price oracles. Given that the issue is exploitable through valid transactions, we assess the severity as HIGH. It is crucial to note that attackers can exploit this vulnerability to manipulate the price oracle.

title: `removeLiquidity` logic is not correct for generalized Well functions other than ConstantProduct
content: The vulnerability lies in the removeLiquidity function of the Well contract. It assumes that the amount of each reserve token returned to a liquidity provider is directly proportional to the fraction of LP tokens being burned (Δx = l/L * x, Δy = l/L * y). This proportionality holds for the constant‑product well function because the invariant is linear in the reserves, but it does not hold for general well functions that are non‑linear, such as the quadratic well used by Numoen. Because the contract does not query the well function when calculating the withdrawal amounts, it applies a fixed linear formula regardless of the underlying invariant. As a result, when a provider removes liquidity from a pool that uses a non‑linear well function, the token amounts returned are mis‑computed, the pool’s invariant is violated, and the total value of the reserves can be altered. In the demonstrated test, after adding liquidity the invariant remains zero, but after a normal removeLiquidity call the invariant becomes a large positive number, indicating that the pool’s accounting no longer matches the mathematical definition of the well. This can be exploited by an attacker who first adds liquidity to a pool with a non‑linear well function and then withdraws using the buggy removeLiquidity, effectively extracting more tokens than the protocol’s economics allow. The impact is a loss of funds for liquidity providers and a breach of the protocol’s core accounting guarantees. The bug manifests only when the pool is instantiated with a well function that does not satisfy the linearity assumption; for constant‑product pools the issue is invisible, making it easy to miss during casual testing. The vulnerability was discovered during a security audit by constructing a mock quadratic well and observing the invariant after removal. Because the UI typically shows the expected token balances after withdrawal, the underlying invariant violation may go unnoticed until a deeper invariant check is performed. The proper fix is to extend the IWellFunction interface with a method that, given an amount of LP tokens to burn, returns the exact reserve amounts that should be withdrawn, and to use this method inside removeLiquidity (or to redesign removeLiquidity to delegate the entire calculation to the well function). This change restores correctness for any well function, preserving the invariant and protecting user funds.
summary:
The protocol intends to provide a generalized framework for constant-function AMM liquidity pools where various Well functions can be used. Currently, only the constant-product type Well function is defined, but we understand that more general Well functions are intended to be supported.

The current implementation of `Well::removeLiquidity` and `Well::getRemoveLiquidityOut` assumes linearity while getting the output token amount from the LP token amount to withdraw. This holds well for the constant product type, as seen below. If we denote the total supply of LP tokens as $L$, the reserve values for the two tokens as $x, y$, and the invariant is $L^2=4xy$ for `ConstantProduct2`.
When removing liquidity of amount $l$, the output amounts are calculated as $\Delta x=\frac{l}{L}x, \Delta y=\frac{l}{L}y$. It is straightforward to verify that the invariant still holds after withdrawal, i.e., $(L-l)^2=(x-\Delta x)(y-\Delta y)$.

But in general, this kind of _linearity_ is not guaranteed to hold.

Recently, non-linear (quadratic) function AMMs have been introduced by some new protocols (see [Numoen](https://numoen.gitbook.io/numoen/)). If we use this kind of Well function, the current calculation of `tokenAmountsOut` will break the Well's invariant.

For your information, the Numoen protocol checks the protocol's invariant (the constant function itself) after every transaction.

The current `Well::removeLiquidity` logic assumes a specific condition on the Well function (linearity in some sense). This limits the generalization of the protocol as opposed to its original purpose. Given that this will lead to loss of funds for the liquidity providers for general Well functions, we evaluate the severity to HIGH.

title: Read-only reentrancy
content: The vulnerability is a read‑only reentrancy flaw in the removeLiquidity function of the Well contract. The function updates the internal reserve accounting only after it has transferred token amounts to the caller. Because the contract calls external token contracts (via safeTransfer) before setting the new reserve values, a malicious token that implements the ERC‑777 hooks can execute a callback during the transfer. The callback can invoke getReserves on the Well while the reserves are still reflecting the pre‑transfer state. This violates the Checks‑Effects‑Interactions pattern: the effect (updating reserves) is performed after the interaction (token transfer). The root cause is the ordering of state updates relative to external calls. An attacker can deploy a Well with a callback‑enabled token, add liquidity, and then call removeLiquidity. During the token transfer, the callback reads stale reserves and can feed them to price‑pump contracts that rely on getReserves, causing the pump to compute incorrect prices or manipulate on‑chain oracle values. From a user perspective the symptoms may include unexpected zero or dramatically altered reserve values displayed in the UI, refunds that are lower than expected, or a situation where a user expects to receive a certain amount of tokens but receives none. The impact ranges from incorrect pricing and potential loss of value for liquidity providers to broader protocol risk if downstream oracle‑dependent contracts trust the manipulated price data. The issue was discovered during a security audit by Cyfrin, which added a test harness that deployed a mock ERC‑777 token with a fallback that called getReserves, demonstrating that the reserves read as zero before the transfer and as the full amount after, confirming the re‑entrancy window. Because the re‑entrancy is read‑only, it does not revert the transaction and therefore can be subtle and hard to notice in normal operation. The vulnerability belongs to the class of read‑only re‑entrancy bugs where state is read before it is correctly updated, breaking the Checks‑Effects‑Interactions pattern. The recommended mitigation is to move the reserve update before any external token transfer, i.e., follow the Checks‑Effects‑Interactions pattern, ensuring that getReserves always returns the post‑transfer state. Updating reserves first eliminates the window where a callback can observe stale data, thereby protecting price pumps and oracle calculations.
summary:
The current implementation is vulnerable to read-only reentrancy, especially in [Wells::removeLiquidity](https://github.com/BeanstalkFarms/Wells/blob/e5441fc78f0fd4b77a898812d0fd22cb43a0af55/src/Well.sol#L440).
The implementation does not strictly follow the [Checks-Effects-Interactions (CEI) pattern](https://fravoll.github.io/solidity-patterns/checks_effects_interactions.html) as it is setting the new reserve values after sending out the tokens. This is not an immediate risk to the protocol itself due to the `nonReentrant` modifier, but this is still vulnerable to [read-only reentrancy](https://chainsecurity.com/curve-lp-oracle-manipulation-post-mortem/).

Malicious attackers and unsuspecting ecosystem participants can deploy Wells with ERC-777 tokens (which have a callback that can take control) and exploit this vulnerability. This will lead to critical vulnerabilities given that the Wells are to be extended with price functions as defined by pumps - third-party protocols that integrate these on-chain oracles will be at risk.

Pumps are updated before token transfers; however, reserves are only set after. Therefore, pump functions will likely be incorrect on a re-entrant read-only call if `IWell(well).getReserves()` is called but reserves have not been correctly updated. The implementation of `GeoEmaAndCumSmaPump` appears not to be vulnerable, but given that each pump can choose its approach for recording a well's reserves over time, this remains a possible attack vector.

Although this is not an immediate risk to the protocol itself, read-only re-entrancy can lead to critical issues, so we evaluate the severity as HIGH.

title: Possible reentrancy during redemption/swap
content: The vulnerability is a reentrancy flaw that can be triggered during the redemption or swap operations of the transmuter contract. The root cause is that the contract transfers collateral tokens to the caller inside a loop after burning the agToken, but it does not protect the function with a reentrancy guard and it performs external calls (ERC777 token hooks or LibManager.release) before all internal accounting variables are fully updated. Because ERC777 tokens invoke a recipient hook on transfer, a malicious contract can execute a second redemption call from within that hook while the first redemption is still in progress. The protocol’s normalizer is updated only once for the total amount being redeemed, and the second call sees a stale view of the remaining collateral balances, causing the calculation of the second payout to be based on an incorrect pool size. As a result the attacker can receive more collateral than entitled, effectively draining assets from the pool. This issue manifests when a user redeems agToken for collaterals that include a token with a callback mechanism, or when a managed collateral release triggers an external call. From the user’s perspective the symptom is that a redemption that should return a certain amount of collateral instead returns a larger amount, or that the protocol’s total collateral balance unexpectedly decreases. The impact is a loss of funds for the protocol and any other token holders, breaking the accounting guarantees of the system. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the flow of external calls inside the redemption logic and identified that the contract assumed no callbacks would occur. It is hard to notice because most ERC20 tokens do not have hooks, so standard testing may not reveal the reentrancy path. The recommended mitigation is to apply the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern or, more simply, to add a nonReentrant modifier to the redeem and swap functions, ensuring that no second entry can occur until the first call finishes, or to restrict the set of accepted collateral tokens to those without callback capabilities.
summary: Redeemers might charge more collaterals during redemption/swap by the reentrancy attack.

title: The first disputer might lose funds although his dispute is valid
content: The vulnerability is a race‑condition and state‑overwrite bug in thedispute mechanism of the contract. The contract is designed to allow a single user to lock a fixed amount of tokens as a deposit when calling disputeTree, storing the caller address in a single variable called disputer. The business rule is that while a dispute is active, no other dispute should be accepted, and when the governor later calls resolveDispute with a flag indicating the dispute is valid, the stored disputer should receive the deposited tokens back. However, the implementation does not enforce the single‑dispute invariant: disputeTree can be invoked again even when disputer is already set. A second caller can therefore overwrite the disputer address before resolveDispute is executed. If an attacker observes a legitimate dispute transaction and front‑runs it with their own disputeTree call, the contract will record the attacker as the current disputer. When the governor finally resolves the dispute as valid, the refund is sent to the attacker, while the original, valid disputer loses the deposit despite having a correct claim. This can be exploited by any party capable of front‑running the transaction ordering, typically a bot or a miner. The impact is a loss of the deposited tokens for honest disputers, a breach of the expectation that a valid dispute will be reimbursed, and a potential erosion of trust in the protocol’s governance and dispute‑resolution process. The bug manifests only when resolveDispute is called after a second dispute has been submitted but before the first dispute is resolved, i.e., during the dispute period while the contract still holds a non‑zero disputer address. All users who attempt to dispute the tree are affected, but the first disputer suffers the loss. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the dispute logic, where the lack of a guard against re‑entering disputeTree was noted. It is subtle because the refund logic appears correct at a glance and the contract does not emit the disputer address or amount in the Disputed event, making it difficult to trace which address should receive the refund. The bug belongs to the class of “single‑slot race conditions” where mutable state is overwritten without proper access control, violating accounting assumptions that a deposit is tied to the party that posted it. The recommended fix is to add a requirement that disputer must be the zero address before accepting a new dispute, or to use a more robust data structure that tracks multiple concurrent disputes, and to emit events that include the disputer and amount for transparency. Additionally, a recovery function such as recoverERC20 can be used by governance to manually return funds to the original disputer, but the primary mitigation is to prevent the state overwrite from occurring in the first place.

title: Poor detection of disputed trees allows claiming tokens from a disputed tree
content: The vulnerability is an improper validation of the Merkle tree state during reward claims. The contract determines the active Merkle root by checking only whether the current block timestamp is past the end of the dispute period. It does not verify whether a dispute has actually been opened, which is indicated by the disputer address being set. As a result, when a tree is disputed close to the end of its dispute window and the governor or guardian takes time to resolve the dispute, the timestamp condition becomes true while the disputer flag remains non‑zero. The getMerkleRoot function then incorrectly returns the disputed root instead of falling back to the previous safe root. An attacker controlling a trusted externally owned account can submit a malicious Merkle root that allocates the entire contract balance to themselves, trigger a dispute, and wait for the dispute period to expire. Because the contract still treats the disputed tree as valid, the attacker can successfully claim the full amount before the dispute is resolved. This leads to loss of funds for legitimate users, emptying the distribution contract and breaking the accounting assumptions that only undisputed trees may be used for claims. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the dispute handling logic and noticed that the disputer address was never checked in the root selection routine. It is hard to notice because the function appears to respect the dispute period, giving a false sense of safety, while the missing guard condition is subtle. The bug belongs to the class of state‑validation errors where a required invariant (no active dispute) is not enforced before performing a critical operation. From a user perspective, a malicious claim succeeds and the expected reward for honest participants disappears, often showing as a zero balance or missing refund. The correct fix is to modify the root‑selection logic to also require that the disputer address is zero before returning the current Merkle root, thereby ensuring that any tree with an active dispute is never used for claims.
summary: Users can claim rewards from a Merkle tree that’s being disputed. This can potentially lead to loss of funds since a malicious trusted EOA can claim funds from a malicious tree while it’s being disputed.

title: In `LlamaRelativeQuorum`, the governance result might be incorrect as it counts the wrong approval/disapproval
content: The vulnerability resides in the way the LlamaRelativeQuorum strategy calculates voting power for approval and disapproval. The contract records the total approval and disapproval supply at action creation by calling getRoleSupplyAsNumberOfHolders, which returns the raw count of role holders. However, when the actual votes are tallied, the functions getApprovalQuantityAt and getDisapprovalQuantityAt return the raw quantity associated with each holder, which can be greater than one when a holder has been granted additional weight. This mismatch means that the numerator (total approvals) is measured in weighted units while the denominator (total supply) is measured in simple headcount. As a result, a single holder with a quantity greater than one can satisfy a quorum that was intended to require a majority of distinct holders. The bug can be exploited by an attacker who holds a higher quantity: by casting a single weighted approval they can trigger the condition totalApprovalQuantity/totalApprovalSupplyAtCreationTime ≥ minApprovalPct, causing an action to be queued even though the required percentage of distinct holders has not voted. The impact is that governance decisions may be approved with far fewer participants than intended, undermining the security and trust model of the DAO, potentially allowing malicious proposals to pass and exposing funds to unauthorized actions. The issue manifests whenever the policy assigns quantities greater than one to any role holder while the relative quorum strategy is used; it does not appear when all quantities are exactly one. Affected parties include all DAO participants, the protocol’s governance layer, and any assets that can be moved by approved actions. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the supply calculation in validateActionCreation with the vote‑counting logic and noticed the inconsistent metric. It is subtle because both functions appear to return a “quantity” and the code comments refer to percentages, leading reviewers to assume the same unit is used on both sides. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that an action becomes approved after only one vote, even though the UI or documentation indicates that a majority of holders is required; users may see an unexpected “action queued” message or a proposal passing with an apparently insufficient number of approvals. The correct fix is to align the metrics: either change getApprovalQuantityAt and getDisapprovalQuantityAt to return a constant value of 1 for any positive quantity (or the maximum value for forced roles) so that each holder contributes a single unit, or modify the supply calculation to use the total weighted quantity instead of the raw holder count. This ensures that the percentage comparison uses a consistent denominator and numerator, restoring the intended quorum semantics.
summary: In `LlamaRelativeQuorum`, the governance result might be incorrect as it counts the wrong approval/disapproval.

title: Anyone can change approval/disapproval threshold for any action using LlamaRelativeQuorum strategy
content: An external function called validateActionCreation in the LlamaRelativeQuorum strategy is intended to be invoked only when a new governance action is created. Its purpose is to record the total supply of the approval and disapproval roles at that moment, storing them in the mappings actionApprovalSupply and actionDisapprovalSupply. Because the function is declared external and has no access restriction, any address can call it after the action has been created. By calling the function again, an attacker can overwrite the stored supply values with the current role supply, which may be lower if a role holder has been revoked or if the supply has otherwise changed. The quorum calculation later multiplies the required percentage by the stored supply, so reducing the stored supply lowers the absolute number of votes needed for approval or disapproval. Consequently an action that originally required all ten policy holders to approve can become approved after only nine votes once a holder is revoked and the attacker updates the supply. This breaks the core governance invariant that the approval threshold is fixed at creation time, allowing unauthorized actions to pass, potentially triggering protocol state changes, fund transfers, or contract upgrades without the intended consensus. The bug manifests when a role holder is removed or the role supply changes after an action is queued; any user can trigger the exploit by sending a transaction to validateActionCreation with the action identifier. The affected parties include all participants of the Llama protocol that rely on the relative quorum strategy, the protocol itself, and any downstream contracts that assume correct governance outcomes. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where the lack of an access control check on an apparently harmless external function was identified as a logical flaw. Because the function does not emit events and only updates internal mappings, the change can go unnoticed in the UI, leading users to see an action marked as Approved even though the visible vote count is insufficient. The vulnerability belongs to the class of unrestricted state‑modifying external functions that allow post‑creation manipulation of immutable governance parameters. The recommended mitigation is to restrict validateActionCreation so that only the core contract (LlamaCore) can invoke it, for example by making the function internal or adding an onlyCore modifier, thereby preserving the snapshot of role supplies at action creation.
summary: Anyone can change approval/disapproval threshold for any action using LlamaRelativeQuorum strategy.

title: There is a vulnerability in the `executeFlashloan` function of the `PeUSDMainnet` contract. Hackers can use this vulnerability to burn other people’s eUSD token balance without permission
content: The vulnerability resides in the flash‑loan entry point of the PeUSDMainnet contract. The executeFlashloan function accepts an arbitrary address as the FlashBorrower receiver and then charges the flash‑loan fee by calling the burnShares function of the EUSD token, passing the receiver address as the target of the burn. Because PeUSDMainnet holds the minter role of EUSD, the burnShares call succeeds without any permission check, and the EUSD contract’s transferFrom implementation allows the minter to move tokens from any address without a prior allowance. An attacker can therefore invoke executeFlashloan with a victim address that holds eUSD and that implements only a fallback function, causing the contract to bypass the onFlashLoan check. When the flash‑loan fee is calculated (for example 5 % of a large loan amount), the fee is deducted from the victim’s balance via burnShares, effectively destroying the victim’s eUSD tokens. This attack can be carried out whenever the attacker can supply a receiver contract that does not revert on the onFlashLoan call, which includes many proxy contracts that expose a generic fallback. From the user’s perspective the symptom is a sudden loss of eUSD balance – the balance may drop to zero or a large portion may disappear without any transaction initiated by the user. The impact is a direct loss of funds, erosion of trust in the protocol’s accounting, and potential legal liability for the platform. The flaw was discovered during a formal audit when the code was examined for flash‑loan fee handling and the interaction with the EUSD token’s mint‑vault privileged functions was traced. The issue is subtle because the fee is taken via an internal burn rather than an external transfer, making it easy to miss in transaction logs, and the fallback contract masks the missing onFlashLoan implementation. To remediate the problem the flash‑loan logic should be constrained so that the receiver is always the caller (msg.sender), removing the external receiver parameter entirely. This ensures that only the initiator of the flash loan can be charged the fee, preventing any third‑party from being forced to lose tokens. The fix also aligns the flash‑loan design with standard expectations that the borrower pays the fee, restoring correct accounting and protecting user balances.
summary: The `executeFlashloan` function of the `PeUSDMainnet` contract is used to provide users with the flash loan function. There is a loophole in the logic and hackers can use this loophole to burn other people’s eUSD token balance without permission.

title: doesn’t calculate the current borrowing amount for the provider, including the provider’s borrowed shares and accumulated fees due to inconsistency in `collateralRatio` calculation
content: The vulnerability is an inconsistency in the way the protocol computes the collateral ratio for borrowers versus liquidity providers. For borrowers, the liquidation() function determines the collateral ratio by dividing the value of the deposited asset (multiplied by the current price and a scaling factor) by the total amount owed, which is obtained from the getBorrowedOf() helper. This helper adds the principal borrowed, any fees already stored, and newly accrued fees, thus reflecting the true debt of the borrower. In contrast, the rigidRedemption() function that evaluates a provider’s collateral ratio only divides the deposited asset value by the raw borrowed principal (borrowed[provider]), completely ignoring the accumulated fees and newly accrued fees. The root cause is the use of two different formulas for the same economic concept – collateral ratio – where one formula omits fee components. An attacker can exploit this mismatch by inflating the fee component (for example, by triggering actions that increase _newFee) while the provider’s ratio is still calculated on the lower principal amount. The protocol will then believe the provider is over‑collateralised and allow a redemption or avoid liquidation, but the actual debt is higher. When the provider later attempts to redeem or when a liquidation is finally triggered, the protocol will discover the shortfall, causing the provider’s collateral to be seized or to disappear, effectively stealing funds from the provider. The impact is a loss of collateral for liquidity providers and a breach of the accounting guarantees that the protocol promises, potentially undermining trust in the system. This condition occurs whenever a provider’s collateral ratio is checked – specifically in the rigidRedemption() path – while borrowers are evaluated through liquidation(). The affected parties are the liquidity providers who supply assets to the pool, the borrowers who rely on correct liquidation logic, and any users of the protocol who expect that collateral ratios are calculated consistently. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where the auditors compared the two ratio calculations and noticed the omission of fee terms in the provider path. It is hard to notice because both calculations look syntactically similar and the UI typically displays a single collateral‑ratio figure, masking the underlying discrepancy. To remediate, the protocol should use the same total‑debt calculation (borrowed + stored fees + newly accrued fees) for both borrowers and providers, i.e., replace the direct borrowed[provider] reference with a call to getBorrowedOf(provider) or an equivalent aggregation. This ensures that the collateral ratio reflects the true economic exposure, preventing providers from unintentionally losing funds due to an understated debt. The bug belongs to the class of accounting inconsistencies where fee accruals are omitted from debt calculations, leading to wrong collateral‑ratio assessments, refund calculation errors, and potential fund disappearance.
summary: doesn’t calculate the current borrowing amount for the provider, including the provider’s borrowed shares and accumulated fees due to inconsistency in `collateralRatio` calculation.

title: Incorrectly implemented modifiers in `LybraConfigurator.sol` allow any address to call functions that are supposed to be restricted
content: The vulnerability resides in the access‑control modifiers defined in LybraConfigurator.sol, namely onlyRole(bytes32) and checkRole(bytes32). These modifiers are intended to restrict sensitive functions such as initToken and setProtocolRewardsPool to accounts that hold a specific governance role. However, the implementation merely calls GovernanceTimelock.checkOnlyRole (or a similar helper) without asserting its result. Because the call is not wrapped in a require or otherwise examined, the modifier always succeeds regardless of the caller’s actual role. Consequently, any external address can invoke functions that should be exclusive to the DAO or timelock executor. The root cause is a missing enforcement statement inside the modifier, turning what appears to be a role check into a no‑op. An attacker can exploit this by simply sending a transaction to the configurator contract; the contract will accept the call and execute the privileged logic. In practice this means a random user can replace the protocol’s EUSD token address, point the rewards pool to an address they control, or otherwise reconfigure core protocol parameters. The impact is severe: protocol governance is bypassed, funds intended for the official rewards pool may be diverted, token references can be corrupted, and the overall trust model of the system collapses. The issue manifests whenever a function protected by onlyRole or checkRole is called – there is no condition under which the check blocks an unauthorized caller. All participants that rely on the assumption that only the DAO can change configuration – token holders, liquidity providers, and downstream contracts – are affected because the protocol state can be altered arbitrarily. The flaw was discovered during a systematic audit using Foundry tests; by impersonating a random address with vm.prank the auditor observed that initToken and setProtocolRewardsPool executed without reverting, proving the modifiers were ineffective. The problem is subtle because the code compiles without warnings and the modifier name suggests proper access control, making it easy to overlook during manual review. To remediate, the modifiers must explicitly enforce the role check, for example by writing require(GovernanceTimelock.checkOnlyRole(role,msg.sender),"Not Authorized") inside onlyRole and similarly for checkRole, or by having the called function revert on failure. This change restores the intended gatekeeping, ensuring that only accounts with the designated role can perform configuration changes, thereby preserving protocol integrity and preventing unauthorized fund redirection.
summary: The modifiers `onlyRole` (bytes32 role) and `checkRole` (bytes32 role) are not implemented correctly. This would allow anybody to call sensitive functions that should be restricted.

title: The Constructor Caveat leads to bricking of Configurator contract.
content: The vulnerability is that the configurator contract, which is intended to be used behind a TransparentUpgradeableProxy, performs its critical state initialization inside the constructor of the logic contract. In the proxy pattern, the constructor of the implementation is executed only when the implementation contract is deployed, not when the proxy delegates calls. Consequently, the governance timelock address and the curve pool address that are set in the constructor never become part of the proxy’s storage. When the proxy is instantiated, those storage slots contain the default zero value, so the contract believes that the governance address is the zero address and that the timelock is uninitialized. Any function that checks msg.sender against the governance address or that interacts with the timelock therefore reverts or behaves incorrectly. An attacker can trigger a revert by calling functions that require a valid governance address, effectively bricking the configurator and preventing the protocol from adding tokens, setting parameters, or executing upgrades. The impact is that the protocol’s configuration layer becomes unusable, which can halt token issuance, freeze upgrades, and potentially lock user funds that depend on those configurations. The issue appears during deployment of the proxy, before any user interaction, and is visible to anyone who attempts to call initToken or other governance‑restricted functions: the call fails with a revert because the stored address is zero. The problem was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, which observed that the constructor code never runs in the proxy context and that the test suite reproduced a revert when initToken was called. Because the bug resides in the deployment flow rather than in runtime logic, it may be missed by casual testing that only interacts with the implementation contract directly. The proper fix is to move all state‑setting logic out of the constructor and into an external initializer function that is called exactly once after the proxy is linked to the implementation, using OpenZeppelin’s Initializable pattern or a custom guard that prevents re‑initialization. By ensuring that the governance address and other critical parameters are written to the proxy’s storage, the contract will behave as intended and the configuration functions will be usable.
summary:
In Solidity, code that is inside a constructor or part of a global variable declaration is not part of a deployed contract’s runtime bytecode. This code is executed only once, when the contract instance is deployed. As a consequence of this, the code within a logic contract’s constructor will never be executed in the context of the proxy’s state. This means that any state changes made in the constructor of a logic contract will not be reflected in the proxy’s state.

  1. This will lead to governance timelocks contract and the `curvePool` contract contain default values of zero values.
  2. As a result, all the functions that rely on governance will be broken, since the governance address is set to zero address.

title: Making `_totalSupply` and `_totalShares` imbalance significantly by providing fake income leads to stealing fund
content: The vulnerability is an accounting imbalance between the protocol’s total supply of synthetic eUSD and the total number of shares that represent ownership of the underlying stETH collateral. The root cause is that the contract allows a malicious actor to inject artificial excess income – for example by transferring stETH directly to the contract before any genuine deposits exist – which inflates the stETH balance without a corresponding increase in the share count. The excessIncomeDistribution function then calculates the number of shares to be burned based on the ratio of totalSupply to totalShares, but when the ratio is large the integer division rounds down to zero, meaning that a user can “burn” zero shares while still receiving a proportional amount of stETH. An attacker can exploit this by first depositing a tiny amount of ETH to mint a minimal number of shares, then sending additional stETH to create fake income, calling excessIncomeDistribution to convert that income into eUSD, and finally invoking redemption (rigidRedemption) or liquidation functions with an eUSD amount equal to totalSupply/totalShares. Because the share conversion yields zero, the attacker receives stETH without any share reduction, repeatedly draining the protocol’s collateral while the internal accounting variables remain out of sync. The impact is that funds disappear from the protocol: honest users who later deposit and borrow see their balances reduced, receive fewer shares than expected, or cannot withdraw their collateral because the share pool has been depleted. The bug manifests only when the protocol is freshly launched or when totalSupply greatly exceeds totalShares, and when the attacker can directly transfer stETH to the contract. All depositors, borrowers, and token holders are affected because the protocol’s accounting invariants are broken, leading to loss of value and loss of trust. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the logic of excessIncomeDistribution and the redemption path, noticing that the share‑to‑eUSD conversion could return zero under certain ratios, a subtle rounding error that is easy to miss in testing. It is hard to notice because the contract state variables appear internally consistent, yet the external effect – receiving assets without share burn – is hidden. The recommended fix is to make the _repay function return the exact number of burned shares and to use that amount for all subsequent calculations in liquidation and redemption, ensuring that the share reduction matches the withdrawn value. Additionally, the excessIncomeDistribution logic should include a fallback that treats a zero‑share result as a 1‑to‑1 conversion, preventing division‑by‑zero style rounding. Enforcing that excess income cannot be added before any real deposits, or requiring a non‑zero totalShares before allowing redemption, would also mitigate the attack vector. In summary, the protocol’s accounting model can be deliberately skewed, allowing an attacker to steal stETH and synthetic eUSD without burning any shares, violating the fundamental business logic that each share must be backed by collateral.
summary: If the project has just started, a malicious user can make the `_totalSupply` and `_totalShares` imbalance significantly by providing fake income. By doing so, later, when innocent users deposit and mint, the malicious user can steal protocol’s stETH without burning any shares. Moreover, the protocol’s income can be stolen as well.

title: `EUSD.mint` function wrong assumption of cases when calculated sharesAmount = 0
content: The vulnerability resides in the token minting routine that converts a requested eUSD amount into an internal share amount. The contract assumes that a calculated share amount of zero can only happen when the total token supply is also zero, and in that case it defaults to a 1‑to‑1 conversion. In reality, because the conversion uses integer division, the expression totalShares * mintAmount / totalSupply can round down to zero even when totalSupply is non‑zero. This situation arises after the protocol’s burnShares operation reduces the number of outstanding shares while leaving the total eUSD supply unchanged, causing the price of a single share to become very high. When a user then mints a relatively small amount of eUSD, the division truncates to zero, the contract mistakenly treats the case as a fresh supply, and assigns shares equal to the eUSD amount. The result is that the attacker receives far more shares than warranted – effectively minting shares at a 1‑to‑1 ratio despite a high share price. From a user’s perspective the protocol appears to give them an unexpectedly large share balance for a tiny deposit, or conversely the protocol’s accounting shows an inflated share count that dilutes existing holders. The impact is a potential loss of value for all token holders because the attacker can acquire cheap shares, increasing the total share count without a proportional increase in eUSD backing, thereby reducing the value of each share. The flaw manifests only when totalSupply is positive, totalShares is low, and the mint amount is small enough that totalShares * mintAmount < totalSupply, a condition that is rare and therefore easy to overlook. It was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena through logical review and a concrete Foundry test that demonstrated the rounding error after a burnShares call. The issue is hard to notice because the contract’s comment explicitly states the zero‑share case is tied to a zero supply, misleading reviewers, and because the erroneous path is only taken under specific state changes. To remediate, the mint function should explicitly verify that a zero share result does not occur when totalSupply is non‑zero and either revert the transaction or skip minting, or the conversion formula should be adjusted to use rounding up or a minimum share allocation check. This class of bug belongs to arithmetic rounding errors that lead to under‑allocation of internal accounting units, breaking the invariant that each share is backed by a proportional amount of eUSD and violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions.
summary:
* `Mint` function might calculate the `sharesAmount` incorrectly.
  * User can profit by manipulating the protocol to enjoy 1-1 share-eUSD ratio even when share prices is super high.

title: `_voteSucceeded`
content: The vulnerability lies in the governance contract’s internal vote‑success check. The function that determines whether a proposal has passed compares the number of votes stored at index 1 with the number stored at index 0 and returns true when the former is greater. In this contract the vote mapping is defined such that index 0 represents the count of "for" votes and index 1 represents the count of "against" votes. Consequently the success condition is inverted: a proposal is considered successful when it has more against votes than for votes. This logical inversion breaks the intended voting process because proposals that the community overwhelmingly rejects are executed, while proposals that receive majority support are discarded. The bug is triggered each time a proposal’s voting period ends and the contract evaluates _voteSucceeded to decide whether to enact the proposal. All participants in the governance system—token holders, proposal creators, and the protocol itself—are affected because the outcome of governance decisions no longer reflects the expressed preferences of the voters. The issue was uncovered during a formal audit when the auditor compared the public view function that reports forVotes and againstVotes with the internal success check and noticed the mismatch. It can be hard to spot in normal operation because the UI correctly displays the vote tallies, yet the execution result contradicts those numbers, leading users to see proposals they voted for being rejected and proposals they voted against being approved. Exploitation is straightforward: an attacker can craft or promote a malicious proposal and simply gather enough opposition votes, which the contract mistakenly treats as support, causing the proposal to pass without needing any genuine backing. The impact includes unauthorized protocol upgrades, fund transfers, or parameter changes that were never intended by the community, effectively compromising the protocol’s security and trust model. To remediate, the comparison should be swapped so that the function returns true when the count of for‑votes exceeds the count of against‑votes, aligning the logical condition with the semantic meaning of the stored vote indices. This correction restores the intended governance semantics, ensuring that proposals only pass when they have genuine majority support.
summary: As a result, voting process is broken, as it won’t execute proposals with most of `forVotes`. Instead, it will execute proposals with most of `againstVotes`.

title: Governance wrongly calculates `_quorumReached`
content: The vulnerability lies in the governance contract’s quorum verification routine, which mistakenly adds only the counts of against votes and abstain votes when determining whether a proposal has reached the required quorum. In a correctly designed system, quorum should be measured against the total number of votes cast – the sum of for, against and abstain votes – because the purpose of quorum is to ensure that a sufficient portion of the voting population has participated, regardless of how they voted. The root cause is a logical error in the _quorumReached function: it references the supportVotes array indices that correspond to against (index 1) and abstain (index 2) instead of aggregating all three categories. As a result, the condition for quorum becomes "againstVotes + abstainVotes >= requiredQuorum". This means that quorum is considered reached only when at least one third of all votes are either against or abstain, which contradicts the intended governance model where any combination of votes that reaches the quorum threshold should be acceptable. An attacker can exploit this by casting a large number of abstain or against votes to artificially satisfy the quorum requirement while the number of supporting votes remains low, allowing a malicious proposal to be approved despite lacking genuine community backing. Conversely, honest proposals that receive many supporting votes may never meet quorum if the number of against or abstain votes is insufficient, causing legitimate governance actions to stall. The impact is high because it undermines the integrity of the decision‑making process, potentially leading to the execution of proposals that do not reflect the true will of token holders, and may affect the allocation of funds, protocol upgrades, or other critical actions. The bug manifests whenever a proposal’s vote tally is evaluated, i.e., during every call to _quorumReached, which occurs at the end of the voting period before a proposal can be queued or executed. All participants in the governance system – token holders, proposal creators, and the protocol itself – are affected because the outcome of votes cannot be trusted. The issue was discovered during a formal audit where the auditors compared the contract’s implementation against the documented governance specifications and identified the mismatch in vote aggregation. It can be hard to notice because the contract may still appear to function in simple test cases where the numbers of against and abstain votes happen to satisfy the quorum condition, masking the logical flaw. The proper fix is to replace the erroneous sum with a reference to the totalVotes field, ensuring that the quorum check compares the total number of votes cast against the required threshold. This aligns the implementation with standard governance patterns and restores confidence that proposals are approved only when a sufficient portion of the community has participated, regardless of vote direction. The bug belongs to the class of logical miscalculations in voting quorum logic, where an incorrect subset of vote categories is used to assess participation, leading to accounting errors and potential governance manipulation. From a user’s perspective the symptoms may include proposals that never pass despite many affirmative votes, or proposals that pass with almost no support, creating confusion when the UI reports "quorum reached" while the supporting vote count is near zero. The discrepancy violates the fundamental business rule that quorum should reflect overall participation, not a specific vote type, and can cause funds to be moved or protocol changes to be enacted without genuine consensus.
summary: For some reason it is calculated as sum of `againstVotes` and `abstainVotes` instead of `totalVotes` on proposal. As the result, quorum will be reached only if >=1/3 of all votes are abstain or against, which doesn’t make sense.

title: A new era might be triggered despite a significant value being held in the previous era
content: The vulnerability originates from the protocol’s era‑transition mechanism, which automatically starts a new staking or drafting era whenever the current staking or draft rate exceeds a predefined percentage threshold after a Reserve Token (RSR) seizure. The logic assumes that a rate above the threshold indicates that little value remains in the current era, so resetting the era is safe. However, the implementation only checks the rate and ignores the absolute amount of value still locked. If a previous seizure has already pushed the rate close to the threshold, even a modest subsequent seizure can push the rate just over the limit while a large amount of stake or draft tokens remains. When this happens the contract calls the function that begins a new era, which clears all balances associated with the previous era. Consequently, users who still have significant holdings see their balances become zero, effectively losing their funds. The exploit can be triggered by an attacker who initiates a small seizure at a moment when the rate is near the threshold, causing the automatic era reset and wiping out all existing stakes. This condition occurs only when the rate is close to the threshold and a seizure event is processed; it does not require any special privileges beyond the ability to trigger a seizure, which is part of the protocol’s normal operation. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when the auditors constructed a proof‑of‑concept scenario: a maximum stake rate of 1e9, a seizure that raised the rate to 91e7, followed by normal staking that rebuilt a large total stake, and finally a 10 % seizure that pushed the rate to 1.01e9, triggering a new era and erasing the accumulated value. The bug is subtle because the threshold check appears reasonable on its own and the wiping of balances only occurs after a legitimate protocol event, making it easy to overlook during testing. To remediate the problem, the protocol should decouple era initiation from a simple rate comparison and introduce additional safeguards such as a migration path that allows users to transfer their holdings into the new era, or a governance‑controlled function that validates that the total value to be wiped is negligible before allowing a new era to start. In essence, the contract must enforce that a new era is only begun when both the rate exceeds the threshold and the remaining locked value is below an acceptable limit, thereby preventing unexpected loss of funds and preserving the intended accounting guarantees of the staking and drafting system.
summary: When RSR seizure occurs the staking and drafting rate is adjusted accordingly, if any of those rates is above some threshold then a new era begins (draft or staking era accordingly), wiping out all of the holdings of the current era. The assumption is that if the rate is above the threshold then there’s not much staking or drafts left after the seizure (and therefore it makes sense to begin a new era). However, there might be a case where a previous seizure has increased the staking/draft rate close to the threshold, and then even a small seizure would make it cross this threshold. In that case the total value of staking or drafts can be very high, and they will all be wiped out by starting a new era.

title: Custom redemption might revert if old assets were unregistered
content: The vulnerability resides in the custom redemption logic of the protocol, specifically in the function that builds the list of ERC20 tokens to be returned to a redeemer. The code creates an array (erc20sAll) whose length is taken from the current size of the asset registry, assuming that this size matches the number of assets that may appear in any basket. When governance removes an asset from the registry but the old basket still contains that asset, the basket’s composition becomes larger than the registry size. During the loop that populates erc20sAll the function attempts to write more entries than the array can hold, causing an index‑out‑of‑bounds revert. This situation can be triggered when a governance vote unregisters a token, the basket switch is recorded, but rebalancing is paused so the contract still holds the old basket composition. Any user who tries to redeem using the custom redemption path under these conditions will see the transaction fail with a low‑level out‑of‑bounds error, receiving no assets even though they expected a full redemption. From the user’s perspective the UI reports a failed transaction, often with a generic “revert” message, and the user’s balance appears unchanged or zero for the redeemed amount, creating confusion and a temporary denial of service. The root cause is a mismatch between the dynamic set of assets in a basket and the static size of the asset registry used to allocate the return array, a classic off‑by‑size bug. The issue was discovered during a code audit that examined the assumptions of quoteCustomRedemption and reproduced the failure with a concrete scenario involving USDC, USDT, and DAI. The bug is hard to notice because the function silently skips unregistered assets in the final output, so the error only surfaces when the basket contains more assets than the registry size, a relatively rare state. The impact is limited to denial of service for custom redemption; funds are not lost because the revert prevents any transfer, and governance can re‑register the asset to restore functionality. The recommended mitigation is to decouple the array length from the registry size, for example by allowing the caller to specify the desired length or by filtering out unregistered assets before constructing the array, ensuring that the loop never writes beyond the allocated storage. This aligns the implementation with the intended accounting model where the redemption calculation must handle dynamic basket compositions safely.
summary: `quoteCustomRedemption()` works under the assumption that the maximum size of the `erc20sAll` should be `assetRegistry.size()`, however there can be cases where an asset was unregistered but still exists in an old basket, making the size of the old basket greater than `assetRegistry.size()`. In that case the function will revert with an index out of bounds error.

title: `VaultProxy` implementation can be initialized by anyone and self-destructed
content: The vulnerability originates from the VaultProxy implementation contract being left uninitialized after the VaultFactory deployment. Because the factory never invokes the initialise functionon the newly created implementation, the contract does not disable its initializer and any address can subsequently call initialise and supply arbitrary arguments. One critical argument is the _staderConfig address, which determines the contract that the fallback function will delegatecall to. An attacker can pass a malicious contract whose fallback contains a selfdestruct call. When a user later triggers the fallback of the VaultProxy implementation—by calling a non‑existent function—the proxy’s fallback delegatecalls the attacker‑controlled contract, causing the selfdestruct to execute in the context of the implementation. This erases the bytecode at the implementation address. All vault instances created by the factory are simple clones that forward calls to this single implementation address, so after the selfdestruct every proxy forwards to an empty address. Calls to the proxies appear to succeed (the low‑level call returns true) but no business logic is executed, resulting in user‑facing symptoms such as transactions that return success while balances remain unchanged, refunds that never arrive, or vault functions that silently do nothing. The impact is that the entire vault system becomes non‑functional, preventing withdrawals, reward distribution, or any state‑changing operation, effectively locking user funds and breaking protocol guarantees. The issue occurs whenever the factory is deployed without calling initialise on the implementation and the implementation does not protect its initializer. It affects all participants that rely on the vaults—stakers, delegators, and the protocol itself. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the factory‑proxy relationship and noticed that the initialise function was never called and that the contract did not inherit OpenZeppelin’s Initializable pattern. The problem is subtle because the proxy still returns a successful call flag, giving the impression that operations succeeded, while in reality no code runs. To remediate, the implementation should inherit Initializable, invoke _disableInitializers in its constructor, and protect initialise with the initializer modifier, or the factory should call initialise at deployment time, ensuring the implementation cannot be re‑initialized by an attacker.
summary: When the `VaultFactory` contract is deployed and initialized, the `initialise` method on the newly created `VaultProxy` implementation contract is never called. As such, anyone can call that method and pass in whatever values they want as arguments. One important argument is the `_staderConfig` address, which controls where the `fallback` function will direct `delegatecall` operations. If an attacker passes in a contract that calls `selfdestruct`, it will be run in the context of the `VaultProxy` implementation contract and will erase all code from that address. Since the clones from the `VaultProxy` contract merely delegate calls to the implementation address, all subsequent calls for all created vaults from that implementation will be treated like an EOA and return `true`, even though calls to functions on that proxy were never executed.

title: POSU-1 | willPositionCollateralBeSufficient Validation Bypassed
content: The vulnerability lies in the collateral‑sufficiency validation that decides whether the remaining collateral for a position after a modification is enough to support its leverage. The validation logic ignores two critical deductions: the execution fees that will be taken from the position’s collateral and any negative price impact that can reduce the collateral’s effective value. Because of this omission, a trader can submit a decrease order that passes the check, even though after the fees and price impact are applied the collateral falls below the required safety threshold. An attacker can therefore craft a position‑reduction transaction that appears valid, but once executed leaves the position under‑collateralized, exposing it to liquidation or loss of funds. The impact is that positions that should be flagged as unsafe remain open, potentially causing the trader’s balance to shrink unexpectedly and increasing systemic risk for the protocol. The condition under which this occurs is any scenario where a position is decreased and the contract evaluates collateral sufficiency without accounting for pending fees or adverse price impact. From a user’s perspective the symptoms may include a balance that drops more than expected after closing or shrinking a trade, or a position that remains open despite appearing to be under‑collateralized. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the validation routine with the protocol’s accounting assumptions and noticed that the safety check returned true while the post‑transaction state violated the leverage requirements. The problem is hard to notice because the check itself succeeds and no error is emitted; the discrepancy only becomes visible after the transaction when fees are deducted, making it easy to miss in standard testing. The recommended remediation is to extend the collateral‑sufficiency check to incorporate all deductions that will affect the position, including execution fees and any negative price impact, ensuring that the post‑transaction collateral never drops below the required threshold. This flaw belongs to the broader class of insufficient collateral validation or accounting‑logic bypass bugs, where safety checks ignore downstream state changes, leading to money disappearing or positions becoming unsafe.
summary: The willPositionCollateralBeSufficient validation aims to decide whether or not the collateral amount that remains for a position will be sufficient for it's leverage. However in many cases this validation allows decrease orders which will put the position’s collateral below the “sufficient threshold”. This is because the willPositionCollateralBeSufficient validation excludes fees that will be subtracted from the position's collateral as well as negative price impact that can be applied to the position's collateral.

title: ORDH-1 | Keeper Griefed With orderUpdatedAtBlock
content: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service style gas‑griefing issue that occurs when an order remains in the order store after the execution transaction reverts with the OracleBlockNumbersAreSmallerThanRequired error. The root cause is that the contract does not clear or invalidate the order when the oracle block number validation fails, and the executionFee attached to the order is left untouched. An attacker can exploit this by front‑running a keeper’s execution transaction, updating the order’s orderUpdatedAtBlock to a higher value, and then allowing the keeper’s transaction to reach the oracle block validation step. Because the validation fails, the transaction reverts, the keeper has spent a large amount of gas on price‑setting and swap‑path processing, but the order stays in the store with the same executionFee. The attacker can repeat this pattern, repeatedly causing the keeper to waste gas without paying any additional fee, and finally cancel the order to retrieve the original executionFee. The impact is that keepers lose gas repeatedly, potentially making order execution economically unviable and creating a denial‑of‑service condition for the protocol. The issue manifests when orders require many price updates, such as those with long swapPath arrays, because the expensive computation occurs before the oracle block check. Affected parties include the keeper bots that execute orders, the protocol that relies on timely order processing, and any users whose orders become stuck or delayed. The problem was discovered during a security audit that examined the order execution flow and noticed that the order store was not pruned on revert. It can be hard to notice because the order appears to be pending as usual and the executionFee is still present, while the only symptom is an unusually high gas consumption on failed execution attempts.
