To remediate, the contract should either require a non‑refundable payment (for example, a WNT deposit) when an order is updated, thereby disincentivising repeated front‑running, or move the oracle block number validation to the beginning of the execution routine so that the transaction aborts before any costly operations are performed. Additionally, clearing the order or marking it as invalid on revert would prevent the same order from being retried indefinitely.
summary: Orders will remain in the order store when the OracleBlockNumbersAreSmallerThanRequired error occurs during execution. Therefore a malicious user can cause the keeper to continuously expend gas to attempt to execute an order without requiring any additional executionFee. Consider the following scenario: A malicious user frontrun’s the keepers execution tx and updates their order, updating the orderUpdatedAtBlock. Now the keeper's tx goes through all of the price setting and order execution logic up to the oracle block number validation. Then the order execution tx reverts, the keeper has spent a significant amount of gas but the order still remains, with the same executionFee still attached. The malicious user may continue to do this and continue to gas grief the keeper. The malicious user can then cancel their order at any time to receive their executionFee back. The scenario can be exacerbated with an order that requires many prices to be set where the malicious user includes a maximum length swapPath that requires many prices.

title: MKTU-1 | Borrowing Fees Avoided Due To Skip
content: The vulnerability is a borrowing‑fee bypass that occurs when the contract’s skipBorrowingFeeForSmallerSide flag is active and the cumulative borrowing factor for a side has not been updated before the side becomes the smaller open‑interest (OI) side. The root cause is that fee accrual is tied to a cumulativeBorrowingFactor that is only incremented when the side remains the larger OI; when a trader deliberately shifts the larger OI to the opposite side, the contract skips the fee update for the now‑smaller side. An attacker can exploit this by first building a large position on the side that currently holds the greater OI, allowing borrowing fees to accrue but remain un‑solidified because the cumulative factor has not been refreshed. The attacker then opens a position on the opposite side, causing the original side to become the smaller OI. Because the skip flag prevents fee calculation for the smaller side, the attacker can subsequently close the original position and pay zero borrowing fees. The impact is a loss of expected fee revenue for the protocol, an unfair advantage for the attacker, and a breach of the accounting assumptions that borrowing fees are always collected proportionally to open interest. The condition under which this occurs is when cumulativeBorrowingFactorUpdatedAt for the larger side is stale and skipBorrowingFeeForSmallerSide is enabled. All users of the protocol are potentially affected because the fee‑collection mechanism is compromised, but the exploit specifically benefits traders who can manipulate OI direction. The issue was discovered during a targeted audit that included a test case reproducing the scenario, and it is subtle because the fee‑calculation logic appears correct for normal flows; the bypass only manifests when the side switches from larger to smaller, a situation that may not be exercised in routine testing. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a trader expects to see a borrowing‑fee deduction when closing a position, but the balance remains unchanged, effectively receiving a free trade. This class of bug can be described as a conditional fee‑skip or accounting‑state‑inconsistency caused by asymmetric update rules. To remediate, the protocol should ensure that borrowing‑fee factors are updated for both long and short sides on any position increase or decrease, removing the ability to skip fee calculation when a side becomes smaller, thereby preserving the invariant that all accrued fees are eventually collected.
summary: Users who have accumulated a large amount of borrowing fees can avoid paying these fees as long as the cumulativeBorrowingFactor has not yet been incremented and skipBorrowingFeeForSmallerSide is enabled. Consider the following scenario: Long OI > Short OI. Trader A has a large long position that has accumulated a significant amount of borrowing fees. These borrowing fees have not been “solidified” by the update of any other long position. Therefore the cumulativeBorrowingFactor has not yet been incremented to account for Trader A’s accumulated borrowing fees since the last recorded cumulativeBorrowingFactorUpdatedAt for longs. Trader A opens another short position shifting the larger side to be the opposite of the first position. Trader A then closes the first position and pays 0 borrowing fees.

title: crvRewardsContract `getReward` can be called directly, breaking vaults `claimRewards` functionallity
content: The vulnerability is an unrestricted access control flaw in the external Convex reward pool contract that the Amphora vault uses to collect CRV and CVX rewards. The vault’s claimRewards function expects to be the only caller of the reward pool’s getReward method, passing the vault’s own address as the recipient. Because getReward is a public function without any restriction on the caller, any external account can invoke it on behalf of the vault. An attacker can monitor when the vault has accrued rewards and call getReward(address(vault),false) before the vault executes its own claimRewards. This front‑runs the legitimate claim, draining the CRV reward and the derived CVX reward that the vault would later convert into AMPH tokens. When the vault finally runs claimRewards, the call to earned(address(vault)) returns zero, the internal counters stay at zero, and the subsequent AMPH claim fails. From a user’s perspective the UI shows no AMPH tokens being minted after a claim, or a “rewards: 0” line even though the deposit should have generated rewards. The impact is limited to loss of protocol‑level rewards – user deposits remain safe – but the protocol’s incentive model is weakened and token holders receive fewer AMPH tokens than expected. The issue occurs whenever the vault has pending rewards and an attacker can submit a transaction before the vault’s claimRewards call. It was discovered during a Code4rena audit that examined the vault’s claimRewards implementation and noticed that the external reward contract does not enforce any caller restriction. The problem is subtle because the function is designed to be called by the vault, so the disappearance of rewards can be mistaken for a normal zero‑balance state; there is no explicit event indicating an unauthorized claim. The bug belongs to the class of “missing access control on external reward claims” or “reward hijacking via unrestricted public function”. To remediate, the vault should either implement its own internal claim mechanism that does not rely on an external contract’s unrestricted function, or the reward pool should be modified to restrict getReward to a whitelist that includes only the vault address. Adding a check that the caller is the authorized vault, or using a pull‑pattern where the vault first verifies the reward balance before claiming, would prevent an attacker from front‑running the claim and ensure that rewards are only transferred when intended.
summary: crvRewardsContract of convex can be called by anyone on behalf of Vault, this will allow malicious users to call `getReward` and break the Vault `claimRewards` functionality.

title: Rounding error in `WUSDA` can result in loss of user funds, especially when manipulated by an attacker
content: The vulnerability is a rounding error caused by the use of Solidity’s integer division in the conversion routine that maps USDA tokens to wrapped WUSDA tokens. The private function that computes the amount of WUSDA to mint performs a multiplication of the deposited USDA amount by a fixed maximum supply constant and then divides by the total USDA supply, without any additional precision scaling. Because Solidity truncates the result toward zero, when the deposited USDA amount is small relative to the total USDA supply, or when the total supply is artificially inflated within a single block, the division can round down to zero or to a value far smaller than expected. This occurs both in the deposit path, where a user may receive little or no WUSDA for the USDA they supplied, and in the withdraw path, where the contract may attempt to burn zero WUSDA while still releasing USDA, effectively allowing the user to extract value without surrendering the corresponding wrapped tokens. An attacker can exploit this by using a flash loan to temporarily increase the USDA supply, front‑running a victim’s deposit so that the victim’s conversion rounds down to zero, then back‑running a withdraw to capture the victim’s USDA while only burning a minimal amount of WUSDA. The impact is that honest users see their balances unchanged or receive far fewer WUSDA than they paid for, leading to a loss of value that is ultimately absorbed by the protocol’s reserves and other participants. The issue manifests when the contract is called with small deposit amounts, or when the total USDA supply is manipulated in the same block, and it is difficult to notice because the transaction succeeds and emits no error, while the UI may simply show a successful deposit with an unexpectedly low or zero token balance. The bug was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena through analysis of the conversion formula and testing edge cases where the result could be zero. It belongs to the class of arithmetic precision bugs and rounding‑to‑zero errors that violate the accounting assumptions of a one‑to‑one backing between USDA and WUSDA. To remediate, the contract should check for a zero return from the conversion function and revert, employ a higher‑precision scalar (e.g., using a fixed‑point library) to avoid truncation, and introduce safeguards that prevent the total USDA supply from being altered within a single block, such as a multi‑block delay or snapshot mechanism. These measures would restore the expected economic relationship and protect users from receiving no tokens or losing funds due to rounding.

title: Reentrancy issue with the `withdraw` method of USDC. All tokens could be drained.
content: The vulnerability is a classic reentrancy flaw in the withdraw logic of a USDC‑backed protocol. The public withdraw functions forward the request to an internal _withdraw routine that first performs an external token transfer (sUSD.transfer) and only afterwards updates the internal accounting by burning the caller’s balance. Because the external call is executed before the state change, a malicious contract can exploit the fallback function triggered by the token transfer to call withdraw again before the original execution finishes. Each re‑entry repeats the same sequence, allowing the attacker to repeatedly receive tokens while the protocol’s reserveAmount is only decremented after the transfer, eventually draining all USDC held by the contract. The issue occurs whenever a user invokes withdraw or withdrawTo while the contract holds a non‑zero reserve and the attacker’s contract is capable of receiving the transferred tokens and re‑entering the withdraw path. All token holders are affected because the protocol’s total balance can be emptied, leading to loss of user funds and a broken accounting model that assumes a 1‑to‑1 exchange between sUSD and USDC. The flaw was discovered during a formal security audit that inspected the ordering of state updates and external calls. It is hard to notice because the code follows a seemingly reasonable pattern of checking balances, performing the transfer, and then burning tokens, but the critical checks‑effects‑interactions principle is violated. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a successful withdrawal, yet the displayed balance becomes zero or the protocol shows no remaining USDC, contradicting the expectation that a withdrawal only reduces the user’s own balance. The bug belongs to the class of reentrancy vulnerabilities where external calls are made before internal state is secured. To remediate, the contract should either move the _burn operation (or any state mutation that reduces the user’s entitlement) before the token transfer, or employ a reentrancy guard such as OpenZeppelin’s ReentrancyGuard or a mutex pattern. Additionally, following the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern and possibly pausing the contract in emergencies would prevent an attacker from repeatedly invoking withdraw and ensure that funds cannot disappear unexpectedly.
summary: High: All USDC tokens could be drained from the protocol.

title: `expressReceiveToken` can be abused using reentry
content: The vulnerability is a re‑entrancy flaw in the cross‑chain token receipt flow. The function that processes an express token transfer first performs an external token transfer and then calls a helper that ultimately invokes the Axelar gateway, before finally marking the command as executed with _setExpressReceiveTokenWithData. Because the state flag is set after the external calls, an attacker can trigger a second execution of the same command during the gateway call. In practice an attacker (or a malicious gateway operator) can front‑run the AxelarGateway::execute transaction that reports the cross‑chain transfer, call the third‑party contract that implements expressReceiveTokenWithData, and cause that contract to invoke the gateway again while the original command is still unmarked. The re‑entered call to InterchainTokenService::execute transfers the same amount a second time from the token manager to the destination contract. As a result the attacker receives twice the intended amount while the original sender’s funds are deducted only once, effectively stealing the excess tokens. The issue appears when any external party can invoke expressReceiveTokenWithData and when the Axelar gateway permits anyone to call its execute function, which is the case in the current deployment. It also extends to tokens with transfer callbacks such as ERC777, because the same re‑entrancy pattern applies. The bug was discovered during a Code4rena audit by constructing a test that front‑runs the gateway call and observes the double credit in the recipient contract. It is hard to notice because the re‑entrancy spans multiple contracts and occurs across a cross‑chain message, not within a single function’s call stack, and the state update that should prevent re‑execution is placed after the external interactions. The impact is high: funds can be drained from the token manager or from users who rely on the express receipt mechanism, breaking the accounting guarantees of the protocol and violating the expectation that each cross‑chain transfer is settled exactly once. From a user’s perspective the victim sees their token balance reduced unexpectedly while the attacker’s balance grows, and the protocol may appear to have “missing refunds” or “money disappearing”. To remediate, the contract should follow the check‑effects‑interactions pattern by marking the command as executed (or otherwise recording that the transfer has been processed) before any external token transfer or gateway call, and optionally add a re‑entrancy guard. This ensures that any re‑entered call will find the command already marked and abort, preserving the one‑time transfer invariant.

title: ERC777 and similar token implementations allow a stealing of funds when transferring tokens
content: The vulnerability is a re‑entrancy flaw in the TokenManager implementations that handle cross‑chain token transfers. The low‑level _takeToken function determines the amount of tokens transferred by measuring the change in the contract's token balance before and after calling transferFrom on the source‑chain token contract. Because the function does not protect itself against re‑entrancy, a malicious token contract that implements a hook (such as the ERC777 tokensToSend callback) can invoke TokenManager.sendToken again while the original transfer is still in progress. In the nested call the balance delta is calculated only for the re‑entered transfer, while the outer call later observes a larger balance increase that includes both the original and the re‑entered transfer. Consequently the TokenManager emits two cross‑chain messages: one for the amount of the re‑entered transfer and another for the summed balance change. The destination chain therefore credits the attacker with more tokens than were actually burned on the source chain, allowing the attacker to receive extra tokens without paying for them. This issue occurs whenever the TokenManager interacts with a token that executes external code during transfer, such as ERC777 or any custom token with similar hooks, and it is not limited to ERC20 tokens that lack callbacks. The affected parties are the TokenManager contracts (LiquidityPool and LockUnlock implementations), the InterchainTokenService that mints tokens on the destination chain, and any user who sends tokens across chains, as the protocol’s accounting can be subverted and funds can be effectively stolen. The flaw was discovered during a security audit by Code4rena when the auditors examined the balance‑difference logic of _takeToken and crafted a malicious ERC777 contract to trigger the re‑entrancy. The problem is hard to notice because each individual balance change appears correct and typical ERC20 tokens do not expose the hook, so the double‑counting only manifests with tokens that allow callbacks. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a transfer that should move a certain amount of tokens results in the recipient receiving more tokens than expected, while the sender’s source‑chain balance reflects only the amount actually sent. This violates the fundamental accounting assumption that the amount burned on the source chain equals the amount minted on the destination chain. The recommended mitigation is to add a re‑entrancy guard (for example OpenZeppelin’s ReentrancyGuard) to the _takeToken functions, or to restructure the code so that the amount to be transferred is computed before any external call and the contract follows the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern, thereby preventing the balance‑delta manipulation that enables the exploit.
summary: A malicious actor can trick a `TokenManager` into thinking that a bigger amount of tokens were transferred. On the destination chain, the malicious actor will be able to receive more tokens than they sent on the source chain.

title: Pumps are not updated in the shift
content: The vulnerability consists of an oracle‑update omission in the Well contract: when the shift() or sync() functions modify the pool reserves, the contract does not call the internal routine that updates the attached Pump with the previous block's reserve snapshot. The design of the contract expects the Pump to be refreshed with the prior‑block reserves whenever reserves change, so that the Pump’s price calculation reflects the true state before any new values are applied. Because shift() and sync() skip this step, a user can invoke shift() to set the reserves to arbitrary values within the same block, then perform a swapFrom or swapTo operation that triggers the Pump update using those manipulated reserves. The Pump therefore records a false price, allowing the attacker to profit from arbitrage or to cause other participants to receive incorrect pricing. The impact includes potential loss of funds for liquidity providers and traders, distorted market prices, and a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees. The condition occurs any time a participant calls shift() or sync() in a block where the reserves have been altered; no special permissions are required. The affected parties are anyone interacting with the pool – liquidity providers, traders, and the protocol itself – because the Pump data is used for pricing, fee calculation and external oracle feeds. The issue was uncovered during a Code4rena audit, where a test case demonstrated that after a shift the Pump still reported the original reserves, enabling the attacker to manipulate the Pump’s internal state while the visible pool balances appeared unchanged. The bug is subtle because the contract’s external behavior (reserve balances) looks correct, while the hidden Pump state diverges, making the problem hard to notice without inspecting the Pump’s stored reserves. The recommended remediation is to invoke the Pump‑updating helper inside both shift() and sync() so that the Pump always receives the correct previous‑block reserve snapshot before any new reserve values are applied. This aligns the oracle with the contract’s accounting assumptions and prevents price manipulation. From a user’s perspective the symptom may be a trade that seems to execute at a normal price but later the reported pool price is wildly off, or a user receiving less output than expected because the oracle has been skewed. The flaw belongs to the class of “oracle update omission” or “state‑inconsistent oracle” bugs, where a price‑feeding component is not synchronized with underlying state changes, violating the business logic that reserves and price feeds must stay consistent.
summary:
The `Well` contract mandates that the `Pumps` should be updated with the previous block’s `reserves` in case `reserves` are changed in the current block to reflect the price change accurately.

However, this doesn’t happen in the `shift()` and `sync()` functions, providing an opportunity for any user to manipulate the `reserves` in the current block before updating the `Pumps` with new manipulated `reserves` values.

title: User can steal tokens by using duplicated ERC20 tokens as parameter in `NounsDAOLogicV1Fork.quit`
content: The issue resides in the quit function of the DAO governance contract, where a caller can supply an array of ERC20 token addresses that are intended to be withdrawn from the treasury. The function only checks that each supplied address belongs to a whitelisted set, but it does not verify that the array contains unique entries. As a result, an attacker can include the same token address multiple times. The contract later iterates over the supplied array and, for each entry, calculates a proportional share of the token balance based on the number of NFTs being quit. Because the calculation is performed for every array element, each duplicate entry causes an additional payout of the same token amount. Consequently, a malicious user can receive several times the amount of a token they are entitled to, potentially draining the entire balance of that ERC20 token from the treasury. The vulnerability is triggered whenever a user calls quit and passes a list of ERC20 tokens; it does not depend on any external state beyond the standard subset check. All token holders and the DAO treasury are affected because the stolen tokens reduce the overall assets available to the protocol. The flaw was discovered during a security audit when a test case deliberately supplied the same token address three times and observed that the caller received three times the expected balance. The problem is subtle because the subset verification appears correct, and the duplicate‑free requirement is not obvious from the code, making it easy to overlook during manual review. To remediate the issue, the contract should enforce uniqueness of the ERC20 token list, for example by invoking a duplicate‑detection routine or by using a data structure that guarantees a set of addresses. This ensures that each token is accounted for exactly once, preserving the intended proportional distribution of assets and preventing unauthorized token extraction.
summary: Calling [NounsDAOLogicV1Fork.quit](https://github.com/nounsDAO/nouns-monorepo/blob/718211e063d511eeda1084710f6a682955e80dcb/packages/nouns-contracts/contracts/governance/fork/newdao/governance/NounsDAOLogicV1Fork.sol#L206-L216) by using duplicated ERC20 tokens, malicious user can gain more ERC20 tokens than he/she is supposed to, even drain all ERC20 tokens.

title: The `_currentExchangeRate` of the Vault contract can’t increase and will always be lower than or equal to `_assetUnit`
content: The vulnerability is a logical constraint in the Vault contract that prevents the internal exchange rate from ever increasing beyond the base asset unit. The function that computes the current exchange rate first determines the amount of assets that can be withdrawn from the underlying yield vault. It then forces this withdrawable amount to be no larger than the amount that corresponds to the total supply multiplied by the last recorded exchange rate. Because the withdrawable amount is capped, the subsequent calculation of exchange rate (withdrawableAssets * assetUnit / totalSupply) can never produce a value higher than the previously recorded rate. Consequently, when the vault becomes under‑collateralized – that is, when the computed exchange rate falls below the asset unit – the contract has no mechanism to raise the rate back up, effectively locking the vault in a state where additional collateral cannot be recognized. An attacker or a market event that pushes the vault into this state can therefore prevent future yield from being reflected in share values, causing users to receive fewer assets than expected on withdrawal, or to see their balances appear stagnant despite accrued interest. The issue was uncovered during a Code4rena audit when an assert was added that demonstrated the exchange rate never exceeds the asset unit, and all tests still passed, making the bug subtle. It is hard to notice because the function returns the asset unit when the supply or withdrawable amount is zero, and the cap does not produce an outright error. The bug violates the core accounting assumption that the exchange rate should be monotonic non‑decreasing as the vault earns yield. The recommended fix is to remove the code that artificially limits the withdrawable assets, allowing the exchange rate calculation to reflect the true growth of the underlying assets.
summary: The `_currentExchangeRate` of the Vault contract can not increase and will always be lower than or equal to `_assetUnit`. Therefore, when the vault is under-collateralized (`_currentExchangeRate` < `_assetUnit`), it can’t be further collateralized.

title: A malicious user can steal other user’s deposits from Vault.sol
content: The vulnerability is an accounting mismatch caused by truncating the number of shares to a 96‑bit unsigned integer when burning them during a withdrawal. The Vault contract stores shares as a uint256 but the internal _burn function casts the amount to uint96 before reducing the holder’s balance. Because type(uint96).max is the largest value that can be represented, a malicious actor can deposit the maximum amount of underlying assets twice (or more via flash‑loan tricks) so that the total deposited shares exceed the uint96 limit. When the attacker later calls withdraw with an amount that corresponds to the full deposited balance, the contract correctly transfers the underlying assets but only burns type(uint96).max shares due to the cast. The remaining shares stay in the attacker’s account, allowing them to call withdraw again and extract assets that belong to other users. This can happen whenever a user is able to make multiple deposits that together exceed the 96‑bit share ceiling, which is feasible because each individual deposit is limited only by the uint96 maximum. The impact is that the attacker can drain the vault of funds belonging to honest participants, effectively stealing deposits. From a user’s perspective the UI may show that a withdrawal succeeded and the user received the expected amount, yet the vault still reports that the user holds shares, and other users may see their balances drop to zero without any action on their part. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit when the withdrawal logic was examined and the cast to uint96 was identified as a truncation point. It is hard to notice because the contract does not revert on the mismatch and the share balance appears to be positive after withdrawal, which can be missed by superficial tests. The bug belongs to the class of integer truncation/overflow vulnerabilities that break accounting invariants. To remediate, the contract should avoid converting the share amount to a smaller type when burning, either by using uint256 throughout or by adding explicit checks that prevent withdrawals that would leave unburned shares exceeding the actual amount withdrawn.
summary:
When the `Vault.withdraw()` function is called, a maximum of `type(uint96).max` shares are burnt subsequently: `Vault.withdraw()`-> `Vault._withdraw()`-> `Vault._burn` burns `uint96(_shares)`, see [Vault.sol line 1139](https://github.com/GenerationSoftware/pt-v5-vault/blob/b1deb5d494c25f885c34c83f014c8a855c5e2749/src/Vault.sol#L1138-L1139).

A malicious user can exploit this in the following way:

  1. A malicious user deposits, for example, two times the value of `type(uint96).max` underlying assets into the Vault; calling the function `Vault.deposit()` two times. They can’t deposit more in a single transaction because `type(uint96).max` is the maximum value to deposit.
  2. Then, the malicious user calls `Vault.withdraw()` with a higher value of assets to withdraw more than `type(uint96).max`. For example, they withdraw (`2 * type(uint96).max`), which is the total amount of assets they deposited before.
  3. Now what happens, is the Vault.sol contract only burns `type(uint96).max` shares for the user, but transfers `2 * type(uint96).max` underlying assets to the malicious user, which is the total amount they deposited before.
  4. This happens because `Vault._burn()` only burns `uint96(shares)` shares of the malicious users - see Vault.sol line 1155.
  5. Now, the malicious user has still vault shares left but they withdrew the total amount of their deposited assets.
  6. Now, the vault transferred the total amount of the malicious user’s assets back to them and the malicious user still has shares left to withdraw; with even more assets that are now being stolen from assets deposited by other users.
  7. Or, if the malicious user was the first depositor, they wait until another user deposits and the malicious user can now withdraw the other users deposited assets since the malicious user still has Vault shares left.
  8. Or, if the malicious user is not the first depositor, they use a `flashLoan` or `flashMint` to deposit multiple times `type(uint96).max` assets into the vault. Then, they can withdraw their deposit, pay back the `flashLoan` or `flashMint` and they will still have enough vault shares left to steal all other users assets by withdrawing them.

In this way, other user’s deposited assets can be stolen, as explained above.

title: `_amountOut` is representing assets and shares at the same time in the `liquidate` function
content: The vulnerability resides in the liquidate function of the Vault contract where the input parameter _amountOut is treated interchangeably as an asset amount and as a share amount. In a vault architecture, assets (the underlying token) and shares (the accounting token representing a proportional claim on the assets) are linked by a conversion rate that is normally calculated through functions such as _convertToShares or _convertToAssets. The code, however, uses the raw _amountOut value directly in three distinct contexts: it is compared against the liquidatable yield, which is an asset quantity; it is used to compute the yield fee, which expects a share quantity; it is compared with the vault's total asset balance, again an asset quantity; and finally it is minted to the liquidated account as a share amount. Because the same numeric value cannot simultaneously represent both units without applying the conversion formula, the function’s logic diverges from the intended accounting model. An attacker or a careless caller can trigger the function with a _amountOut that is interpreted as a share amount while the contract treats it as an asset amount in the earlier checks, allowing the minting of more shares than the underlying assets would justify. This can lead to an inflation of share supply, dilution of existing shareholders, and potential loss of assets when the vault later redeems those shares. The issue manifests whenever liquidate is invoked with a non‑zero _amountOut and the caller passes the vault’s own share token as _tokenOut, which is the normal usage pattern. It was discovered during a manual audit when the reviewer noticed contradictory comments and mismatched unit usage in the code. The bug is subtle because the variable name _amountOut does not convey its unit, and the function contains several conditional checks that appear reasonable in isolation, making the mixed‑unit misuse easy to overlook. To remediate, the function should first convert the supplied _amountOut into the appropriate asset representation (e.g., _amountOutToAsset) using the vault’s conversion routine, then use that asset value for all asset‑related comparisons and calculations, while retaining the original share value for minting. In other words, separate variables must be introduced for asset and share quantities, and each part of the logic must consistently reference the correct one, thereby restoring the invariant that shares are always backed by a proportional amount of assets and preventing unintended share inflation.
summary: In the `liquidate` function from the `Vault` contract, the input argument `_amountOut` is used as if it was representing a value of asset amounts and share amounts at the same time; which is impossible as there is a conversion rate between them. This error will make the `liquidate` function behave in an expected manner, not the one that was intended.

title: `Vault.mintYieldFee` function can be called by anyone to mint `Vault Shares` to any recipient address
content: The vulnerability resides in an external function that mints vault shares representing accrued yield fees. The function accepts a caller‑supplied address as the fee recipient and does not enforce any access control, allowing any external account to invoke it. Because the implementation uses the supplied address instead of the immutable _yieldFeeRecipient state variable set at contract deployment, an attacker can specify their own address (or any address they control) as the recipient. When the vault is collateralized and the number of shares requested does not exceed the currently accrued _yieldFeeTotalSupply, the call succeeds, the internal fee counter is decreased, and new shares are minted to the attacker’s address. This effectively transfers the protocol’s yield fee to an arbitrary party, draining the fee pool without affecting the underlying collateral. From a user’s perspective the expected fee balance remains zero or unchanged, while the attacker’s balance suddenly increases, leading to symptoms such as “my fee balance is empty” or “unexpected shares appear in my wallet”. The issue was discovered during a formal audit (Code4rena) where the lack of access control and the mismatch between the function parameter and the stored fee recipient were identified as logical flaws. It is hard to notice because the function appears to perform a legitimate mint operation and only reverts on obvious under‑collateralisation or overshoot of the fee supply, which are not triggered in a normal exploit. The bug belongs to the class of unauthorized minting or access‑control bypass vulnerabilities, where a contract allows arbitrary address specification for privileged token creation. To remediate, the function should eliminate the external _recipient parameter, use the immutable _yieldFeeRecipient state variable for minting, and optionally restrict the function to authorized callers (e.g., internal or only governance). This ensures that yield fees are always credited to the intended recipient and prevents malicious actors from stealing them.
summary:
The `Vault.mintYieldFee` external function is used to mint `Vault shares` to the yield fee `_recipient`. The function is an external function and can be called by anyone since there is no access control. The function will revert only under following two conditions:

  1. If the Vault is under-collateralized.
  2. If the `_shares` are greater than the accrued `_yieldFeeTotalSupply`.

The issue with this function is, it allows the caller to set the `_recipient` (address of the yield fee recipient). It does not use the `_yieldFeeRecipient` state variable, which was set in the `Vault.constructor` as the `yield fee recipient`. 

Which means, anyone can steal the available `yield fee` from the vault (as long as the above two revert conditions are not satisfied) by `minting shares` to their own address or to any address of their choice.

title: Delegated amounts can be forcefully removed from anyone in the `TwabController`
content: The vulnerability resides in a public sponsor function that allows an arbitrary caller to force a delegation change for any user without requiring the user’s consent or a non‑zero deposit. The root cause is that the contract does not verify whether the target address has already delegated to the sponsorship address before overwriting the delegation, and delegations to the special sponsorship address are not tracked in the TwabController. Consequently, an attacker can invoke the function with a zero amount for a victim, causing the victim’s delegated balance to be set to zero and the delegate pointer to be redirected to the untracked sponsorship address. This removal of delegated power reduces the total delegated supply in the TwabController to zero, enabling the attacker to become the sole holder of the remaining delegated amount and to manipulate the lottery or any other logic that depends on delegated voting power. The issue manifests whenever a user has an active delegation and the sponsor function is called; it affects all participants of the vault, the lottery mechanism, and any downstream protocol that relies on correct accounting of delegated balances. The problem was discovered during a security audit when a proof‑of‑concept test demonstrated that calling sponsor with a zero amount instantly erased a user’s delegate balance. The bug is subtle because the function appears to be a harmless deposit helper and a zero amount seems innocuous, so the silent loss of voting power can go unnoticed by users. To remediate, the sponsor function should either reject calls that would force a delegation change without an existing delegation to the sponsor, or it should be limited to the caller’s own address, removing the ability to specify an arbitrary receiver. In broader terms, this is an unauthorized state manipulation bug that allows forced delegation removal, a form of privilege escalation that breaks the accounting invariants of the system. From the user’s perspective the UI would show their delegated power dropping to zero, lottery entries disappearing, and expected rewards not being received, contrary to the expectation that their delegation remains intact unless they explicitly change it.
summary:
The `sponsor` function in the `Vault.sol` contract allows anyone to remove another user’s delegation by forcing them to delegate to the sponsor address. `_sponsor` will deposit some amount from the caller for the target user and then force a delegation to the sponsor address (`address(1)`).

However, this amount can just be 0 and so it becomes a function to simply force a removal of a delegation. The full delegated power gets removed, because delegations to the sponsor address are not tracked.

As such, it becomes possible to call the `sponsor` function for every user and make the total delegated power supply in the `TwabController` equal to 0. The attacker can then be the only one with some delegated amount that is equal to 100% of the total supply, manipulating the process of the lottery.

Rectifying the delegation requires manual interaction from the user and the exploit can be repeated anytime and continuously, further manipulating the values in the `TwabController`.

title: Resetting delegation will result in user funds being lost forever
content: The vulnerability is that resetting a delegation to the default value (address(0)) causes the delegated balance to be transferred to the zero address, effectively burning the funds. The contract uses address(0) as a sentinel meaning self‑delegate. When a user has previously delegated their balance to another address and later calls the delegate function with _to = address(0) to reset the delegation, the internal _transferDelegateBalance moves the entire delegated amount to address(0). Because the zero address holds no private key, the tokens become unrecoverable. After this transfer the stored delegate for the user is still address(0); any subsequent attempt to delegate to the user’s own address or to any other address triggers the SameDelegateAlreadySet check and reverts, leaving the user unable to move the balance again or to withdraw from the vault. The impact is a permanent loss of the user’s deposited assets, which appears to the user as a zero balance, failed delegation transactions, and inability to withdraw. The bug manifests only when a user who has an active delegation tries to reset it by using the default sentinel value; it does not affect users who never delegated or who explicitly delegate to a non‑zero address. The issue was discovered during a security audit (Code4rena) by reviewing the delegate logic and noticing that address(0) is treated both as a sentinel and as a valid target for the delegate function. The problem is subtle because the UI may present reset delegation as a legitimate action, and the zero‑address sentinel is a common pattern, making the loss of funds easy to overlook. The vulnerability belongs to the class of sentinel‑value misuse or self‑delegate sentinel mis‑handling bugs, where a special value that represents a default state is incorrectly allowed as an explicit target, leading to unintended state transitions. To fix the issue, the contract should reject delegations to address(0) and require users who want to delegate back to themselves to pass their own address explicitly. This prevents the transfer of funds to an irretrievable address and restores the expected business logic that a user’s balance can always be reclaimed by delegating to a valid address.
summary: The default delegate value for a user is `address(0)`, which maps to the user delegating to themselves. If a user had delegated to another address and wanted to reset their delegated balance back to themselves, they would lose all of their funds contributed to the vault.

title: `_requireVaultCollateralized`
content: The vulnerability is an invariant‑check ordering flaw in the vault contract. The internal function that verifies a vault remains sufficiently collateralized, _requireVaultCollateralized(), is invoked at the start of the mintYieldFee() and liquidate() functions. Both of these functions subsequently modify the vault’s state – mintYieldFee() increases the protocol’s fee share balance and liquidate() reduces the vault’s collateral or increases its debt. Because the collateralization check runs before these state changes, the contract does not guarantee that the vault is still safe after the operation completes. An attacker can call either function with parameters that push the vault’s collateral‑to‑debt ratio below the required threshold, causing the vault to become under‑collateralized without triggering a revert. This can lead to unintended liquidations, loss of user funds, or the minting of yield fees that exceed the actual value of the underlying assets. The issue manifests whenever mintYieldFee() or liquidate() are executed with values that reduce collateral or increase obligations, which is a common scenario in normal protocol operation. All vault owners and participants are affected because the safety guarantees of the vault are broken, potentially resulting in missing balances, zeroed refunds, or unexpected fee allocations. The problem was discovered during a Code4rena audit through logical analysis of the function flow rather than through a failing test case, making it subtle: the transaction succeeds, no error is emitted, yet the vault’s accounting is compromised. Detecting the bug is difficult because the contract does not emit an event or revert when the vault becomes unsafe after the function finishes; the invariant is only checked at the beginning, giving a false sense of security. The correct mitigation is to move the collateralization verification to the end of each function, or to perform an additional check after the state‑changing operations, ensuring that the vault’s collateralization ratio is still satisfied before the transaction is finalized. Conceptually, this belongs to the class of “post‑condition invariant violation” bugs where safety checks are placed before mutable operations, allowing the system to enter an invalid state after execution. From a user’s perspective, the symptoms may appear as a vault that can be liquidated despite having sufficient collateral before the call, or as a situation where a user expects a fee to be minted based on their share but receives an incorrect amount, effectively causing funds to disappear or be allocated incorrectly.
summary: The `liquidate()` and `mintYieldFee()` functions could leave the vaults under-collateralized.

title: Increasing reserves breaks PrizePool accounting
content: The vulnerability is an accounting mismatch in the prize pool contract that occurs when the reserve is increased through the public increaseReserve function. The root cause is that the internal accounting routine that calculates the pool's accounted balance does not incorporate reserve injections performed via increaseReserve, so the variable that tracks the total accounted tokens remains unchanged while the actual token balance of the contract grows. An attacker can exploit this by first calling increaseReserve to transfer prize tokens into the contract and increase the reserve, and then invoking the contributePrizeTokens function (or any similar path that uses the delta between the real token balance and the accounted balance). Because the accounted balance does not reflect the newly injected reserve, the delta includes the attacker’s own contribution, allowing the attacker’s vault to claim those tokens as if they were newly earned prize liquidity. The impact is that the prize pool’s real token holdings become lower than the amount the protocol believes it has, leading to reduced or missing prize payouts for users, potential loss of funds for participants, and a breach of the protocol’s financial guarantees. This condition occurs whenever any address is permitted to call increaseReserve – a permissionless entry point – and later calls a function that distributes the perceived excess balance. The affected parties include the prize pool contract itself, any vaults that can call contributePrizeTokens, and ultimately the end‑users who expect their prizes to be funded correctly. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when the auditors checked the invariant that the contract’s token balance must equal the sum of available tier liquidity and the reserve; the invariant failed after a manual reserve injection. The bug is subtle because the contract’s balance appears correct during normal draw closures, and only diverges after an external reserve increase, making the discrepancy easy to miss in routine testing. To remediate, the contract should update its accounted balance whenever the reserve is increased, for example by tracking total reserve injections and adding that amount to the accounted balance calculation, thereby preserving the accounting invariant and preventing double counting of the same tokens. This fix restores the logical accounting model where every token held by the contract is reflected in the internal accounting state, ensuring that prize distribution matches the actual token pool.
summary: When anyone calls the `increaseReserve` method in `PrizePool.sol` the accounted balance in the prize pool isn’t properly updated. This allows a vault to effectively steal the prize token contribution and this contribution gets distributed during draws; effectively double counting the initial injection into the reserves. The actual prize token balance of the prize pool will be below the accounted balance of the prize pool as time goes on.

title: `Vault` is not compatible with some ERC4626 vaults
content: The Vault contract implements a share‑based accounting model where the number of shares a depositor receives is calculated by converting the deposited asset amount using a current exchange rate. The exchange rate is obtained by calling an internal function that multiplies the amount that the underlying ERC4626 yield vault reports as maxWithdraw for the Vault contract by the asset unit and divides by the total supply of shares. This design assumes that maxWithdraw returns the full amount of assets that are actually owned by the Vault, including any accrued yield. However, some ERC4626 implementations, such as DnGmxSeniorVault, deliberately limit the value returned by maxWithdraw when the vault has borrowed a portion of the deposited capital or enforces a withdrawal cap. When maxWithdraw reports a value that is lower than the true asset balance, the computed exchange rate drops below one. The lowered rate is then stored as the last recorded exchange rate and is used for all subsequent deposit and withdrawal calculations. As a result, depositors who later withdraw their shares receive fewer assets than they originally supplied, effectively losing funds. The problem manifests only when the underlying vault cannot honour a full redemption at the moment of the rate calculation, which may happen intermittently depending on borrowing activity or withdrawal limits. Users experience the issue as a discrepancy between the amount they expect to receive and the amount actually transferred; a user may see their balance reduced to zero or receive a partial refund despite having deposited the full amount. The vulnerability was discovered during a security audit by Code4rena, where the auditors traced the flow from _convertToShares through _currentExchangeRate and identified the reliance on maxWithdraw as the root cause. The bug is subtle because the Vault contract’s internal accounting appears consistent and no explicit error is thrown; the loss is encoded in the silently adjusted exchange rate. To remediate the issue, the contract should not rely on maxWithdraw for the exchange rate, but instead use a method that reflects the true total assets held, or add explicit checks that reject underlying vaults that do not guarantee full redemption, or cap the exchange rate to prevent it falling below the asset unit. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of accounting mismatches caused by incompatible external token standards, where a contract assumes a certain behavior from an interface that is not universally enforced.
summary: Depositors can lose funds.

title: CBEthCollateral and AnkrStakedEthCollateral _underlyingRefPerTok is incorrect
content: The vulnerability resides in the way CBEthCollateral calculates the reference amount per token (_underlyingRefPerTok). The function uses the exchangeRate reported by the Coinbase manager, which only reflects the ratio between cbETH and the underlying staked ETH2, not the market price of cbETH against ETH. Because the reference unit is mismatched, the computed ref/tok rate is systematically higher than the true value. When the unstake queue for ETH2 grows, the premium embedded in the exchangeRate also grows, further inflating the reported rate. An attacker can therefore deposit cbETH as collateral and mint more rTokens than the actual value of the deposited assets. Even if the cbETH token were to default or lose value, the CBEthCollateral contract never transitions to the DISABLED state because its internal check relies on the inflated exchangeRate. The exploit can be carried out whenever the unstake delay changes or the queue length spikes, which are normal network conditions. Users who interact with the protocol expecting their deposited collateral to be fully backed may see their rTokens over‑issued, leading to a dilution of the protocol’s backing and potential loss of funds for honest participants. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by comparing the on‑chain exchangeRate with the independent Chainlink cbETH/ETH price feed and noticing a consistent discrepancy (e.g., 1.045264 vs 1.0438). Because the contract does not expose the reference rate directly, the problem is subtle and may not be evident from UI screens that simply show a single exchangeRate value. The bug belongs to the class of oracle‑mispricing or reference‑unit mismatch vulnerabilities, where an internal price source does not reflect the true market price used for accounting. To remediate, the contract should obtain the cbETH/ETH price from a reliable oracle such as Chainlink, or redefine the reference unit to be the staked ETH2 amount, ensuring that the calculated ref per token matches the economic reality. In practice, fixing the oracle source or adjusting the reference unit will prevent the protocol from issuing rTokens at an inflated rate, preserving the intended collateralisation guarantees.
summary: The `_underlyingRefPerTok` will return a higher ref/tok rate than the truth. And the premium is positively correlated with the unstake delay of eth2. When the unstake queue suddenly increases, the attacker can uses cbeth to issue more rtokens. Even if the cbETH has defaulted, the CBEthCollateral will never mark the state as DISABLED because the `CBEth.exchangeRate()` is updated by coinbase manager and it only represents the cbETH / staked eth2 rate instead of the cbETH/ETH rate.

title: CurveVolatileCollateral Collateral status can be manipulated by flashloan attack
content: The vulnerability resides in the way CurveVolatileCollateral determines whether its underlying pool has become de‑pegged. The contract computes the proportion of each underlying token in the pool and compares it to an expected equal‑weight value (one‑third for a three‑asset pool). If any token’s observed share exceeds the expected share by more than a fixed threshold (default 5 %), the internal function _anyDepeggedInPool returns true, causing the refresh routine in the parent CurveStableCollateral to mark the collateral status as IFFY. Because the check is performed on the instantaneous token balances, an attacker can temporarily distort the balance distribution using a flash loan. By borrowing a large amount of one asset, depositing it into the pool, and immediately calling refresh, the attacker forces the observed share of that asset to exceed the threshold, triggering the IFFY status. After the flash loan is repaid, the pool’s balances return to normal, but the contract has already recorded a de‑peg condition. Once the delayUntilDefault period elapses, the alreadyDefaulted function marks the collateral as DISABLED, prompting the protocol’s basket manager to rebalance and sell off all CurveVolatileCollateral holdings. From a user’s perspective this appears as a sudden change of collateral status, unexpected rebalancing, and potentially a loss of value or a zero payout when trying to withdraw or redeem assets. The impact is high because the protocol may liquidate a large amount of collateral at unfavorable prices, harming all participants who rely on the stability of the basket. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by analysing the de‑peg detection logic and realizing that flash‑loan‑induced temporary imbalances are not filtered out. It is hard to notice because the imbalance exists only for a single block, leaving no obvious on‑chain trace once the loan is repaid, and the status change is delayed by the default timer. The bug belongs to the class of flash‑loan‑induced state manipulation or economic oracle manipulation, where a contract trusts a short‑term snapshot of on‑chain data without smoothing or external verification. To remediate, the de‑peg check should be hardened by using a time‑weighted average, requiring multiple consecutive violations before marking IFFY, increasing the threshold, or incorporating an external price oracle that is resistant to flash‑loan attacks. Additionally, the contract could ignore balance changes that occur within the same transaction as a refresh call, or enforce a cooldown period before status updates, thereby preventing an attacker from exploiting transient distribution spikes.
summary: Attacker can make the CurveVolatileCollateral enter the status of IFFY/DISABLED. It will cause the basket to rebalance and sell off all the CurveVolatileCollateral.

title: ConvexStakingWrapper.sol after shutdown，rewards can be stolen
content: The vulnerability is an accounting bypass that appears after the ConvexStakingWrapper contract is put into shutdown mode. When the shutdown flag is true, the internal _checkpoint function returns immediately, skipping the logic that updates each account's reward_integral_for value during token transfers. Reward calculations in the contract rely on the difference between a global reward_integral (which continues to grow while rewards are accrued) and the per‑account reward_integral_for that should be refreshed on every transfer. Because the checkpoint is disabled, a user who receives tokens after shutdown gets a reward_integral_for of zero while the global reward_integral retains its pre‑shutdown value. The attacker can then call claimRewards, receiving balance × (global_integral − 0), effectively stealing the entire pool of pending rewards. This can be repeated by moving tokens to fresh addresses, each time harvesting the full reward integral without any prior contribution. The issue manifests only after the contract’s shutdown function has been invoked; normal operation before shutdown does not exhibit the problem, making it easy to miss during routine testing. Users see normal token balances but unexpectedly large reward claims, while legitimate stakers see their expected rewards disappear. The bug was discovered during a security audit that examined the shutdown path and noticed that the checkpoint guard prevented reward state updates. It is hard to notice because the UI still shows correct balances and the contract continues to accept transfers, giving a false sense of safety. The flaw belongs to the class of “state‑update omission after pause/shutdown” bugs, where critical accounting is deliberately or inadvertently disabled, allowing reward theft. To remediate, the checkpoint logic must remain active after shutdown, or transfers should be prohibited, or the contract should explicitly set reward_integral_for for recipients to the current global integral before allowing a claim. Ensuring that reward accounting is consistent regardless of the contract’s lifecycle state will prevent the reward integral bypass and protect the protocol’s reward pool.
summary: After shutdown, checkpoints are stopped, leading to possible theft of rewards.

title: TOFT in
content: The vulnerability resides in the removeCollateral function of the TapiocaOFT contract, which forwards a market address supplied by the caller to an internal market module without any validation. When removeCollateral is invoked, the contract first approves the supplied market address to spend a specified amount of the TOFT token, then calls the market’s removeCollateral function. Because the market address is unchecked, an attacker can deploy a malicious market contract that implements removeCollateral to transfer the approved TOFT tokens to an address of their choice. The exploit works by the attacker passing their malicious market as the removeParams.market argument, causing the contract to approve the attacker’s contract and then immediately invoke its removeCollateral implementation, which calls transferFrom to move the entire approved balance. This results in the complete loss of TOFT held by the TapiocaOFT contract, effectively stealing all funds that were intended to be withdrawn as collateral. The issue occurs whenever a user calls removeCollateral with a market address that is not trusted, which can happen on any chain where the contract is deployed because the function does not enforce a whitelist or any access control on the market parameter. Users are affected because they expect the function to safely return their collateral, but instead their token balance becomes zero and no funds are received. The problem was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where a Foundry test demonstrated that a malicious market could drain the contract’s entire TOFT balance. The flaw is subtle because the approval and external call appear legitimate and the contract’s logic otherwise follows the intended cross‑chain flow, making the missing validation easy to overlook. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of unchecked external contract calls and improper access control, where user‑controlled input is used to authorize token transfers without verification. To remediate the issue, the contract should restrict the market address to a known whitelist of trusted market contracts, or otherwise enforce that only authorized markets can be passed to removeCollateral, thereby preventing arbitrary contracts from receiving approval and stealing tokens.
summary: The `TOFT` available in the `TapiocaOFT` contract can be stolen when calling `removeCollateral()` with a malicious market.

title: `exitPosition` in `TapiocaOptionBroker` may incorrectly inflate position weights
content: The vulnerability resides in the exitPosition function of the TapiocaOptionBroker contract, where the routine that updates the pool's cumulative weight mistakenly uses the pool's current average magnitude instead of the specific weight contributed by the exiting participant. As a result, when a user who entered the pool with a relatively small weight exits, the contract subtracts a much larger value – the average magnitude that reflects later, larger participants – from the cumulative total. This premature removal inflates the remaining cumulative weight, causing subsequent participants to appear to have disproportionate influence or power in the pool. The bug is triggered when a participant calls exitPosition after other participants with higher magnitudes have already joined, because the average magnitude has been updated to reflect those later participants. In practice, a user such as Alice who entered with a weight of 10 and later exits while Bob has already contributed a weight of 50 will cause the pool.cumulative to be reduced by 50 instead of 10. Consequently, a later participant like Charlie, who only contributed a weight of 20, will find the pool.cumulative lower than expected, granting him more relative voting or reward power than the protocol's accounting logic intends. The impact includes distorted reward distribution, potential over‑allocation of voting rights, and a breach of the economic assumptions that the pool’s weight reflects the true sum of active positions. Users experience symptoms such as their expected share of rewards being reduced, their voting power appearing higher than justified, or the pool showing an inconsistent cumulative value after exits. The issue was uncovered during a Code4rena audit through systematic testing that revealed the cumulative inflation when exitPosition was called under varying participation scenarios. It is hard to notice because the cumulative variable still holds a numeric value that seems plausible, while the underlying weight composition is silently corrupted. The proper remediation is to record each participant’s exact weight at the time of participation and to subtract that stored weight when the participant exits, rather than relying on the mutable average magnitude. This class of bug falls under incorrect state update due to misuse of aggregate metrics, a common pattern where global averages are applied to individual removals, leading to accounting mismatches and unintended privilege escalation within decentralized finance protocols.
summary:
```solidity
Users who `participate()` and place stakes with large magnitudes may have their weight removed prematurely from `pool.cumulative`, hence causing the weight logic of participation to be wrong. `pool.cumulative` will have an incomplete image of the actual pool hence allowing future users to have divergent power when they should not. In particular, this occurs during the `exitPosition()` function.
```

title: The amount of debt removed during `liquidation` may be worth more than the account’s collateral
content: The vulnerability resides in the liquidation routine of the lending contract, where the amount of debt that can be erased (borrowPart) is converted into a collateral share that is taken from the borrower. The conversion adds liquidation fees and a bonus multiplier, but the code does not enforce that the resulting collateralShare is bounded by the borrower’s actual collateral balance. Consequently, when market prices move sharply and the computeClosingFactor function yields a large borrowPart, the added fees and bonus can inflate the collateralShare so that it represents a value greater than the borrower’s total collateral. The contract then simply caps the collateralShare to the borrower’s balance, removes that amount of collateral, and records the larger borrowPart as repaid debt. This mismatch means the protocol removes more debt than the value of collateral actually taken, effectively allowing debt to disappear without an equivalent loss of assets. An attacker can trigger liquidation on an under‑collateralised position, causing the protocol to write‑off debt while only seizing a fraction of the required collateral, leading to a net loss of funds for the protocol and its lenders. The issue manifests when a price drop or aggressive liquidation parameters cause the closing factor to produce a borrowPart that, after fees and bonuses, exceeds the borrower’s collateral. All participants who rely on the accounting invariants of the protocol—borrowers, lenders, and the protocol treasury—are affected because the accounting guarantees are broken. The flaw was discovered during a Code4rena audit through a crafted proof‑of‑concept that simulated a 120 % price drop and observed a revert triggered by a require statement checking that collateralShare and borrowPart have equal worth. The problem is subtle because the liquidation flow appears to take collateral from the user, yet the invariant that debt removed equals collateral taken is silently violated, making it easy to miss in manual review. To remediate, the calculation of borrowPart must be constrained so that the resulting collateralShare, after applying fees and bonuses, never exceeds the borrower’s actual collateral. In practice this means recomputing borrowPart based on the available collateral, incorporating fees and bonuses into the bound, and adding explicit checks that enforce collateralShare ≤ userCollateral before proceeding with the liquidation. This restores the intended accounting relationship where the value of debt erased matches the value of collateral seized, preventing the protocol from losing funds.
summary:
```solidity
The contract decreases user’s debts but may not take the full worth in collateral from the user, leading to the contract losing potential funds from the missing collateral.
```

title: Incorrect solvency check because it multiplies collateralizationRate by share not amount when calculating liquidation threshold
content: An incorrect solvency check occurs in the market contract when determining whether a CDP can be liquidated. The check multiplies the user’s collateral share by the collateralizationRate (scaled by precision constants) before converting the share to an amount. Because the collateralizationRate is a ratio that should be applied to a monetary amount, applying it to a share distorts the computed collateral value. The conversion from share to amount uses a fixed‑point ratio that is deliberately offset (totalAmount++ and totalShares+=1e8) to prevent 1:1 attacks, so the share‑based calculation under‑estimates the true collateral value. As a result the contract may deem a position solvent when it is actually under‑collateralised, or vice‑versa, allowing a liquidator to trigger liquidation at an incorrect threshold. In practice a borrower whose collateral appears sufficient may be liquidated, losing part of their collateral, while the protocol may lose revenue because liquidations occur too early. The bug manifests whenever the _isSolvent function is called, which happens during liquidation eligibility checks, borrow, repay, or any operation that queries solvency. It affects all users of the market, the protocol’s liquidity pool, and any third‑party liquidators. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena when the test suite compared the result of the share‑based calculation with an amount‑based calculation and observed a mismatch. The problem is subtle because the arithmetic uses large precision constants and the conversion function hides the share‑to‑amount ratio, making the error hard to spot by visual inspection. The vulnerability belongs to the class of incorrect financial ratio application or misuse of share versus amount in collateral valuation. An attacker can exploit it by opening a position that is close to the liquidation threshold, then waiting for the protocol to mis‑classify the position as solvent and force a liquidation at a favorable price, effectively stealing collateral. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a healthy collateralisation ratio while the transaction reverts with a solvency error or, conversely, a liquidation transaction may succeed unexpectedly, resulting in a loss of collateral. The fix is to perform the collateral valuation using the actual amount obtained from the share‑to‑amount conversion, and only then apply the collateralizationRate, ensuring that the same unit is used on both sides of the comparison. All other functions that compute liquidation thresholds, such as _computeMaxAndMinLTVInAsset and _computeMaxBorrowableAmount, should also be audited to guarantee they use amounts rather than shares.

title: Ability to steal user funds and increase collateral share infinitely in BigBang and Singularity
content: The vulnerability resides in the addCollateral functions of the BigBang and Singularity market contracts. These functions accept a share parameter that represents the amount of YieldBox shares to be locked as collateral. When a caller passes a value of zero for share, the function defers the calculation of the actual share amount to an internal routine that calls YieldBox.toShare after the allowedBorrow modifier has already executed. The allowedBorrow modifier is intended to enforce that the caller is authorized to borrow a specific number of shares, but because it receives the original share argument (zero), the check always succeeds and no allowance is deducted. Consequently, an attacker who has been granted approval to move another user’s YieldBox assets (via setApprovalForAll or allowanceBorrow) can invoke addCollateral with share set to zero, causing the contract to transfer the victim’s shares to the attacker’s address while the internal accounting records the attacker’s collateral share as if they had supplied the assets themselves. This flaw enables two distinct attack vectors: (1) direct theft of another user’s YieldBox shares by adding collateral on their behalf, resulting in the victim’s balance dropping to zero and the attacker receiving the underlying collateral; (2) repeated calls with share equal to zero allow the attacker to inflate their own collateral share without bound because each call adds newly calculated shares to the totalCollateralShare while the allowedBorrow check never limits the amount. The inflated share grants the attacker proportionally larger borrowing power, ultimately permitting unlimited minting of USDO or borrowing of assets from the Singularity market. The issue manifests whenever the addCollateral function is called with a zero share and the caller possesses the necessary token approvals. It affects any user who has approved the market contract to manage their YieldBox assets, as well as the protocol itself, which can become insolvent due to uncontrolled borrowing capacity. The bug was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where test cases demonstrated that a malicious actor could steal shares and increase collateral share indefinitely. The problem is subtle because the share parameter appears optional and the conversion to actual shares happens after the security‑critical modifier, giving a false sense of protection. Detecting the flaw requires tracing the order of operations and understanding that the modifier validates the pre‑conversion value rather than the effective share amount. To remediate, the contract should compute the share amount before invoking allowedBorrow, or move the allowedBorrow check to occur after the toShare conversion, and additionally enforce that share cannot be zero when the caller is not the owner. A more robust solution is to validate that the caller either supplies a non‑zero share or that the calculated share matches the authorized allowance, thereby preventing unauthorized transfer of shares and unbounded collateral inflation.

title: BalancerStrategy `_withdraw` uses `BPT_IN_FOR_EXACT_TOKENS_OUT` which can be attack to cause loss to all depositors
content: The vulnerability resides in the withdrawal routine of the BalancerStrategy contract. The strategy records each depositor's entitlement in terms of Balancer Pool Tokens (BPT) but, when a withdrawal is requested, it calculates the amount of BPT to burn by using the BPT_IN_FOR_EXACT_TOKENS_OUT exit kind, which derives the required BPT from the amount of ETH (or other token) the caller wants to receive. Because the calculation is based on a single‑sided token amount rather than the exact BPT balance, an attacker can deliberately unbalance the underlying pool, for example by swapping large amounts of the other pool token, so that the proportional share of BPT needed to extract a given amount of ETH becomes much larger than the BPT actually owned by the strategy. When the strategy executes its _withdraw function it therefore burns all of its BPT, effectively taking value from other liquidity providers and leaving the strategy with insufficient assets to cover its recorded shares. The result is a total loss of the deposited tokens for every user of the strategy; balances may appear to be reduced to zero or withdrawals may return far less than expected. The exploit can be carried out whenever the pool is not perfectly balanced and the contract permits single‑sided exposure, which is the case for the current implementation. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by inspecting the join/exit enum usage and noticing the mismatch between deposit accounting (EXACT_TOKENS_IN_FOR_BPT_OUT) and withdrawal accounting (BPT_IN_FOR_EXACT_TOKENS_OUT). It is difficult to detect from the UI because the withdrawal transaction itself does not revert and may even report a successful amount withdrawn, while the hidden accounting error silently drains value from the pool. The proper mitigation is to use the EXACT_BPT_IN_FOR_TOKENS_OUT exit kind and to denominate the strategy in LP tokens, thereby ensuring that withdrawals are based on the exact BPT amount owned and eliminating the single‑sided exposure that enables the manipulation. This class of bug falls under incorrect LP‑token accounting and withdrawal slippage manipulation, where the contract trusts a formula that can be skewed by external pool state, violating the fundamental accounting assumption that each BPT represents a fixed proportion of the pool assets.
summary:
Withdrawals can be manipulated to cause complete loss of all tokens.

The BalancerStrategy accounts for user deposits in terms of the BPT shares they contributed, however, for withdrawals, it estimates the amount of BPT to burn based on the amount of ETH to withdraw, which can be manipulated to cause a total loss to the Strategy.

Deposits of weth are done via userData.joinKind set to `1`, which is extracted here in the generic Pool Logic:  
<https://etherscan.io/address/0x5c6ee304399dbdb9c8ef030ab642b10820db8f56#code#F24#L49>

The interpretation (by convention is shown here):  
<https://etherscan.io/address/0x5c6ee304399dbdb9c8ef030ab642b10820db8f56#code#F24#L49>

```solidity
enum JoinKind { INIT, EXACT_TOKENS_IN_FOR_BPT_OUT, TOKEN_IN_FOR_EXACT_BPT_OUT }
```

Which means that the deposit is using `EXACT_TOKENS_IN_FOR_BPT_OUT` which is safe in most circumstances (Pool Properly Balanced, with minimum liquidity).

title: Usage of `BalancerStrategy.updateCache` will cause single sided Loss, discount to Depositor and to OverBorrow from Singularity
content: The vulnerability originates from the way the BalancerStrategy calculates the value of its holdings in a Balancer pool. The contract stores a cached balance that is derived from a call to vault.queryExit, which simulates withdrawing the LP tokens in a single‑sided manner (i.e., as if only one asset were removed). Because the price is computed from a single‑sided exit, the cache can be manipulated by changing the internal composition of the pool before the cache is refreshed. An attacker can perform a swap that skews the pool’s token ratios, or can send additional ETH to the pool, causing the simulated exit value to be artificially high. The updateCache function is invoked only after a deposit operation (inside _deposited) and therefore runs too late to reflect the true state of the pool at the moment the deposit is recorded. The YieldBox contract later reads the cached balance through a view function, accepts the inflated number without any verification, and uses it to determine how many shares to mint or how much borrowing power to grant. Consequently, an attacker can trigger a sandwich sequence: first imbalance the pool, then cause updateCache to store an inflated balance, deposit into YieldBox to obtain an oversized credit, rebalance the pool back to normal, and finally withdraw or borrow against the overstated balance, extracting value from other users. The impact is multi‑faceted: depositors may receive fewer assets than expected, borrowers can be over‑borrowed leading to protocol insolvency, and liquidators can profit from unfair liquidations. The issue manifests whenever the strategy’s cache is refreshed after a deposit while the pool can be externally rebalanced, affecting any user who interacts with the YieldBox or relies on the strategy’s reported balance. It was discovered during a Code4rena audit by analysing the logical flow of updateCache and noticing that the single‑sided pricing model does not reflect the true reserve ratios. The bug is subtle because the cached value appears consistent with the queryExit call, and the view‑only nature of the balance check prevents on‑chain disputes, making the manipulation hard to detect from the outside.
