This _will_ create market-related periods of insufficient collateral, leading to regular (albeit temporary) DoS of the bonding mechanism which can impact the `ETH` peg of the `DpxEthToken` (not to mention the poor optics for the project).

title: The settle feature will be broken if attacker arbitrarily transfer collateral tokens to the PerpetualAtlanticVaultLP
content: The vulnerability is an accounting invariant violation in the PerpetualAtlanticVaultLP contract. The contract keeps an internal variable _totalCollateral that records the amount of collateral that should be held. When a loss is settled, the function subtractLoss checks that the ERC‑20 balance of the collateral token held by the contract exactly equals _totalCollateral minus the loss, using a strict equality (==) comparison. Because the check requires exact equality, any external transfer of collateral tokens into the vault changes the on‑chain balance without updating _totalCollateral. An attacker can arbitrarily send a small amount of the collateral token (e.g., 1 wei of WETH) to the vault LP contract. After the transfer, collateral.balanceOf(address(this)) becomes larger than the expected value, causing the require statement to revert with "Not enough collateral was sent out". The revert propagates to RdpxV2Core.settle, which then aborts the settlement process and halts the protocol. This can be triggered at any time after a position is ready to settle, simply by sending tokens to the vault address; no special permissions are required. The affected parties are all users who rely on the settle function to receive their payouts, as the protocol becomes unable to distribute funds, effectively locking user balances. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where a test case demonstrated that an arbitrary token transfer caused settle to revert. The bug is hard to notice because the contract does not provide a function to reconcile the internal accounting with the actual token balance, so the mismatch remains hidden until a settlement is attempted. The proper fix is to relax the invariant check to allow the on‑chain balance to be greater than or equal to the expected amount (using >=) and to adjust _totalCollateral accordingly, or to implement a synchronization mechanism that updates the internal accounting when external token transfers occur. In user‑facing terms, a trader expects a settlement to credit their account, but instead receives no funds and sees the transaction fail with an error, leading to confusion and potential loss of confidence. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “invariant violation due to strict equality on external token balances”, which can cause funds to become inaccessible when external token transfers are possible.
summary: `RdpxV2Core.settle` reverts and the protocol stops.

title: `UniV3LiquidityAMO::recoverERC721` will cause `ERC721` tokens to be permanently locked in `rdpxV2Core`
content: The vulnerability consists of a permanent lock of ERC721 tokens when the UniV3LiquidityAMO contract calls its recoverERC721 function. The function is intended to allow an admin to retrieve NFTs that were accidentally sent to the AMO, but it transfers the tokens to the RdpxV2Core contract. RdpxV2Core inherits AccessControl, ContractWhitelist, ERC721Holder and Pausable, none of which implement any method to move, approve or otherwise manage ERC721 assets. ERC721Holder only implements onERC721Received, which permits the contract to receive NFTs but provides no outbound transfer capability. Consequently, once an NFT is sent to RdpxV2Core, there is no public or internal function that can transfer it out, nor can the contract approve another address to spend it. An attempted workaround using approveContractToSpend fails because the function expects an ERC20 amount, validates that the amount is greater than zero, and reverts when called with an NFT tokenId. The result is that the NFT becomes irretrievable, effectively disappearing from the protocol’s accounting. This issue was discovered during a formal audit when the code of RdpxV2Core was examined and the lack of any ERC721 handling logic was noted. The problem is subtle because the contract compiles without errors and the recoverERC721 function appears to perform a sensible recovery, yet the destination contract is incapable of releasing the assets. Users who rely on the admin’s ability to recover NFTs would see the token balance drop to zero after the recoverERC721 call and receive no refund or transfer, violating the expectation that the admin can return the NFT. The impact is a loss of the NFT’s value, which may be significant for high‑value collectibles or protocol‑specific positions. The vulnerability affects the protocol’s administrators, token holders, and any party that may accidentally send NFTs to the AMO. To remediate, the protocol should either add an ERC721 withdrawal function to RdpxV2Core or modify recoverERC721 so that it sends the NFTs directly back to the caller (or another address that can manage them). This change restores the ability to move the tokens and aligns the contract’s behavior with its intended recovery logic.
summary:
`UniV3LiquidityAMO::recoverERC721` is a function created in order to be able to recover `ERC721` tokens from the `UniV3LiquidityAMO` contract. It can only be called by admin and will transfer all `ERC721` tokens to the `RdpxV2Core` contract. The problem is, that it won’t be possible to do anything with these tokens after they are transferred to `rdpxV2Core`.

Indeed, `RdpxV2Core` inherits from the following contracts:

  * `AccessControl`,
  * `ContractWhitelist`,
  * `ERC721Holder`,
  * `Pausable`

and no contract from this list implement any logic allowing the NFT transfer (only `ERC721Holder` has something to do with NFTs, but it only allows to receive them, not to approve or transfer).

Moreover, `rdpxV2Core` also doesn’t have any logic allowing transfer or approval of NFTs:

  * there is no generic `execute` function there
  * no function implemented is related to `ERC721` tokens (except for `onERC721Received` inherited from `ERC721Holder`)
  * it may seem possible to do a dirty hack and try to use `approveContractToSpend` in order to approve `ERC721` token. Theoretically, one would have to specify `ERC721` `tokenId` instead of `ERC20` token amount, so that `IERC20WithBurn(_token).approve(_spender, _amount);` in fact approves `ERC721` token with `tokenId == _amount`, but it fails with `[FAIL. Reason: EvmError: Revert]` and even if it didn’t, it still wouldn’t be possible to transfer `ERC721` token with `tokenId == 0` since there is `_validate(_amount > 0, 17);` inside `approveContractToSpend`

title: Users can get immediate profit when deposit and redeem in `PerpetualAtlanticVaultLP`
content: The vulnerability is an ordering flaw in the deposit function of the PerpetualAtlanticVaultLP contract that allows a user to obtain an immediate profit by depositing and redeeming in the same block. The function first calls previewDeposit, which calculates the number of shares to mint based on the current total collateral, and only afterwards calls updateFunding, which adds newly accrued funding to the vault’s total collateral. Because the share price is computed before the funding increase, the user receives a slightly lower amount of shares for the assets supplied. When the same user calls redeem in the same block, updateFunding has already increased the total collateral, so the conversion from shares back to assets uses a higher denominator, resulting in more assets being returned than were originally deposited. This creates a profit without any market movement. The issue occurs whenever deposit and redeem are executed within the same block and the funding update condition is met, which can be triggered by any participant but is especially attractive to bots that can front‑run or sandwich other users’ transactions. The impact is a direct loss of collateral from the vault, erosion of trust in the protocol, and a potential drain of funds if the attack is repeated at scale. The bug was discovered during a Code4rena audit by writing a Foundry test that measured the balance before and after a deposit‑redeem sequence and observed a positive delta of roughly 0.02 ETH. The problem is subtle because the deposit and redeem calls appear normal and the profit per transaction is small, making it easy to miss in manual testing. The flaw belongs to the class of state‑inconsistency or ordering bugs, where a contract’s internal accounting is updated out of sync with user‑visible calculations, leading to exploitable arithmetic discrepancies. From a user’s perspective the UI would show a normal deposit confirmation followed by a redeem that returns more tokens than were supplied, violating the expectation that “what I put in is what I get out”. To remediate the issue the funding update must be performed before the share preview calculation, ensuring that both deposit and redeem use the same up‑to‑date total collateral value. Alternatively, the contract could lock the funding state for the duration of the deposit‑redeem cycle or compute shares after the funding adjustment, thereby eliminating the profit window.
summary: Due to wrong order between `previewDeposit` and `updateFunding` inside `PerpetualAtlanticVaultLP.deposit`. In some case, user can get immediate profit when call `deposit` and `redeem` in the same block.

title: Bond operations will always revert at certain time when `putOptionsRequired` is true
content: The vulnerability is a deterministic denial‑of‑service condition that occurs when the contract’s putOptionsRequired flag is true and a bond operation attempts to purchase put options from the PerpetualAtlanticVault during a short window before the next funding payment. The root cause is that the calculatePremium function forwards the raw timeToExpiry value (nextFundingPaymentTimestamp() ‑ block.timestamp) to the option pricing library without enforcing a minimum duration. The pricing library expects the time to expiry expressed in days multiplied by a precision factor; when the raw value is less than 864 seconds (approximately fourteen minutes) the conversion yields a zero timeToExpiry, which triggers a revert inside OptionPricingSimple.getOptionPrice. An attacker does not need to supply malicious input – the revert is triggered purely by blockchain time, making the bug easy to hit for any user who initiates a bond in that interval. Exploitation consists of a user calling bond while putOptionsRequired is true; the internal call to _purchaseOptions invokes PerpetualAtlanticVault.purchase, which calculates premium with the too‑small timeToExpiry, causing the transaction to revert. The impact is that legitimate users cannot complete bond transactions for roughly fourteen minutes each funding epoch (weekly in the current deployment), resulting in lost opportunity to acquire rDPX, no receipt tokens are minted, and the protocol’s liquidity provisioning is temporarily halted. The condition affects any participant trying to bond when the flag is active; funds are never transferred because the whole transaction reverts, but the user experience is a sudden failure with no receipt token and a generic revert message. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by reproducing the edge case in a Foundry unit test that warped the block timestamp to just before the funding deadline and observed the expected revert. It is hard to notice in normal testing because the problematic time window is narrow and only appears at a specific point in the funding cycle. To remediate, the calculatePremium function should enforce a lower bound on timeToExpiry (e.g., clamp values below 864 seconds to 864) before passing it to the pricing library, ensuring the pricing formula always receives a non‑zero expiry and preventing the revert. This class of bug is a time‑dependent input validation error that leads to a denial‑of‑service by violating the business assumption that options can always be priced, breaking the accounting flow that expects a premium to be deducted from the WETH reserve.
summary: when `putOptionsRequired` is `true`, there is period of time where bond operations will always revert when try to purchase options from perp atlantic vault.

title: Incorrect precision assumed from RdpxPriceOracle creates multiple issues related to value inflation/deflation
content: The vulnerability is a precision mismatch between the RdpxEthPriceOracle and the contracts that consume its price data. The oracle returns prices with 18 decimal places (1e18 precision) while RdpxV2Core, UniV2LiquidityAmo, ReLp and PerpetualAtlanticVault all assume the values are expressed with 8 decimal places (1e8 precision), as documented in their NatSpec comments. This discrepancy originates from an oversight in the oracle implementation and the reliance on a mock oracle during testing that used the wrong scale. When a contract reads the 1e18 price and treats it as 1e8, every downstream calculation that divides or multiplies by 1e8 produces values that are off by a factor of 1e10. For example, getRdpxPrice() returns an inflated price, causing calculateBondCost() to deflate the required rdpx amount, calculateAmounts() to inflate the rdpxRequiredInWeth, and _transfer() to inflate rdpxAmountInWeth which can lead to under‑flow errors. In the AMO, getLpPriceInEth() overestimates the LP token value, making reLP() report excessively high minimum token amounts. In the perpetual vault, getUnderlyingPrice() returns a value ten‑billion times larger than expected, which inflates the premium calculation in calculatePremium(). From a user’s perspective this manifests as unexpected zero or tiny refunds, excessively high premium quotes, LP token balances that appear larger than they should be, or transactions that revert due to under‑flow. The bug affects any participant interacting with the core protocol – bond purchasers, liquidity providers, option traders and vault users – because the core accounting logic is corrupted. It was discovered during a formal audit when reviewers compared the NatSpec precision declarations with the actual return values of the oracle and observed that the mock oracle used in tests hid the problem. The issue is subtle because both the oracle and the consuming contracts compile and run without errors; only the financial outcomes reveal the mismatch, making it easy to miss in functional testing. The proper fix is to align the precision expectations: either modify the oracle to return 1e8 values or, more appropriately, update all consuming contracts to handle 1e18 precision consistently, adjusting division factors and any scaling logic accordingly. This correction restores the intended accounting invariants and prevents inflated or deflated price‑derived calculations, ensuring that users receive correct refunds, premiums and LP valuations.
summary:
The `RdpxEthPriceOracle`, available in the audit repo [here](https://github.com/dopex-io/rdpx-eth-oracle/blob/5762c2339b1c45b87ff4db172e43cef4a0ff603a/src/RdpxEthOracle.sol), provides the `RdpxV2Core`, the `UniV2LiquidityAmo` and the `PerpetualAtlanticVault` contracts the necessary values for `rdpx` related price calculations.

The issue is that these contracts expect the returned values to be in `1e8` precision (as stated in the natspec [here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/eb4d4a201b3a75dd4bddc74a34e9c42c71d0d12f/contracts/core/RdpxV2Core.sol#L1224), [here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/eb4d4a201b3a75dd4bddc74a34e9c42c71d0d12f/contracts/amo/UniV2LiquidityAmo.sol#L378) and [here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-dopex/blob/eb4d4a201b3a75dd4bddc74a34e9c42c71d0d12f/contracts/perp-vault/IPerpetualAtlanticVault.sol#L20C1-L24C65)). But the returned precision [is actually `1e18`](https://github.com/dopex-io/rdpx-eth-oracle/blob/5762c2339b1c45b87ff4db172e43cef4a0ff603a/src/RdpxEthOracle.sol#L243).

This difference creates multiple issues throughout the below contracts:

Contract | Function | Effect  
---|---|---  
`rdpxV2Core.sol` | `getRdpxPrice()` | Returns an `1e18` value when `1e8` expected  
| `calculateBondCost()` | Deflates the `rdpxRequired`  
| `calculateAmounts()` | Inflates the `rdpxRequiredInWeth`  
| `_transfer()` | Inflates `rdpxAmountInWeth` and may cause possible underflow  
`UniV2LiquidityAmo` | `getLpPriceInEth()` | Overestimates the lp value  
`ReLp.sol` | `reLP()` | Inflates min token amounts  
`PerpetualAtlanticVault.sol` | `getUnderlyingPrice()` | Returns `1e18` instead of `1e8`  
| `calculatePremium()` | Inflates the premium calculation

title: The peg stability module can be compromised by forcing lowerDepeg to revert
content: The vulnerability resides in the accounting logic of the peg stability module that relies on a global counter called totalWethDelegated. The root cause is that the withdraw function does not decrease this counter when a delegate withdraws its WETH, leaving totalWethDelegated inflated even though the underlying WETH has been returned to the caller. Because the sync function later uses totalWethDelegated to adjust the contract's internal WETH reserve, the inflated counter causes the reserve value to be artificially reduced, potentially to zero. When extreme market conditions trigger the lowerDepeg function, which attempts to buy back and burn dpxETH to restore the dpxETH/ETH peg, the contract performs arithmetic that assumes the reserve is sufficient. The artificially low reserve leads to an under‑flow error, causing the lowerDepeg transaction to revert. An attacker can exploit this by first calling addToDelegate to increase totalWethDelegated, then immediately calling withdraw, which does not correct the counter, and finally invoking sync to corrupt the reserve balance. By repeating the add‑to‑delegate and withdraw steps, the attacker can inflate totalWethDelegated with only a small amount of WETH, making the attack cheap. The impact is that the protocol loses the ability to defend the peg, potentially leaving users with a broken price relationship, missing refunds, or zero balances where funds should exist. The issue is observable from a user’s perspective as a sudden drop in displayed WETH reserves, failed peg‑restoration transactions, or unexpected reverts when the admin attempts to execute lowerDepeg. The flaw was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena through manual testing of edge‑case flows involving delegate management and reserve synchronization. It is hard to notice because the withdraw function appears to succeed and the delegate’s balance is correctly transferred, while the internal accounting variable silently diverges. The bug belongs to the class of state‑inconsistency and accounting‑misalignment vulnerabilities, where a public state variable is not kept in sync with external token movements. To remediate, the withdraw function must correctly decrement totalWethDelegated by the amount actually withdrawn, ensuring that subsequent sync calls reflect the true reserve balance and that lowerDepeg can execute without arithmetic errors.
summary: In a scenario where extreme market conditions necessitate the execution of the `lowerDepeg` function to restore the dpxETH/ETH peg, an attacker can exploit the flawed interaction between the `addToDelegate`, `withdraw`, and `sync` functions to force a revert on the admin’s attempt to restore the peg. As a result, the protocol will not be able to effectively defend the peg, leading to potential disruptions in the protocol’s peg stability module.

title: `ReLPContract` wrongfully assumes protocol owns all of the liquidity in the UniswapV2 pool
content: The vulnerability resides in the re‑LP logic of the protocol’s liquidity management contract. The contract retrieves the total reserves of a UniswapV2 pair and then assumes that the entire pool of LP tokens belongs to the protocol’s AMO (Automated Market Operations) component. This assumption is baked into the formula that calculates how many LP tokens must be withdrawn (lpToRemove) when a user bonds with the re‑LP feature enabled. Because the protocol may only own a fraction of the total LP supply, the calculation can produce a value that exceeds the actual balance held by the AMO. When this oversized lpToRemove amount is passed to the ERC20 transferFrom call, the transfer fails due to an under‑flow or insufficient allowance, causing the transaction to revert. The revert manifests as a denial‑of‑service condition: any attempt to bond while re‑LP is active will fail, preventing users from completing the operation and effectively freezing the re‑LP pathway. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when the auditors added console logs and observed that the computed lpToRemove (e.g., 1.78e19) was larger than the AMO’s LP balance (e.g., 2.23e18). The bug is subtle because the contract correctly reads the pool reserves, yet the subsequent ownership assumption is hidden in the business logic, making it easy to overlook during code review. The impact is that users see their bond transaction revert, receive no tokens, and may lose confidence in the protocol; the protocol itself cannot process re‑LP bonds until the logic is corrected. The root cause is an incorrect accounting assumption – the protocol treats the whole pool as its own, violating the invariant that only the portion of LP tokens actually owned can be transferred. To fix the issue, the calculation must be based on the AMO’s actual LP balance rather than the total pair supply, ensuring that lpToRemove never exceeds the owned amount. This change restores correct accounting, prevents under‑flows, and eliminates the DoS scenario, aligning the contract’s behavior with the intended financial model where only owned liquidity can be re‑LPed.
summary: Possible full DoS for `ReLPContract`

title: When price is within position’s range, `deposit` at TokenisableRange can cause loss of funds
content: The vulnerability resides in the deposit routine of a tokenised Uniswap V3 range position. The function expects the caller to supply positive amounts for both tokens (n0 and n1) when the pool price is inside the position’s tick range. Inside the routine the contract reads the current pool price from slot0, calls LiquidityAmounts.getAmountsForLiquidity to compute the amount of each token that corresponds to the existing liquidity, and then scales the pending fees (fee0 and fee1) proportionally to the supplied amounts using the formula newFee0 = n0 * fee0 / (token0Amount + fee0) (and similarly for token1). This calculation assumes that token0Amount and token1Amount are both non‑zero. If, between the moment the transaction is signed and the moment it is executed, the pool price moves outside the position’s range, one of the token amounts returned by getAmountsForLiquidity becomes zero. When token1Amount is zero, the denominator of the second formula collapses to fee1, causing newFee1 to equal n1 – the entire amount the user intended to deposit is treated as a fee. The contract then deducts this fee from n1, leaving the user with no token1 deposited while still being charged the full amount. From the user’s perspective the transaction appears to succeed, but the expected token balance is missing or reduced to zero, effectively “funds disappear”. The issue is triggered only when price slippage or a front‑running trade pushes the price out of the tick range during execution, a condition that is not obvious during static analysis because the price is read from the pool at runtime. The bug was uncovered during a security audit that simulated price movement and observed the fee‑clawback logic misbehaving. It is hard to notice because under normal market conditions the price stays within the range and the fee calculation yields reasonable values. The root cause is the reliance on a volatile on‑chain price to compute fee proportions without safeguarding against zero token amounts, leading to a division‑by‑zero‑like situation and an excessive fee charge. To remediate, the contract should avoid using the pool’s instantaneous price for fee scaling; instead it should compute fees based on oracle‑derived stable prices or on the amounts the user actually supplied, and it must enforce that both token amounts are greater than zero before applying the proportional fee formula. Adding explicit checks that reject a deposit when either token amount returned by getAmountsForLiquidity is zero, or capping the fee to the supplied amount, eliminates the possibility of charging the full deposit as a fee and restores the intended accounting guarantees.
summary: When slot0 price is within the range of tokenized position, function `deposit` needs to be called with both parameters, `n0` and `n1`, greater than zero. However, if price moves outside the range during the transaction, user will be charged an excessive fee.

title: Unused funds are not returned and not counted in `GeVault`
content: The vulnerability in GeVault is an accounting and fund‑return flaw that can cause a portion of a user’s deposited tokens to become permanently locked inside the contract and omitted from the reported total value locked (TVL). The root cause is that the depositAndStash routine forwards token amounts to a Uniswap V3 pool without first ensuring that the amounts are balanced according to the pool’s current price. Uniswap V3 only accepts a pair of tokens in a ratio that matches the pool’s price; when the supplied amounts are not perfectly balanced, the TokenisableRange.deposit call returns the excess (unspent) tokens to the GeVault contract. Because GeVault’s deposit() function does not capture or forward these returned tokens back to the depositor, and because the getTVL() and getTickBalance() calculations only sum the liquidity that was successfully added to the pool, the leftover tokens remain invisible to the TVL metric and are never accounted for during withdrawal. An attacker or any user can trigger this situation by depositing an unbalanced amount, then invoking the rebalance() flow which removes liquidity from all ticks and redeploys assets in equal halves. The redeployment may again produce unspent tokens that stay trapped. When the user later calls withdraw(), the contract computes the payout based on the TVL that excludes the hidden tokens, so the user receives less than originally deposited. From the user’s perspective the UI may show that the deposit was accepted, but on withdrawal the balance appears reduced or the refund is partially missing, leading to confusion and perceived loss of funds. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that traced the flow of tokens through deposit(), rebalance(), and deployAssets(), noticing that the safeTransfer calls in TokenisableRange.deposit return excess tokens that GeVault never handles. The bug is subtle because the contract does not emit events for the hidden tokens and the TVL figure looks correct, making the loss hard to detect without deep inspection of the token flows. To remediate, the contract should either return any unspent tokens to the original depositor within depositAndStash, or adjust the accounting logic to include those tokens in the TVL calculation, and add tests to guarantee that rebalancing never leaves residual balances. This class of bug falls under improper handling of external contract return values and inaccurate accounting of assets, which violates the fundamental business logic that every deposited token must be either invested or refundable.
summary: Users can lose a portion of their deposited funds if some of their funds haven’t been deposited to the underlying Uniswap pools. There’s always a chance of such event since Uniswap pools take balanced token amounts when liquidity is added but `GeVault` doesn’t pre-compute balanced amounts. As a result, depositing and withdrawing can result in a partial loss of funds.

title: Overflow can still happen when calculating `priceX8` inside `poolMatchesOracle` operation
content: An overflow vulnerability exists in the price calculation performed by the poolMatchesOracle function of the GoodEntry vault. The function reads the sqrtPriceX96 value from a Uniswap V3 pool, scales it down by dividing by 2**12, squares the result and then multiplies by a factor derived from the token decimals to obtain a price expressed with 8 decimal places (priceX8). Because the scaling factor (2**12) is far smaller than the factor required to keep the intermediate product within the 256‑bit unsigned integer range, the multiplication and squaring can exceed the maximum uint256 value before the final division by 2**168 is applied. When the overflow occurs the arithmetic wraps or reverts, causing priceX8 to be incorrect or the whole transaction to fail. The bug is triggered when the pool contains assets with a large disparity in decimal places, such as WBTC (8 decimals) paired with WETH (18 decimals), and when the sqrtPriceX96 value is large, as demonstrated by the test case that reproduces an overflow with the real WBTC/WETH pool data. The overflow prevents the contract from correctly comparing the on‑chain price with the Chainlink oracle price, so the rebalance decision logic may never evaluate to true. As a result the vault can stay in an unbalanced state, exposing users to stale pricing, potential arbitrage loss, or even permanent loss of funds if the contract relies on periodic rebalancing to maintain collateral ratios. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by inspecting the arithmetic expression and reproducing the failure with a unit test that triggered an arithmetic over/underflow exception. The problem is subtle because the overflow happens only for certain token pairs and does not manifest as an obvious error message; it simply causes the transaction to revert, which can be mistaken for a generic failure. The correct mitigation is to use the scaling factor recommended by the Uniswap V3 library (for example, FullMath.mulDiv with the library’s Q96 constant) or to apply a larger down‑scaling (such as dividing sqrtPriceX96 by 2**96 before squaring) so that the intermediate product stays within the uint256 range. By adopting the library’s price‑calculation routine or by explicitly matching the scaling used in the official Uniswap SDK, the overflow is eliminated and the price comparison works as intended, restoring the vault’s ability to rebalance safely.
summary: `poolMatchesOracle` is used to compare price calculated from uniswap v3 pool and chainlink oracle and decide whether rebalance should happened or not. `priceX8` will be holding price information calculated using `sqrtPriceX96` and when operations is performed, it will try to scale down using `2 ** 12`. However, the scale down is not enough and overflow can still happened.

title: TokenisableRange’s incorrect accounting of non-reinvested fees in “deposit” exposes the fees to a flash-loan attack
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect accounting of fees that have not been reinvested when a user calls the deposit function of a TokenisableRange contract. The contract is supposed to collect trading fees from a Uniswap V3 pool on every liquidity event and, when the accumulated fees represent more than 1 % of the pool’s liquidity, automatically reinvest them. However, the 1 % check is performed on the raw token amounts of fee0 and fee1 rather than on their combined market value. When the price of the underlying assets moves sharply after fees have been accrued, the monetary value of the fees can far exceed the intended 1 % threshold while the contract still treats the fees as below the limit, so no reinvestment occurs. At the same time, the minting of TokenisableRange liquidity tokens is down‑scaled only when the full amount of deposited liquidity is added to the pool; a user can supply a negligible amount of the second token (for example a few wei of WETH) to bypass the down‑scaling logic and receive a proportional share of the undistributed fees essentially for free. An attacker can combine these two weaknesses in a single deposit‑withdraw cycle, often funded by a flash loan, to claim the majority of the fee balances (fee0 and fee1) that are sitting in the contract. From the user’s perspective the contract may appear to accept a normal deposit, but after withdrawal the attacker’s wallet shows a large increase in token balances while the victim sees no compensation for the lost fees. The impact is a loss of protocol‑owned fees, potentially several percent of the total pool value, and a breach of the economic assumption that fees are either reinvested or fairly distributed among liquidity providers. The issue was discovered during a security audit that exercised realistic market conditions and observed that the fee‑value check did not consider oracle prices. It is hard to notice because the raw fee amounts may be small and the price deviation is not obvious from on‑chain data alone. The bug belongs to the class of incorrect value‑based accounting and incomplete token‑mint scaling errors. To remediate, the contract should calculate the fee threshold using the current market price of each token via a reliable oracle and always adjust the minted liquidity tokens by the value of any undistributed fees, regardless of how small the supplied secondary token amount is.
summary:
The `TokenisableRange` is designed to always collect trading fees from the Uniswap V3 pool, whenever there is a liquidity event (`deposit` or `withdraw`). These fees may be reinvested in the pool, or may be held in form of `fee0` and `fee1` ERC-20 balance held by the TokenisableRange contract.

When a user deposits liquidity in the range, they pay asset tokens, and receive back liquidity tokens, which give them a share of the TokenisableRange assets (liquidity locked in Unisvap V3, plus fee0, and fee1).

To prevent users from stealing fees, there are several mechanisms in place:

1. fees are, as said, always collected whenever liquidity is added or removed, and whenever they exceed 1% of the liquidity in the pool, they are re-invested in Uniswap V3. The intention of this check seems to be limiting the value locked in these fees
2. whenever a user deposits liquidity to the range, the LP tokens given to them are scaled down by the value of the fees, so the participation in fees “is not given away for free”

Both of these mechanisms can however be worked around:

1. the 1% check is done on the `fee0` and `fee1` **amounts** compared to the theoretical pool amounts, and **not on the total value of the fees** as compared to the total value locked in the pool. This means that when the price changes significantly from when fees were accumulated, the combined value of the fees can exceed, potentially by much, the 1% intended cap, without the reinvestment happening before liquidity events. A malicious user can then monitor and act in such market conditions.
2. the downscaling of the LP tokens minted to the user happens only if none of the provided liquidity is added to the pool fees instead of the Uniswap V3 position. The user can send just a few wei’s of tokens to short-circuit the downscaling, and have a share of fees “for free”.

Given a TokenisableRange contract in the right state (high value locked in fees, but still no reinvestment happening) a user can maliciously craft a `deposit` and `withdraw` sequence (why not, with flash-loaned assets) to steal most of the fees (`fee0`, `fee1`) held by the pool before distribution.

title: V3Proxy swapTokensForExactETH does not send back to the caller the unused input tokens
content: The vulnerability resides in the V3Proxy contract function that swaps an arbitrary amount of an ERC‑20 token for a fixed amount of native ETH (swapTokensForExactETH). The function accepts a maximum input amount (amountInMax) from the caller, transfers that full amount to the proxy, and then performs an exact‑output swap on Uniswap V3. After the swap the contract calculates the actual amount of tokens consumed (amounts[0]) but fails to return the difference (amountInMax‑amounts[0]) to the caller. Consequently the surplus tokens remain locked inside the proxy contract. The root cause is improper handling of excess input funds: the contract does not include a refund step after the swap, leaving the leftover tokens unrecoverable by the user. An attacker can exploit this by deliberately supplying a much larger amountInMax than required, causing the proxy to retain the excess tokens on each call. Repeating the call drains tokens from any user who trusts the proxy to perform exact‑output swaps. The impact is a loss of user assets – the user receives the expected ETH but sees a larger-than‑expected reduction in their token balance, effectively “funds disappear”. This occurs whenever the function is invoked with a path of length two, the second token being WETH, and the caller supplies an amountInMax that exceeds the true required input for the desired ETH output. All users of the proxy, especially those swapping stablecoins for ETH, are affected. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit through a unit test that checked the caller’s token balance after the swap; the test revealed that the excess tokens were not returned. The bug can be hard to notice because the transaction does not revert and the ETH transfer succeeds, so a UI may display a successful swap while the token balance silently shrinks. To remediate, the contract should explicitly transfer the unused portion of the input token back to the caller after the swap, or alternatively compute the exact required input before transferring any tokens, thereby ensuring that no funds remain unintentionally locked. This class of bug is commonly referred to as an “excess input token lock” or “missing refund” vulnerability, which violates the expected accounting invariant that the sum of tokens sent in equals the sum of tokens sent out plus the amount actually used for the swap.
summary: The `V3Proxy` `swapTokensForExactETH` function swaps an unspecified amount of a given ERC-20 for a specified amount of the native currency. After the swap happens, however, the difference between the amount taken from the caller (`amountInMax`) and the actual swapped amount (`amounts[0]`) is not given back to the caller and remains locked in the contract.

title: Incorrect Solidity version in FullMath.sol can cause permanent freezing of assets for arithmetic underflow-induced revert
content: The vulnerability is an arithmetic underflow caused by compiling the Uniswap V3 FullMath library with Solidity version 0.8.x, which introduces automatic overflow and underflow checks. FullMath is designed to perform 512‑bit multiplication and division using unchecked arithmetic; when compiled with Solidity 0.8 or later the built‑in checks trigger a revert whenever an intermediate value would overflow. In the TokenisableRange contract the helper function LiquidityAmounts.getAmountsForLiquidity is called to convert pool liquidity into token amounts. If the current sqrt price (sqrtRatioX96) is lower than the lower bound of the configured price range (sqrtRatioAX96), the calculation underflows and the function reverts. This revert propagates to higher‑level functions such as returnExpectedBalanceWithoutFees, getTokenAmountsExcludingFees, claimFee, deposit and withdraw. Because deposit and withdraw invoke claimFee on every operation, a price that stays outside the range makes every deposit or withdrawal transaction revert, effectively locking the underlying assets in the contract until the market price moves back into the range. In real markets the price can remain permanently on one side of the range, so the assets may be frozen forever. From a user’s point of view a deposit or withdrawal simply fails with a revert, the UI shows no change in balance, and the user may see their tokens appear to disappear or become inaccessible. The issue was discovered during a security audit that included a proof‑of‑concept test using real‑world Uniswap V3 slot0 data, which demonstrated that the underflow occurs with actual market prices. The bug is hard to notice because it only manifests under specific price conditions and the revert message does not reveal the underlying arithmetic problem. The proper fix is to restore the original FullMath implementation that is compiled with a Solidity compiler version earlier than 0.8.0, or alternatively wrap the arithmetic in an unchecked block, although the latter is not recommended. By using the correct library the phantom overflow behavior is restored, the underflow no longer triggers a revert, and deposits and withdrawals work as intended regardless of price movements, preserving the protocol’s accounting guarantees and preventing permanent asset lockup.
summary:
`TokenisableRange` makes use of the `LiquidityAmounts.getAmountsForLiquidity` helper function in its [`returnExpectedBalanceWithoutFees`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-goodentry/blob/71c0c0eca8af957202ccdbf5ce2f2a514ffe2e24/contracts/TokenisableRange.sol#L338), [`getTokenAmountsExcludingFees`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-goodentry/blob/71c0c0eca8af957202ccdbf5ce2f2a514ffe2e24/contracts/TokenisableRange.sol#L371C31-L371C31) and [`deposit`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-goodentry/blob/71c0c0eca8af957202ccdbf5ce2f2a514ffe2e24/contracts/TokenisableRange.sol#L240C18-L240C18) functions to convert UniswapV3 pool liquidity into estimated underlying token amounts.

This function `getAmountsForLiquidity` will trigger an arithmetic underflow whenever `sqrtRatioX96` is smaller than `sqrtRatioAX96`, causing these functions to revert until this ratio comes back in range and the math no longer overflows.

Such oracle price conditions are not only possible but also likely to happen in real market conditions, and they can be permanent (i.e. one asset permanently appreciating over the other one).

Moving up the stack, assuming that `LiquidityAmounts.getAmountsForLiquidity` can revert (which is shown in the below PoC with real-world conditions), both the [`returnExpectedBalanceWithoutFees`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-goodentry/blob/71c0c0eca8af957202ccdbf5ce2f2a514ffe2e24/contracts/TokenisableRange.sol#L338) and [`getTokenAmountsExcludingFees`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-goodentry/blob/71c0c0eca8af957202ccdbf5ce2f2a514ffe2e24/contracts/TokenisableRange.sol#L371C31-L371C31) functions can revert. In particular, the former [is called by the `claimFee()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-goodentry/blob/71c0c0eca8af957202ccdbf5ce2f2a514ffe2e24/contracts/TokenisableRange.sol#L187) function, which is always called when [depositing](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-goodentry/blob/71c0c0eca8af957202ccdbf5ce2f2a514ffe2e24/contracts/TokenisableRange.sol#L227) and [withdrawing](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-goodentry/blob/71c0c0eca8af957202ccdbf5ce2f2a514ffe2e24/contracts/TokenisableRange.sol#L293) liquidity.

The root cause of this issue is that the FullMath.sol library, [imported from UniswapV3](https://github.com/Uniswap/v3-core/blob/main/contracts/libraries/FullMath.sol) was [altered to build with solidity v0.8.x](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-08-goodentry/blob/71c0c0eca8af957202ccdbf5ce2f2a514ffe2e24/contracts/lib/FullMath.sol#L2), which has under/overflow protection; the library, however, makes use of these by design, so it won’t work properly when compiled in v0.8.0 or later:
```solidity
/// @dev Handles "phantom overflow" i.e., allows multiplication and division where an intermediate value overflows 256 bits
library FullMath {
```
When the fair exchange price of the pool backing the TokenisableRange’s falls outside the range (higher side), the `deposit` and `withdraw` will always revert, locking the underlying assets in the pool until the price swings to a different value that does not trigger an under/overflow. If the oracle price stays within this range indefinitely, the funds are permanently locked.

title: Underflow in `updateTranscoderWithFees` can cause corrupted data and loss of winning tickets
content: The vulnerability is an arithmetic underflow that occurs in the function responsible for updating a transcoder’s reward balance when a winning ticket is redeemed. The root cause is the use of a generic percentage library that defines its divisor as one million, while the protocol’s specification requires a 27‑digit precision divisor. Because the contract calls the generic library to compute the portion of rewards that should go to the treasury, the calculated treasury share is orders of magnitude larger than intended. When the contract then subtracts this oversized treasury amount from the total rewards, the subtraction underflows, producing a wrap‑around to a very large number or causing a revert, depending on the Solidity version. This underflow can be triggered every time the updateTranscoderWithFees function is executed after a transcoder has missed a scheduled reward distribution, which is a normal path defined in the protocol’s reward‑recalculation logic. The impact is that the reward accounting becomes corrupted: the transcoder’s reward balance may be reduced to zero, the ticket is marked as redeemed, and the expected payout never reaches the delegator or transcoder. From a user’s perspective the symptom is a missing or zero reward after a winning ticket claim, with no error message other than a possible transaction failure. The parties affected include transcoders, delegators who stake through them, and the protocol treasury that relies on accurate fee accounting. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when the auditors compared the contract’s implementation against the LIP‑92 specification and noticed the mismatch between MathUtils and PreciseMathUtils. The bug is subtle because the underflow only manifests when the reward amount is smaller than the incorrectly computed treasury share, a condition that occurs consistently after a skipped round but may not be obvious during normal testing. To remediate the problem the contract should replace the generic percentage calculation with the precise library that uses the correct 27‑digit divisor, or add explicit checks to ensure the treasury portion never exceeds the total rewards before subtraction. This change restores correct arithmetic, prevents reward loss, and aligns the implementation with the protocol’s accounting assumptions.
summary: `updateTranscoderWtihFees` can underflow because MathUtils is used instead of PreciseMathUtils.

title: By delegating to a non-transcoder, a delegator can reduce the tally of someone else’s vote choice without first granting them any voting power
content: The vulnerability is an accounting flaw in the governance voting logic that allows a delegator who is not a transcoder to modify the vote tally of another participant without first receiving any voting power themselves. The root cause is a missing validation step: when a delegator casts a vote, the contract checks whether the address they have delegated to has already voted, but it does not verify that this delegate is a registered transcoder before subtracting the delegate’s vote weight from the tally. Because non‑transcoder delegates never receive the delegated stake as voting power, the subtraction operation reduces the tally of the delegate’s chosen option by the full weight of the delegator’s stake, effectively removing votes that never belonged to the delegator. An attacker can exploit this by delegating a large amount of stake to a non‑transcoder delegate who has already voted, then casting their own vote. The contract will execute the subtraction logic, decreasing the previously recorded tally for the delegate’s choice and adding the attacker’s weight to the opposite side, resulting in a net gain of voting influence that exceeds the attacker’s actual stake. This manipulation can double‑count votes, distort governance outcomes, and allow a malicious party to sway proposals without proper authority. The issue manifests whenever a delegator (Bob) votes after delegating to a delegate (Alice) who is not a transcoder and whose vote has already been recorded. All participants in the governance process, including token holders and protocol maintainers, are affected because the final vote counts no longer reflect the true distribution of delegated stake. The flaw was discovered during a formal security audit that examined the vote‑handling routine and identified the missing transcoder check as a logical oversight. It is hard to notice because the contract does not emit an error; the tally simply changes in an unexpected direction, which may be attributed to normal voting dynamics. To remediate, the vote‑override function should include a condition that confirms the delegate is a transcoder before applying any subtraction to the tally, ensuring that only entities with actual voting power can influence the accounting. Conceptually, this is a role‑based validation bug in a delegated voting system, where the accounting of delegated stakes is performed without proper authority checks, leading to vote tally manipulation and potential governance compromise.
summary:
A delegate can subtract their own voting weight from the voting choice of another delegate, even if that user isn’t a transcoder. Since they are not a transcoder, they don’t have their votes initially increased by the amount delegated to them, voting weight is still subtracted from the tally of their vote choice.

Maliciously, this could be used to effectively double one’s voting power, by delegating their votes to a delegator who is about to vote for the choice which they don’t want. It can also occur accidentally, for example when somebody delegates to a transcoder who later switches role to delegate.

title: Too many rewards are distributed when a draw is closed
content: The vulnerability is an over‑allocation of rewards that occurs when a prize pool draw is closed through the rngComplete function. The contract closes the draw, which automatically adds the amount stored in reserveForOpenDraw to the pool's main reserve, and then mistakenly calculates the reward amounts using a futureReserve value that adds reserveForOpenDraw a second time. This double‑counting of the pending reserve means the reward fraction is applied to tokens that have not yet been minted, resulting in reward recipients receiving more tokens than the protocol’s accounting rules allow. The root cause is a logical error in the reward calculation order: the code uses prizePool.reserve() + prizePool.reserveForOpenDraw() after closeDraw has already incorporated reserveForOpenDraw into reserve(), effectively counting the same tokens twice. An attacker can exploit this by first calling computeRewards to see the inflated reward amount, then triggering rngComplete (or a relayer calling it) to close the draw and claim the excess tokens. The impact is that the protocol distributes extra tokens, draining the prize pool’s reserves faster than intended and breaking the economic guarantees of the lottery. This condition occurs every time a draw is closed while the reward calculation uses the futureReserve expression, affecting any participant who receives rewards, as well as token holders who rely on the pool’s integrity. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, and it can be subtle because the reward numbers appear plausible and the over‑payment may be small per draw, making it hard to notice without detailed accounting checks. From a user perspective the symptoms are unexpectedly large reward payouts, a rapid decrease in the pool’s visible balance, or draws that seem to give out more tokens than the advertised prize structure. The bug belongs to the class of accounting miscalculations where pending funds are double‑counted, leading to reward over‑distribution. To fix the issue the reward calculation should use only the current reserve after closeDraw, removing the addition of reserveForOpenDraw, so that RewardLib receives the correct reserve amount and the reward fraction is applied to the true available token pool.
summary:
A relayer completes a prize pool draw by calling `rngComplete` in `RngRelayAuction.sol`. This method closes the prize pool draw with the relayed random number and distributes the rewards to the RNG auction recipient and the RNG relay auction recipient. These rewards are calculated based on a fraction of the prize pool reserve rather than an actual value.

However, the current reward calculation mistakenly includes an extra `reserveForOpenDraw` amount just after the draw has been closed. Therefore the fraction over which the rewards are being calculated includes tokens that have not been added to the reserve and will actually only be added to the reserve when the next draw is finalised. As a result, the reward recipients are rewarded too many tokens.

title: `rngComplete` function should only be called by `rngAuctionRelayer`
content: The vulnerability is an unauthorized function call flaw in the rngComplete routine of the prize‑pool contract. The function is intended to be invoked only by a designated relayer after a random number is supplied, and it distributes the auction reward to the address supplied as _rewardRecipient. Because the implementation contains no access‑control check on msg.sender and accepts the reward recipient as an unrestricted argument, any external account can call rngComplete before the legitimate relayer does and supply an address of its own choosing. When this happens the contract records the attacker’s address as the recipient, calculates the reward fraction, and then withdraws the allocated reward from the prize‑pool reserve to that address. The true auction winner therefore receives no payout while the attacker receives the full reward. This issue occurs whenever the auction sequence has not yet been marked as completed and the relayer has not yet called the function; under those conditions any caller can trigger the reward distribution. The affected parties are the participants who expect to receive the auction reward, the prize‑pool’s accounting logic, and any users relying on the relayer to enforce correct reward flow. The flaw was discovered during a Code4rena audit that examined the function signature and noticed the absence of a modifier or explicit sender verification. It can be hard to notice because the function appears to be part of the normal auction lifecycle and emits events that look legitimate, masking the fact that the reward recipient can be arbitrarily changed. The bug belongs to the class of missing‑access‑control or privilege‑escalation vulnerabilities where a public function performs privileged state changes without restricting the caller. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a user who should receive a reward sees a zero balance or no token transfer after the draw, while an unexpected address suddenly receives a large amount. The expectation that the contract will automatically credit the correct winner is violated, breaking the business rule that auction rewards are allocated to the designated winner. The recommended remediation is to enforce that only the authorized rngAuctionRelayer can invoke rngComplete, for example by adding a require or revert that checks msg.sender against the stored relayer address, and optionally removing the external _rewardRecipient parameter or validating it against the auction’s recorded winner before distributing funds.
summary: The `rngComplete` function is supposed to be called by the relayer to complete the Rng relay auction and send auction rewards to the recipient, but because the function doesn’t have any access control it can be called by anyone, an attacker can call the function before the relayer and give a different `_rewardRecipient` and thus he can collect all the rewards and the true auction reward recipient will not get any.

title: Lack of Balance Validation
content: The contract implements a constant‑product style liquidity pool that must keep the ratio of token Y to token X inside a predefined interval [MIN_M,MAX_M). This invariant is enforced by an internal routine called _checkBalances(), which is invoked only from the swap and LP‑token‑minting paths. The depositGivenInputAmount() and withdrawGivenOutputAmount() entry points, however, call a lower‑level routine _reserveTokenSpecified() and never trigger the balance check. As a result, a malicious or careless user can supply a deposit amount or request a withdrawal amount that pushes the pool’s internal reserves so that y/x falls below MIN_M (or above MAX_M). Because the contract does not revert in these cases, the pool’s accounting state becomes inconsistent: subsequent swaps may be priced incorrectly, the pool may appear to have sufficient liquidity while actually being under‑collateralised, and users can receive zero or dramatically reduced output tokens. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are missing refunds, unexpected zero balances, or swaps that return far less than expected, effectively making funds disappear. The flaw is triggered only when the deposit or withdrawal functions are called with extreme values that violate the ratio; normal‑sized operations stay within the safe range and therefore the bug can remain hidden during routine testing. The issue was uncovered during a formal audit by running property‑based tests that deliberately forced the ratio outside the allowed interval and observed that the contract did not revert as it should. Detecting the problem in production is difficult because the pool may continue to operate, but the hidden invariant breach can be exploited repeatedly to drain value or break the market‑making guarantees. The proper remediation is to invoke the same balance validation after the reserve updates in both depositGivenInputAmount() and withdrawGivenOutputAmount(), ensuring that any state change that could affect the y/x ratio is checked against the MIN_M and MAX_M bounds before the transaction is finalized. This brings the functions into the same safety class as the swap and LP‑minting paths and restores the intended accounting guarantees of the protocol.
summary:
The pool’s ratio of y to x must be within the interval `[MIN_M, MAX_M)`, which will be checked by the `_checkBalances()` function. External view functions will call the `_swap()`, `_reserveTokenSpecified()` or `_lpTokenSpecified()` functions to get the specified result. However, `_checkBalances()` is only used in the `_swap()` and `_lpTokenSpecified()` functions. There is no balance validation for `depositGivenInputAmount()` and `withdrawGivenOutputAmount()` functions, which use the `_reserveTokenSpecified()` function.

If there are no other validations outside of these two functions, user deposits/withdrawals may break the invariant, i.e. the pool’s ratio of y to x is outside the interval `[MIN_M, MAX_M)`.

title: User doesn’t have to deposit for a week into the market to get their weekly reward from the `LendingLedger`
content: The vulnerability resides in the way the LendingLedger contract determines a lender’s weekly CANTO reward. Rewards are allocated per epoch that is defined as a whole week, and the contract computes the eligible time by truncating the deposit timestamp to the start of the week. Because of this rounding, a user can deposit a fraction of a second before the week ends (for example at 23:59:59) and withdraw immediately after the new week begins (00:00:00). The contract still treats the deposit as having been present for the entire week and therefore credits the full weekly reward even though the actual holding time was only a second. The root cause is the use of a coarse, week‑aligned time bucket without accounting for the precise duration a deposit was active within that bucket. An attacker can exploit this by repeatedly performing end‑of‑week deposits and withdrawals, harvesting rewards that are disproportionate to the liquidity actually provided. The impact is a systematic over‑allocation of reward tokens, which reduces the pool available for honest liquidity providers and defeats the economic incentive model of veRWA that relies on time‑weighted balances. The condition occurs whenever the reward period is measured in whole weeks and the contract rounds timestamps down to the week start; it affects any lender interacting with the market, the protocol’s token economics, and ultimately CANTO holders who expect rewards to reflect genuine liquidity provision. The issue was discovered during a security audit when a test case demonstrated that a lender could claim a full‑week reward after depositing for only one second. It is subtle because the reward distribution appears correct for most users, and the edge case only manifests at the exact week boundary, making it easy to overlook in routine testing. From a user’s perspective the symptom is an unexpected increase in CANTO balance after a very short deposit, contradicting the expectation that rewards are earned only after a full week of participation. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of time‑bucket rounding errors where accounting periods are coarsely aligned, leading to inaccurate proportional calculations. The proper fix is to replace the week‑level truncation with a precise, per‑second accounting of deposit duration, or to split the epoch reward proportionally based on the actual fraction of the week the deposit was active, ensuring that rewards are truly time‑weighted and that no user can claim more than their real contribution warrants.
summary: In the `LendingLedger` contract, a user is rewarded with CANTO tokens depending on how long he has his deposit in the market. Rewards are distributed for each week during which the deposit was inside the market. However, the user can cheat this condition because we are rounding down to the start of the week, so the user can deposit at 23:59 at the end of the week and withdraw at 00:00 and still get rewarded as if he had his deposit for the whole week.

title: Voters from VotingEscrow can vote infinite times in vote _for_ gauge_weights
content: The vulnerability is an unlimited vote‑inflation flaw in the interaction between a token‑locking escrow contract and a gauge controller that determines reward distribution. The escrow contract lets a token holder lock assets and optionally delegate the associated voting power to another address. The gauge controller reads the voting power of a voter by querying the current timestamp (or the current block) instead of a snapshot taken a fixed number of blocks in the past. Because the snapshot is taken at the moment of each call, a user can vote for a gauge, immediately delegate the same voting power to a fresh address, and have that address cast another vote using the same underlying lock. By repeating the delegate‑vote cycle arbitrarily many times, the attacker can multiply the effective weight of a single lock by the number of delegations performed. The inflated weight is then used by downstream contracts such as a lending ledger to calculate token rewards, allowing the attacker to claim far more tokens than their actual locked stake justifies. The issue manifests whenever a lock exists, the delegate function is available, and the gauge controller does not enforce a voting window or a historical snapshot. It affects all participants that rely on gauge weights for fair reward allocation, including regular users, lenders, and the protocol’s economic model. The flaw was discovered during a formal audit when a test case demonstrated that a single lock could be used to increase a gauge’s relative weight from the expected 50 % to over 95 % by performing twenty delegations. The problem is subtle because the gauge weight appears to grow smoothly and there is no explicit counter that limits the number of votes per lock, making the inflation easy to miss in routine monitoring. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of vote‑replay or vote‑inflation attacks caused by using mutable state (current block) to compute voting power instead of an immutable snapshot. To remediate, the protocol should compute voting power from a block that is a fixed distance in the past, enforce a one‑vote‑per‑lock‑per‑period rule, and optionally define a governance‑controlled voting window during which votes are accepted. This prevents an attacker from repeatedly delegating and voting within the same period, thereby preserving the intended accounting relationship between locked tokens and gauge weight and protecting the fairness of reward distribution.
summary: Delegate mechanism in `VotingEscrow` allows infinite votes in `vote_for_gauge_weights()` in the `GaugeController`. Users can then, for example, claim more tokens in the `LendingLedger` in the market that they inflated the votes on.

title: When adding a gauge, its initial value has to be set by an admin or all voting power towards it will be lost
content: The vulnerability is an initialization flaw in the gauge‑weight tracking logic of the voting contract. When a new gauge is added, the mapping that stores the most recent timestamp at which the gauge’s weight was recorded (time_weight) is left at its default value 0. The private function _get_weight reads this timestamp, expects it to be non‑zero, and then iterates week by week to update the bias and slope values that represent the gauge’s voting power. Because the initial timestamp is zero, the loop runs for the maximum 500 iterations, but the condition that would write a new timestamp (t > block.timestamp) is never satisfied, so time_weight remains 0 and the function returns a bias of 0. Consequently any vote cast for the newly added gauge is ignored; get_gauge_weight reports 0, reward calculations that depend on the weight allocate nothing, and users see their voting power disappear. This situation occurs between the moment add_gauge is called and the moment an admin manually invokes change_gauge_weight (or a similar initialization routine). The affected parties are gauge creators, token holders who lock voting power, and the protocol itself because rewards are not distributed as intended. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by writing tests that added a gauge, voted, and observed a zero weight, confirming that the missing initialization caused the loss of voting power. The bug is subtle because the contract does not revert or emit an error; it simply returns 0, making it easy to miss in casual testing. The proper fix is to ensure that add_gauge either calls change_gauge_weight with an initial weight (typically 0) or directly sets time_weight to the next weekly checkpoint, guaranteeing that _get_weight has a valid starting timestamp. By initializing the timestamp, the bias calculation will correctly reflect votes, the gauge weight will be non‑zero after voting, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions about vote‑based reward distribution will hold.
summary: Voting power towards gauges will be lost and project will not work properly

title: Delegated votes are locked when owner lock is expired
content: An issue exists in the VoteEscrow contract where the delegate() function enforces that the lock belonging to the delegatee must have an end timestamp greater than the current block time. This rule is applied even when a user attempts to undelegate by delegating back to themselves. If the original lock has expired before the user removes the delegation, the require statement rejects the transaction with a Delegatee lock expired error. Because the contract also checks the delegatee field in withdraw() and only allows withdrawal when the caller is the current delegatee, the user is unable to call withdraw() after the lock expires. Consequently the user’s tokens and associated voting power remain locked indefinitely. The root cause is a missing exemption for the undelegation path in the expiration check, which treats undelegation as a normal delegation. The bug can be triggered when a token holder delegates their voting power, lets the lock period run out, and later tries to either re‑delegate to another address or simply undelegate. From the user’s perspective the UI will show a normal balance, but attempting to withdraw or to change the delegate will revert with an error, leading to confusion as the funds appear to be stuck. The problem was identified during a formal audit by Code4rena, and it may be hard to notice because the contract does not emit a specific event for the failure and the error message does not clearly indicate that the lock has already expired. The vulnerability belongs to the class of delegation‑state‑validation bugs where business‑logic constraints are applied uniformly without considering special cases, breaking the accounting assumption that a user can always retrieve their assets after the lock expires. To remediate, the contract should either skip the expiration check when the caller is undelegating (i.e., when the target address equals msg.sender) or introduce a short grace period that allows the undelegate operation even if the lock end time has passed. Adding explicit handling ensures that users can always recover their tokens and voting power after a lock expires, restoring the intended withdrawal flow.
summary: In `delegate()` of VoteEscrow.sol, a user is able to delegate their locked votes to someone else, and undelegate (i.e. delegate back to themselves). When the user tries to re-delegate, either to someone else or themselves, the lock must not be expired. This is problematic because if a user forgets and lets their lock become expired, they cannot undelegate. This blocks withdrawal, which means their tokens are essentially locked forever.

title: It is possible to DoS all the functions related to some gauge in `GaugeController`
content: The vulnerability is an integer underflow in the weight‑updating routine of a gauge controller contract that can permanently disable all operations related to a specific gauge. The root cause is that the internal function that computes the total weight for a gauge iterates over weekly checkpoints and subtracts a slope value derived from pending weight changes without first verifying that the stored slope is large enough. When governance reduces a gauge’s weight, it can set the stored bias to a lower value while leaving the slope unchanged, and later a subsequent governance increase may leave the slope at zero while the bias remains positive. If any pending weight change for a future week still has a non‑zero amount, the subtraction of that amount from a zero (or very small) slope triggers an unsigned integer underflow. This underflow occurs every time the weight‑calculation function is called, causing the function to revert and preventing any further calls that rely on it, such as voting, checkpointing, weight changes, or gauge removal. From a user’s perspective the gauge appears to be frozen: attempts to vote for the gauge, change its weight, or even remove it revert with an arithmetic error, and any funds that were delegated to the gauge cannot be withdrawn or re‑allocated, effectively locking user voting power and breaking the protocol’s incentive mechanism. The issue manifests only after a sequence where governance first lowers the gauge weight (or a malicious actor front‑runs a weight reduction) and later raises it while there remain pending weight changes for future weeks. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the weight‑update loop and identified that the code does not guard against the slope becoming smaller than the pending change. The bug is subtle because the loop normally processes a large number of weeks and the underflow only appears under specific state transitions, making it easy to miss in routine testing. The proper fix is to ensure that the slope subtraction is performed only when the stored slope is at least as large as the pending change, otherwise the slope should be set to zero, thereby preventing the underflow and preserving the ability to interact with the gauge. This class of bug belongs to unchecked arithmetic in state‑update loops that can lead to denial‑of‑service conditions in decentralized finance contracts.

title: Users may be forced into long lock times to be able to undelegate back to themselves
content: The vulnerability originates from a business‑logic check in the VotingEscrow (verwa) contract that only permits a delegation when the target lock expires at the same time or later than the source lock. The code enforces require(toLocked.end >= fromLocked.end, "Only delegate to longer lock"); which blocks a user from delegating to an address with a shorter or equal lock period. In the verwa implementation any change to a lock automatically extends its expiry by five years, a rule that was inherited from the original FiatDAO design but applied uniformly to all lock modifications. When a user delegates their voting power to another participant whose lock ends later, the delegator’s lock remains shorter. After some time, if the delegator wishes to undelegate back to themselves by calling delegate(msg.sender), the same check is triggered and the transaction reverts because the delegator’s lock end is still earlier than the delegatee’s lock end. Because the contract forces any lock adjustment to add five years, the only way to satisfy the check is to extend the delegator’s lock by an additional five years, which many users consider unacceptable. This situation can force users to remain delegated to an unwanted address or to lock their tokens for an excessively long period, effectively immobilising their funds. The impact is financial: users cannot retrieve voting power or withdraw tokens without incurring a five‑year lock extension, exposing them to market volatility and potential loss of value. The condition occurs when a delegator’s lock and the delegatee’s lock are created in different epochs, the delegatee’s lock ends later, and the delegator later attempts to undelegate. All participants who rely on the VotingEscrow for governance or token staking are affected, including regular token holders and protocol operators. The issue was discovered during a security audit that compared the verwa contract against the reference FiatDAO implementation and identified that the original “extend by one week” workaround no longer applied because verwa adds five years on any change. The bug is subtle because the require statement appears to enforce a sensible invariant, yet its interaction with the five‑year extension rule creates an unintended lock‑time enforcement problem that is not exercised by typical unit tests. To remediate, the delegate function should be modified to allow a user to delegate back to themselves regardless of lock length, for example by relaxing the require condition to permit self‑delegation or by checking that the target address is the caller before enforcing the longer‑lock rule. This change restores the intended flexibility of undelegating without forcing an unnecessary five‑year lock extension, aligning the contract’s behavior with the original business logic and protecting users from being trapped in an overly long lock period.
summary: Due to a check requiring users only be able to delegate to others or themselves with longer lock times and verwa’s restrictions of all changes increasing lock times by 5 years users may be forced to remain delegated to someone they do not wish to be or extend their lock much longer than they wish.

title: lack of access control in `LendingLedger.sol#checkpoint_lender` and function `checkpoint_market`
content: An absence of access control on the public checkpoint_market and checkpoint_lender functions allows any address to invoke them with an arbitrary forwardTimestampLimit. The functions are intended only to advance the internal epoch bookkeeping for a market or a lender, but because the caller is not validated and the timestamp is only checked for being a multiple of a week, an attacker can supply a past timestamp such as 0. When called with 0, the internal variables lendingMarketTotalBalanceEpoch and lendingMarketBalancesEpoch are set to zero. Subsequent calls to sync_ledger or claim calculate rewards based on these epoch values; with the epoch reset to zero the reward formula yields zero, effectively griefing the user’s reward. The impact is that a legitimate depositor sees no reward payout despite having accrued entitlement, and the protocol’s accounting state becomes inconsistent. The issue manifests when a malicious actor deliberately invokes the checkpoint functions after deposits have been made, before any claim is attempted. It was discovered during a Code4rena test‑coverage competition where a proof‑of‑concept showed that calling the functions with forwardTimestampLimit = 0 reduced the claimed reward from six ether to zero. The bug is subtle because the functions do not revert; they silently corrupt the epoch history, making the problem hard to notice without inspecting internal state. The proper mitigation is to restrict these functions to privileged roles (e.g., governance or the market contract), to verify that the market is whitelisted, and to enforce that the forward timestamp is not earlier than the current epoch, thereby preventing the epoch counters from ever decreasing.
summary:
_Note: This audit was preceded by a [Code4rena Test Coverage competition](https://code4rena.com/test-coverage). While auditing was not the purpose of the testing phase, relevant and valuable findings reported during that phase were eligible to be judged. This finding [H-07] was discovered during that period and is being included here for completeness._

User’s claim and `sync_lender` will be griefed at low cost.

title: If governance removes a gauge, user’s voting power for that gauge will be lost
content: An on‑chain governance system allows ve token holders to allocate voting power to individual gauges. The contract stores the amount of power a user has already committed and checks that the sum of new allocations does not exceed the user’s total ve balance. When governance removes a gauge, the implementation deletes the gauge entry but does not clear the per‑user record that marks the user’s power as already used for that gauge. As a result, the contract still believes the user’s voting power is fully consumed, and any subsequent call to vote_for_gauge_weights reverts with “Used too much power”. This behaviour occurs for any non‑malicious gauge removal and prevents the user from reallocating their ve power to remaining gauges. From a user perspective the UI will show that the user cannot assign any more votes, even though their ve balance is unchanged, leading to a situation where “my voting power disappears” or “I cannot vote for other gauges”. The impact is a loss of governance influence and may indirectly affect reward distribution that depends on gauge weights. The issue was discovered through a targeted test that removed a gauge after a user had voted 100 % for it and then attempted to vote elsewhere, observing the revert messages. The bug is subtle because gauge removal is an infrequent operation and the error messages do not explicitly reference the stale allocation, making it easy to overlook during normal usage. The vulnerability belongs to the class of state‑inconsistency bugs where cleanup logic is missing after a mutable entity is deleted. To remediate, the contract should reset or subtract the user’s allocated power for a gauge when that gauge is removed, and update the internal accounting of used voting power so that the remaining balance can be freely re‑distributed to other gauges.
