By moving the state changes ahead of the minting logic, the limit check cannot be bypassed, restoring the intended economic guarantees of the collection.
summary: An attacker can reenter the `MinterContract::mint` function, bypassing the `maxCollectionPurchases` check and minting the entire collection supply.

title: Attacker can drain all ETH from `AuctionDemo` when `block.timestamp == auctionEndTime`
content: The vulnerability consists of two interacting bugs that together allow an attacker to drain all ether from the AuctionDemo contract. The first bug is a time‑boundary error in the claimAuction function: it uses a non‑strict comparison (>=) to determine whether the auction has ended, which permits a caller to invoke claimAuction at the exact block.timestamp equal to the auctionEndTime. The second bug is an improper state update before external calls when processing refunds. In claimAuction (and similarly in cancelBid) the contract does not set the auction status to false before sending ether back to the bidder, so a malicious participant can trigger a second refund path after the first one has already transferred funds. When an attacker waits until the block timestamp matches the auction end time, they can place multiple bids, call claimAuction to receive refunds for the non‑winning bids, and then call cancelAllBids to obtain refunds for all of their bids again. Because the contract’s balance is not protected against this double‑refund scenario, the attacker ends up receiving the sum of all their bids plus the winning bid, while the contract balance is reduced to zero and honest users retain only the amount they originally spent. This issue manifests only when the exact end‑time condition is met, which is a rare edge case that can be missed during normal testing. It affects any participant in the auction, the auction owner who loses expected revenue, and the overall protocol integrity because funds disappear from the contract. The flaw was discovered during a Code4rena audit through targeted testing of the claimAuction logic and inspection of the refund flow. It is hard to notice because the equality check appears harmless and the missing state flag is a subtle omission that does not raise a compiler warning. The problem belongs to the class of time‑boundary and improper‑state‑update bugs that enable double‑spend or re‑entrancy‑like attacks. To remediate, the claimAuction function should require a strict greater‑than comparison (>) to exclude the exact end time, and the contract should update the auction status to false before performing any external ether transfers, mirroring the pattern used in cancelBid. This ensures that once a refund is processed the auction cannot be claimed again, preventing the attacker from draining the contract.
summary: It’s possible to drain all ETH from the `AuctionDemo` contract. There are two bugs that make it possible when they’re exploited together.

title: Adversary can block `claimAuction`
content: The vulnerability resides in the auction contract’s claimAuction function, which follows a push‑style refund pattern. When an auction ends, the function iterates over every stored bid and attempts to send the corresponding ether back to each bidder by invoking a low‑level call with value. Because the contract does not isolate each refund in a separate pull‑based function and does not limit the amount of gas forwarded, a malicious bidder can deploy a contract that deliberately reverts or consumes all gas in its receive/fallback function. When claimAuction reaches the malicious bidder’s entry, the external call fails and, depending on the implementation, may cause the whole transaction to revert or exhaust the block gas limit, preventing the loop from completing. Consequently, all other non‑winning bidders who have not cancelled their bids are unable to receive their refunds, effectively locking their funds in the auction contract. This denial‑of‑service condition occurs whenever at least one participant supplies a contract that behaves adversarially during the refund phase, which can be triggered by placing a minimal bid (as low as 1 wei) and then remaining in the auction until the claim phase. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the refund logic and identified the lack of a pull‑based claim mechanism and unchecked external calls. It is subtle because the code appears to handle refunds correctly by emitting events and capturing the success flag, yet the success flag is never acted upon, and the loop’s unbounded nature hides the potential for a single malicious callback to halt the entire process. The impact is high: honest participants may lose access to their deposited funds, the auction may become unusable, and the protocol’s reputation suffers. To remediate, the contract should replace the push‑style loop with a pull‑based design, providing each bidder with an individual claim function (similar to the existing cancel‑bid functions) that they can invoke independently. Additionally, the contract should enforce a minimum bid amount, limit gas forwarded in external calls, and verify the success of each transfer, reverting only the individual refund rather than the whole auction. This change restores the expected behavior where users initiate their own refunds, eliminates the single point of failure, and aligns the contract with established best practices for handling untrusted external calls.
summary:
`claimAuction()` implements a push-strategy instead of a pull-strategy for returning the bidders funds.

This gives the opportunity for an adversary to DOS the function, locking all funds from other participants.

This finding differs from the automated findings report [M-01](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-nextgen/blob/main/bot-report.md#m-01-unchecked-return-value-of-low-level-calldelegatecall), and [L-18](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-nextgen/blob/main/bot-report.md#l-18-gas-griefingtheft-is-possible-on-an-unsafe-external-call), as it has a different root cause, can’t be prevented with any of the mitigations from the bot, and also highlights the actual High impact of the issue.

title: Multiple mints can brick any form of `salesOption` 3 mintings
content: The vulnerability resides in the time‑window calculation used by sales option 3 of the minting contract. When a collection performs more than one mint batch, the contract computes the timestamp of the last successful mint as allowlistStartTime plus the product of the configured timePeriod and the expression (current circulating supply minus one). This expression treats the total number of minted tokens as if each token consumed one timePeriod slot, which is only correct for a single‑token mint per period. After the first batch (for example 500 tokens), the calculation yields an artificial lastMintDate that is many minutes – in the example 499 minutes – later than the real whitelist window. Subsequent mint attempts compare the stored timeOfLastMint with the current block.timestamp, causing the subtraction (block.timestamp - timeOfLastMint) to underflow and revert. The result is that any user trying to mint after the first batch encounters a transaction revert with an underflow error, effectively bricking the whitelist and potentially the entire public sale. The issue occurs only when sales option 3 is selected, the collection has a non‑zero timePeriod, and more than one mint batch is scheduled, which is a common pattern for collections that spread their sale over several days. Affected parties include the collection owner, whitelisted participants, and any public buyers because they are unable to acquire NFTs despite expectations that the sale continues. The problem was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, reproduced with a test that performs two successive mints and observes the underflow revert. It is hard to notice because the calculation looks plausible and only fails after the first batch, presenting as a generic revert rather than a clear logic error. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of arithmetic miscalculations that cause time‑based logic overflow or underflow, breaking business rules that assume a linear progression of mint windows. From a user’s perspective the UI reports a failed mint, often with no clear message, while the user expects to receive an NFT during the whitelist period; instead the balance remains unchanged and the transaction reverts. The proper fix requires redesigning the time‑window logic so that the lastMintDate is derived from the actual timestamp of the most recent successful mint or from a fixed increment per mint event, rather than from the total circulating supply. A more extensive refactor of the sales option implementation is needed to ensure that multiple mint batches do not distort the allowed time window.
summary: As explained by the sponsor, some collections might want to conduct multiple mints on different days. However, due to the way `salesOption` 3 works, these multiple mints might encounter issues.

title: Permanent DoS due to non-shrinking array usage in an unbounded loop
content: The vulnerability is a permanent denial‑of‑service condition caused by the use of dynamically growing arrays that are never cleared and are iterated over in unbounded for‑loops. The contract stores bids for each token in an array that can increase without bound because every call to participateToAuction pushes a new entry but no function ever removes elements after the auction finishes. Functions such as returnHighestBid, returnHighestBidder, claimAuction and cancelAllBids loop over the entire length of this array to compute the highest bid or to process refunds. When an attacker repeatedly calls participateToAuction with minimal (dust) amounts, the array length grows until the gas required to iterate over all entries exceeds the block gas limit. At that point, any call that invokes one of the loops runs out of gas and reverts. Because claimAuction relies on returnHighestBid, the winner or an admin attempting to claim the auction will experience a transaction failure, effectively locking the auction forever. The impact is that legitimate participants cannot receive their winnings or refunds, balances appear unchanged, and the UI may show generic transaction‑failed errors or missing funds. This condition occurs only after the array has been inflated beyond what the gas limit can accommodate, which may not be obvious during normal testing because the loops appear correct for small arrays. The issue was discovered by an automated findings tool that flagged the unbounded loops over a non‑shrinking array. It is hard to notice because the code does not contain explicit size checks and the problem only manifests under extreme, attacker‑driven growth. The bug belongs to the class of unbounded iteration over ever‑growing data structures, violating the assumption that the collection size remains bounded for reasonable gas consumption. To remediate, the contract should either shrink or delete the array entries after the auction ends, replace the array with a mapping that does not require iteration, impose a hard cap on the number of bids, or redesign the logic to avoid iterating over the entire collection in a single transaction. Such changes restore the ability of winners and admins to claim or cancel auctions and prevent permanent lock‑out of funds.
summary:
_Note: this finding was reported via the winning [Automated Findings report](https://gist.github.com/code423n4/b979a00ee3ea3f7d36ee39e2a536ba8a). It was declared out of scope for the audit, but is being included here for completeness._

There are some arrays that can grow indefinitely in size, as they never shrink. When these arrays are used in unbounded loops, they may lead to a permanent denial-of-service (DoS) of these functions.

title: Incorrect calculations for Surplus Auction creation cause massive surplus imbalances
content: The vulnerability resides in the surplus auction creation logic of the AccountingEngine contract. The code incorrectly compares the configured surplusTransferPercentage against a constant representing one hundred times the fixed‑point base (ONE_HUNDRED_WAD) instead of the base unit (WAD). Because ONE_HUNDRED_WAD equals 100 × 1e18, the condition "if (_params.surplusTransferPercentage < ONE_HUNDRED_WAD)" is always true for any valid percentage value, including the maximum allowed 100 % (1e18). Consequently the contract always enters the auction branch even when the intention is to transfer the entire surplus directly. In the same branch the amount to sell is calculated with ONE_HUNDRED_WAD‑_params.surplusTransferPercentage, which inflates the value by a factor of up to one hundred. For example, with a surplusAmount of 3 e18 and a transfer percentage of 100 % the computed _amountToSell becomes 297 e18 instead of the expected 0, creating a surplus auction that claims far more coins than actually exist. This mis‑calculation breaks the protocol’s accounting invariants: the surplus auction house believes it holds an oversized amount of surplus, leading to distorted debt‑settlement logic, potential over‑allocation of tokens, and a mismatch between on‑chain balances and the protocol’s internal accounting. The issue manifests whenever the surplusTransferPercentage is set to its upper bound, the surplus amount is non‑zero, and the cooldown period has elapsed – essentially any normal execution of auctionSurplus after a surplus accrues. All participants that rely on correct surplus handling – token holders, borrowers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the protocol may appear to have excess funds that do not exist, causing unexpected auction outcomes, missing refunds, or even loss of funds if the inflated auction is later settled incorrectly. The flaw was discovered during a formal audit by reviewing the percentage logic and noticing the misuse of ONE_HUNDRED_WAD, a subtle mistake that is easy to overlook because the constant name suggests a percentage but its magnitude is off by two orders of decimal places. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are a surplus auction with an absurdly large amount, a situation where a user expects a direct transfer of surplus but instead sees an auction event, or where balances displayed in the UI do not match the actual token holdings. The root cause is a wrong constant used for both the comparison and the arithmetic expression. The recommended remediation is to replace ONE_HUNDRED_WAD with WAD in the conditional check and in the calculation of _amountToSell, thereby ensuring the percentage logic operates on the correct scale and preventing the creation of oversized auctions. This change restores the intended business rule that a 100 % transfer bypasses the auction and that any partial transfer sells only the appropriate fraction of surplus, preserving accounting integrity and user expectations.
summary:
There are two big issues in `AccountingEngine.sol::auctionSurplus()` when calculating values for the creating a Surplus Auction; specifically in [Lines 213 - 217](https://github.com/open-dollar/od-contracts/blob/dev/src/contracts/AccountingEngine.sol#L213-L217).

  1. The first issue is the `if` statement at [line 213](https://github.com/open-dollar/od-contracts/blob/dev/src/contracts/AccountingEngine.sol#L213-L217) which incorrectly checks if `_params.surplusTransferPercentage` is less than `ONE_HUNDRED_WAD` when it should check if it is less than `WAD`.

            if (_params.surplusTransferPercentage < ONE_HUNDRED_WAD) {

The maximum value for `_params.surplusTransferPercentage`, as checked by the function at [line 199](https://github.com/open-dollar/od-contracts/blob/dev/src/contracts/AccountingEngine.sol#L199), is `1e18` so the check at [line 213](https://github.com/open-dollar/od-contracts/blob/dev/src/contracts/AccountingEngine.sol#L213-L217) will always return `TRUE`.

However, the check should return `FALSE` when `_params.surplusTransferPercentage` is `1e18` or `100%` because in that case an auction shouldn’t be created; rather the full `surplusAmount` should be transferred to `extraSurplusReceiver` in the next code block.

  2. The second issue is the use of `ONE_HUNDRED_WAD` to calculate `_amountToSell` at [Line 215](https://github.com/open-dollar/od-contracts/blob/dev/src/contracts/AccountingEngine.sol#L213-L217) which results in a hugely inflated figure in the newly created surplus auction.

The use of `ONE_HUNDRED_WAD` causes the calculated figure to be `100 times` greater than it should be.
    
        _amountToSell: _params.surplusAmount.wmul(ONE_HUNDRED_WAD - _params.surplusTransferPercentage)

title: Missing debt check lets users start a debt auction of non-existent debt
content: The vulnerability is a missing validation step that permits the AccountingEngine contract to start a debt auction even when the contract does not hold enough bad debt to satisfy the required minimum bid (debtAuctionBidSize). The root cause is that the check confirming sufficient unqueued and unauctioned debt is performed before the internal _settleDebt call, but not re‑evaluated after settlement. _settleDebt reduces the amount of bad debt that is available for auction; if the reduction brings the balance below the minimum threshold, the contract still proceeds to create the auction because the post‑settlement condition is never verified. An attacker can trigger the auctionDebt function, which internally calls _settleDebt and then immediately starts the auction without the second check. As a result, the auction is created with a debt amount of zero or an amount smaller than the required bid size. Bidders can then purchase what appears to be debt but actually represents no underlying liability, causing the protocol token to be minted or transferred at an inflated rate, effectively diluting existing token holders. This issue manifests whenever the protocol attempts to auction debt that has just been settled and the remaining bad debt falls below the configured minimum. All participants who rely on the auction mechanism – including token holders, borrowers, and liquidity providers – are affected because the economic assumptions of the auction (that each bid corresponds to real debt) are broken. The flaw was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena when test cases demonstrated that a direct call to auctionDebt succeeded without reverting, contrary to the expected behavior of the two‑step flow that includes an external settleDebt call. The problem is subtle because the contract already contains a pre‑settlement check, leading reviewers to assume the invariant holds after settlement as well. To remediate, the contract should repeat the debt‑availability check after _settleDebt returns, ensuring that debtAuctionBidSize is still less than or equal to the current unqueued, unauctioned debt before creating the auction. This change restores the intended accounting guarantees and prevents creation of auctions for non‑existent debt, thereby protecting token value and protocol integrity.
summary:
The `AccountingEngine.sol` contract serves as the protocol’s central component responsible for initializing both debt and surplus auctions. Debt auctions are consistently initiated with a predefined minimum bid referred to as debtAuctionBidSize. This is done to ensure that the protocol can only auction debt that is not currently undergoing an auction and is not locked within the debt queue, as articulated in the comment found on `IAccountingEngine:248`: “It can only auction debt that has been popped from the debt queue and is not already being auctioned”. This necessity prompts the check on AccountingEngine:181:

`if (_params.debtAuctionBidSize > _unqueuedUnauctionedDebt(_debtBalance))`

This check verifies that there is a sufficient amount of bad debt available to auction.

The issue stems in line 183, where `_settleDebt` is called, this aims to ensure that only bad debt is considered for the auction. However, if the remaining bad debt, after settlement, falls below the specified threshold `(debtAuctionBidSize <= unqueuedUnauctionedDebt())`, the auction still starts with an incorrect amount of bad debt coverage, diluting the protocol Token when it is not yet needed.

title: The 51% majority can hijack the party’s precious tokens through an arbitrary call proposal if the `AddPartyCardsAuthority` contract is added as an authority in the party.
content: The vulnerability is an unchecked arbitrary‑call path that allows a majority of party members to hijack the party’s precious NFT tokens. The core of the problem is that the ArbitraryCallsProposal contract does not verify the target of each call, so an attacker can include a call to the AddPartyCardsAuthority contract. AddPartyCardsAuthority is designed to add new party members and assign them voting power, but when it is invoked through an arbitrary proposal it can mint a new governance NFT with voting power equal to the total voting power of the party. Because the proposal engine treats proposals that achieve unanimity as special – they bypass the normal execution delay and the safeguards that protect precious token transfers – the attacker who now controls the entire voting weight can submit a second arbitrary‑call proposal that transfers every precious token held by the party to an address they control. The attack proceeds in two stages: first a proposal is submitted that calls AddPartyCardsAuthority to create an attacker account with astronomical voting power; the proposal is accepted by the existing members and executed, resulting in a de‑facto unanimous vote. In the second stage the attacker, now holding total voting power, creates an arbitrary‑call proposal that invokes the ERC‑721 transferFrom function on each precious token, moving them out of the party contract. The impact is the complete loss of the party’s valuable NFTs – users see their balances become zero and the party no longer holds the assets it was supposed to protect. This can happen whenever the AddPartyCardsAuthority contract is added as an authority and the proposal engine allows arbitrary calls without restriction, especially when the execution delay is set to zero or can be bypassed by a unanimous vote. The affected parties are the token holders, the governance participants, and any downstream protocol that relies on the integrity of the party’s asset pool. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where a proof‑of‑concept test demonstrated the two‑step exploit. It is hard to notice because arbitrary calls are intended to be flexible and the authority contract appears benign; the lack of explicit checks means the dangerous combination is hidden in normal governance flow. To remediate, the contract should either forbid arbitrary calls to authority contracts that can modify voting power, add explicit validation that proposals affecting precious tokens cannot be marked as unanimous, enforce a non‑zero execution delay for any call that moves assets, or require a separate multi‑signature guard for token transfers. In short, the bug is a privilege‑escalation through unchecked arbitrary calls that breaks the accounting assumptions of the party’s governance model, allowing an attacker to steal all precious tokens.
summary:
There is no check on the [`ArbitraryCallsProposal`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-party/blob/main/contracts/proposals/ArbitraryCallsProposal.sol) contract that prevents the calling of the [`AddPartyCardsAuthority`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-party/blob/main/contracts/authorities/AddPartyCardsAuthority.sol) contract. This allows the 51% majority, through an arbitrary call proposal, to hijack ALL of precious tokens of the party.

They can achieve this by going through the following steps:

  1. Create an `ArbitraryCallsProposal` to simply mint a governance NFT token for an arbitrary user with an astronomical voting power, which gives the arbitrary user an ability to pass and bypass the execution delay of any proposal.
  2. The newly-created arbitrary user will create an `ArbitraryCallsProposal` with multiple arbitrary calls with a goal of transferring all of the party precious tokens to themselves.
  3. The newly-created arbitrary user will then vote on the `ArbitraryCallsProposal` proposal they just created.
  4. The proposal will pass and be marked as a unanimously voted proposal, allowing them to bypass all of the safeguards in place to prevent the hijacking of precious NFT tokens through a non-unanimously voted proposal.

title: Single host can unfairly skip veto period for proposal that does not have full host support
content: The vulnerability is a governance logic flaw that allows a single host to bypass the mandatory veto period for a proposal that has met the voting threshold but has not received acceptance from all designated hosts. The root cause is that the contract’s acceptance check uses the current host status rather than a snapshot of host membership taken at the moment the proposal was created. When a host abdicates its role to another address and then casts an acceptance vote from the new address, the contract increments the number of accepted hosts based on the updated host list, causing the count of accepted hosts to equal the total number of hosts even though one original host never accepted. This mis‑alignment makes the protocol treat the proposal as "Ready" for execution, effectively skipping the veto window that is intended to give all hosts a chance to block harmful or exploitative proposals. An attacker can exploit this by crafting a malicious proposal (for example using hidden CREATE2 and SELFDESTRUCT calls) that appears benign to voters, then using a compromised host to abdicate and re‑accept, thereby eliminating the veto period with minimal cost. The impact is severe: proposals that should have been halted can be executed, potentially resulting in unauthorized asset transfers, loss of funds, or protocol state corruption. The issue manifests when a proposal passes the vote threshold, at least one host has not accepted, and a host performs an abdication followed by an acceptance from a new address. All participants in the governance process—hosts, token holders, and end‑users—are affected because the security guarantees of the veto mechanism are broken. The flaw was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where a proof‑of‑concept test demonstrated the host‑abdication trick. It is hard to notice because the contract appears to correctly track the number of hosts and accepted hosts, and the acceptance logic seems to work under normal circumstances; only the dynamic change of host membership reveals the inconsistency. This class of bug belongs to improper state snapshotting and race‑condition‑like logic errors, where the system relies on mutable state rather than immutable snapshots for critical security checks. From a user’s perspective, a proposal may suddenly show a "Ready" status and be executable even though one of the original hosts never voted, leading to unexpected execution of malicious code and disappearance of funds. To remediate, the acceptance logic should be tied to a snapshot of host membership taken at proposal creation (or at the block just before proposal execution) so that only hosts that were members at that snapshot can contribute to the acceptance count, preventing a host from swapping addresses to artificially satisfy the acceptance requirement.
summary:
After a proposal passes the vote threshold, there is a delay before it can be executed so that hosts get a chance to `veto` it if they wish. If all hosts voting in favour of the proposal, then this veto period is skipped.

However, a single host can ensure the veto period is skipped even if no other hosts `accept` the proposal. The veto period is in place to prevent harmful/exploitative proposals from being executed, even if they are passed; therefore, a malicious/compromised host being able to skip the veto period can be seriously harmful to the protocol and its users. The [Tornado Cash governance hack](https://medium.com/coinmonks/tornado-cash-governance-hack-ec77ebb3aa68) from May 2023 is a relevant example, during which the attacker was able to steal around `$`1 million worth of assets.

This attack has a very low cost and a very high potential impact. If a malicious proposal is crafted in the same way used by the Tornado Cash attacker using hidden `CREATE2` and `SELFDESTRUCT` operations, then it is entirely feasible that it would meet the voting threshold, as many voters may not be savvy enough to spot the red flags.

title: Borrowers can escape from paying half of the penalty fees by closing the market, and those remaining penalty fees will be covered by the lender who withdraws last
content: The vulnerability is that when a market is closed while it is still in a delinquent state, the contract calculates the total debt using the current scale factor but does not take into account any remaining penalty time (state.timeDelinquent). As a result the borrower only pays the principal and the portion of the delinquency fee that has already accrued, while the remaining half of the penalty continues to accrue after closure. Because the base interest is set to zero on closure, the only fee that keeps growing is the delinquency fee, and the contract does not require the borrower to settle it. Consequently the unpaid penalty is effectively transferred to the lenders: every lender that withdraws before the last one receives their principal plus the accrued penalty, but the final lender receives less than expected because part of the market’s assets have been consumed by the unpaid penalty. From a user perspective the borrower appears to have repaid the full debt when the market is closed, but later the market balance is insufficient to cover the last lender’s withdrawal, leading to a shortfall that the last lender must absorb. The issue occurs only when closeMarket() is called after the market has entered delinquency and the grace period timer has not yet counted down to zero. It was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena through a test that fast‑forwarded time and observed that the scale factor and total debt kept increasing after closure. The bug is subtle because the contract emits an event indicating the market is closed and the total assets equal the reported debt, giving the impression that all obligations are settled, while the hidden penalty accrual is not visible in the state. The root cause is the omission of a check for remaining delinquency time in the closure logic and the reliance on a scale factor that continues to grow while penalties are still owed. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “incomplete settlement on contract termination” or “post‑closure fee accrual” bugs, where fees that should be settled before termination are left to accrue and are unintentionally shifted to other participants. The impact is financial loss for the last withdrawing lender and a breach of the protocol’s economic guarantees. A proper fix would require the closeMarket() function to either forbid closure while state.timeDelinquent is greater than zero or to compute and collect the full outstanding delinquency fee (including the portion that would accrue during the remaining grace period) before allowing the market to be closed, possibly by adding a buffer amount or by adjusting the scale factor to zero out pending penalties.

title: `codehash` check in factory contracts does not account for non-empty addresses
content: The vulnerability stems from an incorrect assumption about the semantics of the .codehash property used in several factory contracts. The code checks whether an address already hosts a contract by comparing its codehash to bytes32(0). According to EIP‑1052, an address that has no code returns the hash of empty data (keccak256("") ) when the account exists but is not empty, i.e., it has a non‑zero balance or a non‑zero nonce. Consequently, an address that has received even a single wei will report a non‑zero codehash even though no contract code is present. The factory functions – deployController, deployMarket and createEscrow – rely on the .codehash != bytes32(0) test to decide whether a CREATE2 deployment is allowed. An attacker can pre‑emptively fund the deterministic address that will be generated by CREATE2, causing its codehash to become keccak256("") . When the legitimate borrower later calls the deployment function, the check incorrectly believes a contract already exists and reverts with ControllerAlreadyDeployed or MarketAlreadyDeployed, or in the escrow case it skips contract creation and returns the address. This results in a denial‑of‑service condition: the borrower can never deploy a controller, markets cannot be created, and escrow contracts are never instantiated, leaving any tokens sent to the escrow address permanently locked because no code can handle withdrawals. The issue manifests only when the deterministic address is funded before the legitimate call, which is feasible because the salt is derived from known values (borrower address, asset, name, etc.). Users experience failed transactions with error messages indicating the contract already exists, or see their market tokens disappear into an address with no code. The bug was discovered during a security audit that included unit tests reproducing the front‑running scenario. It is hard to notice because checking .codehash against zero is a common pattern and developers may overlook the special case defined by EIP‑1052. The proper fix is to treat both bytes32(0) and keccak256("") as indicators of an empty account, or to use address.code.length != 0 for a more reliable presence‑of‑code test. By correcting the empty‑address detection, the factories will no longer reject legitimate deployments and escrow contracts will be correctly created, preserving protocol functionality and user funds.
summary:
```solidity
In `WildcatMarketControllerFactory.sol`, registered borrowers can call `deployController()` to deploy a `WildcatMarketController` contract for themselves.

The function checks if the `codehash` of the controller address is `bytes32(0)` to determine if the controller has already been deployed:

[WildcatMarketControllerFactory.sol#L287-L296](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-wildcat/blob/main/src/WildcatMarketControllerFactory.sol#L287-L296)
    
    // Salt is borrower address
    bytes32 salt = bytes32(uint256(uint160(msg.sender)));
    controller = LibStoredInitCode.calculateCreate2Address(
        ownCreate2Prefix,
        salt,
        controllerInitCodeHash
    );
    if (controller.codehash != bytes32(0)) { // auditor: This check
        revert ControllerAlreadyDeployed();
    }

This same check is also used in `deployMarket()`, which is called by borrowers to deploy markets:

[WildcatMarketController.sol#L349-L353](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-wildcat/blob/main/src/WildcatMarketController.sol#L349-L353)
    
    bytes32 salt = _deriveSalt(asset, namePrefix, symbolPrefix);
    market = LibStoredInitCode.calculateCreate2Address(ownCreate2Prefix, salt, marketInitCodeHash);
    if (market.codehash != bytes32(0)) {
        revert MarketAlreadyDeployed();
    }

This check also exists in `createEscrow()`, which is called by markets to deploy an escrow contract whenever a sanctioned lender gets blocked:

[WildcatSanctionsSentinel.sol#L104-L106](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-wildcat/blob/main/src/WildcatSanctionsSentinel.sol#L104-L106)
    
    escrowContract = getEscrowAddress(borrower, account, asset);
    
    if (escrowContract.codehash != bytes32(0)) return escrowContract;
```
However, this `<address>.codehash != bytes32(0)` check is insufficient to determine if an address has existing code. According to [EIP-1052](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-1052), addresses without code only return a `0x0` codehash when they are **empty**:

In case the account does not exist or is empty (as defined by [EIP-161](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-161)) `0` is pushed to the stack.

In case the account does not have code the keccak256 hash of empty data (i.e. `c5d2460186f7233c927e7db2dcc703c0e500b653ca82273b7bfad8045d85a470`) is pushed to the stack.

As seen from above, addresses without code can also return `keccak256("")` as its `codehash` if it is non-empty. [EIP-161](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-161) states that an address must have a zero ETH balance for it to be empty:

An account is considered _empty_ when it has **no code** and **zero nonce** and **zero balance**.

As such, if anyone transfers 1 wei to an address, `.codehash` will return `keccak256("")` instead of `bytes32(0)`, making the checks shown above pass incorrectly.

Since all contract deployments in the protocol use `CREATE2`, a malicious attacker can harm users by doing the following:

  * For controller deployments:

    * Attacker calls [`computeControllerAddress()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-wildcat/blob/main/src/WildcatMarketControllerFactory.sol#L342-L347) to compute the controller address for a borrower.
    * Attacker transfers 1 wei to it, causing `.codehash` to become non-zero.
    * When `deployController()` is called by the borrower, the check passes, causing the function to revert.
  * For market deployments:

    * Attacker calls [`computeMarketAddress()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-wildcat/blob/main/src/WildcatMarketController.sol#L221-L228) with arguments such that the deployment salt is the same.
    * Attacker transfers 1 wei to the resulting market address, causing `.codehash` to become non-zero.
    * When `deployMarket()` is called by the borrower, the function reverts.
  * For escrow deployments:

    * Attacker calls [`getEscrowAddress()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-wildcat/blob/main/src/WildcatSanctionsSentinel.sol#L61-L85) with the `borrower`, sanctioned `lender` and market/asset address to compute the resulting escrow address.
    * Attacker transfers 1 wei to the escrow address, causing `.codehash` to become non-zero.
    * When either [`nukeFromOrbit()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-wildcat/blob/main/src/market/WildcatMarketConfig.sol#L74-L81) or [`executeWithdrawal()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-10-wildcat/blob/main/src/market/WildcatMarketWithdrawals.sol#L123-L188) is called, `createEscrow()` simply returns the escrow address instead of deploying an escrow contract.
    * The market tokens and/or funds of the lender are transferred to the escrow address, causing them to be unrecoverable since the escrow contract was never deployed.

Note that for controller deployments, since the salt is fixed to the `borrower` address and cannot be varied, the DOS for `deployController()` is permanent. This effectively locks the `borrower` out of all protocol functionality forever since they can never deploy a market controller for themselves.

title: Borrower has no way to update `maxTotalSupply` of `market` or close market.
content: Borrower has no way to update maxTotalSupply of market or close market. The vulnerability is a missing administrative interface in the WildcatMarketController contract. The market contract defines setMaxTotalSupply and closeMarket functions that are protected by an internal access control allowing only the controller to call them. However, the controller does not expose any external function that the borrower (the entity that created the market) can invoke. As a result, once a market is deployed the borrower cannot increase the maximum total supply to raise additional capital, nor can they decrease the limit to stop paying interest on unused capacity, nor can they close a market that is no longer needed. The root cause is the absence of a public wrapper with the onlyBorrower modifier. Exploitation consists of the borrower being forced to keep the market open with a fixed maxTotalSupply, causing continuous accrual of interest on the unused portion of the supply. From a user perspective the borrower sees interest charges even though no assets are being utilized, and may notice that the market balance remains locked and cannot be withdrawn or closed. The impact is economic loss: funds remain idle, interest accrues unnecessarily, and the protocol’s capital efficiency is reduced. The condition occurs whenever the borrower wishes to adjust supply limits or retire a market, which is a common operational need. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the access control flow and noticed that the only functions that can change these parameters are internal to the market and not reachable by the borrower. The problem is subtle because the functions exist and are correctly guarded, but the lack of a forwarding function makes the capability effectively unavailable, which can be overlooked in a quick code review. The recommended remediation is to add two thin wrapper functions in WildcatMarketController – setMaxTotalSupply(address market, uint256 _maxTotalSupply) and closeMarket(address market) – each protected by the onlyBorrower modifier and calling the corresponding market functions. This restores the intended governance model, allowing the borrower to raise more assets, reduce the supply cap, and close markets when they are no longer needed, eliminating unnecessary interest charges and aligning the contract behavior with business expectations.
summary:
Without the ability to update `maxTotalSupply`, `borrower` has no way to raise more assets in a specific market. Even worse, `borrower` has to pay extra interest for unused assets all the time because `borrower` has no way to reduce the max total supply of the market.

Similarly, `borrower` has to pay extra interest to the no-longer-used market all the time because there is no way to close it.

title: When `withdrawalBatchDuration` is set to zero lenders can withdraw more then allocated to a batch
content: The vulnerability originates from the way the Wildcat protocol handles withdrawal batches when the configuration parameter withdrawalBatchDuration is set to zero. In normal operation a non‑zero duration creates a time window during which a batch’s accounting fields – especially the normalizedAmountPaid that represents the total assets actually paid out for the batch – are frozen before any lender can execute a withdrawal. When the duration is forced to zero, the batch expires immediately and lenders are allowed to call queueWithdrawal and executeWithdrawal in the same block. Because the contract updates the batch’s scaledTotalAmount before it finalises the normalizedAmountPaid, a second lender that joins the same expiry can calculate its withdrawable amount using the original normalizedAmountPaid (which only reflects the first lender’s payout) while the denominator of the pro‑rata formula now includes the combined scaled amounts of both lenders. The formula newTotalWithdrawn = normalizedAmountPaid * scaledAmount / scaledTotalAmount therefore yields a value that, when summed across all lenders in the batch, can exceed the actual paid assets. An attacker can submit multiple withdrawal requests in a single block, each receiving a share of the batch that together surpasses the batch’s paid balance, effectively creating an over‑withdrawal condition. The impact is a breach of a core protocol invariant – that withdrawals may not exceed the assets counted as paid for the batch – which can lead to funds disappearing from the market, other pending batches becoming under‑funded, and ultimately a loss of confidence in the protocol’s accounting integrity. This bug only manifests when withdrawalBatchDuration is zero and multiple withdrawals share the same expiry timestamp, affecting any lender using the market and the protocol’s overall liquidity pool. It was discovered during a security audit that examined edge‑case parameter settings and identified that the existing expiry check (if expiry > block.timestamp) allowed immediate execution, missing the case where expiry equals the current block timestamp. The issue is subtle because the same code works correctly for typical non‑zero durations, so the over‑withdrawal scenario is not obvious during routine testing. To remediate the problem the contract should prevent execution when expiry is equal to the current timestamp (changing the check to expiry >= block.timestamp) or disallow a zero‑duration configuration altogether, and ensure that the normalizedAmountPaid is updated atomically with respect to the scaledTotalAmount before any withdrawal calculation is performed, thereby guaranteeing that each lender can only withdraw their true pro‑rata share of the batch’s paid assets.

title: Lenders can escape the blacklisting of their accounts because they can move their MarketTokens to different accounts and gain the `WithdrawOnly` Role on any account they want
content: The vulnerability allows alender who has been flagged as sanctioned by the Chainalysis oracle to bypass the market’s blacklisting mechanism and still withdraw funds. The root cause is the public WildcatMarketController.updateLenderAuthorization function, which any address can call. This function iterates over a list of markets and forwards a boolean flag derived from the controller’s internal _authorizedLenders set to WildcatMarket.updateAccountAuthorization. When the lender address is not present in _authorizedLenders, the flag is false, and the market’s updateAccountAuthorization routine interprets a false _isAuthorized value as a command to assign the WithdrawOnly role to the supplied account. Because the caller can choose any target address, a sanctioned lender can first transfer all of its MarketTokens to fresh accounts that hold no role, then invoke updateLenderAuthorization with those accounts as the "lender" argument. The market will grant each of those accounts the WithdrawOnly role, which permits only withdrawals and no further deposits. The lender can then queue and execute withdrawal requests from any of the newly funded accounts, effectively escaping the sanction. This attack can be performed after the lender’s original address has been marked as sanctioned but before the nukeFromOrbit function fully blocks the account, or even after nukeFromOrbit because the tokens have already been moved. From a user perspective the expected behaviour is that a sanctioned account becomes unable to move funds; instead the user sees their tokens disappear from the original address yet remains able to pull the same amount out of other addresses, leading to confusion and a false sense of security that the protocol is enforcing sanctions. The impact is that the protocol’s compliance enforcement is broken, allowing malicious or sanctioned actors to extract value that should have been frozen, potentially resulting in financial loss and reputational damage. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the interaction between the sanctions sentinel and the controller’s authorization update logic; it is subtle because the false flag is not an error but is interpreted as a legitimate role change, making it easy to overlook during testing. To remediate, the updateLenderAuthorization function should be restricted to a trusted caller (e.g., only the borrower or a whitelisted admin) and the market’s updateAccountAuthorization logic should not automatically grant WithdrawOnly on a false flag without explicit revocation semantics. In other words, the protocol must enforce proper access control on role‑changing functions and separate the concepts of “authorized” and “withdraw‑only” to prevent arbitrary role escalation by sanctioned lenders.
summary: Lenders can escape the sanctioning of their account in any market.

title: Borrower can drain all funds of a sanctioned lender
content: The vulnerability is a logic error in the way a sanctions escrow is created when a lender is blocked for sanctions. When the market’s internal _blockAccount routine calls the external WildcatSanctionsSentinel.createEscrow function, it passes the arguments in the order (account, borrower, asset) while the sentinel contract expects (borrower, account, asset). This mismatch swaps the identities of the sanctioned lender and the market borrower inside the escrow’s temporary parameters. As a result, the escrow’s canReleaseEscrow check queries the sentinel to see whether the borrower (who is not sanctioned) is blocked, which returns false, allowing the escrow to be released immediately. The borrower can then call releaseEscrow, which transfers the entire balance that originally belonged to the sanctioned lender to the borrower’s address. The flaw is triggered whenever a lender is marked as sanctioned and the market’s nukeFromOrbit (or any function that blocks the account) is invoked. From the user’s point of view the sanctioned lender sees their market token balance drop to zero and is unable to retrieve it even after the sanction is lifted, while the borrower suddenly gains a large amount of tokens and can withdraw the underlying assets. The impact is a complete loss of funds for the affected lender and an unauthorized gain for the borrower, effectively allowing fund theft. The issue was uncovered during a Code4rena audit by inspecting the parameter ordering in the escrow creation call and observing that the escrow’s release logic behaved incorrectly. It is difficult to notice because the escrow contract is created successfully and the sanction check appears to pass, masking the swapped roles. The proper remediation is to align the argument order between the market’s _blockAccount function and the sentinel’s createEscrow interface, ensuring that the borrower and account parameters are passed in the correct positions, or to modify the sentinel to accept the current ordering. Conceptually, the fix restores the intended invariant that only a sanctioned account’s escrow can be released after the sanction is cleared, preventing the borrower from draining the lender’s funds.
summary:
The `WildcatMarketBase#_blockAccount()` function that is used to block a sanctioned lender contains a critical bug. It incorrectly calls `IWildcatSanctionsSentinel(sentinel).createEscrow()` with misordered arguments, accidentally creating a vulnerable escrow that enables the borrower to drain all the funds of the sanctioned lender.

The execution of withdrawals (`WildcatMarketWithdrawals#executeWithdrawal()`) also performs a check if the `accountAddress` is sanctioned and if it is, then escrow is created and the amount that was to be sent to the lender is sent to the escrow. That escrow, however, is also created with the `account` and `borrower` arguments in the wrong order.

That means whether or not the borrower has anything to do with a sanctioned account and their funds ever, that account will never be able to get their money back in case their sanction gets dismissed.

title: `VoteKickPolicy._endVote()` might revert forever due to underflow
content: The vulnerability is an arithmetic underflow that can occur in the VoteKickPolicy contract when the function _endVote attempts to distribute rewards after a flagging vote. The root cause is the way the minimum stake required for an operator is calculated in StreamrConfig.minimumStakeWei. The formula multiplies the total flagger and reviewer rewards by 1 ether and then divides by the slashing fraction. When the slashing fraction is a small value such as 3 % the division truncates the result, rounding the required stake down. Consequently the amount of stake that is considered “at risk” for the target operator (targetStakeAtRiskWei) can be smaller than the sum of the rewards that must be paid to the flagger and reviewers. During _endVote the contract subtracts the total rewards from targetStakeAtRiskWei using unchecked arithmetic. Because the rewards exceed the available stake, the subtraction underflows, causing the transaction to revert. The revert stops the vote finalisation, meaning the flagging process never completes and the malicious operator is never kicked out of the system. This effect is only observable when the slashing fraction is set to a low value that triggers rounding; with the default 10 % fraction the calculation yields a sufficient stake and the bug does not manifest, which makes the issue easy to miss during casual testing. The impact is that the protocol’s governance mechanism for removing misbehaving operators can be blocked, potentially allowing a rogue operator to remain active indefinitely and preventing flaggers and reviewers from receiving their expected rewards. Users of the protocol – operators, flaggers, reviewers, and any participants relying on the kick‑out logic – are affected because the expected state transition (operator removal and reward distribution) does not happen, leading to missing payouts and a false sense of security that the system is still enforcing its rules. The problem was discovered during a formal audit that examined edge‑case values for the slashing fraction and identified the rounding discrepancy. It is hard to notice because the underflow only triggers for specific parameter configurations and does not appear with the typical default settings. To remediate the issue the minimumStakeWei function should be changed to round up instead of down, ensuring that the calculated stake at risk is always at least as large as the total rewards. Alternatively, the reward distribution logic in _endVote could include a safety check that verifies sufficient stake before performing the subtraction, or use safe‑math operations that revert with a clear error message rather than silently underflowing. By guaranteeing that targetStakeAtRiskWei >= totalRewards, the vote finalisation will succeed, the operator can be removed when appropriate, and flaggers and reviewers will receive the payouts they expect.
summary:
** In `onFlag()`, `targetStakeAtRiskWei[target]` might be less than the total rewards for the flagger/reviewers due to rounding.

```solidity
File: contracts\OperatorTokenomics\StreamrConfig.sol
22:     /**
23:      * Minimum amount to pay reviewers+flagger
24:      * That is: minimumStakeWei >= (flaggerRewardWei + flagReviewerCount * flagReviewerRewardWei) / slashingFraction
25:      */
26:     function minimumStakeWei() public view returns (uint) {
27:         return (flaggerRewardWei + flagReviewerCount * flagReviewerRewardWei) * 1 ether / slashingFraction;
28:     }
```

- Let's assume `flaggerRewardWei + flagReviewerCount * flagReviewerRewardWei = 100`, `StreamrConfig.slashingFraction = 0.03e18` (3%), `minimumStakeWei() = 1000 * 1e18 / 0.03e18 = 10000 / 3 = 3333`.
- If we suppose `stakedWei[target] = streamrConfig.minimumStakeWei()`, then `targetStakeAtRiskWei[target] = 3333 * 0.03e18 / 1e18 = 99.99 = 99`.
- As a result, `targetStakeAtRiskWei[target]` is less than total rewards (=100), and `_endVote()` will revert during the reward distribution due to underflow.

The above scenario is possible only when there is a rounding during `minimumStakeWei` calculation. So it works properly with the default `slashingFraction = 10%`.

** The `VoteKickPolicy` wouldn't work as expected and malicious operators won't be kicked forever.

title: Possible overflow in `_payOutFirstInQueue`
content: The vulnerability is an arithmetic overflow in the exchange‑rate conversion routine that is invoked by the internal payout function. When the contract attempts to compute the amount of operator tokens to return for a given amount of data wei, it multiplies the supplied data amount by the total supply of operator tokens before dividing by the value without earnings. Because the multiplication is performed without overflow protection, supplying an extremely large data amount – for example the maximum uint256 value that can be passed to the undelegate() entry point – causes the product to exceed the 256‑bit limit and triggers a revert. The revert propagates back to the _payOutFirstInQueue() routine, which is responsible for processing the first entry in the delegation queue. As a result, every subsequent call to _payOutFirstInQueue() also reverts, effectively freezing the queue logic forever. This means that delegators who attempt to undelegate their tokens receive no payout, their balances appear unchanged, and the protocol cannot process any further withdrawals or refunds. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the streamr v2.0 contracts, where the auditor noticed that the operatorTokenToDataInverse() view function performed an unchecked multiplication that could overflow. The bug is subtle because it only manifests with extreme input values that are unlikely to appear in normal operation, and typical unit tests may not cover the edge case of type(uint256).max. From a user’s perspective the UI would show a successful undelegate transaction but the expected refund would never arrive, leaving the user’s balance at zero or unchanged, which contradicts the expectation that a withdrawal returns the correct amount. The class of bug is an unchecked arithmetic overflow leading to a denial‑of‑service condition in a financial queue. To remediate the issue the contract should enforce a ceiling on the amount of data wei passed to the conversion function, or rearrange the calculation to perform division before multiplication, or use Solidity 0.8+ built‑in overflow checks, thereby guaranteeing that the conversion never reverts and the payout queue can continue processing withdrawals.

title: Wrong validation in `DefaultUndelegationPolicy.onUndelegate()`
content: The vulnerability resides in the onUndelegate function of the staking contract, where the validation logic mixes two unrelated token units. The function receives an amount parameter that represents a quantity of the DATA token, while the balanceOf(owner) call returns the Operator token balance held by the operator. The require statement then compares the Operator token balance after the undelegation (balanceAfter) with the total supply after the undelegation (totalSupplyAfter) multiplied by a minimum self‑delegation fraction, but the amount subtracted from both balances is expressed in DATA tokens. Because DATA and Operator tokens are not interchangeable, the arithmetic produces an incorrect balanceAfter value that is effectively unrelated to the actual Operator token holdings. As a result, whenever the operator owner attempts to undelegate any amount, the condition 1 ether * balanceAfter >= totalSupplyAfter * minimumSelfDelegationFraction() is evaluated against a mismatched value and almost always fails, causing the transaction to revert with the error_selfDelegationTooLow message. This bug was discovered during a manual audit by Cyfrin, where the logical inconsistency between token types was identified. The issue is subtle because the code compiles and the require statement appears to enforce a sensible business rule – that the operator must retain a minimum fraction of the total supply – yet the underlying units are wrong, making the check ineffective. From a user perspective, an operator attempting to withdraw or reduce their delegation sees no change in their balance, receives an error, and may believe that their funds are locked or that the protocol is malicious. The impact is limited to the operator role: the operator cannot reduce its stake, potentially locking up capital and preventing normal delegation management, which can affect the overall liquidity and trust in the protocol. The bug violates the accounting assumption that self‑delegation is measured in the same token as the total supply. To remediate, the validation should first convert both sides of the comparison to the same token denomination – either by converting the DATA amount to Operator tokens using the appropriate exchange rate or by performing the self‑delegation check using only Operator token balances – ensuring that the minimumSelfDelegationFraction constraint is applied to comparable quantities.

title: Malicious target can make `_endVote()` revert forever by forceUnstaking/staking again
content: The contract implements a flagging mechanism where a flagger can start a vote to kick a target operator. When the vote ends, the internal function _endVote updates accounting variables that track locked stakes and forfeited stakes. The function decides whether the flagger or the target is "gone" by checking if their current staked balance (stakedWei) is zero. If the flagger is gone, the flagger’s locked stake is moved to forfeitedStakeWei; otherwise it is deducted from lockedStakeWei. The same logic is applied to the target. The vulnerability arises because the decision is based on the current staking balance rather than the actual state of the locked stake. If a target operator calls forceUnstake during the voting period, the contract’s Sponsorship._removeOperator resets lockedStakeWei[target] to zero while the target’s stakedWei becomes zero as well. The attacker can then immediately stake again, restoring a positive stakedWei but leaving lockedStakeWei[target] at zero. When _endVote later runs, the condition targetIsGone evaluates to false (because stakedWei is now positive) and the code attempts to subtract targetStakeAtRiskWei[target] – the amount that was originally locked – from lockedStakeWei[target], which is still zero. This subtraction underflows, causing the transaction to revert. Because the revert happens inside the vote‑finalisation routine, the vote can never be completed, leaving the flagging process stuck indefinitely. A malicious operator can therefore avoid being kicked and continue to collect operator rewards without ever facing a slash, effectively bypassing the governance safeguard. The issue manifests only when the specific sequence (flag, forceUnstake, restake, vote end) occurs, making it easy to miss in standard testing. From a user perspective the UI would show a flagging vote that never resolves, or a transaction that repeatedly fails with a revert, while the flagged operator remains active and continues earning rewards. The root cause is an arithmetic underflow caused by inconsistent state management – the contract assumes that a non‑zero staked balance guarantees a corresponding locked stake, which is not true after a forceUnstake followed by a new stake. To remediate, the unlock logic in _endVote should rely on the stored lockedStakeWei value (or a dedicated flag indicating whether the stake was already moved to forfeited) rather than the current staked balance, and it should guard against underflow by checking that the subtraction amount does not exceed the available locked stake. This change restores the intended accounting invariants and prevents the vote‑finalisation routine from being permanently blocked.

title: `TokenSaleProposal::buy` implicitly assumes that buy token has 18 decimals resulting in a potential total loss scenario for Dao Pool
content: TokenSaleProposalBuy::buy function assumes that the amount parameter is expressed with 18 decimal places regardless of the actual decimals of the purchase token. The internal helper _sendFunds calls safeTransferFrom with amount.from18(token.decimals()), which converts the supplied 18‑decimal amount to the token's native decimals. Because the caller provides the raw amount without first normalising it to 18 decimals, tokens that have fewer than 18 decimals (for example USDC with 6 decimals) cause the conversion to truncate to zero. When the conversion result is zero, the transfer of funds to the governance pool effectively sends no tokens, while the buyer still receives the full amount of DAO tokens according to the exchange rate. This creates a scenario where a user can acquire DAO tokens for free, resulting in a total loss of value for the DAO pool. The vulnerability manifests whenever a purchase token with non‑18 decimals is used and the buyer supplies the amount in the token's native precision instead of 18‑decimal precision. It affects any participant who attempts to buy DAO tokens with such a token, the DAO treasury, and any downstream protocol that relies on the integrity of the token sale proceeds. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the conversion logic and identified that the amount is never validated or normalised before the conversion. The bug is subtle because the function call succeeds and no revert occurs; the only symptom is that the DAO pool balance does not decrease while the buyer’s claim balance increases, which may be overlooked in normal testing. The root cause is an implicit design decision that all token amounts are 18 decimals, which is not true for many ERC20 tokens. To fix the problem the contract should either require callers to always provide amounts in 18‑decimal format and perform a safe conversion that reverts when the result is zero, or, preferably, redesign the logic so that amounts are supplied in the token’s native decimals and the protocol performs the conversion centrally. Using a safe conversion function such as from18Safe that checks for zero output, or adding an explicit revert when amount.from18(token.decimals()) == 0, mitigates the loss. The broader class of bug is an incorrect assumption about token decimal handling leading to rounding‑to‑zero errors and unintended fund loss.

title: Attacker can combine flashloan with delegated voting to decide a proposal and withdraw their tokens while the proposal is still in Locked state
content: The vulnerability is a governance token lock bypass that arises from the combination of flash‑loaned voting power and the ability to delegate and undelegate that power within the same block. The GovPool contract permits a user to deposit voting tokens, delegate the voting power to another address, and later undelegate and withdraw the same tokens while a proposal remains in the Locked state. Because the contract does not enforce a separation between delegation, voting, and withdrawal, an attacker can obtain a large amount of voting tokens through a flash loan, deposit them into the pool, delegate the power to a slave contract, and have the slave cast a vote that immediately satisfies the quorum. The proposal therefore transitions from Voting to Locked in a single transaction. At that point the attacker undelegates the voting power and withdraws the flash‑loaned tokens before the proposal is finalized, repaying the loan and keeping the governance outcome they forced. This attack can be executed atomically, making it difficult to detect during normal operation. The impact is that an attacker can manipulate any proposal, approve malicious changes, and temporarily remove a large amount of tokens from the pool, causing token balances to disappear for honest participants and breaking the expected accounting guarantees of the governance system. The issue occurs whenever a proposal is in the Voting phase and the contract allows delegation and undelegation in the same block, combined with a flash‑loan source of voting tokens. It affects the protocol’s governance integrity, token holders who rely on locked voting power, and any user who expects their deposited tokens to remain locked until a proposal is resolved. The flaw was discovered during a security audit by Cyfrin, which demonstrated the attack with a custom contract and unit test. The problem is hard to notice because the contract’s state transitions appear correct – the proposal does reach Locked – and the token balances are restored after the transaction, masking the temporary misuse of voting power. To remediate, the protocol should prevent delegation or undelegation and deposit or withdrawal actions from occurring in the same block, enforce that tokens remain locked for the full lifetime of a proposal, and add checks that disallow withdrawals while a proposal is in the Locked state. In broader terms, this is a class of governance‑state race condition where token lock assumptions are violated by rapid state changes enabled by flash loans and delegated voting.
summary:
** Attacker can combine a flashloan with delegated voting to bypass the existing flashloan mitigations, allowing the attacker to decide a proposal & withdraw their tokens while the proposal is still in the Locked state. The entire attack can be performed in 1 transaction via an attack contract.

** Attacker can bypass existing flashloan mitigations to decide the outcome of proposals by combining flashloan with delegated voting.

title: Attacker can destroy user voting power by setting `ERC721Power::totalPower` and all existing NFTs `currentPower` to 0
content: The vulnerability is a permission‑less manipulation of the ERC721Power contract that allows an attacker to reduce the global voting power (totalPower) and the individual power of every existing NFT (currentPower) to zero. The root cause is a subtle mismatch between two time checks: the view function getNftPower returns zero when block.timestamp is less than or equal to powerCalcStartTimestamp, while the state‑changing function recalculateNftPower only returns zero when block.timestamp is strictly less than powerCalcStartTimestamp. When an attacker invokes recalculateNftPower for each token in the exact block where block.timestamp equals powerCalcStartTimestamp, the function proceeds, subtracts the NFT’s maximum power from totalPower, adds the newly calculated power (which is zero), and writes zero into the NFT’s currentPower field. By iterating over all token IDs, the attacker can set totalPower and every currentPower to zero in a single transaction without any special privileges. This results in the complete loss of voting power for all holders of ERC721Power NFTs: users who expect their NFTs to contribute voting weight suddenly see their voting power drop to zero, proposals become impossible to create, and the DAO becomes effectively bricked. The attack only succeeds on the precise block when the power calculation period starts, making it hard to detect during normal operation because the condition is fleeting and the contract otherwise behaves correctly. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the time‑based logic and confirmed the exploit with a dedicated attack contract and test harness. Because the state change is irreversible without redeploying the NFT contract, the bug violates the protocol’s accounting assumptions that voting power can only decrease over time due to collateral withdrawal, never be abruptly erased. The recommended fix is to harmonize the timestamp comparison in both functions—using the same inequality (e.g., <=) or restructuring the logic so that recalculateNftPower does not execute when the power calculation has just started—thereby preventing the zero‑power reset at the boundary block.

title: Under-funded eth distribution proposals can be created causing claiming rewards to revert
content: The vulnerability consists of the ability to create an ETH distribution proposal that is under‑funded because the contract function that finalises the proposal does not verify that the amount of ether declared for distribution matches the ether actually supplied in the transaction. The root cause is a missing equality check between the parameter `amount` and `msg.value` in the `execute()` routine of the distribution proposal contract. An attacker who controls a GovPool can therefore submit a proposal promising a certain reward, then call `execute()` with a lower `msg.value`, resulting in a proposal that records a reward amount larger than the ether held by the contract. When users later vote on the proposal and attempt to claim their share through `claim()`, the claim function attempts to transfer more ether than is available and reverts with an error such as "Gov: failed to send eth". From the user’s perspective the UI shows a reward amount, the user votes expecting to receive it, but the claim transaction fails and the user’s balance remains unchanged, effectively losing the promised payout. This issue manifests only for proposals funded with ether and only when the execution step is performed with insufficient funds; it does not affect token‑based distributions. Anyone who can create a GovPool – typically the protocol owner or a malicious actor – can exploit this flaw to lure participants into voting on fake incentives, thereby extracting votes without paying rewards. The problem was discovered during a security audit by Cyfrin, where a test case demonstrated that an under‑funded proposal causes `claim()` to revert. The bug is subtle because the proposal appears valid on‑chain and in the UI, and the mismatch between declared reward and actual funding is not emitted as an event, making it hard to detect without inspecting the contract state. Conceptually, the fix is to enforce a strict check that `amount == msg.value` for ether‑funded proposals, causing the transaction to revert if the funding is insufficient, and optionally to validate funding at proposal creation time. By adding this validation the protocol regains its economic guarantees, prevents denial‑of‑service of reward distribution, and restores confidence that voting incentives will be honoured.
summary:
** It is possible to create under-funded eth distribution proposals as `DistributionProposal::execute()` [L62-63](https://github.com/dexe-network/DeXe-Protocol/tree/f2fe12eeac0c4c63ac39670912640dc91d94bda5/contracts/gov/proposals/DistributionProposal.sol#L62-L63) doesn't check whether `amount == msg.value`. If `msg.value < amount` an under-funded distribution proposal will be executed.

This opens up an attack vector where a malicious GovPool owner can provide fake incentives to users to make them vote on proposals. At the time of reward distribution, owner can simply execute a distribution proposal without sending the promised amount as reward. As a result, users end up voting for a proposal and not getting paid for it.

** Users can't claim their rewards as `DistributionProposal::claim()` will revert for under-funded distribution proposals. Since anybody can create a `GovPool`, there is a potential for loss to users due to malicious intent.

title: Attacker can bypass token sale `maxAllocationPerUser` restriction to buy out the entire tier
content: The vulnerability resides in the token‑sale contract’s enforcement of the per‑user allocation cap for each sale tier. The contract defines a maxAllocationPerUser value that is intended to limit the total amount of tokens any single participant can acquire from a given tier. However, the implementation only checks the amount being purchased in the current transaction against the cap and does not aggregate the participant’s previous purchases in that tier. As a result, an attacker can split the intended maximum purchase into many smaller transactions, each individually below the limit, and cumulatively acquire the entire token supply of the tier. This bypass is possible whenever the sale is active, the tier parameters include a non‑zero maxAllocationPerUser, and the contract does not maintain a running total per user per tier. The issue was discovered during a security audit when a test case demonstrated that a user could execute a series of buys of 25 wei each, bypassing the 100‑wei cap and eventually claiming the full 1000‑wei tier allocation. From a user’s perspective the contract appears to enforce a restriction – a single purchase larger than the cap is rejected with a “wrong allocation” error – but after several small purchases the attacker ends up owning all tokens, causing other legitimate participants to see the tier sold out and receive an “insufficient sale token amount” error when they try to buy. The impact is severe: other users are permanently blocked from acquiring any tokens in the affected tier, the token distribution model is broken, and the attacker may obtain a controlling share of the token supply, potentially leading to market manipulation. The bug is subtle because the per‑transaction check gives the impression of a proper limit, making it easy to overlook the missing cumulative accounting. The proper fix is to track the total amount each address has purchased in a tier and enforce that the sum of the previously purchased amount and the new request does not exceed maxAllocationPerUser. This change restores the intended economic guarantees of the sale and prevents a single participant from monopolising a tier’s tokens.
summary:
An attacker can bypass the token sale `maxAllocationPerUser` restriction to buy out the entire tier by doing multiple small buys under this limit.

Permanent grief for other users who are unable to buy any of the exploited tier's tokens. Depending on the total supply a buyer could take control of the majority of the tokens by scooping them all up in a token sale, preventing them being distributed as intended and having monopoly control of the market. The `maxAllocationPerUser` restriction is not working as intended and can easily be bypassed by anyone.

title: A malicious DAO Pool can create a token sale tier without actually transferring any DAO tokens
content: The vulnerability consists of a token‑sale tier creation function that allows a DAO pool owner to register a new sale tier without guaranteeing that the required amount of DAO tokens has actually been transferred to the TokenSaleProposal contract. The root cause is that the implementation performs a low‑level call to the ERC20 token’s transferFrom function but never validates that the contract’s token balance has increased by the expected totalTokenProvided amount. Because the call’s return value is deliberately ignored and no post‑transfer balance check is performed, a malicious ERC20 contract can override transferFrom to return a success flag while leaving the token balances unchanged. When such a custom token is used, the DAO pool owner can create a “fake” tier that appears on‑chain, and naive participants will be led to believe that the pool holds sufficient DAO tokens to satisfy future claims. In reality the TokenSaleProposal contract holds fewer tokens than required, so any attempt by participants to claim their allocated DAO tokens will fail, resulting in a permanent denial‑of‑service condition for those claims. The issue manifests whenever a DAO pool owner supplies an ERC20 token that does not follow the standard transfer semantics, especially when the contract relies on a low‑level call without balance verification. It affects all users who join the affected token sale, the DAO pool itself, and the broader protocol because the perceived token availability is false. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the createTier function and noted a developer comment explicitly stating that the return value is not checked, prompting a deeper review of balance handling. The problem is subtle because the transaction does not revert and the tier creation event is emitted, giving the impression that the transfer succeeded, while the underlying accounting is broken. To remediate, the contract should record the token balance of the TokenSaleProposal before the transfer, execute a safeTransferFrom (or an equivalent checked call), then read the balance again and require that the increase matches totalTokenProvided, adjusting for fee‑on‑transfer tokens where necessary. This ensures that the tier cannot be created unless the correct amount of DAO tokens is truly deposited, preserving the integrity of the sale and preventing users from receiving zero tokens or experiencing a DOS when claiming their entitlement.

title: Attacker can use delegation to bypass voting restriction to vote on proposals they are restricted from voting on
