Every time the `deposit()` function is called, a new element is added to `positionAccounts`, `mapPositionAccountPdaAta`, and `mapPositionAccountLiquidity`, which decreases the available storage by `64 + 32 + 32 = 128` bits. This means that the contract will run out of space after at most `80000 / 128 = 625` deposits. Once the storage limit is reached, no further deposits can be made, effectively causing a permanent DoS condition. This could be exploited by an attacker to block the contract’s functionality at a very small cost.

title: CM can `delegatecall` to any address and bypass all restrictions
content: The GuardCM contract is intended to act as a transaction filter for the Community Multisig (CM) by checking each outgoing call in the GnosisSafe before it is executed. The checkTransaction function explicitly rejects delegatecall operations only when the destination address equals the timelock owner, assuming that the timelock is the only place where delegatecall could be dangerous. Because the guard does not verify the operation type for any other target address, the CM can issue a delegatecall to an arbitrary contract. An attacker can deploy a small contract that contains a function which writes zero to the storage slot that holds the guard address inside the safe, effectively deleting the guard. By submitting a transaction that delegatecalls this malicious contract, the guard variable is cleared, after which the CM is free to invoke any timelock function such as schedule or scheduleBatch without restriction. The vulnerability is triggered whenever the guard is active (not paused) and the CM submits a transaction with Enum.Operation.DelegateCall to a non‑owner address. The impact is a privilege‑escalation path that allows the CM, which already holds the privileged role in the timelock, to remove the only remaining safeguard and gain unrestricted control over protocol functions, potentially leading to unauthorized fund transfers, treasury pauses, or other state changes that violate the protocol’s business logic. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by adding a test that performs a delegatecall to a contract that clears the guard storage slot; the test showed that a previously reverted schedule call becomes successful after the guard is removed. The bug is subtle because the guard appears to enforce strict target and selector checks, yet the missing generic delegatecall prohibition is easy to overlook in code review. From a user perspective the symptom is that a transaction that should be blocked (for example a call to pause the treasury) suddenly succeeds, and the UI may show that the guard address is now zero or missing. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “improper access control via unchecked delegatecall” and violates the assumption that only the timelock needs protection from delegatecall. The recommended fix is to reject all delegatecall operations regardless of the target address, or to add an explicit check that the operation is not DelegateCall before any other logic, thereby eliminating the bypass vector.
summary: The [`GuardCM`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-12-autonolas/blob/main/governance/contracts/multisigs/GuardCM.sol) contract is designed to restrict the Community Multisig (CM) actions within the protocol to only specific contracts and methods. This is achieved by implementing a [`checkTransaction()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2023-12-autonolas/blob/main/governance/contracts/multisigs/GuardCM.sol#L387) method, which is invoked by the CM `GnosisSafe` [before every transaction](https://github.com/safe-global/safe-contracts/blob/186a21a74b327f17fc41217a927dea7064f74604/contracts/GnosisSafe.sol#L147-L167). When `GuardCM` is not paused, the implementation restricts calls to the `schedule()` and `scheduleBatch()` methods in the timelock to only specific targets and selectors, performs additional checks on calls forwarded to the L2s and blocks self-calls on the CM itself, which prevents it from unilaterally removing the guard: ```solidity if (to == owner) { // No delegatecall is allowed if (operation == Enum.Operation.DelegateCall) { revert NoDelegateCall(); } // Data needs to have enough bytes at least to fit the selector if (data.length < SELECTOR_DATA_LENGTH) { revert IncorrectDataLength(data.length, SELECTOR_DATA_LENGTH); } // Get the function signature bytes4 functionSig = bytes4(data); // Check the schedule or scheduleBatch function authorized parameters // All other functions are not checked for if (functionSig == SCHEDULE || functionSig == SCHEDULE_BATCH) { // Data length is too short: need to have enough bytes for the schedule() function // with one selector extracted from the payload if (data.length < MIN_SCHEDULE_DATA_LENGTH) { revert IncorrectDataLength(data.length, MIN_SCHEDULE_DATA_LENGTH); } _verifySchedule(data, functionSig); } } else if (to == multisig) { // No self multisig call is allowed revert NoSelfCall(); } ``` However, a critical oversight in the current implementation allows the CM to perform `delegatecall`s to any address but the timelock. As can be seen above, `DelegateCall` operations are only disallowed when the target is the timelock (represented by the `owner` variable). What this effectively means is that the CM cannot run any `Timelock` function in its own context, but it can `delegatecall` to any other contract and hence execute arbitrary code. This allows it to trivially bypass the guard by delegating to a contract that removes the guard variable from the CM’s storage. The CM holds all privileged roles within the timelock, which is in turn the protocol’s owner. This means that the CM can potentially gain unrestricted control over the entire protocol. As such, this vulnerability represents a significant risk of privilege escalation and is classified as high severity.

title: Wrong invocation of Whirpools’s updateFeesAndRewards will cause it to always revert
content: The vulnerability originates from an incorrect sequence of calls in the withdraw routine of a lockbox that interacts with the Orca Whirlpools pool. When a user attempts to withdraw the full amount of liquidity from a position, the contract calculates a remainder (positionLiquidity‑amount) that becomes zero. The code then unconditionally invokes the pool’s updateFeesAndRewards function before the position is closed. Whirlpools’ updateFeesAndRewards is designed to operate only on positions that still hold a positive liquidity amount; if the supplied position has zero liquidity the function reverts. Consequently, the withdraw transaction fails and the user’s funds remain locked in the lockbox, effectively making the deposited assets unwithdrawable. This failure mode is triggered only when the withdrawal amount exactly matches the remaining liquidity, so partial withdrawals succeed and the bug can be easily missed during routine testing that does not cover the edge case of a full exit. The issue was discovered during a security audit that exercised the withdraw path with a full‑liquidity removal and observed a revert from the external pool call. From a user’s perspective the UI would show a successful request but the transaction would revert, leaving the balance unchanged or appearing as zero after the attempt, contrary to the expectation that the funds would be returned. The bug violates the accounting assumption that fees and rewards can be updated independently of liquidity state, breaking the protocol’s invariant that a position can always be closed. The recommended remediation is to remove the explicit updateFeesAndRewards call from the withdraw flow, relying instead on the decreaseLiquidity operation—which already updates fees and rewards—or to guard the call with a check that the remainder is greater than zero. By correcting the order of operations, the contract will allow users to fully withdraw their deposits without encountering a revert, restoring the intended financial flow and preserving protocol safety.
summary: Deposits will be unwithdrawable from the lockbox.

title: Bonds created in year cross epoch’s can lead to lost payouts
content: The vulnerability originates from the way the bonding program tracks the amount of Olas that can be allocated to bonds through the variable known as effectiveBond. EffectiveBond is calculated at the beginning of each epoch by adding the projected inflation for that epoch, regardless of whether the projected amount can actually be minted in the current calendar year. Because the Olas token contract enforces a yearly inflation ceiling, any portion of the projected amount that belongs to the next year cannot be minted until that year begins. When an epoch spans the boundary between two years – a situation that appears after the ninth year of the protocol when a fixed‑supply schedule is in place – effectiveBond may include Olas that are not yet mintable. The contract that creates bonds checks only that effectiveBond is greater than or equal to the requested bond amount, reduces effectiveBond accordingly, and records the deposit as successful. Later, when the treasury attempts to mint the Olas needed to satisfy the bond payout, the Olas contract performs an inflationControl check. If the amount exceeds the yearly allowance, the mint function returns silently without reverting. Consequently, the bond deposit is recorded, but the actual Olas are never created, so the depositor’s later claim yields zero tokens. The same silent failure can affect agent or component owners who are supposed to receive top‑up rewards, causing their reward claims to return nothing. From a user’s perspective the UI shows a successful bond deposit and a normal vesting period, yet when the claim transaction is executed the user receives no Olas and their balance remains unchanged, contradicting the expectation of a payout. The issue was discovered during a formal audit that examined the interaction between epoch checkpointing, effectiveBond updates, and the yearly inflation schedule. It is difficult to notice because the mint function does not revert on failure, so no error is emitted and the transaction appears successful. The root cause is an accounting mismatch: effectiveBond assumes future mintable supply, while the inflation control enforces a hard yearly cap. To remediate the problem the bonding logic should be refactored to separate bond allocations by calendar year, ensuring that effectiveBond only counts Olas that are actually mintable in the current year, or the contract should revert when the mint operation cannot satisfy the required amount, thereby preventing silent loss of payouts. This class of bug can be described as an over‑allocation of future token supply combined with silent failure on minting, leading to lost rewards and broken financial guarantees in a token‑bonding system.
summary: Bond depositors and agent/component owner’s may never receive the payout Olas. Incorrect inflation control.

title: Withdrawals can be frozen by creating null deposits
content: The contract allows a user to create a liquidity position with zero LP tokens because the deposit routine only validates that the supplied liquidity does not exceed the uint64 maximum and does not enforce a lower bound. As a result a mapping entry is written with a liquidity value of 0, which the contract later treats as a valid position identifier. The withdrawal function determines whether a position exists by reading the stored liquidity; a value of 0 is interpreted as “no token account” and triggers a revert with the message No liquidity on a provided token account. Since the contract iterates linearly over all stored positions, encountering the artificially created zero‑liquidity entry causes the entire withdraw transaction to fail and prevents any subsequent positions from being processed. This effectively freezes all withdrawals, leaving users unable to retrieve their LP tokens or any associated funds. The issue manifests when an attacker or any user deliberately makes a deposit of exactly zero liquidity, after which any call to withdraw will revert once the loop reaches that entry. The bug was uncovered during a security audit that examined input validation in the deposit path and the existence check in the withdraw path. It is difficult to spot because a zero value is also the default for unmapped keys, so the code mistakenly conflates an uninitialized entry with a deliberately created empty position. The vulnerability belongs to the class of denial‑of‑service bugs caused by missing lower‑bound checks and improper existence verification. From a user perspective the UI will show a normal balance before the withdraw attempt, but the transaction will revert and the balance will remain unchanged, leading to confusion and the perception that funds have disappeared. The proper fix is to add an explicit check that the deposited liquidity is greater than zero (and optionally to guard the withdrawal loop against zero‑liquidity entries), ensuring that only positions with positive liquidity are recorded and that the existence test correctly distinguishes between absent and intentionally empty positions.
summary: It won’t be possible to withdraw any LP token after doing a deposit of $0$ liquidity, leading to withdrawals being effectively freezed.

title: The `userGaugeProfitIndex` is not set correctly, allowing an attacker to receive rewards without waiting
content: The vulnerability resides in the reward accounting logic of the ProfitManager contract. When a user calls claimGaugeRewards for the first time before any gauge weight has been recorded, the contract checks if the user's gauge weight is zero and returns early without initializing the userGaugeProfitIndex. Because the index remains zero, a later call after the gauge profit index has advanced will treat the zero value as the default initial index (1e18) and compute a positive reward delta, allowing the caller to claim the full accrued rewards without having waited for the profit to mature. The root cause is the missing initialization of userGaugeProfitIndex when _userGaugeWeight is zero, combined with the assumption that a zero index always corresponds to a fresh user. An attacker can exploit the flow by first letting the protocol notify profit for a gauge, then voting for the gauge (incrementGauge) which triggers a first claimGaugeRewards call that returns early, leaving the index at zero. A subsequent claimGaugeRewards call will set the index to the baseline 1e18, compare it with the already increased gaugeProfitIndex, and transfer the difference as rewards. This can be performed in a single transaction, resulting in the attacker receiving matured yield that should belong to legitimate participants. The impact is that the attacker drains the reward pool, causing other users to receive no rewards and potentially causing ERC20 transfer failures due to insufficient balance. The condition occurs only when a user has never held a gauge weight before the first profit notification and calls claimGaugeRewards before voting. The affected parties are any token holders who rely on the profit sharing mechanism, the protocol’s economic model, and the integrity of the reward distribution. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena when testing edge‑case sequences of profit notification and gauge voting. It is subtle because the early‑return path looks harmless and the zero index is later interpreted as a valid baseline, making the bug easy to miss in casual testing. The proper fix is to ensure that whenever claimGaugeRewards is invoked and the stored userGaugeProfitIndex is zero, it is immediately set to the current gaugeProfitIndex before any reward calculation, regardless of the user’s gauge weight. This aligns the contract with the generic class of “uninitialized accounting index” bugs where a missing initialization leads to an inflated reward calculation. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a user who expects to receive a proportional share of profit may see a sudden, unexplained increase in their token balance, while other users see their balances stay at zero or experience transfer reverts. The expectation that rewards accrue only after a waiting period is violated, effectively allowing “funds disappear” for honest participants and “reward theft” for the attacker.

title: The creation of bad debt
content: The vulnerability is a logical accounting error that occurs during the liquidation auction of an under‑collateralised loan. The protocol records the borrower’s outstanding debt in a field called callDebt at the moment the loan is flagged for auction. This value is calculated using the creditMultiplier that was current when the loan was called. However, the creditMultiplier can change later when the system records bad debt and marks down the value of the Credit token. Because callDebt is a static snapshot, any subsequent markdown makes the actual debt (principal adjusted by the new multiplier) larger than the stored callDebt. During the first phase of the auction the contract expects bidders to supply exactly callDebt amount of Credit in exchange for a portion of the collateral. If the updated principal exceeds callDebt, the onBid logic computes a negative profit‑and‑loss (pnl) value and reverts unless the collateral to return to the borrower is zero – a condition that only holds in the second phase when the entire collateral is offered. Consequently, bids can only succeed in the second phase, forcing liquidators to accept the full collateral for a reduced Credit payment and creating additional bad debt for the protocol. The impact is that the protocol may lose value because the debt owed is understated, users see their collateral sold at a discount, and the system’s accounting invariants are broken. The issue manifests whenever a markdown of Credit larger than the accrued interest on existing loans occurs while those loans are already in auction. It affects borrowers (who may lose more collateral than expected), lenders (who receive less repayment), and the protocol’s overall solvency. The flaw was discovered through static analysis of the getLoanDebt and onBid functions and confirmed with a targeted test that simulates a markdown during an active auction. It is hard to notice because the callDebt field appears correct at the time of the call and the auction proceeds normally until the markdown changes the multiplier, at which point only the second phase behaves differently. The bug belongs to the class of snapshot‑state‑stale‑value vulnerabilities where a value is cached and not refreshed after a dependent global parameter changes. To fix the issue the protocol should recompute the debt against the current creditMultiplier at each step of the auction rather than relying on a stored snapshot, or alternatively update callDebt dynamically whenever the multiplier changes, ensuring that the amount of Credit required from bidders always reflects the true outstanding debt.

title: Users staking via the `SurplusGuildMinter` can be immediately slashed when staking into a gauge that had previously incurred a loss
content: The vulnerability concerns the SurplusGuildMinter contract, which allows users to stake Credit tokens into a gauge that tracks profit and loss. When a user stakes through the minter, the contract calls getRewards to determine whether the user should be considered slashed based on the gauge's last recorded loss. The function retrieves the gauge's lastGaugeLoss value and compares it to the lastGaugeLoss field stored in a freshly created memory struct called userStake. Because this struct is newly allocated, all of its fields, including lastGaugeLoss, are initialised to zero. Consequently, if the gauge has ever experienced a loss in its history, the condition lastGaugeLoss > 0 evaluates to true and the slashed flag is set, even though the user has never been exposed to that loss. The contract then proceeds to delete the user's stake, zeroing out the stored credit and guild balances and preventing any future withdrawal. This behaviour is triggered whenever a gauge that previously incurred a loss is re‑onboarded or when a user stakes into any gauge with a non‑zero loss history via SurplusGuildMinter. The impact is that users lose their deposited Credit, receive no guild rewards, and cannot unstake their position, while the protocol’s internal guild buffer is not replenished. From the user’s perspective the UI shows a successful stake transaction followed by an empty balance and missing rewards, contradicting the expectation that the stake should be retained and withdrawable. The issue was discovered during a security audit that exercised staking, loss, off‑boarding, and re‑on‑boarding scenarios, revealing that the slashing logic incorrectly uses an uninitialised struct rather than the persisted user stake data. The bug is hard to notice because the contract does not revert; it silently clears the stake, making the loss appear as a normal state change rather than an error. The root cause is an initialization and logic error in the loss‑detection routine, a classic case of incorrect state handling that leads to false‑positive slashing. The recommended fix is to initialise the userStake.lastGaugeLoss field to the current block timestamp (or the stored value for the user) when a new stake is created, and to compare the gauge's lastGaugeLoss against this stored value instead of against zero. This aligns the behaviour with the GuildToken.incrementGauge logic, ensuring that only users who were present during an actual loss are subject to slashing, and restores the intended accounting guarantees of the protocol.

title: Liquidations can be prevented by frontrunning and liquidating 1 debt
content: The vulnerability originates from an incorrect accounting assumption in the PosManager contract that tracks a position's accrued interest via the field __posBorrInfos[_posId].borrExtraInfos[_pool].totalInterest. The updatePosDebtShares function assumes that converting debt shares to a debt amount with ILendingPool.debtShareToAmtCurrent always yields a non‑decreasing value, because normal borrowing only adds debt over time. However, when a liquidation reduces the outstanding debt, the conversion can produce a smaller amount than before. If an attacker front‑runs a legitimate liquidation by submitting a tiny liquidation call (for example 1 wei of debt) before the intended larger liquidation, the first call removes a small share of debt and updates the stored totalInterest based on the reduced amount. The subsequent liquidation then encounters a mismatch: the shares are now worth less, the totalInterest is stale, and the contract reverts. This allows the attacker to prevent the second liquidation from succeeding, effectively blocking the protocol’s enforcement of health‑factor thresholds. The same effect can be achieved with a partial liquidation that leaves enough interest unaccrued to keep the stored lastDebtAmt higher than the current debt, again causing the invariant to break. From a user perspective, a liquidator sees a transaction revert with no obvious error, while a borrower may notice that an under‑collateralized position remains active, leading to confusion such as “my position should have been liquidated but nothing happened” or “my collateral is still locked after I tried to liquidate”. The impact is that the protocol’s risk management fails: positions that should be closed stay open, lenders’ collateral may become under‑secured, and the accounting of accrued interest becomes inaccurate, potentially causing funds to become stuck or mis‑reported. The issue was discovered during a security audit when a test case reproduced a revert after a front‑run liquidation, highlighting the hidden assumption about monotonic debt growth. It is hard to notice because most normal operation only increases debt, so the edge case of debt reduction during liquidation is rarely exercised. The recommended mitigation is to update the stored totalInterest only when the current debt amount exceeds the previously recorded debt amount, or to recalculate it correctly on each repayment, thereby removing the reliance on a monotonic increase and preserving the invariant even after partial or front‑run liquidations.
summary: Users can avoid being liquidated if they frontrun liquidation calls with a liquidate call with 1 wei. Or, they may do a partial liquidation and avoid being liquidated before the interest reaches the value of the debt pre liquidation. The total interest stored in `__posBorrInfos[_posId].borrExtraInfos[_pool].totalInterest` would also be wrong.

title: wLp tokens could be stolen
content: The vulnerability is a logical access‑control flaw in the removeCollateralWLpTo function of the position manager contract. The function is intended to let a position owner withdraw wrapped LP (wLp) tokens that were supplied as collateral, but it does not verify that the supplied tokenId actually belongs to the position being operated on unless the withdrawal empties the entire wrapped balance (newWLpAmt == 0). Because the ownership check is only performed in the full‑withdrawal branch, an attacker can call the core contract’s decollateralizeWLp or liquidateWLp paths with a tokenId that belongs to a victim’s position while specifying an amount that leaves at least one wLp token behind. The contract then proceeds to harvest any accrued rewards and unwrap the requested amount to the attacker’s address, effectively draining the victim’s LP tokens and associated rewards. This can be triggered whenever a position holds wLp collateral and another user can create a separate position with a minimal dust amount of wLp, then invoke the removal function with the victim’s tokenId and an amount slightly smaller than the victim’s total balance. The impact is the loss of the victim’s underlying LP tokens and any earned rewards, which may appear to the user as a sudden disappearance of balance or a zero‑return on a withdrawal request. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena when testing edge‑case interactions between decollateralizeWLp and the internal bookkeeping of token ownership. It is hard to notice because the transaction does not revert and the contract still reports a successful withdrawal, making the theft look like a normal operation from the UI perspective. Users see their wrapped LP balance reduced unexpectedly, often without any error message, leading to confusion and potential panic. The bug belongs to the class of missing authorization checks or improper state validation, where the contract assumes that the caller’s position implicitly owns the tokenId. The correct mitigation is to add an explicit verification that the position’s collateral mapping contains the tokenId before any amount is transferred, regardless of whether the withdrawal is full or partial. By enforcing this check, the contract would reject attempts to remove collateral that does not belong to the caller, preserving the integrity of the accounting and preventing unauthorized draining of LP assets.

title: `_handleRepay` of `MoneyMarketHook` does not consider the actual debt shares of the `posId` inside the position manager and could lead to a user’s tokens getting stuck inside the hook
content: The MoneyMarketHook contract contains a logic flaw in its internal repayment handling routine. When a user initiates a repay operation, the hook calculates the amount of underlying tokens to pull from the caller by converting the shares supplied in the request to a token amount, but it never checks how many debt shares are actually recorded for the position in the core position manager. If the recorded debt shares are lower than the shares requested – for example because a liquidator has already reduced the position’s debt in a front‑run liquidation – the hook will still transfer the larger token amount from the user to itself. The excess tokens are not forwarded to the lending pool and remain locked inside the hook contract because the subsequent internal repay function only uses the minimum of the requested and actual shares. From the user’s point of view the transaction appears successful, yet the expected reduction in debt is smaller than anticipated and the transferred tokens are missing from the wallet, effectively disappearing into the hook. This situation can occur whenever a repay is performed after the position’s debt has changed without the hook re‑validating the current debt state. The vulnerability was discovered during a manual audit that compared the share‑to‑amount conversion in the hook with the share lookup in the position manager and identified the missing consistency check. The bug is hard to notice because the transaction does not revert; the UI may report a successful repayment while the user’s balance shows an unexplained loss. The issue belongs to the class of accounting‑mismatch or fund‑locking bugs where on‑chain accounting data is not synchronized with external state before token transfers. To remediate, the hook should retrieve the actual debt shares from the position manager, cap the shares to be repaid at that value, and either refund any surplus tokens to the caller or ensure the excess amount is not transferred in the first place. Because the hook is upgradeable, a patched version could also include a rescue function to recover tokens that became stuck.
summary: When users construct repay operations via `MoneyMarketHook`, it doesn’t consider the actual debt shares of the position inside the `InitCore` and `PosManager`. This could lead to users’ tokens getting stuck inside the `MoneyMarketHook` contract.

title: If the borrower enters token blacklist, LP may never be able to retrieve Liquidity
content: The contract allows a borrower to close a position either voluntarily through closePosition() or involuntarily through liquidatePosition(), which both eventually call an internal _closePosition() routine. At the end of the routine the protocol calculates any profit that must be refunded to the borrower and attempts to transfer the owed amount using Base.refundWithCheck, which in turn calls a private refund() function that invokes TransferHelper.safeTransfer. The logic assumes that the token transfer will always succeed, but it does not handle the case where the token is on a blacklist that blocks outgoing transfers. If the borrower’s address is listed on the blacklist for either token0 or token1 (for example USDC), the safeTransfer call reverts. Because the revert is not caught, the entire _closePosition() call reverts, preventing the function from completing. As a result the liquidity that the LP originally supplied remains locked in the contract, the borrower never receives the expected profit, and the protocol cannot liquidate the position to recover funds. This situation can only arise after a borrower opens a position with a non‑blacklisted token and later becomes blacklisted before the position is closed or liquidated, making it a rare but critical edge case. The vulnerability was discovered during a manual audit that examined the refund path and identified the missing error‑handling for blocked token transfers. It is hard to notice because the failure only manifests under the specific condition of a post‑opening blacklist entry, and the revert looks like a generic transaction failure rather than a systematic liquidity‑locking bug. To remediate the issue the contract should not rely on a direct transfer succeeding; instead it should catch transfer failures (e.g., using try/catch) and record the owed amount in a claim mapping that borrowers can withdraw later, or adjust the tokenOwed accounting for LPs. Additionally, the recipient of refunds should be fixed to the borrower to avoid bypassing blacklist checks, and alternative safe‑transfer mechanisms should be considered. Implementing a claim‑based fallback restores the ability of LPs to eventually retrieve their liquidity and prevents permanent loss of funds due to blacklist‑induced reverts.

title: openPosition
content: The vulnerability originates from the way the contract records fee growth information when a leveraged position is opened. When openPosition is called, the function Base.prepareLeverage reads feeGrowthInside0LastX128 and feeGrowthInside1LastX128 directly from the Uniswap position manager (UNI_POSITION_MANAGER.positions). However, these fee‑growth values are only updated when the position manager executes a state‑changing operation such as increaseLiquidity, decreaseLiquidity or collect. If no such operation is performed after a swap that generates fees, the values returned by positions() remain stale. Consequently the contract stores an outdated fee‑growth snapshot in the lien record. When the borrower later closes the position, Base.getOwedFee computes the fee owed by taking the difference between the current pool fee growth and the stale snapshot. Because the snapshot is lower than the actual fee growth, the calculated difference is larger than it should be, causing the borrower to pay extra fees to the liquidity provider. The bug manifests only when a position is opened after a swap that changes the pool’s fee growth but before any collect call that would synchronize the fee‑growth fields. Users see a discrepancy between the fees they expect to owe and the higher amount actually deducted; the protocol’s accounting assumptions that fees are calculated from the latest growth values are violated, leading to funds disappearing from the borrower’s perspective. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by writing a test that logged the fee‑growth values before and after a swap and after a collect call, showing that the values do not change after the swap until collect is invoked. The problem is subtle because the fee‑growth numbers are large and the difference may be small relative to total fees, making it hard to notice in UI balances. The vulnerability belongs to the class of stale‑state or race‑condition bugs where a contract reads outdated on‑chain data for financial calculations. To remediate, the contract should ensure that the latest fee‑growth values are fetched by invoking a synchronising function such as LiquidityPosition.collectLiquidity (or any other call that updates the position manager) before calling Base.prepareLeverage, thereby guaranteeing that the stored snapshot reflects the current pool state and that fee calculations are accurate.

title: liquidatePosition
content: The vulnerability resides in the liquidation routine of the Particle protocol where the function liquidatePosition ultimately forwards an arbitrary calldata blob (params.data) to the Base.swap implementation. The protocol assumes that the caller will provide a well‑formed swap description, but it never validates the contents of the data field. Because the swap is performed through a generic DEX aggregator (e.g., 1inch or Uniswap V3 router) the liquidator can craft a custom swap that routes through a malicious pool containing a fake ERC20 token. The fake token implements a transfer callback that, during the swap, re‑enters the liquidation flow and supplies just enough amountReceived to satisfy the repayment check, while the remaining swapped value stays with the liquidator. In practice the attacker creates a fake pool where token0 is the malicious ERC20 and token1 is WETH, supplies the full collateral plus any premium as the swap amount, and encodes a call to the router that swaps this amount for the fake token. When the fake token’s transfer is executed, it triggers a secondary transfer of the required repayment amount back to the ParticlePositionManager, allowing the liquidation to succeed. The excess value (collateral + premium − repayment) is retained by the attacker, effectively stealing profit from the borrower. This can be executed whenever a loan has expired and the RenewalCutoffTime flag is set, because any address is permitted to call liquidatePosition. The affected parties are borrowers who expect to receive their full collateral after liquidation, lenders who rely on correct debt settlement, and the protocol itself which may incur unexpected bad‑debt or loss of funds. The issue was discovered during a security audit when the auditors constructed a proof‑of‑concept using a fake ERC20 and a fake Uniswap V3 pool to demonstrate profit extraction. The problem is subtle because the swap call appears legitimate and the protocol only checks that the amountReceived meets a minimum threshold; it does not verify that the swap path or token contracts are trustworthy. From a user’s perspective the borrower sees a reduced balance after liquidation – the expected collateral is partially missing, and the protocol’s accounting no longer matches the original loan terms. This class of bug can be described as an “unrestricted external call with unchecked calldata leading to profit‑stealing via malicious token callbacks”. To remediate the issue the protocol should eliminate the arbitrary data parameter from the liquidation path, enforce that the swap uses only known token pairs and a fixed amount, whitelist a single trusted router (e.g., Uniswap’s SwapRouter) or perform the swap internally, and add strict validation of slippage and return amounts. By removing the ability for a liquidator to supply custom calldata, the protocol prevents re‑entrancy through malicious token callbacks and ensures that liquidation proceeds only with the intended asset exchange, preserving borrower funds and protocol integrity.
summary:
When the Loan expires, and `RenewalCutoffTime` has been set, anyone can execute the liquidation method `liquidatePosition()`.  
Execution path: `liquidatePosition()` -> `_closePosition()` -> `Base.swap(params.data)`

The problem is that this `params.data` can be arbitrarily constructed by the liquidator. As long as there is enough `amountReceived` after the exchange for repayment, it will not `revert`.

In this way, you can maliciously construct `data` and steal the extra profit of the liquidator. (At least `amountReceived` must be guaranteed)

Assume:

collateral + tokenPremium = 120  
repay minimum `amountReceived` only need 100 to swap  
so borrower Profit 120 - 100 = 20

1. create fakeErc20 and fakePool (token0 = fakeErc20,token1 = WETH)
2. execute liquidatePosition():pool = fakePool , swapAmount = 120 (all collateral + tokenPremium)
3. in fakeErc20.transfer() reentry execute reply 100 equivalent `amountReceived` (transfer to ParticlePositionManager)
4. liquidatePosition() success , steal 120 - 100 = 20

title: Underflow could happened when calculating Uniswap V3 position’s fee growth and can cause operations to revert
content: The vulnerability is an arithmetic underflow in the calculation of a Uniswap V3 position’s fee growth inside a range. The contract reproduces the logic from Uniswap’s PositionValue library, which originally relied on unchecked subtraction of 256‑bit unsigned integers. In Solidity versions 0.8 and later, arithmetic operations are checked by default and will revert when an underflow occurs. The function getFeeGrowthInside subtracts the fee growth recorded outside the lower and upper ticks from each other or from the global fee growth, depending on the current tick position. When the current tick lies outside the position’s range, the subtraction can produce a negative result in unsigned arithmetic, triggering an underflow. Because the code does not use an unchecked block, the EVM throws an exception and the whole transaction reverts. This behaviour manifests during any operation that queries fee growth, such as liquidation, reclaiming liquidity, or fee collection. From a user’s perspective the expected outcome – for example a liquidation that repays a debt and returns collateral – fails silently; the transaction reverts and the UI may show an error like “insufficient repay” or simply no action taken, leaving the user’s funds locked or unclaimed. The impact is high because critical protocol functions become unreliable, especially for pools with low fee tiers where the fee‑growth values are small and the subtraction more likely to underflow. The issue was discovered during a security audit that referenced a known Uniswap core issue (issue #573) and was reproduced with a test that forces the underflow condition. It is hard to notice because the underflow only occurs for specific tick configurations that may not be exercised in normal testing, and the revert message does not directly point to an arithmetic problem. The proper mitigation is to wrap the fee‑growth calculations in an unchecked block, allowing the subtraction to wrap around modulo 2^256 as intended by the original Uniswap implementation. This restores the expected accounting behaviour, prevents unexpected reverts, and ensures that fee‑related operations such as liquidation, fee collection, and liquidity reclamation function correctly.
summary: When operations need to calculate Uniswap V3 position’s fee growth, it used similar function implemented by [uniswap v3](https://github.com/Uniswap/v3-periphery/blob/main/contracts/libraries/PositionValue.sol#L145-L166). However, according to this known issue : <https://github.com/Uniswap/v3-core/issues/573>. The contract is implicitly relies on underflow/overflow when calculating the fee growth, if underflow is prevented, some operations that rely on fee growth will revert.

title: Incorrect amounts of ETH are transferred to the DAO treasury in `ERC20TokenEmitter::buyToken`
content: The vulnerability resides in the ERC20TokenEmitter contract’s buyToken function, where the ETH allocated for creators is split into a direct payment and a portion intended to purchase governance tokens. While the direct payment is correctly forwarded to the creators address, the remaining creator share – the amount that should be used to mint governance tokens – is never transferred to the DAO treasury. Instead, this ETH stays locked inside the ERC20TokenEmitter contract. The root cause is an omission in the transfer logic: only the buyer’s share (toPayTreasury) is sent to the treasury, and the creators’ token‑purchase share (creatorsEthAfterDirectPayment) is omitted from the call to treasury.call. An attacker does not need to perform any special steps; any call to buyToken with non‑zero creatorRateBps and entropyRateBps automatically triggers the leak, because the function calculates a creator portion, sends the direct payment, but fails to move the residual ETH to the treasury. The impact is a systematic reduction of treasury funds – each token purchase leaves a chunk of ETH stranded in the emitter contract, decreasing the protocol’s available capital and breaking the accounting assumption that all ETH used to mint governance tokens ends up in the treasury. From a user’s perspective, the symptoms are that after a purchase the DAO treasury balance is lower than expected while the emitter contract holds a non‑zero ETH balance; buyers receive the correct amount of tokens, creators receive their direct payment, but the protocol’s accounting shows missing funds. The issue was discovered during a security audit and confirmed with a unit test that measured balances before and after a purchase, revealing the value leak. It can be hard to notice because the contract still holds the ETH, so no explicit loss is visible on the external transaction trace, and the token minting proceeds normally. The bug belongs to the class of “incorrect fund allocation” or “partial transfer omission” bugs, where a calculated share of value is never forwarded to its intended recipient. To remediate, the transfer to the treasury should be amended to include both the buyer’s share and the creators’ token‑purchase share, i.e., treasury.call{value: toPayTreasury + creatorsEthAfterDirectPayment}(). This ensures that all ETH used for token issuance is accounted for in the treasury, restoring the intended financial flow and eliminating the leak.

title: `ArtPiece.totalVotesSupply` and `ArtPiece.quorumVotes` are incorrectly calculated due to inclusion of the inaccessible voting powers of the NFT that is being auctioned at the moment when an art piece is created
content: The vulnerability consists of an incorrect calculation of the total voting power and the quorum threshold for each art piece when it is created. The contract determines the total vote supply by adding the ERC20 token supply to the weighted ERC721 token supply. However, the calculation does not exclude the ERC721 token that is simultaneously transferred to the AuctionHouse contract for the piece that is being auctioned. Because the AuctionHouse contract cannot vote and the future buyer of the NFT is only granted voting rights from the block at which the art piece was created, the voting power attached to that NFT is permanently inaccessible for the newly created piece. As a result, the stored totalVotesSupply value includes voting weight that no participant can actually exercise, and the quorumVotes value, which is derived from totalVotesSupply, is inflated. When the community casts votes, the observable vote count may appear sufficient, but the protocol still rejects the piece because the reachable voting power is lower than the recorded quorum requirement. This mismatch makes it harder or even impossible for an art piece to satisfy the quorum, causing auctions to stall and potentially locking funds that would otherwise be released. The issue occurs each time a new NFT is minted and immediately placed in the AuctionHouse at the moment of piece creation. It affects all participants who rely on the voting mechanism – artists, voters, and anyone with funds locked in the auction process. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that examined the logic of vote weight calculation and identified that the totalSupply of the ERC721 token was used without filtering out tokens held by the auction contract. The bug is subtle because the totalSupply function returns a correct numeric value, and the UI may display a quorum percentage that seems achievable, masking the fact that part of the supply is unusable. To remediate the issue, the contract should compute the vote weight by subtracting the balance of the ERC721 token held by the AuctionHouse (or otherwise exclude any tokens that cannot vote at the creation block) before applying the weight multiplier and deriving the quorum. This adjustment restores the alignment between the recorded quorum and the actually available voting power, ensuring that the protocol’s business logic for reaching quorum and triggering auctions functions as intended.

title: `VerbsToken.tokenURI`
content: An unsanitized JSON injection vulnerability exists in the function that creates an art piece metadata. The contract stores the raw strings supplied for the image and animationUrl fields and later builds the token metadata by concatenating those strings into a JSON object that is base64‑encoded and returned by tokenURI. Because the contract does not escape characters such as quotation marks, commas or colons, an attacker can embed additional JSON fragments in the image or animationUrl value. When the tokenURI is decoded by a front‑end application, the injected fragment overwrites the original image field, causing the NFT to display a different picture or animation than the one that was voted on. If the front end parses the tokenURI with a vulnerable method such as eval, the injected payload can even execute arbitrary JavaScript, potentially stealing funds from the user’s wallet. The bug is triggered during the createPiece call, which accepts any string for the metadata fields, and manifests after the voting period when the token is minted and tokenURI is queried. All participants who rely on the displayed artwork are affected: collectors receive NFTs with unexpected content, the protocol may be exposed to legal liability for hosting illicit images, and users may be tricked into signing malicious scripts. The issue was discovered during a security audit that included a proof‑of‑concept test where the animationUrl field contained a string that injected a new image entry, resulting in the tokenURI returning a JSON object with the fake image link. The problem is subtle because the metadata is base64‑encoded, so a casual inspection of the on‑chain data does not reveal the injection, and the contract itself does not perform any validation. The vulnerability belongs to the class of JSON injection and improper input sanitisation. The recommended mitigation is to treat all user‑controlled fields as untrusted, escape or strip dangerous characters, or use a proper JSON encoder instead of manual string concatenation, thereby guaranteeing that the generated token metadata cannot be altered by crafted input.
summary:
`CultureIndex.createPiece()` function doesn’t sanitize malicious charcacters in `metadata.image` and `metadata.animationUrl`, which would cause `VerbsToken.tokenURI()` suffering various JSON injection attack vectors.

  1. If the front end APP doesn’t process the JSON string properly, such as using `eval()` to parse token URI, then any malicious code can be executed in the front end. Obviously, funds in users’ connected wallet, such as Metamask, might be stolen in this case.
  2. Even while the front end processes securely, such as using the standard builtin `JSON.parse()` to read URI. Adversary can still exploit this vulnerability to replace art piece image/animation with arbitrary other ones after voting stage completed.

That is the final metadata used by the NFT (VerbsToken) is not the art piece users vote. This attack could be benefit to attackers, such as creating NFTs containing same art piece data with existing high price NFTs. And this attack could also make the project sufferring legal risks, such as creating NFTs with violence or pornography images.

More reference: <https://www.comparitech.com/net-admin/json-injection-guide/>

title: Malicious delegatees can block delegators from redelegating and from sending their NFTs
content: The vulnerability is a delegation‑locking flaw in the ERC‑721 based voting contract of the Revolution protocol. When a token holder (delegator) calls the delegate function, the contract records the delegate address and also updates an internal lock that prevents further changes to the delegation state. The contract does not forbid delegating to the zero address (address(0)). By delegating to a malicious address, the attacker can subsequently call delegate(address(0)) on its own account. Because the contract treats a delegation to address(0) as a final state rather than an “undelegate” operation, the internal lock is set to a value that blocks any later attempts by the original delegator to change its delegate or to transfer the underlying NFTs. As a result, the delegator’s voting power remains attached to the attacker forever and the delegator’s NFTs become non‑transferable; attempts to call delegate or transferFrom revert. This can be triggered whenever a user delegates votes to any address that is under the attacker’s control, and the attacker subsequently self‑delegates to address(0). The affected parties are any token holder who uses delegation, as well as the protocol’s governance process because votes can be permanently captured. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit; a reproducible test case shows that after delegation the victim loses the ability to redelegate and to move any of his NFTs, effectively freezing his assets. The bug is subtle because delegating to address(0) is often interpreted as “clear delegation”, yet the contract’s logic mistakenly treats it as a terminal state that also disables transfer checks. The flaw belongs to the class of “delegation‑locking” or “immutable delegation” bugs where a state transition makes future state changes impossible. To remediate, the contract should reject delegations to address(0) or, alternatively, implement explicit “undelegate” logic that does not set an immutable lock, and ensure that token transfer functions do not depend on the delegate’s current address. By preventing the zero‑address delegation, the protocol restores the ability of users to redelegate and to transfer their NFTs, eliminating the risk of permanent asset freeze.
summary: If user `X` delegates his votes to `Y`, `Y` can block `X` from redelegating and even from sending his NFT anywhere, forever.

title: GMXFuturesPoolHedger's _increasePosition can
content: The vulnerability resides in the pool hedger’s internal _increasePosition routine, which adds margin to an existing futures position without verifying that the collateral actually received from the LiquidityPool is sufficient to keep the resulting leverage within safe bounds. The function requests a certain amount of quote collateral, calls liquidityPool.transferQuoteToHedge, and only checks that the returned amount is non‑zero; any positive amount, even a dust amount, is accepted. Because the code never compares the received collateral against the size increase, a situation can arise where the position is enlarged with far too little margin, pushing the leverage close to or beyond the liquidation threshold. When market prices move, such an over‑leveraged position can be liquidated automatically, causing the hedging position to disappear while the underlying option exposure remains. From a user perspective the contract may appear to have opened a larger position, but later the hedge is lost, balances drop to zero, and the protocol may suffer massive losses or even insolvency as the net position becomes effectively naked. The flaw is triggered during normal workflow whenever the LiquidityPool has limited free liquidity, so the transfer returns less than requested but still greater than zero. It is hard to notice because the contract does not emit a warning for low collateral and the UI may simply show a successful position increase, while the hidden leverage metric is dangerously high. The issue was identified during a security audit that examined the hedger’s margin handling logic. To remediate, the contract should compute the prospective leverage after receiving collateral and reject the increase if the leverage would exceed a predefined maximum (for example the market’s maxLeverage setting). Alternatively, it could require manual collateral top‑up when the received amount is insufficient, ensuring that the hedge never operates with an unsafe leverage ratio.

title: updateCollateral can be used to modify the to-
content: updateCollateral function allows a user to request an increase of quote collateral that is transferred to the GMXFuturesPoolHedger. The liquidity pool tracks the amount of quote used as collateral with a variable called usedDeltaLiquidity, which is consulted by the internal _getTotalPoolValueQuote routine to compute the pool's total quote value. When a collateral increase request is pending, the transferred quote is already moved out of the pool but usedDeltaLiquidity is not incremented until the request is settled. Consequently, during the pending window the pool's accounting believes that more quote is still available than actually is, inflating the reported total pool value. An attacker can exploit this timing gap by calling updateCollateral and, before the pending request resolves, depositing liquidity or minting LP shares based on the overstated pool value. The attacker receives a larger share of the pool than their contribution warrants, effectively creating shares out of thin air and diluting honest participants. The impact is a loss of economic value for legitimate LPs, potential fund misallocation, and a breach of the protocol's accounting invariants. The condition occurs whenever a collateral update is in flight, i.e., after the request is submitted to the GMX position router but before the callback updates usedDeltaLiquidity. The vulnerability was discovered during a manual audit when the reviewer noticed that the variable tracking used liquidity was never adjusted for pending transfers. Because the discrepancy exists only for a short, asynchronous period, it may not be visible in normal operation and can be missed without careful state‑transition analysis. The proper fix is to include the pending delta amount in the total pool value calculation, for example by adding a pendingDeltaLiquidity term to the value returned by _getTotalPoolValueQuote or by updating usedDeltaLiquidity immediately when the transfer is initiated. This change ensures that the pool's accounting reflects the true amount of quote locked as collateral at all times, preventing the creation of excess LP shares and preserving the integrity of the protocol's financial logic.
summary:
When calling updateCollateral, a request is submitted to Gmx position router, and
some quote amount is transferred either in or out of the liquidity pool to the
GMXFuturesPoolHedger.
In LiquidityPool.sol: _getTotalPoolValueQuote uses the variable usedDeltaLiquidity
to track available quote amounts used on GMX as collateral.
The variable usedDeltaLiquidity will not be increased during the period in which
the request for increase is pending, but the quote will be sent to
GMXFuturesPoolHedger. A malicious user can call updateCollateral before
depositing into the LP, getting more shares.

title: hedgeDelta() calculates collateralDelta inac-
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect calculation of the collateral delta inside the hedgeDelta routine of the GMXFuturesPoolHedger contract. When a hedge position incurs a negative unrealised profit‑and‑loss (PNL), the routine derives a collateralDelta value from the GMX Vault without adjusting for the loss. As a result the contract attempts to reduce the position’s collateral by an amount that is larger than the actual collateral remaining after accounting for the negative PNL. This mismatch triggers a revert in the Vault’s _reduceCollateral function, causing hedgeDelta calls to fail permanently for that position. The root cause is a logical error in the accounting logic: the code assumes that the collateralDelta can be applied directly, ignoring that a negative PNL effectively reduces the usable collateral. Exploitation occurs when market movements create a sufficiently large adverse price change – for example a long position that experiences a sharp price drop – which makes the unrealised PNL negative enough that the computed collateralDelta exceeds the adjusted collateral. An attacker does not need to interact directly with the contract; simply causing or waiting for a large price swing can push the system into this state. When the failure happens, any attempt to hedge the position reverts with a message indicating that the contract cannot subtract the collateralDelta, and the UI may show a generic “hedge failed” or “transaction reverted” error. From the user’s perspective the expected outcome – a new hedge that reduces exposure – never materialises; balances appear unchanged, and the position remains exposed to further market risk. Liquidity providers and protocol participants are affected because the hedging mechanism, which is supposed to protect LP capital, becomes inoperable, potentially leading to amplified financial losses. The issue was discovered during integration testing (IntegrationTestsGMX.ts) when adjusting the price change from 1300 to 1200 caused the test to hit the failure path at Vault.sol line 1039. It is hard to notice in normal operation because the bug only manifests under extreme price moves that generate a large negative PNL, a scenario that may not be exercised in routine tests. The bug belongs to the class of arithmetic/accounting mismatches where delta calculations do not correctly incorporate loss adjustments, leading to under‑flows or reverts. To remediate, the collateralDelta computation must be modified to factor in the negative PNL, applying the same adjustment logic used by GMX Vault’s _reduceCollateral method so that the collateral is never reduced below the amount actually available after accounting for losses. This conceptual fix restores the integrity of the hedging process and aligns the contract’s accounting with the protocol’s financial safety assumptions.
summary:
GMXFuturesPoolHedger does not calculate the collateralDelta correctly when the
hedge position has a negative PNL. A price change in either direction that creates a
big enough collateralDelta could create a scenario where the system can not be
hedged anymore, and calls to hedgeDelta() will always fail.
The scenario can be reproduced by setting the price change in the if spot price
decreases, hedger needs to long less test case to 1200 instead of 1300 in
IntegrationTestsGMX.ts on line 553. The following output below contains the
position when the price is updated and hedgeDelta() is called, as well as relevant
output from GMX Vault when position execution calls decreasePosition() and
subsequently _reduceCollateral() where the call fails at Vault.sol#L1039.

pos.collateral 13512
pos.averagePrice 1614
pos.entryFundingRate 0
pos.unrealisedPnl -3738
pos.isLong true
-- Call Vault.decreasePosition ---

--- Reducing position.collateral ---
