The system can not hedge its position anymore if the negative PNL is too big in
proportion to its size. This could lead to increased financial losses for Lyra LPs.

title: processWithdrawalQueue can permanently fail
content: The contract implements a two‑step withdrawal mechanism where a user first initiates a withdrawal request and, after a mandatory delay, calls processWithdrawalQueue() to receive the quoted asset. The queue is processed strictly in chronological order; each entry is handled one after another without the ability to address a specific request by identifier. The internal helper _transferQuote() converts the internal amount to the quote asset’s decimals and then calls quoteAsset.transfer(to,amount). If the transfer returns false, the function reverts with QuoteTransferFailed. Because processWithdrawalQueue() does not catch this revert, a single failing transfer aborts the entire processing loop, leaving the queue halted at the offending entry. This situation can arise when a user who holds LP tokens is blacklisted by the quote asset (USDC) and attempts to withdraw; the blacklist causes the token transfer to fail, triggering the revert. Consequently, every withdrawal that was queued after the blocked entry remains unprocessed, effectively locking the funds of all subsequent users. From a user’s perspective the UI will show a pending withdrawal that never resolves, the expected balance does not change, and the user receives no funds despite having waited the required delay. The vulnerability was identified during a manual audit that examined the withdrawal flow and noticed the lack of error handling around the token transfer. It is difficult to detect in normal operation because only withdrawals involving a blacklisted address fail, which may be a rare or hidden condition. The issue belongs to the class of queue‑stalling denial‑of‑service bugs where an unhandled exception in a sequential processor prevents progress for later items. To remediate, the contract should wrap the transfer call in a try/catch (or check the boolean return) and, on failure, skip the problematic withdrawal, optionally removing it from the queue or marking it as failed, so that subsequent withdrawals can continue. This change restores the intended guarantee that a single faulty request does not freeze the entire liquidity pool.
summary:
Withdrawals are made in a two-step process. First, a user starts the withdrawal,
and if the initial validation succeeds, the withdrawal is added to queuedWithdrawals.
After a withdrawal delay, a user can call processWithdrawalQueue(). This function
does not allow a user to process the withdrawal based on an id but processes
withdrawals in chronological order. When a user wants to withdraw funds, all other
withdrawals that were initiated before need to be processed first. This can be
problematic if one of the withdrawals fails for an unforeseen reason because then,
the withdrawal queue is stuck, and no other withdrawals after the failing one can
take place. Such a scenario could occur when a user with LP tokens gets
blacklisted and initiates a withdrawal. USDC is planned to be the quote asset, and
it has a blacklist function that has been used in the past for various reasons.
_transferQuote() is called when a withdrawal is processed as part of
processWithdrawalQueue(). It attempts a token transfer and expects it to succeed in
line 1060. It has no mechanism to handle a failing transfer and skip the queue.
The withdrawal queue could become permanently stuck, and users will not be able
to withdraw their funds anymore from the LiquidityPool contract.
sol#L428
```solidity
function _transferQuote(address to, uint amount) internal {
    amount = ConvertDecimals.convertFrom18(amount, quoteAsset.decimals());
    if (amount > 0) {
        if (!quoteAsset.transfer(to, amount)) {
            revert QuoteTransferFailed(address(this), address(this), to, amount);
        }
    }
}
```
sol#L1057-L1064

title: Multiple update position requests can be cre-
content: The vulnerability resides in the updateCollateral() function that is responsible for adjusting positions on the GMX PositionRouter to match the target leverage of a liquidity pool. The function does not verify whether a pending order already exists before it creates a new update‑position request or before it calls the internal _closeSecondPosition() helper. As a result, when two positions are open simultaneously, an attacker can invoke updateCollateral() repeatedly, causing each call to overwrite the stored pendingOrderKey. Overwriting the key makes previously created pending orders impossible to cancel with cancelPendingOrder() and allows many pending orders to accumulate on the PositionRouter. This situation can unbalance the hedging position, push the exposure beyond the intended leverage range and eventually trigger liquidation of the pool’s collateral. The issue appears only when the contract holds more than one open position and the caller repeatedly triggers the function; under normal single‑position operation the missing check is not exercised. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that examined the control flow of updateCollateral() and noticed that the only leverage check occurs in _getCurrentLeverage() on line 305, while no guard exists for pending orders. Because the contract silently overwrites the pendingOrderKey without emitting an error, the problem can be hard to notice until a liquidation event occurs. From a user perspective the symptoms are unexpected pool liquidation, loss of funds, or a situation where a user attempts to cancel a pending order and receives no response, leading to a perception that “my refund or hedge disappeared”. The root cause is a missing pending‑order existence check, which is a classic example of a race‑condition or state‑clobbering bug in state‑ful contract logic. The recommended remediation is to add a guard that verifies no pending order is active before any new request is issued, especially before calling _closeSecondPosition(), and to ensure that only one pending order can exist at any time. This aligns the contract’s behavior with the intended business logic that each leverage adjustment should be processed sequentially and cancellable.

title: H-01 wstETH-ETH Curve LP Token Price can
content: The vulnerability is a view‑only reentrancy flaw that allows an attacker to manipulate the virtual_price of the wstETH‑ETH Curve liquidity‑provider (LP) token. The LP token’s value is derived from a contract‑internal variable called virtual_price, which the RiskEngine reads to assess the collateral value of accounts that use the LP token as security. The root cause is that the pool’s remove_liquidity function sends ETH to the caller before it updates its internal accounting of wstETH balances. Because the external call to the RiskEngine can be triggered during this window, a malicious contract can re‑enter the RiskEngine while the pool’s state is partially updated. By supplying a large amount of ETH (for example via a flash‑loan or by impersonating the GMX Vault) the attacker can artificially depress the virtual_price, causing the RiskEngine to believe that the collateral value has dropped dramatically. The engine then flags the position as under‑collateralised and initiates a liquidation. From the user’s perspective the symptom is an unexpected liquidation: the user sees their LP token balance unchanged, receives no refund, and their account is marked as liquidated even though the on‑chain accounting of their deposited assets appears correct. The impact is that any account that relies on the wstETH‑ETH LP token as collateral can be forced into liquidation with a relatively small cost – roughly 60 basis points of the ETH used to manipulate the price, which translates to about $90 k for a 14.5 k ETH attack that can suppress the virtual_price by more than 10 %. The condition for exploitation is that the attacker can call remove_liquidity and, in the same transaction, invoke the RiskEngine before the pool finishes updating its internal balances. This scenario was discovered during a security audit that included manual testing of re‑entrancy vectors and simulation of infinite‑borrow attacks. The bug is hard to notice because the virtual_price is not exposed to an external oracle; it is a derived value that can change silently during internal operations, and the pool does not emit explicit warnings when the price is being artificially lowered. To remediate the issue the protocol should either protect the virtual_price with a trusted price feed such as a Chainlink oracle or a time‑weighted average price (TWAP), and/or redesign the remove_liquidity function to follow the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern, updating all internal balances before making any external calls, and adding a non‑reentrant guard around the RiskEngine invocation. In short, the flaw is a re‑entrancy‑based price manipulation that breaks the accounting assumptions of the liquidation engine, allowing unfair liquidations and loss of user funds.
summary: The wstETH-ETH LP token is priced via it's virtual_price. Through what Chainalysis called View only Reentrancy, we can reduce the value of virtual_price, causing the RiskEngine to trigger a liquidation event. Per some testing I made, we know that the Debt for such an account will be denominated WETH, this price cannot be tampered. However, the price of the ETH-wstETH LP Token can be manipulated by calling the RiskEngine while reEntering from the POOL.remove_liquidity function. This is possible because the function will send ETH first, before updating it's internal wstETH balances. To test the maximum impact I simulated borrowing an infinite amount of WETH (by impersonating the GMX Vault). If that amount of ETH were available on Arbitrum, we can achieve over 10x in price suppression, effectively making any "normal" account instantly liquidatable. The estimated cost of the attack is 60 BPS of the total ETH used (due to price impact). Because of the price manipulation, we can trigger unfair liquidations to our advantage, because the cost of manipulation is in the 50BPS range, any time a big enough deposit is made, it becomes profitable to force liquidate them. In the theoretical scenario shown below (borrowing from GMX Vault), I can effectively liquidate any account using the token. A more pragmatic scenario is listed below as well

title: Non terminal tokens received via Balancer batchSwap()
content: The vulnerability originates from Balancer's batchSwap function, which can return multiple token amounts in a single transaction. When a user constructs a multi‑step swap that yields intermediate tokens not already present in the protocol's registered asset list, those tokens are transferred to the user's external address but are never added to the internal accounting structures used by the RiskEngine. The RiskEngine calculates a user's collateral by iterating only over the assets recorded in the account's asset list; any token that arrives outside this list is ignored, causing the protocol to perceive a lower collateral balance than the user actually holds. This discrepancy can be exploited by crafting a batchSwap where the user receives a non‑terminal token (for example, USDC) as an intermediate output while only the terminal token (such as WETH) is registered. The user sees the expected token in their wallet, but the protocol’s balance view omits the intermediate token, potentially triggering a premature liquidation event. The impact is that users may be liquidated despite having sufficient overall value, leading to loss of funds and undermining confidence in the protocol’s risk management. The issue occurs whenever batchSwap is invoked with steps that produce token outputs not previously listed in the account’s assets, especially when using the “max amount” mode that automatically forwards any surplus to the user. It affects any participant who relies on batchSwap for complex swaps, the protocol’s risk engine, and downstream liquidators. The bug was discovered during a security audit through a targeted Foundry test that demonstrated the mismatch between transferred tokens and internal balances. It is subtle because the transferred tokens appear in the user’s wallet, so the UI may show the correct holdings, while the protocol’s internal state remains out‑of‑sync, making the problem hard to notice without deep inspection of the accounting logic. To remediate, the contract should ensure that all tokens received from batchSwap are reflected in the account’s asset list, for example by invoking Balancer’s canBatchSwap static call to obtain the assetDeltas array and updating the tokensIn and tokensOut sets accordingly. This class of bug is an accounting‑registration mismatch where external token transfers are not synchronized with internal collateral accounting, violating the fundamental assumption that a user’s on‑chain balance equals the protocol’s recorded balance.
summary:
Balancer's batchSwap() function is able to return multiple tokens along the token in the swap. The result is that other tokens received from a user's trade will not be registered with the protocol or included in their account. Balancer's batchSwap() functionality takes in an array of BatchSwapSteps, each of which dictates a pool to use for the swap, assets to swap to and from, an amount, and some additional user data (which is currently unused by Balancer). For users who would like all their funds to move from step to step (swapping all of their input token from their first step, for the maximum amount of the output token steps after the first, and it will automatically use the maximum amount. Alternatively, users are able to provide their own amounts in each step. Any amount returned from a step that is not used for the next step is sent to user. Here is a simple example:
• Step 1: Trade 400 BAL for max WETH (returns ~1.7)
• Step 2: Trade 1 WETH for max USDC (returns ~1575)
• Result: 400 BAL is inputted, and both 0.7 WETH and 1575 USDC are returned
Here is a gist with a standalone Foundry test that can be run to show this behavior. In this case, USDC) would be returned in the tokensIn[] array. While the user's WETH would be transferred to account, it would not be registered with the protocol to count in the account balance or interact with. If a user uses Balancer's batchSwap() functionality with returned intermediate tokens that are not in the account's asset list already, the user may get liquidated sooner than expected as RiskEngine.sol:_getBalance() only counts in the assets in the assets list.

title: Precision differences when calculating user-
content: The vulnerability is a precision‑scale mismatch in the calculation of the user collateral ratio (userCollateralRatioMantissa) performed during borrowing and liquidation. The contract divides the raw debt amount, expressed in the loan token’s native decimal precision, by the raw collateral balance, expressed in the collateral token’s native precision, without first normalising both values to a common scale. Because Solidity integer division truncates toward zero, when the two tokens have very different numbers of decimals – for example a 6‑decimal stablecoin such as USDC paired with an 18‑decimal meme token such as SHIB – the numerator (debt * 10^18) can be many orders of magnitude smaller than the denominator (collateral amount), causing the division to evaluate to zero. This results in the protocol reporting a collateral ratio of 0 % even though the user holds a healthy amount of collateral. The bug can be exploited by simply opening a position with a high‑precision collateral and a low‑precision debt; any attempt to liquidate that position will fail because the protocol’s invariant that every under‑collateralised loan is liquidatable is broken. Consequently, debt may remain forever outstanding, collateral may become effectively locked, and the protocol’s risk model collapses. The issue manifests whenever a borrower uses a token pair whose decimal precisions differ significantly, which includes many real‑world pairs (e.g., USDC/SHIB, USDT/APE). Users see their collateral ratio displayed as zero, receive error messages when trying to trigger liquidation, and may notice that their position cannot be closed despite being under‑collateralised. The problem was discovered during a manual audit of the borrow and liquidate functions, where the auditor observed that the ratio calculation used raw token values and that integer division could truncate to zero for certain token pairs. It is hard to notice because most common token pairs have similar precisions, so the bug only appears with extreme precision differences, which are less frequently tested. The proper fix is to normalise both debt and collateral amounts to a common 18‑decimal precision before performing the division, ensuring that the ratio reflects the true economic relationship regardless of token decimals. This class of bug is known as a precision‑loss or scaling‑mismatch error, common in financial smart contracts that handle assets with heterogeneous decimal places. It violates the business logic that collateral must always be sufficient to cover debt and that liquidations must be possible, leading to funds disappearing from the protocol’s risk‑management perspective.
summary:
When calculating userCollateralRatioMantissa in borrow and liquidate. It divides the raw debt value (in loan token precision) by the raw collateral balance (in collateral precision). This skew is fine for a majority of tokens but will cause issues with specific token pairs, including being unable to liquidate a subset of positions no matter what. /Pool.sol#L474
When calculating userCollateralRatioMantissa, both debt value and collateral values are left in the native precision. As a result of this certain token pairs will be completely broken because of this. Other pairs will only be partially broken and can enter state in which it's impossible to liquidate positions. Imagine a token pair like USDC and SHIB. USDC has a token precision of 6 and SHIB has 18. If the user has a collateral balance of 100,001 SHIB (100,001e18) and a loan borrow of 1 USDC (1e6) then their userCollateralRatioMantissa will actually calculate as zero:
1e6 * 1e18 / 100,001e18 = 0
There are two issues with this. First is that a majority of these tokens simply won't work. The other issue is that because userCollateralRatioMantissa returns 0 there are states in which some debt is impossible to liquidate breaking a key invariant of the protocol. Any token with very high or very low precision will suffer from this. Some token pairs will always be/will become broken

title: First depositor can abuse exchange rate to
content: The vulnerability is a share‑ratio manipulation bug that appears in vault‑style contracts which issue proportional shares for deposited assets. When the very first depositor contributes an extremely small amount, such as a single wei, the contract records this deposit and then allows the same address to make an additional donation that does not generate new shares but increases the total asset balance of the vault. Because the conversion from assets to shares is performed using integer division with truncation, the tiny initial deposit creates a disproportionately large share‑to‑asset exchange rate. Subsequent users who deposit larger amounts receive shares calculated at this inflated rate, meaning they receive fewer shares than they should for the value they contributed. When later users withdraw, the inflated exchange rate causes the vault to allocate more assets to the first depositor’s shares, effectively allowing the first depositor to extract value that belongs to later participants. The impact is a loss of funds for anyone who deposits after the attacker, as the attacker can claim a disproportionate portion of the vault’s assets. This condition occurs only after the vault has been created and before any substantial liquidity has been added, i.e., when the first deposit is extremely small and the contract does not enforce a minimum deposit or lock a portion of the initial contribution. The affected parties are regular users of the vault, the protocol that relies on fair share accounting, and any token holders expecting correct proportional ownership. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the share‑minting logic and identified that the integer division could truncate to zero when the deposit amount is tiny, leading to an inflated exchange rate. It can be hard to notice because the contract may appear to work correctly for normal deposit sizes, and the problem only manifests when an attacker deliberately seeds the vault with a minimal amount. The bug violates the fundamental accounting assumption that each share represents a constant fraction of the total assets; the truncation breaks this invariant and allows the attacker to “steal” assets. From a user’s perspective, a later depositor may see their balance disappear after a withdrawal, or notice that the amount they receive is far less than expected, even though the UI shows a successful deposit. The expected behavior is that each depositor receives shares proportional to their contribution, but the reality after exploitation is that the first depositor can withdraw more than their fair share, effectively causing funds to disappear for others. The recommended mitigation is to prevent the share‑to‑asset ratio from being established on a negligible first deposit. This can be achieved by locking a small, non‑trivial amount of the initial deposit, enforcing a minimum deposit size, or initializing the vault with a seed balance that sets a sane exchange rate before any user deposits. By ensuring that the first conversion does not suffer from truncation, the share accounting remains accurate and the vault remains safe for all participants.
summary: Classic issue with vaults. First depositor can deposit a single wei then donate to the vault to greatly inflate share ratio. Due to truncation when converting to shares this can be used to steal funds from later depositors. See summary. First depositor can steal funds due to truncation

title: Malicious user can finalize other’s withdrawal
content: The vulnerability is an off‑by‑gas error in the OptimismPortal contract that allows a third‑party attacker to finalize another user’s withdrawal with slightly less gas than the amount the withdrawing user specified. The contract checks that gasleft() is at least user‑provided gasLimit plus a constant buffer (20 000 gas) before it writes the l2Sender storage slot and performs other bookkeeping. Those operations consume about 5 122 gas, so when the contract later forwards gasleft()-20 000 to the target call, the actual gas supplied to the external contract is user‑gasLimit‑5 122. If the user set the gasLimit only a few thousand gas above the true execution cost, the require check succeeds but the external call runs out of gas and reverts. Because the OptimismPortal does not replay failed withdrawals, the ETH that was meant to be withdrawn remains locked in the portal contract forever. The bug is triggered when a malicious actor calls finalizeWithdrawalTransaction on behalf of the victim with a gas amount that passes the initial check but is insufficient for the later call. From the user’s perspective the withdrawal transaction simply reverts; the UI shows no funds received and the user’s L1 balance does not change, contrary to the expectation that the withdrawal would succeed. The issue was discovered during a security audit and reproduced with a Foundry test that varied the gas supplied to the portal. It is hard to notice because the contract emits the standard "insufficient gas to finalize withdrawal" error only when the initial check fails; in the vulnerable range the transaction passes the check and then fails silently, leaving the funds stuck. The problem belongs to the class of gas‑accounting bugs where the contract assumes that the gas available after internal operations is still at least the user‑specified limit. The proper mitigation is to separate the buffer used for the pre‑call bookkeeping from the buffer used for the external call, or otherwise account for the exact gas consumed between the check and the call so that the forwarded gas is never less than the declared limit. Fixing the bug restores the guarantee that a withdrawal either succeeds or, if it fails, the user can retry without losing funds.
summary:
Transactions to execute a withdrawal from the Optimism Portal can be sent with 5122 less gas than specified by the user, because the check is performed a few operations prior to the call. Because there are no replays on this contract, the result is that a separate malicious user can call finalizeWithdrawalTransaction() with a precise amount of gas, cause the withdrawer’s withdrawal to fail, and permanently lock their funds.
Withdrawals can be initiated directly from the L2ToL1MessagePasser contract on L2. These withdrawals can be withdrawn directly from the OptimismPortal on L1. This path is intended to be used only by users who know what they are doing, presumably to save the gas of going through the additional more “user-friendly” contracts.
One of the quirks of the OptimismPortal is that there is no replaying of transactions. If a transaction fails, it will simply fail, and all ETH associated with it will remain in the OptimismPortal contract. Users have been warned of this and understand the risks, so Optimism takes no responsibility for user error.
However, there is an issue in the implementation of OptimismPortal that a withdrawal transaction can be executed with 5122 gas less than the user specified. In many cases, this could cause their transaction to revert, without any user error involved. Optimism is aware of the importance of this property being correct when We want to maintain the property that the amount of gas supplied to the call to the target contract is at least the gas limit specified by the user.
We can do this by enforcing that, at this point in time, we still have gaslimit + buffer gas available.
This property is not maintained because of the gap between the check and the execution.
The check is as follows, where FINALIZE_GAS_BUFFER == 20_000:
require(
gasleft() >= _tx.gasLimit + FINALIZE_GAS_BUFFER,
"OptimismPortal: insufficient gas to finalize withdrawal"
);
After this check, we know that the current execution context has at least 20,000 more gas than the gas limit. However, we then proceed to spend gas by (a) assigning the l2Sender storage variable, which uses 2900 gas because it’s assigning from a non-zero value, and (b) perform some additional operations to prepare the contract for the external call.
The result is that, by the time the call is sent with gasleft() - FINALIZE_GAS_BUFFER gas, gasleft() is 5122 lower than it was in the initial check.
Mathematically, this can be expressed as:
• gasAtCheck >= gasLimit + 20000
• gasSent == gasAtCall - 20000
• gasAtCall == gasAtCheck - 5122
Rearranging, we get gasSent >= gasLimit + 20000 - 5122 - 20000, which simplifies to gasSent >= gasLimit - 5122.
For any withdrawal where a user sets their gas limit within 5122 of the actual gas their execution requires, a malicious user can call finalizeWithdrawalTransaction() on their behalf with enough gas to pass the check, but not enough for execution to succeed.
The result is that the withdrawing user will have their funds permanently locked in the OptimismPortal contract.

title: Withdrawals with high gas limits can be bricked
content: The vulnerability is a gas‑forwarding mismatch in the OptimismPortal withdrawal path that can permanently lock a user’s funds. When a user initiates a withdrawal they specify a gasLimit that the portal contract checks with a simple require statement: gasleft() must be at least gasLimit plus a small buffer. The contract then forwards the remaining gas (minus the buffer) to the target L2 contract using a low‑level call. However, the EVM limits the amount of gas that can be sent to an external call to 63/64 of the caller’s remaining gas. For withdrawals with a gasLimit larger than roughly 952,192 units, the 1/64 portion that is withheld can exceed the hard‑coded buffer, meaning the actual gas forwarded is smaller than the user‑specified limit. The require check still passes because it does not account for the 63/64 rule, so the call later runs out of gas and reverts. Because the OptimismPortal does not replay failed withdrawals, the ETH that was supposed to be transferred remains trapped in the portal contract, effectively bricking the withdrawal. This can be triggered deliberately by a malicious actor who calls finalizeWithdrawalTransaction with a carefully chosen gas amount that passes the check but causes the forward to be insufficient, locking the withdrawer’s funds forever. The issue was discovered during a security audit by Sherlock through targeted tests that varied the gas supplied to the portal and observed the mismatch between the check and the actual forwarded gas. It is hard to notice because the transaction appears to succeed up to the require, and the failure occurs only inside the low‑level call, which silently reduces the gas without an explicit error message. The impact is that users expecting a successful withdrawal receive no ETH, see their balance unchanged, and cannot recover the locked funds without a contract upgrade or administrative intervention. The bug belongs to the class of “insufficient gas forwarding due to EVM 63/64 stipend limitation” and violates the business assumption that the portal will always forward at least the gas limit declared by the user. The recommended fix is to adjust the gas check to multiply the required amount by 64/63, ensuring that enough gas remains after the EVM’s automatic reduction before the external call is made.
summary:
Transactions to execute a withdrawal from the Optimism Portal require the caller to send enough gas to cover gasLimit specified by the withdrawer. Because the EVM limits the total gas forwarded on to 63/64ths of the total gasleft() (and silently reduces it to this value if we try to send more) there are situations where transactions with high gas limits will be vulnerable to being reverted. Because there are no replays on this contract, the result is that a malicious user can call finalizeWithdrawalTransaction() with a precise amount of gas, cause the withdrawer’s withdrawal to fail, and permanently lock their funds.

Withdrawals can be withdrawn from L2's L2ToL1MessagePasser contract to L1's OptimismPortal contract. This is a less "user-friendly" withdrawal path, presumably for users who know what they are doing.

One of the quirks of the OptimismPortal is that there is no replaying of transactions. If a transaction fails, it will simply fail, and all ETH associated with it will remain in the OptimismPortal contract. Users have been warned of this and understand the risks, so Optimism takes no responsibility for user error.

In order to ensure that failed transactions can only happen at the fault of the user, the contract implements a check to ensure that the gasLimit is sufficient:
```solidity
require(
    gasleft() >= _tx.gasLimit + FINALIZE_GAS_BUFFER,
    "OptimismPortal: insufficient gas to finalize withdrawal"
);
```
When the transaction is executed, the contract requests to send along all the remaining gas, minus the hardcoded FINALIZE_GAS_BUFFER for actions after the call. The goal is that this will ensure that the amount of gas forwarded on is at least the gas limit specified by the user.

Optimism is aware of the importance of this property being correct when they write “We want to maintain the property that the amount of gas supplied to the call to the target contract is at least the gas limit specified by the user. We can do this by enforcing that, at this point in time, we still have gaslimit + buffer gas available.”

The issue is that the EVM specifies the maximum gas that can be sent to an external call as 63/64ths of the gasleft(). For very large gas limits, this 1/64th that remains could be greater than the hardcoded FINALIZE_GAS_BUFFER value. In this case, less gas would be forwarded along than was directed by the contract.

Here is a quick overview of the math:
• We need X gas to be sent as a part of the call.
• This means we need X * 64 / 63 gas to be available at the time the function is called.
• However, the only check is that we have X + 20_000 gas a few operations prior to the call (which guarantees that we have X + 14878 at the time of the call).
• For any situation where X / 64 > 14878 (in other words, when the amount of gas sent is greater than 952_192), the caller is able to send an amount of gas that passes the check, but doesn't forward the required amount on in the call.

For any withdrawal with a gas limit of at least 952,192, a malicious user can call finalizeWithdrawalTransaction() with an amount of gas that will pass the checks, but will end up forwarding along less gas than was specified by the user. The result is that the withdrawing user can have their funds permanently locked in the OptimismPortal contract.

title: Causing users lose their fund during finalizing
content: The vulnerability is a logical flaw in the cross‑domain message finalisation flow that allows a malicious actor to mark a legitimate user withdrawal as completed while the actual fund transfer never occurs. The root cause is the presence of a reentrancy guard inside the CrossDomainMessenger.relayMessage function, which blocks a nested call to the same messenger during the execution of OptimismPortal.finalizeWithdrawalTransaction. When the inner call is blocked, the contract does not propagate the failure back to the outer call, so the outer transaction finishes successfully and records the withdrawal as finalised even though the inner call that would move the funds was aborted. An attacker can exploit this by first sending a message that deliberately reverts, causing the system to store the message as failed. After the challenge period for a victim’s withdrawal has elapsed, the attacker rewrites the payload of the failed message to contain the victim’s withdrawal transaction and then re‑relays the message with a flag that prevents the revert. The messenger calls the attacker contract, which in turn calls OptimismPortal.finalizeWithdrawalTransaction with the victim’s data. The inner call succeeds up to the point where it attempts to invoke CrossDomainMessenger.relayMessage again, at which moment the reentrancy guard rejects the call. Because this rejection is not caught, the outer transaction reports success and the system marks the victim’s withdrawal as finalised. From the user’s perspective the UI shows a successful withdrawal, but the expected funds never appear on L1, effectively disappearing. The impact is loss of funds for any user whose withdrawal is processed in this manner, and the protocol’s accounting invariants are broken because a withdrawal is recorded without the corresponding token movement. The issue manifests only after the challenge period has passed and when an attacker can control a previously failed cross‑domain message, making it hard to notice because the transaction receipt contains no revert and the state flag appears correct. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the interaction between the reentrancy guard and the message‑retry logic. To remediate, the finalisation routine should detect the specific reentrancy‑guard revert (for example using a try/catch around the inner call) and revert the outer transaction, or redesign the flow to avoid calling the messenger from within a messenger‑protected context, ensuring that a failed inner call always aborts the whole withdrawal process.

title: Signers can bypass checks and change thresh-
content: The vulnerability is a post‑execution invariant bypass that allows signers of a multi‑owner safe to change the contract's signature threshold despite a guard that is supposed to prevent such changes. The guard function checkAfterExecution compares the safe's current threshold with a value returned by an internal helper _getCorrectThreshold, which calculates the expected threshold based on the number of valid owners after the transaction and the configured minimum and maximum limits. Because the helper is called after the transaction has already modified the owners list, the computed threshold can legitimately match the new owner count, allowing the check to pass even though the threshold has been reduced. This happens when a signer includes a call to removeOwner (or a sequence of removeOwner calls via multicall) within the same transaction that is being validated. The root cause is that the invariant does not capture the pre‑transaction threshold value; it only ensures that the post‑transaction threshold equals the post‑transaction owner count bounded by the limits. An attacker can therefore lower the threshold by removing owners, gaining disproportionate control over future executions because fewer signatures are required. From a user’s perspective the UI may still display the threshold as unchanged during the transaction, but after confirmation the threshold appears lower than expected, violating the assumption that signers cannot alter the security parameter. This can lead to a situation where a single malicious signer can approve and execute arbitrary transactions, potentially draining funds or altering protocol state. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the guard’s logic and identified that the threshold comparison does not preserve the original value. It is subtle because the check appears to succeed and no explicit error is thrown, making it easy to miss in functional tests that only verify successful execution. The proper fix is to capture the safe's threshold before the transaction executes (e.g., in checkTransaction) and compare the post‑execution value against this stored snapshot, ensuring that any change to the threshold is detected and rejected. Conceptually, this bug belongs to the class of invariant‑violation or state‑mutation‑bypass flaws where a contract validates a condition after a mutable operation without preserving the pre‑state, allowing an attacker to manipulate critical parameters such as quorum thresholds.

title: HatsSignerGate + MultiHatsSignerGate: more signers than expected
content: The vulnerability is that the HatsSignerGate and MultiHatsSignerGate contracts can end up with more valid signers than the configured maxSigners limit. The root cause is that the claimSigner functions do not reconcile the current signer count before performing the maxSigners check, and the internal accounting of valid signers can become stale when the underlying Safe owners are modified (for example via Safe.addOwnerWithThreshold) without updating the hat‑wearer status. An attacker or any user can trigger the situation by adding an extra owner to the Safe while the number of hat wearers remains at the limit, then later re‑wearing the hat, causing the contract to believe fewer signers are active than actually are. When a new signer calls claimSigner, the contract thinks the limit has not been reached, allows the claim, and the total number of owners and valid signers both exceed maxSigners. Subsequent calls to reconcileSignerCount revert because validSignerCount > maxSigners, effectively freezing all transaction execution until a signer voluntarily renounces his hat, which is unlikely. The impact is a denial‑of‑service for the protocol: no further Safe transactions can be executed, and existing signers may lose their signing privilege. The condition occurs whenever the Safe’s owner set is changed independently of the hat system, such as through Safe.addOwnerWithThreshold, and the contract’s internal signer count is not refreshed. All owners and signers are affected, as the protocol cannot process any further operations. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the interaction between claimSigner and reconcileSignerCount and identified a mismatch in state after owner changes. It is hard to notice because the contract still reports a lower signer count, so the maxSigners check passes, and the problem only surfaces later when reconcileSignerCount is invoked, producing a revert that looks unrelated to the original claim. The proper fix is to invoke reconcileSignerCount at the start of claimSigner (and similarly in MultiHatsSignerGate) and to use the refreshed maxSigners value for subsequent logic, ensuring that the contract never allows more valid signers than the configured limit. In user‑facing terms, a user may see that a transaction to add a new signer succeeds, but later any attempt to execute a Safe transaction fails with a MaxSignersReached error, and signers may find that their signing rights disappear unless they manually give up their hat. This bug belongs to the class of state‑inconsistency between access‑control tokens and on‑chain role counters or accounting mismatch leading to denial‑of‑service.

title: HatsSignerGateBase: valid signer threshold can be bypassed
content: The vulnerability is a mismatch between the signature verification performed by a Gnosis Safe and the additional guard logic implemented in the HatsSignerGate (HSG) contract. The Safe checks that the first *threshold* signatures in the submitted signature blob are valid signatures from owners, while the HSG guard iterates over *all* signatures and counts any that belong to a currently valid signer, without ensuring that the same subset of signatures is being examined. Because the HSG does not restrict its validation to the first threshold signatures, an owner who has been removed from the valid signer set but remains listed as an owner in the Safe can still cause a transaction to be accepted. The attacker can append a fresh signature from the removed signer together with one or more previously recorded signatures from valid signers, thereby satisfying both the Safe’s check (which only looks at the first threshold signatures) and the HSG’s count (which scans the entire list). The guard also fails to verify that the recovered address is non‑zero, allowing a zero‑address signer to be counted as valid. This flaw can be triggered whenever an owner’s signer hat is revoked but the owner is not yet removed from the Safe’s owner list, and when the transaction sender supplies more signatures than the threshold. From a user’s perspective the transaction appears to have been approved normally, yet the contract may execute actions that were not authorized by any current valid signer, leading to unexpected fund transfers, loss of assets, or the accidental transfer of the signer hat to the zero address. The issue was discovered during a security audit by Sherlock, who noted that the two verification steps were applying different criteria, making the problem subtle and easy to miss because both components report success independently. The root cause is the guard’s use of an unrestricted signature count and its lack of checks for signature data integrity and zero‑address recovery. To remediate, the HSG should be modified to evaluate only the first *threshold* signatures – the same set that the Safe validates – and to remove redundant length checks that are already performed by the Safe. Aligning the verification logic eliminates the possibility for revoked signers to bypass the threshold and restores the intended security guarantees of the multi‑signature wallet.
summary:
differently which opens the door to exploitation.
I will show how this allows a valid signer that has become invalid but not yet removed from the owners of the Safe to continue signing transactions. The invalid signer can effectively sign transactions as though he was valid.
Also there is the possibility of valid signers calling Safe.addOwnerWithThreshold.
When an owner is added to the Safe but not a valid signer he can still sign transactions and the HSG will not recognize that there are not enough valid signatures.
To summarize, the issue is caused by this:
1. Signatures are first checked by the Safe then by the HSG logic
2. We can pass an arbitrary amount of signatures when executing a transaction
3. The Safe checks that the first threshold signatures are valid. However the HSG logic checks that ANY of the signatures are signed by valid signers. The HSG logic does not check the same signatures as the Safe.
Essentially the Safe and HSG logic are applying different checks to different signatures.
A transaction is executed by calling Safe.execTransaction
First the signatures are checked by the Safe then the checkTransaction function is executed on the guard (HatsSignerGate)
The HatsSignerGate then executes countValidSignatures to check if enough signatures were signed by valid signers
With all prerequisites out of the way, we can now get into the actual issue.
The Safe calls checkNSignatures to check if the first threshold signatures in the signatures bytes are valid
So if threshold=5 but we provide say 7 signatures, the last two signatures are not checked. If the first 5 signatures are valid the check passes successfully.
The issue is that the HSG countValidSignatures function iterates over ALL signatures and tries to find enough valid signers such that threshold is reached.

5. Bob calls Safe.execTransaction. The Safe checks the first 3 signatures to be valid signatures from owners. The check passes. The HSG checks that there are at least 3 signatures signed by valid signers. Which also passes.
Important: Bob can pass a 4th signature from a previous transaction because two of the signature types used in HSG do not check that the correct data has been signed https://github.com/Hats-Protocol/hats-zodiac/blob/9455cc0957762f5dbbd8e62063d970199109b977/src/HatsSignerGateBase.sol#L561-L568.

Owners of the Safe that are not valid signers can sign transactions.

title: Signers can brick safe by adding unlimited additional owners
content: The vulnerability is that the contract allows the number of owners (signers) to exceed the immutable maxSigners limit by adding owners through the execTransaction path, because checkAfterExecution does not verify that the owner set remained within the limit. The root cause is the absence of a validation step after a transaction that may modify the owners array, combined with a threshold‑checking function that only compares the safe’s threshold to a target value and does not enforce the maxSigners constraint when owners are added via execTransaction. An attacker who controls at least one signer can collude with other signers to call execTransaction with data that adds additional owners, possibly using hats that are already marked as valid. If the safe’s threshold is already at the targetThreshold, or if the new owners are currently disabled, the internal _getCorrectThreshold logic returns a value that passes the threshold check, allowing the owners to be added. Once the total valid signer count exceeds maxSigners, the reconcileSignerCount function invoked by checkTransaction reverts with MaxSignersReached on every subsequent transaction. As a result, all future executions fail, the safe becomes unusable, and any funds held by the safe are effectively frozen. This condition can be triggered unintentionally if signers mistakenly add too many owners, or deliberately as a ransom attack where colluding signers freeze the contract to demand that the hat‑wearers renounce their hats. The issue is hard to notice because the contract already contains several signer‑related checks, and the addition of owners via execTransaction appears legitimate; only after a transaction is processed does the over‑limit condition surface, causing a generic revert. The vulnerability was identified during a security audit that examined the flow of owner management functions and the interaction between checkAfterExecution, checkTransaction, and the threshold logic. To remediate, the contract should enforce that the number of owners does not exceed maxSigners after any state‑changing operation, for example by adding a validation step in checkAfterExecution or by prohibiting owner addition through execTransaction altogether. Making maxSigners adjustable by an authorized admin or providing a mechanism to safely reduce the signer set without trapping funds would also mitigate the risk. In user terms, a participant may see transactions suddenly revert with a MaxSignersReached error, balances appear unchanged, and attempts to withdraw or execute proposals fail, giving the impression that “my funds disappeared” or “the contract is stuck”.

title: Other module can add owners to safe that push
content: An unsafe interaction between the HatsSignerGate module and other modules attached to a Gnosis Safe allows owners to be added without the module’s maxSigners check. The HatsSignerGate module enforces a limit on the number of valid signers (maxSigners) by comparing the count of owners that are wearers of a specific immutable hat against this limit whenever a transaction is processed. The module only validates owners that are added through its own claimSigner() function. However, any other module that has permission to call the Safe’s addOwner or similar functions can add additional owners directly, bypassing the claimSigner() path. When the total number of owners that satisfy the hat requirement exceeds maxSigners, the reconcileSignerCount() routine triggers a revert with MaxSignersReached, causing every subsequent transaction to fail. Because the Safe’s execution flow always calls checkTransaction() before a transaction is executed, the failure is deterministic and blocks all activity. The impact is that the Safe becomes permanently bricked: funds remain locked, users see transaction failures with no obvious indication that the problem is an excess of owners, and the expected behavior of successful execution is violated. The condition occurs only when the Safe is configured with the HatsSignerGate module, an immutable hat, and at least one additional module capable of adding owners. Affected parties include the Safe administrator, any hat wearers, and downstream protocol users who rely on the Safe to move funds. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the interaction between claimSigner() and external owner‑addition mechanisms. It is hard to notice because the revert surface is a generic “MaxSignersReached” error that does not point to a configuration problem, and the UI may simply report a failed transaction. The bug belongs to the class of insufficient cross‑module state validation or configuration‑locking vulnerabilities, where one component assumes exclusive control over a critical invariant. From a user perspective the symptoms are transactions that revert, balances that appear unchanged, and an expectation that a submitted operation will succeed, but instead the Safe reports an error and no funds move. A proper fix would enforce the maxSigners constraint across all possible owner‑addition paths, either by preventing other modules from adding owners, by adding a fallback mechanism that can reduce the signer count when the limit is exceeded, or by allowing an admin to remove excess owners without requiring hat wearers to renounce their hats.
summary:
If another module adds owners to the safe, these additions are not checked by our module or guard's logic. This can result in pushing us over maxSigners, which will cause all transactions to revert. In the case of an immutable hat, the only way to avoid the safe being locked permanently (with all funds frozen) may be to convince many hat wearers to renounce their hats.
When new owners are added to the contract through the claimSigner() function, the total number of owners is compared to maxSigners to ensure it doesn't exceed it. However, if there are other modules on the safe, they are able to add additional owners without these checks.
In the case of HatsSignerGate.sol, there is no need to call claimSigner() to "activate" these owners. They will automatically be valid as long as they are a wearer of the correct hat.
This could lead to an issue where many (more than maxSigners) wearers of an immutable hat are added to the safe as owners. Now, each time a transaction is processed, checkTransaction() is called, which calls reconcileSignerCount(), which has the following check:
```solidity
if (validSignerCount > maxSigners) {
    revert MaxSignersReached();
}
```
This will revert.
Worse, there is nothing the admin can do about it. If they don't have control over the eligibility address for the hat, they are not able to burn the hats or transfer them. The safe will be permanently bricked and unable to perform transactions unless the hat wearers agree to renounce their hats.
The safe can be permanently bricked and unable to perform transactions unless the hat wearers agree to renounce their hats.

title: Price of voltGNS share is calculated incorrectly
content: The vulnerability lies in the way the price of the voltGNS share token is calculated inside the contract. The price function adds the amount of GNS that is held in the vault (totalStaked) and then divides this sum by the total supply of shares, which is a standard approach for share‑based tokens. However, the contract also maintains a separate variable called boostedGNS – an amount of GNS that the contract owner can deposit without receiving any additional shares. Because boostedGNS is included in totalStaked but is never deducted when the price is computed, the reported price is artificially inflated. When the owner later calls unboostGNS to withdraw the boosted amount, the totalStaked drops while the totalSupply remains unchanged, causing the price to fall sharply. This sudden price drop can trigger massive liquidation events for users who have taken loans against voltGNS collateral in the VoltaVault contract, often without any warning. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are a rapid decrease in the apparent value of their collateral, unexpected liquidation notices, or receiving far fewer GNS than expected when redeeming shares. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the price calculation logic, where the auditor noticed that the boostedGNS balance was never accounted for in the denominator of the price formula. The flaw is hard to spot because the formula superficially appears correct – it uses total assets over total shares – but the hidden reserve of owner‑deposited GNS silently skews the result. The bug belongs to the class of accounting or price‑oracle manipulation vulnerabilities, where hidden reserves break the invariant that each share represents an equal claim on the underlying assets. To remediate the problem the price calculation must subtract the boostedGNS amount from totalStaked before dividing by totalSupply, or alternatively the protocol should mint proportional shares for any owner‑deposited GNS so that the reserve is reflected in the share supply. Either approach restores the invariant that the share price reflects only the assets that are actually claimable by token holders, preventing the owner from arbitrarily influencing the price and protecting users from unexpected liquidations.
summary:
Forget to deduct the boostedGNS when calculating price
The price of voltGNS is updated whenever the function voltGNS.swapToGNS() is called.
The function firstly calculates the totalStaked which is amount of gns staking in gnsVault plus with amount of gns which was swapped from pendingDai. Then the price will be determined by dividing totalStaked with totalSupply() of the vault.
At the first glance, this formula seem right when calculating the price using the total underlying assets and the total shares supply. So it means that if I withdraw all the totalSupply shares, I can receive all the totalStaked. Unfortunately this won't be happened because of the boostedGNS. The boostedGNS is amount of gns which is deposited by the owner and no share will be minted for the him. Furthermore this amount can be deposited / withdrew at anytime whenever the owner wants.
This boostedGNS mechanism can lead to the big issue for the VoltaVault contract which uses the voltGNS as collateral. When the owner calls unboostGNS(), it can make the voltGNS.price() lose a lot of value. That will make the big liquidation events occured for a lot of users without noticing them.
The price of a token should depend on the fluctuation of the market, and should not depend on the single individual like owner. Malicious owner can abuse this to make profit.
When owner calls unboostGNS() can incur a immediate liquidation for users without their preparation.

title: Liquidator receives less collateral then he should
content: The vulnerability is a misallocation of collateral during the liquidation process of a vault. When the function that handles liquidation is executed, the contract first collects the debt from the liquidator and then attempts to split the seized collateral between the liquidator and the protocol according to a discount model described in the documentation. The root cause is an incorrect arithmetic formula used to compute the liquidator discount and the protocol fee. The code calculates a discount based on the minimum collateral percentage, then derives a protocol fee as 1e18 minus half of the remaining discount. Because the discount is derived as 100e18 * 1e18 / minimumCollateralPercentage, the resulting value is larger than intended, and the subsequent fee calculation makes the protocol fee close to the full discount amount. Consequently, the protocol receives the majority of the collateral (for example 83.33% of a 100‑ether collateral) while the liquidator receives only a small remainder (16.67%). This behaviour contradicts the documented expectation where the liquidator should obtain half of the discount (approximately 17% of the collateral) and the protocol the other half. The flaw can be exploited simply by calling the liquidation function; the liquidator pays the debt but is rewarded with far less collateral than promised, effectively losing a large portion of the value they expected to acquire. The impact is a financial loss for any participant acting as a liquidator, reducing incentives to perform liquidations and potentially undermining the economic model of the protocol. The issue manifests whenever a vault becomes eligible for liquidation, i.e., when its loan‑to‑value ratio reaches the minimum collateral percentage (for instance 150%). All users who attempt to liquidate such vaults are affected, and the protocol’s reputation may suffer because the fee distribution does not match the advertised terms. The problem was discovered during a manual audit by comparing the on‑chain calculation with the protocol’s documentation and reproducing the numbers in a simple test contract on Remix, which showed the protocol receiving the larger share. The bug is subtle because the arithmetic expressions compile without error and the resulting numbers appear plausible, making it easy to overlook without a direct reference to the intended split. To fix the issue, the contract should reverse the allocation logic: compute the liquidator’s share as half of the discount and assign the remaining half to the protocol, or directly swap the amounts transferred so that the liquidator receives collateralExtract ‑ protocolEarned and the protocol receives protocolEarned as defined by the correct fee formula. This adjustment aligns the on‑chain behavior with the documented economic model, ensuring that liquidators receive the expected discounted collateral and that protocol fees are correctly sized.

title: If another module adds a module, the safe will
content: The vulnerability is a logic flaw in the module‑guarding mechanism of a Gnosis‑compatible safe that relies on a hash comparison of the module list before and after a transaction. The guard records the keccak256 hash of the first *enabledModuleCount* modules, then after the transaction it recomputes the hash using *enabledModuleCount + 1* to detect any newly added module. The root cause is that the safe’s internal counter *enabledModuleCount* is only incremented when a module is added through the public enableNewModule() function. If another already‑authorized module adds a new module by calling a lower‑level function that bypasses enableNewModule(), the counter stays unchanged while the actual module array grows. Consequently the “before” hash is calculated over a truncated list, the “after” hash includes the extra entry, and the two hashes never match. This mismatch triggers the guard’s revert (SignersCannotChangeModules) on every subsequent transaction, effectively bricking the safe. The exploit can be carried out by a malicious signer who convinces an existing module to add a new module, or by any module that possesses the ability to call the internal addModule routine. From a user’s perspective, any attempt to execute a transaction results in an immediate revert with a generic “signers cannot change modules” error; the UI may show that the transaction cannot be submitted, balances remain displayed but become inaccessible, and users receive no confirmation that their action succeeded. The impact is severe: all assets held by the safe become permanently locked because the guard prevents any further state‑changing calls, and there is no built‑in recovery path. The condition under which this occurs is narrow – it requires a safe that employs this specific hash‑based guard and also has at least one module capable of adding another module without using the public enable function. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the interaction between module pagination, the enabledModuleCount variable, and the guard logic. It can be hard to notice because the guard appears to protect against unauthorized module changes, yet the failure manifests only as repeated transaction reverts, which may be attributed to other causes such as gas limits or network congestion. To remediate, the guard logic must be redesigned so that it either validates the full module list length, uses a deterministic source of truth for module additions, or outright forbids any module from adding other modules on safes that rely on this guard. In practice this means either removing the pagination‑based hash check, ensuring that any module addition updates the enabledModuleCount, or prohibiting the deployment of additional modules on safes that employ this protection, thereby eliminating the possibility of a hidden module count mismatch and preventing the safe from becoming permanently bricked.

title: Signers can bypass checks to add new mod-
content: The vulnerability allows signers of a Gnosis Safe‑like contract to bypass the post‑execution module invariant by exploiting a re‑entrancy flaw in the guard logic. The contract records a hash of the currently enabled modules in checkTransaction() and stores it in a private variable. After the user‑initiated transaction finishes, checkAfterExecution() recomputes the hash and reverts if it differs, intending to prevent signers from adding or removing modules. However, the guard that should prevent nested calls – the _guardEntries counter – is only incremented on entry and decremented on exit, without ever enforcing that the counter is zero before a new entry. Consequently, a signer can craft a multicall that first adds a malicious module, then invokes execTransaction() again within the same outer call. The inner call updates the stored hash to include the new module, so when the outer checkAfterExecution() runs the hashes match and the restriction is silently bypassed. This re‑entrancy path lets any signer that meets the threshold install an arbitrary module, which in turn can execute transactions with unlimited privileges, effectively lowering the safe’s threshold to one and removing any guard checks. From a user’s point of view the transaction appears to succeed, but afterwards the safe’s module list has changed without any visible warning, leading to loss of control over funds and potential theft. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the interaction between the module snapshot logic and the re‑entrancy counter. It is difficult to notice because the hash comparison succeeds, giving no error, and the guard variable does not overflow, so no obvious revert occurs. The proper mitigation is to replace the incremental guard with a classic non‑reentrant pattern, for example requiring _guardEntries to be zero at the start of checkTransaction() or setting it to one and checking for underflow on exit, ensuring that any nested call will cause the guard to fail. Additionally, the snapshot of the module list should be immutable for the duration of the outer transaction, for example by storing it in memory and not overwriting it on re‑entrant calls. By applying a robust re‑entrancy guard and protecting the module hash snapshot, the protocol can enforce that signers cannot add new modules and thereby preserve the intended security guarantees.
summary:
The checkAfterExecution() function has checks to ensure that new modules cannot be added by signers. This is a crucial check, because adding a new module could give them unlimited power to make any changes (with no guards in place) in the future. However, by abusing reentrancy, the parameters used by the check can be changed so that this crucial restriction is violated.
The checkAfterExecution() is intended to uphold important invariants after each signer transaction is completed. This is intended to restrict certain dangerous signer behaviors, the most important of which is adding new modules. This was an before execution to the has of the modules after.
```solidity
(address[] memory modules,) = safe.getModulesPaginated(SENTINEL_OWNERS, enabledModuleCount);
_existingModulesHash = keccak256(abi.encode(modules));
```
After:
```solidity
(address[] memory modules,) = safe.getModulesPaginated(SENTINEL_OWNERS, enabledModuleCount + 1);
if (keccak256(abi.encode(modules)) != _existingModulesHash) {
    revert SignersCannotChangeModules();
}
```
/// @notice Post-flight check to prevent safe signers from removing this contract guard, changing any modules, or changing the threshold
Why Restricting Modules is Important
Modules are the most important thing to check. This is because modules have unlimited power not only to execute transactions but to skip checks in the future.
Creating an arbitrary new module is so bad that it is equivalent to the other two issues together: getting complete control over the safe (as if threshold was set to 1) and removing the guard (because they aren't checked in module transactions).
However, this important restriction can be violated by abusing reentrancy into this function.
Reentrancy Disfunction
To see how this is possible, we first have to take a quick detour regarding reentrancy. It appears that the protocol is attempting to guard against reentrancy with the guardEntries variable. It is incremented in checkTransaction() (before a transaction is executed) and decremented in checkAfterExecution() (after the transaction has completed).
The only protection it provides is in its risk of underflowing, explained in the // leave checked to catch underflows triggered by re-erntry attempts
However, any attempt to reenter and send an additional transaction midstream of another transaction would first trigger the checkTransaction() function. This would increment _guardEntries and would lead to it not underflowing.
In order for this system to work correctly, the checkTransaction() function should simply set _guardEntries = 1. This would result in an underflow with the second decrement. But, as it is currently designed, there is no reentrancy protection.
Using Reentrancy to Bypass Module Check
Remember that the module invariant is upheld by taking a snapshot of the hash of the modules in checkTransaction() and saving it in the _existingModulesHash variable.
However, imagine the following set of transactions:
• Signers send a transaction via the safe, and modules are snapshotted to _existingModulesHash
• The transaction uses the Multicall functionality of the safe, and performs the following actions:
• First, it adds the malicious module to the safe
• Then, it calls execTransaction() on itself with any another transaction
• The second call will call checkTransaction()
• This will update _existingModulesHash to the new list of modules, including the malicious one
• The second call will execute, which doesn't matter (could just be an empty transaction)
• After the transaction, checkAfterExecution() will be called, and the modules will match
• After the full transaction is complete, checkAfterExecution() will be called for the first transaction, but since _existingModulesHash will be overwritten, the module check will pass
Any number of signers who are above the threshold will be able to give themselves unlimited access over the safe with no restriction going forward.

title: Safe can be bricked because threshold is up-
content: The vulnerability is a logic error in the safe’s threshold‑adjustment routine that can permanently brick the contract. The code is supposed to compute a new threshold as the lower of the current number of valid signers and a configured targetThreshold, storing this value in a temporary variable called newThreshold. However, when the contract later calls the safe’s changeThreshold function it mistakenly passes the raw validSignerCount instead of newThreshold. As a result, if the number of valid signers exceeds the targetThreshold, the safe’s internal threshold is set to a value higher than the maximum allowed by the protocol. The subsequent checkAfterExecution routine validates that the threshold does not exceed the configured maximum and will revert any transaction that violates this rule. Because the threshold has been set above the allowed maximum, every transaction submitted to the safe reverts, effectively locking the safe and any assets it holds. This situation occurs only when the safe is configured with a single hat signer and the eligibility module cannot reduce the signer count, meaning the oversized threshold cannot be corrected by removing signers, and the targetThreshold cannot be raised enough to accommodate the new value. Users attempting to execute any operation will see transactions fail with a generic revert, experience missing balance updates, and may perceive that their funds have disappeared even though they remain locked in the contract. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the intended threshold logic with the actual function call and identified the typo. It is hard to notice because the threshold appears to increase rather than decrease, and the failure only manifests later when the safe enforces its maximum‑threshold rule. To remediate, the contract should pass newThreshold to changeThreshold, add explicit bounds checks before updating the threshold, and consider adding a fallback mechanism to lower the threshold if it ever exceeds the allowed maximum. This class of bug falls under improper state update due to a variable‑mix‑up, leading to invariant violation and permanent loss of functionality.

title: Unlinked tophat retains linkedTreeRequests,
content: The vulnerability originates from the unlinkTopHatFromTree function, which is intended to restore a tophat’s full self‑sovereignty after it has been detached from an admin tree. While the function correctly deletes the linkedTreeAdmins entry, it fails to clear the linkedTreeRequests mapping that stores a pending request to link the tophat to a new admin. Because the request remains in storage, a previously authorized admin (or any address that knows the request value) can later call approveLinkTopHatToTree and successfully link the tophat to their own hat, thereby hijacking admin control without the tophat’s consent. The root cause is a stale state – a leftover permission request that is not removed during the unlink operation. Exploitation proceeds by first having the current admin create a link request via requestLinkTopHatToTree, then unlinking the tophat, after which the request persists. At a later time the same admin or a malicious actor invokes approveLinkTopHatToTree, passing the stored request identifier, which passes the linkage check and re‑establishes admin authority. The impact is a loss of sovereignty for the tophat owner: the hat that was expected to be independent can be taken over, potentially compromising governance decisions, fund management, or any privileged actions tied to the hat. This occurs whenever a tophat is unlinked while a link request is pending, which can happen for any domain that has previously been linked. The affected parties include the hat owners, protocol participants relying on the hat’s autonomy, and any users whose assets or permissions are governed by the hat. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s state‑reset logic, where the unlink function was examined and the omission of linkedTreeRequests was noted. The bug is subtle because the unlink transaction emits an event indicating the hat is now linked to zero, giving the impression that all relationships have been cleared, while the hidden request remains invisible to most front‑ends. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after unlinking, the hat appears to have no admin, yet later the admin role is suddenly assigned to an unexpected address, resulting in “admin rights disappear and reappear under a stranger”. The expectation that unlinking fully isolates the hat is violated, breaking the accounting assumption that no pending linkage survives a detach operation. The recommended remediation is to delete the linkedTreeRequests entry in the unlinkTopHatFromTree function, ensuring that all pending linkage state is cleared and the hat truly regains self‑sovereignty. This class of bug is a stale state or leftover permission request that enables privilege escalation, similar to other cases where state is not fully reset after a role change.

title: voltGNS#withdraw and redeem take fees from
content: The vulnerability originates from the fee handling logic in an ERC4626 vault that permits an approved spender to withdraw or redeem shares on behalf of another account. When a third‑party address calls the withdraw or redeem function, the contract calculates a fee and then invokes internal helpers sendWithdrawFees and sendRedeemFees. These helpers incorrectly transfer the fee amount from msg.sender – the caller – instead of from the actual share owner whose tokens are being withdrawn. As a result, the operator or relayer that initiates the operation bears the cost that the protocol intended to charge the vault participant. This misallocation of fees violates the accounting assumptions of ERC4626, where fees are expected to be deducted from the user whose balance is reduced. The flaw can be exploited whenever the allowance mechanism is used: any approved contract or external account can trigger a withdrawal or redemption for a victim and will see its own balance reduced by the fee amount. In practice, services that act as custodians or relayers may notice unexpected fee deductions, leading to loss of funds, increased operational costs, or denial‑of‑service if the fee‑paying address runs out of balance. The issue appears only when withdraw or redeem is called by an address other than the token holder, making it invisible to tests that only cover direct user calls. It was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the fee‑transfer functions and identified the use of msg.sender instead of the owner parameter. Detecting the problem is difficult because the transaction succeeds and the fee is transferred, but the affected party is not the one whose shares were moved, so standard balance checks on the user may not reveal the discrepancy. The proper remediation is to modify sendWithdrawFees and sendRedeemFees so that they debit the fee from the owner argument – the account whose shares are being withdrawn or redeemed – rather than from msg.sender, thereby aligning fee collection with the intended economic model. This class of bug can be described as a fee misallocation or improper use of msg.sender in delegated operations, leading to the wrong party paying protocol fees and breaking user expectations such as "my withdrawal should only cost me the fee" versus the reality where a third‑party pays it, causing symptoms like unexpected balance reductions on relayer wallets, missing fees for users, or failed transactions due to insufficient fee balance on the caller.
summary:
ERC4626 vaults allow approved users to withdraw shares on behalf of another user. When this occurs fees are charged to msg.sender rather than the owner.
#L152-L162
sendWithdrawFees and sendRedeemFees transfers fees from msg.sender rather than the specified owner. This is problematic when a user withdraws/redeems on behalf of another user because they will be forced to pay the fees instead.
Wrong user pays fees when one users withdraws/redeems on behalf of the other

title: PerpDespository#reblance and rebalanceLite
content: The contract exposes an unpermissioned function that rebalances the perpetual depository by swapping assets and then settling any quote‑token shortfall. The caller can pass an arbitrary address that is used as the source of the shortfall repayment. Internally the function builds a swap request with user‑controlled parameters (amount, minimum output, price limit and pool fee) and, after the swap, calculates a shortfall. If the shortfall is positive the contract calls transferFrom on the quote token, pulling the required amount from the address supplied by the caller. Because the function has no access control and the account argument is not validated, a malicious actor can invoke the function with a victim’s address that has previously granted an allowance to the depository. By crafting hostile swap parameters and front‑running (sandwiching) the legitimate rebalance transaction, the attacker can inflate the shortfall to the full allowance amount and force the victim to transfer all approved tokens to the contract, effectively stealing the funds. This vulnerability manifests whenever any user approves the depository to spend their quote token, which is a normal operation for many perpetual protocols. The impact is a loss of the approved balance, leaving the victim with a zero or reduced token balance and no receipt of the expected rebalance outcome. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the rebalancing logic and noticed that the account parameter was passed unchecked to transferFrom. It is subtle because the function’s purpose is to correct PnL, so developers may assume that only the contract itself should be affected, overlooking that an external caller can dictate who pays the shortfall. The bug belongs to the class of “unrestricted external account parameter leading to unauthorized token transfer” and violates the accounting assumption that only the contract’s own funds are used to settle rebalancing. To remediate, the contract should replace the user‑supplied account with msg.sender, enforce that only authorized roles (e.g., the protocol’s treasury or a designated keeper) can call the function, and remove the ability to specify an arbitrary payer.
