Adding proper access control and ensuring that transferFrom is only invoked against the caller’s own allowance will prevent the shortfall from being charged to an unsuspecting third party and restore the intended economic safety of the rebalancing process.

title: Malicious user can use an excessively large _-
content: The vulnerability originates from the fact that the _toAddress parameter of the OFTCore sendFrom function is defined as a bytes calldata with no length restriction. Because the LayerZero messaging protocol enforces a blocking order—each message must be processed successfully before the next one—receivers normally implement a try‑catch pattern to avoid a single failure halting the whole channel. However, if the try‑catch itself reverts, the protocol falls back to its original blocking behavior. An attacker can exploit the unrestricted size of _toAddress by submitting a sendFrom request that includes an extremely large byte array. When this oversized payload is transmitted from a source chain with a high block gas limit (for example Arbitrum) to a destination chain with a much lower gas limit (for example Optimism), the transaction on the destination side runs out of gas and cannot be executed. Since the message never succeeds, the nonce remains stuck and the non‑blocking fallback cannot be triggered, effectively freezing the communication channel for that direction. This condition can be reproduced for any pair of chains where one chain permits larger gas consumption than the other, leading to a permanent blockage of cross‑chain transfers. From a user perspective, tokens appear to be burned on the source chain while no corresponding receipt or balance update occurs on the destination chain, resulting in missing funds, zero balances where a transfer was expected, and an overall loss of confidence in the protocol. The issue was identified during a security audit by the researcher Sherlock, who noted that the lack of validation on the _toAddress length makes the problem subtle and easy to overlook, especially because the function signature looks innocuous and the protocol’s normal non‑blocking guarantees give a false sense of safety. The attack does not require any special privileges; any user can craft the oversized payload. Mitigation consists of imposing a reasonable upper bound on the length of the _toAddress field—such as 32 bytes, which matches the maximum address size used on supported EVM‑compatible chains—thereby preventing the creation of payloads that exceed the destination chain’s gas capacity and preserving the intended non‑blocking behavior of LayerZero.
summary:
By default layerZero implements a blocking behavior, that is, that each message must be processed and succeed in the order that it was sent. In order to circumvent this behavior the receiver must implement their own try-catch pattern.
If the try-catch pattern in the receiving app ever fails then it will revert to its blocking behavior. The _toAddress input to OFTCore#sendFrom is calldata of any arbitrary length. An attacker can abuse this and submit a send request with an excessively large _toAddress to break communication between network with different gas limits.
```solidity
function sendFrom(address _from, uint16 _dstChainId, bytes calldata _toAddress,
    uint _amount, address payable _refundAddress, address _zroPaymentAddress,
    bytes calldata _adapterParams) public payable virtual override {
    _send(_from, _dstChainId, _toAddress, _amount, _refundAddress,
        _zroPaymentAddress, _adapterParams);
}
```
The _toAddress input to OFTCore#sendFrom is a bytes calldata of any arbitrary size. This can be used as follows to break communication between chains that have different block gas limits.
Example: Let's say that an attacker wishes to permanently block the channel Arbitrum -> Optimism. Arbitrum has a massive gas block limit, much higher than Optimism's 20M block gas limit. The attacker would call sendFrom on the Arbitrum chain with the Optimism chain as the destination. For the _toAddress input they would use an absolutely massive amount of bytes. This would be packed into the payload which would be called on Optimism. Since Arbitrum has a huge gas limit the transaction would send from the Arbitrum side but it would be so big that the transaction could never succeed on the Optimism side due to gas constraints.
Since that nonce can never succeed the communication channel will be permanently blocked at the Optimism endpoint, bypassing the nonblocking behavior of layerZero.
Users can still send messages and burn their tokens from Arbitrum -> Optimism but the messages can never be received. This could be done between any two chain in which one has a higher block gas limit. This would cause massive loss of funds and completely cripple the entire protocol.
Massive loss of user funds and protocol completely crippled

title: RageTrade senior vault USDC deposits are sub-locked due to underflow in withdrawal
content: The vulnerability resides in the senior vault’s withdrawal guard logic. The contract enforces a maximum utilization ratio of 90%, meaning the vault must keep at least ten percent more USDC deposits than the amount loaned to the junior vault. The beforeWithdraw hook calculates the utilization after the requested assets have already been subtracted from totalAssets and reverts if totalUsdcBorrowed() exceeds the allowed threshold. Because the check is performed on the post‑withdrawal balance, any withdrawal that would push the utilization even slightly above the 90 % limit triggers a revert, effectively preventing the user from pulling out any USDC when the vault is already highly utilized. This creates a “sub‑locked” state where large deposits become inaccessible, especially during market stress such as a de‑peg of the UXD token, because the protocol cannot free collateral that is needed to stabilize the system. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the DnGmxSeniorVault.sol source, where the logical condition in beforeWithdraw was identified as overly restrictive and prone to underflow‑style failures. It is hard to notice because the function is internal and only executed during a withdrawal; normal operation with low utilization passes silently, so tests that do not simulate a near‑capacity scenario miss the problem. The impact is that users see their USDC balance remain unchanged or become zero after a withdrawal attempt, receiving a MaxUtilizationBreached revert, and the protocol loses the ability to rebalance assets, potentially leading to collateral being locked and the overall system becoming unstable. To remediate, the utilization check should be based on the pre‑withdrawal asset amount or include a safety margin that allows limited withdrawals even when utilization is close to the limit. Additionally, monitoring tools should be added to prevent deposits that would push utilization into a locking region, and a fallback mechanism should be provided to move a portion of USDC out of the vault in emergencies. In summary, the bug is a classic business‑logic enforcement error where a post‑action constraint blocks legitimate operations, resulting in funds disappearing from the user’s perspective and breaking the accounting assumptions of the vault.

title: USDC deposited to PerpDepository.sol are ir-redeemable
content: The vulnerability consists of a permanent lock‑up of USDC that is sent to the PerpDepository insurance vault. The contract adds USDC to its internal collateral pool when it rebalances negative profit‑and‑loss positions through functions that swap base assets for quote assets. However, the accounting variable that tracks how much insurance has been deposited (insuranceDeposited) is only decreased when the owner calls withdrawInsurance and is never increased when USDC is injected by the rebalancing logic. Consequently the withdrawInsurance routine can only release an amount that is less than or equal to the original insuranceDeposited value, even though the vault’s actual USDC balance may be larger. The positive‑PNL rebalancing path that previously allowed USDC to leave the system has been disabled, leaving withdrawInsurance as the sole exit mechanism, which is now ineffective. This mismatch between the recorded insurance amount and the real token balance means that any USDC added after deployment becomes irretrievable. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the state changes of the rebalancing functions with the withdrawal logic and noticed that the insuranceDeposited counter never reflects the new deposits. It is hard to notice because the contract’s external interface still reports a successful withdrawal call, but the funds never leave the vault, and the USDC balance silently grows without a corresponding increase in the withdrawable allowance. Exploitation does not require an attacker; the protocol itself becomes unable to redeem the locked USDC, causing the overall collateral pool to be effectively reduced. Over time the system’s delta‑neutral position cannot be liquidated and the UDX token becomes under‑collateralized, exposing users to loss of value and potentially causing a cascade of failures in the ecosystem. From a user’s perspective the expected behavior – that deposited USDC can be reclaimed or that the protocol can maintain its collateral ratio – is violated; users may see their UDX value drop or receive no refund when they anticipate a 1:1 redemption. The bug belongs to the class of accounting‑state mismatch or “locked‑funds” vulnerabilities where internal bookkeeping does not reflect actual token balances. The recommended remediation is to adjust the accounting so that any USDC added to the insurance vault is recorded as part of insuranceDeposited, or to redesign withdrawInsurance to allow redemption of the full USDC balance on a 1:1 basis, thereby restoring the ability to retrieve the locked funds and preserving the protocol’s collateral integrity.

title: PerpDepository#getPositionValue uses incor-rect TWAP interval
content: The vulnerability originates from an incorrect time‑weighted average price (TWAP) interval being used when calculating a perpetual position's value in the PerpDepository contract. The function getPositionValue calls getMarkPriceTwap with a hard‑coded argument of 15, which the exchange interprets as a 15‑second TWAP. According to the protocol specification, the mark price must be derived from a 15‑minute (900‑second) TWAP to reflect a stable market price. Because the contract uses the short‑interval TWAP, the reported mark price can diverge significantly from the intended 15‑minute average, especially during periods of rapid price movement. This discrepancy propagates to the unrealized profit‑and‑loss calculation and the final position value returned to callers. An attacker or a market participant can exploit the flaw by creating a temporary price spike or dip that lasts less than a minute; the contract will read the inflated or deflated 15‑second TWAP, compute an erroneous position value, and consequently trigger larger than expected rebalances, margin calls, or liquidations. The impact is that traders may see their position value jump unexpectedly, receive excessive rebalancing actions, or be liquidated with insufficient collateral, effectively causing loss of funds. The issue manifests whenever getPositionValue is invoked—typically during margin checks, rebalancing, or settlement—under volatile market conditions. All users of the PerpDepository, the clearing house risk engine, and the broader protocol are affected because the accounting assumptions about collateral adequacy are broken. The problem was discovered during a manual audit when the reviewer noticed the hard‑coded constant 15 and compared it against the documented 15‑minute TWAP requirement. It can be hard to notice because the returned price still appears plausible and only deviates noticeably during short‑term volatility, making the bug subtle in normal operation. To remediate, the contract should retrieve the TWAP interval from the ClearingHouseConfig (which can be updated by governance) or replace the constant with the correct 900‑second value, ensuring that the mark price always reflects the intended 15‑minute average. This class of bug falls under incorrect parameter usage and hard‑coded constants that lead to miscalculation of oracle‑derived values, violating the protocol’s accounting logic and exposing users to unexpected financial loss.

title: User specified slippage allows frontrunning
content: The vulnerability is an authorization and slippage manipulation flaw in the rebalance and rebalanceLite functions of the PerpDepository contract. These functions accept an arbitrary account address as a parameter that determines from which account the assets are taken, while the actual caller (msg.sender) is not required to match that address. Because any user can call the functions, an attacker can target a victim who has previously granted a non‑zero token allowance to the PerpDepository. By watching the mempool, the attacker can copy the victim’s pending rebalance transaction, increase the gas price to be mined first, and set the amountOutMinimum (the slippage protection) to zero. The attacker’s transaction then executes the Uniswap swap without any minimum‑output check, allowing the attacker to extract value from the pool while the victim’s transaction later executes with a worse price, effectively sandwiching the victim’s trade. The impact is that the victim’s token balance is reduced unexpectedly; the user receives less or no output from the swap, and the protocol suffers a loss of funds and a breach of trust. The condition for exploitation is that the victim has approved the PerpDepository to move tokens and that the rebalance call is observable in the mempool. The affected parties are any token holder who has granted allowance, as well as the overall protocol and its users. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the function signatures and the flow of funds, noting that the source account is supplied by the caller rather than derived from msg.sender and that there is no enforcement of a slippage limit. The bug can be hard to notice because the functions appear to be internal utilities and the missing slippage check does not raise an error; the transaction succeeds while silently draining value. To remediate, the contract should replace the external account parameter with msg.sender, ensuring that only the caller’s own approved balance can be used, and should enforce a reasonable amountOutMinimum or otherwise protect against zero‑slippage swaps. In generic terms, this is an authorization bypass combined with a front‑running‑friendly slippage setting, a class of vulnerability where user‑controlled parameters allow an attacker to manipulate trade execution and steal funds.
summary:
rebalance and rebalanceLite can be called by any user. Assets are taken from a user specified account address which has approved PerpDepository. If an address has a non-zero approval for PerpDepository, a frontrunner can use rebalance to transfer funds and profit by sandwiching the Uniswap pool swap.
When mint or redeem is called in UXDController, msg.sender is where the value is coming from. But rebalance allows for the caller to specify the account where funds are coming from. This means msg.sender can be any address. This allows for different scenarios where a frontrunner can profit with these steps.
1. a frontrunner detects a call of rebalance transaction in the mempool for a certain account address
2. the frontrunner duplicates the transaction but increases the gas amount (to allow frontrunning the original transaction) and changes the amountOutMinimum value to zero
3. the frontrunner can profit by sandwiching the Uniswap swap which now has no slippage setting
4. The user will lose value
An account that is used in rebalance can lose value

title: UserManager's cancelVouchInternal breaks up vouch accounting
content: The vulnerability resides in the internal function that removes a voucher relationship between a staker and a borrower. When cancelVouchInternal is executed, it correctly swaps the last element of the vouchers array into the slot of the removed voucher, but it updates the bookkeeping data with the wrong index. Specifically, the code reads the index of the removed voucher from voucherIndexes and then uses that same index to modify the vouchees array, even though voucherIndexes and vouchees are independent structures with their own ordering. Moreover, after moving the last voucher into the vacated slot, the function deletes the original voucherIndexes entry but fails to rewrite the voucherIndexes entry for the moved voucher, leaving a stale reference. As a result, the voucherIndexes mapping still points to the old position of the moved voucher, while the vouchees entry is updated using an unrelated index derived from voucherIndexes. This mismatch corrupts the accounting of locked stakes and trust values. The bug manifests whenever a voucher that is not the last element in the borrower’s vouchers list is cancelled; the subsequent insertion of a new voucher (a normal operation) causes the stale index to reference an incorrect locked amount. Consequently, trust can be reported as lower than the actual locked amount, cancellation of the old voucher may become blocked, and the staker’s funds can become effectively frozen because the protocol believes a non‑zero lock still exists. The impact is limited to the specific borrower‑staker pair whose voucher was removed, but because the protocol relies on this accounting for all trust and stake calculations, the error can propagate to other protocol invariants, allowing a borrower to retain trust that should have been removed and potentially lock additional funds from the staker. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the UserManager contract, where the auditor noticed that the array‑swap pattern used for removal did not symmetrically update both index mappings. The problem is subtle because the swap‑and‑pop technique is a common idiom and the code appears to delete the relevant mapping entry, giving a false sense of correctness. However, the stale index only becomes visible later when other functions read the outdated voucherIndexes entry, making it hard to detect through simple unit tests. To remediate the issue, the removal logic must update both the voucherIndexes entry for the moved last voucher and the corresponding vouchees entry using the correct vouchee index, ensuring that all parallel structures stay in sync after the swap. In practice this means assigning the new voucher index to voucherIndexes[borrower][lastVoucher.staker].idx and updating vouchees[lastVoucher.staker][voucheeIndexes[borrower][lastVoucher.staker]].voucherIndex accordingly. The bug belongs to the class of bookkeeping errors caused by inconsistent updates of parallel arrays or mappings after element removal, often referred to as stale pointer or index mismanagement bugs. From a user’s perspective the symptoms include a UI that still shows an active vouch after a cancellation request, a borrower’s trust value appearing higher than the actual locked stake, or a staker’s balance remaining unchanged while the protocol reports a non‑zero lock, effectively freezing the funds. The protocol’s core trust‑vouch accounting logic is violated, leading to potential financial loss and loss of confidence in the system.

title: Staker can manipulate lockedCoinAge and earn extra rewards
content: The vulnerability is an arithmetic manipulation of the lockedCoinAge accumulator used to compute reward multipliers for stakers. The root cause is that the timestamp field vouch.lastUpdated, which should be refreshed each time the voucher contributes to the lockedCoinAge total, is only updated in the unlock path and not when the lock flag is true and the voucher’s trust value is already fully locked (vouch.trust == vouch.locked). Because updateLocked adds (block.number‑_max(lastWithdrawRewards, vouch.lastUpdated)) * vouch.locked to stakers[vouch.staker].lockedCoinAge before the voucher logic runs, a malicious staker can repeatedly trigger updateLocked with lock==true while keeping vouch.lastUpdated unchanged. Each call therefore re‑adds the same block‑difference multiplied by the locked amount, allowing the attacker to grow lockedCoinAge to an arbitrarily large value simply by performing many small borrow transactions. The inflated lockedCoinAge inflates the lendingRatio used in _getRewardsMultiplier, which in turn multiplies the reward calculation, enabling the attacker to claim an arbitrarily large amount of UNION tokens – effectively draining the entire reward pool. The exploit is viable whenever a voucher’s trust is fully locked, the borrower calls borrow() with an amount above the minimum threshold, and the contract’s updateLocked function is invoked with the lock flag set to true. The affected parties include legitimate stakers who lose their expected rewards, borrowers who may see reduced incentives, and any token holder relying on the integrity of the reward distribution. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the UserManager.updateLocked logic, where the missing vouch.lastUpdated assignment was identified as a logical flaw. It is hard to notice because the lockedCoinAge variable normally grows over time, so the extra increments appear as a natural increase rather than a malicious one. The recommended fix is to always assign vouch.lastUpdated = block.number after the lockedCoinAge accumulation, regardless of the lock flag, ensuring that each block interval is counted only once and preventing the accumulator from being artificially inflated. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “state‑update omission” leading to unbounded reward multiplier escalation, violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions that rewards are proportional to genuine locked stake over time.

title: Staker can perform rewards withdrawal every
content: The vulnerability is a reward‑withdrawal timing manipulation that lets any staker repeatedly claim the full UNION reward without suffering the penalty normally applied to frozen coin age (bad‑debt) balances. The root cause lies in the reward accounting logic of _getEffectiveAmounts and _getCoinAge, where the time interval used for frozenCoinAge calculation (repayDiff) is compared against the protocol‑wide overdueBlocks threshold using the condition overdueBlocks < repayDiff. Because the variable lastWithdrawRewards, which influences repayDiff, is stored in a mapping that the staker can update by calling withdrawRewards, the attacker can keep repayDiff continuously below overdueBlocks by invoking withdrawRewards at intervals of overdueBlocks‑1 blocks or faster. As a result the frozenCoinAge accumulator remains zero even when the staker’s borrowers have overdue debt, so the effective locked amount and the reward multiplier are computed as if no bad debt existed. An attacker can therefore harvest full rewards on each claim, inflating the total UNION emission. The impact is monetary loss for all UNION holders: the extra tokens dilute the share of honest participants and effectively steal value from the protocol’s token economics. The bug manifests when a staker calls withdrawRewards frequently; from the user’s perspective the UI shows normal or even higher reward balances while the protocol’s accounting assumes a penalty that never materialises. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the reward‑distribution code, and it is hard to notice because the reward numbers appear legitimate and no explicit error is raised. To fix the problem the accounting should retain cumulative effective, locked and frozen coin‑age values across reward claims instead of resetting them on each withdrawal, and the reward period should be derived from the difference between the current block and the last claim point without allowing the claimant to manipulate the underlying timestamps. This change removes the ability to keep the frozenCoinAge counter at zero and restores the intended penalty for overdue debt, preserving the integrity of the token emission schedule.

title: WNT in depositVault can be drained by abus-
content: The contract’s createDeposit function accepts a struct called CreateDepositParams that contains fields initialLongToken, initialShortToken and executionFee. Inside the function the code determines which side of the market is the native wrapped token (WNT) by comparing market.longToken and market.shortToken to the address returned by TokenUtils.wnt. If the long side is WNT the code subtracts params.executionFee from the amount recorded for the initialLongToken, otherwise it subtracts the fee from the amount recorded for the initialShortToken. Crucially, the implementation never checks that the token supplied in initialLongToken or initialShortToken actually matches the market’s long or short token. An attacker can therefore supply a cheap token such as USDC as initialLongToken while the market’s long token is WNT. The executionFee, which can be set to any value, is then deducted from the USDC amount, but later when the attacker calls cancelDeposit the contract repays the executionFee in WNT from the depositVault. By providing a USDC amount that is equal to or larger than the vault’s WNT balance and setting executionFee to that balance, the attacker can trigger a cancelDeposit that transfers the entire WNT reserve to the attacker, effectively draining the vault. This flaw occurs whenever a market contains WNT as either its long or short token and the createDeposit function is called without proper validation of the token addresses supplied in the parameters. The vulnerability was discovered during a security audit when the auditor crafted a proof‑of‑concept test that minted USDC, used it as the initialLongToken, set a large executionFee, and successfully emptied the vault. The issue is subtle because the token transfer logic appears to handle the correct amounts, yet the mismatch between token types allows the fee to be paid out in a different, more valuable asset. The impact is a loss of all native token liquidity held by the depositVault, compromising user funds and the protocol’s economic guarantees. To remediate, the contract should enforce that initialLongToken equals market.longToken and initialShortToken equals market.shortToken before applying any fee deductions, or it should condition the fee subtraction on the actual token address being WNT. In other words, the fee must only be taken from the WNT amount that is truly deposited, preventing an attacker from swapping a low‑value token for a high‑value fee repayment.

title: Collateral cannot be claimed because there
content: The vulnerability is a claimability logic error in the collateral withdrawal path of a synthetic market contract. The contract stores a claimable amount for each user and applies a configurable claimable factor to determine how much of that amount can actually be withdrawn. By default the factor is initialised to zero and, critically, the contract does not expose any function that allows the designated config keeper to modify this factor. When a user attempts to claim collateral, the code reads the stored factor, multiplies the claimable amount by the factor (which remains zero), and then checks whether the adjusted claimable amount is greater than or equal to the amount already claimed. Because the adjusted amount is always zero, the condition is always true and the function reverts with a CollateralAlreadyClaimed error, preventing any withdrawal. This flaw originates from a missing setter for the claimable factor, a configuration key that is never made writable, and the assumption that the factor will be set elsewhere. Exploitation is straightforward: any user who is entitled to collateral – for example after a large liquidation that creates a capped price impact – will see a non‑zero claimable balance in the UI but any on‑chain claim transaction will fail, resulting in a permanent loss of principal. The impact is a loss of user funds, erosion of trust in the protocol, and potential legal exposure because the protocol promises collateral return after liquidation. The condition occurs whenever the system records a positive claimable amount, which typically happens after sizable liquidations that happen periodically in volatile markets. All users with open positions that become under‑collateralised are affected, but the most visible effect is on liquidity providers who rely on the ability to retrieve their collateral. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the reviewer noticed that the claimable factor key was never added to the list of allowed configuration keys, meaning it could never be updated from its default zero value. The bug is subtle because the UI may correctly display a claimable balance, yet the on‑chain logic silently blocks the withdrawal, making it easy to miss without a deep code review. To remediate, the contract should expose a secure setter for the claimable factor (restricted to the config keeper) and ensure the factor is initialised to a non‑zero default that reflects the intended business rule. Alternatively, the entire market module could be redeployed with corrected logic, after winding down existing positions and allowing users to withdraw their collateral under the new code. This class of bug falls under mis‑configured state variables and missing access control for critical economic parameters, leading to a denial‑of‑service style loss of funds.

title: Collateral cannot be claimed due to inverted
content: The vulnerability is an inverted comparison in the collateral‑claim routine of the market contract. When a user (or liquidity provider) attempts to claim collateral that has become claimable after a liquidation, the code retrieves the total claimable amount, applies the claimable factor and then compares the adjusted amount with the amount already claimed. The check is written as `if (adjustedClaimableAmount >= claimedAmount) revert ...`, which is the opposite of the intended logic. Because the claimed amount starts at zero, any positive adjusted claimable amount satisfies the condition and the transaction reverts with CollateralAlreadyClaimed, preventing the user from receiving any of the owed collateral. This bug originates from a simple logical error – the comparison operator was flipped – and it manifests only when the system tries to release collateral that exceeds the capped price‑impact threshold, a situation that occurs during large liquidations. An attacker does not need to act; any legitimate user who follows the normal claim flow will be blocked, resulting in principal loss as the funds remain locked in the contract. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a “Claim” button, but the transaction fails and the user receives no tokens, often with an error that suggests the collateral has already been claimed even though it has not. The issue is hard to notice because the revert message is misleading and the condition appears syntactically correct; only a careful audit or testing of edge‑case liquidation scenarios reveals that the comparison is reversed. The bug violates the core accounting assumption that claimable collateral can be withdrawn up to the amount available, breaking the contract’s financial guarantees. The recommended fix is to invert the comparison to `adjustedClaimableAmount <= claimedAmount` (or to restructure the logic so that the claim proceeds only when the adjusted amount is greater than the already claimed amount). In practice the fix may require winding down open positions, forcing LPs to withdraw their collateral, and redeploying the corrected contract.

title: Fee receiver is given twice the amount of bor-
content: The vulnerability is an accounting error that causes the fee receiver to receive twice the amount of borrowing fees that it is entitled to, while the user who opens or modifies a position is charged twice for the same fee component. The root cause lies in the calculation of the total net cost of a position change: the contract first computes a borrowingFeeAmount that already includes the portion destined for the fee receiver (borrowingFeeAmountForFeeReceiver). It then adds this full borrowingFeeAmount to the totalNetCostAmount while also adding the feeReceiverAmount, which itself already contains borrowingFeeAmountForFeeReceiver. As a result, the borrowing fee portion is counted twice – once directly and once through the feeReceiverAmount – leading to an over‑allocation of fees to the fee receiver and an over‑charging of the user. An attacker does not need to invoke a special function; the bug is triggered automatically whenever a position incurs borrowing fees. The user experiences a higher than expected cost: the UI may show a larger fee deduction, the position may be opened with less remaining collateral than anticipated, or a transaction may revert due to insufficient balance. The impact is that users lose extra funds that should have remained in their position, while the fee receiver (often the protocol treasury or a designated address) gains an unintended surplus. This condition occurs whenever the borrowing fee calculation is performed, i.e., on every leveraged trade that involves borrowing. The affected parties are borrowers, liquidity providers, and any participant relying on the protocol’s fee accounting. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the fee distribution logic and identified that the totalNetCostAmount expression summed both fees.feeReceiverAmount and fees.borrowingFeeAmount, despite the latter already being partially accounted for in the former. The bug is subtle because the individual fee components appear correct in isolation, and the double counting only becomes evident when the aggregate cost is compared against expected values. To remediate the problem, the totalNetCostAmount should be recomputed using the already‑adjusted pool fee amount (fees.feeAmountForPool) instead of adding the raw borrowingFeeAmount again, or alternatively subtract the duplicated portion from the sum. This change ensures that each fee component is counted exactly once, preserving the intended economic model where the user pays the correct fee and the fee receiver receives only its rightful share. The flaw belongs to the class of double‑counting or over‑allocation bugs in financial smart contracts, where a value is inadvertently added multiple times to an aggregate, breaking accounting invariants and leading to fund loss for end users.

title: Accounting breaks if end market appears mul-
content: The vulnerability is an accounting inconsistency that occurs during multi‑hop token swaps when a market appears more than once in the swap path. The swap routine iterates over an array of markets and calls an internal _swap function for each hop. Inside _swap the contract updates the internal pool balance for the output token and, unless the receiver address equals the market’s own token contract, it transfers the calculated amountOut to the receiver. When the next hop in the path is the destination market, the condition "receiver != marketToken" evaluates to false, so the transfer is skipped, but the accounting variables are still incremented as if the tokens had been moved. Consequently the destination market’s internal accounting shows a higher token balance than the actual token holdings, while subsequent markets record lower balances than they truly possess. This mismatch can be triggered deliberately by an attacker who performs a series of swaps that loop through the same market multiple times, paying the normal swap fees to avoid detection. By repeatedly causing the same market to be processed as both an intermediate and final hop, the attacker can drain the pool’s collateral tokens without the contract detecting the loss, leading to a state where liquidity providers cannot withdraw their positions because token transfers revert due to insufficient balance. The impact is a loss of funds for users attempting to exit positions, under‑collateralisation of the market, and a breakdown of the protocol’s accounting guarantees. The issue manifests only when the swap path contains duplicate market entries and the final hop points to a market that has already been visited earlier in the same transaction. All participants that rely on accurate pool balances – liquidity providers, traders, and the protocol’s risk engine – are affected. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the swap logic, where the auditor noticed that the conditional transfer check does not consider the case where the receiver is the market token itself, yet the accounting update is unconditional. Because the token balances appear correct on‑chain until a withdrawal is attempted, the problem can remain hidden for extended periods, especially in low‑volume markets. The proper fix is to make the loop aware that it is processing the final hop and either skip the accounting update for that hop or adjust the condition so that token transfers and balance updates stay in sync. In other words, the contract should only update internal accounting when an actual token transfer occurs, or explicitly handle the case where the receiver is the market token to prevent phantom token creation. This class of bug is a token accounting mismatch caused by inconsistent state updates during multi‑step swaps, leading to “funds disappear” symptoms where users see zero balances or failed withdrawals despite the protocol reporting positive reserves.
summary:
accounting breaks
When doing a swap, every market in the provided array of markets has _swap() called, with the input token amount currently residing in the market address of the market, which converts the token to the output token. When the next market isn't array, to be processed on the next iteration, and the pool's balance of input/output market, no transfer is done, but the balance is still updated (to account for tokens being taken out as either a swap order, or a swap into a position's collateral token).
market appears multiple times in the swap path, markets that appear in the array, after the extra destination market, will have updated their accounting of received tokens, without actually receiving tokens.
Token accounting will be broken, because the destination market will have extra tokens that its tracking of its own pool amounts doesn't know about (and can't be updated to know about), and subsequent markets in the chain will have fewer tokens than their pool amount accounting believes it does.
An attacker, if they're willing to incur the expense of swap fees, can perform swaps back and forth through the same market multiple times (to minimize swap impact fees), and cause a pool to have zero collateral tokens remaining, meaning LP market tokens are unable to withdraw their funds because token transfers will revert, and nobody will be able to exit their positions for the affected markets, since no collateral tokens will be available. There also will be an undercollateralization, because the reserves calculation will be wrong.
Even through normal use, if a user does this, they'll be able to get their funds, since LPs are providing swap liquidity, but when it comes time to wind down the market, the last to withdraw will not be able to get their funds.
Tokens aren't transferred to the next market if the next market is the destination market of the swap:
```solidity
// File: gmx-synthetics/contracts/swap/SwapUtils.sol : SwapUtils._swap()
#1
// the amountOut value includes the positive price impact amount
if (_params.receiver != _params.market.marketToken) {
    MarketToken(payable(_params.market.marketToken)).transferOut(
        cache.tokenOut,
        _params.receiver,
        cache.amountOut,
        _params.shouldUnwrapNativeToken
    );
}
cts/swap/SwapUtils.sol#L240-L248
```

title: Pool value calculation uses wrong portion of
content: The vulnerability is an accounting error in the function that calculates the total value of a liquidity pool. The code aggregates the long and short token USD values and then adds the borrowing fees multiplied by a factor that represents the portion of fees destined for the fee‑receiver address. Borrowing fees are split into two components: the amount that belongs to the pool and the amount that is sent to a designated fee‑receiver. By applying the fee‑receiver factor to the total borrowing fees, the calculation actually adds the fee‑receiver’s share instead of the pool’s share. Consequently the reported pool value is inflated by the fee‑receiver portion and the pool’s true share of the fees is omitted. This mis‑calculation is used by getPoolValue() to determine how many pool shares to mint on deposit and how many collateral tokens to return on withdrawal, as well as to display market token valuations. When a user deposits collateral, the contract may mint more shares than the economic value warrants, allowing the user to later withdraw a larger amount of collateral than they are entitled to; conversely, other users may receive fewer shares and suffer a principal loss. The impact is that liquidity providers can experience unexpected gains or losses, the accounting invariants of the protocol are broken, and the overall trust in the pool’s pricing is compromised. The bug manifests whenever borrowing fees are present and the fee‑receiver factor is non‑zero, i.e., during normal operation of leveraged positions that generate fees. It was discovered during a manual audit of the market utilities library, where the auditor noticed that the factor was applied to the total fee amount rather than to the fee‑receiver portion. The error can be subtle because the pool still appears to function and the discrepancy may be small on a per‑transaction basis, making it hard to detect without precise accounting checks. The correct fix is to subtract the fee‑receiver’s share from the total borrowing fees, or equivalently add only the pool’s portion of the fees, as shown by replacing the line that adds Precision.applyFactor(totalBorrowingFees, feeReceiverFactor) with totalBorrowingFees minus that factor. This restores the proper accounting of pool value, ensures that share minting and redemption reflect the true economic contribution, and prevents inadvertent over‑ or under‑payment to liquidity providers. The issue belongs to the class of incorrect fee allocation bugs where a contract mistakenly attributes revenue to the wrong stakeholder, violating business logic that assumes fees are split according to predefined ratios.

title: Limit orders can be used to get a free look
content: The vulnerability is a price‑manipulation weakness in the limit‑order workflow of the GMX synthetic exchange. The contract allows a user to call the updateOrder function, which immediately rewrites the orderUpdatedAtBlock field without any enforced waiting period before the order can be executed by a keeper. Execution of a limit order is permitted only when the oracle price that the keeper supplies is signed for a block range that is strictly greater than the last update block. Because the oracle signs future prices for a range of blocks, there is an inherent time gap between when a price for block N is archived and when the next price for block N+1…N+k becomes available. An attacker can observe the upcoming signed price, then repeatedly update the order (for example by changing the amount by one wei) in each block, keeping the order’s last‑updated block just behind the oracle’s minimum block number. This “free look” lets the attacker decide in the next block whether the price is favorable and, if so, let the keeper execute the order; if not, the attacker can update again. The root cause is the absence of a minimum block‑age or delay constraint on order updates, combined with the oracle’s future‑price signing scheme. Exploitation requires monitoring the oracle’s price feed, sending cheap update transactions each block, and finally allowing execution when the price moves in the attacker’s favor. The impact is that the counter‑party on the opposite side of the trade receives a worse price, effectively losing capital, while the attacker extracts value without paying the usual market spread. This can be especially profitable for large positions or when price gaps are significant enough to outweigh the gas cost of the updates. The issue manifests when a user places a limit‑decrease or limit‑swap order that relies on future oracle prices; the user may notice that their order can be tweaked repeatedly and that the execution seems delayed until a favorable price appears, which is contrary to the expectation that the order should execute as soon as the price condition is met. The problem was discovered during a security audit that examined the validateOracleBlockNumbers checks and noticed that the updateOrder function modifies orderUpdatedAtBlock directly, bypassing any delay logic. Because the behaviour appears normal – the contract simply allows order updates – it can be hard to spot without tracing the timing relationship between updates and oracle block numbers. To remediate, the protocol should enforce a minimum number of blocks (or a time‑lock) between the last order update and any subsequent update, similar to the REQUEST_EXPIRATION_BLOCK_AGE used for market‑order cancellations, or otherwise separate the update and execution phases so that an attacker cannot continuously shift the order’s timestamp to gain a free look at future prices. This class of bug falls under mutable order parameters with insufficient time‑locking, leading to price‑manipulation or free‑look attacks.

title: Incomplete error handling causes execution
content: The vulnerability is an incomplete error‑handling flaw in the GMX protocol’s callback mechanism. When a user‑controlled contract is invoked as a callback for deposit, withdrawal, order execution or order cancellation, the protocol wraps the call in a try/catch block and forwards any revert data to ErrorUtils.getRevertMessage. This helper assumes the revert follows the standard Solidity Error(string) ABI layout and directly decodes the payload with abi.decode. A malicious callback can deliberately craft a revert payload that passes the selector check (0x08c379a0) but contains malformed offset or length fields that cause abi.decode to revert itself. Because the decode is performed inside the catch clause, the failure propagates and makes the outer execution or cancellation revert as well. The bug is triggered only when the attacker supplies such a malformed revert reason; otherwise normal callbacks work. It was discovered during a manual audit of the error‑handling utilities, where the auditor noticed that the function does not validate the size of the encoded data before decoding. The issue is subtle because the revert still appears to be a regular error string, so developers may not notice that the decoding step itself can fail. Exploitation allows an attacker to block keepers from successfully executing or cancelling orders by forcing the error‑handling routine to revert on every callback. Consequently, orders remain in an unprocessed state, enabling the attacker to time order execution or cancellation to their advantage, and keepers repeatedly spend gas on transactions that always revert, potentially draining their funds. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are missing order updates, “nothing happens” when trying to execute or cancel, and unexpected loss of keeper rewards. The underlying class of bug is unsafe parsing of external data without bounds checking, a form of unchecked revert‑message decoding. The recommended mitigation is to validate that the offset and length fields extracted from the revert payload are smaller than the total payload size before calling abi.decode, or to replace the direct decode with a safer parsing routine that gracefully handles malformed data.

title: Incorrect nextOpenInterestvalues set for priceImpact
content: An incorrect calculation of the next open‑interest values in the pricing utility causes the price‑impact algorithm to use a zero value for the side that did not receive the user’s trade. The function getNextOpenInterestParams receives the current long and short open‑interest and a flag indicating whether the trade is long. It only updates nextLongOpenInterest when the trade is long, or nextShortOpenInterest when the trade is short, leaving the other variable at its default of 0. Consequently, when the market already has a large open‑interest on the opposite side, the subsequent price‑impact formula compares the current long and short totals with a next‑side value of zero. This makes the boolean isSameSideRebalance evaluate incorrectly, flips the sign of the price‑impact, and inflates its magnitude. A user who should receive a positive impact for adding liquidity instead sees a large negative impact, effectively losing funds. The bug manifests whenever a trade changes the open‑interest on one side while the opposite side retains a non‑zero balance, especially in markets with high total open‑interest. It affects any participant who relies on the price‑impact feedback, the protocol’s accounting, and ultimately the funds held in the contract. The issue was uncovered during a manual audit of the PositionPricingUtils contract, where the logical flow of getNextOpenInterestParams was examined and the missing assignment was identified. Because the price‑impact is a derived value, the error can be subtle and may only become apparent under extreme market conditions, making it hard to detect through routine testing. The proper fix is to compute both nextLongOpenInterest and nextShortOpenInterest based on the trade size: the side matching the trade direction should be increased by the absolute USD delta, while the opposite side should retain its current value. This ensures that the price‑impact calculation receives accurate next‑state values and the boolean isSameSideRebalance reflects the true market state. In generic terms, the vulnerability is a state‑update omission that leads to an incorrect accounting of future market exposure, causing erroneous pricing and potential loss of user capital.

title: Incorrect parameter ordering in function call
content: The vulnerability is a logical error caused by passing arguments to a cross‑contract function in the wrong order. In PositionUtils.updateTotalBorrowing the developer forwards the current position's borrowingFactor and sizeInUsd to MarketUtils.updateTotalBorrowing, but the MarketUtils signature expects the previous position size first and the previous borrowing factor second. Because these two values are swapped, the internal accounting routine receives a mismatched size and factor, leading to an incorrect calculation of the market's total borrowing amount. This miscalculation can occur whenever a position is modified – for example when a trader increases or decreases the size of a position – because the updateTotalBorrowing helper is invoked on every size change. The root cause is a simple parameter ordering mistake that compiles without error and therefore may remain unnoticed during normal testing. Exploitation does not require a malicious transaction; any legitimate position update will feed wrong data into the accounting logic, causing the protocol to record either a higher or lower total borrowing than actually exists. The impact is that the protocol’s risk metrics become inaccurate, potentially allowing positions to become under‑collateralised or causing the system to allocate too much borrowing capacity. Users may observe that their borrowing balance changes unexpectedly, that fees are higher than anticipated, or that their position is liquidated without a clear reason. From a protocol perspective, the total borrowing figure stored in the DataStore diverges from the true economic state, breaking the fundamental accounting invariants on which the market relies. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the GMX synthetics contracts, where the auditor noticed that the argument list in PositionUtils did not match the definition in MarketUtils. Because the bug does not trigger a revert, it can be hard to spot without careful code review or runtime accounting checks. To remediate the problem, the call in PositionUtils must be rewritten so that the arguments are passed in the exact order defined by MarketUtils.updateTotalBorrowing – i.e., previous position size first, then previous borrowing factor – and the change should be covered by unit tests that verify the total borrowing calculation against known inputs. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of parameter‑ordering mistakes that lead to accounting errors, and fixing it restores the integrity of the borrowing accounting, ensuring that users receive the correct borrowing updates and that the protocol’s risk model remains sound.
summary:
The ordering of parameters in function call made in updateTotalBorrowing() in PositionUtils.sol is incorrect. The function call of updateTotalBorrowing() in PositionUtils.sol has a different parameter ordering to the one defined in the actual function being called in MarketUtils.sol. More specifically, params.position.borrowingFactor() and params.position.sizeInUsd() are swapped around.

Updating the total borrowing function with incorrect parameter values would upset the internal accounting of the system and would result in loss of user funds.

Loc:
n/gmx-synthetics/contracts/position/PositionUtils.sol#L460-L474
gmx-synthetics/contracts/market/MarketUtils.sol#L1773-L1793

In PositionUtils.sol
```solidity
function updateTotalBorrowing(
    PositionUtils.UpdatePositionParams memory params,
    uint256 nextPositionSizeInUsd,
    uint256 nextPositionBorrowingFactor
) internal {
    MarketUtils.updateTotalBorrowing(
        params.contracts.dataStore,
        params.market.marketToken,
        params.position.isLong(),
        params.position.borrowingFactor(),
        params.position.sizeInUsd(),
        nextPositionSizeInUsd,
        nextPositionBorrowingFactor
    );

```

In MarketUtils.sol
```solidity
function updateTotalBorrowing(
    DataStore dataStore,
    address market,
    bool isLong,
    uint256 prevPositionSizeInUsd,
    uint256 prevPositionBorrowingFactor,
    uint256 nextPositionSizeInUsd,
    uint256 nextPositionBorrowingFactor
) external {
    uint256 totalBorrowing = getNextTotalBorrowing(
        dataStore,
        market,
        isLong,
        prevPositionSizeInUsd,
        prevPositionBorrowingFactor,
        nextPositionSizeInUsd,
        nextPositionBorrowingFactor
    );
    setTotalBorrowing(dataStore, market, isLong, totalBorrowing);
}
```

title: No slippage for withdrawal without swap
content: The vulnerability originates from the withdrawal routine of a market contract that allows liquidity providers to burn LP tokens and receive the underlying long and short tokens. When a user initiates a withdrawal, they may optionally supply swap paths (longTokenSwapPath and shortTokenSwapPath) to convert the received tokens into other assets. If the user does not provide any swap path, the contract still invokes the generic SwapUtils.swap function, but because the path array is empty the function simply transfers the tokens to the receiver without performing any slippage verification. The contract accepts user‑specified minimum amounts (minLongTokenAmount and minShortTokenAmount) intended to protect against adverse price movement, yet there is no post‑transfer check that the actual received amounts satisfy these minima when no swap path is supplied. Consequently, a malicious actor who can front‑run the transaction can manipulate the market price or token balances between the time the withdrawal is signed and when it is executed, causing the user to receive fewer long or short tokens than expected. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a successful withdrawal but the balance of the withdrawn token may be lower than anticipated, or in extreme cases the user may receive zero of one token type, leading to a feeling that funds have disappeared. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the withdrawal logic and noticed the absence of a slippage guard in the branch where swap paths are omitted. It is difficult to notice because the same swap function is called in both cases, and the missing check is hidden behind an empty array condition rather than an explicit omission. The bug belongs to the class of “missing slippage protection” or “unchecked output amount” vulnerabilities, where a contract fails to enforce user‑defined lower bounds on token outputs. To remediate, the withdrawal implementation should, after the token transfer, compare the actual amounts received with minLongTokenAmount and minShortTokenAmount and revert the transaction if either bound is not met, thereby restoring the intended slippage protection for both swapped and non‑swapped withdrawals.
summary:
No slippage for withdrawal without swapping path. When user withdraws, he should provide amount of LP tokens, that he wants to burn. According to that amount, output amount of long and short tokens of the market will be calculated for him.

In case if user wants to swap this short/long tokens to another tokens, then he can provide longTokenSwapPath/shortTokenSwapPath array. If he doesn't want to swap them, but just receive without swapping, he doesn't provide that array. No matter if he provided swap path or no, swapping will be called.

Then inside SwapUtils.swap in case if no swap path is provided, then function will just send tokens to receiver. One of parameters of SwapUtils.swap function is minOutputAmount. This parameter is important as it stands as slippage protection. In case if swap path is not provided, then amount will not be checked for that slippage. If swap path present, then slippage check will be done. So in case if no swap path is provided, then slippage provided by user will not be checked, as inside WithdrawalUtils._executeWithdrawal there is no any check that user received minShortTokenAmount and minLongTokenAmount. Because of that user can be frontrunned and lose some funds. There is no slippage check in case if user doesn't provide swap path.

title: Incorrect function call leads to stale borrow
content: The vulnerability consists of an inaccurate fee calculation caused by calling a stale state‑reading function when determining total borrowing fees for a market. The contract’s getTotalBorrowingFees routine multiplies the current open interest by a cumulative borrowing factor obtained from getCumulativeBorrowingFactor and then subtracts the total borrowing amount. However, getCumulativeBorrowingFactor returns the factor as of the last explicit update and does not incorporate the borrowing factor that has accrued since that timestamp. The correct value requires adding the pending delta, which is provided by getNextCumulativeBorrowingFactor. Because the stale factor is used, the resulting fee amount under‑represents the true fees owed. This mis‑calculation occurs every time the fee‑query function is invoked, typically during liquidity‑provider reward distribution or when a user queries pending fees. The root cause is a logical error in the accounting flow: a time‑dependent variable is read without applying the elapsed‑time adjustment, leading to stale data being used in a financial formula. From an attacker’s perspective the bug does not require a direct exploit; instead it allows borrowers to effectively pay fewer fees than the protocol intends, while liquidity providers receive a token that reflects a lower pool value because pending fees are omitted from the accounting. The impact is a systematic under‑payment of fees, which translates into reduced returns for LPs, potential mis‑pricing of the pool’s share token, and a gradual erosion of the protocol’s revenue model. The issue is observable from the user’s point of view as a discrepancy between expected and actual earnings: a liquidity provider may notice that their LP token balance or the amount received on withdrawal is lower than anticipated, or that the pool’s total value seems to stagnate despite ongoing borrowing activity. The problem was discovered during a manual audit when the reviewer compared the fee‑calculation logic against the intended economic model and identified that the function used to fetch the borrowing factor did not account for the elapsed seconds since the last update. The bug can be hard to spot because the contract still returns a numeric fee value that appears plausible at a single snapshot, and the UI may display the fee without indicating that it is stale. The appropriate remediation is to replace the call to getCumulativeBorrowingFactor with getNextCumulativeBorrowingFactor (or an equivalent calculation that adds the pending delta) so that the fee computation always reflects the most recent borrowing factor, thereby ensuring accurate accounting and protecting LP interests. In broader terms, this is a classic case of stale‑state usage in a time‑sensitive financial contract, where failing to incorporate the latest state leads to incorrect accounting and economic loss.

title: Unpaid funding fees from wrong calculation
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect funding‑fee accounting bug in the market contract that determines how much a trader must pay to cover the funding cost of an open position. The root cause is that the calculation uses the combined open interest of both the long and short token pools when dividing the total funding amount (cache.fundingUsd). This division produces a single value (cache.fundingUsdForLongCollateral) that is then applied to both collateral types, even though a trader can only settle the fee with the collateral token of his own position. Because the fee is spread over the total interest of both sides, the portion that each trader actually pays is only a fraction of the amount that should be collected. An attacker can exploit this by opening a position and simply paying the reduced fee, effectively receiving the remainder of the funding payment for free. The impact is twofold: first, the protocol’s accounting becomes inconsistent over time, as the pool that should receive the full funding amount receives only a partial payment, which can eventually lead to insolvency or unexpected shortfalls. Second, the protocol loses revenue because users consistently under‑pay the fees they owe, reducing the variable fundingAmountPerSizePortion that should be deducted from the collateral. The bug manifests only when a user is required to pay funding fees; it does not affect the claim path where users receive funding, because both sides can be claimed. It is triggered whenever a position is open and the funding interval elapses, and it affects any trader, liquidity provider, or downstream protocol that relies on correct fee collection. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the MarketUtils library, where the auditor noticed that the fee‑payment path used the total open interest instead of the per‑side interest, a subtle mistake that does not raise immediate errors in the UI. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a funding fee amount, but the actual balance deducted from the trader’s collateral is smaller than expected, leading to a situation where “my balance does not decrease as much as the fee shown” or “the protocol seems to give me extra funds”. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of accounting misallocation or fee‑calculation errors, where a shared pool metric is incorrectly applied to individual participants. To remediate the issue the funding‑fee formula should be rewritten so that the fee owed by a trader is proportional only to the open interest of the token they are using as collateral, rather than the aggregate of both sides. In practice this means computing separate funding amounts for long and short collateral pools and charging each trader the exact amount due for their specific side, thereby restoring correct accounting and preventing revenue leakage.
summary:
The vulnerability starts at the function getNextFundingAmountPerSize: cts/market/MarketUtils.sol#L912. Basically, GMX is handling incorrectly the way on how they calculate the FundingFees to be paid because they calculate the amount using the getOpenInterest from both the short and long tokens.

The detailed issue here is that GMX is incorrectly handling the calculation with the getOpenInterest (the open Interest) of the two tokens, short and long. They are dividing the cache.fundingUsd for the interest of the two tokens: cts/market/MarketUtils.sol#L953-L957. After dividing, you get the cache.fundingUsdForLongCollateral which is basically the amount that has to be paid or paidTo for any of both collaterals and positions. That is a big problem in one case, when users need to pay those fees. When the user does have to pay the fundingFees. Because customers can only pay those fundingFees for their collateral token, not for both.

As said, this is not an issue when users do receive the fundingFees because you can claim both tokens, but it is an issue when paying the fees. This will result in less fundingFees being paid by users.

2 Impacts:
1. A mismatch in the pools accounting will occur over time which might have unexpected results in terms of insolvencies.
2. High because users are not paying the fees that they should pay, so there is an economic damage. Specifically because the bug just described, does reduce the variable fundingAmountPerSizePortion : cts/market/MarketUtils.sol#L963-L966 which is what user pays for the collateral token. As said before, the amounts are being divided by the entire interest, therefore, just a small part only a portion of the FundingFees will be paid, meanwhile the entire amount can be claimed.

title: Creating an order of type MarketIncrease opens
content: The vulnerability is an unbounded swap path length in the createOrder function for market‑increase orders. When a user creates a MarketIncrease order, the contract records the initial collateral and, if the collateral token is not the native wrapped token, it also records a separate execution‑fee transfer. The function does not limit the size of the address[] swapPath supplied in the order parameters. An attacker can provide a swapPath that is deliberately long, approaching the block gas limit. During order execution the contract invokes a callback contract supplied by the caller; the callback consumes the remaining gas and can exceed the block’s gas limit, causing the execution to revert. Because the order remains pending, the price oracle values used for the order become stale after several blocks. When the attacker later modifies the callback’s gas usage (for example by flipping a switch) the order can be executed again, this time with the old price data. The result is that the attacker can open a leveraged position at a price that no longer reflects the market, effectively allowing a trade with no risk or with an artificial profit. From a user’s perspective the order appears to be created successfully, but the first execution fails with an out‑of‑gas error, the order stays in the system, and later it is filled at a price that is different from the one shown at the time of creation, leading to unexpected gains or losses. The impact is that the protocol’s accounting assumptions about price freshness and collateral adequacy are broken, enabling an attacker to extract value without providing the expected risk. The issue occurs only for MarketIncrease orders that use a custom swapPath and a callback contract; other order types are not affected because they either do not record a separate execution fee or they have a fixed swap path length. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit when the reviewer noticed that the swapPath array is accepted without any length check and that the callback gas limit is configurable by the caller. It is hard to notice because the contract’s normal operation works with short paths, and the gas‑limit exhaustion only manifests under extreme, deliberately crafted inputs. The recommended mitigation is to enforce a maximum length on the swapPath (for example, require(swapPath.length < MAX_PATH_LENGTH)) and to validate that the callback gas limit cannot be set to a value that would cause the transaction to exceed the block gas limit. This prevents the creation of orders that can be forced to execute with stale prices and eliminates the risk of free or risk‑free trades caused by gas‑limit manipulation.

title: Underestimated gas estimation for executing
content: The vulnerability is an under‑estimation of the gas required to execute a withdrawal request. The contract uses a helper function that adds a static gas limit and the caller‑provided callback gas limit, but it ignores the additional gas that token‑swap operations consume at the end of the withdrawal flow. Because the estimated gas is lower than the real consumption, the validation step that checks whether the execution fee supplied by the user covers the estimated gas accepts fees that are insufficient for the actual work. When a keeper later calls the execution function, the protocol pays the keeper only the fee that was declared, which may be far below the gas actually spent on the swap. Consequently the keeper is under‑compensated and may refuse to execute, causing the withdrawal to stall or revert. From the user’s perspective the withdrawal appears to be submitted successfully, the fee they paid looks reasonable, but the funds never arrive or the transaction fails with an out‑of‑gas error, leaving the user with a pending request and no refund. The issue is discovered during a manual audit that compared the gas‑estimation logic for deposits (which correctly includes swap gas) with the withdrawal path and noticed the missing component. It is hard to notice because the estimation function is internal and the discrepancy only manifests when the swap is large enough to exceed the static margin, a condition that may not be reproduced in simple unit tests. The root cause is a logical omission: the gas model assumes that withdrawals never perform token swaps, while the actual implementation does. The class of bug is a gas‑estimation mis‑calculation that leads to economic under‑payment and potential denial‑of‑service. To remediate, the estimation routine should be extended to add the expected gas cost of the swap steps, for example by reusing the same methodology applied to deposit estimation or by measuring the swap gas in a sandbox and adding a safety margin. This ensures that the execution fee validation reflects the true cost, that keepers receive fair compensation, and that users’ withdrawals succeed without unexpected failures.
summary:
The GasUtils.estimateExecuteWithdrawalGasLimit function underestimates the gas
estimation for withdrawal execution, as it does not take into account token swaps,
unlike the gas estimation in the GasUtils.estimateExecuteDepositGasLimit function
(used to estimate executing deposits).
When creating a withdrawal request, the WithdrawalUtils.createWithdrawal
function estimates the gas required to execute the withdrawal and validates that
the paid execution fee (params.executionFee) is sufficient to cover the estimated
gas and to compensate the keeper executing the withdrawal fairly.
However, the GasUtils.estimateExecuteWithdrawalGasLimit function used to
estimate the gas for executing withdrawals does not account for token swaps that
can occur at the end of the withdrawal logic and therefore underestimates the gas
estimation.
Token swaps are performed in the WithdrawalUtils._executeWithdrawal function in
lines 354 and 365.
The keeper executing withdrawals receives fewer execution fees and is not fully
compensated for the gas spent. Moreover, users can pay fewer execution fees than
expected and required.

The gas estimate calculated in the GasUtils.estimateExecuteWithdrawalGasLimit

title: ADL operations do not have any slippage protection
content: The vulnerability consists of missing slippage protection on Auto‑Deleveraging (ADL) operations. When the ADL keeper creates an ADL order it builds a market‑decrease order with the acceptable price set to an extreme value (zero for longs, the maximum uint256 for shorts) and the minimum output amount forced to zero. Because the order does not enforce any price ceiling or output floor, the execution can occur at any market price, even if the price has moved dramatically due to a spike or a cascade of exits. The root cause is that the ADL utility function creates the order without referencing the position’s entry price or a bounded impact factor, and the only post‑execution checks relate to global metrics rather than the individual position’s profitability. An attacker or a malicious keeper could trigger the ADL order when the market price is unfavorable, causing the user’s expected gain to be eroded or turned into a loss. From a user’s point of view the contract may appear to have successfully closed the position, but the UI will show that the received amount is far lower than anticipated, sometimes even zero, leading to a sudden disappearance of funds. This situation can arise when the price impact factor becomes large – for example, after a rapid price surge combined with many simultaneous ADL executions following mass exits. The affected parties are any traders whose positions are subject to ADL, the protocol that promises fair liquidation, and ultimately the end‑users who lose expected proceeds. The issue was identified during a manual audit that inspected the ADL order construction and noticed the absence of any slippage guard. It is difficult to notice in normal operation because ADL is performed by an internal keeper and the contract does not emit explicit warnings about the lack of price limits. To remediate the problem the protocol should introduce a maximum position impact factor for ADL, similar to the existing limit for liquidations, and enforce a non‑zero minimum output amount or a bounded acceptable price that reflects the position’s entry price. This change would ensure that ADL executions cannot arbitrarily consume the user’s gains and would align the execution with the intended economic guarantees of the system.
summary:
ADL operations do not have any slippage protection. ADL orders, generated by the ADL keeper, are forced to allow unlimited slippage, which means the user may get a lot less than they deserve.

There may be a large price impact associated with the ADL order, causing the user's large gain to become a loss, if the price impact factor is large enough, which may be the case if the price suddenly spikes up a lot, and there are many ADL operations after a lot of users exit their positions.

Any price is allowed, and the minimum output amount is set to zero:
```solidity
// File: gmx-synthetics/contracts/adl/AdlUtils.sol : AdlUtils.createAdlOrder()

    Order.OrderType.MarketDecrease, // orderType
    Order.DecreasePositionSwapType.NoSwap, // decreasePositionSwapType
    params.sizeDeltaUsd, // sizeDeltaUsd
    0, // initialCollateralDeltaAmount
    0, // triggerPrice
    position.isLong() ? 0 : type(uint256).max, // acceptablePrice
    0, // executionFee
    0, // callbackGasLimit
    0, // minOutputAmount
    params.updatedAtBlock // updatedAtBlock
```
