cts/adl/AdlUtils.sol#L141-L153

The only checks after the ADL order completes are related to global metrics, not position-specific ones.

title: Tracking of the latest ADL block use the wrong block number on Arbitrum
content: The vulnerability stems from the contract’s reliance on the native block identifier when tracking the most recent Automated Deleveraging (ADL) block on Arbitrum. Instead of using the layer‑2 specific block number provided by the Chain abstraction, the code records block.timestamp (or block.number) which on Arbitrum reflects the L1 block timestamp or L1 block number. Because L1 blocks are produced far more slowly than L2 blocks, the stored value is dramatically older than the actual L2 block height that the oracle uses for price timestamps. Consequently, when the protocol later checks whether ADL should be enabled, it compares the stale L1 block number against fresh L2 oracle block numbers and incorrectly determines that the ADL condition is satisfied. This logic error allows the ADL keeper to execute ADL orders at any time, even when market conditions do not warrant liquidation. From a user’s perspective, positions may be closed or liquidated unexpectedly, balances can drop to zero, and refunds that should be withheld may be processed, violating the expected accounting guarantees of the platform. The issue was uncovered during a security audit when the reviewer noticed the mismatch between the block source used for ADL state updates and the rest of the code base, which consistently calls Chain.currentBlockNumber(). The bug is subtle because both block.timestamp and block.number are valid Solidity globals, and on many EVM chains they correspond to the same block height, making the discrepancy easy to overlook in testing. The impact is high: any user with an open position can suffer premature ADL execution, leading to potential loss of capital and erosion of trust in the protocol’s safety mechanisms. The fix is conceptually straightforward – replace the direct use of block.timestamp/block.number with the Chain.currentBlockNumber() abstraction wherever the latest ADL block is recorded, ensuring that the same L2 reference is used throughout the system. This aligns the ADL enablement check with the oracle’s L2 timestamps and restores the intended business logic that ADL only triggers under genuine over‑exposure conditions.

title: Keepers can be forced to waste gas with long revert strings in callbacks
content: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service style gas exhaustion that occurs when a contract executes a user‑provided callback inside a try‑catch block with a fixed gas stipend (callbackGasLimit). The callback is intended to be harmless, but if the external contract deliberately reverts with an extremely long error string, the revert handling code must (1) execute the failing call, (2) decode the revert data to obtain the message, and (3) emit an event that includes the same message. Each of these three steps consumes gas proportional to the length of the revert string, effectively tripling the gas cost of the callback. Because keepers (off‑chain bots that execute orders) allocate a budget based on an estimate that assumes a modest revert message, a malicious user can inflate the revert string up to the full callbackGasLimit, causing the keeper to spend far more gas than anticipated. This can happen during order cancellation, frozen‑order handling, or any lifecycle step that invokes a user‑supplied callback. The affected parties are the keepers that run the protocol, the protocol itself (which may fail to process orders), and ultimately users whose orders are delayed or blocked, leading to missed trading opportunities or price‑impact manipulation. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the callback wrapper logic and measured gas consumption of the revert‑message extraction routine. It is hard to notice because the contract still functions correctly when callbacks succeed; only when a deliberately crafted revert occurs does the gas usage spike, and the extra cost is hidden inside the internal error‑handling path. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are orders that appear to be stuck, callbacks that emit large error strings, and keepers reporting out‑of‑gas failures despite having sufficient gas for the normal path. Users expect an order to be cancelled or frozen promptly, but instead the transaction reverts with a long message and no state change, effectively making funds unavailable until the price moves to a more favorable level. This violates the protocol’s accounting assumptions that callbacks are cheap and cannot affect the economic outcome of an order. The conceptual fix is to account for the worst‑case gas cost of the revert handling during gas estimation, for example by multiplying the estimated callback gas by three or by imposing a maximum length on revert strings before emitting them. Alternatively, the protocol could avoid propagating user‑provided revert messages in events or could cap the gas used for decoding and emitting error data, thereby preventing a malicious actor from forcing excessive gas consumption.

title: Limit orders are broken when there are price gaps
content: The vulnerability concerns limit and stop‑loss orders that rely on two oracle‑provided prices – a primary and a secondary price – to be on opposite sides of the user‑specified trigger price. The contract enforces a strict “straddle” rule: the earlier price must be on one side of the trigger and the later price on the other side. When a market moves sharply between the block in which the order is submitted and the next block, both oracle prices can end up on the same side of the trigger (for example, both above the trigger for a decreasing order). Because the validation logic does not account for such price gaps, the condition fails and the function reverts with an InvalidOrderPrices error. This means the order never executes even though the user’s stop‑loss or limit condition was mathematically satisfied before the price jump. The impact is that a user who expected their position to be closed or reduced remains fully exposed, potentially leading to liquidation or unexpected loss of funds. The bug manifests only when the oracle price experiences a discontinuity large enough to push both prices beyond the trigger, a scenario that is rare in normal market conditions and therefore easy to miss during routine testing. From the user’s perspective the order appears to be pending and then silently disappears or reverts, with no execution and no clear error message in the UI, creating confusion and a false sense of security. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the order‑execution path and identified that the straddle check could reject valid orders under price‑gap conditions. It belongs to a class of input‑validation bugs where overly strict constraints reject legitimate inputs, specifically a price‑gap handling flaw. To remediate, the contract should relax the straddle requirement when both prices are worse than the trigger and simply use the trigger price as the execution price, thereby allowing the order to be fulfilled even in the presence of abrupt price movements. This change aligns the on‑chain logic with the intended business rule that a limit or stop‑loss order should execute whenever the market price crosses the trigger, regardless of how the crossing occurs.

title: Malicious revert reasons with faked lengths can disrupt order execution
content: The vulnerability is an out‑of‑gas denial‑of‑service caused by maliciously crafted revert reasons in user‑supplied callbacks that are executed during order processing. When a callback reverts, the protocol captures the revert data and attempts to decode it as a Solidity string using abi.decode(result,(string)). The decode routine reads the first 32‑byte word as the declared length of the string and then reads that many bytes from memory. Because the revert data is stored in a mutable memory array, an attacker can supply a short byte payload but set the length field to an extremely large value. The decoder therefore tries to read far beyond the actual data, exhausting the remaining gas and causing the whole transaction to revert with an out‑of‑gas error before any further logic can run. This occurs inside the try‑catch block that is meant to isolate callback failures, so the protective wrapper is bypassed when the decode itself runs out of gas. The impact is that order‑related operations such as execution, liquidation, automatic deleveraging, freezing, pausing bypass, and cancellation can be halted indefinitely. From a user’s perspective an order may appear to be stuck, a liquidation may never happen, or a cancellation may silently fail, while the UI shows no explicit error message because the revert reason cannot be decoded. The affected parties include any participant relying on the protocol’s order lifecycle – traders, liquidators, and the protocol itself – because the bug resides in a shared utility (ErrorUtils.getRevertMessage) used across many callbacks. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the handling of external callback revert data. It is hard to notice because the transaction simply runs out of gas without emitting a readable revert string, making the failure look like a generic out‑of‑gas problem rather than a targeted attack. The proper mitigation is to enforce a maximum allowable length for any decoded string, validate the declared length against this cap, and truncate or reject overly long payloads before calling abi.decode. By bounding the length, the decoder cannot be forced to read arbitrary memory, preserving the intended isolation of callback failures and preventing denial‑of‑service attacks on order execution.
summary:
Malicious revert reasons with faked lengths can be used in the various order callbacks to disrupt order execution
For most order-related operations, the user is allowed to provide the address of a contract on which a callback is triggered, whenever anything related to an order changes. These callbacks are executed with a limited amount of gas, under a try-catch block, in order to ensure that the user-supplied callback cannot affect subsequent processing. Whenever the callback reverts, the revert reason is fetched so that it can be emitted.
The code that parses the return bytes uses abi.decode(result, (string)) to parse the "string", which relies on the first word of the data, to figure out how many bytes long the string is. Because the results variable is a memory variable, rather than calldata, any read past the end of the bytes is allowed, and is considered as value zero byte slots. If a malicious callback provides a reason "string" that is only a few bytes long, but sets the length to a very large number, when the decode call is made, it will try to read a string of that provided length, and will eventually run out of gas.
In this case, the callback will revert with an out of gas error, and there won't be a string to parse.
A malicious user can use this attack in many different places, but they all stem from the bug in ErrorUtils.getRevertMessage(). One such attack would be that a user can prevent themselves from being liquidated or ADLed, by providing a malicious string in the revert reason in their CallbackUtils.afterOrderExecution() callback.
Other places include the freezing of orders, bypassing pauses by having resting orders that can never execute until allowed, and preventing orders from being canceled when their normal execution reverts.

title: User-supplied slippage for decrease orders is ignored
content: The vulnerability is a slippage‑control bypass that occurs when a user creates a decrease‑position order and supplies a minimum output amount (minOutputAmount) to limit how much price impact they are willing to accept. The contract logic that executes the two internal swaps – one that converts realised profit to the collateral token and another that converts withdrawn collateral back to the profit token – hard‑codes the minOutputAmount parameter to zero instead of using the user‑provided value. Because the swap handler receives a zero tolerance, the swap can execute with unlimited slippage, meaning the actual amount received may be far lower than the user expected, or even zero. This flaw is rooted in the DecreasePositionCollateralUtils library where the SwapUtils.SwapParams struct is constructed with a literal 0 for minOutputAmount, and there is no subsequent check that the swap output meets the user’s original requirement. An attacker can exploit the bug by front‑running or sandwiching the user’s transaction: after the user’s order is placed, the attacker moves the market price, causing the subsequent swap to yield a much smaller amount. Since the contract does not enforce the user‑specified slippage limit, the swap succeeds and the protocol transfers the reduced amount back to the user, effectively stealing part of the user’s collateral or profit. The impact is that users who attempt to close or reduce their positions may receive less collateral than anticipated, see their balances shrink unexpectedly, or in extreme cases receive nothing, leading to a loss of funds that appears as a “missing refund” or “funds disappear” symptom in the UI. The issue manifests whenever a decrease order is processed, regardless of the market conditions, and affects any participant who relies on the slippage protection offered by the minOutputAmount field. It was discovered during a manual audit of the GMX synthetic contracts when the auditor inspected the DecreasePositionCollateralUtils functions and noticed the hard‑coded zero value and the absence of any validation against the order’s slippage parameter. The bug can be hard to notice because the transaction does not revert; it simply completes successfully while delivering a lower output, which may be interpreted as a normal market loss rather than a contract flaw. To remediate the issue, the contract should propagate the user‑supplied minOutputAmount into the swap parameters and enforce a check that the actual swap output is greater than or equal to this threshold, reverting the transaction otherwise. This would restore the intended slippage protection and prevent unlimited price impact, aligning the on‑chain behavior with the user’s expectations and the business logic that guarantees a minimum return when decreasing a position.

The user-supplied minOutputAmount order parameter for controlling slippage is ignored when a user decreases their position
There are no checks that the amount out matches the user-supplied value during order creation, and in fact infinite slippage is allowed during the swap of PNL and collateral, ensuring there are opportunities for sandwiching.

title: Adversary can brick bounty payouts by call-
content: The vulnerability originates from a token‑handling routine that is intended to receive only ERC20 tokens as bounty rewards but uses a generic interface that also matches ERC721 contracts. The function that records incoming funds calls transferFrom and balanceOf on the supplied token address. Because ERC721 implements both of these methods (transferFrom works with a token ID and balanceOf returns the owner’s token count), an attacker can supply an ERC721 contract address and a valid token ID, causing the bounty contract to accept the NFT as if it were an ERC20 amount. The root cause is the absence of explicit token‑type validation and a single whitelist that does not differentiate between fungible and non‑fungible assets. When the bounty is later claimed, the payout logic invokes the ERC20‑only transfer method to send the reward. Since ERC721 contracts do not implement transfer, the call reverts, aborting the entire payout transaction. As a result, the bounty becomes permanently unclaimable and all assets that were deposited – both the mistakenly added NFT and any legitimate ERC20 tokens – become locked in the contract. This failure manifests only after a claim attempt; the initial deposit appears successful because the ERC721 functions satisfy the generic checks, making the issue hard to notice during normal operation. The impact is high: users expecting a reward receive nothing, the UI may show a successful claim transaction but no change in balance, and the protocol loses the ability to distribute the bounty, effectively “bricking” the reward mechanism. The bug belongs to the class of token‑type confusion or improper interface usage, where a contract assumes a single token standard without enforcing it. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the token‑receiving and payout paths and identified that the whitelist allowed any contract with the required functions. To remediate, the contract should maintain separate whitelists for ERC20 and ERC721 tokens, enforce that only ERC20‑compatible contracts are accepted in the ERC20 bounty flow, and add explicit checks (e.g., interface detection or try/catch on transfer) before recording a reward. By preventing NFTs from being deposited as ERC20 rewards, the payout functions will always be able to execute the expected transfer, preserving the integrity of the bounty system and avoiding permanent fund loss.
summary:
recieveFunds is only meant to be called with an ERC20 token but _receiveERC20 is generic enough to work with an ERC721 token. An adversary could call this with an ERC721 token to add it as a bounty reward. The problem is that the payout functions would completely break when trying to send it as a payout. The result is that afterwards the bounty would be completely broken.
plementations/BountyCore.sol#L197-L209
BountyCore#_receiveERC20 makes two calls to the underlying token contract. The first is the transferFrom method which exists functions identically to the ERC20 variant using token id instead of amount.
plementations/BountyCore.sol#L291-L299
The other call that's made is balanceOf which is also present in ERC721
plementations/BountyCore.sol#L221-L228
On the flipside, when withdrawing and ERC20 it uses the transfer method which doesn't exist in ERC721. The result is that ERC721 tokens can be deposited as ERC20 tokens but can't be withdrawn. Since the contract will revert when trying to payout the ER721 token all payouts from the bounty will no longer work.
Submitting as high risk because when combined with refund locking methods it will result in all deposited tokens being stuck forever.
Bounty will be permanently unclaimable

title: Tier winner can steal excess funds from tiered
content: The vulnerability resides in a tiered percentage bounty contract that takes a single snapshot of the total token balances when the bounty is closed and then uses that snapshot to compute each tier winner’s payout. The root cause is that the snapshot is performed only once and the contract does not account for later changes to the pool caused by refundable deposits whose expiration has passed. Because the contract allows new deposits to be added after the bounty is closed, an attacker who is also a tier winner can artificially inflate the recorded prize pool with a short‑lived deposit, claim a percentage of the inflated amount, and then immediately refund the temporary deposit. The exploitation flow is as follows: (1) the bounty creator funds the contract with an initial prize; (2) the initial deposit expires and becomes refundable before the bounty is officially settled; (3) the attacker is added as a tier winner; (4) the attacker deposits a large amount of the payout token with an expiration of only one block, thereby increasing the total balance that the snapshot will record; (5) the attacker calls the claim function, which uses the inflated snapshot to calculate a payout that is much larger than the legitimate share; (6) in the next block the attacker refunds the temporary deposit, withdrawing the extra funds and leaving the contract with little or no remaining balance. The impact is that the entire bounty pool can be drained, legitimate participants receive no reward, and the protocol loses trust in its incentive mechanisms. This condition occurs only when the main deposit has become refundable (i.e., its lock period has ended) before the bounty is closed, and when the contract permits additional deposits after closure. All parties that rely on the bounty – the competition creator, other contestants, and any downstream contracts that expect the bounty to retain funds – are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the interaction between DepositManagerV1 and ClaimManagerV1 and noticed that the balance snapshot does not reflect subsequent refunds. It is subtle because the snapshot appears correct at the moment of claim, so the contract seems to pay the correct percentage, yet the total pool later shrinks, effectively stealing funds. To remediate, the contract should enforce a minimum lock period for any deposit that remains after a tiered bounty is closed, prevent new deposits after closure, or recompute payouts after any refund to ensure that the payout percentage is applied to the actual remaining balance. In user‑facing terms, a participant may see that after claiming a prize the contract balance drops to zero, the expected refund never arrives, or the winner receives an unexpectedly large amount, indicating a breach of the intended accounting logic. This class of bug can be described as a “snapshot‑inflation” or “post‑snapshot refund” economic manipulation, where the accounting assumptions of a fixed prize pool are violated by allowing mutable deposits after the snapshot.
summary:
Total funds used to calculate the percentage payment is set when the bounty is closed. If the main deposit is refundable by the time when the bounty is closed, a tier winner could exploit the bounty to steal all the funds in the contract.
plementations/TieredPercentageBountyV1.sol#L123-L136
When a tiered bounty is closed, the balances of each payout token is snapshot.
plementations/TieredPercentageBountyV1.sol#L104-L120
These balance snapshots are used to calculate the amount to pay of each payout token. The balances are only snapshot once and don't change when deposits are refunded. A tier winner can abuse this structure to steal excess funds from the contract if there are any expired deposits. This would be accomplished by using a very short-lived deposit to artificially inflate the prize pool before claiming and refunding to drain all available funds.
Example: User A creates a competition with 10,000 USDC in prizes. The contest goes longer than expected and their deposit becomes available for refund. User B wins 3rd place which entitles them to 10% of the pool. User A makes a call adding User B as the winner of tier 2 (3rd place). User B calls DepositManagerV1#fundBountyToken to fund the bounty with 90,000 USDC and a _expiration of 1 (second). They then call ClaimManagerV1#permissionedClaimTieredBounty which snapshots the total bounty at 100,000 USDC and entitles User B to 10,000 USDC (10%) of winnings. The next block User B calls DepositManagerV1#refundDeposit and refunds their deposit. Since the initial 10,000 USDC deposit has expired, User B withdraws the other 90,000 USDC in the contract. This leaves the bounty with no funds.
Tier winner can steal all funds in the percentage bounty during claim if initial deposit is expired

title: Adversary can permanently break percent-
content: The vulnerability is a logic flaw that allows a bounty contract to become permanently unable to distribute rewards when it handles an ERC20 token that rejects zero‑value transfers. The contract records every token that is ever deposited in a list called tokenAddresses. When a deposit is later refunded, the token’s balance in the contract drops to zero but the token address remains in the list because the code does not remove entries with a zero funding total. During a payout, the contract iterates over tokenAddresses and calls the ERC20 transfer function with the amount stored in fundingTotal for each token. If fundingTotal is zero, the contract still attempts a transfer of 0 tokens. Some ERC20 implementations are written to revert any transfer call with an amount of zero, so the call fails and the entire payout transaction reverts. An adversary can exploit this by deliberately depositing a token that has the zero‑transfer revert behaviour, then triggering a refund. The token stays in the list with a zero balance, causing every subsequent payout attempt to revert, effectively bricking the payout mechanism. The impact is that all future claimants are unable to receive any rewards and the locked funds cannot be recovered because the contract has no function to clear or remove zero‑balance tokens. The condition occurs only when the token does not support zero transfers and the contract’s refund logic does not prune empty token entries. This issue was discovered during a manual audit of the TieredPercentageBountyV1.sol implementation, where the code paths for handling fundingTotals and token removal were examined. It is hard to notice because many popular ERC20 tokens allow zero transfers, so the bug does not manifest in typical testing. The bug belongs to the class of “zero‑value transfer” or “accounting logic” vulnerabilities where assumptions about token behaviour are violated, leading to a mismatch between expected refund logic and actual token contract semantics. From a user’s perspective the UI would show that a claim is submitted but the transaction reverts, resulting in no tokens being received and balances appearing unchanged. Users expect a refund or bounty payout, but instead receive nothing and the contract appears to be stuck. To remediate the issue the contract should (1) remove a token from tokenAddresses when its balance becomes zero after a refund, and (2) add a guard in the internal transfer routine to skip calls when the transfer amount is zero, thereby preventing the revert and preserving the ability to process other token payouts.

Some ERC20 tokens don't support 0 value transfers. An adversary can abuse this by adding it to a percentage tier bounty then refunding it. This is because after the refund the token will still be on the list of tokens to distribute but it will have a value saved of 0. This means that no matter what it will always try to transfer 0 token and this will always revert because the specified token doesn't support zero transfers.

An adversary can purposefully trigger these conditions by making a deposit with ERC20 token that has this problem. This will add the ERC20 token to tokenAddresses and cause the contract to try to send 0 when making a payout.
Payouts will become completely bricked, with no way to recover since fundingTotals can't be set anywhere else.

title: Adversary can permanently break reward dis-
content: The vulnerability resides in the way the bounty contract determines the amount of tokens that will be distributed to winners when a competition is closed. At the moment closeCompetition is invoked the contract records a snapshot of the current token balance for each reward token and later uses that snapshot as the total pool from which payouts are calculated. Because the snapshot is taken before any post‑close refunds are allowed, the contract assumes that the recorded balance will remain available until all winners claim their rewards. An attacker can exploit this assumption by making a deposit of a token that initially has a zero balance, setting the competition expiration to a very short interval (for example one second), and then, after the competition has been closed, invoking the refund function to return the deposited amount. The refund reduces the contract’s actual token holdings below the amount recorded in the snapshot, so when a winner later calls claimReward the contract attempts to transfer more tokens than it holds. This mismatch causes the transfer to revert, and the claim transaction fails. For ERC20 tokens the shortfall can be remedied by sending additional tokens to the contract, but the contract’s receive function is disabled for native MATIC, meaning that the contract cannot be funded with native currency after the shortfall occurs. Consequently an attacker who uses native MATIC as the deposit can permanently break the payout mechanism, leaving all future rewards unclaimable. The issue is triggered only after the competition has been closed and a refund is processed; it does not affect the normal deposit or claim flow before closure. Users, bounty participants, and the protocol itself are affected because legitimate winners receive no reward, balances appear to be zero, and the protocol’s economic guarantees are violated. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the interaction between the closeCompetition snapshot logic and the refund pathway. It can be difficult to notice because the contract behaves correctly under normal operation, and the failure only manifests when a post‑close refund is performed, a scenario that may not be covered by typical unit tests. The root cause is the reliance on a static balance snapshot without protecting that balance from later reduction. To remediate the issue the contract should either disable refunds after the competition is closed or redesign the payout calculation to use the actual balance at claim time, ensuring that the contract never attempts to transfer more tokens than it currently holds. This class of bug is a “post‑close balance depletion” or “snapshot‑based payout” vulnerability, where accounting assumptions are broken by later state changes, leading to failed payouts and potential loss of funds.
summary:
When closeCompetition is called for TieredPercentageBountyV1 it takes a snapshot of the current token balance. Afterwards it uses this number to calculate the payouts. When a deposit is refunded after the competition is closed then the contract won't have enough funds to pay users.
To exploit this an adversary can make a deposit for a token that has a current balance of zero using a expiration of 1 second. After the competition closes they refund their deposit. Now when the contract tries to give payouts to the winners it will try to payout a token that it no longer has any of, causing it to revert anytime someone tries to claim a payout.

title: Adversary can break any bounty they wish by
content: The contract implements a bounty system where a funder deposits an NFT as collateral. The deposit is recorded in an internal list called nftDeposits. When the funder requests a refund, the function refundDeposit transfers the NFT back to the funder but fails to delete the corresponding entry from nftDeposits. Later, when a claimant successfully completes the bounty, the claim manager iterates over nftDeposits and attempts to transfer each recorded NFT to the winner. Because the refunded NFT entry remains, the loop tries to transfer an NFT that the contract no longer owns. The transfer call reverts or silently fails, causing the entire payout routine to stop and leaving any remaining NFTs locked in the contract. An adversary who can trigger a refund on any deposited NFT can therefore break the payout mechanism for that bounty, and when combined with other locking mechanisms the effect can be that all deposited NFTs become unrecoverable. The issue occurs whenever a refund is processed before a claim is resolved. It affects all participants: funders who expect their NFT to be returned and later reclaimed, claimants who expect to receive the pledged NFTs, and the protocol itself because the bounty becomes unfulfillable. The problem was discovered during a manual audit of the BountyCore and ClaimManagerV1 contracts, where the audit team noticed that the refund function does not update the deposit registry. The bug is subtle because the contract still holds a reference to the NFT, but the asset is no longer present, so the failure only appears at claim time, making it easy to miss in basic testing. The vulnerability belongs to the class of state‑inconsistency or stale‑reference bugs, where on‑chain bookkeeping diverges from actual token balances. From a user perspective the UI may show that a bounty is still active, but when a winner tries to claim the reward the transaction reverts and no NFT is transferred, leading to confusion such as 'my reward never arrived' or 'the bounty seems stuck'. The correct mitigation is to remove the deposit entry from nftDeposits (or mark it as cleared) as part of the refund process, ensuring that the claim loop only iterates over NFTs that are still held by the contract. This restores consistency between the contract’s internal state and its token holdings and prevents an attacker from permanently breaking payouts.

Refunding an NFT doesn't remove the nftDeposit so the contract will try to payout an NFT it doesn't have if the NFT has been refunded.

ager/Implementations/ClaimManagerV1.sol#L150-L165
When any bounty is claimed it loops through nftDeposits and attempts to transfer an NFT for each one. The problem is that if an NFT has been refunded the deposit receipt will still exist but the contract won't have the NFT. The result is that all payouts will be permanently broken.
Submitting as high risk because when combined with refund locking methods it will result in all deposited tokens being stuck forever.
Adversary can permanently break payouts on any bounty

title: Adversary can lock every deposit forever by
content: The vulnerability is an integer overflow that leads to a denial‑of‑service condition in the deposit‑refund workflow. DepositManagerV1 allows a caller to specify an _expiration value that is forwarded unchanged to BountyCore.receiveFunds, where it is stored in a mapping called expiration. When a user later requests a refund, BountyCore.getLockedFunds computes the lock period by adding the stored deposit timestamp (depositTime) to the stored expiration value. Because the addition is performed without a safety check, an attacker can create a deposit with _expiration set to the maximum uint256 value. The sum depositTime+expiration then exceeds the uint256 range, causing an arithmetic overflow that triggers a revert in getLockedFunds. As a result, DepositManagerV1.refundDeposit always reverts for any deposit that references the corrupted entry, breaking the refund mechanism for all users. The impact is that tokens deposited into the bounty pool become permanently unrecoverable through the normal refund path, effectively locking the funds forever. This condition occurs whenever a malicious deposit with an extreme expiration is present; it does not depend on timing or other state changes. The affected parties are depositors and any protocol participants who rely on being able to retrieve their funds, as the contract’s accounting assumptions that a deposit is unlockable after a finite period are violated. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the parameter flow from DepositManagerV1 to BountyCore and identified the unchecked arithmetic in the lock‑time calculation. It is hard to notice because typical test cases use reasonable expiration values, and the overflow only manifests with the maximum possible value, which normal usage rarely reaches. The bug belongs to the class of unchecked integer overflow leading to denial‑of‑service or fund‑locking bugs. From a user’s perspective the UI would show a transaction failure when trying to claim a refund, with no funds being returned and balances appearing unchanged despite a successful deposit. Users expect to receive their deposited tokens back after the lock expires, but instead the contract reverts and the funds remain stuck. To remediate the issue the contract should enforce an upper bound on the expiration parameter, for example by requiring the value to be less than or equal to type(uint128).max, or by using Solidity’s built‑in checked arithmetic to prevent overflow before storing the expiration. This ensures that the lock‑time calculation cannot overflow and that refunds remain functional.
summary:
DepositMangerV1 allows the caller to specify _expiration which specifies how long the deposit is locked. An adversary can specify a deposit with _expiration = type(uint256).max which will cause an overflow in the BountyCore#getLockedFunds subcall and permanently break refunds.

DepositManagerV1#fundBountyToken allows the depositor to specify an _expiration which is passed directly to BountyCore#receiveFunds.

BountyCore stores the _expiration in the expiration mapping.

When requesting a refund, getLockedFunds returns the amount of funds currently locked. The line to focus on is depositTime[depList[i]] + expiration[depList[i]]

To exploit this the user would make a deposit with _expiration = type(uint256).max which will cause a guaranteed overflow. title: Refunds can be bricked by triggering OOG (out of gas)
content: The vulnerability is an unbounded iteration in the refund logic of the DepositManager contract that can cause out‑of‑gas (OOG) reverts and prevent any refunds from being processed. The contract stores every deposit in a dynamic array that grows without any explicit limit because the receiveFunds function does not enforce a maximum number of entries. When a user or an attacker creates a large number of deposits, the array becomes sufficiently long that the refundDeposit function, which calls getLockedFunds and iterates over the entire list, consumes more gas than the block gas limit. The transaction then runs out of gas, reverts, and no tokens are transferred back to the original depositor. This situation can be triggered deliberately by an adversary who spams the contract with many small deposits, or it can happen unintentionally as the protocol matures and the deposit list simply grows over time. The impact is that legitimate users who expect a refund see their transaction fail, their UI may display an error or simply show no change in balance, and the funds remain locked in the contract indefinitely. The issue affects all participants who rely on the refund mechanism, including bounty hunters, token holders, and the overall protocol reputation. It was discovered during a manual audit when the reviewer noticed that getLockedFunds contains a for‑loop over the full deposit list and that no bounds are enforced on the size of that list. Because the loop works correctly for small arrays, the problem is not obvious during normal testing and only manifests when the array reaches a size that exceeds the gas budget, making it hard to detect without stress testing. The bug belongs to the class of unbounded loop or gas‑limit denial‑of‑service vulnerabilities, where a contract’s logic can be forced into a state that exceeds the blockchain’s gas constraints. From a user’s perspective the expected behavior – receiving a refund after calling the function – is replaced by a silent failure: the transaction reverts, the UI may report “refund failed” or simply show no balance change, leading to confusion and loss of trust. To remediate the issue the contract should avoid iterating over an unbounded collection. Practical fixes include imposing a hard cap on the number of deposits that can be recorded, using a pagination or batch‑processing approach for refunds, storing aggregate balances per bounty instead of a global list, or switching to a pull‑payment model where each depositor can claim their own refund individually without requiring a loop over all entries. Any of these approaches eliminates the possibility of a single transaction exhausting the block gas limit and ensures that refunds remain available even as the contract scales.
summary:
The DepositManager contract is in charge of refunding tokens from the individual bounties. This function ends up running a for loop over an unbounded array. This array can be made to be sufficiently large to exceed the block gas limit and cause out-of-gas errors and stop the processing of any refunds.
The function refundDeposit() in DepositManager.sol is responsible for handling refunds, through the following snippet of code, nager/Implementations/DepositManagerV1.sol#L152-L181 We are here interested in positManager/Implementations/DepositManagerV1.sol#L171-L172 which calculates available funds. If we check the function getLockedFunds(), we see it run a for loop plementations/BountyCore.sol#L333-L352 This loop is running over the list of ALL deposits. The deposit list is unbounded, since there are no checks for such limits in the receiveFunds() function. This can result in a very long list, causing out-of-gas errors when making refund calls.
Inability to withdraw funds. Can be forever locked into the contract.

title: Earlier users in rollover queue can grief later users
content: The vulnerability is a queue‑reordering flaw that allows users who appear earlier in the rollover queue to unintentionally or deliberately prevent later users from receiving their expected fund rollover. The contract maintains a mapping called rolloverAccounting that records, for each epoch, the highest queue index that has been processed. When a participant removes (delists) themselves from the queue, the implementation swaps the last enlisted user into the vacated slot instead of preserving the original ordering. Because the processing function mintRollovers() is called with a fixed number of operations rather than explicit start and end indexes, the contract may advance the processed index past the position of the delisted user while the swapped‑in last user has not yet been processed. If the earlier user delists after the contract has recorded progress up to their own index but before the last user’s turn, the boolean that would mark the last user as processed never flips, leaving that user’s funds unrolled for the current epoch. From a user’s perspective the expected behaviour – an automatic rollover of their balance at the end of each epoch – is broken; the affected user sees no change in their balance, may even observe a zero‑return when a refund was anticipated, and must manually delist and re‑enlist to trigger a new rollover, defeating the purpose of the feature. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit that examined the queue management logic and identified that the combination of index replacement and operation‑count‑based processing creates a race condition where later entries can be skipped. It is difficult to notice because the contract correctly processes earlier entries and the overall accounting appears consistent, masking the fact that a subset of users never receives their rollover. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of mutable‑queue‑state vulnerabilities where reordering of elements after a removal leads to incomplete processing of pending actions. The proper mitigation is to replace the operation‑count approach with explicit start and end indexes and to track, via a boolean mapping, whether each user’s rollover has already been executed, thereby preventing the last user from being silently omitted when earlier participants leave the queue.
summary:
The current implementation enables users who are earlier in the queue to grief those who are later.
There is a rolloverAccounting mapping that, for every epoch, tracks the current index of the queue for which mints have been processed up to thus far.
When a user delists from the queue, the last user enlisted will replace the delisted user's queue index.
It is thus possible for the queue to be processed up to, or past, the delisted user's queue index, but before the last user has been processed, the processed user delists, thus causing the last user to not have his funds rollover.
Whether accidental or deliberate, it is possible for users to not have their funds rollover.

title: Bounties can be broken by funding them with malicious ERC20
content: The vulnerability is a token‑bricking flaw that allows an attacker to render a bounty contract unusable by funding it with a malicious ERC20 token. The DepositManagerV1 contract accepts deposits of any token as long as the internal flag tokenAddressLimitReached is false, which is the default state for most deployments. Because the contract does not verify the behaviour of the supplied token, a malicious contract can be created that deliberately reverts on any transfer call. When a winner later tries to claim a reward, the ClaimManagerV1 contract iterates over all deposited tokens and uses the Address.safeTransfer helper to move each token to the recipient. SafeTransfer propagates any revert from the token, and the claim function does not catch these errors. Consequently, if even a single deposited token reverts, the entire claim transaction reverts, preventing any reward from being paid out. This situation effectively bricks the bounty: the reward balance appears on‑chain, but users receive nothing, balances may show zero for winners, and the funds remain locked in the contract until the bounty’s expiry timestamp, which can be arbitrarily long. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the token‑handling logic and identified that the deposit check always passes and that claim processing lacks failure handling. It is hard to notice because the malicious token behaves like a standard ERC20 during deposit, only failing on transfer, so normal testing with well‑behaved tokens does not expose the problem. The impact is loss of expected payouts, potential loss of user trust, and indefinite locking of value in the protocol. The flaw belongs to the class of “untrusted token transfer” bugs where contracts assume external token contracts are well‑behaved and do not protect against reverts. To remediate, the claim logic should wrap each token transfer in a try‑catch (or low‑level call with return‑value checking) and either skip failing tokens or revert with a clear error, and the deposit function should optionally whitelist known safe tokens or enforce a token interface check. This change ensures that a malicious ERC20 cannot prevent other legitimate tokens from being claimed and that users receive the rewards they expect.
summary:
Any malicious user can fund a bounty contract with a malicious ERC20 contract and prevent winners from withdrawing their rewards.
The DepositManagerV1 contract allows any user to fund any bounty with any token, as long as the following check passes in fundBountyToken function nager/Implementations/DepositManagerV1.sol#L45-L50 This check always passes as long as tokenAddressLimitReacehd is false, which will be the case for most cases and is a reasonable assumption to make.
The claims are handled by the claimManagerV1 contract, which relies on every single deposited token to be successfully transferred to the target address, as can be seen with the snippet below, taken from the function _claimAtomicBounty ager/Implementations/ClaimManagerV1.sol#L123-L134 and the claimBalance function eventually ends up using the safeTransfer function from the Address library to carry out the transfer as seen in BountyCore.sol:221 https://github.com/syCore.sol#L221-L228 However, if any of the tokens end up reverting during the safeTransfer call, the entire claiming call is reverted. It is quite easy for an attacker to fund the bounty with such a malicious contract, and this would essentially brick the bounty preventing the claims from being processed. This will also lock up the funds in the contract until expiry, which can be an indefinite amount of time.
This attack can be carried out in the following bounty types:
1. AtomicBountyV1
3. TieredPercentageBounty
by using malicious ERC20 tokens following the same attack vector.
Bricking of bounty and lock up of funds until expiry timestamp

title: Funds can be stolen because of incorrect update of rollover index
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect update of the rollover index that governs which queue entry is considered active for a given owner. When an owner who already has a rollover entry calls the enlistInRollover function, the contract overwrites the existing queue item with new asset and epoch values, but it also unconditionally sets the ownerToRollOverQueueIndex mapping to the length of the rollover queue. This causes the index to point to the newly appended (or empty) slot instead of the slot that was just updated. The notRollingOver modifier later retrieves a queue item using getRolloverIndex, which now returns the wrong identifier. Consequently the modifier checks the wrong epoch and asset balance, allowing the condition that should block withdrawals to be bypassed. An attacker who is a depositor can therefore call withdraw and retrieve assets that the protocol intended to lock for the rollover period. The impact is that funds that should remain locked disappear from the protocol’s accounting, effectively enabling theft of locked assets. The bug manifests only when an owner already has a rollover entry and attempts to re‑enlist; users without a prior entry are not affected. It affects any participant who relies on the rollover mechanism to secure their assets, as well as the overall integrity of the protocol’s financial guarantees. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by Sherlock, who noticed that the ownerToRollOverQueueIndex assignment was placed outside the conditional that distinguishes between updating an existing entry and creating a new one. Because the mapping is updated in both branches, the logical error is subtle and may not be caught by simple unit tests that only verify successful enlisting. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after initiating a rollover they can still withdraw the same amount, seeing no lock applied and potentially observing a balance that remains unchanged while the protocol’s internal state believes the assets are locked. This violates the business rule that assets must be frozen for the duration of the rollover, breaking accounting assumptions and exposing the protocol to loss. The recommended fix is to move the assignment of ownerToRollOverQueueIndex into the else branch that handles the creation of a new queue entry, leaving the index unchanged when an existing entry is updated. This ensures that the notRollingOver modifier always references the correct queue item and that withdrawals are correctly blocked while a rollover is active.

title: depositFee can be bypassed via deposit queue
content: The vulnerability consists of a fee‑bypass that arises from the way the protocol charges a dynamic deposit fee and processes queued deposits. The contract charges a deposit fee that grows linearly during the deposit window and applies this fee when a user calls the direct deposit function. However, the system also supports a deposit queue where a user can first place a deposit into the queue (using a zero‑epoch deposit call) and later have a relayer mint the queued deposit with mintDepositInQueue. Because the queue operates under a FILO ordering, a transaction that contains both the queue deposit and the mint call processes the mint before the fee calculation is performed. As a result, the user’s deposit is recorded without any fee being deducted, even though the fee period is active and non‑zero. The attacker can also capture the relayer fee that would normally be paid to the entity that processes the queue, effectively paying zero fees while still receiving the full benefit of the deposit. This flaw was discovered during a manual audit when the reviewer noticed that the fee logic is only tied to the direct deposit path and does not account for the mintDepositInQueue path, and that the ordering of operations allows both calls to be combined in a single transaction. The issue is subtle because the fee appears to be enforced on every deposit event, yet the queue path is an alternative route that is not obvious from the fee‑charging code. From a user’s point of view the symptom is that a deposit that should have reduced the user’s balance by the fee amount instead leaves the balance unchanged, and the protocol’s fee revenue is reduced. The impact is a loss of expected fee income for the protocol, which can affect the economics of relayers and any downstream incentives that rely on that revenue. The bug belongs to the class of “fee‑exemption through alternative execution path” or “economic bypass via transaction ordering”. To remediate the problem the fee calculation should be applied to queued deposits as well, or the protocol should take a proportion of the relayer fee, or the ordering logic should be changed so that a mintDepositInQueue cannot be executed in the same transaction that creates the queue entry, thereby preventing the fee bypass.
summary: The deposit fee can be circumvented by a queue deposit + mintDepositInQueue() call in the same transaction. A deposit fee is charged and increases linearly within the deposit window. However, this fee can be avoided if one deposits into the queue instead, then mints his deposit in the queue. Loss of protocol fee revenue.

title: Malicious seller forced break lockCapital()
content: The vulnerability resides in the protocol’s capital‑locking routine that is triggered when a lending pool transitions from the Active state to Late. The lockCapital() function iterates over all active protection entries and, for each entry, calls calculateRemainingPrincipal() to determine how much of the protected principal is still outstanding. calculateRemainingPrincipal() first checks whether the caller (the buyer) is the current owner of a specific NFT that represents the protection position by invoking the ERC‑721 ownerOf() method. If the NFT has been burned – which is possible when the token’s principal has been fully redeemed – the ownerOf() call reverts with the standard “ERC721: owner query for nonexistent token” error. Because the revert is not caught, the entire lockCapital() execution aborts, preventing the protocol from changing the pool status to Late and from locking the required capital. Consequently, the seller continues to earn the premium amount indefinitely, while the buyer loses any compensation that would have been paid out after the Late transition. This flaw can be exploited in two ways: a legitimate buyer who unknowingly burns their protection NFT (for example, after redemption) unintentionally disables compensation for all other buyers of the same pool; a malicious seller can deliberately purchase a protection, immediately burn the associated NFT, and force the lockCapital() call to fail, thereby keeping the premium flow while depriving honest buyers of their expected refunds. The issue arises from an unchecked assumption that the NFT always exists and that ownerOf() will succeed, which is not true for burned tokens. It is discovered through static analysis of the contract code during an audit, and it may be hard to notice because the failure only manifests when a token is burned – a relatively rare event that does not affect the normal execution path. The impact is a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees: funds that should be locked and later redistributed to buyers remain unlocked, premium income is improperly retained by the seller, and the protocol’s state machine becomes stuck in Active. To remediate, the contract should handle the possibility of a missing token, for example by wrapping the ownerOf() call in a try/catch block, checking token existence before the call, or prohibiting burning of protection NFTs altogether. The fix restores the intended business logic that a Late transition always locks the appropriate capital and ensures that buyers receive their rightful compensation.
summary: Malicious burn nft causes failure to lockCapital() seller steady earn PremiumAmount, buyer will be lost compensation When the status of the lendingPool changes from Active to Late, the protocol will call ProtectionPool.lockCapital() to lock amount lockCapital() will loop through the active protections to calculate the lockedAmount. The code is as follows: ```solidity function lockCapital(address _lendingPoolAddress) external payable override onlyDefaultStateManager whenNotPaused returns (uint256 _lockedAmount, uint256 _snapshotId) { .... uint256 _length = activeProtectionIndexes.length(); for (uint256 i; i < _length; ) { ... uint256 _remainingPrincipal = poolInfo .referenceLendingPools .calculateRemainingPrincipal( //<----------- calculate Remaining Principal _lendingPoolAddress, protectionInfo.buyer, protectionInfo.purchaseParams.nftLpTokenId ); ``` The important thing inside is to calculate the _remainingPrincipal by referenceLendingPools.calculateRemainingPrincipal() ```solidity function calculateRemainingPrincipal( address _lendingPoolAddress, address _lender, uint256 _nftLpTokenId ) public view override returns (uint256 _principalRemaining) { ... if (_poolTokens.ownerOf(_nftLpTokenId) == _lender) { //<------------call ownerOf() IPoolTokens.TokenInfo memory _tokenInfo = _poolTokens.getTokenInfo( _nftLpTokenId ); .... if ( _tokenInfo.pool == _lendingPoolAddress && _isJuniorTrancheId(_tokenInfo.tranche) ) { _principalRemaining = _tokenInfo.principalAmount - _tokenInfo.principalRedeemed; } } } ``` GoldfinchAdapter.calculateRemainingPrincipal() The current implementation will first determine if the ownerOf the NFTID is _lender There is a potential problem here, if the NFTID has been burned, the ownerOf() will be directly revert, which will lead to calculateRemainingPrincipal() revert, and lockCapital() revert and can't change status from active to late Let's see whether Goldfinch's implementation supports burn(NFTID), and whether ownerOf(NFTID) will revert 1. PoolTokens has burn() method, if principalRedeemed==principalAmount you can burn it ```solidity contract PoolTokens is IPoolTokens, ERC721PresetMinterPauserAutoIdUpgradeSafe, HasAdmin, IERC2981 { ..... function burn(uint256 tokenId) external virtual override whenNotPaused { TokenInfo memory token = _getTokenInfo(tokenId); bool canBurn = _isApprovedOrOwner(_msgSender(), tokenId); bool fromTokenPool = _validPool(_msgSender()) && token.pool == _msgSender(); address owner = ownerOf(tokenId); require(canBurn || fromTokenPool, "ERC721Burnable: caller cannot burn this token"); require(token.principalRedeemed == token.principalAmount, "Can only burn fully redeemed tokens"); _destroyAndBurn(tokenId); emit TokenBurned(owner, token.pool, tokenId); } ``` https://github.com/goldfinch-eng/mono/blob/88f0e3f94f6dd23ebae429fe09e2511650df893a/packages/protocol/contracts/protocol/core/PoolTokens.sol#L199 2. ownerOf() if nftid don't exists will revert with message "ERC721: owner query for nonexistent token" ```solidity contract ERC721UpgradeSafe is Initializable, ContextUpgradeSafe, ERC165UpgradeSafe, IERC721, IERC721Metadata, IERC721Enumerable { ... function ownerOf(uint256 tokenId) public view override returns (address) { return _tokenOwners.get(tokenId, "ERC721: owner query for nonexistent token"); } ``` https://github.com/goldfinch-eng/mono/blob/88f0e3f94f6dd23ebae429fe09e2511650df893a/packages/protocol/contracts/external/ERC721.sol#L136-L138 If it can't changes to late, Won't lock the fund, seller steady earn PremiumAmount So there are two risks 1. normal buyer gives NFTID to burn(), he does not know that it will affect all protection of the lendingPool 2. Malicious seller can buy a protection first, then burn it, so as to force all protection of the lendingPool to expire and get the PremiumAmount maliciously. buyer unable to obtain compensation Suggested try catch for _poolTokens.ownerOf() If revert, it is assumed that the lender is not the owner buyer will be lost compensation.

title: Sandwich attack to accruePremiumAndEx-
content: The vulnerability is a sandwich‑style manipulation of the ProtectionPool’s premium‑accrual routine that allows a malicious participant to increase the pool’s exchange rate between sToken shares and the underlying asset and then withdraw more underlying than they originally deposited. The root cause lies in the way accruePremiumAndExpireProtections() adds premium directly to totalSTokenUnderlying while the total number of sToken shares remains unchanged. Because the deposit() function mints new shares on a 1:1 basis with the amount of underlying supplied, an attacker can front‑run the premium‑accrual call, deposit a large amount of underlying, and thereby keep the exchange rate unchanged at the moment of deposit. When the premium is later added, the total underlying rises while the share count stays the same, causing the exchange rate to shift in the attacker’s favour. The attacker can then withdraw the same number of shares and receive more underlying tokens than they contributed, effectively stealing value from other pool participants. This exploit can be carried out whenever the pool is in a phase that permits deposits (i.e., not OpenToBuyers) and the premium‑accrual function is scheduled to run in the same block or cycle as a user‑controlled deposit. All users of the ProtectionPool are affected because the unfair profit reduces the amount of underlying that honest participants can redeem for their shares, violating the protocol’s Fair Distribution principle. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the interaction between deposit(), withdraw() and the premium‑accrual logic; it can be hard to notice because the exchange rate appears unchanged immediately after the deposit, and the profit only materialises after the premium is added, a subtle accounting shift that may not be obvious in routine testing. To remediate the problem, the premium should be streamed to the pool over a defined delivery period rather than being added in a single step, thereby removing the incentive for a quick front‑run. Additional mitigations include imposing per‑cycle caps on deposit and withdraw amounts and separating the premium buffer into a temporary contract that releases funds gradually, ensuring that the exchange rate cannot be artificially inflated by a single transaction. In user‑facing terms, a regular participant expects to receive the same amount of underlying when redeeming their shares, but under attack the attacker receives a higher payout while other users see their expected returns shrink, leading to a loss of confidence in the protocol’s fairness.
summary: accruePremiumAndExpireProtections() will increase totalSTokenUnderlying, and thus increase the exchange rate of the ProtectionPool. A malicious user can launch a sandwich attack and profit. This violates the Fair Distribution principle of the protocol: https://www.carapace.finance/WhitePaper#premium-pricing Let's show how a malicious user, Bob, can launch a sandwich attack to accruePremiumAndExpireProtections() and profit. 1. Suppose there are 1,000,000 underlying tokens for the ProtectionPool, and totalSupply = 1,000,000, therefore the exchange rate is 1/1 share. Suppose Bob has 100,000 shares. 2. Suppose accruePremiumAndExpireProtections() is going to be called and add 100,000 to totalSTokenUnderlying at L346. ol/ProtectionPool.sol#L279-L354 3) Bob front-runs accruePremiumAndExpireProtections() and calls deposit() to deposit 100,000 underlying tokens into the contract. The check for ProtectionPoolPhase will pass for an open phase. As a result, there are 1,100,000 underlying tokens, and 1,100,000 shares, the exchange rate is still 1/1 share. Bob now has 200,000 shares. ```solidity function deposit(uint256 _underlyingAmount, address _receiver) external override whenNotPaused nonReentrant { _deposit(_underlyingAmount, _receiver); } function _deposit(uint256 _underlyingAmount, address _receiver) internal { /// Verify that the pool is not in OpenToBuyers phase if (poolInfo.currentPhase == ProtectionPoolPhase.OpenToBuyers) { revert ProtectionPoolInOpenToBuyersPhase(); } uint256 _sTokenShares = convertToSToken(_underlyingAmount); totalSTokenUnderlying += _underlyingAmount; _safeMint(_receiver, _sTokenShares); poolInfo.underlyingToken.safeTransferFrom( msg.sender, address(this), _underlyingAmount ); /// Verify leverage ratio only when total capital/sTokenUnderlying is higher than minimum capital requirement if (_hasMinRequiredCapital()) { /// calculate pool's current leverage ratio considering the new deposit uint256 _leverageRatio = calculateLeverageRatio(); if (_leverageRatio > poolInfo.params.leverageRatioCeiling) { revert ProtectionPoolLeverageRatioTooHigh(_leverageRatio); } } emit ProtectionSold(_receiver, _underlyingAmount); } ``` 4) Now accruePremiumAndExpireProtections() gets called and 100,000 is added to totalSTokenUnderlying at L346. As a result, we have 1,200,000 underlying tokens with 1,100,000 shares. The exchange rate becomes 12/11 share. 5) Bob calls the withdraw() function (assume he made a request two cycles back, he could do that since he had 100,000 underlying tokens in the pool) to withdraw 100,000 shares and he will get 100,000*12/11 = 109,090 underlying tokens. So he has a profit of 9,090 underlying tokens by the sandwich attack. A malicious user can launch a sandwich attack to accruePremiumAndExpireProtections() and profit.

title: When rolling over, user will lose his winnings
content: When a user chooses to roll over assets from a finished epoch to a new epoch, the contract executes mintRollovers. The function first checks whether the previous epoch has been resolved and calculates the number of shares the user is entitled to withdraw (entitledShares) by calling previewWithdraw. If entitledShares is greater than the amount the user originally supplied (queue[index].assets), the contract burns the original shares and then mints new shares for the next epoch. The bug lies in the minting step: instead of minting entitledShares, which include both the original principal and any winnings, the code mints only the original asset amount (assetsToMint = queue[index].assets – relayerFee). Because the original shares have been burned, the user loses the additional shares that represent the winnings and later cannot claim them. The vulnerability is an accounting logic error in the rollover mechanism that truncates rewards. It can be exploited by any participant who rolls over after winning in the previous epoch; the loss occurs automatically without any explicit error, so the user sees no revert but later finds that the reward balance is zero. The impact is loss of earned rewards, effectively making funds disappear from the user’s perspective. The condition for the bug to manifest is that the previous epoch is resolved, the user’s entitledShares exceed the rolled‑over amount, and the user invokes enlistInRollover which queues the assets for rollover. Affected parties are all users of the protocol who rely on the rollover feature, as well as the protocol’s reputation because rewards may be unintentionally forfeited. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by Sherlock, who noticed that the minting calculation used the wrong variable. The problem is subtle because the transaction succeeds and the minted amount matches the input, making the loss of winnings only observable when a later claim returns zero. To remediate, the contract should mint entitledShares (or entitledShares minus any applicable fee) instead of the original assets, or it should allow the user to withdraw the winnings separately before burning the old shares. This class of bug falls under reward‑truncation or incorrect share accounting during epoch rollover, violating the business logic that users should retain both their principal and any earned rewards when moving to a new epoch.
summary: from previous epoch When mintRollovers is called, when the function mints shares for the new epoch for the user, the amount of shares minted will be the same as the original assets he requested to rollover - not including the amount he won. After this, all these asset shares from the previous epoch are burnt. So the user won't be able to claim his winnings. When user requests to enlistInRollover, he supplies the amount of assets to rollover, and this is saved in the queue. rolloverQueue[index].assets = _assets; When mintRollovers is called, the function checks if the user won the previous epoch, and proceeds to burn all the shares the user requested to roll: if (epochResolved[queue[index].epochId]) { uint256 entitledShares = previewWithdraw( queue[index].epochId, queue[index].assets ); // mint only if user won epoch he is rolling over if (entitledShares > queue[index].assets) { ... _burn( queue[index].receiver, queue[index].epochId, queue[index].assets ); Then, and this is the problem, the function mints to the user his original assets - assetsToMint - and not entitledShares. uint256 assetsToMint = queue[index].assets - relayerFee; _mintShares(queue[index].receiver, _epochId, assetsToMint); So the user has only rolled his original assets, but since all his share of them is burned, he will not be able anymore to claim his winnings from them. be burned, but he would receive his entitledShares, and not just his original assets. but entitledShares is sent (unlike minting rollover, which only remints _assets.) _burn(_owner, _id, _assets); _burnEmissions(_owner, _id, _assets); uint256 entitledShares; uint256 entitledEmissions = previewEmissionsWithdraw(_id, _assets); if (epochNull[_id] == false) { entitledShares = previewWithdraw(_id, _assets); } else { entitledShares = _assets; } if (entitledShares > 0) { SemiFungibleVault.asset.safeTransfer(_receiver, entitledShares); } if (entitledEmissions > 0) { emissionsToken.safeTransfer(_receiver, entitledEmissions); } User will lose his rewards when rolling over. if (epochResolved[queue[index].epochId]) { uint256 entitledShares = previewWithdraw( queue[index].epochId, queue[index].assets ); // mint only if user won epoch he is rolling over if (entitledShares > queue[index].assets) { ... _burn( queue[index].receiver, queue[index].epochId, queue[index].assets );

title: Adversary can break deposit queue and cause
content: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition in the deposit queue of the Carousel contract. When a user makes a deposit, the contract calls an internal _mintShares function which forwards to the ERC1155 _mint implementation. The ERC1155 _mint always executes _doSafeTransferAcceptanceCheck, which invokes the onERC1155Received callback on the recipient address. If the recipient contract deliberately reverts in this callback, the entire mint transaction reverts. Because the deposit processing loop does not catch or skip failing deposits and deposits cannot be cancelled, a malicious actor can submit a deposit that points to a contract that always reverts, causing the queue to stall. The queue processes deposits in a first‑in‑last‑out order, so once the attacker’s deposit is placed, all earlier deposits remain unprocessed and the funds remain locked in the contract. Users who deposited before the attacker lose access to their funds, seeing no balance update or receipt, while the UI may show a pending deposit that never completes. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the deposit handling code, where the auditor noticed that the safe‑mint logic from ERC1155 was being reused without considering that the receiver callback can be hostile. The problem is subtle because the ERC1155 standard expects the receiver to be a well‑behaved contract, and the safe‑mint call is usually harmless for normal users, so the denial‑of‑service effect is not obvious from a superficial test. The bug belongs to the class of external‑call‑induced denial‑of‑service or safe‑transfer DoS where a contract’s reliance on a callback that can revert blocks progress. To remediate, the contract should override the internal mint routine to omit the _doSafeTransferAcceptanceCheck when minting shares for deposits, or otherwise isolate the deposit logic from external callbacks, ensuring that a malicious receiver cannot abort the whole queue.

title: The renewal grace period gives users insur-
content: The vulnerability concerns the renewal logic of a protection position in the insurance pool. When a user renews a position, the contract validates that the previous expiration timestamp lies within an allowed grace period relative to the current block timestamp. However, after this check the contract incorrectly sets the start of the new insurance period to block.timestamp instead of the original expiration time. Because the grace period is meant to be a short window during which the user can pay a premium to extend coverage, resetting the start time to the current time means that no premium is collected for the duration of the grace period. Consequently the user receives coverage for free during that window. An attacker can repeatedly renew at the last moment of each grace period, paying only the minimal premium required for the next interval while continuously enjoying coverage that should have been paid for. This results in loss of revenue for the protocol and undermines the economic assumptions of the insurance model. The issue manifests whenever a protection position is renewed within its grace period; it does not affect renewals performed after the grace period has elapsed. All participants who hold protection positions are potentially affected, but the exploit is most profitable for users who can time renewals precisely. The bug was discovered during a manual audit of the ProtectionPoolHelper and ProtectionPool contracts, where the renewal flow was examined and the mismatch between the validation timestamp and the actual start timestamp was observed. The problem is subtle because the contract still enforces the grace‑period check, so the renewal appears legitimate, and the UI may simply show an uninterrupted protection period, making the loss of premium revenue hard to notice. To remediate the issue, the renewal function should calculate the new coverage start as the previous expiration timestamp rather than the current block.timestamp, ensuring that the grace period is billed correctly and that premiums are collected for the entire coverage duration. This class of bug falls under incorrect time‑based accounting or misaligned state updates, where the contract’s accounting logic diverges from the intended business rules, leading to free insurance, missing premium collection, and a breach of the protocol’s financial guarantees.
summary: When a protection position is renewed, the contract checks that the expired timestamp is within the grace period of the current timestamp. The issue is that when it is renewed, it starts insurance at block.timestamp rather than the expiration of the previous protection. The result is that the grace period is effectively free insurance for the user. /ProtectionPoolHelper.sol#L390-L397 When checking if a position can be renewed it checks the expiration of the previous protection to confirm that it is being renewed within the grace period. ol/ProtectionPool.sol#L181-L194 After checking if the protection can be removed it starts the insurance at block.timestamp. The result is that the grace period doesn't collect any premium for it's duration. To abuse this the user would keep renewing at the end of the grace period for the shortest amount of time so that they would get the most amount of insurance for free. One might argue that the buyer didn't have insurance during this time but protection can be renewed at any time during the grace period and late payments are very easy to see coming (i.e. if the payment is due in 30 days and it's currently day 29). The result is that even though technically there isn't insurance the user is still basically insured because they would always be able to renew before a default. Renewal grace period can be abused to get free insurance.

title: Missing validation of snapshotId makes it pos-
content: The vulnerability is an improper state update in the protection pool’s claim logic. When a seller calls claimUnlockedCapital, the contract calculates the amount that can be withdrawn for the current snapshot and then stores the snapshot identifier in a mapping that tracks the last claimed snapshot for each seller and lending pool. The code fails to verify that the snapshot identifier returned by the internal _calculateClaimableAmount function is non‑zero before writing it back. If the calculation yields a zero claimable amount – which happens when the seller has already claimed the capital for the most recent snapshot or when the locked capital flag is false – the mapping is overwritten with zero. As a result the contract believes the seller has never claimed any snapshot and allows the same snapshot to be claimed again. An attacker can therefore trigger a claim that returns zero, reset the last claimed snapshot id, and then repeatedly invoke claimUnlockedCapital to drain the unlocked capital from the protection pool. The impact is that funds that should be locked after a single claim become repeatedly withdrawable, leading to loss of capital for the protocol and unfair advantage for the malicious seller. The issue occurs whenever the snapshot calculation returns zero, which is typical after a lending pool moves from Late back to Active and the locked flag is cleared. It affects any investor or seller that interacts with the protection pool, as well as the overall protocol’s accounting guarantees. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the state‑update sequence and noticed that the snapshot id was written without a guard. It is subtle because a zero‑amount claim does not transfer tokens, so the UI may show a successful transaction with no visible funds moved, making the reset of internal state easy to miss. To remediate, the contract should only update the last claimed snapshot id when the returned snapshot identifier is greater than zero (or greater than the previously stored value), ensuring that a zero‑amount claim cannot reset the accounting record. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of improper state mutation after a no‑op operation, often leading to double‑spending or replay of previously settled actions.
summary: Missing validation of snapshotId makes it possible for the investor/seller to claim unlocked capitals from the same snapshot multiple times Description The seller can call ProtectionPool.claimUnlockedCapital function to claim unlocked capitals. It then calls defaultStateManager.calculateAndClaimUnlockedCapital to calculate the claimable amount, then it transfers the amount to the seller if it is greater than zero. defaultStateManager.calculateAndClaimUnlockedCapital function works as follows: 1. Iterates over all lending pools. 2. For each lending pool calculates the claimable amount for the seller. 3. Updates the last claimed snapshot id for the seller for the given lending pool so it becomes uncalimable next time. However, before updating the last claimed snapshot id, it doesn't check if the returned snapshot Id (from _calculateClaimableAmount function) is zero. This means if it happens that the returned value is zero, the last claimed snapshot id will be reset to its initial value (zero) and the seller can claim again as if s/he never did. • An investor/seller could possibly claim unlocked capitals from the same snapshot multiple times which is unfair. • An attacker could join the pool as seller, later drains the funds from the protection pool whenever any lending pool goes into Late then Active state again. • ProtectionPool.claimUnlockedCapital ```solidity /// Investors can claim their total share of released/unlocked capital across all lending pools uint256 _claimableAmount = defaultStateManager .calculateAndClaimUnlockedCapital(msg.sender);
