if (_claimableAmount > 0) { console.log( "Total sToken underlying: %s, claimableAmount: %s", totalSTokenUnderlying, _claimableAmount ); /// transfer the share of unlocked capital to the receiver poolInfo.underlyingToken.safeTransfer(_receiver, _claimableAmount); } ``` ol/ProtectionPool.sol#L427-L445 • defaultStateManager.calculateAndClaimUnlockedCapital ```solidity /// Calculate the claimable amount across all the locked capital instances for a given protection pool ( uint256 _unlockedCapitalPerLendingPool, uint256 _snapshotId ) = _calculateClaimableAmount(poolState, _lendingPool, _seller); _claimedUnlockedCapital += _unlockedCapitalPerLendingPool; /// update the last claimed snapshot id for the seller for the given lending pool, /// so that the next time the seller claims, the calculation starts from the last claimed snapshot id poolState.lastClaimedSnapshotIds[_lendingPool][_seller] = _snapshotId; ``` faultStateManager.sol#L186-L195 • defaultStateManager._calculateClaimableAmount ```solidity /// Verify that the seller does not claim the same snapshot twice if (!lockedCapital.locked && _snapshotId > _lastClaimedSnapshotId) { ERC20SnapshotUpgradeable _poolSToken = ERC20SnapshotUpgradeable( address(poolState.protectionPool) ); console.log( "balance of seller: %s, total supply: %s at snapshot: %s", _poolSToken.balanceOfAt(_seller, _snapshotId), _poolSToken.totalSupplyAt(_snapshotId), _snapshotId ); /// The claimable amount for the given seller is proportional to the seller's share of the total supply at the snapshot /// claimable amount = (seller's snapshot balance / total supply at snapshot) * locked capital amount _claimableUnlockedCapital = (_poolSToken.balanceOfAt(_seller, _snapshotId) * lockedCapital.amount) / _poolSToken.totalSupplyAt(_snapshotId); /// Update the last claimed snapshot id for the seller _latestClaimedSnapshotId = _snapshotId; console.log( "Claimable amount for seller %s is %s", _seller, _claimableUnlockedCapital ); } ``` faultStateManager.sol#L487-L515

title: Protection sellers can bypass withdrawal delay
content: The vulnerability is a withdrawal‑delay bypass that lets protection sellers withdraw their full sToken balance in every cycle despite the protocol’s intention to enforce a two‑cycle waiting period after a withdrawal request. The root cause is that the internal _requestWithdrawal function only records a single withdrawal request per user for a specific future cycle and overwrites any previous request without keeping track of how much of the user’s balance is already locked by earlier requests. Because the contract does not maintain a separate accounting of “pending withdrawal” versus “available balance”, a user can submit a new request for the full balance in each new cycle, causing the withdrawalCycleDetails mapping for each upcoming cycle to contain the user’s entire balance. When the open period of the next cycle arrives, the contract allows the user to withdraw the amount recorded for that cycle, which is again the full balance, effectively resetting the delay each time. An attacker can therefore call requestWithdrawal at the end of every cycle, wait the minimal open‑period time, and pull out the entire amount repeatedly, draining the protection pool far faster than intended. The impact is a rapid loss of capital from the protected lending pool, erosion of the economic guarantees that protection sellers are supposed to provide, and potential loss of rewards for honest participants whose funds are unexpectedly reduced. The issue manifests whenever a protection seller submits a withdrawal request; there is no penalty or additional check to prevent repeated full‑balance requests, and the contract assumes that a single request per user per cycle is sufficient to enforce the delay. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the withdrawal logic, where the auditor noticed that the code only stores the latest request amount and never aggregates or caps pending withdrawals against the user’s total holdings. This oversight can be hard to detect because the function emits a WithdrawalRequested event that appears to respect the delay, and typical unit tests may only cover a single request scenario, missing the cumulative effect across multiple cycles. To remediate, the contract should track a per‑user pending withdrawal amount that is locked for the required delay, ensure that the sum of pending withdrawals never exceeds the user’s current sToken balance, and optionally impose a penalty such as suspending reward accrual on locked funds during the waiting period. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of accounting‑state‑inconsistency vulnerabilities where delayed actions are not properly recorded, allowing an attacker to repeatedly reset the delay and extract funds. From a user’s perspective, the UI may show a withdrawal request being accepted with a “2‑cycle delay” label, yet the user can actually receive the funds after the next cycle’s open window, contradicting expectations. Other participants may notice their pool balance dropping unexpectedly or see “funds disappear” messages without any explicit error, indicating that the withdrawal delay enforcement is ineffective. The protocol’s business logic that assumes funds are locked for a defined period is violated, breaking the trust model of the protection service.

title: Lending pool state transition will be broken when pool is expired in late state
content: The vulnerability is a state‑machine transition flaw in the lending‑pool management logic. The contract determines a pool’s status by first checking whether the pool is expired and only afterwards checking for a late condition. Because the _getLendingPoolStatus function returns Expired before Late, the DefaultStateManager never sees a transition from Late to Expired or from Active directly to Late when the loan term ends without payment. As a result, capital that should be unlocked when a late pool is repaid, or locked when an active pool becomes late, remains in its previous state indefinitely. This can happen in two concrete scenarios. First, a pool that is already in the Late state reaches its term end or is fully repaid; the status changes to Expired, bypassing the Late‑to‑Expired transition, so previously locked capital is never released. Second, a pool that is still Active reaches its term end without the required payment; the status jumps to Expired instead of Late, preventing the lock‑up of capital that should protect lenders. The bug affects all participants that rely on the state manager – lenders, borrowers, protection‑token holders and the protocol itself – because funds may become permanently inaccessible or protection buyers may not receive compensation. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the ReferenceLendingPools and DefaultStateManager contracts when the auditor noticed that the order of condition checks could skip necessary state transitions. It is hard to notice because the contract simply reports the pool as Expired, which is a valid status, and no explicit error is thrown; the missing transition is silent. From a user’s perspective the UI will show a pool status of “Expired” while expected actions such as unlocking capital or locking protection funds do not occur, leading to symptoms like “my protection claim returns zero” or “my funds are still locked after repayment”. The bug belongs to the class of state‑machine edge‑case errors where missing or mis‑ordered transitions create dead states that break business logic. To remediate, developers should introduce explicit handling for Late‑to‑Expired and Active‑to‑Late transitions, or reorder the status checks so that late conditions are evaluated before expiration. Additionally, the contract should distinguish between expiration due to time and expiration due to full repayment, ensuring that appropriate capital‑movement actions are executed for each case.

title: User can game protection via renewal to get full insurance for free
content: The contract implements an insurance‑like protection mechanism where a user purchases a protectionAmount for a lending position and may later renew that protection. The renewal logic only validates that the caller, the token address and the lending contract match the original position and that the renewal occurs before the grace period expires. It does **not** verify that the new protectionAmount is equal to or less than the amount that was originally purchased. Because of this omission, a malicious user can open many positions with the minimum protection (for example, a protectionAmount of 1) and stagger the expiration of each position so that at any moment a position is about to become overdue. When a payment is about to be classified as late, the attacker calls the renewal function and supplies the maximum possible protectionAmount – typically the full token balance – while paying only the tiny premium associated with the original 1‑unit protection. The protocol then treats the position as fully protected and will reimburse the borrower for the entire loss, even though the premium collected is negligible. From the user’s point of view the expected behaviour is that the premium scales with the amount of protection purchased; instead the user can obtain full coverage for almost no cost, leading to a situation where “the insurance is free”. The vulnerability is a classic case of **missing validation of state‑changing parameters** (here the protection amount) during a state transition (renewal). It is discovered through manual audit of the renewal function in ProtectionPoolHelper.sol where the only checks are time, token and contract address. The bug is hard to notice because the function appears to enforce the usual temporal constraints, and the economic impact is not obvious from the code alone. The impact is severe: the protocol can lose the full value of protected loans without receiving adequate premiums, undermining its financial model and potentially draining funds from the protection pool. The issue affects any borrower or lender that relies on the insurance, as well as the protocol’s overall solvency. To remediate, the renewal routine must enforce that the new protectionAmount does not exceed the amount that was originally purchased (or at most the amount of the expired insurance) and must recalculate the premium based on the renewed amount, ensuring that users cannot increase coverage without paying the corresponding fee. This change restores the intended economic invariant that protection cost is proportional to coverage and prevents free‑insurance exploitation.
summary:
When renewing a position, the new protectionAmount can be higher than what was previously bought. A user can abuse this to get insurance for free. Most of the time they would keep the protection amount at 1 and pay virtually no premium. Since late payments can be seen very far in advance they would simply renew their insurance at the max value of token right before the borrower was officially late and gain the full protection.
ProtectionPoolHelper.sol#L383-L398
When evaluating if a user can renew their insurance only the time, token and lending contract are verified. It never checks the amount of protection that the user is renewing for. This can be abused to renew for MORE protection than originally bought. A user could abuse this to renew right before there was a late payment for the full amount of protection.
They can abuse another quirk of the renewal system to make sure they are always able to renew at any time. Since a user is allowed to open an unlimited number of positions on a single LP token they can open a large number of positions with 1 protection amount. They would space out each protection to expire exactly with the grace period. The result is that they would be able to renew any position at a moment's notice.
They would abuse this by choosing to renew their protection for the max value of the token right before a payment was officially late. This would allow them to collect a full repayment while paying basically nothing in premium.
User can get full protection for free.

title: Fixed title
content: The vulnerability concerns the renewal path of a protection product that guards a lending pool against loss events. When a borrower’s protection expires, the protocol allows a grace period (LateWithinGracePeriod) during which the borrower may still renew the protection. The contract’s renewal function first validates that the caller owns the correct NFT and that the request occurs within the grace period, then forwards the call to a shared internal routine that also creates new protections. This shared routine invokes a verification step that checks the lending pool status and rejects any pool whose status is LateWithinGracePeriod or Late. Because the same verification logic is used for both fresh purchases and renewals, a legitimate renewal request made while the loan is in the grace period is mistakenly treated as invalid and the transaction reverts with a LendingPoolHasLatePayment error. The root cause is the inappropriate reuse of a status‑check that is intended for new protections but is too strict for renewals. Exploitation is straightforward: an existing buyer who has been paying premiums on time attempts to renew exactly when the loan transitions from Active to LateWithinGracePeriod, which can happen within seconds after the previous protection expires. The contract denies the renewal, leaving the buyer without coverage at the moment when risk is highest. The impact is that the buyer loses all previously paid premiums and is exposed to loss events without any recourse; the protocol also suffers reputational damage because users cannot rely on the promised grace‑period renewal window. This condition occurs only when the loan status changes to LateWithinGracePeriod or Late during the renewal window, a timing edge case that may be missed during normal testing because the same verification function appears correct for new purchases. The issue was identified during a formal audit where the flow of renewProtection was examined and the status check was traced to the shared _verifyLendingPoolIsActive function. It is hard to notice because the revert message references a generic late‑payment condition, which seems appropriate for new protections, and the code path is identical for both operations. The proper remediation is to separate the verification logic for renewals from that for new protections, allowing renewals when the pool is in LateWithinGracePeriod or Late while still rejecting truly defaulted or expired pools. Implementing a dedicated verifyLendingPoolIsActiveForRenewal function that omits the LateWithinGracePeriod and Late checks resolves the problem and restores the intended user experience where a buyer can extend coverage during the grace period, preventing loss of premiums and ensuring the protocol’s protection guarantees are honored.

title: Protection seller will lose unlocked capital if it
content: The vulnerability is an accounting error in the calculation of claimable unlocked capital for protection sellers. The function that aggregates unlocked capital iterates over an array of locked capital snapshots, but it stores the intermediate result in a single variable that is overwritten on each iteration instead of being incremented. As a result, only the amount associated with the most recent snapshot is returned, regardless of whether earlier snapshots contain unclaimed capital. This happens when the pool transitions from a locked state to an active state multiple times and a seller does not claim the unlocked capital after each transition. Under these conditions the seller’s claim will miss the earlier unlocked amounts, causing the funds to disappear from the seller’s perspective. The impact is a loss of unlocked capital for any protection seller who fails to claim in every period; the protocol appears to pay out, but the user receives less than expected, often only the last snapshot’s amount, while earlier amounts are silently dropped. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the claim logic, where the loop’s behaviour was examined and it became clear that the variable _claimableUnlockedCapital was being overwritten rather than accumulated. Because the function still returns a non‑zero value, the bug can be subtle and may not raise an immediate error, making it hard to notice without detailed testing of multi‑period scenarios. The flaw violates the business rule that sellers should be able to claim all unlocked capital across snapshots and that no capital should be lost due to timing. To fix the problem the aggregation variable must be incremented for each snapshot, or a separate accounting mechanism should track which snapshots have already been claimed, ensuring that the total claimable amount is the sum of all unclaimed unlocked capital rather than the last entry alone.
summary:
The protection seller will lose unlocked capital if it fails to claim during more than one period. The function DefaultStateManager._calculateClaimableAmount, used by DefaultStateManager.calculateAndClaimUnlockedCapital, which in turn is used by ProtectionPool.claimUnlockedCapital, overrides the claimable unlocked capital on every loop iteration on the lockedCapitals array. As a result, only the last snapshot is returned by this function, regardless if the protection seller has claimed the unlocked capital or not. The purpose of this code was to prevent sellers from claiming the same snapshot twice, but since the _claimableUnlockedCapital variable is being overwritten instead of incremented, on each loop iteration, it will also make sellers lose unlocked capital if they fail to claim at each snapshot. Proof of concept:
1. Pool goes to locked state with snapshotId 1
2. Pool goes to active state
3. Pool goes to locked state with snapshotId 2
4. Pool goes to active state
5. Protection seller calls ProtectionPool.claimUnlockedCapital, but they will only receive what's due from snapshotId 2, not from snapshotId 1
The protection seller will lose unlocked capital if it fails to claim during more than one period.

title: Sybil on withdrawal requests can allow lever-
content: The vulnerability is a withdrawal‑request sybil flaw that allows a single deposit of STokens to be used to generate multiple independent withdrawal requests across different addresses. The contract only verifies that the caller holds a positive SToken balance at the moment a withdrawal is requested, but it does not lock, burn, or time‑lock those tokens. Consequently an attacker can deposit USDC, receive the corresponding STokens, immediately request a withdrawal, transfer the STokens to another address they control, and repeat the request. Because each request is considered valid, the protocol records several pending withdrawals that together exceed the actual deposited amount. The attacker can then deposit new USDC through the same set of addresses within the same block or cycle, inflate the protocol’s leverageRatio or leverageFactor, and obtain a cheaper protection premium. By combining the inflated leverage with a flash‑loan, the attacker can borrow a large amount of USDC, purchase protection at an artificially low price, and unwind the position in the same transaction, repaying the flash‑loan while leaving protection sellers with reduced premiums or even a loss. The issue manifests whenever a user can request a withdrawal and subsequently move the STokens before the withdrawal is settled; it does not require any special permissions and can be executed in a single block if the timing is optimized. All participants who rely on the premium calculation – protection buyers, sellers, and lenders – are affected because the manipulated leverage factor breaks the economic assumptions of the protocol. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the withdrawal logic and noticed that the balance check is performed only at request time without any subsequent state change to prevent reuse. It is hard to notice because the contract’s state appears consistent – the user’s SToken balance remains unchanged until the withdrawal is processed – and no funds are lost directly at the moment of the request. The recommended mitigation is to freeze or burn the STokens associated with a withdrawal request, or to introduce a time‑lock that prevents the same tokens from being used to request another withdrawal until the first one is settled. This change ensures that each deposited token can back at most one pending withdrawal, restoring the intended one‑to‑one relationship between deposits and withdrawal requests and preventing leverage manipulation, premium gaming, and potential denial‑of‑service attacks.
summary:
To be able to withdraw, a user has to request a withdraw first. The only requirement to be able to request a withdraw is to have a balance of SToken when requesting. By requesting withdraws with the same tokens but different addresses, a malicious user can create the option to withdraw during one cycle more than what is deposited in the protocol. They cannot drain the protocol since they only have a limited amount of SToken to burn (required to call withdraw()), but they acquire the ability to deposit new funds and withdraw them in the same block, thus manipulating premium prices. Consider the following scenario: A malicious user wants to manipulate leverageRatio (to get a cheaper premium for example). They deposit 10k USDC into the protocol, and get 10k STokens. They request immediately a withdraw, and transfer STokens to another address and request a withdraw there, repeating the process 10 times. This works since balance is checked on requesting withdrawal but not locked or time-locked. 2 cycles later (actually ~1 cycle if the timing is optimized), they have the ability to take a flashloan for 100k USDC, deposit through the 10 addresses used, enjoy the cheaper premium as a protection buyer due to leverageFactor being high and withdraw all in the same transaction. They can safely repay the flash loan. Protection buyers can use this to:
• game premium prices, meaning that protection sellers get rugged.
• overprotect their lending positions (used in conjunction with HIGH-02, it can drain the whole protection pool if lending pool defaults).
• DOS the protocol by sending the leverage factor very high.

title: Protection buyer may buy multiple protections
content: The vulnerability is an over‑protection flaw in the Carapace protocol’s protection‑purchase logic. The contract verifies that each individual protection request does not exceed the loan’s remaining principal, but it does not keep a running total of protection already purchased for that loan. As a result a malicious buyer can submit several separate protection purchases, each of which passes the single‑request check, and cumulatively obtain protection coverage that is larger than the amount actually lent. This occurs because the function ReferenceLendingPools.canBuyProtection only compares the new protection amount with the current remainingPrincipal and never subtracts previously bought protection from that value. An attacker can therefore repeatedly call the purchase function, stacking protections until the sum of all protections exceeds the loan’s capital. When the underlying Goldfinch loan defaults, the protocol will honor each protection claim, paying out the aggregated amount, which can be greater than the pool’s available capital. The impact is a potential loss of funds for the protocol and its lenders, effectively allowing the attacker to “steal” money by over‑insuring a loan. The issue manifests under normal operating conditions whenever a user is allowed to buy multiple protections for the same loan position; no special privileges are required. It affects any participant who purchases protection, the protocol’s accounting integrity, and ultimately the lenders whose capital backs the pool. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the protection‑purchase flow and noticed that the remainingPrincipal variable was never updated after a protection was bought. Because each transaction appears valid in isolation, the problem can be hard to spot without aggregating state across multiple calls. From a user’s perspective the UI may show several distinct protection entries, and the borrower may expect each to be independent, while the protocol ends up paying out more than it should, leading to missing balances or empty pools after a default. The bug belongs to the class of “cumulative state‑validation” errors where per‑action checks are performed but aggregate constraints are omitted. To remediate the issue the protocol should maintain a total protection amount per loan and enforce that the sum of all protections never exceeds the remaining principal, or alternatively decrement the remainingPrincipal each time a protection is purchased. This ensures that the accounting invariant – total protection ≤ loan capital – holds across multiple purchases, preventing over‑protection and protecting the protocol’s funds.
summary: The Carapace protocol checks that a protection buyer does not buy a protection for an amount greater than remainingPrincipal in the corresponding loan. However it is possible for the buyer to buy multiple different protections for the same Goldfinch loan. The check for the possibility for a user to buy a protection is done in ReferenceLendingPools.canBuyProtection. It checks the protection about to be created does not exceed remaining principal. But it still allows the user to create multiple protections for the same loan position. The malicious user can overprotect their loan position on Goldfinch and thus claim a larger amount on loan default than what they lent. For now as the default using all funds deposited into the protocol reaching leverageRatioFloor and not allowing any new protections to be bought.

title: Too many active protections can cause the
content: The vulnerability is an unbounded iteration over a dynamic array of protection records inside the ProtectionPool contract. The contract stores each purchased protection in an array and later iterates over the entire collection in two critical functions: lockCapital() and _accruePremiumAndExpireProtections(). Because the array length is not limited, an attacker or a legitimate user can cause the array to grow arbitrarily large. When the number of stored protections approaches the block gas limit, the loops consume more gas than the block allows, causing the transaction to run out of gas and revert. This situation occurs whenever lockCapital() is called to lock deposited tokens or when the contract tries to accrue premiums and expire old protections. The revert prevents the contract from performing its core accounting, effectively rendering the ProtectionPool unusable. Users who have purchased protection expect their tokens to be locked and to receive coverage in case the underlying pool defaults; instead they see their transactions fail, their balances remain unchanged, and no coverage is provided. The impact is severe: protection buyers are left unprotected, deposited funds cannot be locked, and the protocol may lose trust because a core safety mechanism is broken. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that identified loops over an unbounded array, matching the pattern described in SWC‑128 (Unexpected Ether consumption due to unbounded loops). The bug is hard to notice because the contract works correctly with a small number of protections, and the failure only appears after the array grows beyond a certain size, which may not be exercised in typical test scenarios. Conceptually, the fix requires either imposing a hard cap on the number of active protections so that the gas consumption of the loops stays safely below the block limit, or redesigning the logic to avoid iterating over the entire array—for example by using a mapping with per‑protection bookkeeping, processing protections in batches, or employing a queue that limits the number of items processed per call. By eliminating the need to traverse an unbounded collection, the contract can reliably lock capital and accrue premiums without risking out‑of‑gas reverts, restoring the intended protection functionality and preserving user funds.
summary: There are two instances where the ProtectionPool contract loops over an unbounded array. These can cause the transaction to exceed it, exceeding it will make the transaction revert, see https://swcregistry.io/docs/SWC-128. Both in lockCapital() and in _accruePremiumAndExpireProtections() the contract loops over the unbounded array of protections. If there are too many protections the transaction will revert because it exceeds it. Both the lockCapital() and _accruePremiumAndExpireProtections() functions are critical components of the contract. Them not being accessible renders the contract useless. Protection buyers won't be covered in case of the underlying pool defaulting because the deposited tokens can't be locked up.

title: Rogue plugin can become unremovable and
content: The vulnerability resides in the plugin management design of the StakingModule contract. The module allows external plugins to be attached, but removal of a plugin is gated by a require check that the plugin reports itself as deactivated via IPlugin.deactivated(). If a plugin becomes malicious – for example after a buggy upgrade or because its owner deliberately changes its behaviour – it can permanently return false for deactivated() and also return the maximum uint256 value (2**256‑1) from its claim() function. The claim() return value is summed into a total without overflow protection, so the addition overflows and causes the surrounding transaction to revert. In addition, the module calls IPlugin.requiresNotification() and IPlugin.notifyStakeChange() for every plugin during staking, exiting and migration operations. A rogue plugin that always reverts these calls blocks the internal _notifyStakeChangeAllPlugins loop, which in turn prevents stake(), partialExit(), exit(), claim(), slash() and other core functions from completing. Because the removal function cannot bypass the deactivated() check, the malicious plugin cannot be removed, effectively freezing the entire StakingModule. All stakers see their balances locked, withdrawals become unavailable, and the protocol’s accounting logic is broken – users expect to be able to claim rewards or exit their position but receive no response or a transaction that reverts. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the plugin lifecycle and identified that the contract trusts plugin‑provided boolean flags without any fallback mechanism. It is difficult to notice in normal operation because the plugin interface appears benign and the failure only manifests when the plugin returns unexpected values, which may be indistinguishable from a temporary failure. The recommended mitigation is to add a force‑removal option that allows an authorized role to bypass the deactivated() requirement, or to redesign the plugin interface to include safe arithmetic checks and to ensure that a single misbehaving plugin cannot halt the entire module. In essence, the bug is a classic case of an untrusted external component being given too much control over core protocol flow, leading to a denial‑of‑service and permanent fund lockup.

title: CollateralManager#commitCollateral can be
content: The vulnerability resides in the CollateralManager contract where the public function commitCollateral allows a caller to attach additional collateral to a loan without verifying the current state of that loan. Because the function does not check whether the loan identified by the supplied bidId is still pending, has already been accepted, or is otherwise active, a borrower (or any user with access to the function) can invoke commitCollateral after the loan has been filled. This missing state validation constitutes an improper access‑control or business‑logic flaw: the contract assumes that collateral can only be added before acceptance, but the code does not enforce that assumption. An attacker can exploit the flaw by submitting a malicious token as collateral after the loan is active. The malicious token is crafted so that when the escrow later attempts to withdraw it during liquidation or loan closure, the transfer reverts, causing the escrow withdrawal to fail. As a result, the liquidation transaction reverts, preventing the lender from recovering the loaned assets and effectively denying service to the protocol. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition that can persist indefinitely; the loan remains in an accepted state but cannot be liquidated, and the funds locked in the escrow become inaccessible. This condition occurs whenever a borrower or any user calls commitCollateral with a bidId that corresponds to an already accepted loan. The affected parties include borrowers who may use the flaw maliciously, lenders who lose the ability to liquidate or recover their funds, and the overall protocol which suffers from reduced trust and potential financial loss. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the flow of collateral handling and noted the absence of a loan‑state guard in commitCollateral. It can be hard to notice because the function appears to work correctly for normal pending bids, and the revert only manifests later during liquidation, a path that may not be exercised in routine testing. To remediate, the contract should enforce a check that the loan is not active before allowing new collateral to be committed, typically by reverting if the loan status is anything other than pending. This aligns the implementation with the intended business rule that collateral may only be supplied before loan acceptance, eliminating the ability to inject malicious assets after the fact and restoring the correct liquidation flow.

title: CollateralManager#commitCollateral can be abused by any caller
content: The vulnerability resides in the CollateralManager contract where the function commitCollateral is declared as public and contains no access‑control checks. As a result any address can invoke the function for any existing bid identifier and supply an arbitrary list of collateral descriptors. The root cause is the missing verification that the caller is either the borrower of the loan, an approved forwarder, or the TellerV2 core contract that coordinates loan lifecycle events. Because the function trusts only the data it receives and does not validate the caller, an attacker can front‑run the normal loan acceptance flow, inject a malicious token as collateral, and manipulate the token’s behaviour after it has been recorded. In a typical exploit the attacker first creates a token that reports an extremely large balance (for example uint256.max) and can be paused after a single transfer. When a borrower creates a loan bid and a lender is about to accept it, the attacker observes the pending bid, calls commitCollateral with the malicious token, and thereby adds the token to the loan before the lender’s acceptance transaction is mined. Once the loan is filled, the attacker pauses the token, which breaks the protocol’s liquidation logic and prevents the loan from being fully repaid using the collateral. The attacker can then demand a ransom to unpause the token, effectively holding the locked collateral hostage. The impact is that lenders may lose the ability to recover their funds through liquidation, borrowers may find their loan unable to be repaid, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions about collateral value and availability are violated. This condition can occur at any time while a bid is open and before it is filled, and it affects any participant that interacts with the loan – borrowers, lenders, and the protocol itself. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that highlighted the lack of any require statement or modifier restricting access to commitCollateral. Because the function appears to perform a benign operation (adding collateral) and does not emit explicit warnings, the problem can be difficult to notice unless one inspects the call‑graph and tests for unauthorized calls. The recommended remediation is to enforce proper authorization by reverting the call unless the sender is the loan’s borrower, an approved forwarder, or the TellerV2 contract, thereby restoring the intended trust model and preventing arbitrary parties from injecting malicious collateral. This class of bug is a classic missing‑authorization vulnerability that enables front‑running and token‑manipulation attacks, leading to scenarios where funds disappear, refunds fail, or collateral becomes unusable, contrary to user expectations that only the legitimate borrower can provide collateral for their loan.

title: CollateralManager#commitCollateral overwrites collateral
content: The vulnerability resides in the collateral management logic of the protocol where the internal function that records a borrower’s collateral does not protect against duplicate entries for the same collateral address. When a borrower (or any actor) calls the commitCollateral routine with a collateral address that has already been stored for a given bid, the mapping that holds the collateral information is overwritten with the new struct, replacing the original amount and token identifier. Because the lender acceptance function (lenderAcceptBid) retrieves the collateral amount directly from this storage without any additional verification, a malicious actor can front‑run the lender’s transaction, submit a second commitCollateral call with a dramatically lower amount, and cause the protocol to escrow only the reduced amount while still disbursing the full loan amount to the borrower. This sequence allows the attacker to obtain a large amount of borrowed assets (for example 10 ETH) while providing only a token amount worth a fraction of the required collateral (for example 1 USDC). The impact is a loss of funds for the lender who expects the borrower to lock sufficient collateral, and a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees that collateral value must cover the loan. The issue manifests when duplicate collateral is committed before the lender calls lenderAcceptBid, and when the protocol does not enforce that the collateral information supplied by the lender matches the originally committed values. It affects any lender who relies on the protocol to enforce proper collateralization, as well as the overall trustworthiness of the lending market. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the flow of collateral commitment and bid acceptance and identified that the storage write operation unconditionally overwrites existing entries. The problem is subtle because overwriting a mapping entry is a normal Solidity operation and no explicit error is raised, making it easy to miss without tracing the state changes across transactions. To remediate the issue, the contract should either prevent overwriting of existing collateral entries or require the lender to provide the expected collateral address and amount during bid acceptance, with a check that the stored values match these expectations. Additionally, the protocol could enforce a one‑time commit per collateral address per bid or emit a distinct event when an attempt to overwrite occurs, allowing external monitoring to detect suspicious activity. In essence, the bug is a classic “state overwrite” or “missing integrity check” that breaks the accounting invariant that collateral value must be at least the loan value, leading to scenarios where users see their funds disappear or loans being granted with insufficient security.

title: _repayLoan will fail if lender is blacklisted
content: The vulnerability resides in the internal loan repayment routine that directly transfers the lending token from the borrower to the recorded lender using a safeTransferFrom call. Because the routine does not mediate the transfer through an escrow, the call will revert if the token contract enforces a blacklist, as many stablecoins such as USDC do. The lender address is obtained from the bid record, and if the lender is a manager contract it can forward the loan ownership to any address, including one that is blacklisted by the token. By moving the loan to a blacklisted address, the lender can make the safeTransferFrom fail for every subsequent partial or full repayment and also for the liquidation path that would normally transfer the token to the lender. As a result the repayment transaction reverts, the loan never reaches a PAID state, and the borrower is unable to trigger the withdraw function that releases the collateral. From the borrower’s point of view the UI shows a repayment failed error or simply does not allow the withdrawal, leading to a situation where the collateral appears to disappear or become permanently locked. The attack can be performed at any time, for example after the borrower has almost fully repaid the loan, giving the lender a guaranteed griefing vector that forces a default and potentially allows the lender to claim the collateral. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the TellerV2 contract where the repayment flow was traced and the interaction with blacklisted token contracts was examined. It is subtle because the failure only manifests when a blacklisted address is involved, which may not be obvious during normal testing with non‑blacklisted tokens. The root cause is the lack of an intermediate escrow or pull‑based payment model; the contract assumes that a direct transfer will always succeed. To remediate, the protocol should adopt a push‑pull pattern: the borrower deposits the repayment amount into a trusted escrow (for example the TellerV2 contract itself) and the lender later pulls the funds, or the contract holds the repayment until the lender withdraws it. This way the repayment can only fail if the escrow itself is blacklisted, which is under the protocol’s control, eliminating the lender‑controlled blacklist attack.

title: Malicious user can abuse UpdateCommitment
content: UpdateCommitment is a function that allows a lender to modify certain fields of an existing loan commitment. The function checks that the caller is the original lender and that the principal token address and market identifier remain unchanged, but it does not verify that the lender field supplied in the new Commitment struct matches the original lender. Because of this missing validation, a malicious actor who is the current lender can submit a Commitment where the lender address is replaced with an arbitrary victim address. The contract accepts the update, overwriting the stored commitment with the attacker‑provided data. Subsequent loan execution logic, which assumes that the stored lender field correctly identifies the party entitled to receive the principal, will then transfer funds to the attacker’s address or lock the victim’s funds, effectively allowing the attacker to hijack the commitment and drain assets. The vulnerability manifests whenever updateCommitment is called; it does not depend on specific token values or market conditions, only on the ability to craft a Commitment with a different lender. Users who rely on the UI to see their own address as the lender may notice that after an update their balance becomes zero or that expected refunds never arrive, because the contract now points to a different owner. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the function’s require statements and identified the absent check for _commitment.lender. It can be hard to notice because the function appears to allow legitimate updates and the UI may not display the altered lender field prominently. The bug belongs to the class of improper access‑control or authorization checks, where a critical ownership attribute is not protected. To remediate, the contract should require that _commitment.lender equals msg.sender and also equals the stored lender before performing the assignment, ensuring that the lender cannot be changed through an update.

title: All allowances to DepositStableCoinToDealer
content: The vulnerability is an unchecked external call in the DepositStableCoinToDealer and GeneralRepay helper contracts that enables an attacker to execute an arbitrary contract call using user‑controlled parameters. The contract receives a bytes‑encoded parameter that is decoded into a swap target address and calldata, then it performs a low‑level call to that address without any validation or whitelist. Before the call, the contract approves the same target address to spend the deposited stable‑coin amount on behalf of the contract. Because the approval is granted to an address supplied by the caller, a malicious actor can set the swap target to the token contract itself and craft calldata that triggers a transferFrom from any user who has previously approved the helper contract. The root cause is the combination of (1) granting token allowance to an arbitrary address and (2) invoking that address with unchecked calldata, which together break the assumption that only a trusted swap router will be called. An attacker can exploit the bug by first waiting for a victim to approve the helper contract for a certain amount of USDT, then submitting a deposit transaction where the swap target is the USDT token contract and the calldata calls transferFrom(victim, attacker, amount). The contract will approve the token contract to spend the victim’s tokens and then execute the call, resulting in the token contract moving the approved amount from the victim to the attacker. The impact is a loss of the victim’s approved stable‑coin balance; from the user’s perspective the expected outcome – a successful swap into the dealer or bank – is replaced by a zero balance or missing funds, with no error message other than a possible revert if the call fails. The issue manifests whenever a user calls the deposit function after having set an allowance for the helper contract, and the attacker can supply any swap target address. All users who have granted allowances to the contract are potentially affected, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions that deposited funds are safely swapped are violated. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the source lines where the contract decodes the parameters and performs the low‑level call, noting the lack of any address validation or function selector checks. The problem is subtle because the call appears to be a normal swap operation, and the approval‑reset pattern (approve 0 then approve amount) is a common practice, making the malicious use of the same pattern less obvious. To remediate, the contract should restrict the swap target to a known whitelist of trusted router contracts, validate calldata against expected function signatures, and avoid granting token allowances to addresses supplied by external callers. Additionally, using safe‑swap libraries that encapsulate the approval and call logic can prevent arbitrary external calls and protect user allowances from being hijacked.

title: Escrow approvals are not cleared when club is
content: The vulnerability is a persistent‑approval flaw in the club escrow system. When a club token (ERC20 or ERC721) is transferred, any approvals that were granted by the previous owner are not automatically revoked. As a result, the former owner retains the ability to invoke approved functions on the club’s assets – such as withdrawing players, tokens or other value – even after the club has been sold to a new holder. The root cause is that the escrow contract does not clear or reset the approval mappings when ownership of the club identifier changes, treating the approval state as independent of token ownership. An attacker can exploit this by first acquiring a club, setting an approval for themselves (or a malicious contract), then selling the club to an unsuspecting buyer. After the sale, the attacker invokes the lingering approval to drain all assets that were associated with the club, leaving the new owner with an empty or partially emptied club. The impact is high: funds, player NFTs, and any ERC20 balances linked to the club can be stolen, effectively nullifying the buyer’s purchase and undermining trust in the protocol. The condition under which this occurs is any club transfer that does not trigger a revocation of existing approvals; it affects all participants who buy or sell clubs, as well as the overall protocol’s reputation and financial safety. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the escrow’s state‑transition logic and noticed that approval mappings were never updated on transfer events. Because the contract continues to function normally from the user interface – the buyer sees the club listed but later observes missing players or zero balances – the problem can be hard to notice until after the assets have been drained. The bug belongs to the class of “approval persistence” or “missing revocation” vulnerabilities, where access control state is not tied to ownership changes, violating the fundamental accounting assumption that only the current owner can manage the club’s assets. From a user’s perspective, the expected behavior is that after purchasing a club, they should have exclusive control over its assets; in reality, the previous owner can still move those assets, leading to symptoms such as “my club shows no players after I bought it” or “my balance is suddenly zero”. To remediate the issue, the escrow design must be changed so that any approval granted on a club identifier is automatically cleared or transferred in a controlled manner when the club token changes hands. This can be achieved by resetting approval mappings in the transfer hook, using ERC721’s _beforeTokenTransfer or ERC20’s _beforeTokenTransfer callbacks, or by implementing a dedicated revocation function that is called as part of the sale process. Ensuring that approvals are tightly coupled to the current owner will restore the intended security guarantees and prevent malicious draining after a sale.
summary:
Escrow approvals remain even across club token transfers. This allows a malicious club owners to sell their club then drain everything after sale due to previous approvals.
ERC20 and ERC721 token approval persist regardless of the owner of the club. The result is that approvals set by one owner can be accessed after a token has been sold or transferred. This allows the following attack:
1) User A owns clubId = 1
2) User A sets approval to themselves
3) User A sells clubId = 1 to User B
4) User A uses persistent approval to drain all players and tokens
Malicious approvals can be used to drain club after sale

title: Malicious users can honeypot other users by
content: The vulnerability is a front‑running or race‑condition style honeypot that arises because the escrow component of the club marketplace does not lock the tokenized assets during a sale transaction. The root cause is a design separation where the club contract and the escrow contract are independent and the escrow owner (typically the seller) retains unrestricted permission to transfer the underlying player tokens at any time, including immediately before or even within the same block as a purchase. An attacker can monitor the mempool for a pending club purchase, then quickly invoke the escrow’s token‑withdrawal function to move all player tokens out of the escrow before the sale is finalized. This can be done in a single block, effectively allowing the seller to keep the assets while the buyer receives an empty club. The impact is that a buyer who believes they are acquiring a club with valuable assets ends up with a club that contains no players, resulting in a loss of the purchase price and a breach of the protocol’s economic guarantees. The condition occurs whenever a club is listed for sale and the escrow does not enforce an atomic transfer of assets; it can be triggered by any user with owner privileges on the escrow, which is typically the seller. All participants in the marketplace – buyers, sellers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the trust model assumes that assets are transferred together with ownership. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the escrow’s access controls and noticed that the withdrawal function was not gated by any sale‑in‑progress flag. It may be hard to notice in normal operation because the contract behaves correctly when no concurrent purchase is observed; only under the specific timing of a front‑run does the bug manifest, making it appear as a sudden “empty club” symptom rather than a deterministic failure. From a user’s perspective the UI would show a successful purchase transaction, but the club’s player list would be empty, contradicting the expectation that the purchased club contains the advertised assets. This violates the fundamental accounting assumption that the value of a club is the sum of its player tokens and that ownership transfer preserves that value. To remediate the issue the escrow logic should be redesigned to lock or escrow the player tokens for the duration of a sale, enforce an atomic swap of ownership and assets, or employ a commit‑reveal scheme that prevents the seller from withdrawing until the buyer’s transaction is irrevocably mined. Such a redesign would eliminate the ability for a malicious seller to execute a honeypot attack and restore confidence that purchases deliver the expected assets.
summary:
Since the club and escrow are separate and tokens can be transferred at any time by the owner, it allows malicious users to honeypot victims.
Tokens can be transferred out of the escrow by the owner of the club at anytime. This includes right before (or even in the same block) that the club is sold. This allows users to easily honeypot victims when selling clubs:
1) User A owns Club 1
2) Club 1 has players worth 5 ETH
3) User A lists Club 1 for 2.5 ETH
4) User B buys Club 1
5) User A sees the transaction in the mempool and quickly transfers all the players out
6) User A maintains all their players and User B now has an empty club
Malicious users can honeypot other users

title: MarginTrading.sol: Missing flash loan initiator check
content: The vulnerability is an unchecked flash‑loan initiator in the MarginTrading contract. The executeOperation callback is intended to be invoked only when the contract itself initiates the flash loan, but the code does not verify that the caller (the initiator address passed by Aave) matches the contract address. Because Aave allows any address to be specified as the receiver of a flash loan, an attacker can request a flash loan with the MarginTrading contract set as the receiver while the attacker is the actual initiator. The callback then runs with the attacker‑controlled parameters, allowing the attacker to perform a malicious swap that extracts part of the borrowed assets before the loan is repaid. The borrowed amount is repaid from the MarginTrading contract’s balances, not from the attacker, so the contract’s position can be closed or partially closed without the owner’s consent, and excess funds can be siphoned away. This can happen whenever a flash loan is taken against the contract, i.e., any time the executeFlashLoans function is callable, and there is an open margin position with assets that can be swapped. Users of the protocol see their DAI balance reduced unexpectedly, or a margin position that appears to be closed while they receive no profit. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that noted the missing _initiator check, a known mistake highlighted in Aave documentation. It is hard to notice because the flash‑loan callback is executed in the same transaction and the contract’s internal accounting appears consistent after repayment, masking the theft. The proper fix is to enforce that the initiator address equals the contract’s own address, ensuring only self‑initiated flash loans are processed. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of “unrestricted external callback” or “missing access control on flash‑loan receiver”, which breaks the assumption that only trusted code can trigger sensitive state changes. Exploiting the bug allows an attacker to steal funds, close positions without permission, and violate the protocol’s accounting guarantees.
summary:
The MarginTrading.executeOperation function is called when a flash loan is made (and it can only be called by the lendingPool).
The wrong assumption by the protocol is that the flash loan can only be initiated by the MarginTrading contract itself.
However this is not true. A flash loan can be initiated for any receiverAddress.
This is actually a known mistake that devs make and the aave docs warn about this (although admittedly the warning is not very clear):
https://docs.aave.com/developers/v/2.0/guides/flash-loans
So an attacker can execute a flash loan with the MarginTrading contract as receiverAddress. Also the funds that are needed to pay back the flash loan are pulled from the receiverAddress and NOT from the initiator:
https://github.com/aave/protocol-v2/blob/30a2a19f6d28b6fb8d26fc07568ca0f29 18f4070/contracts/protocol/lendingpool/LendingPool.sol#L532-L536
This means the attacker can close a position or repay a position in the MarginTrading contract.
By crafting a malicious swap, the attacker can even steal funds.
Let's assume there is an ongoing trade in a MarginTrading contract:
daiAToken balance = 30000
wethDebtToken balance = 10
The price of WETH when the trade was opened was ~ 3000 DAI
In order to profit from this the attacker does the following (not considering fees for simplicity):
1. Take a flash loan of 30000 DAI with MarginTrading as receiverAddress with mode=0 (flash loan is paid back in the same transaction)
2. Price of WETH has dropped to 2000 DAI. The attacker uses a malicious swap contract that pockets 10000 DAI for the attacker and swaps the remaining 20000 DAI to 10 WETH (the attacker can freely choose the swap contract in the _params of the flash loan).
3. The 10 WETH debt is repaid
4. Withdraw 30000 DAI from Aave to pay back the flash loan
The attacker can close trades, partially close trades and even steal funds. debt on behalf of the MarginTrading contract)

title: claimCOMPAndTransfer() COMP may be locked
content: The vulnerability is a front‑running race condition in the claimCOMPAndTransfer function that can cause COMP rewards to become permanently locked in the contract. The function is intended to claim newly accrued COMP incentives from the Compound Comptroller and immediately transfer the claimed amount to the treasury manager. It does this by recording the contract's COMP balance before the claim, invoking COMPTROLLER.claimComp, recording the balance after the claim, and then calculating netBalance as the difference. The root cause is that COMPTROLLER.claimComp is a public function that any address can call at any time, and the contract does not protect the balance‑difference calculation from being altered by external calls before it executes. An attacker who can front‑run the manager’s transaction can call COMPTROLLER.claimComp on the same contract first, draining all pending COMP rewards. When the manager’s claimCOMPAndTransfer transaction runs afterwards, the balance before and after the call are identical, so netBalance is zero and the subsequent safeTransfer never executes. As a result, the COMP that was supposed to be transferred remains locked inside the contract, effectively disappearing from the treasury’s perspective. This issue manifests whenever the manager contract invokes claimCOMPAndTransfer while an adversary can submit a preceding transaction that also calls claimComp on the same address. The affected parties are the protocol’s treasury manager, any downstream users who rely on the receipt of COMP incentives, and the overall protocol revenue model that expects these incentives to be harvested and redistributed. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that examined the interaction between the reward‑claiming function and the public claimComp entry point, noting that the balance‑delta logic does not account for external calls. The bug can be hard to notice because the code appears to safely transfer only newly claimed tokens, and the contract’s COMP balance does not change after the manager’s call, giving the impression that nothing went wrong. To remediate the issue, the contract should not rely on a net balance delta that can be manipulated; instead it should transfer the entire COMP balance (or use a pull‑pattern where the manager explicitly withdraws the known amount) after claiming, or enforce that claimComp cannot be called by third parties during the critical window, for example by using a reentrancy guard combined with a single‑step claim‑and‑transfer operation. This would prevent an attacker from front‑running the claim and ensure that COMP rewards are always transferred out as intended, preserving the protocol’s accounting integrity and preventing funds from becoming locked.

title: Partial liquidations are not possible
content: The issue is a liquidation dead‑lock caused by an overly strict enforcement of the protocol's minimum‑borrow rule. In the vault valuation logic the system calculates the maximum amount a liquidator may deposit to reduce an under‑collateralised position. If the liquidator’s deposit is smaller than this calculated maximum, the code forces the liquidator to wipe out the entire outstanding debt. At the same time, a separate check ensures that after liquidation the remaining debt must be either zero or greater than the protocol‑defined minimum borrow size. Because the maximum deposit amount can be lower than the total debt, a liquidator may be unable to provide enough funds to clear the debt completely, while the post‑liquidation check prevents a partial reduction that would leave a non‑zero debt below the minimum threshold. The result is a state where the vault account cannot be liquidated at all: the transaction reverts with a “Must Liquidate All Debt” error, yet the liquidator cannot supply enough capital to satisfy the full‑liquidation requirement. This dead‑lock can occur for vault positions whose debt is close to the minimum borrow size (for example within 20 % of the threshold) and where discounting of future cash flows reduces the present‑value debt below the minimum. Users who rely on liquidations to protect their collateral – such as liquidity providers or borrowers – may see their positions remain under‑collateralised, leading to unrecoverable bad debt for the protocol and potential loss of funds for LPs who must cover the shortfall. The vulnerability was discovered during a manual audit of the vault liquidation flow, where the auditor observed that certain edge‑case debt amounts triggered a revert despite the presence of sufficient collateral. The bug is subtle because the logic appears to protect against under‑collateralisation, yet the interaction between the maximum deposit calculation and the minimum‑borrow guard creates an impossible condition that only manifests for a narrow range of debt values. To remediate the issue the liquidation factor calculation should be adjusted to allow partial liquidations that bring the debt down to, but not below, the minimum borrow size, or the minimum‑borrow check should be relaxed when a partial liquidation would leave a healthy position. In essence, the contract must treat the minimum‑borrow constraint as a lower bound for the *post‑liquidation* debt rather than an absolute barrier that prevents any reduction below that threshold, thereby restoring the ability to partially liquidate and eliminating the dead‑lock scenario.
summary:
Due to an incorrect implementation of VaultValuation.getLiquidationFactors(), Notional requires that a liquidator reduces an account's debt below minBorrowSize. This does not allow liquidators to partially liquidate a vault account into a healthy position and opens up the protocol to an edge case where an account is always ineligible for liquidation. While VaultValuation.getLiquidationFactors() might allow for the resultant outstanding debt to be below the minimum borrow amount and non-zero, deleverageAccount() will revert due to checkMinBorrow being set to true. Therefore, the only option is for liquidators to wipe the outstanding debt entirely but users can set up their vault accounts such that that maxLiquidatorDepositLocal is less than each of the vault currency's outstanding debt.
acts-v2/contracts/internal/vaults/VaultValuation.sol#L240-L270
File: VaultValuation.sol
```solidity
240: int256 maxLiquidatorDepositLocal = _calculateDeleverageAmount(
241:     vaultConfig,
242:     h.vaultShareValueUnderlying,
243:     h.totalDebtOutstandingInPrimary.neg(),
244:     h.debtOutstanding[currencyIndex].neg(),
245:     minBorrowSize,
246:     exchangeRate,
247:     er.rateDecimals
248: );
249:
250:
251: if (depositUnderlyingInternal < maxLiquidatorDepositLocal) {
252:     // If liquidating past the debt outstanding above the min borrow, then the entire
253:     // debt outstanding must be liquidated.
254:
255:     // (debtOutstanding - depositAmountUnderlying) is the post liquidation debt. As an
256:     // edge condition, when debt outstanding is discounted to present value, the account
257:     // may be liquidated to zero while their debt outstanding is still greater than the
258:     // min borrow size (which is normally enforced in notional terms -- i.e. non present
259:     // value). Resolving this would require additional complexity for not much gain. An
260:     // account within 20% of the minBorrowSize in a vault that has fCash discounting enabled
261:     // may experience a full liquidation as a result.
262:     require(
263:         h.debtOutstanding[currencyIndex].sub(depositUnderlyingInternal) < minBorrowSize,
264:         "Must Liquidate All Debt"
265:     );
266: } else {
267:     // If the deposit amount is greater than maxLiquidatorDeposit then limit it to the max
268:     // amount here.
269:     depositUnderlyingInternal = maxLiquidatorDepositLocal;
270: }
```
If depositUnderlyingInternal >= maxLiquidatorDepositLocal, then the liquidator's deposit is capped to maxLiquidatorDepositLocal. However, maxLiquidatorDepositLocal may put the vault account's outstanding debt below the minimum borrow amount but not to zero. However, because it is not possible to partially liquidate the account's debt, we reach a deadlock where it isn't possible to liquidate all outstanding debt and it also isn't possible to liquidate debt partially. So even though it may be possible to liquidate an account into a healthy position, the current implementation doesn't always allow for this to be true. Certain vault positions will never be eligible for liquidation and hence Notional may be left with bad debt. Liquidity providers will lose funds as they must cover the shortfall for undercollateralised positions.

title: Vault accounts with excess cash can avoid
content: The vulnerability concerns a logical dead‑lock in the vault settlement and liquidation workflow of the protocol. When a vault account is settled, any excess cash that resides in one of the vault’s currencies may be transferred out. This transfer can change the account’s collateral composition: the cash balance in the withdrawn currency drops while the debt exposure in the other currency remains unchanged. After the transfer, the contract calls IVaultAccountHealth.checkVaultAccountCollateralRatio to verify that the account still satisfies the required collateral ratio. If the withdrawal has made the account under‑collateralised, this check reverts, causing the settlement transaction to fail. The problem is compounded by the private function _authenticateDeleverage, which forbids any deleveraging or liquidation of a vault account that has not been settled first. Because settlement now reverts when the collateral ratio is violated, a liquidator cannot invoke deleveraging either, leaving the account in a state where it cannot be settled nor liquidated. This creates a situation where vault accounts that hold excess cash in one currency and significant debt in another become permanently stuck, preventing the protocol from recovering the debt and potentially leading to accrued bad debt. The issue manifests when an account is otherwise considered healthy before settlement, but the act of withdrawing the excess cash pushes it into an unhealthy state. Users experience symptoms such as transaction reverts during settlement, inability to trigger liquidation, and balances that appear unchanged or zero despite having cash. The bug belongs to the class of accounting‑logic errors where state transitions are ordered incorrectly, violating business assumptions that settlement should never render an account un‑liquidatable. It was discovered during a manual audit of the VaultAccountAction and VaultLiquidationAction contracts, where the interaction between settleVaultAccount, the collateral‑ratio check, and the deleverage authentication was examined. The flaw is subtle because each individual check appears correct in isolation, but their combination creates a dead‑lock that is not obvious from simple unit tests. To remediate the issue, the protocol should introduce a liquidation path that either performs the collateral‑ratio verification after the liquidator has purchased vault shares (thereby restoring health) or separates the settlement step from the collateral check, allowing a liquidator to settle and then immediately offset debt without triggering a revert. In essence, the fix requires re‑ordering or relaxing the collateral‑ratio enforcement during settlement so that accounts with excess cash can still be liquidated safely.

title: repayAccountPrimeDebtAtSettlement() user
content: The vulnerability resides in the settlement routine that repays a vault account’s prime‑debt and is intended to return any residual cash to the user. The function calculates a variable called primeCashRefund, which should represent the amount of cash that exceeds the account’s debt after repayment. However, due to a coding mistake the contract assigns netPrimeDebtChange the same value as accountPrimeStorageValue and then computes primeCashRefund as netPrimeDebtChange.sub(accountPrimeStorageValue). Because netPrimeDebtChange is equal to accountPrimeStorageValue, the subtraction always yields zero, so the refund amount is always zero. The root cause is a misuse of variables – the code should have used netPrimeDebtRepaid, the actual amount repaid, instead of netPrimeDebtChange. This logic error is triggered only when netPrimeDebtRepaid is less than the account’s stored debt, a condition that occurs during normal vault settlement when a user has over‑paid or has residual cash. When the condition is true the contract proceeds to the refund branch, calls TokenHandler.withdrawPrimeCash with a zero amount, and marks the transfer as successful, giving the appearance that the operation succeeded while the user receives no funds. From the user’s perspective the UI shows a successful settlement but the expected cash back never arrives; balances appear unchanged or the user sees a missing residual amount, effectively causing funds to disappear. The issue was discovered during a manual code review by the audit team, who noticed a spelling‑like error in the arithmetic expression. It is hard to notice because the transaction does not revert, no explicit error is emitted, and the only symptom is the absence of the expected refund. The bug belongs to the class of arithmetic/logic errors that break accounting assumptions, leading to incorrect financial outcomes. To remediate the problem the refund calculation must be corrected to use netPrimeDebtRepaid.sub(accountPrimeStorageValue) before converting the amount back to cash, ensuring that any genuine residual cash is transferred back to the user.

title: VaultAccountSecondaryDebtShareStorage.maturity
content: The vulnerability is a premature clearing of the secondary‑borrow maturity field in a vault account when a liquidation operation reduces only one of the two secondary debt shares. The root cause lies in the _reduceAccountDebt function, which constructs a two‑element PrimeRate array but populates only the element that corresponds to the currency being reduced. The second element remains uninitialized, yet the updateAccountSecondaryDebt routine later reads both debt shares using both prime rates. Because the missing prime rate causes VaultStateLib.readDebtStorageToUnderlying to return zero for the untouched debt share, the contract believes that both accountDebtOne and accountDebtTwo are zero. Consequently, the internal helper _setAccountMaturity sets the stored maturity to zero even though the second debt share still holds a non‑zero value in memory. This state inconsistency occurs during liquidation or deleveraging when a liquidator clears one secondary currency but not the other. From a user’s perspective the vault account appears to have no maturity, yet it still carries debt; attempts to settle the secondary borrow revert because the settleSecondaryBorrow function checks that a zero maturity must be accompanied by zero debt. The impact is that vault accounts with remaining secondary debt become unsolvable – they cannot be settled, cannot exit the vault, and the user’s assets remain locked in the protocol. The bug was discovered during a manual audit of the liquidation flow, where the auditor observed that after a successful deleverage call the maturity field was cleared while a secondary debt balance persisted. The issue is subtle because a zero maturity is a normal indicator of a fully repaid position, so the inconsistency may not be evident until later settlement logic fails. To remediate the problem the contract should retrieve and pass both prime rates for the secondary currencies, ensuring that readDebtStorageToUnderlying receives valid data for both debt shares, or the _setAccountMaturity logic should be hardened to clear maturity only when both debt values are truly zero after proper conversion. This class of bug is an accounting state‑inconsistency error caused by incomplete data propagation, leading to corrupted vault account state and potential fund lockup.

title: StrategyVault can perform a full exit without
content: The vulnerability is a missing validation of secondary debt when a StrategyVault performs a full exit for a vault account. In the Notional protocol, vaults are allowed to borrow a secondary currency in addition to the primary debt, and the protocol expects the vault to repay the secondary debt before the account is considered closed. The exit logic only checks that the primary debt (accountDebtUnderlying) and the vault share balance are zero before resetting the account maturity, but it never verifies that the secondary debt balances are also zero. This omission originates from the fact that the full‑exit path trusts the StrategyVault implementation to have cleared secondary obligations, yet the Notional contract does not enforce this invariant. An attacker can exploit the flaw by opening a secondary borrow, then triggering a full exit through the StrategyVault while leaving the secondary debt non‑zero. Because the Notional contract does not reject the exit, the protocol records a negative secondary balance, effectively creating bad debt that is not covered by any collateral. The impact is that the protocol’s accounting becomes inconsistent, the overall solvency of Notional may be reduced, and other users could bear the loss of the uncovered secondary loan. The condition for exploitation requires a vault that uses secondary borrowing, an outstanding secondary debt, and the ability to invoke the full‑exit function (redeeming all shares). The affected parties include the Notional protocol, its lenders, and any participants in leveraged vaults that rely on the isolation guarantees of the design. The issue was discovered during a security audit performed by Sherlock, who noted that the code only validates the primary debt and vault shares (line 271) and does not include a check for secondary debt. The bug can be hard to notice because the primary debt check passes, and the secondary debt is managed by a separate module, so the failure does not surface in the main contract’s state variables. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after exiting a vault the UI shows a zero balance and no remaining shares, yet the protocol’s internal accounting shows an outstanding secondary liability, meaning “funds disappear” or “debt remains unpaid”. To remediate the issue, the exit routine should be extended to query the secondary debt balances (both components if applicable) and require them to be zero before allowing the maturity to be cleared, thereby restoring the intended isolation of leveraged vaults and preventing the creation of bad debt.

title: Unable to transfer fee reserve assets to trea-
content: The vulnerability resides in the internal function that attempts to move fee reserve assets from the protocol’s fee pool to the treasury manager contract. The function calls a library routine to withdraw cash, expecting the routine to return a positive integer representing the amount transferred. In reality the library routine returns a signed integer that is zero or negative because the amount is expressed as a debit (negative) when redeeming assets. The code then checks that the returned value is greater than zero with a require statement. Because the value is never positive, the require condition always fails and the transaction reverts. Consequently any call that relies on this internal function – including the public transferReserveToTreasury entry point – cannot succeed, meaning the fee reserve assets are permanently locked in the contract. The root cause is an incorrect sign handling: the contract treats a negative redemption amount as a positive transfer without applying a negation. This logical error is subtle because the function signature returns a signed integer and the developer may have assumed the library would already provide a positive amount. The bug is discovered during a manual audit of the fee‑handling code where the return value of the withdraw routine was examined and found to be non‑positive. From a user’s perspective the treasury manager sees no increase in its balance after a fee transfer, the UI may display a zero fee balance even though fees have been accrued, and the protocol’s accounting reports show a discrepancy between expected revenue and actual treasury holdings. The impact is high because the protocol cannot move collected fees to its treasury, potentially starving the protocol of revenue, breaking incentive mechanisms, and causing accounting mismatches that could affect downstream contracts. The issue occurs whenever the protocol attempts to redeem and transfer any fee reserve asset, regardless of currency or amount. To remediate the problem the sign of the value returned by the withdrawal routine should be inverted before the require check, or the require condition should be rewritten to accept a negative value and treat its absolute magnitude as the transferred amount. In conceptual terms the fix is to correct the sign handling so that the transferred amount is interpreted correctly and the require statement can succeed, allowing fee assets to be moved to the treasury as intended.

title: Excess funds withdrawn from the money mar-
