The bug belongs to the class of state‑inconsistency or accounting‑mismatch vulnerabilities, where a contract’s internal ledger is not kept in sync with external token holdings. To remediate the issue the finishLiquidation() function should include a statement that writes the new token balance back to the pool’s storage, ensuring that the internal record always reflects the true ERC20 balance after any liquidation. Proper unit tests and invariant checks that compare the stored balance with the token contract’s balanceOf should be added to prevent regression.
summary: In D3Liquidation's finishLiquidation() function, update pool's token balance is missing. After finishLiquidation, there will be unequally of pool's token balance record and IERC20(token).balanceOf(pool), which will causing serious problems.

title: Bypass the blacklist restriction because the
content: The vulnerability is a blacklist bypass that occurs because the token contract does not enforce the blacklist restriction when tokens are minted or burned. The root cause lies in the _beforeTokenTransfer hook, which returns early for minting (from == address(0)) and burning (to == address(0)) operations, skipping the call to the transferRestrictor that checks the blacklist mapping. As a result, a blacklisted address can still receive newly minted dShares or have its tokens burned without triggering the AccountRestricted revert. An attacker can exploit this by creating a buy order that designates a non‑blacklisted receiver while the order originates from a blacklisted account; when the order is filled, the protocol mints dShares to the receiver, effectively allowing the blacklisted user to obtain tokens indirectly. Similarly, a blacklisted user can front‑run a blacklist transaction, open a sell order, and later have the escrowed dShares burned without any blacklist verification, receiving the payment token despite the protocol’s stated policy that blacklisted accounts cannot send or receive tokens. The impact is that the protocol’s compliance guarantees (OFAC, AML, and other security requirements) are broken, enabling illicit funds to move through the system and exposing the platform to regulatory risk. The issue manifests only during minting and burning paths; normal transfers are correctly blocked, which makes the bug easy to miss during routine testing because the most common token flow appears safe. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the whitelist/blacklist logic and noticed the early return in the _beforeTokenTransfer function. The problem is hard to notice because the code intentionally skips restrictions for mint and burn, a pattern that many developers assume is harmless. To remediate, the contract should perform a blacklist check on the recipient address during minting and on the sender address during burning, and it should also prevent blacklisted accounts from creating buy or sell orders. Conceptually, this is an access‑control bypass where validation is omitted in privileged lifecycle functions, a class of bugs often referred to as “missing authorization on mint/burn”. From a user’s perspective, a blacklisted user may still see their order filled, receive dShares, or cash out, contrary to the expectation that they would be blocked and receive zero tokens or no payment. The discrepancy between the protocol’s promise (blacklisted accounts cannot send or receive) and the observed behavior (tokens move through mint/burn) constitutes a serious compliance violation.

title: ProcessWithdrawals is still DOS-able
content: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition in the withdrawal processing routine of the VUSD contract. The contract maintains a queue of pending withdrawals and processes them sequentially by calling each recipient’s fallback/receive function while forwarding the remaining gas. Because the implementation does not limit the amount of gas that can be consumed by an external call, a malicious receiver can deliberately consume an amount of gas that exceeds the block gas limit (approximately 30 million gas on Ethereum). An attacker creates a contract whose receive function runs a long loop, for example 150 000 iterations, which uses more than 30 million gas. When the attacker requests a withdrawal to this contract via the withdrawTo function, the malicious entry is placed in the queue. When the protocol later calls processWithdrawals, the call to the malicious contract exhausts the available gas, causing the entire transaction to revert. As a result, the queue cannot advance, and all subsequent legitimate withdrawals remain stuck. Users experience the symptom of “withdrawal pending forever” – their UI shows a pending request, their balance does not decrease, and they receive no funds. The protocol’s assets become effectively locked and may be considered burnt because no one can process the queue. This issue was discovered during a Foundry test where a malicious contract recorded gas usage greater than the Ethereum block limit, leading to an out‑of‑gas revert. The problem is hard to notice in normal operation because withdrawals succeed when recipients are well‑behaved; only a deliberately gas‑heavy contract triggers the failure, and the revert appears as a generic out‑of‑gas error rather than a queue‑specific problem. The bug belongs to the class of gas‑griefing or withdrawal‑queue DoS vulnerabilities, where unbounded external calls allow an attacker to halt protocol functionality. To remediate, the contract should either eliminate the withdrawal queue and transfer assets immediately, enforce a fixed gas stipend for each external call, allow users or an admin to skip or remove malicious entries, or redesign the withdrawal mechanism to a pull‑based model that does not rely on iterating over a mutable queue. These measures would prevent a single malicious receiver from consuming excessive gas and ensure that legitimate withdrawals can continue to be processed.

title: Failed withdrawals from VUSD#processWithdrawals
content: The contract contains a withdrawal processing routine that iteratesover pending withdrawal requests and attempts to transfer the requested amount to each recipient using a low‑level call. If the external call returns false, the code merely emits a WithdrawalFailed event and moves on to the next entry without adjusting the contract’s reserve or recording the failure for later handling. Because there is no mechanism to retry or reclaim the amount, any withdrawal that fails becomes permanently locked inside the contract. The root cause is the absence of proper error handling for failed external calls: the function does not revert, does not deduct the amount from the reserve on failure, and does not persist the failed request in a retry queue. An attacker or a legitimate user can trigger the failure by withdrawing to a contract that deliberately reverts in its fallback function, consumes all gas, or otherwise rejects the call. When this happens, the transaction completes successfully from the perspective of the caller, the WithdrawalFailed event is logged, but the user receives no funds and the contract’s accounting no longer reflects the locked amount. The impact is that users who initiate withdrawals may see their balances unchanged, experience a “withdrawal failed” event without any refund, and the protocol loses access to the locked tokens, potentially reducing total liquidity and breaking accounting assumptions that reserves equal outstanding withdrawals. This condition occurs whenever a withdrawal address is unable to accept ether or the call fails for any reason; it is not limited to a specific amount or timing. All users who request withdrawals are affected, and the protocol’s overall health may degrade as more funds become unrecoverable. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the processWithdrawals function, where the lack of a retry or compensation path was noted. It can be hard to notice because the transaction does not revert, the event may be ignored, and the contract’s public state appears unchanged, giving a false impression that withdrawals succeeded. To remediate, the contract should record failed withdrawals in a pending list and allow authorized actors or the users themselves to retry the transfer, or alternatively fallback to sending the native token (VUSD) directly to the user on failure, ensuring that the reserve is correctly updated and that no funds remain permanently inaccessible. This class of bug falls under improper handling of external call failures leading to permanent fund loss, a common pattern in pull‑payment implementations that lack robust failure recovery.

title: Rogue validators can manipulate funding rates
content: The vulnerability consists of a privileged order‑matching mechanism that allows any validator on the Hubble exchange to control how liquidation and regular trades are settled. Because validators are the sole actors that can submit matching orders, they can create their own orders at prices that are deliberately advantageous and still remain within the protocol‑defined spread of up to twenty percent from the oracle price. The root cause is the combination of (i) exclusive matching rights granted to validators, (ii) the absence of any economic penalty such as slashing or token depreciation for misbehaviour, and (iii) the fact that the matching logic lives in a smart‑contract layer that is not part of the consensus protocol, so violating it does not trigger block rejection. An attacker who becomes a validator – which is trivial on Hubble because any node that stakes the required amount can join – can exploit this by first posting a low‑price order when a liquidation event occurs. For example, if the market price of WETH is 2000 USDC and a user must sell 100 ETH, the validator can place an order at 1980 USDC, match the liquidation to that order, and then immediately sell the acquired ETH on the open market at the true price, pocketing a profit of roughly 20 USDC per ETH. In a second attack vector the validator can submit tiny orders at the extreme ends of the allowed twenty‑percent spread, thereby skewing the time‑weighted average price (TWAP) that the protocol uses to compute funding rates. By inflating or deflating the mark price, the validator can force funding rates to move dramatically, causing leveraged positions to be liquidated faster and creating additional liquidation profit opportunities. The impact is that ordinary users receive a worse liquidation price than the market would provide, see unexpected spikes in funding rates, and may lose more collateral than anticipated. The protocol’s accounting assumptions – that the mark price reflects a fair market value and that funding rates are unbiased – are broken, leading to loss of trust and potential capital outflow. The issue was identified during a security audit (Sherlock) that examined the validator privilege model and the economic incentives surrounding it. It is difficult to detect in production because the manipulated prices still lie within the permitted spread, so they appear as legitimate trades, and there is no on‑chain evidence of misbehaviour due to the lack of slashing or consensus‑level enforcement. To remediate the problem the order‑matching design should be re‑engineered to remove exclusive validator control, enforce tighter price bounds, incorporate on‑chain verification of oracle consistency, and introduce economic penalties such as slashing or collateral requirements that can be seized when a validator deviates from fair matching. In broader terms the bug belongs to the class of privileged‑actor price manipulation and funding‑rate distortion vulnerabilities, where a party with special rights can bias market‑derived parameters to extract value at the expense of regular participants.
summary:
Validators are given the exclusive privilege to match. Any validator can abuse this privilege to manipulate funding rates and profit unfairly from liquidations. Normally validators are fully trusted but in the circumstances of these smart contracts and the chain it's deployed on, practically anyone can become a validator and abuse this privilege.
Consider the following attack vectors:
1) Profiting unfairly from liquidation. Assume the current mark price for WETH is 2000. A user is liquidated and 100 ETH needs to be sold. Assume there are available orders that can match this liquidation at 2000. Instead of matching it directly, the validator can create his own order at 1980 and match the liquidation to his own order. He can then immediately sell and match with the other available orders for a profit of 2,000 (20 * 100) USDC.
2) Manipulation of funding rate. Validators are allowed to match non-liquidation orders at up to 20% spread from the oracle. This makes it incredibly easy for validators to manipulate the markPriceTwap. By creating and matching tiny orders at the extremes of this spread they can dramatically skew the funding rate it whatever way they please. Max funding rates can liquidate leveraged positions very quickly allowing that validator to further profit from their liquidations.
Now we can discuss how just about anyone can become a validator and abuse this privilege with zero consequences.
First we need to consider the typical methodology for ensuring validators behave and why NONE of those factors apply in this scenario. 1) "Slash validators that misbehave." Hubble mainnet is a fork of the AVAX C-Chain which is different from most chains in the fact that AVAX validators can’t be slashed. 2) "Validators are forced to hold a volatile protocol token that would depreciate if they are publicly observed misbehaving." On Hubble mainnet the gas token is USDC so it would not depreciate in the event that validators misbehave. 3) "Blocks that break consensus rules are rejected." The Hubble exchange smart contracts are not part of the consensus layer so abusing validator privilege as described aren't breaking any consensus rules and would therefore be accepted by honest validators.
Second we consider the ease of becoming a validator. Hubble mainnet is a fork of AVAX and uses it's same consensus mechanism. This allows any node who posts the required stake to become a validator for the network. This allows anyone with access to any decent level of capital to become a validator and begin exploiting users.
Validators can manipulate funding rates and profit unfairly from liquidations

title: setSymbolsPrice() can use the priceSig from multiple times
content: The vulnerability resides in the function that records a price signature (setSymbolsPrice) used for liquidation calculations. The code only checks that the timestamp of the supplied price signature is not later than the allowed liquidation deadline, but it does not enforce a lower bound on the timestamp. As a result, an attacker can replay a previously signed priceSig that was created at any earlier point in time. The verification routine (LibMuon.verifyPrices) validates the cryptographic signature and the internal consistency of the arrays, yet it never validates that the timestamp falls within a recent, expected window. Consequently, a malicious actor can submit a stale priceSig whose upnl field contains a large negative value, causing the liquidation logic to interpret the position as overdue and trigger a LiquidationType.OVERDUE. This forces the protocol to liquidate the counter‑party (partyB) under false pretenses, potentially draining their collateral or reducing their balance to zero. The impact is severe: users of the protocol may lose funds unexpectedly, the accounting model that assumes price data reflects the current market is broken, and the trust in the liquidation mechanism is undermined. The issue manifests whenever setSymbolsPrice is called with a priceSig whose timestamp is older than the current liquidation timestamp for the party; there is no safeguard preventing such replay. It affects any participant that relies on the liquidation process, especially the counter‑party whose position is liquidated (partyB). The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the timestamp checks and noticed the missing lower‑bound condition. Because the signature itself is valid, the bug can be subtle and may not raise obvious errors; the contract behaves as designed, yet the business logic is violated, making the problem hard to spot without a focused review of time‑range validation. The appropriate remediation is to enforce that priceSig.timestamp is greater than or equal to the stored liquidationTimestamp for the party, thereby preventing the use of stale signatures. This class of bug is a replay‑or‑stale‑data vulnerability where time‑based constraints are incomplete, leading to incorrect financial calculations and unintended liquidations.

title: liquidatePositionsPartyB can be used by malicious liquidator to manipulate upnl
content: The vulnerability is a logical flaw in the two‑step liquidation workflow that allows a malicious liquidator to manipulate the unrealized profit‑and‑loss (upnl) reported for the counter‑party (PartyA) while PartyB is being liquidated. The process starts with liquidatePartyB, which transfers most of PartyB’s funds to PartyA, and then liquidatePositionsPartyB can be called repeatedly with an arbitrary list of position identifiers until every active position of PartyB is closed. The contract and the off‑chain muon application do not verify whether a position’s counterparties are currently in a liquidation state when calculating upnl or when allowing position‑closing operations. Because of this missing check, after the first step but before all positions are liquidated, PartyA can still perform actions such as deallocating funds based on a temporarily inflated upnl that only includes the subset of positions the attacker chose to liquidate. A malicious liquidator can therefore select only those PartyB positions that are losing for PartyA, leaving the profitable positions untouched and artificially boosting PartyA’s reported profit. PartyA can then deallocate its maximum allocated balance, effectively withdrawing funds that should be locked against the still‑open profitable positions. Once the remaining PartyB positions are finally liquidated, PartyA’s upnl collapses into a large bad debt, while the allocated balance remains zero, causing the counterpart (PartyB) to lose the profit it was owed. The bug is triggered whenever a liquidation is in progress and the contract does not enforce a liquidation‑status guard on upnl calculations, close‑position requests, or the liquidatePositionsPartyA function. It affects any PartyA that holds a losing position against a PartyB that becomes liquidatable, and it can be combined with other missing checks to drain the entire protocol. The issue was discovered during a security audit that exercised the liquidation flow and observed that upnl values could be altered by selectively liquidating positions. It is hard to notice because the upnl appears correct at the moment of deallocation and the UI may show a normal profit, while the underlying accounting is inconsistent. The flaw belongs to the class of state‑validation race conditions where a contract fails to lock or verify the liquidation status of involved parties before performing accounting‑sensitive operations. The recommended remediation is to introduce a temporary locked status for any party whose counter‑party is being liquidated, preventing upnl calculations and position‑closing actions until the liquidation completes, and to add explicit liquidation‑status checks in both the on‑chain functions (liquidatePositionsPartyB, requestToClosePosition, fillCloseRequest, liquidatePositionsPartyA) and the off‑chain muon upnl calculation logic. This ensures that unrealized profit is never computed on positions that are in the middle of a liquidation, preserving accounting integrity and preventing fund theft.

title: PartyA and PartyB nonce is not incremented
content: The contract implements a dual‑party liquidation mechanism where each party (PartyA and PartyB) signs off on its unrealised profit‑and‑loss (UPnL) using a nonce‑based replay‑protected signature. The vulnerability arises because none of the liquidation functions increment the nonce of either party after state‑changing actions such as adjusting allocated balances, deleting positions, or modifying UPnL. Consequently, a signature that was valid before liquidation remains valid afterwards, even though the underlying financial state has been altered. An attacker who controls both parties and the liquidator can exploit this by first creating opposite positions that make PartyA liquidatable, then performing a liquidation that inflates PartyB’s allocated balance without changing PartyB’s nonce. The attacker then re‑uses the previously obtained PartyB signature, which still matches the unchanged nonce, to call a deallocation function and withdraw the inflated balance. Because the deallocation logic trusts the signature rather than the current balance, the protocol transfers more funds than are actually deposited, allowing the attacker to drain all protocol assets. This attack can be carried out whenever a liquidation function modifies a party’s financial state but fails to bump its nonce, which includes liquidatePartyA, liquidatePositionsPartyA, liquidatePartyB and related pending‑position functions. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the signature verification flow and noticed that nonce updates were omitted despite state changes. It is hard to notice because the contract still enforces liquidation status checks, giving a false sense of safety, and the nonce omission does not cause immediate reverts; the problem only manifests when an old signature is replayed after liquidation. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are a missing or zero balance after a seemingly successful withdrawal, or an unexpectedly large allocated balance that can be withdrawn, contradicting the expectation that only deposited funds are withdrawable. The bug belongs to the class of replay‑protected signature misuse where nonce management is inconsistent with state mutations, breaking the accounting invariant that a signature must reflect the current balance. The proper fix is to increment the nonce of every party whose financial state is altered by a liquidation call, ensuring that any previously signed UPnL data becomes stale and cannot be reused to authorize further transfers. By coupling nonce updates with balance changes, the protocol restores the guarantee that signatures are bound to the exact state at the time of signing, preventing the described fund‑stealing scenario.

title: LibMuon Signature hash collision
content: The vulnerability is a hash‑collision weakness in the LibMuon signature scheme. The library builds the message hash with keccak256(abi.encodePacked(...)) and does not prepend any function‑specific identifier or type tag. Because abi.encodePacked concatenates the raw binary representation of each argument, different argument layouts – especially when dynamic arrays are involved – can produce exactly the same byte sequence. Consequently two distinct logical messages, such as a price‑verification payload and a profit‑and‑loss verification payload, may generate an identical hash. The root cause is the lack of a domain separator or explicit type prefix, which makes the hash ambiguous. An attacker who obtains a legitimate signature for one function (for example a SingleUpnlAndPriceSig) can reuse that signature as a valid proof for another function (such as verifyPrices) because the verifier recomputes the same hash from the forged data. Exploitation proceeds by crafting a payload whose fields are rearranged to match the byte layout of a different function, submitting the reused signature, and passing the verifyTSSAndGateway check. The impact is that the protocol can be tricked into accepting unauthorized price updates or profit‑and‑loss reports, potentially leading to incorrect accounting, unauthorized fund movements, or loss of user balances. The bug manifests whenever a signature is verified using the vulnerable hash construction – i.e., any call to verifyPrices or verifyPartyAUpnlAndPrice – and when the attacker can control at least one of the dynamic array arguments. All participants that rely on the integrity of these signatures – the protocol itself, its users, and any downstream contracts – are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the auditor wrote a small test that showed two different encodePacked calls producing the same keccak256 hash, confirming that the signatures are interchangeable. Because hash collisions are not obvious from the contract’s external behaviour, the problem can remain hidden until a crafted exploit is attempted. The bug belongs to the class of “signature domain‑separation failures” or “abi.encodePacked collision” bugs, where the message format does not uniquely identify the operation. From a user’s perspective the symptom may appear as unexpected price changes, a profit‑and‑loss value that seems to have been altered without any transaction, or a balance that suddenly moves without a visible cause – the user expects a legitimate update but receives an unauthorized one. To remediate the issue the contract should adopt a collision‑resistant message encoding: either switch to abi.encode (which includes length information) or prepend a unique string identifier for each function before hashing, thereby ensuring that each logical message maps to a distinct hash domain. This change restores the cryptographic guarantee that a signature can only be used for the exact operation it was created for, eliminating the possibility of signature reuse across different function calls.

title: depositAndAllocateForPartyB is broken due to
content: The vulnerability is a precision mismatch in the combined depositAndAllocateForPartyB function. The function receives a single amount parameter that the caller supplies in the token’s native decimal format (for USDC this is 6 decimals). It forwards this raw amount unchanged to two internal helpers: depositForPartyB, which internally converts the amount to the protocol’s 18‑decimal accounting representation, and allocateForPartyB, which assumes the amount is already expressed in 18‑decimal precision. Because the same unscaled value is passed to allocateForPartyB, the protocol interprets a 6‑decimal value as an 18‑decimal one, resulting in an allocation that is off by a factor of 10^12. For example, a user intending to allocate 1,000 USDC (1,000 × 10⁶) ends up allocating only 1 × 10⁻⁹ USDC. The bug is triggered whenever a user or an external contract calls depositAndAllocateForPartyB with a token that has fewer than 18 decimals, which includes most stablecoins. The impact is that the allocated balance, which is used to assess health factors and to prevent liquidation, is effectively unchanged, leading users to believe their position is safer than it actually is. In a liquidation scenario, a user may call the function to boost the allocated balance, see the event emit the expected amount, but the protocol records a negligible increase, causing a false sense of security and potentially resulting in liquidation and loss of funds. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the AccountFacet implementation, where the auditor noticed that the two internal calls expect different decimal precisions. The problem is subtle because the deposit step succeeds and the emitted events show the correct amount, masking the mis‑allocation. The bug belongs to the class of decimal‑precision mismatch or unit conversion errors, where inconsistent handling of token decimals leads to incorrect accounting. To fix the issue, the amount must be converted to 18‑decimal precision before it is passed to allocateForPartyB, either by reusing the scaling logic from depositForPartyB or by performing an explicit conversion in depositAndAllocateForPartyB. After the fix, the allocated balance will correctly reflect the user’s intended amount, preserving the protocol’s accounting invariants and preventing unintended liquidations.

title: Accounting error in PartyB's pending locked
content: The vulnerability is an accounting inconsistency in the contract that manages pending locked balances for the counter‑party (PartyB) when a position is only partially filled. The root cause is that the code subtracts only the portion of the locked value that has been filled (lockedValuefilled) from PartyB’s pendingLockedBalance, while the remaining unfilled portion (lockedValueunfilled) is never removed because the newly created quote is not added to PartyB’s pending quote list. Consequently, PartyB’s pendingLockedBalance retains the full amount of the original locked value even though no pending quote exists for PartyB. This can be exploited whenever PartyB participates in a partial fill: each execution inflates PartyB’s pendingLockedBalance by the unfilled amount, silently reducing the available balance reported by the partyBAvailableForQuote function. Over time the inflated pending locked balance can consume all of PartyB’s allocated funds, preventing the account from opening new positions, de‑allocating, or withdrawing assets, effectively causing a loss of assets for PartyB. The issue manifests only under the condition that a partial fill occurs; full fills correctly clear the pending balance. It affects any PartyB account that engages in partial fills, the protocol’s accounting invariants, and any downstream logic that relies on the available balance calculation. The bug was discovered during a manual audit of the openPosition function where the state transitions of pendingQuotes and pendingLockedBalances were traced. It is hard to notice because the visible pending quote list for PartyB becomes empty, giving the impression that no funds are locked, while the internal pendingLockedBalance still holds a non‑zero value. To remediate the problem the contract should subtract the total locked value (lockedValuetotal) from PartyB’s pendingLockedBalance when a partial fill occurs, ensuring that both the filled and unfilled portions are correctly accounted for, and optionally add the new quote to PartyB’s pending quote list if required by the protocol’s design. This correction restores the integrity of the accounting model, prevents silent balance inflation, and protects PartyB’s assets from being unintentionally locked away.
summary:
Accounting error in the PartyB's pending locked balance during the partial filling of a position could lead to a loss of assets for PartyB.

```solidity
    uint256 quoteId,
    uint256 filledAmount,

) internal returns (uint256 currentId) {
    // ...SNIP...

    // ...SNIP...
    quoteLayout.quoteIdsOf[quote.partyA].push(currentId);
    // ...SNIP...
    } else {
        accountLayout.pendingLockedBalances[quote.partyA].sub(filledLockedValues);
        accountLayout.partyBPendingLockedBalances[quote.partyB][quote.partyA].sub(
            filledLockedValues
        );

```
() Parameter Description ()
quotecurrent Current quote (Quote ID = 1)
quotenew Newly created quote (Quote ID = 2) due to partially filling
lockedValuetotal 100 USD. The locked values of quotecurrent
lockedValuefilled 30 USD. lockedValuefilled = lockedValuetotal × filledAmount / quote.quantity
lockedValueunfilled 70 USD. lockedValueunfilled = lockedValuetotal - lockedValuefilled
pendingLockedBalancea 100 USD. PartyA's pending locked balance
pendingLockedBalanceb 100 USD. PartyB's pending locked balance
pendingQuotesa PartyA's pending quotes. pendingQuotesa = [quotecurrent]
pendingQuotesb PartyB's pending quotes. pendingQuotesb = [quotecurrent]
()
Assume the following states before the execution of the openPosition function:
• pendingQuotesa = [quotecurrent]
• pendingQuotesb = [quotecurrent]
• pendingLockedBalancea = 100 USD
• pendingLockedBalanceb = 100 USD
When the openPosition function is executed, quotecurrent will be removed from pendingQuotesa and pendingQuotesb in Line 156.
If the position is partially filled, quotecurrent will be filled, and quotenew will be created with the unfilled amount (lockedValueunfilled). The quotenew is automatically added to PartyA's pending quote list in Line 225.
The states at this point are as follows:
• pendingQuotesa = [quotenew]
• pendingQuotesb = []
• pendingLockedBalancea = 100 USD
• pendingLockedBalanceb = 100 USD
Line 238 removes the balance already filled (lockedValuefilled) from pendingLockedBalancea. The unfilled balance (lockedValueunfilled) does not need to be removed from pendingLockedBalancea because it is now the balance of quotenew that belong to PartyA. The value in pendingLockedBalancea is correct.
The states at this point are as follows:
• pendingQuotesa = [quotenew]
• pendingQuotesb = []
• pendingLockedBalancea = 70 USD
• pendingLockedBalanceb = 100 USD
In Line 239, the code removes the balance already filled (lockedValuefilled) from pendingLockedBalanceb.
The end state is as follows:
• pendingQuotesa = [quotenew]
• pendingQuotesb = []
• pendingLockedBalancea = 70 USD
• pendingLockedBalanceb = 70 USD
As shown above, the value of pendingLockedBalanceb is incorrect. Even though PartyB has no pending quote, 70 USD is still locked in the pending balance.
1) quotecurrent has already been removed from pendingQuotesb in Line 156
2) quotenew is not automatically added to pendingQuotesb. When quotenew is created, it is not automatically locked to PartyB.
3) pendingQuotesb is empty
As such, lockedValuetotal should be removed from the pendingLockedBalanceb instead of only lockedValuefilled.
Every time PartyB partially fill a position, their pendingLockedBalanceb will silently increase and become inflated. The pending locked balance plays a key role in the protocol's accounting system. Thus, an error in the accounting breaks many of the computations and invariants of the protocol.
For instance, it is used to compute the available balance of an account in partyBAvailableForQuote function. Assuming that the allocated balance remains the same. If the pending locked balance increases silently due to the bug, the available balance returned from the partyBAvailableForQuote function will decrease. Eventually, it will "consume" all the allocated balance, and there will be no available funds left for PartyB to open new positions or to deallocate+withdraw funds. Thus, leading to loss of assets for PartyB.

title: Liquidation can be blocked by incrementing
content: The vulnerability is a race‑condition that allows a party whose account is liquidatable to block the liquidation process by deliberately changing the on‑chain nonce that is embedded in the off‑chain signature used for liquidation verification. The liquidation functions liquidatePartyA and liquidatePartyB compute a hash that includes the current nonce of the target party (PartyA or PartyB) and then verify a Muon signature against that hash. When a liquidator submits a liquidation transaction, a malicious party can monitor the mempool, front‑run the transaction and send a separate transaction that increments its nonce (for example by performing a dust transfer, opening and closing a dummy position, or calling requestToClosePosition followed by requestToCancelCloseRequest). Because the nonce stored on‑chain is now different from the nonce that was signed, the signature verification fails and the liquidation call reverts. This can also be achieved on chains without a public mempool by repeatedly sending nonce‑incrementing transactions each block, as long as the gas cost is acceptable. The issue occurs only when liquidation eligibility is determined off‑chain and the on‑chain nonce is expected to stay in sync with the signed value. It affects liquidators, counterparties that rely on realized profits (PartyB), and the overall fairness of the protocol because blocked liquidations prevent the realization of unrealized profits and may cause loss of expected revenue. The problem was discovered during a security audit that examined the liquidation facet and the LibMuon signature verification logic. It is hard to notice because legitimate‑looking actions such as small token transfers or dummy position updates can silently change the nonce, making the exploit blend with normal activity. To remediate, the protocol should avoid using a mutable on‑chain nonce in off‑chain signatures for liquidation eligibility, either by moving the liquidation check entirely on‑chain, using a nonce that cannot be manipulated by the target, or by designing the verification to be atomic with the liquidation execution. In short, the bug is a nonce‑mismatch front‑running attack that blocks liquidation, violates the accounting assumption that a liquidatable account can always be liquidated, and leads to unexpected zero payouts for liquidators and reduced profits for counterparties.

title: Liquidation of PartyA will fail due to underflow
content: The vulnerability is an arithmetic underflow that occurs during the liquidation of PartyA when the contract attempts to subtract a profit amount from PartyB’s allocated balance using unsigned integer arithmetic. The root cause is the lack of a safety check before performing the subtraction; the code assumes that PartyB always has enough allocated funds to cover the profit that PartyA earned. When PartyA realizes a large profit – for example, a sudden price spike that generates a $3,000 gain – the liquidation logic tries to deduct the same $3,000 from PartyB’s allocated balance. If PartyB’s balance is only $1,000, the subtraction underflows, causing the transaction to revert. The exploit scenario is straightforward: an attacker or any participant can trigger a liquidation with a position that yields a profit larger than the counter‑party’s allocated balance, causing the underflow and preventing the liquidation from completing. As a result, the assets that should be transferred from PartyA (the debtor) to PartyB (the creditor) remain locked in the contract, leading to a loss of expected funds for the creditor and a failure of the protocol’s accounting guarantees. This failure manifests to users as a liquidation transaction that reverts, with no funds moving and possibly a UI message indicating “liquidation failed” or simply no change in balances. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the LiquidationFacetImpl contract, where the auditor identified that the subtraction is performed without verifying that the balance is sufficient. The bug can be hard to notice because it only manifests under extreme profit conditions, which may be rare in normal operation, and the revert does not provide a clear error message about insufficient balance. To remediate, the contract should enforce a check that caps the deduction at the available allocated balance, or use safe‑math patterns that prevent underflow, ensuring that the amount subtracted never exceeds the current balance. This aligns the implementation with the intended business logic that a creditor can receive at most the amount they are owed, preserving the integrity of the liquidation process and preventing assets from becoming permanently stuck.

title: Wrong accounting of the storage balances re-
content: The vulnerability is an accounting inconsistency in the protocol’s storage of debt balances that can cause the system to appear in debt even after a borrower has repaid the bad debt associated with a closed position. The root cause lies in the way the contract updates two separate mappings: one that tracks the total amount of liquidity borrowed from providers (total_debt_amount) and another that records bad debt accrued when a position is closed at a loss (bad_debt). When a position is fully closed and the swap that settles the position returns less than the outstanding debt, the contract correctly calculates the shortfall, records it as bad debt, and uses the received amount to repay liquidity providers. However, the implementation fails to subtract the newly recorded bad debt from total_debt_amount. Because total_debt_amount continues to include the bad debt amount, the protocol’s global debt figure remains inflated after the repayment, preventing liquidity providers from withdrawing the full amount of funds they are entitled to. This flaw can be exploited by simply closing a position that results in bad debt; the protocol will then be stuck with an artificial debt balance that blocks full withdrawals, effectively locking user funds. The impact is that liquidity providers may see their balances reduced, receive less than expected when withdrawing, or be unable to withdraw at all, even though the underlying bad debt has been settled. The condition occurs whenever a position is closed with a loss that generates bad debt, i.e., when amount_out_received from the swap is lower than the position’s debt. All participants who provide liquidity are affected because the protocol’s accounting error limits the amount they can reclaim. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the debt‑repayment flow and identified that the bad_debt entry was never reconciled with total_debt_amount. It can be hard to notice because the contract still records a repayment event and the bad_debt mapping shows a zero balance after settlement, giving the impression that the debt has been cleared, while the total_debt_amount remains overstated. To fix the problem, the contract should either deduct the bad debt amount from total_debt_amount when it is recorded or, as recommended, repay the full position debt amount before closing the position rather than only the amount received from the swap. This ensures that the global debt accounting reflects the true outstanding obligations and allows liquidity providers to withdraw their full entitled balances. The bug belongs to the class of accounting or state‑inconsistency errors where related state variables are not kept in sync, leading to mismatched balances and violated business logic that assumes total_debt_amount always equals the sum of outstanding principal plus accrued interest.
summary:
Wrong accounting of the storage balances results for the protocol to be in debt even when the bad debt is repaid.
When a position is fully closed, it can result in accruing bad debt or being in profit and repaying the borrowed liquidity which all depends on the amount_out_received from the swap.
In a bad debt scenario the function calculates the bad debt and accrues it based on the difference between the position debt and the amount out received from the swap. And after that repays the liquidity providers with the same received amount from the swap.
The mapping total_debt_amount holds all debt borrowed from users, and this amount accrues interest with the time.
Prior to closing a position, the bad debt is calculated and accrued to the mapping bad_debt, but it isn't subtracted from the mapping total_debt_amount which holds all the debt even the bad one accrued through the time.
As the bad debt isn't subtracted from the total_debt_amount when closing a position, even after repaying the bad debt, it will still be in the total_debt_amount, which will prevent the full withdrawing of the liquidity funds.
The issue leads to liquidity providers unable to withdraw their full amount of funds, as even after repaying the bad debt it will still be in the total_debt_amount mapping.

title: Leverage calculation is wrong
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect leverage calculation in the contract's internal _calculate_leverage function. The function is supposed to return the ratio between the current value of a trader's position and the trader's margin (the amount of collateral that remains after subtracting the borrowed debt). Instead of using the total position value as the numerator, the code uses the sum of the debt value and the margin value. Because the debt token and the position token are priced independently via Chainlink feeds, the sum of debt and margin does not equal the actual position value when the two assets move at different rates. Consequently the computed leverage can be higher or lower than the true leverage. An attacker or market movement that causes the price of the position token to diverge from the price of the debt token will cause the contract to report an inflated leverage figure. The liquidation engine relies on this figure, so a trader may be liquidated prematurely, lose their collateral, or be allowed to open a position that is effectively more leveraged than the protocol permits. The bug manifests when _position_value > _debt_value (i.e., the position is not underwater) and the assets involved have non‑correlated price movements. Users see symptoms such as an unexpectedly high leverage number, a liquidation that occurs even though the margin appears sufficient, or a sudden disappearance of their funds after a price swing. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s math, where the formula was compared against the financial definition of leverage. It is subtle because the numbers can be close under stable market conditions, making the error easy to miss in routine testing. The proper fix is to replace the numerator with the actual position value, i.e., return position_value / (position_value – debt_value), or equivalently position_value / margin_value, and to ensure that all values are derived from the same valuation basis. This correction restores the intended accounting relationship and prevents unfair liquidations and over‑leveraged exposure.

title: Vault: _update_debt does not accrue interest
content: The vulnerability resides in the vault’s debt‑updating routine, where the function responsible for accruing interest updates the timestamp before calculating the interest owed. Specifically, the _update_debt routine sets last_debt_update for a given debt token to the current block.timestamp and then immediately calls _debt_interest_since_last_update. The interest calculation multiplies the elapsed time (block.timestamp minus last_debt_update) by the current per‑second interest rate and the total debt amount. Because the timestamp was just overwritten, the elapsed time is always zero, causing the function to return zero interest. As a result, the total_debt_amount is increased by zero, meaning that debt fees are never accrued. This logical ordering error is a classic example of a state‑update‑before‑computation bug, often seen in financial smart contracts where timing variables are mishandled. The impact is that borrowers can hold positions indefinitely without incurring any interest, leading to a systematic loss of revenue for the protocol and an unfair advantage for malicious actors who can exploit the missing fee. Users observing their vault balances will see that their principal remains unchanged while the expected interest component never appears, contradicting the protocol’s advertised fee model. The issue manifests whenever _update_debt is invoked, which is the normal path for interest accrual, making the bug pervasive across all debt tokens. It was uncovered during a manual audit when the auditor noticed that the interest‑accrual function always returned zero despite non‑zero debt balances and elapsed time. The problem is subtle because the contract’s state appears consistent – balances are non‑zero and timestamps are updated – yet the accounting logic silently fails, making it hard to detect through simple balance checks. To remediate, the contract should first compute the pending interest using the stored last_debt_update, add the resulting amount to total_debt_amount, and only then update last_debt_update to the current block.timestamp. This ensures that the elapsed time reflects the true period since the previous accrual and that interest is correctly charged, restoring the intended economic behavior of the vault.
summary:
```solidity
def _update_debt(_debt_token: address):
    ...
    self.last_debt_update[_debt_token] = block.timestamp
    ...
    self.total_debt_amount[_debt_token] += self._debt_interest_since_last_update(
        _debt_token
    )
```
_update_debt call _debt_interest_since_last_update to accrue interest but _debt_interest_since_last_update always return 0 in _update_debt. _update_debt sets self.last_debt_update[_debt_token] to block.timestamp and then calls _debt_interest_since_last_update. _debt_interest_since_last_update always returns 0. because block.timestamp - self.last_debt_update[_debt_token] is always 0.
```solidity
def _debt_interest_since_last_update(_debt_token: address) -> uint256:
    return (
        (block.timestamp - self.last_debt_update[_debt_token])
        * self._current_interest_per_second(_debt_token)
        * self.total_debt_amount[_debt_token]
        / PERCENTAGE_BASE
        / PRECISION
    )
```
Debt fee is not accrued.

title: Adversary manipulate the middle path when
content: The vulnerability resides in the execute_dca_order function where the caller supplies an arbitrary _uni_hop_path array that defines the multi‑hop swap route for Uniswap V3. The contract only checks that the first element matches the order's token_in and the last element matches token_out, but it does not validate any intermediate token. Because the path is user‑controlled, an adversary can insert a malicious token as the middle hop, create a custom liquidity pool for that token with extreme price ranges, and thereby distort the effective price of the overall swap. When a regular user triggers a DCA order expecting a USDC‑to‑WETH trade, the attacker’s crafted path (USDC → MYTOKEN → WETH) is accepted, the router executes the multi‑hop swap using the attacker‑controlled pool, and the user receives far fewer WETH than anticipated. The slippage and TWAP checks only enforce a minimum amount out for the final token and cannot detect that the intermediate token was priced unfavorably, so the protection mechanisms appear to work while the user still loses value. This issue manifests whenever execute_dca_order is called by any address, because the function is external and non‑restricted, allowing anyone to supply a malicious path. The affected parties are the end users who place DCA orders, the protocol that routes swaps through the contract, and any funds locked in the DCA vault. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that highlighted the lack of validation on the intermediate hop and the possibility of price manipulation through a custom token. The problem is subtle because the transaction does not revert and the recorded slippage is within the configured bounds, making the loss look like normal market variance. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of untrusted input leading to price‑oracle manipulation, often referred to as a path injection or swap‑route tampering vulnerability. From the user’s perspective the UI shows a successful swap but the received amount is unexpectedly low or even zero, contradicting the expectation that the contract will honor the quoted rate. To remediate the issue the contract should either compute the swap path internally based on a whitelist of allowed intermediate tokens, enforce that only known safe routes are used, or replace the user‑provided path with an oracle‑derived price check and a minimum output range for the final token. Removing the ability for arbitrary callers to specify the path or restricting it to a vetted list eliminates the attack surface and restores confidence that the DCA order will execute at a fair rate.
summary:
```solidity
@external
@nonreentrant('lock')
def execute_dca_order(_uid: bytes32, _uni_hop_path: DynArray[address, 3], _uni_pool_fees: DynArray[uint24, 2], _share_profit: bool):
    ...
    # ensure path is valid
    assert len(_uni_hop_path) in [2, 3], "[path] invlid path"
    assert len(_uni_pool_fees) == len(_uni_hop_path)-1, "[path] invalid fees"
    assert _uni_hop_path[0] == order.token_in, "[path] invalid token_in"
    assert _uni_hop_path[len(_uni_hop_path)-1] == order.token_out, "[path] invalid token_out"
    ...
    # Vyper way to accommodate abi.encode_packed
    path: Bytes[66] = empty(Bytes[66])
    if(len(_uni_hop_path) == 2):
        path = concat(convert(_uni_hop_path[0], bytes20), convert(_uni_pool_fees[0], bytes3), convert(_uni_hop_path[1], bytes20))
    elif(len(_uni_hop_path) == 3):
        path = concat(convert(_uni_hop_path[0], bytes20), convert(_uni_pool_fees[0], bytes3), convert(_uni_hop_path[1], bytes20), convert(_uni_pool_fees[1], bytes3), convert(_uni_hop_path[2], bytes20))
    min_amount_out: uint256 = self._calc_min_amount_out(order.amount_in_per_execution, _uni_hop_path, _uni_pool_fees, order.twap_length, order.max_slippage)
    uni_params: ExactInputParams = ExactInputParams({
        path: path,
        recipient: self,
        deadline: block.timestamp,
        amountIn: order.amount_in_per_execution,
        amountOutMinimum: min_amount_out
    })
    amount_out: uint256 = UniswapV3SwapRouter(UNISWAP_ROUTER).exactInput(uni_params)
    ...
```
Adversary manipulate the middle path when calling execute_dca_order, resulting user loss, benefiting the attacker. Allowing anyone to call the execute_dca_order function with a custom _uni_hop_path introduce security issue. If an attacker constructs a malicious path with their own token in the middle, they could manipulate the liquidity and perform an exploit. The _uni_hop_path parameter in execute_dca_order is really dangerous input which can be manipulated by attacker. For example a user want to Dca USDC -> WETH by posting post_dca_order with _token_in is USDC, and _token_out is WETH, and with the min_amount_out generated from _calc_min_amount_out which is based on twap and slippage percentage (in contrary, LimitOrders.vy use input min_amount_out for token out from the post_limit_order function, thus will not facing same effect like this issue). When attacker see this Dca order, they can create a new ERC20 MYTOKEN (and will provide liquidity in uniswap) and plan to attack the Dca by selecting his own token as the middle path, so execute_dca_order will be executed using USDC -> MYTOKEN -> WETH path. Since attacker can manipulate the liquidity of MYTOKEN in Uniswap, resulting user will get bad swap amount due to the custom path provided by attacker. Slippage and twap length as protection are not enough, because the middle token path is the problem here. Moreover, using twap with twap_length can also be manipulated by preparing / pre-attack pool since the last_execution and seconds_between_executions is known, also the order's twap_length is visible, so attack scenario can prepared beforehand. Steps: 1. A malicious user creates a custom token called "MYTOKEN" and provides liquidity for it on Uniswap v3. They allocate liquidity to create extreme price ranges for MYTOKEN. 2. A regular user intends to swap USDC to WETH. 3. The malicious user intercepts the transaction and modifies the path by adding intermediate token with MYTOKEN. The new path becomes USDC -> MYTOKEN -> WETH. 4. Uniswap v3 receives the modified path and attempts to execute the swap based on the provided path. 5. Uniswap v3 calculates the best available price based on the modified path, which includes MYTOKEN. 6. Due to the manipulated liquidity pool of MYTOKEN, the price of MYTOKEN is significantly skewed, leading to an unfair price for the regular user executing the multi-hop swap. 7. The malicious user takes advantage of the distorted liquidity pool by executing multi-hop swaps involving MYTOKEN at highly advantageous prices. 8. Innocent users who unknowingly interact with the manipulated liquidity pool may receive unfavorable prices for their USDC to WETH swaps, leading to financial losses. In this scenario, the malicious user modifies the path of the multi-hop swap by replacing the intended intermediate token with MYTOKEN. As a result, the malicious user exploits the manipulated liquidity pool and executes trades at favorable prices, while causing losses for other traders and disrupting the market equilibrium. User will get a bad rate (far from the normal rate) due to middle token rate is manipulated, thus losing his asset.

title: reduce_margin_by_amountin Vault.reduce_position
content: The vulnerability resides in the function that reduces an existing leveraged position by selling a portion of the position token and decreasing both the debt and the margin. The contract attempts to keep the leverage ratio unchanged after the reduction, but it calculates the amounts to subtract from margin and debt incorrectly. The root cause is that the margin‑to‑debt ratio is taken from the pre‑reduction state and then applied directly to the total amount received from the swap, without accounting for the fact that the swap output should be split according to the proportion of the position that is being closed. As a result, the function may reduce the margin by the full swap output while leaving the debt unchanged, or otherwise allocate the swap proceeds in a way that changes the leverage. In the concrete example used in the audit, a position with 9,000 USDC debt and 9,000 USDC margin receives 9,000 USDC from the swap. The code computes a margin‑debt ratio of 0.5 and then reduces the margin by 9,000 USDC (the full amount) and the debt by 0, which doubles the effective leverage. An automated test that checks the post‑reduction debt and margin values fails, demonstrating that the expected proportional reduction (e.g., both margin and debt decreasing to 6,000 USDC) does not occur. The impact is that users see their leverage unexpectedly increase, which can lead to insufficient collateral, higher liquidation risk, or loss of funds when market prices move against the position. The bug manifests whenever a caller invokes the reduction function with a non‑zero amount, especially when the swap output is comparable to the existing margin. All users who open leveraged positions are affected because the protocol’s accounting assumptions about constant leverage are violated. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by writing a targeted unit test that compared the expected and actual debt after reduction. It is hard to notice because the function emits no error and the state changes appear plausible; only precise accounting checks reveal the discrepancy. The proper fix is to recompute the margin‑debt ratio after the swap or, more robustly, to calculate the reduction amounts based on the fraction of the position being closed, ensuring that margin and debt are reduced proportionally and the leverage ratio remains unchanged. In generic terms, this is a proportional‑allocation bug in a financial contract that breaks the invariant that debt‑to‑margin ratio stays constant after a partial unwind, leading to unexpected leverage shifts and potential fund loss.
summary:
In Vault.reduce_position, some position tokens are sold and debt and margin are reduced. The remaining amount of debt and margin should maintain the same leverage as before. However, the reduced amount is wrongly calculated and as a result, the leverage is changed. Suppose that the debt amount is 9000 USDC and the margin amount is also 9000 USDC. And the amount_out_received is 9000 USDC. Let’s take a look of the calculation: We can find out that the reduced amount of margin is 9000 and the reduced amount of debt is 0. The leverage is changed. I also wrote a test to demonstrate the issue. (The test case is different from the previous case)
def test_reduce_position(vault, owner, weth, usdc, mock_router, eth_usd_oracle):
    eth_usd_oracle.set_answer(9000_00000000)
    assert vault.swap_router() == mock_router.address
    uid, amount_bought = vault.open_position(
        owner,
        # account
        weth,
        # position_token
        2 * 10**18,
        # min_position_amount_out
        usdc,
        # debt_token
        9000 * 10**6,
        # debt_amount
        9000 * 10**6,
        # margin_amount
    )
    position_before = vault.positions(uid)
    position_amount_before = position_before[6]
    assert position_amount_before == 2 * 10**18
    margin_amount_before = position_before[3]
    assert margin_amount_before == 9000 * 10**6
    debt_amount_before = vault.debt(uid)
    assert debt_amount_before == 9000 * 10**6
    vault.reduce_position(uid, int(position_amount_before/3), 6000 * 10**6)
    position_after = vault.positions(uid)
    debt_amount_after = vault.debt_shares_to_amount(usdc.address, position_after[4])
    print(debt_amount_after)
    assert debt_amount_after == pytest.approx(6000 * 10**6, abs=10000000) # is 9000 * 10**6
    margin_amount_after = position_after[3]
    print(margin_amount_after)
    assert margin_amount_after == pytest.approx(6000 * 10**6, abs=1000000)
    position_amount_after = position_after[6]
Besides, I want to mention that the usage of pytest.approx is incorrect in assert debt_amount_after == pytest.approx(6000 * 10**6, 10000000). If the approximation means 6000 * 10 ** 6 ± 10000000, it should be pytest.approx(6000 * 10**6, abs=10000000). On the other hand, pytest.approx(6000 * 10**6, 10000000) considers numbers within a relative tolerance of the expected value. The approximation 6000 * 10 ** 6 ± (6000 * 10**6 * 10000000) has too large of a range of values. The reduced amounts of debt and margin are wrongly calculated. The leverage is changed after reduce_position.

title: Vault: The attacker can sandwich attack him-
content: The vulnerability is a sandwich‑style manipulation of the token swap that the Vault contract performs when opening, reducing or closing a leveraged position. The contract calls an external MarginDex swap function and only checks the maximum leverage before the swap, assuming the amount received will match the amount sent. Because the slippage argument is supplied by the caller and is not bounded, an attacker can set it to an effectively infinite value and front‑run or sandwich the swap with a large opposing trade. The manipulated swap returns only a tiny fraction of the expected tokens, but the Vault records the full intended amount in the position’s accounting. Consequently the position becomes under‑collateralised: the recorded collateral appears sufficient according to the pre‑swap leverage check, yet the actual assets are far lower. When the attacker later closes or reduces the position, the protocol attempts to settle using the insufficient assets, creating a bad debt that can be drained from the Vault. The issue occurs whenever a user opens, reduces or closes a position because the contract does not re‑validate the health of the position after the swap nor compare the execution price to an oracle reference. All participants who rely on the Vault – lenders, traders and the protocol itself – are affected because the accounting mismatch can erase user balances, leave refunds at zero, and ultimately allow an attacker to siphon funds. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the flow of open_position and noticed that the slippage parameter was unchecked and that no post‑swap liquidation check was performed. It is subtle because the transaction does not revert; the swap succeeds, the position is recorded as opened, and only later does the under‑collateralisation become apparent when the position is settled. To remediate, the contract should invoke the liquidation check after the swap completes, enforce a reasonable slippage limit, and verify that the execution price does not deviate excessively from a trusted oracle price before allowing a close or reduce operation. This transforms the vulnerable pattern into a standard safeguard against price‑manipulation and ensures that the accounting reflects the true value of the assets held, preventing funds from disappearing due to a swap‑price attack.
summary: The attacker could call MarginDex to open/close positions in Vault. The swap slippage is controlled by the attacker. He can set the slippage to infinite to steal from swaps and leave a bad position/debt. In open_position of Vault, max_leverage is first checked to ensure the position that is about to open will be healthy. Then token is borrowed and swapped into position token. The attacker can set slippage to infinite and sandwich attack the swap to steal almost all of the swapped token. Then the amount swapped out is recorded in position and the position will be undercollateralized. Swaps in close_position and reduce_position are also vulnerable to this sandwich attack. The attacker can attack to steal from swap and make a bad debt. The protocol could be drained because of this sandwich attack.

title: reduce_position doesn’t update margin map-
content: The vulnerability resides in the function that reduces a leveraged position by selling a portion of the position token for the debt token. The routine correctly calculates how much of the received amount should be treated as margin repayment (reduce_margin_by_amount) and decreases the position’s internal margin_amount field accordingly. However, the contract maintains a separate per‑account margin ledger (self.margin[account][debt_token]) that represents the amount of collateral a user can later withdraw. The code never adds the reclaimed margin back into this ledger. As a result, after a user calls the reduction function, the internal accounting shows a lower margin_amount but the external margin mapping remains unchanged, effectively locking the reclaimed collateral inside the vault. The root cause is an omitted state update – a missing write to the margin mapping – which creates an inconsistency between the position’s internal state and the protocol‑wide accounting of user balances. An attacker (or any user) can trigger the function with any _reduce_by_amount, causing the contract to silently swallow part of the user’s collateral; the user will later attempt to withdraw and receive less than expected, often zero, because the reclaimed margin was never credited. The impact is loss of user funds: margin tokens that should be withdrawable become permanently inaccessible, violating the protocol’s guarantee that collateral can be reclaimed after reducing leverage. This condition occurs every time reduce_position is executed, regardless of the size of the reduction, and affects any account that holds a leveraged position. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the updates to position.margin_amount with the updates to the global margin mapping and noticed the discrepancy. It can be hard to notice because the contract still emits events that suggest the margin was reduced, and the UI may only display the new position size, not the underlying ledger balance, leading users to believe their funds are safe. The bug belongs to the class of accounting‑state‑inconsistency vulnerabilities, where a logical operation updates one representation of a value but fails to synchronize another representation that is used for withdrawals. To remediate, the contract should credit the reclaimed margin back to the user’s margin ledger (self.margin[account][debt_token] += reduce_margin_by_amount) immediately after decreasing position.margin_amount, ensuring that the external accounting matches the internal state and that users can withdraw the expected amount of collateral.
summary:
```solidity
debt_amount: uint256 = self._debt(_position_uid)
margin_debt_ratio: uint256 = position.margin_amount * PRECISION / debt_amount
amount_out_received: uint256 = self._swap(
    position.position_token, position.debt_token, _reduce_by_amount,
    min_amount_out
)
# reduce margin and debt, keep leverage as before
reduce_margin_by_amount: uint256 = (
    amount_out_received * margin_debt_ratio / PRECISION
)
reduce_debt_by_amount: uint256 = amount_out_received - reduce_margin_by_amount
position.margin_amount -= reduce_margin_by_amount
burnt_debt_shares: uint256 = self._repay(position.debt_token, reduce_debt_by_amount)
position.debt_shares -= burnt_debt_shares
position.position_amount -= _reduce_by_amount
```
reduce_position function decrease the margin amount of the position but doesn't add it back to the user's margin mapping, making it impossible to withdraw the margin. After selling some position tokens back against debt tokens using reduce_position function, debt_shares and margin_amount are reduced proportionally to keep leverage the same as before: Vault.vy#L313-L330. However, even though some of the margin have been paid back (position.margin_amount has been reduced), self.margin[position.account][position.debt_token] mapping hasn't been updated by adding reduce_margin_by_amount which would allow the user to withdraw his margin. Users will lose their margin tokens.

title: Interest calculated is amplified by multiple of 1000
content: The vulnerability is a precision‑mismatch arithmetic error in the function that calculates accrued interest on outstanding debt. The contract multiplies the elapsed time, the per‑second interest rate and the total debt amount, then divides the product by two constants: PERCENTAGE_BASE (which has two decimal places) and PRECISION (1e18). The per‑second interest rate, however, is expressed with a precision of twenty‑three decimal places because it is derived from a yearly rate that uses PERCENTAGE_BASE_HIGH (five decimal places). Dividing by the lower‑precision PERCENTAGE_BASE therefore removes only twenty digits of precision instead of the required twenty‑three, causing the final result to be inflated by roughly a factor of one thousand. This amplified interest is added to the debt balance each time the _debt_interest_since_last_update function is called, so any normal update – whether triggered by a borrower, a liquidator or an automated keeper – will cause the recorded debt to grow far beyond the expected 3 % annual rate. From a user’s perspective the balance may suddenly jump to an enormous value, liquidation warnings may appear unexpectedly, and share tokens that represent a portion of the pool can appear to be worth zero. The bug breaks the core accounting assumptions of the protocol: interest should be proportional to time and rate, but the mis‑scaled calculation makes interest effectively thousands of percent per year, potentially bricking the leverage, liquidation and share mechanisms. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the auditor compared the on‑chain per‑second interest constant (expected 9.512937595129375e15) with the result of the interest‑accrual formula and observed a thousand‑fold discrepancy. It is hard to notice because short‑interval tests may not expose the scaling error and the large numbers can be mistaken for normal growth in a high‑value system. The correct fix is to replace the division by PERCENTAGE_BASE with a division by PERCENTAGE_BASE_HIGH (or otherwise align the denominator’s precision with the numerator), thereby restoring the intended scaling and preventing the interest amplification. This class of bug is commonly known as a precision or unit‑conversion error, where mismatched decimal bases cause arithmetic overflow or unintended scaling.
summary:
Interest calculated in the _debt_interest_since_last_update function is amplified by multiple of 1000, hence can completely brick the system and debt calculation. Because we divide by PERCENTAGE_BASE instead of PERCENTAGE_BASE_HIGH which has more precision and which is used in utilization calculation. Following function calculated the interest accured over a certain interval :
```solidity
def _debt_interest_since_last_update(_debt_token: address) -> uint256:
    return (
        (block.timestamp - self.last_debt_update[_debt_token]) *
        self._current_interest_per_second(_debt_token) *
        self.total_debt_amount[_debt_token]
    ) / PERCENTAGE_BASE / PRECISION
```
But the results from the above function are amplified by factor of 1000 due to the reason that the interest per second as per test file is calculated as following:
```solidity
# accordingly the current interest per year should be 3% so 3_00_000
# per second that is (300000*10^18)/(365*24*60*60)
expected_interest_per_second = 9512937595129375
assert (
    expected_interest_per_second
    == vault_configured.internal._current_interest_per_second(usdc.address)
)
```
So yearly interest has the precision of 5 as it is calculated using utilization rate and PERCENTAGE_BASE_HIGH_PRECISION is used which has precision of 5, and per second interest has precision = 23. But if we look at the code:
```solidity
(block.timestamp - self.last_debt_update[_debt_token]) *
self._current_interest_per_second(_debt_token) *
self.total_debt_amount[_debt_token]
/ PERCENTAGE_BASE
/ PRECISION
```
We divide by PERCENTAGE_BASE that is = 100_00 = precision of => 2 And than by PRECISION = 1e18 => precision of 18. So accumulated precision of 20, where as we should have divided by value precised to 23 to match the nominator. Where is we should have divided by PERCENTAGE_BASE_HIGH instead of PERCENTAGE_BASE. Hence the results are amplified by enormous multiple of thousand. Interest are too much amplified, that impacts the total debt calculation and brick whole leverage, liquidation and share mechanism.

title: All fund from Teller contract can be drained
content: The vulnerability is a repeated‑claim flaw in the Teller contract that allows a malicious receiver to drain all collateral held by the contract. The contract’s reclaim function transfers the full amount of the payout or quote token to the option receiver after expiry, but it never updates the option’s state – specifically it does not burn or otherwise invalidate the option token that represents the claim. Because the option token’s totalSupply remains unchanged, the same amount can be transferred again on every subsequent call. An attacker can exploit this by deploying an option where they control the receiver address, waiting until the option expires, and then invoking reclaim repeatedly. Each call reads the same totalSupply value and transfers the same collateral amount, effectively emptying the Teller contract of all funds that were ever deposited for any option. The impact is severe: all users’ deposited funds can disappear, leaving the protocol without collateral and causing loss of value for option writers and holders. The issue occurs only after the option’s expiration timestamp and only when the caller is the designated receiver, but because there is no one‑time guard, the condition can be satisfied indefinitely. The affected parties include option creators, option holders, and any third‑party relying on the Teller contract for secure collateral management. The flaw was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the lifecycle of option tokens and noticed that the reclaim logic lacked a burn or state‑change step. It can be hard to notice because the function appears to perform a legitimate transfer and does not emit an event indicating a one‑time claim, so normal monitoring may not reveal repeated withdrawals. To remediate, the contract should mark the option as claimed by burning the option token or setting a reclaimed flag before transferring funds, ensuring that subsequent calls to reclaim are rejected. This class of bug is commonly known as an “unrestricted re‑claim” or “missing burn” vulnerability, where the accounting invariant that each token can be redeemed only once is broken, leading to double‑spending of collateral and violation of the protocol’s financial guarantees. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that funds that were expected to be locked become unavailable or disappear, and a user who expects a single payout may see the contract balance drop to zero after a malicious party repeatedly calls reclaim.

title: All funds can be stolen from FixedStrikeOp-
content: The vulnerability is an arithmetic manipulation caused by unchecked reliance on the payout token's decimals value. The contract's create, exercise and reclaim logic call payoutToken.decimals() at runtime and use the returned value to compute how many quote tokens must be locked or released. Because any address can be supplied as the payout token and there is no whitelist, an attacker can deploy a malicious ERC20 whose decimals function returns an arbitrary large or small integer. During the create call the attacker makes decimals return a very large number, causing the contract to think that a huge amount of quote tokens is required while actually pulling zero DAI from the attacker, yet minting option tokens to him. Later, before exercising or reclaiming, the attacker changes the decimals return value to a very small number, causing the contract to calculate a massive payout amount in DAI based on the same option balance. The contract then transfers the inflated amount to the attacker, draining all collateral. This can be exploited by any user because the deploy, create and exercise functions are public and lack access control. The impact is total loss of the contract's collateral, typically DAI, with negligible gas cost. The issue occurs whenever the contract interacts with a payout token whose decimals are not trustworthy, i.e., when the token is not whitelisted or its decimals are not cached. The affected parties are token holders, option buyers, and the protocol that relies on the contract for collateralized options. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the arithmetic flow and noticed that the decimals value is fetched on each call without validation. It is hard to notice because the decimals function is part of the ERC20 interface and most tokens implement it correctly; the contract does not emit any warning when a malicious token is used. To remediate, the contract should store the decimals of the payout token at deployment time, or better, enforce a whitelist of known safe tokens and avoid using external token metadata in critical calculations. By fixing the reliance on a mutable external value, the arithmetic integrity of the option pricing and collateral release is restored, preventing the possibility of draining funds.

title: Lack of segregation between users' assets and
content: The vulnerability is a mixing of users' swapped assets with the protocol fee pool, which allows the contract owner to withdraw both the fee and the users' tokens in a single operation. The root cause is that the LimitOrderRegistry contract stores native ETH and wrapped ETH (WETH) received as fee together with the ETH/WETH that belong to users after a limit order is fulfilled, without any accounting separation. Because the withdrawNative function transfers the entire native ETH balance and the entire WETH balance to the owner, an owner who calls this function before a user invokes claimOrder can empty the contract of the user’s swapped tokens. An attacker (or the owner) can simply trigger withdrawNative at any time, causing the user’s assets to be sent to the owner’s address. The impact is that users who have placed limit orders lose the tokens they expected to receive; when they later call claimOrder the transaction reverts due to insufficient balance, and the lost assets cannot be recovered. This situation occurs whenever the fee is collected in ETH or WETH and the contract does not keep a separate ledger for fees, which is typical in setups that automatically swap a portion of collected ETH/WETH to LINK for upkeep. The affected parties are the users who submit limit orders, any investors relying on the protocol, and the protocol itself because the loss of user funds undermines trust. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the flow of fee collection and withdrawal.
