Thus, the totalAssetscached will deviate from totalAssetsactual. This difference could be arbitrated or exploited by malicious users for their gain.
Certain actions such as previewDeposit, previewMint, previewWithdraw, and previewRedeem functions rely on the totalAssetscached value while other actions such as _withdraw and _calcUserWithdrawSharesToBurn functions rely on totalAssetsactual value.
The following shows one example of the issue.
The previewDeposit(assets) function computed the number of shares to be received after depositing a specific amount of assets:
shareReceived = (assetsdeposited / totalAssetscached) * totalSupply
Assume that totalAssetscached < totalAssetsactual, and the values of the variables are as follows:
• totalAssetscached = 110 WETH
• totalAssetsactual = 115 WETH
• totalSupply = 100 shares
Assume Bob deposited 10 WETH when the total assets are 110 WETH (when totalAssetscached < totalAssetsactual), he would receive:
shareReceived = (10ETH / 110ETH) * 100e18 shares = 9.090909091e18 shares
If a user deposited 10 WETH while the total assets are updated to the actual worth of 115 WETH (when totalAssetscached == totalAssetsactual, they would receive:
shareReceived = (10ETH / 115ETH) * 100e18 shares = 8.695652174e18 shares
Therefore, Bob is receiving more shares than expected.
If Bob redeems his nine (9) shares after the totalAssetscached has been updated to totalAssetsactual, he will receive 10.417 WETH back.
assetsReceived = (9.090909091e18 shares / (100e18 + 9.090909091e18) shares) * (115 + 10) ETH = (9.090909091e18 / 109.090909091e18) * 125ETH = 10.41666667 ETH
Bob profits 0.417 WETH simply by arbitraging the difference between the cached and actual values of the total assets. Bob gains is the loss of other vault shareholders.
The totalAssetscached can be updated to totalAssetsactual by calling the permissionless LMPVault.updateDebtReporting function. Alternatively, one could also perform a sandwich attack against the LMPVault.updateDebtReporting function by front-run it to take advantage of the lower-than-expected price or NAV/share, and back-run it to sell the shares when the price or NAV/share rises after the update.
One could also reverse the attack order, where an attacker withdraws at a higher-than-expected price or NAV/share, perform an update on the total assets, and deposit at a lower price or NAV/share.
Loss assets for vault shareholders. Attacker gains are the loss of other vault shareholders.

title: Gain From LMPVault Can Be Stolen
content: The vulnerability is that the LMPVault's updateDebtReporting function can be called by any address without restriction. Because the function adds newly claimed reward tokens to the vault's total assets before any snapshot of share ownership is taken, an attacker can deposit a huge amount of capital (or use a flash loan) immediately before the call, receive a proportional share of the newly added assets, and then withdraw the same amount of shares in the same transaction or block. This results in the attacker capturing almost the entire gain that should have been distributed to existing shareholders. The attack works because the vault does not enforce any deposit‑withdrawal separation, does not charge fees, and lacks a snapshot mechanism that would weight rewards by the length of time a share has been held. When the attacker’s large deposit inflates the total share count, the net asset value per share only increases marginally, allowing the attacker to withdraw a huge amount of ether while the legitimate users see only a tiny increase in their NAV. The impact is that honest participants receive far less profit than expected; in the example, a user who owned all 100 shares would receive only 0.003 WETH instead of the 30 WETH of rewards. The issue is observable from the UI as a user receiving almost no extra balance after a reward distribution, or seeing their share price barely move despite a large reward being queued. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the vault’s accounting logic, where the auditor noted that updateDebtReporting is public and that the contract does not prevent immediate withdrawals after a deposit. The problem can be hard to notice because the contract’s state changes appear normal – total assets increase and share price updates – but the distribution of the gain is skewed. To remediate, the function should be restricted to a trusted role, a fee should be applied on deposits or withdrawals, deposits and withdrawals should be forced into separate blocks, and a snapshot of share balances should be taken before rewards are added so that only holders at the time of the reward receive the appropriate portion. This class of bug is a profit‑stealing or share‑dilution attack caused by missing access control and accounting safeguards.

title: Incorrect pricing for CurveV2 LP Token
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect pricing calculation for Curve V2 liquidity provider (LP) tokens caused by using the wrong quote currency when retrieving the internal price oracle value. In Curve V2 pools the second token in the coins array (for example frxETH) is priced against the first token (for example rETH), meaning the oracle should return a price expressed as frxETH per rETH. The contract registers each pool with tokenToPrice set to the second token, but the getPriceInEth function later calls the system registry’s root price oracle with getPriceInEth(poolInfo.tokenToPrice). This call returns the price of the second token in terms of ETH, not in terms of the first token as required. Consequently the assetPrice variable holds a value that represents frxETH = ETH instead of frxETH = rETH, and the LP price formula (2 * virtualPrice * sqrt(assetPrice) / 10**18) produces a systematically biased result. The bug manifests whenever the oracle is used to compute LP token value – during debt calculations for derivative vaults, rebalancing logic, NAV and share calculations for LMPVaults, and the amount of assets a user receives on withdrawal. Users may see withdrawals that are larger or smaller than expected, vaults may become over‑ or undervalued, and strategies could execute unprofitable rebalances, potentially leading to loss of assets. The issue occurs under normal operation after a pool is registered; it is not triggered by a special edge case but by the inherent mismatch between the pool’s pricing convention and the generic getPriceInEth call. It was discovered during a manual audit of the oracle integration where the developer’s comment about pricing the second token in the first token was not reflected in the implementation. The problem is subtle because the returned price is still a plausible ETH‑denominated value, so the mispricing can go unnoticed until financial metrics diverge. To remediate, the getPriceInEth function should be updated to obtain the price of the second token expressed in the first token, either by calling a dedicated price‑in‑base‑currency oracle or by inverting the ETH‑based price, ensuring the assetPrice reflects frxETH = rETH. This correction aligns the oracle output with the pool’s pricing model and restores accurate LP token valuation, preventing incorrect NAV, faulty debt assessments, and potential fund loss.

title: Incorrect number of shares minted as fee
content: The vulnerability resides in the fee‑minting logic of the vault contract, where the number of shares issued to the fee sink is calculated with a simplistic proportional formula that ignores the dilution effect caused by the new shares. The code multiplies the fee amount by the current total supply and divides by the total assets, yielding shares2mint = (fees * totalSupply) / totalAssets. Because the newly minted shares increase the total supply, the actual value of those shares after minting is lower than the fee amount taken, resulting in a shortfall (for example, 2 shares are minted for a 20 WETH fee but their post‑mint value is only about 19.6 WETH). The root cause is the use of an incorrect arithmetic relationship that does not preserve the invariant that the fee‑collector’s share value equals the fee amount. An attacker or any participant can exploit this by triggering profit distribution events, causing the protocol to mint fewer shares than required and thereby reducing the fee revenue that should be allocated to the designated sink address. The impact is a systematic under‑allocation of fees, which translates into lost revenue for the protocol and its stakeholders, potentially eroding trust and affecting token holder returns. The bug manifests whenever the vault records a positive profit and attempts to mint fee shares – essentially any fee collection cycle. The affected parties include the protocol itself, the fee sink (often a treasury or reward contract), and indirectly the token holders who rely on accurate fee accounting. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by the security researcher Sherlock, who identified a mismatch between the expected fee value and the actual share value after minting. It can be hard to notice because the share price appears to adjust smoothly, and the discrepancy is a subtle arithmetic error rather than an outright failure, making it easy to overlook in routine testing. The recommended remediation is to replace the current formula with one that accounts for the dilution effect, such as shares2mint = (profit * performanceFeeBps * totalSupply) / ((totalAssets * MAX_FEE_BPS) - (performanceFeeBps * profit)), which aligns the minted share value with the exact fee amount. This approach mirrors the fee calculation used by Lido and ensures that the fee collector receives the full economic value of the fee. In summary, the bug is a miscalculated share‑minting routine that leads to fee loss, violates the protocol’s accounting assumptions, and should be fixed by adopting the correct dilution‑aware formula.

title: Maverick oracle can be manipulated
content: The vulnerability is that the price oracle for a Maverick pool derives its ETH price by taking the pool’s token reserves and multiplying them by external token price feeds. Because the reserves are directly affected by swaps, an attacker who can move a large amount of tokens into the pool can temporarily distort the reserve balance, causing the oracle to return a manipulated price. The root cause is the reliance on on‑chain reserve quantities that are not protected against short‑term price impact, combined with a simple multiplication with static external prices. An attacker can execute a flash‑loan, perform a large swap that pushes the price of the higher‑value token down (or the lower‑value token up), read the altered price from getPriceInEth, and then reverse the swap to repay the loan, all within one transaction. This manipulation can be used to lower the reported value of a position, which reduces the totalDebt calculation in a lending vault and allows the attacker to mint more vault shares than warranted, or conversely to inflate the reported value and extract excess tokens on withdrawal. The issue manifests whenever the oracle is queried after a sizable swap, especially in contexts where the oracle feeds debt or reward calculations. Users of the protocol, such as lenders, borrowers, and token holders, may see their balances change unexpectedly: a borrower may receive more shares for the same deposit, or a withdrawer may obtain more tokens than should be due. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the oracle’s reliance on mutable pool state and verified that a flash‑loan attack could alter the reserves. Because the price deviation exists only for a short window and the oracle does not include any time‑weighted averaging or sanity checks, the manipulation can be subtle and may not be obvious from normal UI metrics, making it hard to detect without targeted testing. The bug belongs to the class of “oracle manipulation via on‑chain state dependence” or “price feed that trusts volatile pool reserves”. To remediate, the oracle should compute value using a time‑weighted average of reserves, incorporate a TWAP from the pool, or source prices from a trusted external market feed that is not directly manipulable by a single transaction. In short, the contract currently trusts a mutable variable that can be altered by an attacker, leading to incorrect accounting and potential loss of funds.
summary:
In the MavEthOracle contract, getPriceInEth function utilizes the reserves of the Maverick pool and multiplies them with the external prices of the tokens (obtained from the rootPriceOracle contract) to calculate the total value of the Maverick position.
However, the reserves of a Maverick position can fluctuate when the price of the Maverick pool changes. Therefore, the returned price of this function can be manipulated by swapping a significant amount of tokens into the Maverick pool. An attacker can utilize a flash loan to initiate a swap, thereby changing the price either upwards or downwards, and subsequently swapping back to repay the flash loan.
Attacker can decrease the returned price of MavEthOracle by swapping a large amount of the higher value token for the lower value token, and vice versa.
Here is a test file that demonstrates how the price of the MavEthOracle contract can be manipulated by swapping to change the reserves.
There are multiple impacts that an attacker can exploit by manipulating the price of MavEthOracle:
• Decreasing the oracle price to lower the totalDebt of LMPVault, in order to receive more LMPVault shares.
• Increasing the oracle price to raise the totalDebt of LMPVault, in order to receive more withdrawn tokens.
• Manipulating the results of the Stats contracts to cause miscalculations for the protocol.

title: Aura/Convex rewards are stuck after DOS
content: The vulnerability is a reward‑distribution logic flaw that allows an attacker to permanently lock Convex rewards inside the Tokemak liquidation contract. The root cause is twofold: the public getReward function in the reward contract does not restrict the _account parameter, so any caller can request rewards on behalf of any address, and the ConvexRewardsAdapter calculates the amount of newly claimed tokens by comparing the token balance of the target account before and after the claim (balanceBefore/after). Because the accounting relies on the external token balance of the account rather than an internal ledger, an adversary can invoke the external Convex contract’s getReward method with the Tokemak contract address as the recipient. This transfers the earned reward tokens directly to the Tokemak contract without invoking the internal reward‑claimed hook that would normally update the accounting state. When Tokemak later executes its own claimRewards routine, the balance difference for each reward token is zero, so the adapter records no amount claimed and the rewards remain stuck in the LiquidationRow contract, never being forwarded to the MainRewarder. The impact is that users who are supposed to receive Convex rewards see their balances stay unchanged, effectively losing the earned incentives; the protocol’s accounting assumptions are violated because the expected flow of “earned → claimed → distributed” is broken. The issue manifests whenever the adapter uses the balance‑before/after pattern and the external Convex contract permits arbitrary reward claims. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the reward‑claiming path and noticed that the getReward function lacks any access control and that the balance‑diff method does not account for external transfers. The bug can be hard to notice because the transaction does not revert and no explicit error is emitted; the contract simply reports zero claimed amount while the tokens sit idle. To remediate, the contract should stop using balanceBefore/after for reward accounting and instead rely on a trusted internal accounting variable or on the contract’s own token balance after the claim. Additionally, the getReward function should be restricted to authorized callers or limited to the caller’s own address, and any external token transfer must trigger the appropriate accounting hook to keep the reward ledger consistent.

title: Destination Vault rewards are not added to
content: The vulnerability resides in the withdraw routine of the LMPVault contract, where rewards received from a Destination Vault are not correctly accounted for when the amount of assets pulled exceeds the amount that was originally planned to be pulled. The function first records any extra base‑asset that arrives as a reward by adding the difference between the post‑withdraw balance and the pre‑withdraw balance (minus the explicit amount pulled) to the variable that tracks idle increase. However, if the total assets pulled (info.totalAssetsPulled) becomes larger than the target amount (info.totalAssetsToPull), the code overwrites the previously calculated idle increase with a simple subtraction (info.idleIncrease = info.totalAssetsPulled - info.totalAssetsToPull) and also caps totalAssetsPulled to the target value. This assignment discards the reward portion that should have been added to idle, effectively reducing the recorded idle increase and leaving the reward amount unaccounted for. Because the recover function cannot extract the base asset from the vault, the unrecorded reward becomes permanently locked inside the contract. The root cause is a logical error: using an assignment instead of an additive update when handling the excess‑pull scenario, combined with a recovery path that does not consider the base asset. An attacker or a user can trigger the condition by withdrawing shares that generate a reward from the Destination Vault, causing totalAssetsPulled to exceed totalAssetsToPull. The contract then silently drops part of the reward, so the user’s balance appears lower than expected and the protocol loses the reward permanently. This issue manifests only during withdrawals that yield extra rewards; normal withdrawals where the pulled amount matches the target do not expose the bug. All participants who rely on the vault – token holders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because their accounting is off and some assets become frozen. The problem was discovered during a manual audit by Sherlock, who noticed that the idle increase calculation was overwritten in the excess‑pull branch, contradicting the earlier additive logic. The bug is subtle because the contract still reports a non‑zero idle increase, making the loss of a portion of the reward easy to miss in routine checks. To remediate, the assignment should be changed to an additive operation (info.idleIncrease += info.totalAssetsPulled - info.totalAssetsToPull) so that any excess assets are correctly added to idle, and the recover function should be extended to allow extraction of the base asset, ensuring that rewards are never permanently locked.

title: Liquidations miss delegate call to swapper
content: The LiquidationRow contract is responsible for orchestrating the liquidation of vault rewards. Its public function liquidateVaultsForToken gathers the total balance to liquidate and then calls a private helper _performLiquidation. Inside this helper the contract invokes IAsyncSwapper(asyncSwapper).swap(params) expecting the swapper to exchange the collected tokens for the target asset. However, the contract never transfers the collected tokens to the swapper, nor does it invoke the swapper via delegatecall. The async swapper implementation used elsewhere in the codebase (for example in LMPVaultRouter.swapAndDepositToVault) relies on delegatecall so that the swap logic runs in the context of the caller and can access the caller’s token balances. By calling the swapper with a normal external call, the swapper executes with its own storage context and therefore sees a zero balance for the token it is supposed to swap. The swap function checks that the amount received is at least the requested buyAmount and reverts when the balance is insufficient. Consequently the liquidation transaction reverts, leaving the rewards that were supposed to be claimed stuck inside LiquidationRow. This denial‑of‑service style bug prevents any liquidator from successfully executing liquidateVaultsForToken, meaning vault owners cannot receive their expected rewards and the protocol’s accounting becomes inconsistent. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the reviewer noticed that no token transfer precedes the swap call and that the swapper is never invoked with delegatecall, a pattern that is used in a different contract. The problem is subtle because the existing unit tests employ a mock swapper that simply mints tokens without checking balances, so the bug does not surface in the test suite. To remediate the issue the call to the async swapper should be changed to a low‑level delegatecall, mirroring the implementation in LMPVaultRouter, or the contract should explicitly transfer the tokens to the swapper before invoking its swap function. Either approach ensures that the swapper operates on the correct token balance, allowing the liquidation to complete and the rewards to be distributed as intended. From a user’s perspective the UI would show a liquidation attempt that never finalises, balances remaining unchanged, and possibly an error message indicating a revert. The bug belongs to the class of context‑mismatch or delegatecall misuse vulnerabilities where a contract calls external logic without preserving the caller’s execution context, leading to token handling errors and locked funds.

title: When queueNewRewards is called, caller could
content: The vulnerability resides in the reward‑queueing function of a token reward contract. The function is intended to accept a caller‑provided amount of new reward tokens, add any previously queued rewards that are already held by the contract, and then either distribute the total immediately or store it for later distribution. The root cause is a logic error in the final token transfer: after the internal variable newRewards is increased by the amount of already queued rewards, the contract calls safeTransferFrom with the inflated newRewards value instead of the original amount supplied by the caller. Because the queued rewards are already owned by the contract, pulling them again results in a double‑count of those tokens. When queuedRewards is non‑zero, two outcomes are possible. If the caller does not have enough balance or allowance for the inflated amount, the transfer reverts, causing a denial‑of‑service for legitimate callers. If the caller does have sufficient funds, the contract withdraws more tokens than the caller intended, effectively stealing the excess amount. The exploit can be triggered by any whitelisted address that calls the function while queuedRewards is non‑zero; the attacker does not need to manipulate the contract state beyond the normal queuing logic. The impact is loss of user funds or failed transactions, breaking the economic assumptions of the reward system where queued rewards are assumed to be already accounted for. The condition occurs only after at least one reward period has left a non‑zero queuedRewards balance, which may not be exercised in early testing, making the bug easy to miss. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the reward distribution logic, where the auditor noticed that the transfer amount was calculated after the queued amount had been added. The problem is subtle because the function works correctly when queuedRewards is zero, giving a false sense of correctness. The proper fix is to transfer only the original newRewards amount supplied by the caller (the startingNewRewards variable) and keep the queued amount internal to the contract, thereby preventing double‑counting and ensuring that only the intended tokens are moved. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of “incorrect accounting of already‑held assets leading to double‑withdrawal” and violates the contract’s business logic that queued rewards should not be re‑collected from the caller.

title: Curve V2 Vaults can be drained because
content: The vulnerability resides in the CurveV2CryptoEthOracle contract that registers Curve V2 pools for price oracle purposes. The registerPool function accepts a flag called checkReentrancy that is intended to be true only for pools that contain the native ETH sentinel address (0xEeeeeEeeeEeEeeEeEeEeeEEEeeeeEeeeeeeeEEeE). The code enforces this by reverting if neither token of the pool matches that sentinel address. However, all Curve V2 pools that accept ETH actually use the wrapped ETH (WETH) token address instead of the sentinel address. Because of this mismatch, a pool that uses WETH can be registered with checkReentrancy set to true without triggering the revert, and the oracle later assumes that the pool is safe from reentrancy because it believes the pool contains native ETH. In the getPriceInEth routine the contract performs a read‑only reentrancy test by calling cryptoPool.claim_admin_fees() when checkReentrancy is enabled. When the pool’s functions are invoked with the use_eth flag set to true (a feature that allows the pool to accept raw ETH via msg.value and to send raw calls back to the caller), the raw call can invoke an attacker‑controlled contract. This raw call bypasses the intended reentrancy protection because the oracle never checks for reentrancy on WETH pools. An attacker can therefore deposit shares at the correct price, trigger a view‑only reentrancy by removing liquidity with use_eth true, manipulate the price returned by getPriceInEth, and then withdraw shares at an inflated price. The inflated price causes the protocol to credit the attacker with more assets than their share entitlement, effectively draining the LMPVault. The impact is that the vault’s balance can shrink unexpectedly, users may see their deposits disappear, and the protocol can lose a large portion of its assets. The flaw occurs whenever a Curve V2 pool that uses WETH is registered with checkReentrancy enabled and an attacker can cause a raw call through the use_eth flag. It affects all depositors and the protocol’s overall safety. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the expected ETH sentinel with the actual token addresses used by Curve V2 pools and traced the reentrancy logic in the oracle. It is hard to notice because the reentrancy guard is only a view‑only check and the raw call path is hidden behind a Python‑style keyword argument, making the vulnerability non‑obvious in a quick code scan. The proper mitigation is to replace the sentinel ETH address with the WETH address in the reentrancy check, or to disable the checkReentrancy flag for pools that use WETH, and to add explicit reentrancy protection for any function that can perform a raw call back to the caller. In short, the bug is a mismatch between token identification and reentrancy assumptions that enables a read‑only reentrancy attack, leading to price manipulation and potential loss of funds.

title: updateDebtReporting can be front run,putting
content: The vulnerability resides in the vault’s accounting routine that updates the debt of each destination vault. The function responsible for this, updateDebtReporting, accepts a caller‑supplied list of destination addresses and only recalculates the debt for the entries that appear in the list. Because the list is not forced to contain every active destination, an attacker can submit a transaction that supplies a list limited to the destinations that generated a profit during the current accounting period. By front‑running a legitimate updateDebtReporting call, the attacker causes the protocol to record profit only for the selected vaults, while the loss incurred by the other vaults is ignored. Immediately after the malicious update, the attacker withdraws his share. The protocol’s fee logic interprets the reported profit as real earnings, mints fee shares and distributes them to the fee sink, effectively rewarding the attacker with extra assets. Subsequent legitimate updates that include the loss‑bearing destinations then allocate the remaining loss to honest liquidity providers, who receive less than they should. From a user’s perspective the attacker sees a higher balance after withdrawal – for example, a deposit of 1000 assets may be redeemed for roughly 1020 – while other users experience a reduced payout, sometimes receiving zero or a significantly lower amount than expected. The issue occurs only when the vault holds multiple destination vaults with differing performance and when an attacker can control transaction ordering, i.e., can front‑run the updateDebtReporting call. It affects any participant who relies on the vault’s accounting, including depositors, the protocol’s fee collector, and the overall health of the vault. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that simulated a scenario where one destination earned 5 % profit and another lost 10 %. The attack is subtle because the function signature appears benign – it merely accepts an array – and the accounting discrepancy only becomes visible after withdrawals, making it easy to miss in routine testing. The root cause is the lack of a guarantee that all active destinations are accounted for during a debt update, allowing selective reporting. To remediate, the function should be redesigned to operate without an external list, automatically iterating over the full set of registered destinations, thereby preventing partial updates. Conceptually, the fix enforces atomic, complete accounting of all positions before any withdrawal, eliminating the opportunity for profit‑skimming via front‑running.

title: Incorrect approach to tracking the PnL of a DV
content: The vulnerability concerns the way a Destination Vault (DV) profit and loss (PnL) is tracked inside a liquidity mining pool (LMP) vault. The contract stores a snapshot called updatedDebtBasis that represents the debt value of the DV at the last rebalancing. When a user attempts to withdraw, the code checks whether the current debt value (currentDvDebtValue) is lower than this snapshot; if it is, the contract treats the DV as being in a loss and limits the amount of shares that can be burned. The root cause is that the snapshot is refreshed to the current debt value immediately after any rebalancing, even when the underlying loss has not been compensated by an appreciation of the underlying LP tokens. Consequently, a DV that is still underwater can be incorrectly marked as not in loss because currentDvDebtValue becomes equal to updatedDebtBasis after the update, despite the fact that the loss of several ether remains. An attacker can exploit this by triggering a small rebalancing that adds a few LP tokens, causing the condition to evaluate to false, and then withdraw all of the DV shares. This locks in the hidden loss and forces the remaining shareholders to bear the deficit. The impact is a reduction of the effective value of the LMP vault for honest participants, potential loss of funds, and a breach of the accounting assumptions that a loss must be covered before full withdrawals are allowed. The issue manifests only after a rebalancing event; before that the contract correctly limits withdrawals. It affects any user holding shares in the LMP vault, as well as the protocol’s overall capital integrity. The problem was discovered during a manual audit of LMPDebt.sol, where the conditional logic at line 275 was examined and found to reset the loss flag prematurely. The bug is subtle because the comparison itself looks correct, and the UI may still display normal balances, making the loss invisible to users. To remediate, the protocol should adopt a more sophisticated PnL tracking mechanism that only clears the loss flag when the price of the underlying LP tokens has appreciated enough to cover the deficit, for example by maintaining a cumulative loss accumulator or by not overwriting the debt basis until the loss is truly resolved. This would preserve the intended business logic that users can only withdraw the amount that is actually available, preventing hidden loss write‑offs and ensuring accurate accounting.
summary:
Let DVA be a certain destination vault.
Assume that at T0, the current debt value (currentDvDebtValue) of DVA is 95 WETH,
and the last debt value (updatedDebtBasis) is 100 WETH. Since the current debt
value has become smaller than the last debt value, the vault is making a loss of 5
WETH since the last rebalancing, so DVA is sitting at a loss, and users can only burn
a limited amount of DestinationVault_A's shares.
Assume that at T1, there is some slight rebalancing performed on DVA, and a few
additional LP tokens are deposited to it. Thus, its current debt value increased to
98 WETH. At the same time, the destInfo.debtBasis and destInfo.ownedShares will
be updated to the current value.
Immediately after the rebalancing, DVA will not be considered sitting in a loss since
the currentDvDebtValue and updatedDebtBasis should be equal now. As a result,
users could now burn all the DVA shares of the LMPVault during withdrawal.
DVA suddenly becomes not sitting at a loss even though the fact is that it is still
sitting at a loss of 5 WETH. The loss has been written off.

A DV might be incorrectly marked as not sitting in a loss, thus allowing users to

title: Inflated price due to unnecessary precision
content: The contract inflates the reported token price by applying an unnecessary 1e18 scaling factor during the initialization of the pricing statistics. The getPriceInEth function already returns a value with 18 decimal places, so multiplying the accumulated price by 1e18 before dividing by the sample count creates an average price that is larger by exactly 1e18. This arithmetic mismatch causes the fast and slow filter prices to be set to values that are many orders of magnitude higher than the true market price. The bug manifests after the initialization phase when the sample counter reaches the configured INIT_SAMPLE_COUNT (18). At that moment the code computes averagePrice = existing._initAcc * 1e18 / INIT_SAMPLE_COUNT, stores the inflated value in existing.fastFilterPrice and existing.slowFilterPrice, and later uses these values in the exponential filter formula. Because the prior filter values are astronomically large, the subsequent filtered price calculation produces a result such as 1.34e36 wei (approximately 1.34e18 ETH) even though the real price is only a few ETH. The protocol relies on these filtered prices to decide whether a rebalance proposal is profitable. An attacker who can trigger a rebalance during the post‑initialization phase can cause the strategy to believe a trade is highly profitable, leading to execution of an unprofitable swap and loss of vault assets. Users observing the UI would see the token price displayed as an absurdly high number, or they might notice that expected returns are zero or negative despite market conditions indicating otherwise. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the arithmetic handling of price values and identified the redundant scaling. It is hard to notice because the overflow does not occur; the numbers remain within the uint256 range, and the contract does not emit explicit warnings. The vulnerability belongs to the class of unit‑mismatch or precision bugs where values are multiplied or divided by an incorrect factor, breaking the intended accounting assumptions. To remediate, the average price should be calculated without the extra multiplication, i.e., averagePrice = existing._initAcc / INIT_SAMPLE_COUNT, and the filter values should be set from this correctly scaled average. This restores the invariant that all price variables share the same 18‑decimal precision and prevents inflated pricing from corrupting the protocol’s decision logic.

title: Immediately start getting rewards belonging
content: The vulnerability is an accounting error in the reward distribution logic of a vault‑rewarder system. When a user mints new vault shares, the ERC20 _mint function first increases the user’s token balance and then triggers the _afterTokenTransfer hook, which automatically calls the rewarder’s stake function on the user’s behalf. Inside stake, the contract calls _updateReward before actually recording the new stake amount. _updateReward reads the current rewardPerToken value, which already reflects rewards accrued for the current block, and computes the user’s earned amount as balance × (rewardPerToken − userRewardPerTokenPaid). Because the user’s balance has already been increased but userRewardPerTokenPaid is still zero, the calculation attributes the full current reward per token to the newly minted shares, granting the user an immediate reward of balance × rewardPerToken (for example 100 × r). This reward is not earned and can be withdrawn, effectively allowing a new participant to claim tokens that belong to the reward pool. The bug occurs whenever a fresh user receives shares via minting or any operation that stakes tokens before the reward snapshot is taken. It affects all participants of the vault because the over‑issued rewards reduce the pool available to legitimate stakers, potentially draining the reward contract. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that traced the flow from ERC20 _mint through the _afterTokenTransfer hook into MainRewarder.stake and observed that _updateReward was invoked prior to the internal balance update. The problem is subtle because the stake function appears to follow a typical pattern, and the reward calculation itself is mathematically correct for existing balances; only the ordering of state updates creates an unintended credit. To fix the issue, the rewarder should update the user’s reward state after the balance has been increased, or it should maintain its own internal accounting of balances and total supply so that the snapshot is taken against the correct pre‑stake state. In practice this means moving the call to _updateReward to after _stake, or redesigning _stake to adjust _totalSupply and _balances before calling _updateReward, thereby ensuring that newly minted shares start with zero pending rewards. The bug belongs to the class of “reward snapshot before balance update” or “premature reward accrual” errors, which violate the business rule that rewards are earned only for time held, not for instantaneous allocation. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after receiving newly minted shares, the UI may show a large reward balance that can be claimed immediately, contrary to the expectation that rewards accrue over time. This discrepancy can lead to users withdrawing unearned tokens and the protocol losing funds.

title: liquidatePartyArequires signature which doesn't
content: The vulnerability is an unfair liquidation flaw that stems from the liquidation signature lacking any reference to the current nonces or state of the parties involved. Because the signature only contains static fields such as the unrealized profit and loss (upnl) and the liquidation type, it can be generated when a party appears liquidatable, but it does not capture any subsequent state changes that may occur before the transaction is mined. In the described scenario, PartyA is initially liquidatable with an upnl of -100 and a liquidator obtains a valid signature. At the same time PartyB fulfills PartyA’s request to close half of the position, which reduces PartyA’s allocated balance and upnl, making PartyA solvent again. However, the liquidation transaction still executes using the stale signature, calculates an available balance based on the old allocated amount, classifies the liquidation as OVERDUE, and zeroes PartyA’s balance while giving PartyB only a partial profit and leaving the liquidator without the expected fee. The impact is that PartyA loses all of its funds despite being solvent moments before, PartyB receives less than its rightful profit, and the liquidator receives no compensation, effectively stealing value from all participants. This condition occurs whenever a liquidation request is signed and submitted while another transaction that modifies the same account’s balances can be mined first, a race‑condition enabled by the missing nonce fields. The affected parties are any user whose position can be closed, the counterparties that share the position, and the liquidators who rely on correct fee calculation. The issue was uncovered during a systematic audit by reproducing the race in a test suite that deliberately interleaved a close‑position request with a liquidation call. It is hard to notice because on‑chain balances after the close appear correct, yet the liquidation still succeeds due to the outdated signature, making the loss look like a protocol‑level bug rather than a simple accounting error. The proper mitigation is to bind the liquidation signature to the current nonces of both parties, or otherwise enforce an on‑chain state check that rejects liquidation if the account’s balance or nonce has changed since the signature was produced, thereby preventing execution based on stale data and preserving the intended business logic of only liquidating truly insolvent positions.
summary:
Example Scenario:
1. PartyA: allocated=109, upnl=-99, cva+lf=10. To avoid liquidation, partyA tries to close 50% of its position, submitting requestToClosePosition
2. PartyA: allocated=109, upnl=-100, cva+lf=10. PartyA becomes liquidatable
3. Liquidator submits liquidating transaction (with upnl=-100), but partyB at the same time fulfills partyA request
4. partyB transaction executes first, partyA has: allocated = 59, upnl=-50, cva+lf=5 (not liquidatable anymore)
5. Liquidator transaction executes (with upnl=-100): 4.1. Available Balance = 59-5 - 100 = -46 4.2. Liquidation type = OVERDUE (46 > 5), deficit = 41 4.3. Corresponding partyB receives 50 - 50*46/100 = 27 4.4. PartyA allocated balance is set to 0 4.5. Liquidators receives 0 (because it's OVERDUE liquidation)
The result:
1. PartyA was solvent just before the liquidation, but was still liquidated, losing all funds
2. PartyB has received 27 instead of full 50 profit (even though partyA had enough funds)
3. Liquidator didn't receive any fee, although it should have received it as partyA had enough funds.
All 3 parties have lost funds. Protocol basically stole those funds.
Unfair liquidation for partyA, loss of funds for liquidator and partyB in many possible situations during partyA liquidation - happening by itself or caused by malicious actors.

title: liquidatePositionsPartyA limits partyB loss to
content: The vulnerability resides in the liquidation routine that processes each open position of a counter‑party (PartyA) independently when calculating the amount to deduct from the counterpart’s (PartyB) allocated balance. The contract computes a separate amountToDeduct for every position, using the allocated balance of PartyB at that moment, instead of first aggregating the signed profit‑and‑loss (PnL) of all positions belonging to the same PartyB. As a result, when PartyA holds both a large negative unrealised PnL position and a large positive one, the liquidation of the negative position does not reduce PartyB’s allocated balance because the balance is zero at that point. The subsequent liquidation of the positive position then credits PartyB with the full positive amount, ignoring the earlier loss. Consequently PartyB’s recorded balance can become far larger than the net sum of its unrealised PnL plus credit‑line (cva+liquidity‑fund), effectively creating phantom funds that never entered the protocol. This over‑crediting inflates the protocol’s apparent liabilities while the actual pool of assets remains unchanged, opening the door to a systemic shortfall: later users attempting to withdraw may find insufficient liquidity, potentially triggering a bank‑run scenario. The flaw manifests whenever a party has multiple positions with opposite signs and the liquidation order processes the losing position first while the counterpart’s allocated balance is zero. It affects any user who is the counter‑party to a liquidated participant, as well as the overall protocol health because the accounting invariants (total assets = total liabilities) are broken. The issue was uncovered during a manual audit of the symmetrical update logic, where the auditor observed that the total signed PnL for PartyB was not taken into account before updating balances. The bug is subtle because the contract still updates balances without reverting, and the per‑position accounting appears correct in isolation, making the inconsistency hard to spot without a holistic view of all positions. To remediate, the liquidation code should first sum the signed PnL of all positions belonging to a given PartyB, compute a single net amountToDeduct, and then apply that net adjustment to the allocated balance. This ensures that gains and losses offset correctly and prevents the creation of artificial credit. In broader terms, the problem belongs to the class of accounting‑logic errors where per‑item updates are performed without respecting aggregate constraints, leading to balance inflation and violation of financial guarantees.
summary:
Example Scenario:
Position 1: upnl = -960, cva+lf = 10, mm=10 Position 2: upnl = +1000, cva+lf = 10, mm=10 Total cva+lf = 20, total mm=20 PartyB has allocated balance = 0 (available = 0 + 1000 - 960 = 40 >= 20 - not liquidatable) Party A is liquidated:
1. Position 1 is liquidated. amount = 960 amountToDeduct = 0 (because partyB allocated balance = 0) partyB allocatedBalance remains 0
2. Position 2 is liquidated. amount = 1000 partyB allocatedBalance increases by 1000 (is set to 1000)
The result: PartyB should have a balance of less than 60 (upnl+cva), but it has 1000 instead!
In some situations during partyA liquidations, PartyB balance is increased significantly while no funds enter the protocol, meaning protocol debt to users increases and is greater than protocol funds. This can cause a bank run, since the last users to withdraw will be unable to do so.

title: when reservedUntilTokenId > 100 first funder
content: The vulnerability is an allocation misalignment caused by using the reservedUntilTokenId value directly as the starting base token identifier when initializing founder vesting schedules. Because the contract later treats token identifiers modulo 100, any reservedUntilTokenId greater than 99 produces a baseTokenId that lies outside the valid range of the tokenRecipient mapping. The first call to _getNextTokenId receives this out‑of‑range identifier, stores the founder in tokenRecipient[200] (for example) but the minting logic in _isForFounder later reduces the token id with %100, so the entry at index 200 is never consulted. As a result the first founder receives one token less than intended (e.g., 9 % instead of 10 %). The root cause is the missing modulo operation when initializing baseTokenId, creating a mismatch between the indexing scheme used for reservation and the indexing scheme used for minting. An attacker or a misconfigured deployment can trigger the condition simply by passing a reservedUntilTokenId value larger than 99, which silently drops the first allocation without reverting. The impact is a loss of ownership of a portion of the NFT for the affected founder, breaking the protocol’s accounting assumptions and potentially reducing the perceived value of the collection. The bug manifests only when the initialization parameter exceeds the 0‑99 range; under normal values the contract behaves as expected. It affects any founder whose allocation is calculated first, as well as downstream users who rely on the correct distribution of tokens. The issue was discovered during a manual audit and confirmed with a unit test that inspected the public tokenRecipient mapping and observed a non‑zero entry at index 200 that never resulted in a minted token. Because the contract never accesses indices above 99 in the minting path, the problem can be hard to notice without explicit inspection of the storage layout. The appropriate fix is to normalize the starting identifier, for example by setting baseTokenId to 0 or by applying a %100 operation to reservedUntilTokenId before the loop, ensuring that all entries written to tokenRecipient are within the range that the minting logic will ever query. This correction restores the intended founder share and aligns the allocation logic with the protocol’s accounting model.

title: Adversary can permanently brick auctions due
content: The vulnerability is an arithmetic precision mismatch that occurs duringthe settlement of an auction when the contract attempts to deposit reward funds in a batch. The auction logic calculates a total reward amount by multiplying the final bid by the sum of all reward basis‑point percentages and then dividing by a constant representing 100 percent (BPS_PER_100_PERCENT). Separately, each individual reward (builder, referral, founder) is calculated with the same multiplication and division but using its own percentage. Because Solidity integer division truncates toward zero, the three individual calculations can lose up to one wei each, while the combined calculation may lose a different amount. The ProtocolRewards contract later checks that the ether sent with the batch deposit (msg.value) is exactly equal to the sum of the individual amounts array. When the rounding loss makes the summed amounts differ from the previously computed totalRewards, the equality test fails and the function reverts with INVALID_DEPOSIT. An adversary can deliberately choose a final bid value that forces this off‑by‑one‑wei condition, causing the depositBatch call inside the _settleAuction function to always revert. As a result the auction cannot be settled, rewards are never distributed, and the auction state becomes permanently stuck – effectively bricking the auction. The impact is that users who win an auction see no reward, the protocol’s accounting is broken, and funds remain locked in the contract. The bug affects any participant who relies on the auction settlement, including bidders, reward recipients, and the protocol governance that expects auctions to close. It was discovered during a manual audit when the reviewer noticed that the totalRewards variable was derived from a summed percentage while the individual amounts were computed separately, leading to a potential mismatch. The issue is subtle because the discrepancy may be as small as a single wei, which can be overlooked in typical testing with larger values. To fix the problem the totalRewards should be built incrementally by adding each individual reward amount, guaranteeing that the sum of the amounts array always matches the value sent, or the deposit function should allow a small tolerance or use a rounding‑up strategy. In essence, the bug is a classic integer‑division rounding error that violates the contract’s accounting invariants, causing reward distribution to fail and auctions to become irrecoverable.

title: Registering/Revoking of keys susceptible to
content: The contract provides two public functions, registerSigningKey and revokeSigningKey, that allow a user to add or remove an authorized signing key for their account. Both functions accept an off‑chain signature that proves the caller’s consent, but the signed message does not contain any replay‑prevention field such as a nonce or a unique identifier. Because the contract does not record whether a particular signature has already been processed, any previously valid signature can be submitted again at a later time. An attacker who can observe a legitimate transaction – for example, the registration of a key by Alice – can extract the signature data from the transaction receipt and replay it to the contract. In a replay registration scenario the attacker submits the same registration signature after Alice has revoked the key, causing the key to be added back to Alice’s approved list without her consent. In a replay revoke scenario the attacker re‑uses the revocation signature after Alice has re‑registered the key, causing the key to be removed again. The vulnerability therefore allows a malicious party to manipulate the set of authorized signing keys of any user, potentially enabling unauthorized actions that rely on those keys, such as signing withdrawals or other privileged operations. From the user’s perspective the expected behavior – a key that has been revoked stays revoked, or a newly added key remains active – is violated; users may see a key disappear and later reappear, or see a key they thought was active suddenly revoked without any action on their part. The issue was discovered during a security audit when the auditors replayed captured signatures in a test harness and observed that the contract accepted them. The bug is subtle because the signatures themselves are cryptographically valid and the contract emits the correct events, so a superficial inspection may not reveal that the same signature can be reused indefinitely. The root cause is the absence of a nonce or other monotonic counter in the signed payload, which is a common pattern for preventing replay attacks. To remediate the issue the contract should incorporate a per‑account nonce (or a global incrementing counter) into the data that is hashed and signed for both registration and revocation, and the contract must verify that the nonce supplied in the transaction matches the current stored nonce and then increment it. This ensures that each signed message can be processed only once, eliminating the possibility of replaying old signatures and protecting the integrity of the key management system.

title: Adversary can reenter takeOverDebt() during
content: The vulnerability is a re‑entrancy flaw in the function that transfers an outstanding debt to a new borrower (takeOverDebt). The contract postpones updating its internal borrowing records until after it makes an external call during the repayment process. When a liquidatable position is repaid, the function performs a UniV3 token swap that transfers a custom attacker‑controlled token. This transfer hands execution control back to the attacker before the borrowing storage is cleared. Because takeOverDebt lacks a nonReentrant guard, the attacker can invoke it during this callback, moving the loan to a secondary address while the original repayment continues. The storage cleanup (removing the borrowing key) is performed only after the re‑entered call returns, and the key‑removal routine does not revert if the key is already missing, allowing the repayment to finish successfully. As a result the same liquidity‑provider (LP) position is liquidated twice: the attacker receives the LP tokens from the first liquidation, then the contract refunds the same LP amount again after the re‑entered takeover, creating a net deficit in the vault’s token balances. The impact is that the vault can be drained of the target token, other users lose their collateral, and the protocol’s accounting invariants are broken – users expect their deposited LP to be returned once, but they receive nothing while the attacker walks away with extra LP. The flaw manifests only when a position becomes liquidatable and the repay() function is called, which triggers the external swap. It affects any borrower, the vault’s liquidity pool, and ultimately the protocol’s users. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that traced the control flow of repay() and observed that storage updates occur after an external token transfer, and that the key‑removal helper silently succeeds even when the key is absent. The problem is subtle because the re‑entrancy occurs deep inside a multi‑step financial operation, and the missing revert in the key‑removal function masks the abnormal state, making the bug hard to notice in normal testing. The correct mitigation is to protect takeOverDebt (and any other functions that can be called during external interactions) with a re‑entrancy guard such as the nonReentrant modifier, and to ensure that borrowing state is updated before any external call and that key removal reverts on unexpected conditions. In abstract terms, this is a classic re‑entrancy attack combined with improper state handling and silent failure of a data‑structure cleanup routine, leading to double‑spending of LP assets and a vault deficit.

title: Creditor can maliciously burn UniV3 position
content: The vulnerability originates from the contract’s reliance on the ERC721.ownerOf function to identify the creditor of a loan that is represented by a Uniswap V3 position NFT. The ERC721.ownerOf implementation reverts when it is called with a tokenId that no longer exists, such as after the NFT has been burned. In the LiquidityManager and LiquidityBorrowingManager contracts, the repayment and liquidation logic iterates over all active loans and calls ownerOf for each loan’s tokenId to verify the caller’s rights and to transfer rewards. When a creditor (or any malicious actor) deliberately burns the NFT that backs a loan, every subsequent call to ownerOf for that tokenId reverts, causing the entire repayment or liquidation loop to fail. As a result, the protocol cannot process repayments, liquidations, or emergency withdrawals for any loan that references the burned token, effectively locking the associated funds. The impact is that lenders cannot retrieve their capital, borrowers cannot repay, and the protocol’s liquidity management becomes dead‑locked. This condition occurs only when the NFT is burned, which may be rare and therefore easy to overlook during testing, especially because ownerOf normally succeeds for valid tokens. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the repayment flow and noticed that ownerOf is called without any existence check or error handling. It is hard to notice because the revert only happens for a specific edge case (burned token) and does not affect normal operation. To remediate, the contract should store the original creditor address at loan creation and use a try‑catch or existence check (e.g., ERC721._exists) before calling ownerOf. If the call reverts or the token does not exist, the stored creditor should be used as a fallback, ensuring that repayment and liquidation logic can continue even when the NFT is no longer present. This class of bug is a “missing existence check on external token ownership query” that leads to a denial‑of‑service and fund‑lockup scenario, violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions that each loan always has a reachable creditor address.

title: No slippage protection during repayment due
content: The contract that handles loan repayment performs an internal token swap to convert the held collateral (holdToken) into the sale token needed to restore liquidity. The amount of sale token expected from the swap is calculated on‑the‑fly using the current sqrtPrice obtained from the Uniswap V3 pool’s slot0() function. This price is then used to compute a minimum amountOut value (amountOutMinimum) as a simple percentage of the expected output. Because the same mutable price is used both to determine the expected output and to set the minimum acceptable output, the slippage check becomes ineffective: the calculated amountOutMinimum will always be satisfied as long as the swap executes at the current price. An attacker can therefore front‑run (sandwich) the repayment transaction, briefly moving the pool price by performing a large trade before the repayment. When the repayment transaction runs, the manipulated price is read from slot0, causing the contract to believe the sale token amount is still acceptable and to accept a much worse rate. The swap succeeds, but the repayer receives fewer sale tokens than anticipated, reducing the profit that would otherwise be earned from restoring liquidity. This loss is observable as a small reduction in the user’s sale‑token balance after repayment (for example, a difference of roughly 0.0000049 WETH, equivalent to about 8 USD in the reported test). The issue manifests only when the repayment logic relies on the instantaneous pool price and does not enforce an independent slippage bound or use a time‑weighted average price (TWAP). It affects any user who repays a loan through the contract, the protocol’s economic model, and potentially the overall health of the liquidity pool because the expected profit incentive is eroded. The vulnerability was discovered during a security audit by reviewing the repayment code path and reproducing a sandwich scenario in a test environment, where the profit loss became evident despite the transaction appearing successful. The problem is subtle because the transaction does not revert and the UI shows a successful repayment, making the profit reduction easy to overlook. To remediate, the contract should avoid reading the volatile slot0 price at execution time; instead it should query the Uniswap V3 oracle for a TWAP over a reasonable interval, and it should set amountOutMinimum based on a price observed before the repayment transaction begins, optionally adding an explicit slippage buffer. This change restores proper slippage protection, prevents price manipulation, and aligns the repayment outcome with the protocol’s intended accounting logic.

title: old borrowing key is used instead ofnewBorrowingKey
content: The vulnerability originates from a logic error in the borrowing management flow of the protocol. When a user attempts to transfer or refinance an existing loan, the contract first removes the credentials associated with the current borrowing key by calling _removeKeysAndClearStorage with the old borrower address, the old borrowingKey and the list of old loans. Afterwards, a new borrowing key is generated in _initOrUpdateBorrowing using the holdToken, saleToken and the address of the new borrower. However, instead of using this freshly created newBorrowingKey when the contract records the loan information, the implementation mistakenly passes the previously deleted old borrowing key to _addKeysAndLoansInfo. As a result, the tokenId of each old loan is mapped to the stale borrowing key inside the tokenIdToBorrowingKeys mapping. From a user perspective this manifests as a loan that appears to have been transferred or refinanced, yet the on‑chain record still points to an invalid or deleted borrowing key. Consequently, subsequent operations that rely on the borrowing key – such as repayment, liquidation or claim of collateral – fail because the contract cannot locate valid credentials for the loan. The impact is that funds may become effectively locked, borrowers may be unable to repay or retrieve collateral, and an attacker who can guess or reuse the old key could potentially manipulate the loan state. The bug is triggered only when the update flag is false (i.e., during a refinancing or transfer path) and the old borrowing key has already been cleared, making the condition relatively narrow but still high‑severity because it breaks core accounting guarantees. The issue was discovered during a manual audit where the flow of key generation and storage updates was traced and the mismatch between the key used for deletion and the key used for insertion was observed. It is subtle because the contract does not emit an explicit error; the state simply becomes inconsistent, which can be hard to detect without deep inspection of the mapping contents. The correct remediation is to replace the reference to the old borrowing key with the newly generated newBorrowingKey when invoking _addKeysAndLoansInfo, ensuring that the loan records are always associated with a valid, active borrowing credential. Conceptually, this belongs to the class of state‑inconsistency bugs where a resource identifier is incorrectly reused after its lifecycle has ended, violating the protocol’s invariant that each loan must be linked to a currently authorized borrowing key.
summary:
The old borrowing key credentials are deleted in _removeKeysAndClearStorage(oldBorrowing.borrower, borrowingKey, oldLoans);

title: It is possible to frontrun liquidations with self
content: The vulnerability is that the liquidation routine clears the warning flag unconditionally after performing a repayment, even if the account remains under‑collateralized. Borrower.warn stores a timestamp indicating when the grace period expires by encoding block.timestamp + LIQUIDATION_GRACE_PERIOD into slot0. Borrower.liquidate calls an internal _repay and then overwrites the warning bits with SLOT0_DIRT without checking the post‑repayment health of the account. As a result an attacker can trigger a liquidation transaction that repays only a tiny amount, clears the warning, and then let the block finish. Any subsequent liquidation attempt in the same block or after the grace period will find the warning cleared and revert with the “Aloe: grace” error, effectively denying liquidation of an unhealthy position. This front‑running attack creates a denial‑of‑service condition: the protocol cannot liquidate risky accounts, allowing borrowers to accumulate large bad‑debt positions. When the warning is missing, users attempting to withdraw may see their balances stuck or receive no funds, and the protocol may run out of liquidity, leading to a potential bank run where early withdrawers are paid but later ones receive nothing. The issue was discovered during an audit by constructing a test that calls warn, skips the grace period, then calls liquidate with an exaggerated strain parameter to clear the warning and verifies that a second liquidation reverts. The bug is subtle because the warning flag is intended only as a timing guard, and developers may assume it is cleared only after a successful liquidation; the unconditional clearing violates that expectation. The class of bug is an improper state transition that enables a race condition and front‑running, a form of denial‑of‑service through state flag manipulation. To remediate, the contract should only clear the warning flag if the account is healthy after the repayment, or defer clearing until a successful liquidation has been confirmed, thereby preserving the grace‑period guard and preventing the front‑run attack.

title: Oracle.sol: manipulation via increasing Uniswap
content: The vulnerability resides in the price oracle that reads Uniswap V3 observations to compute a time‑weighted average price (TWAP) and implied volatility. The oracle’s observe function treats every slot in the circular observation array as valid, even when the slot has never been initialized. Uniswap V3 allows any address to call increaseObservationCardinalityNext, which expands the array and leaves newly added slots with a timestamp of 1 and all other fields set to zero, while the initialized flag remains false. Because the oracle does not check this flag, a crafted seed value can cause the algorithm to select one of these empty slots as the left‑hand observation during a binary‑search style lookup. When this happens the oracle incorporates a zero tick cumulative and zero seconds‑per‑liquidity value into its arithmetic, producing a corrupted price and volatility output. An attacker can trigger the condition by first expanding the observation cardinality, then performing swaps that move the pool’s current observation index to a position where the uninitialized slot lies on the left side of the search window, and finally calling the oracle with a seed that points to the vulnerable index. The manipulated TWAP can be inflated or deflated arbitrarily, which downstream contracts use for liquidation thresholds, collateral valuation, and debt calculations. Consequently a user may see a liquidation occur at a price far from market reality, receive no funds when expecting a refund, or see their collateral seized while the protocol records an unrealistically high asset value. The issue appears only when the observation array contains uninitialized entries and the attacker can influence both the pool state and the seed parameter; it is difficult to notice because the oracle still returns a numeric price rather than reverting, and the zero values blend into normal low‑liquidity observations. The bug was uncovered during a manual audit of the Oracle.consult and Oracle.observe implementations, where the lack of an initialized‑check was observed. To remediate, the observe routine must skip any observation whose initialized flag is false, and the contract should either restrict who can increase the observation cardinality or enforce that newly added slots are populated before they can be read. This class of flaw is an oracle manipulation vulnerability caused by reading uninitialized data structures, breaking the fundamental accounting assumption that every price observation reflects a real market state.

title: Borrower's modify, liquidate and warn functions
content: The vulnerability is an accounting mismatch that allows a borrower to create unrepayable debt by exploiting the fact that the contract uses a stale value (borrowBalanceStored) to calculate liabilities in the modify, liquidate and warn functions. The stored borrow balance is only updated during an explicit accrueInterest call and therefore reflects the debt at the last interest accrual, while the current borrow balance (borrowBalance) includes interest that has accrued since then. A malicious user can borrow the maximum amount allowed at the highest leverage, add a small safety margin, and then wait for a period of market inactivity during which interest accrues. After this idle period the actual borrow balance exceeds the stored balance by more than the allowed leverage. Because the contract still bases collateral checks and withdrawal limits on the outdated stored balance, the attacker can withdraw assets that appear to be safely collateralised but are in fact insufficient to cover the real debt. The account remains apparently healthy and is not liquidatable because liquidation also relies on the stored liabilities. Once the attacker triggers an explicit accrueInterest on the lender, the stored balance catches up to the real debt, the account becomes liquidatable and a liquidation can be performed, leaving the borrower with a large residual debt and zero assets. The protocol’s other users suffer because the bad debt reduces the lender’s total assets, meaning that later depositors may be unable to withdraw their funds, potentially causing a bank‑run scenario. The issue was discovered during an audit by reproducing the exploit in a test contract (Exploit.t.sol) that demonstrates the sequence of borrowing, waiting, withdrawing, and forced liquidation. It is hard to notice because the UI and on‑chain queries that read borrowBalanceStored report a healthy collateralisation ratio, and the warning mechanisms also use the stale value, so no alert is raised until interest is manually accrued. The root cause is the reliance on borrowBalanceStored in the internal _getLiabilities routine instead of the up‑to‑date borrowBalance that incorporates accrued interest. The recommended remediation is to replace borrowBalanceStored with borrowBalance when computing liabilities, ensuring that all collateral checks, withdrawals, warnings and liquidations use the current debt figure. This class of bug falls under stale‑state or accounting‑mismatch vulnerabilities that break the invariant that assets must always cover liabilities, leading to unexpected fund loss and violation of the protocol’s financial guarantees.

title: IV Can be Decreased for Free
content: The vulnerability consists of a free manipulation of the implied volatility (IV) metric that the protocol uses to calculate loan‑to‑value (LTV) and to estimate the probability of insolvency. IV is derived from a formula that divides a constant by the product of the time elapsed and the total liquidity (tickTvl) present in a single tick spacing. Because the calculation uses only the on‑chain state of the current block, an attacker can artificially inflate tickTvl by depositing a large amount of liquidity into that specific tick, invoke the contract’s update function, and then withdraw the liquidity within the same block. This sequence reduces the denominator of the IV formula, causing IV to drop dramatically without any price movement or trading activity. The drop in IV directly raises the LTV, allowing borrowers to obtain up to the maximum 90 % leverage even for highly volatile assets, effectively bypassing the protocol’s risk controls. As a result, a borrower can avoid liquidation despite adverse market conditions, and the protocol’s insolvency estimation based on IV becomes unreliable, turning a designed five‑sigma insolvency event into a likely occurrence. The issue is hard to notice because the IV value changes appear to be a normal market‑driven adjustment, yet no price data is altered; only the liquidity distribution is manipulated, which is not obvious from external observations. The flaw was identified during a security audit that examined the IV computation and its reliance on a single‑block, single‑tick liquidity snapshot. To remediate the problem, the protocol should replace the instantaneous tick liquidity with a time‑weighted average of in‑range liquidity over a recent window, preventing a single block’s liquidity injection from having a disproportionate effect on IV. In user terms, a borrower may expect a loan to be liquidated when the market crashes, but instead sees the loan remain safe or be able to borrow far more than intended, indicating that the system’s accounting assumptions about volatility and collateral safety have been broken.
summary:
The liquidity at a single tickSpacing is used to calculate the IV. The more liquidity is in this tick spacing, the lower the IV, as demonstrated by the tickTvl dividing the return value of the estimate function:
```solidity
return SoladyMath.sqrt((4e24 * volumeGamma0Gamma1 * scale) / (b.timestamp - a.timestamp) / tickTvl);
```
Since this is using data only from the block that the function is called, the liquidity can easily be increased by: 1. depositing a large amount liquidity into the tickSpacing 2. calling update 3. removing the liquidity active liquidity tick. Therefore, the capital cost required to massively increase the liquidity is low. Additionally, the manipulation has zero cost (aside from gas fees), as no trading is done through the pool. Contrast this with a pool price manipulation, which costs a significant amount of trading fees to trade through a large amount of the liquidity of the pool. Since this manipulation costs nothing except gas, the IV_CHANGE_PER_UPDATE which limits the amount that IV can be manipulated per update does not sufficiently disincentivise manipulation, it just extends the time period required to manipulate. Decreasing the IV increases the LTV, and due to the free cost, it's reasonable to increase the LTV to the max LTV of 90% even for very volatile assets. Aloe uses the IV to estimate the probability of insolvency of loans. With the delay inherent in TWAP oracle and the liquidation delay by the warn-then-liquidate process, this manipulation can turn price change based insolvency from a 5 sigma event (as designed by the protocol) to a likely event.
• Decreasing IV can be done at zero cost aside from gas fees.
• This can be used to borrow assets at far more leverage than the proper LTV
• Borrowers can use this to avoid liquidation
• This also breaks the insolvency estimation based on IV for riskiness of price-change caused insolvency.

title: _killWoundedAgents
content: The vulnerability resides in the private function that removes wounded agents from the game. The routine decides which agents to kill by checking only the agent's status flag for being wounded, but it does not verify when the wound occurred. Because the contract records the round number at which an agent became wounded (woundedAt), the missing check allows the kill logic to treat any agent that is currently marked as wounded as eligible for death, regardless of whether the agent was healed in a later round and then wounded again. The function is invoked after a new round's random word is fulfilled; the contract first determines the set of newly wounded agents for the current round and then calls the kill routine for agents that have been wounded for a predefined number of rounds. Since the kill routine does not compare the stored woundedAt value with the round identifier passed to it, an agent that was healed in a previous round and subsequently wounded again in the same round can be killed immediately, even though it has not satisfied the required waiting period. This timing mismatch means that a player who pays tokens to keep an agent alive and even performs a heal operation can see the agent die instantly, resulting in unexpected loss of tokens and premature removal from the game. The issue was discovered during a manual audit and reproduced with a proof‑of‑concept test that repeatedly healed and re‑wounded agents across rounds, observing that the contract emitted a Killed event for agents that should have been safe. The bug is subtle because the status flag alone appears sufficient to indicate a wounded agent, so developers may not notice that the temporal condition is required for correct game economics. It belongs to the class of logical state‑transition errors where a state change is applied without validating the associated timestamp or epoch, breaking the intended accounting assumptions of delayed death after a wound. To remediate, the kill routine should also compare the agent's woundedAt field with the round identifier supplied to the function, ensuring that only agents that have remained wounded for the exact number of rounds defined by the protocol are removed. Adding this temporal guard restores the intended game flow where healed agents survive until they are wounded for the required duration, preventing inadvertent token loss and preserving fairness for all participants.

title: Winning agent id may be uninitialized when
content: The vulnerability is an uninitialized winning agent identifier that prevents the grand prize from being claimed. In the claimGrandPrize function the contract reads agents[1].agentId to verify that the caller owns the winning agent. Because the agentId field is never set during the game, its default value is zero, which is defined as an invalid identifier with no associated owner. When the function subsequently calls the internal ownership check with this zero identifier, the check fails and the transaction reverts, leaving the prize pool locked forever. This occurs after the game has been declared over and a legitimate winner attempts to claim the reward. The affected party is the winner, who expects to receive the prize but instead receives a revert and sees no change in balance, while the protocol suffers from a locked fund that undermines trust. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the claim logic and noticed that the agentId was not initialized before being used. It can be hard to notice because the revert path is only triggered under the specific condition of a zero identifier, which may not be exercised in typical test scenarios. The bug belongs to the class of uninitialized state variable or improper default value errors that break business logic and accounting assumptions, effectively causing “funds disappear” or “prize claim fails” symptoms.
