This issue is most clearly demonstrated with a mint of a single wei. The single wei will be insufficient to cover the entire underAllocation, as a result, the caller is errantly required to provide the entire underAllocation amount in GM tokens to mint the specified single wei of GMI.

Similarly, this issue is present with withdrawals, where redeeming a single wei of shares will result in the withdrawer receiving the entire over-allocation amount.

This is a fundamental accounting error and will significantly affect the assetVault share values and the GMI valuation over time.

title: AGV-1 | Mishandling Of Gas Stipends
content: The vulnerability is a mis‑calculation of the gas payment required from users in an asynchronous keeper‑driven protocol. The contract checks that the ether sent with a request (msg.value) is greater than or equal to a variable named gas, which actually represents a raw gas amount measured in gas units, not a monetary value in wei. Because the check treats gas units as if they were wei, the required payment is orders of magnitude smaller than the real cost of executing the keeper’s transaction. When a user submits a deposit or withdrawal request, the contract accepts the request even though the user has supplied only a tiny fraction of the needed ether. The keeper later executes the request, paying the full gas cost at the prevailing gas price, while the protocol never recovers those fees. This results in a systematic loss of funds on every request that is processed, potentially draining the protocol’s treasury over time. The issue occurs whenever the asynchronous model relies on users pre‑paying gas and the contract uses the flawed require(msg.value >= gas) check. It affects all participants: users think they are paying a correct fee, keepers incur unreimbursed gas, and the protocol suffers a financial shortfall. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that compared the semantics of the gas variable with the economic model of the system. It is hard to notice because the required ether amount is extremely small – often less than a billionth of a cent – so the transaction appears to succeed without any obvious error, and UI components may simply display a generic “fee paid” message. The bug belongs to the class of “incorrect unit handling” or “under‑charging due to unit mismatch” vulnerabilities, where a numeric value representing one unit (gas) is mistakenly interpreted as another unit (wei). An attacker could exploit this by submitting requests with the minimum possible ether, causing the protocol to lose the keeper’s gas on each execution. To remediate, the contract should convert the gas amount into a monetary value before performing the check, for example by requiring msg.value >= gas * tx.gasprice (or an equivalent safe conversion) so that the ether sent truly covers the expected execution cost. This change restores the intended economic balance, ensures keepers are reimbursed, and prevents systematic fund loss.
summary:
The protocol charges users an amount for gas since the protocol employs an asynchronous model where keepers pick the transactions up and execute them. The protocol checks whether the user has sent enough ETH in msg.value and if so adds their transaction to the uncompleted transaction queue.

The issue here comes in due to how those gas fees are handled. The following checks whether the user has sent enough funds to cover the gas to be expended by the keeper:
```solidity
require(msg.value >= gas, "AggregateVault: !gasRequirement");
```
The issue with the above check is that it assumes that gas is in terms of ETH instead of in gas units as it is.

Given that the gas stipend for a request is within the 100,000 - 1,000,000 range the transaction's gas cost on the user's side will be extremely low - less than a billionth of a cent since ETH is in 18 decimals. This will cause the protocol to lose funds in keeper gas fees on every deposit/withdrawal request that gets executed.

title: RH-2 | Wrong Withdrawal Fee Calculation Parameters Passed
content: The vulnerability is a fee‑calculation mismatch in the withdrawal path of the vault contract. The protocol’s fee logic expects a raw amount of the native token to be supplied to the previewWithdrawalFee function, but the calling code passes the number of vault shares instead. Because each share represents a growing portion of the underlying assets as the vault’s total value locked (TVL) increases, the share count is larger than the equivalent native token amount. Consequently the fee routine treats the share count as if it were a native token amount, dramatically under‑estimating the withdrawal fee. This can be exploited when an attacker or any user initiates a withdrawal after the vault has accrued significant yield; the contract will charge a fee based on the inflated share number, resulting in a fee that is far lower than the protocol’s configured percentage. The impact is a systematic loss of revenue for the protocol, as the fees collected on withdrawals are consistently below the intended level. The condition for the bug to manifest is any state where the share‑to‑asset conversion rate exceeds one, i.e., when the vault’s TVL has grown. All participants that rely on the fee model – the protocol itself, token holders, and potentially the governance that funds operations – are affected because the economic assumptions of the fee model are broken. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the fee‑preview interface with the underlying fee‑calculation contract and noticed a type mismatch. It is hard to notice because the fee appears correct when the vault is small; the discrepancy only becomes visible after the vault accumulates yield, making it a subtle accounting error rather than an outright runtime exception. The bug belongs to the class of unit‑mismatch or parameter‑type errors, where a value expressed in one unit (shares) is mistakenly used as another unit (native tokens), violating the accounting invariant that fees must be proportional to the actual asset amount withdrawn. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a normal withdrawal amount but the fee deducted is unexpectedly low, leading to a perception that “the protocol is giving me a free withdrawal” while in reality the protocol is losing money. The correct mitigation is to convert the share quantity to its underlying native‑token value before invoking the fee‑preview function, ensuring that the fee calculation receives the proper unit and that the protocol’s fee policy is enforced as intended.
summary:
The protocol charges users fees on deposit and withdrawal. Those fees are based on the percentages set by the protocol and on the size in the asset vault's native token of the amount being deposited/withdrawn.

The issue here is due to a share size being passed to the aggregateVault.previewWithdrawalFee function even though the function that calculates the said fee - VaultFees.getWithdrawalFee() assumes it is a native token amount.

As the vault's TVL grows and more yield is gained through its strategies, each share will be worth more. However, this will not be represented when calculating the withdrawal fee as the calculations will think that the amount of shares passed in is the native token amount.

This directly impacts the protocol as the fees it will receive on withdrawal will be substantially lower than expected leading to a loss of fees for the protocol.

title: GMXL-1 | Withdrawals Apply _minOutputAmount To One Side
content: The vulnerability resides in the withdrawal routine of the GMXL contract, specifically in the executeInitiateUnwrapping function where a single _minOutputAmount parameter is used to validate the amount of tokens returned to the user. In GMX, a withdrawal is split into two separate token streams: a short token portion that is transferred directly to the caller and a long token portion that is first swapped into the short token (or vice‑versa) via a predefined swap path. After the split, the contract checks the short token output against minShortTokenAmount and the long token output against minLongTokenAmount. Because the code only propagates the original _minOutputAmount to one side of the split, the other side is validated against a zero minimum. Consequently, when a user requests a withdrawal with a non‑zero _minOutputAmount, the portion of the short token that is transferred directly from GMX must satisfy the entire minimum, while the portion that arrives after the swap is effectively unchecked. This mismatch often causes the minimum‑output validation to fail, causing the transaction to revert even though the total amount received would meet the user’s expectation. The root cause is a logical error in how the minimum output constraint is distributed across the two token streams; the contract assumes a single output amount can be applied to a split withdrawal, which contradicts the underlying accounting model of GMX. An attacker could exploit this by submitting a withdrawal request with an artificially high _minOutputAmount, forcing the transaction to revert and potentially locking user funds in the contract, leading to a denial‑of‑service condition for legitimate users. From the user’s perspective the symptoms are a failed withdrawal transaction, often with an error message indicating that the minimum output was not met, or a situation where the short token balance appears to drop to zero after the call while no funds are received. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the flow of token amounts through the unwrapping logic and identified the inconsistency between the single‑parameter validation and the dual‑token split. It can be hard to notice because the contract still performs a swap and may return some tokens, giving the impression that the withdrawal succeeded, while the overall minimum‑output requirement is silently violated. The proper remediation is to refactor the logic so that the _minOutputAmount can be allocated between minLongTokenAmount and minShortTokenAmount, ensuring that each side of the split is validated against an appropriate portion of the user‑specified minimum, thereby preserving the intended accounting guarantees and preventing unintended reverts.
summary:
In the executeInitiateUnwrapping function the withdrawalParams are created with a
_minOutputAmount that can only apply to either the shortToken output or the longToken output.
However withdrawals in GMX remove a split of the shortToken and longToken. The resulting
shortToken and longToken are then subjected to the longTokenSwapPath and shortTokenSwapPath,
the outputs of which are validated against the minLongTokenAmount and minShortTokenAmount
respectively.
Therefore even though the outputs are swapped to the same token, take for example the short token,
the short token that is directly removed from GMX will be validated against the entire
_minOutputAmount and the short token that is received from the portion that was removed as the
longToken and swapped to the shortToken will be validated against a minShortTokenAmount of 0.
This results in the withdrawal likely failing the minimum output validation as the portion of short
token that is directly removed from GMX is unlikely to solely pass the _minOutputAmount validation.
Additionally, there can be no minimum output that applies to the portion of funds that are swapped
which is exactly the portion that ought to be validated.

title: GMXL-2 | Redemptions Incorrectly Appear Unpaused
content: The vulnerability is a logical error in the function that determines whether GM token redemptions are paused. The contract uses the current profit‑and‑loss‑to‑pool factor to decide if withdrawals are allowed, but it only compares the long‑side factor against the maximum PnL threshold and mistakenly also checks the ADL threshold, which does not influence withdrawal execution on GMX. For short positions the code compares the short factor against the same long threshold instead of the short‑specific maxPnlForWithdrawals value. Consequently, when the short PnL‑to‑Pool factor exceeds its true withdrawal limit, the function still reports that redemptions are unpaused. In addition, the check does not verify that the market itself is enabled or that the withdrawal feature is active, both of which can be disabled by GMX. Under these conditions a user sees a UI indicating that a redemption can be performed, initiates the transaction, and then the call reverts on GMX because the underlying withdrawal is actually paused. From the user’s perspective the balance appears unchanged, the expected refund is zero, and gas is spent for no result. The impact is high because users may adjust collateral or attempt to zap into GM tokens under the false assumption that withdrawals are possible, potentially leading to liquidation risk or loss of opportunity. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the pause‑logic and cross‑checked it with GMX’s withdrawal rules. It is hard to notice because the contract does not emit a specific error for the pause state; the failure only surfaces when the external GMX call reverts. The proper fix is to fetch the maxPnlForWithdrawals separately for long and short positions, compare each side’s PnL‑to‑Pool factor against its correct threshold, and additionally confirm that the market and withdrawal flags are enabled in the datastore before reporting that redemptions are unpaused.
summary:
The function isExternalRedemptionPaused is used to determine if GM withdrawals are currently
paused, utilizing the current PnL-to-Pool Factors as one validation for a paused state.
The validation only compares against the maxPnlForAdl and maxPnlForWithdrawals with isLong =
true, although the threshold factor may be different with isLong = false. This is incorrect as the
shortPnlToPoolFactor should be compared against the MAX_PNL_FACTOR_FOR_WITHDRAWALS for
isLong = false as in MarketUtils.validateMaxPnl
Furthermore, the condition verifies that the shortPnlToPoolFactor or the longPnlToPoolFactor
should not exceed the maxPnlForWithdrawals, as GMX will revert on withdrawal execution when the
threshold is passed. However, the check also looks at the maxPnlForAdl, which does not impact
withdrawal execution on GMX.
As a result, redemptions may appear possible when the PnL-to-Pool Factor exceeds both the
maxPnlForWithdrawals and maxPnlForAdl, although that is not the case and the withdrawal will fail.
Additionally, GMX can disable withdrawal creation, execution, or a market entirely which should also
be included to verify that redemptions are paused. Because the market appears unpaused, users can
modify their collateralization when liquidations aren’t possible, or zap into more of the irredeemable
GM tokens across Dolomite.

title: AIMUTI-1 | Severely Undercollateralized Positions Cannot Be Liquidated
content: The vulnerability is an edge‑case failure in the liquidation workflow of the protocol where a position that is exactly equal to the amount the liquidator wants to seize cannot be liquidated. The liquidation routine always builds a fixed sequence of four actions – two call actions followed by two sell actions – assuming that after the first pair there will be a remaining amount to process. When the total available user amount matches the requested liquidation amount, the second pair receives a zero input value. Because the underlying AsyncIsolationModeUnwrapperTraderImpl still creates these zero‑amount actions, the call to the market contract is executed with a zero amount, causing the transaction to revert. As a result the first set of actions succeeds in clearing the withdrawal position, but the second set fails, leaving the account in a state where it still holds a positive balance in the GM market and cannot be vaporized. This situation can be triggered by an attacker who deliberately creates a severely under‑collateralized position and then initiates liquidation with an amount that exactly equals the available collateral. The impact is that the under‑collateralized position remains open, the liquidator’s transaction fails, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions are broken because funds that should have been seized remain locked. Users see a failed liquidation transaction, their balances appear unchanged, and the protocol cannot enforce its liquidation guarantees, potentially exposing the system to insolvency risk. The bug was discovered during a manual audit when the liquidation proxy was exercised with boundary values; the failure is subtle because most liquidation amounts do not hit the exact‑match condition, so the problem only appears in this narrow scenario. The issue belongs to the class of off‑by‑zero or zero‑amount handling bugs where code assumes a positive amount without checking for equality, leading to invalid external calls. To remediate, the unwrapping logic should skip the creation of the second call and sell actions when the difference between the input amount and the available amount is zero, or the liquidation proxy should be adjusted to generate a two‑step action array instead of a fixed four‑step array. As a temporary workaround, dummy no‑op actions can be inserted to preserve the expected array length without causing side‑effects. Properly fixing the logic restores the ability to liquidate positions at any amount, ensures that under‑collateralized accounts can be cleared, and aligns the protocol’s accounting with its business rules.
summary:
During liquidation, an issue appears when the total available user amount to liquidate is equal to the
input liquidation amount. The input liquidation amount is passed to the liquidate function from the
LiquidatorProxyV4WithGenericTrader contract when liquidating a position.
Liquidation always creates a second set of call and sell actions. When the amounts are equal, the
second call and sell action will be executed with 0 as input. This results in execution failing because
the first set of actions clears the withdrawal position.
It is also worth mentioning that the account is not vaporizable in this state since it still holds a
positive balance in the GM market.

title: AIMUTI-2 | Withdrawal Keys Misused by Differing Subaccount in Liquidations
content: The vulnerability concerns the handling of withdrawal keys during a liquidation on a vault that contains multiple sub‑accounts. The contract stores a withdrawal request together with a key that identifies the sub‑account that originated the request. When a liquidation is performed, the internal function _callFunction is invoked without checking that the stored account number of the withdrawal matches the account number supplied in the liquidation call. As a result, a malicious actor can trigger a liquidation on account A while supplying the withdrawal key that belongs to a different account B. The contract then clears the withdrawal information of account B, even though the liquidation was intended for account A. If account B later attempts to retry its pending withdrawal, the stored withdrawal data is empty and the retry fails. Because the failure occurs inside the liquidation path, the vault’s state becomes inconsistent: the cleared withdrawal prevents any further unwrapping or retry operations for any sub‑account, effectively freezing the entire vault. The issue manifests only when two sub‑accounts have pending, retryable withdrawals that share the same output token and when at least one of the accounts becomes liquidatable. Under these conditions, an attacker can repeatedly misuse withdrawal keys to block the vault, causing user‑facing symptoms such as “withdrawal failed”, “balance remains unchanged”, or “no funds can be withdrawn”. The impact is severe because all operations from any sub‑account are blocked, funds become inaccessible, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions about withdrawals and liquidations are violated. The bug was discovered during a manual security audit by the Guardian team, who noted that the logic for normal unwrapping correctly validates the account number, but the liquidation branch omitted this check, making the problem hard to notice in routine testing. To remediate the issue, the _callFunction implementation should verify that the stored accountNumber matches the _accountInfo.number whenever the call originates from a liquidation operation, ensuring that a withdrawal key cannot be applied to a different sub‑account. This additional validation restores the integrity of the withdrawal bookkeeping and prevents the vault from being hijacked and frozen.
summary:
When a liquidation is executed on an account from a vault with multiple accounts, a malicious actor
can pass the withdrawal key belonging to an account that is different from the one being liquidated
and block the vault.
Consider the scenario where a vault has accounts A and B:
By liquidating account A using account B’s key, account B’s withdrawal information is cleared. If
account B has a withdrawal that needs to be retried, the execution will fail as the stored withdrawal
information is empty.
Even if account B becomes liquidatable and uses account A’s key to perform the liquidation, that will
fail because DolomiteMargin would interpret that as a borrow increase in an unborrowable market.
This happens when account A’s withdrawal is for a larger amount that account B’s.
The vault remains frozen and all operations from any sub-accounts are blocked. Such a hijacked
liquidation can occur when both withdrawals have the same output token and are both retryable. The
withdrawal can be retryable from either an on-going liquidation or from a failed withdrawal of a
healthy position.

title: ORDM-5 | Impossible to Liquidate When Fee is Greater Than PnL
content: The vulnerability is an arithmetic underflow that occurs during the liquidation of a position when the fee amount charged in collateral exceeds the net profit before fees. In the _liquidatePosition routine the contract emits a PnlRealized event that records the realized profit as netPnl - feesInCollateral. Solidity 0.8+ performs checked arithmetic, so if feesInCollateral is larger than netPnl the subtraction underflows and the transaction reverts. The root cause is that the liquidation logic assumes netPnl will always be greater than or equal to feesInCollateral, but the helper function _getNetProfitOrLossIncludingFees can set isNetProfit to false and produce a fee value that is larger than the positive netPnl when the position is only marginally profitable before fees. When this condition is met, the event emission triggers a revert, preventing the liquidation from completing. The impact is that a position that appears liquidatable remains stuck on-chain; the protocol cannot collect the collateral, resulting in lost yield for the protocol and its liquidity providers. The bug manifests only for positions where the fee component outweighs the raw profit, so it may not be obvious during normal operation and can be missed because the failure happens after state updates, at the point of event logging. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a liquidation request succeeded but the transaction fails silently, leaving balances unchanged and yielding no reward. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the liquidation flow and identified the unsafe subtraction in the event emission. It is hard to notice because the contract does not revert earlier in the logic, and the underflow only surfaces when the specific profit‑fee relationship occurs. To remediate, the contract should avoid calculating netPnl - feesInCollateral in the event, either by emitting a separate liquidation event that reports the net profit without subtraction, or by adding a guard that checks the relationship before performing the subtraction, or by using unchecked arithmetic with explicit handling of negative results. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of unchecked arithmetic or unsafe event logging that can cause transaction reverts and block critical protocol operations.
summary:
In the _liquidatePosition function the PnlRealized event is emitted which includes the pnlInCollateral. This is calculated by taking the netPnl and subtracting feesInCollateral. However, the feesInCollateral may be greater than netPnl, causing an underflow revert.
```solidity
emit PnlRealized(_positionId, false, netPnl - feesInCollateral, feesInCollateral, executionPrice);
```
In the _getNetProfitOrLossIncludingFees function which is called in _liquidatePosition, if the position is in profit excluding fees it will enter the inner if-statement the isNetProfit will be set to false and feesInCollateral will be greater than netPnl. At the end of the _liquidatePosition function when the PnlRealized event is emitted the transaction will revert, making any liquidation impossible until the position is completely underwater, leading to a loss of yield for the protocol and LP's.

title: ORDM-2 | Position Created Without Reserves
content: The vulnerability consists of creating a trading position without first checking that the Vault holds enough liquidity to cover the potential profit or loss of that position. The root cause is a missing validation step that should compare the amount of open interest or the size of the new position against the current reserve balance of the Vault. Because the contract does not enforce this check, a trader can open a position even when the Vault balance is zero or insufficient to satisfy the market’s profit‑and‑loss calculations. An attacker or any user can exploit the flaw by submitting an open‑position transaction; the contract will accept it, record the position, and later attempt to settle it against a reserve that does not exist. When the position should generate a profit for the trader, the contract cannot transfer the funds, leaving the trader with a stuck position that yields no payout. Conversely, when the Vault later receives enough funds for a withdrawal, the settlement logic will drain those newly added reserves to satisfy the outstanding position, effectively stealing the liquidity providers’ deposited capital. The impact is twofold: traders may be unable to realize legitimate profits and become locked in a dead position, while liquidity providers risk losing their entire contribution because the Vault’s funds are redirected to cover under‑collateralized positions. The condition occurs whenever the open‑interest exceeds the Vault’s current balance, which can happen at any time after the contract is deployed, especially in low‑liquidity markets. All participants—traders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself—are affected because the accounting assumptions that profits are always payable from the Vault are violated. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that reviewed the position‑opening flow and noticed the absence of a reserve‑sufficiency guard. It can be hard to notice because the contract may appear to function correctly in normal scenarios where the Vault is well‑funded; the bug only surfaces under edge‑case conditions of low or zero reserves. To remediate, the contract should enforce a rule that the total open interest or the size of any new position does not exceed a safe percentage of the Vault’s available funds, thereby creating a liquidity buffer and ensuring that every position can be settled without draining LP capital. This class of bug is commonly referred to as an under‑collateralized position opening or missing reserve validation, and it breaks the fundamental business logic that user deposits are protected and that profits are always payable.
summary: A user’s position is created without taking the funds in the Vault into account. As a result, a trader may open a position when the Vault has zero funds, or not enough funds to support the market’s PnL. Users will be unable to realize their profits and be stuck with their position. Furthermore, as soon as there are enough reserves in the Vault for withdrawal, the Vault’s funds will be drained and LP’s will lose their deposited funds.

title: ORDM-3 | Trapped collateralDelta With Increase Order
content: The vulnerability concerns the handling of the opening fee for position‑modifying orders in the protocol. When a user submits an increase order, the contract expects the caller to provide a deltaCollateral amount that covers the opening fee. If the supplied deltaCollateral is smaller than the required opening fee, the order can be created but the contract does not allow the user to cancel it. Consequently, if market conditions prevent the order from being executed, the user’s collateral becomes permanently locked in the contract. The same code path also treats decrease and close orders differently: cancelling those orders does not charge any opening fee, which contradicts the behaviour of increase orders and creates an accounting mismatch. The root cause is an inconsistent fee‑charging logic that only validates the fee for increase orders at order creation time, while the cancellation routine for other order types bypasses the fee entirely. An attacker could exploit this by deliberately submitting an increase order with an insufficient deltaCollateral value, causing the order to remain pending forever and trapping the user’s funds. The impact is that users may lose access to part of their collateral, reducing confidence in the platform and potentially affecting overall liquidity. The issue manifests whenever the deltaCollateral parameter is less than the opening fee and the order cannot be fulfilled; it also appears when a decrease or close order is cancelled, because no fee is deducted, leading to a discrepancy in the protocol’s accounting model. The problem was discovered during a manual security audit performed by the Guardian team, who noticed that the cancellation path does not revert the fee logic and that the UI does not warn users about the minimum collateral requirement. Because the contract silently rejects cancellation without an explicit error, the condition can be hard to spot for end‑users who simply see their funds disappear from their wallet. To remediate the issue, the fee handling should be refactored so that the opening fee is either required up front for all order types (increase, decrease, close) or, alternatively, charged only at execution time while ensuring that a minimal execution fee is always retained. This unified approach would prevent orders from becoming irrevocably stuck and would align the accounting of fees across all order flows, restoring the expected behaviour that a user can always cancel a pending order and retrieve any unspent collateral.
summary: If a user creates an increase order and provides a deltaCollateral that is less than their openingFee, they cannot cancel this order and their funds will be stuck if the order cannot be executed. Additionally, there is no opening fee charged when a decrease or close order is cancelled. This is in contradiction to the behavior of increase orders.

title: VAULT-1 | Withdrawal Cooldown Can Be Bypassed
content: The vulnerability is a withdrawal cooldown bypass in the ParifiVault contract. The contract’s cooldown() function only verifies that the caller’s token balance is non‑zero before recording a timestamp, but it does not record the amount of shares that the caller holds nor enforce a per‑address withdrawal limit after the cooldown period. Because of this, an attacker can create many auxiliary addresses, each holding a trivial amount of share tokens (for example 1 wei), call cooldown() from each address, and then rotate the addresses to satisfy the expiry‑window check. When the attacker later wants to withdraw liquidity, they can transfer all of their real share balance to one of the pre‑warmed addresses and call withdraw() or redeem() without waiting for the intended cooldown delay. The contract therefore allows a depositor to sidestep the intended time lock, extract reserves immediately, and leave other participants without liquidity. The issue can be amplified with a flash‑loan: an attacker flash‑loans a large amount of tokens, deposits them, triggers a fee distribution that raises the value‑per‑share, and then withdraws the inflated shares through a pre‑warmed address, pocketing the profit. The impact is that traders who rely on the cooldown to protect their positions may find the vault drained of reserves, resulting in lost profits or inability to withdraw. The bug manifests whenever a user with a non‑zero balance calls cooldown; the contract does not check the actual share amount, so even a single wei is sufficient to satisfy the condition. It affects any participant who deposits LP tokens, the vault’s overall liquidity, and ultimately the protocol’s trustworthiness. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the logic of the cooldown and withdrawal functions and identified that the balance check is insufficient. Because the contract does not emit explicit warnings when the cooldown is bypassed, the behavior can be hard to notice in normal operation; the vault appears to accept withdrawals normally, but the intended delay is silently ignored. To remediate, the contract should record the exact amount of shares that entered cooldown and enforce that only that amount (or less) can be withdrawn after the cooldown expires, or reset the cooldown timer whenever shares are transferred or deposited, thereby preventing the use of multiple addresses to circumvent the lock. In generic terms, this is a time‑lock bypass caused by an incomplete state check, leading to premature fund extraction and a violation of the protocol’s accounting assumptions about delayed withdrawals.
summary:
In ParifiVault, the cooldown function only checks that the balance of a sender is not 0. It does not check how many tokens the user has or the amount that could be withdrawn after the cooldown period. A user may:
Prepare X addresses for which it sends 1 WEI of share tokens
Call the ParifiVault.cooldown function from each address
Rotate this system in order to also bypass the expiry window constraint
Whenever a user wishes to withdraw any amount of LPs, they send all token shares to one of the pre-warmed addresses and withdraw reserves
Because the cooldown can be avoided, a depositor can view a profitable position but withdraw their liquidity without waiting. This is extremely detrimental to traders as they will be unable to withdraw their profits due to the lack of reserves.
Due to the bypassed cooldown, profit from the vault may also be extracted with the following steps:
Flash-loan a large amount of tokens
Deposit the tokens into the vault
Create a new position that triggers [fee distribution](https://github.com/GuardianAudits/PariFi-10-2023/blob/main/src/OrderManager.sol#L684-L687) and increases the value per share
Withdraw tokens using a pre-warmed address and profit

title: ORDM-4 | Execution Fee May Be Circumvented
content: The vulnerability is a missing enforcement of the execution fee in the order settlement logic. The contract only deducts an execution fee when the order explicitly contains a non‑zero fee value, as shown by the conditional check if (_order.executionFee != 0) { _chargeExecutionFee(...); }. Because there is no rule that forces the fee field to be greater than zero, a malicious or careless user can submit an order with executionFee set to zero and avoid paying the fee that is intended to compensate keepers for executing the order. This omission originates from a business‑logic flaw: the protocol assumes that the fee will always be provided, but the code does not validate that assumption. An attacker can exploit the flaw by creating orders that appear normal but carry a zero execution fee; keepers will still be called to settle the order, yet they receive no compensation. Consequently, the protocol must still cover the gas cost of the transaction and any oracle price‑update fee that is charged per execution, leading to a gradual erosion of the treasury. The impact is that keepers become under‑remunerated, may stop servicing the system, and the protocol’s funds can be drained over time. The issue manifests whenever an order is placed without a non‑zero execution fee, which is allowed by the current validation logic. All participants are affected: users can submit fee‑free orders, keepers lose expected payment, and the protocol’s economic model is broken. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that examined the fee‑charging path and noticed the lack of a minimum‑fee requirement. It can be hard to notice because the code appears to charge a fee, but the conditional guard silently skips the charge when the fee is zero, which may be interpreted as a legitimate optional field. To remediate, the contract should store the required execution fee in a dedicated state variable and enforce that every incoming order supplies a fee that matches this value (or at least a non‑zero minimum). The fee should be charged unconditionally, ensuring that keepers are always compensated and that the protocol’s accounting assumptions remain intact. This class of bug is commonly referred to as an “optional fee enforcement” or “missing mandatory payment validation” flaw, where a financial incentive is unintentionally optional, leading to fund loss and broken incentive alignment.

title: STEA-1 | stETH Price Hardcoded To 1 ETH
content: The vulnerability consists of a hard‑coded assumption that one stETH token is always worth exactly 1e18 wei, i.e., a 1:1 price with ETH. This assumption is embedded in the stETH adapter’s value() function, which returns a constant instead of querying a live market price. Because stETH is a rebasing token whose balance grows with staking rewards, its market price can drift above or below the 1:1 peg. When the actual stETH price is lower than the hard‑coded value, deposits of stETH are converted into more protocol shares than the economic value warrants, effectively diluting existing shareholders. Conversely, withdrawals return fewer ETH‑equivalent assets to the user, causing a loss of funds. When the price is higher than the assumed 1:1 rate, the opposite occurs: depositors receive fewer shares than they should, and withdrawers obtain a larger amount of ETH than justified, again eroding the value of the remaining shares. An attacker can exploit this by timing deposits or withdrawals to coincide with periods of price deviation, extracting profit at the expense of honest participants. The issue manifests only when the stETH/ETH price diverges from the hard‑coded constant, a condition that can persist for hours or days depending on network conditions and reward accrual. All users who interact with the protocol—depositors, withdrawers, and liquidity providers—are affected because the accounting logic no longer reflects the true value of their holdings. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that compared the adapter’s return value against a reliable on‑chain price feed and observed mismatches. It is subtle because the price of stETH typically stays close to parity with ETH, so the constant appears correct under normal conditions, making the bug easy to overlook in casual testing. The proper remediation is to replace the constant with a dynamic price source, such as the stETH/ETH Chainlink price feed, ensuring that the value() function always reflects the current market rate. This change restores the intended accounting guarantees, prevents share dilution or inflation, and aligns user expectations (receiving the correct amount of shares or ETH) with actual protocol behavior. The bug belongs to the class of hard‑coded price oracle errors, where static values replace live market data, leading to incorrect financial calculations and potential fund loss.
summary: stETH is a rebasing token. It distributes staking rewards through increasing the balances of users with their accrued APR daily. Since the total supply of stETH represents the total staked ETH plus the staking rewards it has a price that is usually very close to that of ETH. The issue arises due to the price of stETH being hardcoded to 1e18. Even though the token is loosely pegged to ETH, 1 stETH ≠ 1 ETH. 1. When price of stETH < the price of ETH: A. Deposits in stETH will mint more to the user than supposed to, devaluing the shares. B. Withdrawing in stETH will make users receive less than intended, thus losing them funds. 2. When price of stETH > ETH: A. Depositing stETH will output less shares than should, thus damaging the depositor. B. Withdrawing stETH will be more profitable than should be, thus devaluing the shares.

title: VLT-1 | restETH Becomes Cheaper Upon Withdrawals
content: The vulnerability concerns the restETH token price distortion that occurs when a user initiates a withdrawal through the withdrawUsingEigenShares function. The contract reduces the total assets reported by the Eigenlayer StrategyManager immediately when the withdrawal is queued, but the corresponding restETH shares are only burned later in the completeWithdraw function after the withdrawal finishes. This timing mismatch creates a temporary inconsistency: the denominator of the restETH price (total supply of shares) remains unchanged while the numerator (total assets) drops, causing the calculated price of each restETH share to fall unexpectedly. An attacker can exploit this by repeatedly queuing withdrawals to force the price down, then buying restETH at the artificially low price and later redeeming it after the price normalises, effectively extracting value from the protocol. The impact is that honest users who simply request a withdrawal see their token value decrease before the withdrawal completes, leading to lower redemption amounts, potential loss of confidence, and broken accounting assumptions that total assets should match share supply. The issue manifests only during the window between the call to withdrawUsingEigenShares and the execution of completeWithdraw, and it affects any holder of restETH as well as the protocol’s overall liquidity and pricing oracle. It was discovered during a manual audit that compared the share‑burning logic in the restETH contract with the asset‑reduction logic in the StrategyManager, revealing that the two operations are not synchronised. Because the price drop is subtle and only visible in on‑chain data, it may go unnoticed by users who do not monitor token price after queuing a withdrawal. The proper fix is to align the accounting by burning the appropriate amount of restETH shares at the same moment the total assets are reduced, or alternatively to defer the asset reduction until the shares are burned, thereby preserving the invariant that share price remains stable throughout the withdrawal lifecycle. This class of bug is a temporal accounting inconsistency that violates the expected one‑to‑one relationship between token supply and underlying assets, leading to a “price‑drop on withdrawal” symptom where users expect their restETH value to stay constant but instead see it shrink temporarily.
summary: In the completeWithdraw function the restETH shares are only burned upon completion of the withdrawal. However the shares attributed to the Vault contract in the Eigenlayer StrategyManager contract are reduced upon the queuing of a withdrawal. The strategy contract will often refer to the StrategyManager.stakerStrategyShares to produce the shares result (see [StrategyBase)](https://github.com/Layr-Labs/eigenlayer-contracts/blob/m2-mainnet/src/contracts/strategies/StrategyBase.sol). Therefore the totalAssets value is reduced immediately upon calling the withdrawUsingEiganShares function, while the corresponding decrease in the restETH supply only occurs when the withdrawal is completed in the completeWithdraw function. As a result, the price of restETH will errantly drop when users initiate a withdrawal with the withdrawUsingEiganShares function.

title: VLT-2 | Vault Can Be Drained Through Overlooked Mint Function
content: The vulnerability resides in the RestEthVault contract that implements the ERC4626 standard for tokenized vaults. The contract provides an adapter for each liquid staking token (LST) it supports and sets the flagship LST as the underlying asset. However, the developer forgot to override the ERC4626.mint(uint256,address) function. As a result, when shares are minted through this entry point the vault assumes a 1:1 parity between the amount of LST deposited and ETH value, ignoring the actual market price of the LST. If the flagship LST temporarily trades at a premium relative to ETH, an attacker can deposit a small amount of ETH, receive shares that are incorrectly valued at the higher LST price, and immediately sell those shares using the withdrawUsingAssets function. Because the mint function does not apply the correct price feed, the attacker extracts more ETH than was supplied, after accounting for the protocol’s withdrawal fees. The attack requires existing liquidity in the vault, so the attacker typically back‑runs a legitimate deposit transaction to ensure sufficient assets are available. The impact is a potential complete drainage of the vault’s funds, harming all users who have deposited assets, as the vault’s accounting assumptions are broken and the protocol can lose the value of the underlying LST. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that compared the contract’s implementation against the ERC4626 specification and identified the missing override. It is subtle because the mint function is rarely called directly by end‑users; most interactions go through higher‑level deposit functions, so the price mismatch is not obvious in normal operation. From a user’s perspective the symptom may appear as a sudden loss of balance after a deposit, or an unexpected profit when withdrawing, both of which contradict the expectation that deposits and withdrawals are value‑preserving. The bug belongs to the class of “incorrect asset valuation in tokenized vaults” where a standard function is left unimplemented, leading to a mismatch between on‑chain accounting and external price feeds. To remediate the issue the contract should explicitly override ERC4626.mint and compute the required LST amount using the adapter’s price oracle, ensuring that share issuance reflects the true market value of the underlying asset.
summary: The RestEthVault contract Vault has an adapter for each LST it supports, including for the flagship asset, that will be set as the ERC4626 vault asset. The contract mistakenly does not overwrite the ERC4626.mint(uint256,address) function, meaning that when receiving shares through that function, the required asset LST asset amount will be mapped as a parity of 1:1 with ETH. If the flagship LST has a moment when it is valued higher than ETH, by depositing through this function an attacker could then instantly resell the shares, using the withdrawUsingAssets function for a profit, after fees. The attack would require that funds be existing in the vault, thus back-running any deposit call and would require the difference in price in the flagship LST and ETH so that it is profitable after withdraw fees.

title: update_market
content: The vulnerability originates from a mismatch between the unit used to represent an epoch in the reward‑distribution routine and the unit expected by the GaugeController’s weight query function. In the update_market function the contract computes an epoch value by rounding the current block number down to the nearest BLOCK_EPOCH interval (a weekly block count) and then passes this value directly to gaugeController.gauge_relative_weight_write. The GaugeController, however, interprets its second argument as a Unix timestamp (seconds) and internally aligns it to a weekly boundary using the constant WEEK (7 days). Because a block number is far smaller than a Unix timestamp, the internal alignment yields a timestamp that falls in the year 1970, where the stored weight points are empty, resulting in a weight of zero. Consequently the cantoReward calculation, which multiplies the block delta, the per‑block reward, and the returned weight, evaluates to zero for the affected market. This means that users who have supplied assets to the market receive no Canto rewards despite the contract believing it has performed the accounting correctly. The issue is triggered whenever update_market is called after the market’s lastRewardBlock has advanced, which is the normal operation of the protocol, so the bug can affect any whitelisted market over its lifetime. It is difficult to notice because the function updates internal accounting variables without emitting explicit warnings, and the UI may simply show that rewards have not increased, which could be mistaken for normal variance. The root cause is the use of block numbers instead of timestamps to represent epochs, a classic units‑mismatch bug that breaks the business logic that rewards must be proportional to the gauge’s voting weight for the current week. To remediate, the contract should store and pass a proper time‑based epoch (e.g., block.timestamp rounded to the nearest week) when querying the gauge controller, ensuring that the weight lookup aligns with the controller’s expectations and that the reward formula yields the intended non‑zero amount. This correction restores the accounting invariant that total supplied assets earn rewards proportional to their gauge weight, preventing total loss of rewards for users.

title: EWT-1 | All Attempted Withdrawals Will Fail in EigenLayer M1
content: The vulnerability consists of a complete failure of the withdrawal pathway for users who have restaked assets in the EigenLayer system. When a staker invokes the public function withdrawUsingEigenShares, the contract internally calls a helper routine named _queueWithdraw. This routine attempts to forward the withdrawal request to the DelegationManager by invoking delegationManager.queueWithdrawals with the formatted request data. The root cause is that the currently deployed DelegationManager contract, which belongs to the first‑generation (M1) EigenLayer deployment, does not implement the queueWithdrawals function at all. Because the Rest Vault contract was written against an interface that assumes the presence of this function – an interface that is only satisfied by the later M2 version – the external call resolves to a non‑existent entry point and the EVM throws a revert. Consequently, every attempt to withdraw eigen shares reverts, leaving the user’s balance unchanged and the requested funds locked inside the Rest Vault. The impact is that any participant who tries to retrieve their restaked assets receives a transaction failure, sees no change in their UI balance, and may be left with the impression that the protocol is withholding funds. This condition occurs every time the withdrawUsingEigenShares path is exercised, regardless of the amount or the user’s role, because the missing function is a hard requirement of the withdrawal flow. The issue was discovered during a security audit when the auditors executed withdrawal scenarios and observed consistent reverts. It can be hard to notice in static analysis because the contract compiles against an abstract interface that declares queueWithdrawals, so the mismatch only surfaces at runtime. The bug belongs to the class of interface‑mismatch or upgrade‑incompatibility defects, where a contract assumes the existence of a function that is not present in the deployed implementation. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are a failed transaction, a UI that may still show a pending withdrawal request, and an expectation of receiving funds that is not met – effectively “funds disappear” from the user’s perspective. To remediate the problem the Rest Vault should be made upgradeable so that, when EigenLayer migrates to the M2 contracts, the reference to the DelegationManager can be updated to point to a version that implements queueWithdrawals. Additionally, a fallback withdrawal path could be added that uses the current M1 StrategyManager’s queueWithdrawal and completeQueuedWithdrawal functions, thereby providing a functional withdrawal mechanism until the full upgrade is performed.
summary: When a staker wants to withdraw their eigen shares through function withdrawUsingEigenShares, the function _queueWithdraw is called which queues a withdrawal through the delegation manager: delegationManager.queueWithdrawals(arrayify(withdraw)); However, the currently deployed M1 DelegationManager does not support function queueWithdrawals and all calls to it will revert. Consequently, users are entirely unable to withdraw their restaked assets.

title: GLOBAL-1 | Issuance Withdrawals Can Be Trapped
content: The vulnerability is a withdrawal‑trapping bug that occurs when a user initiates a withdrawal through the Issance contract, which queues the request in the Vault contract. The Issance contract is set as the owner of the queued withdrawal, and the Vault exposes a public completeWithdraw function that anyone can call. Because the Vault does not verify that the caller is the Issuance contract, an attacker can invoke completeWithdraw on behalf of any queued withdrawal, supplying the victim’s parameters. When the function executes, the Vault transfers the withdrawn assets to the Issance contract address, but the Issance contract’s internal pendingWithdraws mapping is never updated, since the call bypasses the Issance’s withdrawal‑completion logic. As a result, the funds become locked inside the Issance contract with no record that the withdrawal was fulfilled, and the original requester sees their pending withdrawal remain indefinitely. The root cause is the lack of proper access control and accounting synchronization between the two contracts: the Vault trusts the caller to be the legitimate owner, while the Issance assumes that only it will trigger completions. Exploitation is straightforward: an attacker monitors the queue, selects a victim’s withdrawal request, and calls completeWithdraw directly, causing the victim’s assets to be sent to a contract that does not credit them. The impact is that users lose access to their funds, the protocol’s liquidity is reduced, and the accounting invariants that guarantee that every queued withdrawal will eventually be settled are broken. This condition appears whenever withdrawals are queued via Issance and the Vault’s completeWithdraw function remains publicly callable. Affected parties include any user who has a pending withdrawal, the protocol’s overall fund pool, and any downstream services that rely on accurate balance information. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the interaction between Issance and Vault and identified that the pendingWithdraws state in Issance could be circumvented. It is hard to notice because the transfer event shows assets moving to the Issance contract, which looks legitimate, while the internal pendingWithdraws entry still shows a pending request, giving the impression that the withdrawal simply has not been processed yet. From a user’s perspective the symptom is a withdrawal that never resolves: the UI continues to display a pending status, the expected balance does not increase, and the user receives no tokens despite the contract having transferred them elsewhere. The expected behavior is that after a withdrawal is queued, the user eventually receives the funds and the pending entry is cleared; the reality is that the funds disappear into a contract that does not credit the user. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “accounting mismatch” or “withdrawal trapping” vulnerabilities where external calls can bypass internal state updates. The recommended remediation is to refactor the integration so that only the Issance contract can invoke the Vault’s completeWithdraw function, or to have the Vault call back into Issance to update the pendingWithdraws mapping whenever a withdrawal is completed, thereby preserving accounting consistency and preventing funds from being trapped.
summary: Anyone may complete a withdrawal that was queued through the Issuance contract by calling the completeWithdraw function on the Vault contract directly. Because the owner is the Issuance address for withdrawals done through the Issuance contract, a user can complete a withdrawal for another user and their funds will be sent to the Issuance contract and stuck. Furthermore, the pendingWithdraws for the true owner will not be updated in the Issuance contract.

title: GLOBAL-2 | stETH Rebase Frontrunning
content: The vulnerability stems from the way the protocol handles the daily stETH rebase, which updates the token balance to reflect staking yield. In the Vault contract, the total value of the vault is calculated after the rebase, but the withdrawal fee is not sufficient to offset the increase in value. An attacker can deposit a different liquid staking token, such as rETH, just before the rebase, then withdraw after the rebase when the vault’s reported value has risen due to the stETH yield. Because the fee does not capture the extra value, the attacker extracts more rETH than they originally supplied, effectively stealing a portion of the rebase profit. In the Issuance contract, the completeWithdrawEarly function allows a buyer to purchase a user’s pending stETH withdrawal before the rebase is recorded. By front‑running the rebase, the attacker can buy the pending withdrawal at the pre‑rebase price, and once the rebase occurs the assets are worth more, giving the attacker a discounted acquisition of higher‑value stETH. This exploitation is possible only around the predictable daily rebase event, making the attack timing‑dependent. Users who have deposited tokens or requested withdrawals may notice that their balances are lower than expected, that a pending withdrawal disappears, or that they receive less stETH than anticipated after a withdrawal. The issue was discovered during a security audit by Guardian, who identified the logical flaw in the accounting model and the lack of protective fees. It can be hard to detect because the rebase is a normal operation and the profit extracted may appear as a small, seemingly legitimate yield. The bug belongs to the class of rebase‑timing front‑running or value‑extraction vulnerabilities, where state‑dependent accounting allows an attacker to profit from predictable state changes. To mitigate the problem, the protocol should either increase the withdrawal fee to make extracting the rebase profit unprofitable, introduce a protocol fee on buyers of pending withdrawals, or redesign the accounting so that the vault value and withdrawal calculations are based on a snapshot taken before the rebase, preventing the attacker from benefiting from the post‑rebase value increase.
summary: stETH rebases once a day to reflect the yield earned from staking ETH. This creates issues in the Vault and Issuance contracts. Firstly, in the Vault contract a malicious actor may deposit a different LST, say rETH, before the stETH rebase and withdraw more rETH directly after the stETH rebase -- as the value of the vault has increased by the stETH yield. Secondly, a malicious actor may frontrun the stEth rebase and use the completeWithdrawEarly function in the Issuance contract to buy out a user's stETH pending withdrawal before the rebase is recorded, therefore obtaining the assets at a discount.

title: ISU-1 | Tokens Stolen When Completing Withdraw
content: The vulnerability resides in the withdrawal finalisation function of the Issuance contract, which is intended to release tokens to the original requester after a withdrawal request has matured. The function incorrectly transfers the token amount to the caller of completeWithdraw instead of verifying that the caller is the owner of the pending withdrawal. This missing ownership check is the root cause: the contract trusts the external caller without confirming that msg.sender matches the withdrawal record’s beneficiary. An attacker can therefore invoke completeWithdraw with any identifier of a queued withdrawal, regardless of who created it, and receive the full token amount. Exploitation is straightforward – the attacker watches for a withdrawal that has entered the mature state, calls completeWithdraw with the corresponding request ID, and the contract sends the tokens to the attacker’s address. The impact is a direct loss of user funds: legitimate users see their expected refunds disappear, their balances remain unchanged, and the attacker’s balance increases by the stolen amount. The bug manifests only after a withdrawal has been queued and matured, i.e., when the contract permits completion. All participants who rely on the contract to safely return their tokens – individual users, liquidity providers, and the broader protocol – are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the flow of withdrawal finalisation and noticed the absence of an explicit owner validation. Because the function performs a token transfer without any visible guard, the problem can be subtle in normal operation; only when a malicious party actively calls the function does the loss become apparent, making it easy to miss in routine testing. The vulnerability belongs to the class of authorization or access‑control bugs, specifically an “missing ownership check” that allows arbitrary callers to claim assets. From a user’s perspective the symptom is a missing refund: a user initiates a withdrawal, expects to receive tokens after the maturity period, but instead receives zero tokens while the attacker’s wallet shows an unexpected increase. To remediate, the contract should enforce that the caller of completeWithdraw is the recorded owner of the withdrawal request, typically by comparing msg.sender with the stored beneficiary address and reverting if they differ. This change restores the intended business logic that only the rightful owner can claim the funds, preventing unauthorized token extraction.
summary: The Issuance contract was created to facilitate early buyouts of pending withdraws. The function completeWithdraw must be called after a withdraw has matured from a queued state. This function incorrectly sends the funds to the caller of the function, rather than the owner of the pending withdraw. This makes it possible for anyone to call this function, with any non-pending withdraw and steal the funds.

title: ISU-2 | All Early Withdrawals Fail
content: The vulnerability resides in the early withdrawal mechanism of the Issuance contract. The function completeWithdrawalEarly is intended to let a participant purchase the right to execute another participant’s pending withdrawal by providing an equivalent amount of LST/ETH. The business rule requires that the pending withdrawal be associated with a valid root identifier; only withdrawals that have a root set should be processed. However, the contract implements the check in reverse: it proceeds only when the root is not set, and reverts when a root exists. This inverted condition means that any legitimate early withdrawal request that carries a proper root is rejected, while malformed or non‑existent withdrawals may pass. As a result, users attempting to buy out a withdrawal experience a transaction revert and receive no funds, effectively creating a denial‑of‑service (DoS) against the early‑withdrawal feature. The impact is that the protocol’s intended liquidity‑sharing mechanism is broken, users cannot retrieve their assets early, and the protocol may lose trust because the advertised buy‑out functionality does not work. The bug manifests whenever a user calls completeWithdrawalEarly with a pending withdrawal that has a non‑zero root, which is the normal case. All participants who rely on early withdrawals—individual investors, liquidity providers, and any downstream contracts that assume the function works—are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual audit where the logic of the root‑validation condition was examined and found to be opposite to the specification. Because the function simply reverts with no explicit error message, the failure can be mistaken for a generic out‑of‑gas or network issue, making it hard to spot without reviewing the source. The class of bug is an inverted conditional or improper input validation, a common logical error where a boolean expression is negated unintentionally. To fix the problem, the contract should verify that the root of the pending withdrawal is set (i.e., not the zero address) before proceeding, and revert with a clear error such as UnknownRoot() when the root is missing. Replacing the current check with if (pendingWithdraws.owner(root) == address(0)) revert UnknownRoot(); restores the intended behavior, allowing legitimate early withdrawals to succeed and preventing the DoS condition.
summary: The completeWithdrawalEarly function from the Issuance contract allows users to "buy out” the withdrawal of someone else in return for the withdrawal's equivalent in their desired LST/ETH. It checks the opposite of what it should. Only withdrawals that have a set root should continue being executed, when the check is doing quite the opposite. This will completely DoS the function from being used as intended and will further introduce unexpected behavior.

title: ISU-3 | Unbounded Call Leads To Gas Griefing and DoS
content: The contract implements an early‑withdrawal mechanism where a caller can invoke completeWithdrawalEarly to buy out another user’s pending withdrawal. The function determines the value of the withdrawal and then sends that value to the original owner either by calling ERC20.transfer for token payouts or by using address.call when the payout is in native ETH. The call to address.call is performed without specifying a gas stipend, which means the callee can consume up to 63/64 of the remaining gas. Because the call is unbounded, a malicious recipient can deliberately use a large amount of gas or deliberately revert the call. If the recipient spends excessive gas, the transaction becomes prohibitively expensive for the caller, effectively griefing them. If the recipient reverts, the entire completeWithdrawalEarly call fails, preventing the early‑withdrawal from being completed and causing a denial‑of‑service condition. This issue appears only when the withdrawal was queued with wantsEth set to true, but the underlying pattern is a classic push‑payment design that gives the receiver unrestricted control over execution. From a user’s perspective the expected outcome – receiving the equivalent ETH or LST – may not happen; the transaction may either run out of gas, cost an unexpectedly high fee, or simply revert, leaving the user with no funds received and possibly a failed transaction. The vulnerability was discovered during a manual audit that examined the payment flow and identified the lack of a gas limit on the external call. It can be hard to notice because address.call is a common idiom for sending ETH and the code does not contain explicit checks for gas consumption or revert handling. The root cause is the push‑payment model combined with an unbounded external call, which violates the protocol’s accounting assumption that the payout will always succeed with predictable gas usage. The recommended mitigation is to replace the push model with a pull pattern, allowing the original owner to claim their payout in a separate transaction, or to enforce a fixed gas stipend on the call, thereby preventing the recipient from exhausting gas or forcing a revert that blocks the operation.
summary: Issuance.completeWithdrawalEarly() is used to “buy out” a withdrawal from someone in return for the equivalent the withdrawal's value in the LST of the withdrawal or in ETH if the withdrawal was queued with wantsEth = true. That equivalent value gets sent to the oldOwner of the withdrawal either through and ERC20.transfer or through an address.call in the case of ETH. Calling an address through address.call() without a gas stipend allows the call recipient to use as much as 63/64 of the gas left for execution. This allows the recipient to do two things: 1. Maliciously expend gas in order to make the transaction be very expensive for the caller. 2. Trigger a revert, which will make the transaction fail and disallow it from being completed, thus causing DoS.

title: update_market
content: The vulnerability is an accounting error in the market reward update routine. The function that advances a market’s reward state calculates a variable called nextEpoch by adding the fixed epoch length to the current loop index (i + BLOCK_EPOCH). The index i represents the last processed block, which may lie anywhere inside the current epoch. Because the code uses i instead of the epoch start timestamp, the computed nextEpoch can be offset beyond the true boundary of the weekly epoch. When the loop crosses an epoch boundary, the blockDelta that is used to compute the reward for the current epoch is therefore larger than it should be, causing the contract to credit the market with rewards for blocks that belong to the next epoch at the old reward rate. In the example where the previous epoch paid 100 Canto per block and the new epoch pays zero, the buggy calculation adds three blocks of reward (100 × 3) instead of the correct single block (100 × 1). The root cause is the misuse of a spot‑time variable (i) for epoch alignment rather than the deterministic epoch start (epoch). An attacker can trigger the update_market function exactly after an epoch transition, causing the contract to over‑mint reward tokens and inflate the accCantoPerShare value. This inflated share value later distributes more rewards to lenders than they are entitled to, breaking the protocol’s accounting guarantees and potentially draining the reward pool. The bug manifests only when the lastRewardBlock is not aligned with the epoch start and a call to update_market spans the epoch boundary; normal updates within a single epoch appear correct, making the issue hard to notice. It was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, which added a test that rolls the blockchain to a point just before an epoch change, calls update_market, then rolls past the boundary and observes an unexpected increase in accCantoPerShare. From a user perspective the symptom is that the displayed reward balance jumps suddenly, often showing a larger-than‑expected amount after a week rolls over, while later rewards may be missing because the accounting has been exhausted. The bug belongs to the class of “epoch‑boundary accounting mis‑calculation” bugs, where reward accrual logic fails to correctly segment time intervals. The recommended fix is to compute nextEpoch from the epoch start (epoch + BLOCK_EPOCH) instead of from the loop index, ensuring that blockDelta never spans more than one epoch and that rewards are calculated with the correct per‑block rate for each epoch. Properly fixing the calculation restores the invariant that accCantoPerShare reflects the exact amount of rewards earned per share of market supply, preserving the protocol’s economic model and preventing unintended token inflation.

title: Whitelisted accounts can be forcefully DoSed from buying `curveTokens` during the presale
content: The vulnerability is a permanent denial‑of‑service condition that can be triggered against accounts that are whitelisted for a token presale. The contract keeps, for each holder, an array called ownedCurvesTokenSubjects that records every token subject for which the holder ever owned a curve token. When a holder buys a curve token for the first time, the contract adds the subject to this array via an internal function that iterates over the whole storage array. The array is never shrunk: when a holder sells, transfers or otherwise disposes of all tokens of a given subject, the address remains in the list because no pop operation is ever performed. Moreover, the same internal function is called during any transfer to a recipient, meaning that any external party can cause a new subject address to be appended to the recipient’s array. An attacker can therefore create a large number of dummy token subjects, acquire a single token of each, and then transfer all of them in one transaction to a whitelisted account. Each transfer invokes the add‑subject routine, inflating the ownedCurvesTokenSubjects array without bound. Because the add routine reads the array from storage and loops over it, the gas cost of the loop grows linearly with the array length. When the whitelisted account later attempts to purchase the real presale token, the contract again iterates over the now‑massive array, causing the transaction to run out of gas and revert. From the user’s perspective the purchase simply fails with an out‑of‑gas error, even though the user expects to receive the presale tokens. The impact is that the whitelisted participant is forced to miss the presale and must resort to a different address during the open sale, effectively losing the privileged opportunity. The issue occurs only when the contract’s presale buying function is used, the victim account is whitelisted, and an attacker can transfer arbitrary curve tokens to that account. It affects any participant that relies on the whitelist mechanism and any protocol that assumes the whitelist provides exclusive access. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that examined the handling of ownedCurvesTokenSubjects and noticed that the array only grows and is never cleaned up. The bug is hard to notice because the array growth is not visible on‑chain until the gas limit is exceeded, and the contract does not emit any warning when the list becomes large. The root cause is the combination of an unbounded storage array, lack of removal logic, and the fact that external transfers can arbitrarily extend the list. The recommended fix is to add logic that removes a subject from the ownedCurvesTokenSubjects array whenever the holder’s balance for that subject drops to zero, for example by popping the entry in the sellCurvesToken and _transfer functions. A more robust solution is to replace the dynamic array with an EnumerableSet, which provides constant‑time add, contains and delete operations and prevents uncontrolled growth. Implementing these changes restores the intended business logic that a whitelist grants exclusive buying rights and eliminates the possibility of a forced denial‑of‑service attack.
summary: Whitelisted accounts can be DoSed from buying `curveTokens` during the presale by a malicious party, as a result, the user who owns the whitelisted account will be forced to miss the presale and it will be able to acquire the `curveTokens` only during the open sale using a different account.

title: Unrestricted claiming of fees due to missing balance updates in `FeeSplitter`
content: The vulnerability resides in the fee distribution mechanism of the FeeSplitter contract, which uses an accumulator pattern to allocate rewards to token holders based on the time they hold a balance. The contract maintains a cumulative fee per token value and a per‑account offset that records the accumulator snapshot at the last balance change. The root cause is that the function responsible for updating this per‑account offset, onBalanceChange, is only invoked during buy and sell operations performed by Curves._transferFees and is never called when tokens are transferred, deposited, or withdrawn. Consequently, when a holder moves tokens to a fresh address, the new address’s userFeeOffset remains at its default value of zero while the cumulative fee accumulator may already contain a large amount of accrued fees. The claimFees function then calculates the claimable amount using the current token balance multiplied by the difference between the cumulative fee and the zero offset, allowing the new address to withdraw the full amount of fees as if it had held the tokens since the beginning of the reward period. An attacker can repeatedly transfer the same tokens to newly created accounts, invoke claimFees from each account, and drain the FeeSplitter of all accumulated fees. From a user’s perspective the contract appears to grant large, unexpected fee payouts to accounts that have only just received tokens, violating the expectation that fees are earned proportionally to holding duration. The impact is a loss of matured yield for all legitimate participants, effectively stealing funds from the protocol. The issue manifests whenever token balances change without a corresponding onBalanceChange call – i.e., during any standard ERC20 transfer, deposit, or withdrawal. It was discovered through extensive community testing and audit reviews that highlighted the missing state update. The bug is subtle because the fee claim logic itself works correctly; the problem lies in the missing bookkeeping step, which may not be obvious without tracing balance‑change pathways. The vulnerability belongs to the class of missing‑state‑update or accumulator‑reset bugs that enable unauthorized reward extraction. To remediate, the contract must invoke onBalanceChange (or an equivalent updateFeeCredit) for both sender and receiver on every token transfer, as well as on deposit and withdrawal operations, ensuring that each account’s fee offset accurately reflects its actual holding period before any claim is allowed.

[3](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-01-curves-findings/issues/134)), [0xMAKEOUTHILL](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-01-curves-findings/issues/144), [ptsanev](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-01-curves-findings/issues/109), [Kow](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-01-curves-findings/issues/92), [israeladelaja](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-01-curves-findings/issues/91), [rvierdiiev](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-01-curves-findings/issues/68), kutugu ([1](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-01-curves-findings/issues/45), [2](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-01-curves-findings/issues/41)), [DarkTower](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-01-curves-findings/issues/874), [peanuts](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-01-curves-findings/issues/1523), [d3e4](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-01-curves-findings/issues/1462), [0x0bserver](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-01-curves-findings/issues/1437), [Aymen0909](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-01-curves-findings/issues/1312), [0xE1](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-01-curves-findings/issues/1232), [Soul22](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-01-curves-findings/issues/1123), and [0xStalin](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-01-curves-findings/issues/1066)**

The `FeeSplitter` contract is designed to distribute fees among token holders. It employs an accumulator pattern to distribute rewards over time among users who do not sell or withdraw their tokens as ERC20s. This pattern works by maintaining an accumulator representing the cumulative total of the reward rate over time, and updating it for each user every time their balance changes.

However, the current implementation does not update the accumulator associated with each user during token transfers, deposits, or withdrawals. The [`onBalanceChange()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-01-curves/blob/516aedb7b9a8d341d0d2666c23780d2bd8a9a600/contracts/FeeSplitter.sol#L96) function, which is responsible for updating the accumulator following changes in a user’s balance, is exclusively called from [`Curves._transferFees()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-01-curves/blob/516aedb7b9a8d341d0d2666c23780d2bd8a9a600/contracts/Curves.sol#L218), which is only called during buy and sell transactions.
