This oversight can be easily exploited to drain the `FeeSplitter` contract of its fees. An attacker could repeatedly transfer the same tokens to new accounts and claim fees every time. This is possible because `data.userFeeOffset[account]` will be zero for every new account they transfer to, while the claimable rewards are [calculated](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-01-curves/blob/516aedb7b9a8d341d0d2666c23780d2bd8a9a600/contracts/FeeSplitter.sol#L63-L87) using the current balance returned by the Curves contract.

Since there is no limit to the amount of rewards that may accumulate in the `FeeSplitter` contract, this can be considered loss of matured yield and is hence classified as high severity.

title: Attack to make `CurveSubject` to be a `HoneyPot`
content: The vulnerability is a honey‑pot condition that can be introduced into any CurveSubject by the subject’s creator. The root cause lies in two design choices in the Curves contract: first, the internal fee‑distribution function _transferFees always attempts to forward the referral fee to a stored referralFeeDestination address, even when the calculated referralFee amount is zero; second, the contract allows the creator of a CurveSubject to change the referralFeeDestination address at any time through setReferralFeeDestination. Because the call to the referral destination is unconditional and its success is required (the transaction reverts on failure), a malicious destination contract can be crafted to reject the call when a sell operation triggers the fee transfer. The attacker deploys a contract (EvilReferralFeeReceiver) that implements a receive fallback which reverts unless the caller is explicitly allowed. By updating the referralFeeDestination to this contract, the protocol enters a state where any user attempting to sell their Curve tokens causes the referral fee transfer to fail, resulting in a revert with CannotSendFunds. Consequently, users can still buy tokens – the buy path sends the referral fee to the malicious contract but the contract’s receive function permits the transfer – but they are unable to sell, effectively locking their liquidity. The impact is that token holders lose the ability to exit their position, funds become effectively frozen, and the creator can sell their own holdings (being on an allowlist) at a higher price, profiting at the expense of other participants. This condition occurs whenever the referral fee is zero or non‑zero and the destination contract is set to a malicious implementation, and it can be triggered at any time by the subject creator. The affected parties include all buyers of the CurveSubject, the protocol’s economic model, and any DAO or governance entity that assumes free bidirectional trading. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the fee‑distribution logic and identified the unconditional call, then confirmed exploitability with a proof‑of‑concept test that demonstrated the honey‑pot behavior. The bug is subtle because the referral fee may be zero, leading developers to assume the call is harmless, and because the ability to change the destination address is not obviously dangerous. To remediate, the contract should avoid making an external call when the referral fee amount is zero, employ a safe ETH transfer pattern such as Solady’s forceSafeTransferETH, and restrict or remove the ability for arbitrary creators to modify the referral fee destination after deployment. These changes would prevent a malicious contract from causing sell operations to revert and restore the intended bidirectional liquidity of Curve tokens.
summary: Any `CurveSubjects` could be turned to a `HoneyPot` by the creator of `CurveSubject`, which causes that users can only buy but can’t sell the curve tokens any more. Then malicious creators can sell their own tokens at a high price to make profit.

title: Unauthorized Access to `setCurves` Function
content: The vulnerability is an unauthorized access flaw in the fee distribution contract where the function that updates the reference to the external Curves contract can be called by any address. Because the function lacks any access‑control modifier, a malicious user can replace the legitimate Curves contract with a counterfeit one that the attacker controls. The counterfeit contract allows the attacker to set arbitrary values for the token balance and total supply that the fee splitter uses to compute each holder’s claimable fees. By inflating these values the attacker can cause the fee calculation routine to return an excessively large amount for the attacker’s address, while legitimate users receive little or no fees. The issue occurs whenever the contract is deployed and before the owner or a trusted manager restricts the setter function; any user can invoke setCurves at any time. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the contract’s public interface and identified that setCurves is not protected by onlyOwner or onlyManager modifiers. The problem is hard to notice because the function does not emit obvious events and the fee calculation appears correct when the legitimate Curves contract is in place, so the misbehaviour only surfaces after the reference is switched. The impact is financial loss for token holders, as the attacker can claim fees that belong to the whole pool, effectively draining funds. This class of bug is an improper access‑control vulnerability that permits unauthorized state mutation, breaking the accounting assumptions that fees are distributed proportionally to actual token holdings. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a normal fee balance for the attacker, while other users see their expected fees disappear or remain zero, contradicting the expectation that fees are automatically allocated. The recommended remediation is to restrict the setCurves function to privileged roles, such as the contract owner or an authorized manager, by applying the onlyOwner or onlyManager modifier, thereby preventing arbitrary replacement of the Curves contract and preserving the integrity of fee calculations.
summary:
The `FeeSplitter.sol` contract, which is responsible for fee distribution and claiming, contains a significant security vulnerability related to the `setCurves` function. This function allows updating the reference to the `Curves` contract. However, as it currently stands, any user, including a malicious actor, can call `setCurves`. This vulnerability can be exploited to redirect the contract’s reference to a fake or malicious `Curves` contract (`FakeCurves.sol`), enabling manipulation of critical calculations used in fee distribution.

The exploit allows an attacker to set arbitrary values for `curvesTokenBalance` and `curvesTokenSupply` in the fake `Curves` contract. By manipulating these values, the attacker can falsely inflate their claimable fees, leading to unauthorized profit at the expense of legitimate token holders.

title: Malformed equate statement
content: The contract contains two access‑control modifiers that are intended to restrict function execution to privileged accounts, but the implementation is flawed. Each modifier evaluates a boolean expression – `msg.sender == owner` for the onlyOwner modifier and `managers[msg.sender] == true` for the onlyManager modifier – without using a require or revert statement. Because the expression result is not checked, the modifiers do not enforce any restriction; they simply compute a value that is discarded. This logical omission means that any address can call functions guarded by these modifiers, effectively bypassing the intended ownership or manager checks. An attacker can exploit the bug by invoking a protected function directly; the transaction will not revert even if the caller is not the owner or a registered manager. The impact is severe: privileged operations such as fund withdrawals, parameter changes, or administrative actions can be performed by unauthorized parties, leading to potential loss of assets, protocol state corruption, or complete takeover of contract governance. The vulnerability manifests whenever a function is marked with onlyOwner or onlyManager, which is common in contracts that rely on role‑based access control. All users of the contract, as well as the protocol operators, are affected because the security guarantees promised by the contract’s interface are broken. The issue was discovered during a manual audit review where the modifier bodies were inspected and found to lack a require statement. It can be hard to notice because the syntax looks superficially correct – the modifiers are declared and referenced – yet the missing require is a subtle logical error that does not produce a compiler warning. From a user’s perspective, actions that should be restricted (for example, only the owner can pause the contract or withdraw fees) appear to work for any address, leading to unexpected behavior such as unauthorized withdrawals or configuration changes. The bug violates the fundamental business logic that only trusted roles may perform sensitive operations, breaking accounting assumptions and trust in the system. The recommended remediation is to replace the bare equality checks with explicit require statements that revert when the caller is not authorized, thereby restoring proper access control enforcement.
summary: _Note: This finding was reported via the winning[Automated Findings report](include%20link%20to%20bot-report.md%20file). It was declared out of scope for the audit, but is being included here for completeness._

title: Anyone can update the address of the Router in the DcntEth contract to any address they would like to set.
content: The vulnerability is an unrestricted access control on the function that updates the router address in the DcntEth contract. Because the setRouter function is declared public without any modifier restricting callers, any external account can invoke it and replace the stored router address with an arbitrary contract controlled by the attacker. The DcntEth contract relies on the router address to gate the mint and burn functions; only the router is supposed to be able to call these privileged methods. When the router address is overwritten, the attacker’s contract becomes the authorized router, allowing the attacker to call mint and create unlimited DcntEth tokens or call burn to destroy tokens held by the legitimate DecentEthRouter. This can be exploited by first calling setRouter with a malicious address, then invoking the mint function to inflate the token supply and withdraw the underlying WETH or ETH that was deposited as liquidity, or by calling burn to sabotage liquidity pools and cause denial‑of‑service for addLiquidity and removeLiquidity operations. The impact includes loss of the entire total value locked (TVL) of the Decent ETH token, unauthorized token creation, forced token burns that break accounting, and failed liquidity operations that revert, leaving users unable to add or withdraw funds. The condition for exploitation is simply that the contract is live and the setRouter function is callable by anyone; no special permissions or prior state are required. All participants who interact with the DecentEthRouter – liquidity providers, traders, and the protocol itself – are affected because their balances may be drained or their transactions may revert unexpectedly. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the visibility of state‑changing functions and noted the absence of an onlyOwner or similar guard on setRouter. It is hard to notice in normal operation because the function appears benign and the router address is not frequently displayed in UI, so the contract may appear to work correctly until an attacker actively changes the address and triggers abnormal mint or burn behavior. The proper remediation is to introduce a robust access‑control mechanism (for example, onlyOwner or a role‑based guard) on setRouter so that only trusted governance or deployment accounts can modify the router address, and to consider adding events and checks that validate the router address before critical operations. This class of bug is an unauthorized privileged function vulnerability that breaks the intended trust model of the contract, leading to token accounting errors, fund disappearance, and broken liquidity functionality.
summary: By allowing anybody to set the address of the Router contract to any address they want to set it allows malicious users to get access to the mint and burn functions of the DcntEth contract.

title: Due to missing checks on minimum gas passed through LayerZero, executions can fail on the destination chain
content: The vulnerability originates from a missing validation of the minimum gas amount that must be supplied to the destination chain when using LayerZero’s cross‑chain messaging through the DecentEthRouter contract. The router assumes that a caller will first query estimateSendAndCallFee() to obtain the native and ZRO fees and will then add those values to a hard‑coded constant GAS_FOR_RELAY before passing the sum as the _dstGasForCall argument of bridge() or bridgeWithPayload(). Because this assumption is not enforced, a user can provide an arbitrary, possibly very low, _dstGasForCall value. The contract simply adds the constant (100 000 gas) to the supplied value and forwards the total to LayerZero without checking whether it meets the minimum required by the destination chain. If the supplied gas is insufficient, the destination execution reverts with an out‑of‑gas error. LayerZero nevertheless marks the message as delivered, transitioning its state from INFLIGHT to STORED. A STORED message blocks any further messages from the same source to that destination chain until the blocked message is manually retried and succeeds. Consequently, a malicious or careless user can cause a denial‑of‑service condition that permanently blocks the cross‑chain channel, preventing legitimate transfers and potentially locking funds that were expected to arrive on the other chain. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a successful transaction on the source chain while the recipient sees no funds, a pending or failed status, or an unexpected zero balance, contradicting the expectation that the bridge will deliver the assets. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined LayerZero integration patterns and observed that the DecentEthRouter does not enforce any lower bound on the gas parameter, contrary to LayerZero’s documentation. The problem is subtle because the source transaction does not revert, making the failure appear as a silent message‑store rather than an obvious error. To remediate the flaw, the contract should require that _dstGasForCall be at least the sum of the estimated native and ZRO fees, or make the fee‑estimation step mandatory. Additionally, a maximum gas consumption check should be added at the executor level to guarantee that enough gas remains after any arbitrary call to store a failed message, or a fixed safe gas margin should be enforced. Implementing these checks restores the intended accounting guarantees of the bridge and prevents the channel from being blocked by insufficient gas provision.
summary:
```solidity
In LayerZero, the destination chain’s function call requires a specific gas amount; otherwise, it will revert with an out-of-gas exception. It falls under the responsibility of the User Application to ensure that appropriate limits are established. These limits guide relayers in specifying the correct gas amount on the source chain, preventing users from inputting insufficient values for gas.

The contract logic in `DecentEthRouter`, assumes that a user will first get their estimated fees through `estimateSendAndCallFee()` and pass it as an argument in either `bridge()` or `bridgeWithPayload()` to be added to the calculation together with the hardcoded `GAS_FOR_RELAY` so that it can be passed as the adapter params when `CommonOFT.LzCallParams` is called, although this is not enforced and is left on the user’s responsibility.

A user can pass an arbitrary value as the `_dstGasForCall` argument to be added to the hardcoded `GAS_FOR_RELAY` fee, thus sending less gas than required which can lead to out-of-gas exceptions.

Once the message is received by destination, the message is considered delivered (transitioning from INFLIGHT to either SUCCESS or STORED), even though it threw an out-of-gas error.

Any uncaught errors/exceptions (including out-of-gas) will cause the message to transition into STORED. A STORED message will block the delivery of any future message from source to all destination on the same destination chain and can be retried until the message becomes SUCCESS.

As per: https://layerzero.gitbook.io/docs/faq/messaging-properties
```

title: When `DecentBridgeExecutor.execute` fails, funds will be sent to a random address
content: The vulnerability is a misrouted refund bug in the DecentBridgeExecutor contract used by the Decent cross‑chain bridge. When a cross‑chain transfer is executed, the bridge builds a payload that contains a field called “from” which is set to msg.sender on the source chain – the DecentBridgeAdapter contract address. On the destination chain the DecentEthRouter decodes this payload and forwards the same “from” value to DecentBridgeExecutor.execute. If the low‑level call performed by _executeEth or _executeWeth fails, the executor attempts to refund the amount by sending it to the address stored in the “from” parameter. Because that address is the adapter contract on the source chain and not the user’s refund address, the funds are transferred to an unrelated contract that has no logic to receive them, resulting in permanent loss. The bug occurs whenever the target call reverts or returns false, which can happen due to insufficient gas, a revert in the called contract, or any other execution failure. A user who initiates a cross‑chain transfer expects that a failed call will be refunded to their own address, but instead the balance disappears and the UI shows a successful transaction with no received funds. The issue was discovered during a security audit that traced the payload construction in _getCallParams and compared it with the refund logic in DecentBridgeExecutor. It is hard to notice because the source‑chain transaction emits no error and the refund address is not logged, so the loss appears as a silent disappearance of funds. The bug belongs to the class of “incorrect refund address” or “misrouted funds” vulnerabilities, which violate the accounting assumption that the sender of a failed cross‑chain call is the rightful recipient of the refund. To remediate, the executor should be called with the actual user refund address – for example by passing the user’s address instead of the adapter address – or the bridge should ensure that the same address is used on both chains (e.g., by deploying contracts with CREATE2 so the address is deterministic). Correcting the refund address restores the intended business logic that failed transfers are safely returned to the initiator, preventing total loss of user funds.
summary:
```solidity
When the `DecentBridgeExecutor._executeWeth/_executeEth` target call fails, a refund is issued to the `from` address.

However, this address is wrongly set, so those refunds will be permanently lost.
```

title: Users will lose their cross-chain transaction if the destination router do not have enough WETH reserves.
content: The issue is a cross‑chain fund loss bug in the DecentEthRouter contract that occurs when the destination router does not hold enough WETH to satisfy the incoming amount and the message type is not a simple ETH transfer. The router’s onOFTReceived function checks the WETH balance and, if it is lower than the amount received, it falls back to transferring the wrapped token representation (dcntEth) to the address stored in the _to variable. For simple ETH transfers _to is the user, but for calls that include a payload (msgType != MT_ETH_TRANSFER) the _to address is the destination bridge adapter – an execution target that has no mechanism to withdraw or forward the dcntEth token. Consequently the dcntEth is locked in a contract that cannot be accessed by the original sender, effectively causing the cross‑chain transaction to be lost. The root cause is the misuse of the _to parameter as a refund destination and the lack of a proper fallback path when WETH reserves are depleted. Exploitation does not require an attacker; it happens automatically whenever the destination router’s WETH balance falls below the transferred amount while a payload‑based message is processed. From the user’s perspective the transaction appears successful on the source chain, but the destination wallet receives no ETH or WETH, the balance remains unchanged, and the UI may show a completed transfer while the funds have disappeared. The impact is loss of user funds and broken cross‑chain accounting, undermining trust in the bridge. The bug was discovered during a security audit that traced the control flow of onOFTReceived and the bridge executor’s _executeWeth function, revealing that the fallback transfer targets an address that cannot redeem the token. The problem is subtle because the fallback path is only triggered under low‑reserve conditions, making it easy to miss in normal testing. The recommended mitigation is to include a dedicated refund address in the payload and replace the use of _to with this address when the WETH balance is insufficient, ensuring that the dcntEth is returned to the original sender or another recoverable account. This change restores the intended business logic that users should either receive their ETH/WETH after the router is refilled or be able to send the token back to the source chain, preventing silent fund loss.

title: MarginTradingHook#updateOrder lacks access control
content: The vulnerability resides in the function that allows a user to modify an existing order in a margin‑trading contract. The function checks that the order is currently active and that the caller has an opened position, but it does not verify that the position identifier belonging to the caller matches the position identifier stored inside the order data structure. Because of this missing ownership check, any participant who holds any active position can supply the identifier of another user’s order and successfully overwrite the order’s parameters such as trigger price, limit price, collateral amount and the token to be received. An attacker can therefore hijack a stop‑loss or take‑profit order that belongs to a different trader, change the price thresholds to values that cause premature liquidation or unfavorable execution, and potentially force the victim to lose collateral or miss a profit opportunity. The issue manifests only when the order is in the Active state and the caller’s position identifier is non‑zero, conditions that are common in a live trading environment. All users who open positions are affected because they can be either the victim of a tampered order or the attacker who can manipulate others’ orders. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit by Code4rena when the reviewers noticed that the updateOrder routine performed only a generic position existence check and then added a test case that demonstrated a cross‑account update. The problem is subtle because the function appears to enforce reasonable constraints – active order and existing position – which can give a false sense of security, making the missing equality comparison easy to overlook. To remediate the issue, the contract should enforce proper ownership by adding a requirement that the stored initPosId inside the order equals the initPosId derived from the caller’s address, mirroring the check used in the cancelOrder function. This change restores the intended access control, ensuring that only the creator of an order can modify its parameters, and prevents unauthorized manipulation that could lead to unexpected order execution, loss of funds, or broken accounting assumptions in the protocol.

title: Order’s creator can update `tokenOut` to arbitrary token
content: The vulnerability is an unauthorized token substitution bug that allows the creator of a limit order to change the output token (tokenOut) to any ERC‑20 token after the order has been created. The root cause is that the updateOrder function does not verify that the new tokenOut address matches one of the two assets (baseAsset or quoteAsset) that belong to the margin position associated with the order. Because the check that exists during order creation is omitted in the update path, a malicious order creator can call updateOrder with an arbitrary token address, and the contract will accept it. An attacker can exploit this by front‑running the executor’s fillOrder call: just before the executor attempts to settle the order, the creator submits an updateOrder transaction that swaps tokenOut for a high‑value token that the executor’s hook is already approved to spend. When fillOrder runs, the protocol transfers the collateral amount using the newly set tokenOut, causing the executor to send out the high‑value token instead of the intended low‑value token, or vice‑versa. The impact is a loss of funds for the executor or the protocol, incorrect balances for users, and a breach of the accounting assumptions that each order should deliver a specific asset. The condition for exploitation is that the order is still active, the creator has the ability to call updateOrder, and the executor’s hook has a blanket allowance for the attacker’s chosen token. The affected parties include order creators, executors, any users relying on the order’s promised token, and the overall protocol’s liquidity pool. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the validation logic of order creation with that of order updates and noticed the missing asset check. It can be hard to notice because the UI typically displays the token chosen at creation, and the tokenOut field is not visibly immutable, so a user may not realize it can be altered later. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after an order is filled they receive zero of the expected token or a completely different token, and the protocol’s balance appears to have shrunk unexpectedly. The bug belongs to the class of “mutable parameter injection” or “unauthorized state change” vulnerabilities where a critical parameter is allowed to be changed without proper authorization checks. To remediate, the updateOrder function should enforce the same asset whitelist check as order creation (i.e., require that the new tokenOut equals either the baseAsset or the quoteAsset of the associated margin position) or, preferably, make tokenOut immutable after order creation, thereby preventing any post‑creation substitution of the output token.
summary: When an order is created, it checks whether the `order.tokenOut` is equal to `marginPos.baseAsset` or `_tokenOut` is equal to `marginPos.quoteAsset`. However, when `tokenOut` is updated via `updateOrder`, it can be changed to an arbitrary token. This has the potential to be exploited by changing `tokenOut` to a high-value token right before the executor executes the `fillOrder`.

title: `fillOrder` executor can be front-run by the order creator by changing order’s `limitPrice_e36`, the executor’s assets can be stolen
content: The vulnerability is a front‑running manipulation of a mutable slippage protection parameter called limitPrice_e36 that is used to compute the amount of tokens (amtOut) transferred to the order creator when an executor calls fillOrder. The contract allows the order creator to update limitPrice_e36 after the order has been placed, and the fillOrder implementation does not re‑validate this value against the original constraints before performing the calculation. Because amtOut is directly derived from limitPrice_e36, an attacker who is also the order creator can observe a pending fillOrder transaction, submit a transaction that changes limitPrice_e36 to a more favorable value, and have the pending fillOrder execute with the altered price. This results in a larger amtOut being sent to the attacker and a corresponding loss for the executor, effectively stealing the executor’s assets. The issue occurs whenever the order is still mutable and the executor relies on the current limitPrice_e36 without additional checks. It primarily affects executors (liquidity providers, bots, or any user filling orders) who expect to receive a certain token amount, but instead see their balance decrease or receive nothing, while the order creator receives an unexpectedly high payout. The problem was discovered during a Code4rena audit by analyzing the fillOrder logic and noticing the heavy reliance on a mutable limitPrice_e36. The bug is subtle because the arithmetic appears correct and the contract does not emit obvious warnings; the manipulation only becomes visible after the executor’s funds are missing. This class of bug falls under mutable parameter abuse leading to front‑run attacks, similar to price‑or‑oracle manipulation where a value that should be immutable is changed after a dependent transaction is queued. To remediate, the protocol should lock limitPrice_e36 at order creation or enforce that fillOrder checks the current limit price against the originally supplied minimum/maximum bounds, reverting the transaction if it has been altered. Alternatively, the updateOrder function could be redesigned to cancel the existing order and create a new one, preventing in‑place modification of the critical slippage parameter.
summary: `limitPrice_e36` acts as slippage protection for the order creator, depending on the trade/order position (whether long or short). A higher or lower limit price impacts the `tokenOut` amount that needs to be transferred to the order’s creator. However, when the executor executes `fillOrder`, it can be front-run by the order creator to update `limitPrice_e36` and steal tokens from the executor.

title: All orders can be hijacked to lock rental assets forever by tipping a malicious ERC20
content: The vulnerability is an order‑hijacking flaw that allows a malicious actor to lock rental assets forever by injecting a malicious ERC20 token into the consideration array of a Seaport order, a technique known as “tipping”. The root cause lies in the way the Create contract validates orders: the order hash that is signed by the offerer only incorporates the original length of the consideration items (totalOriginalConsiderationItems) and therefore ignores any additional items that a fulfiller may append during fulfillment. The zone logic receives the full list of consideration items, but it does not enforce that the list matches the original length, nor does the signed RentPayload depend on the consideration items. Consequently, a fulfiller can extend the consideration array with an arbitrary ERC20 token after the order has been signed. If the added token is crafted to revert on transfer, the rental stop process, which attempts to transfer the token from the escrow back to the offerer, will fail. The stopRent call then reverts, leaving the rented NFT or other assets trapped in the escrow contract with no mechanism to recover them. This exploit can be carried out whenever the protocol uses the unrestricted “tipping” feature of Seaport and the Create contract’s zone does not restrict consideration extensions. Users who rent out assets, lenders who provide NFTs, and the protocol itself are affected because assets become permanently inaccessible, breaking the expected business logic that rentals can be ended and funds returned. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by tracing the order validation flow, noticing that the order hash calculation discards extra consideration items, and confirming that the zone parameters accept the full array without validation. The problem is subtle because the order appears correctly signed and the extra tip is not reflected in the hash, so the exploit only manifests later when the escrow tries to move the malicious token. To remediate, the protocol should either disable the tipping feature entirely or add explicit checks that the number of consideration items received by the zone matches the original count, rejecting any additional items. A whitelist of allowed tokens or a restriction that only pre‑declared consideration items can be transferred would also prevent a malicious ERC20 from being introduced, thereby restoring the guarantee that rentals can be stopped and assets returned safely.

title: Incorrect `gnosis_safe_disable_module_offset` constant leads to removing the rental safe’s `module` without verification
content: The vulnerability originates from an incorrectly defined constant that determines the calldata offset used when the Guard contract validates a Gnosis Safe disableModule transaction. The constant gnosis_safe_disable_module_offset was set to 0x24, which points to the first parameter (prevModule) of the disableModule(address prevModule, address module) function instead of the second parameter (module) that actually identifies the module to be removed. When the Guard's _checkTransaction routine encounters a disableModule call, it extracts an address from calldata using this offset and stores it in the variable extension. Because the offset points to prevModule, the Guard ends up checking the whitelist status of the previous module address rather than the target module address. Consequently, a module that is not whitelisted can be removed without triggering a revert, while a whitelisted previous module may cause a false negative and block legitimate removals. This mis‑validation can be exploited by an attacker who crafts a disableModule transaction where the prevModule argument is a whitelisted address; the Guard will approve the transaction and the unsafe module will be disabled. The impact is that protected extensions of a rental safe can be removed arbitrarily, breaking the expected security guarantees of the protocol and potentially leading to loss of functionality or indirect fund loss. The bug manifests whenever the Guard processes a disableModule call, i.e., any transaction that attempts to remove a module from a Gnosis Safe managed by the protocol. It affects all users of the rental safe who rely on the whitelist to control which modules can be added or removed, as well as the protocol itself because the integrity of its module management is compromised. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the constant value was examined and a proof‑of‑concept transaction demonstrated that the wrong address was being checked. The problem is subtle because the function selector matches and the calldata layout appears correct at a glance, making the error easy to miss in testing, especially since the original test suite assumed a single‑parameter version of disableModule. To remediate the issue, the offset constant must be updated to 0x44, which correctly points to the module argument (32 bytes for the calldata length, 4 bytes for the selector, plus 32 bytes for the first argument). This change restores proper whitelist verification, ensuring that only authorized modules can be disabled. In user‑facing terms, a user may see a module disappear from the UI even though they never approved its removal, or a transaction may revert unexpectedly when trying to disable a legitimate module because the Guard is checking the wrong address. The bug belongs to the class of calldata‑offset mis‑alignment errors that lead to incorrect parameter extraction and faulty access control checks.
summary:
The `gnosis_safe_disable_module_offset` constant was incorrectly specified to point at an incorrect function parameter of the `disableModule(address prevModule, address module)`.

Specifically, the offset constant will point at the `prevModule` (1st param) instead of the `module` (2nd param).

title: Escrow contract can be drained by creating rentals that bypass execution invariant checks
content: The vulnerability resides in the escrow module that holds ERC20 tokens for rental payments. The contract records a rental by updating storage and increasing an internal balance for the escrow, but it relies on a list of executions generated during order matching to verify that the promised token transfers actually occurred. Because the matching logic calculates the total number of executions by counting distinct from‑to pairs, an attacker can craft a pair of orders where the offerer and the consideration recipient are the same address. In that situation the execution list becomes empty, its length is zero, and the invariant check that validates the expected receivers is skipped entirely. The contract therefore believes the rental has been funded, writes the rental data to storage and credits the escrow balance with the declared amount, even though no ERC20 transfer was performed and the NFT never left the attacker’s wallet. After the rental is stored, the attacker can invoke the stop‑rental function; the escrow logic assumes a legitimate payment was made and releases the recorded amount to the caller, effectively draining all tokens that were previously credited. The bug manifests only when orders can be matched with identical from and to addresses, which makes the execution list empty and bypasses the recipient verification step. Users experience a situation where they expect their NFT to be transferred to a safe and their token balance to be locked, but the NFT remains in their possession and the escrow balance shows no incoming transfer. Later, when the rental is stopped, the tokens that were supposedly locked disappear from the escrow contract, leaving the protocol with missing funds and breaking accounting assumptions. The issue was discovered during a security audit that exercised the order‑matching flow and observed that storage updates occurred without any transfer events. It is difficult to notice because the contract emits no events for the phantom rental and the escrow balance appears to increase only in internal bookkeeping, not in on‑chain token balances. The proper fix is to ensure that the invariant checks are performed regardless of the execution list length, to require that each offer and consideration results in an explicit execution even when the sender and receiver are identical, and to update the escrow balance only after a successful token transfer has been confirmed. Adding explicit validation that the escrow’s token balance matches the amount actually transferred, and rejecting rentals that produce a zero‑length execution set, would close the attack surface and restore the intended economic guarantees.
summary: The Escrow contract where ERC20 tokens are escrowed for payments can be completely drained.

title: Development Team might receive less SALT because there is no access control on `VestingWallet#release`
content: The vulnerability is an unrestricted token release function in the VestingWallet contract that allows any address to call release() and transfer the vested SALT tokens directly to the beneficiary address, which in this deployment is the Upkeep contract. The root cause is the absence of any access control or caller verification on VestingWallet.release, combined with the integration logic in Upkeep that assumes it is the sole entity that will invoke release and subsequently forward the received tokens to the managedTeamWallet’s mainWallet. When an external actor invokes release before Upkeep.performUpkeep is executed, the VestingWallet sends the vested amount to Upkeep, but Upkeep does not have a mechanism to detect that the tokens arrived outside its normal workflow, and therefore it never forwards the balance to the development team. As a result, the released SALT becomes locked inside the Upkeep contract, the team’s mainWallet balance remains zero, and the expected periodic reward appears to disappear. This situation occurs each time the vesting schedule becomes releasable – typically on a yearly basis – and can be triggered by any participant who discovers the public release function. The affected parties are the development team and any stakeholders relying on the correct distribution of the 10 million SALT reward; end‑users of the protocol are not directly impacted. The issue was discovered during a security audit when the auditors simulated a premature release call and observed that the Upkeep contract retained the tokens without forwarding them. The bug is subtle because VestingWallet contracts often intentionally expose release without restrictions, and the problem only manifests due to the specific beneficiary configuration and the missing forwarding logic in Upkeep. To remediate, the deployment should set the managedTeamWallet as the beneficiary of the VestingWallet, or the Upkeep contract should include explicit access control on release and a safe‑transfer routine that moves any received SALT to the team’s mainWallet. Conceptually, the fix is to enforce that only the authorized contract can trigger token release or to ensure that any tokens arriving in Upkeep are automatically routed to the intended recipient, thereby preventing the loss of rewards and restoring the expected accounting behavior where the team receives the vested SALT as scheduled.
summary: The Development Team could potentially incur a loss on their SALT distribution reward due to the absence of access control on `VestingWallet#release()`.

title: First Liquidity provider can claim all initial pool rewards
content: The vulnerability is an unfair reward allocation bug that allows the very first liquidity provider to claim the entire amount of rewards that have been deposited into a staking pool. The root cause lies in the accounting logic for virtual rewards: when a user’s share is increased, the contract only calculates and adds a virtualRewards entry if the pool already has a non‑zero totalShares value. For an empty pool, existingTotalShares equals zero, so the conditional block that computes virtualRewards is skipped. Consequently, the first depositor’s userShare becomes equal to totalShares, while their virtualRewards remains zero. The reward‑claim function later computes a user’s pending reward as (totalRewards * userShare / totalShares) minus virtualRewards. Because virtualRewards is zero for the first user, the subtraction does not reduce the calculated share, and the user can withdraw the full pool of rewards. This situation is triggered when the first liquidity provider deposits before any other participants and after the contract’s upkeep routine has transferred reward tokens into the pool. The protocol’s timer for reward distribution starts at contract deployment, which may allow the upkeep function to fund the pool with the maximum daily reward before any liquidity exists, further amplifying the impact. Affected parties include liquidity providers, the protocol’s reward emission schedule, and any token holders relying on fair distribution. From a user’s perspective the UI may show an unexpectedly large reward balance for the first provider, while later providers see little or no rewards, violating the expectation that rewards are shared proportionally. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by inspecting the _increaseUserShare and userRewardForPool functions and noticing that the virtualRewards calculation is bypassed for the initial depositor. It can be hard to notice because the reward formula works correctly once the pool has at least one existing share; only the edge case of the first deposit exhibits the flaw. To remediate, the contract should ensure that virtualRewards are correctly initialized for the first user, for example by computing virtualRewards after totalShares has been updated or by applying a baseline virtualRewards entry even when totalShares is zero. Adjusting the upkeep timer to start after the pool becomes active, or resetting the timer during the bootstrap phase, also mitigates the problem by preventing a large reward injection before any liquidity is present. Properly fixing the accounting logic restores proportional reward distribution and aligns the protocol with its intended economic model.

title: The use of spot price by CoreSaltyFeed can lead to price manipulation and undesired liquidations
content: The vulnerability stems from the way the protocol obtains asset prices through a component called CoreSaltyFeed. CoreSaltyFeed reads the instantaneous spot price supplied by a Chainlink oracle, while the protocol’s internal accounting, collateral valuation and liquidation logic rely on a time‑weighted average price (TWAP) that updates more slowly. Because the spot price can be altered quickly by an attacker who can feed manipulated data to the oracle or create large trades that shift the pool’s price, a temporary divergence can be created between the spot price and the TWAP. When the protocol uses the manipulated spot price to assess the health of a loan, it may incorrectly deem a well‑collateralised position as under‑collateralised, triggering a liquidation or allowing the attacker to extract value through arbitrage. The exploit works by repeatedly swapping a token pair in small steps to move the spot price by a few percent, then performing a liquidation or reverse swap before the TWAP catches up. The impact is that honest users can see their collateral liquidated unexpectedly, their balances reduced to zero, or funds disappear from their accounts, while the attacker profits from the price swing. This condition occurs whenever the system reads the spot price for critical decisions and the TWAP update interval is longer than the time needed to manipulate the spot price. All users who provide collateral, the DAO and the protocol itself are affected. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit when a test suite demonstrated that a series of small swaps could move the price by several percent with low gas cost, revealing that the reliance on the spot price created an attack surface that is not obvious from the presence of a reputable oracle. The bug is hard to notice because the protocol appears to use a trusted price feed and a TWAP, leading reviewers to assume price stability, yet the mixed use of spot and averaged prices allows a subtle manipulation. To remediate, the spot‑price feed should be replaced with an oracle that offers stronger resistance to manipulation, such as Band Protocol, or the protocol should base all critical calculations on the TWAP exclusively. Additional safeguards like price deviation checks, longer observation windows, or limiting the influence of a single price update can also mitigate the risk.
summary: When the price moves, Chainlink instantly reports the spot price, while the TWAP slowly changes the price. The spot price of CoreSaltyFeed can be manipulated, allowing an attacker to move the price in a desired direction.

title: First depositor can break staking-rewards accounting
content: The vulnerability originates from the way the SALTY staking contract calculates and stores virtual rewards for each user. When a user’s share amount increases, the contract computes a virtual reward amount using the formula virtualRewardsToAdd = Math.ceilDiv(totalRewards * increaseShareAmount, existingTotalShares). This value is then added to two state variables that are declared as uint128. Because the multiplication totalRewards * increaseShareAmount can easily exceed the 128‑bit limit, especially when the first depositor artificially inflates the totalRewards by sending a large amount of SALT tokens before any other shares exist, the resulting virtualRewardsToAdd overflows the uint128 range. The overflow is silent: the value is truncated when cast to uint128, corrupting the accounting of both the user’s virtual rewards and the pool’s totalRewards. As a consequence, the contract believes that far more rewards are owed than the actual SALT balance holds. When later users deposit and the contract attempts to distribute the inflated rewards, the claim function reverts with “ERC20: transfer amount exceeds balance”, effectively locking the rewards and causing a loss of matured yield. The bug is triggered on a newly created pool when the first depositor can set an excessively high rewards‑to‑shares ratio, either by donating a large amount of SALT or by exploiting the unrestricted addRewards function. All participants in the affected pool – liquidity providers, token holders and the protocol itself – are impacted because the UI may display large reward numbers while the underlying token balance is insufficient, leading to failed claims and user confusion. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit through logical analysis and a proof‑of‑concept test that demonstrated the sum of claimable rewards exceeding the contract’s SALT balance. It is hard to notice because the overflow does not throw an error at the point of calculation; only later, when a claim is attempted, does the contract revert. The problem belongs to the class of arithmetic overflow and unchecked casting bugs that break financial accounting invariants. To remediate, the contract should store virtual rewards and user shares using a 256‑bit type, enforce safe casting, and restrict the addRewards entry point so that the initial rewards‑to‑shares ratio cannot be manipulated by an arbitrary first depositor. Additionally, initializing pools with a minimal, non‑zero share count and a bounded reward amount would prevent the ratio from being set to an extreme value, preserving the integrity of reward distribution.
summary:
Staking in SALTY pools happens automatically when adding liquidity. In order to track the accrued rewards, the code “simulates” the amount of virtual rewards that need to be added given the increase of shares and lend this amount to the user. So, when computing the real rewards for a given user, the code will compute its rewards based on the `totalRewards` of the given pool minus the virtual rewards. The following code computes the virtual rewards for a user:

```solidity
uint256 virtualRewardsToAdd = Math.ceilDiv( totalRewards[poolID] * increaseShareAmount, existingTotalShares );
```

Basically, it aims to maintain the current ratio of `totalRewards` and `existingTotalShares`. The issue with this is that allows the first depositor to set the ratio too high by donating some SALT tokens to the contract. For example, consider the following values:

```solidity
uint256 virtualRewardsToAdd = Math.ceilDiv( 1000e18 * 200e18, 202 );
```

The returned value is in order of 39-40 digits. Which is beyond what 128 bits can represent:

```solidity
user.virtualRewards += uint128(virtualRewardsToAdd);
totalRewards[poolID] += uint128(virtualRewardsToAdd);
```

This will broke the reward computations. For a more concrete example look the PoC.

title: User can evade `liquidation` by depositing the minimum of tokens and gain time to not be liquidated
content: The vulnerability is a liquidation‑evasion flaw in the CollateralAndLiquidity contract. The contract stores a timestamp called user.cooldownExpiration for each position and requiresthat any share‑increase operation that uses the cooldown flag can only be executed after this timestamp has passed. The internal function _increaseUserShare, which is called by depositCollateralAndIncreaseShare, updates user.cooldownExpiration to block further modifications for a period defined by stakingConfig.modificationCooldown(). When a user is under‑collateralised and a liquidation transaction is submitted, the liquidator calls _decreaseUserShare with the useCooldown flag set to true. Because the same cooldown check is performed, an attacker can front‑run the liquidation by calling depositCollateralAndIncreaseShare with a dust amount of collateral just before the liquidation is executed. This call resets user.cooldownExpiration to a future time, causing the subsequent liquidation call to revert with the error 'Must wait for the cooldown to expire'. The exploit works whenever the attacker can submit a transaction that is mined before the liquidation transaction, which is typical in a public mempool. The impact is that liquidations can be avoided, leaving the protocol with positions that remain under‑collateralised and potentially accumulating debt, while liquidators receive no reward and users see their liquidation attempts fail. The issue is discovered by an audit test (testUserLiquidationMayBeAvoided) that reproduces the revert. It is hard to notice because the cooldown mechanism is intended for normal share adjustments and the liquidation path reuses the same internal function without considering that an attacker could manipulate the timestamp. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a user as liquidatable but the transaction fails, the liquidator receives no funds, and the under‑collateralised user retains their position. The bug belongs to the class of business‑logic state‑manipulation vulnerabilities, specifically a cooldown bypass that breaks accounting assumptions about when a position can be forced closed. The recommended fix is to call _decreaseUserShare with the useCooldown flag set to false during liquidation, or otherwise separate the cooldown logic from liquidation so that the timestamp check does not block forced closures.

title: When borrowers repay USDS, it is sent to the wrong address, allowing anyone to burn Protocol Owned Liquidity and build bad debt for USDS
content: When a borrower calls the repayUSDS function, the contract transfers the specified amount of USDS from the borrower to the USDS token contract instead of to the Liquidizer contract that is responsible for tracking how much USDS should be burned. At the same time the function calls liquidizer.incrementBurnableUSDS, which increases the internal variable usdsThatShouldBeBurned. Because the transferred USDS never arrives in the Liquidizer, the contract’s USDS balance remains unchanged while the burnable amount grows. During each upkeep cycle the Liquidizer checks whether its USDS balance is at least the amount recorded in usdsThatShouldBeBurned. If the balance is insufficient, the contract withdraws a percentage of its Protocol Owned Liquidity (POL) and swaps it for USDS so that the shortfall can be burned. Consequently, every repayment that does not actually increase the Liquidizer’s USDS balance forces the protocol to liquidate POL to cover the artificial deficit. An attacker can exploit this mismatch by repeatedly borrowing the maximum amount of USDS and immediately repaying it. Each repayment inflates usdsThatShouldBeBurned without providing any USDS to the Liquidizer, causing the contract to repeatedly withdraw and burn POL. Over many iterations the POL pool can be exhausted, leaving the protocol unable to cover bad debt generated by liquidations. This situation can depress the market price of USDS because the protocol loses the safety buffer normally provided by POL. The vulnerability was discovered during a formal audit when a test script performed a loop of borrow‑repay operations and observed that usdsThatShouldBeBurned grew far beyond the Liquidizer’s actual USDS balance, eventually causing the POL withdrawal logic to fail. The bug is subtle because the repayment transaction succeeds and the transferred USDS appears in the USDS contract, so users see no immediate error; the internal accounting mismatch is hidden from external observers, making the drain of liquidity difficult to detect during normal operation. To remediate the issue the repayment flow must be corrected so that the repaid USDS are sent directly to the Liquidizer, or the accounting logic must be adjusted to decrement usdsThatShouldBeBurned when USDS are transferred elsewhere. Aligning the token flow with the burn accounting eliminates the unnecessary POL liquidation and restores the protocol’s ability to cover bad debt.

title: H-01 | Compounding Rewards Dilutes Rewards For Others
content: The vulnerability is an economic flaw in the reward distribution mechanism where rewards are not locked for the duration of the staking lock period and can be claimed at any time. Because the contract calculates each participant’s share of the reward pool based on the current total supply of staked tokens, a user who holds a large proportion of the total supply can repeatedly claim their accrued rewards, immediately restake those rewards (or swap them into the staking token) while their original stake remains locked for the 13‑week period. This continuous compounding increases the attacker’s relative share of the pool, causing the effective reward per token for all other participants to shrink. The root cause is the absence of a snapshot or lock on the reward balance during the reward interval, allowing the reward‑to‑stake ratio to be manipulated after each claim. An attacker can exploit the flaw by: (1) staking a large amount, (2) waiting for rewards to accrue, (3) claiming the rewards before the lock expires, (4) immediately restaking or swapping the claimed tokens back into the staking token, and (5) repeating the cycle throughout the reward period. Each iteration inflates the attacker’s share of the total supply, thereby diluting the rewards that are distributed to honest stakers. The impact is a disproportionate allocation of the fixed reward pool: honest users receive less than the proportionate amount they expect, potentially seeing their pending rewards drop to near zero while the attacker’s earnings grow dramatically. This situation occurs whenever the reward token is the same as the staking token or can be converted to it, and when the protocol permits reward claims before the end of the lock period. All participants in the pool, the protocol’s reputation for fair reward distribution, and any downstream applications that rely on predictable yields are affected. The issue was identified during a manual audit that examined the reward accounting logic and noticed that the contract does not enforce a claim‑after‑lock rule. It can be hard to notice because the contract still emits correct reward events and the attacker’s activity looks like normal claiming and staking, while the cumulative effect on other users’ balances is only visible over the full reward period. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a normal accrual of rewards, but after the attacker’s repeated compounding the displayed pending reward for other users may suddenly shrink or disappear, contradicting the expectation that rewards are proportional to stake. To remediate the flaw the protocol should either lock rewards until the end of the lock period, use a snapshot of total supply taken at the start of the reward interval to compute shares, or prohibit restaking of claimed rewards within the same reward window. Any of these approaches would prevent the attacker from inflating their share and restore fair, predictable reward distribution.
summary:
In the rewards system, rewards are not locked and can be claimed at any point in time, even if the user's staking tokens are locked for the 13 week period.
A user with a large portion of the totalSupply may continuously claim their rewards and lock those tokens to gain an even greater portion, whether it be directly staking if the reward token matches the staking token, or with a swap to the staking token from the reward token.
This will ultimately dilute the rewards for other users in the reward period while massively swaying the rewards towards themselves.
The change in distribution is at the expense of other staked users, as there is a set amount to be distributed and the final rewards are dramatically skewed towards the user due to their continuous compounding while other staked users have their rewards fractionalized.

title: A locked fighter can be transferred; leads to game server unable to commit transactions, and unstoppable fighters
content: The contract implements a rule that fighters locked in a battle may not be transferred to another address. This rule is enforced in the overridden transferFrom and safeTransferFrom functions by calling an internal check _ableToTransfer before performing the token movement. However, the contract inherits OpenZeppelin’s ERC721 implementation, which also provides a public safeTransferFrom function that accepts an additional bytes data argument. Because the developer did not override this four‑parameter version, the function remains available without the custom transferability guard. As a result, a malicious or careless user can invoke safeTransferFrom(address from,address to,uint256 tokenId,bytes data) and move a locked fighter despite the intended restriction. The root cause is an incomplete override of all ERC721 transfer entry points, leaving an unchecked transfer path. Exploitation consists of calling the inherited safeTransferFrom with any data payload, bypassing the _ableToTransfer check, and causing the fighter to change ownership while still marked as locked. When the game server later attempts to process a battle outcome involving that fighter, it may be unable to commit the transaction because the fighter’s state no longer matches the server’s expectations. This leads to several observable impacts: the server stalls on win or loss resolution, the transferred fighter becomes “unstoppable” – a losing transaction cannot be finalized – and the fighter can be used as a “poison pill” to block another player’s progress. From a user perspective the affected player may see their fighter disappear from their inventory or appear in another wallet without consent, and the game may refuse to execute actions involving that fighter, producing error messages or silent failures. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the contract’s transfer functions and noticed that the four‑parameter safeTransferFrom was not overridden. It is easy to miss because the function signature differs only by an extra data parameter, which is often overlooked when reviewing inheritance hierarchies. To remediate the problem, the contract should either override the full safeTransferFrom with data and enforce the same _ableToTransfer check, or move the transferability validation into a universal hook such as _beforeTokenTransfer that is executed for every transfer path. By ensuring that every possible ERC721 transfer entry point respects the lock condition, the invariant that locked fighters cannot be moved is restored and the game server can reliably commit battle outcomes.
summary:
```solidity
FighterFarm` contract implements restrictions on the transferability of fighters in functions [transferFrom()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-02-ai-arena/blob/70b73ce5acaf10bc331cf388d35e4edff88d4541/src/FighterFarm.sol#L338-L348) and [safeTransferFrom()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-02-ai-arena/blob/70b73ce5acaf10bc331cf388d35e4edff88d4541/src/FighterFarm.sol#L355-L365), via the call to function [_ableToTransfer()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-02-ai-arena/blob/70b73ce5acaf10bc331cf388d35e4edff88d4541/src/FighterFarm.sol#L539-L545). Unfortunately this approach doesn’t cover all possible ways to transfer a fighter: The `FighterFarm` contract inherits from OpenZeppelin’s `ERC721` contract, which includes the public function [safeTransferFrom(…, data)](https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts/blob/ecd2ca2cd7cac116f7a37d0e474bbb3d7d5e1c4d/contracts/token/ERC721/ERC721.sol#L175-L183), i.e. the same as `safeTransferFrom()` but with the additional `data` parameter. This inherited function becomes available in the `GameItems` contract, and calling it allows us to circumvent the transferability restriction. As a result, a player will be able to transfer any of their fighters, irrespective of whether they are locked or not. Violation of such a basic system invariant leads to various kinds of impacts, including:

  * The game server won’t be able to commit some transactions;
  * The transferred fighter becomes unstoppable (a transaction in which it loses can’t be committed);
  * The transferred fighter may be used as a “poison pill” to spoil another player, and prevent it from leaving the losing zone (a transaction in which it wins can’t be committed).

Both of the last two impacts include the inability of the game server to commit certain transactions, so we illustrate both of the last two with PoCs, thus illustrating the first one as well.
```

title: Non-transferable `GameItems` can be transferred with `GameItems::safeBatchTransferFrom
content: The vulnerability is a missing business‑rule enforcement in the batch transfer function of an ERC1155‑style GameItems contract. The contract defines a boolean attribute called transferable for each item type and correctly checks this flag in the single‑item safeTransferFrom implementation, reverting when an item is marked non‑transferable. However, the safeBatchTransferFrom function is not overridden to perform the same check, and the internal _safeBatchTransferFrom routine also lacks a requirement that each id being transferred is marked transferable. As a result, an attacker or any user can call safeBatchTransferFrom with a list that includes non‑transferable item IDs and the call will succeed, moving items that were intended to be locked. The root cause is the omission of the transferable flag verification in the batch transfer path, which violates the contract’s intended accounting logic that certain game assets cannot change owners. Exploitation is straightforward: a user first marks an item as non‑transferable via adjustTransferability(false) and then invokes safeBatchTransferFrom with that item’s id. The transaction does not revert, the balances are updated, and the item appears in the recipient’s account. From the user’s point of view the expected behaviour is a revert and the item staying in the original wallet, but instead the balance becomes zero for the sender and the item shows up for the receiver, effectively “funds disappear” from the sender and appear elsewhere. This issue was discovered during a security audit when a test case demonstrated that safeTransferFrom correctly reverted while safeBatchTransferFrom transferred the same non‑transferable token. The bug can be hard to notice because developers often assume that ERC1155’s batch function inherits all checks from the single‑transfer implementation, overlooking the need to duplicate custom business rules. The impact is high: it breaks the game’s economic model, allows unauthorized redistribution of locked assets, and could be abused to steal or manipulate in‑game items. The proper fix is to override safeBatchTransferFrom (or the internal _safeBatchTransferFrom) and insert a require statement that checks the transferable flag for each id before performing the balance updates, thereby ensuring that the same restriction applies to both single and batch transfers.
summary: The `GamesItems` contract fails to appropriately override and include essential checks within the `safeBatchTransferFrom` function, enabling the transfer of non-transferrable Game Items.

title: Players have complete freedom to customize the fighter NFT when calling `redeemMintPass` and can redeem fighters of types Dendroid and with rare attributes
content: The vulnerability resides in the redeemMintPass function of the FighterFarm contract, which allows a holder of a mint‑pass NFT to supply arbitrary fighter type identifiers and DNA strings when burning the pass for a new fighter NFT. Because the contract does not bind the mint‑pass token to a predefined set of fighter properties, the caller can choose any fighter type supported by the system – for example, the value 1 corresponds to the Dendroid class – and can also provide a DNA value that was previously observed to generate rare physical attributes. The attribute generation logic in AiArenaHelper is deterministic, meaning that supplying the same DNA input reproduces the same rarity profile. Consequently, a malicious player can copy DNA values from earlier transactions that produced rare fighters and reuse them in redeemMintPass, obtaining additional rare NFTs at no cost. This breaks the sponsor’s expectation that players should not be able to customise fighter properties during redemption and undermines the intended scarcity model of the game. The flaw is triggered whenever redeemMintPass is called; there is no signature verification or other integrity check to ensure that the fighter type and DNA match the original mint‑pass metadata. Any user who possesses a valid mint‑pass can exploit the issue, leading to an unfair advantage, inflation of rare NFTs, and potential loss of revenue or trust for the protocol. The problem was discovered during a security audit when the auditors crafted a test that passed a custom fighterTypes array containing the Dendroid identifier and reused a known rare DNA string, resulting in successful minting of a rare fighter. The issue is subtle because the function’s purpose – burning a pass and minting a fighter – appears benign, and the deterministic attribute generation is not obvious from the external interface. To remediate, the contract should cryptographically bind the mint‑pass to the exact fighter properties that the holder is entitled to, for example by requiring a signed claim that includes the allowed fighter type and DNA, similar to the existing claimFighters implementation. This would prevent users from arbitrarily selecting types or copying rare DNA values, restoring the intended economic model and protecting users from receiving unexpected or overly powerful NFTs.
summary:
The function [redeemMintPass](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-02-ai-arena/blob/cd1a0e6d1b40168657d1aaee8223dc050e15f8cc/src/FighterFarm.sol#L233-L262) allows burning multiple mint passes in exchange for fighters’ NFTs. It is mentioned by the sponsor that the player should not have a choice of customizing the fighters’ properties and their type. However, nothing prevents a player from:

  1. Providing `uint8[] fighterTypes` of values `1` to mint fighters of types _Dendroid_.
  2. Checking previous transactions in which the [`dna` provided](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-02-ai-arena/blob/cd1a0e6d1b40168657d1aaee8223dc050e15f8cc/src/FighterFarm.sol#L237) led to minting fighters with rare physical attributes, copying those Dnas and passing them to the [redeemMinPass](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-02-ai-arena/blob/cd1a0e6d1b40168657d1aaee8223dc050e15f8cc/src/FighterFarm.sol#L237) to mint fighters with low rarity attributes. That is because creating physical attributes is [deterministic](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-02-ai-arena/blob/cd1a0e6d1b40168657d1aaee8223dc050e15f8cc/src/AiArenaHelper.sol#L83-L121), so providing the same inputs leads to generating a fighter with the same attributes.

title: Since you can reroll with a different fighterType than the NFT you own, you can reroll bypassing maxRerollsAllowed and reroll attributes based on a different fighterType
content: The vulnerability resides in the reRoll function of the fighter NFT contract. The function accepts a fighterType parameter supplied by the caller but does not verify that this parameter matches the actual type of the token identified by tokenId. Because the contract stores the allowed number of rerolls in a mapping keyed by fighterType, an attacker who owns a token of one type can pass the fighterType of another type that has a higher maxRerollsAllowed value. The require check therefore compares the token's current reroll count against a larger limit, allowing the attacker to exceed the intended maximum number of rerolls. After the payment is processed the contract calls internal routines that generate element, weight and physical attributes based on the supplied fighterType. Consequently the token can receive attributes that are calculated with the rules of a different class, such as a rarer element or a different generation weight. This flaw originates from missing validation of the relationship between tokenId and fighterType, an instance of improper input validation that breaks business logic. Exploitation is straightforward: the token owner calls reRoll repeatedly until the stored count reaches the original limit, then invokes reRoll once more with the alternate fighterType, causing numRerolls to increase beyond the intended cap and causing the token's attributes to be overwritten with values that would not be possible for its original class. The impact is that users can obtain more rerolls than the protocol permits and can artificially upgrade their NFTs, leading to an unfair advantage, potential devaluation of other tokens and disruption of the economic model that relies on rarity and generation constraints. The issue appears only when the contract owner has increased the maxRerollsAllowed for a particular fighterType, for example by incrementing the generation of that type. Any token holder of a different type can then exploit the mismatch. From a user perspective the symptom is that a token that should stop rerolling after a few attempts continues to accept reroll requests and suddenly shows an unexpected element or weight that does not match its class, contrary to the expectation that the NFT's attributes remain within its original tier. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that included a proof‑of‑concept test where the attacker called reRoll with a different fighterType and observed the counter exceed the limit and the attributes change. The problem is subtle because the function signature looks legitimate and the only visible check is the reroll count against a limit, which passes when the wrong type is supplied. To remediate the issue the contract should either remove the fighterType argument from reRoll and derive the type from the stored token data, or add an explicit require that the supplied fighterType matches the token's stored fighter type before checking the reroll limit and before invoking the attribute generation functions. This ensures that the business rules governing maxRerollsAllowed and attribute calculation are enforced consistently.
summary: Can reroll attributes based on a different fighterType, and can bypass maxRerollsAllowed.

title: Malicious user can stake an amount which causes zero curStakeAtRisk on a loss but equal rewardPoints to a fair user on a win
content: The vulnerability is a rounding precision bug that creates an asymmetric reward‑penalty relationship in the staking logic of the RankedBattle contract. The function that calculates the staking factor rounds a zero result up to one, while the function that determines the current stake at risk rounds the value down. When a user stakes an extremely small amount – for example one wei of the NRN token – the square‑root based staking factor evaluates to zero, is forced to one, and the subsequent calculation of curStakeAtRisk is rounded down to zero. As a result the user’s stake at risk becomes zero on a loss, meaning no tokens are transferred to the risk address, yet the same user receives the full amount of reward points that a normal participant would earn for a win. This discrepancy allows a malicious participant to accumulate ranking points without any financial exposure, effectively gaming the ELO system and undermining the economic incentives of the protocol. The issue manifests only for tiny stake amounts that are below the precision threshold of the fixed‑point arithmetic (less than 1e18 wei), which makes it easy to overlook during casual testing. It was discovered during a formal audit when test cases compared three staking scenarios and observed that a 1‑wei stake yielded the same reward points as a near‑full 4‑NRN stake while incurring no loss on defeat. The bug is hard to notice because the rounding logic appears harmless and small‑stake transactions are uncommon, so the zero‑loss outcome does not raise immediate alarms. The impact is that an attacker can inflate their reward points and potentially manipulate rankings or earn disproportionate rewards without risking capital, which can distort competition and reduce confidence in the protocol’s fairness. The affected parties include any user who can submit a stake, the protocol’s ranking mechanism, and any downstream contracts that rely on the integrity of reward distribution. To remediate, the contract should enforce a minimum stake amount (e.g., 4 NRN) and remove the artificial rounding‑up of the staking factor, instead requiring the computed factor to be strictly greater than zero. Additionally, the calculation of curStakeAtRisk must guarantee a non‑zero value whenever reward points are awarded, and any excess stake beyond the minimum could be returned to the user. These changes close the rounding loophole and restore a balanced risk‑reward model.
summary:
The [_getStakingFactor()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-02-ai-arena/blob/main/src/RankedBattle.sol#L530-L532) function rounds-up the `stakingFactor_` to one if its zero. Additionally, the [_addResultPoints()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-02-ai-arena/blob/main/src/RankedBattle.sol#L439) function rounds-down the `curStakeAtRisk`.  
Whenever a player loses and has no accumulated reward points, 0.1% of his staked amount is considered “at risk” and transferred to the `_stakeAtRiskAddress`. However due to the above calculation styles, he can stake just `1 wei` of NRN to have zero `curStakeAtRisk` in case of a loss and in case of a win, still gain the same amount of reward points as a player staking `4e18-1` wei of NRN.   

Let’s look at three cases of a player with ELO as 1500:

Case | Staked NRN | stakingFactor calculated by the protocol | Reward Points accumulated in case of a WIN | NRNs lost (stake at risk) in case of a LOSS  
---|---|---|---|---  
1 | 4 | 2 | 1500 | 0.004  
2 | 3.999999999999999999 | 1 | 750 | 0.003999999999999999  
3 | 0.000000000000000001 | 1 | 750 | 0  
  
As can be seen in Case 2 vs Case 3, a player staking `0.000000000000000001 NRN` (1 wei) has the same upside in case of a win as a player staking `3.999999999999999999 NRN` (4e18-1 wei) while their downside is `0`.

title: `FighterFarm::reRoll` won’t work for nft id greater than 255 due to input limited to uint8
content: FighterFarm::reRoll is intended to let the owner of a fighter NFT request a new random set of traits by paying a reroll cost. The function accepts the token identifier as a uint8 parameter. Because a uint8 can only represent values from 0 to 255, any NFT whose identifier is larger than 255 triggers a type‑conversion overflow when the caller passes the value. The Solidity runtime reverts the transaction with a panic error, so the require checks are never reached and the reroll logic is never executed. As a result, owners of higher‑indexed fighters cannot invoke the reRoll feature; their transactions fail, they lose the gas spent on the call, and the game’s promised ability to improve or refresh a fighter’s attributes is effectively unavailable for those tokens. The problem appears only after the collection grows beyond 255 items, which makes it easy to miss during early testing when all token IDs fit in the range. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the type of the tokenId argument with the type used elsewhere in the contract (ownerOf expects a uint256). The bug belongs to the class of integer‑size mismatches that cause denial‑of‑service or functionality loss.
