To fix the problem, the tokenId parameter should be changed to uint256 (or to the same unsigned integer type used throughout the contract) so that any valid token identifier can be passed without overflow. After the change, owners of any token, regardless of its numeric value, will be able to call reRoll, pay the reroll cost, and receive new traits as intended, restoring the expected user experience and preserving the economic model of the protocol.
summary: `FighterFarm::reRoll` uses uint8 for nft id as input, which will stop people calling this function who owns id greater than 255. It will lead to not being able to use the reRoll to get random traits, which could have been better for there game performance.

title: Fighters cannot be minted after the initial generation due to uninitialized `numElements` mapping
content: The contract defines a public mapping that stores the number of possible element types for each fighter generation. Only generation 0 is populated in the constructor, leaving every other generation with the default value of zero. When a new fighter is minted the contract reads this mapping to compute the element identifier by taking the DNA modulo numElements[generation]. Because the mapping entry for any generation beyond zero is zero, the modulo operation attempts to divide by zero, which Solidity treats as a panic and causes the transaction to revert. As a result, once the protocol tries to introduce a new generation of fighters, the minting function cannot succeed; users see transactions fail and no new fighters can be created. This effectively blocks the evolution of the game and can lock user funds that are sent for minting. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the initialization logic of the mapping. It is subtle because the mapping is public and appears to be correctly defined, yet the lack of initialization for later generations is not obvious without tracing the minting path. The bug belongs to the class of uninitialized state‑variable errors that lead to division‑by‑zero panics. From a user’s perspective the UI would show a “mint” button that appears to work, but the transaction reverts and the user receives no fighter and may lose the gas spent, creating a mismatch between the expectation of receiving a new NFT and the reality of getting nothing. The root cause is the missing setter or initialization for numElements for each new generation. To remediate, the contract should provide an admin‑only function that allows the number of elements to be set for any generation before minting, or initialize the mapping for all planned generations in the constructor, and include checks that prevent a zero value from being used in the modulo operation.

title: Player can mint more fighter NFTs during claim of rewards by leveraging reentrancy on the `claimRewards
content: The vulnerability is a reentrancy flaw in the reward‑claiming function of the fighting game contract. When a round ends, winners are allowed to call claimRewards to receive a fixed number of fighter NFTs. The function iterates over the list of rewards, mints an ERC‑721 token for each reward, and then updates a state variable that records how many rounds have been claimed. Because the mint operation triggers the ERC721Receiver callback on the recipient contract, a malicious winner that is itself a contract can execute additional calls to claimRewards from within onERC721Received before the original function finishes updating its bookkeeping. This re‑entry allows the attacker to repeat the mint loop multiple times for the same round, effectively inflating the number of NFTs received beyond the amount they are entitled to. The root cause is the classic checks‑effects‑interactions issue: the contract updates the claim‑tracking variable after performing an external call (the NFT mint), giving the external contract a window to re‑enter. The attack works only when the winner is a contract capable of receiving ERC‑721 tokens and invoking claimRewards again, and the number of possible re‑entries is bounded by the round identifier, which determines how many mint iterations are performed. In practice, an attacker can end up with, for example, seven NFTs when only three were owed, as demonstrated by the test suite. The impact is a distortion of the game’s economics: the attacker gains an unfair advantage, the total supply of fighter NFTs is artificially increased, and honest participants receive a smaller share of value. The issue was discovered during a security audit that included reentrancy testing; it is subtle because the minting logic appears internal and the state variable seems protected, yet the external callback provides an unexpected entry point. The bug belongs to the class of reentrancy vulnerabilities that arise from improper ordering of state updates and external calls. To remediate, the contract should follow the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern by updating the claim‑tracking state before invoking any external contract, or protect the function with a nonReentrant guard (e.g., OpenZeppelin’s ReentrancyGuard). This prevents the attacker’s contract from re‑entering claimRewards during the mint process, ensuring that each winner receives exactly the number of NFTs they earned and preserving the intended accounting of rewards.
summary:
When a fighting round ends, winners for the current round get picked and allocated respective rewards. These rewards are fighter NFTs that can be claimed by such winners. When you claim your rewards for a round or several rounds, the `numRoundsClaimed` state variable which stores the number of rounds you’ve claimed for gets updated to reflect your claim and each winner can only ever claim up to the amounts they win for each given round. That means if you try to batch-claim for two given rounds for which you won 2 fighter NFTs, your NFT count after the claim should be whatever your current balance of NFT is plus 2 fighter NFTs.

The issue here is that there’s a way to mint additional fighter NFTs on top of the fighter NFTs you’re owed for winning even though the `claimRewards` function has implemented a decent system to prevent over-claims. For one, it’s relatively complex to spoof a call pretending to be the `_mergingPoolAddress` to mint but a malicious user doesn’t need to worry too much about that to mint more fighters; they just need to leverage using a smart contract for engineering a simple reentrancy.

title: Holders array can be manipulated by transferring or burning with amount 0, stealing rewards or bricking certain functions
content: The vulnerability originates from the token contract’s _beforeTokenTransfer hook, which adds a recipient address to an internal holders array whenever the recipient’s balance is zero. The check does not consider the transfer amount, and the ERC20 standard permits transfers and burns with an amount of zero. Consequently, an attacker can invoke a zero‑value transferFrom or burn(0) to insert arbitrary addresses – including their own address multiple times or the zero address – into the holders list without changing any balances. During reward distribution, the contract iterates over the holders array and calculates each recipient’s entitlement based on their current token balance. Because duplicate entries cause the same address to be processed repeatedly, the attacker receives the full reward multiple times, effectively stealing funds that should be shared with other legitimate holders. In addition, populating the array with many zero‑address entries inflates its size, leading to out‑of‑gas reverts or complete failure of the distributeToAllHolders function, which constitutes a denial‑of‑service condition. The issue manifests whenever a zero‑amount transfer or burn is executed, which can happen at any time after a holder is approved. All token holders and the protocol’s reward mechanism are affected because the accounting invariant that each holder appears exactly once in the array is broken. The flaw was discovered during a security audit by inspecting the _beforeTokenTransfer implementation and confirming that zero‑value operations are allowed; a proof‑of‑concept test demonstrated duplicate entries and a reverted distribution call. The problem is subtle because zero‑value transfers do not modify balances and therefore appear harmless in normal transaction logs, making the corruption of the holders list easy to overlook. To remediate, the hook should only push a new address when the transfer amount is greater than zero, the recipient is not the zero address, and the recipient is an approved holder; additional safeguards can prevent the zero address from ever being added. This class of bug is an array‑injection or state‑corruption issue caused by improper handling of zero‑value token operations, violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions that each holder receives a single, proportional reward. From a user’s perspective the symptoms include receiving more reward tokens than expected, seeing distribution transactions revert unexpectedly, or observing that other users receive no rewards while the attacker’s balance grows disproportionately.

title: `MagnetarMintXChainModule.sol`:`mintBBLendXChainSGL` can be used to manipulate user positions by abusing whitelist privileges
content: The vulnerability is an authorization bypass that stems from a whitelist‑based access control in the Magnetar cross‑chain modules. The internal _checkSender function only permits an operation when the caller is either the account owner or a contract that has been added to a trusted whitelist. Because the whitelist check is performed on the immediate caller (the USDO contract) and not on the user address embedded in the payload, a malicious actor can craft a cross‑chain compose message that specifies any victim address in the data.user field of the depositYBLendSGLLockXchainTOLP call. When the attacker invokes mintBBLendXChainSGL on chain A, the Magnetar contract forwards a message through the USDO contract to chain B, where the whitelisted USDO contract executes depositYBLendSGLLockXchainTOLP with the attacker‑chosen data.user. The victim must have previously granted the Magnetar contract allowance to move their tokens, so the call silently transfers tokens from the victim’s balance and alters their market position without any on‑chain signature from the victim. This can happen whenever a whitelisted contract is allowed to forward arbitrary payloads and the target function does not verify that data.user matches msg.sender or that the caller is authorized to act on behalf of that user. The impact is loss of tokens, unexpected zero balances, and corrupted loan or liquidity positions for any user whose allowance is in place, effectively breaking the protocol’s accounting guarantees. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the access‑control logic of cross‑chain functions and noticed that the whitelist check does not cascade to the user field inside the composed message, making the flaw subtle and easy to miss because the transaction appears to be initiated by a trusted contract. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after approving the protocol they may see their balance drop to zero or a loan position disappear even though they never submitted a withdrawal, violating the expectation that only they can move their assets. The bug belongs to the class of “privileged‑contract‑parameter‑tampering” or “whitelist abuse” vulnerabilities where a trusted contract can be tricked into acting on arbitrary accounts. To remediate, the contract should enforce that the user address in the payload equals msg.sender or is otherwise explicitly authorized, add a second‑level check inside the cross‑chain compose handling, and consider limiting or removing the blanket whitelist privilege for functions that move user funds.

title: Missing check on helper contract allows arbitrary actions and theft of assets
content: The vulnerability is an unchecked external contract reference in the MagnetarOptionModule's exitPositionAndRemoveCollateral function. The function receives a struct containing externalData, which includes addresses for bigBang, singularity and marketHelper. While bigBang and singularity are verified against a whitelist, marketHelper is never validated. As a result, an attacker can supply a malicious contract address as marketHelper. The malicious helper can craft arbitrary module and calldata payloads that are later passed to bigBang_.execute, which executes them without further verification because the call originates from the privileged Magnetar contract that already holds user allowances. By returning a borrow or removeCollateral payload targeting another user's position, the attacker can cause the Magnetar contract to transfer collateral or borrow USDO on behalf of the victim, effectively stealing assets. This occurs whenever a user calls exitPositionAndRemoveCollateral with any marketHelper address, and the contract assumes the helper is trustworthy. The impact is loss of collateral or unauthorized borrowing, leading to funds disappearing from the victim's account. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit that compared the handling of marketHelper across modules and noticed the missing whitelist check. The bug is hard to notice because other modules correctly whitelist marketHelper, giving a false sense of safety, and the execution path involves delegated calls that hide the origin of the payload. The proper mitigation is to enforce a whitelist or explicit validation of the marketHelper address before invoking its functions, and to consider additional checks on the generated calldata to ensure it does not perform unauthorized actions. This class of bug belongs to unchecked external contract references leading to arbitrary call injection, similar to delegatecall or multicall injection vulnerabilities. From a user perspective, a user may see their balance drop to zero or their collateral removed without any explicit transaction, expecting a repayment but receiving no funds. The protocol's business logic that assumes only approved helpers can construct market calls is violated, breaking accounting guarantees.

title: Absence of restrictions on the sender of the `twTAP.claimRewards`
content: The vulnerability resides in the reward‑claiming function of the twTAP contract. The function claimRewards(uint256 _tokenId, address _to) is intended to transfer the reward accrued by a specific position to a designated recipient. However, the function only verifies that the destination address _to is either the owner of the position or an address approved by the owner; it does not restrict who may invoke the function. Because the caller (msg.sender) is not checked, any external account can trigger the claim on behalf of any approved recipient. This missing access‑control creates a race condition: an attacker can observe a legitimate user’s workflow that first grants approval to the TapTokenReceiver contract and then expects the contract to call claimRewards on the destination chain. Between the approval transaction and the internal call that actually pulls the reward, the attacker can submit a separate transaction calling twTAP.claimRewards(_tokenId, TapTokenReceiver). By doing so the attacker forces the reward to be transferred to the TapTokenReceiver contract before the contract’s internal logic runs. When the contract later executes its internal _claimTwpTapRewardsReceiver function, the call to twTap.claimRewards returns zero for all reward amounts because the rewards have already been drained, leaving the intended receiver with no tokens and causing the reward tokens to become permanently locked in the contract. The issue manifests only when the permission‑granting step and the reward‑claiming step are executed in separate transactions, which is the case for cross‑chain messages that are composed of a permit message followed by a claim message. From a user’s perspective the UI will show that the reward balance is zero after the approval, even though the protocol reports that rewards were distributed. The impact is high because funds can be permanently lost for any user who relies on the cross‑chain claim flow, and the problem is difficult to notice because the contract does not emit an explicit error; it simply returns zero amounts. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the interaction between the TapTokenReceiver contract and the twTAP reward contract, revealing that the only guard in place is a check on the recipient address, not on the caller. The root cause is an absent sender restriction, which allows front‑running attacks. To remediate the issue the claimRewards function should enforce that the caller is authorized to claim on behalf of the position, for example by requiring that msg.sender has permission for the tokenId in addition to the _to address, or by redesigning the flow to use a pull‑based pattern where the contract itself initiates the claim after the approval is securely recorded. The proposed fix in the original report, which adds a _requireClaimPermission(msg.sender, _tokenId) check, is insufficient because in the intended usage msg.sender equals _to, so the same vulnerability persists. A robust solution must either bind the claim to the approved contract or employ a nonce/commit‑reveal scheme to prevent front‑running, ensuring that rewards cannot be intercepted and that users receive the amounts they expect.

title: Incorrect approval mechanism breaks all Magnetar functionality
content: The vulnerability consists of an approval mismatch in the Magnetar contract suite. Magnetar is designed to grant permission to external contracts so they can move tokens that Magnetar holds. Originally the external contracts used standard ERC20 approvals or YieldBox approvals, but a later refactor changed those contracts to rely on a custom permit function called permitC for token transfers. Magnetar was never updated to issue permitC approvals, and therefore continues to set only ERC20 allowances or YieldBox allowances. The root cause is a stale integration: the approval logic was not synchronized with the new token‑transfer interface of the dependent contracts. When Magnetar calls functions such as _depositYBLendSGL or _wrapSglReceipt, it sets an allowance for the target contract (Singularity or TOFT) using the old mechanism. The target contracts, however, attempt to pull tokens via permitC, which checks for a different kind of permission that Magnetar never granted. As a result, the token transfer calls revert or silently fail, breaking the entire workflow of the Magnetar system. This can be exploited by any user or contract that expects a successful deposit, wrap, or withdrawal; the operation will appear to succeed on the front‑end but the underlying token movement does not occur, leaving user balances unchanged. The impact is a denial‑of‑service style failure: users cannot deposit assets, cannot receive expected receipts, and may see their balances remain at zero despite successful transaction receipts. The condition under which the bug manifests is any interaction where Magnetar hands out an approval to a contract that now requires permitC – essentially all current Magnetar functionality. Affected parties include end‑users of the protocol, token holders, and the protocol itself because core financial flows are halted. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by manually inspecting the approval code paths and comparing them with the token‑transfer implementations of the target contracts. It is hard to notice because the contract does emit approval events that look correct, and the UI may report a successful transaction, yet the token movement never happens, creating a silent failure. To remediate, Magnetar must be refactored to issue permitC approvals wherever it currently uses ERC20 or YieldBox approvals, ensuring that the permission model matches the expectations of the dependent contracts. This class of bug falls under mismatched authorization interfaces, where an outdated approval mechanism is used after downstream contracts change their token‑transfer logic. From a user’s perspective, a deposit transaction may complete but the deposited amount does not appear in the protocol, the expected receipt token is not minted, or balances stay at zero, contradicting the expectation that “my funds are now in the system”. The failure violates the fundamental accounting assumption that an approved contract can move the specified tokens, leading to funds that appear to be locked or vanished from the user’s perspective.
summary:
The Magnetar contract hands out approvals to various contracts so that the target contracts can use any tokens held currently by the Magnetar contract.

The issue is that at some point of time, all the target contracts were refactored to use `permitC` to handle token transfers. However, this change wasn’t reflected in the Magnetar contracts. Thus, instead of handing out `permitC` approvals, Magnetar hands out normal ERC20 approvals or yieldbox approvals. This essentially breaks the whole system.

There are numerous instances of this in the codebase. Essentially, almost every approval in the Magnetar contract is incorrect. Below are some examples, however the entire codebase needs to be checked for approvals and corrected.

The `_depositYBLendSGL` function in `MagnetarAssetCommonModule.sol` contract gives approval to the singularity contract via yieldbox. However, if we check the `_addTokens` function in the singularity contract below, we see the token transfers actually take place via `pearlmit`/`permitC`.

```solidity
_setApprovalForYieldBox(singularityAddress, yieldBox_);
```

Since the Magnetar contract does not give `permitC` approval to the singularity contract, and instead only gives yieldbox approval, the singularity contract is unable to transfer tokens from the Magnetar contract.

Similarly, in the `_wrapSglReceipt` function, the Magnetar gives approval to the TOFT contract vie ERC20 approval:

```solidity
IERC20(sgl).approve(tReceiptAddress, fraction);
```

But if we check the TOFT contract, we see the tokens are transferred via `permitC` and not with the raw tokens:

Since the Magnetar contract does not hand out the `permitC` approvals, most of the token transfers via Magnetar will fail.

title: `_vested
content: The vulnerability is an over‑vesting arithmetic error in the internal _vested function of a token vesting contract. The function is intended to compute the maximum claimable amount for a beneficiary based on the total allocation, the vesting start time, the cliff, the duration and an optional initial unlock time offset. The root cause is that the check which determines whether the schedule is fully vested does not incorporate the __initialUnlockTimeOffset value. The code uses the condition block.timestamp >= _start + _duration to decide that the entire amount is vested, but _start has been later adjusted by subtracting the offset for the partial‑vesting calculation. Consequently, when the current block timestamp falls in the interval between (_start - __initialUnlockTimeOffset + _duration) and (_start + _duration) the function treats the schedule as still partially vested and applies the linear formula (_totalAmount * (block.timestamp - _start)) / _duration. Because _start is smaller by the offset, the numerator becomes larger than intended, producing a result that can exceed the original _totalAmount. An example with _totalAmount 500, duration 1000, __initialUnlockTimeOffset 100, start 1000 and block.timestamp 1999 yields a calculated vested amount of 549.5, which is 49.5 tokens more than the maximum entitlement. An attacker or any user can exploit this by invoking the claim function after the offset‑adjusted vesting period but before the original end time, thereby receiving more tokens than they are entitled to. The impact is inflation of the token supply, loss of economic guarantees, and potential depletion of protocol funds. The bug manifests only when an initial unlock offset is configured and the timestamp is in the narrow window described, making it easy to miss in standard testing that focuses on pre‑cliff, fully vested, and normal linear periods. It was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where the logical inconsistency between the offset handling and the fully‑vested check was identified. The issue is hard to notice because the formula appears mathematically correct in isolation and the off‑by‑offset condition only affects a specific edge case. To remediate, the fully‑vested condition must be updated to include the offset, i.e., block.timestamp >= _start - __initialUnlockTimeOffset + _duration, ensuring that once the adjusted schedule has elapsed the function returns exactly _totalAmount and never exceeds it. This correction aligns the accounting logic with the intended business rule that no user can claim more than the total allocated amount, preserving token economics and protocol safety.

title: Attacker can use `MagnetarAction.OFT` action of the Magnet to perform operations as any user including directly stealing user tokens
content: The vulnerability is a combination of two access‑control flaws in the Magnetar contract that together allow an attacker to act as any user and steal tokens or collateral. First, the internal function that processes cross‑chain OFT actions does not verify that the calldata supplied matches the expected function signatures of the target contract; it only checks that the target address is present in the Cluster whitelist. Because of this missing selector validation, an attacker can craft an OFT action that calls any whitelisted contract with arbitrary data, effectively bypassing the intended permission model. Second, the Magnetar contract itself is added to the same whitelist, which means that when Magnetar calls itself the msg.sender of the sub‑call is also a whitelisted address. The internal _checkSender routine only reverts when the caller is not the whitelisted sender, so a self‑call skips this check and allows the attacker to supply a victim’s address as the logical sender without triggering a revert. By exploiting these two weaknesses, an attacker can construct a payload where the withdraw flag is set, causing the collateralWithdrawReceiver to be the Magnetar contract itself, and then direct the subsequent cross‑chain withdrawal to an address under the attacker’s control. The result is that user‑deposited collateral or tokens are transferred to the attacker’s wallet on the destination chain, while the victim sees their balance drop to zero and receives no refund. This issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit when an integration test revealed that Magnetar was unintentionally whitelisted, and the missing function‑selector check was identified as a logical flaw. The bug is hard to notice because the whitelist check passes and the call appears legitimate, masking the unauthorized behavior. To remediate, the contract should enforce explicit validation of allowed function selectors for OFT operations, exclude the Magnetar address from the whitelist, and add a strict check that the logical sender matches an authorized user or is explicitly approved. In broader terms, the problem belongs to the class of improper access control combined with unchecked external calls, where whitelist misconfiguration and absent calldata validation enable arbitrary code execution and fund theft, violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions and user expectations of safe cross‑chain transfers.

title: Incorrect math means `data.removeAndRepayData.removeAssetFromSGL` will never work once SGL has accrued interest
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect mathematical conversion used when a user attempts to remove assets from the Singularity (SGL) module. The contract computes a share value by converting the desired withdrawal amount to YieldBox shares with a rounding‑down operation, then passes that share directly to Singularity’s removeAsset function, which expects a fraction of the total assets rather than a raw share count. Because the fraction is calculated against the sum of the current elastic balance and the shares representing borrowed interest, any accrued interest changes the denominator, causing the share value to be too low. As a result, once Singularity has generated any interest, the removeAsset call no longer removes the intended amount; it may remove nothing or an amount far smaller than requested. This occurs under the condition that the protocol has performed any operation that adds interest to the total borrow elastic, which modifies the internal accounting used for the fraction calculation. Users attempting to withdraw after interest accrual experience a mismatch between the amount they expect and the amount actually transferred, often seeing a zero or unexpectedly reduced balance while the transaction reports success. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by analysing the _removeAsset internal logic and testing scenarios where interest accrues, revealing that the fraction and share values diverge after a few interest‑generating operations. The bug is subtle because initial withdrawals may appear correct due to rounding coincidences, making it hard to notice until interest accumulates. It belongs to the class of accounting or rounding bugs where a value representing a proportion is incorrectly derived from a discrete token count, violating the protocol’s financial invariants and breaking the guarantee that users can retrieve their deposited assets. To remediate, the contract should compute the correct fraction using the dedicated getFractionForAmount helper (or an equivalent precise conversion) and ensure that the value passed to removeAsset matches the expected unit, handling rounding edge cases appropriately. This fix restores the alignment between requested withdrawal amounts and the internal accounting, allowing users to reliably withdraw their funds after interest accrues.
summary:
The code to remove shares from Singularity is as follows:

```solidity
singularity_.removeAsset(data.user, removeAssetTo, share);
```

Where `share` is computed in this way:

```solidity
uint256 share = yieldBox_.toShare(_assetId, _removeAmount, false);
```

The line is calculating: The (incorrectly rounded down) amount of shares of Yieldbox to burn in order to withdraw from Yieldbox the `_removeAmount`.

But the code is calling:

`singularity_.removeAsset(data.user, removeAssetTo, share);`

This is asking Singularity to remove a % (part) of the total assets in Singularity. Due to this, the line will stop working as soon as singularity has had any operation that generated interest.

title: `IMarket.execute.selector`, `_checkSender` bypass allows to execute arbitrary operations
content: The contract exposes an execute function that is intended to be callable only by a privileged entity called Magnetar. Before performing the requested operation, the function extracts an address from the supplied calldata (using abi.decode on bytes 4‑36) and compares it with msg.sender via an internal _checkSender routine. Because the calldata slice is interpreted incorrectly, an attacker can craft a payload where the decoded address exactly matches the caller’s address, thereby satisfying the require(msg.sender == entry) check without actually being Magnetar. This flaw allows any external account that can construct such a payload to bypass the sender verification and invoke execute with arbitrary parameters. In practice the attacker can encode a function selector followed by a 32‑byte word that contains their own address, making the length of the calldata equal to the address value, which satisfies the check. Once the check is bypassed, the attacker can call execute to perform any market operation that Magnetar is authorized to perform, such as transferring tokens that have been approved to the contract. The impact is the potential theft of any token balances that the contract can move, effectively allowing funds to disappear from users or other participants. The vulnerability manifests whenever execute is called with crafted calldata; it does not depend on the specific token or market state, only on the ability to supply the malformed calldata. It affects all users whose assets are managed by the market, the protocol’s integrity, and any role that relies on Magnetar’s exclusive authority. The issue was discovered during a security audit when the auditors noticed that the calldata slicing logic did not enforce the intended sender restriction and could be manipulated. Because the check appears to compare a decoded address with msg.sender, developers may assume it is safe, making the bug subtle and easy to overlook. The correct mitigation is to remove the execute command from the set of publicly reachable commands or to replace the address‑based check with a robust authentication mechanism that cannot be satisfied by crafted calldata, such as using msg.sender directly without decoding, or employing signature‑based authorization. In summary, the bug is a sender‑validation bypass that enables arbitrary execution of privileged operations, leading to unauthorized token transfers and loss of funds, and it belongs to the class of improper input validation and access‑control flaws.
summary: Because of an incorrect interpretation of `calldata` for the `execute` signature, we are able to bypass the `_checkSender` and perform arbitrary `execute` operations as Magnetar.

title: Funds can be stolen through remote transfer functionality
content: The vulnerability is an authorization bypass in the cross‑chain remote‑transfer flow of the TapiocaOmnichainSender/Receiver contracts. When a user composes a message, the encoding routine stores the original msg.sender as srcChainSender_ inside the payload. Later, on the destination chain, the receiver extracts this srcChainSender_ value and uses it as the owner of the funds for a remote‑transfer operation (MSG_REMOTE_TRANSFER). The contract assumes that srcChainSender_ is the legitimate initiator and therefore skips the usual allowance check when the owner equals srcChainSender_. An attacker can craft a composed message that declares a victim’s address as the owner while sending a zero amount in the first hop, which passes the transfer validation. Because srcChainSender_ is now the victim, the subsequent composed call can transfer the victim’s entire token balance to the attacker without any approval. This exploit can be triggered whenever a user is allowed to include an arbitrary composed message with a remote‑transfer operation, and it does not require any special privileges. The impact is that tokens held by an honest user on one chain can be silently moved to the attacker’s address on another chain, resulting in loss of funds and a mismatch between the UI balance (showing a sudden zero or reduced balance) and the expected accounting. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by analysing the message‑encoding logic and noticing that srcChainSender_ is taken from msg.sender without further verification, a subtle flaw that can be missed by standard tests because a zero‑amount transfer appears harmless. The bug belongs to the class of cross‑chain authentication errors where user‑controlled data is trusted for permission checks, effectively breaking the business rule that only the token owner or an approved spender may move funds. From a user perspective, the symptom is an unexpected disappearance of tokens after initiating a cross‑chain operation, with no error message. The correct mitigation is to pass the true initiator address to the internal remote‑transfer function and enforce allowance checks against that address, or to validate that srcChainSender_ matches msg.sender before using it for privileged actions. This ensures that only the actual caller can authorize a remote transfer and restores the intended accounting guarantees across chains.
summary:
User can send LZ message through any `Oft` token using the `TapiocaOmnichainSender.sendPacket` function. User provides params that should be used and also provides [composed message](https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapioca-periph/blob/032396f701be935b04a7e5cf3cb40a0136259dbc/contracts/tapiocaOmnichainEngine/TapiocaOmnichainSender.sol#L57C75-L57C86) if he needs to send it.

What is important for composed message is [during crafting message](https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapioca-periph/blob/032396f701be935b04a7e5cf3cb40a0136259dbc/contracts/tapiocaOmnichainEngine/BaseTapiocaOmnichainEngine.sol#L166-L172), `msg.sender` is stored as `srcChainSender_`. In this way we know who have triggered composed call.

```solidity
function encode(
    bytes32 _sendTo,
    uint64 _amountShared,
    bytes memory _composeMsg
) internal view returns (bytes memory _msg, bool hasCompose) {
    hasCompose = _composeMsg.length > 0;
    // @dev Remote chains will want to know the composed function caller ie. msg.sender on the src.
    _msg = hasCompose
        ? abi.encodePacked(_sendTo, _amountShared, addressToBytes32(msg.sender), _composeMsg)
        : abi.encodePacked(_sendTo, _amountShared);
}
```

The amount that should be sent to other chain is burnt (if any) and LZ call [is sent](https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapioca-periph/blob/032396f701be935b04a7e5cf3cb40a0136259dbc/contracts/tapiocaOmnichainEngine/TapiocaOmnichainSender.sol#L73-L74). On another chain, the call will be handled [by `TapiocaOmnichainReceiver._lzReceive` function](https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapioca-periph/blob/032396f701be935b04a7e5cf3cb40a0136259dbc/contracts/tapiocaOmnichainEngine/TapiocaOmnichainReceiver.sol#L72C14-L72C24). This function [will mint tokens to recipient](https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapioca-periph/blob/032396f701be935b04a7e5cf3cb40a0136259dbc/contracts/tapiocaOmnichainEngine/TapiocaOmnichainReceiver.sol#L85). If the composed message was included, then it will [sent it to endpoint](https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapioca-periph/blob/032396f701be935b04a7e5cf3cb40a0136259dbc/contracts/tapiocaOmnichainEngine/TapiocaOmnichainReceiver.sol#L93-L98), so it can be triggered later.

When composed message is triggered, then [`lzCompose` function](https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapioca-periph/blob/032396f701be935b04a7e5cf3cb40a0136259dbc/contracts/tapiocaOmnichainEngine/TapiocaOmnichainReceiver.sol#L120C14-L120C23) handles it. As you can see, the function retrieves `srcChainSender_` to know who was initiator of compose call on source chain. Then [`_lzCompose` function](https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapioca-periph/blob/032396f701be935b04a7e5cf3cb40a0136259dbc/contracts/tapiocaOmnichainEngine/TapiocaOmnichainReceiver.sol#L139) continue processing of message.

Using [`msgType`](https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapioca-periph/blob/032396f701be935b04a7e5cf3cb40a0136259dbc/contracts/tapiocaOmnichainEngine/TapiocaOmnichainReceiver.sol#L148C17-L148C25) user can provide operation he wants to execute on target chain. One of operations [is `MSG_REMOTE_TRANSFER`](https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapioca-periph/blob/032396f701be935b04a7e5cf3cb40a0136259dbc/contracts/tapiocaOmnichainEngine/TapiocaOmnichainReceiver.sol#L154) that allows to remotely send tokens to another chain. The flow is next: on chain A user initiates compose call to chain B, that will send his tokens on chain B to chain A, or will use allowance to send tokens of other user on chain B to chain A. Let’s check how it works.

First, the function should [transfer tokens from owner to `address(this)`](https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapioca-periph/blob/032396f701be935b04a7e5cf3cb40a0136259dbc/contracts/tapiocaOmnichainEngine/TapiocaOmnichainReceiver.sol#L218-L220). This function receives owner of funds and `_srcChainSender` as inputs [to check allowance](https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapioca-periph/blob/032396f701be935b04a7e5cf3cb40a0136259dbc/contracts/tapiocaOmnichainEngine/TapiocaOmnichainReceiver.sol#L287-L289). As you can see, in the case of if `_srcChainSender` is owner then we don’t need any approve.

After transfer is done to `address(this)` then the [contract can send them back to chain A](https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapioca-periph/blob/032396f701be935b04a7e5cf3cb40a0136259dbc/contracts/tapiocaOmnichainEngine/TapiocaOmnichainReceiver.sol#L223C9-L225). So the function [burns tokens](https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapioca-periph/blob/032396f701be935b04a7e5cf3cb40a0136259dbc/contracts/tapiocaOmnichainEngine/TapiocaOmnichainReceiver.sol#L250) and crafts message to another chain and it can have composed call again; which means that [it will include `_srcChainSender`](https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapioca-periph/blob/032396f701be935b04a7e5cf3cb40a0136259dbc/contracts/tapiocaOmnichainEngine/TapiocaOmnichainReceiver.sol#L266C96-L266C111), so the contract on chain A knows who initiated the call.

The problem is that `_srcChainSender` that will be included is [owner of funds on chain B](https://github.com/Tapioca-DAO/tapioca-periph/blob/032396f701be935b04a7e5cf3cb40a0136259dbc/contracts/tapiocaOmnichainEngine/TapiocaOmnichainReceiver.sol#L224C13-L224C37), which is incorrect.

Here’s the described attack flow:

1. Victim has funds on chain A, that attacker is going to steal to chain B.
2. Attacker on chain A initiates compose call with victim as owner of funds and provides amount `0` as amount to transfer of chain B.
3. Compose call succeed on chain B as it is possible to transfer `0` tokens and then another compose message was included, which transfers all tokens from victim to attacker on chain B.
4. Because `_srcChainSender` was set to victim on first compose call. Then the next compose call on chain A will think that victim is initiator of remote transfer, which means that no allowance will be checked.
5. Funds are stolen to attacker address on chain B.

title: Adversary can steal approved `tOLP`s to Magnetar via `_paricipateOnTOLP`
content: The vulnerability resides in the Magnetar contract’s internal function that processes participation on a tOLP NFT. The function accepts a user‑supplied token identifier and a lockDataTarget address, then calls the ERC‑721 approve method on the supplied lockDataTarget without verifying that the caller actually owns the specified tOLP token. Because there is no ownership check, an attacker who has not minted a tOLP NFT can supply any arbitrary token ID and a malicious lockDataTarget contract that implements approve without reverting even when the caller is not the token owner. The function then invokes the option broker’s participate method, which locks the supplied tOLP token and mints an oTAP NFT that is transferred to the attacker’s address. From the user’s perspective the expected behavior is that their tOLP NFT remains in their wallet after participation, while they receive an oTAP NFT as a reward. In practice the user’s original NFT disappears, the balance for that token becomes zero, and the attacker ends up holding the newly minted oTAP NFT. The impact is the loss of the user’s NFT, which may represent significant value, and a breach of the protocol’s accounting assumptions that a participant’s token cannot be transferred without explicit consent. The flaw occurs whenever the function is called with a zero‑minted tOLP state and an attacker can control the lockDataTarget parameter; the contract does not enforce that the supplied lockDataTarget corresponds to the actual ERC‑721 contract that holds the token. This issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by noticing the missing ownership verification before the approve call. It is hard to notice because the approve call succeeds silently and no explicit transfer event is emitted, so the UI may simply show that the participation succeeded while the original NFT silently vanishes. The recommended remediation is to add a check that the caller (or the supplied user address) is the current owner of the tOLP token ID before performing the approve, and to restrict or validate the lockDataTarget address so that only the legitimate ERC‑721 contract can be used. In broader terms, this is a classic missing access‑control bug on ERC‑721 token handling that allows unauthorized approval and subsequent transfer of assets.

title: Adversary can utilise approved to Magnetar `oTAP` and `tOLP` NFTs
content: The Magnetar contract is designed to let users batch calls to the Tapioca option broker and liquidity provision contracts by first granting the Magnetar contract allowance over their oTAP and tOLP NFTs. Inside Magnetar the private function _processTapTokenOperation checks only that the target contract is whitelisted and that the calldata matches one of a few permitted selector signatures, then forwards the call with _executeCall. Crucially the function does not verify that the caller of Magnetar actually owns the NFT referenced in the forwarded calldata. The underlying Tapioca contracts (for example the exerciseOption function) perform an ownership check against msg.sender, but when the call is proxied through Magnetar the msg.sender seen by the Tapioca contract is the Magnetar contract itself, which has been approved by the NFT owner. As a result any attacker who knows that a victim has approved Magnetar can craft a call to Magnetar that includes the victim’s token ID and cause the Tapioca contract to treat Magnetar as an authorized operator and execute the option exercise on the victim’s behalf. The attacker can therefore trigger an exercise of the victim’s option, withdraw the entitled tap amount, or otherwise manipulate the position without the victim’s consent. This vulnerability manifests whenever a user has granted Magnetar allowance over their NFTs, which is a normal prerequisite for legitimate batching. The impact is an unauthorized transfer of value: the victim loses the right to exercise the option, their eligible tap amount may be reduced to zero, and the protocol’s accounting of option positions becomes inconsistent. Users may notice that their option appears exercised in the UI, that their balance of eligible tap amount disappears, or that they receive an unexpected payment. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the proxy logic of Magnetar and identified the missing ownership check, a classic confused‑deputy or authorization‑bypass pattern where a privileged contract is used as a deputy without proper validation. The bug is hard to spot because the downstream contract’s own checks appear correct in isolation, and the proxy hides the fact that the effective caller is different. To remediate, Magnetar should enforce that the original caller is the owner of the NFT referenced in the calldata before forwarding the call, for example by querying the NFT contract’s ownerOf function or by requiring that the caller be the same address that approved the NFT. Adding this explicit access control eliminates the unauthorized use of approved NFTs and restores the intended security model.

title: Adversary can steal user’s NFT’s if they have set Magnetar as `isApprovedForAll == true`
content: The vulnerability is an authorization bypass that allows an attacker to steal ERC721 tokens when a user has granted the Magnetar contract universal approval (isApprovedForAll) for their NFTs. Magnetar is designed as a router that can execute a variety of permit operations, and its internal _processPermitOperation function accepts calldata for several selectors, including the ERC721.approve selector. The function only checks that the first argument decoded from the calldata matches msg.sender, assuming this argument represents the token owner. However, for ERC721.approve the first argument is the address to be approved, not the token owner. Consequently, an attacker can craft a permit call where the calldata encodes ERC721.approve(to=attacker, tokenId). Magnetar decodes the first argument, sees that it equals the attacker’s address, and the check passes. The contract then forwards the call to the NFT contract. Inside the ERC721 implementation, the require statement permits the call if the caller is either the token owner or an operator approved for all; because Magnetar is an approved operator for the victim, the internal check succeeds and the token is approved to the attacker. The attacker can then transfer the token out of the victim’s wallet. This exploit occurs whenever a user has set Magnetar as an operator for all of their NFTs, which is a common expectation for router contracts that need to manage multiple assets. The affected parties are any users who have granted Magnetar universal approval, the protocol that relies on Magnetar for asset management, and the NFTs themselves, which can be transferred without the owner’s consent. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit while reviewing the permit handling logic and noticing that ERC721.approve was treated as a safe operation despite its owner‑check semantics. The bug is subtle because approve is often considered a harmless permission change, and the whitelist check in Magnetar gives a false sense of security, making the flaw easy to overlook in testing. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are a missing NFT, a zero balance for a token that was never sold, or an unexpected approval shown in the UI, leading to confusion and potential financial loss. The vulnerability belongs to the class of improper authorization checks and privilege escalation through operator patterns. To remediate, the contract should reject any calldata that uses the ERC721.approve selector, or it should enforce that the caller of the permit operation is the actual token owner rather than an arbitrary address, thereby preventing operators from abusing the approve function to hijack tokens.

title: Exploitation of the receive Function to Steal Funds
content: The vulnerability is a reentrancy guard bypass in the WiseLending contract caused by the receive function resetting the internal sendingProgress flag that is used by the _sendValue helper to indicate an ongoing external ETH transfer. The syncPool modifier sets sendingProgress to true before the call and resets it to false after the call, intending to block re‑entrant calls while value is being sent. However, an attacker can trigger the receive fallback by sending a small amount of ETH directly to the contract (excluding transfers from the WETH address), which invokes _sendValue and clears the sendingProgress flag while a previous external call is still in progress. This allows the attacker to re‑enter functions protected by the syncPool guard, such as withdrawExactAmountETH. By re‑entering during the payout, the attacker first resets the guard, then calls paybackBadDebtForToken to settle their own loan that has become bad debt, earning a 5 % incentive and extracting the ETH that was just sent to them. The attack flow is: a user deposits ETH, borrows a portion, initiates withdrawExactAmountETH, the contract sends ETH via _sendValue, the attacker’s receive function is triggered with a tiny ETH transfer, sendingProgress is cleared, the attacker re‑enters and calls paybackBadDebtForToken, receives the borrowed amount plus incentive, the health check passes, and the original withdrawal completes, letting the attacker walk away with their original deposit plus the borrowed amount and incentive. The impact is that an attacker can effectively steal funds from the pool, receiving more ETH than they originally deposited, while the protocol’s accounting appears consistent because the health check runs after the external call. The condition occurs whenever the contract performs an external call that uses _sendValue, which is also used by the receive fallback for any plain ETH transfer that is not from the WETH address. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a successful withdrawal but the contract’s total ETH balance is reduced, leading to missing liquidity or unexpected zero balances. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the syncPool reentrancy modifier and traced the state changes of sendingProgress across the receive fallback. It is hard to notice because the reentrancy guard appears to be in place and the external call succeeds, while the guard variable is silently reset by a separate code path that is not obvious from the modifier alone. The bug belongs to the class of reentrancy guard bypasses where a secondary entry point resets the guard flag, allowing nested calls into protected functions. To remediate, the _sendValue helper should perform an explicit reentrancy check before modifying sendingProgress, or the receive function should be excluded from resetting the flag, ensuring that the guard remains set for the entire duration of the external transfer. In short, the contract’s accounting assumptions that a user’s position remains healthy after a withdrawal are violated because the attacker can manipulate the guard and extract additional value.

title: User can erase their position debt for free
content: The vulnerability originates from a missing validation in the routine that removes a token from a user's position. When a position is being reduced, the internal function _removePositionData receives a token address (_poolToken) and assumes that this token is present in the user’s token list. If the supplied token is not actually part of the position, the function still proceeds to delete the last entry in the list, because it only checks the length of the list and never confirms that the token matches. This flaw is triggered through the public entry point FeeManager.paybackBadDebtNoReward, which allows an attacker to specify any token and a share amount of zero. When the position has a non‑zero bad‑debt flag, the call reaches _corePayback, which subsequently invokes _removePositionData with the attacker‑chosen token. Because the position contains only one borrow token, the length‑equals‑one branch executes and the contract deletes the borrow record without verifying the token identity. As a result, the protocol’s accounting state is corrupted: the user’s debt entry is erased while the collateral remains, making the system believe the borrower has no outstanding liability. From a user perspective the symptom is that a large debt disappears instantly and the collateral appears free, contrary to the expectation that the debt must be repaid. The impact is severe – an attacker can effectively steal the borrowed amount, causing funds to disappear from the protocol and undermining trust in the lending platform. The issue occurs only when a position has bad debt, the attacker can call the payback function with an arbitrary token, and the position’s token list length is one. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the flow of payback functions and identified the lack of existence checks. The bug belongs to the class of improper input validation leading to state corruption, specifically a token‑removal logic error. It is hard to notice because the function appears to handle single‑token positions correctly, yet the missing check creates a silent state change without emitting an error. The correct mitigation is to verify that the token passed to _removePositionData is indeed present in the user’s token array and to revert the transaction if it is not, thereby preventing unauthorized deletion of debt records.
summary:
When the pool token stops being used in the position, the `_removePositionData` function is called. However, it assumes that `poolToken` that is passed as a parameter always exists in user token array, which is not always the case. In the case of function `FeeManager.paybackBadDebtNoReward()`, which indirectly calls `_removePositionData`, insufficient validation doesn’t check if repay token is in user array, which results in zeroing out information about user debt.

Free elimination of user debt.

title: Incorrect bad debt accounting can lead to a state where the `claimFeesBeneficial` function is permanently bricked and no new incentives can be distributed, potentially locking pending and future protocol fees in the `FeeManager` contract
content: The vulnerability originates from an inconsistency in the way the protocol records bad debt during partial liquidations. When a position becomes under‑collateralised, the global variable totalBadDebtETH is increased by the amount of newly created bad debt, while the per‑position mapping badDebtPosition is overwritten with only the most recent shortfall. Because liquidations can be partial, a position may incur bad debt several times; each liquidation adds to totalBadDebtETH but the mapping keeps only the last value, and it can even be reset to zero when the loan‑to‑value reaches exactly 100 %. The payback functions that reduce totalBadDebtETH are limited to the amount stored in badDebtPosition, so any excess “fake” bad debt that remains in the global counter can never be cleared. As a result, totalBadDebtETH stays greater than zero permanently. The contract contains a guard in claimFeesBeneficial that reverts with ExistingBadDebt whenever totalBadDebtETH is non‑zero, and the incentive distribution logic only runs when totalBadDebtETH equals zero. Consequently, once the accounting error occurs, beneficiaries and incentive owners are unable to claim protocol fees or rewards; calls to claimFeesBeneficial revert, and claimIncentives returns NoIncentive, leaving users with zero balances despite fees having been accrued. The issue was discovered during a formal audit and reproduced with a Forge test that simulates a market crash, partial liquidations, and subsequent fee claims. It is hard to notice because the global bad‑debt counter appears as a normal accounting figure and no user principal is lost; the symptom is a silent loss of yield and locked incentives. The bug affects the entire protocol, not just the liquidated position, because the global flag blocks fee distribution for all beneficiaries. The root cause is the failure to adjust totalBadDebtETH by the difference between the new and previous per‑position bad debt during liquidation, unlike the correct logic used in the fee‑manager helper when bad debt is repaid. A proper fix is to compute the delta between the newly calculated shortfall and the previously recorded badDebtPosition and apply that delta to totalBadDebtETH (increasing or decreasing as needed), ensuring that when a position’s bad debt is cleared or reduced, the global counter is updated accordingly. This restores the ability of the protocol to claim fees and distribute incentives once the bad‑debt state is accurate.

title: Liquidators can pay less than required to completely liquidate the private collateral balance of an uncollateralized position
content: The vulnerability originates from an incorrect handling of uncollateralized positions during liquidation. In the WiseLending protocol a user can separate his deposits into a private (pure) balance that is excluded from collateral calculations and a normal balance that can be used as collateral when the position is marked as collateralized. When a user explicitly uncollateralizes his position, only the private balance should be considered as collateral for liquidation. The contract computes the liquidation percentage based on the full collateral returned by getFullCollateralETH, which correctly reports only the private balance for an uncollateralized position. However, later in the internal function that determines the amount the liquidator receives, the same percentage is applied to both the private balance and the normal balance because the check for an uncollateralized flag is performed too late. As a result, the liquidator can claim a portion of the normal balance in addition to the private balance while only paying for the private portion. An attacker can trigger a liquidation on an uncollateralized, under‑collateralized position, set the removal percentage such that the calculated extra cash‑out from the normal balance is positive, and then drain the private balance without covering the full value of the assets taken. In practice a user may deposit equal amounts into private and normal balances, borrow against the private balance, and after a price move become liquidatable. The liquidator pays only the amount required to liquidate the private collateral (e.g., 50 % of the private balance) but receives an additional amount from the normal balance, effectively stealing funds. The impact is a loss of private funds for the user and an increase in protocol bad debt. The bug manifests only when a position is uncollateralized and liquidatable; collateralized positions are unaffected. It was discovered during a formal audit by reproducing the scenario in a unit test that showed the liquidator earning more than the amount paid. The issue is subtle because the liquidation percentage calculation appears correct and the extra cash‑out path is hidden behind internal bookkeeping, making it easy to overlook. The proper fix is to move the uncollateralized check to the beginning of the receive‑amount calculation so that the extra cash‑out logic is bypassed entirely for uncollateralized positions, ensuring that only the private balance can be reduced during liquidation.

title: Wrong use of `nftID` to check if a `PowerFarm` position is an Aave position
content: The vulnerability originates from an identifier mismatch in the PowerFarm contracts where the mapping that records whether a position is an Aave position (isAave) is keyed by the internal keyId of the PowerFarm NFT, but several functions mistakenly query this mapping using the external WiseLending nftId. The root cause is that the keyId, which is the index of the PowerFarm NFT, is linked to the WiseLending nftId through the farmingKeys mapping, yet the code continues to use the WiseLending nftId as the lookup key. This incorrect lookup causes the isAave flag to be read as false for genuine Aave positions, leading to a cascade of logical errors. When a user creates an Aave‑backed PowerFarm position, functions such as getLiveDebtRatio, manuallyPaybackShares, and the liquidation pathway retrieve zero borrow shares because they consult isAave with the wrong identifier. Consequently, the debt ratio reported to the user is zero, manual repayment attempts revert due to arithmetic underflow, and liquidation attempts revert with the custom DebtRatioTooLow error even though the position is technically eligible for liquidation. The impact affects any user holding an Aave PowerFarm position, the protocol’s accounting integrity, and liquidators who are unable to enforce collateral enforcement, potentially leaving funds locked or unaccounted for. The bug manifests only for Aave‑type positions; non‑Aave positions operate correctly, making the issue subtle and easy to miss during casual testing. It was discovered through targeted unit tests that exercised the Aave path, revealing zero ratios and revert patterns. The class of bug can be described as an identifier‑based mapping misuse or key mismatch, a common source of accounting failures in smart contracts. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are a debt ratio that reads zero, inability to manually repay borrowed shares, and liquidation transactions that fail with an unexpected error, contradicting the expectation that the protocol should allow repayment and liquidation. The fix consists of consistently using the internal keyId when accessing the isAave mapping across all affected functions, thereby aligning the logical flag with the correct position identifier and restoring correct borrow‑share calculations, repayment flows, and liquidation logic.
summary:
When a `PowerFarm` position is created its `keyId` is used as a key in the `isAave` mapping to indicate if it is an Aave position or not. The `keyId` is the index of the Power Farm NFT linked with the position.

[PendlePowerManager.sol#L129-L130](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-02-wise-lending/blob/79186b243d8553e66358c05497e5ccfd9488b5e2/contracts/PowerFarms/PendlePowerFarm/PendlePowerManager.sol#L129C1-L130C1)

```solidity
    isAave[keyId] = _isAave;
```

The `keyId` is also linked with another `nftId`. This other `nftId` is used to hold the `keyId`s Power Farm position in the `WiseLending` contract. They are linked together in the `farmingKeys` mapping of the `MinterReserver` contract.

[MinterReserver.sol#L88C1-L91C46](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-02-wise-lending/blob/79186b243d8553e66358c05497e5ccfd9488b5e2/contracts/PowerFarms/PowerFarmNFTs/MinterReserver.sol#L88C1-L91C46)

```solidity
    uint256 keyId = _getNextReserveKey();

    reservedKeys[_userAddress] = keyId;
    farmingKeys[keyId] = _wiseLendingNFT;
```

The issue is the check if a position is an Aave position is done using the `WiseLending` `nftId` instead of the Power Farm’s `keyId`. This occurs five times in the code:

It is used in `getLiveDebtRatio()` to know the pool token borrowed so the `borrowShares` can be retrieved.

[PendlePowerFarm.sol#L64-L70](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-02-wise-lending/blob/79186b243d8553e66358c05497e5ccfd9488b5e2/contracts/PowerFarms/PendlePowerFarm/PendlePowerFarm.sol#L64-L70)

```solidity
    uint256 borrowShares = isAave[_nftId]
        ? _getPositionBorrowSharesAave(
            _nftId
        )
        : _getPositionBorrowShares(
            _nftId
    );
```

It is used in `_manuallyPaybackShares()` to know the pool token to pay back.

[PendlePowerFarm.sol#L127-L129](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-02-wise-lending/blob/79186b243d8553e66358c05497e5ccfd9488b5e2/contracts/PowerFarms/PendlePowerFarm/PendlePowerFarm.sol#L127-L129)

```solidity
    if (isAave[_nftId] == true) {
        poolAddress = AAVE_WETH_ADDRESS;
    }
```

It is used in `checkDebtRatio()` to know the pool token borrowed so the `borrowShares` can be retrieved.

[PendlePowerFarmMathLogic.sol#L396-L402](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-02-wise-lending/blob/79186b243d8553e66358c05497e5ccfd9488b5e2/contracts/PowerFarms/PendlePowerFarm/PendlePowerFarmMathLogic.sol#L396-L402)

```solidity
    uint256 borrowShares = isAave[_nftId]
        ? _getPositionBorrowSharesAave(
            _nftId
        )
        : _getPositionBorrowShares(
            _nftId
    );
```

It is used in `_coreLiquidation()` to select a token to payback and to know the pool token borrowed so the `borrowShares` can be retrieved.

[PendlePowerFarmLeverageLogic.sol#L575-L590](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-02-wise-lending/blob/79186b243d8553e66358c05497e5ccfd9488b5e2/contracts/PowerFarms/PendlePowerFarm/PendlePowerFarmLeverageLogic.sol#L575-L590)

```solidity
    address paybackToken = isAave[_nftId] == true
        ? AAVE_WETH_ADDRESS
        : WETH_ADDRESS;

    paybackAmount = WISE_LENDING.paybackAmount(
        paybackToken,
        _shareAmountToPay
    );

    uint256 cutoffShares = isAave[_nftId] == true
        ? _getPositionBorrowSharesAave(_nftId)
            * FIVTY_PERCENT
            / PRECISION_FACTOR_E18
        : _getPositionBorrowShares(_nftId)
            * FIVTY_PERCENT
            / PRECISION_FACTOR_E18;
```

These have the following effects:

* For `getLiveDebtRatio()`, users would get zero when they try to retrieve their debt ratio.
* For `_manuallyPaybackShares()` users won’t be able to pay back their shares manually from the `PowerFarm` contract since it’ll fetch zero shares as borrow shares.
* The last two instances are used in liquidation and allow a malicious user to have a position that can’t be liquidated even though it is eligible for liquidation. The malicious user can:

  1. Create an Aave `PowerFarm` position.
  2. The position becomes eligible for liquidation after some price changes.
  3. Liquidators cannot liquidate the position because the call to `_coreLiquidation` first calls `checkDebtRatio()` which uses the wrong `borrowShares` to calculate the debt ratio and returns true. Thus, causing a revert.

        revert DebtRatioTooLow();

title: H-01 | Weth Transferred From The Wrong Address
content: During execution of the Router contract's createPoolETH function, the implementation first calls the WETH contract's deposit() method, sending the native Ether supplied by the caller and receiving an equivalent amount of WETH that is held by the Router. Immediately afterwards the code invokes WETH.safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, newPool, amount) assuming that the Router itself should be the source of the tokens. Because safeTransferFrom pulls tokens from the address that gave an allowance – in this case the original caller – the caller's approved WETH balance is also transferred to the pool. As a result the caller ends up paying twice: once through the Ether that was deposited and again through the approved WETH allowance. The Ether that was deposited into the Router is never forwarded to the pool and becomes unrecoverable, effectively disappearing from the user's perspective. This bug manifests whenever a user creates a new pool with ETH and has previously granted the Router an allowance for WETH. Users who have not set an allowance are not affected, which can make the problem easy to miss during testing because the transaction may succeed without obvious revert. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the router's pool‑creation logic, where the flow of funds was traced and the mismatch between the source of the WETH transfer and the deposited Ether was identified. The vulnerability belongs to the class of token‑transfer mis‑routing bugs, where a contract mistakenly pulls tokens from an external address instead of its own balance, leading to double payment and loss of native assets. From a user’s point of view the UI may show that the pool creation transaction succeeded, but the user's wallet balance is reduced by the amount of Ether sent plus the same amount of WETH, and the pool contains only a single WETH amount. The expected behavior is that the pool receives the WETH equivalent of the Ether sent, and the user’s balance is reduced only by that amount. To remediate the issue the router should transfer the WETH it holds (the result of the deposit) to the newly created pool, for example by calling safeTransfer from the Router contract itself, rather than safeTransferFrom from msg.sender. This ensures that only the deposited Ether is converted to WETH and moved once, eliminating the double‑payment and preventing loss of funds.
summary: In the Router.createPoolETH function, a deposit to the weth contract is made but then a subsequent weth safeTransferFrom is made from the msg.sender to the newly created pool. As a result, users may accidentally pay twice for the WETH the pool should be created with if they had approved the Router contract. The native Ether sent to the Router will be lost.

title: H-02 | twapUpdate Overﬂow DoS
content: The vulnerabilityis a denial‑of‑service condition caused by an unchecked cumulative price accumulator in the MagicLP contract. Every time the pool’s reserve is changed via setReserve or when the pool state is synchronized via sync, the internal function _twapUpdate adds the latest price contribution to a variable called _BASE_PRICE_CUMULATIVE_LAST_. This variable is defined as a uint256 and is intended to grow indefinitely. In older DODO v2 contracts compiled with legacy Solidity versions, arithmetic overflow would silently wrap around, allowing the accumulator to continue operating even after exceeding the maximum uint256 value. MagicLP, however, is compiled with a newer Solidity version where arithmetic is checked by default; an addition that exceeds 2^256‑1 triggers a revert. Because the contract does not place the addition inside an unchecked block or otherwise guard against overflow, once the cumulative value reaches the uint256 ceiling the next _twapUpdate call reverts, preventing any further execution of setReserve, sync, or any function that depends on them. The result is that the pool becomes permanently non‑functional: users cannot add or remove liquidity, trades cannot be executed, and balances appear frozen. The condition can be triggered by any participant who can invoke setReserve or sync, meaning an attacker could deliberately call these functions repeatedly to accelerate the accumulator’s growth and force the overflow earlier than it would occur naturally. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the arithmetic in _twapUpdate and compared the contract’s Solidity version with the expected overflow behaviour. It is hard to notice because the overflow may require a very large number of updates to manifest, which typical unit tests or short‑term simulations may not reach. To remediate the problem the addition should be wrapped in an unchecked block (or the accumulator should be periodically reset or capped) so that overflow wraps safely instead of reverting, restoring the contract’s intended continuous‑price‑tracking behaviour. This class of bug falls under unchecked arithmetic leading to denial‑of‑service, where a monotonically increasing counter exceeds its type limit and halts contract logic, violating the business assumption that price cumulative data can grow without bound.
summary: In MagicLP.sol, _twapUpdate is called every time setReserve or sync is called. The update adds to _BASE_PRICE_CUMULATIVE_LAST_ which is an ever increasing value. In DODO v2, because they use an older version of solidity, it is desired and expected for this value to overﬂow once it has hit the max of type.uint256. However for MagicLP which uses a newer solidity version, this cannot overﬂow and all contract functionality will be bricked.

title: H-03 | previewAddLiquidity Incorrect quoteBalance
content: The vulnerability resides in the previewAddLiquidity view function of a liquidity‑pool contract. The function is supposed to compute an estimated quote token balance (quoteBalance) that represents the current amount of quote tokens held by the pool plus the amount of quote tokens that the caller intends to add (quoteInAmount). Instead, the implementation adds the base token amount (baseInAmount) to the existing quote token balance. This mismatch between the intended variable (quoteInAmount) and the used variable (baseInAmount) is the root cause. Because previewAddLiquidity is used by front‑ends and external callers to display how many LP tokens will be minted for a given deposit, the incorrect calculation can mislead users about the expected outcome. An attacker or a careless user can supply a baseInAmount that is larger than the actual quoteInAmount, causing the preview to report a higher quoteBalance than will actually be present after the transaction. When the real addLiquidity call is executed, the pool will receive fewer quote tokens than the preview suggested, resulting in the user receiving fewer LP tokens or, conversely, the pool minting more LP tokens than justified, which distorts the pool’s accounting and can lead to fund loss or unfair advantage for a malicious actor. The impact is primarily on liquidity providers who rely on the preview for accurate pricing; they may experience unexpected loss of value, and the protocol’s invariant calculations become unreliable. The issue manifests whenever previewAddLiquidity is called, which is typically before any liquidity addition. It affects any participant that queries the function, including UI components, bots, and other contracts that depend on the estimate. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit where the variable names were compared against the function’s documentation and the surrounding code. Because the function does not modify state, the error does not cause an immediate revert, making it easy to overlook during testing; the discrepancy only becomes apparent when the actual addLiquidity transaction is executed and the returned LP token amount differs from the preview. To remediate, the calculation should be changed to add quoteInAmount to the existing quote token balance, i.e., quoteBalance = IMagicLP(lp)._QUOTE_TOKEN_().balanceOf(address(lp)) + quoteInAmount. This aligns the preview with the real token flow, restores accurate accounting, and prevents users from being misinformed about the amount of liquidity they will receive. The bug belongs to the class of incorrect input‑parameter usage or mis‑referenced variable errors that lead to inaccurate financial estimations in smart contracts.
summary: In the previewAddLiquidity function the quoteBalance is intended to account for the current balance of the quote tokens in the LP as well as the new quote tokens which will be added to the LP. However the quoteBalance is the balance of quote tokens + the baseInAmount: uint256 quoteBalance = IMagicLP(lp)._QUOTE_TOKEN_().balanceOf(address(lp)) + baseInAmount;

title: H-04 | Lacking Gas Yields Claiming Logic
content: The vulnerability consists of a missing gas‑yield claiming mechanism in several core contracts of the Abracadabra and Mimswap ecosystems, specifically the MIM FeeRateModel, FeeRateImplementation, BlastTokenRegistry and SPELL contracts. These contracts are integrated with the Blast protocol, which automatically accrues gas‑yield rewards whenever certain state‑changing actions occur – for example each token transfer, approval, or swap operation generates a small amount of gas‑yield that is credited to the contract’s internal balance. The root cause is that the contracts contain no public or internal function that forwards the accrued gas‑yield to an address that can actually receive it, nor do they invoke the Blast claim interface after each accrual event. Consequently, the rewards accumulate silently in the contract’s internal accounting but remain locked, because there is no path for the protocol or its users to extract them. An attacker or a malicious actor could deliberately trigger a high volume of transfers, approvals or swaps to inflate the amount of unclaimed gas‑yield, thereby inflating the apparent profitability of the system while the actual rewards stay inaccessible. The impact is primarily economic: token holders, liquidity providers and the protocol treasury lose the opportunity to collect the gas‑yield that should have been distributed, reducing overall incentive alignment and potentially eroding user confidence. This condition manifests whenever any of the affected contracts processes a transaction that triggers gas‑yield accrual – essentially on every normal operation of the MIM token and the Mimswap swapping engine. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit that examined the integration points with the Blast protocol and noticed the absence of any claim‑related code paths. Because the contracts do not emit events or revert when yields are generated, the problem can be hard to notice; the system appears to function correctly while silently hoarding rewards. To remediate the flaw, the contracts should be extended with a proper claim function that calls the Blast token’s claim interface and transfers the accrued yield to a designated beneficiary, and the claim should be invoked after each accrual event or made available through an explicit user‑triggered transaction. This change restores the intended accounting model where gas‑yield rewards are realized and distributed, aligning the protocol’s economic incentives with its design.
summary: There are several contracts in the Abracadabra and Mimswap systems that cannot claim gas yields as they accrue.
