The original Uniswap OracleLibrary applies a correction that decrements the tick by one in this exact situation, but the examined implementation omits that step. Consequently the calculated tick is higher than it should be, which translates into a higher quoted price for the reference pool. This inflated price can be observed by users as a larger than expected asset value, allowing borrowers to obtain more credit or lenders to receive less value when liquidating positions. The bug manifests only when a non‑zero TWAP window is used and the price moves downward such that the cumulative tick delta is negative with a non‑zero remainder. It affects any participant that relies on the oracle – borrowers, lenders, and any contract that uses the price for accounting or collateral checks. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when the auditors compared the implementation against the reference Uniswap library and noticed the missing rounding‑down correction. Because the price deviation may be small and only appears under specific market conditions, it can be difficult to detect through casual testing; the oracle still returns a plausible price most of the time. The proper remediation is to replicate the Uniswap rounding logic: after computing the signed delta, if the delta is negative and the remainder of the division is non‑zero, decrement the tick before converting it to a sqrt price. This adjustment restores the correct floor rounding behavior and eliminates the opportunity for price manipulation and arbitrage that stem from the over‑estimated price.

title: Owner of a position can prevent liquidation due to the `onERC721Received` callback
content: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that allows the owner of a Uniswap V3 liquidity position, when represented as an ERC721 token, to block the liquidation of an under‑collateralised loan. The liquidation routine calls a private function that attempts to return the NFT to the borrower using the ERC721 safeTransferFrom method. SafeTransferFrom invokes the onERC721Received callback on the recipient contract and requires that the callback return the exact selector defined by the ERC721Receiver interface. Because the protocol assumes the borrower will accept the NFT, it does not verify the return value beyond the standard check. If the borrower is a contract that deliberately implements onERC721Received to return an incorrect selector, the safeTransferFrom call reverts with the error "ERC721: transfer to non ERC721Receiver implementer". This prevents the cleanup step of the liquidation, leaving the loan in an under‑collateralised state that cannot be resolved. The impact is that lenders cannot recover their collateral, the protocol’s accounting assumptions that collateral can always be reclaimed are broken, and a malicious borrower can effectively freeze the position, causing a DoS on the liquidation mechanism. The issue occurs only when the borrower is a contract capable of overriding the ERC721Receiver callback; it does not affect EOAs that automatically accept ERC721 transfers. It was discovered during a formal audit by constructing a malicious borrower contract that returns an invalid selector and confirming that liquidation reverts in a Foundry test. The problem is subtle because safeTransferFrom is normally reliable and developers may not anticipate a borrower deliberately breaking the callback contract. To remediate, the protocol should avoid pushing the NFT back to the borrower during liquidation. A pull‑over‑push pattern can be used: the contract should approve the NFT for the borrower and emit an event, allowing the borrower to withdraw the token later, or the liquidation logic should use a non‑safe transfer that does not invoke the callback, or include explicit checks that the transfer succeeded regardless of the receiver implementation. This change ensures that liquidation can always proceed and that collateral can be reclaimed even if the borrower contract is malicious, restoring the intended accounting guarantees of the vault.
summary:
When liquidating a position, `_cleanUpLoan()` is called on the loan. This attempts to send the uniswap LP position back to the user via the following line:
```solidity
nonfungiblePositionManager.safeTransferFrom(address(this), owner, tokenId);
```
This `safeTransferFrom` function call invokes the `onERC721Received` function on the owner’s contract. The transaction will only succeed if the owner’s contract returns the function selector of the standard `onERC721Received` function. However, the owner can design the function to return an invalid value, and this would lead to the `safeTransferFrom` reverting, thus being unable to liquidate the user.

title: Gas issuance is inflated and will halt the chain or lead to incorrect base fee
content: The vulnerability resides in the fee‑adjustment routine that runs inside the L2 anchor() function. Instead of issuing a fixed amount of gas equal to config.gasTargetPerL1Block for each L1 block, the code multiplies the target by the difference between the current L1 block identifier and the lastSyncedBlock value. Because lastSyncedBlock is only refreshed every five L1 blocks, a sequence of five consecutive anchor() calls causes the contract to issue fifteen times the intended gas amount (3 × the expected issuance). This over‑issuance inflates the internal gasExcess variable, which in turn drives an incorrect 1559 base‑fee calculation. When the computed base fee is compared to the actual block.basefee, the two values diverge. If the client enforces the match, the mismatch triggers a revert (L2_BASEFEE_MISMATCH) and the protocol halts; if the client accepts the flawed value, the chain continues but with a severely deflated base fee that breaks the economic assumptions of the protocol. The bug is triggered whenever anchor() is called on multiple L1 blocks before lastSyncedBlock is updated – essentially any period shorter than the BLOCK_SYNC_THRESHOLD. All participants are affected: users see transactions fail or fees drop to near zero, validators cannot produce new blocks, and the protocol becomes unavailable, effectively freezing any funds locked on the chain. The issue was uncovered during a formal audit when the auditors compared the calculated base fee against block.basefee and observed a systematic mismatch, then reproduced the problem with a small test that logged the cumulative issuance over five blocks. It is difficult to spot in production because the mismatch only appears after a handful of blocks and the symptom – a reverted transaction or an unexpectedly low fee – can be mistaken for a transient network glitch. The proper fix is to issue exactly config.gasTargetPerL1Block per L1 block, removing the multiplication by the block delta and ensuring lastSyncedBlock is updated each block or the calculation is otherwise bounded. In generic terms the bug belongs to the class of economic‑logic errors where a scaling factor is applied incorrectly, leading to an accounting imbalance that violates the protocol’s fee‑adjustment invariants. From a user’s perspective the expected behaviour is a stable, predictable fee and continuous block production; the reality can be a transaction that reverts with a base‑fee mismatch error, a block whose base fee is near zero, or a chain that stops advancing, effectively making funds inaccessible until an upgrade or manual intervention restores the correct fee logic.
summary: The base fee calculation in the `anchor()` function is incorrect. Issuance is over inflated and will either lead to the chain halting or a severely deflated base fee.

title: Validity and contests bond ca be incorrectly burned for the correct and ultimately verified transition
content: An issue exists in the Taiko L1 proving contract where validity bonds and contest bonds can be permanently burned even when the transition that triggered the bond loss is later verified as the correct and final transition. The root cause is that the contract’s bond‑return logic only considers the liveness bond when a guardian overrides a proof; it does not take the history of the final verified transition into account. When a lower‑tier prover submits a transition, a higher‑tier challenger can contest it, and later a guardian (or any top‑tier prover) can submit a higher‑tier proof that overwrites the earlier transition. At verification time the contract refunds only the liveness bond to the last prover (the guardian) and calculates the amount to return based on the current slot’s validityBond and livenessBond fields. Because the guardian is now recorded as the prover, the original prover’s validity bond and any contest bond that a challenger posted are deducted or never returned, and the remaining funds are sent to the guardian contract, which has no function to recover them. This results in the original prover seeing a reduction in their token balance, often with no explicit error message, and the challenger losing their contest bond even though their challenge was correct. The vulnerability manifests whenever a transition is contested by a higher tier and subsequently overridden by a guardian, which is a rare but possible sequence. All participants who stake validity or contest bonds – provers, challengers, and token holders – are affected because their economic incentives are broken and funds can disappear silently. The issue was discovered during a formal audit and reproduced with a Forge test that shows the prover’s balance decreasing after verification. It is hard to notice because the contract does not emit an event indicating a bond burn, and the loss is reflected only as a lower token balance. The proper fix is to extend the guardian’s refund path so that it can return both validity and contest bonds in the same way it returns liveness bonds, and to ensure that rewards are kept in the main contract rather than being locked in the guardian contract when an override occurs. In conceptual terms the bug belongs to the class of “incorrect bond handling after state override” where accounting assumptions about final state are violated, leading to unexpected fund loss and broken business logic.

title: Users will never be able to withdraw their claimed airdrop fully in ERC20Airdrop2.sol contract
content: An ERC20 airdrop contract defines a claim period and a subsequent withdrawal window during which the allocated tokens become linearly unlockable. The contract enforces that the withdraw function may only be called while the current time is strictly greater than the claim end and strictly less than the sum of claimEnd and the withdrawalWindow. Because the condition uses a strict “<” comparison for the upper bound, the exact moment when the tokens are fully unlocked (timestamp equal to claimEnd + withdrawalWindow) does not satisfy the modifier and the call reverts. As a result, a user who waits until the tokens are completely vested cannot execute the withdrawal, and can only withdraw a fraction of the entitled amount before the window closes. The impact is that eligible participants lose part or all of their airdrop allocation; the loss is larger for users who claim early or who try to withdraw only after full vesting. The bug is triggered only when block.timestamp reaches or exceeds the end of the withdrawal window, a situation that normal users cannot reliably time because blockchain timestamps are only controllable by miners within a small range. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when the test suite demonstrated that a claim of 100 tokens resulted in only 50 tokens being withdrawable after the window elapsed, and a subsequent call reverted with the "WITHDRAWALS_NOT_ONGOING" error. The problem is subtle because the contract appears to allow withdrawals throughout the window, yet the off‑by‑one comparison silently blocks the final withdrawal. The correct fix is to relax the upper‑bound check, for example by allowing a small buffer after the window or by using a “<=” comparison, so that users can still call withdraw when the tokens are fully unlocked. This class of bug is an off‑by‑one timing error in access‑control modifiers that enforce withdrawal periods, and it violates the business logic that users should be able to retrieve the full amount once the vesting schedule is complete. From a user’s perspective the UI would show that the airdrop is claimable, the user claims, but later the balance either remains unchanged or only partially increases, contrary to the expectation of receiving the full allocated tokens.
summary:
**Context:** The ERC20Airdrop2.sol contract is for managing Taiko token airdrop for eligible users, but the withdrawal is not immediate and is subject to a withdrawal window.

Users can claim their tokens within claimStart and claimEnd. Once the claim window is over at claimEnd, they can withdraw their tokens between claimEnd and claimEnd + withdrawalWindow. During this withdrawal period, the tokens unlock linearly i.e. the tokens only become fully withdrawable at claimEnd + withdrawalWindow.

**Issue:** The issue is that once the tokens for a user are fully unlocked, the [withdraw()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-03-taiko/blob/f58384f44dbf4c6535264a472322322705133b11/packages/protocol/contracts/team/airdrop/ERC20Airdrop2.sol#L88) function cannot be called anymore due to the [ongoingWithdrawals modifier](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-03-taiko/blob/f58384f44dbf4c6535264a472322322705133b11/packages/protocol/contracts/team/airdrop/ERC20Airdrop2.sol#L39) having a strict `claimEnd + withdrawalWindow < block.timestamp` check in its second condition.

**Impact:** Although the tokens become fully unlocked when block.timestamp = claimEnd + withdrawalWindow, it is extremely difficult or close to impossible for normal users to time this to get their full allocated claim amount. This means that users are always bound to lose certain amount of their eligible claim amount. This lost amount can be small for users who claim closer to claimEnd + withdrawalWindow and higher for those who partially claimed initially or did not claim at all thinking that they would claim once their tokens are fully unlocked.

title: Taiko L1 - Proposer can maliciously cause loss of funds by forcing someone else to pay prover’s fee
content: The issue is an economic mis‑allocation bug that lets a block proposer force another address to pay the prover fee for a block proposal. In the block‑proposing flow the library copies the caller‑supplied params.coinbase into the internal metadata only when the field is zero, using the statement if (params.coinbase == address(0)) { params.coinbase = msg.sender; }. Because the check does not reject a non‑zero value, a malicious proposer can supply any address as coinbase. Later, when an AssignmentHook’s onBlockProposed callback pays the assigned prover, the contract uses the metadata field _meta.coinbase as the source of ERC20 token transfers: IERC20(assignment.feeToken).safeTransferFrom(_meta.coinbase, _blk.assignedProver, proverFee). Consequently the token transfer is taken from the address stored in coinbase, not from the proposer who triggered the hook. An attacker can therefore approve the hook contract to spend a large allowance of victim tokens, propose a block with the victim’s address as coinbase, and cause the victim’s allowance to be drained to pay the prover fee. The vulnerability manifests only when the fee is paid in ERC20 tokens and when the hook is invoked with a non‑zero coinbase value. It affects any user who has granted the hook contract a token allowance, as well as the protocol’s economic guarantees because fees may be paid by parties that never proposed a block. The bug was discovered during a security audit that examined the interaction between the proposing library and the AssignmentHook callback; the logic appeared harmless at first glance because the defaulting to msg.sender seemed reasonable, making the problem easy to overlook. From a user’s perspective the symptom is a sudden reduction of token balance after a block is proposed by someone else, contrary to the expectation that fees are only deducted from the proposer’s own account. The root cause is an improper validation of a user‑controlled address that is later used as the payer in a token transfer, a classic case of incorrect authorization or payment‑to‑arbitrary‑address vulnerability. To remediate, the contract should enforce that the coinbase field always equals msg.sender, ignoring any externally supplied value, for example by resetting the field whenever it does not match msg.sender. This ensures that only the actual proposer can be charged for the fee and prevents forced fee extraction from unrelated accounts.

title: Signatures can be replayed in `withdraw`
content: The vulnerability is a signature replay flaw in the withdraw function of the TimelockTokenPool contract. The function accepts an off‑chain signed message that authorises a token transfer, but it does not keep any state that prevents the same signed message from being processed more than once. Because there is no nonce, timestamp, or other replay‑prevention mechanism, an attacker who obtains a legitimate withdrawal signature from a user can submit that signature repeatedly and cause the contract to transfer the authorized amount each time. This can be exploited by simply calling withdraw with the same parameters and signature in a loop, or by forwarding the signature to other accounts. The impact is that the pool can lose more tokens than the user intended, effectively allowing funds to disappear from the contract and leaving users with reduced balances or zero refunds. The issue manifests whenever a user signs a withdrawal request and the contract processes it without checking whether the signature has already been used. All users who rely on signed withdrawal messages are affected, as are the protocol’s overall token accounting and any parties that trust the pool’s integrity. The flaw was discovered during a formal security audit that examined the signature verification logic and noticed the absence of a replay‑prevention field. It can be hard to notice because the transaction succeeds, the UI may show the correct amount withdrawn, yet the pool’s total balance shrinks unexpectedly. The bug belongs to the class of replay attacks on signed messages, similar to missing nonce bugs in off‑chain authorization schemes. To remediate, the contract should incorporate a unique identifier such as a per‑user nonce, a global counter, or a timestamp that is included in the signed payload and checked before processing. Once a signature is used, the corresponding nonce should be incremented or the signature marked as spent, preventing any further execution with the same data. This change restores the intended accounting guarantees and ensures that a user’s signed withdrawal can only be executed once.
summary: Signatures can be replayed in `withdraw()` to withdraw more tokens than the user originally intended.

title: `paymaster` will refund `spentOnPubdata` to user
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect refund calculation in the zkSync bootloader when a transaction is executed with a paymaster. The bootloader collects the gas spent on publishing data (pubdata) at the end of the transaction, but the value passed to the paymaster’s postTransaction function – _maxRefundedGas – is computed as gasLeft plus reservedGas without subtracting the amount of gas that was actually spent on pubdata (spentOnPubdata). Because the paymaster uses this _maxRefundedGas to determine how much ETH to return to the caller, the paymaster ends up refunding the pubdata cost as well. The root cause is that the refundCurrentL2Transaction routine does not include spentOnPubdata in the maxRefundedGas argument and later adds the full reservedGas and remaining gas to the totalRefund before subtracting spentOnPubdata only for the operator‑provided refund path. An attacker can craft a transaction that includes a paymaster and consumes pubdata, causing the contract to calculate a much larger refund than it should. The extra ETH is transferred directly to the refundRecipient (either the original sender or the paymaster), effectively draining funds from the operator or the protocol treasury. This issue manifests when a transaction with a paymaster finishes and the system attempts to reimburse the caller; the user may see a higher balance than expected, or a refund that exceeds the actual gas cost, while the protocol’s accounting shows a deficit. It was discovered during a Code4rena audit by inspecting the bootloader’s YUL code and noticing that the spentOnPubdata value is never deducted from the amount handed to the paymaster. The bug is subtle because the refund still follows the normal ETH transfer path, so there is no explicit error flag, and the over‑refund can be mistaken for a normal reward. To fix the problem, the bootloader must compute the maximum refundable gas as gasLeft + reservedGas – spentOnPubdata before passing it to the paymaster, or otherwise ensure that the totalRefund calculation always subtracts the pubdata cost. In conceptual terms, the bug belongs to the class of “incorrect accounting of gas‑related refunds” where the system refunds more than the net gas expenditure, violating the economic assumptions of the protocol and breaking the invariant that total refunds cannot exceed the sum of reserved and remaining gas after accounting for pubdata usage.

title: Attacker can drain protocol tokens by sandwich attacking owner call to `setPositionWidth` and `unpause` to force redeployment of Beefy's liquidity into an unfavorable range
content: The vulnerability resides in the StrategyPassiveManagerUniswap contract where the public functions setPositionWidth and unpause trigger a redeployment of the Beefy liquidity position based on the current pool tick without enforcing the onlyCalmPeriods modifier. Because the contract does not verify that the pool price remains stable between reading the slot0 tick and executing the liquidity deployment, an attacker can manipulate the pool price by performing a large trade immediately before the owner’s transaction (front‑run) and then execute a second trade after the owner’s transaction (back‑run). In the front‑run step the attacker swaps a large amount of USDC for WBTC, exhausting the WBTC reserve in the pool and driving the WBTC price upward. When the owner subsequently calls setPositionWidth or unpause, the strategy reads the now‑inflated tick and redeploys its liquidity, allocating the protocol’s USDC into a range that is extremely favorable to the attacker. The attacker then back‑runs the owner’s call, swapping the accumulated WBTC back for USDC at the inflated price, effectively draining the protocol’s token balances. The impact is a near‑complete loss of the vault’s underlying assets: the LP balances for WBTC and USDC drop to near zero, users see their deposited funds disappear, and the protocol suffers a large financial loss (hundreds of thousands of USDC in the demonstrated tests). This condition occurs whenever the owner invokes setPositionWidth or unpause during normal operation, because those functions lack the calm‑period guard and therefore allow external price manipulation between the tick read and the liquidity deployment. The affected parties include the protocol’s token holders, the Beefy vault, the strategy contract, and any users who have deposited assets. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Cyfrin, which added a targeted forge test that reproduced the sandwich attack and observed the token drain. The bug is subtle because the functions appear to be simple administrative calls and do not emit warnings about price volatility, making it easy to overlook the missing invariant check. It belongs to the class of price‑manipulation or state‑inconsistency bugs where a contract assumes external state remains unchanged across a multi‑step operation. To remediate, the onlyCalmPeriods modifier should be applied to setPositionWidth and unpause, or more robustly to the internal _setTicks routine that performs the tick read and liquidity deployment, ensuring that no external actor can alter the pool price between these steps. This change restores the intended accounting invariant that the protocol’s liquidity is always added at a fair market range, preventing the attacker from forcing an unfavorable range and protecting user funds from disappearing after routine administrative actions.
summary:
When the owner of the `StrategyPassiveManagerUniswap` contract calls `setPositionWidth` and `unpause` an attacker can sandwich attack these calls to drain the protocol's tokens. This is possible because `setPositionWidth` and `unpause` redeploy Beefy's liquidity into a new range based off the current tick and don't check the `onlyCalmPeriods` modifier, so an attacker can use this to force Beefy to re-deploy liquidity into an unfavorable range.

Attacker can sandwich attack owner call to `setPositionWidth` and `unpause` to drain protocol tokens.

title: No slippage parameter on UniswapV3 swaps can be exploited by MEV to return fewer output tokens
content: The vulnerability is a missing slippage protection and deadline check in the Uniswap V3 swap helper used by Beefy Finance’s fee‑charging and reward‑conversion routines. The swap function is invoked with amountOutMinimum set to zero, meaning the contract accepts any amount of output tokens regardless of market price at execution time. Because there is no minimum‑output constraint or timestamp deadline, a miner‑extractable‑value (MEV) actor can front‑run, sandwich, or delay the transaction so that the pool price moves unfavourably between the moment the contract calls the swap and the moment it is actually executed. In a sandwich attack the attacker trades ahead of the swap to push the price against the contract, then trades back after the swap, causing the contract to receive fewer tokens than expected. A validator or sequencer that withholds the transaction can also execute it later when market conditions have deteriorated, again yielding a reduced amount. The issue manifests when the protocol attempts to convert accrued fees or reward tokens into the native token; the caller expects a certain amount based on the quoted price, but receives a smaller amount or even zero, effectively causing fees to disappear. This loss is subtle because the transaction does not revert; it simply returns less value, making the bug hard to notice during normal testing. The impact is a reduction of protocol revenue, lower returns for users, and potential long‑term erosion of vault balances, especially on low‑cost L2 or alternative L1 chains where the attacker’s gas expense is minimal. The bug was identified during a security audit by Cyfrin, who noted the absence of a slippage parameter and deadline as a logical flaw in the fee‑swap flow. To remediate, the swap call should include a properly calculated minimum‑output amount (slippage tolerance) and a deadline timestamp that limits how long the transaction can be pending, ideally derived off‑chain to avoid on‑chain manipulation. Adding these checks restores the intended accounting guarantees that the protocol receives at least the expected amount of tokens, preventing MEV‑driven token loss and aligning actual outcomes with user expectations.
summary:
`UniV3Utils::swap` performs a [swap](https://github.com/beefyfinance/experiments/blob/14a313b76888581b05d42b6f7b6097c79f3e65c6/contracts/interfaces/exchanges/UniV3Utils.sol#L22) with `amountOutMinimum: 0`. This function is called by `StrategyPassiveManagerUniswap::_chargeFees` [L375](https://github.com/beefyfinance/experiments/blob/14a313b76888581b05d42b6f7b6097c79f3e65c6/contracts/protocol/concliq/uniswap/StrategyPassiveManagerUniswap.sol#L375), [L389](https://github.com/beefyfinance/experiments/blob/14a313b76888581b05d42b6f7b6097c79f3e65c6/contracts/protocol/concliq/uniswap/StrategyPassiveManagerUniswap.sol#L389) and `BeefyQIVault::_swapRewardsToNative` [L223](https://github.com/beefyfinance/experiments/blob/14a313b76888581b05d42b6f7b6097c79f3e65c6/contracts/protocol/qidao/BeefyQIVault.sol#L223).

Due to the [lack of slippage parameter](https://dacian.me/defi-slippage-attacks#heading-no-slippage-parameter) an MEV attacker could sandwich attack the swap to return fewer output tokens to the protocol than would otherwise be returned. For `StrategyPassiveManagerUniswap` the reduced output tokens applies to the protocol's fees.

Whether the attack will be profitable or not will depend on the gas cost the attacker has to pay; it may well be that on L2s and Alt-L1s where Beefy intends to deploy, it will be profitable to exploit these swaps with the small pool manipulation `onlyCalmPeriods` may allow because the gas costs are so low.

Combined with a lack of effective deadline timestamp, malicious validators could also hold the swap transaction and execute it at a later time when it would return a reduced token amount than if it had been executed immediately. The `onlyCalmPeriods` check wouldn't appear to provide any protection against this since the swap would still be executed in a calm period, just at a later time when it would return less tokens than the caller expected when they called it.

The previous state could also arise organically due to a sudden and sustained spike in gas costs for example from a popular and prolonged NFT mint; the transaction could be organically delayed and executed at a later time resulting in a worse swap than would have occurred had it been executed when it was supposed to.

title: Queued transfers can become stuck on the source chain if Transceiver instructions are encoded in the incorrect order
content: The vulnerability concerns the handling of queued outbound token transfers in the NTT Manager when multiple transceivers are used. The contract expects the list of transceiver instructions supplied by the sender to be sorted in strictly increasing order of their registration index. This ordering is enforced by the parsing routine that iterates over the encoded instructions during the execution of a queued transfer; if an instruction index is not greater than the previous one the routine reverts with UnorderedInstructions. However, the same ordering check is omitted when the transfer is initially queued for delayed execution. Consequently, a user can submit a transfer that passes the initial queuing step – the manager locks the user's tokens and records the transfer – but later, when the queued transfer is processed by calling completeOutboundQueuedTransfer, the parsing routine detects the out‑of‑order indices and aborts. The abort leaves the locked tokens permanently held by the NTT Manager because there is no fallback path to release them. The root cause is the missing validation of instruction ordering at the point where the transfer is added to the outbound queue, combined with the assumption that the queued data will always be well‑formed. An attacker (or a careless user) can exploit this by deliberately encoding the transceiver instructions in a jumbled order, for example by swapping the positions of two instructions. When the outbound capacity limit forces the transfer to be queued, the transaction succeeds, the user’s balance becomes zero, and the contract’s token balance increases, giving the impression that the transfer is in progress. Later, the completion step fails with a revert, and the funds remain inaccessible, effectively creating a denial‑of‑service condition for the affected user and reducing the overall liquidity of the protocol. This issue manifests only when the outbound limit is exceeded (triggering queuing) and when more than one transceiver is configured, making it easy to miss during casual testing because the initial transfer does not revert. It was discovered during a formal audit by Cyfrin, which reproduced the failure with a unit test that intentionally encoded the instructions in reverse order and observed the revert on completion. The problem is subtle because the contract does not emit a clear error at the queuing stage, and the user sees no immediate indication that the transfer will later fail. To remediate, the manager should verify that the transceiver instruction list is correctly ordered before adding a transfer to the outbound queue, or enforce ordering at the encoding layer, thereby preventing malformed queued messages from ever being stored. This class of bug falls under “incorrect input validation for delayed execution paths” and can lead to funds being locked, refunds not being delivered, and accounting inconsistencies within cross‑chain token bridges.

title: Queued transfers can become stuck on the source chain if new Transceivers are added or existing Transceivers are modified before completion
content: The vulnerability concerns delayed outbound transfers that are placed in a queue when the requested amount exceeds the current outbound capacity of the NTT manager. The contract records the transfer together with a set of transceiver instructions that are encoded according to the list of enabled transceivers at the moment of queuing. Because the rate‑limit duration (typically 24 hours) postpones execution, the configuration of the NTT manager can be altered – new transceivers may be added or existing ones removed – before the queued transfer is finally processed. When the manager later attempts to parse the stored instructions, it allocates an array whose length matches the *current* number of enabled transceivers. If the stored payload contains fewer instructions than the new array length, the parsing loop writes to an index that does not exist, triggering an out‑of‑bounds revert. Consequently the queued transfer cannot be completed, the delivery price cannot be calculated, and the funds that were locked in the NTT manager remain permanently stuck. The issue is discovered during a formal audit by reproducing the scenario in a test that adds a third transceiver after queuing a transfer that only contains two instructions, then removes one of the original transceivers and finally attempts to complete the transfer, which reverts with an index‑out‑of‑bounds error. The bug is subtle because it only manifests after a time delay and only when the contract’s transceiver set changes, making it easy to miss during normal functional testing. Users experience the problem as a transfer that appears to be queued successfully, but later the transaction fails and their token balance in the NTT manager stays reduced while their external balance shows zero, effectively “funds disappear”. The affected parties are the senders of the queued transfers, any downstream protocol that relies on timely cross‑chain delivery, and the overall trustworthiness of the bridge. The root cause is a mismatch between the snapshot of transceiver configuration stored at queuing time and the live configuration used at execution time. To remediate, the contract should either store a snapshot of the transceiver list with each queued transfer, validate that the number of provided instructions matches the current configuration before queuing, or modify the price‑estimation routine to safely handle missing instructions (for example by treating absent indices as zero‑cost placeholders). This prevents the out‑of‑bounds access and ensures that queued funds can always be released, preserving accounting integrity and user expectations that a queued transfer will eventually be executed or refunded.

title: Wrong `PoolSize` increment in `Goldilend.repay()`
content: The vulnerability is an accounting error in the repay function of the Goldilocks lending contract. When a borrower calls repay, the contract calculates the interest that corresponds to the amount being repaid and stores it in a local variable named interest. However, instead of adding this calculated interest to the global poolSize variable, the code mistakenly adds the original total interest recorded in the loan struct (userLoan.interest). This mismatch means that for any partial repayment the poolSize is increased by more than the actual interest that was transferred back to the pool. The root cause is a simple variable misuse: the developer referenced the stale loan record instead of the freshly computed interest value. An attacker or any borrower can exploit this by repaying only a portion of the loan, causing the poolSize to be inflated artificially. The inflated poolSize is later used to determine share distributions, liquidity checks, and withdrawal limits, so the protocol may think it has more funds than it really does. This can lead to over‑payment of protocol fees, insufficient liquidity for other borrowers, and potentially allow malicious actors to withdraw more than their entitlement. The bug manifests only when repay is called with an amount smaller than the total borrowed amount; full repayment does not trigger the mis‑calculation because the interest values coincide. All participants who rely on correct pool accounting – lenders, borrowers, and the protocol’s fee collectors – are affected because the internal accounting no longer reflects reality. The issue was discovered during a formal security audit performed by Cyfrin, who noted that the comment in the code explicitly warned that the wrong variable was used. Because poolSize is an internal state variable, the problem is not immediately visible to users; it only becomes apparent when subsequent functions that depend on poolSize behave unexpectedly, such as incorrect fee payouts or failed withdrawals. To remediate the issue, the contract should update poolSize using the locally computed interest variable (interest) rather than the stale userLoan.interest value, ensuring that only the actual repaid interest is added to the pool’s balance. This correction restores the intended accounting invariants and prevents the pool from being overstated, thereby preserving the protocol’s financial integrity.

title: Users can extend an expired boost using invalidated NFTs.
content: The vulnerability is a logical flaw in the boost‑extension mechanism that allows a user to keep a boost active even after the NFTs that originally granted the boost have been invalidated. The contract stores the boost parameters, including the boost magnitude, in a struct associated with the user. When a user calls the internal _buildBoost function after their current boost has expired, the code copies the previously stored boostMagnitude without checking whether the partner NFTs are still valid. It then optionally adds the magnitude of any newly supplied NFTs, but if the caller supplies empty arrays the old magnitude is reused unchanged. Because the contract never re‑validates the stored partnerNFTs or clears the old boostMagnitude, an attacker can first create a boost with a legitimate NFT, later have that NFT invalidated via adjustBoosts, wait for the boost to expire, and then call boost() with no NFTs to extend the boost indefinitely. This can be exploited repeatedly, effectively granting a perpetual boost that should have been removed when the NFT was invalidated. The impact is that malicious users retain privileged boost benefits (such as higher rewards or lower fees) forever, breaking the intended accounting and economic model of the protocol. The condition occurs only after a boost has expired and the associated NFTs have been marked invalid, but the contract’s logic does not enforce a re‑check at that point. All users who rely on the boost system are affected because the integrity of the boost calculation is compromised, and the protocol’s fairness is undermined. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the boost‑building routine and noticed that the old magnitude is used without validation. It can be hard to notice because the contract still appears to function correctly for normal users; only when an NFT is invalidated and a boost is later extended does the discrepancy become visible, often manifesting as a boost that never expires or rewards that are higher than expected. The proper fix is to re‑evaluate the validity of all partner NFTs each time a boost is extended, reset or recompute the boostMagnitude based on currently valid NFTs, and clear any stored data that references invalidated NFTs before constructing a new boost. This aligns the implementation with the intended business rule that only active, valid NFTs may contribute to a boost’s magnitude, preventing perpetual boost extensions and preserving the protocol’s economic guarantees.

title: Team members can't unstake the initial allocation forever.
content: The vulnerability consists of a logic error in the contract’s vesting calculation that permanently blocks team members from withdrawing any staked tokens. When a user invokes the unstake() function, the contract calls an internal helper _vestingCheck() to determine how much of the user’s balance is currently vested. The helper contains a guard clause that checks if the caller has a non‑zero entry in the teamAllocations mapping and, if so, immediately returns 0. This unconditional return bypasses the normal vesting formula that is applied to seed investors, meaning that for every team member the function reports that no amount is vested regardless of the elapsed time, the vesting schedule, or the amount originally allocated. Consequently, when a team member calls unstake() the contract calculates a vested amount of zero and the transaction completes without reverting, leaving the user with no tokens returned. The problem is compounded by the stake() function, which only blocks seed investors from staking additional tokens but does not prevent team members from adding extra stakes. If a team member stakes more tokens after the initial allocation, those extra tokens are also subject to the same _vestingCheck logic and become permanently locked as well. The issue manifests whenever a team member attempts to unstake, whether immediately after the initial allocation or after any subsequent stake, and it affects any address recorded in the teamAllocations mapping. From a user’s perspective the UI will show a successful unstake transaction but the balance will not change, leading to confusion as the expected refund or withdrawal never arrives. The bug was identified during a security audit by Cyfrin, and because the function silently returns zero rather than throwing an error, it can be difficult to detect through normal testing; the contract appears to behave correctly on the surface while silently withholding funds. This flaw violates the core business logic that team members should be able to retrieve their vested tokens according to the same schedule as other investors, breaking accounting assumptions and undermining trust in the protocol. To remediate the issue, the early return for team members should be removed and the vesting calculation should be applied uniformly to both seed investors and team members, or a separate but equivalent vesting schedule should be implemented for the team. Additionally, the stake() function should be updated to either prevent team members from adding extra stakes or to ensure that any additional stakes are also subject to a proper vesting schedule, thereby avoiding permanent lock‑up of funds.

title: In `GovLocks`, it shouldn't use a `deposits` mapping
content: The vulnerability originates from the contract’s use of a separate `deposits` mapping to record how many underlying LOCK tokens each address has contributed, while the `govLocks` token itself is fully transferable. When a user deposits LOCKs, the contract increments `deposits[msg.sender]` and mints an equal amount of govLocks. However, the contract does not adjust the `deposits` entry when govLocks are transferred between accounts. Consequently, a holder who acquires govLocks through a transfer (for example, by buying them from another user) will have a positive govLock balance but a zero entry in the `deposits` mapping. The `withdraw` function checks the `deposits` mapping and subtracts the requested amount before burning the govLocks and returning the underlying LOCKs. Because the mapping still shows zero, the subtraction underflows or triggers a revert, preventing the holder from withdrawing any LOCKs. This mismatch between the token balance and the internal accounting state can be exploited by any participant who receives govLocks via transfer: they simply call `withdraw` and the transaction fails, effectively locking their underlying assets forever. The impact is that users lose the ability to redeem their deposited LOCKs, leading to funds being permanently inaccessible while still retaining voting power. The issue manifests whenever govLocks are transferred after deposit, which is allowed by the token’s ERC‑20‑like transfer functions. All token holders, delegators, and the protocol that relies on the ability to exit their position are affected. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the deposit and withdraw logic and noticed that the `deposits` mapping was never updated on token transfers, a classic double‑bookkeeping or accounting‑mismatch bug. It can be hard to notice because the deposit and withdraw functions appear symmetric and the contract otherwise behaves correctly for direct depositors; only secondary holders encounter the problem. From a user’s perspective the UI would show a normal govLock balance, but attempting to withdraw would either revert with an error or result in no LOCKs being returned, contradicting the expectation that “I can always burn my govLocks to get back my LOCKs”. The bug violates the fundamental business assumption that each govLock is backed 1:1 by a deposited LOCK. The recommended remediation is to eliminate the `deposits` mapping entirely and rely on the token’s balance ledger for accounting, or alternatively update the mapping on every transfer so that the internal record always mirrors the actual govLock holdings. Either approach restores the invariant that a holder’s withdrawable amount equals their govLock balance, preventing funds from becoming irretrievable.

title: `Goldilend.lock()` will always revert
content: The vulnerability resides in the token‑locking workflow of the Goldilocks contract. The public lock(uint256 amount) function is intended to let a user deposit iBGT tokens, receive a minted representation, and stake the deposited tokens in an external iBGTVault. However, the implementation calls an internal helper _refreshiBGT before the actual token transfer from the user. _refreshiBGT first approves the vault to spend the specified amount and then immediately invokes iBGTVault.stake. Because the contract has not yet called SafeTransferLib.safeTransferFrom to pull the iBGT tokens from the caller, its balance is still zero at the moment stake is executed. The vault’s stake function checks that the caller holds the required tokens and therefore reverts due to insufficient balance. This ordering mistake causes lock() to revert on every invocation, preventing any user from successfully locking iBGT. The root cause is a logical sequencing error: external state‑changing calls are performed before the contract holds the necessary assets. Exploitation is trivial – an attacker does not need to craft any special input; simply calling lock with any amount triggers the revert, effectively a denial‑of‑service on the deposit path. The impact is that users cannot lock tokens, their UI will show a transaction failure or a generic “revert” message, and the protocol cannot accept new deposits, breaking its intended economic model. The issue affects all participants who rely on the lock function – token holders, liquidity providers, and any downstream contracts that expect minted iBGT to be backed by real assets. It was discovered during a manual audit where the flow of funds was traced and the premature stake call was identified as the failure point. The bug can be hard to notice because the approve call succeeds and the stake call appears syntactically correct; only at runtime does the vault detect the missing balance and revert, which may be mistaken for a vault‑side problem. To remediate, the contract should first transfer the user’s iBGT tokens into its own balance, then perform the approval and stake operation, or alternatively separate the staking step into a distinct function that is called after the deposit succeeds. Conceptually, the fix is to ensure that any external contract that requires a token balance is called only after the contract actually holds the required tokens, preserving the atomicity of the deposit‑and‑stake sequence and restoring the intended functionality of the lock mechanism.

title: Some functions of `Goldilend` will revert forever.
content: The Goldilend contract contains three public functions—multisigInterestClaim, apdaoInterestClaim and sunsetProtocol—that are intended to move ibgt tokens from the protocol to privileged addresses. The code assumes that the contract itself holds the ibgt balance, but in reality all ibgt tokens are stored in a separate iBGTVault contract. Each function reads an internal claim amount, resets the claim variable to zero and then calls SafeTransferLib.safeTransfer to send ibgt directly from the Goldilend address. Because the Goldilend contract does not hold any ibgt, the transfer attempts to move more tokens than are available, causing the SafeTransferLib call to revert. The revert is not caught, so the transaction fails and the function cannot be executed again, effectively locking the claim forever. This denial‑of‑service condition occurs whenever the privileged caller (the multisig, the APDAO address or the timelock) tries to claim accrued interest or to execute the protocol sunset. The affected parties are the protocol’s governance participants and any users who expect to receive their interest payouts; from a user perspective the UI would show a claim button that appears to work but results in no funds being received, often with an error like “transfer failed” or a silent revert. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Cyfrin, where the auditors noted that the contract never interacts with the vault before attempting a transfer. It can be hard to notice because the function signatures look correct and the claim variables are updated, giving the impression that the claim succeeded, while the underlying token balance check is hidden inside the library call. The bug belongs to the class of “missing asset withdrawal before external transfer” or “incorrect accounting of token custody”, which violates the protocol’s financial logic that accrued interest should be payable. To remediate, each function must first invoke the vault’s withdraw method for the exact amount to be sent, thereby moving the ibgt tokens into the Goldilend contract before the safeTransfer call. After the withdrawal, the transfer will succeed and the claim can be completed, restoring the intended flow of interest distribution and allowing the sunset procedure to release remaining assets.

title: H-01 | minimumCredit Inaccurately Restricts Backing For Shorts
content: The vulnerability lies in the way the contract computes the minimumCredit value that defines the lowest amount of credit capacity the market must retain. The function mixes the total market size and the current index token price in a single formula, applying the same calculation to both long and short open interest. Because short positions are valued at their cost‑basis rather than the current market price, the formula incorrectly inflates the amount of backing liquidity that should be reserved for shorts when the index price rises. For example, if a market has ten index tokens of short open interest and the market size is ten, a doubling of the index price causes the minimumCredit calculation to treat the short exposure as if it were worth twice its original cost, even though shorts are in a loss and can only gain up to their entry cost. This mis‑representation leads the system to believe that less credit is available than actually is, causing legitimate short traders to receive “insufficient credit” errors, preventing them from opening or maintaining positions, and potentially locking liquidity that should be usable elsewhere. The issue manifests whenever the index token price moves upward relative to the short positions, affecting any user attempting to trade shorts, liquidity providers whose capital is unnecessarily tied up, and the protocol’s overall market health. It was discovered during a manual audit by the Guardian team, who noticed that the credit‑capacity check behaved inconsistently under price changes. The bug is subtle because the formula appears reasonable at a glance and the UI only shows a reduced credit amount without explaining the cause. To remediate, the calculation must separate long and short open interest: reserve liquidity for longs based on openInterestInTokens multiplied by the current price, and reserve liquidity for shorts based on the aggregate position cost (entry price times size), as done in the GMX V2 system. This class of bug belongs to inaccurate financial accounting logic where a single metric is used for heterogeneous position types, leading to wrong backing requirements, broken accounting assumptions, and user‑visible symptoms such as missing funds, zero balances, or unexpected denial of short trades.
summary:
The minimumCredit function defines an amount which the available credit capacity cannot go below
depending on the size of the market and the current index price. However this calculation perturbs
the amount that ought to be reserved for shorts.
For example:
• A market has 10 index tokens as short open interest.
• The market size is 10.
• The price of the index token doubles.
• The minimum credit is now a ratio based on the 10 tokens of short open interest, now valued at
twice the price.
This inaccurately represents the amount of backing liquidity that ought to be reserved for the market
as shorts can only ever gain up to their cost-basis and when the price of the index token rises, shorts
are in a loss.

title: H-02 | Liquidation Computes Utilization Before Updating Market Size
content: The vulnerability resides in the liquidation workflow of the market contract where the utilization metric is recomputed before the market size is adjusted to reflect the removed position. Utilization is a ratio of total borrowed or open exposure to the available market capacity, and it is used by the protocol to determine margin requirements for all remaining traders. In the current implementation, the function that prepares a liquidation (updateMarketPreLiquidation) calls market.recomputeUtilization while the market.size variable still contains the amount that is about to be liquidated. Consequently, the utilization rate is calculated using the old, larger market size, leaving the utilization value unchanged after the liquidation completes. This occurs whenever a liquidation reduces the market size, especially in scenarios where utilization was already high and a large position is removed; the expected drop in utilization that would relax margin constraints for other traders does not happen. As a result, traders continue to be assessed against an artificially high utilization, which can cause their positions to be deemed under‑collateralised and trigger further liquidations that are not economically justified. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the liquidation path, where the auditor noticed that the utilization metric did not change after a simulated large liquidation despite the market size being reduced. The bug is subtle because the contract does not revert or emit an error; the state simply remains inconsistent with the intended accounting model, making it hard to spot without explicit checks of the utilization value before and after liquidation. To remediate the problem, the recomputeUtilization call should be moved to occur after market.size (and any related skew variables) have been updated, ensuring the utilization rate reflects the new market state. This class of bug can be described as an ordering error in state updates that leads to incorrect financial metrics, breaking the protocol’s accounting assumptions and potentially causing funds to disappear from traders’ safety buffers due to unfair liquidations.
summary:
During liquidatePosition, updateMarketPreLiquidation is called to perform pre-steps and validation,
including the recomputation of utilization. market.recomputeUtilization is incorrectly called before
market.size is reduced by the liquidation size. The new utilization rate should be calculated with the
new market size, similar to settleOrder in OrderModule.sol.
By calling recomputeUtilization before updating size, the liquidation leaves utilization rate unchanged
when it should have reduced it, affecting all remaining traders.
Assume the utilization rate was very high, and a large position was just liquidated. This should in
effect bring down utilization rate and improve the margins of all other traders. However, due to this
error, the margins of all other traders remain unchanged, which could then lead to unfair liquidations.

title: H-03 | sUSD Drained From Vault When Liquidating Margin Only
content: The vulnerability resides in the liquidation eligibility check of the margin trading module. The contract marks a position as liquidatable when the calculated discountedMarginUsd equals zero, without verifying that the remaining collateral can cover the liquidation keeper reward or any sudden drop in collateral price. Because the discountedCollateralUsd is computed by multiplying the available collateral amount by a discounted price that is expressed with 18‑decimal precision, a collateral asset whose market price falls below 1e18 results in a discounted price that rounds to zero. Consequently, even a position that holds only a single wei of collateral can produce a discountedCollateralUsd of zero, making discountedMarginUsd zero as well. An attacker can exploit this by depositing a negligible amount of low‑price collateral, triggering the isMarginLiquidatable function to return true, and then calling the liquidation routine. The attacker receives the keeper fee and is able to withdraw sUSD from the V3 pool, effectively draining funds while the victim’s account appears to have sufficient margin. The impact is a loss of protocol‑owned sUSD, creation of bad debt, and a breach of the accounting assumption that margin must always be able to cover liquidation costs. This condition occurs only when the collateral price is sufficiently low to cause rounding to zero and when the liquidation logic relies solely on a zero discountedMarginUsd threshold. Users experience a situation where their positions are liquidated despite having a non‑zero balance, leading to unexpected zero refunds or missing funds. The issue was uncovered during a manual audit that examined the margin‑liquidation path and identified the missing safety check. It is difficult to notice because the zero‑margin condition looks legitimate on the surface and the rounding error is subtle. The proper remediation is to require that discountedMarginUsd be greater than the keeper reward (and optionally a safety margin for price slippage) before allowing margin‑only liquidation, and to enforce a minimum collateral amount that can survive any price‑impact scenario before a position becomes liquidatable. This changes the vulnerability class from an unchecked zero‑margin liquidation to a robust collateral‑coverage validation, aligning the contract’s behavior with the intended business logic that liquidation should only occur when the position truly cannot satisfy its obligations.
summary:
In the isMarginLiquidatable function, accounts are determined to be liquidatable when they have a
discountedMarginUsd of 0. However this puts the protocol at risk of taking on bad debt as there is
no requirement that the margin is able to cover liquidator fees as well as potential instantaneous
collateral price decreases.
Furthermore, an issue arises with low price collateral assets. An attacker can deposit a very small
amount of collateral (1 wei), and the validation for isMarginLiquidatable will return true, as the
discountedCollateralUsd will be 0 when collateral price is below 1e18:
discountedCollateralUsd += available.mulDecimal(discountedCollateralPrice);
The attacker will then liquidate the account and earn keeper fees, withdrawing sUSD from the V3
pool.

title: H-04 | minimumCredit Backed By Trader sUSD Collateral
content: The vulnerability resides in the way the BFP market calculates its credit capacity against the required minimum credit. In the current implementation, sUSD that traders deposit as collateral is added to the market’s creditCapacity and then compared with the minimumCredit threshold that is meant to guarantee sufficient backing liquidity. Because trader‑provided sUSD can be withdrawn if the market’s isCapacityLocked check fails, it should not be counted as locked backing. By mistakenly treating this potentially removable collateral as part of the protected liquidity, the protocol may appear to satisfy the minimumCredit requirement while, in reality, the market is under‑collateralised. Moreover, profits that are settled to sUSD for traders are not included in the minimumCredit accounting, meaning that even when the market seems funded, there may be insufficient liquidity to cover those payouts. This logical flaw can be exploited when a market is opened or when its credit capacity is re‑evaluated: an attacker or a sequence of trader deposits can push the reported creditCapacity above the minimumCredit without actually providing the necessary locked funds. If the market later fails the capacity‑locked validation, the trader‑provided sUSD may be withdrawn, leaving the market without the liquidity needed to honour positions or settle profits. The impact is that the protocol’s backing liquidity can become inadequate, potentially causing trader positions to be under‑funded, profits to be unpaid, and in extreme cases, funds to disappear from the market. The issue manifests whenever the market relies on the creditCapacity check – typically at market creation, after large trader deposits, or during periodic capacity validations. All participants who rely on the market’s solvency – traders, liquidity providers, and end‑users – are affected because the market may report a healthy state while actually being vulnerable to loss. The flaw was discovered during a security audit by the Guardian team through logical analysis of the credit accounting flow; it is subtle because the on‑chain numbers for creditCapacity look correct, yet the underlying assumptions about collateral lock‑up are violated, making the problem hard to spot from a UI perspective. From a user’s point of view the market may appear active, but when attempting to withdraw or settle, users might receive zero or a reduced amount, experience unexpected liquidations, or see their profits not being paid. This class of bug falls under improper collateral accounting and insufficient validation of backing liquidity. To remediate, the protocol should either exclude trader‑deposited sUSD from the creditCapacity used for minimumCredit validation, lock that collateral when the market is operating, or adjust the minimumCredit calculation to explicitly account for settled profits and subtract any trader‑provided collateral that is not guaranteed. A conservative approach is to require that the creditCapacity includes only locked backing liquidity, ensuring that the minimumCredit threshold truly reflects the amount of funds that cannot be withdrawn, thereby restoring the intended safety guarantees.
summary:
In the BFP market, sUSD collateral is deposited by traders and counted towards the creditCapacity of
the market. This creditCapacity is ultimately compared against the minimumCredit to validate that
there is sufficient backing liquidity to safely operate the market.
However trader collateral should not be included in this validation as it cannot be locked in the event
that the market's isCapacityLocked validation fails, failing to safely back the market with a minimum
amount of liquidity and adequately back trader’s positions. Additionally trader’s profits which are
settled to sUSD ought to always be able to be covered by backing liquidity, however this amount is
not accounted for in the minimumCredit.

title: H-05 | minimumCredit Reserves Not Validated Upon Position Increase
content: The vulnerability consists of a missing validation step that should ensure the market’s minimum credit requirement is always covered by the available credit capacity before a trader is allowed to open a new position or increase an existing one. The root cause is that the contract does not re‑evaluate the invariant that the total minimumCredit, which represents the amount of liquidity that must be reserved to back all open positions, stays less than or equal to the market’s creditCapacity after a position size change. Because this check is omitted, a trader can submit orders that push the minimumCredit above the backing liquidity without any rejection. An attacker can repeatedly increase position sizes, deliberately inflating the required reserve while the actual liquidity pool remains unchanged. As the gap widens, the market becomes under‑collateralized and can enter an insolvent state. When insolvency occurs, any attempt to withdraw sUSD collateral is effectively denied – the withdrawal transaction either reverts or returns zero – and profitable positions cannot be settled because the contract lacks sufficient backing funds to pay out gains. This situation manifests to users as unexpected zero payouts, missing refunds, or the inability to retrieve deposited collateral, contrary to the expectation that a settled trade will always result in a correct transfer of funds. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit that examined the market’s accounting logic and identified that the minimumCredit validation is only performed on order creation but not on subsequent position increases. The bug is subtle because the contract still accepts orders and appears functional until the liquidity shortfall becomes large enough to trigger a failure, making it easy to miss during casual testing. To remediate the problem, the contract should enforce the minimumCredit ≤ creditCapacity condition for every state‑changing operation that alters position size, rejecting any order that would violate this invariant. In broader terms, this is a classic example of an insufficient collateral or liquidity validation flaw, where accounting assumptions about reserved backing are broken, leading to fund disappearance and denial‑of‑service for withdrawals and settlements.
summary:
Traders are allowed to open and settle orders even when the existing market positions cannot be
adequately supported by the liquidity backing the BFP market. Even if the existing minimumCredit is
too large for the backing creditCapacity, traders can continue to increase the market size and
therefore increase the uncovered gap between the minimumCredit and the lacking creditCapacity.
As a result the BFP market can easily become insolvent in the event that traders continue to open
positions without consideration for the backing liquidity. This leads to a market state where sUSD
collateral withdrawals are DoS'd as well as any settlement for positions in a profit.

title: Design flaw and mismanagement in vault licensing leads to double counting in collateral ratios and positions collateralized entirely with kerosine
content: The vulnerability is a design flaw in the protocol’s vault licensing and deployment logic that allows collateral to be counted twice when calculating the Collateralization Ratio (CR) and also permits positions to be collateralized entirely with the endogenous kerosene token. The root cause is that the DeployV2 script registers WETH vaults with both the KeroseneManager and the VaultLicenser, which populates the same vault address in two separate mappings – one used for price calculation (vaultsKerosene) and one used for external collateral accounting (vaults). Because the CR calculation sums the values from both mappings, a vault that appears in both is double‑counted, inflating the reported CR. Additionally, the script mistakenly licenses kerosene vaults through the VaultLicenser instead of the KeroseneManager, causing those vaults to be treated as normal external collateral. An attacker can exploit this by calling the add and addKerosene functions with the same vault identifier, causing the protocol to believe a position is far more over‑collateralized than it actually is. This prevents legitimate liquidations, leading to a situation where a position that is under‑collateralized appears safe, and may later default, causing loss of funds for lenders. The issue manifests when the deployment script runs and when users are able to register vault IDs through both licensing pathways; any position that includes a vault present in both mappings is affected. The affected parties include borrowers, lenders, and the protocol itself, as the inflated CR undermines the economic guarantees of the system. The flaw was discovered during a formal audit and reproduced with unit tests that demonstrated double counting and full kerosene collateralization. It is hard to notice because the CR calculation itself does not raise errors; the numbers simply look higher than expected, and the UI may display a healthy ratio while the underlying risk is hidden. To remediate, the licensing design should be re‑thought: separate the mapping used for price oracle calculations from the mapping used for external collateral licensing, ensuring that kerosene vaults are never added to the external collateral set. The DeployV2 script should call a dedicated function (e.g., addVaultForOracleCalculation) for vaults that should only influence price feeds, and use the standard add function only for legitimate external collateral vaults. This separation prevents double counting and stops kerosene vaults from being used as primary collateral, restoring correct CR computation and liquidation safety.
summary:
Due to a design flaw in the protocol’s management of vault licensing and the deploy script, a significant risk exists where collateral can be counted twice in the calculation of the Collateralization Ratio. This occurs because WETH vaults are incorrectly licensed to both the `KeroseneManager` and `VaultLicenser`, allowing users to register the same asset and their NFT ID in both Kerosene vaults and normal vaults. This can allow users to exploit this to greatly inflate their CR calculations, misleading the protocol into considering a position more secure than it truly is, which can prevent necessary liquidations and pose significant risk to the protocol.

However, a user can also register his ID and the `keroseneVault` as a normal `vault` because the script calls the licensing function for the `kerosineVaults` using the `VaultLicenser` rather than the `kerosineManager`. This can lead to positions entirely collateralized with kerosene token. Which is not what protocol intends to do and is very risky as the kerosene token is endogenous and has a manipulable asset price.

title: Inability to perform partial liquidations allows huge positions to accrue bad debt in the system
content: The vulnerability is a limitation in the liquidation mechanism that prevents partial liquidations of vault positions. The liquidate function always burns the entire amount of DYAD that was minted for a given DNft identifier by calling dyad.burn with dyad.mintedDyad(address(this), id) as the amount. Because the function does not accept a user‑specified amount, a liquidator can only liquidate a position by covering the full outstanding debt. This design choice becomes a problem when a vault holds a very large amount of minted DYAD – often the case for whale accounts – because a liquidator is unlikely to have enough DYAD, even with flash‑loan techniques, to match the whole debt. When the collateral ratio of such a vault falls below the minimum threshold, the protocol attempts to call liquidate, but the call cannot succeed because the required burn amount is too large. Consequently the vault remains under‑collateralised, no collateral is transferred to the liquidator, and the system records bad debt that accumulates over time. The impact is that the protocol’s accounting invariants are violated: the expected reduction of debt and corresponding increase in collateral for the liquidator never occurs, leading to a situation where funds appear to disappear from the system’s balance sheet. Users who rely on liquidation to protect their positions may see their collateral stay locked, while the protocol’s overall health degrades as more large, un‑liquidated positions appear. The issue was discovered during a security audit when the code of liquidate was examined and it was noted that the burn call always uses the total minted amount, offering no path for partial repayment. The bug is subtle because normal‑sized positions can be liquidated successfully, so tests that only cover typical cases may not reveal the problem. To remediate, the liquidation routine should be refactored to accept a burn amount parameter, calculate the proportional share of collateral based on the amount actually burned, and adjust reward calculations accordingly. This change restores the ability to partially liquidate oversized positions, prevents the buildup of bad debt, and aligns the contract’s behaviour with the intended economic model of maintaining sufficient collateralisation at all times.
summary:
The [liquidate()](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-dyad/blob/cd48c684a58158de444b24854ffd8f07d046c31b/src/core/VaultManagerV2.sol#L205) function allows liquidators to burn DYAD on behalf of an DNft id and receive collateral in return.

The issue is that the current functionality only allows burning of the whole DYAD amount minted by the DNft id. This means that partial liquidations cannot be performed and prevents liquidators from liquidating DYAD minted by whales that hold huge positions in the system. Since the liquidations cannot be performed unless the liquidator can match up to the collateral deposited and DYAD minted by the whale, the system will be undercollaterized causing bad debt to accrue.

The effect of this issue will increase as more such positions exist in the system that cannot be liquidated by the liquidators.

title: Attacker can make `0` value `deposit`
content: The vulnerability originates from an improper access‑control check on the deposit function of the VaultManagerV2 contract. The function is protected by the isValidDNft modifier, which only verifies that the supplied DNFT identifier exists, but it does not confirm that the caller is the actual owner of that DNFT. Consequently, any address can invoke deposit on behalf of any DNFT, even with an amount of zero. When a zero‑value deposit is executed, the contract records the current block number in the idToBlockOfLastDeposit mapping. This state change interferes with later calls to withdraw or redeemDyad, which contain a safeguard that reverts if a withdrawal is attempted in the same block as the most recent deposit. An attacker can front‑run a legitimate user’s redeemDyad or withdraw transaction, submit a zero‑value deposit for the same DNFT, and thereby cause the subsequent user‑initiated call to hit the same‑block check and revert. From the user’s perspective the transaction fails with a generic revert (DepositedInSameBlock or VaultHasAssets), the expected collateral is not returned, and the vault removal operation is blocked even though the user holds no assets. In a worst‑case scenario the forced revert can leave the user’s collateralization ratio below the required minimum, opening the door for a liquidation attack. The issue also manifests when an attacker deposits a single wei before a user attempts to remove a vault; the presence of any non‑zero asset balance triggers a revert in the remove function, effectively denying the user the ability to cleanly exit the protocol. This bug belongs to the class of authorization bypass and state‑manipulation vulnerabilities, where insufficient ownership checks allow an adversary to alter protocol state without contributing value. It is difficult to notice because zero‑value transfers are normally allowed and do not raise immediate red flags, yet they silently corrupt the block‑level deposit tracking used for security checks. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the modifiers applied to critical functions and traced the interaction between deposit, withdraw, and remove logic. To remediate the issue, the deposit function should enforce the same ownership verification as withdraw and remove (i.e., use isDNftOwner), ensuring that only the rightful DNFT holder can modify the deposit state. Additionally, the contract could reject zero‑value deposits or separate the same‑block check from deposit tracking to prevent front‑running manipulation. Fixing the access control restores the intended business logic that users can only affect their own vaults, preserves collateral ratios, and prevents denial‑of‑service or liquidation attacks caused by malicious zero‑value deposits.
summary: Function [`deposit()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-dyad/blob/cd48c684a58158de444b24854ffd8f07d046c31b/src/core/VaultManagerV2.sol#L119) uses modifier [`isValidDNft()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-dyad/blob/cd48c684a58158de444b24854ffd8f07d046c31b/src/core/VaultManagerV2.sol#L42) instead of [`isDNftOwner()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-dyad/blob/cd48c684a58158de444b24854ffd8f07d046c31b/src/core/VaultManagerV2.sol#L39), which allows anyone to call [`deposit()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-dyad/blob/cd48c684a58158de444b24854ffd8f07d046c31b/src/core/VaultManagerV2.sol#L119) on behalf of any DNft id.

title: Attacker can frontrun user’s withdrawals to make them revert without costs
content: The vulnerability originates from a flash‑loan protection mechanism that records the block number of the most recent deposit for each dNft token identifier in a mapping called idToBlockOfLastDeposit. The deposit function is publicly callable by anyone who can supply a valid dNft id, and it unconditionally writes the current block number into this mapping before performing any checks on the caller or the vault being used. When a withdrawal is later attempted, the withdraw function compares the stored block number with the current block and reverts with the error DepositedInSameBlock if they match. Because the mapping can be overwritten by any external address, an attacker can front‑run a legitimate user’s withdrawal by calling deposit on the same dNft id in the same block, using a fake vault and a fake ERC‑20 token that the attacker controls. This action updates idToBlockOfLastDeposit to the current block, causing the subsequent withdrawal attempt by the rightful owner to fail instantly, even though no assets are transferred from the attacker. The impact is a denial‑of‑service on the user’s funds: the user sees a transaction revert, receives no tokens, and their balance remains unchanged, contrary to the expectation that a withdrawal would succeed.
