Malicious or compromised token owners can trap funds in a contract by adding the contract address to the blocklist. This could potentially be the result of regulatory action against the contract itself, against a single user of the contract (e.g. a Uniswap LP), or could also be a part of an extortion attempt against users of the blocked contract.

If a user whose address has been blocklisted is added to a `withdrawQueue` inside the `AccountingManager` contract, all other users that are in that same queue will not be able to withdraw, as the `executeWithdraw` function will revert when it tries to do [`baseToken.safeTransfer`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-noya/blob/main/contracts/accountingManager/AccountingManager.sol#L428) call on the blocklisted address.

title: Loss of funds in `PendleConnector.depositIntoMarket`
content: The vulnerability resides in the depositIntoMarket function of the PendleConnector contract, where it transfers a user‑specified amount of SY and PT tokens to a Pendle market, calls market.mint with those amounts as upper‑bound desires, and then immediately invokes market.skim. The developer assumed that skim would return any surplus SY or PT that were not consumed by the mint operation back to the connector, but the actual implementation of skim forwards any excess tokens to the Pendle treasury. Consequently, when the mint call does not use the full supplied amounts – which is common because mint treats the inputs as maximum limits – the leftover tokens are permanently redirected away from the caller. This mis‑understanding of the market’s accounting logic creates a loss‑of‑funds condition: users see their deposited tokens disappear from their balance, the expected LP tokens are minted with less underlying collateral, and the surplus ends up in the treasury or can be captured by an attacker through MEV. The issue is triggered whenever depositIntoMarket is used with amounts that exceed the market’s optimal liquidity ratio, a situation that can arise naturally due to market price fluctuations or user error. It affects any participant who relies on the connector to provide accurate accounting of deposited assets, including end‑users, protocol integrators, and the treasury itself. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract’s expectations with the actual behavior of the skim function in the Pendle core code. It is subtle because the call to skim does not revert or emit an obvious error; the tokens simply vanish from the caller’s perspective, making the problem easy to miss in functional testing. To remediate the issue, the connector should stop calling skim and instead compute the exact amounts of SY and PT that will be consumed by the market using the MarketMathCore.addLiquidity helper, passing those precise values to market.mint. This ensures that no surplus tokens are sent to the treasury and that the accounting remains consistent with user expectations. In broader terms, the bug belongs to the class of “incorrect handling of surplus token returns” or “mis‑assumed token reclamation” vulnerabilities, where a contract relies on a function to refund excess assets but the function actually redirects them, breaking the intended financial flow and potentially enabling fund loss or theft.
summary: `PendleConnector` contracts can lose out on funds when minting LP tokens.

title: Incomplete TVL Calculation in `AerodromeConnector::_getPositionTVL` Function
content: An incomplete Total Value Locked (TVL) calculation exists in the AerodromeConnector contract. The function that reports the TVL only reads the balance of the liquidity‑token held directly in the Aerodrome pool, while the liquidity that has been deposited into the gauge contract is ignored. The root cause is that _getPositionTVL does not query the gauge’s balance of the same token, even though the stake() function transfers the tokens to the gauge via a deposit call. An attacker or a protocol that relies on the TVL metric can exploit this omission by staking liquidity, causing the reported TVL to be lower than the actual amount locked. Because many protocol components – such as share‑allocation, reward distribution, or governance weight – are derived from the TVL, the under‑reporting can lead to users receiving fewer rewards than they are entitled to, dashboards showing a smaller total value, or mis‑priced positions. The bug manifests only after liquidity has been staked in the gauge; before staking the calculation is correct. It affects any user who stakes through the connector, the protocol’s accounting logic, and any external services that consume the TVL value. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the stake() implementation, which moves tokens to the gauge, with the TVL routine that only checks the pool balance. The discrepancy is subtle because the contract still holds a non‑zero balance and the gauge balance is not visible in the same storage slot, making the under‑estimation easy to miss in casual testing. The proper fix is to add the gauge’s token balance to the pool balance before converting reserves to value, i.e., balance = pool.balanceOf(this) + gauge.balanceOf(this). This brings the TVL calculation in line with the actual assets locked and restores correct reward and share calculations. The vulnerability belongs to the class of accounting or metric‑miscalculation bugs where a subset of assets is omitted from a financial aggregate.
summary: The [AerodromeConnector::stake](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-noya/blob/9c79b332eff82011dcfa1e8fd51bad805159d758/contracts/connectors/AerodromeConnector.sol#L100) function allows to stake liquidity tokens to the gauge pool. However, the [AerodromeConnector::_getPositionTVL](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-noya/blob/9c79b332eff82011dcfa1e8fd51bad805159d758/contracts/connectors/AerodromeConnector.sol#L125) function, which is responsible for calculating the Total Value Locked (TVL), does not take into account the liquidity tokens deposited in the gauge pool. This oversight will result in an incorrect calculation of the TVL, which could negatively impact the overall functionality of the protocol that utilizes the TVL metric.

title: `PendleConnector` incorrectly sends the redeemed `PT` tokens to the market
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect token routing bug in the PendleConnector contract when it attempts to burn a Pendle liquidity provider (LP) position. The contract calls the market.burn function with the market address as the receiver of the PT (principal token) instead of using its own address. Because the burn function expects the first parameter to receive SY tokens and the second parameter to receive PT tokens, passing address(market) for the PT receiver causes the newly minted PT tokens to be transferred back to the market contract rather than to the PendleConnector. This mis‑routing is the root cause: a simple parameter mix‑up in the call to market.burn. An attacker or any manager with permission to invoke burnLP can trigger the function, causing the PT tokens to be locked inside the market where they are not accessible to the connector. The impact is a loss of value for the connector and for any user who expected to receive PT tokens after burning their LP; from the user’s perspective the balance of PT remains zero or the refund amount is missing even though the transaction succeeded. The bug manifests whenever burnLP is executed, which occurs after the connector transfers the LP tokens to the market and then calls market.burn. It affects the PendleConnector contract, its manager role, and any downstream users or protocols that rely on the connector to retrieve PT tokens. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where the auditor noted that the second address argument was set to address(market) instead of address(this). The problem is subtle because the ERC20 transfer of LP tokens succeeds and no revert is thrown, so the loss of PT tokens can be easily overlooked. To fix the issue the contract should pass its own address as the PT receiver, i.e., call market.burn(address(this), address(this), amount) or otherwise ensure that the PT tokens are sent to the connector. This correction restores the intended accounting flow where burning LP yields SY and PT tokens back to the connector, preserving user balances and protocol integrity. The bug belongs to the class of “incorrect parameter ordering” or “token mis‑routing” vulnerabilities that break financial accounting assumptions and cause funds to disappear from the expected holder.
summary: Burning a Pendle LP will donate the `PT` tokens to the market instead of withdrawing them to the `PendleConnector` which leads to a loss of funds for the Connector.

title: A Vault can steal all funds from another Vault through the Registry’s flash loan contract due to insufficient access control in `Connector.sendTokensToTrustedAddress`
content: The vulnerability is an improper access‑control flaw in the generic connector function that moves tokens to a trusted address. The BaseConnector.sendTokensToTrustedAddress routine trusts only that the caller is the flash‑loan contract registered in the Registry, but it does not verify that the caller is authorized to move the specific token balance belonging to a particular vault. Because any vault keeper can invoke BalancerFlashLoan.makeFlashLoan and supply arbitrary destination connectors and calldata, a malicious keeper can embed a call to another vault’s connector inside the flash‑loan callback. When the flash‑loan contract executes the supplied calldata, the target connector (C‑2) sees the Registry’s flash‑loan address as msg.sender and therefore permits the transfer of its entire token holding to the flash‑loan contract. The attacker’s own connector (C‑1) then pulls those tokens out of the flash‑loan contract and repays the loan, keeping the stolen amount. This sequence can be performed whenever a vault’s keeper is able to start a flash loan, which is the normal operation of the system, making the exploit blend into legitimate activity. The impact is that the attacker can drain all tokens held by any other vault’s connector, effectively stealing user funds and breaking the accounting guarantees of the protocol. The issue affects all vaults that rely on the Registry’s flash‑loan address and any token holders whose assets are managed by those vaults. It was discovered during a Code4rena audit by reviewing the interaction between the Registry, the BalancerFlashLoan contract and the BaseConnector implementation. The problem is subtle because the token transfer appears as a normal part of a flash‑loan repayment flow and no explicit error is raised, so observers may assume the movement is legitimate. The recommended mitigation is to add a strict authorization check in sendTokensToTrustedAddress, ensuring that only the vault that owns the connector or a designated role can request a transfer, or to validate that the token being moved belongs to the caller’s vault before allowing the operation. In abstract terms the bug belongs to the class of “privileged function misuse due to missing access control”, where a function intended for internal trusted transfers can be hijacked to move assets from unrelated contracts. From a user perspective the symptoms are a sudden disappearance of token balances after a flash‑loan transaction, a missing refund or yield, and a vault UI showing zero or reduced holdings despite no explicit withdrawal request.
summary: The keeper of a Vault can steal all funds from another Vault.

title: PrismaConnector are not able to claim surplus collateral in recovery mode
content: The vulnerability consists of the PrismaConnector contract being unable to forward calls to the TroveManager.claimCollateral function, which is responsible for returning surplus collateral to borrowers after a liquidation that occurs while the protocol is in Recovery Mode. In Recovery Mode, when a vault’s Individual Collateral Ratio falls below the Global Total Collateral Ratio, the vault can be liquidated, but the protocol caps the liquidation loss at 110 % of the collateral, leaving any excess collateral (the surplus balance) to be reclaimed by the borrower. The TroveManager correctly records this surplus in the mapping surplusBalances, and the claimCollateral function can transfer the amount to a receiver. However, the PrismaConnector does not expose any method that calls claimCollateral, nor does it provide a way for users interacting through the connector to retrieve the surplus. As a result, the surplus balance remains permanently locked in the TroveManager contract for any vault that was liquidated through the connector. The issue is discovered during a security audit that examined the recovery‑mode liquidation flow and noticed that the connector’s public interface lacks a claim function. It may be hard to notice because the TroveManager code contains the claim logic, and the connector appears to handle other vault operations, so a reviewer could assume the claim path is reachable. The impact is that borrowers who expect to receive the leftover collateral after liquidation receive nothing; from the user’s perspective the UI may show a claimable amount but the transaction to withdraw fails or is unavailable, leading to funds effectively disappearing. The problem affects any user of the PrismaConnector who experiences a liquidation in Recovery Mode, and it undermines the protocol’s guarantee that surplus collateral is returned, potentially eroding trust. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “missing external call / inaccessible withdrawal” bugs, where a contract records a balance but does not provide a public method to withdraw it, violating accounting assumptions that recorded balances are always claimable. To remediate, the connector should implement a public function that forwards the caller’s request to TroveManager.claimCollateral, optionally passing the caller’s address as the receiver, and ensure that surplusBalances can be cleared and transferred. Adding proper access control and event emission will allow users to retrieve their surplus collateral and restore the intended economic behavior.

title: `AccountingManager::resetMiddle` will not behave as expected
content: The vulnerability resides in the AccountingManager contract where the resetMiddle function is used to reposition the middle index of either the deposit or withdrawal queue. When the function is called for the withdrawal queue, it updates withdrawQueue.middle but fails to reset the accounting variable currentWithdrawGroup.totalCBAmount that tracks the total base token amount required for the current group of withdrawals. This omission creates a state inconsistency: after a reset, the next call to calculateWithdrawShares will add the newly calculated assetsNeededForWithdraw to the stale totalCBAmount value that still contains the amount from the previous calculation. Consequently the protocol believes it needs to withdraw more base tokens than actually required. The root cause is an incomplete reset of the withdrawal group state; the function checks bounds and the isStarted flag but does not clear the cumulative amount field. Exploitation is straightforward for any manager with permission to call resetMiddle: by resetting the middle index without resetting totalCBAmount, the manager can cause the accounting to double‑count the required withdrawal amount. When calculateWithdrawShares runs again, the inflated totalCBAmount leads the protocol to request excess funds from its connectors, reducing potential yield and, in extreme cases, exceeding the total value locked (TVL). If the inflated amount surpasses TVL, the vault cannot satisfy the withdrawal request and the user’s funds remain locked until new deposits arrive. The issue manifests under the condition that the manager invokes resetMiddle for the withdrawal queue while currentWithdrawGroup.isStarted is false and the new middle index lies within the allowed range. It affects the protocol’s financial integrity, the manager’s ability to correctly process withdrawals, and ultimately the users who expect to receive their funds. The bug was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where the missing reset line was highlighted with an audit comment. It can be hard to notice because external balances and UI may still display correct values, while the internal accounting diverges, leading to unexpected larger withdrawal amounts or failed withdrawals that appear as “insufficient funds” errors. From a user’s perspective, a withdrawal may revert, return zero tokens, or remain pending indefinitely, contradicting the expectation that the request will be fulfilled promptly. The vulnerability belongs to the class of accounting state‑inconsistency bugs where a reset operation does not fully clear all related state variables. The proper remediation is to reset currentWithdrawGroup.totalCBAmount to zero when the withdrawal queue middle is reset, ensuring that subsequent share calculations start from a clean slate and that the protocol’s accounting matches the actual token flows.

title: `SNXConnector.sol` TVL calculation is incorrect
content: The vulnerability lies in the way the contract calculates the total value locked (TVL) for a user’s position. The function that reports TVL adds the values returned by the Synthetix core proxy as totalDeposited plus totalAssigned, but the implementation of getAccountCollateral defines totalDeposited as the sum of totalAssigned and the amount that is available for delegation. Consequently, totalAssigned is counted twice, inflating the reported collateral amount. In addition, the TVL routine completely ignores the debt that is created when a user mints SUSD. The mintOrBurnSUSD function already registers the newly minted SUSD in the registry, which means the debt side of the balance sheet is never subtracted from the TVL calculation. The result is an over‑statement of the protocol’s locked value. This mis‑calculation can be exploited by an attacker who mints SUSD without providing additional collateral; the protocol’s TVL metric will rise even though the underlying collateral has not increased, potentially leading to inflated rewards, misleading governance metrics, or a false sense of safety for other participants. The impact is primarily on the accuracy of on‑chain analytics, reward distribution that depends on TVL, and the overall health checks that assume the protocol is fully collateralised. The bug manifests whenever the _getPositionTVL view is called after a mint operation, which is a common path for dashboards and incentive calculations. Users of the protocol see a higher TVL figure than the real amount of collateral, may be told they are earning more rewards than they actually are, and could later experience a correction that reduces their apparent balance. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the SNXConnector contract, where the auditor noticed that the TVL function summed two variables that already overlap and that no debt term was considered. It is hard to notice because the numbers still look plausible and the double counting is subtle without a deep inspection of the underlying storage layout. To fix the problem the TVL calculation should use a single source of truth for collateral – either totalDeposited or totalAssigned – and then subtract the current debt of the account, which can be obtained from a view‑compatible debt‑reading function or by storing the debt value separately. In conceptual terms the TVL should be computed as collateral value minus outstanding minted SUSD debt, ensuring that the protocol’s accounting reflects both sides of the balance sheet correctly.

title: `Registry.sol#updateHoldingPosition` remove position logic is incorrect: should use `ownerConnector` instead of `calculatorConnector` when calculating `holdingPositionId`
content: The vulnerability resides in the logic that removes a holding position from the vault's holdingPositions array. When a position that is not the last element is removed, the contract swaps the element at the target index with the last element and then pops the array. The code then updates the mapping that tracks which position identifier is stored at which index. However, the identifier (holdingPositionId) is recomputed using the field calculatorConnector, which points to the AccountingManager contract, instead of using ownerConnector, which holds the address of the connector that actually owns the position. Because the two fields differ for most token‑holding positions, the mapping is updated with an incorrect key. As a result the internal index for the swapped position becomes stale, causing subsequent removals to delete the wrong array entry. This mis‑alignment propagates to the total value locked (TVL) calculation performed by the AccountingManager: the protocol believes a position has been removed while the underlying tokens are still held by a different connector, leading to a TVL that drops to zero or otherwise becomes inaccurate. The bug is triggered only when a non‑terminal position is removed, which is a common scenario during token migrations or connector rebalancing. Users experience symptoms such as a sudden disappearance of their reported balances, a dashboard showing zero TVL despite deposited assets, or refunds that never arrive. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by constructing a test that moved assets across three connectors; after two sequential removals the TVL incorrectly reported zero. The problem is subtle because the contract does not revert or emit an explicit error; the state appears consistent but accounting data is corrupted, making it hard to detect without explicit TVL checks. The correct fix is to recompute holdingPositionId with the ownerConnector field when updating the isPositionUsed mapping, ensuring the mapping key matches the actual owner of the position. This change restores the integrity of the position index and guarantees that TVL reflects the true amount of assets held by the protocol.

title: `BalancerConnector::_getPositionTVL` is calculated incorrectly
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect calculation of the total value locked (TVL) for Balancer LP positions inside the BalancerConnector contract. The function that returns the TVL multiplies the token value by the LP balance and then divides by the token weight before dividing by the pool total supply. Balancer’s vault already returns token balances that are proportional to their weights, so applying the weight a second time artificially reduces the computed amount to roughly the weight fraction of the true balance. This double‑weighting occurs whenever _getPositionTVL is called for a weighted pool, which includes most multi‑asset Balancer pools. An attacker or a user can observe that the reported TVL is far lower than the actual market value of the underlying assets; the protocol that relies on this figure for collateral checks, liquidation thresholds, or reward distribution will therefore treat the position as under‑collateralised. In practice a user may see their LP position value displayed as a fraction of a cent, may be unable to withdraw the expected amount, or may be liquidated despite holding sufficient assets. The issue was discovered during a security audit by comparing the Balancer documentation, which shows that TVL should be calculated as the sum of balances multiplied by price divided by total supply, with the connector’s implementation that incorrectly incorporates the weight field. Because the contract does not emit an explicit error and only returns a smaller number, the problem can be subtle and may only be noticed when users compare on‑chain values with external price feeds. The bug belongs to the class of financial‑formula errors where a parameter is applied twice, leading to an accounting mismatch. The correct fix is to remove the weight division and compute TVL using the raw token balances with proper decimal scaling, matching the Balancer reference implementation. By doing so the reported TVL will reflect the true market value, preventing false liquidation and ensuring accurate accounting.
summary:
```solidity
BalancerConnector misuses the weight of pool tokens, leading to decreased TVL of these positions.
```

title: `BalancerConnector` has incorrect implementation of totalSupply, positionTVL and total TVL will be invalid
content: The BalancerConnector contract calculates a user position value and the overall protocol TVL by reading the ERC20 totalSupply of a Balancer pool token. In modern Balancer weighted and stable pools the token supply is split into a pre‑minted amount and the actual circulating amount that reflects protocol fees. The ERC20 totalSupply function returns the sum of both, while the correct metric for valuation is totalActualSupply (also called getActualSupply). Because the connector uses totalSupply, the denominator in the positionTVL formula is inflated, causing the computed TVL and individual share values to be lower than they should be. This mis‑calculation occurs whenever the connector interacts with pools that implement pre‑minted BPT, which includes most recent Balancer pools. Liquidity providers and any protocol component that relies on the reported TVL for fee distribution, reward allocation or risk assessment are affected. From a user perspective the UI may display a higher total pool value than what is actually withdrawable, withdrawals can return less than expected or even appear to be zero, and balances may seem to disappear after certain operations. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit that compared the connector code with Balancer documentation and observed a discrepancy between totalSupply and totalActualSupply on a live pool. The bug is subtle because totalSupply returns a plausible large number, making the error easy to miss unless the specific pool type is examined. The vulnerability belongs to the class of accounting errors caused by using an inappropriate supply metric, similar to using totalSupply of a rebasing token for valuation. To remediate, the connector should replace the call to IERC20(pool).totalSupply() with the pool’s totalActualSupply (or getActualSupply) function for compatible pools, and adjust the TVL calculation accordingly. This change restores the invariant that the denominator reflects only the circulating shares, ensuring accurate TVL reporting, correct reward distribution, and preventing users from receiving less than their rightful share.
summary:
```solidity
`BalancerConnector` has incorrect implementation of totalSupply, positionTVL and total TVL will be invalid.
```

title: SiloConnector `_getPositionTVL` miscalculate the TVL position
content: The vulnerability resides in the SiloConnector contract's internal function that reports the total value locked (TVL) for a position. The function iterates over each asset returned by the Silo protocol and adds together the balances of two share tokens – collateralToken and collateralOnlyToken – as if they were amounts of the same underlying asset. It then multiplies those share balances by the market price of the underlying token, without converting the share tokens to their underlying amounts. Because each share token has its own exchange rate and represents a different portion of the protocol's accounting (total deposits, collateral‑only deposits, and total borrow amount), the calculation produces a TVL that can be significantly higher or lower than the real value. The AccountingManager and the ERC‑4626 share‑price logic rely on this TVL to mint and redeem vault shares. When the TVL is inflated, the contract may mint more shares than the underlying assets justify; when it is deflated, users redeem fewer assets than they expect. An attacker can exploit the mismatch by depositing assets that are represented only by the collateralOnlyToken, which does not earn interest, causing the TVL to be overstated, then redeeming shares later to extract excess value. The impact is a distortion of the share price, potential loss of user funds, and a breach of the protocol’s accounting invariants. The bug appears whenever the connector’s _getPositionTVL function is called – typically during every deposit, withdrawal, or accounting snapshot – and affects any user who interacts with the vault, as well as the protocol’s overall asset accounting. It was discovered during a manual audit that compared the Silo protocol’s internal accounting fields with the values returned by the connector, revealing that the share‑token balances were being summed incorrectly. The issue is subtle because the three tokens share the same underlying asset, so a superficial inspection may not notice the differing exchange rates, and the resulting TVL discrepancy can be hidden by other protocol operations. The proper fix is to convert each share‑token balance to its underlying asset amount using the token’s exchange rate, sum the true underlying deposits (totalDeposits plus collateralOnlyDeposits), and then subtract the true underlying borrow amount before applying the price conversion. In other words, the TVL calculation must operate on underlying token quantities, not on share‑token balances, and must treat collateral‑only deposits separately from interest‑bearing deposits. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that the vault’s share price appears unusually high, yet when a user attempts to withdraw they receive less of the base token than expected, or the displayed balance may drop to zero despite a prior deposit. This constitutes a classic accounting‑logic bug where share‑token accounting is conflated with underlying asset accounting, leading to incorrect valuation and potential fund loss.
summary:
```solidity
`_getPositionTVL` from SiloConnector calculates wrongly the position’s TVL thus affecting the share price at which shares are minted / redeemed from the protocol.
```

title: It is possible to open insolvent position in Silo connector, due to missing check in borrow function
content: The vulnerability resides in the SiloConnector contract that mediates interactions with the Silo protocol. When a manager calls the borrow function, the contract forwards the request to the underlying Silo contract but does not perform any post‑borrow solvency verification. The protocol’s own SolvencyV2 library defines a minimum health factor that must be respected to keep a position adequately collateralised. In the repay function the connector correctly checks this health factor after the repayment and reverts if the position remains insolvent, but the borrow function lacks an analogous check. As a result, a caller can open a new borrowing position that is already under‑collateralised according to the protocol’s accounting rules. The root cause is the omission of a call to SolvencyV2.isSolvent (or an equivalent health‑factor assertion) after the borrow operation. An attacker or careless user can exploit this by borrowing more assets than the deposited collateral can support, causing the connector’s internal accounting to record an insolvent position from the outset. The impact includes the possibility of under‑collateralised debt remaining on the protocol, which may later be liquidated or cause loss of funds for the connector’s users. The issue manifests when the manager invokes borrow with an amount that would breach the minimum health factor; the transaction succeeds, the user receives the borrowed tokens, but the position is flagged as insolvent when later inspected. Users see the expected borrowed amount in their wallet yet the UI or health‑factor query reports a zero or below‑threshold health factor, contradicting the expectation that borrowing is only allowed when sufficient collateral exists. The bug was discovered during a formal audit when a test case called borrow, then queried SolvencyV2.isSolvent and observed a false result, indicating that the position was already insolvent. Because the borrow function does not revert, the problem can be subtle and may only be noticed when a later operation (such as repay) triggers a solvency check and fails. To remediate, the borrow function should be amended to invoke the same solvency verification used in repay, reverting the transaction if the health factor falls below the required minimum, and updating the token registry accordingly. This change restores the invariant that all positions opened through the connector must satisfy the protocol’s collateralisation rules, preventing the creation of insolvent debt and protecting user funds.

title: `PrismaConnector` can mint a position below the desired health factor
content: The vulnerability resides in the PrismaConnector contract’s adjustTrove function, which is intended to let a user borrow additional ULTRA tokens or repay existing debt while keeping the trove’s collateral ratio (also called health factor) above a predefined safety threshold. The code obtains the health factor by calling ITroveManager.getNominalICR, a view that returns a nominal collateral ratio that does not incorporate the current market price of the collateral token. Because the nominal ratio is calculated with a default or stale price, its value is systematically lower than the true collateral ratio returned by getCurrentICR when a realistic price is supplied. Consequently, the comparison `if (minimumHealthFactor > healthFactor)` almost always fails, causing the function to revert with IConnector_LowHealthFactor even when the trove is well‑collateralised. The root cause is the misuse of an inappropriate oracle‑independent metric to enforce a safety check. An attacker does not need to manipulate any state; simply invoking adjustTrove – either to borrow or to repay – triggers the revert, effectively freezing the connector’s ability to manage its position. Users experience a situation where a transaction that should succeed (e.g., borrowing 1 ULTRA or repaying 1 ULTRA) fails with a low‑health‑factor error, despite the UI showing sufficient collateral and the underlying trove having a healthy ratio. This leads to funds being locked in the connector, prevents legitimate users from adjusting their positions, and can undermine confidence in the protocol’s reliability. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit when a test case that opened a trove with ample collateral still caused adjustTrove to revert. It is hard to notice because the revert message mentions health factor, which appears correct, yet the underlying calculation is silently using the wrong function. The proper fix is to replace the call to getNominalICR with a price‑aware call such as getCurrentICR, passing the current collateral price obtained from the value oracle, and to relax the health‑factor check for repayment operations. Adding explicit getter functions for the collateral token and the current ICR in the TroveManager interface enables the connector to perform an accurate safety check, restoring the ability to borrow, repay, and withdraw collateral as intended, and eliminating the unintended lock‑up of user funds.

title: In Dolomite, when opening a borrow position, the holding position in the Registry will never be updated due to the `removePosition` flag being set to true
content: In the Dolomite connector a borrow position is created by calling openBorrowPosition, which subsequently invokes registry.updateHoldingPosition with the boolean flag removePosition set to true. The removePosition flag is intended to signal that a position should be removed from the registry, typically when the position is fully closed or the token balance becomes zero. By setting this flag to true during the opening of a borrow position, the registry’s internal circuit‑breaker logic interprets the call as a removal request. The circuit‑breaker checks if the position index is zero and the flag is true, and if so it returns type(uint256).max, preventing any further updates to the isPositionUsed mapping that records that the holding position exists. Consequently the newly opened borrow position is never recorded in the Registry’s holdingPositions array. This omission means that any downstream logic that relies on the Registry – for example, strategies that monitor positions to trigger timely repayments or liquidations – will not see the open borrow position. When the protocol later attempts to close the position, the Registry still believes the position does not exist, which can cause the close operation to fail, potentially leading to forced liquidations, bad debt, or loss of collateral. The vulnerability manifests whenever any user or manager opens a borrow position through the connector, regardless of market or amount, and it affects all participants whose positions are managed by the affected vault. It was discovered during a Code4rena audit by inspecting the flag usage in the openBorrowPosition function and tracing the registry’s updateHoldingPosition implementation. The bug is subtle because the UI may show that a borrow position was opened, yet the internal accounting appears unchanged, giving no immediate error signal. The proper fix is to pass false for the removePosition flag when updating the holding position during an openBorrowPosition call, ensuring the position is added to the Registry, while retaining true for genuine removal scenarios such as closing or emptying a position. This change restores correct accounting, prevents hidden positions, and aligns the Registry’s state with the protocol’s business logic for borrowing and repayment.
summary:
```solidity
Whenever some of the connectors opens or closes a position, it is updated in the registry.

Usually if/when a position is closed (all asset amount withdrawn / borrow position closed in its entirety, etc.), the holding position is updated with the flag `true` for `bool removePosition`.

In Dolomite, whenever we open a new borrow position, the flag is also set to `true` which means that the position should be removed, and again when closing the borrow position, the flag is also set to `true`.

This will lead to that position never being accounted for in the Registry.
```

title: Numerous errors when calculating the TVL for the MorphoBlue connector
content: The MorphoBlue connector miscalculates the protocol's total value locked (TVL) because three independent logic errors combine to produce an accounting mismatch. First, the conversion routine that translates collateral amounts into loan‑token equivalents ignores the differing decimal precision of the two assets; when a collateral token such as USDC (6 decimals) is paired with a loan token such as DAI (18 decimals) the raw numbers are treated as if they share the same scale, causing the TVL to be inflated by several orders of magnitude. Second, the function that aggregates a position’s TVL adds the borrowed amount instead of subtracting it, so any borrowing operation artificially raises the reported TVL while repayments lower it, the opposite of the intended accounting rule. Third, during a withdrawal the internal registry that tracks token balances is updated only for the collateral token; the loan token balance is left unchanged, which means that when a user withdraws the loan token the TVL is recorded as roughly half of its true value. These defects manifest whenever a market involves tokens with different decimal places, when a position is borrowed or repaid, or when a loan token is withdrawn. Users who deposit assets receive a number of protocol shares that is derived from the erroneous TVL; because the TVL can be too high, a depositor may be granted more shares than their contribution warrants, while a withdrawer may receive either fewer shares or an excess of base tokens depending on whether the TVL is under‑ or over‑estimated. The impact is a breach of the fundamental accounting invariant that each share should represent a proportional claim on the underlying assets, leading to potential over‑allocation of value to some participants and under‑allocation to others. The issue was uncovered during a systematic audit by Code4rena, where test cases that mixed USDC and DAI revealed dramatic TVL spikes and sign‑reversal behavior. Because TVL is an internal metric not directly displayed to end‑users, the bug can remain hidden until edge‑case interactions expose the discrepancy, making it difficult to notice in routine operation. To remediate the problem the conversion routine must normalize amounts by dividing by 10**(collateralDecimals) and multiplying by 10**(loanDecimals), the borrow amount must be subtracted from the TVL aggregation, and the withdrawal logic must invoke the token‑registry update for both collateral and loan tokens. Correcting these logical flaws restores the invariant that deposited value equals issued shares and that withdrawals return the correct proportion of base tokens, preserving the protocol’s economic integrity.
summary:
There are numerous issues when calculating the TVL for the MorphoBlue connector

  1. decimals are not considered in the function `convertCToL` this means that if the loanToken and collateralToken have a different number of decimals the TVL calculation will be wrong.
  2. borrowAmount is added rather than subtracted when calculating the TVL. This means that any borrowing will increase the TVL and any repaying will decrease the TVL
  3. When withdrawing the function `_updateTokenInRegistry` is only called for the collateralToken and not the loanToken. This means that if the loanToken is withdrawn the TVL will be less than it should be.

If the TVL is incorrect, users will receive an incorrect number of shares when depositing and an incorrect number of base tokens when withdrawing. The below table shows the possible scenarios.

User | TVL lower than expected | TVL higher than expected  
---|---|---
Deposits | Receives more shares than should be entitled to | Receives fewer base tokens than should be entitled to  
Withdraws | Receives less shares than should be entitled to | Receives more base tokens than should be entitled to

title: `_getPositionTVL` of `UNIv3Connector` wrongly assumes ownership of all liquidity of the provided ticks inside `positionManager`
content: The vulnerability resides in the TVL calculation routine of the UniV3 connector, specifically the internal function that determines the value of a position. The routine queries the Uniswap V3 pool for the total liquidity that exists between two tick boundaries and then assumes that the entire amount of liquidity returned belongs to the connector’s own position. This assumption is incorrect because the pool aggregates liquidity from all participants that share the same tick range, regardless of who owns each share. The root cause is the construction of a pool position key from the connector’s position manager address together with the lower and upper tick values, and then calling pool.positions with that key. The key does not identify a single NFT or a specific owner; it identifies the whole tick range, so the liquidity value includes contributions from unrelated LPs. An attacker can exploit this by creating a separate UniV3 position that uses the same tick range but is owned by a different address. When the connector later calls the TVL function, it will read the combined liquidity, add it to its own reported assets, and thereby inflate the protocol’s total value locked. This inflated TVL can be used by the protocol’s accounting logic to grant higher borrowing limits, distribute larger fees, or present a healthier solvency picture to users and investors. The impact is that the protocol may appear to hold more assets than it actually does, leading to potential over‑leveraging and, in worst‑case scenarios, insufficient funds to satisfy withdrawals or settle debts. The condition occurs every time the _getPositionTVL function is invoked, which is typically during deposit, withdrawal, or valuation operations. All users of the protocol, lenders, and token holders are affected because the mis‑reported numbers can change the economic outcomes of their interactions. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit when the reviewer examined the logic that builds the pool position key and noticed that it does not verify ownership of the liquidity. The bug is subtle because the function returns a plausible numeric TVL; without a separate sanity check, the over‑statement can go unnoticed. To remediate the problem, the connector should query the positions manager’s positions getter, which returns the exact liquidity owned by the connector’s NFT, or otherwise track the tokenId‑specific liquidity directly, ensuring that only the connector’s own share is counted. This class of bug falls under incorrect accounting of shared resources, where exclusive ownership is incorrectly assumed, leading to inflated asset valuations and potential protocol insolvency. From a user’s perspective the symptom may be that a deposited position is displayed with a higher value than the amount that can actually be withdrawn, or that after a withdrawal the balance unexpectedly drops to zero because the protocol had counted liquidity that was never its own.
summary: When `_getPositionTVL` is called, it queries position information from the pool using the calculated key. However, it assumes that all liquidity within the provided ticks in the `positionManager` is owned by the connector.

title: Decreasing a position in PendleConnector will remove it even if there’s still a stake at Penpie
content: The vulnerability resides in the PendleConnector contract that manages Pendle market positions. When a caller invokes decreasePosition with the closePosition flag set to true, the function checks whether the market is empty by calling isMarketEmpty. The isMarketEmpty routine examines the balances of the three core tokens of the market – the standardized yield token, the principal token and the yield token – as well as the market token balance held directly by the connector. However, it completely ignores any balance that the connector may have deposited in the external Penpie staking pool for that market. As a result, if the connector still holds a stake in Penpie, the isMarketEmpty function incorrectly returns true, causing the connector to call registry.updateHoldingPosition with the flag that removes the holding position from the AccountingManager. This logical omission leads to the market being removed from the connector’s list of active holdings even though a stake remains in Penpie. From a user perspective the UI will show that the market has disappeared from the portfolio and the reported total value locked (TVL) for the connector drops, while the underlying LP tokens are still locked in the Penpie pool and cannot be accounted for or withdrawn correctly. The impact is a mismatch in accounting, under‑reporting of TVL, loss of visibility of staked assets and potential inability to claim rewards that depend on the recorded holdings. The bug manifests only when closePosition is true and there is a non‑zero balance in the Penpie pool; otherwise the original logic works as intended. It affects any protocol component that relies on the AccountingManager’s TVL, including investors, auditors and downstream applications that display portfolio data. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by inspecting the logic of decreasePosition and noticing that the external staking balance was not considered. It can be hard to notice because the connector’s direct token balances are zero, which is the usual indicator of an empty market, while the hidden stake resides in a separate contract that is not obvious from a simple balance check. The class of bug is an incomplete state validation or logical omission where external asset holdings are not included in emptiness checks. To remediate, the isMarketEmpty (or the related isMarketOpen) function should be extended to also query the Penpie staking helper for the connector’s balance in that pool and require it to be zero before treating the market as empty. This ensures that a market is only removed when all associated assets, including those locked in external staking contracts, have been fully withdrawn, preserving accurate TVL reporting and preventing accidental removal of active positions.
summary: `decreasePosition()` will falsely remove the market as a holding position, ignoring the staked Pendle market LP tokens at Penpie and thus that stake won’t be counted towards the TVL of the connector and the TVL of the AccountingManager the connector belongs to.

title: Invalid calculation of position TVL in Pendle connector
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect calculation of the position total value locked (TVL) inside the Pendle connector contract. The root cause is a misunderstanding of the semantics of the helper functions getLpToAssetRate and getPtToAssetRate, which return the price of a liquidity‑provider (LP) token or principal token (PT) expressed in the underlying asset (for example USDT). The connector code treats these rates as if they were expressed in SY tokens, multiplying the LP balance by the returned rate and dividing by 1e18, which leads to a systematic under‑ or over‑estimation of the value of LP and PT holdings when they are converted to SY for TVL aggregation. An attacker or any participant can trigger the mis‑calculation by depositing LP tokens into the market, minting PT and YT, and then depositing the resulting SY and PT back into the market; the connector’s internal _getPositionTVL function will then report a TVL that is significantly lower than the actual economic value of the assets held. The impact is that the protocol’s reported TVL, which is used for reward distribution, governance thresholds and risk monitoring, becomes inaccurate; users may see their position value drop on dashboards, receive fewer rewards than expected, or be misled about the health of the protocol. The bug manifests whenever the connector holds LP or PT tokens and calls the faulty conversion logic, as demonstrated by a unit test where TVL drops from roughly 100 USDC to 59 USDC after a market deposit. The affected parties include protocol managers, liquidity providers, and any stakeholder that relies on TVL‑based metrics. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by writing a test that compared the accounting manager’s TVL against expected balances and observing the unexpected drop. It is hard to notice because TVL is an aggregate figure and the discrepancy may be masked by other assets, while the function name getLpToAssetRate suggests it already provides a SY‑compatible rate. The bug belongs to the class of financial conversion or unit‑mismatch errors, where a price feed is interpreted in the wrong unit. From a user perspective the UI may show a lower position value, missing rewards, or a balance that appears unchanged while the protocol reports a loss. The correct fix is to refactor the _getPositionTVL implementation so that it acknowledges that getLpToAssetRate and getPtToAssetRate return values in the underlying asset and then converts those amounts to SY using the appropriate SY‑to‑asset price, or to use a helper that directly provides the SY price per LP/PT. This adjustment restores accurate TVL accounting and aligns the protocol’s reported metrics with the true economic value of the assets.
summary:
Pendle connector allows protocol managers to deposit some underlying asset in return for some SY tokens, which can be used to mint PT and YT tokens. PT and YT can be deposited in markets and in return for LP tokens and some claimable rewards. These LP tokens should be considered when calculating the TVL of the position, to do this the protocol is using `getLpToAssetRate`, which from the [docs](https://docs.pendle.finance/Developers/Helpers/PendleRouterStatic#overview):

`getLpToAssetRate`: Serves the same purpose, but in terms of SY’s asset.

This means that it returns the price of LP in terms of the underlying asset (which is USDT in the below example); however, the protocol is using this function assuming that it returns the price of LP in terms of SY, through:

`SYAmount += lpBalance * IPMarket(market).getLpToAssetRate(10) / 1e18;`

The above also applies to `getPtToAssetRate`.

This will cause an inaccurate representation of the Connector’s TVL affecting the whole protocol’s TVL.

title: Invalid handling of holding positions in `DolomiteConnector::transferBetweenAccounts`
content: The vulnerability originates from the DolomiteConnector contract when it invokes the Dolomite protocol function transferBetweenAccounts to move collateral from one internal account to another that shares the same owner. After the transfer, the connector fails to inform the protocol’s registry about the new holding position of either the source or the destination account. The registry continues to associate the collateral with the original account identifier, so the protocol’s accounting layer still calculates total value locked (TVL) based on the stale position. As a result, the TVL reported for the connector – and consequently for the whole Dolomite system – can drop dramatically, even to zero, despite the assets still being present in the destination account. This discrepancy occurs whenever a manager uses transferBetweenAccounts to re‑allocate funds across accounts, because the connector does not call registry.updateHoldingPosition for the affected accounts. Users observing the UI will see their deposited balance disappear or the protocol TVL suddenly collapse, which contradicts the expectation that funds remain locked and visible after a transfer. The issue was uncovered during a Code4rena audit by writing a test that deposits DAI, transfers the full amount to a second account, and then asserts that the accounting manager’s TVL reads zero while the underlying DolomiteMargin balances show the collateral residing in the new account. The problem is subtle because the underlying balances are correct; only the accounting cache that drives TVL is out of sync, making the bug easy to miss unless the TVL metric is explicitly checked after a transfer. The class of bug can be described as an accounting state inconsistency or stale holding‑position update, where internal state changes are not propagated to external accounting registries. To remediate the issue, the connector should update the holding position for both the old and new accounts after a successful transfer, using registry.updateHoldingPosition with the appropriate account identifiers and market data, thereby ensuring that TVL reflects the true distribution of collateral across accounts.
summary:
In Dolomite protocol, `transferBetweenAccounts` transfers the collateral from 1 account to another under the same owner. So the owner of both accounts still owns these funds regardless of the account they’re deposited in. In `DolomiteConnector`, when calling `transferBetweenAccounts` the protocol isn’t updating the holding position of either account.

So when the manager moves the collateral to account ID 1 for example, the protocol doesn’t know about the new holding position (which is the position related to account ID 1) and will remain calculating the TVL according to the old holding position (account Id 0), even if the whole amount of account 0 was moved to account 1.

This will cause an inaccurate representation of the Connector’s TVL affecting the whole protocol’s TVL.

title: `SettleLongPremium` is incorrectly implemented: premium should be deducted instead of added
content: The vulnerability resides in the premium settlement routine for long option positions. The function responsible for finalising the premium, which should reduce the holder’s balance by the amount of premium owed, mistakenly adds the premium to the holder’s account. The root cause is an incorrect sign handling: the code forwards the realised premium value directly to the collateral token’s exercise call instead of negating it, so the protocol treats a debit as a credit. An attacker or any user with a long option can invoke the settlement function repeatedly, each call crediting the premium amount to their balance. Because the function does not enforce a one‑time settlement or check that the premium has already been accounted for, the extra credits accumulate, draining the protocol’s collateral pool. From a user’s perspective the UI would show an unexpected increase in token balance after settlement – the user expects the premium to be deducted or at most to receive the payoff, but instead sees a sudden boost (for example, a 33 342‑unit increase observed in the test). This breaks the accounting assumptions of the option contract, leading to funds disappearing from the protocol treasury while the user’s balance inflates. The issue manifests whenever the settleLongPremium function is called for a long option after expiry, and it affects all long option holders, the protocol’s collateral reserves, and any downstream participants relying on correct premium accounting. It was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where a proof‑of‑concept test measured the balance before and after three settlement calls and observed a net increase instead of the expected deduction. The bug can be subtle because the function name suggests a normal settlement and the positive balance change may be mistaken for a reward, making it easy to overlook during manual testing. The correct mitigation is to invert the sign of the realised premium before invoking the collateral token’s exercise method, ensuring that the premium is subtracted from the holder’s balance as intended, and to add appropriate checks that prevent multiple settlements of the same premium.
summary: `SettleLongPremium` is the function intended to settle premiums for long option holders. When called, it should deduct the premium from the option owner’s account, but the current implementation adds the premium instead.

title: Overflow in `CollateralTracker` allows minting shares for free
content: The vulnerability is an arithmetic overflow in the CollateralTracker contract that occurs inside an unchecked block when calculating the amount of underlying assets that correspond to a requested number of shares. The root cause is the use of an unchecked multiplication (shares * DECIMALS) without protecting against overflow, combined with a custom mulDivRoundingUp function that assumes the intermediate product fits into the uint256 range. When an attacker supplies an extremely large share amount, the multiplication wraps around, producing a much smaller product. Consequently the previewMint function returns an asset value that is far lower than the true value of the minted shares – often as low as one unit – while the mint function only checks that the returned asset amount does not exceed type(uint104).max. Because the overflowed asset value passes this check, the contract mints a huge number of shares for essentially no collateral. An attacker can then call the withdrawal logic to claim the full underlying collateral against the artificially inflated share balance, effectively draining the pool. The impact is that funds belonging to honest users can be stolen, leading to a total loss of collateral for the protocol. The condition occurs whenever the mint function is called with a share amount large enough to cause the multiplication to overflow, which is possible because the contract does not enforce an upper bound on the share input before the unchecked block. The affected parties are all users who deposit collateral, the protocol’s economic model, and any token holders relying on the share‑to‑asset accounting. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when the auditors crafted a proof‑of‑concept test that minted shares using type(uint).max/10000+1 and observed that the returned asset amount was only one, while the share balance increased by the full amount. The bug is subtle because the overflow happens inside a low‑level arithmetic routine and the contract still reports a successful mint, making it easy to miss during casual testing. To remediate, the unchecked block should be removed or replaced with safe arithmetic that checks for overflow, and the previewMint calculation should enforce that the share input cannot cause the intermediate product to exceed the maximum representable value. In broader terms, this is a classic unchecked overflow leading to a mis‑calculation of token accounting, allowing free minting of shares and subsequent unauthorized withdrawal of assets, violating the protocol’s accounting invariants and user expectations that each minted share is backed by a proportional amount of collateral.
summary: Malicious actors can mint huge amounts of shares for free and then withdraw all collateral.

title: Withdrawals can be locked forever if recipient is a contract
content: The vulnerability originates from the use of Solidity's low‑level transfer function in the claim() routine of the WithdrawQueue contract. Transfer forwards a fixed stipend of 2300 gas to the recipient address, which is sufficient for a simple externally owned account but insufficient for any contract that implements a receive() or fallback function requiring more than the stipend. When a user initiates a withdrawal from a contract wallet—such as a multisig or smart‑contract based wallet—the contract address is recorded as the withdrawal requester. After the cooldown period the same contract must call claim() to receive the ETH. Because claim() executes payable(msg.sender).transfer(amount), the Ethereum Virtual Machine attempts to deliver the ETH with only 2300 gas. If the recipient contract’s receive() logic consumes more gas (for example, a Safe that needs over 6 k gas to forward the call and emit an event), the transfer reverts with an out‑of‑gas error. The transaction therefore fails and the ETH remains locked inside the WithdrawQueue contract with no further mechanism to retrieve it. From a user’s perspective the expectation is that the claimed amount will be transferred to their wallet, but instead the UI shows no change in balance and the withdrawal appears stuck forever. The impact is a permanent loss of funds for any participant using a contract account as the withdrawal destination. The issue was discovered during a security audit that exercised withdrawals from a multisig contract and observed the revert caused by the gas stipend limitation. It is hard to notice because transfers to regular accounts succeed, and the failure only manifests when the recipient is a contract with non‑trivial fallback logic. The bug belongs to the class of gas‑stipend limitations where transfer or send are used instead of call, leading to locked assets when the recipient cannot execute with the provided gas. The recommended remediation is to replace transfer with a low‑level call that forwards all available gas and checks the returned success flag, thereby allowing any contract to receive the ETH and execute its receive logic safely.
summary:
The [`WithdrawQueue`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L303) contract allows users to request withdrawals of their ezETH tokens in exchange for a selected asset, such as ETH or an ERC20 token. After a cooldown period, users can call the [`claim()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/519e518f2d8dec9acf6482b84a181e403070d22d/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L279) function to receive their withdrawn assets.

When the selected asset is ETH, the `claim()` function sends the ETH using the low-level `transfer()` function:

```solidity
payable(msg.sender).transfer(_withdrawRequest.amountToRedeem);
```

However, `transfer()` only forwards 2300 gas, which is not enough for the recipient to execute any non-trivial logic in a `receive()` or fallback function. For instance, it is not enough for Safes (such as [this one](https://etherscan.io/address/0xd1e6626310fd54eceb5b9a51da2ec329d6d4b68a) in use by the protocol) to receive funds, which require `>` 6k gas for the call to reach the implementation contract and emit an event:

Note: to view the provided image, please see the original submission[here](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo-findings/issues/612).

In this case, the impact is higher than that reported by [4naly3er](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/4naly3er-report.md#m-4-call-should-be-used-instead-of-transfer-on-an-address-payable) because `claim()` requires the caller to be the same address that initiated the original withdrawal request via `withdraw()`.

If a user calls `withdraw()` from a contract account like a multisig or smart contract wallet that has a `receive()` function requiring `>2300` gas, their subsequent `claim()` call will fail permanently. The withdrawn ETH will be locked in the `WithdrawQueue` contract forever, leading to loss of funds.

title: Incorrect calculation of queued withdrawals can deflate TVL and increase ezETH mint rate
content: The vulnerability originates from an incorrect accounting routine used to compute the protocol’s total value locked (TVL) and the amount of ezETH that can be minted against deposited collateral. The function that aggregates a token’s underlying balance adds the value of shares held by the strategy and, when applicable, the value of shares that have been queued for withdrawal. However, the condition that decides whether queued shares should be added checks the mapping entry for the contract’s own address (address(this)) instead of the specific token address. Because the contract never records queued shares under its own address, the check always evaluates to zero, causing the function to ignore any pending withdrawals for that token. As a result, when a user or the operator queues a withdrawal, the amount that is slated to leave the system is omitted from the TVL calculation. The protocol therefore reports a lower TVL than the actual assets under management. Since the ezETH minting formula uses the reported TVL as a denominator, a deflated TVL inflates the mint rate, allowing more ezETH to be minted per unit of collateral than intended. An attacker can trigger withdrawals for a chosen token, watch the TVL drop, and then deposit additional collateral to receive an oversized amount of ezETH, effectively diluting existing holders and stealing value from the protocol. The impact is economic: users may receive more ezETH than they should, the protocol’s accounting becomes inconsistent, and the perceived health of the system is misrepresented, potentially leading to loss of confidence and financial loss for honest participants. The bug manifests whenever the RestakeManager calls getTokenBalanceFromStrategy while there are queued withdrawals for any supported collateral token. It is difficult to notice because the TVL simply appears lower; the UI may show a reduced total locked amount without obvious error, and the minting process still succeeds, masking the underlying mis‑calculation. The issue was discovered during a formal audit, where a Foundry proof‑of‑concept demonstrated that after queuing a withdrawal of 50 stETH the reported TVL fell from 100 stETH to 50 stETH, confirming that the queued amount was ignored. To remediate, the accounting function must reference the queuedShares entry for the token address (queuedShares[address(token)]) when deciding whether to add the pending withdrawal value, ensuring that all assets slated to leave the protocol are correctly reflected in the TVL and that the ezETH mint rate remains accurate.

title: ETH withdrawals from EigenLayer always fail due to `OperatorDelegator`’s nonReentrant `receive`
content: The vulnerability originates from the use of a nonReentrant guard on the OperatorDelegator contract’s receive function, which is invoked during the completion of a queued ETH withdrawal from EigenLayer. When an admin calls completeQueuedWithdrawal with the receiveAsTokens flag set to true and the withdrawal includes any amount of ETH, the delegationManager triggers a call to the receive fallback of OperatorDelegator. Because receive is marked nonReentrant, the re‑entrant call that is required to forward the ETH to the restake manager is blocked, causing the ETH transfer to fail silently. As a result, the withdrawn ETH becomes permanently stuck in the EigenLayer contract, the withdrawal queue never clears, and users see no change in their balances despite a successful transaction. The issue occurs only when the withdrawal contains ETH and the caller is the EigenPod contract; withdrawals that involve only ERC20 tokens are unaffected. This bug was discovered during a security audit that exercised the withdrawal path on a mainnet fork and observed that the ETH never arrived. It is difficult to notice because the transaction does not revert; it simply leaves the ETH locked, leading users to believe the withdrawal succeeded while their funds are inaccessible. The problem belongs to the class of reentrancy‑guard misuse on fallback functions, where a protective modifier unintentionally prevents a legitimate internal re‑entrancy required by the business logic. Users experience the symptom of initiating a withdrawal, receiving a transaction receipt, but seeing their ETH balance remain unchanged and the protocol’s withdrawal queue stay full. The expected behavior—receiving the withdrawn ETH back—does not occur, violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions that deposited ETH can always be redeemed. To remediate, the nonReentrant modifier should be removed from the receive function entirely, or applied conditionally only when the caller is not the EigenPod, thereby allowing the required internal re‑entrancy while still protecting against external re‑entrancy attacks.

title: Withdrawals logic allows MEV exploits of TVL changes and zero-slippage zero-fee swaps
content: The vulnerability is a withdrawal amount pre‑calculation flaw in which the protocol computes the amount of assets a user can redeem at the moment a withdrawal request is submitted, using the current oracle price and total value locked (TVL) rather than at the later claim stage. Because the price of the underlying ezETH token or any supported liquid staking token (LST) can change between request and claim, an attacker can manipulate the oracle or exploit natural price movements to obtain a larger amount of the target asset than was originally deposited, all without paying fees. The exploit works by observing a pending price‑increase transaction (for example a Chainlink price update or EigenLayer reward distribution), depositing the asset just before the price rises, and immediately submitting a withdrawal request after the price change. The contract credits the request with the higher post‑change price, and when the claim is finally processed the attacker receives the inflated amount, effectively stealing value from honest participants. A similar attack can be performed when a LST price drops sharply due to slashing, an exploit, or liquidity stress: the attacker borrows or purchases the LST, inflates its reported price, deposits it, and requests a withdrawal of another asset such as ETH, receiving more than the fair value. The impact is that funds disappear from the pool, honest users receive less or even zero assets when they claim, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions about one‑to‑one redemption are broken. The issue manifests whenever the oracle price or TVL changes between the request and claim, which can happen within the same block, making it exploitable by front‑running bots or MEV actors. All users who deposit or withdraw are affected, as are the protocol’s overall capital and any downstream applications that rely on its stability. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit by Code4rena when the withdrawal logic was examined and the timing of the redemption calculation was noted. It is hard to notice because the UI shows a successful request and no explicit error, yet the underlying accounting is subtly altered. To remediate, the contract should recompute the redemption amount at claim time and enforce that the lower of the two values is used, optionally adding a rate‑limit or short delay on deposits to prevent rapid price swings. This aligns the design with a safe oracle‑price‑based redemption model rather than a zero‑slippage, zero‑fee DEX, eliminating the class of price‑manipulation and front‑running vulnerabilities.
summary:
Deposit and withdrawal requests can be done immediately with no costs or fees, and both use the current oracle prices and TVL calculation ([`deposit`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/RestakeManager.sol#L499-L504), and [`withdraw`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L217)). Crucially, the [withdrawal amount is calculated at withdrawal request submission time](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L220C1-L224C11) instead of at withdrawal claim time. Any small change in either ezETH value or in the price of a collateral token can be exploited at no cost by MEV. Specifically, if the price increases, a deposit is made before the increase, and a withdrawal request immediately after.

Additionally, in case of a supported LST’s sudden change in price (for example, due to price manipulation, an exploit of that LST, due to consensus layer penalties (slashing), or liquidity issues), external holders of that LST may frontrun the change, deposit the LST into Renzo, and immediately request a withdrawal of another asset (e.g., native ETH). In such situations, Renzo functions as a **zero-slippage zero-fees oracle-price-based DEX** for LSTs and ETH up to the TVL cap for the affected LST. Zero-slippage zero-fee oracle-price-based designs are notoriously vulnerable to both oracle manipulation and oracle latency attacks if not carefully prevented.

title: Withdrawals of rebasing tokens can lead to insolvency and unfair distribution of protocol reserves
content: The vulnerability resides in the WithdrawQueue contract that manages user withdrawals of various assets, including liquid staking derivatives (LSDs) that implement a rebasing mechanism such as stETH. When a user calls withdraw(), the contract queries an oracle to compute a fixed token amount (amountToRedeem) that represents the value of the user’s ezETH share in the chosen output asset. This amount is stored directly in a WithdrawRequest struct and later transferred to the user in claim() via a standard ERC‑20 transfer. The root cause is that the contract treats rebasing tokens as if their balances were static, ignoring that the underlying token balance can change between the time the withdrawal request is recorded and the moment it is claimed. Rebasing tokens keep a constant number of shares while the underlying pooled ETH value per share can increase or decrease after events such as slashing or reward distribution. Because the WithdrawQueue records a fixed token amount rather than the corresponding share count, a negative rebasing event (for example a 10 % slashing of the stETH pool) reduces the contract’s actual stETH balance while the stored amountToRedeem remains unchanged. When the first claimant executes claim(), the contract transfers the originally recorded amount, which now represents a larger proportion of the remaining pool than intended. Consequently the protocol disburses more value than it holds, causing later claimants to either receive less than expected or encounter a transfer failure. From the user’s perspective the symptoms are a missing or zero balance after a claim, or an unexpected revert when trying to withdraw, while the protocol’s reserves become under‑collateralised and may even become insolvent. The issue manifests only for assets that rebase; non‑rebasing tokens such as wBETH behave correctly because their token balance tracks value one‑to‑one. The problem was uncovered during a formal audit by simulating a negative rebasing event in a Foundry test, which showed that early withdrawers could extract the full pre‑rebasing amount while later withdrawers were left with insufficient funds. The bug is subtle because the contract’s balance checks occur at request time, giving a false sense of safety, and the rebasing adjustment is not visible on‑chain until after the event. The recommended mitigation is to store and transfer the user’s entitlement in terms of shares rather than a fixed token amount. By converting the oracle‑derived value to stETH shares with getSharesByPooledEth() at withdrawal time and later transferring those shares with transferShares(), the protocol ensures each user receives a proportional slice of the current pool regardless of rebasing. Similar share‑based accounting should be applied to claimReserve and buffer calculations. This change restores accounting integrity, prevents unfair profit extraction, and protects the protocol from insolvency caused by rebasing token dynamics.
summary:
The [`WithdrawQueue`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol) contract allows users to withdraw their funds in various tokens, including liquid staking derivatives (LSDs) such as stETH. The [`withdraw()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L206) function calculates the amount of the specified `_assetOut` token equivalent to the ezETH being withdrawn [using](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L229) the `renzoOracle.lookupTokenAmountFromValue()` function. This amount is then stored in the `amountToRedeem` field of a new `WithdrawRequest` struct, which is added to the user’s `withdrawRequests` array and the token’s `claimReserve`.

When the user later calls [`claim()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L279), the contract transfers the `amountToRedeem` to the user via the [`IERC20.transfer()`](https://github.com/code-423n4/2024-04-renzo/blob/main/contracts/Withdraw/WithdrawQueue.sol#L305) function.

However, this implementation does not properly handle rebasing tokens like stETH. The stETH balance of the `WithdrawQueue` can change between the time a withdrawal is recorded and when it is claimed, even though the contract’s stETH shares remain constant.

If the stETH balance decreases during this period due to a rebasing event (e.g., a slashing of the staked ETH), the `amountToRedeem` stored in the `WithdrawRequest` may exceed the contract’s actual stETH balance at the time of claiming. As a result, the withdrawal can fail or result in the user receiving a larger share of the total protocol reserves than intended.

The issue can be illustrated by comparing the behavior of withdrawals for non-rebasing and rebasing LSDs:

1. Non-rebasing LSD (e.g., wBETH):

   * User A requests a withdrawal of 10 wBETH (worth 10 ETH) from the protocol.
   * While the withdrawal is pending, wBETH’s underlying staked ETH suffers a 50% slashing event.
   * The price of wBETH drops to 0.5 ETH per token due to the slashing.
   * When User A claims their withdrawal, they receive 10 wBETH, which is now worth only 5 ETH.
   * User A bears the loss from the slashing event.
2. Rebasing LSD (e.g., stETH):

   * User B requests a withdrawal of 10 stETH (worth 10 ETH) from the protocol.
   * While the withdrawal is pending, the underlying staked ETH suffers a 50% slashing event.
   * Everyone’s stETH balances are rebased to maintain the ETH peg, so the protocol’s stETH balance is halved.
