The impact is that the user receives far fewer output tokens than expected, effectively losing value; from the user’s perspective the UI may show a successful swap but the received amount is dramatically lower or even zero, contradicting the expectation of a fair market rate. This condition occurs whenever a MarketSwap order is still executable after its requestExpirationTime and the contract does not enforce a maximum oracle timestamp. All users who place MarketSwap orders and any protocol relying on accurate price feeds are affected, as the flaw undermines the accounting assumptions that the price used for a swap reflects the market at the time of order execution. The issue was discovered during a security audit that reviewed the order‑processing logic and identified the missing maxOracleTimestamp check. It can be hard to notice because the transaction does not revert and the price discrepancy may only become apparent after the swap, especially if the UI does not display the age of the oracle price. The recommended remediation is to add a validation step that ensures the oracle timestamp used for a MarketSwap order does not exceed the order’s requestExpirationTime, thereby guaranteeing that only fresh, authorized price data can be used for execution. This class of bug falls under insufficient input validation and time‑based oracle validation errors, which can lead to price manipulation and financial loss.
summary: In the processOrder function for swap orders, the price timestamp validation includes no maxOracleTimestamp validation for MarketSwap orders. As a result a keeper may accidentally or maliciously execute a MarketSwap order when it is far past its request expiration age, with prices that are significantly unfavorable for the user.

title: H-08 | Atomic Withdrawal Feature Unusable
content: The vulnerability concerns the atomic withdrawal feature of the protocol. When a user invokes the executeAtomicWithdrawal function, the modifier withOraclePrices triggers a call to the internal _validatePrices routine in Oracle.sol. This routine checks that the price provider supplied by the keeper matches the provider stored for each token. For regular token operations the stored provider is the dataStreamProvider, but for atomic withdrawals the protocol uses a distinct priceFeedProvider. Because the validation logic always compares the keeper‑provided address against the dataStreamProvider entry (oracleProviderForTokenKey), the check fails for atomic withdrawals. The mismatch causes the transaction to revert before any funds are transferred, making the atomic withdrawal path effectively unusable. The root cause is an incorrect validation condition that does not distinguish between normal and atomic withdrawal contexts, leading to a business‑logic violation where the promised atomic exit mechanism cannot be executed. The issue manifests only when the atomic withdrawal action is attempted; normal withdrawals continue to work as expected. Users experience a failed transaction, often seeing a generic “revert” error or a UI message such as “withdrawal failed”, while their balances remain unchanged. From the auditor’s perspective the problem was discovered by tracing the call stack during a security review and noticing that the provider comparison never succeeds for the atomic path. The bug is subtle because the same validation code is reused for multiple actions, so the failure is hidden unless the specific atomic withdrawal flow is exercised. To remediate the issue the validation should be altered to compare the keeper‑provided address with the isAtomicOracleProviderKey entry when the action is an atomic withdrawal, thereby allowing the correct priceFeedProvider to be accepted. Conceptually this belongs to the class of improper configuration validation bugs that break a specific feature by applying a generic check to a specialized case, resulting in functional denial of service for users attempting the atomic withdrawal.
summary: During executeAtomicWithdrawal modifier withOraclePrices is used which when we follow the call trace we will reach the _validatePrices function in Oracle.sol. In this function we check the provider for the given tokens to validate that it is indeed the same provider given by keeper. The problem is, the normal providers for tokens will be the dataStreamProvider while for atomic withdrawals they will be the priceFeedProvider. Hence keeper provided provider won't match this provider in dataStore which will lead to reverts for all atomic withdrawal calls.

title: H-09 | Migration Inconsistencies
content: The vulnerability stems from a migration window in which both the legacy contract and the upgraded contract are simultaneously active and can be invoked by keeper bots. Because the two contracts implement different business logic, the system can produce inconsistent outcomes for the same user action. Borrowing fee calculations are performed with distinct formulas in each contract, so a borrower may be charged a higher or lower fee depending on which contract the keeper routes the request to, and the market token price derived from those fees can diverge, breaking the protocol’s pricing invariants. In the legacy contract, excess fees are automatically transferred to a designated fee collector, whereas the new contract forwards those fees to a receiver address; integrators that have already switched to the new flow may lose the ability to collect excess fees when the old contract still processes transactions. Additionally, take‑profit and stop‑loss orders opened through the new contract are registered in an auto‑cancellation list that is cleared only when the same contract processes the closing or liquidation. If a keeper closes the position using the old contract, the entry remains in the list, causing the system to think the order is still pending and potentially opening unintended positions for the user later. The issue manifests only while both contracts are live, which typically occurs during a planned upgrade or migration phase. Users experience symptoms such as unexpected borrowing costs, missing fee payouts, or spontaneous position openings that were never requested. The problem is hard to detect because each contract functions correctly in isolation; the inconsistency only appears when the two are interleaved, a scenario that may not be exercised in standard unit tests. The root cause is the lack of a coordinated deprecation strategy and the absence of state synchronization between the contracts. To remediate, the protocol should ensure that only one contract is operational at any time, defer activation of parameters like optimalBorrowingFactor until the legacy contract is fully retired, and provide clear communication to integrators and users about the temporary inconsistencies. Alternatively, a bridging layer could be introduced to reconcile fee calculations and order bookkeeping across both versions during the migration period, but the simplest and safest approach is to avoid overlapping usage altogether.
summary: According to documentation there is a time where both old contracts and new contracts are live and used by keepers. This can create massive inconsistency in the system such as: 1. Borrowing fee calculations are different between systems which will lead to both different borrowing fee's for users between systems and also different market token pricing's for the system which can have catastrophic effect. 2. While old system continue to send excess fees to account, new system will send them to receiver. Which can be especially problematic for integrators who changed their system according to new implementation and can't send excess fees to receiver anymore. 3. Take profit and stop-loss orders that are opened with new contracts will be added to autoCancelList but if the position is closed/liquidated with the old keeper, this lost won't be cleared. Which in turn, users can experience unexpected position openings in the future if they continue to use the system.

title: H-01 | Borrowing Fees Increase Based On Incorrect Rate
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect ordering of state updates that leads to inaccurate borrowing fee calculations. When a position is updated, the contract calls a function that increments a cumulative borrowing factor based on the current borrowing rate, which itself depends on the proportion of pool liquidity that is currently borrowed. The rate should be applied to the time elapsed since the last update, using the utilization that existed during that interval. However, deposit and withdrawal operations change the pool’s utilization but do not update the cumulative borrowing factor before the state change. Consequently, the next time the funding and borrowing state is refreshed, the contract uses the new utilization value for the entire elapsed period, even though that utilization only applied after the deposit or withdrawal. This mismatch causes borrowing fees to be over‑charged after withdrawals (because the rate appears higher than it actually was) and under‑charged after deposits (because the rate appears lower). The impact is that borrowers may see unexpectedly high fees, potentially pushing near‑liquidation positions into liquidation, while the protocol may suffer from accounting inconsistencies and loss of trust. Attackers can exploit the step‑wise fee jump by timing large deposits or withdrawals to create a temporary rate shift and then trigger a funding update, profiting from arbitrage or forcing liquidations. The issue manifests whenever a user performs a deposit or withdrawal and a subsequent funding update occurs, which is common in protocols that integrate with GMX where large liquidity movements are frequent. It affects all borrowers, liquidity providers, and any downstream contracts that rely on correct fee accounting. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the sequence of calls in the funding update logic and identified that the cumulative borrowing factor was not refreshed early enough. Because the fee discrepancy only appears after sizable liquidity changes, it can be hard to notice and may be mistakenly attributed to market volatility. The bug belongs to the class of state‑ordering or race‑condition errors where a stale rate is applied to a new time interval, violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions that fees are proportional to actual utilization over time. From a user’s perspective the symptoms include higher than expected borrowing costs, sudden liquidation warnings, or refunds that seem too low after a deposit. The correct mitigation is to update the funding and borrowing state before any deposit or withdrawal modifies the pool’s liquidity, ensuring the cumulative borrowing factor reflects the true utilization for the elapsed period.
summary: When a position is updated the updateFundingAndBorrowingState function is called which updates CUMULATIVE_BORROWING_FACTOR based on the recent rate as well as the time since the last update. The rate of which the CUMULATIVE_BORROWING_FACTOR will increase is dependent on what percentage of the pools liquidity is being borrowed. The higher the percentage the higher the rate. By updating the CUMULATIVE_BORROWING_FACTOR before any changes to the state that could affect rate the borrowing fees can correctly be calculated. The issue however is that this is not the case everywhere. When a user withdraws or deposits they will change the rate. As they withdraw the rate will increase and as they deposit the rate will decrease. However because the CUMULATIVE_BORROWING_FACTOR is not updated before a deposit/withdraw, the next time it is updated the rate will use the new value not the value that was actually representative of the elapsed time. Leading to excessive fees being charged if a withdraw occurs, or insufficient fees being charged if a deposit occurs. With protocols integrating into GMX large deposits or withdraws will occur which will have a larger impact on the inaccuracy of the fees. The excessive fees being charged would lead to near liquidateable positions to become unexpectedly pushed to a liquidateable state. This step-wise jump in borrowing fees can also lead to arbitrage opportunities where attackers can profit off the inaccurate jump by making timely orders and deposits.

title: H-02 | Atomic Providers Cannot Be Configured
content: The vulnerability is a configuration error in the function that sets the atomic price feed provider. Instead of writing to the storage slot that controls the atomic oracle provider, the code writes to the slot used for the generic oracle provider flag. Because the atomicOracleProvider variable is never updated, the contract cannot record any provider that is authorized to supply prices for atomic withdrawals. The root cause is a copy‑paste mistake where the identifier is mismatched, leading to a logical disconnect between the intended configuration and the actual state change. An attacker or a legitimate user cannot exploit this directly to steal funds, but the bug effectively disables the atomic withdrawal feature: when a user initiates an atomic withdrawal, the contract attempts to fetch a price from the atomic oracle provider, finds none, and typically falls back to a default or reverts, resulting in a zero or missing payout. The impact is that users expecting an instant, on‑chain price‑based withdrawal receive nothing or experience a failed transaction, breaking the business logic that assumes a reliable price feed for atomic exits. This condition occurs whenever the contract owner or governance tries to register or update an atomic oracle provider after a signal event; the call silently succeeds but has no effect. All participants who rely on atomic withdrawals – traders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the feature is effectively turned off while the contract appears to accept configuration. The issue was discovered during a manual audit where the reviewer compared the storage keys used in the setter function against the intended state variables and noticed the mismatch. Because the function does not emit an error and the storage write succeeds, the problem can be hard to notice without inspecting the contract’s internal state or testing the atomic withdrawal path. The proper remediation is to replace the incorrect key with the correct atomic provider key, ensuring that the atomicOracleProvider variable is written correctly. Conceptually, this is a misconfiguration bug where a setter writes to the wrong storage slot, a class of errors common in contracts that manage multiple similar flags or addresses. From a user’s perspective the UI may show the atomic withdrawal option, but after confirming the transaction the user receives no funds or sees a reverted transaction, contrary to the expectation that the withdrawal should complete instantly with the correct amount. The failure violates the accounting assumption that a valid price feed will always be available for atomic exits, leading to a silent loss of functionality rather than a direct loss of assets.
summary: In the setAtomicOracleProviderAfterSignal function the isOracleProviderEnabledKey is used instead of the isAtomicOracleProviderKey. As a result the atomicOracleProvider value cannot be set, preventing any price feed provider from atomic withdrawal use, and disallowing the atomic withdrawal feature.

title: H-03 | Users Can Use Shift To Avoid Deposit Fees
content: The vulnerability allows a user to bypass the SwapPricingType.TwoStep deposit fee by exploiting the shift mechanism. In the contract the function that executes a shift does not call the shift vault’s recordTransferIn routine at the start of the operation. Fee calculation is performed in _executeDeposit by calling SwapPricingUtils.getSwapFees, which distinguishes three fee types: TwoStep, Atomic, and a zero‑fee path for shifts. Because the shift path never records incoming tokens before the fee is computed, any tokens that are sent directly to the shift vault before the keeper runs are later accounted for as part of the shift deposit and are treated as having paid the zero‑fee rate. An attacker can front‑run the keeper transaction, transfer a large amount of the long and short assets to the shift vault, and then let the keeper execute the shift. When recordTransferIn is finally called after the withdrawal step, the protocol records the transferred amount as a normal deposit but does not apply the TwoStep fee, effectively allowing the attacker to deposit millions of dollars with no fee. The impact is a loss of expected fee revenue for the protocol and an unfair advantage for users who discover the trick, while honest participants continue to pay the normal fee. The issue manifests only when a shift is executed and the vault receives external tokens before the shift logic runs; under normal deposit calls the fee is correctly applied. It is hard to notice because the shift and deposit code paths are separate and the fee‑exempt flag for shifts gives the impression that no fee should ever be charged for that path. The bug was identified during a security audit that examined the interaction between the shift executor and the fee calculation routine. To remediate the problem the shift executor should invoke shiftVault.recordTransferIn for both the long and short tokens at the beginning of executeShift, ensuring that any tokens arriving in the vault are accounted for before the fee logic runs and that the TwoStep fee is applied consistently.
summary: Users can avoid the SwapPricingType.TwoStep fee on deposits by utilizing shift and its lack of fees. Inside _executeDeposit, SwapPricingUtils.getSwapFees calculates the fee that users would pay for depositing into the exchange. Where there are 3 fees - TwoStep, Atomic, and 0 fee for shifts. Users can abuse the lack of fee for shifts by simply front-running the keeper and sending their desired tokens to the shiftVault. When the keeper calls executeShift, these tokens would be accounted for as deposited from the shift when recordTransferIn is executed. This way, users can avoid paying the SwapPricingType.TwoStep fee. For Example: 1. User makes a deposit of 1 USDC into the USDC:WETH vault. 2. User creates a shift for the same market. 3. User sees keeper TX and front-runs with 10,000 USDC and 2 WETH. 4. Keeper executes shift: 1. In the middle of the shift after the withdrawal, the tokens are recorded from the ShiftVault. 2. The recorded change is 10,001 USDC and 2 WETH. 5. The shift deposits the USDC and WETH while avoiding the fee.

title: H-04 | Cant set data stream through config
content: The vulnerability is a logical error in the setDataStream function that prevents a new data stream from being added through the configuration interface. The function includes a guard that is intended to verify that the data stream has not already been set, but the guard checks a constant key generated by Keys.dataStreamIdKey(token) instead of querying the actual data store where the stream identifiers are recorded. Because the generated key is never zero, the condition that should allow a fresh insertion is always evaluated as false, causing the function to reject every attempt to register a stream. This mistake originates from an incorrect reference to storage; the contract looks at the wrong variable, so the existence test is effectively meaningless. An attacker or honest user cannot exploit the bug to steal assets, but the flaw can be used to deny service by blocking the addition of required data feeds. When the contract is called, it silently fails or returns an error, leaving the caller with the impression that the operation succeeded while the internal state remains unchanged. As a result, the protocol’s accounting and business logic that depend on external data streams—such as price oracles—break down, leading to missing or zeroed values in user interfaces, failed calculations, and potentially halted functionality for any component that expects fresh feed data. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the configuration pathways and identified that the guard never evaluates to true. It can be hard to notice because the function does not revert with a clear message; instead it simply prevents the update, which may be interpreted as a normal condition by callers. To remediate the problem, the contract should reference the actual data store mapping that holds the stream identifiers and check whether the entry for the given token is empty (e.g., address(0) or zero) before allowing a new stream to be set. This change restores the intended behavior, ensures that data streams can be added when appropriate, and aligns the implementation with the protocol’s expectation that configuration updates succeed when the stream is not already present.
summary: When the setDataStream function is called there is a check that ensures the dataStream is not already set. However the check incorrectly does not reference the dataStore instead the check only uses the Keys.dataStreamIdKey(token) key. Which will never return 0. Which means the check will always fail and Data Streams will not be able to be added via the config.

title: H-05 | GMOracleProvider Reverts Due To Incorrect Validation
content: The vulnerability resides in the price‑aggregation contract that receives signed price ranges (minPrice and maxPrice) from a set of oracle keepers. The contract expects each keeper to submit a pair of values that are later sorted in ascending order before the signature validation routine (validateSigner) checks that the price at a given index matches the signature at the same index. Because the implementation validates the minPrice array and the maxPrice array independently against the same signer list, sorting the two arrays separately destroys the one‑to‑one relationship between a keeper’s signature and its price pair. In practice an order keeper will sort the minPrices array and the maxPrices array independently to satisfy the “ascending order” requirement, which results in a mismatched ordering: the minPrice at index i no longer belongs to the signer whose signature is stored at index i, and the same holds for maxPrice. When validateSigner is called, the contract compares a price that originated from keeper A with a signature that belongs to keeper B, causing the check to fail and the transaction to revert. The bug can be triggered simply by providing correctly signed price ranges but allowing the sorting step to rearrange the arrays, which is the normal behaviour of most order‑keeping implementations. Consequently, any attempt to update the oracle feed may revert, preventing the protocol from receiving fresh price data. This can freeze trading, cause order execution failures, and ultimately lead to loss of opportunity or stranded funds for users who rely on timely price updates. The issue is discovered during a manual audit that examined the validation logic and identified the implicit assumption that the ordering of price arrays is preserved after sorting. It is hard to notice because the revert appears as a generic “invalid signature” error, which may be attributed to a malformed request rather than a deeper ordering problem. The vulnerability belongs to the class of data‑integrity bugs where an ordering assumption breaks the association between signed data and its signer. To remediate, the contract should preserve the pairing of minPrice, maxPrice, and signer before any sorting operation, for example by validating each keeper’s price pair in its original order or by using a structure that keeps the three elements together and sorting only after the signature check. This ensures that the signature always corresponds to the exact price range it signed, eliminating the mismatch that leads to reverts.
summary: GMOracleProvider get signed prices from Oracle keepers and tries to validate them with validateSigner(). What is expected from Order Keepers is providing both minPrices and maxPrices in ascending order for a token. The problem occur because these minPrices and maxPrices are validated against their corresponding index in the signers and signatures array. But it is not guaranteed and in most cases won't be possible to both sort minPrices and maxPrices while protecting their corresponding signatures in the correct index. Consider the following scenario: • Oracle Keeper 1 signs minPrice = 1003, maxPrice = 1010 • Oracle Keeper 2 signs minPrice = 1004, maxPrice = 1011 • Oracle Keeper 3 signs minPrice = 1005, maxPrice = 1009 Here when Order Keeper sort both prices in ascending order they will be sorted as follows: minPrice = [Keeper1 minPrice, Keeper2 minPrice, Keeper3 minPrice] maxPrice = [Keeper3 maxPrice, Keeper1 maxPrice, Keeper2 maxPrice] Hence in validateSigner call, prices and respective signatures won't match and call will revert. If on the other hand Order Keeper does not sort the order as above, then sorting check will fail and transaction will again revert.

title: A malicious staker can delay the increase of any delegator's voteWeight as much as he wants
content: The vulnerability is a logical flaw in the delegation mechanism that allows a malicious staker to arbitrarily reduce the effective staking duration (the variable representing stakeTime) of any delegator, which in turn delays or suppresses the growth of the delegator’s voteWeight. The root cause is that when a user delegates tokens to a delegator the contract decreases the delegator’s stakeTime to reflect the added delegation, but when the same user later undelegates, the contract only reduces the delegator’s balance and never restores the previously decreased stakeTime. Because stakeTime is used in the formula votePower = balance * t / (t + HalfTime), repeatedly delegating and undelegating can drive t to an arbitrarily low value, causing the votePower to stay low or approach zero regardless of how long the delegator has been holding tokens. An attacker can exploit this by repeatedly performing a delegate‑then‑undelegate cycle on the same delegator, either within a single transaction or across multiple transactions, each cycle further shrinking t. The impact is that the affected delegator’s voting power does not increase as expected, effectively silencing their influence in governance, skewing proposal outcomes, and potentially allowing the attacker to control protocol decisions. This condition occurs whenever the contract’s delegation functions are used and the stakeTime variable is not correctly restored on undelegation, affecting any token holder who relies on delegated voting power. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the interaction between setUserVoteDelegate/unsetUserVoteDelegate and stake/withdraw functions and identified the asymmetric handling of stakeTime. It can be hard to notice because the votePower appears to change gradually and may be mistaken for normal staking decay; there is no explicit error or revert, only an unexpected reduction in voting power. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that their voteWeight remains low or even drops to near zero despite holding a substantial balance for an extended period, leading to situations where a user expects to be able to vote but receives no voting power. The bug belongs to the class of “state‑inconsistent accounting” or “mutable time‑based weight manipulation” vulnerabilities, where a contract’s accounting variable is improperly updated on opposite actions. To remediate the issue the contract should ensure that any decrease in stakeTime caused by delegation is symmetrically restored when the delegation is removed, or alternatively compute voteWeight based on immutable timestamps rather than a mutable stakeTime variable, thereby preventing external manipulation of the voting weight calculation.
summary: When a staker delegates his balance to a delegator, the time duration variable `_weights[delegate].stakeTime` is decreased. However, when undelegating only the balance is decreased. This makes it possible a malicious user can decrease `_weights[delegate].stakeTime`. He can expand the impact of this attack by repeating delegating and undelegating. A malicious user can delay the increase of any delegator's `voteWeight` as much as he wants.

title: Malicious users can double their voting power.
content: The vulnerability is a vote‑weight inflation caused by a delegation cycle in the governance contract. When the function that returns a delegatee's voting power calculates the result, it adds the delegatee's own vote weight to the weight that is delegated to it, without checking whether the delegatee has itself delegated its votes to another address. Because the contract does not forbid a delegate from delegating further, two or more participants can create a circular delegation (for example Alice delegates to Bob and Bob delegates back to Alice). In this situation each call to the vote‑weight function counts the other party's weight as well as the caller's own weight, effectively doubling the voting power of every address in the cycle. The root cause is the unconditional addition of ownVoteWeight and the lack of a mechanism to enforce an acyclic delegation graph. An attacker can exploit the bug by registering two accounts as delegates, establishing a mutual delegation, and then voting with the inflated weight, which can sway governance proposals, approve upgrades, or change protocol parameters with far fewer genuine votes than required. The issue manifests only when both participants are recognized as delegates and the contract’s getDelegatedVoteWeight function is invoked; normal delegation to a non‑delegate does not trigger the problem. All token holders who are allowed to delegate, the governance process, and any decisions that rely on vote tallies are affected. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that examined the delegation logic and noticed that the function adds the delegatee's own weight even when the caller is already a delegate of that address. Because the inflated totals still appear as plausible numbers, the bug can be hard to notice without explicit testing of cyclic delegations. To remediate, the contract should either forbid a delegate from delegating to another address, prevent self‑delegation cycles, or compute delegated vote weight without adding the delegatee's own weight unless the delegate is the caller itself. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of delegation‑cycle or double‑counting vulnerabilities, where a graph‑based permission model fails to enforce acyclicity, leading to accounting errors that break the assumption that each token's voting power is counted exactly once. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a normal token balance but report a voting power that is unexpectedly high, contradicting the expectation that delegating simply transfers weight without multiplication. The mismatch between expected and actual vote totals can cause proposals to pass with far fewer participants, undermining the protocol’s security guarantees.

title: The delegator resetting self-delegation causes multiple issues in the protocol
content: The vulnerability is a delegation state inconsistency that arises when a delegator resets its self‑delegation flag without the protocol verifying that the delegator is still considered self‑delegated at the moment vote power is modified. The root cause is the absence of a guard in three core functions – the routine that clears a user’s vote delegate, the internal withdrawal routine, and the internal staking routine – that should confirm the delegator’s self‑delegation status before adjusting delegated balances. Because this check is missing, the contract assumes a non‑zero delegated balance even after self‑delegation has been disabled, leading to under‑flow reverts when the code tries to subtract from zero and, more critically, allowing an attacker to repeatedly stake, modify delegation, and withdraw without the delegated balance being correctly accounted for. An attacker can exploit the flaw by first delegating to a target (e.g., Bob), then having the target reset its self‑delegation, after which the attacker stakes tokens, receives voting power as if still self‑delegated, and subsequently changes the delegation to another party. By looping this process, the attacker accumulates unlimited voting power, which can be used to sway governance decisions. At the same time, legitimate users experience failed withdrawals because the contract attempts to deduct a delegated amount that no longer exists, resulting in transaction reverts and funds appearing to be stuck. The issue manifests only when the self‑delegation flag is toggled after delegations have been established, so it may be missed during casual testing that does not cover this specific sequence. It was discovered during a formal audit by Cyfrin when the auditors exercised delegation reset scenarios and observed unexpected reverts and inflated voting power. The bug is hard to notice because the contract does not emit explicit warnings; the failure appears as a generic arithmetic error, and the voting power inflation does not immediately break any invariant until a governance action is taken. To remediate, each of the affected functions should first verify that the delegator’s self‑delegation is still active; if it is not, the function must either abort with a clear error or adjust the internal accounting to reflect the loss of delegated balance. Additionally, resetting self‑delegation should automatically clear any outstanding delegated balances or prevent further staking until the state is reconciled. This correction restores the invariant that delegated balances are only manipulated while the delegator is self‑delegated, preventing both under‑flow reverts and infinite voting‑power accumulation, and thereby preserving the protocol’s accounting integrity and user trust.
summary:
Whenever the vote power of delegators are changed, the validity of self-delegation of the delegator is not checked, which results in issues in multiple parts of the protocol.

- `unsetUserVoteDelegate`: It does not allow stakers to unset delegation through the function because it tries to subtract delegated balance from zero.
- `_withdrawFor`: It does not allow stakers to withdraw their assets because it tries to subtract delegated balance from zero.
- `_stakeFor`: It allows malicious stakers to get infinite voting power by repeating staking & modifying delegator & withdrawal process.

It allows attackers to repeat issues in `_stakeFor` to accumulate voting power, also it causes reverts in withdrawals.

title: H-01 | Keeper's Not Remunerated For Cancellation Callback
content: The vulnerability is an incentive misalignment in the order cancellation flow where the gas used by the keeper to execute the cancellation callback is not compensated. The contract bundles the gas required for the callback inside the order’s executionFee, but after the callback runs the payExecutionFee function refunds any unused portion of the executionFee back to the user. Because the refund calculation does not exclude the gas actually spent on the callback, the keeper’s gas cost is mistakenly returned to the user instead of being paid to the keeper. This design flaw occurs whenever an order is cancelled and the cancellation callback is invoked. A keeper that triggers the callback will see the gas it spent deducted from the executionFee that is later refunded, resulting in a net loss for the keeper. The impact is that keepers may refuse to perform cancellations, leading to delayed or missing order cancellations, reduced reliability of the protocol, and potential economic loss for the keepers themselves. The issue was discovered during a security audit by Guardian, who noticed that the fee accounting logic does not correctly separate callback gas from the refundable portion of the executionFee. Because the contract still appears to return the unused fee to the user, the problem can be subtle and may only be observed as unexpected negative profit for keepers. The bug belongs to the class of fee misallocation or incentive‑alignment bugs where accounting assumptions about gas reimbursement are violated. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a keeper who expects to be reimbursed for the gas spent on a cancellation receives no compensation, effectively seeing “funds disappear” from its balance after the operation. The correct mitigation is to redesign the cancellation flow so that the callback gas is either excluded from the refundable executionFee or explicitly paid to the keeper before any refund is issued, ensuring that the keeper is properly remunerated for the gas it consumes.
summary: The callback gas amount is included inside an order’s executionFee, however the payExecutionFee function will refund the not used part of executionFee to the user. Since this unused part includes callback gas, the keeper will not be remunerated for the gas spent during the cancellation callback.

title: H-03 | getLiquidityForReserve DoS
content: The vulnerability resides in a liquidity‑calculation routine that determines how much liquidity corresponds to a given amount of token1 for a price range. The function receives a lower price (sqrtPriceL) and an upper price (sqrtPriceU) but does not verify that the upper bound is strictly greater than the lower bound. When the two prices are equal – which can happen when a caller supplies an anchor range of zero width or when the current pool price exactly matches the lower tick price – the internal call to the library that computes liquidity for amount1 receives identical bounds. The library assumes a positive price interval and performs arithmetic that divides by the difference between the bounds; with a zero interval the division yields a revert or an overflow, causing the whole call to fail. Because the failing call is made inside getLiquidityForReserves, any higher‑level operation that depends on this helper (such as quoting, position updates, or swap simulations) also fails, effectively denying service to users and halting core protocol functionality. From a user’s perspective the UI may show “no liquidity available”, trades may be rejected, or expected refunds may never be calculated, leading to confusion and potential loss of confidence. The issue was uncovered during a manual audit that examined edge‑case handling of price ranges. It is subtle because normal operation always provides a non‑zero interval, so the bug only appears under rare but valid conditions. The root cause is a missing validation check that upperPrice must be greater than lowerPrice. The recommended mitigation is to insert a guard that compares the two prices and returns zero liquidity (or reverts) when the interval is non‑positive, thereby preventing the unsafe library call and preserving protocol availability. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of unchecked input leading to arithmetic errors and denial‑of‑service conditions in financial smart contracts.
summary:
In the getLiquidityForReserves function there is no validation that the lower price and upper price provided to the getLiquidityForAmount1 function are not equal. This is possible either with an anchor range that has no width or when the active price is exactly that of the lower tick price for a range.
This behavior results in a DoS of several key functionalities of the system when these edge cases are hit.

title: H-04 | Leverage And Deleverage Are Sandwichable
content: The vulnerability concerns the leverage and deleverage operations that rely on a flash‑borrow/repay swap where the parameter maxAmountIn is automatically set to the amount being borrowed for a leverage call or to the amount of unlocked collateral for a deleverage call. Because this limit is derived from the transaction’s own intent and not from a user‑controlled bound, a malicious actor can observe a pending transaction, front‑run it with a large opposing swap, and push the on‑chain price far enough that the amount of reserves required by the swap exceeds the supplied maxAmountIn. When this happens the swap either returns zero output or reverts with an insufficient‑reserves error, leaving the original caller with no borrowed tokens after a leverage request or with a failed repayment after a deleverage request. The root cause is the unchecked reliance on external price movement and the absence of a configurable cap on the input amount, which makes the function economically sandwichable. The exploit can be carried out in a single block: the attacker submits a price‑impacting trade, the victim’s transaction executes with its default maxAmountIn, the price has already moved, the swap cannot deliver the expected amount, and the victim ends up with an empty balance change while still incurring debt or losing collateral. The impact is that users expecting to receive a loan or to have their collateral returned see no change in their balances, may be left with an outstanding position, and the protocol may accumulate stuck positions that reduce overall liquidity. This condition occurs only when the transaction is exposed to front‑running and the price can be moved sufficiently within the same block, which is why it may not appear in normal testing. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the economic flow of the leverage/deleverage functions and identified that the maxAmountIn parameter is not user‑configurable. It is hard to notice because the functions behave correctly under benign market conditions; the failure only manifests under adversarial price manipulation. To remediate, the contract should allow callers to specify an amountInMaximum that cannot exceed the borrowed amount or unlocked collateral, and it should enforce that this user‑provided cap is respected by the swap. Additionally, exposing parameters such as sqrtPriceLimitX96 and a deadline for the swap would give callers control over price slippage and execution timing, providing stronger protection against MEV‑style sandwich attacks. This class of bug is an economic or price‑manipulation vulnerability where default swap limits enable a sandwich attack, violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions that a leveraged position will always receive the requested funds.
summary:
In the leverage and deleverage functions traders flash borrow and repay using a swap where the maxAmountIn is the borrowed amount for borrows and the unlocked collateral amount for repayments.
This allows malicious actors to frontrun these actions and push the price far enough such that these limits are hit. In the case of borrowing, this leaves the borrower with no funds received from the action as the reservesNeeded can be pushed to the maximum of the entire newPrincipal_.

title: H-05 | removeAllFrom DoS With External Liquidity
content: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition in the removeAllFrom function of a liquidity management contract. The function is designed to return early when the calculated amount of liquidity to remove (liquidityToRemove) is zero, but this amount is derived from the actual liquidity reported by the external Uniswap pool rather than the contract's internal accounting. An attacker can deposit a small amount of external liquidity, causing the external query to return a non‑zero value even though the internal getLiquidity mapping shows that the system holds no liquidity. When removeAllFrom is invoked, the early‑return check is bypassed, the contract proceeds to withdraw the attacker’s malicious liquidity, and then attempts a second removal of zero liquidity after the internal balance has already been depleted. This second call to the Uniswap pool reverts with the NP error, causing the whole transaction to fail. From a user perspective the transaction simply reverts with an obscure NP error and no funds are transferred, leading to a situation where legitimate users see their withdrawal attempts fail and balances remain unchanged. The issue occurs whenever removeAllFrom is called while the internal liquidity record is empty but external liquidity exists, which can be induced by a malicious actor adding liquidity to the pool. The bug was discovered during a security audit by the Guardian team, and it can be hard to notice because the early‑return logic appears correct at first glance; the failure only manifests after the internal state has been altered and the external call is made. The root cause is the reliance on external state for the early‑return condition instead of also checking the internal accounting after the removal step. To remediate, a second early‑return should be added immediately before the internal _removeLiquidity call, checking again if liquidityToRemove is zero and returning the appropriate values, thereby preventing the erroneous external call and eliminating the denial‑of‑service vector. This class of bug falls under improper handling of external contract responses and insufficient validation of internal state before performing external operations, which can break business logic that assumes a successful removal when no liquidity actually exists.
summary:
In the removeAllFrom function, the function is short circuited if there is 0 liquidityToRemove, however this value is based upon the amount that is deployed in Uniswap.
Therefore a malicious actor may add to this amount in order to stop this early return check from triggering when the getLiquidity mapping reports that there is no liquidity deployed there for the system.
In this scenario the function execution continues on to remove all of the attacker’s malicious liquidity from the range and then attempts to remove 0 liquidity from the range after it has been depleted.
This second attempt to remove liquidity will revert with the NP error from Uniswap.

title: H-06 | Migration Cannot Be Done
content: The vulnerability resides in the migration routine that builds the initial distribution of spot tokens and credit tokens for each participant. During migration the contract owner calls an allocate function before the pool is launched. The function is supposed to reject only allocations that are completely empty, i.e., where both spot and credit amounts are zero. However the implemented check uses a logical OR: it reverts if the spot amount is zero OR the credit amount is zero. Consequently, any user who holds only spot tokens or only credit tokens triggers the revert, even though the allocation is valid for a single‑asset holder. Because the allocate call processes the entire list of users in a single transaction, the revert caused by a single malformed entry aborts the whole migration, preventing the pool from being launched. The impact is that the migration cannot be completed, leaving the protocol in an uninitialized state and potentially locking user funds until the bug is fixed. All participants, the contract owner, and any downstream contracts that rely on the pool being live are affected. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the migration logic and identified that the validation condition did not match the intended business rule. It can be hard to notice because the condition appears to guard against empty allocations, which is a reasonable safety check, yet the logical operator is wrong. From a user’s perspective the UI may show that their spot or credit balance is supposed to be migrated, but after the migration attempt the transaction fails and no assets are transferred, leading to confusion such as “my funds disappeared” or “the migration gave me zero balance”. The bug belongs to the class of input‑validation errors where an incorrect boolean expression causes legitimate inputs to be rejected. To remediate, the condition should be changed to revert only when both spot and credit are zero, i.e., using a logical AND, thereby allowing allocations that contain a non‑zero amount of either asset and enabling the migration to succeed.
summary:
During the migration process, the owner will construct the initial distribution of spot and credits and it will be done with allocate function. This can only be called before the pool is launched, and the pool will be deployed later.
Users might have both spot and credit to be distributed. But a user can also have only spot or only credit. However, the check that ensures the allocation is not empty is incorrect, and the allocate function will revert if a user has only spot or only credit.
The whole migration process will be disrupted even if just one user has only spot or only credit.

title: H-07 | Premium Compounding Is Incorrect
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect compounding of the liquidity premium used by the protocol when calculating the threshold for deploying liquidity across price ranges. The root cause lies in the getCurrentThreshold function, which applies the powWad helper with a numerator of 1e16 – a value smaller than the fixed‑point scaling factor of 1e18. Because the base supplied to powWad is less than one, each exponentiation step reduces the premium instead of increasing it as the distance between the active tick and the floor tick grows. Consequently, the premium that should rise with larger tick gaps actually shrinks, causing the computed liquidity threshold to be lower than intended. This faulty threshold is used by the sweep and slide mechanisms that rebalance liquidity; with a decreasing premium, those mechanisms allocate insufficient liquidity, and the protocol never reaches the designed maximum of roughly 1.1 × anchor liquidity during discovery. The impact is that liquidity providers receive lower than expected returns, the protocol may appear under‑capitalized, and users could see their balances remain static or even appear to lose potential earnings because the system believes less liquidity is needed. The bug manifests whenever the active tick moves away from the floor tick, i.e., during any normal price movement that triggers a sweep or slide operation. All participants that rely on correct liquidity provisioning – the protocol itself, its liquidity providers, and downstream users – are affected. The issue was discovered during a manual audit where the auditor noticed that the premium value behaved opposite to the specification; existing unit tests only verified that the function returned a value, not that the value increased with tick distance, making the defect easy to miss. From a user’s perspective the UI may show that the pool’s liquidity has not grown despite market movement, or that expected yield calculations remain flat, contradicting the expectation that returns should improve as the price range widens. The bug belongs to the class of arithmetic scaling errors in fixed‑point exponentiation, often referred to as “incorrect compounding” or “inverse growth” bugs. To remediate, the formula must be rewritten so that the base supplied to powWad is greater than one (for example by using a numerator of 1e18 or adjusting the exponent logic) ensuring that the premium compounds positively. Comprehensive test coverage should be added to assert that the premium strictly increases with tick distance and that the resulting liquidity thresholds respect the intended 1.1 × anchor bound.
summary:
The protocol deploys liquidity to ranges based on a liquidity premium and this premium supposed to be compounding when the difference between the activeTick and the floorTickL increases.
However, due to incorrect usage of the powWad in the getCurrentThreshold function, premium decreases instead of increasing. The reason of this behaviour is the numerator (1e16) in the formula is smaller than 1e18 and it causes result to decrease in every power.
As a result of this, all liquidity managements in sweep and slide will be incorrect, and the maximum liquidity in discovery range will never pass 1.1 * anchor liquidity during these operations.

title: H-08 | bAsset Shorts Can Make A Guaranteed Profit
content: The vulnerability is an economic arbitrage flaw that allows a participant to generate a guaranteed profit by shorting a synthetic asset (bAsset) when the protocol’s liquidity management creates a rapid and asymmetric shift between two internal pools, commonly referred to as the discovery pool and the anchor pool. The root cause lies in the Baseline V2 design where, after a user borrows bAssets from a lender, the system immediately permits a large reallocation of liquidity (the slide operation) that moves the anchor price upward while simultaneously draining liquidity from the discovery pool. Because the borrowed assets are purchased while the discovery pool still holds high liquidity, the buyer can push the anchor price up, and then sell the same amount back into the anchor pool where liquidity is lower, resulting in a lower average sell price. When the slide later restores discovery liquidity at the lower price, the attacker can repurchase the bAssets at a cheaper average cost and repay the loan at the higher original price, pocketing the price delta as a risk‑free profit. This sequence can be exploited step‑by‑step: (1) borrow bAssets from a lender; (2) buy enough bAssets to raise the anchor price; (3) sell the same quantity into the anchor pool where the price impact is adverse to the attacker; (4) allow the slide to shift discovery liquidity back down; (5) buy back the borrowed amount at the reduced price and settle the loan. The impact is that the attacker extracts value from the protocol without bearing market risk, effectively draining liquidity from lenders and eroding confidence in the system’s accounting guarantees. The condition for the exploit is the presence of immediate, large liquidity shifts after a borrowing event, which the protocol assumes are neutral but in practice create a price asymmetry. All participants who provide liquidity or rely on fair pricing—particularly lenders like Alice—are affected because their expected return is reduced while the attacker walks away with a profit. The issue was uncovered by the Guardian audit team through a targeted proof‑of‑concept test that simulated the described sequence of actions. It can be difficult to notice because the price movements appear normal on a per‑transaction basis and the protocol’s internal accounting does not flag the temporary imbalance as an error; only a systematic analysis of the liquidity flow reveals the guaranteed profit path. To remediate, the protocol should redesign its liquidity management so that large rebalancing cannot occur instantly after a borrow, for example by smoothing the slide over multiple blocks, imposing caps on the amount of liquidity that can be shifted in a single operation, or decoupling borrowing from immediate price impact. In generic terms, the bug belongs to the class of flash‑loan‑style arbitrage vulnerabilities where asymmetric liquidity across price zones enables risk‑free profit, violating the business logic that borrowed assets should be repaid at comparable market value and that the system’s internal pricing should be invariant to internal rebalancing.
summary:
In the Baseline V2 system it is possible for a user to arbitrage the system in order to make guaranteed profit on a short.
This arbitrage can occur with the following actions:
1. Bob borrows X bAssets from Alice
2. Bob buys Y bAssets to move the anchor up after sweeping
3. Bob sells Y bAssets and achieves a lower pool price than before his buy because:
   - The anchor has moved up, meaning there is less capacity for the same amount of liquidity (though in many cases this is offset by discovery surplus)
   - On his buy he was buying in the discovery (higher liquidity) and on his sell he was selling in the anchor (lower liquidity)
4. Slide moves the discovery liquidity back down so that Bob is able to buy the bAssets back at a lower average price, due to higher liquidity at a lower price.
5. Bob can pay back the bAssets he borrowed from Alice while the bAsset price is lower than when he borrowed, representing a profitable short.
Bob has made a guaranteed profit of the delta on this short.

title: H-09 | Deleverage Can Break Through Floor Tick
content: The vulnerability occurs in the deleverage routine of the protocol where the function relies on a flash swap to sell bAsset collateral before the borrowed reserves are re‑added to the virtual floor liquidity (floor tick). The root cause is a mismatch in accounting: the floor tick is calculated without including the borrowed reserves that are still pending, so the contract assumes there is enough liquidity to execute the flash swap when, in fact, the available capacity may be insufficient. An attacker or any user can trigger the deleverage on an account that holds a large amount of borrowed reserves; the flash swap then attempts to sell the collateral against a liquidity pool that does not meet the required size, causing the swap to fail or to execute with insufficient depth. This can leave the account under‑collateralised, result in the user receiving no funds, or cause the collateral to be lost, effectively making funds disappear. The issue manifests only when the deleverage function is called and the borrowed reserves have not yet been added back to the floor tick, a condition that is not obvious from the UI because the floor tick is a virtual construct and the flash swap may succeed in many ordinary cases. The bug was discovered during a security audit by the Guardian team while reviewing the logical flow of the deleverage mechanism. It is hard to notice because the failure is conditional on the size of the borrowed reserves relative to the floor tick and does not produce a clear error message; the transaction may simply revert or complete with zero payout, which looks like a normal failure to the user. To remediate, the contract should enforce a check that the real liquidity available (excluding the virtual floor) can comfortably cover the sale of the bAsset collateral before performing the flash swap, or the deleverage feature should be removed in favour of a manual process or a periphery contract that performs a naive deleverage without flash swapping. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of liquidity‑accounting errors where virtual liquidity floors are mis‑used, leading to violations of the protocol’s accounting invariants and causing unexpected loss of user funds.
summary: When deleveraging an account, the floor tick can be breached because the account’s borrowed reserves have not yet been added to the floor tick, therefore the capacity cannot handle the flash swap — which assumes there is enough liquidity to sell the bAsset collateral before the borrowed reserves have been re-added.

title: H-10 | Borrows In The Floor Invalidate Baseline Value
content: The vulnerability is a logical accounting flaw in the borrowing mechanism of a baseline liquidity pool that uses a floor position to guarantee a minimum amount of liquidity. When a user borrows assets while the pool price is still inside the floor range, the implementation moves the borrowed amount from the floor reserves into a set of virtual reserves but does not deduct the removed amount from the floor’s effective liquidity. Consequently, the floor position appears to retain its original reserve size even though part of it has been taken away. As the market price climbs out of the floor range, additional real reserves are expected to flow into the floor, but because the virtual reserves have already been stretched by the earlier borrow, the floor’s true capacity shrinks. This mismatch breaks the capacity invariant – the mathematical guarantee that the floor always holds enough liquidity to back the baseline value of the bAsset. When the invariant is violated, the baseline value that the protocol uses for accounting and pricing becomes incorrect, potentially allowing positions to become under‑collateralised, causing users to receive less than expected on withdrawals or to see their balances disappear. The bug can be triggered whenever a borrow is executed inside the floor range and the price subsequently moves upward toward the upper tick of that range. An attacker could deliberately borrow large amounts from the floor, watch the price drift upward, and then exploit the weakened capacity to extract value or cause the protocol to liquidate honest users. The issue was discovered during a formal audit of the _leverage function, where the auditors noticed that the capacity check did not consider the reduction of floor liquidity caused by borrowing, and that additional reserves entering the floor as price rises could mask the invariant breach. The problem is subtle because the contract still reports that the floor holds its original reserves, so surface‑level balance checks appear normal, making the bug hard to notice without deep invariant analysis. To remediate, the _leverage function should validate that a borrow will not cause the capacity invariant to be violated at any intermediate price tick up to the upper bound of the floor. This validation must ignore any hypothetical capacity increase that would arise from future reserves entering the floor, because such gains can conceal the moment when the invariant actually breaks. In essence, the fix requires a proper accounting of floor liquidity after each borrow and a pre‑emptive check that the floor’s capacity remains sufficient throughout the price trajectory, thereby preserving the baseline value integrity of the bAsset.
summary:
Upon borrowing reserves are transferred out of the floor position and are accounted for in the virtual reserves. When a borrow occurs within the floor position, the reserves removed from the floor will not contribute towards the floor liquidity, therefore not requiring additional reserves to enter the floor upon swaps which move the price upwards out of the floor.
As a result, when reserves are moved into the virtual reserves and price moves upwards out of the floor, the virtual floor reserves are increasingly stretched wider across the floor. As a result the virtual floor reserves offer a smaller amount of liquidity and capacity as the price increases.
This can lead to an invalidation of the capacity invariant of the system, which ultimately invalidates the baseline value of the bAsset.

title: H-11 | Shorts Profit Because Of Fixed Anchor Width
content: The vulnerability is a deterministic arbitrage arising from a fixed maximum width imposed on the anchor price in the Baseline V2 system. Because the anchor cannot expand beyond a predefined distance from the floor, a liquidity gap is created between the anchor level and the floor level. When a market participant with a short position pushes the market price down into the floor region, the system’s automatic liquidity rebalancing mechanism detects the gap and adds discovery liquidity to fill it. This rebalancing lowers the price at which bAsset tokens can be bought back, allowing the short trader to close the position at a price lower than the entry price, guaranteeing a profit regardless of external market conditions. The exploit can be carried out simply by moving the price into the floor, waiting for the liquidity refill, and then purchasing the bAsset tokens. The impact is that short traders can earn risk‑free profit while long position holders and liquidity providers suffer reduced returns or loss of capital, effectively distorting the intended market dynamics. The condition for the attack is that the protocol enforces a hard cap on anchor width and that the discovery liquidity is allowed to flow into the gap without additional checks. Any user who expects the price to reflect true market supply and demand may instead see an abrupt price drop to the floor followed by a rapid rebound, leading to confusion when their long position loses value or when they observe unusually high short profits. The issue was discovered during a security audit by the Guardian team, who noted that the combination of a static anchor width and an automatic liquidity refill creates a predictable profit loop that is not obvious from surface‑level testing. Because the price movement appears normal and the profit is realized automatically, the bug can be hard to detect without a detailed analysis of the liquidity accounting logic. To remediate the problem the protocol should either remove the hard maximum width on the anchor or modify the discovery‑liquidity rebalancing so that it does not fill the gap in a way that creates a guaranteed arbitrage, for example by capping the amount of liquidity added or by making the anchor width dynamic based on market conditions. In broader terms the flaw belongs to the class of “fixed‑parameter liquidity gap” bugs where static constraints on price bands enable deterministic profit extraction through automated market‑making mechanisms.
summary: In the updated Baseline V2 system the anchor is now limited to a distinct maximum width. This introduces an arbitrage whereby shorts can make a guaranteed profit by moving price into the floor, over the liquidity gap between the anchor and floor, rebalancing liquidity to fill in the gap, and buying bAsset tokens back at a lower price as the liquidity for the discovery has filled in the previous gap in the liquidity structure.

title: H-12 | Anchor Liquidity Can Be Removed
content: The vulnerability resides in the slide routine that re‑positions the anchor of a concentrated liquidity pool. The routine determines the amount of liquidity for the new anchor by copying the reserve values of the previously active anchor. Because the previous anchor is artificially limited by a maximum width, the market price can be pushed below that anchor when an external participant creates a position outside the current range. When this happens the previous anchor’s reserves drop to zero. The slide function does not check for this condition and therefore assigns the new anchor a reserve balance of zero, which translates into zero effective liquidity for the new price range. An attacker can deliberately open an out‑of‑range position, cause the price to slip below the current anchor, and then trigger the slide operation. The result is that the pool appears to have moved its anchor but actually holds no liquidity, so subsequent swaps either revert or execute against an empty pool, causing traders to receive no output and liquidity providers to see their capital become inaccessible. This flaw is discovered during a manual audit by the Guardian team, and it is subtle because the slide transaction itself succeeds and the contract state changes appear normal; only the hidden zero‑reserve condition reveals the loss of liquidity. The issue belongs to the class of “anchor‑based liquidity misallocation” bugs where state derived from a potentially empty source is used without validation. From a user perspective the UI may show the anchor moved as expected, yet the pool balance displayed as zero or trades returning nothing, violating the expectation that moving the anchor preserves existing liquidity. The root cause is the reliance on reserve values rather than a guaranteed positive liquidity metric. To remediate, the slide logic should be rewritten to allocate the new anchor based on actual liquidity amounts (e.g., total token amounts supplied) or to enforce a minimum reserve check, falling back to the last non‑zero anchor when necessary, thereby preventing the creation of a zero‑liquidity anchor.
summary:
In the slide function the anchor position is allocated based on the reserves of the previous anchor.
However the previous anchor may have zero reserves, since it is capped to a maximum width, and the price is able to go below the anchor, between the gap if another actor creates an outside position.
As a result, the slide function will read that the anchor has 0 reserves and assign the new anchor to have 0 reserves and thus 0 liquidity.

title: H-01 | DoS Via External Liquidity By Predicting Positions
content: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that arises from an accounting mismatch in the protocol’s liquidity tracking. The contract stores the amount of liquidity available for each price range in a mapping called getLiquidity. When external liquidity is added to a range using the addReservesTo or addLiquidityTo functions, the mapping is updated with the new total liquidity, including the externally supplied amount. The protocol assumes that the liquidity recorded in getLiquidity belongs to the system and can be safely swept during the sweep operation, which collects fees and rebalances positions. An attacker can exploit this by first adding external liquidity to the range that will become the protocol’s anchor after a bump, then triggering the bump so that the anchor range coincides with the maliciously funded range. When the anchor’s addLiquidityTo call runs, the contract records the attacker’s external liquidity as if it were internal, inflating the getLiquidity entry. Later, when sweep attempts to transfer the recorded amount, the internal accounting believes there is more liquidity than actually belongs to the system, causing an arithmetic underflow and a revert. The impact is that the sweep function fails, effectively halting fee collection and position rebalancing, which can freeze user withdrawals and disrupt normal market‑making activity. This condition occurs only when external liquidity can be injected into a range that will later be promoted to the anchor and when the sweep is subsequently called. All participants that rely on the protocol’s ability to sweep – liquidity providers, traders, and the protocol itself – are affected because the contract becomes unusable until the bug is fixed. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by the Guardian team, who traced the flow of liquidity updates and identified that the mapping update does not distinguish between internal and external contributions. The bug is subtle because the mapping appears to reflect the correct total liquidity, and the underflow only manifests during a rarely exercised sweep, making it easy to miss in routine testing. The class of bug can be described as an accounting mismatch that leads to an underflow when external deposits are mistakenly treated as internal reserves. From a user’s perspective the symptom is a transaction that reverts with an underflow error when attempting to sweep, often reported as “transaction failed” or “insufficient liquidity”, and balances may appear to drop to zero unexpectedly. To remediate the issue the protocol should separate externally added liquidity from the internal liquidity accounting for any range that may become the anchor, for example by moving that amount into a bufferedReserves variable before the sweep, ensuring that sweep only operates on genuine system reserves and preventing the underflow condition.
summary:
Users adding external liquidity to the protocol's positions should not affect the market making operations, as the liquidity for each range is tracked by the getLiquidity mapping in the BPOOL contract storage.
The issue relies on the way this mapping is updated after an operation completes. When using addReservesTo or addLiquidityTo this mapping will be updated with the new real position liquidity, including externally added liquidity.
An attacker can DoS the sweep operation by following these steps:
1. Add ext liquidity to the projected ANCHOR range after a bump (lowerTick + 1 TS, upperTick).
2. Execute bump(), now the ANCHOR range is the same as the projected one, which we just maliciously added liquidity to.
3. Now the addLiquidityTo function call for the ANCHOR range records the malicious liquidity as belonging to the system.
4. sweep now reverts with underflow.

title: H-02 | Slide Allows Anchor To Exceed Discovery
content: The vulnerability is an invariant violation in the slide function of the protocol's liquidity management. The slide function is intended to shift the anchor position along the price curve while preserving the total amount of liquidity allocated to the anchor and discovery pools. The implementation records the amount of reserves that belong to the anchor (anchorReserves) before the slide, removes the liquidity, performs the slide, and then adds the previously recorded reserves back to the new anchor position. Because the slide moves the anchor leftwards, the same amount of reserves is added to a position that now represents a smaller price range. Consequently the anchor pool ends up holding more liquidity than before, while the discovery pool is constrained by a rule that its new liquidity may not exceed the old discovery liquidity. This creates a state where anchorLiquidity > discoveryLiquidity, breaking the protocol’s accounting assumptions that discovery liquidity is always at least as large as anchor liquidity. The bug occurs whenever an operator calls the slide function with a leftward shift while also removing and re‑adding liquidity in the same transaction. An attacker could trigger the slide repeatedly to inflate the anchor pool, effectively creating phantom liquidity that can later be withdrawn or used to manipulate price calculations, leading to loss of funds for users or incorrect pricing of swaps. The impact includes potential over‑allocation of assets to the anchor pool, distortion of the price curve, and the possibility of draining funds from the discovery pool because the protocol may allow withdrawals based on the inflated anchor balance. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the BaselineV2.1 contract where the auditor noticed that the invariant “anchorLiquidity ≤ discoveryLiquidity” could be violated after a slide operation. The problem is subtle because the code appears to preserve reserves, and the slide logic is complex, making the mismatch hard to detect through simple unit tests. To remediate, the contract should either stop enforcing the condition that new discovery liquidity must be less than or equal to the old value, or it should stop re‑adding the full anchorReserves after the slide and instead recalculate the appropriate amount based on the new price range, thereby keeping the liquidity distribution consistent. In summary, the bug is a liquidity‑distribution invariant breach caused by improper handling of anchor reserves during a leftward slide, which can lead to phantom liquidity, pricing errors, and potential fund loss.
summary:
When removing and adding back liquidity to the anchor position in the slide function, the anchorReserves are tracked and added back to the adjusted anchor position.
However the anchor position has moved leftwards after the slide, therefore the liquidity for the anchor position will increase as the reserves are maintained.
As a result, since the new discovery liquidity cannot increase past the old discovery liquidity, the protocol can enter a state where the anchor liquidity is greater than the discovery liquidity.

title: H-08 | Protocol Loses Blast Points And WETH Rebasing Yields
content: The vulnerability consists of the protocol treating Blast's rebasing WETH token as a regular reserve token and assuming that any holder, including smart contracts, can automatically claim the Blast points that are generated by the token's rebasing mechanism. In reality the Blast points system requires a specific Blast Points API that is only implemented by externally owned accounts or contracts that explicitly adopt the IERC20Rebasing interface. The BPOOL contract, which is the largest liquidity provider for the Thruster pools, does not implement this API, so when the pool's constructor marks the WETH yield as claimable the protocol attempts to allocate the earned points to BPOOL. Because BPOOL cannot respond to the Blast Points callbacks, the points become unclaimable and are effectively lost. The root cause is the mismatch between the token's rebasing behavior and the contract's interface: the code uses a standard ERC20 interface for the reserve token and does not perform any verification that the recipient contract supports the Blast Points API. An attacker does not need to actively exploit the bug; the loss occurs automatically whenever a contract address provides liquidity to a Thruster pool that uses the rebasing WETH token. The impact is that the protocol and its liquidity providers miss out on the incentive rewards that were expected, reducing overall profitability and potentially misleading users who see no points or zero additional balance despite providing assets. The condition under which the issue manifests is when a significant portion of the pool's liquidity is supplied by contracts rather than EOAs, or when the protocol deploys liquidity to any Uniswap‑like fork that uses the same rebasing token. The problem was discovered during a security audit that compared the protocol's integration documentation with the actual contract code and identified that the reserve token was handled as a plain ERC20. The bug is hard to notice because the missing points are not reflected in on‑chain balances and no explicit error is thrown; users only observe that their expected reward balance stays at zero. To remediate the issue the protocol should interact with the reserve token through the IERC20Rebasing interface, ensure that any contract acting as a liquidity provider implements the Blast Points API, and configure the pool so that only claimable addresses receive the rebasing yields. In short, the flaw is a classic case of an incentive‑allocation mismatch caused by using an inappropriate token interface, leading to unclaimed rewards and lost economic value.
summary: The reserve token in the protocol is Blast’s rebasing WETH token, which has automatic rebasing by default (not like the native ETH with void by default) for both EOAs and smart contracts. Normally, these reserve tokens are not held in the Baseline contracts. They are deployed into the Thruster pools, which set their WETH yield configuration as claimable in their constructor, as liquidity. So, Thruster pools earn rebasing yields from liquidity providers’ assets, and the factory owner of the pool can claim these yields. According to [Thruster docs](https://docs.thruster.finance/incentives/blast-points-and-gold#blast-points), liquidity providers earn Blast points depending on their WETH balances since they help Thruster to earn yields. Thruster says the system is automatic, but there are some checks: “Pools with a significant amount of liquidity providers being contracts (not EOAs) need to be manually verified to ensure that the Points are claimable by the contracts”. BPOOL contract itself will be the biggest liquidity provider but it has no way to claim Blast points. Therefore, the Thruster protocol [will not allocate](https://docs.thruster.finance/integration/blast-points-for-thruster-lp-integrations) these earned points to Baseline. ”…it should not be allocated to a contract address that does not support the Blast Points API as those Points then become unclaimable or transferable…”. This would also be a case if the protocol decides to deploy liquidity in another Uniswap fork.

title: H-01 | Anchor Liquidity Is Incorrectly Calculated After Sweep
content: The vulnerability concerns the calculation of anchor liquidity during the sweep operation of a liquidity pool. When sweep is executed, discovery liquidity is rebalanced into the anchor and floor segments and the anchor tick range is expanded. Instead of using the pool’s manageLiquidityFor function, the code calls manageReservesFor with the new reserve amount (newReservesA). Because the tick range has been widened, the amount of reserves required to keep the anchor liquidity constant or increase it also grows.
