The implementation does not verify that newReservesA is sufficient for the larger range; it merely adds any surplus discovery reserves (surplusReservesD), which may be small or zero. Consequently, each sweep can cause the anchor’s reported liquidity to drop. From a user’s perspective the UI may show that after a sweep the anchor liquidity has decreased, leading to unexpectedly high slippage, thin order books, and price volatility between the floor and discovery zones. Traders and liquidity providers are affected because the thin anchor range degrades trading conditions and can be exploited by repeatedly triggering sweeps to shrink the anchor liquidity, potentially allowing price manipulation. The issue was uncovered during a security audit that examined the rebalancing logic and identified the mismatch between tick‑range expansion and reserve management. It is subtle because the sweep function appears to add liquidity, yet the net effect is a reduction, which may not be obvious without inspecting the underlying liquidity calculations. The proper mitigation is to compute the exact reserve amount needed to preserve the anchor liquidity for the new tick range, add any surplus on top of that amount, and then redeploy the anchor liquidity using the correct liquidity‑management call. This ensures that the anchor segment remains adequately funded and prevents the thin‑range, high‑volatility condition.
summary: During sweep, discovery liquidity is rebalanced into anchor and floor liquidity. Anchor’s tick range is also increased. It was observed that anchor’s liquidity could decrease post-sweep which is undesirable. The issue stems from the increased anchor tick range and calling BPOOL.manageReservesFor(Range.ANCHOR, Action.ADD, newReservesA); instead of BPOOL.manageLiquidityFor(). There is no guarantee that newReservesA is sufficient to maintain or increase anchor’s liquidity, given the new tick range. Although surplusReservesD (surplus reserves in discovery) is added to newReservesA, this may not be sufficient as surplus could be small or even zero. As a result, every time sweep is called anchor liquidity could decrease, leading to a very thin anchor range and poor trading conditions where price fluctuates wildly between floor and discovery.

title: H-02 | Invalid Leverage Factor Calculation
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect calculation of the leverage factor used to scale the liquidity premium during sweep or slide rebalancing operations. The contract intends to compute the leverage factor as a fixed‑point multiplier representing the ratio of total collateral to the circulating external bAssets, expressed with 18 decimal places. The correct formula should multiply the ratio by 1e18 (or add 1e18 to a properly scaled division) so that a ratio of 5 yields a 5x multiplier (5e18). Instead, the implementation first computes the raw ratio (totalCollateral / (bAssetsCirculating‑totalCollateral)) and then adds a raw 1e18 constant to the result, producing a value of 1e18 + 5 rather than 5e18. This off‑by‑scale error means the multiplier is orders of magnitude smaller than intended, causing the protocol to apply an almost negligible premium when a substantial premium should be applied, or conversely to misprice positions if the code later interprets the value as a fixed‑point number. The bug manifests whenever a sweep or slide rebalance is executed, because those functions call the faulty leverage factor routine. Users experience symptoms such as receiving far lower refunds or payouts than expected, seeing their balances shrink unexpectedly after a rebalance, or observing that the protocol’s advertised leverage (e.g., 5x) does not match the on‑chain calculations. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the InitializeProtocol.sol contract, where the auditor noticed that the function returned leverageFactor_ += 1e18 instead of scaling the ratio correctly. It can be hard to notice because the contract still compiles and the returned value is a valid uint256; only when the premium is applied does the discrepancy become visible, often only under specific collateral ratios. Exploitation is possible by an attacker who can trigger rebalances at advantageous times, causing the protocol to under‑ or over‑charge liquidity premiums, potentially leading to loss of funds or unfair advantage. The root cause is a misuse of fixed‑point arithmetic: adding a raw 1e18 constant to an already unscaled ratio rather than using a proper fixed‑point division. The conceptual fix is to compute the multiplier using a reliable fixed‑point library, such as FixedPointMathLib, ensuring the ratio is scaled before adding the base unit, i.e., leverageFactor = 1e18 + totalCollateral.divWad(bAssetsCirculating‑totalCollateral). This correction restores the intended 5x (or N‑x) multiplier behavior, aligns on‑chain calculations with business logic, and prevents incorrect premium application that could otherwise erode user funds or break accounting assumptions.
summary: The leverage factor is calculated as the ratio between the totalCollateralized and the spot supply (externally owned bAssets). Whenever sweep or slide rebalances are executed, the leverage factor will act as a multiplier for the liquidityPremium. The main issue relies on the calculation of this multiplier. The first part of the formula correctly calculates the ratio: leverageFactor_ = totalCollateral / (_bAssetsCirculating - totalCollateral); But the value returned by the function is: leverageFactor_ += 1e18; This means that if the ratio is 5, the leverage factor will be 1e18 + 5 instead of 5e18 or a 5x multiplier. The issue can also be found at [InitializeProtocol.sol#L166](https://github.com/GuardianAudits/baseline-team-1-pocs/blob/main/src/policies/InitializeProtocol.sol#L166) as well.

title: H-03 | Interest Free Borrowing Due To TimeslotLib
content: The vulnerability is a boundary‑condition flaw in the interest calculation of the CreditFacility borrowing flow. When a user has an active credit account that expires on a given day, the protocol computes the interest for any additional borrowing based on the number of days remaining until expiry. On the final expiry day the variable daysRemaining is zero, so the formula yields an interest amount of zero. Because the contract does not check whether daysRemaining is zero before allowing a new borrow, a user can request extra reserves on that last day without extending the expiry and will be charged no interest for the new amount. An attacker can combine this with an immediate repayment in the same transaction, effectively borrowing for free and only paying gas. By repeatedly performing such zero‑interest borrows from the FLOOR and ANCHOR pools, the attacker inflates the protocol’s borrowing capacity while draining the ANCHOR reserves that underpin the price oracle, creating an arbitrage window for other actors to extract value. The issue occurs only when a borrow is initiated on the exact expiry day of a credit slot and no additional days are added. It affects any participant who can open a credit account, as well as the protocol itself because it loses expected interest revenue, sees its reserve accounting distorted, and becomes vulnerable to price manipulation. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit by the Guardian team, who noticed that the TimeslotLib library returns zero for daysRemaining on the expiry day and that the borrowing function does not guard against this case. The bug is subtle because the UI shows a normal borrowing operation and the zero interest amount may be interpreted as a promotional feature rather than a calculation error, making it easy to miss in routine testing that does not cover the expiry‑day edge case. To remediate, the contract should reject any borrow request when daysRemaining equals zero unless the caller also extends the credit term, or the interest formula should be adjusted to use the original credit duration rather than the remaining days. This class of bug is a missing‑validation / boundary‑condition error that violates the business rule that every borrowed amount must accrue a proportional interest charge, leading to unexpected “free loan” behavior, missing interest fees, and potential reserve depletion.
summary: Users can borrow reserves from CreditFacility using bAssets as collateral. A small interest will be paid based on the credit amount and the days added. The issue arises when users borrow more reserves with an existing credit account, without adding more days to expiry time. The protocol will try to calculate the interestOnNewCollateral based on the daysRemaining, but this value is 0 as there won't be any days remaining during the last expiry day. Any user borrowing during the last expiry day of the account, and does not add more days to the expiration, will effectively pay no interest for the new credit. Users might take advantage of this issue, by borrowing reserves from the FLOOR and ANCHOR, and repaying them in the same transaction to the FLOOR, and only pay gas fees. This will cause the capacity to be increased at will, as well as reduce the ANCHOR reserves that support the current price, opening the opportunity for arbitrageurs to extract reserves from the protocol.

title: H-04 | Incorrect Calculation of Upper Tick in Anchor Range
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect calculation of the upper tick for the ANCHOR liquidity range in the MarketMaking policy. The function that determines the next highest initialized tick, which must be a multiple of the protocol‑defined TICK_SPACING, rounds the current tick toward zero when the tick value is negative. Because negative ticks should be rounded up (toward zero) rather than down, the function returns a tick that is one spacing unit too low. This mis‑calculation only manifests when the active price tick is negative; when the price is positive the upper tick is computed correctly. As a result, when the market price resides in the FLOOR range and the active tick is negative, the ANCHOR range does not disappear as intended. Consequently the sweep‑rebalance operation can be triggered while the price is still inside the ANCHOR range. The rebalance logic checks only the reserves held at the ANCHOR position and ignores the amount of liquidity that has been removed as bAssets, which are then burned. From a user perspective the symptom is that a position that should have been closed or re‑balanced appears to remain active, and after a sweep rebalance the user may see their balance reduced or even disappear without any explicit withdrawal. The impact is a loss of funds because bAssets are unintentionally burned, violating the protocol’s accounting assumptions that liquidity removal is always accounted for before burning. The bug occurs during the rebalancing step, specifically when the contract calls the internal _getUpperAnchorTick function while the checkpoint tick is negative. It was discovered during a manual audit that compared the documented behaviour of getTickBoundaries with the actual implementation and observed that the anchor range behaved inconsistently for negative price ticks. The issue is hard to notice because the contract operates correctly for the majority of price movements (positive ticks) and the erroneous path is only exercised under specific market conditions that may not appear in routine testing. The class of bug is a sign‑aware rounding error in boundary calculation, a common source of off‑by‑one or off‑by‑sign defects in financial smart contracts. To remediate, the formula should be refactored so that for any tick value it first checks whether the tick is already aligned with TICK_SPACING and, if not, adds the spacing in the direction that moves toward the next higher multiple, handling negative values by rounding up rather than down. This ensures the ANCHOR upper tick is always the correct next initialized tick, preventing the anchor range from persisting incorrectly and eliminating the unintended burning of bAssets.
summary: The MarketMaking policy deploys liquidity to FLOOR, ANCHOR and DISCOVERY positions when rebalancing and their tick boundaries are calculated based on the getTickBoundaries function. The upper tick of ANCHOR (lower tick of DISCOVERY is calculated based on _getUpperAnchorTick which is suppose to return the next highest initialized tick that is a multiple of TICK_SPACING as stated in the docs. Although the _getUpperAnchorTick works with positive ticks, it does not return the correct value for negative ticks. This is due to the fact that the function is rounding the current tick down in absolute value, but negative ticks should be rounded up. When the active tick is in the FLOOR range, the ANCHOR range will disappear when the active tick is positive, but it won't when its negative. This also creates an unexpected scenario where the sweep rebalance operation can be executed when the price is at ANCHOR range. This operation will only check the reserves at ANCHOR, but not the liquidity removed as bAssets, which will be burned.

title: H-05 | Migration Process Can Be DoS’d
content: During the migration of a Uniswap‑style pool the protocol performs three distinct actions: it first creates the pool (initialization), then distributes spot tokens and creates internal credit records, and finally deploys the intended liquidity to the pool. Because these steps are executed in separate transactions and are not atomic, there is a measurable time window between the pool being initialized and the liquidity actually being added. In that window the pool contains no real liquidity and the active tick is set to a predefined INITIAL_ACTIVE_TICK. An attacker can exploit this gap by adding a tiny amount of liquidity to any tick of their choosing and performing a swap before the third step completes. The swap changes the active tick because the pool, although empty, will accept the trade for a negligible amount of wei. The migration process does not verify that the active tick after step one still matches the expected INITIAL_ACTIVE_TICK before proceeding to step three, so it continues to deploy liquidity based on outdated assumptions. Two harmful outcomes are possible. If the attacker swaps below the floor tick, the liquidity deployment succeeds but the price ratio between the discovery and anchor ranges becomes astronomically large, breaking the intended pricing model. If the attacker swaps far above the floor tick, the active tick ends up outside the discovery range and the liquidity deployment fails, effectively halting the pool’s operation. From a user perspective this manifests as swaps that either revert with extreme price slippage or a pool that appears to be dead, showing zero balances or refusing trades. The root cause is the non‑atomic migration design and the missing check that the active tick remains unchanged before liquidity is added. The issue was uncovered during a manual security audit that examined the migration flow and identified the lack of safeguards. It can be difficult to notice because the attacker uses only a few wei, leaving no obvious loss of funds, and the contract does not emit explicit warnings about the tick mismatch. To remediate the problem the migration should be refactored into a single atomic transaction or, at minimum, include a validation step that aborts the deployment if the current active tick differs from the expected INITIAL_ACTIVE_TICK. This eliminates the window for malicious swaps and restores the intended accounting guarantees of the protocol.
summary: During the migration process, the protocol will: 1. Initialize the pool 2. Distribute spot tokens and create credits 3. Deploy liquidity to the pool This migration is not atomic and will take some time, which means there will be a lag between the initialization of the Uniswap pool and deploying liquidity to the pool. In this period, an attacker can add liquidity to any tick he wants, perform a swap, and change the active tick. Since the pool is empty, this can be done with only a few wei. Attacker injects a swap between steps 1 and 3 above but the migration process continues, and there is no check regarding whether the current tick is the same as INITIAL_ACTIVE_TICK. There are two possible impacts depending on which way the swap is performed by the attacker. 1. If the attacker swaps below the floor tick, the liquidity deployment will be successful, but the ratio between discovery and anchor will be enormous. 2. If the attacker swaps way above, liquidity deployment will fail due to active tick being in the discovery range.

title: H-06 | Interest Formula Favours Longer Credits
content: The vulnerability is a mis‑calculated interest formula used for credit positions in the protocol. The contract is supposed to pay interest upfront based on a linear rate defined by the INTEREST_PER_DIEM variable and the length of the credit. Instead, the conversion from daily or monthly rates to yearly rates uses incorrect multipliers: the yearly interest is computed as roughly 348.6 times the daily rate rather than the correct 365, and as roughly 11.6 times the monthly rate rather than the correct 12. This error causes longer‑duration credits – such as yearly or multi‑month loans – to receive about a 4.5 % discount on the expected interest. The root cause is a faulty arithmetic expression that does not properly scale the per‑diem or per‑month interest to the full credit period, effectively favouring borrowers who select longer terms. An attacker or any user can exploit this by simply choosing a longer credit term, thereby receiving less interest expense than the protocol intended, which reduces the protocol’s revenue stream. The impact is a systematic loss of roughly 3‑5 % of the expected interest income, which directly lowers the baseline token value that is funded by both LP fees and credit interest. The condition under which the bug manifests is any credit whose length exceeds a single day or month, because the erroneous conversion factor is applied during the interest calculation step. All participants – borrowers, liquidity providers, and token holders – are affected because the reduced interest revenue diminishes the token’s inflationary rewards and may cause the token price to drift downward. The issue was discovered during a formal audit of the BaselineV2 contract where the auditor compared the documented interest model with the on‑chain implementation and identified the mismatch in conversion constants. The bug can be hard to notice because the contract still pays interest and the discrepancy is relatively small on a per‑transaction basis, making it appear as normal variance rather than a systematic error. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a borrower who expects a certain amount of interest for a yearly credit receives a lower amount, and token holders may observe a slower growth of token balances than advertised. The vulnerability belongs to the class of financial‑logic errors where incorrect scaling of rates leads to revenue leakage. To remediate the issue the interest calculation should be rewritten to use the exact number of days in a year (365) and the exact number of months in a year (12) when converting per‑diem or per‑month rates, ensuring that the interest rate remains constant regardless of credit length. This conceptual fix restores linearity of the interest model and eliminates the unintended discount for longer credits.
summary: The protocol has a credit feature and the interests for these credits are paid upfront. Interest is meant to be linear based on INTEREST_PER_DIEM variable and credit length. However, interest formula favours longer credits due to an error in it. Currently: • Yearly credit interest is ~348.6 * daily interest instead of 365. • Yearly credit interest is ~11.6 * monthly interest instead of 12. This means ~4.5% discount in interest when taking yearly credits. The protocol has two major revenue streams: LP fees and credit interests. This income is used to increase the baseline value of the token. Due to this formula favouring longer credits, protocol loses ~3-5% of it’s expected interest revenue (exact number will be affected by average credit length).

title: H-07 | All Gas Yields Earned On Blast Are Lost
content: The vulnerability consists of a misconfiguration of the contract’s gas‑claim mode on the Blast execution layer. Blast offers a mechanism whereby a smart contract can reclaim a portion of the gas it spends, typically between fifty and one hundred percent, by setting its gas mode to a claimable state. By default, however, the gas mode is Void, which directs all consumed gas to the sequencer and prevents any reclamation. In the examined protocol the developer never invoked the configuration function on the BLAST system contract (address 0x4300000000000000000000000000000000000002) that would switch the contract from Void to a claimable mode. Consequently, every transaction executed by the protocol incurs a cost that is permanently transferred to the sequencer, and the protocol forfeits the expected supplemental income that would otherwise be added to its BLV token balance. The issue manifests whenever the protocol performs on‑chain operations on Blast; under those conditions the contract’s gas fees are silently lost, leading to a systematic reduction in revenue. Users of the protocol do not see any direct symptom in the UI, but they may notice that the protocol’s token balance does not grow proportionally to activity, or that expected refunds are missing. The problem was identified during a security audit that reviewed the deployment checklist and noted the absence of a call to the BLAST configuration function. Because the loss is economic rather than a functional failure, it can be easy to overlook; the contract still operates correctly, and no transaction reverts, so the missing income does not raise immediate alarms. To remediate the issue, the contract should be updated to call the appropriate method on the BLAST contract to set its gas mode to a claimable setting before any gas‑intensive operations are performed. This change will enable the protocol to capture the entitled portion of gas fees, aligning the implementation with the business assumption that gas consumption generates additional revenue. Past gas fees that were spent while the contract remained in Void mode cannot be retroactively reclaimed, so the loss is irreversible for those transactions, but future operations will benefit from the corrected configuration.
summary: This protocol will be deployed on Blast, which provides a feature to claim gas fees consumed by smart contracts. Contracts can claim 50% to 100% of gas fees depending on the claim rate. The default gas mode for contracts on Blast is Void, and all consumed gas is sent to the sequencer. For these gas fees to be claimed, smart contracts must be configured by interacting with the BLAST contract at 0x4300000000000000000000000000000000000002 address.

title: H-01 | Invalid Portion Burned
content: The vulnerability is a scaling error in the calculation of the portion of a reserve that should be burned during the contract’s reheat operation. The code stores the minimum and maximum allowed portions as .05 ether and .15 ether, which represent 5 % and 15 % when interpreted with a denominator of 1e18 (the standard wei scaling for ether values). However, the reheat function computes the reserveSize using a denominator of 100e18, effectively treating the stored values as if they were expressed in hundredths of a percent. As a result the actual portion that is burned is two orders of magnitude smaller than intended – roughly 0.05 % to 0.15 % instead of 5 % to 15 %. This mismatch originates from an incorrect assumption about the unit of the portion variables and manifests whenever the reheat function is invoked. An attacker or any user can exploit the bug by triggering reheat expecting a substantial burn of the reserve; the contract will only burn a negligible amount, leaving excess tokens in the system. The impact is a distortion of the protocol’s token‑omics: the supply reduction that should occur does not happen, potentially inflating the token supply, reducing expected fee revenue, and breaking accounting assumptions that rely on a specific burn rate. Users may notice that after a reheat transaction the visible reserve balance has decreased far less than the advertised 15 % burn, or that expected refunds or fee adjustments are missing. The issue was uncovered during a manual audit when the reviewer compared the comment on line 150 (which states the portion should be 15 %) with the actual arithmetic and observed the denominator mismatch. Because the contract still performs a burn, albeit a tiny one, the problem can be subtle and may not raise an immediate alarm, especially if the UI only shows the final balance without highlighting the percentage change. To remediate the bug, the denominator in the reserveSize calculation should be changed to 1e18, aligning the scaling with the ether‑based portion values, or alternatively the portion constants should be re‑defined to match the 100e18 denominator. This class of bug falls under “unit‑conversion or scaling errors” where percentages are mis‑represented, leading to incorrect financial calculations and broken business logic.
summary: In the reheat function the reserveSize is computed with a denominator of 100e18, however the minPortion and maxPortion are assigned to as .05 ether and .15 ether respectively in the constructor. The comment on line 150 indicates that the portion ought to be 15% rather than 0.15%, therefore the portion is a factor of 100x smaller than it ought to be.

title: H-02 | YesArena Block Stuﬃng Attack
content: The vulnerability is a block‑stuffing manipulation of the YesArena game on the Blast chain. The contract determines the winner based on which address is recorded as the “winner” after a deposit, while a second address holds the “hotPotato” role. Because the game only checks the order of deposit calls within a fixed two‑minute window, an attacker who controls two separate addresses can first deposit with address A to become the hotPotato, then deposit with address B to make A the winner and B the new hotPotato. After establishing this favorable state, the attacker floods the network with a large number of low‑value, gas‑wasting transactions that fill every block for the remaining two minutes. Since the blockchain continues to produce blocks but all of them contain only the attacker’s filler transactions, no other participant’s deposit can be included before the window expires, effectively locking the winner role to the attacker. The root cause is the reliance on block inclusion order without any protection against deliberate block saturation, combined with a short, static time window that does not adapt to network congestion. Exploitation requires only the ability to send many transactions quickly; no special privileges are needed. The impact is a loss of fairness: honest users who try to deposit during the final minutes see their transactions either delayed or dropped, they receive no chance to become the winner, and the protocol’s reward distribution becomes skewed toward the attacker. From a user’s perspective the UI may show that deposits are pending for an unusually long time, the “you are not the winner” message never appears, and the expected reward never arrives even though the user has funded the contract. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the game’s timing logic and identified that the two‑minute window can be monopolised by transaction spamming. It is hard to notice because the blockchain continues to function normally; there is no explicit error, only an unexpected lack of new winners. The bug belongs to the class of time‑window manipulation and denial‑of‑service attacks that exploit predictable state transitions. To mitigate the problem the protocol should extend the game timer each time a deposit is recorded, enforce a minimum block interval between winner changes, introduce randomness or commit‑reveal schemes, or limit the number of transactions an address can submit within the window. These changes raise the cost of block stuffing and restore the intended probabilistic fairness of the arena.
summary:
A malicious actor may significantly increase their odds of winning the YesArena at the end of the game time by using two addresses to ensure they control both the winner and hotPotato addresses and then submitting many transactions to stuff Blast blocks for the next 2 minutes. For example:
• Bob calls deposit with address A, A is now the hot potato
• Bob calls deposit with address B, A is now the winner & B is the hot potato
• Bob submits many gas waster transactions to stuff the next 2 minutes of Blast blocks until he is the winner
This can significantly reduce the chances that other actors have at getting a deposit call recorded before the 2 minutes is over.

title: When `sellCreditMarket`
content: The vulnerability resides in the fee calculation performed by the accounting library when the sellCreditMarket function is used to sell credit for a specific amount of cash (szaUSDC). The contract computes the swap fee with the expression Math.mulDivUp(cashAmountOut, swapFeePercent, PERCENT) in the original code, but the correct economic model requires the fee to be calculated on the net amount after the fee is taken, i.e. cashAmountOut * swapFeePercent / (PERCENT‑swapFeePercent). By using the plain denominator PERCENT the contract under‑charges the fee, especially in the branch where the caller requests an exact cash amount (exactAmountIn=true). The root cause is an arithmetic mistake: the denominator does not account for the fee being taken out of the cash amount, leading to a lower fee than the protocol’s specification. An attacker can exploit this by invoking sellCreditMarket with exactAmountIn set to true and specifying a cash amount that triggers the faulty branch. The contract will then credit the seller with more cash than it should, while the feeRecipient receives a smaller fee than documented. The impact is a loss of revenue for the protocol: each affected trade yields a fee shortfall that accumulates over many transactions, reducing the funds available to the feeRecipient and potentially destabilising the economic incentives of the system. The bug manifests only when the function is called to sell credit for a predetermined cash amount, either in the no‑fractionalisation case (cashAmountOut equals maxCashAmountOut) or when cashAmountOut is below the fragmentation‑adjusted maximum. Users of the protocol – lenders, borrowers and the feeRecipient – are affected because balances may not match the expected accounting rules; a user may notice that they receive slightly more cash than anticipated while the fee shown on‑chain is lower than the protocol’s fee table. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when the auditors compared on‑chain fee outcomes with the fee tables published in the protocol documentation and observed a discrepancy in Example 2. It is hard to notice because the deviation is small (often a few hundred thousand units on a million‑scale transaction) and the UI typically displays only the net cash received, not the detailed fee breakdown. To remediate, the fee formula should be corrected to use the denominator (PERCENT‑swapFeePercent) and to incorporate the fragmentation fee consistently in both the credit amount and fee calculations. This class of bug belongs to arithmetic or rounding errors in fee logic, where an incorrect denominator leads to under‑charging. The failure mode can be described as “funds disappear from the fee pool” or “refund calculation error” because the protocol pays out more cash than it should while collecting insufficient fees, violating the intended accounting invariants.
summary: The protocol might receive a lower fee than expected when `sellCreditMarket()` is called to sell credit for a specific cash amount.

title: Risk of overpayment due to race condition between `repay` and `liquidateWithReplacement` transactions
content: The vulnerability is a race condition that occurs when a borrower tries to repay a debt position at the same time a keeper bot executes the liquidateWithReplacement function. The liquidateWithReplacement operation replaces the unhealthy borrower with a new one but deliberately keeps the same debt position identifier and the same future value. Because the repay function only checks the debt position identifier and does not verify that the caller is still the borrower of that position, a repayment transaction that is mined after the liquidation will credit the caller’s funds against the new borrower’s debt. As a result the original borrower unintentionally pays the debt of the replacement borrower, effectively repaying more than twice the amount they owed because the liquidation also distributes a reward to the liquidator. This can be triggered whenever two transactions – a repayment and a liquidation – are submitted in close temporal proximity, which is common when users receive UI alerts that their position is liquidatable and attempt to repay immediately while a keeper bot is also monitoring the same condition. If an attacker observes the pending repayment in the mempool, they can front‑run the transaction with a liquidation, causing the borrower to lose funds. The impact is that the borrower’s balance is reduced by an amount greater than the original debt, often appearing as a missing or zeroed balance after the transaction, while the liquidator gains the reward. The issue affects any user who holds a debt position, the protocol’s accounting logic, and lenders who expect repayment on the original schedule. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the interaction between the repay library and the liquidation library and identified that the borrower address is not part of the repayment validation. The bug is subtle because the protocol emits an event updating the borrower, but the UI may not highlight the change before the repayment is processed, leading users to believe they are repaying their own debt. Conceptually, the fix is to require both the debt position ID and the borrower address in the repayment call and to validate that the supplied borrower matches the current owner of the position, thereby preventing a repayment from being applied to a different borrower after a replacement liquidation. This change restores the intended accounting invariant that a repayment always reduces the debt of the borrower who initiated it and eliminates the over‑payment scenario.
summary:
* **Likelihood** : Medium - Users and liquidation bots are likely to call their respective functions around the same time.
* **Impact** : High - Users end up repaying more than double their future value.

title: The collateral remainder cap is incorrectly calculated during liquidation
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect calculation of the collateral remainder cap that is applied when an overdue loan is liquidated. The contract is supposed to split the collateral that remains after the liquidator receives the debt amount plus a reward between the borrower and the protocol, but the cap that limits the protocol’s share is computed using the full liquidation collateral ratio (for example 130%) instead of the excess portion above the debt (30%). This root‑cause stems from a formula that multiplies the debt amount by the liquidation ratio directly, rather than by the difference between the liquidation ratio and 100 percent. When the cap is too large, the protocol can claim a larger slice of the remaining collateral, and borrowers with a higher collateral ratio lose more than those with a lower ratio even though both positions have the same debt size. An attacker can trigger liquidation on any overdue position that is not underwater; the contract will then allocate an inflated protocol fee, effectively stealing additional collateral from borrowers who over‑collateralised their loan. The impact is that users see less collateral returned than expected, with higher‑CR users experiencing a disproportionate loss, which undermines the economic incentive to provide ample collateral and may erode confidence in the protocol’s fairness. The condition for exploitation is that the loan is overdue, the borrower’s collateral ratio exceeds the liquidation threshold, and the liquidation function is called. Affected parties include borrowers whose collateral is partially confiscated, the protocol fee recipient that receives an unintended excess, and liquidators who may benefit from the mis‑allocation. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when test cases showed that two borrowers with identical debt but different collateral ratios received different protocol profit amounts, revealing that the cap calculation was using the full 130 percent instead of the 30 percent excess. The bug is subtle because the cap calculation appears syntactically correct and only diverges in edge cases where collateral ratios differ, making it easy to overlook without comparative testing. To remediate, the cap should be computed as debt × (crLiquidation − 100 percent) / 100 percent, or equivalently using the excess collateral ratio, ensuring that only the surplus above the debt is eligible for protocol fees. This adjustment restores the intended accounting logic where the protocol’s share is limited to the excess collateral, aligning user expectations with actual outcomes and preserving the incentive for higher collateralisation.
summary:
When a position is overdue, it can be liquidated even if the owner has a sufficient collateral ratio. Some rewards are sent to the liquidator as an incentive and some fees are assigned to the protocol. However, the calculation of the protocol fee is flawed due to an incorrect collateral remainder cap calculation.

Imagine the collateral ratio for liquidation is set at 130%. The collateral equivalent to the debt should be paid to the protocol, and the excess collateral (30%) can be the remainder cap. Currently, the entire 130% is treated as the remainder cap, leading to an unfair situation where a user with a 150% collateral ratio experiences more loss than a user with a 140% CR.

This discourages users with higher CRs, who generally contribute to the protocol’s health. If higher CRs result in greater losses, it disincentivizes users from providing sufficient collateral to the protocol.

title: Users won’t liquidate positions because the logic used to calculate the liquidator’s profit is incorrect
content: The vulnerability is an arithmetic scaling error in the liquidation routine that calculates the liquidator’s profit. The contract determines the amount of collateral assigned to a debt position and converts the debt amount from the debt token (USDC with 6 decimals) to the collateral token (ETH with 18 decimals). Because the conversion does not correctly align the differing decimal precisions, the resulting debt value expressed in collateral units is off by a factor of 1e12. Consequently, the profit formula – which adds a reward based on the difference between assigned collateral and the converted debt – yields a reward that is orders of magnitude smaller than intended. This mis‑calculation removes the economic incentive for external actors to call the liquidation function when a borrower’s collateral ratio falls below the protocol‑defined threshold. In practice, a liquidator who initiates a liquidation transaction receives a profit that is effectively zero, often displayed in the UI as a negligible amount or even zero, while the borrower’s unhealthy position remains on‑chain. The issue manifests only when a position becomes liquidatable; the faulty profit computation is triggered during the executeLiquidate call. Affected parties include borrowers whose positions stay underwater, liquidators who are not compensated, and the protocol itself, which risks insolvency if unhealthy positions accumulate. The problem was uncovered during a Code4rena audit when the auditors observed logs showing a future value of 82814071 USDC converting to 82814071000000000000 wei, yet the assigned collateral was 100000000000000000000 wei, resulting in a profit that was many orders of magnitude smaller than expected. The bug is subtle because the numbers involved are large and appear correct at a glance; only a careful inspection of token decimal handling reveals the discrepancy. To remediate, the profit calculation must normalize all amounts to a common unit before performing arithmetic, either by scaling the USDC amount to 18‑decimal precision or by converting the ETH amount to 6‑decimal precision, and then applying the reward formula on these aligned values. This class of bug falls under unit‑mismatch or scaling errors, which break accounting assumptions that collateral value and debt value are comparable on a one‑to‑one basis. By fixing the decimal alignment, the protocol restores proper incentives for liquidators, ensuring that unhealthy positions are promptly cleared and the system remains solvent.
summary: Liquidation is crucial, and all liquidatable positions must be liquidated to maintain the protocol’s solvency. However, because the liquidator’s profit is calculated incorrectly, users are not incentivized to liquidate unhealthy positions. This issue has a significant impact on the protocol.

title: A malicious user can steal money out of the vault and other users
content: A rebasing token such as AMPL is whitelisted in the Thorchain router contract and is treated as a regular ERC‑20 token. The contract records the amount a user deposits and then grants the router an allowance equal to that recorded amount. The implementation assumes that the token balance associated with the recorded amount remains constant after the deposit. Because a rebasing token changes the relationship between its internal "gons" balance and the external fragment balance whenever a rebase occurs, the recorded amount no longer reflects the actual token balance held by the contract. When a rebase reduces the fragment value, the contract’s internal balance is effectively larger than the allowance that was granted, allowing a malicious actor to approve a rogue router for the original deposited amount and then call transferFrom to move tokens out of the contract. The attacker can front‑run a rebase, deposit a known amount, wait for the rebase to change the conversion factor, and then use the stale allowance to steal tokens that belong to other users or to lock funds if the rebase increases the conversion factor. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that a legitimate depositor sees only a fraction of the expected balance when withdrawing (for example, a user deposits 1,000 AMPL but can only withdraw 500) while the attacker’s balance increases by the same amount. The impact is a direct theft of funds – up to 50 % of the victim’s deposit in the demonstrated scenario – and can also lead to a denial‑of‑service when the contract’s balance grows but the allowance does not, preventing legitimate withdrawals. The vulnerability is triggered only when a rebasing token is used, the router grants a static allowance based on the pre‑rebase deposit amount, and the contract does not recalculate or adjust allowances after a rebase. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the safeTransferFrom helper, which correctly returns the actual amount received but the surrounding logic still relies on the original deposit amount. The bug is subtle because the contract’s balanceOf view returns the correct external fragment balance, masking the internal mismatch between allowance and actual token holdings. To remediate the issue the contract must stop assuming a constant token balance after a deposit; it should either recompute the allowance based on the current token balance after each rebase, use the amount returned by safeTransferFrom for all subsequent calculations, or explicitly forbid rebasing tokens unless proper handling logic is added. Implementing a mechanism that tracks the real fragment balance or that resets allowances after a rebase would close the attack vector and restore the intended accounting guarantees of the vault.
summary: A malicious user can steal money out of other users and the vault when a rebasing token like AMPL is used. That particular token is whitelisted as seen [here](https://gitlab.com/thorchain/thornode/-/blob/develop/common/tokenlist/ethtokens/eth_mainnet_latest.json?ref_type=heads).

title: ThorChain will be informed wrongly about the unsuccessful ETH transfers due to the incorrect events emissions
content: The Router contract emits a TransferOut event that ThorChain uses to record an outbound transfer. In the transferOut function the contract first attempts to send native ETH to the destination address using the .send method, which forwards only 2300 gas and returns a boolean indicating success. If the send fails, the function refunds the ETH back to the calling vault but still emits the TransferOut event with the original to address unchanged. Because the event is emitted before the success check and the to field is not updated to the vault address, ThorChain parses the log and assumes the funds were successfully delivered to the intended recipient. This breaks the invariant that only events reflecting actual successful transfers should populate the txInItem structure. The bug can be triggered by sending ETH to a contract that either reverts or consumes more than 2300 gas in its fallback, causing .send to return false. The contract then bounces the ETH back to the vault, but the event still reports the original destination. From a user perspective the UI shows a successful outbound transaction, the memo and amount appear correct, yet the recipient balance remains unchanged and the vault balance is reduced only by gas, leading to apparent loss of funds. The protocol updates its accounting based on the false event, which may result in vaults being credited for funds that never left the vault, breaking accounting assumptions and potentially exposing user assets to loss. The issue was discovered during a security audit by testing a contract (named Navich) that deliberately rejects ETH, revealing that the TransferOut event reports the wrong to address while the ETH is actually returned. The problem is subtle because the transaction does not revert and no error is emitted, so standard monitoring that relies on events will not notice the failure. The vulnerability belongs to the class of premature event emission or false‑positive accounting bugs, where logs are emitted before confirming the underlying state change. A correct fix is to emit the TransferOut event only after a successful transfer, or to revert the transaction on failure, or to adjust the to field to the vault address when a bounce‑back occurs, and to ensure the log parser validates that the recorded recipient matches the actual holder of the funds.

title: Most users won’t be able to claim their share of Uniswap fees
content: The vulnerability concerns the fee‑claiming routine of a Uniswap V3 based liquidity‑vesting contract. The contract is supposed to let every liquidity provider withdraw the portion of protocol fees that corresponds to their current position, regardless of any pending vesting schedule. In practice the claim() function first burns the caller’s liquidity, then adds the accumulated fee amounts (fees0 and fees1) to a variable called collect0/collect1 and finally invokes pool.collect to transfer those tokens to the contract. The root cause is that the amount passed to pool.collect is calculated using the total liquidity of the position (positionLiquidity) instead of the actual liquidity that is being claimed (liquidity2Claim). As a result the contract attempts to collect the full fee entitlement for the whole position each time a claim is made, even after a previous claim has already withdrawn those fees. When the first user calls claim, the pool returns the expected fee tokens and the contract’s internal balance is reduced to zero. A subsequent user calling claim for a different tokenId triggers the same collect call, but the contract no longer holds the required fee tokens, causing the pool’s safe‑transfer to revert with the error code “ST”. This failure also blocks the vesting withdrawal path because the contract cannot satisfy the fee transfer that is part of the vesting logic. The impact is that legitimate users see their expected refunds disappear; the UI may show a successful claim transaction for the first user, while later users receive a reverted transaction and see no tokens credited, effectively losing access to their share of fees. The issue manifests only when multiple distinct tokenIds share the same underlying Uniswap pool and claim sequentially, which is a common scenario in multi‑investor offerings. It was discovered during a systematic forge test that simulated two investors claiming fees after a flash‑loan generated fee accrual; the second claim consistently reverted. The bug is subtle because the first claim succeeds and the code appears to follow the Uniswap fee‑collection pattern, making the over‑collection logic easy to overlook. To remediate, the contract should compute fees based on the exact amount of liquidity being claimed, limit the collect parameters to the caller’s entitlement, and reset fee‑tracking variables after each successful claim. In broader terms, this is a classic case of improper accounting of shared resources leading to double‑spending of fee tokens, violating the contract’s financial invariants and breaking user expectations that “my share of fees should always be claimable”.
summary:
Users should be able to claim Uniswap fees for their current liquidity position regardless of their pending vestings, or cliff. But most users won’t be able to claim those Uniswap fees.

It is also possible that they won’t be able to claim their vesting if they accumulate sufficient unclaimed Uniswap fees.

title: Vultisig whitelisting can be bypassed by anyone
content: The vulnerability is a whitelist bypass that allows any address to participate in the token sale during the designated whitelist launch phase, even if the address is not listed in the contract's whitelist. The root cause lies in the contract's whitelist verification logic, which checks the stored whitelist index of the recipient against a configurable upper bound (_allowedWhitelistIndex). When the upper bound is set, the condition "_whitelistIndex[to] == 0 || _whitelistIndex[to] > _allowedWhitelistIndex" treats a zero index (meaning the address is not whitelisted) as acceptable because the second part of the OR expression is false and the first part evaluates to true only when the index is zero. Consequently, the check does not reject non‑whitelisted accounts once the limit is configured, effectively turning the whitelist into a no‑op. An attacker can exploit this by simply calling the purchase function with any address after the allowed index is set, thereby bypassing the intended 3 ETH per‑account limit and acquiring tokens that should be reserved for legitimate whitelisted participants. The impact is that the token price can be distorted, legitimate users lose their allocation opportunity, and the overall fairness of the launch is compromised. This condition is active only during the WL Launch window, as indicated by the launch timeline diagram, and it affects all participants, the protocol’s token economics, and any investors expecting a protected allocation. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, where a unit test demonstrated that a non‑whitelisted account could call the whitelist check successfully after the allowed index was set. The bug is subtle because the code appears to enforce a whitelist, but the logical operator order and the handling of a zero index mask the flaw, making it easy to miss during manual review. To remediate, the contract should explicitly reject any address whose whitelist index is zero, regardless of the allowed index, for example by reverting when "_whitelistIndex[to] == 0" or when the index exceeds the allowed limit. This ensures that only addresses explicitly added to the whitelist can purchase during the protected phase, preserving the intended allocation limits and protecting the token sale’s economic integrity.
summary:
Whitelist launch will be bricked. Anyone can buy tokens, and also bypass the 3 ETH limit by buying via other non-whitelisted accounts. This will have an impact on price and ruin the opportunities of legit whitelisted users.

[Here’s a diagram](https://docs.vultisig.com/vultisig-token/launch#launch-liquidity) on the timelines of the launch. “WL Launch” is the affected phase.

title: Adversary can prevent the launch of any ILO pool with enough raised capital at any moment by providing single-sided liquidity
content: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that allows an adversary to block the launch of any Initial Liquidity Offering (ILO) pool even after the pool has reached its fundraising target. The root cause is that the ILOManager contract validates the Uniswap V3 pool price at launch by reading the current sqrtPriceX96 from the pool and comparing it with the price that was cached when the project was created. When the pool contains little or no liquidity, an attacker can perform a cost‑free swap that pushes the price to an extreme tick because the AMM price is determined solely by the ratio of reserves. After the price is manipulated, the attacker can add single‑sided liquidity (only the raise token) in a tick range that lies outside the manipulated price but still below the original expected price. This single‑sided liquidity locks the price because any attempt to swap back to the original price would require the opposite token (the sale token) which is not available – all sale tokens are held in the ILO pool awaiting the launch. Consequently, when the ILOManager calls launch, the price check fails and the transaction reverts with the UV3P error, preventing the token launch. The impact is a protocol‑wide denial of service: users who have contributed gas and funds to the sale cannot claim refunds or receive the launched token, leading to wasted gas, loss of confidence, and potential damage to the token’s market perception. The attack can be executed at any moment, including immediately before the launch deadline, and the cost to the attacker is negligible – only a minimal amount of the raise token is needed to mint the single‑sided liquidity. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, which included a proof‑of‑concept test that demonstrated the price manipulation and the subsequent failure to revert the price. The bug is hard to notice because the pool may appear to have a valid price before the launch and the added liquidity can be very small, making it easy to overlook in normal monitoring. To remediate, the protocol should enforce a minimum amount of liquidity before allowing a launch, use a time‑weighted average price or a price oracle that is not directly manipulable by a single swap, reserve a small amount of the sale token to enable price correction, or wrap the sale token in a mintable proxy that can be used to restore the expected price. These measures would raise the cost of the attack and prevent the price from being locked by single‑sided liquidity, thereby restoring the ability to launch the ILO pool as intended.

title: Math error in creator payment calculation
content: The vulnerability is a mathematical error in the calculation of the maximum amount that can be paid to a content creator in the Tunnl protocol. The contract stores the total offer value as maxValueUsdc, which already includes a flat fee and an advertiser percentage fee. When the protocol prepares a Chainlink Functions request it derives maxCreatorPayment by subtracting the flat fee and then dividing by 10000 plus s_config.creatorFeePercentageBP. The intended denominator should be 10000 plus the advertiser fee percentage that belongs to the specific offer (s_offers[offerId].advertiserFeePercentageBP). By using the creator fee percentage instead, the contract either inflates the payable amount when the creator fee is lower than the advertiser fee, causing the fulfillment logic to revert with an “Exceeds max” error, or deflates the amount when the creator fee is higher, resulting in the creator receiving less than the advertised amount. This mis‑calculation occurs every time sendFunctionsRequest() is called, i.e., after a successful verification of an offer, and it is hidden because the value is only logged and the test suite supplies a mocked fulfillment amount that does not reflect the real maxCreatorPayment. The bug affects advertisers who expect their full budget to be spent, creators who expect to receive the promised payment, and the protocol itself because payouts may fail or be systematically under‑paid, breaking the economic model. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by Cyfrin, which noticed the wrong configuration variable being used and confirmed the problem by logging the computed maxCreatorPayment. It is hard to notice because the incorrect value is not compared against the stored maxValueUsdc and the existing unit tests use an artificial payout amount, so the discrepancy does not surface in the test run. The vulnerability belongs to the class of fee‑calculation bugs where an incorrect percentage is applied in an arithmetic expression, leading to wrong accounting and potential loss of funds. From a user’s perspective the creator may see a zero or reduced balance after a payout, the advertiser may see leftover funds or a transaction revert, and the UI may show a successful campaign while no funds are actually transferred. The correct fix is to replace s_config.creatorFeePercentageBP with the advertiser fee percentage stored in the offer (s_offers[offerId].advertiserFeePercentageBP) and to compute the payment using the proper formula that subtracts the creator fee after the advertiser fee has been accounted for. This change restores the intended accounting logic, ensures that the maximum creator payment never exceeds the offer budget, and prevents under‑payment of creators.

title: H-01 | Valor Emitted Without Cap
content: The vulnerability is an unbounded token emission bug. The contract is designed to limit the total amount of Valor that can be emitted by keeping a running total (totalValorEmitted) and comparing it against a predefined maximum (maximumValorEmission) before each new emission. Because the totalValorEmitted state variable is never updated after an emission, its value remains zero forever. Consequently the comparison always succeeds, effectively removing any cap on the amount of Valor that can be minted. An attacker or any caller with permission to trigger emissions can repeatedly invoke the emission function, causing the contract to create an unlimited number of tokens. This can lead to uncontrolled inflation, dilution of existing holders' balances, loss of economic guarantees, and potential loss of trust in the protocol. The issue manifests whenever the emission routine is executed, regardless of the amount being emitted, because the guard condition is always satisfied. It affects all token holders, the protocol’s token economics, and any downstream contracts that rely on a bounded supply. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the state updates and noticed that totalValorEmitted was read but never written. It can be hard to notice because the contract may still appear to function correctly for small emissions and no explicit overflow occurs. The proper fix is to update the totalValorEmitted variable each time an emission occurs, for example by adding totalValorEmitted += valorEmission in the internal accounting routine, thereby restoring the intended supply cap enforcement. This class of bug is a missing state‑update or accounting omission that defeats a logical invariant designed to enforce a maximum supply.
summary: The system uses two variables to calculate the valor emission, totalValorEmitted and maximumValorEmission, and performs a check to validate if the new emission and the total emitted will not surpass the max value. The issue is that totalValorEmitted state variable is never updated, so it's value is always 0. Therefore, the valor cap validations are non existent, and the system can emit valor indefinitely.

title: H-02 | Claim Rewards Callback Message Not Executable
content: The vulnerability concerns the cross‑chain reward claim flow for the esORDER token in an omnichain ledger system. When a user initiates a claim for esORDER rewards, the contract first stakes the claimed amount and then attempts to send a ClaimRewardBackward message back to the Vault chain via LayerZero. The receiving function vaultRecvFromLedger in the ProxyLedger contract contains a strict validation that the incoming message must reference the native ORDER token and have a positive amount. Because the backward payload carries the esORDER token, the require statement (message.token == LedgerToken.ORDER && message.tokenAmount > 0) fails, causing the callback to revert. This revert does not discard the message; instead, it remains pending in the LayerZero queue, blocking any subsequent messages from being processed on the destination chain until the failed message is manually cleared. Consequently, users who try to claim esORDER rewards experience a silent failure: the claim appears to succeed on the source chain, but the reward never arrives and the cross‑chain pathway becomes stalled. The impact is a denial‑of‑service condition for all reward‑related communications, potentially locking funds that depend on the backward callback and breaking the accounting assumptions that rewards are automatically transferred after staking. The issue manifests whenever the claim function is called with esORDER as the reward token, regardless of the amount, and affects any participant who expects to receive or restake esORDER rewards, as well as the Vault chain that relies on the backward message to update its state. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the message handling logic and identified the mismatch between the expected token type and the actual payload. The problem is subtle because the initial staking step succeeds, giving the impression that the operation completed, while the failure occurs only in the asynchronous cross‑chain callback, making it hard to detect without inspecting the LayerZero message queue. To remediate the issue, the claim routine should bypass the backward message when the reward token is esORDER, for example by returning early after the staking step or by adding an explicit else branch that only sends the ClaimRewardBackward payload for ORDER tokens. This change ensures that only valid messages are sent to the Vault chain, preventing the require check from failing and keeping the LayerZero pathway clear for future messages.
summary: Users can claim ORDER and esORDER rewards based on the merkle distributions. The issue arises when claiming esORDER, as the amount claimed will be staked, but will also try to send a ClaimRewardBackward payload to the Vault chain. The internal vaultRecvFromLedger in ProxyLedger contract will fail as this callback performs the following check: require(message.token == LedgerToken.ORDER && message.tokenAmount > 0, "InvalidClaimRewardBackward"); Therefore, every esORDER claim request will block the LayerZero pathway for the destination chain, as no new messages can be executed before clearing the failed one.

title: H-03 | Partial Vesting Claim Requests DoS’ed
content: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that occurs when a user attempts to claim a portion of their vested ORDER tokens before the linear vesting period has completed. The contract logic routes the claimed portion to the user on the vault chain, but any remaining unclaimed amount is transferred directly to an orderCollector address on the ledger chain via a safeTransfer call in OmnichainLedgerV1. Because OmnichainLedgerV1 never holds a balance of ORDER tokens, the safeTransfer always reverts whenever there is a non‑zero unclaimed remainder. Consequently, any partial‑claim request triggers a transaction failure, preventing the user from receiving any tokens and forcing them to wait until the full 90‑day vesting period expires before a claim can succeed. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the interaction between the vesting module and the cross‑chain ledger, noting that the ledger contract’s balance check was never satisfied. It is hard to notice because the UI may display the correct claimable amount, yet the transaction silently fails on the back‑end transfer. The impact is that users cannot retrieve partial vesting rewards, effectively locking their funds for the entire vesting term and breaking the expected accounting model where users can withdraw earned portions early. The affected parties are token holders who try to claim early, as well as the protocol that promises flexible vesting. The bug belongs to the class of improper handling of partial withdrawals leading to transfer failures due to missing asset custody. To remediate, the safeTransfer should be moved to a component that actually holds the tokens (such as LedgerOCCManager) and OmnichainLedgerV1 should expose a function allowing the unclaimed portion to be transferred to the collector, ensuring that the ledger contract has a sufficient token balance before attempting the transfer.
summary: Partial vesting claim requests occur when users claim before the vesting linear periods. When these claims are executed ORDER tokens are sent to the user in vault chain, but unclaimed amounts are transferred directly to the orderCollector in the ledger chain. The issue is that OmnichainLedgerV1 will never have ORDER token balance, so the safeTransfer will always fail as long as there is unclaimed amount. Therefore, users will need to wait for the full 90 days vesting period to be over as no partial claims are possible.

title: H-04 | Dust Amount DoS
content: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition caused by the way the contract handles a tiny residual, called a dust amount, when transferring OFT tokens. In the OCCManager and LedgerOCCManager modules the variable that represents the total amount to be sent (amountLD) is set to the same value as the dust amount that must be subtracted before the transfer. After the subtraction a slippage check verifies that amountLD‑dustAmount is at least a configured minimum (minAmountLD). Because amountLD and dustAmount are equal, the resulting net amount is zero, which is always lower than minAmountLD, causing the transaction to revert. This logic error appears whenever a user’s balance contains any non‑zero dust component – for example after unstaking or vesting esOrder tokens – and prevents any subsequent staking, withdrawing, or claiming operation. From the user’s point of view the UI may show a positive balance, but the transaction fails with a generic revert and the expected funds never leave the contract, leading to the perception that “my withdrawal returns nothing” or “my claim does not work”. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the cross‑chain ledger contracts, where the auditor noticed that the same variable was used for both the total amount and the dust amount, a pattern that is easy to miss because the dust value is usually very small and does not affect normal accounting. The bug belongs to the class of precision‑or rounding‑related denial‑of‑service bugs, where an invariant check (minimum transfer amount) is unintentionally triggered by a negligible remainder, breaking business logic that assumes any positive balance can be moved. Exploitation does not require malicious intent; any user with a dust balance will experience the failure, effectively locking their funds until the contract logic is changed. The impact is that users cannot retrieve or re‑stake their tokens, which can halt vesting schedules and reduce confidence in the protocol. To remediate the problem the contract should separate the cleared transfer amount from the dust amount, for example by passing the net amount (amountLD‑dustAmount) as the minAmountLD, or by tracking dust in a dedicated state variable and crediting it back to the user’s balance after the transfer. This prevents the slippage check from rejecting legitimate transfers while still allowing the protocol to account for the tiny remainder.
summary: When the OFT token receives a request to send amountLD of tokens, it will deduct some dust amount from that. After that a slippage check is performed and if amountLD - dustAmount is less than a given minAmountLD, the transaction will revert. The problem found in OCCManager and LedgerOCCManager is that both amountLD and dustAmount are set to the same value. This will result in inability to transfer tokens when there is a dust amount present, meaning no staking, withdrawing, claiming can be performed with these amounts. Ignoring the UX issues, this can be quite problematic for unstaking and vesting esOrder. Imagine that a user has some esAmount that they unstake and vest. After the vesting period ends, the user is not able to claim their order tokens because esAmount has dust amount to be removed.

title: H-05 | Missing whenNotPaused Modifier Causes Loss Of Funds
content: The vulnerability is a missing pause guard on several core functions of the cross‑chain ledger system. Contracts that inherit the OpenZeppelin Pausable pattern implement pause and unpause, but the whenNotPaused modifier is omitted from user‑facing functions such as send, stake and sendUserRequest in OrderOFT, OrderAdapter and ProxyLedger. The root cause is an inconsistent application of the pause check: OmnichainLedgerV1 correctly uses whenNotPaused while ProxyLedger does not. When the contract owner activates a pause on both the source ledger (OmnichainLedgerV1) and the proxy ledger, the proxy still accepts calls to stake or send. These calls burn the caller’s tokens on the source chain, attempt to mint them on the destination chain, and then revert because the destination ledger is paused. The revert aborts the staking logic, leaving the minted tokens unassigned and the burned tokens unrecoverable. From the user’s point of view the expected outcome – a successful stake or transfer – does not happen; the UI may show a transaction receipt but the token balance becomes zero and no staking record appears. The impact is a loss of user funds, broken accounting across chains, and erosion of trust in the protocol’s emergency controls. The issue manifests only when the owner pauses the system, a scenario that is typically exercised during emergencies or upgrades, making it easy to miss during normal testing. It was discovered during a security audit that compared the pause implementation across contracts. The bug belongs to the class of missing access‑control checks that lead to state inconsistency and fund loss. To remediate, every external function that changes token state should be protected with the whenNotPaused modifier, and the pause logic should be enforced uniformly across all contracts that participate in cross‑chain operations, ensuring that no token burn can occur while the corresponding mint or stake is disabled.
summary: Several contracts in the repository inherit Pausable from OpenZeppelin and correctly implement the pause and unpause functions. However, the modifier whenNotPaused is not implemented in core contracts such as OrderOFT, OrderAdapter and ProxyLedger. The modifier should be added to user-facing functions to allow the owner to pause operations in the event of an emergency for example. A more critical issue also exists because OmnichainLedgerV1 correctly implements the whenNotPaused modifier while ProxyLedger does not. If the owner were to pause both contracts, users would still be able to call functions like stake on the ProxyLedger which would execute successfully but revert on destination chain. User's tokens would lose funds as their tokens would be burned on source chain, minted on destination chain but never staked on the user's behalf.

title: H-01 | Layerzero Pathway will be Continuously Blocked
content: The vulnerability is a pathway‑blocking flaw in the Omnichain Fungible Token (OFT) implementation that uses LayerZero ordered delivery. The contract permits the caller to specify any address as the destination recipient, including the zero address. When a cross‑chain transfer is initiated with the zero address, the source chain increments the outbound nonce and sends a packet to the destination chain. On the destination chain the OFT’s _mint function from OpenZeppelin reverts because minting to address(0) is prohibited. Because LayerZero delivers messages in order, the failed packet occupies the next expected nonce, causing every subsequent packet with a higher nonce to be held indefinitely. An attacker can repeatedly submit such malformed packets, keeping the nonce occupied and effectively halting all cross‑chain token movements. The impact is that legitimate users see their transfers remain pending, UI shows no balance change, and the protocol’s bridge becomes unusable, potentially freezing funds across all supported chains. The issue occurs whenever the contract does not validate the recipient address before constructing the cross‑chain payload and when ordered delivery is enabled. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the OFT’s cross‑chain send logic. The problem is subtle because address(0) is a syntactically valid address and the revert only happens on the remote chain after the nonce has already been consumed, making the failure appear as a network or gas issue rather than a contract bug. The correct mitigation is to add an explicit check that the destination recipient is not the zero address before sending the packet, or to switch to unordered delivery or to catch the revert and advance the nonce safely. By preventing zero‑address minting, the pathway remains open and the accounting assumptions of token supply and user balances are preserved.
summary:
Currently, the OFT contract allows anyone to set the address(0) as a token recipient on the destination chain. However, this is a transaction that will always revert because the OpenZeppelin's implementation does not allow minting to the 0 address. An attacker can leverage this to block the LayerZero pathway. An example:
- The nonce on both chains is 5.
- An attacker successfully sends their minting tx and the nonce becomes 6.
- The transaction is received on the destination chain, but fails.
- Since the app uses ordered delivery, all subsequent transactions will be blocked until 6 is resolved. As a result, an attacker can keep blocking the LayerZero pathway.

title: H-02 | [_acceptNonce](https://github.com/GuardianAudits/oft-team-1-pocs/blob/e8b7aad0b1e812be934e5c180f2a2569b044bb37/contracts/OrderAdapter.sol#L106C1-L115C6) Should Not Be Called
content: The vulnerability originates from the contract’s internal function that accepts a nonce, _acceptNonce, being invoked when the contract owner performs privileged actions such as burning, nilifying or clearing a packet nonce. In the ordered delivery mode the protocol enforces a strict sequential rule: a nonce can only be accepted if it equals the current maximum received nonce plus one. When the owner calls burn, the target nonce is always lower than the stored maxReceivedNonce, and when nilify or clear are used the function attempts to accept a nonce that does not satisfy the max+1 condition. Consequently, _acceptNonce reverts, preventing the intended state change. This mismatch creates a divergence between the OrderOFT contract’s view of the highest received nonce and the LayerZero messaging layer’s view, causing subsequent cross‑chain messages to be rejected permanently. The issue can be triggered by any delegate address that is authorized to invoke the owner‑only functions, meaning an external actor could deliberately call burn, nilify or clear to force the contract into a state where no further packets are processed, effectively a denial‑of‑service. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are missing or delayed transfers, balances that appear unchanged despite a transaction, and error messages indicating a revert on nonce acceptance. Users expect their cross‑chain operation to complete, but instead the contract blocks further execution, violating the fundamental accounting assumption that every sent packet will eventually be received and processed. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the interaction between owner‑controlled nonce manipulation functions and the ordered delivery enforcement logic. It is subtle because the functions appear to perform legitimate administrative tasks, yet the hidden call to _acceptNonce introduces a hidden dependency on the ordering invariant that is not obvious from the external interface. The recommended remediation is to stop calling _acceptNonce inside these privileged functions and to provide an explicit setter that can safely adjust the maxReceivedNonce mapping when administrative actions are required, thereby preserving the ordered delivery invariant while allowing legitimate state updates without triggering reverts.
summary:
[OrderOFT](https://github.com/GuardianAudits/oft-team-1-pocs/blob/e8b7aad0b1e812be934e5c180f2a2569b044bb37/contracts/OrderOFT.sol#L82-L97) and [OrderAdapter](https://github.com/GuardianAudits/oft-team-1-pocs/blob/e8b7aad0b1e812be934e5c180f2a2569b044bb37/contracts/OrderAdapter.sol#L83C1-L98C6) allow the owner to burn, nilify, skip and clear nonces. When doing so, a call to _acceptNonce is initiated. This is problematic for:
- burning: The nonce to be burnt will always be less than the maxReceivedNonce. However, in ordered delivery the _acceptNonce function reverts if the specified nonce is not max + 1. This will result in burning not working when ordered delivery is turned on.
- nilifying: The _acceptNonce will let us nilify only the packet with nonce = max + 1. After nilifying the maxReceivedNonce will be set to the nilified nonce. Now even if the nilified package gets reverified, it will not be possible to execute it.
- clearing: If there is a need to clear a nonce which is bigger than maxNonce + 1, it will be impossible because of the ordered nonce. In addition, these actions can be initiated by a delegate address and not by the OFTApp directly. This will cause a discrepancy between the OrderOFT and LayerZero maxReceivedNonce and the messaging will be blocked because acceptNonce will always revert from this moment on.

title: Function `claimEffectiveBalance()` may consistently revert, making it impossible to complete queue withdrawals
content: The vulnerability is a logical error in the claimEffectiveBalance function that can cause the function to revert every time it is called, effectively preventing any queued withdrawal from being completed and locking users' ETH. The root cause is the mismatch between the index used to remove an element from the delayedEffectiveBalanceQueue array (always index 0) and the index used to read the withdrawal that is passed to completeQueuedWithdrawal (the loop variable i). Because the array is shifted each time an element at index 0 is removed, the withdrawal stored in variable withdrawal no longer corresponds to the element that was just removed.
