After the first iteration, the function may attempt to complete a withdrawal that has already been processed in a previous call. Since completeQueuedWithdrawal can only be called once for a given withdrawal, the second call reverts. This can be exploited simply by invoking claimEffectiveBalance repeatedly; after the first successful iteration the next call will hit the mismatched index, trigger the revert, and stop the loop, leaving the remaining withdrawals in the queue forever. The impact is that users who have queued withdrawals see no funds returned, their balances appear unchanged, and the protocol’s accounting is broken because effective balances are never released. The condition under which this occurs is when the delayedEffectiveBalanceQueue contains at least one withdrawal that has already been completed but remains in the array due to the incorrect removal logic. All participants who rely on the queue – delegators, token holders, and the protocol itself – are affected because the contract can no longer release locked ETH. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by Cyfrin, where the auditor noticed that the loop removes the first element while still referencing the i‑th element for completion, leading to a state drift that is not obvious from the surface logic. The bug is hard to notice because the code appears to iterate over the queue and the removal operation seems correct at a glance; however, the subtle shift of indices only manifests after the first iteration. To fix the problem the function should use a consistent index for both removal and completion, for example by always processing the element at index 0, or by iterating backwards and removing the processed element after a successful call, or by swapping the last element into the removed slot. In any case the removal and the call to completeQueuedWithdrawal must refer to the same withdrawal object. This class of bug is an index‑misalignment error in queue processing that leads to double‑execution of a one‑time operation, causing transaction reverts and fund lockup.

title: Delayed rewards can be claimed without updating internal accounting
content: The vulnerability is an accounting inconsistency that arises when delayed rewards are claimed on the EigenLayer Delayed Withdrawal Router without passing through the contract's own claimRewards function. The root cause is that claimRewards updates internal variables such as delayedRewards, reservedFeeBalance and emits a RewardsClaimed event only after it invokes the router’s claimDelayedWithdrawals method. Because the router permits any caller to specify an arbitrary recipient address, an attacker can call claimDelayedWithdrawals directly with the contract address as the recipient. This external call transfers the pending reward tokens to the contract but bypasses the internal bookkeeping performed in claimRewards, leaving delayedRewards unchanged even though the funds have already been received. An exploit therefore consists of three steps: (1) identify the amount of delayed rewards owed to the contract, (2) invoke the router’s claimDelayedWithdrawals function with the contract address, and (3) collect the transferred tokens while the contract’s accounting still reports the same delayedRewards balance. The impact is that the protocol’s view of total stake becomes inflated, reward distribution calculations may allocate too much to other participants, and users may see their expected future rewards disappear because the system believes the rewards are still pending. The bug manifests whenever the router’s claim function is called directly, which can happen at any time after rewards become claimable. All parties that rely on the contract’s accounting – the protocol itself, stakers, and downstream contracts – are affected because the reported stake and fee balances no longer reflect reality. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by Cyfrin when the team noticed that the contract’s balance could increase without a corresponding reduction in delayedRewards. It is hard to notice because the external balance change is visible on‑chain, but the internal state variables are not automatically synchronized, and no event is emitted to signal the mismatch. The appropriate remediation is to decouple reward receipt from the router call and move the accounting updates to a dedicated receive or fallback function that only accepts ether or tokens from the known router address, or to enforce that only the contract’s own claimRewards function can trigger a claim by adding access control or validation of the caller. In generic terms, this is a classic case of missing state synchronization after an external token transfer, leading to stale accounting data and potential financial mis‑representation. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after a reward claim the UI still shows the same pending reward amount, or a user may receive no additional payout later because the system believes the reward has not yet been claimed, effectively causing funds to disappear from the expected reward pool.

title: Anyone can submit proofs via  EigenPod `verifyAndProcessWithdrawals` to break the accounting of `withdrawRewards`
content: The vulnerability is an improper access control that allows any address to call EigenPod.verifyAndProcessWithdrawals and submit withdrawal proofs, bypassing the intended onlyReporter gate of CasimirManager.withdrawRewards. The root cause is that the EigenPod contract does not restrict who can invoke the proof‑verification function, so external actors can trigger partial or full validator withdrawals without the CasimirManager contract updating its delayedRewards bookkeeping. When proofs are submitted directly to EigenPod, the delayedRewards variable remains unchanged, which means the subsequent accounting fields rewardStakeRatioSum and latestActiveBalanceAfterFee are no longer consistent with the actual state of the validator. As a result, any later attempt to claim rewards through CasimirManager.withdrawRewards reverts because the withdrawal has already been marked as processed, even though the reward balance that should have been credited was never recorded. From a user’s perspective this appears as a situation where a reward claim transaction fails with a revert, the expected reward amount is missing, or the UI shows a zero balance after a withdrawal that seemed to succeed. The impact is that rewards can become permanently locked, the protocol’s accounting invariants are broken, and all participants who rely on the withdrawRewards path – including validators, reporters, and token holders – may be unable to retrieve earned rewards. The issue manifests whenever a pod owner is expected to be the sole entity submitting proofs; because the contract does not enforce this, any external caller can trigger the state change at any time. The bug was discovered during a security audit by Cyfrin, which noticed that the withdrawRewards function is protected by an onlyReporter modifier while the underlying proof‑processing function is publicly callable, creating a mismatch between the two contracts’ state updates. This type of flaw is hard to notice because the withdrawal itself succeeds, but the accounting discrepancy only surfaces later when users attempt to claim rewards, leading to silent loss of funds. To remediate the problem, the protocol should either restrict access to EigenPod.verifyAndProcessWithdrawals to the pod owner or ensure that CasimirManager’s delayedRewards (and related accounting variables) are updated even when proofs are submitted directly, for example by tracking eigenWithdrawals.delayedWithdrawals and delayedWithdrawalsCompleted within EigenLayer and using that data to compute delayedRewards correctly. In essence, the fix restores proper synchronization between the withdrawal processing and reward accounting logic, eliminating the state desynchronization that currently allows rewards to disappear from the system.
summary:
`CasimirManager::withdrawRewards` is an `onlyReporter` operation that performs the key tasks below:
1. Submits proofs related to the partial withdrawal of a validator at a given index.
2. Updates the `delayedRewards` based on the last element in the array of `userDelayedWithdrawalByIndex`.
Note that anyone, not just the pod owner, can submit proofs directly to `EigenPod::verifyAndProcessWithdrawals`. In such a case, the `delayedRewards` will not be updated, and the subsequent accounting during report finalization will be broken.
Any attempt to withdraw rewards by calling `CasimirManager::withdrawRewards` will revert because the withdrawal has already been processed. Consequently, `delayedRewards` will never be updated.
This same issue is applicable when submitting proofs for processing a full withdrawal. Critical accounting parameters that are updated in `CasimirManager::withdrawValidator` are effectively bypassed when proofs are directly submitted to EigenLayer.
If `delayedRewards` is not updated, the `rewardStakeRatioSum` and `latestActiveBalanceAfterFee` accounting will be broken.

title: Front-run withdrawValidator by submitting proofs can permanently DOS validator unstaking on EigenLayer
content: The vulnerability is a front‑run denial‑of‑service condition in the CasimirManager.withdrawValidator function. The function assumes that the withdrawal proofs it receives have not been verified on EigenLayer yet. It calls eigenPod.verifyAndProcessWithdrawals, which reverts if the supplied proofs have already been processed. An attacker who monitors the mempool can submit the same proofs directly to EigenLayer before the legitimate transaction is mined. When the original withdrawValidator transaction later executes, the verification step detects that the proofs are already verified and triggers a revert, causing the whole withdrawal call to fail. Because the function also calculates the finalEffectiveBalance as the difference between the updated and initial withdrawable balance, a revert or an empty proof results in a zero balance, preventing the queuing of a delayed withdrawal. Consequently, validators that should be unstaked remain locked, users see no change in their balances, and the protocol may face insolvency risk if withdrawals are permanently blocked. The issue occurs whenever a validator withdrawal is processed and can be exploited with negligible cost by front‑running the transaction. It affects the Casimir protocol, its stakers, and the EigenLayer infrastructure. The bug was discovered during a security audit by Cyfrin, where the logical assumption that proofs are unique was identified as missing. The problem is subtle because the revert only happens when a proof is duplicated, which may appear as an occasional transaction failure rather than a systematic flaw. To remediate, the verification and queuing steps should be separated, already‑verified proofs should be caught with try‑catch logic, and event emissions should be used to safely queue withdrawals without relying on a single verification call.

title: Incorrect accounting of `tipBalance` can indefinitely stall report execution
content: The vulnerability is an accounting mismatch in the CasimirManager contract that can cause the reporting process to stall indefinitely. The contract’s receive fallback function adds the incoming ether amount to a variable called tipBalance whenever the sender is not the DelayedWithdrawalRouter. The developers assumed that all ether deposits, whether partial rewards or full withdrawals, would be routed through the DelayedWithdrawalRouter. This assumption holds for partial withdrawals but fails for full withdrawals, where the EigenPod itself sends ether directly to the manager. As a result, tipBalance is increased even when the contract’s actual tip pool has not grown, inflating the recorded tip balance. When the contract owner later calls claimTips, tipBalance is reset after applying a fee, but the withdrawnEffectiveBalance variable, which is updated in claimEffectiveBalance, is based on the previously inflated tipBalance. Because withdrawnEffectiveBalance is supposed to be backed by the contract’s ETH balance at all times, the inflated tipBalance creates a situation where the invariant that the contract’s total ETH balance is greater than or equal to withdrawnEffectiveBalance can be violated. When this invariant breaks, the fulfilUnstakes function, which relies on accurate accounting of effective balances, may revert, causing the report execution to halt. From a user’s perspective, withdrawals may appear to succeed but later the protocol stops processing further reports, leaving users with missing or frozen funds and no visible refunds. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the flow of ether through the receive function and the subsequent accounting in claimEffectiveBalance. It is subtle because the receive function is a generic fallback that only conditionally updates tipBalance, making the bug easy to overlook unless the exact source of ether deposits is traced. The bug belongs to the class of “incorrect accounting of incoming funds due to faulty assumptions about caller identity,” which can lead to balance inconsistencies and stalled protocol logic. To remediate the issue, the contract should only increase tipBalance when the sender is neither the DelayedWithdrawalRouter nor the EigenPod, ensuring that tipBalance always reflects the true amount of tip ether held by the contract and preserving the critical balance invariant.

title: Function `getTotalStake()` fails to account for pending validators, leading to inaccurate accounting
content: The contract’s accounting routine getTotalStake is responsible for reporting the total amount of ETH that the CasimirManager considers to be staked. It aggregates several components: the unassigned balance, the capacity of validators that are ready, the balance of already active validators, delayed and withdrawn balances, and a few fee adjustments. However, the function omits the ETH that is locked in validators that have been deposited but not yet activated – the pending validators. In the lifecycle of a validator, users deposit ETH, the contract marks the validator as ready, a reporter then calls depositValidator which moves the validator to a pending state while the 32 ETH is transferred to the beacon deposit contract, and finally activateValidator moves the validator to the active set and updates the active balance. Because getTotalStake only adds the ready and active validator capacities, any validator that is stuck in the pending state is invisible to the total‑stake calculation. When a report is finalized, the protocol uses the value returned by getTotalStake to compute rewardStakeRatioSum, which determines how gains and losses are proportionally distributed among participants. If pending validators exist, the reported totalStake is lower than the real amount of ETH that is effectively locked, causing the divisor in the reward formula to be too small. Consequently, the rewardStakeRatioSum is inflated, leading to over‑allocation of rewards to reporters or stakers, or under‑allocation of penalties, depending on the sign of the gain or loss. This mis‑allocation can be exploited by deliberately keeping validators in the pending state before finalizing a report, thereby reducing the apparent total stake and inflating the reward share for the attacker’s address. The issue manifests only when at least one validator is pending at the moment of report finalization; otherwise the calculation appears correct. Users of the protocol – stakers, reporters, and any downstream contracts that rely on accurate reward distribution – are affected because they may receive more or less ETH than the protocol’s economic model intends. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit by Cyfrin, who noted that the pendingValidatorIds array is never referenced in the total‑stake computation. It is subtle because the contract does not expose the pending validator count directly in UI elements, and the totalStake value may still look reasonable, making the accounting error easy to miss during routine testing. To remediate the problem, the accounting function should be extended to include the capacity of pending validators (pendingValidatorIds.length * VALIDATOR_CAPACITY) so that the totalStake reflects all ETH that is locked, regardless of activation state, thereby restoring correct reward calculations and preserving the intended economic guarantees of the protocol.

title: Hardcoded cluster size in `withdrawValidator` can cause losses to operators or protocol for strategies with larger cluster sizes
content: During the execution of the withdrawValidator function the contract calculates the amount that a validator owes to the protocol (the shortfall from the 32 ether cap) and then attempts to recover that amount from the operators that are linked to the validator. The code uses a hard‑coded constant of 4 when it computes the per‑operator recovery amount (recoverAmount = owedAmount / 4) and also caps the total collateral that can be taken to four times the collateral unit. This assumption is only correct for strategies whose cluster size is exactly four operators. When a strategy uses a larger cluster, the division by a fixed 4 under‑allocates the amount each operator should return and the earlier cap limits the total amount the protocol can reclaim. As a result, operators that belong to larger clusters lose a higher percentage of their deposited collateral than intended, and the protocol may recover less than the actual shortfall, leaving a net loss of funds. The problem manifests whenever withdrawValidator is called for a validator that belongs to a cluster whose size differs from four, which can happen in normal operation of the protocol. The issue was discovered during a security audit by Cyfrin, which flagged the hard‑coded operator size as a logical flaw. Because the function still reports the correct owedAmount, the mis‑calculation is not obvious from the UI; users see the expected shortfall amount but the contract silently reduces the amount taken from operators, making the bug hard to notice without inspecting the arithmetic. The vulnerability belongs to the class of hard‑coded constants that cause incorrect financial accounting, often referred to as a parameterization or scaling bug. From a user’s perspective an operator may notice an unexpected reduction in their collateral balance after a validator withdrawal, or the protocol may observe that the recovered funds are lower than the calculated shortfall, effectively causing funds disappear or refund calculation error. To remediate the issue the contract should replace the literal 4 with the actual clusterSize supplied by the strategy (for example, using cluster.size or a similar variable) when computing recoverAmount and when determining the maximum collateral that can be taken. This change aligns the recovery logic with the real number of operators, restores correct accounting, and prevents unintended loss of collateral.

title: A malicious staker can force validator withdrawals by instantly staking and unstaking
content: The issue is an economic grief vulnerability that allows a malicious participant to force honest validators to exit the Beacon Chain by exploiting the way the contract calculates the number of required validator exits during an unstake request. The root cause lies in the requestUnstake function, which determines the required exits based solely on the current expected withdrawable balance – a value that does not take into account a stake that has just been deposited. Because there is no lock‑up period or additional accounting safeguard, an attacker can deposit a small amount of ETH, immediately call requestUnstake, and cause the contract to believe that the withdrawable balance is insufficient. The logic then computes a non‑zero requiredExits value and invokes exitValidators, which forces an existing validator to leave the active set. This can be repeated with larger deposits, each time triggering additional forced exits. The impact is that honest stakers lose potential rewards, operators are forced to deregister their validators, and the protocol incurs high gas costs for each unnecessary exit. The vulnerability manifests whenever a user can call requestUnstake shortly after a deposit, i.e., in the absence of any minimum time or block delay. It affects all participants in the staking pool – the malicious staker, genuine validators, their operators, and the overall protocol economics. The flaw was discovered during a security audit by Cyfrin, where the logical relationship between deposited stakes and withdrawable balance was examined and found to be inconsistent. The problem is subtle because the contract appears to allow unstake requests at any time, and the exit logic is hidden behind internal accounting; users only notice the symptom that their validator is unexpectedly exited and their rewards stop accruing, often accompanied by higher gas fees. To remediate, the protocol should introduce an unstake lock period that prevents immediate withdrawal after a deposit, and/or adjust the accounting to remove ETH from readyValidators instead of exiting active validators, thereby avoiding the need to force a validator exit. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of withdrawal manipulation or economic grief attacks caused by improper state accounting, where the contract’s incentive‑compatible assumptions about validator availability are violated, leading to loss of yield and unnecessary protocol overhead.

title: Attacker can cause a DOS during unstaking by intentionally reverting the transaction when receiving ETH
content: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition that arises when the contract fulfills unstake requests by directly sending ETH to the beneficiary using a low‑level call and immediately reverting the whole transaction if the call fails. The root cause is the combination of a push‑style payment (the contract initiates the transfer) and a FIFO processing queue that requires each earlier request to succeed before any later request is handled. An attacker can exploit this by registering a malicious address whose fallback or receive function deliberately reverts, causing the low‑level call to return false. Because the function checks the return value and reverts on failure, the entire unstake processing routine aborts, leaving the queue stuck at the offending request. As a result, every subsequent unstake request remains unprocessed, effectively locking all users’ staked funds. This situation occurs whenever the contract processes an unstake entry and the recipient’s contract or address rejects the incoming ETH transfer. All stakers, the protocol’s liquidity pool, and any user expecting to withdraw their stake are affected. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the internal fulfillUnstake logic and identified that a revert in the receive function propagates through the FIFO queue. It can be hard to notice because normal users experience successful withdrawals, while the problem only manifests when a malicious address is present in the queue. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a transaction failure, “unstake failed”, or a pending request that never resolves, and the user’s balance appears unchanged despite having initiated a withdrawal. The bug belongs to the class of push‑payment denial‑of‑service flaws where a contract’s reliance on external calls for value transfer makes the whole system vulnerable to a single misbehaving recipient. To remediate, the contract should adopt the pull‑over‑push pattern: record the amount owed and let each user claim their ETH via a separate withdraw function, or at minimum handle failed transfers without reverting the entire queue (for example by logging the failure and moving on). This eliminates the single point of failure and restores correct accounting, ensuring that funds are not unintentionally locked.

title: Operator is not removed in Registry when validator has `owedAmount == 0`
content: The vulnerability originates from the way the CasimirManager contract handles the finalisation of a validator withdrawal. After a validator is fully withdrawn, the manager calculates an owedAmount based on the difference between the required 32 ETH deposit (VALIDATOR_CAPACITY) and the validator’s final effective balance. If the final balance is lower than 32 ETH, owedAmount is positive and the code iterates over the validator’s operatorIds, calling registry.removeOperatorValidator for each operator with a non‑zero recoverAmount. The removeOperatorValidator function not only transfers collateral but also updates each operator’s internal accounting, specifically decrementing operator.validatorCount. However, when the final effective balance is equal to or greater than 32 ETH, owedAmount becomes zero and the conditional block is skipped, meaning removeOperatorValidator is never invoked. Consequently, operator.validatorCount is never decremented, leaving the operator’s record in the CasimirRegistry in an inconsistent state. From a user’s perspective the validator appears to have been removed, but the operator is unable to withdraw the collateral that should have been released; the UI may still show the operator holding the same amount of locked collateral or a validator count that never drops. This discrepancy can cause funds to remain permanently locked, reducing liquidity and potentially breaking business assumptions that each validator corresponds to a withdrawable collateral slice. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the withdrawal flow and noticed that the state‑update function was gated behind a positive owedAmount check. It is subtle because no transaction reverts and no explicit error is emitted – the contract simply fails to update a bookkeeping variable, making the bug easy to miss in functional testing. The proper remediation is to ensure that registry.removeOperatorValidator is called for every removed validator, even when owedAmount equals zero, passing a recoverAmount of zero so that the operator’s validatorCount is correctly decremented and collateral can be released. Alternatively, the manager could directly update the operator’s validatorCount when owedAmount is zero, but the essential fix is to guarantee that the state‑cleanup logic always runs regardless of the owed amount.

title: Accounting for `rewardStakeRatioSum` is incorrect when a delayed balance or rewards are unclaimed
content: The vulnerability is an accounting defect that causes the protocol’s reward‑to‑stake ratio (rewardStakeRatioSum) to be inflated when delayed balances or delayed rewards are not claimed before a new reporting period begins. The root cause is an incorrect assumption in the contract logic that any delayed effective balance and any delayed reward will have been swept prior to the start of the next report. In reality those funds remain locked for several days, and the reporting routine adds them to the accounting a second time. This double counting occurs because the startReport step records the swept balance based on the current delayed reward amount, while the finalizeReport step later adds the same reward again to the rewardStakeRatioSum without checking whether it has already been accounted for. An attacker or any user can exploit the bug by simply allowing a report to be generated while the previous rewards are still pending; each subsequent report will increase rewardStakeRatioSum even though no new rewards were earned. The impact is that the internal representation of each user’s stake becomes larger than the actual deposited amount, leading to over‑payment when a user unstakes – users may receive more ETH than they originally contributed. The condition for the bug to manifest is a sequence of reports with no intervening claim or sweep of the pending rewards, which is a normal situation when validators do not perform actions for a few days. All stakers, the protocol’s accounting layer, and any downstream contracts that rely on the rewardStakeRatioSum are affected because the inflated ratio propagates to reward calculations and UI displays. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by Cyfrin, where a crafted scenario demonstrated that after three consecutive reports without claiming rewards, rewardStakeRatioSum grew without bound while the underlying balances remained unchanged. The bug is subtle because each individual report appears consistent – the swept balance and active balance values match expectations – yet the cumulative ratio diverges over time, making it hard to spot without long‑term observation. To remediate the problem the accounting logic must be revised so that delayed balances and delayed rewards are only incorporated once, for example by tracking whether a reward has already been swept and excluding it from subsequent report calculations, or by resetting the delayed reward counter after each sweep. This correction restores the invariant that rewardStakeRatioSum reflects only newly earned rewards and prevents users from receiving more ETH than they are entitled to, preserving the protocol’s financial integrity.
summary:
** The current accounting incorrectly assumes that the delayed effective balance and delayed rewards will be claimed before any new report begins. This is inaccurate as these delayed funds require a few days before they can be claimed. If a new report starts before these funds are claimed, the `reportSweptBalance` will account for them again. This double accounting impacts the `rewardStakeRatioSum` calculation, leading to inaccuracies.

** The accounting for `rewardStakeRatioSum` is incorrect, which leads to an inaccurate user stake. Consequently, users may receive more ETH than anticipated upon unstaking.

title: Incorrect accounting of `reportRecoveredEffectiveBalance` can prevent report from being finalized when a validator is slashed
content: An accounting error exists in the contract that finalizes validator reports. When a validator is slashed, the contract records the loss by decreasing the cumulative reward‑to‑stake ratio (rewardStakeRatioSum) and the variable that tracks the active balance after fees (latestActiveBalanceAfterFee). The slashed amount is later reimbursed by the node operator’s collateral, which is reported in the variable reportRecoveredEffectiveBalance. The implementation fails to add this recovered balance back into rewardStakeRatioSum and latestActiveBalanceAfterFee. As a result, the net change calculated during finalizeReport can become negative enough to cause an unsigned integer underflow, especially when the last validator in a pool is withdrawn after a slashing event. The underflow aborts the finalizeReport transaction, preventing the report from being marked as finalized. Because a finalized report is required to activate new validators and to start the next reporting period, the protocol can become stuck: users see no new validator slots, withdrawals may revert, and pool balances appear lower than expected. The bug is subtle because the numbers look correct before the final adjustment step; only when the recovered balance is omitted does the arithmetic overflow manifest, making it hard to detect through casual testing. The issue was uncovered during a systematic audit that simulated slashing and withdrawal scenarios. To remediate, the recovered effective balance must be incorporated into the reward‑adjustment formulas, i.e., rewardStakeRatioSum should be increased by a proportion of reportRecoveredEffectiveBalance and latestActiveBalanceAfterFee should be incremented accordingly. This brings the accounting back into alignment with the business logic that slashing losses are fully compensated, eliminating the underflow risk and allowing reports to finalize normally.

title: Attacker can burn `USDToken` from any user
content: The vulnerability is an unauthorized token burn flaw in the USDToken contract. The burn function is publicly callable and accepts an arbitrary address argument instead of implicitly using msg.sender. Because there is no access control modifier (such as onlyOwner or a role check), any external account can invoke the function and specify any target address together with a burn amount. This design mistake allows an attacker to reduce the token balance of any holder at will. Exploitation is straightforward: the attacker sends a transaction calling burn(victimAddress, amount) where amount is less than or equal to the victim’s balance. The contract then decreases the victim’s balance and the total supply without any permission check, causing the victim’s funds to disappear. The impact is a loss of USDToken holdings for honest users, potentially leading to zero balances or unexpected reductions, which contradicts the expectation that only the token owner can destroy their own tokens. The issue can be triggered at any time after deployment because the function lacks any temporal or state‑based guard. All token holders and any protocol components that rely on USDToken balances are affected. The flaw was identified during a formal security audit performed by Cyfrin, where the source code was examined and the missing access control was noted. Because the function signature appears normal and the contract does not emit a special warning, the problem can be hard to notice in routine testing; the transaction succeeds and the balance change may only be observed later through UI discrepancies. To remediate, the contract should enforce proper authorization, for example by restricting the burn function to a privileged role or by removing the address parameter and using msg.sender so that only the token holder can burn their own tokens. This aligns the implementation with the intended business logic that token destruction is a self‑service operation, preserving accounting integrity and preventing arbitrary fund loss.
summary:
```solidity
[USDToken::burn](https://github.com/zaros-labs/zaros-core-audit/blob/de09d030c780942b70f1bebcb2d245214144acd2/src/usd/USDToken.sol#L21-L24) has:
* no access control meaning anyone can call it
* arbitrary address parameter, not using `msg.sender`
```
Anyone can call `USDToken::burn` to burn the tokens of any user.

title: Attacker can steal user deposited collateral tokens by updating account nft token to a custom attack contract address
content: An unrestricted configuration function allows any address to replace the contract that represents trading accounts (the NFT token). Because the function does not check the caller, an attacker can point the system to a malicious ERC721 contract they control. The attacker then mints an NFT with the same token identifier that belongs to a victim’s trading account, and calls the engine’s account‑transfer notification, causing the engine to believe the account has been transferred to the attacker. Once the engine records the attacker as the owner of the account, the attacker can invoke the standard withdraw routine and extract the collateral that the victim previously deposited. The vulnerability is triggered whenever the configuration function is called, which is typically only during system setup, but the missing access control makes it callable at any time by any user. The impact is that user‑deposited funds can be drained without any on‑chain warning; from the user’s perspective the balance shown in the UI drops to zero after a seemingly normal withdrawal attempt, or the user receives no funds when trying to withdraw. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the contract’s administrative functions and noticed the absence of an onlyOwner modifier. It is hard to notice because the function itself does not emit any event indicating a change of the NFT contract, and the subsequent transfer of ownership follows the normal ERC721 flow, so the malicious activity blends with legitimate operations. The proper mitigation is to restrict the configuration function to privileged accounts, typically by adding an onlyOwner or similar access‑control modifier, and to emit an event whenever the account token address is changed so that any unexpected change can be detected. This class of bug falls under unauthorised configuration change or privilege escalation via mutable contract reference, which can lead to theft of user collateral, breach of accounting assumptions, and loss of trust in the protocol.
summary:
`GlobalConfigurationBranch.setTradingAccountToken` has [no access control](https://github.com/zaros-labs/zaros-core-audit/blob/de09d030c780942b70f1bebcb2d245214144acd2/src/perpetuals/branches/GlobalConfigurationBranch.sol#L147-L153) meaning an attacker could update the account nft token to an arbitrary address.
An attacker can use a custom attack contract to steal user deposited collateral.

title: `TradingAccount::withdrawMarginUsd` transfers an incorrectly larger amount of margin collateral for tokens with less than 18 decimals
content: The vulnerability is a decimal‑scaling mismatch in the function that withdraws margin collateral expressed in USD. The protocol stores collateral amounts using a fixed‑point type (UD60x18) that always assumes 18 decimal places, even for tokens whose native precision is lower, such as USDC with 6 decimals. When the function calculates the required amount of collateral to satisfy a USD withdrawal, it correctly works with the 18‑decimal representation, but before transferring the tokens it calls the ERC‑20 safeTransfer with the raw 18‑decimal value instead of converting it back to the token’s native precision. As a result, the contract sends a much larger integer number of token units than intended. The bug can be exploited whenever a user triggers a margin withdrawal for a low‑decimal token, for example during liquidation or settlement. An attacker can request a modest USD amount, the contract will compute a tiny 18‑decimal collateral amount, but will actually transfer the full token balance because the scaling step is missing. This allows the caller to drain more collateral than they are entitled to, corrupting the internal margin‑collateral accounting and leaving the protocol with a deficit that other users cannot recover. The issue occurs only for collateral tokens whose decimals are less than 18 and only when the withdrawMarginUsd path is executed; tokens with 18 decimals are unaffected because the scaling factor is effectively 1. All users of the protocol who rely on correct margin accounting are affected, as the bug can lead to loss of funds for honest participants. The problem was identified during a formal audit by Cyfrin, who noted that the safeTransfer line contains a comment flagging the wrong amount. It is hard to notice because the internal balance variables still appear correct in the 18‑decimal space, while the external token transfer silently moves an oversized amount, making UI balances look inconsistent only after the fact. From a user’s perspective the UI may show that a withdrawal of, say, 0.00001 USDC was requested, but the wallet receives the full 10 000 USDC, and the protocol’s recorded collateral balance only decreases by the tiny scaled amount, leaving a mismatch that can be observed as “my balance didn’t change after I withdrew” or “the protocol shows I still have collateral even though I received it”. The bug belongs to the class of decimal‑conversion or unit‑mismatch errors, where internal accounting uses a different precision than external token transfers. To remediate, the contract must convert the computed 18‑decimal amount back to the token’s native decimal representation before calling safeTransfer, typically by dividing by 10^(18‑tokenDecimals) or by using a library that handles token‑specific scaling. This ensures that the amount sent on‑chain matches the intended USD‑derived collateral amount and preserves the integrity of the margin accounting system.

title: Impossible to liquidate accounts with multiple active markets as `LiquidationBranch::liquidateAccounts` reverts due to corruption of ordering in `TradingAccount::activeMarketsIds`
content: The vulnerability originates from the liquidation routine that iterates over a trader's active market identifiers while assuming the list order stays constant throughout the loop. The contract stores these identifiers in an OpenZeppelin EnumerableSet, a data structure that deliberately does not guarantee element ordering and whose remove operation uses a swap‑and‑pop technique. When the liquidation code closes a position, it calls a function that removes the corresponding market id from the set. This removal instantly reshuffles the remaining ids, breaking the original ordering. Because the outer for‑loop still indexes the set based on its original length, the next iteration may read an index that no longer exists, causing an out‑of‑bounds panic and reverting the whole liquidation transaction. The bug manifests only when an account holds positions in more than one market; a single‑market account liquidates correctly, making the problem easy to miss during casual testing. An attacker (or any user) can open positions in two or more markets, let the positions become under‑collateralised, and then trigger liquidation. The protocol will attempt to liquidate but will revert, leaving the positions open and the account effectively immune to forced closure. This defeats the core risk‑management assumption that under‑collateralised accounts can always be liquidated, potentially allowing unsafe positions to persist and exposing the system to systemic loss. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when the auditors added a test that opened two manual positions and observed a panic with the message "array out‑of‑bounds access" during liquidation. From a user perspective the liquidation transaction simply fails, the UI may show an error or no change in balances, and the trader sees their positions remain despite being flagged as liquidatable. The root cause is the misuse of an unordered set for ordered iteration. To remediate, the contract should either replace the EnumerableSet with a data structure that preserves order, defer removal of market ids until after the iteration completes, or copy the set contents into a memory array and iterate over that immutable snapshot. Any of these approaches restores a stable iteration order and prevents the revert, re‑enabling reliable liquidation of multi‑market accounts.

title: Attacker can perform a risk-free trade to mint free USDz tokens by opening then quickly closing positions for markets using negative `makerFee`
content: The vulnerability is a fee‑calculation flaw that allows an attacker to mint USDz tokens without taking market risk by exploiting a negative maker fee in a perpetual market. The contract’s getOrderFeeUsd function is designed to reward traders who flip the market skew, but it incorrectly permits a negative makerFee value and also applies the maker fee even when the market skew is zero and the order is a buy. Because the fee is stored as a signed integer, a negative makerFee creates a credit for the trader each time a position is opened or closed. An attacker can open a market order in a market that has been configured with a negative makerFee, receive a fee credit, and then immediately close the opposite position, receiving a second credit. The net effect is that the attacker’s collateral balance after the two trades is higher than the amount initially deposited, effectively minting free USDz. This can be performed with minimal exposure to price movements if the two trades are executed in rapid succession, ideally within the same block, although the real system’s keeper design may force the trades into separate blocks, still leaving a very short window of market risk. The issue impacts any user who can create a market order in a negatively‑fee‑configured market, the protocol’s token economics (inflating the supply of USDz), and ultimately the security of the whole platform. It was discovered during a security audit when the auditors modified the market configuration to set makerFee to a negative value and observed that the test account’s USDz balance increased after an open‑then‑close sequence. The problem is subtle because fee logic normally rewards activity, so a negative fee may appear as a harmless incentive, and the accounting checks do not flag a credit as an error. To remediate, the protocol should forbid negative maker or taker fees by using an unsigned integer type for fee parameters, and/or enforce a minimum holding period before a position can be closed so that a rapid open‑close loop cannot be used to harvest fee credits. In user‑facing terms, a trader expects to trade BTC for USDz and later receive the same amount back (minus fees), but instead sees their USDz balance grow unexpectedly, indicating a free‑mint scenario that violates the intended accounting model of the platform.
summary:
Attacker can perform a risk-free trade to mint free USDz tokens by opening then quickly closing positions in markets using negative `makerFee`; this is effectively a free mint exploit dressed up as a risk-free "trade".
The attacker can effectively perform a risk-free or minimal-risk trade to harvest free tokens via the negative `marginFee`; in the PoC the attacker was able to profit $796.
One potential invalidation for this attack vector is that in the real system the protocol controls the keepers who fill orders so an attacker couldn't force both trades into the same block in practice.
The real-world flow would go like this:
1) Attacker creates market order to buy (block 1)
2) Keeper fills buy order (block 2)
3) Attacker creates market order to sell (block 3)
4) Keeper fills sell order (block 4)
So it couldn't be done in one block in practice which means the attacker would be exposed to market movements for a tiny amount of time and that it isn't flash loan exploitable.
But it still seems quite exploitable to mint free tokens with very little exposure to market movements especially as the attacker is able to harvest the maker fee on both transactions by exploiting these 2 Low findings:
* `PerpMarket::getOrderFeeUsd rewards traders who flip the skew with makerFee for the full trade`
* `PerpMarket::getOrderFeeUsd incorrectly charges makerFee when skew is zero and trade is buy order`

title: `TradingAccountBranch::depositMargin` attempts to transfer greater amount than user deposited for tokens with less than 18 decimals
content: The vulnerability resides in the depositMargin function, which incorrectly uses a scaled token amount when transferring collateral, leading to an over‑transfer for tokens whose native decimals are less than 18. The root cause is a mismatch between the conversion of the user‑provided amount to a fixed‑point UD60x18 representation (which multiplies the amount by 10^(18‑tokenDecimals)) and the subsequent use of that scaled value directly in the safeTransferFrom call. Because the scaled value is cast back to a uint256 without re‑adjusting to the token’s native precision, the contract attempts to pull far more tokens than the user intended. Exploitation occurs when a user deposits a token such as USDC (6 decimals) and supplies an amount like 1 000 000 (representing 1 token). The conversion multiplies this by 10^12, producing 1 000 000 000 000 000 000, which the contract then tries to transfer. If the user has approved at least that inflated amount or granted an infinite allowance, the transfer succeeds and the protocol receives a multiple of the intended deposit, effectively stealing the excess tokens. The impact is that users lose a larger amount of collateral than expected, the protocol’s accounting becomes inconsistent (recorded margin does not match actual token balance), and downstream risk calculations such as liquidation thresholds may be corrupted. The bug manifests only for collateral tokens with fewer than 18 decimals and when the caller supplies a normal amount while the contract uses the scaled UD60x18 value for the external token transfer. Affected parties include any user depositing such tokens, the protocol’s risk engine, and traders relying on correct margin data. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that flagged the conversion comment and the subsequent transfer line as using the wrong variable; the problem is subtle because the conversion function is intended for internal accounting, making it easy to overlook that the scaled amount should not be used for an ERC‑20 transfer. The fix is to pass the original unscaled amount to safeTransferFrom, keeping the scaled UD60x18 value only for internal calculations. This aligns the token transfer with the token’s native decimal precision and prevents over‑withdrawal. The bug belongs to the class of decimal‑mismatch or unit‑conversion errors where a higher‑precision representation is mistakenly used for an external token operation. From a user’s perspective the UI shows a normal deposit amount, but after the transaction the wallet balance is reduced by a much larger number, or the transaction reverts if the allowance is insufficient, leading to confusion and potential loss of funds.

title: `GlobalConfiguration::removeCollateralFromLiquidationPriority` corrupts the collateral priority order resulting in incorrect order of collateral liquidation
content: An issue exists in the protocol's global configuration component where the list that determines the order in which different collateral types are liquidated is stored in an OpenZeppelin EnumerableSet. EnumerableSet is designed for constant‑time add, remove and existence checks, but it explicitly does not preserve the insertion order of elements. Its remove operation implements a swap‑and‑pop technique: the element to be deleted is replaced by the last element in the internal array and the array length is reduced. Consequently, when a collateral type is removed from the priority set, the relative ordering of the remaining collaterals is shuffled. The contract assumes that the set maintains a stable ranking (for example, collateral A is always liquidated before collateral B), and many downstream functions read the element at index 0 as the highest‑priority collateral. After a removal, the contract may mistakenly select a lower‑priority or even an unintended collateral as the first to be liquidated. This can cause the protocol to liquidate assets that are less valuable or that the user did not intend to be used, potentially leading to higher slippage, loss of capital, or failure to meet liquidation requirements. The bug manifests only when a collateral type is deregistered or disabled; if the set is never modified, the ordering appears correct, making the problem easy to miss during casual testing. It was discovered during a formal audit when the auditors wrote a small Foundry test that added several addresses to the set, removed the first one, and observed that the element at index 0 changed to the last address, confirming the swap‑and‑pop behavior. Because the contract does not emit an explicit warning and the UI typically shows only the list of active collaterals, users may see a collateral disappear from the configuration page while the liquidation engine suddenly starts using a different asset, leading to unexpected funds disappear or wrong asset liquidated symptoms. The vulnerability belongs to the class of ordering‑assumption bugs where a data structure that does not guarantee order is used to enforce business logic that relies on a stable sequence. To remediate, the protocol should replace the EnumerableSet with a structure that preserves insertion order, such as an array with explicit index management or a linked list, or redesign the removal process to rebuild the set without invoking the swap‑and‑pop operation. Ensuring that the priority list remains consistent after any modification will align the contract’s behavior with the expected liquidation policy and prevent accidental liquidation of unintended collateral.

title: Trader can't reduce open position size when under initial margin requirement but over maintenance margin requirement
content: The vulnerability consists of an over‑restrictive margin validation that is applied when a trader tries to decrease an existing position. In the perpetual contracts implementation the functions that create market orders and that fill orders unconditionally verify that the account satisfies the initial margin requirement, regardless of whether the order is opening a new position, increasing an existing one, or decreasing it. As a result, when a trader’s position has incurred a loss that brings the collateral below the initial margin threshold but still above the maintenance margin threshold, any attempt to reduce the size of that position triggers the same initial‑margin check, causing the transaction to revert with an InsufficientMargin error. The root cause is a missing conditional branch that should switch the margin rule to the maintenance‑margin level for position‑size‑reduction orders. An attacker does not need to craft a special payload; any legitimate user who is trying to manage risk can be blocked. The impact is that the trader cannot scale down exposure to a losing position before it becomes liquidatable, effectively forcing the position to remain open until liquidation occurs, which may lead to unnecessary loss of funds. The bug manifests only when the account is under‑collateralised with respect to the initial margin but still meets the maintenance margin, and when the order type is a reduction of an existing position. Users observe a transaction that reverts with an InsufficientMargin message, see no change in their position size, and may later receive a liquidation notice that could have been avoided. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by constructing a test that opens a position, moves the price against it to create negative PNL, and then attempts a partial close; the test consistently reverts. The problem is subtle because margin checks are expected for new positions, so developers may overlook the need for a different rule when shrinking exposure. To remediate, the order‑creation and settlement logic should detect when the order reduces an existing position and, in that case, validate against the maintenance‑margin requirement instead of the initial‑margin requirement, allowing the reduction as long as the account remains above the maintenance threshold. This change restores the intended business logic that traders can safely downsize losing positions while still respecting the protocol’s safety margin.
summary:
[`OrderBranch::createMarketOrder`](https://github.com/zaros-labs/zaros-core-audit/blob/de09d030c780942b70f1bebcb2d245214144acd2/src/perpetuals/branches/OrderBranch.sol#L204-L208) and [`SettlementBranch::_fillOrder`](https://github.com/zaros-labs/zaros-core-audit/blob/de09d030c780942b70f1bebcb2d245214144acd2/src/perpetuals/branches/SettlementBranch.sol#L130-L139) always enforce the initial margin requirement, even when a trader is reducing the size of a previously opened position.
When a trader's position has negative PNL and no longer satisfies the initial margin requirement, the trader may wish to reduce the position size before their position continues to deteriorate and goes below the maintenance margin requirement which would cause their position to be liquidated.
However in this case when the trader attempts to reduce their position size the transaction will always revert since `OrderBranch::createMarketOrder` and `SettlementBranch::_fillOrder` always enforce the initial margin requirement even when reducing already opened positions.
Hence a trader is unable to scale down their exposure to a losing position that is not yet subject to liquidation.

title: `WellUpgradeable` can be upgraded by anyone
content: The vulnerability concerns the upgrade mechanism of the WellUpgradeable contract, which inherits from OpenZeppelin's UUPSUpgradeable and OwnableUpgradeable. In a UUPS proxy the internal function _authorizeUpgrade must enforce an access restriction, typically by applying the onlyOwner modifier, to ensure that only a privileged account can change the implementation address. In the current implementation the function is overridden but contains no such restriction, meaning that the public upgradeTo and upgradeToAndCall methods can be called by any address. An attacker can therefore submit a transaction from an arbitrary account that calls upgradeTo with the address of a malicious implementation contract. Once the proxy points to the malicious code, the attacker can alter business logic, steal deposited tokens, block legitimate withdrawals, or otherwise break the expected behavior of the protocol. From a user’s point of view the contract may appear to work normally until the upgrade occurs; after the upgrade a user may notice that balances that previously held tokens are now zero, that withdrawal calls revert, or that the contract returns unexpected values, effectively causing funds to disappear. The issue manifests only when the upgrade functions are invoked, which can be hidden during routine testing because the proxy pattern masks the missing access control. The flaw was discovered by a unit test that performed an upgrade from a non‑owner address and verified that the implementation pointer changed, demonstrating that the access check is absent. Detecting this problem can be difficult because the upgrade functions are part of the proxy infrastructure and do not emit obvious warnings; the missing onlyOwner check is a subtle omission. The correct remediation is to override _authorizeUpgrade and include a proper access‑control modifier such as onlyOwner or a role‑based check, thereby restricting upgrades to authorized accounts and restoring the intended security guarantees of the UUPS upgrade pattern.
summary:
`WellUpgradeable` is an upgradeable version of the `Well` contract, inheriting from OpenZeppelin’s `UUPSUpgradeable` and `OwnableUpgradeable` contracts. According to OpenZeppelin’s documentation for `UUPSUpgradeable.sol` ([here](https://docs.openzeppelin.com/contracts/4.x/api/proxy#UUPSUpgradeable:~:text=The%20_authorizeUpgrade%20function%20must%20be%20overridden%20to%20include%20access%20restriction%20to%20the%20upgrade%20mechanism.) and [here](https://docs.openzeppelin.com/contracts/4.x/api/proxy#UUPSUpgradeable-_authorizeUpgrade-address-)), the internal `_authorizeUpgrade` function must be overridden to include access restriction, typically using the `onlyOwner` modifier. This must be done to prevent unauthorized users from upgrading the contract to a potentially malicious implementation.

However, in the current implementation the `_authorizeUpgrade` function is overridden with custom logic but lacks the `onlyOwner` modifier. As a result, the `upgradeTo` and `upgradeToAndCall` methods can be invoked by any address, allowing anyone to upgrade the contract, leading to the deployment of malicious code and compromise the integrity of the contract.

title: Incorrectly assigned `decimal1` parameter upon decoding
content: The vulnerability is a logical error in the routine that decodes token decimal information from a byte array. The function extracts two unsigned integers, decimal0 and decimal1, but it mistakenly checks the first value twice when deciding whether to replace a zero with the default of 18. As a result, if the second token reports a decimal value of zero or any value different from 18, the code overwrites it with 18 regardless of the actual token precision. This occurs because the condition `if (decimal0 == 0) { decimal1 = 18; }` uses the wrong variable, so the intended safeguard for decimal1 is never executed. The bug propagates to every calculation that relies on the decoded decimals, such as reserve scaling, LP token supply, rate computation and ratio‑based swaps. When a token with fewer than 18 decimals (for example a 6‑decimal stablecoin) is used, the protocol treats its reserves as if they were 18‑decimal values, causing the internal accounting to either over‑inflate or under‑inflate the token amount. In the extreme case where decimal1 is actually zero, the contract attempts to scale using a factor of zero, which can trigger arithmetic under‑flow or overflow errors, as demonstrated by a failing unit test that reverts with a panic. The impact is high because the mis‑scaled reserves lead to incorrect price calculations, potentially allowing an attacker to manipulate trades, extract value from liquidity providers, or cause swaps to fail. The issue manifests whenever the decode routine is invoked, which is in many core functions of the Stable2 contract suite. Users of the protocol—liquidity providers, traders and any party interacting with the pool—are affected because they may receive incorrect amounts, see their balances appear larger or smaller than expected, or experience transaction reverts. The flaw was discovered during a formal audit when a test case that supplied zero decimals for the second token caused a panic due to arithmetic under‑flow. It is hard to notice in normal operation because most ERC‑20 tokens use 18 decimals, so the bug remains silent unless a token with a non‑standard decimal count is involved. To remediate the issue, the conditional check must be corrected to examine decimal1 instead of decimal0, assigning the default of 18 only when decimal1 equals zero, and the function should retain proper validation that both decimals are within the allowed range. This change restores accurate scaling, prevents price distortion, and eliminates the risk of arithmetic failures caused by an incorrect decimal assumption.
summary: Impact is high as lots of functions depend on the `decodeWellData`, and as such will be fed incorrect data about `token1`’s decimals. This can lead to potential overvaluation or undervaluation of the token’s amount and prices, depending on the context with which its used. It also ignores the fact that `decimals1` can return a 0 value and as such will work with that for scaling, rather than scaling it to 18. This also depends on the `decimal0` being 0;

title: Mismatch between yield amount deposited in shares calculation and `getAccountYieldBalance`
content: The vulnerability is a mismatch between the amount of yield that is recorded when a deposit ismade and the value returned by the getAccountYieldBalance view function. When a user stakes an NFT, the YieldStakingBase contract calls the underlying yield source (Etherfi or Lido) and receives a number of minted shares that represent the deposited ETH. Because the share‑to‑asset ratio of these protocols is less than one and changes over time, the number of shares returned on each deposit is smaller than the actual ETH amount sent. The contract, however, treats the returned share count as if it were the raw asset amount and stores it as the user’s yield balance. Later, when totalAssets is calculated, the contract reads the real ETH balance of the yield source, not the share count, and uses that value to compute the yield owed to each NFT. As a result, the accounting for each staked NFT diverges: the first NFT receives a higher recorded yield that can be claimed immediately, while subsequent NFTs appear to have a loss or even a negative yield. This discrepancy can be exploited by withdrawing the excess from the first NFT, which effectively reduces the collateral backing the later NFTs and may push them into liquidation. The impact is that users may receive more funds than they are entitled to from one position while other positions become under‑collateralised, leading to unexpected liquidation, loss of expected yield, or disappearance of funds from the user’s perspective. The bug manifests whenever more than one NFT is deposited into the same YieldAccount, i.e., when the protocol processes multiple deposits in a single pool. It affects NFT owners, borrowers, and the overall protocol because the core accounting assumption that deposited assets equal recorded shares is violated. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by Code4rena, which reproduced the problem with a test that showed different yieldAmount values for two NFTs that were staked with identical underlying amounts. The bug is subtle because the UI may display the correct total ETH balance while the internal per‑NFT accounting is wrong, making the error hard to notice without detailed inspection of share‑to‑asset conversions. To fix the problem, the contract should record the actual ETH amount deposited (or correctly convert shares back to assets) when updating the yield balance, and the getAccountYieldBalance function must reflect the same accounting model, ensuring that assets and shares are consistently treated throughout the protocol.
summary: Mismatch between the return amount in all yield Etherfi and Lido assets and the `getAccountYieldBalance()` call causes the yield amount of each staked nft to the same `YieldAccount` to be incorrect, leading to the possibility of withdrawing the excess for some nfts while being closer to liquidation on others

title: `isolateRepay`
content: The vulnerability resides in the isolateRepay operation of the lending pool. The function accepts an array of NFT token IDs and an onBehalf address that indicates whose isolated borrow balance will be reduced. The implementation only checks that onBehalf is non‑zero, but it does not verify that the caller is the owner of the supplied NFTs or that onBehalf matches the NFT owner. Because the contract stores each borrower’s scaled isolated debt in a mapping (userScaledIsolateBorrow) and later uses that value during repayment and liquidation, an attacker can call isolateRepay with a victim’s NFT ID while setting onBehalf to the victim’s address or to any other address. The call will decrement the victim’s scaled debt even though the attacker never supplied collateral for that address. When the victim later attempts a legitimate repayment or when the protocol tries to liquidate the position, the stored debt value may have been reduced below the actual loan amount, causing an unsigned integer underflow. The underflow can make the protocol think the loan is fully repaid, skip liquidation, or corrupt accounting, effectively allowing the attacker to erase part of another user’s debt and potentially steal the collateral or cause loss of funds. The bug appears only when isolateRepay is invoked with mismatched onBehalf and NFT owner; normal usage where onBehalf equals the owner works as intended, making the issue easy to miss during casual testing. It was discovered during a formal audit that examined input validation logic and noticed the missing ownership check. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “missing authorization” or “improper access control” bugs, specifically where a function that mutates a per‑user balance does not enforce that the caller is authorized to modify that balance. From a user’s perspective, a borrower may see that a repayment they performed on behalf of another address unexpectedly reduces their own debt, or that a liquidation transaction reverts with an underflow error, leading to a situation where their collateral is not returned or the protocol reports an inconsistent balance. The expected behavior is that a repayment reduces only the caller’s own isolated borrow balance; the actual behavior allows arbitrary reduction of any user’s balance. The fix is to add a check that the owner field of each NFT token matches the onBehalf address (or that the caller is the owner), thereby ensuring that only the rightful borrower can repay their own isolated loan.

title: `erc721DecreaseIsolateSupplyOnLiquidate`
content: The vulnerability is a state‑reset omission in the ERC‑721liquidation path of the BVault contract. When an NFT that was supplied in isolate mode is liquidated via isolateLiquidate(supplyAsCollateral=false), the internal function erc721DecreaseIsolateSupplyOnLiquidate iterates over each tokenId, clears the owner field and resets the supplyMode flag, but it fails to clear the lockerAddr field that records which contract is currently holding the token. As a result the tokenData entry ends up with owner set to address(0) and supplyMode cleared, while lockerAddr still points to the pool manager address. Because the lockerAddr is not reset, the token is considered "locked in use" by later validation logic. When the user later tries to deposit the same NFT again (for example in cross‑supply mode) the deposit function does not check lockerAddr, so the token appears to belong to the user and the contract accepts the deposit. However any subsequent withdraw or other isolate‑mode operations invoke validateWithdrawERC721, which requires tokenData.lockerAddr to be address(0). The stale lockerAddr causes the require to revert with ASSET_ALREADY_LOCKED_IN_USE, effectively freezing the NFT. The bug can be triggered for any user who supplies an ERC‑721 token in isolate mode and later experiences liquidation, or who manually calls the isolateLiquidate path. The impact is that the user’s NFT becomes unusable: the UI may show the NFT as owned, but on‑chain checks prevent withdrawal, transfer, or further protocol interactions, leading to a denial‑of‑service style loss of access to the asset. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by inspecting the state updates performed after liquidation and noticing that lockerAddr was never cleared. It is hard to notice because the token is transferred back to the user and no event signals that the lock flag remains set, and the deposit function does not validate the locker address, so the problem only surfaces later when a withdraw is attempted. The proper fix is to reset tokenData.lockerAddr to address(0) in both erc721DecreaseIsolateSupplyOnLiquidate and the related erc721DecreaseIsolateSupply function, and to ensure any other paths that release isolation also clear this field. Optionally, deposit functions should also verify that lockerAddr is zero before accepting a token, providing an additional safety net. This class of bug is an incomplete cleanup of mutable state after a lifecycle transition, leading to stale references that break invariant checks and cause asset lock‑up.

title: Revert due to underflow error, leading to lock of the liquidated NFT
content: The vulnerability is an arithmetic underflow that occurs when the liquidation routine tries to decrease the stored total bid amount using the accumulated borrow amount instead of the actual bid amount. In the isolated NFT lending flow, a liquidator can start an auction for a collateral NFT and place a bid that is stored in assetData.totalBidAmout. Over the auction period (up to seven days) the outstanding loan balance grows because interest is continuously added to the scaled amount. When the auction ends and the winning liquidator calls executeIsolateLiquidate, the contract recomputes the current borrowAmount and then calls erc20TransferOutBidAmountToLiqudity with vars.totalBorrowAmount as the amount to subtract from assetData.totalBidAmout. If the accrued borrowAmount exceeds the original bid, the subtraction underflows, causing a revert (arithmetic error) and preventing the function from completing. As a result the NFT remains locked in the protocol, the liquidator cannot withdraw the collateral, and the pool’s liquidity accounting becomes inconsistent. The issue manifests only after time has passed and interest has accumulated, making it easy to miss during short‑term testing. It was discovered during a Code4rena audit and reproduced with a Foundry proof‑of‑concept that advances the blockchain time until the borrow amount overtakes the bid. The bug belongs to the class of accounting‑logic errors where a contract uses an outdated or wrong monetary variable for balance adjustments, leading to underflow/overflow and state lock‑up. From a user’s perspective the transaction simply reverts with an arithmetic error, the expected NFT transfer never happens, and the user sees no funds returned despite having won the auction. The protocol’s business logic that the winning bid must always cover the debt is violated because the code does not enforce this invariant at liquidation time. The recommended fix is to subtract the stored bid amount (vars.totalBidAmount) from assetData.totalBidAmout while still adding the actual borrowed amount to availableLiquidity, thereby preserving accounting consistency and preventing the underflow.
summary:
The `IsolateLogic.sol#executeIsolateAuction()` is triggered by liquidators to launch a new auction or just participate in an existing one for isolated lending. Each NFT token has a predefined auction duration `nftAssetData.auctionDuration`, the MAX duration is 7 days. In the period of (e.g.) 7 days, the `borrowAmount` will keep increasing due to the interest:

```solidity
File: GenericLogic.sol#calculateNftLoanLiquidatePrice()

279:     vars.borrowAmount = nftLoanData.scaledAmount.rayMul(vars.normalizedIndex);
```

If the liquidator is the first bidder, the bid price must be greater than borrowed debt and the liquidate price. Otherwise, the liquidator will just try to outbid the last bidder, by at least 1%.

At the end of `executeIsolateAuction()`, it will transfer the underlying asset from the liquidator to escrow and increase the value of `assetData.totalBidAmout` by the bid amount from the liquidator (Note: remember the last point).

```solidity
File: IsolateLogic.sol#executeIsolateAuction()

269:     VaultLogic.erc20TransferInBidAmount(debtAssetData, params.msgSender, vars.totalBidAmount);
```

After 7 days, the liquidator who wins the auction will invoke `IsolateLogic.sol#executeIsolateLiquidate()` to implement the liquidation. It will calculate the `borrowAmount` and check for any remaining or extra amount.

```solidity
File: IsolateLogic.sol#executeIsolateLiquidate()

427:       vars.borrowAmount = loanData.scaledAmount.rayMul(vars.normalizedIndex);
```

Then, because the bid is already in the pool, it will sub-call to `VaultLogic.sol#erc20TransferOutBidAmountToLiqudity()` to increase liquidity in the pool `assetData.availableLiquidity` and decrease the `assetData.totalBidAmout` value.

The issue is here, is about how much `totalBidAmout` has decreased. In the below code snap is passing `totalBorrowAmount` to `erc20TransferOutBidAmountToLiqudity()`:

```solidity
File: IsolateLogic.sol#executeIsolateLiquidate()

464:     VaultLogic.erc20TransferOutBidAmountToLiqudity(debtAssetData, vars.totalBorrowAmount);
```

The `vars.totalBorrowAmount` is just the value of `vars.borrowAmount` (in case of one NFT in the liquidation). As we mentioned above, the borrowed amount will keep increasing over time and it will exceed the saved value in `assetData.totalBidAmout` (check the above note). This will lead the transaction to revert:

```solidity
File: VaultLogic.sol

503:   function erc20TransferOutBidAmountToLiqudity(DataTypes.AssetData storage assetData, uint amount) internal {
504:     assetData.totalBidAmout -= amount;
505:     assetData.availableLiquidity += amount;
506:   }
```

There are multiple scenarios to reach this point (revert):

  * The auction ends with only one bidder (the first bidder wins it), so the rest of the time (until the auction ends) the borrowed amount will keep accumulating interest.
  * The auction ends, but the borrowed amount exceeds the winner’s bid price (due to accumulated interest).

The liquidator wins the auction but he can’t withdraw/unlock the NFT, due to an **Arithmetic over/underflow** and fails when reducing the `assetData.totalBidAmout` value in `erc20TransferOutBidAmountToLiqudity()`.

title: Bad debt is never handled which places insolvency risks on BendDAO
content: Bad debt is never handled in the BendDAO lending pool, meaning that when a borrower’s collateral value drops sharply or the outstanding debt grows beyond the value of the supplied collateral, the liquidation routine only repays the portion of the debt that can be covered by the remaining collateral. For ERC20 positions the LiquidationLogic executes a partial liquidation that clears debt up to the available collateral and then reverts because no collateral is left, leaving the excess debt untouched. For ERC721 positions the liquidation price is derived from the debt amount, so if the collateral token is not sufficiently valuable the liquidation does not occur at all. The root cause is the absence of any mechanism—such as a reserve pool, supply‑index adjustment, or DAO‑treasury repayment—to absorb or redistribute the residual debt. An attacker or market event that drives the price of the collateral down can therefore create “bad debt” that the protocol cannot repay. Because the protocol’s liquidity pool is reduced by the unpaid debt, subsequent withdrawal requests from other users may fail or be permanently blocked, effectively DoSing honest users. From a user’s point of view the symptom is a withdrawal transaction that either reverts or returns zero funds, even though the user’s deposit balance appears unchanged. The impact is a loss of confidence, potential loss of access to funds, and a systemic insolvency risk for the whole protocol. The issue was discovered during a Code4rena audit by inspecting the LiquidationLogic library and observing that the function executeCrossLiquidateERC20 allows only partial liquidation and that no fallback path exists for the remaining debt. The problem is hard to notice because the liquidation itself succeeds and no explicit error is emitted; the failure only becomes visible later when liquidity is insufficient for withdrawals. The vulnerability belongs to the class of bad‑debt handling or insolvency bugs where the accounting assumptions that total debt must be covered by collateral are violated. To remediate the issue the protocol should introduce a bad‑debt handling flow, for example by allocating a reserve that absorbs the leftover debt, by decreasing the supply index to spread the loss among suppliers, or by having the DAO treasury actively repay the debt through a cross‑repay function. This would ensure that all debt is cleared, that liquidity remains sufficient for withdrawals, and that the protocol’s accounting invariants are restored.
summary: Bad debt is never handled, which may happen whenever the collateral asset price crashes or the debt value spikes. Whenever this happens `ERC20` positions will be partially liquidated and `ERC721` positions will not be profitable for liquidation, which means the debt will not be repaid. When this happens, the protocol will not have enough liquidity to fulfill withdrawals, DoSing them forever or until the price comes back up again.

title: Users cannot unstake from YiedlETHStakingEtherfi.sol, because YieldAccount.sol is incompatible with ether.fi’s WithdrawRequestNFT.sol
content: The vulnerability is an incompatibility between the YieldAccount contract used by BendDAO’s YiedlETHStakingEtherfi and the ERC721 safe‑mint mechanism employed by Ether.fi’s WithdrawRequestNFT. When a user calls unstake, the protocol routes the call through YieldStakingBase → YieldEthStakingEtherfi → LiquidityPool → WithdrawRequestNFT.requestWithdraw. The requestWithdraw function attempts to create a withdrawal‑request NFT by calling the internal _safeMint function, which first mints the token and then checks that the recipient implements the ERC721Receiver interface via onERC721Received. YieldAccount, which is cloned for each user, does not inherit OpenZeppelin’s ERC721Holder nor does it implement onERC721Received, so the _checkOnERC721Received call fails and the transaction reverts.
