Likelihood: Medium + Impact: High = Severity: High. marketHelper isn't checked to be whitelisted in leverageUpReceiver(): /tOFT/modules/TOFTMarketReceiverModule.sol#L74-L79 ```solidity function leverageUpReceiver(bytes memory _data) public payable { /// @dev decode received message LeverageUpActionMsg memory msg_ = TOFTMsgCodec.decodeLeverageUpMsg(_data); /// @dev 'market' _checkWhitelistStatus(msg_.market); ``` It is used to craft call sequence for market, that can be arbitrary this way (which, similar to misplacing to as mentioned above): /tOFT/modules/TOFTMarketReceiverModule.sol#L88-L93 ```solidity { (Module[] memory modules, bytes[] memory calls) = IMarketHelper(msg_.marketHelper).buyCollateral( msg_.user, msg_.borrowAmount, msg_.supplyAmount, msg_.executorData ); IMarket(msg_.market).execute(modules, calls, true); } ``` And in marketRemoveCollateralReceiver(): /tOFT/modules/TOFTMarketReceiverModule.sol#L161-L165 ```solidity function marketRemoveCollateralReceiver(bytes memory _data) public payable { /// @dev decode received message MarketRemoveCollateralMsg memory msg_ = TOFTMsgCodec.decodeMarketRemoveCollateralMsg(_data); _checkWhitelistStatus(msg_.removeParams.market); ``` Where it can, as an example, place msg_.user as to, still calling withdraw from magnetar: /tOFT/modules/TOFTMarketReceiverModule.sol#L172-L197 ```solidity { uint256 share = IYieldBox(ybAddress).toShare(assetId, msg_.removeParams.amount, false); approve(msg_.removeParams.market, share); (Module[] memory modules, bytes[] memory calls) = IMarketHelper(msg_.removeParams.marketHelper) .removeCollateral(msg_.user, msg_.withdrawParams.withdraw ? msg_.removeParams.magnetar : msg_.user, share); IMarket(msg_.removeParams.market).execute(modules, calls, true); } { if (msg_.withdrawParams.withdraw) { _checkWhitelistStatus(msg_.removeParams.magnetar); bytes memory call = abi.encodeWithSelector(MagnetarYieldBoxModule.withdrawToChain.selector, msg_.withdrawParams); MagnetarCall[] memory magnetarCall = new MagnetarCall[](1); magnetarCall[0] = MagnetarCall({ id: MagnetarAction.YieldBoxModule, target: address(this), value: msg.value, allowFailure: false, call: call }); IMagnetar(payable(msg_.removeParams.magnetar)).burst{value: msg.value}(magnetarCall); } } ``` I.e. the assumption that the calls is constructed by regular white-listed MarketHelper to follow the operation logic is broken: cts/markets/MarketHelper.sol#L119-L128 ```solidity function removeCollateral(address from, address to, uint256 share) external pure returns (Module[] memory modules, bytes[] memory calls) { modules = new Module[](1); calls = new bytes[](1); modules[0] = Module.Collateral; calls[0] = abi.encodeWithSelector(SGLCollateral.removeCollateral.selector, from, to, share); } ```

title: exerciseOptionsReceiver() Lack of Ownership
content: The vulnerability resides in the USDO contract function exerciseOptionsReceiver, which is invoked when a cross‑chain message of type MSG_TAP_EXERCISE is processed. The function assumes that the caller has already obtained permission to operate on a specific oTAP token ID by calling oTAP.permit, but it never verifies that the address supplied in the _options.from field (or the message sender) actually owns or is approved for that token. Because the permit signature is public, any actor who can observe the signature – for example a front‑runner – can reuse it in a crafted cross‑chain message that calls exerciseOptionsReceiver with their own address as the beneficiary. The contract then calls the external option broker to exercise the option and subsequently refunds any unused payment tokens to the address stored in _options.from. As a result, an attacker can exercise an option that belongs to a legitimate user, receive the exercised assets, and potentially receive a refund that should have gone to the rightful owner. The impact is the unauthorized transfer of option value and associated payment tokens, effectively causing loss of funds for the original token holder. This scenario occurs whenever an option owner approves the USDO contract via oTAP.permit and the same transaction (or a subsequent cross‑chain message) triggers exerciseOptionsReceiver; the lack of an ownership or approval check makes the flow exploitable. The affected parties include option owners, any user of the USDO protocol who relies on cross‑chain exercise, and the protocol itself because the accounting of exercised options becomes inconsistent. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the cross‑chain message handling logic, where the auditor noticed that the permit step is public and that the subsequent call does not enforce any access control. The bug can be hard to notice because the permit function appears legitimate and the contract’s refund logic masks the loss – the victim may simply see a missing or reduced balance without an obvious error. The proper remediation is to add an explicit check that the owner of the oTAP token ID matches _options.from, or that the caller is authorized via standard ERC‑721 approval mechanisms, before invoking the external exerciseOption call. This aligns the implementation with the intended business rule that only the token holder (or an approved operator) may exercise the option, restoring correct accounting and preventing unauthorized asset movement.
summary: In UsdoOptionReceiverModule.exerciseOptionsReceiver(): For this method to execute successfully, the owner of the oTAPTokenID needs to approve it to address(usdo). Once approved, anyone can front-run execute exerciseOptionsReceiver() and utilize this authorization. In USDO.lzCompose(), it is possible to specify _msgType == MSG_TAP_EXERCISE to execute USDO.exerciseOptionsReceiver() across chains. ```solidity function exerciseOptionsReceiver(address srcChainSender, bytes memory _data) public payable { ... ITapiocaOptionBroker(_options.target).exerciseOption( _options.oTAPTokenID, address(this), //payment token _options.tapAmount ); _approve(address(this), address(pearlmit), 0); uint256 bAfter = balanceOf(address(this)); // Refund if less was used. if (bBefore > bAfter) { uint256 diff = bBefore - bAfter; if (diff < _options.paymentTokenAmount) { IERC20(address(this)).safeTransfer(_options.from, _options.paymentTokenAmount - diff); } } ... ``` For this method to succeed, USDO must first obtain approve for the oTAPTokenID. Example: The owner of oTAPTokenID is Alice. 1. alice in A chain execute lzSend(dstEid = B) with • composeMsg = [oTAP.permit(usdo,oTAPTokenID,v,r,s) 2.exerciseOptionsReceiver(oTAPTokenID,_options.from=alice)] oTAP.revokePermit(oTAPTokenID)] 2. in chain B USDO.lzCompose() will • execute oTAP.permit(usdo,oTAPTokenID) • exerciseOptionsReceiver(srcChainSender=alice,_options.from=alice,oTAPTokenID ) • oTAP.revokePermit(oTAPTokenID) The signature of oTAP.permit is public, allowing anyone to use it. This opens up the possibility for malicious users to front-run use this signature. Let's consider an example with Bob: 1. Bob in Chain A uses Alice's signature (v, r, s): • composeMsg = [oTAP.permit(usdo, oTAPTokenID, v, r, s), exerciseOptionsReceiver(oTAPTokenID, _options.from=bob)] 2. In Chain B, when executing USDO.lzCompose(dstEid = B), the following actions occur: • Execute oTAP.permit(usdo, oTAPTokenID) • Execute exerciseOptionsReceiver(srcChainSender=bob, _options.from=bob, oTAPTokenID) As a result, Bob gains unconditional access to this oTAPTokenID. It is advisable to check the ownership of oTAPTokenID is _options.from before executing ITapiocaOptionBroker(_options.target).exerciseOption(). The exerciseOptionsReceiver() function lacks ownership checks for oTAP, allowing anyone to use oTAPTokenID.

title: Claim functions don't validate if the epoch is
content: The vulnerability resides in the claim functions of the vault contract, which allow a user to claim a deposit or redemption without verifying that the associated epoch has already been settled. The root cause is the absence of a check against the current, unsettled epoch before converting the stored request balances to shares or assets. The conversion helpers _convertToShares and _convertToAssets deliberately return zero when the request belongs to the current epoch, but the surrounding claim logic does not enforce this rule, so a claim can be executed while the epoch is still open. When this happens the contract reads uninitialized snapshot values, the conversion yields zero, and the claim transaction succeeds while the user receives no shares or assets. From the user’s perspective the pending request disappears from the vault, yet the expected funds are not transferred, leading to a situation where “my deposit claim returned zero shares” or “my redemption claim gave me nothing”. The impact is a loss of funds for any account that makes a claim in the same epoch as the request, and the problem is amplified by the claimAndRequestDeposit function, which lets an attacker invoke a claim on behalf of any other address. An attacker can therefore wipe another user’s pending deposit by calling claimAndRequestDeposit with the victim’s address, causing the victim’s request balance to be cleared while the attacker receives nothing. The issue manifests when the vault is closed, a deposit or redemption request is created, and the claimant calls claimDeposit, claimRedeem, or claimAndRequestDeposit before the epoch is settled. It was discovered during a security audit by exercising the claim functions in the same epoch and observing that the contract emitted a successful claim event but transferred zero value. The bug is subtle because the transaction does not revert; it merely produces a zero payout, which can be mistaken for a normal outcome. To remediate, the claim functions must explicitly check that the request’s epoch identifier is not the current epoch and revert if it is, thereby preventing zero‑conversion claims and protecting users from inadvertent or malicious fund wipes. This class of bug falls under “epoch‑validation missing” or “unsettled‑state claim” errors, where business logic assumes that a request can only be settled after a snapshot is taken, but the contract fails to enforce that assumption, breaking accounting invariants and allowing funds to disappear without error.
summary: Both claim functions fail to validate if the epoch for the request has been already settled, leading to loss of funds when claiming requests for the current epoch. The issue is worsened as claimAndRequestDeposit() can be used to claim a deposit on behalf of any account, allowing an attacker to wipe other's requests. When the vault is closed, users can request a deposit, transfer assets and later claim shares, or request a redemption, transfer shares and later redeem assets. Both of these processes store the assets or shares, and later convert these when the epoch is settled. For deposits, the core of the implementation is given by _claimDeposit(): ```solidity function _claimDeposit( address owner, address receiver ) internal returns (uint256 shares) { shares = previewClaimDeposit(owner); uint256 lastRequestId = lastDepositRequestId[owner]; uint256 assets = epochs[lastRequestId].depositRequestBalance[owner]; epochs[lastRequestId].depositRequestBalance[owner] = 0; _update(address(claimableSilo), receiver, shares); emit ClaimDeposit(lastRequestId, owner, receiver, assets, shares); } ``` ```solidity function previewClaimDeposit(address owner) public view returns (uint256) { uint256 lastRequestId = lastDepositRequestId[owner]; uint256 assets = epochs[lastRequestId].depositRequestBalance[owner]; return _convertToShares(assets, lastRequestId, Math.Rounding.Floor); } ``` ```solidity function _convertToShares( uint256 assets, uint256 requestId, Math.Rounding rounding ) internal view returns (uint256) { if (isCurrentEpoch(requestId)) { return 0; } uint256 totalAssets = epochs[requestId].totalAssetsSnapshotForDeposit + 1; uint256 totalSupply = epochs[requestId].totalSupplySnapshotForDeposit + 1; return assets.mulDiv(totalSupply, totalAssets, rounding); } ``` And for redemptions in _claimRedeem(): ```solidity function _claimRedeem( address owner, address receiver ) internal whenNotPaused returns (uint256 assets) { assets = previewClaimRedeem(owner); uint256 lastRequestId = lastRedeemRequestId[owner]; uint256 shares = epochs[lastRequestId].redeemRequestBalance[owner]; epochs[lastRequestId].redeemRequestBalance[owner] = 0; _asset.safeTransferFrom(address(claimableSilo), address(this), assets); _asset.transfer(receiver, assets); emit ClaimRedeem(lastRequestId, owner, receiver, assets, shares); } ``` ```solidity function previewClaimRedeem(address owner) public view returns (uint256) { uint256 lastRequestId = lastRedeemRequestId[owner]; uint256 shares = epochs[lastRequestId].redeemRequestBalance[owner]; return _convertToAssets(shares, lastRequestId, Math.Rounding.Floor); } ``` ```solidity function _convertToAssets( uint256 shares, uint256 requestId, Math.Rounding rounding ) internal view returns (uint256) { if (isCurrentEpoch(requestId)) { return 0; } uint256 totalAssets = epochs[requestId].totalAssetsSnapshotForRedeem + 1; uint256 totalSupply = epochs[requestId].totalSupplySnapshotForRedeem + 1; return shares.mulDiv(totalAssets, totalSupply, rounding); } ``` the amounts owed to the user: _convertToShares() and _convertToAssets() use the settled values stored in epochs[requestId] to convert between assets and shares. However, there is no validation to check if the claiming is done for the current unsettled epoch. If a user claims a deposit or redemption during the same epoch it has been requested, the values stored in epochs[epochId] will be uninitialized, which means that _convertToShares() and _convertToAssets() will use zero values leading to zero results too. The claiming process will succeed, but since the converted amounts are zero, the users will always get zero assets or shares. This is even worsened by the fact that claimAndRequestDeposit() can be used to claim a deposit on behalf of any account. An attacker can wipe any requested deposit from an arbitrary account by simply calling claimAndRequestDeposit(0, account, ""). This will internally execute _claimDeposit(account, account), which will trigger the described issue. CRITICAL. Requests can be wiped by executing the claim in an unsettled epoch, leading to loss of funds. The issue can also be triggered for any arbitrary account by using claimAndRequestDeposit().

title: Calling requestRedeem with _msgSender() != owner
content: The vulnerability is an accounting mismatch in the redeem workflow of AsyncSynthVault. The contract allows a token holder (owner) to grant allowance of its vault shares to another address. When the delegated address calls requestRedeem and passes the owner’s address as the source of shares, the internal function _createRedeemRequest records the epoch identifier in the mapping lastRedeemRequestId using the owner key instead of the receiver key. Consequently the vault believes that the owner has no pending redeem request, while the receiver’s pending balance is recorded but never linked to a request ID. When claimRedeem is later called, the contract looks up lastRedeemRequestId for the caller (the receiver) which is still zero, so the redeem logic reads a zero balance and mints no assets. The shares remain locked in the vault forever, and both the original owner and the delegated user end up with zero vault shares and zero underlying tokens. This can be triggered whenever an allowance is used to request a redeem on behalf of another address, i.e., during any epoch after the vault is closed and before settlement. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by testing the flow with two accounts and observing that after a successful requestRedeem the subsequent claimRedeem returned no tokens. The bug is subtle because the request appears to succeed – the pendingRedeemRequest function reports a non‑zero amount – yet the later claim silently fails, making it easy to miss in casual testing. The root cause is a wrong key used when updating the lastRedeemRequestId mapping; the contract should store the epoch ID for the receiver, not the original owner. Fixing the bug requires changing the assignment to lastRedeemRequestId[receiver] = epochId, thereby correctly linking the pending balance to a claimable request. As a class of vulnerability, this is an “incorrect state tracking” or “mis‑attributed request identifier” bug that breaks the accounting invariant that each pending redeem request must be claimable by the address that holds the pending balance. From a user perspective the symptoms are that after delegating shares and requesting a redeem, the user sees a pending amount but receives no tokens when claiming, and both parties lose their vault shares. The loss is permanent because the contract provides no function to withdraw or reassign the locked shares.
summary: The requestRedeem function in AsyncSynthVault.sol can be invoked by a user on behalf of another user, referred to as 'owner', provided that the user has been granted sufficient allowance by the 'owner'. However, this action results in a complete loss of balance. The _createRedeemRequest function contains a discrepancy; it fails to update the lastRedeemRequestId for the user eligible to claim the shares upon maturity. Instead, it updates this identifier for the 'owner' who delegated their shares to the user. As a result, the shares become permanently locked in the vault, rendering them unclaimable by either the 'owner' or the user. This issue unfolds as follows: 1. The 'owner' deposits tokens into the vault, receiving vault shares in return. 2. The 'owner' then delegates the allowance of all their vault shares to another user. 3. When epochId == 1, this user executes The requestRedeem , specifying the 'owner''s address as owner, the user's address as receiver, and the 'owner''s share balance as shares. 4. The internal function _createRedeemRequest is invoked, incrementing epochs[epochId].redeemRequestBalance[receiver] by the amount of shares, and setting lastRedeemRequestId[owner] = epochId. 5. At epochId == 2, the user calls claimRedeem, which in turn calls the internal function _claimRedeem, with owner set to _msgSender() (i.e., the user's address) and receiver also set to the user's address. 6. In this scenario, lastRequestId remains zero because lastRedeemRequestId[owner] == 0 (here, owner refers to the user's address). Consequently, epochs[lastRequestId].redeemRequestBalance[owner] is also zero. Therefore, no shares are minted to the user. Proof of Code : The following test demonstrates the claim made above : ```solidity function test_poc() external { // set token balances deal(vaultTested.asset(), user1.addr, 20); // owner vm.startPrank(user1.addr); IERC20Metadata(vaultTested.asset()).approve(address(vaultTested), 20); // owner deposits tokens when vault is open and receives vault shares vaultTested.deposit(20, user1.addr); // owner delegates shares balance to user IERC20Metadata(address(vaultTested)).approve( user2.addr, vaultTested.balanceOf(user1.addr) ); vm.stopPrank(); // vault is closed vm.prank(vaultTested.owner()); vaultTested.close(); // epoch = 1 vm.startPrank(user2.addr); // user requests a redeem on behlaf of owner vaultTested.requestRedeem( vaultTested.balanceOf(user1.addr), user2.addr, user1.addr, "" ); // user checks the pending redeem request amount assertEq(vaultTested.pendingRedeemRequest(user2.addr), 20); vm.stopPrank(); vm.startPrank(vaultTested.owner()); IERC20Metadata(vaultTested.asset()).approve( address(vaultTested), type(uint256).max ); vaultTested.settle(23); // an epoch goes by vm.stopPrank(); // epoch = 2 vm.startPrank(user2.addr); // user tries to claim the redeem vaultTested.claimRedeem(user2.addr); assertEq(IERC20Metadata(vaultTested.asset()).balanceOf(user2.addr), 0); // however, token balance of user is still empty vm.stopPrank(); vm.startPrank(user1.addr); // owner also tries to claim the redeem vaultTested.claimRedeem(user1.addr); assertEq(IERC20Metadata(vaultTested.asset()).balanceOf(user1.addr), 0); // however, token balance of owner is still empty vm.stopPrank(); // all the balances of owner and user are zero, indicating loss of funds assertEq(vaultTested.balanceOf(user1.addr), 0); assertEq(IERC20Metadata(vaultTested.asset()).balanceOf(user1.addr), 0); assertEq(vaultTested.balanceOf(user2.addr), 0); assertEq(IERC20Metadata(vaultTested.asset()).balanceOf(user2.addr), 0); } ``` To run the test : 1. Copy the above code and paste it into TestClaimDeposit.t.sol 2. Run forge test --match-test test_poc --ffi The shares are locked in the vault forever with no method for recovery by the user or the 'owner'.

title: Exchange rate is calculated incorrectly when
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect exchange rate calculation between vault shares and underlying assets when the vault is in a closed state. The contract stores snapshot variables for total assets and total supply and adds a constant offset of 1 to each snapshot inside the previewSettle function. The conversion helpers _convertToAssets and _convertToShares add the same offset again, resulting in a double‑increment of the cached totals. Because the exchange ratio is derived from these snapshots, the double increment skews the ratio whenever the share‑to‑asset price deviates from 1:1. When the vault is closed, a user who requests a deposit receives more shares than the deposited assets merit, while a user who requests a redemption receives fewer assets than they are entitled to. The discrepancy accumulates in the claimable silo, allowing an attacker to deposit the minimal amount needed for one share across many addresses, claim the inflated shares after the vault reopens, and immediately redeem them for a profit, effectively stealing value from honest users. The issue appears only when the vault is closed and the exchange rate is not exactly 1:1; it does not affect operations while the vault is open or when the rate is 1:1. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that examined the accounting logic of AsyncSynthVault and identified the redundant +1 operation. It is subtle because the extra unit is small and the contract’s public view functions hide the internal snapshot values, making the mis‑balance hard to notice until a large number of deposits are processed. The impact includes accounting inconsistencies, loss of user funds, inability for users to redeem their shares, and a vector for profit‑making attacks that require no minting of new shares. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “incorrect accounting due to double counting of state variables” or “snapshot mis‑adjustment”. To remediate, the conversion functions should return zero for a zero request identifier and must not add the extra 1 to the cached totals; the snapshot should be taken only once in previewSettle. Additionally, initializing the vault with a zero‑balance deposit and enforcing a zero‑asset balance before the first real deposit can prevent the offset from being applied on an empty vault. From a user perspective, a depositor may see that they receive more shares than expected, while a redeemer may notice that the amount of assets returned is lower than anticipated, sometimes even zero, leading to confusion and loss of confidence.
summary: The exchange ratio between shares and assets is calculated incorrectly when the vault is closed. This can cause accounting inconsistencies, funds being stolen and users being unable to redeem shares. The functions AsyncSynthVault::_convertToAssets and AsyncSynthVault::_convertToShares both add 1 to the epoch cached variables totalAssetsSnapshotForDeposit, totalSupplySnapshotForDeposit, totalAssetsSnapshotForRedeem and totalSupplySnapshotForRedeem. This is incorrect because the function previewSettle, used in _settle(), already adds 1 to the variables: ```solidity ... uint256 totalAssetsSnapshotForDeposit = _lastSavedBalance + 1; uint256 totalSupplySnapshotForDeposit = totalSupply + 1; ... uint256 totalAssetsSnapshotForRedeem = _lastSavedBalance + pendingDeposit + 1; uint256 totalSupplySnapshotForRedeem = totalSupply + sharesToMint + 1; ... ``` This leads to accounting inconsistencies between depositing/redeeming when a vault is closed and depositing/redeeming when a vault is open whenever the exchange ratio assets/shares is not exactly 1:1. If a share is worth more than one asset: • Users that will request a deposit while the vault is closed will receive more shares than they should • Users that will request a redeem while the vault is closed will receive less assets than they should When the ratio between shares and assets is not 1:1 the protocol calculates the exchange rate between assets and shares inconsitently. This is an issue by itself and can lead to loss of funds and users not being able to claim shares. It can also be taken advantage of by an attacker to steal shares from the claimable silo. the attacker is not required to mint any share.

title: Two Pyth prices can be used in the same trans-
content: The vulnerability is a price‑manipulation flaw that allows an attacker toexploit the pull‑based Pyth oracle model used by OracleMaker and SpotHedgeBaseMaker contracts. The contracts accept a signed price from an off‑chain provider and only verify that the price is not older than a configurable maxAge. No additional freshness or monotonicity checks are performed, and the same transaction can call the contract’s updatePrice function multiple times with different signed prices. Because the deposit() function calculates the number of LP shares based on the price that is stored at the moment of the call, and the withdraw() function redeems collateral using the price stored at the moment of withdrawal, an attacker can supply a low price, deposit funds (or flash‑loaned funds) to receive a large amount of LP shares, then immediately update the price to a higher value and withdraw the same shares for a larger amount of collateral. The protocol does not charge any fee for deposit or withdrawal, and the whitelist that could restrict who may call these functions is not enforced, so any address can perform the sequence. The attack can be executed entirely within a single block because the block timestamp does not change between the two price updates, making the maxAge check pass for both readings. The result is that value that should have been allocated to honest LPs is siphoned off by the attacker, effectively causing funds to disappear from the pool. This issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the accounting logic of the maker contracts and identified that the price used for share issuance and redemption is taken from a mutable state variable without sufficient protection. The flaw is subtle because price updates are expected to occur many times per second, and the maxAge constraint gives a false sense of security, so developers may not notice that two distinct prices can be injected in the same transaction. To remediate, the protocol should restrict price updates to trusted relayers, enforce that a single price is used for the whole lifecycle of a deposit‑withdrawal pair, add a fee or slippage protection, and optionally lock the price for a short period after a deposit. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of oracle‑staleness or price‑replay attacks where mutable on‑chain price state is abused to manipulate accounting calculations.

title: Funding Fee Rate is calculated based only on
content: The vulnerability stems from the way the perpetual market calculates its funding fee rate. The protocol determines the funding rate solely from the net position imbalance of the Oracle Maker, while the fee itself is charged to every open position in the market, regardless of which maker supplied the liquidity. Because the rate does not take into account the positions held through the Spot‑Hedge (HSBM) maker, an attacker can artificially inflate the funding rate by opening a very large long position on the Oracle Maker. The attacker then immediately closes that long and simultaneously opens an opposite short position on the Spot‑Hedge maker within the same block. Since the funding rate is still derived from the Oracle Maker’s skew, the extreme rate persists for the next block and is paid by all long positions, including those of honest users. This creates several attack vectors. In a griefing scenario the attacker’s manipulation makes the funding cost for longs so high that many long positions become under‑collateralised and are liquidated in the following block, draining users’ margin and potentially causing loss of funds. In a profit‑seeking scenario the attacker also opens a short on the Spot‑Hedge maker, captures the inflated funding fee for a single block, then closes the short at the start of the next block, extracting the fee differential as profit while only suffering the spread loss between the two makers. A third variant involves depositing a large amount into the Oracle Maker, withdrawing it after one block, and benefitting from the sudden increase in share value caused by the high funding fee that is accounted for in the share price calculation. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the funding‑fee logic, where the auditor noticed that the rate calculation referenced only the Oracle Maker’s settled margin and ignored pending margin, leading to a circular dependency that was deliberately avoided but introduced a blind spot. The bug is subtle because the funding fee appears to behave normally under typical market conditions; only when an attacker can move large volumes within a single block does the discrepancy become exploitable, making it hard to detect through routine testing. The impact is severe: honest traders may see their funding fees spike unexpectedly, positions become liquidatable without warning, and the protocol’s PnL pool can be drained, reducing the value available for withdrawals. Affected parties include any user holding long positions, liquidators, and the protocol’s treasury. To remediate the issue the funding rate calculation should be made symmetric, incorporating the net position skew of all makers or, alternatively, charging funding fees only to positions that contributed to the skew that generated the rate. This change would prevent a single maker from unilaterally dictating the fee and would align the economic incentives across the whole market, eliminating the possibility of the described manipulation.
summary:
The fact that the Funding Fee rate is calculated only based on the Oracle Maker's position skew enables an exploiter to open a large long position on the Oracle Maker that generates an extreme funding fee paid by long takers, and then close the position (+open an opposite one) on the SpotHedge maker within the same block while maintaining the funding fee value and direction. This can be used to generate various attacks as detailed below.
Perpetual uses funding fee to balance between long and short positions, mainly to balance/reduce exposure of the Oracle Maker (from the docs: "In our system, having a funding fee will be beneficial for the Oracle Pool"). Presumably for this reason the funding rate is calculated based only on the Oracle Maker's position skew as can be seen in this code snippet taken from the getCurrentFundingRate to OracleMaker in the code):
```solidity
// we can only use margin without pendingMargin as totalDepositedAmount
// since pendingMargin includes pending borrowingFee and fundingFee,
// it will be infinite loop dependency
uint256 totalDepositedAmount = uint256(_getVault().getSettledMargin(marketId, fundingConfig.basePool));
```
However, the funding fee applies to any position in the market (as can be seen in the Vault::settlePosition function) which enables an exploiter to create a very high funding rate for a low cost by opening a large long position on the oracle maker and close the position immediately after on the HSBM maker (possibly also opening a short depending on the type of attack). Since the opposite position does not affect the funding rate (as it is settled with the SpotHedge maker), the funding rate will maintain its extreme value and its direction.
This maneuver can generate multiple types of attacks that can be conducted individually or combined:
A. Griefing/Liquidation attack - The attacker creates an extreme funding rate that causes immediate loss to position holders of the attacked direction, possibly making many positions liquidatable on the next block. This attack is conducted as follows:
A.1. Attacker opens a maximal long position on the oracle maker creating an extremely high funding rate paid by longs. A.2. Attacker closes their long position using the HSBM maker. This means the extreme high funding rate is unaffected since its calculated based on the oracle maker only. (A1 and A2 can be done in an atomic transaction from an attacker contract).
A.3. Starting from the next block any long position in the system incurs a very high cost per block, likely making many positions liquidatable immediately.
A.4. The cost for the attacker is only the negative PnL caused by the spread between the oracle and HSBM makers. The attacker can offset the cost and make a profit by running a transaction at the start of the next block that liquidates all positions that were liquidated by the move (the attacker has information advantage over other liquidators and are likely to win the liquidations).
B. Profiting from large funding fee within one block by also opening a short (exfiltrating funds from the PnL pool).
B.1. the attack starts similarly to A: the attacker opens a maximal long position on the OM and then a counter short position on the HSBM maker, only this time the attacker also opens a short on the SpotHedge maker that gains the attacker funding fees starting from the next block.
B.2. The attacker can close the short position at the start of the next block to reduce risk, taking profit from the fee paid for the one block, in addition to liquidating any affected positions as in scenario A.
B.3. The cost of attack: negative PnL caused by spread between the two makers, plus borrowing fee. However because borrowing fee does not grow exponentially with utilization rate like the funding fee, it is covered by the funding fee with a profit.
C. Profiting from a large deposit to the oracle maker/withdraw within one block.
C.1. The attack runs the same as scenario A, only the attacker also makes a large deposit to the oracle maker, and withdraws on the next block.
C.2. Since share values take into account pending fees, the share value will increase significantly from one block to the next because the oracle maker will also get a high funding fee within that one block (this is because oracle maker also holds a large short position as a result of the attackers initial position, that gets paid no expected loss to share value between these two blocks
The POC below shows how with reasonable market conditions the attacker can make a significant profit, specifically using only attack type B.
The various possible attacks detailed above generate immediate profits to the exploiter that can be withdrawn immediately if enough PnL exists in the pool, diluting the PnL pool on the expense of users and causing them financial loss from not being able to withdraw their profits. In addition, as detailed above many positions can be made liquidatable following the attack causing further damage.

title: Pool can be drained
content: The vulnerability is a drainable pool condition that allows an attacker to extract more assets than legitimately deposited by exploiting the fact that the contract only enforces per‑swap limits such as maxNotionalSwap and maxGamma, but does not enforce a cumulative limit across multiple swaps executed within the same transaction. The root cause is that the AMM pricing formula and the limit checks are applied independently to each individual swap, so an attacker can split a large trade into many small trades that each stay under the configured thresholds. By using a flashloan to obtain a large amount of the base token, the attacker performs a series of partial swaps that gradually push the pool price in their favor, then swaps back a small amount of the quote token to receive a disproportionately large amount of the base token, repaying the flashloan and keeping the surplus. This sequence can be repeated in a single transaction, bypassing the intended protection mechanisms. The impact is that the pool’s reserves can be drained, causing users to see their balances disappear, prices deviate dramatically, and expected refunds or swaps return zero or far less than anticipated. The condition occurs whenever the contract permits multiple swaps in one transaction without aggregating the notional amount, and when the price‑impact calculation does not account for the cumulative effect of sequential swaps. It affects any participant that relies on the pool for fair pricing, including regular users, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself, as the drained assets reduce overall liquidity and can lead to loss of funds. The issue was discovered by reproducing a previously reported exploit, using a test that flash‑loans a large amount, performs ten partial swaps, and then swaps back a small amount of USDC to obtain an order‑of‑magnitude excess of WOO. The bug is hard to notice because each individual swap appears to respect the limits and the price change per swap is modest, masking the overall manipulation that only becomes evident when the series is considered as a whole. To remediate, the contract should enforce a cumulative notional limit per transaction, incorporate a check that the total outflow cannot exceed the pool’s reserves, adjust the pricing formula to reflect the impact of sequential swaps, and possibly restrict flashloan usage or require a single‑swap path for large trades, thereby preventing the attacker from fragmenting a large exploit into many small, allowed operations.

title: Tax refund is calculated based on the wrong
content: The vulnerability concerns the calculation of a tax refund that users can claim after a private sale period ends. The contract determines the amount of tax to return based on the user’s remaining USDC balance (left) and a tax‑free allocation (taxFreeAllc). The logic assumes that if the user’s allocated share (s.share) is less than or equal to the tax‑free allocation, the full tax amount is refunded, otherwise the refund is computed as (left * tax) / POINT_BASE. This formula is flawed because it ignores the tax that should be refunded for the tax‑free allocation itself when the user’s share exceeds the tax‑free allocation. In practice, a user who deposits more than the amount actually used in the sale receives a refund only for the unused portion, while the tax that should be reclaimed on the tax‑free portion is omitted. For example, a user deposits 1000 USDC, the sale uses only 500 USDC (s.share = 500, left = 500), and the user has a 400 USDC tax‑free allocation. The correct refund should cover tax on the 500 USDC left plus tax on the 400 USDC tax‑free allocation, but the contract only returns tax on the 500 USDC left, resulting in a shortfall. The issue manifests after the private period when the sale is oversubscribed and the user’s share is lower than the deposited amount. It affects any participant who relies on the tax refund mechanism, leading to a loss of expected funds and a breach of the protocol’s financial guarantees. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the refund logic and identified the missing addition of the tax‑free allocation in the refund formula. Because the code path is only exercised in an oversubscription scenario, the bug can be subtle and may not be caught by simple unit tests that use balanced inputs. The vulnerability belongs to the class of accounting or arithmetic bugs where a formula omits a term, causing an under‑payment. To remediate, the refund calculation should be changed to include both the leftover amount and the tax‑free allocation, for example: refundTaxAmount = ((left + taxFreeAllc) * tax) / POINT_BASE; This adjustment ensures that users receive the full tax they are entitled to, restoring the intended economic behavior of the protocol.

title: If token does not oversell, users cannot claim
content: The vulnerability resides in the token sale contract’s claim function, where a mandatory require statement checks that a variable named left is greater than zero before any tax refund can be processed. The variable left is only assigned a non‑zero value when the private sale has oversold the total token supply (state.totalPrivateSold > state.totalSupplyInValue). If the sale does not oversell, the internal _claim routine returns left as zero, causing the require(left > 0, "TokenSale: Nothing to claim") to revert the transaction. Consequently, even users who have paid a tax on their deposit and are entitled to a tax‑free allocation cannot receive their refund unless the oversell condition is met. The root cause is an unnecessary guard that ties the ability to claim a refund to an unrelated oversell flag, effectively blocking legitimate refunds in normal sale scenarios. An attacker does not need to exploit the contract actively; the bug manifests automatically for any depositor when the sale does not oversell, resulting in funds that remain locked in the contract and users seeing no refund despite having a positive tax amount. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the claim flow and noticed that the left variable is only populated under the oversell branch. It can be hard to notice because the claim function otherwise appears to work, and the revert message "TokenSale: Nothing to claim" may be interpreted as a generic error rather than a logical flaw. The impact is that users experience a missing refund, their balances appear unchanged, and the protocol’s promised tax‑free allocation is broken, violating the business logic that tax should be returned on the refundable portion of a deposit. To remediate, the require check on left should be removed or altered so that a refund can be issued even when left equals zero, and the refund calculation should be based on the user's share rather than the leftover amount, ensuring that tax refunds are always claimable regardless of oversell status.

title: Reentrancy in Vesting.sol:claim() will allow users
content: The vulnerability is a classic reentrancy flaw in the claim() function of a vesting contract. The function calculates the amount of tokens or native BNB that a user is entitled to based on elapsed vesting points, then sends that amount to the caller using a low‑level .call() before it updates the user’s vesting index (s.index) and the amount already claimed. Because the external call is performed prior to the state change, a malicious contract can receive the transferred funds, execute its fallback function, and invoke claim() again while the original call is still on the stack. The second invocation sees the same s.index value as the first call, passes the “already claimed” check, recomputes the same pctAmount and triggers another .call(), allowing the attacker to repeat the process until the contract balance is exhausted. This can happen whenever a user claims native BNB (identified by address(1)) or any token that is transferred via a .call‑style transfer, and the contract holds sufficient unclaimed balance. The impact is that funds disappear from the vesting contract, honest participants receive less or no tokens, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions are broken because the vesting schedule no longer reflects reality. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit when the reviewer noticed that the external call precedes the update of the user’s index, violating the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern. It can be hard to spot because the function otherwise appears to enforce proper vesting checks and uses safeTransfer for ERC20 tokens, giving a false sense of safety. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after a claim the contract balance may become zero unexpectedly, or a user may receive multiple payouts for the same vesting period, effectively “draining” the contract. The bug belongs to the reentrancy class of vulnerabilities, where an external call allows the callee to re‑enter the vulnerable function before critical state variables are updated. To remediate, the contract should update s.index and s.amountClaimed before performing any external transfer, adopt the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern, and optionally protect the function with a ReentrancyGuard modifier. This ensures that even if a malicious contract re‑enters, the state will already reflect that the claim has been processed, preventing further payouts.

title: Underlying LP value can be manipulated to drain
content: The vulnerability originates from the way the Orange and Teahouse vault contracts calculate the total value of their underlying liquidity provider (LP) positions. Both contracts read the current price information directly from the Uniswap V3 pool’s slot0() function – specifically the sqrtPriceX96 field – and use this instantaneous price to convert the amount of token1 held into an equivalent amount of token0. Because slot0 reflects the most recent swap price, an attacker can deliberately execute a large trade on one of the underlying pools to push the price away from its market equilibrium. After the price is distorted, the vault’s totalAssets (or estimatedValueInToken0) function reports a higher aggregate value for the LP tokens than actually exists in the pool. The protocol then uses this inflated figure to determine each LP’s share price. If the system contains multiple vaults that each reference separate pools but share a common accounting model, the attacker can manipulate the price in one pool, causing the global LP valuation to rise, and then withdraw from a second vault that is linked to an unmanipulated pool. The withdrawal extracts more assets than the attacker contributed, while the manipulated pool can later be restored to its original price, leaving the protocol with a net loss. From a user’s perspective the vault appears to hold the correct balance, but after the attack the user’s share may be drained, balances become zero, or expected refunds are missing. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the Copra Finance contracts, where the auditor noticed that the valuation logic relied on a mutable on‑chain price source rather than a trusted oracle or time‑weighted average. The problem is hard to spot because the price manipulation can be performed in a single transaction and the vault’s accounting still reports a consistent total value; only after the cross‑vault withdrawal does the discrepancy become evident. This class of bug is an “oracle manipulation via direct on‑chain price feed” that leads to incorrect asset accounting and potential fund drainage. To remediate, the contracts should replace the direct slot0 price with a secure external price oracle such as Chainlink, or compute a time‑weighted average price (TWAP) that cannot be altered by a single trade, ensuring that LP share valuation reflects a stable market price rather than a transient swap price.

title: Malicious Data Injection via
content: The vulnerability is an unchecked data injection flaw in the TeahouseLiquidityWarehouse contract that allows an attacker to embed malicious swap instructions into the generic calldata accepted by functions such as deactivate(), liquidate(), withdrawLender() and withdrawBorrower(). The root cause is that these functions forward the supplied bytes directly to an internal multicall routine without any validation of the content, enabling the attacker to craft a call to the UniswapV3Swap router with arbitrary pool addresses, amounts and price limits. When the malicious calldata is executed, the multicall performs a swap that moves assets out of the warehouse into a pool where the protocol receives little or no value, effectively draining the stored tokens. This can be exploited whenever a user or an automated process invokes any of the affected functions with attacker‑controlled calldata; no specific pre‑condition other than the ability to submit the transaction is required. The impact is a loss of liquidity: users who expect to withdraw their funds may see their balances reduced to zero, receive no refund, or observe that a withdrawal returns far less than anticipated. The protocol’s accounting assumptions that assets are only swapped under controlled, slippage‑limited conditions are violated, breaking the business logic that guarantees fair value for swaps. The issue was discovered during a manual security audit that highlighted the lack of input sanitisation before low‑level calls. It can be hard to notice because the functions appear benign and the swap is performed through a trusted external router, so a transaction may look like a normal swap on the surface while actually moving funds to the attacker. To remediate, the contract should implement strict validation of the calldata passed to multicall, whitelist only approved function selectors, verify that swap paths correspond to known pool addresses, enforce reasonable slippage limits, and consider using a safe‑call wrapper that restricts execution to a predefined set of safe operations. In generic terms, this is a classic unchecked external‑call or data‑injection bug that enables unintended token transfers and financial loss. From the user’s perspective the failure mode manifests as missing balances, zero refunds, or unexpected token deductions after a transaction that was expected to be harmless.
summary: deactivate() and liquidate() functions as well as withdrawLender and withdrawBorrower functions allow attacker to inject malicious bytes calldata data. This specifically pertains to the execution of multicall in the Teahouse Liquidity Warehouse extension, where malicious swap data can lead to adverse swaps via uniswapV3Swap, resulting in a drain of assets. The TeahouseLiquidityWarehouse contract facilitates interactions through multicall, which includes swap operations. Malicious actors can exploit the deactivate() or liquidate() functions by passing in crafted swapData that triggers detrimental swaps, draining assets without the protocol receiving the intended swap outcomes. This vulnerability stems from the lack of validation on the swapData passed into multicall, which can include calls to uniswapV3Swap with specifically crafted parameters. This vulnerability will lead to significant financial losses by enabling attackers to execute swaps that deplete the protocol's assets without receiving fair value in return.

title: Highest bidder can withdraw his collateral due
content: The vulnerability is a logical flaw in the English periodic auction contract that allows the current highest bidder to cancel all of their bids, withdraw the locked collateral, and remain recorded as the winning bidder. The root cause is that the internal _cancelAllBids function iterates over every auction round up to the current round and releases any collateral it finds without checking whether the caller is the highest bidder for the active round, and it does not reset the highestBids mapping. An attacker who has placed the highest bid can invoke the public wrapper that calls _cancelAllBids (or a similar cancelAllBidsAndWithdrawCollateral function), causing the contract to mark the attacker’s collateral as available for withdrawal while still keeping their address in the highestBids slot. The attacker then withdraws the full amount of their bid, effectively paying nothing for the asset. When the auction later settles, the contract treats the attacker as the winner and attempts to transfer the bid amount from the contract balance to the previous highest bidder, but the withdrawn funds are no longer present, leading to failed or under‑funded withdrawals for other participants. This results in free acquisition of the auctioned token for the malicious bidder and a loss of locked collateral for honest bidders, potentially draining the contract balance if repeated. The issue occurs whenever the highest bidder calls the cancellation routine before the round is finalized; it affects all participants in the auction, the protocol’s economic guarantees, and any funds locked as collateral. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that compared the checks in _cancelBid with the implementation of _cancelAllBids and noticed the missing require statement. It can be hard to notice because the function appears to only clean up old rounds, and the missing check does not raise an error for non‑highest bidders, making the behavior seem normal during routine testing. To remediate, the contract should enforce the same prohibition that exists in _cancelBid inside _cancelAllBids, either by adding a require that the caller is not the current highest bidder for each round, by skipping the current round entirely, or by resetting the highestBids entry when a cancellation is performed, thereby preserving the invariant that the highest bidder cannot withdraw collateral while still being declared the winner.

title: Index logic is flawed
content: The vulnerability is a precision and scaling flaw in the calculation of the liquidity index used by the protocol to track accrued interest and rebasing rewards. The index is supposed to be a Ray‑scaled value (1e27) that never falls below this baseline because it represents a cumulative multiplier applied to user balances. The root cause is that the code that incorporates claimable rebasing rewards converts the reward amount into a percentage of total pool holdings and then multiplies the existing liquidity index by this percentage. When the claimable amount is small relative to the pool size, the percentage (claimedInterestIndex) becomes a value far smaller than 1e27, and due to integer division it can even round down to zero. Multiplying the previous index by a sub‑baseline factor drives the new liquidity index below 1e27 or to zero. This violates the invariant that the index must stay above the Ray unit, breaking the core accounting logic that assumes a monotonic increase. An attacker or even a regular user triggering a reward claim with a tiny amount can cause the global liquidity index to collapse, after which all subsequent interest calculations return zero or negative values. The impact is severe: user balances appear to lose accrued interest, withdrawals, deposits, and borrowing operations may revert or behave incorrectly because the protocol relies on the index to compute amounts. The condition occurs whenever the claimable rewards are insufficiently large compared to the total pool holdings, which is a realistic scenario for low‑volume pools or after many small reward distributions. All participants of the pool are affected because the index is stored at the reserve level and shared across users. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the index‑update logic, where the auditor observed that the claimedInterestIndex could be less than the Ray unit and that the subsequent multiplication could produce a zero index. The bug is hard to notice because the contract does not emit explicit warnings when the index drops, and the erroneous values may only surface later as failed transactions or missing interest. Conceptually, the fix is to ensure that any percentage derived from rewards is normalized to the Ray scale before multiplication, or to guard against under‑flow by capping the minimum index at 1e27 and handling zero‑reward cases without altering the index. In other words, the protocol must treat the liquidity index as a strictly non‑decreasing Ray‑scaled accumulator and avoid applying a factor that can reduce it below the baseline. From a user’s perspective, the symptom is that after claiming a small reward, their balance may show no increase, or operations such as withdraw or borrow may fail with “insufficient liquidity” errors, effectively making funds appear to disappear. This class of bug falls under improper scaling and precision handling in financial index calculations, leading to a breakdown of the protocol’s accounting guarantees.

title: Borrow index isn't updated correctly
content: The vulnerability is an accounting inconsistency in Aave V2 when a rebasing token is used as collateral or supplied. The protocol correctly accrues the rebasing reward by increasing the liquidityIndex, but the borrowIndex, which tracks the growth of borrowed positions, is not updated with the same rebasing amount. This mismatch originates from the borrow index calculation that only compounds the variable borrow rate and ignores the claimable amount from the rebasing token, while the liquidity index logic explicitly incorporates the rebasing reward. As a result, after each rebasing event the perceived supply balance grows faster than the borrowing side, causing the liquidityIndex to run ahead of the borrowIndex. Borrowers therefore do not receive the extra APY generated by the rebasing token, and they have no incentive to claim the reward, while suppliers see inflated interest. Over time the divergence can become large enough that the protocol believes it has more assets than are actually available, allowing withdrawals that exceed the real pool and potentially leading to insolvency. The issue manifests when any rebasing token such as USDB, WETH (treated as rebasing), or stETH is supplied, and the contract executes the claimableAmount logic; the borrow side remains unchanged. Users experience symptoms like unexpectedly high supplied balances, withdrawals that fail or return zero, and a supply APY that appears higher than the borrow APY. The problem was discovered during a security audit of Seismic Finance’s integration with Aave V2, where the auditor compared the liquidity index update code with the borrow index update code and noted the missing rebasing adjustment. Because the indices are large numeric values, the discrepancy may remain hidden until a significant rebasing event occurs, making it hard to notice in routine testing. The recommended mitigation is to avoid using raw rebasing tokens with Aave V2 and instead employ non‑rebasing wrapper tokens (NrETH, NrUSDB, wstETH) or to extend the protocol’s accounting to also update the borrowIndex with the rebasing reward, ensuring both indices reflect the same growth and preserving protocol solvency. This class of bug can be described as an asymmetric index update or rebasing token accounting mismatch, which violates the fundamental accounting assumption that supply and borrow growth are tracked consistently.

title: Claiming rebasing token rewards in ReserveL-
content: The vulnerability originates from the ReserveLogic::_updateIndexes routine that attempts to claim rebasing token rewards for a reserve that holds a rebasing underlying asset such as USDB or WETH. The implementation mistakenly queries the rebasing token’s getClaimableAmount function with address(this), which in this context is the LendingPool contract, instead of the AToken address that actually owns the underlying balance. Because the rebasing token only permits accounts configured with YieldMode.CLAIMABLE to query claimable amounts, the call reverts with NotClaimableAccount when the LendingPool address is used. A second mistake is that the code calls the rebasing token’s claim function directly from the LendingPool, passing the AToken address as the recipient. The LendingPool does not hold the underlying balance, so the claim cannot be executed even if the first call succeeded. In addition, the constant addresses for USDB and WETH are hard‑coded to the wrong network values, further preventing correct identification of the rebasing tokens. When a reserve with a rebasing underlying token triggers _updateIndexes – for example during a deposit, withdrawal, or any operation that updates liquidity indexes – the erroneous calls cause the entire transaction to revert. As a result, liquidity providers do not receive the additional rebasing rewards that should be accrued to the AToken, breaking the accounting model that expects these rewards to be added to the pool’s liquidity index. Users see symptoms such as a zero claimable amount, missing balance updates, or a transaction that fails unexpectedly after a small deposit. The issue was discovered during a manual audit and reproduced with a Forge test that deliberately corrected the token addresses and observed a revert when the pool attempted to claim rewards. The bug is subtle because the code compiles and the logic appears correct at a glance; the failure only manifests for specific rebasing assets and only when the internal claim path is exercised. To remediate, the getClaimableAmount call must be made with the AToken address, the claim function should be invoked by the AToken itself (or via a proper internal call that respects the token’s ownership model), and the constant addresses for the rebasing tokens must be updated to the correct network values. This fixes the claim flow, restores proper reward accrual, and aligns the protocol’s accounting with its business logic that LPs earn rebasing interest.

title: Malicious user can overtake a prefunded auc-
content: The vulnerability originates from the way the AuctionHouse contract records a newly created auction in the lotRouting mapping. When the auction() function is called, the return variable lotId is declared at the function signature level and therefore starts with the default value 0. The contract then creates a local storage pointer with the statement Routing storage routing = lotRouting[lotId]; before the lotId variable is updated to the next available identifier by incrementing the internal lot counter. As a result, the routing pointer always references lotRouting[0] for the first line of code in the function, regardless of the actual lot identifier that will later be assigned. This off‑by‑one error means that the first auction created after the contract is deployed, as well as any subsequent auction that is created before the lotId variable is reassigned, will write its seller address and other metadata into the same storage slot (index 0). An honest user who creates a prefunded auction therefore deposits funds that are recorded under lotRouting[0]. A malicious actor can then create a second auction with the same base token but without prefunding; because the routing pointer still points to lotRouting[0], the attacker becomes the recorded seller of that lot while the prefunded amount remains unchanged. By calling cancel(0, …) the attacker triggers the contract’s cancellation logic, which transfers the stored funding to the current seller – now the attacker – leaving the original user with a zero balance. The attack can be carried out simply by submitting two transactions in quick succession: first a legitimate prefunded auction, then a malicious auction that overwrites the routing entry, and finally a cancellation of the overwritten lot. The impact is a direct theft of the prefunded funds, loss of trust for users who rely on the auction mechanism, and potential financial damage to the protocol if such auctions are common. The issue is discovered during a manual audit and reproduced with a Forge test that demonstrates the overtake and fund transfer. It is subtle because the mapping index 0 is a valid entry and the contract does not perform any explicit check that the routing entry being written corresponds to the newly generated lot identifier. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after creating a prefunded auction they see their token balance drop to zero after another user cancels an apparently unrelated auction, and the protocol appears to have transferred the funds to the attacker without any error messages. The bug belongs to the class of storage‑slot mis‑alignment or improper initialization bugs, where a variable is used before it is correctly set, leading to unintended overwrites of critical state. The correct mitigation is to ensure that the lot identifier is incremented and stored before any routing storage pointer is created, or to compute the routing entry after the lotId has been assigned. Additionally, the contract should validate that the seller recorded in the routing entry matches the caller who created the auction and that prefunded amounts are bound to the correct lot identifier, preventing an attacker from hijacking the funding by simply overwriting the first slot.

title: Incorrect prefundingRefundcalculation will dis-
content: The contract contains an arithmetic error in the calculation of the prefundingRefund value inside the claimProceeds function. The code adds the current routing.funding balance to the amount already sent (payoutSent_) and then subtracts the total quantity sold (sold_). Because routing.funding is reduced each time a bid payout is claimed, it may already be lower than the sold amount when claimProceeds is finally executed. In that situation the expression routing.funding + payoutSent_ - sold_ becomes a negative number, but the variables are unsigned (uint96). The unchecked block then causes an under‑flow, wrapping the value to a very large number and triggering a revert when the subsequent subtraction routing.funding -= prefundingRefund is performed. The bug appears only when all bidders have claimed their payouts before the seller calls claimProceeds, which is a realistic execution order. As a result the seller’s transaction reverts, no proceeds are transferred, and the funds remain locked in the contract. Users see the expected payout disappear, the UI may show an error or simply no change in balance, and the seller receives nothing despite having sold assets. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the state changes of routing.funding across claimBids and claimProceeds. It is hard to notice because the arithmetic looks correct in isolation and the unchecked block suppresses Solidity’s built‑in overflow checks. Conceptually the bug belongs to the class of unsigned integer under‑flow errors caused by incorrect accounting of prefunded capacity. The correct approach is to compute the refund based on the original prefunded capacity rather than the mutable routing.funding value, for example by using capacity - sold_ plus any curator‑fee adjustments. Fixing the calculation eliminates the under‑flow, restores the ability of sellers to claim proceeds, and preserves the intended accounting invariants of the protocol.

title: [M-1]
content: The vulnerability resides in the claimProceeds function of the auction contract, where a refund of the prefunded base token is sent without first verifying that the amount to transfer is non‑zero. The function computes prefundingRefund as routing.funding + payoutSent_ - sold_. In normal operation routing.funding holds the amount of base token that was deposited to guarantee the auction, and payoutSent_ tracks how much of that funding has already been paid out. When the auction settles completely, payoutSent_ equals sold_, leaving routing.funding at zero. Under these conditions prefundingRefund evaluates to zero. The contract then calls a generic Transfer.transfer helper with a zero amount. Certain ERC20 tokens – including many that conform to the ERC20 Metadata standard and have 6‑18 decimals as listed in the protocol’s README – deliberately revert when a transfer of zero tokens is attempted. Because the contract does not guard against a zero‑value transfer, the call reverts, aborting the claimProceeds execution after the seller’s quote‑token payout has already been sent. As a result the seller’s remaining base‑token funds stay locked inside the contract forever, and the seller receives no refund despite the protocol indicating that a refund should be available. The issue is triggered only when the auction finishes with no leftover funding, which is a legitimate and common scenario for successful auctions. It affects any user acting as a seller who expects to receive back any unused base‑token capital, and it also harms the protocol’s reputation because funds appear to disappear from the user’s perspective. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that compared the contract logic with the documentation and identified that the README explicitly permits tokens that revert on zero transfers, yet the code does not handle that case. The bug can be hard to notice because the transfer of zero tokens is a no‑op for many ERC20 implementations, so tests that use well‑behaved tokens pass, masking the failure for tokens that enforce a revert. To remediate, the contract should check that prefundingRefund is greater than zero before invoking the transfer, or use a safe‑transfer wrapper that silently skips zero‑value transfers. This change aligns the implementation with the intended business logic that sellers receive any unused funding and prevents permanent locking of assets caused by a zero‑transfer revert.

title: Module's gas yield can never be claimed and
content: The vulnerability is a misconfiguration of the gas‑yield mechanism in the modules that are intended to run on the Blast network. By default the Blast protocol defines a yield mode called 'VOID', which disables the accumulation and claiming of gas and ether rewards. The constructor of the modules only calls IBlast.configureGovernor to set the auction house as the governor, but it never invokes IBlast.configureClaimableGas to switch the yield mode from 'VOID' to 'CLAIMABLE'. Because the auction‑house contract does not expose any function to change the yield mode, the modules remain in the 'VOID' state for the lifetime of the deployment. Consequently, any gas that would have been generated by the Blast network is never recorded, and the claimGasYield function in the auction house always reverts. The issue manifests when a user or protocol operator attempts to claim gas yield and receives no funds, often seeing a zero balance or an empty transaction log, which can be mistaken for a normal state rather than a loss. The root cause is the omission of a required initialization step and the absence of an administrative interface to modify the yield mode after deployment. This bug is hard to notice because the contract does not throw an error; it simply never accrues yield, so standard testing that only checks for successful transactions may miss the problem. The impact is economic: the protocol forfeits the expected gas revenue, reducing overall profitability and potentially breaking business logic that assumes periodic yield collection. The affected parties include the protocol developers, the auction‑house governor, and any token holders who expect the protocol to generate additional ether from gas yields. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the constructor code and the BlastGas abstract contract, where the missing configureClaimableGas call was identified. To remediate, the constructor should invoke configureClaimableGas before setting the governor, or a separate governance function should be added to allow the auction house to enable claimable yield after deployment. This change ensures that the modules transition to the 'CLAIMABLE' mode, allowing the auction house to successfully claim and distribute gas yields as intended.
summary:
Module's gas yield can never be claimed
The protocol is meant to be deployed on blast, meaning that the gas and ether balance accrue yield.
By default these yield settings for both ETH and GAS yields are set to VOID as default, meaning that unless we configure the yield mode to claimable, we will be unable to recieve the yield. The protocol never sets gas to claimable for the modules, and the governor of the contract is the auction house, the auction house also does not implement any function to set the modules gas yield to claimable.
```solidity
constructor(address auctionHouse_) LinearVesting(auctionHouse_) BlastGas(auctionHouse_) {}
```
The constructor of both BlastLinearVesting and BlastEMPAM set the auction house here BlastGas(auctionHouse_) if we look at this contract we can observe the above.
BlastGas.sol
```solidity
constructor(address parent_) {
    // Configure governor to claim gas fees
    IBlast(0x4300000000000000000000000000000000000002).configureGovernor(parent_);
}
```
As we can see above, the governor is set in constructor, but we never set gas to claimable. Gas yield mode will be in its default mode which is VOID, the modules will not accue gas yields. Since these modules never set gas yield mode to claimable, the auction house cannot claim any gas yield for either of the contracts.
Additionally the auction house includes no function to configure yield mode, the auction house contract only has a function to claim the gas yield but this will revert since the yield mode for these module contracts will be VOID.
Gas yields will never acrue and the yield will forever be lost

title: Auction creators have the ability to lock bid-
content: The vulnerability is a state‑transition flaw in the batch auction contract that allows the auction creator to cancel an auction after the scheduled conclusion time, effectively locking bidders’ quote tokens inside the auction house. The root cause is an off‑by‑one error in the _revertIfLotConcluded check, which only reverts when the current block timestamp is strictly less than the conclusion timestamp. When block.timestamp becomes equal to the conclusion, the check passes, allowing cancelAuction to be called. The cancel function then sets the auction capacity to zero and marks the status as Claimed, bypassing the intended restriction that cancellations are only permitted before the auction starts. Because the auction never reaches the Decrypted or Settled states, the subsequent refundBid and claimBids functions remain blocked – they each call _revertIfLotConcluded or _revertIfLotNotSettled, both of which now revert due to the zero capacity or unchanged status. As a result, bidders cannot retrieve their deposited quote tokens, and the tokens remain permanently locked in the contract. This condition occurs precisely at the moment the auction’s conclusion timestamp is reached, and it can be triggered by any creator with the internal cancelAuction permission. Users who placed bids see their balances unchanged after the auction ends, receive no refund, and may notice that the auction is no longer live despite having participated. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the lifecycle checks for auction cancellation and bid settlement, and it is subtle because the contract’s public interface appears to prevent cancellation after start, yet the timing edge case is not obvious from a surface‑level review. The bug belongs to the class of improper state validation or time‑based access control errors, where boundary conditions are incorrectly handled, leading to a violation of the business rule that funds must be recoverable after an auction finishes. To remediate, the _revertIfLotConcluded function should reject calls when block.timestamp is greater than or equal to the conclusion timestamp, and the cancel logic should enforce that capacity is non‑zero and status is not already Claimed. Additionally, the auction settlement flow should ensure that a private key cannot be submitted without triggering decryption, preventing the creator from stalling the transition to Settled. Properly fixing these checks restores the guarantee that bidders can always claim or refund their tokens once the auction ends, aligning the contract’s behavior with expected auction economics.

title: Bidders can not claim their bids if the auction
content: The vulnerability originates from an incorrect state transition in a batch auction contract. After the auction has been settled, the contract expects bidders to claim their bids only while the auction status remains Settled. However, the auction creator is allowed to claim the proceeds first, which updates the auction status to Claimed. Because the claimBids function explicitly checks that the auction status is Settled, any subsequent attempt by bidders to retrieve their quote tokens or receive allocated base tokens is rejected, leaving their funds permanently locked in the auction house. This flaw occurs when the creator exercises the right to claim proceeds before any bidder has exercised their claim, a scenario that is permitted by the contract’s public interface and was uncovered during a systematic audit that added a test reproducing the sequence: settle the auction, invoke claimProceeds, then attempt claimBids, which triggers a WrongState revert. The issue is subtle because both operations are documented as being order‑agnostic, yet the underlying state machine does not support the claimed order, making the problem easy to miss during casual testing. From a user’s perspective, a bidder who expects to receive a refund of their quote tokens or to obtain the purchased base tokens instead sees no transaction outcome, their balance on the auction house remains unchanged, and the UI may show no error other than a generic revert. The impact is a loss of access to funds for all bidders who have not yet claimed, effectively freezing their assets and undermining trust in the auction protocol. The bug belongs to the class of “incorrect state‑machine enforcement” or “logic ordering vulnerability” where a contract’s state variable is set to a terminal value that prevents other legitimate actions. To remediate, the contract should either allow claimBids when the status is Claimed, separate the proceeds claim from the bidder claim by using distinct status flags, or enforce a strict ordering that requires all bidder claims to be completed before the creator can claim proceeds. Implementing one of these fixes restores the intended invariant that every participant can retrieve their rightful funds regardless of the order in which claims are made.

title: Bidders' funds may become locked due to in-
content: The vulnerability is an allocation inconsistency in the auction contract’s MaxPriorityQueue that can cause bidders’ quote tokens to become permanently locked. Bids are ordered by a cross‑multiplication comparison (q1*b2 < q2*b1) and, when the products are equal, the queue breaks the tie by preferring the higher bid identifier. Separately, the claim logic computes a price using Math.mulDivUp(q,10**baseDecimal,b) and allows a claim when the computed price is greater than the marginal price or when it is equal and the bid identifier is less than or equal to the stored marginalBidId. Because the two calculations use different rounding semantics, a bid whose exact price equals the marginal price can be placed after the marginal bid in the priority queue yet still satisfy the claim condition. When this happens, the contract treats the later bid as a winner, allowing it to withdraw base tokens. If the total amount of base tokens required by all winning bids exceeds the finite supply, the last bidders – including those that are not true winners – receive no payout and their quote tokens remain locked in the auction house. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when a test case demonstrated that a bid with a marginal price but a higher identifier could be claimed, exhausting the token pool and leaving earlier bidders with zero payout. The problem is hard to notice because the price check appears correct on its own and the queue ordering seems deterministic; only the subtle rounding mismatch reveals the overflow.
