title: Not transferring collateral when submitting
content: An attacker can exploit the fact that Teller does not escrow collateral at the moment a borrow request (submitBid) is created. The contract only checks that the borrower’s address holds the required collateral tokens, but it does not transfer them into an escrow contract. Consequently, a borrower can submit a request offering a valuable NFT, for example a Uniswap V3 liquidity‑position NFT, as collateral, wait for a lender to call lenderAcceptBid, and then front‑run that transaction to modify or drain the NFT’s value before the escrow step (collateralManager.deployAndDeposit) is executed. When the lender’s transaction finally runs, the contract pulls the NFT from the borrower, but the NFT now represents little or no value, while the borrowed funds have already been sent to the borrower. The lender therefore receives the loan amount without receiving the promised security, resulting in a loss of the lent assets. This situation occurs only when collateral is not locked at request time and the collateral asset can be altered by its owner, such as NFTs that represent mutable positions. The vulnerability was discovered during a security audit that examined the flow of collateral handling and identified a race condition between submitBid and lenderAcceptBid. It is difficult to notice because the initial balance check passes, no error is thrown, and the UI still displays the original high‑value collateral, giving the lender a false sense of security. The bug belongs to the class of improper collateral escrow and front‑running race conditions, violating the protocol’s accounting assumption that collateral value is static between request creation and acceptance. From a user perspective, a lender sees an attractive loan backed by an NFT worth X ETH, expects to be protected by that amount, but after the transaction the NFT is worth near zero and the lender’s balance is reduced by the loan amount. The correct mitigation is to require the borrower to transfer or lock the collateral into the Teller escrow at the time of submitBid, and to allow withdrawal only after the bid expires without acceptance, thereby eliminating the window for the borrower to manipulate the collateral after the request is posted.
summary:
Currently, Teller does not require collateral to be transferred when a bid request with collateral is submitted. Instead, the collateral is pulled from the borrower when the bid is accepted by the lender in a different transaction. This pattern allows attackers to leverage certain collaterals to perform honeypot-style attacks. The current flow to create a bid in Teller putting some collateral consists in the following steps:
1. Call submitBid with an array of Collateral. This creates the bid request, but does not transfer the collateral to Teller. Instead, Teller only check that Teller performs is checking the collateral balance of the borrower to guarantee that he actually owns the collateral assets.
2. After submitting the bid request, an interested lender can lend his assets to the borrower by calling lenderAcceptBid. This is the step where collateral will actually be transferred from the borrower, as shown in the following code snippet:
```solidity
// TellerV2.sol
function lenderAcceptBid(uint256 _bidId)
external
override
pendingBid(_bidId, "lenderAcceptBid")
whenNotPaused
returns (
uint256 amountToProtocol,
uint256 amountToMarketplace,
uint256 amountToBorrower
)
{
...
// Tell the collateral manager to deploy the escrow and pull funds from the borrower if applicable
collateralManager.deployAndDeposit(_bidId);
...
}
```
Although this pattern (checking the borrower’s collateral balance in step 1 to ensure he actually owns the assets) might look like a correct approach, it’s actually incorrect and can lead to honeypot-style attacks when specific NFTs are used as collateral. Consider the following scenario: a malicious borrower holds a Uniswap V3 liquidity position NFT with liquidity worth 10 ETH. He decides to trick borrowers in Teller, and submits a loan request asking for only 1 ETH (a very attractive offer, given that on default, the lender will gain access to 10 ETH worth of collateral):
1. Borrower creates the borrow request by calling submitBid. submitBid then checks and guarantees that the borrower indeed holds the Uniswap liquidity position.
2. After some time, a lender sees the borrow request and decides that they want to lend their assets to the borrower by calling lenderAcceptBid, as the Uniswap liquidity position (which is worth 10 ETH) is attractive enough to cover the possibility of borrowed assets never being repaid.
3. The malicious borrower then frontruns the lender transaction and decreases the Uniswap liquidity position to nearly 0 (because collateral has not been transferred when submitting the bid request, the NFT owner is still the borrower, hence why liquidity can be decreased by him).
4. After decreasing the Uniswap position liquidity, the lender’s lenderAcceptBid transaction actually gets executed. Uniswap’s liquidity position NFT gets transferred to Teller from the borrower, and the borrowed funds are transferred to the borrower.
As we can see, not transferring the collateral when the bid request is submitted can lead to these type of situations. Borrowers can easily trick lenders, making them believe that their loaned assets are backed by an NFT worth an X amount, when in reality the NFT will be worth nearly 0 when the transactions actually get executed. High. Attackers can easily steal all the borrowed assets from lenders with no collateral cost at all, given that the collateral NFT will be worth 0 when the borrow is actually executed.

title: burnSharesToWithdrawEarnings burns before math,
content: The vulnerability is an arithmetic ordering error in the withdraw‑earnings routine. The function that processes a partial withdrawal first burns the caller’s shares, thereby reducing the total supply, and only afterwards computes the principal per share using the reduced supply. Because the pool’s total estimated value is unchanged while the share count is lower, the derived share‑price inverse becomes smaller, which inflates the amount of underlying tokens calculated for the withdrawal. As a result a user who withdraws, for example, 20 % of the shares receives roughly 25 % of the pool’s principal, effectively being overpaid. This overpayment can be triggered any time the burnSharesToWithdrawEarnings function is called with a non‑zero amount, so any holder can exploit the mis‑order to extract more value than their proportional ownership. The impact is a systematic loss of funds from the pool, potentially leading to insolvency if multiple users repeat the exploit. The bug affects all token holders, the protocol’s accounting guarantees, and any downstream contracts that rely on correct share valuation. It was discovered during a security audit when the auditor traced the math of the withdrawal path and noticed that the share‑price calculation used the post‑burn total supply. The issue is subtle because the individual formulas appear correct in isolation; only the sequence of operations creates the discrepancy, making it easy to miss in casual testing. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a normal withdrawal request but the received token amount is higher than expected, while the pool balance drops more than anticipated, leading to confusing “extra” payouts or missing funds for other participants. The class of bug is a share‑price mis‑calculation caused by premature state mutation, a common pattern in financial smart contracts where snapshots must be taken before mutating balances. The recommended remediation is to compute the withdrawal amount using the share supply before burning, or to perform the burn after the principal calculation, thereby preserving the correct proportional relationship between shares and underlying assets.
summary:
The burnSharesToWithdrawEarnings function burns shares before calculating the share price, resulting in an increase in share value and causing users to be overpaid. When burnSharesToWithdrawEarnings burns shares and subsequently calculates the principal per share, the share amount is reduced but the principal remains the same, leading to a decrease in the sharesExchangeRateInverse, which increases the principal paid. Principal is calculated using _valueOfUnderlying, where the formula is:
```solidity
uint256 principalTokenValueToWithdraw = (amount * 1e36) / sharesExchangeRateInverse();
```
The problem arises in sharesExchangeRateInverse which uses the reduced share count:
```solidity
return 1e72 / sharesExchangeRate();
```
Where sharesExchangeRate is defined as:
```solidity
rate_ = (poolTotalEstimatedValue * 1e36) / poolSharesToken.totalSupply();
```
Example:
• 1k shares and 10k principal.
1. Alice withdraws 20% of the shares.
2. 200 shares are burned, reducing the supply to 800.
3. Calculation for principal:
rate_ = (10_000e18 * 1e36) / 800e18 = 1.25e37 sharesExchangeRateInverse = 1e72 / 1.25e37 = 8e34 principalTokenValueToWithdraw = 200e18 * 1e36 / 8e34 = 2500e18
4. Alice withdraws 25% of the pool's principal, despite owning only 20% of the shares. This flaw results in incorrect calculations, allowing some users to withdraw more than their fair share, potentially leading to insolvency.

title: Anyone can steal pool shares from lender group
content: An attacker can obtain pool shares without providing the required principal tokens because the contract uses a plain ERC20 transferFrom call that returns a boolean and does not check the result. When the principal token is a non‑reverting token such as ZRX, transferFrom returns false on insufficient balance but the transaction continues. The addPrincipalToCommitmentGroup function therefore mints pool share tokens for the caller even though no tokens were transferred into the escrow. The attacker can then call burnSharesToWithdrawEarnings, burn the minted shares and receive principal tokens that belong to other lenders. This results in theft of assets, incorrect accounting of totalPrincipalTokensCommitted and totalPrincipalTokensWithdrawn, and a loss of confidence for all participants. The vulnerability appears only when a token that does not revert on failure is used as the principal token; the contract assumes that transferFrom will either succeed or revert. Because the return value is ignored, the failure is silent and no error event is emitted, making the bug hard to notice during normal testing. The issue was discovered during a security audit that included a custom NoRevertToken PoC demonstrating that a call with an amount larger than the caller’s balance does not revert and still leads to share minting. To remediate, the contract should use a safe transfer helper that checks the boolean result and reverts on false, or replace the call with SafeERC20’s safeTransferFrom, ensuring that token transfer failures abort the whole operation.

title: Borrowers can brick the commitment group
content: The vulnerability is an accounting mismatch that can be triggered by a borrower who first takes a loan directly from the core TellerV2 contract and then registers a repayment listener that points to a LenderCommitmentGroup (LCG). The function setRepaymentListenerForBid only checks that the caller is the lender recorded on the bid, which is true for a normal LCG‑originated loan, but it does not verify that the lender is the LCG itself. When the borrower later repays the loan, the repayment callback inside the LCG is invoked and the LCG updates its totalPrincipalTokensRepaid and totalInterestCollected counters. Because the original borrowing did not go through the LCG, its totalPrincipalTokensLended counter was never increased. The result is a discrepancy where totalPrincipalTokensRepaid grows without a matching increase in totalPrincipalTokensLended. This causes the helper function getTotalPrincipalTokensOutstandingInActiveLoans to underflow, which can render the LCG contract permanently unusable (bricked). At the same time, the inflated totalInterestCollected makes share values appear higher than they are backed by, creating artificial profit that is not supported by any real principal. The issue occurs whenever a borrower calls setRepaymentListenerForBid after a direct TellerV2 borrow and then repays that loan. It affects any user who interacts with the LCG – borrowers can exploit it to disrupt the commitment group, and lenders may see their expected accounting and profit calculations become incorrect. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit by the researcher Sherlock, who noticed that the repayment listener setter does not restrict the caller to the commitment group contract. The problem is subtle because the function’s require statement appears to enforce a sensible rule (only the bid lender may set the listener), which is true for the intended workflow, so the mismatch only surfaces when the borrowing path is altered. To remediate, the setter should be limited to calls originating from the LCG (for example by adding an onlyCommitmentGroup modifier) or the accounting logic should be adjusted to ensure that any repayment reported through a listener also updates the totalPrincipalTokensLended counter. In practice, the fix prevents borrowers from arbitrarily attaching LCG callbacks to loans they obtained outside the group, thereby preserving the invariant that totalPrincipalTokensLended equals totalPrincipalTokensRepaid and eliminating the underflow and unbacked profit generation. From a user perspective the bug manifests as a commitment group that suddenly stops accepting new bids, balances that appear unchanged or zero after repayment, and profit numbers that look unexpectedly high, all of which contradict the user’s expectation that repayments simply reduce the outstanding principal.

title: liquidateDefaultedLoanWithIncentive sends
content: The vulnerability resides in the liquidation path of defaulted loans. The function intended to reward a liquidator by transferring the seized collateral to the caller instead forwards the collateral to the lender’s commitment group (LCG). This occurs because the internal helper _lenderCloseLoanWithRecipient receives a _collateralRecipient argument but never passes it to the collateral manager; the call collateralManager.lenderClaimCollateral(_bidId) always withdraws the assets to the lender address stored in the loan record. Consequently, when a liquidator invokes liquidateDefaultedLoanWithIncentive, the collateral is not credited to the liquidator, yielding zero profit. The root cause is a missing use of the recipient parameter and an accounting path that does not update totalPrincipalTokensRepaid, breaking the protocol’s incentive model and causing inaccurate utilization metrics. An attacker (any party able to call the liquidation function) can trigger the function on a defaulted loan, causing the collateral to be locked away from the liquidator and eventually leading to loss of liquidity for lenders, as the protocol cannot recover the collateral through proper accounting. The impact includes loss of expected profit for liquidators, reduced incentive to perform liquidations, potential accumulation of unrecovered collateral, inflated utilization ratios, and eventual bricking of the contract where loans cannot be closed properly. The issue manifests when a loan is in default and a liquidator attempts to liquidate; the UI may show a successful liquidation transaction but the user’s balance does not increase, and the lender’s pool may show higher utilization without corresponding collateral return. The problem was discovered during a manual audit of the liquidation flow, where the code path was traced and the recipient argument was found unused. Because the transaction does not revert and appears successful, the bug can be hard to notice without inspecting internal state changes or accounting variables. The proper fix is to modify _lenderCloseLoanWithRecipient (and any related helper) so that the collateral is transferred to the address supplied in _collateralRecipient, and to ensure that totalPrincipalTokensRepaid is updated accordingly. In generic terms, this is an incentive‑misalignment bug caused by an incorrect destination address in a fund‑transfer routine, leading to accounting inconsistencies and loss of expected rewards.

title: Drained lender due to LenderCommitmentGroup_Smart::acceptFundsForAcceptBid() _collateralAmount by STANDARD_EXPANSION_FACTOR multiplication
content: The vulnerability is an under‑collateralisation bug in the LenderCommitmentGroup_Smart contract. The function that checks whether the borrower supplied enough collateral multiplies the required collateral amount by a constant called STANDARD_EXPANSION_FACTOR (1e18). The price conversion routine that derives the collateral requirement from the Uniswap V3 sqrtPriceX96 value already returns a value with 2**96 extra precision, which is later cancelled by UNISWAP_EXPANSION_FACTOR. Because the extra 1e18 factor is not compensated, the contract believes that a borrower needs far less collateral than the economic reality. As a result a borrower can provide a dust amount of WETH (or the opposite token) and still be allowed to draw the full principal amount of DAI. The exploit consists of calling acceptCommitmentWithRecipient (or acceptFundsForAcceptBid) with a normal principal amount while supplying collateral that is off‑by a factor of 1e18 smaller than required. The protocol then transfers the principal to the borrower, updates the lender’s share balance, and the lender’s escrow ends up holding almost no collateral. From the user’s perspective the lender’s balance drops to zero, the borrower receives the full loan despite posting almost no collateral, and any subsequent liquidation attempts fail because there is no collateral to seize. The bug occurs whenever the contract calculates collateral for a loan using the price‑from‑sqrtX96 helper and then applies STANDARD_EXPANSION_FACTOR, which is the case for all markets that rely on this helper. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by reproducing a test where 10 000 DAI were borrowed with only 4 WETH, confirming that the lender was drained. The problem is subtle because the price calculation appears mathematically correct and the extra factor is hidden in a constant, making the under‑collateralisation easy to miss in code review. The correct fix is to remove the multiplication by STANDARD_EXPANSION_FACTOR from the collateral requirement check, or to adjust the calculation so that both precision factors cancel out, thereby restoring the intended collateral‑to‑principal ratio. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of arithmetic scaling errors that break financial invariants, leading to loss of funds and violation of the protocol’s accounting assumptions.

title: LenderCommitmentGroup_Smart picks the wrong price
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect worst‑case price selection in the function that computes the amount of collateral required for a loan. The contract is supposed to protect lenders by using the most unfavorable price from a Uniswap pool – the minimum price when the loan principal is token0 and the maximum price when the principal is token1 – so that the borrower must provide the largest possible amount of collateral. The implementation mistakenly uses Math.min for token0 and Math.max for token1, which actually selects the most favorable price for the borrower. As a result the calculated collateral amount is lower than it should be. This mis‑calculation can be exploited by a borrower who first obtains a flash‑loan, manipulates the pool price, and then borrows from the LenderCommitmentGroup_Smart contract with insufficient collateral, effectively receiving principal for near‑zero cost and leaving the lender under‑collateralized. The impact is that the lender’s collateral pool can be drained, LPs in the referenced Uniswap pool lose value, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions about over‑collateralisation are violated. The bug manifests whenever acceptFundsForAcceptBid() is called, i.e., when a borrower accepts a loan commitment, and the price oracle returns a spot price and a TWAP price. Users see the loan succeed but the required collateral appears normal, while the lender later discovers that the collateral balance is insufficient or that the loan was repaid with far less value than expected. The issue was discovered during a security audit by Sherlock, who added logging to the price variables and observed that the worstCasePairPrice variable actually held the best price for the borrower. The problem is subtle because the code comments claim a worst‑case price is being used, and the min/max functions are syntactically correct, making the logical error easy to miss. The proper fix is to invert the use of Math.min and Math.max: when the principal token is token0 the contract should take the maximum of the TWAP and immediate price, and when the principal token is token1 it should take the minimum. This change restores the intended over‑collateralisation guarantee and prevents borrowers from exploiting price manipulation to drain funds.

title: Interest rate in LenderCommitmentGroup_Smart may be gamed
content: The vulnerability is a manipulation of the interest‑rate mechanism in the LenderCommitmentGroup_Smart contract. The contract derives the loan interest directly from the pool utilization ratio, which is calculated as the amount of outstanding principal divided by the total estimated pool value (principal plus accrued interest minus liquidation premiums). Because the calculation uses the most recent on‑chain values and there is no restriction on when a lender can deposit, borrow, or withdraw shares, a borrower can artificially lower the utilization ratio and therefore obtain a much lower interest rate without taking any additional risk. The attack proceeds by first depositing a sizable amount of principal to receive pool shares, then borrowing the full amount of that principal while the utilization ratio is still low, and finally withdrawing the shares before the pool’s exchange rate is recomputed. The contract incorrectly burns the pool‑shares token prior to calculating the exchange rate, which means the withdrawn amount is based on a stale, favorable rate. As a result the borrower receives a loan at a reduced interest rate while the pool’s earnings for legitimate liquidity providers are diminished. This flaw manifests whenever a participant can perform a deposit, borrow, and share‑withdraw sequence within the same block or across consecutive blocks without any time‑based constraints. It affects all users of the lending pool: honest liquidity providers see their expected yield drop, and borrowers can obtain loans at rates that were never intended by the protocol. The issue was discovered during a security audit when the auditor simulated the described sequence in a unit test and observed that the minimum interest rate reported by the contract dropped to an unexpectedly low value, allowing the attacker to borrow at that rate and then withdraw the underlying principal. The problem is subtle because the utilization ratio appears to be a standard metric and the share‑burn operation is a routine accounting step, making the incorrect ordering of operations easy to overlook. To remediate the issue the protocol should enforce a delay or time‑lock on share burning after a loan is taken, or otherwise ensure that the exchange rate used for withdrawals is computed on the pre‑withdrawal pool state. In user‑facing terms, a lender may notice that after a loan is taken the pool balance shown in the UI drops to zero or that their accrued interest is far lower than expected, while a borrower may see that they can obtain a loan with a surprisingly low interest rate and still retrieve their original deposit, effectively receiving a free discount on borrowing costs.

title: liquidateDefaultedLoanWithIncentive can be abused to avoid interest payment
content: The vulnerability is an accounting omission in the liquidation routine of the LenderCommitmentGroup contract. When a defaulted loan is liquidated through the function liquidateDefaultedLoanWithIncentive, the contract calculates the amount that must be repaid by calling getAmountOwedForBid with the boolean flag set to false. This flag tells the helper function to return only the principal component of the debt and to ignore any interest that accrued during the borrowing period. The root cause is a logical error: the developer passed the wrong argument, causing the liquidation logic to treat the loan as if only the principal were owed. An attacker can exploit this by triggering liquidation on a defaulted loan, paying back only the principal, and receiving the liquidation incentive while the accrued interest remains unpaid. Because the TellerV2 contract’s own liquidation path requires repayment of both principal and interest, the discrepancy allows the liquidator to shift the unpaid interest to the rest of the lending pool, effectively spreading bad debt among all lenders. The exploit works whenever a loan is in default and the liquidator calls liquidateDefaultedLoanWithIncentance; no additional conditions are required. The parties affected are borrowers (who avoid interest), liquidators (who profit from the incentive and the interest shortfall), and lenders (who lose the expected interest revenue and see the pool balance shrink). The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the call to getAmountOwedForBid and noticed the false argument, a detail that can be easy to miss because the function still repays the principal and the transaction appears successful. The impact is a financial loss to the lending pool, distortion of interest accounting, and erosion of confidence in the protocol’s fairness. To remediate, the amountDue calculation must include accrued interest, for example by invoking getAmountOwedForBid with true, or by otherwise ensuring that the liquidation routine repays both principal and interest consistently with the TellerV2 contract. This class of bug is a typical under‑payment or interest‑exclusion error in loan settlement logic. From a user’s perspective, a lender may notice that after a liquidation the expected interest payout is missing or that the pool balance drops unexpectedly, while a borrower may see that no interest is charged after liquidation, contrary to the protocol’s business rules that liquidations should settle the full debt.

title: Malicious actor can steal funds using dex and data arguments in swapFromDexAndBond
content: The vulnerability resides in a swap helper function that accepts a user‑supplied DEX contract address and an arbitrary calldata blob, then forwards the calldata to the supplied address using a low‑level functionCall. Because the contract does not validate that the address is a trusted DEX nor that the calldata matches an expected swap interface, an attacker can supply any contract address and any encoded function call. In practice this means the Zapper contract can be tricked into executing token transfer or approval functions on ERC‑20 contracts for which it already holds allowance from users. The root cause is the unchecked external call that treats the DEX parameter as a trusted component, violating the principle of least privilege. An exploit proceeds as follows: the attacker calls swapFromDexAndBond, sets the dex parameter to the address of a token contract (for example WETH), and encodes a transferFrom call that moves tokens from the Zapper’s balance or from a user who previously approved the Zapper. When the Zapper executes dex.functionCall(data) the token contract processes the transfer, sending the specified amount to the attacker’s address. Because users normally approve the Zapper to spend their tokens in order to perform swaps, the malicious call can drain those approved balances without the user’s consent. The impact is the loss of user funds and, in a secondary scenario, the loss of any idle tokens held by the Zapper itself. The issue manifests whenever a legitimate user invokes the swapFromDexAndBond function; the malicious call is indistinguishable from a normal swap request from the perspective of the caller, so the funds disappear silently and the UI may simply show a successful transaction while the user’s token balance is reduced or becomes zero. The problem was discovered during a manual security audit that examined the function’s external call pattern and identified the lack of address whitelisting. It is hard to notice because the function does not revert on unexpected calldata and the token contracts do not emit warnings when called via a generic functionCall; the only symptom is an unexpected reduction in token balances. To remediate, the contract should restrict the dex parameter to a predefined list of trusted DEX router contracts, validate that the calldata matches an approved swap signature, or replace the low‑level call with a typed interface that only permits the intended swap functions. This eliminates the ability for an attacker to invoke arbitrary token methods and restores the intended business logic that the Zapper only performs swaps, not token transfers on behalf of users.

title: Incorrect accounting of cost share requests
content: The vulnerability is an inconsistent accounting error in the cost‑share request workflow of the protocol. When a user creates a cost‑share request, the contract stores the amount that will be paid out (requestPayout) in the CostShareRequest struct, but later internal functions such as setAvailableBenefits and incrementCounts use the original claimAmount, which is defined to be 10 % higher than requestPayout. This mismatch causes the protocol to deduct only 90 % of the user’s availableCostShareBenefits when a claim is denied, effectively stealing a tenth of the funds that the user has already paid for. In addition, the incrementCounts function adds the full claimAmount to the global variable openPWPRequestAmount, while the corresponding decrementCounts function subtracts only requestPayout. Because the subtraction is 10 % smaller, openPWPRequestAmount never returns to zero even after all claims are closed. The persistent non‑zero value skews the calculation of fShare and the price of the FSD token, forcing the protocol to hold ever more ether to keep the required ratio above one. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are a sudden reduction of the displayed available cost‑share balance after a denied claim, and a UI that may still indicate open requests even though the user has no active claims. The issue occurs every time a cost‑share request is opened and later denied or finalized, and it accumulates over time as more requests are processed. All members who purchase memberships with cost‑share benefits are affected, as are the protocol’s economic model and any token holders relying on correct pricing. The bug was discovered during a security audit by Sherlock through unit‑test execution that revealed mismatched values and unexpected state after claim denial. It is hard to notice because the loss is only 10 % and only manifests after a claim is rejected, which may be a rare event in normal operation. The root cause is the misuse of two semantically different variables (requestPayout vs claimAmount) in separate accounting functions, leading to an off‑by‑10 % error and a stale open‑request counter. To fix the issue the contract should consistently use requestPayout for all accounting updates, including setAvailableBenefits, incrementCounts, and decrementCounts, ensuring that the amount added to and removed from openPWPRequestAmount is identical and that availableCostShareBenefits are adjusted by the correct payout amount. This correction restores proper accounting, prevents unintended fund loss, and eliminates the artificial inflation of protocol‑wide metrics that could otherwise jeopardize the system’s stability.

title: Bonder can bypass the 1% of capital pool unbonding limit
content: The vulnerability consists of a bypass of the intended 1 percent daily unbonding limit on the FairSide token contract. The contract’s unbond function checks that the amount a single staker attempts to withdraw, added to that staker’s previously unbonded amount, does not exceed one percent of the total capital pool. This check is performed only against the caller’s own state (staker.amountUnbonded) and the current reserve balance, without any aggregation of unbonding activity across the whole protocol or across a time window. Because the limit is enforced per address rather than globally, an attacker can split the total amount of tokens they control among many self‑owned addresses, invoke unbond from each address, and stay under the per‑address 1 percent threshold on every call. The cumulative effect is that the attacker can withdraw a total amount far larger than the intended limit, draining liquidity from the pool. When a large unbond transaction appears in the mempool, other participants may rush to unbond pre‑emptively to avoid a bigger loss, amplifying the liquidity pinch. The impact is a reduction of available capital for all contributors, potential inability to fulfill redemption requests, and a loss of confidence in the protocol’s accounting guarantees. The issue manifests whenever the unbond function is called and the attacker controls multiple addresses; it does not require any special permissions or external contracts. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the logic of the unbond limit and noticed that the check does not consider global or temporal aggregation. The bug is subtle because each individual transaction passes the contract’s require statement, making it appear as a correct operation from the perspective of a single user. Conceptually, the flaw belongs to the class of “per‑entity limit bypass” bugs where a global constraint is incorrectly scoped to a single entity. To remediate, the protocol should enforce the 1 percent cap on the total amount unbonded across all users within a defined period (for example, per day) or introduce a global counter that is updated before each unbond. Alternatively, the same restriction could be applied in the token’s _beforeTokenTransfer hook to prevent mass transfers that would enable the same bypass. Proper accounting of cumulative unbond volume would align the contract’s behavior with the intended business logic that only a small fraction of the pool may be withdrawn at any time, preserving liquidity and protecting contributors.

title: Uniswap and 1inch swap function in Zapper send wrong tokenMinimum
content: The vulnerability resides in the Zapper contract functions that perform a token swap on Uniswap V3 or 1inch and then immediately call the FairSide token's bondTo function. Both swapFromUniswapAndBond and swapFrom1inchUnoswapAndBond take the amount of WETH (or the generic swapped token) returned by the DEX call and pass that value as the second argument to FSD.bondTo. The bondTo interface, however, expects the second argument to be the minimum amount of FSD tokens that must be minted, which is used as slippage protection for the bonding step. Because the contract supplies the swapped output amount instead of a user‑defined minimum FSD amount, the slippage check is effectively bypassed. If the market price of FSD moves unfavourably between the swap and the bond, the bondTo call may mint fewer FSD tokens than the user anticipates, causing the user to receive less than expected or, in the opposite direction, to trigger a revert when the minted amount is lower than the supplied tokenMinimum. This logic error can be exploited by MEV bots that front‑run the transaction, manipulate the price, and capture the difference, leading to potential token loss for honest users. The issue manifests whenever a user invokes the Zapper swap‑and‑bond flow, which is a core user‑facing feature for acquiring FSD through a single transaction. Affected parties include any user who relies on the Zapper UI to receive a guaranteed minimum amount of FSD after swapping, as well as the protocol itself because the unexpected reverts can halt bonding activity and erode trust. The bug was discovered during a manual audit of the contract source, where the auditor noticed that the parameter name tokenMinimum was being populated with the swapped token amount rather than a calculated minimum FSD amount. The problem is subtle because the function signatures match and the code compiles without warnings; only a careful review of the business logic reveals the mismatch. From a user perspective the symptoms are a missing or reduced FSD balance after a successful swap, or a transaction that fails with a revert despite the swap succeeding, which appears as “funds disappear” or “bonding failed”. The vulnerability belongs to the class of parameter‑misuse or slippage‑protection bypass bugs, where a function receives an incorrect argument that defeats intended safety checks. To remediate, the contract should expose a slippage parameter to the caller, compute the appropriate minimum amount of FSD tokens based on the expected price impact, and pass that computed value to bondTo, thereby restoring the intended protection against adverse price movements.

title: User can bypass copay and get 100% coverage
content: The vulnerability consists of an incorrect validation of a user’s cost‑share entitlement in the FairSideClaim contract. When a user opens a Cost Share Request via openPWPRequest, the contract calculates a payout amount (requestPayout) by applying a 10 % haircut to the submitted claimAmount (requestPayout = claimAmount * 0.9). The subsequent check compares the user’s availableCostShareBenefits against this reduced requestPayout instead of the original claimAmount. Because the check uses the already‑discounted value, an attacker can inflate the claimAmount to exactly availableCostShareBenefits * 10/9. After the 0.9 multiplication, requestPayout equals the full available benefit balance, the if‑statement passes, and the contract records a cost‑share request for the entire benefit amount. This allows the user to bypass the intended 10 % copay and receive 100 % coverage, resulting in a loss of funds for the protocol. The issue occurs whenever a cover holder calls openPWPRequest with a claimAmount that satisfies the described relationship; no additional constraints are required. Affected parties include any cover holder able to submit claims, the protocol’s treasury that funds the payouts, and downstream insurers that rely on the correct risk‑sharing model. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the claim‑processing logic, where the auditor noticed that the validation step used the haircut‑adjusted amount rather than the original claim amount, a subtle arithmetic mismatch that can be easily overlooked because the 10 % haircut is a legitimate business rule elsewhere in the code. The bug belongs to the class of financial‑logic errors where validation is performed on a transformed value rather than the original, leading to mismatched accounting units. From a user’s perspective the UI may display a full refund where a partial reimbursement (with a 10 % user contribution) was expected, violating the business rule that only 90 % of a claim should be covered by the protocol. The attack flow is: (1) attacker reads their availableCostShareBenefits B; (2) computes inflated claimAmount = B * 10/9; (3) calls openPWPRequest with this claimAmount; (4) validateCSR multiplies by 0.9, producing requestPayout = B; (5) the if‑statement passes because B <= B; (6) createCostshareRequest records a request for B, which is later paid out, draining the protocol of the full benefit amount. The recommended fix is to compare the user’s available benefits against the original claimAmount (or otherwise ensure that the same value is used consistently in both the haircut calculation and the eligibility check), thereby preventing the copay bypass.

title: Free CSB and bypass of maximum CSB per wallet
content: The vulnerability is a logical accounting flaw that allows a user to obtain cost‑share benefits (CSB) without paying for them and to exceed the protocol‑defined maximum of 100 ether per wallet. The contract deducts the requested claim amount from the member’s available CSB when a cost‑share request is created, and restores the same amount if the request is denied. The maximum‑benefit check is performed only during purchase, renewal and top‑up operations; it is not re‑evaluated when benefits are restored after a denial. Consequently, an attacker can repeatedly (1) purchase the full 100 ether of CSB, (2) open a cost‑share request that consumes the entire balance, (3) top up the membership with another 100 ether, and (4) trigger a denial that restores the previously deducted amount. By looping these steps, the attacker can accumulate an arbitrary amount of virtual CSB, effectively receiving free coverage and bypassing the per‑wallet cap. The flaw also permits opening cost‑share requests after a membership has expired, allowing a user to renew with a minimal payment, receive a denial, and regain the full original CSB, again resulting in free coverage. The impact includes unlimited virtual coverage that can be backed by the bonding‑curve reserve, potential draining of that reserve if large requests are approved, violation of the core invariant that limits coverage to 100 ether, and the inability of honest users to unbond because the protocol’s accounting assumes a bounded CSB amount. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit that examined the flow of CSB adjustments and identified that the restoration logic does not respect the maximum‑benefit constraint. It is hard to notice because the contract correctly enforces the limit during explicit top‑up calls, giving the impression that the cap is always respected, while the indirect restoration path bypasses the check. To remediate, the protocol should enforce the maximum‑benefit limit on every state change that modifies available CSB, including restorations after denied requests, and consider disabling top‑ups or renewals for cover IDs that have pending cost‑share requests. This class of bug can be described as an invariant‑violation or accounting inconsistency where virtual balances are manipulated without proper bounds, leading to symptoms such as users receiving no payout when they expect a refund, balances appearing to reset to zero after a request, or coverage amounts exceeding advertised limits.

title: Wrong calculation in the cover cost during membership top-up
content: The vulnerability is a mis‑calculation of the prorated cover cost that is applied when a user tops up an existing membership before the original expiration date. The contract computes a daily cost by dividing the annual cover price by the constant MEMBERSHIP_DURATION, which represents the number of seconds in a year, but it then multiplies this daily cost by the number of days remaining, which is derived by dividing the remaining time by 86400 (the number of seconds in a day). Because the daily cost is expressed in per‑second units while the remaining time is expressed in whole days, the resulting rate is orders of magnitude lower than it should be. This unit mismatch is the root cause of the bug. An attacker can exploit the flaw by initiating a top‑up at any point before the membership expires; the contract will charge a fee that is far below the proportional amount that should be owed for the remaining coverage period. From the user’s point of view the contract appears to accept a very small payment and the transaction succeeds, leading the user to believe they have paid a fair price, while in reality they have been undercharged. The impact is a systematic loss of premium revenue for the protocol, which can erode the capital pool that backs the cover and affect other stakeholders such as stakers and insurers. The condition under which the bug manifests is when block.timestamp is less than the membership’s expiry timestamp and the calculated daysRemaining is greater than zero; in that branch the faulty formula is used. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by the researcher Sherlock, who wrote a Hardhat test that compared the expected half‑year cost with the actual cost returned by the contract and observed a large discrepancy. The problem is subtle because the contract still returns a non‑zero fee and the arithmetic does not overflow, so the error can be missed without a precise reference calculation. To remediate the issue the daily cost must be expressed in the same time unit as the remaining period, for example by multiplying the annual cover price by 86400 before dividing by MEMBERSHIP_DURATION, or by converting the remaining time to seconds before applying the per‑second rate. This correction aligns the units, ensures that a top‑up for half a year costs roughly half of the full‑year premium, and restores the intended economic guarantees of the membership model. The bug belongs to the class of unit‑conversion or arithmetic‑precision errors that break business logic assumptions about proportional pricing, leading to under‑charging and potential fund depletion.

title: Reentrancy in distributePremium allows attacker
content: The vulnerability is a classic reentrancy flaw that occurs in the premium‑distribution routine of the membership management flow. When a user purchases, renews or tops‑up a membership the contract first calls the internal function that refunds any excess ETH sent (distributePremium). This refund is performed with a plain external call (sendValue) before the contract updates the critical state variables that track how many memberships a user owns (userMembership) and the aggregate cost‑share benefit (totalPWPCSB). Because the external call hands control back to the caller, a malicious user can invoke the purchaseMembership function again from within the refund callback, re‑entering the contract while the bookkeeping variables still hold their pre‑refund values. The root cause is the ordering of operations: the contract sends ether before it records the new membership and before it increments the total cost‑share counter, violating the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern. An attacker can therefore bypass the per‑user wallet limit (maxCoverWallet) and the global capital‑pool validation (validateCapitalPool) that ensures the ratio of available capital to cost‑share benefits stays above a safety threshold. By repeatedly re‑entering, the attacker can create an arbitrary number of memberships, inflate the apparent coverage without increasing the underlying capital pool, and consequently drive the FSHARE ratio below the required 100 % level, exposing the protocol to insolvency. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are confusing: the transaction appears to succeed, the user receives a refund, but the contract’s internal accounting does not reflect the new membership, leading to missing balances, zero‑price token minting, or unexpected token price behavior. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the membership lifecycle functions, where the auditor noticed that the refund call preceded state updates and that the contract lacked any reentrancy guard. The flaw can be subtle because the external call is a simple value transfer that normally seems harmless, and the contract does not emit explicit events indicating a state change before the refund, making the race condition hard to spot in normal testing. To remediate, the contract should either enforce that the sent value matches exactly the required fee (eliminating the need for a refund) or, more robustly, apply a reentrancy guard (e.g., OpenZeppelin’s nonReentrant modifier) to all entry points that involve external calls and state updates, and reorder the logic so that all critical storage writes occur before any external ether transfer. This aligns the code with the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern and prevents an attacker from exploiting the refund path to manipulate membership limits and capital‑pool invariants.

title: getTokenFShare will never increase past floor
content: The vulnerability resides in the calculation of the token share (FShare) that is used to derive the spot price of the FSD token in the FairSideNetwork contract. The function getTokenFShare multiplies the total premium‑weighted coverage sum (totalPWPCSB) by 100 using ABDKMath64x64.mul, which treats the second argument as a signed 64.64‑fixed‑point number. Supplying the integer 100 therefore causes the library to first multiply the values and then scale the result down by 1e18, effectively dividing totalPWPCSB by 1e16. As a consequence the computed fShare is orders of magnitude smaller than intended, often close to zero. The contract then applies a hard floor of 2500 ETH, so the final fShare value is always the floor regardless of the actual coverage purchased. This mis‑calculation propagates to the getFSDPrice routine, which uses the fShare to determine how much a user must pay for membership cover or to request a claim. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a normal price, but the underlying contract enforces a price that is either dramatically undervalued or over‑priced, leading to users either overpaying for protection or the protocol receiving insufficient compensation for risk. The issue appears only when the fShare calculation is executed, which is on every cover purchase and claim request, and it affects all participants—members, claimants, and the protocol’s treasury. It was discovered during a manual audit when the auditor noticed that the ABDKMath multiplication was used with a plain integer and that the resulting value was far below the expected range, triggering the floor condition every time. The bug is subtle because the code compiles without warnings and the floor guard masks the arithmetic error, making the price look plausible on the surface. To remediate, the calculation should either use plain integer multiplication (totalPWPCSB * 100) or, if fixed‑point arithmetic is required, multiply by 100 ether (or the appropriate 1e18 scaling factor) so that the result reflects the true share value. Correcting the formula restores the intended price curve, ensures that users pay the correct amount, and prevents the protocol from suffering unintended financial loss due to a systematic pricing error.
summary:
In FairSideNetwork - getTokenFShare() is used to get the FSHARE to calculate the
FSD token spot price getFSDPrice. The spot price is used to calculate the amount
the user needs to pay when paying for membership cover and requesting claims.
However, the getTokenFShare calculation of total cost share benefits is incorrect
which leads the FSHARE to always be the floor price 2500 ETH.
The formula for calculating the fshare is as follows:
https://github.com/FairSideNetwork/FairsideContractsV2/blob/main/2/contracts/network/FairSideNetwork.sol#L929
```solidity
function getTokenFShare() internal view returns (uint256) {
    uint256 fShare = totalPWPCSB.mul(100) / fsd.gearingFactor();
    // Floor of 2500 ETH
    if (fShare < getFshareFloor()) fShare = getFshareFloor();
    return fShare;
}
```
Notice that totalPWPCSB.mul(100) is using ABDK math. The result of
totalPWPCSB.mul(100) actually divides totalPWPCSB by 1e16 instead. This is because
mul multiplies totalPWPCSB and 100 then scales down 1e18.
Even if the maximum amount of coverage (100 ETH) is purchased by 1 billion users,
the resultant fshare is much under the floor value (2500 ether):
```solidity
uint256(1_000_000_000 * 100 ether).mul(100) = 10000000000000 (0.00001 ether)
```
Fshare will never represent a price on the curve as it's supposed to. Incorrect price
will be set for purchasing cover and requesting coverage.

title: Membership top-up on the last day of the duration
content: The vulnerability concerns the calculation of a prorated membership top‑up fee when a user attempts to extend a membership on the final day of its current period. The contract checks whether the current block timestamp is greater than or equal to the stored membership duration and, if not, proceeds to compute a fee based on the remaining days. The root cause is the use of integer division on the expression (duration‑block.timestamp)/86400 to obtain daysRemaining. When the top‑up is performed on the last day, the subtraction yields a value smaller than one day, and integer division truncates the result to zero. The subsequent conditional "if (daysRemaining == 0) { return fee; }" therefore returns the full annual fee instead of a proportional amount. This logic flaw allows a user who expects to pay only for the few hours or minutes left in the membership to be charged the entire yearly cost, resulting in an unexpected loss of funds. The issue manifests only under the specific condition that the top‑up transaction occurs after the membership start time but before the exact expiration timestamp, i.e., within the final 24‑hour window. It was discovered during a security audit when the test suite artificially advanced time to the last day of a 365‑day membership and observed that the estimated cost returned the full amount rather than a reduced figure. The problem is subtle because the code appears to handle the "expired" case correctly and the developer may assume that a zero‑day remainder naturally maps to a zero‑cost scenario, overlooking the fact that a zero‑day remainder should instead trigger a proportional calculation based on seconds or a special‑case handling. From the user’s perspective the UI would display a normal top‑up prompt, the user would confirm the transaction expecting a small payment, but the wallet balance would decrease by the full yearly premium, leading to confusion and potential loss of trust. The bug belongs to the class of arithmetic‑rounding or time‑granularity errors that cause incorrect fee computation at boundary conditions. To remediate the issue the contract should either forbid top‑ups when the remaining time is less than a full day, or, preferably, perform the prorated calculation using seconds (or a higher‑precision unit) so that any remaining fraction of the period is correctly accounted for. Additionally, the conditional logic should be revised to ensure that a zero‑day remainder does not default to the full fee, and comprehensive tests covering the final‑day edge case should be added.

title: TotalPWPCSB is never decremented
content: The vulnerability is an accounting inconsistency in the FairSide network where the global counter that tracks the total Cost Share Benefits (totalPWPCSB) is only ever increased and never decreased. The contract adds the benefit amount each time a membership is purchased, topped‑up or renewed via setCoverCounts, but it never subtracts the amount when a membership expires or when a claim reduces the available benefits. Because the variable is used to enforce a maximum total benefit limit and to compute the fShare factor that drives the FSD token price and staking reward ratios, the unchecked growth eventually pushes totalPWPCSB against its hard cap, causing new memberships to be rejected with a “max total cost share benefits reached” error. At the same time, the inflated fShare makes the denominator of the pricing formula grow faster than the numerator, driving the token price toward zero and collapsing the getNetworkFshare ratio, which in turn reduces calculateSmartStakingReward to near‑zero values. The issue manifests when any membership expires or a claim is processed, but because the decrement logic is missing, the state diverges from the protocol’s accounting assumptions. All participants—potential members, token holders, and stakers—are affected: users attempting to join receive a transaction revert, existing users see their token price drop dramatically, and staking rewards become negligible. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that inspected state‑changing functions and noticed that totalPWPCSB is never written to in any exit path. It is hard to notice in normal operation because the variable is internal and the cap may not be reached for a long time, so the contract appears to work until the limit is finally hit. The bug belongs to the class of missing state‑update or invariant‑violation bugs, where a global accounting variable is not kept in sync with the actual resources it represents. An attacker could deliberately inflate totalPWPCSB by repeatedly purchasing or topping‑up memberships, forcing the cap to be reached and causing the token price to collapse, effectively denying service to legitimate users and devaluing the token. The correct remediation is to add logic that decrements totalPWPCSB when a membership expires and when increaseOrDecreaseCSB is called with the decrease flag, ensuring that the global counter always reflects the sum of active Cost Share Benefits. This restores the intended economic behavior, prevents the cap from being prematurely hit, and keeps token pricing and reward calculations within expected bounds.

title: Malicious users can drain the contract's funds
content: The vulnerability is a reentrancy flaw in the buy function of a trading‑card contract that uses an ERC1155 token. The contract calculates the price of each card from a bonding‑curve sequence that depends on the current supply. Because the function calls the ERC1155 _mint routine before it updates the supply‑dependent price, the _mint call triggers the ERC1155Receiver callback on the buyer contract. A malicious buyer can implement onERC1155Received to call buy again before the original call finishes, thereby purchasing additional cards while the price variable still reflects the original supply. As a result the attacker can acquire multiple cards while paying only the price of the first card, causing the contract to receive less ether or ERC20 tokens than it should. The attack works whenever the buy function performs an external call (the mint callback) before it records the new supply or locks reentrancy, and when the token follows the ERC1155 safe transfer pattern. Users see the symptom that they receive more cards than the amount they paid, while the contract’s balance is lower than expected; the protocol loses funds because the bonding‑curve accounting is bypassed. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that included a proof‑of‑concept attacker contract that reentered the buy function via onERC1155Received. The flaw is subtle because the price calculation appears correct for a single purchase and the external call is hidden inside the mint routine, making it easy to miss in a superficial review. The bug belongs to the class of reentrancy vulnerabilities combined with mutable pricing logic such as bonding‑curve or arithmetic‑sequence pricing. To remediate, the contract should follow the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern: update the supply and compute the new price before invoking any external contract, and it should also protect the buy function with a non‑reentrant guard such as OpenZeppelin’s ReentrancyGuard. By moving state updates ahead of the _mint call or by disabling callbacks during mint, the attacker can no longer purchase extra cards at a reduced price, restoring the intended accounting and preventing fund drainage.

title: The Rounding Done in Protocol's Favor Can Be
content: The vulnerability is a rounding and price‑inflation bug that appears when a market’s totalSupply of share tokens is zero. Because the protocol calculates the value of one share by dividing the total assets by totalSupply, a zero denominator causes the share price to be treated as infinitely large. An attacker can exploit this by minting a single wei of share in a newly created throw‑away account, using that share as collateral to borrow the entire pool of assets, and then withdrawing only the minimal amount of the underlying asset that is allowed by the withdrawal check. The withdrawal logic rounds the required share redemption up to the next whole wei, which burns the single wei of share even though its implied value is huge. After the burn the throw‑away account holds no collateral but retains a large debt, while the original account, which never borrowed, now owns all the shares and can withdraw the full amount of assets, including the borrowed tokens transferred from the throw‑away account. This sequence drains the whole protocol whenever a market’s totalSupply reaches zero. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined edge‑case arithmetic in the short‑fall and withdrawal functions. It is difficult to notice because the operations involve only one‑wei amounts and the rounding behaviour is hidden behind internal accounting checks, making the protocol appear healthy while the value of a single share is massively overstated. The impact is a complete loss of funds for all users of the affected market, as the attacker can walk away with the entire asset balance. The bug belongs to the class of rounding‑up and division‑by‑zero price manipulation vulnerabilities that break accounting invariants such as share value equals total assets divided by totalSupply. To remediate, the protocol must prevent totalSupply from ever being zero, enforce a minimum non‑zero supply, use safe arithmetic that caps share price when supply is low, and adjust the withdrawal rounding to avoid burning shares whose nominal value exceeds the withdrawn assets. Proper checks should also ensure that collateral valuation cannot be inflated by a single‑wei share when the market is empty.
summary:
• When the totalSupply of a market is 0, an attacker can take advantage of #1 and #2 to drain the entire protocol.
• The attacker inflates the value of 1 share to a large value, making it sufficient to borrow all the borrowable assets using stealth donation as described in #1 using the original account.
• They create a throwAway account and mint 1 wei of share to that account as well.
– They put up this 1 wei of share as collateral, borrow all the available assets, and transfer them to the original account.
– Abandon the market by withdrawing only 1 wei of asset which is allowed, because 1 wei of asset won't be enough to make the position unhealthy (checked using auditor.shortfall at the start of the withdrawal). However, this results in 1 whole wei of share (worth a large value) being burnt due to rounding up. See #2.
– As a result, the throwaway account will now have 0 collateral and a lot of debt.
• The original account now has the claim to all the assets as they are the only holder of shares. Since the original account never borrowed, they are able to withdraw all the assets. Additionally, they receive all the borrowed assets that the throwaway account sent to it.
• If the totalSupply of a market is 0, the whole protocol can be drained.
