title: Unassigned pool earnings can be stolen when
content: The vulnerability is an accounting flaw that allows an attacker to capture earnings that were left unassigned in the pool after a borrowed maturity is liquidated. The root cause is that the Market contract’s noTransferRepayAtMaturity function is invoked with the canDiscount flag set to false during liquidation, which deliberately skips the conversion of unassigned earnings into the earningsAccumulator. As a result, those earnings remain in a temporary pool variable and are not deducted from the amount that should be repaid to the liquidated position. After liquidation, the pool’s accrueEarnings routine eventually moves the unassigned earnings into floatingAssets, where they become claimable by any subsequent deposit or borrow operation at the same maturity. An attacker can exploit this by first borrowing a minimal amount at the target maturity, thereby creating a floatingBackupBorrowed value that exceeds the current supply (which may be zero after liquidation). The attacker then deposits a tiny principal at the same maturity; the deposit logic treats the previously unassigned earnings as a fee owed to the depositor and credits the attacker with the full amount. In the provided proof‑of‑concept, depositing only one unit of principal yields a position value of roughly 6.66e18, effectively stealing the pool’s fee. The impact is that the protocol’s fee pool can be drained by repeatedly performing the borrow‑deposit sequence, reducing the returns of legitimate lenders and potentially exhausting the earnings that should be distributed to users. The condition for exploitation is the presence of non‑zero unassigned earnings after a liquidation where canDiscount is false, combined with a low or zero supply at the targeted maturity. All participants who rely on the fee distribution – lenders, borrowers, and token holders – are affected because the protocol’s accounting invariants are broken and the expected fee revenue disappears. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by the Sherlock team when a test case in Market.t.sol demonstrated that a single‑unit deposit could claim the entire liquidated fee. The flaw is subtle because the unassigned earnings are an internal bookkeeping field that is not exposed in the UI, making the loss of fees appear as a normal market fluctuation rather than a malicious extraction. To remediate the problem, the liquidation path must be changed so that any unassigned earnings are immediately transferred into the earningsAccumulator (or an equivalent over‑time accumulator) before the liquidation completes, ensuring that they cannot be reclaimed by later deposits. This change restores the intended accounting flow where fees are accrued over time and only distributed according to the protocol’s rules, eliminating the opportunity for a zero‑principal attacker to siphon funds.

title: The quantity is calculated incorrectly when
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect calculation of the quantity of eETH shares that are returned when a user deposits ETH to obtain weETH. The contract assumes that the value returned by Etherfi LiquidityPool.deposit (and the analogous stETH.submit) represents the actual amount of eETH tokens, but the LiquidityPool implementation returns the number of shares minted, which is not equal to the underlying token balance. This mismatch occurs in the depositEth function when the predefined pool is set to weETH. The internal call _ethTOeEth forwards the deposited ETH to the Etherfi liquidity pool, receives a share count, and passes that share count directly to _eethTOweEth, which in turn calls weETH.wrap. The wrap function expects a true eETH token amount, converts it to shares internally, and mints weETH accordingly. Supplying a share count instead of an amount causes two possible failure modes: if the share count is lower than the actual eETH balance, the wrap call will mint fewer weETH tokens than the user deposited, effectively leaving a portion of the user’s assets stranded in the pool; if the share count is higher than the actual eETH balance, the wrap call will revert because the liquidity pool cannot provide enough eETH to satisfy the requested amount, causing the whole transaction to fail. The bug is triggered only when depositing ETH into the weETH pool; deposits to wstETH are handled correctly because the conversion function _ethTOstEth explicitly measures the token balance before and after the operation. Users are affected because they may receive less weETH than expected, see their balance reduced unexpectedly, or experience transaction reverts with no clear error message. The protocol’s accounting is also compromised because the internal accounting variables totalValueInLp and totalValueOutOfLp are updated based on share quantities that do not reflect the true token amounts, breaking the invariant that totalValueOutOfLp should equal the total weETH supply. The issue was discovered during a manual audit when the reviewer compared the behavior of the mock liquidity pool used in tests (which returns the minted amount directly) with the real Etherfi implementation (which returns shares). The discrepancy is subtle because both functions share the same interface and the tests passed, making the bug easy to overlook. To remediate the problem, the conversion routine should be changed to return the actual eETH balance increase rather than the raw share count, for example by recording the eETH balance before and after the deposit and returning the difference, mirroring the approach used for stETH. Alternatively, the wrap function could be modified to accept share quantities and perform the appropriate conversion internally. Either way, the contract must ensure that the quantity passed to weETH.wrap represents a true token amount, preserving user expectations that depositing a given amount of ETH yields an equivalent value of weETH and maintaining correct accounting throughout the protocol.

title: Many cases stEth::transferFrom will transfer
content: The vulnerability originates from the way the stETH token represents balances as shares rather than raw wei. When a user calls the depositStEth function, the contract forwards the user‑specified _amount to IERC20(stETH).safeTransferFrom, expecting that exactly _amount of stETH will be transferred to the contract. However, because stETH rounds share conversions, the actual number of wei received can be one or two wei less than the requested amount. The contract does not verify the post‑transfer balance; it simply passes the original _amount to the internal _stEthTOwstEth function, which calls the wstETH wrapper with the same _amount. The wrapper requires that the contract hold at least the amount being wrapped. If the transferred amount is short by even a single wei, the wrap call reverts, causing the whole deposit transaction to fail. This mismatch creates a denial‑of‑service condition for the farming contract: legitimate deposits can be rejected whenever the rounding error occurs, effectively freezing the pool and preventing users from adding liquidity. The issue was discovered during a security audit of the Sophon farming contracts and is documented in a prior Lido DAO discussion, where it was classified as high severity. It is hard to notice because the shortfall is only one or two wei, which does not appear in typical balance checks and may only surface sporadically depending on the exact amount being deposited. From a user’s perspective, the UI may show a successful approval but then the transaction reverts with no obvious reason, leaving the user with a failed deposit and potentially a loss of gas. The business logic assumes a one‑to‑one relationship between the amount requested and the amount received, violating the accounting invariant that the contract’s stETH balance equals the sum of deposited amounts. To remediate, the contract should either use Lido’s transferShares function, which transfers the exact share amount, or implement a “balance‑before‑and‑after” check (FoT approach) to adjust the amount passed to the wrapper based on the actual received balance, ensuring that the wrap call never receives a larger amount than the contract holds.

title: Malicious users can bypass the blacklist.
content: The vulnerability stems from implementing a blacklist using the AccessControlUpgradeable role mechanism, where the BLACKLISTED_ROLE is assigned to addresses that should be prohibited from transferring tokens. The contract enforces the restriction through a modifier that checks the sender and receiver are not holding the BLACKLISTED_ROLE before allowing a token transfer. However, AccessControlUpgradeable provides a public renounceRole function that lets any address voluntarily revoke any role it currently possesses, including the BLACKLISTED_ROLE. Because the blacklist check only verifies that the address does not currently hold the role, a blacklisted user can simply call renounceRole(BLACKLISTED_ROLE, msg.sender) to remove the blacklist flag from themselves and then proceed with transfers that should have been blocked. This flaw can be exploited whenever a blacklisted address is able to execute a transaction; the attacker first renounces the blacklist role and then invokes a token transfer, which passes the onlyNotBlacklisted checks and succeeds. The impact is that the protocol’s compliance and anti‑money‑laundering controls are effectively bypassed, allowing malicious actors to move funds that were intended to be frozen, potentially facilitating theft, fraud, or regulatory violations. The issue manifests whenever the contract relies on role‑based blacklisting without preventing role renunciation, affecting any user that has been placed on the blacklist as well as the broader protocol and its stakeholders who trust the blacklist to enforce restrictions. The problem was discovered during a manual audit of the token’s transfer hooks, where the reviewer noticed that the onlyNotBlacklisted modifier ultimately calls onlyNotRole, which in turn can be satisfied after a user renounces the role. The bug is subtle because role revocation is a standard feature of AccessControl and appears harmless, making it easy to overlook that a blacklist should be immutable. To remediate, the protocol should avoid using roles for blacklisting altogether, replace the role with a dedicated mapping that only privileged accounts can set or clear, or override the renounceRole function to reject attempts to renounce the BLACKLISTED_ROLE. Conceptually, the fix ensures that once an address is marked as blacklisted, the status cannot be voluntarily removed, thereby restoring the intended transfer blocking behavior and preserving the integrity of the protocol’s compliance mechanisms.

title: Multihop trade allows bypassing fees by set-
content: The vulnerability is a fee‑bypass flaw in the multihop trade function that permits a trader to specify two swap operations that share the same input token but produce two different output tokens. The contract’s logic selects the fee token from the last operation, so an attacker can route the bulk of the input amount to the desired token in the first operation and send only a dust amount to a second, fake output token that is used as the fee token. After the two swaps are executed, the protocol charges fees only on the tiny dust output, leaving the large amount of the desired token locked inside the contract. Because the contract does not enforce that consecutive operations with identical input tokens must also have identical output tokens, the residual balance violates the core invariant that no token should remain in the contract after a trade. The attacker can then perform a third, minimal‑value swap that uses the locked token as the output token and pays the fee in the original input token (or another dust token). This final dust swap triggers the contract to release the entire locked balance to the attacker while only a negligible fee is taken, effectively allowing the trader to bypass fees completely. The impact is that protocol revenue is lost, the economic model is broken, and any user relying on fee collection may be defrauded. The issue occurs whenever the takeTokensAndTrade (or similar) function accepts a list of operations without validating that the output token remains constant for identical input tokens, and when the fee token can be arbitrarily chosen per operation. It affects the protocol itself, its token holders, and any participants expecting to pay the advertised fee. The flaw was discovered during a security audit through a proof‑of‑concept test that demonstrated the dust‑swap technique and observed that the contract retained a non‑zero balance of the intended output token after the initial trade. The problem is subtle because the fee is taken from a dust amount, making the discrepancy easy to overlook in normal usage and because the contract’s balance checks only verify that the final fee token balance is zero, not that other token balances are cleared. To remediate, the contract should enforce that for a series of operations sharing the same input token, the output token must also be identical, or it must reset cumulative accounting and reject mismatched output tokens. Additionally, after completing a multihop trade the contract should assert that no residual token balances remain, thereby preserving the fee collection invariant and preventing the described fee‑avoidance attack.
summary: A trader can bypass fees by setting two different output tokens for the same input token. Then only the second (fake) output token will be charged fees, and the first (real) output token remains in the contract. The trader can then retrieve the real output token by simply trading dust amount with the same output token (as outlined by the README). By setting the second output token's trade to an extremely small value in the initial trade, the trader can bypass fees completely. Consider the following scenario. Alice wants to trade 1 ETH into USDC. If she trades through Maradona as normal, she will have to take the full fee. Alice can set up the following trade through takeTokensAndTrade() to dodge fees: • Two operations • Operation 1: – ETH to USDC – Amount in = 0.9999999999999 ETH • Operation 2: – ETH to USDT – Amount in = 0.0000000000001 ETH • Fee token: USDT What will happen is that: • The two operations are performed in order: – (almost) 1 ETH gets traded into USDC – Dust amount of ETH gets traded into dust amount of USDT • After the swaps are completed, some fees are charged from the output USDT (which is a dust amount), and the rest is returned to Alice • The remaining USDC are stuck in the contract However, Alice can now perform a trade using dust amount of input ETH to USDC (and with ETH as the fee token), and the contract's entire USDC balance will be sent back to Alice, for another dust amount of ETH fee. • Breaks core invariant of the protocol that there should be no set of inputs that leaves balance within the contract • Fees can be bypassed completely

title: Fees can be bypassed by 99.99% by setting
content: The vulnerability is a fee‑bypass flaw in the multihop trade logic of the Maradona paymaster contract. It allows an attacker to construct a trade consisting of multiple hops where the final hop is configured with a ratioBps value of 1 and the fee token set to the same token that is used as the fake output of that hop. Because the contract only validates that the cumulative ratio of each hop reaches 10000 before a new input token is processed, it does not enforce that the total ratio after the last hop also equals 10000 when the hop uses contract funds. Consequently the contract treats almost the entire output amount as contract‑owned funds, takes a fee on only the tiny 1 bps portion that is swapped to the fee token, and returns that small amount to the user. The remaining 99.99 % of the expected output stays in the contract but can be retrieved later by the attacker through a dust trade that uses the same token as output. The root cause is insufficient validation of the ratioBps sum and of operations that use contract funds in a multihop context. Exploitation proceeds by submitting a legitimate first hop (e.g., ETH→USDC with ratioBps = 10000) followed by a malicious second hop (USDC→USDT with ratioBps = 1 and useContractFunds = true). The contract swaps the ETH, takes a negligible fee on the 0.01 % of USDC that is converted to USDT, and leaves the bulk of the USDC locked in its balance. From the user’s perspective the expected output token is largely missing; the user receives only a tiny amount of the fee token and may notice that the contract’s balance of the output token has increased unexpectedly. The protocol’s fee revenue is severely reduced, breaking the economic invariant that fees are collected on the full trade amount. The issue was discovered during a security audit when the auditors added a PoC test that demonstrated the 99.99 % fee evasion and the subsequent retrieval of the locked funds. The bug is hard to notice because the contract still returns a non‑zero amount and the balance change can be attributed to normal trade activity. To remediate, the contract should enforce after processing all hops that the total ratioBps equals 10000 regardless of whether contract funds are used, and it should prohibit a hop that both uses contract funds and specifies a non‑zero ratioBps or sets the fee token as the output token of that hop. In other words, the validation logic must ensure that no operation can artificially shrink the fee base by diverting the majority of the output into contract‑owned balance.

title: ERC20-only trades can be done on Maradona
content: The Maradona paymaster contract is designed to accept a sequence of swap operations that must begin with native ETH and then continue chaining swaps where each hop’s input token is the previous hop’s output token. In practice the contract only enforces that the first operation’s inputToken equals address(0) (ETH) and that the cumulative ratio of all hops reaches 100 % before a new split may start. However, the implementation does not verify that the input token of a new split matches the output token of the preceding hop. Consequently an attacker can craft a multi‑hop trade where the first hop trades a dust amount of ETH for a fake ERC20 token via a malicious Balancer pool, and the second hop uses the contract’s internal funds flag (useContractFunds) to supply an arbitrary ERC20 token such as WBTC as the input for a second swap. Because the contract never checks that the second hop’s input token equals the first hop’s output token, the two swaps are effectively independent, allowing ERC20‑only trades to be executed while the fee calculation is performed only on the tiny ETH amount. This breaks several protocol invariants: trades are no longer required to start with ETH, non‑chained swaps that the README explicitly forbids become possible, and protocol fees are bypassed. From a user’s perspective the transaction appears to succeed – the trader receives the expected output token – but the contract may retain leftover tokens (e.g., the fake token) and the fee paid is far lower than intended, effectively “money disappears” from the protocol’s fee pool. The vulnerability was discovered during a security audit when the auditors constructed a proof‑of‑concept that leveraged a custom Balancer pool and a mock ERC20 token to demonstrate the attack. The issue is subtle because the contract’s state variables (cumRatio, canBeFromEth, mustUseContractFunds) give the impression that token continuity is enforced, yet the missing explicit token‑match check allows the exploit to slip through. To remediate the flaw the contract should add a validation step inside the split‑reset branch that requires op.inputToken to equal swapOps[i‑1].outputToken, and should ensure that any new split can only be started when the previous output token is ETH or when the contract’s internal flag permits it. This change restores the intended invariant that each hop’s input token must be the previous hop’s output token, preventing arbitrary ERC20‑only trades and re‑establishing correct fee accounting.
summary: Per the Maradona code: dit-v1/contracts/Paymaster/Maradona.sol#L283 require(ops[0].inputToken == address(0), "Maradona: first operation must be from eth"); Thus it can be inferred that Maradona should only support trades beginning with ETH. Per the contest README: Q: Please discuss any design choices you made. The idea is to chain swaps one after the other so: we always swap with tokens inside the contract (e.g. you can't do wETH->USDC and DAI->wBTC in the same transaction), and the check for minAmountOut is only done in the last output overriding anything in between. Also, we decided to override every minAmountOut check for each hop except for the last one. Any vulnerability related to this should be reported as an issue. We show that it is still possible do trades similar to WETH->USDC and DAI->wBTC in the same transaction. We also extend on this fact, and show a way to perform arbitrary ERC20 trades at a cost of dust ETH amounts only using the Maradona contract. This attack also has a side effect of bypassing protocol fees. In the following branch: dit-v1/contracts/Paymaster/Maradona.sol#L377-L384 // Check if last start address is different that the current start address // If it is, we reset the cumRatio and cumOutputAmount if (i > 0 && op.inputToken != lastAddress) { require(cumRatio == 10000, "Maradona: cumRatio is not 10000"); cumRatio = 0; prevCumOutputAmount = cumOutputAmount; cumOutputAmount = 0; canBeFromEth = false; mustUseContractFunds = true; } If the new input token is different from the old input token, then a new split begins, with the previous output amount. However, there is no validation that the new input token matches the old output token. Therefore any trades similar to ETH->USDC and DAI->wBTC in the same operation, that should not have been supported, is now possible. There is still a restriction that the code takes the USDC output amount as the first trade to be DAI's input amount for the second trade (see prevCumOutputAmount = cumOutputAmount; and the line below) dit-v1/contracts/Paymaster/Maradona.sol#L389-L391 if (op.useContractFunds) { the second hop onwards, overwrite amountIn } However, by utilizing Balancer's architecture, we show that it is possible to set up a fake Balancer pool and a fake ERC20 token, to trick Maradona contract into using our supplied amount of DAI for the second operation. • Breaks protocol invariant, that Maradona is supposed to work with trades starting with ETH only • Breaks protocol invariant, that a non-chain trade as shown in the README example should not work • Breaks protocol invariant, that balances should not be left in the contract after a trade • Renders the Messi contract obsolete • Bypassing of protocol fees and all other types of fees

title: Fees can be charged on a worthless token by exploiting permissionless AMMs
content: The vulnerability is a fee‑bypass flaw that arises from the way the Maradona contract validates the token used to pay protocol fees. The contract permits the fee token to be either the native ETH (represented by address(0)) or the output token of the final operation in a multihop trade, without any additional checks on the token’s economic value or source of liquidity. Because permissionless automated market makers such as Uniswap V2/V3 and Balancer allow anyone to create a new ERC20 token and a corresponding liquidity pool, an attacker can deploy a worthless token, become the sole liquidity provider of a pool that pairs this token with a legitimate asset (for example USDC), and then construct a trade route where the final hop outputs the worthless token. When the trade is executed, the protocol calculates fees based on the amount of the output token, which in this case is the attacker‑controlled token that has no market value. Consequently, the protocol receives only the junk token as fee while the attacker withdraws the valuable asset from the pool without any fee deduction. From a user’s perspective the expected fee on USDC never appears; the user sees the full USDC amount transferred into the pool and receives no fee charge, leading to the impression that the swap succeeded without cost. The impact is a loss of fee revenue for the protocol and a breach of the economic assumptions that fees are taken from valuable assets. The issue manifests whenever a multihop swap is performed and the fee token is set to the output token of the last hop, which can be any ERC20 token created by an adversary. It was discovered during a manual audit of the fee‑validation logic, where the simple equality check was identified as insufficient. The bug is hard to notice because the fee token matches the expected output token format, and the contract does not verify that the token has any liquidity or intrinsic value. The flaw belongs to the class of “fee token spoofing” or “fee bypass via malicious output token” vulnerabilities. To remediate, the contract should restrict fee tokens to a whitelist of trusted assets (for example only ETH) or enforce that fees are always collected in a predetermined, value‑backed token, thereby preventing arbitrary ERC20 tokens from being used to evade fees.
summary: Due to the permissionless nature of UniV2/UniV3/Balancer, and by the fact that the user is free to choose the input (ETH) or the output token as fees, the Maradona contract can be tricked into receiving a worthless token as fee, effectively allowing the user to bypass any associated fees. The Maradona contract allows for creating multihop trades. While the input token must be ETH, the output token may be any token, and the trader is free to choose whether they want the input token or the output token to serve as protocol fees dit-v1/contracts/Paymaster/Maradona.sol#L288-L290 if (!validateFeeToken(feesTokenAddress, ops)) { revert("Maradona: fee token must be either eth or output token"); } dit-v1/contracts/Paymaster/Maradona.sol#L102-L105 // @dev this function validates if the fee token is either the input or output token, regardless of the type of operation (claim, swap, bridge) function validateFeeToken(address feeTokenAddress, OperationParameters[] memory ops) internal pure returns (bool) { return (feeTokenAddress == address(0) || feeTokenAddress == ops[ops.length - 1].outputToken); } However, because it is permissionless to create an ERC20 token, and create a pool of it on a supported AMM, anyone can create a new pool with their own token/their desired output token, become the sole LP there, and force the protocol into taking their worthless token as fee. This is equivalent to bypassing fee completely. The protocol will receive only worthless tokens as fees, effectively allowing complete fee bypassing.

title: If there's enough balance in feeToken prior to the swap, fees are charged early and ETH remains stuck
content: The vulnerability is a premature fee‑charging logic error that can cause a portion of the user’s input ETH to become permanently locked in the contract and subsequently withdrawn by an attacker. The contract attempts to collect protocol fees before executing any swap operation. It does this by calling tryToChargeFees with the fee token address and a computable fee amount that is derived from the expected output token amount. When the fee token happens to be the same token that will be received from the swap (for example DAI when swapping ETH for DAI) and the contract already holds enough of that token before the swap begins, the fee is taken immediately from the contract’s balance. After the fee is successfully charged, the code subtracts the fee amount from the first swap operation’s amountIn field, which represents the amount of ETH the user supplied. Because the fee was already paid in DAI, the subtraction artificially reduces the ETH amount that will be sent to the swap router, leaving the difference (the fee amount expressed in ETH) stranded inside the contract. An attacker can exploit this by front‑running the user’s transaction, sending a small amount of the output token (e.g., 0.01 DAI) to the contract just before the user’s swap. This satisfies the fee‑availability check, causing the contract to charge the fee early, reduce the user’s ETH input by the same amount, and then leave that ETH idle in the contract. The attacker can later call a public skim function or otherwise withdraw the trapped ETH, resulting in a direct loss of funds for the honest user. The issue manifests only when the fee token equals the output token and the contract’s balance of that token is sufficient before the swap. It affects any user performing a swap that involves ETH as the input and a fee token that is also the output, as well as the protocol itself because the unexpected ETH drain undermines its accounting guarantees. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the ordering of fee collection and swap execution and identified that the fee‑charging step does not consider the token flow semantics. The problem is subtle because the fee appears to be correctly deducted, yet the user’s ETH balance after the transaction is lower than expected, and the UI may still report a successful swap, making the loss easy to overlook. To remediate, the contract should defer fee collection until after the swap has produced the output token, or explicitly skip the pre‑swap fee charge when the fee token is the same as the output token. Additionally, the logic that subtracts fees from the input amount should be removed or guarded so that it only applies when the fee is taken from the input token, ensuring that no residual ETH can be left behind. This correction restores the intended accounting model where fees are taken from the token that the user actually receives, preventing the possibility of funds disappearing or being skimmed by malicious actors.
summary: If there's enough balance in feeToken prior to the swaps, fee will actually be charged from the ETH Even if the feeToken is the outputToken, the contract will attempt to charge fees prior to the swaps. (succeeded, feesCharged) = tryToChargeFees( feesTokenAddress, computableFeeAmount, feeRateBps, feeReceiver, receivingUser, false, false ); if (succeeded) { if (swapOps.length > 0) { require(swapOps[0].amountIn > feesCharged, "Maradona: cannot subtract fee from input swap"); swapOps[0].amountIn -= feesCharged; } else { require(bridgeOp.amountIn > feesCharged, "Maradona: cannot subtract fee from input bridge"); bridgeOp.amountIn -= feesCharged; } } The problem is that if for some reason there's enough balance of said feeToken prior to the swap, the fees will be charged. While this is not immediately a problem, if we look right after the tryToChargeFees function, we'll see that if it has succeeded, swapOps[0].amountIn will be decreased. This amount of ETH will then remain within the contract and can be skimmed by any user at any time. 1. User wishes to swap 1 ETH for DAI. Fee is 1%. 2. Attacker front-runs transaction and sends 0.01 DAI to the contract. 3. tryToChargeFees executes before the swap. Since the amount to execute on is computableFeeAmount, fee is calculated as 0.01 DAI. Since the contract has enough DAI, it sends the DAI now. 4. Since tryToChargeFees has executed, swapOps[0].amountIn will be decreased by 0.01 ETH. This 0.01 ETH will remain within the contract 5. The attacker can then skim the 0.01 ETH. Loss of funds

title: User can avoid paying fees by sending the ETH separately from the swap transaction
content: The vulnerability is a fee‑calculation bypass that allows a user to pay far less than the intended protocol fee when performing a multi‑step swap that is paid in ETH. The contract’s takeTokensAndTrade function only checks that msg.value (the ETH sent with the transaction) is sufficient to cover the fee for the first swap operation. If the swap consists of several consecutive swapOps, the fee is attempted a second time after all swaps have completed via tryToChargeFees. At that point the fee amount is recomputed based on the amount of tokens received from the final swap, but the payment is still taken from the original msg.value. Because the fee is now expressed as a percentage of the output token amount, the required ETH fee can be dramatically smaller than the fee that should have been charged on the original input ETH. Consequently, a user can send just enough ETH to satisfy the first, insufficient check, let the first fee attempt fail, let the swaps execute, and then pay a tiny fee that is calculated on the output token amount. In the example, a user swaps 1 WETH for 4000 USDC, should pay a 1 % fee of 0.01 WETH, but only pays 40 µWETH (0.00000004 WETH), losing over 99.9999999 % of the expected fee revenue. The issue occurs only when fees are denominated in ETH (feesTokenAddress == address(0)) and when the swap involves more than one swap operation. Any participant who can craft such a multi‑swap transaction can exploit the bug, resulting in reduced fee collection for the protocol and potential loss of yield for token holders. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit that examined the fee‑charging logic and noticed that the second fee check uses the post‑swap token amount instead of the original ETH amount. It is hard to notice because the transaction does not revert; the user receives the expected token amount and a fee is still deducted, albeit an unexpectedly small one, so UI‑level symptoms may simply show a normal swap with a tiny fee deduction. To remediate, the contract should compute the required fee based on the total value that will be swapped (or on the final token amount if fees are taken in that token) before any swaps occur, and enforce that msg.value (or the appropriate token balance) is at least that amount. Alternatively, the fee logic should be moved to a single, deterministic point that uses a consistent base amount, preventing the double‑check bypass. This class of bug falls under improper fee validation and inconsistent accounting, where the protocol’s accounting assumptions about fee bases are violated, leading to revenue leakage.
summary: User can avoid paying fees by sending the ETH separately from the swap transaction When user calls takeTokensAndTrade, it only verifies that enough msg.value is sent for the first swapOp. However, eth -> token swap can happen in multiple consecutive swap operations. If msg.value is not enough to cover the fees prior to the swaps, fees will simply not be taken and transaction will continue. After the swapOps finish, tryToChargeFees will be invoked again. However, this time the amount on which the call will be attempted is the received token amount. Imagine the following scenario: User wishes to swap 1WETH -> 4000 USDC 1. User sends 1 WETH to the contract 2. User calls takeTokensAndTrade with 2 swapOps - first one has amountIn = 40e6 wei, second one has 1e18 - 40e6. msg.value == 40e6. feesTokenAddress == address(0). 3. Fees are calculated as 1% = 0.01 WETH. First tryToChargeFees call fails as msg.value is not enough to cover the fees. 4. Swap execute. 4000 USDC is received (4000e6). 5. tryToChargeFees is called again. However, this time the amount on which fees will be calculated is 4000e6. 1% of that is 40e6. Since msg.value is enough to cover that, 40e6 is paid in fees. In the end the user did a swap for 1 WETH and should've paid 0.01e18 WETH in fees but paid only 40e6 (over 99.9999999% less) Loss of yield

title: mustUseContractFunds restrictions can be skipped due to check-before-set
content: The contract implements a loop that processes a series of swap operations (swapOps) and is supposed to enforce a rule that, after the first split operation, every subsequent operation must use the contract’s own funds (mustUseContractFunds flag). The intended rule is enforced by a require statement that checks op.useContractFunds only when mustUseContractFunds is true. However, the require is evaluated before the code that sets mustUseContractFunds to true for the following iterations. When the input token changes (i>0 && op.inputToken != lastAddress) the contract resets accounting variables and then sets mustUseContractFunds = true, but this assignment happens after the require for the current iteration. Consequently, the current operation can set useContractFunds to false and still pass the check, allowing a malicious user to craft a swapOps array where a later operation bypasses the fee‑collection logic. For example, an attacker can submit ops[0] with ETH input, ops[1] with useContractFunds true, and ops[2] with useContractFunds false; the third operation will not be forced to use contract funds, reducing the amount of ETH counted for fees. The vulnerability stems from a check‑before‑set ordering mistake, a classic logic‑flow bug where state is updated after it is validated. It can be exploited whenever a sequence of swaps includes a token change that triggers the flag reset, which is a common pattern in multi‑hop trades. The impact is that the protocol may collect insufficient fees, leading to revenue loss and potential imbalance in accounting, as the contract’s internal accounting assumes all later swaps are funded by the contract. Users may notice that expected fees are not deducted, or that the contract’s balance after a trade is lower than anticipated, violating the business rule that fees must always be taken. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by Sherlock, who noticed that the require statement appears before the flag assignment and that the flag’s purpose is not enforced for the iteration that triggers it. The bug is subtle because the require condition looks correct in isolation and typical unit tests may not cover multi‑step swaps with token changes, making the flaw easy to miss. To remediate, the require that enforces mustUseContractFunds should be moved after the flag is set, or the flag should be set before the loop iteration begins, ensuring that every operation after a token change is validated against the updated rule. In broader terms, this is a state‑transition ordering vulnerability where a security‑critical condition is checked before the relevant state variable is updated, allowing an attacker to bypass intended restrictions.

title: A malicious executor can delete the fees been
content: The vulnerability is an economic manipulation that allows a malicious executor of the ArrakisStandardManager contract to delete the fees that are accrued for the pool manager. The root cause is that the ValantisHOTModule.swap function accepts an arbitrary router address and payload, then performs three steps: it withdraws liquidity from the pool, executes the supplied payload via a low‑level call to the router, and finally deposits the resulting token balance back into the pool. A slippage check is performed after the payload execution, requiring the output token balance to increase by at least the expected minimum return, which is forced to be at least one unit. Most admin functions called through the router would fail this check because they do not transfer tokens, but the SovereignPool.claimPoolManagerFees function does transfer the manager fees to the caller (the module). When a malicious executor includes a payload that calls claimPoolManagerFees, the module receives the fees during step two, satisfying the slippage condition, and then re‑deposits those fees into the pool in step three. As a result, the fees that should be claimable by the pool manager are effectively erased from the manager’s balance and become part of the pool’s liquidity. Additionally, the poolManager variable is set to address(0) during the attack, causing any function protected by the onlyPoolManager modifier to revert, which breaks expected pool management operations. The issue occurs during a rebalance transaction where the executor role, although described as restricted, can supply a malicious payload. It is hard to notice because the rebalance call succeeds, no revert is emitted, and the pool’s token balances appear normal while the manager’s fee accounting shows a zero balance. The impact is loss of all accrued manager fees for the affected vault and disruption of pool manager functionality. The vulnerability was discovered through manual audit and a proof‑of‑concept test that demonstrated the fee‑stealing flow. To fix the issue, the module should reject any router address that points to the pool it is managing, preventing the module from calling claimPoolManagerFees on its own pool, and the design should enforce that only legitimate swap operations that respect accounting invariants are allowed. This class of bug falls under unchecked external calls with insufficient validation of side‑effects, leading to unauthorized fund redirection and accounting violations.
summary: The contest README states that the executor of ArrakisStandardManager is a RESTRICTED role during rebalance action on vaults. ArrakisStandardManager::rebalance() with a malicious payload, which ends up stealing the accrued manager fees and re-depositing them into the pool’s liquidity. On calling rebalance(), it makes a call to the module, with provided payloads_ from the executor: (bool success,) = address(module).call(payloads_[i]); For this attack, the payload’s function signature will be of the swap() function in the ValantisHOTModule. The swap() function essentially does these 3 things: 1. Withdraw liquidity from the pool (via ALM) 2. Do an arbitrary call to an arbitrary address (router_.call(payload_)) 3. Deposit the resulting balance back into the pool (via ALM) The intended functionality is that in step 2, a call is made to a router which swaps the tokens to rebalance the funds. However, a malicious executor can use this arbitrary call to execute any admin function in other contracts (HOT, SovereignPool) that only this module is allowed to call. The issue with the above is that the swap() function has a slippage check after step 2: if (zeroForOne_) { if (balance1 < _actual1 + expectedMinReturn_) { // require(balance1 >= _actual1 + expectedMinReturn_); revert SlippageTooHigh(); } } else { if (balance0 < _actual0 + expectedMinReturn_) { revert SlippageTooHigh(); } } This means that in order for the swap() to not revert, the balance of the output token must increase by at least expectedMinReturn_ during step2. Now due to the _checkMinReturn check that is done at the start of swap(), the expectedMinReturn_ must be at least 1. Hence, in step 2, trying to call admin functions like HOT.setFeeds() will revert since no tokens are sent in to the contract during this call, so it fails the slippage check shown above. This is the case for most admin functions except for two, one of which is SovereignPool.claimPoolManagerFees: ```solidity function claimPoolManagerFees( uint256 _feeProtocol0Bips, uint256 _feeProtocol1Bips ) external override nonReentrant onlyPoolManager returns (uint256 feePoolManager0Received, uint256 feePoolManager1Received) { (feePoolManager0Received, feePoolManager1Received) = _claimPoolManagerFees( _feeProtocol0Bips, _feeProtocol1Bips, msg.sender ); } ``` We can see that the pool manager fees are sent to msg.sender which is the module. This will increase the module’s balance during step 2, allowing it to pass the slippage check. Then, these claimed manager fees will be deposited back to the pool in step3, effectively deleting the accrued manager fees. (All of this is proven in the coded PoC) In addition to the above fund loss, since poolManager is updated to address(0), any onlyPoolManager functions within the pool will revert. 100% of the fees which are meant for the Arrakis manager are re-deposited into the pool by a malicious executor and never claimable by the manager.

title: Incorrect handling of first deposit for new module
content: An incorrect handling of the first deposit in a newly‑installed module allows the entire liquidity of the Arrakis pool to be withdrawn to the ArrakisStandardManager. The contract code assumes that when the flag notFirstDeposit is false the reserves returned by pool.getReserves() are only dust left after a previous withdrawal. When a new module is set via ArrakisMetaVault.setModule, the old module withdraws all liquidity and transfers it to the new module, which then calls initializePosition to deposit the full amount. Because the boolean notFirstDeposit is never reset, the first deposit logic treats the full reserves as dust and executes the dust‑removal branch, calling alm.withdrawLiquidity with the full reserve amounts and sending the tokens to the manager. Consequently the pool becomes empty, the vault’s share value drops to near zero and users receive no tokens for their deposits. The issue was discovered during a functional audit that exercised module replacement and observed that the manager balance increased by the full pool amount after the first mint. The bug is subtle because the code path is only exercised after a module change, a scenario that is not covered by typical tests, and the manager is a trusted contract, so the loss is not immediately obvious. An attacker can further exploit the situation by calling ArrakisStandardManager.rebalance with a payload that sets the pool’s manager to address(0). This causes pool.claimPoolManagerFees to revert, which in turn makes withdrawManagerBalance revert, preventing the trusted manager from returning the funds. The result is a denial‑of‑service that locks the withdrawn liquidity forever unless a new vault is deployed and the manager manually recovers the tokens. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “incorrect initialization state handling” and “assumption‑based fund routing” bugs, where state variables are not reset after a contract upgrade, leading to mis‑classification of legitimate balances as dust. To fix the issue the code must reset or correctly initialize the notFirstDeposit flag when a new module is installed, and the dust‑removal logic should verify that the reserves are indeed negligible before withdrawing, or be disabled for the first deposit after a module change. Additionally, the manager‑withdrawal flow should be hardened against reverts caused by pool manager changes, for example by separating fee collection from the manager balance recovery or by protecting the manager address from being set to zero.
summary: See detail. (uint256 _amt0, uint256 _amt1) = pool.getReserves(); if (!notFirstDeposit) { if (_amt0 > 0 || _amt1 > 0) { // #region send dust on pool to manager. address manager = metaVault.manager(); alm.withdrawLiquidity(_amt0, _amt1, manager, 0, 0); // #endregion send dust on pool to manager. } _amt0 = _init0; _amt1 = _init1; notFirstDeposit = true; } This code assumes that the reserves of the pool (_amt0, _amt1) will be dust amounts. The case that the protocol did not consider: This module could be a new module that was set via ArrakisMetaVault.setModule(). When setModule() is called, it withdraws all the liquidity through the old module: _module.withdraw(module_, BASE); // BASE means withdraw 100% of the liquidity // the new module (module_) is the receiver of the liquidity (_module is the old module, and module_ is the newly set one) Then, all the funds are directly transferred to the new module, and initializePosition is called to deposit it into the pool. This issue is that the notFirstDeposit boolean is still false, indicating that the first deposit has not yet occured. Then when the first deposit occurs in the module, the ‘dust removal’ logic shown earlier is triggered in the the new module. However all the liquidity from the old module has been deposited via the new one. This means that _amt0 and _amt1 will not be dust, as they represent the entire liquidity of the pool. Then, as shown in the PoC, the ‘dust removal’ logic withdraws the entire liquidity of the pool, and sends it to the manager of the meta vault (ArrakisStandardManager). So far, while this is already a severe error, it’s not all bad since the owner of ArrakisStandardManager is trusted, and they can withdraw the funds via withdrawManagerBalance() and return the funds so that users don’t lose any funds. However, it gets even worse, because a malicious executor can DOS the withdrawManagerBalance() function for that specific vault. There is a PoC for the • Malicious executor calls ArrakisStandardManager.rebalance(), with malicious payload • It ends up calling pool.setPoolManager(address(0)) • Now pool.claimPoolManagerFees() will revert since the ValantisHOTModule is no longer the pool manager • Hence, withdrawManagerBalance() will revert since it requires pool.claimPoolManagerFees() to be called via the module. pool to make the managerFee variable non-zero so that the expectedMinReturn passed in to within ValantisHOTModule.swap() of 1 can be met. (see PoC to understand) 100% of the pool liquidity is lost after the first deposit occurs in a new module. It is sent to the ArrakisStandardManager. The value of everyone’s shares in the vault goes to effectively zero. Then due to the DOS by the malicious executor, the funds cannot be withdrawn from the manager by calling withdrawManagerBalance(vault). The only way would be to deploy an entirely new vault with the same token0 and token1, and then calling withdrawManagerBalance(newVault) to collect the tokens from the ArrakisStandardManager contract.

title: Through rebalance(), an executor can drain
content: The vulnerability is an economic drain that can be triggered by a malicious executor during the rebalance operation of an ArrakisStandardManager vault. The root cause is the lack of validation on the router address supplied to the ValantisHOTModule.swap function and the allowance for the HOT.depositLiquidity call to be executed while the pool reserves are temporarily zero. Because the pool calculates its reserves for rebase tokens directly from the token balance of the pool contract, an attacker can artificially inflate the reserves by sending a tiny amount of a rebase token to the pool after liquidity has been withdrawn. The swap function then performs an arbitrary call to the attacker‑controlled router, which uses the inflated reserves to mint a large amount of vault shares at a negligible price (the price is derived from the near‑zero reserves). After the swap completes and the liquidity is re‑deposited, the attacker burns the freshly minted shares and extracts almost the entire pool balance, losing only a few wei of each token. This attack requires at least one rebase token in the pool, the executor role to be unrestricted during rebalance, and the router parameter to be unchecked. The impact is a loss of over 99 % of the vault’s assets and the associated fees, affecting all token holders, the vault manager, and the protocol’s reputation. The issue was discovered during a security audit and demonstrated with a proof‑of‑concept test that shows the pool TVL dropping from thousands of dollars to a few tens after a single transaction. The bug is hard to notice because the pool’s reserves appear zero during the withdrawal step, and the swap function’s external call looks legitimate, masking the manipulation of token balances. To remediate, the protocol should forbid HOT.depositLiquidity during rebalance, enforce a whitelist or other validation on the router address, and ensure that share minting cannot occur when the pool’s total deposit amount is effectively zero, thereby preventing cheap share creation and subsequent fund drainage.
summary:
The contest README states the following:
Executor of ArrakisStandardManager is RESTRICTED during rebalance action on vaults.
This is a complex attack performed by a malicious executor to drain a vault during rebalance.
It requires at least one of the tokens to be a rebase token, since it requires the pool reserves to be increased without calling HOT.depositLiquidity()
On calling rebalance(), it makes a call to the module, with provided payloads_ from the executor:
(bool success,) = address(module).call(payloads_[i]);
For this attack, the payload’s function signature will be of the swap() function in the ValantisHOTModule
The swap() function essentially does these 3 things:
1. Withdraw liquidity from the pool (via ALM)
2. Do an arbitrary call to an arbitrary address (router_.call(payload_))
3. Deposit the resulting balance back into the pool (via ALM)
The intended functionality is that in step 2, a call is made to a router which swaps the tokens to rebalance the funds. However, since the router_ param is not checked, a malicious executor can pass in any address they want.
After step 1, the pool’s reserves for both tokens is 0. Then in step 2, the executor can mint vault shares at a very cheap price, since the price depends on the pool’s reserves.
Attack Details
However, when pool reserves are equal to 0, depositing liquidity will fail due to the error: SovereignPool__depositLiquidity_zeroTotalDepositAmount. To solve this, the executor must be able to somehow slightly increase the values returned by pool.getReserves()
For non-rebase tokens, the only way would be to increase reserve0 or reserve1 in the pool, but this would require depositing liquidity, which would revert since the reserves are 0.
However for rebase tokens, the reserves are calculated via:
reserve = _token0.balanceOf(address(this));
This can be inflated by the executor since they simply have to send the token to the pool.
Now after step2, the swap() function also has a check to ensure that expectedMinReturn_ is met.
To ensure that this doesn’t revert, the executor simply passes expectedMinReturn=1 (0 can’t be used due to _checkMinReturn()) and amountIn=1, and sends 1 wei of the output token to the module, to meet the minimum expected return.
preventing this attack, since the attacker redeems their vault shares after the rebalance is over.
Summary of Attack (see PoC for implementation):
1. Malicious executor calls ArrakisStandardManager.rebalance()
2. ValantisModule.swap() is called, with expectedMinReturn=1 and amountIn=1 and zeroToOne=false
3. This executes router_.call(payload), which calls mintFreeShares() on the attacker’s fake router contract
1. This function call first sends 1 wei of token0 and token1 to the SovereignPool, so that the reserves are non-zero
2. Then, it mints 100e18 vault shares, for the price of 100 wei (since the liquidity was withdrawn in step1 of the swap() function)]
3. It sends 1 wei of token0 to the module, so that the expectedMinReturn_ check does not revert
4. The remainder of ValantisModule.swap() occurs, re-depositing funds into the pool.
5. Attacker calls Vault.burn(100e18, attacker) to burn the 100e18 shares, stealing over 99% of the vault’s funds.
Ultimately, the attacker is able to steal 99% of the pool’s reserves, while spending 100 wei of each token, which is a negligible cost.
100% of the fees which are meant for the Arrakis manager are re-deposited into the pool by a malicious executor and never claimable by the manager.
While restricting router_ to a whitelist technically prevents the attacks, it also hinders the functionality of the protocol and is an overly restrictive solution, and is definitely not optimal. Since there are already various checks during rebalance, it is clear that the protocol intent was to allow the executor to provide any router_ as long as it meets constraints like expectedMinReturn_ and the vault TVL does not drop significantly after the rebalance.
The attacks show features that the protocol did not consider (1. minting cheap shares from the vault, or 2. calling admin-only functions), so additional checks should be added to prevent these attacks.
This means that the reports should not be duplicated, since their attack methods and root causes are different.

title: ArrakisMetaVault::setModule Malicious execu-
content: The vulnerability resides in the module‑upgrade mechanism of the Arrakis vault system. When an admin whitelists a new module and later calls the manager’s setModule function, the manager forwards a call to the module’s withdraw routine and then executes an arbitrary list of payloads supplied by the caller. Because the manager does not verify that the token reserves transferred to the new module match the vault’s expected balance, a malicious executor can craft a payload array that first re‑initialises a position in the new module (or does nothing) and then immediately calls the module’s withdraw function with an attacker‑controlled recipient. This sequence moves the entire vault balance out of the pool and into an address of the attacker, effectively draining all user funds. The flaw is a logical omission: the setModule flow assumes the new module will behave honestly and does not enforce any post‑transfer accounting checks. Exploitation requires only that a legitimate module be whitelisted – a condition that is normally satisfied during routine upgrades – after which the attacker invokes setModule with the malicious payloads. The impact is total loss of deposited assets, leaving liquidity providers with a zero balance and breaking the protocol’s accounting guarantees. The issue was discovered during a security audit when the reviewer noticed that the manager executes external calls without validating the resulting reserves. It is hard to notice because the upgrade transaction appears normal; the malicious calls are embedded in the payload array and the manager does not emit explicit warnings about unexpected withdrawals. To remediate, the manager should compare the vault’s token balances after the new module is set against the pre‑upgrade totals, reject the upgrade if they differ, and restrict the executor role to trusted callers or limit the payloads to a safe whitelist. In essence, the bug is an unchecked external call during a module swap that enables a “withdraw‑after‑upgrade” attack, violating the fundamental business rule that a vault’s assets must remain intact after a module change.
summary:
A malicious executor, after a new module is whitelisted by an admin, can drain the vault by calling ArrakisStandardManager.setModule() with a malicious payloads_.
The setModule() function of the ArrakisStandardManager contract allows an executor to set a new module for a vault: ArrakisStandardManager.sol#L438.
It calls ValantisModule.withdraw(), to withdraw the funds from the pool and transfer to the new module: ValantisHOTModule.sol#L235.
Once the vault's funds are in the new module, the first malicious payloads_ is executed and calls ValantisModule::initializePosition to deposit the liquidity back into the pool: ValantisHOTModule.sol#L148.
Lastly, the second payloads_ of the malicious executor gets executed and calls ValantisModulePublic::withdraw which calls ValantisModule::withdraw on the new module and withdraws all funds to an arbitrary address: ValantisHOTModule.sol#L203.
Theft of all funds in the vault.
Scenario
1. Owner whitelists a legitimate new module with ArrakisMetaVault::whitelistModules.
2. Malicious public vault executor calls ArrakisStandardManager::setModule with a malicious payloads_.
1. It calls ArrakisMetaVault::setModule.
2. It calls ValantisModulePublic::withdraw which calls _module.withdraw(module_, BASE) to withdraw all vault's funds from old to new module.
3. Malicious executor has provided two payloads
1. The first one calls ValantisModule::initializePosition to deposit liquidity into the new pool.
2. Then the second malicious payloads_ is executed and contains a call to ValantisModule::withdraw with attacker as the receiver direct theft of funds, the executor can also call withdrawManagerBalance which would transfer all the balance of the module to the manager. Or also not call any function at all (payloads is an empty array), and leave the balances in the module.

title: Adding liquidity can be DoSed due to calcula-
content: Adding liquidity to the Arrakis vault can be unexpectedly reverted because the router contract calculates the required token amounts using a rounding‑down strategy, while the downstream mint and deposit functions round up. When a user supplies the maximum token amounts (amount0Max and amount1Max), the router’s _getMintAmounts() function may report that slightly fewer tokens are needed (for example 1e18‑1 wei of each token). The router then pulls exactly that amount from the user and forwards it to the vault. Inside the vault, the mint function recomputes the proportion and the deposit function in the ValantisHOTModulePublic contract independently rounds the required amounts up, expecting the full 1e18 wei of each token. Because the router only holds 1e18‑1 wei, the deposit call fails and the whole transaction reverts. This mismatch is a classic rounding‑inconsistency bug that manifests as a one‑wei shortfall, which is easy to miss during testing because the difference is tiny and the revert message may be generic. The vulnerability can be exploited to perform a denial‑of‑service attack: an attacker can repeatedly trigger the mismatched calculation, preventing legitimate liquidity providers from adding funds, effectively freezing the growth of the pool. The impact is that users attempting to add liquidity see their transactions revert, receive no shares, and lose only the gas spent, while the protocol suffers from reduced liquidity and potential loss of revenue. The issue occurs whenever the pool reserves and vault totalSupply are not perfectly aligned, such as when they contain an extra unit of token due to prior operations. It affects liquidity providers, the vault contract, and any downstream users relying on the added liquidity. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that traced the flow of token amounts across the router, vault, and hot‑module contracts and identified the divergent rounding behaviours. Because the discrepancy is only a single wei, it does not cause overt token loss, making it hard to notice without detailed accounting. The proper remediation is to make the amount calculations consistent across all involved functions, for example by updating _getMintAmounts() to round up or by using a shared arithmetic library that guarantees identical rounding semantics, thereby ensuring that the router always supplies at least the amount required by the downstream contracts.
summary:
When users add liquidity, they send tokens to the ArrakisPublicVaultRouter contract. The ValantisHOTModulePublic contract then takes the required tokens from the ArrakisPublicVaultRouter contract. However, due to a calculation mismatch, the required amount is often greater than the user-sent amount, causing the transaction to be reverted.
Let's consider following scenario:
1. The current state:
• pool: reserve0 = 1e18 + 1, reserve1 = 1e18 + 1
• vault: totalSupply = 1e18 + 1
2. Bob calls the ArrakisPublicVaultRouter.addLiquidity() function with the following parameters:
• amount0Max = 1e18, amount1Max = 1e18
3. At L139, the _getMintAmounts() function returns:
• (sharesReceived, amount0, amount1) = (1e18 - 1, 1e18 - 1, 1e18 - 1)
4. The router contract takes token0 and token1 from Bob in amounts of 1e18 - 1 each and calls the _addLiquidity() function with above parameters.
5. In the _addLiquidity() function, ArrakisMetaVaultPublic.mint(1e18 - 1, Bob) is invoked at L898.
6. In the ArrakisMetaVaultPublic.mint() function:
• at L58, the proportion is recalculated as 1e18 - 1
• _deposit(1e18 - 1) is called at L71
• in the _deposit() function, ValantisHOTModulePublic.deposit(router, 1e18 - 1) is invoked at L150
7. In the ValantisHOTModulePublic.deposit() function:
• amount0 = 1e18, amount1 = 1e18(at L71, L73)
• at L79, L80, it takes token0 and token1 from the router in amounts of 1e18 each
Finally, the process fails because there is only 1e18 - 1 in the router, as mentioned in step 4.
This problem occurs because the calculations in the ArrakisPublicVaultRouter._getMintAmounts() function rely on rounding down. In contrast, the proportion calculation in the ArrakisMetaVaultPublic.mint() function and the amount calculations in the ValantisHOTModulePublic.deposit() function are based on rounding up.
Adding liquidity can be DoSed due to the calculation mismatches.

title: ArrakisMetaVaultPrivate::fund No slippage con-
content: The vulnerability is a front‑running slippage‑control weakness in the private‑vault deposit function of ArrakisMetaVaultPrivate. Because the contract does not expose any minimum‑share or price‑range checks when a vault owner calls the fund (depositLiquidity) method, an attacker can submit a transaction that changes the pool price immediately before the deposit is executed. In the described scenario the attacker swaps a large amount of one token to push the pool price far outside the expected bounds, then the victim’s deposit is processed at this manipulated price. The victim’s liquidity is therefore added at an unfavorable rate, creating a highly unbalanced position where one side of the supplied assets is over‑exposed. The attacker can then back‑run the transaction, swapping the over‑exposed asset for the other token and extracting profit, while the depositor ends up with fewer shares than expected or even a net loss of value. This issue occurs whenever a private vault owner deposits liquidity without explicit slippage limits, and it can be triggered by any participant who can front‑run the deposit transaction, which is common in public mempools. The affected parties are the vault owner (who loses value) and any users relying on the private vault’s accounting, as the protocol’s accounting assumptions about balanced liquidity are violated. The problem was discovered during a manual audit that simulated deposit and swap sequences using a Uniswap V3 reference script, revealing that the price bounds supplied to the deposit function are not enforced. The bug is subtle because the contract does not revert or emit an obvious error; the pool state simply changes and the depositor receives fewer assets, which may be mistaken for normal market movement. The class of bug is a missing slippage protection / price‑oracle validation flaw in a liquidity‑adding function. To remediate, the deposit interface should require the caller to specify acceptable lower and upper sqrt‑price bounds (e.g., _expectedSqrtSpotPriceLowerX96 and _expectedSqrtSpotPriceUpperX96) and should revert if the current pool price falls outside these limits, thereby preventing deposits at manipulated prices. From a user’s perspective the symptom is that after depositing, the expected amount of liquidity tokens or the value of the deposited assets appears lower than anticipated, sometimes showing a zero or negative net gain, and the user may see their balance shrink without a clear on‑chain error. This violates the business logic that a deposit should not lose value due to price manipulation, breaking the accounting guarantees of the vault.
summary:
An attacker can front-run a deposit transaction for an ArrakisMetaVaultPrivate, forcing the depositor to deposit in an unbalanced way. This increases liquidity around an unfavorable price, leading to a loss of one side of the provided liquidity.
The owner of a private vault has full ownership of the shares of liquidity, so they are not even calculated explicitly. It is thus not possible to quantify the slippage control as a minimum amount of shares minted.
However, by providing liquidity around an unfavorable price, the owner of the vault exposes one side of his liquidity to be backrun, as we will see in the concrete example below.
An attacker can manipulate the price at which liquidity is added, leading to potential losses for the depositor.

title: Vault portion calculation in
content: The vulnerability resides in the calculation of the vault portion used by the PrizePool contract when determining how much of the total contributed assets belong to the vault. The function that computes the start draw identifier for the accounting range reads a value that can be overwritten in the circular buffer that stores total contributions, but the same identifier is not applied when reading the vault‑specific and donation‑specific accumulators. Because the total accumulator is updated every draw while the vault and donation accumulators are only updated when a contribution occurs, after the buffer wraps around (365 draws) the oldest draw entry in the total accumulator is replaced, whereas the vault accumulator may still contain the original entry. Consequently the contract sums a longer period for the vault than for the total, inflating the vault’s share. An attacker can trigger this condition by letting the pool run for more than 365 draws without making a vault‑related contribution each day, or by deliberately timing contributions to keep the vault accumulator stale. When the inflated vault portion is later used to compute a user’s share of the prize, the user receives a higher probability of winning than the protocol intends, and in extreme cases the mismatch can cause an under‑flow in the total‑supply calculation, leading to a revert that prevents any prize from being claimed. The issue appears only after the circular buffer has been filled, i.e., after the 365th draw, and is therefore hard to notice during short‑term testing because the numbers look correct for the first year of operation. It was discovered during a formal audit by reviewing the range‑start‑draw logic and adding a test that simulated 366 consecutive draws, which exposed the discrepancy between the total and vault portions. The bug belongs to the class of accounting‑window mismatches caused by inconsistent handling of circular buffers, a subtle state‑synchronisation error that violates the invariant that the vault portion must be computed over the same draw range as the total contribution. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a normal prize balance but the underlying calculation gives them a larger chance to win, or the claim transaction may fail with an underflow revert, effectively making the prize disappear. The correct fix is to cap the range size used to compute the inclusive start draw identifier to the size of the circular buffer (365 draws) so that both total and vault accumulators reference a draw that is guaranteed to still exist in the buffer. By ensuring the start identifier is never older than the oldest entry, the vault portion will be calculated over the same period as the total, restoring the intended accounting guarantees.

title: Unfair Manipulation of Winning Chances Due
content: The vulnerability is an economic manipulation flaw in the PoolTogether prize pool deployed on Blast where the prize token, WETH, is a rebasing token that automatically increases its balance in Automatic mode. The contract exposes a public function, contributePrizeTokens, that allows any caller to transfer any amount of the token balance that has grown since the last accounting (the delta balance) into an arbitrary vault’s accumulator. Because the delta balance includes the yield generated by the rebasing token, a malicious participant can repeatedly call this function, specifying their own vault address and the exact amount of newly minted yield. By doing so they siphon the automatically generated yield from the prize pool and credit it to their vault, inflating their contribution share while simultaneously reducing the share of all other vaults. The inflated share expands the malicious vault’s winning zone – the portion of the total ticket‑weighted average balance (TWAB) that determines prize eligibility – and shrinks the winning zones of honest participants. From a user’s perspective the symptom is a lower than expected chance of winning a prize despite having contributed the same amount of tokens; legitimate users may see their odds drop or feel that “nothing happens” when they keep contributing. The flaw occurs whenever the prize token is in Automatic rebasing mode and the contributePrizeTokens function is callable by anyone without checks on the source of the contributed amount. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the accounting logic of the prize pool and noticed that the delta balance is not restricted to genuine deposits. The issue is hard to notice because the token balance naturally grows, making the extra yield appear legitimate, and the contract does not emit any warning that the yield has been redirected. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of “unchecked rebasing token yield siphon” or “inflation attack” where economic state can be artificially inflated by an attacker. To remediate the problem the protocol should configure the WETH token to Claimable mode so that rebasing does not affect the raw balance, expose a dedicated claimYield function that sends the claimable amount to a neutral address (e.g., a donator or the prize pool itself), and restrict contributions to only genuine deposits or require proof of ownership. This prevents arbitrary capture of rebasing yield and restores fairness to the prize distribution mechanism.
summary:
• The PoolTogether protocol on Blast will use WETH as it's prize token as mentioned by sponsor, which generates yield over time. This yield can be stolen and used to manipulate the vaults' winning chances unfairly. By contributing the stolen yield to their own vault, users can inflate their vault's portion, increasing their chances of winning prizes while decreasing the chances for other legitimate users. This undermines the fairness of the prize distribution.
• The PoolTogether protocol will be deployed on Blast, and as the sponsor mentioned, WETH will be the prize token.
• WETH on Blast is a rebasing token that automatically generates yield over time. WETH holders have three Yield Modes for rebasing: Void, Automatic, and Claimable. The Default mode is Automatic, which means the balance will increase over time by the yield generated.
• The prizePool will hold WETH as the prize token and will generate yield over time. However, this yield can be stolen by anyone, as they can contribute it to their own vault by calling the contributePrizeTokens() function, passing their vault and the amount of yield generated.

```solidity
function contributePrizeTokens(address _prizeVault, uint256 _amount) public returns (uint256) {
    uint256 _deltaBalance = prizeToken.balanceOf(address(this)) - accountedBalance();

    if (_deltaBalance < _amount) {
        revert ContributionGTDeltaBalance(_amount, _deltaBalance);
    }
    uint24 openDrawId_ = getOpenDrawId();
    _vaultAccumulator[_prizeVault].add(_amount, openDrawId_);
    _totalAccumulator.add(_amount, openDrawId_);
    emit ContributePrizeTokens(_prizeVault, openDrawId_, _amount);
    return _deltaBalance;
}
```

• The idea is that this yield is generated from all vault contributions. However, a malicious user can exploit this feature to their advantage. While this might be considered a missing feature (not benefiting from yield) in different protocol contexts, within the PoolTogether on Blast scenario, it has a detrimental effect. The malicious user's ability to exploit the yield generation artificially inflates their vault's portion compared to other vaults. This act will decrease other vaults portions consequently increases the malicious user vault portion, thus increase his chances of winning prizes and decrease others chances.
• For the malicious user's vault, the increase in their contribution portion will lead to a higher winning zone thus more chances to win. Conversely, for other vaults, the decrease in their contribution portions will lead to a smaller winning zone reducing their chances of winning.
• This manipulation undermines the fairness of the prize distribution. Not only will the yield be stolen from all vaults contributions and not be spread to them proportionally, but it will also affect their winning chances by decreasing them. This gives the malicious user an unfair advantage by increasing their likelihood of winning at the expense of others.

Scenario
Normal Case
• Let's say from draw 4 to draw 40, we have:
– vault1.contributionBetween = 100
– vault2.contributionBetween = 100
– totalContributionBetween = 200
• To calculate their portions:
– v1.portion = 100 / 200 = 0.5
– v2.portion = 100 / 200 = 0.5
Assuming the TWAB balance is 500 for both vaults and they both have 1 user for easy calculation (so users twab also 500), and ignoring the odds scaling:
• winningZone(vault1[user]) = 500 * 0.5 = 250
• winningZone(vault2[user]) = 500 * 0.5 = 250

Yield Stolen Case
• Now let's assume that a malicious user continuously steals yield during this period (from draw 4 to draw 40)
Notice that the yield will be generated for all the PrizePool balance (probably more than 200 which totalContribution in this period):
• When we get the contribution of vault3 (malicious vault) for this period (from draw 4 to 40), we get:
– vault3.contribution = 50
• Now let's recalculate the vaults' portions again:
– vault1.contributionBetween = 100
– vault2.contributionBetween = 100
– vault3.contributionBetween = 50
– totalContributionBetween = 250
• To calculate their portions:
– v1.portion = 100 / 250 = 0.4
– v2.portion = 100 / 250 = 0.4
– v3.portion = 50 / 250 = 0.2
Assuming the TWAB balance is 500 for all vaults:
• winningZone(vault1[user]) = 500 * 0.4 = 200
• winningZone(vault2[user]) = 500 * 0.4 = 200
• winningZone(vault3[maliciousUser) = 500 * 0.2 = 100
• Notice how the malicious user now has a chance to win without any contribution from it's vault (only stolen yield), and how legitimate users vaults' chances have decreased.
• Malicious actors can steal yield generated by the prize pool, inflating their vault's portion and unfairly increasing their win chances. This decreases legitimate players' portion and winning probabilities.

title: Draw auction rewards likely exceed the available reserve
content: The vulnerability is an over‑allocation of auction rewards caused by the contract’s reward‑fraction logic allowing the sum of all start‑draw and finish‑draw fractions to exceed 1.0. The root cause is that the functions that compute the individual rewards return fractional values in the range [0,1] but the contract never validates that the total of those fractions stays within the unit interval before distributing the amounts. An attacker or any user can trigger several startDraw calls before a finishDraw is executed; each call adds its own fraction to the internal list. When the cumulative fraction is greater than one, the subsequent reward calculation multiplies the available reserve by a total fraction larger than 1, resulting in either (i) the contract attempting to transfer more tokens than are present in the prize‑pool reserve, which leads to an InsufficientReserve revert and prevents the draw from being awarded, or (ii) the contract silently over‑paying participants because the transfer succeeds before the reserve check, effectively creating tokens out of thin air. The impact is two‑fold: participants may receive more reward than intended, breaking the accounting guarantees of the prize pool, and the protocol may become unable to award draws when the reserve is exhausted, causing draws to fail and users to receive no payout. The condition under which this occurs is when multiple startDraw auctions are opened before the corresponding finishDraw, especially when the total reserve is close to the configured maxRewards cap. All participants, the prize‑pool contract, and token holders are affected because the invariant that total distributed rewards ≤ available reserve is violated.
