title: Lack of slippage control on _redeemPT function
content: The vulnerability consists of a missing slippage protection in the internal _redeemPT routine of the Pendle principal‑token vault. The function calls SY.redeem with the parameter minTokenOut forced to zero, which disables any check that the amount of underlying token returned after redeeming PT shares meets a user‑specified minimum. Because the redemption may involve external swaps, staking withdrawals or other on‑chain operations, the actual amount received (netTokenOut) can be lower than expected due to normal market movement or a malicious sandwich/MEV attack. The code that follows _redeemPT – either the instant redemption path that trades the output token for a borrow token, or the withdraw path that forwards the redeemed amount to an external SY withdraw – accepts the returned netTokenOut unconditionally. Consequently, a user who initiates a redemption or a withdrawal may receive fewer tokens than anticipated, potentially even zero, without any revert or error. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a successful transaction but the balance of the expected token does not increase, or it drops unexpectedly, leading to the perception that “my funds disappeared” or “my refund is missing”. The issue is triggered whenever the vault redeems PT shares, i.e., during any call to _executeInstantRedemption or _initiateWithdrawImpl, and it affects all participants holding vault shares, the protocol’s accounting, and any downstream contracts that rely on the redeemed amount. The flaw was identified during a manual audit that inspected the source code and noticed the hard‑coded zero in the minTokenOut argument, a pattern that is easy to overlook because the function still returns a value and does not revert. The problem is subtle because the contract does not emit a warning or error when slippage occurs; the loss is only observable after the transaction completes. To remediate, the contract should propagate a user‑defined minimum output amount through the redemption call, enforce that the actual netTokenOut meets or exceeds this threshold, and revert otherwise. This aligns the implementation with standard slippage‑control patterns used in DeFi swaps and prevents accidental or adversarial loss of assets.

title: The withdrawValue calculation in _calculateValueOfWithdrawRequest
content: The vulnerability lies in the way the vault contract calculates the monetary value of a pending withdrawal request when the request has been split but not yet finalized. The internal function _calculateValueOfWithdrawRequest delegates to _getValueOfWithdrawRequest for all cases that are not explicitly finalized. In the split‑withdraw scenario, _getValueOfWithdrawRequest reads the total amount of the underlying token that the request is asking for (tokenOutSY or an equivalent amount) and multiplies it by the current oracle price, without taking into account the proportion of vault shares that actually belong to the caller (w.vaultShares). Consequently the function returns the full withdrawal value instead of the fractional value that corresponds to the caller’s share. This logical error originates from an incorrect assumption that the stored token amount always represents the caller’s entitlement, which is only true for non‑split or finalized requests. An attacker can exploit the bug by creating a split withdraw request, leaving it in the non‑finalized state, and then invoking functions that rely on the over‑estimated value – for example, liquidation checks or reward calculations. Because the protocol believes the user holds more collateral than they truly do, liquidation may be skipped, allowing the user to retain an under‑collateralised position and potentially withdraw more assets than entitled. The impact is an over‑estimation of user assets that can lead to missed liquidations, protocol under‑collateralisation and financial loss for other participants. The condition occurs whenever a withdraw request has the hasSplit flag set and the split has not been marked as finalized; the same pattern is repeated across several vault implementations (PendlePTKelpVault, PendlePTStakedUSDeVault) that share the same helper library. Users of the vault, the protocol’s risk engine and any lenders are affected because the accounting invariants are broken. The issue was discovered during a manual audit by the researcher Sherlock, who traced the call flow and identified that the valuation function ignored the vaultShares field. It is subtle because normal withdrawals (non‑split or finalized) produce correct numbers, so standard unit tests that do not cover split‑withdraw paths may not reveal the discrepancy. To remediate, the calculation should be rewritten to multiply the caller’s vaultShares by the oracle price (as done in the EtherFiVault implementation) or otherwise scale the total token amount by the share proportion before applying price conversion. In short, the bug is a mis‑valuation of split, non‑finalized withdrawal requests that inflates reported balances and undermines liquidation logic.

title: Kelp:_finalizeCooldown cannot claim the withdrawal
content: The vulnerability resides in the KelpCooldownHolder contract that mediates a two‑step withdrawal from rsETH to stETH and finally to ETH via LidoWithdraw. The internal function _finalizeCooldown is responsible for claiming the ETH that LidoWithdraw has released, but it is hard‑coded to claim only the first (index‑0) withdrawal request returned by LidoWithdraw.getWithdrawalRequests. When more than one withdrawal request exists for the same holder, any request that is not at position zero is silently ignored. An attacker can exploit this by submitting a tiny “dust” withdrawal request for the holder before the legitimate large request is created. Because the dust request occupies index zero, the subsequent legitimate request is placed at index one and never claimed. The contract then attempts to finalize the cooldown, finds no claimable request at index zero, and the withdrawal remains unclaimed. The vault’s accountWithdrawRequest is cleared, the only‑vault modifier prevents a second call, and the rescueTokens function cannot retrieve the stETH because it has already been transferred to LidoWithdraw. From a user perspective the vault appears to have processed the withdrawal but the expected ETH never arrives; balances stay unchanged and the user sees a pending withdrawal that never resolves. The impact is a denial‑of‑service that permanently locks the funds belonging to the vault and its users, effectively making the stETH and the resulting ETH unrecoverable. The issue occurs whenever the holder can receive multiple withdrawal requests, which is possible because any external address can call LidoWithdraw.requestWithdrawals on behalf of the holder. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the withdrawal flow and confirmed the bug with a proof‑of‑concept that creates a dust request and verifies that the real request ID is not at index zero. The problem is subtle because the contract behaves correctly in the common single‑request case, and the dust request amount is so small that it does not raise immediate suspicion. The bug belongs to the class of “incorrect request indexing” or “hard‑coded assumption of single pending request” vulnerabilities, where logic assumes a single element in a list and fails when the list grows. To remediate, the contract should either iterate over all pending requests and claim each one, or store the specific requestId generated in the triggerExtraStep and claim that exact request during finalization, thereby removing the reliance on a fixed index and preventing the DoS vector.
summary:
If an adversary calls LidoWithdraw.requestWithdrawals with some dust stETH amount and the KelpCooldownHolder's address, the withdrawal will be locked. It cannot be rescued via rescueTokens, since it does not have the logic to claimWithdrawal, therefore the withdrawal will be locked permanently.

The KelpCooldownHolder is responsible to withdraw from rsETH to stETH via WithdrawManager, and then withdraw stETH to ETH via LidoWithdraw. Since it is two step process, the KelpCooldownHolder implements triggerExtraStep. After the first withdrawal request is finalized, the triggerExtraStep should be called to initiate the second withdrawal request.

-vaults-private/contracts/vaults/staking/protocols/Kelp.sol#L83
The KelpCooldownHolder._finalizeCooldown will be called when the exitVault is called to finalize the process by LidoWithdraw.claimWithdrawal and send the claimed ETH back to the vault.

-vaults-private/contracts/vaults/staking/protocols/Kelp.sol#L100
This KelpCooldownHolder._finalizeCooldown is, however, hardcoded to claim the 0-th request from the LidoWithdraw.getWithdrawalRequests, thus if there are more than 1 withdrawal requests for this KelpCooldownHolder, all the requests but the 0-th request will be ignored.

An adversary can abuse this fact by requesting withdrawal for the KelpCooldownHolder before the triggerExtraStep is called. In that case the real withdrawal request will not be the 0-th, and will be ignored.

After the finalize on the dust withdrawal is done, the accountWithdrawRequest on the PendlePTKelpVault will be deleted and this finalizeCooldown on the holder cannot be called again since it has onlyVault modifier. The rescueTokens will not help, as the stETH is already transferred to LidoWithdraw.

A malicious actor can use dust amount of stETH to freeze withdrawal from the KelpPTKelpVault. The frozen withdrawal will be locked permanently.

title: Lido withdraw limitation will brick the with-
content: The vulnerability is a missing enforcement of Lido withdrawal amount limits in the wrapper contract's initiateWithdraw implementation. Lido requires that each withdrawal amount bebetween a configurable minimum and maximum, that withdrawals are not paused, that the caller holds enough stETH, and that the contract has transfer approval. The wrapper forwards a requestWithdraw call without checking these constraints. When a user with a share amount below the minimum or above the maximum initiates a withdrawal, the request succeeds and the rsETH tokens are transferred to the wrapper, starting the cooldown period. After the cooldown, the user must call triggerExtraStep to complete the withdrawal, but Lido's internal checks reject the amount, causing the call to revert. Because the wrapper does not handle the revert, the pending withdrawal remains forever unclaimed, effectively locking the user's funds and preventing any further deposits or liquidations while the request is pending. This creates a denial‑of‑service condition for the affected account and can freeze assets in the protocol. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the documented Lido constraints with the wrapper's code and identified that the constraints were not validated before initiating the withdrawal. The bug is hard to notice because the initial transaction appears successful and no error is emitted until the later step, which may be executed days after the request. The class of bug is an input‑validation omission that leads to a post‑condition failure and violates the protocol’s accounting assumptions that every withdrawal request can be fulfilled. From a user’s perspective the UI shows a pending withdrawal that never resolves, balances appear unchanged, and attempts to claim or interact with the vault result in transaction reverts with no funds returned. To remediate, the wrapper should enforce the same minimum and maximum limits as Lido before calling requestWithdraw, split oversized requests into multiple smaller ones, reject undersized requests, or add deposit limits that prevent users from creating unfulfillable withdrawal requests.
summary:
Lido withdraw limitation will brick the withdrawal process due to unenforced constraints.
Lido protocol has limitation regarding the requestWithdraw function. However some of these limitation have not been considered in the _initiateWithdrawImpl leading to users being unable to claim their vault shares even after the cooldown. Lido has stated the following withdraw limitation in their docs:
1. withdrawals must not be paused
2. stETH balance of msg.sender must be greater than the sum of all _amounts
3. there must be approval from the msg.sender to this contract address for the overall amount of stETH token transfer
4. each amount in _amounts must be greater than MIN_STETH_WITHDRAWAL_AMOUNT and lower than MAX_STETH_WITHDRAWAL_AMOUNT (values that can be changed by the DAO) Extracted from here(https://docs.lido.fi/contracts/withdrawal-queue-erc721#requestwithdrawals)
Consider the following scenario:
1) A user who has shares representing stETH less than the MIN_STETH_WITHDRAWAL_AMOUNT or more than the MAX_STETH_WITHDRAWAL_AMOUNT calls initiateWithdraw. The withdraw will be initiated successfully and the rsETH to withdraw will be sent to the holder contract which is going to start the cooldown.
2) However after the cooldown has passed the user will call the triggerExtraStep function which will always result in revert because of the Lido requirements regarding the amount to be withdrawn (mentioned in point 4).
The user will experience a full DOS of the protocol. They will have a pending withdraw that will never finish, which will result in their funds being locked forever. They will not be able to liquidate or deposit because of the pending withdraw. The function triggerExtraStep will always revert and the tokens from Kelp will never be claimed, because of Lido's limitation. - High

title: Selling sUSDe is vulnerable to sandwich at-
content: Selling a staked version of USDe (sUSDe) through the instant redemption path of the Notional leveraged vault is vulnerable to sandwich attacks because the first trade that swaps sUSDe for sDAI on Curve does not enforce any slippage limit. The contract only checks a minimum purchase amount in the second trade, which converts the unwrapped DAI into the borrow token, but this second trade is skipped when the borrow token is DAI itself. Consequently, when a user redeems and the borrowed token is DAI, the transaction executes a single trade without any protection against price movement between the time the transaction is submitted and the time it is mined. A malicious MEV bot can observe the pending transaction, front‑run it with a large trade that moves the sUSDe/sDAI pool price, and then back‑run the user’s transaction, causing the user to receive far fewer DAI than expected or even zero. From the user’s perspective the UI shows a successful redemption but the received amount is dramatically lower than the expected minimum, effectively making funds disappear. The issue occurs only in the instant redemption flow, only when the borrow token is DAI, and only because the contract assumes the second trade will always provide slippage safety. It was discovered during a manual audit of the leveraged vault code where the trade logic was examined and the conditional execution of the second leg was noted. The bug is subtle because the presence of a slippage check in the second leg gives a false sense of security, masking the fact that the first leg can be exploited when the second leg is bypassed. To remediate, the contract should enforce a slippage constraint on the sUSDe→sDAI swap, for example by adding a minimum amount‑out check comparable to the minPurchaseAmount parameter, or by explicitly requiring the DAI amount received to meet the user‑specified minimum. This would align the protection model with the business logic that users expect to receive at least a certain amount of borrowed token when they redeem, preventing the sandwich attack vector and preserving accounting integrity.

title: EtherFiLib::_initiateWithdrawImpl will revert
content: EtherFiLib::_initiateWithdrawImpl contains a logic flaw that assumes the amount ofeETH received from unwrapping weETH is exactly equal to the amount requested for transfer. Because eETH is a rebasing token, the unwrap operation actually transfers shares and the resulting token balance can be lower by one or two wei due to rounding. The function first unwraps a specified amount of weETH, stores the returned value as eETHReceived, approves that exact amount to the LiquidityPool, and then calls requestWithdraw with eETHReceived. If the real balance after unwrapping is slightly less than eETHReceived, the LiquidityPool transfer fails because the contract does not hold enough eETH, causing the whole transaction to revert. This creates a denial‑of‑service condition: users who try to withdraw see their transaction fail, receive no funds, and the protocol’s withdrawal pipeline becomes blocked. The bug manifests only when the underlying asset is a rebasing token such as stETH or eETH, and the discrepancy is tiny (1‑2 wei), making it easy to miss in normal testing or UI checks. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the token accounting logic. The issue violates the fundamental accounting assumption that tokens sent equals tokens received, breaking the protocol’s guarantee that a withdrawal request will be honored. To remediate, the contract should measure the actual eETH balance after the unwrap (for example by recording the balance before and after the call) and approve/withdraw exactly that amount, rather than the nominal amount returned by the unwrap function. This change ensures that the LiquidityPool receives a transferable amount that truly exists, eliminating the revert and restoring correct withdrawal behavior.

title: Incorrect valuation of vault share
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect valuation of vault shares that arises when the contract converts a withdrawal amount expressed in the redemption token (RT) to the borrowed token (BT) using an oracle price that is returned with 18‑decimal precision, but the conversion formula does not account for the differing token precisions. The root cause is a missing scaling factor for the borrowed token’s native precision (6 decimals) and the redemption token’s native precision (18 decimals) together with the constant EXCHANGE_RATE_PRECISION, which leads to a multiplication by 1e12 that inflates the computed value of a split‑finalized withdraw request. An attacker can exploit this by submitting a withdraw request that, after the flawed calculation, appears to be worth far more BT than the actual RT deposited. The contract then records an over‑inflated collateral amount for the attacker, allowing them to borrow significantly more BT than should be permitted. The impact is that the protocol’s accounting is broken: users may see their collateral reported as huge numbers, loans are granted against phantom value, and assets can be drained from the vault. The condition under which the bug manifests is any situation where borrowToken and redeemToken differ and the oracle price is fetched via Deployments.TRADING_MODULE.getOraclePrice, which always returns a rate with 18‑decimal precision. All participants who rely on the vault’s collateral – borrowers, lenders, and the protocol itself – are affected because the inflated collateral undermines the security model. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the arithmetic in WithdrawRequestBase.sol and identified that the formula (s.totalWithdraw * rate * w.vaultShares) / (s.totalVaultShares * Constants.EXCHANGE_RATE_PRECISION) does not normalize the units of rate, totalWithdraw, and vaultShares, resulting in a value that is off by a factor of 1e12. The bug is hard to notice because the numbers involved are large and the contract uses high‑precision arithmetic throughout, masking the unit mismatch. To fix the problem, the conversion formula must be adjusted to include the borrowed token precision (BORROW_PRECISION = 1e6) and the redemption token precision (REDEMPTION_PRECISION = 1e18) in the denominator, effectively scaling the rate back to the correct unit basis. Conceptually, the fix restores proper unit handling so that the value of a withdraw request is computed in the same decimal space as the borrowed token, preventing collateral over‑inflation and preserving the protocol’s accounting invariants. This class of bug is a precision‑handling or units‑mismatch arithmetic error, often seen in cross‑token calculations where token decimals differ and oracle prices are expressed with a fixed precision.

title: Loss of rewards due to continuous griefing at-
content: The vulnerability is a rounding‑to‑zero error in the reward accounting logic of the vault contract on L2 networks such as Arbitrum. The contract calculates the amount of reward tokens claimed by taking the difference between the token balance after a claim and the balance before the claim, then divides this amount by the total number of vault shares (scaled to 1e8 precision) to update the per‑share reward accumulator. Because transaction fees on Arbitrum are very low, a malicious actor can invoke the public claimRewardTokens function on every block. Each invocation transfers only a tiny fraction of a reward token, often far smaller than the total vault share denominator. When the integer division is performed, the result is rounded down to zero, so the accumulatedRewardPerVaultShare is not increased. The same rounding problem occurs in the emission‑based accumulation path, where the time elapsed since the last accumulation is only a few seconds, producing a similarly tiny numerator that also rounds to zero. As a result, legitimate vault participants see their expected rewards disappear; the UI may show zero pending rewards or a missing refund even though they have deposited assets. The issue manifests whenever the claim function is called frequently with small reward amounts, which is feasible on L2 due to cheap gas. It affects all users of the vault, the protocol’s incentive model, and any downstream contracts that rely on accurate reward distribution. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that examined the reward‑claiming functions and identified the integer‑division pattern combined with low‑value claims. It is hard to notice because each individual claim appears to succeed and the loss is only observable over many blocks as a gradual erosion of reward balances. The root cause is the use of fixed‑point arithmetic with insufficient precision for the ratio of claimed tokens to total shares, coupled with a permissionless claim entry point that can be abused to force the calculation into the zero‑rounding regime. A conceptual fix is to restrict who can trigger the claim, introduce a minimum claim threshold, or redesign the accounting to use higher‑precision arithmetic or cumulative accounting that does not rely on per‑claim division. Permissioning the claimRewardTokens function to a whitelisted bot or adding a time‑based throttling mechanism would mitigate the griefing vector and prevent the rounding‑to‑zero loss of rewards.

title: Users can deny the vault from claiming reward
content: The contract implements a reward‑claiming routine that measures how many reward tokens were received by taking a snapshot of each token balance before calling an external reward pool, then calling the pool’s getReward function, and finally measuring the balance after the call. The difference (balanceAfter‑balanceBefore) is recorded as the amount claimed for the vault. Because the external reward pool’s getReward function is public and can be invoked by any address, a malicious actor can submit a transaction that calls getReward directly before the vault’s _claimVaultRewards transaction is mined. This front‑running causes the external pool to transfer the pending reward tokens to the vault ahead of the vault’s own claim. When the vault later executes its _claimVaultRewards logic, the before‑after snapshot sees no change in the token balances, so the computed reward amount is zero. The vault therefore records that no rewards were claimed and the tokens that arrived earlier remain locked in the vault with no mechanism to distribute them, effectively losing the assets for the protocol and its users. The issue occurs whenever the vault attempts to claim rewards from Convex or Aura pools and relies on a balance‑difference calculation without protecting the call from external pre‑emptive execution. It affects any user who expects to receive reward tokens from the vault, as they will see their expected rewards disappear or be reported as zero, breaking the accounting assumptions that rewards are transferred only during the vault’s claim. The flaw was discovered during a security audit, referencing a similar incident in a previous Notional V3 contest, and is hard to notice because the contract does not revert or emit an error; it simply records a zero reward, which may look normal in logs. To remediate, the reward‑claiming logic should avoid using a before‑after balance delta that can be neutralised by front‑running. Instead, it should either use the total token balance after the external call, employ a pull‑based accounting model, or restrict the getReward call to the vault itself via access control or a re‑entrancy guard, ensuring that only the intended claim transaction can trigger the reward transfer.

title: Malicious users can steal reward tokens via
content: The vulnerability is a re‑entrancy flaw in the reward‑distribution logic of a single‑sided liquidity vault. When a user redeems vault shares, the contract first transfers the accrued reward tokens and only afterwards updates the internal accounting of shares and reward debt. Because the reward token transfer is performed via a low‑level call that can invoke a callback (for example an ERC777 or a malicious ERC20 with a transfer hook), a malicious token can re‑enter the vault contract during the transfer and call the public claimAccountRewards function before the share balance has been reduced. The claimAccountRewards function reads the total vault shares and the caller’s share balance from storage, which at that moment still reflect the pre‑redeem state, and then calculates the reward entitlement using the stale values. Consequently the attacker can claim the same reward amount a second time, effectively stealing the difference between the old and the new rewardsPerVaultShare. In the example, a user with 100 shares and a debt of 100 reward tokens redeems 90 shares when rewardsPerVaultShare has doubled from 1.0 to 2.0. The first claim correctly transfers 100 tokens, but the re‑entered call sees the old share count (100) and the updated debt (20) and computes an additional 180 tokens, which are also transferred. The protocol loses those tokens and other shareholders receive a smaller share of the reward pool. The issue manifests only when the reward token’s transfer can trigger external code, making it easy to miss during normal testing because the transfer errors are deliberately ignored and the accounting appears consistent on the surface. It was discovered during a manual audit that examined the ordering of state updates and external calls. The flaw violates the fundamental accounting assumption that a user’s reward entitlement is based on the current share balance after any share‑changing operation. To remediate, the claimAccountRewards function (and any other entry point that can be reached during a token transfer) must be protected with a re‑entrancy guard, or the contract should follow the checks‑effects‑interactions pattern by updating the share balance and reward debt before performing any external call. Additionally, the vault could restrict reward tokens to those without transfer callbacks or use a pull‑based reward claim that separates token transfer from share updates, thereby eliminating the re‑entrancy window.

title: Wrong decimal precision resulted in the price
content: An oracle used by the Notional leveraged vaults calculates the price of a Pendle principal token (PT) by multiplying the PT‑to‑asset rate, the USD price of the underlying asset and a fixed 1e18 scaling factor, then dividing by the product of the Chainlink USD‑price scaling (baseToUSDDecimals) and the PT token’s decimal scaling (ptDecimals). The implementation incorrectly assumes that the PT‑to‑asset rate returned by Pendle’s getPtToAssetRate function is expressed with the same number of decimals as the PT token itself. In reality the rate is always reported with 18 decimals. When the PT token has fewer decimals – for example a PT with 6 decimals – the denominator uses 1e6 while the numerator already contains a 1e18 factor, causing the computed price to be inflated by roughly 10^(18‑6)=10^12. The inflated price is then used as the collateral value for vault accounts. As a result, a borrower can appear to have far more collateral than actually exists and can borrow amounts that far exceed the true value of the deposited PT, allowing the borrower to extract assets from the protocol. The bug manifests only when the oracle is queried for PTs that do not use 18 decimals; for PTs with 18 decimals the calculation happens to be correct, which makes the problem easy to miss during testing. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the PendlePTOracle contract when the auditor examined the price‑calculation formula and compared the expected magnitude of the result with the on‑chain value returned for a 6‑decimal PT. The discrepancy was large (≈10^29 instead of ≈1), indicating a decimal‑scaling error. Exploitation requires a malicious user to supply a PT with non‑standard decimals as collateral, trigger the oracle price read, and then open a leveraged vault using the overstated collateral. The protocol suffers loss of funds because the vault can be liquidated or the borrower can withdraw the borrowed assets before the error is detected. Users see unusually high collateral valuations and may be able to borrow far more than they expect, but the protocol’s accounting assumptions about one‑to‑one value between PT and underlying asset are violated. The fix is to adjust the formula so that the PT rate is first normalized to the PT’s decimal precision, i.e., divide the rate by 1e18 (or multiply the denominator by 1e18) before applying the ptDecimals factor, ensuring that the final price is expressed in the correct number of decimals regardless of the PT’s own decimal count.

title: Compound v2 Empty Markets Exploit.
content: An empty‑market rounding bug in the redeemUnderlying logic of the Deepr protocol (a Compound v2 fork) allows an attacker to extract all assets from a market that has zero liquidity but a non‑zero collateral factor. The function calculates the number of cToken shares to burn by dividing the requested underlying amount by the stored exchange rate, but it truncates the division result (rounds down) instead of rounding up. When the market holds no underlying tokens, the exchange rate can be artificially inflated, causing the division to underestimate the required shares by as little as one wei. Because the protocol only checks that the caller’s share balance is sufficient, the attacker can redeem a tiny amount of underlying while burning fewer shares than required, and repeat the operation until the total supply of cTokens is exhausted, effectively draining the whole market. This flaw is triggered only when a market reaches a state of zero liquidity; such a state can occur if all users withdraw their deposits or if the market is newly created without an initial seed. The vulnerability was discovered during a manual audit of the contract’s accounting functions, where the rounding behavior of div_ was noted as inconsistent with the Compound reference implementation. It is hard to notice because the loss per iteration is minimal (one wei of shares) and the protocol’s events still report successful redemptions, so normal monitoring may not flag abnormal activity until the balance disappears. The impact is severe: any user who supplies collateral to the affected market can see their funds vanish, and the protocol’s overall solvency is compromised because the collateral factor permits borrowing against a market that no longer holds assets. To remediate, the rounding in the share‑burn calculation must be changed to round up (or use a ceiling division) so that the exact amount of shares corresponding to the redeemed underlying is always consumed, and the protocol should enforce a non‑zero minimum liquidity invariant or seed new markets with a small amount of tokens sent to the zero address before enabling a collateral factor. This class of bug belongs to the broader category of accounting rounding errors that break the invariant that total underlying equals total shares multiplied by exchange rate, leading to funds disappear or refund calculation error symptoms where users receive less or no underlying tokens despite a successful transaction.

title: Non-functional vote() if there is one bribe rewarder
content: The vulnerability is an incorrect authorization check placed in the BribeRewarder contract’s deposit function, which is invoked by the voter contract during a vote. The deposit function requires that the caller be the owner of the NFT associated with the vote, but when the voter contract calls deposit, msg.sender is the voter contract itself, not the NFT holder. Consequently, any vote that targets a pool containing at least one bribe rewarder triggers a revert with the error BribeRewarder__NotOwner, preventing the vote() function from completing. This occurs because the access control intended for claim operations was mistakenly applied to deposit, a function that should accept calls from the voter contract to record bribe contributions. An attacker can exploit this by registering a bribe rewarder on a pool, causing all subsequent votes on that pool to fail, effectively creating a denial‑of‑service condition for the governance process. The impact is that users attempting to vote see their transactions revert, receive no voting power, and observe no change in their balances or token allocations, contrary to the expectation that a vote would be recorded. The issue manifests only when a pool has one or more bribe rewarders attached; pools without bribe rewarders operate normally. It affects any participant who tries to vote, the governance protocol that relies on votes to make decisions, and potentially the overall health of the system because voting may be stalled. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that exercised the vote flow with a mock bribe rewarder and observed the revert. It can be hard to notice because the deposit function appears to be an internal bookkeeping call, and the revert only surfaces when the specific condition of a bribe rewarder is present, making it easy to miss in casual testing. The proper fix is to remove the ownership check from the deposit function and relocate it to the claim function where it belongs, or to whitelist the voter contract as an authorized caller for deposit, thereby restoring the intended flow where votes can be recorded while still protecting claim operations.

title: A voter lose bribe rewards if another voter voted
content: The vulnerability resides in the reward accounting logic of the BribeRewarder contract. The contract stores a single global variable, _lastUpdateTimestamp, which is used to compute the amount of unclaimed bribe rewards for a given period. Because this timestamp is not scoped to a specific period identifier, when the contract advances to a new voting period and updates _lastUpdateTimestamp, the previous period’s timestamp is overwritten. Consequently, any rewards that were accrued during the earlier period but have not yet been claimed become impossible to calculate, leading to a reduction or complete loss of those rewards. The flaw is triggered when a voter deposits or votes in period N+1 before voters who participated in period N have claimed their pending rewards. The later deposit updates the global timestamp, causing the reward calculation for period N to ignore the time interval that belongs to it. As a result, users who expect to receive the full bribe reward for the first period may only receive a fraction of it, or even zero, while the contract’s balance still holds the tokens. From a user’s perspective the UI will show a lower token balance after a claim than anticipated, violating the expectation that “my reward should be fully paid out”. The issue was discovered during a formal audit by reproducing the scenario with a Forge test that deposited votes across two periods and observed that the claimed amounts for the first period dropped from 75e17 and 25e17 to 50e17 and 0 respectively. The problem is subtle because the reward calculation appears correct for each individual period when examined in isolation; only when multiple periods interact does the overwritten timestamp become apparent. This class of bug can be described as an accounting or state‑scoping error, where a mutable global state is incorrectly shared across distinct logical epochs. To remediate the issue the contract should store the last update timestamp per period, for example by using a mapping from period identifier to timestamp, or otherwise redesign the reward calculation so that it does not rely on a single mutable timestamp that spans multiple periods. Such a fix restores the ability to correctly compute and distribute rewards for each period, ensuring that voters receive the full amount they are entitled to and preserving the economic integrity of the protocol.

title: Wrong call order for setTopPoolIdsWithWeights,
content: The vulnerability originates from an incorrect sequence of function calls used to update pool weights and reward accrual in the MasterChef contract. The contract distributes LUM tokens to a set of top‑ranked farms based on a per‑second emission rate (lumPerSecond) multiplied by each pool’s weight divided by the total weight of all top pools. Rewards are minted when the updateAll function is invoked, which calculates the amount earned since the pool’s lastUpdated timestamp. The documented workflow requires the caller to first updateAll for the old pool identifiers, then call setTopPoolIdsWithWeights to assign new weights, and finally updateAll for the newly‑added pools. This order is flawed because when setTopPoolIdsWithWeights is executed before the new pools are updated, the lastUpdated timestamp of those pools remains at the moment they were created, not at the moment the weight change occurs. Consequently, the subsequent updateAll call applies the new weight retroactively over the entire elapsed interval since the pool’s creation, causing rewards to be calculated for a period during which the pool was not actually part of the top‑ranked set. The result is an inflation of minted LUM tokens: pools that have just entered the top list receive rewards for time periods before they were eligible, while pools that have left the top list may retain accrued rewards that should have been halted. From a user’s perspective this manifests as unexpectedly high pending rewards or balances that increase dramatically without any additional staking activity, breaking the expectation that rewards grow proportionally to the time a pool remains in the top set. The impact is high because the protocol’s emission schedule can be exceeded by a factor of two or more, draining the token supply, distorting tokenomics, and potentially devaluing LUM for all participants. The issue appears whenever the admin follows the documented call order, which is the normal operational procedure for rotating top pools every two weeks, making it easy to trigger unintentionally. It was discovered during a security audit through a proof‑of‑concept test that compared the correct and incorrect call sequences, revealing that the wrong order yields 3000 LUM minted over a 1000‑second interval where only 1000 LUM should have been emitted. The bug is hard to notice because the reward numbers still look plausible and the over‑minting is spread across multiple pools, masking the discrepancy in aggregate emission statistics. The proper mitigation is to ensure that all pools—both those being removed and those being added—are updated before any weight changes are applied. This can be achieved by calling updateAll for the union of old and new pool identifiers prior to invoking setTopPoolIdsWithWeights, or by embedding the updateAll logic directly inside setTopPoolIdsWithWeights and validating that each pool’s lastUpdated timestamp is recent. By synchronising timestamps with weight updates, the contract will correctly calculate rewards only for the time intervals during which a pool actually holds a weight, preserving the intended emission rate and preventing accidental over‑distribution of LUM.
summary:
The Masterchef contract allows people to stake an admin-selected token in farms to earn LUM rewards. Each two weeks, MLUM stakers can vote on their favorite pools, and the top pools will earn LUM emissions according to the votes. Admin has to call setTopPoolIdsWithWeights to set those votes and weights to set the reward emission for the next two weeks.
Per the documented call order for setTopPoolIdsWithWeights:
```solidity
/**
* @dev Set farm pools with their weight;
*
* WARNING:
* Caller is responsible to updateAll oldPids on masterChef before using this function
* and also call updateAll for the new pids after.
*
* @param pids - list of pids
* @param weights - list of weights
*/
```
We show that this call order is wrong, and will result in wrong rewards distribution.
There is a global parameter lumPerSecond, set by the admin. Whenever updateAll is called for a set of pools:
• Let the total weight of all votes across all top pools be totalWeight
• Let the current weight of a pool Pid be weightPid. This weight can be set by the admin using setTopPoolIdsWithWeights
• Pool Pid will earn totalLumRewardForPid = (lumPerSecond * weightPid / totalWeight) * (elapsed_time), i.e. each second it earns lumPerSecond times its percentage of voted weight weightPid across the total weight all top pools totalWeight.

title: Voters will lose all bribe rewards forever if they
content: The vulnerability is an out‑of‑bounds array access in the reward‑claiming routine of a bribe‑reward contract. The contract stores a fixed‑size rewards array that is sized only for the periods that were originally advertised as bribe periods (for example periods 1‑5). The claim() function determines the last finished voting period by calling Voter.getLatestFinishedPeriod() and then iterates from the contract’s _startVotingPeriod up to that value, summing the rewards for each period. Because the loop does not cap the iteration at the contract’s own _lastVotingPeriod, once two voting periods have elapsed after the final advertised bribe period, the loop reaches a period identifier that has no corresponding entry in the rewards array. The internal index calculation (periodId‑_startVotingPeriod) then produces an index that is equal to the length of the array, causing a Solidity index out of bounds revert. The revert aborts the whole claim transaction, so any rewards that were still unclaimed for earlier periods become permanently inaccessible. From a user’s perspective the contract silently accepts a claim call, but after the seventh voting period the transaction reverts and the user receives no tokens, even though the UI may still show a non‑zero pending reward balance. The issue is triggered only after the blockchain advances past the last bribe period plus two additional voting cycles, which can be hard to notice because the contract continues to work correctly for the first two periods after the advertised end. The bug belongs to the class of incorrect loop bounds leading to array‑index overflow and violates the accounting assumption that the reward data structure contains an entry for every period the claim loop may address. It was discovered during a manual audit of the BribeRewarder contract when the auditor examined the interaction between the claim loop and the Voter contract’s period calculation. The problem may remain hidden in production because the revert only occurs after a delay, and users may assume that a failed claim is a temporary network issue rather than a permanent loss of funds. The proper fix is to constrain the loop’s endPeriod to the contract’s own _lastVotingPeriod, ensuring that the loop never accesses an index beyond the allocated rewards array. By adding a simple min‑check (if endPeriod > _lastVotingPeriod then endPeriod = _lastVotingPeriod) the contract will stop iterating over non‑existent periods, allowing users to claim all accrued rewards at any time before the final period ends.

title: Voting does not take into account end of stak-
content: The vulnerability lies in the voting logic of the Voter contract, which accepts a staking position as proof of voting power but fails to verify that the remaining lock period of that position exceeds the length of the current voting epoch. The protocol documentation requires that a valid Magic LUM staking position must have an overall lock longer than 90 days and that the remaining lock time be longer than the epoch duration, yet the contract only checks the initial lock duration and the total lock duration at the moment of voting. Consequently, a user can submit a vote with a stale position whose lock has already expired or will expire during the epoch. After casting a vote, the user can withdraw the original position, create a new staking position with the same amount of tokens, and cast a second vote within the same epoch because the contract only records a single vote per tokenId per period and does not consider that the tokenId may have been destroyed and replaced. This breaks the invariant that each stake may vote only once per epoch and allows double‑voting with the same balance, inflating the vote weight of chosen pools. The impact is that pool selection for LUM emissions can be manipulated, giving an unfair advantage to parties that exploit the timing loophole. The issue occurs whenever a staking position satisfies the minimum lock requirement but its remaining lock is shorter than the epoch, which can happen every 90 days for a 2‑week lock configuration. It affects any user holding a staking NFT, the protocol’s governance outcomes, and ultimately the fairness of token emissions. The flaw was discovered during a security audit that compared the on‑chain checks with the documented requirements and reproduced the exploit in unit tests. It is hard to notice because the contract does emit no explicit error for a stale lock, and the UI may simply show a successful vote while the underlying lock condition is violated. To remediate, the contract must enforce the invariant that the remaining lock period is greater than the epoch length before accepting a vote, and it should prevent voting with a position that was created after the epoch started or that has been withdrawn and re‑created within the same epoch. This can be achieved by adding a check against the current block timestamp and the position’s startLockTime, and by tracking votes per address or per stake lifecycle rather than only per tokenId per period. The fix restores the intended business logic that each stake can contribute voting power exactly once per epoch, preserving the fairness of pool selection and emission distribution.

title: Funds unutilized for rewards may get stranded
content: The vulnerability is that reward tokens deposited to a BribeRewarder contract can become permanently stranded when they are not fully consumed during the bribe periods. The root cause is that the contract enforces funding of the total amount per period but does not provide any mechanism to withdraw leftover tokens, and the reward calculation uses integer division (amountPerPeriod / duration) which truncates fractional emissions, leaving a residual amount that is never emitted. Additionally, if a voting pool receives no voters in a given period, the full per‑period allocation is considered spent even though no distribution occurs, and the contract does not roll the unused portion into later periods. An attacker or even an honest bribe provider cannot extract these leftovers because the contract lacks a sweep or rescue function. The impact is that the bribe provider loses the unutilized tokens permanently, which may be a substantial amount especially when a pool becomes inactive or is removed. The condition occurs after the bribe cycle is started and any period ends without any voter, or when the integer division rounding leaves a remainder. All parties that fund the contract—typically token holders or protocol participants—are affected because their deposited rewards never reach any voter and simply disappear from the contract balance. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the fundAndBribe and _calculateRewards logic and noticed the absence of any token recovery path. It can be hard to notice because the contract’s balance appears to hold the expected amount at the start, and there is no visible error; only after periods finish does the balance stay unchanged despite expectations of reward distribution. The bug belongs to the class of “fund‑locking due to missing sweep function and rounding‑induced token loss”. From a user perspective, a bribe provider may see that after a bribe period the contract still holds the same amount of tokens, receives no refunds, and the intended voters receive zero rewards, violating the expectation that deposited tokens are either distributed or returned. To remediate, the contract should implement a recovery or sweep method that allows the original funder (or a designated role) to withdraw any leftover reward tokens, and the reward calculation should be adjusted to account for fractional emissions, for example by using a cumulative accounting approach or by rounding up the per‑second emission. This would prevent permanent loss of funds and align the contract’s behavior with the intended economic model.

title: Attacker can block all votes to a specific pool
content: The vulnerability is an arithmetic overflow in the reward‑distribution logic of the MagicSea bribing system that can be used to deny‑of‑service the voting process for a chosen liquidity pool. The root cause is that the BribeRewarder contract accepts any ERC20 token as a reward and calculates a per‑share debt value (accDebtPerShare) by multiplying the total reward amount by a precision factor and dividing by the total supply of deposited tokens. Because the calculation uses unchecked arithmetic, an attacker can supply a token with a total supply equal to type(uint256).max and a total deposit of only one wei. This makes accDebtPerShare become an astronomically large number. When a legitimate user later votes and the contract attempts to compute deposit * accDebtPerShare, the multiplication overflows the 256‑bit integer range, causing the transaction to revert. The overflow is triggered inside the internal getDebt function, which shifts the product after multiplication, but the overflow occurs before the shift. The impact is that any vote for the targeted pool during the affected period fails, effectively blocking all voting activity for that pool. By repeating the attack across multiple pools or periods, an attacker could halt the entire governance or reward‑distribution mechanism of the protocol. The condition for exploitation is minimal: the attacker only needs to be able to create a BribeRewarder with a custom token, mint the maximum token amount, fund the rewarder, and cast a single minimal vote to initialise the inflated accDebtPerShare. No external permissions or time‑based constraints are required. Users experience a generic transaction failure – the vote transaction reverts with an arithmetic error, no vote is recorded, and expected bribe rewards are not received, which may appear as “my vote did not go through” or “I got no reward”. The issue was discovered during a security audit when the auditor examined the reward‑calculation functions and noticed the lack of bounds on totalRewards and the use of unchecked arithmetic. It is hard to notice because normal operation with reasonable token amounts works correctly; the overflow only manifests after an attacker deliberately injects an extreme token supply. The bug belongs to the class of unchecked arithmetic overflow leading to denial‑of‑service, especially in systems that allow unbounded external token inputs. To remediate, the protocol should restrict which tokens can be used for bribing (e.g., a whitelist), enforce reasonable caps on reward amounts, and employ safe‑math checks or require that totalRewards be less than a safe multiple of totalSupply before performing the multiplication. Upgrading the contracts to include these safeguards would prevent the overflow and restore normal voting functionality.

title: Wrong calculation of Accure Reward in
content: The vulnerability is an accounting logic error in the reward‑accrual routine of the staking protocol. The contract calculates a user’s accrued reward based on a variable called globalTotalStaked, which is intended to represent the total amount of tokens actively staked across the system. However, the function that updates the global total does not first subtract the amount of tokens that have just been frozen for a user. As a result, when a user freezes tokens and then immediately triggers the _accrueRewards function, the contract reads a stale globalTotalStaked value that still includes the newly frozen tokens. This inflated total is then used to compute the reward amount and to update the inflation index, causing the system to allocate more reward tokens than the user is actually entitled to. The root cause is the incorrect ordering of state updates: the global total is queried before the frozen balance (_totalFrozen) is reconciled, violating the invariant that globalTotalStaked should equal totalStaked minus totalFrozen. An attacker can exploit this by freezing a large amount of tokens and calling the reward‑claim function before the protocol’s batchUpdateFrozenInfo routine adjusts the frozen counters, thereby receiving excess reward tokens. The impact includes unintended token inflation, loss of value for honest participants, and a breach of the protocol’s economic assumptions about fair reward distribution. The bug manifests only when the reward‑accrual path is executed after a freeze operation but before the global total is refreshed, meaning that users who do not interact with the freeze‑then‑claim sequence are unaffected. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the Comptroller and UserManager contracts, where the auditor observed that the globalTotalStaked value used in _accrueRewards did not reflect the most recent frozen amounts. Because the reward calculation appears to succeed and the UI simply shows a reward amount, the problem can be subtle and may go unnoticed until the extra tokens are minted and the inflation becomes apparent. To remediate the issue, the contract should retrieve the global total only after all frozen balances have been updated, or directly compute the effective total as totalStaked minus totalFrozen at the point of reward calculation. This ensures that the reward formula uses an accurate representation of the currently staked capital, restoring the intended accounting guarantees and preventing users from claiming rewards on tokens that are no longer eligible for inflation.

title: VouchFaucet can be immediately drained by
content: The vulnerability is an unchecked token claim in the faucet contract that allows any address to withdraw an arbitrary amount of any ERC20 token. The root cause is that the claimTokens function checks the amount already claimed against a per‑token maximum but never updates the claimedTokens mapping after a successful claim. Because the mapping always returns zero, the require statement effectively becomes require(0 <= maxClaimable), which is always true regardless of the amount requested. An attacker can therefore call claimTokens with a large amount, receive the tokens via the ERC20 transfer, and repeat the call until the contract balance is exhausted. This can happen in a single transaction or across multiple transactions and does not depend on any special privileges; any external account can invoke the function. The impact is that the faucet’s token reserves disappear, breaking the intended distribution model and leaving legitimate users unable to obtain the limited amount they expect. Users would see the contract balance drop to zero, their own claim succeed with far more tokens than allowed, or conversely, the contract may appear empty when they try to claim. The issue was discovered during a security audit when the test suite demonstrated that setting a max claimable amount of one token unit still allowed a caller to claim three units. The bug is hard to notice because the require statement appears to enforce a limit, giving a false sense of safety, while the missing state update silently defeats the check. To fix the problem the contract must record the new total claimed amount before transferring tokens and verify that this new total does not exceed the configured maximum. Adding a re‑entrancy guard, a global cap, or a cooldown period can further harden the faucet against abuse. In generic terms the flaw belongs to the class of accounting or state‑inconsistency bugs where a critical invariant is not maintained due to an omitted state mutation, leading to unrestricted asset transfer.

title: Repaying a Loan with Permit in UErc20.sol Wrongly
content: The vulnerability is a mismatched decimal scaling bug in the loan‑repayment path that uses ERC20 permits. When a borrower calls the function that permits a token transfer and then repays a loan, the contract scales the principal amount to the internal 1e18 representation but leaves the accrued interest in the token’s native decimal format. Because the interest value is not multiplied by the same scaling factor, the protocol records an interest amount that is too small for tokens with fewer than 18 decimals (for example USDC or USDT with 6 decimals) and too large for tokens with more than 18 decimals. The root cause is the call to _repayBorrowFresh with decimalScaling(amount, underlyingDecimal) for the amount while passing the raw interest returned by calculatingInterest(borrower). An attacker or honest user can exploit this by repaying a loan with a low‑decimal token and receiving a refund of interest that should have been paid to lenders, or by overpaying interest with a high‑decimal token, thereby reducing the pool of funds available to other lenders. The impact includes users paying an incorrect interest amount, excess interest becoming trapped in the contract without an owner, and the protocol’s profit and interest‑sharing calculations becoming inaccurate. The condition occurs whenever the repayBorrowWithERC20Permit function is used, i.e., when a borrower supplies a permit signature and the contract attempts to accrue interest before repayment. All borrowers, lenders and the protocol itself are affected because the accounting invariants that guarantee that total interest earned equals interest distributed are broken. The issue was discovered during a formal security audit (Sherlock) that compared the implementation against the reference UToken contract where interest is correctly scaled. The bug is subtle because the function signatures appear correct and the permit flow works; only the hidden scaling mismatch causes the accounting error, which may not be visible until a repayment is performed and the pool balances are examined. To fix the problem, the interest value must be scaled using the same decimal factor as the principal before being passed to _repayBorrowFresh, ensuring that both amount and interest are expressed in the same 1e18 internal unit. This aligns the repayment logic with the reference implementation and restores correct interest distribution and pool balance consistency.

The issue arises because the amount to repay is scaled to 1e18, but the interest is not, leading to users passing incorrect interest amounts based on the token's decimal places. This can result in users paying significantly less interest than they should for tokens with fewer decimal places (e.g., USDC, USDT) or more than they should for tokens with more decimal places.
The core of the problem lies in the different scaling applied to the amount and interest during the repayment process. In UErc20.sol, the function _repayBorrowFresh is called with the amount scaled to 1e18 but the interest remains unscaled, which causes incorrect interest calculations.

title: The _totalStaked tracker calculation is incor-
content: The vulnerability is an accounting mis‑calculation in the way the protocol tracks the total amount of tokens that are currently staked. The UserManager contract keeps a variable that records the aggregate staked balance in a scaled form (actualAmount). When a debt write‑off operation is performed, the code subtracts the unscaled nominal amount (amount) from this aggregate counter instead of the correctly scaled value (actualAmount). Because the aggregate counter is later used by the Comptroller contract to compute a global inflation index, the mismatch causes the inflation index to be artificially increased. This inflated index is then used in reward calculations, leading to rewards being over‑issued or, conversely, to users seeing their accrued rewards reduced unexpectedly. The bug manifests whenever any user triggers a debtWriteOff, and can be amplified by repeatedly calling the unrestricted batchUpdateFrozenInfo function, which forces the Comptroller to update its inflation index based on the corrupted total‑staked value. Affected parties include stakers, reward claimants, and any external system that relies on the reported total‑staked amount for accounting or risk assessment. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the Union Finance v2 contracts, where the auditor noticed that the subtraction in debtWriteOff used the wrong variable and that the subsequent call to updateTotalStaked propagated the error. The problem is subtle because the contract still updates the per‑account staked balances correctly; only the global aggregate is wrong, so normal UI balances appear unchanged while the hidden inflation index diverges. The impact is high: an inflated inflation index can cause the protocol to mint excessive reward tokens, diluting existing holders, or can lead to accounting inconsistencies that break trust in the protocol’s financial statements. The bug belongs to the class of “incorrect scaling of accounting variables” or “global state mis‑alignment due to mixed units”. To remediate, the write‑off logic must subtract the scaled actualAmount from the total‑staked counter, ensuring both per‑account and global counters use the same unit. After fixing, the Comptroller’s inflation index will be calculated from a correct total‑staked value, restoring accurate reward accrual and preventing unintended inflation of token supplies.

title: Referrer can get less referral reward due to
content: The vulnerability is a referral‑reward misallocation that occurs in the onFlowChanged routine of the protocol. When a trader creates or updates a token flow, the contract retrieves the current referrer address and then immediately passes that address to getOrCreateSleepPod, a helper that creates a dedicated "pod" contract for any address that does not already have one. If the referrer is already a pod (which happens after the first flow change because the stored referrer value has been replaced by the pod address), the helper treats the pod itself as a regular user and creates a new pod for it. This newly created pod address is then written back into the referral record and used for subsequent emission‑unit updates. As a result, the original referrer (the human user who should receive the 5 % extra BORING token) is replaced by an intermediate pod address, and each subsequent flow change creates another nested pod. The emission treasury therefore credits the reward to the newest pod rather than the intended referrer, causing the original referrer to receive fewer tokens than expected. The issue manifests only after a trader performs a second or later flow modification; the first flow works correctly because the stored referrer is still the user’s address. Affected parties include the referrer, the trader, and the protocol’s accounting logic, because the referral accounting diverges from the business rule that a referrer should earn a fixed percentage of the trader’s flow. The bug was discovered during a manual audit of the onFlowChanged function, where the auditor noticed that the referrer field is overwritten with the result of getOrCreateSleepPod and that the subsequent emission update logic compares the new referrer against the old one, leading to a cascade of pod‑for‑pod creations. The problem is subtle because the UI still shows the correct referral link and the trader’s flow proceeds normally; only the referral reward amount is reduced, which may be observed as missing or lower‑than‑expected BORING tokens in the referrer’s balance. To fix the issue, the contract should preserve the original user address when updating emission units and only convert that address to a pod after the referral logic has been applied, or alternatively store the pod address separately and never feed a pod address back into getOrCreateSleepPod. This prevents nested pod creation and ensures that referral rewards are credited to the intended referrer, restoring the intended accounting guarantees.

title: DistributionFeeDIP does not update previous
content: The vulnerability is an accounting flaw in the distribution fee module where the contract fails to update the stored distributor address for a trader after a flow change. The root cause is that the internal mapping $.distributors[torex][trader] is never reassigned to the new distributor inside updateDistributionStats, leaving the previous distributor entry unchanged (typically address(0)). Because the mapping is not updated, every subsequent flow update treats the old distributor as still active. The function therefore continues to credit the old (zero) address with a negative flowRate while adding the new flowRate on top of the existing credit for the current distributor. This results in the distributor’s recorded flowRate growing cumulatively with each update, and the pseudo‑distributor (address(0)) accumulating an increasingly negative flowRate. If the negative value exceeds the int128 limit, an underflow occurs that can halt the protocol’s fee accounting, effectively a denial‑of‑service. Exploitation is straightforward: an attacker who can trigger onInFlowChanged (for example by opening or modifying a flow) can repeatedly set a distributor address, causing the distributor’s recorded flowRate to inflate arbitrarily while the protocol’s totality stats become inconsistent. From a user perspective the symptoms are misleading fee balances – a distributor may appear to have earned far more than expected, while the protocol may show missing or negative fee totals, leading to failed claims or zero payouts. The issue manifests whenever a trader updates a flow and supplies a new distributor in the userData field; it does not require any special conditions beyond the normal flow‑update path. All participants that rely on accurate distribution statistics – the protocol itself, fee claimers, and end‑users expecting correct fee allocations – are affected. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the Super Boring contract suite, where the auditor noticed that the event DistributorUpdated was emitted but the underlying storage variable was never written. The bug is subtle because the contract still emits an update event, giving the impression that state was changed, and the arithmetic appears correct on a per‑call basis, masking the cumulative error. The proper fix is to assign the new distributor to the mapping after the accounting adjustments, i.e., $.distributors[torex][trader] = distributor, ensuring that future updates reference the correct address and that flowRate deltas are applied only once. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of stale‑state or mapping‑update errors that break invariant maintenance in accounting contracts, leading to inflated rewards and potential protocol‑wide DoS.

title: Torex flow created with zero address referrer
content: The vulnerability originates from the InitialStakingTIP library where a new SleepPod is created for a staker without first verifying that the staker address is non‑zero. When a user creates a Torex flow and supplies the zero address as the referrer, the onFlowCreated callback eventually calls getOrCreateSleepPod with the zero address. Because the code only checks whether a SleepPod already exists (address(p) == address(0)) and does not exclude the zero address, a SleepPod is instantiated for address(0). All referrer rewards that would normally be credited to a legitimate referrer are instead accumulated in this SleepPod. Since the zero address is not owned by any external account, the rewards become permanently inaccessible, effectively locking them forever. The issue can be triggered simply by submitting a flow with a missing or intentionally zero referrer; no special permissions or external conditions are required. The impact is a loss of earnings for any staker who expected to receive referrer incentives, as the protocol’s accounting records show rewards being allocated while the user sees no increase in balance or receives a zero payout. From a user’s perspective the UI may display a normal flow creation, but later the expected referral bonus never appears, leading to confusion or suspicion that funds have vanished. The bug was discovered during a manual audit of the SuperBoring contracts, where the auditor noticed that the SleepPod creation logic lacked a guard against a zero‑address staker. It is subtle because the zero address is a syntactically valid address, so the contract does not revert and the reward accounting proceeds without obvious errors. The proper mitigation is to add an explicit check that the staker (or referrer) is not the zero address before creating a SleepPod, as shown in the provided diff. This change prevents the creation of an unreachable reward container and restores the intended business logic that referrer rewards must be claimable by a real participant.
