title: Red Stone Oracle Can Time Travel
content: The vulnerability is a price‑manipulation flaw in the Redstone oracle integration that allows an attacker to repeatedly overwrite the stored price within the three‑minute validity window of a price observation. The root cause is that the updatePrice function records a synthetic timestamp (block.timestamp‑THREE_MINUTES) without tracking the actual timestamp of each individual observation, and it does not enforce any cooldown between successive updates. Consequently, any caller can submit a fresh, valid observation, then immediately submit another observation that also falls inside the same three‑minute validity period, and later revert to the original observation, effectively “time‑traveling” the oracle price back and forth. An attacker can exploit this by feeding a low price, executing a trade that benefits from the undervalued asset, then feeding a higher price before the transaction settles, or by performing the entire sequence atomically within a single transaction. The impact is that users may receive incorrect trade execution prices, experience unexpected loss of funds, or see their balances change dramatically without any market movement; the protocol’s accounting assumptions about price stability over the validity period are broken. This condition occurs whenever the oracle update function is called more than once within the three‑minute window, which is allowed by the contract logic. All participants that rely on the oracle – traders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are affected because the price feed can be arbitrarily warped. The issue was discovered during a security audit that included a proof‑of‑concept test harness capable of generating mock Redstone payloads with custom timestamps; the test demonstrated that the price could be toggled between two values and back again, confirming the manipulation. The flaw is subtle because the contract appears to enforce a freshness check, yet the check only uses a static offset and does not validate that the new observation is newer than the previously stored one, making the problem easy to miss in casual review. To remediate, the contract should enforce that at least the full THREE_MINUTES interval has elapsed since the last successful update before accepting a new observation, and reject any premature update silently (without reverting) so that price data cannot be overwritten within the validity period. This change restores the intended guarantee that price data remains stable for the duration of its validity window and prevents arbitrary price warping.

title: User's can seize more assets dur-
content: The vulnerability is an over‑seizure flaw in the liquidation routine of the protocol. During liquidation the contract computes the maximum value of collateral that may be taken by multiplying the value of debt repaid by a factor that accounts for the liquidation discount. The computation iterates over the array of DebtData supplied by the liquidator and, for each entry, adds the value of the amount specified. If the amount field is set to type(uint256).max the code substitutes the current borrow balance of the position for that pool. The flaw arises because the routine assumes that each pool identifier appears only once in the DebtData array and that the max sentinel will always represent the *current* debt at the moment of the check. An attacker can first repay a partial amount of the debt and then include a second entry for the same pool with type(uint256).max. The first entry records the partial repayment, while the second entry is interpreted as the full outstanding debt before the partial repayment is taken into account, causing the debtRepaidValue to be double‑counted. Consequently the calculated maxSeizableAssetValue is inflated, and the subsequent check that the seized collateral value does not exceed this limit is bypassed. The liquidator can therefore seize far more collateral than the protocol’s economic model permits – in the extreme case the entire collateral of the borrower can be taken. From the borrower’s point of view the expected behaviour (only a portion of the collateral proportional to the debt plus discount) is violated; the user sees their collateral balance drop to zero or an unexpectedly large amount is transferred away, receiving no refund or compensation. The issue manifests whenever a liquidation is performed, the liquidator can control the DebtData array, and the protocol allows the max sentinel to be used. It was discovered by the audit team through a targeted test (testHash_LiquidateExcessUsingDouble) that demonstrated the double‑counting effect. The bug is subtle because the use of type(uint256).max is a legitimate way to indicate “repay all” and the validation logic appears sound at a glance; duplicate pool identifiers are not explicitly prohibited, making the over‑seizure condition easy to miss. To remediate the problem the contract should enforce that each poolId appears at most once in the debtData array, for example by requiring the array to be strictly ordered and unique, or by aggregating duplicate entries before the valuation step. Additionally, the calculation of debtRepaidValue should be based on the actual post‑repayment balance rather than the pre‑repayment snapshot when type(uint256).max is used, ensuring that the maximum seizable collateral cannot be artificially inflated. This correction restores the intended accounting guarantees and prevents borrowers from losing excess collateral during liquidation.

title: Rounding error due to internal accounting when total supply of a pool is zero
content: The vulnerability is a rounding‑down error in the pool’s internal accounting that can be triggered when the total supply of the pool is effectively zero. The contract calculates the number of shares to mint from a deposit using a formula that divides the total number of shares by the total amount of assets, applying integer division that always rounds down. When an attacker first creates a situation where totalDepositShares equals one and totalDepositAssets equals two (for example by depositing a tiny amount of collateral, borrowing, repaying, and then transferring a few wei directly into the pool), the conversion formula yields a share price that is slightly lower than the true value. By repeatedly depositing a quantity equal to totalDepositAssets+1 and immediately withdrawing a single share, the attacker forces the contract to mint exactly one share each time because the integer division discards the fractional remainder. The pool’s total asset balance therefore grows while the total share count remains constant at one, inflating the apparent asset‑per‑share ratio. Subsequent honest users who later deposit into the pool receive shares based on the distorted ratio, causing a portion of their deposited assets – up to roughly one‑third in the worst‑case scenario – to be silently reallocated to the attacker’s share. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are a missing or reduced balance after a deposit, unexpected loss of up to 33 % of the funds, and shares that appear to be correctly issued but are worth far less than expected. The issue occurs only under the specific condition that the pool’s total supply is zero or can be forced to a minimal non‑zero value, which makes it easy to overlook during normal operation because the rounding discrepancy is only a few wei. It was discovered during a security audit that included targeted testing of edge‑case supply values and manual manipulation of the pool’s balance. The bug is hard to notice because the rounding error is deterministic yet tiny, and it only becomes exploitable after the attacker has set up the initial state. To remediate the problem the contract should either prevent deposits when totalSupply is zero, enforce a minimum non‑zero supply before allowing share calculations, or modify the conversion routine to use ceiling division or a safe‑math library that preserves the fractional component, thereby eliminating the systematic rounding‑down bias. In broader terms the flaw belongs to the class of accounting‑precision bugs where integer division leads to systematic under‑allocation of value, breaking the economic invariants of the protocol and allowing value extraction through repeated small‑scale operations.

title: Fee Precision Loss Disrupts Liquidity and Liquidations
content: The vulnerability is a systematic precision loss in the calculation of borrowing and funding fees that affects every pool and position on the protocol. The root cause is twofold: first, the constant DENOM used to scale fee rates is set to 1e9, which limits the smallest representable fee per block to 10‑7 % (approximately 1.578 % annualised on a 2‑second block interval). Any fee rate that falls below this granularity is rounded down to zero, meaning that periods with low funding or borrowing rates generate no fee at all. Second, the utilization percentage that drives dynamic fee formulas is computed by dividing reserves by 100, providing only two decimal places of precision. This coarse rounding can truncate utilization values (for example 1.9999 % becomes 1 %), which in turn reduces the derived fee rates by whole percentage points. When both sources of rounding interact, the effective fee can be under‑paid by tens of percent or even 100 % for certain market conditions. The bug can be exploited simply by opening positions that fall into the low‑rate regime; an attacker does not need to craft a special transaction, they only need to trigger the normal fee‑accrual path while the protocol’s calculations round the fee to zero. The impact is material under‑payment of fees to liquidity providers and funding recipients, leading to reduced incentives for providing liquidity and increased counter‑party risk. Moreover, because liquidations rely on accrued borrow fees to become profitable, the rounding error delays liquidation events, sometimes extending the time to liquidate a position by 20 % or more, which can allow losing positions to survive market volatility longer than intended. The condition occurs whenever the annualised fee rate is below the interval defined by DENOM or when utilization is calculated with only two‑digit precision, which is common for low‑interest environments. All users of the protocol—traders, LPs, and funding recipients—are affected because the fee shortfall is applied globally across pools. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when the auditors wrote isolated unit tests for the fee‑calculation contracts and observed that two different interest scenarios produced identical utilization values and identical fee outputs, contrary to expectations. The problem is hard to notice in production because the fee discrepancy manifests as a gradual erosion of expected earnings rather than an outright failure; users see lower rewards or slower liquidations but may attribute it to market conditions. The bug belongs to the class of rounding‑and‑precision errors in financial smart contracts, where fixed‑point arithmetic with insufficient scaling leads to loss of fractional values. From a user’s perspective, the symptoms are: LPs receive less than the advertised reward (e.g., expecting 11.3 % annual return but receiving only 9.5 %), borrowers see their positions remain open longer than the protocol’s liquidation model predicts, and funding rates sometimes appear to be zero despite non‑zero market utilization. The expectation that fees scale linearly with utilization is violated; instead, the protocol applies a step‑function due to rounding, breaking the accounting assumptions of continuous fee accrual. To remediate, the protocol should increase the precision of the DENOM constant by at least three orders of magnitude (e.g., using 1e12 instead of 1e9) and compute utilization with three additional decimal places (e.g., dividing by 100 000 rather than 100). This change reduces the rounding error by three orders of magnitude, ensuring that even very small fee rates are represented accurately and that utilization reflects true market conditions, thereby restoring correct fee distribution and timely liquidations.

title: A Reserve Borrow Rate can be manipulated during liquidation
content: The vulnerability is a borrow‑rate manipulation that occurs during the liquidation process of a reserve. When a liquidation is executed the contract calls an internal function that repays the debt of the liquidated position. The function calculates the number of debt shares that have been burnt and mistakenly stores this burnt amount in the variable that represents the next total debt shares of the reserve. The interest‑rate model later reads this variable to compute the next borrow rate, assuming it contains the total remaining debt shares. Because the burnt amount is usually smaller than the total debt, the borrow rate is recomputed with a reduced denominator, causing the reported borrow rate to drop dramatically. An attacker can trigger a liquidation on his own unhealthy position, deliberately limit the amount of debt that is covered in the liquidation, and thereby force the protocol to record a much lower borrow rate for that reserve. After the rate has been lowered the attacker can continue borrowing or repaying at the artificially cheap rate, reducing the interest that would otherwise be owed and extracting value from the protocol. The issue only manifests when the liquidation logic updates the reserve’s nextDebtShares field; normal borrowing or repayment paths are unaffected. Any user who can initiate a liquidation – typically any other participant in the market – can exploit the bug against a target borrower, and the protocol itself loses revenue because the interest calculation no longer reflects the true outstanding debt. The problem was discovered during a manual audit by inspecting the _repayDebtTokens implementation and confirmed with a test that shows the borrow rate before liquidation dropping from a high value to a much lower one after a single liquidation call. The bug is subtle because the borrow rate is a derived value that is not directly displayed in the UI; only a developer looking at the reserve data or a test that logs the rate can see the unexpected change. The correct fix is to update the nextDebtShares field with the total debt shares stored in the reserve’s supply structure instead of the burnt amount, ensuring the interest‑rate model receives the proper total debt figure. In generic terms the flaw belongs to the class of ‘incorrect state update during accounting’ bugs where a temporary variable is written back to persistent storage, leading to mis‑calculation of financial metrics.

title: User can sandwich their own position close to get back all of their position fees
content: The vulnerability is a fee‑extraction manipulation that allows an attacker to recover virtually all borrowing fees associated with a leveraged position by temporarily providing a large amount of liquidity and then closing the position before the fees are permanently locked in the pool. The root cause is that the protocol only distributes borrowing fees to liquidity providers at the moment a position is closed, and the distribution is calculated solely on the current share of LP tokens without considering how long each provider has supplied liquidity. Because LP tokens can be minted and withdrawn instantly, an attacker can use a flash‑loan to inject a massive amount of capital, obtain a dominant share of the pool, close the position, trigger the fee distribution, and then withdraw the LP tokens while still holding the borrowed capital. The fees that would normally be retained by the protocol are therefore paid back to the attacker, effectively allowing the user to avoid paying any borrowing fees. This attack can be carried out whenever flash‑loan providers are available and the protocol does not enforce a minimum lock‑up period or a gradual fee accrual mechanism. The impact is a loss of revenue for the protocol and a reduction of incentives for honest liquidity providers, potentially leading to under‑funded fee pools and degraded market quality. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the fee accounting logic, where the auditor noticed that fees are held inside the position until closure and that the distribution formula does not weight providers by time. The problem is subtle because the fee distribution appears correct for normal users; only a malicious sequence of actions reveals the manipulation. To remediate the issue the protocol should adopt a gradual fee distribution model, such as per‑block accrual, or enforce a minimum staking period for newly added liquidity, or exclude liquidity added in the same block from receiving fees, thereby preventing an attacker from capturing the entire fee share with a single flash‑loan operation.

2. Close their position and let the fees be distributed (with most going back to them as they've got majority in the pool)
3. Withdraw their LP tokens
4. Pay back the flashloan

title: Interest rate is updated before
content: The vulnerability is an ordering flaw in the repayment flow of the lending pool. When a borrower calls the repay function, the contract updates the reserve’s interest rates before it has reduced the recorded total debt. The interest‑rate calculation reads the cached nextDebtShares value, which still reflects the pre‑repayment debt amount. Consequently the new liquidity and borrow rates are computed as if the debt had not changed, treating the repayment as a fresh liquidity injection rather than a debt reduction. This stale‑state usage allows the protocol to keep charging interest on a debt that is already zero. The bug manifests whenever a repayment clears a user’s outstanding borrow – including the special case where the caller passes type(uint256).max to repay the full amount. Under these conditions the protocol emits a correct Repay event, transfers the assets, but the subsequent call to updateInterestRates uses the old debt figure, leaving the reserve’s utilization unchanged. Suppliers who have provided liquidity therefore continue to accrue interest based on the previous, higher utilization, even though no borrowers remain. From a user’s perspective a supplier sees their supplied balance grow unexpectedly or, when trying to withdraw, encounters a revert because the pool’s internal accounting shows more shares than the actual token balance. The impact is a distortion of the accounting model: interest is over‑distributed to early suppliers and under‑distributed to later ones, and in extreme cases funds can become locked because the pool believes it owes more interest than it holds. The issue was discovered during a formal audit and reproduced with a test that repays a loan, skips time, forces a reserve update and then observes that the supplier’s accrued interest continues to increase and withdrawal fails. The problem is hard to notice because the interest‑rate values appear to update normally and the repayment transaction succeeds, hiding the fact that the underlying debt metric was never refreshed. The bug belongs to the class of state‑ordering or stale‑cache vulnerabilities, where a contract reads a value that should have been updated earlier in the same transaction. The correct fix is to move the call that updates the reserve’s interest rates to after the debt balance and cache variables have been refreshed – for example by updating cache.nextDebtShares (or the equivalent debt state) before invoking updateInterestRates, or by separating the two steps into distinct transactions. In conceptual terms the protocol must ensure that any interest‑rate computation uses the most recent debt snapshot, guaranteeing that interest accrues only on actual outstanding borrowings and that suppliers receive interest that matches the true utilization of the pool.

title: Wrong calculation of sup- ply/debt balance of a position, disrupting core system functionalities Found by 000000, 0xAlix2, A2-security, BiasedMerc, Bigsam, DenTonylifer, Honour, JCN, JuggerNaut63, KupiaSec, Nihavent, Obsidian, Tendency, TessKimy, Varun_05, almurhasan, charlesjhongc, coffiasd, dany.armstrong90, denzi_, dhank, ether_sky, iamnmt, jah, joshuajee, lemonmon, neon2835, oxelmiguel, perseus, silver_eth, trachev
content: The vulnerability consists of an incorrect calculation of a position’s supply and debt balances inside the core library that provides these values to the rest of the protocol. The two functions responsible – one that returns the supply balance and one that returns the debt balance – mistakenly return the raw share amount (self.supplyShares or self.debtShares) instead of converting those shares into the underlying asset amount using the current liquidity index. The root cause is a misunderstanding of the share‑to‑asset conversion: the code adds an “increase” term that is derived from the difference of ray‑multiplied shares, but then returns the original share count plus that increase, which still yields a share quantity rather than an asset quantity. Because every component that relies on these helpers (withdrawal logic, repayment logic, reward distribution, NFT position accounting and vault total‑asset calculation) expects an asset amount, the protocol consistently works with a value that is far lower than the real balance. An attacker or honest user can trigger the bug simply by performing normal operations – for example, supplying assets, borrowing, accruing interest and then attempting to withdraw or repay the full debt. The exploit manifests as a failure to fully repay a loan even when the caller passes type(uint256).max, leaving a residual debt that can be observed in the contract’s state. Similarly, withdrawals may revert or return less than expected because the contract believes the position holds insufficient supply. Reward calculations that depend on the reported balance become inaccurate, potentially rewarding users with too few or too many tokens. The impact is therefore systemic: lenders may be unable to retrieve their full deposits, borrowers may be stuck with lingering debt, NFT‑based positions may display incorrect balances, and the protocol’s accounting invariants are broken, which could erode trust and lead to capital loss. The condition under which the bug appears is any call to getSupplyBalance or getDebtBalance with the current liquidity index (or any other index) – essentially every read of a position’s balance. All participants that interact with the pool – regular users, NFT position owners and the protocol itself – are affected. The issue was discovered during a thorough audit when reviewers wrote a test that attempted a full‑repay using UINT256_MAX; the test logged a non‑zero debt after the repayment, confirming that the balance returned by the library was wrong. The bug is subtle because the contract’s external view functions still return a non‑zero number, so the discrepancy can be hidden as “dust” and may not be obvious from UI displays that round small amounts. To remediate the problem the balance functions must be rewritten to return the asset amount directly by multiplying the stored shares by the supplied index (self.supplyShares.rayMul(index) and self.debtShares.rayMul(index)) and removing the erroneous addition of the original share value. This change restores the correct accounting semantics, allowing withdrawals, repayments and reward calculations to operate on the true asset balances and re‑establishing the protocol’s financial integrity.

title: Full Liquidation Won't Sweep the
content: The vulnerability is a unit‑mismatch bug in the liquidation workflow where debt and collateral values are handled as share quantities instead of actual asset amounts. The root cause is that the internal function _calculateDebt returns the borrower’s debtShares and the amount of debt to liquidate as shares, but these values are never converted to asset units using the current borrow index. Likewise, the collateral balance supplied to _calculateAvailableCollateralToLiquidate is taken as supplyShares without converting to asset amounts via the liquidity index. The subsequent liquidation logic treats these share values as if they were asset amounts, feeding them into repayDebt and other accounting functions that expect real token quantities. When a liquidator attempts a full liquidation – i.e., covers the maximum liquidatable debt – the protocol repays only a fraction of the actual debt because the share‑to‑asset conversion is missing. The remaining debt shares stay in the borrower’s position, but the borrowing flag is cleared because the code checks whether the original userDebt equals the actualDebtToLiquidate, a comparison that succeeds when both are expressed in shares. This incorrectly marks the user as no longer borrowing, causing the protocol to calculate a lower total debt, an inflated health factor and LTV, and to treat the position as healthy despite an outstanding obligation. The bug manifests only when a liquidation request specifies an amount that would fully cover the debt according to the share‑based calculation; under partial liquidations the mismatch is less visible. It affects borrowers whose positions are liquidated, liquidators who trigger the operation, and the overall pool because the accounting errors propagate to risk metrics and can enable under‑collateralized positions. The issue was discovered during a manual audit and reproduced with a focused test case that logged the borrow index, debt shares before and after liquidation, and the borrowing flag, revealing that a significant amount of debt remained while the flag was false. The problem is hard to notice because the external view of the position shows zero asset debt, while the internal share balance still holds value, and the flag change masks the residual liability. The correct fix is to convert shares to assets before any arithmetic in the liquidation path, for example by using getDebtBalance(borrowIndex) for debt and getSupplyBalance(liquidityIndex) for collateral, ensuring that all subsequent calculations operate on true token amounts. This aligns the liquidation logic with the protocol’s accounting model and prevents false clearing of borrowing status, preserving accurate health factor, LTV, and overall pool safety.

title: Liquidation can be DOSed due to
content: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition affecting the liquidation process of a multi‑asset lending pool. The root cause is that the protocol uses the same asset reserves for both lending/borrowing operations and for holding users’ collateral deposits, without any mechanism to prevent the portion of the reserve that backs collateral from being borrowed or withdrawn. Because the pool administrator can only disable borrowing for an entire reserve, an attacker can supply collateral to a reserve, then borrow from that same reserve (or withdraw the supplied assets) to drain the liquidity that is supposed to back the collateral. When a liquidation is later attempted, the protocol tries to transfer the collateral from the depleted reserve to the liquidator, but the reserve no longer holds enough of the asset, causing the liquidation call to revert. From the user’s point of view, a borrower who is under‑collateralised expects the protocol to liquidate the position and recover the debt, yet the liquidator receives an error, the collateral remains locked, and the borrower’s debt stays unchanged. This results in bad debt for the protocol, potential loss of funds for lenders, and undermines the economic assumptions that collateral can always be sold to cover a default. The issue can occur in any normal operation of a pool that contains at least two asset reserves, each of which is permitted to accept collateral and to be used for borrowing, which is the intended design of the protocol. It was discovered during a security audit when a test case demonstrated that after an attacker borrowed against the same reserve that held a victim’s collateral, the subsequent liquidation reverted. The problem is subtle because the reserve may be partially or fully drained through legitimate borrowing activity, making it hard to distinguish malicious intent from normal market dynamics. To remediate, the protocol should enforce a separation of concerns: collateral deposits must be locked in a portion of the reserve that cannot be borrowed or withdrawn, or the system should track per‑account collateral balances and prevent those specific amounts from being used for lending. This could be achieved by introducing a collateral‑only flag for each deposit, by maintaining distinct liquidity pools for lending and for collateral, or by adding fine‑grained access controls that block borrowing against assets that are earmarked as collateral. Implementing such a safeguard would ensure that, even if the overall reserve is heavily borrowed, the collateral needed for liquidation remains available, preserving the protocol’s ability to recover bad debt and protecting users’ funds.

title: An attacker can hijack the Cura
content: The vulnerability resides in the CuratedVault contract’s totalAssets view function, which aggregates the balances of all positions in the withdraw queue without first updating the pool’s liquidityIndex (or reserve). Because the liquidityIndex reflects the accrued interest over time, failing to refresh it means the function reports a stale total asset value that does not include the most recent yield. When a user deposits after the yield has accrued, the contract calculates the number of shares to mint based on this outdated totalAssets figure. Consequently, the new depositor receives a larger share of the vault than they should, effectively capturing a portion of the matured yield that rightfully belongs to earlier participants. An attacker can exploit this accounting mismatch by taking a flash loan, depositing the borrowed amount at the moment after yield accrual but before the reserve is updated, and then immediately redeeming the inflated shares. The attacker’s profit equals the fraction flashLoanAmount/(flashLoanAmount+totalAssets) of the accrued yield, which can be substantial when the pool’s interest rate is high or when the time interval between updates (T2‑T1) is large, such as in low‑activity pools. The impact is a direct loss of accrued interest for legitimate users, reducing their expected returns and potentially eroding confidence in the protocol. The issue manifests when the vault’s totalAssets is queried or used for share calculations without a preceding forceUpdateReserve call; from a user’s perspective the UI may show the same vault balance before and after a deposit, yet the underlying accounting has shifted, leading to unexpected zero or reduced refunds. The bug was discovered during a formal audit and reproduced with a proof‑of‑concept test that demonstrated a flash‑loan attacker profiting from the stale index. It is hard to notice because the function is read‑only and appears to simply sum balances, so the missing update step is not obvious without inspecting the interaction between liquidityIndex and share minting logic. The proper remediation is to force an update of the pool’s reserve (or liquidityIndex) at the beginning of totalAssets, ensuring that the reported asset total always reflects the latest accrued yield before any share calculations are performed. This aligns the contract with the expected accounting guarantees of ERC‑4626, where totalAssets must represent the current value of all underlying assets, thereby preventing yield hijacking and preserving fair distribution of interest among all participants.

Attack Path

• The pool has high interest rate.
• T2 - T1 is large. This is the case for the pool with low interactions.
When X is a considerable amount, the amount of hijacked funds could be greater than the cost of the attack, then the attacker will benefit from the attack.

title: LiquidationLogic@_burnCollateralTokens
content: The vulnerability resides in the liquidation routine of the protocol where the function that burns a liquidator’s collateral tokens does not include the protocol liquidation fee in the amount of collateral that is withdrawn from the borrower’s position. When the protocol fee percentage is non‑zero, the fee amount is transferred to the treasury but the internal accounting of supply shares is left unchanged because the withdrawCollateral call is made with only the net collateral amount (vars.actualCollateralToLiquidate). As a result the pool’s total supply shares and the liquidator’s share balance are inflated relative to the actual underlying assets held by the pool. This mismatch allows a liquidated actor to later withdraw more assets than they are entitled to, effectively letting the fee be reclaimed by the liquidator or other users and causing the pool to become insolvent. The issue manifests during any liquidation that includes a protocol fee, which is a common configuration for many lending markets. It affects borrowers who become liquidated, liquidators who receive the inflated shares, and all other depositors whose withdrawals may be short‑changed. The flaw was discovered during a security audit when a test that enabled a 5 % liquidation fee produced a failed assertion: the pool balance after liquidation did not match the expected amount, exposing the accounting error. The problem is subtle because the fee transfer appears to succeed and no explicit error is thrown; the discrepancy only shows up in aggregate share calculations, making it hard to notice in normal operation. Conceptually the fix is to adjust the withdrawCollateral call to include the fee amount (vars.liquidationProtocolFeeAmount) so that the total shares burned reflect the true amount of collateral removed from the pool, thereby keeping the supply accounting consistent with the underlying token balances. This class of bug is an accounting inconsistency caused by neglecting fee deductions in token burn logic, leading to money disappearing from the pool and violating the protocol’s accounting invariants.

title: Malicious pool deployer can set
content: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service caused by unrestricted upgrade of the interest rate strategy contract. The pool configurator permits the pool creator to call setReserveInterestRateStrategyAddress with any address. Because the protocol later calls IReserveInterestRateStrategy.calculateInterestRates during updateInterestRates, a malicious strategy that simply reverts makes every call to updateInterestRates fail. After users have deposited into the vault, the attacker replaces the strategy with the reverting contract. When a user later initiates a withdrawal, executeWithdraw invokes updateInterestRates, which triggers the revert, so the transaction aborts and no tokens are transferred. From the user’s point of view the withdrawal transaction fails with a generic revert and the displayed balance remains unchanged, contrary to the expectation that the funds would be returned. The impact is that deposited assets become permanently inaccessible as long as the malicious strategy remains, effectively locking the pool’s liquidity. The condition for exploitation is that the pool deployer retains the privileged role that can change the interestRateStrategy address after deposits have been made. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the configurator’s permission model and the reliance on an external contract for rate calculation. It can be hard to notice because the revert appears as a generic error without indicating that the rate‑calculation contract is at fault, and the loss of funds is only observed when a withdrawal is attempted. The bug belongs to the class of “unrestricted external contract reference” or “upgradeable contract DoS” where an attacker can point a critical protocol component to a contract that always reverts. To remediate, the protocol should restrict the setReserveInterestRateStrategyAddress function to only accept addresses that are part of a vetted whitelist, or make the strategy immutable or governed by a multi‑signature process, thereby preventing a malicious deployer from inserting a reverting contract.
summary:
Once vault depositors have deposited funds into a pool, a malicious pool creator can upgrade the interestRateStrategy contract (using PoolConfigurator.setReserveInterestRateStrategyAddress()) to make all calls to it revert.  
As a result any function of the protocol that calls updateInterestRates() will revert because updateInterestRates() makes the following call:  
(vars.nextLiquidityRate, vars.nextBorrowRate) = IReserveInterestRateStrategy(_reserve.interestRateStrategyAddress).calculateInterestRates( /* PARAMS */ );  
The main impact is that now withdrawals will revert because executeWithdraw() calls updateInterestRates() which will always revert, so the funds that vault users deposited into this pool are lost forever.  
Allowing the pool deployer to specify any interestRateStrategyAddress  
Internal pre-conditions  
External pre-conditions  
Attack Path  
1. Vault users deposit into the pool  
2. the deployer sets their interestRateStrategy contract to make all calls to it revert  
3. All calls to withdraw funds from the pool will revert, the vault depositors have lost their funds  
All the funds deposited to the pool from the vault will be lost

title: When bad debt is accumulated
content: The vulnerability is an accounting flaw that prevents bad debt from being shared among all depositors in a lending pool. When a liquidation results in a shortfall – the liquidator repays less than the total debt – the contract continues to calculate each user’s withdrawal amount as the product of their share balance and the current liquidity index. This formula does not subtract the outstanding bad debt from the pool’s total assets, so the first users who withdraw after the shortfall can redeem their shares at the pre‑shortfall rate and receive the full amount they deposited. Later users, who withdraw after the pool’s assets have been depleted by the unrecovered debt, receive a reduced amount or may even be unable to withdraw at all. The impact is that funds effectively disappear for the last withdrawers, violating the protocol’s expectation that losses be socialised across all participants. The issue occurs only after a bad‑debt liquidation and when multiple depositors are present; early withdrawers escape the loss while later withdrawers bear the entire shortfall. Depositors, especially those who wait to withdraw, are affected because their balances may be lower than expected or may revert entirely. The flaw was discovered during an audit by constructing a proof‑of‑concept where two users supplied equal amounts, a liquidation repaid only part of the debt, and the first user withdrew the full amount while the second could withdraw only a fraction. The problem is subtle because normal withdrawals succeed and the pool appears healthy until a later user experiences a loss, making it easy to miss during routine testing. To fix the issue the protocol must adjust the accounting so that any bad debt is deducted from the pool’s total assets before computing per‑share value, for example by updating the liquidity index or applying a loss factor that is applied uniformly to all share balances, thereby socialising the loss among every depositor.
summary:
When bad debt is accumulated, it should be socialised amongst all suppliers.  
The issue is that the protocol does not do this, instead only the last users to withdraw funds will feel the effects of the bad debt.  
If a pool experiences bad debt, the first users to withdraw will experience 0 loss, while the last to withdraw will experience a severe loss.  
The withdrawn assets is calculated as shares*liquidityIndex which does not take into account bad debt  
This means that even if bad debt accrues, the first users to withdraw will be able to withdraw their shares to assets at a good rate, leaving the last users with all the loss.  
Internal pre-conditions  
External pre-conditions  
Attack Path  
This attack path is shown in the PoC:  
1. User A supplies 50 ETH to the pool  
2. User B supplies 50 ETH to the pool  
3. A bad debt liquidation occurs, so the liquidator only repaid 64 ETH out of the 100 ETH  
4. User A is still able to withdraw their 50 ETH  
5. User B is left with less than 14 ETH able to be withdrawn  
Huge fund loss for the suppliers last to withdraw  
Early withdrawers effectively steal from the late withdrawers

title: Liquidated positions will still ac-
content: The vulnerability consists of rewards continuing to be allocated to an NFT‑backed position after that position has been liquidated because the contract that stores per‑NFT balances is never updated when liquidation occurs. The root cause is that the NFTPositionManager contract, which holds the _balances mapping used in the reward formula, does not receive a callback from the liquidation routine, so the balance value remains equal to the pre‑liquidation amount. The reward calculation multiplies this stale balance by the difference between the global reward per token and the user‑specific paid amount, which yields a positive reward amount even though the position no longer holds any collateral. An attacker can exploit this by opening a leveraged position, allowing the collateral price to drop, triggering liquidation, and then simply waiting for the reward period to elapse before calling the claim function. The user will receive reward tokens that should have been forfeited, effectively stealing value from the protocol and other participants. This scenario occurs whenever a position becomes under‑collateralized, the price feed reflects a sufficient drop, and a liquidator calls the liquidation function. Affected parties include the protocol (loss of reward tokens), other users sharing the reward pool, and any user whose position is liquidated. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the reward accrual path and noticed that the balance variable is never cleared on liquidation. It is hard to notice because the UI may still display the NFT as existing and the reward balance as growing, which can be mistaken for normal accrual. The bug belongs to the class of stale‑state or missing‑state‑update errors that cause over‑allocation of rewards. From the user’s perspective, the expectation is that rewards stop once the position is liquidated, but the reality is that the reward balance continues to increase and can be withdrawn, leading to unexpected token gains. The attack flow can be described as: (1) open a leveraged position, (2) let the collateral price fall, (3) trigger liquidation, (4) do nothing else, (5) allow the reward period to run, (6) claim the inflated rewards. The recommended mitigation is to have the liquidation function invoke a callback on the rewards manager to reset the user’s balance to zero or mark the position as inactive before any further reward calculations, thereby aligning the reward accounting with the actual collateral state.
summary:
The NFTRewardsDistributor contract which is responsible for managing a users rewards using a masterchef algorithm does not get updated when a users underlying position in a pool is liquidated. This results in the position wrongfully continuing to accrue rewards with an outdated asset balance.  
The choice to neglect updating the NFTPositionManager contract when a position is liquidated is the root cause of this issue due to the NFTPositionManager contract not containing up-to-date user balances for calculating rewards.  
```solidity
function earned(uint256 tokenId, bytes32 _assetHash) public view returns (uint256) {
    return _balances[tokenId][_assetHash].mul(rewardPerToken(_assetHash).sub(userRewardPerTokenPaid[tokenId][_assetHash])).div(1e18).add(
        rewards[tokenId][_assetHash]
    );
}
```
The above calculations are done in NFTRewardsDistributor.sol:98 to determine an NFT position's rewards. Due to this bug, the users balance _balances[tokenId][_assetHash] will be incorrect, leading to overinflated rewards.  
Internal pre-conditions  
1. User needs to have a position NFT registered with the NFTPositionManager contract  
2. The NFTPositionManager needs to have rewards accrual enabled for there to be any impact  
3. The users NFT position needs to be liquidated due to their position being unhealthy  
External pre-conditions  
1. Users collateral assets need to drop in enough in price to make their position liquidatable  
2. Any user needs to liquidate the users position  
Attack Path  
1. User creates a position  
2. The NFTPositionManager contract will start accruing rewards for the user  
3. The users position's collateral drops in price enough to make their position unhealthy  
4. The user gets liquidated  
5. The user will continue to accrue rewards pertaining to their NFT's position for as long as they wish because the NFTPositionManager believes they are still providing collateral and borrowing assets.  
6. The user withdraws their accrued rewards whenever they wish  
The liquidated user will essentially be able to steal rewards from the protocol/other users since their position won't be backed by any collateral.

title: Function executeMintToTreasur
content: The vulnerability resides in the pool’s accounting routine that mints accrued fees to the treasury. In the function that transfers those fees, the contract reduces the global supply share counter (totalSupply.supplyShares) without simultaneously crediting any account – specifically the treasury’s share balance is never increased. Because the protocol assumes that the minted shares exist and can be burned, the totalSupply.supplyShares value can become lower than the sum of all individual balances. This invariant violation is the root cause of the bug. When a user initiates a withdrawal (or the simplified withdraw function), the pool calls the faulty mint‑to‑treasury routine. The routine subtracts shares from the global counter while no user’s balance is adjusted, so the next withdrawal attempts to reconcile the mismatch. If the pool is close to empty, the last one or two users will encounter an under‑flow in totalSupply.supplyShares, causing the transaction to revert. From the user’s point of view the withdrawal fails, no assets are transferred, and the user’s balance appears unchanged – effectively the funds become locked in the pool. The issue was discovered during a systematic audit of the pool logic, where the relationship between totalSupply.supplyShares and the aggregate of individual supplyShares was examined and found to be broken by the mint‑to‑treasury path. The bug is subtle because it only manifests under specific conditions (non‑zero accrued treasury shares and a withdrawal that triggers the mint routine) and does not affect normal operations when the pool has ample liquidity. It belongs to the class of accounting invariant violations where a global accounting variable is updated inconsistently with per‑account state, leading to a “balance sheet mismatch”. To remediate the problem the mint‑to‑treasury function must either credit the treasury’s share balance before reducing the global counter, or avoid modifying totalSupply.supplyShares altogether and instead adjust only the underlying asset balance. In short, the function should keep the invariant that totalSupply.supplyShares equals the sum of all users’ supplyShares, ensuring that withdrawals succeed and funds remain accessible.
summary:
The incorrect reduction in PoolLogic::executeMintToTreasury will cause failure of some (likely to be the last) user's withdrawal, and the fund will be locked.  
The totalSupply.supplyShares is supposed to be the sum of balances.supplyShares, as they are always updated in tandem:  
acts/core/pool/configuration/PositionBalanceConfiguration.sol#L94-L95  
acts/core/pool/configuration/PositionBalanceConfiguration.sol#L48-L49  
If this is not held, then some users will not be able to withdraw their collateral, as the totalSupply.supplyShares will underflow and revert.  
However in the PoolLogic::executeMintToTreasury updates the totalSupply.supplyShares without updating any user's balance. It is because it incorrectly assumes that there is share to be burned, even though the accrued amount was never really minted to the treasury (in that the treasury's share balance was not added). If it is so, that share should be burned from the treasury.  
Also, for example, when premium is added via flashloan, the premium is counted as /zerolend-one/contracts/core/pool/logic/FlashLoanLogic.sol#L118  
Therefore, when the underlying asset is transferred out via executeMintToTreasury, the underlyingBalance should be updated accordingly.  
Internal pre-conditions  
Non-zero accruedToTreasuryShares  
External pre-conditions  
Attack Path  
1. Anybody calls withdraw or withdrawSimple, it will reduce the asset's totalSupply.supplyShares incorrectly.  
The last user(s) who is trying to withdraw will fail, and their fund will be locked

title: Market coordinator can steal all market collateral
content: The vulnerability is a design flaw in the market’s fee architecture that allows a market coordinator to expropriate the entire collateral pool of a market. The protocol defines an adiabatic fee that is charged to takers when they increase the market skew and paid to takers when they reduce skew, with the intention of incentivising risk‑reducing trades. Because the coordinator is granted unrestricted authority to modify risk parameters, including the adiabatic fee rate, the coordinator can first set the adiabatic fee to zero, open very large maker and taker positions that incur no fee, and then, after the positions have been settled for one oracle interval, raise the adiabatic fee to its maximum allowed value (for example 1%). When the coordinator subsequently closes the positions, the fee that is now owed to the taker is credited to the market’s global exposure field. That exposure is supposed to be covered by the market owner, but the contract permits the coordinator to withdraw the amount that was added to exposure, effectively moving the newly created fee revenue into the coordinator’s own balance. By repeating the cycle, the coordinator can drain the market’s token balance while the individual user accounts still show positive collateral, leaving users unable to withdraw because the market no longer holds any tokens. The attack can also be performed by an external user who front‑runs a scheduled fee increase, opening a delta‑neutral taker position before the fee change and then closing it after the fee rises, thereby extracting the fee differential at the expense of the owner’s exposure. The issue manifests whenever risk parameters are updated via the Global.update call, which adjusts the global exposure based on the new adiabatic fee. It is discovered through audit testing that manipulates fee parameters and observes the resulting exposure accounting. The problem is hard to notice because the fee change itself is a legitimate operation and the collateral balances of individual accounts appear correct; only the aggregate market token balance reveals the loss. The impact is severe: all market collateral can be stolen, leaving the market insolvent and users with unrecoverable funds. The affected parties are market participants who deposit collateral, the market owner who is left with a negative exposure, and any protocol that relies on the coordinator’s fee‑setting authority. A conceptual fix requires redesigning the adiabatic fee mechanism so that fee rate changes cannot create net positive exposure for the coordinator, for example by removing adiabatic fees, capping the exposure that can be generated by a fee change, or forcing the coordinator to post collateral that covers any exposure created by their parameter updates. In short, the bug is a classic “fee manipulation” or “parameter abuse” vulnerability that breaks the accounting invariants of the market and enables the coordinator to steal funds.

panprog Summary The README states the following:
Q: Please list any known issues and explicitly state the acceptable risks for each known issue. Coordinators are given broad control over the parameters of the markets they coordinate. The protocol parameter is designed to prevent situations where parameters are set to malicious steal funds. If the coordinator can operate within the bounds of reasonable protocol parameters to negatively affect markets we would like to know about it
Even when protocol parameters are reasonable, market coordinator can steal all market funds by utilizing the adiabatic fees change. The adiabatic fees are fees taken from takers when they increase skew (difference between open longs and shorts) and paid to takers when they decrease skew to incentivize orders which reduce price risk for makers. The issue is that market coordinator can set adiabatic fees to 0, open large maker/taker positions (taker position paying 0 adiabatic fees), then immediately set adiabatic fees to max possible (e.g. 1%) and close taker/maker positions (receiving the adiabatic fee). This fees difference when adiabatic fees are changed by market coordinator is subtracted from market's global exposure, which is supposed to be paid/received by the owner. I.e. when adiabatic fees are increased, this increases exposure to be paid by the owner with coordinator being able to withdraw this amount to himself (up to total market's collateral available), meaning coordinator can steal all market funds.
Root Cause The root cause is the protocol design of adiabatic fees, it's hard to pinpoint any specific code which is the root cause.
When market risk parameters are updated, Global.update is called with new risk parameters, which changes the global exposure:
nnial-v2/packages/perennial/contracts/types/Global.sol#L54-L56
This global exposure has to be covered or received by owner by calling
/blob/main/perennial-v2/packages/perennial/contracts/Market.sol#L329-L339
Since market coordinator can change adiabatic fees, this allows market coordinator to control the owner's exposure, which is essentially what lets coordinator to take advantage of this and steal funds.
Internal pre-conditions Coordinator is malicious OR User front-runs adiabatic fees increase transaction
External pre-conditions None.
Attack Path
1. Coordinator sets adiabatic fees and all the other fees to 0, also increases makerLimit to large amount to cause larger impact
2. Coordinator opens large maker position and large taker position (paying 0 fees)
3. Wait for 1 oracle version to settle maker and taker positions
4. Coordinator sets adiabatic fees to max allowed value (e.g. 1%)
5. Coordinator closes taker position, settles it, closes maker position, settles it
6. At this point maker should have about the same amount of collateral as deposited, and taker should have deposited collateral + adiabatic fees paid to taker for closing the position. Both maker and taker accounts withdraw all collateral. Most likely total collateral will be higher than the market has, so simply withdraw all collateral market has
At this point all funds are stolen by coordinator (and if not - simply repeat from step 1 until all funds are stolen). The other users will have positive collateral balances, but they will be unable to withdraw anything since market token balance will be 0 (market owner will have large negative exposure).
Alternative attack scenario:
1. Coordinator wants to increase adiabatic fees
2. User listens to coordinator transaction and front-runs it by creating huge taker position (possibly 2 taker positions - long+short to be delta-neutral, also maybe maker position if necessary, to be able to open large taker positions). This doesn't need to be classic front-run, maybe the coordinator will announce risk parameter changes in the forum or somewhere, and user opens these positions in anticipation of adiabatic fees increase
3. Coordinator transaction to increase adiabatic fees goes through
4. User closes his positions, receiving large profit from adiabatic fees only (which should more than cover all the other fees, and market price risk can be neutralized by opening delta-neutral positions), at the expense of the owner's exposure
Impact All market collateral token balance is stolen.

title: Market coordinator can liquidate all users in
content: The vulnerability is an unchecked governance‑parameter abuse that allows a market coordinator to arbitrarily raise margin ratios, maintenance ratios, minimum USD amounts and fee percentages without any upper bound or delay. Because the RiskParameter contract only enforces a lower limit (preventing values from being set to zero) and lacks a timelock or sanity caps, a malicious coordinator can set these parameters to extreme values such as a 1000% margin requirement. When the margin and maintenance ratios are increased dramatically, every existing position in the market becomes under‑collateralised, triggering the protocol’s liquidation logic. The coordinator can then call the liquidation function on all maker positions, collect the maximum liquidation fee, open a tiny maker position for themselves, and subsequently liquidate every taker position. The fees earned from each liquidation (often a percentage of the notional, e.g., 1%) are accumulated in the coordinator’s sole maker account, which can then be closed and the collateral withdrawn. This sequence results in at least a one‑percent loss of total market value, all user positions being closed, and users seeing their balances drop to zero or receive only a negligible payout. The attack can be carried out by any coordinator with permission to modify market parameters; no external conditions are required. All market participants—makers, takers, and any users holding collateral—are affected because the protocol assumes that parameter changes are reasonable and that users are given notice before such changes. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the risk‑parameter design and noted the absence of an upper limit and a timelock. It is hard to notice because the contract permits parameter updates as part of normal market governance, so a sudden increase may be mistaken for a legitimate market adjustment rather than a malicious act. To remediate, the protocol should enforce reasonable upper caps on margin, maintenance and minimum values, and introduce a timelock or multi‑signature approval process for any coordinator‑initiated parameter change, thereby giving users advance warning and preventing instantaneous forced liquidations. This class of bug falls under unchecked configuration or governance‑parameter abuse, where economic assumptions of the system (stable collateral requirements and fair fee structures) are violated, leading to unexpected fund disappearance and broken accounting logic from the user’s perspective, who expects their positions to remain healthy unless market conditions change, not because a coordinator arbitrarily altered protocol settings.

title: Market coordinator can steal all market col-
content: The vulnerability is a design flaw in the market’s risk‑parameter system that allows a market coordinator to manipulate the fee‑scale and maker‑limit values to arbitrarily low numbers. The fee calculation for both taker proportional fees and maker proportional fees multiplies the absolute order size by the price and then by (orderSize/scale). When scale is set to 1, the fee becomes essentially orderSize² × price × feeRate, which can easily exceed 100 % of the position value. Because the contract only checks that the scale is larger than a percentage of the makerLimit, and because there is no upper bound on the makerLimit itself, a malicious coordinator can first open a large maker position, settle it, then open a large taker position that remains unsettled, and finally change the risk parameters so that makerLimit and scale are both set to 1. At the next oracle settlement the taker position is charged an astronomically high fee, creating a huge bad‑debt balance for the taker, while the maker (controlled by the coordinator) receives a profit larger than the total market collateral. The coordinator can then withdraw the inflated maker balance, effectively stealing all funds that were deposited in the market. This attack works whenever the coordinator has permission to update risk parameters and there are no additional checks on the magnitude of scale relative to the actual open positions. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the validation logic of RiskParameter.sol and the fee formulas, noting that the scale limit is derived only from makerLimit and that the proportional fee formula is unbounded. The issue is hard to notice because the fee parameters appear to be normal percentages in the UI, and the excessive fees only manifest after the coordinator changes the parameters, which may happen in a single transaction. From a user’s point of view a taker sees their balance drop to a large negative number or receives no payout after settlement, while a maker sees an unexpected large profit and can withdraw more than the total collateral. Honest participants who only deposited collateral see their funds disappear. The bug belongs to the class of “unbounded fee calculation” or “parameter manipulation leading to fee overflow”. To remediate the problem the protocol should enforce strict validation of the fee‑scale against the current global position sizes, cap the proportional and adiabatic fees to a maximum percentage, limit the range of makerLimit and efficiencyLimit, and redesign the fee formulas to be percentage‑based with hard caps so that fees can never exceed the position value regardless of scale settings.

panprog Summary The README states the following:
Q: Please list any known issues and explicitly state the acceptable risks for each known issue. Coordinators are given broad control over the parameters of the markets they coordinate. The protocol parameter is designed to prevent situations where parameters are set to malicious steal funds. If the coordinator can operate within the bounds of reasonable protocol parameters to negatively affect markets we would like to know about it
Market coordinator can set both makerLimit and scale for takerFee at very low amount (like 1), which will charge absurdly high taker proportional fee to existing positions, because proportional fee formula is change.abs().mul(price).muldiv(change.abs(), scale).mul(fee), i.e. the fee is (order_size)^2 * price * fee when scale is 1. The same issue is with maker proportional fee and taker adiabatic fee - all of them multiply by order size divided by scale.
The only limitation for scale setting is that it must be larger than some percentage of makerLimit and there is no limitation on makerLimit:
self.makerLimit.div(self.efficiencyLimit).mul(protocolParameter.minScale);
if (self.takerFee.scale.lt(scaleLimit) || self.makerFee.scale.lt(scaleLimit)) revert RiskParameterStorageInvalidError();
This allows to set any scale amount, the makerLimit just has to be set to a similar amount, or alternatively efficiencyLimit can be set to a huge amount (there is only downside limitation for it), which will make scaleLimit very low, allowing very low scale values.
Market coordinator can abuse this by opening large maker position (settling it), opening large taker position (unsettled), changing risk parameter makerLimit and scale to 1, then at the next oracle version the large taker position will be settled using scale = 1, charging fees much higher than 100%, putting taker position into huge bad debt, while all makers will have huge profit (larger than market collateral), which coordinator can immediately withdraw from his maker position, stealing all market collateral.
Root Cause The exact root cause is hard to determine here. It might be the lack of risk parameter settings validations: the only scale check is against scaleLimit calculated from makerLimit, but there is no conditions on makerLimit itself: nnial-v2/packages/perennial/contracts/types/RiskParameter.sol#L159-L161
On the other hand, it's probably hard to set correct protocol-wide limitation for this, so maybe the issue is with the design of the proportional and adiabatic fees, where the order_size / scale multiplication is quite dangerous as it is unlimited.
Internal pre-conditions Coordinator is malicious.
External pre-conditions None.
Attack Path
1. Coordinator opens large maker position, settles it
2. Coordinator opens large taker position (but doesn't settle it yet)
3. Coordinator sets risk parameter: makerLimit = 1, takerFee.scale = 1 and takerFee.proportionalFee set to max.
4. Coordinator commits oracle version of the taker position, settles maker+taker positions: taker is in huge bad debt, maker is in huge profit (larger than all market collateral)
5. Coordinator withdraws all market collateral
Alternatives:
• Setting takerFee.scale = 1 and efficiencyLimit to a very high value.
• All taker trades after the scale = 1 is set will incur huge fee, so it's possible to have settled taker position before the risk params change, and then close it by liquidation, incurring huge fees. Coordinator doesn't even have to open his own taker position, he can simply liquidate any large existing taker.
• Use adiabatic fees scale instead of taker proportional fees
• Use maker proportional fees (and use only maker accounts)
Impact All market collateral stolen.
Additional impact: if the market is part of any vault, almost all this vault funds can be stolen. This can be done by forcing the vault to re-balance (depositing or withdrawing some amount), which will charge huge fees, making vault's collateral in the market negative. Next re-balance will add more collateral into the market, which can be stolen again, repeated until most vault funds are stolen.

title: Maliciously specifying a very large intent.price
content: The vulnerability is an unchecked price parameter in the market order creation flow. When a user creates an intent, the contract only checks that the supplied collateral exceeds the product of the intent position and the last known market price. It does not validate how far the intent.price can deviate from the current market price. As a result an attacker can submit an order with an arbitrarily large intent.price while providing only a modest amount of collateral that satisfies the minimal position‑based check. During settlement the protocol computes profit and loss as (intent.price - lastVersion.price) multiplied by the position. Because the price difference is huge, the calculated pnl becomes extremely large and is added to the local collateral balance of the party that settles the order. The attacker can then withdraw the inflated collateral, effectively stealing funds that were never backed by sufficient risk margin. This flaw occurs whenever the market contract accepts a new order without imposing a bound on intent.price or requiring collateral that covers the potential price swing. All participants that rely on the market’s accounting – including honest traders, liquidity providers, and the protocol itself – are exposed to loss of funds. The issue was discovered during a security audit when a test case deliberately set intent.price to 1.25 × 10^12 while the market price remained at 123, resulting in a collateral increase from 10 000 to over 6 250 000 000 000 after settlement. The problem is subtle because the order submission appears normal; the UI shows no error and the large price value does not trigger an overflow or revert, making it easy to miss in casual testing. The root cause is the absence of a validation rule that ties the allowed price range to the current market price and the lack of collateralization logic that secures the price delta. To remediate, the contract should enforce that intent.price stays within a reasonable band around lastVersion.price (for example by limiting the percentage deviation) and that the required collateral is calculated based on the maximum possible pnl derived from that band. In other words, the price field must be treated as a bounded input and the collateral model must be updated to cover the worst‑case profit or loss that could arise from the allowed price range. This class of bug is a price‑validation and under‑collateralization flaw that can lead to arbitrary fund extraction through manipulated settlement calculations.

in CheckpointLib.sol#L79

This value is counted towards the collateral local.collateral.

title: Lack of access control in the
content: The vulnerability is an unrestricted access control flaw in the MarketFactory.updateExtension function, which allows any external caller to add or remove entries in the extensions mapping without owner verification. The root cause is the omission of the onlyOwner modifier after the Perennial 2.3 update introduced a new authorization mechanism for signers and extensions. Because the extensions mapping is consulted by the MarketFactory.authorization routine, an address listed in extensions is treated as a protocol‑wide operator for every account. An attacker can therefore call updateExtension with their own address and set the boolean flag to true, instantly becoming an authorized operator for all user accounts. Once registered as an extension, the attacker can invoke market functions that rely on the authorization check, such as withdrawing collateral or executing trades on behalf of any user. The impact is the potential loss of all funds held by affected accounts, as the contract will accept the attacker’s calls as legitimate operator actions. This condition occurs whenever the contract is deployed with the vulnerable version of MarketFactory and no additional guard (e.g., a pause or multi‑sig) prevents arbitrary calls to updateExtension. All users, including token holders, traders, and any role that relies on the market’s collateral safety, are affected because their balances may be drained without any on‑chain indication. The issue was discovered during a security audit that reviewed the new authorization flow and noticed that the updateExtension function lacked any access restriction. The bug is subtle because the extensions mapping is not directly exposed in the UI, and the contract does not emit warnings when an unauthorized address is added, making the exploit invisible to casual observers. Conceptually, the flaw belongs to the class of “missing access control” or “privilege escalation” bugs where a privileged operation is callable by any actor. From a user’s perspective, the expected behavior is that only the contract owner or a designated governance entity can designate operators; in reality, a malicious actor can become an operator, causing funds to disappear, withdrawals to fail, or collateral to be transferred without consent. The proper remediation is to protect the updateExtension function with an onlyOwner (or equivalent role‑based) modifier, ensuring that only authorized governance can modify the extensions mapping, and to consider adding events or safeguards that alert when extensions are changed.

title: Market coordinator can set staleAfter to a huge
content: The vulnerability consists of an unchecked risk parameter called staleAfter that a market coordinator can set to any uint24 value. Because the contract does not validate this parameter, a coordinator can assign an extremely large timeout, effectively telling the market that price data may remain stale for an arbitrarily long period. The root cause is the absence of a sanity check in the RiskParameter contract where staleAfter is stored. An attacker who controls the coordinator role can exploit this by first opening a large long position and a matching short position from two accounts, creating a delta‑neutral portfolio that locks a substantial amount of market collateral. After the positions are opened the market is left idle long enough for the external price oracle to move far away from the last committed price, which is easy to achieve in thinly traded markets or during rapid price swings lasting only a few minutes. The coordinator then sets staleAfter to its maximum value (e.g., uint24.max) together with minimal margin and maintenance requirements, and withdraws the maximum collateral from the position that is currently profitable given the stale price. When the next oracle update is committed, the withdrawn position is marked as bad debt because the price used for liquidation is now far from the stale price. The coordinator subsequently closes the opposite position, extracting the remaining collateral. Because the bad‑debt amount equals the profit of the two combined positions, the coordinator can end up extracting more than the total collateral that was originally deposited, effectively stealing all market funds. The attack can be repeated until the market’s collateral pool is empty. The impact is a total loss of market collateral for all users who supplied liquidity, while the coordinator walks away with the stolen assets. The condition required for the exploit is a period of inactivity that allows the price to diverge beyond the margin requirement, a situation that occurs frequently in real‑world markets. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the risk‑parameter validation logic; it is hard to notice because staleAfter is not used in most normal operations and the contract does not emit any warning when an extreme value is set. The vulnerability belongs to the class of unchecked parameter bugs that enable economic attacks by manipulating risk settings. To remediate the problem the contract should enforce reasonable upper bounds on staleAfter, require governance approval for extreme values, and possibly add runtime checks that reject staleAfter values that would allow price data to remain stale longer than a predefined safe window.

title: Perennial account users with rebalance group
content: The vulnerability originates from the rebalance logic of perennial accounts that are organised into a rebalance group. The function that decides whether a market can be rebalanced, RebalanceLib.checkMarket, evaluates only the percentage difference between the target collateral and the actual collateral, without enforcing any minimum absolute value. Consequently, when a group contains one market with a tiny amount of collateral and the remaining markets hold zero collateral, the percentage calculation reports a 100 % imbalance and the controller marks the group as re‑balancable. The controller then attempts to pull the surplus from the market with collateral and push it to the markets that are deficient. Because the target collateral for the empty markets is also zero, the computed imbalance for those markets is zero, so the net effect of the transfer is that the tiny amount of collateral is moved back into the owner’s perennial account, leaving the markets empty again. An attacker can exploit this by first donating an arbitrarily small amount of DSU (or USDC) to any market in the victim’s empty group – a donation is allowed by the market’s updateContext checks, which permit a sender to deposit value without changing the position. After the donation, the attacker calls the incentivised rebalanceGroup function, which executes the described transfer and restores the group to its original empty state while the victim’s perennial account now holds the donated amount. By repeating the donate‑and‑rebalance cycle, the attacker can drain the entire balance of the victim’s perennial account, because each iteration extracts a small slice of the remaining funds. The impact is a complete loss of the user’s DSU and USDC holdings, manifested to the user as a sudden drop of their account balance to zero or missing refunds when they attempt to withdraw. The issue only manifests when the account owner has activated a rebalance group whose markets are all empty (or have been emptied by withdrawals, liquidation, or simply never funded) while the perennial account still contains funds. The affected parties are the account owners, the protocol’s accounting layer, and any downstream users relying on the integrity of the rebalance mechanism. The flaw was discovered during a manual audit of the controller and rebalance library, where the logical relationship between percentage‑based thresholds and absolute collateral values was examined. It is difficult to notice because the rebalance operation appears to succeed, no error is thrown, and the transferred amount can be extremely small, making the balance change look like a normal fee or rounding error. To remediate the issue, the protocol should introduce a minimum absolute rebalance amount check, ensure that markets with zero collateral are excluded from rebalance calculations, or require that the target collateral be non‑zero before a rebalance is permitted. This prevents attackers from leveraging the percentage‑only check to repeatedly siphon funds from empty groups.

title: Frequency-dependent TaxCalc
content: The vulnerability resides in the TaxCalculator contract where the function that updates the compounded interest factor uses a discrete arithmetic expression with an incorrect scaling divisor. Instead of dividing the per‑second rate by 10,000, the code divides by 1,000, and then multiplies the result by the elapsed time period before adding it to the previous factor. Because the function is invoked each time a collection checkpoint is created – for example when a user creates, cancels or fills a listing – the interest multiplier is recomputed at a frequency that depends on marketplace activity rather than on the passage of real time. When the collection utilization is high (around 90 %) and checkpoints occur frequently (e.g., daily), the erroneous formula inflates the effective interest rate dramatically; a test case shows users can lose roughly 3200 % more than expected over a year. Conversely, if the protocol expects compound interest but checkpoints are sparse, the same mis‑scaled calculation can reduce the protocol’s earned interest by up to 42 % per year. The bug is a classic case of a financial‑logic error: an inaccurate compounding model caused by a wrong divisor and a discrete update that does not reflect continuous accrual. It manifests as users receiving higher fees than advertised, balances decreasing faster than anticipated, or refunds appearing smaller or missing. The issue is hard to notice because the contract still records a numeric interest factor, so the discrepancy only becomes apparent after prolonged operation or when comparing expected versus actual returns. No external attacker is required; the flaw is deterministic and affects every participant who interacts with the collection. The proper fix is to replace the discrete update with either a correctly scaled addition (using the proper divisor) for simple non‑compound interest, or to implement a mathematically sound compounding method such as per‑second exponentiation or continuous compounding, which also reduces gas consumption. By aligning the calculation with the intended financial model, the protocol will charge users the advertised rate and collect the expected interest, restoring trust in the system’s accounting assumptions.
