When an investor uses a smart contract wallet such as a multisig or account abstraction wallet, the contract may be deployed at a different address on the other chain. Consequently, the bridge registers the encoded address as belonging to the investor and issues the destination‑chain tokens to it. If another user, for example an attacker, controls an externally owned account that coincidentally has the same address on the destination chain, the bridge will allocate the tokens to that attacker. Exploitation follows a simple flow: the investor initiates a bridge transaction, the bridge payload includes the investor’s source address, the destination contract receives the payload, adds the address to the investor’s record, and mints tokens to that address. Because the address is not owned by the investor, the tokens become inaccessible to them and may be controlled by a third party. The impact is loss of funds, unauthorized control of minted tokens, and a breach of the protocol’s accounting guarantees that tokens issued to an investor are held by that investor. This condition occurs whenever a smart contract wallet is used on the source chain and the destination chain does not have a matching deployment of that wallet. Users of standard externally owned accounts are not affected, making the bug subtle and hard to notice; the UI may show a successful bridge and a token balance on the destination chain, yet the investor cannot interact with those tokens. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that highlighted the assumption in the payload encoding and the subsequent updateInvestor call. It may evade detection in automated testing because the address format is syntactically correct and the transaction succeeds. To remediate, the bridge should require investors to supply an explicit destination address that is verified to be under their control, possibly by a prior address‑credential bridging step, and should not rely on _msgSender() for cross‑chain token delivery. This change prevents the mismatch and ensures that token issuance aligns with the investor’s actual wallet on the target chain.
summary:
Investors using smart contract wallets may have their destination chain tokens issued to an address they don't control  
Description: SecuritizeBridge::bridgeDSTokens encodes _msgSender() in the payload message to be destination address for bridged tokens delivered on the destination chain; this is expected to represent the investor's wallet address:
// Send Relayer message
wormholeRelayer.sendPayloadToEvm{value: msg.value} (
    targetChain,
    targetAddress,
    abi.encode(
        investorDetail.investorId,
        value,
        _msgSender(), // @audit destination address of bridged tokens
        investorDetail.country,
        investorDetail.attributeValues,
        investorDetail.attributeExpirations
    ), // payload
    0, // no receiver value needed since we"re just passing a message
    gasLimit,
    whChainId,
    _msgSender()
);
SecuritizeBridge::receiveWormholeMessages executed on the destination chain adds the address to the investor's account and issues tokens to it:
address[] memory investorWallets = new address[](1);
investorWallets[0] = investorWallet;
// @audit assumes investor controls same wallet address
// on destination chain - not necessarily true for smart contract wallets
registryService.updateInvestor(investorId, investorId, country, investorWallets, attributeIds,
    attributeValues, attributeExpirations);,!
dsToken.issueTokens(investorWallet, value);
Impact: If the investor's wallet is a smart contract wallet (multisig/AA wallets - which can have different addresses on different chains), there is no guarantee that the investor will have their smart wallet contract deployed at the same address on the destination chain.
In an unlikely worst-case scenario, the address on the destination chain is owned by a different EOA user who is not an investor. This causes SecuritizeBridge::receiveWormholeMessages to give a foreign user control over the original investor's account because it registers the foreign user's address as belonging to the investor on the destination chain:
• Alice uses a Gnosis Safe at 0xAAA... on Ethereum  
• Alice bridges her DSTokens to Arbitrum  
• Bob (malicious) controls EOA 0xAAA... on Arbitrum (same address, different controller)  
• The bridge registers 0xAAA... on Arbitrum as Alice's wallet  
• Bob now controls all of Alice's tokens on Arbitrum

title: Burn and seize functions can be DoS when investor has several wallets that they control
content: The vulnerability is a balance‑checking mismatch in the token contract’s burn (and analogous seize) functions. Instead of verifying that the amount to be burned is covered by the investor’s total balance across all registered wallets, the code checks only the balance of the specific wallet address that initiates the call (`_tokenData.walletsBalances[_who]`). This root cause stems from the contract storing per‑wallet balances separately from an aggregated investor balance, but mistakenly using the former for critical admin operations. An investor who controls multiple wallets can transfer all tokens from the wallet they intend to use for burning to another of their wallets, leaving the caller’s wallet balance at zero while the investor’s overall balance remains unchanged. When a burn is attempted from the empty wallet, the `require` statement fails with “Not enough balance,” causing the transaction to revert. The impact is a denial‑of‑service (DoS) condition: administrators cannot burn or seize tokens, and an attacker could front‑run a burn transaction by moving tokens between wallets just before execution, effectively blocking the operation. This occurs whenever an investor has more than one registered wallet and moves tokens away from the wallet used for the burn or seize call. The affected parties include token holders, protocol administrators, and any downstream systems that rely on burning or seizing tokens for compliance or supply management. The issue was discovered during a security audit and demonstrated with a proof‑of‑concept test that registers an investor with three wallets, issues tokens, transfers the full amount to a secondary wallet, and then observes the burn revert. The bug is subtle because the UI may correctly display a zero balance for the calling address, leading users to believe they have no tokens, while the aggregate investor balance still shows the correct amount; the mismatch is not obvious without inspecting the contract’s internal accounting. To remediate, the contract should validate burn and seize amounts against the investor’s total balance (`investorsBalances[investorId]`) or provide functions that iterate over all wallets belonging to an investor (e.g., `burnAll`, `seizeAll`). Additional mitigations include restricting the ability to add unlimited wallets, performing sensitive admin actions through private mempools to prevent front‑running, and ensuring that balance checks reflect the business logic that an investor’s tokens are fungible across their wallets. This class of bug is a typical accounting or balance‑validation error where per‑entity state is incorrectly used for global operations, leading to unexpected failures and potential loss of functionality.

title: Uninitialized CCTP domain mapping can send USDC to the incorrect blockchain
content: The vulnerability is an uninitialized CCTP domain mapping in the USDCBridgeV2 contract that can cause USDC to be sent to the wrong blockchain. The contract maintains a public mapping from Wormhole chain identifiers (uint16) to Circle CCTP domain identifiers (uint32). When the mapping entry for a given target chain has never been set, Solidity returns the default value 0 for the uint32. Circle’s CCTP protocol defines domain 0 as the Ethereum mainnet, so the bridge’s internal function getCCTPDomain returns 0 for any unconfigured chain. The bridge then calls Circle’s depositForBurn with this domain value, causing the USDC to be burned on Ethereum instead of being minted on the intended destination chain such as Avalanche. This occurs whenever an admin fails to initialize the mapping via setBridgeAddress or removes an entry without clearing the domain mapping. From a user’s perspective, a transaction appears successful, the source balance is reduced, but the expected USDC never appears on the destination chain, leading to the perception that funds have disappeared. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that flagged the direct return of the mapping value without validation, noting that the default zero value maps to a real domain. The bug is hard to notice because the contract does not revert; it merely misroutes the funds, and the on‑chain logs show a normal depositForBurn call. The impact is high because users can lose assets across chains, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions that a domain identifier uniquely identifies the target blockchain are violated. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “uninitialized storage leading to default‑value misuse” and “incorrect domain routing” bugs. To remediate, the getCCTPDomain function should enforce that a zero domain is only acceptable for Wormhole’s Ethereum chain identifier (ID 2) and reject all other cases with a clear error. Additionally, administrative functions should always set a valid CCTP domain when adding a bridge address and delete the domain entry when removing a bridge, ensuring the mapping cannot remain in an undefined state.
summary:
USDCBridgeV2::chainIdToCCTPDomain maps Wormhole chain IDs to Circle's CCTP domain IDs:
```solidity
mapping(uint16 => uint32) public chainIdToCCTPDomain;
function getCCTPDomain(uint16 _chain) internal view returns (uint32) {
    return chainIdToCCTPDomain[_chain]; // @audit returns 0 if not set!
}
```
Impact: When this mapping isn't initialized for a wormhole chain id, it returns 0 by default (Solidity's default value for uint32). However Circle's CCTP domain 0 is Ethereum mainnet. So if a mapping has not been configured for a given wormhole chain id e.g. (6 for Avalanche), USDCBridgeV2::_transferUSDC will happily send USDC to Ethereum instead of Avalanche:
```solidity
circleTokenMessenger.depositForBurn(
    _amount,
    getCCTPDomain(_targetChain), // @audit 0 by default = Ethereum mainnet
    targetAddressBytes32, // mintRecipient on destination
    USDC, // burnToken
    destinationCallerBytes32, // destinationCaller (restrict who can mint)
    0,
    1000
);
```

title: Missing Chainlink oracle staleness check
content: The vulnerability is a missing oracle freshness validation in the ChainlinkFeedLibrary.getPrice function. The function retrieves the latestRoundData from a Chainlink price feed but does not examine the updatedAt timestamp or the answeredInRound field, both of which are provided specifically to detect stale or incomplete data. Because the library ignores these fields, it may return a price that has not been refreshed for an extended period. This occurs whenever the feed experiences a delay in updates and the contract subsequently calls getPrice; the condition is triggered under normal blockchain operation when no new price is posted within the expected interval. The root cause is a logical oversight: the developer assumed that latestRoundData always yields fresh data and omitted the necessary time‑based checks. An attacker who can either manipulate the feed timing or simply wait for a period of inactivity can cause the contract to consume an outdated price. The protocol then uses this stale price in critical calculations such as asset valuations, margin requirements, liquidation thresholds, or swap rates. As a result, users may experience unexpected liquidations, trades executed at unfavorable rates, or balances that appear to disappear, violating the business logic that assumes prices reflect the current market. From a user perspective the UI may show a normal price feed but the underlying transaction settles with a wrong amount, leading to confusion and potential loss of funds. The issue was discovered during a security audit when a test case mocked a feed that returned a price with an updatedAt timestamp one day old; the getPrice call succeeded and returned the stale price, demonstrating the lack of a staleness guard. The bug is hard to notice because the price value itself looks plausible and no explicit error is thrown. To remediate, the getPrice function should enforce that updatedAt is newer than block.timestamp minus a configurable MAX_STALENESS threshold and that answeredInRound is at least as large as the roundId, reverting or returning an error when these conditions are not met. This aligns the implementation with the standard Chainlink oracle usage pattern and restores confidence that the protocol operates on fresh, reliable price data.
summary:
The getPrice function in ChainlinkFeedLibrary fetches the latest price from a Chainlink feed using latestRoundData, but does not check if the returned data is stale. Chainlink feeds can become stale if no new price updates have occurred for a significant period, which may result in outdated or inaccurate price information being used by the protocol. The Chainlink interface provides updatedAt and answeredInRound fields specifically to help consumers detect stale or incomplete data, but these are ignored in the current implementation.  
Impact: The protocol may use outdated or stale price data, leading to incorrect valuations, margin calculations, or other critical logic. This can be exploited by attackers if they can manipulate or anticipate periods of feed staleness. Users and integrators may be exposed to increased risk due to reliance on old price information.

title: Country updates is not reducing from the storage the prev country
content: The vulnerability is an accounting flaw in the compliance service that leads to double counting of investors when they change their jurisdiction. The root cause is that the function responsible for adjusting investor statistics after a country change receives the previous country as an argument but deliberately ignores it, only calling the routine that increases the counters for the new country. Consequently, the counters for accredited investors, US investors, EU retail investors per country, and Japan investors are incremented without a corresponding decrement for the former country. This occurs whenever an investor with a non‑zero token balance invokes the RegistryService.setCountry() function, which forwards the previous country to the compliance service. Because the previous‑country decrement step is missing, each country change inflates the jurisdiction‑specific totals, causing the protocol to believe it has more investors in a region than actually exist. The impact includes inaccurate compliance reporting, potential violation of regulatory caps on investor numbers, and the risk that token issuance may be halted or that the platform could be deemed non‑compliant. The issue was discovered during a security audit and reproduced with a proof‑of‑concept test that showed the US investor count remaining at one after moving the same investor to Japan. The bug is hard to notice because the counters may appear correct after a single change and only diverge after multiple updates. To fix the problem, the adjustInvestorCountsAfterCountryChange function must first call the decrement routine for the previous country (if it is non‑empty) before incrementing the counters for the new country, thereby restoring proper accounting and ensuring that investor limits reflect the true distribution across jurisdictions.

title: AccessControlManager is in charge of managing roles and permissions for accounts to determine what users can call on which contracts
content: The vulnerability resides in the AccessControlManager contract that builds role identifiers by encoding a target contract address together with a function selector. When the grantCall function is invoked with the special inputs address(0) and bytes4(0) – which represent permission to call the fallback function on any contract – the internal roleFor routine produces a 32‑byte value of zero because both the shifted address part and the selector part are zero. In this system the constant DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE is defined as bytes32(0), so the subsequent grantRole call unintentionally assigns the full administrative role to the specified account instead of a narrowly scoped permission. This occurs only under the edge case where both parameters are zero, making it easy to miss during normal testing because most calls use non‑zero addresses and selectors. An attacker or a careless developer can trigger the bug by granting fallback permission, thereby receiving admin rights that allow them to grant or revoke any other role, effectively taking control of the permission hierarchy. From a user perspective the symptom is that an account that was supposed to have a single limited capability suddenly can change roles, leading to unexpected admin actions such as authorizing other accounts to call restricted functions. The impact is high because the admin role can be used to compromise the entire protocol’s access control. The issue was discovered through static analysis and a proof‑of‑concept test that called grantCall with address(0) and selector 0, confirming that the target account gained DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE and could then grant permissions to others. Detecting the problem is difficult because the zero role value is a valid identifier in the role mapping and does not raise an error by itself. The proper mitigation is to add a validation step before granting any role, rejecting transactions where the computed role equals DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE, for example with a require statement that reverts on role == DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE. This change prevents the accidental assignment of admin privileges and restores the intended fine‑grained permission model.

title: Disabling an asset via STBL_Register::disableAsset with active deposits can DOS user withdrawals
content: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition caused by the asset disabling function in the registry contract allowing an asset to be marked as DISABLED even when users still have active deposits. The root cause is that the disableAsset routine only checks the current status flag and does not verify whether the total deposited balance for the asset is zero before changing its status. When an asset is disabled in this way, the withdrawal (exit) function in the core contract, which is protected by a modifier that requires the asset to be ACTIVE, will revert with an asset‑disabled error. Consequently, any user attempting to withdraw their funds receives a transaction failure, sees no change in their balance, and perceives that their money has disappeared or become inaccessible. This situation occurs whenever an administrator or privileged role calls disableAsset on an asset that still holds user deposits, a scenario that may be rare and therefore hard to notice until a withdrawal is attempted. The affected parties include depositors who cannot retrieve their funds, the protocol which may lose credibility, and any downstream applications that rely on successful withdrawals. The issue was identified during a security audit by cross‑referencing the asset status checks in the disableAsset function with the isValidIssuer modifier in the exit function. It is subtle because the disabling operation itself succeeds without error, masking the problem until a user interaction triggers the revert. To remediate, the disableAsset function should be amended to include a guard that prevents disabling while deposits exist, or to enforce a grace period that allows pending withdrawals before the asset can be fully disabled. Alternatively, an emergency withdrawal path could be provided to unblock users in case of accidental disabling. This class of bug falls under improper state transition validation, where a contract permits a state change that invalidates subsequent business‑logic operations, leading to locked funds and a breach of the protocol’s accounting assumptions.

title: Division by zero in CompensationPriceFinder
content: The vulnerability is a division‑by‑zero error in the CompensationPriceFinder::_zeroForOneGetFinalCompensationPrice function. The routine calculates a variable A as the difference between the accumulated input amount sumX and the virtual reserve threshold rangeVirtualReserves0. When sumX is exactly equal to rangeVirtualReserves0, A becomes zero. The code then proceeds to compute the final compensation price using the formula (-L + sqrt(D)) / A and calls Math512Lib.div512by256 with A as the divisor. Because the implementation does not check for the zero case, the divisor is zero and the library throws a DivisorZero exception, causing the whole transaction to revert. This bug originates from an unchecked arithmetic assumption that A is always positive; the edge case where A equals zero was not handled. An attacker or any user can trigger the revert by constructing a swap that makes sumX match the virtual reserve exactly, which may happen naturally when the price reaches a boundary defined by the protocol. Exploitation does not steal funds, but it prevents the swap from completing, leading to a denial‑of‑service condition for trades at that precise price point. Users experience a transaction that fails with a DivisorZero error, see no output tokens, and lose the gas spent, contrary to the expectation that the swap would succeed and deliver the calculated compensation. The issue was discovered through a manual code audit that identified the missing zero‑check in the arithmetic branch. It can be hard to notice because the condition requires an exact equality, which may occur infrequently in normal operation, and the revert message may be obscured by generic error handling. The bug belongs to the class of arithmetic edge‑case vulnerabilities, specifically division‑by‑zero due to unchecked denominator values. To remediate, the contract should add an explicit branch that detects A == 0 and either applies the linear solution of the underlying equation or returns a safe fallback price, thereby guaranteeing that no division by zero can occur. This fix restores the intended business logic that a price is always computable and prevents swaps from unexpectedly reverting, preserving protocol availability and user confidence.

title: donation attack on strategy withdrawal
content: The vulnerability is a donation‑attack exploitation that breaks the withdrawal logic of a tranche‑based strategy. The contract enforces a post‑withdrawal invariant that the total supply of tranche shares must never fall below a constant MIN_SHARES. This check is implemented in an internal view function that reverts with MinSharesViolation when totalSupply() < MIN_SHARES. The root cause is that the share‑to‑asset ratio is calculated from total assets reported by the strategy, but the contract does not prevent external parties from inflating total assets without receiving corresponding shares. An attacker can donate a token (sUSDe) directly to the strategy, which increases the strategy’s asset balance while leaving the share supply unchanged. After this donation, the attacker makes a tiny deposit (for example 1.1 USDe) that, because of the inflated asset pool, results in the tranche minting only a single wei of shares. This extreme dilution of the exchange rate means that any subsequent legitimate deposit mints an insufficient number of shares, keeping the overall share supply below MIN_SHARES. When a user later attempts to withdraw, the _onAfterWithdrawalChecks function detects the low share supply and reverts, causing the withdrawal to fail and the assets to remain locked in the strategy contract. The impact is that user‑deposited funds become inaccessible, effectively freezing the capital of all participants in the tranche. The issue occurs whenever an external donation is made to the strategy before the tranche has accumulated enough shares to satisfy the MIN_SHARES threshold, and it can be triggered by a single transaction that combines the donation and a minimal deposit. It was discovered during a security audit that exercised edge‑case deposit and withdrawal sequences and observed the MinSharesViolation error being triggered unexpectedly. The bug is subtle because the contract appears to function correctly under normal deposit‑withdrawal flows; only when the asset pool is artificially inflated does the share supply fall short, a condition that may not be obvious from the UI or standard tests. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “share‑dilution” or “donation‑attack” bugs where external asset injection breaks accounting invariants. From a user’s perspective, the symptoms are withdrawals that revert with an obscure error, balances that appear unchanged after a deposit, or a zero share balance despite having supplied assets. The business logic that each share represents a proportional claim on the underlying assets is violated, undermining trust in the protocol’s accounting. To remediate the issue, the contract should ensure that the share supply cannot be reduced below the minimum bound, for example by performing an initial dummy deposit of at least one full USDe at deployment (using an unusable address as the receiver) so that the minted shares satisfy MIN_SHARES from the outset, and by carefully configuring the deployment script to set proper approvals and prevent unauthorized donations. This conceptual fix restores the invariant that totalSupply() >= MIN_SHARES, preventing the withdrawal check from reverting and keeping user funds accessible.

title: ComplianceServiceRegulated applies double locking to investor transferable tokens leading to DoS of transfers
content: The vulnerability is a double‑locking accounting error in the ComplianceServiceRegulated contract that causes a denial‑of‑service for token transfers. The function getComplianceTransferableTokens obtains the investor's transferable balance from the InvestorLockManager, which already excludes tokens locked at the wallet level, and then iterates over issuance records to add the same locked tokens again as compliance locks. Because the same locked amount is counted twice, the calculation transferable = balanceOfInvestor - min(totalLockedTokens, balanceOfInvestor) often reduces to zero even when the investor actually holds transferable tokens. This occurs when an investor owns multiple wallets and a new issuance of locked tokens is added; the aggregated locked amount exceeds the aggregated transferable amount, so the compliance module reports no transferable tokens. As a result, any transfer attempt is reverted with an “Under lock‑up” error, effectively DoS‑ing the investor’s ability to move funds. The bug was discovered during a security audit that exercised token issuance, lock periods, and compliance queries, revealing that after issuing locked tokens the complianceTransferableTokens function returned zero while the lock manager still reported a positive transferable balance. The issue is hard to notice because the UI may still display a positive balance, yet transfers fail, leading to user confusion and panic. It affects all investors, especially those with multiple wallets, and violates the business logic that locked tokens should only be counted once in compliance checks. The recommended mitigation is to replace the call to getLockManager().getTransferableTokens with a call to the token’s balanceOfInvestor, thereby using the total token balance as the base and applying only the compliance‑specific locks, which removes the double counting. Until the fix is applied, funds remain in the wallets but cannot be transferred, and a contract upgrade or administrative intervention is required to restore normal operation.

title: Bridging DSToken back-and-forth between chains causes totalIssuance cap to be reached, preventing further issuances and cross-chain transfers
content: The vulnerability is an accounting flaw in a capped token that uses the StandardToken totalIssuance variable to enforce a maximum supply. totalIssuance is intended to record the cumulative number of tokens ever minted and is not decreased by burns, but the SecuritizeBridge contract calls DSToken.issueTokens on the destination chain each time tokens are received via cross‑chain bridging. Because the bridge never decrements totalIssuance on the source chain, every round‑trip transfer artificially inflates the totalIssuance on both the source and destination chains. When the accumulated count reaches the hard‑coded cap, the token’s require check fails, causing any further issuance or bridge transaction to revert. This can happen without any malicious actor; a user who repeatedly bridges the same tokens back and forth will eventually trigger the cap. The impact is that legitimate users see their balances unchanged while the contract believes the supply limit has been exhausted, leading to failed bridge transfers, blocked minting, and potentially locked funds on the chain where the cap was hit. The condition occurs whenever the token implements a fixed cap based on totalIssuance and the bridge uses the standard issue function for receipt handling. Affected parties include token holders, the bridge operator, and any protocol components that rely on the ability to mint or move tokens across chains. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the interaction between the token’s cap enforcement and the bridge’s receipt logic. It is hard to notice because external balances appear correct and burns do not affect totalIssuance, so the growing internal counter is not visible to users. Conceptually, the bug belongs to the class of double‑counting or supply‑cap accounting errors in cross‑chain token bridges. An attacker could exploit the situation by simply performing many bridge cycles to force the cap, effectively DoS‑ing the bridge and preventing further token movements. To remediate, the bridge should decrement totalIssuance on the source chain when tokens leave, or the token should provide a custom issuance path for bridging that does not increment totalIssuance. Alternatively, a separate counter for bridged tokens can be maintained and the cap check adjusted to exclude those amounts, ensuring that the cap reflects only truly newly minted supply rather than transferred tokens.
summary:
StandardToken::totalIssuance is not decreased by burns but is used to enforce maximum cap, since totalIssuance is supposed to track the total number of tokens ever issued, not the current "supply". However there is an interesting consequence to this when considering cross-chain bridging via SecuritizeBridge; receiveWormholeMessages calls DSToken::issueTokens on the destination chain which increases StandardToken::totalIssuance.

Impact: Consider this scenario:
• Alice bridges from Ethereum -> Arbitrum with 1000 DSToken  
• Alice bridges back from Arbitrum -> Ethereum with the "same" 1000 DSToken  
• Alice keeps doing this over and over again  

This process continually increases the totalIssuance on both chains, even though it is just the same tokens going back and forth; at some point this will cause the cap to be hit on one of the chains. This doesn't even require malicious investors, just investors who bridge back-and-forth frequently. Once the cap is hit further issuances and cross-chain transfers will revert on that chain.

title: euRetailInvestorsCount Underflow
content: The vulnerability is an integer underflow in the euRetailInvestorsCount accounting variable that tracks the number of retail investors for each EU‑compliant country. The root cause is missing logic in the investor‑count adjustment routine: when a qualified EU investor who holds tokens is downgraded to a retail status, the contract fails to increment the retail counter for that country. Consequently the system believes there is one fewer retail holder than actually exists. An attacker can trigger the flaw by first having a retail investor transfer a portion of its tokens to a qualified investor, then re‑classifying that qualified investor to retail while it still holds the received tokens, and finally having the original retail investor transfer its entire remaining balance. At the moment of the final transfer the contract attempts to decrement the euRetailInvestorsCount for the country, which is already zero, causing an underflow that reverts the transaction. From the user’s perspective the balance appears correct, but the transfer button may be disabled or the transaction fails with an unexpected revert, leading to symptoms such as “funds disappear” or “cannot send tokens”. The impact includes halted transfers for affected investors, inconsistent regulatory reporting, and potential denial‑of‑service for EU retail participants. The issue was discovered through targeted testing that simulated qualification status changes and token movements, revealing that the retail counter became negative and that subsequent transfers reverted. It is hard to notice because the token balances themselves remain unchanged and only the internal counter misbehaves, which is not directly visible in standard UI elements. The bug belongs to the class of accounting or state‑management errors that cause integer underflows. The proper fix is to modify the adjustInvestorsCountsByCountry function to increment euRetailInvestorsCount whenever a qualified investor is converted to retail and holds a non‑zero balance, ensuring the counter accurately reflects the true number of retail holders before any decrement operation.

title: Frontrunning to Block Junior Tranche Withdrawals
content: The vulnerability is a front‑running denial‑of‑service on junior‑tranche withdrawals caused by the way the contract computes the maximum withdrawable amount. In the accounting module the junior tranche’s maxWithdraw is limited so that after a withdrawal the junior net asset value (jrtNav) must remain at least a fixed percentage (minimumJrtSrtRatio, default 5%) of the senior net asset value (srtNav). The check reads the current NAV values directly from storage at the moment the withdraw function is executed. Because a senior‑tranche deposit updates srtNav via an internal balance‑flow routine, an attacker who sees a victim’s junior withdrawal pending in the mempool can submit a large senior deposit in the same block. This deposit inflates srtNav before the victim’s transaction is processed, raising the minimum required junior NAV and causing the maxWithdraw calculation to return zero or a value lower than the victim’s requested amount. When the withdraw function then compares the requested baseAssets to maxAssets, the condition fails and the contract reverts with ERC4626ExceededMaxWithdraw. The impact is that legitimate junior investors are unable to withdraw their funds, effectively trapping liquidity and creating a denial‑of‑service. The issue occurs whenever the contract uses up‑to‑date NAVs for the ratio check and does not snapshot the state before processing a withdrawal. All junior tranche participants, as well as the protocol’s overall liquidity guarantees, are affected. The flaw was discovered during a security audit by writing a Foundry test that reproduces the attack: an attacker deposits a calculated amount into the senior tranche, then the victim’s junior withdrawal reverts and the post‑attack maxWithdraw reads as zero. The problem is subtle because the ratio check appears mathematically sound; however, the reliance on mutable state within the same transaction makes it exploitable. To remediate, the contract should compute the maximum junior withdrawal based on a snapshot of NAVs taken before any state‑changing operations in the block, or separate the senior‑deposit logic so it cannot influence junior withdrawals within the same block. Alternative mitigations include adding a re‑entrancy guard, enforcing a minimum time delay between senior deposits and junior withdrawals, or redesigning the accounting rule to use immutable parameters that cannot be manipulated by front‑running.

title: Hard-coding 0 max fee with fast finality is incompatible
content: The vulnerability consists of a hard‑coded maximum fee of zero combined with a fixed fast‑finality threshold of 1000 in the USDCBridgeV2 contract’s call to Circle’s TokenMessenger.depositForBurn. Circle’s CCTP specification defines fast messages as those with a minFinalityThreshold of 1000 or lower and states that the applicable fee must be obtained from an off‑chain API before each transaction. In practice the API returns a minimum fee of 1 USDC (or 1 unit of the token) for fast finality on most domain pairs, while the contract forces the maximum fee to be zero. When a user initiates a cross‑domain transfer with fast finality, the depositForBurn call fails because the required minimum fee exceeds the supplied maximum fee, causing the transaction to revert or automatically fall back to standard finality. If the standard‑finality fee ever becomes greater than zero, the automatic downgrade is no longer possible and every attempted transfer will revert, effectively denying service to all users. From the user’s perspective the bridge UI reports a failed transaction, the expected USDC balance on the destination chain never appears, and the source balance may appear unchanged, leading to confusion and loss of confidence. The issue was discovered during a security audit that inspected the bridge’s fee handling logic and compared it against Circle’s technical guide. The bug is subtle because a fee of one unit is small and may be overlooked, and the contract’s fallback to standard finality can mask the problem until fee parameters change. The root cause is the use of immutable literals for fee and finality instead of dynamically fetching the current fee basis points from Circle’s API and calculating an appropriate maximum fee. The vulnerability belongs to the class of hard‑coded parameter and accounting logic errors that break business assumptions about fee coverage. The recommended remediation is to retrieve the current fee bps from the Circle API for the selected input and output domains, multiply it by the transfer amount to compute a realistic maximum fee, and pass both the calculated fee and the desired finality threshold as arguments to depositForBurn, or at minimum expose a setter that allows the maximum fee to be updated without redeploying the contract.
summary:
Hard-coding 0 max fee with fast finality is incompatible as this combination commonly has minimum fees of 1  

Circle's CCTPv2 Technical Guide provides the following relevant information:
- Messages with minFinalityThreshold of 1000 or lower are considered Fast messages
- Messages with minFinalityThreshold of 2000 are considered Standard messages (in practice everything > 1000 is considered Standard)
- The applicable fee should be retrieved every time before executing a transaction using this API  

The provided API requires specifying the CCTP input and output domains. Using the wget form of the API, the minimum fees for fast finality (1000) are typically 1:
```bash
wget --quiet \
--method GET \
--header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
--output-document \
- https://iris-api-sandbox.circle.com/v2/burn/USDC/fees/0/1
[{"finalityThreshold":1000,"minimumFee":1},{"finalityThreshold":2000,"minimumFee":0}]%
```
```bash
wget --quiet \
--method GET \
--header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
--output-document \
- https://iris-api-sandbox.circle.com/v2/burn/USDC/fees/0/5
[{"finalityThreshold":1000,"minimumFee":1},{"finalityThreshold":2000,"minimumFee":0}]%
```

Impact: Many CCTP cross-domain transfers have a minimum fee of 1 for fast finality, but `USDCBridgeV2::_-transferUSDC` hard-codes a maximum fee of 0 with fast finality 1000:
```solidity
circleTokenMessenger.depositForBurn(
    _amount,
    getCCTPDomain(_targetChain),
    targetAddressBytes32, // mintRecipient on destination
    USDC, // burnToken
    destinationCallerBytes32, // destinationCaller (restrict who can mint)
    0, // @audit maximum fee
    1000 // @audit fast finality
);
```
This combination is incompatible and will result in many cross-domain transfers unable to use fast finality, reverting to standard finality. If the minimum fee for standard finality ever becomes > 0, this would cause all attempted cross-domain transfers to revert since the automatic downgrade to standard finality would no longer be possible.

title: Historical token issuances become subject to new lock-up requirements when users change residency
content: The vulnerability is a temporal lock‑up misapplication that causes all historical token issuances to be subject to the lock period associated with the investor's current residency rather than the period that was in effect when each issuance was created. The root cause lies in two functions: checkHoldUp determines a lock period at transfer time by inspecting a flag that reflects the investor's present country and then selects either the US or non‑US lock duration; this single duration is subsequently supplied to getComplianceTransferableTokens, which iterates over every issuance but uses the same lock time for each entry. Consequently, when an investor changes residency after receiving tokens, the contract retroactively applies the new, often longer, lock period to earlier issuances that should have already unlocked. Exploitation occurs during a normal transfer call: the compliance service calculates total locked tokens by adding the value of every issuance whose timestamp falls within the current lock window, which, due to the bug, includes tokens that are legally free. The impact is that users see a zero or reduced transferable balance, experience failed transfers, and may be unable to move funds that should be liquid, creating liquidity freezes and potentially violating securities regulations that mandate lock‑up periods based on the investor’s status at issuance. This condition manifests whenever an investor updates their residency profile after having received tokens, a scenario common in cross‑border investment platforms. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the compliance logic and identified that the lock period parameter is derived from current state rather than persisted issuance data. It can be hard to notice because the UI simply reports a locked balance without exposing per‑issuance lock details, leading users to assume a contract‑wide lock rather than a bug. The appropriate remediation is to store the applicable lock period at the moment each issuance is recorded and to reference that stored value when evaluating lock status, thereby ensuring that each token batch is unlocked according to the regulatory regime that applied at its creation. This class of bug falls under improper temporal state handling and lock‑up period misapplication, where business logic assumes a static rule but the implementation dynamically rewrites historical constraints, breaking the expectation that "tokens issued under a six‑month lock become transferable after six months" and instead enforcing "all tokens follow the current lock rule".

title: Insufficient duration validation in STBL_Register::setupAsset can lock user withdrawals
content: The vulnerability is an insufficient validation of the relationship between two time‑based parameters – duration and yieldDuration – in the asset registration functions of the STBL protocol. Because the contract does not enforce that yieldDuration must be less than or equal to duration, an asset can be configured where the required waiting period for yield (yieldDuration) is longer than the overall allowed holding period (duration). The withdrawal function in the issuer contract checks two conditions: it reverts if the current block timestamp is greater than depositBlock + duration (withdraw after the overall period) and it also reverts if the timestamp is less than depositBlock + yieldDuration (withdraw before the yield period). When yieldDuration exceeds duration both conditions are simultaneously true for any timestamp, meaning the logical “both false” requirement is never satisfied. An honest user cannot find any moment when the withdrawal is permitted, effectively locking the deposited funds forever. This situation occurs only after an asset has been set up with the invalid parameters, which can happen during normal registration or later when the setDurations function is called. The affected parties are the users who have deposited NFTs or tokens into the asset, the protocol that promises redeemable yields, and any downstream contracts that rely on the ability to withdraw. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the withdrawal logic and noticed the contradictory time checks. It is hard to notice because the code compiles and the checks appear reasonable in isolation; only the combination of the two inequalities creates the impossible window. From a user’s perspective the UI would show a pending withdrawal that never completes, balances remain unchanged, and the user may see error messages such as “Yield duration not reached” even after the asset’s overall duration has passed. The bug belongs to the class of “invalid parameter relationship” or “logical time‑window inversion” bugs that break business logic assumptions about fund availability. To remediate, the registration and duration‑setting functions should include a validation step that rejects any configuration where yieldDuration is greater than duration, or automatically clamp the values, thereby guaranteeing that a non‑empty withdrawal window always exists.

title: Incomplete validation in OpNetVaultAutoDeploy allows invalid burner configuration for registering operators with auto vault deployments
content: The vulnerability is an incomplete validation in the OpNetVaultAutoDeploy contract that permits an invalid burner configuration to be accepted during auto‑deployment setup. Specifically, the _validateConfig function checks collateral, epoch duration, slashing window compatibility and the relationship between the withSlasher flag and the burner hook flag, but it omits any verification of the burner address itself. When an administrator creates a configuration with withSlasher set to true, isBurnerHook set to true, and burner equal to the zero address, the validation routine mistakenly considers the configuration valid. Later, during vault creation, the BaseSlasher contract’s _initialize function reads the burner address from the newly instantiated vault. Because the burner is zero while the burner hook flag is true, the function reverts with the NoBurner error. This revert aborts the entire vault deployment, causing the registerOperator call to fail and leaving the operator without a vault. The impact is a denial‑of‑service for all operators attempting to register in auto‑deployment mode: users see no vault address, their registration transactions revert, and any funds they intended to lock remain unspent, creating confusion and a perception that the protocol is broken. The issue occurs only when the specific combination of flags (withSlasher and isBurnerHook) is enabled and the burner address is not provided, a scenario that can be set by any privileged account that manages the auto‑deploy configuration. It affects protocol administrators, operators, and end‑users who rely on automatic vault provisioning. The flaw was discovered through manual code review during a security audit, where the reviewer noted the missing burner address check despite the later reliance on a non‑zero burner. The bug is subtle because the configuration appears syntactically correct and passes all existing checks, so the failure only surfaces at deployment time, making it hard to detect without thorough testing. To remediate, the validation function should be extended to reject configurations where withSlasher and isBurnerHook are true while burner equals address(0), thereby enforcing the protocol’s accounting assumption that a valid burner contract must exist whenever a burner hook is enabled. Adding this check prevents the NoBurner revert, restores reliable vault deployment, and eliminates the denial‑of‑service condition.

title: Investor Counter Decrement DoS
content: The vulnerability is an accounting logic error in the compliance service that incorrectly decrements the global investor counters when an investor transfers their entire token balance either between two of their own wallets or to the same wallet (self‑transfer). The root cause is the `recordTransfer` function, which checks only the amount transferred and the sender’s balance without first verifying whether the sender and receiver belong to the same investor identity. As a result, a transfer that empties the sender’s balance triggers `adjustTotalInvestorsCounts` with a decrement operation even though the investor still holds the same total amount across multiple addresses. This flaw can be exploited by any participant who moves their full balance between owned wallets or performs a self‑transfer, causing the on‑chain investor counter to drop to zero while token balances remain unchanged. The immediate impact is a denial‑of‑service: subsequent compliance checks read the corrupted counter and reject further transfers for all users, often reverting with messages such as “Not enough investors”. Additionally, the inaccurate counter can allow the investor limit mechanism to be bypassed, undermining regulatory compliance. The issue occurs during normal transfer operations and is triggered only when the transferred amount equals the sender’s entire balance; it is hard to notice because balances appear correct and the contract does not emit explicit warnings, so developers may assume the system is functioning normally. The bug was discovered through targeted unit tests that performed full‑balance transfers among wallets of the same registered investor, revealing that the investor count unexpectedly fell to zero. To remediate, the contract should first retrieve the investor identifiers for both `_from` and `_to` addresses and skip the decrement logic when they are identical. Refactoring helper functions to accept investor IDs directly can also improve gas efficiency. Conceptually, the fix restores proper accounting by ensuring that the global investor count only changes when an investor truly exits the system, preserving the expected behavior that users retain their balances and that compliance limits remain enforced.

title: Changing investor country to the same country inflates investor count
content: The vulnerability is a logical error in the compliance accounting of a regulated token platform where changing an investor’s country to the same value unintentionally inflates the per‑country investor count. The root cause lies in the function adjustInvestorCountsAfterCountryChange, which increments the investor counter without first verifying that the new country differs from the previous one. This function is invoked by RegistryService.updateInvestor and RegistryService.setCountry, both of which can be called by an admin to modify attributes such as accreditation status while leaving the country unchanged. Because the guard is missing, each call adds one to the country‑specific tally, causing the stored count to diverge from the actual number of investors. An attacker or careless admin can exploit this by repeatedly updating an investor’s non‑country fields, thereby driving the counter up until it reaches the configured MAX_INVESTORS_IN_CATEGORY limit. When the limit is hit, the compliance check completeTransferCheck aborts token transfers, leading to blocked trades and potentially frozen funds. The issue manifests when the UI or compliance queries report a higher investor count than expected, for example showing two US investors when only one exists, and when transfers suddenly fail with a max‑investor error despite no new investors being added. The bug was discovered through a unit test that called setCountry with the same country value and observed the count increase. It can be hard to notice because the increment occurs silently during routine attribute updates, and the symptom only appears when the artificial limit is reached. To fix the problem, the adjustInvestorCountsAfterCountryChange routine should either revert or simply skip any counter adjustments when the supplied _country equals _prevCountry, thereby preserving the invariant that the investor count reflects distinct investors per jurisdiction. This correction restores accurate compliance accounting, prevents false max‑investor errors, and ensures that legitimate transfers are not blocked due to an inflated counter.
summary:
Changing investor country to the same country inflates investor count.  
Impact: Inflating the investor count will erroneously trigger **MAX_INVESTORS_IN_CATEGORY** error in `ComplianceServiceRegulated::completeTransferCheck`. This does not require any error on the admin's part since the admin can call `RegistryService::updateInvestor` where the country remains the same but other investor properties are being changed, and this ends up calling `ComplianceServiceRegulated::adjustInvestorCountsAfterCountryChange` and inflating the investor count.

title: Investor can prevent themselves from being removed by making removeInvestor revert
content: An investor removal denial-of-service vulnerability exists in the RegistryService contract. The removeInvestor function is designed to delete an investor only when the stored walletCount for that investor equals zero. However, the contract also provides an addWalletByInvestor function that any registered investor can call without restriction, allowing the investor to increase their own walletCount arbitrarily. Only accounts with the EXCHANGE role are permitted to call removeWallet, so an investor who has added one or more wallets cannot have those wallets removed by themselves. When an administrator or exchange tries to invoke removeInvestor, the require statement investors[_id].walletCount == 0 fails and the transaction reverts with the message \"Investor has wallets\". This creates a permanent denial-of-service condition: the investor can deliberately add wallets to block their own removal, and the system has no mechanism to force wallet deletion before investor deletion. The impact is that compliance or governance processes that rely on being able to purge inactive or malicious investors are blocked, potentially leaving stale data and preventing reclamation of associated resources. The issue is discovered during a manual audit of role-based access controls and invariant checks. It is hard to notice because the removal logic appears correct at a glance, while the unrestricted wallet-addition path is overlooked. From a user perspective, an admin expects the investor to be removed but receives a revert and sees the investor still listed, leading to confusion. The bug belongs to the class of \"inconsistent state-based access control\" or \"removal condition bypass\" vulnerabilities where state can be manipulated by an unprivileged actor to violate removal preconditions. To remediate, the contract should either restrict addWalletByInvestor to privileged roles, require that wallets be removed (or transferred) before an investor can be deleted, or modify removeInvestor to handle existing wallets safely, for example by automatically cleaning up wallet entries or by allowing exchange-role accounts to force wallet removal. Ensuring that the invariant walletCount == 0 cannot be violated by the same entity that later triggers the removal check eliminates the DoS vector and restores the intended business logic that an investor can be fully deregistered when no wallets remain.

title: Self-triggered Licredity::_afterSwap back-run enables LP fee farming
content: The vulnerability is a self‑triggered back‑run embedded in the Licredity::_afterSwap hook that activates whenever the pool price reaches or falls below the parity level of one (sqrtPriceX96 <= ONE_SQRT_PRICE_X96). The root cause is the hook’s logic that, upon detecting a low price, constructs and executes an exact‑out swap that pushes the price back up to the maximum allowed sqrt price. This secondary swap pays the standard Uniswap V4 swap fees to the liquidity providers in the pool. An attacker who supplies a dominant share of liquidity on both sides of the parity tick can exploit this by first performing a trade that nudges the price just below one, thereby earning fees on their own trade, and then allowing the automatic back‑run to execute, which generates a second set of fees that also accrue to the attacker’s liquidity. After the back‑run restores the price to at least one, the attacker redeems their liquidity positions via Licredity::exchangeFungible at an approximately 1:1 rate, recovering the principal while retaining both fee legs. This loop can be repeated indefinitely as long as the attacker can steer the price slightly under one, resulting in a steady extraction of value from other traders and the protocol’s stabilization mechanism. The impact is an economic drain: regular users see reduced net output from swaps, their balances may appear unchanged while the pool’s fee pool is siphoned, and the protocol’s fee distribution becomes skewed toward the attacker. The condition occurs only when the price crosses the parity threshold, making it hard to detect because the price is immediately corrected and the extra fees are indistinguishable from normal accrual unless the liquidity distribution is examined. The issue was discovered during a security audit that included a proof‑of‑concept test demonstrating fee mining with dominant liquidity. It belongs to the class of “self‑triggered fee‑extraction” bugs where contract hooks unintentionally reward privileged participants. To remediate, the back‑run should be removed or swaps that would end below the parity price should be rejected, access to liquidity provision around the critical tick should be restricted, or the fee logic should be altered so that swaps initiated by the contract itself do not generate LP fees. From a user’s perspective, trades near the 1:1 price may result in unexpectedly low returns or missing balances, contrary to the expectation that a swap at parity yields equal value. The bug violates the accounting assumption that fees are proportionally shared among all liquidity providers and that price stability mechanisms do not create profit opportunities for a single actor.

title: Math512Lib sqrt512 and div512by256 Vulnerability
content:
The vulnerability resides in the Math512Lib library, specifically in the sqrt512 function and the div512by256 routine that together compute high‑precision square roots and 512‑by‑256 division used by the protocol’s price‑finding logic. sqrt512 assumes that the initial guess for the square root, derived from a left‑shift based on the index of the most‑significant set bit of the upper 256‑bit limb (x1), is always larger than that limb and fits within 256 bits. When the most‑significant bit index is odd, the shift rounds down, producing a guess that can be smaller than x1. This causes the subsequent division floor(([x1 x0]) / root) to generate a quotient that does not fit in 256 bits (≥ 2^256), leading to an arithmetic overflow or an incorrect root that is significantly smaller than the true value. The Newton‑Raphson iteration therefore does not remain strictly monotonically decreasing and may converge to a wrong result.
In parallel, div512by256 attempts to emulate Solady’s 512‑by‑256 division but incorrectly builds the remainder. The assembly code truncates the high 128 bits of the combined remainder before applying addmod, using a shifted version of x1 instead of the actual remainder r1. This truncation changes the value of r, causing the low digit y0 to be biased upward or downward and allowing the high digit y1 to be non‑zero when the mathematical expectation is zero (i.e., when the dividend fits in 256 bits). Consequently, the long‑division invariant is broken and the computed quotient can be too wide.
Both bugs manifest only under specific edge conditions: an odd most‑significant bit in the upper limb for sqrt512, and inputs where the upper 256‑bit part of the dividend is less than or equal to the divisor for div512by256. These conditions are tied to the protocol’s liquidity distribution because the values fed into the library (L ± sqrt(D) and related terms) depend on reserve balances and tick ranges. An attacker could influence the liquidity layout to create the offending bit pattern, causing the effective price calculation to deviate. Users experience the impact as incorrect compensation or pricing – for example, a trade that should yield a certain amount of tokens may result in a smaller payout, or a compensation claim may return less than the rightful amount, appearing as a missing or zero balance.
The issue was discovered through extensive fuzz testing and targeted unit tests that varied the most‑significant bit of the upper limb, revealing arithmetic reverts and mismatched division results. It is hard to notice in normal operation because the bug only triggers on rare bit patterns; the contract does not revert in many cases but silently returns a wrong price, making the symptom subtle.
To remediate, the initial square‑root guess must be forced to be larger than the upper limb, for instance by adjusting the shift when the bit index is odd or by adding a safety margin. The division routine must be corrected to compute the remainder using the full 256‑bit high part, as shown in the recommended addmod expression that includes both r1 and the full 256‑bit mask. These conceptual fixes restore monotonic convergence of sqrt512 and accurate long‑division in div512by256, eliminating the price‑calculation errors and protecting users from incorrect compensation.

title: Tranche::maxMint for Junior Tranches is at risk of overflow when the jrNav falls below 1:1 rate to JR_Shares
content: The vulnerability resides in the junior tranche’s maxMint function, which determines the maximum number of shares that can be minted by converting the protocol’s reported maximum deposit amount into shares. The CDO contract reports its maximum deposit as type(uint256).max, representing an effectively unlimited amount. Under normal conditions the junior tranche’s net asset value (jrtNav) yields a share‑to‑asset conversion rate of at least 1:1, so converting type(uint256).max assets to shares produces a value that fits within the uint256 range. However, the junior tranche is designed to absorb losses or fund senior‑tranche APR, actions that reduce the junior NAV and consequently lower the share‑to‑asset ratio below parity. When this ratio falls below 1:1, the conversion of the unlimited asset amount to shares requires multiplying by a factor greater than one, which exceeds the uint256 capacity and triggers an arithmetic overflow. The overflow causes the maxMint call to revert, effectively denying any further minting operations for the junior tranche. From a user’s perspective the symptom is a transaction that reverts without a clear error message, often observed after a loss event where the junior balance appears to drop or where a mint attempt returns zero shares. The impact is a denial‑of‑service on the minting path; existing funds remain safe but users cannot acquire new junior shares until the NAV recovers or the bug is fixed. The issue was discovered during a targeted audit that simulated a 10 % loss on the junior strategy, reproducing the overflow condition. It is hard to notice because the overflow only manifests after a specific state change (NAV < 1) and the revert message does not directly indicate an overflow. Conceptually, this is an unchecked arithmetic overflow in a conversion routine that assumes a non‑decreasing share price. The recommended mitigation is to treat the unlimited deposit case as a special branch: when the underlying CDO’s maxDeposit returns type(uint256).max, the function should return type(uint256).max directly instead of performing the share conversion, thereby avoiding the overflow and preserving the intended unlimited minting capability.
summary:
Given that the system is composed of two tranches (Senior and Junior), and all the assets deposited among the two Tranches are polled together on the Strategy, the actual totalAssets() for each Tranche is calculated using the corresponding NAVs (srtNav and jrtNav). The Junior Tranche has the peculiarity that can be used to:
1. Fund the Senior's target APR when the generated APR is not enough.
2. Cover losses by taking the hit first and covering as much as possible to limit/reduce the loss for the Seniors.
Any of the above two events results in a decrease in the jrtNav, which is translated into the totalAssets() for the Junior Tranche being decremented. As a result, the JR Shares to assets decrements and can cause the share<=>assets rate to fall below 1:1.
When the JR_Shares<=>assets falls below 1:1, maxMint() results in overflow because the underlying Math methods implemented for the conversions of shares to assets, and the fact that assets to be converted is set as type(uint256).max

title: NAVs or APRs are updated using an outdated accounting on certain operations
content: The vulnerability consists of stale‑state accounting updates in several core functions that modify Net Asset Values (NAVs) or Annual Percentage Rates (APRs) without first synchronising the internal accounting state to the latest market data. Functions such as setReserveBps, setRiskParameters, reduceReserve, updateAprs and onAprChanged write new parameters to storage while relying on NAV and APR values that were last refreshed at an earlier point in time. Because the contract does not recalculate the NAVs after a change in the sUSDe↔USDe exchange rate, or accrue interest up to the current block before applying a new APR, the subsequent arithmetic operates on outdated numbers. This leads to mis‑allocation of rewards and profits between the Senior (SR) and Junior (JR) tranches: a lowered APR is applied to a longer accrued period, causing SR holders to receive fewer rewards than expected, while an increased APR benefits SR at the expense of JR, reducing JR profits. When reserves are reduced, the contract subtracts an amount from reserveNav and nav that was computed using a stale rate, potentially decreasing tranche balances incorrectly. The impact is that users may see lower payouts, zero withdrawals, or unexpected balance reductions, effectively causing funds to disappear from the accounting perspective. The issue manifests whenever a rate change or APR adjustment occurs between two accounting updates, which can happen frequently in a live protocol. All tranche holders, the protocol itself, and any downstream applications that rely on accurate accounting are affected. The bug was discovered during a manual audit that traced the execution flow of the listed functions and identified the missing state‑refresh calls. It is hard to notice because the contract’s external view functions still return values that appear consistent, while the internal ledger diverges only after a sequence of operations, making the discrepancy visible only in later calculations. The proper mitigation is to update the internal NAVs and accrued APR calculations before any parameter change, ensuring that the accounting reflects the current market rate and time‑weighted interest. Conceptually, this is a classic stale‑state or race‑condition bug in financial smart contracts, where state is not atomically refreshed before dependent updates, violating the business logic that assumes accounting always reflects the latest asset values and interest rates.
summary:
Description: The next list of functions makes changes either to the NAVs or APRs, or both of them, but none of those variables are updated before the update is reflected on the storage, which means, the accounting is updated using outdated values that don't reflect the current value.  
• Accounting::setReserveBps()  
• Accounting::setRiskParameters()  
• Accounting::reduceReserve()  
• Accounting::updateAprs()  
• Accounting::onAprChanged()  
For example, when reducing reserves, the reserveNav and nav are updated, but those variables were not previously updated, which means that the update to reserveNav and nav is made on outdated values since the last time those navs were updated.  
• Since the last update, the sUSDe <=> USDe rate could've changed, but that difference is not reflected on the navs prior to updating them to subtract the amount by which the reserves are been reduced.  
Another example is when updating APRs:  
• If the APR is lowered, SR Tranche will loss on rewards because the lower APR will be applied to a higher time period.  
• If the APR is increased, JR Tranche will loss on profits because the higher APR will be applied to a higher time period benefiting the SR Tranche at the expense of the JR Tranche.  
Impact: Update of accounting with outdated data can result in unexpected outcomes and potentially messing up the accounting for operations afterwards. Updating APRs without updating the internal accounting causes that the new APR is applied to calculations until an update occurs.  
• If the APR was lowered, SR Tranche will loss on rewards because the lower APR will be applied to a higher time period.  
• If the APR was increased, JR Tranche will loss on profits because the higher APR will be applied to a higher time period benefiting the SR Tranche at the expense of the JR Tranche.

title: Combination of Ownable and AccessControl can cause loss of admin functionality
content: The vulnerability arises from combining an Ownable (2‑step) upgradeable pattern with AccessControlUpgradeable in the same contract and then protecting admin‑management functions with onlyOwner while those functions internally invoke grantRole or revokeRole. Granting or revoking a role in AccessControl requires the caller to hold the role’s admin, which by default is DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE. Consequently, a caller must simultaneously satisfy the owner check and possess DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE. When the owner address is changed without also updating the DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE membership, the two identities diverge. The new owner can no longer call the wrappers because the internal AccessControl check fails, and a holder of DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE who is not the owner cannot perform upgrades because _authorizeUpgrade is restricted to onlyOwner. This dual‑requirement creates a hidden dependency that can lock out legitimate governance actions. The issue is discovered during an audit that added a test transferring ownership and then attempting to grant an admin role, which reverted with AccessControlUnauthorizedAccount. It is hard to notice because each modifier works correctly in isolation; only their interaction reveals the problem. The impact includes loss of ability to manage roles, inability to upgrade the contract, and an enlarged attack surface due to redundant wrappers, potentially leaving the protocol unable to respond to emergencies or implement improvements. Affected parties are the contract owner, any address holding DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE, protocol participants relying on upgrades, and ultimately users whose funds may become inaccessible if the contract cannot be upgraded or managed. The bug belongs to the class of role‑based access control misconfigurations where multiple authorization mechanisms are unintentionally combined, leading to a dual‑authorization requirement. From a user’s perspective, after an ownership transfer the UI may still show the new owner as the admin, but attempts to add or remove admins result in a transaction that reverts with no explicit error message, effectively making the “owner” powerless and causing confusion such as “my admin button does nothing” or “funds disappear because I cannot upgrade the contract”. To remediate, the contract should unify its access control model, preferably by removing Ownable and gating privileged functions with onlyRole(DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE), including upgrade authorization. Alternatively, if Ownable must be retained, the code should synchronize role membership on ownership changes by granting DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE to the new owner and revoking it from the old one, or by enforcing that at least one address always retains DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE to prevent permanent lockout. Removing the redundant wrappers also reduces bytecode size and attack surface, aligning the contract’s behavior with its intended business logic of centralized governance via a single admin role.
summary:
Description: BasisTradeTailor and BasisTradeVault mix Ownable(2Step)Upgradeable with AccessControlUpgradeable. Several admin wrappers are onlyOwner but internally call grantRole / revokeRole, which themselves require the caller to hold the role’s admin (usually DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE). Example:
```solidity
function grantAdmin(address account) external onlyOwner {
    grantRole(ADMIN_ROLE, account); // requires DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE too
}
```
This creates a dual requirement: the caller must be both owner and DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE. If those identities diverge (e.g., ownership transferred without also granting default admin), governance gets brittle and confusing.  
Impact: The “Owner” may be unable to manage roles (grant/revoke admin/agent) and a DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE holder who isn’t owner can’t upgrade (since _authorizeUpgrade is onlyOwner) as well as extra wrappers duplicate functionality and enlarge the attack surface/bytecode/ABI for no gain.

title: precision loss causes systematic under-reporting of voting power for high decimal tokens
content: The vulnerability is a precision‑loss rounding error that systematically under‑reports voting power for tokens whose decimal precision exceeds the protocol’s base of 24 decimals. The root cause lies in the Scaler.scale function, which when faced with a tokenDecimals greater than targetDecimals performs a plain integer division by 10^(decimals‑targetDecimals). Because Solidity integer division truncates any fractional remainder, any stake that is smaller than this divisor is reduced to zero before the voting power is recorded. This bug manifests whenever a token with more than 24 decimals is used as collateral and the holder’s raw balance is less than 10^(tokenDecimals‑24). In practice, a user who deposits, for example, 999,999 units of a 30‑decimal token sees a divisor of 1,000,000; the division yields 0, so the protocol reports zero voting power despite the user holding a substantial economic value. From the user’s perspective the UI shows no voting power, the expected ability to vote is missing, and the balance appears unchanged, creating confusion and a feeling that the system is broken or malicious. The impact is that legitimate stakeholders lose influence in governance, potentially allowing other participants with larger or differently scaled stakes to dominate decisions, and the protocol’s accounting assumptions about proportional voting power are violated. The issue was discovered during a security audit when the auditors wrote a proof‑of‑concept test that deposited a sub‑divisor amount and observed a voting power of zero. The bug is hard to notice because token balances remain correct and only the derived voting power is affected, which may only be visible in governance dashboards. To remediate, the protocol should either restrict tokens to a maximum of 24 decimals or adjust the normalization logic to ensure that any non‑zero stake yields at least a voting power of one, for example by applying a rounding‑up formula or by explicitly checking for a zero result and returning a minimum of one. This class of bug falls under integer‑division rounding errors and precision loss in fixed‑point arithmetic, common in financial smart contracts that convert between token precisions.

title: ComplianceServiceRegulated::preIssuanceCheck allows issuance to non-accredited investors
content: The vulnerability resides in the compliance service of a regulated token platform where the preIssuanceCheck function does not enforce the same accreditation and regional minimum token‑holding rules that are applied during transfers by completeTransferCheck. When the platform configuration enables ForceAccredited or ForceAccreditedUS, completeTransferCheck correctly blocks transfers to non‑accredited investors, but preIssuanceCheck omits this verification, allowing token issuance to any address regardless of its accreditation status. Similarly, completeTransferCheck checks that the recipient’s balance after a transfer meets a region‑specific minimum (for example the US minimum token holding), whereas preIssuanceCheck only validates a generic global minimum. As a result, an issuer can request token issuance that brings a US investor’s balance below the legally required minimum. The flaw originates from missing conditional logic in preIssuanceCheck, likely introduced during refactoring or incomplete code reuse. Exploitation occurs when an attacker or a careless operator calls the issuance routine while the force‑accredited flags are active; the contract skips the accreditation guard and the regional minimum guard, resulting in tokens being minted to unqualified investors or in amounts that breach regional thresholds. The impact includes regulatory non‑compliance, potential legal liability for the platform, and erosion of investor protection because users may receive tokens they are not permitted to hold. The issue manifests only during the issuance flow, not during normal transfers, making it difficult to detect unless both paths are tested. It was discovered during a security audit that compared the logic of completeTransferCheck with preIssuanceCheck and identified the missing checks. To remediate, the same accreditation verification (checking the accredited flag for the recipient) and the same region‑specific minimum‑holding verification should be added to preIssuanceCheck, ensuring that issuance respects the configured compliance policies. From a user’s perspective, a non‑accredited investor may unexpectedly see a token balance appear, or an investor may receive fewer tokens than required to satisfy a regional minimum, contradicting the expectation that the platform enforces compliance rules before crediting any tokens.

title: Proxy reuse without implementation check inside UnstakeCooldown leads to execution on outdated/vulnerable logic
content: The vulnerability consists of reusing previously created proxy contracts from a per‑user pool without verifying that those proxies still delegate to the current implementation of the token logic. Each proxy is a clone whose target implementation address is permanently embedded in its bytecode at creation time. When the contract owner calls the setImplementations function to upgrade the implementation for a token, the mapping implementations[token] is updated, but the existing proxies in users’ pools retain the old address. Consequently, when a user later initiates an operation that requires a proxy, the system may pop an outdated proxy from the pool and execute the call against the obsolete implementation. This occurs because the reuse routine lacks a check that the proxy’s embedded implementation matches the latest implementations[token] entry. The impact is that users can experience inconsistent behavior: some transactions are processed by the new logic while others are handled by the old, potentially vulnerable code.
