From a user’s perspective, the UI may show a successful pledge and token balance increase even though the user never signed the required paperwork, violating the expectation that signing all documents is mandatory before acquiring tokens. To remediate, the contract should reject any pledge where hasSignedDocs reports missing signatures, for example by reverting with a NotAllDocumentsAreSigned error, and ensure that adminTransferFrom is called with checkTC set to true so that the terms‑and‑conditions check cannot be bypassed.

title: DocumentManager::hasSignedDocs incorrectly returns true when there are no documents to sign
content: The vulnerability resides in a document‑signature verification routine that reports a signer as having completed all required documents even when the system contains no documents at all. The root cause is an unconditional return of true after a for‑loop that iterates over the stored document hashes. When the hash array length is zero the loop body is never executed, so the function reaches the final statement return(true,0x0) and signals success. This logic flaw can be exploited by any caller that relies on the routine to gate privileged actions such as token transfers, role changes, or other protocol functions that require a signed agreement. An attacker can simply ensure that the document list is empty—either by invoking the contract before any documents are added or by removing all documents if the protocol permits—and then call the downstream function; the upstream contract will mistakenly believe the user has satisfied the signature requirement and will allow the prohibited operation. The impact is that unauthorized actions are permitted, breaking the intended compliance model and potentially leading to loss of funds or violation of regulatory assumptions. The condition occurs whenever the document storage is empty, which may be the case immediately after deployment or after all documents have been cleared. All participants that depend on the signature check—protocol developers, users, auditors, and any integrated dApp—are affected because they receive a false indication that the user’s obligations are fulfilled. The issue was discovered during a formal audit when a unit test called the verification function with an empty document array and observed an unexpected true result. Because the function returns a boolean without any explicit error, the problem can be subtle and may not surface in normal operation until edge‑case testing is performed. To remediate, the routine should first verify that the document collection is non‑empty; if it is empty it must either revert with a clear error such as EmptyDocument or return (false,0x0) to accurately reflect that no signatures exist. This change restores the intended business logic that a user cannot be considered signed until at least one document requiring a signature is present, preventing the false‑positive UI messages like “All documents signed” and ensuring that downstream permission checks enforce the correct constraints.

title: Check return value when calling Allowlist::exchangeAllowed and RemoraToken::_exchangeAllowed to prevent unauthorized transfers
content: The vulnerability consists of an unchecked boolean return from the Allowlist.exchangeAllowed function within the RemoraToken contract. Allowlist.exchangeAllowed is designed to enforce a policy that only permits token transfers when both participants are registered and share the same domestic attribute; it reverts only for unregistered users and otherwise returns true or false based on the domestic match. The token contract’s adminTransferFrom, as well as internal helpers such as _exchangeAllowed used by transfer and transferFrom, invoke this view function but discard its boolean result, assuming that a failed check would automatically revert. Because the function does not revert on a false result, the token contract proceeds with the transfer even when the allowlist policy denies it. This flaw allows transfers between two allowed accounts whose domestic fields differ, effectively bypassing the intended compliance rule. The impact is that unauthorized token movements can occur, leading to potential loss of funds, violation of regulatory or business constraints, and erosion of trust in the protocol’s enforcement mechanisms. The issue manifests whenever both sender and receiver are registered but belong to different domestic groups; under those conditions the allowlist would return false, yet the token transfer succeeds without any error or warning. Users experience symptoms such as balances decreasing without a corresponding authorized receipt, or transfers completing despite expectations that they should be blocked. The problem was discovered during a security audit that flagged the missing boolean check comment. It can be hard to notice because the transaction does not revert and no explicit error is emitted, making the behavior appear normal in logs while silently violating policy. The correct mitigation is to enforce the allowlist decision by checking the returned boolean and reverting when it is false, or to redesign Allowlist.exchangeAllowed to revert on policy violations instead of returning a value. Implementing a require(IAllowlist(allowlist).exchangeAllowed(from,to),"Transfer not allowed") or similar guard restores the intended security guarantees and aligns the contract’s behavior with its business logic.

title: DividendManager::distributePayout will always revert after 255 payouts, preventing any future payout distributions
content: The vulnerability is an arithmetic overflow caused by storing the payout sequence counter in an 8‑bit unsigned integer (uint8) inside the DividendManager contract. Each time the distributePayout function is executed, the internal variable _currentPayoutIndex is incremented and used as the key for a mapping that records payout information. Solidity version 0.8 and later automatically reverts on overflow, so when the counter reaches its maximum representable value of 255 and a subsequent call attempts to increment it to 256, the transaction aborts. This bug originates from an inappropriate choice of data type for a value that is expected to grow beyond a few hundred entries, a common oversight when the developer assumes that the number of dividend rounds will remain low. An attacker does not need to actively exploit the condition; the contract simply becomes unusable for any further payout distribution once the limit is hit. The impact is that all future dividend payouts are blocked, leaving token holders without the expected payments, causing balances shown in user interfaces to remain unchanged even though new payouts are announced, and potentially breaking business logic that assumes continuous dividend streams. The condition occurs after exactly 255 successful calls to distributePayout, which may happen in long‑running protocols or in contracts that issue frequent small payouts. All participants who rely on the dividend mechanism—investors, protocol operators, and downstream applications—are affected because the protocol can no longer fulfill its financial obligations. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that inspected the storage layout of the HolderManagementStorage struct and noticed that _currentPayoutIndex was declared as uint8 while the surrounding fields left ample unused bits in the same storage slot, indicating that a larger type could be used without extra gas cost. The bug can be subtle because the contract functions correctly for the first 255 payouts, giving a false sense of security, and only fails later when the counter overflows, which may be far after deployment. To remediate the problem, the counter should be redeclared using a larger unsigned integer type such as uint16, uint32, or uint56, and any mappings that index by this counter must be updated to use the same larger key type. This change eliminates the overflow risk while preserving the existing storage layout, ensuring that dividend distributions can continue indefinitely and that the contract’s accounting remains consistent with its business expectations.

title: Impossible for user to get refund after re‑joining a rescheduled game which is subsequently cancelled
content: The vulnerability is an accounting flaw in the game session manager that makes it impossible for a participant to receive a second refund after re‑joining a game that has been rescheduled and later cancelled. The root cause is a per‑game, per‑player boolean flag (hasRefunded) that is set to true when a refund is issued on leaving a rescheduled game, but the flag is never cleared when the same player joins the game again. Because the refund and cancellation functions check this flag and revert with an AlreadyRefunded error if it is true, any subsequent attempt to claim a refund – either by leaving the rescheduled game a second time or by invoking the cancellation‑refund path – is blocked. An attacker does not need to exploit the bug; a legitimate user who follows the normal flow of joining, leaving, re‑joining, and then experiencing a cancellation will find their entry fee permanently trapped in the contract. The impact is that user funds disappear from the user’s balance and remain locked in the session manager, violating the protocol’s expectation that entry fees are always refundable on cancellation. The condition occurs only after a user has already been refunded once for a given game and then re‑joins that same game; it does not affect users who never leave or who never re‑join. All participants who might need to re‑enter a rescheduled match are affected, as are the protocol’s overall accounting guarantees. The issue was discovered through a unit test that simulated the full lifecycle: a user joins, the game is rescheduled, the user leaves and receives a refund, the user joins again, and finally the game is cancelled. The test observed that the second refund call reverted, indicating the bug. This type of problem is hard to notice because the single‑join/leave path works correctly; only the combination of refund followed by a new join triggers the hidden state inconsistency. The correct remediation is to reset the hasRefunded flag to false whenever a player joins a game, ensuring that each new participation starts with a clean refund state. Conceptually, the fix restores idempotent refund logic and aligns the contract’s behavior with the business rule that a user should be able to receive a refund for each distinct participation in a game.
summary: Impossible for user to get refund after re‑joining a rescheduled game which is subsequently cancelled.

title: Forwarders can lose payouts of the holders forwarding to them
content:
The vulnerability is a logical inconsistency in the payout forwarding mechanism of a token contract. A holder can designate a forwarder address to receive all of its distribution payouts. The contract tracks two separate values for each holder: the token balance (which determines holder status) and a calculatedPayout field that records the amount of payouts earned but not yet claimed. When a forwarder claims its accumulated payouts, its payoutBalance becomes zero and it may subsequently transfer all of its PropertyToken balance to another address, causing its token balance to drop to zero. At this point the contract removes the forwarder’s holder status and, because the balance is zero and payoutBalance returns zero, the internal _updateHolders function calls deleteUser to clean up the holder record.
The problem arises when, after this cleanup, time passes and the original holder continues to earn payouts that are still forwarded to the same forwarder address. The forwarder, although no longer a holder, receives credit for these new payouts in its calculatedPayout field, but its token balance remains zero. When the forwarder later receives tokens again (regaining holder status) and immediately empties its balance a second time within the same distribution index, the contract again sees a zero token balance and a zero payoutBalance (because payoutBalance only looks at the current payout index, not the pending calculatedPayout). Consequently, deleteUser is invoked a second time while calculatedPayout is still non‑zero. This deletes the forwarder’s holder record and discards the pending payout amount, causing the holder’s forwarded payouts to be permanently lost.
Exploitation requires the specific sequence: (1) forwarder holds tokens and is a holder, (2) holder sets forwarder, (3) payouts are credited to forwarder, (4) forwarder claims payouts, (5) forwarder empties its token balance and loses holder status, (6) further distributions occur, (7) forwarder receives new payout credit while still having zero token balance, (8) forwarder regains holder status by receiving tokens, (9) forwarder empties its balance again before the contract records the newly earned payout, triggering deleteUser. The impact is loss of funds: the holder’s payouts that were supposed to be forwarded disappear from the system. Users experience symptoms such as receiving no refund or payout despite being entitled, seeing their balance remain zero, or observing that previously earned payouts are missing.
The issue is hard to detect because it only manifests after a precise series of state changes that may not be covered by standard tests. It violates the accounting assumption that a holder’s calculated payout is preserved as long as the holder has any pending amount, regardless of token balance. The recommended mitigation is to augment the cleanup condition in _updateHolders to also require that holderStatus.calculatedPayout be zero before calling deleteUser. This prevents the contract from deleting a holder record that still has pending payout credit, thereby preserving the forwarder’s accrued payouts and maintaining consistent state.
summary:
A holder can have a designated forwarder who will accumulate the payouts earned by the holder.  
The vulnerability identified in this report is when the designated forwarder has no pending payouts to claim and zeroes out his PropertyToken's balance, and, time passes (while forwarder is still accumulating the payouts of the holder) and then it becomes a holder again, but on the same distributionIndex the forwarder zeroes out his balance again.  

The combination of these steps leads the contract's state to an inconsistent state that ends up causing the unclaimed accumulated payouts to be lost.  

The steps that lead the contracts to the inconsistent state are:  

1. forwarder has balance, it is a holder  
2. holder sets a forwarder  
3. payouts for holder are computed and credited to forwarder  
4. forwarder claims payouts, and gets computed all pending payouts  

   • At this point, payoutBalance of forwarder would be 0  

5. forwarder zeros out his balance, and gets removed the isHolder status (no longer a holder)  
6. distributions passes  
7. payouts for holder are computed and credited to the forwarder  
8. forwarder gets a balance and regains holder status  

   • lastPayoutIndexCalculated = currentPayoutIndex  

9. forwarder zeros out his balance again  

   • payoutBalance(forwarder) is called but returns 0 because lastPayoutIndexCalculated == current‑PayoutIndex  

   • so, balance == 0 and payoutBalance() returns 0, deleteUser(forwarder) gets called  

10. As a result of step 10, the payouts earned by the holder get lost  

Impact: Forwarders can lose holders' payouts

title: RemoraToken Transfer Bricking
content: The vulnerability is a transfer‑bricking logic error in the RemoraToken contract. When a token holder is not on the whitelist, the transfer, transferFrom and adminTransferFrom functions automatically invoke the internal _unlockTokens routine with the full amount requested for the transfer. The contract does not first determine how many of the holder’s tokens are already unlocked. Consequently, if the holder’s unlocked balance is smaller than the transfer amount – for example because none of the tokens are currently unlockable or only a subset is locked – the _unlockTokens call reverts with an InsufficientTokensUnlockable error. This revert aborts the entire transfer, leaving the sender’s balance unchanged. The bug manifests under two typical conditions: (1) the sender has enough total tokens to cover the transfer but has no unlockable tokens, and (2) the sender has a mixture of locked and unlocked tokens such that the locked portion is less than the transfer amount, yet the contract still tries to unlock the full amount. Users experience the symptom of a transaction that appears to succeed on the UI but actually fails, showing no change in balance and often no clear error message. From a business‑logic perspective the contract violates the fundamental accounting assumption that a transfer should succeed whenever the sender’s total balance is sufficient and the required unlocked amount is available. The issue was discovered during a security audit through unit‑test simulations that deliberately removed a holder from the whitelist and attempted transfers, causing the contract to revert. The problem is subtle because the external balance check passes, masking the internal unlock failure until the transaction reverts. The affected parties include any token holder who loses whitelist status, the protocol that relies on token mobility, and downstream applications that assume transfers are always possible. To remediate, the transfer logic should first compute the sender’s unlocked balance (balance minus locked tokens) and only call _unlockTokens for the shortfall needed to satisfy the transfer, or skip the unlock call entirely when the unlocked balance already covers the amount. This change ensures that only the necessary tokens are unlocked, prevents unnecessary reverts, and restores the expected transfer behavior.

title: LockUpManager::_unlockTokens returns if lockUpTime == 0
content: The vulnerability is an early‑return logic error in the internal token unlock routine of the LockUpManager contract. The function checks a global lockUpTime variable and immediately returns when lockUpTime equals zero (or when the requested amount is zero). This guard was intended to skip processing when no lock period is configured, but it also prevents the subsequent loop that iterates over each individual token lock from executing. The root cause is the assumption that a zero lockUpTime implies that no locks exist, which is false if locks were created while lockUpTime was non‑zero. An attacker or protocol administrator can change lockUpTime to zero after users have locked tokens. When a user later attempts to unlock or withdraw those tokens, the function returns without modifying the stored lock records, leaving the locks permanently recorded. From the user's perspective the contract still reports a non‑zero locked amount while the actual token balance may have been reduced by normal transfers. The protocol invariant that the amount of tokens a user has locked must be less than or equal to the user's token balance is therefore violated. When the contract later computes the unlocked balance as balance minus getTokensLocked(sender), the subtraction can underflow, causing transfer transactions to revert with an arithmetic error. This manifests as users being unable to send tokens, seeing their usable balance appear as zero, or experiencing unexpected transaction failures. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that flagged the early‑return statement as suspicious because it bypasses the unlocking logic. It can be hard to notice because setting lockUpTime to zero looks benign and does not affect immediate token transfers; the problem only surfaces after state changes and subsequent unlock attempts. The impact is classified as high because it can freeze user funds and break core accounting, leading to denial‑of‑service conditions. The recommended mitigation is to remove the early return for lockUpTime == 0 and allow the function to iterate over all stored locks, clearing any that are eligible, or to enforce that lockUpTime cannot be set to zero while active locks exist. This correction restores the invariant that locked tokens never exceed the holder's balance and prevents funds from becoming permanently inaccessible.

title: Forwarder can befrozen and still receive and claim payouts while frozen
content: The vulnerability is an inconsistency in the freeze logic of a token payout forwarding mechanism. When a holder is designated as a payout forwarder, the contract records a frozenIndex that indicates the payout round at which the address was frozen. The payoutBalance function only blocks payouts for addresses whose frozenIndex is zero, meaning they were frozen before any payout was calculated. Consequently, if the forwarder is frozen after it has already participated in at least one payout, the frozenIndex becomes non‑zero and the eligibility check passes, allowing the forwarder to continue receiving and claiming forwarded payouts despite being frozen. This occurs because the claimPayout function does not re‑verify the frozen status, relying solely on payoutBalance, which contains the flawed condition. An attacker can exploit this by first allowing a forwarder to receive a payout, then freezing the address to bypass any compliance or sanction mechanisms, and still claim subsequent distributions. The impact is that funds intended to be blocked by a freeze can still be withdrawn, breaking the protocol’s accounting assumptions and potentially leading to loss of assets or regulatory violations. The bug manifests only after the first payout has been distributed; before any payout, freezing correctly prevents receipt. Users see a discrepancy where a frozen forwarder still shows a positive payout balance and can claim tokens, contrary to the expectation that freezing stops all payouts. The issue was discovered during an audit through unit tests that froze a forwarder before and after a payout and observed differing behaviours. It is hard to notice because the freeze appears to work in the initial state, and the logic error is hidden in the subtle use of frozenIndex. To remediate, the contract should treat any frozen address as ineligible for receiving or claiming payouts regardless of when it was frozen, either by removing the frozenIndex check or by resetting calculated payouts upon freezing, and by adding explicit frozen‑status guards in the claim function. This aligns the implementation with the intended business rule that freezing fully disables payout forwarding and claimability.
summary:
If the forwarder is frozen before the first payout then they don't receive and can't claim any payouts while frozen.  
But if the forwarder is frozen after the first payout, then they do receive and can claim payouts while frozen.

title: Forwarder can be set to frozen address
content: The vulnerability is a forwarding‑to‑frozen‑address flaw in the dividend distribution logic. The contract’s setPayoutForwardAddress function does not verify whether the supplied forwarding address has been frozen, allowing a user or an attacker to designate a frozen holder as the recipient of forwarded payouts. When a dividend payout is executed, the system forwards the allocated amount to the designated address; if that address is frozen, the token transfer is silently dropped because frozen accounts are prohibited from receiving tokens. Consequently, both the original user’s payout balance and the frozen forwarder’s balance remain zero. If the user later removes the forwarding relationship while the forwarder is still frozen, the previously lost payout is not automatically re‑credited, leaving the user with no claimable tokens. This scenario can be reproduced by first minting tokens to a user and a separate forwarder, freezing the forwarder, setting the user’s payout forward address to the frozen forwarder, funding a payout, and observing that both balances stay at zero even after removing the forward. The root cause is the missing frozen‑address check and the absence of a fallback or reclamation path for payouts sent to frozen accounts. The impact is loss of dividend tokens for any holder that relies on forwarding, breaking the protocol’s accounting guarantees and potentially eroding user trust. The issue manifests whenever the protocol permits both freezing of holders and forwarding of payouts, and it is discovered through targeted audit tests that simulate the freeze‑then‑forward sequence. Because the contract does not revert or emit an error, the loss can be subtle and may only be noticed when users report missing balances. To remediate, the setPayoutForwardAddress function should revert if the target address is frozen, and the system should consider automatically cancelling or re‑routing existing forwards when an address becomes frozen, thereby preserving the intended accounting behavior and preventing token disappearance.
summary: Forwarder can be set to frozen address; this is not ideal and can result in lost tokens in a worst-case scenario.

title: Fee calculations break when token decimals are different from 18
content: The vulnerability is a decimal‑scaling mismatch in the fee controller. The contract assumes every ERC‑20 token has 18 decimals when converting a token‑amount fee to a USD‑denominated value. The code divides the product of fee amount and oracle price by 10**18, which correctly removes the oracle’s 18‑decimal scaling, but it never accounts for the token’s own decimal count. For tokens with fewer than 18 decimals (e.g., USDC, USDT with 6 decimals) the division leaves the result smaller by a factor of 10**(18‑decimals), producing a fee that is orders of magnitude lower than intended. Conversely, for tokens with more than 18 decimals the fee becomes inflated. The error propagates when a strategy step executes multiple actions involving different tokens: each action returns a fee expressed in its own mis‑scaled unit, and the step aggregates them by simple addition. The aggregated fee therefore mixes wei‑USD values that are not comparable, allowing a user to set a maxFeeInUSD that appears sufficient while the contract only charges the correctly scaled portion, effectively bypassing the fee limit. From the user’s perspective the UI may show a near‑zero fee for USDT trades, or an unexpectedly high fee for exotic high‑decimal tokens, and automations may revert with FeeExceedMaxFee even though the supplied max fee seems generous. The issue was discovered during a manual audit of the FeeController’s calculateFee and calculateTokenAmount functions, where the constant 10**18 was identified as a hard‑coded assumption. The bug is subtle because the contract still compiles and runs, and the discrepancy only becomes visible when tokens with non‑standard decimals are used, which may not be covered by typical test suites. The vulnerability belongs to the class of unit‑mismatch or decimal‑handling bugs, similar to incorrect token‑price conversions. To fix it, the contract must query each token’s decimals via IERC20Metadata.decimals() and use that value as the scaling factor when converting between token units and the 18‑decimal USD reference. This ensures that fee calculations are performed in a consistent unit, preventing under‑charging, over‑charging, and fee‑limit bypasses. The affected parties include protocol operators who lose revenue, users who may be over‑charged or see their transactions revert, and any downstream contracts that rely on the aggregated fee value.
summary:
feecontroller.calculatefee()_and_calculatetokenamount()_implicitly_treat_every_erc-20_as_if_it_had_18_decimals,_but_many_popular_assets_(usdc/usdt_=_6,_etc.)_do_not._inside_calculatefee_the_line `uint256 _feeInUSD = _feeAmount * _tokenPrice / 10**18;`  
divides by 1e18 to cancel the oracle’s 18-dec scaling, but completely ignores the token’s own decimals. When the token has fewer decimals the resulting “USD value” is shrunk by 10**(18‑decimals); when it has more decimals it is bloated.  
Because _executeStep() adds the individual action fees returned by _executeAction(), any step that mixes tokens of different precision sums numbers that are not expressed in the same unit:  

Token Decimals | Fee for $100 volume at 1 % (expected $1 = 1e18) | Fee actually returned  
--- | --- | ---  
USDT 6 | 1 × 10¹ | 1 × 10 (1 e12 × too low)  
DAI 18 | 1 × 10¹ | 1 × 10¹ (correct)  

When a strategy step executes an action in USDT followed by an action in DAI the total fee becomes:  
`total = 1e6 (USDT) + 1e18 (DAI) = 1000000000001000000 wei‑USD`  
but the semantically correct amount should be `2 × 10¹`.  

Down‑stream effects:  
* StrategyBuilderPlugin.executeAutomation() compares the aggregated fee against the user‑supplied maxFeeInUSD. A user can set maxFeeInUSD = 1.1e18 and still execute both actions (paying the DAI part only) because the mis‑scaled USDT fee barely moves the total.  
* The executor misses on revenue on every 6/8/12‑dec token; conversely users of exotic high‑decimal tokens may be over‑charged and see their automations revert with FeeExceedMaxFee().

title: Automation DoS via blacklisted or reverting fee recipients
content: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service caused by the fee distribution function handling ERC‑20 and native token transfers in a push‑payment model without proper error handling. The function attempts to forward tokens using safeTransferFrom and ETH using transfer to several parties such as beneficiary, creator, vault and a burner address. If any of these destinations is black‑listed by tokens like USDT or USDC, the ERC‑20 transfer returns false and safeTransferFrom reverts; similarly, the native transfer forwards only 2300 gas, so a contract wallet whose receive or fallback function consumes more gas or deliberately reverts will cause the transfer to fail. Because the code does not wrap each transfer in try/catch or use a pull‑payment pattern, a single failing recipient aborts the entire handleFee execution, preventing any fees from being distributed and effectively blocking all future executeAutomation calls for the affected strategy. The issue manifests when a black‑listed address or a malicious contract is set as one of the fee recipients, which can be done by an attacker controlling a blacklist feature or by deploying a contract with a reverting fallback. From a user perspective, expected refunds or fee payouts never arrive, balances appear unchanged, and the automation UI shows failed transactions. The bug is hard to notice in normal testing because transfers usually succeed; it only appears under the specific condition of a failing recipient. It was discovered during an audit that examined the fee handling logic and identified the unchecked external calls. The vulnerability belongs to the class of unchecked external call or push‑payment DoS bugs, violating the assumption that all recipients will accept funds. To remediate, the contract should adopt a pull‑payment model where each party claims its fees, or at minimum wrap each transfer in a try/catch (or use a safe native transfer library) so that a single failure does not revert the whole operation, and replace transfer() with a method that forwards sufficient gas and checks success.

title: DoS of strategy execution due to array indices out of bounds
content: The vulnerability is an off‑by‑one array index validation error in the StrategyBuilderPlugin contract. The internal function that checks whether a step’s condition results point to a valid next step compares each result index with the maximum step index using a strict greater‑than operator, while the maximum is supplied as the length of the steps array. Because Solidity arrays are zero‑based, the highest valid index is length‑1, but the check allows an index equal to the length. Consequently, a strategy can be created with a condition result that references an out‑of‑bounds step. When the strategy is later executed, the contract attempts to read or write at this invalid index, causing an out‑of‑bounds revert. The execution transaction fails entirely, so no token transfers or state updates occur. From a user’s perspective the strategy appears to do nothing: the expected token receiver balance remains zero, and the user receives no confirmation of successful execution. The impact is a denial‑of‑service (DoS) condition for any strategy that contains such an invalid index, potentially blocking legitimate users from using the protocol until the faulty strategy is removed or corrected. The bug manifests only when a step index equal to the array length is supplied, a scenario that may not be covered by typical tests, making it hard to notice. It was discovered during a manual audit when reviewers examined the validation logic and crafted a proof‑of‑concept test that deliberately set the result indices to the array length, causing execution to revert. The issue belongs to the broader class of off‑by‑one errors and improper bounds checking that lead to out‑of‑bounds array accesses. To remediate, the validation should reject indices that are greater than or equal to the array length (using >=) or should pass the highest permissible index (length‑1) as the limit. This change ensures that any attempt to create a strategy with an invalid next‑step reference is blocked at creation time, eliminating the execution‑time revert and restoring correct protocol behavior.

title: Volume-based fee can be bypassed with a wrapper contract
content: The vulnerability is a fee‑bypass flaw that arises from the way the protocol’s _executeAction function determines which fee to charge. The function relies on FeeController.getTokenForAction to map a (target contract address, function selector) pair to a specific token whose balance change will be measured to calculate a volume‑based fee. If the mapping does not contain the pair, the function falls back to a static minimum fee defined for the fee type. An attacker can exploit this by wrapping any high‑value operation—such as a large deposit to Aave, a withdrawal, or a token swap—inside a helper contract whose address and selector are not registered in the FeeController. The wrapper receives the user’s funds, forwards them to the external protocol, and then returns the resulting tokens, but because the (wrapper, function) pair is unknown, getTokenForAction returns (address(0), false). Consequently, the protocol charges only the minimum flat fee instead of the intended percentage of the transferred volume, which can be orders of magnitude lower (for example, paying a few dollars instead of a 1 % fee on a $100 000 deposit). This bypass can be performed repeatedly, leading to substantial revenue loss for the protocol’s executors and undermining the economic assumptions of the fee model. The issue occurs whenever an action is executed through an unregistered contract, affecting any user who interacts via such a wrapper and, more importantly, the protocol itself because it receives far less fee income than expected. It was discovered during a security audit that examined the fee calculation logic and identified that the mapping check is the sole gatekeeper for volume‑based fees. The flaw is subtle because the contract still emits the ActionExecuted event and the transaction succeeds, so users see no error and may assume the fee was correctly applied. From a user’s perspective, the symptom is that a large operation appears to be charged only a negligible fee, contrary to the documented fee schedule. The bug belongs to the class of “incorrect fee gating” or “fallback‑to‑flat‑fee” vulnerabilities, where business logic assumes exhaustive registration of all fee‑relevant actions. To remediate, the design should be changed so that either all possible actions are registered, or the fee calculation does not rely on a whitelist but instead derives the fee from the actual token flow regardless of the caller, or enforces a minimum percentage fee even when the mapping is missing. Such changes would close the bypass vector and restore the intended fee economics.

title: An attacker can drain the entire protocol balance of sUSDe during the yield phase due to incorrect redemption accounting logic in pUSDeVault::_withdraw
content: The vulnerability is an accounting logic error in the pUSDeVault::_withdraw function that occurs during the protocol’s YieldPhase. When a user redeems yUSDe (or pUSDe) shares, the contract calls previewYield to calculate the accrued sUSDe yield and then adds this yield amount to the assets variable that represents the amount to be withdrawn. The code subsequently calls an internal _withdraw helper, passing the inflated assets value as the baseAssets parameter. Inside this helper the contract subtracts baseAssets from the internal depositedBase counter, which is supposed to track only the principal amount of USDe held by the vault. Because the inflated assets include both principal and yield, depositedBase is reduced by more than the actual principal withdrawn. This mismatch can cause depositedBase to underflow or become far smaller than the real balance. The underflow either blocks further redemptions or, when the underlying USDe pool is large enough, allows an attacker to redeem far more sUSDe than they are entitled to, effectively draining the protocol’s sUSDe balance. The problem is amplified by the rounding behavior of sUSDe.previewWithdraw, which rounds up the amount of sUSDe that must be burned to satisfy the requested USDe amount; the contract transfers this rounded‑up amount to the user while still subtracting the full inflated assets from depositedBase, further inflating the apparent yield. The bug is triggered only after the contract has entered the YieldPhase, when yield has been accrued, and when a redemption call includes the yield calculation. It affects all depositors of pUSDe and yUSDe, as well as the protocol treasury, because the totalAssets view becomes inaccurate and the protocol can lose user funds. The issue was discovered during an audit and reproduced with a Forge test that simulated yield accrual, multiple redemptions, and observed the depositedBase variable shrinking to near zero while users received far less USDe than expected. The bug is hard to notice because external token transfers still succeed and the mismatch is internal to accounting state, only visible through balance queries or after many redemptions. The correct mitigation is to separate principal from yield: include the yield only when previewing the sUSDe withdrawal but pass only the base (principal) assets to the internal _withdraw so that depositedBase is decremented correctly. This restores accurate accounting, prevents underflow, and stops the possibility of draining the vault.

title: Yield Phase Withdrawal Issue
content: The vulnerability is a withdrawal failure that occurs during the yield phase of a meta‑vault that aggregates assets from multiple supported ERC4626 vaults. The root cause is a missing call to redeemRequiredBaseAssets inside the internal _withdraw function when the vault is in yield mode. When the yield phase is activated, the base USDe token is staked into a separate staking vault (sUSDe), leaving the meta‑vault with a zero USDe balance. The contract still reports a high totalAssets value because it sums the assets of each supported vault, and maxWithdraw is calculated from this sum. If a new supported vault is added while the yield phase is active, the meta‑vault accepts shares from that vault but never redeems the underlying USDe before a withdrawal request. Consequently, a user who is entitled to withdraw a certain amount sees the UI indicate a positive withdrawable balance, yet the withdrawal transaction reverts with an ERC20InsufficientBalance error because the contract lacks the actual USDe to transfer. The impact is that users cannot retrieve the assets they deposited, leading to funds appearing to be stuck or vanished, and shares disappearing from their personal wallets as they are held by the meta‑vault address. This issue is discovered through an audit test that simulates deposits, activation of the yield phase, addition of a new supported vault, and subsequent withdrawal attempts, which all revert despite correct accounting. The bug is hard to notice because totalAssets and maxWithdraw still return expected values, masking the underlying balance deficiency. To fix the problem, the withdrawal logic must invoke redeemRequiredBaseAssets to pull back enough USDe when the balance is insufficient, or the protocol should prohibit adding new supported vaults during the yield phase (except for the designated staking vault). By ensuring the contract’s internal accounting matches the actual token balances, withdrawals will succeed and the protocol will uphold its financial guarantees.
summary: During the yield phase, when using supported vaults, users can't withdraw vault assets they are entitled to.

title: DoS of meta vault withdrawals during points phase if one vault is paused or attempted redemption exceeds the maximum
content: The vulnerability is a denial‑of‑service condition affecting withdrawals from a meta‑vault that aggregates several ERC‑4626 vaults. The root cause lies in the internal function redeemRequiredBaseAssets, which uses ERC4626Upgradeable.previewRedeem to estimate how many base assets can be withdrawn from each underlying vault. According to the ERC‑4626 specification, previewRedeem must ignore user‑specific limits such as maxWithdraw and must never revert because of pause states or other withdrawal caps. The implementation incorrectly treats the preview value as a guaranteed amount, assuming that any shortfall will be covered by the other vaults. When an underlying vault is paused, or when a hack or administrative action reduces its maxWithdraw limit, previewRedeem can return a number larger than the actual withdrawable amount. The code then attempts to withdraw the full requested baseTokens from that vault. Because the vault’s withdraw call either reverts (if withdrawals are disabled) or returns less than requested, the subsequent ERC‑20 transfer that settles the user’s withdrawal fails with an insufficient‑balance error. This failure blocks the entire withdrawal operation, even though other vaults may have sufficient assets to satisfy the request. The issue manifests during the points phase when the meta‑vault relies on multiple underlying vaults to provide liquidity. Users experience symptoms such as transactions reverting with ERC20InsufficientBalance or ERC4626ExceededMaxWithdraw, UI showing a zero or missing refund despite a positive balance, and an inability to withdraw funds. The problem was discovered during a security audit that included a proof‑of‑concept test using a mock ERC‑4626 contract capable of pausing withdrawals and artificially lowering maxWithdraw. The bug is hard to notice because previewRedeem returns a plausible value and does not revert, giving the impression that the withdrawal logic is sound. The impact is that funds become effectively locked for users until the paused vault is re‑enabled or the contract is patched, violating the protocol’s accounting assumption that the sum of underlying balances always covers liabilities. To fix the issue, the code should replace previewRedeem with an availability‑aware query such as maxWithdraw, which respects pause states and withdrawal caps, and should iterate over vaults, withdrawing only when a vault reports sufficient withdrawable assets, falling back to other vaults when one fails. This change restores correct accounting, prevents the denial‑of‑service, and ensures that users receive the expected refunds.
summary:
Description: pUSDeVault::_withdraw assumes any USDe shortfall is covered by the multi-vaults; however, redeeemRequiredBaseAssets() does not guarantee that the required assets are available or actually withdrawn, so the subsequent ERC-20 token transfer could fail and DoS withdrawals if the ERC-4626 withdrawal does not already revert. Usage of ERC4626Upgradeable::previewRedeem in redeemRequiredBaseAssets() is problematic as this could attempt to withdraw more assets than the vault will allow. Per the ERC-4626 specification, previewRedeem():
• MUST NOT account for redemption limits like those returned from maxRedeem and should always act as though the redemption would be accepted, regardless if the user has enough shares, etc.
• MUST NOT revert due to vault specific user/global limits. MAY revert due to other conditions that would also cause redeem to revert.
So an availability-aware check such as maxWithdraw() which considers pause states and any other limits should be used instead to prevent one vault reverting when it may be possible to process the withdrawal by redeeming from another.

title: Value leakage due to pUSDe redemptions rounding against the protocol/yUSDe depositors
content: The vulnerability is a rounding‑bias bug that appears when the pUSDeVault contract processes redemptions after the system has entered the YieldPhase. In that phase the internal _withdraw function adds any accrued yield to the assets amount and then calls sUSDe.previewWithdraw to determine how many sUSDe shares must be burned to satisfy the requested USDe amount. previewWithdraw implements Math.Rounding.Up, meaning it rounds the required share amount upward to the next integer. The contract then transfers this rounded‑up share quantity to the user. Because the rounding is performed in favor of the redeemer, the protocol effectively gives away a small excess of sUSDe on each redemption. This excess is taken from the pool that backs yUSDe depositors, causing value to leak from the system to pUSDe redeemers. The bug is triggered only after the vault transitions to the YieldPhase and when redemptions are executed through the _withdraw path that uses previewWithdraw; it does not affect deposits or redemptions in the pre‑deposit phase. The issue was uncovered during a security audit and reproduced with unit tests and fuzzing (Forge test and Echidna), where the reported USDe amount differed from the actual amount after redemption. From a user’s perspective the symptom can be an unexpectedly larger USDe payout for a redemption, or conversely, other users seeing smaller balances than expected, violating the protocol’s fairness guarantees. The problem is subtle because the rounding discrepancy is typically a few wei per transaction, making it hard to notice without precise accounting checks, yet it accumulates over many redemptions and can become financially significant. The root cause is the misuse of a rounding‑up conversion function where a rounding‑down conversion is required. The correct mitigation is to replace the call to previewWithdraw with convertToShares (or an equivalent function that uses Math.Rounding.Down), ensuring that the number of sUSDe shares burned never exceeds the exact amount needed. This change restores proper accounting, prevents value leakage, and aligns the contract’s behavior with the intended business logic that redemptions should be value‑preserving for all participants.

title: pUSDeVault::startYieldPhase should not remove supported vaults from being supported or should prevent new supported vaults once in the yield phase
content: The vulnerability is a state‑transition logic error in the pUSDeVault contract where the function startYieldPhase unintentionally removes all currently supported vaults from the protocol’s whitelist while still allowing new vaults to be added during the same phase. The root cause is that startYieldPhase calls MetaVault.removeVaultAndRedeemInner, which clears the supported‑vault set without checking whether the contract is entering a yield phase, and the contract does not enforce a restriction on addVault while the yield phase flag is active. An attacker or the contract owner can trigger the yield phase, causing every vault that was previously accepted for deposits to become unsupported. Because the vault list is cleared, any subsequent deposit transaction is rejected and reverts, leading users to see no shares credited, balances appearing unchanged, or deposits failing with no obvious error. The impact is that user deposits revert until the owner manually re‑adds each vault, disrupting normal operation and potentially eroding user trust. This condition occurs whenever startYieldPhase is executed and the protocol remains in the yield phase while addVault remains callable. The affected parties include the protocol owner, who must perform costly re‑configuration, and all users attempting to deposit USDe, who experience failed transactions and may perceive that their funds disappear. The issue was discovered during an audit test that verified the supported‑vault flag before and after invoking startYieldPhase, revealing that the flag was cleared and could be reset later, contradicting the intended accounting flow. The bug is subtle because the removal of vaults may appear intentional for asset conversion, yet the ability to re‑add them later creates an inconsistent state that is not obvious without explicit checks. Conceptually, this is a business‑logic inconsistency and a configuration‑state management flaw, similar to a “phase‑transition” bug where configuration changes are not properly locked during critical phases. To remediate, the contract should either retain the supported‑vault status after converting assets, ensuring deposits continue to be accepted, or it should block any addVault calls while the yield phase flag is set (except for the designated sUSDe vault), thereby preserving a consistent set of supported vaults throughout the yield phase.
summary:
The intention of pUSDeVault::startYieldPhase is to convert assets from existing supported vaults into USDe in order to then stake the vault's total USDe into the sUSDe vault. However because this ends up calling MetaVault::removeVaultAndRedeemInner, all the supported vaults are also removed after their assets are converted.  
But new vaults can continue to be added during the yield phase, so it makes no sense to remove all supported vaults at this time.  
Impact: The contract owner will need to re-add all the previously enabled supported vaults causing all user deposits to revert until this is done.

title: pUSDeVault::maxWithdraw doesn't account for withdrawal pausing, in violation of EIP-4626
content: The vulnerability resides in the maxWithdraw function of the pUSDeVault contract, which calculates the maximum amount a user can withdraw without taking the global withdrawal pause flag into account. According to the EIP‑4626 standard, maxWithdraw must consider both global and user‑specific limits and must return zero when withdrawals are disabled, even temporarily. The root cause is that the implementation resides in a subclass that overrides maxWithdraw but does not query the withdrawalEnabled state that is managed in the PreDepositVault base contract. As a result, when an administrator disables withdrawals via setWithdrawalsEnabled(false), maxWithdraw continues to report the full theoretical withdrawable balance based on the user's share holdings. An attacker or honest user can query maxWithdraw and be led to believe that a certain amount is available, but any subsequent call to withdraw will revert because the underlying pause logic blocks the operation. This discrepancy can break downstream protocols that rely on maxWithdraw for accounting, risk limits, or UI display, leading to transaction failures, wasted gas, and user confusion. The issue manifests whenever withdrawals are paused; it does not affect the withdraw function itself, which correctly enforces the pause, but it misrepresents the state through the view function. The bug was discovered during an audit by writing a test that deposits funds, pauses withdrawals, and then checks the return value of maxWithdraw, which incorrectly returned the deposited amount instead of zero. The problem is subtle because the view function does not cause a revert, so developers may not notice the inconsistency unless they compare the view output with actual withdraw behavior. To remediate, maxWithdraw should be overridden in the contract where the pause flag is stored (PreDepositVault) and should return zero whenever withdrawals are disabled, thereby aligning with the EIP‑4626 specification and restoring correct expectations for users and integrators.
summary:
pUSDeVault::maxWithdraw doesn't account for withdrawal pausing, in violation of EIP-4626 which can break protocols integrating with pUSDeVault.  
EIP-4626 states on maxWithdraw:  
MUST factor in both global and user-specific limits, like if withdrawals are entirely disabled (even temporarily) it MUST return 0.

title: Future epoch cache manipulation via calcAndCacheStakes allows reward manipulation
content: The vulnerability is that the middleware function that calculates and caches stake totals does not check whether the epoch argument refers to a past or current epoch. Because of this, an attacker can call the function with a future epoch, causing the contract to store the current stake snapshot under that future epoch. Subsequent reward calculations and operator‑stake queries for that epoch read the cached value instead of the real stake at the time the epoch is processed. The root cause is the missing epoch‑validation check before caching, combined with a flag that marks the total stake as cached and makes the getter return the cached value unconditionally. An attacker can exploit this by invoking calcAndCacheStakes for a far‑future epoch while holding a large stake, then later withdrawing or reducing the stake before the epoch is reached. The cached high stake remains locked in the reward formula, inflating the attacker’s share of rewards. The impact is that reward distribution becomes inaccurate, allowing reward inflation, and node‑rebalancing logic that relies on up‑to‑date stakes may be skipped, leaving the protocol in an inconsistent state. The bug manifests when users see their expected rewards reduced or missing, while the attacker receives a larger payout; from a UI perspective a user may notice that their reward balance does not increase despite having deposited stake, or that the protocol reports higher total stakes than actually exist. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that examined the calcAndCacheStakes implementation and noticed the absence of a check against the current epoch. It is hard to notice because the function works correctly for past and current epochs, and the cached flag is only set once, so the incorrect values persist silently. The vulnerability belongs to the class of “epoch‑validation missing” or “cache poisoning” bugs, where stale data is written to a cache that is later trusted for accounting. To fix it, the contract should enforce that the supplied epoch is less than or equal to the current epoch before allowing caching, and optionally clear or forbid caching for future epochs altogether. Adding a require(epoch <= getCurrentEpoch()) prevents future‑epoch caching and ensures that reward calculations always use up‑to‑date stake data.

title: Blacklisted implementation versions are accessible through migrations
content: The vulnerability is a missing validation in the VaultFactory contract that allows vault owners to migrate an existing vault to a contract implementation that has been explicitly blacklisted. The factory maintains a blacklist of versions that are considered vulnerable or deprecated, and it correctly checks this list when a new vault is created through the create function. However, the migrate function, which is used to upgrade an existing vault to a newer implementation, does not perform the same blacklist verification. As a result, an owner can call migrate with a blacklisted version number, and the factory will blindly forward the upgrade request to the proxy, causing the vault to inherit the code of the prohibited implementation. This occurs whenever a version has been added to the blacklist and a vault owner initiates a migration after that point. The affected parties include vault owners, users of the vaults, and the overall protocol because the security barrier intended to prevent deployment of known‑bad code can be bypassed. The impact is that a vault may be upgraded to a version containing known security flaws, leading to potential loss of funds, unauthorized actions, or broken functionality. From a user’s perspective the UI will show the vault’s version number changing to the blacklisted value, and users may experience unexpected behavior such as inability to withdraw, incorrect accounting, or outright loss of assets, contrary to the expectation that upgrades are safe and vetted. The issue was discovered during a manual audit that compared the logic of create and migrate and was confirmed with a proof‑of‑concept test where a vault created at version 1 was successfully migrated to version 2 after the latter had been blacklisted, and the state variables of the blacklisted implementation were applied. The bug is subtle because the presence of a blacklist check in one entry point (create) creates an implicit assumption that all upgrade paths are protected, which is not true. To remediate, the migrate function should include the same blacklist guard as create, rejecting any newVersion that is marked as blacklisted and reverting with a clear error. This aligns the upgrade logic, restores the intended security guarantee, and prevents vaults from being moved onto vulnerable implementations, thereby preserving the protocol’s accounting integrity and user trust.
summary:
The VaultFactory contract implements a blacklisting mechanism to prevent the use of vulnerable or deprecated contract versions. However, the blacklisting check is only applied when creating new vaults through the `create` function, but is entirely absent from the `migrate` function.  
This allows vault owners to bypass the blacklist restriction by migrating their existing vaults to versions that have been explicitly blacklisted, potentially due to security vulnerabilities or other critical issues.  

Consider following scenario:  
• A vault is created with version 1  
• Version 2 is blacklisted in the factory  
• Despite being blacklisted, the vault can successfully migrate to version 2  
• The migrated vault fully inherits the functionality of the blacklisted implementation  

The intended security barrier provided by blacklisting can be completely bypassed, opening potential attack vectors even after vulnerabilities have been identified.

title: In DelegatorFactory new entity can be created for a blacklisted implementation
content: The vulnerability is a missing blacklist verification in the DelegatorFactory.create function, which allows the deployment of new delegator entities based on implementation types that have been explicitly marked as prohibited. The root cause is that the create routine clones the implementation contract and registers the entity without first checking the blacklisted mapping, so a call to blacklist(type) only sets a flag that is never consulted. An attacker or any user can exploit this by supplying the identifier of a blacklisted implementation; the factory will clone and initialize the contract as if it were allowed. The impact is that unsafe, deprecated, or malicious contract code can be instantiated, potentially bypassing governance controls, leading to loss of funds, unexpected contract behavior, or the introduction of backdoors. This occurs whenever the create function is invoked after a type has been blacklisted, regardless of the caller’s role, affecting all users of the protocol who rely on the factory to enforce security policies. The issue was discovered during a security audit that included unit tests exercising the blacklist function; the test showed that after calling blacklist the subsequent create call did not revert, revealing the logical omission. The bug is subtle because the blacklist state appears to be updated correctly, yet the creation path does not reference it, making the failure easy to miss in manual reviews. To remediate, the factory should perform a check such as `if (blacklisted[type_]) revert DelagatorFactory__TypeBlacklisted();` before cloning the implementation, thereby enforcing the intended restriction. This class of bug belongs to access‑control or policy‑enforcement failures where state is updated but not enforced, leading to a mismatch between expected business logic (prohibited implementations cannot be deployed) and actual contract behavior (they can). From a user’s perspective the UI may display a new delegator address even though the type was supposed to be blocked, transactions may succeed unexpectedly, and subsequent interactions with the newly created contract could result in missing balances or failed calls, violating the expectation that blacklisted contracts are inaccessible.
summary:
The current implementation of DelegatorFactory::create fails to verify whether the specified implementation type has been explicitly blacklisted. This creates a security and consistency risk where blacklisted contract types can still be deployed, potentially bypassing governance or security restrictions.  
Impact: The lack of a blacklist check in the create function allows the creation of contracts based on implementation types that may have been deemed unsafe, deprecated, or otherwise restricted.

title: Timestamp boundary condition causes reward dilution for active operators
content: The vulnerability is a boundary‑condition error in the AvalancheL1Middleware contract that causes operators and vaults to be considered active at the exact timestamp when they are disabled. The private helper _wasActiveAt uses the comparison disabledTime >= timestamp, which returns true when disabledTime equals the epoch start timestamp. As a result, the stake of a just‑disabled operator is still added to the totalStake computed in calcAndCacheStakes, and similarly disabled vaults are included in getOperatorStake. This inflated totalStake is later used in the Rewards contract’s _calculateOperatorShare function to determine each operator’s share of the epoch rewards. Because the denominator is larger than it should be, the share allocated to genuinely active operators is diluted, often to the point where the computed reward amount is zero. The bug manifests when an operator or vault is disabled exactly at the beginning of an epoch; the contract treats them as active for that epoch, inflates the total stake, and consequently locks the expected rewards in the Rewards contract. Users experience symptoms such as receiving no tokens after claiming, seeing their reward balance remain zero despite the UI indicating an entitlement, or observing that the total stake reported by the system exceeds the sum of active participants. The issue was discovered during a security audit that examined the reward‑distribution logic and identified the off‑by‑one error in the timestamp comparison. It is hard to notice because the condition only triggers at precise epoch boundaries, which may not occur frequently in normal testing. The bug violates the business assumption that only active operators at the epoch start should contribute to the reward pool, breaking the accounting model that distributes rewards proportionally to stake. To remediate, the comparison should be changed to disabledTime > timestamp so that entities disabled at the epoch start are excluded from the stake calculation. After fixing the condition, the contract must recalculate cached stakes for affected epochs and, if possible, redistribute the previously diluted rewards to the rightful operators.

title: Immediate stake cache updates enable reward distribution without P-Chain confirmation
content: The vulnerability is an immediate stake‑cache update bug that allows reward distribution to be based on unconfirmed stake changes. When an operator calls the stake‑update entry point, the middleware writes the requested new stake into its nodeStakeCache for the next epoch before the asynchronous P‑Chain transaction that actually changes the validator’s weight has been confirmed. The reward calculation function later reads this cached value without verifying the confirmation status, so it attributes a larger effective stake to the operator. This creates a temporal window where the accounting used for rewards diverges from the true state on the P‑Chain. An operator can therefore receive a reward boost in the epoch following the stake‑update call, even if the P‑Chain later rejects the update or takes multiple epochs to confirm it. The impact is that operators may earn rewards that are not backed by real stake, draining the reward pool and breaking the economic assumptions of the protocol. The issue occurs only for validators with a pending weight‑update; validators without pending updates are unaffected. It was discovered during a security audit by inspecting the middleware’s initializeValidatorStakeUpdate function and observing that nodeStakeCache is set immediately, and then confirming through a test that getOperatorUsedStakeCachedPerEpoch returns the unconfirmed stake. The bug is subtle because the rebalancing logic in forceUpdateNodes correctly skips pending validators, giving the impression that pending updates are handled consistently, while the reward path lacks this guard. From a user’s perspective the UI may show a higher reward or a larger balance after a stake increase, contradicting the expectation that rewards correspond to confirmed stake. The class of bug is a state‑synchronisation flaw between off‑chain cache and on‑chain source of truth, specifically a premature cache write leading to accounting inconsistency. The recommended fix is to defer updating nodeStakeCache until after the P‑Chain confirms the weight change, for example by moving the cache write into a completion callback such as completeStakeUpdate, and ensuring that the cache for the current epoch always reflects the rolled‑over value from the previous epoch regardless of pending updates. This aligns reward calculations with the verified validator state and eliminates the reward‑inflation attack vector.

title: Vault rewards incorrectly scaled by cross-asset-class operator totals instead of asset class specific shares causing rewards leakage
content: The vulnerability is a reward‑scaling bug in the vault reward distribution contract. The contract calculates an operatorBeneficiariesShare for each operator by aggregating the operator’s proportional stake across all asset classes and then stores this total in a single mapping. Later, when computing the reward share for an individual vault, the code multiplies the vault’s stake by the operator’s aggregated share and the vault’s asset‑class share. Because the operator’s share includes stake from unrelated asset classes, the vault’s reward is unintentionally diluted. The root cause is the misuse of a cross‑asset‑class operator total in a context that requires an asset‑class‑specific operator share. This flaw can be exploited whenever an operator holds asymmetric stake across multiple asset classes: an attacker (or any operator) can cause vaults belonging to a particular class to receive less than their entitled portion of the epoch’s rewards. The impact is systematic under‑distribution of rewards; a portion of the allocated rewards becomes undistributed and effectively disappears from users’ balances. From a user’s perspective, vault owners may see lower than expected payouts, sometimes even zero rewards, despite having staked the full amount and expecting the advertised asset‑class share. The protocol’s accounting no longer matches the intended allocation model, breaking the business logic that each asset class receives its predefined share of the total rewards. The issue occurs during the reward distribution phase of each epoch, specifically in the internal functions _calculateOperatorShare and _calculateAndStoreVaultShares. It affects all participants who stake through vaults, the operators managing those vaults, and the overall integrity of the protocol’s reward economics. The bug was discovered through a manual audit and reinforced by a proof‑of‑concept test that demonstrated a 7.5 % leakage of rewards in a scenario with three asset classes and operators holding stakes in multiple classes. The problem is hard to notice because the total rewards allocated to the epoch appear correct, while the per‑vault breakdown is subtly off, and the discrepancy is hidden in the undistributed rewards pool. To remediate, the contract should track operator shares per asset class rather than a single aggregated value. Introducing a mapping keyed by epoch, operator, and asset class and using this granular share in the vault reward calculation eliminates the cross‑asset dilution and restores correct reward distribution.

title: Division by zero in rewards distribution can cause permanent lock of epoch rewards
content: The vulnerability is a division‑by‑zero error in the rewards distribution logic of the protocol. The function that calculates an operator's share iterates over the list of asset classes returned by the middleware, which always reflects the current set of classes. When the contract attempts to distribute rewards for a historical epoch, it may encounter asset classes that were either newly added after that epoch or deactivated, both of which have a total stake of zero for the epoch in question. The calculation multiplies the operator's stake by a basis‑points denominator and then divides by the total stake; if total stake is zero, the internal Math.mulDiv function performs a division by zero and the transaction reverts. This mismatch between the current asset‑class list and the historical stake data creates a scenario where the entire rewards distribution for that epoch fails, effectively locking the rewards forever. The issue can be triggered whenever an admin adds a new asset class, deactivates an existing one, or any asset class ends up with zero stake, even though a minimum stake requirement exists but is not actively enforced. From a user's perspective, expected rewards never arrive, balances remain unchanged, and the UI may show a zero payout despite eligibility. The protocol’s operators, delegators, and any participants relying on epoch rewards are affected because the rewards for that epoch become permanently unavailable until the contract is patched. The bug was discovered during a security audit that examined the reward‑calculation paths and identified missing zero‑stake checks. It is subtle because the code appears to handle normal cases correctly, and the division‑by‑zero only manifests under specific state changes that are legitimate in protocol upgrades. To remediate, the contract should include explicit guards that skip asset classes with a total stake of zero (or set their share to zero) and also verify that operatorActiveStake is non‑zero before performing similar calculations. By adding these checks, the distribution can continue for the remaining valid asset classes, preventing a denial‑of‑service condition and ensuring that rewards are correctly allocated according to the protocol’s accounting rules.
summary:
Description: In the Rewards::_calculateOperatorShare() function, the system fetches the current list of asset classes but attempts to calculate rewards for a historical epoch:
```solidity
function _calculateOperatorShare(uint48 epoch, address operator) internal {
    // ... uptime checks ...
    uint96[] memory assetClasses = l1Middleware.getAssetClassIds(); // @audit Gets CURRENT asset classes
    for (uint256 i = 0; i < assetClasses.length; i++) {
        uint256 operatorStake = l1Middleware.getOperatorUsedStakeCachedPerEpoch(epoch, operator,
            assetClasses[i]);,!
        uint256 totalStake = l1Middleware.totalStakeCache(epoch, assetClasses[i]); // @audit past epoch
        uint16 assetClassShare = rewardsSharePerAssetClass[assetClasses[i]];
        uint256 shareForClass = Math.mulDiv(
            Math.mulDiv(operatorStake, BASIS_POINTS_DENOMINATOR, totalStake), // ← DIVISION BY ZERO
            assetClassShare,
            BASIS_POINTS_DENOMINATOR
        );
        totalShare += shareForClass;
    }
}
```
This creates a mismatch where:
- Deactivated asset classes remain in the returned array but have zero total stake  
- Newly added asset classes are included but have no historical stake data for past epochs  
- Asset classes with zero stake for any reason cause division by zero  

Consider following scenario:  
- Epoch N: Normal operations, operators earn rewards, rewards distribution pending  
- Epoch N+1: Protocol admin legitimately adds a new asset class for future growth  
- Epoch N+2: New asset class is activated and configured with rewards share  
- Epoch N+3: When attempting to distribute rewards for Epoch N, the system:  
  - Fetches current asset classes (including the new one)  
  - Attempts to get totalStakeCache[N][newAssetClass] which is 0  
  - Triggers division by zero in Math.mulDiv(), causing transaction revert  

Similar division by zero checks are also missing in _calculateAndStoreVaultShares when operatorActiveStake == 0.

Impact: Adding a new asset class ID, deactivating or migrating an existing asset class ID or simply having zero stake for a specific assetClassId (though unlikely with minimum stake requirement but this is not enforced actively) are all instances where reward distribution can be permanently DOSed for a specific epoch.

title: If multiple users call DefaultSession::assertResults all but the first caller lose their bonds
content: The vulnerability is a duplicate‑assertion bug in the DefaultSession contract that allows multiple users to call the permissionless function assertResults for the same sessionId after the game has ended. The root cause is the absence of any guard that prevents more than one in‑process or resolved assertion for a given session. When the first caller submits a correct assertion, the optimistic oracle resolves it, and recordResults stores the winners for that session. If a second user later calls assertResults with the same parameters, the oracle also resolves the second assertion, but the callback recordResults attempts to write winners again. The function contains a require check that winners[sessionId].length == 0, which fails because the winners are already recorded, causing the callback to revert. The revert prevents the bond that the second caller transferred in USDC from being returned, so the user loses the $250 bond. This impact manifests as funds disappearing from the user’s balance; the user expects the bond to be refunded after a successful assertion but receives nothing, often seeing a zero or reduced USDC balance. The issue occurs only when the session state is Ended, the same sessionId is used, and multiple distinct callers invoke assertResults with identical result data. It affects any participant who attempts to assert results after another participant has already done so, as well as the protocol’s overall accounting because it breaks the one‑to‑one relationship between a session and its recorded result. The bug was discovered during an audit that exercised the function with two successive calls in a test suite, revealing that the second call caused a revert in the callback. It can be hard to notice in production because the first call behaves correctly and the failure happens deep inside a callback, which may not surface as an obvious error to end users. To fix the issue, the contract should either prevent multiple concurrent or subsequent assertions for the same sessionId—by tracking pending assertions and rejecting duplicates—or modify the callback to return silently when winners are already recorded instead of reverting, thereby ensuring that later callers do not lose their bonds. This class of bug is a re‑entrancy‑like state‑management flaw where insufficient uniqueness checks lead to unintended fund loss and broken business logic.

title: Inaccurate uptime distribution in UptimeTracker::computeValidatorUptime leads to reward discrepancies
content: The vulnerability resides in the uptime accounting routine of the rewards subsystem. The function that computes a validator’s uptime takes the total amount of time reported since the previous checkpoint and distributes that amount evenly across every epoch that has elapsed, without checking whether the validator was actually online during each individual epoch. This root cause – a missing activity verification step – leads to uptime being credited to epochs where the validator was offline and to being split across epochs that have different reward rates. An attacker does not need to exploit the contract; the bug can be triggered simply by the normal operation of validators that are active in some epochs but not others. When the Rewards contract later reads the per‑epoch uptime values to calculate payouts, it multiplies the incorrectly attributed uptime by the epoch‑specific reward factor. Consequently, a validator that was active only in a high‑reward epoch may have part of its uptime incorrectly assigned to a lower‑reward epoch, resulting in a lower overall reward. From a user’s perspective the symptoms are a lower than expected token balance after a distribution, or even a zero payout despite having been online, and the UI may show uptime numbers that do not match the validator’s actual online periods. The issue occurs whenever computeValidatorUptime is called after more than one epoch has passed since the last checkpoint, which is a common situation in a rolling epoch system. All validators, protocol participants, and downstream reward recipients are affected because the accounting error can distort the fairness of the reward pool, potentially rewarding inactive validators and penalising honest ones. The flaw was discovered during a formal audit that included unit tests reproducing the scenario: the test warped the blockchain time across multiple epochs, recorded uptime, and then compared the expected versus actual reward amounts, revealing a discrepancy. The problem is subtle because the contract does not emit explicit warnings; the even split looks plausible and the total uptime across epochs remains correct, masking the mis‑allocation. To remediate, the uptime computation should be redesigned to record and attribute uptime on a per‑epoch basis, cross‑referencing validator activity logs or status flags so that only epochs where the validator was truly active receive uptime credit. This change restores the integrity of the reward calculation, ensures that rewards are proportional to actual contribution, and preserves the economic incentives of the protocol.
summary:
The UptimeTracker::computeValidatorUptime function calculates a validator's uptime by evenly distributing the total recorded uptime across all epochs between the last checkpoint and the current epoch. However, it does not verify whether the validator was actually active during each of those epochs. As a result, uptime may be incorrectly attributed to epochs where the validator was offline or inactive.  
This flaw becomes significant when the uptime data is used by the Rewards contract to determine validator rewards. Since reward values can differ substantially between epochs, attributing uptime to the wrong epochs can misrepresent a validator's actual contribution.
